أب:
Know that the letters hamza and bā' in the doubled root have two origins: one is pasture, and the other is intent and readiness.

As for the first, it is God's saying: {and fruit and fodder} [ʿAbasa: 31]. Abū Zayd al-Anṣārī said: I have not heard al-abb mentioned except in the Qur'an. Al-Khalīl and Abū Zayd said: al-abb is pasture, on the pattern fa'l.

Ibn Durayd cited, in a line of verse:
Our stock is Qays and Najd is our home; we have the pasture there, and the watering place.

Shubayl ibn 'Azra cited, for Abū Dūwād, in a line of verse:
It grazes on the meadow of al-Ḥazn, on its pasture's watercourses, among a herd of wild asses that guard each other.

Meaning: they guard one another. One says ṣaḥibaka llāh, meaning God protect you.

Abū Isḥāq al-Zajjāj said: al-abb is all the herbage that livestock graze on. This is how it was related from Ibn 'Abbās, God be pleased with him.

That is the first origin. As for the second, al-Khalīl and Ibn Durayd said: al-abb is the verbal noun of abba fulānun ilā sayfihi — when he brought his hand back to his sword to draw it. Al-abb, in Ibn Durayd's account, is yearning toward one's homeland; and al-abb, in both their accounts, is readying oneself to set out. Al-Khalīl alone said: abba hādhā l-shay' — when it became ready and its course was set straight — ibāba being the verbal noun.

He cited, for al-A'shā, in a line of verse:
I cut ties, though I did not cut them with you — like one who cuts ties, a brother who has folded his flank and set himself to go.

Hishām ibn 'Uqba said, concerning al-ibāba, in a line of verse:
The one present readied himself to depart, his readiness plain, and an intention struck down the ropes of the tent.

Some people mentioned that gazelles do not come to water, and no watering-place is known for them. They said: this is why the Arabs said of gazelles: if it finds [water] there is no gulping, and if it lacks it there is no yearning for it. Its meaning: if it finds water it does not gulp it down, and if it does not find it, it does not set itself to seek it. God knows best whether this is true.

Al-abb is also intent, aim. One says abibtu abbahu, ammamtu ammahu, ḥammamtu ḥammahu, ḥaradtu ḥardahu, and ṣamadtu ṣamdahu — all meaning I aimed straight for it.

The rajaz-poet said, describing a wolf, in a line of verse:
It passed by, bold, like the rope of the bucket-well, and made straight for my sheep and made straight for me.

Meaning: it aimed at them and aimed at me.
أبت: The letters hamza, bā' and tā' are a single root, and it is heat and its intensity. Ibn al-Sikkīt and others said: abata yawmunā ya'butu — our day grew intensely hot, so it is abit [scorching]. He recited, in a line of verse: a resting herd, lying still in a barren waste, over which the sun has blazed with scorching heat. One says: yawmun abtun (a scorching day) and laylatun abtatun (a scorching night). And rajulun ma'būt — a man struck by the heat. Abū 'Alī al-Aṣfahānī said: al-abta is like al-waghra, the fierce heat of midsummer.
أبث: This chapter is left unaddressed by al-Khalīl. Al-Shaybānī said: al-abith is the lively, high-spirited one. He said, in a line of verse: 'Ammār rose lively and restless, eating meat left overnight that had already turned. This chapter is left unaddressed by al-Khalīl, and the word is not found in Ibn Durayd either. Al-kabith is [meat] that has gone off and smells strong; al-kabith is found neither in al-Khalīl nor in Ibn Durayd. And one who cannot keep still from high spirits is called abith. Al-Shaybānī said: "aṣabtu ibilan abāthā" — I came upon camels abāthā, meaning kneeling herds, well-fed. And nāqatun abitha — a restless, high-spirited she-camel.
أبد:
The letters hamza, bā', and dāl, in their formation, point to length of time and to wildness. They say al-abad is time, eternity, plural ābād. The Arabs say abadun abīd, just as they say dahrun dahīr [enduring time]. Al-abda is a deed that lasts forever. Ta'abbada al-ba'īru means the camel turned wild. In the hadith: "These beasts have their wild fits, like the wild fits of wild game." Ta'abbada al-manzilu means the dwelling-place became deserted. Labīd said:
The abodes have grown desolate, both their alighting-place and their standing-place ... at Minā — its Ghawl and its Rijām have both turned to wilderness.
Ibn al-A'rābī said: al-ibid is livestock capable of bearing young, like a female slave, a mare, or a she-donkey, because they bear young every year. And one says ta'abbada wajhuhu, meaning his face grew rough/chapped.
أبر:
The letters hamza, bā' and rā' — their pattern points to pricking a thing with something sharp-pointed.

1. Al-Khalīl said: al-ibra — the needle, well known; and one who sells them is an abbār.
2. al-abr — the scorpion's sting with its stinger; it "abrs" [stings].
3. al-abr — the pollinating of palm trees; one says abarahu abran, and abbarahu ta'bīran. Al-Khalīl said: al-abr is also the tending of crops with whatever sets them right — watering and care. Ṭarafa said, in a line of verse: and I have the noble stock in which the tender sets right the crop of the one who seeks tending. Al-mu'tabir is the one who seeks to have his crop tended.
4. Al-Khalīl said: al-mā'bir — acts of tale-bearing; singular mi'bar. Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse: that is from a word of mine that reached you, and from enemies smuggling their tale-bearing in to you. And one says "innahu ladhū mi'bar" — he has a talebearing tongue — when he is a gossip. A poet said, in a line of verse: and whoever has a talebearing tongue, words will come to him, whether by chance or by intent.
5. Al-Khalīl said: al-ibra is also a small bone level with the end of the forearm bone, running from the arm to the fingertip. A poet said, in a line of verse: where al-ibra meets al-qabīḥ [another bone of the wrist].
6. And it is said: ibrat al-lisān — the tongue's "needle" — is its tip.
أبز: The letters hamza, bā' and zā' point to restlessness, speed, and unsettledness. Al-Khalīl said: a person ya'bizu [darts restlessly] in his running, resting a while and then moving on again at times. Al-Farrā' said: al-abazā and al-qafazā are nouns from "the horse bounded" and "it leapt." Al-abz is leaping. Abū 'Amr said: najībatun abūz — a fine she-camel that endures with remarkable patience; it has shown that restless endurance. He said, in a line of verse: I gave a morning drink to Ḥamal ibn Kūz from a spirited, wondrously enduring mount, Wakrā. Al-Shaybānī said: al-ābiz is one who wrongs his companion and speaks ill of him indirectly. One says: I see you speaking ill of him.
أبس:
The letters hamza, bā' and sīn point to overpowering. From it one says: abasa al-rajulu al-rajula — the man overpowered [another] man. A poet said, in a line of verse: lions of battle, never assailed with overpowering force.

1. al-abs — any rough, harsh ground.
2. One says abastu meaning ḥabastu, I detained/held back; and ta'abbasa al-shay' — the thing changed/altered. Al-Mutalammis said, in a line of verse: have you not seen that al-Jawn [a mountain] stands firm and fixed — the days circle round it, and it does not change. And it is also said with a yā': "lā yata'ayyasu," already discussed in its own place.
أبش: The letters hamza, bā' and shīn are not a root, because the hamza in it stands in for a hā'. Ibn Durayd said: abashtu al-shay' and habashtuhu — I gathered the thing together.
أبض:
The letters hamza, bā' and ḍād point to a span of time, and to something related to the groin area of the belly.

1. al-ubḍ — time, its plural ābāḍ. Ru'ba said, in a line of verse: through a long stretch we lived by that span of time.
2. al-ibāḍ — a rope by which a camel's fetlock is tied up to its upper leg; one says abaḍtuhu, I hobbled it.
3. And the inner side of a camel's knee is called al-ma'biḍ.

And the diminutive of al-ibāḍ is ubayyiḍ. A poet said, in a line of verse: I say to my companion, as night grows dark: your little black hobble-rope — do not let it be lost. He means: guard your black hobble-rope so it is not lost.

And Labīd said, in a line of verse: as if its choice white camels were mata'abbiḍāt, and, tethered together, as still as little heaps of dust-covered earth. Muta'abbiḍāt means hobbled, held fast by the hobble-ropes. He means: as if, in this state and bound by ropes, they were like little mounds of packed dust.
أبط:
The letters hamza, bā' and ṭā' are a single root, and it is a person's armpit, or a borrowed use of the word for something else.

1. al-ibiṭ — the armpit, well known. Ta'abbaṭtu al-shay' — I tucked the thing under my armpit. Ibn Durayd said: ta'abbaṭa sayfahu — he slung his sword on, because it then sits under his armpit. And anything you sling on in the place a sword goes, you have "ta'abbaṭ"-ed it. Al-Hudhalī said, in a line of verse: I drank from its gathered water and turned away from it, my slung-on companion a white, sharp-cutting sword. Some said: his word for that sword means "it is at the side of my armpit." Others said: it means attributed to his armpit, then lightened in form.

2. The borrowed use: al-ibiṭ of sand-dunes — where the bulk of a dune breaks off and only a thin, spread-out remnant stays, joined to the hard flat ground; the place where its bulk breaks off is called al-ibiṭ, its plural al-ābāṭ. Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse: and a dust-grey barren plain, its mirage running over the trailing edges of the dune-flanks, their backs raised in ridges.
أبق:
The hamza, bā' and qāf indicate a slave's fleeing, and severity/firmness in a matter. abaqa al-ʿabd, ya'biqu, abqan and abaqan — the slave fled.

A rajaz-poet said, in a line of verse:
Hold fast to your sons, ʿAmr — I am fleeing ... a bolt of lightning, flashing over the land of the ghouls.

1. ʿabd abūq and abbāq — a slave [prone to] fleeing.
2. Abū Zayd said: ta'abbaqa al-rajul — the man hid himself.

Al-Aʿshā said:
But death came to him — it is not to be hidden from.

Another [poet] said:
Indeed Bahān said — and why do you hide? — you have known comfort, though comfort does not suit you.
(This line is obscure; the sense above is my best rendering of it.)

Some of them said: it is said to a man, "There is such-and-such in you," and he answers, "By God, mā ata'abbaq" — meaning "I do not deny it." And it is said to him, "O son of so-and-so," and he answers, "Mā ata'abbaq minhā" — meaning "I do not deny her."

3. Al-Khalīl said: al-abaq — the bark of hemp.
4. Abū Ziyād said: al-abaq — a plant whose stalks are pounded until the bark comes free of it, becoming hemp.

Ru'ba said:
Eight lean [she-camels], like ropes of hemp.

Zuhayr said:
The knots of the leather strap and of the hemp-rope have been made fast.
أبك: The letters hamza, bā' and kāf are a single root, and it is fatness. One says: abika al-rajul — the man grew fat.
أبل:
The letters hamza, bā' and lām are a construction built on three origins: one about camels, one about making do without something, one about heaviness, and one about overcoming. Al-Khalīl said: al-ibil (camels) is well known.

1. ibil mu'abbala — camels made into separate droves, group by group; this description is used only for camels. A man who owns camels is called ābil.
2. Abū Zayd said: al-ibil is used for both the old and the young of the species; it has no singular of its own form, and its plural is ābāl. A poet said: "Their camels (ābāluhum) have already drunk by the fire — and fire may cure the burning thirst."
3. Ibn al-A'rābī said: a man is ābil if he owns camels, and abil (on the pattern fa'il) if he is skilled at herding them; the verb is abila ya'balu. He is among the most skilled of people with camels (ābal al-nās). They say: "he is more skilled [with camels] than Ḥunayf al-Ḥanātim" [a proverb].
4. al-ibilāt — camels.
5. abbala — said of a man whose camels grew numerous, so he is mu'abbil; māl mu'abbal is said specifically of camels, meaning their great numbers, so many that some crowd upon the backs of others.
6. fulān lā ya'tabil — so-and-so cannot keep his seat on camels, i.e. cannot manage riding them.

Abū 'Alī al-Aṣfahānī related from al-'Āmirī: al-abala is like giving camels their due care — doing right by looking after them. Abū Nakhīla used to say: "The wealth most deserving of good care and shelter is wealth that pays blood-money and stops bloodshed, by which women are given as dowries, by which God is worshipped in the sky, whose milk is a cure and whose urine is medicine, and to own it is honour."

Abū Zayd said: they say "so-and-so has ibil," meaning he has a hundred camels — the word ibil is used as a name for a hundred camels, as hunayda is [a name for a hundred of something else]. The Messenger of God, God's blessing and peace upon him, said: "People are like a hundred camels among which you will not find a single one fit to ride." Al-Farrā' said: they say "so-and-so yu'abbil against so-and-so," meaning he piles exaggeration on him; its sense is inflating and magnifying [a matter]. A poet said: "May God reward a companion well — whenever he comes he settles the matter, and pays no attention to the words of the one who exaggerates (al-mu'abbil)."

He said: from this the camel (al-ibil) was named, for the greatness of its build. Al-Khalīl said: a camel is ābil when it stays in a place without leaving, making do without water. A man ta'abbala from a woman [withdrew from her] as a wild animal makes do without water; from this is the hadith: "Adam, peace be upon him, withdrew (ta'abbala) in grief over his slain son for days, not approaching Eve." Labīd said: "And when I stirred my stirrup, it quickened its pace — or my saddle-girths, at the running of a dark [donkey] that had already gone without water (abal)." He means a donkey that made do without water. From this one says: abala ya'bilu wa ya'bulu ubūlan. Al-'Ajjāj said, [describing] the hides of the pregnant she-camels (al-mukhāḍ) that go without water (al-ubbāl).

Ibn al-A'rābī said: abalat ta'bilu ablan — when an animal grazed on pasture, whether the pasture was green or dry; if it eats the green pasture that is called al-juz'. Abū 'Ubayd said: ibil awābil, ubbal, and ubbāl all mean going without water. He cited: "by it both months of spring passed without her needing water (abalat)." Al-Aṣma'ī said: ibil mu'abbala means numerous, as one says ghanam mughannama (abundant sheep) and baqar mubaqqara (abundant cattle); it is also said to mean "kept as accumulated wealth." Ibn al-A'rābī said: nāqa abila means a strong she-camel.

They say "he has neither hābil nor ābil" — al-hābil is the resourceful one who can be relied on to provide for him; al-ābil is the herdsman.

Al-Khalīl said, on God Almighty's words {birds in flocks (ṭayran abābīl)} [al-Fīl: 3]: meaning following one after another; the singular is ibbāla or ibbawl. Al-Khalīl said: al-abīl is one of the chiefs of the Christians, also called al-abīliyy. Al-A'shā said: "and what is a monk (aybuliyy), upon a temple he built, and set up crosses in, and stayed" — he means abīliyy, but under metrical necessity moved the yā' forward, as one says aynuq [for she-camels] whose true form is anwuq. 'Adiyy said: "Indeed I, by God — so accept my oath — swear by a monk (abīl) who, whenever he prays, groans."

Some said: ta'abbala 'alā al-mayyit means he grieved over the dead; and abbaltu al-mayyita is like abbantuhu (I gave his eulogy). As for the line: "Two clans — of them one forsakes me and does not answer me, and another, wronged among them (musta'bal), is denied and treated unjustly" — it is said the poet meant by al-musta'bal the man who is wronged.

Al-Farrā' said: al-abalāt are grudges, singular abala. Al-'Āmirī said: qaḍā abalatahu min kadhā means he satisfied his grudge over such a thing; he said it names a trait of ill-will, not of good. Abū Zayd said: they say "mā lī ilayka abila" (with fatḥa on the alif and kasra on the bā'), meaning "I have a need of you." And they say "anā aṭlubuhu bi-abila," meaning I pursue him out of a grievance (tira). Ya'qūb said: Ublā is a place-name. Al-Shammākh said: "then she vanished at Ublā, one night then another, at Ḥādha, and crossed intentions away from their [former] intentions."

It is said: aballa ar-rajulu ya'bilu ablan, when he prevailed and resisted. Al-abala is heaviness/burden; and in the hadith: "Any wealth whose due [zakāh] has been paid, its burden (abala) has been lifted." Al-ibbāla is a bundle of firewood.
أبن:
The letters hamza, bā' and nūn point to mentioning [someone], to knots, and to following after a thing.

1. al-uban — knots in wood. A poet said, in a line of verse: a branch of sarā'-wood, with few knots.
2. al-uban — [also] enmities.
3. "fulānun yu'banu bi-kadhā" — so-and-so is spoken of with such-and-such, meaning he is blamed for it. And it is related, describing the Messenger of God's gathering, peace be upon him and his family: "in it, women under protection are not spoken ill of" — meaning they are not mentioned with blame.
4. al-ta'bīn — praising a man after his death. A poet said, in a line of verse: by my life, it is not my habit to eulogize the dead, nor to grieve wildly over what has struck and pained me.
5. "hādhā ibbānu dhālika" — this is the ibbān of that, meaning its proper time.
6. And one says: abbantu atharahu — I followed his trace; and abbantu al-shay' — I watched the thing closely. Aws said, in a line of verse: those who see him say: that is a rider, watching a figure standing on high ground.
أبه: The letters hamza, bā' and hā' point to being noticed/prominent and to loftiness. "Mā abahtu bihi" — I did not take notice of it, meaning I did not know its whereabouts and was not acquainted with it. And al-ubbaha is majesty.
أبو:
The letters hamza, bā', and wāw point to nurturing and feeding. Abawtu al-shay'a ābūhu abwan means I fed it; the father is named ab from this. In the relative adjective from ab, one says abawiyy. A she-goat is abwā' when pain strikes her from smelling the urine of wild goats.

Al-Khalīl said: al-ab is well known, plural ābā' and ubuwwa. A poet said:
I spare Nizār of Syria — for their Nizār ... is the fatherhood of my fathers, and I am the pillar of it.
He said: you say ta'abbaytu aban, I took a father for myself, just as tabannaytu ibnan and ta'ammahtu umman. He said: in poetry it is permissible to say hādhāni abāka [these two are your father], meaning abawāka [your two fathers], and ra'aytu abīka, meaning abawayka. A poet said:
And he is redeemed by the two fathers and the maternal uncle.
In the plural, abūna is also permitted; hā'ulā'i abūkum means ābā'ukum.

Abū 'Ubayd: mā kunta aban wa-laqad abayta ubuwwatan [you were not a father, but you have become one]. Abawtu al-qawma means I was a father to them. A poet said:
We lead them and we father them all together ... just as leather straps are cut from a single hide.
Al-Khalīl said: fulānun ya'bū al-yatīm, meaning he nurtures the orphan as a father nurtures his own child.
أبي:
The letters hamza, bā', and yā' point to refusal. Abaytu al-shay'a ābāhu [I refused the thing]. A people are abiyyūn or ubāt [refusers, proud of spirit]. A poet said:
One who refuses humiliation, from a people who refuse it too.
Al-ibā' is: you offer a man a thing and he refuses to accept it, so you say mā hādhā al-ibā', with either damma or kasra, following the Arab pattern for words of the form fa'ala yaf'alu.

1. Al-abiyya, among camels, is the intractable one.
2. Al-Liḥyānī said: a man is abayān when he refuses things; mā'un ma'bāt, on the pattern of ma'bāh, means water the camels refuse to drink.
3. Ibn al-Sikkīt said: akhadhahu abā'un, when he refuses food.
4. Abū 'Amr said: al-awābī, among camels, are the ḥiqāq, the jidhā', and the thinnā' — when the stallion mounts one and she does not conceive, she is called āwābī until she conceives once; after that she is no longer called that. Its singular is ābiya.
5. It would not be far-fetched that al-ubā' follows this same pattern — a pain that afflicts goats from smelling the urine of wild goats. A poet said:
So I said to Kannāz, "Dismount!" for indeed ... it is an affliction — I do not think the sheep are free of it.
6. Al-abā' is the tips of reed-canes, singular abā'a; then the reed-thicket itself came to be called abā'a, just as a thicket is called arāka. A poet said:
The brother of the reed-thicket, when he saw his companions ... lying in ranks around him, like idhkhir grass.
It is also possible he meant by al-abā'a spears, likening them to reeds for their abundance. A poet said:
Whoever is pleased by a striking that scatters its parts, one against another ... like the crackling of burning reeds.
أت: Ibn Durayd said: attahu ya'uttuhu — when he overcame him in speech, or silenced him with argument. Nothing else has come in this chapter, and I take the hamza to be converted from an 'ayn.
أتب:
The letters hamza, tā' and bā' are a single root, and it is something the armpit is wrapped in — a garment [shift] not stitched at the two sides.

1. al-itb — Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse: one of those women of modest gaze, such that if a year-old ant crept over her shift, it would leave a mark. Al-Aṣma'ī said: it is the same as al-baqīra — a cloak that is taken and slit, then a woman throws it over her neck, without sleeves or an opening for the head. Abū Zayd said: attabtu al-mar'ata u'attibuhā — I dressed the woman in the itb.
2. Al-Shaybānī said: al-ta'attub is when a man puts the strap of his bow across his chest and slips his shoulders out of it, so that the bow rests on his shoulder-blades.
3. Al-Numayrī said: al-mi'tab is a wrap; he "ta'attaba" it when he threw it under his armpit and then wrapped himself in it.
4. And rajulun mu'attab al-ẓahr, also mu'tab — one whose back is bent forward, stooped. A poet said, in a line of verse: on a young, still-suckling [creature], its back stooped. (The animal named here is unclear in the text.)
أتل:
The letters hamza, tā' and lām point to a single root, and it is slowness and sluggishness.

1. Abū 'Ubayd said: al-atalān is taking short, close steps in anger; one says atala ya'tilu, and atana ya'tinu. He recited, in a line of verse: I find that I never come to you except as if I had done wrong — or else you are angry, taking short angry steps.
2. It is also a sluggish, heavy walk. He recited, in a line of verse: what is wrong with you, O she-camel, that you plod slowly with me across al-Dahnā', lagging behind?
3. Abū 'Alī al-Aṣfahānī said: atala ya'tilu utūlan — the man lagged behind and fell back. A poet said, in a line of verse: and I filled its belly until it grew heavy and lagged.
أتم:
The letters hamza, tā' and mīm point to one part of a thing joining together with another part.

1. al-atam, in stitching, is when two stitched holes tear open and become one.
2. From this comes al-mar'a al-atūm — a woman who has been torn through, her two passages having become one.
3. Abū 'Amr said: al-utum is a variant form of al-'utum, the wild olive tree.
4. And one says: atama bi'l-makān — he dwelt in the place; and al-atam [is also said to mean] dwelling.
5. al-ma'tam — women gathering together, whether for a happy or a sad occasion; so said al-Qutabī, and he recited, in a line of verse: a gentle, deliberate woman of Rabī'a ibn 'Āmir struck him [with love], one who sleeps late into the morning, amid a gathering of women, what a gathering! He means: among women, what women!

And Ru'ba said, in a line of verse: when its gathering of owls calls out over the hard flat ground, it sets the caves echoing, its dull-voiced ones calling to each other. He likened the owls to women wailing in mourning. His words "it set the caves echoing" mean that when the owls call, they set the caves echoing back in answer — that is the sound you hear from a mountain or a cave after your own voice.
أتن:
The letters hamza, tā' and nūn are a single root, and it is the female donkey, or something to which this name was applied by borrowing.

1. Al-Khalīl said: al-atān — the she-ass, well known; its plural al-utun. Ibn al-Sikkīt said: one says "this is an atān" and "three ātun," and the plural is utun, or utn in the lightened form; the form atāna is not permitted, because atān is a noun reserved for the female alone. Abū 'Ubayd said: ista'tana fulānun atānan — so-and-so acquired a she-ass for himself. And of a [male] donkey mistaken for or treated as a she-ass, one says ista'tana al-ḥimār.
2. al-ma'tūnā' — she-asses [collectively].
3. atān al-ḍaḥl — a large rock standing in shallow water, covered over with algae. Aws said, in a line of verse: with a sturdy she-camel, like the rock in shallow water, hardened by the black water-plants gnawing it, as if pounded with a crushing-stone.
4. Yūnus said: al-atān is the standing-place of the water-drawer at the mouth of the well.
5. Al-Naḍr said: al-atān — the base of a camel-litter, its plural al-utun.

Abū 'Ubayd said: al-atanān is taking short steps in anger; one says atana ya'tinu. But this does not belong to this root, because the nūn stands in for a lām, and the original form is al-atalān, already discussed [under the root for slowness].
أته: The letters hamza, tā' and hā' — it is said that al-ta'attuh is pride and haughty self-conceit.
أتو:
The letters hamza, tā', wāw, alif and yā' point to a thing's coming, its keeping company, and its yielding.

1. al-atw — going straight and steadily in one's course; one says atā al-ba'īru ya'tū, the camel went steadily. A poet said, in a line of verse: they set out trusting, following it from behind however it went steadily, swift, easy in its swaying gait, hard-striking. And one says: how fine is the steady motion of its forelegs in its gait. Muzāḥim said, in a line of verse: there is no reaching stride like its stride when it goes away, and no steady pace like its pace when it comes toward you.
2. And the Arabs say: atawtu fulānan in the sense of "I came to him." A poet said, in a line of verse: O my people, what is between me and Abū Dhu'ayb — I used to come to him from a distant absence.
3. Al-Ḍabbī said: of a waterskin, when it is churned, one says "its flow has come."
4. Al-Khalīl: al-itāwa — tax, and a bribe, and a fee paid for a task, and any levy apportioned among a people and collected from them in this way. A poet said, in a line of verse: they pay the tribute, humbled. He recited, in a line of verse: in every market of Iraq there is a tribute, and on everything a man sells, a toll of a dirham. Al-Aṣma'ī said: one says atawtuhu atwan — I gave him the tribute.
أتي:
You say: so-and-so came to me [atānī] — one act of coming is itiyānan, atyan, atyatan, or atwatan, but one does not say itiyānatan for a single instance except under a poet's necessity, and that is a poor use. This is because verbal nouns, when made to denote a single instance, are formed back onto the pattern of their verb — that is, when the verb is on the pattern fa'ala. But when extra letters enter the verb beyond that, their extra letters are carried into the singular verbal noun too, as in our saying iqbālatan wāḥidatan [a single approach].

A poet said, about al-atī, in a line of verse:
Indeed I, and Ibn Ghallāq's coming to host me ... am like one feeling a dog for fatness, hoping to find marrow in its tail.

Al-Liḥyānī reported the form itiyānatan as also used.

1. Abū Zayd said: one says tinī bi-fulānin, meaning "bring so-and-so to me" [i'tinī]; for two people, tiyānī bihi; for a group, tūnī bihi; to a woman, tīnī bihi; to a group of women, tīnananī.
2. I approached the matter [atū al-amr] from its proper approach [ma'tāhu] and its proper way [ma'tātihi]. He said, in a line of verse:
And a need I spent the night keeping silent over ... I approached it alone, by its proper way.
3. Al-Khalīl said: I "ātaytu" so-and-so regarding his affair — mu'ātāt — meaning good compliance with him. One does not say wātaytahu except in an ugly dialect found in Yemen. Forms like āsaytu, ākaltu, āmartu, ākhaytu are only turned into wāw-forms by lightening the hamza, as in yuwākilu, yuwāmiru, and the like.
4. Al-Liḥyānī said: "You did not come to us until we ista'taynāka [pressed you to come]" — meaning we found you slow in coming and asked you to come.
5. One says ta'atta li-hādhā al-amr, meaning: go gently about this matter.
6. Al-ītā' is giving. You say ātā yu'tī ītā'an.
7. You say hāti in the sense of āti [give, bring], on the pattern fā'il, the hā' having replaced the alif.
8. You say ta'attā li-fulānin amruhu — his affair came right for him — and God atta-hu ta'tiyatan, made it come right for him. From this comes the saying:
And time came right for him [tatā] until he recovered.
This is a lightened form of ta'attā. Labīd said:
With a well-strung bow, whose grip her thumb managed easily.
9. Al-Khalīl said: al-atiyy is what falls into a river — wood or leaves — and dams up the water. You say atti li-hādhā al-mā', meaning: clear the way for this water to flow. Among common people al-atiyy is the channel that carries water to the trough; its plurals are al-utiyy and al-ātā'.
10. Al-atiyy also means a flood that comes from a land other than your own. Al-Nābigha said:
She let go the path of a flood-channel that had been holding it back ... and raised it up to the two curtains, then the piled goods.
Some said he meant the channel of the nu'ā [the trench dug round a tent against rain], which is its course; others said he meant whatever dams the channel — leaves or grass. I attaytu for the water — tatiyatan — when I directed a channel for it.
11. Al-Liḥyānī: a man is atiyy when he is effective, gets things done.
12. Al-Khalīl said: a man is atiyy, meaning a stranger among a people, not one of them; and atāwiyy means the same. Al-Aṣma'ī recited:
Do not ever equate strangers, buffeted by a cold shifting wind ... with the people settled at home.
In the hadith of Thābit ibn al-Daḥdāḥ: "He is only a stranger [atiyy] among us."
13. Al-itā' is the growth or yield of crops and palms. One says nakhlun dhū itā'in, meaning palms with good yield. Al-Farrā' said: the land and the palms atat atwan [yielded well], and the water atā itā'an, meaning it increased. He said, in a line of verse:
Some talk has no substance to hold it together ... like a flood of water that leaves no increase behind.
Another said:
There I do not care for irrigated palms, nor rain-fed ones ... however great their yield.
أث:
This chapter branches from gathering together and softness, and it is a single root.

1. aththa l-nabtu athan — Ibn Durayd said: the plant grew thick and abundant.
2. nabtun athīth — a thick plant; and anything pressed down and matted is athīth; it has been athtitha ta'thīthan.
3. athāth al-bayt — the household furnishings, from this. It is said its singular is athātha; it is also said it has no singular of its own root.

The rajaz-poet said, concerning al-athīth, in a line of verse:
They beat down its thick growth until you see its standing stalks uprooted.

Meaning: torn out, uprooted.

4. nisā'un athā'ith — women plump and soft of flesh.

He cited, in a line of verse:
Among what I love are the heavy, plump women, whose haunches, sunk in the soft ground, make them sway. [uncertain: the exact sense of "al-awā'ith" here]

Concerning al-athāth, al-Thaqafī said, in a line of verse:
Did the litters stir your longing, the day they departed, with their fine adornment of furnishings?

This is how the line is transmitted in Mu'jam al-Buldān (307:8:8), but in Lisān [al-'Arab] (19:8) it reads: bi-dhī l-ra'yi — and al-ra'y is whatever good state and visible fine clothing the eye takes in. Al-Mubarrid noted, in al-Kāmil (377), that bi-dhī l-ra'yi is the correct transmission.
أثر:
The letters hamza, thā', and rā' have three roots: putting a thing before another, reporting a thing, and the lasting mark a thing leaves behind.

Al-Khalīl said: laqad athirtu bi-an af'ala kadhā, meaning I have resolved and set my mind to do such-and-such. You say: if'al yā fulānu hādhā āthiran mā, and āthira dhī athīrin, meaning: even if you have chosen that other act, do this one anyway, come what may. Ibn al-A'rābī said: its meaning is do it before anything else. 'Urwa ibn al-Ward said:
And they said, "What do you wish?" and I said, "To take my ease" ... until the morning, first thing of all.
Al-āthir is on the pattern fā'il. As for 'Umar's hadith: "I have not sworn, since that, either āthiran or dhākiran" — he means by āthiran: reporting from someone else that he swore by it, that is, he did not say "So-and-so said, by my father, I will surely do such-and-such", from your saying atharu al-ḥadītha [I relate the report], and ḥadīthun ma'thūr [a transmitted report]; and "nor dhākiran" means: I did not mention that of myself.

1. Al-āthir, said by al-Khalīl, is what wears down the callus of a camel's foot.
2. Al-athīr, among beasts, is the one whose track in the ground, from its pad or hoof, is deep and large.
3. Al-athar, said by al-Khalīl, is what remains visible of anything, or what is no longer visible after some trace of it lingers; al-athār is the same word, like al-falāḥ and al-falaḥ, or al-sadād and al-sadad.
4. Athar al-sayf is the stroke of a sword. They say: "Who will buy my sword, and here is its mark?" — said proverbially of the tried and tested.
5. Al-mi'thara is a knife used to mark the underside of a camel's footpad, so that wherever it goes it may be known by its mark; plural al-ma'āthir.
6. Al-athar, said by al-Khalīl, also means pursuit and following; it has two forms, athar and ithr, and no verb is derived from it in this sense — one says dhahabtu fī itrihi [I went in pursuit of him]. They say: "She leaves the source and pursues the trace" — said of one who leaves the easy path for the hard one.
7. Al-athīr is the one dear to you, whom you favour [tu'thiruhu] with your bounty; a woman is athīra, verbal noun al-athara — "'indanā athara" [we hold him dear]. Abū Zayd said: a man is athīr on the pattern fa'īl, plural athīrūn, described as bayyin al-athara; another plural of al-athīr is uthara'. Al-Khalīl said: istaathara Allāhu bi-fulānin means he died while there is hope for him of Paradise; in the hadith: "When God claims something for Himself, then leave it be" — meaning: if He forbids something, abandon it. Abū 'Amr ibn al-'Alā': akhadhtu dhālika bi-lā atharatin 'alayka, meaning I did not favour myself over you in it. A man is athur, on the pattern fa'ul, meaning one who favours himself over his companions. Al-Liḥyānī said: akhadhtuhu bi-lā uthrā 'alayka, and recited:
So I said to him, "O wolf, is there in you a brother ... who shares equally, without favouring himself over you, and without stinginess?"
In the hadith: "You will see after me a favouring of self" — meaning those who keep the spoils for themselves. Ibn al-A'rābī said: āthartuhu bi-l-shay'i īthāran, and it is al-athara and al-ithra, plural al-ithar. A poet said:
They did not favour you with it, when they put you forward for it ... no, rather, for themselves was the favouring.
8. Al-athāra is a remnant left over from a thing, plural athārāt; from this comes God's saying, Almighty: {Or a remnant of knowledge} [al-Aḥqāf: 4]. Al-Aṣma'ī said: al-ibilu 'alā athāratin means the camels are on old stored fat. A poet said:
And one with stored fat, that has grazed upon ... fresh growth, still in its sheaths, doubled over.
9. Al-Khalīl said: al-athr in a sword is something like what is called al-firind [the watered pattern]; a sword is called ma'thūr for this. One says atharat al-sayfa āthuruhu athran, meaning I polished it until its pattern showed. Al-Farrā': al-athar is also said with a short vowel. He recited:
The sword-polishers polished them and brought them out ... so they all came showing their pattern.
He said al-Farrā' used to say athar al-sayf with the vowel-movement, and would recite:
As though they were white Yemeni swords ... clean their edges, their pattern still holding.
Al-Naḍr said: al-ma'thūra, among wells, are those dug in secret before you, then buried over, and you happened upon them and saw the traces of the ropes and cords — that is al-ma'thūra. Al-Kalbī related: uthirtu bi-hādhā al-makān, meaning I stayed fixed there. And he recited:
If you wish, let there be God's protection between us ... and the greatest of pledges, and a covenant of shelter — a truce; then I turned away and did not leave ... my young she-camel with any ill remaining behind her.
Abū 'Amr said: ṭarīqun ma'thūr means a path with a fresh track. Abū 'Ubayd said: when the milk separates from the butter and is drawn off clear, it is called al-uthr. Al-Aṣma'ī said it is al-uthr with a damma; Ya'qūb said it with a kasra; its plural is al-uthūr. A poet said:
They come away content, all of them ... at my command, whether I command or merely advise. And you are always put last in every affair ... the full milk-skins and the buttermilk keep you occupied.
Tuwāribuka means: they concern/press you, from al-arab, meaning need. Al-jawāzim are skin-vessels filled with milk.
أثف:
The letters hamza, thā' and fā' point to gathering together and to firmness.

Al-Khalīl said: one says ta'aththaftu bi'l-makān — I settled and stayed in the place; and athafa al-qawmu ya'thifūna — the people held back and fell behind. And ta'aththafa al-qawmu — the people gathered together. Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse: even if enemies gathered round you with aid — meaning they surrounded you on every side, becoming like the three stones set around a cooking pot.

1. al-uthfiyya — a stone set up for a cooking pot to stand on [one of a set of three]. One says qidrun muthaffāh — a pot set on its stones. And they also say mu'aththafa, though muthaffāh is the more familiar, more widely used form. Some Arabs say mu'athfāh, sounding like the pattern muf'alāh, though its true grammatical shape is mu'af'ala: athfā yuthfā follows the pattern af'ala yuf'alu, but speakers sometimes drop the alif that af'ala yu'af'alu would properly keep, because af'ala has already been carried out of the three-letter root pattern into a four-letter one. The same thing happens with kisā'un mu'arnab, a cloak lined with rabbit fur [arnab]: there they keep the alif that belongs to arnab itself (on the af'ala pattern), and instead drop the hamza of mu'af'al. And rajulun mu'anmal describes a man with thick fingertips. A poet said, in a line of verse: and stones set glowing over the fire, just as cooking-stones are set up as a hearth. Abū 'Ubayd said: it is also said ithfiyya, with the i-vowel.
2. Abū Zayd said: al-athāfī [in the sky] are stars positioned opposite the "head of the pot" [a constellation], just like the stones set round a pot; and al-qidr, "the pot," is also the name of a circle of stars.
3. Al-Farrā' said: al-muthaffāh is a branding mark shaped like the three cooking-stones; it is also called al-athāfī.
4. He said: and one says imra'atun muthaffāh — a woman whose three husbands have died [leaving her three times a widow]; and rajulun muthaffan — a man who has married three women in succession.
5. Abū 'Amr: athafahu ya'thifuhu — he pursued him. He said: al-athif is one who follows a people; one says "marra ya'thifuhum wa-yuthaffīhim" — he passed by, following them. Abū Zayd said: athafahu ya'thifuhu — he drove him off.

Ibn al-A'rābī said, quoting a saying: "there remains of the sons of so-and-so a rough uthfiyya" [a hard core] — said when a large number of them remains, a formidable body of people.

6. Abū 'Amr said: al-mu'aththaf, among men, is the short, broad, fleshy one. He recited, in a line of verse: not one to be humbled by the cold — thick-set, fat with his own flesh.
أثل:
The hamza, thā' and lām indicate the root/base of a thing, and its being gathered together.

1. Al-Khalīl said: al-athl — a tree resembling the tamarisk, but larger than it, and better in its wood, from which fine drinking-bowls are made.
2. Abū Ziyād said: al-athl — one of the thorn-trees, tall and reaching upward, with long, fine fronds and no thorns.

The Arabs say, "He is fond of whittling at his athla," meaning he is fond of running him down and reviling him. Al-Aʿshā said:
Will you not stop whittling at our athla? You do it no harm, so long as the camels [still] creak.

3. Al-Khalīl said: athala, ta'thīlan — so-and-so's wealth grew abundant and his standing improved.
4. al-muta'aththil — one who piles up wealth upon wealth.
5. athala Allāhu mulkaka — may God "athala" your rule, meaning magnify it and increase it.

A line:
He built up a great dominion of Khindif's line.

6. Abū ʿAmr said: al-athāl — glory, or wealth (Al-Aṣmaʿī gave the hamza both with i and with u).
7. athalat kulli shay' — the athala of anything is its root.
8. ta'aththala fulān — so-and-so acquired a foundation of wealth.
9. al-muta'aththil, among the branches of a tree, is the thick, luxuriant one.

A line:
And the root grows its branch thick and luxuriant, while the fingertips of the palm are not all equal.

10. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: athaltu ʿalayhi al-duyūn, ta'thīlan — I piled up debts against him, meaning I heaped them upon him.
11. athaltuhu bi-rijāl — I strengthened him with men, meaning I increased his numbers through them.

Al-Akhṭal said:
Do you revile a people who strengthened you through [the tribe of] Nahshal? Had it not been for them, you would have been mere dependents, like [the tribe of] ʿUkl.

12. ta'aththaltu li-l-shitā' — I "ta'aththaltu" for winter, meaning I made ready for it.
13. Abū ʿUbayda said: Uthāl is the name of a mountain.

Ibn al-Aʿrābī, on the line:
Kaʿb piles the debt upon me — but my Lord will change how it plays out.
said: tu'aththilu means she fastens it upon me.

14. Ibn al-Aʿrābī and Al-Aṣmaʿī said: ta'aththaltu al-bi'r — I dug the well.

Abū Dhu'ayb said:
They had sent their advance-party ahead, and they dug out a well, drawing its water like elderly slave-women [at their work].

This fits the pattern of the root, because that is bringing out what had already been laid up within it.
أثم:
The letters hamza, thā', and mīm point to a single root, which is slowness and lagging behind. One says nāqatun āthimatun, a she-camel that lags behind. Al-A'shā said:
When the lagging she-camels lie about the midday heat.
Al-ithm [sin] is derived from this, because the one who commits sin lags behind and is slow in reaching what is good.

Al-Khalīl said: athima fulānun means he fell into sin; when he restrains himself and holds back from it, one says ta'aththama, just as ḥarija means he fell into constraint and taḥarraja means he kept himself far from constraint. Abū Zayd said: a man is athīm or athūm.

Some people related from al-Akhfash — though I do not know how sound this is — that al-ithm means wine, and on this basis he explained God's word, Almighty: {Say: My Lord has only forbidden shameful acts, what is apparent of them and what is hidden, and sin} [al-A'rāf: 33]. And they recited:
I drank the ithm until my reason went astray ... that is what ithm does to reason.
If this is sound, then it follows the same pattern, because wine casts the one who drinks it into sin.
أثن: The letters hamza, thā' and nūn are not a root; only one word came into it by substitution of letters. They say al-uthun as a variant form of al-wuthun [idol]. And they say al-uthna is a thicket of ṭalḥ-trees [acacia]. We stipulated, at the start of this book of ours, that we would reason by analogy only from sound, established speech.
أثوى: The letters hamza, thā', wāw and yā' are a single root, in which the wāw and yā' intermix. They say athā 'alayhi ya'thī — he informed against him, slandered him. And they recite, in a line of verse: and I will not be for you a tale-bearer, a slanderer. Al-nayrab is tale-bearing. And a poet said, in a line of verse: indeed a man who slanders the chiefs of his own people deserves, by my life, to be blamed and reviled.
أج:
Hamza and jīm have two origins: a rustling sound, and intensity — whether of heat or of saltiness.

1. ajja l-ẓalīm, ajīj, and ajj — the male ostrich ran; that is when you hear the rustle of its running.
2. al-ajīj — the roar of the smith's bellows, from the rustle of the fire.

The poet said, describing a she-camel, in a line of verse:
So she went off in the evening, the tips of the waymarker-stones standing raised, roaring as the startled ostrich roars.

Another said, describing a horse, in a line of verse:
As if the coming and going of his breath were the roar of a blazing fire driven on by the north wind.

3. ajjat al-qawm — the rustle of people's walking and the mingling of their talk. All this from Ibn Durayd.
4. al-mā' al-ujāj — salty water. Some said: al-ujāj is water that is hot, blazing, ablaze — from ta'ajjajati l-nār, the fire blazed.
5. al-ajja — intense heat. From it one says i'tajja l-nahār i'tijājan, the day grew fiercely hot.

Ḥumayd said, in a line of verse:
And the flame of strife blazes fiercely.

Dhū l-Rumma said, concerning al-ajja, in a line of verse:
Until, when the roaring heat of summer rose against him, with a fierce heat that made the water and the moist dates sizzle.

'Ubayd ibn Ayyūb al-'Anbarī said, mourning a cousin of his, in a line of verse:
I was away and did not witness it; had I been present, it would have eased the roaring blaze of my heart.
أجأ: Ajā' — a mountain belonging to [the tribe of] Ṭayy'. And we have already said that the names of places can scarcely be reasoned about by analogy. A poet said, about Ajā', in a line of verse: and from Ajā', around me, are mountain-ridges, as if they were troops of horses, some bay, some chestnut-red.
أجح: The letters hamza, jīm and ḥā' are a branch form, not a root, because the hamza in it stands in for a wāw. So al-ujāḥ is a screen, and its true origin is wujāḥ, already discussed under the letter wāw.
أجد: The letters hamza, jīm and dāl are a single root, and it is something bound together — for al-ijād is the arch that is built into a structure; and for this reason a she-camel is called ujud [firmly knit]. Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse: so turn away from what you see, since there is no bringing it back, and carry the saddle-frame on a sturdy, firmly-knit she-camel. And one says: she is mu'jadat al-qarā, firm-backed. Ṭarafa said, in a line of verse: reddish-brown of beard, firm of back, long-striding in her hind leg, swift-moving in her foreleg. And it is also said that she is one whose spine is as firm as a single bone without a joint. This is something the scholars of language all agree on.
أجر:
The letters hamza, jīm, and rā' are two roots that can be joined in meaning: the first is payment for work, the second is the setting of a broken bone.

As for payment: it gives al-ajr and al-ujra. Al-Khalīl used to say: al-ajr is recompense for work; the verb is ajara ya'juru ajran, and the one paid is ma'jūr. Al-ajīr is the one hired. Al-ujāra is what you give as wages for work. Others said: from this too comes a woman's bridal payment, for God Almighty says: {Give them their wages} [al-Nisā': 24].

As for the setting of a bone: one says ujirat yaduhu [his hand was set/healed]; some say ajarat yaduhu.

These, then, are the two roots. What joins them is that a worker's wage is, as it were, a thing by which his condition is "set right" for the toil that befell him in his work.

Al-ijjār [flat rooftop] is a Syrian word, though the people of the Ḥijāz sometimes used it too. It is related that the Messenger of God, God bless him and his family and grant him peace, said: "Whoever spends the night on a rooftop with nothing to keep his feet from falling is free of any claim of protection." We have not counted it among words of this chapter's pattern, since it is not speech of the desert Arabs — some people even say injār instead, which further weakens its standing. If someone should ask: how can this be, when the Messenger of God himself used it? The answer is: this is like his saying, "Rise, for Jābir has made you a sūr" — and sūr is a Persian word for a wedding feast. If you find the word in poetry, the same explanation applies. Abū Bakr ibn Durayd recited:
Like Abyssinians ranked upon a rooftop.
He likened the necks of the horses to Abyssinians standing in a row on a rooftop, looking out.
أجص: The letters hamza, jīm and ṣād are not a root, because nothing came from this pattern except al-ijjāṣ [the plum]. And it is said that it is not an Arabic word, since the jīm rarely occurs together with the ṣād.
أجل:
Know that the letters hamza, jīm, and lām point to five distinct words that can scarcely be traced to one another by any common pattern — each is a root in itself, and your Lord does what He wills.

1. Al-ajal is the furthest point of a time set for a debt or anything else. Al-Khalīl gave its full conjugation: ajila hādhā al-shay'u, ya'jalu; the noun is al-ājil, opposite of al-'ājil [the immediate]; al-ajīl is what is deferred, put off to a later time. A poet said:
And the furthest point of what is deferred is the pit of ruin.
Their word ajal, used in answering ["yes, indeed"], belongs to this chapter too, as though the speaker means: it has come to its end, reached its furthest point.

2. Al-ijl is a herd of wild cattle, plural ājāl. Ta'ajjala al-ṣuwār means the herd formed into a group.

3. Al-ajl is the verbal noun of ajala 'alayhim sharran, he brought evil upon them and dug it up for them. Khawwāt ibn Jubayr said:
And a household of a righteous family, between whom ... they had fought, over an immediate wrong that I brought upon them — meaning: I who brought it upon them.

4. Al-ijl is a pain in the neck. It is related from Abū al-Jarrāḥ: "I have an ijl, so treat me [ajjilūnī]" — meaning: cure me of it.

5. Al-ma'jal is something like a wide trough into which the water of a well or channel is gathered for some days, then let out to flood the crops; plural ma'ājil. They say ajjil li-nakhlatika, meaning: make for your palm-tree something like a trough.

These are the roots. Two words remain. One belongs to letter-substitution: their saying ajalū māhum ya'jilūnahu ajlan, meaning they withheld it, whose true root is with the letter zā': azalūhu. It is possible that this word and ma'jal al-mā' share one derivation, since water too is "held back" in it.

The other is their saying min ajli dhālika fa'altu kadhā [because of that, I did such-and-such], carried on the pattern of ajaltu al-shay'a, I brought it about — so its meaning is [from] an ujila kadhā fa'altu, that is, from what was brought about.

As for Ajalā, on the pattern fa'lā, this is a place-name, and place-names are for the most part simply given, not derived by pattern. A poet said:
Sulaymā alighted at the side of al-Jarīb ... at Ajalā, the encampment of the stranger.
أجم:
The letters hamza, jīm and mīm never stray from gathering together and intensity.

1. As for gathering: al-ajama — a thicket where trees grow densely together; its plural al-ājām.
2. So too al-ujum — a fortress; and likewise uṭum and āṭām [same meaning]. In a hadith: "until she was hidden by the fortresses of Medina." Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse: and at Taymā', he left there no palm-trunk, nor any fortress, but built up firm with quarried stone. That is a place where building and people are gathered together.
3. As for intensity: their saying "ta'ajjama al-ḥarr" — the heat intensified. And from this: ajimtu al-ṭa'ām — I grew weary/sick of the food; that is a thing that weighs intensely on a person.
أجن: The letters hamza, jīm and nūn make a single word. Ajana al-mā' — the water went stale, and this is the correct, eloquent form. And sometimes they said it went stale in a different vowelling, and it [the water] is ajūn, stale. A poet said, in a line of verse: like a frog in stale water, croaking. As for al-mi'jana, the fuller's beating-stick, that has already been discussed under the letter wāw. And al-ijjān [a washtub] is a word the scholars of language scarcely vouch for as sound.
أح:
Hamza and ḥā' have a single origin, and it is the imitation of the sound of coughing and what resembles it — thirst and rage — all of it close to one another.

1. fī qalbī 'alayhi uḥāḥ — al-Kisā'ī said this means: rancor and enmity in my heart toward him.
2. al-uḥāḥ — al-Farrā' said: thirst.
3. sami'tu li-fulānin uḥāḥan wa aḥīḥan — Ibn Durayd said this is when one groans in pain from rage or grief.

He cited, in a line of verse:
He folds his ribs over his groaning rage.

4. Uḥayḥa — a man's name, derived from this.
5. aḥḥa aḥḥan — said to imitate the sound of coughing.

He said, in a line of verse:
From clearing his throat and coughing he all but mimics the cough of one choked and hoarse.

Some mentioned that it is also said with a long vowel: āḥ. He cited, in a line of verse:
As if the sound of her milk drawn out were the cough of an old man of Banū l-Julāḥ, who says, after coughing, 'āḥ'.
أحد: The letters hamza, ḥā', and dāl are a branch, whose true root is the letter wāw: waḥada [to be alone, one], already discussed under the letter wāw. Al-Duraydī said: mā ista'ḥadtu bi-hādhā al-amr means: I did not deal with it alone.
أحن:
The letters hamza, ḥā' and nūn are a single word. Al-Khalīl said: al-iḥna is the grudge held in the chest. Another recited, in a line of verse:
Whenever there is a grudge in your cousin's chest ... do not stir it up, its buried thing will one day show.
And another said, on the plural of iḥna, in a line of verse:
You were only ever a people among whom were grudges ... which you kept pursuing, would the pursuing ever end.
One says: aḥina ʿalayhi ya'ḥanu iḥnatan, he held a grudge against him. Abū Zayd said: āḥantuhu mu'āḥanatan, meaning I treated him as an enemy. And sometimes they said aḥina to mean he grew angry.
Know that the hamza does not combine with the ḥā' except in what we have mentioned here, because of how close these two letters are to one another.
أخ:
As for hamza and khā', they are two origins: one is groaning or aversion, and the other origin is a particular food.

1. akhkh — Ibn Durayd said: a word said when groaning. I take it to be a later coinage.
2. akhkh — it is also said this is a word uttered at feeling aversion to something.

He cited, in a line of verse:
And union with the fair women was an 'akhkh' [a thing shunned].

Dakhtanūs bint Laqīṭ was married to 'Amr ibn 'Amr ibn 'Udas, an old man; he laid his head in her lap and breathed as a sleeper breathes, and she said 'akhkh!' He said, 'akhkh, by God, at you!' — and he heard it, so he opened his eyes and divorced her. She then married 'Amr ibn Ma'bad ibn Zurāra. Horsemen of Bakr ibn Wā'il raided them and took her among those taken. The clan mounted, and 'Amr ibn 'Amr caught up and fought for her until he took her back, and said, as he returned with her, in a line of verse:
Which of your two husbands did you find better — the one huge in member and organ, or the one who advances on the armored warriors on foot?

She said: that one for that, and this one for this.

3. al-akhīkha — flour on which water is poured, then thinned with oil or clarified butter and drunk.

He said, in a line of verse:
The old man's belching after the akhīkha-gruel.
أخذ:
The letters hamza, khā', and dhāl are a single root from which branches spread that are close in meaning. As for akhadha: the origin sense is seizing a thing, collecting it, gathering it in. You say akhadhtu al-shay'a ākhudhuhu akhdhan. Al-Khalīl said: it is the opposite of giving, and it is taking hold. He said: al-ukhda is a charm that seizes the evil eye or the like. Al-mu'akhkhadh is a man whom a woman "seizes" from his own judgment and from other women, as though he were held back from them.

1. Al-ikhādha — though Abū 'Ubayd says al-ikhādh, without the tā' — is a gathering-place of water resembling a pool. Al-Khalīl said: because a person "takes" it for himself; it may also be called ikhādh because it is "taken" from water. Abū 'Ubayd and others recited, from 'Adī ibn Zayd describing rain:
So it filled it, like tufted wool, from the meadow ... and the pools did not stint the gathered water.
Its plural is ukhudh. Al-Akhṭal said:
So he stayed watching from a height while the pools had grown warm ... thinking the way to the pools was worn smooth.
Masrūq ibn al-Ajda' said: "I have likened the Companions of Muḥammad, God bless him and his family and grant him peace, to nothing but these gathered pools: one pool suffices a single rider, another suffices two riders, and another suffices a great crowd of people." This same pattern is used of diseases that "seize" upon things, and elsewhere too, though the underlying sense is one.

2. Al-ākhidh, said of camels, is one that has begun to put on fat; the plural is al-awākhidh. Al-Khalīl said: a camel is akhidha ya'khadhu akhdhan, so it is akhidh — a state resembling madness that seizes it; this also happens to sheep.

If someone should ask: this pattern has held true up to here, so what of ramad [eye-inflammation]? For it is said al-ukhudh means ramad and al-akhidh means one afflicted by it. The answer: diseases are named this way because they "seize" upon a person and take hold in him. The commentators on the poetry of Hudhayl, on Abū Dhu'ayb's line —
He casts his eyes at what is hidden from view, his gaze ... lowered, as one "seized" whose eyes are inflamed, droops —
meant that the wild donkey casts his eyes at everything that vanishes from him, his gaze lowered, like one "overtaken" whose inflammation has grown severe — that is, whose "seizing" by it has grown severe; the inflammation "took hold" [istakhadha] in him, so kasafa means he lowered his head, also said to mean he closed his eyes. This confirms that it is called ukhudh because the disease "takes hold" [yasta'khidh] in it. This word — istakhadha — is well known. Ibn Abī Rabī'a said:
To them — whenever sleep takes hold among them ... while I have a sitting-place, were it not for my longing, harder to bear.

3. Nujūm al-akhdh, the stars of "taking", are the mansions of the moon, following the same pattern, because the moon "takes" its place every night in one of these mansions. A poet said:
The stars of the "taking" failed to bring rain, except a faint one ... a faint one of a dry season, whose dripping brings no increase.
أخر:
The letters hamza, khā', and rā' are a single root to which its branches return: it is the opposite of coming before. This is a principle taken from al-Khalīl, for he said: al-ākhir is the opposite of al-mutaqaddim [what comes first], and al-ukhur is the opposite of al-qudum: you say maḍā qudaman [he went forward] and ta'akhkhara ukhuran [he went back]. He said: a saddle has its ākhira [back part] and its qādima [front part], and its mu'akhkhar and its muqaddam. He said: the lightened form mu'khir occurs nowhere in their speech except in mu'khir al-'ayn and muqdim al-'ayn [the outer and inner corners of the eye].

From this same pattern: bi'tuka bay'an bi-akhiratin, meaning on deferred payment; mā 'araftuhu illā bi-akharatin, meaning I only came to know him later. Al-Khalīl said: fa'ala Allāhu bi-l-akhir, meaning may God do ill to the farthest-off one; ji'tu fī ukhrayātihim, ukhrā al-qawm [I came among the last of them]. A poet said:
I am the one born among the last of the camels.

Ibn Durayd says: al-ākhir follows after al-awwal [the first]. This is close to what has already been said, except that our saying qāla ākhiru al-rajulayni and qāla al-ākhiru fits Ibn Durayd's account better. Ukhar means: another group of things.
أخو: The letters hamza, khā', and wāw are not a root, because in our view the hamza here is substituted for a wāw; this has been discussed, with its explanation, in the chapter of the letter wāw. Al-ākhiya [a tethering-loop] is likewise from that root, not its own.
أد:
As for hamza and dāl in the doubled root, they are two origins: one is a thing's greatness, intensity, and recurrence; the other is bolting, fleeing.

1. al-idd — a monstrous, grave matter; that is the first.

God Almighty said: {you have brought forth a monstrous thing} [Maryam: 89], meaning something grave, of unbelief.

Ibn Durayd cited, in a line of verse:
O mother, I have undertaken a monstrous matter — I saw a man broad-armed, sturdy, fair, bright of brow, valiant, and I got from him a sip and a coolness.

Al-Khalīl cited, in a line of verse:
And we guard against indecency and vile things, and the gravest of grave matters, and the calamities. [uncertain: exact force of "al-idad al-idād"]

2. addati l-nāqa — the she-camel repeated her yearning-cry.
3. al-add — strength, said by Ibn Durayd, who cited, in a line of verse:
They stripped from me both vigor and strength, after I had been sturdy and stalwart.

That is the first origin. As for the second, Ibn Durayd said: addati l-ibil, when the camels bolted, fled.

As for Udd ibn Ṭābikha ibn Ilyās ibn Muḍar, Ibn Durayd said: the hamza in Udd is [really] a wāw, for it is from wudd, love, and it has been mentioned in its own chapter.
أدب:
The letters hamza, dāl and bā' are a single root whose branches all return to it. Al-adb is that you gather people to your food; it is called al-ma'daba and al-ma'duba. Al-ādib is the one who calls people to it.
Ṭarafa said, in a line of verse:
In the season of want we call out to everyone widely ... you will not see the caller among us holding anyone back.
Al-ma'ādib is the plural of al-ma'duba. A poet said, in a line of verse:
As if the hearts of the birds, deep in their nest ... were date-stones scattered by some of the feast-tables.
From this same reasoning comes al-adab too [refined conduct], because it is a thing everyone agrees is good. As for the ḥadīth of ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd, "This Qur'ān is God's banquet (ma'dubat Allāh), so learn from His banquet" — Abū ʿUbayd said: whoever says ma'duba means the feast a person prepares, calling people to it; from it one says adabtu ʿalā al-qawm ādibu adban, I hosted a feast for the people. He then mentioned Ṭarafa's line above, and then mentioned a line of ʿAdī's, in a line of verse:
Loud, its downpour answered by a drum ... for a feast-table's company, and a reed-pipe.
He said: and whoever says ma'daba is going by al-adab, treating it as a noun of place formed from it. And it is said: al-idb means wonder, astonishment — if that is so, it is because people gather together for it.
أدر:
The letters hamza, dāl and rā' are a single word: it is al-adra and al-adara, a hernia. One says adira ya'daru, and he is ādaru, hernia-afflicted.
A poet said, in a line of verse:
I was told that ʿUtba the shoemaker had threatened me ... how many a hernia-stricken fool there is, worse off than Maythā'.
أدل:
The letters hamza, dāl and lām are a single root from which two words branch that are close in meaning though far apart in outward appearance. Al-idl is sour milk. The Arabs say: he brought idla that cannot be borne [in sourness] — meaning because of how sour it is. Ibn al-Sikkīt said: al-Farrā' said, al-idl is a pain in the neck.
So the meaning, in being something disliked, is one and the same. And on Abū ʿUbayd's report there is a better line of reasoning than what we have given — indeed it is the true origin. Abū ʿUbayd said: when milk clots together, part upon part, without actually curdling apart, it is idl. This fits better with what al-Farrā' said, because pain in the neck can come from the veins pressing close together and twisting.
أدم:
The letters hamza, dāl, and mīm are a single root, and it is agreement and harmony. This is the sense of the Prophet's words, God bless him and his family and grant him peace, to al-Mughīra ibn Shu'ba, when he proposed to a woman: "Look at her, for it is more fitting that harmony be established between you two." Al-Kisā'ī said: yu'dam means love and accord come to be between them; one says adama ya'dimu adman. Abū al-Jarrāḥ al-'Uqaylī said the like.

Abū 'Ubayd said: I take this to be from adm al-ṭa'ām [the seasoning of food], because food's goodness comes from its seasoning; one says ṭa'āmun ma'dūm [seasoned food]. Ibn Sīrīn said, of the food for the expiation of an oath: "a seasoned meal, until they are satisfied." He said: some person of knowledge told me that Durayd ibn al-Ṣimma wished to divorce his wife, and she said: "O father of so-and-so, will you divorce me? By God, I have fed you my best-seasoned food and confided in you what I kept hidden, and I came to you free, with no previous tie." Abū 'Ubayd said: one also says ādama Allāhu baynahumā yu'dimu īdāman, so he is mu'dam baynahumā. The poet said:
And fair women give love only to one who is himself made lovable.

From this chapter too: ja'altu fulānan adamata ahlī, meaning I made him their equal, sound because it brings harmony between them. Al-adama is the means to a thing, because one at odds with another cannot use him as a means.

If someone should ask: on what basis do you derive al-adama, when it also means the inner layer of skin? Al-adama fits better against the flesh than does al-bashara [the outer skin], and for this Adam, peace be upon him, was named [Ādam], because he was taken from the adama of the earth [its fertile inner layer]. It is also said to mean the fourth layer of the earth. The Arabs say mu'dam mubshar, meaning one who combines the softness of the adama and the roughness of the bashara. As for the dark-brown colour, al-ādam, it is so called because it is the predominant colour among the children of Adam. Some say adīm al-arḍ and adamatuhā, meaning its surface.
أدو:
The letters hamza, dāl and wāw are a single word. Al-adw is like guile and cunning evasion. One says adā ya'dū adwan.
A poet said, in a line of verse:
I lay in wait for him, that I might seize him ... but no — the young man was too wary.
This is derived from al-adāh, a tool, because a tool performs works by which what is wanted is reached, and guile and deceit likewise perform works. Al-Khalīl said: the alif in al-adāh is without doubt a wāw, because its plural is adawāt. One says: a working man is mu'din, ʿāmil. And adāt [al-ḥarb] is the weapon.
A poet said, in a line of verse:
I pass by, resolved, with young men beside me ... some of them armed, and some bare-handed.
From this chapter also: istaʾdaytu ʿalā fulānin, meaning istaʿdaytu, I sought redress against so-and-so — as though you were asking, by it, for a means that would give you power over your adversary. And ādaytu fulānan means I helped him.
He said, in a line of verse:
I shall indeed bring you along, with a hard, driving pace.
أدي:
The letters hamza, dāl and yāʾ are one root: the reaching of a thing to another, or its arriving there of its own accord. Abū ʿUbayd said: the Arabs say of milk, when it reaches the state of curdling, that is, when it thickens: qad adā, yaʾdī, udyan. Al-Khalīl said: addā fulānun yuʾaddī mā ʿalayhi, adāʾan wa-taʾdiyatan, so-and-so discharged what was owed by him. You say: fulānun ādā li'l-amānati minka, so-and-so is more faithful in returning trusts than you. Another recited (the final word of this line I am not certain of — it may be a name):

He delivered to Hind her greetings ... and said: this is from my farewell
أذ:
As for hamza and dhāl, it is not a root — the hamza in it is converted from hā', and it has been mentioned under hā'.

1. adhdha ya'uddhu adhdhan — Ibn Durayd said: it means he cut, like hadhdha.
2. shafratun adhūdh — a sharply-cutting blade.

Al-Mufaḍḍal cited, in a line of verse:
He cuts with the blade, a fine cutting, of udder-teat and belly-fat and liver-lobe.
أذن:
The letters hamza, dhāl, and nūn are two roots close in meaning though far apart in form: one is the ear of anything that has an ear, the other is knowledge; the whole chapter branches from these two. Their closeness lies in this: it is by the ear that knowledge of everything heard comes about.

1. Al-udhun [ear] is well known and feminine. One who has an ear is ādhan, a female with an ear is adhnā'. Salama recited from al-Farrā':
Like the ostrich, while she was sound ... eared, until fate and madness overcame her (he meant al-junūn, madness). She came to buy a horn or replace it ... while time in it brings both the gain and the loss of a sale. So it was said: your two ears are a wrong, then they were cut off ... down to the ear-canal, so no horn, and no ear.
2. A man who listens to everyone is udhun. God Almighty said: {And among them are those who trouble the Prophet, saying, "He is an ear"} [al-Tawba: 61].
3. Al-udhun also means the handle of a jug — a metaphor.
4. Al-adhan means listening, said adhan because it comes about through the ear. Among what came as metaphor is the hadith: "God has not given ear to anything as He has given ear to a prophet chanting the Qur'an aloud." 'Adī ibn Zayd said:
O heart, distract yourself with idle pleasure ... my concern is in hearing and in listening.
And also:
And a hearing the old man gives ear to ... and talk like sweet wine, well told.

The other root is knowledge and informing. The Arabs say qad adhintu bi-hādhā al-amr, meaning I knew of it. Ādhananī fulānun means he informed me; the verbal noun is al-adhn and al-īdhān. Fa'alahu bi-idhnī means he did it with my knowledge — it may also mean with my permission, which is close to the same sense. Al-Khalīl said: from this comes udhina lī fī kadhā [I was given leave for such-and-such].

5. Al-adhān [the call to prayer] is the name for the act of calling, just as al-'adhāb is the name for the act of tormenting. Sometimes it is turned into the pattern fa'īl: adhīn. A poet said:
Until, when the call was cried out.
The correct account is that al-adhīn here is al-adhān, on the evidence already given. Al-adhīn also means the place the call reaches from every direction. A poet said:
Ground swept clean of gravel had become an open place ... and there was no suspicion in it, to be feared or doubted.
Al-adhīn also means the caller himself. The rajaz poet said:
So it recoiled from him upon her in a roar, utterly ... and the caller of the settlement did not call —
meaning the mu'adhdhin of the houses built of clay, mudbrick, and stone.

6. As for His saying, Almighty: {And when your Lord proclaimed: if you are grateful, I will surely increase you} [Ibrāhīm: 7] — al-Khalīl said: al-ta'adhdhun comes from your saying la-af'alanna kadhā, meaning by it the binding certainty of the act, that I will surely do it without fail. This is one opinion; clearer still is al-Farrā''s: ta'adhdhana rabbukum means your Lord made known. The Arabs sometimes use the pattern tafa''altu in the sense of af'altu; likewise aw'adanī and tawa''adanī [he threatened me] — this is common.

7. Ādhinu al-rajul is a man's chamberlain — this too belongs to the chapter.
أذي: The letters hamza, dhāl, and yā' are a single root, and it is a thing you find distasteful and cannot settle upon. You say ādhaytu fulānan ūdhīhi [I harmed so-and-so]. One says ba'īrun adhin and nāqatun adhiyatun, said of a camel that will not settle in one place though it is not in pain, as though it suffers [ya'dhā] from its place.
أر:
This chapter has a single origin, and it is a thing's being stirred up by kindling and heating.

1. al-arr — copulation. One says arrahā ya'urruhā arran. al-mi'arr — one much given to copulation.

Al-Aghlab said, in a line of verse:
She was joined with a heavy, virile stallion, thick of joints, and how sturdy a build!

2. al-arr — kindling fire. One says arra l-rajulu l-nāra, when he kindled it.

Abū l-Ḥasan 'Alī ibn Ibrāhīm al-Qaṭṭān recited to us — he said Tha'lab dictated to us —, in a line of verse:
A night-traveler's night stirred longing in a night-traveler, though it had all but passed or gone by ... as if a jealous, quarrelsome woman of al-Ḥīra had spent the night fanning a flame beneath him.

3. al-arr — treating a she-camel when her ability to bear young has stopped: a branch of qatād-thorn is taken and moistened, then salt is sprinkled on it, and her vulva is pricked with it until it bleeds. One says nāqatun ma'rūra, a she-camel so treated; and the thing used for the treatment is al-irār.
أرب:
The letters hamza, ra' and ba' have four origin senses that their branches go back to: need, intelligence, a share, and binding.

As for need: al-Khalil said: al-arab is need. "ma arabuka ila hadha" — what is your need for this. Al-ma'raba, al-ma'ruba and al-irba all mean need. God, Most High, said: {those male attendants who have no need of women} [an-Nur: 31]. And in the proverb: "need, not warm welcome" — meaning: it is need that brought you, not affection.

Al-irb is intelligence. Ibn al-A'rabi said: intelligence too is called irb and irba, just as need is called irba and irb. The adjective from al-irb is arib; the verb is aruba. Ibn al-A'rabi said: aruba the man, ya'rubu, irab — he grew intelligent. From this root too, success and skill at a thing: aribtu bi-shay' — I became skilled at it.

Qays said, in a line of verse:
I grew skilled at warding off war when I saw it — for all my warding off, it only drew nearer.

One says: arabtu 'alayhim — I triumphed over them. Labid said, in a line of verse:
And a young man's life is pledged to the stake of one skilled at the game.

From this root too, al-mu'araba — outwitting, cunning; so al-Khalil said. And likewise what came in the hadith: "to outwit the clever man is folly."

As for a share: it and a limb of the body belong to one root, since both are a part of a thing. Al-Khalil and others said: al-urba is the winner's share of the slaughtered camel, in the game of chance. Ibn Muqbil said, in a line of verse:
They do not rejoice when their winner wins — nor is the winner's own share ever kept from them.

And from this, what came in the hadith: "he was the most in command of you, of his irb" — meaning, of his limb. One says: a limb is mu'arrab — full of flesh, complete. Al-Kumayt said, in a line of verse:
And Yuhabir snatched out two limbs from it — while 'Abd al-Qays kept a limb full and whole.

Meaning: a generous share fell to them. One says: ariba — his limbs fell away from him (said as a curse). 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said to a man: "May your hands be cut off — do you ask me about a thing I myself asked the Messenger of God about?" One says ariba, from this.

As for binding and being strict: Abu Zayd said: aruba the man, ya'rubu — when he grew rigid, stingy and obstinate. From this root too, at-ta'rib — setting people against one another; one says arrabtu 'alayhim. ta'arraba fulanun 'alayna — so-and-so grew difficult and contrary toward us. Al-Asma'i said: ta'arrabtu fi hajati — I was firm and persistent in my need; arrabtu al-'uqda — I tightened the knot, one that does not come undone except by deliberate untying.

The collar of a horse or dog is called urba because it is knotted around its neck. Al-Mutalammis said, in a line of verse:
Were you a hunting dog, you would wear a collar — its knot fastened at the end of the leash.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: al-urba is the opposite of al-unshuta, the slip-knot — that is, it is a knot that holds fast. And he recited, in a line of verse:
And a firm knot, whose joints my cunning has mastered — no hasty knot of a fool, nor of the ill-tempered.

Al-Khalil said: al-musta'rib, among bowstrings, is the strong, excellent one. He said, in a line of verse: "from a firmly-twisted, well-drawn pull." As for Ibn Muqbil's line:
High-nosed men, whom the striking of the gambling-arrows, and their persistence over the stake, make forget to turn aside —

it was said this means: they complete their share; and it was said: they press hard over the stake. And he said, in a line of verse:
They do not rejoice when their winner wins — nor is their hard-won share ever kept from them.

Meaning: they are generous; no hardship comes upon them to spoil their affairs. Ibn al-A'rabi said: a man is arib when his affairs are firmly managed. From this root too, aribtu bi-kadha — I sought help by means of it. Aws said, in a line of verse:
And I mastered my cares by means of a sturdy, swift she-camel, not sluggish under a rider.

Al-lajun: the sluggish one. From this root too, al-urba, the extraordinary calamity — they said it is so named for the tightness of its knot, as if it cannot be undone. Ibn Ahmar said, in a line of verse:
When my night grew dark, and I was certain it was the great calamity — it came bringing with it the worst of disasters.

These, then, are the origin senses of this root. From one of them comes Irab, a place-name, after which "the Day of Irab" is named: the day al-Hudhayl ibn Hassan al-Taghlibi raided the Banu Yarbu' and attacked them. Of this al-Farazdaq said, in two lines of verse:
And it was as if the banners of Hudhayl, when they appeared above the army, were swooping eagles;
they came to Irab with a great host of Wa'il, loud at evening, strong against their rivals.

Then Jaz' ibn Sa'd ar-Riyahi raided, with the Banu Yarbu', against Bakr ibn Wa'il while they were away from camp, and took their captives and their goods. The two sides then met at Irab and made peace: Jaz' released what he held of Yarbu's captives and goods, and they let al-Hudhayl bring his horses and camels to the water. Of this day Jarir said, in a line of verse:
And we it was who caught up with Ibn Hisn and his kinsmen — and we it was who kept the captives from being taken, on the Day of al-Araqim.
أرث:
The letters hamza, rā' and thā' indicate the striking of fire, or the kindling of enmity. Al-Khalīl said: arrathtu al-nār, I struck it alight.
ʿAdī said, in a line of verse:
And she has a gazelle that kindles longing in her ... wearing, fastened at the throat, a necklace.
The noun is al-urtha. And in the proverb: "Slander is the kindling-stick of enmity." Al-Shaybānī said: al-irāth is what you stoke a fire with. He said: al-ta'arruth is bursting into flame.
A poet said, in a line of verse:
At the top of Dhū al-Majāza there stands a lone tree ... whose disgrace has long lain heavy on the people of al-Majāza.
And had they struck it with axes, and burned it ... at its root, until its fire caught and blazed.
One says arrith nāraka ta'rīthan, kindle your fire well. As for al-urtha, it is the boundary-line. As for al-irth, inheritance, it does not belong to this chapter, because its alif is a substitute for a wāw, and it has been dealt with in its own place. As for their saying naʿjatun arthā', it is a ewe whose white patches blaze out within her black, and this does belong to the chapter; it too is called al-urtha, and a ram of that colouring is ārath.
أرج:
The letters hamza, rā' and jīm are a single word: it is al-araj, which, along with al-arīj, is the scent of perfume.
Al-Hudhalī said, in a line of verse:
As if upon her there were a musk-pouch's fragrant scent ... a scent rising from between her two shoulder-blades.
أرخ:
The letters hamza, rā' and khā' are a single Arabic word: it is al-irākh, the wild cow.
Al-Khansā' said, in a line of verse:
And a wailing you sent up, like that of the wild cows ... the wide-eyed ones had set their young at ease.
As for ta'rīkh al-kitāb, dating a document, it has been heard in use, but it is not Arabic, nor has it been heard from anyone of pure eloquent speech.
أرز:
The letters hamza, rā' and zā' are a single root whose pattern never fails to hold: it is gathering together and pressing close. The Messenger of God, God bless him and his family and grant him peace, said: "Indeed Islam draws in toward Medina as the snake draws in to its hole." They say: so-and-so araza, when he shrinks into himself out of stinginess. Some of them used to say: "So-and-so, when asked, draws back — and when invited, seizes the chance." A man is arūz when he does not open himself up to generosity.
A poet said, in a line of verse:
That one is a miser, drawn tightly in upon himself.
Meaning that he does not open up, but rather draws part of himself against part. Al-Khalīl said: they say so-and-so reached the top of the mountain only drawn-in — meaning contracted, not stretching out in his stride, from the severity of his exhaustion; he has become exhausted and drawn-in. And they say a she-camel is āriza al-faqāra, drawn-in at the vertebrae, when they are firm and interlock one into another.
Zuhayr said, in a line of verse:
