With vertebrae drawn close and firm, not betrayed by ... any slackening on the journey, nor any emptiness of strength.
As for their calling a cold night āriza, this too is from the same, because the flank draws in upon itself from the cold.
أرس: The letters hamza, rā' and sīn are not Arabic. It is said that al-arārīs are the farmers, and that the word is Levantine.
أرش:
The letters hamza, rā' and shīn could be a root; some scholars of the language made it instead a branch, claiming that the true origin is al-harsh, and that the hamza stands in place of the hā'. This seems to me plausible, because these two letters — I mean the hamza and the hā' — are close to one another: they say iyyāka and hiyyāka, araqtu and haraqtu.
Whichever it is, the word belongs to the chapter of stirring up trouble. One says arrashtu al-ḥarb wa'l-nār, meaning I kindled them.
He said, in a line of verse:
I was not one of those who stirred up war between them ... but Masʿūd and Jundub, the two of them, were the ones who brought it on.
And arsh al-jināya is its blood-compensation, and this too is something that provokes dispute and incitement — so the chapter is one.
أرض:
The letters hamza, rā', and ḍād are three roots: one that branches out with many issues, and two others that do not follow any wider pattern — each is simply a word as the Arabs happened to place it.

As for these latter two:
1. Al-arḍ is a head-cold. A man is ma'rūḍ, meaning stricken with a head-cold. This is one of the two roots, and of it the Hudhali poet said:
You were ignorant of your snuff, until you supposed ... you had been given a head-cold, when you had not.
2. The other is trembling. One says bi-fulānin arḍun, meaning he has a trembling. Dhū al-Rumma said:
When she caught a faint sound from their hoofbeats ... she was like one seized by trembling, or by fever.

As for the first root: it is everything that lies low and faces the sky. One says of the upper part of a horse "its sky", and of its legs "its earth". A poet said:
And a bay horse like brocade — as for his sky, it was glossy; as for his earth, it was dust-pale.
His "sky" is his upper parts, his "earth" is his legs.

Al-arḍ is also this ground we stand on; its plural is araḍīn, though it never comes in that plural in the Book of God. This is the root, and from it branches:
1. Arḍun arīḍatun, said of land when it is soft and good. Imru' al-Qays said:
Broad lands, and soft good earth ... where the torrents of rain-showers spread, in a wide open space.
2. A man arīḍ for good, meaning fit for it, likened to soft good land.
3. Ta'arraḍa al-nabt, said of a plant when it becomes possible to graze or cut it; a kid is arīḍ when it is able to graze such a plant.
4. Al-irāḍ, a great spread of hair-cloth or wool.
5. Fulānun ibnu arḍin, meaning a stranger. A poet said:
A stranger came to us seeking provisions, after ...
6. Ta'arraḍa fulānun, said when he stayed close to the ground. A man of Banū Sa'd said:
And a companion I roused to rise up ... he got up without stumbling, and did not cling to the ground.
أرط:
The letters hamza, rā' and ṭā' are a single word with no further derivation: it is al-arṭā, the tree; one of it is arṭāh, and the dual is arṭātān, and the plural arṭayāt. It also occurs as arṭā with nunation. Abū ʿAmr said: arṭāh and arṭā — the alif was not added to it to mark the feminine.
Al-ʿAjjāj said, in a line of verse:
In a bed rich with ḍāl-trees, and leafy arṭā.
The word both takes and does not take full declension. One says: this is much arṭā (masculine form) and this is much arṭā (feminine form). One says arṭat al-arḍ, the ground grew arṭā, so it is murṭi'a.
Al-Khalīl mentioned a word which, if it is sound, belongs to substitution, where the hamza has been put in place of a hā'. Al-Khalīl said: al-arīṭ is the barren man, and he recited, in a line of verse:
What can you hope for from the barren one?
The true origin of it is al-haraṭ: one says naʿjatun hariṭa, a ewe that is wasted thin, whose meat is of no use, worn out. And a man yahriṭu in his speech when he talks in confused, jumbled fashion. This has been mentioned in its own place.
أرف: The letters hamza, rā' and fā' are a single root, not extended by analogy and nothing branches from it. One says urrifa ʿalā al-arḍ, when boundary-markers are set upon it. And in the ḥadīth: "Any property that has been divided and boundary-marked carries no right of pre-emption," and "the boundary-markers (al-uruf) cut off every right of pre-emption."
أرق:
The letters hamza, rā' and qāf are two roots: one is the fleeing of sleep by night, the other a kind of colour.
The first is their saying ariqtu araqan, and arraqanī al-hammu yu'arriquni, worry kept me sleepless.
Al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse:
I lay sleepless — and what is this wakeful insomnia ... I have no sickness in me, and no beloved I long for.
One also says āraqanī. Ta'abbaṭa Sharran said, in a line of verse:
O ʿĪd, what ails you, of longing and sleeplessness ... and the passing of a phantom over the terrors of night, ever treading.
A man is ariq and āriq, on the patterns faʿil and fāʿil.
He said, in a line of verse:
So I spent the night in the sleeplessness of the restless, tossing man.
The second root is in the words of the speaker, in a line of verse:
And he leaves the rival with his fingertips gone yellow ... as if on his two garments there were a splash of arqān.
It is said that al-arqān is a red tree. Abū Ḥanīfa said: from this too is al-arqān that strikes crops, a yellowing that comes over them; one says zarʿun ma'rūq, and it has been uriqa. Al-Liḥyānī reported the words al-irāq and al-arq for it.
أرك:
The letters hamza, rā' and kāf are two roots from which the branches spread: one is a tree, the other is staying in one place.

The first is al-arāk, a well-known tree.

1. Ibn al-Sunnī told us, from Ibn Musabbiḥ, from Abū Ḥanīfa Aḥmad ibn Dāwūd, who said: the singular of al-arāk is arāka, and a woman was named Arāka after it. He said: one also says i'taraka al-arāk when the arāk tree became fully grown. Ru'ba said, in a line of verse:
from the thorn-trees and the fully-grown arāk.
2. Abū 'Amr said: camels that eat the arāk are called arākiyya and awārik. In the hadith: "The Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, was brought at ʿArafa the milk of arāk-grazing camels."
3. arḍun arika — land abundant in arāk. Camels that graze on arāk are also called arika, just as one says ḥāmiḍ [sour-plant grazer] from al-ḥamḍ. Abū Dhu'ayb said, in a line of verse:
she chooses from the milk of the arāk-grazing camels in summer... [line appears cut off in the source].

The second root is staying in one place. Ibn al-Sunnī told me, from Ibn Musabbiḥ, from Abū Ḥanīfa, who said: al-Kisā'ī classed the arākiyya camels as taken from al-urūk, meaning staying. Abū Ḥanīfa said: this is not taken from the word al-arāk, nor does it mean they stay specifically among arāk trees — rather this word applies to anything staying put, even a man staying in his house; one says from it araka ya'riku and ya'ruku, urūkan. Kuthayyir said, describing the women's litters, in a line of verse:
and above the tribe's camels, fair women, as though — by their markings — they were the white gazelles of the tamarisk grove, the ones that stay put.

The proof that Abū Ḥanīfa was right is their naming the bed inside the bridal canopy arīka, plural arā'ik. If someone objects that Abū 'Ubayd claimed one says of a wound, when it heals and mends, araka ya'ruku urūkan — the answer is: this belongs to the second root, because when a wound heals its swelling and its rising above the skin settles down.

From this same root is the derivation of the name Arīk, a place. A poet said, in a line of verse:
so she passed by Kushub at dawn, and drew level, alongside Arīk, in the late afternoon.

As for the letters hamza, rā' and lām — that is neither a root nor a branch, though they said Arul is a mountain; but it is actually spelled with a kāf.
أرم:
The letters hamza, rā' and mīm are a single root: it is the stacking of one thing upon another in height, and then the pattern holds the same at its top as at its bottom. One further branch grows from it: taking the whole of a thing, whether by eating or otherwise.
The explanation of that is that al-arm is the place where the plates of the skull meet, and a large head is mu'arram; a helmet or shell that is mu'arrama is wide at its top. Al-irm is the way-marker — stones piled together as if they were a standing man. One says irami and arami; these are also hummocks, like al-ayārim.
He said, in a line of verse:
... its hump, like the ayram.
Abū Zayd said: al-urūm are the ridges on the skull of an aged camel. Al-arūma is the base of every tree; the base of one's lineage is arūma, and likewise the base and gathering-point of anything at all. Al-urram, in al-Khalīl's account, is stones, and he recited, in a line of verse:
Gnawing the stones at us, out of spite.
It is also said that al-urram is the molar teeth; one says huwa yaḥruqu ʿalayhi al-urrama, he grinds his teeth at him. If that is so, it is because they clamp down (ta'rim) on whatever they bite.
He said, in a line of verse:
I was told that Sulaymā's in-laws had done nothing ... but spend the night furious, grinding their teeth.
Aramathumu al-sana means the drought wiped them out utterly; such years are called sunūn awārim. A cutting knife is sikkīn ārim. Arama mā ʿalā al-khiwān means he ate everything that was on the table. Their saying arama ḥablahu comes from the same, because the strands are gathered together and firmly twisted. And so-and-so, of a woman, is ḥasanat al-arm, meaning well formed in the twisting-together of her flesh. Abū Zayd said: mā fī fulānin irmun — with the alif carrying a kasra and the rā' still — because a tooth ya'rimu, wears down by grinding. Arḍun ma'rūma is land whose growth has all been eaten away, so that neither root nor branch is left in it.
He said, in a line of verse:
And we graze bare every sprouting plant, down to the pasture.
أرن:
The letters hamza, rā' and nūn are two roots: one is liveliness, the other a shelter that a wild creature or something else retreats into.
As for the first, al-Khalīl said: al-aran is liveliness; arina ya'ranu aranan. Al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse:
You see him, when his companions set out in the morning ... with both his flanks like the lively young lamb's.
The second root is in the words of the speaker, in a line of verse:
How many a shelter I have stripped of its midday resting-place ... when the noble wild game, denied their coverts, grew wary.
He meant the burrow — that is, how many a burrow I have stripped of being called a resting-place, from al-qaylūla, the midday rest. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: al-mi'rān is the shelter cattle take among the trees. And the place a chameleon retreats into is called urna.
Ibn Aḥmar said, in a line of verse:
And the chameleon lingered at its shelter ... looking sideways, its throat-pulse beating.
أرو: As for the letters hamza, rā' and wāw — there is nothing to them but al-arwā, the mountain-goats; it is not a root that anything is derived from, nor is anything measured against it. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: al-urwiyya is the female of the wild goats, and three up to ten of them are arāwī; when they are more than that, they are al-arwā. Abū Zayd said: both the male and the female are called urwiyya.
أري:
As for the letters hamza, rā' and yā', they are a root indicating steady attachment and persistence. Al-Khalīl said: ary al-qidr is what sticks to the sides of the pot from the broth, and likewise honey that clings to the sides of the honeycomb-frame.
Al-Hudhalī said, in a line of verse:
The gatherers' honey clinging to the crest of a high place ... where the vultures perch, as though it were a settled procession.
He means: the vultures came down there because of its ruggedness, as though it were a procession, sitting cross-legged, at rest. Another said, in a line of verse:
Of what clings and what runs down.
Meaning: what sticks and what flows; its clinging is its i'tirā'.
Zuhayr said, in a line of verse:
They watch its flashes of lightning, while the south wind sprinkles ... its clinging moisture on its brows — the clouds.
This is ary of the clouds, borrowed in meaning from what came before. From this chapter too is al-ta'arrī, watchful expectation.
He said, in a line of verse:
He does not wait about, watching for what is in the pot ... nor does he clutch at his ribs from the bite of hunger.
He means: he eats plain bread and does not wait for the food of others, nor for what is in their pots. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: ta'arrā bi'l-makān means he stayed in the place, and ta'arrā ʿan aṣḥābihi means he fell behind his companions. One says baynahum ary ʿadāwatin, meaning a lasting enmity between them; and ary al-nadā is what settles of dew on trees and rock and grass and keeps on clinging, one part to another.
Al-Khalīl said: āriyy al-dābba, the animal's stall, is a well-known word, built on the pattern fāʿūl.
He said, in a line of verse:
It keeps returning to folds that have a stall.
Abū ʿAlī al-Aṣfahānī said, on the authority of al-ʿĀmirī: al-ta'riya is that you rest a length of wood, which has a strong rope folded around it, in a dug pit, then heap earth over it, then tie the camel to it so that it grows docile and its wild spirit breaks. One says arri li-baʿīrika wa awkid lahu, secure it well for your camel. Al-īkād and al-ta'riya are the same thing, and it can be done for gazelles too.
He said, in a line of verse:
And the dust-coloured gazelles knew that he ... had a firmly-fastened snare among the young trees.
أز:
Hamza and zāy indicate moving, causing to move, and disturbing.

1. al-azz — al-Khalīl said: a person's driving another person to something gently and by cunning. al-shayṭānu ya'uzzu l-insāna 'alā l-ma'ṣiyati azzan, the devil incites a person to sin.

God Almighty said: {Do you not see that We have sent the devils upon the disbelievers, inciting them with incitement} [Maryam: 83]. The exegetes said: it means driving them on with agitation.

Ibn Durayd cited, in a line of verse:
Neither deceit nor divination take hold among us, nor the enemies' agitating clamor.

2. al-azz — Ibn al-A'rābī said: milking a she-camel forcefully.

He cited, in a line of verse:
Fierce in the milking of her hindquarters, as if, when the two rough milkers set upon her, she were the loud cry of a returning traveler.

3. al-azz — Abū 'Ubayd said: joining one thing to another.
4. al-azz — al-Khalīl said: the boiling of a cooking-pot; also called al-azīz.

In the hadith: he would pray, and in his chest was a bubbling like the bubbling of a cooking-pot, from weeping.

5. al-azz — Abū Zayd said: the sound of thunder. One says azza ya'izzu azzan wa azīzan.
6. al-azīz — Abū Ḥātim said: intense cold. One says laylatun dhātu azīzin, a night of biting cold, but not yawmun dhū azīzin, a day of it.
7. al-azīz — he said: intensity of travel. One says azzatnā l-rīḥ, the wind drove us on.
8. baytun azazun — Ibn Durayd said: a house packed full of people.
أزب:
The letters hamza, zā' and bā' are two roots: shortness and fineness and the like, and the other root is liveliness and clamour in wanton excess.
Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: al-izb is the short man. He recited, in a line of verse:
And I despise, among Hudhayl, every short man ... short of stature, you would take him for a child.
Al-Khalīl said: al-izb is the one fine in the joints, and the root is the same one. It is also said to mean the miser. From this same reasoning: al-mīzāb, the water-spout, plural al-ma'āzīb, named for its fineness and the narrowness of the water's channel through it.
The second root: al-Aṣmaʿī said: al-uzbiyy is speed and liveliness. The rajaz-poet said, in a line of verse:
... until its swift vigour came, along with the strain.
Al-Kisā'ī said: uzbiyy and azābiyy mean clamour. A bow that has uzbiyy has a loud, ringing sound.
He said, in a line of verse:
As if its ringing sound, when it twanged ... were the blow struck by seekers on the track of what they had found.
Abū ʿAmr said: al-azābiyy is wanton transgression.
He said, in a line of verse:
A woman of wanton excess, and of ill repute ... marked, among what is on her, by something dark and foul.
أزح: The letters hamza, zā' and ḥā'. One says azaḥa, when he falls behind and lags from something, ya'ziḥu. And azaḥa, when he draws in on himself and one part of him comes close to another.
أزد: A tribe-name; its true letter is sīn, not zā', and this has been dealt with in its own place.
أزر:
The letters hamza, za' and ra' are a single root: strength and intensity.

1. ta'azzara an-nabt — the plant grew strong and thick.

'Ali ibn Ibrahim al-Qattan recited to us, saying Tha'lab dictated to us, in a line of verse:
The plants grew so strong and thick upon it that its hillocks seemed alive, and the sheep, sleeping within it, could no longer be seen.

He is describing the abundance of the plants, such that the sheep sleep in it and cannot be seen. Al-azr — strength. Al-Ba'ith said, in a line of verse:
I braced my strength for him, with the resolve of a determined man, against a matter of his that had turned grave.
أزف:
The letters hamza, zāy and fā' indicate nearness and approach. One says: azifa al-raḥīl — the departure drew near. God Almighty said: {The Approaching Hour has drawn near (azifat al-āzifa)} [al-Najm: 57], meaning the Resurrection.

As for al-muta'āzif, it belongs to this same sense: one says "a man is muta'āzif," meaning short, of compact build. Umm Yazīd ibn al-Tathriyya said: "a young man cut like the cut of a sword, neither muta'āzif nor loose-fleshed at the throat and collarbones." Al-Shaybānī said [the word instead describes one] narrow/difficult in temperament, and cited: "great in the breadth of chest, not muta'āzif, wide of gait, and not stiff-handed or short (mujaddhar)." Al-mujaddhar is the short one; al-jādī is the withered/dry one. This line says nothing about temperament, only about physical build — the poet meant simply "the short one."

One says: ta'āzafa al-qawm — the people drew close to one another. Al-Shaybānī said: azafanī fulān, meaning so-and-so hurried me — yu'zifu īzāfan. Al-mā'āzif are filthy places, singular ma'zafa. He cited: "as though his two garments, when he wraps himself in them, are on a dung-beetle that haunts the filthy places (al-mā'āzif) with a foul smell." And that scarcely occurs except in a cramped, narrow space.
أزق:
The letters hamza, zā' and qāf are one single pattern and one root: it is narrowness. Al-Khalīl and others said: al-azq is the tightness of battle, and for that reason the place of fierce fighting is called al-ma'ziq. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: one says istu'ziqa ʿalā fulānin when the space grows too narrow around him and he cannot break free. It occurs in al-ʿAjjāj's poetry, in a line of verse:
[a wearying labour] he grows weary of, and narrowness.
أزل:
As for the letters hamza, zā' and lām, they are two roots: hardship, and lying. Al-Khalīl said: al-azl is hardship; one says they are in azl of livelihood, meaning they are in a year of drought or trial.
He said, in a line of verse:
Nizār's two sons relieved the tremors ... from those at prayer, and relieved a hardship pressing hard.
Al-Shaybānī said: azaltu al-māshiya wa'l-qawm azlan, I put the livestock and the people under want. Uzilat al-ibil, the camels were kept back from pasture. Ibn Durayd recited, in a line of verse:
Khashshāf swore, and he kept his word ... that he would let it graze only a stinted grazing.
One says uzila al-qawmu yu'zalūna when they are struck by drought.
He said, in a line of verse:
So let them be brought low, and their milking-beasts run dry ... and their little one be fed on nothing but thin, watered milk.
Al-samār is diluted milk, mostly water. Al-āzil is the man struck by drought.
A poet said, in a line of verse:
Of those camped for the spring pasture, and of one struck by want ... when the night wraps him round, like one groaning.
Al-Khalīl said: one says azaltu al-farasa when you shorten its tether and then turn it loose to graze. Abū al-Najm said, in a line of verse:
It has not grazed hemmed in, nor yet been set loose.
As for the lying, that is al-izl. Ibn Dāra said, in a line of verse:
They say Laylā's love and affection is a lie ... but they have lied — there is no lie in her affection.
As for al-azal, meaning eternity, its origin is not one reached by analogy but is a compressed, altered expression: it was originally lam yazal, he has not ceased to be, and they wanted to form a relational word from it, but it would not come out smoothly, so they related it instead to yazala, then turned the yā' into a hamza and said azaliyy — just as, relating a spear to Dhū Yazan, they said azaniyy.
أزم:
As for the letters hamza, zā' and mīm, they are a single root: narrowness, and the close, tight clinging of one thing to another with force. Al-Khalīl said: azamtu, wa anā āzim. Al-azm is a fierce bite. The horse ya'zimu on the crosspiece of its bit.
Ṭarafa said, in a line of verse:
Big-framed, and stallions well-guarded, of Awjan stock ... biting hard upon the racecourse.
Al-ʿĀmirī said: one says azama ʿalayhi when he bites down and does not open his mouth. Abū ʿUbayd said: azama ʿalayhi is to clamp with the mouth, and bazama is to do so with the front of the mouth. And restraint from food, abstaining, is called azm from this, as if a person holds his own mouth shut. One says azama al-rajulu ʿalā ṣāḥibihi, meaning he clung fast to him, and āzamanī kadhā, meaning he bound that upon me. And the year of famine is azma, for the hardship in it.
He said, in a line of verse:
... when the hardships of every year press hard.
Abū ʿAmr recited, in a line of verse:
The blows of harsh time have spared ... something of her yet, and the passing of hardship's misfortunes too.
Al-Aṣmaʿī said: a year is azūm and azām, said with the lighter case-ending.
He said, in a line of verse:
She kept back food for her, and did not waste it ... on the morning of dread, when it turned hard and harsh.
And al-amr al-azūm is the dreadful, detestable matter. Al-Khalīl said: azamtu al-ʿinān wa'l-ḥabl — I am āzim and it is ma'zūm — when I have twisted its cord tightly and firmly. Al-ma'zim is the narrow, rugged pass of a valley; al-ma'zimān are two such narrow passes within the sacred precinct.
أزى:
The letters hamza, zā', and what follows them of the weak letters, are two roots to which every branch of this whole chapter returns, once looked at closely: one is a thing's parts packing together into each other, the other is standing directly opposite something.
Al-Khalīl said: azā al-shay'u ya'zī, when part of it packs tightly against another part and draws together.
He said, in a line of verse:
... so he is a man packed close, his flesh drawn tight together.
Al-Shaybānī said: azati al-shamsu li'l-maghīb azyan, the sun drew close to setting. Azā al-ẓillu ya'zī azyan wa uzuwwan, when the shade shrank. Another recited, in a line of verse:
Make haste with your two old ones, before the shade shrinks away ... for youth is fast departing from them both.
And when water grows less, one likewise says azā; the pattern of reasoning is the same. So too azā al-māl, wealth dwindled.
He said, in a line of verse:
... until his counted holdings had dwindled away.
From this chapter too is al-Farrā's saying: aza'tu ʿan al-shay'i, when I flinched back from a thing, because in flinching one draws in and pulls together. That is one of the two roots.
The other is al-izā', which is facing directly opposite. One says āzaytu fulānan, meaning I stood facing him. As for al-qayyim, the one placed in charge of something, being called al-izā' — this too is from the same, because the one in charge of a thing always stands facing it, watching over it. Likewise izā' al-ḥawḍ, the trough's inlet, because it faces what is opposite it.
A poet said of al-izā' meaning the one in charge, in a line of verse:
A keeper of a livelihood, whose belt never once ... grows slack, and in her there is resolve, while she sits at her post.
Abū al-ʿUmaythil said: al-Aṣmaʿī asked me about the rajaz-poet's line describing a trough, in a line of verse:
Its inlet like the striving polecat.
I said: al-izā' is where the bucket empties into the trough. He said to me: how does he liken the bucket's emptying-place to a polecat? I said: what do you have on it? He said to me: rather he meant the water-drawer, from your saying so-and-so is izā' of property, when he takes charge of it and manages it — and he likened him to the polecat for the sharpness of its smell. As for izā' al-ḥawḍ, it is where the water pours into it; one says āzaytu al-ḥawḍ īzā'an.
Al-Hudhalī said, in a line of verse:
By my father's life for Laylā — indeed fate has led him ... to a grave, water poured out for him among the mountain-slopes.
And you say āzaytu when you pour onto the inlet. Ru'ba said, in a line of verse:
We draw water from a rain-fed pool, and we pour it in.
Some say: rather it comes from your saying azaytu ʿalā ṣanīʿi fulān, meaning I matched or doubled it; if so, it is because each of two matching things stands opposite (izā') the other. And one says nāqatun aziyya, a she-camel that will drink from nowhere but the trough's own inlet.
أس:
Hamza and sīn indicate a foundation, something firmly fixed and established.

1. al-uss — the foundation of a building, its plural āsās; the singular is also said asās, with a short alif, and its plural usus.
2. al-uss — a man's origin, his lineage.
3. al-uss — the face of time, of fortune. One says: kāna dhālika 'alā ussi l-dahr, that happened in ancient times.

Al-Kadhdhāb al-Ḥirmāzī said, in a line of verse:
A foundation of glory, firm and fixed, whose towering top has reached the sky.

As for al-ās [myrtle], this is not its chapter; it has been mentioned in its own place.
أسد:
The letters hamza, sīn and dāl indicate the strength of a thing, and for that reason the lion was named al-asad, for its strength; and from it is derived everything that resembles it. One says ista'sada al-nabtu, the plant grew vigorous and strong.
Al-Ḥuṭay'a said, in a line of verse:
In a place where the wadi-beds grow thick and vigorous, its low ground green ... its blossoms leaning toward the sun, radiant.
One says ista'sada ʿalayhi, he grew bold and emboldened against him. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: asadtu al-rajula is like sabaʿtuhu [I likened him to a beast of prey]. And Asd, with the sīn quiescent, are the people also called al-Azd, and perhaps this belongs to the chapter.
As for al-isāda, it does not belong to this chapter, because its hamza is converted from a wāw. And likewise al-usdiyy, in al-Ḥuṭay'a's words, in a line of verse:
Consuming the choicest of the herd, like al-usdiyy — the hands of the pack-camels have made it ... humbled, and rough with wear.
أسر:
The letters hamza, sīn and rāʾ are one root, a steady sense-pattern: confinement, restraint. From this: al-asīr, the captive — they used to bind him with rawhide thongs, called al-isār, so that anyone taken, even unbound, came to be called asīr. Al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse:

Poetry has fettered me in its house ... just as the binding-women fettered the donkey

meaning he has reached the utmost devotion to it. The Arabs say asara qatabahu, he fastened his pack-saddle. God, Most High, said: {and We have made firm their frame} [al-Insān: 28] — some say He meant man's physical creation, others that He meant the passages of the two bodily outlets. Usrat al-rajul: his close kin, because he draws strength from them. You say asīr, plural asrā, and asārā with a fatḥa. Al-usr is retention of urine.
أسف:
The letters hamza, sīn and fā' are a single root indicating a loss one grieves over, yearning regret, and things like that. One says: asifa ʿalā ash-shay' ya'safu asafan — like talahhafa, he grieved with regret.

1. al-asif — the angry one. God Most High said: {And when Mūsā returned to his people, angry, grieving [asifan]} [al-A'rāf: 150]. Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
I see a man among them grief-stricken [asīf], as if he presses to his sides a stained hand —
meaning he is the angry one.
2. It is said that al-usāfa is land that grows nothing at all; this fits the pattern, because vegetation has passed it by.
3. Likewise al-jamal al-asīf — the camel that hardly ever grows fat.

As for the "follower/servant" and their naming him asīf, that does not belong to this root, because there the hamza is converted from an ʿayn, and it has been mentioned in its own place.
أسك: The letters hamza, sīn and kāf — its formation is attested in the two books [of reference]. The people of language said: al-ma'sūka is the woman [performing circumcision] whose cutting-stroke missed and struck somewhere other than the place meant to be cut.
أسل:
The letters hamza, sīn and lām indicate the sharpness of a thing together with its length and fineness. Al-Khalīl said: al-asal is spears — he said they were so named by likening them to al-asal of plants; every plant with long thorns has thorns called asal. Al-asala is the fine, narrow part of the forearm; al-asala is also the fine, narrow part of the tongue. They said: anything sharpened to a point is mu'assal.
Muzāḥim said, in a line of verse:
Its two hindmost molars rival the front teeth when it champs ... with an edge fine as the buckle-tongue of the pointed weapon-strap.
Yubārī means it rivals, matches. Sadīsāhā are two molars at the back of the mouth that have grown long enough to come level with the canine teeth — these are the shabā mentioned. Al-ibzīm is the piece of metal you see fitted fine and narrow on a belt, which holds it fastened when drawn tight.
أسم: The letters hamza, sīn and mīm are a single word: it is Usāma, one of the names of the lion.
أسن:
The hamza, sīn and nūn are two roots: one is the spoiling of something, the other is "cause" (al-sabab).

The first: asana al-mā', ya'sinu and ya'sunu — the water spoiled/went stale; this is the well-known form, though asina is also said. God, exalted is He, said: {of water not stale} [Muḥammad: 15]. asina al-rajul — the man fainted from the [foul] smell of a well.

Here are two flawed words that do not belong to the root: one is al-usun, meaning leftover fat — its hamza stands in for an ʿayn, the true form being ʿusun. The other is ta'assana, ta'assunan, said of one who fell ill and grew slow; the reason for this is that Abū Zayd said it is really ta'assara, ta'assuran [with rā'].

The other root: al-āsān — ropes.

A line:
I used to love the woman of al-Nāqimiyya for a long while — but now the ropes of parting have begun to snap.

This is used figuratively in their saying, "He is on āsān from his father," meaning [following] his ways.
أسو:
The letters hamza, sin and waw are a single root indicating medical treatment and setting right. One says 'asawtu l-jurh' — I treated the wound, and for this the physician is called 'al-asi'. Al-Hutay'a said:
They are the ones who treated the wound to the crown of the head, when the physicians and the healers had all shirked from it.
Meaning: the ones who treat/care for it. Al-Umawi said this. One says 'asawtu l-jurha asw an wa asa' — I treated the wound. Al-A'sha said:
With him are piety and God-fearing, and the mending of the rift, and the bearing of burdens for one weighed down.

One says 'asawtu bayna l-qawm' — I made peace between the people. From this root: 'li fi fulanin uswa' — I have in so-and-so an example, that is, I follow his example. 'Assaytu fulanan' — I consoled so-and-so, from the same root, meaning I said to him: let so-and-so be your example, for he was afflicted just as you were, and yet was content and accepted it. From this root too: 'asaytuhu bi-nafsi' — I shared his affliction as my own [comforted him by likening my own state to his].
أسي: The letters hamza, sīn and yā' are a single word: it is sorrow. One says asītu ʿalā al-shay'i āsā asan, meaning I grieved over it.
أش:
Hamza and shīn indicate movement toward an encounter.

1. ashsha l-qawmu ya'ushshūna ashshan — Ibn Durayd said: when some of a people rose up against others for harm, not for good.
2. al-ashāsh — others said: like al-hashāsh, cheerful readiness.

In the hadith: when he saw some ashāsh in his companions, he would admonish them.
أشا: The letters hamza, shin and alif. Al-ashā' are young palm trees, the small ones; the singular is ashā'a.
أشب:
The letters hamza, shin and ba' point to mixing and entangling.

1. 'īṣ ashib — a thicket, meaning tangled and dense; and so-and-so came with a great, entangled number of people.
2. ta'ashshaba l-qawm — the people mixed together.
3. ashabtu fulānan āshibuhu — I blame him, as if I had pinned an ugly thing on him and blamed him for it.

Abū Dhu'ayb said, in a line of verse:
Those near her blame me concerning her ... though if they knew, they would not blame me with any real cause.

4. al-ushāba — the mixed rabble of people, as in this saying:
I trusted him for victory, when it was said that tribes from Ghassān had gone to war ... not a mixed, motley crowd.
أشر:
The letters hamza, shin and ra' are a single root indicating sharpness.

1. huwa ashir — he is insolent from ease, hasty, sharp-tempered; one says ashira, ya'sharu.
2. naqa mi'shir — a she-camel of great mettle, on the pattern mif'il from al-ashar.

Aws said, in a line of verse:
A lean, swift she-camel, whose sire and dam are of one thoroughbred line, her uncles on both sides the same — sturdy and mettlesome.

3. rajul ashir and ashur — a man, in two vocalizations of the same word.
4. al-ushr — a fineness and sharpness at the edges of the teeth.

Tarafa said, in a line of verse:
The sun replaced what grew there with a white frost, polished at its sharp edge.

5. asharu al-khashaba bi-l-mi'shar — I sawed the piece of wood with the saw — from this same root.
أشف: The letters hamza, shin and fa' are not an original word, so we have not mentioned it as a root. What was heard using these letters is al-ishfā, the awl — a cobbler's needle.
أص:
As for hamza and ṣād, it has two meanings: one is a thing's root and its gathered mass, and the other origin is trembling.

1. al-iṣṣ — the lexicographers said: the root, the origin.
2. aṣūṣ — said of a she-camel compactly built.

The plural of al-iṣṣ, meaning origin, is āṣāṣ.

He said, in a line of verse:
Summits of glory that towered over their foundations, and a might unyielding, that bows to none.

3. al-aṣīṣ — the base of a wine-jar, in which drink is put.

'Adī said, in a line of verse:
When shall I see drinking companions gathered around the wine-jar's base?

That is one origin. As for the other, they said: aflata fulānun wa lahu aṣīṣ, meaning he escaped, trembling.
أصد:
The letters hamza, ṣād and dāl: something that encloses something.

1. aṣīda — what they call an enclosure or pen, named for enclosing what is in it.
2. al-uṣda — a small shirt worn by young girls; one says 'ṣabiyyatun dhātu mu'aṣṣad', a girl wearing a mu'aṣṣad.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
I fell in love with Laylā while she still wore the mu'aṣṣad ... and her breasts had not yet shown their shape to her peers.
أصر:
The letters hamza, ṣād and rā' are a single root from which branch things close to one another. Al-aṣr is restraint and inclination, and what shares their meaning. The explanation is that a covenant is called iṣr, and kinship is called āṣira, and every bond, kinship-tie, and covenant is an iṣr — the whole chapter is one [meaning].

The Arabs say: "no āṣira (bond of kinship) inclines me (tā'ṣirunī) toward so-and-so," meaning no kinship draws me to him. Al-Ḥuṭay'a said: "they showed me kindness without a bond of kinship (āṣira), for the bonds (al-awāṣir) had already grown weighty," meaning they were kind to me without covenant or kinship.

Al-ma'ṣir [a restraining barrier] is from this, because it is a thing by which something is confined. As for their saying that a heavy covenant is an iṣr, this too is from this root, because covenant and kinship carry a burden (iṣr) that ought to be borne. One says: aṣartuhu, I restrained him.

From this chapter also is al-iṣār, the tent's guy-rope, plural uṣur; it is also said to be the peg of the guy-rope. As for al-A'shā's line: "this one prepares fodder (al-khalā) for them, and sets the guy-rope (al-iṣāra) between them" [meaning obscure to me beyond this].
أصل:
The letters hamza, ṣād, and lām are three roots, far apart from one another: the foundation of a thing; the snake; and the part of the day after the afternoon.

1. Al-aṣl is the foundation of a thing. Al-Kisā'ī said, of their saying "lā aṣla lahu wa-lā faṣla lahu" [he has neither root nor branch]: al-aṣl here means lineage, al-faṣl means eloquence. One says majdun aṣīl [rooted, well-established glory].
2. Al-aṣala is the great snake. In the hadith mentioning the Antichrist: "It is as though his head were an aṣala."
3. Al-aṣīl is the part of the day after the afternoon, plurals uṣul and āṣāl; also aṣīl and aṣīla, plural aṣā'il. A poet said:
By my life, you are indeed the house whose people are honoured ... and I sit in its shade in the late afternoons.
أض:
Hamza and ḍād have two meanings: compulsion and breaking, and they are close to each other.

1. aḍḍanī ilā kadhā ya'uḍḍunī aḍḍan — Ibn Durayd said: when it forced me toward it.

Ru'ba said, in a line of verse:
While she sees one in need, driven by compulsion.

Meaning: compelled.

2. al-aḍḍ — he said: also breaking. One says aḍḍahu, exactly like haḍḍahu.
3. al-aḍāḍa — Abū Zayd related: compulsion.

He said, in a line of verse:
A time when I did not resist compulsion, with kohl-black eyes that had no white in them.
أضا: The letters hamza and ḍād, with a weak letter after them, are a single word: al-aḍāh, a place where water collects and stands, like a pool. Abū ʿUbayd said: al-aḍāh is standing water, from a flood or otherwise; its plural is aḍan, and the plural of al-aḍā is iḍā', with a long final vowel, which is an unusual form.
أضم:
The letters hamza, ḍād and mīm are a single root and a single word, and it is grudge, rancor. One says 'aḍima ʿalayhi' — when he bore a grudge against him and grew furious.

Al-Jaʿdī said, in a line of verse:
I rebuke the hidden enemy when he speaks ill of you behind your back ... a rebuke from me, despite my own rancor.
أط:
Hamza and ṭā' have a single meaning, which is the sound a thing makes when it groans and creaks.

1. aṭṭa l-raḥlu ya'iṭṭu aṭīṭan — the saddle creaked, that is when it is new and you hear a creaking from it. Any sound resembling that is aṭīṭ.

The rajaz-poet said, in a line of verse:
At the hours of the evening milking they pant heavily from the bloated fullness of the creaking, overladen camels.

He describes camels whose bellies are full. yaṭḥarna means they breathe hard, like groaning. al-inā is the time of the evening drink. al-aṭṭāṭa is the she-camel whose creaking you hear.

In the hadith: until its creaking is heard from the crowding — meaning the gate of Paradise.

2. aṭṭat al-shajara — the tree creaked, when it groaned and bent.

The rajaz-poet said, in a line of verse:
My lote-tree knew me and creaked, and after it I too went grey, and it greyed as well.
أطر:
The letters hamza, ṭā' and rā' are a single root, and it is the bending of one thing over another, or its enclosing of it.

1. iṭār — the people of the language say: anything that encloses a thing is an iṭār, a rim or frame. What surrounds the lip along its edge is also called an iṭār. One says 'the sons of so-and-so are an iṭār to the sons of so-and-so' when they settled around them.

Bishr said, in a line of verse:
The clan, the clan of Banū Subayʿ, settled among us as stragglers ... and we were an enclosing rim around them.

2. aṭartu l-ʿūda — I bent the stick; such a stick is then ma'ṭūr. From this comes the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him and his family: "until you take hold of the wrongdoer's hands and bend him firmly toward the truth" — meaning: bend him.
3. aṭartu l-qawsa — I bent the bow.

Ṭarafa said, in a line of verse:
As if the two coverts of a ḍāla tree flanked it ... and the bent bows lay beneath a firm, sturdy back.

4. uṭra — the sinew-wrapping that gathers the arrow's notch; from it one says 'aṭartu al-sahma aṭran', I fitted the notch of the arrow.
5. al-ta'aṭṭur — I heard ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm al-Qaṭṭān say he heard Thaʿlab say: al-ta'aṭṭur means lingering, tarrying.

One word has strayed from this chapter: al-aṭīr, which is a fault or sin. One says 'akhadhanī bi-aṭīri ghayrī', meaning: he held me to account for someone else's fault. This is how they explained the saying of ʿAbdallāh ibn Salama, in a line of verse:
And if I grow great, it is not for the fault of a burden ... that a sturdy blade parts from my shoulder.
أطل:
The letters hamza, ṭā' and lām are a single root and a single word: al-iṭil and al-iṭl, which is the flank; its plural is āṭāl. Likewise al-ayṭal.

Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
He has the flanks of a gazelle and the shanks of an ostrich ... the loose stride of a wolf and the quick trot of a young fox.

This word is not to be taken as a model for others.
أطم:
The letters hamza, ṭā' and mīm point to confinement and enclosing a thing.

1. al-uṭum — a fortress, plural āṭām.

Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
And at Taymā' he left no palm trunk standing ... nor any fortress except one built up with stone.

2. al-uṭām — from this same chapter: constipation, the withholding of the bowels.
3. al-aṭīma — the hearth where fire is kindled, plural al-aṭā'im.

Al-Asʿar said, in a line of verse:
In a position of sharp edge, as if ... the men there stood upon the hearths, amid the blaze.
أف:
As for hamza and fā' in the doubled root, they have two meanings: one is aversion to a thing, and the other is the present moment.

1. affa ya'uffu affan — Ibn Durayd said: when he expressed aversion from distress or irritation. rajulun affāf, a man much given to expressing aversion.

Al-Farrā' said: uffi, with the case-ending but without the nūn, and uffin, with the case-ending and the nūn — because it is treated as a sound, the way sounds are given case-endings, as one says ṭāqi ṭāqi. Some Arabs say: uffun lahu. He said: some Arabs also said: do not say to him uffan or tuffan, treating it like a noun. He said: the Arabs say: he began to express aversion at a smell he noticed, and he expresses aversion at a hardship that befalls him.

Mutammim ibn Nuwayra said, when 'Umar asked him about his brother Mālik: He would ride the slow, heavy-footed camel, and lead along the slow horse, and carry across his back the ungainly, swaying spear, and wear the ill-fitting cloak, between two leaking waterskins, on a cold, wet night, and would greet the clan in the morning laughing, without groaning and without expressing aversion.

2. al-uff and al-tuff — al-Khalīl said: one is the dirt under the fingernails, the other is the dirt of the ear.

He said, in a line of verse:
Upon them be the curse and the expression of disgust.

Ibn al-A'rābī said: one says affan lahu wa tuffan, and affatan lahu wa tuffatan.

3. al-afaf — Ibn al-A'rābī said: irritation, vexation.
4. al-ya'fūf — from this same pattern: the quick-tempered.

The other meaning: their saying jā'a 'alā ta'iffati dhāka wa afafihi wa iffānihi, meaning at its proper time.

He said, in a line of verse:
At the time of estrangement, and a moment alone.
أفد:
The letters hamza, fā' and dāl point to a thing drawing near and being close at hand.

One says afida al-raḥīl — the departure has come close. And al-afid is someone in a hurry.

Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
The setting-out has come close upon us — except that our mounts have not yet stirred with our saddles on them, though they are as good as gone.

A bedouin woman sent her daughter to the neighbour with this message: "My mother says: give me a breath or two of time, so that I may work my hide with it — for I am in haste."
أفر:
The letters hamza, fā' and rā' point to lightness and to mixing together.

One says afara al-rajul — the man was quick and light in service. Al-mi'far is a servant. Al-ufra is a mixing-up, a confusion.
أفق:
The letters hamza, fā' and qāf are a single root, indicating the remoteness between the extremities of a thing and its wideness, and the reaching of a limit. From this are al-āfāq: the outlying regions and edges; and the āfāq of a Bedouin tent are its sides, not its roof. He cited a line describing tent-poles [obscure to me in its exact sense]: "and one worn thin by travel among people, who left him no turning-about of the sky's horizons unfaced." For this reason one says: afaqa al-rajul, the man went off travelling in the land.

Abū Bakr Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq al-Dīnawarī related to me, reading it to him: Abū 'Abdillāh al-Ḥusayn ibn Musabbiḥ told me: I heard Abū Ḥanīfa say: the sky has horizons (āfāq) and the earth has horizons. As for the horizons of the sky, they are as far as sight reaches of it together with the face of the earth on every side — the boundary between what is hidden of the celestial sphere and what shows of the earth. The rājiz-poet said: "before the nearing of the horizon (al-ufuq) to its [star] Gemini," meaning before Gemini's rising, since both rising and setting occur at the horizon. And [another], describing the sun: "so it sits on the horizon like the eye of a cross-eyed man." And another: "until, when the western view had turned to blood from the sun's redness, when the horizon (al-ufuq) had made it vanish (ightālahā)" — its "making it vanish" means causing it to disappear.

He said: as for the horizons of the earth, they are its outer edges from wherever they encircle you. The rājiz-poet said: "enough for you, instead of some visiting of the horizons (al-āfāq), is a tawny [thing] from what Ibn Mikhrāq wore threadbare." One says of a man, when he belongs to one of the horizons: ufuqiyy or afaqiyy; and likewise of a star, when its course lies close to the horizon and does not pass overhead in the middle of the sky, it is ufuqiyy or afaqiyy. Here ends Abū Ḥanīfa's speech.

It is said: al-āfiq is the man who has reached the utmost limit of generosity, and a woman is āfiqa. Al-A'shā said: "one to whom tribute is brought, from all between 'Umān and Malaḥ" [describing such a man]. Abū 'Amr [said]: al-āfiq is like al-fā'iq (the one who surpasses); one says afaqa ya'fiqu afqan, he overcame; and al-ufuq [also] means overcoming. One says "farasun ufuq," on the pattern fu'ul, meaning an outstanding horse.

As for al-A'shā's line: "nor King al-Nu'mān, the day I met him in his splendour, giving out the tribute-ledgers (al-quṭūṭ) and ya'fiqu" — al-Khalīl said its meaning is that he takes tribute from the regions (al-āfāq). He said: the singular of al-āfāq is ufuq, a region among the regions of the earth. Ibn al-Sikkīt said: "a man is afaqiyy," of the people of the distant regions — formed irregularly against the normal pattern; it is also said ufuqiyy.

Ibn al-A'rābī said: the afaq of a road is its clear track; one says "I sat on the afaq of the road," its track. From this chapter also is Ibn al-A'rābī's saying: al-afaqa is the flank/hip-hollow, plural al-afaq. He cited a line naming the flesh by the ribs and the afaq [obscure in full sense]. And one says: "I drank until I filled my two afaqatān [both flanks]." Abū 'Amr and others said: a bucket is afīq when it holds more than the other buckets. He cited: "it is not [just] a bucket — it is the surpassing one (al-afīq)." For this reason tanned hide is also called al-afīq, plural afaq, and ufuq is also allowed.

This is what belongs to the language and its derivation. As for the Day of al-Ufāqa, it is one of the Arabs' battle-days — it is the Day of al-'Uẓālā, the Day of A'shāsh, and the Day of Mulayḥa; Ufāqa is a place. Its story was that Bisṭām ibn Qays came forward with three hundred horsemen, watching for Banū Yarbū' to come down into the rough ground. The first of them to appear were Banū Zubayd, until they made camp in the enclosure at al-Ufāqa. Bisṭām came forward keeping watch and saw the dark encampment at the enclosure of al-Ufāqa, and saw a boy among them, and said to him: "Who are these?" He said: "Banū Zubayd." He said: "Then where are Banū 'Ubayd and Banū Aznam?" He said: "At the meadow of al-Thamad." Bisṭām said to his people: "Obey me and seize this isolated clan of Zubayd, for safety is one of the two prizes." They said: "Your nerve has failed you — rather we shall pick off Banū Zubayd, then pick off the rest of them, the way truffles are gathered." He said: "I fear that tomorrow spear-thrusts will meet you that will make you forget the spoils!"

A mare belonging to Usayd ibn Ḥinnā'a sensed the horsemen and pawed the ground with her hoof, so Usayd mounted and made for Banū Yarbū', calling: "To arms! O clan of Yarbū'!" Before the heat of midday had risen, they had caught up with each other at al-Ghabīṭ. Al-Uḥaymir ibn 'Abdillāh came and charged Bisṭām on his chestnut mare — they claim al-Uḥaymir never thrust with a spear but that it broke, so he was called "Breaker of Spears" — and when he swooped to spear Bisṭām, Bisṭām and those with him fled, after those of them who were killed had been killed. A poet said of this: "If there is any blame in the army of al-Ghabīṭ, then the army of al-'Uẓālā was more disgraced and more blameworthy. Abū al-Ṣahbā' fled when the battle grew fierce, and threw down his armour and gave himself up. Had it been a mere sparrow you would have taken it for one marked out, calling to 'Ubayd and Aznam." This day is the Day of al-Iyād, of which Jarīr says: "Mujāshi' was not present on the Day of al-Iyād, nor was he of nobility, on the day the spearheads dripped blood."
أفك:
The letters hamza, fā', and kāf are a single root, pointing to the overturning of a thing and turning it away from its direction. One says ufika al-shay'u [the thing was overturned]. A man is afika when he lies; al-ifk is lying. Afaktu al-rajula 'an al-shay'i means I turned him away from it. God Almighty said: {They said, "Have you come to us to turn us away from our gods?"} [al-Aḥqāf: 22]. A poet said:
If you have been turned away from the noblest choice ... then others too have been turned away.
Al-mu'tafikāt are the winds that shift and blow from different directions. They say: "When the shifting winds increase, the earth grows fertile."
أفل:
The letters hamza, fā' and lām are two roots: one is disappearance (going out of sight), and the second is the young ones among camels.

As for disappearance, one says: the sun afalat (set), meaning it disappeared, and stars are described as uffal (setting). Anything that disappears is āfil.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Leave Su'dā be — for separation grants only the meeting of the Pleiades: once, then it sets.

Al-Khalīl said: when the seed settles in the depth of the womb, it has afala (gone out of sight, settled).

1. al-afīl — the second root. It is the weaned young camel (al-faṣīl); the plural is al-ifāl.

Al-Farazdaq said, in a line of verse:
The pick stud of the she-camels came before their young, striding swiftly, and they came behind him, hurrying too.

Al-Aṣma'ī said: al-afīl is the ibn makhāḍ (a camel colt in its second year, so called because its mother is pregnant again) and the ibn labūn (a camel colt in its third year, so called because its mother is now nursing a new calf); the female is afīla. Once it grows beyond that stage it is no longer called afīl.

Ihāb ibn 'Umayr said, in a line of verse:
They stood, at the wide open ground of the ravine's slope, upright — coming to water on the eighth day, and their young ones crying.

Thāmina means: coming to water after eight days. Muthūluhā means: their standing upright.

And in the proverb: "The great stud camel comes only from the young weanling," meaning: the great one begins as the small one.
أفن:
The letters hamza, fā' and nūn point to a thing being emptied and drained out.

1. al-afan — a lack of intelligence; a man of this kind is ma'fūn, feeble-minded.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
I was told that ʿUtba the braggart threatened me ... how many a swollen, feeble-minded man there is, from Maytha'!

And it is said that a ma'fūn walnut is one with nothing inside its shell. The origin of all this is in their saying:

2. afana l-faṣīlu mā fī ḍarʿi ummihi — the young weaned camel drank all that was in its mother's udder.
3. afana l-ḥālibu l-nāqata — the milker left nothing in her udder.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
When she is milked dry, her milk satisfies your household ... but when her milking is delayed, her yield overflows the skin.

4. afanati l-nāqatu — some said this of a she-camel whose milk grew scant; she is then afina, in the shortened form.
أقر:
Uqur is a place. Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
I truly warned Banū Dhubyān away from Uqur ... and away from their spring grazing there in every barren season.

This is not an [original] root.
أقط:
The letters hamza, qāf and ṭā' point to mixing and being mixed.

They said: al-aqiṭ is milk that has been churned, then cooked, then left until the whey drains out of it; a piece of it is an aqiṭa. Aqaṭtu al-qawm aqṭan — I fed people that. Food that is ma'qūṭ has been mixed with aqiṭ.

A poet said, in two lines of verse:
The hollow-bellied one has come to you, hungry, brimming over with the froth of the pot, and at times she takes her morning drink —
mixed with aqiṭ, and she went back to being the slaughterer of the one who does the slaughtering.

Al-ma'qiṭ is the place of battle, which is a narrow place, because they are all mixed together in it.
أقن:
The letters hamza, qāf and nūn are a single word that nothing else is measured against.

Al-uqna is a pit in the backs of the rocky uplands, narrow at its mouth; sometimes it is a sheer drop between two peaks or two crags.

Al-Ṭirimmāḥ said, in a line of verse:
In the jagged edges of pits, with the droppings of birds between them, like the fast of the ostrich.
أك:
As for hamza and kāf, the meaning is intensity — of heat and otherwise.

1. al-akka — Ibn al-Sikkīt said: fierce, smothering heat. One says aṣābatnā akkatun min ḥarrin, fierce heat struck us; hādhā yawmun akkun and yawmun dhū akkin, this is a day of akka.
2. al-akka — Ibn al-A'rābī said: bad temper and shortness of breath.

He cited, in a line of verse:
When the heavy drinker is seized by an akka, leave him be until he vomits it all up.

3. i'takka l-rajul — Ibn al-A'rābī said: when a man's legs knocked together.

He said, in a line of verse:
In his leg, from his arousal, a knocking together.

4. al-akka — al-Khalīl said: a grievous calamity among the calamities of fate. One says i'takka fulānun min amrin armaḍahu i'tikākan, so-and-so was distressed by a matter that tormented him.
5. yawmun 'akkun akkun, and 'akīkun akīkun — Ibn Durayd said: both mean a day of intense heat.
أكد: The letters hamza, kāf and dāl are not a root, because the hamza is turned from a wāw. One says wakkadtu al-'aqd — I made the contract binding. It has been dealt with in its own chapter.
أكر:
The letters hamza, kāf and rā' are a single root, and it is digging.

Al-Khalīl said: an ukra is a hole dug beside a pool or a watering trough so that the water may settle clear in it. One says ta'akkartu ukratan — I dug such a hole. The ploughman, al-akkār, is named from this.

Al-Akhṭal said, in a line of verse:
A slave to a foreigner of the two forts, a ploughman.

Al-'Āmirī said: I found water in an ukra up in the mountain — a hollow in the smooth rock about the size of a bowl.
أكف: The letters hamza, kāf and fā' are not a root, because the hamza is turned from a wāw. One says wikāf and ikāf — a pack-saddle.
أكل:
The letters hamza, kāf and lām are a chapter with many branches, and the root is a single word whose meaning is diminishing — one thing being taken away bit by bit.

Al-Khalīl said: al-akl (eating) is well known; an akla is one time of it, and an ukala is a noun, like a mouthful. One says rajul akūl of a man who eats a great deal. Abū 'Ubayd said: al-akala is the plural of ākil (an eater); they say "they are no more than the eaters of one head" — that is, a handful of men. Al-akīl is the one who eats with you. Al-ma'kal is what is eaten, like al-maṭ'am. Al-mu'kil is the one who feeds. In the hadith: "God has cursed the one who consumes usury and the one who feeds it to him." Al-ma'kala is a means of living.

Mā dhuqtu akālan — I have tasted nothing that is eaten. Al-ukl, as Ibn al-A'rābī reported, is a living the kings used to grant to the nobility, such as villages; the plural is ākāl.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Your army, inherited and newly won, is of the lords — the people of the domed tents and of the granted estates.

Abū 'Ubayd said: they say "you have made me eat what I did not eat" — that is, you have laid a claim against me falsely. Al-akūla is the ewe pastured to be eaten, not for selling or breeding; they say "pasture and no ewe for the pot" — meaning wealth heaped up with nobody to spend it. Akīl al-dhi'b is the sheep or anything else the wolf eats, when you mean the thing eaten, male and female alike; when you mean it as a noun you say akīlat dhi'b. Abū Zayd said: al-akīla is the lion's prey. Akā'il al-nakhl are the palms held back to be eaten from. Al-ākila, on the pattern fā'ila, is the grazing beast; it is also called al-ikla. Al-akila, on the pattern fa'ila, is the she-camel whose young one's fur grows inside her belly and hurts her and eats at her.

One says i'takalat al-nār — the fire blazed up fiercely; and i'takala al-rajul — the man's anger blazed up. The ember tatakkal, that is, it glows; and the sword's watered pattern tatakkal along its blade.

Aws said, in a line of verse:
When it is drawn from the scabbard its pattern glows along it, over the like of a silver bowl, glowing.

It is said of perfume, when its scent blazes out, that it tatakkal. One says akalat al-nār al-ḥaṭab — the fire ate the firewood; and ākaltuhā — I fed it to it. Ākaltu bayn al-qawm — I set people against one another. Lā tu'kil fulānan 'irḍak — do not trade insults with so-and-so and so let him eat away at your honour. Al-mu'kil is the tale-bearer.

Fulān dhū uklatin fī al-nās — a man with a share of eating among people — is said of one who backbites them. Al-ukl is a man's portion and what he is given of this world; he is dhū ukl, and a people are dhawū ākāl.

Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
Around me are the men of granted estates, of Wā'il, like the night for number — settled and nomad alike.

One says thawb dhū ukl — a garment with much yarn in it; rajul dhū ukl — a man of judgement and understanding; and likewise a palm tree, and a crop.

Al-ukāl is an itch; one says an itching struck him in his head. Al-akal in a hide is a thin place whose surface you take to be sound, but when it is worked its flaw shows. Bi-asnānihi akal — his teeth are eaten away, and ukilat asnānuhu ta'kal akalan.

Al-Farrā' said: a knife is called ākilat al-laḥm, the flesh-eater; and from this is the hadith that 'Umar said: one of you strikes his brother with the like of a flesh-eater, then thinks I shall not have him killed for it. Abū Ziyād said: al-mi'kala is a pot smaller than the large one — the pot a clan finds it easy to cook in.

Ukul al-shajara is a tree's fruit. God says: {It brings forth its fruit at every season by the leave of its Lord} [Ibrāhīm: 25].
أكم:
The letters hamza, kāf and mīm are a single root: a thing gathering together and rising a little.

Al-Khalīl said: an akama is a hillock of the rocky ground; the plural is ākām and akam. Ista'kama al-makān — the place became like a hillock. It is also given the plural al-ākām.

Abū Khirāsh said, in a line of verse:
Nor is he the red-legged one that stayed as though, on the jutting hillocks, he were a stone.
He means a falcon. Iḥza'alla means stood upright. A naṣīl is a stone about a cubit long.

Of this same measure are al-ma'kamatān: the two pieces of flesh joining the rump to the two sides of the back.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
When the wind strikes her through the shift, her haunches stand out — and loose garments in the wind are put to shame.
أكن: The letters hamza, kāf and nūn are not a root, because the hamza in it is turned from a wāw. The root is wukna, which is a bird's nest. It has been dealt with in the chapter of wāw.
أل:
Hamza and lām in the doubled root have three origins: gleaming with a quivering motion, sound, and a bond that is kept and upheld.

1. alla l-shay'u — al-Khalīl and Ibn Durayd said: when it gleamed.
2. al-alla — Ibn Durayd said: the spear was named this for its gleam.
3. alla l-farasu ya'illu allan — when the horse's gait shook and quivered.
4. allat farā'iṣuhu — his shoulder-flesh gleamed and quivered as he ran.

He said, in a line of verse:
Until I shot her while her shoulder-flesh quivered, and her back seemed like a slab for grinding marble.

5. alla l-rajulu fī mishyatihi — the man quivered in his gait.
6. al-alla — al-Khalīl said: the spear, its plural ilāl.

He said, in a line of verse:
Its thunderheads flash in the clouds like Abyssinians standing with spears and lances.

7. al-alīla and al-alīl — the spear is also called this.

He said, in a line of verse:
He defends the honor of your father's sons, and stabs with the spear and the lance.

He said: al-alla was so named because it is fine, slender at the head.

8. alla l-rajulu bi-l-alla, meaning: he stabbed.

It was said to an Arab woman who had grown weak-minded with age: so-and-so has sent to ask for your hand. She said: would you hurry me before I know my mind and take care — may he have neither fetter nor spear!

9. al-ta'līl — he said: your sharpening or tapering a thing, like the tip of the reed pen.
10. al-mu'allal — also: sharpened, pointed. One says udhunun mu'allala, meaning a pointed ear.

Ṭarafa said, in a line of verse:
Two pointed ears in which noble breeding is known, like the two ears of a gazelle alone at Ḥawmal.

11. udhunun ma'lūla, and farasun ma'lūl — both meaning pointed.

He said, in a line of verse:
Pointed of ears, dark-rimmed of eye.

12. yawmun alīl — said of a harsh, grievous day.

Al-Afwah said, in a line of verse:
With every youth of wide reach, who rises to the raids on the direst of days.

13. al-alal and al-alalān — al-Khalīl said: the two faces of a knife, and the two faces of anything broad and flat.

Al-Farrā' said: from this, the two layers of flesh that meet with a gap between them, found in the shoulder-blade — when one is peeled from the other, water flows out between them — are called alalān.

A woman said to her neighbor: do not give your co-wife the shoulder-cut as a gift, for water runs between its two alal-layers — meaning: give her something worse than it.

As for the sound-meaning, they said, regarding the line of verse:
And a stabbing whose two alal-cries the girl of the clan makes many, following it with wailing —

it is an imitation of the sound of one who wails.

He said: al-alīl is groaning, as in the line of verse:
If you see me, you will find me groaning much.

Ibn Mayyāda said, in a line of verse:
Say to her: what do you bid a lover be, who after the sleeping of eyes has only groaning?

Ibn al-A'rābī said: in his chest is groaning and clanging. 'I heard the alīl of water,' meaning its sound. It is also said al-alīla is bereavement.

He cited, in a line of verse:
Mine is the wailing grief if my mother's kin are killed, and mine is the wailing grief if they are not killed.

They said: rajulun mi'all, a man much given to talk, who assails people with his tongue.

Al-Farrā' said: al-all is raising the voice in supplication and weeping. One says from it: alla ya'illu alīlan.

In the hadith: your Lord marvels at your crying out, and your despair, and how quickly He answers you.

They cited, for al-Kumayt, in a line of verse:
And what are you, in a dark and dusty night, when the full-bosomed maiden cries out her two alal-cries?

The third meaning: al-ill is lordship, divinity. Abū Bakr said, when Musaylima's words were mentioned to him: this did not come forth from divine [inspiration].

God Almighty said: {they observe toward a believer neither a bond nor a covenant} [al-Tawba: 10]. The exegetes said: al-ill is God, exalted be His praise. Some said: it is kinship, closeness of blood-relation.

He said, in a line of verse:
They severed, in undutifulness, the bond that was between us, and kept faith with neither covenant nor pact.

Ibn al-A'rābī said: al-ill is any bond between two people.

He cited, in a line of verse:
By your life, your bond among Quraysh is like the bond of a young camel to the chick of an ostrich.

Al-ill also means: a covenant.

Among what departs from these origins is their saying alila l-siqā': the waterskin's smell changed, went bad. It could belong to one of the three, for Ibn al-A'rābī mentioned that it is a skin whose two alal-layers have spoiled — that is, when water gets in between the hide and the flesh-side.

Ibn Durayd said: the Arabs would lighten [pronounce without doubling] al-ill.

Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
Fair of reputation, who fears not leanness, who cuts no tie of kinship, and who betrays no bond.
ألب:
The letters hamza, lām and bā' have to do with gathering together, with inclining, with returning, and with what resembles that.

Al-Khalīl said: al-ilb is leaning towards a side; one says his leaning is with him, and "they became one ilb against him" in enmity and mischief.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And people are banded against us over you — we have no shield but our swords and the points of our spears.

Al-Shaybānī: ta'allabū 'alayhi — they gathered against him; and alabū ya'libūn alban.

It is said that al-alba is famine, so named because people band together in it.

Ibn al-A'rābī said: alaba means he returned. He said: a man of Banū Ḍabba told me a story and then began another; I asked him about the first and he said, "He will come back to you presently" — that is, return to you.

Ibn al-A'rābī recited, in a line of verse:
Do you not know that talk, tomorrow and the day after, bands together as hunted beasts band together —
that is, one part joins itself to another.

Of this same measure is their saying fulān ya'lubu ibilahu — he drives his camels together. And from it too is Ibn al-A'rābī's saying rajul ilbu ḥarb of a man who rallies men in war and gathers them. And from it their saying alaba al-jurḥ ya'lubu alban of a wound that begins to heal and then festers again underneath.

As for their calling the space between the fingers ilb, that is from this too, because it is where the fingers meet.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Until it was as though the two leagues were a finger's width.

What Ibn al-Sikkīt reported — layla alūb, a cold night — may belong to this chapter, because one who feels the cold draws himself together and huddles; and it may belong to the chapter of substitution, the hamza standing for a hā', which has been dealt with in its own chapter.

And the rajaz-poet's line:
Rejoice at a drawer of water, an alūb —
is said to mean the man who sends the buckets down one after another, as people band together one to another.
ألت:
The letters hamza, lām and tā' are a single word pointing to falling short. One says alatahu ya'lituhu — he made it less.

God says: "He will not diminish anything of your deeds for you" — that is, He will not stint you.
ألس: The letters hamza, lām and sīn are a single word, and it is treachery. The Arabs call treachery als; they say: "he does not deceive and he does not betray."
ألف:
The letters hamza, lām and fā' are a single root pointing to one thing joining itself to another — and to great numbers of things as well.

Al-Khalīl said: alf (a thousand) is well known; the plural is ālāf. Ālafat al-ibil, with a long vowel, means the camels came to a thousand.

Ibn al-A'rābī said: ālaftu al-qawm — I made them a thousand; and ālaftuhum — I made them a thousand by adding someone other than myself; and ālafū — they became a thousand. The like of it is akhmasū and amā'ū. This is a sound measure, because a thousand is the gathering of hundreds.

Al-Khalīl said: alaftu al-shay' ālafuhu — I grew used to a thing, I grew fond of it. Al-ulfa is the verbal noun of i'tilāf, coming together in fellowship. Your ilf and your alīf is the one you are close to. Anything of which you have joined one part to another, you have allaftahu ta'līfan — put it together.

Al-Aṣma'ī: one says alaftu al-shay' ālafuhu ilfan and I am ālif; and ālaftuhu and I am mu'lif.

Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
Of those that keep to the sand — a dusky, noble one, on whose colour the light of the forenoon shows clear.

Abū Zayd said: the people of the Ḥijāz say ālaftu al-makān wa-l-qawm — I grew attached to the place and the people. And ālaftu ghayrī too — I brought someone else to grow attached.

Al-Khalīl said: awālif al-ṭayr are the birds that keep to Mecca and elsewhere.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Keeping to Mecca, of the grey doves.

One says ālafat hādhihi al-ṭayr mawḍi'a kadhā, and they are mu'lifāt, because they never leave it.

As for His saying, exalted be He: {For the keeping together of Quraysh} [Quraysh: 1] —

Abū Zayd said: al-ma'laf is the sheltering tree that game draws near to out of its attachment to it, and so comes close.
ألق:
The letters hamza, lām and qāf are a root pointing to lightness and giddiness, and to flashing quickly.

Al-Khalīl said: al-ilqa is the she-demon, and the she-wolf, and the bold woman — for the mischief in them.

Ibn al-Sikkīt said: the plural is ilaq.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
He was in earnest, and a she-demon of the demons was in earnest.

He said: one says imra'a alaqā of a woman quick to spring. Some said: rajul allāq — a great liar; and alaqa bi-l-kadhib ya'liqu alqan.

Abū 'Alī al-Aṣfahānī said, on the authority of al-Qarī'ī: ta'allaqat al-mar'a when she girded herself for a quarrel, made ready for mischief and raised her head. Ibn al-A'rābī said: its meaning is that she became like the ilqa. Ibn al-Sikkīt mentioned imra'a ilqa and rajul ilq.

Of this same measure: i'talaqa al-barq i'tilāqan when it flashed, and ta'allaqa ta'alluqan.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
At one moment he listens, at another he crosses soft ground — as though he were a star flashing over the sand.
ألك:
The letters hamza, lām and kāf are a single root, and it is the carrying of a message.

Al-Khalīl said: al-alūk is a message, and it is al-ma'lauka on the pattern maf'ula.

Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
Carry a word from me to you, 'Uyayna — the reciters will bear it to you on my behalf.

He said: a message is called alūk only because it is turned over in the mouth — taken from the Arabs' saying that a horse ya'luku the bit and ya'lukuhu, when it chews the iron.

He said: a poet is allowed to treat ma'laka as masculine.

'Adī said, in a line of verse:
Carry al-Nu'mān a message from me: that my imprisonment and my waiting have gone on long.

And the Arabs' saying "alikni ilā fulān" means: carry my message to him.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Carry my word to her — by your life, young man — with the token of how she came to us with gifts.

Abū Zayd said: alaktuhu ulīkuhu ilākatan when I sent him. Yūnus ibn Ḥabīb said: istal'aka fulān li-fulān — he went with his message; the regular form would be ista'laka.
ألم:
The letters hamza, lām and mīm are a single root, and it is pain.

Al-Khalīl said: al-alam is pain; one says waja' alīm, a painful hurt. The verb from alam is alima — he was in pain — and he is alim. The transitive form is alīm, so by this measure it is fa'īl in the sense of muf'il — the pattern of "painful" carrying the force of "causing pain". So too wajī' in the sense of mūji'.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Is it from Rayḥāna that the caller comes, the hearing one —
putting samī' (hearing) in the place of musmi' (making heard).

Ibn al-A'rābī said: 'adhāb alīm means a punishment that causes pain; and rajul alīm and mu'lam mean a man in pain. Abū 'Ubayd said: one says alimta nafsak, in the way you say safihta nafsak — you have brought pain upon yourself.

The Arabs say: "the free man gives, and the slave's heart aches."
أله:
The letters hamza, lām and hā' are a single root, and it is worship — the giving of oneself in service.

Al-ilāh is God, exalted be He, and He is named so because He is the One worshipped. One says ta'allaha al-rajul — the man devoted himself to worship.

Ru'ba said, in a line of verse:
How fine are the well-favoured women who anointed themselves — they gave praise, and drew back from my devotion.

Al-ilāha is the sun, so named because a people used to worship it.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
We raced the sun, lest it should turn home.

As for their saying aliha ya'lahu of bewilderment, that does not belong to this chapter, because there the hamza stands for a wāw. It has been dealt with in its own chapter.
ألوى:
The letters hamza and lām, with a weak letter after them, are two roots far apart from one another: one of them is striving hard and going to the utmost, and the second is the opposite of the first — falling short.

Of the first: their saying ālā yūlī of a man who swears an oath — an aliyya or an ilwa.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Word came to me from al-Nu'mān of the wrong of an oath, wronging by it a man of Tihāma after one of Najd.

And another said, of al-alwa:
He gives my words the lie and breaks my oath.

Aliyya is taken as fa'ūla, and alwa as fa'la, like qadma. One says yu'lī and ya'talī, and yata'allā when going to the utmost.

Al-Farrā' said: one says i'talā al-rajul when he swears; and in the Book of God: {And let not those of you who have bounty swear off} [al-Nūr: 22]. Sometimes they give alwa the plural ulā. And he recited:
A little, like the loosening of the oaths — then a startled disposition drew it in as a bird draws in.
He said: an oath is called alwa, ulwa, ilwa and aliyya.

Al-Khalīl said: one says mā alawtu 'an al-juhd fī ḥājatik — I have not fallen short of any effort in your need — and mā alawtuka nuṣḥan — I have not stinted you good counsel.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
We gave our utmost, we did not hold it back —
that is, we left no effort undone.

Abū Zayd said: one says alawtu fī al-shay' ālū when I fall short in it. And in the proverb: "if not a favoured one, then no swearing off" — meaning: if favour has passed you by, do not swear off showing affection to people.

Al-Shaybānī: ālaytu — I was slow and hung back.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
My sons neither held back nor did wrong.

Allā al-kalb 'an ṣaydihi — the dog fell short of its quarry; and likewise the hawk and its kind.

One of the bedouin said, in a line of verse:
And I, when her distance outstrips me, am one who falls short in visiting her, and is blamed for it.
أم:
The letters hamza and mīm are a single root, branching into four chapters: the origin, the point of return, the group, and religion — these four are close to one another. After that come three further senses: stature, a span of time, and aim.

Al-Khalīl said: al-umm is the singular [mother], and its plural is ummahāt; sometimes they said umm and ummāt.

A poet said, in a line of verse combining both forms of the word:
When mothers' [ummahāt] faces turn ugly ... you dispelled the darkness with your mother [ummātikā].
He used both ummahāt and ummāt for "mothers" in the same line.

Al-Rā'ī said, in a line of verse: their mothers [ammātuhunna] and their sires [ṭarquhunna] were choice studs.

The Arabs say "lā umma lahu" (he has no mother) both in praise and in blame. Abū 'Ubayda said: "mā kunti umman wa-laqad amamti umūmatan" — you were not a mother, but you have now become one, a mother. So-and-so [a woman] taʾummu so-and-so, meaning she nourishes him — that is, she is a mother to him, feeding and raising him.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
We mother them and father them together ... just as straps are cut from the hide.
That is, we are mothers and fathers to them.

And he recited, in a line of verse:
Seek out Abū Nakhla, from among those who would father you ... for they all deny you your own father.

One says umm and umma, with the tā' marbūṭa. A poet said, in a line of verse:
You received her from a mother of yours whose veil was long fought over in the markets.

Al-Khalīl said: anything that other things attach to and gather around, the Arabs call that thing an umm. And from this:

1. umm al-ra's — the brain, the "mother of the head." One says "amamtu fulānan bi'l-sayfi wa'l-'aṣā amman" — I struck so-and-so with the sword or staff, a blow that reached the brain.
2. al-amīm — one who has been struck on the brain (al-ma'mūm); it is also the stones with which heads are crushed. A poet said, in a line of verse: with siege engines and with amā'im [head-crushing stones].
3. al-shajja al-āmma — a head-wound that reaches the "mother of the brain"; it is also called al-ma'mūma. A poet said, in a line of verse: he probes a wound reaching the brain, with a hollow in its depth — and the physician's backside, its speck, is like earth-truffles [maghārīd]. (This line is obscure; the sense is uncertain.)
4. Abū Ḥātim said: ba'īr ma'mūm — a camel whose backbone had bones removed so that its hump's ridge was gone. A poet said, in a line of verse: he is neither ma'mūm [with a ruined back] nor ajabb [with a cut-off hump].
5. Al-Khalīl said: umm al-tanā'if — the harshest and farthest reach of the waterless deserts.
6. umm al-qurā — Mecca; and every city is the "mother" of the villages around it. So too umm ruḥm [a place-name].
7. umm al-Qur'ān — the opening chapter of the Book [al-Fātiḥa].
8. umm al-kitāb — what is in the Preserved Tablet.
9. umm al-rumḥ — the banner of a spear and what is wound around it. A poet said, in a line of verse: they stripped the spear, its banner still on it, from the rebel's hand, before the affair had gone on long.
10. umm mathwan — what the Arabs call the woman whose house one lodges in [a hostess]; the man is abū mathwan [a host].
11. Ibn al-A'rābī said: umm mirzam — the north wind. A poet said, in a line of verse: when he spends winter evenings at al-Ḥalā'a, umm mirzam [the north wind] strips the skin off the top of his nose.
12. umm kalba — fever. Concerning this is the Prophet's saying, peace be upon him, to Zayd al-Khayl: "What a fine young man he will be, if he survives umm kalba [the fever]." So too umm mildam [another name for fever].
13. umm al-nujūm — the sky. Ta'abbaṭa Sharran said, in a line of verse: he sees the desolate wild as pleasant company, and finds his way where umm al-nujūm, the interlaced [stars], found its way.

Abū Bakr ibn al-Sunnī told us, al-Ḥusayn ibn Musabbiḥ told us, from Abū Ḥanīfa, who said: umm al-nujūm is the Milky Way, because no patch of sky has more stars gathered in it than that. Ta'abbaṭa Sharran said this too, in the line already given. And Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse: with unkempt men who cut across the wasteland's heads, when umm al-nujūm, the interlaced [stars], has turned [ḥawwalat]. "Ḥawwalat" means it inclines/shifts.

14. umm kifāt — the earth.
15. umm al-qurād — a hollow at the back of the pastern above the hoof, where ticks gather like in a little dish. Abū al-Najm said, in a line of verse: [its trace touches] the ground, from the dusty umm al-qurād.
16. umm al-ṣadā — the same as umm al-dimāgh, the "mother of the brain."
17. umm 'uwayf — a small speckled creature that, when it sees a person, stands on its tail and spreads its wings; it is used as a proverb for cowardice. A poet said, in a line of verse: O umm 'awf, spread your two cloaks — the commander stands over you. It is also said to be the locust.
18. umm ḥumāris — a small black creature with many legs.
19. umm ṣabbūr — a confused, tangled affair; it is also said to be a hill with no way through it.
20. umm ghaylān — a tree thick with thorns.
21. umm al-luhaym — death.
22. umm ḥubayn — an animal.
