23. umm al-ṭarīq — the main part of a road.
24. umm waḥsh — the open desert waste; so too umm al-ẓibā' [mother of the gazelles]. A poet said, in a line of verse: my need mattered little to umm al-ẓibā', when [the wind] sent dust over it and the tall palm shed [its leaves]. (This line is obscure.)
25. umm ṣabbār — a lava-field. Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse: it fends people off from us when we ride it against wrongs — it is called umm ṣabbār.
26. umm 'āmir and umm al-ṭarīq — the hyena.
27. Ya'qūb said: umm aw'āl — a specific named hill. A poet said, in a line of verse: and umm aw'āl is like it, or nearer.
28. umm al-kaff — the hand. A poet said, in a line of verse: he has no finger on umm kaff.
29. umm al-bayḍ — the [female] ostrich. Abū Du'ād said, in a line of verse: he came running to us, spreading out like umm al-bayḍ [the ostrich]... (the line is cut off in the text).
30. umm 'āmir — the desert waste.
31. umm kulayb — a small shrub with yellow blossom.
32. umm 'iryaṭ — the scorpion.
33. umm al-nadāma — haste.
34. umm qash'am, umm khashshāf, umm al-raqūb, umm al-raqim, umm arayq, umm rubayq, umm jundab, umm al-balīl, umm al-rubays, umm ḥabawkarā, umm adraṣ, and umm na'ād — all of these are names for calamity.
35. umm farwa — the ewe.
36. umm suwayd and umm 'izm — the lower part of a person.
37. umm jābir — [the tribe of] Iyād.
38. umm shamla — the cold north wind.
39. umm ghirs — the well.
40. umm khurmān — a particular named road.
41. umm al-hashīma — a great tree among dried-out trees. Al-Farazdaq said, describing a cooking pot, in a line of verse: when it is fed umm al-hashīma [dry wood], it rumbles, just as umm al-ḥiwār, the mother of the wrapped-up young camel, rumbles.
42. umm al-ṭa'ām — the belly. A poet said, in a line of verse: I raised him when he was like a fledgling, his bones tiny, his belly [umm al-ṭa'ām] such that you could see down through his skin.

Al-Khalīl said: al-umma is religion. God Almighty said: {We found our fathers following a religion} [al-Zukhruf: 22]. Abū Zayd related: "lā umma lahu" — he has no religion. And the Prophet, peace be upon him and his family, said of Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl: "He will be raised on the Day of Judgment as a community unto himself alone."

Likewise everyone who follows a true religion differing from all other religions is called an umma. And any people attributed and traced back to something are an umma; and every generation of people is a separate umma. In a hadith: "Were it not that these dogs are a community among the communities, I would have ordered them killed; but kill every pure black one among them."

As for His saying, {mankind was a single community} [al-Baqara: 213], it is said this means they were disbelievers, so God sent the prophets bringing good news and warning. And it is said: rather, everyone who was with Noah, peace be upon him, in the ark was a believer, and afterward they became divided. And it is said, concerning {Indeed Abraham was a community} [al-Naḥl: 120] — meaning a leader by whom guidance is found, and he is the cause of people's gathering together. And al-umma can also mean a group of scholars, as in His saying: {Let there be among you a community calling to what is good} [Āl 'Imrān: 104].

Al-Khalīl said: al-umma is also stature. The Arabs say: so-and-so is ṭawīl al-umma, tall of stature, and they are ṭiwāl al-umam. Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse: and the Mu'āwiya, the most noble people, are handsome of face, tall of stature.

Al-Kisā'ī said: a man's umma is his body and his face. Ibn al-A'rābī said: al-umma is obedience, and also the learned man. Abū Zayd said: one says "he is ḥasan ummat al-wajh," handsome in the cast of his face — meaning [his face] follows the accustomed pattern. (The exact sense of the phrase that follows this in the Arabic is uncertain.) "There is no umma for the sons of so-and-so" means: they have no clear direction they aim toward, but they blunder about like a blind she-camel groping at random. Al-Liḥyānī said: "mā aḥsana ummatahu" means how good his character is.

Abū 'Ubayd said: al-ummī in the language is one attributed to the natural condition people are born in — one who does not write; he is, in not writing, still as he was born. He said: as for al-Nābigha's line of verse, "Does one of umma sin while obedient?" — whoever reads it with the u-vowel meant the custom of a kingdom; whoever reads it with the i-vowel made it mean a religion, from "following as a leader," as in your saying "i'tamma bi-fulānin immatan" — he followed so-and-so as a leader. And al-umma in His saying, {and he remembered after a time} [Yūsuf: 45], means after a span of time.

And al-imām is anyone who is followed as a model and put forward in affairs. The Prophet, peace be upon him, is the imām of imāms; the caliph is the imām of the subjects; and the Qur'an is the imām of the Muslims. Al-Khalīl said: al-imma is a blessing. Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse: your raid struck a blessing and swept it away. He said: and the cord by which building is set straight/plumbed is called imām.

Al-Khalīl said: al-amām is what is in front. One says "ṣadruka amāmuka" (your chest is your front), putting amāmu in the nominative because he made it a noun; and one says "akhūka amāmaka" (your brother is ahead of you), putting it in the accusative because, used as a description, it means "in front of him." As for Labīd's line of verse, "So it went about, thinking each of its two open flanks — behind it and in front of it — was the source of danger," he made "behind" and "in front" refer back to the two flanks, as you would say "each of your two sides — your right and your left — is the source of danger," meaning its master and the one responsible for it.

Abū Zayd said: "imḍi yamāmī" has the sense of "imḍi amāmī" (go ahead of me). One also says yamāmī and yamāmatī. A poet said, in a line of verse: say "here I am, at your call," and listen ahead of me [yamāmatī]. (This line is obscure.)

Al-Aṣma'ī said, quoting a saying: "Ahead of her, a slave-woman met her work" — meaning wherever she turned, she found work waiting for her. And they say: "Ahead of you, you will see your trace" — meaning you will see what you have sent ahead. Abū 'Ubayda said: and among their proverbs: "Gently — in time it becomes clear which is Umāma and which is Hind." He means: be deliberate in the matter and do not hurry, and it will become clear to you.

Al-Khalīl said: al-amam is something slight and trifling. One says: "I did something that is neither amam nor beneath it." And al-amam is also something near, within reach. A poet said, in a line of verse: a woman of Kūfa, her dwelling far off — her house is neither amam [near] nor ṣaqab [close by].

Abū Ḥātim said: Abū Zayd said: one says amam meaning both small and great — it is one of the words with opposite meanings. Ibn Qamī'a said, using it for "small," in a line of verse: alas for my youth — when I lost it, I had not lost, in its place, even a small thing.

Al-Khalīl said: al-amam is also a due measure, moderation. Yūnus said: "this is a matter that is ma'mūm" — one that people take as their model, that people follow. Abū 'Amr said: rajulun mi'amm — a man who makes his way across lands without a guide. A poet said, in a line of verse: beware the wide-wastes traveler, the confident wayfinder.

And God Almighty said: {nor those making for the Sacred House} [al-Mā'ida: 2] — the plural of āmm, those who yaʾummūn [make for] the House of God, meaning they set out toward it.

Al-Khalīl said: al-tayammum runs along the same lines as seeking out deliberately. One says: "tayammam amran ḥasanan" — seek out a good course; and "tayammamū aṭyaba mā 'indakum taṣaddaqū bihi" — seek out the best of what you have and give it in charity. And al-tayammum with clean earth [the dry ablution] comes from this same meaning: seek out the best and cleanest of it and aim for it deliberately. So al-tayammum came, on common people's tongues, to mean simply the act of wiping oneself with earth, so that they say "so-and-so has done tayammum with dust." And God Almighty said: {then seek out clean earth} [al-Nisā': 43], meaning: aim deliberately for it.

A poet said, in a line of verse: if my best horsemen have indeed been struck down, then deliberately, with open eyes, I set my aim on Mālik.

And one says: "yammamtu fulānan bi-sahmī wa-rumḥī" — I aimed my arrow and spear deliberately at so-and-so, choosing him over anyone else. A poet said, in a line of verse: I aimed the spear at him from the side, then said to him: this is manliness, not the game of sliding down slopes.

Whoever, in this sense, says "ammamtuhu" instead of "yammamtuhu" has erred, because he said "from the side," and that can only be from one side, and he did not aim at what was directly in front of him.

Al-Kisā'ī said: al-umāma is eighty [head] of camels. A poet said, in a line of verse: he was gracious and gave me generously, and gave me besides eighty camels [umāma], their drivers driving them to me.

And al-umm also means the head, the chief; one says "huwa ummuhum," he is their head. Al-Shanfarā said, in a line of verse: and a mother of dependents I have witnessed feeding them — when she fed them she measured carefully and gave little. By "mother of the dependents" he meant their chief, the one who saw to their affairs; it is said this was Ta'abbaṭa Sharran.
أمت: The hamza, mīm and tā' are a single root, not extended by analogy: al-amt. God, exalted is He, said: {you will see in it no crookedness and no unevenness} [Ṭā-Hā: 107]. Al-Khalīl said: crookedness (ʿiwaj) and unevenness (amt) mean one thing. Others said — meaning the same thing — that al-amt is for a place to be raised in one spot and low in another.
أمد: The letters hamza, mīm and dāl: al-amad is the furthest point, the limit. It is a single word; nothing else is built on it by analogy.
أمر:
The letters hamza, mīm and rā' are five roots: al-amr, meaning one matter among affairs; al-amr, the opposite of forbidding; al-amar with a fatḥa on the mīm, meaning growth and blessing; a mark or sign; and wonder.

As for the single one of the affairs, it is their saying: this is a matter I was pleased with, and a matter I am not pleased with. And in the proverb: 'Some matter has brought you.' And of this, in the proverb: 'For some reason is he made a chief who is made a chief.' The amr that is the opposite of forbidding is your saying, do such a thing. Al-Aṣma'ī said: one says, I have over you one amra that is obeyed - that is, I have it against you that I command you once and you obey me. Al-Kisā'ī said: so-and-so yu'āmiru nafsayhi, he takes counsel with his two selves - one self commands him to do one thing and another self commands him to do another. And he said: he is amūr, much commanding of what is right, and nahiyy, much forbidding of what is wrong, one of a people who are umur. Of this section are al-imra and al-imāra, command and the office of a commander, and the one who holds it is amīr and mu'ammar. Ibn al-A'rābī said: ammartu fulānan - I made so-and-so a commander. And amartuhu and āmartuhu all have one meaning. Ibn al-A'rābī said: amura fulānun 'alā qawmihi - when he became commander over his people. And of this section is al-immar, the man who never stops asking people for their opinion and ends at what they say. Al-Aṣma'ī said: al-immar is the man weak in judgement, the fool who hears the talk of this one [and the talk of that one] and does not know what to take hold of. A poet said, in a line of verse:
I am no man of stiff joints, no weak-witted immar, who when he is led against his will goes meekly along.

And the Arabs say: 'When Sirius rises at dawn and you see no rain with it, then send after them neither an immara nor an immar.' He means: do not send out among your camels a man who has no sense.

As for growth: al-Khalīl said: al-amar is growth and blessing, and a woman is amira, that is, blessed for her husband. And amira al-shay' - the thing became many. And the Arabs say: 'Whoever is few is abased, and whoever grows many prevails' - that is, whoever becomes many overcomes. And you say: amira banū fulānin amaratan, that is, they became many and their cattle bore young. Labīd said, in a line of verse:
If they are envied they are brought low, and if one day they grow many, they come at last to ruin and to nothing.

Al-Aṣma'ī said: the Arabs say, 'The best of wealth is a pollinated row of palms, or a blessed and fertile filly' - and she is the one with many young, the blessed one. And one says: amara Allāhu mālahu and āmarahu - God made his property many. And from it comes 'a blessed and fertile filly'. And of the first sense: {amarnā mutrafīhā} [al-Isrā': 16]. And whoever reads it (ammarnā), its interpretation is: we set them in authority.

As for the mark and the appointed time: al-Khalīl said: al-amāra is the appointed time. Al-'Ajjāj said, in a line of verse:
To a term, and the term of my span.

Al-Aṣma'ī said: al-amāra is the sign. You say, set between me and you an amāra and an amār - a sign. A poet said, in a line of verse:
When the sun spreads its light over the lands, that is the sign of my greeting to you, so greet me back.

And al-amār - the amār of a road is its landmarks, the singular being amāra. Ḥumayd ibn Thawr said, in a line of verse:
In the middle of an open plain, as though a landmark in it, when it came into view, were a rutting stallion swaggering.

And al-amar and al-ya'mūr are also the marker. One says: I have set between me and him an amār, a time, an appointment and a term - all of that is amār. As for wonder, it is the word of God Most High: {laqad ji'ta shay'an imran} [al-Kahf: 71].
أمع: The letters hamza, mīm and ʿayn: this is not a root. What has come from it is 'rajulun immaʿa' — a man of weak judgment, who says to everyone, 'I am with you.' Ibn Masʿūd said: 'Let none of you be an immaʿa.' The origin is 'maʿa' (with), and the hamza is an added letter.
أمل:
The letters hamza, mim and lam are two origin senses: the first is steadying oneself and waiting; the second, a long ridge of sand.

As for the first, al-Khalil said: al-amal is hope. One says ammaltuhu u'ammiluhu ta'miilan, and amaltuhu amuluhu amlan and imlatan, on the pattern of "jilsa." This carries within it something of waiting. He also said: at-ta'ammul is steadying oneself in looking closely.

He said, in a line of verse:
Look carefully, my friend — do you see any of the litter-borne women, setting out from above Jurthum?

Al-Marrar said, in a line of verse:
Consider carefully what you say — for you were once a falcon, one who looks little before he strikes.

Al-qutami: the falcon, satisfied with a single glance.

The second origin sense: al-Khalil said: al-amil is a long ridge of sand set apart from the main body of sand, on the pattern "fa'il," plural umul. Ibn al-A'rabi recited, in a line of verse:
And I had crossed, with hardship, the greatest of the sand-ridges.

Tajashshamtu: I forced my way through with hardship. Amil al-umul: the greatest of them. And he said, in a line of verse:
And it swerved away in fright, not turning aside — like lightning crossing a well-marked ridge of sand.

Al-Asma'i said: in the proverb, "there was, between the two sand-ridges, room" — meaning: there was open space in the land.
أمن:
The letters hamza, mīm and nūn are two roots close to one another: one of them is trustworthiness, which is the opposite of treachery, and its meaning is the stillness of the heart; the other is holding something true. The two meanings, as we said, lie near together.

Al-Khalīl said: al-amana is from safety. Al-amān is the granting of safety. Al-amāna is the opposite of treachery.

One says amintu al-rajul amnan, amanatan and amānan; and āmananī yu'minunī īmānan. The Arabs say rajul ummān of a man who is trustworthy.

Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
And I have been at the trustworthy merchant's, his drink much resorted to.

And of one who is trustworthy: laqad amuna.

Abū Zayd said: al-amīn is the one who is trusted.

Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
And I was his trusted one, had you not betrayed him — but the Yemeni has no trustworthiness in him.

And Ḥassān said, in a line of verse:
And a trusted man to whom I gave my heart's secret to keep — and he kept it as the trusted keeps the truster.
The first is the object and the second the subject: as though he said, the keeping by the trusted of the one who trusts.

A house that is āmin is one that has safety in it. God says: {My Lord, make this land safe} [Ibrāhīm: 35].

Al-Liḥyānī recited, in a line of verse:
Do you not know, Asmā' — woe to you — that I swore an oath never to betray the one who trusts me —
that is, my āmin.

Al-Liḥyānī and others said: rajul umana is one whom people trust and whose mischief they do not fear; and amana, with a fatḥa, is one who believes whatever he hears and calls nothing false, trusting people.

As for their saying a'ṭaytu fulānan min āmani mālī, they said its meaning is: of what is dearest to me. And though this is so, the meaning is the meaning of the whole chapter, because what is dearest to a man is what his soul is at rest in.

And they recited the speaker's line, in a line of verse:
We guard our honour with the dearest of our wealth, and in the battle we trail our spears and call out our name.

And in the proverb: "the wary man is come at from the side he felt safe on." And they say: "the man of Balī is your brother — and do not trust him," meaning it as a warning.

As for holding true: the saying of God, exalted be He: {And you would not believe us} [Yūsuf: 17] — that is, hold us true.

Some of the people of knowledge said that al-Mu'min among the names of God, exalted be He, is that He makes true what He has promised His servant of reward. Others said: He is mu'min to His friends, giving them safety from His punishment and doing them no wrong — and this comes back to the first meaning.

And from it is al-Nābigha's line, in a line of verse:
And the giver of safety to the birds that take refuge, which the riders of Mecca stroke, between the thicket and al-Sa'd.

Of the second root — and God knows best — is our saying in supplication: "Āmīn." They said its explanation is: O God, do it. And it is said to be one of the names of God, exalted be He.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Fuṭḥul and his mother's son have drawn far from me — āmīn! — and God has made the distance between us greater still.

Sometimes they lengthen it, and the proof of that is the line:
My Lord, never strip me of her love — and God have mercy on a servant who said Āmīn.
أمه: As for the letters hamza, mīm and hā': they have mentioned, on the reading of those who read God's words wa-ddakara ba'da amah in that way, that it is forgetting. One says amihtu when I forgot. This is a single word that nothing else is measured against.
أموى:
As for the letters hamza and mīm with a weak letter after them, they are a single root, and it is the bondage of a bondwoman.

Al-Khalīl said: an ama is a woman in bondage. You say aqarrat bi-l-umuwwa — she acknowledged her bondage.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
As bondwomen are led to the wedding feasts.

And you say ta'ammaytu fulāna — I made her a bondwoman; and likewise ista'maytu.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
They are content with being made slaves and bondwomen.

And if it were said ta'ammat — she became a bondwoman — that would be correct too.

And he said of al-ummī, in a line of verse:
When they ran together like the wild ass in a desert of driving dust.

And laqad amiti wa-ta'ammayti umuwwatan.

Ibn al-A'rābī said: one says ista'mat when she came to resemble bondwomen, and she is not musta'miya when she does not resemble them — and likewise a slave who is musta'bid.
أن:
The letters hamza and nūn doubled are a single root, and it is a sound made in pain. Al-Khalīl said: one says "anna al-rajulu ya'innu anīnan wa-annatan wa-annan" — the man groaned; that is his sound made in pain. Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse: she complains of the nose-peg and the track worn by the two girth-straps, as the ailing sick man groans to those who visit him.

1. rajulun annān — a man who groans much.
2. Al-Liḥyānī: one says "the bow groans a groan" when its sound is soft and drawn-out. A poet said, in a line of verse: it groans when it draws the roped [creature], groaning as a weeping woman groans who has just lost someone dear. Ya'qūb said: al-annāna, among women, is one whose husband has died and who marries again, so that whenever she sees the new husband she wails and says "God have mercy on so-and-so" [her first husband].

As for the letters hamza and hā', they are not a single root, because imitations of sounds are not roots that can be reasoned from by analogy; but they say "ahha ahhatan wa-āhatan" — he sighed. Muthaqqib said, in a line of verse: when I rise to saddle her by night, she sighs the sigh of a grieving man.
أنب:
The letters hamza, nūn and bā' are a single word. 'Annabtuhu ta'nīban' means: I rebuked him and blamed him. Al-unbūb is what lies between each two joints of a reed or cane. They claim that al-anāb is musk, though God knows best whether that is true. They recite the saying of al-Farazdaq, in a line of verse:
As if it were an ostrich egg washed with rain-cloud water ... and Dārī musk mixed with old wine.
أنت:
The letters hamza, nūn and tā' are absent from al-Khalīl's book in this arrangement, and likewise from Ibn Duraid's. Others said: he groans with effort, meaning he strains. They also said: al-ma'nūt is the one struck by the evil eye — this is from Abū Ḥātim. It is also said: al-ma'nūt is that which is decreed, fated. A poet said:
Far off from it is its fated water.
أنث:
As for the letters hamza, nūn and thā', al-Khalīl and others said: al-unthā, the female, is the opposite of the male. And one says a sword is anīth al-ḥadīd when its iron is soft, "female". And al-unthayān are the two testicles. And al-unthayān are also the two ears.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And we, when the tyrant turned his cheek away in scorn ... struck him beneath the two ears, upon the nape.

And arḍ anītha is land with good growth.
أنح:
The letters hamza, nūn and ḥā' are a single root, and it is the sound of throat-clearing and straining.

1. anaḥa ya'naḥu anḥan — one says this when he cleared his throat from sickness or breathlessness, without groaning outright.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
You see the crowd standing, straining and groaning at it ... the way one straining at a hard task does, when its grips grow tight.

Abū ʿUbayd said: it is a sound accompanied by throat-clearing, and its verbal noun is al-unūḥ. Al-fi'ām is the crowd; they were groaning as they strained at it — he means, at the siege engine.

2. al-āniḥ — Abū ʿAmr said: on the pattern of fāʿil, this is the one who, when asked for something, clears his throat out of stinginess; it is said 'ya'naḥu' and 'ya'niḥu' alike, just like 'yazḥaru.'
3. al-annāḥ — the intensive form of the same. A poet said:
He is not a stingy grumbler of ample paunch ... harsh toward his kinsman, slow of glance.

4. al-anūḥ — Al-Naḍr said: among men, this is one who, when he carries a load, says 'aḥ, aḥ.' A poet said:
Men of great burden — no groaning weakling nor short-legged, crouching man can bear loads like theirs.

Al-jādhī is the short, crouching man.
أنس:
The letters hamza, nūn and sīn are a single root, and it is the showing of a thing, and everything that runs against the way of wildness. They said: al-ins are the opposite of the jinn, and they were so named for their being visible. One says ānastu al-shay' — I saw the thing. God the Exalted said: {and if you perceive in them sound judgement} [al-Nisā': 6]. And one says ānastu al-shay' — I heard the thing; and this is borrowed from the first. Al-Ḥārith said:
She caught a faint sound, and the hunters startled her at eventide, and the coming of night had drawn near.

And al-uns is a man's ease with a thing, when he does not shy away from it. And the Arabs say kayfa ibnu insika? — how is the son of your fellowship? — when he asks a man about himself. And one says insān, insānān and anāsiyy — a human being, two of them, and many. And insān al-ʿayn is the pupil, the little one that is in the black of the eye. Ibn insika is written in al-Mukhaṣṣaṣ (13: 200) as ibn insika and ibn ansika.
أنض:
The letters hamza, nūn and ḍād are a single word, not to be taken as a model for others. One says 'laḥmun anīḍ' — meat that still has rawness in it, meaning it is not fully cooked. Zuhayr said, in a line of verse:
He turns a mouthful over in his mouth, in it something underdone ... it has gone rank, and beneath the flank it sits as a sickness.

You say 'ānaḍtuhu īnāḍan' — I left it undercooked — and 'anuḍa anāḍatan' — it was undercooked.
أنف:
The letters hamza, nūn and fā' are two roots from which all the questions of this chapter branch: one is taking a thing from its beginning, and the other is the nose belonging to every creature that has a nose. Its underlying sense is delimitation.

As for the first: al-Khalīl said: ista'naftu such-and-such, meaning I returned to its start, and i'tanaftu i'tināfan [the same]. Mu'tanaf al-amr is what is begun in a matter. From this chapter also is their saying "fa'ala kadhā ānifan," he did such-and-such just now, as if it were its very beginning. God Almighty said: {They said to those given knowledge, "What did he say just now (ānifan)?"} [Muḥammad: 16].

The second root is al-anf, the nose, well known; the counted plural is ānuf, the ordinary plural unūf. A camel that is ma'nūf is one led by a ring through its nose, because when the nose-peg wounds it, it becomes obedient. A camel is anif or ānif (short and long forms). From this is the hadith: "Muslims are gentle and easy, like the anif camel — if led it follows, if made to kneel it kneels." A man is unāfiyy, great of nose. Anaftu the man: I struck his nose. A woman is anūf: pleasant in the scent of her nose.

As for their saying "anifa min kadhā" (he disdained such a thing), this too is from al-anf, like their saying of the arrogant man "warima anfuhu," his nose swelled. The nose in particular is mentioned rather than the rest of the body because one says "shamakha bi-anfihi," he raised his head in pride, which comes from anger. He cited: "and he is not to be provoked when his nose has swollen," meaning: he is not addressed while angry. And one says: "his pain is where the healer cannot place his nose" — said of what has no remedy.

Abū 'Ubayda said: Banū Anf al-Nāqa are Banū Ja'far ibn Quray' ibn 'Awf ibn Ka'b ibn Sa'd. It is said they slaughtered a she-camel they had won as spoils in a raid, while Ja'far ibn Quray' had stayed behind; he came, and nothing remained of the she-camel but the nose, so he took it, and they named him for it. This is Abū 'Ubayda's account. Al-Kalbī said: they were so named because Quray' ibn 'Awf slaughtered a she-camel and had four wives; he sent meat to them all except Umm Ja'far, so she said [to her son]: "Go and ask your father for meat." He went, and nothing remained but the nose; he took it, it stuck to him [as a nickname], and he was mocked with it — they kept mocking them with it, until al-Ḥuṭay'a said: "a people who are the nose, while others are the tails — and who would equal the tail to the she-camel's nose?" — so it turned into praise for them.

The Arabs say: "so-and-so is my anf," meaning my glory and my pride. A poet said: "and my pride (anfī) is in the gathering, and my boasting." Al-Khalīl said: anf al-liḥya (the nose of the beard) is its tip, and the anf of anything is its beginning. He cited: "and the hand has already taken from the tip of your beard." Anf al-jabal (the nose of the mountain) is its beginning, what first appears of it to you. He cited: "take the front of Harshā or its rear, for on both sides of Harshā there is a way."

Ya'qūb said: anf al-bard (the nose of the cold) is its harshest point; "he came running at anf al-shadd" means at its hardest pace. Anf al-arḍ (the nose of the land) is what faces you of its bare, open ground. A man is mi'nāf: one who travels at the anf of the day, its very beginning. Wine is unuf at the very first that comes from it. He cited a line describing wine the colour of gazelle's blood, aged, from the wine of 'Āna or the vineyards of Shibām. A girl is unuf: newly come into her youth.

Ibn al-A'rābī said: annaftu al-sirāj, I sharpened the lamp-wick's tip and trimmed it even; from this one says in praise of a horse "unnifa ta'nīf al-sayr," meaning it was shaped and evened as a leather strap is evened. Al-Aṣma'ī said: a spearhead (sinān) that is mu'annaf means sharpened. He cited a line about a resonant bow and an arrow like the sharpened sword of the Ḥimyarite. And al-ta'nīf in the hock [of a horse's leg] is trimming it fine, which is thought desirable in a horse.
أنق:
The letters hamza, nūn and qāf point to a single root, and it is being pleased with something, finding it pleasing.

1. al-anaq — Al-Khalīl said: being pleased with a thing; you say 'aniqtu bihi' and 'anā ānaqu bihi anaqan,' and 'anā bihi aniqun,' meaning: pleased. And 'ānaqanī yūniqunī īnāqan' — it pleased me.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
When she came out of her tent, her charm delighted the eye ... and the ostrich eggs pleased her.

2. aniq — a thing is aniq, and a plant is aniq, both meaning pleasing, lovely. And he said of al-aniq:
Neither trustworthy is his companion, nor is he pleasing.

3. ta'annaqtu al-makān — Abū ʿAmr said: 'aniqtu al-shay' ānaquhu' means: I loved it, and 'ta'annaqtu al-makān' means: I loved the place. This is from al-Farrā'.

Al-Shaybānī said: he seeks out al-anaq eagerly — al-anaq being the best of pasture and the like, meaning to select the finest of it. A poet said:
Your cousins have come, seekers of the choicest pasture.

One word has strayed from this root: al-anūq, the vulture. In the proverb: 'He sought the eggs of the anūq' — meaning he sought something impossible. It is said that she does not lay eggs; and it is also said that rather, no one is able to get at her eggs. A poet said:
He sought the piebald wild-ass mare, and when he could not get her, he set out to seek the eggs of the anūq.
أنك: The letters hamza, nūn and kāf have no root in them, except that al-ānuk has been mentioned. It is said to be pure lead; and it is also said that it is rather a kind of lead.
أنى:
The letters hamza, nūn, and whichever weak letter follows them have four origins: slowness and what resembles it, such as forbearance; a period of time; the attaining or ripening of a thing; and a container.

As for the first: Al-Khalīl said: al-anāh is forbearance, and its verb is ta'annā and ta'ayyā. He recites the saying of al-Kumayt, in a line of verse:
Stop at the abodes as a visitor stops ... and be patient, for you are not a lowly man.

It is also transmitted as 'wa ta'ayya.' Lingering patiently over matters is called al-ta'annī.

The Messenger of God, peace and blessings upon him and his family, said to a man who stepped over people's necks on a Friday: 'I saw you cause harm and delay' — meaning: you came late and were slow. Al-Ḥuṭay'a said, in a line of verse:
I delayed the evening meal until Suhayl rose ... or until al-Shiʿrā, so my delay grew long.

One says, from al-anāh, 'rajulun aniyyun dhū anātin' — a man of forbearance. A poet said:
Be forbearing, for the man of sound judgment and slow deliberation is the most forbearing.

It was said to Ibnat al-Khuss: 'Does the two-year-old she-camel conceive?' She said: 'Yes, but her conceiving is aniyy' — meaning slow. One also says: 'So-and-so's good comes slowly [aniyy]' — meaning slow. And al-anā is from al-anāh, deliberateness. A poet said:
The deliberation grew long, and haste parted ways with what was right.

Another poet said:
With patience and forbearance, and awaiting them tomorrow ... I am neither slack nor an inexperienced weakling.

One says of a man: 'He is a man of anāh,' meaning he does not hurry in matters, and he is ānin, dignified. Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
Gentleness is a blessing, and patience is good fortune ... so be patient, with gentleness, and you will meet success.

'Ista'naytu fulānan' means: I did not hurry him. A forbearing, blessed woman is called anāh, plural anawāt. Abū ʿUbayd said: al-anāh is a woman who has a certain languor when she rises.

As for time: al-inā and al-anā is an hour of the hours of the night, plural ānā'; every inan is an hour. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: one says 'uniyy' for all of them together. A poet said:
Would that I had a drinking-companion from Ghaniyy like my own ... a true companion, laughing at every hour,
when the water-buckets were carried by their ropes.

He means: at whatever hour you came to him, you found him laughing.

As for the attaining or ripening of a thing: this is al-inā. You say 'intaẓarnā inā al-laḥm' — we waited for the meat to be ready. You say 'mā anā laka' and 'lam ya'ni laka,' meaning: it has not yet come due for you. God Almighty said: {Has the time not yet come for those who believe} [al-Ḥadīd: 16], meaning: it has not come due. 'Āna ya'īnu' means the same. 'Ista'naytu al-ṭaʿām' means: I waited for the food to be ready. {boiling water, at its extreme heat} [al-Raḥmān: 44] — its heat has reached its limit. The verb is 'anā l-mā'u l-musakhkhanu ya'nī' — the heated water reaches its boiling point. And {a spring, boiling} [al-Ghāshiya: 5].

ʿAbbās said, in a line of verse:
Openly, while the horses' backs are covered ... with boiling-hot blood, and simmering blood pooling from within.

Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: one says 'āna ya'īnu aynan' and 'anā laka ya'nī anyan,' meaning: it came due. One says 'atayt fulānan āyinatan baʿda āyinah,' meaning: from time to time, and also 'tāratan baʿda tārah,' turn after turn. God Almighty said: {without waiting for it to be ready} [al-Aḥzāb: 53].

As for the container: it is al-ināʾ, with a long final vowel, from al-āniya, vessels. Al-awānī is a plural of a plural — the pattern fiʿāl is pluralized as afʿila.
أهب:
The letters hamza, hā' and bā' are two words of distinct origin.

1. al-ihāb — Ibn Duraid said: al-ihāb is the hide before it is tanned, plural ahab. It is one of the words pluralized on the pattern fa'al whose singular is fa'īl, or fa'ūl, or fi'āl: adīm/adam, afīq/afaq, ʿamūd/ʿamad, ihāb/ahab. Al-Khalīl said: every hide is called ihāb, plural ahab.
2. al-ta'ahhub — the second word. Al-Khalīl said: 'ta'ahhabū li-l-sayr' — they made ready for the journey. 'Akhadha fulānun uhbatahu' means: so-and-so took up his equipment, his readiness. One also drops the alif and says 'hubatahu.'
أهر: The letters hamza, hā' and rā' are a single word, not found in al-Khalīl nor Ibn Duraid. Others said: al-ahara is household furnishings, household goods.
أهل:
The letters hamza, hā' and lām are two roots far apart. One of them is al-ahl, the family. Al-Khalīl said: a man's ahl is his wife. And al-ta'ahhul is marrying. And a man's ahl are the people closest to him. And ahl al-bayt are the dwellers in the house. And ahl al-islām are those who hold that religion. And the plural of ahl is ahlūn; and al-ahālī is the plural of the plural.

Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
Three households I outlived and lost, and God was the One turned to for help.

And you say ahhaltuhu li-hādhā al-amr ta'hīlan — I made him fit for this matter. And makānun āhilun, ma'hūlun — an inhabited place.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Long ago it was peopled, and now it has become a grazing ground for wild goats.

And the rajaz poet said, in a line of verse:
I knew the dwellings at al-Naṣriyya, empty now, and they had once been peopled places of theirs.

And everything among the beasts and others, when it keeps to a place, is āhil and ahlī, tame. And in the hadith: «He forbade the flesh of domestic donkeys.» And some of them said: the Arabs say "āhalaka Allāhu fī al-janna īhālan" — that is, may God give you a wife in it.

The other root is al-ihāla. Al-Khalīl said: al-ihāla is the fat of the tail and the like, which is taken, cut up and melted down. That is al-ihāla, and al-jamīl, and al-jumāla.
أهن:
The letters hamza, hā' and nūn are a single word, not to be taken as a model for others. Al-Khalīl said: al-ihān is al-ʿurjūn, the stalk above the small stems of the date cluster, that is, of the palm tree. A poet said:
She has a forearm like the palm-stalk ... smooth, and a belly that stayed slim.

The plural for small numbers is āhina, and the general plural is uhun.
أو: A word of doubt and of permission.
أوب:
The letters hamza, wāw and bā' are a single root, and it is returning; then things are derived from it that sound a little far off, though the origin is one.

Al-Khalīl said: āba fulān ilā sayfihi — so-and-so put his hand back to his sword to draw it. Al-awb is the swinging back of the forelegs and the legs in travelling. Ka'b ibn Zuhayr said, in lines of verse:
As though the swing of her two forelegs, when she had sweated ... and the mirage had wrapped itself about the hills,
were the swing of the hands of a grey-haired woman who has lost her child and wails ... who passed the night, and stricken, bereaved women answered her.

The verb from it is al-ta'wīb, and for this reason they call travel by [day ta'wīb, and travel by] night is'ād. And a poet said, in a line of verse:
Two days: a day of standing-places and assemblies ... and a day of marching against the enemy, a day's hard travel.

He said: a single instance of it is a ta'wība. Al-ta'wīb is also the glorifying of God, in His words, exalted: {O mountains, echo praises with him, and you birds} [Saba': 10]. Al-Aṣma'ī said: awwabtu al-ibil — I brought the camels back in the evening to their resting-place. And one says ta'awwabanī — he came to me by night. A poet said, in a line of verse:
My old sickness came upon me by night and stayed till the last dark ... I fear my sickness will come back on me and lay me low again.

Abū Zayd said: al-Aṣma'ī used to explain every verse in which "al-iyāb", the returning, is mentioned as being with the night, and he would argue from the line:
A sickness came upon me by night, pouring down.
and so he explained everything of the kind in the poems. I said to him: al-iyāb is only returning, at whatever time a man returns; you say qad āba al-musāfir — the traveller has come back. It was as though I wanted to make it plain to him, so I said: 'Abīd's line:
Everyone who is absent returns ... but he whom death takes away does not return —
is this in the evening? He set about arguing with me over it, so I said: then God's words, exalted, {Indeed to Us is their return} [al-Ghāshiya: 25] — is this in the evening? He fell silent. Abū Zayd said: yet most of it does come as he said — may God have mercy on us and on him.

Al-ma'āb is the place of return. Abū Ziyād said: ubtu al-qawma — that is, I returned to the people. A poet said, in a line of verse:
How, and from where, has delight come back to you?

Abū 'Ubayd said: the outlet by which the flour comes from the millstone is called al-ma'āb, because whatever was under the millstone returns to it. Al-Khalīl said: and you say ābat al-shamsu iyāban — when the sun disappears into its ma'āb, that is, its place of setting. Umayya said, in a line of verse:
And he saw the setting of the sun at its going down.

Al-Naḍr said: al-mu'awwiba is the sun, and its ta'wīb is what lies between the east and the west; it toils through its day and returns at sunset. And one says "they came from every awb" — that is, from every side and quarter; and that too is from this. Al-awb is bees. Al-Aṣma'ī said: they were named so for their returning to the hive, since they come back from their pastures. It is as though the singular of al-awb were ā'ib, as one says [ābaka Allāh] — may God put you far away. A poet said, in a line of verse:
May God put you far! Why not — while the nights come unawares ... to visit, and in the days there are things to keep you from us.
أود:
The hamza, wāw and dāl are a single root: bending and curving. udtu al-shay' — I bent a thing. ta'awwada al-nabt — the plant bent and curved, [as if it] "folded and turned."

A poet said:
If what you have left of me were hung on a stem of thumām-grass, its stem would not [even] bend.

To this belongs ādanī al-shay', ya'ūdunī — a thing weighed on me, as though it grew heavy upon you until it bent and curved you.

Awd is a tribe, and it is possible its name is drawn from this. Ūd is a place.

A line:
Was it love — did I see you at Rāmatān and Qūd, or at al-Junayna, in the watercourses of Ūd?
أور:
The letters hamza, wāw and rā' are a single root, and it is heat. Al-Khalīl said: al-uwār is the heat of the sun, and the heat of an oven. One says 'arḍun awira' — a hot land. He said: sometimes they pluralize al-uwār as al-uwur. Uwāra is a place.

The Day of Uwāra: this was when ʿAmr ibn al-Mundhir al-Lakhmī fostered a son of Zurāra ibn ʿUdus called Asʿad. When the boy grew up, a large-humped she-camel passed by him and he threw a stone at her udder. Her owner, Suwayd, one of the Banū ʿAbdallāh ibn Dārim, set upon him and killed him. Suwayd then fled and made his way to Mecca. Zurāra was at that time with ʿAmr ibn al-Mundhir, and he concealed the killing of his son Asʿad.

Then ʿAmr ibn Milqaṭ al-Ṭā'ī came — he bore a grudge against Zurāra — and said, in a line of verse:
Who will carry word to ʿAmr, that ... no man is made to endure forever;
here, the last-born son of his mother lies ... on the slope, below Uwāra;
and the misfortunes of the days leave ... nothing behind but stone.

ʿAmr ibn al-Mundhir said: 'Zurāra, what do you say to this?' He said: 'He lies; you know his enmity toward me.' ʿAmr said: 'You speak truly.' But when night fell, Zurāra slipped away and made off, joining his people. He did not stay long before he fell ill and died.

When word of his death reached ʿAmr, he raided the Banū Dārim — he had sworn to kill a hundred of them. He came and made camp at Uwāra; they had already fled and scattered, but he killed ninety-nine of them. Then a poet from the Barājim came to him to praise him; ʿAmr seized him and killed him too, to make up the hundred, saying: 'It is the wretched man who comes as the Barājim's envoy.'

Al-Aʿshā said concerning this, in a line of verse:
And we shall be counted among the forebears, equal ... to Minqar and the Banū Zurāra —
sons of a people killed ... on the day of al-Quṣayba, from Uwāra.

And al-uwār also means a place. A poet said:
Of those raised without hardship ... whose abodes are al-Qaṣīma, then al-Uwār.
أوس:
The letters hamza, wāw and sīn are a single word: the gift. They said: 'ustu l-rajula a'ūsuhu awsan' — I gave to the man. Al-aws is also said to mean compensation. Al-Jaʿdī said, in a line of verse:
Three households I lost ... and God alone was the one sought for compensation.

Meaning: the one from whom compensation is sought. Aws is also [a name for] the wolf, and its derivation may be from what we have mentioned; its diminutive is Uways. A poet said:
What has Uways done today among the flock?
أوق:
The letters hamza, wāw and qāf have two origins: the first is heaviness, the second is a low, sunken place.

As for the first: al-awq is heaviness. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: one says 'āqa ʿalayhim,' meaning: it grew heavy upon them. A poet said:
Wandering she-camels, fate weighed heavily upon them ... swaying, from fear of what befell the others.

He means: what fate brought down upon the first one weighed most heavily on them, so they feared the like of it for themselves.

Yaʿqūb said: one says 'awwaqtu al-insān,' when you load a person with more than he can bear. As for al-ta'wīq regarding food, it too is from this, because it places a weight upon the soul — meaning delaying it and reducing it. A poet said:
Ḥutrūsh ibn ʿAzza was indeed content ... with a straitened life, other than the life he has now.

And the rajaz poet said:
It weighed hard on your uncle that you should go hungry, or that you should spend a night without your evening drink, or that you should be seen gloomy, uncheered.

As for the second: al-ūqa is a low place where water gathers, plural al-uwaq. Ru'ba said, in a line of verse:
And the hunter plunged in among the hollows.

It is also said that al-ūqa is a well.
أول:
The letters hamza, wāw and lām are two roots: the beginning of a matter and its end.

As for the first, it is al-awwal, which is the start of a thing; and the feminine is al-ūlā, on the patterns afʿal and fuʿlā; and the plural of al-ūlā is ūlayāt, like al-ukhrā, the last. As for al-awā'il, some of them say that the building of "awwal" is founded on a hamza, a wāw and a lām, and that is the [right] word; and some of them say it is founded on two wāws with a lām after them. And the Arabs have said awwala for the feminine, and pluralised it awwalāt. And he recited, describing a camel, in a line of verse:
Dark brown, known by his firsts, his forebears; his father's pride goes to the sons of his daughters —
that is: his father's pride is plain in his offspring.

Abū Zayd: a nāqa awwala and a jamal awwal — when the two of them go ahead of the camels. And the pattern in its plural is awāwil, except that every wāw that falls at the end, or near it, after a quiescent alif is turned into a hamza.

Al-Khalīl: ra'aytuhu ʿāman awwala yā fatā — I saw him last year, young man — because awwal is on the pattern of afʿal; and whoever gives it tanwīn treats it as indefinite.

Abū al-Najm said, in a line of verse:
He has tasted no dregs since the year before.

Ibn al-Aʿrābī: khudh hādhā awwala dhāti yadayn, and awwala dhī awwal, and awwala awwal — that is, before everything. And they say: "As for first of all, I praise God."

And the prayer called al-ūlā was so named because it was the first prayer that was prayed. Abū Zayd said: the people of the Days of Ignorance used to call Sunday al-Awwal. And they recited about it, in a line of verse:
I hope that I may live, and that my day may fall on al-Awwal, or on Ahwan, or on Jubār.

The second root: al-Khalīl said: al-ayyil is the male of the mountain goats, and the plural is ayā'il. And it was called ayyil only because it goes back (ya'ūlu) to the mountain to take refuge.

Abū al-Najm said, in a line of verse:
As though upon the tails of those long unmated, from the summer's dirt, were the horns of the mountain goat.
He likened what had stuck to their tails of their dung and dried there to the horns of wild goats.

And their saying āla al-labanu — the milk thickened — is of this chapter, and that is because it does not thicken [except] at the end of its course.

Al-Khalīl said, or another: al-iyāl, on the pattern fiʿāl, is a vessel in which drink is gathered for days until it comes good.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
He breaks the seal when it has grown old, and after one steeping he makes another.

And āla ya'ūlu — that is, he returned. Yaʿqūb said: it is said "awwala al-ḥukma ilā ahlihi" — that is, he returned the judgement and gave it back to them.

Al-Aʿshā said:
I return the judgement to its own people.

Al-Khalīl said: āla al-labanu ya'ūlu awlan wa-uwūlan — it thickened; and so too a plant. Abū Zayd said: āla al-labanu ʿalā al-iṣbaʿ, and that is that it curdle, so that when you put your finger in it, it is said āla ʿalayhā. And āla al-qaṭirān — when the tar thickened. And āla jismu al-rajul — when the man's body grew lean. And that is of the chapter, because it turns and shrinks, that is, it goes back to that state.

And al-iyāla, the governing of people, is of this chapter, because the return of the flock is to the one who tends it. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: āla al-rajulu raʿiyyatahu ya'ūluhā — when he governed them well.

The rajaz poet said, in a line of verse:
He governs them, the first of those who govern.

And the Arabs say among their proverbs: "ulnā wa-īla ʿalaynā" — that is, we governed and others governed us. And of the saying of Labīd:
With a wetted stick that her thumb works into shape —
they said it is on the pattern iftaʿala from altuhu, that is, I set it right. And rajulun ā'ilu mālin, on the pattern of khā'ilu mālin — that is, one who manages it. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: it is said radadtuhu ilā ā'ilatihi — that is, to his nature and his disposition.

And a man's āl, the people of his house, is from this too, because to him is their return and to them is his. And this is the sense of their saying yāla fulān — O family of so-and-so.

And Ṭarafa said, in a line of verse:
You reckon a glance at her a piece of courage — O my people, for youth in its full flush!

And the proof that this is from the first, lightened from it, is the saying of a poet, in a line of verse:
Your duty was to say to Bāriq: O family of Yāriq, why was Jarīr reviled?

And a man's āl, his person, is from this too. And so is the āl of everything. And that is because they speak of him by his āl, and they are his kin: they say āl Abī Bakr, and they mean Abū Bakr. And in this there is a little obscurity.

Al-Khalīl said: the āl of a mountain are its edges and its sides.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
As though the mountain's high crag, in the mirage when it appeared, were a great swaying camel with two loads.

And the āl of a camel are its flat bones and what juts out from the sides of its frame.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Of those which, when their temper has softened, still keep after it a frame and a toughened hide.

And another said:
You see he has a frame and a long, tall body.

And the āl of a tent are its poles.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Nothing was left but the poles of a well-ordered tent, black stones over myrtle, and a broken trench.

And al-āla is a state.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
I shall carry myself upon a course — be it against me or for me.

And from this chapter is the ta'wīl of speech, which is its outcome and what it comes back to, and that is His saying, exalted be He: {hal yanẓurūna illā ta'wīlahu} — do they wait for anything but its outcome? [al-Aʿrāf: 53]. He is saying: what it comes back to at the time of their being raised and brought forth.

And al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse:
Except that her love kept coming back, as the spring-born young camel keeps coming back, and then it was fostered.
He means its return and its outcome. And that is from āla ya'ūlu.
أون:
The letters hamza, wāw and nūn are one word pointing to gentleness. One says āna ya'ūnu awnan, when he goes gently. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And a journey that had little ease in it.

And it is said to the traveller: un ʿalā nafsika — that is, go easy on yourself. And untu a'ūnu awnan; and a man is ā'in, one who goes gently.
أوه:
The letters hamza, waw and ha' are a word that is not an origin sense to build analogies on. Ta'awwaha — he said "awwah" or "awh"; the Arabs say this in pain or grief.

He said, in a line of verse:
Whenever I rose to saddle her by night, I groaned the groan of a grieving man.

God, Most High, said: {Indeed Ibrahim was one much given to lament and supplication, forbearing} [at-Tawba: 114] — meaning: much given to supplication and lament to God. Awwah has several forms: with the first vowel long and the waw doubled; with the first vowel short and the waw doubled; with the first vowel long and the waw single. And awhi, with the waw quiet and the ha' carrying a short i; and awwih, with the waw doubled carrying a short i and the ha' quiet; and ah and aw; and awtah.
أوى:
The letters hamza, wāw and yā' have two origins: one is gathering together, the other is compassion.

Al-Khalīl said: one says 'awā l-rajulu ilā manzilihi' and 'āwā ghayrahu,' with the verbal nouns uwiyyan and īwā'an; one also says 'awā iwā'an,' though al-uwiyy is the better form. God Almighty said: {when the youths took refuge in the cave} [al-Kahf: 10], and He said: {and We gave the two of them refuge on a hillside} [al-Mu'minūn: 50]. Al-ma'wā is the place where anything takes refuge, by night or day. 'Awati l-ibilu ilā ahlihā ta'wī uwiyyan' — the camels returned to their people; such a camel is āwiya.

Al-Khalīl said: al-ta'awwī is gathering together. One says 'ta'awwati l-ṭayru' — when the birds drew close together; they are then uwiyy and muta'awwiyāt. A poet said:
As the kites drew near together in flocks.

He likened each of the three gathered hearth-stones to a kite.

The other origin is their saying 'awaytu li-fulānin āwī lahu ma'wiyatan' — meaning to feel tenderness and mercy for him; the verbal noun is also given as ayyatan. Abū ʿUbayd said: one says 'ista'waytu fulānan,' meaning: I asked him to show me compassion. A poet said:
And even had I asked him for compassion, he would not have shown it to me.
أي: A word of wonder and of questioning. One says ta'ayyaytu — on the pattern of tafa''altu — meaning I lingered. This is in the speaker's line of verse: and I knew it was not a place for lingering. As for ta'ayyaytu and al-āya [a sign/verse], that has already been discussed in its own place. And ā' — with a long final vowel — is a tree; this is in the line of verse: a knock-kneed, close-cropped-eared [beast], grazing for itself at al-Sīy on tannūm-shrub and ā'-tree. Al-Khalīl said: the imitation of the clamor of armies and the like is called ā'. A poet said, in a line of verse: in a loud, tumultuous host, its horses' neighing heard by night at its edges as āʾ. And we have already said that imitations of sounds are not roots that can be reasoned from by analogy.
أيد:
The letters hamza, yā' and dāl are a single root, pointing to strength and to guarding. One says ayyadahu Allāh, that is, God gave him strength. He, Most High, said: {and the heaven, We built it with might} [al-Dhāriyāt: 47]. This is the sense of strength. As for the guarding, al-iyād is anything that blocks a thing off and guards it. Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
We drove him away from fair eggs on a sandy slope, which had gathered around them, out of its own soil, a guarding bank.
أير:
The letters hamza, yā' and rā' are a single word, and it is the wind. There is disagreement about it: some said it is a hot wind, bearing scorching heat. If that is so, then the yā' was originally a wāw, and the explanation of that has already passed under the letters hamza, wāw and rā'. Others said: it is the cold north wind, in the dialect of Hudhayl. A poet said, in a line of verse:
We are generous when the east wind blows ... and we hold steady in worth when the north wind blows.
أيس:
The letters hamza, yā' and sīn are not a root to be taken as a model for others; only two words have come from it that I do not think belong to the true speech of the Arabs, and we have mentioned them only because al-Khalīl mentioned them.

Al-Khalīl said: 'ays' is a word that has fallen out of use, except that the Arabs say: 'Bring it from wherever it is or is not.' Ays was used only in this saying; its meaning is like [ḥaythu], meaning being, existing, having. He said: 'lays' means 'no ays,' meaning: no being found.

The other word is al-Khalīl's statement that al-ta'yīs is finding something scanty; one says 'mā ayyasnā fulānan,' meaning: we found nothing of good in him.

Another word occurs in the saying of al-Mutalammis, in a line of verse:
The days circle around him, and nothing wears him down.

Abū ʿUbayda said: this means nothing affects him. And he recited:
If you were a boulder of solid rock, nothing would wear it down — meaning: nothing affects it.
أيض: The letters hamza, yā' and ḍād are a single word pointing to returning and going back. One says 'āḍa ya'īḍu' — when he returned. From this comes their saying 'qāla dhāka ayḍan' (he said that also) and 'faʿalahu ayḍan' (he did it also).
أيق:
The letters hamza, yā' and qāf are a single word, not to be taken as a model for others. Al-Khalīl said: al-ayq is al-waẓīf, the place on a horse's leg where the shackle sits. Al-Ṭirimmāḥ said, in a line of verse:
The wild oryx stood, locking every fettered leg ... as tightly set as the pastern-bone of a gilded-coated, still-standing horse.

Al-Aṣmaʿī and Abū ʿAmr said: al-ayq is al-qayn, the place of the shackle on the shank.
أيك:
The letters hamza, yā' and kāf are a single root, and it is a coming-together of trees, a thicket.

1. al-ayka — a thicket that grows sidr (lote-trees) and arāk (the toothstick tree). Al-Khalīl said this.
2. ayyika — another way of saying [ayka]; it is made up of soft, tender trees.

The scholars of tafsīr said: they were people of a tangled, thickly-grown tree — meaning God's saying {The companions of the Thicket denied} [al-Shuʿarā': 176]. Abū Ziyād said: al-ayka is a mass of arāk trees.

Al-Akhṭal said, about palm trees, in a line of verse:
The picker nearly loses his way amid its thicket ... when its doves' cooing calls out to each other in the evening.
أيم:
The hamza, yā' and mīm are three entirely distinct roots: smoke, the snake, and the woman without a husband.

The first: Al-Khalīl said: al-īām — smoke. Abū Dhu'ayb said:
When he drove them out with smoke, they clustered in huddled groups, humbled and downcast.
He means the honey-gatherer drove the bees out with smoke. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: āma, ya'ūmu, īāman — the man smoked the hive so its bees would leave and he could harvest its honey; he is āyim, and the bees are ma'wūma, or if you like, mu'wam ʿalayhā.

The second: al-aym, among snakes, is the white one. A poet said:
As though its nose-rein were a bold white snake, swaying among dense, coiling folds.
Ru'ba said:
[She has] a belly like a snake, a stalk-slender waist, and a soft haunch that quivers as it sways.
Yūnus said: it is the small white snake. Banū Tamīm say ayn [with nūn]. Al-Aṣmaʿī said its true form is doubled: one says ayyim and aym, like hayyin and hayn.

A line:
...but for [she-camels] surly as worn-out things, used by night to the watering-place of a coiling snake.

The third: al-ayyim — a woman with no husband, or a man with no wife. God, exalted is He, said: {and marry off those among you who are unmarried} [al-Nūr: 32]. āmat al-mar'a, ta'īmu, ayma and uyūman — the woman remained without a husband.

A poet said:
O Fāṭima, I am dying — so remain unwed [after me], and do not grieve: every woman, in the end, is left a widow.
أين:
The letters hamza, yā' and nūn indicate weariness, and the nearness of a thing.

As for the first: al-ayn is weariness. It is said that no verb is built from it, yet they have said āna yaʾīnu aynan, he grew weary. As for nearness, they said: āna laka, yaʾīnu aynan, the time has come for you.

As for the snake called al-ayn, that is a substitution of letters, the true original being mīm [in place of the nūn].

A poet said, in a line of verse:
He travels by night over the ayn-snakes and other snakes, going barefoot ... my soul be your ransom, one who journeys on foot.
أيه: The letters hamza, yā' and hā' are not a single root, for it is the imitation of a sound. One says: ayyaha taʾyīhan, when he shouted, made a noise. We have already said that sounds like this cannot be used as a basis for deriving a root.
أيى:
The letters hamza, yā' and yā' are a single root, and it is looking, gazing. One says: taʾayyā yataʾayyā taʾayyiyan, meaning: he tarried, lingered.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Stand at the abodes as a visitor stands ... and linger, for you are not lowly.

Labīd said, in a line of verse:
And I lingered over it, returning ... while shadows of dusk lay upon the ground.
He means: I departed unhurriedly, calmly.

Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: taʾayyaytu [al-amr] means: I waited for its right time to come.

ʿAdī said, in a line of verse:
I waited from them for the outcome, and I did not cease ... holding back from myself one who was constant and one who was contending.

And one says: this is not a dwelling of lingering, meaning: a stopping place.

And another root, and it is deliberate intent. One says taʾāyaytu, on the pattern of tafāʿaltu, its origin being taʿammadtu āyatahu wa-shakhṣahu, I purposely set my aim on its mark and its form.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
With it I take aim at every direction and every parting of ways.

They said: al-āya is the sign, and this is called āya maʾāya, just as one says ʿalāma muʿlama, a marked sign. And one has said ayyaytu, meaning: I set up a sign.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Convey, on your part, to Banū Tamīm ... by the sign of how much you love food.

They said: the origin of āya is aʾya, on the pattern of aʿya, with two hamzas, and the second was softened so the word lengthened. Sībawayh said: the middle letter of āya is a wāw, because a word whose middle letter is wāw and whose final letter is yāʾ is more common than one whose middle and final letters are both yāʾ, just as shawaytu (I roasted) is more common in speech than ḥayītu (I lived).

Al-Aṣmaʿī said: āyat al-rajul is his person, his bodily form. Al-Khalīl said: kharaja al-qawmu bi-āyatihim, meaning: with their whole company.

Burj ibn Mushir said, in a line of verse:
We went out from the two passes — no tribe like us ... with our whole company, driving on the milk-laden riding camels.

From this too is āyat al-Qurʾān, a verse of the Qurʾan, because it is a group of letters, and its plural is āy. And iyāt al-shams is its light, and that too is from this, because it is like a mark for it.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
The sun's light gave it drink, all but its gums [the rest of this line is unclear to me].

The book of hamza is complete, and the book of bā' follows it.
اعرنزمت:
The nose-tip and the jowl, when they grow thick and firm. He said:
The fire of al-Sharawrā was kindled by heads with great jaws, their jowls swollen firm.
This is a blend formed from ʿaraza and razama. As for razama, it means he gathered together — from it the bundle of clothes was named, which we have already mentioned. As for ʿaraza, it is from ʿaraza, when it contracted and drew together.
اعلنكس: Hair, when its blackness deepens and it grows thick, is described as iʿlankasa. This belongs with the previous root; the lām stands in place of the rāʾ, and we have already explained it. I say ʿarkastu al-shayʾ, I gathered a thing's parts one upon another; this is from ʿakasa and rakasa, both already explained.
بأس:
The letters bā', hamza and sīn are a single root, hardness and [what] resembles it. So al-ba's is hardness in war. And a man dhū ba's and ba'īs is a brave man. And ba'asa ba'san; and if you describe him with bu's you say ba'usa. And al-bu's is hardness in living. And al-mubta'is is the iftaʿala form built from dislike and grief. He said, in a line of verse:
Whatever God apportions, accept it without repining at it, and sit as a noble man, at ease of mind.
بأو: The letters bā’, hamza and wāw are a single word, and it is al-ba’w, which is self-conceit.
بب:
The letters bāʾ and bāʾ, doubled, are not a true root, for it is the imitation of a sound. Al-Khalīl said: al-babba is the roaring of a stallion in its reverberation. Ruʾba said, in a line of verse:
A white-lipped one, loudly roaring, drives them on, bellowing ... when he calls them, they come forward without holding back.

And they have said: a man is babb, meaning: fat, plump; and one of them used to be nicknamed "Babba."
بت:
The letters bā' and tā' have two aspects, two roots: one is cutting, the other a kind of clothing.

As for the first: they said al-batt is total, complete cutting. One says batattu al-ḥabl and abtattu, I cut the rope completely. One says: I gave him this grant decisively, once and for all. "Al-battata" is derived from cutting, but it is used for any matter that is carried through and never returned to. One says: so-and-so cut off from so-and-so, so he withdrew and drew back.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
He settled among Jusham, and cut himself off, withdrawing ... with his bond, from the heights of the noble, illustrious ones.

Al-Khalīl said: abatta fulānun ṭalāqa fulānata, meaning: he pronounced a decisive, final divorce. Al-Kisāʾī said: the Arabs' speech is abtattu ʿalayhi al-qaḍāʾa, with an alif, while the people of the Ḥijāz say batattu, anā abuttu. And one says: ḍaraba yadahu fa-abattahā wa-battahā, meaning: he cut it off. And anything you carry through and finish, you have "batatta" it.

Al-Khalīl and others said: a very foolish man is called bātt; a drunk man is called bātt, meaning: cut off from work; and a drunk man who "does not batt" is one who settles nothing. Abū Ḥātim said: the camel called al-bātt is the one that stops moving from exhaustion, until it dies. And in the hadith: "the one whose mount has broken down [al-munbatt] has neither crossed land nor kept his mount's back sound" — that is the one who exhausted his riding animal until its back gave way, and he was left stranded by it.

Al-Tamīmī said: "this is an overloaded camel, and I fear that if I put a load on it I will batt it," meaning: I will finish it off. Mubdaʿ means overburdened; from this is the saying "I have been overburdened."

Al-Naḍr said: the worn-out camel called al-bātt is the emaciated one that cannot move.

1. battāt — travel-provisions, so called because they are a sign of parting.
2. battathu ahluhu — his family provisioned him for a journey. Al-Khalīl said this.

A poet said, in a line of verse [I am unsure of the exact sense of this line]:
Father of five, whom they all circle round together ... tomorrow, not one of them will have provisions.

Abū ʿUbayd said, and in the hadith: "no tithe is taken on al-batāt," meaning household goods — that is, no alms-tax is due on it. Al-ʿĀmirī said: al-batāt is provisions of food and drink; and one says tabattata al-rajulu li'l-khurūj, meaning: he made himself ready for departure.

Al-ʿĀmirī said: one says ḥajja fulānun ḥajjan battan, meaning: alone, and likewise for anything single of its kind. He said: a man is called batt, meaning alone; and a shirt is batt, meaning single, with nothing else worn over it.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Many a fair woman, wearing a single garment.

Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: aʿṭaytuhu kadhā fa-battat bihi, meaning: he kept it entirely to himself.

Among what falls outside this chapter is their saying: ṭaḥana bi'l-raḥā battan, when he moved his hand away toward his left [while grinding], and shazran, when he moved it away toward his right.
بتر:
The bā', tā' and rā' are a single root: cutting before completing it.

1. al-sayf al-bātir — the sharp-cutting sword.
2. abtar — said of a man with no offspring, and of anyone whose trace of good has been cut off.

In the hadith: "Kill the [snake] with the two stripes, and the short-tailed one."

3. Ziyād gave his "cut-off sermon" (al-khuṭba al-batrā'), because he did not open it with praise of God, exalted is He, and prayer upon the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace.
4. rajul ubātir — a man who severs his ties of kinship, cutting them off.

A line:
Severing the bonds of kin — swift, and thorough about it.
بتع: The letters bāʾ, tāʾ and ʿayn are a single root, indicating strength and firmness. Al-bataʿ is length of the neck together with firmness of its base. And everyone strong in the joints is called batiʿ. As for al-bitʿ, they say it is a fermented drink made of honey, mead. And it is possible it was named so for a reason connecting it to this same sense of strength.
بتك:
The bā', tā' and kāf are a single root: cutting. They say: bataktu al-shay', abtukuhu, batkan — I cut a thing.

1. Al-Khalīl said: al-batk — the cutting of the ear. In the Qur'an: {and they will surely cut into the ears of cattle} [al-Nisā': 119].
2. al-bātik — the cutting sword.
3. al-batk — to grip hair, or feathers, or the like, then pull it toward you so that it tears out at its root, meaning it is severed and plucked away. Each portion of it is a bitka, plural bitak.

Zuhayr said:
Until, when the boy's hand swooped down at it, it flew off — leaving in his hand torn tufts of its plumage.
بتل:
The letters ba', ta' and lam are one root, indicating the setting apart of a thing from another.

1. bataltu ash-shay' — I separated it from another.
2. "he divorced her batta batla" — finally, decisively.
3. Mary the Virgin is called al-Batul from this, because she set herself apart, having no husband.
4. nakhla mubtil — a palm tree from which the young shoot growing beside it has been separated off.

The Hudhali poet said, in a line of verse:
Is that your way, when her camels were brought near, like the young she-camel set apart from the herd?

5. al-batila — any limb, compact with its own flesh, plural bata'il, as if, from the abundance of its flesh, it stood apart from the limb beside it.
6. "a woman mubattalat al-khalq" — full-limbed, each limb distinctly and fully formed.
7. at-tabattul — sincerity of intention toward God and devoting oneself wholly to Him.

God, Most High, said: {and devote yourself to Him utterly} [al-Muzzammil: 8] — meaning: cut yourself off, for Him, from all else.
بث:
The letters bā' and thā' are a single root, and it is the scattering of a thing and making it manifest. One says: they scattered the horses in the raid. And the hunter loosed his dogs upon the game.

Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
So he loosed them upon it, and they went on with it ... slender-jointed [hounds], free of any defect [I am unsure of the exact sense of "free from ḥarad" here].

God Almighty created creation and scattered them upon the earth for their livelihood. And when goods are spread out through the corners of a tent or house, they are mabthūth. And in the Qurʾan: {and carpets spread far and wide} [al-Ghāshiya: 16], meaning: many, scattered.

Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: tamrun bathth, meaning: dates scattered, not gathered into store. He said: and one says bathathtu al-ṭaʿāma wa'l-tamr, when I turned it over and threw some of it upon the rest; and bathathtu al-ḥadītha, meaning: I spread it, made it known.

As for al-bathth meaning grief, it too is from this, because it is something one complains of, discloses, and makes manifest. God Almighty said, in the story of the one who said: {I only complain of my anguish and my grief to God} [Yūsuf: 86].

Abū Zayd said: one says abaththa fulānun shuqūrahu wa-fuqūrahu ilā fulānin, yubiththu ibthāthan. And al-ibthāth is that he complains to him of his poverty and his misfortune.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And I weep for him, until, from what I pour out of my grief, its very stones and its playgrounds nearly speak back to me.

And a woman said to her husband: "By God, I have fed you my seasoned food, and I have disclosed to you what I kept hidden, utterly, holding nothing back" [I am unsure of the exact sense of the closing phrase of this saying].
بثا:
The letters bā', thā' and alif are a single word, not analogised upon and nothing is derived from it: it is al-bathā', easy land — a particular piece of land. He said, in a line of verse:
I raised my eyes toward her, while between us stood gathered troops, and horsemen raiding at al-Bathā'.
بثر:
The letters bā', thā' and rā' are a single root, and it is the breaking-out of a thing, with continuity, ease, and abundance.

1. bathara jilduhu — his skin broke out in blisters. Al-Khalīl said this.
2. al-bathr — small pustules, one of them a bathra. Al-Khalīl said this.
3. bathara jilduhu buthūran, fa-huwa bāthir; and buthira, so it is mabthūr — his skin broke out (in pustules), and he is bāthir; or it was made to break out, and it is mabthūr. Abū ʿAlī al-Aṣfahānī said this.
4. al-mā' al-bathr — water that oozes up and remains standing on the surface of the ground like green scum, raised above the level of the ground. They say: the pool turned to bathr. Abū ʿAlī also said this.
5. mā'un bathrun kathīr — water that seeps up abundantly. Abū Zayd said this.

Al-Hudhalī said, in a line of verse:
So it turned them away from al-Sawā', whose water is bathr, and a broad, clear road crossed it.

And one says: bāthir and bāthiʿ — of a thing when it shows itself and protrudes.
بثع: The letters bā', thā' and ʿayn are a single word pointing to the like of the root before it. One says: shafatun bāthiʿa, a full lip — that is, a lip that is filled out.
بثق: The letters bā', thā' and qāf point to a breaking-open in water and other things. Al-bathq is the breaching of water; it is sometimes vowelled bithq, but the form with fatḥa is the more correct.
بثن: The letters bā', thā' and nūn are a single root pointing to ease and softness. One says: arḍun bathna, easy land, and its diminutive is buthayna. A woman was named Buthayna after this. Al-bathaniyya is a kind of wheat, named after a place. From this too is the ḥadīth of Khālid ibn al-Walīd: Umar put me in charge of Syria, but when he had settled in and turned to easy living and honey, he removed me and put another man in my place.
بج:
The letters bā' and jīm are a single root, and it is opening up, splitting. From this is their word for stabbing: bajj.

Ruʾba said, in a line of verse [I am unsure of the precise sense of this fragment]:
Striking on the heads, and piercing, and gashing.

Abū ʿUbayd said: it is a stab that reaches the interior of the body without passing through it; one says from it bajajtuhu abujjuhu bajjan. And one says a man is abajj, when he is wide at the corner of the eye.

Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: al-bajj is cutting and splitting the skin and flesh so that blood shows. Al-Aṣmaʿī cited, in a line of verse:
And she came as though the dark lion had gashed her ... its fresh shoots, and the swaying fruit-clusters.
He is describing a ewe: she is so abundant in milk that even if she had not grazed, she would come with her udders full from her own abundance, as though she had grazed on these very plants, and as though her udders had been split open and swollen.

1. yabujju ibilahu — he waters his camels, giving them their fill.
2. bajajtu al-ibila bi'l-māʾi bajjan — I gave the camels their fill of water.
3. bajjahā al-ʿushbu — the pasture filled her out with fat.
4. al-bajbāj — the body filled out with fat; its plural is bajābij.
5. ʿaynun bajjāʾ — a wide eye, like najlāʾ; and a man wide-eyed is bajīj al-ʿayn.

A line of verse:
The silk veil is over one well-proportioned ... bright-faced, wide-eyed, radiant.

As for their calling the fool al-bijbāj, it is possibly from this chapter, because his mind never rests, so he opens up into the doors of ignorance; and it is also possible that it is anomalous, not from this root.

Among what falls outside this chapter is al-bajja, the name of a god that was worshipped in the pre-Islamic age.
بجح:
The letters bā', jīm and ḥā' are a single word. One says: bajaḥa bi'l-shay', when he rejoiced in it; and yubajjaḥu bi-kadhā, he is made joyful by such a thing. In the ḥadīth of Umm Zarʿ: "bajjaḥanī fa-bajaḥtu" — he made me glad, so I rejoiced. Al-Rāʿī said:
It was not poverty from the land of the clan that drove us to you — rather, in being near you we take pride.
بجد:
The letters bā', jīm and dāl are two roots: one is the inner depth of a matter, its hidden part; the other is a kind of garment.

As for the first, it is their saying: huwa ʿālimun bi-bajdati amrika wa-bujdatihi — he knows the inner depth of your affair, its hidden part. And they say of the skilled guide: "huwa ibnu bajdatihā", as if he had grown up in that land.

The other root is al-bijād, a striped cloak, plural bujd. The poet said:
With bread, or dates, or clarified butter, or the thing wrapped up in the bijād.
From this too is their saying: bajada bi'l-makān, he settled and stayed at the place.
بجر: The letters bā', jīm and rā' are a single root, and it is the knotting-together and gathering of a thing. A man whose navel protrudes, with veins gathered around it, is called al-abjar, and that swelling is al-bujra. The Arabs say: "afḍaytu ilayhi bi-ʿujarī wa-bujarī" — I disclosed to him all my affairs. From this chapter too is al-bajārā, calamities, because they are tangled, confused matters; the singular of it is bujriyy.
بجس:
The bā', jīm and sīn: the bursting open of something, with water in particular.

1. Al-Khalīl said: al-bajs — a split opening in a waterskin, a rock, or the ground, from which water wells up; if nothing wells up, it is not "inbijās."

Al-ʿAjjāj said:
And how the water-drawer's two buckets burst open.

He said: inbijās is the general word, while nubūʿ, springing forth, belongs specifically to a spring. God, exalted is He, said: {and there gushed forth from it twelve springs} [al-Aʿrāf: 160].

2. tabajjasa al-gharb — the [drawn] bucket burst open. "This is land that bursts forth with springs"; "the cloud bursts forth with rain."
3. Yaʿqūb said: "He brought us a bowl of tharīd that was oozing" — from the abundance of fat in it.

It is reported of a man called Abū Turāb, whom we ourselves do not know, that he said: bajastu al-jurḥ is like baṭaṭtuhu — I lanced the wound.
بجل:
The letters bā', jīm and lām are three roots: one is sufficiency and being reckoned enough; the second is a great thing; the third is a vein.

The first is their saying bajal, meaning ḥasb, "enough". From it one says: abjalanī kadhā, as one says kafānī and aḥsabanī, it was enough for me. Al-Kumayt said:
To him are the watering-places of the needy, and from him comes the sufficing return.
Thaʿlab said: bajal means ḥasb. He said: I never heard it put in construct except in a single line, the saying of Labīd:
Enough for me now, of life — enough.
So Thaʿlab said. And Ṭarafa said:
Indeed I was given to drink a thing black as pitch — enough for me of that drink, enough!
And Bajīla is a tribe; it may be derived from this root, or from the one after it.

The second root is their calling a great man bajāl and bajīl. And al-bujl is a great slander. Its evidence is the saying of Abū Duwād:
You spoke a great falsehood — you spoke a lying word.

The third root is a vein in the inner part of the forearm. A poet said:
The leftover flow of the ravening abjal vein went out to them.
بجم: The letters bā', jīm and mīm are a single root, and it belongs to gathering. A large gathering is called bajm. From this too: bajjama fī naẓarihi — that is, when he narrowed his eyelids together and looked.
بح:
The letters bā' and ḥāʾ are two roots: one is that the voice of a speaker is not clear, husky; the other is the wideness and spaciousness of a thing.

The first is al-baḥaḥ, the verbal noun of al-abaḥḥ, the hoarse one. You say from it baḥḥa yabuḥḥu baḥaḥan wa-buḥūḥan; and when it comes from illness it is al-buḥāḥ.

A line of verse:
And I have grown hoarse from calling out to your gathering: is there any champion to duel?

And a lute is abaḥḥ, when there is coarseness in its sound. Al-Kisāʾī said: mā kunta abaḥḥa wa-laqad baḥiḥta, with kasra, tabuḥḥu baḥaḥan wa-buḥūḥatan. And al-buḥḥa is the noun for this; one says bihi buḥḥatun shadīdatun, he has a severe hoarseness. Abū ʿUbayda said: baḥaḥtu, with fatḥa, is also a dialect form.

A poet said, in lines of verse:
When the fair woman does not wash her hands, and her sight is not confined behind a veil, they fed their guests young weaned camels, with gaming-arrows [the stakes of a game of chance] — the dark-skinned tribe lives off their surplus.
Al-rabaḥ is the weaned young of camels; al-buḥḥ are gambling arrows. Al-Shaybānī said this.

Al-Aṣmaʿī said, on the words of the poet:
And a female reproacher who rose at night to blame me ... and in her hand a fragment [of meat], husky-dull, dripping with fat.
Al-radhūm is dripping with fat. He says: she blamed him for slaughtering his wealth for his guests, and in her hand were fragments of the meat, and she said: is such a thing to be slaughtered? And we think that the fat, fleshy one was called abaḥḥ [dull-sounding, muffled] in contrast to their saying of the emaciated one: he is bones that rattle.

And the other root is al-buḥbūḥa, the middle of a house, and the middle of a people's encampment.

Jarīr said, in a line of verse:
My people are Tamīm, the people who drive Taghlib away from the very center of the encampment.
