And al-tabaḥbuḥ is being firmly settled in a dwelling and a stay. Al-Farrāʾ said: one says naḥnu fī bāḥati al-dāri, with a doubled ḥāʾ, meaning the widest part of it. And for that it is said: fulānun yatabaḥbaḥu fī al-majdi, meaning: he expands, flourishes, in glory. And a bedouin said, of a woman whom labour pains had struck: "I left her stretching out at ease in the hands of the midwives."
بحت:
The letters bā', ḥā' and tā' point to the purity of a thing, and that nothing else is mixed into it. Al-Khalīl said: al-baḥt is a pure thing, and misk baḥt is pure musk; it takes neither a diminutive nor a dual form. Al-ʿĀmirī said: bāḥatanī al-amr — he was open with me about the matter, made it plain, and did not hide it from me. Al-Aṣmaʿī said:
So-and-so fed his mount purely on ḍarīʿ and other plants — that is, aṭʿamahā iyyāhu baḥtan, fed it that alone, unmixed. Mālik ibn ʿAwf said:
Indeed Thumāla defended the valley of Wajj with swift horses that were not fed ḍarīʿ alone —
that is, they were not fed ḍarīʿ unmixed with anything else. And one says: ẓulmun baḥt, sheer injustice mixed with nothing; bardun baḥtun wa-maḥt, true, genuine cold; ḥubbun baḥt likewise; and ʿarabiyyun baḥtun wa-maḥḍun wa-qalb, a pure Arab. And the plural takes the same form as the singular.
بحث:
The bā', ḥā' and thā' are a single root: stirring something up.

1. Al-Khalīl said: al-baḥth — your searching for something in the dirt; also, to ask about something and seek word of it. istabḥith ʿan hādhā al-amr — seek information about this matter; anā astabḥithu ʿanhu — I seek information about it. baḥathtu ʿan fulān, baḥthan — I inquired about so-and-so.

A proverb: "Like the one digging up a knife" — said of one whose death comes by his own hand. Its origin is with the wild bull: a knife is buried for it in the dirt, and it digs it up, not knowing, and is slaughtered with it.

A line:
Do not be like the bull for whom the iron of death was buried, and yet went on digging it up.

2. He said: al-baḥth is done only with the hand; with the foot it is called al-faḥṣ.
3. Al-Shaybānī said: al-baḥūth, among camels, is one that, as it walks, digs at the dirt with a foreleg, again and again, throwing it behind itself.

A line:
They dig, a digging — [obscure image, rendered uncertainly: like anklets gone astray].

4. baḥatha ʿan al-khabar — he inquired after the news, meaning he sought word of it.
5. Al-Duraydī: it is said, "I left him at the digging-grounds of the wild oxen," meaning in a place where no one knows where he is.
6. Abū Zayd said: al-bāḥithā' — on the pattern of al-qāṣiʿā' — the dirt the jerboa piles up [at its burrow]; the plural is bāḥithāwāt.
بحر:
The letters bā', ḥā' and rā'. Al-Khalīl said: the sea was called baḥr because of its istibḥār, that is, its spreading out and its wideness. And one says istabḥara fulān fī al-ʿilm - so-and-so ranged widely in knowledge; and tabaḥḥara al-rāʿī fī raʿy kathīr - the herdsman ranged widely in abundant pasture. Umayya said, in a line of verse:
Call your sheep to a herbage in which they may range widely, between the watercourses, and pen them at Jildān.

And tabaḥḥara fulān fī al-māl - so-and-so ranged widely in wealth. A man is baḥr when he is generous; they named him so because his hand overflows with giving as the sea overflows. Al-ʿĀmirī said: abḥara al-qawm - the people took to the sea; and abarrū - they took to the land. Abū Zayd said: baḥirat al-ibil - the camels ate the trees of the sea-coast. And baḥira al-rajul - the man swam in the sea until his swimming failed him. Water is said to have istabḥara when it has grown heavy after being sweet, and mā' baḥr means salt water. A poet said, in a line of verse:
The water of the land has turned to brine, and it has added to my sickness that the sweet drinking place has turned salt.

He said: and all rivers are biḥār - seas. Al-Farrā' said: al-baḥra is the meadow. Al-Umawī said: al-baḥra is the town; and one says hādhihi baḥratunā - this is our town. Some of them said: al-baḥra is a wide open hollow of the ground. Al-Nimr ibn Tawlab said, in a line of verse:
As though she were a Daqrā, its growth imagined - untrodden fresh growth, the plants of its hollows burying the ḍāl trees.

The second root is a disease. One says baḥirat al-ghanam and abḥarūhā, when they have eaten herbage with dew upon it and have sickened from it, and that is that their bellies grow hollow and their bodies waste away. Al-Shaybānī said: baḥirat al-ibil - when the camels eat dew-wet growth, and there come out of their bellies creatures like snakes. Al-Ḍabbī said: al-baḥar in sheep is the counterpart of al-suhām in camels; there is no baḥar in camels and no suhām in sheep.

Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: rajul baḥir - a man who has been struck with wasting sickness. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And of my lads there is one sick in the lungs and one wasted.

Al-Ziyādī said: al-baḥr is the yellowing of the colour. And al-saḥīr is the one who complains of his lungs.

If someone says: where does this stand in relation to the origin you mentioned, the spreading out and the widening? He is answered: all of it is carried back to the sea, because sea water is not drunk, and if it is drunk it brings on disease. So too every salt water, even if it is not the water of the sea.

Of this chapter is al-rajul al-bāḥir, who is the fool, and that is because he spreads himself wide in his ignorance where a sensible man does not. And of this chapter is baḥartu al-nāqa baḥran, which is the slitting of her ear; she is al-baḥīra. The Arabs used to do this to a camel when she had borne ten times: she was not ridden and no use was made of her back. God - exalted is He - forbade them that, and said: {God has not appointed any baḥīra} [al-Mā'ida: 103]. As for al-dam al-bāḥir and al-baḥrānī - blood so described - a group said: it is what is intense in redness. The soundest word on it is that of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muslim: that baḥrānī blood is ascribed to al-baḥr. He said: and al-baḥr is the depth of the womb - so the matter has come back to the first chapter. Al-Khalīl said: rajul baḥrānī is one ascribed to al-Baḥrayn; and they said baḥrānī to make a difference between him and the one ascribed to the sea. Of this chapter is their saying laqītuhu ṣaḥrata baḥrata - I met him face to face, openly. As for the saying of Dhū al-Rumma, in a line of verse:
In a land of choice soil, whose earth is watered by the spring rains, sweet ground from which saltness and brine are far away -
he means by al-baḥr every salt water. And al-baḥr is the well-watered cultivated country.
بحن: The letters bā', ḥā' and nūn are a single root pointing to bigness. One says: jullatun baḥwana, a huge palm-fibre basket. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: the Arabs say of a bucket, when it is great and draws much water: "innahu la-baḥwan", on the pattern of jadwal.
بخ:
The letters bāʾ and khāʾ. There is a report about them that is not a true root to be reasoned from, and I do not think it is genuinely Arabic — and it is their word, on praising a thing: bakh; and bakhbakha fulānun, when he said it over and over.

A line of verse:
Between al-Ashajj and Qays is a lofty one — well done, well done, to his father and to the newborn.

And sometimes they said bakhin.
A line of verse:
Its supporters are the noblest of supporters — well done to you, well done, to a vast, generous sea.

As for their saying "bakhbikhū ʿankum min al-ẓahīra," meaning: cool off, [take shelter] from the noon heat, it is not a true root, because it is a reversal of khabb, and that has been dealt with in its own chapter.
بخت:
The letters bā', khā' and tā' are a word mentioned by Ibn Durayd, who claimed that al-bukht, a kind of camel, is sound Arabic, and cited as evidence:
The milk of the bukht camels, in bowls of khalanj-wood.
بخد: There is nothing in this chapter but a single foreign word, not analogised upon. They said: imra'atun bakhandāh — a woman heavy in the hips.
بخر: The letters bā', khā' and rā' are a single root: it is a scent, or a vapour that rises. From this is al-bukhār, vapour, and from it al-bakhūr, incense, with fatḥa on the bā'; Thaʿlab used to say it is on the pattern faʿūl, like al-barūd and al-wajūr. As for their calling the clouds that come before summer "banāt bakhr", that is not from this chapter, for that bā' is substituted from a mīm, and the origin is makhr; its derivation, with its evidence, has been given in its own chapter.
بخس:
The letters ba, kha and sin are a single root: it is deficiency. God, Most High, said: {and they sold him for a paltry price} [Yusuf: 20], meaning a diminished price. From this root, their saying of marrow: 'bakhkhasa tabkhisan' — when it withdraws into the wrist-bones and the eye-socket, that being when it diminishes and vanishes from the rest of the body. A poet said:
They do not complain of toil so long as they are not depleted — as long as marrow remains in wrist-bone or eye-socket.
بخص: The letters bā', khā' and ṣād are a single word: it is a particular kind of flesh. One says of the flesh of the eye: bakhaṣa. And bakhaṣtu al-rajul — when I struck that flesh of his. Al-bakhaṣa is the flesh of the inner pad of a camel's foot. And bakhaṣ al-yad is the flesh at the base of the fingers, on the side next to the palm.
بخع:
The letters ba', kha' and 'ayn are one root: killing, and what comes close to it of humiliation and subjugation.

Al-Khalil said: bakha'a ar-rajulu nafsahu — the man destroyed his own soul, from rage, out of the intensity of his grief. Dhu ar-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
O you who destroy yourself with grief, over a thing that fate has carved away from your grasp.

From this, God's saying, Most High: {so perhaps you will destroy yourself with grief, following after them} [al-Kahf: 6].

Abu 'Ali al-Asfahani said, as told to us by Abu al-Fadl Muhammad ibn al-'Amid, from Abu Bakr al-Khayyat, from him: ad-Dabbi said: bakha'tu adh-dhabiha — I cut through the bone of the slaughtered animal's neck; it is then mabkhu'a. And nakha'tuha is a lesser cut than that, because an-nukha' is the white cord running through the neck and the vertebrae of the back. Al-bikha', with a ba': the sinew that runs along the spine.

Abu 'Ubayd said: bakha'tu lahu nafsi wa-nushi — I gave him my utmost effort and sincere counsel. Ard mabkhu'a — land whose full capacity has been exhausted by cultivation. bakha'a li bi-haqqi — he acknowledged what was due to me.
بخق:
The letters bā', khā' and qāf are a single root and a single word. One says: bakhaqtu ʿaynahu — when you strike his eye until it is blinded. Ru'ba said:
And his eyes bear none of the blemishes of bakhq.
بخل:
The letters bā', khā' and lām are a single word, and it is al-bukhl and al-bakhal, stinginess. A man is bakhīl and bākhil, a miser. And if that is his settled way, he is bakhkhāl, a great miser. Ru'ba said, in a line of verse:

So that one is a great miser, tight and shrinking as a stubborn rock.
بخو: The letters bā', khā' and wāw are a single word, not analogised upon. Ibn Durayd said: al-bakhw is a spoiled, over-ripe fresh date; one says ruṭabatun bakhwa, a spoiled fresh date.
بد:
The letters bāʾ and dāl, doubled, are a single root, and it is separation and the distancing of two things from each other. One says: a horse is abadd, meaning: wide apart between its two legs. And baddadtu al-shayʾa, when I dispersed it.

From this is the hadith of Umm Salama: "O girl, give it out to them, date by date," meaning: distribute it among them one date at a time.

And from it is the saying of al-Hudhalī, in a line of verse:
So he dealt out to them their deaths, scattered ... one fleeing with his last breath, one kneeling, crouched down.
Meaning: he distributed death among them. And one says: farraqnāhum badādi. A line of verse: They fell back, scattered, before the spears, each apart.

And you say: bādadtuhu fī al-bayʿi, meaning: I traded with him in direct exchange.

If someone asks about their saying "lā budda min kadhā," there is no escaping such-and-such, it too is from this chapter, as though meaning: there is no parting from it, no distance from it. The reasoning holds.

And likewise their calling the vast open desert "badbad," named for the great distance between its edges. And al-bāddān are the inner parts of the two thighs, from this, named for the gap between them.

Two words fall outside this root: their calling a man of great build "abadd." A line of verse: obstinate, walking with the gait of the great-built man. And their saying: mā laka bihi badad, meaning: you have no strength against it.
بدأ:
The letters bā', dāl and hamza are about the opening of a thing. One says bada'tu bi-l-amr and ibtada'tu — I began with the matter — from al-ibtidā', beginning. And God, exalted be He, is al-Mubdi' and al-Bādi', the One who originates and begins. God, mighty and majestic, said: {Indeed it is He who originates and brings back} [al-Burūj: 13], and He said, exalted be He: {how He began the creation} [al-ʿAnkabūt: 20].

And a wondrous matter is called badī', as though, from the wonder of it, one begins with it.

ʿAbīd said, in a line of verse:
Neither a thing to begin with nor a wonder.

And the chief is called al-bad', because one begins with mentioning him.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
You see us counted second when their chief man comes, but their chief, if he comes to us, is counted second.

And you say abda'tu min arḍin ilā ukhrā, ubdi' ibdā'an — when you go out from one land to another.

And al-bud'a is a share, and this too belongs here, because everyone who has a share is begun with in the mention before anyone else, and he is the one most important to him.

The poet said, in a line of verse:
So I gave its choice share to a watcher leaning in, while the fire scorched his face with its blaze.

And al-budū' are the joints of the fingers, one of them a bad', like badʿ. I think it is one of those words given a hamza when the hamza is not original to it. They were only called budū' because they stand out and show, so it belongs then to the first section.

And of what falls outside this root, and I do not know what it is derived from, is their saying budi'a, so he is mabdū' — when a man has the smallpox or the measles.

The poet said, in a line of verse:
As though the outer surfaces of his skin had been struck with pox from what it meets of the blaze of her arrows.
بدح:
The letters bā', dāl and ḥā' are a single root to which similar branches are traced back; everything beyond that is carried upon it or substituted from it. The root itself is softness, pliancy, and ease. Al-Hudhalī said:
As if the onrush of the flood had stretched out over them, when the great surges drove it on across the soft open ground.
From this they then derived their calling a big-bodied woman baydaḥ. Al-Ṭirimmāḥ said:
I am jealous even of myself for Salma, alone with my thoughts of her, though every fair, full-bodied woman should offer herself to me.
Abū Saʿīd said: al-badḥā' among women is the one wide in the haunch. He said:
Full-hipped, whom her two thighs do not cover.
One says: badaḥat al-mar'a, and tabaddaḥat — when her walk became graceful. The poet said:
They sway on legs whose anklets make no sound, with the gait of young foals at water, wary of the mud.
Another said:
They follow the easy, swaying gait of a gentle mount, led by a guide, with a watchful eye glancing about.
Tabaddaḥa — it spread itself, eased out. From this chapter too is Al-Khalīl's saying: al-badḥ is your striking someone with a thing that has some softness in it, as when you take a melon and strike a person with it. And you say: I saw them pelting each other playfully with unripe dates, pomegranates, and the like.
This is the root that is the mainstay of the chapter.

As for the remaining words: their saying badaḥahu al-amr is really with a ḥā' substituted from a hā', the origin being badahahu, already treated. Likewise their saying ibtadaḥta al-shay' — when you began it of your own initiative — is in origin ibtadaʿta and ikhtalaqta, you originated and invented it. The poet said:
O you who ask about the noble chief — he is indeed among Murād, with nothing invented in it.
Likewise al-badḥ, which is the inability to bear a burden once a man has taken it up, and likewise a camel's inability to carry its load. The poet said:
How many a bright, noble chief is there at al-Maʿn who, when burdened with heavy loads, does not fail to bear them.
This belongs with the letter ʿayn, that is, the failing already mentioned, when an animal tires and is worn out. As for the poet's saying:
By the estrangement from Shaʿthā', and the bond that she severed suddenly —
this is from the hā' root, as if she had taken him by surprise, already mentioned. As for what Abū ʿUbayd related of their saying badaḥtuhu bi'l-ʿaṣā, meaning I struck him with it, this is carried upon their saying badaḥtuhu bi'l-rummāni wa-shibhihā, I struck him with a pomegranate and the like, and that is the original sense.
بدر:
The bā', dāl and rā' are two roots: one is the completeness and fullness of something, the other is hastening toward something.

The first: they call anything complete a badr. The full moon (al-badr) was named badr for its completeness and fullness. Ten thousand dirhams is called a badra, because it is the full round number, its uttermost limit. ʿayn badra — a full [round] eye.

A poet said:
And an eye, round and full, beneath a brow where the lashes were set close.

The skin of a young lamb is called a badra — taken by analogy with the [ten-thousand] count, as though so named because it holds that many [coins as a purse]. They say ghulām badr of a boy full of youthful vigour.

As for Badr the place, it is a well-known watering place, named after a man called Badr. As for al-bawādir, of a person or otherwise, it is the plural of bādira — the flesh between the shoulder and the neck, belonging to this root because it is full.

A poet said:
And the horses came, their shoulder-flesh reddened.

The other root: they say badartu towards a thing, and bādartu — I hastened to it. A slip is called a bādira because it bursts from a person in a moment of sharpness and anger. "There were bawādir from him" means there were lapses. badarat dam'atuhu, and bādarat — his tear came first/rushed out — it is a bādira, plural bawādir.

Kuthayyir said:
When it is said, "This is ʿAzza's dwelling," longing draws me toward it, and the rushing tears hasten me on.
بدع:
The letters bā', dāl and 'ayn are two roots: one is the starting of a thing and making it without any model before it, and the other is being cut off and worn out.

The first is their saying: abda'tu the thing, in word or deed, meaning: I began it without any prior model. And God is badī' (the Originator) of the heavens and the earth. The Arabs say: so-and-so ibtada'a a well, meaning: he dug it out and brought forth its water for the first time. And so-and-so is a bid' in this matter [the first to do it]. God Almighty said: {Say: I am not a novelty among the messengers} [al-Aḥqāf: 9], meaning: I am not the first.

The other root is their saying: ubdi'ati the riding-mount, meaning: it grew exhausted and broke down. And ubdi'a bi- the man, meaning: his mount grew exhausted or broke down and he was left stranded, unable to go on. In the hadith: a man came to him and said, "O Messenger of God, I have been stranded, so carry me." It is said: al-ibdā' (being stranded) happens only through lameness [of the mount]. From part of this the word al-bid'a (innovation) is derived.
بدغ: The letters bā', dāl and ghayn hold no genuinely original word, for in one of its roots the dāl is substituted from a ṭā': that is their saying badigha al-rajul, when a man is smeared with evil, and he is badigh among men — this is in origin with ṭā', and has been treated in its own chapter (baṭagha). Two words remain in doubt: one is their saying al-badagh, crawling along the ground; the other their saying "inna banī fulānin la-badighūn", when they are fat and their state is good. God knows best whether that is sound.
بدل:
The letters bā', dāl and lām are a single root, and it is one thing standing in the place of another that has gone. One says: this is the badal of the thing and its badīl, its substitute. And they say baddaltu al-shay' when you change it, even if you bring no substitute for it. God, exalted be He, said: {Say: it is not for me to change it of my own accord} [Yūnus: 15]. And abdaltuhu when you bring a substitute for it. The poet said:
The dismissal of the governor for the governor put in his place.
بدن:
The letters ba', dal and nun are one root: the bulk of a thing apart from its extremities.

1. badan al-insan — a person's body, plural abdan.
2. the aged mountain-goat is called badan from this.

The poet said, in a line of verse:
The rock ledge has closed in around her and the old goat — be diligent, for every worker there is a reward: the head, the shanks, and the hide.

It was so named because when they wish to emphasize a thing's description, they call it by the name of its whole kind — just as they say of a man emphatically described: "he is a man" — likewise the massive mountain-goat is called badan. Likewise al-badana, the camel or cow offered to the sacred House, is so named because they used to fatten it.

3. rajul badan — an aged man.

The poet said, in a line of verse:
Is there any seeking back youth once it has passed? Or why does the grey-haired old man weep?

4. rajul badin and badīn — large of frame and body; one says baduna, from this.

In the hadith: "indeed I have grown stout." People also transmit it as "I have aged." They say baddana — he grew old.

The poet said, in a line of verse:
And I had thought that grey hair, and age, and care, were things that make a companion forget.

5. the coat of mail is called al-badan, because it encloses the body.
بده:
The letters bā', dāl and hā' are a single root pointing to the first of a thing, and to that which takes one by surprise. One says: bādahtu fulānan bi'l-amr — when I surprised him with the matter. And fulānun dhū badīha — when a matter surprises him, he is not confounded by it. And al-budāha is the first burst of a horse's running. Al-Aʿshā said:
Except the first dash, or the second burst, of a swimming, full-limbed horse.
بدو:
The letters bā', dāl and wāw are one root, and it is a thing's showing itself. One says badā al-shay' yabdū, when it appears, so it is bādin. And what is other than settled life was called badw from this, because they are in the open of the land and are not in villages whose buildings cover them. And al-bādiya is the opposite of al-ḥāḍira, the settled country. The poet said, in a line of verse:
Whoever is taken with the life of towns, what men of the desert do you take us to be?

And you say badā lī fī hādhā al-amr badā', that is, my mind about it changed from what it had been.
بذ: The letters bāʾ and dhāl are a single root, and it is overcoming, subduing, and humbling. One says: badhdha fulānun aqrānahu, when he overcame his rivals — he is bādhdh, yabudhdhuhum. And to this goes back their saying: huwa bādhdh al-hayʾa, and badhdh al-hayʾa bayyinu al-badhādha, meaning: time has worn him down, so he is overcome, subdued — and here the active-participle form carries a passive sense.
بذأ: The letters bā', dhāl and hamza are a single root: it is a thing's departure from the way of being praised. You say: huwa badhī' al-lisān — he is foul-tongued. And badha'tu ʿalā fulān abdha'u budhā'an — I spoke ill of him. And one says: badha'tu al-makān abdha'uhu — when you came to a place and did not find it agreeable.
بذج:
The letters bā', dhāl and jīm are a single root, not from the speech of the Arabs but an arabised word: it is al-badhaj, one of the young of sheep, plural bidhjān. The poet said:
Our neighbour-woman has perished from want — and if she hungers, she eats a young goat, or a lamb.
بذح:
The letters bā', dhāl and ḥā' are a single root: it is splitting, cutting, and what is close to that. Abū ʿAlī al-Aṣfahānī said: al-ʿĀmirī said: badhaḥtu al-laḥm — when you cut the meat into strips. He said: al-badḥ is the split; and one says: aṣābahu badḥun fī rijlihi — he suffered a crack in his leg. And he cited:
I shall surely brand Ḥarzam with a branding-mark, three of them, at the cut of the incision.
Abū ʿUbayd said: badhaḥtu lisāna al-faṣīl badḥan — done at the time of splitting and tethering [a weaned camel's tongue, to stop it suckling]. And close to this chapter is their word for the chafing of the two thighs: madhaḥ.
بذخ: The letters bā', dhāl and khā' are a single root: it is loftiness and self-magnification. One says: badhakha — when he grew haughty; and fulānun [fī] bādhikhin min al-sharaf — so-and-so is in a lofty state of nobility, that is, elevated.
بذر: The letters bā', dhāl and rā' are a single root: it is the scattering of a thing and its dispersal. One says: badhartu al-badhra abdhuruhu badhran, I sowed the seed; and baddhartu al-māla ubaddhiruhu tabdhīran, I squandered the wealth. God Almighty said: {And do not squander wastefully; the squanderers are the brothers of the devils} [al-Isrā': 26]. Al-budhur are people who cannot keep a matter secret and do not guard their tongues. 'Alī, peace be upon him, said: "Those are the lamps of the darkness, neither gossips (al-masāyīḥ) nor tale-spreading blabbermouths (al-madhāyī' al-budhur)" — al-madhāyī' are those who spread news about, and al-budhur are those just described [who cannot keep a secret]. Badhdhar is a place-name, and it may be derived from the root already given. The poet said: "May God water watering-places I have known the location of — Jurāb, and Malkūm, and Badhdhar, and al-Ghamr."
بذع: The letters bā', dhāl and ʿayn are a single word about which there is doubt, not analogised upon. They say: badhaʿtuhu wa-abdhaʿtuhu — when I frightened him.
بذل: The letters bā', dhāl and lām are a single word: it is the abandoning of the safeguarding of a thing. One says: badhaltu al-shay' badhlan, so I am bādhil and it is mabdhūl; and ibtadhaltuhu ibtidhālan. And so-and-so came in his mabādhil — the clothes he wears for everyday, rough use. They are also called maʿāwiz, which has been treated in its own chapter.
بر:
The letters bāʾ and rāʾ, doubled, are four roots: truthfulness; the imitation of a sound; the opposite of the sea; and a plant.

As for truthfulness: their saying ṣadaqa fulānun wa-barra; barrat yamīnuhu, his oath was true, fulfilled; and abarrahā, he carried it out truthfully. And you say: barra Allāhu ḥajjaka wa-abarrahu, and ḥijjatun mabrūra, meaning: it was accepted, as a truthful deed is accepted. From this is their saying yaburru rabbahu, meaning: he obeys Him — it is from truthfulness.

A line of verse:
O God, were it not that Bakr stands before You ... people would obey You or defy You.

And from it is God Almighty's saying: {Righteousness is not that you turn your faces towards the east and the west} [al-Baqara: 177]. And as for al-Nābigha's saying: "upon them, disheveled men, making for their birr" — they said he meant obedience, and it is also said he meant the pilgrimage.

And their calling the swift, generous, winning horse "al-mubirr" is from this, because when it runs it proves true, and when it carries a load it proves true.

Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: I asked a bedouin: do you know the generous winning horse from the slow, base-bred one? He said: Yes. I said: describe them to me. He said: "As for the generous one, it is compact like a wild donkey, refined in gait — when it runs it stretches out at full speed, and when it stands, it stands straight and smooth. As for the slow, base-bred one, it has a worn croup, a thick nose, a coarse neck, and much noise — if you hold it back it says 'let me go,' and if you let it go it says 'hold me back.'"

And the origin of al-ibrār is what we mentioned of overcoming and subduing, and it too goes back to truthfulness. Ṭarafa said, in a line of verse:
They remove harm from the one harmed among them ... and they prevail over the one who defiantly resists.

And from this chapter is their saying: huwa yaburru dhā qarābatihi, he is dutiful to his kinsman, its origin being truthfulness in affection. One says: rajulun barrun wa-bārrun; and barartu wālidī, I was dutiful to my father, and barartu fī yamīnī, I was true to my oath. And abarra al-rajulu waladu awlādan abrāran, a man had children who became dutiful.

Abū ʿUbayda said: Barra is a proper name for dutifulness, a definite noun that takes no case-ending. Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
The day we took our two separate paths between us ... I carried Dutifulness (Barra), and you carried Wickedness (Fajār).

As for the imitation of a sound: the Arabs say "he does not know hirr from birr" — al-hirr being the call used to drive sheep, and al-birr the sound made in driving them; and it is [also] said: he does not know the one who dislikes him from the one who is dutiful to him. And al-barbara is much talk and clamour of the tongue.

A line of verse [I am unsure of the exact sense of this fragment]:
By ʿAḍr, every foul-mouthed, clamorous one.

And a man is barbār, and a woman barbāra. Perhaps the derivation of al-Barbar [the Berbers] is from this. As for Ṭarafa's saying, in a line of verse:
But he called forth from Qays ʿAylān a band ... driving the barābir in the heights of the Ḥijāz —
it is said this is the plural of burbur, the young of small livestock; they said this too is from the sound, because al-barbara is the sound made by goats.

And the third root is the opposite of the sea. Abarra al-rajulu, he went onto dry land; abḥara, he went onto the sea. Al-barriyya is the open desert. Al-barr is the opposite of shelter. And the Arabs use it as an indefinite noun, saying kharajtu barran and kharajtu baḥran. God Almighty said: {Corruption has appeared on land and sea} [al-Rūm: 41].

As for the plant: from it is al-burr, wheat, the singular being burra. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: abarrat al-arḍu, when its wheat grew abundant, just as one says abhamat, when its buhmā grass grew abundant. And al-burbūr is coarsely-ground wheat. Bread is called "ibn burra" and "ibn ḥabba," both indeclinable. Al-Shaybānī said: "he is shorter than a burra," meaning a single wheat-grain, that is, a burra is the extreme of shortness.

Al-Khalīl said: al-barīr is the fruit of the arāk tree. Al-Nābigha said: She nibbles its berries and roams about among it.

Abū Ziyād al-Kilābī said: al-barīr has smaller berries than al-mard and al-kabāth, as though they were small beads. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: al-barīr is the name for the ripened fruit of the thorny trees; when it fully ripens, its blackness deepens. Bishr said, in a line of verse:
He saw a fair pearl, its colour set off ... by fine hair, dark as the ripened berries of the arāk, braided.
He is describing her hair.
برأ:
As for the letters bā', rā' and hamza, they are two roots to which the branches of the chapter come back. One of them is creating: one says bara'a Allāh al-khalq yabra'uhum bar'an - God created the creation. And al-Bāri' is God, exalted be His praise. God, exalted is He, said: {So turn in repentance to your Maker} [al-Baqara: 54]. And Umayya said, in a line of verse:
The Creator, the Maker, the Fashioner.

The other root is drawing away from a thing and parting from it. Of that is al-bur', which is soundness from sickness. One says bari'tu and bara'tu. Al-Liḥyānī said: the people of the Ḥijāz say bara'tu min al-maraḍ abru'u burū'an; and the people of al-ʿĀliya say [bara'tu abra'u] bar'an. And of that is their saying bari'tu ilayka min ḥaqqika - I have cleared myself towards you of your due. And the people of the Ḥijāz say anā barā'un minka, and others say anā barī'un minka. God, exalted is He, said in the tongue of the people of the Ḥijāz: {I am quit of what you worship} [al-Zukhruf: 26]; and in more than one place of the Qur'an: {I am quit} [al-Anʿām: 78]. So whoever says anā barā' makes no dual of it and no feminine, and they say naḥnu al-barā' wa-al-khalā' - we are clear and free of this. And whoever says barī' says barī'ān and barī'ūn, and bura'ā' on the measure of buraʿā', and burā' with no ajr, in the manner of burāʿ, and birā' like birāʿ. And of that is al-barā'a, being clear of a fault and of what is hateful, and from it only bari'a yabra'u is said. And bāra'tu al-rajul, that is, I cleared myself towards him and he towards me. And the woman bāra'at her husband upon parting; and likewise I bāra'tu my partner, and abra'tu from the debt and from the guarantee. And it is said that al-barā' is the last night of the month, so named because the moon clears itself of the month. A poet said, in a line of verse:
On a day when the last night of the month is of ill omen.

Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: the barā' day is the lucky one, that is, it is clear of what is disliked. Al-Khalīl said: al-istibrā' is that a man buy a slave-girl and not lie with her until she menstruates. And this is from the chapter, because she has been cleared of the doubt that keeps the buyer from going in to her. And the bur'a of the hunter is his hide, which is his covered pit, and the plural is bura'. And it is from the chapter, because every man has drawn away from it and left it. A poet said, in a line of verse:
In it are hunters' hides like young palm shoots wrapped about.
برت: The letters bā', rā' and tā' are a single root, and it is for a thing to penetrate deeply, unseen. From this is al-burt, which is the axe, and the guide is likened to it, because he penetrates deep into the land and finds his way in the darkness.
برث: The letters bā', rā' and thā' are a single root, and it is soft, level ground. Soft, level ground is called barth, plural birāth. Ru'ba made its plural al-barārith, and it is said that this is an error.
برج:
The letters ba, ra and jim are two roots: one is prominence and appearing; the other is a stronghold and a refuge.

From the first: al-baraj is width and largeness of the eye together with intense blackness of its black and intense whiteness of its white. From it: al-tabarruj, a woman's displaying of her charms.

The second root: al-burj, one of the mansions of the sky. The origin of al-burooj [these mansions] is fortresses and castles. God, Most High, said: {even if you had been in towering strongholds} [al-Nisa': 78]. One says of a garment decorated with the image of towers: 'thawbun mubarraj'.
برح:
The letters bā', rā' and ḥā' are two roots from which many branches emerge. The first: departure, emergence, and uncovering. The second: severity, greatness, and the like.

As for the first, al-Khalīl said: baraḥa yabraḥu barāḥan, when he sought to move from his place; abraḥtuhu, I made him move. Al-'Āmirī said: a man says to his slow riding-camel: "do not move off in a way that does one any good" [a set phrase used of a sluggish mount]. And one says "mā baraḥtu af'alu dhālika," meaning "I did not cease doing that." God Almighty said, narrating the words of some people: {We will not cease (lan nabraḥa) to remain devoted to it} [Ṭāhā: 91], meaning we will not stop. He cited: "and I will not cease (fa-abraḥu), as long as God preserves my people, by praise of God, girded and excellent," meaning I will not stop. Mujīd: a man with a fine racehorse; muntaṭiq: one who has bound on his belt.

The Arabs say "baraḥa al-khafā'u," the hidden matter became uncovered. He cited: "the concealment has become uncovered, and I have no endurance left." Al-Farrā' said: baraḥa, with a fatḥa, also means "passed by"; from this al-bāriḥa (yesterday evening) is named. They said: al-bāriḥa is the night before your night, a description so dominant it came to function as a name; its origin is from baraḥa, it departed its place. Abū 'Ubayda said, of the proverb "How much tonight resembles yesterday-night!" — said of one who awaits some good, like something before, and it comes just the same.

Abū 'Ubayd said: al-birāḥ is open confrontation; one says "bāraḥa birāḥan," he confronted openly. And I think al-bāriḥ, the opposite of al-sāniḥ [an omen-creature crossing left to right, versus right to left], is from this, because it is something that emerges and shows itself. Al-Khalīl said: al-burūḥ is the verbal noun of al-bāriḥ, opposite of al-sāniḥ, said of gazelles and birds taken as a bad or good omen. He cited a line about them passing sometimes as bāriḥ, sometimes as sāniḥ omens.

The Arabs say in their proverbs: "he is like the bāriḥ of the mountain-goat, rarely seen" — said of one hardly ever seen, or of something that happens from him only once in an age. Its origin is that mountain-goats dwell in the mountains and their peaks, so people scarcely ever see them pass as sāniḥ or bāriḥ except once in a long while. [Ibn Fāris notes he has already discussed people's disagreement about this in the chapter on the letter sīn, when discussing al-sāniḥ.] It is also said that "he is like the bāriḥ of the mountain-goat" carries a double ill-omen: because the mountain-goat is itself taken as a bad omen wherever it appears, so when it also passes as bāriḥ, that is a still greater sign of ill fortune.

The other root: Abū 'Ubayd said: one says "mā abraḥa hādhā al-amr," how impressive this matter is. He cited from al-A'shā: "so you made a lord great (abraḥti rabban) and made a neighbour great (abraḥti jāran)" — they said its meaning is "you made great," the sense being the same [as abraḥa = made impressive/great]. Ibn al-A'rābī said: one says "abraḥtu bi-fulān," I burdened him with more than he could bear, so he grew distressed (tabarraḥa) by it and it grieved him. He cited a line about burdening one who was planted and favouring the one who plants [sense unclear to me in full]. Ibn al-A'rābī also: al-barīḥ is exhaustion. Abū Wajza said, of a worn riding-camel, with it sweat (al-masīḥ) and exhaustion (barīḥ) and clamour. Al-masīḥ: sweat.

Abū 'Amr: one says "abraḥta lu'man" and "abraḥta karaman" [you were extremely mean; you were extremely generous]. One says "barḥā lahu," said when you are amazed at someone. A camel is called burḥa, from al-buraḥ, meaning choice/excellent; "give me from the burḥ of your camels" means from the best of them.

Al-Khalīl said: one says "barraḥa fulānun tabrīḥan fa-huwa mubarriḥ," when he does harm through persistence; the noun is al-barḥ. Dhū al-Rumma said: "and passion is a hardship (barḥ) upon whoever pursues it." Al-tabārīḥ: hardship and difficulty. "He struck him a severe blow (ḍarban mubarriḥan)." "This matter is harder (abraḥ) on me than that." Dhū al-Rumma said: "groaning, and much complaint by day, upon me — and what the night brings is harder (abraḥ) still," meaning harder.

One says: "I met from him al-buraḥīn and al-baraḥayn and banāt barḥ and barḥan bāriḥan" [set phrases for severe trouble]. From this chapter also are al-bawāriḥ, [a name for certain] winds, because they carry dust for the intensity of their blowing. Dhū al-Rumma said: "no — rather it is the longing from a home changed, sometimes by cloud and sometimes by a dust-bearing wind (bāriḥ)."

As for the saying of one who addresses the archer when he misses, "barḥā," on the pattern fa'lā — Ibn Durayd and others said it belongs to this chapter, as though he meant "a severe stroke," i.e. hard/harsh.
برخ: The letters bā', rā' and khā' are a single root — if it is genuine Arabic, it is growth and increase. It is said that it comes from baraka (blessing), and that it is a Nabataean word.
برد:
The letters bā', rā' and dāl are four roots: one is the opposite of heat, the second is stillness and steadiness, the third is a worn garment, and the fourth is agitation and movement. The branches go back to these.

As for the first, al-bard is the opposite of heat. One says barada, so it is bārid; and barada al-mā'u ḥarārata jawfī yabruduhā — the water cooled the heat in my belly. A poet said:
set free my young she-camel among the mounts, for she will cool livers with grief, and make mourners weep.
Another said:
if the coolness of water were, to a hot and thirsty man, strange to me — it would indeed be strange.

1. baradtu ʿaynahu bi-l-barūd — I treated his eye with a cooling remedy.
2. al-barada — indigestion, a feeling of fullness from overeating.
3. saḥābun barid — a cloud carrying hail.
4. al-abradān — the two cool ends of the day, morning and evening. A poet said:
when the arṭā shrub pillows its two cool ends, the cheeks of wide-eyed gazelles rest on the sand.
It is also said al-baradān.
5. Swords are called al-bawārid: some say this means "the killing ones," others say it is because the touch of iron is cold. And he recited:
and that the Commander of the Faithful choked me, the choking of the two of them, with the sharp cold-touched blades.
6. One says jā'ū mubridīna — they came when the heat had died down.

As for the second root, al-bard is sleep. God Most High said: {They will not taste therein coolness nor drink} [an-Naba': 24]. The poet said:
if you wish, I shall forbid women to you; and if you wish, I shall not taste cool water nor sleep.

1. barada ash-shay' — the thing lasted. Abū 'Ubayda recited:
today is a day whose scorching wind endures; whoever grieves today, do not blame him —
bārid here meaning "enduring."
2. barada lī ʿalā fulānin min al-māli kadhā — such-and-such wealth became fixed as owed to me by so-and-so, meaning it became settled.
3. barada fī yadī kadhā — such-and-such came into my possession.
4. They say barada ar-rajul when the man died. This could be from this root ("became settled/still") or from the one before it (related to "cold").

As for the third, al-burd is a well-known garment. He said:
and I do hope that my dust-cloud will be wrapped around one wearing a cloak from Salāmān, or a burd.
And burdā al-jarāda — the two wings of the locust.

The fourth root is barīd al-ʿasākir — the courier of the armies, because he comes and goes. He said:
a phantom vision of Umm as-Salsabīl, while between her and me is a month's journey, for the wavering courier.
It is possible that al-mibrad, the file, comes from this, because the hand moves it back and forth when it is used.
برز:
The letters bā', rā' and zāy are a single root, and it is a thing's showing itself and coming out into view — a rule that does not fail. One says baraza al-shay' fa-huwa bāriz — the thing came out, so it is out in the open. So too a thing's standing out alone from its like, as in the single combat of two horsemen, since each of them steps out alone from his company toward his opponent. Al-barāz is open, wide ground, because it lies exposed, being neither a hollow nor a cleft nor a pit. One says imra'a barza, that is, a woman of standing who comes out and sits in the courtyard of her house. Some said: rajul barz and imra'a barza, both described as open of manner and sound of mind. In al-Khalīl's book: rajul barz, a pure and chaste man. This is the analogy of the rest of the chapter, because the man with something to hide pushes himself out of sight and conceals himself. One says barraza al-rajul wa-l-faras when the man and the horse outstrip the rest, and that is [of] the chapter. One says abraztu al-shay' ubrizuhu ibrāzan — I brought the thing out. And al-mubrawaz has also come. Labīd said, in a line of verse:
Or a fresh track of gold upon its tablets, the writing spread out open and the writing sealed up.
Al-mubrawaz is the one out in the open; al-makhtūm is the one not out in the open. Others said al-mubrawaz is the unrolled, spread-open one. That is a good view.
برس: The letters bā', rā' and sīn are a single root pointing to ease and softness. Abū Zayd said: barrastu al-makān — when you make a place smooth and soft. He said: from this comes the name Bursān, a tribe of al-Azd. And al-burs is cotton; the derivation holds throughout. Among what strays from this root is their saying: mā adrī ayyu al-barāsā' wa'l-barnasā' huwa — I do not know which of mankind he is.
برش: The letters bā', rā' and shīn are a single word: it is for a thing to have scattered white spots. Jadhīma was leprous, and so was nicknamed al-Abrash.
برص:
The letters ba', ra' and sad are one root: that there be, in a thing, a patch differing from the rest of its color — from this, al-barasi, leprosy or vitiligo.

1. they sometimes called the moon abras, for its markings.
2. al-barisi is like al-basisi, a gleam — the same derivation.

He said, in a fragment of verse: "upon his cheek there is forever a gleam."

3. al-birasi — bare patches within sand that grow nothing.
4. sam abras — the spotted house-lizard, well known.

Al-Qutaybi said: its plural is al-abarisi. And he recited, in a line of verse:
By God, if I were given wholly to this, I would be a slave who eats geckos.

Tha'lab said, in the Book of al-Fasih: it is sam abras, sama abras (dual), and sawamm abras (plural).
برض:
The letters bā', rā' and ḍād are a single root pointing to the scantiness of a thing, and taking it little by little. Al-Khalīl said: al-tabarruḍ is reaching sufficiency from a scant livelihood, seeking it here and there, a little at a time. Likewise: tabarraḍa al-mā' min al-ḥawḍ — when the water in a trough is scant, it is poured into the water-skin from here and there. He said:
I used to seek her out little by little before I won her — how much more so now that her rope is bound to mine!
He means: I used to pursue her from time to time — how much more so now that we are tied to one another. And al-ibtirāḍ comes from this. And one says: qad baraḍa fulānun lī min mālihi, wa-huwa yabruḍu barḍan — when he gives you a little of it. He said:
By your life, I, in my pursuit of Salmā, am truly like one scooping a little from a scant, doubtful pool.
Thamad means a small standing pool of water. Ru'ba says:
At the perennial spring, it drew out no small, scant pools, little by little.
From this chapter too: baraḍa al-nabātu yabruḍu burūḍan — the first thing the livestock graze upon. And al-bāriḍ is the first shoot to appear of al-buhmā grass. He said:
It grazed on the first shoots of the buhmā, on lush growth and unripe buds, and on firm-tipped shoots, until their sharp points made it turn away.
برع:
The letters bā', rā' and ʿayn are two roots: one is volunteering a thing without it being obligatory, and the other is excelling and surpassing merit.

Al-Khalīl said: one says baraʿa yabraʿu, burūʿan and barāʿatan — and he yatabarraʿu, gives of his own accord, from himself, by giving.

Al-Khansā' said, in a line of verse:
Enduring, handsome, of noble root, excelling, pious — a refuge for widows, orphans, and the neighbor.

He said: al-bāriʿ is the one of noble root, sound of judgment. And one says: something was given to a person as a natyā' by way of tabarruʿ (volunteering), when it was not asked for.
برق:
The letters ba, ra and qaf are two roots from which branches spread: one is the flashing/gleaming of a thing, the other the combination of black and white in a thing. Everything beyond these is a figure of speech carried upon these two roots.

As for the first: Al-Khalil said: al-barq is the flash of the cloud. One says 'baraqa l-sahabu barqan wa bariqan'; he said 'abraqa' is also used. Some said one says 'barqatun' for a single occurrence of the flash, and 'burqatun' [with damma] when meaning the amount of lightning. One says: 'I will not do it as long as a star flashes in the sky' — that is, as long as one rises. 'Atana 'inda mabraqi l-subh' — he came to us at the flashing of dawn, that is, when it broke. Al-Lihyani: 'abraqa l-rajul' — the man aimed toward the lightning when he saw it. Al-Khalil said: al-bariqa is the cloud that has lightning in it. Anything whose color glitters is 'bariq', 'yabruqu bariqan'. Swords are called 'bawariq'. Al-Asma'i: one says 'abraqa fulanun bi-sayfihi' — so-and-so made his sword flash/gleam. One says 'ra'aytu l-bariqa' — I saw the gleam of swords. One says 'a bariqa passed by us tonight', that is, a cloud with lightning in it, and I do not know where it struck. The Arabs say: 'sweeter than the water of al-bariqa.'

One calls a sword, and anything that gleams, 'ibriq' — they even call a beautiful, radiant woman 'ibriq'. A line (obscure, rendered as best as can be made out):
The dwelling-place of the radiant, swaying-gaited one at evening.
Al-khawzal is a woman who sways as she walks. Another line, describing a hunt (obscure, rendered as best as can be made out):
A hunter set his dogs upon it while it was unwary — dogs leashed with leather straps, coursing the thicket — and it slipped away, gleaming like the ewer, over the rise.

Abu 'Ali al-Asfahani said: one says 'abraqati l-sama' 'ala biladi kadha' — the sky flashed lightning over such a land. 'Abraqtu' — I was struck by lightning. 'Abraqtu bi-baladi kadha' — I was rained upon in such a land. Al-Khalil said: when one threatening intensifies his threat, one says 'abraqa wa ar'ada' — he flashed and thundered. A line:
Flash and thunder, O Yazid — your threat does not harm me.
One also says 'baraqa wa ra'ada' without the extra letter. A line (obscure, rendered as best as can be made out):
And if I set Faris before you, then thunder there as you please, and flash.

Abu Zayd, on the authority of al-Asma'i: 'baraqati l-sama'' — the sky came with lightning; likewise 'ra'adat', and 'baraqa l-rajul wa ra'ada' [of a man threatening]. Al-Asma'i did not recognize the forms 'abraqa' and 'ar'ada'. A line:
How far our lands lie from you! So flash lightning in your own land, as you please, and thunder.
And he paid no heed to al-Kumayt's saying: 'Flash and thunder, O Yazid...' [the same line as before].

Abu Zayd said: Abu Zayd reported this to us on the authority of the Arabs. Then a Bedouin of Banu Kilab came to us, in the state of pilgrim consecration. We wished to question him, so Abu Zayd said: let me question him myself, for I am gentler with him. He said to him: how do you say, 'you indeed flash [threats] and thunder'? He said: 'in blustering speech?' — meaning the language of threatening. He said: yes. He said: I say, 'you indeed flash and thunder.' I reported this to al-Asma'i, and he said: I know only 'baraqa' and 'ra'ada' [without the extra letter].

From this root, Al-Khalil said: 'abraqati l-naqa' — the she-camel struck her tail, once against her vulva and once against her rump; she is then 'baruq' and 'mubriq'. Al-Lihyani said: one says of a she-camel that raises her tail as if pregnant though she is not: 'abraqati l-naqa', so she is 'mubriq' and 'buruq'; her opposite is 'al-miktam' [one that shows no such sign though she is pregnant].

Ibn al-A'rabi said: 'baraqat', without the extra letter, so she is 'bariq' — when she flicks her tail without having conceived. Some said: 'barraqa l-rajul' — the man produced something baseless. Ibn al-A'rabi related that a man did something, and one of his companions said to him: 'you have flashed and you have sweated' — meaning: you made a show of something without substance; and 'you sweated' means you gave little, from their saying (obscure, rendered as best as can be made out): do not fill the bucket, but give sparingly into it — do you not see the effect on the one who draws the water?

Al-Khalil said: a man who is perpetually timorous is 'al-baruq'. A line:
He startles every faint-hearted, timid one.
A person left as if stunned is said to have 'his sight flash' ('bariqa basaruhu'), so he is 'bariq' — frightened, dumbfounded. So too is the explanation given by those who recite {when the sight is dazzled} [al-Qiyama: 7] with one vowelling; but those who recite it with the other vowelling say it means: you see it glisten from the intensity of its fixed stare, unable to bear it. A line:
When Ibn 'Umayr came to me, pleading, I gave him a white she-camel from among them, and he was dazzled [with astonishment].
That is, out of his amazement at it. 'Barraqa bi-'aynihi' — he made his eye glitter from the intensity of his gaze. A line:
And she took to clapping with her hand, and began flashing her eyes, toward the commander, seeking her release.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: 'baraqa l-rajul' — the man's eyes receded into his head, his reason left him. Al-Yazidi said: 'baraqa wajhahu bi-l-duhn' — he made his face gleam with oil, 'yabruqu barqan', and it has a sheen ('bariq'); likewise 'baraqtu l-adima abruquhu barqan' — I gave the hide a sheen, and 'barraqtuhu tabriqan' [the same, intensified].

Abu Zayd said: 'baraqa ta'amahu bi-l-zayt awi-l-samn aw dhawbi l-ihala' — he drizzled his food with oil, ghee, or rendered fat, putting only a little of it in.

Al-Lihyani said: 'bariqa l-siqa'u yabraqu baraqan wa buruqan' — the waterskin, struck by heat, had its butter melt and separate out. Ibn al-A'rabi said: one says 'zubdatun bariqa' and 'siqa'un bariq' when they have been affected by heat; they sometimes say 'zubdun mubriq' [the same]. The 'ibriq' [pitcher/ewer] is well known and belongs to this root [as something that gleams].

Abu Zayd said: al-barwaq is a weak plant. The Arabs say: 'more thriving/grateful than a barwaq-plant', because when the sky withholds rain it still turns green, and it is said that if heavy rain strikes it, it dies. A poet, describing a battle, said:
The hands of the men fly off in it, as though, in the terror, they flew off like the stalks of the barwaq-plant.
Al-Aswad, describing a woman, said:
She got an evening meal of crushed colocynth-seed and barwaq-plant, and she got a meal of three kinds of meat.
He said 'three kinds of meat' because the one who fed her was a hunter.

Ya'qub said: 'bariqati l-ibilu tabraqu baraqan' — the camels' bellies ached from it [from eating the plant].

As for the second root, Al-Khalil and others said: the eye is called 'barqa'' for its blackness and whiteness together. A line:
And a stream descending from the top of Barqa', brought down by fear of parting from a departing beloved.
[Al-munhadir here means the flowing tear.] They said al-baraq is the verbal noun of al-abraq said of ropes and mountains — a rope twisted with strength from a black strand and a white strand. Of mountains: those that have white streaks and black streaks. Barqa' land is streaked ground — a patch with black stones mixed through with white sand. Each distinct such patch is a 'burqa'; when it widens it is called al-abraq, al-abariq, al-barraq. A line:
Ours are the strongholds from Busra to Hajar, on to al-Yamama, then the sandy tracts, then the streaked lands.
Al-burqa is what has gone white in a black rope's twisted strand.

Abu 'Amr al-Shaybani said: al-buraq is what pours down the flash-flood from the direction of the mountain. A line (fragment, obscure): as though it were at the pouring flood-channels...

Qutrub said: al-abraq is a mountain that faces you for a day and a night, smooth, unclimbable. Abu Ziyad al-Kilabi said: al-abraq in the land is high ground with stones, its lower parts sand, where people settle; it is named after the mountains. And since it was originally a descriptive quality that became a fixed designation, it was pluralized like nouns, so they said al-abariq, just as they said al-abatih and al-adahim for the plural of al-adham [meaning a fetter], and al-asawid for the plural of al-aswad meaning the snake. Al-Ra'i said (a line, obscure, rendered as best as can be made out): after their silence they poured forth at a stony tract of Dhu l-Abariq, when they had grazed at Haqila.

Qutrub said: Banu Bariq are a clan of Yemen, of the Ash'arites. Bariq was [the name of] Sa'd ibn 'Adi, who settled at a mountain called Bariq, and was named after it. His descendants are called Banu Bariq, known by it.

Some Bedouin said: al-abraq and al-abariq are among the finest lands for vegetation — land half stone and half white earth tinged with red, scattered with loose red stones. When there is sand together with stones, that too is 'abraq'. When one means the land specifically [as feminine], one says 'barqa''. Al-abraq can also be a towering landmark of stone in two colors, or of clay and stone together. Al-abraq and al-burqa, plural al-buraq, al-biraq, al-barqawat.

Al-Asma'i said: al-burqan is what has turned yellow among locusts and taken on streaked markings and blackened. One says: 'I saw much streaked young locust in the land', singular 'burqana', as one says 'zabyatun udmana' and 'zibaun udman' [color-terms for gazelles]. Abu Ziyad said: al-burqan has black and white in it, like the streaking of a sheep. Al-Asma'i said: also 'barqa''. Abu Ziyad said: it remains, when it first emerges, white for seven days, then black for seven, then it becomes 'burqan' [streaked].

Al-barqa' among sheep is like al-balqa' among horses [both meaning piebald].
برك:
The letters bā', rā' and kāf are one root, and it is a thing's staying firm; then it puts out branches that come near to one another. One says baraka al-baʿīr yabruku burūkan - the camel knelt down. Al-Khalīl said: al-bark falls upon those of the he-camels and she-camels that kneel at the water or in the open waste, from the heat of the sun or from being full; the single one is bārik and the female bārika. And he recited about al-bark also, in a line of verse:
Kneeling camels sleeping in an empty waste, over which the sun was made to burn by the still, breathless heat.

Al-abt is fierce heat with no wind. Abū al-Khaṭṭāb said: al-bark is the many camels that drink and then kneel in the resting-place by the water; they are not called bark except so. Al-Khalīl said: abraktu al-nāqa fa-barakat - I made the she-camel kneel and she knelt. He said: and al-bark is also the camel's breast-bone and his chest, with which he crushes whatever is beneath him. You say: he rubbed it and crushed it with his bark. The poet said, in a line of verse:
So it struck them down where they stood and pressed its chest upon them, and gave the plunder to any nobody, son of nobody.

And al-birka is what of the skin of the belly is next to the ground, and what is next to it of the chest, in every beast. And its derivation is from the mabrak of camels, which is the place where they kneel; the plural is mabārik. Yaʿqūb said: the birka of a horse is where its two chest-muscles stand out from below, as far as the two veins under the upper arms, as far as the folds of the forelegs on the inner side.

Abū Ḥātim said: al-bark, with a on the bā', is the chest; and when you put the hā' in, you say it with i on the bā'. Some of them said: al-bark is the breast-bone. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: the people of Kufa used to call Ziyād the hairy-chested. Yaʿqūb said: the Arabs say: this is a matter my camels do not kneel over - that is, I do not come near it and do not accept it. And they also say: this is a matter over which the girded grey camels do not kneel - which is said of a matter when it grows grave and hard. And that is because camels, when they find a thing strange, shy away from it.

Abū ʿAlī said: he singled out camels because they will hardly kneel in a rough kneeling-place; they seek only soft ground, tasting the earth with their foot-pads, and if it is soft they kneel in it. Abū Zayd said: among the rain-stars of al-Jawzā' there is one called al-Burūk, and that is because the rains of al-Jawzā' do not fall until there is in them a day and a night in which the camels kneel down from the fierceness of its cold and its rain. He said: and al-Burak is ʿAwf ibn Mālik ibn Ḍubayʿa, so named on the day of Qiḍḍa, because he hamstrung his camel on a hill-pass and stayed where he was, and said: I am al-Burak; I kneel wherever I am overtaken.

Al-Khalīl said: one says ibtaraka al-rajul upon another man, running him down and reviling him. And they ibtarakū in the war, when they knelt upon their knees and then fought, ibtirākan. And al-barākā' is a noun from that. Bishr said about it, in a line of verse:
And nothing saves a man from the floods of battle but kneeling to the fight, or flight.

Abū ʿUbayda said: they say barāki barāki, meaning kneel down. Yaʿqūb said: one says baraka fulān upon the matter, and bāraka, both alike, when he keeps steadily at it. And ibtaraka the horse in his running, that is, he strove hard. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And they run with us, striving hard.

Al-Khalīl said: one says abraka al-saḥāb, when the cloud keeps pouring rain upon the place. Another said: rather one says ibtaraka. And that is the sound form. And he recited, in a line of verse:
A hoarse-sounding downpour, settled over it, strips the pebbles off it, as though it were one scraping out a hollow, or a boy at his rolling game.

As for al-Kumayt's words, in a line of verse:
One having a birka that has not fallen short by a span, filled out for her by the successive milkings at their settled times.

Al-wuẓub means the constant ones. For the birka, as it is said, is that she be milked before she rises.

Al-Aṣfahānī said, on the authority of al-ʿĀmirī: one says ḥalabtu al-nāqa birkatahā, and ḥalabtu al-ibil birkatahā, when you milk the milk that has gathered in her udder in her kneeling-place. And that is only said of the early mornings. And nothing is called birka except what has gathered in her udder by night and is milked in the early morning. One says: milk for us from the birak of your camels.

Al-Kisā'ī said: al-birka is that the she-camel's milk flows while she is kneeling, and he makes her stand and milks her. Al-Kumayt said, in a line of verse:
The milch-camel of your bounty does no harm.

Al-Khalīl said: al-birka is like a trough dug out in the ground, and no sides are made for it above the surface of the earth. The Kilābīs said: al-birka is the cistern, and its plural is birak, except that the cistern is not lined, while this one is lined with baked brick.

Al-Khalīl said: al-baraka is from increase and growth. And al-tabrīk is that you call down blessing. And {Blessed is God} [al-Aʿrāf: 54] is glorifying and exalting. And it has been explained as: God is exalted. And God knows best what He meant.

Abū Zayd said: ṭaʿām barīk, that is, food that has blessing in it.
بركلة:
It is a person’s walking in water and mud. The bā’ is added, and it is really from "tarakkala," when he struck with one of his two legs and drove it into the ground while digging. Al-Akhṭal said, in a line of verse:
She was raised, and in her lap was raised the son of a city-dweller ... who remains, upon his spade, striding on.

And among this is their saying (balsama) the man — his face turned sour. The mīm in it is added, and it is really from al-mublis, the sorrowful, grieving, regretful one. He said, in a line of verse:
And in the faces is a yellow pallor and dejection (iblās).

And among this is the she-camel (al-bal‘ak), the one slack of flesh. The lām is added, and it is al-ba‘k, which is gathering-together. Already mentioned.

And among this is (al-balqa‘), that in which there is nothing. The lām is added, and it belongs to the chapter of bā’, qāf and ‘ayn.

And among this is (tab‘atharat nafsī) [my soul was scattered]. The ‘ayn is added, and it really belongs to bā’, thā’ and rā’. Its explanation has already passed.
برم:
The letters ba', ra' and mim indicate four origin senses: making a thing firm; distress at a thing; the mixing of two colors; and a kind of plant.

As for the first: al-Khalil said: abramtu al-amr — I made the matter firm. Abu Ziyad said: al-mabarim are the thick spindles on which a woman twists her thread, made of acacia wood. abramtu al-habl — I twisted the rope firm. Al-mubram is spun thread, twisted from two strands, the opposite of as-sahil, spun on a single strand.

As for distress: baramtu bi-l-amr — I grew weary of the matter; abramani — it wearied me. He said: and they say "I hope I do not abram from asking about such a thing," meaning: grow weary.

He said, in a fragment of verse: "so do not blame me — I have grown weary of my own scheming."

Al-Khalil said: baramtu bi-kadha, meaning I was vexed by it, noun baram. Another poet recited, in a couplet:
What do you counsel of a soul that has grown weary of itself, as if 'Urwa al-'Udhri's love-sickness had taken hold of her —
smitten with one whose grazing-ground is Turban, then al-Hidmala, at the first cold, is where she begins.

abramani ibraman — he wearied me. Ibn at-Tathriyya said, in a line of verse:
And when I came, she spoke words to me that wore me down, and I found no answer for them.

As for the mixing of two colors: al-barimayn are the two strands of anything made of two mixed elements, like the blackness of night mixed with the whiteness of day; likewise tears mixed with kohl are called barim. 'Alqama said, in a line of verse:
With the eyes of an oryx, from which the tears fall — two mingled strands, of tears and kohl.

Abu Zayd said: for this reason the dawn, at its first showing, is called barim, for the mixing of its whiteness with the blackness of night. He said, in a line of verse:
In haste, while dawn showed — as though, against a dark and unbroken night, it were a mingled strand.

Al-Khalil said: the Arabs say "these are the barim of a people," meaning: a mixed band of them, of every kind. Layla said, in a line of verse:
O you frustrated stallion, twisting his head, to lead a mixed band from the people of the Hijaz.

Abu 'Ubayd said: one says "roast us some of its two barims," meaning: from the liver and the hump. Al-barim: a herd of gazelles. He said: al-barim is also a thing a woman ties around her waist, strung with beads. Al-Farazdaq said, in a line of verse:
Brought forth to view, no veil set before her, when the bent nursing-mother's waist-band swings.

The fourth origin sense: al-barama — the sweetest-smelling of it is the blossom of the salam acacia; the foulest-smelling is the blossom of the 'urfut, white like the blossom of the myrtle. Ash-Shaybani said: abrama at-talh — the talh-tree first put forth its fruit. Abu Ziyad said: al-barama is the blossom from which the grape-cluster emerges. Abu al-Khattab: al-baram also means grape-berries once grown past the bud stage, the size of ants' heads.

Departing from these origin senses: al-buram, the large tick. The Arabs say: "he clings closer than a buram." And likewise al-burma, the cooking-pot.
بروى:
The letters bā', rā', and the weak letter after them — wāw or yā' — are two roots: one is the shaping of a thing by carving, and the second is presenting oneself before something and imitating it.

The first root is their saying barā al-ʿūd yabrīhi baryan — he whittled the stick — and likewise the pen. Some people say yabrū, and they are the same people who say for al-burr (wheat) yaqlū; with the yā' (yabrī) is more correct.

Al-Aṣmaʿī said: one says barаytu al-qawsa baryan wa-burāyatan — I whittled the bow — and the name for what falls from it, the shavings, is al-burāya. They extend this until they say "rain that has burāya", meaning it scrapes and peels the ground.

Al-Khalīl said: al-bariyy is the arrow whose whittling has been completed, but which has not yet been fledged with feathers and not yet fitted with a head.

Abū Zayd said: the Arabs say "give the bow to its whittler" (aʿṭi al-qawsa bāriyahā), meaning: entrust the matter to the one who knows it.

As for their saying of the camel that it has burāya, this too is from this root, meaning it has been worn down by a thorough wearing. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: it is said of a camel, when it still holds up under travel, that it has burāya.

Al-Aʿlam said, in a line of verse:
With flesh worn smooth, hollow-limbed, it spent the day among tall colocynth plants.

This is when flesh wears away from it bit by bit — it is not worn down all at once at the start of its journey; rather flesh goes from it and some leanness (burāya) is left, then more goes and leanness remains again. A man too can be said to have burāya, worn lean.

From this root also is al-bura, a ring put in the nose of a camel. One says: nāqa mubrāh (a she-camel fitted with a nose-ring), jamal mubrā (a he-camel fitted with one).

A poet said, in a line of verse:
I brought up a nose-ringed she-camel, her ribs seeming like the strung bows the Māsikha bowyers make.

This nose-ring is called mabruwwa, meaning made, crafted. One says: abraytu al-nāqata ubrīhā ibrā'an — I fitted the she-camel with a nose-ring — when you put a ring in her nose.

Al-bura is also a ring of gold or silver, when thin and bent at both ends together; its plurals are al-burā, al-burūn, and al-birūn. Every ring is a bura.

Abū ʿUbayd said: "the one with the nose-ring" (dhū al-bura) is the man mentioned by ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm, in a line of verse:
And the one with the ring, of whom you have been told — through him we are protected, and we protect those who take refuge.

He was a man of Taghlib who had put a ring in his own nose because of a vow he owed. It is also said al-bura was a sword — he had a sword called al-Bura.

Al-burā' is the shavings scraped off, and it belongs to this root. A poet of Hudhayl said, in a line of verse:
His parted hair scorched, like pale-colored shavings.

From this root also, al-barā means mankind (creation), and al-barā means dust. One says "in his mouth is al-barā" — a curse, may his mouth be filled with dust — because mankind is made from it.

The other root is imitation in action and presenting oneself before something. Al-Khalīl said: one says bārayta fulānan, meaning: you matched him. Al-mubārāh is for a man to match another, doing as he does. From this is their saying: so-and-so matches (yubārī) his neighbors, and matches the wind, meaning: he gives as much as the wind blows.

A poet said, in a line of rajaz verse:
A swimmer matches her pace as she swims.

That is: he keeps abreast of her. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: one says inbarā lahu and barā lahu, meaning: he presented himself before him, and he said, in a line of verse:
A fast-running female ostrich, presenting herself before a male ostrich.

Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
A small-headed, patch-colored, submissive female ostrich presents herself before him.

Ibn al-Sikkīt said: one says tabarraytu maʿrūfa fulānin and tabarraytu li-maʿrūfihi, meaning: I sought out his kindness. He said, in a line of verse:
And a beloved family whose affection I sought out, and to whom I gave my utmost effort and my gifts in that affection.

One says ahl and ahla, both meaning family.

A poet said, in a line of rajaz verse:
And he, when he gives himself over to youthful ease, and puts on his shirt without buttoning it, and trails the ends of his cloak along the ground.
بز:
The letters bāʾ and zāy are a single root, and it is bearing, appearance, in the way of clothing or weaponry. One says: huwa bazzāz, yabīʿu al-bazz, he is a cloth-merchant, selling bazz [cloth goods]. And fulānun ḥasanu al-bizza, so-and-so is of fine dress. And al-bazz is also weaponry.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
As though, when they set out, I had entrusted my gear ... to a swooping, seeking eagle.
He means: as though my clothes and weapons, when I set out swiftly, were upon an eagle, because of my swiftness. And his word "swooping": you hear a sound from its wing as it swoops down. And their saying bazaztu al-rajula, meaning: I stripped him of his goods, is from this, since it is an act done upon his bazz, just as one says raʾastuhu, I struck his head.

Among what falls outside this chapter is al-bazbaza, swiftness in travelling.
بزخ: The letters bā', zāy and khā' are a root close to the one before it. Al-bazakh is the chest jutting out and the back sinking in; one says a man is abzakh and a woman bazkhā'. A woman is said to tabāzakhat when she moves her rump as she walks.
بزر:
The letters bā', zāy and rā' are two roots: one belongs to seeds, the other to the tools used in pounding something.

The first is well known. Al-Duraydī said: the common people's saying bazr al-baql (seed of the vegetable) is an error — it is properly badhr. In al-Khalīl's book: al-bazr is every seed that is sown; one says badhartuhu and bazartu al-qidr bi-abzārihā — I seasoned the cooking-pot with its spices.

The second root: al-baizara is the fuller's wooden beater, with which he pounds cloth — hence Aws said, in a line of verse:
With their hands, beaters.

One says: bazartuhu bi-l-ʿaṣā — I struck him with the stick.
بزع: The letters bā', zāy and ʿayn are a single root, and it is wit. A witty person is called bazīʿ, and a boy is said to tabazzaʿa when he becomes witty — this is said only of the young. They sometimes say tabazzaʿa al-sharr, the trouble grew worse, when it became severe; if this is sound, it is a second root.
بزغ:
The letters ba', za' and ghayn are one root: the rising and appearing of a thing.

1. bazaghat ash-shams and bazagha nab al-ba'ir — the sun rose, and the camel's tooth broke through.
2. they say of the farrier, when he has opened the animal's vein for bloodletting, "he has bazagha-ed it" — the same derivation.
بزق: The letters bā', zāy and qāf are a single root, and it is the casting out of a thing. One says bazaqa al-insān, like baṣaqa, he spat. The people of Yemen say bazaqa al-arḍ when he sowed it, scattering seed on it.
بزل:
The letters bā', zāy and lām are two roots: the opening of a thing, and the second, strength and power.

As for the first: one says bazaltu al-sharāba bi-l-mibzal abzuluhu bazlan — I tapped the wine with the tapping-tool. From this is their saying bazala al-baʿīr, the camel's canine tooth broke through — split open — which happens in its ninth year. A shajja bāzila is a head-wound whose blood flows out. Inbazala al-ṭalʿ — the palm-spathe split open. From this root also is al-ba'zala, the fast gait, because one who hurries opens up in his stride. He said, in a line of verse:
She turned away angrily, walking with the bāzila gait.

The second root: their saying "a matter with bazl", meaning severity. ʿAmr ibn Shaʾs said, in a line of verse:
They split open the head of the great affair after the millstone of hardship had turned in the matter of severity.

From this too is their saying "so-and-so is quick to rise to a bazlā' (weighty matter)", when he is capable of bearing great affairs. Some said, and this belongs to the same root: "a man of bazlā'" means a man of sound judgment. Abū ʿUbayd cited, in a line of verse:
Indeed, when a people are occupied by their own concerns, I am one broad in ways open, quick to rise to weighty matters.
بزم: The letters bā', zāy and mīm are a single root: holding fast and gripping. One says bazama ʿalā al-shay' when he gripped it with the front of his mouth. Al-ibzīm (the buckle) is genuine, eloquent Arabic, derived from this. Al-bazīm is the leftover of provisions, so named because it is held back from being spent.
بزو:
The letters bā', zāy and wāw are a single root, and it is a bodily posture marked by the chest thrust out, or by tallness, or something similar. A man whose back is sunken in and whose chest juts out is called abzā. Kuthayyir said, in a line of verse:
Among the people, one abzā, stooped, hollow within.

Some said: tabāzā is when he moves his rump as he walks. Abū ʿUbayd said: al-ibzā' is for a person to raise his rear; from it one says abzā yubzī. Al-bāzī (the falcon) yabzū in its tallness, or in its tameness — it may also be called al-bāz without a yā', in poetic necessity. ʿAntara said, describing a horse, in a line of verse:
As though he were a falcon of an overcast day, atop a lookout post, that has driven off the sandgrouse — seasoned to hunting in the open desert, gorged.

The falcon is keener in seeking prey on overcast days; "seasoned to hunting in the open desert" (ḍārī samlaq) means habituated to hunting in the samlaq, open desert flatland. Sanaq means gorged. I myself think that describing it as gorged is not a fitting description.

They say: "I took from so-and-so the bazw of such a thing," meaning the amount it reaches and rises to. They sometimes say abzaytu bi-fulān, when you overpowered him by force; this too is from this root, because it means to rise over him and overcome him.
بس:
The letters bāʾ and sīn are two roots: one is driving; the other is crumbling a thing and mixing it.

The first is God Almighty's saying: {and the mountains are crumbled [bussat]} [al-Wāqiʿa: 5] — it is said: they were driven along. And it came in the hadith: "A people will come from Medina, driving along, while Medina would be better for them, if only they knew." And from it is the saying of Abū al-Najm: and the snakes of the loose, shifting sand-dune moved along — meaning: they went along.

And the other root is their saying: bussat al-ḥinṭatu wa-ghayruhā, meaning: it was crumbled. And God Almighty's saying {and the mountains are crumbled} [al-Wāqiʿa: 5] is explained this way too. And that mixture is called al-basīsa.

A poet said: Do not bake bread — but crumble and mix [the roasted meal with water]. He means: do not bake, for that would delay you — rather mix the meal with water and eat.

As for their saying bassa bi'l-nāqati wa-abassa bihā, when he called her for milking, it is from the first root. And among the proverbs of the Arabs: "I will not do that as long as a slave calls a she-camel for milking."

A poet said, in a line of verse:
May God curse whoever among us seeks reconciliation ... as long as the one calling for milking circles round the black she-camel.
بسأ: The letters bā', sīn and hamza are a single root, and it is familiarity with a thing. One says basa'tu bihi and also basi'tu. A nāqa basū' is a she-camel that does not resist the milker.
بسر:
The letters ba', sin and ra' are two origin senses: freshness, a thing's being before its proper time; and a thing's stillness, its lack of motion.

The first: anything fresh and green is called busr; a plant is busr when moist; water is busr when newly fallen from the clouds. ibtasara al-fahlu an-naqata — the stud camel covered the she-camel while she was not yet in heat. The sun, at the first moment of its rising, is called busra. From this, basara ar-rajulu al-haja — the man sought the need before its proper time or place. Its derivation is sound, because it is as if he sought it before it had ripened. Al-basr also: drinking the milk in the waterskin before it has soured — drinking it before its time.
بسط:
The letters bā', sīn and tā' are a single root, and it is the stretching out of a thing, whether in breadth or otherwise. Al-bisāt is what is spread out. Al-basāt is the earth, and it is al-basīta. One says makānun basīt and basāt, a wide place. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Between the hand of al-Hajjāj and its reaching me lies a wide stretch of ground for the feet of the fast camels.
And the hand of so-and-so is bist, when he is a big spender; and al-basta in everything is wideness; and he is broad of body, of arm's reach and of knowledge. God Most High said: {and increased him in breadth of knowledge and body} [al-Baqara: 247]. And of this root, and returning to it, is their word for the she-camel that is left with her young and not kept from it: bust, also read bist.
بسق:
The bā', sīn and qāf are a single root: the rising and height of something.

1. Al-Khalīl said: basaqat al-nakhla, busūqan — the palm tree grew tall and reached its full height. In the Qur'an: {and tall palm trees} [Qāf: 10], meaning towering ones.
2. Yaʿqūb said: nakhla bāsiqa, nakhīl bawāsiq, the verbal noun being al-busūq. He said: basaqa al-rajul — the man grew tall/eminent; basaqa fī ʿilmihi — he rose high in his learning.
3. Abū Zayd, from al-Muntajiʿ ibn Nabhān: ghamāma bāsiqa — a towering white cloud; the bawāsiq of clouds are their upper reaches.

If someone should say, "But basaqa [to spit] has also come, and does not fit this pattern," he is told: this is not a [true] root-word, but a case of letter-substitution — the sīn stands in place of a ṣād, the true form being baṣaqa.

4. On this same basis they carried over another word: absaqat al-shāt, fa-hiya mubsiq — the ewe "absaqat", so she is "mubsiq", when she brought down milk a month or more before giving birth, so that she could be milked. If this is sound, it is as though she produced busāq, likened to human spittle — and as evidence, they say a girl still a virgin may develop milk in her breast, and is that not just like busāq?
