5. Abū ʿUbayda said: al-mibsāq — a ewe that yields milk before her time. He recited a line — though I mostly think Abū ʿUbayda composed it himself:
And a mubsiq ewe is milked at half her term, yielding before the lamb is even born.
بسل:
The letters ba', sin and lam are one root whose branches are close to one another: prevention and restraint. From this, the Arabs' saying of the forbidden: basl. And anything held back is basl.

Zuhayr said, in a fragment of verse: "and if the two of you keep from them, know they are forbidden." Al-basala, courage, is from this, because it is the holding firm against one's rival.

From this root too: absaltu ash-shay' — I gave the thing up to destruction; absaltu waladi — I pledged my child as security. God, Most High, said: {those are the ones given up to ruin for what they earned} [al-An'am: 70]. 'Awf ibn al-Ahwas then said, in a fragment of verse: "and my giving my sons up to ruin, though they had done no wrong — no matter avenged, no blood spilled."

As for al-busla, the fee paid to one who performs a protective charm — by a fine point of reasoning it could be traced to this root, but the better view, to me, is that it departs from the greater part of the root. Ibn al-A'rabi used to say: al-basal is one repellent of face — and that is a sound derivation, consistent with what has been established here.
بسم: The bā', sīn and mīm are a single root: the parting of the front of the mouth in pleasure, less than laughter. One says basama, yabsimu, tabassama, and ibtasama — he smiled.
بش:
The letters bāʾ and shīn are a single root, and it is a pleasant meeting, and smiling at a person out of joy at seeing him. Ibn Durayd cited, in a line of verse:
The one who asks of him never lacks abundance ... and before it, warmth and a cheerful welcome.
One says: bashsha bihi bashshan wa-bashāsha, he greeted him warmly.
بشر:
The letters bā', shīn and rā' are a single root: the appearing of a thing together with beauty and comeliness. So al-bashara is the outer skin of a person; and from it is a man's bāshara of a woman, and that is his bringing his skin to her skin. And mankind, al-bashar, was called bashar for their being visible. And al-bashīr is the fair of face. And al-bashāra is beauty.

Al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse:
And she saw that grey hair had driven off from him freshness of face and comeliness.

And one says bashshartu fulānan ubashshiruhu tabshīran — I gave so-and-so good news — and that is with good; and sometimes something else, of evil, is carried upon it, and I think that is a kind of taunting. But when the speech is left plain, then al-bishāra is with good and al-nidhāra with what is otherwise. One says absharat al-arḍ — when the land put out its plants. And one says mā aḥsana basharata al-arḍ — how fine the surface of the land is. And one says basharta al-adīm — when you pared the face of the hide. And fulānun mu'damun mubsharun — when he is a complete man, as though he had brought together the softness of the inner hide and the roughness of the outer skin. And it is said that Baḥna ibn Rabīʿa married off his daughter and said to his wife: "Fit her out, for she is the one soft within and firm without."

And some of them related absharta al-adīm, like basharta. And tabāshīr al-ṣubḥ are the first light of dawn; and likewise the first parts of everything. And no verb is formed from it. And al-mubashshirāt are the winds that bring news of rain.
بشع:
The letters bā', shīn and ʿayn are a single root, and it is the repugnance of a thing and its poor going-down the throat.

Al-Khalīl said: al-bashaʿ is a repugnant taste, having dryness and bitterness, like the taste of the bitter halīlaj fruit. He said: one says rajul bashiʿ and imra'a bashiʿa — of foul breath, because he does not pick his teeth or use a tooth-stick. The verbal noun is al-bashaʿ and al-bashāʿa. One says bashiʿa yabshaʿu bashaʿan. Food that is bashiʿ is that which does not go down the throat easily.

Ibn Durayd said: al-bashaʿ is the throat's straitness from coarse food. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: al-bashiʿ is that which does not pass down easily. One says bashiʿa al-wādī bi-l-nās when people crowded into it until it grew too narrow for them. He cited, in a line of verse:
When it meets the branches, it slips free from among them — neither harsh nor rough and coarse.

Al-Duraydī said: bashiʿtu bi-hādhā al-amr, meaning: you were straitened by it. Al-Naḍr said: I carved the body of the wood-stick until its bashaʿ — its knots — were gone. Al-Ḍabbī said: food that is bashiʿ is coarse food that has not been sifted, so it does not go down the throat easily, from its roughness.
بشك: The letters bā', shīn and kāf are a single root, and from it branches what is close to swiftness. One says nāqa bashakā, meaning swift, and imra'a bashakā ʿamūl, a swift and hardworking woman. Ibtashaka fulān al-kadhib — he fabricated the lie. Bashaktu al-thawb — I cut the garment. All this is from al-bashk in gait, the swiftness in moving the legs.
بشم:
The letters bā', shīn and mīm are a single root, and it is a kind of surfeit with some food, which then extends to something else being likened to it. One says bashimtu min al-ṭaʿām, as though you had grown weary of it. Al-Khalīl said: al-basham is used specifically for fatty food. He said: it is said of a young weaned camel: bashima, from drinking too much milk.

What departs from this root is al-bashām, which is a kind of tree.
بص:
The letters bāʾ and ṣād are a single root, and it is the gleam of a thing and its shimmer as it moves. One says: baṣṣa, when it gleamed, yabiṣṣu baṣīṣan wa-baṣṣan.

A line of verse:
Its rind gleams, glossy and bright ... like a sea-pearl, lifted up by the diver.
Al-dulāmiṣ is the glossy, shining one; zahāhā, he raised it, brought it out.

1. al-baṣṣāṣa — the eye.
2. baṣbaṣa al-kalbu — the dog wagged its tail; likewise the stallion.

A line of verse: They wagged their tails when we were driven along.
Ruʾba said, in a line of verse: They wagged with their tails, from thirst and gnats.

3. baṣbaṣa jarwu al-kalbi — the puppy's eyes flickered with a gleam before they opened.
4. khimsun baṣbāṣ — a far journey to water.

Abū Duwād said, in a line of verse:
And I have startled the graceful, slender does, their tails flickering.
They said: he meant to say "I startled the wild cattle," but the metre did not allow it, so he said "daughters of the uncle of the slender ones," meaning the gazelles. And by al-baṣābiṣ he meant their moving of their tails.

5. al-baṣīṣ — trembling, shivering, from the same reasoning.
بصر:
The letters bā', ṣād and rā' are two roots. One of them is knowledge of a thing; one says huwa baṣīrun bihi — he knows it well. From this is al-baṣīra, insight; and also the piece of blood which, when it falls on the ground, spreads out round.

Al-Asʿar said, in a line of verse:
They went off with their baṣā'ir — their blood-traces — upon their shoulders, while mine is borne at a run by a swift, sturdy horse.

And al-baṣīra is a shield, so it is said. And al-baṣīra is a proof. The origin of all of that is the clearness of a thing. And one says ra'aytuhu lamḥan bāṣiran — I saw him with a seeing glance, that is, looking with a hard stare. And one says baṣurtu bi-al-shay' — when you have come to know it and be aware of it; and abṣartuhu — when you saw it.

As for the other root, the buṣr of a thing is its thickness. From it is al-baṣr, which is that one hide be joined to another, the two being sewn as the border of a garment is sewn. And al-baṣīra is what lies between the two cloth-widths of a tent, and that is nearer to the first root. As for al-baṣra, it is soft stone; and when the hā' is dropped you say biṣr, with a kasra on the bā'. This belongs to the second root.
بصط: The letters bā', ṣād and ṭā' are not a root, because the ṣād in it is originally a sīn. One says baṣaṭa meaning basaṭa, he spread out, and "in so-and-so's body there is baṣṭa" like basṭa, stature.
بصع:
The letters bā', ṣād and ʿayn are a single root, and it is a thing coming out with force through a narrow space. Al-Khalīl said: al-baṣʿ is a narrow opening through which water barely passes; one says baṣaʿa yabṣaʿu baṣāʿatan. Al-Khalīl said: one says tabaṣṣaʿa al-ʿaraq min al-jasad when sweat oozes out slightly from the roots of the hair.

Al-Duraydī said: baṣaʿa al-ʿaraq when it seeped out. He mentioned that al-Khalīl used to recite, in a line of verse:
She refuses, when forced, all but the warm water — for that seeps through slowly.

With a ṣād, going by what we have mentioned. But what people generally use is with a ḍād, meaning flowing. Al-Duraydī said: al-baṣīʿ is sweat itself.

What departs from this root: baṣʿ, meaning something. It is related on the authority of Quṭrub: "a biṣʿ of the night has passed", meaning: some of it.
بصق:
The letters bā', ṣād and qāf are a single root sharing with bā', sīn, qāf — the matter between them being close. One says baṣaqa meaning bazaqa and basaqa, he spat. Al-Khalīl said: with the ṣād is better. The noun is al-buṣāq.

Abū Ziyād said: one says abṣaqat al-shāh — the ewe let down her milk before giving birth, so that in the base of her udder there is some milk while what is above it stays empty. He said: this happens to a ewe with little milk when she gives birth. He said: mabāṣīq of the flock give birth many days after their milk comes down, and their milk is only in the base and edge of the udder.

Someone said: baṣaqtu al-shāh — I milked the ewe while she still carried a lamb in her belly. He said: al-baṣūq is the ewe most lacking and least in milk. Al-Duraydī said: buṣāq al-ibil is the pick of the camels, the singular and plural being the same.

As for their calling the white glittering stone "the spittle of the moon" (buṣāqat al-qamar, baṣqat al-qamar), it is likened to human spittle. Al-buṣāq is also a kind of palm-tree, as though by analogy with al-busāq; that is treated under its own entry.
بصل:
The bā', ṣād and lām are a single root. Al-baṣal is the well-known [vegetable, onion]. Labīd likened helmets to it, saying:
Large, pungent [war-gear], bound fast with straps — of Kurdumānī and Turkish make, like onions.
(The exact sense of "Kurdumānī" is unclear to me — likely a place or style of armour-making; I render it uncertainly.)
بض:
The letters bāʾ and ḍād are a single root, and it is the moistness of a thing, as though it were sweating. One says: baḍḍa al-māʾu yabiḍḍu baḍḍan wa-buḍūḍan, when it seeped from a rock or the ground. And among the proverbs of the Arabs: "not even his stone seeps," meaning: no good is to be had from him. And rakiyyun baḍūḍ is a well of little water. And one does not say "baḍḍa al-siqāʾ" nor "al-qirba" of a waterskin — that seeping is called al-rashḥ or al-natḥ; and if it is of oil or clarified butter, it is al-natth and al-matth.

As for their calling a plump body baḍḍ, that too is from this, because from its fatness and fullness it is as though it seeps, so its colour glistens. They said: al-badan al-baḍḍ is the full, plump body, and this is not only for the fair-skinned — it may be said of the fair-skinned and the dark-skinned alike.

Ibn Durayd said: rajulun baḍḍ bayyinu al-baḍāḍa wa'l-buḍūḍa, when he was bright of complexion and plump. A poet, describing a slain man, said, in a line of verse [I am unsure of the exact sense of the second half]:
And a fair, plump one, with the vultures upon him ... and at his side a broken thing.

Abū Zubayd al-Ṭāʾī said, in a line of verse:
O ʿUthm, come to my aid, for my well has gone hard ... and has failed to seep with its water.
بضع:
The letters ba, dad and 'ayn are three roots: the first is a portion of a thing, whether a limb or otherwise; the second is a tract of land; the third is that a thing be remedied, whether by speech or otherwise.

As for the first: Al-Khalil said: 'bada'a l-insanu l-lahma yabda'uhu bad'an', and 'bada'ahu yubaddi'uhu tabdi'an' — he cut the meat into pieces. Al-bad'a is the piece, the cut portion — it is al-habra. They say: so-and-so is strong of build (shadidu l-badi'i wa l-bad'a) when he is fleshy and well fed. A line:
Firm of build, his flesh solid and taut.
He said: 'khazi l-badi'' means strong of flesh. Ya'qub said: al-badi' of flesh is the plural of bad', as one says 'abd' and 'abid' [slave, slaves].

As for al-badi'a, it is the piece cut from a flock of sheep; one says 'firqun bawadi'' [portions cut off from a flock]. Al-Asma'i said: al-bad'a is a gathered piece of meat, its plural bida', as one says badra and bidar [purse of money, and its plural], and it is also pluralized as bad'. Zuhayr said:
Blood by a carcass, birds hopping around it, and cut portions of meat-work in a stretched hide.

From this: their saying 'bada'tu l-ghusna abda'uhu' — I cut the branch. Aws said:
And a splinter cut from the top of a shoot, on a mountain-peak you see crowned with cloud.

As for al-mubada'a, meaning marital intercourse, it is from this root, being a mutual-action form from al-bud', and it is one of the fine euphemisms.

Al-Asma'i said: 'bada'a l-rajulu mra'atahu' — the man had intercourse with his wife, 'bida'an'. In the proverb: 'like one teaching her mother intercourse' — said of a man who teaches someone more knowledgeable than himself. He said: one says 'fulanun maliku bud'iha' — so-and-so holds the right over her marriage. A poet said:
Would that the one who married her, and the one with rights over her, and all their father's sons, had never been created.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: al-bud' is marriage/intercourse, and al-bida' is copulation.

Carried on the first sense: bida'atu l-tajir, a merchant's portion of his wealth [used in trade]. Al-Asma'i said: 'abda'a l-rajulu bida'atan' — the man invested a portion of goods in trade. He said: from this comes their saying, 'like the one carrying dates as merchandise to Hajar' — a proverb for one who brings a thing to people who know it and are more skilled in it than he is. The plural of bida'a is bida'at and bada'i'.

Abu 'Amr said: al-badi' is the one who imports the goods of a settlement. Al-Asma'i said: one says 'ittakhadha 'irdahu bida'atan' — he treated his honor as a piece of merchandise, that is, like a thing bought and sold. Al-Asma'i made explicit what we have said, for in his very wording: al-bida'a was named so only because it is a portion of wealth set aside for trade.

Ibn al-A'rabi said: al-bada'i' are like al-'ala'iq — they are the spare, led camels driven alongside the [main] camels. A line:
Load upon them, for they are spare/led ones — and what God allows to be lost is indeed lost.
And similarly:
He sent it off as a led animal, not knowing that led animals meet [misfortune].

Among the body-parts that are portions of the body: their saying 'al-shajjatu l-badi'a' — a head-wound that splits the flesh but does not lay bare the bone. Al-Asma'i said: it is the one that splits the flesh lightly. From this is the hadith of 'Umar, that he struck the man who had sworn an oath demanding something of Umm Salama, giving him thirty lashes as discipline, 'all of them splitting the flesh and drawing blood' — that is, splitting the skin and bringing down the blood.

From this root: al-bid' in numbers — what is between three and ten. One says al-bid' is seven. They say that is the meaning of His saying, Most High: {a number of years} [Yusuf: 42]. Among their proverbs: [an obscure saying about merchandise being offered up when a person is in need].

As for the second [root, a tract of land]: al-buday' is a place-name; Hassan mentioned it:
Did you question the traces of the abode, or did you not — between al-Jawabi, then al-Buday', then Hawmal.
Badi' too is a place. Badi' is a mountain, mentioned in Labid's poetry. Al-badi' also means the sea. The Hudhali poet said:
He kept watching the sun until it seemed, just above the sea, in its rays, like a dense thicket.
Al-Duraydi said: al-badi' is an island cut off from the [main] land, in the sea. If what Ibn Duraid said is correct, then it returns to the first sense [a cut-off piece].

As for the third root: their saying 'bada'tu min al-ma'' — I drank my fill from the water. Water that is fresh/wholesome is 'ma'un badi''. Al-Asma'i said: 'shariba fulanun fa-ma bada'a' — so-and-so drank but was not satisfied. Al-bad' is the satisfying of thirst. Al-Shaybani said: 'bada'a budu'an', as one says 'naqa'a' [similarly].
بط:
The letters bāʾ and ṭāʾ are a single root, and it is lancing, splitting. One says: baṭṭa al-jurḥa yabuṭṭuhu baṭṭan, meaning: he lanced it. As for al-baṭīṭ, meaning wonder, it too is from this, because it is a matter that has been lanced open, and so disclosed, until it caused astonishment. Al-Kumayt said, in a line of verse:
Have you not marvelled, and seen a wonder ... among those gone by in the passing years?

And whatever else there is of bāʾ and ṭāʾ words beyond this is entirely Persian.
بطأ:
The bā', ṭā' and hamza are a single root: slowness in a matter. abṭa'a, ibṭā'an and buṭ'an — he was slow. A man is baṭī', a people biṭā'.

A line:
And a scattered troop, scattered like locusts, stretched wide — I turned its stragglers back to join its swift ones.
(The image is of gathering back a spread-out group; the exact scene is not fully clear from the line alone.)
بطح:
The letters bā', ṭā' and ḥā' are a single root, and it is the spreading out and extending of a thing.

Al-Khalīl said: al-baṭḥ comes from your saying baṭaḥahu ʿalā wajhihi baṭḥan — he threw him down flat on his face. Al-baṭḥā' is a watercourse containing fine gravel; when it widens and broadens it is called abṭaḥ. Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
As though the anklets and the ivory bands, bent around their limbs, were on an ʿushar bush — a desert shrub, the Sodom-apple — that the flood-course had left standing.

And he said, describing the tabaṭṭuḥ, in a line of verse:
When they lie sprawled flat upon the litters, sprawling like the duck lies flat by the shore.

Tabaṭṭaḥa al-sayl — the flood spread out broadly. Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
May a broadly spreading downpour never cease to fall on you both, from the rain-star of al-Simāk and the rain-star of al-Zubānā.

Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: al-abṭaḥ is the track left by a flood, whether wide or narrow, and its plural is abāṭiḥ. The grammarians said: it was pluralized as the plural of nouns on the pattern afʿal, like al-aḥāmid and al-asāwid, because this pattern so predominates in the meaning that it becomes like a proper noun.

Al-Khalīl said: al-baṭīḥa is the stretch of standing water between Wāsiṭ and Basra, so vast that its two ends cannot be seen; it is where the Tigris and Euphrates drain out. Baṭḥā' Makka, the gravel plain of Mecca, is from this. Al-Duraydī said: "Quraysh of the baṭḥā'" are those who dwell in the gravel plain of Mecca, and "Quraysh of the outskirts" are those who dwell in the area around Mecca. He said, in a line of verse:
Had a band of Quraysh witnessed me — Quraysh of the gravel plain, not Quraysh of the outskirts.

He said: dust too is called al-baṭḥā'. One says: he called for the baṭḥā' of its bark [an obscure phrase; the sense is not clear]. He cited, in a line of verse:
A great drinker of the milk of the milch-camels, who often dwells in the sandy hollows of the gravel plains.

Al-Farrā' said: "There is nothing between me and him but a baṭḥa", meaning the stature of a man — what lies between you and him along the ground is called a baṭḥa, and what lies between you and him in something raised up is called a qāma, a standing-height. Al-buṭāḥ is an illness resembling pleurisy but is not the same; one is said to be mabṭūḥ, afflicted by it.
بطخ: The letters bā', ṭā' and khā' are a single word, and it is al-biṭṭīkh, the melon, and I do not consider it a genuine root, because it is a transposition of al-ṭibbīkh, and this is more regular and better-formed by analogy. It has been written up under its own entry.
بطر:
The letters ba', ta' and ra' are one root: splitting. The farrier, al-baytar and al-mubaytir, is named from this.

An-Nabigha said, in a line of verse:
He pierced the flank-muscle with the comb-spike and drove it clean through — the piercing of a farrier treating al-'adad.

Al-'adad is a disease that afflicts the upper foreleg. Al-batar, insolence from ease — exceeding proper bounds in high spirits — is carried on this same derivation.

As for their saying "his blood went for batar," unavenged, this may depart from the root; or it could be said his blood's course was split open and so it went to waste — that is, when it is declared forfeit, with no compensation owed for it.
بطش: The letters bā', ṭā' and shīn are a single root, and it is seizing a thing with force, mastery and strength. God, exalted, said: {indeed the grip of your Lord is severe} [al-Burūj: 12]. And a hand is *bāṭisha*, a hand that seizes hard.
بطغ:
The letters bā', ṭā' and ghayn are a single root, and it is being smeared with something. A poet said, in a line of rajaz verse:
Were it not for the filth of his backside, he would not have been smeared.
بطل:
The letters bā', ṭā' and lām are a single root, and it is a thing's passing away and the shortness of its staying and lasting. One says baṭala al-shay'u yabṭulu buṭlan and buṭūlan - the thing came to nothing. Satan was called al-Bāṭil - the false one - because his doings have no reality, and nothing that comes of him has any coming back or anything to rely upon. Al-baṭal is the brave man. Those who hold to this reasoning said he was named so because he exposes himself to the places of destruction. And that is sound; one says baṭal bayyin al-buṭūla wa-al-baṭāla - plainly a champion. And they have said imra'a baṭala - a woman champion. As for their saying in the proverb: "Your brother is one under compulsion, not a champion" - there has been disagreement about it. A group said: the proverb belongs to Jarwal ibn Nahshal ibn Dārim, who was a coward of complete build; and that a tribe of the Arabs raided the Banū Dārim, and they and the Banū Dārim fought hard until the slain were many. Jarwal came and saw a man driving a woman in a litter; and when the man saw him he feared him for the fullness of his build, not knowing who he was. Jarwal said: "I am Jarwal ibn Nahshal, of ample noble descent." So the man turned upon him and took him and bound his hands behind him, saying, in a line of verse:
When you see a man in the din of battle, then remind yourself, Jarwal.
Until he brought him to the leader of the army, who had known Jarwal's cowardice, and he said: Jarwal, we never knew you to fight champions and to love single combat! And Jarwal said: "Your brother is one under compulsion, not a champion."

And a group said: rather the proverb belongs to Bayhas, and his story has been told at length elsewhere than in this chapter.

And one says rajul baṭṭāl bayyin al-baṭāla - a man plainly idle and good for nothing. And dhahaba damuhu buṭlan, that is: his blood went unavenged and for nothing.
بطن:
The letters bā', tā' and nūn are a single root that hardly ever fails, and it is the inward side of a thing and the side of it that faces you. Al-batn, the belly, is the opposite of the back. You say batantu al-rajul, when you strike a man's belly. One of them said:
When you strike a laden beast, strike it on the belly.
And the bātin of a matter is its inner part, the opposite of its outward side. And God Most High is al-Bātin, the Inward, because He knows the inside of things through and through. You say batantu hādhā al-amr, when you come to know its inside. And al-batīn is the man with a great belly. And al-mabtūn is the one sick in his belly. And al-mibtān is the one who eats much. And al-mubtin is the one lean of belly. And al-butnān are the inner sides of the feathers of an arrow. And al-batn among the Arabs is a group smaller than a tribe. And al-butayn is a star; it is said that it is the belly of Aries. And al-bitān is the girth of a saddle, which is its band, and that is because it lies along the belly.

And of this chapter is their word for the men close to a man who know the inside of his affair: they are his bitāna. God Most High said: {Do not take as intimates any but your own} [Al 'Imran: 118]. And one says tabattantu al-kala', when you range about in the pasture. A poet said, in a line of verse:
I have ranged about, and under me a strong she-camel, keeping her elbows off her sides, with sinews in them twisted like rope.
بظ: The letters bāʾ and ẓāʾ. It is said that they say: baẓẓa awtārahu li'l-ḍarb, when he tuned his strings ready for playing. And the like of this is not to be relied upon.
بظر: The letters bā', ẓā' and rā' are a single root not to be reasoned from by analogy. Al-buẓāra is the piece of flesh hanging down from a ewe's udder, the teat. Al-buẓāra is also a protruding thing on the upper lip, not found in everyone. ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him, said to Shurayḥ in a legal ruling: "What do you say, O long-lipped slave?" And God knows best.
بظى: The letters bā', ẓā' and the weak letter after them are a single root, and it is a thing's firmness together with softness and suppleness in it. One says baẓiya laḥmuhu, his flesh became firm and full, and "his flesh is khaẓan baẓan", a paired expression for firm and full. They sometimes say khaẓiyat al-mar'a and baẓiyat, and this belongs to the same root, though it is said to be a borrowed, foreign word.
بع:
The letters bāʾ and ʿayn are a single root, according to what al-Khalīl said, and it is heaviness and persistence. Al-Khalīl said: al-baʿāʿ is the heaviness of a rain-cloud from the rain it carries. Imruʾ al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
And it cast down its heavy load in the open plain of al-Ghabīṭ ... like the alighting of the Yemeni trader with his laden packs.

He said: and it is said of a man, when he throws himself down [exhausted]: he has cast his heavy burden upon us. And it is said of a rain-cloud, when it lets fall all the rain within it: it has cast down its heavy burden. One says: baʿʿa al-saḥābu wa'l-maṭaru baʿʿan wa-baʿāʿan, when it persisted heavily in a place.

As for Ibn Durayd, he mentioned none of this, and mentioned, among reduplicated words, al-baʿbaʿa, the rapid repetition of speech. And we have already said that sounds like this cannot be used as a basis for deriving a root.
بعث:
The letters bā', ʿayn and thā' are a single root, and it is stirring up. And one says baʿathtu al-nāqa, when you stirred her up. And Ibn Aḥmar said, in a line of verse:
So I roused her, and she cut short her paces, after the life of the fire had all but gone out for the one seeking light.
بعج:
The letters bā', ʿayn and jīm are a single root, and it is the splitting open of a thing. This and the root mentioned under bā', ʿayn, qāf belong to one and the same valley — they can hardly be told apart.

Al-Khalīl said: baʿaja baṭnahu bi-l-sikkīn — he gashed his belly with the knife, that is, he cut it, split it, and churned it open. He said: tabaʿʿaja al-saḥāb tabaʿʿujan is the cloud's breaking open in release of rain. He said, in a line of verse:
Where the rain-cloud began to pour, or broke open.

Baʿʿaja al-maṭar al-arḍ tabʿījan — the rain gashed open the ground, from the force with which it dug into the stones. A man is called baʿij, as though his belly were slack, split open, from the weakness of his walk. He said, in a line of verse:
A night I walk in peril, walking slowly, gently, like the gait of the baʿij.

Abū ʿAmr related: baʿajtu ilayhi baṭnī, meaning: I laid open my innermost secret to him. And one says baʿajahu ḥuznun — grief tore him open. A "gashed belly" (baṭn baʿīj) has the sense of mabʿūj. Abū Dhu'ayb said, in a line of verse:
And that is a greater loss for you than for him, for he was noble, and my belly is torn open with grief for the noble.

Al-Liḥyānī said: a man is baʿīj and a woman is baʿīj, and women in this state are baʿjā, and likewise the men. It is said this refers to the tearing of the peritoneum and the falling away of what is within it — al-indiyāl meaning the falling away. Al-Khalīl said: bāʿijat al-wādī is where the valley opens out and widens. He said, in a line of verse:
And the naṣī grass of a bāʿija, and salt-marsh growth pooled with water.

Abū Ziyād and Abū Faqʿas said: al-bāʿija is the small, wide hollow — the valley opens out there from one of its two sides; it is among the places where naṣī grass grows. It is also said: al-bāʿija is the far end of the sand, a place between soft, level ground and rugged ground, sometimes raised, sometimes sloping down. Al-Naḍr said: al-bāʿija is a low-lying place among the sands, shaped like a depression, ground packed down with no ridges, growing rimth and ḥamḍ shrubs and the choicest herbage.

Everything else left aside in this category is like what has already been mentioned. Bāʿijat al-Qirdān is a place-name, in the saying of Aws, in a line of verse:
Then Bāʿijat al-Qirdān, then al-Mutathallim.
بعد:
The letters bā', 'ayn and dāl are two roots: the opposite of nearness, and the counterpart of 'before'.

They said: al-bu'd is the opposite of nearness, and al-bu'd and al-ba'ad are perishing. And they said of the words of God Most High, {kamā ba'idat Thamūdu} [Hūd: 95], that is, as Thamūd perished. And the analogy of that is one. Al-abā'id, the far ones, are the opposite of al-aqārib, the near kin. A poet said, in a line of verse:
If you do not rub away at your side some of what troubles you from your nearest kin, the far ones will shoot at you.

And you say: stand aside, ghayra bā'idin - that is, not in humiliation. And stand aside, ghayra ba'īdin - that is, stay near.

As for the other, it is your saying, he came min ba'du, afterwards, just as you say for its opposite, min qablu, beforehand.
بعر:
The letters ba', 'ayn and ra' are two origin senses: camels, and dung.

1. ba'ir — a camel; plurals ab'ira, aba'ir, bu'ran.

One of the thieves said, in a couplet:
Indeed I would be ashamed before God to be seen dragging a rope with no camel on it,
and to beg a mean man for his camel — while my Lord's camels are many throughout the land.

2. al-ba'r — dung, well known.
بعص: The letters bā', ʿayn and ṣād are a single root, and it is agitation. Abū Mahdī said: tabaʿṣaṣa al-shay' — it writhed and squirmed in the hand; likewise tabaʿṣaṣa fī al-nār, said of something thrown into the fire, when it begins darting about with no real running to it. The hare tatabaʿṣaṣu in a person's hand. It is also said of a snake, when struck, that it writhes and lashes its tail — it has tabaʿṣaṣat.
بعض:
The letters bā', ʿayn and ḍād are a single root, and it is the dividing of a thing into parts. Every portion of it is a baʿḍ, a part.

Al-Khalīl said: the baʿḍ of anything is a portion of it. You say: a girl, parts of her resemble other parts of her. And baʿḍ is masculine. You say: this house, part of it is joined to part. And baʿʿaḍtu al-shay' tabʿīḍan — when you break the thing up into parts.

It is said that the Arabs attach baʿḍ as a connective just as they attach mā, as in His saying, exalted be He: {fa-bi-mā raḥmatin mina Allāh} — so by a mercy from God [Āl ʿImrān: 159] — and {mimmā khaṭī'ātihim} — because of their sins [Nūḥ: 25]. He said: and so too baʿḍ in His saying, exalted be He: {wa-in yaku ṣādiqan yuṣibkum baʿḍu alladhī yaʿidukum} — and if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will strike you [Ghāfir: 28]. And a bedouin said: "I saw crows yatabaʿḍaḍna" — as though he meant that they were taking hold of one another, part at part.

Of what strays from this root is al-baʿūḍa, the mosquito, which is well known; the plural is baʿūḍ.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And I became a slave to the mosquitoes, brought low.

And hādhihi laylatun baʿiḍa — this is a night full of mosquitoes; and mabʿūḍa as well, like their saying makānun sabiʿ and masbūʿ, a place with many lions, and dhi'ib and madh'ūb, a place with many wolves. In the proverb: "You have charged me with the marrow of a mosquito" — said of what cannot be.

Ibn Aḥmar said, in lines of verse:
I was not among my people one given to trickery, had a man who disobeys had any command.
You charged me with the marrow of a mosquito, and I gave it up: there is no success in it and no excuse.

And the People of the Mosquito are a folk whom Khālid ibn al-Walīd killed in the wars of apostasy, and of them the poet says, in a line of verse:
Over the like of the People of the Mosquito, then, scratch your face in grief.
بعط: The letters bā', ʿayn and ṭā' are not a root, because the ṭā' in abʿaṭa is substituted from a dāl. One says abʿaṭa fī al-sawm, he named an outrageous price in bargaining, like abʿada.
بعق:
The letters bā', ʿayn and qāf are a single root, and it is the splitting and opening of a thing; it is then extended to cover whatever is close to that meaning.

Al-Khalīl said: al-buʿāq is a loud noise, and heavy rain is al-buʿāq. Baʿaqa al-wābil — the downpour burst open suddenly. Abū Ziyād said: al-buʿāq is the fiercest of rains, and one says "land that has been mabʿūqa", struck by such rain. He said: al-inbiʿāq is for something to burst upon you suddenly. He cited, in a line of verse:
While a man is at ease, a sudden calamity of death alarms him — he had not feared its bursting-forth.

One says baʿaqtu al-ibil, meaning: I slaughtered them. In the hadith: "Who are these who yabʿaqūna our milk-she-camels?" — meaning: who slaughter them. Its origin is from the flowing of blood.

Abū ʿAlī said: al-baʿq is the split found in the back of the hoof. Some Bedouin related: baʿaqtu fulānan ʿan al-amr baʿqan, meaning: I tore it open and exposed it for him. Munbaʿaq al-mafāza is the wide-open stretch of the desert. Jandal al-Ṭuhawī said, in a line of verse:
For the wind, in its unknown bursting-place, are trailing tracks with fluttering skirts.

Al-Ḍabbī said, in a saying: "Near us there was a she-wolf given to raiding; she came, she and her mate, by night, and baʿaqā our sheep" — meaning: the two of them tore open their bellies.
بعك:
The letters bā', ʿayn and kāf are a single root, gathering together crowding, jostling, and mixing. Al-Duraydī said: al-baʿak is coarseness of body and stiffness; from it is derived Baʿkak, the name of a man from Quraysh.

Someone else said: I left him in the baʿkūkat of the people, meaning the gathered mass of their dwellings; and we hold that he vocalized the bā' with a fatḥa and made the pattern faʿlūla, treating it as one of the verbal-noun patterns, like sāra sayrūratan and ḥāda ḥaydūdatan, and qaylūlatan. He cited, in a line of verse:
They come out from the crowded mingling — like the shed skins of thin, worn-out snakes.

But the Basrans reject this pattern for verbal nouns except for weak-lettered roots. Some scholar said: buʿkūkatu al-shay' is its middle. ʿUbayd ibn Ayyūb said, in a line of verse:
And, O Lord, if You do not pardon me, You will cast me into the Fire, into its close-pressing midst.

One says: he fell into baʿkūkā', meaning trouble and uproar. Al-Farrā' said: al-baʿkūka is the crowding of camels when gathered together, and it is also said to mean the group of them, plural baʿākīk.

Abū Zayd said: al-bāʿik among men is one utterly foolish, ruined by folly, and this too belongs to that root, because he is mixed up, confused.
بعل:
The letters ba, 'ayn and lam are three roots: the first is companion/master — the husband is called 'ba'l'; they also used to name some of their idols Ba'l. From this: al-bi'al, a man's amorous dealings with his household. In hadith, concerning the days of tashriq: 'they are days of eating, drinking, and conjugal delight.' Al-Hutay'a said:
How many a chaste, married woman have I left, such that when night grew dark she found none to share intimacy with.

The second root: a kind of bewilderment/confusion. One says 'ba'ila l-rajul' — the man became bewildered. Perhaps from this too comes their saying of a woman who does not know how to wear her clothes: 'ba'ila'.

The third root: al-ba'l of land — elevated land that rain reaches only once a year. A poet said:
When we climbed atop a broad, unirrigated plateau, you would think upon us the shells of cracked eggs.

Carried on this third root: al-ba'l — that which drinks by its own roots from the earth, without being watered by rain; this occurs in his saying, peace and blessings be upon him and his family, concerning the tithe of date-palms: 'whatever drinks by ba'l, on it is the tenth [tithe].' Ibn Rawaha said:
There I care not for palm-trees watered [by irrigation] nor for those unwatered, even if the vessel [of yield] be great.
بعوي:
The letters bā', ʿayn, wāw and yā' are two roots: committing an offense, and taking a thing as a loan or by wagering.

The first root is their saying baʿawtu abʿū wa-abʿā, meaning: you committed a crime. ʿAwf ibn al-Aḥwaṣ said, in a line of verse:
And my abandoning my sons without any crime they had committed, nor any blood that had been shed.

They said: from this too is baʿawtuhu bi-ʿaynī, meaning: I struck him, spotted him with my eye.

The second root is al-baʿw. Al-Khalīl said: it is the loan; one says istabʿaytu minhu, meaning: I borrowed from him. He also said al-baʿw is wagering; one says baʿawtuhu baʿwan, meaning: I won something from him, I bested him at gambling. He said, in a line of verse:
The heart grew sober after intimacy, and its ardor turned back, and what Tumāḍir had won from it was given back to it.

Al-Aṣmaʿī said: one says abʿaytu fulānan farasan, in the sense of akhbaltuhu, I lent him it as a loan, that being when you lend him it so he may raid upon it. Al-istibʿā' is for a man to borrow a horse from another to race upon it. One says istabʿaytuhu fa-abʿānī — I asked to borrow it from him and he lent it to me; and that is al-baʿw. Al-Kumayt said, in a line of verse:
That the two of them might borrow a solid-black, nose-ringed dog — and whoever's forebears were elephant-like fools will turn out foolish too.
بغ:
The letters bāʾ and ghayn, doubled, are two distinct roots according to al-Khalīl and Ibn Durayd. The first is al-baghbagha, the imitation of a kind of rumbling, bellowing roar. Al-Khalīl cited, in a line of verse [I am unsure of the exact sense of this fragment]:
With a rumbling, bellowing roar, a deep resounding bellow.

And the second root, mentioned by Ibn Durayd, who said: al-baghbagh, its diminutive bughaybigh, is a well close to the surface.

A line of verse:
Many a water of yours in the mountains ... a shallow well, drawn up with a rope.
بغت:
The letters bā', ghayn and tā' are a single root on which nothing further is built by analogy. From it is al-baght, which is that a thing should come upon one suddenly.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And the greatest thing of all is when the sudden blow falls upon you.
بغث:
The letters bā', ghayn and thā' are a single root, indicating the lowliness and weakness of a thing.

1. bughāth al-ṭayr — birds that neither hunt nor can defend themselves.
2. al-baghthā' — a name given to the mixed common rabble of people, their lowest sort.
3. al-abghath — a place with sand, called this because it is soft, not firm.
بغر:
The letters bā', ghayn and rā' are a single root, and it contains words close to one another in meaning, concerning drinking.

1. al-baghar — a person's drinking without ever having his thirst quenched; it afflicts camels too. A man was taunted, and it was said of him: "His father died of overeating, and his mother died of unquenched thirst."
2. baghara al-naw' — said when the star's rain-season broke out with rain.
3. bughirat al-arḍ — said, some report, when the rain has softened the ground.
بغز:
The letters bā', ghayn and zā' are a root, and it is like liveliness and boldness in speech.

Ibn Muqbil said, in a line of verse:
You would think it, in its boldness by night, gone mad.

1. al-bāghiz — the foul-mouthed, obscene man, they said.

All of this goes back to boldness.
بغش:
The letters bā', ghayn and shīn are a single root, and it is weak rain, called al-baghsh.

1. arḍ mabghūsha — ground rained on lightly.

It came in poetry: maṭar bāghish — a lightly-falling rain.
بغض:
The letters bā', ghayn and ḍād are one root, and it indicates the opposite of love. One says abghaḍtuhu ubghiḍuhu — I hated him.

As for his saying, in a line of verse:
and among the vicissitudes of fate is that she should strike you with hatred, and hurling from her, and that you should be watched —
it was said that al-bighḍa here means "enemies," and it was said he meant "people of hatred." And they sometimes said baghuḍa jadduhu — his fortune turned wretched, just as they say ʿathara [he stumbled, his luck failed]. And God knows best.
بغل: The letters bā', ghayn and lām indicate strength in the body. From this comes al-baghl, the mule. Some said it is named this for the strength of its build. Others said it is named baghl from al-tabghīl, a certain kind of gait. What we hold is that al-tabghīl is derived from the gait of the mule.
بغم:
The letters bā', ghayn and mīm are a minor root, and it is a sound, and something resembling it that is not fully distinct.

1. al-bughām — the sound a she-camel repeats. The cry of a doe (female gazelle) is also called bughām.
2. baghūm — said of a doe (female gazelle) that has this cry.

A poet said, about a she-camel, in a line of verse:
You took my mount's low cry for a young kid's bleating ... but it is not — confound anyone but you — the kid's bleating.

Also carried by this root is their saying baghamtu li-l-rajuli bi-l-ḥadīth, said when you speak to a man without making the matter plain to him.
بغو: The letters bā', ghayn and wāw contain nothing but al-baghw. Ibn Durayd mentioned that it is dates before their dryness is complete.
بغي:
The letters bā', ghayn and yā' are two roots: one of them is the seeking of a thing, and the second a kind of spoiling.

Of the first: baghaytu al-shay'a abghīhi — when you seek it. And one says baghaytuka al-shay' — when I seek it for you; and abghaytuka al-shay' — when I help you to seek it. Al-bughya and al-bighya are the need. And you say mā yanbaghī laka an tafʿala kadhā — it is not fitting for you to do such a thing. And this is one of the verbs of yielding: you say baghaytuhu fa-inbaghā, as you say kasartuhu fa-inkasara — I broke it and it broke.

The second root: their saying baghā al-jurḥ — when the wound goes on to spoiling; then what comes after this is derived from it. Al-baghī is the immoral woman; you say baghat tabghī bighā'an, and she is a baghī. And from it is that a man should wrong another. And from it is baghy al-maṭar, and it is the violence of the rain and its main body; and when a thing has baghy in it, some spoiling must come of it.

Al-Aṣmaʿī said: dafaʿnā baghya al-samā'i khalfanā, that is, the main body of its rain.

And al-baghy is wrongdoing. A poet said:
But the young man Ḥamal ibn Badr did wrong, and wrongdoing's pasture is deadly.

And sometimes they called the horse's prancing and friskiness baghy.

Al-Khalīl said: but one does not say farasun bāghin.
بق:
The letters bāʾ and qāf, according to al-Khalīl and Ibn Durayd, are two roots: one is opening up in a thing, whether in word or deed; the other is a slight, trifling thing.

As for the first: their saying baqqa yabuqqu baqqan, when he was generous, giving abundantly. And likewise baqqat al-samāʾu baqqan, when it came with heavy rain. The rajaz-poet said:
He spread out good for us and lavished it ... so all creation eats of His provision.

1. baqqa fulānun ʿalaynā kalāmahu — he multiplied his talk upon us.
2. al-baqbaqa — much talk; one says rajulun baqāq wa-baqbāq.

The rajaz-poet said [I am unsure of the exact sense of this line]:
And I have led on, with the wrapped-up sick one ... silent among the riders, yet talkative at the halting-place.

3. baqbaqat al-māʾi — its sound in movement; and of the cooking-pot, its sound in boiling.

And the other root is al-baqq, the gnats, the singular baqqa. The rajaz-poet said: They flick with their tails, from thirst and gnats. And from this chapter is al-baqāq, the odds and ends of household goods.
بقر:
The letters bā', qāf and rā' are two roots — and some people have joined them and claimed that it is a single root — and that is al-baqr, cattle. The second root is widening a thing and opening a thing up.

As for al-baqar, it is the collective of baqara, the cow, and its plural also is al-baqīr and al-bāqir, as you say ḥamīr, donkeys, and ḍa'īn, ewes. A poet said, in a line of verse:
They strike the tails of the cattle that lie up in their shelters.
And he said of al-bāqir, in a line of verse:
What fault is it of his that the cattle refused the water? And they refuse the water only so as to be driven to it.
Al-bāqir among cattle is like al-jāmil among camels. Abū 'Ubayda said: the male too is called baqara, as a cock is called dajāja, a hen.

Al-Aṣma'ī said: one says, I saw belonging to the sons of so-and-so baqar and baqīr and bāqir and bāqūra, all meaning cattle. He said: and ubqūr, on the pattern of um'ūz, a herd of goats. He said: and Ibn [Abī] Ṭarafa recited to me, in a line of verse:
I quieted them with words until they were like hornless cattle that the pastures have made calm.
He said: al-bawāqir is a plural with no singular, though it may be the plural of bāqira. He said: and al-baqīr has no singular, and it is a plural like al-ḍa'īn, ewes, and al-shawī, sheep.

One says baqira al-rajul when a man looks at many cattle all at once and loses his wits.

Among what has been carried onto this chapter is their word for dependants, al-baqara. One says so-and-so came driving a baqara, that is, a large household. Yūnus said: al-baqara is the woman.

As for the second root, al-tabaqqur is spreading wide and opening out, from baqartu al-baṭn — I split the belly open. Al-Aṣma'ī said: tabaqqara fulān fī mālihi, that is, he squandered it. To this is referred the hadith of the Prophet, God bless him and give him peace: 'that he forbade tabaqqur in family and property.'

Al-Aṣma'ī said: one says nāqa baqīr of the she-camel whose belly is split open for her young. And fitna bāqira, a strife like a disease of the belly. And al-muhr al-baqīr is the foal whose mother dies before the birth, so her belly is split open and it is taken out.

Abū Ḥātim said of the foal, when it comes out of its mother's belly still in the caul and the membrane and its body falls to the ground: it is baqīr, and its opposite is al-salīl.

Of this chapter is their saying baqqarū mā ḥawlahum, that is, they dug up what was around them; one says, how much have you dug for your palm shoots. Al-buqqayrā is a game of theirs: they beat out rings on the ground like the marks of hooves. Ṭufayl said, in a line of verse:
They swerved, and they never cease, around Mutāli', to have a playing ground like the marks left by the man who beats out rings.
And from it are the words of al-Khuḍrī, in a line of verse:
Bound at her flanks is a smooth-shaven, moon-pale thing, coarse and shaggy, like the ring-scratching of a child.
This is the second root. Whoever joined the two together held that cattle were so called because they split the ground open; but that is nothing.

Among what strays from the chapter is their saying bayqara, when a man moves away from one land to another. And one says bayqara, when he throws himself in the way of destruction. And the words of Imru' al-Qays are recited, in a line of verse:
Has the news reached her — and calamities are many — that Imru' al-Qays son of Tamlik has gone off far away?
One says bayqara, that is, he came to the land of Iraq. It is also said bayqara, when he runs with his head hanging down from weakness. A poet said, in a line of verse:
As one who walks to al-Jalsad goes with head bowed low.
Ibn al-A'rābī said: bayqara — he drove himself on. And to some of what has gone before goes back al-Baqqār, which is a place. Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
Stinking of the rust of iron, as though under their mail they were the jinn of al-Baqqār.
And Baqar is the name of a sand hill. A poet said, in a line of verse:
The two dunes of Baqar keep the sweeping winds off it, and a high hill of the two Firindāds, packed hard.
بقع:
The letters bā', qāf and 'ayn are a single root to which all its branches go back — though some of them seem distant, the kind is one: colors differing from one another. Like al-ghurāb al-abqa', the crow that is black with white on its chest.

1. One says ghurābun abqa' — a pied crow, and kalbun abqa' — a pied dog.
2. Someone said to al-Ḥajjāj, about the horsemen of Ibn al-Ash'ath: 'I saw a people who were bug' (patchy).' He said: 'What is al-bug'?' He said: 'They had patched their clothes from hardship.'
3. And in the hadith: 'It is near that the buq'ān (pale-skinned people) of the people of Syria will be set to rule over you.' Abū 'Ubayd said: he meant the Byzantines and the Slavs, and by the word he meant their whiteness.
4. Al-Khalīl said: al-buq'a is a patch of ground unlike the ground next to it; its plurals are biqā' and buqa'.
5. Abū Zayd said: it is also al-baq'a, with a fatḥa on the bā'.
6. Abū 'Ubayda said: al-abqa' among horses is one whose body has scattered patches differing from its main color.
7. Abū Ḥanīfa said: al-baq'ā', among lands, is one where rain has struck part of it and not another part; likewise mubaqqa'a. It is said: arḍun baqi'a when it has patches of plant growth in it; and it was also said this means bare land with nothing in it — but the first is more correct.
8. Ibn al-A'rābī said: al-baq'ā', of land, is al-ma'zā' — hard ground with pebbles and stones.
9. Al-Khalīl said: al-baqī' of land is a place with the stumps of trees of various kinds; from this Baqī' al-Gharqad in Medina was named.
10. Abū Zayd said: every hollow tract of land and district is a baqī'.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Many a baqī' — had I called out into its hollow,
a noble man would have come to me, nodding his head, eyes lowered.

And in the proverb: 'His fatness saved a donkey at al-Baqī'.'

Al-bāqi'a is a calamity. One says baqa'athum bāqi'a, meaning a calamity struck them — it is a thing that clings until its trace is gone.

Ibn al-A'rābī said: sanatun baq'ā' means a year of drought.

Abū 'Ubayda said: Banū al-Baq'ā' are Banū Hāriba ibn Dhubyān, and their mother was al-Baq'ā' bint Salāmān ibn Dhubyān.

Bishr said of them, in a line of verse:
We did not perish for Murra's sake when they turned away;
they went off in the manner of Hāriba's people, and hid away.

Abū al-Mundhir said: Hāriba's people are called 'al-Baq'ā'', and they are few. He said: 'I have never seen a man of Hāriba at all.'

Al-Ḥuṣayn ibn Ḥumām said of them, in a line of verse:
And Hāriba of al-Baq'ā' — their assembly came to be,
ahead of the people's assemblies, an assembly set foremost.

Some said: Baq'ā' is a village among the villages of al-Yamāma.

He said, in lines of verse:
But word has reached me that Yaḥyā —
evil is said of him in Baq'ā'.
So I said to him: avoid everything
that could be held against you — for the free man is free.

Ibn al-Sikkīt said: one says buqi'a fulānun bi-kalāmi saw'in, meaning he was struck with evil talk — this comes from the origin sense we mentioned.

As for their saying ibtuqi'a lawnuhu (his color changed), it may be from this, or it may be a case of letter-substitution, since they also say imtuqi'a lawnuhu.

Al-Kisā'ī said: when the color changes from grief or fright striking someone, it is said: ibtuqi'a.

Ibn al-A'rābī said: one says lā adrī ayna saqa'a wa-baqa'a, meaning 'I don't know where he went.'

Another said: one says baqa'a fī l-arḍi buqū'an, when someone vanished and his trace was gone.

One of the Bedouin said: al-buq'a, among men, is the one who talks a great deal, wandering off from his subject — one who throws out speech with no known beginning or end.

Some said: baqa'a l-rajula means he swore an oath to him.

And 'āmun abqa' wa-arbad — a year is called this when it has no rain in it.
بقل:
The letters bā', qāf and lām are a single root, and it belongs to plants; to it all the branches of this entry go back.

Al-Khalīl said: al-baql, among plants, is what is neither a small shrub nor a large tree. He distinguished between al-baql and small shrubs by the thickness of the stem — rains and winds do not break their stalks; you see them standing — whatever has been eaten, has been eaten, and whatever remains, remains.

1. Al-Khalīl said: ibtaqala l-qawm — the people did this when they grazed their animals on baql (fresh green herbs); and camels tabtaqilu and tatabaqqalu, meaning they eat the baql.
2. Abū al-Najm said, in a line of verse: 'She grazed on green herbs, at the very start of the grazing season.'
3. Al-Khalīl said: abqalati l-arḍ and baqalat — the land did this when it grew baql; it is then mubqila. Al-mabqala and al-baqqāla mean a place with baql.
4. Abū al-Ṭamaḥān said, about a place green with baql, in a line of verse: 'He spent the spring season atop 'Ar'ar and its plain, then the flocks of Mawliyy al-Asirra, green with herbs.' (This line is obscure; the place-names are uncertain.)
5. Al-Farrā' said: arḍun baqilatun and baqīlatun — land abundant in baql.
6. Al-Shaybānī said: baqala l-ḥimār — the donkey did this when it ate baql, yabqulu. Some said: abqala l-makān — a place did this when it grew rimth (a desert shrub); they then call it bāqil, and we do not know them to say baqala l-makān — they treat it the same way as a'shaba l-balad fahuwa 'āshib (the land grew abundant grass, so it is 'āshib), and awrasa l-rimth fahuwa wārisun (the rimth turned green, so it is wārisun).
7. Abū Ziyād said: al-baql is a name for anything that first sprouts. From this it is said of a young man's face, when hair first grows on it: baqala yabqulu buqūlan wa-baqlan — it sprouted. And baqala nābu l-ba'īr means the camel's tooth came through.
8. Al-Shaybānī said: al-khalā (dry standing grass) is not called baql unless it is moist.
9. Al-Khalīl said: al-bāqil is what comes out on the sides of trees when the days of spring draw near and sap runs in them — you see on their sides something like the eyes of locusts, before the leaves become visible; that is al-bāqil. The tree is then said to have abqala. At that point it is said: the tree has become a single baqla (a single mass of green growth).
10. Abū Zayd said: the rimth, when it first sprouts, is called bāqil — that is when rain has struck it until you see on its branches something like ants' heads, and that is the best it ever is. Then it becomes ḥāniṭ, then wārisun (later ripening stages); once it passes that, it spoils and the camels stop eating it.

As for Bāqil, he was a man proverbial for inarticulateness.
بقي:
The letters bā', qāf and yā' are a single root, and it is lasting.

Al-Khalīl said: one says baqiya al-shay'u yabqā baqā'an — the thing lasted — and it is the opposite of perishing. He said: and the speech of Ṭayyi' is baqā yabqā, and so too is their way in every word with a kasra before it: they make it an alif, as in baqā and raḍā. They did that only because they dislike a kasra and a yā' coming together, so they put a fatḥa before the yā', and the yā' turns into an alif; and they say jārāt for jāriya, bānāt for bāniya, and nāṣāt for nāṣiya.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And it was not out of any sparing of me that Khālid turned away, but the crushing lions came between him and me.

By al-baqiyya here he means al-buqyā, sparing him. And the Arabs say: nashadtuka Allāha wa-l-buqyā — I ask you by God and by mercy. And sometimes they say al-baqwā.

Al-Khalīl said: istabqaytu fulānan — that is that you pardon his slip so as to keep his affection.

Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
You are not one who keeps a brother if you do not gather him up over his flaws; which of men is the faultless one?

And the Arabs say: he yabqī the thing with his eye, when he is looking at it and watching it.

Al-Kumayt said, in a line of verse:
She passed the day, and he passed it thirsty upon a rise, watching him with parched, unwatered eyes.

He is describing the wild ass, that he wanted to bring his she-asses down to the water from above a rise, and waited for the sun to set. In the same way, so-and-so spent the night yabqī the lightning, when he took to looking at it, where it flashes.

Al-Fazārī said, in a line of verse:
A flashing lightning stirred me tonight, and I passed the night watching it, my eye pouring down.

Ibn al-Sikkīt said: baqaytu fulānan abqīhi — when you keep an eye on him and wait for him. And one says: ibqi lī al-adhāna — watch out for the call to prayer for me.

And this was recited, in a line of verse:
I kept on watching the litters until they were like the weaver's cross-threads that the weavers work away.

Of this is the hadith of Muʿādh, may God be pleased with him: "We waited for the Messenger of God, God bless him and his family and grant them peace" — he means, we waited on him. And this goes back to the first root, because waiting is a part of staying firm and lasting.
بك:
The letters bāʾ and kāf, doubled, are a single root that combines crowding and overcoming. Al-Khalīl said: al-bakk is breaking the neck. And it is said Mecca was named Bakka because it used to break the necks of tyrants when they transgressed there unjustly, without being given respite. And it is also said: it was named Bakka because people crowd against one another there in the circumambulation, meaning: they push. Al-Ḥasan said: meaning they press together there from every direction. And it is also said: Bakka is on the pattern faʿla, from bakaktu al-rajula, when I pushed him back and put him down.

A line of verse:
When thirst grips the fellow drinker, leave him be, until he pushes his way through the press.

And another said, in a line of verse:
The herd crowds at the trough for their second and their first drink ... while short of driving them off is a resting-place that lulls to sleep.
tabukku, they crowd upon it. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: tabākkat al-ibilu, when the camels crowded upon the water and drank. And a man is abakk, powerful, overpowering, its plural bukk. And one says: bakkahu, when he overcame him.

Al-Farrāʾ said: the thick rope is called al-abakk. And al-abakk, in al-Aṣmaʿī's account, is thickly clustered trees. He is explaining the poet's saying, in a line of verse [I am unsure of the exact sense of this line]:
A group like the wild asses of the thicket ... with no young one among them, and none aging either.
بكت: The letters bā', kāf and tā' are a single word not subject to further derivation, and it is al-tabkīt — sharp rebuke, and overcoming someone with an argument.
بكر:
The letters bā', kāf and rā' are a single root to which two branches go back, both of them from it. The first is the beginning of a thing and its start. The second is derived from it, and the third is a likening.

The first is al-bukra, which is the early morning, and the plural is al-bukar. Al-tabkīr and al-bukūr and al-ibtikār are going out at that time. Al-ibkār is the early morning, just as al-iṣbāḥ is a name for the dawn. And bākartu al-shay' when you go early to it.

Abū Zayd said: abkartu al-wird ibkāran — I came early to the watering; and abkartu al-ghadā' — I took the morning meal early; and bakartu 'alā al-ḥāja — I went early about the need; and abkartu ghayrī — I made another go early; bakartu and abkartu. And one says a man is bakir or bakur, a man given to early rising, as one says ḥadhir and ḥadhur, wary.

Al-Khalīl said: ghayth bākūr is the rain that comes early at the beginning of the first autumn rains; and it is also the cloud that travels at the start of the night and the start of the day. A poet said, in a line of verse:
The wind dragged its trailing edge over her, and early night-travelling clouds passed her on from one to another.
One says a cloud is midlāj bakūr, travelling by night and coming early. And one says bakkarat al-amṭār tabkīran and bakarat bukūran when the rains come before their time.

Al-Farrā' said: abkara al-saḥāb, and bakara, and bakkara; and bakarat al-shajara, and abkarat, and bakkarat tubakkir tabkīran, and bakarat bukūran, and she is bakūr, when the tree is quick with its fruit and its ripening; and if that is her habit she is mibkār; and the plural of bakūr is bukur. The Hudhalī said, in a line of verse:
That is your way, when in the morning they were driven aside, like the early-bearing trees that let their fruit fall.

The first date of the season is a bākūra, and it is said it is al-bakīra and the plural al-bakā'ir. And one says a land is mibkār when it puts forth growth at the first growth of the earth. Al-Akhṭal said:
Rain that showed itself again and again in a soft, early-bearing hollow.

So this is the first origin, and what comes after it is derived from it. From it is al-bakr among camels, the one that has not yet cut its eye-tooth. That is because it is in the freshness of its age and the beginning of its life, and this is the meaning that joins it to what came before it. When it cuts that tooth it is a jamal, a full-grown camel. Al-bakra is the female, and when she cuts that tooth she is a nāqa, a she-camel. Abū 'Ubayda said: its plural is bikār, and the smallest number is three, abkur.

From it is the proverb: 'the age of his young camel told me the truth.' Its origin is that a man haggled with another over a bakr he wanted to buy, and asked the seller about its age, and the seller told him other than the truth and said: it is a bakr, a young one — while it was worn out with age. So the buyer looked into its teeth and said: 'the age of his bakr told me the truth.'

Al-Tamīmī said: the camel is called bakr from the time it is ridden until it enters its fourth year, and the female is bakra; and the qa'ūd is the bakr. He said: and the Arabs say: 'better watered than the bakr of Habannaqa.' He was the man who was counted a fool, and his bakr used to come away from the water with those going away, having drunk its fill, then go back down with those coming to the water before it reached the pasture.

Al-Khalīl said: al-bikr among women is she who has never been touched at all. Abū 'Ubayd said: when a woman has borne one child she is a bikr still. Al-Khalīl said: one is called bikr, whether a boy or a girl. And it is said: the strongest of people is a firstborn son of two firstborns. He said: and a bikr cow is a young one that has not carried. Al-bikr of every affair is its first. And he says: this affair is neither bakīr nor thaniyy, in the sense that it is neither first nor second. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Standing at the doors, seekers of a need, a need that is middling among needs, or a first one.

Al-bikr is the vine that has borne fruit for the first time. Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
A little blue-eyed one, safe from its going unsold, picked it out from the first of the vintages.

Al-Khalīl said: 'asal abkār is honey made by the abkār of the bees, that is, their young ones; and it is said, rather, that the abkār are the young girls who tend it. So this is the second origin, and it is not far from the analogy of the first.

As for the third, it is al-bakara, the pulley over which water is drawn. If someone were to say that it was lent the name of the bakra of she-camels, that would be a view to hold. Al-bakara is well known. Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
As though her forepart, when her bridler stood up, were a sheave-frame set upon a crooked pulley.

And there are rings in the ornament of a sword called bakarāt. And all of that has one and the same origin.
بكع:
The letters bā', kāf and 'ayn are a single root, and it is repeated striking, or repeated giving, or something like that.

1. al-bak' — Al-Khalīl said: forceful, repeated striking. One says baka'nāhu bi-l-sayfi wa-l-'aṣā bak'an — we struck him repeatedly with sword and stick.
2. Also carried by this reasoning is Abū 'Ubayd's saying: al-bak' is to confront a man with what he dislikes.
3. Al-Tamīmī said: a'ṭāhu al-māla bak'an wa-lam yu'ṭihi nujūman — he gave him the money all at once, not in instalments; this comes from the first sense, because it follows through on him as a whole, without pausing between.
4. One says baka'tuhu bi-l-amr, meaning bakkattuhu — I rebuked him sharply over the matter.
5. Al-'Uklī said: baka'ahu bi-l-sayf — he cut him with the sword.
بكل:
The letters bā', kāf and lām are two roots: one is mixing and things like it, and the other is deriving benefit from a thing and profiting by it.

1. al-bakīla — wheat that is taken and ground together with dried curd, then mixed (tubkal) with water, that is, blended, and then eaten. It was recited: An angry man, for whom the bakīla was not seasoned with fat.
2. al-bakla and al-bakāla — flour mixed with roasted grain-meal and moistened with oil or clarified butter, as Abū Ziyād said. Abū Zayd said the same word is used when sheep are mixed in among goats.

Ibn al-A'rābī reported of a woman thought foolish, who said, in a line of verse:
Then I am no daughter of Za'bala, if I do not change my bikla, if I do not make myself equal to the tall ones.
She means: if I do not change the confused talk I mix into my speech, and do not seek noble qualities, then I am no daughter of Za'bala — Za'bala being her father.

Al-Liḥyānī claimed that al-bikla means one's manner and dress, and explained the woman's saying on this basis.

Abū 'Ubayd said: al-mutabakkil is one who mixes up his speech confusedly.
3. From this chapter is Abū Zayd's saying: tabakkala al-qawmu 'alā al-rajuli — said when people set upon a man together with beating, abuse, and overpowering, because that, coming from a group, is itself a kind of mixing together.

As for the second root, they said: al-tabakkul is gaining and earning a livelihood. Aws said, in a line of verse:
Over the best merchandise she has seen, for one seeking to sell it, or to profit by it.
Al-Khalīl said: al-insān yatabakkal, that is, he seeks a way to gain.
بكم: The letters bāʾ, kāf and mīm are one root, of limited use: muteness. Al-Khalīl said: al-abkam is the mute man who does not speak; when a person refrains from speech from ignorance or deliberately, it is said bakima ʿan al-kalām. It is also said of one who cannot speak clearly: innahu la-abkam. Al-abkam, in exegesis, refers to one born mute. Al-Durayd said: it is said bakīm in the sense of abkam, with the plural abkām, like sharīf and ashrāf.
بكوء:
The letters bā', kāf, wāw and hamza are two roots: one is weeping, and the other is a thing's diminishing and scarcity.

1. bakā yabkī [bukā'] — to weep. Al-Khalīl said: it comes both shortened (bukā) and with a final glottal stop (bukā'). One says bākaytu fulānan fa-bakaytuhu — I outdid so-and-so in weeping, meaning I wept more than he did.
The grammarians said: whoever shortens the word treats it like words for ailments and diseases; whoever lengthens it with the glottal stop treats it like words for sounds, such as thughā' (bleating), rughā' (braying) and du'ā' (calling). They recited, showing both forms: My eye wept, and its weeping was its due, yet weeping and wailing avail nothing.
Al-Aṣma'ī said: bakaytu al-rajula and bakkaytuhu both mean I wept over him; and abkaytuhu means I did to him what made him weep.
Ya'qūb said: al-bakkā' is a man among the Arabs after whom a clan is named, so that they say Banū al-Bakkā' — he is 'Awf ibn Rabī'a ibn 'Āmir ibn Ṣa'ṣa'a, so named because his mother remarried after his father's death; 'Awf entered the house while her new husband was with her, and thought he meant to kill her, so he wept the fiercest weeping.

The other root is their saying, of a she-camel with little milk: she is bakī'a, and bakuʾat tabkuʾu bakā'atan (with a lengthened final vowel). It was recited:
Its resting-place is nearer to its pasture ... even if, for want of milk, every milked beast were driven far off.
He means: its resting-place, in a household that keeps it well, is nearer to finding rich pasture.
Abū 'Ubayd said, of the Prophet's saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "We company of prophets are bikā' [sparing of tears], for their tears are few."
Zayd al-Khayl said, in a line of verse:
They said: 'Āmir has marched against you with a thousand, or a bukā, of which few remain.
His word bukā means a shortfall; its true form has the glottal stop, from bakaʾat al-nāqatu tabkaʾu, said when a she-camel's milk grows scant; also bakuʾat tabkuʾu. And he said:
Our milch-camel is but a dark, wide-mouthed jar, its little jar following behind it.
And when she gives little milk, or fails altogether, the clay seal is broken from the side of another jar.
And al-As'ar al-Ju'fī said, in a line of verse:
Yet how many a band of travellers met with scant provision; they toiled on while their night's luck grew scant, until it failed.
He said: ḥārada means the rain in it grew scant; and bakā means the same, but with the glottal stop dropped.
بل:
The letters bāʾ and lām, doubled, have five roots, making up the bulk of this chapter.

The first is moisture. One says: balaltu al-shayʾa abulluhu. Al-billa is moisture, and the bāʾ may also take ḍamma, so one says bulla. And sometimes they use it for the remaining moisture in the stomach of an animal. The rajaz-poet said: and the moisture of the wild, thirst-enduring animals left it. And one says: dhahabat ablālu al-ibili, meaning: the fluids that were in their bellies. Al-Ḍabbī said: there is no she-camel among the herd that comes to water while moisture remains in her, except al-Ṣahbāʾ, meaning: she endures thirst.

And from this is the sense of a gift, a favour. Al-Khalīl said: it is said of a man, when his condition improves after emaciation: he has become moist again, restored. And they say: "I will not do such-and-such as long as the sea moistens a tuft of wool." And it is said of the miser: "his one hand does not moisten the other," meaning he gives nothing. And from it: "keep your ties of kinship moist, even with no more than a greeting." And one says: lā tabullika ʿindī bālla wa-lā bilāl wa-lā balāli, on the pattern of ḥadhāmi.

A line of verse:
No, by God, O son of Abū ʿAqīl ... after this, no favour of ours shall reach you again among us.

And among the proverbs of the Arabs: "travel some miles, and you will find something to moisten your throat." Al-Khalīl said: billat al-lisān is its falling correctly on the places of the letters, and its fluency in speech; one says: mā aḥsana billata lisānihi, how fluent his tongue is. Abū Zayd said: al-billa is the sap of the samur tree. And one says: aballa al-ʿūdu, when the moisture of the rain ran through it. Al-Kisāʾī said: inṣarafa al-qawmu bi-billatihim, meaning: they departed while still having something left of themselves. And one says: iṭwi al-thawba ʿalā bullatihi, meaning: fold the garment while some dampness remains in it, so that it does not crease and break; its origin is in a waterskin that dries and shrivels, so that when one wants to use it, it is dampened again. And from this is their saying: ṭawaytu fulānan ʿalā bilālihi, meaning: I bore with him despite his ill conduct; and one says ʿalā bullatihi wa-bululatihi.

They recited:
And I have borne with you despite your faults ... and I knew well what mischief was in you.

Abū Zayd said: one says: mā aḥsana balala al-rajuli, meaning: how well he bears, endures — with fatḥa on both lāms. As for their calling the cold wind balīl, al-Aṣmaʿī said: it is a cold wind that comes in winter, bringing dampness with it. Al-Hudhalī said: and a cold, damp, gusting wind drove it along.

And the second root: recovery from illness. One says: balla wa-aballa wa-istaballa, when he recovered.

A line of verse:
When he recovers from an illness he has, he thinks he is saved ... while the illness that will kill him is still in him.

And the third root: taking a thing and going off with it. One says: balla fulānun bikadhā, when it fell into his hand. Dhū al-Rumma said: she got hold of it, being neither reckless nor trembling. And they say: "if he gets hold of it, he will surely get what he wishes." And from it is his saying, in a line of verse:
Know that over you is a driver ... who has taken firm hold, clinging to the hindquarters of the riding-beasts, close behind.

And one says: innahu la-ballun bi'l-qarīna, he is well able to handle his companion. They recited:
And I am well able to handle her, as long as she holds back ... and if I break with her, I break decisively.

And another said, in a line of verse:
ʿUrayna got the better, in the encounter, of a horseman ... neither reckless nor trembling, nor hesitant.

And they say: innahu la-yabullu bihi al-khayru, meaning: good agrees with, suits, him.

And the fourth root: al-balal, the verbal noun of al-aball among men, the bold, forward one who feels no shame and takes no care. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Will you not fear God, O family of ʿĀmir ... does the resolute, shameless one fear God?

And it is said: he is the immoral one, fierce in dispute; and it is also said: he is the wary, shrewd one. And one says: aballa al-rajulu yubillu iblālan, when he overcame and wore out an opponent. Abū ʿUbayd said: a man is aball, and a woman ballāʾ, meaning: one whose full measure cannot be reached.

And what comes after this is the imitation of sounds and things, not true roots to be reasoned from. Abū ʿAmr said: al-balīl is a sound like a moan. Al-Marrār said, in a line of verse:
Thirsting, each of them like a mother mourning her calf's stuffed hide ... when she moans, you hear from her a low groaning.

Al-Liḥyānī said: balīl al-māʾ is its sound. And al-ḥamām al-muballil is the dove that never stops cooing.

A line of verse:
They startle, with their calling, the goats of the heights ... and, from the side of the valley, the doves that never cease their cooing.

And Bābil is a place. And al-bulbul is a bird. And al-balbala is the whispering of anxieties in the breast, and it is also called al-balbāl. And balbalat al-alsun is their confusion in speech. And one says: balbala al-qawmu, and that is their uproar. And al-bulbul, of men, is the light, agile one, likened to the bird called al-bulbul, its origin being the sound it makes, and its plural is balābil.

A line of verse:
You will overtake what ʿUmāra and his son defend ... swift she-camels at an easy pace, and disheveled, light-footed men.
بلأص: Not a root, because the hamza is substituted from a hā’, and the ṣād is substituted from a sīn.
بلت:
The letters bā', lām and tā' are a single root, and it is cutting off. It appears to be a metathesis of batala [to sever completely].

1. One says takallama ḥattā balita — he spoke until he fell silent [was cut off]. Al-Shanfarā said, in a line of verse: ...over her mother, and if she speaks to you, she falls silent.
2. As for their saying mahr maḍmūn muballat [a bride-price fully guaranteed and settled], it too belongs here, because it is "cut off," wholly discharged — though there is some doubt about this word. They recited: She was married for nothing but a fully-settled bride-price.
3. It is said that al-balīt is pasturage of two years' standing, and it too belongs here, because it grows brittle and breaks apart. It was said, in a line of verse: They grazed on the old dry pasture a while, then we cut across the faint, effaced tracks of the valleys with them.
بلج:
The letters bā', lām and jīm are a single root that follows a regular pattern of derivation, and it is the clarity and brightness of a thing.

1. al-balaj — brightness; from it, inbilāj al-ṣubḥ, the breaking of dawn's light. It was said: Until the bright neck of dawn appeared.
The Arabs say: "Truth is bright, and falsehood stammers [is confused]." It was said: Have you not seen that you find truth bright, while you find a people's falsehood stammering and confused?
2. One who does not have his eyebrows joined together is called ablaj, and the brightness between them is called bulja. It was said: Bright, his light between his two brows; when he oversteps, whatever falls short of him is set aside.
بلح:
The letters bā', lām and ḥā' are a single root, and it is slackness in a thing, exhaustion, and lack of firmness; every branch of this chapter goes back to it.

1. al-balaḥ (also al-khalāl), one al-balaḥa — the fruit of the palm while it is still green and small, like unripe sour grapes. Abū Khīra said: the fruit of the salam tree [a kind of acacia] is called al-balaḥ while it has not yet split open; once it splits open it is al-barama. Abū 'Ubayda: ablaḥat al-nakhla, said of a palm tree when it puts out its balaḥ.
Abū Ḥātim said: moist earth, once it dries out, is said to have balaḥa buluḥan. It was recited: Until the branch craved the morning drink, and the earth had dried hard for it.
2. From this chapter is balaḥa al-rajul, said of a man when he is stopped short by exhaustion and cannot move. Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse: And when one of them is loaded with a burden, his joints ache from it, and he gives out. Another said, in a line of verse: The protection of the family of La'y has failed — it turns back neither sheep nor camel.
3. Al-Shaybānī said: one says balaḥa when he stubbornly refuses.
4. Quṭrub said: balaḥa al-mā', the water grew scarce; and balaḥat al-rakiyya, the well ran low. It was said: What is wrong with you, that you will not fill up, O Muḍabbaḥ? You used to rise, while the well ran dry.
5. One says balaḥa al-zand, said when the fire-stick fails to spark.
6. Al-'Āmirī said: one says balaḥat 'alayya rāḥilatī, said when my mount grew weary and would not go along with me.
7. One says balaḥa al-ba'īr and balaḥa al-rajul, said when he has nothing left. It was said: Acknowledging the loss in his wealth, when the stubborn, worn-out camel collapsed.

Falling outside this chapter: al-bulaḥ, a bird; and al-balaḥlaḥa, a shallow bowl with no depth to it.
بلخ: The letters bā', lām and khā' are a single root, and it is arrogance. One says rajul ablakh, an arrogant man; and taballakha means he acted arrogantly.
بلد:
The letters bā', lām and dāl are a single root whose branches come close together when you look into its analogy, and the root is the breast.

One says waḍa'at al-nāqa baldatahā bi'l-arḍ, when the she-camel kneels down and sets her chest on the ground. Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
She was made to kneel and cast down one balda upon another balda — a place where sounds are few but for her groaning.

And one says taballada al-rajul, when a man puts his hand on his chest in his perplexity over a matter. Al-ablad is the man whose eyebrows are not joined; the space between his brows is called bulda. And it is from this root, because that resembles bare open ground, al-balda. Al-balda is also the star; they say it is the balda of the Lion, that is, its chest. And al-balad is the chest of the villages, the chief of them.

As for the saying of Ibn al-Riqā', in a line of verse:
After decay had covered over its ablād.

That too is from this. And they said: rather al-balad is a trace or mark, and its plural is ablād. But the first statement follows the analogy better. And one says ballada al-rajul bi'l-arḍ, when he clings close to the ground. A poet said, in a line of verse:
When the man of sense does not contend with the fool of the people, and the landmarks cling low at night like little hills.

He means: as though they were stuck fast to the ground. And a man of Tamīm said, describing a watering trough, in a line of verse:
And a low-lying trough between two waterless wastes in a place of death, which I came up beside with a tall camel of mighty build.

He is speaking of a trough clinging to the ground. And one says ablada al-rajul iblādan, exactly like taballada. And al-mubālada with swords is like al-mubālaṭa, fighting it out. Some of them said it is derived from the first sense, as though they kept to the ground and fought upon it. And al-bālid, by analogy, is the one who dwells in a town.
بلز:
The letters bā', lām and zā' are not a root; it contains a few minor words.

1. al-biliz — a short woman.
2. al-bal'az — a short man, they say.
