3. al-bal'aza — eating.

There is doubt about all of this.
بلس:
The letters bā', lām and sīn are one root, and what comes after it cannot be relied upon.

The root is despair. One says ablasa when he despaired. God Most High said: {when they are, in it, despairing} [al-Mu'minūn: 77]. They said: from this the name Iblīs is derived, as if he despaired of God's mercy.

1. From this root: ablasa ar-rajul — the man fell silent.
2. From it also: ablasat an-nāqa, she being miblās — the she-camel did not bellow, from the intensity of her heat.

As for the saying of Ibn Aḥmar, in a line of verse:
turn back, daughter of al-balas, the doubtful one, for the small may yet grow, and the broken may yet be mended —
it is said that al-balas means "the gloomy, downcast one."
بلص:
The letters bā', lām and ṣād contain words that, in my judgement, mostly cannot be relied upon, yet are close to one another in sense.

1. ballaṣat al-ghanam, said when sheep's milk grows scarce.
2. tabalaṣat al-ghanam al-arḍ, said when sheep leave nothing ungrazed on the ground.
3. tabalaṣtu al-shay', I sought the thing out in secret.

There is doubt about this, in my view.
بلط:
The letters bā', lām and ṭā' are a single root, and the matter here is close to the one before it.

1. al-balāṭ — anything a house's floor is paved with, of stone or otherwise, they said. Ibn Muqbil said, in a line of verse: In a raised building, its pavement close-fitted, whose keepers used to be brought offerings. He means: it is a shrine built for Christians who worship in it, in a raised structure closely set together. Layyāq means "closely fitted" — one says mā yalīqu bika kadhā, meaning "it does not stick to you [does not suit you]." He is describing the beauty of the place, and its being furnished with offerings and lamps. If this account is sound — though al-balāṭ is, to my mind, a loanword — then from it comes al-mubālaṭa: two men striking at each other while standing on the balāṭ, being, in their closeness, like two things stuck together.
2. ablaṭa al-rajul, he became poor, so he is mubliṭ; this comes from the first sense, as though he became so poor he stuck to the bare pavement — like tariba, said when someone becomes poor enough to be stuck to the bare dust.
As for Imru' al-Qays's saying, in a line of verse: I came down upon 'Amr ibn Darmā' at Bulṭa — it is said this is the name of a known hill; it is also said that bulṭatan means "suddenly, unexpectedly." The first is more correct.
بلع: The letters bā', lām and 'ayn are a single root, and it is swallowing something. One says: bala'tu l-shay'a ablaʿuhu — I swallowed the thing. Al-bālū', the drain, comes from this, because it swallows water. Sa'd Bula' is a star. Al-bula' is the hole in the upright post of the pulley-frame; the reasoning is the same, because it 'swallows' the piece of wood that passes through it. As for their saying balla'a l-shaybu fī ra'sihi (grey hair spread through his head), that is close in reasoning to this — when it covers his head, it is as if it has 'swallowed' it.
بلعوم:
Al-bul‘ūm is the passage of food in the throat. It may be shortened, so one says bul‘um. It is not obscure that this is taken from bali‘a [he swallowed], except that something was added to it, of the kind added for intensifying its meaning. This, and what resembles it, is a preamble to what follows.

Among this is (buḥtur), the short one, compact in build. This is blended from two words: from bā’, tā’ and rā’, from "batartuhu fa-butira" [I cut it off, so it was cut short] — as though he were denied length, so his form was cut short. And the second word is ḥā’, tā’ and rā’, from "ḥatartu" and "aḥtartu," that is, that one does not give more to anyone. One says "aḥtara ‘alā nafsihi [wa-‘iyālihi]," he restricted provision upon himself and his family. So this meaning came to apply to the short man, because he was not given what the tall man was given.

Among this is (baḥtharatu) a thing, when you scatter it. And al-baḥthara is turbidity in water. This is blended from two words: from "baḥathtu al-shay’ fī al-turāb" [I dug into the thing in the dust], already explained among the triliteral roots, and from al-bathr, which appears on the body — sound, well-known Arabic. That is because it appears scattered over the skin.

Among this is (al-ba‘thaqa), and its meaning is the coming out of water from a trough. One says "tab‘athaqa al-mā’ min al-ḥawḑ" when water burst from the trough, when a side of it broke and the water came out from it. That is blended from two words: ba‘aqa and bathaqa. One says "inba‘aqa al-mā’," it burst open, already explained among the triliteral roots, and "bathaqtu al-mā’," which is al-bathq, already mentioned.

Among this is (al-burjud), a striped cloak. It is carved from two words: from al-bijād, the cloak, already explained, and from al-burd [another kind of cloak]. The resemblance between them is close.

Among this is (ablandaḥa), meaning: it grew wide, spacious. It is blended from two words: from al-badāḥ, open, spacious land, and from al-balad, open bare ground. Their meanings have already been explained.

Among this is their saying: he struck him, so (bakhdha‘ahu). This is from your saying "khudhdhi‘a," when it was gashed and cut up. And from this:
Both of them, brave in combat, were gashed.
Already explained — and from "budhi‘a," one says "budhi‘ū fa-ibdha‘arrū," when they scattered.

Among this is their saying (balṭaḥa) the man, when he threw himself upon the ground. It is blended from "buṭiḥa" and "ublita," when he clung to the pavement (balāṭ) of the ground.

Among this is their saying (bazmakha) the man, when he grew arrogant. It is blended from their saying "zamakha," when he held his nose high in pride, and he is "zāmikh," and from their saying "bazakha," when he leaned back, and "mashā mutabāzikhan," when he affected an upright bearing. Already explained.

Among this is their saying: his flesh (tabalkhaṣa), when it grew thick. That is from two words: from al-lakhaṣ, abundance of flesh — one says "ḍar‘ lakhīṣ" [a thick, fleshy udder] — and from al-bakhaṣ, the flesh of the forearm, the eye, and the roots of the fingers.

Among this is (tabaz‘ara), meaning: his temper turned bad. This is from al-za‘ar and al-za‘āra, and al-tabazzu‘. Already explained, each in its place among the triliteral roots.

Among this is (al-birqish), a bird. It is from two words: from "raqashtu" a thing, which is like inscribing, and from al-barash, the difference of two colors [mottling]; it is well known.

Among this is (al-bahnasa), swaggering. It is from al-bahs, a description of the lion, and from "banasa," when he lagged behind. Its meaning is that he walks with an affected slowness, in an air of self-importance and pride.

And close to this is their saying (balhasa), when he hurried. It is from "bahasa" and from "baliha," the description of the foolish one.
بلغ: The letters bā', lām and ghayn are a single root, and it is reaching a thing. You say balaghtu al-makān, when you reached it. And drawing near may be called bulūgh by right of nearness. God, exalted be He, said: {And when they reach their term, keep them honourably} [al-Ṭalāq: 2]. And of this chapter is their saying: he is aḥmaq bilgh and balgh — that is, for all his foolishness he reaches what he wants. And al-bulgha is what one gets by of livelihood, as though it is meant that he reaches the rank of the wealthy man when he is content and satisfied. And likewise al-balāgha, the eloquence for which a man of fluent tongue is praised, because by it he reaches what he wants. And lī fī hādhā balāgh — that is, a sufficiency. And their saying ballagha al-fāris means that he stretches out his hand with his horse's rein so as to add to its running. And their saying taballaghat al-qilla bi-fulān, when want has pressed him hard, is because it comes to its utmost in him and reaches its limit.
بلق:
The letters bā', lām and qāf are a single root, regular and consistent in its derivations, and it is opening.

1. One says ablaqa al-bāb and balaqahu, he opened it all the way. It was said: The fortress breached, and the door thrown wide open.
2. al-balaq — a large tent, from this same root.

The use of al-balaq for piebald coloring [white patches on an animal] may seem remote from this, but it is close: al-bahīm [an all-dark animal] is derived from the root meaning "sealed, undifferentiated," so when part of it turns white, it is like a thing being opened.
بلم:
The letters bā', lām and mīm are two roots: one is swelling, or something resembling it, and the second is a plant.

1. balam — a disease that takes hold in a she-camel's womb-passage. One says ablamat al-nāqa, said of the she-camel when this afflicts her. Al-Farrā': ablamat and balimat, said when her vulva swells.
Abū 'Ubayd said: from this comes their saying lā tuballim 'alayhi, meaning: do not make it look worse than it is.
Abū Ḥātim said: ablamat al-bakra, said of a young she-camel that has never once conceived; she is mublim, and the noun is al-balama.
Ya'qūb said: ablama al-rajul, said of a man whose two lips swell; I saw his lips mublamatayn (swollen). Al-iblām also means falling silent — one says ablama when he fell silent.

The second root: al-ablam is a kind of palm-leaf strip. Abū 'Amr said: one says iblim, ablam, and ublum. From it is the proverb: "The property is between me and you, the split of the ublama" — meaning, in two halves, because the ublama, when split lengthwise, splits into two equal halves from its beginning to its end. Some render it in the nominative and say: "The property between me and you is the split of the ublama," meaning: it is so [divided evenly].
بله:
The letters bā', lām and hā' are a single root, and it is something like guilelessness and heedlessness.

1. al-balah — Al-Khalīl and others said: weakness of mind. The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Most of the people of Paradise are al-buluh [the simple-hearted]" — meaning those who were shrewd in the matter of the next life, though simple in the matter of this world.
2. Al-Zibriqān ibn Badr said: "The best of our children is the ablah, the sound-minded one" — meaning that, from the intensity of his modesty, he appears simple, yet he is in fact sound of mind. One also says shabāb ablah, youth described this way for the guilelessness in it. The life of the ablah has few cares. Ru'ba said, in a line of verse: After the fresh, guileless youth had passed.
3. As for their saying "balha," it may be an irregular form; it is possible, though a stretch, to bring it back within this root's pattern, with the meaning "leave aside." This is what came in the hadith: "God the Exalted says: I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and what has never occurred to a human heart — balha [leave aside] what I have shown them" — meaning, leave aside what I have shown them, give it no further thought.
بلوي:
The letters bā', lām, wāw and yā' are two roots: one is a thing wearing out, and the second is a kind of testing; informing/telling is also carried under this second sense.

1. As for the first: Al-Khalīl said: baliya yablā, so it is bālin (worn out); al-bilā is its verbal noun. With a fatḥa on the first letter it is al-balā', and some said this is simply another form of the same word. It was recited: The passing of the nights and the turning of circumstances wear a man out as a shirt is worn out.
2. al-baliyya — the riding-beast that, in the pre-Islamic age, used to be tied at its owner's grave, with a wrapping (waliyya) fastened over its head, and was given neither fodder nor water until it died. Abū Zubayd said, in a line of verse: Like the baliyyas, their heads in their wrappings, facing the burning wind with bare cheeks. Some of these beasts were instead hamstrung at the grave until they died. It was said: The hamstrung beast staggers there over the shafts of spears, as the baliyyas staggered when hamstrung by a grave. One says of this ballaytu al-baliyya, I performed this rite on the mount.
Al-Yazīdī said: the Arabs used to skin a man's riding-beast after his death, stuff it with thumām grass, and leave it on his path to the meeting-place; they claimed it would be raised up together with him on Judgement Day, and that whoever this was not done for would be raised on foot, without a mount.
Ibn al-A'rābī said: one says balla 'alayhi al-safaru and ballāhu, both meaning the journey wore him out. It was recited: Two crook-necked young she-camels, worn down by continual night-travel, then by pressing on through the midday heat — meaning, it wore the two of them out.
Al-Khalīl said: one says nāqa bilwu safar, like niḍwu safar, meaning the journey has worn her down; and bilyu safar, on the authority of al-Kisā'ī.
3. As for the second root, it is their saying buliya al-insān and ubtuliya, from testing, that is, trial. It was said: I have been tried, and the loss of a loved one is a trial; how many a noble soul is tried, then bears it patiently. Al-balā' occurs both in good and in ill: God the Exalted is said to try His servant balā'an ḥasanan (with a good trial) and balā'an sayyi'an (with an evil trial), and this goes back to the same root, because through it a servant's patience and gratitude are put to the test.
Al-Ja'dī said, of al-balā', that it is testing, in a line of verse: The trial has been enough for me, and I am a man who, once matters become clear to him, does not doubt.
Ibn al-A'rābī said: it is also called al-bilwa, al-baliyya, and al-balwā. They said, of Zuhayr's saying: So He gave the two of them the best of the trial He tries [His servants] with — meaning: He gave the two of them the best of the gift with which He tests His servants.
Al-Aḥmar said: the Arabs say nazalat balā'i, on the pattern of the name Ḥadhāmi.
4. Also carried under this chapter is their saying ablaytu fulānan 'udhran, meaning: I made it known to him and made it plain, as between him and me, so that no blame remains against me afterward.
Abū 'Ubayd said: ablaytuhu yamīnan, meaning I put his mind at ease with an oath. Aws said, in a line of verse: It is as though the freshness of the abode informs you of them, a man clear in his oath, swearing after your pact.
Ibn al-A'rābī said: yublīka means "informs you." The Arabs say: ablinī kadhā, meaning "tell me such-and-such"; and the other replies lā ublīka, "I will not tell you." From this is the hadith of Umm Salama, when she related the Prophet's saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "Among my Companions are some who will not see me again after I part from them." 'Umar asked her: "Am I one of them?" She said: "No — and I will never inform anyone after you," meaning, I will never tell.
Ibn al-A'rābī said: one says ibtalaytuhu fa-ablānī, meaning I sought news from him and he informed me.

A mention of what falls outside these two roots: Al-Khalīl said: one says al-nās bi-dhī baliyyin and dhī biliyyin, meaning the people are scattered. Abū Zayd said: they are also bi-dhī baliyyān, said when they are far apart from one another, separate bands with no leader to gather them. From this is the hadith of Khālid, when 'Umar removed him from command in Syria: "That is when the people are bi-dhī baliyyin wa-dhī ballā [scattered, leaderless]."
Al-Kisā'ī recited, of a man who sleeps too long, in a line of verse: He sleeps while the people move on, until it is said: they have reached dhī billiyān.
As for balā (the word meaning "yes"), it does not belong to this chapter at all; its origin is bal.
And Baliyy ibn 'Amr ibn al-Ḥāff ibn Quḍā'a — the adjectival form from it is Balawī. Al-Ablā' is the name of a well. Al-Ḥārith said, in a line of verse: Then the meadows of the sand-grouse, then the valleys of al-Shurbub, then al-Shu'batān, then al-Ablā'.
بن:
The letters bāʾ and nūn, doubled, are a single root, and it is staying and dwelling, and to it go back all the matters of this chapter. Al-Khalīl said: al-ibnān is staying; one says: abannat al-saḥābatu, when it stayed in place; and abanna al-qawmu bi-maḥallatin, they settled at an encampment.

A line of verse: O riders, staying at the sandy slope.

1. bannana al-rajulu — so he is mubannan, when he ties up a ewe to fatten it up.

A line of verse: My people reproach me for fattening a sheep — but does anyone fatten the lowly ones except the noble?

2. al-banān — the tips of the fingers on the two hands. Al-Khalīl said this. In God Almighty's saying {And strike off from them every fingertip} [al-Anfāl: 12], al-banān means the extremities, that is, the hands and feet. He said: in poetry, al-banāna, with a tāʾ, may occur for a single finger.

He said, in a line of verse:
O God, You have honoured the sons of Kināna ... no tribe has, over them, so much as the length of a finger.
Meaning: no one has over them the advantage of a single finger's-width.

And he said, in a line of verse:
When she saw the rust of iron upon his skin ... his colour was ashen, and his fingers were short.

Abū Isḥāq Ibrāhīm ibn al-Sarrī al-Zajjāj said: the singular of al-banān is banāna. Its meaning in God Almighty's saying {And strike off from them every fingertip} [al-Anfāl: 12] is the fingers and the other limbs generally. And the derivation of al-banān is only from their saying abanna bi'l-makān, when he stayed, remained; for the fingertips are that upon which everything relies for staying settled and for life itself.

3. al-banna — the scent from the droppings of cattle, sheep, and gazelles; it may also be used for perfume, so one says: I find in this garment a pleasant scent of apple or quince.

He cited, in a line of verse [I am unsure of the exact sense of this fragment]:
A scent clung to the tail-tuft, lingering.
This too is from the first root, because the scent lingers, stays. And the rajaz-poet said, of al-ibnān, which is staying, in a line of verse:
Young she-camels that do not complain of exhaustion ... that do not wait for the man who lingers behind.

Abū ʿAmr said: al-banīn, of men, is the intelligent, composed one. He said: it is derived from al-banna. And al-bunāna is the lush, richly-flowered meadow. From this is [the name of] Thābit al-Bunānī, who was of the descendants of Saʿd ibn Luʾayy ibn Ghālib; he had a nursemaid called Bunāna. And this too is from the first root, because a lush meadow never lacks a pleasant scent.
بنج:
The letters bā', nūn and jīm are a single word that, to my mind, is not a true root, and I do not know how it fits the pattern of the language; but it has been mentioned.

1. al-binj — one's origin, one's stock. One says raja'a ilā binjihi, he returned to his roots.
بند: The letters bā', nūn and dāl are a Persian root, with no cause to mention it here.
بنس: The letters bā', nūn and sīn are a single word. One says bannasa 'an al-shay' tabnīsan, said when he holds back and lags behind a thing.
بنق:
The letters bā', nūn and qāf are a single word, and I take it to be one of the marginal words, not a central one.

1. al-banīqa — the shirt's collar-slit. It is also said: al-banīqa is any patch set into a garment, like the labina [an inserted panel] and the like — and it has come this way in poetry. It was said: The night draws to me the first stirrings of her love, as the banā'iq [collar-flaps] draw together the buttons of a shirt.
بنك: The letters bā', nūn and kāf are a single word, and it is their saying tabannaka bi-l-makān, he settled and stayed in the place. This word is like the one before it [marginal].
بنو:
The letters bā', nūn and wāw are a single word, and it is a thing generated from another thing, like a human being's son and the like. The origin of its verbal root is banawa, and the adjectival form from it is banawiyy; likewise the adjectival form from bint (daughter) and from bunayyāt al-ṭarīq [the little side-tracks of a road]. So the origin of the word is what we have mentioned; the Arabs then branch out from it, naming many things "ibn [son of] such-and-such," and other things "built as" such-and-such.

1. ibn dhukā' — the morning; dhukā' being the sun, because it dhakū (blazes) as fire blazes. It was said: The son of dhukā' lies hidden behind a covering [of night].
2. ibn turnā — the base, contemptible man. Abū Dhu'ayb said, in a line of verse: For ibn turnā, if I come to you, wards off from me a harsh, grievous word — sharp, from barraḥa bihi, he dealt harshly with him.
3. ibn thaʾdāʾ — the son of a slave-woman.
4. ibn al-mā' — a bird [a waterfowl]. It was said: I came upon it by cutting straight across, while the Pleiades were, as it were, a circling waterbird atop the crown of the sky.
5. ibn jalā — the morning. It was said: I am ibn jalā, and the climber of the mountain-passes; whenever I set down my turban [remove my disguise], they know me.
6. ibn mulimma — one who, when misfortune (mulimma) befalls him, dispels it. And ibn aḥdhār — the wary, cautious man. From this is al-Nābigha's saying, in a line of verse: Tell Ziyād — a man's appointed time overtakes him — had you been shrewd, or been ibn aḥdhār [a son of caution] ...
7. ibn aqwāl — the stubborn arguer.
8. ibn al-falāt — one who cuts recklessly across open wasteland.
9. ibn ghabrā' — the poor man with no shelter but the bare earth and its dust. Ṭarafa said, in a line of verse: I have seen the sons of ghabrā' [the destitute] not disown me, nor the people of that spread-out tent.
10. ibn al-sabīl — the traveller. And ibn layl — one who journeys by night. And ibn 'amal — one devoted earnestly to his work. The rajaz-poet said: O Sa'd, O son of toil, O Sa'd.
11. They say: huwa ibn madīna, said of one learned about a city; and ibn bajdatihā likewise means one learned about it — bijdat al-amr being its inner knowledge.
12. They say of one noble on both sides, father and mother: huwa ibn iḥdāhā.
13. huwa ibn khalāwa — one innocent of a matter. And ibn ḥabba — for bread. And ibn na'āma — for the road, because they call the foot na'āma [ostrich]. It was said: And ibn al-na'āma [my own two feet] was my mount that day.
14. In the proverb: "ibnuka ibnu būḥika," meaning: your son is the son of your own self, the one you fathered.
15. The night on which the moon rises is called faḥmat ibn jamīr. It was said: Their day is a pitch-black night, and their night — even when there is a full moon — is faḥmat ibn jamīr [black as moonless dark]. He is describing a band of thieves.
16. ibn ṭāb — a variety of date-palm cluster in Medina.

Everything else in this chapter that we have left unmentioned is scattered elsewhere in the book, and we have omitted it here to avoid over-length.

Falling outside this root: al-mabnāt, a spread hide or leather mat. The poet said, in a line of verse: Upon the back of a fresh mabnāt, its straps new, a seller circles round it amid the bundled wares.
بني:
The letters bā', nūn and yā' are a single root, and it is the building of a thing by joining part of it to part. You say banaytu al-binā', abnīhi - I build the building. And Mecca is called al-Baniyya. And one says a bow is bāniya, and it is the one that has settled onto its string, and that is when its string is nearly cut through from clinging to it. And Ṭayyi' say bānāt in place of bāniya; and that is the wording of Imru' al-Qays, in a line of verse:
Not settling upon its string.

And one says bunya and bunan, and binya and binan with a kasra on the bā', just as one says jizya and jizan, and mishya and mishan.
به:
The letters bāʾ and hāʾ, doubled, are not a true root, for it is the imitation of a sound, or the modelling of one word upon another. Al-bahbaha is the roaring of a stallion. A poet said, in a line of verse [I am unsure of the exact sense of this fragment]:
With a rumbling, bellowing roar, a deep resounding bellow.

Abū Zayd said: al-bahbaha is loud, many sounds. And al-bahbaha is a large multitude of creatures. As for their calling the bold, big-bodied man "al-bahbahī," it is from this, because he roars in his speech.

A line of verse:
You never see him, in any turn of fate ... except that he goes forth boldly, with a mighty, bold spirit.

And their saying tabahbaha al-qawmu, when they rose to nobility, is also from the modelling of one word upon another, its origin being bakhbakhū, from their saying, in exalting and honouring: bakhin bakhin, well done, well done. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Do you not see that I am, from Zubayd, at a summit ... where my kinfolk branched out and rose to prominence?
بهأ:
The letters bā', hā' and hamza are a single root, and it is familiarity, being at ease with someone.

1. The Arabs say bahaʾtu bi-l-rajul, I grew at ease with the man. Al-Aṣma'ī said, in the Book of Camels: nāqa bahā' (with a lengthened final vowel), said of a she-camel that has grown used to her milker; he said this comes from bahaʾtu, meaning I grew at ease with him.
2. al-bahā' — beauty and comeliness; and it belongs to this same root, because whoever looks at it feels at ease.
بهت: The letters bā', hā' and tā' are one root, and it is like bewilderment and confusion. One says buhita al-rajulu yubhatu bahtan — the man was struck dumb. And al-bahta is confusion. As for al-buhtān, it is lying. The Arabs say: yā la-l-bahīta — that is, O the lie!
بهث: The letters bā’, hā’ and thā’ are not a root. A man has been named Buhtha.
بهج: The letters bā', hā' and jīm are a single root: it is joy and freshness. One says "nabātun bahīj," a fresh, beautiful plant. God Almighty said: {And We caused every delightful (bahīj) kind [of plant] to grow in it} [Qāf: 7]. Al-ibtihāj, joy, is from this too.
بهر:
The letters bā’, hā’ and rā’ are two roots: one is overcoming and loftiness, the other is the middle of a thing.

As for the first, the people of language say: al-bahr is overcoming. One says "a dazzling light" (ḍaw’ bāhir). And from this is their saying in cursing: "bahran lahum," meaning overcoming, defeat. He said, in a line of verse:
And my grandfather to my people, when they sold my life’s blood ... for a young woman — overcoming be upon them, then overcoming again.
He is calling down ill upon them.

And Ibn Abī Rabī‘a said, in a line of verse:
Then they said, "Do you love her?" I said, "Overwhelmingly" ... as many as the sand, the pebbles and the dust.

Some said its meaning is "overcoming be upon you." Others said its meaning is "a love that has overcome and overwhelmed." Others said its meaning is "I said that openly, not concealing it." He said: and from this is "so-and-so was ubtuhira with so-and-so-woman," meaning he became notorious for her. One says "ubtuhira bi-shay’," he became known for a thing and it overcame him. And from this is "the dazzling moon" (al-qamar al-bāhir), meaning the manifest one. The Arabs say: "Husbands are three: a husband of overcoming (bahr), a husband of time (dahr), and a husband of bride-price (mahr)."

Al-bahr is said of the one whose beauty dazzles the eyes. Of them is one who is kept as a resource against time and its misfortunes, and of them is one in whom there is nothing but that the bride-price be taken from him.

And to this chapter belongs their saying "so-and-so was ubtuhira with so-and-so-woman." What is claimed of that may be a lie. Tamīm said, in a line of verse:
... when the spear-points cross one another ... and there is no boastful false claim in me, even if I praised them.
Meaning: no false claim overcomes in that. And al-Kumayt said, in a line of verse:
It is ugly for one like me to describe the young woman ... whether by boastful claim or by false imputation.

As for the other root: their saying for the middle of a valley and the middle of everything is buhra. One says "the night ibhārra" when it reaches its middle. And from this is the hadith: "The Prophet, God’s blessings and peace be upon him and his family, traveled one night until the night ibhārra." Al-abāhir is a term for certain feathers in a bird’s wing. And from some of this is the derivation of the name Bahrā’.

As for al-buhār, the measure by which things are weighed, its origin, in my view, is not Bedouin.
بهز: The letters bā’, hā’ and zā’ are a single root, and it is overcoming and pushing with violence.
بهس: The letters bā’, hā’ and sīn are a single word: it is said that the lion is called Bayhas.
بهش:
The letters bā’, hā’ and shīn are two things: one is something like joy, the other is a kind of tree.

The first is their saying "bahasha ilayhi," when he saw him and was pleased by him and smiled at him. And from this is the hadith of al-Ḩasan: "The Prophet, God’s blessings and peace be upon him and his family, used to let his tongue hang out, so the child would bahash at him [smile with delight]." And from this is his saying, in a line of verse:
And when you see those who bahash [delight] toward high rank —

The second is al-bahsh, which is al-muql [doum-palm fruit] while it is moist; when it dries it is called khashl. ‘Umar said — word having reached him that Abū Mūsā had recited a passage of the Qur’an in the dialect of his own people — "Abū Mūsā was not among the people of al-bahsh." He means: he was not from the people of the Ḩijāz, for al-muql grows there — meaning: the Qur’an came down in the dialect of the Ḩijāz, not of Yemen.
بهصلة:
Buhṣula is the short woman, and a buhṣul donkey is a short one.

Al-bukhnuq is the short face-veil. Al-Farrā' said: al-bukhnuq is a piece of cloth a woman wears to protect her headscarf from oil.

Al-bal'ath is the one of bad character.

Al-bahkatha is speed.

Al-baḥzaj is the young of the cow, and so too al-burghuz.

A man bardhana when he became heavy and sluggish.

Al-barāziq are the groups of people.

Al-burzul is the huge one.

A bir'is she-camel is one abundant in milk.

He barshaṭa the meat: he shredded it into strips.

A man barshama when he fell silent and showed grief; and he barhama, when he kept his gaze fixed steadily.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
A gaze, slow and gentle — he stared fixedly.

Al-barqaṭa is a short, close-stepping gait.

And God knows best what is correct.

(Here ends the Book of the Letter Bā')
بهظ: The letters bā’, hā’ and ẓā’ are a single word, and it is their saying "bahazahu al-amr," when the matter weighed heavily upon him. And "this is a burdensome matter" (amr bāhiẓ).
بهق:
The letters bā’, hā’ and qāf are a single word, and it is a blackness that comes over the skin, or a color that differs from the skin’s own color. Ru’ba said, in a line of verse:
As though on the skin were the mottling of vitiligo.
بهل:
The letters bā', hā' and lām. Three roots: the first is leaving something alone, the second is a kind of prayer, and the third is scantness of water.

As for the first: they say bahaltuhu, meaning I left him to himself and his own will. From this comes al-nāqa al-bāhil, the she-camel that carries no brand-mark, or as it is also said, no udder-tie on her. From this too is the hadith of the woman who said to her husband: 'I told you my secrets, I fed you my best food, and I came to you bāhilan — untied, with no cord on me,' meaning: unrestrained, free to be let go — he meant by it to divorce her.

As for the second: al-ibtihāl is earnest, humble pleading in prayer. Al-mubāhala goes back to this too, for each of two people who mubāhala one another calls down a curse upon the other. God Most High said: {Then let us earnestly invoke, and place the curse of God upon the liars} [Āl 'Imrān: 61].

The third is al-bahl, which is a small amount of water.
بهم:
The letters bā', hā' and mīm: for a thing to remain such that the way to approach it is not known. One says "this is an obscure matter (amrun mubham)." From this is al-buhma: the solid rock with no crack in it, and by it the brave man who cannot be reached from any direction is compared. Some said: al-buhma is a company of horsemen. From this too is al-bahīm: a colour unmixed with any other, whether black or otherwise. "Abhamtu al-bāb": I locked the door.

What falls outside this root: al-ibhām, the thumb, among the fingers; al-bahm, young sheep; al-buhmā, a kind of plant — one says "abhamat al-arḍ," the land grew abundant in its buhmā-plant. He cited a line [describing an envoy well cared-for, and garments] which I cannot render with confidence in full.
بهن:
The letters bā’, hā’ and nūn are a single word, and there is also an irregularity in it: al-bahnāna is said of a laughing woman, and it is also said to mean a sweet-smelling woman. And his saying, in a line of verse:
Did she not say, "Bahān," while she did not run away ... you have grown old, and comfort no longer suits you.
He meant the name we have mentioned, but brought it out on the pattern fa‘āl.
بهو:
The letters bā', hā' and wāw are a single root, and it is a room or tent, and things like it.

1. al-bahw — the front room set before the rest of the house.
2. al-bahw — the wild bull's lair.
3. al-bahw — the resting-place of the unborn young, between the two hip-bones of a pregnant female.
4. al-bahw — also said of the inner cavity of a human being or other creature.
بهي:
The letters bā', hā' and yā' are a single root, and it is a thing's being empty and left unused.

1. bayt bāhin — a house, said when it is empty, with nothing in it. They say: "Goats leave [tents] empty, they do not build them" — meaning that no tents are made from goat-hair, and goats climb up onto tents and tear them apart.
2. In one hadith: "abhū al-khayl," meaning: leave the horses unused, turn them loose.
3. Sometimes they say bahiya al-bayt bahā'an, said when the house becomes full of holes and torn.
بو:
Al-bawwu is a single word, not a root with branches, and it is the skin of a young camel, stuffed, to which the she-camel is made to incline when her own young has died. Al-Kumayt said, in a line of verse:
Wrapped up, like the stuffed calf-skin, between the two wet-nurses.

And ash is called "bawwu al-athāfī" [the calf-skin of the hearthstones], by comparison.
بوأ:
The letters bā', wāw and hamza are two origins: the first is returning to a thing, and the other is two things being equal.

The first is al-bā'a and al-mabā'a, which is the dwelling-place of a people, where they settle at the head of a valley or on the slope of a mountain. One says qad tabawwa'ū — they have taken up their dwelling; and bawwa'ahum Allāh ta'ālā manzila ṣidq — God Almighty settled them in a place of truth. Ṭarafa said, in a line of verse:
Good is their dwelling-place, easy ... and they have paths, if you wish, in wild and rugged country.

And Ibn Harma said, in a line of verse:
She was settled in the very heart of her clan ... so her dwelling among her people was complete.

Al-mabā'a is also the resting-place of camels, where they kneel down at the watering-places. One says aba'nā al-ibil, nubī'uhā, ibā'atan — with the long vowel — when you make them kneel one against another. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Two neighbours between whom there is bad blood ... yet they kneel their camels together in one narrow fold.

And a poet said, in a line of verse:
They have a dwelling with a broad camel-yard, well peopled.

Al-Aṣma'ī said: one says qad abā'ahā al-rā'ī ilā mabā'ihā — the herdsman brought them to their resting-place — fa-tabawwa'athu, and they settled in it; and bawwa'ahā iyyāhu tabwī'an. Abū 'Ubayd said: one says fulān ḥasan al-bī'a, on the pattern fi'la, from your saying tabawwa'tu manzilan — I took a dwelling. And bāta fulān bi-bī'ati sū' — so-and-so passed the night in a bad lodging. A poet said, in a line of verse:
I spent the day at Dhū al-Arṭā, just above Muthaqqab ... in a bad lodging, dead or as good as dead.

And one says huwa bi-bī'ati saw' with the same meaning. Abū Mahdī said: one says bā'at 'alā al-qawmi bā'atuhum when their camels come home to them in the evening. From this chapter is their saying abi' 'alayhi ḥaqqahu — give him back his right — like ariḥ 'alayhi ḥaqqahu. And qad abā'ahu 'alayhi when he returned it to him. From this chapter is their saying bā'a fulān bi-dhanbihi — so-and-so came back bearing his sin — as though he had returned to his lodging carrying his sin. And qad bu'tu bi-al-dhanb, I have come back bearing the sin; and the Jews came back bearing the wrath of God Almighty.

The other origin is the Arabs' saying inna fulānan la-bawā'un bi-fulān — that if he were killed for him he would be his equal. And one says aba'tu bi-fulān qātilahu — I killed his killer for him. And istaba'tuhum qātila akhī — I demanded of them that they hand him over bound. And istaba'tu bihi is like istaqadtu — I sought retaliation for him. A poet said, in a line of verse:
If you kill al-Walīd from among us, then we ... have taken for him slain men whose noses are brought low.

And Zuhayr said, in a line of verse:
I have never seen a people take a sacrificial victim captive ... nor have I seen a neighbour of the house given up in retaliation.

And you say bā'a fulān bi-fulān when he is killed for him. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Will kings not leave off from us, and guard themselves ... against what is forbidden us, so that blood is not matched with blood?
That is, before the bloods are matched; when they are made equal in the killing, they have been matched.

From this chapter is the Arabs' saying kallamnāhum fa-ajābūnā 'an bawā'in wāḥid — we spoke to them and they [all] answered us with one and the same answer. And hum fī hādhā al-amri bawā' — they are in this matter equal and each other's like. In the hadith: «that he ordered them to be equal one with another» — that is, that they be matched in retaliation. From it is the saying of Muhalhil to Bujayr ibn al-Ḥārith: "Be given up in return for the sandal-strap of Kulayb." And he recited, in a line of verse:
So I said to him: be given up for a man you are not the like of ... even if you are enough to satisfy one who seeks blood.
بوب:
The letters bā', wāw and bā' are a single root, and it is your saying tabawwabtu bawwāban, that is, I took a doorkeeper for myself. And the alif of al-bāb, the door, is originally a wāw which was turned into an alif. As for al-Bawbāt, it is a place, and it is the first thing that appears from Qarn to al-Ṭā'if.

Al-Mutalammis said, in a line of verse:
You will never travel the roads of al-Bawbāt heading for Najd ... as long as you live, ʿAmr, and as long as you are given life, Qābūs.
بوث: The letters bā’, wāw and thā’ are a root that is not strong, but they say "bātha ‘an al-amr bawthan," when he searched into it.
بوج: The letters bā’, wāw and jīm are a good root, and it is from gleaming. The Arabs say "tabawwaja al-barq tabawwujan," when the lightning flashed.
بوح:
The letters bā’, wāw and ḥā’ are a single root, and it is the spaciousness of a thing, its coming forth and its being manifest. Al-būḥ is the plural of bāḥa, which is the open courtyard of a house. And in the hadith: "Clean your courtyards, and do not leave them like the courtyard of the Jews." And they say, among their proverbs: "Your son is the son of your courtyard (būḥika)," meaning the one you fathered in the courtyard of your house.

From this chapter is ibāḥa of a thing [permitting it], that is, that it is not forbidden to him, so his affair in it is open, not restricted. And by the same reasoning they say "istabāḥūhu," meaning they plundered it. He said, in a line of verse:
Until they laid open the family of ‘Awf by force ... with the Mashrafī swords and the supple spear-shafts.

And Ibn al-A‘rābī claimed that al-Bahdalī told him: al-bāḥa is a cluster of palm trees. And he cited, in a line of verse:
He gave, and gave me a hand, and a house ... and a courtyard of palms which he granted as property.
"The hand" here is the gathering of his people and his helpers.
بوخ: The letters bā’, wāw and khā’ are an eloquent word, and it is stillness. One says "bākhat al-nār bawkhan," the fire died down, its heat stilled. Likewise the heat of the day. One says "bākha" when he grew exhausted, because his movements slacken and grow feeble.
بور:
The letters bā', wāw and rā' are two roots: one is the destruction of a thing and what resembles it — its being disused and left empty; the other is the testing and trial of a thing.

As for the first, al-Khalīl said: al-bawār is destruction. One says bārū, and they are būr, meaning lost, destroyed. Abārahum fulān — so-and-so destroyed them. Būr may be used for one or many, women or men alike. God Most High said: {and you were a ruined people} [al-Fatḥ: 12]. Al-Kisā'ī said: from this is the hadith: "he used to seek refuge from the ruin of a widow left unmarried" — that is, that she become unwanted and find no husband.

1. Ya'qūb said: al-būr is the corrupt man in whom there is no good. 'Abd Allāh ibn az-Ziba'rā said, in a line of verse:
O messenger of the King, my tongue mends what it once tore, now that I am ruined.
2. Abū Zayd said: one says innahu la-fī ḥūrin wa būrin — meaning "in loss and waste."
3. al-bā'ir — goods that find no buyer. One says bārat al-biyāʿāt — the goods went unsold. From this is {the house of ruin} [Ibrāhīm: 28].
4. arḍun bawārun — land in which there is no crop.
5. Abū Ziyād said: al-būr, of land, is the barren kind, unfit to be worked; such lands are called arāḍūn abwār. From this is the letter of the Messenger of God, God bless him and his family and grant him peace, to Ukaydir: "Indeed the barren land and the untraceable land belong to us."
6. Al-Yazīdī said: al-būr is land left fallow for a year so it may be sown the year after; likewise al-bawār.
7. Abū 'Ubayd said, from al-Aḥmar: nazalat bawārun ʿalā an-nās — meaning calamity fell upon the people. He recited:
she was slain, and it became mutual wrongdoing and aggression — indeed mutual wrongdoing between friends is ruin.

The second root is testing and trial. One says burtu fulānan and burtu mā ʿindahu — I tested him, I tried what he had.

1. burtu an-nāqata fa-anā abūruhā — I brought the she-camel near the stallion, to see whether she is pregnant or not; likewise al-faḥl mibwar — the stallion is skilled at telling the two states apart. A poet said:
with a thrust like the ears of the wild ass, whose remainder [is]; and a thrust like the spurting of the she-camels being tested.
2. One says bāra an-nāqata bi-l-faḥl [the same meaning].

As for his saying:
one remembered for her twin foals, propped up along the back, toward whom the guarded, noble she-camels are brought to be tested —
he means: the noble, guarded she-camels are sought out on the strength of her description, from your saying burtu an-nāqa.
بوش: The letters bā’, wāw and shīn are a single root, and it is the gathering together of different sorts of people. One says "bawsh bā’ish" [a mixed rabble]. It is not, in our view, from the pure speech of the Arabs.
بوص:
The letters bā’, wāw and ṣād are two roots: one is something belonging to the limbs, the other is about outrunning.

The first is al-būṣ, which is a woman’s buttocks. He said, in a line of verse:
Wide of buttocks — when she turns her back ... slender-waisted, small in the embrace.
Al-būṣ is also a color, a complexion.

As for the other root: al-bawaṣ is escaping and outrunning. One says "bāṣanī" [he outran me]. And from this is their saying "khims bā’iṣ," meaning a hard-driving, hurrying stage of a journey.
بوع:
The letters bā’, wāw and ‘ayn are a single root, and it is the extension of a thing. Al-baw‘ is from your saying "bu‘tu al-ḥabla baw‘an," I stretched the rope, when you extend your arm-span (bā‘) with it. Al-Khalīl said: al-baw‘ and al-bā‘ are two dialect forms, but they use al-baw‘ for the bodily build. As for extending the bā‘ in generosity and the like, they only say "karīm al-bā‘" [generous of reach]. He said, in a line of verse:
He has, in glory, precedence and reach.

Al-bā‘ is also the verbal noun of "bā‘a yabūu‘u," and it is the extending of the arm-span. Camels "tabūu‘u" [extend their stride] in their gait. Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
... with the stretch of the pace, if the girth grew slack.

A man "yabūu‘u" with his wealth when he extends his reach with it. He said, in a line of verse:
I feared that I would meet death and not attain ... from wealth that by which I could rise and extend my reach.

And Ibn al-A‘rābī cited, in a line of verse:
And a thing bargained over, that is bargained for though it is cheap ... it is measured by the spans of hands, and crossed over.
He is describing an open wasteland in which the camels graze freely. "Cheap" means: it does not refuse. "Tubā‘u" means: the camels extend their spans (abwā‘) by it. "Tumsaḥ" means: it is cut across.

Abū ‘Ubayd said: "bu‘tu al-ḥabla abūu‘uhu baw‘an," when you extend one of your two hands until it becomes a bā‘ [full arm-span]. Al-Liḥyānī: one says he is long of arm-span, al-bā‘ and al-baw‘. One "bā‘a" in his walk, "yabūu‘u baw‘an," and "tabawwa‘a tabawwu‘an," and "inbā‘a," when he lengthens his strides. He said, in a line of verse:
He combines forbearance and calm together ... then he springs forth as the brave man springs.

The Arabs say, among their proverbs: "mukhranbiq li-yanbā‘a." Al-mukhranbiq is the one who lies low, silent. His saying "li-yanbā‘a" means: so that he may leap up. It is used as a proverb for the man who lies in wait for a calamity he intends.

Abū Ḩātim said: "baw‘ al-ẓaby" is the gazelle’s running short of a full sprint; al-nafz is its reaching the utmost of galloping.

Al-Liḥyānī: one says, "By God, they will never reach his stride (baw‘)," meaning they will never attain what he attained. Abū Zayd said: "a camel that is buwā‘," meaning large-bodied. One says "the oil inbā‘a" when it flows. He said, in a line of verse:
And a supple, pliant-jointed shaft as though ... it were draped by flowing oil, spilling.

One says "a horse that is bayyi‘," meaning wide of stride; it is from al-baw‘. Al-‘Abbās ibn Mirdās said, in a line of verse:
Upon the back of a bare-backed mare, noble of build ... like the point of the tall spear-shafts, wide of stride.
بوغ: The letters bā’, wāw and ghayn are a single root, and it is the stirring up of a thing. One says "tabawwagha" when it stirred up, like "tabayyagha." Al-bawghā’ is dust whose cloud rises up.
بوق:
The letters bā’, wāw and qāf are not a root relied upon, and in my view there is no sound word in it. They have mentioned that al-būq is lying and falsehood. And they mentioned a line of verse by Ḩassān:
... except what they spoke was a lie (būqan), and it was not so.
If this is sound, then it seems to be an imitation of a sound.

As for their saying "bāqathum bā’iqa," a calamity that befalls, meaning a disaster — this is not a genuine root; I take it to be substituted from jīm, and al-bā’ija is like a rupture and a defect. It has already been mentioned earlier.
بوك: The letters bā’, wāw and kāf are not a root; it is a euphemism for the act. One says "bāka al-ḥimār al-atān" [the donkey mated with the she-donkey].
بول:
The letters bā', wāw and lām are two roots: one is a liquid that trickles out, and the second is the mind, one's inner thought.

The first is al-bawl (urine), which is well known. So-and-so is ḥasan al-bīla, meaning good in the manner of urinating. He is seized by buwāl if he urinates a lot. Sometimes they used the word for progeny.

Al-Farazdaq said, in a line of verse:
My father is the one of abundant offspring, Mujāshi', in every land where no other stallion sires.

Al-Aṣma'ī said: the drops of mules are called "urine of mules," and from this the mirage was called "urine of mules," by way of comparison. It was compared to the urine of mules because the seed of mules is false — it does not impregnate — and the mirage is likewise deceptive, without substance.

Ibn Muqbil said, in a line of verse:
In the highland of Ḥimyar, where the mirage lies — however you made your way there, at nightfall, was that parting.

Ibn al-A'rābī said: fat is bawwāla (quick-melting) when it melts fast.

He said, in a line of verse:
When al-Nathūl said to al-Jamūl: "O daughter of fat, melt away in the throat."

Al-Jamūl is a lump of fat that is cooked; al-Nathūl is the woman who takes it out of the pot. A waterskin is called bawwāl if it gushes with the drink inside it; this occurs in the poetry of 'Adī.

As for the second root, it is al-bāl: the state of mind, the inner concern. One says: "it never crossed my bāl," meaning: it was never placed in my thought. If someone objects that Al-Khalīl said that bāl al-nafs is concern/caring, and from it "mā bālaytu" (I did not care) and "it did not cross my bāl" are derived — the answer is: it is the same meaning we have given, since caring means that what falls into one's mind weighs on him, so it goes back to what we said. The verbal noun is al-bāla and al-mubālāh.

From this is the saying of Ibn 'Abbās, when asked about performing ablution with milk: "I do not care about it in the least — be lenient, and leniency will be shown to you." They say "lam ubāli" and, shortened, "lam ubal."

Carried on this same meaning is al-bāl, ease of life; one says: he is at ease of mind, comfortable of mind.
بوم:
The letters bā’, wāw and mīm are a single word not to be analogized from. Al-būm is the male of al-hām [owl], and it is the plural of būma [owl]. He said, in a line of verse:
Often I trudge on through the far, unknown wasteland as I make my way ... in the shade of a dark-green tree where the owls call out to their kin.
They said: the plural of al-būm is abwām. He said, in a line of verse:
In a wasteland where, at the voice of the jinn in its terrors ... there is a moaning, and for the owls in it there is a wailing.
بون:
The letters bā’, wāw and nūn are a single root, and it is distance. Al-Khalīl said: one says "baynahumā bawn ba‘īd" and "buwan" — on the pattern of ḥawr and ḥuwar — and "bayn ba‘īd" also, meaning a difference.

Ibn al-A‘rābī said: "bānanī fulān yabūnunī," when he grew distant from you or cut you off. He said, and also "bānanī yabīnunī," likewise.

If it is asked: how then can al-biwān [tent-pole] be reckoned to this? It is said in reply: it is not far-fetched, for al-biwān is the pole among the poles of the tent, by which the tent is raised up and held aloft, and that gap it creates is al-bawn.

Abū Mahdī said: al-biwān is a pole raised on the foremost guy-rope, in the middle of the strip of cloth by which the tent is draped. He said: that is what is known as al-biwān. He said: then the rest of the poles are called buwan and biwānāt. And he cited, in a line of verse:
And his sitting-place beneath the foremost tent-pole.
And another said, in a line of verse:
He walks to her tent-pole with the gait of the lazy one.

And from this chapter is al-bāna, which is a kind of tree. As for Dhū al-Bān, it was among the lands of Banū al-Bakkā’. The poet said of it, in a line of verse:
And my longing for her, in the days of Dhū al-Bān, was led astray by her ... a commander whose heart toward me was whole.
And Buwāna is a valley belonging to Banū Jusham.
بوه:
The letters bā’, wāw and hā’ are not, in my view, a root; it is speech like mockery and derision. They say of a man in whom there is no good and no benefit: "būha." He said, in a line of verse:
O Hind, do not marry a worthless man (būha) ... whose lock of hair [as a child] was reckoned a poor thing.
And like it is their saying that al-būh is a bird like al-būma [the owl]. He said, in a line of verse:
Like the owl beneath the sprinkled shade.
He said: he means: it is as though I were a bird whose feathers had molted from old age, so water was sprinkled on it so that its feathers would grow back faster. He said: this is done especially with hawks. They said: and it is this that Imru’ al-Qays meant, likening the man to it, and this shows what we have said. Likewise al-būha is what the wind carries off of dust. One says: "more insignificant than a wisp of wool in a cloud of blown dust."
بيء:
The letters bāʾ-yāʾ-bāʾ and bāʾ-hamza are not true roots to be reasoned from, because they are isolated, individual words. They say "hayyu bnu bayyin" for one who is unknown. And they say: biʾbaʾtu al-ṣabiyya, meaning: I said "bābā" to him. Al-Aḥmar said: bāʾbaʾa al-rajulu, he hurried. And one says: tabaʾbaʾnā, when we hurried. And al-buʾbuʾ is the fine, noble master. And al-buʾbuʾ is the origin, the essence.

A line of verse: At the very heart of glory, and the centre of generosity.

And God knows best.
بيت:
The letters bā', yā' and tā' are a single root, and it is the place of shelter, the place of return, and the gathering of the household. One says bayt, and buyūt and abyāt. And from it a line of poetry is called a bayt, by way of likeness, because it is the gathering place of the words, the letters and the meanings, on a particular condition, namely the metre. And it is that which the one who said this meant, in a line of verse:
And many a verse I have built on the back of a riding-camel, with a brown thing split at the nostrils that bleeds.
By the brown thing he meant the pen. And al-bayt is a man's household, those with whom he spends the night. And one says: so-and-so has not the bīta of one night — that is, food or anything else to pass the night on. And bayyata al-amr, when he planned it by night. God, exalted be He, said: {when they plot by night what does not please Him of speech} [al-Nisā': 108] — that is, when they gather in their houses. Only that this is kept to the night; of the day one says ẓalla. And al-bayyūt is water that has stayed the night. And al-bayyūt is the matter its owner passes the night over, troubled by it. Umayya said, in a line of verse:
And I make the hollow of her back my provision, when I fear the night-brooded, baffling matter.
And al-bayāt and al-tabyīt is that you come upon the enemy by night, as though you took him in his house. And it is related from [Abū] ʿUbayda that he said: buyyita al-shay' when it is measured out and planned, and that is likened to the measuring out of lines of poetry. And this is not far from the root we laid down and reasoned upon.
بيح: The letters bā’, yā’ and ḥā’ are neither a root nor a branch; there is nothing in it but al-biyāḥ, which is a kind of fish.
بيد:
The letters bā', yā' and dāl are a single root, and it is for a thing to perish. One says: bāda l-shay'u baydan wa-buyūdan, when it perishes. Al-baydā' (the open desert waste) comes from this too — the connection in meaning between the two is clear. It is said that al-baydāna is the wild she-ass that dwells in the baydā'.

As for their word bayd, it comes in the sense of ghayr (except, however). One says: fu'ila kadhā bayda annahu kāna kadhā — such-and-such was done, except that such-and-such was so. It occurs in the hadith of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him and his family: 'We are the last, yet the foremost on the Day of Resurrection, except that they were given the Book before us, and we were given it after them.'

And he said, in a line of verse:
I did that on purpose — except that I,
I think, had I perished, you would not have shown me [grief].

This departs from the first reasoning given for the root. And were it said that this is a separate root in its own right, that would not be far-fetched.
بيص:
The letters bā’, yā’ and ṣād are not a root, because bayṣa is an echo-word following ḥayṣa. One says "the people fell into ḥayṣa bayṣa," meaning confusion. He said, in a line of verse:
It did not entangle me in confusion (ḥayṣa bayṣa) that clings fast.
بيض:
The letters bā', yā' and ḍād are an origin, and something derived from it, and something likened to the derived.

The origin is al-bayāḍ, whiteness among colours. One says ibyaḍḍa al-shay' — the thing turned white. As for what is derived from it, it is al-bayḍa, the egg of a hen and of other creatures, and the plural is al-bayḍ; and what is likened to that is bayḍat al-ḥadīd, the iron helmet.

Of metaphor is their saying about the man who is mighty in his place: he is bayḍat al-balad, the egg of the town, that is, he is kept and guarded as the egg is kept. One says ḥamā bayḍat al-islām wa-l-dīn — he protected the sheltered heart of Islam and of the religion. But when they speak of the lowly, weakened man as being bayḍat al-balad, they mean that he is left alone and by himself, like an egg left out in the open ground. And for that reason the egg is called al-tarīka, the one left behind. This has been explained in its own place.

One says bāḍat al-buhmā when the buhmā grass drops its sharp points. And bāḍa al-ḥarr — the heat grew fierce; and what is meant by that is that it has settled in, as though it laid eggs and hatched them and made the place its home.
بيظ: The letters bā’, yā’ and ẓā’ are a word I do not know in sound Arabic speech, and even if they had mentioned it, there would be no ground for establishing it. They said: al-bayẓ is the stallion’s fluid.
بيع:
The letters bā', yā' and ʿayn are a single root, and it is the selling of a thing; and buying too is sometimes called bayʿ. The meaning is one.

The Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: "Let none of you sell against the sale of his brother." They said: its meaning is, let him not buy against his brother's buying.

And one says biʿtu al-shay' bayʿan — I sold the thing; but if you offer it for sale you say abaʿtuhu.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
I was content with the gifts of the bay horse, so whoever would sell a horse, our fine one is not for sale.
بيغ: The letters bā’, yā’ and ghayn are not a root. What has come regarding it is tabayyugh al-dam, its surging. They said its origin is tabaghghā, with the yā’ brought forward and the ghayn placed after — like your saying jadhaba and jabadha, and mā aṭyabahu and aytabahu.
بين:
The letters bā', yā' and nūn are a single root, and it is a thing's being far off and its being uncovered. So al-bayn is parting; one says bāna yabīnu baynan wa-baynūnatan — he parted, parting. And al-bayūn is the well that is deep down. And al-bīn is a stretch of ground as far as the eye can reach. He said:
In the highland of Ḥimyar, where mules' urine is upon it — how did you cross that stretch of land in the night?

And bāna al-shay' and abāna — the thing became clear and showed itself. And so-and-so is abyanu than so-and-so, that is, plainer in his speech than he. As for al-bā'in in milking . . . .
تأر:
The letters tā', hamza and rāʾ are one word. One says atʾartu ʿalayhi al-naẓar, if I fixed my gaze sharply on him.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
I kept watching them while the mirage lifted them up, until my fixed gaze grew dim at the edge of my eye.

As for their saying ittaʾaba, meaning he felt shy, that belongs to another place, in the book of the wāw.
تأم:
The letters tā', hamza and mīm are a single word, and it is al-taw'amān: two children born in one womb. One says "the woman gave birth to twins" (at'amat al-mar'a), and she is mut'im, a mother of twins. Al-tu'ām is the plural.

A poet, Suwayd, said, in a line of verse:
Like the Tu'āmiyya, if you draw close to her...

It is said that al-Tu'ām is the chief town of Oman.
تب: The letters tā' and bā' are a single word, which is al-tibāb, meaning loss and ruin. 'Tabban lilkāfir' means ruin be upon the disbeliever. God Almighty said: {and they added to them nothing but ruin} [Hūd: 101], meaning causing loss. And a word has come opposite to these two in meaning: they say 'the matter istatabba' when it became settled and arranged smoothly. If this is sound, then this chapter has two senses: loss, and being set right.
تبر:
The letters tāʾ, bāʾ and rāʾ are two roots far apart: one is destruction, the other a mineral substance from the earth.
The first: tabbara Allāhu ʿamala al-kāfir, He destroyed and nullified it. God, Most High, said: {Indeed, these — destroyed is what they are engaged in, and false is what they used to do} [al-Aʿrāf: 139].
The other root: al-tibr, gold or silver not yet worked.
تبع:
The letters tā', bā' and 'ayn are a single root from which nothing in the section strays, and it is following after and coming behind. One says tabi'tu fulānan when you came behind him [and] ittaba'tahu. And atba'tuhu when you caught up with him. The root is one, except that they made a difference between coming behind and catching up, so they altered the form by the slightest alteration. God said: {fa-atba'a sababan} [al-Kahf: 85], [and] {thumma atba'a sababan} [al-Kahf: 89]. The meaning of this, on this reading, is catching up; and among the people of Arabic there are those who make the meaning in both one and the same.

Al-tubba' in the saying of the speaker, in a line of verse:
He comes down to the waters in a small band and in a scouting party, as the sandgrouse comes to water when the shade shrinks away.

It is the shade, and it is always following the person. And this analogy is truer than a sandgrouse. Al-tabī' is the calf of a cow when it follows its mother, and it is what is due on thirty head. And some of the jurists used to say: it is the one whose horns and ears are level. This is by the way of legal ruling, not by the analogy of the language.

Al-taba' are the legs of a beast, and they were so called because one of them follows another. Al-tabī' is the helper, because his help follows him. And al-tabī' is the one who owes you property, so that you follow him up for it. And in the hadith: 'The delay of a rich man is wrongdoing, and when one of you is referred on to a solvent man, let him follow it up.' He means: when he is referred on, let him accept the transfer.
تبل:
The letters tā', bā' and lām are words close to one another in sound and meaning, and they mean the opposite of soundness and safety.

1. al-tabl — enmity.
2. al-tabl — love overwhelming the heart; one says "a heart matbūl," a heart overcome by love.

One says "time consumed them" (tabalahum al-dahr afnāhum) — wore them away.

They explained al-A'shā's line, in a line of verse:
Is it because she saw a night-blind man harmed ... by the turns of fate, and a treacherous, wasting time?
تبن:
The letters tā', bā' and nūn are words very different from one another in meaning, and that is evidence that some Arab speech is set down by pure convention, without analogy or derivation.

1. al-tibn — the well-known thing, straw, the chaff of grain.
2. al-tibn — the largest of drinking-bowls, one that can nearly give twenty people their fill.
3. al-taban — sharp understanding, and likewise al-tabbāna. One says "tabina li-kadhā," he grasped such a thing with sharp understanding.

It is possible that this tā' is a substitute for a ṭā'.

Sālim ibn 'Abd Allāh said: "We used to say such-and-such, until you became sharp-witted (tabbantum)" — meaning: you looked closely, with your sharp understanding.
تجر: The letters tā', jīm and rā': trade, al-tijāra, is well known. One says tājir and tajr, a trader and traders, as one says ṣāḥib and ṣaḥb, a companion and companions. And a tā' with a jīm after it is hardly ever seen.
تحت: The letters tā', ḥā' and tā' are one word: taḥt al-shay', beneath the thing. And al-tuḥūt are the low ones among people. In the hadith: "The mountain goats perish and the low ones come to the top." Al-wuʿūl, the mountain goats, are the great and the high-standing.
تحم: Al-atḥamī is a kind of striped cloak.
تخ: The letters tā' and khā', doubled, are not a root that other words can be measured against or derived from, and what has been mentioned of it is not something to be relied upon. They said: al-takhtakha is the imitation of a sound. And al-takhkh is sour dough; one says takhkha, tukhūkha (it turned sour), and its owner atakhkhahu, itkhākhan (he made it sour).
تخذ: The letters tā', khā', and dhāl are a single word: takhidhtu the thing and ittakhadhtuhu both mean I took it, I adopted it.
تخم:
The letters tā', khā', and mīm are a single word that does not branch further. Al-tukhūm are the markers of land and its boundaries. In the hadith: 'Cursed is he who alters the boundary-markers of the land.' Some said he meant the boundaries of the sacred sanctuary. Others said it is when a man enters into the boundaries of another and seizes them wrongfully.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
O sons, do not wrong the boundary-markers ... for wronging the boundary-markers carries a binding penalty.

As for al-tukhma [indigestion], it belongs in its chapter in the Book of the Letter Wāw.
تر:
The letters tā' and rā' are close to what came before. In it, from the sound original language, there is one word: their saying 'a body with tarāra' — meaning it has fatness and plumpness. One says: it tarra (became plump).

A poet said, in a line of verse:
We wake in the morning being the plumpest of things ... and pass the evening being lean and worn out.

As for al-tarātir, they are great matters, but this is not a true root, because the rā' here stands in for a lām.

And their saying 'the date-stone tarrat from its crushing-stone, tatirru' — this is close to what came before. Likewise the thread called 'al-turr', which the builder stretches taut — hardly anything like it can be verified. Likewise their saying that al-utrūr is the young boy — and were it not that we found this in their books, it would be more correct to disregard it. And how can something be sound when its only evidence is a verse of poetry like this:

I seek refuge in God and in the commander ... from the officer of the watch and from al-utrūr.

And similar to it is what was related from al-Kisā'ī: 'the man tarra from his country' — meaning he went far away; and 'the judgment atarrahu' — meaning it drove him far away.
ترب:
The letters tā', rā' and bā' are two roots: one is dust and what is derived from it, and the other the equality of two things.

The first is al-turāb, dust, which is also al-tayrab and al-tawrāb. And one says tariba al-rajulu when he became poor, as though he stuck to the dust; and atraba when he became rich, as though he came to have of wealth as much as there is dust. And al-tarbā' is the earth itself. And one says a wind is triba when it comes carrying dust.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
No, rather it is longing, from a dwelling worn away — one time by cloud, another time by a hot dusty wind.

As for the other root: al-tirb is the companion of one's own age, and the plural is atrāb. From it is al-tarīb, the chest, where the heads of the bones are level with one another.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Her two breasts stood out over the upper chest.

And from it are al-taribāt, the fingertips; one of them is a triba.

Of what has strayed from this chapter is al-turba, a plant.
ترج: The letters tā', rā', and jīm — there is nothing in this except 'Tarj', which is a place-name. And al-utrujj [the citron] is well-known.
ترح:
The letters tā', rā', and ḥā' are two related words. Al-Khalīl said: al-tarah [grief] is the opposite of joy. They say: 'After every joy comes a grief, and after every delight comes a tear.' A poet said, in a line of verse:

There is no joy but that a grief will follow it ... and nothing flourishing but that soon it will fall to ruin.

The other word: al-nāqa al-mitrāḥ is the she-camel whose milk quickly dries up; its plural is matārīḥ.
ترز:
The letters tā', rā', and zāy are a single sound word. Tariza the thing means it became hard and solid. And anything firmly set is tāriz. And the dead is called tāriz, because it has stiffened. A poet said, in a line of verse:

It is as though the wild game that is shot at is tāriz [rigid].

And Imru' al-Qays said — and this shows that al-tāriz means hard and solid:

With a stout she-camel whose running has hardened her flesh ... like a dead thing, as though she were the beam of a weaver's loom.

And one says: the woman atrazat her rope — meaning she twisted it into a very tight twist. And she atrazat her dough — when she kneaded it firmly.
ترس:
The letters tā', rā', and sīn are a single word, which is al-turs, the shield, a well-known thing. Its plurals are tirasa, tirās, and turūs.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
As though a sun had come down as many suns ... our coats of mail, and the helmets, and the shields.
ترش: The letters tā', rā', and shīn are neither a root nor a branch, except that Ibn Durayd mentioned that al-tarash is rashness and impulsiveness; one says tarisha, yatrashu, tarashan. And I do not know what it is.
ترص:
The letters tā', rā', and ṣād are a single root, and it is soundness and firmness of make. One says: the thing taruṣa; and atraṣtuhu means I made it firm and sound, so it is mutraṣ. And anything whose making you have made firm, you have atraṣta it. Al-Khalīl recited:

And bind your hands with the firm, well-made knot.
ترع:
The letters tā', rā', and 'ayn are a root whose sense applies consistently, and it is the opening up of a thing. So al-tur'a is the door, and al-tarrā' is the gatekeeper.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
I was kept from visiting you by a fortress, firmly built ... which, whenever I move my legs within it, clamors.

Hard, and set solid with mortar and stone ... having battlements, watch-post above watch-post.

Its gatekeeper offers me the choice between a ring ... that bites hard when it closes, and a fettering shackle plated with iron.

The Messenger of God, God's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, said: 'This pulpit of mine is a gate among the gates of Paradise.' And al-tara' is rushing headlong into evil, and a man is described as tari'. This belongs to the same sense, because it involves an opening up toward what is not proper — and this word is hardly ever used for something good.

From this chapter also: atra'tu the vessel means I filled it. And a bowl is mutra'a [brimming]. A poet said:

Had he been alive, he would have brought them a brimming bowl in the morning.

And al-tara' is fullness. One says the vessel tari'a [became full]. Some scholars of language used to say: I do not say tari'a, but rather utri'a [it was filled]. This too belongs to the chapter, because when it is filled it hastens to overflow.

Al-tur'a — plural tura' — are the mouths of streams. And one says a swift pace is described as atra'. A poet said:

And he spread himself over the ground with a swift, sweeping pace.

And the underlying sense throughout is one.
ترف: The letters tā', rā' and fā' are one word, and it is al-turfa, the good thing set apart for someone. One says a man mutraf — pampered; and tarrafahu ahluhu, when his family pamper him with good food and with a thing given to him alone. And in the book of al-Khalīl: al-turfa is the little something in the upper lip. This is a mistake; it is only al-tufra, and it has already been mentioned.
ترق: The letters tā', rā' and qāf contain nothing but al-tarquwa, the collarbone. Al-Khalīl held that it is on the pattern fa'luwa, a bone connecting the hollow of the throat and the shoulder.
ترك:
The letters tā', rā' and kāf: al-tark is the leaving of a thing alone, and that is the reasoning of the chapter; and for that reason the egg left out in the open ground is called tarīka. Al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse:
And many a waterless waste where the eye is bewildered in its midst ... and where you find ostrich eggs left lying.

And tarkat al-silāḥ, and it is the helmet, is carried upon this and likened to it; and the plural is tark. Labīd said, in a line of verse:
A great rank-smelling one, bound up with its thongs ... a Qurdumānī coat, and helmets like onions.

And tarāki means "leave off". A poet said, in a line of verse:
Leave them, leave off these camels of theirs ... do you not see death at their haunches?

And tarikat al-mayyit is what a dead man leaves of his estate. And al-tarīka is a meadow that people overlook and do not pasture on. And in the book ascribed to al-Khalīl: one says taraktu al-ḥabl shadīdan, that is, I made the rope tight. But I do not think this is from al-Khalīl's speech.
تره:
The letters tā', rā', and hā' are a word that is not a root with branches from it. They said: al-tarrahāt, and al-turrah, are false and worthless matters. Ru'ba said, in a line of verse:

And a truth that is not the speech of falsehood.

They said: its singular is turraha. He said: and some people made its plural al-tarārīh. He said, in a line of verse:

Bring back the camels of the sons of al-A'raj, from nearby ... before the empty talk, and after the claim.
تسع: The letters ta, sin and 'ayn are a single word, meaning nine, in counting. One says 'tasa'tu l-qawma' — I became their ninth. 'Atsa'tu l-shay'' — I completed a thing that was eight, into nine. Al-tis' is three nights of the month, the last of them being the ninth night. 'Tasa'tu l-qawma atsa'uhum' — I took a ninth of their wealth [as a tithe].
تع:
The letters tā' and 'ayn belong to sound original speech, and their sense is unsettledness and being forced. One says a man ta'ta'a when he becomes clumsy and stumbling in his speech. And anyone who is compelled in a matter until he becomes unsettled has been tu'ti'a. In the hadith: 'until the weak person's right is taken from the strong, without tut'ta'' [without being pushed around]. And one says the horse ta'ta'a when it stumbled and floundered.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
It flounders in soft, loose ground when it climbs it ... and it stumbles even on the straight road.

And one says: the people fell into ta'ātī', meaning false rumors and confusion.
تعب:
The letters tā', 'ayn, and bā' are a single word, and it is exhaustion, such that one says: ta'iba ta'aban, and he is ta'ib [weary]; one does not say mat'ūb. And I at'abtuhu, it'āban, means I wearied him. As for their saying 'the bone uti'iba', meaning it broke again after having been set, this is not from this root; it is rather a metathesis of u'tiba, and it has already been mentioned in its own chapter. A poet said, in a line of verse:

Whenever he sees a glimpse of her, his heart breaks ... over her, like the re-breaking of a bone already shattered and weary.
تعر: The letters tā', 'ayn, and rā' amount to nothing, except Ti'ār, which is a mountain.
تعس:
The letters tā', 'ayn and sīn are a single word, and it is stumbling headlong. One says: ta'asahu Llāhu wa-at'asahu — God cast him down.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
At dawn we routed their host at Mutāli' —
they returned in headlong ruin, under the worst of omens.
تعص: The letters tā', 'ayn, and ṣād are a single word. Ibn Durayd mentioned that al-ta'iṣ is the one who complains of his neck from walking.
تغ: The letters tā' and ghayn are not a root. They say: al-taghtagha is the imitation of a sound, or of laughter.
تف: The letters tā' and fā' are like what came before. Except that they say: al-tuff is the dirt under the fingernail.
تفث: The letters tā', fā' and thā' are a single word, in God Most High's saying: {then let them accomplish their tafath} [al-Ḥajj: 29]. Abū 'Ubayda said: it is the clipping of nails, the trimming of the mustache, the smelling of perfume, and everything forbidden to a person in the state of iḥrām, except intercourse. He said: no verse of poetry has come citing this word that could be relied upon.
تفح: The letters tā', fā' and ḥā' are one word, and it is al-tuffāḥ, the apple.
تفر:
The letters tā', fā' and rā' are one word, and it is al-tafira, the little dip beneath the nose in the middle of the upper lip.

1. al-tafra — from a human, this same feature; from a camel it is called al-nuʿw. Abū ʿUbayd said this.
2. al-tafira — a plant, the most loved grazing to the herds.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
It has tafira-plants beneath it, and the shorter ones beside them, reaching toward fresh new growth not yet caught by the hooked sticks.
تفل:
The letters tā', fā', and lām are a single root, and it is the foulness of a thing and its offensiveness. So al-tafal is a foul, offensive smell. A woman is described as tafila and mitfāl [not perfumed]. The Messenger of God, God's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, said: 'Do not keep the maidservants of God from the mosques of God, and let them go out, when they go out, tafilāt' — meaning not wearing perfume. And I atfaltu the thing [left it unperfumed]. A poet said, in a line of verse:

O son of the one who hunts the hyraxes ... and leaves ambergris and musk-pouches unscented.

And Imru' al-Qays said:

When she turns away, full-figured, not unperfumed.

From this chapter also: tafalta with the thing, when you spat it from your mouth in disgust for it. A poet said, in a line of verse:

And from the depths of water whose surface is covered with a year's growth of algae ... whenever the people's water-drawer tastes of it, he spits it out.
تفه: The letters tā', fā', and hā' are a single root, and it is the scantiness of a thing. One says: the thing tafiha, so it is tāfih [trifling], when it becomes little. In the hadith, speaking of the Qur'an: 'It does not become trifling, and it does not wear out.' And in another hadith: 'The hand used not to be cut off for a trifling thing.'
تق: The letters tā' and qāf are like what came before. They say: he tataqtaqa from the mountain, when he fell.
تقد: The letters tā', qāf and dāl. They say al-tiqda is a plant. This and its like are things not worth pursuing further.
تقن:
The letters tā', qāf and nūn are two roots: the first is making a thing exact and sound, and the second is mud and silt.

As for the first: atqantu l-shay'a — I made the thing exact. A man is tiqn, meaning skilled. Ibn Tiqn was a man famed for excellent archery, proverbial for it. A poet said, in a line of verse: 'He shoots with it, more accurately than Ibn Tiqn.'

As for the mud and silt: one says taqqanū arḍahum, when they improved their land with that substance — and that substance is al-tiqn.
تك: The letters tā' and kāf are not a root. What weakens its case further is that tā' and kāf rarely combine at the start of a word. Yet al-tikka [a waistband] has been transmitted, and 'takaktu the thing' means I trod on it. And al-tākk is the fool. Whatever God, glorious is His majesty, wills to be sound is sound.
تل:
The letters tā' and lām, doubled, are a sound root, and it points to standing upright, and to the opposite of standing upright.

As for standing upright: it is al-tall, a well-known word [a mound]. And al-talīl is the neck. And I talaltu the thing in his hand [placed it into his hand]. And al-taltala is unsettledness, which follows the same sense.

As for its opposite: talla-hu means he threw him down. This is a kind of contrast within the same root. And al-mitall is the spear with which one is thrown down. God Almighty said: {and he laid him down on his brow} [al-Ṣāffāt: 103]. Then Labīd said:

Steady of heart, guarding their exposed flank ... I wheel the dark one with a well-proportioned, thrusting spear.

He means: I wheel it, and with me is a spear, mitall [ready for felling].
تلد:
The letters tā', lām and dāl are a single root, and it is staying, remaining in place.

1. talada — they say 'so-and-so talada among the sons of so-and-so,' yatlidu, if he settled and stayed among them.
2. atlada — if he acquired wealth for himself.
3. al-tilād — the wealth you yourself produced and built up in your own possession.
4. māl mutlad — long-held, inherited wealth.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
If time itself had wealth of its own long keeping, then Sakhr would have been the wealth time had acquired.

5. al-talīd — what you bought young, and it grew up in your keeping.
6. al-atlād — a group among the Arabs, a tribe so named.
تلع:
The letters tā', lām and ʿayn are a single root, and it is stretching and rising upward in height. One says atlaʿati al-ẓabya, the doe raised its neck high.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
I remembered you when she raised her neck from her covert, and remembering you is a strange stupor upon me.

1. jīd talīʿ — a long neck.

Al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse:
The day Qutayla showed us a long neck, adorned by necklaces.

2. al-atlaʿ — the long-necked one.

One says tatālaʿa fī mishyatihi, if he stretched his neck out as he walked. And so-and-so stayed fixed in his place and mā tatallaʿa, if he did not want to leave.

Abū Dhuʾayb said, in a line of verse:
They came down to water while al-ʿAyyūq sat like the watcher over the gamblers, behind the star, not craning its neck.
