3. Mutāliʿ — a mountain.

It is said that al-taliʿ is the one who often looks around himself.

And from this root: talaʿa al-nahār and atlaʿa, if the day spread out and rose.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
As if they, in the shimmering haze when the forenoon rose, were ships afloat, dressed in their coverings.

As for their saying 'he is taliʿ toward evil,' it is possible this comes from the same root, because he is forever on the lookout for evil. And it is possible the lām here stands in place of a rā', so the word is really al-tariʿ, which has already been discussed.

4. al-talʿa — raised, rugged ground, sometimes broad, where floodwater winds about before draining down into a talʿa lower than it. It is fine ground for plants to grow.

Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
Ḥusum has been effaced of Fartanā, then al-Fawāriʿ, then the two flanks of Arīk, then the flowing talʿa-valleys.
تلف: The letters tā', lām and fā' are one word, and it is a thing's passing away. One says talifa yatlafu talafan, it perished. And arḍ matlafa — a deadly wasteland; plural matālif.
تلم:
The letters tā', lām and mīm are not a root, and there is no sound or correct speech built on them. Ibn Durayd said, of al-talām, that it means al-talāmīdh, the students.

He cited, in a line of verse:
Like the [word uncertain] in the hands of the students.

And in the book attributed to al-Khalīl: al-talam is the mark cut by ploughing, in the language of the people of Yemen. He mentioned much the same about al-talām as Ibn Durayd had. But there is nothing in any of that to rely on, since al-tilmīdh, 'student,' is not a word from the speech of the Arabs.
تله:
The letters tā', lām and hā' are not a root in themselves. That is because they say taliha, if he became bewildered, then they say the tā' there stands in for a wāw. And they said: al-talah stands in for al-talaf, loss, meaning the same thing, and they recite:
By it she crossed the deceiving reach of every place of bewilderment.

But the correct wording, as Abū ʿUbayd transmitted it, is 'every mīlah' (waymark) in place of 'matlah.' He said: those are the lands that make a person wander lost. Al-wālih is the one who is bewildered.
تلو:
The letters tā', lām and wāw are one root, and it is following. One says talawtuhu, when you followed him. And of it is the tilāwa of the Qur'an, its recitation, because one verse is made to follow another. As for their saying talawtu al-rajula atlūhu tilwan, when you forsake a man and leave him, if that is sound then it is the measure of the root, because he was his companion and with him, so when he broke off from him and left him he came to be behind him, in the place of the one who follows.

Of this section are al-taliyya and al-tulāwa, which are the remainder, because the remainder follows what went before it. Ibn Muqbil said, in a line of verse:
O Ḥurr, the last remnants of youth have gone by this evening; I am left with neither sight nor trace of them.
And of what holds good in this is what al-Aṣma'ī related: a need of mine remained, and I go after its remains. And al-talā' is protection given, because it is followed up and sought; one says atlaytuhu dhimmatan, I gave him a covenant. And al-mutālī is the one who answers his fellow back in singing; the two were so named because each of them follows the other. Al-Akhṭal said:
Or the singing of one answering in turn.
تم:
The letters tā' and mīm are a single root that is regularly applied, and it points to completeness. One says: the thing tamma, when it became complete, and I atmamtuhu — I completed it.

1. Al-tamīma — an amulet. It is as though they mean by it the completion of the medicine and the cure that is sought. In the hadith: 'Whoever hangs an amulet, may God not complete his affair for him.'
2. Al-tamīm — also, something hard and solid.

One says a pregnant woman is mutimm [carrying to term]; and 'she gave birth litamām' [at full term]; and 'the night of full completion' is called laylat al-timām and nothing else.

Completing the shares in the gambling-game (tatmīm al-aysār) is that you feed them the winnings of your arrow, without holding back any of it. Al-Nābigha said:

Indeed I complete my shares of the gambling-game and grant them ... doubled gifts, and clothe the great bowl in leather.

3. Al-mustatimm — the one who seeks some wool or hair with which to finish weaving his cloak. Abū Duwād said:

They are like eggs in their nesting-hollows, from which ... no strap is given to one who seeks to complete his need.

And what is given is called al-timma and al-tumma.

As for their saying al-mutatammim, meaning the one broken up and shattered, this may belong to this same root, because a thing reaches its limit until it breaks apart. But it is also possible that the tā' here stands in place of a thā', as if it were mutathammim — and this is the more likely view. In it, this is recited:

Like the re-breaking of the exhausted, shattered one.
تمر:
The letters tā', mīm and rā' are one word, and other words are then derived from it: it is al-tamr, dates that are eaten. The one who has dates is called tāmir, and the one who feeds them to others is also called tāmir. One says tamartuhum, atmiruhum, if you fed them dates.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
You deceived me, and claimed that you had milk in summer, and dates besides.

1. al-mutammir — the one who dries them, the dates. One says tummira al-laḥm, if the meat was dried; the word is taken from al-tamr.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
She has strips of meat that she dries.

2. al-mutmir — one with abundant dates. One says atmara, just as one says albana if his milk became abundant, and albaʾa if his colostrum became abundant.
3. al-tammār — the one who sells dates.
4. al-tamriyy — the one who loves dates.
تمك: The letters tā', mīm and kāf are one word, and it is a thing's rising up. One says tamaka al-sanām, if the hump rose high; and it is sanām tāmik, a raised hump. Ibn Durayd mentioned: atmakahā al-kalaʾ, the pasture made it plump. God knows best.
تمه: The letters tā', mīm and hā' are one word, indicating a thing's change for the worse. One says tamiha al-ṭaʿām, if the food spoiled. And tamiha al-laban — the milk's smell changed. And shāh mitmāh — a ewe whose milk changes as soon as it is milked. Al-tamah in milk is like al-namas in fat [al-namas is an obscure word here, rendered as best as can be told].
تن: The letters tā' and nūn are two words whose root I do not know. Except that they call one's agemate 'al-tinn'. And they say: 'the illness atannahu' — when it wore him down, and he barely grows up.
تنأ: The letters tā', nūn and hamza are one word. One says tanaʾa bi-l-balad, if he settled in the land, and he is a tāniʾ, a resident.
تنخ: The letters tā', nūn and khāʾ are one word, and it is staying, residing. One says tanakha bi-l-makān tunūkhan, and tatannakha tatannukhan, if he resided there. By this Tanūkh was named — tribes of the Arabs who gathered and made a pact together, fa-tanakhū, meaning they settled in their places.
تنف:
The letters tā', nūn and fāʾ are one word: al-tanūfa is open wasteland, and so too al-tanūfiyya.

Ibn Aḥmar said, in a line of verse:
How much wasteland lies between me and Laylā — shimmering ground where travellers dedicate their vows.

And Ibn Qutayba transmitted it as 'tanūfā' and said: a high mountain pass. He said some people say 'yanūfā' instead.

He cited, in a line of verse:
It is as if Banū Nabhān's neighbour was carried off by an eagle of Tanūfā, not the eagle of al-Qawāʿil.

Al-Qawāʿil are small mountain passes. He means: as if their neighbour was borne away by this eagle. And similar is the saying of al-Musayyab, in a line of verse:
You are the faithful one, never to be blamed, while some others keep their word the way the eagle of Malāʿ keeps its word.

He said: Malāʿ is treated grammatically the way Ḥadhām is, as a fixed name that does not decline. One says imtalaʿahu, meaning he snatched it away.
ته:
The letters tā' and hā' are not a root, and no word branching from it has come. They only say: al-tahātuh is falsehood. Al-Quṭāmī said, in a line of verse:

What we were tried with, of her promises, was nothing ... but empty falsehood and a sickly wishful hope.

They said: and al-tahtaha is a stammer in the tongue.
تهم:
The letters tā', hāʾ and mīm are a single root, and it is spoiling brought on by heat. Al-taham is intense heat together with stillness of the wind, and by this Tihāma was named. One says atham al-rajul, the man went down to Tihāma.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
If you go down to Tihāma, I go up to Najd, against you; and if you go to ʿUmān bearing evil with you, I go to Iraq.

And one says tahima al-ṭaʿām, the food spoiled. And Abū ʿAmr related: 'when they went down to the Ḥijāz they said athamūhu,' as if meaning they found it unwholesome.
تو: The letters tā' and wāw are a single word, which is al-tawwu, meaning the single, unpaired one. In the hadith: 'The circumambulation is tawwun' [done singly, without pause]. And one says: 'he traveled a tawwan journey' — meaning he did not stop along the way; but if he stopped somewhere and set out on another journey, it is not tawwun.
توب: The letters tā', wāw and bā' are one word pointing to returning. One says tāba min dhanbihi, that is, he turned back from it — yatūbu ilā Allāhi tawbatan wa-matāban — and he is tā'ib, one who turns back. And al-tawb is al-tawba, repentance. God, exalted, said: {wa-qābili al-tawb} [Ghāfir: 3].
توت: The letters tā', wāw and tā' are not a root. In it is al-tūt, which is a fruit, the mulberry.
توخ: The letters tā', wāw and khāʾ are not a root. A word was mentioned in the book of al-Khalīl which I take to be a copyist's error. He said: 'the finger sank (tākhat) into the soft thing.' But this word is really spelled with a thāʾ — thākhat.
تور:
The letters ta', waw and ra' are not an origin sense to build on. Al-Khalil, in this section, mentioned something not truly of its root: "the wild game istaw'arat," took fright and scattered — that belongs under its own proper entry.

Ibn Durayd mentioned a word it would have been better to pass over. He said: at-tawr is a go-between among a people, sound Arabic. He said, in a line of verse:
And the go-between is set to work between us — one both the sender and the one sent to are content with.

And it is said that al-tara, a turn or an instance, has a waw as its root letter — the explanation of that belongs elsewhere; the text here does not give it.
توس: The letters tā', wāw and sīn: nature, disposition — and it is not a root, because the tā' here stands in for a sīn, and the word is really al-sūs.
توع:
The letters tā', wāw and ʿayn are one word. Abū ʿUbayd said, from Abū Zayd: atāʿa al-rajul itāʿatan, if he vomited. And from this is the saying of al-Quṭāmī, in a line of verse:
Its veins spew clotted blood, vomited forth.

Al-Khalīl mentioned another word, sounder than this one. He said: al-tawʿ is your breaking off a piece of curdled milk or clarified butter with a scrap of bread, to scoop it up with.
توق:
The letters tā', wāw and qāf are a single root, and it is the soul's longing; other things are then carried along from it. One says tāqa al-rajul, yatūqu. Al-tawq is the soul's longing for a thing, and it is also called al-tuʾūq. Nafs tāʾiqa — a longing soul.

Ibn al-Sikkīt said: tuqtu and taʾiqtu both mean 'I longed.'

Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: tāqa yatūqu, if he gave freely of his own life. And likewise rāqa yarīqu, and fāqa yafīqu or yafūqu.
تول: The letters tā', wāw and lām are a word I do not take to be sound, though it has been transmitted. They said: al-tiwala is a kind of sorcery. And they said it is something a woman puts on her neck to make herself more pleasing to her husband.
تولب:
Al-tawlab is the young of the cow. Analogy requires that the tā' here be a substitute for a wāw, with the wāw after it extra, as though the word were on the pattern fawʿal from walaba, "he returned." Its pattern is thus the same as that of al-tabī' (a calf, a "follower"). If someone takes this view, he would not be far off.

As for tibrāk, the tā' in it is extra; it is on the pattern tifʿāl from baraka, "he settled and stayed." It belongs properly under the letter bā', but it is mentioned here for its form.

Al-turnūq is the mud that remains in the course of water once it has receded; the tā' and the wāw in it are both extra, and it is from al-ranq, murkiness.

The rest of these words, which are few, are set down by pure convention.

Among them: itla'abba, said of a matter when it became straight and went smoothly.

What follows are words of more than three letters whose first letter is tā':

Tiryam is a place. A poet said, in a line of verse:
In the valleys of Tiryam their skulls lay unburied.

As for al-tarabūt among camels, the tame, docile one — if someone said it comes from tā', rā' and bā', as though the camel is made so submissive that it presses close to the ground (al-turāb, dust), that would be a reasonable view.

Itmahalla — said when something stood upright.

Al-ta'lab is a well-known kind of tree.

Al-taw'abāniyyān are the two front teats of an udder. Ibn Muqbil said, in a line of verse:
She passed by the hillocks of Hirr one evening, having two front teats not yet grown coarse.

It is possible that the tā' here is extra and the true root is al-wa'b. Al-wa'b is something hollowed out cup-shaped, and it has been mentioned in its own place. God knows best what is correct.

Here ends the Book of the Letter Tā'.
توه: The letters tā', wāw and hāʾ are not a root. They said tāha yatūhu, the same as tāha yatīhu. It is a case of one letter substituted for another, and this has already been discussed.
توي:
The letters tā', wāw and yāʾ are one word, and it is a thing's coming to nothing. One says tawiya yatwā tawan and tawāʾan.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And it was for their mother that the loss came to be.

The verse as printed appears cut short here.
تيح:
The letters tā', yāʾ and ḥāʾ are a single root, and it is their saying tāḥa fī mishyatihi yatīḥu, if he swayed as he walked. Faras mityaḥ and tayyaḥān — a horse that veers playfully as it goes, leaning to either side. Rajul mityaḥ and tayyaḥān — a man who is bold and forward in everything.

A poet said of al-mityaḥ, in a line of verse:
Is it after the departing litters that your eye is glancing? Yes — no matter; your heart is restless.

And he said of al-tayyaḥān, in a line of verse:
By my warding blame off my lineage and my wealth, and off the thrusts of a proud, bold man.

And one says atāḥa Allāhu taʿālā al-shayʾ yutīḥuhu itāḥatan, if He decreed it. And once He has decreed a thing for someone, He has inclined it toward him. And tāḥa al-shayʾ nafsuhu — the thing itself came to pass.
تير: The letters tā', yāʾ and rāʾ are one word: al-tayyār is the wave of the sea that throws up spray. That is said to be its breathing. The wave that does not 'breathe' is called al-aʿjam, the mute one.
تيز:
The letters tā', yāʾ and zāʾ are one word. They said al-tayyāz is a thick-bodied man.

Al-Quṭāmī said, in a line of verse:
When the thick-muscled man came, we said: away, away — he found no room in his arm for it.
تيس: The letters tā', yāʾ and sīn are one word: al-tays, well known, among gazelles, goats and wild mountain goats. One of their proverbs is 'a she-goat that made herself a billy-goat' (ʿanzun istatyasat), said when a she-goat became bold and lively like a billy-goat. It is used as a proverb for a lowly person who puts on airs of strength.
تيع:
The letters tā', yāʾ and ʿayn are a single root, and it is a thing's agitation. One says tatāyaʿa al-baʿīr fī mishyatihi, if the camel shook its flanks as it walked; and the drunk man tatāyaʿu in his walking, if he flung himself about. Al-tatāyuʿ is headlong rushing into evil, and it is said to mean sheer obstinacy. In the ḥadīth: 'What makes you rush headlong into lying, as the moth rushes headlong into the fire?' Al-tatāyuʿ is never said of good.

Straying from the root: al-tīʿa, forty head of sheep, which is what came in the ḥadīth: 'On the tīʿa, one ewe is due.'
تيم:
The letters tā', yāʾ and mīm are a single root, and it is enslavement. One says tayyamahu al-ḥubb, if love enslaved him. The people of language said: from this comes Taym Allāh, meaning ʿAbd Allāh, servant of God.

Straying from this chapter: al-tīma, the ewe kept beyond the forty — or, it is said, the ewe a man milks at home. And ittāma al-rajul, if he slaughtered his tīma.

Al-Ḥuṭayʾa said, in a line of verse:
The neighbour-woman of the family of Laʾy does not slaughter her home-ewe, but they see to her provisioning instead.
تين:
The letters tā', yā' and nūn are not a root, except for al-tīn, the fig, which is well known. Al-Tīn is also a mountain.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Tawny, thirsty camels, they came to al-Tīn from the side,
driving along a thin cloud, its water cool.
تيه: The letters tā', yā' and hā' are a sound word, and it is a kind of bewilderment. Al-tīh and al-tayhā' are the open desert waste in which a person loses his way.
ثأ: The letters thā' and hamza are two words that are not a root. One says "tha'tha'tu bi'l-ibil," I shouted at the camels; and "I met so-and-so and tha'tha'tu from him," meaning I feared him.
ثأد:
The thā', the hamza, and the dāl are a single word from which derivation runs, and it is dampness and the like.

Al-tha'd is dampness. Al-tha'id is the moist, soft ground. One says tha'ida l-makānu, yatha'adu — the place grew damp. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Is Suwayd anything but a lurking lion —
the ground grew damp about him, so he moved off to graze.

As for al-tha'dā', on the pattern faʿalā' or faʿlā', it is the slave-woman, following the same pattern, and the two senses are one. It was said to ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may God be pleased with him: "You were no son of a slave-woman in that matter" [meaning: you were not found lowly or incapable]. Sometimes they invert it and say da'thā'. And they recite, in a line of verse:
We were no sons of a slave-woman, when
we settled every score with spear-points.
ثأر:
The thā', the hamza, and the rā' are a single root: the sought-after blood-vengeance. One says tha'artu fulānan bi-fulānin when you kill the killer of so-and-so. Qays ibn al-Khaṭīm said, in a line of verse:
I avenged ʿAdiyy and al-Khaṭīm, and did not neglect
the charge the elders set me to fulfil.

One says huwa l-tha'ru l-munīm — it is the vengeance that, once achieved, lets its seeker sleep. In the reflexive form one says itta'artu. Labīd said, in a line of verse:
And the old she-camels, should they come upon a worn bone of mine
after death — know that I used to seek vengeance.

As for their saying istatha'ara fulānun fulānan, when he called on him for help, this too belongs here, as though he were calling him to the pursuit of vengeance. A poet said, in a line of verse:
When a caller for help came to them, his aid was
a cry: up, and fly out, every sturdy, capable one!

Al-thu'ra is also blood-vengeance. A poet said, in a line of verse:
O sons of ʿĀmir, was I ever base in seeking my vengeance?
ثأط:
The thā', the hamza, and the ṭā' are a single word, not a root. Al-tha'ṭa is mud, plural tha'ṭ. They recite, in a line of verse:
In a spring of thick clay and black mire.
We say it is not a root because they also pronounce it with a dāl, as though it belongs to the chapter of letter-substitution.
ثأي:
The thā', the hamza, and the yā' are a single word indicating corruption and a tear.

Al-tha'y, on the pattern of al-thaʿy, is a rent. One says atha'ati l-khārizatu l-kharza, tuth'īhi — the seamstress tore the stitching. One says atha'aytu fī l-qawmi ithā'an — I inflicted a wound among the people. A poet said, in a line of verse:
What a ravage, what a rending —
ending in killing and captivity!
ثب: The letters thā' and bā' are a word not found in the two books, and if it is sound, it points to a thing reaching its limit. One says "thabba al-amr," when the matter was completed. It is said that al-thābba is a decrepit old woman, and they say: "is she young (shābba) or old (thābba)?"
ثبت:
The letters thā', bā' and tā' are a single word, and it is the lasting of a thing.

One says thabata thabātan wa thubūtan — it stayed firm. And a man is thabt and thabīt, steady. Ṭarafa said about al-thabīt, in a line of verse:
The dull-witted man has no heart in him, and the steady man — his own understanding has steadied him.
ثبج:
The letters thā', bā' and jīm are one word from which other words branch, and it is the main part of a thing and its middle.

1. Ibn Duraid said: the thabaj of everything is its middle.
2. A man is athbaj and a woman thabjā' when he or she is great in girth, big-bellied.
3. thabaja — said of a man when he squats down on the tips of his feet, as if he were cleaning himself an odd number of times, as in the ritual of istinjā'.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
When the armoured warriors crouched down on their knees, I hunched, O 'Amr, the hunching of the wood-gatherer.
This is said only because he juts out his back and midsection — his thabaj.

4. The plural of al-thabaj is athbāj and thubūj, and a people called thubj is the plural of athbaj.
5. tathabbaja — said of a man with a stick, when he set it across his back and put his hands behind it.
6. The thabaj of sand is its main bulk, and likewise the thabaj of the sea is its main body.

As for their saying thabbaja al-kalām tathbījan, it is that one does not deliver speech in its proper shape. Its origin is from this root, because it is as if he gathers it all together and brings it out bunched up, neither summarised nor set out in detail.
ثبر:
The letters thā', bā' and rā' are three roots: the first is ease, the second is destruction, and the third is persevering at a thing.

Easy, level land is ath-thabra. Thabra is a well-known place. The rajaz poet said:
I saved myself and abandoned his reckoning — how fine a young man, I left him at Thabra; the noble free man will never surrender a maiden.

Ibn Durayd said: ath-thabra is soil resembling lime; when a palm's root reaches it, it stops growing further, so they say: "the palm reached a thabra-layer of the ground."

Thabīr is a well-known mountain. Mathbir an-nāqa — the place where the she-camel drops her young. Thabara al-baḥr — the sea ebbed, and that uncovers a soft, level stretch of ground.

As for destruction: ath-thubūr; a man mathbūr is one who is ruined. In the Book of God Most High: {they called out there for ruin} [al-Furqān: 13].

As for the third: one says thābartu ʿalā ash-shay' — I persevered at the thing, kept steadily at it. Ibn Durayd mentioned: tathābarat ar-rijāl fī al-ḥarb — the men leapt at each other in battle; this belongs to this last root.
ثبن:
The letters thā', bā' and nūn are one root, and it is a container among containers.

1. al-thabn — your taking up a fold in your waist-wrap, in which you put what you have gathered of fresh dates or the like. In the hadith: "Let him eat, and not take up a thibān" [a pouch made from a folded garment].
2. al-mathbana — Ibn Duraid gave this by the same analogy, though he himself thought it was probably not genuine: a pouch in which a woman keeps her mirror and her implements. He claimed it is a word of the Yemeni dialect.
ثبي:
The letters thā', bā' and yā' are a single root, and it is persisting in something. Al-Khalīl said this. He also said: al-tathbiya is persisting in a thing, and al-tathbiya is also praising a person while he is still alive. He cited a line of verse by Labīd:
He keeps up praise from a noble man, and his saying:
'Come, enjoy this fine greeting, and drink.'
This is a sound root.

As for al-thuba, it is a troop of horsemen — they form a thuba; its plurals are thubāt and thubūn. 'Amr said, in a line of verse:
As for the day we feared for them,
our horsemen came to be in bands, in troops.

Al-Khalīl said: al-thuba is also the thuba of a watering-trough, its middle, to which the water returns. This is Al-Khalīl's own reasoning for the matter, and it shows that the letter dropped from al-thuba is a wāw before the bā', since he held it to be from yathūbu (it returns).

He said after that: as for common speakers, they form its diminutive as thubayya, following the surface spelling. Those who say thuwayba as the diminutive of the trough-sense thuba are keeping to the strict rule, restoring the missing letter to its place — just as they said ruwayyi'a as the diminutive of rawiyya, because it is from rawwa'tu (I deliberated).

What I hold is that the origin of the trough-thuba and the horsemen-thuba is one and the same, with no difference between them. The diminutive in both is thubayya, and its reasoning is what we opened this entry with, in speaking of al-tathbiya — it is from thabbā 'alā l-shay'i, when he persisted in a thing. As for deriving thuwayba from rawiyya, holding it to be from rawwa'tu, that is open to question.
ثتن:
The letters thā', tā' and nūn are not a root. They say: thatina al-laḥm — the meat went rotten and foul. And thatinat lathatuhu — his gum went slack and stank.

A line of verse says:
A gum that had gone rotten, foul with rot.

We said it is not a root only because they say sometimes thatinat and sometimes thanitat — the same two letters transposed.
ثج:
The letters thā' and jīm are a single root, and it is the pouring of a thing. One says "thajja al-mā'," he poured out the water; and "water thajjāj" means pouring copiously. God Almighty said: {and We have sent down from the rain-clouds pouring water} [al-Naba': 14]. One says "the valley was crammed full with the rush of water" (iktaẓẓa al-wādī bi-thajīj al-mā'), when it reached its two banks.

Abū Dhu'ayb said, in a line of verse:
It watered the mother of 'Amr at the end of every night, with dark rain-clouds whose water pours down.

And in the hadith: "The best of the Hajj is al-'ajj and al-thajj." Al-'ajj is raising the voice in the talbiya, the pilgrim's call; al-thajj is the flowing of the blood of the sacrificial animal. From this too is the hadith about the woman with prolonged bleeding: "I am pouring it out, a real pouring."
ثجر:
The letters thā', jīm and rā' are a single root, pointing to the wideness and breadth of a thing.

1. thajrat al-wādī — the middle of the valley, the part of it that widens out.
2. waraq thajr — broad leaves. Anything you make broad, you have "thajjartahu."
3. thujrat al-naḥr — the middle of the upper chest, and what is around the throat area of it.
4. al-thujar — thick, heavy arrows.

One says "in his flesh there is tathjīr," meaning slackness.

As for their saying "the water inthajara," it gushed and overflowed, and "the blood inthajara from the stab-wound," this is not from this root, because the thā' in it is a substitute for a fā'. Likewise al-thajīr.
ثجل:
The letters thā', jīm and lām are a root pointing to the largeness of a hollow thing, and from there it is extended to things that are not hollow.

1. al-thujla — largeness of the belly. One says "a man athjal," and "a woman thajlā'." A water-skin thajlā' is a wide one. Abū al-Najm said, in a line of verse:
The gait of the water-carrying camels, with the wide water-skin.
It is also transmitted as "al-anjal," and this has been mentioned elsewhere.

2. julla thajlā' — a large palm-basket. He said, in a line of verse:
They spent the night feeding their guest small dry dates, while they themselves had the fine dates in large baskets.

This pattern of word-formation is left unused by al-Khalīl, and that is strange.
ثجم:
The letters thā', jīm and mīm are not a root; it is the continuation of rain for days. One says "athjamat al-samā'," when the sky kept raining for days without letting up. I take it that the thā' here is a shift from a sīn, except that once it is turned into a thā', it is put into the pattern af'ala.

Here is another word, and God knows best if it is sound: they said al-thajm is quickness in turning away from a thing. God knows best.
ثحج: The letters thā', ḥā' and jīm. Ibn Durayd mentioned, under thā', ḥā' and jīm, a word he claimed belonged to Mahra ibn Ḥaydān. They say "thaḥajahu bi-rijlihi," when he struck him with his foot. Abū Bakr [Ibn Durayd] has gone rather far in citing this — as far as he could.
ثخن:
The letters tha', kha' and nun indicate a thing's weightiness combined with heaviness.

1. thakhuna ash-shay' thakhana — the thing became thick, dense.
2. the forbearing, steady man is thakhin.
3. cloth dense in weft and warp, from the excellence of its weave, is thakhin.
4. athkhantuhu — I weighed him down, incapacitated him.

God, Most High, said: {until he has thoroughly subdued them in the land} [al-Anfal: 67] — because the slain man has been so weighed down that no movement is left in him. "I left him muthkhan," meaning: beaten down.

Some said: the unarmed man, with no weapon on him, is called thakhin — and this fits the root's derivation, because his movement lessens, out of fear for himself.
ثدق:
The letters thā', dāl and qāf are a single word. "Thadaqa al-maṭar," the rain poured. A cloud is thādiq. Thādiq is also the name of a horse, as though its owner likened it to a cloud.

He said, in a line of verse:
She spent the night blaming me over Thādiq, that he be sold — my defiance of her had grown serious.
That is, my defiance of her. "Li-yushrā" means "to be sold."
ثدم: The letters thā', dāl and mīm are a word that is not a root. They claim that al-thadm is the same as al-fadm, a dull, clumsy man. If this is sound, it belongs to the category of letter-substitution.
ثدن: The letters thā', dāl and nūn are a word. They say al-thadin is a man abundant in flesh. It is also said that al-thadan is rather the change of odor of meat, meat going off.
ثدي:
The letters thā', dāl and yā' are a single word: it is al-thady, a woman's breast. The plural is athdin. Al-thadyā' is a woman large in the breast.

A distinction was then made between this and what belongs to a man: for a man it is called al-thundu'a, with damma and a hamza, or al-thanduwa, with fatḥa and no hamza.
ثر:
The letters thā' and rā' are an analogy that never fails, and it is the copiousness of an abundant thing. One says "cloud tharr," meaning copious. And "'ayn tharra," a cloud that rises from the direction of the qibla.

'Antara said, in a line of verse:
Every copious cloud rained generously upon it, and they left every hollow like a silver coin.

One says "tharartu al-shay'" and "tharraytuhu," meaning I moistened it. A she-camel tharra is one abundant in milk. A stab-wound tharra is one that let blood flow copiously and abundantly.

Al-tharthār is a man much given to talk. In the hadith: "The most hateful of you to me are the tharthārūn, the pompous talkers." Al-Tharthār is also the name of a particular valley.

Al-Akhṭal said, in a line of verse:
By my life, Sulaym and 'Āmir met, on the side of al-Tharthār, the bawling of a young camel.
ثرب:
The letters thā', rā' and bā' are two words unrelated in origin, with no branches to either.

Al-tathrīb is blame, taking someone to task over a sin. God Most High said: {No blame upon you today} [Yūsuf: 92]. This is one root.

The other is al-tharb, a thin fat that covers the stomach-lining and intestines; its plural is thurūb.
ثرد:
The letters thā', rā' and dāl are a single root: the crumbling of a thing, and what resembles that. One says "tharadtu al-tharīd athruduhu," I crumbled the tharīd, bread crumbled in broth. It is also said, and this is from the same analogy, that al-tharad is a cracking of the two lips.

It came in the hadith concerning the slaughter of an animal: "Whatever slits open the veins of the throat is lawful, so long as it is not muthrad" — meaning that the blade must not be blunt, causing the place of slaughter to be crushed, the way a thing cracks and splinters when torn roughly rather than cut cleanly.
ثرم: The letters thā', rā' and mīm are a single word from which other words are derived. One says "tharamtu al-rajul fa-tharima," I broke his front tooth and he became gap-toothed; and "tharamtu thaniyyatahu fa-ntharamat," I broke his incisor and it broke off. Al-Tharmā' is a watering-place belonging to Kinda.
ثروى:
The letters thā', rā' and the weak letter are a single root: abundance, the opposite of dryness.

Al-Aṣma'ī said: "tharā al-qawm yathrūna," said of a people when they grew numerous and increased. "Athrā al-qawm," when their wealth grew abundant. "Tharā al-māl yathrū," when the wealth increased. "Tharawnā al-qawm," when we outnumbered them, that is, we were more than them.

One says "the thing between me and so-and-so is muthrin," meaning it has not been cut off; the origin of this is to say "the moisture of the earth between me and him has not dried up." Jarīr said, in a line of verse:
Do not let the moist ground between us dry out, for what is between me and you remains abundant.

Abū 'Ubayda said: among their proverbs, for a man's fear that his companion will cut him off, is "lā tūbis al-tharā baynī wa-baynaka," do not let the moist ground between us dry — meaning: let the matter between us not be severed.

Al-māl al-thariyy is abundant wealth. In the hadith of Umm Zar': "and he brought back to me abundant livestock." From this too a man is named Tharwān, and a woman Tharwā, then, in the diminutive, Thurayyā.

One says "tharraytu al-turba," I moistened the soil; "tharraytu al-aqiṭ," I poured water on the dried curd-cheese and kneaded it. One says "the moisture of water appeared on the horse," when it grew damp with its own sweat.

Ṭufayl said, in a line of verse:
They fended off as the fifth-time-watered camels are fended off, while the sweat-moisture already showed, trickling from their flanks.

One says "the two moistures met," which is when the rain comes and sinks into the ground until it meets the ground's own dampness. One says "arḍ tharyā'," a land possessing moisture.

Al-Kisā'ī said: "thariytu bi-fulān fa-anā tharin bihi," meaning I am made independent of other people by him. "Tharā Allāhu al-qawm," God made the people numerous. Al-tharā' is abundance of wealth.

'Alqama said, in a line of verse:
They desire abundance of wealth wherever they know it to be, while the flush of youth in them is a wondrous thing.
ثط: The letters thā' and ṭā' are a single word: al-thaṭaṭ is thinness of the beard. Such a man is thaṭṭ.
ثطأ: The letters thā', ṭā' and hamza are a word not to be relied upon. One says "thaṭa'tuhu," I trampled him underfoot.
ثطع: The letters thā', ṭā' and 'ayn are similar to what came before, except that they say "thaṭa'a al-rajul," the man exposed his rear. "Thuṭi'a," when he caught a head-cold. Other than this is sounder than it, though it has indeed been said. God knows best.
ثع: The letters thā' and 'ayn are a single word: al-tha'' is vomit. One says "tha'' tha''atan," when he vomited once.
ثعب:
The letters tha', 'ayn and ba' are a root indicating the stretching-out of a thing and its spreading — whether in water or otherwise.

Al-Khalil said: tha'abtu al-ma' atha'abuhu — I made the water burst forth so that it gushed out, like blood gushing from the nose. From this, math'ab is derived, the channel for rainwater.

Fitting under this too: ath-thu'ban, the huge, long serpent — by the same derivation, in its outstretched form and movement. He said, in a fragment of verse: "upon a track winding like the serpent of the thicket." Water too is sometimes called tha'b, a gushing stream; its plural is ath-thu'ban.
ثعر: The letters thā', 'ayn and rā' are a formation which, if sound, points to meanness and smallness. Al-thu'rūrān are like the two small nipple-like teats that flank a ewe's udder. On this analogy they call a short man thu'rūr.
ثعط:
The letters thā', 'ayn and ṭā' are a sound word. One says "tha'iṭa al-laḥm," when meat spoiled and went rank. He said, in a line of verse:
Eating meat left overnight that has gone rank.

Among what is carried onto this same meaning is al-tha'īṭ, fine dust that the wind blows about.
ثعل:
The letters thā', 'ayn and lām are a single root, and it is extra growth and an irregular state.

1. al-tha'al — an extra tooth, an irregularity among the teeth in where they grow in. One says "tha'ila al-rajul" and "tha'ilat sinnuhu," his tooth grew irregularly — he ya'thalu tha'alan; such a man is ath'al, a woman is tha'lā', and the plural is al-thu'l. Al-tha'al may also occur in the teats of a she-camel or cow, an extra growth on the two teats.

Al-Khalīl said: al-thu'lūl is an angry man. He recited, in a line of verse:
He is not a thu'lūl when asked and begged from, nor sullen one day when the guest has drawn near.

On this same analogy is a word al-Khalīl mentioned: that al-ath'al is a great chief, when he has excess of generosity.

2. Among what is derived from it is Thu'al, a clan of the Arabs. Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
I set down my two saddle-bags among Banū Thu'al; the noble is, for the noble, a fitting place to alight.

One says "ath'ala al-qawm," when the people disagreed among themselves.
ثعلب:
1. thaʿlab — the outlet by which water drains away from the threshing-floor. This is taken from thaʿaba, to gush out, with the lām in it an added letter.
2. thaʿlab al-rumḥ — the socket of a spear[-head]. This is a blend of al-thaʿb and al-ʿalb: in its shape it resembles al-mathʿab, a water-spout, and it is maʿlūb — al-ʿalb has been explained under its own root. Another view is that it is a blend of al-ʿalb and al-thalb, which is a weak, soft-shafted spear, its tip being thin, which makes it thalib, feeble.

3. al-thurmuṭa — mud and wetness. This word too is a blend of two words, from al-tharṭ and al-ramṭ, both meaning to smear or stain. One says thuriṭa fulān when he was smeared with a fault, and likewise rumiṭa.

4. ithbajarra — said of a people in their affair, when they doubted it and wavered from fright and terror. This is a blend of al-thabaj and al-thujra, because they draw back and gather together. The explanation of both those words has already passed.

The Book of Thā' is complete.
ثعم:
The letters thā', 'ayn and mīm are not a root to be relied upon. Ibn Durayd did not mention it as a root at all. Al-Khalīl, for his part, placed it once among the unused forms — so we were informed on his authority — and it was reported from him another time that al-tha'm is pulling out and dragging; one says "tha'amtuhu," meaning I pulled it out and dragged it. It was reported from him too that one says "the land of Banū So-and-so tatha''amat So-and-so," when it delighted him and drew him and pulled him toward it.

Some said: this is a copying error, and it is really "tana''amathu fa-tana''ama" — meaning it showed him what pleasure it held for him, so he sought that pleasure, that is, he made the sole of his foot work at walking toward it. To me this is no better than the first version. No transmission of any of it has been established as sound.
ثغا:
The thā', the ghayn, and the weak letter are a root indicating sound.

1. al-thughā' — the bleating of sheep.
2. al-thāghiya — the ewe.

One says, "mā lahu thāghiyatun wa lā rāghiyatun" — he has neither ewe nor she-camel.
ثغب:
The thā', the ghayn, and the bā' are a single root, and it is a pool of water in rugged ground. It is called thaghb or thagab, its plural thighāb or athghāb, and one also says thighbān. 'Ubayd said, in a line of verse:
And indeed she settles there, as though its froth were
a pool whose clearness is stirred through with wine.
ثغر:
The thā', the ghayn, and the rā' are a single root indicating an opening and a parting.

1. al-thaghr — a gap among the passes of a country. Also thughrat al-naḥr — the hollow of the breastbone, plural thughar. A line of verse is quoted:
And at times in the hollows of the throats.
2. al-thaghr — a person's front teeth. One says thughira al-ṣabiyy when a child's teeth fall out, and ittha'ghara when they grow back after falling — though some also say ittha'ghara for the falling itself. A poet said, in a line of verse:
A horse with all its teeth grown, bared on one side,
and a four-year-old, its side not yet shed.

One also says: the men of one clan met the men of another and thagharūhum — they blocked the way out against them, so they did not know which way to break through. A poet said, in a line of verse:
They routed their rivals with a jagged blade
and an edge, and hemmed the people in until they fell back.
ثغم:
The thā', the ghayn, and the mīm are used in a single word, al-thaghāma — a tree white in its fruit and its blossom, to which greying hair is likened. In the hadith: the Messenger of God, God bless him and his family and grant him peace, was brought Abū Quḥāfa [on the day of the Conquest of Mecca], and it was as though his head were thaghāma, so he was ordered to change its colour.

Ibn Durayd overlooked this word and did not mention it, despite how well known it is. And it has been said that al-thaghim is a fierce hunting dog, though I did not find this in the two reference books. If it is sound, it belongs to the chapter of letter-substitution, because the thā' stands in for a fā' — and it has been mentioned in its place.
ثفر:
The thā', the fā', and the rā' are a single word indicating the hindmost part.

Al-thafar is the crupper-strap of a riding animal. One says istathfarat al-mar'atu bi-thawbihā when a woman wraps herself in her garment, then folds the end of the wrap back between her legs and tucks it into the waistband behind her. Al-thafr is the private part of a beast of prey or another animal. A poet said, in a line of verse:
May God repay, on her account, the two one-eyed men with reproach,
and ʿAbda with reproach for the private part of the crooked young cow.
ثفروق: al-thafrūq is the stem-cap of the date. This word is a blend [manḥūt] made from al-thafr, which is the rear or hindmost part, and from faraqa, to separate — because it is something at the rear of the date that comes away, separating from it. This is a plausible explanation, not far-fetched.
ثفل:
The thā', the fā', and the lām are a single root: a thing that settles beneath another thing, whether from murkiness or something else. One says huwa thuflu l-qidri — it is the pot's sediment, meaning what settles as dregs.

1. al-thifāl — the piece of hide laid beneath the millstone. It is also said to be a piece of fur set beside the millstone. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Its millstone-mat lies to the east of Najd,
and all of Quḍāʿa is its feeding-mouth.
Another poet said, in a line of verse:
So it grinds you as the millstone grinds upon its mat,
and conceives though barren, then bears, and bears twins.
2. al-thafāl — the slow camel; the naming holds, for from slowness it seems to settle beneath its load, hardly ever moving.
ثفن:
The thā', the fā', and the nūn are a single root: a thing's clinging fast to another thing. Al-Khalīl said: thafinat al-ba'īr are the parts of a camel's body that touch the ground and so grow thick and calloused, like the two knees and others.

He and others said: thafantu l-shay'a bi-l-yad, athfinuhu — I struck the thing with my hand. He said of al-thafina, in a line of verse:
He leaned upon five level parts —
the breastbone-pad, and calluses worn smooth.

One says thāfantu ʿalā l-shay' — I kept steadily at the thing. And they say thāfantuhu ʿalā l-shay' — I helped him with it. That follows the same sense.
ثفي:
The thā', the fā', and the weak letter are a single root: al-uthfiyya — a hearthstone, plural athāfiyy. Sometimes they lighten the word, though that is not the better usage.

1. al-mar'a al-muthaffiya — a woman whose three husbands have died [leaving her].
2. al-rajul al-muthaffī — a man whose three wives have died [leaving him].

They also say, by way of metaphor, "there remained of the sons of so-and-so a rough uthfiyya," when a number of them remained.

Al-thafā' is a plant, and does not belong to this root. In the hadith: "What healing is there in the two bitter things: ṣabr and thafā'?" They said: it is mustard.
ثقب:
The letters thā', qāf and bā' are a single word, and it is for a thing to pass through. One says thaqabtu al-shay'a athqubuhu thaqban, I pierced the thing.

Al-thāqib, in His words, the Exalted: {the piercing star} [al-Ṭāriq: 3] — they said it is a star whose light passes through all the heavens.

One also says thaqabtu al-nāra, meaning you kindled it up; that act is called thuqba or dhukwa. This is said because its light passes through.
ثقف:
The letters thāʾ, qāf and fāʾ are one word to which the branches return: the setting straight of a thing's crookedness. It is said thaqqaftu al-qanāt, when you straightened the crookedness of a spear-shaft. A poet said, in a line of verse:

The straightener looks along the joints of his spear-shaft ... until his tool sets right its warp

And thaqiftu hādhā al-kalāma min fulānin, I picked up this saying from so-and-so. A man is thaqif laqif, one who grasps whatever he hears, evenly and accurately. It is said thaqiftu bihi, meaning you got hold of him. A poet said, in a line of verse:

But if you get hold of me, then kill me ... and if I am not caught, you will see how I fare

If it is asked what connects this to the first sense — the answer is: has he not, in 'thaqifa'-ing him, held him fast? And likewise one who gets the better of a thing holds it fast. So the sense-pattern takes both together as one.
ثقل:
The letters thā', qāf and lām are a single root from which branch words close to one another in sense, and it is the opposite of lightness. And for that reason the jinn and mankind are called al-thaqalān, the two weighty ones, for the greatness of their number. And the athqāl of the earth are its treasures, in His saying, exalted: {and the earth brings forth its burdens} [al-Zalzala: 2]; and it is said they are the bodies of the children of Adam. God, exalted, said: {and it carries your burdens} [al-Naḥl: 7], that is, your bodies.

And al-Khansā' said, in a line of verse:
Is it after the son of ʿAmr, of the house of al-Sharīd ... that the earth has decked itself out with its burdens?

That is, it adorned its dead with him. And one says: the people set off with their thaqla, that is, with their baggage; and: I find in myself a thaqala, a heaviness. So they say, by way of distinguishing the forms, though the reasoning is one and the same.
ثكل: The thā', the kāf, and the lām are a single word indicating the loss of a thing, seemingly reserved for the loss of a child. One says thakilathu ummuhu, tathkaluhu, thaklan — his mother lost him. To his mother belongs al-thukl, bereavement. If a speaker says it of another who is not truly his child, he only means it in that borrowed sense; the true origin is what has been stated.
ثكم: The thā', the kāf, and the mīm are a single word: the gathering-place of a thing, its main part. One says tanaḥḥa ʿan thakami l-ṭarīq — move off the thakam of the road, meaning its main, well-trodden part.
ثكن:
The thā', the kāf, and the nūn are a single word indicating the gathering-place of a thing. One says tanaḥḥa ʿan thakani l-ṭarīq — move off the thakan of the road, meaning its main, well-trodden part.

Al-thuknah is a flock, and a group, plural thukan. Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
He grapples an ash-grey, dark dove,
to catch her among a flock in a pigeon-house.
ثل:
The letters thā' and lām are two distinct roots: one is gathering, the other is falling, demolition, and humiliation.

The first: al-thalla is a flock of sheep. Some say this name applies specifically to the woolly sheep; that is why they say "ḥabl thalla," a rope of wool, and "a cloak good in its thalla," its wool. A poet said, in a line of verse:
They have paired me with a wretched, feeble man, worn out like the wet rope of the flock's wool.

Al-thulla is also a group of people. God Almighty said: {a group from the first generations and a group from the later ones} [al-Wāqi'a: 39].

The second: "thalaltu al-bayt," I demolished the house. Al-thulla is the earth thrown up from a well. Al-thalal is destruction.

Labīd said, in a line of verse:
We struck hard among Murād a great striking, and Ṣudā', bringing them to ruin.

One says "thulla 'arshuhu," when a person's condition worsened. Zuhayr said, in a line of verse:
You two came to the aid of al-Aḥlāf whose support had already been brought down, and of Dhubyān, when their feet slipped on the sandal.

Some said "thulla 'arshuhu" (and also "'urshuhu") means he was killed. They cited, in a line of verse:
And 'Abd Yaghūth, the birds circling around him, his two neck-joints struck down by the sharp, well-made sword.

The two 'urshān are the place where the neck is set into the shoulders.
ثلب:
The thā', the lām, and the bā' are a sound word, regular in its pattern, concerning the limpness of a thing and its being frayed.

1. al-thalib — the limp spear. Al-Hudhalī said, in a line of verse:
And a straight spear of Khaṭṭ-reed,
neither flawed nor limp.
2. al-thilb — the very old, worn-out one; one says thaliba, thalban.

One says thalabtuhu when you find fault with him. He is dhū thalibatin — a man with a fault, and that follows the same pattern, for it wears him down and frays him.

A woman is thālibatu l-shawā, meaning one whose feet are cracked. A poet said, in a line of verse:
A woman of cracked feet bore Ghassān,
enduring of night-travel, her neck knowing no vine.

Al-thalab is grime; one says innahu la-thalibu l-jild — his skin is grimy and roughened. The pattern is the same throughout.
ثلث:
The letters thā', lām and thā' are one word, and it is in number; one says two and three. And al-thulāthā' is one of the days. A poet said, in a line of verse:
[They said] his Tuesday is wealth and a feast, and every one of his days is a Tuesday.

And thālithat al-athāfī is the jutting spur of the mountain, to which two rocks are joined and then the cooking-pot is set upon them. And it is what al-Shammākh meant, in a line of verse:
Two neighbours of stone stayed on at their two camping grounds, dark red above, black where the fire burned beneath them.

And al-thalūth of camels is the one that fills three vessels when she is milked. And al-mathlūtha is the water-skin made of three hides. And a rope is mathlūth when it is of three strands.
ثلج:
The thā', the lām, and the jīm are a single root: the well-known snow, from which the words gathered in its chapter branch out. One says arḍun mathlūjatun when snow has fallen upon land.

If they say rajulun mathlūju l-fu'ād, he is the dull, incapable man — from the same pattern, meaning that his heart is as though struck by snow, so that its warmth has cooled and it has gone numb. A poet said, in a line of verse:
He woke with a heart chilled and swollen.

And if they say thalija bi-khabarin atāhu, he was gladdened by news that reached him — this too belongs to the root, because when distress settles on the heart it brings a burning ache, and when its opposite arrives, the coolness of joy comes. This is common in their speech: do you not see that in cursing someone they say, "May God heat his eye," and in blessing him they say, "May God cool his eye"? On this pattern they also say ḥafara ḥattā athlaja — he dug until he reached the gathered clay, moist as snow.
ثلط: The thā', the lām, and the ṭā' are a single word: the dung of the camel and of the cow.
ثلغ: The thā', the lām, and the ghayn are a single word: the crushing of a thing. One says thalaghtu ra'sahu — I crushed his head. What has fallen from ripe dates and split open they call muthallagh.
ثلم: The thā', the lām, and the mīm are a single root: a chipping that occurs at the edge of a thing, like the thulma at the rim of a vessel. Sometimes a gap is also called thulma even when it is not at an edge. A vessel is munthalim or mutathallim — chipped.
ثم:
The letters thā' and mīm are a single root: gathering with pliancy. One says "thamamtu al-shay' thamman," when he gathered it. It is mostly used of grass. A handful of grass is called al-thumma.

1. al-thumām — a weak, frail shrub, and a man is sometimes named after it. A poet said:
She made for it two sticks, one of nasham-wood and another of thumām.

2. al-thumām — some said it is what is broken off the branches of a tree and laid down for stacking clothes on; once it has dried it is called thumām.

One says "thamamtu al-shay' athummuhu thamman," when he gathered it and mended it. A verse is recited — God knows best whether it is sound:
I attended to my needs and spurned Bishr; wretched indeed is the resting-place of the starving travelers.

"Thammat al-shāh al-nabt bi-fīhā" — the ewe pulled up the plant with her mouth.

From this too is the hadith: "We were the people of its thamm and ramm," its gathering and mending — meaning we used to gather it thoroughly, that is, we took full charge of it.
ثمأ:
The thā', the mīm, and the hamza are a single word, not itself a root but a branch of the one before it.

Thama'a liḥyatahu — he dyed his beard; the hamza seems to stand in for a ghayn. One says thama'tu l-kam'ata fī l-samni — I dropped the truffle into the clarified butter, though there is something uncertain in this. If it is sound, it belongs to this chapter, because the truffle is as though dyed by the butter.
ثمد:
The thā', the mīm, and the dāl are a single root: the small amount of a thing.

1. al-thamd — water that is little, with nothing to replenish it.
2. thamadat fulānan al-nisā' — the women exhausted his seed/strength [through repeated intercourse].
3. mathmūd — a man so much asked of that what he has runs out. A line of verse was recited of al-mathmūd:
Or like the water of the drained well after it was full,
its flow now scant, its tears sparse, not returning.
4. al-thāmid — a young weaned lamb just beginning to graze, because what it takes is little.

Anomalous to the chapter is al-ithmid, the well-known [antimony/kohl]; some philologists said it belongs here, because what is used of it is little — but this cannot be settled with certainty.
ثمر:
The letters thā', mīm and rā' are a single root, and it is a thing that comes out of another thing, gathered together, and then other things are carried upon it by borrowing.

Al-thamar, fruit, is well known. One says thamara, and thamar, and thimār, and thumur. And the tree that is thāmir is the one that has reached the time when it bears fruit. And al-muthmir is the one that has fruit on it. So said Ibn Durayd. And thammara al-rajul mālahu: he tended his property in the best way. And it is said in prayer: "May God make his wealth grow", that is, increase it. And al-thamīra of milk is when it begins to gather and becomes like the white pith of the palm; and this is the reasoning. And the knot of a whip is called a thamara, and that is by likeness.

And of what falls outside the chapter is laylat ibn thamīr, and it is the moonlit night. And I do not know what its origin is.
ثمغ:
The thā', the mīm, and the ghayn are a single word, not to be extended by analogy nor branched from.

One says thamaghtu l-thawba thamghan — I dyed the garment with a deep, saturating dye. A poet said, in a line of verse:
I left the sons of al-Ghuzayyil without any pride,
as though their beards had been dyed with wars, a deep yellow dye.

There is here also a word not from this chapter, though still known: al-Kisā'ī said thamaghat al-jabal is its summit, with a thā'. Al-Farrā' said: what I heard is namagha, with a nūn.
ثمل:
The thā', the mīm, and the lām are a root that extends by regular analogy: a thing that remains and stays fixed, whether in small amount or great. One says dāru banī fulānin thamalun — the dwelling of so-and-so's sons is a settled home.

1. al-thamīla — what remains of fodder in the stomach; every remainder is a thamīla. It is so named because it stays, and the camels then drink relying on that remainder — otherwise they would need no drink at all, for how would they drink upon nothing? From this comes the saying fulānun thimālu banī fulān — so-and-so is the mainstay of his people, on the same pattern, for he is relied upon as the camels rely on that remaining fodder. Abū Ṭālib said of al-thimāl, of his nephew the Messenger of God, God bless him and his family and grant him peace, in a line of verse:
A fair man, by whose face the clouds are asked for rain,
the mainstay of orphans, a shelter for widows.
2. al-thamla — the remainder of water.
3. al-thumāl — poison left to steep. Al-Hudhalī said, in a line of verse:
And after a little while he gave her to drink, together with another,
from a swift, deadly, bitter, steeped poison.
4. al-thumla — the remainder of tar left in the vessel. A poet said, in a line of verse:
As the remnant is smeared round in the tar.
Here al-thamala is the rag with which a camel is smeared with tar; it took the name of the tar by association. It is sometimes also called mithmala.
5. al-thamil — the drunk man, so named for the remainder of drink that intoxicated and thickened his senses. A poet said, in a line of verse:
I said to the people at our home, when they had grown drunk:
sheathe your swords — but how does a drunken drinker sheathe his?
6. al-thumāla — froth. Athmala l-labanu — the milk frothed; this draws on the root sense, though froth itself is short-lived. A poet said, in a line of verse:
When the froth's skin touches its muzzle,
it turns its two lips aside for the clear milk beneath, and bows to it.
Here he called the froth khirshā' [a membrane] and gave the milk the name thumāla. The two senses are close.
ثمن:
The letters thā', mīm and nūn are two roots: one of them is what is given in exchange for what is sold, and the other is a part out of eight.

The first is their saying bi'tu kadhā wa akhadhtu thamanahu — I sold such a thing and took its price. And Zuhayr said, in a line of verse:
And the prices of the sacrificial camels grew dear.

Whoever narrates it with a ḍamma, athmun, it is the plural of thaman, a price. And whoever narrates it with a fatḥa, athman al-budn, means the dearest of them in price.

As for al-thumun, it is one part out of eight. One says thamantu al-qawm athmunuhum when you take an eighth of their wealth. And al-thamīn is the eighth. A poet said, in a line of verse:
I am not of you and you are not of me, if [ever] an eighth of my wealth flies away.

And al-Shammākh or another said, in a line of verse:
And the like of the nobles of your people will never be raced, not to a quarter of the wager nor to an eighth.

And of what stands apart from the chapter is Thamīna, which is a town. And the Hudhalī said, in a line of verse:
With a truer courage than the friend of Thamīna, and keener when the hand loses its grip on the sword-hilt.

And from it also is al-mithmana, which is like a nosebag.
ثن:
The letters thā' and nūn are a single root, and it is a growth, whether of hair or of something else.

1. al-thunna — as regards hair, the hair overhanging the back of a mount's pastern.
2. al-thinn — apart from hair, dry, crumbled plant matter. He recited:
They kept striking the crumbled dry stalks of al-thinn, after the lush, murmuring meadow.

As for al-thunna, it is also what lies below the navel, on the lower belly of a mount — perhaps so named for the fine hairs that are there.
ثنت:
The thā', the nūn, and the tā' are a single word. Thanita l-laḥmu — the meat's smell changed [it spoiled]. Sometimes they say thatina instead. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And his gums went rank, dirḥāyah.
[This last word is obscure in the source and is left as printed.]
ثني:
The letters thā', nūn and yā' are a single root, and it is the repeating of a thing twice, or the making of it two things, either following one another or distinct. That is your saying thanaytu al-shay' thanyan, I doubled the thing. And al-ithnān, two in number, are well known. And al-thinā and al-thunyān are the one who comes after the chief, as though he were his second.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
You see us as seconds when their foremost man comes ... while their foremost man, if he comes to us, counts as a second.

It is also related as: "our second, if he comes to them, counts as their foremost". And al-thinā is a matter repeated twice. The Messenger of God, God's blessing and peace be upon him and his family, said: "There is no thinā in the alms", meaning that they are not taken twice in one year.

And Maʿn said, in a line of verse:
Is it for the sake of Bakr that you cut me to pieces with blame? ... By my life, her blaming was a second time over.

And al-Namir b. Tawlab said, in a line of verse:
And when you do not hit upon right guidance ... some of the blame comes round a second time.

And it is said a woman is thiny when she has borne two, and one does not say thilth, nor beyond that. And al-thināya is a rope of hair or of wool; it may be that it was so named because it is doubled, or because it can be doubled.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
[And] the rough stone and the doubled rope.

And al-thunyā of a slaughtered camel is the head or some other part when its owner reserves it for himself.

And the sense of al-istithnā', exception, follows the analogy of the chapter, in that its mention is doubled, once in the whole and once in the detail; for when you say "the people went out", Zayd and ʿAmr are among the people, and when you then say "except Zayd", you have mentioned Zayd a second time, an open mention. For that reason some of the grammarians said that it went out of what it had entered into, so that what governs it governs it as "twenty" governs the word dirham in "twenty dirhams". And this is sound, straight speech.

And al-mithnāt is the end of the nose-rein at the nose-peg, as though it were the second of the rein. And al-mathnāt is what is read of the Book and repeated. God, exalted, said: {And We have given you seven of the mathānī} [al-Ḥijr: 87], meaning that the reciting of them is doubled and repeated.
ثهل: The thā', the hā', and the lām are a single word: a mountain called Thahlān, which is well known. It has also been said — though I do not think it correct — that al-thahal is a spreading-flat upon the face of the earth.
ثوب:
The letters thā', wāw and bā' are a sound analogy from a single root, and it is returning and coming back. One says thāba yathūbu when he returned. And al-mathāba is the place to which people return. God, exalted, said: {And when We made the House a place of return for men, and a sanctuary} [al-Baqara: 125]. The people of commentary said: mathāba means they return to it and never have their fill of it. And al-mathāba is the standing-place of the water-drawer at the mouth of the well, and it is from this, because he returns to it; the plural is mathābāt.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And there is no remnant left for the standing-places of the well-frames ... when the props have been drawn out from beneath the frames.

And some people said: al-mathāba is a great number of people. If that is sound, it belongs to the chapter, because they are the company to which one returns. And one says thāba al-ḥawḍ, when the trough filled up.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
If your trough does not fill up before the drinking.

And it is so, as though it had been empty and then the water returned into it, or it came back full after having been empty. And al-thawāb, reward and recompense, is a thing that is returned to. And it is said that al-mathāba is the hunter's snare; if this is sound, it is because it is the place to which the game returns, by way of metaphor and likening.

The rajaz-poet said, in a line of verse:
When, oh when, will the snare be looked in upon ... perhaps some doddering old fellow has been caught.

By "old fellow" he means the mountain goat that he hunts. And it is said that al-thawāb is honey; and it belongs to the chapter, because the bees return to it.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
So it is sweeter than honey when ... you taste her mouth, by Him who creates souls.

They said: and the singular is thawāba. And Thawāb is the name of a man who used to be made a proverb for obedience, so it is said: "more obedient than Thawāb".

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And all my life I never used to obey a woman ... yet today I have become more obedient than Thawāb.

And al-thawb, the garment that is worn, may be from this same analogy, because it is worn and then worn again and returned to. And they sometimes express the soul by the word thawb, so it is said: he is clean of garment.
ثوخ:
The thā', the wāw, and the khā' are not a root, because their saying thākhati l-iṣbaʿ — the finger sank in — is simply a substitution for sākhat, with a sīn. Sometimes they say it with a tā': tākhat. The true root throughout all of this is the wāw. Abū Dhu'ayb said, in a line of verse:
So the finger sinks into it.
ثور:
The letters thā', wāw and rā' are two roots which, with a little thought, can almost be joined into one: the first is a thing's rising up and stirring, the second is a kind of animal.

The first: their saying thāra ash-shay' yathūru thawran, thu'ūran, and thawarānan — the thing stirred up, rising. Thāratil-ḥaṣba tathūru — the measles rash flared up. Thāwara fulānun fulānan — so-and-so leapt at so-and-so, as if each rose up against the other. Thawwara fulānun ʿalā fulānin sharran — so-and-so stirred up evil against so-and-so, brought it into the open. It is possible that ath-thawr, in the usage of those who say it means "pond-scum/algae," comes from this, because it is a thing that has risen up over the surface of the water.

The second: ath-thawr, plural ath-thīrān — the bull; also pluralized al-athwār. As for their calling a chief thawr — this is by way of comparison, if the Arabs indeed use it so; though I myself have not seen a sound transmission of it.

As for the saying of the poet, in a line of verse:
as for me and my killing of Sulayk, then binding his blood-price — like the bull that is struck, when the cows shy away from the water —
some said: this means the star called ath-Thuwār itself, because they say a jinn rides on its back, so the cattle refuse to drink. It is from the saying:
and what is his fault, that the cattle shied from the water — they shy from the water only so that it be struck.
Others said it means the algae, already mentioned. Thawr is a mountain. Thawr is also a tribe among the Arabs — this too by way of comparison. As for ath-thawr [in yet another sense], it is a lump of dried curd. It is possible that it is from... [the entry breaks off unfinished in the source].
ثول:
The thā', the wāw, and the lām are a single word indicating disturbance, to which its branches return.

1. al-thawal — a disease that afflicts the ewe, so that its limbs go slack; it can also occur in males, and one says tays athwal — a slack-limbed billy-goat. Sometimes the foolish man, slow to any good, is also called athwal, from the same sense of disturbance.
2. al-thawl — a swarm of bees, from the same root, because when it gathers it grows agitated, one part jostling over another.

One says tathawwala l-qawmu ʿalā fulānin tathawwulan — the people swarmed together upon so-and-so.
ثوم: The thā', the wāw, and the mīm are a single word: al-thūma, from among the plants [garlic]. Sometimes they also call the pommel of a sword's hilt thūma, though that is not the true root sense.
ثوي:
The letters thā', wāw and yā' are a single sound word pointing to staying in a place.

One says thawā yathwī, so he is thāwin, one who stays.

And a poet said, in a line of verse:
Asmā' has given us notice of her parting; many a one who stays is wearied of by his staying.

And one says athwā as well.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
He stayed, and made his night short so that he might be provisioned; then he went, and broke the promise made of Qutayla.

Al-thawiyya and al-thāya are the fold of the sheep. And al-Thawiyya is a place. And umm mathwā al-rajul is the mistress of the house where a man lodges. The analogy of it all is one. And al-thāya also: stones raised up for the shepherd, that he may come back to them at night, being a landmark for him.
ثيل: The thā', the yā', and the lām are a single word: al-thīl, the sheath of a camel's penis. Al-thīl is also a plant that entwines upon itself; its derivation and that of the word before it are one and the same. It is not far-fetched that this yā' is a turning of a wāw, from their saying tathawwalū ʿalayhi — they gathered together upon him.
جأ:
The letters jīm and hamza are not a root, because it is the imitation of a sound. One says "jaʾjaʾtu bi-l-ibil" when I called the camels to drink. The noun is al-jīʾ. A line runs:
And never, upon the calls of jīʾ nor of hīʾ, was my praising of you.
جأب:
The letters jim, hamza and ba' are two words. One of them indicates earning. One says ja'abtu ja'ban, meaning I earned and worked. He said:

God sees my work and my earning.

The other sense is unrelated to this: it is the donkey among the wild donkeys -- the tough, hardy one. And al-maghra, red ochre, is pronounced with the hamza or without it.
جأث: The letters jim, hamza and tha' are a single word indicating terror. One says ju'itha yuj'athu, when a person was terrified. And in the hadith: "I was struck with terror at it."
جأز: The letters jim, hamza and za' name a kind of ailment. They said: al-ja'z is like the choking that seizes the chest at the onset of rage. One says ja'iza al-rajul -- the man was seized with this choking.
جأف: The letters jim, hamza and fa' are a single word indicating terror. The fa' seems to stand in place of the tha'. One says ju'ifa al-rajul, like ju'itha.
جب:
The letters jīm and bā', doubled, are two roots: the first is cutting, the second is the gathering of a thing.

The first: al-jabb is cutting; one says "jababtuhu ajubbuhu jabban." A castrated one is majbūb, clearly so [al-jibāb, castration]. One says "jabbahu" when he surpassed him in beauty or otherwise, as if he cut him off from rivalling or competing with him. A line runs: "She cut off all the women of the world by that means — so that, beside her, they are all like mere lovers." She had measured her hips with a cord and sent word to them: is there one among you like her? There was not, so she surpassed them all. This is like another's saying: "Ḥabāba, daughter of Jazʾ, gave the people of Jalājil a long cord as a gift." al-jabab — that a camel's hump is cut off; the camel is ajabb, the she-camel jabbāʾ.

The second root: al-jubba, well known, because it envelops the body and gathers it within itself. al-jubba is also that into which the socket of a spear fits, the part that takes the spearhead. al-jubjuba — a sack of hides in which soil is gathered when it is carried off. al-jubjuba — also the stomach-lining in which meat is put, preserved meat. "jabba al-nās al-nakhl," when they pollinated the palms — that is the season of al-jibāb. al-jabūb — hard, rugged ground, so named for its compactness. Abū Khirāsh said, describing an eagle that lifted up its prey and then let it drop, and it struck the ground:
It met it on a bare, open waste, and struck the hard ground between its eyes.
al-majabba — the main track of a road, its gathering-point. al-jubb — the well. "jabbaba tajbīban" — he fled, because he draws himself together for flight and gathers himself up. al-jubāb — something that gathers on camels' milk like cream, though camels have no true butter. A poet said: "The saliva binds his mouth fast, as fast as the jubāb clings to the lips of the milk-skin." Ibn Duraid said: al-jibjāb is abundant water, and likewise al-jabājib.
جبأ:
The letters jim, ba' and hamza are two roots. One of them is drawing back from a thing. One says jaba'tu 'an al-shay' -- I flinched from it, when you shrink back timidly. And al-jubba', contracted and with the hamza, is the coward. He said, in a line of verse:

I am not, before the turns of fate, a coward, nor am I, before God's bounty, one who despairs.

One also says jaba'at 'ayni 'an al-shay' -- my eye recoiled from the thing, when it started back from it. And sometimes they say the opposite of this: jaba'tu 'ala al-qawm -- I came upon the people from above, looking down on them.

Anomalous to this root is al-jab' -- the truffle, three of them being thalathatu ajbu'. And ajba'ati al-ard -- the land abounded in truffles.

Also anomalous is their saying ajba'tu -- when you buy a standing crop before its produce has ripened; some say it without the hamza. And it is related in the hadith: "Whoever practises ijba' has practised usury." It is possible the hamza was dropped here because the word was paired with arba.
جبت: The letters jīm, bā' and tā' are a single word. Al-jibt is the sorcerer, and it is also said to mean the soothsayer.
جبذ: The letters jim, ba' and dhal are not a root, because it is a single word with its letters reversed. One says jabadhtu al-shay', meaning the same as jadhabtuhu -- I pulled it.
جبر:
The letters jīm, bā' and rā' are a single root, and it is a kind of greatness, height and straightness. So *al-jabbār* is that which has grown tall and gone beyond the hand's reach; one says *faras jabbār* and *nakhla jabbāra*, a tall palm. And *dhū al-jubbūra* and *dhū al-jabarūt*, the possessor of might, is God, whose praise is exalted. A poet said, in a line of verse:
For if you anger me, the very pebbles will be angry with you, and so will the possessor of might, the lofty one.

And one says of it *jabriyya* and *jabarūwa* and *jabarūt* and *jubbūra*. And *jabartu al-ʿaẓma fa-jubira* — I set the bone and it was set. A poet said, in a line of verse:
God has set the religion right, and it was set right.

The splints of wood with which a broken bone is bound are called *jibāra*; the plural is *jabā'ir*. And the bracelet was likened to it and so called *jibāra*. And a poet said, in a line of verse:
And she showed you a hand in its dye, and a wrist that filled the bracelet.

Among what stands apart from this chapter is *al-jubār*, which is a loss that goes unpaid for. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: "The well is *jubār*, and the mine is *jubār*." As for the well, it is the ancient one from of old, whose digger and owner are not known; a man or something else falls into it, and that is unpaid for. And the mine is *jubār*: a people dig it for a wage and it caves in on them, and that is *jubār*, because they are working for a wage.

And one says *ajbartu fulānan ʿalā al-amr* — I forced so-and-so to the matter — and that only comes about by mastery and a kind of setting oneself above him.
جبز: The letters jim, ba' and za' are not, in my view, a root -- although they say al-jabiz is dry bread; but this is doubtful. And some people say al-jibz is the base, ignoble man. If this is correct, then the za' stands in place of a sin [so the word is really jibs].
جبس: The letters jim, ba' and sin are a single word: al-jibs, which is the base, ignoble man -- also said to mean the coward.
جبع: The letters jim, ba' and 'ayn: it is said there are two words in it. One of them is al-jubba', from arrows -- one that has neither feather nor head. And it is said al-jubba'a is the short woman.
جبل:
The letters jīm, bā' and lām are a root that runs steady and can be reasoned upon, and it is the gathering of a thing in height. Al-jabal - the mountain - is well known, and al-jabal is also the great and numerous company. A poet said, in a line of verse:
As for Quraysh, you will never meet them but that they are the best of those who go barefoot and who wear sandals,
And nothing but that they are the mountain of God, which the mountains fall short of, so that no mountain matches it.

A she-camel with a huge hump is called jabala. Some said: the hump itself is jabla. And imra'a jabla - a woman huge in build. And he said of the she-camel, in a line of verse:
And the hump rose high upon a great frame, like a smooth bare rock among the crags of [al-Ṣajan].

Al-jibilla is the created nature. Al-jibill is the numerous company. God - exalted is He - said: {And he led astray from among you many a jibill} [Yā-Sīn: 62], and (jubull) as well. One says ḥafara al-qawm fa-ajbalū, when they dug and reached hard ground.
جبن: The letters jīm, bā' and nūn are three words, none measured against the others. Al-jubn is what is eaten (cheese) — its nūn is sometimes doubled, with the bā' vowelled with ḍamma. Al-jubn is also the quality of al-jabān, cowardice. Al-jabīnān are the two sides of the forehead, right and left; each one is a jabīn.
جبه:
The letters jīm, bā' and hā' are a single word, and other things are then likened to it. Al-jabha is the forehead, and by extension a body of horsemen. Al-jabha, among people, is a group. Al-jabha is also a star — it is said to be the forehead of Leo.

From this entry is their saying jabahnā l-mā'a, when we came to water that had no rope-and-post rig or drawing-tool over it. This belongs to the same entry, because they faced it head-on with nothing between them to help draw the water.

The Arabs say: 'Every jābih gets one jawza (one turn), then it is announced that his turn is over.' Al-jābih is as we described. Al-jawza is the amount he drinks there before he passes on.
جبي:
The letters jīm, bā' and the weak letter that comes after them are a single root, pointing to gathering a thing together and to coming together.

One says jabaytu al-māl ajbīhi jibāyatan — I collected the money. And jabaytu al-mā' fī al-ḥawḍ — I gathered the water in the watering trough. The trough itself is a jābiya.

Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
A great bowl goes round in the evening to the family of al-Muḥallaq, like the cistern of the old Iraqi man, brimming full.

Al-jabā, with a short ending, is the ground around a well. Al-jibā, with i on the jīm, is what has been gathered of water in a trough or elsewhere. It is also called jibwa and jibāwa. Al-Kisā'ī said: jabaytu al-mā' fī al-ḥawḍ jiban — I gathered the water in the trough. And jabbā yujabbī is said when a man prostrates himself; and that is a drawing of himself together.
جث:
The letters jīm and thā' point to the gathering of a thing; it is a sound analogy.

al-juththa — a person's body, when sitting or lying down. al-juthth — a raised mound of earth, like a hillock. Ibn Duraid said: I reckon that juththa, of a man, is from this. One says al-jathth is a kind of debris mixed into honey — this is what al-Hudhalī mentioned: "The ropes did not rest until they had set it down beside the swarm, clearing away its debris and tending to it." One says al-jathth is also wax; the same analogy holds. One says a plant is juthājith, meaning thick-grown; perhaps al-jathjāth, a plant, is from this. "juthithtu min al-rajul" — you were startled by the man, because one who is frightened draws himself together.

If someone should ask: how do you fit onto this analogy "jathathtu al-shayʾ" and "ijtathaththuhu," I uprooted the thing, and al-jathīth, young palm-shoots, and al-mijaththa, the iron tool a thing is uprooted with? The answer is that its analogy is that of this same root, because a thing is not majthūth, uprooted, unless it has been pulled up with all its roots and rootlets, so that nothing of it is left — so it comes back to what we set down as the root sense.
جثر: The letters jim, tha' and ra' are a word about which there is doubt. Ibn Durayd said: a jathr place is ground mixed with salty soil.
جثل:
The letters jim, tha' and lam are a sound root indicating the softness of a thing. One says sha'r jathl -- hair that is abundant and soft. And ijtha'alla al-nabt -- the plant grew tall. And ijtha'alla al-ta'ir -- the bird ruffled up its feathers.

Anomalous to this root is the saying "thakilat-hu al-jathal" -- may al-jathal, a name for his mother, be bereaved of him. And al-jathla is said to be the black ant.
جثم:
The letters jīm, thā' and mīm are a sound root indicating the gathering together of a thing.

1. al-juthmān — a person's body.
2. jathama — he pressed himself flat to the ground.
3. jathama aṭ-ṭā'ir yajthumu — the bird crouched down on the ground.
