In the hadith: "He forbade al-mujaththama" — an animal held down and shot at until death.
جح:
The letters jīm and ḥā' point to the greatness of a thing. The chief among men is called al-jaḥjāḥ, plural jaḥājiḥ and jaḥājiḥa.

Umayya said, in a line of verse:
What lords, mighty chiefs, were at Badr and al-'Aqanqal, marzbāns!

1. ajaḥḥat — said of a female when she conceived and neared her time of delivery, that being when her belly grows large from the size of the young within her. The plural [of the participle] is majāḥḥ. In the hadith: "He passed by a woman who was mujiḥḥ" [big-bellied with child]. This is what al-Khalīl mentioned.
2. Ibn Duraid added something open to question. He said jaḥḥa al-shayʾ means he dragged the thing — then excused himself by calling it a word of the Yemeni dialect.
3. al-juḥḥ — small, young melons.
جحد:
The letters jīm, ḥā' and dāl are a root that points to scarcity of good. One says 'ām jaḥid — a year of little rain. And a man is jaḥd or jaḥid, poor; and one says jaḥida and ajḥada. Ibn Durayd said: al-jaḥd in everything is fewness. The poet said:
And as long as he lives he will see nothing but want.

Al-Shaybānī said: [ajḥada al-rajul and jaḥada when he is stripped bare and his wealth goes. And he recited a line of al-Farazdaq]:
And many a fair woman of the people of Medina, who has never tasted hardship, nor followed the pack-beasts of a destitute man.

From this chapter is al-juḥūd, denial, which is the opposite of acknowledging, and it only happens when the denier knows that the thing is true. God Almighty said: {And they denied them, though their own souls were convinced of them} [al-Naml: 14]. And no denier ever brought any good at all.
جحر: The letters jīm, ḥā' and rā' are a root pointing to the narrowness of a thing, and to hardship. al-jiḥara is the plural of juḥr, a burrow. "ajḥara fulānan al-fazaʿ wa-l-khawf" — fright and fear drove him into hiding. majāḥir al-qawm — their hiding-places. "jaḥarat ʿaynuhu" — his eye sank, became sunken. al-jaḥra — a harsh, hard year.
جحس: The letters jīm, ḥā' and sīn are not a root. That is because they said al-jiḥās, then they said the sīn stands in for the shīn. Ibn Duraid said: "juḥisa jilduhu" is like "juḥisha," meaning his skin was scraped.
جحش:
The letters jīm, ḥā' and shīn are very far apart in sense.

al-jaḥsh, the donkey-foal, is well known. The Arabs say "he is juḥayshu waḥdih" as blame, just as they say "nasīju waḥdih" as praise — this is one sense. A different word: they say "juḥisha" when his skin was scraped. In the hadith: he, God bless him and his family and grant him peace, fell from a horse, and his side was scraped. A different word again: "jāḥashtu ʿanhu," you defended him. One says "so-and-so encamped jaḥīshan" — from the word just before, used when he camped apart, off to one side. Al-Aʿshā said: "When the tribe encamped, al-Jaḥīsh settled off to the side."

As for al-jaḥwash, the boy before he has grown sturdy, this belongs to the root of al-jaḥsh; letters were only added to its shape so that he not be called directly "a donkey-foal" — the meaning is otherwise the same. A line runs: "We killed Mukhlid, and the two sons of Ḥurāq, and another, a boy, just past weaning."
جحظ: The letters jīm, ḥā' and ẓā' are one word: "jaḥaẓat al-ʿayn," said of an eye when its ball grew large and bulged out.
جحف:
The letters jīm, ḥā' and fā' are a single root, and its sense is taking a thing away entirely, consuming it whole.

1. sayl juḥāf — a flood that sweeps away everything and carries it off.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
She has haunches like the smooth rock of a watercourse, laid bare by a devastating flood.

Al-Juḥfa was named because the flood swept away its people — that is, it carried them off.

2. ajḥafa bi-l-shay' — to sweep a thing away, to make off with it.
3. mawt juḥāf, like jurāf — a sweeping, devouring death.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And how many have slipped from it, from the sweeping-away of fates.

4. al-juḥāf, from this same chapter — a disease that strikes a person in his belly and gives him diarrhea; the sense is the same.
5. jaḥaftu lahu — I scooped something out for him.

And another root: veering and turning aside. From it:

6. al-jiḥāf — when the bucket strikes the mouth of the well as the water is drawn.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Straightening its two rims against the striking of the well-mouth.

7. tajāḥafa al-qawm fī al-qitāl — the people fell upon one another in the fighting, each leaning against the other with swords and sticks.
8. jāḥafa al-dhanb — he leaned toward, inclined to, sin.
9. fulānun yujḥifu li-fulān — so-and-so leans together with so-and-so against someone else.
جحل:
The letters jīm, ḥā' and lām point to the greatness of a thing.

1. al-jaḥl — the large waterskin.
2. al-jayḥal — the huge rock.
3. al-jaḥl — the large yaʿsūb (a large hornet).
4. al-jaḥl — the chameleon.

Dhū al-Rummah said, in a line of verse:
When the labour of bearing its load was done and they showed themselves, the chameleon (al-jaḥl) climbed high upon its perch.

As for their saying jaḥḥaltu al-rajul, meaning I threw him down, it comes from this, because the one thrown down must draw himself in and curl up.

Al-Kumayt said, in a line of verse:
Abū al-Shaʿthā' turned aside, disheveled and bleeding, and Abū Jahl lay slain, thrown down.

And straying from this root: al-juḥāl, the deadly poison.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
He gave him the poison, the deadly poison, to drink.
جحم:
The letters jīm, hā' and mīm: the greater part of this is heat and the fierceness of it. Al-jāhim is the place of fierce heat. Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
They make ready for the battle before the meeting of it, on the morning when hardship comes on and death is blazing.
And from it Hell, al-jahīm, is called jahīm. And of this chapter, and it is not far from it, is al-jahma, the eye; and it is said that it is in the tongue of Yemen. However that may be, it is from this root, because the two eyes are two burning lamps. A poet said, in a line of verse:
O my eye, weep for Umm 'Āmir, the prey of wolves in one of the watercourses.
They said: the jahmatā of the lion are its two eyes, in all the tongues. And this is sound, because its eyes are always burning. And one says jahhama al-rajul, when a man opens his eyes wide like one staring, and the eye is jāhima. Al-juhām is a sickness that strikes a man in his eyes so that his eyes swell. Al-ajham is the one whose eye is very red together with its wideness, and a woman is jahmā'. And jahhamanī bi-'aynihi, when he looks hard at me. As for their saying ajhama 'an al-shay', when he holds back from it, that is not a root, because that is turned about from ahjama. And it has been mentioned in its own chapter.
جحمظت:
[One says jahmazat] a boy, when you bind his hands to his feet and throw him down.

And al-jukhdub is a small creature, also called jukhadib, plural jakhadib.

And al-ju'shum is the one small of body, thin of flesh.

And al-jalanfa' is the thick-set one among camels [and al-jukhdub is the massive camel]. He said, in a line of verse: a heavy-treading one, massive of ribs, a jukhdub.

And one says of a people ijlakhamma, when they grew arrogant. He said, in a line of verse: we strike their assembled ranks when they grow arrogant.

And al-ji'thn is the roots of silliyan grass. And al-jalsad is the name of an idol. He said, in a line of verse -- the first half is missing from the text: "...like one who turns aside walking toward al-Jalsad."

And al-jirsam is deadly poison.

Here ends the Book of Jim.
جحن:
The letters jīm, ḥā' and nūn are a single root, and it is poor growth and the smallness of a thing in itself.

1. al-jaḥan — poor nourishment.
2. al-jaḥin — the poorly-nourished one.

Al-Shammākh said, in a line of verse:
Its flanks had sweated, and it gave freely of its yield — the fare of a stunted, meagre one.

Al-qatīn is the one who eats little. He is describing a tick, calling it jaḥin because of its poor nourishment.

3. al-mujḥan, of plants — the short one that has not reached its full growth.

As for jaḥwān, its derivation is from al-jaḥwa, which is the palm-spathe, the sheath that encloses the palm's flower cluster.
جخ:
The letters jīm and khā'. Al-Khalīl mentioned two roots: the first is moving off and turning away from a place, the second is shouting.

1. jakhkha — a man moves from one place to another. In the hadith: "When he prayed, he would jakhkha," meaning he moved from place to place.
2. al-jakhjakha — the second root: shouting and calling out. They say: "If glory pleases you, then jakhjikh among Jusham," meaning: shout and call out among them. It could also mean: and move over to them.
3. Ibn Duraid added: jakhkha bi-rijlihi — he kicked up dust with his foot; and jakhkha bi-bawlihi — he made his urine froth. If this is sound, the first belongs to the first root, since kicking up dust moves it from place to place, and the second belongs to the second root, since frothing must be accompanied by a sound.
4. al-jakhjakha — also, the sound of water breaking apart; this too belongs to the same root.

As for their saying "I jakhjakhtu the man," meaning I threw him down, it is not far-fetched to trace it by the same analogy to the first root mentioned from al-Khalīl.
جخر:
The letters jīm, khā' and rā': an ugliness in a thing when it widens.

1. jakhkharnā al-bi'r — we widened the well.
2. al-jakhar — a fault they describe in the mouth: they said it is its wideness, and they also said it is a change in its odour.
جخف:
The letters jīm, khā' and fā' are one word, and it is arrogance.

1. fulānun dhū jakhf wa-jakhīf — so-and-so is arrogant, full of threats.

They say jakhafa al-nā'im when the sleeper snores in his sleep. And God knows best.
جد:
The letters jīm and dāl are three roots: the first is greatness, the second is fortune, the third is cutting.

The first, greatness: God, exalted is His praise, said, reporting one who said: {and that He — exalted is the majesty of our Lord} [al-Jinn: 3]. One says "jadda al-rajul fī ʿaynī," meaning he grew great in my eyes. Anas ibn Mālik said: "A man, when he had recited Sūrat al-Baqara and Āl ʿImrān, jadda among us," meaning he grew great in our hearts.

The second, wealth and fortune. The Messenger of God, God bless him and his family and grant him peace, said in his supplication: "lā yanfaʿu dhā l-jaddi minka al-jadd" — meaning: the wealthy man's wealth does not benefit him against You; only acting in obedience to You benefits him. "So-and-so is ajadd than so-and-so" and "aḥaẓẓ than him" mean the same thing.

The third, cutting. One says "jadadtu al-shayʾ jaddan," and the thing is majdūd and jadīd, meaning cut off. A poet said, in a line of verse:
My love for Sulaymā refused to perish, and her bond, though it grew worn, stayed ever freshly cut.
It is not far-fetched that al-jidd, seriousness in a matter, and exerting oneself in it, comes from this — because he cuts it off decisively and resolves upon it firmly. From this comes your saying "ajiddaka tafʿalu kadhā?" — are you in earnest doing such-and-such? — meaning: is it seriousness from you, is it a firm decision from you, is it resolve from you? Al-Aʿshā said:
Are you in earnest that you did not hear the charge of Muḥammad, the Prophet of God, when he charged and called to witness?
And he said:
Are you in earnest that you did not close your eyes one night, to sleep it through along with her sleeping?

al-judd, the well, belongs to this root too, on the same analogy, but it is pronounced with ḍamma on the jīm. Al-Aʿshā said of it, in a line of verse:
The doubtful well, that had been spared the downpour of the roaring rain-cloud, was not made [its equal].
And the well: the ground is cut through for it.

1. al-jadjad — level, flat ground. A poet said: "Its sleeves pour down over the man, as the flood-channel pours over the level ground."
2. al-jadad — the same as al-jadjad. The Arabs say: "Whoever travels the level ground is safe from stumbling," and they say: "Gently — they are climbing onto the level ground." One says "ajadda al-qawm" when the people came onto level ground.
3. al-jadīd — the surface of the earth. A line runs: "...except the surface of the earth, or the back of the hand."
4. al-judda — from this too; every judda is a path or a stripe. al-judda is also the streak that runs along a donkey's back.
5. al-jaddāʾ — land with no water in it, as if the water had been judda, cut off, from it. From this also al-jadūd and al-jaddāʾ, said of a ewe whose milk has dried up and whose udder has withered.
6. al-jidād and al-jadād — the harvesting of dates from the palm.
7. jāddat al-ṭarīq, the highway — its main, level stretch, as if cut off from the rest, and also because it is travelled and worn smooth by travel. From this too comes al-judda: the side of anything is its judda, like the judda of a water-skin, which is the place cut at its edges.

As for Al-Aʿshā's saying, in a line of verse: "He lit his tent with the lamp, while night submerged its judād" — it is said that this word is Nabataean, meaning the cords tied to a tent. This, to me, is nothing; rather it is genuine Arabic, from al-jadd, cutting, because the cords are cut evenly, in a level way.

Their saying "thawb jadīd," a new garment, is from this too, as if its weaver had just now cut it off the loom. This is the origin; then everything time had not yet worked upon came to be called jadīd. That is why night and day are called "the two new ones," al-jadīdayn and al-ajaddayn, because each of them, whenever it comes, is new. The origin of al-judda is what we have said.

As for al-Ṭirimmāḥ's saying: "She gathers the ripened fruit of its juddād, singly or in twin clusters of the barm-shrub" — it is said that al-juddād means small trees. To me too that is so, by way of comparison with the juddād of a tent, the cords — the explanation of which has already passed.
جدب:
The letters jīm, dāl and bā' are a single root pointing to the scarcity of a thing.

1. al-jadb — the opposite of abundance; a barren place is makān jadīb.

And on its pattern: al-jadb, meaning fault-finding and disparagement. One says jadabtuhu — I found fault with him. In the hadith: "He found fault with (jadaba) their talk after the night prayer" — meaning he disparaged it.

Dhū al-Rummah said, in a line of verse:
Ah, what a smooth cheek, and soft speech, and a nature whose fault-finder busies himself with falsehood.

That is, he busied himself with falsehood when he found no way to the truth.
جدث: The letters jīm, dāl and thā' are a single word: al-jadath is the grave, plural ajdāth.
جدح:
The letters jīm, dāl and ḥā' are a single root: a stick with which medicine is stirred, having three notches marking its measure.

1. al-majdūḥ — a drink taken in the time before Islam: a she-camel would be sought out and bled, her blood taken into a vessel, and this was drunk in time of drought.
2. al-mijdaḥ and al-mujdaḥ — a star-cluster, being three stars as though they were the three stones a cooking pot stands on over the fire; the sense is the same.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
When the mijdaḥ sinks low.

3. al-mijdaḥ — a branding mark used on camels, in this shape. One says ajdaḥtu al-baʿīr — I branded the camel with the mijdaḥ mark.
جدر:
The letters jīm, dāl and rā' are two roots. The first is al-jidār, the wall; its plurals are judur and judrān. Al-jadr is the base of a wall. In the hadith: "Water [your land], O Zubayr, and let the water return to the wall's base." Ibn Durayd said: al-Jadara is a clan of al-Azd who built the wall of the Ka'ba. From this is al-jadīra, something set up for sheep like a pen. And Jadar is a village.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Oh, pour us in the morning a strong wine of Jadar, with the water of a rain-cloud — my idle talk outrunning the truth.

From this chapter is their saying: he is jadīr with such a thing, meaning: worthy of it, deserving of it — something that ought to be affirmed and one's affairs built upon. They say: al-jadīra is [one's] nature.

The second root is the appearing of a thing, whether a plant or something else. Al-judariyy (smallpox) is well known, also called al-jadariyy. A ewe is called jadrā' if it has that disease. Al-jadar is a lump that appears on the body. Al-jadr is also plant growth; one says: a place ajdara or jadara, meaning: its plants sprouted.

Al-Ja'dī said, in a line of verse:
You would love it, when the plants sprout, that you had, among the family of Ja'da, uncles on both sides.

Al-jadr is also the mark of a bite on a donkey's neck.

Ru'ba said, in a line of verse:
Or one whose two sides of the neck bear the bite-mark, folded up with rage.

This belongs to the same pattern because that bite mark makes the skin swell up, as though it were smallpox scars.
جدس: The letters jīm, dāl and sīn are one word: al-arḍ al-jādisa, land in which nothing grows.
جدع:
The letters jīm, dāl and ʿayn are a single root, and it is a kind of cutting. One says jadaʿa anfahu yajdaʿuhu jadʿan — he cut off his nose.

1. jadāʿ — a severe year, because it takes wealth away, as though it had cut it off.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
I have sworn to prove faithless in a year of jadāʿ, even if promised mother-camels ready to bear young.

2. al-jadiʿ — the poorly-nourished one, as though his nourishment had been cut off from him.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
One clad in a worn garment, her forearms bare, quiets with water a poorly-fed young ass.

3. jādaʿa fulānun fulānan — so-and-so quarrelled with so-and-so; this belongs to the same chapter, as though each of them sought to cut the other off.

They say: I left the land of the sons of so-and-so, its vipers biting at one another.

4. al-mujaddaʿ, of plants — that whose top has been eaten away while its lower part remains.
5. kala' judāʿ — sickly pasture, as though it were cut off because of its poorness and unwholesomeness.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And the aftermath of my enmity is sickly, cut-off pasture.

And straying from this root: al-majdūʿ, the one held in prison.
جدف:
The letters jīm, dāl and fā' are words entirely separate, none measured against another; this occurs often in their speech.

1. al-mijdāf — the oar of a ship. The two wings of a bird are its mijdāfān. From this one says jadafa al-ṭā'ir when the bird draws back its wings to fly.

How far this is from their saying that al-judāfā is the spoils of war, and from their saying that al-tajdīf is ingratitude for a blessing! And in the hadith: "Do not show ingratitude (lā tujaddifū) for God Most High's blessing" — meaning, do not belittle it.
جدل:
The letters jīm, dāl and lām are a single root, and it belongs to the chapter of a thing's being firmly made together with an extension in it, and of a quarrel drawn out and speech gone over again and again. That is the analogy we have mentioned.

A tightly twisted rein is called jadīl. And al-jadwal is a small river, and it is drawn out, and its water is stronger in the holding together of its parts than water that spreads out and runs loose. And a man is majdūl when he is spare of build without being wasted. And a boy is jādil when he grows strong. And al-judūl are the limbs, the singular being jidl. And al-jādil among the young of camels is the one above the rāshiḥ. And a coat of mail that is majdūla is one firmly made. And one says jadala al-ḥabb fī sunbulih, the grain grew strong in its ear. And al-ajdal is the falcon, so named for its strength.

Dhū al-Rumma said, mentioning wild asses in their running, in a line of verse:
As though they were the hind feathers of an eager falcon ... which turned aside so that the male bustard might outrun it over the stony ground.

Al-kharab is the male of the bustard. He meant: the bustard turned aside to outrun it, and the falcon pursues it.

And from the chapter is al-jadāla, which is the ground, and it is hard.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
I ride one mount after another ... and leave the helpless man upon the ground.

And for that reason one says ṭaʿanahu fa-jaddalahu, he thrust at him and threw him to the ground. And al-mijdal is the castle, and it is the analogy of the chapter.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
In a castle whose building is raised high ... the bird's claw slips off it.

And al-jadāl is unripe dates, the singular being jadāla, and that is because it is hard and not ripened, and it is in its first state while it is still green.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Its unripe dates fall upon the hands of the water-drawers.

And Jadīl is a well-known stallion camel. Al-Rāʿī said, in a line of verse:
Reddish-brown camels tracing their line to Shadqam and to Jadīl.
جدم:
The letters jīm, dāl and mīm point to meanness and shortness of stature.

1. rajul jadama — a short man.
2. al-shāh al-jadama — the poor, stunted ewe.
جدوى:
The letters jīm, dāl and the weak letter are five distinct roots.

1. al-jadā, in its shortened form — general rain, and a generous gift. One says ajdaytu ʿalayhi, I gave generously to him. And al-jadā', in its lengthened form — benefit, sufficiency, which follows the same pattern as the shortened form before it.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Little was his benefit to Mālik, when war blazed up with its firebrands.

2. al-jādī — saffron.
3. al-jady — the kid goat, well known. And al-jidāya — the young female gazelle.
4. al-jadiyya — a clot of blood.
5. jidyatā al-sarj — the two pads of the saddle, which lie beneath its two flaps.
جذ:
The letters jīm and dhāl are one root, either breaking or cutting.

1. One says "jadhadhtu al-shayʾ," I broke it. God, exalted is He, said: {and He made them broken pieces, save one great one of theirs} [al-Anbiyā': 58], meaning: he smashed them. And "jadhadhtuhu," I cut it off — and from this His saying: {a gift uninterrupted} [Hūd: 108], meaning: not cut off.
2. One says "mā ʿalayhi judhdha," meaning he has nothing covering him of clothes, as if meaning a rag or the like.
3. al-jadhīdha — grain that is broken up and made into sawīq, a meal of roasted, crushed grain.
4. judhādh — the ore-stones of gold, so called because they are broken up and dissolved down. Al-Hudhalī said: "as the pounders were plied upon the gold-ore." al-masāḥin are the implements with which gold-ore is pounded, the singular is misḥana.
5. al-mujdhawdhī — it is not far-fetched that this too is from the root: one who clings to his saddle, not leaving it, sitting upright upon it. One says "ijdhawdhā," because when he is so, it is as if he has cut himself off from everything and set himself upright for his journey on his mount. A line of verse runs: "Are you not clinging steadily to the saddle? Then you have no share but what you have been granted."
جذب:
The letters jīm, dhāl and bā' are a single root pointing to the severing of a thing.

1. jadhabtu al-shay' ajdhibuhu jadhban — I pulled the thing.
2. jadhabtu al-muhr ʿan ummihi — I weaned the colt from its mother. One says nāqa jādhib when her milk has grown scant, plural jawādhib. This follows the pattern of the chapter, because when her milk lessens it is as though she has drawn it in to herself.

And straying from this root: al-jadhab, the coarse palm-heart, singular jadhaba.
جذر:
The letters jīm, dhāl and rā' are a single root, and it is the base of everything, to the point that the base of the tongue is called jidhr.

Ḥudhayfa said: the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him and his family, told us that trustworthiness descended into the base (jidhr) of men's hearts. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: al-jadhr is the base of everything.

Zuhayr said, in a line of verse:
And two ears that show their noble breeding in them, down to the base, polished and sharpened at the joints.

And in the book attributed to al-Khalīl: al-jadhr is the base of reckoning; one says ten times ten is a hundred. As for al-majdhūr and al-mujaddar, it is said to mean the short one; if that is correct, it belongs to this chapter, as though he were the base of something the rest of which has departed from him.
جذع:
The letters jīm, dhāl and 'ayn are three roots. One indicates the newness of age and its freshness: al-jadha' from sheep or goats is one that has reached two years; from camels, one that has reached five years. Time/fate is called "the ever-fresh, unlucky one" (al-azlam al-jadha') because it is [always] new. He cited: "O Bishr, had I not held a certain standing among you, the ever-renewing fate would have thrown its hands upon me." Some said he meant by it the lion.

One says: "he is jadha' in this matter," when he has newly taken it up.

The second root: jidh' al-shajara, the trunk of a tree. The third: al-jadh', from your saying "jadha'tu the thing," meaning you rubbed/scraped it. He cited a line I cannot render with confidence, about the length of the rubbing of a wild ass's [flank?]. And their saying in proverbs, "take from Jidh' what he gives you," for it is the name of a man.
جذف:
The letters jīm, dhāl and fā' are one word, pointing to hastening and cutting. One says jadhaftu al-shay' — I cut the thing.

Al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse:
Sitting, with the drinking-companions beside him, with no lack, brought a wrapped wine-jar.

One also says it with dāl in place of dhāl.

1. jadhafa al-rajul — the man hastened. Ibn Durayd said: jadhafa al-ṭā'ir, when the bird beats its wings swiftly; this happens most when one of its wings has been clipped. From this comes the derivation of mijdāf, the oar of a ship. He said it is a known Arabic word.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Its whip, when moved, nearly slips loose from its knots and from the hand.

He means the she-camel: he made the whip like an oar for her. It is said with both dhāl and dāl, two correct forms of the word.
جذل:
The letters jīm, dhāl and lām are a single root: the fixed, upright base of a thing.

1. al-jidhl — the stump of a tree; and the base of anything is its jidhl.

Ḥubāb ibn al-Mundhir said, when the Anṣār disagreed over the pledge of allegiance: I am its well-rubbed stump. He said this because such a stump is fixed in a wall so that mangy camels rub against it; he meant: my counsel is sought for healing, as mangy camels seek healing by rubbing against that stump.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
It found by the water a firmly-planted little stump.

He means it stands fixed, not leaving its place, like the stump that has been driven in, that is, made firm.

As for al-jadhal, meaning joy, it is possible this comes from the same root, because the joyful person stands upright, while the grieving one clings low to the ground. This belongs to what is merely possible, not to what is established as fact.

2. They said: al-jidhl is what juts out and shows from the top of a mountain, plural al-ajdhāl.
3. fulānun jidhlu māl — so-and-so tends property well, when he manages it carefully. This follows the pattern of the chapter, as though in his watching over it he were a jidhl that does not move.
جذم:
The letters jīm, dhāl and mīm are a single root: cutting.

1. jadhamtu al-shay' jadhman — I cut the thing.
2. al-jidhma — a cut piece, of rope or otherwise.
3. al-judhām — leprosy, named for the cutting-off of the fingers it causes.
4. al-ajdham — one whose hand has been cut off.

In the hadith: "Whoever learns the Qur'an then forgets it will meet God Most High as ajdham."

Al-Mutalammis said, in a line of verse:
I was no different from one whose hand was cut off by his own other hand, and so he became maimed.

5. injadhama al-ḥabl — the rope snapped.

Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
Suʿād departed, and her bond was cut, and she alighted at al-Shar', then the two lowlands of Iḍam.

6. al-ijdhām — swiftness in travel; this belongs to the chapter.
7. al-ijdhām — also, ceasing from a thing.
جذو:
The letters jīm, dhāl and wāw are a root indicating standing erect. One says: jadhawtu 'alā aṭrāfi aṣābi'ī, meaning I stood up on my toes.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Whenever I wished, the village headmen would sing to me,
and a cymbal-player poised on the edge of a camel's foot-pad. (This image is obscure.)

Al-Khalīl said: one says jadhā yajdhū, like jathā yajthū (to kneel), except that jadhā indicates staying fixed in place more strongly.

What Al-Khalīl said here is evidence for us in some of what we have set out about the principles of language. Al-Khalīl, in our view, is a leading authority on this subject.

He said: one also says jadhā l-qurādu fī janbi l-ba'īr — the tick clung fast to the camel's side, from how tightly it sticks. And jadhat ẓalifatu l-ikāfi fī janbi l-ḥimār — the edge-board of the pack-saddle stuck into the donkey's side.

The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him and his family, said: 'The likeness of the hypocrite is the likeness of the cedar tree, standing fixed upon the ground, until it is uprooted all at once.' By al-mujdhiya he meant the one standing firm.

From this entry: tajādhā l-qawmu l-ḥajar, when people took turns lifting a stone to test their strength.

As for their saying rajulun jādhin, meaning a man of short reach, this in my view is from the same root, because a reach, when it is not long and extended, is like a thing jutting up, standing erect.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
The caliphate was never confined,
ever, to a short-armed man, charged with stinginess.
جر:
The letters jīm and rā' are one root, and it is the stretching and dragging of a thing. One says "jarartu al-ḥabl," I pulled the rope. Laqīṭ said, in a line of verse:
She drew the rope of the proud one taut between us, so that we see from her neither clear despair nor hope.

1. al-jarr — the foot of a mountain, from this root, as if it were something dragged, drawn down. A line runs: "And I crossed a valley and a jarr."
2. al-jarūr, among horses — one that resists being led. It has two explanations: that it is [the pattern] faʿūl in the sense of the passive, as if it is forever being dragged; or that it is jarūr in the active sense, because it drags its leader toward itself.
3. al-jarrār — the great army, because it drags its followers along and is itself drawn along. A line runs: "You will regret it, when our vanguard comes upon you, with a vast, straggling army, loud with neighing."
4. al-jurjūr — by the same analogy, a great herd of camels. A line runs: "A hundred, a great herd, from their giving."
5. al-jarīr — a leather rope that goes round a she-camel's neck; a man is named Jarīr after it.
6. al-jarīra — a wrong a person drags upon himself, a fault, because it is something he draws onto himself.
7. al-jirra — the cud of livestock, because it is drawn up.
8. The Milky Way is named majarra because it is like the trace of dragging.
9. al-ijrār — that the tongue of a young camel-calf is pulled out and then pinned, so that it cannot suckle. A line runs: "as the back of the pulled tongue was pinned." Some said al-ijrār is that it is pulled and then slit. On this basis 'Amr's line was explained: "Had my people's spears given me speech, I would have spoken — but the spears instead were left thrust through me." He means: had they fought, I would have boasted of it in my poetry; but their spears were left in me, as if they had cut off my tongue from boasting of them.

One says "ajarrahu al-rumḥ" when he speared him and left the spear in him, trailing. A line runs: "and in the fight we drag the spears along, and lay claim to glory." And another: "and they left Naḍla on the battlefield, dragging the spearheads like a wood-gatherer" — and this is a proverb. The origin is what we have said, of dragging a thing.

One says "jarrat al-nāqa," the she-camel, when her time to give birth came and passed and she did not give birth until some days after — she has jarrat her pregnancy, dragged it out. In the hadith: "There is no alms-due on jārra camels" — those led along by their halters, as if meaning those under loads, though it is also said they are rather the people's own riding-camels.

10. "ajrartu fulānan al-dayn" — you deferred a debt for him, like the ijrār of a trailing spear or halter-rope. From this too, "ajarra fulān fulānan aghānī," when he kept the songs coming for him one after another. A line runs: "When he had settled what he owed of me, he kept the songs coming for me, one after another, that the singer never tires of."
11. You say: "It was such-and-such in olden times, and halumma jarran to this day," meaning: that has drawn on to today, unbroken, uncut off.
12. al-jarr, also of camels — that they graze while on the move, dragging their loads.
13. al-jārūr — so it is said — a channel a flood cuts through.
14. al-jurra — a stick about a forearm long, with a snare at its top and a rope at its middle, buried as a trap for gazelles; when a gazelle is caught, it struggles a while, dragging the peg toward itself as the peg drags it, until the peg overpowers it and it comes to rest, caught. The Arabs make a proverb of it for one who opposes his people's opinion and then comes back around to their word: "He struggled against the jurra, then made peace with it."
15. al-jarra, the pottery jar, because it is always dragged along for drawing water.
16. al-jarr — something made from the skinned hock of a camel, in which a woman keeps her spare garment, hanging it from the back of her pack-bundle when travelling; it always dangles and sways. A line runs: "Your husband, O one of the gleaming teeth, the even-set teeth, the noble brow — he grew weary, so we bound him hanging as the jarr hangs, then lashed him fast over it with a rope."
17. rakī jarūr — a well deep at the bottom, worked by rope and beast, its water always drawn up by dragging.
18. al-jarra — the loaf drawn out of the hot embers. A line runs: "And a companion I kept, a sly wretch — I doctored him when he complained and ached, with a loaf like a reclining stallion."

As for al-jarjara, the sound a camel makes over and over in its throat, it too belongs to this root, because it is a sound that is dragged out; but since it is repeated, it is said jarjara, just as one says ṣalla and ṣalṣala. Al-Aghlab said: "He gurgled, in a throat like a great jar, and a head like an overturned cooking-pot." From this too the hadith: "He who drinks from vessels of silver is only gurgling the fire of Hell into his belly." This root has held, throughout, to one running analogy.
جرب:
The letters jīm, rā' and bā' are two roots: one is a plain thing over which something of its own kind spreads, like a plant; the other is something that holds something within it.

The first: al-jarab, well known, something that grows on the skin of its own kind. One says baʿīr ajrab, plural jarbā.

Al-Qiṭirān said, in a line of verse:
I am al-Qiṭirān, and the poets are mangy, and in al-Qiṭirān is a cure for the mangy.

Carried onto this by comparison: their calling the sky jarbā', its stars likened to the mange of a mangy animal.

Usāma ibn al-Ḥārith said, in a line of verse:
It showed him, of the mangy sky, in every view, streaks — and so his resting place was the still, unmoving day.

Al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse:
Reaching for a dog among their dwellings, and it nearly soared up to the mangy sky, then rose.

Al-jirba — a level cultivated plot; this follows the same pattern, because it is a plain surface over which what grows upon it spreads.

Al-Asʿar said, in a line of verse:
As for when it feeds, it is like a fox of the plot, or a wolf of the watering-place, moving briskly and lightly.

Al-ʿajrama is swift movement with lightness. Abū ʿUbayd used to say: al-jirba is the cultivated field.

Bishr said, in a line of verse:
Upon a plot over which its buckets pass, watering the furrows.

Abū Ḥanīfa said: the Milky Way is called jirbat al-nujūm, the plot of the stars.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And the plot of stars failed to give rain, so no wild mountain-goat drinks from the yielding of the south wind.

Khayyuhā means that it does not rain; mary al-janūb is the south wind drawing forth the rain.

The other root: al-jirāb, well known — a sack. Jirāb al-bi'r — the inside of the well, from its top to its bottom. Al-jarabba — a herd of donkeys; this belongs to the chapter before it, because there is a gathering-together in that. And sometimes they called strong people, when gathered together, jarabba.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
We have no poverty driving us to complaint — a hardy band, like the donkeys of al-Abakk.
جرج:
The letters jīm, rā' and jīm are one word: al-jādda, the beaten track, is called jarajah.

Some people claimed this is something Abū ʿUbayd miscopied; but the matter is not as they said — al-jarajah is correct. And on its pattern is Jurayj, a man's name.

It is said that al-jarij means unsteady.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Her anklet on her leg, not unsteady.

It is possible to say this is a substitution for marij.

Ibn Durayd said: al-jarj is stony ground.

As for al-jurja, for something like a saddlebag or chest, I do not think it is genuinely Arabic. Yet Aws did say, in a line of verse:
Three fine striped garments, and a jurja, and a dark honeycomb treated with the honey of the west wind's bees.
جرح:
The letters jīm, rā' and ḥā' are two roots: one is earning, and the second is cutting the skin.

The first is their saying: ijtaraḥa, meaning: he worked and earned. God, mighty and glorious, said: {Or do those who commit evil deeds reckon...} [al-Jāthiya: 21]. This is called ijtirāḥ because it is work done with al-jawāriḥ, the limbs that do the earning. Al-jawāriḥ among birds and beasts of prey are those used for hunting.

The other is their saying: he jaraḥahu (wounded him) with an iron blade, a wounding; the noun is al-jurḥ. One says: he "wounded" a witness, meaning he rejected his testimony by spreading something unseemly about him. So-and-so istajraḥa, meaning: he did something for which he could be discredited.

As for the saying of Abū 'Ubayd concerning the hadith of 'Abd al-Malik: "I have preached to you, and preaching has only increased you in istijrāḥ" — he took it to mean a decrease in goodness. The meaning is sound, but the wording does not point to it. What 'Abd al-Malik meant is what we have explained: that preaching only increases in you what earns you being "wounded" and attacked, just as hadiths are impugned. Abū 'Ubayd said: he means that they are many and the sound ones among them are few. In our view the meaning here is as we said before: that they became so numerous that scholars were forced to impugn some of them as unsound.
جرد:
The letters jīm, rā' and dāl are a single root, and it is for the outside of a thing to show, with nothing covering it. Other things sharing this sense are then carried on it.

1. tajarrada — one says tajarrada al-rajulu min thiyābihi, yatajarradu tajarrudan: a man stripped off his clothes.
2. al-jarīd — some philologists said al-jarīd is palm-frond stalks, one of them called a jarīda, named so because its leaflets have been stripped off it.
3. al-jarad — wide open land, named so because it stands out and shows plainly, with nothing covering it.
4. ajrad — one says a horse is ajrad when its coat is fine and thin; such a horse is described as ḥasan al-jurda, fine in its smoothness, and al-mutajarrad.
5. jārūd — an ill-omened man, as though he strips things bare and scrapes them away.
6. jārūda — a year of drought, from the same sense.
7. al-jarād — locusts, well known. Land struck by locusts is majrūda. Some scholars said it is called jarād because it strips (yajrudu) the land bare, eating everything on it.
8. al-jarad — a skin condition, for a person's skin to break out from eating locusts.
9. jarīd — this belongs to the root, following its regular pattern: they say ʿām jarīd, a complete year, because it ran its full course and came out clear (jarīd), not accused of falling short.
10. From this too: “I have not seen him for ajradān and jarīdān,” meaning two complete days — the meaning being what was just given.
11. injarada — from the same sense, injarada bi-nā al-sayru means the journey stretched on with us.

As for their saying, of a thing that has gone off with no trace of it to be found, “I do not know which locust-swarm carried it away” — this is a proverb, and the locust meant is this same well-known locust.
جرذ: The letters jīm, rā' and dhāl are one word: al-juradh, one of the jirdhān, rats; and from it is named al-jarad, the ailment that takes hold in the legs of a riding animal. As for their saying rajul mujarradh, meaning seasoned, well-tried, that belongs to letter-substitution, and is not itself a root.
جرز:
The letters jīm, rā' and zā' are a single root, and it is cutting. One says jarazttu al-shay'a, meaning I cut the thing.

1. jurāz — a sword called jurāz is a cutting sword.
2. juruz — land called juruz has no plants on it, as though it were cut off from growth.
3. majrūza — al-Kisā'ī and al-Aṣmaʿī said land called majrūza, from juruz, is land the rain has not reached; it is also said to mean land whose plants have been eaten away.
4. al-jarūz — a man called jarūz is one who, when he eats, leaves nothing on the table; the word is used the same way for a woman or a she-camel. A poet said: “You see the old woman, sly, a big eater.” And the Arabs say in a proverb: “A hateful woman will not be satisfied except with jarza” — meaning that from the intensity of her hatred and envy she is not satisfied with those she hates except by wiping them out entirely.
5. al-jāriz — a severe, cutting cough, called so because it cuts the throat. Al-Shammākh said: “She has, in the windpipe and the nostrils, a jāriz.”
6. jāriza — rough, dry land surrounded by sand.
7. jāriz — a barren woman.
8. dhū jaraz — something rough and hard, said also of a camel: in my view this is taken from the jāriza land, rough ground, already mentioned.
جرس:
The letters jīm, rā' and sīn are a single root, and it is about sound; everything after that is carried upon it.

They said: al-jars is a faint sound. One says mā samiʿtu lahu jarsan, I heard no sound from him, and samiʿtu jarsa al-ṭayr, I heard the sound of birds' beaks upon something they were eating. One says ajrasa al-ṭā'ir, the bird made a sound.

1. Carried on this: their calling bees jawāris, meaning eating ones, because at such times they make the faintest sound.

Abū Dhu'ayb said, describing bees, in a line of verse:
There linger over the fruit-laden branches sounding bees, still nursing their brood, tawny-winged, downy-necked.

2. al-jaras — that which is hung upon camels.

In the hadith: "The angels do not accompany a travelling party that has a bell (jaras) with it."

One says jarastu bi-l-kalām, I spoke words. And ajrasa al-ḥaly, the ornament made a sound.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
You hear the ornament, when it whispers and shakes on their necklaces, making its sound.

And straying from this root: al-rajul al-mujarras, the seasoned, well-tried man. And the meaning of jars min al-layl is a stretch of the night.
جرش:
The letters jīm, rā' and shīn are a single root, and it is jarsh al-shay': to pound a thing coarsely, without refining the pounding. One says jarashtuhu, and it is jarīsh. Al-jurāsha is what falls from the pounded thing. jarrashtu al-ra's bi-l-mushṭ — I combed the head until much scurf came off it. Al-Khalīl mentioned that al-jarsh also means eating.

And straying from this root: al-jirishshā, meaning the self.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
To it belongs the self, and its yearning surged forth.

As for their saying maḍā jarsh min al-layl, a stretch of the night passed, this too strays from the root we have mentioned.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Until, when she was left at Jarsh.
جرض:
The letters jīm, rā' and ḍād are two roots: one is a kind of choking, the other is about largeness.

As for the first, they say jariḍa bi-rīqihi — he choked on his own saliva.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
It is as though the young man had never lived a single night among people, when the two jaws part at the moment of choking.

Al-Khalīl said: al-jaraḍ is when a person swallows his saliva out of grief and sorrow. One says māta fulānun jarīḍan — so-and-so died choked with grief.

As for the second: their saying baʿīr jirwāḍ, a thick, massive camel. Al-jurā'iḍ — the huge camel, also said to mean the voracious eater. And naʿja jurā'iḍa — a large ewe.
جرع:
The letters jīm, rā' and 'ayn indicate scantness of a thing drunk. One says: jari'a l-shāribu l-mā'a yajra'uhu, and jara'a yajra'u — the drinker swallowed a mouthful of water.

As for al-jar'ā', it is a sand-tract that grows nothing — this is because, though the rain does it some good, it is as if it were never watered at all.

Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
Did nothing draw tears from your eyes but a campsite
at Jumhūr Ḥuzwā, or at Jar'ā' Mālik?

From this entry is their saying: 'So-and-so escaped by a mouthful's breadth at the chin,' meaning the last gasp that leaves the throat. So said al-Farrā'.

One says nūqun majārī' — she-camels scant in milk, as if their udders held only a mouthful.

What departs from this root is al-jara' — a twist in one strand of a rope, standing out above the rest of the strands.
جرف:
The letters jīm, rā' and fā' are a single root: taking a thing entirely, sweeping it all up.

One says: jaraftu l-shay'a jarfan, when you carried it all off. A jurāf sword is one that cuts through everything.

Al-jurf is a place being eaten away by a flash-flood. Jarrafa l-dahru mālahu — time swept away his wealth, wiping it out. Wealth like this is mujarraf.

A jurāf man is one much given to intercourse, as if he sweeps it up wholesale.

From this entry: al-jurfa is when a strip of skin is cut from a camel's thigh and gathered up on its thigh as a mark.
جرل:
The letters jīm, rā' and lām are two roots: one is stones, the other a colour among colours.

The first: al-jarwal and al-jarāwil are stones. One says arḍ jarila when it has much stony ground. Al-ajrāl is the plural of al-jaral, a stony place.

Jarīr said, in a line of verse:
Of every high-withered mount, even if the distance is far, sound of hoof, threading through the stony ground.

The other: al-jiryāl, the red dye; and for this wine was called jiryāl.

As for al-Aʿshā's saying, in a line of verse:
And a well-aged wine, of what Bābil ages, like the blood of a slaughtered beast — I stripped it of its jiryāl.

Some said he meant its colour, that is its redness; they related from him an account that indicates he meant its colour.
جرم:
The letters jīm, rā' and mīm are a single root to which the branches go back. Al-jirm is cutting. The cutting of date-palms is called al-jirām and al-jarām. And one says: the time of the jarām has come. And jaramtu ṣūfa al-shāt - I sheared the sheep's wool and took it. Al-jurāma is what falls of the dates when they are cut. And it is said: al-jurāma is what is picked up of the stumps of the fronds after the cutting. And one says sana mujarrama, a complete year, as though it had been cut off at its fullness. It is from tajarrama al-laylu - the night went away. Al-jarām and al-jarīm are dry dates. All of this agrees in wording, in meaning, and in the way it is measured.

Among what is brought back to it is their saying jarama, that is, he earned; because what a man takes for himself is as though he had cut it off. And fulān jarīmatu ahlihi - he is the earner for his family. A poet said, in a line of verse:
The earner for a fledgling on the head of a mountain peak; you see on the bones of what she has gathered dripping fat.
He is describing an eagle. He says: she is the earner for a nāhiḍ - he means her chick. Al-jurm and al-jarīma are sin, and that is from the first sense, because sin is an earning, and earning is a cutting off. And they said about their expression lā jarama that it is from their saying jaramtu, that is, I earned. And they recited, in a line of verse:
I dealt Abū 'Uyayna such a thrust as earned Fazāra, after it, that they should be angry -
meaning: it earned them anger. And the body is a jirm, because it has a size and a cut shape. And one says mashyakha jilla jarīm, elders great of body.

As for their saying of a man with a fine voice, "he is of good jirm", some people said: the voice itself is called al-jirm. Sounder than that is the word of Abū Bakr ibn Durayd: that it means the goodness of the voice's coming out of the body. And Banū Jārim are among the Arabs. Al-jārim is the earner, and it is what the sayer said:
And al-Jārimī is its chief.
And jarm is earning, and by it Jarm was named; they are two clans, one among Quḍā'a, the other among Ṭayy.
جرن:
The letters jīm, rā' and nūn are a single root pointing to softness and ease.

1. al-jarīn — the threshing-floor, called this because it is a place that has been made smooth and even.
2. al-jārin, of garments — that which has become worn and soft. jaranat al-dirʿ — the coat of mail grew supple and smooth.
3. jirān al-baʿīr — the front of a camel's neck, from its slaughtering-place, plural jurun.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Be wary, O my two neighbours, for I have seen the neck of the old camel about to grow tame.

And some mentioned that al-jārin is the young of the snake. If that is correct, it belongs to this chapter, because it is soft to the touch and smooth.
جره: The letters jīm, rā' and hā' are one word: al-jarāhiya. Abū ʿUbayd said: jarāhiyat al-qawm is their clamour and their talk done openly rather than in secret. And if someone were to say that this is a metathesis of al-jahr, al-jahrā' and al-jahāra, that would be a plausible view.
جرو:
The letters jīm, rā' and wāw are a single root: the small one of a dog's young, and then other things are carried upon it by comparison. Al-jarw is used for a dog and others. One says sabuʿa mujriya and mujrin when it has its young one with it.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And a mother-beast drags my flesh to gathered young ones.

This is the origin. Then the small cucumber is called al-jirwa.

In the hadith: "The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was brought young ones, downy" — and likewise jarw al-ḥanẓal (the colocynth) and jarw al-rummān (the pomegranate), meaning they were small.

Banū Jirwa is a clan of the Arabs. One says alqā al-rajulu jirwatahu — the man cast down his young one, meaning he steadied his resolve and bore patiently with the matter, as though he had tethered a puppy and settled it. This is a comparison.
جري:
The letters jīm, rā' and yā' are one root, and it is the running and flowing of a thing. One says jarā al-mā'u yajrī jaryatan and jaryan and jarayānan - the water ran. And habit is called al-ijriyyā, and that is because it is the course along which a man runs. Al-jarī is the agent who acts for another, and he is plainly of jirāya, agency; you say jarraytu jariyyan and istajraytu, that is, I took a man as my agent. And in the hadith: "Let Satan not take you as his agents." The agent was called jarī because he runs in the course of the man who appointed him, and the plural is ajriyā'.

As for the ship, it is al-jāriya, the runner, and so is the sun, and that is the measure of the word. And the jāriya among women is from that too, because she is taken to run in service, and she is plainly of jirā', girlhood. He said, in a line of verse:
The fair women have grown past their youth and their girlhood has grown long, and they were reared among slaves and small herds of camels.
And one says: that was in the days of her jirā', that is, her girlhood. As for al-jirriyya, which is the crop of a bird, the origin that is relied upon in it is that the jīm is put in place of a qāf, as though its origin were qirriyya, because it gathers a thing, that is, collects it; then they turned the qāf into a jīm, as they do with those two letters.
جز: The letters jīm and zāy are one root, and it is the cutting of a thing made of many weak strands. One says "jazaztu al-ṣūf jazzan," I sheared the wool — this is the season of al-jazāz and al-jizāz. al-jazūza — sheep whose wool is sheared. al-juzāza — what falls away from a hide when it is cut, the trimmings. This is carried by the same analogy; the origin of al-jazz is what I have said. al-jazīza — a lock of wool, plural jazāʾiz.
جزأ:
The letters jīm, zāy and hamza are a single root: it is making do with a thing. One says "ijtaza'tu bi-shshay' ijtizā'an," I was satisfied with it; and "ajza'anī al-shay' ijzā'an," it was enough for me. He cited lines of verse: "I have sworn I will never betray, in [time of] scarcity, even if I am offered mother she-camels in return — for betrayal among peoples is a disgrace, and the free man makes do (yajza'u) with the shank of poor meat," meaning: he is content with it. Al-juz' is a grazing animal's independence from water because it eats green fodder. Some mentioned, about God's words {and they assigned to Him a portion (juz'an) from among His servants} [al-Zukhruf: 15], that it is from this — since they claimed He chose daughters over sons. God is exalted, greatly exalted, above what the idolaters say. Al-juz' [also] means a part or portion of a thing.

What falls outside this root: al-juz'a, the handle of a knife; one says "ajza'tuhā ijzā'an," when you gave it a handle. It may also be that it was so named because it is a part of the tool, a portion of it.
جزح:
The letters jīm, zāy and ḥā' are one word, not branching and not measured against anything else. One says jazaḥa lahu min mālihi — he cut off a share for him from his wealth. Al-jāziḥ — the one who cuts off a share. It occurs in the poetry of Ibn Muqbil, in a line of verse:
Truly a giver, from the store of inherited wealth, cutting off a portion for the one hard-pressed.
جزر:
The letters jīm, zā' and rā' are a single root, and it is cutting.

1. One says jazartu l-shay'a jazran, I cut the thing — a cutting. From this the slaughtered animal (jazūr) was named jazūr.
2. al-jazara — the sheep that its owners go to and slaughter.
3. jazaran, in the saying "the sons of so-and-so left the sons of so-and-so jazaran" — meaning they killed them and left them as prey for the beasts of prey.
4. al-juzāra — the extremities of the camel: its feet and its head. It was named juzāra because the butcher (jazzār) takes them, so they are his juzāra — just as one says of a worker, he took his 'umāla, his wage. So if you say "a horse thick of juzāra", you mean the thickness of its legs and feet and the abundance of its sinew. The head is not included in this, because a big head is a fault in horses.
5. The island (jazīra) was named jazīra for being cut off.
6. jazara l-nahru, the river jazara, when its water lessened — a jazr.
7. al-jazr is the opposite of al-madd, the ebb as against the flood-tide.
8. One says ajzartuka shātan, I gave you a sheep to slaughter, when you handed someone a sheep for him to slaughter. It is called al-jazara, and this word is used only of sheep. Some scholars said: that is because the sheep is kept only for slaughter. It is not said of the she-camel or the male camel, because they are kept for other work.
جزع:
The letters jīm, zā' and ʿayn are two roots: one is cutting across/breaking off, the other is a kind of gemstone.

As for the first, they say jazaʿtu al-ramlata, meaning you crossed the sand dune; from this comes jizʿ al-wādī, the place where the valley is crossed from one side to the other; it is also said to mean its bend. If that is so, it is because it breaks off from being straight and curves.

Al-jazaʿ is the opposite of patience — the breaking off of one's strength to bear what has befallen him.

Al-juzʿa is a small quantity of water, following the pattern of the root.

As for the other root, al-jazʿ/juzʿ is the well-known banded bead. One says busra mujazzaʿa, an unripe date, when ripening has reached halfway through it, at which point it resembles the banded bead.
جزل:
The letters jīm, zāy and lām are two roots: one is the largeness of a thing among things, the other is cutting.

The first: al-jazl — what is large among firewood; then it was used by extension, so one says ajzala fī al-ʿaṭā', he gave generously. From this comes al-ra'y al-jazl, the weighty opinion, which belongs to the second root, to be mentioned below.

As for the saying, in a line of verse:
Ah for your pot, ah for it — when, in time of drought, the large logs were chosen.

He singled out al-jazl because poor meat is slow to cook, so large firewood is sought for it.

The other root: the Arabs say jazaltu al-shay' jizlatayn — I cut the thing into two pieces. And this is the season of al-jizāl, meaning the cutting of the dates.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Until, when the time came for its harvesting.

From this chapter: al-jazal, when a sore strikes a camel's withers, a piece of bone comes out from it, and its place sinks in. A camel so affected is ajzal.

Abū al-Najm said, in a line of verse:
It leaves the hump like the back of the sunken-withered camel.

Al-jizla — a portion of dried dates.

As for their saying jazl al-ra'y, it is possible this belongs to the second root, meaning it is a decisive, cutting opinion.

And straying from this root: al-jawzal, the young of the dove.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Sulaymā said: I do not love the young dove, nor do I love little fish as food.

It is also said: al-jawzal is poison.
جزم:
The letters jīm, zāy and mīm are a single root: cutting. One says jazamtu al-shay' ajzimuhu jazman. Al-jazm in grammatical inflection is so called because the inflection has been cut off from it. Al-jizma — a portion of sheep. From this: jazamtu al-qirba, I filled the waterskin, said of the moment when the drawing of water is cut off, finished.

Ṣakhr al-Ghayy said, in a line of verse:
When I had filled my waterskin with it, I made for a watering-place, or another instead.

And they say: al-jazma is a single meal. If that is correct, it follows the pattern of the chapter, because it happens once and is then cut off. From this too comes their saying jazzama al-qawm, the people gave up, were unable.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
But I went on and did not give up, and patience was the custom of our forebears.
جزي:
The letters jīm, zāy and yā': a thing standing in the place of another and requiting it.

One says jazaytu fulānan ajzīhi jazā'an — I repaid so-and-so — and jāzaytuhu mujāzātan, with the same sense. And one says: this is a man jāzīka min rajul — that is, he is enough for you. Its meaning is that he stands in the place of every other man, as you say kāfīka (your sufficiency) and nāhīka (your stopping-point) — that is, it is as though he forbids you to seek anyone else along with him.

And you say jazā ʿannī hādhā al-amra yajzī — this matter settled the account for me — just as you say qaḍā yaqḍī, he discharged, he discharges. And tajāzaytu daynī ʿalā fulān, that is, I claimed my debt from so-and-so. The people of Medina call the one who claims a debt al-mutajāzī. God, exalted be His praise, said: {wa-ittaqū yawman lā tajzī nafsun ʿan nafsin shay'an} [al-Baqara: 48] — that is, no soul discharges anything for another.
جس: The letters jīm and sīn are one root, and it is discerning a thing by a light touch. One says "jasastu al-ʿirq," I felt the pulse, and so with other things, jassan. al-jāsūs, the spy, is [the pattern] fāʿūl from this, because he seeks out by stealth and subtlety what he wants to learn. It is related from al-Khalīl that the senses, man's faculties of perception, are sometimes called jawāss. Ibn Duraid said: al-jass can also be with the eye — and this confirms what al-Khalīl said. He cited: "So they banded together, then scrutinised him with their eyes."
جسأ: The letters jīm, sīn and hamza point to hardness and toughness. One says jasā l-shay'u, when it grew hard, and also jasa'a with the hamza. And jasa'at yaduhu, his hand grew hard and callused.
جسد:
The letters jīm, sīn and dāl indicate the gathering of a thing together, and its firming up. From this is jasad al-insān, the body of a person. Al-mijsad is the garment that lies next to the body. Al-jasad and al-jasid, said of blood, is what has dried; it is called jasid and jāsid.

Al-Ṭirimmāḥ said, in a line of verse:
Of it, some is dried blood and some is fresh blood.

Some said: al-jasad is blood itself, and al-jasid is the dried part.

Outside this chapter is al-jasād, meaning saffron. If you say "al-mijsad" with the mīm carrying a kasra, it is the garment that lies next to the body — this according to the Kufan grammarians. The Basran grammarians, however, know only "mujsad," meaning [a garment] soaked through with dye.
جسر:
The letters jīm, sīn and rā' point to strength and boldness. Al-jasra is the strong she-camel — it is said she is bold in travelling. Sulbun jasr means strong. He said:
The place of her saddle-load is jasr.
And al-jisr, the bridge, is well known. Ibn Durayd said: it is, with the jīm carrying a fatḥa, what the common people call jisr — it is al-qanṭara, the arched bridge. Al-jasāra is boldness, and from it "Jasr" is derived, a tribe's name. Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
And she settled among the Banū al-Qayn ibn Jasr
... and from them troubles have arisen for us.
جسم:
The letters jīm, sīn and mīm indicate a thing gathering together into a mass.

Al-jism is every perceptible physical body. Ibn Durayd said this.

Al-jasīm is one great in body; likewise al-jusām.

Al-jusmān is the physical form.
جش:
The letters jīm and shīn are one root, and it is crumbling apart. From it one says "jashashtu al-ḥabb," I coarsely ground the grain. al-jashīsha — something cooked from grain once coarsely ground. Describing a voice they say ajashsh, hoarse, because it breaks up in the throat — do you not see them say "a husky, cracked reed-pipe"? One says a horse has an ajashsh voice, and a cloud is ajashsh [rumbling]. A line runs: "with a husky-voiced, swift horse, which, coming on the camp by night, neighs."

As for their saying "jashashtu al-biʾr," when you clean out a well, it too is from this, because the shaft crumbles as it is cleared. Abū Dhuʾayb said: "They said, once the well was cleaned out, 'bring them to water!' — yet there was not in it the least drop enough for one who came to drink."
جشأ:
The letters jīm, shīn and hamza are a single root, and it is the rising of a thing. One says jashsha'at nafsī, my soul rose, when it rose up from grief or fright. As for jāshat, without the hamza, that is not from this — that is only its nausea, its queasiness. Abū 'Ubayd said: ijtasha'atnī l-bilādu wa-ijtasha'tuhā, the land "ijtasha'at" me and I "ijtasha'tu" it, when it did not agree with you — because when that is so, you rise from it and recoil from it. Some said: jasha'a l-qawmu min baladin ilā baladin, the people "jasha'ū" from one land to another, when they went out from it.

From this same reasoning comes tajashsha'a, tajashshu'an, belching, and the noun is al-jushā'. And of this chapter is al-jash', said with the hamza or without it: the thick bow. Abū Dhu'ayb said:
In his hand is a thick bow, deep of sound and cutting.
جشب:
The letters jīm, shīn and bā' point to roughness in a thing. One says ṭaʿāmun jashibun, food, when it is without any relish. Al-mijshāb is the coarse, thick one. He said:
She turns to you a side that is slender, not coarse.
جشر: The letters jīm, shīn and rā' are a single root pointing to the spreading and the emergence of a thing. One says jashara l-ṣubḥu, the dawn jashara, when it lit up. From this comes their saying iṣṭabaḥnā l-jāshiriyyata, we took our morning drink at al-jāshiriyya — a drink taken with the dawn. And aṣbaḥa banū fulānin jasharan, the sons of so-and-so became jashar, when they went out from the settlement and then stayed on, not returning to their tents; and likewise al-māl al-jashar, livestock that grazes out in front of the tents. Al-jashshār is the one who takes the livestock out to al-jashr, the open pasture.
جشع:
The letters jīm, shīn and ʿayn are a single root, and it is intense greed. One says rajulun jashiʿun bayyinu l-jashaʿ, a man plainly greedy, and qawmun jashiʿūn, a greedy people. Suwayd said, in a line of verse:
And the hunting dogs among them have greed.
جشم:
The letters jīm, shīn and mīm are a single root, and it is the sum of the body. One says alqā fulānun ʿalā fulānin jushamahu, so-and-so threw his jusham — his bodily weight — upon so-and-so, meaning he cast his burden onto him. And jushamu l-baʿīri is the camel's chest, and a man was named "Jusham" from this. As for their saying tajashshamtu l-amra, its meaning is: I bore it with my jusham until I had done it. And jashshamtu fulānan kadhā means I burdened so-and-so with such a thing, that is, I charged him to carry its weight upon himself. He said:
I swear, no calamity I burdened him with
... that would weigh down noble men, but he bore it.
جص: The letters jīm and ṣād do not make up a genuine word. al-jiṣṣ, gypsum, is an arabised, foreign word; the Arabs [also] call it al-qiṣṣa. jaṣṣaṣa al-jarw is a puppy opening its eyes. And al-ijjāṣ [the plum]. In all of this there is doubt.
جض: The letters jīm and ḍād are close to the one before it. They say "jaḍḍaḍa ʿalayhi bi-l-sayf," meaning he charged at him with the sword.
جظ: The letters jīm and ẓā', if sound, are a kind of coarseness. It is related in a hadith: "The people of the Fire are every jaẓẓ, arrogant one," and it is explained that al-jaẓẓ is the big-bodied one. They also say "jaẓẓa" when he had intercourse. All of this is close, one sense to another.
جع:
The letters jīm and ʿayn are one root, and it is an unwelcome, disliked place. Al-Khalīl said: al-jaʿjāʿ is a bad couching-place for camels. It is said of a slain man: "he was left at al-jaʿjāʿ" [left where he fell, on bare ground]. Abū Qays ibn al-Aslat said, in a line of verse:
Whoever tastes war will find its taste bitter, and it will leave him on the bare ground [where he fell].

Al-Aṣmaʿī said: it is also confinement. A line runs: "when they made the camels kneel, between couching and confinement." Ibn Ziyād wrote to Ibn Saʿd: "jaʿjiʿ with al-Ḥusayn," peace be upon him — as if meaning: force him onto rough, uneasy ground. Some said al-jaʿjaʿa here means to harass and unsettle; one says "jaʿjaʿtu al-ibil," when you drove the camels to make them kneel. Abū Dhuʾayb said, of the jaʿjaʿa that marks a bad end:
So it dealt out death to each of them in its own way — one fleeing with the last of his breath, another crouched down, collapsed.
جعب:
The letters jīm, ʿayn and bā' are a single root, and it is gathering. Ibn Durayd said: jaʿabtu l-shay'a jaʿban, I gathered the thing. He said: and that is said only of a small amount. This is correct. From it comes al-juʿba, the quiver for arrows. Al-jiʿāba is the craft of making quivers; the maker is al-jaʿʿāb, and his verb is jaʿʿaba yujaʿʿibu tajʿīban. One says al-jiʿibbā and al-jiʿibbā': the lower part of a person. Al-Khalīl quoted a line of verse about it that seemed to be fabricated and contained indecency, so we have not given it here.

Standing outside this chapter is al-juʿabā, a kind of ant, which follows the same pattern as al-juʿbūb, a base and lowly person — because he is drawn in on his own meanness, not open-handed in generosity.
جعد:
The letters jīm, ʿayn and dāl are a single root, and it is a drawing-in, a contraction, in a thing. One says shiʿrun jaʿdun, curly hair, the opposite of al-sabṭ, straight hair. Al-Khalīl said: jaʿuda yajʿudu juʿūdatan, and jaʿʿadahu ṣāḥibuhu tajʿīdan, his companion curled it. And he quoted:
A young, supple girl has enthralled me
... with jet-black hair that its curling adorned.

Carried on this same chapter is their saying nabātun jaʿdun, a crimped plant, and rajulun jaʿdu l-aṣābiʿ, a man curled of fingers — a way of saying he is stingy. As for Dhū al-Rumma's saying, "and the muzzles were wrapped in the curled foam" — he means the foam that gathers on the camel's muzzle, layer upon layer. This is sound, as a comparison. As for their calling the wolf "Abū Jaʿda", it was said he was nicknamed so for his stinginess, and this is nearer the truth than their saying that al-jaʿda is the ewe-lamb and the wolf was nicknamed after it. Al-jaʿda is also a plant, and perhaps it was so called because it grows curled.
جعر:
The letters jīm, ʿayn and rā' are two distinct roots.

The first is excrement — what is in the belly. One says rajulun mijʿārun, a man given to frequent defecation. Jaʿara l-kalbu jaʿran yajʿaru, the dog defecated. Al-jāʿiratān are the two spots on a donkey's hindquarters, above its two thighs, where it is branded. Banū al-Jaʿrā', of Banū al-'Anbar, is a nickname for them. Durayd said:
Ask Hawāzin — has word reached her
... of what al-Jaʿrā' did to me alone?

The second: al-jiʿār is the rope the water-drawer ties around his waist at the well, so that he does not fall in. He said:
The waist-rope will not save me from fate
... even were I bound with a well-twisted, sturdy cord.
جعس: The letters jīm, ʿayn and sīn point to baseness, meanness and vileness.
جعش: The letters jīm, ʿayn and shīn follow the same pattern as the one before it.
جعظ:
The letters jīm, ʿayn and ẓā' are a single root pointing to bad character, and refusal, and driving off. One says rajulun jaʿẓun, a man of bad character. Jaʿaẓtuhu ʿani l-shay'i, I drove him off from the thing, and likewise ajʿaẓtuhu. He said:
And the two Jufra they defended, driving off [the attackers].
He means: they drove them back from it.

As for the letters jīm and ghayn, they have no root at all in speech. What Ibn Durayd said about al-jaghb, that it means one given to disturbance — that is a kind of letter-substitution that Ibn Durayd invents and uses on his own.
جعف: The letters jīm, ʿayn and fā' are a single root, and it is uprooting a thing and throwing it down. One says jaʿaftu l-rajula, I threw the man down, when you throw him down after uprooting him from the ground. Al-injiʿāf is the being uprooted; one says injaʿafati l-shajaratu, the tree was uprooted. In the hadith: "The likeness of the hypocrite is the likeness of the arza-tree, standing firm on the ground, until its uprooting comes all at once." And Juʿfī is a tribe.
جعل:
The letters jīm, ʿayn and lām are words that hold to no one measure; they do not resemble one another. So al-jaʿl is the palm-trees that grow past the reach of the hand, and one of them is a jaʿla. And it is his saying:
Or its small palms and its tall ones come out even.

And al-jaʿwal is the young of the ostrich. And al-jiʿāl is the rag by which the cooking-pot is taken down off the hearth-stones. And al-juʿl, al-jaʿāla and al-jaʿīla are what is set for a man in return for a thing he does. And jaʿaltu al-shay' — I made the thing. Al-Khalīl said: except that jaʿala is more general — you say jaʿala yaqūlu, he began to say, and you do not say ṣanaʿa yaqūlu. And a bitch is mujʿil when she wants the male. And al-Juʿala is the name of a place. He said:
And after it, the year we spent the spring at al-Juʿala.

So this section, as you see, does not resemble itself part for part.
جعم:
The letters jīm, ʿayn and mīm are two roots: old age, and greed for eating.

The first is the saying of al-Khalīl: al-jaʿmā', among women, is she whose mind has failed her from old age, and one does not say rajulun ajʿam of a man. And the aged she-camel is called al-jaʿmā'.

The second is the saying of al-Khalīl and others: jaʿimati l-ibilu, the camels jaʿimat, when they find no ḥamḍ and no ʿiḍāh to graze, so they gnaw bones instead — that from their eagerness for whatever they can eat. Al-Khalīl said: jaʿima yajʿamu jaʿaman, when he craves meat intensely, and in all of that he is a great eater. A man is jaʿim and a woman jaʿima, and bihā jaʿam means a coarseness of speech from a wide throat. Al-'Ajjāj said:
When the two Dhuhl craved every craving
— meaning they craved fighting as one craves meat. This is what al-Khalīl mentioned.

As for Abū Bakr, he mentioned something I hope is correct, though I think he dictated it as he recalled it from memory: he said jaʿima yajʿamu jaʿaman, when he does not desire food. He said: and I reckon it among the words that carry opposite meanings, because they sometimes called the voracious man jaʿim too. He said: and one says juʿima, so he is majʿūm, when he likewise does not desire it. This is Abū Bakr's account, and the true usages of the language do not rest on "I reckon" and "I think." As for his saying jaʿamtu l-baʿīr, like ka'amtuhu — perhaps this is an analogy in the chapter of letter-substitution that he found agreeable and so made into a usage of his own. God knows best whether it is sound.
جعن: The letters jīm, ʿayn and nūn are a thing with no root behind it. And Jaʿwana is the name of a place. So al-Khalīl said.
جف:
The letters jīm and fā' are two roots. The first is your saying "jaffa al-shayʾ," it dried, "yajiffu, jufūfan."

The second: al-juff, the sheath of the palm-spathe, its covering. One says al-juff is also something hollowed out of a palm trunk. al-juff — half a water-skin, made into a bucket. As for their calling a large group of people juff, as in al-Nābigha's line, "in the juff of Thaʿlab, comers to the bitter waters" — it is from this, because a group is something people cling to and gather round, as if it were the gathering-place of those who take refuge in it.

al-jafjaf, raised ground, belongs to the first root, because such ground, being raised, holds less moisture. Jufāf al-Ṭayr is a place-name. The poet said:
He saw not the fire that showed itself to him beyond Jufāf al-Ṭayr, except in doubt.
جفر:
The letters jīm, fā' and rā' are two roots: one describes something hollow, the other is the leaving of a thing.

The first: al-jafr is a well that has not been lined with stones. Carried on this too is al-jafr, said of the young of a sheep whose two flanks have widened out — jafara janbāhu — and it stays "jafr" until it becomes a yearling. A boy too is called jafr from this. Al-jafīr is like the quiver (al-kināna), but wider, holding many arrows. A horse is mujfar when it is large in al-jufra, which is its flank.

As for the second root: their saying ajfartu l-shay'a, I cut it off, and ajfaranī man kāna yazūrunī, the one who used to visit me ajfaranī — that is, he stopped visiting and left me. And ajfartu l-shay'a lladhī kuntu astaʿmiluhu, I abandoned the thing I used to use. From this comes jafara l-faḥlu ʿani l-ḍirābi, the stallion jafara from mating, when he holds back and abstains. He said:
And Suhayl has shown itself to the night traveller, as though
... a choice, noble stallion, following the she-camels, abstaining.
جفز: The letters jīm, fā' and zā' cannot be valid speech, except for what Ibn Durayd brings — that al-jafz is speed. I do not know what to make of it. And likewise his saying about al-jifs, that it is a dialect form of al-jibs, a worthless man; and likewise al-jafs, which he makes mean gathering.
جفل:
The letters jīm, fā' and lām are a single root, and it is the gathering of a thing, which may then move as one body in going away or fleeing. Al-jafl is the cloud that has poured out all its water — for once it has poured it out, it "injafala", moved off and passed on. A wind that is mujfil or jāfila is one quick in passing. Al-jufāl is what a flood casts off from its scum and debris. It is related of Ru'ba the poet that he used to recite the verse as: {as for the foam, it goes away as refuse} [al-Raʿd: 17] — a variant of the usual reading. One says injafala l-nāsu, the people injafalū, when they went away. Al-jafalā is inviting people to your food generally, all of them together, the opposite of al-naqarā, inviting them selectively. Ṭarafa said:
We, in the season of want, call all to our table
... you will not see the caller among us being choosy.
And ẓalīmun ijfīlun is a male ostrich that flees from everything — because it draws itself together as it flees and darts off — and by this word the coward too was called ijfīl. One says of the night, when it turns and departs: it injafala.

Al-Khalīl said: al-jufāla, of people, is the crowd, whether coming or going. One says akhadha juflatan min ṣūfin, he took a shorn portion of wool — that is, a fleece-cutting of it. Al-jufāl is hair that is thick and gathered together. Dhū al-Rumma said:
Over the two sides [of the back], hanging down thick and full.
جفن: The letters jīm, fā' and nūn are a single root, and it is something that encircles a thing and holds it in. Al-jafn is the eyelid, which holds in the eye. Al-jafn is also the scabbard of a sword. Jafn is also a place-name. The grapevine was called jafn because it winds around whatever it clings to — that can be seen for yourself.
جفو:
The letters jīm, fā' and the weak final letter indicate a single root: a thing recoiling away from another thing. From this: jafawtu l-rajula ajfūhu — I estranged the man; he shows plain al-jifwa, that is, al-jafā' (estrangement).

Jafā l-sarju 'an ẓahri l-faras — the saddle sat clear of the horse's back, not touching it, and ajfaytuhu — I made it sit clear. Likewise anything that does not stay pressed against another thing is said to jafā 'anhu yajfū — draw away from it.

Abū al-Najm said, describing a herdsman, in a line of verse:
Hard of staff, holding himself apart from courting women,
like the falcon that holds itself apart from chasing small sparrows.

He means: he has no skill at flirting with women; he keeps his distance from them just as the falcon keeps its distance from chasing the dukhkhal, a small bird, also called ibn tamra — literally 'son of a date-palm.'

Al-jafā' is the opposite of kindness. Al-jufā' is what a flash-flood casts aside; al-jafā' (estrangement) is derived from this.

This pattern holds consistently even in the hamzated form: one says jafa'tu l-rajula, when you threw him down and struck him against the ground. Ijtafa'tu l-baqlata, when you pulled the plant up out of the ground. Ajfa'ati l-qidru bi-zabadihā, when the cooking-pot threw off its scum, ijfā'an.

From this is his saying, peace and blessings be upon him and his family: 'As long as you do not drink it morning or evening, or pull up plants with it' — according to the version of those who transmit it with a jīm.

From this entry too: tajaffa'ati l-bilād, when a land's good has gone from it. And he cited, in a line of verse:
And when she saw that the land had lost its good,
Umm Ḥanbal complained to us of her hard life —
meaning: its green plants had all been eaten away.
جل:
The letters jīm and lām are three roots.

The first: "jalla al-shayʾ," it became great. jullu al-shayʾ — the greater part of a thing. jalāl Allāh — His majesty; He is Possessor of Majesty and Honour. al-jalal — a great matter. al-jilla — mature, old camels. A line runs: "Or let my camels turn their weapons on me one day, be it for the old among them or the young." al-jallāla — the huge she-camel. al-jalīla — the opposite of the small one. One says "he has neither daqīqa nor jalīla," meaning: he has neither she-camel nor sheep. "I came to so-and-so, and he neither ajallanī nor aḥshānī," meaning: he gave me nothing, small or great, of the mature stock or the young. "So-and-so adaqqa and ajalla," when he gave both little and much. A line runs: "Ah, who will help an eye that never sees the peaks of al-Ḥimā, nor the mountain of al-Rayyān, but it streams — persistent when it pours, copious when it weeps; it wept, and wept both little and much." He means: it shed both the small measure of weeping and the great. One says: "I did that from your jalāl," meaning: because of your greatness in my heart. Kuthayyir said: "and my honouring of enemies is on account of her greatness."

The second root: something that envelops another thing, like jull al-faras, the horse's covering-cloth, and like al-mujallil, the rain that covers the earth with water and plant growth. From it, al-julūl, the sails of ships. Al-Qaṭāmī said: "In one with sails, whose companion death singles out, when the sailor, from its terrors, makes the sign of prayer." The singular is jull.
