The third root, from sound: a cloud is mujaljil when it rumbles. al-juljul, the small bell, is derived from it. From this root, "jaljaltu al-shayʾ fī yadī," when you mixed it and then shook it. A line runs: "So he shook it twice, then let it go, as it was cast, roughly shaped, untrimmed." It is possible that juljulān al-simsim, the sesame seed, is from this, because it rattles in its pod when it dries. Also carried on this: their saying "I struck the juljulān of his heart," meaning its innermost kernel. From it too, al-jull, the stalks of standing crop, because the wind, striking it, sets it rattling — though it is also possible this belongs to the first root, on account of its bulk. From it, al-jalīl, which is thumām, a coarse rush. A line runs: "Ah, would that I knew whether I shall ever spend a night in a valley, with idhkhir-grass and jalīl-rush about me."

As for al-majalla, a written page, it stands outside this root, unless it is attached to the first, for the great worth and majesty of knowledge. Abū ʿUbayd said: every book, among the Arabs, is a majalla. Also outside this root: al-jilla, dung.
جلب:
The letters jīm, lām and bā' are two roots: one is bringing a thing from one place to another; the other is something that covers over another thing.

The first is their saying jalabtu al-shay'a jalban, I brought the thing in [from elsewhere]. A poet said, in a line of verse:
It was granted him, from his land and his sky ... for the bringers-in may bring a thing from far away.

Al-jalab, forbidden in a hadith, is for the zakat-collector to refrain from going to the owners of livestock at their watering-places to take the alms-due, and instead order them to drive their herds to him, taking the alms-due only then. It is also said this word instead concerns horse-racing: for a man to set up another man to shout and drive at his horse during the race, so that the horse being driven-on runs faster.

The second root: al-julba is a piece of hide put over a pack-saddle. Al-julba is also the scab over a wound as it heals; one says jalaba al-jurḥu or ajlaba, the wound scabbed over. Jilb al-raḥl is the wooden frame of a camel-saddle; it seems to be named so by closeness [to the sense of covering]. Al-julb is a thin cloud lying across the sky, with no water in it.

Abū ʿAmr said: al-julba is a cloud that looks like a mountain; likewise al-julb. He quoted, in a line of verse:
I am not a julb, a julb of wind and cold ... nor a bare, hard rock set apart from all good.

From this too comes the derivation of al-jilbāb, the long garment, plural jalābīb. He quoted, in a line of verse:
The vultures walk toward it, unconcerned ... like the walk of young girls wearing their long garments.
He means: the vultures are in an empty place with nothing to frighten them, so they are unworried and unhurried.
جلج: The letters jīm, lām and jīm are not a root, because they in fact hold two separate words. Ibn Durayd said: al-jalaj is like al-qalaq, restlessness. If that is sound, then the jīm here stands in place of a qāf. And the other word is al-jalaja, the head — one says "for every jalaja in the division, such-and-such," meaning per head. This is not established as sound, and it may be something taken into Arabic from a foreign tongue.
جلح:
The letters jīm, lām and ḥā' are a single root, and it is being stripped bare and the uncovering of one thing from another. Al-jalaḥ is the loss of the hair from the front of the head, and a man with it is ajlaḥ. Al-sunūn al-majāliḥ are the years that strip away livestock. Al-sayl al-julāḥ is the violent flood that sweeps everything before it, carrying it off. One says jalaḥa l-mālu l-shajara yajlaḥuhu jalḥan, the livestock jalaḥa the trees, when it eats off their tops, and the tree is then majlūḥ. Al-ajlaḥ, of howdahs, is the one with no dome over it. This is the steady, regular pattern.

Carried on this too is their saying fulānun mujallaḥun, when he presses ahead firmly in a matter, like the tajlīḥ of a wolf — and this only comes by casting off the veil of shame. From this too is al-tajlīḥ in travel, meaning hard, driving travel, because it strips a man bare for the journey and draws him tight into it. In this chapter too is al-nakhla al-mijlāḥ, the palm tree that does not mind drought, and al-nāqa al-mijlāḥ, the she-camel that gives milk freely in winter — of this same chapter, as though she were tough, tough of face, unconcerned by hardship.
جلخ: The letters jīm, lām and khā' are not a root, and there is no sound Arabic word in them. If there is anything to it, the khā' stands in place of a ḥā', and that has already been discussed.
جلد:
The letters jīm, lām and dāl are a single root, and it points to strength and hardness.

Al-jild, the skin, is well known, and it is stronger and harder than the flesh beneath it. Al-jalad is the hardness of the skin. Al-ajlād is the body; a man's body is called his ajlād and his tajālīd. Al-mijlad is a piece of leather that the wailing woman holds and strikes her face with it at a mourning. A poet said, in a line of verse:
They came out trailing their garments and brought out a mijlad, a strip of leather, and the yellow marked rods went round about them.

About al-jalad there are two sayings. One of them is that the hide of a camel or of some other beast is flayed off and another animal is clothed in it. A poet said:
As though he were in a jalad, a hide hanging loose about him.

The second saying is that the hide of a camel calf is stuffed with thumām grass or something else, and its mother is made to lean over it so that she takes to it as her own. Al-'Ajjāj said, in a line of verse:
I have seen myself a prey for the fair women for a time, as though upon me there were a jalad.
He means: they take to me and lean towards me as the she-camel takes to the stuffed hide.

Ibn al-A'rābī used to say that al-jild and al-jalad are one and the same, as one says shibh and shabah. Ibn al-Sikkīt said: this is not known.

One says jallada al-rajulu jazūrahu — the man skinned his slaughter-camel — when he pulls its hide off it. One does not say salakha jazūrahu of a slaughter-camel. One says a horse is mujallad when it does not flinch at the stroke of the whip. One says a she-camel is dhāt majlūd when she is strong. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Of those which, when their temper has softened, still keep after that their frame and their strength.

It is said that al-jalad among camels are the big ones, with no young among them. Al-jalad is also hard, rough ground. Al-jilād among camels are those that give less milk than the khūr; the single one is a jildah.
جلذ:
The letters jīm, lām and dhāl point to what the letters before them point to, namely strength. Al-jildhā'a is hard, rugged ground. Al-juldhiyya is the strong, swift she-camel. Al-juldhī is a strong, swift pace. He said:
You shall press on with a swift, strong night-march to the water.
As for Ibn Muqbil's saying, "the striking of the bells, in which the hands of al-jalādhī do not slacken, and jawn that do not cease" — he is speaking there of Christians. Al-jalādhī are his people and his attendants. Ibn al-A'rābī said: he was named juldhī only because he had shaved the middle of his head, so that spot was likened to the smooth stone, which is also called al-juldhī.

Ibn al-A'rābī said: we always took al-jawn, in this line, to mean doves — "mā yuʿaffīna" being about their cooing — until I was told, by one of Ibn Muqbil's descendants, that al-jawn means lamps, so named for their whiteness. "Mā yuʿaffīna" means: what goes out, fades. And what is meant is that these attendants do not slacken in striking the bells. One says ijlawwadha, when he moved quickly.
جلس:
The letters jīm, lām and sīn are a single word and a single root, and it is being raised up in something. One says: jalasa l-rajulu julūsan, the man sat up — that is done from a state of sleep or lying down; but if he was standing, the state opposite to that would be called al-qu'ūd (sitting down).

One says qāma (he stood) and qa'ada (he sat); from this comes al-muqīm and al-muq'id.

Al-jilsa is the manner in which a sitting person sits; one says jalasa jilsatan ḥasanatan, he sat in a good posture. Al-jalsa is a single instance of sitting.

One also says jalasa l-rajulu, when a man came to Najd — this fits the pattern of the root, since Najd is the opposite of al-Ghawr (the lowland), and it lies high. Najd is also called al-jals.

From this comes the hadith: 'He gave them the mines of al-Qabaliyya, both their lowland and their highland parts.'

The Hudhalī poet said, in a line of verse:
Whenever we take to the highland, we are never without
Sulaym and Hawāzin, near our tents, coming and going.

Another said, in a line of verse: 'And to the right of the one who has gone up to the highland.'

And he said, in a line of verse:
Tell al-Farazdaq — folly is just as its name says —
if you dislike what I have commanded you, then go up to the highland.
He means: go to Najd.

Abū Ḥātim said: Umm al-Haytham said: jalasati l-rakhama, when the vulture squatted down to roost.

Al-jals is rough, hard ground. From this comes their saying nāqatun jalsun, a she-camel that is tough and sturdy. This pattern holds consistently, as you see.

As for al-A'shā's line of verse:
We have jullasān there, and violets,
and basil, and marjoram richly patterned —
it is said that this word is Persian, being gulshan, meaning scattered rose-petals.
جلط: The letters jīm, lām and ṭā' are a root — rare, but of a steady pattern — and it is the stripping bare of a thing. One says jalaṭa ra'sahu, when he shaved his head, and jalaṭa sayfahu, when he drew his sword.
جلع:
The letters jīm, lām and ʿayn are a single root, close to the one before it. One says of a woman with little shame: jaliʿa, as though she had cast off the veil of modesty. And one says jaliʿa famu fulānin, when his lip drew back and his teeth showed.

Al-Khalīl said: al-mujālaʿa is people quarrelling with one another over drink or over a division of something. He said:
Nor is he foul-mouthed and quarrelsome over drink.
جلف:
The letters jīm, lām and fā' are a single root pointing to cutting and to scraping. One says jalafa l-shay'a jalfan, when he stripped it away entirely — a stronger word than al-jarf, scraping. A man is mujallaf when time has jallafahu, stripped him bare, come upon and taken away his wealth. This is al-Farazdaq's line:
And the bite of time, son of Marwān, has left
... of wealth nothing but what is utterly ruined or stripped bare.
Al-jilfa is a piece cut off from a thing. Al-jilf is the skinned carcass with neither head nor legs — and for this they say huwa jilfun jāfin, he is coarse and rough — it was so named because its extremities have been cut off.
جلق:
The letters jīm, lām and qāf are neither a root nor a branch. Jillaq is the name of a town, and it is not an Arabic word. He said:
God's blessing on a band I once caroused with
... one day at Jillaq, in bygone times.
جلم:
The letters jīm, lām and mīm are two roots: one is cutting, the other is the gathering of a thing.

The first: jalamtu l-sanāma, I cut off the hump. Al-jalam is well known — shears, with which one cuts or shears.

The other is their saying akhadhtu l-shay'a bi-jalamatihi, I took the thing entire, all of it. Jalamatu l-shāti is the sheep's skinned carcass once its shanks and joints have been taken from it. It is said that al-jilām are the kid-goats, in al-A'shā's line:
Lean, their yearlings are like the kid-goats
... the riding-gear has already worn sores upon them.
This perhaps belongs under the second root, or else stands apart from it.
جله:
The letters jīm, lām and hā' are a single root pointing to the baring, the uncovering, of a thing. Al-jalah is the receding of the hair from the two sides of the head. Ru'ba said:
When she saw me — worn of the gilded sheen
... shining at the bare, smooth patches of my receded brow.
Jalhatā l-wādī are its two sides, when there is hardness of rock in them. That is taken from their saying jalahtu l-ḥaṣā ʿani l-makāni, when you clear the gravel away from a place.
جلو:
The letters jīm, lām and the weak final letter are one root, following a consistent pattern: the uncovering and appearing of a thing.

1. jalawtu al-ʿarūs jalwatan wa jalā'an — I unveiled the bride.
2. jalawtu as-sayf jalā'an — I polished the sword.
Al-Kisā'ī said: as-samā'u jalwā' — the sky is clear.
3. One says tajallā ash-shay' — the thing became uncovered.
4. A man is ajlā when the hair at the front of his head has receded; that is al-jalā. He said, in a line of verse:
from the receded hairline, and the visible traces of grey hair.

From this root: jalā al-qawm ʿan manāzilihim jalā'an — the people departed, driven out from their dwellings; ajlaytuhum anā ijlā'an — I drove them out.

They say: huwa ibnu jalā — "he is a son of jalā," when his affair cannot be hidden, on account of his fame. He said, in a line of verse:
I am the son of jalā and the climber of mountain-passes; whenever I remove my turban, you will know me.

One also says jalā al-qawm, and ajlaytuhum anā, and jalawtuhum, all meaning "I drove them out." Abū Dhu'ayb said, in a line of verse:
so when he drove them out with smoke, they scattered into separate groups, humiliation and dejection upon them.
جم:
The letters jīm and mīm, doubled, are two roots: the first is the abundance and gathering of a thing, the second is being without weapons.

The first: al-jamm, abundant. God, exalted is His praise, said: {and you love wealth with an abounding love} [al-Fajr: 20]. al-jimām — fullness. One says a vessel is jammān when it has reached its jimām, brimful. A line runs: "Or like the water of a well drawn dry after being full to the brim, its flow choked off, scant, not returning." One says the horse is in its jamām; al-jamām is rest, because it is then composed, its limbs still — and this fits the analogy of the root. al-jumma — the people who collect contributions for blood-money, because they gather together for it. A line runs: "and a jumma asked of me, and I gave." al-jamīm — a thick growth of buhmā-grass. A line runs: "It grazed on the young shoots of buhmā-grass, thick-grown, and on busra and ṣamʿāʾ, until their points made it shy away." al-jumma, of a person — the gathered mass of the hair of his forelock. al-jamma, of a well — the place where its water gathers. al-jamūm — a well abundant in water; "jammat jumūman." A line runs: "the churning of the buckets swells its abundance." al-jamūm, among horses — one whose burst of speed, once spent, is at once renewed — pointing again to abundance and gathering. Al-Namir ibn Tawlab said: "abundant in its running, its tail raised, you would think the white of its blaze a lamp." al-jumjuma — the human skull, because it gathers together the plates of the head. al-jamjama — a well dug in salt-flat ground. "jamma" and "ajamma" — a horse, when it is left unridden, is from this root, because its strength returns to it and gathers. jamājim al-ʿArab — the great tribes that gather the sub-clans together, so that a man is attributed to them rather than to the sub-clans, as with Kalb ibn Wabra: one says "Kalbī" and need not trace himself to any of its sub-clans. al-jammāʾ al-ghafīr — the multitude of people. Some said it is [also] al-bayḍa, the iron helmet, because it gathers in the hair of the head. From this root, "ajamma al-shayʾ," it drew near.

The second root: al-ajamm — one who carries no spear with him in war. al-shāh al-jammāʾ — the sheep or goat with no horn. It came in the hadith: "We were commanded to build mosques jumman," meaning that their walls should carry no battlements.
جمح:
The letters jīm, mīm and ḥā' are a single, consistent root: a thing going headlong forward by overpowering force. One says jamaḥati l-dābbatu jimāḥan, when the mount overpowered its rider until it got the better of him. A horse like this is jamūḥ.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Swift-swimming, headstrong, its full gallop
like the crackling roar of burning palm-fronds.

Jamaḥa l-ṣabiyyu l-ka'ba bi-l-ka'b, when a boy struck one knucklebone with another to knock it from its place in the game. This is open to question, since it is more properly said with another word, and has been mentioned elsewhere.

Al-jummāḥ is an arrow with a ball of clay like a pellet fixed on its head, that boys shoot with.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Will it carry me to them by morning —
a young ostrich, its head like a clay-headed arrow?

Some philologists said: al-jamūḥ is one who rides after his own whims.

As for God Most High's saying: {they would turn to it, racing headlong} [al-Tawba: 57], he meant: hurrying. It is the same sense.

And he said, in a line of verse:
I threw off restraint, headlong, and no rebuke of any rebuker
could turn me back from the fair women, like statues.

Jamaḥati l-mar'atu ilā ahlihā — the woman bolted off to her family, went without permission.
جمخ: The letters jīm, mīm and khā' are one word, perhaps belonging to the chapter of letter-substitution. They say jāmakhtu al-rajul, meaning I vied with him, boasting against him. We say it belongs to substitution because the mīm may be a change from an original fā' — the word being al-jafkh and al-jakhf, with the same meaning.
جمد:
The letters jīm, mīm and dāl are a single root, and it is a liquid thing solidifying, from cold or otherwise. One says: jamada l-mā'u yajmudu — the water froze.

Sanatun jamād is a year scant in rain — this is carried over from the first sense, as if its rain had solidified and stopped.

Al-Shaybānī used to say: al-jamād is land that has not been rained on.

The Arabs say to a miser: 'jamādi lah' — meaning: may his state never stop being frozen; it is the opposite of ḥamādi, a word of praise.

Al-Mutalammis said, in a line of verse:
'Frozen be her state, frozen' — and never say
of her, whenever she is mentioned, 'praised be.'
جمر:
The letters jīm, mīm and rā' are a single root indicating a gathering together.

1. al-jamr — the ember of fire, well known; one ember is a jamra.
2. al-jummār, also called jāmūr — the pith of the palm tree, the soft heart at its top.
3. jammara fulānun jayshahu — said of a man when he held his army back on campaign and did not let them return home.
4. hāfirun mujmar — a hoof that is tough, firm, hard, compact.
5. al-jamarāt al-thalāth — the three [heaps] at Mecca that are pelted [in the pilgrimage], named from this too, for the gathering together of the pebbles there.

As for the jamarāt of the Arabs, some said: when a tribe has three hundred horsemen, it is a jamra. Others said: any tribe that banded together and fought others while allying with no one else, they are a jamra.

Abū 'Ubayd used to say: the jamarāt of the Arabs are three — Banū Dabba ibn Udd, Banū Numayr ibn 'Āmir, and Banū al-Ḥārith ibn Ka'b. Two of these jamras were put out and one remained. Dabba was put out because it allied with al-Ribāb; Banū al-Ḥārith was put out because it allied with Madhḥij; and Numayr remained, not put out, because it allied with no one.

6. jammarat al-mar'a sha'rahā — said of a woman when she gathered her hair and bound it at the back of her neck.
7. jamīr al-qawm — the gathering-together of a people.
8. ajmara al-qawm 'alā al-amr — they came to agreement together on the matter.
9. Ibn Jamīr — the dark night.
جمز:
The letters jīm, mīm and zā' are a single root, and it is a kind of gait.

One says jamaza al-ba'īr jamzan — a camel's gait, and it is faster than the pace called al-'anaq. The camel of al-Najāshī was named Jammāz for the swiftness of its going.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
I am al-Najāshī, upon Jammāz — Ibn Ḥassān swerved away from my war-chant.

A donkey that is jamazā is a swift one.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
As if I, and my saddle, when I startled her, were upon a swift wild ass grazing the sands, needing no water.

One word strays from this pattern: al-jumza, a lump of pressed dates.
جمس:
The letters jīm, mīm and sīn are a single root, from jumūs al-shay', a thing's congealing.

One says jamasa al-wadak — the fat congealed, set hard. Al-jamsa is the unripe date once it has begun to turn soft, while still hard.
جمش:
The letters jīm, mīm and shīn are a single root, and it is a kind of shaving.

One says jamashtu al-sha'r — I shaved the hair; sha'run jamīsh is hair that has been shaved. In the hadith: "if you see a ewe at the waste of al-Jamīsh" — al-khabt is open desert waste, and al-jamīsh is ground with no plant growth on it. A year that is jamūsh is one that has shaved the plants bare.

Ru'ba said, in a line of verse:
Or like the clean shave of the depilatory paste.

Two words stray from this chapter: al-jamsh, milking with the fingertips; and al-jamsh, a sound.
جمع:
The letters jīm, mīm and ʿayn are a single root pointing to a thing's being drawn together. One says jamaʿtu al-shay' jamʿan — I gathered the thing. And al-jummāʿ is a mixed body drawn from scattered tribes.

Abū Qays said, in a line of verse:
Then it cleared away, and we had the upper hand, from among a gathering that was no mixed rabble.

And of a woman who dies with a child in her belly it is said: she died bi-jumʿ. And it is said that it is a woman's dying untouched by any man. And from this is the saying of al-Dahnā': "I am with him bi-jumʿ."

And al-jāmiʿ is the she-ass at her first conception. And a qidr jimāʿ and jāmiʿa is a great cooking-pot. And al-jamʿ is every kind of date-palm whose name is not known; one says how much jamʿ there is in the land of the sons of so-and-so, of palms that came up from date-stones. And one says ḍarabtuhu bi-jumʿi kaffī and bi-jimʿi kaffī — I struck him with my closed fist. And you say nahbun mujmaʿ — booty gathered up together.

Abū Dhu'ayb said, in a line of verse:
And it is as though she, at the bend, the bend of Nubāyiʿ, and the folk of Dhī al-Kharjā', were booty all gathered up.

And you say istajmaʿa al-farasu jaryan — the horse gathered himself for a run. And Jamʿ is Mecca, so called for the gathering of people there; and likewise the day of [the Gathering, Friday]. And ajmaʿtu ʿalā al-amr ijmāʿan, and ajmaʿtuhu — I resolved upon the matter.

Al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥilliza said, in a line of verse:
They settled their affair by night, and when they came into the morning there was an uproar among them.

And one says falātun mujmiʿa — a desert in which people keep together and do not scatter, for fear of losing the way. And al-jawāmiʿ are shackles. And al-jamʿā' among beasts and others is the one from whose body nothing has gone.
جمل:
The letters jīm, mīm and lām are two roots: one of them is gathering together and largeness of build, and the other is beauty.

The first is your saying ajmaltu al-shay' — I summed the thing up — and hādhihi jumlat al-shay', this is the sum of it. And ajmaltuhu — I gathered it in. God Most High said: {and those who disbelieved said: if only the Qur'an had been sent down upon him all at once} [al-Furqān: 32].

And it may be that al-jamal, the camel, is from this, for the largeness of its build. Al-jummal is a thick rope, and that too is from this. And it is said ajmala al-qawm — the people's camels grew many. Al-jumālī is the man of great build, as though he were likened to a camel; and likewise a she-camel is jumāliyya. Al-Farrā' said: (jimālāt) is the plural of jamal. And al-jimālāt are the ropes and cables gathered together.

The other root is al-jamāl, beauty, which is the opposite of ugliness. A man is jamīl and jumāl. Ibn Qutayba said: its origin is from al-jamīl, which is the melted grease of fat. What is meant is that the water of plumpness runs in his face. And it is said jamālaka an taf'ala kadhā, that is, be seemly and do not do it. Abū Dhu'ayb said, in a line of verse:
Be seemly, O wounded heart; you will meet the one you love and find rest.

And a woman said to her daughter: "lā tajammalī wa-ta'affafī" — that is, eat the jamīl, which is the melted fat we mentioned, and drink the 'ufāfa, which is what is left over of the milk.
جمن:
The letters jīm, mīm and nūn hold nothing but al-jumān, which is pearl.

Al-Musayyab said, in a line of verse:
Like a pearl of the sea, brought up by its diver from the deep of the sea.
جمي:
The letters jīm, mīm and the weak letter are one word, and it is al-jamā', which is a person's shape or figure. The jīm is sometimes said with damma [jumā'].

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And a round loaf like the boss of a shield.
جن:
The letters jīm and nūn are one root, and it is covering and concealment.

al-janna — what the Muslims will attain in the hereafter, a reward hidden from them today. al-janna — the garden, likewise, because the trees, with their leaves, conceal. Some say that al-janna, among the Arabs, is [also] tall palm trees, citing Zuhayr's line: "As if my two eyes were the two worn buckets of the watering-camels, watering a lofty grove of tall palms." al-janīn — the child in its mother's womb. al-janīn — also the one laid in the grave. al-janān — the heart. al-mijann — the shield. Anything one shields oneself with, of weaponry, is a junna. Abū ʿUbayda said: al-silāḥ is what one fights with, al-junna what one shields oneself with. A line runs: "Where you see the horses, grim with their riders, rising up with Indian blades and shields." al-jinna — madness, because it covers over the reason. janān al-layl — its blackness, its concealing of things. A line runs: "Had it not been for the covering dark of night, our galloping would have overtaken, at Dhū al-Rimth and al-Arṭā, ʿIyāḍ ibn Nāshib." One also says junūn al-layl, the same meaning. One says "janna al-nabt junūnan" when a plant grew vigorous and put out its blossom — possibly a metaphor from madness, as a person goes mad and becomes agitated, while the origin of junūn remains concealment, as we said; the analogy holds. janān al-nās — the bulk of the people, also called al-sawād. al-majanna — madness. As for the serpent called al-jānn, it is named by comparison to a single one of the jinn. The jinn were named thus because they are hidden from the eyes of creation. God, exalted is He, said: {he sees you, he and his tribe, from where you do not see them} [al-Aʿrāf: 27]. al-janājin — the bones of the chest.
جنأ:
The letters jīm, nūn and hamza are a single root, and it is bending over a thing, leaning over it in tenderness.

One says jani'a 'alayhi yajna'u jana'an — he stooped, grew hunched. A man is adna' or ajna' with the same meaning. And tajāna'tu 'alā al-rajul — you leaned over the man, protecting him. Al-turs al-mujna', the curved shield, is from this.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And a curved, dark-brown shield, battered by blows.
جنب:
The letters jīm, nūn and bā' are two roots close to each other. One of them is the side or quarter, and the other is distance.

As for the quarter, that is al-janāb. One says hādhā min dhālika al-janāb, that is, from that quarter. And so-and-so sat janbatan, when he keeps apart from people. And in the hadith: keep to sitting apart, for it is chastity.

And of the chapter is al-janb, the side of a person and of others. And of this is the janb forbidden in the hadith: that a man lead alongside his own horse, at a race, another horse, for fear of being outstripped, so that he may shift over onto it. And al-janab is that a camel's thirst grows so fierce that his lung sticks to his side. And one says janiba yajnabu. A poet said, in a line of verse:
As though his limp were there for all to see, or he were a camel with his lung stuck to his side.

And al-majnab is abundant good, as though it were at a person's side. And janabtu al-dābba, when you lead the beast at your side. And so too janabtu al-asīr - I led the captive along. And the shield was called mijnab because it is at a person's side.

As for distance, that is al-janāba. The poet said, in a line of verse:
Do not deny me a gift because I am far off in kin, for I am a man who is a stranger among the tents.

And it is said that al-junub, the man who has lain with his wife, is derived from this, because he keeps far from what others come near to, of the prayer and the mosque and other than that.

And of what strayed from the chapter is the south wind, rīḥ al-janūb. One says juniba al-qawm - the south wind struck the people; and ajnabū, when they entered into the south wind. And their saying jannaba al-qawm, when the milk of their camels grows little. And this, in my view, is not from the chapter. But if someone were to say that it is from distance, as though their milk had grown little and so gone away, that would be a way of taking it. And Janb is a tribe, and the relative name from it is Janbī. And it is derived from some of what we have mentioned.
جنث:
The letters jīm, nūn and thā' are a single root, and it is origin and soundness.

1. jinth — the origin or root of anything.
2. al-junthī — the maker of chain-mail, so called because he makes the mail sound and secure.

As for his saying:
The mail-maker made firm, against its weak points, every stud — which rings out when pressed.
He meant the mail-maker, that is: he made firm its rivets, which are the studs. Whoever puts al-junthī in the accusative case meant the sword instead, making the verb belong to every stud, so that the meaning of "made firm" becomes "held off" — he is saying: it is mail whose studs stop the sword from working on it.

And a poet said, of the sword:
But it is a market whose trade is carried on in a junthiyya-sword, which the polishers have brought to purity.
جنح:
The letters jīm, nūn and ḥā' are one root pointing to leaning and to wrongdoing. One says janaḥa ilā kadhā, that is, he leaned towards it. And the two wings were called janāḥān because of their leaning out on the two sides. And al-junāḥ is sin, so named for its leaning away from the road of the truth.

And this is the root; then things are derived from it. So a stretch of the night is called junḥ and jinḥ, as though it were likened to the wing, which is one part of the bird's body. And al-jawāniḥ are the ribs, because they lean. And juniḥa al-baʿīr, when his ribs are broken by a heavy load. And janaḥat al-ibil in their going, when they hurried. And this is from the wing, as though they had set their wings to work.
جند: The letters jīm, nūn and dāl indicate gathering together and helping. One says: they are his jund, that is, his helpers and supporters. And al-ajnād are the ajnād of Syria, and they are five: Damascus, Ḥimṣ, Qinnasrīn, al-Urdunn and Palestine; each one of these is called a jund. And Janad is a town. And al-janad is rough ground with white stones in it; and this may be from the chapter, and it may be a case of letter-substitution, the original being al-jalad, hard ground.
جنز:
The letters jīm, nūn and zā' are one word. Ibn Durayd said: janaztu al-shay' ajnizuhu janzan — you covered it, concealed it — and from this comes the derivation of al-janāza, the funeral bier.

Al-Khalīl's view differs from this. He said: al-janāza is the dead person, and also anything that weighed heavily on a people and grieved them is called a janāza.

He cited:
I never feared that I would become a burden upon you — and who is not deceived by the turns of fate?

He said: as for al-jinaza [with kasra], it is the wood of the bier. He said: and the Arabs say, "rumiya bi-janāzatihi fa-māta" — he was struck down by his janāza and died [said of sudden collapse]. He said: al-janāza with fatḥa on the jīm has become current on people's tongues, but the careful scholars reject it.
جنس:
The letters jīm, nūn and sīn are a single root, and it is a kind or a sort of a thing.

Al-Khalīl said: every sort is a jins, and it applies to people, birds, and things generally; the plural is ajnās.

Ibn Durayd said: al-Aṣma'ī used to reject the common people's saying "hādhā mujānis li-hādhā" [this is akin to that], saying it is not correct Arabic. And I say: this is a mistake laid on al-Aṣma'ī, for he is the one who composed the Book of Kinds, and he was the first to bring this term into the language.
جنف:
The letters jīm, nūn and fā' are a single root, and it is leaning aside/deviation.

One says janifa when someone turns aside and wrongs others, deviating unjustly. God the Exalted, glorious is His praise, said: {but whoever fears from a testator an unjust deviation} [al-Baqara: 182].

A man is ajnaf when there is a lean in his frame; it is said this applies only to height — a stoop or bend.

One says tajānafa ʿan kadhā when he turned away from something. A poet said, in a line of verse:
My she-camel turned away from the heart of al-Yamāma ... yet she did not turn from its people for anyone but you.
جنه:
The letters jīm, nūn and hā' are not a root, and to my mind it is not even genuine speech of the Arabs — except that some people claimed that al-junah is the khayzurān, a cane. They recited:
In his hand a cane whose scent is fragrant — in the hand of a noble man, in whose nose is haughtiness.
جني:
The letters jīm, nūn and yā' are a single root, and it is taking fruit from its tree; other things are then carried on this. You say janaytu al-thamarata ajnīhā, and ijtanaytuhā, I picked the fruit. Fruit called janiyy is fruit picked fresh, at its right time.

Carried on this sense: janaytu al-jināyata ajnīhā, I committed the offence — the same word for picking extended to bringing about a wrong.
جه: The letters jīm and hā' are not a root, because it is the imitation of a sound. One says "jahjahtu bi-l-sabuʿ" when you shouted at a predator [to drive it off]. A line runs: "then it came, undeterred by the shout or the jahjaha." Some related "tajahjaha ʿan al-amr" — he desisted from the matter, stopped. If this is sound, it belongs to the class of correspondence, since you say "I jahjahtu at him" and so "he tajahjaha," was driven off.
جهد:
The letters jīm, hā' and dāl - their origin is hardship, and then what is near to it is carried upon it. One says jahadtu nafsī and ajhadtu - I wore myself out. Al-juhd is what one has the capacity for. God - exalted is He - said: {And those who find nothing but their juhd - their utmost} [al-Tawba: 79].

And it is said that al-majhūd is the milk whose butter has been taken out, and that hardly comes about except with hardship and toil. Al-Shammākh said, in a line of verse:
She comes at morning, her udders holding draughts of good taste, sweet, not stripped of its butter.

Among what comes near this chapter is al-jahād, which is hard ground. And fulān yajhadu al-ṭaʿām, when he falls upon the food with much hard eating. Al-jāhid is the greedy one. And marʿan jahīd is a pasture that the herds fell upon because of its sweetness and ate up.
جهر:
The letters jīm, hā' and rā' are a single root, and it is making a thing public, uncovering it, and its being high. One says jahartu bi-al-kalām — I spoke out openly with the words. And rajul jahīr al-ṣawt — a man with a loud voice. A poet said, in a line of verse:
I speak out aloud while they speak low ... and how far apart are the loud voice and the whispered speech.

From this chapter: jahartu al-shay' when it looms great in your eye. And jahartu al-rajul likewise. A poet said, in a line of verse:
As though its great bulk were so to whoever saw it plain.

As for al-'ayn al-jahrā', it is the eye that cannot see in the sun. And one says ra'aytu juhra fulān — that is, his outward look. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And what the people hid was what follows upon the outward look.
That is, they will not be able to hide anything of what is known of him and of what follows upon his outward look. And one says jahīr bayyin al-jahāra of a man of fine appearance. Abū al-Najm said, in a line of verse:
I count whiteness in women a fine appearance ... but nobility I know upon the brown-skinned.

And one says jaharnā banī fulān — that is, we came upon them in the morning unawares. It belongs to this chapter, that is, we came to them at morning; and the morning is jahr. And a company of people is called al-jahrā'. And it is said that al-jahrā' is the broad rising ground.
جهز:
The letters jīm, hā' and zā' are a single root: something that is held firmly and gathered together, such as al-jahāz (household goods, one's gear). I jahhaztu so-and-so [equipped him], meaning: I took on the task of preparing his travel gear.

As for their saying of the camel when it bolts, "it struck off with its gear," this is a proverb, meaning: it carried its equipment and went off. Abū 'Ubayda said: among the proverbs of the Arabs, "So-and-so struck off with his gear" is said of estrangement and drawing away. The origin is what we have mentioned.
جهش:
The letters jīm, hā' and shīn are a single root, and it is readying oneself to weep.

One says jahasha yajhashu and ajhasha yujhishu — he made ready to weep.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
My very soul rose complaining to me, on the edge of tears — 'and I have carried you seven years after seventy.'
جهض:
The letters jīm, hā' and ḍād are a single root, and it is a thing's leaving its place swiftly.

One says ajhaḍnā fulānan 'an al-shay' — we drove him away from it and overcame him regarding it. Ajhaḍat al-nāqa — the she-camel miscarried her young; she is mujhiḍ. As for their saying, of one hard and bold of heart, "innahu la-jāhiḍ, wa fīhi juhūḍa wa jahāḍa," this too is from the same root — as if his heart, from its sharpness, leaps from its place.
جهف:
The letters jīm, hā' and fā' are not a root; it belongs instead to the chapter of letter-substitution.

One says ijtahaftu al-shay' — you seized it violently. The origin is ijtaḥaftu [with ḥā'], which has already been mentioned.
جهل:
The letters jīm, hā' and lām are two roots: one of them is the opposite of knowledge, and the other is lightness and the opposite of settledness.

The first is al-jahl, the opposite of knowledge. And a waterless waste with no landmark in it is called a majhal.

The second is their word for the stick with which embers are stirred: a mijhal. And one says istajhalat al-rīh al-ghusn, when the wind moves the branch so that it shakes. And of it is the saying of al-Nābigha, in a line of verse:
Love has called you, and the dwelling-places have made you light-headed; and how should a man play the youth when grey hair is over all of him?
And it is of the chapter, because its meaning is: they made you light and stirred you up. And al-majhala is the thing that drives you to folly.
جهم:
The letters jīm, hā' and mīm indicate the opposite of cheerfulness and openness.

1. rajulun jahm al-wajh — a man disagreeable, scowling of face.
2. jahmat al-layl, also juhmatuh — the stretch of night between its start and its first quarter.
3. jahamtu al-rajul, also tajahhamtuhu — you met the man with a scowling face.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
So do not scowl at us, Umm 'Amr — for we bear the malady of a gazelle whose limbs have not failed it.

And from the same, his saying:
And a land that meets the harsh one with a scowl —
meaning: it meets him with what he dislikes.

4. al-jahām — cloud that has poured out all its water, so called because its good is now little and no longer looked to.
5. al-jahūm — the incapable, helpless one; close in meaning to the last.
جهن: The letters jīm, hā' and nūn are one word. They said jāriyatun juhāna, meaning a young girl. They said: from this comes the derivation of the name Juhayna.
جهو:
The letters jīm, hā' and the weak letter indicate a thing's being uncovered.

One says ajhat al-samā' — the sky cleared of cloud. A tent that is muj-hin has no covering over it. Al-bayt jahiya yajhā — the house fell into ruin; it is jāhin. And it is said that al-jahwa is the buttocks, laid bare.
جو:
The letters jīm and wāw are one thing, and it is that which encloses something on its sides. al-jaww — the expanse of the sky, that which arches over the earth on every side; jaww al-bayt, the space within a house, is from this too.

As for al-juʾjuʾ, the breast, it is spelled with a hamza, though it may be carried on the same analogy.
جوب:
The letters jīm, wāw and bā' are a single root, and it is the cutting through of a thing. One says jubtu al-arḍ jawban — I cut across the land; so I am jā'ib and jawwāb. Al-Jaʿdī said, in a line of verse:
Abū Laylā came to you, cutting the darkness with him ... the darkness of the night, a crosser of the wilderness, strong and heavy.

And one says: "Have you a jā'ibat khabar?" — that is, a piece of news that travels the lands. And al-jawba is like a low open hollow, and it is of the chapter, because it is like a hole cut in the ground. And al-jawb is a mail garment that a woman wears, and it is majūb, cut out, named with the verbal noun. And al-mijwab is an iron tool with which a thing is cut, that is, stitched and pieced together.

And there is another root, and it is the exchange of speech. One says kallamahu fa-ajābahu jawāban — he spoke to him and he answered him with an answer; and the two answered one another, tajāwabā mujāwabatan. And al-mujāba is the answer. And they say in a proverb: "He heard badly, so he answered badly." And al-Kumayt said to Quḍāʿa about their moving over to Yemen, in a line of verse:
And none whom you call upon for help ... is quicker to answer you than the hadīl dove.
The Arabs say: there was in Noah's ark — peace be upon him — a young bird; it flew and fell into the water and drowned, so all the birds weep for it. And about it the poet says, in a line of verse:
I said: does a sorrowing one weep, remembering ... a hadīl that has perished, before ever Tubbaʿ was?
جوت:
The letters jīm, wāw and tā' are not a root, because the word imitates a sound, and sounds are not measured by the rules of derivation, nor is anything measured against them.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
As you startled the thirsty beasts, parched with thirst, with the jawt-sound.

Abū 'Ubayd said: al-Kisā'ī used to recite this line putting the word in the accusative, saying "kamā ru'ta bi'l-jawta," reciting it fixed with the alif and lām.
جوح:
The letters jīm, wāw and ḥā' are a single root, and it is uprooting something entirely.

One says jāḥa al-shay' yajūḥuhu — he destroyed it utterly, uprooted it. From this comes the derivation of al-jā'iḥa, a calamity that sweeps everything away.
جوخ:
The letters jīm, wāw and khā' are, to my mind, not a root, because part of the word is an Arabicized foreign word, and part of it is doubtful. If it is sound Arabic, then it is a kind of tearing open.

One says jākha al-sayl al-wādī yajūkhuhu — the flood tore away the banks of the valley.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
So the rock, from the floods' tearing, has gained a gash.

Ibn Durayd mentioned it; another mentioned tajawwakhat al-bi'r — the well caved in. The Arabicized word from this is al-jawkhān, the threshing floor.
جود:
The letters jīm, wāw and dāl are a single root, and it is being open-handed with a thing, and giving abundantly.

One says a man is jawād, clearly generous, and a people are ajwād.

Al-jawd is heavy, abundant rain.

Al-jawād is a swift, fast horse, plural jiyād. God the Exalted said: {when there were shown to him in the evening the standing steeds, the swift ones} [Ṣād: 31].

The verbal noun is al-jawda, excellence.

As for their saying “so-and-so yujādu towards such a thing,” it is as though he is being driven towards it.
جور:
The letters jīm, wāw and rā' are a single root, and it is swerving away from the road. One says jāra jawran — he swerved.

From this chapter is ṭa'anahu fajawwarahu — he stabbed him and knocked him down. It is possible that this belongs to the chapter of letter-substitution, as though the jīm stood in place of a kāf.

As for al-ghayth al-jiwarr, which is abundant rain, it is anomalous beside the origin sense we have set down. It may belong to another chapter, that of jīm, hamza and rā'; for Ibn al-Sikkīt mentioned that they say huwa ju'ar, on the pattern fu'al. If it is so, then it is from al-ju'ār, which is a cry, as though the rain cries out when it strikes. And he recited:
Do not give him to drink the downpour of a moaning, roaring cloud.
جوز:
The letters jīm, wāw and zā' are two roots: one is the cutting through of a thing, the other is the middle of a thing.

As for the middle: al-jawz of anything is its middle. Al-jawzā' is a ewe whose middle is white. Al-Jawzā' is also a star [constellation]; some said it was named so because it crosses the jawz of the sky, meaning its middle; others said it was named so for the three stars in its middle.

The other root: juztu al-mawḍiʿ — I passed through the place, I travelled in it; ajaztuhu — I passed beyond it and crossed it; ajaztuhu also means I went all the way through it. Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
so when we had crossed the open ground of the tribe, and there bore with us a hollow valley with rugged, winding sand-hills.
Aws ibn Maghrā' said, in a line of verse:
...until it is said: let the family of Ṣafwān pass —
praising them for letting pilgrims travel through safely.

Al-jawāz: the water given to livestock and crops. One says istajaztu fulānan fa-ajāzanī — I asked so-and-so for water-passage, and he granted it, when he gives you water for your land or livestock. Al-Qaṭāmī said, in a line of verse:
[and they said]: Fuqaym is the keeper of the water, so ask Ubāda for passage — indeed the one seeking passage stands at [his] quarter —
meaning "direction."
جوس:
The letters jīm, wāw and sīn are a single root, and it is passing through the midst of something. One says: jāsū khilāla l-diyāri yajūsūn — they went rampaging through the homes. God Most High said: {and they rampaged through your homes} [al-Isrā': 5].

As for al-jūs, it is not a root of its own, since it is an echo-word following al-jū' (hunger); one says: jū'an lahu wa-jūsan lahu — 'hunger and jūs be upon him.'
جوظ:
The letters jīm, wāw and ẓā' are a single root for an ugly trait, never used in praise.

Some said: al-jawwāẓ is the man heavy with flesh, who struts arrogantly in his walk. One says jāẓa yajūẓu jawaẓānan.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Raising up by it the muscular, strutting one.

And it is said al-jawwāẓ is the glutton; and it is said it means the immoral, depraved man.
جوع: The letters jīm, wāw and ʿayn are one word. Al-jūʿ [hunger] is the opposite of being full. One says: ʿāmu majāʿatin wa majūʿatin — a year of famine.
جوف:
The letters jīm, wāw and fā' are a single word, and it is the hollow interior of a thing. One says: this is jawf al-insān, the inside of a person, and the jawf of anything.

Ta'natun jā'ifa — a stab-wound that reaches the interior of the body. Qidrun jawfā' — a cooking pot with a wide interior.

Jawf 'Ayr is a place that a man named Ḥimār kept as his protected preserve. And in the proverb: 'more empty than the hollow of 'Ayr.'

Its origin: a man who kept a valley of his as a protected preserve. His story has been told in Kitāb al-'Ayn.
جول:
The letters jīm, wāw and lām are a single root, and it is circling round.

One says jāla yajūlu jawlan and jawalānan; ajaltuhu — I made it circle. This is the origin, and other words branch from it.

1. al-jūl — the side of a well, for a well has sides one goes around.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
He charged me with a matter of which my father and I were innocent — he charged me with it out of the very side of the well [i.e. out of nowhere].

2. al-mijwal — the pool, because the water circles within it; a coat of mail is sometimes likened to it for the clearness of its colour.
3. al-mijwal — the shield.
4. al-mijwal — a loose shirt, in which its wearer has room to move.

Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
When she moved supplely between a shift and a loose gown.

5. jawalān — small livestock, the young of the flock, so called because they move about among the grown beasts.

Al-Farrā' said: mā li-fulānin jūl, meaning he has no settled judgement — this too is drawn from the root given, because a man of sound judgement turns his opinion over and works it through.

As for al-Jawlān, it is a place, a proper name.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Those who lost him returned with clear knowledge — and resolve and generosity were left behind at al-Jawlān.
جون:
The letters jīm, wāw and nūn are a single root. Some grammarians claimed that al-jawn is an Arabicized word, being the colour the Persians call "al-kūnah," meaning the colour of a thing; he said that this is why one says al-jawn al-aswad [the black jawn] and al-jawn al-abyaḍ [the white jawn]. But this is talk with no real meaning.

Among the people of language as a whole, al-jawn is a name applying to both black and white — an instance of the class where two opposite things are called by one name, like al-nāhil and al-ẓann and the rest of that class.

Al-jawna is the sun. Some said it was so named for its whiteness. From this comes the account of the coat of mail shown to al-Ḥajjāj, which he could hardly see for its clarity; someone present said to him, "inna al-shams jawna," meaning clear, possessed of dazzling radiance. Others said it was named jawna instead because it turns black when it sets.

As for al-jūna, it is well known [a chest or basket], and perhaps it too is an Arabicized word; its plural is juwan.

Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
And the exchange of blows was over what was in the jūna-chests.
جوي:
The letters jīm, wāw and yā' are a root indicating dislike of a thing.

One says ijtawaytu al-bilād — you found the land disagreeable and wished to leave it, even while living there in comfort; also jawītu, with the same sense.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
I sickened of its fare and turned from it in aversion — though I had, had I wished, a remedy for it.

From this comes al-jawā, sickness of the heart. As for al-jiwā', it is open, wide land, and that word is anomalous, straying from the root given here.
جيأ: The letters jīm, yā' and hamza are two words with no reasoning between them. One says jā'a yajī'u majī'an — he came, coming. And one says jā'ānī fa-ji'tuhu, that is, he strove to outdo me in coming often [and I outdid him]. And al-jay'a is the verbal noun of jā'a. And al-ji'a is the gathering of water around the fort and the like. And it is said it is ji'a with a kasra and a doubled letter.
جيب: The letters jīm, yā' and bā' are a root that may belong to the category of one letter standing in for another. Al-jayb is the neck-opening of a shirt. One says "jibtu al-qamīṣ," I cut out its opening, and "jayyabtuhu," I made an opening for it. This shows that its origin is a wāw, and it carries the sense "I tore/cut" — which has already been mentioned [elsewhere in the book].
جيد:
The letters jīm, yā' and dāl are a single root, and it is the neck. One says jīd, plural ajyād. Al-jayd is length of neck. Al-jaydā' is a woman long of neck.

As for al-A'shā's line of verse: 'the men of Iyād with their ajyād' — it is said that this word is an Arabicized loanword, and that he meant cloaks.
جير:
The letters jīm, yā' and rā' are one word. Jayri means "truly."

A poet said, in a line of verse:
She said, 'You have grieved,' and I said, 'Truly — grieving, yes, it is from that, indeed it is.'

As for al-jayyār, quicklime plaster, it is an Arabicized word.

Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
With clay, and quicklime-plaster, and lime, and baked brick.

As for al-jā'ir, what a person feels in his breast of the heat of anger or grief, its root belongs to the chapter of wāw, and it has already been mentioned.
جيز: The letters jīm, yā' and zā' — the origin of its yā' is a wāw, and it has already been mentioned.
جيس: The letters jīm, yā' and sīn — the origin of its yā' is a wāw, and it has already been mentioned.
جيش:
The letters jīm, yā' and shīn are a single root, and it is boiling and surging up.

One says jāshat al-qidr tajīshu jayshan wa jayashānan — the cooking pot boiled over.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Our pot boiled over with them one day until night, striking the vertebrae of backs and thrusting.

From this comes their saying jāshat nafsuhu — his soul churned, as if it boiled. And al-jaysh, the army, belongs to this chapter too, being a mass of men that surges.
جيض:
The letters jīm, yā' and ḍād are a scant usage, indicating a kind of gait.

One says mashā mishyatan jiyaḍḍan — a walk with a swagger in it. And jāḍa yajīḍu — he passed by as a fleeing man passes.
جيل:
The letters jim, ya' and lam indicate gathering. Al-jil is the group. And al-jil is this nation -- they are the brothers of the Daylam, and it is said that Imru' al-Qays meant them in his saying, in a line of verse:

Jilan gathered around it at its cutting-time ... and the water was turned about in it until it grew confused.

As for al-jay'al, which is the hyena, it does not belong to this root.
حأ: The letters ḥā' and hamza name a tribe. A poet said, in a line of verse: I sought vengeance among Ḥakam and Ḥā'.
حب:
The letters ḥā' and bā' are three origins: one is lastingness and clinging fast, another is the grain of a thing that has grain, and the third is a description of shortness.

1. al-ḥabb — the well-known grain, of wheat and barley.
2. al-ḥibb, with kasra — the sprouting of sweet herbs, one al-ḥibba. The Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, said of a people: "They come out of the Fire and sprout as al-ḥibba sprouts on silt left by a flood." Some scholars said: everything that has grain, the name of its grain is al-ḥibba; but wheat and barley are called ḥabb and nothing else.
3. ḥabbat al-qalb — the black speck at the heart's core; it is also said to be its core/fruit.
4. al-ḥabab — the even, close-set ranking of the teeth.

Ṭarafa said, in a line of verse:
And when she laughs she shows al-ḥabab
... like musk chewed fine, mixed with cool water.

As for lastingness: al-ḥubb and al-maḥabba (love) are derived from aḥabbahu, meaning he clung fast to it. Al-muḥibb is the camel that tires and so stays fixed in its place. A poet said, in a line of verse:
She overcame the women of the worlds with the rope
... and so they, all of them, become like al-muḥibb thereafter.

It is also said al-muḥabb, with fatḥa. It is said aḥabba the camel, when it stood still and refused to move. They said: al-iḥbāb in camels is like al-ḥirān (balking) in beasts of burden. A poet said, in a line of verse:
A blow struck at the bad camel when it balked

that is, when it stood still. Thaʿlab recited, for a bedouin woman speaking to her father:
Oh father, oh dear father
... you have made me fine except for the neck,
So adorn it too, father
... until the suitor comes,
With camels muḥabḥaba.

Its meaning is that from their fatness they stand still. It has also been transmitted with khā', "mukhabkhaba," which has a different meaning, already mentioned in its own entry. He also recited:
One held fast, like the stillness of the sick man — his only grief being that he finds no one to grapple with him.

As for the description of shortness: al-ḥabḥāb is the short man. From this is the saying of al-Hudhalī, in a line of verse:
My night-travel, when night closes in, upon al-muqarrana, al-ḥabāḥib

Al-muqarrana are the mountains that draw close to one another, as if they had been paired together. Al-ḥabāḥib are the small ones, plural of ḥabḥāb.

I think ḥabāb al-māʾ (the water's bubbling froth) is from this too, though it could also belong to the first section, as if [the bubbles] were little grains. They have also said ḥabāb al-māʾ is its main bulk, as in the saying:
Her breastbone cleaves the water's bulk with her
... as the plough-blades part the soil by hand.

Al-Ḥubāḥib is a man's name, derived from some of what was mentioned above. It is said he was a man whose fire gave no benefit, so every fire that gives no benefit came to be named after him. Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
It cuts through the doubled-woven Saluqi mail
... and they kindle, upon the flat stone, the fire of al-Ḥubāḥib.

What falls outside this root is al-ḥubāb, the snake. They said al-ḥubāb is also the name given to a devil, because the snake is a devil. He recited:
She plays with a pair of Hadrami blades, as though it were
... the writhing of a devil among desolate castor-plants.
حبج: The letters ḥā', bā' and jīm are not, in my view, a root to rely on, nor one that branches out, and I do not know how sound their saying is: ḥabaja al-'alam, the marker appeared; ḥabajat al-nār, the fire flared up suddenly; ḥabijat al-ibil, when the camels ate al-'arfaj and their bellies ached — all of this is close alike in weakness. As for ḥabaja bihā, the jīm there is substituted for a qāf.
حبر:
The letters ḥā', bā' and rā' are a single root, regular and consistent, and it is a trace or mark of beauty and splendor. Al-ḥabār is a trace. A poet described a horse, in a line of verse:
The farrier did not turn over the ground around it ... nor was there any mark left there by its two tethering-ropes.
Then this branches out. The one thing written with is called ḥibr (ink).

1. ḥibr and ḥabr — the one who writes with the ink; that is, the scholar, plural aḥbār.
2. al-ḥabr — beauty and splendor. One says dhū ḥibrin wa sibrin, possessed of beauty and bearing. In the hadith: "A man comes out of the Fire whose ḥibr and sibr have gone" — meaning his beauty and bearing.

Ibn Aḥmar said, in a line of verse:
We wore its splendor until we were claimed ... for deeds and appointed terms already decreed for us.

3. al-muḥabbar — the thing that is adorned. Ṭufayl al-Ghanawī used to be called Muḥabbir, because he used to adorn and embellish poetry.

The word may also come, by the same reasoning, in a sense that is not beauty. So they say ḥabira al-rajulu, when a man's skin has had sores that healed but left marks. Al-ḥibr is also the yellowness that gathers on teeth. A garment described as ḥabīr, from the first sense, is new and fine. Al-ḥabra is joy. God Almighty said: {so they are in a meadow, made joyful} [al-Rūm: 15]. One also says qidḥ muḥabbar for an arrow-shaft well trimmed and shaped. Land described as miḥbār grows plants quickly. And a cloud called ḥabīr is one heavy with water.

What falls outside this chapter is their saying mā fīhi ḥabarbar, meaning "there is nothing in it at all." Al-ḥubārā is a bird, the bustard. They say, "So-and-so died of the grief of the ḥubārā," because it sheds its feathers along with the rest of the birds, but its feathers are slow to grow back; so when the other birds fly and it cannot fly, it dies of grief. A poet said:
Zayd is dead of the grief of the ḥubārā ... when Hunayda departs, or nearly so.
"Nearly so" translates muqārib. Al-Rā'ī said of the ḥubārā:
I swore to them that they would not think my insult ... was like the eyes of a bustard caught in a hunter's snare.
She saw a man running toward her, and she stared wide-eyed ... at him, the corners of her rolling eyes turned on him.
She strikes out with her legs, and her feathers are already wet ... with a spray like the lather of washed hair...
[The line breaks off here in the source.]
Al-mu'zib is the hunter, so called because he does not go home to his family. Ḥamlaqat means she rolled back the inner corner of her eye. The sense is that your cursing me will not pass for nothing, so that I should be like the bustard, who has no recourse when caught in the snare except to roll her eyes — she is among the most abject of birds. Tanūshu bi-rijlayhā means she strikes with her two legs. Al-ghisl is the mallow plant used to wash hair; he means she has soiled her own feathers. Al-Kumayt said something like it:
The bustard's warning-display, seen from afar, puffed up ... for a blue one whose talons are treated with dye.
حبس:
The letters ḥā', bā' and sīn. One says ḥabastuhu ḥabsan, I confined him.

Al-ḥabs is that which is held as an endowment. One says aḥbastu farasan fī sabīli'Llāh, I dedicated a horse as an endowment in the way of God.

Al-ḥibs is a reservoir for water, plural aḥbās.
حبش:
The letters ḥā', bā' and shīn are a single word indicating gathering together. Al-aḥābīsh are groups who have gathered from various tribes.

Ibn Rawāḥa said, in a line of verse:
And we came upon a surging wave of the sea — motley bands, some of them unarmed and some in armour.
حبص: The letters ḥā', bā' and ṣād are not a root. They claim there is a single word in it. Ibn Durayd mentioned: ḥabaṣa al-faras, when the horse ran a hard run.
حبض:
The letters ḥā', bā' and ḍād are two roots: one is movement, the other is deficiency.

The first: al-ḥabaḍ is movement. From it is al-ḥābiḍ, the arrow that falls short in front of the archer, that being its falling short of the target. One says ḥabaḍa mā' al-rakiyya, the well's water diminished.

From the second one says: aḥbaḍa fulānun bi-ḥaqqī, meaning he voided it. As for al-maḥābiḍ, which are al-mashāwir, sticks with which honey is drawn out, it is possible these belong to the first sense.

Ibn Muqbil said, in a line of verse:
As if their sounds, from wherever you hear them, were the sound of the honey-sticks drawing the combs out.
حبط:
The letters ḥā', bā' and ṭā' are a single root pointing to a thing coming to nothing, or to pain. One says aḥbaṭa Allāh 'amal al-kāfir — God made the unbeliever's deed come to nothing.

As for the pain: al-ḥabaṭ is that a beast eats until its belly is blown up by it. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: «Among what the spring growth brings forth is that which kills by bloating, or comes near to it.»

Al-Ḥārith was called al-Ḥabiṭ because he was on a journey and something like this befell him. And these are the people of Tamīm who are called al-Ḥabiṭāt.

Among what comes close to this chapter is ḥabiṭa al-jild — when the skin has had wounds in it which healed and left their marks behind.
حبق: The letters ḥā', bā' and qāf are not, in my view, a root to be relied on, nor does it have a clear meaning. But they say ḥabbaqa matā'ahu, when he gathered his belongings together, and I do not know how sound this is.
حبك:
The letters ḥā', bā', and kāf are a root that fits a clear, consistent pattern: making a thing firm along a stretch, running evenly. One says a camel is maḥbūk al-qarā, meaning its back is firm.

From al-iḥtibāk is al-iḥtibāʾ, wrapping oneself tightly with a garment; this fits the root's pattern.

Regarding ḥubuk al-samāʾ in His saying, Exalted is He: {by the sky, full of ḥubuk} [al-Dhāriyāt: 7] — some said this means: of fine, firmly-made structure; others said al-ḥubuk means bands, singular ḥabīka, meaning the paths of the stars. One says a cloak is muḥabbak, meaning striped.
حبل:
The letters ha, ba and lam are a single root indicating the stretching-out of a thing; other senses are then carried upon it, and the branches all return to the one reference point.

Al-habl is the rope, well known, plural hibal. Al-habl is the tendon along the neck and shoulder. Al-habl is a long ridge of sand.

Carried on this: al-habl meaning covenant/pact. Al-A'sha said:
And when the pacts of one tribe pass her beyond it, she takes up, toward you, the pacts of the next.
He means safe-conduct and pledges of protection: that is, she is escorted from one tribe until she reaches another, and that tribe escorts her in turn until she arrives.

Al-hibala is the hunter's snare. One says 'ihtabala l-sayd' — he caught the game in a snare. Al-Kumayt said:
Do not liken me, in my hoping for your affection, to one who hopes to snare the eggs of the female vulture [on a sheer cliff].
Do not liken me to one who hoped for what cannot be; because the vulture cannot be reached, so whoever hopes to catch her upon her eggs hopes for the impossible.

As for Labid's saying:
And I go out at dawn, and I never lack a companion whose pasterns are not long.
He means by 'muhtabal' the pasterns [of the leg], because the snare-cord is fastened there when [the animal] is hobbled.

One says of one who stands his ground, not fleeing: 'habilu barah', as if he were snared, that is bound with ropes. Some claim the lion too is called 'habilu barah'.

Derived from this root: al-hibl, with kasra on the ha, meaning calamity. A line:
Do not be hasty, O 'Azz, to make out whether what has come is sincere advice from the slanderers, or calamity.
Its sense, in my view, is that when a person is struck by calamity it is as though he has been snared, fallen into the trap, like the game that is caught. This is not far-fetched.

From this root: al-habal, pregnancy, because the days are drawn out by it. The grapevine too is called habla and habala, and belongs to this root, because in its growth it is like ropes. Al-hublah is the fruit of the acacia tree. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas said: 'We used to go on campaigns with the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him and his family, with no food but the acacia-fruit and the leaves of the samur tree.' And I reckon that al-hublah, an ornament set in necklaces, is from this too, perhaps likened to its fruit. A line:
And adorning her throat is bright jewelry, and necklaces of hublah-ornament and strung beads.
حبن:
The letters ḥā', bā' and nūn are a single root, holding two words, one carried on the other.

1. al-ḥibn — like a boil in the body; some say instead that al-aḥban is the man afflicted with dropsy (fluid retention).
2. umm ḥubayn — a creature the size of a person's palm.
حبو:
The letters ḥā', bā' and the weak letter are a single root, and it is nearness and closeness; everything that draws near is ḥābin.

1. ḥabiyy al-saḥāb — the low fringe of cloud, named for its nearness to the horizon.
2. ḥabawtu al-rajul — I gave the man a gift, ḥubwatan or ḥibwatan; the noun is al-ḥibā'. This only happens out of affection and drawing close.
3. iḥtabā al-rajul — the man gathered his back and legs together with a garment, sitting wrapped up; the name for this is al-ḥibwa or al-ḥubwa, two dialect forms.
4. al-ḥābī — the arrow that creeps along toward the target.
5. ḥabawtu lil-khamsīn — a saying of the Arabs, meaning you are drawing near to fifty (years of age).

Al-Aṣma'ī mentioned a word that may seem outwardly somewhat far from this root, but in truth is not far: he said fulānun yaḥbū mā ḥawlahu, meaning he protects and guards what is around him.

Ibn Aḥmar said, in a line of verse:
And the she-camels went out at evening, with no stallion to guard them, and no man prowling among them by night in search of milk.

They also say — and this is the regular analogy — that al-ḥibā, written short with the ḥā' vowelled with a kasra, means specifically a king's due share, plural aḥbā'. Some said instead that its singular is ḥaba', with a hamza, written short. It was named this for its nearness and closeness. So nothing in this chapter has been left unaccounted for. God knows best.
حبوكر:
Ḥabawkar — calamity.

One says iḥbanṭā, said when someone swelled up like an angry man. The pattern of this word has already been given, under al-ḥabaṭ.

One says: mā lī min hādhā al-amri ḥuntāl — meaning, I have no way out of this matter.

Al-ḥunẓab is the male locust. Al-ḥurbuth is a plant. Ḥaḍājir is the hyena. Al-ḥazanbal and al-ḥabarkal both mean the short man.

The principle in these sections is: whatever does not have a derivation that holds up in the way we have been setting out remains open to question, except what the great and trusted scholars themselves transmitted. God knows best.

(The Book of Ḥā' is complete.)
حت:
The letters ḥā' and tā' are a single root, and it is the falling of a thing, like leaves and the like; whatever is close to that sense is carried along with it.

1. al-ḥatt — the shedding of leaves from a branch. The tree taḥātta (shed its leaves).
2. It is said "ḥattahu miʾata sawṭin" (he gave him a hundred lashes ḥattan), meaning he hastened them, as if that were taken from the shedding of leaves — the sense is close.
3. faras ḥatt — a swift horse, one that presses on its running at speed, ḥattan; plural aḥtāt.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
On one whittled-swift, hollow-reed of limb
that lingered among tall shrub of colocynth.

And Ḥutāt is a man's name, from this.
حتا: The letters ḥā', tā' and hamza are a single word and not a root; I think it belongs to the chapter of letter-substitution, substituted from a kāf. They say aḥta'tu al-thawb iḥtā'an, when you twisted the cloth — on the thinking that it is substituted, from aḥka'tu al-'uqda, I tightened the knot, the explanation of which has already passed. And he says... (the text breaks off here in the source).
حتد:
The letters ḥā', tā' and dāl are a single root, and it is the settling and firmness of a thing.

1. al-ḥatd — staying in a place; ḥatada yaḥtidu.
2. al-maḥtid — the origin; one says huwa fī maḥtidi ṣidqin, he is of a sound origin.
3. al-ḥutud — a spring whose water never runs dry, which fits the analogy of the chapter.
حتر:
The letters ḥā', tā' and rā' are two roots: one is the encircling of a thing by another and its going round it, the other is the lessening and diminishing of a thing.

The first:
1. al-ḥatār — what surrounds the eye from the inner eyelid, plural ḥutur.
2. ḥatār al-ẓufr — what surrounds the nail.
3. al-ḥatār (a further sense) — the fringe and border of a strip of cloth, plural ḥutur.
4. al-ḥutur — what is attached to the bottom of a tent when it rises off the ground and draws in, to act as a screen, according to Abū Zayd al-Kilābī; one says ḥatartu al-bayt, I fitted the tent with this.
5. al-ḥatr — fixing the eye intently on a thing when looking at it, according to some philologists; one says ḥatira yaḥtiru ḥatran, and this fits the analogy of the chapter.
6. aḥtartu al-'uqda — I made its knot firm; this belongs to the first sense, because a knot is only made by one thing going round another.

The second root: aḥtartu al-qawm, or aḥtartu lil-qawm, when you make their food fall short.

Al-Shanfarā said, in a line of verse:
And many a mother of a household have I seen providing for her family: when she fed them, she gave short measure and gave little.

They also say al-ḥutra is al-wakīra (a modest feast for moving into a house); one says ḥattir lanā, give us a small meal — this is not far-fetched, because al-wakīra is the least of feasts and invitations. They say al-ḥatra is a single suckling. And they say mā ḥatartu al-yawma shay'an, meaning I have tasted nothing today.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
You are the lords, the rain-givers, when the she-camel's young does not spend the evening having tasted even a little.

He means: she had no abundant milk, nor even a little, to suckle her young with.
حتف: The letters ḥā', tā' and fā' are a single word, not to be reasoned from by analogy, because no verb is formed from it. It is al-ḥatf, plural ḥutūf, and it is death.
حتك:
The letters ḥā', tā' and kāf indicate closeness of step and smallness.

1. al-ḥatk — taking short strides and quickly lifting and setting down the foot; it is a sound, well-known word, from which is formed al-ḥatakān, distinct from al-ḥayakān (mentioned under ḥ-y-k).
2. al-ḥawātik — the young of the ostrich.
3. al-ḥawtak — the short man.
حتل:
The letters ḥā', tā' and lām are not, in my view, a root, and I am not even confident of what is related about it. It is said to indicate smallness and littleness.

1. al-ḥawtal — a boy nearing puberty.
2. ḥawtal — said for the chicks of the sand-grouse (al-qaṭā); in my view this is a misreading, and it is really ḥawtak, with a kāf, which has already been mentioned.
3. ḥatala lahu — he gave him something; and this is nothing solid.
حتم:
The letters ḥā', tā', and mīm are not, in my view, a true root; I mostly think that this too belongs to the substitution of tā' for kāf, except that what it carries is the making firm of a thing. One says ḥattama ʿalayhi, he decreed it upon him as binding, and its origin, as we have said, is ḥakama, he ruled — its explanation has already passed.

Al-ḥātim is the one who settles a matter. As for their naming the crow ḥātim, this is from the same root, because they claim it decrees parting [an omen of separation] — like a ruling coming from it. A poet said, in a line of verse:
I went out early, though I never used to go out heeding a warning-bird or a crow of ill omen.

In this branch there is another word, also close to the case of substitution. They say al-ḥutāma is what remains of food on the table — this, in my view, belongs instead to the root with ṭāʾ, because it is something that crumbles and breaks apart. Its explanation has already passed.
حتن:
The letters ḥā', tā' and nūn are a single root indicating the equality of things.

1. al-ḥatin — the match, the equal; one says humā ḥitnāni, the two of them are equal.
2. taḥātanū — they became equal to one another.
3. waqa'at al-nabl fī al-hadaf ḥatnā — the arrows fell on the target ḥatnā (on the pattern fa'lā), when their landing places fell close together.

And everything none of whose parts differs from another is muḥtatin.
حتو:
The letters ḥā', tā' and the weak letter after it are a single root, indicating intensity.

1. al-ḥatw — running hard; ḥatā yaḥtū ḥatwan.
2. al-ḥatw (a second sense) — gripping the fringe of a cloak with the hand; one says ḥatawtuhu.

As for al-ḥatiyy, it is said to be the crushed pulp of the fruit of the doum-palm (al-muql), and this is irregular. It may be permissible to draw an analogy for it to a chapter with some roughness in its sense.

Al-Hudhalī said, in a line of verse:
May I have no good of myself, if I feed your alighting guest the husk of al-ḥatiyy while I have stored-up wheat with me.
حث:
The letters ḥā' and thā' are two origins: one is urging someone on to a thing, and the other is dried-up remains of a thing's dried-out part.

The first: their saying "ḥathathtuhu ʿalā (the thing), aḥuthhu" — I urged him on to it. From it is al-ḥathīth; it is said "he went off ḥathīthan," meaning hastening. Salāma said, in a line of verse:
He went off in haste, and this gray hair pursues him
... if the racing of the male partridges could ever catch him.

From it also is al-ḥathḥatha, the flickering of lightning in the clouds.

As for the other: al-ḥuthth is dried-up, broken plant matter; it is also said al-ḥuthth is dry, coarse sand. A poet said, in a line of verse:
until al-ḥuthth is seen where the rain of the Pleiades has dried up
حثر:
The letters ḥā', thā' and rā' are a single root, indicating a granular clumping in a thing, and coarseness.

1. ḥathirat 'aynu al-rajul ḥatharan — a man's eye becomes coarse, when its lids thicken from weeping or from soreness.
2. ḥathira al-'asal — the honey granulates.
3. al-ḥawthara — one of a man's members (organs); this is not part of the chapter's analogy.
4. al-ḥawāthir — a people (tribe) from 'Abd al-Qays.
5. ḥuthārat al-tibn — the crumbled remains of straw, its chaff.
حثل:
The letters ḥā', thā', and lām are a single root, indicating badness and meanness.

1. ḥuthālat al-burr — the bad, inferior part of wheat.
2. ḥuthālat al-duhn and the like — its dregs/sediment.
3. al-muḥthal — one poorly fed, badly nourished.

Mutammim said, in a line of verse:
And a widow walking with a disheveled, poorly-fed child,
like the chick of a bustard, its head all matted.

He likened him to the chick of a bustard because it is ugly in appearance, its feathers plucked.
حثم:
The letters ḥā', thā', and mīm indicate intensity.

1. al-ḥathma — a hillock; a woman was named "Ḥathma" after it.
2. Some philologists said: ḥathamtu al-shay'a ḥatham — I rubbed/kneaded the thing.
حثوى:
The letters ḥā', thā', and the weak letter indicate the scattering of something light that floats and drifts away.

1. al-hathā — chaff, finely crushed straw.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And dust-grey, wind-worn ground — you see upon it
chaff that the wind has driven from every channel.

And a poet said, in a line of verse (rajaz):
As if it were a sack full of chaff.

2. One says ḥathā t-turāba yaḥthūhu — he scatters/throws the dust.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
The fort is nearer, if you wanted it,
than your throwing dust on the rider.

3. One also says ḥathā yaḥthī ḥathyan — and this is the more correct form.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
I scatter, upon Daysam, some of the soft moist earth.

4. One says arḍun ḥathwā' — land with much dust/dirt.
حج:
The letters ḥā' and jīm are four origins.

The first is intent — heading toward something — and every such intent is ḥajj. A poet said, in a line of verse:
I witness, of ʿAwf, many an encampment
... heading for al-Zibriqān's saffron-dyed cloak.

Then this name became specific to heading for the Sacred House for the rites of pilgrimage. Al-ḥajīj is the pilgrim body. A poet said, in a line of verse:
I remembered you while the pilgrims raised their clamor
... in Mecca, and hearts throbbed with it.

They are also called al-ḥujj. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Pilgrims, camped at the foot of Dhū l-Majāz

Among their proverbs: "He persisted, and so he prevailed." Another of their proverbs: "You have let the pilgrims hear it" — said when someone has let out a secret, meaning: if you let the pilgrims hear it, you have let all creation hear it.

From this root is al-maḥajja, the main track of a road. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Convey from me to Ḥurayth a message
... you have swerved from the straight course of the road.

It is possible that al-ḥujja (proof, argument) is derived from this, because it is aimed at, or by means of it the sought-after truth is reached. It is said "ḥājajtu fulānan fa-ḥajajtuhu," meaning I argued with so-and-so and defeated him by argument; that triumph occurs in a dispute; plural ḥujaj; the verbal noun is al-ḥijāj.

From this root: "ḥajajtu al-shajja" — I probed the head-wound, when you probe it with a probe, because you intend to learn its extent. A poet said, in a line of verse:
He probes a brain-deep wound, at whose bottom lies crumbling matter

It is also said that it is rather the pouring of clarified butter onto the blood of the wound so that its extent shows and can be lifted out with a wad of cotton. Abū Dhu'ayb said, in a line of verse:
Musk was poured upon it until it seemed
... a healer probing the wound down to the membrane of the brain.

The second origin: al-ḥijja, which is the year. It is possible this could be joined to the first origin, because the pilgrimage in the year occurs only once, so the year seems to have been named ḥijja after the pilgrimage held within it. A poet said, in a line of verse:
They wear smooth hard pearls every year
... even were their necks bare of ornament.

Some said he meant "the year"; others said al-ḥijja here means the earlobe. It is also said al-ḥijja is the bead or pearl hung in the ear. Both these views are open to question.

The third origin: al-ḥijāj, the bone that curves around the eye. One with a large ḥijāj is called aḥajj; the plural of ḥijāj is aḥijja. Abū ʿAmr claimed that a hollowed-out place, a cavity in rock, is also called ḥajjāj.

The fourth origin: al-ḥajḥaja is holding back/retreating. It is said: "they charged at us, then held back." Al-muḥajḥij is the one who cannot follow through. A poet said, in a line of verse:
A resounding blow, not one that holds back

It is said "I do not ḥajḥij in such-and-such," meaning I do not doubt. They say: "Let no wavering and no hesitation carry you away." A ḥajḥaj man is a worthless man.
حجا:
The letters ḥā', jīm, and the weak letter are two closely related roots: one is the encircling of a thing by another and clinging to it, the other is intent and deliberateness.

As for the first: al-ḥajwa is the pupil of the eye, because it is from aḥdaqa bi-shay' — to encircle a thing. The outlying districts and edges of a land that surround it are called aḥjā'.

Ibn Muqbil said, in a line of verse:
The outlying edges of the lands do not shelter a man,
nor are ladders built for him up to the skies.

It is possible that al-ḥajāh belongs to this same root — the bubble that forms on water from raindrops, because it is round.

The second root is their saying: taḥajjaytu al-shay' — when you sought it out deliberately and set your mind to it.

Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
So she came, in the dim early dawn, making deliberately for the watering-place.
