They say ḥajītu bi-l-makān and taḥajjaytu bihi — I stayed on deliberately at the place.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Where a silent one lingers deliberately at the ravine.

Al-ḥajw bi-shay' is cherishing a thing, being loath to part with it; one says ḥaji'tu bihi, meaning I was loath to give it up. After this a man was named Ḥajwa. And ḥaja'tu bihi — a different word — means: I rejoiced in it.

We have said the two roots are close, and to one who looks closely the underlying pattern in both is one and the same.

As for al-uḥjiyya and al-ḥujayyā — the riddle people put to one another, one of them saying "uḥājīka mā kadhā" [I put this riddle to you] — it may be that this falls outside these two roots, or it may be referred back to them, in which case uḥājīka means: aim, look, and apply yourself deliberately to knowing what I am asking you.

From this too: anta ḥajin an taf'ala kadhā — you are fit to do such-and-such, just as one says ḥarīy, worthy.
حجب: The letters ḥā', jīm and bā' are one root, and it is preventing. One says ḥajabtuhu ʿan kadhā — that is, I kept him from it. And ḥijāb al-jawf is what screens between the heart and the rest of the inward parts. And al-ḥājibān are the two bones above the eyes, with the hair and the flesh. And this is by likeness, as though the two of them screened off a thing that would reach the eyes. And so too ḥājib al-shams, the rim of the sun: it is only likened to the eyebrow of a man. And so too al-ḥajaba, the head of the hip: a likening also, for its jutting out.
حجر:
The letters ḥā', jīm and rā' are a single root running straight through, and it is preventing and closing round a thing.

Al-ḥajr is a man's lap, and its ḥā' may be given a kasra. And one says ḥajara al-ḥākimu ʿalā al-safīhi ḥajran — the judge placed the foolish spender under restraint; and that is his preventing him from dealing with his own wealth. And the mind is called ḥijr because it prevents a man from doing what he should not, just as it is called ʿaql, a tether, by likeness to the hobble. God, exalted be He, said: {Is there in that an oath for one who has a mind?} [al-Fajr: 5]. And Ḥajr is the chief town of al-Yamāma.

Al-ḥajar, stone, is well known, and I think that the whole chapter is carried over onto it and taken from it, for its hardness and firmness. And the rule for its plural in the smaller number is aḥjār; al-ḥijāra also has a rule, as one says jamal and jimāla, and it is rare. And al-ḥijr is the mare; she is kept safe and grudged to others. And al-ḥājir is what holds water in a low-lying place, and its plural is ḥujrān. And ḥajrat al-qawm is the side of their dwelling, and it is what they protect. And al-ḥujra among buildings is well known. And ḥajjara al-qamaru when a ring formed around it.

Of what is derived from this is their saying: ḥajjartu ʿayna al-baʿīr, when you brand round it with a round branding iron. And maḥjir al-ʿayn is what goes round the eye, and it is the part that shows out of the face-veil. And al-Ḥijr is the ḥaṭīm of Mecca, which is the part enclosed round the House. And al-ḥijr is kinship; and its rule is the rule of the chapter, because it is a bond and something to be defended, protected and guarded.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
They want to drive him far from me, though he is of near descent to me and of kinship.

And al-ḥijr is what is forbidden. A man would meet a man he feared in the sacred months and say: ḥijran — that is, forbidden; and its meaning is: it is forbidden to you to reach me with any harm. So when the Day of Resurrection comes, the idolaters see the angels of punishment and say: {a forbidding barrier} [al-Furqān: 22], supposing that this will help them in the next world as it used to help them in this one. Of this are the words of the speaker, in a line of verse:
Until we called upon ties of kinship that were between us of old, and their speaker said: I am under protection.

And al-maḥājir are gardens; one of them is a maḥjir.

Labīd said, in a line of verse:
A great strong she-camel, full-grown, waters the gardens.
حجز:
The letters ḥā', jīm and zā' are a single root, applied consistently, and it is coming between two things and separating them.

This is their saying ḥajaztu bayna al-rajulayn, I separated the two men, meaning each is kept from the other. The Arabs say ḥajāzayka, on the pattern of ḥanānayka, meaning: separate the people. Al-Ḥijāz is named so because it separates Najd from al-Sarāh, the western mountain range.

Ḥujzat al-izār is the waist-fold of the lower wrap-garment, where it is tied. Ḥujzat al-sarāwīl is the waistband of the trousers, where the drawstring sits; this is by resemblance, as though it separates the upper part of the body from the lower.

It is said: “there was rimmiyā between the people, and it then turned into ḥijjīzā” — meaning they threw missiles at each other and were then kept apart from one another.

As for the words of the one who said, in a line of verse:
Thin-soled in sandals, clean are their waist-folds ... they are greeted with sweet basil on the feast day.
This word — ḥujuzāt, plural of ḥujza — is used figuratively for chastity, meaning they are men of clean conduct.
حجف:
The letters ḥā', jīm, and fā' make up a single word with no wider pattern — it is al-ḥajafa, the small shield made by layering two hides together to form it. Its plural is ḥajaf.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Would the people bar us from the water of the Euphrates,
while among us are swords, and among us are shields?
حجل:
The letters ḥā', jīm, and lām — discussion of it converges from one direction only, and weakly. It is said, tentatively and provisionally, that it is something that encircles something else.

1. al-ḥijl — the anklet, which encircles the shin.
2. al-ḥajala — the bride's curtained canopy.
3. "So-and-so passed by, yaḥjulu in his walk" — meaning he strutted/swaggered. This fits the pattern described, as if he were turning about himself.
4. taḥjīl of a horse — whiteness that encircles its fetlocks.
5. al-ḥawjala — the small glass flask.

A poet said, in a line of verse (rajaz):
As if his two eyes, from their sunkenness,
were two hollows in the smooth face of a pierced rock —
is that so, or are they the two flasks of a bottle?

'Alqama said, in a line of verse:
As if their eyes held little flasks within them.

Among what falls outside this root is al-ḥajal, this bird [the partridge]. And from this root is al-Aṣma'ī's saying: ḥajjalat al-'ayn — the eye sank, became sunken.
حجم:
The letters ḥā', jīm, and mīm are a single root, and it is a kind of restraint and turning away.

1. One says aḥjamtu 'an al-shay' — I held back from the thing, when you drew back from it.
2. ḥujima al-ba'īr — the camel's mouth was bound shut with leather and palm-fibre.

Among what falls outside this root is al-ḥawjama — the red rose, plural ḥawjam. And al-ḥajm is the act of the cupper [one who performs cupping, drawing blood by suction].
حجن:
The letters ḥā', jīm, and nūn are a single root, indicating a bending.

1. al-ḥajan — the crookedness of a piece of wood and the like.
2. al-miḥjan — a stick or staff with a hooked head.
3. iḥtajantu bihā al-shay' — I took hold of the thing with it.
4. al-ḥajināt — a name for hooked claws.

'Ajjāj said, in a line of verse:
With hooked claws that pierce through the waists.

5. aḥjana al-thumām — the thumām plant put out its shoot; and perhaps that shoot is itself called ḥajnā', the bent one.
6. iḥtajantu al-shay'a li-nafsī — I drew the thing toward myself, that being your inclining it to yourself.
7. They say: iḥtajana 'alayhi ḥajnatan, just as one says ḥajara 'alayhi — he placed a restraint on him.

And from this root is their saying ghazwatun ḥajūn, said when you make apparent an aim toward one thing and then turn aside toward another. One says: ghazāhum ghazwan ḥajūnan — he raided them with such a raid.
حد:
The letters ha' and dal are two roots: the first is prevention, the second is the edge of a thing.

1. al-hadd -- the barrier between two things. A man is mahdud when he is deprived of good fortune. They say "he is indeed unlucky and deprived," as though he were denied provision. The doorkeeper is called haddad, because he keeps people from entering. Al-A'sha said, in a line of verse: we rose, before our rooster had crowed, to a dark wine-jar, by its keeper.

Al-Nabigha spoke of hadd in the sense of prevention: except Solomon, when the King said to him: rise among creation and restrain it from folly.

Another said, in a line of verse: O Lord, whoever hid the ascent from me -- grant him a quarrelsome wife, to whom he will be, for as long as she lives, a keeper. That is, he would be her doorkeeper, so that she could not escape.

Iron, hadid, was named for its resistance, hardness and strength. Al-istihdad is the use of iron, for shaving. One says a woman haddat or ahaddat over her husband, in mourning, when she denies herself adornment and dye. Al-muhadda is opposition, as though it were mutual prevention -- though it may also belong to the second root.

One says: "I have no hadad or muhtadd from this matter," meaning no turning away from it and no escape. One says hadadan, meaning "God forbid" -- its origin is from prevention. Al-Kumayt said, in a line of verse: God forbid that your bounty among us should be cut short, or come to us meanly measured.

The punishment, hadd, of the offender is so called because it prevents him from repeating the offense. Al-Duraydi said: one says "this is a hadad matter," meaning inaccessible.

2. As for the second root: their saying hadd al-sayf, the edge of a sword, and hadd al-sikkin, the edge of a knife. And hadd al-sharab, the sharpness of a drink. Al-A'sha said, in a line of verse: many a cup, like the rooster's eye, whose sharpness I met at first light.

Hadd al-rajul is a man's fierce vigor -- a metaphor from the blade. Carried from this too is al-hidda, the sharpness of temper that comes over a person from impulsiveness. One says hadadtu 'ala al-rajul ahiddu hiddatan -- I grew sharp with the man.
حدأ:
The letters ḥā', dāl and hamza are a single root: a bird, or something likened to it.

1. al-ḥidaʾa — the well-known bird, the kite. Plural al-ḥidaʾ. A poet said, in a line of verse: as the sheltering kites draw close to one another.
2. al-ḥadaʾa — something likened to it, with some of its vowelling changed: something like an axe or pick with which stones are chiseled. A poet said, in a line of verse: like the sharpened pick.

What falls outside this root: "ḥadi'a bi-al-makān" — he clung fast to the place.
حدا:
The letters ḥā', dāl, and the weak letter that follows are a single root, and it is driving [something] along. It is said "ḥadā bi-ibilihi" — he urged on his camels and sang to them. It is said of the wild ass, when he leads his she-asses ahead, that he drives them on. A poet said, in a line of verse:
driver of three, of the lean long-backed she-asses

It is said of an arrow in flight that its feathers drive it on, and its head guides it. It is said "ḥadawtuhu ʿalā kadhā," meaning I drove him and roused him to it. The north wind is called ḥadwā', because it drives the clouds along, that is, it herds them. Al-ʿAjjāj said, in a line of verse:
A driving north wind that came from the heights of Ṭūr

Their saying "[so-and-so] yataḥaddā so-and-so," when he competes with him and contests supremacy with him, is from this root, because in doing so it is as if he drives him on to the matter. It is said "anā ḥudayyāka li-hādhā al-amr," meaning: come forward against me in this. ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm said, in a line of verse:
a challenge to all people, every one of them together
حدب:
The letters ḥā', dāl and bā' are a single root, and it is a thing rising up. Al-ḥadab is what rises up from the ground.

God Most High said: {and they will come rushing down from every rising ground} [al-Anbiyā': 96].

Al-ḥadab is also a hump in the back; one says ḥadiba and iḥdawdaba. Nāqatun ḥadbā' is a she-camel whose hip-bones show, from thinness; likewise al-ḥidbār. One says: hunna ḥudbun ḥadābīr — they are humped and worn thin.

As for their saying ḥadiba 'alayhi, when someone showed tender care and concern for another, this too is from the same root, because it is as if he bent low over the other out of concern — and that resembles a hump.
حدث: The letters ḥā', dāl and thā' are a single root, and it is a thing's coming to be when it had not been. One says ḥadatha amrun baʿda an lam yakun - a matter came about after it had not been. Al-rajul al-ḥadath is the young and fresh in years. Al-ḥadīth - talk - is from this, because it is speech in which one thing comes into being after another. And rajul ḥadath is one whose talk is good. And rajul ḥidthu nisā' is a man who talks much with women. And one says hādhihi ḥiddīthā ḥasana - this is fine talking - on the pattern of khiṭṭībā, and by it talk is meant.
حدج:
The letters ḥā', dāl and jīm are a single root close to "ḥadaqa bi-l-shay'," said when [the eyes] encircle a thing, staring fixedly at it. Al-taḥdīj in looking is like al-taḥdīq, staring.

From this root: al-ḥidj, one of the women's riding-litters. It is said "ḥadajtu al-baʿīr," when you fasten the litter onto the camel. Al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse:
Say to Maythā': what is the matter with her
... is it by night that her camels are fitted with litters?

From this root also: al-ḥadaj, the colocynth (bitter-apple) once it has hardened and firmed; we say this belongs here because it is round.
حدر:
The letters ḥā', dāl and rā' are two origins: descent, and fullness.

The first: "ḥadartu al-shay'" — I brought the thing down. Al-ḥudūr is the act of the one descending. Al-ḥadūr, with fatḥa on the ḥā', is the place one descends from.

The second origin is their calling a full thing ḥādir. It is said "a full, round eye," meaning full. Its supporting citation has already been given earlier. A she-camel is ḥādirat al-ʿaynayn when her eyes are full; she is called ḥadrā' for that. It is said al-ḥaydara is the lion, and it is possible this is derived from here.

From it: "his skin ḥadara" — it swelled. "Aḥdartuhu," when you struck him until you left a mark on him. Al-ḥadra, with a quiescent dāl, is a sore that comes up on the inside of the eyelid. It is said "a tribe dhū ḥudūra," meaning one that is numerous and closely gathered. A poet said, in a line of verse:
I am of a people whose spears hunt down, at morning's break
... him who is numerous and angered.

Al-ḥudra is a small herd of camels, named so for being gathered together.

What falls outside this root: al-ḥādūr, the earring. It is recited:
distanced in the shoulder from her earring
حدس:
The letters ḥā', dāl and sīn are a single root resembling casting and speed, and the like. Al-ḥads is conjecture; its analogy fits the root, because we say "he cast with conjecture," as though he threw it. Al-ḥads is also swiftness of travel. A poet said, in a line of verse:
as though she, after swift travel...

It is said "ḥadasa bihi al-arḍa ḥadsan," when he threw him down to the ground. [text broken] ... you see among them one thrown down and another throwing.

From it also: "ḥadastu fī labbat al-baʿīr," when you stab into the camel's throat-pit. "Ḥadastu al-shay'a bi-rijlī" — I trod on the thing with my foot. "Ḥadastu al-nāqa," when you made the she-camel kneel down. "Ḥadastu bi-sahmī" — I shot with my arrow.
حدق: The letters ḥā', dāl and qāf are a single root: a thing that surrounds another thing. One says "ḥadaqa al-qawmu bi-r-rajul" and "aḥdaqū bihi," the people surrounded the man. He cited: "those who feed [guests] are Banū Ḥarb, while death has surrounded me (ḥadaqat), and I have found my helpers slow." Ḥadaqat al-'ayn, the pupil of the eye, is from this — the black part, because it surrounds [the tiny reflected image seen in it]; plural ḥidāq. He cited: "and the eye, after them, as though its pupils (ḥidāqahā) had been sewn shut with thorns, sore and weeping." Al-taḥdīq: intensity of staring. Al-ḥadīqa: land with trees on it. Al-ḥindīqa: the pupil of the eye.
حدل:
The letters ḥā', dāl and lām are a single root, and it is a leaning/tilt. It is said "rajulun aḥdal," when there is a tilt in his side; that is al-ḥadal. Abū ʿAmr said: al-aḥdal is one whose shoulders and neck stoop forward over his chest. It is said "a bow muḥdala or ḥadlā'," when its tip curves down.

Al-ḥadl is the opposite of justice. Abū Zayd said: "ḥadala ʿan al-amr, yaḥdilu ḥadlan" — he turned away unjustly from the matter. He is indeed ḥadl [biased], not just.

What falls outside this root, and I do not know whether it is sound or not, is their saying: al-ḥawdal is the male of monkeys.
حدم:
The letters ḥā', dāl and mīm are a single root: the intensifying of heat. It is said "iḥtadama al-nahār" — the heat of the day intensified. "Iḥtadama al-ḥarr" — the heat intensified. "Iḥtadamat al-nār" — the fire blazed up. Fire has a ḥadama, which is its intensity; it is also said to be the sound of its blazing.

Al-Khalīl said: "the sun aḥdamat the thing, so it iḥtadama," and "his chest iḥtadama with rage." As for the iḥtidām of blood, some said its redness intensified until it turned black; but the correct view is that its heat intensifies. Al-Farrā' said: "qidrun ḥudama," said of a cooking pot quick to boil; the opposite of al-ṣalūd (slow to boil).
حذ:
The letters ha' and dhal are a single root indicating cutting, lightness, and speed -- nothing departs from it.

1. al-hadhdh -- cutting.
2. al-ahadhdh -- that which has had its tail cut off. The sand-grouse is called haddha', for the shortness of its tail. He said, in a line of verse: short-tailed going away, earless-seeming coming toward you -- for the water at her breast there is a wondrous marking.
3. amr ahadhdh -- a matter in which no one has any hold, because it has been finished and settled. He said, in a line of verse: when we have crossed the sand-dune and its soft sand, we have before us a swift, decisive, plunging matter.

Al-Khalil said: al-ahadhdh is that which nothing can cling to. The heart is called ahadhdh. He said: and a qasida haddha' is a poem so excellent that no fault can attach to it. And al-haddha' is the disavowed oath by which a right is wrongfully cut off.

From this section, in the doubled form: qarab hadhhadh, meaning swift and brisk.

And in the hadith of 'Utba ibn Ghazwan: "Truly the world has given notice of its parting and has turned away swiftly, leaving nothing of itself but the last dregs left in a vessel."
حذر:
The letters ḥā', dhāl and rā' are a single root, and it is from guarding oneself and being on the watch.

One says ḥadhira yaḥdharu ḥadharan — he was wary. And a man is ḥadhir and ḥadhūr and ḥidhriyān: watchful, on his guard.

And ḥadhāri means "beware".

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Beware of our spears, beware.

And it has been read: {and indeed we are all wary} [al-Shuʿarā': 56] — they said: prepared and ready. And (ḥadhirūn): fearful. And al-maḥdhūra is terror. As for al-ḥidhriya, it is rough ground; and it may be that it was named so because one is wary of walking on it.
حذق:
The letters ḥā', dhāl and qāf are a single root, and it is cutting. It is said "ḥadhaqa al-sikkīnu al-shay'," when the knife cuts the thing. A poet said, in a line of verse: That is a knife sharp upon the throat.

By this same analogy: the man ḥādhiq in his craft is the skilled one, because he "cuts through" the matter, leaving nothing in it to catch on. From it: ḥidhq al-Qur'ān (mastery of learning the Qur'an by heart). By its analogy also: al-ḥudhāqī, the eloquent of tongue, because he separates matters, cutting them clean. For that reason the tongue is called a joint-separator. The whole root is one and the same sense.

From this root: "ḥadhaqa fāhu al-khall," when vinegar makes his mouth sting sharply — that is like a cutting sensation occurring in it.
حر:
The letters ha' and ra', in the doubled root, have two origins.

The first is what is opposite to servitude, and freedom from fault and deficiency. One says huwa hurrun bayyinu al-hururiyyati wal-hurriyyati -- he is clearly a free man. One says tin hurr -- clay with no sand in it. And "so-and-so spent a hurra night," when her husband did not come to her on the first night; but if he did reach her, she spent a shayba' night. He said, in a line of verse: suns that ward off every hurra night, disappointing the hope of the wayward, jealous man.

And hurr al-dar is the middle of the house. Much has been carried on this pattern: the young of the snake is called hurr. He said, in a line of verse: coiled within its den, like the coiling of the hurr among the salam-trees.

And the male of the qamari dove is called saq hurr. Humayd said, in a line of verse: nothing stirred this longing but a dove that called saq hurr in sorrow and in song.

A woman is hurratu al-dhifra, meaning fine of the place behind the ear where the earring rests. He said, in a line of verse: and the earring in the fine place behind her ear hangs loose -- its cord has slackened, so it swings free.

And hurr al-baql is the herb that is eaten uncooked. As for Tarafa's saying: let not your love be a disease within me -- this is not, Mawiyya, becoming of you -- this belongs to the root, meaning: this is not fine or fitting of you. One says harra al-rajul yaharru, from al-hurriyya.

The second origin is the opposite of cold. One says "this is a day of harr," and "a hot day." Al-harur is the hot wind that blows by day or night. From it is al-hirra, thirst. They say, as a proverb: "a hot thirst under a cold chill."

From this section too is al-harir -- al-mahrur, the one seized with rage over some matter that has befallen him; and a woman is harira. He said, in a line of verse: they went out harira women and showed patient endurance, and the yellow gaming-arrows were passed among them -- meaning by "the yellow lettered ones," the divination-arrows.

Al-harra is land of black stones. In my view this too belongs to the root, as though it were scorched. Al-Kisa'i said: Nahshal ibn Harri, with the ra' doubled, as though named after al-harr. Al-Kisa'i also said: hararta ya yawmu taharru, and hararta tahirru, when the heat of the day grew intense.
حرب:
The letters ḥā', rā' and bā' are three roots: one of them is stripping a man of what he has, another is a small creature, and the third is a part of a sitting-place.

The first is *al-ḥarb*, war. It is derived from *al-ḥarab*, which is plundering. One says *ḥarabtuhu mālahu* — I stripped him of his property — and *ḥuriba māluhu*, his property was taken from him, *ḥaraban*. *Al-ḥarīb* is the man who has been plundered. A man who is *miḥrāb* is brave, forward in the business of war and takes it in hand himself. A man's *ḥarība* is the property he lives on, so that if he is stripped of it he never stands up again after it. One says *asad ḥarib* — a lion whose rage is so fierce that it is as though he had been *ḥuriba*, robbed of something. The same is said of a man, *al-ḥarib*.

As for the small creature, it is *al-ḥirbā'*, the chameleon. One says *arḍ muḥarbi'a* of a land when its chameleons are many. From this, by likeness, the studs of coats of mail are called *al-ḥirbā'*. And so too *ḥarābiyy al-matn* — the fleshy muscles of the back.

The third is *al-miḥrāb*, the front of the sitting-place, where the chief sits; the plural is *maḥārīb*. They say that *al-miḥrāb* is the upper chamber, in His words, exalted: {so he came out to his people from the miḥrāb} [Maryam: 11]. And a poet said, in a line of verse:
The mistress of an upper chamber — when I came to her I never met her unless I climbed a ladder.

Among the words that stand apart from these roots is *al-ḥurba*. Ibn Durayd mentioned that it is the black sack. And he recited:
And many a companion I have kept company with, one not far off — you see him propped between the two black sacks.
حرت: The letters ḥā', rā' and tā' are a single root, and it is rubbing. It is said "ḥaratahu ḥartan," when he rubbed it hard.
حرث:
The letters ḥā', rā' and thā' are two roots that stand apart: one of them gathering and earning, and the other that a thing be made lean.

The first is al-ḥarth, which is earning and gathering, and from it a man is named Ḥārith. And in the hadith: "Work for your world as though you will live forever, and work for your hereafter as though you will die tomorrow."

And of this section is the ploughing of crops. And the woman is the husband's tilth; this is a likening, and that is because she is the sown ground of his child. God, exalted be He, said: {your women are a tilth for you} [al-Baqara: 223]. And al-aḥritha are the grooves in which the bowstring runs in the notches of the arrow, because they gather it in.

As for the other root, one says ḥaratha nāqatahu — he made his she-camel lean; and aḥrathahā too. Of this is the saying of the Anṣār when Muʿāwiya said to them: what has become of your watering camels? They said: we wore them down on the day of Badr.
حرج:
The letters ḥā', rā' and jīm are a single root, and it is the bulk of this section and the point its branches return to, and that is a thing's crowding together and its narrowness.

From it is al-ḥaraj, the plural of ḥaraja, which is a thicket where trees stand close together. In the plural one also says ḥarajāt.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
O thickets of the clan on the day they loaded up at Dhū Salam, may no spring rain water you.

And one says ḥirāj as well.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
He caught sight of a clan whose herds were like close-standing thickets.

And from this: al-ḥaraj is sin, and al-ḥaraj is narrowness. God, exalted be He, said: {and whoever He wishes to lead astray, He makes his breast tight and constricted} [al-Anʿām: 125]. And one says ḥarijat al-ʿayn taḥraj — that is, the eye is dazzled and at a loss. And you say ḥarija ʿalayya ẓulmuka — your wronging me is forbidden. And one says aḥrajahā bi-taṭlīqa — that is, he made her forbidden to himself by a pronouncement of divorce. And they say aksaʿahā bi-l-muḥrijāt, meaning with three pronouncements of divorce. And al-ḥaraj is the bier on which the dead are carried. And a covered camel-litter is a ḥaraj.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
If you should see me in Jābir's saddle, on a litter like a cage, with my grave-clothes flapping.

And a she-camel is ḥaraj and ḥurjūj — lean and spare, and that is from the packing together of her bones and her flesh. And from it is al-ḥarij, the man who hardly ever leaves off fighting.

And of what falls outside this section is their saying that al-ḥirj is a cowrie shell, the plural aḥrāj. And it is said that it is the dog's share of the flesh of the hunted game.

Jaḥdar said, in a line of verse:
And my going forward to the lion, shuffling in my bonds, until I fight him for the shares of the kill.

And it is said that al-ḥirj are the snares that are set up.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
As though they were the snare of a trapper.
حرد:
The letters ḥā', rā', and dāl are three origins: intent, anger, and withdrawal.

The first is intent. One says ḥarada ḥardahu, meaning he made straight for it, intending it. God Almighty said: {and they went early, determined in their intent} [al-Qalam: 25]. And a poet said, in a line of verse:
A flood came, sent from God, making straight for the fruitful garden.
From this branch too is al-ḥurūd, the hindquarters of camels, the singular of which is ḥird.

The second is anger. One says ḥarida al-rajulu, the man grew angry (ḥardan, with the rā' unvowelled). Al-Ṭirimmāḥ said, in a line of verse:
And the son of Salmā, in anger.
One also says an angry lion, asadun ḥārid. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Perhaps one day you will see me as though my sons around me were the angry lions.

The third is withdrawing and turning aside. One says so-and-so camped ḥarīdan, meaning apart from the rest. A lone star is called kawkabun ḥarīd. Jarīr said, in a line of verse:
We build our tents on the very track of the enemy; we seek no one's protection, and we do not camp apart.
Abū Zayd said: al-ḥarīd here means one who has moved away from his people — one says ḥarada ḥurūdan. He means: we do not camp apart from our own people out of weakness or humiliation, but because of our strength and our numbers.

Al-muḥarrad, of anything, is that which is bent. One says ḥāradat al-nāqa, the she-camel's milk grew scant, because she has turned away from the flow of milk she used to give; likewise ḥāradat al-sana, the year, when its rain grows scant. A rope is muḥarrad when it is braided so that a twist develops in it from its own crookedness.
حرذ: The letters ḥā', rā' and dhāl are not a root, and there is no sound Arabic word from it. They have said that al-ḥirdhawn is a small creature.
حرز:
The letters ḥā', rā' and zāy are a single root, from guarding and being on guard. It is said "ḥaraztuhu" (I kept it safe) and "iḥtaraza huwa" — he was on his guard.

Some hold that this zāy is substituted for a sīn, and that the origin is al-ḥars (guarding); this is a valid view. In al-Khalīl's book it is said that al-ḥaraz is a rubbed walnut used in play, plural aḥrāz. We say: this is not to be relied upon, and it has no [real] place here.
حرس:
The letters ḥā', rā' and sīn are two roots: one is guarding, the other is a span of time.

The first: ḥarasahu yaḥrusuhu ḥarsan — he guarded it. Al-ḥaras are the guards.

As for ḥarīsat al-jabal, which occurs in the hadith, it is said to be a sheep that night overtakes before it returns to its fold, so that it is as if it had only been watched over there, not properly secured. Abū 'Ubayda said, on ḥarīsat al-jabal: some take it to mean the theft itself; one says ḥarasa yaḥrisu ḥarsan, when he stole.

If this is correct, it is close to the same root, because the thief watches the thing as if he were guarding it, until he can get hold of it. But the first explanation is more correct.

That is the philologists' statement that al-ḥarīsa is the thing being watched over. So it is said: 'there is no hand-cutting penalty for what is [merely] watched over on the mountain,' because that is not a place of secure keeping.
حرش:
The letters ḥā', rā' and shīn are a single root to which the branches of this entry all return: it is a mark and a notching-roughness.

Al-ḥarsh is a mark; from it a man is named Ḥirāsh. For that reason they call a gold coin aḥrash, because it has roughness on it. They call the spiny-tailed lizard aḥrash, because its skin has roughness and ridging on it. From this root: "ḥarashtu (the lizard)" — that is, you stroke its burrow-hole and move your hand until it thinks it is a snake, so it puts out its tail and you seize it; that stroking leaves a mark, so it belongs to the analogy mentioned.

Al-ḥarīsh is a spotted kind of snake. They sometimes say "a snake ḥarshā'," as they say raqṭā' (spotted). A poet said, in a line of verse:
With a rough-skinned, well-worn snake, whose hiss when startled
... is like water poured onto embers.

Al-ḥarshā' is also a seed-plant resembling mustard. Abū al-Najm said, in a line of verse: and its mustard-like seed fell away from the ḥarshā' of Falj.

As for their saying "ḥarrashtu baynahum," when you incite people and cast enmity between them, it belongs to this root, because that is like a notch that occurs in breasts and hearts. From this too: their naming al-nuqba, the first appearance of mange, ḥarshā'. It is said "a mange-spot ḥarshā'," a pustular spot not yet smeared with ointment. A poet said, in a line of verse:
until it is as though Muʿabbad shields himself behind me
... having on him a rough mange-spot that has met no ointment.

As for his saying: as scatters the carded [wool full of] al-ḥarāshīn — it is said this is something in cotton that carding-mallets cannot soften, which can only be from roughness in it.
حرص:
The letters ḥā', rā' and ṣād are two roots: one is splitting, the other is greed.

The first: al-ḥarṣ, splitting. One says ḥaraṣa al-qaṣṣār ath-thawb — the fuller tore the garment, when he split it. Al-ḥāriṣa, among head-wounds, is the kind that tears the skin. From this also al-ḥarīṣa and al-ḥāriṣa — a cloud that scrapes the surface of the ground from the force of its rainfall. He said:
the pouring-down of a scouring rain.

As for greed and excess in craving: one says ḥaraṣa, meaning he was greedy, yaḥriṣu, ḥirṣan; so he is ḥarīṣ. God Most High said: {even if you are eager for their guidance} [an-Naḥl: 37]. One also says ḥuriṣa al-marʿā — the pasture was grazed completely bare, nothing left of it; that belongs to this root too, as though it were scraped from the face of the ground.
حرض:
The letters ḥā', rā' and ḍād are two roots: one is a plant, the other indicates ruin, loss, destruction, weakness, and the like.

As for the first: al-ḥurḍ is potash-plant (al-ushnān), and the one who processes it is al-ḥarrāḍ. Al-iḥrīḍ is the safflower dye-plant. He cited: "blazing like the blaze of al-iḥrīḍ."

The second root: al-ḥaraḍ is one on the verge of ruin. God Almighty said: {until you become wasted away (ḥaraḍan)} [Yūsuf: 85]. One says "ḥarraḍtu fulānan 'alā kadhā," I incited so-and-so to do such-and-such; some people claimed this belongs to the same root. Abū Isḥāq al-Baṣrī al-Zajjāj said: that is because if he disobeys he has thereby been ruined. And God's words {urge (ḥarriḍ) the believers to fight} [al-Anfāl: 65] — because if they disobey they will be destroyed. The rest of the chapter is close to this: they say "huwa ḥurḍa," of one who hands out the gambling-arrows for others to cast; it is said he never eats meat bought with money, but only what he is given, so he is called ḥurḍa, because there is no good in him.

From this chapter also is their saying, of one who does not fight and has neither ability nor weapon: ḥaraḍ. Al-Ṭirimmāḥ said: [describing] protectors against the weak, worthless ones (al-a'rāḍ). One says "ḥaraḍa the thing" and "aḥraḍahu ghayruhu," it decayed and another caused it to decay. "Aḥraḍa the man": a bad child was born to him. And sometimes they said "ḥaraḍa al-ḥālibān al-nāqa," the two milkers milked the she-camel's milk out completely.
حرف:
The letters ḥāʾ, rāʾ and fāʾ are three roots: the edge of a thing, turning-aside, and the measuring-out of a thing.
The edge: ḥarf of anything is its edge, like a sword's. From this: al-ḥarf, a single aspect — 'he is on one ḥarf regarding his affair,' meaning one course only. God, Most High, said: {And among the people is he who worships God on an edge} [al-Ḥajj: 11], meaning on one aspect only — the servant owes obedience to his Lord in both ease and hardship, and if he obeys in ease but disobeys in hardship, he has worshipped God 'upon a ḥarf.' Do you not see that He, Most High, then said: {but if a trial befalls him, he turns back on his face} [al-Ḥajj: 11]. A she-camel is called ḥarf — some said the lean one, likened to a sword's edge; others said the massive one, likened to a mountain's ridge, that is, its flank. Aws said, in a line of verse:

A ḥarf-camel — her brother is her father, of well-bred stock ... and her uncle on both sides is one, long-striding, swift

And Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr said, in a line of verse:

A ḥarf-camel — her brother is her father, of well-bred stock ... and her uncle on both sides is one, lean-flanked, swift

The second root: turning away from a thing. One says inḥarafa ʿanhu, yanḥarifu, inḥirāfan; and ḥarraftuhu ʿanhu, I turned him away from it. From this comes muḥārif, said of one whose livelihood has been turned away from him; likewise taḥrīf al-kalām is the turning of speech from its true direction. God, Most High, said: {they distort the words from their places} [al-Nisāʾ: 46].
The third root: al-miḥrāf, an iron probe for gauging wounds in treatment. A poet said, in a line of verse:

When the physician probes it with his two probes ... it grows worse, beyond the tapping or the moving of it, with pain

Some have claimed al-muḥārif (the poor, unlucky man) comes from this, as though his provision were measured out against him as a wound is measured with the probe.
From this chapter too: 'so-and-so yaḥrufu for his family,' meaning he earns their living. Better than this, though, is to say the fāʾ here stands for a thāʾ, and it is from ḥaratha, he earned and gathered. Sometimes they say aḥrafa fulānun iḥrāfan, when his wealth grew and prospered. So-and-so is ḥarīfu fulānin, his business-partner. All this comes from ḥarafa and iḥtarafa, he earned a living, and the origin is what has been described.
حرق:
The letters ḥā', rā' and qāf are two roots. One of them is the rubbing of one thing against another with heat and burning, and many branches go back to it. The other is something of the body.

The first is their saying ḥaraqtu al-shay', when you file a thing and rub part of it against part. The Arabs say: 'he grinds the urram at you in rage', and that is when a man rubs his teeth one against the other. Al-urram are the teeth. A poet said, in a line of verse:
I was told that Sulaymā's in-laws had passed the night in anger, grinding their teeth.
Some read {We shall surely file it away, then We shall scatter it} [Ṭā-Hā: 97]; they said its meaning is, we shall file it down with files. Al-ḥaraq is fire. Al-ḥaraq is also a burn in a garment. Al-ḥarūqā' is this thing called al-ḥurrāq, tinder. The analogy of all of that is one.

Of this chapter is their calling ḥariq the man whose hair breaks and falls away. A poet said, in a line of verse:
With the hair broken at the partings, like whitish-red parings.
Al-ḥurqān is chafing between the two thighs, and it comes from the rubbing of one against the other. One says faras ḥurāq when a horse burns along in its running. And saḥāb ḥariq when a cloud has fierce lightning. Aḥraqanī al-nās bi-lawmihim — the people galled me with their blame. It is said that al-muḥāraqa is a kind of sexual intercourse. And mā' ḥurāq is water salt with a sharp saltiness.

As for the other root, it is al-ḥāriqa, the sinew that is in the hip. One says rajul maḥrūq when his hip sinew is torn through. A poet said, in a line of verse:
He shoves along with the crook like a man whose hip sinew is torn.
حرك:
The letters ḥā', rā', and kāf are a single root: movement (ḥaraka) is the opposite of stillness.

1. al-hārikān — the two points where the shoulders meet, at the withers, because they are always in motion.
2. al-harākīk — the same as al-harāqif, the hip bones; the singular is harkaka.
حرم:
The letters ḥā', rā' and mīm are one root, and it is forbidding and making strict.

Al-ḥarām is the opposite of the lawful. God, exalted, said: {wa-ḥarāmun ʿalā qaryatin ahlaknāhā} [al-Anbiyā': 95]. And it was read: wa-ḥirmun. And a sawṭun muḥarram is a whip not yet made supple. Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
She shies at my hand and at the stiff, unsoftened lash.

Al-qaṭīʿ is the whip, and al-muḥarram is the one not yet worked and not yet made supple.

And al-ḥarīm is the ḥarīm of the well, and it is what lies around it; it is forbidden to anyone other than its owner to dig in it. And the two ḥarams are Mecca and Medina, named so for their inviolability, and because it is forbidden that anything be newly brought about in them, or that a wrongdoer be sheltered there. And aḥrama al-rajulu bi-l-ḥajj — the man entered the consecrated state for the pilgrimage — because what was lawful to him of hunting and of women and other things becomes forbidden to him. And aḥrama al-rajul — the man entered the sacred month. A poet said:
They killed Ibn ʿAffān the caliph while he was in the sacred state, and he passed on, and I have not seen his like slain.

And it is said that al-muḥrim is the one who has a covenant of protection. And one says aḥramtu al-rajula — I beat him at a game — as though you had forbidden him what he had hoped for from you. And likewise ḥarima huwa yaḥramu ḥaraman — when he does not win. And the reasoning is one: it is as though he was kept from what he had hoped for.

And ḥaramtu al-rajula al-ʿaṭiyyata ḥirmānan — I withheld the gift from the man — and aḥramtuhu, and it is a poor form of speech. A poet said:
And I was told of her that you had withheld her from her own people, so that she might marry among another folk.

And maḥārim al-layl are its frightening places, which it is forbidden to the coward to travel. And Thaʿlab recited:
By God, sleep, and white women with rounded arms, are easier than a night of young she-camels hurrying on;
the frightening places of the night are for them a trackless waste, at the hour when the cautious, half-hearted man is asleep.

And of consecration for the pilgrimage one says qawmun ḥurum and ḥarām, and rajulun ḥarām. And a rajulun ḥaramī is one attributed to the sacred territory. Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
At the voice of a woman of the sacred territory, who said, when they had set off: is there among your light-burdened riders one who seeks hides?

And al-ḥarīm is that whose touching has been forbidden, so that one is not brought near it. And the Arabs, when they made the pilgrimage, used to cast off the clothes they had on and not wear them in the sacred territory; and a garment, when its wearing is forbidden, is called al-ḥarīm. A poet said:
Grief enough for me is my passing by it, as though it were a thing cast down before the hands of those circling, a forbidden garment.

And one says: between the people is a ḥurma and a maḥrama, and that is derived from its being forbidden to let it go to waste and to leave off keeping it.

And it is said that al-ḥarīma is the name of what has escaped of everything hoped for and desired.

And among the odd words of the section is al-ḥayrama: the cow.
حرن:
The letters ḥā', rā' and nūn are a single root: one thing clinging to another, hardly parting from it. Al-ḥirān (balking) in a riding-beast is well known; it is said "ḥarana" and "ḥaruna." Al-maḥārin, of bees, are those that cling fast to the honeycomb and do not leave until removed. A poet said, in a line of verse: the sound of the honey-scrapers as they pull away the clinging bees.

Likewise al-Shammākh's saying, in a line of verse:
Arwā is no dearer to us, however precious she is
... than a hobbled, balking beast

She is the one that will not leave the mountaintop. It is said "ḥarana in a sale," meaning he held firm and would neither raise nor lower the price.
حروى:
The letters ḥā', rā' and the weak letter after them are three origins: the first is a kind of heat, the second is nearness and intent, the third is returning.

The first: al-ḥarw. From your saying "I found in my mouth ḥarwa and ḥarāwa," a burning sting from something eaten, like mustard and the like. By this analogy: ḥarāt al-nār, the blazing of a fire. From it also: al-ḥarra, noise and clamor.

As for nearness and intent: their saying "anta ḥarā an tafʿala kadhā" — you are apt to do such-and-such. This word is not put in the dual or plural, but if you say ḥariyy, you say ḥariyyān and ḥariyyūn and aḥriyā' for the group. You say "this matter is a maḥrāh for such-and-such." From it: their saying "he yataḥarrā the matter," meaning he seeks/aims at it. It is said that al-ḥarā, written short, is the place of the eggs, the [bird's] scratched-out nest-hollow. From it: "he taḥarrā at the place" — he lingered. From it: their saying "I alighted bi-ḥarāhu wa-bi-ʿarāhu," meaning at his courtyard/vicinity.

The third: their saying "ḥarā al-shay', yaḥrī ḥaryan," when a thing shrinks back and diminishes. "And time made it shrink." The viper that has grown old and whose body has wasted is called ḥāriya. In imprecation against someone they say: "May God strike him with a wasted viper," because it wastes away with the passing of time and shrinks, and that is the more vicious kind. And in the hadith: "When the Messenger of God, God bless him and his family and grant him peace, died, Abū Bakr's body began to waste away until he joined him."
حز:
The letters ha' and za' are a single root: notching a thing with iron or otherwise, from which other senses branch. One says hazaztu fi al-khashaba hazzan -- I notched the wood. And when the camel's elbow strikes its callus-pad and leaves a mark on it, it is said "bihi hazz." Al-huzzaz is the rankling grief within the self, for it notches the heart and other things. Al-Shammakh said, in a line of verse: when he sold her, the eye overflowed with tears, and in the breast was a rankling grief of reproach, biting deep.

Al-hazaza is from this too. Anything that chafes in your breast has "hazza." And from it is the hadith of 'Abd Allah: "Sin is what notches the hearts." From this root too is al-haziz, rugged, uneven ground, plural ahizza. He said, in a line of verse: at the ahizza of al-Thalabut.

From it too is al-hazaz, dandruff on the head. One says "I came at an unwelcome hazza," meaning a state and a time -- and I do not think it is said of a good state. He said, in a line of verse: and at what notch of passing time does it come apart?
حزب:
The letters ḥā', zāy and bā' are a single root, and it is the gathering together of a thing.

From this is al-ḥizb, a group of people. God Most High said: {kullu ḥizbin bimā ladayhim fariḥūn} — every party rejoicing in what it has [al-Mu'minūn: 53]. And a portion of anything is a ḥizb; one says: he recited his ḥizb, his set portion, of the Qur'an. Al-ḥizbā' is rough hard ground. Al-ḥazābiya is the donkey that is compact in build.

And of this chapter is al-ḥayzabūn, the old woman. They added to it the yā', the wāw and the nūn, as they do in the like of this, so that it should be stronger in the description they intend.
حزر:
The letters ḥā', zāy and rā' are two origins: one is a thing's intensifying, the other is a kind of exercising judgment.

The first origin: al-ḥazāwir, hillocks, singular ḥazwara. From it: the boy al-ḥazwar, when he has grown sturdy and strong; plural ḥazāwira. From it also: "ḥazara al-labanu wa-l-nabīdh," when milk or date-wine turned strongly sour; it is ḥāzir. A poet said, in a line of verse: after that which passed sourness and turned strongly sour.

As for the third [origin]: their saying "ḥazartu al-shay'," when you estimate it; I am a ḥāzir. It is permissible to relate to this their calling the choicest of property ḥazarāt. And in the hadith: "The Prophet, God bless him and his family and grant him peace, sent out a collector of alms-tax and said: Do not take anything from people's choicest wealth. Take the old worn-out camel, the young camel, and the one with a defect." So al-ḥazarāt are the choicest [property], as though the alms-collector exercises his judgment and so [would otherwise] take the choicest [which he is here told not to].
حزق:
The letters ḥā', zāy and qāf are a single root, and it is a thing's gathering together. From it, al-ḥizaq: bands/groups of people. ʿAntara said, in a line of verse: Yemeni bands, for a mumbling foreigner.

Al-ḥazīqa, of palm trees, is a cluster. From it also: al-ḥuzuqqa, the short man, named so because his frame is drawn together compactly. Al-ḥazq is stringing the bow tightly with the bowstring. The man al-mutaḥazziq is one who grips tight, out of stinginess, what is in his hands. They say: al-ḥāziq is the one whose boot has grown tight and pinches him. The analogy throughout this root is one and the same.
حزك: The letters ḥā', zāy and kāf are a single word, which I take to belong to the category of letter-substitution, and not to be a true root. It is al-iḥtizāk, that is, wrapping oneself tightly with a garment. Either the kāf stands for a mīm [it is really al-iḥtizām], or the zāy stands for a bā' and it is really al-iḥtibāk. Al-iḥtibāk has already been discussed in its own entry.
حزل: The letters ḥā', zāy and lām are a single root: a thing's rising. It is said "iḥza'alla," when it rose up. "The camels iḥza'allat over the ground while traveling" — they rose up [into a visible line]. "The mountain iḥza'alla" — it appeared raised up in the mirage.
حزم:
The letters ḥā', zāy and mīm are a single root, tying a thing and binding it together — a consistent analogy.

Al-ḥazm is soundness of judgment, likewise al-ḥazāma, this being its being drawn together and not scattered or wavering. The girth-strap of a saddle is from this. Al-mutaḥazzim is one girded up. Al-ḥuzma, of firewood or the like, is well known. Al-ḥayzūm and al-ḥazīm are the chest, because it is where its bones gather and are bound together. The Arabs say: "I have girded my chest for this matter" [I resolved firmly on it].

Abū Khirāsh, describing an eagle, said, in a line of verse:
She saw prey about to escape, so she drew in
... supple feathers to her breast

That is, the quarry was about to escape her. Al-raṭīb means soft/supple. That is, she folded her wing when she saw the quarry, in order to swoop down.

As for the sayer's words: "I made ready Ḥuzma, and she is muqraba" — she is a mare, and her name is derived from what we have mentioned.

Al-ḥazam is like a choking tightness in the chest; it is said "ḥazima yaḥzamu ḥazaman"; that only comes from something gathering there. As for al-ḥazm, rugged high ground, it may be from this, or it may be that the nūn was turned into a mīm, the original being ḥazn (rough ground), and they turned it to mīm because al-ḥazm, as they say, is higher than al-ḥuzn.
حزن: The letters ḥā', zāy and nūn are a single root, and it is roughness in a thing and hardness in it. From that is al-ḥazn, which is the rugged part of the ground. And al-ḥuzn - grief - is well known; one says ḥazananī al-shay' yaḥzununī - the thing grieved me; and they have also said aḥzananī. And ḥuzānatuka are your family and those you grieve for.
حزوى:
The letters ḥā', zāy and the weak letter after them are a root with few words, and it is rising. It is said "ḥazā al-sarābu al-shay'a, yaḥzūhu," when the mirage lifts the thing, making it appear raised. From it: "ḥazawtu al-shay'a" and "ḥazaytuhu," when you estimate its measure. It belongs to this root because you do that and then raise it up [in reckoning] so that its amount may be known.

They have also made a hamzated word of this, saying: "ḥaza'tu al-ibil, aḥza'uhā ḥaz'an," when you gather the camels and drive them; that too is a rising in their pace. As for al-ḥazā', it is a plant.
حس:
The letters ha' and sin are two roots: the first is overpowering a thing by killing or otherwise, the second is the imitation of a sound made at pain or the like.

The first: al-hass is killing. God Almighty said: {when you were slaying them by His leave} [Al 'Imran: 152]. From it is the hadith: "Slay them with the sword." And in the hadith about locusts: "when the cold strikes it dead." Al-hasis is the slain man. Al-Afwah said, in a line of verse: and every rival has now fallen, slain.

One says the cold is a "mahassa" for plants, killing them. From this too is hasastu al-shay' min al-lahm -- to put a piece of meat on the live coal; and hashhashtu also means the same. The Arabs say: "do that before the husas of the gamblers," meaning before they put the meat of their slaughtered camel on the fire.

From this section too is their saying ahsastu, meaning I came to know of the thing. God Almighty said: {do you perceive any one of them} [Maryam: 98]. This is carried on their saying "I killed the matter with knowledge," meaning mastered it thoroughly -- so it returns to the root sense mentioned. The five senses are called al-hawass: touch, taste, smell, hearing and sight. From this too is their saying: "from where did you perceive this news," meaning where did you learn of it.

From this section too is their calling the one who drives off hunger by his generosity hashas. He said, in a line of verse: and remember Husayn among the departing host, and before him Hasan, and 'Utba, the generous, the hashas.

The second root: their saying hassi, a word said at the onset of pain. One says hasistu lahu, fa-ana ahissu, when you feel tenderness for someone, as though your heart aches with pity for him. From this too is al-hiss, a pain that seizes a woman at childbirth. One says inhassat asnanuhu -- his teeth fell out. He said, in a line of verse: in the ancient mine of kingship, unshakeable, neither uprooted nor loosened.

From this section, and not far from it, is al-husas, ill-temper. He said, in a line of verse: many a drinking-companion of yours has husas -- his drink is like the notch of the razors. And al-husas is also said to mean bad luck. This may belong either to this root or to the first, since it takes away good fortune.
حسب:
The letters ḥā', sīn and bā' are four roots.

The first: counting. You say ḥasabtu al-shay'a aḥsubuhu ḥasban wa-ḥusbānan — I counted the thing. God, exalted, said: {al-shamsu wa-l-qamaru bi-ḥusbān} [al-Raḥmān: 5]. And of the reasoning of the section is al-ḥisbān, supposing; it was set apart from counting by a change of vowel and of form, but the meaning is one, because when he says ḥasibtuhu kadhā — I supposed it to be so — it is as though he said: it is among the things I count as coming to be.

Of the section is al-ḥasab, that which is counted up in a man. The lexicographers said: its meaning is that he counts up noble forefathers.

Of this section too is their saying iḥtasaba fulānun ibnahu — when his son dies grown. That is, he counts him among the things stored up for him with God, exalted. Al-ḥisba is your counting on the reward. And so-and-so is ḥasanu al-ḥisba in a matter, when he manages it well; and this is not from counting on the reward. This too belongs to the section, because when a man manages a matter well he knows the count of everything and its place in judgement and in what is right. The reasoning is all one.

The second root: sufficiency. You say shay'un ḥisāb, that is, a thing that is enough. And one says aḥsabtu fulānan — when you give him what satisfies him; and likewise ḥassabtuhu.

A woman said, in a line of verse:
We feed the child of the tribe if he is hungry, and we satisfy him if he is not hungry.

The third root: al-ḥusbān, which is the plural of ḥusbāna, and it is the small cushion. And ḥassabtu al-rajula uḥassibuhu — when you seat him on it and prop him with it. From it is the saying of the poet:
On the morning he lay in the sand with no cushion under him.

And another said:
O ʿĀm, had our spears been able to reach you, and the camels dancing on to Minā and then to al-Ghabghab,
you would have felt in the hollow of your foot the thrust of a burning, thirsting avenger, or you would have lain with no cushion under you.

And of this root is al-ḥusbān: small arrows shot from the Persian bows, the single one a ḥusbāna. The two were set apart only because these are small and those [large].

From it is their saying aṣāba al-arḍa ḥusbān, that is, locusts. And His word, exalted: {wa-yursila ʿalayhā ḥusbānan mina al-samā'} [al-Kahf: 40] was explained as hail.

The fourth root: al-aḥsab is the one whose skin has turned white from a disease so that his hair is spoiled, as though he were a leper. A poet said:
O Hind, do not marry a dull weakling, whose birth-hair upon him is patchy white.

And there does sometimes occur among the roots of the sections this spread that you see among these four roots.
حسد: The letters ḥā', sīn and dāl are one root, and it is envy.
حسر:
The letters ḥā', sīn and rā' are a single root, and it is from uncovering a thing. [One says ḥasartu 'an al-dhirā'] — that is, you bared the forearm. Al-ḥāsir is the man who has neither coat of mail nor helmet on him. One says ḥasartu al-bayt — I swept out the house. It is said that al-miḥsara is the broom. And so-and-so is karīm al-maḥsar — generous in what is laid bare of him, that is, karīm al-makhbar: when you uncover his character you find a generous man there.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
She lay sleepless, and I do not know whether sickness is her ailment, or it is from parting with a brother generous in what is found beneath the surface of him.

Also of this root is al-ḥasra — grieving regret over a thing that has slipped away. One says ḥasirtu 'alayhi ḥasaran wa-ḥasratan, and that is the laying bare of his condition in his distress and his want of patience. From it comes a she-camel described as ḥasrā, when she goes lame. And ḥasara al-baṣar, when the sight tires out, and it is ḥasīr; that is the laying bare of its condition in the shortness and weakness of its seeing. Al-muḥassar is the one made small and despised, as though he had been laid bare, that is, made a man of regret. We have already explained it.
حسف:
The letters ḥā', sīn and fā' are a single root, and it is something that peels off from a thing and falls away. From it: al-ḥusāfa, what falls away from dates and fruit. It is said "inḥasafa al-shay'," when a thing crumbles in your hand.

As for al-ḥasīfa, which is enmity, it is possible it belongs to this root. But what I hold is that it belongs to the category of letter-substitution, and the origin is al-ḥasīka, the kāf having been substituted with fā'. Al-ḥasīka and its analogy are discussed after this entry. It is said al-ḥasaf is thorns, and that belongs to this root.
حسك: The letters ḥā', sīn and kāf come from the roughness of a thing; its branches do not go beyond this. From it: al-ḥasak, the burr of the saʿdān plant, named so for its roughness and the thorns upon it. From it also: al-ḥasīka, which is enmity, and the roughness gathered in the heart. From it also: al-ḥiskik, the hedgehog. The analogy throughout all of it is one and the same.
حسل:
The letters ḥā', sīn and lām are a root with few words, and it is the young of the ḍabb (spiny-tailed lizard), called al-ḥisl, plural ḥusūl. They say in the proverb: "I will not come to you [as long as] the young lizard [keeps] its tooth," meaning: I will never come to you — because the ḍabb never loses a tooth. The ḍabb is nicknamed Abū al-Ḥisl.

Al-ḥasīl is the young of cattle, having no singular of its own form. A poet said, in a line of verse: and they, like the tails of young cattle, went off.
حسم:
The letters ḥā', sīn, and mīm are a single root: cutting a thing off completely.

1. al-ḥasm — cutting.
2. ḥusām — the sword, so named from this; one also says its ḥusām is its edge — either way it comes from cutting.
3. ḥusūman, in His saying, Exalted is He: {and eight days, in unbroken succession} [al-Ḥāqqa: 7] — it is said these are the consecutive ones, one running into the next. It is also said al-ḥusūm means ill fortune, or that they were so named because they cut off good fortune from their people — this latter view fits the root better.
4. maḥsūm — a child poorly nourished, as though his growth were cut off when his food was cut off.
5. al-ḥasm — to cut a vein and cauterize it with fire so its blood does not flow; for this reason one says, cut this matter off from yourself (iḥsim ʿanka), meaning end it and spare yourself its trouble.
حسن:
The letters ḥā', sīn and nūn are a single root. So al-ḥusn, beauty, is the opposite of ugliness. One says, a man is ḥasan and a woman ḥasnā' and ḥussāna. A poet said, in a line of verse:
The dwelling of the girl to whom we used to say: O gazelle without ornament, fair of neck.

And there is nothing in this section but this. And they say: al-Ḥasan is a mountain, and a ridge among the ridges of sand. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Woe to the mother of the earth for what she has covered over, on the morning when the road pressed hard by al-Ḥasan.

Al-maḥāsin, the good points of a man and of other things, are the opposite of al-masāwī, the bad points. Al-ḥasan of the forearm is the half that is next to the wrist, and I think it was named so as a counterpart to the other half, because they call the half that is next to the elbow al-qabīḥ, the ugly, and it is what is called kisr qabīḥ. A poet said, in a line of verse:
If you were an ass you would be an ass of humiliation, and if you were a bone of the forearm you would be the ugly one.
حسوى:
The letters ḥā', sīn and the weak letter after them are a single root, from which words are then derived: it is the sipping of a liquid thing, like water and milk and the like; from it is said "ḥasawtu al-laban ḥaswan" (I sipped the milk).

It is said in the proverb: "For the like of this I used to feed you sips." The origin: the horseman feeds his horse with milk, sipping it into him, then he comes to need it in pursuit or flight, so he says: "For this I used to do with you what I did." Then that is said of anyone groomed for a purpose.

The Arabs say in their proverbs: "He conceals a sip within a show of merely skimming the froth," meaning he pretends to be only taking the milk's froth, when what he actually wants is to drink the milk itself. This is said of one who schemes, showing one thing while intending another. They say: "sleep like a bird's sip," meaning very little. They say: "I drank ḥaswan and ḥasā'an" [a sip, and broth].

Ibn Judʿān used to be called "the sipper of gold," because he had a golden vessel he sipped from.

Al-ḥisy is a place where, when its sand is cleared away, its water springs forth. A poet said, in a line of verse:
It fills up as al-ḥisy fills, its buckets surge forth
... cooled from beneath by a thicket and a sandy watercourse.

This too belongs to the first sense, as though its water is sipped. What is also carried on this: "iḥtasaytu al-khabar" and "taḥassaytu," like taḥassastu (I sought news out); and "ḥasītu bi-l-shay'," like ḥasistu (I sensed the thing). A poet said, in a line of verse:
except that the noble riding-camels sensed it
... and so eyed it warily.

It is also possible this belongs to the category where they turn a doubled letter into a yā' upon doubling, like "qaṣṣaytu aẓfārī" (I trimmed my nails) and "taqaḍḍā al-bāzī" (the falcon swooped in its dive); it is close to both explanations. And Ḥisy al-Ghamīm is a place name.
حش:
The letters ha' and shin are a single root: a plant or the like that dries up, and this is then borrowed for other things while the sense stays one.

1. al-hashish -- dried-up plants.
2. al-hishash / al-mihashsh -- its container. He said, in a line of verse: between the two flanks of a huge, gruff old bull-camel.
3. hishasha of a person or anything else: its two sides, from Abu Malik -- as though likened to the two sides of a bundle of hashish.
4. al-hushsha -- a hilltop where plants grow and turn white with dried grass on top. He said, in a line of verse: so al-Hushsha, black, from the back of the landmark.
5. al-muhashsh among people: the small man, as though he had dried up and shrunk.

He said, in a line of verse: how ugly a husband -- shrivelled, misshapen. One says istahashshati al-ibil -- the camels' pasterns grew fine from their bulk or their fatness. They also say istahashsha sa'iduha kaffaha, when the forearm grows large so the hand looks small by comparison. He said, in a line of verse: when its two veins swell they start together -- when the two lean over, its cheeks grow thin.

One says hashashtu al-nar, when you stoke a fire, and this belongs to the root mentioned, as though you made its kindling like dry grass that it feeds on. He said, in a line of verse: they did not lose courage that we would press upon them, but they saw a fire being stoked and fanned.

And hashsha al-rajulu sahmahu, when he fixes its feathers along its sides. From this section too: a horse mahshush al-zahr bi-janbayhi, when it is broad and hollow-flanked. He said, in a line of verse: from the withers, broad-flanked, spacious-sided.

And the saying of al-Hudhali: concerning the man of Mazin for whom I gathered up the wealth of this poor, unlucky man, whose inherited stock was scant -- he means: I added to this poor man's wealth, since he had been captured and ransomed with his own property.

One says hushshati al-yad, when the hand grows numb and dry, as though likened to dried grass. And ahashshati al-hamil, when a pregnant animal goes past the time of birth and the young dries up inside her.

Anomalous to this root is al-hushasha, the last remnant of life. He said, in a line of verse: God has refused to leave me any remnant of life -- so patience, then, for what God has willed for me, patience.
حشب:
The letters ḥā', shīn and bā' are close in meaning to what came before. One says al-ḥawshab is the man who is big-bellied. He said, in a line of verse:
And a running pack drags — dragging my flesh toward big-bellied ones.

Al-ḥawshab is also the packing of the hoof; and it is said, rather, that it is a bone inside the hoof, between the sinew and the cannon-bone. Ru'ba said, in a line of verse:
In a pastern that does not complain of the ḥawshab.
حشد: The letters ḥā', shīn and dāl are close in meaning to what came before. One says ḥashada al-qawm, when the people gathered and were quick to help one another. A she-camel ḥushūd is one whose milk gathers quickly in her udder. Al-ḥashd: those who have mustered. This, although it lies within the meaning of what came before it, carries a further sense too: cooperation. One says a cluster of dates is ḥāshid or ḥāshik: massed and heavy in what it bears.
حشر:
The letters ḥā', shīn and rā' are close in meaning to the one before them, with an added meaning too: driving, rousing, and being roused.

The people of the language say: al-ḥashr is gathering together with driving, and every gathering is a ḥashr. The Arabs say ḥasharat al-sana māla banī fulān - the year gathered up the property of so-and-so's people, as though it swept it together; it carried it off and finished it. Ru'ba said, in a line of verse:
Nothing escaped that sweeping-up of hers, neither wild beast nor any living creature of the creatures.

One says udhun ḥashra - an ear whose make is drawn tight together. A poet said, in a line of verse:
She has an ear drawn tight and fresh, like the husk of a markh branch when it has turned yellow.

Among the names of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, is al-Ḥāshir, the Gatherer. It means that people will be gathered at his feet, as though he goes before them on the Day of Rising with them behind him. It may also be that, since he was the last of the prophets, people were gathered in his time.

Ḥasharāt al-arḍ are the small creatures of the ground - jerboas, lizards and the like - named so because of how many they are and how they are driven along and roused up. Al-ḥashwar among men is the one huge in build, or huge in the belly.

Among what departs from the origin sense is their calling a light, nimble man ḥashr. And al-ḥashr among the feathers of an arrow is what is fine and slender. A spearhead is ḥashr, that is, thin; and one says ḥashartuhu - I made it thin.
حشف:
The letters ḥā', shīn and fā' are a single root indicating slackness, weakness, and being worn out.

First of that: al-ḥashaf, the worst kind of dates. They say in their proverbs: "Both bad dates and short measure too?" — for a man who combines two bad things at once. Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
As though the hearts of birds, moist and dry, lay by their nest
... jujube-fruit, and worn-out ḥashaf dates.

He mentioned their hearts because that is the choicest part of a bird, and it is what they bring to their chicks. It is said "ḥashifa khilfu al-nāqa," when a she-camel's teat's milk dried up.

Al-ḥashīf is a worn-out, threadbare garment. "The man taḥashshafa" — he wore the threadbare garment. A poet said, in a line of verse:
He draws the worn garment close over her, to conceal her and himself
... being one who wears ragged clothes.

Al-ḥashafa is an old, aged woman; also dried-out leaven; also a soft crumbling rock with level ground around it.
حشك:
The letters ḥā', shīn and kāf are a single root, and it is the gathering together of a thing.

1. One says ḥashaktu al-nāqa, when you leave a she-camel without milking her, so her milk gathers; she is then maḥshūka.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
She went out in the morning, maḥshūka, her udder full.

2. Ḥashaka al-qawm, when the people ḥashadū — gathered and rallied together.
3. Ḥashakat al-saḥāba: the cloud's water became abundant.
4. From this comes their calling a palm tree heavy with fruit ḥāshik.
5. Ḥashakat al-samā': the sky brought its rain.
6. Sometimes this was extended further, so they said qawsun ḥāshika, meaning a bow that shoots far, reaching a distant mark.
7. Ḥashshāk is a river.
حشم:
The letters ḥā', shīn and mīm are a shared root, and it is anger, or something close to it.

The people of the language said: al-ḥishma is a drawing back and a shyness. Others said: it is anger. Ibn Qutayba said: it has been related from some of the eloquent Arabs that a certain thing is among what yuḥshim the sons of so-and-so, meaning: angers them. Another said that the Arabs know al-ḥishma as nothing but anger, and that when they call a man's ḥasham his servants, they mean only that these are the people for whom he grows angry, and who grow angry for him.

Abū 'Ubayd said: Abū Zayd said: ḥashamtu al-rajul, aḥshimuhu, and aḥshamtuhu — this is when a man sits with you and you hurt him, letting him hear what he dislikes. Ibn al-A'rābī says: ḥashamtuhu fa-ḥashama means: I put him to shame. And aḥshamtuhu means: I angered him.

He recited, in a line of verse:
By your life, Abū Khubayb's bread-cake is slow to bake, and its eater [al-akīl, the one who eats it] is put to shame.
حشن:
The letters ḥā', shīn and nūn are a single root, and it is a thing changing because of the dirt clinging to it. From it is then derived:

1. As for the first, Al-Khalīl related their saying: ḥashina al-siqā', when a waterskin was filled with milk and not looked after with washing, so that its outside changed and stank.
2. As for the underlying pattern, Abū 'Ubayd said: al-ḥishna — with the ḥā' before the shīn — is a grudge. He recited:
Truly, I see no one carrying a grudge in his heart, suppressing it, but the buried thing in him will show.
3. Someone else said: from this too comes their saying: so-and-so spoke to so-and-so until he ḥashshana his chest, filling it with rancor.
حشوى:
The letters ḥā', shīn and the weak letter after them are a single root — sometimes hamzated, in which case the two meanings still remain close. It is that a thing be placed fully into a container. One says ḥashawtuhu, aḥshūhu, ḥashwan — I stuffed it.

1. Ḥishwat al-insān wa'l-dābba: the intestines of a person or of an animal.
2. So-and-so is min ḥishwati banī fulān — meaning among the basest of them. This is said because what things are stuffed with is never the finest of the goods, but the poorest of it.
3. Al-miḥshā: what a woman stuffs herself with to make her buttocks look larger; the plural is al-maḥāshī. He said, in a line of verse:
Abundant [hair], with no need of the padding.
4. Al-ḥashā: a person's ḥashā [flank], plural aḥshā'.
5. Al-ḥashā also means the region, the quarter — and this belongs to the pattern of the root, because every region has its people, as though they had filled it. One says mā adrī bi-ayyi ḥashan huwa — I do not know in which quarter he is. He said, in a line of verse:
In which region did the parting companions spend the evening?

From the hamzated form, which is not far from the root's pattern, comes their saying ḥasha'tuhu bi'l-sahm, aḥsha'uhu — when you strike a man in the side with an arrow. He said, in a line of verse:
I will surely strike your side with a broad arrowhead — a wolf's bite, Uways, out of folly.

From this too comes ḥasha'tu al-mar'ata, said as a euphemism for intercourse.

Al-ḥashā, without the hamza, is shortness of breath. One says ḥashiya yaḥshā ḥashan, so he is ḥashsh, as you see.

As for al-Nābigha's line:
Gather your miḥāsh [troops], O Yazīd, for I have made Yarbū' and Tamīm ready against you —
this has two readings. One is that its mīm is a root letter, already discussed in its own place. The other is that the mīm is an added letter, making it a noun of the mif'al pattern from al-ḥashw — as though he meant the rabble, the mixed riff-raff — and it should properly have been miḥshā, but he inverted it.
حص:
The letters ha' and sad, in the doubled root, have three origins: the first is a share, the second the clarity and firm establishment of a thing, the third the departure and diminishing of a thing.

1. The first: al-hissa, a share. One says ahsastu al-rajul, when you give a man his share.
2. The second: their saying hashasa al-shay' -- the thing became clear. God Almighty said: {now the truth has become clear} [Yusuf: 51]. From this hashasa also means: to move a thing until it settles firmly in place.
3. The third: al-hass and al-husas, running fast. Inhassa al-sha'r 'an al-ra's -- the hair fell out from the head. A man ahass has little hair. Hassat al-bayda sha'ra ra'sihi -- the helmet wore off the hair of his head. Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat said, in a line of verse: the helmet has worn the hair from my head, so that I taste no sleep but a doze.

Al-hasasa is also going far off across the land. A man ahass and a woman hassa' means ill-omened, as though good fortune has departed from them. From this section too: "so-and-so yahussu," when he protects no one. He said, in a line of verse: I withhold protection and grant none -- and whoever I do protect is not like one deceived by false hope.

Al-ahassan are the slave and the donkey, because their prices keep pace with their wear until they grow old, their value drops, and they die. One says sana hassa' -- a barren year with no good in it.

Anomalous to this root is their calling wars, a yellow dye-plant, huss. He said, in a line of verse: mixed wine, as though al-huss were in it, when the water blended with it, warmed.
حصب:
The letters ḥā', ṣād and bā' are one root, a kind of matter found on the ground; from it is derived al-ḥaṣbā', a kind of pebble.

1. ḥaṣabtu ar-rajul bi-l-ḥaṣbā' — I pelted the man with pebbles.
2. rīḥun ḥāṣib — a wind that comes bringing dust.
3. al-ḥaṣba — a rash breaking out on the body, likened to gravel.
4. al-muḥaṣṣab, at Minā, is the place of the pebble-throwing. Dhū ar-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
I see my she-camel at al-muḥaṣṣab, yearning stirred in her, by the departure of the Yemeni traveller and the repeated cooing —
meaning the party of Yemenis when they set off homeward; al-hadīl here is the sound of doves — he means she recalled the birds among her people and longed for them.

5. From this root: al-iḥṣāb — a person's stirring up gravel against his enemy.
6. arḍun maḥṣaba — land abundant in pebbles.
7. Their saying ḥaṣṣaba al-qawmu ʿan ṣāḥibihim yuḥaṣṣibūn — their turning away from him hastily, like al-ḥāṣib, the strong wind; this too fits the pattern of the root.
8. It is said that al-ḥaṣib, among milks, is that which will not yield its cream; this too belongs to the root, as though from its coldness it hardens until it becomes like gravel and yields no cream.
حصد:
The letters ḥāʾ, ṣād and dāl are two roots, quite different from each other: the cutting of a thing, and its being made firm.
The first: ḥaṣadtu al-zarʿ wa-ghayrahu, ḥaṣdan, I harvested the crop and other things — this is the harvest-season, zaman al-ḥaṣād and al-ḥiṣād. In the hadith: 'What throws people down on their faces into the Fire, if not the harvests of their tongues?' — al-ḥaṣāʾid, plural of ḥaṣīda, everything said against people with the tongue and thereby cut down on them. One says ḥaṣadtu and iḥtaṣadtu; a man is muḥtaṣid. A poet said, in a line of verse:

We are but like the tender stalk of a crop ... whenever it is ready, its reaper comes

The other root: their saying ḥablun muḥṣadun, a rope tightly twisted. From this chapter too: shajaratun ḥaṣdāʾ, abundant in leaves; a coat of mail dirʿun ḥaṣdāʾ, firmly made; and istaḥṣada al-qawm, when a people banded firmly together.
حصر:
The letters ḥāʾ, ṣād and rāʾ are one root: gathering, confinement, restraint. Abū ʿAmr said: al-ḥaṣīr is the flank of an animal. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: al-ḥaṣīr is what lies between the vein showing crosswise on a camel's or horse's flank and, upward from there, to where the flank ends — all of it al-ḥaṣīr. Either way it belongs to the sense of 'gathering,' being where the ribs come together.
Al-ḥaṣr: an impediment in speech, as though speech were held back from him. Al-ḥaṣar: tightness of the chest. From this chapter too: al-ḥuṣr, retention of the bowels, said ḥuṣira and uḥṣira. The she-camel al-ḥaṣūr is narrow in her teat-orifice, the sense-pattern being one. Al-iḥṣār is when a pilgrim is barred from the House by illness or the like; some say illness ḥaṣarahu while an enemy aḥṣarahu.
Abū ʿUbayd related from Abū ʿAmr: ḥaṣaranī al-shayʾ and aḥṣaranī, meaning it confined me, citing Ibn Mayyāda:

And Laylā's estrangement was not because she had grown distant ... from you, nor because preoccupations had confined you

The matter of ḥaṣarahu against aḥṣarahu is, to my mind, thoroughly ambiguous — some conflate the two, others distinguish them, and neither position contradicts the sense-pattern described; the whole points to confinement.
From this chapter too: al-ḥaṣūr, the man who does not go in to women — some say it follows the pattern faʿūl in the sense of mafʿūl, as though he were held back; others say he holds himself back from them, as a man is called ḥaṣūr when he withholds his generosity and does not bring out what boon-companions bring out. Al-Akhṭal said, in a line of verse:

and a companion, generous with the wine-cup, who kept me company ... not withholding, nor unruly with it

From this chapter too: al-ḥaṣir bi'l-sirr, one who keeps a secret close. Jarīr said, in a line of verse:

The slanderers sought me out but found ... one close-mouthed with your secret, O Umaym, tight-lipped

Al-ḥaṣīr in His saying, Mighty and Majestic: {and We have made Hell a confinement for the disbelievers} [al-Isrāʾ: 8], meaning a place of confinement. Al-ḥaṣīr in Labīd's line (the text before me gives only this much, and it looks cut off):

At the gate of the enclosure stood — the king

Al-ḥiṣār: a stuffed cushion placed at the front of a camel-litter; one says of the camel iḥtaṣarat al-baʿīru iḥtiṣāran.
حصف:
The letters ḥā', ṣād and fā' are a single root, and it is a firmness in a thing, along with hardness and strength. Soundness of mind is called ḥaṣāfa, and vigorous running is iḥṣāf. One says a horse miḥṣaf and a she-camel miḥṣāf. One also says a squadron maḥṣūfa, when its men are massed together and there is little gap between them. Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
Its scattered bands return to a tightly-massed body, a formidable one, whose onslaught the mailed warriors dread.
It is also said makhṣūfa, with khā', which follows a different pattern, already mentioned in its own place.

One says istaḥṣafa al-zamān 'alā banī fulān, when the times grew hard on them, and farjun mustaḥṣif, meaning tight. He said, in a line of verse:
And when you thrust, you thrust into a tight place, full to the touch, plastered with perfume.

Al-ḥaṣaf is small pustules that make the skin tighten.
حصل:
The letters ḥā', ṣād, and lām are a single root that fits a clear pattern: gathering a thing. For this reason the bird's crop is called ḥawṣala, because it gathers into it. One says ḥaṣṣaltu al-shayʾa taḥṣīlan, I gathered the thing.

Some people of language claim that the origin of taḥṣīl is extracting gold or silver from stone or from the dust of a mine; the one who does this is called al-muḥaṣṣil. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Is there not a man — may God reward him well — who will point the way to a woman refining ore who stays up through the night?
If this is so, then it fits the pattern, and the whole branch is built on it.

Al-ḥaṣal is unripe green dates, before they firm up and their stalk-caps appear; the singular is ḥaṣala. A poet said, in a line of verse:
From them falls the withered unripe date and the green unripe date.
Al-sadā is the withered unripe date, singular sadāh. This too, I mean al-ḥaṣal, belongs to the root, because it is gathered from the palm tree.

Among what falls outside this root, and I do not know what it is derived from, is their saying: the horse ḥaṣila, when its belly aches from eating dirt.
حصم:
