The letters ḥā', ṣād and mīm are a root with few words to it, beyond that it concerns a thing breaking. One says inḥaṣama al-'ūd, when the stick broke. Ibn Muqbil said, in a line of verse:
And a whiteness my hair brought on, like the broken stalks of the harvest.
Among what is derived from it is ḥuṣām al-dābba, its dung. The pattern here is close to the root.
حصن:
The letters ḥā', ṣād and nūn are a single root that follows one analogy, and it is guarding, protecting and keeping safe.

Al-ḥiṣn, the fortress, is well known, and the plural is ḥuṣūn. Al-ḥāṣin and al-ḥaṣān are the chaste woman who guards her private parts. A poet said, in a line of verse:
No chaste woman of Rabī'a bore me, if I ever side with desire so as to follow it.

And Ḥassān said about al-ḥaṣān, in a line of verse:
Chaste and grave, no suspicion is thought of her, and she rises in the morning hungry from the flesh of heedless women.

And the verb from this is ḥaṣuna. Aḥmad b. Yaḥyā Tha'lab said: every chaste woman is muḥṣana and muḥṣina, and every married woman is muḥṣana and nothing else. He said: and everything kept guarded is called muḥṣan, and people have mentioned that a lock is called muḥṣan. And one says aḥṣana al-rajul so that he is muḥṣan. And this is one of the words that came on the pattern af'ula so that it is muf'al.
حصوى:
The letters ḥā', ṣād and the weak letter are three roots: the first is prevention, the second is counting and being able to encompass a thing, and the third is something among the parts of the earth.

1. The first is al-ḥaṣw. Al-Shaybānī said it is prevention; one says ḥaṣawtuhu, meaning I prevented him. He said, in a line of verse:
Do you not fear God, when you withheld my due from me without any wrong, and thwarted me?

2. The second root: aḥṣaytu al-shay', when you counted it and could master its count. God, exalted is He, said: {He knew that you would never be able to count it} [al-Muzzammil: 20]. And He said: {God has counted it and they have forgotten it} [al-Mujādila: 6].

3. The third root: al-ḥaṣā, well known [pebbles/gravel]. One says arḍ maḥsāh, when it has gravel in it. It has also been said ḥaṣiyat taḥṣā.

Among what is derived from it is al-ḥaṣāh: one says mā lahu ḥaṣāh, meaning he has no sense. This comes from the same root, because pebbles have firmness and hardness in them, and al-ḥaṣāh also means sense, because by it a man holds himself together and gains strength of self. He said, in a line of verse:
Truly a man's tongue, when he has no ḥaṣāh, stands as witness against his own faults.
Every piece of musk is also called a ḥaṣāh, but this is a comparison, not the root pattern.

When hamzated, its root sense is a thing gathering together. One says aḥsa'tu al-rajul, when you gave a man his fill of water, and he himself ḥaṣi'a — drank his fill. One says ḥaṣa'a al-ṣabī min al-laban, when a child nursed until his stomach was full, and likewise a kid.
حض:
The letters ha' and dad are two roots: the first is urging someone toward a thing, the second is a low, settled ground.

1. The first: hadadtuhu 'ala kadha, when you spur him and urge him toward it. Al-Khalil said: the difference between al-hadd and al-hathth is that al-hathth applies to travel, driving on and everything, while al-hadd does not apply to travel or driving.
2. The second: al-hadid, the settled surface of the ground. He said, in a line of verse: I came down to him, standing on the low ground.
حضب:
The letters ḥā', ḍād and bā' are two roots: the first is what feeds a fire, and the second is a kind of sound.

The first is in His saying, exalted be His praise, of "the ḥaḍab of Hell" — they said it means the fuel. What fires are stoked with is called miḥḍab. Al-A'shā's line is recited:
So do not be, in our war, a stoker of the flames, setting your people apart into rival factions.

The second, the sound, is as in their calling the sound of a bow ḥiḍb, plural aḥḍāb. As for their saying that al-ḥiḍb is the snake, there is dispute over it, and if it is sound, it is an irregular departure from the root.
حضج:
The letters ḥā', ḍād and jīm are a single root, indicating the lowliness of a thing, its falling, and its departure from the way that is chosen. The Arabs say: inḥaḍaja al-rajul, and others too, when he fell on his side, and ḥaḍajtu bihi al-arḍ — I threw him down to the ground. One says: this is one of so-and-so's ḥaḍajāt, meaning one of his falls — and this applies both to speech and to action.

Al-ḥiḍj is what remains of water in the camels' troughs, plural aḥḍāj. A lowly man is called ḥiḍj. Ḥaḍajtu al-thawb means you struck it with the miḥḍāj while washing it — that being the piece of wood used for the striking.

As for their calling a large waterskin ḥiḍāj, it is close to this root, because it sags and slumps down. As for their saying ḥaḍajtu al-nār, meaning I kindled it, it may belong to this root, and it is also possible that it belongs to the category of letters substituted for one another.
حضر:
The letters hā', dād and rā' are the bringing of a thing, and its coming, and the witnessing of it. And there may come what is far from this, though the root is one.

Al-hadar is the opposite of desert life. And settled life in the hadar is al-hidāra. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Whoever is pleased by settled life, then what men of the desert do you see in us!
Abū Zayd said it with a kasra, and al-Asma'ī said it is al-hadāra with a fatha. As for al-hudr, which is running, that too is of the chapter, because a horse and others bring forward what they have of it; one says ahdara al-faras, and it is a horse that is mihdīr, quick in running, and mihdār. And one says hādartu al-rajul, when you run with him. And the Arabs' saying "milk is attended" means that it is much subject to harm; and they say that the jinn attend it. And they say: "privies are attended". And some people interpreted His words, exalted: {And say: My Lord, I take refuge with You from the promptings of the devils, and I take refuge with You, my Lord, lest they be present with me} [al-Mu'minun: 97], as meaning: lest they touch me with harm. And the whole chapter is one, and that is because they come to him with harm. And one says al-hādir, and that is the great settled clan. Hassān said, in a line of verse:
Ours is a full settlement and a desert camp, as though it were the household of God in glory and honour.
And some people relate it:
. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
as though it were the peaks of Radwā in glory and honour.
And Quraysh rejected that and said: what glory and honour have the peaks of Radwā? And al-hadīra is a company that is not large. A poet said, in a line of verse:
He comes down to the waters with a small band and with a scouting party, like the sand-grouse coming to water when the shade has shrunk away.
And it is said that al-muhādara is the seeking to overcome; and hādartu al-rajul: I knelt facing him before a ruler or a judge.

And one says alqat al-shāt hadīratahā, the ewe cast her hadīra, and it is what she throws out after the young, of the afterbirth and the rest. And this is sound reasoning, and that is because those things are called al-shuhūd, the witnesses, and they have been mentioned in their chapter.

And a man's hadra is his courtyard. And al-hadīra is what gathers of matter in a wound. And one says hadarat al-salāt, the prayer has come; and the tongue of the people of Medina is hadirat. And all of them say tahdur. And this is of the rare things that come in speech on the pattern fa'ila yaf'ulu. And of the sound verbs, those without a weak letter, one single word has come in this way, and it has been mentioned in its chapter. And one says rajulun hadir when he is not fit for travel. And this is like their saying rajulun nahir, when he is fit for the works of the day and not of the night. A poet said:
You are no man of the night, but I am a man of the day.
And they say that al-hadr is fat in the flank and above it. And of what falls outside the chapter is al-Hadr, which is a fortress, in the words of 'Adī, in a line of verse:
And the lord of al-Hadr, when he built it, and when the Tigris was made to bring in tribute to him.
And al-Khābūr, and of the odd ones out, and it may be that hadāri is carried upon what came before it; and it is a star. And the Arabs say: "Hadāri and al-Wazn are two makers of oaths"; and that is because people swear about them that they are Suhayl, since they resemble it. And al-muhlif is the thing that drives one to swearing. A poet said, in a line of verse:
A bay that leaves no room for oaths, but like the colour of wars-dye poured over leather.
And the hidār of camels are the white ones. The Hudhalī said:
Their black ones and their white ones.
حضل: The letters ḥā', ḍād and lām are a single word, not a root, and nothing is generalized from it. One says ḥaḍilat al-nakhla, when the bases of a palm tree's fronds spoiled.
حضن:
The letters ḥā', ḍād and nūn are a single root that can be generalized, and it is the guarding and safekeeping of a thing.

Al-ḥiḍn is what lies below the armpit down to the waist. One says iḥtaḍantu al-shay' — I put it in my ḥiḍn.

As for al-Kumayt's line of verse:
And a waste of desert, whose two flanks of darkness I crossed quietly, when the bird of the night can see —
he means by it that he crossed it. The bird of the night is the bat. The sides of anything are its aḥḍān.

From this root: ḥaḍanat al-mar'a waladahā, a woman cradled her child, and likewise ḥaḍanat al-ḥamāma bayḍahā, the dove brooded on her eggs. Al-muḥtaḍan is the ḥiḍn. He said, in a line of verse:
Broad in the haunch when she turns away, slender at the waist, full at the side.

Ḥaḍan is a mountain in Najd, and it is the first of Najd. The Arabs say: "He has reached Najd, whoever has seen Ḥaḍan." One says imra'atun ḥaḍūn, bayyinat al-ḥiḍān — a woman clearly possessed of ḥiḍān, the caring, nurturing quality this root names.

As for their saying ḥaḍantu al-rajul 'an al-rajul, meaning you set him aside from him, it is a doubted word, and I found many scholars denying it. If it is sound, the pattern in it runs true, as though the thing were guarded away from him and kept from him, not given into his reach. Its verbal noun is al-ḥaḍn and al-ḥaḍāna.

It is said al-ḥaḍan is ivory, in the speaker's line:
She smiled at the flash of lightning, baring her teeth, and revealed a pure white like al-ḥaḍan.
It is also said al-ḥaḍan is the base of a mountain. If what we mentioned about ivory is sound, then it is an irregular departure from the root.
حضى: The letters ḥā', ḍād and the weak letter are a single root, and it is the stirring up of a thing, said especially of fire. One says ḥaḍawtu al-nār, when you kindled it. The stick used to stir the fire is al-miḥḍā'. It is also said ḥaḍa'tuhā, with the hamza, and the stick is then miḥḍa', on the pattern mif'al — sometimes lengthened too, though the first form is better.
حط:
The letters ha' and ta' are a single root: bringing a thing down from a height. One says hatattu al-shay' ahuttuhu hattan. God Almighty's saying {hitta} [al-Baqara: 58] -- they say its meaning is: O God, lift off from us our burdens.

From this section too: their saying of a girl mahtutatu al-matnayn, as though her back had been smoothed with the mihatt, a planing tool. He said, in a line of verse: white, smooth-backed, tender, plump of hindquarters, not gaunt from bearing young.

From this section too: their saying of a man huta'it, meaning small, short, as though he had been pressed down.

From this section too: their calling a swift, noble she-camel hatut, as though she is forever setting down a load in some land.

Anomalous to this analogy is al-hatat, a pimple that appears on the face. Al-Hudhali said, in a line of verse: and a face I once approached by night, Umaym's, clear, smooth, not harsh, without any pimples. And it is also transmitted as: like the disc of the sun, without any pimples.
حطأ:
The letters ḥā', ṭā' and hamza are a root that can be generalized, and it is the sinking down and falling of a thing. One says ḥaṭa'tu al-rajul bi'l-arḍ — I struck him down to the ground. Al-Ḥuṭay'a is the short man. Tha'lab said: the poet was named al-Ḥuṭay'a for his squat ugliness.

Abū Zayd said: al-ḥaṭī' among men, on the pattern fa'īl, is the base man.

Ibn 'Abbās said: "The Messenger of God, peace and blessings upon him and his family, took me by the back of the neck and gave me a ḥaṭ'a, and said: Go and call so-and-so for me." He means: he gave me a push.

One says ḥaṭa'at al-qidr bi-zabadihā — the pot threw off its foam. And ḥaṭa'a al-rajul al-mar'a — he had intercourse with her.
حطب:
The letters ḥā', ṭā' and bā' are a single root, and it is firewood; what resembles it is then carried on this.

Al-ḥaṭab is firewood, well known. One says ḥaṭabtu aḥṭibu ḥaṭban, I gathered firewood. Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
Whenever we rode out, our family's children would say ... come, until the game arrives, let us gather firewood.

One who talks confusedly, mixing things up, is called a “night wood-gatherer” — someone who gathers firewood in the dark grabs anything, good or bad, without seeing.

One says ḥaṭabanī ʿabdī, my slave “wooded” me, when he brought you firewood. A line of verse is quoted:
A cunning glutton — when hungry, he cries; he neither gathers firewood for the people nor gives them water.

A place called ḥaṭīb is one rich in firewood. A she-camel called muḥāṭiba is one that eats dry thorns.

Regarding His words, the Exalted: {and his wife, the carrier of firewood} [al-Masad: 4] — they said this is a figure of speech for gossip-carrying. One says ḥaṭaba fulānun bi-fulānin, so-and-so “wooded” so-and-so, meaning he informed against him or stirred up trouble against him.

It is said al-aḥṭab means severely emaciated, and likewise al-ḥaṭib, as though such a person is likened to dry firewood.

What was said above about gossip is supported by the words of a poet:
One of the fair women, not won by a warrior's coat of mail ... nor one who went about among people carrying damp firewood.
حطم:
The letters ḥāʾ, ṭāʾ and mīm are one root: the breaking of a thing. One says ḥaṭamtu al-shayʾ, ḥaṭman, I broke it. A thing crushed within itself is ḥaṭim. A horse worn down by old age is called ḥaṭim; it is also said al-ḥaṭam is an ailment afflicting an animal's legs, or a weakness — such a horse is ḥaṭim. Al-ḥuṭma: a harsh year, for it breaks everything. Al-ḥuṭam: a rough driver who crushes some camels against others. A poet said, in a line of verse:

The night has wrapped it up with a rough driver

The Fire was named al-Ḥuṭama for its crushing of whatever it meets. A herd of camels is also called ḥuṭama, for crushing whatever it meets. Ḥuṭmat al-sayl: the main crashing force of a flood. This is not itself a root, being a metathesis of al-ṭuḥma. As for al-ḥaṭīm, it is possible this comes from the root — it is al-ḥijr, the wall by the Kaʿba, so named for how many people crowd repeatedly around it, as if being crushed there.
حظ: The letters ha' and za' are a single root: a share and good fortune. One says fulan ahazz min fulan -- so-and-so is luckier than so-and-so, and he is mahzuz. The plural of hazz is ahazin, against the regular analogy. Abu Zayd said: a man haziz jadid, when he has a share of provision. One says haziztu fi al-amr ahazzu. He said: and the plural of al-hazz is ahuzz.
حظر:
The letters ḥā', ẓā' and rā' are a single root, indicating prohibition/fencing off.

One says ḥaẓartu al-shay'a aḥẓuruhu ḥaẓran, I forbade the thing; I am ḥāẓir, and the thing is maḥẓūr, forbidden. God the Exalted said: {and never is the gift of your Lord withheld} [al-Isrā': 20].

Al-ḥiẓār is an enclosure built round sheep or other livestock with branches or fresh or dried wood; it is scarcely ever built except with fresh wood, which then dries. The one who builds it is called al-muḥtaẓir. God the Exalted said: {and they became like the dried-up debris of the pen-builder} [al-Qamar: 31] — meaning the one who makes the enclosure for the sheep, which then dries and crumbles.

One says “so-and-so came with fresh fencing-wood” when he came out with an outrageous lie. One says “he is lighting a fire in the enclosure” when someone is spreading gossip; its supporting example has already passed.
حظل:
The letters ḥā', ẓā' and lām are a single root, close to what came before. Al-ḥaẓl is jealousy, and the preventing of a woman from freely acting and moving. He said:
So he ḥaẓl-s, or grows jealous.

Abū 'Ubayd said: ḥaẓaltu 'alayhi is like ḥaẓartu — I forbade him. It is said, of his line "so he ḥaẓl-s, or grows jealous," that it means stinginess, and this seems the sounder reading, since he said "or grows jealous." Stinginess goes back to the sense of preventing already given. The proof of this is their saying ḥaẓalān and ḥaẓlān. He said, in a line of verse:
Umm Mughallis taunts me with stinginess, so I said to her: why do you cast my own fault back at me?
حظوى:
The letters ḥā', ẓā' and the weak letter after them are two roots: one is closeness to a thing and standing, the other a kind of weapon.

The first: their saying rajulun ḥaẓiyy, when he has standing and ḥuẓwa — favor; and imra'atun ḥaẓiyya. The Arabs say: "unless favored, then do not fail to try." He means: if you have no favor, do not fail to seek closeness. Mā alawtu means: I did not fall short.

The other root: al-ḥiẓā', plural of ḥiẓwa, is a small headless arrow, shot for practice. Some scholars of language said every shoot growing at the base of a tree is called ḥaẓwa, plural ḥaẓawāt. Aws said, in a line of verse:
He learned it in its thicket while it was a young shoot, in a valley with tall nab' trees [a bow-wood tree] and hithyal [another plant].
When a man is taunted with weakness it is said to him: "your arrows are only ḥiẓā'." Children's arrows too are called ḥiẓā'. From this comes the proverb: "one of Luqmān's little arrows." Abū 'Ubayd said: al-ḥuẓayyāt are the throwing-arrows that have no heads.
حف:
The letters ha' and fa' are three roots: the first a kind of sound, the second something surrounding a thing, the third hardship in living.

Explanation: the first, al-hafif, the rustle of trees and the like, and likewise the rustle of a bird's wing.

The second: their saying haffa al-qawm bi-fulan, when they surrounded him. God Almighty said: {and you see the angels surrounding the Throne on every side} [al-Zumar: 75]. From this too, hifafa of anything are its two sides. Tarafa said, in a line of verse: as though the two wings of a soaring hawk had folded around its two sides, stitched fast to the shaft with a needle.

From this section too: "he is on the hafaf of a matter," meaning on one side of it -- every side of a thing surrounds it. From this section too, their saying: "so-and-so yahuffuna wa yaruffuna," as though he takes us in and gives to us and provides for us.

The third: al-hufuf and al-hafaf, hardship and dryness of living. Abu Zayd said: haffat arduna wa qaffat, when its herbage dries up -- it is like al-shazaf. One says "they are in a hafaf of living," meaning hardship and dearth. This is then extended so that one says "so-and-so's head is mahfuf and haff," when it has gone long without oil; then one says haffat al-mar'a wajhaha min al-sha'r, when a woman removes the hair from around her face; and ihtafaftu al-nabt, when you clip the plant.
حفت: The letters ḥā', fā' and tā' are not a root, and there is little to say about it. Al-ḥafaytā' is the short man.
حفث:
The letters ḥā', fā' and thā' indicate something showing softness and pliancy. One says ḥafith al-karish [the stomach] for its faḥith [its lining, or the matter inside it]. Al-ḥuffāth is a snake that neither harms nor is feared. He said, in a line of verse:
Do they still boast, when they have seen their harmless snake bitten, and the fierce one has finished him off?
This line's exact sense is uncertain. It is said of a man growing angry: "his ḥuffāth has bristled up."
حفد:
The letters ḥā', fā', and dāl are a root indicating quickness in work, and gathering together.

1. al-ḥafada — helpers, because gathering together and quickness of movement combine in them; the singular is ḥāfid. Speed in obedience is ḥafd, and for this reason one says in the qunūt prayer: "To You we hasten and we speed." A poet said, in a line of verse:
O son of she who rode a swift, quick-paced camel.
Regarding His saying, Exalted is He: {and made for you, from your wives, sons and ḥafada} [al-Naḥl: 72] — it is said they are helpers, and this is the correct view; it is also said they are in-laws by marriage, and also that al-ḥafada are grandchildren, the children of one's children.
2. al-miḥfad — a measure by which things are measured out.
3. In the branch of speed and quickness one speaks of a sword that is muḥtafid, meaning quick to cut.
4. al-ḥafadān — quickening one's pace to catch up.
حفر:
The letters ḥā', fā' and rā' are two roots: one is digging a thing, which is uprooting it from below; the other is the beginning of a matter.

The first: ḥafartu al-arḍa ḥafran, I dug the ground. Ḥāfir al-faras is the horse's hoof, from this, as though it digs the ground with it. From this root also: al-ḥafr in the mouth, tooth decay. One says ḥufira fūhu yaḥfiru ḥafran, his teeth decayed.

Al-ḥafar is the earth taken out of a hole, like rubble; it is also said to be the name of the place that was dug. A line is quoted:
They said, we have arrived, and this is the dug-out trench.

One says aḥfara al-muhru li'l-ithnā' wa'l-irbāʿ, the colt reached the digging stage for its second or fourth set of teeth, when some of its teeth fall out to make room for new ones growing in.

It is said: there is no pregnant female but that pregnancy digs into her and wears her down, except the she-camel, who grows fat on it. The meaning of “digs into her” is that it makes her thin.

The second root is al-ḥāfira, in His words the Exalted: {are we indeed to be restored to our former state?} [al-Nāziʿāt: 10]. It is said this means the first, former state — that is, shall we live again after we have died? It is also said al-ḥāfira comes from their saying “so-and-so went back on his ḥāfira,” meaning he returned by the same road he had taken; and “the old man went back on his ḥāfira” when he grew decrepit and senile.

Their saying “cash at the hoof” means: the horse's hoof will not move from its spot until you pay me its price in cash. Because horses were held in such high regard among them, they were not sold on credit. This usage then became common, so that it came to be said of things other than horses as well.
حفز:
The letters ḥā', fā' and zā' are a single word, indicating urging on and what is close to it. Al-ḥafz is your urging a thing on from behind. A man yaḥtafizu in his sitting when he means to rise, as though an urger had urged him and a pusher had pushed him. One says: the night drives the day on and urges it forward. One says ḥafaztu al-rajul bi'l-rumḥ — I drove the spear into the man. Al-Ḥawfazān was named from this, rarely so formed. He said, in a line of verse:
And we drove al-Ḥawfazān back with a thrust that gave him to drink dark blood, streaked, from deep within.
حفس: The letters ḥā', fā' and sīn are not a root. A short man is called ḥayfas.
حفش:
The letters ḥā', fā' and shīn are a single root, indicating gathering. One says: they yaḥfishūn against you, meaning they muster against you. The flood ḥafash-ed the water from every side into a single pool. He said, in a line of verse:
On the evening we set out toward them, and they toward us, as the gathering floods filled the watercourse.
One says the horse came yaḥfishu, meaning it came with one burst of running after another. Al-ḥifsh is a small tent, named so because its sides are drawn together — or, it is said, because things are gathered and stored in it. Taḥaffashat al-mar'a li'l-rajul means she showed him affection, because she gathers herself for him.
حفص: The letters ḥā', fā' and ṣād are not a root, and there is no pattern in it to generalize from. A leather basket is called ḥafṣ. A hen is called Umm Ḥafṣa. It is said that the young of the lion is called ḥafṣ. There is question over all of this.
حفض:
The letters ḥā', fā' and ḍād are a single root, indicating the falling and the lightness of a thing. Al-ḥafaḍ is household baggage, and for this the camel that carries it is called ḥafaḍ. The pattern is as we said, since al-aḥfāḍ are called al-asqāṭ, the discarded things.

One says ḥafaḍtu al-'ūd, when you bent it. The rajaz-poet said:
If you see how time has bent me down, curved and low.
Al-Aṣma'ī said: ḥafaḍtu and ḥaffaḍtuhu, light and doubled, mean: you threw it down. And he recited:
If you see how time has bent me down, cast low.
Meaning: it cast me down. Al-aḥfāḍ, in 'Amr ibn Kulthūm's line of verse:
And we, when the tent-pole of the tribe falls upon the baggage, protect whoever is near us —
are the camels newly broken to riding. It is also said that al-aḥfāḍ are the tent-poles.
حفظ: The letters ḥā', fā' and ẓā' are a single root pointing to the watching over of a thing. One says ḥafiẓtu al-shay' ḥifẓan — I kept and guarded the thing. And anger is al-ḥafīẓa, and that is because that state calls a man to watch over a thing. Anger is called al-iḥfāẓ; one says aḥfaẓanī — he angered me. And al-taḥaffuẓ is little heedlessness, being on one's guard. And al-ḥifāẓ is the keeping watch over affairs.
حفل:
The letters ḥā', fā' and lām are a single root, and it is gathering. One says ḥafala al-nās wa-ḥtafalū, when people gathered in their assembly, and the assembly place is a maḥfil. Al-muḥaffala is a ewe that has been ḥuffilat — meaning her milk has been made to gather in her udder. Taṣriya and taḥfīl of this kind were forbidden. One says lā taḥfil bihi, meaning do not care about it; this too comes from the root, meaning: do not let your concern gather over it, since one whom a matter befalls gathers himself in concern for it.

As for their calling broken straw-chaff ḥufāla, this is not from the root — it belongs instead to the substitution of one letter for another, since the original is ḥuthāla, with the thā' changed to fā'.

From the root: a man dhū ḥafla, when he goes to great lengths in what he undertakes, gathering for it both his judgment and his action. Iḥtafala lahum means he managed their affair well. Iḥtafala al-wādī bi'l-sayl means the valley filled with the floodwater. Taḥaffala, meaning he adorned himself, is from this too, because he gathers together for himself all that is fine.

As for ḥafaltu al-shay', meaning you polished it, this too belongs to the root, and the pattern holds true, since polishing gathers a thing's brightness and light by clearing away its tarnish. Bishr said, in a line of verse:
He saw a white pearl, her color set off by soot-black hair, curled, like ravens among wild fruit.
Al-muqaṣṣab means curled. By the pearl he meant a woman. "Soot-black sets off her color" means the hair, whose blackness increases her whiteness, as though it had polished her — and this is very fine speech.
حفن:
The letters ḥā', fā' and nūn are a single word, generalizable, and it is the gathering of a thing in the palm or otherwise. Al-ḥafna is a fill of both palms of food. One says ḥafantu al-shay' ḥafnan, with my two hands.

From this comes the report of Abū Bakr: "We are only a handful among the handfuls of God, exalted." Its meaning is that God, exalted, when He wills, admits His creatures into Paradise, and that this is as easy for Him as a single handful. Iḥtafantu al-shay' li-nafsī means you took it for yourself.

It is also said that al-ḥufna is a pit. If this is sound, it admits of two possibilities: one, that it belongs to the substitution of letters, the nūn standing for a rā'; or that it belongs to the root already given, since a pit too gathers a thing, whether water or something else. Al-ḥaffān does not belong to this root — it was mentioned already elsewhere, its nūn being an added letter.
حفى:
The letters ḥā', fā' and the weak letter after them are three roots: prevention, thoroughness in asking, and al-ḥafā', the opposite of wearing footwear.

1. The first: ḥafawtu al-rajul min kulli shay' — you deprived him of everything.
2. The second root: ḥafītu ilayhi fi'l-waṣiyya — I went to great lengths in the bequest. Taḥaffaytu bihi and aḥfaytu mean: I went to great lengths in honoring him. Al-ḥafiyy is one who is thorough and persistent in asking. Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
If you ask about me — how many an asker, most earnest, has asked about al-A'shā, wherever he journeyed on.
Some said, and this too is from the root: ḥafītu bi-fulān and taḥaffaytu, meaning you took great care of him. Al-ḥafiyy also means one who is well informed about a thing.
3. The third root: al-ḥafā, short vowel, is the verbal noun of al-ḥāfī. One says ḥafiya al-faras — its hoof was worn. Aḥfā al-rajul — his mount became footsore. Al-Kisā'ī said: ḥāfin bayyinu l-ḥifya wa'l-ḥifāya. One says ḥafiya yaḥfā of one who has neither leather sock nor sandal on his feet. As for one made footsore by much walking, he is ḥafin bayyinu l-ḥafā', short vowel.

As for the hamzated form, al-ḥafa', short, is the root of the white, moist reed that is eaten. On this his saying, peace and blessings upon him and his family, was explained: "as long as you do not pull it up by the root, it is yours to deal with." One says iḥtafa'tuhu, when you pulled it up by the root.
حق:
The letters ha' and qaf are a single root indicating the soundness and correctness of a thing. Al-haqq is the opposite of falsehood; every branch of it then returns to this by good derivation and skilled fitting-together. One says haqqa al-shay' -- the thing became due. Al-Kisa'i said: the Arabs say "you well know the due that is upon you, yet excuse yourself with what you have." And they say: "when he recognized the due from me, he gave way."

One says haqqa fulanun fulanan, when each of two men lays claim to the same thing; when one overcomes the other in the right, one says haqqahu and ahaqqahu. Ihtaqqa al-nas min al-dayn, when each claims the right for himself.

In the hadith of 'Ali, peace upon him: "When women reach the nass al-hiqaq, the father's kin has the better right to arrange marriage." Abu 'Ubayd said: he means reaching maturity and the attainment of reason. Al-hiqaq is when this one says "I have the better claim" and those others say "we have the better claim" -- haqaqtuhu hiqaqan. Whoever transmits it as "nass al-haqa'iq" means the plural of al-haqiqa.

One says of a man who disputes over small things: "he is nazaq al-hiqaq." One says ta'na muhtaqqa, when a spear-thrust reaches the belly-cavity by its force; it is also said to be the thrust made at haqq al-warik, the hip-socket. Al-Hudhali said, in a line of verse: and indeed, when the spear-points were bared toward her, some thrusts went deep, some only grazed. Some said: al-muhtaqq is the one who is killed on the spot. One says thawb muhaqqaq, when it is tightly, firmly woven. He said, in a line of verse: put on the skin of your father's face -- we have spared you the tightly-woven, thin garments.

Al-hiqqa, among the young of camels, is the one that has become fit to be ridden or loaded; plural al-hiqaq. Al-A'sha said, in a line of verse: and they, whatever they are, when the wine grows dear and their wineskins and their measures worth a hiqq are set up -- he means: a skin of it is sold for the price of a hiqqa camel.

Fulan hami al-haqiqa, when he defends what it is due for him to defend; al-haqiqa is also said to be the banner. Al-Hudhali said, in a line of verse: protector of what is due, swift to reach the place of thirst, eager for the burden of vengeance -- no coward, no laggard.

Al-ahaqq, among horses, is the one that does not sweat; this belongs to the root, because that comes from its hardness, strength and soundness. A man of the Ansar said, in a line of verse: and a sturdy one, high at the withers, bounding, bay-coloured, neither ahaqq nor shai't. Its verbal noun is al-haqaq. Some said: al-aqdar is the horse whose hind hooves' fall outpaces the fall of its forefeet.

Al-ahaqq is when this hind footfall exactly matches the forefoot's print. And al-shai't is when the fall of the hind hoof falls short of the fall of the fore hoof.

Al-haqqa is the Resurrection, because it makes every matter certain -- God Almighty said: {but the sentence of punishment was realized against the disbelievers} [al-Zumar: 71]. Al-haqhaqa is the harshest and most exhausting pace for the mount's back. In the hadith of Mutarrif ibn 'Abd Allah to his son: "the best of affairs are their middle course, and the worst pace is al-haqhaqa."

Al-huqq is the meeting-point of any two bones except the back; and this only happens where it is hard and strong. From this too, al-huqq of wood, as though it were the meeting and fitting-point of a thing; it is feminine, plural huqaq. It occurs in the poetry of Ru'ba: "the exact fitting of the huqaq."

One says fulan haqiq bi-kadha and mahquq bihi. Al-A'sha said, in a line of verse: she indeed deserves to answer his call, and to know that whoever is helped by God is granted success.

Some scholars said, on God Almighty's saying, in the story of Moses, peace upon him: {bound to speak} [al-A'raf: 105]: he said it means "incumbent upon me." Whoever reads it haqiqun 'ala, its meaning is "eager for."

Al-Kisa'i said: huqqa laka an taf'ala hadha -- it is fitting for you to do this -- and huqiqta. One says haqqan la af'alu dhalika, in an oath. Abu 'Ubayda said: they also insert the lam, saying la-haqqun la af'alu dhaka, giving it the nominative without nunation. One says haqaqtu al-amr and ahqaqtuhu, meaning I was certain of it.

Al-Kisa'i said: haqaqtu hadhar al-rajul and ahqaqtuhu -- I did what he had been warned against. One says ahaqqati al-naqa min al-rabi' -- the she-camel grew fat from the spring pasture.

A man said to a man of Tamim: "What is a hiqqa that has become hiqqa alongside three hiqaq?" He said: it is a young she-camel with two others alongside her, in the same spring -- she grew fat before they did, then came into heat before they did, then conceived before they did.

Abu 'Amr said: istahaqqa laqahuha, when her conception became due. Ahaqqat -- she entered her third year. And she has reached her hiqqa when she becomes a hiqqa camel. Al-A'sha said, in a line of verse: tied up in her hiqqa-year in the palm-fibre rope, until her back teeth grew old with use. One says asanna al-sinn: the tooth grew in.
حقب:
The letters ḥā', qāf and bā' are a single root, indicating holding back/withholding.

One says ḥaqiba al-ʿāmu, the year was ḥaqib, when its rain was withheld; and ḥaqiba al-baʿīru, the camel was ḥaqib, when its urine was retained.

From this root: al-ḥaqab, a rope with which the saddle is tied to the camel's belly, so that the girth-strap will not pull it forward.

As for al-aḥqab, the wild donkey, there is disagreement over the meaning: some said it is named so for the whiteness of its flanks, others for the thinness of its flanks. The female is ḥaqbā'. If this belongs to the root, it is because that is the place [the flank] tied with a ḥiqāb, a rope. A line is quoted:
As though she were a ḥaqbā', pale-flanked, piebald at the rump.

From this root: al-ḥaqība, the saddlebag, well known. From this too: iḥtaqaba fulānun al-ithma, so-and-so “packed up” sin, as though he gathered it into a saddlebag. Iḥtaqabahu min khalfihi, he carried him behind him as a rider; al-muḥqab is the one carried as a passenger behind.

As for time: a period is ḥiqba, plural ḥiqab. Al-ḥuqb is eighty years, plural aḥqāb, named for the years and months gathered together within it. It is also said al-ḥiqāb is a mountain. A tall hill rising into the sky is called ḥaqbā'. A line is quoted:
The ḥiqāb held her fast, together with her body. [The exact sense of this line is unclear to me.]
حقد:
The letters ḥāʾ, qāf, and dāl are two roots: one is malice, and the other is not finding what one seeks.

The first is al-ḥiqd, whose plural is al-aḥqād. The second is their saying aḥqada al-qawmu, when they sought gold-ore in the mine and did not find it.
حقر: The letters ḥāʾ, qāf, and rāʾ are a single root, deeming a thing small. One says shayʾun ḥaqīr, meaning a small thing, and anā aḥtaqiruhu, meaning I deem it small. As for their calling the name of the sky Ḥāqūra, I do not think that correct; and if it is correct, then perhaps it is a name taken as such, without derivation.
حقط: The letters ḥāʾ, qāf, and ṭāʾ are not a root, and I do not think al-ḥayquṭān — the male of the durrāj [francolin] — is correct either.
حقف:
The letters ḥā', qāf, and fā' are a single root indicating a thing's leaning and its curve. One says iḥqawqafa al-shayʾu, the thing curved, so it is muḥqawqif or ḥāqif. From this is the hadith: "He passed by a gazelle lying curled up (ḥāqif) in the shade of a tree," meaning one that had bent and curled itself up in its sleep.

For this reason curving sand is called ḥiqf, plural aḥqāf. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And when we crossed the open ground of the encampment, and the hollow of Khabt turned us toward it — a place of piled, curving dunes.
It is also transmitted as "of rugged hills." Another poet said, in a line of verse:
Like the crescent moon's arc, curving until it bent.
حقل:
The letters ḥā', qāf and lām are a single root, and it is the land, and what is close to it. Al-ḥaql is the good cultivated plot. It is said: "only the fertile plot grows the herb." Ḥaqīl is a place. He said, in a line of verse:
From Dhū l-Abāriq, when they grazed at Ḥaqīl.
Al-muḥāqala, which was forbidden, is selling standing grain in the ear for wheat or barley.

From this root: their saying ḥaqila al-faras, according to some, when a pain struck its belly from eating soil; the root sense there is the earth.

One says ḥawqala l-shaykh, when the old man leaned with his hands on his waist as he walked; that gait is al-ḥawqala, apparently taken from his closeness to the ground. As for their calling a small glass bottle ḥawqala, its origin is al-ḥawjala, with the jīm perhaps changed to qāf.
حقم: The letters ḥā', qāf and mīm are neither a root nor a branch. They say al-ḥaqm is a bird.
حقن: The letters ḥā', qāf and nūn are a single root, and it is the gathering of a thing. Anything that is gathered and bound together is said to be ḥuqin, and for this the one who withholds milk is called ḥāqin. One speaks of al-laban al-ḥaqīn: milk whose fresh milk has been poured onto its curdled milk. Al-ḥawāqin are what lies below the belly. Some said: al-ḥāqinatān are what lies beneath the two collarbones.
حقو:
The letters ḥāʾ, qāf, and the weak letter are a single root, and it is one of the parts of the body.

Al-ḥiqw is the waist, and the place where the waist-wrap is tied. For that reason the thin part of an arrow next to the feathers is also called ḥaqwan. As for the hadith "that the Messenger of God, God bless him and his family and grant him peace, gave the women who washed his daughter a ḥaqwa" — it is explained in the commentary as meaning the waist-wrap (izār), whose plural is ḥiqiyy. This too is called ḥiqw only because one ties the waist (al-ḥiqw) with it. As for al-ḥaqwa, it is a pain that afflicts a person in his belly; one says of it ḥuqiya al-rajulu, so he is maḥquww.
حك:
The letters ha' and kaf are a single root: two things meeting so that each rubs against the other. Al-hakk is your rubbing one thing against another. One says "no hakka remains in his mouth," meaning no tooth. Ahakkani ra'si fa-hakaktuhu -- my head itched so I scratched it. One says "such-and-such hakka in my breast," when your heart is not at ease over it, as though a thing had pierced your breast and rubbed there.

Al-hukaka is what falls off from two things when you rub them together. Al-hakik is a hoof worn thin. They say -- and this is the root's core sense -- "so-and-so yatahakkaku bi," meaning he rubs, provokes trouble, against me. Al-Farra' said: he is truly a rubber of trouble, a rubber of malice.
حكد: The letters ḥāʾ, kāf, and dāl are a letter of the chapter of substitution [where one sound stands in for another]. Al-maḥtid [origin, lineage] is called al-maḥkid. This has already been explained in its own chapter.
حكر: The letters ḥāʾ, kāf, and rāʾ are a single root, and it is withholding. Al-ḥukra is withholding food, waiting for it to become dear — that is al-ḥukr. Its origin in the speech of the Arabs is al-ḥakar, which is standing, gathered water, as though it were hoarded (uḥtukira) because of its scarcity.
حكل:
The letters ḥāʾ, kāf, and lām are a sound root, applied by analogy, and it is a thing that is not clear.

It is said that al-ḥukl is a thing among animals that has no speech, such as ants and the like. A poet said, in a line of verse:

If I had been given the knowledge of al-ḥukl
the knowledge of Solomon, the speech of ants.

One also says fī lisānihi ḥuklah, meaning a foreign accent in his speech. And one says aḥkala ʿalayya al-amr, when a matter becomes obstructed and obscure.

Falling outside this chapter is their calling a short man ḥankal.
حكم:
The letters ḥā', kāf and mīm are a single root, and it is preventing. The first of that is al-ḥukm, judgement, which is preventing wrongdoing. The ḥakama of a riding beast, the curb at its jaw, was so called because it holds the beast back; one says ḥakamtu al-dābba and aḥkamtuhā. And one says: ḥakamtu al-safīh and aḥkamtuhu, when you take hold of the fool's hands and restrain him. Jarīr said, in a line of verse:
O sons of Ḥanīfa, restrain your fools; I fear for you that I may grow angry.

Al-ḥikma, wisdom, follows this same analogy, because it prevents ignorance. And you say: ḥakkamtu fulānan taḥkīman - I held him back from what he wants. And ḥukkima fulānun fī kadhā, when the matter is put into his hands. Al-muḥakkam is the tried and tested man ascribed to wisdom. Ṭarafa said, in a line of verse:
Would that the wise old man and the one who is preached to had their two voices under the earth, when falsehood is uncovered.

By al-muḥakkam he meant the old man ascribed to wisdom. And in the hadith: 'Paradise belongs to the muḥakkamūn - and they are a people who were given the choice between being killed and holding fast to Islam, and unbelief, and they chose to hold fast to Islam along with being killed, and so they were called al-muḥakkimīn.'
حكى:
The letters ḥāʾ, kāf, and what follows them, a weak letter, are a single root, and in it is a kind of hamzated word close in meaning to the weak one — it is making a thing firm, by a knot or by settling it.

One says ḥakaytu al-shayʾa aḥkīhi, and that is doing as the first one did. In the hamzated form one says aḥkaʾtu al-ʿuqdata, when you made the knot firm. And one says aḥkaʾtu ẓahrī bi-izārī, when you tied it firmly. ʿAdiyy said:

Yes, God has favored you
above whoever tied a back firmly with a waist-wrap.

And another said:

He tied my rope firmly to his rope in my two hands
and he tied firmly, in my sandal, its strap, for a foot.
حل:
The letters ha' and lam have many branches and questions, but their whole origin, in my view, is the opening of a thing -- nothing departs from it.

One says halaltu al-'uqda ahulluha hallan -- I undid the knot. The Arabs say: "O one who ties, remember also to undo." Al-halal, opposite of al-haram, belongs to the root mentioned, as though from halaltu al-shay', when you make it permitted and open it wide for some purpose.

Halla means: he alighted, settled. This belongs to this root because the traveler binds and ties his load, and when he alights he undoes it; one says halaltu bil-qawm. Halil of a woman is her husband; halila of a man is his wife -- they were so named because each of them alights beside the other.

Abu 'Ubayd said: whoever camps beside you and is your neighbour is your halil. He said, in a line of verse: and I am not one of two shabby garments who lulls his neighbour-wife to sleep when the sleepers are quiet -- he means his neighbour.

It is also said the wife is called halila because each of the two undoes the waist-wrap of the other. Al-hulla is well known, and it is never less than two garments. It is also possible to carry this on the root, saying: since they are two, there was a gap between them.

From this root too: al-ihlil, the outlet of urine, and the outlet of milk from the udder. From this root too: tahalhala 'an makanihi, when he moved away from his place. He said, in a line of verse: Thahlan of the peaks does not budge.

Al-hulahil is the chief, the leader, and this belongs to the root -- not closed off and forbidding like the miser, firm and dry. Al-hilla is the settled encampment of the Arabs. Al-A'sha said, in a line of verse: there was indeed, in Shayban, had I but known, tents, and a settled clan, and tribes.

Al-mahalla is the place where a people settle. A settled clan is hayyun hilal. Halla al-dayn -- the debt fell due. Al-hill is what lies beyond the sacred precinct of Mecca. A man muhill is one out of the state of ihram, and muhrim is one in it. Hill and halal mean the same, and correspondingly hirm and haram. In the hadith: "The Messenger of God, peace and blessings upon him and his family, married Maymuna while both were in the muhill state, not in pilgrim consecration."

A man muhill has no covenant, and muhrim has one. He said, in a line of verse: they set al-Qanan on their right, and its rugged tract, and how many at al-Qanan, some out of covenant, some bound by one. Some said: muhill means one who considers my blood lawful to shed, and muhrim means one who considers it forbidden.

Al-hullan is the kid that is cut from its mother's belly at birth. He said, in a line of verse: he presents to him the foreleg of the young goat as an honour, whether it was slaughtered or was a hullan.

This too belongs to the root. Hallaltu al-yamin uhallilha tahlilan -- I released the oath from its binding force. Fa'altu hadha tahillata al-qasam, meaning I did only as much as would release my oath, without going further. From it: "No believer loses three children and is touched by the Fire, except for the brief span that fulfills the oath" -- meaning: by only so much as God's Almighty oath is fulfilled, from His saying {and there is not one of you but shall come to it} [Maryam: 71], that is, he will not come to it except by the measure that releases the oath.

This usage then grew common until it was said of anything not done to the full: tahlil. One says darabtuhu tahlilan, and "this she-camel's footfalls came down tahlilan," when she did not press hard on the ground. It occurs in the words of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr: their footfall on the ground is light.

As for Imru' al-Qays's saying: like the first-borne of a mixed white streaked with yellow, nourished by clear running water, unspoiled -- there are two views on it: one, that he meant something slight, related to the taste we mentioned; the other, that it means un-grazed-over, so that it does not spoil or grow turbid.

One says ahallati al-shat, when milk descends into a ewe's udder without her having given birth. Al-hilal is the gear, the furnishings, of a camel-saddle. Al-A'sha said, in a line of verse: as though she had not met six months of hardship, when she set down her gear beside you.

Al-Qasim ibn Ma'n transmitted it this way; others transmit it with a jim instead. Al-hilal is also a kind of women's riding-seat. He said, in a line of verse: a camel with its riding-seat, left behind, its load scattered.

I found in some books, from Sibawayh: huwa hillata al-ghawr, meaning its intended direction. And he cited: he journeyed by night after the stars had set, and after the Pleiades seemed, in the direction of the low ground, like a sieve -- meaning: its intended direction.
حلب:
The letters ḥāʾ, lām, and bāʾ are a single root, and it is drawing a thing out.

1. *al-ḥalab* — the milking of sheep and goats; it serves both as a noun and as a verbal noun.
2. *al-miḥlab* — the vessel that is milked into.
3. *al-iḥlāba* — that you milk for your family while you are out at pasture, and send the milk to them. One says aḥlabahum iḥlāban [he sent them milk].
4. *nāqa ḥalūb* — a she-camel giving milk; when this is made into a noun one says "this is al-ḥalūba belonging to so-and-so."
5. *nāqa ḥalbāna* — like al-ḥalūb.

One says aḥlabtuka: I helped you milk the she-camel. Aḥlaba al-rajul, when his camels gave birth to females, and ajlaba, when they gave birth to males — because their young would then be driven off (tujlab) and sold.

From this chapter, and derived from it, is al-muḥlib, the helper. [A poet] said:

He signaled to them with al-Aṣamm's flash, and they came forward,
proud-nosed men — no helper comes to him for aid.

That is when a helper comes to you from outside your own people; it belongs to this chapter because, as I have mentioned, it is from support and seeking support.

Al-ḥalba is horses gathered for a race from every direction, just as one says of a people who come from every direction to give aid: "they have gathered (aḥlabū)."
حلت: The letters ḥāʾ, lām, and tāʾ are not, in my view, a sound root. A few words have come from it: al-ḥiltīt is a resin. One says ḥalata daynahu: he paid off his debt; ḥalata fulānan, when he gave him something; and ḥalata al-ṣūf: he stripped the wool.
حلج: The letters ḥāʾ, lām, and jīm are not, in my view, a root. One says ḥalaja al-quṭn: he ginned the cotton. And ḥalaja al-khubza: he rounded the loaf of bread. And ḥalaja al-qawmu yaḥlijūna laylatahum, when they traveled through their night. All of this needs further examination.
حلز: The letters ḥāʾ, lām, and zāʾ are a sound root. One calls a short man ḥillizz; it is also said he is the bad-tempered one. One says al-ḥalz is peeling; ḥalaztu al-adīm, I peeled the hide. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: from this comes [the name of the poet] al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥillizah.
حلس:
The letters ḥāʾ, lām, and sīn are a single root, and it is a thing that clings to a thing.

Al-ḥils is the ḥils of the camel, which is what lies beneath the pack-saddle's padding. Aḥlastu fulānan yamīnan, that is when you make him swear it again and again, binding it firmly on him; it is also said, meaning the same, "rather I made it binding on him." Istaḥlasa al-nabt, when the plant growth covers the ground, that being as though it forms a ḥils for it — we have already explained this. Banū fulān are aḥlās al-khayl, meaning those who keep horses and stay constantly on their backs; that is why people say "lasta min aḥlāsihā" [you are not one of its regulars]. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muslim said: its origin is from al-ḥils. He said: al-ḥils is also a rug spread out in the house. They say "kun ḥilsa baytika," meaning stay in it the way a rug stays in place. Al-ḥals is the brave man, and the greedy man — because out of his eagerness he clings to what is eaten.
حلط:
The letters ḥāʾ, lām, and ṭāʾ are a single root: striving hard at a thing, with an oath or with distress. One says aḥlaṭa, when he strove hard and swore. Ibn Aḥmar said:

So we and they were like the two sons of Subāt, who parted,
separate, then one went to Najd and the other to Tihāma.
The man of Tihāma then cast down his stakes,
while this one swore firmly: I will not budge from my place —

and: "I will not go back the way I came."

From this chapter comes their saying: "The first sign of helplessness is confusion, and the worst speech is excess." Al-ikhtilāṭ here means anger.
حلف:
The letters ḥā', lām and fā' are a single root, and it is keeping close company. One says ḥālafa fulānun fulānan when he keeps close to him.

From this chapter is al-ḥalif, the oath; one says ḥalafa yaḥlifu ḥalifan. That is because a man is bound to hold firm to it. Its verbal noun is al-ḥalif, and al-maḥlūf as well. One says this thing is muḥlif when it is doubtful, so that people swear opposing oaths about it. A poet said, in a line of verse:
A bay mare that leaves no room for men to swear against each other, but like the colour of undiluted wine with which the hide has been steeped.

Among what strays from this chapter is their saying he is ḥalīf al-lisān when he is sharp of tongue. And of the anomalous is al-ḥulafā', a plant; the single one is a ḥalfā'a.
حلق:
The letters ḥā', lām and qāf are three roots: the first is the removal of hair from the head, then other senses are carried over from it. The second indicates a rounded tool or instrument. The third indicates height.

The first: ḥalaqtu ra'sī aḥliquhu ḥalqan, I shaved my head. Rough cloaks that wear away hair by their roughness are called maḥāliq. He cited a line I cannot render with confidence. And they say "iḥtalaqat al-sana al-māl," when a year [of drought] stripped away the livestock entirely. Carried over from this also: "ḥaliqa qaḍību al-ḥimār," when a donkey's member reddened and its skin peeled; it is said it was called ḥaliqa for its peeling, not its reddening.

The second root: al-ḥalqa, an iron ring. All weaponry/armour together is also called al-ḥalaqa. Al-ḥilq: a ring of authority [a signet], because it is round. Camels that are muḥallaqa are branded with the ḥalaq, a ring-shaped mark. He cited a line about a ring-branded animal whose ownership the witness-marks (al-'awādhīr) settle between claimants.

The third root: al-ḥāliq is a high, overlooking place. One says "ḥallaqa," when he went up onto a ḥāliq. Al-Hudhalī said: "had my mother not borne me, the far-flying [bird/fate] would have carried me off, among the clan of Kalb" — his mother was of Kalb, and a man of Kalb had captured him meaning to kill him, but when he named his lineage, the man spared him; he means: had my mother not been of Kalb, I would have perished. One says "ḥallaqat bihi al-mughrib," as one says "shālat na'āmatuhu" [idioms for ruin/death]. Al-Nābigha said: "when he goes to war with the army, flocks of birds fly high above him, guided by other flocks" — because vultures, eagles, and carrion-birds follow armies awaiting the slain, to descend on them. Then he said: "wings certain that their [prey's] people, when the two hosts meet, will be first to be defeated."
حلك: The letters ḥāʾ, lām, and kāf are a word indicating blackness. One says "huwa ashaddu sawādan min ḥalaki al-ghurāb" [he is blacker than the blackness of the crow] — meaning its blackness. And one says "huwa aswadu ḥulkūk" [he is intensely black].
حلم:
The letters ḥā', lām and mīm are three roots: the first is leaving off haste, the second the boring through of a thing, and the third the seeing of a thing in sleep. They are very far apart from one another, and they show that some of the language is not by rule, even though most of it does run by rule.

The first: al-ḥilm is the opposite of rashness. One says ḥalumtu ʿanhu aḥlumu, so I am ḥalīm, forbearing.

The second root: their saying ḥalima al-adīmu when the hide is bored through and spoiled; and that is when little creatures get into it and ruin it.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
You, with your letter to ʿAlī, are like a woman tanning a hide when the hide is already riddled through.

And the third: he has ḥalama in his sleep, ḥulman and ḥuluman — he dreamt. And al-ḥalam are small ticks. And al-ḥalama is a little creature.

Carried over onto this are the ḥalamatān of the breast, the two nipples. As for their saying taḥallama when he grew fat, it is only that he filled out, as though he were a swollen tick.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Up to a year in which its ticks had not grown fat.

And one says a camel is ḥalīm, that is, fat.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Of the fat in the backs of every well-fleshed one.

And al-ḥālūm is something like dried curd. And I do not think it is sound Arabic.
حلن: The letters ḥāʾ, lām, and nūn — if you take the nūn as extra, then we have already mentioned this word before. And if you take the nūn as original, then it is on the pattern fuʿʿāl, and it is the young goat, and the word is not a root that can be measured by analogy. This has already passed in its own chapter.
حلو:
The letters ḥāʾ, lām, and what follows them, a weak letter, are three roots: the first is the pleasantness of a thing together with the soul's inclination toward it; the second is adorning a thing; and the third — which is hamzated — is driving a thing away.

The first is al-ḥulw, the opposite of bitter. One says istaḥlaytu al-shayʾ [I found the thing sweet], and ḥalā fī fammī yaḥlū [it grew sweet in my mouth]. Al-ḥalwāʾ, what is eaten, is said both with and without the long vowel at the end. One says ḥaliya bi-ʿaynī yaḥlā [it was pleasing to my eye]. Taḥālat al-marʾa, when a woman displayed sweetness, as one says tabākā [feigned weeping] and taʿālā [made himself out as high] — that is, showing openly something whose like is not normally hidden. Abū Dhuʾayb said:

So take her in charge; I am trustworthy, and truly
when the like of her feigns sweetness, I do not go near her.

From this chapter comes ḥalawtu al-rajula ḥulwānan, when you gave him something — "and the Messenger of God, God bless him and his family and grant him peace, forbade the ḥulwān of the soothsayer" — that is, what is given to him for his soothsaying. Aws said:

As if I had sweetened the poetry, the day I praised him,
like the sheen of a bare, hard rock, its moisture spent.

Al-ḥulwān is also a man taking something from his daughter's bridal dower for himself, and that is a disgrace among the Arabs. A woman said, praising her husband:

He does not take the ḥulwān from my daughters.

The second root: al-ḥuliyy, a woman's jewelry, is the plural of ḥaly, as one says thady/thudiyy [breast/breasts] and ẓaby/ẓubiyy [gazelle/gazelles]. Ḥallaytu al-marʾa [I adorned the woman]. And this is ḥilyat al-shayʾ, meaning its description. One says ḥilyat al-sayf [the fittings of the sword], and one does not say ḥuliyy al-sayf.

The third root is driving a thing away. One says ḥallaʾtu al-ibila ʿan al-māʾ, when you drove the camels away from the water. [A poet] said:

Driven off from the way to the water, chased away.

And what is peeled from a hide is called al-ḥulāʾa, on the pattern fuʿāla; one says from it ḥalaʾtu al-adīma, I peeled the hide. And al-ḥalūʾ, on the pattern faʿūl, is that you rub a stone against a stone, and one with sore eyes uses their scrapings as kohl; one says from it aḥlaʾtu al-rajul. And one says ḥalaʾat al-arḍ, when you struck the ground.

Falling outside this chapter: ḥalaʾahu miʾata dirham, when he paid him a hundred dirhams in cash; and ḥalaʾahu miʾata sawṭ, he struck him a hundred lashes.
حم:
The letters ha' and mim show great variation, because its chapters branch out considerably. One of its roots is blackness, another is heat, a third is nearness and presence, a fourth is a kind of sound, and a fifth is intention.

As for blackness: al-humam is charcoal. Tarafa said, in a line of verse: did the abandoned campsite grieve you, or its age, or ashes, worn away, its charcoal cold? From it too is al-yahmum, smoke. Al-himhim is a black plant, and everything black is himhim. One says hammamtuhu, when you blacken his face with soot, which is al-sukham. From this section too: hammama al-farkh, when a chick's feathers first appear. He said, in a line of verse: a chick fledged, like curled tufts.

As for heat: al-hamim is hot water; al-istihmam is washing with it. From it too is al-hamm, the fat of the tail-fat rendered down -- what remains after the rendering is hamm, singular hamma. From it too is al-hamim, sweat. Abu Dhu'ayb said, in a line of verse: she withholds her milk when provoked to anger -- all but the sweat, for that oozes out.

From it too is al-humam, fever in camels. One says ahammati al-ard, when it becomes fever-ridden. Al-Khalil cited, concerning al-hamm, in a line of verse: press its two sides together, pressing them as an old woman presses the fat into a vessel, full.

As for nearness and presence, they say ahammat al-haja, meaning the need became pressing; ahamma al-amr, the matter drew near. He cited: greet that gazelle, so fully grown -- if that is the parting, it has now truly drawn near.

As for the sound: al-hamhama is the neighing-murmur of a horse at feeding-time.

As for intention: their saying hamamtu hammahu, meaning I aimed at his aim. Tarafa said, in a line of verse: I made it the aim of her chest, in the evening, a steady rain that soaks it through.

Anomalous to these sections is their saying: the man divorced his wife and hammamaha, when he gave her a garment or the like as a parting gift. He said, in a line of verse: you are the one who granted Zayd, after I had resolved to give the old woman only a parting gift.

As for their saying ihtamma al-rajul, its first letter (the deeper ha' sound, ha') here stands in place of a different, softer h-sound letter -- it is really from ihtamma, he was distressed, concerned.
حمد:
The letters ḥā', mīm and dāl are one word and one root, pointing to the opposite of blame. One says ḥamidtu fulānan aḥmaduhu. And a man is maḥmūd and muḥammad when his praiseworthy qualities, not his blameworthy ones, are many. Al-A'shā said, praising al-Nuʿmān ibn al-Mundhir — and it is said that he set him above all who praised him that day with this word of his — in a line of verse:
To you, may you be spared cursing, was her weariness: to the glorious one of noble stock, the generous, the much-praised.
And for this that we have mentioned our Prophet, may God bless him and his family and give them peace, was named Muhammad. And the Arabs say ḥumādāka an tafʿala kadhā — that is, your utmost, and the praiseworthy, not the blameworthy, deed from you. And one says aḥmadtu fulānan, when you find him praiseworthy, as one says abkhaltuhu when you find him miserly, and aʿjaztuhu [when you find him] incapable. And this is a reasoning that runs steadily through all the qualities. And ahyajtu al-makān, when you find it dried up, its plants withered. He said, in a line of verse:
And he found al-Khalṣā' dried up, from Dhāt al-Buraq.
And if someone asks about their saying al-ḥamda for the sound of fire flaring up, he is answered: this is not of the chapter, because it is of the transposed words, and its origin is ḥadama. And that has been mentioned in its own place.
حمر:
The letters ḥāʾ, mīm and rāʾ are, in my view, one root: what is known by redness. It may also be made two roots, the other being a kind of animal.
The first: redness in colours, well known. The Arabs say 'beauty is red,' because souls scarcely dislike the colour red. You say rajulun aḥmar, and aḥāmir [as a plural]; if colour is meant you say aḥmar. The evidence for al-aḥāmira is Al-Aʿshā's line of verse:

Indeed the three red things have destroyed ... my wealth, and I was long devoted to them

he treated al-aḥāmira as specific nouns, not adjectives — had he meant adjectives he would have said ḥumr. Al-ḥamrāʾ means the non-Arabs, so named because fair colouring predominates among them; from this comes their saying to ʿAlī, God be pleased with him: 'this ḥamrāʾ has overpowered you in our favour' (the exact force of this saying is not fully certain to me). It is said mawtun aḥmar, a violent death, said when death is described as harsh. ʿAlī said: 'Whenever the fighting grew fierce, we would shield ourselves behind the Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, and none of us was ever nearer to the enemy than he.'
From this chapter too: their saying waṭʾatun ḥamrāʾ, said of a fresh footprint, and waṭʾatun dahmāʾ, an old, faded one. A harsh year is sanatun ḥamrāʾ; for this the fierce heat of midsummer is called ḥamārra. This is said because redness is the colour they find most wondrous, so when they wish to describe a thing intensely they describe it with redness or a word resembling it.
As for calling an unarmed man aḥmar, it is possible this is a comparison to the non-Arabs, not noted for courage as the Arabs were. A poet said:

and the spears will make trial of the ruddy, cowardly ḍayāṭira

Al-ḍayāṭira is the plural of ḍayṭār, the huge-bodied coward who cannot properly bear arms. A poet said:

The ḍayāṭirūn of Fuʿāla stood forth against us ... yet what good is a ḍayṭār turning over a flat stone

And their saying ghaythun ḥimirr, a violent downpour that strips the earth's surface, belongs to the same intensifying pattern.
As for the second root: al-ḥimār, well known [the donkey]. One says ḥimār, ḥamīr, ḥumur, and ḥumurāt, as one says ṣaʿīd, ṣuʿud, and ṣuʿudāt. A poet said, in a line of verse:

When the finch sings in other than a meadow ... woe to the people of sheep and donkeys

meaning: when the season is a drought with no meadow, and the finch sings elsewhere, then woe to those who own sheep and donkeys, for there is no pasture.
Carried under this chapter too is their name for a small creature: ḥimār qabbān, the woodlouse. A poet said:

O wonder — indeed I have seen a wonder ... a woodlouse driving along a hare

From this too: al-ḥimār, something placed around a water-trough so its water does not spill, plural ḥamāʾir. A poet said (this couplet's precise images are not fully certain to me):

And a bogging place between wasteland and a deathly spot ... I crossed it with a mighty, towering frame

as though the trailing edges high on its trough-rims ... were the hems of fine cloth, of silk and linen

As for calling a half-bred horse miḥmar, this too belongs to the chapter. From this chapter too: al-ḥimārān, two stones on which curd-cheese is dried, called together with the stone above them al-ʿulāh. A poet said:

The shepherd's sheep avail him nothing there ... nor his two stones, nor his ʿulāh

Al-ḥammāra: stones set up around a house, plural ḥamāʾir. A poet said (obscure to me in its precise sense):

a house of deaths, whose stone-circles were piled high

As for their saying 'emptier than the inside of a donkey,' its story has been told in the chapter of the letter ʿayn.
حمز:
The letters ḥāʾ, mīm, and zāʾ are a single root, and it is sharpness in a thing, like pungency and the like. Al-ḥamza is a pungency in a thing. One says sharābun yaḥmizu al-lisān [a drink that stings the tongue]. From it comes al-ḥamza, an edible plant that stings the tongue — "Anas ibn Mālik said: 'The Messenger of God, God bless him and his family and grant him peace, nicknamed me after a plant I had picked'" — and he was known by the kunya Abū Ḥamza. Al-Shammākh said, describing a man who sold [a bow] and grieved over it:

When he sold it, his eye overflowed with tears,
and in his heart a stinging ache from reproach.

As for their calling a sharp-hearted, quick-witted man ḥamīz — he is ḥamīzu al-fuʾād — that belongs to this chapter too, because that comes from keenness and sharpness, and the sense in it is the same throughout.
حمس:
The letters ḥāʾ, mīm, and sīn are a single root indicating severity.

1. *al-aḥmas* — the brave man.
2. *al-ḥamas* and *al-ḥamāsa* — bravery and severity.
3. *rajulun ḥamis* — a man of this kind. [A poet] said: "And the like of me was thrust in among the resolute, staunch leader." One also says "bi-l-ḥamis al-baʾīs" [the resolute, harsh one].
4. *taḥammasa al-rajul* — he became stubborn, unyielding.
5. *al-ḥums* — Quraysh, because they were strict in their religion, that is, they held firm. Some said: al-ḥumsa is sanctity, and they were called ḥums only because they resided within the sacred precinct.
6. *ʿāmun aḥmas* — a hard year.
7. *arḍūn aḥāmis* — harsh lands.

Some people claimed that al-ḥamīs is the oven; others said it is spelled with the [dotted] shīn instead. Whichever it is, it is sound: if it is with sīn, it belongs to what we have mentioned, from the intensity of its fire's blaze; and if it is with shīn, it is from aḥmashtu al-nār wa-l-ḥarb [I stoked the fire, I stoked the war].
حمش:
The letters ḥāʾ, mīm, and shīn are two roots: one is the blazing and stirring-up of a thing, the other is thinness.

The first: their saying aḥmashtu al-rajul, I angered him. Istaḥmasha al-rajul, when he blazed with anger. [A poet] said: "Indeed, when he incites me, I incite him in turn." From this chapter: ḥamashtu al-shayʾ, I gathered it.

The second root: their calling one with thin legs ḥamsh, and one says ḥamushat qawāʾimuhu, his legs grew thin. From this chapter: their saying litha ḥamsha, gums with little flesh on them.
حمص: The letters ḥāʾ, mīm, and ṣād are not a root to be measured by analogy, and what analogy there is in it may come from dryness in a thing. They say inḥamaṣa al-waram, when a swelling subsided — this is the soundest thing said about it. Al-ḥamaṣīṣ is an edible plant.
حمض: The letters ḥāʾ, mīm, and ḍād are a single sound root, something among tastes. One says shayʾun ḥāmiḍ [a sour thing], and fīhi ḥumūḍa [sourness in it]. Al-ḥamḍ, among plants, is what has saltiness in it; al-khulla is whatever is other than that. The Arabs say: al-khulla is the camels' bread, and al-ḥamḍ is their fruit; they turn to al-ḥamḍ only when they have tired of al-khulla. All of this concerns plants; none of the great trees is called ḥamḍ or khulla.
حمط:
The letters ḥāʾ, mīm, and ṭāʾ are not a root and not a branch, and there is no sound usage in them, except for something among plants or trees. A certain kind of snake is called shayṭān al-ḥamāṭ. Derived from that is their saying "aṣabtu ḥamāṭata qalbihi," meaning the blackness of his heart, as they say ḥabbata qalbihi [the kernel of his heart]. Al-ḥamāṭa, as it is said, is a pain in the throat, though that is not the sound meaning; if it is sound, then it is taken from a plant that perhaps has a pungent taste.

As for their saying al-ḥamaṭīṭ and al-ḥimṭāṭ: the first is a plant, and the second is a worm found in grass, marked with colors — there is no point in mentioning it.
حمق: The letters ḥāʾ, mīm, and qāf are a single root indicating the stagnation of a thing, and weakness and deficiency. Al-ḥumq is deficiency of intellect. The Arabs say inḥamaqa al-thawb, when a garment wore out; and inḥamaqat al-sūq, the market went stagnant.
حمل:
The letters ḥā', mīm and lām are one root pointing to the lifting and carrying of a thing. One says ḥamaltu al-shay'a aḥmiluhu ḥamlan - I carried the thing. Al-ḥaml is what is in a belly, or on top of a tree. One says a woman ḥāmil and ḥāmila, pregnant. Whoever says ḥāmil says: this is a description that belongs only to females. Whoever says ḥāmila builds it on ḥamalat, she carried, so she is ḥāmila. He said, in a line of verse:
Fate laboured for him with a day that came due; and every bearing woman has her full term.
Al-ḥiml is what is on a back or on a head. Al-ḥamāla is that a man takes on himself a blood-price and then goes about gathering it; and standing surety is ḥamāla, and the meaning is one, and it is the measure of the section.

And among what is joined to this meaning is the woman called al-muḥmil, who lets down her milk without being pregnant. One says aḥmalat tuḥmil iḥmālan. And that is said of the she-camel too. Al-ḥumūl are the camel litters, whether there were women in them or not. And taḥāmaltu, when you force yourself to a thing in spite of hardship. And Ibn al-Sikkīt said about al-A'shā's line:
Let me not know you, if our enmity grows hard and help is sought from you in return, to be borne with in anger -
that al-iḥtimāl is anger. He said: and one says uḥtumila, when a man became angry. This is a sound measure, because they say: anger carried him off, and anger lifted him, that is, when it stirred him up. Al-ḥimāla and al-miḥmal are the strap of a sword. And of that is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:
Until my tears wetted my sword-strap.
Al-ḥamūla are the camels on which loads are carried, whether there is a load on them or not. And al-ḥamūla are the camels with their loads; and the loads themselves are ḥamūla. And one says aḥmaltu fulānan, when you helped him with the load. And ḥamīl al-sayl is what the torrent carries of its scum. And in the hadith: "A people come out of the Fire and sprout as the grain-seed sprouts in the scum carried down by a torrent." So al-ḥamīl is what the torrent has carried of scum. For that reason a man of doubtful descent who is taken in is called ḥamīl. Al-Kumayt said, reproaching Quḍā'a for going over to the Yemen, in a line of verse:
Why have you come down, with no poverty and no hardship upon you, to the station of the one carried in by the flood?

As for their saying al-Aḥmāl - they are of Banū Yarbū', namely Tha'laba, 'Amr, al-Ḥārith the father of Salīṭ, and Ṣubayr - it is said that their mother carried them on her back on one of the days of alarm, so they were called al-Aḥmāl. And it was they that Jarīr meant by his saying:
O sons of Qufayra, who will hold our watering back, or who will stand up to the might of the Aḥmāl?
And one says adalla 'alayya fa-ḥamaltu idlālahu and iḥtamaltu idlālahu, with one meaning: he presumed upon me and I bore his presuming. And he said, in a line of verse:
She presumed and I did not bear it, she spoke and I did not answer; by her father's life, I am indeed a wrongdoer.
And the measure runs straight through everything we have said. As for the young lamb, al-baraq, it is called ḥamal, and that is derived from carrying, as though one said the ewe carried a ḥaml, and the thing carried is a ḥaml and a ḥamal - as one says nafaḍtu al-shay'a nafḍan, I shook the thing, and the thing shaken is nafaḍ; and ḥasabtu al-shay'a ḥasban, I counted the thing, and the thing counted is ḥasab; and it is a straight pattern. Then a likeness is made to this, and one of the towers of the sky is called Ḥamal, the Ram. Al-Hudhalī said, in a line of verse:
Like white garments whose colour was made bright by the pouring rain of the sagging-bellied Ḥamal.
حن:
The letters ha' and nun are a single root: tenderness and compassion, sometimes with a sound of grief. Hanin of the she-camel is her yearning for her homeland. Some said this may also occur without a sound. As for the sound, it is like the hadith about the hanin of the tree-trunk which the Messenger of God, peace and blessings upon him and his family, used to lean against, before the pulpit was made for him and he stopped leaning on it.

Al-hanan is mercy. God Almighty said: {and tenderness from Us} [Maryam: 13]. One says hananaka, meaning "Your mercy." He said, in a line of verse: neighbouring the Banu Shamaja ibn Jarm -- Your mercy, our Lord, O source of mercy.

And hananayka, meaning mercy after mercy, compassion after compassion. Tarafa said, in a line of verse: O Abu Mundhir, you have destroyed us -- spare some of us; hananayka -- some harm is lighter than more.

Al-hanna is a man's wife, its derivation being from al-hanin, because each of the two yearns for the other. Al-hanun is a wind that, when it blows, sounds like the moaning of camels. He said, in a line of verse: a wandering, moaning wind stirs it.

A bow, qaws hannana, moans, because it moans when the string is loosed. He said, in a line of verse: and at my shoulder is a moaning bow, of nab' wood, that a seller in the market of Mecca chose out for me.

Anomalous to this root: tariq hannan, meaning a clear, plain road.
حناتم: Ḥanātim — black clouds. Everything black is called ḥantam. Likewise the Arabs reckon green as a shade of black, and from this jars were named ḥanātim: in the Jāhiliyya [the pre-Islamic era] jars were green, so the Arabs called them ḥanātim.
حنب: The letters ḥāʾ, nūn, and bāʾ are a single root indicating what the one before it indicated, that is, crookedness in a thing. Al-muḥannab is a horse with its legs set wide apart without splaying, and that is praise. It is said that al-ḥanab is crookedness in the two shanks. Al-Khalīl said, of taḥnīb in horses, that it only describes strength, and that there is no crookedness in it — this is contrary to what the philologists said.
حنث:
The letters ḥā', nūn and thā' are a single root, and it is sin and wrongdoing.

One says ḥanitha fulānun fī kadhā, meaning he sinned in such a matter. From this, their saying “the boy reached al-ḥinth” means he reached an age at which the recording pen began writing down his obedience and disobedience, and his sins began to be recorded against him. From this too, al-ḥinth in an oath is breaking it. This is the sense of sin.

As for their saying “so-and-so yataḥannathu from such a thing,” it means he is shunning sin. The difference between athima [he sinned] and ta'aththama [he shunned sin] is that ta'aththum means turning away from sin, just as one says ḥarija and taḥarraja: ḥarija means he fell into wrongdoing, while taḥarraja means he turned away from wrongdoing. This applies to a known set of words that all follow the same pattern.

From this too, al-taḥannuth, meaning devotion, withdrawing to worship. And from this the hadith: that the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, used to go to the cave of Ḥirā' and devote himself to worship there for a number of nights.
حنج: The letters ḥāʾ, nūn, and jīm are a single root indicating leaning and crookedness. One says ḥanajtu al-ḥabl, when you twisted the rope; it is maḥnūj. Ḥanajtu al-rajula ʿan al-shayʾ: I turned him away from it. Aḥnaja fulānun ʿan al-shayʾ: he turned aside. As for their calling one's origin ḥinj, perhaps that belongs to the chapter of substitution. And if it is sound, its measure is a single measure, because every branch inclines toward its root and returns to it.
حنذ:
The letters ḥā', nūn, and dhāl are a single root: thoroughly cooking a thing. One says roasted meat is ḥanīdh, meaning thoroughly cooked — that is, when stones are heated and placed on it until it is cooked through.

One also says ḥanadhtu al-farasa, I made the horse gallop, when you run it a lap or two and then pile blankets on it until it sweats; such a horse is maḥnūdh or ḥanīdh.

As for their saying Ḥanadh, it is a place-name. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Be pollinated, best of palm trees — be pollinated from Ḥanadh, and raise high.
They say: "When you pour a drink, iḥnidh," meaning use little water and much of the wine. This too belongs to the root, because the drink keeps its strength when it is not diluted with water.
حنر: The letters ḥāʾ, nūn, and rāʾ are a single word — were it not that it occurs in a hadith, there would be no reason to mention it, because in the speech of the Arabs a rāʾ hardly ever comes after a nūn. What occurs in the hadith is: "Had you prayed until you became like al-ḥanāʾir" — it is said that these are bows, the singular being ḥanīra. It is possible that the rāʾ is, as it were, stuck onto the word, and that it goes back to what we have mentioned of ḥanaytu al-shayʾ and ḥanawtuhu.
حنش: The letters ḥāʾ, nūn, and shīn are a single sound root, and it belongs to the chapter of hunting, when you catch something. Abū ʿAmr said: al-ḥanash is anything hunted among birds and creeping creatures. Others said: al-ḥanash is the snake, and that is the [main] analogy. As for their saying ḥanashtu al-shayʾ, when you bent it — if that is sound, it belongs to the chapter of substitution, and perhaps it comes from ʿanashtu or ʿanajtu.
حنط: The letters ḥāʾ, nūn, and ṭāʾ are not that root which can be measured from or measured by; in it is the sense of a grain or something resembling one. Al-ḥinṭa [wheat] is well known. One says of al-rimth [a desert shrub], when it whitens and ripens, that it has ḥaniṭ. Some mentioned that one says aḥmaru ḥāniṭ, as one says aswadu ḥālik [intensely black]. This is based on al-ḥinṭa being called al-ḥamrāʾ [the red one] — this has already been mentioned.
حنف:
The letters ḥā', nūn and fā' are a straight root, and it is leaning.

A man who walks on the backs of his feet is called aḥnaf. Some people said — and I think it the sounder view — that al-ḥanaf is a crookedness in the foot turning inward. A man is aḥnaf, that is, with legs that lean, and that happens by the fronts of his feet drawing close together and his heels standing apart.

Al-ḥanīf is the one who leans toward the straight religion. God Most High said:
{but he was ḥanīf, a Muslim} [Āl 'Imrān: 67].
