This is the origin; then its explanation is widened, so it is said that al-ḥanīf is the devout worshipper, and it is said he is the circumcised man, and it is said he is the one straight in his way. And it is said huwa yataḥannaf — he seeks out the straightest of roads.
حنق:
The letters ḥā', nūn and qāf are a single root, and it is the tightness of a thing. One says: lean horses are maḥāniq (tucked-up, narrow in the flank). Anger (al-ḥanaq), in the sense of rage, goes back to this, because it is a tightness in temperament, with no give and no room to spread.

A poet said, in a line of verse, on their saying muḥnaq:
What harm would it have done you, had you spared him? And sometimes a young man spares, even while he is enraged, filled with wrath.
حنك:
The letters ḥā', nūn, and kāf are a single root: it is a body part, and then things close to it are built upon it by the path of derivation.

The origin of al-ḥanak is the human palate, the back of the mouth. One says ḥannaktu al-ṣabiyya, I chewed dates and rubbed it on the baby's palate — so the child is muḥannak; and ḥanaktuhu, so he is maḥnūk. One says: "he is blacker than the ḥanak of the crow," meaning its beak; while its ḥalak is its blackness.

One says iḥtanaka al-jarādu al-arḍa, the locusts stripped the land bare, when they consume all its plants; this fits the pattern rightly, because it eats until it fills its palate. Built on this is uprooting a thing entirely, which is iḥtināk; from this, in the Book of God, Exalted is He: {I will surely take hold of his offspring, all but a few} [al-Isrā': 62], meaning: I will lead them all astray, as a thing is uprooted entirely, except a few.

If someone were to say: but we say "experience gave him wisdom," and "age matured him," and "a mature man," from what pattern does this come? It is answered: it belongs to this root, because it is reaching the utmost of a matter and arriving at its limit — just as the locusts strip the plants utterly, reaching their very end.

The leather strap that binds together the wooden frame-pieces of a saddle is called ḥunka, by likeness to the palate, because it is drawn tight and gathered together. One says ḥanaktu al-shayʾa, I understood the thing fully — this too belongs to the root, because when you understand something you have reached its farthest extent. God knows best.
حنو: The letters ḥāʾ, nūn, and the weak letter are a single root indicating bending and curving. One says ḥanawtu al-shayʾa ḥanwan and ḥanaytuhu, when you bent it, bending. Ḥinw al-sarj [the arch of the saddle] is named from this too, its plural aḥnāʾ. From it, ḥanat al-marʾa ʿalā waladihā taḥnū, when she does not remarry after their father's death, out of her tenderness toward them. Nāqa ḥanwāʾ: a she-camel with a curve in her back. Inḥanā al-shayʾu yanḥanī inḥinaʾan, it bent. Al-maḥniyya is the bend of a valley. As for al-ḥanwa and al-ḥinnāʾ [henna], two known plants, it is possible that these fall outside the root as an anomaly.
حوب:
The letters ḥā', wāw, and bā' are a single root that branches into sin, or need, or destitution — and these are all close to one another.

1. al-ḥūb and al-ḥawb — sin. God Almighty said: {indeed, it is a great sin} [al-Nisā': 2], and {a great sin} [al-Nisā': 2].
2. al-ḥawba — one whom a person sins against by mistreating them, such as a mother and the like. So-and-so yataḥawwabu from such a thing, meaning he holds back from it as sinful. In the hadith: "My Lord, accept my repentance, and forgive my sin." It is also said al-taḥawwub means groaning in pain. Ṭufayl said, in a line of verse:
So taste as we tasted, on the morning of Muḥajjar, the rage in our hearts, and the groaning.
3. al-ḥawba — need and destitution. One says: God brought al-ḥawba upon him.

If it is asked: then what pattern accounts for al-ḥawbā', which means the soul, one's very self? The answer: it is the very root itself, because a person's tenderness for his own self is the greatest and most constant of all cases the root covers.

As for their word used to drive camels on, ḥawb — we have already said that such sounds and imitative calls are not taken from any root; any speaker of Arabic can invent the like of it, and it then spreads and becomes common on people's tongues. As for al-Ḥawʾab, it is mentioned in its own place.
حوت:
The letters ḥā', wāw and tā' are a sound root, following a regular pattern; it comes from agitation and evasive dodging. Al-ḥūt is the great fish [i.e. whale], forever restless, never still. The Arabs say: ḥāwatanī fulānun — so-and-so tried to dodge and outmanoeuvre me. This line of verse is recited:
all day, an ash-grey calamity kept dodging me, on the day of ath-Thawiyya, away from my family and my wealth.
حوث:
The letters ḥā', wāw and thā' are scarce, not regular in pattern and not branching out.

1. al-ḥawthā' — the liver and what adjoins it. They say this, and recite: 'the paunch, the liver, and the gullet.'
2. jāriya ḥawthā' — a plump girl. A poet said: 'And she is a virgin, guileless, plump.'
3. tarakahum ḥawthan bawthan — he left them scattered every way, said when he dispersed them.

All of this is close in weakness and scarcity alike. They also say istabthtu al-shay' and istaḥathtuhu, when a thing was lost in the dust and you went looking for it.
حوج: The letters ḥā', wāw and jīm are a single root: it is being compelled toward or in need of a thing. Al-ḥāja, need, plural al-ḥājāt. Al-ḥawjā': need. One says "aḥwaja ar-rajul," he became needy; one also says "ḥāja yaḥūju," meaning he became needy. He cited: "I was content and did not turn you away when you asked, and I became needy (ḥujtu) and did not count debts against you on my fingers." As for al-ḥāj, it is a kind of thorn-plant, and it is irregular, outside the root.
حوذ:
The letters ḥā', wāw and dhāl are a single root, and it concerns lightness, speed, and briskness in a matter.

Al-iḥwādh is swift travel. One says ḥādha al-ḥimāru utunahu yaḥūdhuhā, the wild donkey drove his jennies, when he drove them roughly. Al-ʿAjjāj said, in a line of verse:
He drives them on, and he has a driving swiftness about him.

Al-aḥwadhiyy is one quick and deft in matters, who has mastered things and perfected them. ʿĀ'isha said of ʿUmar: “By God, he was aḥwadhiyy, unique of his kind.” Al-aḥwadhiyyān are the two wings of the sandgrouse. A line is quoted:
On two swift wings she rose up in flight.

From this root: istaḥwadha ʿalayhi al-shayṭānu, Satan overcame him, when he overcame him and drove him to whatever waywardness he wanted.

Also irregular, outside the root's pattern, is their saying: “he is light of ḥādh.” They quote, in a line of verse:
Light of ḥādh, a swift long-strider ... a servant to his companions, no ordinary servant.
[I am not fully sure of the sense of “a swift long-strider” here — the phrase is obscure to me.]

Also irregular: al-ḥādh, which is a kind of tree.
حور:
The letters ḥā', wāw and rā' are three roots: one of them is a colour, the second is returning, and the third is that a thing turns round.

As for the first, al-ḥawar is intense white of the eye set within intense black of it. Abū 'Amr said: al-ḥawar is that the eye should be black all over, like the eyes of gazelles and cattle, and there is no ḥawar in the children of Adam. He said: women are called ḥūr al-'uyūn only because they are likened to gazelles and cattle. Al-Aṣma'ī said: I do not know what ḥawar in the eye is.

One says ḥawwartu al-thiyāb — I whitened the clothes. The companions of Jesus, peace be upon him, are called al-ḥawāriyyūn because they used to whiten clothes, that is, bleach them. This is the origin, and then every helper was called a ḥawārī. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family, said: 'Al-Zubayr is my aunt's son and my ḥawārī, my helper, from my community.' Al-ḥawāriyyāt are white women. A poet said, in a line of verse:
So tell the white women to weep for others than us, and let none weep for us but the barking dogs.

Al-ḥuwwārā of food is what has been whitened. And iḥwarra al-shay' — the thing turned white, iḥwirāran. A poet said, in a line of verse:
O Ward, one day I shall die; then who is the ally of the whitened bowl?
That is, the bowl made white with hump fat. And some of the Arabs call the star known as Jupiter al-aḥwar.

It is possible to carry back to this origin al-ḥawar, which is hide tanned with something other than qaraẓ leaves and which is soft; and perhaps there is a colour there too. Al-'Ajjāj said, in a line of verse:
With hooked talons that pierce the breasts, as though they were tearing soft ḥawar leather along with the flesh.
He means: this falcon tears open the middles of the birds, as though he were tearing ḥawar leather with them, that is, he is swift in tearing them.

As for returning, one says ḥāra when he returned. God Almighty said: {Indeed he thought he would never return. Nay} [al-Inshiqāq: 14]. The Arabs say 'falsehood is in ḥūr', that is, in returning back and in loss; every loss and turning back is ḥūr. A poet said:
The blame remains, and the people's provision is gone to nothing.
Al-ḥawr is the verbal noun of ḥāra ḥawran, he returned. One says: '[we seek refuge with God] from ḥawr after kawr', and that is decrease after increase. One also says ḥāra ba'da mā kāra — he decreased after he had increased. And you say: I spoke to him and he did not return me a word — ḥawāran, and ḥiwāran, and maḥūratan, and ḥawīran.

The third origin is al-miḥwar, the piece of wood on which the pulley turns. And one says ḥawwartu al-khubzata taḥwīran when you shape the dough and make it round to put it in the hot ashes.

Among what strays from this chapter is ḥuwār of a she-camel, which is her young one.
حوز:
The letters ḥā', wāw, and zā' are a single root: gathering and coming together. Any gathering-place or district is called ḥawz or ḥawza. One says so-and-so protected al-ḥawza, meaning the territory. A woman made it a figure for what she must guard, and said, in a line of verse:
So I kept throwing dust in his face, driving him from myself, and guarding the territory of the one who is away.

1. taḥawwazat al-ḥayya — the snake coiled/twisted. Al-Qutāmī said, in a line of verse:
She drew away from me for fear that I would corner her, just as the viper draws aside for fear of one who strikes.
2. ḥāzahu ḥawzan — anyone who gathers a thing to himself has taken possession of it.
3. ḥawz — a man's natural disposition.
4. al-ḥūzī — one who draws apart from people and keeps to himself. Al-ʿAjjāj's line of verse is transmitted, in a line of verse:
He gathers them together, and he has his own way of driving them.
This describes the donkey that gathers his she-asses and drives them along.
5. al-aḥwazī, among men, is like al-aḥwadhī [the capable, efficient man]; the underlying pattern is the same.
حوس:
The letters ḥā', wāw and sīn are a single root: mixing with a thing and treading on it. One says ḥustu al-shay' ḥawsan.

1. al-taḥawwus — like hesitating over a thing; it is when a man stays despite meaning to travel, because something has come up to occupy him.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Go — the time has come for you, O one who lingers!

2. al-aḥwas — the one who gallops constantly, and the bold man whom nothing daunts.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Bold in the darkness, with the wavering spear.

3. ḥawwās — he is this by night, one who prowls.
حوش:
The letters ḥā', wāw and shīn are a single word. Al-ḥūsh means wild game. A wild, untamed thing is called ḥūshiyy.

ʿUmar said of the poet Zuhayr: “He did not pile his rhymes together clumsily, nor did he chase after strange, obscure words, nor did he praise a man except for what was truly in him.”

Ibn Qutayba said: the camels called ḥūshiyya are named after al-ḥūsh; it is said they are the stallions of the jinn's livestock, which mated with certain camels, so those camels were named after them. Ru'ba said, in a line of verse: “She pulled our millstone from the lands of al-ḥūsh.” I think this is a case of letter-inversion, like jadhaba and jabadha, which both mean to pull.

The root sense of the word, if it is sound, is gathering: one says ḥushtu al-ṣayda and aḥashtuhu, when you closed in on the game from around it and drove it together, to steer it into the trap.

Iḥtawasha al-qawmu fulānan means they put him in their midst. One says taḥawwasha ʿannī al-qawmu, the people kept their distance from me. “So-and-so does not yanḥāshu from a thing” means he does not draw back from it, from how little he cares about it. A line is quoted:
A fair woman who does not shrink back from us — though her mother, when she saw us, would draw sharply away from us in alarm.

It is said al-ḥuwāsha is a matter in which there is sin; this belongs to the root, because a person draws himself together and shrinks back from it. A line is quoted:
You wanted a sinful thing and were ignorant of what was right ... and you preferred jesting, without approval.

It is also said al-ḥuwāsha means shyness; this too belongs to the root, because the one who feels shame draws himself back from a thing.

Al-ḥawsh is for a person to eat from the sides of the food until he exhausts it. Al-ḥā'ish is a cluster of palm trees, with no singular form.
حوص:
The letters ḥā', wāw and ṣād are a single word indicating narrowness in a thing.

1. al-ḥawṣ — sewing; ḥuṣtu al-thawb ḥawṣan, that being bringing together the two edges of what is being sewn.
2. al-ḥawaṣ — narrowness of the outer corners of the two eyes, in their sunkenness; a man with it is aḥwaṣ. Some say instead that al-aḥwaṣ is one narrow in only one eye.
حوض:
The letters ḥā', wāw and ḍād are a single word, and it is a hollow dug into the ground.

1. al-ḥawḍ — the water trough. Istaḥwaḍa al-mā': he made himself a trough.
2. al-muḥawwaḍ — like the ḥawḍ, made for a palm tree so it may drink from it.
3. yuḥawwiḍu ḥawālay fulāna — so-and-so 'makes a trough around' a certain woman, said when he is in love with her.
4. ḥawḍ al-ḥimār — 'the donkey's trough,' said of a man sunken in the chest; it is an insult.
حوط: The letters ḥā', wāw and ṭā' are a single word, and it is a thing going round about a thing. So al-ḥawṭ is from ḥāṭahu ḥawṭan, he guarded and encompassed it. And the he-ass yaḥūṭu ʿānatahu, he keeps his herd of she-asses together, that is, he gathers them. And ḥawwaṭtu ḥā'iṭan, I built a wall round. And it is said that al-ḥuwāṭa is an enclosure made for grain. And al-ḥawṭ is a round thing of silver that a woman hangs upon her forehead.
حوق:
The letters ḥā', wāw and qāf are a single root close to the one before it.

1. al-ḥūq — what surrounds the glans.
2. al-ḥawq — sweeping the house.
3. al-miḥwaqa — the broom.
4. al-ḥuwāqa — the sweepings.
حوك: The letters ḥā', wāw and kāf: the joining of one thing to another. From this is ḥawk al-thawb wa-l-shi'r, the weaving of cloth and of poetry.
حول:
The letters hā', wāw and lām are a single root, and it is movement in a turning. Al-hawl is the year, and that is because it hawl, that is, it goes round. And one says hālat al-dār and ahālat and ahwalat: a year came upon it. And ahwaltu anā bi'l-makān and ahaltu, that is, I stayed in it a year. One says hāla al-rajul fī matni farasihi yahūlu hawlan and hu'ūlan, when he leaps upon its back; and ahāla likewise. And hāla al-shakhs yahūlu, when the figure moves; and so is everything that shifts from one state. And from it is their saying istahaltu al-shakhs, that is, I looked to see whether it moves. And al-hīla, al-hawīl and al-muhāwala, contrivance, are all of one way, and it is the reasoning we have mentioned, because a man goes round about a thing to get at it. Al-Kumayt said, in a line of verse:
And her of the two names, whose colours are many: she is thought a fool, though her cunning is plain.
She of the two names is the vulture, because she is rakhama and anūq. She is thought a fool though she has cunning, because she keeps to the tops of the mountains, and migrates among the first that migrate, and returns among the first that return, and loves her young, and broods over her eggs, and lets none near her but her mate. And al-huwalā' is what comes out with the young, and it wraps it about.
حوم:
The letters ḥā', wāw and mīm are a single word close to the one before it, and it is circling around a thing. One says ḥāma al-ṭā'ir ḥawla al-shay' yaḥūmu, the bird circled around the thing.

1. al-ḥawma — the thick of the fighting, because the fighters circle round one another.
2. al-ḥawm — a huge herd of camels.
3. al-ḥawmāna — a round patch of ground; they say sand encircles it.
حوى:
The letters ḥā' and wāw, with the weak letter after it, are a single root, and it is gathering. One says ḥawaytu al-shay' aḥwīhi ḥayyan, when you gather a thing.

1. al-ḥawiyya — one of al-ḥawāyā, which are the intestines; this belongs to the sense of gathering. They call the single one ḥāwiyā'.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
As if the creaking of the grain in its belly were the hissing of vipers or the rattle of scorpions.

2. al-ḥawiyya (in another sense) — a cloth wound around the camel's hump, on which one then rides.
3. al-ḥayy — one of the encampments of the Arabs.
4. al-ḥiwā' — the single tent or dwelling.

All of this belongs to the analogy of this chapter.
حي:
The letters ḥā' and yā', with the weak letter [alif], are two roots: one is the opposite of death, and the other is shame (al-istiḥyā'), which is the opposite of shamelessness.

As for the first: al-ḥayāh (life) and al-ḥayawān (animal life), the opposite of death and of deadness (al-mawatān). Rain is called ḥayan, because by it the land is given life. One says nāqa muḥyin or muḥyiya, a she-camel whose young almost never die. You say: I came to the land and aḥyaytuhā, when you found its plants alive and fresh.

The other root: their saying istaḥyaytu minhu, I felt shame before him. Abū Zayd said: ḥayītu minhu aḥyā, when you feel shame. As for ḥayā' al-nāqa, the she-camel's vulva, it is possible this too is from this root — as if it were reasoned that, were she among those who feel shame, she would be ashamed of it showing and being uncovered.
حيث: The letters ḥā', yā' and thā' are not a root, because it is a word set for every place, and it is left vague. You say uqʿud ḥaythu shi'ta - sit wherever you wish; and it takes a u at the end. And al-Kisā'ī reported the a in it too.
حيد:
The letters ḥā', yā', and dāl are a single root: leaning and turning away from the straight path. One says ḥāda ʿan al-shayʾ, yaḥīdu, ḥaydatan wa ḥuyūdan, he swerved away from the thing.

1. al-ḥayūd — one who swerves often; likewise al-ḥayadā, on the pattern faʿalā. The Hudhalī poet said, in a line of verse:
Or a tawny lion, guarding his own bulk, a heavy, swerving beast among the pit-traps.
2. al-ḥayd — a jutting ridge on a mountain, plural ḥuyūd and aḥyād.
3. al-ḥuyūd — the ridges on a gazelle's horn, the rings in it.

All of this goes back to a single root.
حير:
The letters ḥā', yā', and rā' are a single root: wavering back and forth over a thing. From this is al-ḥayra, bewilderment; one says ḥāra fī al-amr, yaḥīru, he was confused over the matter, and taḥayyara, yataḥayyaru, he became bewildered.

Al-ḥayr and al-ḥāʾir are a low place where water collects and swirls about. Qays said, in a line of verse:
She steps on two reed-stalks, fed by abundant water in the open ground of a swirling, brimming pool.

Anything that is full is called mustaḥīr, and this fits the pattern rightly, because when it is full its parts wash back and forth over one another, like the pool where the water swirls when it is full. Abū Dhuʾayb said, in a line of verse:
And her youthfulness brimmed over at its fullest.
حيز: The letters ḥā', yā' and zā' are not a root, because its yā' is in truth a wāw. From this is al-ḥayyiz, the region or area, and inḥāza al-qawm, the people withdrew — this has been mentioned in its own chapter.
حيس: The letters ḥā', yā' and sīn are a single root, and it is mixture. Abū Bakr said: ḥistu al-ḥabl, when you twisted a rope, aḥīsuhu ḥaysan — and this is the basis of what has been said, because when a rope is twisted its strands interlace and mix. Al-ḥays is well known, and belongs to this chapter, because it is things mixed together. Abū 'Ubayd related, of a man whom slave-women surrounded from every side: maḥyūs, saying he was likened to ḥays.
حيص:
The letters ḥā', yā' and ṣād are one root: turning aside into wrongdoing and hesitant confusion. One says ḥāṣa ʿan al-ḥaqq yaḥīṣu ḥayṣan — he turned away wrongfully from the truth. He said, in a line of verse:
and if ʿĀmir should turn away from death...
And they also transmit:
by an honest scale, that does not miss so much as a barley-grain.

From this root is their saying: waqaʿū fī ḥayṣa bayṣa — they fell into a tight, confusing hardship. Al-Hudhalī said, in a line of verse:
I have been one who goes out and comes in, a shrewd dealer — no tight confusing predicament, no crushing hardship, ever trapped me.
حيض: The letters ḥā', yā' and ḍād are a single word. One says: the samura tree ḥāḍat, meaning: a red liquid came out of it. For that reason a menstruating woman is called ḥā'iḍ, comparing her blood to that liquid.
حيط: The letters ḥā', yā' and ṭā' are not a root, because its origin, in al-ḥiyāṭa, al-ḥīṭa and al-ḥā'iṭ, is throughout from a wāw. This has been mentioned in its own chapter.
حيف: The letters ḥā', yā', and fā' are a single root: leaning. One says ḥāfa ʿalayhi, yaḥīfu, he was unjust to him — from leaning against him. From this too is taḥayyaftu al-shayʾa, I took from it at its edges; this fits the root's pattern, because it leans away from the middle toward the sides.
حيق: The letters ḥā', yā' and qāf are one word, and it is a thing coming down upon a thing. One says *ḥāqa bihi al-sū'u yaḥīq* — the evil came down on him. God, exalted, said: {and evil plotting comes down on none but its own people} [Fāṭir: 43].
حيك:
The letters ḥā', yā' and kāf are a single root, and it is a kind of walking. One says ḥākin — huwa yaḥīku fī mashyihi ḥayakānan, when he moves his shoulders and his body as he walks.

1. al-ḥayk — the taking-hold of a saying in the heart; one says mā yaḥīku kalāmuka fī fulānin, your words do not take hold in so-and-so. I say it is from this because walking is a taking-hold along the path one walks in.
2. ḍarabahu fa-mā aḥāka fīhi al-sayf — he struck him and the sword did not take hold in him.
حين:
The letters ḥā', yā' and nūn are one root, and then other things are carried upon it; and the root is time. So al-ḥīn is time, whether little of it or much. And one says ʿāmaltu fulānan [muḥāyanatan] - I dealt with him by fixed terms, from al-ḥīn. And aḥyantu bi-al-makān - I stayed in the place for a time. And ḥāza ḥīna kadhā, that is, the time of such a thing drew near. A poet said, in a line of verse:
My putting Jamīl out of mind would be an hour of time that has not come, and whose hour has not come either.

And one says ḥayyantu al-shāt, when I milked the ewe time after time. And one says ḥayyantuhā, meaning I set a fixed time for her. And al-ta'fīn is that you set her no fixed time in which to milk her. Al-Mukhabbal said, in a line of verse:
If she is milked at no set time, that milking gives your household its fill; and if a time is set for her, her set milking runs over the milk-skin.

And al-Farrā' said: al-ḥīn is of two kinds. There is a ḥīn whose limit is not fixed, and that is the commoner; and a ḥīn that God, exalted is He, mentioned: {It brings forth its fruit at every season} [Ibrāhīm: 25]. And this one is bounded, because it is six months.

As for what is carried upon this, it is their calling destruction ḥayn; and that is by the reasoning, because when it comes there must be a time for it, so it is as though it were named with the name of the verbal noun.
خأ:
The letters khā' and a stretched hamza do not form a root that follows a regular pattern; only a single expression is mentioned under it, and its soundness is not known.

They said: khā'ibaka 'alaynā — meaning, hurry up.

And they cited, for al-Kumayt, in a line of verse:
Calling out with your khā'ibak — come on, hurry!
[The sense of this line is not clear even in the source text.]
خام:
As for the letters khāʾ, alif and mīm, they are turned from a yāʾ. Al-khāma is the fresh, moist shoot of a plant or a crop. The Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, said: "The likeness of the believer is the likeness of the khāma of the crop."

Al-Ṭirimmāḥ said, in a line of verse:
We are indeed like the khāma of a crop:
whenever its time comes, its reaper comes to it.

This is from al-khāʾim, the coward who has no movement in him.

As for the letters khāʾ, alif and fāʾ, they are a single word, and it is al-khāfa, the leather satchel in which honey is gathered when harvested. This is taken by analogy from khayf al-ḍarʿ, the skin of the udder; the pattern is the same.
خب:
The letters khā' and bā' are two roots: the first is that a thing extends lengthwise, the second is a kind of deception.

1. al-khabība and al-khubba — a track that runs through the sand.
2. From this, a strip of cloth torn lengthwise is likened to it.
3. al-khabība of meat — a long slice of it, by the same likeness.
4. al-khibb — deception; al-khibb — the deceiver. This is derived from khabba al-baḥru — the sea grew turbulent. And al-khibb befell them.
5. al-khabab — a kind of trotting gait.
6. One says jā'a mukhibban — he came at a trot.
7. From it: khabba al-nabt — the plant, when it dried up and was uprooted [by wind], as if it were trotting; one imagines it walking.

Ru'ba said, in a line of verse:
And the tips of the awns went trotting over the hard ground.

8. al-khabkhaba — the looseness and agitation of a thing.

All of this goes back to what has been described, because deception is unsettled, not firmly fixed on anything sound.

9. As for what al-Farrā' related — "lī min fulānin khawābb," meaning kinship ties, singular khābb — this belongs, in my view, to the first root, because it is a bond that extends and connects.

As for their saying "khabkhibū 'ankum min al-ẓahīra," meaning cool off through the midday heat, this is not from this root; it is a metathesized form, already discussed elsewhere.
خبأ:
The letters khā', bā', a weak letter, and the hamza indicate concealing a thing. From this: khabaʾtu al-shayʾa akhbaʾuhu khabʾan, I hid the thing. Al-khubaʾa is a young woman who is kept hidden from view.

From this branch too is al-khibāʾ, a tent of hair-cloth; one says akhbaytu ikhbāʾan, and khabbaytu, and takhabbaytu, all of these when you pitch yourself a tent.
خبت: The letters khā', bā' and tā' are a single root indicating humble submission. One says "akhbata yukhbitu ikhbātan," when he submitted humbly; "akhbata lillāhi ta'ālā," he submitted humbly to God. He, exalted is His mention, said: "and give good tidings to the humbly submissive (al-mukhbitīn)." Its origin is from al-khabt, a waterless desert with no vegetation. From this also is the hadith: "even at khabt al-jamīsh" [a barren waste] — do you not see that he called it jamīsh, as though the vegetation had been plucked (jumisha) from it, meaning shaved?
خبث: The letters khā', bā' and thā' are a single root pointing to the opposite of what is good and wholesome. One says khabīth — that is, not wholesome. And akhbath when a man's companions are foul. From this comes the seeking of refuge from al-khabīth al-mukhbith. Al-khabīth is foul in himself, and al-mukhbith is he whose companions and helpers are foul.
خبج: The letters khāʾ, bāʾ and jīm are not a root to be reasoned from, and I do not think there is any sound speech in it. One says khabaja, when he broke wind. Sometimes they say khabajahu bi-l-ʿaṣā, he struck him with the stick. And they say al-khabājāʾ, of stallions, is the one much given to covering — this is as we have said, unless the hadith is sound from the Prophet, God bless him and his family and grant him peace, that he said: "When the prayer is set up, Satan turns away, having a khabaj like the khabaj of a donkey." 'When the prayer is set up, Satan turns away, breaking wind like a donkey breaks wind.' If this is sound, then what is sound is what he, peace and blessings be upon him — by our fathers and mothers be he ransomed — said.
خبر:
The letters khā', bā' and rā' are two roots: the first is knowledge, and the second points to softness, looseness and abundance.

The first is al-khubr: knowledge of a thing. You say: I have khibra and khubr of so-and-so. And God - exalted - is al-Khabīr, that is, the one who knows everything. And God - exalted - said: {And none informs you like one well-acquainted} [Fāṭir: 14].

The second root is al-khabrā', and it is soft ground. 'Ubayd said, describing a horse:
Clinging to the thrust, firm-footed on the soft ground.
And al-khabīr is the ploughman, and he is from this, because he sets the land right and makes it soft and loose. And on this runs the whole of this section; for they say al-khabīr is the ploughman because he works the land as a khabīr, that is, he tills it. As for al-mukhābara which has been forbidden, it is share-cropping for a half of the land's yield, or a third, or less than that, or more. And it is also called al-khibr. And some people said: al-mukhābara is derived from the name of Khaybar.

And from the abundance we mentioned comes their calling a she-camel of much milk khabr. And likewise a great water-skin is a khabr; the plural is khubūr.

And from the softness we mentioned comes their naming butter-froth khabīr. And al-khabīr is soft plants. And in the hadith: "and we pluck the soft green growth."

And al-khabīr is the camel's fur. The rajaz poet said:
Until, when it flew off from her fur -
And one says a place khabir, when it is warm and sheltered, with many trees and much water. And I have known the land to be so. And this is the measure of the section.

And among what strays from the root is al-khubra, and it is the sheep that a group of men buy to slaughter and share out its meat. He said, in a line of verse:
When you have made the sheep a khubra for the people, then look to your own affair; I am going about mine.
خبز:
The letters khā', bā', and zā' are a single root indicating striking a thing with the hand. The camels takhabbazat the saʿdān-thistle, when they beat it down with their legs. From this: the baker khabaza, kneaded, the bread. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Do not knead bread lazily, and do not grind meal carelessly, and do not linger too long where the camels kneel.
One says: al-khabz is the camel striking the ground with its forelegs.
خبس:
The letters khāʾ, bāʾ and sīn are a single root indicating taking a thing by force and overpowering.

1. takhabbastu al-shayʾa — I took it by force; that thing is called khubāsa.
2. al-khubāsa — plunder, spoils. One says ikhtabasa al-shayʾa, he took it by overpowering.
3. asadun khabūs — a lion given to seizing by force.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
But I am a fierce, bold one,
upon rivals daring, seizing.
خبش: The letters khā', bā' and shīn are not a root. Sometimes they said: khabasha the thing — he gathered it. And this is nothing.
خبص: The letters khā', bā' and ṣād are close to the one before it. They say: khabaṣa the thing — he mixed it.
خبط:
The letters khā', bā', and ṭā' are a single root indicating treading and striking. One says khabaṭa al-baʿīru al-arḍa bi-yadihi, the camel struck the ground with its leg. One says khabaṭa al-waraqa min al-shajar, he beat leaves down from a tree, when he strikes it so the leaves fall.

This may be extended, so that a disease resembling madness is called al-khubāṭ, as though the person flails about. God Almighty said: {except as one stands who is beaten down by Satan's touch} [al-Baqara: 275].

Whatever remains of food or other things is called khibṭa. Al-khibṭa is also scant water, because it gets churned up and cannot resist being disturbed.

As for their saying ikhtabaṭa fulānun fulānan, so-and-so came to him seeking his generosity — the origin is that whoever travels by night to a man, or travels at all, must necessarily tread the ground; the expression was then shortened, so that one coming to seek a favor is called mukhtabiṭ.

It is also said al-khibṭa is a rainfall that spreads widely over the land, so named because it beats down upon the ground, striking it.

Some transmitted from al-Shaybānī that al-khābiṭ means the sleeper, and cited from him, in a line of verse:
By night, they crush the sprawled-out snake beneath them.
If this is correct, it is because the sleeper presses the ground with his body, as though striking it. It may also be that al-shujāʿ al-khābiṭ [the snake so called] is named because it is trodden underfoot by passers-by, as the speaker said, in a line of verse:
By the forenoon she severs the necks of the weaver-birds, and by the dark of night she crushes the viper of the sandy wastes.

As for al-khibāṭ, it is a branding mark on the thigh, so named because the thigh is struck with it.
خبع: The letters khā', bā' and ʿayn are not a root, because the ʿayn in it is substituted from a hamza. One says khaba'tu al-shay' and khabaʿtuhu, both meaning I hid the thing. And one says khabaʿa al-rajulu bi-l-makān: he stayed in that place. And sometimes they said khabaʿa al-ṣabiyyu khubūʿan, which is when a child is choked from weeping. If this is sound, it belongs to this chapter, as if his weeping had been hidden away.
خبق:
The letters khā', bā' and qāf are a small root indicating being raised up. Al-khibiqqā is a kind of raised, lofty gait. A poet said, in a line of verse:
He runs the khibiqqā and the difiqqā, exultant.
And from this chapter, al-khibaqq and al-khibiqq: the tall man, and likewise the tall horse.
خبل:
The letters khā', bā' and lām are a single root indicating impairment of the limbs.

Al-khabal is madness. One says ikhtabalahu al-jinn, the jinn drove him mad. A jinn that does this is called khābil, plural khubbal. Al-khabal also means impairment of the limbs. One says khubilat yaduhu, his hand was maimed, when it was cut off and ruined. Aws said, in a line of verse:
Sons of Lubaynā, you are not worth a hand ... except a hand crippled at the upper arm.
Meaning: ruined at the upper arm.

One says “so-and-so is khabāl on his family,” meaning a burden to them, of no use to them at all. “The mire of khabāl” mentioned in the hadith is said to be the pus of the people of Hellfire.

Irregular, outside the root's pattern: al-ikhbāl, said to mean a man dividing his camels into two halves, breeding one half each year, as is done with land in farming. It is also said al-ikhbāl is for a man to lend another a she-camel to ride, or a horse to raid upon. Zuhayr's line is quoted:
There, if they are asked to lend property, they lend it ... and if they are asked, they give; and if they gamble, they pay generously.
خبن:
The letters khā', bā' and nūn are a small single root indicating gripping and diminishing.
1. One says khabantu the thing when you grip it.
2. And khabantu the garment when you raised its lower hem until it drew in, after you had sewn and finished it.
3. Al-khubna is the fold of a man's garment, where he carries things; it is so named because a thing is tucked into it. You say: he lifted it into his khubna. In the hadith: "let him eat from it, and not take away a khubna."
4. And it is said that the khubn of a water-skin is the part below the ear-loop.
As for their saying khabantu al-rajul, like ghabantuhu — I cheated him — it may be from letter-substitution, or it may be because when a man cheats another he has tucked away from him part of his due.
خت:
The letters khā' and tā' do not form a root, because its tā' stands in for a sīn.

One says khatīt, meaning khasīs, mean/lowly. And akhatta Allāhu ḥaẓẓahu means: God made his lot mean. This is in the dialect of those who say marartu bi-l-nāt, meaning bi-l-nās, by the people.

They also mentioned that they say akhatta fulān — he felt ashamed. If this is sound, its meaning is that he did something shameful, of a kind one feels ashamed of.

They cited, in a line of verse:
Whoever has among his forebears one who was mean,
you, O Walīd, are still proud of them.

Meaning: you yourself bring no shame from your forebears.
ختا: The letters khā', tā' and the weak or hamzated letter are not a root. Sometimes they said ikhtata'tu lahu ikhtitā'an, meaning I deceived him (khataltuhu).
ختر:
The letters khā', tā', and rā' are a root indicating slackness and weariness. One says takhattara al-rajulu fī mishyatihi, the man takhattara in his walk, when he walks with the gait of a lazy man.

From this branch too is al-khatr, treachery, because when a man khatara, he has held back from keeping faith. Al-khattār is the treacherous man. God Almighty said: {and none rejects Our signs except every treacherous, ungrateful one} [Luqmān: 32].
ختع:
The letters khā', tā' and ʿayn are a single root indicating a raid, and entering into what conceals the one who enters it. He says khataʿa al-rajulu khutūʿan, when he rode into darkness.
1. Al-khaytaʿa — a piece of hide the archer wraps on his hand when shooting.
2. And by extension, the female leopard is called al-khatʿa, for her boldness and daring.
Al-ʿAjjāj said, of the guide already mentioned, in a line of verse:
She wearied the guides of the open waste, the bold ones.
ختل: The letters khā', tā' and lām are a small root with a single word in it, which is al-khatl. Some people said it is deception. And al-Khalīl used to say: takhātala means to deceive while off guard.
ختم:
The letters khā', tā', and mīm are a single root, and it is the reaching of the end of a thing. One says khatamtu al-'amal [I finished the work], khatama al-qāri'u al-sūra [the reciter completed the sūra]. As for al-khatm, meaning stamping a thing with a seal, this too belongs to the same chapter, because stamping a thing only comes after reaching its end, for safekeeping. Al-khātam is derived from this, because by it a thing is sealed. One says al-khātim, al-khātām, and al-khaytām. A poet said:
You took my seal-ring without right.
The Prophet, God bless him and his family and grant him peace, is khātam al-anbiyā' [the seal of the prophets], because he is the last of them. Khitām of any drink is its end. God Almighty said: {its seal is musk} [al-Muṭaffifīn: 26], meaning: the last thing they find of it, when they drink it, is the scent of musk.
ختن:
The letters khā', tā' and nūn are two words.
1. Khatn al-ghulām — the boy who has reached the age to be circumcised. And al-khitān is the place cut on the male member.
2. Al-khatan — the relative by marriage, the one who marries into the tribe.
خث:
The letters khā' and thā' do not form a sound root or branch worth pursuing, but what is said of it is mentioned here.

They say: al-khuth is what is kneaded from cow-dung and used to plaster something — but this report is not reliable. It is also said that al-khuth is the debris left by a flood, which then dries and turns black.
خثا: The letters khā', thā' and the weak letter are not a root. Sometimes they said a woman is khathwā': slack-bellied. And the singular of al-akhthā' is khithy, dung. And it is nothing. God knows best.
خثر: The letters khā', thā' and rā' are a root indicating thickness in a thing along with slackness. One says khathira al-labanu — the milk thickened — and it is khāthir. Some related: khathira fulānun fī l-ḥayy, when he stayed in the encampment and hardly left. And this is nothing.
خثل: The letters khā', thā' and lām are a single word, not to be reasoned from by analogy. Al-Kisā'ī said: khathalat al-baṭn is what lies between the navel and the pubic bone; it is also said khathlah, and the lighter form is the more common.
خثم: The letters khā', thā' and mīm are not a root. Sometimes they called thickness of the nose al-khatham, and the man with it is akhtham.
خج:
The letters khā' and jīm are a root indicating agitation and rapid, uneven movement.

1. A wind is called khajūj, one that veers as it blows. Al-Aṣma'ī used to say al-khajūj is a wind that blows forcefully.
2. al-khajkhaja is drawing back and feeling shy.
3. They said: khajkhaja al-rajulu — when he did not reveal what was on his mind.
4. One says ikhtajja al-jamalu fī sayrihi — when it did not go straight in its course.
5. A khajjāja man — a fool.

The whole root is one [these senses all trace back to the same idea].
خجا:
The letters khā', jīm and the weak or hamzated letter are not a root.
1. They say rijlun khuja'a, meaning a foolish man.
2. And khaja'a al-faḥlu unthāhu, when the stallion mated with his female.
3. And faḥlun khuja'a: a stallion much given to mating.
خجل:
The letters khā', jīm and lām are a root indicating agitation and hesitation.
1. Some related: "upon him a garment that is khajil," when it was not cut evenly but hung loose and disturbed on him when worn.
2. And from this is al-khajal that comes over a person, which is to remain stunned, not speaking. One says from it: khajila. The Messenger of God, peace and blessings upon him, said to the women: "Indeed when you go hungry you become abject, and when you are full you become khajiltunna." Al-Kumayt said, in a line of verse:
They were not abject when misfortune struck them at the clash of wars, nor were they khajilū.
It is said that khajiltunna here means baṭirtunna wa-ashirtunna — you grew insolent and elated — and that follows the pattern of the chapter.
3. And one says from it: khajila al-wādī, when the buzzing of its flies grows loud.
4. And one says akhjala al-ḥamḍ: the shrub grew tall — and that follows the pattern too, because when it grows tall it sways.
خد:
The letters khā' and dāl are a single root, and it is the tapering of a thing and its running downward.

1. al-khadd — a person's cheek, after which al-mikhadda, the pillow, is named.
2. al-khadd — a furrow.
3. al-akhādīd — furrows in the ground.
4. al-takhaddud — the wasting away of flesh from emaciation.
5. "a woman mutakhaddida" — emaciated.
6. al-khidād — a branding-iron, one of the branding-irons; it is perhaps applied to the cheek. One says from it: ba'īrun makhdūd, a branded camel.
خدب:
The letters khā', dāl and bā' are two roots: one is unsteadiness and softness in a thing, the other is a split in a thing.

The first: *al-khadab* is rashness. In accounts of the Arabs: "there was in Nu'āma khadab", meaning rashness — perhaps in his wars — and that supports what we have said. From it, a camel is *khidabb* when heavy with flesh, for when flesh is abundant it grows soft and unsteady.

From this first sense one says a man is *akhdab* and a woman *khadbā'*. Al-Aṣma'ī said a coat of mail can be *khadbā'*, meaning soft.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
A soft coat of mail, driven down by the sword-belt of an Indian blade.

One says *khadaba* of a man when he lied, because lying is unsteady, not straight. An old man is *khidabb*, described the way the camel is described. Some said: there is *khadab* in his tongue, meaning length.

As for the other root: *al-khadb* with the eye-tooth is the splitting of skin together with flesh. One says a strike is *khadbā'* when it plunges into the body's interior. *Al-khadb* is also hard milking, as if it means splitting the udder by the force of the milking.

What falls outside this chapter as an anomaly is their saying "turn back to your *khaydaba*", meaning your first road. Al-Shaybānī said *al-khaydab* is the clear road. If that is sound, it in fact returns to the pattern, because a road splits the earth.
خدج: The letters khā', dāl and jīm are a single root denoting deficiency. One says a she-camel *khadajat* when she drops her young before term. If she drops it lacking in form even at full term, she has *akhdajat*. Ibn al-A'rābī said: the summer season *akhdajat* when its rain fell short. In the hadith: "Any prayer in which the Opening of the Book was not recited is *khidāj*" — deficient.
خدر:
The letters khā', dāl, and rā' are two roots: darkness and concealment; and slowness and staying in place.

1. al-khudāriyy — the dark night.
2. al-khudāriyya — the eagle, named for its colour.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
A dark, broad-winged eagle, whose feathers a day's cloud,
heavy with successive showers, has soaked through.

3. One says: al-yawmu khadir — the day is overcast.
4. al-layla al-khadira — a dark, rainy night; one says akhdarnā when the rain covered/shaded us.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Among them a soft, tender woman, as if her brow
were the sun of the day, dimmed by the overcast dark.

Another said, in a line of verse:
And they shield the fire, though there is no darkness needing it.

Similar, or close to it, is Ṭarafa's line:
Like mangy pregnant camels on an overcast day.

5. al-khidr — a woman's curtained chamber.
6. A lion is called khādir, because the thicket is his concealing chamber.

The second root: akhdara fulānun fī ahlihi — he settled and stayed among his family.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
As if beneath me were a swift-running falcon,
that had stayed put five days, tasting no food.

7. khadira al-ẓaby — the gazelle fell behind from the herd.
8. al-khādir is said to mean the bewildered one.
9. khadirat rijluhu — his leg went numb; khadira al-rajulu — a man, from a numbness that comes over him.

Ṭarafa said, in a line of verse:
She crossed through the night to our camp,
at night's end, with a drowsy young gazelle.

He means: as if it were sleepy.

10. Wild she-asses are called banāt Akhdar, named after a stallion called Akhdar; for this they are called al-akhdariyya.
خدش:
The letters khā', dāl, and shīn are a single root, and it is the scratching of one thing by another.

1. One says khadashtu al-shay'a khadshan; the plural of al-khadsh is khudūsh.
2. The tips of grain-awns are called al-khādisha, because they scratch.
3. The camel's withers are called mikhdash, for their scantiness of flesh, and because they scratch the mouth of the one gnawing meat off the bone there.
خدع:
The letters khā', dāl and ʿayn are one root; al-Khalīl mentioned its underlying pattern. Al-Khalīl said: al-ikhdāʿ is the concealing of a thing. He said: for this the storeroom was named al-makhdaʿ. The whole root proceeds on what al-Khalīl mentioned.

1. khadaʿtu ar-rajul — I deceived the man, outwitted him.
2. "War is trickery" and "trickery" [both forms of khudʿa].
3. khadaʿa ar-rīqu fī al-fam — the saliva hid in the mouth, staying concealed down the throat. He said, in a line of verse:
sweet of saliva, when the saliva hides.
4. "mā khadaʿat bi-ʿaynayya naʿsatun" — meaning no drowsiness has come into my eyes. He said, in a line of verse:
I stayed sleepless, and no drowsiness crept into my eyes; and whoever meets what I have met must surely stay sleepless.
5. al-akhdaʿ — a hidden vein in the back of the neck. A man is makhdūʿ when his akhdaʿ vein has been cut.
6. So-and-so has a khuluqun khādiʿ — a deceptive character, when he affects a manner not his own; this belongs to the root, because he hides the opposite of what he shows.
7. It is said that al-khudʿa means Time/Fate, in the saying:
O my people, who will excuse me from Time's trickery?
by way of comparison, as though Time deceives and tricks.
8. ghūlun khaydaʿ — a treacherous ghoul, as though it ambushes and deceives.
9. Some claimed one says dīnārun khādiʿ, meaning a coin short in weight — as though it showed itself full and hid its shortfall, until the scale revealed it.

From this root also is al-khaydaʿ, the mirage — the same underlying pattern.
خدف: The letters khā', dāl and fā' are a single root. Ibn Durayd said: al-khadf is speed in walking, and from it comes the name Khindif.
خدل: The letters khā', dāl and lām are a single root, denoting fineness and softness. One says a woman is khadla, meaning fine-boned while her flesh has fullness in it; she is described plainly by the terms khadal and khadāla. It is related from al-Sijistānī that a grape can be khadla, meaning shrivelled and puny.
خدم:
The letters khā', dāl and mīm are a single root, regular in its pattern, and it is one thing encircling another.

1. *al-khadam* — anklets, one of them a *khadama*.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
They paw at the ground pawing, like the digging of anklets gone astray.

2. *al-khadmā'* — a ewe whose lower legs turn white.
3. *al-mukhaddam* — the place on the leg where the anklet sits. A horse is called *mukhaddam* when its white marking circles above the hair of its fetlock.

Al-Khalīl said: *al-khadama* is a well-made strap like a ring, tied around a camel's wrist, to which the sandal-strap is then tied. He said the anklet (*khalkhāl*) was named *khadama* for that reason.

4. *al-arahh al-mukhaddam* — a wide-hooved mountain goat whose whiteness surrounds its lower legs.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
It wears out the wide-hooved *mukhaddam*.

5. *al-khidma* — service, from this same chapter.
6. *al-khādim* — the servant, also derived from it; because the servant circles around the one he serves.
خدن:
The letters khā', dāl and nūn are a single root, and it is companionship.

Al-khidn is the companion. One says khādantu al-rajula mukhādanatan, I befriended the man. Khidn al-jāriya is the man who converses and keeps company with a young woman.

Abū Zayd said: khādantu al-rajula means I made friends with the man. A man called khudana is one who has many companions.
خذا:
The letters khā', dhāl, a weak letter and a hamza denote weakness and softness.

1. *khadhā... yakhdhū khadhwan* — it went slack.
2. *khadhiya... yakhdhā* — the same, in another verb-form.
3. *yanama khadhwā'* — a soft plant, an herb.
4. *udhun khadhwā'* — a drooping ear; and a drooping ear is disliked in a horse.

From this same chapter:
5. *khadhi'tu* and *khadha'tu akhdha'u* — I submitted to him, abjectly, as *khudhū'* or *khadh'*.
6. *istakhdhaytu* and *istakhda'tu* — two dialect forms, the people leaning more toward dropping the hamza in it.

Kuthayyir said, in a line of verse:
You did not cease with the people until they became, as if from fear, birds that hawks had made cower.
He used the hamza here. One says *akhdaytu* so-and-so, meaning I abased him.
خذع:
The letters khā', dhāl and 'ayn denote cutting a thing. One says he *khadda'ahu* with the sword, meaning he struck him with it. The line of Abū Dhu'ayb is related:
And both of them, heroes of the encounter, were *mukhadda'* —
meaning as if each had been struck with the sword again and again. One says a plant is *mukhadda'* when its top has been eaten off. Some people misspelled this word as *mujadda'*, and that is wrong.
خذف:
The letters khā', dhāl and fā' are a single root denoting throwing. One says *khadhaftu* with a pebble when you fling it from between your two forefingers.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
As if the pebbles behind her and before her, when her leg flings them up, were the flick of a left-handed man.

1. *al-mikhdhafa* — what is also called *al-miqlā'*, the sling.
2. an *atān* (she-donkey) is *khadhūf* — meaning fat.

Abū Ḥātim said: al-Aṣma'ī said this is meant to say that if she were struck with a pebble it would sink into her belly from the abundance of her fat. What he relates here from these scholars, though little, supports the soundness of the method of derivation we follow — like what we mentioned just before from al-Khalīl in the chapter of *al-ikhdā'*, and like what al-Aṣma'ī said of the fat she-donkey.

3. *al-khadhafān* — a kind of gait in camels, with little forward throw to it.
خذق: The letters khā', dhāl and qāf are not a root; rather the word in it belongs to the chapter of letter-substitution. One says a bird *khadhaqa* when it excreted. I take this to be *khazaqa* originally, with the zāy replaced by dhāl.
خذل: The letters khā', dhāl and lām are a single root indicating the abandoning of a thing and desisting from it. Al-khidhlān: withholding help. One says "khadhalat al-waḥshiyya," of a wild animal that stayed behind with her young; she is khadhūl. He cited: "one who stays behind (khadhūl), watching over a herd in a thicket, reaching for the tips of the thorn-fruit and going about." From this chapter also: "takhādhalat rijlāhu," his legs grew weak, from a line about a leg weakened, not through lameness. And another said, of fallen ones scattered by misfortune, weak (mutakhādhil). A man is khudhala, one who continually abandons others.
خذم:
The letters khā', dhāl and mīm denote cutting. One says *khadhamtu* a thing, meaning I cut it.

1. *sayf mikhdham* — a sharp, cutting sword.
2. *al-khadhmā'* — a she-goat whose ear is split crosswise without full separation.
3. *al-khadham* — speed of gait; and it belongs to this chapter.
خر:
The letters khā' and rā' are a single root, and it is agitation and falling, accompanied by a sound.

1. al-kharīr — the sound of water.
2. 'aynun kharrāra — a murmuring spring; one says kharrat takhirr — it murmured/gushed.
3. One says of a man, when his stomach is upset and rumbles: taḳharkhara.
4. kharra — when he fell.

Abū Khirāsh said, describing a sword, in a line of verse:
With it I leave the armoured warrior upon his hands,
falling — you would take him for a fresh-poisoned vulture.

Qashīb is poison mixed with the bait for it; one says qashaba lahu, when poison was mixed for it. This is done so that it may be trapped by it. Similar to it is a line of Ṭufayl's:
He clothed her in the moist plumage of every young vulture rising to its nest, and every dark, poisoned one.

Al-muqashshab is a vulture for which poison has been laid in carrion, so that it may be trapped. Nāhiḍ means young in age. A vulture, when it grows old, turns black.

5. One says: kharra al-mā'u al-arḍa — the water cut through the ground.
6. al-akhirra, singular kharīr — low, sunken places between two hillocks, running in a line.

Al-Aḥmar said: I heard one of the Arabs reciting Labīd's line: "at the akhirra of al-Thalabūt."

7. al-khurr of the millstone — the place into which the wheat is thrown [the hopper]. This fits the pattern of the root, because the grain pours down (yakhirru) into it.
8. khurr al-udhun — the ear's opening, likened to that hopper.
خرب:
The letters khā', rā' and bā' are a root indicating breaking a gap into something, and piercing it.

Al-khurba is the hole. Al-ʿabd al-akhrab is a slave with a pierced ear. Al-khurb is the socket of the hip. Al-khurba is also the loop of a water-skin.

From this root, which is the core sense: al-kharāb, ruin, the opposite of habitation. Al-khurb is the point where a great mass of sand-dune breaks off. Al-khārib is specifically a camel-thief; this fits the pattern, because theft is like making a breach in someone's property.

Irregular, outside the root's pattern: al-kharab, the male houbara bustard, plural khirbān. Akhrub is a place-name. A line is quoted:
We went out racing the wild game between Thuʿāla ... and Ruḥayyāt, to the mountain pass of Akhrub.
خرت:
The letters khā', rā' and tā' are a root denoting perforation and the like.

1. *al-khurt* — the eye of a needle.
2. *al-akharāt* — the rings at the ends of straps.
3. *al-khirrīt* — the skilled guide, expert in showing the way; named so because he cuts through the wasteland as if entering its holes and passages.
4. *kharatnā al-arḍ* — we came to know the land so well that its paths were never hidden from us.
خرث:
The letters khā', rā' and thā' are a single word, meaning the discarded odds and ends of a thing. The discarded remnants of a house's furnishings are called *khurthiyy*.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And all the furnishings of the house became *khurthiyy* — worthless remnants.
خرج:
The letters khā', rā' and jīm are two roots, and it is possible to join them together, except that we have taken the plain road. The first is passing out of a thing, and the second is the difference of two colours.

As for the first, it is our saying kharaja, yakhruju, khurūjan - he went out. And al-khurāj is a boil on the body. Al-kharāj and al-kharj are the tribute, because it is property that the giver brings out. Al-khārijī is the man who has made himself a chief with no ancestry behind him, as though he came out by himself, and he is like the one of whom it is said, in a line of verse:
The soul of 'Iṣām made 'Iṣām a lord.

And al-khurūj is the coming out of a cloud; one says, how fine is its coming out. And so-and-so is the khirrīj of so-and-so when he learns from him, as though it were he who brought him out from the bounds of ignorance. And one says a she-camel is mukhtarija when she comes out in the shape of a he-camel. Al-kharūj is the she-camel that goes out from among the camels and kneels off to one side; and it is from going out. Al-kharīj, as they say, is a game of the young men of the Arabs, in which one says: kharāji, kharāji. Al-Hudhalī said, in a line of verse:
I lay wakeful for it at nightfall, as though they were flashing streamers among which the call of kharīj is made.

And Banū al-Khārijiyya are a tribe, and the relative adjective from it is khārijī.

As for the other root: al-kharaj is two colours, between black and white; one says an ostrich hen is kharjā' and a male ostrich is akhraj. And it is said that al-kharjā' is the ewe whose legs are white up to her flank.

Of this section: an earth is mukharraja when its plants are in one place and not in another. And the grazing beasts kharrajat the pasture, when they ate some of it and left some. And that is what we mentioned of the difference of two colours.
خرد:
The letters khā', rā' and dāl are a single root, meaning the guarding of a thing from being touched.

1. *al-jāriya al-kharīda* — the girl who has never been touched.

Ibn al-A'rābī related: a pearl is *kharīda* when it has not been pierced; he said every unmarried woman is *kharīda*.

2. *jāriya kharūd* — a bashful girl; and it belongs to this chapter.

Ibn al-A'rābī said: a man *akhrada* when he spoke little; one says, what is the matter with you, so quiet? This follows the pattern given, because in it is a guarding of speech and of the tongue.
خرز:
The letters khā', rā' and zāy denote gathering one thing to another and joining it to it.

1. *kharz al-jild* — stitching leather, from this.
2. *al-kharaz* — beads, well known, because they are strung and set one against another.
3. the vertebrae of the back are *kharaz*, for being arranged in a row.
4. *kharazāt al-malik* — the king's beads: whenever a king among them completed a year of rule, a bead was added to his crown, so that the number of years of his reign would be known by it.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
He tended the beads of kingship twenty years, and twenty more, until he perished, gray hair spreading over him.
خرس:
The letters khā', rā' and sīn are three roots: the first a kind of vessel, the second the absence of speech, the third a kind of food.

The first: *al-khars*, with the rā' unvowelled, is the large jar, and its maker is called *al-kharrās*.

The second: *al-kharas* in the tongue is the loss of speech. This is carried over, so:

1. a troop is *kharsā'* when it falls silent from the abundance of its armour, having no clatter of weapons.
2. milk is *akhras* when it is thick and makes no sound in the vessel as it is drawn.
3. a cloud is *kharsā'* when it has no thunder in it.

The third: *al-khurs* and *al-khursa* are food prepared for a woman who has given birth; that food is her *khursa*.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
If the woman in childbirth was not given food to mark her firstborn, and her weaned child was not quieted with a scrap of food.

Some people claimed that a young woman is called *khurūs* in the early days of her first pregnancy, and they cited:
Your worst is close at hand, and your milk is the milk of a *khurūs* among the young rabbits, a firstborn.
One also says *al-khurūs* is the one scant in milk.
خرش:
The letters khā', rā' and shīn are a single root, denoting a swelling in a thing together with holes in it.

The origin is *al-khirshā'*, the skin a snake sheds; everything sharing that quality is then likened to it, so foam is called *al-khirshā'*.

Muzarrid said, in a line of verse:
When the froth of the milk touches his nose, he curls back his two lips for the clear milk and is content.

One says the sun rose *fī khirshā'*, meaning in a haze of dust. And a man throws down the *kharāshī* of his chest, meaning thick spit. This is the origin.

As for their saying "a dog of Khirāsh", that is with us a matter of letter-substitution.

The rajaz poet said:
As if her two teats, whenever they gave milk, were two dogs of Khirāsh, roused, then growling.

It may also be from *kharashtu* a thing, meaning you scratched it — and that belongs to the first sense, as if when scratched it startles and swells and tears open. As for their saying *ikhtarashtu* a thing, meaning you earned it, that too is with us a matter of letter-substitution: it is really *iqtarasha*, mentioned in its own chapter. Ibn al-A'rābī used to say *ikhtarasha* means earned, and used to relate the saying: "many a breast opened, and plunder acquired, and a lizard hunted out of its hole" — others relate it as "and plunder *iqtarasha*".

*Al-khirāsh* is a light branding-mark. *Al-kharasha* is a kind of fly, and it may belong to some of what has already been mentioned.
خرص:
The letters khā', rā' and ṣād are roots very different from one another.

The first is al-kharṣ, guessing the amount of a thing.

1. kharaṣtu al-nakhl — I guessed the palm trees, meaning I estimated their fruit.
2. al-kharrāṣ — the liar, named from this, because he says what he does not know and has no right to say.

Another root: a ring of gold is called khurṣ.

Another root: it is every branch put out from a thing that branches.

1. al-kharīṣ, of the sea — an inlet running from it.
2. al-kharṣ — any rod cut from a tree, plural khirṣān.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
You see the straight lance-shafts flung down, as if it were the trimming of twigs by the hands of the women who split palm fronds.

3. From this same root they name the spear al-kharṣ. He said, in a line of verse:
The straightening-frame bit into the Khaṭṭī spear-shafts.
4. al-akhrāṣ — rods the honey-gatherer carries with him.

Another root: al-kharaṣ, a description of one who is hungry and numb with cold. One says kharisa kharṣan.
خرض: The letters khā', rā' and ḍād. Some people claimed that *al-kharīḍ* is a young girl newly come of age, a beautiful one. This is not something to be relied on, and it has no sound derivation behind it.
خرط:
The letters khā', rā' and ṭā' are a single root, regular and consistent, and it is a thing's passing away and slipping out. The branches of this chapter all return to it.

1. *ikhtaraṭtu al-sayf* — I drew the sword swiftly from its sheath.
2. *kharaṭtu 'an al-shajarati waraqahā* — I stripped the tree of its leaves; as if, in doing so, the tree slipped free of them.

Some said *al-kharṭ* is the bark of a stick, and it belongs to this same sense.

3. *al-kharūṭ* — a riding beast that pulls its rein free of its holder's hand and goes off.
4. *ikhrawwaṭa bihim al-sayr* — the journey stretched out.
5. *al-makhrūṭ* — a man long in the face.
6. *istakhraṭa* in weeping — he broke into weeping and persisted in it steadily.
7. *al-kharaṭ* — a disease striking a ewe's udder so her milk comes out clotted like pieces of bowstring; such a ewe is *mukhriṭ*, or *mikhrāṭ* if it is her habit.
8. *al-makhārīṭ* — snakes, once their skins have sloughed off.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Abū Qābūs clothed me in a flowing robe, as if it were the sloughed skin of young *makhārīṭ*.

9. *rajul kharūṭ* — a reckless man, riding his own impulse; and that follows the pattern.
10. *inkharaṭa 'alaynā* — he burst upon us with harsh words.
11. *inkharaṭa jismu fulān* — his body grew thin, as if it had wholly slipped free of its flesh.
12. *kharaṭtu al-faḥl fī al-shawl* — you set the stallion loose among the she-camels.
خرع:
The letters khā', rā' and 'ayn are a single root denoting looseness, and things are then likened to it.

1. *al-khirwa'* — a soft plant; from it comes the word for a woman who is *kharī'*, meaning soft. Al-Aṣma'ī used to deny that *al-kharī'* means the licentious woman, and used to say she is the one who bends and sways from softness.
2. a camel's lip is *kharī'* when it hangs down.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
A drooping [lip] of the she-camel's cheek-strap, its edges swaying, like the folds of a worn-out garment full of creases.

He took this from 'Utayba ibn Mirdās, in his saying, in a line of verse:
She keeps the sharp edge of the fangs from herself with a lip, drooping like the narrow-waisted Aḥwarī sandal-leather.

3. *al-khara'* — looseness in the joints.
4. *al-khurā'* — madness in a she-camel; and it belongs to this chapter.

Among what is likened to this looseness is splitting: one says *kharaʿtuhu fa-nkharaʿa*, I split it and it split.

5. *ikhtaraʿa* a lie — he fabricated it, devised it.
6. *inkharaʿat aʿḍā' al-baʿīr* — the camel's limbs came loose from their places.
7. *al-mukharraʿ* — one of inconsistent character. There is doubt about this word; if sound, it comes from the madness of she-camels above.
8. *khariʿat al-nakhla* — the palm shed its old sheath-base, *takhraʿu* in the present tense.
خرف:
The letters khā', rā' and fā' are two roots: one is that a thing is picked, the other is the road.

The first:
1. *ikhtaraftu al-thamara* — I picked the fruit.
2. *al-kharīf* — the season in which fruit is picked, autumn.
3. *arḍ makhrūfa* — land struck by the autumn rain.
4. *al-mikhraf* — the vessel in which picking is done.

The Messenger of God, God's blessings and peace upon him, said: "The one who visits the sick walks upon the harvesting-grounds of Paradise until he returns." The Arabs say *ukhruf lanā*, meaning pick for us.

5. *al-makhraf*, with the mīm opened, — a grove of palms.

Some people of language said the lamb is called *kharūf* because it grazes here and there.

The other root:
6. *al-makhrafa* — the road.

In the hadith: "you were left upon the like of the *makhrafa* of the livestock", meaning upon the clear, straight road.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
So I struck him with a worn blade — you would think its track a clear road, cut through rugged ground, well-trodden.

7. *al-ikhrāf* — a she-camel giving birth at the same time of year in which she conceived; and this follows the pattern, as if she kept to that same course without deviating.

One word remains in this chapter that is, to us, anomalous and outside the pattern: *al-kharaf*, the corruption of the mind from old age.
خرق:
The letters khā', rā' and qāf are a single root: the tearing of a thing and cutting through it; all its branches go back to that.

One says: kharaqtu the land, meaning I crossed through it. The wind ikhtaraqat the land, meaning it swept through it. Al-mukhtaraq is the place through which the winds sweep.

Ru'ba said, in a line of verse:
And [many a] dust-dark deep desert, empty of any passage through it.

1. al-kharq — a desert waste, because the winds sweep through it.
2. al-khirq — the generous man, as if he breaks through freely in doing good.
3. al-kharq — also the opposite of gentleness, as if the one who does it tears roughly through things.
4. al-takharruq — fabricating lies.
5. rīḥ kharqā' — a wind that does not keep blowing steadily from one direction.
6. al-kharqā' — a woman not skilled at any work.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Clumsy at good — she cannot find her way to it — yet skilled in doing harm, to family and neighbor.

7. al-kharqā', said of sheep and others — the one whose ear is pierced.
8. ba'īr akhruq — a camel whose toe-cleft touches the ground before its whole foot-pad does.
9. al-khirqa — a rag, well known; plural khiraq. Dhū al-Khiraq al-Ṭuhawī was named that for his line of verse: "Upon it are feathers and rags."
10. al-khirqa, said of locusts — a swarm of them.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
There has landed, in the courtyard of Ibn Wāṣil, a swarm of a locust-band, come down to settle.

Al-Farrā' said: one says, "I passed by a kharīq of land between two bare stretches" — land that has grown wide and whose plant growth has become abundant; plural khuruq.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
In wide fertile tracts, one grows full from their soft ramrām plants.

11. al-kharaq — bewilderment and astonishment. One says: the gazelle kharaqa, meaning: the hunter circled around it until it grew stunned and froze to the ground. The same is said, by comparison, of a man: kharaqa in his house, meaning he did not budge.
12. al-khurraq — a bird that presses itself to the ground.

The usage is then broadened, so that al-kharaq is also said to mean shyness. It is related of some of the Arabs: "She has no excessive tallness that mars her, nor shortness that makes her bashful" — meaning: she does not feel shame over it.
13. al-makhārīq — what children play with, made of twisted rags.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Twisted rag-toys, in the hands of our players.
خرم:
The letters khā', rā' and mīm are a single root, a kind of cutting-off.

1. *kharamtu* a thing — I cut it off.
2. *ikhtaramahum al-dahr* — time cut them down.
3. *khurima* a man — the cartilage of his nose was cut, short of full amputation; the description is *akhram*.
4. every cut-off end of a thing is a *makhrim* — so the cut-off spur of a mountain is called *makhrim*.
5. *al-khawrama* — the tip of a person's nose, being its cut-off, furthest part.
6. *akhram al-katif* — the edge of the shoulder-blade's ridge.
7. *yamīn dhāt makhārim* — an oath having ways out (*makhārim*, singular *makhrim*): an oath that admits no interpretation and no atonement has no way out for its meaning and no release from its ruling; but if it can be interpreted, it has *makhārim*, ways out and openings, and becomes like a thing full of holes.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
There is no good in wealth bound by an oath, nor in an oath with no way out — meaning one with no atonement, which binds and constrains.

8. *al-khawram* — a rock full of holes.

Among what runs as a proverb and a comparison is their saying "so-and-so's fire-stick fell still", said when his anger settled.
خز:
The letters khā' and zāy are two roots: one is that something is driven firmly into another, the other is a kind of animal.

1. al-khazz, khazz al-ḥā'iṭ — setting thorns firmly into a wall.
2. One says khazzahu bi-sahmin — he shot him with an arrow and lodged it firmly in him.
3. wa ṭa'anahu bi-l-rumḥi fakhtazzahu — he stabbed him with the spear, driving it firmly in.

Ibn Aḥmar said, in a line of verse:
Until I drove it firmly into his heart with the lance.

As for their saying ba'īrun khuzakhiz, meaning strong/sturdy, this belongs to the root, because its limbs seem to be firmly set in place, made firm.

4. al-khuzaz — the male hare, plural khizzān.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And the sons of Nuwayjiya, who are as though
bare-legged ones marked with white anklets, among the hares.
[The sense of this line is obscure; rendered as closely as the text allows.]
خزب: The letters khā', zāy and bā' denote swelling and a rise in flesh. One says a she-camel *khazibat*, a *khazab*, meaning her udder swelled. The origin is their saying flesh is *khazib*, meaning soft; every soft piece of flesh is *khaziba*.
خزر:
The letters khā', zāy and rā' are two roots: one a kind of cooked dish, the other narrowness in a thing.

The first: *al-khazīr* is flour kneaded with fat; the Arabs used to mock the one who ate it.

The second: *al-khazar* is narrowness and smallness of the eye. One says a man is *akhzar* and a woman *khazrā'*. *Takhāzara* — a man narrowed his eyelids to sharpen his sight.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
When I narrow my eyes, though there is no narrowness of the eye in me.
خزع:
The letters khā', zāy and 'ayn are a single root denoting cutting and being cut off.

1. *takhazza'a fulān 'an aṣḥābihi* — he lagged behind his companions on a journey; and for this the tribe of Khuzā'a was named, because they lagged behind their fellow-travellers and settled at Mecca.

This is the saying of the poet, in a line of verse:
When we came down into the belly of Marr, Khuzā'a lagged behind us with their heavy-laden troops settling.

2. *takhazza'nā al-shay' baynanā* — we divided the thing among ourselves into pieces.
3. *al-khawza'a* — a strip of sand cut off from the main body of the dunes.
خزف: The letters khā', zāy and fā' amount to nothing — not a sound root. Al-khazaf is this well-known thing [pottery], and we do not know whether the word is genuine Arabic or not. Ibn Durayd said: *al-khazf* is the swinging of the hand while walking. This is among the oddities of Abū Bakr [Ibn Durayd].
خزق:
The letters khā', zāy and qāf are a root denoting a thrown thing's passing through, or its sticking fast.

1. *al-khāziq* among arrows — the one that hits the target dead-centre and sticks fast in the target-sheet.
2. *khazaqa al-ṭā'ir* — the bird excreted.
3. *al-khazq* — piercing, stabbing.

The pattern is one and the same throughout.
خزل: The letters khā', zāy and lām are a single root denoting being cut off and weakness. One says *khazaltu* a thing, meaning I cut it off. *Inkhazala* so-and-so, meaning he grew weak.
خزم:
The letters khā', zāy and mīm are a root denoting a thing's being pierced. So everything pierced is *makhzūm*.

1. all birds are *makhzūma*, because the cartilage of their beaks is pierced — for this an ostrich is called *mukhazzam*.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And I raise my voice for the pierced-beaked ostrich.

2. *khazamtu al-jarād fī al-'ūd* — I strung locusts on a stick.
3. *khazamtu al-ba'īr* — I put a hair cord, a *khizāma*, through the cartilage of a camel's nose.

By this pattern a certain tree is named *khazama*, because it has a bark that ropes are twisted from, and such ropes are called *khizāmāt*.

Falling outside this chapter as an anomaly is *al-khazūma*, the cow. And another word: one says *khāzamtu* a man on the road, meaning he takes one path and you take another until the two of you meet in one place. *Akhzam* is a man's name. As for their saying that *al-akhzam* is the male snake, that is a claim open to doubt.
خزن:
The letters khā', zā' and nūn are a root that points to guarding a thing. One says khazantu al-dirham and other things khaznan — I stored it away; and khazantu al-sirr — I kept the secret. A poet said, in a line of verse:
If a man does not keep his tongue guarded over himself, then he is no guardian of anything else.

As for khazina al-laḥm — the meat's smell turned — it is not from this. It is rather from words with their letters transposed, and the original is khaniza. It has been mentioned in its own place. Ṭarafa said, using khuzin:
Then her flesh is not stored away among us; only the hoarder's flesh is stored away.
خزو:
The letters khā', zāy and a weak letter are two roots: one is governance, the other is driving away.

As for the first: their saying *khazawtuhu*, meaning you governed him.

Labīd said, in a line of verse:
And govern her with piety, for God the Most Exalted.

Dhū al-Iṣba' said, in a line of verse:
By God, your cousin — you have not surpassed me in lineage, nor are you my ruler, that you should govern me.

As for the other: their saying *akhzāhu Allāh*, meaning God drove him away and was wrathful with him; the noun from it is *al-khizy*. From this same chapter is their saying a man *khaziya*, meaning he felt shame at the ugliness of his deed — *khazāya* — so he is *khazyān*; because when he does that and feels shame, he draws back and moves away.

Jarīr said, in a line of verse:
And indeed a sanctuary that none but Fartanā protected, nor any but Ibn Dhī al-Kīrayn, is now disgraced, forsaken.
خس:
The letters khā' and sīn are two roots: one is the meanness of a thing, the other is the passing of a thing from hand to hand.

1. al-khasīs — the lowly; one says khassa al-rajulu nafsahu and akhassa, when he did a mean deed.
2. From this root: jāwazat al-nāqatu khasīsatahā — the she-camel passed beyond her lowest age-class, when she passed the ages called ḥiqqa, jadhaʿa and thaniyya and caught up with buzūl [full maturity]. This fits the pattern, because all these ages fall below buzūl.
3. The second root is the Arabs' saying: takhāssa al-qawmu al-amra — the people passed the matter around and competed over it, each wanting to be the one who took it.
4. One says: hādhihi al-umūru khisāsun baynahum — these matters pass by turns among them.

Ibn al-Zib'arā said, in a line of verse:
And gifts pass by turns among them,
and the daughters of fate play with everyone.
خسأ: The letters khā', sīn and hamza indicate driving away. One says: I khasa'tu the dog (drove it off). In the Qur'an: {He said, "Be driven away in it, and do not speak to Me"} [al-Mu'minūn: 108], as one would say: "be gone."
خسر: The letters khā', sīn and rā' are one root pointing to falling short. Of that are al-khusr and al-khusrān, loss, like al-kufr and al-kufrān, and al-furq and al-furqān. And one says khasartu al-mīzān and akhsartuhu, when you make the scale fall short. And God knows best.
خسف:
The letters khā', sīn and fā' are one root pointing to sinking down and going in, and to it the branches of the section go back. So al-khasf and al-khasaf are the sinking in of the surface of the earth. God, exalted be He, said: {so We caused the earth to swallow him and his house} [al-Qaṣaṣ: 81].

And from the section is the eclipse of the moon. And some of the people of the language used to say: al-khusūf is for the moon and al-kusūf is for the sun. And one says a well khasīf, when its stony side is broken so that it falls in, and its water is not drained away. A poet said, in a line of verse:
A copious one, of the deep old wells, the caved-in.

And the eye inkhasafat — it went blind. And the lean one is called khāsif, as though his flesh had sunk and gone in. And from it: he spent the night ʿalā al-khasf, when he spent it hungry, as though what he wanted of food had vanished from him. And he was content with al-khasf — that is, with abasement. And one says: the people fell into akhāsīf of the ground, and that is the soft ground that almost sinks in for its softness.

And of what is carried upon the section is their calling the cloud that [brings] much water khasīf, as though it were likened to the well we have mentioned. And so too their saying a she-camel khasīfa — that is, abundant in milk. As for their saying that al-khasf is the walnut that is eaten, I do not know what that is.
خسق: The letters khā', sīn and qāf are not a root, because the sīn in it stands in for a zāy — the word is altered only to shift part of its meaning. *Al-khāziq* among arrows is the one that sticks fast when it strikes the target; *al-khāsiq* is the one that catches but does not stick fast. It is said — and God knows best whether it is sound — that a she-camel is *khasūq* when she is of bad temper.
خسل:
The letters khā', sīn and lām are a single root indicating weakness and low worth.

1. al-makhsūl — the despised, discarded one.
2. rijāl khussal, muthallal, sukhkhal — weak men.
3. al-kawākib al-makhsūla — the unknown stars, which have no names.

A poet said, in lines of verse:
We are the Pleiades and its Orion, and we are the two bright stars al-Simākān and al-Mirzam.
And you are but obscure stars, seen in the sky, yet unknown.
خش:
The letters khā' and shīn are a single root, and it is entering and penetrating.

1. One says: khashsha al-rajulu fī al-sharr — he entered into trouble.
2. rajulun mikhashsh — a resolute man, bold in venturing into the night.
3. al-khashshā' — the place of wasps, because the swarm burrows into it.

Dhū al-Iṣba' said, in a line of verse:
If you see his arrows, then like a wasps' nest
when its brood is disturbed, stinging fiercely.
[The line is obscure; rendered as closely as the text allows.]

4. al-khashkhāsh — a crowd, because they are a people who gather and intermingle.

Al-Kumayt said, in a line of verse:
And its densely-packed throng, when they encamped.
