5. al-khashsh — putting the khishāsh, a nose-peg, into a camel's nose. One says khashashtuhu, so it is makhshūsh; the peg may be made of wood.
6. khashāsh al-arḍ — the ground's small creatures, its vermin.
7. As for the man called khashāsh, small-headed, it is said with both vowel patterns (khashāsh or khishāsh). This fits the pattern, because he penetrates into a matter as it deserves.

Ṭarafa said, in a line of verse:
I am the capable man you know me for,
sharp as the head of a darting, flickering snake.

And from this root — though outwardly it seems far from the pattern — are al-khushashāwān: two bones that protrude behind the ears. The single one is also called khashshā'. No word of the pattern fu'lā' — with the first letter carrying a u-vowel and the middle letter carrying none — occurs in Arabic besides this one and qūbā' [ringworm], whose more original form gives the middle letter a vowel too.
خشب:
The letters khā', shīn, and bā' are a single root indicating roughness and coarseness.

1. al-akhshab — a rugged, massive mountain. From this is the Prophet's saying, peace be upon him, about Mecca: "It will not pass away until its two akhshab pass away," meaning its two [named] mountains. And a speaker's description of a camel, in a line of verse:
You would think, above the herd of she-camels, it were a rugged mountain.
He likened its height above the she-camels to a mountain.
2. al-khashīb — a sword whose forging has only just begun, and in this state it can only be rough. An arrow is makhshūb or khashīb when it is still being roughly shaped. A camel that is khashīb is coarse. All of this, in my view, is derived from al-khashab, wood.
3. takhashshabat al-ibilu — the camels eat dry, withered pasture.
4. jabhatun khashbāʾ — a forehead that is unpleasant, dry, uneven.
5. ẓalīmun khashīb — a male ostrich that is coarse.

Abū ʿUbayd said: al-khashīb is the sword whose forging has only just begun; then the usage spread until, among them, al-khashīb came to mean the polished, finished sword instead.
خشر: The letters khā', shīn and rā' indicate inferiority and lowness. Al-khushāra is what is left on the table, having no good in it. One says 'khashartu akhshiru khashran' when you leave the poor part behind. And al-khushāra of barley is said to be that which has no kernel, like bran. And 'so-and-so is of the khushāra of people' means he is among their lowest.
خشع:
The letters khā', shīn and 'ayn are a single root pointing to sinking low. One says khasha'a when a man sinks down and lowers his head, yakhsha'u khushū'an. It is close in meaning to khuḍū' (submission), except that khuḍū' is in the body and in admitting one's abasement, while khushū' is in the voice and in the eyes. God Almighty said: {their eyes lowered} [al-Qalam: 43].

Ibn Durayd said: al-khāshi' is the meek man and the one who bows. One says ikhtasha'a fulān, but one does not say ikhtasha'a baṣaruhu — his eye was lowered. And one says khasha'a kharāshiyya ṣadrihi when he throws up sticky phlegm. Al-khush'a is a patch of hard, high ground over which soft ground has got the upper hand. One says quff khāshi' — high stony ground lying flat against the earth. Ibn al-A'rābī said: balda khāshi'a — a dust-coloured land. Jarīr said, in a line of verse:
When the news of al-Zubayr came, they humbled themselves ... the walls of the city and the low-lying mountains.

Al-Khalīl said: khasha'a sanām al-ba'īr — the camel's hump shrank away until little of it was left.
خشف:
The letters khā', shīn and fā' indicate obscurity, concealment, and what is near to that.

1. al-khushshāf — the night bird, well known (the bat).
2. al-mikhshaf — the man bold in going about at night.
3. khashafa yakhshifu khushūfan — said of one who went off into the land; this fits the pattern of the root.
4. al-akhshaf — the camel whose skin is covered by mange, because when it covers him, it has concealed him.
5. sayf khashīf — a sword that cuts true, but with something obscure in its blow.
6. al-khashfa — a sound that is not loud.

Deviating from the root is al-khishf, the fawn of a gazelle; this word is sound. And they say — God knows best — that al-khashīf is snow, and also dried saffron. And 'khashaftu ra'sahu bi'l-hajar' — I struck his head with a stone, when you crushed it. If these three words are sound, then their pattern is a different pattern, from smashing and breaking.
خشل:
The letters khā', shīn and lām are a single root indicating pettiness and smallness. They say: al-khashl is the inferior part of anything. They say its origin is the small ones among the fruit of the muql-tree (dom-palm fruit), and that is al-khashl, one of them being a khashla.

Al-Shammākh said, describing an eagle and its nest, in a line of verse:
You see pieces of snakes in it, their skulls like the stripped khashal.
He means that in its nest are the heads of serpents.

And the studs on jewelry — on anklets and bracelets — are called khashl, either by way of comparison, or because that is the smallest part of the jewelry. Al-Asma'ī used to explain al-Shammākh's line on this basis; he said the poet likened the snakes' heads to that, and this is the more fitting reading.

It is also said that al-khashl is the egg once what is inside it has been emptied out. If this is correct, then nothing is more petty than that — and it fits the pattern of the root.
خشم:
The letters khā', shīn and mīm are a single root indicating elevation.

1. al-khayshūm — the nose.
2. al-khasham — a disease that afflicts it.
3. a man thick in the nose is khushām.
4. al-mukhashsham — one into whose nose the drink has risen, so that he grew drunk.
5. khayāshīm al-jibāl — the noses (jutting spurs) of mountains.

One word deviates from the root, if it is sound: they say 'khashima al-lahm' — the meat spoiled.
خشن:
The letters khā', shīn and nūn are a single root, and it is the opposite of softness.

1. shay' khashin — a rough thing.
2. al-akhshan — they scarcely say anything but this of a stone; the rough one.

A poet said:
The rough stone, and the mountain pass.

3. ikhshawshana al-rajul — the man roughened himself, when he took on hardship and gave up soft living.
4. katība khashnā' — a bristling squadron, meaning one abundant in weapons.
خشي:
The letters khā', shīn and the weak letter point to fear and dread, and then figurative use is carried upon it. So al-khashya is fear. And a man is khashyān, full of fear. And khāshanī fulān fa-khashaytuhu — so-and-so vied with me in fear and I outdid him, that is, I was stronger in fear than he.

And the figurative use is their saying khashītu in the sense of "I knew". A poet said, in a line of verse:
And I knew that whoever follows the guidance ... will dwell in the Gardens with the Prophet Muhammad.
That is, I knew. And one says: this place is akhshā than that, that is, more to be feared.

And of what strays from the chapter, though the two may just possibly be joined at a stretch, is al-khashw: dried-up, poor dates. And khashat al-nakhla takhshū khashwan — the palm bore such dates. And al-khashiyy of meat is the dried.
خص:
The letters khā' and ṣād form a regular, consistent root, indicating a gap and a breach.

1. al-khaṣāṣ — the gaps between the three stones a cooking-pot rests on over the fire.
2. One says of the moon: badā min khaṣāṣati al-saḥāb — it appeared through a gap in the clouds.

Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
It reached its gap and so appeared faint,
weary, while the rest of it slipped entirely away.

3. al-khaṣāṣa — dire poverty.
4. And also: a breach in one's circumstances.
5. From this root: khaṣaṣtu fulānan bi-shay'in khuṣūṣiyyatan [I singled so-and-so out for something specially] — this fits the pattern, because when one thing is singled out a gap is thereby opened between it and the rest, whereas generality is the opposite of that.
6. al-khiṣīṣā — [another word for] being singled out.
خصب: The letters khā', sād and bā' are a single root, and it is the opposite of drought. 'Makān mukhsib' — a fertile place: khasīb. And from this chapter is al-khisāb, the low daqal-variety of palm.
خصر:
The letters khā', sād and rā' are two roots: one is cold, the other the middle of a thing.

As for the first: their saying 'khasira al-insān yakhsaru khasaran' — a person felt pained by cold in his extremities. 'Khasira yawmunā khasran' — our day's cold intensified; and a cold day is 'yawm khasir.'

Hassān said:
Many an uncle of mine — if you had seen him — light of step, on the cold day.

As for the other: al-khasr is a person's waist, or another's, the narrow part above the two hips. Al-mukhassar is the one narrow at the waist; from this comes the mukhassara sandal (narrow at the waist). As for al-mikhsara, it is a rod or staff that the speaker carries when he speaks; plural makhāsir.

A poet said:
When they joined their right hands together with the staffs.

It was named that because it lies level with a person's waist. Al-mukhāsara is for a man to take another's hand and the two to walk together, each one's hand at the other's waist.

A poet said:
Then I walked hand-in-hand with her to the green pavilion, she stepping upon polished marble.

Khasr al-raml — the middle of the sand-dune.

A poet said:
They took the middles of the sand, then crossed it, on every smith-wrought saddle, and a fresh one, and a padded one.

Al-ikhtisār in speech is leaving off what is superfluous in it and condensing its meanings. Some philologists used to say al-ikhtisār is taking the middle parts of speech and leaving its branches. And it is said that al-mukhāsara on a road is like al-mukhāzama, which has already been mentioned. God knows best.
خصف:
The letters khā', ṣād and fā' are a single root indicating one thing being joined to another. It applies consistently and directly.

Al-khaṣf is the patching of a sandal, laying a matching layer over it. Al-mikhṣaf is the awl, the leather-punch. Al-Hudhalī said, in a line of verse:
Until I came to the nest of a powerful eagle ... black, the tip of her beak like an awl.
He means by “the nest of the powerful one” the eagle's nest.

From this root: al-ikhtiṣāf, for a naked person to take broad leaves, or something similar, over his private parts, to cover himself with. Al-khaṣīfa is curdled milk over which fresh milk is poured.

From this root too — though the two differ, the first being the joining of one matching thing to another, the second the joining of one thing to another without matching — is their saying ḥabl khuṣayf, a rope with black and white strands in it. Some philologists said: anything with two colors combined is khuṣayf, most often black and white. A horse is akhṣaf when its white patch rises from its belly up its sides.

From this root: al-khaṣafa, a woven palm-leaf basket for dates, made in overlapping layers. A line is quoted: “She sells her children for baskets and for dates.” [The point of this line is not clear to me.]

Irregular, outside this whole pattern, is their saying of a she-camel when she gives birth after nine months: khaṣafat takhṣifu khiṣāfan; she is khaṣūf.
خصل:
The letters khā', sād and lām are a single root indicating cutting, and a piece cut from a thing; it is then extended to other things by comparison and metaphor.

1. al-khasl — cutting.
2. sayf mikhsal — a sharply cutting sword.
3. al-khusla of hair — well known (a lock).
4. al-khasīla — any piece of flesh that has sinew running through it.

This is the origin.

Among what is carried on this is al-khusal, the hanging tips of tree branches. And from this chapter too is al-khasl in a wager — that is, to win it; what is won is a portion of the thing. Then it came to be said, 'so-and-so has a good khasla and a bad khasla' (a trait). The origin is what we have stated.
خصم:
The letters khā', ṣād and mīm are two roots: one of them is disputing, and the second is the side of a container.

The first is al-khaṣm, the one who disputes with you. The male and the female are alike in this word. Al-khiṣām is the verbal noun of khāṣamtuhu mukhāṣamatan wa khiṣāman. And the plural is sometimes itself pluralized as khuṣūm. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And my adversaries have gone crooked against me.

The second root is al-khuṣm, the side of the load-sack in which the loop is. And it is said that the side of everything is a khuṣm. And akhṣām al-'ayn is what the eyelids close upon. And it is possible to bring the two roots together and lead them back to one meaning: that is because the side of the load-sack leans over toward one of the two halves, and the khaṣm, the disputant, contends on one side; so the root is one.
خصن: The letters khā', sād and nūn are not a root. It contains a single word, if it is sound: they say al-khasīn is the small axe.
خصى: The letters khā', sād and the weak letter form a single word not extended by analogy except metaphorically, namely their saying 'khasaytu al-fahla khasyan' — I castrated the stallion. And 'I disclaim to you any part in castration.' The meaning of 'khasaytu' is a verb derived from al-khusy (the testicle) — it is to do that to him, just as one says 'zahartuhu' and 'batantuhu' when you struck his back or his belly. Likewise 'khasaytuhu': I removed his two testicles.
خض:
The letters khā' and ḍād are two roots: one is the scantiness and flimsiness of a thing, the other is agitation in something accompanied by wetness.

1. al-khaḍaḍ — white beads worn by slave-women.
2. A foolish man is called khaḍḍāḍ.
3. Worthless, trifling talk is called khaḍaḍ.
4. One says: mā 'alā al-jāriyati khaḍāḍun — meaning she wears no jewellery at all. The sense is that she has nothing on her, not even the cheap khaḍaḍ-beads mentioned first.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And if she came out from the fold of the curtain unadorned,
you would say: a gazelle, wearing not even a bead.

5. As for the other root: takhaḍkhaḍa al-mā' — the water sloshed about.
6. al-khaḍkhāḍ — a kind of tar.
7. One says nabtun khuḍakhiḍ, meaning a plant full of moisture. You say: it is as if it sloshes from being so saturated.

One expression falls outside this root, if it is sound: they said khāḍaḍtu fulānan — when you bartered with him, exchanging one thing for another. This is far from the pattern described.
خضب:
The letters khā', dād and bā' are a single root, and it is the dyeing of a thing.

1. khadabtu al-yad — one says 'khadabtu al-yad' and other things, 'akhdibu' — I dye.
2. khādib — the male ostrich, that being when it has eaten the spring herbage so that its two shins turned red or yellow.

Abū Duwād said, in a line of verse:
He has the two legs of a khādib ostrich, one struck suddenly with terror.

It is said only of the male ostrich, not the female.

3. khudaba — a woman who dyes (with henna) often.
4. khadaba al-nakhl — the palm-tree, when its blossom-spathe turns green.
5. khadaba/ikhdaudaba — some said the tree khadaba, yakhdibu, when it turns green, and also ikhdaudaba.
6. al-kaff al-khadīb — the dyed hand, a star, by way of comparison.
7. al-mikhdab — the washtub, called that because what one dyes with is kept in it.
خضد:
The letters khā', ḍād, and dāl are a single, consistent root: the bending of something supple. One says inkhaḍada al-ʿūdu inkhiḍādan, the branch bent without breaking; khaḍadtuhu, I bent it. Sometimes they extended the meaning and said: khaḍadtu al-shajarata, I stripped the tree of its thorns.

A plant that is khaḍīd — the origin is the first sense, because al-khaḍīd is the lush, tender plant that bends because of its suppleness. As for al-Nābigha's saying, in a line of verse:
Fed by every valley, brimming and roaring, carrying piled-up wreckage of thorn-trees and broken branches.
It is said: al-khaḍad is whatever has been broken off any moist green branch.

One says a camel khaḍada the neck of another camel, when two camels fight and one bends the other's neck.
خضر:
The letters khā', ḍād and rā' are one straight root, and other things are carried upon it. So al-khuḍra, greenness, among the colours is well known. And al-khaḍrā' is the sky, for its colour, as the earth is called al-ghabrā', the dust-coloured. And a squadron khaḍrā', when its upper part is the blackness of iron; and that is because everything that differs from white is in the region of black, and for that reason these descriptions overlap, so that black is called akhḍar. God, exalted be He, said, describing the two gardens: {two of a dark green} [al-Raḥmān: 64] — that is, two black ones. And this is from greenness; for the soft well-watered plant is seen, for the depth of its greenness, black from afar. And for that reason the Sawād, the black land of Iraq, was so called, for the many trees in it. And al-Khuḍr are a people who were so called for the darkness of their colours. And al-khuḍra in the markings of horses is a dustiness with darkness mixed into it. As for the saying, in a line of verse:
And I am the green one — who knows me? — green of skin in the house of the Arabs,

he says: I am of pure stock, because the colours of the Arabs are brown. As for the report, "Beware the greenery of dunghills" — that is the beautiful woman in a bad growing-place, as though she were a fresh tree in a heap of dung. And al-mukhāḍara is the sale of fruits before their fitness appears, and it is forbidden. And as for their saying "khuḍr al-mazād", the green ones of the water-skins, it is said that they are the ones in which remains of water stayed so that they turned green with age; and it is said: rather khuḍr al-mazād are the paunches.

And it is said that al-khaḍār is the first herbage.

As for the saying "his blood went khiḍran", said when it is shed unavenged — I suppose it is from the section. He says: his blood went fresh, like the green plant, which when it is cut is of no use afterward, and comes to nothing and withers.

As for their saying that al-khaḍār is milk with much water in it, it is sound and is from the section, because when it is so the water prevails, and water is called al-asmar, the brown. And we have already said that they call the black akhḍar, and for that reason the sea is called khuḍāra.
خضع:
The letters khā', ḍād and ʿayn are two roots: one is a lowering or sinking down in a thing; the other is a kind of sound.

The first is al-khuḍūʿ, submission. Al-Khalīl said: khaḍaʿa khuḍūʿan means humbling oneself and submitting. Ikhtaḍaʿa fulānun means he humbled and lowered himself. A man is akhḍaʿ and a woman khaḍʿā', both meaning content with submission. Al-ʿAjjāj said, in a line of verse:
And I became a slave, submissive, to the mosquitoes ... it sucks at me as a nursing infant suckles.

Another said: khaḍaʿa al-rajulu, the man bowed down; and akhḍaʿahu al-faqru, poverty made him bow down. A man called khuḍaʿa is one who submits to everyone.

Al-Shaybānī said: al-khaḍaʿ is a bending of the neck down toward the chest; one says a man is akhḍaʿ and a neck is khaḍʿā'. Zuhayr said, in a line of verse:
Heavy in the hindquarters going away, deep-bellied coming toward you ... long-necked, with a bend in her neck seen from the side.

Some Bedouin said: al-khaḍaʿ in male ostriches is a bend in their necks. Abū ʿAmr said: al-mukhtaḍiʿ, among birds of prey, is one whose head is lowered toward the tip of its beak. Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
A red-legged hawk, head lowered, swooped down at her ... its beak stained with the blood of prey.

Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: al-akhḍaʿ means lowered. From this the hadith about al-Zubayr: that he was akhḍaʿ [stooped-necked] and ashʿar [hairy].

Abū Ḥātim said: al-khuḍʿān is for camels to lower their necks while traveling, this being their most intense pace. He said: one also says akhḍaʿahu al-shaybu and khaḍaʿahu, grey hair made him bow down.

He said: one says ikhtaḍaʿa al-faḥlu al-nāqata, the stallion camel mounts alongside the she-camel and then presses her down to the ground with his chest.

One says khaḍaʿa al-najmu, the star leaned toward setting. Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
I sent to her while the stars were sinking ... by night, for fear she would stir and be heard.

Ibn Durayd said: khaḍaʿa al-rajulu and akhḍaʿa, the man khaḍaʿa or akhḍaʿa, when his speech became soft. And in the hadith: he forbade a man from softening his voice for a woman other than his wife, meaning softening his speech to her.

As for the other root, al-Khalīl said: al-khayḍaʿa is the mingling clamor of voices in battle or elsewhere; it is also said to mean the dust of the battlefield. What was said about the dust is worth nothing, because it has no basis in the root's pattern, unless by way of association. Labīd said, concerning al-khayḍaʿa: “The strikers of heads beneath the din of battle.” Some said al-khayḍaʿa is the field of battle itself, because in it opponents yield to one another; and on this view the word returns to belonging with the first root.

Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: “the people fell into khayḍaʿa,” meaning uproar and confusion. He also said: al-khaḍīʿa is the sound heard from an animal's belly when it runs, whose source is not known, and there is no verb formed from it.

Al-Khalīl said: al-khaḍīʿa is the raising of the voice in battle or elsewhere; it was then also applied to what is heard from a horse's belly. A line is quoted:
As though the rumbling of the swift horse's belly ... were the howling of a wolf on rugged ground.

Abū ʿAmr said: one also says khaḍaʿa baṭnuhu khaḍīʿatan, his belly made a sound. Some said: al-khaḍūʿ, among women, is one whose sides make a rattling sound like the sound of a horse's belly. Jandal said, in a line of verse:
She is not a black woman, rumbling in the belly-folds ... nor a big flabby-skinned one with a jiggling hide.

Abū ʿUbayda said: al-khaḍīʿatān are two hollow patches of flesh in a horse's flanks, into which air enters, so that a sound is heard from them when it quickens its pace.

Al-Aṣmaʿī said: it is said, “whips have a khaḍʿa, and swords have a baḍʿa” — al-khaḍʿa being the sound of a whip's strike, and al-baḍʿa being a sword's cutting of flesh.
خضف: The letters khā', dād and fā' are not a root, nor was it given attention. They say 'khadifa' where they mean 'khadama' [chewed with the back teeth]. And al-khadaf: melon, as they say.
خضل:
The letters khā', dād and lām are a single root indicating tenderness and moisture.

1. akhdala al-matar al-ard — the rain drenched the land, so it is mukhdil, and the land is mukhdala.
2. ikhdalla al-shay' — the thing became wet.
3. al-khadil — soft, tender plant.
4. al-khadīla — it is said, the meadow.
5. khudulla — a man's wife, from this same sense, just as she is called talla (dewy), because she is like dew in his eye. Every comfort is khudulla.

A poet said:
If I say the day is a day of comfort and no hardship, I meet troublesome matters instead.
خضم:
The letters khā', dād and mīm are two roots: one a kind of eating, the other indicating abundance and fullness.

As for the first: al-khadm, which is chewing with the back teeth. In the hadith: 'You chew with your back teeth while we chew with our front teeth, and the appointed meeting is with God.'

The other root indicates abundance and fullness.

1. al-khidamm — the man abundant in giving.
2. al-khidamm — a great multitude.

A poet said:
So the great host and the great host came together.

3. al-khidamm — the whetstone, called that by comparison, and that fits the pattern of this root, because it is given much water to soak in. His evidence is the saying of Abū Wajza:
Upon a whetstone given turbid water to drink.
4. al-khudumma — the thick bone of the forearm, its stoutest part. It is said that the greater part of anything is its khudumma.
خضن:
The letters khā', dād and nūn are a single sound root. Al-mukhādana is flirtation.

Al-Tirimmāh said:
And a graceful one among them cast words to me — flirting, or gazing toward the speech of the flirter.
خط:
The letters khā' and ṭā' are a single root; it is a mark that extends in a line.

1. al-khaṭṭ — the line a scribe draws.
2. The line drawn by the diviner [in sand-divination].

God Most High said: {or a remnant of knowledge} [al-Aḥqāf: 4] — they said this means the diviner's line. And it is related: "A prophet among the prophets used to draw such lines; whoever draws the like of his line knows the like of his knowledge."

3. al-khiṭṭa — a plot of land a man marks out for himself, because there is a mark drawn out there in a line.
4. And from it, Khaṭṭ al-Yamāma [a place], to which the khaṭṭī spears are attributed.
5. al-khuṭṭa — a situation; one says huwa bi-khuṭṭati sū' — he is in a bad situation, that being a matter marked out for him and against him.

As for al-arḍ al-khaṭīṭa — land that went unrained-on between two lands that were rained on — this does not belong to this root; its second ṭā' is extra, coming instead from akhṭa'a, to miss, as if the rain had missed it. The proof of this is Ibn 'Abbās's saying: "May God make its rain-star miss it" — meaning, when other land is rained on, the rain misses this one and does not fall on it.

As for their saying "in so-and-so's head is a khuṭyah," some said it is really khuṭṭah. If so, then, as already described, it is a matter that is marked and traced out.
خطب:
The letters khā', ṭā' and bā' are two roots. One of them is speech between two people. One says khāṭabahu yukhāṭibuhu khiṭāban — he addressed him. The khuṭba, the public address, is from that. In marriage it is the asking that a woman be given in marriage. God Most High said: {and there is no blame on you in what you hint at of a proposal to women} [al-Baqara: 235]. Al-khuṭba is the speech that is delivered. One says ikhtaṭaba al-qawm fulānan when they invite him to marry the woman of their household. Al-khaṭb is a matter that befalls; it is called that only because of the addressing back and forth and the discussion that happens in it.

As for the other root, it is two colours differing from each other. Al-Farrā' said: al-khaṭbā' is the she-ass that has a black line along her back. The male ass is akhṭab. Al-akhṭab is also a bird, and perhaps two colours differ upon it.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
When the akhṭab, calling upon the great spreading tree, cried out harshly.

Al-khuṭbān is the colocynth when its colours vary. Al-akhṭab is the ass over which a greenish tinge spreads. And every colour resembling that is akhṭab.
خطر:
The letters khā', tā' and rā' are two roots: one is worth and standing, the other agitation and movement.

The first: they call the equal of a thing its khatīr. So-and-so 'has khatar' — a rank and standing that matches him and suits one like him.

The other root is agitation and movement.

1. khatara al-ba'īr bi-dhanabihi, khatarān — the camel swished its tail.
2. khatara bibālī kadhā, khatran — such-and-such passed through my mind, meaning it passed through the heart swiftly, with no lingering and no delay.
3. khatar fī mishyatihi — he swaggered in his gait.
4. rajul khattār bi'l-rumh — a man who goes about with the spear, thrusting.

A poet said:
Bold champions, wielding the spear in the fray.

5. rumh khattār — a spear that quivers.
6. khatara al-dahr khatarānahu — time throbbed its throb, as one says 'it struck its beat.'
7. al-khatra — a passing recollection.

A poet said:
While we were at al-Balākith, then the open plain, hastening, and the she-camels racing swiftly —
a fleeting thought of you passed over my heart at nightfall, and I could not go on.
خطف:
The letters kha, ta and fa are a single root, regular and consistent in its meaning: snatching away with speed and lightness. Al-khatf is snatching. One says 'khatiftuhu akhtafuhu' and 'khataftuhu akhtifuhu' [two forms of the verb]. Lightning that dazzles/snatches the sight is 'barqun khatif'. God, Most High, said: {the lightning almost snatches away their sight} [al-Baqara: 20]. The devil 'snatches' hearing when he steals it by eavesdropping. God, Most High, said: {except one who snatches a snatch} [al-Saffat: 10]. The devil is called al-khattaf; this name occurs in hadith. A swift-moving camel is 'jamalun khaytaf'; that speed is called al-khaytafa. A line:
And a pace, its brisk gait persisting, swift and snatching.
From this comes the name al-khatafa, the root being one, because the swift one keeps his legs on the ground only briefly, as if he snatches [the ground away]. One says 'huwa mukhtafu l-hasha' — he is hollow-flanked, and that is correct too, because it is as if his flesh had been snatched from him, so that it grew thin and shrank.

As for their saying 'rama l-ramiyyata fa-akhtafaha' — he shot at the game and missed it, it is possible this belongs to the root [with the letter substituted], and possible that the letter stands in for the hamza [i.e. from a different root meaning 'to miss']. A line:
Whether he strikes his quarry or misses it.

Al-khuttaf is a bird [the swallow], and the analogy holds soundly, because it snatches things with its claw. The talons of birds of prey are called khatatifuha. A line:
When the snatching talons of his hand seize an opponent, he sees death before his very eyes, black turned red.
Al-khuttaf is [also] a hooked iron implement, because things are snatched up with it, plural khatatif. Al-Nabigha said:
Curved hooks on stout ropes, pulled toward you by yearning hands.
خطل:
The letters khā', tā' and lām are a single root indicating slackness and disorder, a consistent pattern.

1. al-khatal — slackness of the ear; one says 'udhun khatlā''.
2. thulla khutl — sheep with floppy, slack ears.

A poet said:
When the solitary ram lowered its head, pleased by the abundance of the slack-eared flock.

3. rumh khatil — an unsteady, wavering spear.
4. al-khatil — said of the foolish man.
5. al-khatal — corrupt, faulty speech.

Some people claimed the generous man is called khatil, for his quickness to give. A woman said to be khattāla is one open to suspicion, because of her khatal. The origin is one.
خطم:
The letters khā', tā' and mīm indicate the forward projection of a thing, in a protrusion it has.

1. al-makhātim — noses, singular makhtim.
2. rajul akhtam — a man long in the nose.
3. al-khitām — the camel's nose-rope, named that because it falls upon its khatm (muzzle).
4. al-khutma — the jutting spur of a mountain, it is said.

This is the chapter.

One word deviates from it: they said unripe dates (busr) are 'mukhattam' when streaks appear in them.
خطوأ:
The letters khā', tā', the weak letter and the hamza indicate the passing beyond of a thing, and going away from it. One says 'khatawtu akhtū khutwatan.' Al-khutwa is the space between the two legs; al-khatwa is a single instance of it.

Al-khatā' (error) is from this, because it is exceeding the bound of what is right. One says 'akhta'a' when he went beyond what is correct, and 'khati'a yakhta'u' when he sinned — and this fits the pattern of the root, because he abandons the good way.
خظى: The letters khā', zā' and yā' — nothing else falls in this chapter — indicate the compactness of a thing. This is scarcely said except of flesh. One says 'khaziya lahmuhu' when it became compact and firm. 'His flesh is khaza baza' [firm and full]. A man is 'khazawān' when his flesh is piled up, part upon part.
خف:
The letters khā' and fā' are a single root, and it is something opposite to heaviness and weight.

1. One says khaffa al-shay'u yakhiffu khiffatan — the thing became light; it is khafīf or khufāf.
2. One says akhaffa al-rajulu — when his circumstances became reduced.
3. And akhaffa — when his mount was swift/light.
4. khaffa al-qawmu — the people departed.
5. al-khuff [the leather boot] belongs to this root, because the walker moves lightly while wearing it.
6. khuff al-ba'īr, the camel's foot-pad, is from it too. As for al-khuff, a raised strip in the ground longer than a sandal-print, that is a metaphor.
7. al-khiff — the light, nimble one.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
The nimble boy slips down from its back,
while it flings off the garments of the heavy, clumsy rider.

The sounds dogs make are called al-khafkhafa, which is close to this root.
خفت: The letters khā', fā' and tā' are a single root: it is concealment and secrecy. Al-khaft: hushing the voice in speech. "Takhāfata ar-rajulān," the two men spoke in hushed tones. God Almighty said: {they murmur among themselves (yatakhāfatūn)} [Ṭāhā: 103]. Then the poet said: "I speak openly, while for them there is a murmur (takhāfut) — how different is the open voice from the hushed (khaft) speech!"
خفج: The letters khā', fā' and jīm are a single root indicating the opposite of straightness. Al-akhfaj — one crooked in the leg; the verbal noun is al-khafaj. It is said that al-khafaj is trembling — and that fits the same pattern.
خفد: The letters khā', fā' and dāl are a single root, from swiftness. It is said 'khafada al-zalīm' — the male ostrich hastened in its course; for that it is called khufaydad.
خفر:
The letters khā', fā' and rā' are two roots: one is shyness, the other protection, or its opposite.

The first: al-khafar. 'Khafirat al-mar'a' — the woman felt shy, 'takhfaru khafran,' and she is khafira.

A poet said:
Coquetry and shyness adorned them.

The other root: one says 'khafartu al-rajul khufra' when you granted him protection and were his khafīr. 'Takhaffartu bi-fulān' when you sought protection through so-and-so. 'Akhfartuhu' when you sent a protector along with him.

As for the opposite of that: 'akhfartu al-rajul' is when you broke his covenant. This is like the chapter we mentioned regarding 'khafaytu' and 'akhfaytu' [hid / disclosed].
خفع:
The letters khā', fā' and 'ayn are a single root indicating one thing sticking to another because of some harm.

1. inkhafa'a al-rajul — the man, on his bed, when he stuck to it from illness.
2. khafa'a al-rajul — when his belly stuck to his back, from hunger.

Jarīr said:
In comfort, while the guest of Banū 'Iqāl goes hungry.

3. inkhafa'at kabiduhu — his liver, from hunger, meaning it gave out — some mentioned this and cited the same line; it is close to the first sense.
4. al-akhfa' — a man who seems to limp as he walks, according to some.
5. al-khawfa' — the gloomy, dejected one.
6. khafa'tuhu bi'l-sayf — when you struck him with the sword.

The pattern is one throughout.
خفق:
The letters khā', fā' and qāf are a single root to which all its branches return, and it is agitation in a thing.

1. khafaqa al-'alam yakhfiqu — the banner fluttered.
2. khafaqa al-najm — the star sank and flickered.
3. khafaqa al-qalb yakhfiqu khafaqānan — the heart throbbed.

A poet said:
As if a sand-grouse clung by its wing to my liver, from the violence of the throbbing.

4. akhfaqa al-rajul bi-thawbihi — the man flashed his garment about.
5. al-khafq — any striking with something broad; one says 'khafaqa al-ard bi-na'lihi' — he struck the ground with his sandal.
6. rajul khaffāq al-qadam — a man whose forefoot is broad.
7. al-mikhfaq — the broad sword.
8. al-khafqa — it is said, the waterless desert, named that because the winds swirl through it.

From this chapter too: a swift she-camel is 'khafīq.' 'The mirage khafaqa' — it shimmered. 'The man khafaqa a khafqa' — he dozed off. Al-khāfiqān are the two sides of the sky (east and west). A woman 'khaffāqat al-hashā' is slender of belly, as though that part quivers.

As for their saying 'akhfaqa al-rajul' when he went raiding and won nothing, it may be that this deviates from the pattern of the root, or one might say that failing to win anything leaves him in an unsettled state — though that reading is a stretch.

The Messenger of God, God bless him and his family and grant him peace, said: 'Whatever raiding party goes out and comes back without gain has its reward twice over.'

Antara said:
So he comes back once without gain, and profits another time, and he grieves the malicious man over the shrewd one.
خفي:
The letters khā', fā' and yā' are two separate roots that are opposites of each other. The first is covering, and the second is showing.

The first: khafiya al-shay' yakhfā; and akhfaytuhu, and it is fī khifya and khafā', when you have covered it. And they say bariḥa al-khafā', that is, the secret has come out plain and shown itself. And what is behind the ten feathers at the front of a bird's wing is called al-khawāfī. And al-khawāfī are also the palm-branches next to the heart of the palm-tree. And al-khāfī is the jinn. And a man in hiding is called mustakhfin.

The other root: khafā al-barq khafwan, when the lightning flashes; and that is at the least degree of faintness. And one says khafaytu [al-shay'], without the alif, when you have brought it out into the open. And khafā al-maṭar al-fa'r min jiḥaratihinna - the rain drove the mice out of their holes. Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
It drove them out of their burrows, as though a downpour from a piled-up cloud had driven them out.

And on this reading is recited: {Indeed the Hour is coming — I would all but hide it} [Ṭā Hā: 15], that is, I all but show it.
خق:
The letters khā' and qāf are a single root, and it is a hollow in a thing, and a hole.

1. al-ukhqūq — also said al-ikhqīq — a hollow in the ground; plural al-akhāqīq.

It occurs in a hadith: "in the burrows of rats."

2. al-ikhqāq — the widening of the hole of a pulley.
3. From this comes their saying: atānun khaqūq — a she-donkey, when a sound comes from her vulva.
4. A pool, when its water recedes, dries up, and its surface cracks and peels, is called khuqq.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
As if they were walking in a dried, cracked pool-bed.
خل:
The letters khā' and lām are a single root whose branches stay close to one another, coming back either to thinness or to a gap. The whole root holds together closely across all its senses.

1. al-khilāl — singular of al-akhilla, pins.
2. One says fulānun ya'kulu khilalahu wa khulālatahu — meaning what the toothpick brings out from between his teeth.
3. al-khall — your pinning a cloak about yourself with a pin.
4. al-khalīl — the one bound to you as a close friend — this too is from this root, as if the two of you had become pinned together, like the cloak that is pinned shut.
5. al-khall — a lean, thin-bodied man.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
If you should see my body, thin, as if pledged away.

Another said, in a line of verse:
So pour it for me, O Sawād ibn 'Amr —
for my body, since my uncle died, has grown thin.

6. The yearling camel-colt is called khall, because it is thin-bodied.
7. al-khall — a path through sand, because it is narrow.
8. al-khalāl — unripe, green dates.

As for the sense of a gap: al-khalal is the space between two things.

9. One says khallala al-shay'a — when it did not spread over everything, leaving gaps.
10. al-khalla — poverty, because it is a gap in one's condition.
11. al-khalīl — the poor man, in the poet's saying:
And if a poor man comes to him on a day of hunger,
he says: my wealth is neither absent nor withheld.

12. al-khulla — the sheath of a sword, plural khulal.
13. al-khalal are also the straps fitted onto the backs of the two curved tips of a bow, so called for their thinness, as if each strap were itself a khalla.
14. al-khall — a sinew in the neck, connected to the head.
15. al-khalkhāl [the anklet] belongs to this root too, on account of its thinness.
خلب:
The letters khā', lām and bā' are three roots: one is drawing a thing toward yourself, another is a thing that encompasses something, and the third is a defect in a thing.

The first: al-mikhlab, the bird's talon, because it draws things to itself with it. Al-mikhlab is also the sickle that has no teeth. From this chapter is al-khilāba, deception; one says 'khalabahu' with his speech, meaning he beguiled him. By extension from this is derived 'al-barq al-khullab,' lightning that carries no rain, as though it deceives — just as a mirage is called deceptive.

The second: al-khulb, palm-fiber, because it wraps around the tree. Al-khilb, with kasra on the khā', is the membrane enclosing the heart; from it a man is said to be 'khilb of women,' meaning women love him.

The third: al-khulb, mud and black slime — earth that water has spoiled. From it is derived 'khalban,' a foolish woman; this is not from al-khilāba. An emaciated woman is also called khalban.

As for the 'mukhallab' garment, they say it is one of many colors, but that is not so — al-mukhallab is rather the one patterned with designs shaped like talons, just as 'murajjal' is said of one bearing figures of men.
خلج:
The letters khā', lām and jīm are a single root indicating twisting, wringing, and lack of straightness.

1. al-khalīj — water that turns away from the main body of water and settles there.
2. khalījā al-nahr aw al-bahr — the two arms of a river or a sea.
3. fulān yatakhallaju fī mishyatihi — so-and-so sways as he walks.

From this too is their saying 'khalajanī 'an al-amr,' meaning it distracted me — for if it distracted him from the matter, it turned him away from it.

Al-makhlūja is the uneven thrust of a spear, in the words of Imru' al-Qays, in a line of verse:
We thrust them with straight strokes and slanting ones, like the recoil of two coats of mail upon an archer.
Al-sulkā is the straight thrust; al-makhlūja is the slanting, deviating one.

From this too is their saying 'khalajtu al-shay' min yadihi,' meaning I wrested it away; 'khālajtu fulānan,' I contended with him. And in the hadith on reciting the Qur'an: 'Perhaps some of you have contended it away from me.'

Al-khalīj is the halter-rope, named that because it is twisted and twined.

A poet said:
And he spent the night singing while tethered by the halter, as though he were a bay horse, blood-bright, of pure colour, blazed on the brow.

It is said 'the distracting cares (al-khawālij) khalajathu,' just as one says 'the hindering turns of fortune (al-'awādī) 'adathu.'

Al-Hutay'a said:
With a slanting thought that has, despite incapacity, a way out.
He is describing an opinion, likening it to a firmly twined rope — this then is a comparison. It is also possible that, since it was said to have a way out despite incapacity, he called it makhlūja because it had been turned away from that incapacity.

As for their saying 'khulijat al-nāqa' — the she-camel had this said of her when her young was weaned and her milk lessened — this belongs to the chapter, because she was turned away from her young, and her young turned away from her. It is said 'sahāb makhlūj' — scattered cloud; if this is sound it belongs to the chapter too, since one part of it inclines away from another. Al-khalaj is a defect and a disease, and it belongs to the chapter.
خلد:
The letters khā', lām and dāl are one root pointing to lastingness and staying close. So one says khalada — he stayed on — and akhlada likewise. And from it is jannatu al-khuld, the garden of everlasting stay. Ibn Aḥmar said, in a line of verse:
The loved one stayed on, and the dweller there perished, all but camping-grounds, every one of them empty.

And they say rajulun mukhlad and mukhlid — when grey hair is slow in coming to him. And this belongs to the section, because youth has stayed close to him and he has stayed close to youth. And one says akhlada ilā al-arḍ — when he clings to the ground.

God, exalted, said: {wa-lākinnahu akhlada ilā al-arḍ} [al-Aʿrāf: 176]. As for His word, exalted: {wa-yaṭūfu ʿalayhim wildānun mukhalladūn} [al-Insān: 19], [it is] from al-khuld, and it is lasting — that is, they do not die. And others said: it is from al-khilad, and al-khilad is the plural of khilada, and it is the earring. So His word mukhalladūn means wearing earrings and ear-drops. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And women hung with silver, as though their hips were the sand-heaps of the dunes.

And this is sound reasoning, because the earring stays close to the ear.

And al-khalad is the mind, and it was named so because it is settled [in] the heart and fixed.
خلس:
The letters khā', lām and sīn are a single root, and it is snatching and a quick flash.

One says 'ikhtalastu al-shay'' — I snatched the thing. In the hadith: 'There is no hand-cutting punishment for snatching.'

Their saying 'akhlasa ra'suhu' is when white mixed into its black, as though the black had been snatched away, leaving it streaked. Likewise 'akhlasa al-nabt' when its dry growth mixed with its moist growth.
خلص: The letters khā', lām and ṣād are one root, holding steadily, and it is the cleansing of a thing and the purifying of it. They say khallaṣtuhu min kadhā - I freed it clear of such a thing; and khalaṣa huwa, it came clear. And khulāṣat al-samn is what is thrown into the clarified butter, of dates or of parched meal, so that it may be made pure by it.
خلط:
The letters khā', lām and ṭā' are a single root, differing from the chapter before it — indeed opposed to it. You say: I mixed the thing with another, so it became mixed (khalaṭtu ... fakhtalaṭa). A man called mikhlaṭ is one skilled at engaging closely with affairs. Its opposite is al-mizyal, one who keeps apart from them. Aws said:
And if he says to me, "What do you think?", seeking my counsel ... he finds in me, his cousin, a man who both mixes into the matter and keeps clear of it.

1. al-khalīṭ — the neighbor, the one who mingles with you.
2. al-khilṭ — an arrow whose shaft grows up crooked and keeps bending back however much it is straightened. This belongs to the chapter, because it will not settle into being straight and consistent.

One also says istakhlaṭa al-ba'īr, said of a camel when it tires under the pack-saddle upon the she-camel and cannot find its way; so it is set right and gently helped along.
خلع:
The letters khā', lām, and ʿayn are a single, consistent root: separating a thing from what it was wrapped in or wrapped around.

1. khalaʿtu al-thawba, I took off the garment; khuliʿa al-wālī, the governor was deposed. This is scarcely said except of a lesser person deposing one above him — one does not say "the prince khalaʿa his governor," but rather ʿazalahu, he removed him.
2. One says the man ṭallaqa his wife, divorced her; but if it comes from the woman's side, one says khālaʿathu, she sought separation, and she ikhtalaʿat, because she buys herself free of him with something she gives up to him. In the hadith: "Women who seek separation without cause are the hypocrites," meaning those who leave their husbands though the husbands have done them no harm.
3. al-khāliʿ — a half-ripe date that has fully ripened, because it sheds its skin from its own moistness, just as one says the ripe date "burst free" when it comes out of its skin.
4. khalaʿa al-sunbulu — the ear of grain, when it puts out its beard, as though it shed [its sheath] and brought it forth.
5. al-khalīʿ — one whom his own people have cast off: if he commits a crime they are not held responsible for it, and if a crime is committed against him they will not seek redress for him. This is [the poet's] saying, in a line of verse:
And a valley, empty as the belly of a wild donkey, desolate, that I crossed, where the wolf howls like an outcast man, destitute and burdened with dependents.
Al-khalīʿ also means the wolf — indeed it has been well and truly cast off! It is also said al-khalīʿ means the hunter.
6. One says: so-and-so yatakhallaʿu in his walk, meaning he sways, as though his limbs were about to come apart.
7. al-khāliʿ — a disease afflicting the camel: once it kneels down, it cannot rise again, as though its limbs had come apart until it collapses to the ground.
8. al-khawlaʿ — a terror that seizes the heart like a fit of madness; this fits the root's pattern, as though the heart had been wrenched loose.
9. One says the people takhālaʿū, when they broke whatever alliance had been between them.
خلف:
The letters khā', lām and fā' are three roots: one of them is that a thing come after a thing and stand in its place; the second is the opposite of "in front"; and the third is change.

The first is al-khalaf. And al-khalaf is what comes after. They say: he is a khalaf of truth from his father, a good successor; and a khalaf of evil from his father. And when they mention neither truth nor evil, they say khalaf for the good one and khalf for the bad. God, exalted be He, said: {fa-khalafa min baʿdihim khalfun} — then there came after them a successor generation [al-Aʿrāf: 169]. And al-khillīfā is the caliphate; and it was called khilāfa only because the second comes after the first, standing in his place. And you say qaʿadtu khilāfa fulānin — that is, after him. And al-khawālif in His saying, exalted be He: {raḍū bi-an yakūnū maʿa al-khawālif} — they were content to be with those who stay behind [al-Tawba: 87] —
these are the women, because the men are away in their wars, their raids and their trading, and the women come after them in the houses and the dwellings. And for that reason it is said al-ḥayyu khulūf, when the men are absent and the women are staying. And they say in prayer: "khalafa Allāhu ʿalayka" — that is, may God be the one who stands in place for you of the father or close kinsman you have lost. And "akhlafa Allāhu laka" — that is, may He give you in exchange for the thing that is gone something that will come after it and take its place. And al-khilfa is a plant that grows after the dry stubble. And the khilfa of a tree is fruit that comes out after the fruit.

A poet said, in lines of verse:
And she had at al-Māṭirūn, when the ants had eaten what they had gathered,
a second crop; and when she took her spring quarters she settled at Jillaq among the churches.

And Zuhayr said, in what confirms all that we have mentioned, in a line of verse:
In it the wild cows and the white antelopes walk one after another, and their fawns rise up from every resting place.
He is saying: when this one has passed, that one comes after it.

And from this chapter is al-khalf, which is the drawing of water, because the two drawers take turns — this after that, and that after this.

He said, of al-khalf, in a line of verse:
For downy chicks like the young of the sand-grouse, whose water came late, over birds too weak to rise, red in their crops.

One says akhlafa, when he drew water.

The other root is khalf, which is what is not in front. One says hādhā khalfī and hādhā quddāmī — this is behind me and this is before me. And this is well known.

Labīd said, in a line of verse:
So she set off, thinking that at either opening — behind her and before her — was the master of her fear.

And from this chapter is al-khilf, one of the teats of the udder. And it was so named because it lies behind what is after it.

As for the third, it is their saying khalafa fūhu, when his mouth changed in smell, and akhlafa. And that is his saying, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace: "«The change in the mouth of the fasting man is sweeter with God than the scent of musk»". And from it is the saying of Ibn Aḥmar, in a line of verse:
Youth has parted and life has turned away, and the brothers and the age have grown strange.

And from it is al-khilāf, the breaking of a promise. And khalafa al-rajulu ʿan khuluqi abīhi — the man changed from his father's character. And it is said that al-khalīf is the garment whose middle wears out, so the worn part is taken out of it and then it is patched together; so one says khalaftu al-thawb akhlufuhu. And this is a pattern in this root and in the first root.

And one says waʿadanī fa-akhlaftuhu — that is, I found that he had broken his promise to me.

Al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse:
He stayed, and cut his night short so as to make provision, then he went off and broke his appointment with Qutayla.

As for his saying:
My two buckets are a pair that follow one another, and so are their two drawers —
it is because this one comes after that one. And as for their saying ikhtalafa al-nāsu fī kadhā, people differed about such a thing, and al-nāsu khilfatun, people are of differing kinds, it is from the first root, because each one of them puts aside his fellow's word and sets himself in the place of what he has put aside. And as for their calling the pregnant she-camel khalifa, it may be a stray from the root, and it may be gently brought in by saying that she brings a young one, and the young one is a khalaf, a successor — but that is far-fetched. And the plural of khalifa is al-makhāḍ, and they are the pregnant camels.

And of what strays from the three roots is al-khalīf, which is the road between two mountains. As for al-khālifa among the poles of a tent, perhaps it is at the back of the tent, so it is of the chapter of behind and in front. And for that reason they say fulānun khālifatu ahli baytihi, when he is not put forward among them.

And of the chapter of change and spoiling is the camel called al-akhlaf, which is the one that walks lopsided, from a disease that takes hold of it.
خلق:
The letters khā', lām and qāf are two roots: one of them is the measuring out of a thing, and the other the smoothness of a thing.

As for the first, it is their saying khalaqtu al-adīm li-l-siqā' — I cut the leather to measure for the water-skin, when you measure it out. He said:
The women who cut it to measure took no shame in their cutting, and the leak did not lessen its water.
And Zuhayr said:
And you cut out what you have measured, while some people measure and then do not cut.

And of that is al-khuluq, and it is inborn nature, because its owner has had it measured out to him. And so-and-so is khalīq bi-kadhā — fit for such a thing — and akhliq bihi, that is, how fit he is, that is, he is of those for whom that is measured out. And al-khalāq is the portion, because everyone's portion has been measured out for him.

And of the section is a man who is mukhtalaq, full and even in his make. And al-khulq is the making of a lie, and it is its inventing and its contriving and its measuring out in the soul. God the Exalted said: {and you make up a falsehood} [al-ʿAnkabūt: 17].

As for the second root, it is a rock that is khalqā', that is, smooth. And he said:
Time may leave a crack in a smooth firm rock, and bring down from it the white-footed mountain goat with the notched horn.
And one says ikhlawlaqa al-saḥāb — the cloud lay even. And a trace that is mukhlawliq is one that has come level with the ground. And al-mukhallaq is the arrow made smooth and true.

And of this section is akhlaqa al-shay' and khaluqa — the thing wore out. And akhlaqtuhu anā — I wore it out. And that is because when a thing wears out it becomes smooth and its nap goes. And it is said that al-mukhtalaq of everything is what is even. Ru'ba said:
In a thicket of reeds and a lair of even growth.

And al-khalūq, a perfume, is well known, and it is al-khilāq as well. And that is because a thing, when it is smeared with it, becomes smooth. And one says thawbun khalaq and milḥafatun khalaq — a worn garment and a worn wrap; the masculine and the feminine are alike in it. And the arrow made true was called mukhallaq only because it comes to be smooth. As for al-khulayqā' in the horse, it is like the bridge of the nose in a man.
خلم: The letters khā', lām and mīm are a single root indicating intimacy and constancy. Al-khilm — the gazelle's covert; from it was derived al-khilm meaning the close companion. The origin is one.
خلو:
The letters khā', lām and the weak letter are a single root indicating a thing's being bare of a thing. One says he is khilw of such-and-such, when he is free of it. And the house and other things khalat, they empty, takhlū. And al-khalī is the one free of grief. And a woman khaliyya is an indirect way of speaking of divorce, because when she is divorced she has become empty of her husband. And one says khalā lī al-shay' and akhlā, the thing was left free for me.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
O blamer, will the tribes get their share ... of death, or has death been left free for us alone?

And al-khaliyya is the she-camel made to take to a young one not her own, because it is as though she had been emptied of her first young. And al-qurūn al-khāliya are the generations gone by. And al-makān al-khalā' is the place with nothing in it. And one says: there is no one in the house khalā Zaydin and Zaydan, that is, leave off the mention of Zayd, be empty of the mention of Zayd. And one says: do that, and khalāka dhamm, that is, blame has passed you by, and you are free of it and it is free of you.

And of what strays from the chapter is al-khaliyya, the ship, and the beehive. And al-khalā is fresh grass. And they sometimes express a thing that is empty of anyone to guard it by al-khalāt, saying: he is a khalāt for such-and-such, that is, he is one who is coveted and has no one to guard him. And this belongs to the first chapter.

And some people said: al-khaly is cutting, and the sword yakhtalī, that is, it cuts off. So it is as though al-khalā, grass, was so named because it is mown, that is, cut.

And of what strays from the chapter: khalā bihi, when he mocked at him.
خم:
The letters khā' and mīm are two roots: one is a change in smell, the other is the cleaning of something.

1. The first: their saying khamma al-laḥmu — the meat, when its smell turned.
2. The second: their saying khumma al-bayt — the house, when it was swept.
3. khumāmat al-bi'r — what is swept out of a well's earth when it is cleaned.
4. baytun makhmūm — a swept house.
5. One says huwa makhmūmu al-qalb — when his heart is clean of all deceit and corruption.
خمج:
The letters khāʾ, mīm and jīm indicate faltering and a change in condition. Khamaj in a person is faltering. One says fulānun aṣbaḥa khamijan, meaning he became languid. It appears in a line of al-Hudhalī's poetry:
I fear, short of it, the languor.
And they say khamija al-laḥmu, of meat, when it has changed and gone rank.
خمد:
The letters khā', mīm and dāl are a single root, indicating the stilling of motion and a dying down.

Khamadat al-nāru khumūdan, the fire died down, when its flame stilled. Khamadat al-ḥummā, the fever khamadat, when its heat subsided. One who has fainted is said to have khamada.
خمر:
The letters kha, mim and ra are a single root indicating covering, and mixing within concealment.

Al-khamr is the well-known drink. Al-Khalil said: al-khamr is well known; its fermenting/maturing is its working and boiling. Its maker is al-mukhammir. Its khumra is the fermentation and intoxication that veils the heart of the drunk person. A line:
Delightful [wine], whose intoxication struck him at his vital points, so that its fumes scarcely lifted from his heart.
One says 'bihi khumarun shadid' — he has a severe hangover. They say: 'dakhala fi khamari l-nasi wa khamarihim' — he entered into the press/crowd of people. 'Fulanun yadibbu li-fulanin al-khamr' — so-and-so is stalking so-and-so treacherously; that is a figure of speech for plotting a stealthy attack. Its origin is what conceals a person, of trees and thicket. Abu Dhu'ayb said:
Would that they had been wary of their army, that evening they were like the birds hiding in the thicket.
Meaning they are ambushed and concealment is made against them.

Al-khimar is a woman's headscarf. A woman graceful in wearing the headscarf is 'hasanatu l-khimra'. In the proverb: 'the experienced woman is not taught how to wear the headscarf.' Al-takhmir is covering. One says of people who conceal themselves in the thicket of trees: 'they have concealed themselves' (akhmaru). As for their saying 'so-and-so has neither vinegar nor wine', it functions as a proverb, as if they meant: he has neither good nor ill [nothing at all]. Abu Zayd said: 'khamara l-rajulu l-makan' — the man stuck fast to the place and did not leave it.

As for al-mukhammara among sheep — the one whose head turns white while the rest of its body stays dark — it follows the same reasoning as the root, because that whiteness on its head is likened to a woman's headscarf. One says 'khammartu l-'ajin' — I let the dough rest, that is, leave it unused until it improves. One says 'khamarahu l-da'' — the illness settled into him. Kuthayyir said:
Wholesome and pleasant, free of any lurking ailment, is whatever of our honor 'Azza has taken as her due.

Al-Khalil said: al-mustakhmar, in the dialect of Himyar, means the partner/associate. One says 'dakhala fi l-khamar', a hollow where the wolf and the like conceal themselves. A line:
O Zayd and al-Dahhak, journey on — for you two have already passed the hidden stretches of the road.
One says 'ikhtamara l-tibu' and 'ikhtamara l-'ajin' [the perfume matured; the dough rose]. 'Wajadtu minhu khumratan tayyibatan wa khamaratan' — I found from it a pleasant fragrance. Al-mukhamara is drawing near. In the proverb: 'conceal yourself, Mother of 'Amir' — which is [a name for] the hyena. Al-Shanfara said:
Do not bury me — my burial is forbidden to you — but rather, [let me be prey for] 'conceal yourself, Mother of 'Amir'.
Meaning: leave me for the one to whom this is said.

Al-khumra is a kind of cosmetic a woman rubs on her face to improve her complexion. Al-khumra is also the small prayer-mat. In hadith: 'he used to prostrate upon the khumra.'

An anomaly from this root: al-istikhmar, enslavement/subjugation. One says 'istakhmartu fulanan' — I enslaved so-and-so. It occurs in the hadith of Mu'adh: 'whoever enslaves a people' — that is, subjugates them.
خمس:
The letters khā', mīm, and sīn are a single root, concerning number. Al-khamsa [five] is well known. Al-khams is one part of five. Khamastu al-qawma means I took a fifth of their wealth — akhmisuhum. Khamastuhum means I was their fifth — akhmisuhum. Al-khims is one of the intervals between waterings of camels. Al-Khalīl said: it is when the camels drink on the fourth day after the day they left the water, since they count the day of leaving [as the first day].

1. Al-khamīs is Thursday, the fifth day of the week; plurals akhmisā' and akhmisa, like naṣīb, [plural anṣibā'].
2. Al-khumāsiyy and al-khumāsiyya are a boy-slave or girl-slave whose height is five spans. One does not say sudāsiyy or subā'iyy for one who reaches six or seven spans; but elsewhere al-khumāsiyy applies to whatever reaches five, likewise al-sudāsiyy and al-'ushāriyy.
3. Al-khamīs and al-makhmūs, among garments, is one whose length is five cubits. 'Ubayd said:
These carry me, and a white sharp sword ... and a well-tempered spear in a five-cubit shaft.
He means a spear five cubits long. Mu'ādh said to the people of Yemen: "Bring me a khamīs or a labīs, which I will take from you as alms-tax." It is said that the garment al-khamīs was so named because the first to make it was a king in Yemen called al-Khims. Al-A'shā said:
One day you see it like the garments of al-khims ... and another day its leather grown worn.

Falling outside this chapter's pattern: al-khamīs, meaning a large army. From this comes the hadith: "When the Messenger of God, God bless him and his family and grant him peace, looked out over Khaybar, they said: 'Muḥammad, and the army!'" — meaning the army.
خمش:
The letters khāʾ, mīm and shīn are a single root, and it is scratching and what is close to it.
One says khamashtu khamshan, I scratched, a scratch.

1. al-khumūsh — the plural of khamsh.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Hāshim is our grandfather, so if you are angry,
fill your beautiful face with scratches.

2. al-khumūsh — mosquitoes.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
As if the buzzing of the mosquitoes on both its sides
were the buzzing of a caravan of Umaym, laden with clamour.

3. al-khumāsha, plural khumāshāt — a wound of the kind that has no fixed compensation set for it. This follows the pattern of the root, as if it were like a scratch.
خمص:
The letters khā', mīm and ṣād are a single root indicating leanness and sinking-in.

Al-khamīṣ is one lean in the belly; the verbal noun is al-khamṣ. A woman called khumṣāna is slender-waisted. The arch of the foot is called al-akhmaṣ; this fits the root's pattern, because it is sunk in.

From this root: al-makhmaṣa, hunger, because a hungry person is lean in the belly. A hungry person is called al-khamīṣ, and a hungry woman khamīṣa. Al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse:
You spend the winter nights with your bellies full ... while your neighbor-women go hungry, spending the night with lean, empty bellies.

As for al-khamīṣa, it is a black woolen cloak. Al-Aʿshā compared a woman's hair to it, in a line of verse:
When she is unveiled one day, you would think a black cloak lay upon her, and glistening fresh red dye.

If it is asked where this fits the root's pattern, the answer, as far as is possible, is: it may be called khamīṣa because a person wraps himself in it so that it comes to lie at his middle. If that is correct, it belongs to the root; otherwise it is counted among what falls outside it.
خمط:
The letters khā', mīm, and ṭā' are two origins: one is being stripped bare and smoothness; the other is dominance and violent attack.

The first: their saying khamaṭtu al-shāta, meaning when you strip off the sheep's skin and roast it. If only the wool is removed and the skin left on, that is called al-samṭ. The origin of this is from al-khamṭ, which is anything that has no thorns.

The second: their saying takhammaṭa al-faḥlu, the stud camel grows fierce and bellows. Its origin is from takhammaṭa al-baḥr, the sea churns, meaning its heaving and the crashing together of its waves.
خمع:
The letters khāʾ, mīm and ʿayn are a single root indicating a lack of straightness, and crookedness.

1. khamaʿa al-aʿraju — the lame man limped.
2. al-khawāmiʿ — hyenas are called this, because they limp.
3. al-khimʿ — the thief.
4. al-khimʿ — the wolf.

The pattern behind both is one and the same.
خمل:
The letters khāʾ, mīm and lām are a single root indicating lowness, hanging loose, and falling.

1. khamala dhikruhu yakhmulu khumūlan — his renown faded into obscurity.
2. al-khāmil — the hidden, unremarked one; one says huwa khāmilu al-dhikri, he is unremembered; it also names a matter that is not known or spoken of.
3. al-qawlu al-khāmil — subdued, low speech.

In a hadith: "Remember God with a quiet remembrance."

4. al-khamīla — a stretch of loose sand set in a hollow, favourable ground for plants.

Zuhayr said, in a line of verse:
Sand-dunes between which are thickets.

And Labīd said, in a line of verse:
It spent the night, and a steady rain let fall its drizzle,
watering the thickets, its pouring never-ending.

5. al-khaml, with the l unvowelled — the pile of a velvet coverlet or a rug; the down of the ostrich is also called khaml. That follows the pattern of the root, because it hangs loose, falling in softness.

As for al-khumāl, some said it is a limp found in a camel's legs. If that is so, it follows the same pattern, since it is perhaps from slackness. Al-Aʿshā said, about al-khumāl, in a line of verse:
She was not bent down over a young one, nor did ʿUbayd
cut her sinews from slackness.
خن:
The letters khā' and nūn are a single root, and it is the imitation of certain sounds, made weakly.

1. Its origin is khanna — when he wept, khanīn, a stifled sob.
2. al-khankhana — speaking unclearly, without articulating the words plainly.
3. Al-khunnān in camels is said to be like a head-cold in people.
4. al-khunna — like al-ghunna, a nasal twang.
5. al-khanīn is said to mean a stifled laugh.
6. They say al-makhanna is the nose; if so, it is because it is the seat of al-khunna, the nasal twang.
7. One says waṭi'a makhannatahu — he humbled him utterly, as if he had set his feet upon his nose.
خنا:
The letters khāʾ and nūn, with a weak letter after them, indicate corruption and ruin. The calamities of time are called khanan.

Labīd said, in a line of verse:
We reckoned that the ruin of time was heedless.

1. akhnā ʿalayhi al-dahru — time destroyed him.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
It ruined her, the one that ruined Lubad.

2. al-khanā, of speech — its most obscene form. One says khanā yakhnū khanan.
3. akhnā fulānun fī kalāmihi — so-and-so spoke obscenely.
خنب:
The letters khāʾ, nūn and bāʾ are a single root, and it indicates softness and slackness.

1. jāriyatun khaniba — a soft, coquettish girl.
2. rajulun khinnāb — a man bulky in build.

Some related from al-Khalīl that he said it is khinnaʾb, with the khāʾ carrying a kasra and the nūn doubled and hamzed. If this is sound from al-Khalīl, then al-Khalīl is trustworthy; otherwise it is as we have said, without a hamza.

3. al-khinnāb, of men — the foolish one, unsettled, twitching this way and that.
4. al-khinnāb — Al-Khalīl said this is the one with a huge nostril.
5. al-khinnāba — a huge nose-tip.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
I cauterise the spiteful with a scorching brand,
and the wide-nosed fool among them.

Something al-Khalīl did not mention, though it is sound by analogy, is their saying khanabat rijluhu, meaning it weakened, and akhnabtuhā anā, I weakened it.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
My father is the one who weakened Ibn al-Ṣaʿiq's leg,
when the horses became like the sinew of the neck.
خنث:
The letters khāʾ, nūn and thāʾ are a single root indicating bending and doubling over.

1. al-khanith — the slack, bent one.
2. khanathtu al-siqāʾ — I bent the mouth of the waterskin outward and drank from it. If you bend it inward instead, that is qabaʿtahu, a different word.
3. imraʾatun khunuth — a woman who sways.
خنز: The letters khāʾ, nūn and zāʾ are a single word from the class of inverted letters, not a root. One says khaniza al-laḥmu khanazan, of meat, when its smell has changed and it has gone rank. This has already been discussed.
خنزوانة:
Khunzuwāna: pride.
1. Al-khayzurāna — the ship's rudder.
2. Al-khāzibāz — the fly, or its sound. Al-khāzibāz is also a plant. And al-khāzibāz is also a pain that takes hold of the throat. He said, in a line of verse:
O khāzibāz, let go of the jowls!
3. Al-khabranj — one who is well fed and thriving.
4. Al-khafanjal — said of the heavy, foul, splay-legged man; but this is really from al-khafaj, already discussed, because when they wanted to make a word sound worse and uglier they added to it. This one was formed by real derivation.
5. Al-kharfaja — good feeding. And sarāwīl mukharfaja — wide trousers. This one was simply coined, not derived.
6. Al-khaysafūja — the ship's rudder; this belongs to speech one should not bother dwelling on.
7. Khunābis — their name for an ancient thing; this too is a coined word whose derivation is unknown. He said, in a line of verse:
God refused that I be disgraced, and mine is an ancient (khunābis) might.
And God knows best what is correct.
(Here ends the book of the letter khā'.)
خنس:
The letters khā', nūn and sīn are a single root indicating hiding and concealing oneself.

They said: al-khans is going off in secret. One says khanistu ʿanhu, I slipped away from him; and akhnastu ʿanhu ḥaqqahu, I secretly withheld his due from him.

Al-khunnas are the planets, which slip away as they set. Some said they are named so because they hide by day and rise by night. Al-khannās, as a description of Satan, is so called because he withdraws whenever God is mentioned.

From this root: al-khanas in the nose, a sinking-in of the bridge of the nose. All cattle are khuns, snub-nosed.
خنط: The letters khāʾ, nūn and ṭāʾ are a word that is not a root, and it belongs to the class of letter-substitution. One says khanaṭahu, meaning it distressed him, like ghanaṭahu — and it amounts to nothing sound.
خنع:
The letters khāʾ, nūn and ʿayn are a single root indicating abasement, submission, and lowliness. One says khaḍaʿa lahu wa khanaʿa, he submitted and abased himself to him.

In a hadith: "the most abased of names" — meaning the most degrading.

1. akhnaʿatnī ilayhi al-ḥājatu — need forced me to him and abased me before him.
2. al-khāniʿ — the immoral, dissolute one.
3. khanʿa — an act of immorality. One says iṭṭalaʿtu minhu ʿalā khanʿatin, I learned of an immorality of his.

That is in his saying, in a line of verse:
They show no submission toward their women-neighbours.

And from it, another's saying, in a line of verse:
Perhaps one day you will be met with disgrace,
and then your ill-omens will croak at you from a valley.

4. Khunāʿa — a tribe.
خنف:
The letters khāʾ, nūn and fāʾ are a single root indicating a tilt and softness.

1. al-khanūf — a she-camel gentle in her forelegs as she walks; the verbal noun is al-khinaf.

Al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse:
And she scattered the dust with her hind legs, and her forelegs
returned soft in gait, not stiff.

2. al-khinaf — also said of the neck: to tilt it when it is pulled by its rein.
3. al-khanīf — a kind of linen, the worst there is.

In a hadith: "the worn linen tore away from us, and dates burned our bellies."

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Upon one like the worn khanīf, for whom the echo calls,
having troughs, its watering-pools long fouled.
خنق: The letters khā', nūn, and qāf are a single root indicating narrowness. Al-khāniq is a narrow mountain pass. Some scholars said the people of Yemen call an alley khāniq. Al-khanaq is the verbal noun of khanaqahu yakhniquhu khanaqan, he strangled him; some scholars said one does not say khanqan. Al-mikhnaqa is a necklace.
خوب: The letters khāʾ, wāw and bāʾ are a lesser root indicating emptiness and the like. One says aṣābathum khawbatun, meaning what they had was gone and nothing remained. Al-khawba: land that gets no rain between two lands that have been rained on; it is like al-khaṭīṭa, a bare strip left unrained-on.
خوت:
The letters khāʾ, wāw and tāʾ are a single root indicating penetration and passing through with boldness.

1. rajulun khawwāt — a man who does not care what affairs he takes on.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
None finds his way in it but every bold one,
resolute in judgement among men, a khawwāt.

This is the origin. Then one says:

2. khātat al-ʿuqābu — the eagle swooped down; she is khāʾita.

Abū Dhuʾayb said, in a line of verse:
He threw down his sheath and swooped down upon them,
as a greedy, swooping eagle swoops.

3. mā zāla al-dhiʾbu yakhtātu al-shāta baʿda al-shāti — the wolf kept snatching sheep one after another, that is, stealing upon them and preying on them.

As for what Ibn al-Aʿrābī related of their saying khāta yakhūtu, when someone breaks his covenant — this may belong to this chapter, as if he broke faith and passed along the path of his treachery; or the tāʾ may be substituted for a sīn, as if it were khāsa, gone rotten, and when the sīn was turned to tāʾ the pattern changed from yakhīsu to yakhūtu.

4. khāta al-rajulu wa anfaḍa — his provisions ran out. This is from the sīn root.
5. khāta al-rajulu — likewise, when he grew old.

As for their saying that al-takhawwut is diminishment, that in our view belongs to the class of letter-substitution, from either al-takhawwun or al-takhawwuf, both of which have been mentioned in their own chapters.

6. fulānun yatakhawwatu ḥadītha al-qawmi wa yakhtātu — he takes from the people's talk and commits it to memory.

And from the first chapter:

7. hum yakhtātūna al-layla — they travel through the night and cross it.
خوث:
The letters khāʾ, wāw and thāʾ are a lesser root, not regular, and not to be reasoned from. They say khawithat al-marʾatu, when her belly grew large. Or it is said instead that al-khawthāʾ is the soft, plump woman.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Her love and her passion clung to the heart,
while she is a shy young thing, soft.
خوخ: The letters khāʾ, wāw and khāʾ are nothing — not a root. From it is al-khawkh, the peach, and I do not think it is an Arabic word.
خود:
The letters khāʾ, wāw and dāl are a lesser root holding a single word. One says khawwadū fī al-sayr, they plunged ahead in travelling. Its origin is their saying khawwadtu al-faḥla takhwīdan, when you let the stallion loose among the females.

He cited, in a line of verse:
Her stallion was let loose without restraint,
in the land of the well-watered country, rushing like the ostrich.

This is how al-Khalīl cited it; others report it as "wa khawwada faḥluhā" — and her stallion rushed.
خوذ: The letters khāʾ, wāw and dhāl are not a regular root, and not to be reasoned from; it holds only one word, disputed in its meaning. They said: khāwadhtuhu, meaning I opposed him. Some said: khāwadhtuhu, meaning I agreed with him. And they say: khiwādh al-ḥummā is that the fever comes at no fixed time.
خور:
The letters khā', wāw and rā' are two roots: one indicates a sound, the other weakness.

The first is their saying khāra al-thawru yakhūru, the bull lowed. God the Exalted said: {so he produced for them a calf, a body having a low sound} [Ṭāhā: 88].

As for the other: al-khawwār is weak, of anything. One says a spear is khawwār, land is khawwāra, plural khūr. Al-Ṭirimmāḥ said, in a line of verse:
I am the son of the defenders of glory, of the House of Mālik ... when the weak among men start to scatter in fright.

As for their calling a prized she-camel khawwāra, plural khūr, this belongs to the root: because if she is not ʿazūz — al-ʿazūz being narrow in the teat-opening, hard to milk, a word taken from ʿazāz, hard ground — then she is khawwāra, easy-flowing, since the tightness has left her.
خوس:
The letters khāʾ, wāw and sīn are a single root indicating corruption. One says khāsati al-jīfatu, of a carcass, at the first stage it begins to smell — as though it stagnated until it spoiled. Then, carried on this:

1. khāsa bi-ʿahdihi — he broke faith and betrayed, when he goes back on his pledge.
2. al-khaws — treachery.

All of that is close, one sense to another. This is a word shared between wāw and yāʾ, which are near each other, the yāʾ having the greater share in it; it has also been mentioned under the yāʾ.
خوش: The letters khāʾ, wāw and shīn are a root indicating leanness and the like. Al-mutakhawwish is the emaciated one, and for that the two flanks are called al-khawshayn.
خوص:
The letters khāʾ, wāw and ṣād are a single root indicating scantiness, fineness, and narrowness.

1. al-khawaṣ, in the eye — its narrowness and sunkenness.
2. al-khūṣ — the palm-frond, fine and slender.
3. al-takhawwuṣ — taking whatever someone gives you, however little. One says takhawwaṣ minhu mā aʿṭāka wa in qalla.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
O my two companions, draw them close with release,
from every milk-rich, full-uddered one.
He means: bring your camels near, a little at a time, and do not let them crowd upon the trough.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
O you two who drive them, draw them close with release,
and do not drive them as fools drive.

Another said, in a line of verse:
I say to the one driving: draw them close with release;
I fear misfortunes will strike first.

As for their saying akhwaṣa al-ʿarfaju, of the desert shrub, it is derived from akhwaṣa al-nakhlu, the palm put out its fronds, because when the ʿarfaj bursts open it too grows frond-like leaves.
خوض: The letters khā', wāw and ḍād are a single root, pointing to going into the middle of a thing and entering it. One says khuḍtu al-mā' wa-ghayrahu — I waded into the water and into other things. And takhāwaḍū fī al-ḥadīth wa-l-amr, that is, they went into the talk and the matter together and their speech ran into one another's.
خوط:
The letters khāʾ, wāw and ṭāʾ are a lesser root indicating the branching of boughs. Al-khūṭ is the branch, plural khīṭān.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Upon young she-camels like the twigs of the salam tree.
خوع:
The letters khāʾ, wāw and ʿayn are a root indicating diminishment and a tilt. One says khawwaʿa al-shayʾa, when he diminished it.

Ṭarafa said, in a line of verse:
And a herd whose choice camels' fangs were diminished
by the arrow-lot of al-Muʿallā at dusk, and the sifting-arrow.
Khawwaʿa here means diminished; he means by it what is slaughtered from them in the game of chance.

1. al-khawʿ — the bend of a valley.
2. al-khuwāʿ — a snorting sound.

This is more sound by analogy than their saying that al-khawʿ is a white mountain.
خوف: The letters khā', wāw and fā' are a single root pointing to alarm and fright. One says khiftu al-shay' khawfan wa-khīfatan — I feared the thing.
