And the yā' is turned from a wāw because of the kasra. And one says khāwafanī fulānun fa-khuftuhu — so-and-so vied with me in frightening and I outdid him, that is, I was more to be feared than he. As for their saying takhawwaftu al-shay', that is, I took away from it little by little, it is sound and good Arabic, only it is a case of substitution: the original is a nūn, from al-tanaqquṣ, diminishing, and it has been mentioned in its own place.
خوق: The letters khāʾ, wāw and qāf are a lesser root indicating the emptiness of a thing. One says mafāzatun khawqāʾ, when it is empty, waterless, with nothing in it. Al-khawq is a ring of gold; this follows the pattern, because its middle is hollow.
خول: The letters khā', wāw, and lām are a single root, pointing to the tending and looking after of a thing. From this: "He used to attend to them with admonition", meaning he used to look after them with it, from time to time. Fulānun khawliyyu mālin means he tends and improves it. From this too: khawwalaka Allāhu mālan, meaning He granted it to you, because wealth is something to be tended, that is, looked after. From this comes khawal al-rajul, his household servants; its origin is that a single one of them is called khā'il, meaning the shepherd. One says fulānun yakhūlu 'alā ahlihi, meaning he tends to them. Among the eloquent expressions of their speech: takhawwalat al-rīḥu al-arḍa, meaning the wind worked over the land, time after time.
خون:
The letters khā', wāw and nūn are a single root, and it is diminishing. One says khānahu yakhūnuhu khawnan — he betrayed him; and that is a falling short in keeping faith. And one says takhawwananī fulān ḥaqqī — that is, he cut down what was owed me. Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
No — rather it is longing, from a dwelling worn away ... now by cloud, now by a dusty hot wind.

And it is said that al-khawwān is the lion; the rule is the same one. As for what is said, that in the earliest Arabic they used to call the first month of spring [khawwān], there is no sense in it and no reason to busy oneself with it. As for Dhū al-Rumma's line:
Nothing lifts his eye but what wears down his sleep ... a caller calling him by the name of water, bleating —
if by al-takhawwun he meant looking after and tending, as some of the people of learning have said, then it belongs to the substitution of letters, and the original letter is lām — takhawwalahu — and mention of that has already passed. And some of the people of learning say: he means, nothing but what cut short his sleep, his mother's calling to him.

As for the thing eaten upon, some said it is foreign. And I heard 'Alī ibn Ibrāhīm al-Qaṭṭān say: Tha'lab was asked, and I was listening, and it was put to him: may one say that the khiwān, the table, is called khiwān because what is on it is worn down, that is, diminished? He said: that is not far off. And God Almighty knows best.
خوى:
The letters khāʾ, wāw and yāʾ are a single root indicating emptiness and falling.

1. khawat al-dāru takhwī — the house became empty, deserted.
2. khawā al-najmu — the star fell, setting without rain following its setting; also akhwā.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
The stars of the seizing fell, save one faint one,
a faint star of a barren time, whose rain-bearer brings no increase.

3. khawwati al-nujūmu takhwiyatan — the stars tilted toward their setting.
4. khawwati al-ibilu takhwiyatan — the camels' bellies grew lean and hollow.
5. khawiyati al-marʾatu khawan — the woman did not eat at the time of giving birth.
6. khawwā al-rajulu — he spread himself in his prostration, leaving space; and likewise the camel, when it spreads itself as it kneels. This follows the pattern of the root, because in spreading his prostration he leaves the space between his upper arm and his side empty.
7. khawwati al-marʾatu — she did the same, sitting over the censer.
8. khawwā al-ṭāʾiru — the bird let its two wings hang loose.
9. al-khawāh — the sound something makes as it falls.

We have said that most of this does not run to a fixed pattern, and is not a true root.
خيب:
The letters khā', yā' and bā' are a single root, indicating lack of benefit and being deprived.

1. The origin is their saying, of a fire-drill stick that will not strike a spark: it is khayyāb.
2. Then they said: saʿā fī amrin fa-khāba — he strove in a matter and it failed, meaning he was deprived and gained no good from it.
خير:
The letters khā', yā' and rā' - its origin is inclining and leaning towards, and then things are carried onto it. So al-khayr, good, is the opposite of evil, because everyone inclines to it and leans with it towards his fellow. Al-khīra is the choice. Al-khīr is generosity. Al-istikhāra is that you ask for the better of two matters for yourself. And all of this is from al-istikhāra, which is seeking to make a thing incline towards you. And one says istakhartuhu. They said: it is from the istikhāra of the hyena, which is that you put a piece of wood into the hole of its den so that it comes out from one place to another. And al-Hudhalī said, in a line of verse:
Perhaps, if Umm 'Amr has taken in your place another friend, one who reviles me - you are trying to draw her out.

Then the speech is inflected and one says, a man is khayyir and a woman khayyira, meaning excellent, and a people are khiyār and akhyār ... in her goodness, and a woman is khayra in her beauty and her fair looks. And in the Qur'an: {fīhinna khayrātun ḥisān} [al-Raḥmān: 70]. And one says khāyartu fulānan fa-khirtuhu - I contended with him in excellence and proved the better. And you say: ikhtar banī fulānin rajulan - choose a man out of the sons of so-and-so. God Most High said: {wa-khtāra Mūsā qawmahu sab'īna rajulan} [al-A'rāf: 155]. You say huwa al-khīra, light, without doubling, a verbal noun of ikhtāra khīratan, like irtāba rībatan.
خيس:
The letters khāʾ, yāʾ and sīn are a lesser root indicating subduing and softening. One says khayyastuhu, when you have softened it and subdued it. Al-mukhayyas is the prison.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
I wrapped myself around the staff, and knew that I
am a prisoner of the mukhayyas — the prison, should they seize me.

As for their saying khāsa bi-l-ʿahd, we have mentioned it under the wāw; the word is shared between the two. Among the strange things in this chapter is their saying qalla khaysuhu, meaning his grief. Al-khīs is dense, tangled trees.
خيص:
The letters khāʾ, yāʾ and ṣād are a word shared as well, because the wāw has a share in it, and it has been mentioned under al-khūṣ. As for the yāʾ, al-khayṣ is a small gift.

Al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse:
By my life, if he leaves the tribe, departing,
he has gained only a meagre share from ʿUfayra, deprived.

The whole chapter, in both wāw and yāʾ, is one. Among the unusual things in it — and God knows best whether it is sound — is their saying waʿilun akhyaṣ, said of a mountain-goat when one of its two horns stands upright and the other turns forward toward its face.
خيط:
The letters khā', yā' and ṭā' are a single root indicating the stretching-out of a thing in thinness, then it is carried over to whatever stands upright in some of its uses. Al-khayṭ, thread, is well known. Al-khayṭ al-abyaḍ (the white thread) is the whiteness of daylight; al-khayṭ al-aswad (the black thread) is the blackness of night. God Almighty said: {until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread of dawn} [al-Baqara: 187]. What flows [shimmering, like threads] from the heat of the sun is called khayṭ bāṭil. He cited: "you betrayed 'Amr, O Banū Khayṭ Bāṭil, and the likes of you have built houses on betrayal."

As for their saying, of one in whose head grey hair has appeared, "khuyyiṭa," this too belongs to the root, as though what appears is likened to threads. Al-Hudhalī said: "until my temples became threaded (takhayyaṭa) with white." One says "na'āmatun khayṭā'," [describing an ostrich], its khayṭ being the length of its neck. Al-khiyāṭa, sewing, is well known. As for al-khīṭ, with kasra, it is a flock of ostriches, and this fits the pattern of the root, because what is gathered together is like what has been sewn (khīṭa), part to part.

As for al-Hudhalī's line: "he let himself down upon it between a rope (sibb) and a khayṭa, with a smooth [strand] like a low-hanging cloud whose bucket dips" — it has been said al-khayṭa is the rope; if so, this fits the regular pattern of the root. It has also been said al-khayṭa is the tent-peg; we have already said this too is carried over onto the root, because in it there is an extension in an upright form.
خيف:
The letters khāʾ, yāʾ and fāʾ are a single root indicating difference.

1. al-khayaf — that one of a horse's two eyes is blue and the other dark.
2. al-nāsu akhyāf — meaning they differ from one another.
3. al-khayfān — locusts marked with differing streaks.
4. al-khayf — what rises above the streambed of a valley without reaching the height of a mountain; it thus differs from both the plain and the mountain.
5. al-khayf — the skin of the udder, from this, likened to the khayf of the land.
6. nāqatun khayfāʾ — a she-camel with a wide udder-skin.
7. baʿīrun akhyaf — a camel wide in the skin of the sheath.

As for al-khīf, it is the plural of khīfa, fear, and does not belong to this chapter; it has been mentioned in the chapter of wāw after khāʾ, the wāw having become a yāʾ because of the kasra before it.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
So do not sit in dread,
and hide in your heart both longing and fear.
خيل:
The letters khā', yā' and lām are a single root pointing to movement with a shifting of appearance. From that is al-khayāl, and it is a figure. Its origin is what a man pictures in his sleep, because it takes shapes and shifts its colours. One says khayyaltu li-l-nāqa when you set up for her young a scarecrow that frightens the wolf so that it does not come near. Al-khayl, horses, are well known. I heard someone relate from Bishr al-Asadī, from al-Aṣma'ī, who said: I was with Abū 'Amr ibn al-'Alā', and with him was a bedouin boy. Abū 'Amr was asked: why are horses called khayl? He said: I do not know. The bedouin said: for their strutting, ikhtiyāl. Abū 'Amr said: write it down. This is sound, because a man who struts in his walk shifts through colours in his movement. Al-akhyal is a bird, and I think it is many-coloured; it is said to be the shiqirrāq, the green woodpecker. The Arabs take it for an ill omen. One says ba'īr makhyūl when the akhyal alights on a camel's rump and cuts it. Al-Farazdaq said, in a line of verse:
If, Qaṭan, you bring me to him, son of Mudrik, then may you meet an akhyal among the birds of ill omen.
He means: if you bring me to this man I praise, I shall not care that you perish; as Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
When you have brought me to Bilāl, son of Abū Mūsā, then may a butcher stand with an axe between your two joints.
And al-Shammākh said, in a line of verse:
When you have brought me and carried my saddle to 'Arāba, then choke on the blood of your own heart-vein.
One says takhayyalat al-samā' when the sky makes ready for rain, and there must be at that a change of colour. Al-makhīla is the cloud. Al-mukhayyila is the cloud that promises rain. As for their saying khayyaltu 'alā al-rajul takhyīlan, when you turn suspicion upon a man, that is from this, because one says, it looks as though it were so, it is pictured to me that it is so; and from it takhayyaltu 'alayhi takhayyulan, when you read a man's face.
خيم:
The letters khā', yā', and mīm are a single root indicating staying and remaining fixed in place. Al-khayma, the tent, is well known; al-khaym are the wooden poles on which the tent is built. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Nothing remained but the shimmering outline of stacked tent-poles.
One says khayyama bi-l-makān, he settled in the place, and for this reason the tent is called khayma.

Al-khiyam means one's inborn nature, because a person is built upon it and always returns to it.

From this branch too is their calling a coward khāʾim, because from his cowardice he cannot bring himself to move; one says khāma yakhīmu, he held back. As for [the poet's] saying, in a line of verse:
They saw weakness in my leg, and tried to splint it for me, once they saw me holding it raised.
He meant that he was lifting it up, as though he likened it to al-khaym, the tent-poles.

As for the alif that comes after the khā' in this branch, it must be either from roots with an original wāw or an original yā'. The khāl, the mark on the face, belongs to the changing of appearance mentioned elsewhere; from this one says a man is makhīl or makhūl. The diminutive of khāl is khuyayl for those who say makhīl, and khuwayl for those who say makhūl.

As for a man's khāl, his mother's brother, that is from khāʾilu mālin, one who tends and looks after property. Khāl al-jaysh is the army's banner — either from the changing of colors in it, or because the army watches it and looks to it as one tends a thing. Al-khāl is also, it is said, a black mountain — this belongs to the case of letter-substitution.
دأب: The letters dāl, hamza and bā' are a single root, indicating persistence and continuance. Al-da'b is habit and custom. Al-Farrā' said: al-da'b comes from da'abtu, except that the Arabs shifted its sense to mean "habit" or "affair." Da'aba al-rajulu fī 'amalihi means the man was diligent in his work, when he applied himself hard to it. Ad'abtuhu anā id'āban, I drove him hard at it. Al-dā'ibān are the two that are never still: night and day.
دأث: The letters dāl, hamza and thā' are not a root, because al-da'thā' — which is a slave-woman — is a reversal of al-tha'dā'. All the same, they say 'da'thtu al-ṭa'ām', I ate the food.
دأظ:
The letters dāl, hamza and ẓā' are a single word. They say al-da'ẓ is filling. One says 'da'aẓtu al-matā' fī al-wi'ā'', I crammed the goods into the container. He said, in a line of verse:
And the packing in, until no gap remains.
Al-da'ẓ is filling to the full. And al-gharaḍ is a place left that the water does not reach.
دأل:
The letters dāl, hamza and lām indicate lightness and briskness.

1. *al-da'alān* — walking briskly; one says 'da'altu ad'alu' from it.
2. *al-da'l* — stealthy pursuit, deception.
3. *al-du'lūl* — calamity; it is close to this chapter.
4. *al-Du'al* — a tribe.
دأم:
The letters dāl, hamza and mīm indicate one thing following another and things stacking up.

1. *da'amtu al-ḥā'iṭ* — I raised the wall up. Al-Khalīl said this, and it may belong to what we have mentioned, since it is one thing set above another.
2. *tadā'amat 'alayhi al-riyāḥ* — the winds came against him one after another, said when they followed in succession; and 'tada''amat al-amwāj', the waves piled one upon another. He said, in a line of verse:
Beneath the shade of the wave, when it piled up.
3. *al-da'mā'* — the sea itself. Perhaps this sense fits the root even better.
4. *tadā'amtu al-rajul* — I leapt upon the man.
5. *tadā'ama al-faḥl al-nāqa* — the stallion mounted the she-camel.
6. *tadā'amat al-samā'* — the sky's rains came one after another.
دأى:
The letters dāl, hamza and yā' are two roots: one indicates stealthy pursuit, and the other a bone joined to its like, to which something else is likened, and it may be made of wood.

The first is al-da'y, which is stealthy pursuit; one says 'da'aytu ad'ā da'yan', it is stealthy pursuit. And the wolf 'yad'ā', when it stalks its prey stealthily.

As for the other:
1. *al-da'yāt* — the vertebrae of the back, singular da'ya.
2. *Ibn Da'ya* — the crow, because it lands on the da'ya of a camel with a saddle-sore and pecks at it.
3. *al-da'ya*, of a camel — the spot where the wooden frame of the saddle rests and wounds it.
دب:
The letters dāl and bā' are a single root, sound and consistent by analogy, indicating movement over the ground lighter than walking. You say dabba dabīban; and everything that moves on the ground is a dābba. In the hadith: "no daybūb shall enter Paradise, nor qallāʿ" — by al-daybūb is meant the slanderer who creeps among people spreading gossip, and al-qallāʿ is the one who informs on a man to his ruler to have him removed from a position he holds.
1. Nāqatun dabūb — a she-camel that, from the abundance of her flesh, walks only with a creeping gait.
2. "Mā bi-l-dāri dibbiyyun wa-dubbiyyun" — there is no one at all moving in the house.
3. Ṭaʿnatun dabūb — a spear-wound that oozes with blood. Al-Hudhalī said, in a line of verse: On its flat surface, a creeping flow that gushes.
4. "Rakiba fulānun dubbata fulānin, wa-akhadha bi-dubbatihi" — so-and-so followed so-and-so's course, doing as he did, as if walking the way he walked.
5. Al-dubbā' — the gourd. It may be irregular; it is possible it was so named for its smoothness, as if it moves lightly when rolled. Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
When she came forward, you would say she is a gourd, one of the green ones, dipped in the pools.

As for al-dabab, fine down in hair, it belongs to the chapter of letter-substitution, because its dāl stands for a zāy. Al-adbab, among camels, is the shaggy one. In the hadith, if it is sound: "which of you is the companion of the shaggy camel?" As for al-dabūb, it is said to be the deep cave. And this is nothing.
دبج:
The letters dāl, bā' and jīm are a single root indicating something with a fine, handsome surface.

1. *al-dībāj* — well known [a fine brocade cloth].
2. *al-dībājatān* — the two cheeks. Ibn Muqbil said, in a line of verse:
Sweat, checked, runs down upon his two cheeks.
They are also called al-lītān.

As for their saying 'mā bi-l-dāri dibbījun', there is no one in the house — it is said this is with ḥā' [dibbīḥ], and has already been mentioned in its place. If it is with jīm, as some say, then it is not from this root, and it may instead come from 'dibbiyy', from al-dabīb, creeping, with the yā' of the relative adjective changed to jīm, following the dialect of those who do that.
دبح: The letters dāl, bā' and ḥā' are a minor root, and it is bearing down over a thing with the body until you bend fully over it. One says 'dabbaḥa al-rajulu ra'sahu', the man lowered his head, when he bent and dropped it down. And it was forbidden that a man bend low, 'yudabbiḥ', in prayer as the donkey does. And what they say, 'mā bi-l-dāri min dibbīḥin', is from this too, meaning one who dwells in the house, settled and bearing down upon it; and the ḥā' in this word better fits the pattern than the jīm, for the reason we have given.
دبر:
The letters dāl, bā' and rā'. The root of this chapter is that most of it runs on one reasoning, and it is the end of a thing and what is behind it, the opposite of its front. And a few words stray from it, which we shall mention.

The bulk of the chapter is that al-dubur is the opposite of al-qubul, the front. And al-dabīr is what a woman turns backward of her spun thread when she twists it. Ibn al-Sikkīt said: al-qabīl in twisting is what you bring toward your breast, and al-dabīr is what you take back away from your breast. And dābirat al-ṭā'ir is the toe at the back of the bird's foot. And you say: jaʿaltu qawlahu dabra udhunī — I put his word behind my ear, that is, I shut my eyes to it and made myself deaf to it. And dabara al-nahār and adbara, and that is when its end comes, and that is its dubur. And dabbartu al-ḥadīth ʿan fulān when you relate it from him; and it is of the chapter, because the later teller comes behind the first and follows after him. And dābirat al-ḥāfir is what is opposite the back of the pastern. And "may God cut off their dābir" — that is, the last of those left of them. And al-dābir among arrows is the one that goes out past the target, as though it turned its back on the shooter; and it has dabara yadburu dubūran. And al-Dabarān is a star, so named because it comes behind the Pleiades. And dābartu fulānan — I was at enmity with him. And in the hadith: "Do not turn your backs on one another", and it is of the chapter, that being that each of the two leaves off turning his face toward his fellow. And al-tadbīr is that a man manage his affair, and that is because he looks to what its outcome and its end will be, and that is its dubur. And al-tadbīr is a man's freeing his male or female slave ʿan dubur, and that is that the slave be freed after his master's death, as though he says: he is free after my death. And a man is muqābal mudābar when he is noble in lineage from the side of both his parents; and the meaning of this is that whoever of them came before was noble, and whoever came after was likewise. And al-mudābara is the ewe whose ear is slit from the side of its back. And al-dābir among gaming-arrows is the one that does not come out, and it is the opposite of the winning one, and it is of the chapter, because it turned its back on its owner. And al-dābir is the follower; one says dabara dubūran. And in that way is explained His saying, exalted be His praise: "By the night when it turns back" — he says: when it follows the day. And dabara bi-l-qimār when he carries the winnings off. And one says: this matter has neither a front nor a back — that is, it has nothing by which it comes forward so as to be known, and nothing by which it turns away so as to be known. And a man is udābir when he cuts the ties of kinship, and that is because he turns his back on it and does not turn toward it. And al-dabūr is a wind that comes from behind the Kaʿba. And al-dābira is a kind of hold in wrestling. Abū Zayd said: one says "he prays the prayer only dabariyyan", though the traditionists say duburiyyan; and that is when he prays it at the end of its time, meaning that the time has already turned away.

As for the other words, I hold them to stray from the root we have mentioned, and some of them are sound. As for the doubtful one, it is their saying that Dubār is the name of Wednesday, and that the people before Islam used to call it so. In the like of this there is room for doubt. As for the sound one, it is al-dibār, and they are the ridges and beds of a sown field. Bishr said:
Over a green plot whose buckets rise above the ridges.
And of that is al-dabr, and it is much wealth; one says māl dabr, and mālān dabr, and amwāl dabr.
دبس:
The letters dāl, bā' and sīn are a root indicating a pressed juice of a dusky, not-bright colour.

1. *al-dibs* — the syrup [pressed from dates].
2. *al-dubsiyy* — a bird, named for having that colour.
3. *ji'ta bi-umūrin dubsin* — you brought vague matters, said when someone brings them unclear.
4. *adbasat al-arḍ fa-hiya mudbisa* — some scholar said this of land, when the first darkening of new plant-growth was seen on it.
5. *al-dibs* [in the sense of] abundance — this is used by metaphor, the way one also calls a great mass 'al-dahmā'' and 'al-sawād' [both literally 'the black']; so it returns to that same sense.
6. *al-dibāsā'*, on the pattern fa'ālā' — the female locusts.
دبش:
The letters dāl, bā' and shīn are nothing [no sound root]. All the same, they say 'arḍun madbūsha', land whose plants the locusts have eaten. He said, in a line of verse:
In a vast waste, stripped bare by young locusts.
دبغ: The letters dāl, bā' and ghayn are a single word. One says 'dabaghtu al-adīm adbaghuhu wa-adbughuhu dabghan', I tanned the hide.
دبق: The letters dāl, bā' and qāf are nothing [no sound root]. They call diarrhoea al-dabūqā'.
دبل:
The letters dāl, bā' and lām are a root indicating gathering, collecting, and setting right what needs mending.

1. *dabaltu al-shay'* — I gathered the thing, as you gather a mouthful of food with your fingers.
2. *al-dubūl* — the irrigation channels, so named because they are 'tudbal', that is, cleared out and put right.
3. *arḍun madbūla* — land improved with manure or the like. Al-Kisā'ī said this, adding: anything you improve, you have 'dabaltahu' and 'damaltahu' [both meaning you set it right].
4. *al-dawbal* — the small donkey, named for the compactness of its build.
5. *dabila al-ba'īr*, and other animals too — it became full of flesh, when fattened.

Among what falls outside this root is al-dibl, calamity. One says 'dabalahum al-amr min al-sharr', the affair of evil came down upon them, and 'dablan dabīlan', as one says 'thuklan thākilan' [both meaning, roughly, bereavement upon bereavement]. The poet said, in a line of verse:
The thrusting of armoured warriors and the galloping of steeds... and the cry of the nursing women: calamity upon calamity!
دبى:
The letters dāl, bā' and yā' are not a root; rather it is a single word, and other things are then attached to it by comparison.

1. *al-dubā* — locusts, when they stir and move.
2. *adbā al-rimth* — the rimth shrub, when it first begins to split open; likened to al-dubā.
3. *jā'a fulānun bi-daban dabā* — so-and-so came with wealth like the dubā, that is, abundant — as some have mentioned.
4. *arḍun madbāh* — land abundant in dubā.
5. *madbiyya* — land whose plants the dubā has eaten.
دث: The letters dāl and thā' are a single word, which is light rain.
دثأ: The letters dāl, thā' and hamza are not a root, because it belongs to the class of letter-substitution. They say 'maṭarun dathī'un', rain that falls between the hot season and summer. But the true root is 'dafī'', from warmth, al-dif'.
دثر:
The letters dāl, thā’ and rā’ are a single root, regular and consistent [applying by analogy without exception]. It is one thing doubling and piling on another.

1. al-dathr — abundant wealth.
2. al-dithār — what a person wraps himself in, worn over the shi‘ār, the garment worn next to the skin.

As for the poet’s saying ‘wa-l-‘akari l-dathir’ [and the abundant flock], he meant al-dathr, abundant, and shifted the vowel onto the thā’.

3. tadaththara al-faḥlu al-nāqata — the stallion mounted the she-camel and covered her, as though he had become a covering [dithār] for her.
4. tadaththara al-rajulu farasahu — the man leapt onto his horse and rode it.
5. al-dathūr — a man who sleeps a great deal, so named because he wraps himself up [yatadaththaru] and sleeps.

As for their saying rasmun dāthir, a faded trace, this too comes from the root: a trace stays visible until the winds blow over it and the dust-bearing winds come to it, so that it becomes like a covering [dithār] over it, covering it.
دثن: The letters dāl, thā' and nūn are a saying that may well be sound, but as for its following any regular pattern, it does not. They say: 'dathana al-ṭā'ir', the bird hurried in its flight; and 'dathana', he built his nest. The two words resemble each other, and the matter concerning them is weak.
دج:
The letters dāl and jīm are two origins: one is something like a slight creeping motion, and the other is something that covers and conceals.
The first is their saying dajja dajījan, used when a thing creeps along and moves about.
1. al-dājj — those who go along with the pilgrims (al-ḥājj), helping in their trading. In the hadith: "These are the dājj, and not the ḥājj."
As for the hadith of Anas, "I left neither ḥājah nor dājah," that is not from this chapter, because al-dājah is a lightened form of ḥājah, added to it for emphasis.
2. al-dajājah — the hen, well known; so called because it tudajdiju, that is, it comes and goes.
3. al-dajājah — also the ball of thread wound on a spindle; if that use is sound, it is by way of comparison.
4. Their saying "so-and-so has a dajājah," meaning dependents, a household — this too fits the same reasoning, because they crowd toward him.
The other origin is their saying tadajdaja al-layl, said when night grows dark.
1. laylun dajūjiyy — a dark night.
2. dajjajat al-samā' tadjījan — the sky grew clouded.
3. tadajdaja al-fāris bi-shikkatihi — the horseman covered himself in his gear, as though he wrapped himself in it. He is called mudajjij or mudajjaj.
4. mudajjaj — also what they call the hedgehog, from this. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And a mudajjaj running with his gear, his eyes red like a dog's.
5. dajawjāh — a she-camel lying flat spread on the ground; it belongs to this chapter, because it is as though it covers the ground.
دجر:
The letters dāl, jīm and rā' are a root that points to covering, obscurity.

1. al-daijūr — darkness; the plural is daiyājir and daiyājīr.
2. al-dajar — something like bewilderment; this follows the same pattern. One says a man is dajrān, and (plural) dajārā, just as one says ḥayrān and ḥayārā (bewildered).

There is a word here which, if sound, is irregular against the root sense we have given: they say al-dujr is the piece of wood that the plough's iron blade is tied to. I do not think this is from the speech of the Arabs.
دجل:
The letters dāl, jīm and lām are a single root, regular in its pattern, pointing to covering something over and concealing it.

The linguists said: al-dajl is disguising a thing so that it looks other than it is, and for this the liar was named al-dajjāl [the deceiver]. I heard ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm al-Qaṭṭān say: I heard Thaʿlab say: al-dajjāl means the one disguised over. One says a sword is mudajjal when it has been coated with gold. He was asked: can gold itself be called dajjāl? He said: I do not know that.

1. al-dajjāla — a great company of people carrying goods for trade; this belongs to the root.
2. dajjaltu al-baʿīr — I coated the camel with tar; the camel is then mudajjal.

Ibn Durayd said: anything you cover over, you have dajjaltahu. And Dijla [the Tigris] was named so because it covers the land with the great gathering of its water. One says a travelling party is dajjāla when it covers the ground with its crowding. He said, in a line of verse:
A great covering party, one of the largest of companies.

And in Al-Khalīl's book: al-dajjāl is the liar, and his dajal is simply his lying, because he covers truth over with falsehood.
دجم: The letters dāl, jīm and mīm are a single word. One says dujima, meaning he grieved. And they say: I did not hear from so-and-so a dujma, meaning a word. This looks as though it belongs to the pattern of letter-substitution, the original being zujma.
دجن:
The letters dāl, jīm and nūn follow the same pattern as dāl, jīm and lām [covering].

1. al-dajn — the shade of cloud on a rainy day.
2. adjana al-maṭar — the rain went on continuously for days.
3. al-mudājana — keeping good company with someone, mixing well with them.
4. al-dujunna — darkness.

In Al-Khalīl's book he said: had the poet lightened it [the word], that would have been allowed him. Ḥumayd said, in a line of verse:
Until the darknesses of the clouded days cleared away.

5. dajana dujūnan — he stayed on, remained in place.
6. al-shāh al-dājin — the sheep that keeps to the houses, tame and staying close to home.

God knows best.
دح:
The letters dāl and ḥā' are a single root, indicating spreading out and broadening. The Arabs say daḥaḥtu al-bayt, and other things, meaning I widened it. And "his belly indaḥḥa" is said when it broadened out. A bedouin said: "We were rained on for two nights left in the month, and the ground spread out wide with pasture." One also says "the hunter daḥḥa his hide," when he set it low into the ground. Abū al-Najm said, in a line of verse:
A hidden dwelling in the earth, pressed low.
1. al-daḥdāḥ — the short man, so named for being low and thick-set.
2. al-duḥaydiḥa — likewise, a short one.
A poet said, in a line of verse:
Does it deceive you that I am an ugly man, a duḥaydiḥa, while you are a tall, full-figured woman?
دحر: The letters dāl, ḥā' and rā' are a single root: driving away and banishing. God Almighty said: {Get out of it, blamed and banished} [al-A'rāf: 18].
دحز: The letters dāl, ḥā' and zāy are not anything [not a real root]. Ibn Durayd said: al-daḥz is sexual intercourse. This man is fond of the subject of intercourse and pushing, and the subject of gathering up odds and ends and collecting.
دحس:
The letters dāl, ḥā' and sīn are a root, regular and consistent, meaning one thing working its way in between another, quietly and gently.

1. al-daḥs — seeking a thing out in secret.
2. daḥastu bayna al-qawm — I stirred up trouble among the people; this can only be done gently, with a subtle, hidden insinuation.
3. al-daḥs — putting your hand between a sheep's skin and the membrane beneath it, to skin it.
4. al-daḥḥās — a small creature that hides itself in the dust; plural daḥāḥīs.
5. Dāḥis — the name of a horse. He was named this because Ḥawṭ forced himself on his mother — Umm Dāḥis — with water and mud, meaning to draw his own horse's seed out from her womb. There is a story about this.
دحص:
The letters dāl, ḥā' and ṣād are a single word. One says the slaughtered animal daḥaṣa with its leg, yadḥaṣu, daḥṣan, when it thrashes about.

ʿAlqama said, in a line of verse:
The great camel of the sky roared above them, and there was one thrashing about in his war-gear, not stripped of it, and another stripped bare.
دحض: The letters dāl, ḥā' and ḍād are a root indicating vanishing and slipping. One says: his foot daḥaḍat, meaning it slipped. From this: the sun daḥaḍat, meaning it passed its zenith. And so-and-so's argument daḥaḍat, when it did not hold up. God, exalted be His praise, said: {Their argument is refuted before their Lord} [al-Shūrā: 16].
دحق:
The letters dāl, ḥā' and qāf are a pattern close to the one before it.

1. daḥaqa al-shayʾ — the thing shifted and did not stay fixed.
2. al-daḥīq — the far-off, the distant.
3. daḥaqtu ʿanhu yadahu — said when so-and-so did such-and-such and I pulled his hand back from it, meaning I gripped it and drew it away.
4. adḥaqahu Allāh — God drove him far off.
5. daḥaqat al-raḥim — the womb cast out the seed and did not receive it.
6. al-diḥāq — when the female's womb comes out after giving birth, and she does not recover but dies from it; she is then daḥūq.

He said, in a line of verse:
And your mother is the best of women, in that neither the womb-prolapse nor the al-atam [a birth ailment] ever betrayed her.
دحل:
The letters dāl, ḥā' and lām point to a hollow undercut in a thing, and a sinking depression.

1. al-daḥl — a low, sunken place in the ground; plural al-duḥūl.
2. biʾr daḥūl — a well with an undercut hollow in its side, which happens when the water has filled its shaft completely.
3. al-daḥil, describing a person's build — the one with a big belly; this follows the pattern of the root, since it points to a wide, hollowed-out space.
دحم: The letters dāl, ḥā' and mīm are not anything [not a real root]. Though they do say: daḥamahu, meaning he pushed him hard, a violent shove. A man was named for this Daḥmān and Duḥaym.
دحن: The letters dāl, ḥā' and nūn are not a root, because they belong to the pattern of letter-substitution. One says a man is daḥin, which is the same as al-daḥil [big-bellied]; we have already explained it.
دحو:
The letters dāl, ḥā’ and wāw are a single root pointing to spreading out and levelling.

1. daḥā Allāhu al-arḍa yadḥūhā daḥwan — God spread out the earth, laying it flat.
2. daḥā al-maṭaru al-ḥaṣā ‘an wajhi al-arḍ — the rain swept the pebbles off the face of the ground; this is because when that happens, it has levelled the ground.
3. For a horse, when it throws its forelegs forward without lifting its hoof far from the ground, one says: marra yadḥū daḥwan — it went along skimming low over the ground.
4. udḥiyy al-na‘ām — the place where the ostrich lays and hatches its eggs, on the pattern uf‘ūl from daḥawtu, because it scoops the ground out with its foot and then lays its eggs there. The ostrich has no nest.
دخ:
The letters dāl and khā' are not a root from which anything branches, but they say dakhdakhnā al-qawm — dakhdakhah — meaning we humbled them. Al-Shaybānī mentioned that al-dakhdakhah is exhaustion. As for al-dukhkh, it has been mentioned in its own place; it is smoke. He said, in a line of verse:
When the fire's blaze rages, it is covered in smoke.
دخر:
The letters dāl, khā' and rā' are a root indicating abasement. One says: the man dakhara, and he is dākhir, meaning he was abased. Someone else adkharahu, meaning he abased him.

As for al-dakhdār, it is the fine garment that is kept protected.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And it reveals the surface of a fine, new dakhdār garment.

This word has nothing at all to do with the first root, because it is an Arabized foreign word; they say its origin is the Persian "takht dār," meaning: kept safe in a chest.
دخس:
The letters dāl, khā' and sīn are a single root, pointing to being packed tightly together and burrowing into dust or other than it.

1. al-dakhs — a thing burrowing into the dust. For this the rajaz poet named the three stones a cooking pot stands on al-dukhkhas.

This is the origin sense; then everything that gathers together into a thing and enters into it was named from this.

2. al-dakhīs — al-ḥawshab, which is the part of the leg between the shank-bone and the sinew.
3. al-dakhīs, of people — a great number, a large crowd.
4. al-dakhas — a disease in the legs of a riding animal.
5. al-dakhīs — packed, compact flesh; anything fat is dakhīs.
6. al-dakhīs — the flesh of the inner palm of the hand, so it is also said.
7. al-dakhīs, of heaps of sand — abundant, plentiful.
8. kalaʾ daykhas — abundant pasture.

He cited, in a line of verse:
It grazes on ḥaliyy and naṣiyy (types of desert grass), abundant growth.
دخش: The letters dāl, khā' and shīn are not anything [not a real root]. Ibn Durayd claimed that al-dakhash is a verb no longer in use; one says dakhisha, dakhashan, when someone became full of flesh, plump. From it is derived Dakhsham [a man's name].
دخص: The letters dāl, khā' and ṣād are like the one before it. Ibn Durayd mentioned that al-dakhūṣ is a plump young woman.
دخل:
The letters dāl, khā' and lām are a steady root that runs to a regular pattern, and it is entering in. One says dakhala yadkhulu dukhūlan. And al-dukhla, also al-dikhla, is the inward side of a man's affair. You say anā ʿālimun bi-dukhlatihi — I know his inner state. And al-dakhal is a fault in a man's lineage, as though something had entered upon it and spoiled it. And al-dakhal is like al-daghal, corruption, and it is of the chapter, because al-daghal has this same pattern. And it is said that al-madkhūl is the lean, wasted one, and that is sound, because his flesh is as though it had been entered into. And dakhīluka is the one who enters with you into your affairs. And al-dikhāl at the watering is that the camels drink, then be turned back to the trough so that any of them that may not have drunk may drink.

Al-Hudhalī said, in a line of verse:
And she fills out the flanks with a drinking taken in turns.

And it is said that every gathered lump of flesh is a dukhkhala, and by that this bird was called a dukhkhal. And one says dukhila fulānun, and he is madkhūl, when there is something wrong in his mind. And Banū so-and-so are dakhīl among Banū so-and-so, when they trace their descent along with them. And a nakhla madkhūla is a palm rotten within. And al-dukhlul is the one who enters with you into your affairs. And al-dukhkhal of a bird's feathers is what lies between the back feathers and the belly feathers, and it is the best of the plumage. And dākhilat al-izār is the edge of the waist-wrapper that is next to the body. And al-dukhkhal of herbage is what of it has gone in among the roots of the trees.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
The first signs of dark growth gone in among the roots, and of fresh green grass.
دخن:
The letters dāl, khā' and nūn are a single root, and it is what comes from kindling/burning; then everything resembling it — enmity and the like — is compared to it.

1. al-dukhān — smoke, well known. Its plural is dawākhin, against the usual pattern.
2. One says dakhanat al-nār tadkhunu, when a fire's smoke rises.
3. dakhinat tadkhanu — when you throw firewood on a fire and spoil it, so that smoke rises because of that; likewise dakhina al-ṭaʿām yadkhanu, when food is spoiled by smoke.
4. dakhana al-ghubār — the dust rose.
5. In the hadith "hudnatun ʿalā dakhan" (a truce with smoke beneath it): it means a settling upon matters that are disliked.
6. al-dukhna, among colors — a dullness/greyness within blackness: a ewe is dakhnā', a ram is adkhan, a night is dakhnāna.
7. rajulun dakhinu l-khuluq — a man of a dark, foul temperament.
8. Abnā' Dukhān — "the sons of smoke": Ghaniyy and Bāhila [two tribes so nicknamed].
9. al-dukhna — incense with which a house is fumigated.
دد:
The letters dāl and dāl are a single word. Al-dad is amusement and play. The Messenger of God, God bless him and grant him peace, said: "I am not of dad, nor is dad of me." One also says dad, dadan, and dadan [dadanan]. A poet said, in a line of verse:
O heart, distract yourself with dadan — my care is all in listening and in the ear.
And dad — so it is said — is the name of a woman. God knows best.
ددن:
The letters dāl, dāl and nūn are two [separate] words: one of them is amusement and play; one says dadan and dad.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
O heart, distract yourself with amusement — my only concern is in listening and hearing.

From this the blunt sword was named al-dadān, because it is weak, as though it has no sharpness in its striking.

The other word: al-daydan — habit, custom.

God knows best.
در:
The letters dāl and rā', as a doubled root, indicate two origins: one is a thing being generated out of another, and the second is agitation in a thing.

The first: al-darr is the flow of milk. Al-darra — darrat al-saḥāb — is a cloud's pouring rain; one says saḥābun midrār, a cloud that pours heavily.
1. From this comes their saying "lillāhi darruhu" — God's is his output — meaning his deed, as though likened to the milk that comes from milk-yielding animals.
2. And in cursing they say "lā darra darruhu" — may his output not increase — meaning may his good not abound.
3. From this chapter: darrat ḥalūbatu l-Muslimīn, meaning the Muslims' tribute flowed in.
4. And "this market has dirra," meaning brisk trade, as if it had yielded milk — the opposite of ghirār, scarcity. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Alas, my people, Nawār is Nawār no longer... and the market has from her both flow and scarcity.
5. From this: istadarrati l-miʿzā istidrāran, when the she-goat seeks the male, as if she wants his fluid to flow for her.

The other origin: al-darīr, among riding beasts, is the one strong and swift in running. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Swift as a boy's spinning top, that his hands, in steady turns joined by a cord, keep spinning.
1. Al-durdur — where a child's teeth come in. It is from tadardarati l-luḥmatu tadarduran, when the flesh quivered; and dardara al-ṣabiyyu the thing, when he chewed on it, yudardiruhu.
2. Darar al-rīḥ — the quarter the wind blows from.
3. Darar al-ṭarīq — the road's straight course, because it is never empty of those coming and going.
4. Al-durr — large pearls, so named for a shimmer seen in them from their clarity, as though it were water astir. Al-Hudhalī said, of this, in a line of verse:
He brought of it as much as you wished, of oyster-pearl, over which fresh water seems to linger and surge.
He means: it is as if water moved within it, from its clarity and beauty.
5. Al-kawkab al-durriyy — the piercing, shining star, likened to pearl and named for it, for its whiteness.
درب:
The sound part of the letters dāl, rā' and bā' is a single root: being made fond of a thing and clinging to it. One says dariba bi'l-shay', when he clings to it and sticks to it.
1. al-durbah — what they call habit and experience, from this chapter.
2. ṭayrun dawārib bi'l-dimā' — birds made fond of blood, when they have been trained to it.
The poet said, in a line of verse:
They accompany them until they swoop down in their raid, birds of prey fond of blood.
3. darb al-madīnah — the city gate, well known; if this is sound Arabic, it fits the reasoning of the chapter, because people make their way through it, heading for it deliberately.
As for tadarbā al-shay', said when a thing tumbled down, that too has been reported. And al-darbāniyyah is a kind of cattle. And al-dardāb is the sound of the drum. All of this is speech whose sense is not really known.
درج:
The letters dāl, rā' and jīm are a single root pointing to a thing passing on, and to going along in a thing.

From this is their saying daraja al-shay', when it went its way. And raja'a fulān adrājahu, when a man goes back along the road he came by. And daraja al-ṣabiyy, when the small child walks his little walk. Al-Aṣma'ī said: daraja al-rajul, when a man dies and leaves no offspring behind. And madārij al-akama are the paths that cross over a hillock. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Go out across the tracks and keep on, as al-Jawzā' comes out to meet the stars.

As for al-durj, used of certain cases and instruments, if it is sound then it is another root, pointing to covering and hiding. From this is adrajtu al-kitāb, I rolled up the letter, and adrajtu al-ḥabl, I coiled the rope. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Tight-twisted, wound up as a tether-rope is wound.

And of this second chapter is al-durja, rags that are put into the vulva of the she-camel and then drawn out; when the camel smells them she takes them for her young one and yearns over it. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And the rags of fostering were not made for her.
درح:
The letters dāl, rā' and ḥā' likewise form a small root. They call a short man dirḥāyah, who along with that is stout and thickset.
He said, in a line of verse:
A stocky man, when he walks, a dirḥāyah.
God knows best.
درد: The letters dāl, rā' and dāl form a small root, with little to say about it. Al-darad, of the teeth, is their sticking close to the roots after what remains of them has worn away. One says daridat, and she is durd. A man is adrad, and a woman is dardā'.
درز:
The letters dāl, rā' and zāy are nothing — not a root — and I do not think the Arabs spoke it. Except that Ibn al-Aʿrābī related that he said: the Arabs say of low, base people, "They are the sons of Darzah," just as they say of thieves and their like, "the sons of Ghabrā'." He cited, in a line of verse:
The sons of Darzah abandoned you and fled.
درس:
The letters dāl, rā' and sīn are a single root, indicating something hidden, something low, and something worn away. Al-dars is the faint, hidden path. One says darasa al-manzilu, the dwelling-place was effaced.

1. al-darīs — the worn-out garment, of this chapter.

From this too: darasat al-mar'atu, the woman menstruated; it is said her private part is nicknamed "Abū Adrās" [Father of Threshings], from this, connected to menstruation. Darastu al-ḥinṭata wa ghayrahā fī sunbulihā means I threshed the wheat, or other grain, while still in its ear, by treading it underfoot; this is taken to mean it was put under the feet, like a path that is trodden and walked upon. A verse:
A tawny one, from what Ibn Mikhrāq threshed...

Al-dars is also a slight mange found on a camel.

From this chapter too: darastu al-Qur'āna wa ghayrahu, I studied the Qur'an and other things, because the one who studies retraces what he has read, the way a traveler retraces a path he follows.

What falls outside this chapter: al-dirwās, said of a person or animal with a thick neck.
درص:
The letters dāl, rā' and ṣād are not a root that other words are measured against or branch from, but they say al-dirṣ is the young of the mouse, and its plural is diraṣah. And they say "the people fell into umm adrāṣ" when they fell into a place of destruction. That comes from the first sense, because empty, deserted land has young mice in it.
He said, in a line of verse:
Umm Adrāṣ, in a land where men lose their way, is no more treacherous than Qays when night grows dark.
And they say of a man confused about his affair: "The young mouse [durayṣ] lost its burrow."
درع:
The letters dāl, rā' and ʿayn are a single root: something worn as clothing, and other things are then carried onto it by comparison. Al-dirʿ, the iron coat of mail, is feminine, with the plural durūʿ and adrāʿ. And dirʿ al-mar'a, a woman's shift, is masculine.
This is the origin sense. Then one says:
1. shātun darʿā' — a ewe whose head is black and whose rest of the body is white. This follows the same reasoning, because the whiteness of the rest of her body is like a coat of mail she has put on.
2. al-layālī al-durʿ — three nights whose first parts are dark and whose rest is light, likened to the darʿā' ewe. This then is something likened to something already likened to something else.
What departs from the chapter:
1. al-indirāʿ — going ahead in travel.
He said, in a line of verse:
Ahead of the horses, surging forward.
درق:
The letters dāl, rā' and qāf are not, in my view, a root that other words can be measured against. But al-daraqah, the shield, is well known, with the plural daraq and adrāq. Ru'bah said, in a line of verse:
Had he lined up shields, he would have gone past the shields.
And al-dardaq is the young of camels, and small children.
درك:
The letters dāl, rā' and kāf are a single root, and it is one thing catching up with another and reaching it. One says adraktu al-shay' udrikuhu idrākan — I overtook the thing. And it is said: a horse that is darak al-ṭarīda, when no quarry escapes it. And it is said adraka al-ghulām wa-l-jāriya, when the boy and the girl come of age. Tadāraka al-qawm — the last of the people caught up with the first of them. And tadāraka al-tharayān, when the second wetting of the earth catches up with the first rain. As for His words, Most High: {no, their knowledge caught up with them concerning the hereafter} [al-Naml: 66], that is from this, because their knowledge overtook them in the hereafter at a time when it did not profit them.

Al-darak is the piece of rope tied at the end of the well-rope to the crossbar of the bucket, so that the water may not eat away the well-rope. Although it is for this purpose, it is by it that the bucket is caught and brought up.

Of this too is al-darak, which are the dwelling places of the people of the Fire. That is because the Garden [is degrees rising up, and the Fire] is levels going down. God Most High said: {the hypocrites are in the lowest level of the Fire} [al-Nisā': 145]; these are their dwelling places, which they reach and come down to. We seek refuge with God from them!
درم:
The letters dāl, rā' and mīm are a root indicating drawing near and softness. One says dirʿun darimah, meaning a coat of mail that is soft and well-fitted. And al-daramān is taking close, short steps. A man was named Dārim from this.
1. al-daram — a flatness in the anklebone beneath the flesh, so that it has no raised shape. One says of it kaʿbun adram, a flat anklebone.
He said, in a line of verse:
She stood, showing you — for fear it might be cut off — a shapely calf, and a flat anklebone.
2. "His teeth daramat" — one says this when they wear down at the roots and their edges soften.
3. From this too is their saying adrama al-faras, when its tooth falls out, so it passes from being a two-year-old into a four-year-old in its teeth.
4. al-darrāmah — the short woman; in our view this is the same sense of close, short steps, because the short woman walks in this way.
He said, in a line of verse:
Among the fair, no squat, lice-ridden, close-stepping woman outshines the tribe's women in grace and mark.
Then, from what we have mentioned, further words are derived.
1. Banū al-Adram — a tribe.
He said, in a line of verse:
The sons of al-Adram belong to no one.
2. Darim — the name of a man, in the saying of al-Aʿshā:
As was said of the tribe: Darim has perished.
He was a man of Shaybān, who was killed and whose blood was never avenged.
درن:
The letters dāl, rā' and nūn are a sound root, meaning something growing old in a thing along with a change of its color.

1. al-darīn — dried-up herbage left over from the past year. Barren, drought-stricken land is called umm darīn, 'the mother of darīn.'

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Come, let us bind fast our love for Daʿd and set out together as one, while the pasture is at umm darīn.
He means: come, let us hold to our love, our land, and our way of life.

2. al-daran — dirt, grime.
3. durayna — a nickname given to a fool.

As for their saying that al-idrawn means 'the origin' — that is something that has been said, but we do not know what it is.
دره: The letters dāl, rā' and hā' are not a root, because the hā' is substituted for a hamza. One says daraʾa, meaning he appeared, rose up, and this is then turned into a hā', so one says daraha. And al-midrah is the tribe's spokesman, the one who speaks on their behalf.
درى:
The letters dāl, rā', the weak letter, and the hamzated form. As for the one without hamza, it is two origins: one is aiming at a thing and setting oneself toward it in pursuit, and the other is a sharpness found in a thing. As for the hamzated one, it is a single root: pushing a thing away.
The first is their saying: the sons of so-and-so iddaraw a certain place, meaning they set out for it intending a raid or an attack.
He said, in a line of verse:
ʿĀmir came to us from the land of Rām, their quivers hung, seeking us out.
1. al-dariyyah — the animal behind which the hunter of game hides himself in order to shoot it. One says from it daraytu and iddaraytu.
Al-Akhṭal said, in a line of verse:
Even if you struck me true when you shot me with your arrow — the hunter takes his game, yet does not perceive it.
Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: tadarraytu al-ṣayd, when you watched where the game was but had not yet seen it. And daraytuhu, I stalked it by stealth.
As for his saying tadarraytu meaning "I learned," it is because he came to know [dirya] where the thing was — the reasoning is the same. One says daraytu al-shay', I knew the thing, and "God, exalted, adrānīhi," made me know it. God, exalted, said: {Say: had God willed, I would not have recited it to you, nor would He have made you know it} [Yūnus: 16]. And "so-and-so is ḥasan al-diryah," like saying "of good perception."
The other origin is their word for the thing with which the hair is combed and parted: al-midrā, because it is pointed.
1. shātun mudrāt — a ewe with sharp horns.
2. tadarrat al-mar'a — a woman combed out her hair, when she did so.
3. al-midrayān — said to be the two teats of a ewe, and sometimes used for a she-camel's teats.
Ḥumayd said, in a line of verse:
She gives generously from her two teats.
They were called midrayān because, when full, their two ends become pointed.
As for the hamzated form, it is their saying daraʾtu al-shay' — I pushed the thing away. God, exalted, said: {and He wards off from her the punishment} [al-Nūr: 8].
He said, in a line of verse:
You say, when I let loose my saddle-girth for her: is this his religion forever, and my religion?
1. al-darī'ah — the ring used to practice thrusting with a spear.
ʿAmr said, in a line of verse:
I stood as though I were a target for the spears, fighting for the sons of Jarm, though they had fled.
2. "The flood came dar'an" — said when it comes from a distant land.
3. "So-and-so is dhū tudra'" — meaning strong enough to fend off his enemies from himself.
He said, in a line of verse:
I was, in war, possessed of tudra' — yet I was given nothing, nor was I refused.
4. daraʾa — said of one who appears suddenly, unexpectedly; it belongs to this chapter, as though he pushed himself forward, that is, thrust himself out. From this too is dāra'ta so-and-so, meaning you resisted and pushed against him. And when the hamza is softened, it takes the meaning of stealth and deception, going back to the first origin mentioned under daraytu and iddaraytu.
He said, in a line of verse:
What then can the poets perceive of me, when I have passed the age of forty?
5. al-darʾ, meaning crookedness, comes from the same reasoning as pushing, because when a thing bends, it is pushed from the state of straightness into crookedness. And "a road dhū darʾ" means one with breaks and eroded edges, from the same. One also says "I straightened it from its darʾ," meaning I set it right.
He said, in a line of verse:
And we, whenever the tyrant turned his cheek aside in arrogance, would set him straight from his crookedness, and he would be set right.
6. "The camel daraʾa" — said when its back swells up. If this is sound, it belongs to this chapter, because it is pushed outward when it swells.
7. Also from this chapter: "the she-camel adraʾat," so she is mudri', said when she lets her udder hang loose at the time of giving birth.
دس:
The letters dāl and sīn, doubled and matching, are a single root indicating a thing entering under concealment and secrecy. One says dasastu al-shay'a fī l-turābi adussuhu dassan — I buried the thing in the dust. God Almighty said: {does he keep it in disgrace, or bury it in the dust?} [al-Naḥl: 59]. And al-dassāsa is a deaf snake that lives beneath the dust.

As for their saying "dussa al-baʿīr," there are two explanations for it, each following the pattern of this chapter. One: that he has a little mange on him, and if so, it is because that mange is like a slight thing that creeps in unseen. The other: that tar is smeared on the tender parts of the camel's body. From this chapter also: al-dasīs, the one who moves stealthily. And their saying "the vein/bloodline is dassās" — because a trait draws itself out in concealment and subtlety.
دست:
The letters dāl, sīn and tā' are not a root, because al-dast means the open desert, and it is a Persian word arabized. Al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse:
Persia and Ḥimyar and the Arabs alike have known, on the open plain, which of you has come down to stay.
دسر:
The letters dāl, sīn, and rā' are a single root indicating pushing/thrusting. One says dasartu al-shayʾa dasran, when you push a thing with a hard shove. In the hadith: "There is no obligatory alms on ambergris; it is only something the sea dasarahu," meaning cast up and thrust forth. In the hadith of ʿUmar, God be pleased with him: "The thing I fear most for you is that a man be seized and thrust down as the slaughter-camel is thrust down," meaning shoved down.

From this branch too: dasarahu bi-l-rumḥ, he thrust him through with the spear, and a spear used for this is midsar. A poet said, in a line of verse:
From a huge, dark, overwhelming mass — had it thrust its bulk against the peaks of Damkh, they would have been torn up by the roots.
Meaning: had it pushed against them.

A huge, powerful camel is called dawsarī. Dawsar is a name for a battalion, because it drives back enemies.

Among what falls outside the root's core sense, yet is sound: al-disār is a cord of palm-fiber with which the planks of a ship are bound, plural dusur. God Almighty said: {and We carried him upon a thing of planks and cords} [al-Qamar: 13]. And it is said al-dusur means nails.
دسع:
The letters dāl, sīn and ʿayn are a root indicating pushing. One says dasaʿa al-baʿīr bi-jirratihi, said of a camel when it pushes up its cud.
1. al-dasʿ — the coming up of the cud.
2. al-dasīʿah — a man's generosity and noble conduct in his affairs. "So-and-so is ḍakhm al-dasīʿah" — some say this means the [large] bowl, others the table spread of food. Whichever it is, it comes from pushing and giving.
From this is the hadith of the Messenger of God, God bless him, his family, and grant him peace, in his writing between Quraysh and the Anṣār: "The believers' hands are against whoever transgresses against them, or seeks a dasīʿat ẓulm" — meaning here too pushing; that is, he sought to extract something by wrongdoing. And in another hadith: God, exalted, says: "O son of Adam, did I not make you tarbaʿu and tadsaʿu?" His saying tarbaʿu means you take the mirbāʿ, a chief's fourth share of war-spoils; and his saying tadsaʿu means you push forth and give generously.
دسق: The letters dāl, sīn and qāf form a small root indicating fullness. One says: "I filled the trough until it dasiqa," meaning it became so full that its water overflowed and spread. Al-daysaq is the full trough. It is also said that al-daysaq is the shimmering of the mirage over the ground.
دسم:
The letters dāl, sīn and mīm are two origins: one indicates stopping something up, and the other indicates smearing one thing with another.
The first is al-disām, the stopper for anything. Some people said: dasama al-bāb, he shut the door.
The second is al-dasam, well known [grease, fat], so called because it smears onto things.
1. al-dusmah — a base, worthless man; so called because he is as though smeared with vileness.
2. "huwa dasamu al-thiyāb" — said of a treacherous man, as though he has been smeared with something foul.
He said, in a line of verse:
O Lord, indeed al-Ḥārith ibn al-Jahm undertook a pilgrimage in soiled garments.
3. By way of comparison: dasama al-maṭar al-arḍ, said when rain is scant and does not soak the soil.
What departs from the chapter: al-daysam, the offspring of a wolf by a bitch. Al-daysam also names the plant called "bustān afrūz." And it is said that al-daysamah is the ant.
دسوا:
The letters dāl, sīn and the weak letter are a single root, indicating hiddenness and concealment. One says dasawtu al-shay' adsūhu, and dasā yadsū, the opposite of zakā [to grow pure].
As for His word, exalted: {and he has failed who buries it} [al-Shams: 10], the people of learning said the origin is dassasahā, as though he concealed it, because the generous man of hospitality alights in every open, exposed place, and on every high ground, so that guests may come upon him, while the miser alights only in a hollow or hidden spot. So God, exalted, says: {he has succeeded who purifies it, and he has failed who buries it} [al-Shams: 9], that is, concealed it or hid it away. This is the view relied upon. Though some of the people of learning said dassāhā means "he led it astray," and enticed it toward wrongdoing.
He cited, in a line of verse:
And you are the one who led ʿAmr astray, so his wives became widows, abandoned because of him.
دظ: The letters dāl and ẓā' are not a root to be relied on, nor one to reason from by analogy. They mentioned, from al-Khalīl, that al-daẓẓ is routing; one says daẓaẓnāhum, when we routed them. And this is nothing.
دع:
The letters dāl and ʿayn are a single root, sound and consistent by analogy, indicating motion, pushing, and agitation. Al-daʿʿ is pushing; one says daʿaʿtuhu aduʿʿuhu daʿʿan. God Almighty said: {the day they are pushed toward the fire of Hell violently} [al-Ṭūr: 13].
1. Al-daʿdaʿa — shaking a measure so that it takes in the thing fully.
2. Al-daʿdaʿa — a run with a twist to it. One says jafnatun mudaʿdaʿa, a bowl filled by having been shaken; its sense is that it was shaken until it filled.

As for their saying that al-daʿdaʿa is the call used to drive sheep, and that al-daʿdaʿa is your saying "daʿ daʿ" to one who has stumbled, as one says "laʿan" — we have already said that sounds and their imitations can scarcely be reasoned from by analogy, and are not roots on that basis.

As for their calling a short man daʿdāʿ, if that is sound then it comes from substitution of a ḥā': daḥdāḥ.
دعب:
The letters dāl, ʿayn and bā' are a root indicating stretching out and spreading in a thing.
1. al-duʿbūb — the easy, smooth road.
2. farasun duʿbūb — a long-bodied, stretched-out horse, as they sometimes say.
The reasoning of al-duʿābah [jesting, playfulness] comes from this too, because there is in it an easy give and a spreading out.
دعث: The letters dāl, ʿayn and thā' are a single word: al-diʿth, which is rancor.
دعج:
The letters dāl, ʿayn and jīm are a single root indicating a black color.
1. al-adʿaj — the black one.
2. al-daʿaj, in the eye — intense blackness [of the pupil] set against intense whiteness [of the eye].
دعد: The letters dāl, ʿayn and dāl are nothing, not a root. They sometimes name a woman Daʿd.
دعر:
The letters dāl, ʿayn and rā' are a single root indicating something disliked and harmful, and its origin is smoke. One says ʿūdun daʿir, when a piece of wood is heavy with smoke.
Ibn Muqbil said, in a line of verse:
Laylā's wood-gatherers spent the night seeking for her thick logs — neither weak nor smoky.
1. From this too comes the derivation of al-daʿārah, wickedness of character.
2. al-daʿr — corruption, depravity.
3. al-zand al-adʿar — the fire-stick that has been struck many times until its tip has burned and it no longer strikes a spark.
4. Dāʿir — a stud [animal] to whom al-Dāʿiriyyah [a breed] is traced.
دعز: The letters dāl, ʿayn and zāy are nothing, not a root; and no reliance is placed on the claim of those who say it means pushing and copulation.
دعس:
The letters dāl, ʿayn and sīn form a small root indicating pushing and leaving a mark.
1. al-mudāʿasah — thrusting spears at one another, because the one who thrusts pushes the one thrust.
2. rumḥun midʿas, rimāḥun madāʿis — a spear, spears, [used for thrusting].
3. al-daʿs — copulation; this is by way of comparison.
4. al-daʿs — a track, a footprint; this too belongs to the same sense, because whoever leaves the mark pushes the thing at the moment he marks it.
دعص:
The letters dāl, ʿayn and ṣād are a root indicating fineness and softness.

1. al-diʿṣ — what is small and fine of sand.
2. al-daʿṣāʾ — soft, level ground.
3. tadaʿʿaṣa al-laḥm — the meat became overcooked, said when it goes too far in cooking.
4. adʿaṣahu al-ḥarr — the heat struck him dead, said when it killed him, as though it had cooked him and so killed him.
دعض: The letters dāl, ʿayn and ḍād are not a root.
دعظ: The letters dāl, ʿayn and ẓāʾ are not a root. They say: al-daʿẓ is intercourse.
دعق:
The letters dāl, ʿayn and qāf are a single root indicating leaving a mark on a thing and treading it down. A place which animals trample, marking it with their hooves, is called daʿaq.
Ru'bah said, in a line of verse:
Among the traces of tracks, and a trampling ground worn down.
1. shalla ibilahu shallan daʿqan — he drove his camels off hard, when he chased them away.
2. aghāra ghāratan daʿqan — he made a trampling raid.
3. khaylun madāʿīq — horses that trample the ground.
He said, in a line of verse:
They do not concern themselves with driving off the strays by trampling.
دعك:
The letters dāl, ʿayn and kāf are a single root indicating working and rubbing a thing. One says daʿaka the hide or anything else, when he rubbed and kneaded it.
1. tadāʿaka al-rajulān fī al-ḥarb — the two men grappled with each other in battle, when each provoked the other.
2. al-duʿak, on the pattern fuʿal — the weak man.
They cited for Ḥassān, in a line of verse:
And you, when they went to war, were a duʿak.
دعم:
The letters dāl, ʿayn and mīm are a single root: something that stands as support and holding for another thing. One says daʿamtu al-shay' adʿamuhu daʿman, I propped the thing up; it is madʿūm.
1. al-diʿāmatān — the two posts of the pulley.
2. diʿāmat al-qawm — the chief, the mainstay of a people.
3. "there is no daʿm in so-and-so" — meaning he has no strength nor plumpness.
The rājiz said, in a line of verse:
There is no daʿm in me, but Laylā has the daʿm — a girl with flesh upon her hips.
4. Duʿmī — a name derived from this.
دعو:
The letters dāl, 'ayn and the weak letter are a single root, and it is that you incline something towards you by a sound or by words that come from you. You say: da'awtu, ad'ū, du'ā'an - I called. Al-da'wa with a fatḥa is the invitation to food, and al-di'wa with a kasra is the claim to descent. Abū 'Ubayda said: in descent one says di'wa, and in food da'wa. This is the speech of most of the Arabs, except 'Adiyy al-Ribāb, for they put a fatḥa on the dāl in descent and a kasra on it in food.

Al-Khalīl said: al-iddi'ā' is that you claim a right for yourself or for another. You say, he claimed a right, or a falsehood. Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
No, by your father, daughter of the 'Āmirī, the people do not claim that I flee.

And al-iddi'ā' in war is calling out one's lineage, which is that you say, I am the son of so-and-so. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And in the battle we drag our spears and call out our lineage.

And dā'iyat al-laban is what is left in the udder to call down the milk that comes after it. This is a likeness and a comparison. And in the hadith he said to the milker: 'Leave the caller of the milk.'

Then there is carried onto this section whatever resembles it in the analogy we have mentioned, so they say: God called so-and-so with what he hates, that is, He sent it down upon him. A poet said, in a line of verse:
May God call you, hyena, with a viper.

Because when He does that to her, He has inclined it towards her.

And tadā'at al-ḥīṭān, the walls fell one after another, and that is when one falls and then another after it, as though the first had called the second. And they may say: dā'aynāhā 'alayhim, when we pulled them down one after another. And dawā'ī al-dahr are the turns of fortune, as though they incline events towards men. And the sons of so-and-so have adiya, riddles they put to one another, and it is like a puzzle, as though the one asking were calling the one asked to bring out what he has hidden from him. And Abū 'Ubayd recited, from al-Aṣma'ī, a line of verse:
I put it to you as a riddle: what are the things brought along on a night journey, fair themselves, while their traces are not fair?

And of this section: mā bi-l-dāri du'wiyy, there is no one in the house, as though there were no one in it crying out with his call.

And it is carried onto this section by metaphor to say: such a place called so-and-so, when he made for that place, as though the place had called him. And this is of their eloquent speech. Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
The pools called Mayya away, and in her place there came droves of herds of wide-eyed wild cows, lagging behind.
دغر:
The letters dāl, ghayn and rāʾ are a single root, and it is pushing and forcing one's way into a thing. The Messenger of God, God bless him and his family and grant him peace, said to the women: "Do not torment your children with al-daghr."

1. al-daghr — pressing the throat for al-ʿudhra, al-ʿudhra being an ailment that flares up in the throat from blood; one says of the sufferer, huwa maʿdhūr.

Jarīr said, in a line of verse:
Ibn Murra pressed her private parts, O Farazdaq ... the way a doctor presses the swollen throat of one suffering from al-ʿudhra.

2. daghartu al-qawm — I forced my way in on the people, when you enter upon them.

They have a saying: "daghran lā ṣaffan" — meaning: charge upon them, do not line up in ranks facing them.

3. al-daghra — a stealthy snatching, because the snatcher forces himself upon the thing.

And in the hadith: "There is no [hand-cutting] punishment for al-daghra."
دغش: The letters dāl, ghayn and shīn are not a root. They relate the saying daghasha ʿalayhim — no further sense is given for it.
دغص: The letters dāl, ghayn and ṣād are a word said for the flesh that ripples atop a camel's knee: al-dāghiṣa [the kneecap].
دغف: The letters dāl, ghayn and fāʾ are not a root, except that Ibn Durayd claimed that al-daghf is excess in taking a thing.
دغل:
The letters dāl, ghayn and lām are a root indicating confusion and a twisting together of two things that intermingle.

1. al-daghal — tangled, interwoven trees.
2. al-daghal in a thing — corruption in it.
3. adghala fī al-amr — to introduce into a matter something that contradicts it, as they say.
دغم:
The letters dāl, ghayn and mīm are two roots: one is in the chapter of colours, and the other is the entering of something into an opening.

The first: al-dughma in horses is when the colour of the face differs from the colour of the rest of the body, and it is never anything but black. One of the proverbs of the Arabs is: "The wolf is dark-muzzled [adgham]." Its explanation is that it is dark-muzzled whether it has just lapped [eaten] or has not lapped — the dark colour never leaves it, so sometimes it is said that it has eaten when really it is hungry. This is used as a proverb for one who is envied for something he has not attained. From this chapter also: daghamahum al-ḥarr — the heat overcame them, because it changes the colours [of the skin].

The other root: their saying adghamtu al-lijām fī fam al-faras — I put the bit into the horse's mouth, when you insert it into it. From this comes al-idghām among the letters [the merging of one consonant into another in speech]. And al-daghm is the breaking of the nose, crushing it inward.
دف:
The letters dāl and fā' are two roots: one indicates breadth in a thing, the other speed.

The first: al-daff is the flank. Daffā al-baʿīr — the camel's two flanks. A poet said, in a line of verse:
It has a neck that turns with whatever is bound to it, and two flanks that outpace every laden train.
1. One says sanāmun mudaffif, when the hump has slipped down onto the camel's flanks.
2. Al-daff/al-duff — that which is played for amusement.

The second: daffa l-ṭā'iru dafīfan — when a bird glides low over the ground, beating its wings while its feet skim the earth.
1. From this: daffat ʿalaynā min banī fulānin dāffatun, tadiffu dafīfan — a band from so-and-so's tribe came upon us, moving swiftly; their dafīf is their swift travel.
2. And you say dāfaftu l-rajul, when you finish him off quickly. From this is the hadith of Khālid ibn al-Walīd: "whoever has a captive, let him finish him off" — meaning let him dispatch him swiftly. It belongs to this chapter because it hastens his death.
دفأ:
The letters dāl, fā', and hamza are a single root indicating the opposite of cold. Al-difʾ is warmth. One says dafuʾa yawmunā, our day grew warm, so it is dafīʾ; al-Kilābī said dafiʾ. The first form is better known for times and seasons; as for a person, one says dafiʾa, so he is dafʾān and a woman is dafʾā. A garment is dhū difʾ and dafāʾ. "So-and-so has no difʾ on him" means he has nothing to keep him warm. "Such a thing adfaʾanī" means it warmed me; "sit in the difʾ of this wall" means its sheltered lee side.

From this branch too: al-dafaʾī, among rains, is the one that comes in summer. Camels that are mudfaʾa are numerous ones, because some of them warm others with their breath. Al-Umawī said: al-difʾ among the Arabs means the offspring of camels, their milk, and the benefit derived from them. This is His saying, Great is His praise: {for you in them is warmth and other uses} [al-Naḥl: 5]. From this is the hadith of the Messenger of God, peace and blessings upon him and his family: "We have from their difʾ and their harvest whatever they hand over under the covenant."

From this branch too: al-dafaʾ means a stoop, a bending. In the description of the Dajjāl: "that there is dafaʾ in him," meaning a stoop. If this is correct, it fits the pattern, because anything that warms another thing must necessarily cover it and lean over it.
دفا:
The letters dāl, fāʾ and the weak letter [alif] are a root indicating length with a slight curve.

1. al-dafā — the length of a bird's wing; one says ṭāʾirun adfā, a long-winged bird.
2. adfā, of mountain goats — one whose horns are long.
3. dafwāʾ — said of the long-necked, noble she-camel.
4. al-dafwāʾ — the huge, tall tree. From this is the hadith: "He saw a tall tree [dafwāʾ] called Dhāt Anwāṭ."
5. dafwāʾ, said of the eagle — because of the length and curve of its beak.
6. tadāfā al-baʿīr tadāfiyan — the camel went with a swaying, leaning gait.
دفر:
The letters dāl, fāʾ and rāʾ are a single root, and it is a change in smell.

1. al-dafar — stench. They say to the slave-woman: "yā dafāri" [O foul-smelling one].
2. Umm Dafr — a name for the world [this life].
3. katība dafrāʾ — a troop so called, meaning the smells of its iron weapons.

One word has strayed from this chapter, if it is sound: they say dafartu al-rajul ʿannī — I pushed the man away from me.
دفع:
The letters dāl, fā' and ʿayn are a single well-known root pointing to putting a thing aside. One says *dafaʿtu al-shay'a adfaʿuhu dafʿan* — I pushed the thing away. And *dāfaʿa Allāhu ʿanhu al-sū'a difāʿan* — God warded off evil from him. And *al-mudaffaʿ* is the poor man, because he is pushed away from one to another when he asks. And that is what the poet said, in a line of verse:
People are enemies to every man pushed off, empty of hand, and brothers to the man who has much.

And it is he that the poet meant by his words, in a line of verse:
And one beaten who groans with no blow struck, tossed by the tent from tent to tent.

And *al-dufʿa* is a burst of rain, or of blood, or of something else. As for *al-duffāʿ*, it is the great flood. And all of this is derived from the fact that one part of it pushes another. And *al-mudaffaʿ* is the noble camel, the one that whenever he is brought to be loaded is put off and another brought instead, out of respect for him. And he is in the words of Ḥumayd, in a line of verse:
And they brought up for the journey every camel that is spared the load.
دفق:
The letters dāl, fā', and qāf are a single root whose pattern runs consistently: pushing a thing forward. From this: dafaqa al-māʾu, the water gushed forth, so it is māʾun dāfiq; this is a dufqa, a gush of water. Their saying "they came in one dufqa" is built on this, meaning all at once.

A camel is adfaq when its two elbows stand out clear from its sides, because when they stand clear they have pushed and thrust outward from it.

Al-difaqq, among camels, means the swift one. So-and-so walked al-difiqqā, when he moved quickly. Abū ʿUbayda said: al-difiqqā is the utmost pace of the running gait. From this is al-Zibriqān's saying: "she walks at the difiqqā, and she sits in the hunched, cross-legged way."

One says a flood is dufāq, meaning it fills the valley. And "may God dafaqa his soul" is said as a curse calling for his death.
دفل: The letters dāl, fāʾ and lām are not a root that can be measured upon, nor does it have branches. It is only said: al-diflā, which is a tree.
دفن:
The letters dāl, fāʾ and nūn are a single root indicating concealment and obscurity. One says: dufina al-mayyit — the dead person was buried. And this well is dafn: iddafanat [it has silted and filled up on its own].

As for al-iddifān, it is a slave's hiding himself, without meaning outright flight. Some said: al-iddifān is a slave's absconding and going off on his own way. The first is better, on account of what we mentioned from the hadith.

1. al-dāʾ al-dafīn — the hidden ailment whose nature cannot be found.
2. al-dafūn — the she-camel that kneels down among the other camels so that she is in their midst.
3. al-dafanī — a kind of cloth. I heard some people of learning say it is a dye that is soaked into another dye richer than it.
دق:
The letters dāl and qāf are a single root indicating smallness and paltriness. Al-daqīq is the opposite of al-jalīl, the considerable. One says: "so-and-so gave me neither daqīqa nor jalīla" — neither a small thing nor a great one. And adaqqa fulānun wa-ajalla, when he gave both little and much. A poet said, in a line of verse:
One who weeps copiously, streaming when she flows — she wept, giving both little and much in her weeping.
1. Al-daqīq — a man of little good.
2. Al-daqīq — an obscure matter.
3. Al-daqīq — flour.
And you say daqaqtu l-shay'a aduqquhu daqqan — I crushed the thing.

As for al-daqdaqa, it is the sound of riding-beasts' hooves as they move about — so they say. To us the true origin is the same root, because they pound the ground with their hooves, pounding it.
دقر:
The letters dāl, qāf and rāʾ are a root indicating weakness and deficiency.

1. al-daqārīr — falsehoods.
2. al-dawāqīr — as it is said, the plural of dawqara, a low tract of ground that grows nothing.
3. al-diqrāra — the slandering, gossiping man.
4. al-diqrār — a pair of short trousers.

Its pattern follows that of the chapter, on account of its deficiency.
دقس:
The letters dāl, qāf and sīn are close [to being a root].

1. al-duqsa — a small creature.
