2. danqasa al-rajul danqasa — sometimes said with shīn — when he looked from the corners of his eyes; this is not from the genuine speech of the Arabs. Likewise dāl, qāf and shīn.

And they mentioned that Abū al-Duqaysh was asked the meaning of his nickname and said: "I do not know; they are names we hear and are named by." This is very close to being the truth.

3. al-duqsha — a speckled small creature, mentioned by al-Sijistānī.
4. al-daqsh — the same as al-naqsh [marking, patterning].

All of that is forced, and is nothing.
دقع:
The letters dāl, qāf and ʿayn are a single root indicating abasement. Its origin is al-daqʿāʾ, which is dust. One says daqiʿa al-rajul — the man stuck himself to the dust in abasement.

The Messenger of God, God bless him and his family and grant him peace, said to the women: "When you go hungry you become abased [daqiʿtunna], and when you are full you become abashed [khajiltunna]." That is al-daqaʿ.

Al-Kumayt said, in a line of verse:
They were not abased when calamity befell them ... at the outbreak of wars, nor were they abashed.

1. al-madāqīʿ, of camels — those that eat the plants until they press them flat against the ground, from al-daqʿāʾ.
2. al-dāqiʿ, of men — one who pursues the meanest ways of earning.

In one of the dialects: "ramāhu Allāhu bi-l-dawqaʿa" — "may God strike him with al-dawqaʿa" — a word of the pattern fawʿala from al-daqaʿ.
دقل:
The letters dāl, qāf and lām are not a root that can be measured upon, and it has no branches.

1. daqal al-safīna — the mast of the ship.
2. al-daqal — the worst kind of dates.
3. dawqala al-rajul li-nafsihi — said when a man sets something of the food aside especially for himself. This is mentioned from al-Khalīl, though I do not know whether this is soundly attributed to him.
دقم: The letters dāl, qāf and mīm are a minor root with one word in it. One says: daqama asnānahu — he broke his teeth.
دقي: The letters dāl, qāf and yāʾ are one word. daqiya al-faṣīl daqan — the weaned young camel became bloated and sickened from milk. The male is daqin, the female daqiya.
دك:
The letters dāl and kāf are two roots.

The first indicates flattening and being spread level.
1. Al-dukkān — a raised bench, which is well known. Al-ʿAbdī said, in a line of verse: like the mud-plastered bench of the doorkeepers.
2. Al-arḍ al-dakkā' — flat, level, broad ground. God Almighty said: {He made it level} [al-Kahf: 98].
3. Al-nāqa al-dakkā' — the she-camel with no hump.
Al-Kisā'ī said: al-dukk, of mountains, are the broad ones, singular adakk. And farasun adakku l-ẓahr — a horse broad in the back.

The other root is close to the chapter of letter-substitution, as if the kāf here stands in place of a qāf. One says dakaktu l-shay'a like daqaqtuhu — I crushed the thing — and likewise dakaktuhu.
1. Dukka l-rajulu, so he is madkūk, when he fell ill — though it is possible this belongs to the first root instead, as though illness stretched him out flat; so it could bear either sense.
2. Al-dakdāk, of sand, is as if it had been thoroughly pounded, that is thoroughly crushed. The people of the language said: al-dakdāk of sand is what clings to the ground and does not rise. From this is the hadith of Jarīr ibn ʿAbd Allāh, when the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him and his family, asked him about his home at Bīsha, and he said: "level ground and dakdāk, with salam and arāk trees."
3. From this chapter: dakaktu l-turāba ʿalā l-mayyit adukkuhu dakkan, when you heap earth over him; likewise a well that you fill in. It was said this is because the earth is like something pounded.

Among what falls outside these two roots is their saying, if it is sound: amatun midakka, a slave-woman strong for work. And among the irregular sayings: "aqamtu ʿindahu ḥawlan dakīkan" — I stayed with him a complete year.
دكأ: The letters dāl, kāf and hamza are one word: tadākaʾa al-qawm — the people crowded and pressed together.
دكس:
The letters dāl, kāf and sīn are a minor root indicating one thing being overcome by another.

1. al-dukās — what overcomes a person in the way of drowsiness, said Ibn al-Aʿrābī. He recited:
As if from the drowsiness of sleep ... he spent the night sipping two cups of wine.
2. al-dawkas — a great number.
3. al-dakas — the piling of one thing on top of another.

And it is mentioned from al-Khalīl that al-dawkas is the lion; if that is sound, it belongs to this chapter, because of its boldness and its facing dreadful things head-on.
دكع:
The letters dāl, kāf and ʿayn are one word: what they say for an ailment that takes horses and camels in their chests: al-dukāʿ.

Al-Qaṭāmī said, in a line of verse:
You see the horses' chests bulging out from it ... as though afflicted with nuḥāz or dukāʿ.

They also say it is coughing.
دكل:
The letters dāl, kāf and lām are a minor root indicating self-magnification.

1. tadakkala al-rajul — the man became conceited, thinking himself great.
2. al-dakala — a people who, out of their own pride, do not answer the ruler's call.
دكن:
The letters dāl, kāf and nūn are a minor root indicating the stacking of one thing upon another.

1. dakantu al-matāʿ — I stacked the goods, some atop the other.
2. al-dukkān [the shop, the bench] — derived from this, and it is a genuine Arabic word.

Al-ʿAbdī said, in a line of verse:
So my idle deeds remained, and their seriousness ... like the mud-plastered bench of the doorkeepers.
دل:
The letters dāl and lām are two roots: one is making a thing plain by a sign one comes to know, the other is agitation in a thing.

The first: their saying dalaltu fulānan ʿalā l-ṭarīq — I guided so-and-so to the road. Al-dalīl is the sign in a thing. And it is bayyinu l-dalāla wa-l-dilāla — plain in guidance, said with either vowel.

The other root: their saying tadaldala l-shay'u, when it swayed. Aws said, in a line of verse:
Or what of a tribe that let part of their affair slip away, wavering between wrongdoing and obedience.
Al-qusūṭ is wrongdoing; al-dīn is obedience.
1. From this: dalāl al-mar'a — a woman's boldness in coy charm and playfulness, as though she were being contrary while there is no real contrariness in her; and this cannot happen without swaying and agitation.
2. From the same word: fulānun yudillu ʿalā aqrānihi fī l-ḥarb — so-and-so is bold against his rivals in war, like the falcon bold over its prey.

From the first root: al-Farrā' related, of the Arabs, adalla yudillu, said when a man presumes upon a kinship.
دلب: The letters dāl, lām and bāʾ are not a root. Al-dulb, as it is said, is a tree.
دلث:
The letters dāl, lām and thāʾ are a root indicating a surging forth.

1. al-madālith — the channels of a flash flood, singular madlath.
2. al-dilāth — the swift she-camel. One says indalathat al-nāqa tandalithu indilāthan.
3. dalatha al-shaykh — the old man moved slowly [like dalafa], as some related.
4. indalatha fulānun ʿalā fulānin — he bore down and poured himself upon so-and-so.
دلج:
The letters dāl, lām and jīm are a root indicating travel, coming and going — and this was perhaps mostly done in secret.

1. al-dalaj — night travel.
2. adlaja al-qawm — the people travelled the whole night; and if they set out in the last part of the night, they have iddalajū, with the dāl doubled.
3. Abū al-Mudlij — it is said this is [a name for] the hedgehog, and they claim that most of its movement is by night.
4. al-dawlaj — the underground passage.
5. al-dawlaj — also the wild animal's covert.

And this follows the pattern of the chapter, because both are places where one hides oneself. It is then extended within the chapter, so that the one who takes the bucket from the well-head to the trough is called al-dālij, and that place is al-madlaj. The verb is dalaja yadluju dulūjan.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
As if their spears were the ropes of a well ... which have grooves at every place of drawing.

As for al-Shammākh's saying, in a line of verse:
And she complains, through an eye worn out by what wore down her mounts ... while the caller was saying: the people have set out at dawn — "adlijī"
he was relating the caller's voice: that at one time he was calling "the people have set out at dawn," and at another calling "adlijī" [travel by night], giving that command.
دلح:
The letters dāl, lām and ḥā' are a slight root pointing to walking and the heaviness of what is carried.

The Arabs say: the camel dalaḥa with its load, if it walked along heavily under it. A cloud is called daluḥ, as if it runs along carrying its own water. From this comes the hadith of Salmān: that he and Abū al-Dardā' bought meat, and they carried it (tadālaḥāhu) between them on a stick — that is, they carried it and rose up with it. One says a cloud is daluḥ, and clouds are dulaḥ.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
While we were grazing at Falj ... the heavy-laden clouds, full of water, cried out, here it is.
دلس:
The letters dāl, lām and sīn are a root pointing to concealment and darkness.

1. al-dalas — the darkness of night.
2. lā yudālisu — their saying, meaning he does not deceive.
3. al-tadlīs — in a sale, selling something without disclosing its defect, as if he deceived the buyer and brought the thing to him in the dark.

And there is another root pointing to scarcity.

4. tadallastu al-ṭaʻām — the Arabs say this if you took from the food a little at a time. This comes from al-adlās, plants that put out leaves late in the summer.
5. tadallasa al-māl — said of livestock, if it fell upon the adlās.
دلص:
The letters dāl, lām and ṣād point to softness and suppleness.

1. al-dilāṣ — the soft, supple coat of mail.
2. dalaṣat al-suyūl al-ṣakhra — the floods wore the rock smooth, as if they had softened it.

A poet said:
A smooth rock, worn to smoothness by the flood's rushing onset.

3. al-dalīṣ — the shining thing.
4. indalaṣa al-shay' min yadī — said if it slipped out of my hand and fell.

This may be derived from the same root, or the dāl may stand in place of a mīm, from inmalaṣa — and amlaṣat al-mar'a is said of a woman if she miscarried.
دلظ: The letters dāl, lām and ẓā' are a slight root pointing to pushing. One says dalaẓathu dalẓan, if she pushed him. Some report the saying: the army came on yatadalẓā, each part of it pushing against the other.
دلع:
The letters dāl, lām and ʿayn are a slight root pointing to coming out.

1. dalaʿa lisānuhu — his tongue lolled out.
2. dalaʿahu huwa — said if he put it out.
3. al-dalīʿ — the easy road.
4. indalaʿa baṭnuhu — said if his belly stuck out in front of him.
دلف:
The letters dāl, lām and fā' are a single root pointing to advancing gently.

1. al-dalīf — walking slowly; one says dalafa dalīfan; it is a pace above al-dabīb, creeping.
2. dalafat al-katība fī al-ḥarb — the troop advanced in the war.
3. al-dalf — Abū 'Ubayd said al-dalf is advancing; dalafnāhum, we advanced upon them.
4. al-dālif — the arrow that falls short of the target, then glances away from where it landed.
دلق:
The letters dāl, lām and qāf are a single, consistent root pointing to a thing's coming out and its advancing.

1. al-nāqa al-dalūq — the she-camel whose teeth are broken, so that water comes out through her mouth.
2. indalaqa al-sayf min ghimdihi — the sword came out of its sheath without being drawn.
3. indalaqat aqtāb baṭnihi — his intestines came out.
4. indalaqa al-sayl ʿalā al-qawm — the flood poured out upon the people.
5. indalaqa al-jaysh — the army poured forward.

Ṭarafa said, in a line of verse:
Pouring forward in a raid spread wide ... like flocks of birds passing overhead in droves.

6. nāqa dulūq — a she-camel of powerful thrust.
7. al-indilāq — advancing.

'Umāra ibn Ziyād al-'Absī, brother of al-Rabīʿ, used to be called 'Dāliq'.
دلك:
The letters dāl, lām, and kāf are a single root indicating a thing's passing away from another, and it happens only gently. One says dalakat al-shams, the sun passed its zenith; it is also said dalakat means it set. Al-dalak is the time of the sun's declining.

From this branch too: dalaktu al-shayʾa, I rubbed the thing — because when you do this your hand hardly stays still on one spot rather than another. Al-dalūk is whatever a person rubs on himself, of perfume or the like. Al-dalīk is a food made from butter and dates, like a crumbled bread-and-broth dish.

Al-madlūk is a camel that journeys have rubbed down and wearied. It is also said it is one whose knees have dalak, meaning looseness, a lighter condition than al-ṭaraq [a stiffness in the leg]. A horse is madlūk al-ḥajaba, meaning its haunch-bone does not jut out. Land is madlūka, meaning grazed bare, as though it had been rubbed smooth. One says al-dulāka is the last of the milk remaining in the udder, as though named so because the hand rubs the udder to draw it out.

Aḥmad ibn Fāris said: God, Exalted is He, has a secret and a subtlety in every thing. I have reflected on this branch from its beginning to its end, and I find that the dāl, joined with the lām and any third letter, always indicates movement and coming, and going and passing from one place to another. God knows best.
دلم:
The letters dāl and lām are a root indicating length and a drooping in blackness.

1. al-adlam, of men — the tall, black man; and likewise it is said of camels and mountains.

Some people claimed that al-daylam is the blackness and darkness of night. As for ʿAntara's saying, in a line of verse:
A crooked-necked she-camel shying away from the pools of al-daylam
it is said that they [al-daylam] are the enemies. If that is so, then enemies are described with this. Al-Aʿshā said:
They are the enemies, so their livers are black.
Some people said: al-daylam is a place, or a tribe. And one says jāʾa bi-l-daylam, meaning he brought a calamity — this is a comparison.

2. al-dalam — the droop in the lip.
دله:
The letters dāl, lām and hāʾ are a minor root indicating the going away of a thing.

1. dhahaba damu fulānin dalhan — meaning [his blood was shed] in vain, for nothing.
2. dallahahu ʿaqlahu al-ḥubbu wa ghayruhu — love and other things drove his reason away, left him distracted.
دلى:
The letters dāl, lām and the weak letter [yāʾ] are a root indicating the bringing near of a thing and its approach, with ease and gentleness.

One says adlaytu al-dalw, when you let the bucket down into the well; and when you draw it up, you have dalawtu. Al-dalw is also a kind of easy pace. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Do not hurry the pace, and let her go easy.
Al-dalāt is the bucket [dalw] too, its plural al-dilāʾ. As for the saying:
I have sworn never to give any boy for good ... his share of my love [dalātahu]; truly I love al-Aswad.
here he meant by dalātahu his bucketful and his share of affection; and al-Aswad is his son.

1. adlā fulānun bi-ḥujjatihi — so-and-so put forward his proof.
2. adlā bi-mālihi ilā al-ḥākim — he handed his property over to the judge. God, exalted be His praise, said: {and offer it to the judges} [al-Baqara: 188].
3. dalawtu ilayhi bi-fulānin — I sought so-and-so's intercession with him. From this is ʿUmar's saying in his prayer for rain through al-ʿAbbās: "O God, we draw near to You by the uncle of Your Prophet, and the noblest remainder of his forefathers, and the eldest of his men, and we have let ourselves down to You through him, seeking his intercession."

And on this is based their saying jāʾa fulānun bi-l-dalw, meaning a calamity. He recited:
They carry ʿAnqāʾ and ʿAnqafīr ... and the bucket, and al-daylam, and the roaring.

4. dālaytu al-rajul — I dealt gently with the man, humoured him.
5. huwa dallāʾu mālin — he is the manager and keeper of property.
دم:
The letters dāl and mīm are a single root indicating the covering of a thing by smearing it. You say damamtu l-thawb, when you dyed it with any dye; and everything smeared onto a thing is dimām.
1. Al-damdama is destruction. God Almighty said: {so their Lord thundered ruin down upon them for their sin} [al-Shams: 14] — that is, for the punishment and destruction with which He covered them.
2. Qidrun damīm — a cooking pot smeared with spleen.
3. Al-dāmmā' — the jerboa's burrow, because it smooths it out, levelling it thoroughly.
4. A man damīm al-wajh, ugly-faced — it belongs to this chapter, as if his face had been smeared with blackness or ugliness. One says damma wajhuhu yadummu damāma, so he is damīm.
5. Al-daymūma, the waterless desert waste — it belongs to this chapter, because in its flatness it is as though it had been levelled thoroughly, like a thing smeared over.
6. Al-damādim, of land, are gentle rises.
دمث: The letters dāl, mīm and thā' are a single root pointing to softness and ease. Al-damath is softness; one says damitha al-makān yadmathu damathan, and a place is damth or damith — it has sand in it. From this comes the hadith: that the Messenger of God, God bless him and his family and give him peace, turned aside to a soft spot and said, 'When one of you urinates, let him seek out a soft place for it.' Al-damātha is ease of temperament. One says dammith lī al-ḥadīth, meaning make the talk easy and gentle for me.
دمج:
The letters dāl, mīm and jīm are a single root pointing to folding something up and concealing it. One says admajtu al-ḥabl, I wound the rope up, if you rolled it up and twisted it tight.

Al-Aṣma'ī said, about the line of Aws:
You wept over the sealed peace, and from you at Dhū al-Rimth, from Wādī Hubāla, a troop.
He said: it is from dāmajahu dimājan, if he agreed with him on the peace. One says tadāmajū. And fulān 'alā damaj fulān, so-and-so is on so-and-so's course. All that he said here is not far from what we mentioned of hiddenness and concealment.
دمخ:
The letters dāl, mīm and khā' are not a root. It is only Damkh, a mountain, in the saying of the poet:
Sorrow enough, that I stretched up trying to see the peaks of the two waymarks of Damkh, and they did not appear.
دمر:
The letters dāl, mīm and rā' are a single root pointing to entering a house or the like. One says *damara al-rajulu baytahu* when he entered it. And some people made a difference between his entering with permission and without permission, so Abū ʿUbayd said, about the Prophet's hadith, upon him be blessing and peace: "Whoever looks into a people's house without permission has *damara*" — that is, entered. Abū ʿUbayd said: this is when it is without permission; if it is with permission it is not *dumūr*. This is an explanation drawn from the law; as for the rule of the word, it is what we mentioned first. From it come the words of Aws, in a line of verse:
And there met upon him, of the tribe of Ṣubāḥ, a hunter gone into his hide, whose lair had roofing slabs of flat stone.

Al-Shaybānī and al-Aṣmaʿī said: *al-mudammir* is the one who goes into the hunter's pit. And one says *damara al-qunfudh* when the hedgehog enters its hole. And some people said: *al-mudammir* is the hunter who makes smoke with camel hair and the like so that the game will not catch his scent. But what we hold is that *al-mudammir* is the one who goes into his pit, and when he has gone in he makes smoke. *Al-mudammir* is not a description of the one who makes smoke, and the rule does not call for it. And God, exalted, said: {God destroyed them, and for the unbelievers are the like of it} [Muḥammad: 10]. And *al-damār* is ruin. And it is said that *al-tadmuriyy* is a kind of jerboa. If that is sound, it is the rule, because it goes down into its burrows.
دمس:
The letters dāl, mīm and sīn are a single root pointing to the hiddenness of a thing.

1. damastu al-shay' — I hid it.
2. umūr dums, like dubs — matters whose direction could not be made out.
3. damasa al-ẓalām — the darkness grew intense.
4. al-dimās — said to be the underground passage; it belongs to the same idea of being pressed close and hidden.

In the hadith of Jesus, peace be upon him: 'as though he had come out of a dimās.'
دمص: The letters dāl, mīm and ṣād are not, in my view, a root. Some words have been reported about it which, if sound, are close to one another in analogy. They say al-dawmaṣ is an iron helmet, and this points to smoothness in a thing. Then they call a man whose eyebrow is sparse admaṣ, which is close to that. And they say every vein-like streak in a wall is dims. In all of this there is room for doubt.
دمع:
The letters dāl, mīm and ʿayn are a single root indicating water, or a tear.

From this, al-damʿ is the water of the eye, and a single drop is a damʿa. The verb: damaʿat al-ʿaynu damʿan, and damiʿat damaʿan, and damaʿat dumūʿan also — the eye watered. An eye is dāmiʿa; the plural of al-damʿ is dumūʿ.

Al-Khalīl said: al-madmaʿ is where tears gather at the corners of the eye, plural al-madāmiʿ. A woman called damiʿa is one quick to weep, with many tears.

A head-wound called dāmiʿa is said, in al-Khalīl's book, to be one that runs with blood. But the more correct view is that the wound that runs with blood is called al-dāmiya; al-dāmiʿa's case is less severe, being one from which comes what looks like a thin, red-tinged fluid.

Al-Yazīdī mentioned that al-dumāʿ is the trace of tears left on the cheek. A line is quoted:
Oh, for an eye that never stops streaming ... the tears have left their traces upon it.
It is also said [the last word is] dumāʿā. Al-dumāʿ, pronounced either lightly or doubled, is also what oozes from the grapevine during the spring.
دمغ: The letters dāl, mīm, and ghayn are a single word that does not branch out and cannot be used as a pattern for anything else. Al-dimāgh, the brain, is well known. Damaghtuhu: I struck him on the head until I reached the brain. Such a blow is called al-dāmigha.
دمق: The letters dāl, mīm and qāf are not a root, even though they have said damaqa fī al-bayt and indamaqa, meaning he entered. The qāf here is thought to stand in place of a jīm, the true root being damaja, already mentioned.
دمك:
The letters dāl, mīm and kāf point to two meanings: one is strength, the other is speed; and sometimes the two meanings come together.

As for strength: al-damakmak is the strong one. Al-dāmika is calamity, a great and grave matter. Al-midmāk is the piece of wood beneath the feet of the man who draws water at the well.

As for the other meaning, they say the hare damakat, if it hurried in its running. Al-damūk is the great pulley. In it the two meanings meet, strength and speed. Al-damūk is also the millstone, the same in this respect as the pulley.
دمل:
The letters dāl, mīm and lām are a slight root pointing to something gathering together in softness and ease.

1. indamala al-jurḥ — the wound healed, that is its gathering together in soundness and recovery.
2. dumilat al-arḍ bi-l-damāl — the land was manured with al-damāl, which is dung.
3. dāmaltu al-rajul — said if you dealt gently and indulgently with him, the same analogy, because it is a drawing together in ease.
4. al-dummal — the boil, a genuine Arabic word, follows the same analogy of gathering together in softness we mentioned.

Do you not see that Abū al-Najm says:
And the withers swelled up like a boil.
God knows best.
دمن:
The letters dāl, mīm and nūn are a single root pointing to firmness and staying in place.

1. al-dimn — the dung and droppings that pack down in the places where livestock lie; the place itself is called al-dimna, plural dimin.
2. damantu al-arḍ bi-dhālika — I manured the land with it, the same as damaltuhā.
3. al-dimna — the grudge that buries itself in the chest, a likeness to the droppings that pack down in the dimin.
4. dammana fulān finā' fulān — so-and-so haunted and clung to so-and-so's courtyard, if he kept coming to it and stayed close by it.
5. fulān dimn māl — like their saying izā' māl, one who sticks close to the herd; he is named so because he stays close to the property.
6. Dammūn — a place name.

All of this is a single analogy.

7. al-damān — a rot that afflicts palm trees; if the word is sound, it is derived from what we mentioned of al-dimn, because that too inevitably rots.
دن:
The letters dāl and nūn are a single root indicating flattening and lowness.
1. Al-adann — the man bent in the back. One says from it: qad daninta danan.
2. Baytun adann — a low, flattened dwelling.
3. Farasun adann — short in the forelegs; and when it is so, its withers sit low.
4. Al-dandana — hearing an unintelligible murmur from a man, because he lowers and conceals his voice with what he says. From this is the hadith: "as for your murmuring and Muʿādh's murmuring, we do not understand either."

Close to this pattern but not quite it is their name for the blunt sword: dadān. And falling outside the chapter is al-daydan, which is habit.
What can be reasoned to the first root is al-dindin, the blackened, aged plant-growth.
دنب: The letters dāl, nūn and bā' have no root. Even so, they have said rajul dinnaba and dinnāba, meaning the short man. If this word is sound, it comes by substitution, since the true root has a mīm: dinnama.
دنخ:
The letters dāl, nūn and khā' are not a root to be relied on. They have said dannakha al-rajul, if he was humbled and bowed his head. They recited:
When the poets saw me they bowed their heads.
They say al-tadnīkh in a melon is that it caves in toward its inside. They say al-tadnīkh is weakness of sight. One says dannakha fī baytihi, if he stayed at home and did not go out. If what is reported of this is sound, all of it is an analogy pointing to weakness and being broken down.
دنر: The letters dāl, nūn and rā’ are a single word, and it is the dīnār [gold coin]. They say: dannara wajhu fulānin — so-and-so’s face ‘turned to gold’, when it gleamed and shone. And God knows best.
دنس: The letters dāl, nūn and sīn are a single word, al-danas, which is the smearing of something with a foul thing.
دنع: The letters dāl, nūn and ʿayn are a root pointing to weakness, littleness and baseness. Al-rajul al-dani' is the worthless man in whom there is no good. Al-dana' is disgrace. They claim al-dana' is what the butcher discards from the camel when it is slaughtered.
دنف:
The letters dāl, nūn and fā' are a root pointing to a thing's drawing near to its end. One says danifa al-amr, if the matter drew near to being finished and done with. Al-danaf is a persistent illness; the sick man is danaf, as though he has drawn near to his end — the word is not put in the dual or plural. But if you say danif instead, it is put in the dual and plural.

As for al-'Ajjāj's line:
And the sun had nearly become danafā —
it belongs to this chapter too, because he means its yellowing and its nearness to setting. One also says of it adnafat.
دنق: The letters dāl, nūn and qāf are close to what came before. One says danaqa wajh al-rajul, if his face grew yellow from illness. And dannaqat al-shams, if the sun drew near to setting.
دنقش:
[This is one of the entries listing words that do not fit under any three-letter root; it does not open with the usual naming of letters.]

1. A man does danqasha, danqashatan, when he looks and half-closes his eye.
2. al-dahtham, of men — the easy-going, soft-natured one.
3. al-dirfas and al-dirfās — the huge, bulky man.
4. al-darmak — fine white flour.
5. al-durnūk — a kind of cloth with a pile/nap, to which a camel's shaggy coat is likened. He said, in a line of verse: with pile-cloths, and with thick shaggy hair.
6. al-idʿinkār — the surging advance of a flash-flood. It is possible this belongs to the pattern of daʿaka [rubbing, kneading].
7. damkhaqa — a man does this in his walk: he grows heavy and sluggish.
8. al-daghfal — the young of the elephant. al-daghfaliyy — a time of abundance and ease. Al-ʿAjjāj said, in a line of verse: and when people's time was daghfalī. It is possible this word belongs to those formed by adding a dāl, as if from ghafala [to be careless, at ease]; they describe a good, easy season as one of ghafla. He said, in a line of verse: just before experience and forbearance reached me, I was still amid the careless ease of life, before the trials.
9. al-dimaqs — raw silk.
10. al-dardabīs — a calamity; also a decrepit old man.
11. danqastu bayna al-qawm — I stirred up trouble among the people.
12. al-dahārīs — calamities.
13. al-dilqim — a she-camel whose teeth have worn away from old age. It is possible this word is blended from daqamtu fāhu — when you break someone's mouth — and from dalaqa — to slip out — as though her tongue lolls loose.
14. al-dalʿak and al-dalʿas — the bulky woman.
15. darbaḥa — he ran.
16. al-darbala — a manner of walking.
17. al-diraql — a kind of cloth.
18. al-durdāqis — the bone separating the head from the neck. How far this word is from being sound [Ibn Fāris doubts it].
19. al-dulamiz — the strong, resolute one; likewise al-dulāmiz, plural dalāmiz. The poet said, in a line of verse: it baffles even the resolute, sharp ones among the open desert-folk.

God knows best what is correct.
دنم: The letters dāl, nūn and mīm are a root pointing to weakness and littleness. Al-tadnīm is stooping to base matters. Al-dinnāma is the short man; al-Farrā' mentioned it. They also say al-dinnāma is the small ant.
دنى:
The letters dāl, nūn and the weak letter are a single root, each part of it measured against the rest, and it is nearness.

1. al-daniyy — the near one, from danā yadnū, he drew near.
2. al-dunyā, this world — named for its nearness; the word relating to it is dunyāwiyy.
3. al-daniyy, said of men — the weak, lowly one; from the same root, because he is close in origin and rank.

One says dānaytu bayna al-amrayn, I brought the two matters close together. He is ibn 'ammihi dunyā and dinya, his cousin by close kinship.

4. al-daniyy, with a hamza — the base, low one. One says rajul daniyy, and he becomes danu'a yadnu'u danā'a. This too belongs to this chapter, because he is close in rank.
5. al-adna', of men — the one whose upper body is bent over his chest; this too belongs to the chapter, because his top is close to his middle.

One says adnat al-faras, and other animals, if the time of its foaling drew near. Al-daniyya is a disgraceful deed. It comes in the hadith: 'When you eat, danū' — that is, eat from what is nearest to you, what is within reach. One says laqītuhu adnā daniyy, meaning I met him at the very first thing.
ده:
The letters dāl and hā' are not a root to be reasoned from by analogy, nor one that branches into others. It occurs only in their saying tadahdaha l-shay'u, when it rolled — as though al-dahdaha were the sound made there. We have already said that sounds cannot be reasoned from by analogy.

They say: "mā adrī ayyu l-dahdā'i huwa" — I do not know which of the people he is. And al-dahdāh are the young, small camels. And it is said al-dahdahān is a great number of camels.

What shows that this is not a true root is al-Khalīl's statement in his book: as for the line of Ru'ba —
Sayers, save now — never again —
it is said that it is Persian, quoting his nurse's saying. And what al-Khalīl said follows what he had said at the start of the chapter: dah was a word the Arabs used to say — when a man saw his chance for revenge, they would say to him, "O so-and-so, illā dahin fa-lā dah," meaning: if you do not take it now, you never will. All of this points to what we have said.
دهر:
The letters dāl, hā' and rā' are a single root, and it is overpowering and subduing.

Time is named dahr because it comes upon everything and overpowers it. As for the Prophet's saying, peace and blessings be upon him: “Do not curse time, for God is time” — Abū ʿUbayd said its meaning is that the Arabs, when misfortunes struck them, would say “Time destroyed us” and “Time came upon us.” They mentioned this in their poetry. ʿAmr al-Ḍubaʿī said:
The daughters of time struck me from where I could not see ... but how is it for one who is struck yet cannot strike back?
If only I were struck by arrows, I could guard against them ... but I am struck by no arrows at all.

Another poet said:
Time claimed them for itself that morning ... and time strikes at me, while I strike at nothing.
O time, you have brought us much grief ... for our finest men, and wounded us to the bone.
You stripped us of what you will never give back ... O time, you have not been fair in your judgment.

The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, thereby made known that the one who truly does this to them is God, glorious is His praise, and that time itself has no power to act; and that whoever curses the doer of these things has, in effect, cursed his Lord, exalted and high above what the wrongdoers say, greatly exalted.

It may also plausibly be, by the root's pattern, that “al-dahr” is a name taken from the verb, meaning “the one who overpowers,” just as one says a man is ṣawm [fasting] or fiṭr [breaking fast]; so the meaning of “do not curse time” would be: do not curse the Overpowering One who subdues you and overcomes you in your affairs.

One says dahrun dahīr, just as one says abadun abīd. In the Kitāb al-ʿAyn: dahara-hum amrun, meaning a matter befell them. They say “mā dahrī kadhā,” meaning “that is not my concern” — a loose way of putting it, whose real meaning is “that is not what I occupy my time with”; “ambition” itself is not literally called dahr.

Al-dahwara is gathering a thing up and hurling it into a pit; this follows the root's pattern.
دهس: The letters dāl, hā' and sīn are a single root pointing to softness in a place. Al-dahs is the soft place, and likewise al-dahās. Al-duhsa is a colour like the colour of sand.
دهش: The letters dāl, hā' and shīn are a single word, not to be measured against anything else. One says duhisha, if he was astonished, and dahisha dahashan.
دهق:
The letters dāl, hā’ and qāf point to fullness together with a coming and going and a stirring.

1. adhaqtu al-ka’s — I filled the cup. God Most High said: {and a full cup} [al-Naba’: 34].
2. al-dahdaqa — the turning of a large piece of meat in the cooking pot, rising up once and sinking down again.
دهك: The letters dāl, hā' and kāf amount to nothing. Ibn Durayd mentioned dahaktu al-shay' adhakuhu, if you crushed and ground it.
دهل: The letters dāl, hā' and lām amount to nothing. They say marra dahl min al-layl, a stretch of the night passed. They say lā dahl, meaning no harm. This is a Nabatean word with no [Arabic] meaning.
دهم:
The letters dāl, hā’ and mīm are a root pointing to a thing coming upon someone in darkness; it then branches out so that darkness and other things are treated alike. One says: marra dahmun min al-layl — a part of the night passed.

1. al-duhma — blackness.
2. al-duhaymā’ — the diminutive of al-dahmā’, which is a calamity, so named for its darkness.

From this root also:

3. al-dahm — a great number.
4. idhāmma al-zar’ — the crop was overtaken by blackness from being well watered. God, exalted be His praise, said describing the two gardens: {dark green} [al-Raḥmān: 64], meaning the two looked black to the eye, from the watering and the greenness.
5. dahamathum al-khaylu tadhamuhum — the horses came upon them, when they overran them.
6. al-dahmā’ — the cooking pot.
دهن:
The letters dāl, hā' and nūn are a single root, indicating softness, ease, and scantness.

1. al-duhn — oil. One says dahantuhu adhunuhu dahnan, I oiled him/it.
2. al-dihān — what one oils with.

God, mighty and majestic, said: {and it becomes rose-red like oil} [al-Raḥmān: 37]. They said it means the dregs of oil.

3. One says dahanahu bi-l-ʿaṣā dahnan — he "oiled" him with the stick, meaning he struck him lightly with it.
4. Also from this root: al-idhān, from al-mudāhana, which is currying favor. One says dāhantu al-rajul, I dealt smoothly with the man, meaning you were evasive with him and showed him the opposite of what you concealed toward him. This belongs to the root, as though in doing so you were "oiling" him and calming him down.
5. adhantu idhānan — I deceived. From this is His saying, exalted be His praise: {They wish that you would compromise, so they would compromise} [al-Qalam: 9].
6. al-mudhun — the vessel oil is put in. It is one of the words on the pattern mufʿul, among tools, that begins with mīm.
7. By comparison to it, al-mudhun is also a hollow in a mountain where water collects. From this is the hadith of al-Nahdī: "the hollow dried up, and the shrub-stump withered."
8. al-dahīn — a she-camel of little milk.
9. dahana al-maṭar al-arḍ — the rain "oiled" the ground, meaning it wet it only slightly.
10. Banū Duhn — a tribe of the Arabs; ʿAmmār al-Duhnī is named after them.
11. al-Dahnā' — a place, soft sand; the adjective from it is dahnāwī.

And God knows best.
دهى: The letters dāl, hā' and the weak letter are a root pointing to a thing befalling someone in a way that does not please him. One says mā dahāhu, meaning what befell him — it is said only of something bad. Dawāhī al-dahr are the great calamities that befall a person among the turns of time. Al-dahy is sharpness and soundness of judgment; it belongs to the same chapter, because such a person, by his judgment, hits upon what he wants.
دو:
The letters dāl and the weak or hamzated letter after it are close to the chapter before it. Al-daww and al-dawiyya — the waterless desert waste. Some say it is so named because the one alone in it hears something like a dawiyy, a droning sound — so the matter returns again to what we said, that sounds cannot be reasoned from by analogy. The poet said of the dawiyya, in a line of verse:
A desolate waste through which its ostriches walked, like the walk of Christians in soft leather shoes.
1. Al-da'da'a — swift travel.
2. Al-da'da'a — the sound of stones striking in a watercourse.
As for al-da'ādi', they are the three nights at the end of the month, before the nights of the moon's disappearance; this has a sound analogy, because any vessel nearing full is da'da'a — and these nights come as the month nears its completion. As for the one who said they are called da'ādi' for their darkness, that is nothing, with no sound analogy behind it. As for al-dawādī, they are children's swings, and this too is nothing.
دوح:
The letters dāl, wāw and ḥā' are a single word, and it is al-dawḥa: the great tree, plural al-dawḥ. He said, in a line of verse:
It brings the great trees of the kanahbal down onto chins.
دوخ: The letters dāl, wāw and khā' are a single root indicating subduing. One says 'dawwakhnāhum', meaning we subdued them and overpowered them. And 'dākhū', meaning they submitted.
دود: The letters dāl, wāw and dāl are not a root that other words branch from. Al-dūd, the worm, is well known. One says 'dāda al-shay' yadādu' and 'adāda yadīdu', of a thing becoming worm-eaten. And al-dawādī: the traces left by children's swings, singular dawdāt.
دور:
The letters dāl, wāw and rā' are one root pointing to a thing's encircling another thing all round it. One says dāra yadūru dawarānan, it went round. And al-dawwārī is time, because it turns upon men through their states. He said:
And time is a turner upon man.
And al-duwār, with the wāw doubled or single, is a stone that used to be taken from the sanctuary to a place apart and gone round in circuit; and they say it is from going round the Ka'ba, which is circled. And that is his saying:
As the women went round about the duwār.
And another said, in a line of verse:
I left Banū al-Hujaym with a duwār of their own; when their company sets out it goes round.
And the giddiness in the head, al-duwār, is of this section; one says dīra bihi and udīra bihi, so he is madūrun bihi and mudārun bihi. And al-dā'ira in a horse's throat is little hairs that go round, and it is well known. And one says the dawā'ir turned upon them, that is, the hated states came round about them. And al-dār, the house, has a wāw for its origin. And al-dār is the tribe. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: "Shall I not tell you of the best of the dūr of the Anṣār?" - by that he meant the tribes. And of that is the other hadith: "Not a dār remained but a mosque was built in it", that is, not a tribe remained. And al-dārī is the seller of perfume. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: "The likeness of the good companion is the likeness of the dārī: if he does not give you of his perfume, its scent clings to you" - he meant the perfume-seller. And the poet said, in a line of verse:
When the dārī merchant came with a pod of musk, it went running through her parted hair.
And he was called dārī only from al-dār, that is, he lives in a house. And al-dārī is also the man who stays in his house and hardly ever leaves it. He said, in verse:
Wait a little, and the house-dwellers will catch up, the men with the sleek fat horses, the well-provided.
And al-dāra is a level piece of land with mountains going round it, and in the lands of the Arabs there are many dārāt. And the origin of dār is dāra. He said, in two lines of verse:
He has a crier at Mecca, brisk and busy, and another above his dāra calling out,
to great dishes of shīzā wood, filled with the finest of wheat kneaded with honey.
And he said, using dārāt as the plural of dāra:
Wait: even if al-Marawrāt be emptied of them, and its dārāt, then their palm-groves will not be emptied of them.
And the famous dārāt of the Arabs are: dārat Juljul, dārat al-Salam, dārat Wushḥā, dārat Ṣulṣul, dārat Ma'sal, dārat Khanzar, dārat al-Dūr, dārat al-Ja'b, dārat Yam'ūn, dārat Makman, dārat Rahbā, dārat Jawdāt, dārat al-Ar'ām, dārat al-Ruhā, dārat Tīl, dārat al-Ṣafā'iḥ, dārat Haḍb al-Qalīb, dārat Ṣāra, dārat Dammūn, dārat Rumḥ, dārat al-Malika, dārat Malḥūb, dārat Miḥṣar, dārat Ahwā, dārat al-Jumd, dārat Rimrim, dārat Qurḥ, dārat al-Ya'ḍīd, dārat al-Kharj, dārat Radm, dārat Juddā, and dārat al-Niṣāb.
دوس:
The letters dāl, wāw and sīn are a minor root, and it is the treading of a thing. You say 'dustuhu', I trod it; and the thing one threshes with is called midwas. And by extension, they apply the word midwas to the tool the sword-polisher sharpens a sword with, as if, leaning on it, he were like one treading a thing underfoot. He said, in a line of verse:
And a white blade like a pool, upon which so-and-so lingered with the polishing-tools for half a month.
دوش: The letters dāl, wāw and shīn are a single word, from which nothing else branches. One says 'dawishat 'aynuhu tadwashu dawashan', of an eye that grew weak, when it was spoiled by some ailment. And a man is called 'adwash', clearly weak-eyed.
دوف: The letters dāl, wāw and fā' are a single word. One says 'duftu al-dawā' dawfan', I mixed the medicine [with water].
دوق: The letters dāl, wāw and qāf are not a root, nor is there in them anything counted as a genuine word. But they do say: 'mā'iqun dā'iqun', a foolish, silly man.
دوك:
The letters dāl, wāw and kāf are a single root indicating pressing and crowding together.

1. *duktu al-shay' dawkan* — I pressed or pounded the thing.
2. *al-madāk* — the grinding-stone for perfume; a person grinds perfume upon it, 'dawkan'. He said, in a line of verse:
The grinding-stone of a bride, or the stone for colocynth.
3. *bāta al-qawmu yadūkūna dawkan* — the people spent the night in a confused jumble, said when they passed the night in turmoil. From this comes the hadith: that the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said at Khaybar: 'I shall give the banner tomorrow to a man who loves God and His messenger; God will grant victory by his hand.' So the people spent that night in commotion, 'yadūkūn'.
4. *tadāwaka al-qawm* — the people were pressed together tightly, said when they were hard-pressed in a war or a trouble.
دول:
The letters dāl, wāw and lām are two roots: one indicates a thing shifting from one place to another; the other indicates weakness and slackness.

As for the first, the philologists said: indāla al-qawmu, the people indāla, when they moved from one place to another. From this root: tadāwala al-qawmu al-shay'a baynahum, the people took a thing in turn among themselves, when it passed from one of them to another; al-dawla and al-dūla are two dialect variants of the same word. It is also said al-dūla concerns wealth and al-dawla concerns war; both are named so following the root's pattern, because each is something people take in turn, passing from this one to that one and back again.

As for the other root: al-dawīl, of plants, is what has dried up within its own year. Abū Zayd said: dāla al-thawbu yadūlu, the garment wore out. And it is said “his affection began yadūlu,” meaning it began to fade. From this root: indāla baṭnuhu, his belly went slack.
دوم:
The letters dāl, wāw and mīm are a single root pointing to stillness and staying put. One says dāma al-shay' yadūmu when a thing grows still. Al-mā' al-dā'im is still water. 'And the Messenger of God, God bless him and his family and give them peace, forbade that one urinate in still water and then perform ablution from it.' The proof that this reading is right is that it is related in another wording, that he 'forbade that one urinate in standing water.' One says adamtu al-qidr idāmatan when you quiet the boiling of a pot with water. Al-Ja'dī said, in a line of verse:
Their pot boils over at us and we still it, and we cool it away from us when its heat has blazed up.
Among what is carried onto this and has its analogy is a bird's tadwīm in the air, and that is when it wheels high and has, as it were, a pause up there. Of that is their saying dawwamat al-shams fī kabid al-samā', and that is when the sun reaches that place. Those who know about it say that it has there, as it were, a pause, and then it slips down. Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
And the sun, bewildered, hangs still for a while in the sky.
That is, as though it does not move on. As for his words describing dogs, in a line of verse:
Until, when it had wheeled about over the ground, pride came back to him — and had he wished, flight would have saved his life.
it is said that he erred, and that he meant only dawwat, and said dawwamat; this has been mentioned in its own chapter. One says dawwamtu al-za'farān — I stirred saffron into liquid; and that is the analogy, because it comes to rest in what it is stirred into. Wa-stadamtu al-amr, when you go gently with a matter. So they say. The meaning is that when a man goes gently with it and is not rough and not hasty, it lasts for him. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Do not be hasty with your affair, but go gently with it; no one has straightened his staff like the man who takes his time.
As for his words, in a line of verse:
And hope may sometimes keep the greedy man's spittle moist —
they say yudawwimu means it wets; but this is nothing. Yudawwimu means only that it keeps it going, and that is because the man who despairs has his spittle dried up. Al-dīma is a rain that lasts a day and a night or longer.

Of this chapter is that 'Ā'isha [God be pleased with her] was asked about the practice of the Messenger of God, God bless him and his family and give them peace, and she said: 'His practice was a dīma', that is, unbroken. The meaning is that he kept to it, whether he did little of it or much, but he did not break it off. She meant by that his worship, God bless him and give him peace. As for their saying dawwamathu al-khamr, that the wine made him heavy, it is from that, because it thickens him until his movements grow still. Al-da'mā' is the sea, and it may be of the chapter, because it is water that stays, that is neither drawn dry nor moves away. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And the night is like the sea, wearing beneath it a colour like the colour of sudūs, dark blue cloth.
دون:
The letters dāl, wāw and nūn are a single root pointing to nearness and closeness. One says hādhā dūna dhāka — this is nearer than that. And when you wish to make it small you say duwayna. No verb is derived from it. And in urging one on it is said dūnakahu! — that is, take it, come near it and bring it near you. And they say amrun dūn and thawbun dūn — a matter or a garment of little value.

Al-Qutaybī said: dāna yadūnu dawnan — when he grew weak — and udīnu idānatan. And they recited:
And there came upon the herd of wild cows a hard force that was not weakened —
that is, that was not made weak. In his view it is from al-shay' al-dūn, the slight thing. If this is sound, then its pattern is what we have mentioned.
دوه: The letters dāl, wāw and hā' are nothing [no sound root]. They say: al-dawh is bewilderment.
دوى:
The letters dāl, wāw and the weak letter — this is a chapter whose roots are close to one another, and hardly anything in it can be measured by a single analogy, so we have written its words each on its own account.

1. al-dawiyy — the hum of bees, what is heard from them when they gather.
2. al-dawā' — well known, medicine. One says dāwaytuhu udāwīhi mudāwātan wa-dawā'an, I treated him.
3. al-dawāh — the inkwell one writes from; its plural is duwiyy or diwiyy.
Al-Hudhalī said:
I recognised the dwellings, like the writing of the inkwells, which the Himyari scribe had adorned.
4. al-dā' — illness. One says dawiya yadwā; a man is dawin, a woman dawiyya. One says dā'at al-arḍ, and adā'at, and dawiyat dawan, all from al-dā'. One says: taraktu fulānan dawan mā arā bihi ḥayāt, I left so-and-so as dawan, I see no life left in him. The weak, foolish man is likened to this and called dawan.
A poet said, in a line of verse:
And I lead the wrapped-up, feeble one ... silent among the riders, once loud-mouthed back at the camp.
5. dawwā al-ṭā'ir — the bird circled in the air without moving its wings.
6. al-diwāya — the thin skin that rises over curdled milk. One says addawā yaddawī iddiwā'an.
The poet said:
Deceit has shown from you, which you long kept hidden, as a concealing mother hid her son's sickness.
ديث: The letters dāl, yā' and thā' indicate subduing. One says 'dayyathtuhu', I subdued him, from their saying 'ṭarīqun mudayyath', a road that has been worn smooth.
دير: The letters dāl, yā' and rā' — I think it is turned from a wāw, from al-dār and al-dawr, the house and its turning. And from this chapter is al-dayr, the monastery. One says 'mā bihā dayyūrun wa-dayyārun', meaning there is not a soul in it. And from the chapter we have mentioned, Ibn al-A'rābī said: it is said of a man, when he is the head of his companions, 'huwa ra'su al-dayr', he is the head of the circle.
ديص:
The letters dāl, yā' and ṣād are a single root indicating slipping away and breaking loose.

1. *dāṣa yadīṣu dayṣan* — he slipped away, said when he swerved aside.
2. *al-indiyāṣ* — the slipping of a thing out of the hand.
3. *indāṣa 'alaynā fulānun bi-sharrihi* — so-and-so burst upon us with his evil, said when he broke loose upon us suddenly; and one says 'innahu la-mundāṣun bi-l-sharr', he is a man prone to bursting out with evil.
4. *al-dayyāṣ* — the fat man; and *al-dayyāṣa* — the fat woman.

If this last is sound, it is because when such a man is seized, he slips out of the hand, from the abundance of his flesh.
ديف:
The letters dāl, yā' and fā' are nothing [no sound root]. They say: al-diyāfī is a man named for a land in the Jazīra. He said, in a line of verse:
When the old diyāfī camel snuffs at it, it gives a rumbling groan.
ديك: The letters dāl, yā' and kāf are not a root that anything branches from; it is simply al-dīk, the rooster. They also say it is a small bone protruding on a horse's forehead. But this is not sound.
ديل: The letters dāl, yā' and lām do not follow a regular pattern. They say: al-dīl is a tribe, and the relative adjective from it is dīliyy. As for al-du'il, on the pattern fu'il, it is a small creature. The matter is weak on the ground of its pattern, but as for the derivation, it is not far-fetched, and we have already mentioned it under the letters dāl and hamza together with what comes after them.
دين:
The letters dāl, yā' and nūn are one root to which all its branches return. And it is a kind of submitting and lowliness.

Al-dīn is obedience. One says dāna lahu yadīnu dīnan — when he keeps company and submits and obeys. And a qawmun dīn are people obedient and submissive. The poet said, in a line of verse:
And the people, all but us, were submissive.

Al-madīna, the city, is as though it were on the pattern mafʿala; it was named so because the obedience owed to those in authority is carried out in it. And al-madīna is the bondwoman, and the slave is madīn, as though work had made them both lowly. And a poet said, in a line of verse:
She grew up, and there grew up in her lap the son of a bondwoman, who stays at his spade, digging with his foot.

As for the saying of the poet:
O, your heart has been made lowly by Salmā, and made lowly indeed —
its meaning is: O you, your heart has been made lowly, that is, humbled.

As for their saying that a habit is called a dīn, if that is sound it is because the soul, when it grows used to a thing, goes along with it and submits to it. And they recite in this connection:
As was your way with Umm al-Ḥuwayrith before her, and with her neighbour Umm al-Rabāb at Ma'sal.

But the transmission is "ka-da'bika", and the meaning is close.

As for His word, exalted be His praise: {mā kāna li-ya'khudha akhāhu fī dīni al-malik} [Yūsuf: 76], it is said: in his obedience; and it is said: in his judgement. And from it is {māliki yawmi al-dīn} [al-Fātiḥa: 4], that is, the day of judgement. And a people said: the reckoning and the requital. And whichever of these it is, it is a matter that is submitted to. Abū Zayd said: dīna al-rajulu yudānu — when he is made to bear what he dislikes.

Of this section is al-dayn, debt. One says dāyantu fulānan — when you deal with him on credit, whether taking or giving. A poet said, in a line of verse:
I dealt on credit with Arwā, and debts are paid: she put off some of it and paid some.

And one says dintu and iddantu — when you take on a debt; and adantu — I lent and gave on credit. A poet said, in a line of verse:
He borrowed, and the men of old told him that the one lent to is rich and keeps his word.

And al-dayn falls under the steady reasoning of the section, because in it is all lowliness and abasement. And for that reason they say: "Debt is humiliation by day and grief by night."

As for the saying of the poet:
O house of Salmā, empty now — I ask nothing of her but al-Marāna, until she knows the way —
al-Aṣmaʿī said: al-Marāna is the name of his she-camel, and she knew that road, and for that reason he said: I ask nothing of her but al-Marāna. And "until she knows al-dīn" means the state and the matter that she is familiar with. So he meant: I ask nothing to bring me to this house except my she-camel.

And God knows best.
ذأب: The letters dhāl, hamza and bā' are a single root indicating restlessness, and that a thing not keep to one direction in its movement. From this is al-dhi'b, the wolf, so named for its shifting about (tadhau'ub) from no single direction. One says "dhu'iba ar-rajul," when the wolf has struck his flock. One says "tadha''abat ar-rīḥ," the wind came from every side. "Arḍun madh'aba": a land abundant in wolves. "Dhau'uba ar-rajul": he turned into a wicked, wolfish man. The plural of al-dhi'b is adhu'ub, dhi'āb, and dhu'bān. One says "tadhā'abtu al-nāqa tadhā'uban," on the pattern tafā'altu, when you made her foster another's young by disguising yourself to her as a wolf, so that she would be more tender toward it. Some said: al-idhā' is fleeing. He cited: "indeed, when a people's lion flees (adhaba) and his pride collapses and he runs away." This is the origin of the chapter; then a thing is likened to the wolf — al-dhi'ba, of a pack-saddle, is the part beneath the meeting-point of the two side-frames, falling at the weaving-cross (a term whose exact object I am not fully certain of).
ذأر:
The letters dhāl, hamza and rāʾ are one root indicating avoidance and dislike.

1. dhaʾirtu al-shayʾa — I disliked the thing and turned away from it.

And in the hadith: "When the Messenger of God, God bless him and his family and grant him peace, forbade the beating of women, the women grew defiant [dhaʾira] toward their husbands" — meaning they became rebellious, disobedient, and bold.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
News reached us of Tamīm, that they ... grew defiant over the slain of ʿĀmir, and grew angry.

2. nāqatun mudhāʾir — a she-camel that nuzzles [her young] with her nose without her love for it being genuine. It is also said [to mean] rather the one that shies from her young the moment she gives birth to it.

His saying "dhaʾirū li-qatlā" means they grew defiant and took it as an affront; it is also said: anifū [they were indignant].
ذأل:
The letters dhāl, hamza and lām are a root with few words but analogical, indicating speed.

1. dhaʾala yadhʾalu — to walk quickly, with a swaying gait.
2. If it is with a twisted/limping gait, one says yadhʾulu.
3. From this the wolf is named dhuʾālah.
ذأم:
The letters dhāl, hamza and mīm are a root pointing to distaste and fault.

1. adh’amtanī ‘alā kadhā — you forced me, against my liking, to do such-and-such.
2. dha’amtuhu — I belittled him.
3. al-dha’m — fault; one so blamed is madh’ūm.

As for al-dhān, with a nūn, it is not a root of its own, because the nūn in it stands in for a mīm.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
We drove back the massed troop... bearing its blemish and bearing its fault.
[The troop is described as driven back still carrying its flaw upon it, dhānuhā here standing for its fault, with the nūn in place of the mīm.]
ذأى: The letters dhāl, hamza and the weak letter indicate a kind of pace [in travel]. One says dhaʾā yadhʾā dhaʾyan. And al-dhaʾw is [also said to be] hard driving [of animals].
ذب:
The letters dhāl and bā', doubled, are three roots: the first is a little bird, and other things are then carried over to it and likened to it; the second is sharpness; the third is restlessness and motion.

The first: al-dhubāb, well known [the fly]; one of them is a dhubāba, and the plural of the plural is adhibba. Among what is likened to it and carried over from it: dhubāb al-ʿayn, the pupil of the eye. One says dhababtu ʿanhu, meaning I warded something off from him, as though you drove off from him the fly that was troubling him. Al-Nābigha's saying, one that strikes with its lip at the flies — here al-adhibba is the plural of dhubāb. Al-madhbūb, of camels, is the one whose nostril the fly gets into. Al-madhbūb also means the fool, as though he were likened to the fly-plagued camel.

As for sharpness: dhubāb of a camel's teeth is their sharp edge.
A poet said, in a line of verse:
You hear it, when it sings out, like the cooing of doves upon the branches.
And dhubāb al-sayf is the edge of a sword.

The third root: al-dhabdhaba is the swaying of a thing hung in the air. A man who is mudhabdhab is one wavering between two matters. Al-dhabdhab is the male member, because it tadhabdhaba, that is, sways back and forth. Al-dhabādhib are things hung on a litter or on a camel's head. Al-dhabb is the wild bull, also called dhabb al-riyād. Ibn Muqbil said, in a line of verse:
It paces along with it, the dhabb al-riyād, as though it were a Persian youth wearing two bracelets, carrying a spear.
They said it is called dhabb al-riyād because it comes and goes, never settling in one place.

From this third root also comes their saying dhabbat shafatuhu, when his lip shrivelled from thirst. He cited, in a line of verse:
They gave me a long drink after a short one, after my tongue had shrivelled and dried up.
One says dhabba al-nabt, when a plant withered. And dhabba jismuhu, meaning his body wasted away.

From restlessness and motion comes their saying: dhababnā laylatanā, meaning we wore ourselves out travelling through the night. They do not reach water except with a mudhabbib water-skin, meaning a swift one. He said, in a line of verse:
A swift-hurrying one, harmed by my early starts and my midday travel, whenever the fawn cried out from the heat.
And he said:
A red-brown one presses swiftly on behind it, and it manages, with the blow of a wooden mace.

God knows best.
ذبح: The letters dhāl, bā' and ḥā' are a single root, and it points to splitting. Al-dhabḥ is the verbal noun of dhabaḥtu al-shāt dhabḥan — I slaughtered the sheep. Al-dhibḥ is the beast slaughtered. Al-dhubbāḥ is cracks at the roots of the fingers. One says dhubiḥa al-dann when the wine jar is broached. Al-madhābiḥ are small torrents that cut the ground open. Sa'd al-Dhābiḥ is one of the Sa'd stars. Al-dhibaḥ is a plant, and it may be a stray from the root.
ذبل: The letters dhāl, bāʾ and lām are one root indicating shrinking/leanness in a thing.
ذحق: The letters dhāl, ḥāʾ and qāf are not a root. They sometimes say dhaḥaqa al-lisānu, when the tongue peeled from a disease afflicting it.
ذحل: The letters dhāl, ḥāʾ and lām are one root indicating repayment in kind for an offense. One says ṭalaba bi-dhaḥlihi — he sought retaliation for his grievance. God knows best.
ذخر:
The letters dhāl, khā’ and rā’ point to securing a thing so as to keep it safe.

1. dhakhartu al-shay’a adhkharuhu dhakhran — I stored the thing away, keeping it. When you form the ifta‘ala pattern from this you say iddakhartu — I laid something up for myself.
2. al-madhākhir — a term covering a person’s insides and his blood vessels.

Manẓūr said, in a line of verse:
When we gave her a drink of milk mixed with something else, her insides filled up and her jugular vein grew moist with sweat.

They say: mala’a al-ba‘īru madhākhirahu — the camel filled its insides, meaning its belly.

Al-idhkhir, a plant, is not from this root.
ذر:
The letters dhāl and rā', doubled, are a single root pointing to fineness and scattering.

1. al-dharr — small ants, one of which is a dharra.
2. dharartu the salt and the medicine — I sprinkled it.
3. al-dharīra — a well-known fragrant powder.

All of this follows one and the same pattern.

4. dharrat al-shams, dhurūran — the sun rose, that is, a fine, spreading light appeared. This is behind their saying, 'I will not do it while a sunrise gleams,' and 'while the sun's first edge gleams.'
5. It is related from Abū Zayd: dharra al-baql, when the green herbs sprouted up from the ground. This belongs to the root, because they are then small and scattered.

As for their saying dhārrat al-nāqa, she is mudhārr, when a she-camel's temper turns bad, it has been said this word is really the same root but with a doubling [shadda]. If that is sound, it is irregular against the root we have set down. Except that al-Ḥuṭayʾa said:
She flared up at the nose,
lightened [without the doubling]. And I take this to be the correct form; in that case it would come from dhaʾirat, meaning she grew angry, with the hamza lightened. Except that Abū Zayd said: 'in so-and-so's soul there is dhirār,' meaning aversion out of anger, like the dhirār of the she-camel. And this supports the first account. God knows best.
ذرأ:
The letters dhāl, rā' and hamza are two roots: one is a colour tending toward whiteness, the other is like something scattered and sown.

The first: al-dhur'a, whiteness — from gray hair or otherwise. From it, milḥ dharā'āniyy or dharā'āniyy, a kind of whitish salt. Al-dhur'a is whiteness. A man called adhra' is gray-haired; a woman, dhar'ā'. Al-Shaybānī said: a lock of hair called dhar'ā', on the pattern of dhar'ā' meaning white. The verb from it is dhari'a yadhra'u. It is said that among sheep, the dhar'ā' is the one with a white ear.

The second root: their saying dhara'nā al-arḍa, we sowed the land. Crops described as dharī', on the pattern fa'īl. A verse was recited:
You split my heart open, then sowed within it ... your love; so it was stitched, and the splits closed over.

From this chapter too: dhara'a Allāhu al-khalqa yadhra'uhum, God brought the creation into being and multiplied it. God Almighty said: {He multiplies you thereby} [al-Shūrā: 11].

What falls outside the chapter is their saying adhra'tu fulānan bi-kadhā, I made so-and-so keen on such a thing. And it is related from Ibn al-A'rābī: mā baynī wa baynahu dhar', there is a barrier between me and him.
ذرب:
The letters dhāl, rā' and bā' are a single root pointing to the opposite of soundness in how a thing behaves — boldness and rashness toward what should not be done.

1. al-dharab — sickness of the stomach.

Abū Zayd said: 'in so-and-so's tongue there is dharab,' meaning foul, obscene speech. He cited, in a line of verse:
Give me rest, and rest from me, for I am a heavy burden, my tongue is sharp-mouthed.

2. Ibn al-Aʿrābī related: al-dharab is the rust that forms on a sword.
3. One says dhariba al-jurḥ, when a wound keeps widening and will not take medicine.

He said, in a line of verse:
You are the physician for the diseases of hearts, when the lingering, sharp-edged sickness among them is feared.

There remains in this chapter one word whose pattern is not far from all we have mentioned, since it too does not point to soundness: al-dharabayyā, meaning calamity. One says: ramāhu bi'l-dharabayyā, he struck him with calamity.

Al-Kumayt said, in a line of verse:
He struck me with misfortunes from every side, and with the calamity, both the young men of Fihr and its greybeards.
ذرح:
The letters dhāl, rā' and ḥā' — most of this chapter is a single root: scattering a thing over another so as to cover it in a dye.

1. dharraḥtu al-zaʿfarān fī al-māʾ — I put a small amount of saffron into the water.
2. aḥmar dharīḥiyy — deep red, as though redness had been sprinkled over it.
3. al-Dharīḥ — the name of a stud-camel to which certain camels are traced. It is possible this is for his colour, as one says aḥmar [red].

He said, in a line of verse:
A huge, thick-necked one, of the Dharīḥī stock.

4. al-dharāʾiḥ — hills, one of which is a dharīḥa. It may be that these too were named for their colour. God, mighty and glorious, said: {and among the mountains are streaks, white and red} [Fāṭir: 27].
5. Also belonging to this root: al-dharārīḥ (a kind of blister-beetle), one of which is dhurrūḥa, dhurrāḥa, or dhuraḥraḥa. One says dharraḥa ṭaʿāmahu, when he put some of it into his food.

Some relate: ʿasal mudharraḥ, honey that has been thinned with too much water.

God knows best.
ذرع:
The letters dhāl, rā' and ʿayn are a single root, indicating extension and forward movement; the branches all go back to this origin sense.

1. al-dhirāʿ — the human forearm, well known.
2. al-dharʿ — the verbal noun of dharaʿtu al-thawb wa-l-ḥā'iṭ wa-ghayrahu, I measured the garment, the wall, and other things (by the forearm-length).
3. ḍāqa bi-hādhā al-amr dharʿan — his "reach" grew too narrow for this matter, meaning he took on more than he could bear and was overcome.
4. dharaʿahu al-qay' — vomit "outran" him, meaning it came upon him before he could help it.
5. madhāriʿ al-dābba — the legs of a riding animal, singular midhrāʿ.
6. tadharraʿat al-ibil al-mā' — the camels waded into the water with their forelegs.
7. madhāriʿ al-arḍ — the outlying edges of a land, as if each edge of it were like a forearm reaching out.
8. dharaʿtu al-baʿīr — I stepped on the camel's foreleg so that my companion could mount.
9. tadharraʿat al-mar'a al-khūṣ — the woman drew the palm-leaf strips along, meaning she cleaned them, by running them along her forearm.

A poet said, in a line of verse (continuing the same line quoted under the root kh-r-ṣ):
the drawing of twigs along, by the hands of the women who split palm fronds.

10. al-dharīʿa — a she-camel the hunter hides behind while he shoots game, since he moves forward with her, walking alongside her.
11. Also from this root: tadharraʿa al-rajul fī kalāmihi — the man ran on in his speech. al-idhrāʿ is talking a great deal.
12. faras dharīʿ — a horse of wide stride, clearly swift in its going.
13. qawā'im dhariʿāt — legs that are light and quick.
14. al-dhirāʿān — two stars, said to be "the two forearms of the Lion."
15. A woman quick-handed at spinning is called dhirāʿ. Al-Kisā'ī said this.
16. thawr mudharraʿ — a bull is "forearmed," when there are black patches on its forelegs.
17. maṭar mudharriʿ — rain that, when the ground is dug where it fell, is found to have soaked in to the depth of a forearm.
18. al-mudharraʿ, of men — one whose mother is an Arab and whose father is a lowly non-Arab. He is called mudharraʿ after the two markings on the mule's foreleg, since those come from the donkey's side.
19. To a man you promise something ready at hand, one says: "it is yours from me on the rope's forearm-length" — meaning at once, close by.
20. The upper part of the spear-shaft, near the head, is called dhirāʿ al-ʿāmil, the shaft-head's forearm.
21. al-Dhirāʿān — two hills. He said, in a line of verse:
to a cool watering-place between the two Dhirāʿ hills.
22. al-madhāriʿ — the outlying places near the great cities, like al-Qādisiyya is to Kūfa; and madhāriʿ of palm trees are those close to the houses.
23. ziqq midhrāʿ — a waterskin that is long and large.
24. One says dharraʿa lī fulān shay'an min khabar, meaning he informed me.
25. dharraʿa al-rajul fī saʿyihi — the man swung his arms in his running, when he ran and used his arms to help himself, moving them.
26. Of the bearer of good news, when he waves his hand, one says: "the bringer of good news has made the sign" — that is the mark of good tidings.
ذرف:
The letters dhāl, rā' and fā' are three words, not following one consistent pattern.

1. The first: dharafat al-ʿayn damʿahā — the eye shed its tears. And dharafa al-damʿ, yadhrifu, dharfan — the tears flowed. Madhārif al-ʿayn are its tear-ducts.
2. The second: dharafa, yadhrifu, dharafānan — said when someone walked with a weak, faltering gait.
3. The third: dharrafa ʿalā al-miʾa — he went over a hundred, exceeded it.
ذرق: The letters dhāl, rā' and qāf are not anything [not a real root]. As for the word used of a bird's droppings, its true letter is zāy, and it has already been mentioned in its own place. Al-dharaq is a plant; one says adhraqat al-arḍ, when the ground grew it.
ذرو:
The letters dhāl, rā' and the weak letter are two roots: one is a thing overlooking and overshadowing another; the other is a thing falling and scattering.

Al-dhirwa: the highest point of a camel's hump or of anything else, plural dhurā. Al-dharā: anything you shelter behind; you say "I am in the shelter (dharā) of so-and-so." Al-midhrawān: the tips of the two buttocks, because they overlook what lies between them.

As for the other root: one says "dharā nābu al-jamal," when the tip of a camel's tooth breaks off. Aws said: "when a leading stallion-camel among us has the tip of his tooth broken, another stallion bares his teeth among us." From this chapter also: "dharat ar-rīḥu al-shay' tadhrūhu," the wind scattered the thing. Al-dharā is a name for what the wind has scattered. One says "adhrat al-'aynu dam'ahā tudhrīhi," the eye shed its tears. "Adhraytu ar-rajula 'an farasihi": I threw him down from his horse. It is also said al-dharā is a name for what is shed of tears.

From this chapter also is their saying: "balaghanī 'anhu dharwun min qawl," what he lets drop from the edges of his speech, not the whole of it.
ذع:
The letters dhāl and ʿayn, doubled, are a single root pointing to scattering a thing.

One says the wind dhaʿdhaʿat [a thing], meaning it scattered it, so it tadhaʿdhaʿa, meaning it dispersed. Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
A moaning wind scatters it, scattering it about.

1. al-dhuʿāʿ — the gap between one palm tree and the next, as it occurs in Ṭarafa's poetry, though there is disagreement about it; some say it is spelled with a dāl [not ʿayn], and this has already been mentioned.
2. dhaʿdhaʿa al-sirr — Ibn Durayd related this: he divulged the secret, spread it about.
3. al-dhaʿāʿ — scattered groups of people, one of which is a dhaʿāʿa.
ذعر:
The letters dhāl, ʿayn and rā' are a single root pointing to fright, that is al-dhuʿr. One says a man is dhuʿira, so he is madhʿūr.

1. al-dhaʿūr, of camels — one that startles and pulls away if touched.
2. imraʾa dhaʿūr — a woman who is startled at any hint of impropriety.

He said, in a line of verse:
She gives freely of decent talk, but if you seek other than that from her, you are met with alarm, for she is dhaʿūr [easily startled].
ذعط:
The letters dhāl, ʿayn and ṭāʾ are one word. One says dhaʿaṭahu, when he slaughtered him. And dhaʿaṭat-hu al-maniyyah: death killed him. A poet said, in a line of verse:

When they reached their town, they were overtaken ... by death, by the swift slaughtering doom.

Close to this are the letters dhāl, ʿayn and tāʾ; for they say dhaʿatahu yadhʿatuhu, when he strangled him.
ذعف: The letters dhāl, ʿayn and fā' are a single word: al-dhuʿāf is deadly poison. Food that is madhʿūf is poisoned food. A man is dhuʿifa when he was made to drink it.
ذعق: The letters dhāl, ʿayn and qāf are not a root, and there is no established usage in it. But Al-Khalīl claimed that al-dhuʿāf [poison] is a dialect variant of al-dhuʿāq, then said: I do not know whether this is a genuine dialect form or a speech-defect. Ibn Durayd used to say: al-dhuʿāq is like al-zuʿāq, meaning shouting. One says dhaʿaqa and zaʿaqa, meaning he shouted, with the same sense.
ذعن:
The letters dhāl, ‘ayn and nūn are a single root pointing to going along with and yielding.

1. adh‘ana al-rajulu — the man yielded, yudh‘inu idh‘ānan; its base form is dha‘ana, though what is actually used is adh‘ana.
2. nāqatun midh‘ān — a she-camel that is easy-headed and yielding.
ذف:
The letters dhāl and fā' are a single root pointing to lightness and speed.

1. al-dhafīf — a word echoing al-khafīf [the light one]. It is also said al-dhafīf means the swift one.
2. dhaffaftu ʿalā al-jarīḥ — I hastened the wounded man's death, finishing him off quickly. dhufāfa is derived from it.
3. al-dhufāf — little water; and one says miyāh adhiffa, scant waters.

It is related from a Bedouin: al-dhaff is killing. And istadhaffa al-amr — the matter became straight and ready.

4. al-dhifāf — a small amount of anything. They say, mā dhuqtu dhifāfan, meaning I have not tasted the least thing that can be eaten.

Abū Dhuʾayb said, in a line of verse:
They say, now that the well has been cleared out, come and draw — yet there is not the least drop in it for anyone drawing.
He means: there is nothing in it at all.
ذفر:
The letters dhāl, fāʾ and rāʾ are a word indicating a smell.

1. al-dhafar — the sharpness of a pleasant smell.
2. misk adhfar — musk with a strong, pleasant scent, so called.
3. rawḍatun dhafirah — a meadow with a pleasant smell.
4. al-dhafrāʾ — a plant.

As for al-dhifrā, it is the place on the back of a camel's neck where it sweats — that place must have a smell. And al-dhifirr is a camel strong in that place. Then this was carried over as a metaphor, and so a person's [nape] too is called dhifrā.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And the earring, on the soft place of the nape, hangs ... the cord has slipped away from it, so it swings loose.
ذفل:
The letters dhāl, fāʾ and lām are not a root. Even so, they say that al-dhifl is tar. And they recite for Ibn Muqbil, in a line of verse:

The male ostriches walked with it, like dark [camels] ... smeared with the oil of the dark ruhā and with tar, anointed.

God knows best.
ذقن: The letters dhāl, qāf and nūn are a single word to which everything derived in this chapter returns. Al-dhaqan is the chin of a person or other creature: the place where the two jaws meet. One says "nāqatun dhaqūn," a she-camel that shakes her head as she walks. Al-dhāqina: the projecting point of the throat. It occurs in 'Ā'isha's hadith: "The Messenger of God, God's blessing and peace upon him, died between my throat (saḥrī) and my breast (naḥrī), and my ḥāqina and my dhāqina" [naming parts of the throat/collarbone area]. One says "dhaqantu ar-rajula adhqunuhu," when you strike with the heel of your palm against his jaw-hinge. A bucket is dhaqūn when it is not level but bulky and tilted.
ذكا:
The letters dhāl, kāf and the weak letter are one root, regular and analogical, indicating sharpness and penetration in a thing.

1. dhukāʾ — the sun is called this, because it dhakū [blazes] as fire blazes.
2. ibn dhukāʾ — the dawn, because it comes from her [the sun's] light.
3. dhakkaytu al-dhabīḥata udhakkīhā — I slaughtered the sacrificial animal properly.
4. dhakkaytu al-nāra udhakkīhā, and dhakawtuhā adhkūhā — I kindled the fire.
5. al-faras al-mudhakkī — the horse a year past the coming of its permanent teeth; one says dhakkā yudhakkī.

The Arabs say: "jaryu al-mudhakkiyāti ghilāb," and also ghilāʾ — the running of such mature horses is a race for mastery.

6. al-dhakāʾ — sharpness of heart [i.e. of mind].

A poet said, in a line of verse:
It gives him preference, when they strive against each other ... his full maturity of years, and his sharpness of mind.

7. al-dhakāʾ — also quickness of understanding; the verb from it is dhakiya yadhkā.

And of war and of fire one also says adhkaytu [I kindled it]. And the thing with which a fire is kindled is called dhukwah.
ذكر:
The letters dhāl, kāf and rā' are two roots, from which the words of the section branch out. So al-mudhkir is the female that has borne a male. And al-midhkār is the one that bears males as her habit. ʿAdiyy said:
And I have travelled upon a strong she-camel like the anvil of the smith, a bearer of males.

And al-midhkār is also the land that brings forth the coarse plants. And al-mudhakkara among she-camels is the one whose make and whose temper are like the make of the male camel or his temper. Al-Farrā' said: one says kam al-dhikara min waladika? — how many males among your children? — that is, the males. And a sword that is mudhakkar is one with a water upon it; and dhū dhikrin, that is, sharp-cutting.

And dhukūr al-baql are the coarse ones among the plants, such as khuzāmā and uqḥuwān. And aḥrār al-buqūl are those that are soft and choice. And al-Shaybānī used to say: the dhukūr are those with something of bitterness in them.

And the other root: dhakartu al-shay' — I remembered the thing, the opposite of forgetting it. Then upon it was carried al-dhikr with the tongue, mention. And they say ijʿalhu minka ʿalā dhukrin, with a ḍamma on the dhāl, that is, do not forget it. And al-dhikr is high standing and honour; and that is the reasoning of the root. And one says a man is dhakir and dhikkīr, that is, good at remembering, keen.
ذل:
The letters dhāl and lām, doubled, are a single root pointing to submission, abasement, and softness.

1. al-dhull — the opposite of ʿizz [might, glory]. This is a sound pairing of opposites, and it points to a piece of wisdom particular to the Arabs above other nations: for ʿizz comes from ʿazāz, which is hard, unyielding ground, while dhull is the opposite of hardness. It is related that someone said: 'a measure of dhill [with the dhāl carrying a kasra, meaning humbling oneself] preserves one's family and property better.' From this one says: an animal is dhalūl, clearly tame.
2. From the first sense: a man is dhalīl, described by dhull, madhalla, and dhilla [all meaning abasement].
3. What has been trodden down of a road is called dhill.
4. dhullila al-qiṭf, tadhlīlan — a cluster of grapes grew soft and hung down low.
5. One says: 'run matters along their adhlāl,' meaning along their straight, easy course — that is, along the path in which they go smoothly and are led without resistance.
6. Belonging to this root: dhalādhil al-qamīṣ, the part of a shirt nearest the ground at its lower hem; one of these is a dhildhil.
7. They say: idhlawlā al-rajul, idhlīlāʾan, when a man moved quickly. This too belongs to the root.
ذلف: The letters dhāl, lām and fāʾ are one word, not to be reasoned by analogy, and it is al-dhalaf: an evenness at the tip of the nose that is not a thick, coarse edge — and it is the most beautiful of noses.
ذلق:
The letters dhāl, lām and qāf are one root indicating sharpness.

1. al-dhalq — the tip of the tongue.
2. al-dhalāqah — sharpness of the tongue; and everything sharpened is mudhallaq [made sharp].
3. qarn al-thawr mudhallaq — the bull's horn is [described as] mudhallaq.
