4. adhlaqtu al-ḍabb — a verb derived from this: you pour water into the lizard's burrow so that it comes out.
5. al-idhlāq — speed in shooting/throwing.
ذم:
The letters dhāl and mīm, doubled, are a single root, all of it pointing to the opposite of praise.

1. dhamamtu fulānan, adhummuhu — I found so-and-so blameworthy, so he is dhamīm and madhmūm, when he is not praiseworthy.
2. al-dhamma — a well with little water. In the hadith: 'he came upon a dhamma well.' The plural of dhamma is dhimām.

Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
On Ḥimyarī she-camels, as though their eyes were the rims of scanty wells that the water-drawers had emptied dry.
Ankazathā means: they took its water away. Al-mawātiḥ means: the women who draw water.

As for a covenant, it is called dhimām because a person is blamed for failing it. This is a manner of speech the Arabs use, like their saying: so-and-so is ḥāmī al-dhimār, meaning he protects what would provoke anger [if lost], and ḥāmī al-ḥaqīqa, meaning he protects what is rightfully his to guard.

3. ahl al-dhimma — people bound by a covenant. Abū ʿUbayd said: al-dhimma means protection, safe-conduct, as in his saying, God bless him and his family and grant him peace: 'and their pledge of protection is upheld.' They are called ahl al-dhimma because they paid the jizya [tax] and so were secured in their lives and property. One says dhimām, madhamma and midhamma, with fatḥa or kasra; and of dhamm, madhamma with fatḥa only.

It came in the hadith that a man asked the Prophet, God bless him and his family and grant him peace: 'What removes from me the madhamma of nursing?' He said: 'A slave, whether male or female.' By madhammat al-riḍāʿ he means the wet-nurse's due. Al-Nakhaʿī used to explain this hadith: they liked to give the wet-nurse something extra beyond her wage when the child was weaned. So it is as though the man asked: what removes from me the due owed to the woman who nursed me, so that I will have paid her right in full? Al-Qaṭṭān told us this on the authority of the commentator, on the authority of al-Qutaybī. The Arabs say: adhhib madhammatahum bi-shayʾin, meaning give them something, for they hold a dhimām [claim] upon you. One says: do such-and-such, wa-khalāka dhamm, meaning: and no blame falls on you. One says adhamma fulānun bi-fulānin, when he treated him with contempt. And adhamma bihi baʿīruhu, when his camel lagged behind and fell away from the rest of the herd. A thing that is mudhimm is defective. A man who is mudhimm cannot move.

4. Ibn al-Aʿrābī related: a well is dhamīm, the same as dhamma.

Abū al-Ḥasan al-Qaṭṭān recited to us, on the authority of Thaʿlab, on the authority of Ibn al-Aʿrābī:
A hastening [she-camel], racing on, seeking the last scant drops of a well whose water is dhamīm [meagre].
He is describing a sand-grouse.

There remains in this chapter something whose pattern is not far from this, if it is sound: al-dhamīm is a pustule that breaks out on the nose.

Ibn Qutayba related that al-dhamīm is the urine that drips and trickles from a billy-goat's member. Abū Zubayd said, in a line of verse:
You see, behind its udders, a trickle like the dhamīm dripping over the stunted yaʿāmīr.
Al-nasal, from milk, is what drips from it. Al-quzm means the small ones. Al-Shaybānī said: I do not know what al-yaʿāmīr are. I asked, and found no one with any knowledge of it; it is said to mean young sheep.
ذمر:
The letters dhāl, mīm and rāʾ are one root indicating intensity, in physical form and in character alike — from anger and the like.

1. al-dhimr — the brave man.
2. al-dhamr — likewise, urging/inciting.

When it is said that so-and-so yatadhammaru, it is as if he blames himself and grows angry.

3. al-dhimār — everything whose safeguarding, and whose defense when threatened, falls to you as a duty.

As for what we said about intensity of physical form: al-mudhammar is the withers, the neck, and what is around it up to the dhifrā [the nape], which is the base of the neck. One says dhammartu al-salīl, when you feel [an animal's] nape to see whether it is male or female. Uḥayḥa said, in a line of verse:

You do not know, when you feel a newborn's nape ... whether it will be another's, or the young one yours.

They say, when a matter grows severe: "it has reached the mudhammar" [balagha al-mudhammar].

4. rajulun dhamīr and dhamir — a man who is disliked/thought strange.
5. tadhāmara al-qawm — when the people urged one another on.
6. dhamara al-asad — when the lion roared; one says yadhmuru dhamratan.
ذمل: The letters dhāl, mīm and lām are one word, for a kind of gait: al-dhamīl, like the running of camels. One says dhammaltu al-jamal, when you set the camel to the dhamīl pace.
ذمه: The letters dhāl, mīm and hāʾ are not a root, and nothing valid comes from it — except that they say dhamiha, when he grew bewildered/confused; and one says dhamahat-hu al-shams: the sun caused pain in his brain [gave him sunstroke]. God knows best.
ذمى:
The letters dhāl, mīm and the weak letter are one root indicating movement.

1. al-dhamāʾ — movement; one says dhamā yadhmī, when it moved.
2. al-dhamayān — hastening.
3. al-dhamāʾ — also what remains of the breath of life [in a wounded or dying creature], because it is the last of its movement.
4. "khudh mā dhamā laka" — take what rose up for you; it belongs to this chapter because it is what comes into view before you [yasnaḥu].
5. "dhamatnī rīḥu kadhā" — such-and-such a smell hurt/troubled me.
ذن:
The letters dhāl and nūn, doubled, are a root pointing to flowing.

1. al-dhanīn — what runs from the two nostrils. One says dhanna, dhannan; the one afflicted is adhann.

Al-Shammākh said, in a line of verse:
They flee from a hard-driving one that has worn them out, kept them sleepless with a running discharge.

2. It is also called al-dhunān.
3. al-marʾa al-dhannāʾ — a woman whose menstrual flow runs and does not stop.
4. al-dhunāna — what is left of a weak, dying thing.

Among what falls outside this root's pattern — and I have already said that most matters concerning plants do not follow a consistent pattern — is al-dhuʾnūn, a plant. One says the people went out yatadhaʾnanūn, when they went gathering al-dhuʾnūn.
ذنب:
The letters dhāl, nūn and bā' are three roots: one of them is offence, another is the hind part of a thing, and the third is like a share and a portion.

The first is al-dhanb - the sin and the offence. One says adhnaba yudhnibu. The noun is al-dhanb, and he is mudhnib - an offender. The other root is al-dhanab, which is the hind part of beasts, and for that reason followers are called al-dhunābā. Al-madhānib are the channels of the low watercourses, which are the streambeds of the water in them. Al-mudhannib among fresh dates is that of which part has ripened. A horse long in the tail is called dhanūb. Al-dhināb is the tail end of everything. Al-dhānib is the follower; and so too al-mustadhnib, who is the one that keeps at the tails of the camels. The poet said, in a line of verse:
Like the hired man who kept at the tails of the riding beasts.

As for al-Dhanā'ib, it is a place, and about it the sayer said, in a line of verse:
If my night has been long at al-Dhanā'ib, I have wept before now for the short night.

And God knows best.
ذهب:
The letters dhāl, hā' and bā' are a small root pointing to beauty and freshness. Of that is al-dhahab, gold, which is well known; and it is sometimes made feminine, so one says dhahaba, and it is made plural as al-adhhāb. And al-madhāhib are straps gilded over with gold, or gaps in sword-blades. And everything gilded over with gold is a madhhab. Qays said, in a line of verse:
Do you know a trace like the streaking of gilded straps, of 'Amra's camp, desolate, with no place where a rider halts?
And one says a man dhahib, when he sees a mine of gold and is dazzled. And a bay horse mudhhab, when a redness with a tinge of yellow comes over him. As for al-dhihba, it is a heavy shower of rain. And that is the measure of the section, because by it the earth and the plants grow fresh. The plural is dhihāb. Dhū al-Rumma said:
In it are the showers, and the buds have grown thick about it.
This is the greater part of the section. And there remains another root, and it is the going away of a thing, its passing off. One says dhahaba yadhhabu dhahāban and dhuhūban. And so-and-so has gone a good way, dhahaba madhhaban ḥasanan.
ذهر: The letters dhāl, hāʾ and rāʾ are not a root. They sometimes say dhahira fūhu, when his teeth turned black.
ذهل:
The letters dhāl, hā’ and lām are a single root pointing to being kept from a thing, distracted by fright or something else.

1. dhahiltu ‘ani al-shay’i adhhalu — I was distracted from the thing, when I forgot it or was kept busy from it. adhhalanī ‘anhu kadhā — such-and-such distracted me from it. This is the origin.

It is related from al-Liḥyānī: [he came after] dhuhlin min al-layli or dhahlin — a part of the night had passed — just as one says marra hud’un min al-layl, a period of the night’s stillness passed. It may be that this is because of the night’s darkness, and that in it one is distracted [yudhhalu] from things.

Straying from this root is their calling a swift horse dhuhlūl.
ذهن:
The letters dhāl, hāʾ and nūn are a root indicating strength. One says mā bihi dhihn, meaning he has no strength. Aws said, in a line of verse:

I struggle up on a leg that still has strength in it ... while its fellow, the one left behind, has grown weary.

1. al-dhihn — perceptiveness toward a thing, and retaining it.
2. al-dhahan — the same [meaning].

God knows best what is right.
ذوب:
The letters dhāl, wāw and bāʾ are one root, and it is melting (al-dhawb); then what is close to it in meaning is carried over to it metaphorically. One says dhāba al-shayʾu yadhūbu dhawban, and it is dhāʾib [melting/melted].

1. Then they say metaphorically: dhāba lī ʿalayhi min al-māli kadhā — such-and-such wealth became due to me from him; as if, once it became due, it had 'melted' onto him, the way one thing melts onto another.
2. al-idhwābah — butter, at the time it is put into the pot to be melted.
3. al-dhawb — pure honey.

Then, of the sun, when its heat grows intense, they say: dhābat — as if, once its heat reached people's bodies, it had 'melted' upon them. A poet said, in a line of verse:

When the sun blazed fiercely, he sheltered from its scorching heat ... under the branches of a leafed tree of the spring-grazing sand tract.

And they say: adhāba fulānun amrahu, meaning he set his affair right. It belongs to this chapter, because it is as if he did to it what one who renders down clarified butter and the like does, until it becomes pure and sound. From this is the saying of Bishr, in a line of verse:

And you were like the owner of the pot, who, when it boiled over ... did not know whether to bring it down disgraced, or render it further.

Some said: tudhībuhā means tunhibuhā [you make it plunder]; and al-idhābah is plundering — adhabtuhu means I made it plunder for him. And this too belongs to the chapter, as if he had 'melted' it away upon them.
ذود:
The letters dhāl, wāw and dāl are two roots: one is driving a thing away from a thing, and the other is a herd of camels. It is possible the two branches go back to a single root.

The first: their saying dhudtu fulānan ‘ani al-shay’i adhūduhu dhawdan — I drove so-and-so away from the thing, and dhudtu ibilī adhūduhā dhawdan wa-dhiyādan — I drove my camels off, keeping others from them. One also says adhadtu fulānan — I helped so-and-so drive off his camels.

The other root: al-dhawd, from livestock — a small herd of camels. Abū Zayd said: al-dhawd is a number from three up to ten.
ذوق:
The letters dhāl, wāw and qāf are one root, and it is the testing of a thing by way of tasting; then words are derived from it as figures of speech. So one says dhuqtu al-ma'kūla adhūquhu dhawqan - I tasted the food. And dhuqtu mā 'inda fulānin - I put what he has to the test. And in al-Khalīl's book: everything hateful that comes down upon a man, he has tasted it. And one says dhāqa al-qawsa, when he tries how much give the bow has and how strong it is. He said, in a line of verse:
He tried it and it gave him such a share of suppleness as sufficed, and it had a check that kept the arrow from being drawn too deep.
ذوى: The letters dhāl, wāw and yāʾ are one word indicating dryness and desiccation. You say dhawā al-ʿūdu yadhwī, when the twig dried up, and it is dhāwin [withered]. Sometimes they say dhaʾā yadhʾā instead, but the first is better.
ذيأ: The letters dhāl, yāʾ and hamza are one word. tadhayyaʾa al-laḥmu, and dhayyaʾtuhu, when it separated from the bone, [and] when you separated it from the bone.
ذيخ: The letters dhāl, yāʾ and khāʾ are one word with no analogy. Their word for the male hyena is dhīkh, plural dhīyakhah. And they sometimes say dhayyakhtu al-rajula tadhyīkhan, when you humiliated the man.
ذير: The letters dhāl, yāʾ and rāʾ are not a root. They only say dhayyartu aṭbāʾa al-nāqah, when you smeared the she-camel's udders with dung so that the young camel would not suckle. And that [substance] is al-dhiyār.
ذيع:
The letters dhāl, yā’ and ‘ayn are a root pointing to a thing being made apparent, becoming apparent, and spreading.

1. dhā‘a al-khabaru wa-ghayruhu yadī‘u dhuyū‘an — news and other things spread, became public.
2. rajulun midhyā‘ — a man who cannot keep a secret; plural al-madhāyī‘.

In the hadith of ‘Alī, peace be upon him: ‘They are not the wanderers [al-masāyīḥ] nor the reckless spreaders of secrets [al-madhāyī‘ al-budhur].’

There is here also a word carrying this meaning of spreading: they say adhā‘a al-nāsu [mā] fī al-ḥawḍ — the people used up what was in the trough, when they drank all of it.
ذيف: The letters dhāl, yāʾ and fāʾ are one word with no analogy, and it is al-dhīfān, which is deadly poison.
ذيل:
The letters dhāl, yāʾ and lām are a small root, regular and analogical, and it is something that trails low, hanging in a wrap.

1. al-dhayl — from this, the trailing hem of a shirt or the like.
2. dhayl al-rīḥ — the tail of the wind: what drags along the ground from it.
3. farasun dhayyāl — a horse long in the tail.

Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
With every well-tried [horse], like the lion, leaping ... to the limbs of a long-tailed, [thick-tailed] one.

4. If the horse is short [in body] and its tail is long, it is called dhāʾil.
5. mudhāl — their word for a despised/disgraced thing, from this — as if it were not placed among the exalted things.
6. "jāʾa adhyālun min al-nās" — a trailing remnant of people came, meaning a few stragglers of them.
7. al-dhāʾilah, of coats of mail — the one with a long trailing skirt; likewise al-dhāʾil.

A poet said, in a line of verse — the other half is missing:
And the weave of Sulaym, of every hard, trailing [mail-coat] —

8. dhālat al-marʾah — the woman trailed her hems [along the ground]. This is in the poetry of Ṭarafa.

As for the saying of al-Aghlab:
He goes about with a hand and a tail —
he meant the leg, but put dhayl [tail] in its place for the rhyme; for he goes on to say:
Then woe, if the saying of 'woe' could save him.

9. "man yaṭul dhayluhu yantaṭiq bihi" — whoever's train is long girds himself with it: meaning, whoever has abundant means spends his wealth as he pleases.
ذيم: The letters dhāl, yāʾ and mīm are one word, not to be reasoned by analogy nor further derived. One says dhimtuhu adhīmuhu dhayman [I reviled him].
رأ:
The letters rā' and hamza are a root denoting trembling and agitation.

1. ra'ra'at al-'ayn — the eye trembled from its weakness.
2. ra'ra'at al-mar'a bi-'aynihā — the woman flashed her eye brightly.
3. ra'ra'a al-sarāb — the mirage came and went, and glimmered.
4. ra'ra'tu bi-l-ghanam — I called the sheep.

As for al-rā'a, it is a tree, plural rā'.
رأب: The letters rā', hamza and bā' are a single root indicating joining and gathering. You say ra'abtu al-umūra al-mutafarriqata, when you bring scattered matters together gently, as the mender, al-shaʿʿāb, mends the crack of a bowl. That piece of wood used for mending is called ru'ba.
رأد:
The letters rā', hamza and dāl are a small root indicating restlessness and movement.

1. imra'atun ra'datun wa ru'dun — a woman quick to reach youth, who does not remain stunted. This is what we mentioned under movement.
2. al-ra'd and al-ru'd — the base of the jaw.
3. ra'd al-ḍuḥā — its rising, its height. One says tara'ada al-ḍuḥā and tarā'ada.
4. tara'adati al-ḥayyatu — the snake quivered as it glided.

Al-Khalīl used to say: al-ri'd, with hamza, is the agemate, the tirb.
رأس:
The letters rā', hamza and sīn are a root that points to gathering together and to height.

So al-ra's is the head of a man or of anything else. Al-ra's is also a large body of people, as in the line of Ibn Kulthūm:
With a host of the Banū Jusham ibn Bakr ... with whom we pound the soft ground and the rough.

Al-ar'as is the man with a great head. One says ba'īr ra'ūs — a camel with no fat left on him except in his head. And shātun ra'sā' — a ewe whose head has turned black. Al-ra'īs is the one whose [head] has been struck. One says saḥāba rā'isa — a cloud that goes out in front of the other clouds. And one says anta 'alā ri'āsi amrika — you are at the head of your affair. The common people say 'alā ra'si amrika.
رأف:
The letters rā', hamza and fā' are a single word that points to tenderness and mercy, and that is al-ra'fa, compassion. One says ra'ufa yar'ufu ra'fatan and ra'āfatan, on the patterns fa'la and fa'āla. God, mighty and exalted, said: {And let no pity for the two of them take hold of you in the religion of God} [al-Nūr: 2]; and it was also read ra'āfa. A man is ra'ūf, on the pattern fa'ūl, and ra'uf, on the pattern fa'ul. A poet said, using ra'ūf:
He is the All-Merciful; He has been compassionate towards us.

And another said, using al-ra'ūf:
He sees that the Muslims have a right upon him, like the act of a father, compassionate and merciful.
رأل:
The letters rā', hamza and lām are one word indicating the chicks of the ostrich — that is al-ra'l, plural ri'āl, feminine ra'ala.

1. istar'ala al-nabātu — the plant grew tall and became like the necks of the ostrich chicks.
2. dhātu al-ri'āl — a meadow.
3. al-ri'āl — stars.
رأم:
The letters rā', hamza and mīm are a root indicating closeness, nearness and affection. One says of anyone who loves a thing and grows attached to it: qad ra'imahu — he has grown fond of it. Its origin is from their saying ra'ama al-jurḥu ri'mānan, when its mouth closed up for healing.

1. Al-Shaybānī said: ra'amtu shaʿba al-qadaḥi — when you mend the crack of a bowl.

He recited, in a line of verse:
My slain, at the sand-hill of Uwāra, were maimed — they split hearts whose cracks were never mended.

2. al-ru'ma — the glue by which a thing is stuck together.
3. al-ra'm — a young one or offspring that another besides its mother takes to and cares for. One says ra'imat al-nāqatu ri'mānan, the she-camel took to it; ar'amnāhā, we made her take to a ra'm. The she-camel is ra'ūm and rā'ima.
رأى:
The letters rā', hamza and yā' are a root indicating looking and seeing, with the eye or with insight. Al-ra'y: what a person thinks in a matter, plural al-ārā'.

1. One says ra'ā fulānun al-shay'a and rā'ahu, the second being the letters reversed.
2. al-ri'y — what the eye sees of a good appearance.
3. The Arabs say raytuhu in the sense of ra'aytuhu, I saw it.
4. tarā'ā al-qawmu — when some of them saw others.
5. rā'ā fulānun yurā'ī — he made a show of it for others to see. Faʿala dhālika ri'ā'a al-nāsi — he did that for people to see, that is, doing a thing so that people see it.
6. al-ruwā' — a good appearance.
7. al-mir'āh — the mirror, is well known.
8. al-tar'iya — or if you soften the hamza you say al-tariyya — is what a menstruating woman sees of yellowish discharge after the blood of her period, or her seeing some of the signs of menstruation beforehand.
9. al-ru'yā — the dream-vision, is well known, plural ru'an.
رب:
The letters rā' and bā' denote several roots. The first is the mending of a thing and tending to it.

al-rabb is the owner, the creator, the master. al-rabb is also one who sets a thing right; one says rabba fulānun ḍay'atahu, when he tended to the upkeep of his estate. This is a waterskin marbūb (treated) with rubb; and al-rubb is the syrup of grapes and other fruit, because a thing is treated with it. A horse is described as marbūb. Salāma said, in a line of verse: Neither pale-lipped, nor hook-nosed, nor sickly ... given medicine, well cared for, kept in the choicest place of the dwelling.

al-rabb is one who sets a thing right, and God, exalted be His praise, is al-Rabb, because He sets right the states of His creation.

1. al-ribbī — one who knows God well.
2. rababtu al-ṣabiyya arubbuhu, and rabbabtuhu urabbibuhu — I raised the child.
3. al-rabība — the nurse, the one who raises a child.
4. rabīb al-rajul — a man's stepson, his wife's son.
5. al-rābb — the stepfather, the one who takes charge of the rabīb's affairs. In the hadith: "It is disliked for a man to marry the wife of his rābb."

The other root is the clinging to a thing and remaining upon it, close in kind to the first. One says arabbat al-saḥāba, when the cloud lingered over a land.

1. arḍ marabb — land where rain never ceases, for which reason cloud is called rabāb.
2. al-rabāb — cloud hanging below other cloud, white or black, one piece being a rabāba.
3. al-shātu al-rubbā — the ewe kept indoors for her milk, because she arabbat, clings to the house; or, it is said, the one who has recently given birth, in which case she is the one rearing her young, belonging to the first root.
4. al-irbāb — drawing near to a thing.
5. arabbat al-nāqa — the she-camel clung to the stud and grew fond of him; she is murrib.

The third root is the joining of one thing to another, also close in kind to what precedes it; and were the matter looked into closely, the whole chapter would prove to be one single pattern.

1. al-ribāba — the cloth in which the divination-arrows are placed. Al-Hudhalī said, in a line of verse: and they were as though a ribāba, and he as though a gambler casting the arrows and declaring the outcome.
2. al-ribāba — a covenant; those bound by covenant are called arribba. Someone said, in a line of verse: Bahz were their covenant-partners, and the bond of neighborly protection deceived them, for they were a treacherous people. The covenant is called ribāba because it gathers and binds together. As for the saying of 'Alqama, in a line of verse: I was a man whose covenant passed to you ... and before you other guardians raised me, and I went astray — here al-ribāba is the covenant just mentioned, and al-rubūb is the plural of rabb, belonging to the first root.
3. al-ribāb — Abū al-Ḥasan 'Alī ibn Ibrāhīm told us, from 'Alī ibn 'Abd al-'Azīz, from Abū 'Ubayd: al-ribāb is the tithes taken as tax. Abū Dhu'ayb said, in a line of verse: at times she joins with the riders and forms bonds of protection, and her ribāb grants them safe conduct. It is possible this was called ribāb because, once taken, it becomes like a covenant.

Among what departs from these roots:

1. al-rabrab — a herd of wild cattle, though it may be joined to the third root, said to be named for its gathering together, as with al-ribāba.
2. al-rabab — abundant water, named for its gathering together. Someone said, in a line of verse: and the dark-brown wheat-grain, and the gathered water.

As for rubba, it is a word used in speech to make a thing seem few or rare; you say rubba rajulin jā'anī. No derivation is known for it.
ربت:
The letters rā', bā' and tā' are not a root, but belong to the chapter of substitution. One says rabbatahu tarbītan, when he rabbabahu — reared him.

He said:
The grave is a good, silent in-law — there is no rearing for the one placed within it.
ربث:
The letters rā', bā' and thā' are a single root indicating mixing and detainment. You say rabbathtu fulānan urabbithuhu ʿan al-amri, when you detain him from it. Al-rabītha: the matter that detains you. In the hadith: "When it is the day of Friday, Iblīs sends out his troops to the people, and they hold them back with al-rabā'ith" — meaning they remind them of the needs that detain them. One says irbaththa al-qawmu, when they fell into mixed confusion.

He said:
We shot at them until their gathering fell into confusion.
ربج:
The letters rā', bā' and jīm are a single word, if it is sound, indicating bewilderment. Al-Khalīl said: al-tarabbuj is bewilderment.

He said:
I came to Abū Laylā and was not bewildered.

One says, and it is close to that, that al-rabāja is dullness, al-fadāma.
ربح:
The letters rā’, bā’ and ḥā’ are a single root pointing to a surplus gained in a sale.

1. rabiḥa fulānun fī bay‘ihi yarbaḥu — so-and-so profited in his selling, when he gained an excess. tijāratun rābiḥa — trade that yields a profit. One says ribḥ and rabaḥ, just as one says mithl and mathal.

As for al-A‘shā’s saying, in a line of verse: ‘like the cords of al-rabaḥ drawn taut’ — some said al-niṣāḥāt are cords, and that here they are the cords used on wild goats.

2. al-rabaḥ — horses and camels brought in to be sold and traded for profit.

As for the saying: ‘they fed their guests rabaḥan bi-buḥḥin’ [beasts got in trade, hoarse-voiced ones among them — the sense is not fully clear], Ibn Durayd said: straying from this root is al-rubbāḥ, said to mean the monkey.
ربخ:
The letters rā', bā' and khā' are a small root indicating slackness and languor.

1. mashā ḥattā tarabbakha — he walked until he grew languid.
2. al-rabīkh — what they call one with much flesh.
3. al-rabūkh — it is said this is a woman who swoons during intercourse.
ربد:
The letters rā', bā' and dāl are two roots: one is a colour, the other is staying.

1. al-rubda — a dull dark colour mixed into blackness.
2. the ostrich is rabdā', named from this colour.
3. tarabbada — said of a man when his colour changes and darkens in anger.
4. a ewe rabdā' — black, spotted with red and white.
5. al-arbad — a vicious kind of snake, having a rubda mottling in its colour.
6. rabbadat al-shātu — the ewe's udder swelled with milk, and patches of black and white showed in it.
7. al-samā'u mutarabbidatun — the sky clouded over. This belongs to the chapter too.

As for rubad al-sayf, it is the damascening of its blade — a Hudhali word.

He said:
A sharp sword, its blade refined, white and fine, with damascening along its surface.

It is possible to trace this back to the origin we mentioned. So it is said:

As for the other origin, al-mirbad is the place where camels stand; its derivation is from rabada, meaning he stayed. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: rabadahu, when he confined him. Al-mirbad is also the threshing floor. Some people say that al-mirbad is the piece of wood or stick placed at the door of the enclosure, laid across the chests of the camels to keep them from going out — so it was related from Abū Zayd. I think this is a mistake; rather al-mirbad is the pen where the livestock are confined, and the piece of wood is the stick of the mirbad. Do you not see that the poet attributed it to the mirbad? Suwayd ibn Kurāʿ said:
Wayward camels, except for what I set behind them — the mirbad's stick, covering their necks and forelegs.
ربذ:
The letters rā', bā' and dhāl are a root indicating lightness in a thing.

1. al-rabadh — lightness of the legs; one light in the legs is rabidh.
2. al-ribdha — a tuft of wool with which a mangy camel is treated. It is said that the rag of a menstruating woman is called ribdha. Some said: al-ribdha is the rag with which the goldsmith polishes jewelry.
3. al-rabadh — the tufts of wool hung around camels' necks, singular rabadha.

The reasoning in all of it is one, and it goes back to the lightness we mentioned.

Close to this is their saying: fulānun ladhū rabidhātin, meaning he often stumbles in speech — and that comes only from lightness and lack of steadiness.
ربس:
The letters rā', bā' and sīn are a single root mentioned by Ibn Durayd. He said: the origin of al-rabs is striking with the two hands. One says rabasahu bi-yadayhi, he struck him with his two hands. He said: they say dāhiyatun rabsā'u, meaning severe — following the origin we mentioned, as if it batters people with its hands.

Another mentioned, close to what he took as the origin, that al-irtibās is compactness in flesh and other things. One says kabshun rabīsun — a ram, firm and compact.

Among what departs from this is their saying irbassa irbisāsan, when he went off into the land.
ربص: The letters rā', bā' and ṣād are a single root pointing to waiting. From it is al-tarabbuṣ, waiting for something. One says tarabbaṣtu bihi — I waited on him. And al-Sijistānī reported: lī bi-al-Baṣra rubṣa, and lī fī matā'ī rubṣa — that is, in it I have something to wait for.
ربض:
The letters rā', bā' and ḍād are a root indicating stillness and settling.

1. rabaḍat al-shātu — the ewe, and others, crouched down.
2. al-rabīḍ — the group of sheep that are crouching.
3. rabaḍ al-baṭn — what lies against the ground of a camel or other animal when it crouches.
4. al-rabaḍ — what surrounds a city; and the dwelling of any people is a rabaḍ.
5. al-ribḍa — the killing-place of a people slain in a single spot.

As for their saying qirbatun rabūḍun, for a wide waterskin, it belongs to this chapter, as if it is filled and so settles, or is fully watered and so settles.

As for al-rabūḍ, it is the great spreading tree, so named because one takes shelter in it and settles beneath it. Dhū al-Rumma said:
It hollowed out every crouching arṭā-bush.

Al-arbāḍ: the ropes of the saddle, because the load is bound and settled by them. The resting place of sheep is their rabaḍ, because they crouch in it. Some said: arbaḍat al-shamsu, when its heat grew intense, until it made the ewe and the gazelle crouch. Rabḍ al-rajuli and rubḍuhu: his wife — and the reasoning holds firm, because she is his settling place. The proof that this reasoning is sound is that they call the whole dwelling a rabḍ.

He said:
Winter came and I had not yet taken a dwelling — alas for my hands, worn from digging the pits.

As for al-ruwaybiḍa, which came in the hadith "and al-ruwaybiḍa will speak," it is the worthless, contemptible man. He was named that because he crouches on the ground, from his insignificance and lowliness — no attention is paid to him.
ربط:
The letters rā', bā' and ṭā' are a single root, indicating tying fast and being firmly fixed.

1. rabaṭtu al-shay' arbiṭuhu rabṭan — I tied the thing; what it is tied with is ribāṭ.
2. Also from this root: al-ribāṭ — standing guard at the enemy's frontier post, as if they had been tied there and so held firm and stayed at it.
3. rajul rābiṭ al-ja'sh — a man of "tied-fast nerve," meaning strong of heart and spirit.

Labīd said, in a line of verse:
Steady of heart, guarding their exposed flank, I wheel the dark [steed] with a firm, well-built [rein].

Ibn Aḥmar said, in a line of verse:
Steadier of nerve, defending the heights of his people, when [danger presses and] the loincloths are drawn back from what they cover.
(Both lines are terse and I am not fully certain of their exact images — I give the sense as closely as I can follow it.)

4. One says irtabaṭtu al-faras li-l-ribāṭ — I kept the horse tied up ready, for war-service.
5. It is said that al-ribāṭ, of horses, means five mounts or more.
6. "So-and-so's family has a ribāṭ of horses" — as one says tilād, inherited stock — meaning the original stock of horses he owns.

Laylā al-Akhyaliyya said, in a line of verse:
A people whose stock of horses stands amid their tents, and blue-grey spearheads that seem like stars.

7. One says qaṭaʿa al-ẓaby ribāṭahu — the gazelle cut its ribāṭ, meaning its snare.
8. It is reported from al-Shaybānī: mā' mutarābiṭ — water that stands still, going nowhere.
9. They said: al-Rabīṭ is a nickname of al-Ghawth ibn Murr.
10. As for their calling dates rabīṭ — it is said to be dates that have dried out and had water poured on them. This may well be a borrowed word; it is also said to be with dāl, al-rabīd, and is not a genuine root-word here.
ربع:
The letters rā', bā' and ʿayn are three roots: one of them is a part out of four things, another is staying put, and the third is lifting and raising up.

As for the first, it is al-rubʿ, the quarter of a thing. One says rabaʿtu al-qawma arbaʿuhum when you take a quarter of their wealth; and rabaʿtuhum arbaʿuhum when you are the fourth of them. And al-mirbāʿ is from this: it is something the chief used to take, and it is a quarter of the spoil.

ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAnama al-Ḍabbī said, in a line of verse:
Yours is the quarter of it and the choice pieces, and your word, and the share seized on the way, and what is over.

And in the hadith: "I did not make you one who takes a quarter" — that is, who takes the mirbāʿ.

As for Labīd's words:
I turn the black one aside with a marbūʿ mitall —
there are two views. One of them is that he meant the spear, the one that is neither long nor short, as one says a man is rabʿa, of middle height among men. Whoever holds this view takes the bā' to mean "with", as though he said: I turn the black one aside — and it is his horse — and with me is a middling stout spear. The rule of al-rabʿa belongs to the second root. The second view is that he meant a rein of four strands. And this is the more evident of the two.

Of this chapter are the rabāʿiyyāt of the teeth, those next after the front teeth. And al-ribʿ in fever and in coming to water is what happens on the fourth day: that they come to water one day and graze two days, then come to water on the fourth day. And one says rabaʿat ʿalayhi al-ḥummā and arbaʿat — the fever came on him every fourth day. And al-arbiʿā', on the pattern afʿilā', is one of the days; al-arbaʿā', with a fatḥa on the bā', has also been mentioned. Of this chapter is al-rabīʿ, spring, and it is a season out of four seasons; and al-marbaʿ is the people's camping place in that season. And al-rubaʿ is the young camel born in the spring. And a she-camel is murbiʿ when she gives birth in the spring; and if that is her habit, she is mirbāʿ. Of this chapter is arbaʿa al-rajulu, when a child is born to him in his youth, and his children are ribʿiyyūn.

The other root is staying: one says rabaʿa yarbaʿu. And al-rabʿ is a people's dwelling place. Of this chapter: the people are ʿalā rabaʿātihim — that is, upon their first affairs, as though it were the matter they settled upon long ago and forever. And they say: "irbaʿ ʿalā ẓalʿika" — stay where you are and wait. And one says a rain is murbiʿ murtiʿ: al-murbiʿ is the one that keeps whoever it falls on in his camping place from going out to search for pasture, and al-murtiʿ is the one that makes grow what the camels feed on.

The third root: rabaʿtu al-ḥajara, when you lift the stone. From it is the hadith: "that he passed by a people lifting a stone", and "yartabiʿūn" as well. And the stone itself is a rabīʿa. And al-mirbaʿa is the stick with which loads are carried until they are set on the backs of the beasts.

And this was recited:
Where are the two pegs, and where is the carrying-pole, and where is the load of the heavily laden she-camel?

Al-shiẓāẓān are the two sticks put through the loops of the saddle-bag. Al-muṭabbaʿa is the heavily loaded one. Al-wasq is the load. And it is said that al-rabīʿa is the helmet among weapons. And one says rābaʿanī fulānun when he carries the load with you by the mirbaʿa.

Of what has strayed from these roots is al-rabʿa, and it is the space between the stones that hold up the cooking pot.
ربغ: The letters rā', bā' and ghayn are a single word, if it is sound. They say rabīʿun rābighun — a lush spring, abundant — related from Abū Zayd. It was related from Ibn Durayd: al-rabgh is finely-crushed dust.
ربق:
The letters rā', bā' and qāf are a single root: something that goes around something else, like a collar around the neck — then it branches out.

1. al-ribqa — the cord placed around the neck.

In their speech: "the ewes' udders swelled, so tie the ribq, tie the ribq" — said when the sheep's udders swell and the noose-cords are made ready for their young, for they let down their milk at birth.

2. al-rabīqa — the animal tied in the ribqa.

It came in the hadith: "You owe fulfilment of the covenant so long as you do not eat the ribāq" — the plural of ribq, meaning the rope; by it he meant the covenant, comparing what binds the necks to the ribq placed on the necks of young animals.

One says rabaqtu fulānan fī hādhā al-amri, when you cast him into it until he became ensnared. Umm al-Rubayq: a calamity, as if it goes around people until they are ensnared in it.
ربك: The letters rā', bā' and kāf are a word indicating mixing and confusion. Al-rabk: preparing and mixing crumbled bread. What is done that way is called al-rabīka. One says irtabaka fī al-amri, when he could hardly extricate himself from it.
ربل:
The letters rā', bā' and lām are a single root indicating gathering and abundance drawn together.

1. rabala al-qawmu yarbulūna. Al-rabīla — fatness.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
He was not slow-witted, dull-hearted — he wasted his youth in fat living and ease.

2. al-rabala — the inner part of the thigh, plural al-rabalāt. A woman mutarabbila is fleshy; she has tarabbalat. The noun is al-rabāla.
3. al-rabl — kinds of trees that, when the season turns cold and summer withdraws, put out green leaves without rain. One says tarabbalat al-arḍu, the land put out rabl growth.
4. al-ri'bāl — the lion, so named for the gathering-together of his frame.
ربن:
The letters rā', bā' and nūn — if the nūn is taken as original, then it is a single word, al-rubbān. One says akhadhtu al-shay'a bi-rubbānihi, meaning I took the whole of it. Others said: rubbānu kulli shay'in is its newness, its ḥidthān.

Ibn Aḥmar said:
Life is only in its freshness — and you take your share from its branches.

He means by rubbānihi: its newness and freshness.
ربى:
The letters rā', bā' and the weak letter, and likewise the hamzated form of it, indicate a single root: increase, growth and elevation.

1. rabā al-shay'u yarbū — when it increased.
2. rabā al-rābiyata yarbūhā — when he climbed the hillock.
3. rabā — he was struck by al-rabw; al-rabw is shortness of breath from exertion.

He said:
Until it climbed the top of a rise and grew short of breath — it eased from its panting, and did not grow short of breath.
Meaning: it climbed the rise, and was not struck by shortness of breath.

4. al-rabwa and al-rubwa — the raised place, the hillock.

One says arbat al-ḥinṭatu — the wheat throve, it yurbī. Al-ribwa carries the same meaning as al-rabwa also. One says rabbaytuhu and tarabbaytuhu, when I nourished him. This can carry two meanings: one from what we mentioned, because when reared he grows, thrives and increases; the other meaning is from rabbabtuhu, from al-tarbīb, rearing. It may be that one of the two bā's is originally a yā', and both explanations are sound.

5. al-ribā — usury, in wealth and dealings, well known; its dual is ribawān or ribayān.
6. al-urbiyya — belongs to this chapter. One says huwa fī urbiyyati qawmihi, when he is among the high lineage of his family; al-urbiyya is not used of anyone but them.

He recited:
And I, amid Thaʿlaba ibn Ghanm — belong to a high lineage whose branches have spread.

7. al-urbiyyatān — two masses of flesh at the base of the inner thigh, so named for being raised above what is below them.

As for the hamzated form: al-marba' and al-marba'a of the land — the elevated place where a people's lookout stands. Marba'at al-bāzī — the place where the falcon perches.

Imru' al-Qays said:
I go out early with the two hunters beside me, each at his lookout, watching closely.

Anā arba'u bika ʿan hādhā al-amri means I raise you above this matter, I keep you clear of it. Ibn Durayd mentioned: li-fulānin ʿalā fulānin rabā'an, in the extended form, meaning superiority. Abū Zayd said: rābaʾtu al-amra murābaʾatan, meaning I was wary of it and guarded against it — it belongs to this chapter, as though he watches over it. Ibn al-Sikkīt said: mā raba'tu rab'a fulānin, meaning I did not know of him, as though he says: I did not watch him. And from it: faʿala fiʿlan mā raba'tu bihi, meaning I did not suspect it.

God knows best what is correct.
رت:
The letters rā' and tā' are not a root, but they say:

1. al-rutta — haste, or a stammer, in speech.
2. al-rutūt — pigs.
3. al-ratt — Ibn al-A'rābī said it is the chief or leader, plural rutūt.

All of this ought to be looked into with caution.
رتج:
The letters rā', tā' and jīm are a single root indicating closing and narrowness.

1. urtija ʿalā fulānin fī manṭiqihi — when speech closed up on him, he was struck tongue-tied. It comes from artajtu al-bāba, meaning I shut it. One says ratija al-rajulu fī manṭiqihi ratajan.
2. al-ritāj — the shut door, so said al-Khalīl. It was related in the hadith: "Whoever puts his wealth into the ritāj of the Kaʿba" — they said it is the door, but he did not mean the door itself, rather he meant that he made his wealth an offering to the Kaʿba, meaning the vow.

He said, in a line of verse:
When they made me swear, in ʿUlayya, my right hand was inclined toward the side of the bolted ritāj.

3. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: artajat al-nāqatu, when she closed her womb over the water, conceived.
4. artajat al-dajājatu — when her belly filled with eggs.
5. al-marātij — it is said these are the narrow paths.
6. al-ratā'ij — the closely-set rocks.
رتخ: The letters rā', tā' and khā' amount to nothing. Except that they say: rataka al-ʿajīnu ratkhan, when it became thin and runny. Likewise the clay.
رتع:
The letters rā’, tā’ and ‘ayn are a single word pointing to abundance in eating.

1. rata‘a yarta‘u — he ate as much as he wished, which only happens in a time of plenty.
2. al-marāti‘ — places of such free feeding; this is the resting place where a person settles.
رث:
The letters rā' and thā' are a single root, denoting the wearing-out and falling-apart of a thing. al-rathth is a worn-out, decayed thing; one says a rope is rathth, a garment is rathth, a man is rathth al-hay'a (shabby in appearance); it raththa yarithth, rathātha and ruthūtha, it grew worn.

1. al-riththa — the worn-out, cast-off odds and ends of the house, plural rithath. From this comes their saying "he was irtuththa in the battle," because the wounded man falls just as the riththa falls, and is then carried off while rathīth, barely alive.
2. al-riththa — the weak and lowly among people.
3. al-riththa — a foolish woman, it is said; if that is correct, it belongs to this chapter.
رثد:
The letters rā', thā' and dāl are a single root indicating stacking and gathering.

1. rathadtu al-matāʿa — when you stack some of it upon the other. Goods stacked up are rathad. The man was named Marthad from this. Goods are also called rathīd and marthūd.

It is his saying, in a line of verse:
So the two remembered a stacked load, after the sun had cast its right hand into the concealing dark.

2. Al-Kisā'ī related: arthada al-rajulu bi-l-arḍi kadhā, meaning he stayed.
3. al-marthad — it is said this is the noble among men.
4. al-rathad — the weak among people, said of one who said this, by way of comparison, as if they were likened to goods stacked one atop another. They say: taraknā ʿalā al-mā'i rathadan mā yuṭīqūna taḥammulan, we left at the water a mass they could not manage to carry off.
5. al-rathad — also what clings and cakes from moist earth. One says: iḥtafara al-qawmu ḥattā arthadū, meaning they dug until they reached that.
رثع: The letters rā', thā' and ʿayn are a sound root indicating greed and covetousness. So said al-Khalīl: al-rathaʿ is greed and avarice. Al-Kisā'ī said: rajulun rāthiʿun is one who is satisfied with a paltry gift and keeps company with bad companions. One says rathiʿa rathaʿan.
رثم:
The letters rā', thā' and mīm are a small root indicating smearing one thing with another.

1. rathamat al-mar'atu anfahā bi-l-ṭībi — she smeared her nose with perfume.

He said, in a line of verse:
A woman with a fine nose, its bridge smeared with musk.

2. ruthima anfuhu — when it was struck until its blood flowed.
3. al-ratham — whiteness on the upper lip of a horse, that is al-ruthma. It follows the same reasoning, as if the lip had been smeared with white.
رثن: The letters rā', thā' and nūn amount to nothing. They sometimes say: arḍun marthūnatun. Al-rathān, which they claim, is something like fine drizzling rain.
رثى:
The letters rā', thā' and the weak letter are a small root indicating tenderness and compassion. One says rathaytu li-fulānin, meaning I softened, felt tenderness.

1. rathā al-mayyita bi-shiʿrin — he lamented the dead one in verse. Some of the Arabs say rathaʾtu, but that is not the origin.
2. al-rathya — a pain in the joints.

As for the hamzated form, it too is a small root indicating mixing.

3. arthaʿa al-labanu — the milk curdled. The noun is al-rathīʿa. They say in their proverbs: "al-rathī'a is among the things that quench anger."
4. Abū Zayd said: irtathaʿa ʿalayhim amruhum — their affair became confused, and from it is al-rathī'a. One says irtathaʿa fī ra'yihi, meaning he became confused. They yarthiʿūna rathʿan.
5. It is said al-rathī'a is to mix sour milk with sweet.

God knows best what is correct.
رج:
The letters rā' and jīm are a root denoting agitation, and it follows a regular pattern.

1. katība rajrāja — a battle-unit that churns and can hardly move forward.
2. jāriya rajrāja — a young woman whose buttocks quiver as she moves.
3. al-rijrija — the water remaining in a trough.
4. al-rajāj — the weak among men. Someone said, in a line of verse: They came from Nayr and from Suwāj, with a people grown weary of night travel; they are weak men mounted on weak beasts.
5. al-rajj — the shaking of a thing; you say rajajtu al-ḥā'iṭa rajjan, I shook the wall; and irtajja al-baḥr, the sea surged.
6. al-rajraj — describing a thing that quivers. Someone said, in a line of verse: and she clothed with the wrap a lower back that quivered.
7. irtajja al-kalām — speech grew confused and tangled, called that because when it grows muddled it is like the surging sea.
8. al-rijrija — soft, runny tharīd (a bread-and-broth dish).
9. al-rajāja — an emaciated ewe, it is said; if that is correct, then the emaciated one shakes and wobbles.
10. nāqa rajjā' — a she-camel with a great hump, for when a hump grows large it sways and quivers.

As for his saying, "and rijrij hangs in strands between her two jaws" — it is said to mean slobber.
رجب:
The letters rā', jīm and bā' are a root that points to propping one thing up with another and strengthening it.

1. al-tarjīb — propping up a tree when it bears heavily, so that its branches do not break. From this comes the hadith of the Anṣārī man: "I am its well-rubbed post, its propped-up palm shoot," meaning that his opinion should be relied on, just as the palm tree relies on the rujba, the prop, with which it is supported.
2. rajjabtu al-shay'a, I honored the thing greatly — as if you made it a support you lean on for your affair. It is said "innahu la-murajjab," he is greatly honored. What al-Shaybānī related is close to this; he said: al-rajb is awe.
3. rajabtu al-amr, I stood in awe of the matter. The origin of this is the honoring already mentioned, and honoring goes back to what was said about the greatly-honored chief, as if he were the one relied and leaned upon. The senses branch one from another, as has been explained.
4. Rajab, the month, because they used to hold it in great honor; the sacred law has also honored it. When they added Shaʿbān to it, they said "the two Rajabs" (rajabān).

Among what falls outside this root is al-arjāb: the intestines. It is said that it has no singular of its own form. As for al-rawājib, they are the joints of the fingers; and it is also said that al-rājiba is the part of a finger-bone between the two knuckles, between the two joints.
رجح:
The letters rā', jīm and ḥā' are a single root indicating weightiness and increase. One says rajaḥa al-shay'u — it is rājiḥ, when it was weighty; it is from al-rujḥān. As for al-urjūḥa, it has been mentioned in its place.

1. arjaḥtu — when you gave a weighty, generous measure. In the hadith: "Weigh, and give generous weight."
2. nāwa'nā qawman fa-rajaḥnāhum — meaning we were weightier than them.
3. qawmun mirajīḥ — a people weighty in forbearance, singular mirjāḥ.
4. al-arājīḥ — it is said these are camels, for their swaying in their ambling gait as they walk; this belongs to the chapter, because they sway to and fro and their loads sway with them.
5. al-rajāḥ — some mentioned this is a woman heavy in the hips.

He recited, in a line of verse:
And among what I love: heavy-hipped women, full-figured.
رجد: The letters rā', jīm and dāl — one word has been mentioned under it. They said: al-irjād is al-irʿād, trembling, or making something tremble.
رجز:
The letters rā', jīm and zā' are a root pointing to unsteady shaking. Of that is *al-rajaz*: a disease that strikes camels in their hindquarters, so that when the she-camel gets up her thighs tremble.

And from this comes the derivation of *al-rajaz* in poetry, because it is cut short and unsteady. And *al-rijāza* is a cloth in which stones are placed, hung on one of the two sides of the camel-litter when it tips over; and it swings about. And *al-rijāza* is also wool hung on the litter to adorn it. As for *al-rijz*, which is punishment, and which is also the idol, in His words, whose praise is exalted: {and the rujz forsake} [al-Muddaththir: 5] — that is a case of letters exchanged, because its root is with sīn; and it has already been dealt with.
رجس: The letters rā', jīm and sīn are a root pointing to mixing. One says *hum fī marjūsatin min amrihim*, that is, in a confusion. And *al-rajs* is the sound of thunder, and that is because it rolls back and forth. And so too the rumbling of a camel is *rijs*. And a cloud is *rajjās*, and a camel is *rajjās*. And Ibn al-Aʿrābī reported: *hādhā rājisun ḥasan*, that is, a fine thunderer. Of this chapter is *al-rijs*, filth, because it is a smearing and a mixing.
رجع:
The letters rā', jīm and ʿayn are a great root, running steadily and following one measure, pointing to sending back and repeating.

You say rajaʿa yarjiʿu rujūʿan — when he returns. And rājaʿa al-rajulu imra'atahu — the man took his wife back — and that is al-rajʿa and al-rijʿa. Al-rujʿā is returning. Al-rājiʿa is the she-camel that is sold and another like her bought with her price; the second is the rājiʿa, and she has been urtujiʿat, got in exchange. In the hadith: "that the Prophet, God bless him and his family and give him peace, saw among the camels of the alms a big-humped she-camel, and asked about her, and the collector said: I got her in exchange for other camels." And the noun from that is al-rijʿa. A poet said:
Lean, hardy mares bent over the dust-coloured one — no exchanged beasts and no driven herd.

And you say aʿṭaytuhu kadhā thumma irtajaʿtuhu — I gave him such a thing then took it back — which is also sound in its meaning. The poet said, in a line of verse:
The saddle-cloths were shaken out for you as at a settling, and the towns took back their wanderers.

And an imra'a rājiʿ is a woman whose husband has died so that she has gone back to her people. Al-tarjīʿ in the voice is the repeating of it. Al-rajʿ is the beast's drawing back of its forelegs in going. Al-marjūʿ is what is got back of a thing. And al-marjūʿ is the answer to a message.

Ḥumayd said, in a line of verse:
Had any camping-ground ever given an answer back to one who asks, the ground would have pointed to me, or it would have spoken.

And arjaʿa al-rajulu yadahu fī kinānatihi — the man put his hand back into his quiver to take an arrow. And it is the saying of the Hudhalī:
He went to work heedlessly in the quiver, putting his hand back in.

Al-rijāʿ is the return of the birds after their season of departure. Al-rajīʿ is the cud, because its chewing is done over again.

Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
And a waste like the back of a shield, in which there is no fodder but the cud.

Al-rajīʿ of riding beasts is the one you bring back from journey to journey. And arjaʿat al-ibil — when they were lean and then grew fat and their state improved, and that is their returning to their first state.

As for al-rajʿ, it is the rain-giving, and it is the rain, in His word, mighty and majestic: {wa-l-samā'i dhāti al-rajʿ} [al-Ṭāriq: 11], and that is because it gives rain and pours, then returns and gives rain again. And a poet said:
And a barren year came with no rain in it, and no splitting green, that the herdsmen might milk.
رجف: The letters rā', jīm, and fā' are a root pointing to violent shaking. One says rajafat al-arḍu wa-l-qalbu [the earth trembled, and the heart]. The sea is rajjāf for its turbulence. Arjafa al-nāsu fī al-shay'i means the people plunged into rumour and grew agitated about it.
رجل:
The letters rā', jīm and lām: the greater part of their chapter points to the limb, which is the rijl, the leg, of everything that has one. And after that come words that stand apart from it.

So the greater part of the chapter is al-rijl: the leg of a person and of others. And al-rajl is the foot-soldiery. They were called rajl only because they walk on their legs. And al-rujjāl and al-rujālā are men on foot. And al-rajlān is the one going on foot, and the group is rajlā. He said, in a line of verse:
It is binding on me, if I meet Laylā alone, to make the pilgrimage to God's House on foot and barefoot.
Rajaltu al-shāt — I hung the sheep up by its leg. And one says: that was ʿalā rijl fulān — that is, in his time. And al-arjal among beasts is the one with one white leg while the rest of its legs are black; and it is disliked. And al-arjal is also the one with a great leg. And a rajul rajīl and dhū rujla — that is, strong at walking. And rajiltu arjalu rajalan. And tarajjaltu fī al-bi'r, when you climb down into it without being lowered. And irtajala al-faras irtijālan, when it mixes the fast walk with the amble. And arjaltu al-faṣīl — I left the young camel to walk with its mother, suckling whenever it wished. And one says rājil bayyin al-rujla.

And irtajaltu al-rajul — I took him by his leg. Al-Khalīl said: the rijl of the bow is its upper curved end. And rijl al-ṭā'ir, the bird's foot, is a kind of branding-iron. And rijl al-ghurāb, the crow's foot, is a kind of tying up of she-camels' teats. And a ḥarra rajlā' is a lava-field hard to walk in. And all of this goes back to the chapter we have mentioned.

And of what stands apart from that is al-rajul, the single one of the men; and sometimes they say of a woman al-rajula. And of what stands apart from the root also is al-rijla, which is the one called the foolish herb. They said: it was called foolish only because it grows nowhere but in a water-course. And some people said: rather al-rijal are water-courses, the singular of which is rijla.

As for their saying tarajjala al-nahār, when the day rose high, it is from the first chapter, as though a figure of speech — that is, it stood on its leg. And likewise rajjaltu al-shaʿr, combing the hair, is from this, as though it were made strong. And al-mirjal, the cauldron, is derived from this also, because when it is set up it is as though it were stood on a leg.

And of what stands apart from these roots is what al-Umawī related; he said: when sheep bear one after another they say wallidtuhā al-rujaylā'.
رجم:
The letters rā', jīm and mīm are a single root going back to a single sense, and it is [the throwing of] stones; then this is used by transfer.

From this is al-rijām, which is stones. One says rujima fulān — when he is struck with stones. Abū ʿUbayda and others said: al-rijām is a stone tied at the end of a rope and then let down into the well, so that the black mud is stirred about until it rises, and then that water is drawn up and the well is cleaned out. And al-rujma is the grave, and it is said that it is the stones gathered over the grave so that it may be raised in a ridge. And in the hadith: "Do not pile stones on my grave," that is, do not set stones over it; leave it level.

And some of them said: al-rijām is a stone tied to the end of the cross-bar of the bucket, so that it may go down faster.

And what is used by transfer from this is their saying rajamtu fulānan bi-l-kalām — when you abuse him. And it was mentioned in the interpretation of what God, mighty and majestic, related in the story of Abraham, peace be upon him: {if you do not desist I shall surely stone you} [Maryam: 46], that is, I shall surely abuse you; and it is as though, when he abuses him, he has stoned him with words, that is, struck him with them, as a man is stoned with stones. And some people said: la-arjumannaka means I shall surely kill you. And the meaning is close to the first.
رجن:
The letters rā', jīm and nūn are two roots: one, staying; the other, mixing.

The first: their saying rajana bi-l-makāni rujūnan — he stayed there. Al-rājin is the tame one among birds and other animals.

The second: their saying irtajana amruhum — their affair became mixed and confused. It is from their saying irtajanat al-zubdatu, when the butter spoiled during churning.
رجى:
The letters rā', jīm and the weak letter are two distinct roots: one points to hope, and the other to the side of a thing.

The first is al-rajā', which is hope. One says rajawtu al-amra arjūhu rajā'an, I hoped for the thing. Then this is broadened, so that fear is sometimes expressed by rajā' (hope). God Almighty said: {What is it with you, that you do not hope for majesty from God} [Nūḥ: 13], meaning, you do not fear His greatness. Some people say mā arjū meaning "I do not care," and they explained the verse on this basis, and they cited the saying of a poet:
"If bees sting him, he does not mind their sting... and he goes against them, working, among laboring swarms."
They said its meaning is: he did not care.
It is said of a mare, when her foaling draws near: qad arjat turjī irjā'an, she has drawn near to foaling.

As for the other, it is al-rajā, written short: the side of a well, and every side of a thing is a rajā. God, Majestic is His Glory, said: {and the angels are on its sides} [al-Ḥāqqa: 17]. The dual is al-rajawān. A poet said, in a line of verse:
"Let me not be thrown between the two sides, for I... am the least of people whom another could stand in for."

As for the hamzated form, it points to delay. One says arja'tu al-shay'a, I delayed the thing. God, Glorified is His Praise, said: {You may put off whom You wish of them} [al-Aḥzāb: 51]; and from this the Murji'a were named.
Al-Shaybānī said: arja'tu, I delayed it.
رح:
The letters rā' and ḥā' are a root denoting width and spreading out.

1. al-raḥaḥ — the flatness of a hoof or of the front of the foot.
2. wa'l arḥḥ — a mountain-goat with spread-out cloven hooves. Someone said, in a line of verse: Even if people's might were atop a smooth boulder that wearies out the flat-hoofed goat wearing anklets on its legs.
3. taraḥraḥat al-faras — the mare spread her legs apart to urinate.
4. 'aysh raḥrāḥ — an ample, spacious life.
5. Raḥraḥān — a place-name.
رحب:
The letters rā', ḥā' and bā' are a single, regular root indicating spaciousness. From this is al-ruḥb. A raḥb place is a spacious one. Their greeting "marḥaban" means: you have come to spaciousness — you are welcome. Al-ruḥbā is the widest of the ribs in the chest. Al-raḥīb is the big eater, because of the spaciousness of his belly. One says: the house raḥubat, or arḥabat, meaning it became spacious.

In the book of al-Khalīl: Naṣr ibn Sayyār said, "Does entering into obedience to al-Kirmānī make room enough for you?" meaning: does it make things spacious for you? He said this is an irregular word, a verb on the pattern fa'ula used transitively.

Al-raḥba is land often camped on, richly fertile. It is said to horses, urging them on: "arḥibī," meaning: move freely, make room.
رحض:
The letters rā', ḥā' and ḍād are a root that points to washing a thing.

1. raḥaḍtu al-thawb, I washed the garment. A poet said, in a line of verse:
"Deserts alike, as though their mirage were... cloth washed clean by the hands of women washing it."
2. al-mirḥāḍ — what is used for washing, a wash-place.
3. al-ruḥaḍā' — the sweat of fever, which follows the same pattern, as though it washed the body, that is, cleansed it.
رحق: The letters rā’, ḥā’ and qāf are a single word. It is al-raḥīq, one of the names for wine, said to be the finest of it.
رحل:
The letters rā', ḥā' and lām are a single root indicating setting off on a journey. One says: raḥala yarḥalu, a riḥla (he journeyed, a journey). A raḥīl camel is one strong enough for travel; al-riḥla is the setting-off.

As for al-raḥl in "this is the man's raḥl," his dwelling and shelter, this comes from the same root, because the word was said first of a traveler's gear, which stays with him when he travels — he loads it and unloads it when he stops. This is the origin; then it came to be said of a man's dwelling when settled, that it is his raḥl.

As for their calling a beast whose back has turned white "arḥal," this too comes from the same root, because it is compared to a mount that has a riḥāla (a light saddle) on its back. Al-riḥāla is the saddle. It is said metaphorically that so-and-so "saddles" so-and-so with what he dislikes, burdening him with hardship.

Al-muraḥḥal is a kind of Yemeni cloak that has images of travel-gear woven on it. One says: the camels arḥalat, meaning they grew fat after being lean and so became able to bear the journey. Al-riḥāl are also carpets made in al-Ḥīra.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
She spread out over it her cloaks and her carpets.

Al-rāḥila is the riding-camel, male or female. One says: so-and-so rāḥala so-and-so, meaning he helped him with his journey. He raḥḥalahu, meaning he moved him away from his place. He arḥalahu: he gave him a riding-camel. A murḥil man is one who has many riding-camels.

They say, as an insult: "O son of the one where the riders' saddle-gear was thrown down" — pointing by it to something shameful.
رحم:
The letters rā', ḥā' and mīm are a single root pointing to tenderness, kindness and pity. Of that one says raḥimahu yarḥamuhu — he had mercy on him, when he feels tenderness for him and turns to him kindly. And al-ruḥm, al-marḥama and al-raḥma are one in meaning. And al-raḥim is the tie of kinship; then the womb of the female was named raḥim from this, because from it comes what is pitied and felt tender towards — a child. And one says a ewe is raḥūm when her womb pains her after bearing; and she has raḥumat raḥāmatan and ruḥimat raḥman.

And al-Aṣmaʿī said: Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlā' used to recite the line of Zuhayr:
And whose nature is godliness, and whom God and mercy (al-ruḥum) guard from the evil of stumbling.
He said: and I have not heard this word except in this line. And he used to read: {and nearer in mercy} [al-Kahf: 81]. It is as though Abū ʿAmr held that al-ruḥum is mercy. And it is said that Mecca used to be called Umm Riḥm.
رحى:
The letters rā', ḥā' and the weak letter are a single root, and it is al-raḥā, the turning millstone. Then what is close to it in meaning branches from it.

1. raḥā al-ḥarb — the mill of war, that is, its thick of fighting.
2. raḥā al-saḥāb — the mill of the cloud, that is, its circling mass.
3. raḥā al-qawm — the chief of the people, so named because they turn around him as around a millstone.
4. al-raḥā — the round joint at a camel's breastbone, because it is round. A poet said, in a line of verse: "the mill of its breastbone is like the mill that grinds flour."

Al-Khalīl said: al-raḥā, and the dual al-raḥayān; and "three arḥin" for a small number; al-arḥā' for many; and al-arḥiya as though it were the plural of the plural.

5. al-arḥā' — the molar teeth, by way of comparison, as though they grind food like millstones.
6. raḥā is also said, by the same comparison, of a patch of ground that rises above what is around it, like a najfa, a raised mound.

Some philologists say: raḥā, and the dual raḥawān. They said: the Arabs say raḥati al-ḥayyatu tarḥū, the snake coiled, when it curls into a circle.
رخ: The letters rā' and khā' are a rare root, denoting softness. It is said al-rakhākh is ease and softness of life, and rakhkhā' land is soft and loose. It is also said — though this needs looking into — that al-rakhkh is the mixing of a drink.
رخد: The letters rā', khā' and dāl are a single word with no underlying pattern of its own. It is said: al-rikhwadd — one soft-boned, limp-limbed.
رخص:
The letters rā', khā' and ṣād are a root that points to softness, the opposite of hardness.

1. laḥm rakhṣ — tender meat, that is, soft meat.
2. al-rukhṣ — cheapness, the opposite of high price.
3. al-rukhṣa — a dispensation in a matter, the opposite of strictness.

And in the hadith: "God, Glorified is His Praise, loves that His dispensations be taken up, just as He loves that His firm commands be carried out."
رخف:
The letters rā', khā' and fā' are a small root that points to slackness and softness.

1. al-rakhfa — thin, soft butter.
2. arkhaftu al-ʿajīn, I added too much water to the dough until it went slack. From this one says rakhafa yarkhufu, it went slack.
3. ṣāra al-mā'u rukhfatan, the water turned into rukhfa, that is, thin mud.
4. al-rakhfa also names light, hollow stones.
رخل: The letters rā', khā' and lām are a single word, and it is al-rakhil: the female of the young of sheep, while the male is called ḥamal; al-rakhil is pluralized as rikhāl.
رخم:
The letters rā', khā' and mīm are a root that points to tenderness and compassion.

1. alqā fulānun ʿalā fulānin rakhmatahu, so-and-so cast his tender care upon so-and-so, said when he shows compassion and gentleness toward him.
2. al-kalām al-rakhīm — soft, gentle speech. Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
"Soft of speech, faint when she rises to stand... she smiles, showing teeth cool and gleaming."
3. al-rakhama — the bird called al-anūq, the Egyptian vulture. It is said to be so named for its tender care of its egg; it is said that its egg has never once been seen. This is what al-Kumayt meant in his saying, in a line of verse:
"A creature of two names, though its colors differ... called foolish, though its cunning is plain."
4. al-tarkhīm — a term the grammarians use for dropping something off the end of a name when calling out to someone, as in their saying yā Mālik, yā Māl; and yā Ḥārith, yā Ḥār, as though the name, once that part was dropped from it, became soft. Zuhayr said, in a line of verse:
"O Ḥārith, let me not be struck by some calamity from you... that no common man before me, nor any king, has met."

Among what falls outside this root is their saying "shātun rakhmā'," a ewe whose head has turned white.
رخو:
The letters rā’, khā’ and the weak final letter are a root pointing to softness and a slackness of mind. From this: shay’un rikhwun, with the rā’ carrying a kasra. Al-Khalīl said: rakhwun is also said, the two being alternate forms.

1. rakhiya yarkhā, and rakhuwa — it became soft, slack.
2. arkhat al-nāqa — the she-camel’s flank went slack.
3. farasun rikhwun — a horse easy-paced and flowing in its gait, as in Abū Dhu’ayb’s saying, in a line of verse: ‘so she is rikhw, dashing along.’
4. istarkhā bihi al-amr, and istarkhat bihi ḥāluhu — his affair settled into an easy, untroubled state.
5. tarākhā ‘ani al-amr — he held back from the matter and was slow about it.

From this root too, al-rukhā’, the gentle wind. God Most High said: {So We subjected to him the wind, flowing gently by his command wherever he directed} [Ṣād: 36].

Al-irkhā’, in a horse’s running, is not its hardest, most driven gallop. One says farasun mirkhā’, from khaylun marākh, a pace faster than a trot. Abū ‘Ubayd said: al-irkhā’ is letting the horse run at its own pace, without tiring it. And a loosened rope or rein is called urkhiyya, for whatever one has let go slack.
رد:
The letters rā' and dāl are a single root, regular in pattern, meaning the returning of a thing. You say raddadtu al-shay'a arudduhu raddan, I returned the thing.

1. al-murtadd — the apostate, so named because he returned himself to his disbelief.
2. al-ridd — the prop of a thing that holds it back, keeping it from falling and giving way.
3. al-mardūda — the divorced woman. From this comes the hadith in which he said to Surāqa ibn Mālik: "Shall I not tell you of the best charity? Your daughter, returned to you, with no one to provide for her but you."
4. shāt muridd, nāqa muridda — a ewe or she-camel whose udder has swelled with milk, as though she had had no milk and it was returned to her, or she herself returned her milk. Someone said, in a line of verse: she walks, from the swelling of milk, with the gait of the milk-laden.
5. amr lā rādda lahu — a matter with nothing to be gained back from it, no benefit in it.
6. al-radda — a recession in the chin, as though it were pushed back behind itself.
7. al-radda — an ugliness in the face along with some beauty; one says "in her face there is a radda," meaning something there turns the gaze away from her.
8. al-mutaraddid — a person of compact build, as though part of him were folded back onto part.
9. al-mardūda — the razor, it is said, though this needs looking into, because it folds back into its handle.
10. nahr muridd — a river full of water, derived from the ridda of the ewe and the she-camel.
11. rajul muridd — a man whose bachelorhood has grown long, from the same origin, as though his seed had pooled in his loins. Someone said, in a line of verse: she saw a young man in whose loins the water of youth had pooled up, at the very peak of its vigor.
ردب: The letters rā', dāl and bā' are not a root. They call a roof-tile al-irdaba. And al-irdabb is a huge measure used by the people of Egypt.
ردج:
The letters rā', dāl and jīm are not a root. Even so, they say that al-radaj is what a foal expels from its belly the moment it is born. A line of verse is recited:
"She keeps radaj-dung ready in her tent... for the day a suitor should ever come to her."
ردح:
The letters rā', dāl and ḥā' — Ibn Durayd established a root sense for it. He said: its root sense is one thing piling up upon another.

1. katība radāḥ — a squadron thick with horsemen. He also said: it is said that the root sense of al-radāḥ is a great, spreading tree.
2. From this: "so-and-so is radāḥ," meaning generous, abundant in provision.
3. al-radāḥ also names a woman heavy in the hips.
4. radaḥtu al-bayta and ardaḥtuhu, from al-rudḥa, a piece added into a tent, or an extra length added to its poles. Al-Aṣmaʿī recited a line of verse: "a tent of dooms, whose supports have been extended."
5. Ibn Durayd said: radaḥtu al-bayta, said when you plastered mud over it.
ردخ: The letters rā', dāl and khā' are not a root. Even so, they related from al-Khalīl that al-radkh is al-shadkh, crushing.
ردس:
The letters rā', dāl and sīn are a small root that points to striking one thing with another.

1. radastu al-arḍa bi'l-ṣakhrati wa-ghayrihā, I struck the ground with the rock or something else.
2. al-mirdās — a great rock, on the pattern mifʿāl from radastu.
3. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: mā adrī ayna radasa, I do not know where he went off to, meaning he went away.

The underlying pattern is one, because of one who goes off it is said: he went off into the land, and he struck out into the land.
ردع:
The letters rā', dāl and ʿayn are a single root that points to holding back and throwing down.

1. radaʿtuhu ʿan hādhā al-amri fa-rtadaʿa, I held him back from this matter, and he was held back.
2. al-radīʿ — one thrown to the ground. Ibn al-Aʿrābī related this.
3. al-murtadiʿ, of arrows — one whose shaft shatters when it strikes the target.
4. al-murtadiʿ also names one smeared with something. Ibn Muqbil said, in a line of verse: "sweat runs over its two brocade-like cheeks, smeared."

Here al-murtadiʿ means smeared; and it is said that it is from al-radʿ, and al-radʿ is blood — some philologists said this.

5. From this it is said of a slain man: "he rode his own blood." The origin of all this is what was said, that al-radʿ is throwing down, and when someone is thrown down, he is smeared with his own blood, if there is blood there. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: "he rode his own blood" is said when he fell face-down.
6. al-rudāʿ — pain throughout the whole body; this fits the root, because the sick person is as though thrown down. A poet said, in a line of verse:
"Oh my grief, my body-ache has returned to me... and Lubnā's parting was like a deception."
ردغ:
The letters rā', dāl and ghayn are a small root that points to slackness and disorder.

1. al-radgh — water and mud.
2. al-radīgh — the foolish man, since a fool's judgment is disordered.

Among what falls outside this root is al-marādigh: the area between the neck and the collarbone.
ردف:
The letters rā', dāl and fā' are a single, consistent root indicating one thing following another.

1. al-tarāduf — succession, one thing following another.
2. al-radīf — the one who rides behind you on the same mount.
3. The buttocks are called rid[f], from this.

It is said: "a matter befell them, and something greater radifa [followed] after it" — something greater than the first followed it.

4. al-ridāf — the place on a mount where the rider behind sits.
5. "This is a horse that lā yurādifu" — it cannot carry a rider behind it.
6. ardāf al-nujūm — the stars that follow one another in succession.

It is said: "we came to so-and-so and irtadafnāhu" — we seized him.

7. al-radīf — the star that rises in the east just as its counterpart-star sinks in the west.
8. ardāf al-mulūk — in pre-Islamic times, those who would stand in for kings and succeed them.
9. al-ridfān — night and day.
10. In a verse of Labīd, "al-ridf" is the ship's pilot.

"This is a matter with no ridf" means it carries no further consequence.

Al-Aṣmaʿī said: taʿāwanū ʿalayhi, tarādafū, and tarāfadū all mean the same — they helped one another.

11. "The locusts rādafa" [swarmed one after another]. al-murādafa — the male mounting the female.

Abū Ḥātim said: al-radīf is one who brings his gambling-arrow after one or two players have already won, asking them to let his arrow join theirs.

Al-Aṣmaʿī said: al-rudāfā are the camel-drivers who sing to urge the camels on, because when one tires, another takes his place.

Al-Rāʿī said, in a line of verse:
A soft young woman, one of those who at mid-morning hear the rudāfā's verse in soothing song.

12. al-rawāfid — the young shoots that grow stacked upon a palm tree.
ردك: The letters rā', dāl and kāf are not a root, but they say: khalqun murawdak, meaning plump of build. A poet said, in a line of verse: "she rose, showing you her plump form."
ردم:
The letters rā’, dāl and mīm are a single root pointing to closing up a breach.

1. radamtu al-bāba wa-l-thulmata — I closed up the door and the breach. Al-radm is the verbal noun, and al-radm is also the noun for the thing itself.
2. al-thawb al-muraddam — a worn garment patched over.

As for the line: ‘Have the poets left any patched-over place, or did you recognise the abode only by guesswork?’ — on the reading of whoever transmits it this way, it is said that this means words are stuck one onto another, as patches are.

3. ardamat ‘alayhi al-ḥummā — the fever settled on him and persisted without let-up; one says wirdun murdim [an unrelenting bout of thirst] and saḥābun murdim, a cloud that pours without stopping.
ردن:
The letters rā', dāl and nūn — this is a chapter whose words scatter widely; scarcely two of its words meet under one single pattern, so it is written as it stands, without addressing the derivation of its root or its underlying pattern.

1. al-rudn — the front part of a sleeve. One says ardantu al-qamīṣa, I put a rudn on the shirt; the plural is ardān. A poet said, in a line of verse: "and ʿAmra, of the noblewomen among women... her sleeves give off musk."
2. They say al-radan is silk-brocade, as in al-Aʿshā's saying, in a line of verse: "I wore her out and toyed with her... over flat, bare ground like a cloak of radan-silk."
3. al-rumḥ al-rudaynī — the rudaynī spear, named after a woman called Rudayna.
4. Of a camel whose red color has a tinge of yellow mixed in, it is said: "aḥmar rādinī," rādinī-red; a she-camel of this color is rādiniyya.
5. They say al-mirdan is the spindle with which radan-silk is spun, and this is not far-fetched.
6. It is said that al-rādin is saffron. A line of verse is recited: "and she took some rādin and turmeric."
7. It is related from al-Farrā': radina jilduhu radanan, his skin shriveled.
8. al-urdunn — heavy drowsiness. A poet said, in a line of verse: "a heavy drowsiness has seized me." No verb has been heard formed from urdunn.
9. Quṭrub said: al-radan also names the caul that comes out with a child from its mother's belly; the Arabs say "hādhā midraʿu al-radan," this is the garment of the caul.
10. He said: al-radn — stacking up. One says radantu al-matāʿa, I stacked up the goods.
11. He said: al-radn also names the sound of weapons striking against one another.
رده:
The letters rā', dāl and hā' are a small root that points to a hollow in a rock or something else.

1. They said: al-radha — a hollow in smooth rock where rainwater collects; the plural is ridāh.

But what is related from al-Khalīl differs from this; he said: al-radah is something like rough hillocks thick with stones, the singular being radha. He said these are the hills of rough stony ground. Ru'ba said, in a line of verse: "after the piled-up, stony hills."
ردى:
The letters rā', dāl and yā' are a single root that points to throwing, or mutual throwing, and what resembles that.

1. radaytuhu bi'l-ḥijārati ardīhi, I threw stones at him; the stone used for this is mirdāh. al-rady covers three uses that go back to this pattern: the first is radā the stone, throwing it; the second, radā al-farasu, the horse galloped fast; and radat al-jāriyatu, said when a girl lifted one of her legs and hopped on the other, is the third. All of this goes back to the sense of throwing oneself.
2. al-radayān — the running of a donkey between its stall and its rolling-place.
3. al-radā — destruction; one says radiya yardā when he perished; ardāhu Allāhu, God destroyed him.
4. al-taraddī — plunging headlong into a chasm. One says "radiya fī al-bi'r" just as one says "taraddā," he fell into the well. Abū Zayd said this.
5. It is said: "mā adrī ayna radā," I do not know where he went off to; this belongs to the root, its sense being: I do not know where he flung himself.
6. al-radāh — a rock, plural al-radā. A poet said, in a line of verse: "a stud camel among she-camels near birth, like a rock crashing down." When they call a she-camel "mirdāh," they are only comparing her to the rock.
7. rādaytu ʿan al-qawm, said when you threw missiles in defense of the people, on their behalf.

As for Ṭufayl's saying, in a line of verse:
"He is coaxed at the bit's crosspiece, as though... he were being coaxed up the rungs of a stripped palm-trunk,"
this does not belong to this root, because it is a transposition of letters; its meaning is "he is coaxed, persuaded." It has been mentioned in its proper place.

Among what falls outside this root is al-ridā', the cloak that is worn — it is not known what it is derived from, nor under what pattern it falls. It is said "so-and-so is good in his ridya," from the wearing of the cloak. Also outside this root is their saying "ardā ʿalā al-khamsīn," said when someone exceeded fifty years.

As for the hamzated form, it is two very distinct words. One says arda'tu, I ruined something; and radu'a al-shay'u, the thing became bad, so it is radī', bad.
