4. al-murtakiz — dry grass whose leaves have broken up and blown away; its meaning is that what has gone of it has gone, and what remains has stayed fixed [irtakaza].
ركس:
The letters rā', kāf and sīn are a single root, and it is turning a thing on its head and turning its beginning back into its end. God, exalted be His praise, said: {And God turned them back for what they had earned} [al-Nisā': 88], meaning He returned them to their disbelief. One says irtakasa fulānun fī amrin qad kāna najā minhu — so-and-so fell back into a matter he had escaped. al-rakūsiyya — a people who hold a religion between the Christians and the Sabians.

And the Messenger of God, peace and blessings upon him and his family, was brought stones for cleansing, and among them was a piece of dung; he threw it away and said: "It is rikS [filth]." The meaning of that is that it had turned back from being food into something else.
ركض:
The letters rā', kāf and ḍād are a single root indicating forward movement, or setting something moving.

A man is said to "rakaḍa his mount" when he strikes it with his two legs to make it go forward. This grew so common that they came to say "the horse rakaḍa" [it ran], though that is not the original sense.

1. irtikāḍ al-ṣabī — the stirring of an infant in its mother's womb.
2. Al-Khalīl said: rakḍ is also used of a bird beating its wings in flight.
3. "The she-camel arkaḍat" — her young stirs inside her.

In a hadith about the blood of prolonged bleeding [istiḥāḍa]: "it is a rakḍa from Satan" — meaning a thrust, a push.
ركع:
The letters rā', kāf and 'ayn are a single root that points to a bending in a man and in other things. One says raka'a al-rajul when he bends over, and everything that bends is rāki'. Labīd said, in a line of verse:
I tell the tales of the generations that have gone by; I creep along as though, whenever I stand, I were bowing.

In the hadith there is mention of the bowed shaykhs, al-mashāyikh al-rukka', meaning those bent over with age. Bowing in the prayer, al-rukū', is from this. Then the word was turned about, so that the one who prays was called rāki', and the one who prostrates himself in thanks was called rāki'. God Almighty said about Dāwūd, peace be upon him: {so he asked forgiveness of his Lord and fell down bowing and turned in repentance} [Ṣād: 24]. And He said in another place: {and prostrate yourself and bow with those who bow} [Āl 'Imrān: 43]. Some people said its meaning is: prostrate yourself, that is, pray; and bow with those who bow, that is, give thanks to God, exalted be His praise, along with the thankful.

Ibn Durayd said: al-ruk'a is a hollow in the ground; it is a usage of Yemen.
ركل:
The letters rā', kāf and lām are a root pointing to a kind of striking with the foot.

1. *rakalahu* and *rafasahu bi-rijlihi* — he kicked him with his foot.
2. *markalā al-faras* — the two spots on the horse's flanks where the rider strikes with his two feet.
3. *tarakkala 'alā al-shay' bi-rijlihi* — he trod or stamped on the thing with his foot.
4. *tarakkala al-ḥāfir bi-misḥātihi* — the digger struck his spade with his foot, to drive it into the ground.

Al-Akhṭal said, in a line of verse:
She grew up, and in her lap grew a son of the city, who spends his day treading down on his spade.

5. *al-kadīd* — ground that has been trodden and pounded, is called *al-murakkal*.
ركم:
The letters rā', kāf and mīm are a single root indicating the heaping-up of a thing. You say "rakamtu the thing": I threw part of it upon part of it, piling it up.

1. saḥāb murtakim, and rukām — cloud that is piled up, massed cloud.
2. al-rukma — gathered clay or mud.
3. murtakam al-ṭarīq — the trodden track of the road, because travellers pile together upon it.
ركن:
The letters rā', kāf and nūn are a single root indicating strength. Rukn of a thing is its strongest side. "He takes refuge in a strong rukn" means: in might and protection. From this chapter: rakantu ilayhi arkanu (I leaned on him) — a rare verb pattern that takes no guttural letter. So-and-so is rakīn, meaning dignified and steady. Al-mirkan is a wash-tub. One says: a rakīn mountain, meaning it has high peaks.

"Rakantu ilayhi" means I inclined towards him; this belongs to the same root, because he settled toward him and grew firm with him. Al-Khalīl said: [the verb runs] rakana yarkanu, a raknan. In the dialect of the lower tribes of Muḍar: rakina yarkanu. It is also said rakina yarkunu, though this is doubtful. Abū Zayd related: rakina yarkanu.

A she-camel is "murakkanat al-ḍar'" (udder), meaning her udder is swollen, as if it were a rukn.
ركو:
The letters rā', kāf and the weak letter [the final wāw] carry three origin senses: the first, carrying one thing upon another and joining it to it; the second, putting a thing right; the third, a vessel for a thing.

As for the first:
1. *rakawtu 'alā al-ba'īr al-ḥiml* — I doubled the load I put on the camel.
2. *rakawtu 'alayhi al-amr wa-l-dhanb* — I laid the matter, or the offence, upon him, I burdened him with it.
3. *anā murtakin 'alā kadhā* — I am relying on such a thing. "I have no one to rely on but you."
4. *arkayta 'alayya dhanban lam udhnibhu* — al-Farrā' related this: you laid on me a sin I did not commit.
5. *arkaytu ilā fulān* — I took refuge with so-and-so.
6. *arkinī ilā kadhā* — give me respite until such a time, said of a debt owed.
7. *rakawtu 'anhum baqiyyata yawmī* — I remained with them for the rest of my day.

As for putting a thing right:
8. *al-markuww* — the long trough, also said to mean the thing that has been mended.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
A water-drawer stood at the trough, filling it.

9. *rakawtu al-shay'* — when you set it right and mended it.

Suwayd ibn Kurā' said, in a line of verse:
Leave alone people who have spared you their concerns, but your own affair, if you do not mend it, only grows worse.

That is: if you do not put it right.

10. *arkaytu li-fulānin shay'an* — I prepared a thing for him.

As for the other origin sense:
11. *al-rakwa* — a small leather water-vessel, well known; from it comes *al-rakiyy*, a well, because it is, as it were, a container for what is in it.
رم:
The letters rā' and mīm cover four roots: two opposed to each other, and two more opposed to each other. Of the first pair, one is the mending and setting right of a thing, the other is its wearing out. Of the second pair, one is silence, the other its opposite.

Of the first of the first two roots: al-ramm is the mending of a thing; you say ramamtuhu arummuhu, I mended it.

1. aramma al-ba'īr — the camel or other animal grew fat, yurimmu irmāman. Someone said, in a line of verse: He satirized them when his bones had grown fat again ... though had he lived among the Bedouin he would have died of leanness.
2. al-murimm — Abū Zayd said this is the she-camel that has some marrow-fat in her, which is called al-rimm.
3. al-rimm — moist earth, because part of it clings to part. They say: "his is al-ṭimm and al-rimm" — al-ṭimm being the sea, al-rimm the moist earth.

The other of the first two roots is their saying: ramma al-shay'u, when it wore out and decayed.

1. al-ramīm — decayed bones. God Most High said: {He said, who gives life to the bones when they are decayed?} [Yā Sīn: 78]. Likewise al-rimma means decayed bones. "The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, forbade cleaning oneself after relieving oneself with dung or with decayed bone."
2. al-rumma — a worn-out rope. Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse: disheveled, with the last remnant of a worn halter-rope still on him. From this comes the saying "hand it over to him birummatihi" (with its whole rope, i.e. entirely). It is said the origin is that a man sold another a camel with a rope on its neck, and it was said to him: hand it over to him with its rope; this became common in speech, so it was said of anyone who handed something over to another in full: he handed it to him birummatihi, meaning all of it. They said this is the sense al-A'shā intended when he said to the wine-seller, in a line of verse: I said to him, give me this ... for a dark-brown she-camel, led by her rope. He means: sell me this wine for a she-camel, complete with her rope, that is, the whole of her.
3. al-shātu tarummu al-ḥashīsh bi-maramatihā — the sheep gathers grass from the ground with its muzzle. In the hadith cattle are mentioned: "they graze from every kind of tree."

Of the other two roots, the first is from al-irmām, which is silence; one says aramma irmāman, he fell silent. The other is their saying mā tarmarama, meaning he did not move his mouth to speak — this is what Aws said, in a line of verse: and one who wonders at what he sees of our groaning ... yet had war struck him with its hind legs, he would not have made a sound.

As for their saying, "there is neither ḥumm nor rumm from that matter," its meaning is that nothing stands between it and happening; al-rumm here is not a root-word, being a mere echo-word added for rhyme. And they say — if it is correct — na'ja rammā', meaning a white ewe; this departs from the roots that have been mentioned.
رمأ:
As for the letters rā', mīm and hamza, that is a separate root of its own, distinct from the one before it, and it is little used.

1. *rama'at al-ibil tarma'u rumū'an wa-ram'an* — the camels stayed among pasture and herbage.
2. *rama'a fulān fī banī fulān* — so-and-so settled among the tribe of so-and-so.
3. *arama'ati al-akhbār* — the reports became confused, uncertain.
4. *muramma'āt al-akhbār* — the false parts of reports.
رمث:
The letters rā', mīm and thā' are a single root pointing to mending a thing and joining part to part.

1. *ramathtu al-shay'* — I mended it.

Abū Duwād said, in a line of verse:
And a brother whose worn cloak I mended, and whom I counselled faithfully in war.

2. *al-ramath* — timbers bound together and ridden upon, a raft.

In the hadith: "We ride rafts of ours upon the sea" — *armāth* being the plural of *ramath*.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
From my love for Buthayna I wished that we were together on a raft at sea, with no wealth of ours.

3. *al-rimth* — a pasture-plant grazed by camels, [named] because its growth clings together part to part.
4. *ibil ramitha* and *ramāthā* — camels that have eaten rimth and sickened from it.
5. *al-ramath* — also, the remainder of milk left in the udder, because that too is gathered together.
رمج:
The letters rā', mīm and jīm are not a root, though there is something in them that can be accepted and relied on. They do say:

1. *rammaja al-athar bi-l-turāb* — he covered the track over with dust.
2. *rammaja al-suṭūr* — he spoiled, blotted out the lines [of writing].
رمح:
The letters rā’, mīm and ḥā’ are a single word, from which other forms are then derived. The word is al-rumḥ, the spear, well known; plural rimāḥ and armāḥ.

1. al-simāk al-rāmiḥ — a star, named after a star that precedes it as though it were its spear.
2. ramaḥathu al-dābba — the animal kicked him; this too is from this root, because its striking him with its leg is like the spearman’s thrust with his spear.
3. ramaḥa al-jundub — the locust struck the pebbles with its foreleg.
4. al-rammāḥ — one who makes spears; his craft is al-rimāḥa.
5. al-rāmiḥ — one who thrusts with the spear.
6. al-rāmiḥ — also, one who carries it.
7. For the bahmā grass, when it grows too tough for grazing animals to eat, one says: qad akhadhat rimāḥahā — it has taken up its spears.

As a poet said, in a line of verse:
the days when my camels did not take up their weapons against me, neither the old ones among them nor the young.
رمخ: The letters rā', mīm and khā' amount to nothing. It is said that *al-rimkh* is a tree.
رمد:
The letters rā’, mīm and dāl are three roots: one is an illness among illnesses, another a colour among colours, and the third a kind of running.

The first: al-ramad, inflammation of the eye. One says ramida yarmadu ramadan; the sufferer is ramid or armad.

1. al-ramd (with the mīm quiescent) — destruction, ruin, as a poet said: like the remnants of ‘Ād, when ruin covered them.
2. ramadnā al-qawma narmuduhum — we came upon the people to destroy them.

The second: al-ramād, ashes, well known; when it is at its finest it is called rimdid, named for its colour.

3. rammadat al-nāqa tarmīdan — the she-camel, at birth, left only a little milk; this is said by comparison to a colour that comes over her udder.
4. al-armad — anything dust-grey with a dullness in it, from the colour of ash; from this a kind of gnat is called rumd.

Abū Wajza said, describing a hunter, in a line of verse:
his neighbour by night is the viper, and his night-companions are grey gnats leaving on him a sore like mange.

5. al-armidā’ (on the pattern af‘ilā’) — ashes.
6. al-murammad, of roasted meat — that which is buried to cook slowly in the embers. In the proverb: Your brother roasted the meat until, once it was cooked through, he buried it in ash.

As for their saying ‘āmu al-ramāda, the Year of Ashes, some say it was a year of drought that brought ruin [ramd] upon the people; others say it was so named because the drought turned the earth ash-coloured. Abū Ḥātim said: mā’un ramid — water that is stagnant and gone bad.

The third root: al-irmidād, running hard. One says: irmadda al-ẓalīm — the male ostrich ran fast.
رمز:
The letters rā’, mīm and zā’ are a single root pointing to movement and stirring.

1. katībatun rammāza — a battalion that ripples and surges at its edges.
2. ḍarabahu fa-mā irma’azza — he struck him and he did not stir.
3. irtamaza — also, it moved.

They say al-rāmūz is the sea; I take it this occurs in the poetry of Hudhayl.
رمس:
The letters rā', mīm and sīn are a single root pointing to covering and concealing.

1. *al-rams* — dust, earth.
2. *al-riyāḥ al-rawāmis* — the winds that stir up dust and so bury tracks.
3. *ramastu 'alā fulānin al-khabar* — I concealed the news from him.
4. *ramastu al-rajul* and *armastuhu* — I buried the man.
رمش:
The letters rā', mīm and shīn are not from the pure language, nor from what appears in sound, reliable poetry. Yet they do say:

1. *al-ramash* — a curling in the eyelashes, and redness in the eyelids.
2. *ramashahu bi-l-ḥajar* — sometimes said for: he threw a stone at him.
3. *ramashat al-ghanam tarmushu* — related from al-Shaybānī: the sheep grazed a little.
4. *al-ramash* — also, a whiteness that appears in the fingernails of the young.
5. *arḍ ramshā'* — related from al-Liḥyānī: barren land.
رمص:
The letters rā', mīm and ṣād are a small root pointing to casting off discharge.

1. *ramaṣati al-'ayn* — the eye discharged what comes from it during inflammation.
2. Ibn al-Sikkīt said one says: "May God disfigure a mother who *ramaṣat* with him," meaning bore him — if sound, this follows the same pattern, the child being likened to a discharge that is cast off.
3. *ramaṣati al-dajāja* — the hen dropped its dung.

In this chapter there is a further usage pointing to setting right and to good:

4. *ramaṣtu baynahum* — I made peace between them.
5. *ramaṣa Allāhu muṣībatahu yarmuṣuhā ramṣan* — God set his affliction right, mended it.
رمض:
The letters rā’, mīm and ḍād are a consistent root pointing to sharpness in something, whether from heat or otherwise.

1. al-ramaḍ — the heat of stones from the intensity of the sun’s heat.
2. arḍun ramiḍa — ground whose stones are hot.

Some have said that Ramaḍān is derived from the intensity of heat, because when they carried over the names of the months from the old language, they named them after the seasons, and Ramaḍān coincided with the days of the ramaḍ, the burning heat. Its plurals are Ramaḍānāt and Armiḍā’.

3. armaḍahu al-amr — the matter distressed him; ramiḍa lil-amr — he was distressed over the matter.
4. ramiḍa — also, when the ramḍā’ [sun-scorched ground] burned him.
5. ramaḍtu al-laḥma ‘alā al-raḍf — I cooked the meat on heated stones, when you bring it to done.
6. sikkīnun ramīḍ — a sharpened knife; anything sharp is ramīḍ; and I have said ramaḍtuhu, I sharpened it.
7. ramiḍat al-ghanam — the sheep grazed in intense heat until their livers became ulcerated.
8. fulānun yatarammaḍu al-ẓibā’ — so-and-so hunts gazelles in the heat, when he follows and drives them until their legs give way from the scorching ground, then takes them.
9. irtamaḍa baṭnuhu — his stomach went bad, as though some ailment were burning it.

As for their saying: I came to so-and-so and did not find him, so rammaḍtu tarmīḍan — meaning to wait for him — it is possible that this strays from the root, and it is possible that the mīm stands in place of a bā’, as though it were rabbaḍat, from rabaḍa, to crouch down.
رمط: The letters rā', mīm and ṭā' are not a root. They call what gathers of the 'urfuṭ and other thorn-trees a *ramṭ*. And sometimes they say *ramaṭtu al-rajul*, when you found fault with him — a *ramṭ*. There is doubt about this.
رمع:
The letters rā', mīm and 'ayn are a root pointing to agitation and movement.

1. *al-rammā'a* — the part of a person, on a baby's fontanelle, that pulses.
2. *al-rama'ān* — agitation, trembling.
3. *rama'a anf al-rajul yarma'u rama'ānan* — a man's nose twitched, when it moved from anger.
4. "May God disfigure a mother who *rama'at* with him," meaning bore him.
5. *al-yarma'* — thin white stones that glint in the sun.
6. *al-rāmi'* — if sound, one who lowers his head then raises it.
7. *al-rumā'* — a change [pallor, agitation] in the face. The whole chapter is one single sense.
8. *al-murammi'a* — ruin, destruction.
رمغ: The letters rā', mīm and ghayn have no root at all, apart from something Ibn Durayd brings, from *ramaghtu al-shay'*: when you rubbed or kneaded it with your hand, as with a hide or the like.
رمق:
The letters rā', mīm and qāf are a root pointing to weakness and scantness.

1. *tarammaqa al-rajul al-mā'* — he sipped it, sip after sip.
2. *murammaq al-'aysh* — one whose livelihood is meagre.
3. *ramāq* — "his life is nothing but ramāq," meaning just enough to keep the last breath going.
4. *al-ramaq* — what remains of the soul, or of breath.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
People are only ever in scant means or in plenty, and life is nothing but alternation and flow.

5. "The goats' udders have swelled, so ramiq, ramiq" — they used to say this meaning: drink its milk little by little, since goats let down milk some days before giving birth.
6. *al-tarmīq* — work a man does without doing it well.
7. *ḥabl armāq* — a rope that is weak. One says *irmāqqa irmiqāqan* [it grew weak, frayed].
رمك:
The letters rā', mīm and kāf carry two roots: one, a colour among colours; the other, staying in a place.

The first:
1. *al-rumka* — a colour among the colours of camels, a duskier grey than *al-wurqa*.
2. *jamal armak* — a dusky-grey camel; from it derives *al-rāmik* [a black perfume-base].
3. *al-ramaka* — the female of the common pack-horses.

The other root:
4. *ramaka bi-l-makān* — he stayed in the place, so he is *rāmik*.
رمل:
The letters rā', mīm and lām are a root pointing to thinness in a thing whose parts cling closely to one another.

1. *ramaltu al-ḥaṣīr* and *armaltu* — I wove the mat loosely, thinly.

A poet said, in a line of verse: "As if it were the weave of a spider spun thin."

2. *al-ramal* — by likeness to that: light, scant rain, plural *armāl*.
3. *al-raml* — close to this chapter: sand, which is fine-grained.
4. *tarammala al-qatīl bi-damihi* — the slain man was smeared with his own blood; this follows the same pattern as what we mentioned.
5. *al-ramal* — a brisk pace, resembling a run or a walk that lacks steadiness.
6. *al-murmil* — one who has no provisions with him, so named for one of two reasons: either the thinness of his condition, or because his poverty makes him cling to bare sand.
7. *al-armal* — is like *al-murmil*.

Jarīr said, in a line of verse:
These widows — you have seen to their needs — but who is there for the need of this needy man?
رمن:
The letters rā', mīm and nūn form a single word, and it is the pomegranate.

1. al-rummānatān — two hills in the land of the tribe of ʿAbs.

A poet said, in a line of verse [only this half is given]:
At the abode by the two Rummānas, she turns aside.
رمى:
The letters rā', mīm and the weak letter [the final yā'] are a single root, and it is casting a thing away. Derivation and metaphor then build on it.

1. *ramaytu al-shay' armīhi* — I threw the thing.
2. *rimmiyyā*, on the pattern *fi''īlā* — there was mutual throwing (a skirmish) between them.
3. *armaytu 'alā al-mi'a* — I went beyond a hundred.

If it is asked what the sense of this last word is, the answer is: when a thing goes beyond another, it has cast itself forward to the point it reached.

4. *ramaytu*, in the sense of *armaytu*.
5. *al-mirmāt* — the rounded arrowhead, named so because it is shot with.
6. *al-marmāt* — the cloven hoof of a sheep. In the hadith: "If one of them were invited to two marmātayn [two sheep's trotters]..."
7. *al-ramiyya* — the game that is shot at.
8. *al-ramiyy* — a cloud heavy with rain, said to be so called because it forms and then pieces of cloud are cast toward it from here and there until they gather together.

Al-Khalīl said: *ramā yarmī*, with the verbal nouns *rimāya*, *ramy* and *rimā'*. Ibn al-Sikkīt said: *kharajtu atarammā* — I went out to shoot at targets.

9. *armaytu al-ḥajar min yadī irmā'an* — I let the stone fall from my hand.
10. *aramā Allāhu laka* — Abū 'Ubayda said this means: God supported you and worked things for you.
11. *al-rammā'* — increase; we have said its derivation belongs to this root, because it is a thing that casts itself upward.
رن:
The letters rā' and nūn are a single root, denoting a sound.

1. al-irnān — a ringing sound.
2. al-ranna and al-ranīn — the cry of one who grieves.
3. arannat al-qaws — the bow rang out when the archer released the string from it. Someone said, in a line of verse: it rings out a ringing whenever he twangs the string — meaning, when he twangs the bowstring.
4. al-mirnān — the bow, because it has a ringing sound.
5. al-ranan — a small creature, it is said, that lives in water and cries out in the days of summer. Someone said, in a line of verse: nor the wild doves, nor did the ranan cry out for it.

This is the bulk of the chapter, and it follows a regular pattern. A word has been reported whose sense I do not know, and it departs from the pattern if it is correct — I have not heard it myself directly. They said: Jumādā al-Ūlā used to be called Runnā, on the pattern of ḥublā. This is something that ought not to be relied upon.
رنب:
The letters rā', nūn and bā' are a single word, not derived from anything and nothing is derived from it by rule, but other things are likened to it.

1. *al-arnab* — the hare, well known.
2. *arnabat al-anf* — the tip of the nose, likened to it.
3. *arnabat al-raml* — a curved ridge of sand, likened to it.
4. *kisā' mu'arnab* — a cloak whose spun thread is mixed with hare fur.
5. *arḍ mu'arniba* — land abounding in hares.
6. *al-arnab* — also, a kind of plant.
رنح:
The letters rā', nūn and ḥā' are a root pointing to swaying.

1. *tarannaḥa* — he swayed, as a drunken man sways.
2. *runniḥa fulān* — weakness overtook his bones, so he is *murannaḥ*.

Al-Ṭirimmāḥ said, in a line of verse:
Your closest helper — upon him is a howdah-borne woman who reels, when you weep, with the reeling of one made faint.
رنخ:
The letters rā', nūn and khā' are not a root, unless it is something belonging to letter-substitution, carried over on the pattern of the chapter before it, in which case it points to feebleness and weakness.

1. *al-rānikh* — the languid, weak one.
2. *ranakha* — he grew weak.
3. *rannakhtu al-rajul tarnīkhan* — I subdued him, humbled him, so he is *murannakh*.
رند:
The letters rā', nūn and dāl are a small root pointing to a kind of plant.

1. *al-rand* — a fragrant tree among the trees of the wilderness.

'Alī ibn Ibrāhīm told us, from 'Alī ibn 'Abd al-'Azīz, from Abū 'Ubayd, from al-Aṣma'ī, who said: sometimes they called fragrant wood "rand", meaning what is burned as incense. He denied that al-rand is myrtle. Al-Khalīl said: al-rand is a kind of tree, said to be myrtle.

A line of verse: "upon a branch of rand, fresh in growth."

As for the saying of al-Ja'dī, in a line of verse:
[Women] fragrant, nibbling at twigs of rand, with sweet teeth like the thorns of the sayāl tree —

this shows that al-rand is not myrtle.
رنع: The letters rā', nūn and ʿayn are one sound word, and it is al-marnaʿa, for voices that are play and amusement. Al-Farrā' said this. And Abū Ḥātim said: ranaʿa al-ḥarth, when the crop's water is withheld from it and it shrivels. There is doubt about this.
رنف:
The letters rā', nūn and fā' are a small root pointing to the side of a thing.

1. *al-rānifa* — the side of the fat-tail.
2. *al-rānifa* — Al-Khalīl said: the small skin at the tip of the soft cartilage of the nose; also the tip of the ear's cartilage.
3. *al-rānifa* — the fleshy pad of the hand.
4. *rānifat al-kabid* — Abū Ḥātim said: the thin part of the liver.
5. *rawānif al-ākām* — related from al-Liḥyānī: the tops of hillocks.
6. *al-ranf* — is said to be wild marjoram; this is not established.
رنق:
The letters rā', nūn and qāf are a root pointing to the disturbance of a thing whose clarity, if it had been clear, is changed.

1. *al-ranaq* — turbid water.
2. *raniqa al-mā' yarnaqu ranaqan* — the water became turbid.
3. *rannaqa al-nawm fī 'aynihi* — drowsiness settled in his eye, mingling with it.
4. *al-turnūq* — the mud remaining in a watercourse.
5. *rannaqa al-ṭā'ir* — the bird flapped its wing without flying; the origin of the sense of disturbance we gave above.
رنم:
The letters rā', nūn and mīm are a small but sound root in sounds. One says tarannama, when he trilled his voice. And the bird trilled (tarannama) in its cooing. And the bow trilled (tarannamat) — its sound at the moment of release was likened to trilling.

Al-Shammākh said, in a line of verse:
When the archers released the string from it, it trilled ... trilling like a bereaved woman whom funerals have grieved.
رنى:
The letters rā', nūn and the weak letter [the final yā'] are a single root pointing to gazing.

1. *ranā yarnū runūwan* — he looked, gazed.
2. *al-ranā* — the thing you gaze at.
3. *ẓalla fulānun rāniyan* — so-and-so remained gazing, stretching his eyes toward the thing.
4. *arnānī ḥusnu mā ra'aytu* — the beauty of what I saw captivated me.

The saying of Ibn Aḥmar was explained along these lines:
Kingship stretched its tent-ropes over him — a cup that draws the gaze, and a swift, high-bred steed.

It is said this word [for such a cup] was heard from no one but him — as if it were the cup that whoever sees it gazes at, in admiration of it.

5. *fulānun ranuwwu fulāna* — so-and-so constantly gazes at such-and-such a woman.
6. *al-yuranna'* — henna; it may belong to this root, or it may be said to fall outside it.
7. *al-runā'* — a saying that strays from this chapter: the voice.
ره:
The letters rā' and hā', if correct in speech, denote a glimmer of light. One says tarahraha al-shay', when it glistened.

As for the hadith, "When the Messenger of God's chest was opened over his heart, a basin, rahraha, was brought" — al-Qaṭṭān told us, from al-Mufassir, from al-Qutaybī, from Abū Ḥātim, who said: I asked al-Aṣma'ī about it and he did not know it. He said: nor do I know it myself, and I have sought an explanation for it and found none except from one direction, which is that the hā' in it stands in place of a ḥā', as though he meant: a basin, raḥraḥa, was brought, that being a wide one. One says a vessel is raḥraḥ and raḥrāḥ. Someone said, in a line of verse: toward a stand [for a cooking pot] like a wide shield. What I hold on this is that the hadith, if correct, belongs to the first word (rahraha, glimmer), since a basin has a glisten.

Among what departs from the chapter are al-rahrahatān: the two bones that project on the inner sides of the ankles, each facing the other.
رهأ:
The letters rā', hā' and hamza occur only with an extra letter added in, and it is al-rahyaʾa, and this indicates a lack of evenness in a thing.

1. al-rahyaʾa — for one of the two loads on a beast's two sides to be heavier than the other. One says rahyaʾta ḥimlaka, you unbalanced your load; and rahyaʾta amraka, you unbalanced your affair, when you did not set it straight.
2. al-rahyaʾa — also incapacity and sluggishness. One says tarahyaʾa fī amrihi, when he set his mind to a thing then held back from it.
3. al-rahyaʾa — also for the two eyes to well up with tears.
4. tarahyaʾat, said of a cloud — it wavered, when it was in labour with rain.
رهب:
The letters rā', hā' and bā' are two roots. One of them points to fear, and the other to fineness and lightness.

The first is al-rahba, fear: you say rahibtu al-shay' ruhban wa-rahaban wa-rahbatan — I feared the thing. Al-tarahhub is devoting oneself to worship. Also of this root is al-irhāb, which is driving the camels back from the watering trough and keeping them off it.

The other root: al-rahb is the lean, worn-out she-camel. Al-rihāb are thin arrowheads; the single one is rahb. Al-rahāb is a bone in the chest overlooking the belly, shaped like a tongue.
رهج: The letters rā', hā' and jīm are a minor root indicating the stirring up of dust and the like. Al-rahaj: dust.
رهد:
The letters rā', hā' and dāl are a minor root indicating softness, which is al-rahāda. One says hiya rahīda, meaning soft and tender.

As for Ibn Durayd, he mentioned something close to this pattern. He said: one says rahadtu al-shay'a rahdan, when you crushed it with a severe crushing. He said: and al-rahīda is wheat that is pounded and milk poured over it.
رهز: The letters rā', hā' and zāy are a word indicating al-rahz, which is movement.
رهس:
The letters rā', hā' and sīn are two roots: one is fullness and abundance, the other is treading.

The first is their saying: irtahasa al-wādī, the valley filled up; irtahasa al-jarād, the locusts rode one upon another.

The other root: al-rahs is treading. From it, a man called al-rahwas: the big eater.
رهش:
The letters rā', hā' and shīn are a root indicating agitation and movement.

1. al-irtihāsh — for the beast's foreleg to strike against itself in its walking and injure its rawāhish, which are the sinews of the inner forearm. Al-Khalīl said: al-irtihāsh is also a kind of thrusting done sideways. He said, in a line of verse:
Abā Khālid, were it not for my awaiting your help ... I would have taken my spearhead and thrust with it sideways.
He said: and its irtihāsh is the shaking of its two forelegs.
2. a man called ruhshūsh — lively and generous, as if he quivers and delights at generosity and good.
3. al-murtahisha — the bow that, when shot from, shakes so that its string strikes its abhar (its curved inner edge).
4. al-rahīs — the bow whose string strikes its ṭā'if (its outer rim).
5. a she-camel called ruhshūsh — abundant in milk.
رهص:
The letters rā', hā' and ṣād are a root indicating pressing, squeezing and firmness.

1. al-rahṣ — as reported by al-Khalīl, intense squeezing.
2. al-rahaṣ — for a stone to strike a hoof or a soft foot-pad so that its inside is bruised. One says rahaṣahu al-ḥajaru yarhaṣuhu, from al-rahṣa. A beast that has suffered this is called rahīṣ, meaning marhūṣa.
3. al-rawāhiṣ — stones that bruise beasts' feet when they tread on them, singular rāhiṣa. Al-A'shā said:
So bite, if you are angered, the iron of the earth ... with your mouth, and the bruising stones of al-Kulāb.
And "al-Asad al-Rahīṣ" [the Bruised Lion] was one of the horsemen of the Arabs.
4. al-marhaṣ — the place of the bruise. He said, in a line of verse:
Upon mountains that bruise the bruised places.
5. al-rihṣ — the lowest course of stone in a wall. One says yarhaṣu al-ḥā'iṭ, the wall settles firm by what supports it.
6. al-marāhiṣ — ranks or stations; one says marhaṣa and marāhiṣ as one says martaba and marātib. One says: how is so-and-so's marhaṣa with the king, meaning his standing. He said:
Your abandoning eminence flung you among the last of them ... and some people were preferred over you in rank.
رهط:
The letters rā', hā' and ṭā' are a root indicating a gathering among people and other things.

1. al-rahṭ — a band of people, from three up to ten. Al-Khalīl said: what is fewer than seven down to three is called nafar. Pronouncing rahṭ with the hā' left unvoweled is better than pronouncing it fully voweled [ruhuṭ].
2. al-tarhīṭ — Al-Khalīl said this is rolling a mouthful of food together and gathering it up.

A poet said, in a line of verse [only this half is given]:
O you eater who rolls his mouthfuls together!

3. al-rāhiṭā' — one of the jerboa's burrow-holes, between the nāfiqā' and the qāṣiʿā' [its other escape-holes], where it hides its young.
4. al-rihāṭ — Al-Khalīl said this is a hide cut to the length from the waistband down to the knee, then slit into strips like sandal-thongs, worn by a young girl.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
With a blow beneath which heads fall ... and a thrust like the tearing of the rihāṭ.

The singular of rihāṭ is rahṭ.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Whenever I wish it, apart from the pride of kings, I will make you a band gathered together against ḥuyyaḍ.

Al-Khalīl said: al-rihāṭ is a singular, and its plural is arhiṭa. He said: regarding a man's clan you may say "these are your rahṭ" and "your arhuṭ" — both mean the same, the men of your clan gathered together.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Woe to the war that laid whole bands of kinsmen low, so that they [at last] found rest —
meaning: it relieved them of this world through killing.

5. ruhṭa — the jerboa's rāhiṭā' is also called by this name.
رهق:
The letters rā', hā' and qāf are two roots close to one another: one of them is one thing covering another, and the other is haste and delay.

As for the first, it is their saying *rahiqahu al-amr* — the matter came over him. And *al-rahūq* among she-camels is the swift wide-striding one that overtakes you when you draw her out, that is, comes over you from the breadth of her stride. God, whose praise is exalted, said: {and no darkness and no lowness comes over their faces} [Yūnus: 26]. And *al-murāhiq* is the boy who has come close to manhood. And a man *murahhaq* is one at whose house guests alight. And *arhaqa al-qawmu al-ṣalāta* — the people put off the prayer until the time of the next prayer drew near. And *al-rahaq* is haste and wrongdoing. God, exalted, said: {so he fears no loss and no oppression} [al-Jinn: 13]. And *al-rahaq* is haste in lying and in blame. A poet said, in a line of verse:
sound in the flank from reckless wrong.
رهك:
The letters rā', hā' and kāf are a root indicating slackness.

1. al-rahwak — the fat one, among kids and gazelles.
2. al-tarahwuk — moving with slackness.
3. rahaktu al-shay'a — they say this when you crushed a thing.
رهل:
The letters rā', hā' and lām are a word indicating slackness. Al-rahal: slackness from fatness. One says a horse rahil al-ṣadr, slack in the chest.

Abū al-Ḥasan al-Qaṭṭān recited to us, he said 'Alī ibn 'Abd al-'Azīz recited to us, from Abū 'Ubayd, from al-Farrā':
A young man cut like the cutting of a sword, not narrow at the chest ... nor slack in his throat-hollows and his collarbones.
رهم: The letters rā', hā' and mīm indicate fertility and moisture. Al-rihma: rain of small drops; plural riham and rihām. A meadow that has had this rain is called marhūma. Arhamat al-samā', the sky brought rihām-rain. "We alighted with so-and-so, and were on the more fertile of his two sides" — meaning the richer of them.
رهن:
The letters rā', hā' and nūn are a root indicating the fixedness of a thing held by a right or otherwise.

1. al-rahn — the thing that is pledged. You say "rahantu the thing, rahnan"; one does not say "arhantu."
2. al-rāhin — the fixed, lasting thing. "The thing rahana for you" means it stayed in place. "I arhantu it for you" means I made it stay.

Abū Zayd said: "I arhantu in a piece of merchandise" means I bid it up, overpaid for it — the word is used specifically of a high price.

A poet said, in a line of verse [only this half is given]:
Camels of the ʿAyd breed, for which the dinars were bid ever higher.

Abū ʿUbayd's account of this word is an unusual one. But Ibn al-Sikkīt and others said: "urhinat" means it was given as an advance, a loan — and this is the correct view.

3. "They all said: 'arhantu my children'" means I staked them, put them at risk.

As for calling an emaciated person or camel rāhin, this too belongs to the root, because they treated the animal as though its very leanness made it stay fixed in its place, unmoving.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
If you see my body grown thin, held fast by leanness — the glory of men does not lie in fatness.

One says of this "rahana ruhūnan."
رهو:
The letters rā’, hā’ and the weak final letter are two roots: one points to ease, lowness and stillness, and the other to a place that may be either low-lying or raised.

The first: al-rahw — the calm, still sea.

1. ‘ayshun rāhin — an easy, settled life.
2. arhi ‘alā nafsika — go easy on yourself.

Ibn al-A‘rābī said: rahā fī al-sayri yarhū — he went gently, when he was easy-paced in travel.

3. al-faras al-mirhā’ fī al-sayr — a horse that goes with a loose, easy gait, like al-mirkhā’; this is a speed combined with calm, without any restlessness.

As for the place mentioned: al-rahw is low-lying ground, though it is also said to mean raised ground. The one who holds the second view cites this line of verse: ‘The nursing women stay all day at a rahwa’ — he said this is because they are fearful, so they seek out the raised places. And the words of another: ‘And it showed itself — as a blue, hook-beaked bird shaking off the dew shows itself atop a rahwa.’

Al-Khalīl reported: al-rahwa is a standing pool of water.

As for the hadith of the Messenger of God, God’s blessings and peace upon him and his family, when he was asked about [the tribe of] Ghaṭafān and said: ‘A rahwa that gives forth water’ — he meant the high mountain, giving that as a likeness for them. It has also come from him, God’s blessings and peace upon him and his family, that he said: ‘A rough hillock that keeps people away from it.’

Al-Qutaybī said: al-rahwa can mean raised ground, and it can mean low ground; he said it is one of the words that carries opposite meanings.

As for al-rahā’, it is the flat, level desert tract that is rarely without a mirage.

Straying from both roots: al-rahw is also a kind of bird; al-rahw is also a term of reproach for a woman; and jā’at al-khaylu rahwan means the horses came one after another, in succession.
روث: The letters rā', wāw and thā' are two quite distinct words. Al-rawtha: the tip of the nose. And [al-rawtha]: a single piece of dung of beasts.
روج: The letters rā', wāw and jīm are not a root. However al-Khalīl mentioned: rawwajtu al-darāhim, I made the money circulate, and fulānun murawwij, so-and-so is one who makes goods move. And rāja al-shay'u yarūju, when it was moved along briskly. All of this has been said, and God knows best whether it is sound, but I take all of it to be a borrowed word.
روح:
The letters rā', wāw and ḥā' are a great root that runs true, pointing to breadth, room, and steady going. The origin of all of it is al-rīḥ, the wind. And the origin of the yā' in rīḥ is a wāw, and it was only turned into a yā' because of the kasra before it. So al-rūḥ is the spirit of a man, and it is derived from the wind, and so is the whole section. And al-rawḥ is the breath of the wind. And one says arāḥa al-insān, when a man breathes. It is in the poetry of Imru' al-Qays. And one says arwaḥa al-mā'u and other things: its smell changed.

And al-rūḥ is Gabriel, peace be upon him. God, whose praise is exalted, said: {The trustworthy Spirit brought it down upon your heart} [al-Shu'arā': 193]. And al-rawāḥ is the late afternoon; it was so named for the breath of the wind, for the wind mostly blows after the sun's decline. And they went at that time, and that is from the sun's decline until the night. And araḥnā ibilanā: we brought our camels back at that time. As for al-A'shā's saying, in a line of verse:
What omen do you take today from the birds al-ruwaḥ - from the raven of parting, or a buck that crossed from the left? -
some people said: they are the scattered ones. And others said: they are the ones going back at evening to their nests. And al-murāwaḥa between two tasks is that one does this once and that once. And al-arwaḥ is the man who has a spreading in the fronts of his feet. One says rawiḥa yarwaḥu rawaḥan. And a bowl rawḥā' is a shallow one. And one says al-arwaḥ among people is the one whose fore-parts of the feet stand far apart and whose heels come close together; he is plainly of rawaḥ. And one says: so-and-so is stirred to kindness, when a good spirit takes hold of him for it. And rīḥa al-ghadīr: the wind struck the pool. And arāḥa al-qawm: they entered into the wind. And of a dead man, when he has passed away, one says: he has found rest. And one says arāḥa al-rajul, when his breath comes back to him after exhaustion. And arwaḥa al-ṣayd, when the game catches the smell of man. And one says: he came to us with not a smell of blood on his face. And one says araḥtu 'alā al-rajuli ḥaqqahu, when you give a man his right back to him. And I shall do that in sarāḥ and rawāḥ, that is, in ease. And al-marāḥ is where the cattle shelter at night. And al-duhn al-murawwaḥ is perfumed oil. And tarawwaḥa al-shajar, and rāḥa yarāḥu - the meaning of both is that the tree bursts into leaf. He said:
The thorn-trees came into leaf with them, while the root was diseased.
Abū Zayd: arwaḥanī al-ṣaydu irwāḥan, when the game catches your smell. And arwaḥtu min fulānin ṭīban - I smelled sweetness from him. And al-Kisā'ī used to say that in "he did not find the scent of Paradise" the verb is from araḥtu. And it may also be said lam yaraḥ, from rāḥa yarāḥu, when a man finds a smell. And one says: they went out with a riyāḥ of the evening, and with a rawāḥ and an irwāḥ. Abū Zayd said: rāḥat al-ibilu tarāḥu, and araḥtuhā anā, from His saying, majestic His majesty: {when you bring them home} [al-Naḥl: 6]. And rāḥa al-farasu yarāḥu rāḥatan, when the horse is put to stud. And al-marwaḥa is the place through which the wind passes. It is said that this line is 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb's, and it is said rather that he quoted it:
As though her rider were a branch in a windy place, when she bends down with him, or a drunken drinker.
And al-rayyiḥ is that which has rawḥ in it; one says a day rayyiḥ: a pleasant day. And a day rāḥ: one with a strong wind. They said: it was built on their saying kabsh ṣāf, a ram of much wool. As for the saying of Abū Kabīr:
And many a water I came down to aslant, walking like the leopard that feels the piercing cold -
that is his finding of the breath of it. And the tarwīḥa in the month of Ramadan was so named because the people rest after every four bowings. And al-rāḥ is the plural of rāḥat al-kaff, the palm of the hand. 'Ubayd said, in a line of verse:
A low cloud hanging close, its fringe just above the earth; one who stood up could almost push it away with his palms.
And al-rāḥ is wine. Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
And I do drink wine - you know it well - on the day of staying and on the day of departure.
And you say: an affliction came down upon so-and-so, and God, mighty and glorious, was moved with mercy for him and delivered him from it. Al-'Ajjāj said, in a line of verse:
So my Lord was moved and willed mercy for me, and my blessing He completed, and it was complete.
He said: and the explanation of irtāḥa is: He looked upon me and had mercy on me. And al-A'shā said about the aryaḥī, the open-handed man, in a line of verse:
An open-handed, bright-faced man, before whom the people stand still, standing as they stand for the new moon.
Al-Khalīl said: everything wide is called aryaḥ, and a camel-litter aryaḥ. And some of them said a litter arwaḥ. If it were so it would be blame of it, because al-rawaḥ is a splaying out, and that is a fault in a litter. Al-Khalīl said: al-aryaḥī is taken from rāḥa yarāḥu, as one says aṣlatī for al-ṣalt.
رود:
The letters rā', wāw and dāl: most of its chapter [points] to a coming and going that arises from setting out in one direction. You say rāwadtuhu ʿalā an yafʿala kadhā — when you pressed him to do it. Al-rawd is the act of the rā'id, the scout. One says baʿathnā rā'idan yarūdu al-kala' — we sent a scout to seek out pasture, that is, to look and to search.

Al-riyād is the camels' going back and forth in the pasture, coming and turning away. Rādat tarūdu riyādan. Al-marād is the place in which the grazing beasts range. And rādat al-mar'a tarūdu — when a woman goes back and forth to her neighbours' houses. Al-rāda is the gentle wind, because it moves about and does not blow hard. And rā'id al-ʿayn is the mote in the eye that moves about in it. Some of them said: al-irāda, willing, has the wāw for its root, and his proof is that you say rāwadtuhu ʿalā kadhā. And al-rā'id is the wooden bar by which a hand-mill is turned.

As for the saying of the one who said, describing a horse:
Swift both at the urging on and at the gentle pace —
it is from arwadtu fī al-sayr irwādan wa-murwadan, I went gently in travelling; and one says marwadan also. That is from gentleness in going. And one says "rāda wisāduhu" — his pillow shifted — when it does not stay put, as though it comes and goes. And from this chapter is al-irwād in an action: that it be ruwaydan, gently. And rāwadtuhu ʿalā an yafʿala kadhā — when you pressed him to do it. And from this chapter is jāriyatun rūd, a young girl. And the full form of ruwayd is rūd.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
As though she were like one who walks with slow, gentle steps.

And al-mirwad is the eye-pencil.
روز: The letters rā', wāw and zāy are a single word, indicating testing and trying. One says ruztu al-shay'a arūzuhu, when you tested it.
روض:
The letters rā', wāw and ḍād are two roots close to each other in meaning: one indicates spaciousness, and the other softening and ease.

The first: their saying istarāḍa l-makān — the place became spacious. He said: and from it their saying, "do such-and-such as long as the breath is mustarīḍ" — meaning spacious, at ease. He said, in a line of verse:
"Is it rajaz [a simple verse-form] you want, or qarīḍ [composed verse]? Both I do well, at ease."
From this root: al-rawḍa — a meadow. One says arāḍa l-wādī and istarāḍa, when water pooled and stood in it; likewise arāḍa l-ḥawḍ, of a trough. Standing, spread-out water is called a rawḍa. He said, in a line of verse:
"And a meadow-pool from which I watered my worn-out mount."
From this root also: atānā bi-ināin yurīḍu kadhā — he brought us a vessel that is enough for such-and-such. And arāḍahum — he gave them their fill of drink.

As for the other root: their saying ruḍtu l-nāqata arūḍuhā riyāḍatan — I broke in the she-camel, training her.
روع:
The letters rā’, wāw and ‘ayn are a single root pointing to fright, or to the seat where fright settles. From this is al-raw‘.

1. rawwa‘tu fulānan wa ru‘tuhu — I frightened so-and-so.
2. al-arwa‘ among men — one of fine build and striking presence, as though by this he strikes awe in whoever sees him.
3. al-raw‘ā’ among camels — one quick-hearted, easily startled, as though she takes fright at things; the same word is used of a woman who impresses people, like the man described as al-arwa‘.

As for the meaning alluded to, the seat where fright settles, that too is called al-raw‘. One says: waqa‘a dhālika fī rū‘ī — that came into my mind. And in the hadith: ‘The Holy Spirit breathed into my heart [rū‘ī]: no soul shall die until it has received the fullness of its provision, so fear God and be moderate in seeking your livelihood.’
روغ:
The letters rā', wāw and ghayn are a single root indicating swerving and unsteadiness. One says "the fox and the like rāgha, yarūghu" — it swerved, dodged.

1. ṭarīq rā'igh — a slanting road.
2. "So-and-so rāgha toward such a thing" — he inclined toward it secretly.
3. "He tries to turn me from my purpose, and I urīghuhu" — I dodge and evade him.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
They try to turn me away from Sālim, but I turn back to him — he is as close to me as the skin between the eye and the nose.

4. "I rawwaghtu the mouthful with ghee, urawwighuhā, tarwīghan" — I soaked it in fat, turning it round and round in the ghee.
5. "So-and-so rāwagha so-and-so" — he wrestled him, because each tries to turn [yurīghu] the other about.
6. al-riwāgha, al-riyāgha — the place where the sons of so-and-so wrestle.
روق:
The letters rā', wāw and qāf are two roots: one indicates a thing being foremost, the other indicates goodness and beauty.

The first: al-rawq and al-riwāq — the front part of the tent. This is the origin. Then everything that has some degree of being foremost is carried on it.

1. al-rawq — the horn of the bull.
2. "a rawq of the night passed" — meaning a portion of it, the earlier part.
3. rawq al-insān — a person's youth, because it is the foremost part of his life. The word rawq is then borrowed for the body, so one says: he cast his awrāq [his whole self] upon it.

The analogy in all these is one and the same.

As for the saying of al-A'shā — a hard passage, rendered as best as can be made out:
She of the swift bucket, who pelts the foremost with the hindmost ... when the arwāq follow one upon another.
Three things have been said about this:
The first, that he meant the arwāq of the night — no rawq of the night passes but a rawq follows it.
The second, that al-arwāq are the bodies, when they press against one another in travelling.
The third, that al-arwāq are the horns, and that he meant only the crowding together of cattle and gazelles from the heat in their coverts. Whoever held this view placed the completion of the sense in the line that follows it, which is his saying: "in the resting-place of the covert, when the heat blazed, when the shade was gathered in by the leg" — as if he said: the arwāq followed one another to their resting-place in the covert.

4. al-rawaq — for the upper front teeth to be longer than the lower.
5. in what resembles a proverb: "so-and-so ate his rawq", when he lived so long that his teeth crumbled away.
6. one says of the body: he cast his arwāq upon the thing, when he was avid for it.
7. rawwaqa al-laylu — the night is said to do this when it draws out the canopy (riwāq) of its darkness. One also says: he cast his arwiqa.
8. alqā fulānun arwāqahu — said of a man when his running grew intense, because he presses forward and advances with his body. He said:
I cast down my arwāq, the night of Khabt al-Rahṭ.
9. one says: the cloud cast its arwāq, that is, when it persisted with its rain and stayed steady.
10. al-riwāq — a tent like a marquee, carried on a single central pole, plural arwiqa. Riwāq al-bayt: what lies in front of the house.

The other root: their saying rāqanī al-shay'u yarūqunī, when it pleased me. These are youths called rūqa, beautiful ones. From this: rawwaqtu al-sharāb, I strained the drink clear — that is its being made good. Al-rāwūq: the strainer.
رول:
The letters rā', wāw and lām are a root indicating the smearing of one thing with another.

1. rawwaltu al-khubz bi-l-samn — I basted the bread with clarified butter, like rawwaghtu.
2. al-rūwāl — the drool of a beast. One says rawwala fī mikhlātihi, it drooled into its feed-bag.
3. close to this: rawwala al-farasu — said of a horse when it let itself hang loose [an uncertain, likely technical sense].
روم:
The letters rā', wāw and mīm are a root indicating the seeking of a thing. One says rumtu al-shay'a arūmuhu rawman, I sought the thing. Al-marām: the object sought.

Ibn al-A'rābī said: one says rawwamtu fulānan and rawwamtu bi-fulānin, when you made someone seek and pursue a thing.
رون:
The letters rā', wāw and nūn indicate intensity of heat or of sound. They say yawmun arwanān and laylatun arwanāna, meaning intensely hot and oppressive. Al-Qutaybī said: al-arwanān is also the loud sound.

Al-Kumayt said:
There is in it a presence, not of the jinn, that frightens it ... nor any human of loud clamour and noise.
روه: The letters rā', wāw and hā' are not a genuine root, though some say al-rawh is the verbal noun of rāha yarūhu rawhan. He said: it is a word of the Yemeni dialect. They say: rāha al-mā'u 'alā wajhi al-arḍi, the water moved unsettled over the surface of the ground. There is doubt about this.
روى:
The letters rā', wāw and yā' are a single root, from which words are then derived. The origin is what is the opposite of thirst; the word is then used in speech for one who carries what is passed on from him, as if he brings people their fill.

So the origin is rawītu min al-mā'i riyyan, I drank my fill of water. Al-Aṣma'ī said: rawaytu 'alā ahlī arwī rayyan, I brought water to my family. He is called rāwin, from a people called ruwāh, who are those who bring people their water.

That is the origin; then it was likened to the one who brings a people knowledge or news and passes it on (yarwīhi), as if he had brought them their fill of it.
ريب:
The letters rā', yā' and bā' are a small root pointing to doubt, or to doubt together with fear. So al-rayb is doubt. God, exalted be His praise, said: {Alif Lām Mīm. This is the Book, no doubt in it} [al-Baqara: 1], that is, no doubt in it.

Then a poet said, in a line of verse:
They said: we left the people hemmed in about him, so there is no doubt that a slain man lay there.

Al-rayb is also whatever unsettles you in a matter. You say rābanī hādhā al-amr - this matter troubled me - when it brings doubt and fear upon you. And arāba al-rajul: the man became one about whom there is a rība, a suspicion. And qad rābanī amruhu - his affair has made me uneasy. And rayb al-dahr is the turns of fortune of time; and the reasoning is one and the same.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Is it at death and its blows that you grieve, when time gives no redress to the man who frets?

As for the words of the one who said, in a line of verse:
We settled every business in Tihāma and in Mecca, then we let the swords rest.

It is said that here al-rayb means a need. And this is not far-fetched, because the man who seeks a need is in doubt, for the fear he has of missing it.
ريث:
The letters rā', yā' and thā' are a single root indicating slowness, which is al-rayth, the opposite of haste. Labīd said:
Indeed the fear of our Lord is the best of gains ... and by God's leave are my slowness and my haste.

One says from it rātha yarīthu. Istarthtu fulānan: I found so-and-so slow. Some also said istaryatha, though it is not the form in use. One says of a man rayyith, meaning slow.
ريح:
The letters rā', yā' and ḥā' — most of the discussion of this has already passed under rā', wāw and ḥā', because that is the true origin, and the origin of what we mention here now is also wāw; we only write the words as they are pronounced. Al-rīḥ, the wind, is well known, and its derivation has already passed. Al-rayḥān is well known. Al-rayḥān also means provision. And in the hadith: "Indeed the child is among God's rayḥān." And al-rīḥ means victory and strength, in His saying, exalted is He: {so that you should lose heart and your strength should depart} [al-Anfāl: 46]. And the poet said:
Will you two wait a little, for the time of their heedlessness ... or will you two run? For indeed victory belongs to the one who runs.

The origin of all of this is wāw, as has already passed.
ريخ:
The letters rā', yā' and khā' are a single word about which there is doubt.

1. rākha yarīkhu raykhan — for a man to become abased and broken.
2. al-taryīkh — the giving-way of a thing. "They struck so-and-so until they [rayyakhūhu] broke him."
3. rākha al-rajulu yarīkhu raykhan — for a man to become bewildered.
4. rākha al-ba'īru — for a camel to become exhausted.
ريد: The letters rā', yā' and dāl are two words. Al-rayd: the jutting ridge of a mountain. Al-rīd: the peer, one of the same age.
رير:
The letters rā', yā' and rā' are a single word that is not analogised upon nor branched from. Al-rīr: spoiled marrow, also called al-rayr and al-rār. "Arāra Allāhu mukhkha hādhihi al-nāqa" — God made this she-camel's marrow into rīr.

'Alī ibn Ibrāhīm told me: he said, I asked Tha'lab about the saying of the one who said:
May God make your marrow spoiled in the bones of your foot.
And I said to him: is it thus, or:
May God show me your marrow in the bones of your foot?
And which of the two do you prefer? He said: they are the same. And the meaning of arāra is: made thin. And al-sulāmā are the bones of the foot.
ريس:
The letters rā', yā' and sīn are two words far apart in meaning. Al-riyās: the hilt of a sword. He said:
Toward two heroes, both of them stumbling ... each turning the sword's hilt while the sword flashes free.
Another said:
and an elbow like the sword's hilt when it had shrivelled.

The other word: al-rays and al-rayasān: swaggering. He said:
He came to them, among their mounts, swaggering.
ريش:
The letters rā’, yā’ and shīn are a single root pointing to a good state, and to what a person gains of good things. Al-rīsh is ‘the good’; al-riyāsh is wealth.

1. rishtu fulānan arīshuhu raysh an — I saw to so-and-so’s welfare, when you tend to his good condition. This is in his saying:
Give me your bounty, long as you have worn me down; and the best of patrons is one who gives rather than wears away.

Some held that al-rā’ish in the hadith about ‘al-rāshī wa-l-murtashī wa-l-rā’ish’ [the briber, the bribe-taker, and the one who arranges the bribe] is the one who goes between the briber and the bribe-taker. But he is called rā’ish for the reason described above. One says rishtu fulānan, I brought so-and-so some good. This is the sounder of the two views, on the strength of the line: Give me your bounty, long as you have worn me down.

Another poet said:
My good fortune is from you, and my longing is toward you, even if your visits come only now and then.

And also said:
I shall be grateful if you restore my plumage to me, and fix the foremost feathers back into my wing.

2. From this root too: rīsh al-ṭā’ir — a bird’s feathers.
3. rishtu al-sahma arīshuhu raysh an — I fletched the arrow.
4. irtāsha fulānun — so-and-so’s condition improved.
5. al-aryash — one with much hair specifically on the two ears, so they say.

This is the origin of the root. From it a further word was derived: the soft, weak spear is called rāsh, so named because in its weakness it was likened to a feather. From this too, nāqatun rāshshat al-ẓahr — a she-camel weak in the back.
ريط:
The letters rā', yā' and ṭā' are a single word, which is al-rayṭa, meaning any wrap that is not made of two joined pieces; plural rayṭ and riyāṭ.

My father told me, from Abū Naṣr, the son of the sister of al-Layth ibn Idrīs, from Ibn al-Sikkīt, who said: every thin, soft garment is called a rayṭa.
ريع:
The letters rā’, yā’ and ‘ayn are two roots: one is rising and height, and the other is returning.

The first: al-rī‘ — a rise in the ground. It is also said that al-rī‘ is a plural, its singular rī‘a, plural riyā‘. Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse: the wing-feathers overlapping, standing tall above a rī‘a.

From this root too, al-rī‘ means road. God Most High said: {Do you build on every height a landmark, amusing yourselves?} [al-Shu‘arā’: 128] — some said He meant ‘road’, others said ‘a rise in the ground’.

From this root too, al-ray‘ — growth and increase.

1. It is said that the ray‘ of coats of mail is the excess of their sleeves.
2. arā‘at al-ibil — the camels flourished, their young growing many.
3. rā‘at al-ḥinṭa — the wheat thrived.
4. It is said that the ray‘ of a well is the raised bank of earth around its mouth.
5. ray‘ān of anything — its best and earliest part.

As for the other root: al-ray‘ — returning to a thing. In the hadith: a man asked al-Ḥasan about vomiting for one who is fasting, and he said: ‘Did any of it come back?’ — meaning, did it return. And he said, in a line of verse: You hoped Laylā would come back to you — but it is only false hopes that cut men’s necks.
ريف:
The letters rā', yā' and fā' are a single word indicating fertility.

1. arāfat al-arḍ — the land became fertile.
2. aryafnā — when we came to the fertile country, al-rīf.
3. arḍun rayyifa — land of this fertile kind, from al-rīf.
4. rāfat al-māshiya — the livestock grazed the fertile country.
ريق:
The letters rā', yā' and qāf — and words that belong to the wāw-class also enter into this root — are a single root indicating the coming and going of a fluid thing, such as water and the like, from which words are then derived.

1. al-tarayyuq — the coming and going of water over the surface of the ground. One says rāqa al-sarābu fawqa al-arḍi rayqan, the mirage shimmered above the ground.
2. rīq al-insān — a person's saliva, and likewise of others.

The word is then borrowed: they say the rayyiq of everything is its first and best part. "This is the rayyiq of the drink", and "the rayyiq of the rain" is its first part. From this is the saying of Ṭarafa — an obscure line, rendered as best as can be made out:
and my first flush hastened her change of state.
And this is sometimes lightened, so one says rayq. And the line of al-Ba'īth is recited thus — again obscure:
We praised to her the first flush of youth, and she matched it ... with the freshness of youth, in one who keeps the secret, silent.

Ibn Durayd related: akaltu khubzan rayqan, I ate bread plain, without any relish — and this too belongs to the word, meaning it is what mixed with my first saliva alone. And al-mā' al-rā'iq: water drunk on an empty stomach in the morning, without sediment. He said: this is said only of water.

3. al-rā'iq — the free, idle one; it comes from the same word, as if he is still on an empty stomach.

Al-Liḥyānī related: huwa yarīqu bi-nafsihi ruyūqan, meaning he is giving up his soul freely [dying], and this belongs to the first word, because his breath at that point goes back and forth in his chest.
ريم:
The letters rā', yā' and mīm are words of varied origins, such that scarcely two of them ever come together under one derivation.

1. al-raym — the stairway. One says "go up in the raym," meaning climb the steps.
2. al-raym — the bone that remains after the slaughtered camel is divided among its shares.
3. al-raym — the grave.
4. al-raym — an hour of the daytime.
5. One says rīma bi-l-rajuli — a man was rīma, when he was cut off and left stranded.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
The cupbearer who was with me was left stranded.

Ibn al-Sikkīt said: rayyama bi-l-makāni — he stayed there.

6. rayyamat al-saḥābatu wa aghḍanat — the cloud lingered and did not clear, when it persisted without breaking.
7. lā arīmu afʿalu kadhā — I do not cease doing such-and-such, meaning I do not stop.
8. al-raym — the excess. One says "lī ʿalayka raymu kadhā," meaning I have such an excess over you.
رين:
The letters rā’, yā’ and nūn are a root pointing to a covering and a concealment. Al-rayn is a covering over a thing. One says rīna ‘alayhi, as though he were overcome and covered by it.

From this is the hadith of ‘Umar: ‘Beware — al-Usayfi‘, Usayfi‘ of Juhayna, was content with his religion only so far as it being said he outran the pilgrims, [so he ran carelessly into debt], and morning found him qad rīna bihi’ — meaning he had died.

1. rāna al-nu‘āsu yarīnu — drowsiness overcame him.
2. rānat al-khamru ‘alā qalbihi — the wine overpowered his heart.
3. rānat nafsī tarīnu — my stomach turned, felt sick.
4. arāna al-qawmu fa-hum murīnūn — the people’s livestock died off; this follows the same reasoning, because when their livestock died, it was as though they themselves were covered over [rīna] by it.
ريه: The letters rā', yā' and hā' are a word from the chapter of substitution, where one letter stands in for another. One says tarayyaha al-saḥābu, when it tarayyaʿa — became fluid and spread thin. But the true origin is with wāw: tarawwaha, and that has already been discussed.
زأب:
The letters zā', hamza and bā' are two [unrelated] words.

1. za'aba al-shay'a — he carried the thing; al-izdi'āb is the carrying of a load.
2. The other word: za'aba — he drank a strong, heavy draught.

The two have no shared pattern.
زأد:
The letters zā', hamza and dāl are a single word, indicating fright. One says 'zu'ida al-rajulu' — the man was frightened, zu'dan. He said, in a line of verse:
She conceived him on a night of terror, against her will, while the knot of her waist-wrap had not been loosed.
زأر:
The letters zā', hamza and rā' are a single root. 'The lion roared' — za'ara al-asadu za'ran wa-za'īran. Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
I was told that Abū Qābūs threatened me — yet there is no standing still before the roar of the lion.
And from it, he said:
She settled in the land of the roaring [lions], and so, daughter of Makhram, seeking you became hard for me.
From this chapter too is al-za'ra — a thicket; this is like a borrowed use, because lions take shelter in it and roar there.
زأم:
The letters zā', hamza and mīm are a root indicating a sound and speech.

1. al-za'ma — a loud cry.
2. za'ama lī fulānun za'matan — so-and-so threw a word at me, and I do not know whether it is true or false.

Fright, too, is referred to this root: al-za'am. And one says 'az'amtuhu ʿalā kadhā' — I forced him to do such a thing.

Among what is irregular, outside the chapter, is al-za'm: eating heavily. God knows best.
زب:
The letters zāʾ and bāʾ are two origins.

The first indicates abundance in hair, and the word is then extended from there.

1. Al-zabab — length of hair, and its abundance. One says "baʿīrun azabb," a hairy camel.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
You stirred up error, then turned away from it, as the hairy one (al-azabb) turned away from the thrust of spears.

2. From this too, "ʿāmun azabb" — a hairy year, meaning fertile.

The second origin is al-zabīb, well known [raisins], which is then used as a likeness.

1. The two black specks above a snake's eyes are called "zabībatān" — it is the most vicious kind of snake there is. In the hadith: "The hoarded treasure of one of them will come on the Day of Resurrection as a bald serpent with two zabība-specks [above its eyes]."
2. Sometimes the two flecks of foam at the corners of the mouth are called "zabībatān." One says "anshada fulānun ḥattā zabbaba shidqāhu" — so-and-so recited until the corners of his mouth foamed, meaning frothed.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Indeed, when the corners of the mouth foam, and the clamour and the chatter grow many, I am firm of heart, a stone-caster, a striker.

Outside this chapter, not fitting its pattern, is al-zabāb: the mouse [rat], the singular of which is zabāba. It might possibly — though it is a stretch — be from al-zabīb, which has already been mentioned.

And among what is irregular, with no pattern to measure it by: one says "zabbat al-shamsu" and "azabbat" — the sun drew near to setting.
زبد:
The letters zā', bā' and dāl are a single root indicating one thing being produced out of another.

1. zabad al-mā' — the foam of water and the like. One says "azbada, izbādan" — it foamed.
2. al-zubd — butter, also from this. "zabadtu the child, azbuduhu" — I fed him butter.

Sometimes they extended this and derived further from it. Al-Farrā' related from the Arabs: "the sidr tree azbada" when it came into blossom. It is said "so-and-so [a woman] zabadat her waterskin" when she churned it until its butter came out.

3. al-zabd — a gift, also belonging to this root. "zabadtu the man, zabdan" — I gave him a gift.

The Messenger of God, peace be upon him and his family, said: "We do not accept the zabd of the polytheists" — meaning their gifts.
زبر:
The letters zā', bā' and rā' are two roots: one of them points to making a thing firm and tight, and the other points to reading and writing and the like.

The first is their saying *zabartu al-bi'r* — I lined the well, when you build its sides up with stones. From it comes *zubrat al-ḥadīd*, a lump of iron, the piece of it; the plural is *zubar*. Of this chapter too is *al-zubra*, the chest. It is so called because it is like a well that has been *mazbūra*, that is, built up with stones. And it is said that the *zubra* of the lion is the place where his hair gathers thick at his elbows and his chest. A lion is *mazbarāniyy*, that is, huge in the *zubra*.

Of this chapter is *al-zabīr*, which is calamity. Of this chapter also is *akhadha al-shay'a bi-zawbarihi* — he took the thing entire. From it comes what Ibn Aḥmar said in his ode, in a line of verse:
It was reckoned against me, the whole of it.
It is said that its meaning is: it was ascribed to me complete. Of this chapter also is *mā li-fulānin zabr* — so-and-so has no sense and no self-command. From it too is *izba'arra al-shaʿr*, when the hair bristles up and stiffens.

The other root is *zabartu al-kitāb* — I wrote the book. From it comes *al-Zabūr*, the Psalter. And they sometimes said *zabartahu* when you read it. And they say in speech: "I know my own *tazbira*" — that is, my own handwriting.
زبع:
The letters zā', bā' and ʿayn are close to the one before it, indicating rage and a resolve toward evil.

1. tazabbaʿa fulānun — so-and-so made himself ready for evil.
2. tazabbaʿa — he changed [for the worse].

This is in the poetry of Mutammim:
And if you meet him at the drinking-gathering, you will not find him foul-mouthed, nor a filthy man given to rage among the people.
Al-Shaybānī said: al-azbaʿ is a calamity, plural al-azābiʿ. And he recited:
You promised and did not keep faith, and long before that you had promised me — you broke your word to me, and that is one of the calamities.
This, if it is sound, is a case of letters standing in for one another, and belongs to the chapter before it.
زبق:
The letters zā', bā' and qāf are not among the roots one can rely on as sound, and I do not know whether what is said of it is true or not. But they say:

1. zabaqa shaʿrahu — he plucked out his hair.
2. inzabaqa fī al-bayt — he slipped into the house.
3. zabaqtu al-rajula — I confined the man.
زبل:
The letters zā', bā' and lām are a single word. They say 'mā aṣabtu min fulānin zubālan' — I got nothing at all from so-and-so; they say al-zubāl is what the ant carries in its mouth, and it has no derivation. Some have mentioned, if it is sound, 'mā fī al-ināʾi zubālatun' — there is nothing at all in the vessel, when it holds nothing. As for their saying 'zabalta al-zarʿa' — you dunged the crop, when you fertilized it with manure (zibl) — if this is sound then it too belongs to this word, because manure is among the discarded things that count for nothing.

It is also related that al-za'bal is a short man. They recite:
Thick-testicled, a dull clod, a za'bal.
This, and the like of it, is not to be dwelt on.
زبن:
The letters zā, bā and nūn are a single root pointing to pushing away.

1. A she-camel is zabūn, when she pushes at her milker.
2. War is said to "push" people, when it strikes against them; a hard war is called zabūn.
3. A man is dhū zabbūna, when he protects his own side and pushes back in his own defense.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
By fending off blame from my honour with my wealth, and by the fierce pushing-back of one bold and headstrong.

One says "in him is zabbūna", meaning pride, and he is not so except that he pushes back in his own defense.

4. al-zabāniya (the guardian angels of Hell) were named so because they push the people of the Fire into the Fire.
5. al-muzābana — the selling of fruit while still on top of the palm trees, which is the sale the hadith forbids. The scholars said it is so called because of the dispute and pushing-back over the deal that follows from it.
6. al-zabn — they say it also means distance.
7. zubānā of the scorpion (its pincers) — this may also be from this root, as though it pushes away in its own defense with it; or it may be irregular.
زبي:
The letters zā', bā' and yā' indicate harm, not good.

1. laqītu minhu al-azābiyya — I met with harms from him, said when one suffers harm at his hands.
2. al-zubya — a pit that a man digs and hides for hunting; it is dug for the wolf and the lion, and they are caught in it.
3. zabaytu azbī — I drove toward him what he disliked.

He said, in a line of verse:
Take that as your requital, and give judgment to the one who holds it — for it is part of what al-Raqim drives upon you.
زت:
The letters zāʾ and tāʾ are a word with no pattern to measure by. One says "zatattu al-ʿarūsa" when you adorn the bride.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Sons of Tamīm, adorn your girl — for the girl of the encampment is known by her adornment (al-tazattut).

She has become "tazattatat," that is, she adorned herself.
زج:
The letters zāʾ and jīm are a root indicating fineness in a thing.

1. From this, "zujj al-rumḥi wa-l-sahmi" — the ferrule fitted to the spear and the arrow — its plural is "zijāj," with the zāʾ vowelled with a kasra. One says "zajjajtuhu": I fitted it with a zujj. When you pull its zujj off, you say "azjajtuhu."
2. Al-zajaj — the fineness and beauty of the two eyebrows.
3. It is said that al-azajj among ostriches is the one that has white feathers above its eye.
زجر: The letters zāy, jīm and rā' are a word indicating rebuke. Zajartu al-ba'īra ḥattā maḍā, azjuruhu, I drove the camel on with a rebuke until it went. Zajartu fulānan 'ani al-shay'i fa-nzajara, I rebuked so-and-so away from the thing, and he desisted. Al-zajūr, among camels, is the one that knows a person by sight but shies from him by scent.
زجل:
The letters zā', jīm and lām are a root indicating the casting of something and driving it forth.

1. 'qabbaḥa Allāhu umman zajalat bihi' — may God disfigure a mother who cast him forth [in birth].
2. al-zajl — the sending off of a homing pigeon.
3. al-mizjal — the throwing-spear.
4. zajala al-faḥl — the male [animal] cast his seed into the womb.
5. al-zājil — the fluid of the male ostrich, because he casts it forth. Ibn Aḥmar said, in a line of verse:
Nor were the eggs of a shaggy, coarse [ostrich] given to drink of zājil, until we were sated.
It is also said that al-zājil is the marrow of eggs, though the first sense fits the pattern better.

Among what is irregular, outside the chapter: al-zujla — a piece of anything, plural zujal; and al-zi'jīl — a weak man. And from this, if it is sound, al-zājil — a ring at the end of a weight-rope.
زجم:
The letters zā', jīm and mīm are a single root indicating a weak sound.

1. 'mā takallama bi-zajmatin' — he did not speak even a single word.
2. al-zajūm — a bow that does not twang loudly.

God knows best what is correct.
زجى:
The letters zā', jīm and the weak letter are a root indicating the casting of something and driving it along without holding it back.

1. azjati al-baqaratu waladahā — the cow drove her calf along.
2. al-rīḥu tuzjī al-saḥāba — the wind drives the clouds, driving them gently along.
3. al-muzjā — a scant thing, and it follows the pattern of this chapter, meaning something used merely to pass the time. Hence 'hādhihi biḍāʿatun muzjātun' — this is scant merchandise, barely able to be pushed along.
4. zajā al-kharāju yazjū — the tax revenue flowed easily, when its collection became easy.
زح: The letters zāʾ and ḥāʾ indicate distance. One says "zuḥziḥa ʿan kadhā" — he was made to be distanced from such a thing. God Almighty said: {So whoever is removed from the Fire} [Āl ʿImrān: 185] — that is, distanced.
زحر: The letters zā', ḥā' and rā' mean breathing hard — nothing else. One says 'zaḥara yazḥaru zaḥīran' — the sound of his breath when he breathes heavily. And 'zaḥarat al-mar'atu bi-waladihā ʿinda al-wilāda' — the woman strained with her child at birth.
زحف:
The letters zā, ḥā and fā are a single root pointing to surging forward and advancing onward.

1. al-zaḥf — a group advancing toward the enemy.
2. A child "creeps forward" (yazḥafu) on the ground before he can walk.
3. A camel, when it tires and drags its foot, is said to yazḥafu; such camels are zawāḥif, singular zāḥifa.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
On worn-out, dragging camels we drove along, exhausted.

4. One says the young locusts "zaḥafa", when they advance forward in a swarm.
5. al-zāḥif — an arrow that falls short of the target and then creeps forward.

And God knows best what is correct.
زحل:
The letters zā', ḥā' and lām are a root indicating moving aside.

1. zaḥala ʿan makānihi — he moved aside from his place.
2. zaḥalati al-nāqatu fī sayrihā — the she-camel lagged in her pace.
3. al-mazḥal — the place to which one moves aside.
زحم: The letters zā', ḥā' and mīm are a root indicating crowding tightly together. One says 'zaḥamahu yazḥamuhu' — he crowded him, and 'izdaḥama al-nās' — the people crowded together.
زحن: The letters zā', ḥā' and nūn are a root indicating slowness. You say 'zaḥana yazḥanu zaḥnan', and likewise 'al-tazaḥḥun'. One says 'tazaḥḥana ʿalā al-shay'' — he forced himself to it reluctantly, while not wanting it.
زخ:
The letters zāʾ and khāʾ are a minor root indicating pushing and separation.

1. One says "zakhakhtu al-shayʾa" when you push it. In the hadith: "Whoever casts the Qur'an behind his back will be pushed [zukhkha] in the back of his neck."
2. "Zakhkhahā" — he had intercourse with her. Al-mizakhkha — the woman, named from this.
3. From this chapter too, al-zakhkha — rancour and rage.

He said, in a line of verse:
So do not sit nursing rancour, harbouring in your heart both longing and fear.
زخر:
The letters zā', khā' and rā' are a sound root, indicating rising up.

1. zakhara al-baḥru — the sea swelled up, when it surged; it is zākhir.
2. zakhara al-nabātu — the plant grew tall.
3. akhadha al-makānu zukhāriyyahu — the place took on its full bloom, said when the plant grows and puts out its blossom.

Ibn Muqbil said, in a line of verse:
The full blossoming of the plants, as though within it were the finest weave of ʿAbqar and its cut lengths of cloth.
زر:
The letters zāʾ and rāʾ are a minor root indicating intensity and firmness.

Irregular from this is al-zirr — the button of a shirt. From it is then derived:

1. Al-zirr — said to be a bone beneath the heart.
2. Ibn al-Sikkīt said: a man good at tending camels is called "he is a zirr among its zirrs [buttons]" — that is, its mainstay.
3. From this chapter, "zarrat ʿaynuhu" — his eye blazed. One says "ʿaynāhu tazirrāni fī raʾsihi" when his eyes blaze in his head.
4. From this chapter, al-zarr — routing and driving off. One says "huwa yazurru al-katāʾiba bi-sayfihi zarran" — he routs the battalions with his sword.
5. From it, al-zarr — biting. One says "ḥimārun mizarr," a donkey given to biting.
6. It is said al-zarra is the spear.
7. From this chapter, al-zarīr — the shrewd one, sound of judgement.

And God knows best what is correct.
زرب:
The letters zā, rā and bā are a root pointing to a kind of shelter.

1. al-zarb — the pen of sheep, their enclosure.
2. al-zarība — the pit-trap used to catch animals.
3. al-zarība — also the hunter's hide, where he conceals himself waiting for game.
زرح: The letters zā, rā, and ḥā are a single word. Al-zarāwiḥ are small hills.
زرد: The letters zā', rā' and dāl are a single root, indicating swallowing, and the zā' in it stands in place of a sīn. One says 'izdarada al-luqmata yazdaridūhā' — he swallowed the morsel down. It is possible that al-zarad [chain-mail] comes from this, its true letter being sīn, so that the meaning of al-zarrād [mail-maker] is al-sarrād.
زرع:
The letters zāy, rā' and ʿayn are a root pointing to the making of a thing grow.

Al-zarʿ, sown crops, is well known, and its place is al-muzdaraʿ, the sown field. Al-Khalīl said: the origin of al-zarʿ is making grow.
