And some of them used to say: al-zarʿ is the casting of the seed into the ground. And al-zarʿ is a name for what has come up. And the origin in all of this is one.

And Zāriʿ is a dog.
زرف:
The letters zā', rā' and fā' are a root indicating striving and motion.

1. al-zarūf — a she-camel wide of stride and long of leg.
2. zarafa — he leapt.
3. zaraftu al-rajula ʿan nafsī — I pushed the man away from myself.
4. al-zarāfāt — groups of people; they are only called this when they have gathered to strive together toward some matter. It is also said 'zarāffa', with the fā' doubled. Al-Ḥajjāj used to say: 'Beware of me, and beware of these zarāfāt' — meaning those who gather in agitation over sedition and the like.
5. zarifa al-jurḥ — the wound broke open again after it had healed.
زرم:
The letters zā', rā' and mīm are a root indicating cutting off and scarcity.

1. zarima al-damʿ — the tears stopped, when they were cut off, and likewise for anything.

From this is the hadith of the Prophet, peace and blessings upon him and his family, when al-Ḥasan, peace be upon him, urinated on him and he said: 'lā tuzrimū ibnī' — meaning: do not cut off my son's water. 'Zarima al-bawlu nafsuhu' — the urine itself stopped, when it was cut off. He said, in a line of verse:
Or like the water of a well drawn dry after being full, its trickle cut off, returning only scantly.

2. It is also said that al-zarim is the miser — from the same idea.
3. zarima al-kalb — the dog's dung dried hard in its rear end.
زرى: The letters zā, rā, and the weak letter point to holding a thing in contempt and treating it lightly. One says "zarayt ʿalayhi", when you find fault with someone. And "azrayt bihi" means you belittled him, fell short in your regard for him.
زط: The letters zāy and ṭā' are not a root. And "zuṭṭ" is a word of later, non-classical coinage.
زع:
The letters zāy and ʿayn are a root that points to shaking and motion.

1. zaʿzaʿtu al-shay'a and tazaʿzaʿa huwa, I shook the thing, and it shook and became unsteady.
2. sayrun zaʿzaʿ — a hard, fast pace that makes the riding-mounts shake. Al-Hudhalī said, in a line of verse:
"and she paces on, ambling, unsteady... as a rope slips off over the pulley."
زعب:
The letters zāʾ, ʿayn and bāʾ are a single root indicating pushing and mutual pushing.

1. From this, al-zaʿb — pushing. One says "zaʿabtu lahu zaʿbatan min al-māl" — I thrust a lump of wealth on him. The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him and his family, said: "and I will give you a zaʿba [lump sum] of wealth."
2. One says "jāʾa saylun yazʿabu al-wādī" — this with the undotted letter [ʿayn] — meaning it fills it. And "jāʾa saylun yazʿabu," with this same letter, meaning it surges and pushes forward.
3. It is said al-zāʿib is the one who roams the land.

Ibn Harma said, in a line of verse:
The wandering guide well-nigh perishes in it.

4. Al-zāʿibiyya — the spears. Al-Khalīl said: they are named after Zāʿib. It has not become clear whether Zāʿib's identity is that of a man or a place, unless some transmitter has invented it. Others said: al-zāʿibī is that which, when shaken, ripples from its first end to its last, as though this were measured on the mutual surging of water in a wadi, which is its pushing-forward. This is the correct view.
5. One says "zaʿaba al-rajulu al-marʾata" when he had intercourse with her — though this is better said with the letter rāʾ [zaʿara], and that has already been discussed.

There remains in the chapter one word, which, if sound, belongs to the chapter of letter-substitution: they say al-zuʿbūb is the short one among men, and it may perhaps be al-dhuʿbūb [with a dhāl].
زعج:
The letters zāʾ, ʿayn and jīm are a single root indicating unsettling and lack of steadiness.

1. One says "azʿajtuhu uzʿijuhu izʿājan" — I unsettled him.
2. "Azʿajtuhu fa-shakhaṣa" — I unsettled him, so he rose up and departed.

Al-Khalīl said: if one said "inzaʿaja" [in the reflexive], that too would be correct.
زعر:
The letters zāʾ, ʿayn and rāʾ are a minor root indicating bad character and scarcity of good.

1. Al-zaʿāra — fierceness of character, on the pattern of "faʿāla."
2. From this chapter, al-azʿar — a place with little vegetation.

It is said that no verb form is built from al-zaʿāra.

3. From this chapter, al-azʿar — one scant of hair. The woman is "zaʿrāʾ"; one says "zaʿira yazʿaru" [he grew scant of hair].

And God knows best.
زعف:
The letters zāʾ, ʿayn and fāʾ are a minor root.

1. One says "summun zuʿāf" — a deadly poison.
2. "Mawtun zuʿāf" — a swift death.

It seems this may be by way of letter-substitution, with the zāʾ standing in place of a dhāl. One says "azʿaftuhu" and "zaʿaftuhu" when you killed him. And it is related: "zaʿafa fī ḥadīthihi," meaning he lied in his account.
زعق:
The letters zāʾ, ʿayn and qāf are a root indicating intensity — in shouting, or in bitterness, or in salinity.

1. "Ṭaʿāmun mazʿūq" — food with much salt in it.
2. Al-māʾ al-zuʿāq — salty water.

That is in the chapter of tastes.

As for the other sense:

1. "Zaʿaqtu bihi" — I shouted at him.
2. "Inzaʿaqa" — he was struck with terror.
3. Al-zaʿiq — the lively one who is startled along with his liveliness.
4. So-and-so "yazʿaqu dābbatahu" when he drives his mount hard.
5. "Rajulun zāʿiq" — a man given to shouting and startling others.
6. "Azʿaqahu al-khawfu ḥattā zaʿaq" — fear startled him until he cried out.

He said, in a line of verse:
From the terrors of the night, and dread, and the startled cry.

7. It is said al-zuʿāq is skittishness. From it, "waʿilun zaʿʿāq" — a wild goat given to shying.
8. "Muhrun mazʿūq" — a lively colt, startled along with his liveliness.

He said, in a line of verse:
Many a lively colt, given his midday drink or his evening drink, of the milk of dark she-camels with white blazes, until, in winter, he grew like the dhuʿlūq, swifter than the corner of an eye, than a bird, and one fitted with a notched arrow, and than everything created.
زعك:
The letters zāʾ, ʿayn and kāf are a minor root, if sound, indicating tarrying, and meanness, and baseness.

1. They say al-azʿakī is the short, base man. Likewise al-zuʿkūk.
2. Al-Kisāʾī said: it is said of a people "zaʿkatun" when they tarried a while.
3. Al-zaʿākīk, among camels — those of jumbled, uneven build; the singular is zuʿkūk.

He said, in a line of verse:
Its young ones, stunted and misshapen, frisk about.
زعل:
The letters zāʾ, ʿayn and lām are a minor root indicating mirth and lack of settledness, from liveliness.

1. Al-zaʿal — liveliness.
2. Al-zaʿil — the lively one.
3. One says "azʿalahu al-simanu wa-l-raʿyu" — fatness and grazing made him frisky.

Al-Hudhalī said, in a line of verse:
He ate the jamīm [pasture grass grown tall again after grazing], and a long-backed she-ass, straight like a spear-shaft, obeyed him, and the fresh pasture made him frisky.

Ṭarafa said, in a line of verse:
And a place whose male ostriches are frisky, like mangy she-camels heavy with young, on a cold day.

And sometimes this is carried further, so that one writhing from hunger is called "zaʿil."
زعم:
The letters zāy, 'ayn and mīm are two origins: the first is a saying that has no soundness or certainty in it, and the other is standing surety for something.

The first is al-za'm and al-zu'm. This is a saying that rests on nothing sound. God, glorious be His praise, said: {Those who disbelieve claim that they will never be raised up} [al-Taghābun: 7]. And the poet said, in a line of verse:
Ghudāna claimed there is a chief among them ... a huge one — whom a locust's wing would hide.

From this chapter: za'ama fī ghayri maz'am — he set his hopes where there was nothing to hope for. A poet said, in a line of verse:
A vain claim, by your father's life, and no fit place for claiming.

From this chapter is al-za'ūm, the slaughter-camel whose fatness is doubted, so that it is felt over with the hands. And al-taza''um is lying.

The other origin is: za'ama bi-al-shay' when he stood surety for it. A poet said, in a line of verse:
My wife reproaches me about provision, yet ... the sustenance of God's servants rests upon God, as He has undertaken.
That is, as He has stood surety. From this chapter is al-za'āma, which is lordship, because the chief stands as za'īm over affairs, that is, he takes charge of them as surety. And truer than that is the word of God, glorious be His praise: {They said: we miss the king's cup, and whoever brings it shall have a camel-load, and I am surety for it} [Yūsuf: 72]. It is said that al-za'āma is the chief's share of the spoil, and it is said rather that it is the best of the property. Labīd said, in a line of verse:
The arrows of the shares fly out, odd ... and even, and the chieftain's portion goes to the young man.
زغ: The letters zāy and ghayn are not a root. They say: al-zaghzagha is mockery.
زغب: The letters zāʾ, ghayn and bāʾ are a minor root, sound — it is al-zaghab, the first down that grows, among feathers. The vine, too, may "put out down" [yuzghibu] after water has run in it.
زغد:
The letters zāʾ, ghayn and dāl are a minor root indicating a strained sound.

1. From this, al-zaghd — the rumbling groan in which the one groaning strains himself.

Its origin is "zaghada ʿukkatahu" — he squeezed his skin-vessel to press the clarified butter out of it.
زغر:
The letters zāʾ, ghayn and rāʾ are a minor root. One says "zaghara al-māʾu" and "zakhara" [the water surged]. This, in my view, is not by way of letter-substitution, since the pattern of "zaghara" is sound in its own right, and what comes in the quadriliteral chapter will bear this out.

Ibn Duraid mentioned that al-zaghr is seizing by force; one says "zaghartu al-shayʾa zaghran." He said: al-zaghr is an obsolete verb-form. And Zughar is the name of a woman; it is said that the spring of Zughar is named after her.
زغف:
The letters zāʾ, ghayn and fāʾ are a minor root, sound, indicating spaciousness and surplus.

1. From this, al-zaghfa — the coat of mail; its plural is al-zaghf, meaning the roomy kind. Sometimes they said "zaghafa" and "zaghaf."

He said, in a line of verse:
Would the people bar us from the water of the Euphrates, while among us are the swords, and among us the mail-coats?

2. One says "rajulun mizghaf" — greedy, voracious.

Al-Aṣmaʿī said: "zaghafa fī ḥadīthihi" — he added to [exaggerated] his account.
زغل:
The letters zāʾ, ghayn and lām are a root indicating suckling, and pouring [food into a chick's throat], and the like.

1. One says "azghala al-ṭāʾiru farkhahu" when the bird feeds its chick [by regurgitation].

Ibn Aḥmar said, in a line of verse:
So it poured down his throat a gulp — it did not miss the throat, nor did it spill astray.

He said: this is from their saying "azghilī lahu zughlatan min siqāʾiki" — pour him out a little milk from your water-skin.

2. "Azghalat al-marʾatu min ʿazlāʾihā" — the woman poured [milk] from the spout of her water-skin.

And among what is irregular, outside the chapter: al-zughlūl, among men, is the light, nimble one.
زغم:
The letters zāʾ, ghayn and mīm are a minor root indicating the repeating of a muffled sound.

1. They said "tazaghghama al-jamalu" when the camel repeats his groaning faintly, not intensely.
2. From this, al-tazaghghum — suppressed anger, as though in his anger he repeats a sound within himself.
3. Some mentioned "tazaghghama al-faṣīlu li-ummihi" when the weaned camel-calf yearns for its mother with a faint cry.
زف:
The letters zāy and fā' are a root that points to lightness and swiftness in everything.

1. zaffa al-ẓalīmu zafīfan — the male ostrich went zafīf, when it moved swiftly.
2. From this: zuffati al-ʿarūsu ilā zawjihā, the bride was led swiftly to her husband.
3. zaffa al-qawmu fī sayrihim — the people moved swiftly on their journey. He, Glorified is His Praise, said: {and they came toward him, hurrying} [al-Ṣāffāt: 94].
4. al-zafzāfa — a strong wind that has a rushing sound, a zafzafa, that is, a swift lightness; likewise al-zafzaf.
5. They say of one whose composure has gone flighty: "his young ostrich has gone zaff," meaning his wits have taken flight.
6. ziff al-ṭā'ir — the bird's small down-feathers, because they are light.
زفت: The letters zāʾ, fāʾ and tāʾ are nothing, except al-zift [pitch/tar], and I do not know whether it is an Arabic word or not — except that "al-muzaffat" has come in the hadith, meaning [a vessel] coated with pitch. And God knows best what is correct.
زفر:
The letters zā', fā' and rā' are two roots: one indicates a load, the other a kind of sound.

The first — al-zifr, a load, plural azfār. "izdafarahu" — he carried it.

1. A man is named Zufar from this, because he izdafara [shoulders] wealth, being strong enough to bear it.
2. al-zāfira — a man's clan, because they may bear a share of what befalls him.
3. zafrat al-faras — the horse's middle.
4. al-zifr — the waterskin; from this, slave-women who carry waterskins are called zawāfir.
5. al-zufar — also used for a chief, a man of standing.

A poet said [only this half is given]:
The noble, mighty man refuses to be wronged.

The reasoning behind all these senses is one and the same.

6. zifr al-musāfir — the traveller's gear and provisions.
7. al-zufar — the great river, said to be named so because it carries so much water.

[Translator's note: the entry names two roots, one for "a load" and one for "a kind of sound," but only the "load" sense is worked through in the text given to me — the "sound" sense is not explained here.]
زفل: The letters zāʾ, fāʾ and lām are al-azfala, which is the group, the gathering. One says "jāʾū bi-azfalatihim" — they came in their whole group.
زفن: The letters zāʾ, fāʾ and nūn are not, in my view, a root, and there is nothing in it that is of use. They say al-zafn is dancing. And they say al-ziyafn is the strong one. This is not sound.
زفى:
The letters zāʾ, fāʾ and the weak letter indicate lightness and swiftness.

1. From this, "zafat al-rīḥu al-turāba" when the wind drives the dust off the face of the ground.
2. Al-zafayān — the intensity of the wind's blowing.
3. One says "nāqatun zafayān" — a swift she-camel.
4. "Qawsun zafayān" — a bow swift in releasing its arrow.
5. One says "zafā al-ẓalīmu zafyan" when the male ostrich spreads its wing.
زق:
The letters zāy and qāf are a root that points to narrowness.

1. al-zuqāq — an alley, so named for being narrower than the main streets.
2. zaqqa al-ṭā'iru farkhahu, the bird fed its chick.
3. al-ziqq — the skin used as a container.
4. al-tazqīq, of a hide — stripping it off starting from the neck.
زقب: The letters zāʾ, qāf and bāʾ are a word. One says "ṭarīqun zaqab" — a narrow path.
زقل: The letters zāʾ, qāf and lām are nothing. Except that it has been related of some of the Arabs: "zawqala fulānun ʿimāmatahu" when he let the two ends of his turban hang loose from the two sides of his head.
زقم:
The letters zā', qāf and mīm are a minor root indicating a kind of eating.

1. al-zaqm — Al-Khalīl said: the act of eating, from eating al-zaqqūm.
2. al-izdiqām — swallowing.

Ibn Durayd mentioned that some Arabs say "so-and-so tazaqqama the milk," when he drank it to excess.
زقن: The letters zāʾ, qāf and nūn are nothing, except that they sometimes said "zaqantu al-ḥimla azqunuhu" when you carried the load. "Azqantu fulānan" — I helped him with the carrying. And God knows best what is correct.
زقو:
The letters zāʾ, qāf and the weak letter are a minor root indicating a sound among sounds.

1. Al-zaqw is the verbal noun of "zaqā al-dīku yazqū" — the rooster crowed. It is said that every crier is "zāqin."

The Arabs used to say, "he is heavier than the zawāqī" — meaning the roosters — because they used to stay up talking at night, and when the roosters crowed, they would disperse.

2. Al-zuqāʾ — the crowing of the rooster.
زكت: The letters zā, kāf and tāʾ are a root, if it is sound. It is said: zakattu al-ināʾ, I filled the vessel. And God knows best.
زكر: The letters zā, kāf and rāʾ are a minor root, if it is sound, indicating a vessel called al-zukra. It is said: zakkara al-ṣabiyy and tazakkara: his belly became full.
زكل: The letters zāʾ, kāf and lām are not a root, though one word has come from it: al-zawankal, among men, is the short one.
زكم: The letters zāʾ, kāf and mīm have nothing in them except al-zukma and al-zukām [a head-cold]. They use it as a figure of speech, saying: so-and-so is the zukma of his parents, meaning he is the last-born of their children.
زكن:
The letters zā, kāf and nūn are a root disputed in its meaning. Some say it means conjecture; others say it means certainty. The precise scholars among the lexicographers say: zakintu minka kadhā means "I knew that from you." A poet said, in a line of verse:

"My heart will never again return to loving them ... I sensed from them the like of what they sensed."

They said: one does not say azkantu — though al-Khalīl did mention al-izkān. And it is said that al-zakan means conjecture.
زكى:
The letters zā, kāf and the weak letter are a root indicating growth and increase. It is said that purity is the zakāh of wealth. Some said it was named that because it is among what one hopes will bring the zakāʾ of wealth, meaning its increase and growth. Others said it was named zakāh because it is purification. They said the proof of that is His words, exalted be His praise: {Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them to grow} [al-Tawba: 103]. The origin in all of this comes back to these two meanings, growth and purity.

From growth: crops described as zākin, clearly growing. It is said, "It is a matter that will not thrive for so-and-so" (lā yazkū bi-fulānin), meaning it does not suit him. And al-zakā is the even one, meaning a pair.

As for the hamzated word, it is close to what came before it. Al-Farrāʾ said: a man described as zukaʾa has ready cash, and much of it. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: al-zukaʾa is the man of means.

And among what falls outside this chapter altogether is their saying: zakaʾat al-nāqa bi-waladihā, tazkaʾu bihi zakʾan — said of a she-camel when she casts her young out near her hind legs in giving birth.
زل:
The letters zāy and lām are a root that runs consistently by the same pattern in the doubled form, and likewise in every three-letter word where a zāy is followed by a lām. This is among the remarkable things about this root.

1. zalla ʿan makānihi zalīlan wa-zallan, he slipped from his place.
2. al-mā' al-zulāl — sweet water, because it slips easily over the surface of the tongue for its thinness.
3. al-zalla — a mistake, because the one who errs has slipped off the path of what is right.
4. tazalzalati al-arḍu, the earth shook; zulzilat zilzālan, it was made to shake, a quaking.
5. al-mizalla — a slippery place.

As for al-dhi'b al-azall — the wolf, meaning one lean and flat in the haunches — Ibn al-Aʿrābī said it is so named from their saying "zalla" when it ran fast; this is the correct pattern. Then a woman flat in the haunches was compared to it, and so called "zallā'." And if al-arsaḥ, flat-haunched, is as it is said, then this also fits the pattern already mentioned, because the flesh has slipped away from its hindquarters, and likewise from the hindquarters of a woman who is rasḥā', flat in the haunches.

6. al-zulzul — like one restless, because he does not settle in his place.

Among what falls outside this root is al-zalazil: household furnishings and goods, on the pattern faʿalil.
زلج:
The letters zā, lām and jīm are a minor root indicating being driven forward and pushing.

1. al-muzallaj — said of a livelihood: kept going by the bare minimum needed to survive.
2. al-muzallaj — one who is held back from every good thing, from sufficiency and self-sufficient means.

He said, in a line of verse:

"I called for what had befallen me, and there answered me ... a noble one among the young men, not held back."

3. al-zalj — swiftness in walking and elsewhere; anything swift is zālij.
4. an arrow described as zālij — one that shoots swiftly off the bow.
5. al-muzallaj — one pushed away from his due standing.
6. al-mizlāj — the woman thin in the buttocks, as if she were likened, in her slightness, to the swift arrow.
زلح:
The letters zā, lām and ḥāʾ are not a root that runs to a regular pattern in the language, though words have come in it whose soundness God knows best. They say: qaṣʿatun zalaḥlaḥa, a bowl that has no bottom.

Ibn al-Sikkīt said: al-zalaḥlaḥ, of men, is the light, nimble one. And they said: al-zalaḥlaḥ is a valley that is not deep. If this is sound, then the word indicates a thing's spreading flat, with no depth to it.
زلخ:
The letters zā, lām and khāʾ are a root, if sound, indicating a thing's slipperiness.

1. *al-zalkh* — a slippery spot.
2. *biʾrun zalūkh* — a well whose top has a slippery place that makes anyone standing on it slip.
3. *al-zalkh* — your raising your hand in shooting an arrow to the furthest you are able, meaning by it the furthest range.

He said, in a line of verse (the wording is obscure):

"From a hundred shots of zalkh, with a piercing arrow."

4. *al-zalkh* — as some of them said, the furthest limit reached by one who competes at long-range shooting.
5. *al-zullakha* — they say it is an ailment. This is a statement that wants looking into.
زلع:
The letters zā, lām and ʿayn are a root indicating cracking and a thing's leaving its place.

1. al-zalaʿ — the cracking of skin.
2. tazallaʿat yaduhu — his hand became chapped, cracked.
3. zaliʿat jirāḥatuhu — his wound went bad.

Al-Khalīl said: al-zalaʿ is cracking on the back of the hand; if it is on the inside of the palm, it is called kalaʿ.

4. al-zalʿ — snatching something away by stealth.
زلف:
The letters zā', lām and fā' point to pushing forward and moving up close to something. From this one says izdalafa al-rajul — the man came forward. Muzdalifa at Mecca is named from this, because the people draw near to Minā after the departure from 'Arafāt. One says: so-and-so has zulfā with so-and-so, that is, nearness. God, mighty and glorious, said: {And indeed he has nearness with Us} [Ṣād: 25]. Al-zalaf and al-zulfa are a step and a rank. Azlaftu al-rajul ilā kadhā — I brought the man close to such a thing.

As for the words of the poet, in a line of verse:
Until, when the water of the cisterns had dried away, after they had been brimming full like the zalaf.
Some said: al-zalaf are the green basins. If that is so, they were named that because water does not stay in them when they are full, but pushes out over the edge. Others said: al-mazālif are lands between the open desert and the sown country. They were named that for their nearness to the sown country. As for al-zulaf of the night, they are stretches of it, because each stretch of it comes close to the next.
زلق:
The letters zā', lām and qāf are a single root indicating a thing slipping from its place. From that: al-zalaq. One says azlaqat al-ḥāmil, when the pregnant female miscarried her young; and it is said — more correctly — when she expelled the water [of the womb] and did not retain it. al-mazlaqa and al-mazlaq — a place one cannot keep footing on.

As for His saying, exalted be His praise: {And indeed, those who disbelieve would almost make you slip with their eyes} [al-Qalam: 51] — its true meaning is that from the sharpness of their gaze, out of envy, they would almost dislodge you from your place. He said, in a line of verse:
"A look that unseats the very footholds of feet."

It is said that al-zaliq is a man who, on approaching a woman, spends himself before he reaches her. He said, in a line of verse:
"Indeed al-Zubayr is zaliq and zummaliq [hasty, premature]."

Ibn al-A'rābī said: zalaqa l-rajulu ra'sahu — he shaved his head. As for the line of Ru'ba, "as though it were dun and piebald at the zalaq," it is said al-zalaq there is the rump, of that animal and of any riding-beast — named so because the hand slips off it, and likewise whatever rain or dew falls on it. And God knows best.
زلم:
The letters zā', lām and mīm are a root indicating leanness and fineness together with smoothness — though sometimes a word strays from it.

1. al-zalam and al-zulam — a divining arrow-shaft, used to draw lots. They did this in pre-Islamic times, and it was forbidden in Islam by His saying, exalted be His praise: {and that you seek decision by the divining arrows} [al-Mā'ida: 3]. As for the line of Labīd, "its azlām slip on the moist earth," it is said he meant the cow's cloven hooves, by way of comparison.
2. They say rajulun muzallam — a lean, thin man.
3. al-zalama — the small piece of flesh that hangs from a goat's neck; it has two of them.
4. al-zalam also — the dewclaws behind the cloven hoof.
5. al-muzallam — the poorly-fed one, so called because he grows lean and thin from it.

As for their saying "he is the slave, zulmatan," some said it means pure, sheer in servitude — the origin being a comparison to the dewclaws behind the hooves. As for "al-azlam al-jadhaʿ," it is said to mean time, fate; and it is also said the lion is called by this name.
زم:
The letters zāy and mīm are a single root that points to going forward straight and directly.

1. al-zimām — the halter-rope, because the camel moves forward when it is pulled with it, going straight ahead. One says zamamtu al-baʿīra azummuhu, I put a halter on the camel and led it.
2. It is said: "amru banī fulānin zamam," just as one says amam, meaning: close by, direct.
3. They swear, saying: "No, by Him toward whose House my face is zamam," meaning: directly facing it, aimed straight at it.
4. al-zamm — going forward in travel.

Among what falls outside this root is al-zimzima: a group of people. Al-Shaybānī said: al-zimzīm — the large, mature camels.
زمت: The letters zā, mīm and tāʾ are not a root, because the word in it belongs to the category of letter-substitution. They say: rajulun zamīt and zimmīt, meaning silent. The zāʾ here is substituted for a ṣād; the true root is al-ṣamt, silence.
زمج: The letters zā, mīm and jīm amount to nothing. They say: al-zummaj is a bird. Al-zimijjā is the base of a bird's tail; its true form has a kāf: zimikkā. It is said: zamajtu al-siqāʾ, I filled the waterskin — but this is a metathesis; it is really jazamtuhu, which has already been mentioned.
زمح: The letters zā, mīm and ḥāʾ are a single word. They call a short man zummaḥ.
زمخ: The letters zā, mīm and khāʾ are not a root. Al-Khalīl said: al-zāmikh is the one who holds his nose up haughtily; noses described as zummakh are the long ones. If this is sound, its true letter is shīn: shamakha.
زمر:
The letters zā', mīm and rā' are two roots: one indicates scantiness of a thing, and the other a kind of sound.

The first: al-zamar — scantiness of hair. al-zamir — one with little hair. One says rajulun zamiru l-murū'a — a man scant in manly virtue.

The other root: al-zamr and al-zimār — the cry of the ostrich. One says zamarat tazmuru wa tazmiru zimāran.

As for al-zumra, the group of people, it is derived from this second root, because when people gather they raise a clamor, a zimār. As for al-zammāra, which came in the hadith — "he forbade earning from al-zammāra" — they said it means the adulteress. If this is sound, then perhaps her voice's tone was likened to piping [zamr]. But they have also said it is rather al-rammāza, the woman who signals to men with her eyebrows — and this is closer to the truth.
زمع:
The letters zā, mīm and ʿayn are a single root indicating lowness, meagerness and abasement.

1. al-zamaʿ — the small growths behind the cloven hooves of sheep and goats; the base, lowly sort among people were likened to this.

As for al-Shammākh's saying, "ʿikrishatin zamūʿ," al-ʿikrisha is the female hare, and al-zamūʿ is the one having those growths. This belongs to the same chapter.

As for their saying al-zamāʿ, and azmaʿa kadhā, this has two possible explanations: either it is a metathesis of ʿazama, he resolved, or the zāʾ is substituted for a jīm, as though from ijmāʿ al-qawm and ijmāʿ al-raʾy, the people's and the opinion's coming to one accord.

2. zamīʿ — the swift one.

A line is recited:

"One calling to a swift parting, resolute."

They said: al-zamīʿ is the brave man who resolves and then does not turn back; the plural is al-zumaʿāʾ, and the verbal noun is al-zamāʿ. Al-Kisāʾī said: rajulun zamīʿu l-raʾy means one sound in judgement. Its root is what I have mentioned, of metathesis or substitution.

As for the zamaʿ that seizes a person like trembling, that is a report heard, and I do not know its soundness; perhaps it is among what deviates from the root I have set down.
زمق: The letters zā, mīm and qāf amount to nothing, even though they say zamaqa shaʿrahu, when he plucked it out. If this is sound, the true root is zabaqa, already mentioned.
زمك: The letters zā, mīm and kāf: Ibn Durayd and others mentioned that zā, mīm and kāf indicate one thing's interlocking into another. He said: from this comes the derivation of al-zimikkā, the base where a bird's tail grows.
زمل:
The letters zā’, mīm and lām are two roots: one points to carrying a heavy load, and the other to a sound.

The first: al-zāmila — a camel that a man relies on to carry his baggage.

1. izdamaltu al-shay’a — I carried the thing.
2. ‘iyālātun azmila — a large, burdensome household; this belongs to the same root, as though they were a full load that one can barely shoulder or bear.

From this root too, al-zummayl — a weak man who, when some matter presses on him, tazammala, wrapping himself in layer upon layer of clothing until he becomes like a bundle to be carried. Uḥayḥa said, in a line of verse: ‘No, by your father — no lazy, wrapped-up weakling among the young men serves as I do.’

3. al-muzāmala — riding paired as counterweights on a camel, one on each side.

As for the other root: al-azmal, a sound, as in the poet’s saying, in a line of verse: ‘she has, after the evening chill, a low murmuring sound.’

Straying from both roots is al-izmīl, the blade. From it: akhadhtu al-shay’a bi-azmalihi — I took the thing entirely, with everything belonging to it.
زمن:
The letters zā, mīm and nūn are a single root indicating a span of time.

1. al-zamān — time, whether little or much; one says zamān or zaman, plural azmān and azmina.

The poet said, about zaman:

"And I was, for a time, in Iraq ... clean in my encampment, long in lingering." (The last phrase is obscure in the source.)

And he said, about al-azmān:

"The times of Laylā, the year of Laylā and her guardian..." (A fragment; obscure.)

They say: "laqītuhu dhāta l-zumayn," meaning by that the passing of a stretch of time.

As for al-zamāna, the affliction that befalls a person and disables him, its true letter is ḍād — it is al-ḍamāna, and it has been written accordingly under ḍād.
زن:
The letters zāʾ and nūn are a single word; nothing branches from it and nothing is measured by analogy on it. One says "azzantu fulānan bi-kadhā," when you accuse him of it. And he is "yuzannu bihi" — accused of it.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
If you have falsely accused me of it, Juzʾ, then may you meet its like swiftly.
زنج: The letters zā, nūn and jīm amount to nothing — though they do say al-zanaj is thirst, but there is no regular pattern for that.
زنح: The letters zā, nūn and ḥāʾ are like the one before it. Some of them mentioned that al-tazannuḥ is a certain openness in speech.
زند:
The letters zā, nūn and dāl are two roots: one is a body part, which is then used as a likeness for other things; the other is evidence of narrowness in something.

The first: al-zand, the end-bone of the forearm — there are two zands. The fire-stick struck to kindle fire is then likened to it and also called al-zand, the upper one; the lower one is al-zanda.

The other root, al-muzannad:

1. *thawbun muzannad* — a garment, when it is narrow.
2. *ḥawḍun muzannad* — a trough, likewise narrow.
3. *rajulun muzannad* — a man narrow, tight-tempered. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: it is said tazannada fulān, when he is at a loss for an answer and grows angry. ʿAdiyy said:

"So say the like of what they said, and do not tazannad."

4. *al-muzannad* — one who is carried along; it is said zannadtu al-nāqa, when you thread small pegs through the loosened skin at her flanks and bind them with hair — done when her womb has prolapsed after giving birth.
زنر:
The letters zā, nūn and rāʾ are not a root, because a nūn is never followed by a rāʾ in this pattern. However there is one word in this chapter: they say that al-zanānīr are small pebbles that, when the wind blows over them, give off a sound. (Al-Zanānīr is also a place near Jurash.) Ibn Muqbil said, in a fragment that is obscure:

"Zanānīr — the breaths of late summer are upon it..."
زنق: The letters zā, nūn and qāf are a root indicating narrowness or the narrowing of something. They say: zanaqtu al-faras, when you hobble a horse by its four legs. Al-zanaqa is like a narrow, bending passage in a lane or elsewhere. A certain kind of jewelry is called zināq.
زنك: The letters zā, nūn and kāf are not a root, and there is no regular pattern for it. It has been related that al-zawannak is the short, unsightly one.
زنم:
The letters zā’, nūn and mīm are a root pointing to one thing hanging attached to another.

1. al-zanīm — one falsely attached to a lineage not his own. Likewise al-muzannam; the image is drawn from the two zanamas of a goat, the two small flaps that hang from its ear.
2. al-zanama — the piece of flesh that hangs down in the throat.

The poet said of al-zanīm, in a line of verse: ‘A hanger-on the men call in as an extra, just as leg-pieces are added on to widen out a hide.’
زنى:
The letters zā, nūn and the weak letter do not relate to one another, and none of them can be measured against the others.

1. al-zinā — well known. It is said it may be pronounced with a long or a short final vowel. A line is recited, ascribed to al-Farazdaq:

"O Abū Ḥāḍir, whoever fornicates, his fornication becomes known ... and whoever drinks wine will surely grow drunk."

It is said, for the relative adjective from zinā, zinawiyy; and the child is called li-zinya or li-zanya, the fatḥa, zanya, being the more correct.

2. The hamzated word: it is said zanaʾa fī l-jabal, yaznaʾu, zunūʾan and zanʾan, meaning he climbed steeply up the mountain.

3. al-zanāʾ — the short one, of anything. He said:

"And they enter into the confined shade with their heads ... and you would take them for wasted-thin, though they are sound."

And another said:

"And when I was thrown down into one whose bottom is narrow ... dust-dark, dark, among the excavated pits."

4. al-zanāʾ — one holding back his urine. "And the Messenger of God, God's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, forbade that a man should pray while he is zanāʾ."
زهد:
The letters zā, hā and dāl are a root pointing to the scantness of a thing.

1. al-zahīd — a scant, small thing.
2. muzhid — one with little wealth. The Messenger of God (peace and blessings upon him and his family) said: "The best of people is a believer who is muzhid" — that is, one who has little. From this one says azhada izhādan.

Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
They will not seek her secret for wealth's sake, nor give her up for her scantness.

3. al-zahāda — used of this world; al-zuhd — used specifically of religion. Al-Khalīl said this.
4. zahīd (of a man) — one who eats little; he is also narrow of temperament. Al-Liḥyānī said this.
5. al-zahīd (of a valley) — one that takes in little water, so said some.
6. al-zahād — land that runs off (with water) from the least rain.

Close to this root is their saying "take the zahd of what suffices you" — meaning, the amount that suffices you.

It is related from al-Shaybānī — if sound, it is irregular against the root we have established — that he said "zahadtu al-nakhla" of estimating a palm's yield of dates by eye.
زهر:
The letters zā, hā and rā are a single root pointing to beauty, light and clarity.

1. al-zuhara — the star (Venus).
2. al-zahr — the blossom of every plant; one says azhara al-nabātu, the plant blossomed. Some used to say al-nūr is the white blossom and al-zahr the yellow.
3. zahrat al-dunyā — the beauty of this world.
4. al-azhar — the moon.
5. zaharat al-nāru — the fire blazed and gave light; and they say "zaharat bika nārī", my fire has blazed bright because of you.

Irregular against this root is their saying izdahartu bi'l-shay'i, said when you keep and hold onto a thing carefully. The Messenger of God (peace and blessings upon him and his family) said to Abū Qatāda, about the vessel he had given him: "Keep it carefully (izdahir bihi), for it has an importance" — meaning, hold onto it. It is possible that this too may be carried back to the root, because when one keeps a thing carefully it is as though he does so because he finds it beautiful. And a poet said, in a line of verse:
as she guarded it carefully

And perhaps al-mizhar, which is the lute, is carried back to what we have mentioned of the root, for it is close to it.
زهف:
The letters zā, hāʾ and fāʾ are a root indicating a thing's going away. It is said izdahafa l-shayʾ, said when he made off with it. A woman of the Arabs said:

"O who felt for my two little sons, who are ... my hearing and my marrow — for my marrow today is carried off."

And from it is said azhafahu l-mawt, death carried him off; and of this chapter is izdahafahu, when he hurried him along.

He said, in a line whose wording is obscure:

"Your saying of sayings, along with the swearing of oaths ... in it is excess, whatever excess it may be."

Some said: al-izdihāf is padding, exaggeration, in speech. If this is sound, then it is because it is a going away from the truth and an overstepping of it.
زهق:
The letters zāy, hā' and qāf are a single root, indicating going ahead, passing on, and going beyond.

1. zahaqat nafsuhu — his soul departed (he died).
2. zahaqa al-bāṭil — falsehood passed away, meaning it went off.
3. zahaqa al-faras amāma al-khayl — the horse shot ahead of the other horses, meaning it outran and got in front of them.
4. zahaqa al-sahm — the arrow overshot, when it went past the target.
5. faras dhāt azāhīq — a horse of "surges," meaning of running, outstripping, and getting ahead.
6. Also from this root: al-zahq, the bottom of a thing, because a thing goes down and disappears into it when it falls.

Ru'ba said, in a line of verse:
as though their forelegs plunged down into the depth.

7. As for their saying azhaqa inā'ahu — he filled his vessel to overflowing — if that is sound, it belongs to this root, because when it is full it runs over, overflows, and passes on.
8. Also from this root: al-zāhiq, the fat one, because it has gone past the moderate limit until it has packed on flesh.
9. They say zahaqa mukhkhuhu — its marrow "went to fullness," meaning it grew dense.

Zuhayr said, of al-zāhiq, in a line of verse:
the one leading the horses, their heels turned aside — among them the lean and among them the fat, well-greased one.

10. Also from this root: al-zahūq, a well deep at the bottom.

As for their saying "the people are zuhāq mi'a," about a hundred — it is possible, if sound, that it comes from the root we have mentioned, as though their number went forward until it reached that. It is also possible that it comes from letter-substitution, as if the hamza had been changed into a qāf. And it is possible that it is simply irregular.
زهك: The letters zā, hāʾ and kāf have nothing to them, except that Ibn Durayd mentioned that they say zahakat al-rīḥ al-turāb, the wind zahaka'd the dust, like sahakat.
زهل: The letters zā, hāʾ and lām are a word indicating the smoothness of a thing. A horse is described as zuhlūl, meaning smooth.
زهم:
The letters zā, hāʾ and mīm are a single root indicating fatness, grease and the like.

From that: al-zaham, which is the hand becoming greasy from meat. Some mentioned that al-zuhm is specifically the fat of wild game, a name for that alone; and they call the fat one zahim.

As for their report, from Abū Zayd, that al-muzāhama is nearness, and it is said zāhama fulān al-arbaʿīn, meaning he drew near to forty — it is possible this is carried on the root already mentioned, as if he meant smearing himself with it and coming into contact with it. It is also possible that it is by letter-substitution, the mīm standing for a qāf, since al-zāhiq is the very same as al-samīn, the fat one — and we have already mentioned it.
زهو:
The letters zā, hāʾ and the weak letter are two roots: one indicates pride and boasting, the other indicates beauty.

The first: al-zahw, which is boasting. The poet said:

"Whenever I intend other than the pride of kings ... I will make you a band upon ḥuyyaḍ." (The last word is obscure.)

Of this chapter: zuhiya al-rajul, so he is mazhūw, when he grows proud and self-important.

Of this chapter: zahati l-rīḥu l-nabāt, when the wind shook the plant, tazhāhu — the logic being that one made vain by self-admiration goes off swaying from side to side.

The other root: al-zahw, the goodly appearance. From that, al-zahw, the reddening and yellowing of palm fruit as it ripens. Some related zahā and azhā; al-Aṣmaʿī used to say it is only zahā.

As for Ibn Muqbil's saying:

"And never say zahwan, whatever you tell me ... old age has left me no zahw, nor has advancing years."

Some said: al-zahw here means falsehood and lying, and the sense in it is that it belongs to the first chapter, from pride and vanity.

As for al-zuhāʾ, it is an estimate of a number, and it is among what falls outside both roots altogether.
زوج:
The letters zāy, wāw and jīm are a root that points to one thing being paired with another. Of that is [al-zawj, the woman's husband; and the woman is] her husband's zawj, and this is the eloquent usage. God, exalted be His praise, said: {Dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden} [al-Baqara: 35]. And one says so-and-so has two zawj of pigeons, meaning a male and a female. As for His words, mighty and exalted, about plants: {of every delightful zawj} [al-Ḥajj: 5], it is said He meant colour by it, as though He said: of every delightful colour. And it is not far-fetched that this belongs to what we mentioned, because one thing is paired with another that is close to it. And likewise their calling the covering that is thrown over a camel-litter a zawj, because it is a mate to what it is cast over. Labīd said, in a line of verse:
Of every close-wrapped litter whose poles are shaded by a covering over it, a curtain and its cloth.
زوح: The letters zā, wāw and ḥāʾ are a root indicating drawing aside and departing. It is said zāḥa ʿan makānihi, yazūḥu, when he withdrew from his place, and azaḥtuhu, I moved him away. Sometimes they also say azāḥa, yuzīḥu.
زود: The letters zā', wāw and dāl are a root indicating moving on with something good, whether from labor or earning. This is a definition set by al-Khalīl. He said: everyone who moved on carrying something good from labor or earning has tazawwada [provisioned himself]. Others said: al-zawd is the laying-in of al-zād, which is food taken for a journey. al-mizwad — the bag made to hold provisions. And the non-Arabs were nicknamed "the napes of the provision-bags."
زور:
The letters zāy, wāw and rā' are a single root, indicating leaning and turning away. From it, al-zūr, falsehood, because it turns away from the path of truth. Zawwara fulānun al-shay'a tazwīran, so-and-so fabricated the thing — to the point that they say zawwara al-shay'a fī nafsihi, he devised it in his own mind, because he turns it away from the course that would be nearer to the listener's acceptance. As for their calling the idol zūr, that fits the analogy exactly. A verse:
They came with their idols, and we came with the solid one.

1. al-zawar — leaning. One says izwarra 'an kadhā, he turned away from such a thing.
2. al-zā'ir — the visitor, of this chapter, because in visiting you he has turned away from others toward you.

Then, carried further by the same reasoning, the chief of a people, the one in charge of their affairs, is called al-zuwayr, because they all turn away from everyone else toward him. A verse:
By the hands of men with no truce between them ... driving to death the unyielding chief.

They also say, "This is a man with no zawr," meaning he has no place of recourse to return to. Al-tazwīr is the honouring of a visitor. Al-zawr is the visiting party — used for one person, two, a group, and for women alike. A poet said:
Their walk at al-Khubayb sways gently ... as the visiting young women sway together.

As for their saying that al-ziwarr means the strong, powerful one, that is really from al-zawr, the upper chest — an anomaly outside the root we have set down.
زوع:
The letters zā', wāw and ʿayn are a single word. One says 'zāʿa al-nāqata bi-zimāmihā zawʿan' — he pulled the she-camel by her nose-rein, when he tugged her. Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
Pull at the rein — the deep of night lies piled up.
زوف: The letters zā', wāw and fā' are not a root, except that they say 'mawtun zuwāf' — a sudden death, meaning a swift one.
زوق: The letters zā', wāw and qāf are not a root. Their saying 'zawwaqtu al-shay'a' — I adorned the thing and gilded it over — is not from a root either; they say it comes from al-zāwūq, which is mercury. All of this is just talk.
زوك:
The letters zā', wāw and kāf are a word, if it is sound. They say that al-zawk is the walk of the crow, and they recite:
In the shamelessness of an adulteress, and the walk of a crow.
And they say from this 'zawzakat al-mar'a' — the woman hurried in her walk. This chapter is close to the one before it.
زول:
The letters zā', wāw and lām are a single root indicating a thing's moving away from its place. They say: the thing zāla, a zawāl; and the sun zālat from the middle of the sky, tazūlu (it passes its zenith). One says: azaltuhu from the place, and zawwaltuhu from it (I removed it).

Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
And a white fawn that does not shy from us, though its mother, when she sees us, is driven far off in flight from us.

It is said that al-zā'ila is anything that moves.

He recited, in a line of verse:
I used to be a man who once shot at moving creatures, but now I have bid farewell to shooting at moving creatures.

Outside this chapter is their saying: a thing is zawl, meaning astonishing. A zawla woman is one who is nimble.

Al-Ṭirimmāḥ said, in a line of verse:
And a lively one among them cast words to me — flirting in speech, or gazing at the words of one who flirts.
زون:
The letters zā', wāw and nūn are not, in my view, a root. Yet they say: al-zawn is an idol, and at other times they say al-zawn is a house of idols. And they may say 'zānahu yazūnuhu' meaning 'yazīnuhu' — he adorned it.

1. al-ziwanna — a short woman.
2. ziwann — a short man.
3. al-zawanzā — a short man.

All of this is just talk.
زوي:
The letters zā, wāw and yāʾ are a root indicating gathering and coming together. It is said zawaytu l-shayʾ, I gathered it. The Messenger of God, God's blessings and peace upon him and his family, said: "The earth was gathered for me, and I was shown its easts and its wests, and the dominion of my nation will reach as far as was gathered for me of it." He means: the earth was gathered to me.

1. zawā l-rajulu mā bayna ʿaynayhi — he drew his brows together, contracting them.

Al-Aʿshā said:

"Yazīd turns his gaze from me as though ... he had drawn cupping-glasses together, between his eyes, upon me.

So let not what has been drawn together spread out from between your eyes ... and do not meet me except with your nose humbled."

2. inzawat al-jilda fī l-nār — the skin shriveled, contracted, in the fire.
3. zāwiyat al-bayt — the corner of the house, named for the meeting of its two walls.
4. al-ziyy — goodliness of appearance.
5. zawā l-irtha ʿan wārithihi, yazwīhi zayyan — he kept the inheritance away from its heir.

Among what deviates from this root, with no known pattern or derivation, is al-zawzāʾa, meaning driving off skillfully; it is said zawzaytu bihi.

It is said al-zīzāʾ is the tips of feathers. Al-zīzāʾa is a hillock, plural al-zīzāʾ and al-zayāzī, in a line of the Hudhalī poet:

"...and he completes the rugged hillocks of the hills."

And from this, qidrun zūzīya, meaning a huge pot.

And among what has no derivation at all is al-zawʾ, which is death, fate.
زيب:
The letters zā', yā' and bā' are a root indicating lightness, liveliness, and the like; the origin is lightness. They say al-azyab is liveliness, and they say 'a man passed by with azyab' when he passed quickly. From this is their calling a disapproved deed azyab — this fits the pattern, because whoever sees or hears of it makes light of it. He said, in a line of verse:
She lays on the neighbor-woman the fault of the absent men, while she keeps her husband up at night in azyab.
From this chapter too is their calling a lowly man, or one who falsely claims kinship, azyab; and they say of one whose stride draws close together: azyab. I have told you that the whole chapter goes back to lightness and what is close to it.
Among what may fairly be called irregular, outside the chapter, is their calling the south wind azyab.
زيت: The letters za, ya and ta are a single word: al-zayt, olive oil, well known. One says 'zittuhu' — I greased it with olive oil, and it is then 'mazyut'.
زيج: The letters zā', yā' and jīm are not a root. Yet they call the mason's cord al-zīj. I do not know whether it is genuine Arabic or not.
زيح: The letters zā', yā' and ḥā' are a single root, and it is the departure of a thing and its passing away. One says 'zāḥa al-shay'u yazīḥu' — the thing went away, when it departs. And I say 'azaḥtu ʿillatahu fa-zāḥat, wa-hiya tazīḥu' — I removed his ailment, so it went away, and it keeps going away.
زيد:
The letters zā', yā' and dāl are a root pointing to excess. They say zāda al-shay'u yazīdu, the thing increased, so it is zā'id. And these are a people zayd upon such and such a number, that is, more than it. He said, in a line of verse:
And you are a company more than a hundred, so gather your affair into a plot and plot against me.
And one says a thing of many zayāyid, that is, many increases; and sometimes they said zawā'id. And they say of the lion: dhū zawā'id, one with excesses. They said: it is the one that goes beyond bounds in his roaring and his onset. And the she-camel tatazayyad in her walking, when she strains herself beyond her strength. And they relate the line:
So say the like of what they said, and do not go beyond it -
with the yā', as though he meant going too far in speech.
زير:
The letters zā', yā' and rā' are not a root. They say: a man is zīr — one who loves to sit with women and converse with them. In my view its origin is a wāw, from 'zāra yazūru' — he visited — with the wāw turned to yā' because of the kasra before it, as one says 'huwa ḥidthu nisā'' [he is a companion of women]. He said of al-zīr, in a line of verse:
Whoever is a zīr in idle nights, in frivolity and infatuation — then I am not a zīr.
زيغ: The letters zāy, yā' and ghayn are a root pointing to a thing's leaning aside. One says zāgha yazīghu zayghan — he swerved. Al-tazayyugh is leaning to one side, and qawm zāgha, that is, men who swerve away. And zāghat al-shams, and that is when the sun declines and the shadow comes back. God, glorious be His praise, said: {So when they swerved, God made their hearts swerve} [al-Ṣaff: 5]. As for their saying tazayyaghat al-mar'a, that the woman adorned herself, this is from the chapter of letter-substitution: it is a nūn turned into a ghayn.
زيف:
The letters zā', yā' and fā' — there is talk about them, and I do not think any of it sound.

1. dirham zā'if and zayf — a counterfeit coin.
2. zāfa al-jamalu fī mashyihi yazīfu — the camel quickened its pace.
3. al-mar'atu tazīfu fī mashyihā — the woman sways as she walks, as though turning about.
4. al-ḥamāmatu tazīfu ʿinda al-ḥamām — the pigeon does this near the other pigeons.

As for what is related in the saying of ʿAdī, in a line of verse:
They left me beside palaces, and along the flanks of palaces whose overhanging ledges have climbing-stairs.
They say that al-zayf here is the ledge that shields the wall, and it is also read 'li-zayfihinna'. All of this is just talk, and God knows best.
زيل: The letters zā', yā' and lām are not a root; rather the yā' in it is turned from a wāw. That has already been dealt with, and I gave the words of this wording there. Al-tazāyul is parting from one another. One says zayyaltu baynahu — that is, I separated them. God Almighty said: {So We parted them from one another} [Yūnus: 28]. It is said that al-zayal is a wide gap between the two thighs, like faḥaj — bow-leggedness. It is reported from al-Shaybānī, if it is sound, tazāyala fulān 'an fulān — when he holds back from him out of shyness. And that is that same sense, if it is sound.
زيم:
The letters zā', yā' and mīm are a root indicating gathering together. One says 'laḥmun zīyam' — compact, firm flesh. And one says 'the people gathered and became zīyam' [a mass]. Al-Khalīl said, in a line of verse:
And the horses run in a mass around us.
زين:
The letters zāy, yā' and nūn are a sound root pointing to a thing's beauty and to the making of it beautiful. So al-zayn, adornment, is the opposite of al-shayn, disfigurement. One says zayyantu al-shay' tazyīnan — I adorned the thing. And azyanat al-arḍ, and izzayyanat, and izdānat, when its herbage has made it fair. And it is said, if it is sound, that al-zayn is a cock's comb. And they recite:
And you came on a mule with nine men escorting you ... as though you were a cock with a lopsided comb, one-eyed.
سأب: The letters sīn, hamza and bā' are not a root that branches, but they say: sa'abahu sa'ban, meaning he strangled him. And al-sa'b is the water-skin, and likewise al-mis'ab. As for the same word with tā', they also say sa'atahu, meaning he strangled him. In all of that there is room for doubt.
سأد:
The letters sīn, hamza and dāl are two words that do not follow a consistent pattern. Al-is'ād is persistent travel by night. The other word is al-sa'd, the reopening of a wound. And a poet recited:

So I spent that night wakeful, sleepless, meeting what any meeter of it meets, from the sa'd.

And sometimes they said: sa'adat al-ibilu al-mā', meaning the camels shunned the water.
سأل: The letters sīn, hamza and lām are a single word. One says sa'ala yas'alu su'ālan wa-mas'alatan — he asked, asking, a question. And a man is su'ala when he asks a great deal.
سأو:
The letters sīn, hamza and wāw are a word disputed in its meaning. Some said: al-sa'w is one's homeland. Others said: al-sa'w is ambition. A poet said:

As though I, from love of Kharqā', were one struck down, bloodied at the pastern, of far-reaching ambition, love-smitten.

And God knows best what is right.
سب:
The letters sīn and bā': some of the language scholars — I think it was Ibn Duraid — held that the origin sense of this chapter is cutting, from which reviling was then derived. What he said is correct, and most of the chapter is built on it.

1. al-sibb — a woman's head-veil, because it is cut from its loom.

As for the origin sense, al-sabb is wounding; one says "sababtu al-nāqa" — I hamstrung the she-camel, when you wound it.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
What was the fault of the Banū Mālik ... that a youth of theirs was cursed, and so he cursed back?

He means the mutual feuding between Ghālib ibn Ṣaʿṣaʿa and Suḥaym. His saying "subba" means "was cursed"; his saying "sabba" means "wounded". Al-sabb is reviling, and there is no cutting-off sharper than reviling. The one with whom you exchange curses is called a "sibb".

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Do not curse me, for you are no match for my cursing ... my match in cursing is a noble man among men.

It is said: "Do not curse the camels, for in them is the staunching of blood" — this forbids reviling them. As for their calling camels "musabbaba", that comes from what is said in praise of them: "God fight them, how fine their worth is!" — just as one says in astonishment at a person, "God fight him!" This is an exclamation, not a prayer meant literally.

One says "rajul subaba" of a man who curses people a great deal, and "rajul subba" of a man who is cursed a great deal. It is said there was among the tribe an "usbūba", a matter over which they traded curses. It is said "maḍat sabbatun min al-dahr", meaning a stretch of time passed:
And the mention of you, again and again, is a wonder to me.

As for the rope, it is al-sabab; it is possible this is an exception to the origin sense mentioned, and it is possible to say it is a separate root pointing to length and extension.

From this: al-sabab. And from this too: al-sibb, the head-veil already mentioned. The turban too is called "sibb". Al-sibb is also the rope, in the saying of al-Hudhalī, in a line of verse:
He let himself down over her between a rope and a cord.

From this chapter also: al-sibsab, the vast open wasteland, in the saying of Abū Du'ād, in a line of verse:
And a gaping, vast waste, over which ... its dust-swirl runs, a broad plain.

As for al-sabāsib, it is a festival day of theirs, and I do not know what it is derived from.
He said:
They are greeted with fragrant herbs on the day of al-Sabāsib.
سبت:
The letters sīn, bā' and tā' are a single root pointing to rest and stillness. An easy, soft pace is called sabt. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And a she-camel lean in the flanks — as for her day, it is a gentle amble, and as for her night, it is a brisk trot.
Then upon that was carried al-sabt, the shaving of the head. And there is recited about that what confirms this analogy, namely his words, in a line of verse:
He wakes drunk and comes to the evening slack and still.
because at the end of the day he is heavy and moves little; and for that reason a man dazed out of his senses is called masbūt.

As for al-sabt that comes after Friday, it is said that it was named so because creation was finished and completed on Friday, so the day after Friday was not a day in which anything was created. God knows best about that. This is with a fatḥa. As for al-sibt, it is hides tanned with qaraẓ, acacia pods, and it seems to be called sibt because the working of it has been brought to its end, as a fresh date is called munsabita when the ripening has run through it.
سبج: The letters sīn, bā' and jīm are not anything, and have no root in the Arabic language. They say: al-subja is a shirt with a collar-opening; they said it is, in Persian, 'shabī.' And al-sabaj likewise is not anything; so too their saying that al-sabaj is 'the stone of silver.' In all of that there is room for doubt.
سبح:
The letters sīn, bā' and ḥā' are two roots: one of them a kind of worship, and the other a kind of moving swiftly.

The first is al-subḥa, and it is prayer, and it belongs particularly to what is voluntary and not obligatory. The jurists say: the traveller joins the two prayers and does not yusabbiḥ between them, that is, he does not pray a voluntary prayer between them.

Of the section is al-tasbīḥ, and it is the declaring of God, exalted be His praise, far above every evil. And al-tanzīh is a holding far off. The Arabs say subḥāna min kadhā, that is, how far he is from it!

Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
I said, when his boasting reached me: how far from that is ʿAlqama the boaster!

And a people said: its meaning is, how strange of him, when he boasts. And this is close to that, because it is a holding of him far off from boasting.

And among the attributes of God, mighty and majestic, is subbūḥ. Its derivation is from what we mentioned: that He is far above everything not befitting Him. And al-subuḥāt, which came in the hadith, is the majesty of God, exalted be His praise, and His greatness.

The other root: al-sabḥ and al-sibāḥa, which is swimming in water. And al-sābiḥ of horses is the one that stretches its forelegs out well in running. A poet said, in a line of verse:
So you turned away from him while a swift horse carried you off at speed, and the veins of your neck had come level with his ears.

He says: you kept turning round in fear of the spear-thrust, so that your neck-vein came level with your horse's ear.
سبخ:
The letters sīn, bā' and khā' are one root, indicating lightness in a thing. What falls from a bird's feathers is called al-sabīkh.

From this is the hadith: the Messenger of God, peace and blessings of God be upon him and his family, heard ʿĀ'isha praying against a thief who had stolen from her, and he said: "Do not tusabbikhī [lighten his burden] with your prayer against him," meaning: do not lessen it. And it is said in a supplication: "O God, sabbikh the fever away from him," meaning: draw it out and lighten it. And what flies off from cotton when it is carded is also called al-sabīkh. A poet, describing dogs, said:

So they let them loose, scattering the dust as the carding of bow-strings scatters wisps of cotton.

And it has been related of some that he recited: "Indeed for you in the day is a long sabḥ" — and said this carries the sense of al-sabkh, which is being free and unoccupied, for the unoccupied one is light of affair.
سبد:
The letters sīn, bā' and dāl — the greater part of its chapter concerns the growth of hair or the like of it, though a small exception may occur. The root is their saying: mā lahu sabadun wa lā labad. Al-sabad is hair; al-labad is wool/felt.

1. sabbada al-farkh — the chick sabbada, when its feathers appeared and grew spiky.
2. al-subda — the pubic hair.
3. al-subad — a bird, so named for the abundance of its feathers.
4. al-tasbīd — it is said to be the complete shaving off of the hair of the head, and it belongs to this chapter because it is as if one came to his sabad [hair] and shaved and stripped it entirely away. And it is also said that al-tasbīd is frequent washing of the head and applying oil to it.

What deviates from this root is their saying: huwa sibdu asbād, meaning a cunning, formidable one. A poet said:

He confronts a formidable one [sibd] on the rein, headstrong and unyielding.
سبر:
The letters sīn, bā' and rā' contain three unrelated words, none resembling the others.

The first is al-sabr, which is testing a matter and finding out its measure. One says: khabartu mā ʿinda fulānin wa sabartuhu — I found out and tested what so-and-so had. And the instrument by which the depth of a wound is known is called a misbār [probe].

The second word is al-sibr, which is beauty and splendour. The Messenger of God, peace and blessings of God be upon him and his family, said: "A man will come out of the Fire whose hibr and sibr have gone," meaning his learning and his beauty and splendour have gone. Abū ʿAmr said: I came to a tribe of the Arabs, and when I spoke, one of those present said: "As for the tongue, it is that of the desert, but as for the sibr, it is that of the town." Ibn Aḥmar said:

We wore his hibr until we were brought to account for deeds done and terms fulfilled.

The third word is al-sabra, which is the cold morning. The Messenger of God, peace and blessings of God be upon him and his family, mentioned the merit of performing the ablution fully in the cold mornings [al-sabarāt].
سبط:
The letters sīn, bā' and ṭā' are a root indicating the extending-out of a thing; and it is close to the root of bā', sīn and ṭā'.

1. One says shaʿr sabṭ or sabiṭ — hair that is straight, when it is not curly.
2. asbaṭa al-rajul isbāṭan — the man stretched out flat and went limp, after being struck.
3. al-subāṭa — a rubbish-heap, so called because nothing on it is kept or gathered up.

From this is the hadith: "he came to a people's rubbish-heap and urinated standing, because of a pain he had behind his knee."

4. al-sabaṭ — a plant that grows in the sand, said to be a moist kind of ḥalī-plant; it likely has some stretched-out growth to it.
سبع:
The letters sīn, bā' and ʿayn are two steady, sound roots: one of them is in number, and the other is a kind of wild beast.

The first is al-sabʿa, seven. And al-subʿ is a seventh part. And one says sabaʿtu al-qawma asbaʿuhum when you have taken a seventh of their property, or when you were the seventh of them. And from this is their saying: he is subāʿī of body, when he is complete in body. And al-sibʿ is one of the drinking-intervals of camels, being for a number of days known among them.

As for the other, al-sabuʿ is one of the beasts of prey. And a land is masbaʿa when its beasts of prey are many. And from the chapter is sabaʿtuhu, when you fell upon him, as though he likened himself to a beast of prey in his harming and biting. And asbaʿtuhu: I fed him to the beast of prey. And sabbaʿati al-dhi'ābu al-ghanam, when the wolves tore the sheep and ate them.

As for the saying of Abū Dhu'ayb, in a line of verse:
Loud in the gullet, he is never otherwise than as though ... he were a slave of the house of Abī Rabīʿa, musbaʿ

there are several accounts of it. One of them is that it means the pampered one, as though he were a pampered slave who has what he enjoys, so he is never other than brisk. And it is said that it is the herdsman. And it is said it is the one whose mother dies so that another takes over the suckling of him. And it is said al-musbaʿ is one not born of lawful wedlock. And it is said he is the herdsman upon whose flock the beasts of prey have made a raid, so he is shouting at the dogs and the beasts. And it is said he is one who is a slave to seven forefathers. And it is said he is one born after seven months. And it is said al-musbaʿ is the neglected one. And the Arabs say: I will surely do with him the deed of a sabʿa, meaning by it exaggeration in evil. And it is said he meant by al-sabʿa the lioness, meaning sabuʿa and lightening the word.
سبغ: The letters sīn, bā' and ghayn are a single root indicating the completeness and fullness of a thing. One says asbaghtu l-amr, I completed the matter fully; asbagha fulānun wuḍū'ahu, he performed his ablution completely. One says asbagha Llāhu ʿalayhi niʿamahu, God lavished His blessings fully upon him. rajulun musbigh — a man wearing a sābigha, a full-length coat of mail. faḥlun sābigh — long in the jurdān [a stallion camel's sheath]; its opposite is al-kamsh, the short one. One says sabbaghat al-nāqa, when a she-camel miscarried her young after it had already grown hair.
سبق: The letters sīn, bā' and qāf are a single sound root pointing to going before. One says sabaqa yasbiqu sabqan - he went ahead. As for al-sabaq, it is the stake which the one who comes first takes.
سبك:
The letters sīn, bā' and kāf are a small root indicating the utmost thoroughness in melting a thing down.

1. sabaktu — from this: I sabaktu silver or the like, sabkan, meaning I smelted it; and this is also used metaphorically for other than melting.
2. al-sunbuk — the tip of the hoof. As for al-sunbuk of the land, it is a metaphor: a rough, thick patch of little good.
سبل:
The letters sīn, bā' and lām are a single root pointing to the letting down of a thing from a height to below, and to the stretching out of a thing.

The first is from your saying: asbaltu al-sitr - I let down the curtain; and asbalat al-saḥāba mā'ahā and bi-mā'ihā - the cloud let down its water. Al-sabal is heavy rain. And a man's sibāl, his moustaches, are from this, because it is hair that hangs down. And their calling the upper parts of the bucket asbāl is from this, as though it were likened to what we mentioned of a man. A poet said, in a line of verse:
When they sent me down to draw with their buckets, I filled it with blood up to its upper edges.

And what stretches out in length is al-sabīl, which is the road, so called for its stretching out. Al-sābila are those going to and fro along the roads, coming and going. And the ear of corn was called sunbul for its stretching out. One says asbala al-zar', when its ear comes out. Abū 'Ubayd said: sabal al-zar' and its sunbul are the same. And it has sabala and asbala.
سبه: The letters sīn, bā' and hā' are one word, indicating weakness or loss of the mind. Al-sabah is loss of the mind from old age. One says: a man is masbūh or musabbah — close to al-masbūt [one in a stupor], the pattern in both being the same.
سبي:
The letters sīn, bā' and yā' are a root indicating the taking of something from one land to another by force.

1. al-saby — from this: one says sabā the girl, meaning he took her captive, sabyan; he is the sābin [captor], and the one taken is a sabiyya [captive].
2. sabāhā / sabaʾahā — likewise wine, which is carried from one land to another: they distinguish between sabāhā and sabaʾahā.
3. sibā'uhā — as for sibā'uhā, it is its purchase. One says sabaʾtuhā, and this is said only of wine; and they call the wine-merchant al-sabbā'. The pattern in this is one and the same.

What deviates from this root is al-sābiyā', which is the membrane in which the newborn comes; al-sābiyā' is also offspring, the increase of livestock. It is said: so-and-so's family have sābiyā' [young stock] coming to them from their herds. The Messenger of God, peace and blessings of God be upon him and his family, said: "Nine-tenths of provision is in trade, and the remaining part is in al-sābiyā'."

Close to the first chapter is al-asābiyy, which are streaks or tracks. One says asābiyy al-dimā', meaning streaks of blood. Salāma said:

The raiding [horses], with the streaks of blood upon them, as though their necks were the standing-stones of a bound-up shrine.

When what follows the bā' in this word is hamzated, the meaning differs from the first, and there are four different senses:

1. sabaʾtu al-jild — I sabaʾtu the hide, meaning you singed it until part of its surface was burnt.
2. sabaʾtu jildahu — I sabaʾtu his hide, meaning I flayed it.
3. sabaʾa ʿalā yamīn kādhiba — so-and-so sabaʾa upon a false oath, meaning he passed over it unconcerned. From this is derived their saying: insabaʾa al-laban, meaning the milk came out from the udder; and al-masbaʾ is the path on a mountain.
4. The fourth sense is their saying: dhahabū aydiya Saba' [they went the ways of Saba'], meaning scattered — from the dispersal of the people of Yemen. And Saba' is a man who brought together the generality of the tribes of Yemen; their land is also named by this same name.

And God knows best what is right.
ست: The letters sīn and tā' contain nothing but the word "sitta" (six), and the origin of the tā' is a dāl. This has already been discussed in its own chapter.
ستر:
The letters sīn, tā' and rā' form a word indicating covering. You say "satartu the thing, satran" — I covered it.

1. al-sutra — whatever you conceal yourself with, whatever it may be.
2. al-sitār — likewise, a covering, a curtain.

As for al-istār, in their phrase "the istār of the Kaʿba," it most likely comes from "covering," meaning the cloth garment with which the Kaʿba is covered. But some claimed this has nothing to do with clothing, and is instead about a number — they said the Arabs call the number four al-istār, citing as evidence al-Akhṭal's line of verse:
By your life, I, the two sons of Juʿayl, and their mother are indeed a base foursome —

and Jarīr's line:
Al-Farazdaq, al-Buʿayth and his mother, and al-Farazdaq's father were coupled together — an ugly foursome.

They said: so the astār of the Kaʿba are its four walls and sides. This has been said, but God knows best whether it is true.
ستن:
The letters sīn, tā' and nūn are not a root that branches, because it is the name of a plant, called al-astan. Al-Nābigha speaks of it:

They shy from an astan-plant, black at its lower parts, like the slave-women who carry the bundled firewood.
سج:
The letters sīn and jīm are a root pointing to a thing being moderate and level.

1. al-sajsaj — mild air, in which there is no harmful heat or cold. From this is the hadith: "The shade of Paradise is temperate (sajsaj)."
2. arḍ sajsaj — level ground, soft and not hard.

He said:
And the people had crossed the hard stretches of the level ground.

3. sajja al-ḥā'iṭ bi-l-ṭīn — he plastered the wall with clay, when he coated it and made it smooth; this belongs to this chapter. The tool used for that is called "al-misajja".
4. al-sajāj — thin, clear milk.

Close to this chapter is "al-kabsh al-sājisī", the ram thickly covered in wool.

Among what is an exception to the origin sense: their saying "lā afʿalu dhālika sajīsa al-layālī" and "sajīsa al-awjas", meaning "never". "Mā' sajis" is water that has turned bad. Al-sajja was an idol worshipped in the pre-Islamic era. And in a hadith: "Bring out your alms-tax, for God, mighty is His mention, has spared you from al-jabha, al-sajja, and al-bajja" — the hadith explains that these are the names of deities they used to worship in the pre-Islamic era.
سجح:
The letters sīn, jīm and ḥā' are a sound, analogical root, indicating straightness and goodness.

1. al-sujuḥ — the straight thing.
2. "malakta fa-asjiḥ" — it is said, as a saying: "you have gained the upper hand, so asjiḥ," meaning: be good in your pardoning.
3. wajh asjaḥ — a face is asjaḥ, meaning regular and straight in its form. Dhū al-Rumma said:

And a face, like the mirror of the stranger-woman, fair and unmarred.

All this comes from their saying: tanaḥḥa ʿan sujuḥ al-ṭarīq, meaning: step off the road's beaten track, off its straight course.
سجد:
The letters sīn, jīm and dāl are one root, running steadily, pointing to bowing low and lowliness.

One says sajada — when he bows low. And everything that is made low has done sajda. Abū ʿAmr said: asjada al-rajul — when he lowers his head and bends. Ḥumayd said, in a line of verse:
With the loose ends of their reins they bowed low, as the Christians bow to their lords.

And Abū ʿUbayda said the like, and said: an Asadī bedouin recited to me:
And they said to him, bow to Laylā, and he bowed —
meaning the camel, when it lowers its head.

As for their saying asjada isjādan — when he keeps his gaze fixed — this is sound, except that the reasoning requires that to be with a lowering of the eyes, and it is not the staring gaze nor the sidelong one. Pointing to that is his saying:
Has it made you proud toward me that your coquetry with us, and the lowered gaze of your two hunting eyes, wins the day?

And the dirhams of al-isjād are dirhams that had figures on them, among them the figures of their kings, and when they saw them they used to bow down to them. And this was among the Persians. And it is what al-Aswad speaks of:
From the wine of a man of pearl-drops, sweet of voice, girdled, who fetched it for the dirhams of al-isjād.
سجر:
The letters sīn, jīm and rā' cover three roots: filling, mixing, and kindling.

Filling — al-baḥr al-masjūr: the filled, brimming sea.

1. sājir — a place that a flash-flood fills.

A poet [al-Shammākh] said, in a line of verse [only this half is given]:
Every hollow spring, and every filled hollow.

2. al-shaʿr al-munsajir — hair that flows loose and hangs freely from its great abundance.

A poet said, in a line of verse [only this half is given]:
When her flowing hair bends aside.

Mixing:
3. al-sajīr — the close companion and friend, the opposite of al-shajīr [a stranger-companion].
4. ʿayn sajrā' — an eye in which redness mixes into the white.

Kindling — "sajartu the oven," when you light it.

5. al-sujūr — what the oven is kindled with.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And a day like the slave-women's oven, which they kindled, casting thick logs into it until it blazed.

6. al-sijār — also used for al-sujūr [fuel].

Close to this: "the camels istajarat in their swift pace," when they hurried, as though ablaze in their going.

7. "the she-camel sajarat" — when she moaned with a deep, longing cry.
سجع:
The letters sīn, jīm and ʿayn are a single root, indicating a balanced, rhythmic sound.

1. From this comes sajʿ in speech — rhymed prose, made by producing speech with pauses like the rhymes of poetry, as in the sayings: "Whoever has little is humbled, and whoever gives orders may fail" (man qalla dhalla, wa-man amara falla), and "Neither has your water been kept, nor has your filth been cleansed" (lā māʾaki abqayti, wa-lā daranaki anqayti).
2. One says the dove sajaʿat — it cooed — when it made its call.
سجف:
The letters sīn, jīm and fāʾ are a single root: letting a covering thing hang down. One says asjaftu al-sitr — I let the curtain down, I released it.

1. al-sajf and al-sijf — the curtain of the bridal litter.
2. One says asjafa al-layl, like asdafa — night grew dark.
سجل:
The letters sīn, jīm and lām are a single root indicating something pouring out once it has filled up.

1. al-sajl — the great bucket. One says sajaltu al-mā'a fa-'insajala, meaning I poured it out.
2. sajl, said of an udder when it is full.
3. al-musājala — rivalry, boasting; its origin is in buckets: when two men engage in musājala, that is their contest, each wanting to overcome the other.
4. al-shay' al-musjal — a thing given freely to everyone, as though it had been poured out. Muḥammad ibn 'Alī, on His words {Is the reward of goodness anything but goodness?} [al-Raḥmān: 60], said: it is given freely alike to the good man and the wrongdoer. A poet said, of al-musjal, in a line of verse:
And my kindness became something given freely to my people.
5. al-sijill — from al-sajl and al-musājala, being a document that gathers together writings and meanings; it also carries the sense of musājala, since it concerns dispute and rival claims. From this: their saying "the war is sijāl" — a contest, turn for turn, now one way and now the other. In al-Khalīl's book: al-sajl is the filling of the bucket.
6. al-sijjīl — from al-sijill, though it may also be derived from something else already mentioned. They also said al-sijjīl means hard, severe.
سجم:
The letters sīn, jīm and mīm are a single root: the pouring out of something — water or tears. One says sajamat al-ʿaynu damʿahā — the eye poured out its tears.

1. ʿaynun sajūmun — an eye that streams; damʿun masjūmun — tears that are poured out.
2. One says arḍun masjūmatun — land that has been rained upon.
سجن:
The letters sīn, jīm and nūn are a single root, and it is confining. One says sajantuhu sajnan — I imprisoned him. Al-sijn is the place in which a man is imprisoned. God, exalted be His praise, said in the story of Joseph, peace be upon him: {he said: my Lord, prison is dearer to me than what they call me to} [Yūsuf: 33]. It is read with a on the sīn, as a verbal noun, and with i, as the place.

As for the words of Ibn Muqbil, in a line of verse:
A beating that the champions urged upon one another, sijjīn —
it is said that he meant sijjīl, that is, hard and severe. Its mention has already passed. He simply changed the lām into a nūn. The right way of taking this is that it follows the pattern of the first sense, from al-sajn, which is confining, because when a beating is severe the one beaten is held fixed, as though it had imprisoned him.
سجو:
The letters sīn, jīm and wāw are a root pointing to stillness and covering-over.

sajā al-laylu — the night grew pitch dark and still.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
How lovely is the moonlit night, and the still, dark night, and paths like the weaver's cloth.

An eye is sājin, meaning still.
سح:
The letters sīn and ḥā' are a single root pointing to pouring. One says "saḥaḥtu al-mā', asuḥḥu, saḥḥan" — I poured the water out.

1. saḥāba saḥūḥ — a heavily-pouring cloud.
2. shā' sāḥḥ — a fat sheep, as though it pours out fat.
3. faras misaḥḥ — a swift mare, whose running resembles the pouring-down of rain.

One says "saḥsaḥa al-shay'" when a thing flowed. It is said that al-saḥsaḥa is the open courtyard.
سحب: The letters sīn, ḥā' and bā' are a sound root pointing to dragging something spread out and drawing it along. You say *saḥabtu dhaylī bi-l-arḍ saḥban* — I trailed my skirt along the ground.
