And the cloud is called *saḥāb* by likeness to that, as though it dragged itself along in the air, dragging. And they use this figuratively and say *tasaḥḥaba fulān ʿalā fulān*, when he grew bold against him, as though he stretched himself out over him. This is the sound rule. Some people say that *al-saḥb* is eating hard; but I think that is a copyist's slip, because it has no rule behind it — it is only *al-saḥt*.
سحت:
The letters sīn, ḥā' and tā' are a sound root, regular in its pattern. One says su'ḥita al-shay'u, meaning it was utterly wiped out, and usḥita likewise. One says saḥata Allāhu al-kāfira bi-'adhābin, meaning God destroyed him utterly with a punishment. Property is called masḥūt and musḥat, as in al-Farazdaq's line:
The bite of time, son of Marwān, has left of wealth nothing but what is stripped bare or scraped clean.

From this chapter: a man is called masḥūt al-jawf when he never feels full, as though whatever he swallows is wiped out entirely from within him, so that nothing remains there. Property called al-suḥt is anything unlawful whose eater bears the shame of it; it is called suḥt because it has no lasting good in it. One says asḥata fī tijāratihi, meaning he earned suḥt (ill-gotten gain) in his trading, and asḥata mālahu, meaning he ruined his wealth.
سحج:
The letters sīn, ḥāʾ and jīm are a single, sound root, indicating the paring of a thing.

1. One says insaḥaja al-qishr ʿan al-shayʾ — the outer skin was scraped/rubbed off the thing.
2. A donkey is called musaḥḥaj — meaning bitten repeatedly, as though bitten until its hide is scraped raw.
3. A camel is called saḥḥāj when it scrapes the ground with its foot-pad, as if meaning to strip the ground's surface with its pad; and when it does that, it is not long before it goes footsore.
4. A she-camel is called misḥāj when she does that.
سحر:
The letters sīn, ḥā' and rā' are three roots that stand apart from one another: one of them is a limb of the body, another is deceiving and the like of it, and the third is a time of day.

The limb is al-saḥr, and it is what clings to the windpipe and the gullet from the upper part of the belly. And it is said: rather it is the lung. And from it one says of a coward: his saḥr has swelled up. It is called al-suḥr, al-saḥr and al-saḥar.

As for the second, it is al-siḥr, magic. Some people said: it is bringing falsehood out in the shape of truth; and it is said: it is deception. They argued from the saying of the poet, in a line of verse:
If you ask us what we are about, we are but sparrows of this beguiled mankind.
It is as though he meant the deceived man, the one whom the world has deceived and led astray. And it is said that al-musaḥḥar is the one who has been given a saḥr, and whoever has a saḥr cannot do without food and drink.

As for the time, it is al-saḥar and al-suḥra, and that is before the dawn. The plural of saḥar is asḥār. And they say ataytuka saḥara, I came to you at the last of the night, when it is a particular day. But if he means an early morning and some pre-dawn among pre-dawns, he says ataytuka saḥaran.
سحط: The letters sīn, ḥāʾ and ṭāʾ form a word. They say: al-saḥṭ is swift slaughter.
سحف:
The letters sīn, ḥāʾ and fāʾ are a single, sound root: removing one thing from another, uncovering it.

1. From this: saḥaftu al-shaʿr ʿan al-jild — I scraped the hair off the skin — when you strip it off until nothing of it is left. This is in a line of Zuhayr's poetry: "and what was scraped there — the forelocks and the lice."
2. al-sayḥaf — broad arrowheads, in a saying of al-Shanfarā, in a line of verse: "She has a quiver holding thirty broad arrowheads (sayḥaf) ... when she senses the enemy's vanguard, she bristles."
3. al-saḥīfa — one of the saḥāʾif, the streaks of fat that cling to the skin; a she-camel is called saḥūf from this. She is named so because she can be saḥafa'd — that is, scraped clean.
4. al-saḥīfa (a second sense) — a downpour that sweeps away all it passes over.
سحق:
The letters sīn, ḥā' and qāf are two roots: one is remoteness, the other is wearing a thing down until it reaches ruin.

The first: al-suḥq, remoteness. God, exalted be His praise, said: {so away with the companions of the blaze} [al-Mulk: 11]. al-saḥūq — a tall palm tree, named so for how far its top stands from the ground.

The second root: saḥaqtu l-shay'a asḥaquhu saḥqan — I pounded the thing. al-saḥq — a worn-out garment. One says saḥaqahu l-balā fa-nsaḥaqa, decay wore it down and it became worn away. This is used as a metaphor, so that one says the eye "grinds down" its tears — tasḥaqu l-damʿa suḥqan. usḥiqa l-shay', when it shrank and contracted. asḥaqa l-ḍarʿ, when an udder's milk dried up and it wasted away.
سحل:
The letters sīn, ḥā and lām are three roots: one is the scraping of one thing off another, another is to do with sound, and the third is making a thing easy and doing it quickly.

As for the first:
1. "the winds saḥalat the ground" — they scraped its surface off. Ibn Durayd and others said: sāḥil al-baḥr, the seashore, is inverted in its form — in meaning it is masḥūl, scraped, because the water has scraped it. The root of this is "saḥaltu al-ḥadīdata asḥaluhā" — I filed the piece of iron. The filings are called al-suḥāla.
2. al-saḥl — white cloth, as though it had been scraped clean of its dirt and grime; plural al-suḥul.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Like the white cloths, whose colour was made bright by the pouring rain of a heavy, drooping cloud.

The second root:
3. al-saḥīl — the braying of a donkey, and likewise al-suḥāl; for that reason the donkey is called misḥal.
4. al-misḥal — also used for the tongue of an orator, and for the orator himself.

The third root:
5. "saḥalahu mi'atan" — he paid him a hundred dirhams promptly in cash. This is used figuratively, so one says "saḥalahu mi'atan", when he struck him a hundred lashes at once.
6. al-saḥīl — also thread that has been twisted loosely; its opposite is al-mubram and al-barīm, tightly-twisted thread, as in the poetry of Zuhayr:
of loosely-twisted thread and tightly-twisted

Irregular against these roots:
7. al-misḥalān — two rings on the two ends of the bit's crosspiece of a bridle.
8. al-isḥil — a tree.
سحم:
The letters sīn, ḥāʾ and mīm are a single root, indicating blackness.

1. al-asḥam — the black one, having blackness; its blackness is called al-suḥma.
2. Night is called asḥam. A poet said, in a line of verse: "Two who nursed at one mother's breast, sharing her milk — under a black, moonless night, forever, we do not part."
3. al-asḥam — the black cloud. Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse: "under a black cloud, its rain-clouds lowering, pouring down."
4. al-asḥam — the black horn, in a saying of Zuhayr's, in a line of verse: "and its warding [the cow] off from her [calf] with a black, defending horn."
سحن:
The letters sīn, ḥāʾ and nūn are three roots: the first is breaking; the second is colour and shape; the third is mixing.

The first: their saying "saḥantu al-ḥajar" — I broke the stone — when you break it.
1. al-misḥana — the tool stones are broken with, plural masāḥin. A Hudhalī poet said, in a line of verse: "just as the miṣḥana breaks what lies over the crushed grain."

The second root: al-saḥna is the softness of the skin (complexion).
1. al-saḥnāʾ — the appearance, the general look.
2. A mare called musḥana — meaning of fine appearance.

Some people say al-saḥanāʾ is on the pattern faʿalāʾ, with the middle letter open, the way they say thaʾadāʾ for thaʾdāʾ. This has no basis and follows no pattern — it is properly thaʾdāʾ and saḥnāʾ, on the pattern faʿlāʾ.

As for the third root, it is their saying "sāḥantuka musāḥanatan" — I mixed with you, I dealt closely with you.
سحو:
The letters sīn, ḥāʾ and the weak letter are a root indicating the paring of one thing off another, or the taking of a small amount.

1. From this: saḥawtu al-qirṭās ashūhu — I pared the sheet of paper (trimmed its edge); and that paring is called al-siḥāʾa.
2. In the sky there is a siḥāʾa of cloud — a thin wisp of cloud. When you fasten something with the siḥāʾa (the paring/strip), you say saḥaytuhu; and if you said saḥawtuhu, there would be no harm in that either.
3. One says saḥawtu al-ṭīn ʿan wajh al-arḍ bi-l-misḥāh, ashūhu, saḥwan and saḥyan — I scraped the mud off the surface of the ground with the miṣḥāh (the spade) — and also asḥāhu, and asḥīhi: three dialect variants.
4. A man is called usḥuwān — one who eats a great deal, as if he scrapes the food off the face of the table by eating, until the table appears bare.
5. A downpour is called sāḥiya when it strips the surface of the ground.
سخ: The letters sīn and khā' are a root with only a single word in it. It is said that al-sakhākh is soft, fine soil. And they mentioned, if it is sound, "sakhkhat al-jarāda" — the locust struck its tail into the ground, when it dug its tail into the earth.
سخب: The letters sīn, khāʾ and bāʾ form a word not to be generalised as a pattern. They say: al-sikhāb is a necklace of cloves or the like, with no gemstones in it; plural sukhub.
سخت: The letters sīn, khāʾ and tāʾ are not a root, and I do not think the speech built on them is pure [classical] language. They call a hard thing sakht and sikhtīt. Then they say an affair is miskhāt when it has weakened and gone to nothing. These two senses do not agree, and that is why we said this chapter is in itself not a genuine root — even though it was reported from Abū Zayd that iskhātta al-jurḥ means its swelling went down. As for the word sukht that we mentioned from Thaʿlab, at the end of his book, it has been said that it is [the same as] al-sukhd; and on that basis it is among the doubtful words.
سخد:
The letters sīn, khāʾ and dāl are a root. In it is al-sakhd, the fluid that comes out with the newborn.

1. For that reason one says so-and-so became musakhkhad — when he wakes sluggish, heavy in spirit.
2. Sometimes they used the word al-sukhd for what comes out of a newborn's belly before it has eaten. This is disputed: some say sukhd, others say it with a tāʾ, sukht — and that is how it was reported to us from Thaʿlab, at the end of the book he named al-Faṣīḥ.

Some philologists said that al-sukhd is swelling, and that fits the same pattern.
سخر: The letters sīn, khā' and rā' are a steady, straight root pointing to belittling and bringing low. From that is our saying sakhkhara Allāh - mighty and majestic is He - al-shay', and that is when He makes it submit to His command and His will. God - exalted be His praise - said: {And He has made subject to you what is in the heavens and what is in the earth} [al-Jāthiya: 13]. One says rajul sukhra - a man who is put to work under compulsion; and sukhra also when he is one who is mocked. But if it is he who does the mocking, you say sukhara, with a fatḥa on the khā' and the rā'. And one says sufun sawākhir mawākhir. Al-sawākhir are the obedient ships with a fair wind; al-mawākhir are those that plough the water and cleave it. Of this chapter is sakhirtu minhu - I mocked him. And they keep saying sakhirtu bihi as well. In the Book of God - exalted is He: {Then we shall mock you as you mock} [Hūd: 38].
سخف:
The letters sīn, khāʾ and fāʾ are a regular, recurring root, indicating lightness.

1. al-sukhf — lightness in anything, even in clouds. Al-Khalīl said: al-sukhf applies specifically to lightness of mind [feeble-mindedness], while al-sakhāfa applies generally to lightness in anything.
2. One says: I found the sakhfa of one who has been made to hunger — a lightness/faintness that comes over a person when he is hungry.
سخل:
The letters sīn, khāʾ and lām are a regular, sound root that follows a consistent pattern, indicating meanness and weakness.

1. From this: al-sakhl, from the young of sheep — the small, weak one; the female is sakhla.
2. From this too: sakhkhalat al-nakhla — a palm tree is said to do this when it bears shīṣ, unripe dates whose stones have not hardened.
3. al-sukhkhal — worthless, base men; it has no singular of its own form.
4. One says stars are masūkhala when they are obscure/unknown. This is in the saying of the poet: "We are the Pleiades and its Orion, we are the two forearms [stars] and al-Mirzam; and you are obscure stars — seen in the sky, yet unknown."
5. Some mention that the tribe of Hudhayl say: sakhaltu al-rajul — I found fault with the man.
سخم:
The letters sīn, khāʾ and mīm are a regular, straightforward root, indicating softness and blackness.

1. One says hair is sukhāmī — black and soft. That is how it was reported to us from al-Khalīl. But ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm al-Qaṭṭān told me, from ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, from Abū ʿUbayd, who said: al-Aṣmaʿī said: as for hair called al-sukhām, it is soft and fine, and this has nothing to do with blackness.
2. Wine is called sukhāmiyya when it is smooth and easy [to drink]. Ibn al-Sikkīt said: cloth called sukhām is soft; and cotton is sukhām too, as in the line: "soft cotton (sukhāmī) in the hands of the spinners."

What departs from this root is al-sakhīma — a grudge found within the self. One says sakhkhama Allāhu wajhahu — may God blacken his face — this is from al-sukhām, which is the blackness/soot of the cooking-pot.
سخن:
The letters sīn, khāʾ and nūn are a sound, regular, consistent root, indicating heat in a thing.

1. From this: sakhkhantu al-māʾ — I heated the water; water is sukhn and sakhīn.
2. One says: a hot day is sukhn, sākhin and sakhnān; a hot night is sukhna and sakhnāna. One says sakhuna yawmunā — our day grew hot. And sakhinat ʿaynuhu — his eye grew hot/sore, taskhanu; and askhana Allāhu ʿaynahu — may God make his eye sore [a curse]. They say the tear of grief runs hot, citing the saying "may God cool his eye". This is a sound argument.
3. al-miskhana — a small cooking-pot, like a bowl.
4. al-sakhīna — a gruel made from flour. It is said the Quraysh were mocked for eating al-sakhīna, and were nicknamed for it, as in the saying: "What a fight we fought, and no lie in it, over sakhīna — but for the night and the sanctuary [that held us back]."
5. al-tasākhīn — light shoes/boots. It is possible they were named so because they warm the foot as they are worn — and that is not unlikely.
سخي:
The letters sīn, khāʾ and the weak letter are a single root, indicating spaciousness and openness in a thing. The origin of it is their saying: sakhaytu al-qidr and sakhawtuhā — when you make an opening for the fire beneath it [to draw better].

1. sakhāwī al-arḍ: some said al-sakhāwī is the broad expanse of a wasteland. In the saying of some, "sakhāwā al-falā," Ibn al-Aʿrābī said the singular of sakhāwā is sakhwāh. He also said: al-sakhwāʾ is level, easy ground.
2. The philologists said: from this same pattern comes al-sakhāʾ — generosity; one says sakhā yaskhū sakhāwatan and sakhāʾan, both the short and the lengthened form.
3. al-sakhiyy — the generous man.

What departs from this root is al-sakhā, in the short form: a limp that comes when a camel leaps up with its load and a draught of air gets between its hide and its shoulder-blade; such a camel is called sakhin.
سد:
The letters sīn and dāl are a single root pointing to blocking up a gap and making it fit properly. From this: "sadadtu al-thulma saddan" — I blocked up the breach. Every barrier between two things is a "sadd".

1. al-sadīd — one who has "sadād", meaning uprightness, as though there were no gap in him. Correct speech is also "sadād"; one says "qultu sadādan" — I spoke rightly. And "saddadahu Allāhu ʿazza wa jall" — God guided him aright. One says "asadda al-rajul" when a man spoke rightly.

From this chapter: "fīhi sidād min ʿawaz" [with the other vowel on the sīn] — something that fills a want, however imperfectly. Likewise "sidād al-thulma wa-l-thaghr", the stopgap for a breach or a gap in the teeth.

He said, in a line of verse:
They squandered me — and what a young man they squandered! ... for a day of dread and for stopping a gap.

2. al-sudda — like the open courtyard around a house.
3. "istadda al-shay'" — a thing had soundness.
4. al-sudda is also said to mean the door.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
You see the delegations standing at his doorway ... crowding at the door of one who is visited, never a visitor himself.

5. al-sudād — an illness that takes hold in the nose and blocks the breath.
6. al-sadd and al-sudd — locusts filling the horizon.

Their saying "al-sudda" for the door is because it is something that can be closed up. And in a hadith mentioning the destitute: "The disheveled-headed, for whom no doors are opened."
سدج: The letters sīn, dāl and jīm — they say only one form of it is in use, which is al-tasadduj. One says a man is saddāj when he tells falsehoods and strings them together.
سدح:
The letters sīn, dāl and ḥāʾ are a single root, indicating spreading something flat on the ground — as with the sadḥ of a filled water-skin, when it is thrown down on the ground. A slain man is likened to this. Abū al-Najm said, describing a slain man, in a line of verse: "his skull crushed in, or laid out flat (masdūḥ)." As for al-Mufaḍḍal's reading of the line — "between the arāk trees and the palms, the blue spearheads, sharp at their tips, crush them" — it is said that this is a misreading, and that the word is really "tasdaḥuhum" — laid them out flat.

1. al-sadḥ — throwing a man down flat, whether on his face or on his back, so that he does not land seated or curled up.
2. Their saying "so-and-so is sādiḥ," meaning prosperous, comes from this too — because when a man prospers he "insadaḥa" — sprawls out on his back. It is a proverbial saying.
سدخ: The letters sīn, dāl and khāʾ have no basis at all in the speech of the Arabs. And there is no sense to the saying of one who says "insadakha," like "insadaḥa," meaning he sprawled on his back from a blow, or lay flat. And God knows best.
سدر:
The letters sīn, dāl and rā' are a single root indicating something like bewilderment and confusion of judgement. They say al-sādir is the bewildered man. They say sadira baṣaruhu yasdaru, when his sight is dazzled and confused. They say al-sādir is also the man who does not care what he does and is troubled by nothing. Ṭarafa said, in a line of verse:
Heedless, I took my wrongdoing for right guidance ... then I held back, when [the word here is uncertain to me] had already struck.

As for their saying sadarat al-mar'atu sha'rahā, meaning the woman let her hair hang loose, that is a case of letter-substitution, like sadaltu, meaning you let it down. Likewise their saying "he came striking his two asdarān" [striking his own sides — an idiom] is also a case of substitution; the original letter in it is ṣād, and that has been discussed already.
سدس:
The letters sīn, dāl and sīn are a root in numbering: their saying al-sudus, one part of six parts.

1. izār sadīs — a waist-wrap that is "sixed," meaning of six [cubits].
2. al-sids, in the watering-intervals of camels — that the camels stay away from water five days and come to water on the sixth.
3. asdasa al-baʿīr — the camel shed its tooth after the rubāʿiyya tooth, which happens in its eighth year.

As for "six" (sitta), it too comes from this, except that it has been assimilated in pronunciation, as if it were originally sidsa.

Among what falls outside this root: al-sudūs, a kind of cloak (ṭaylasān); and Sadūs as a man's name. Ibn al-Kalbī said: Sadūs, in [the tribe of] Shaybān, is with fatḥa; the one in [the tribe of] Ṭayy is with ḍamma.
سدع: The letters sīn, dāl and ʿayn are not a root one can rely on or generalise from — but al-Khalīl did mention rajulun misdaʿ, saying: it is a man who presses straight ahead on his way. If that is so, it comes from letter-substitution, being from ṣadaʿtu — as if he splits (yaṣdaʿu) the open desert the way a thing is split. It is reported that someone said: "safety to you from every calamity (nakba) and sadʿa," saying: it is like a calamity. This has no sound basis.
سدف:
The letters sīn, dāl and fāʾ are a sound root, indicating the letting-down of one thing over another as a cover for it. One says asdaftu al-qināʿ — I let the face-veil down, I released it.

1. al-sudfa — the mingling of darkness (twilight).
2. al-sadīf — the fat of the camel's hump, as though it were a cover for what lies beneath it; the plural of al-sudfa is sudaf. As in the line: "we, in the planting of young palms, know best among us of racing swift horses in the twilight (sudaf)."

Some people report: asdafa al-fajr, meaning the dawn shone — in the dialect of [the tribe] Hawāzin, not the rest of the Arabs. This has no basis, and it runs against the pattern.
سدك: The letters sīn, dāl and kāf form a single word not to be generalised as a pattern. You say: sadika bihi — when he clung to it.
سدل:
The letters sīn, dāl and lām are a single root, indicating something coming down from a height to a depth, covering it as it comes.

1. From this one says: the night let down its sudūl — its curtains.
2. al-sadl — your letting a garment trail down to the ground.
3. Hair that hangs loosely down over the back is munsadil.
4. al-sidl — the curtain, the covering.
5. al-sidl — a string of gems; plural sudūl.

The pattern behind all of this is one and the same.
سدم:
The letters sīn, dāl and mīm are a root for something whose direction cannot be found.

1. A well is called sudum when it has become filled in with earth.
2. From this too: a camel in rut is called sadim, because when it rages it knows nothing of its own state — like a drunk man who cannot find his way. From this comes the saying of the poet, in a line of verse: "O rutting camel (sadim), tossing its head, meaning to lead a captive away from the people of the Ḥijāz."
سدن:
The letters sīn, dāl and nūn are a single root for one particular thing.

1. al-sidāna is said to be the guardianship [of a shrine].
2. sadanat al-bayt — the custodians of the House [the Kaʿba]; its guardians.
3. They also say al-sadan is the curtain.

If that last is correct, it belongs to the chapter of letter-substitution, its origin being al-sidl.
سدو:
The letters sīn, dāl and wāw are a single root, indicating neglect and heading off aimlessly.

1. From this: al-sadw — following one's own head recklessly while travelling. From this too comes His saying, exalted be His praise: {does man think that he will be left neglected} [al-Qiyāma: 36] — meaning: left alone, neither commanded nor forbidden.

Al-Khalīl said: the children's game with walnuts that is called "zadw" is really al-sadw. If that is correct, it belongs to this chapter, because one releases the walnut from one's hand.

2. From this chapter too: asdā al-nakhl — said of a palm when its date-clusters hang loose, like a thing released from the hand; a single loosened cluster is called al-sadiyya. Abū ʿAmr used to say it is al-sadāʾ, with a lengthened vowel, singular sadāʾa. Abū ʿUbayd said: I do not recall the lengthened form.
3. al-sadā — dew. One says sadiyat laylatunā — our night grew dewy — when its dew was abundant. This belongs to the same idea, because the cloud lets the dew go, and is itself let go by it.
4. From this chapter too: al-sadā — a favour done. One says: so-and-so asdā to so-and-so a kindness — he did him a good turn.
5. From this chapter too: tasaddā fulānun amatahu — so-and-so "tasaddā"'d his slave-girl, when he took hold of her from above, as though he flung himself down upon her. As in the line: "and when I drew near, I tasaddā'd her — one garment I forgot, and one I drag along." Another poet said: "her likeness came over me with sleep, tasaddā'd me, the way mist settles low with clear dew."
سر:
The letters sīn and rā': what its branches share is the concealment of a thing, and what is genuine and settled in it. Nothing that comes from it falls outside this.

1. al-sirr — the opposite of open declaration. One says "asrartu al-shay' isrāran", the opposite of "aʿlantuhu", I made it known.
2. al-sirr — marital intercourse, so named because it is a matter not announced publicly.
3. al-sirār and al-sarār — the night on which the crescent moon hides itself, sometimes one night, sometimes two when the month runs to thirty days.

From this is the hadith: he asked a man, "Did you fast any of the sirar of the month?" The man said, "No." So he said, "When you break your Ramadan fast, then fast two days."

He said, concerning sirar, in a line of verse:
We came upon ʿĀmir's people at dawn, in their encampment ... on bare, swift horses racing between the two edges of the day,
in the evening of the new moon, or of its hiding.

Muḥammad ibn Hārūn al-Thaqafī told me, on the authority of ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, on the authority of Abū l-Ḥasan al-Athram, on the authority of Abū ʿUbayda, who said: "asrartu al-shay'" means I concealed it, while "asrartuhu" means I made it known. And he read: {and they concealed their remorse when they saw the punishment} [Yūnus: 54]. He said: here it means they showed it openly. And he cited the line of Imru' al-Qays:
"...if they were to reveal the place of my killing"
meaning if they were to show it openly.

Then one of the scholars told me, on the authority of Abū l-Ḥasan ʿAbdallāh ibn Sufyān the grammarian, that al-Farrā' said Abū ʿUbayda erred in his interpretation and miscopied the line he cited as evidence. As for the interpretation, al-Farrā' said: "asarrū al-nadāma" means they hid it, for fear of being gloated over. As for the miscopying, what Imru' al-Qays actually said was:
"...if they were to make my killing-place widely visible"
meaning if they were to show it openly. One says "ashrartu al-shay'" when you expose a thing; from this is their saying "ashrartu al-laḥm li-l-shams" — I spread the meat out in the sun. This has already been discussed in its own chapter.

As for the sense we mentioned of the genuine core and settled essence of a thing:

4. al-sirr — the pure essence of a thing.
5. al-surūr, joy, from this, because it is a state free of sorrow.
6. al-surra — a person's navel, the purest and softest part of his body. One says a baby has its "sarar" cut off from it, that being the umbilical cord, plural "asirra". Abū Zayd said: al-sirar is also one of the lines across the palm of the hand.
7. sarārat al-wādī and sirruhu — the best part of a valley.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Why did you not satirize the horsemen of Raḥraḥān ... a handful, driven back and forth in the choicest heart of a valley?

He means: they have a fine appearance, but no substance behind it.

8. al-sarar — an ailment that afflicts a camel in its navel; one says "baʿīr asarr".
9. al-sarr — the verbal noun of "sararptu al-zand" [I struck fire-sticks together for kindling], said when the fire-stick remains "asarr", meaning hollow, and needs mending. One says "surra zanduka fa-innahu asarr" — mend your fire-stick, for it is hollow. One also says "qanāt sarrā'" — a hollow reed. All this comes from al-surra and al-sarar already mentioned.

As for al-asārīr, the creases in the forehead, these are carried on the little creases around the navel. In a hadith: "The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him and his family, came in to ʿĀ'isha, the lines of his face shining with joy." And also carried on what was mentioned: al-asrār, the lines on the inside of the palm, singular "sirr". The origin sense in all of this is one and the same.

Al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse:
So look at a palm and its lines ... will you, if you threaten me, be able to harm me?

As for the tips of sweet basil, it is permissible to call them "surūr" [joys], because they are the freshest and tenderest part of the plant. That is in his saying:
Like the papyrus-reed of the thicket amid the dense growth ... when the water mingles with its tender tips.

As for the sense of settledness mentioned:

10. al-sarīr — the couch of state, plural "sururun" and "asirra". Al-sarīr also means an easy, settled life, because a person settles down upon it and finds his repose there.
11. sarīr al-ra's — the place where the head rests.

He said:
A strike that dislodges the skull from its resting-place.

Some people transmit al-Aʿshā's line with a different word for the last word, meaning "its resting-place" instead of "its tender tips", in which case its meaning would be "its origin, upon which it had settled." And they cited the saying of a poet:
And she left behind a life of ease and comfort ... never fearing, in those days, that her settled state would pass away.

Al-sarar and al-sirar of a baby are what is cut off; al-surra is what remains. From this chapter also: al-sarīr, the sand that lies upon a hillock.

From the first sense: sirr al-nasab — the pure, best part of a lineage.

Dhū l-Iṣbaʿ said, in a line of verse:
And they, in whom they took pride at their children's birth ... are of the pure, unmixed core of lineage.

12. al-sursūr — the wise, perceptive scholar, its origin from "al-sirr", as though he had gained insight into the hidden matters of affairs.

As for al-surriyya [a concubine], al-Khalīl said it follows a particular word-pattern. One says "yutasarraru" and one says "yatasarrā" for taking a concubine. Al-Khalīl said: whoever says "yatasarrā" has erred. Al-Khalīl added nothing beyond this. Al-Aṣmaʿī said al-surriyya comes from al-sirr, meaning marital intercourse, because her master chose her for intimacy, not to trade in her. This is what al-Aṣmaʿī said, and Ibn al-Sikkīt mentioned it in his book.

As for the vowel on the sīn in "al-surriyya" differing from that in "sirr": many word-patterns are altered when forming a relational adjective — one says, for "al-arḍ al-sahla" [level ground], "suhliyy", and for length of life and the extent of time, "duhriyy". Much else is like this. And God knows best.
سرب:
The letters sīn, rā' and bā' are a regular, consistent root, indicating spreading wide and going off through the land. From this: al-sirb and al-surba, a herd of gazelles or of sheep, because it spreads out over the land grazing. Then this was carried over to the sirb of women, a company of them. They say al-sarb, with fatḥa on the sīn, has its origin among camels. From this the Arabs say to a divorced woman: "Go — I shall not call your sarb back," meaning I shall not turn back your camels, let her go where she will. Here al-sirb means the grazing livestock. Abū Zayd said: one says khalli sirbahu, meaning his path, let him go where he wishes. They said it is also said sirb with kasra on the sīn. Dhū al-Rumma's line is recited:
He left clear for her the path of the foremost of the herd.
He explained: meaning the path. One says insaraba al-waḥshiyyu fī sirbihi, the wild creature went off into its track.

From this chapter also: al-sarab and al-sarib, the water that seeps out from a water-skin; it is said saraba sarban. Dhū al-Rumma said:
What ails your eye, that water pours from it ... as though it were a seepage from torn skins.
(with the rā' said either with fatḥa or kasra). One says sarrabtu al-qirbata, meaning I put water in it so that the stitching swells and closes. Al-sarb is the stitching, because water seeps, yansaribu, out of it, that is, escapes. Al-sārib is one going off through the land; one says saraba surūban. God, exalted be His praise, said: {and one who goes openly by day} [al-Ra'd: 10]. A poet said:
How was it you went off, when you were never one to wander ... and dreams draw near yet stay far off.

Al-masraba is the hair growing along the middle of the chest, so named because it looks as though it streams, running down over the chest.

As for their saying āminun fī sirbihi, secure in his sirb — this is with kasra; they said it means secure within himself. This is correct, but there is an implied ellipsis in the phrase, as if to say: his own self is secure wherever it goes off (saraba), that is, wherever it ranges. Likewise huwa wāsi'u al-sirb, meaning the chest — this too is with kasra. They said it is meant that he is slow to anger. This goes back to the same root already given: they say anger does not seize him so that he is thrown into turmoil and the paths close in upon him.
سرج:
The letters sīn, rā' and jīm are a sound root indicating beauty, adornment and comeliness. From this: al-sirāj, the lamp, named for its light and its beauty. From it too: al-sarj, the saddle of a riding animal, being its adornment. One says sarraja wajhahu, meaning he made his face handsome, as though he had made it like a lamp for himself. A verse says:
And dark hair, and a nose-bridge made radiant.
What departs from this root: their calling a habitual way of doing things surjūja.
سرح:
The letters sīn, rā' and ḥā' are one steady root, and it points to release, to setting loose. From it: amrun sarīḥ, a matter with no hindrance or delay in it. Then this is carried over to al-sarāḥ, which is divorce; one says sarraḥtu al-mar'ata, I released the woman. In the Book of God, Most High: {or release them kindly} [al-Baqara: 231]. Al-suruḥ is the fast she-camel. From this chapter too: al-munsariḥ, the naked man who has come out of his clothes. Al-sarḥ: grazing livestock, animals put out to pasture. Al-sāriḥ: the herdsman. It is also said that al-sāriḥ is the man who owns the sarḥ. As for the great tree, it is al-sarḥa, and perhaps this is an irregular outlier from this root; or it may be called sarḥa because its branches spread loose (inṣirāḥ) and go off in every direction. 'Antara said, in a line of verse:

A hero, as if his garments hung upon a great tree ... shod with sandals of tanned leather, having no equal

From this chapter too: al-sirḥān, the wolf, named so because he goes off freely (yansariḥu) after what he seeks; likewise the lion, when it is called sirḥān. As for al-sarīḥa, it is a strip of cloth.
سرد:
The letters sīn, rā and dāl are a consistent, analogically sound root, pointing to the succession of many things, one connected to the next.

1. al-sard — a collective name for coats of mail and similar things made of linked rings. God, great is His majesty, said, concerning David, peace be upon him: {and measure well the links} [Saba': 11]. They said its meaning is: let that be well-measured — the hole not too narrow with the rivet thick, nor the rivet too thin with the hole wide, but everything in due measure.

They said: al-zarrād, the mail-maker, is really al-sarrād, and it is said this variant came about because the rā is close to the sīn in pronunciation.

2. al-misrad — the awl; its derivation from this root is sound.
سرط:
The letters sīn, rāʾ and ṭāʾ are a single, sound root, indicating disappearance in the course of passing and going away.

1. From this: saraṭtu al-ṭaʿām — I swallowed the food — because when a thing is swallowed, it disappears.
2. Some scholars say al-ṣirāṭ [the road/path] is derived from this, because one going along it disappears the way swallowed food disappears.
3. al-sirṭirāṭ, on the pattern fiʿillāl — a sweet confection (al-fālūdh), because it is gulped straight down.
4. al-surāṭ — a sharp sword, cutting and effective on what it strikes. A Hudhalī poet described a sword, in a line of verse: "the colour of salt, its stroke a flash — it strips the flesh clean, a sword that swallows (surāṭī) whole."
سرع:
The letters sīn, rā' and ʿayn are a sound root pointing to the opposite of slowness.

Al-sarīʿ, the swift, is the opposite of the slow. And saraʿān al-nās are the foremost of people, those who go on ahead quickly. And the Arabs say: la-saraʿāna mā ṣanaʿta kadhā — how quickly you did such a thing. As for al-sarʿ among the shoots of a vine, [it is] the quickest thing to come up from it. Like it is al-saraʿraʿ; then the soft, tender person is likened to it.
سرف:
The letters sīn, rā' and fā' are a single root pointing to going beyond the limit, and also to overlooking a thing.

You say: fī al-amri sarafun — in the matter there is excess, that is, going past the proper measure. And it has come in the hadith: "The third washing in the ablution is honour, and the fourth is excess."

As for the overlooking, it is the speaker's words: "I passed by you and sariftukum" — that is, I did not notice you.

Jarīr said, in a line of verse:
They gave a hundred camels driven along by eight men; in their giving there is no reproach and no waste.

And they say that al-saraf is ignorance, and al-sarif is the ignorant man. They argue from Ṭarafa's words, in a line of verse:
A man foolish of heart sees my abuse of him as honey mixed with the water of a cloud.

This goes back to part of what has gone before, and the rule is one. And they say that al-saraf is also craving. In the hadith: "Meat has a craving like the craving for wine" — that is, an addiction. And this is not far from the first word.

Of what has strayed from this chapter: al-surfa, a little creature that eats wood. One says sarafat al-surfatu al-shajarata sarfan when it eats its leaves, and the tree is masrūfa. It is said that it builds itself a fine house. And they say in the proverb: "a better maker than a surfa".
سرق: The letters sīn, rā' and qāf are a root pointing to taking something in hiding and concealment. One says saraqa yasriqu sariqatan — he stole. What is stolen is saraq. Istaraqa al-sam' — when he listens in secret. Among what strays from this chapter is al-saraq, the plural of saraqa, and it is a length of silk.
سرو:
The letters sīn, rāʾ and the weak letter form a chapter of great range; scarcely two words of it come together under one single pattern.

1. al-sarw — generosity joined with manliness; one says sariyy [a noble, generous man], and saruwa — he had that quality.
2. al-sarw — a district of [the tribe] Ḥimyar. Ibn Muqbil said, in a line of verse: "in the sarw of Ḥimyar, the mules' urine is there — how then did you journey by night to that far-off place?"
3. al-sarw — uncovering one thing from another. sarawtu ʿannī al-thawb — I removed the garment from myself, I uncovered it. In the hadith about warm gruel: "it lifts from the sick man's heart" — meaning it removes it. Ibn Harma said: "youth's fleeting shade has slipped from off you, and the departing beloved has drawn near to parting." For that reason one also says surriya ʿanhu — it was lifted from him.
4. al-sirwa — a small creature/insect. One says land is masruwwa, from al-sirwa, when the creature is abundant in it.
5. al-sāriya — the pillar.
6. al-surā — travelling by night; one says sarayt and asrayt. As in the line: "she journeyed by night to you, though she never used to travel by night."
7. al-sarāʾ — a kind of tree.
8. sarāt al-shayʾ — the back, the upper part of a thing.
9. sarāt al-nahār — the day's full height [midday].

What we have listed here is remote, one sense from another, and for that reason we have not forced it onto a single pattern.

1. And when said with a hamza it is further removed still: one says saraʾat al-jarāda — the locust laid its eggs; and when the time for that comes upon it, one says asraʾat.
سطا:
The letters sīn, ṭā', and the weak letter are a root pointing to overpowering and dominance.

1. "saṭā ʿalayhi yasṭū" — he overpowered him, when he overcame him with violent force.
2. faras sāṭin — a horse that outstrips the rest of the horses.
3. "al-faḥl yasṭū ʿalā ṭarūqatihi" — the stallion overpowers the female he covers.
4. "saṭā al-rāʿī ʿalā al-shāh" — the shepherd reached forcibly into the ewe, when her young died in her belly and he reached in and drew it out.
5. "saṭā al-mā'" — the water became abundant, when it increased.

Some of the language scholars said, of a horse described as "sāṭin": it is one that raises its tail while cantering. Al-Shaybānī said: "al-sāṭī" is a camel that, when seized by rut, goes out from one herd of camels to another.

He said:
His head is like that of a rutting, dominant stud-camel.
سطح:
The letters sīn, ṭā and ḥā are a root pointing to the spreading and stretching out of a thing; from it al-saṭḥ, the roof, is well known.

1. The saṭḥ of anything is its upper surface, stretching along with it.
2. insaṭaḥa al-rajulu — a man stretched out on his back and did not move; for that reason the one who lies flat on his back from chronic illness is called saṭīḥ.
3. Saṭīḥ, the soothsayer, was named so because he was created that way, without bones.
4. al-masṭaḥ, with fatḥa on the mīm — the place where dates are spread out to dry.
5. al-misṭaḥ, with kasra on the mīm — the tent; plural masāṭiḥ.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
The fat, cowardly men of Khuzā'a stood in our way — and what good is a fat coward handling a tent?

It was named that because the tent is stretched out by it.

6. al-saṭīḥa — the large water-skin; named so because when it falls it lies flat and spread out, that is, it stretches out.
7. al-suṭṭāḥ — a plant among the plants of the earth, so called because it spreads out over the ground.
سطر:
The letters sīn, ṭā' and rā' are a steady root pointing to a thing standing in a row — like writing, and like trees, and everything that stands in a row. As for al-asāṭīr, they are as though they were things written down out of what is false, and that then became a name for them, belonging to them alone. One says saṭṭara fulān 'alaynā tasṭīran when he comes with falsehoods. And the singular of al-asāṭīr is isṭār and usṭūra.

Among what departs from this chapter is al-musayṭir, who is the one who takes charge of a thing and has mastery over it.
سطع:
The letters sīn, ṭā', and ʿayn are a root pointing to length in a thing and its rising up into the air.

1. al-saṭaʿ — length of the neck. One says "ẓalīm asṭaʿ" [a long-necked male ostrich] and "naʿāma saṭʿā'" [a long-necked female ostrich].
2. al-siṭāʿ — a tent-pole, one of the poles of a tent.

Al-Qaṭāmī said, in a line of verse:
Were they not the very ones who together dealt unjustly ... against al-Nuʿmān, and rushed to seize the tent-pole?

3. saṭaʿa al-ghubār and saṭaʿati al-rā'iḥa — the dust rose up, and the scent rose, when it lifted into the air.
4. al-saṭʿ — the rising of a sound from a thing when you strike something against it; one says "saṭaʿahu".
5. It is said that al-saṭīʿ is the dawn. If this is sound, it fits the reasoning of the chapter, because it too is something that rises and lifts up.

As for al-siṭāʿ in the poetry of the tribe of Hudhayl, it is the name of a specific mountain.
سطل: The letters sīn, ṭā', and lām amount to nothing. Except that they call a certain vessel a "saṭl" or "sayṭal".
سطم:
The letters sīn, ṭā', and mīm are a sound root pointing to the source of a thing and where it gathers together.

1. al-usṭumm — the gathering-place of the sea.
2. "hādhihi usṭummat al-ḥasab" — this is the core of his noble lineage, meaning its very center.
3. "al-nās fī usṭummat al-amr" — the people are at the very center of the matter.
4. al-usṭumm and al-siṭām are said to mean the blade of a sword.

In a hadith: "siṭām al-nās", meaning their sharp edge, their foremost force.
سطن:
The letters sīn, ṭā', and nūn are, in al-Khalīl's view, a true root, because he treats the nūn in it as an original letter. Al-Khalīl said: "usṭuwāna" [pillar] follows a particular word-pattern. One says "hādhihi asāṭīnu musaṭṭana" — these are pillars set up as pillars. He said: one also says "jamal usṭuwān" for a camel that is tall.

He said:
They have tried in me a towering, long-necked one.
سع:
The letters sīn and ʿayn, in the doubled and matched form, point to a single origin sense: a thing passing away. Al-Khalīl said: one says "tasaʿsaʿa al-shahru" — the month has passed away, when most of it has gone. And one says "tasaʿsaʿa al-rajulu mina l-kibar" — the man became unsteady from old age, when his body trembled.

He said:
O Hind, how quickly he has grown feeble and unsteady!
سعد:
The letters sīn, ʿayn and dāl are a root indicating good and joy, the opposite of ill fortune.

1. al-saʿd — good fortune in a matter.
2. al-saʿdān — a plant, among the best pasture. They say in their proverbs: "pasture, but none like al-saʿdān."
3. The suʿūd of the star [the auspicious lunar stations] are ten, such as Saʿd Bulaʿ and Saʿd al-Dhābiḥ; they were named suʿūd for their good fortune.

This is the origin sense; then they called the human forearm sāʿid, because a person draws strength from it for his tasks. For this reason one says sāʿadahu ʿalā amrihi, when he helped him — as if he joined his forearm to the other's forearm. Some said: al-musāʿada is helping in anything, while al-isʿād occurs only in wailing/lamenting together.

4. al-saʿdāna — the kirkira, the callused pad on a camel's chest — named so by comparison to al-saʿdān the plant, for its spreading over the ground.
5. al-saʿdāna — the knot of a sandal-strap that lies against the ground.
6. al-saʿdānāt — the knots in the pan of a balance-scale.
7. Suʿd — a place. Jarīr said, in a line of verse:
"Greet the abodes at Suʿd — for I love, for love of Fāṭima, those very abodes."
8. It is said that al-saʿdāna is the female dove, derived from al-saʿd.
سعر:
The letters sīn, 'ayn and rā' are a single root pointing to [a thing] blazing up, catching fire, and rising.

From this is al-sa'īr, the blaze of a fire. And isti'āruhā is its taking flame. Al-mis'ar is
the wood with which a fire is stirred up. Al-su'ār is the heat of fire. One says su'ira al-rajul, when the hot desert wind strikes a man. And it is said that al-si'rāra is what you see in the sunlight like specks of dust. And sa'artu al-nār and as'artuhā — I kindled the fire — so it is mus'ara and mas'ūra. And one says ista'ara al-luṣūṣ, as though the thieves had caught fire. And ista'ara al-jarab fī al-ba'īr, the mange blazed up in the camel. And al-As'ar al-Ju'fī was so named for his saying, in a line of verse:
Let not the people of the house of Mālik call me away, if I do not set fire upon them and kindle it high.

Ibn al-Sikkīt said: one says sa'arahum sharran, he set evil blazing among them, and one does not say as'arahum. And of this chapter is al-su'r, which is madness, so named because it blazes up within a man. And they say nāqa mas'ūra of a she-camel, and that is for her fierceness, as though she were mad. As for si'r al-ṭa'ām, the price of food, it too is from this, because it goes up and rises. As for masā'ir al-ba'īr, they are its mashā'ir; and it is said: they are its armpits, its groins and the base of its tail where the hair grows thin, and they were so named only because the mange blazes up in them first and blazes up in them most fiercely. And as for the saying of 'Urwa b. al-Ward, in a line of verse:
So they flew off into the lands of al-Yasta'ūr.

They said: he meant al-sa'īr, the blaze. And it is said that it is a place, and it is said that it is a tree called al-yasta'ūr which is used [as] a toothstick.
سعط:
The letters sīn, ʿayn, and ṭā' are a root: that a person be made to take medicine through the nose, and other things are then carried on it.

1. "asʿaṭtuhu al-dawā' fa-staʿaṭahu" — I administered the medicine to him through his nose, and he took it in.
2. al-musʿuṭ — the vessel the nasal medicine, "al-saʿūṭ", is put into. Al-saʿūṭ is the medicine itself, and its underlying verb-form is "saʿaṭa".

Among what is carried on this is their saying "ṭaʿantuhu fa-asʿaṭtuhu al-rumḥ" — I stabbed him and drove the spear into him. And God knows best.
سعف:
The letters sīn, ʿayn, and fā' are two distinct roots: one points to a thing's dryness and raggedness, and the other to a thing being accommodating.

The first:

1. al-saʿaf, plural of "saʿafa" — the branches of a palm tree once they have dried out. The fresh, moist ones are called "al-shaṭb" instead. As for Imru' al-Qays's saying about a mare, "Dried, spreading fronds clothed her face", he means only that he likened her forelock to it.
2. al-saʿfa — sores that break out on a child's head.
3. "suʿifat yaduhu" (al-Kisā'ī's saying) — his hand became chapped, that being the fraying and cracking around the fingernails.
4. nāqa saʿfā' — a she-camel afflicted with "suʿifat saʿafan", a disease that thins the hair of her muzzle. This is particular to she-camels.

The second origin sense: "asʿaftu al-rajula bi-ḥājatihi" — I met the man's need, when you fulfilled it for him. One also says "asʿaftuhu ʿalā amrihi" — I helped him in his affair.
سعل:
The letters sīn, ʿayn, and lām are a root pointing to clamor and a raised voice.

1. One says of a clamorous, loud-mouthed woman that she has become "istasʿalat" — she is likened to the "siʿlāt", a female demon.
2. al-saʿālā — the most wicked of the ghouls.
3. al-suʿāl, coughing, also derived from this, because it is something that rises up.

As for al-Hudhalī's saying, describing a wild donkey:
"...and the fresh green pasture had roused it"
he means the fresh pasture made it lively, until it became like the "siʿlāt" in its movement and liveliness.
سعم: The letters sīn, ʿayn, and mīm are contained in a single word. Al-saʿm is journeying. One says "saʿama al-baʿīr" — the camel journeyed on, when it traveled. A she-camel [good at this] is called "saʿūm".
سعن: The letters sīn, ʿayn, and nūn are contained in a single word. They say "mā lahu saʿna wa lā maʿna" — he has nothing at all, neither little nor much. It is said, if it is sound, that al-suʿn is something like a bucket.
سعو:
The letters sīn, ʿayn, and the weak letter, which is wāw, are two words, if both are sound.

It is related of al-Kisā'ī: "maḍā saʿwun mina al-layl" — a portion of the night passed. Ibn Duraid mentioned that al-saʿw is beeswax, but this is doubtful.

Al-masʿāh is striving in generosity and open-handedness. Al-siʿāya is the collecting of the alms-tax. Siʿāyat al-ʿabd, when a slave has made a contract for manumission, is his working to earn what frees him.

From this chapter also: "sāʿā al-rajulu al-ama" — a man committed fornication with a slave-woman, as though he had striven toward that and she had striven in it too. They said: such mutual striving occurs only with slave-women.
سغ: The letters sīn and ghayn are a root pointing to a thing working its way into another thing with unsteady motion and movement. From this: "saghsaghtu ra'sī bi-l-duhn" — I worked oil into my head, when you soak it thoroughly. Al-Khalīl and others said: "saghsaghta al-shay' fī l-turāb" — you worked a thing into the dust, when you pressed it into it. As for their saying "tasaghsaghat thanniyyatuh" — his front tooth worked loose — it is possible this comes from a letter-substitution, and from the chapter just before this one.
سغب:
The letters sīn, ghayn and bā are a single root pointing to hunger.

al-masghaba — famine. One says saghiba yasghabu sughūban, and he is sāghib or saghbān.

Ibn Durayd said: some philologists said al-saghab is only hunger together with exhaustion. He said thirst is sometimes called saghab too, but that is not the current usage.
سغل:
The letters sīn, ghayn, and lām are a root pointing to poor feeding and a resulting bad state.

1. al-saghil — a child that has been poorly fed. Anything poorly nourished is "saghil".

Salāma ibn Jandal said, describing a horse, in a line of verse:
Not sparse-maned, nor hook-nosed, nor poorly-reared ... given medicine, reared behind the herd, well cared-for.

It is also said that al-saghil is one thin and small in the legs. Ibn Duraid said: al-saghil is one whose flesh is wasted, emaciated, of unsound build.
سغم: The letters sīn, ghayn, and mīm amount to nothing. Except that they use "saghim" for what is otherwise called "saghil", poorly-nourished.
سف:
The letters sīn and fā' are a single root: a thing drawing close to another thing and nearing it. Whatever comes near is then derived from it.

1. asaffa al-ṭā'ir — the bird flew low, when it drew near the ground in its flight.
2. asaffa al-rajulu li-l-amr — the man drew close to the matter, when he approached it.

One says "asaffati l-saḥābatu" — the cloud drew low, when it neared the ground.

Aws said, describing clouds, in a line of verse:
Low-hanging, close above the earth, its trailing fringe ... nearly pushed down by one standing with a raised palm.

3. asaffa al-rajulu al-naẓar — the man kept his gaze fixed, when he sustained it.
4. al-safsāf — a paltry, contemptible matter. It is named so because it comes from a man's "asaffa" toward a low matter.
5. al-musafsifa — the wind that runs low just above the ground.
6. al-siff — the snake called al-arqam, because it clings closely to the ground as it moves.

The reasoning in all of this is one and the same.

As for "safaftu al-khūṣ" — I plaited palm leaves — and "al-safīf", the girth-strap tied round the pack-saddle, these too come from this, because when a thing is woven, every strand of it is drawn close to the rest.

Among what may be carried on this chapter, or may be an exception to it, is your saying "safiftu al-dawā' asuffuhu" — I took the medicine dry. One also says "asaffa wajhahu" — he sprinkled something over his face.

Ḍābi' said, describing a bull, in a line of verse:
Strong is the gleam of his two brows, as though ... he had been dusted with the scorch of a fire, and turned kohl-dark.
سفح:
The letters sīn, fā' and ḥā' are a single root indicating the pouring out of something. One says: he safaḥa blood, meaning he poured it out; "safaḥa the blood" — he shed it. Al-sifāḥ (fornication) is the pouring out of seed without a marriage contract, like something poured out wastefully. Al-Saffāḥ was a man among the chiefs of the Arabs, who poured out water during a raid he waged, and so was named al-Saffāḥ.

As for safḥ al-jabal (the foot of the mountain), it belongs to letter-substitution; its origin is ṣafḥ, mentioned in its own chapter. Al-safīḥ is one of the three [gambling] arrows that carry no share; it is irregular, outside the root we have mentioned.
سفد:
The letters sīn, fā' and dāl are not a single root from which branches spread; rather they hold two words distinct in outward form, though it may be possible to join them by derivation.

1. sifād — the mating of a bird; one says safida yasfadu, and likewise of the billy-goat.
2. al-saffūd — the skewer, well known.

Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
As if, jutting out from its flank, it were a drinking-party's skewer, forgotten by them at the fire-pit.
سفر:
The letters sīn, fā' and rā' are a single root, pointing to uncovering and clearing away. From that is al-safar, travel, called so because people uncover themselves away from their own places. Al-safr are travellers. Ibn Durayd said: a man is safr and a company of people are safr.

Of this root, and it is the origin itself: safartu al-bayt — I swept the house. From it is the hadith: "If only you would give an order about this house and it were swept." And for that reason what falls from the leaves of trees is called al-safīr.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And the withered leaf-fall of the year, its drifting part turning about the mounds of earth, with grey in its colours.

It is called safīr only because the wind sweeps it away. As for their saying safara bayna al-qawm sifāratan, when a man sets things right between people, that is of this root too, because he removed the enmity and disagreement that were there. And safarat al-mar'a 'an wajhihā, when a woman uncovers her face. And asfara al-ṣubḥ — the morning grew bright, and that is the uncovering of the darkness; and a face is musfir when it is shining with joy. And it is said istafarat al-ibil — the camels moved about and went off over the land. The food prepared for a traveller is called sufra. And the leather sheet was named sufra. And it is said a camel is misfar, that is, strong for travel.

Of what strays from this root is al-sifār, an iron piece put in the nose of the she-camel. It is in his words:
What are my camels to me, and what the string of them, and what the nose-iron — foul be the nose-iron.

There is another view about it: that it is a cord whose end is tied to the camel's nose-band and wound round it, and its mouth is made into a rein by it.

Al-safr is writing. Al-safara are the writers, called so because writing uncovers what is needed of the thing written.
سفط:
The letters sīn, fā' and ṭā' amount to nothing, and nothing in this chapter can be relied on, except that they named this [basket] al-safaṭ. And they say: al-safīṭ is the generous man among men. They recited:
He is not a man of resolve, nor a generous one.
And this amounts to nothing.
سفع:
The letters sīn, fā and ʿayn are two roots: one is a colour among colours, the other is taking hold of a thing with the hand.

As for the first:
1. al-sufʿa — blackness; for that reason the three stones a cooking pot stands on over the fire are called sufʿ. From it their saying "I see in him a sufʿa of anger", said when his colour darkens with anger.
2. al-safʿā' — a woman who is sallow and pale; and every falcon is asfaʿ, dark-tinged in colour.
3. al-safʿā' — also the dove, whose dark patch is on her neck, a little below the head and a little above the ring of colour there.
4. al-sufʿa, in the traces left of an abandoned dwelling — what differs in the colour of its ash from the rest of the ground's colour.

Al-Khalīl used to say: al-sufʿa in colour is only a blackness tinged with redness.

As for the other root:
5. safaʿtu al-farasa — to take hold of the front of a horse's head, that is, its forelock. God, exalted be His praise, said: {We will surely seize by the forelock} [al-ʿAlaq: 15]

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Among those bridling their colts, or seizing them by the forelock.

6. The bird "safaʿa" its prey, meaning it struck it.
7. "I safaʿtu so-and-so's head with a stick" — this is carried back to the sense of taking hold with the hand.

In Al-Khalīl's book: ʿUbayd Allāh ibn al-Ḥasan, the judge of Basra, was fond of saying "isfaʿā bi-yadihi fa-aqīmāhu" — take hold of his hand, you two, and stand him up — meaning, take hold of his hand.
سفق:
The letters sīn, fā', and qāf are a small root pointing to the opposite of flimsiness.

1. al-safīq — a variant word for "al-ṣafīq", the opposite of "al-sakhīf", flimsy.
2. "safaqtu al-bāb fa-nsafaqa" — I shut the door firmly, and it shut. This too goes back to that same reasoning.
3. rajul safīq al-wajh — a thick-faced man, said of one with little sense of shame.

From this chapter: "safaqtu wajhahu" — I struck his face.
سفك: The letters sīn, fā' and kāf are a single word. One says safaka damahu yasfikuhu safkan, when he made his blood flow, shed it; likewise tears.
سفل: The letters sīn, fā' and lām are a single root, and it is whatever is the opposite of height. Al-sufl is the lower part of a house or of anything else. Al-sufūl is the opposite of loftiness. Al-safila are the low sort of people; one says he is min safilat al-nās — of the low of the people — and one does not say safila of a single man. Al-safāl is the opposite of eminence. And one says: their affair is indeed in decline. One says qa'ada bi-sufālat al-rīḥ wa-'ulāwatihā — he sat on the downwind side and the upwind side. Al-'ulāwa is the side the wind blows from, and al-sufāla is what lies opposite that.
سفن:
The letters sīn, fā' and nūn are a single root indicating removing a thing from the surface of another, like peeling. Ibn Durayd said: al-safīna (ship) is on the pattern fa'īla with the meaning of the active participle, because it tasfinu the water — as though it scrapes it. Al-saffān is the sailor of the ship. The origin of the chapter is al-safn, planing/scraping; one says: safantu the wood, asfinuhu, a safn — I planed it.

Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
It came stealthily, its belly grazing the ground — you see the dust clinging to it, though not deliberately stuck on.

Al-safan is the iron tool with which one carves.

Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
And every year he has a raid, that scrapes the hind-hooves as the planing-iron scrapes.

And the wind safanat the dust off the surface of the ground, scraping it away.
سفه:
The letters sīn, fā' and hā' are a single root, pointing to lightness and flimsiness. It is a rule that holds throughout. So *al-safah* is the opposite of forbearance. One says *thawb safīh* — a garment of poor weave. And one says *tasaffahat al-rīḥ*, when the wind bends and swerves. Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
They walked as swaying things shake when the winds turn their upper parts aside, at the passing of the scouring winds.

And in his poetry also, in a line of verse:
... its plaited nose-rein unsteady.
He is speaking of the camel's halter and its tossing about. And one says *tasaffahtu fulānan ʿan mālihi* when you cheat him out of it, as though you had swerved him away from it and made him take it lightly. A poet said, in a line of verse:
You beguiled him out of his property when you saw him a youth like the swaying branch of the ban tree.

Some people mentioned that *al-safah* is that a man drinks much water and is never satisfied. If this is sound it is close to that same rule. And Abū Zayd used to say: *sāfahtu al-waṭb* or *al-dann* — when you sit down beside the milk-skin or the jar and drink from it hour after hour. And he recited, in two lines of verse:
Tell me plainly, Umayr: is a knotted spear, unbroken, with a dryness in its shaft,
dearer to you, or a foaming milk-skin that you sit sipping at when the late afternoon leans down?
سفو:
The letters sīn, fā' and the weak letter are a single root indicating lightness in a thing. Al-safw is the verbal noun of safā yasfū safwan, said when someone walks swiftly, and likewise of a bird when it hastens in its flight.

1. al-safā — lightness of the forelock; it is disliked in horses but praised in mules, so one says baghlatun safwāʾ, a mule of light forelock.
2. saffati l-rīḥ — the wind blew the dust, [verbal noun] safyan.
3. al-safā — what the wind scatters of dust.
4. al-safā — the thorn of the buhmā-grass, because when it dries it grows light and the wind scatters it.

Ru'ba said, in a line of verse:
It let the tufts of thorn-down course over the bare ridges.

And from the chapter:

1. al-safā — the dust of the grave.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Grave-dust has come between me and you, and the foes as well; and he who is pledged to the grave-dust is a man of abundant, noble nature.

2. al-safāʾ, with hamza — folly and rashness.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
How many a fool have our spears brought down, who dealt with us foolishly, in heedlessness and folly.
سقب:
The letters sīn, qāf and bā' are two roots: one is nearness, the other indicates something upright and standing.

The first: al-saqab, which is nearness. From it is the hadith, "The neighbour has the better claim by his nearness [saqab]." One says of it saqibati l-dār and asqabat. Al-sāqib — the near one. Some people said: al-sāqib means both the near and the far. The near sense is well known; for the far sense they cited the saying of the poet:
You left your father in the land of the Ḥijāz, and set off toward a distant land.

As for the other root, it is al-saqb and al-ṣaqb, the tent-pole. By comparison to it, al-saqb was named for the young of the she-camel. And one says nāqatun misqāb, said of a she-camel whose bearing is mostly male young — it is his saying:
A blaze-faced one, mostly bearing males, by a stud that also sired males.
This is a verb-form, not a descriptive adjective.
سقر:
The letters sīn, qāf and rā' are a root indicating burning or scorching by fire. One says saqarat-hu l-shams, meaning the sun scorched him, and it is for this that [Hell] is named Saqar.

1. saqarāt al-shams — its blazing heat.

It may also be said with ṣād, and that has been mentioned in its own chapter.
سقط:
The letters sīn, qāf, and ṭā' are a single root pointing to falling, applying consistently. From it: saqaṭa al-shay'u yasquṭu suqūṭan. Al-saqaṭ is shoddy goods. Al-siqāṭ and al-saqaṭ are error in speech or deed. Suwayd said:
How can they hope for my stumbling, after ... gray hair and baldness have covered my head?
Some said al-siqāṭ in speech is the plural of saqṭa, on the pattern of ramla/rimāl.

1. Al-suqaṭ is a child born [miscarried] before it is complete, said with damma, fatḥa, or kasra.
2. Saqṭ al-nār is what falls from it, from the fire-striker.
3. Al-saqqāṭ is a sword that, once past what it strikes, falls through and reaches the ground.
4. Al-sāqiṭa is a man base in his lineage; al-saqīṭa is a base woman.
5. We were told, on the authority passed down from al-Khalīl, that one says saqaṭa al-waladu min baṭni ummihi [the child fell from its mother's womb], and one does not say waqa'a for this.
6. Suqṭ al-raml, siqṭuhu, and saqṭuhu are where its edge comes to an end, its cutoff point; likewise masqiṭ ra'sihi, where he was born; masqiṭ al-sawṭ, where the whip fell; atānā fī masqiṭ al-najm, where the star fell.
7. This deed is masqaṭa for a man, causing him to fall from people's regard — that is, doing what one ought not to do.
8. Al-siqāṭ in a horse is a slackening of its gallop.
9. Aṣbaḥat al-arḍu mubyaḍḍatan min al-saqīṭ, that is, from snow or frost.
10. Siqṭ al-saḥāb is said to be where the edge of a cloud is seen, as though falling upon the earth at the edge of the horizon; likewise siqṭ al-khibā' [the edge of the tent].
11. Siqṭā janāḥay al-ẓalīm are the parts of an ostrich's two wings that drag along the ground, as in the line: "the two trailing edges of the wings of a startled male ostrich." Some scholar said, of the line —
Until, when the dawn shone forth, and there rose up ... from it the darkness of a night with two trailing edges, gathering thick —
it is said na'āmat al-layl means its blackness, and its two siqṭ are its beginning and its end — meaning the night with its two edges had passed, and the dawn had proven true.
سقع: The letters sīn, qāf and ʿayn are not a root, because the sīn in it is substituted from ṣād. One says ṣuqʿ and suqʿ, and ṣaqaʿtuhu and saqaʿtuhu. And mā adrī ayna saqaʿa, meaning I do not know where he went.
سقف:
The letters sīn, qāf and fā' are a root indicating height together with overhanging and bending. From this is al-saqf, the roof of a house, because it is high and overhangs. Al-saqīfa is a roofed shelter. Al-saqīfa is also any wide plank in a structure when it juts out from a wall. The sky is a saqf; God Almighty said: {And We made the sky a protected roof} [al-Anbiyā': 32].

Of this chapter is al-asqaf among men, the tall, stooping man; one says: asqaf, clearly showing that stoop. And God knows best what is correct.
سقل: The letters sīn, qāf and lām are not a root, because the sīn in it is substituted for a ṣād.
سقم: The letters sīn, qāf and mīm are a single root, and it is sickness. One says suqm, saqam, and saqām — three dialect forms.
سقى:
The letters sīn, qāf and the weak letter are a single root, and it is giving a thing water, or the like of it, to drink. You say: saqaytuhu bi-yadī asqīhi saqyan, I gave him drink with my own hand, and asqaytuhu, said when you set aside a share of drink for him.

1. al-suqy — the verbal noun; as in kam siqyu arḍika, how much is your land's share of watering, that is, its portion of drink.
2. asqaytuka hādhā l-jild — I have given you this hide, meaning I have granted it to you to make into a waterskin.
3. saqaytu ʿalā fulān — I said of so-and-so, "May God give him drink," a blessing formula. Al-Akhfash related this.
4. al-siqāya — the place set up for drink during the pilgrimage season.
5. al-siqāya — the drinking-cup. In His mighty and glorious saying: {He put the drinking-cup in his brother's saddlebag} [Yūsuf: 70] — it is the vessel the king used to drink from.
6. saqā baṭnu fulān — so-and-so's belly filled [with fluid], that being a yellow water that collects in it.
7. saqā fulānun ʿalā fulānin bi-mā yakrahu — so-and-so kept repeating to another something he disliked, said when he did it to him again and again.
8. al-saqiyy — papyrus-reed, in Imruʾ al-Qays's saying:
and a calf like the stalk of well-tended, pliant papyrus-reed.
9. al-saqiyy, also on the pattern faʿīl — a cloud heavy with rain.
10. al-siqāʾ — the waterskin, well known; and from this is derived asqaytu l-rajul, said when you backbite a man.

Ibn Aḥmar said, in a line of verse:
Nor, to any I have made my foe, do I give my waterskin to drink.
سك:
The letters sīn and kāf are a regular root pointing to narrowness, closeness, and smallness.

1. al-sakak — smallness of the ear. Such an ear is called "sakkā'".
2. istakkat masāmiʿuhu — his hearing became blocked, said when he went deaf.

Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
And I was told, best of men, that you had blamed me ... and that is the kind of thing that blocks up the ears.

3. al-sikka — the row of palm trees planted in a line, named so for how closely and evenly set they are.
4. sikkat al-darāhim — the coin-die, the iron stamp, from this same root, because of how tightly packed the engraving of its lettering is.
5. al-sakk — fitting an iron bolt to a door, closing it up.
6. al-sakkī — the carpenter.
7. al-sukk — said to be a name for wells whose shaft is of even width throughout.
8. al-sukk — the scorpion's burrow.
9. sukk — said of a coat of mail that is tight, or one whose rings are tight.
10. istakka, said of a plant, when its gaps have closed up.

The reasoning is regular throughout all of this. Among what is carried on it is what Ibn Duraid related: "sakkahu yasukkuhu sakkan" — he cut off both his ears.

Among what is an exception to this chapter: al-sukāk, the space between sky and earth. Al-sukk, a substance used for perfume; it is said to be genuine Arabic.
سكب:
The letters sīn, kāf and bā are a root pointing to the pouring out of a thing. You say: sakaba al-mā'a yaskubuhu, he poured out the water.

A horse is sakb, meaning swift-running, as though it pours out its running the way water is poured — the same way they call it "a sea" for its swiftness.
سكت:
The letters sīn, kāf and tā point to the opposite of speech.

1. sakata yaskutu sukūtan — he fell silent; a man is sikkīt, habitually silent.
2. "He struck him with a sukāta" — with something that silenced him.
3. sakata al-ghaḍabu — the anger fell silent, meaning it subsided.
4. al-sukta — whatever you use to quiet a child.
5. al-sukayt — the tenth horse to finish, when horses run in a race. It is possible it was named so because its owner falls silent from boasting, as one says "such-and-such made him drag", when it stops him from boasting, as though his tongue were dragged into silence.
سكر:
The letters sin, kaf and ra are a single root indicating bewilderment.

From it: al-sukr, from drink. One says 'sakira sukran'; a man much given to drunkenness is 'sikkir'. Al-taskir is bewildering, in His saying, mighty and exalted: {they would surely say, our eyes have only been dazzled} [al-Hijr: 15] and some read it lightened, without doubling the letter; they said its meaning is 'bewitched'.

Al-sikr is that by which water is dammed in the land. Al-sakr is the damming of water; and water, when dammed, becomes agitated/confused. As for their saying 'laylatun sakira', it means the calm, pleasant night, in which there is nothing troubling. Aws said:
Nights are added to it in length; it is neither a pleasant one nor a calm one.

One says 'sakarati l-rih' — the wind died down. Al-sakar is [an intoxicating] drink. Some related that 'sakarahu' means he strangled him; if this is correct, it belongs to this root. And a camel 'strangles/subdues' another with its foreleg, until it nearly kills it. A line (fragment, obscure): a young weak camel is subdued/struck down.
سكف:
The letters sīn, kāf and fā' are not a single root; it holds two words:

1. uskuffat al-bāb — the doorway's threshold, the part that is trodden on; and uskuff al-ʿayn is named by comparison to it.
2. al-iskāf — it is said that among the Arabs every craftsman is called iskāf.

Al-Shammākh's line is recited:
And two forks of mays-wood, shaped by a craftsman.
They said: he meant the bow-maker.
سكم: The letters sīn, kāf and mīm amount to nothing. Though some have mentioned that al-sakm is taking short, close steps.
سكن:
The letters sīn, kāf and nūn are a single root, running steadily, pointing to the opposite of restlessness and motion. One says sakana al-shay' yaskunu sukūnan, so it is sākin, still. And al-sakn is the household who dwell in a house. And in the hadith: 'until a single pomegranate will feed a household.' And al-sakan is fire, in the words of the one who said, in a line of verse:
It has been set straight with fire and with oils.
And it was called sakan for the first sense, namely that the one who looks at it grows still and settles toward it and toward its people. And for that they said: 'More friendly than a fire.' And they say: 'It is fairer than fire in the eye of one who is chilled.' And al-sakan is everything you settle toward of what is loved. And al-sikkīn, the knife, is well known; some of the people of the language said: it is on the pattern fiʿʿīl because it stills the movement of what is slaughtered with it. And of this chapter is al-sakīna, which is gravity and calm. And the sukkān of a ship was so called because it steadies it from tossing; and it is an Arabic word.
سل:
The letters sīn and lām are a single root: drawing a thing out gently and unseen, and other things are then carried on it.

1. salaltu al-shay' asulluhu sallan — I drew the thing out.
2. al-salla and al-islāl — theft.

In a hadith of the Messenger of God, peace be upon him and his family, when he wrote a treaty: "No treachery and no theft." Al-ighlāl is betrayal, and al-islāl is theft.

3. al-salīl — the child, as though he were drawn out from his mother.

A woman of the Arabs said of her son, in a line of verse:
He was drawn out from my heart and my very liver ... a moon beside which the moon itself is nothing.

4. al-silsila — the chain, so named because it is drawn out in a continuous connection. From this too: "tasalsala al-mā' fī l-ḥalq" — the water flowed continuously down the throat. Water is described as "salsal", "salsāl", "sulāsil" when it runs sweet and clear.

Al-Akhṭal said, in a line of verse:
Whenever he feared thirst for her under some star ... he turned toward her a rivulet running in an unbroken stream.

Some of the language scholars said: al-salsala is the continuous connection of one thing to another, and that is why the iron chain is called "silsila", and why the lightning that stretches lengthwise across a cloud is called "silsilat al-barq".

5. al-sāll — a watercourse in the narrow part of a valley, plural "sullān", as though the water slips out from it or into it in a continuous drawing-out.
6. faras shadīd al-salla — a horse with a strong final burst, that being its surge of speed in a race.
7. "kharajat sallatuhu ʿalā jamīʿ al-khayl" — his surge outstripped all the other horses.
8. al-misalla — the needle, well known, so named because it draws the thread through.
9. al-sullā'a — the thorn, from this too, because it has length in it.
10. al-sulāl — a wasting disease, as though the man's flesh had been drawn out of him bit by bit. One says "asallahu Allāh" — God afflicted him with wasting disease.
سلب:
The letters sīn, lām and bā are a single root, and it is the taking of a thing swiftly and by snatching.

1. salabtuhu thawbahu salban — I stripped him of his garment; al-salab is that which is stripped, the spoils. In the hadith: "whoever kills a slain man, the spoils are his."
2. al-salīb — that which is stripped.
3. al-salūb, of she-camels — one whose young is taken from her; plural sulub. aslabat al-nāqa — the she-camel became so.
4. al-salab — also the bark of a tree, belonging to this root too, because it is peeled off the tree, as though the tree has been stripped of it.

The saying of Ibn Maḥkān, in a line of verse:
So he stripped the hide off her as she knelt, the way the hands of a killer strip off the spoils of the slain.

There are two versions of this line: Ibn al-Aʿrābī transmitted "qātil", killer, with a qāf; al-Aṣmaʿī transmitted it with a fā, as "fātil", twister. He used to say: al-salab is tree-bark, and in Medina there is the market of the salab-twisters — so he held that al-fātil is the one who twists the bark into rope. I heard ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm al-Qaṭṭān say: I heard Abū al-ʿAbbās Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā Thaʿlab say: Ibn al-Aʿrābī was mistaken, and what is correct is what al-Aṣmaʿī said.

5. tasallabat al-mar'a — the woman went into mourning-dress, like aḥaddat, she observed mourning. Some said this is from al-sulub, black garments, and what brings it close to the first root is that her garments are likened to al-salab, tree-bark.

Labīd said, in a line of verse:
In black mourning-garments and in worn cloths.

Some said: the difference between iḥdād, mourning, and tasallub is that iḥdād is for a husband, while tasallub may be for someone other than a husband.

6. A horse is salīb — it is said this means long-legged; others said it means light and quick in moving its legs, as one says "a man salīb of the hands with the thrust", and "a bull salīb of the horn with the goring." This is the better and more sound of the two sayings, because it is as though he snatches away the thrust in an instant, as one snatches spoils.
سلت:
The letters sīn, lām and tā' are a single root, and it is stripping and paring a thing away from a thing. One says salatati l-marʾatu khiḍābahā ʿan yadihā, the woman stripped the dye from her hand.

1. salata fulānun anfa fulānin bi-l-sayfi salt an — so-and-so sliced off so-and-so's nose with the sword, said when he took the whole of it off; and the man so treated is aslat.
2. al-saltāʾ — the woman who does not tend to her dye, is called this.

And from the chapter:

1. al-sult — a type of barley that scarcely has husk; the Arabs call it al-ʿuryān, the bare one.
سلج:
The letters sīn, lām and jīm are a root indicating swallowing. One says salaja l-shayʾa yaslajuhu, said when he swallowed it, saljan and salajānan. In their saying: "Taking is a swallow, but repaying is a stalling."

And from the chapter:

1. fulānun yatasallaju l-sharāb — so-and-so keeps at his drink insistently.
سلح:
The letters sīn, lām and ḥā': al-silāḥ, what one fights with. Abū 'Ubayda used to distinguish al-silāḥ from al-junna: al-silāḥ is what one fights with, and al-junna is what one shields oneself with. He argued from the line of verse:
Where you see the horses grim with their riders, rising up with the Indian swords and the shields.

He took this as making the shields distinct from the swords.

Al-islīḥ is a plant that makes camels give abundant milk when they graze on it. The Bedouin woman said: "the islīḥ plant brings froth of milk and easy-flowing milk, and hump-fat and rich fare" [this last phrase is obscure to me and I give it only approximately].
سلخ:
The letters sīn, lām and khā' are a single root, and it is the removal of a thing from its skin. Other senses are then carried upon it.

The original sense: "salakhtu the sheep's hide, salkhan" — I flayed it.

1. al-silkh — the snake's skin, which it sheds.
2. aswad sālikh — a black [venomous snake], so called because it is said to shed its skin every year.
3. Some related "the woman salakhat her dress" — she took it off.

By the same reasoning: "salakhtu the month," when you reach its last day — a figurative use. "The month insalakha" [came to its end], and "the day insalakha from the coming night."

4. nakhla mislākh — a palm tree that sheds its unripe dates while they are still green.
سلس:
The letters sīn, lām and sīn indicate ease in a thing. One says huwa sahlun salis, he is easy and compliant.

1. al-sals — a kind of bead, perhaps named so for the ease with which it is strung.

He said:
And necklaces of ḥublah-beads and sals-beads.
سلط:
The letters sīn, lām and ṭā' are a single root, and it is strength and overpowering. From that is al-salāṭa, from al-tasalluṭ, which is overpowering; and for that reason the ruler is called sulṭān. And al-sulṭān is also the proof or argument. Al-salīṭ among men is the one clear and sharp of tongue. Al-salīṭa is the loud, brawling woman.

Among what departs from this chapter is al-salīṭ: olive oil in the speech of the people of Yemen, and in the speech of others sesame oil.
سلع:
The letters sīn, lām and ʿayn are a root indicating the splitting and opening of a thing.
