1. al-salʿ — a cleft in a mountain shaped like a crack; plural sulūʿ.
2. tasallaʿa ʿaqibuhu — his heel cracked and chapped, said when it split and fissured.
3. salaʿa raʾsahu — he split his head open, said when he cracked it.
4. al-silʿa — a thing for sale, so called because it is not property one keeps hold of, so dealing in it is unrestricted.
5. al-salaʿ — a kind of tree.
سلغ:
The letters sīn, lām and ghayn are not a root, but rather of the substitution kind; its sīn is substituted from ṣād.

1. salaghati l-baqara — the cow shed her tooth, said when her tusk came out, she being sāligh.
2. laḥmun aslagh — meat that is not fully cooked.
3. rajulun aslagh — a man of intense redness.
سلف:
The letters sīn, lām, and fā' are a root pointing to precedence and going before. From it: al-salaf are those who have passed on before us. Al-qawm al-sullāf are those who go ahead. Al-sulāf is what flows from pressed grapes before they are fully pressed. Al-sulfa is food eaten in haste before the main meal. Al-sulūf is a she-camel found at the front of a group of camels when they come to water.

1. From this chapter too: al-salaf in a sale, money paid in advance for something to be bought on deferred delivery. Some call a loan al-salaf, following the same pattern, because it is something given in advance in exchange for something delayed.
2. Outside this pattern: al-silf, meaning silf al-rijāl — the relation between two men, one of whom marries one sister and the other another sister. This follows the pattern of al-sālifatān, the two sides of the neck, one facing the other.
3. Also outside both patterns: al-salf, a leather sack. It is also said the foreskin is called salf. From this comes aslaftu al-arḍa lil-zar', meaning I levelled it in preparation for sowing. It is possible this belongs to the pattern of the first chapter, being something done in advance in preparing it.
سلق:
The letters sīn, lām and qāf contain widely differing words, hardly two of which can be gathered under one single sense; and your Lord, exalted be His praise, does as He wills, and makes His creation speak however He wishes.

1. al-salaq — a low, level tract of ground.
2. al-silqa — the she-wolf.
3. salaqa — he cried out.
4. al-salīqa — one's natural disposition.
5. al-salīqa — also the mark left by the girth-strap on a camel's side.
6. Saluq — a town.
7. al-tasalluq over a wall — climbing over it to get into the house.
8. al-salīq — what falls off a tree, dead leaves or twigs.

An unnamed poet said, in a line of verse:
You hear from it, in the grey fallen brushwood, a crackling like blazing kindled fire.

9. al-sulāq — the peeling of the skin of the tongue.
10. salaqtu al-mazāda — I greased the water-skin, when you oil it.

Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
As though the two of them were the two waterskins of a man in haste, freshly cut, not yet oiled with grease.

11. al-salq — putting one of the two handles of a sack through the other, then folding it back again.
سلك:
The letters sīn, lām and kāf are a root pointing to one thing passing through another. One says salaktu al-ṭarīq aslukuhu — I travelled the road. And salaktu al-shay' fī al-shay' — you made it pass through. Al-ṭa'na al-sulkā is when a man stabs another straight in front of his face. Al-muslaka is a strip torn lengthwise from the side of a garment; it is called that only because of its stretching out, and it is like narrow lanes.

Of what strays from this root is al-sulaka, the female young of the partridge; the male is sulak, and its plural is silkān. And God knows best.
سلم:
The letters sīn, lām and mīm: most of its chapter is from soundness and well-being; and there is in it what strays, but what strays from it is little. So al-salāma is that a man be safe from blight and harm. The people of knowledge said: God, exalted be His praise, is al-Salām, because He is safe from what befalls created things of fault, defect and passing away. God, majestic be His majesty, said: {wa-Allāhu yadʿū ilā dāri al-salām} — and God calls to the House of Peace [Yūnus: 25]; so al-Salām is God, exalted be His praise, and His house is the Garden.

And from this chapter also is al-islām, which is submitting, because the one who submits is safe from refusing and holding back. And al-silām is making peace; the pattern fiʿāl comes often in the sense of doing a thing with another, as in al-qitāl and al-muqātala, fighting. And from the chapter of going along and submitting is al-salam, which is called al-salaf, payment in advance, as though it were wealth handed over that was not withheld from being given. And it is possible that stones were called silām because they are the furthest thing on earth from perishing and passing away, for their hardness and firmness.

As for al-salīm, which is the man bitten by a snake, there are two accounts of the naming. One is that he was given over to what had befallen him. The other is that they took a good omen with safety; and they do sometimes name a thing with names by way of good or ill omen. And al-sullam, the ladder, is well known, and it too is from al-salāma, because the one who comes down it is hoped to come down safe. And al-salāma is a tree, and its plural is salām.

What strays from the chapter is al-salm, the bucket that has a single handle. And al-salam is a tree, one of which is a salama. And al-salāmān is a tree.

And from the first chapter is al-silm, which is peacemaking; it is sometimes made feminine and sometimes masculine. God, exalted be He, said: {wa-in janaḥū lil-salmi fa-ijnaḥ lahā} — and if they incline to peace, incline to it [al-Anfāl: 61]. And al-salima is the stone; of it the poet says, in a line of verse:
That is my friend, and one who reproaches me, throwing at my back with the arrow and with the stone.

And Banū Salima are a clan of the Anṣār; there are no others of that name among the Arabs. And of the proper names: Salmā, a woman; and Salmā, a mountain. And Abū Sulmā, the father of Zuhayr, with a ḍamma on the sīn — there is no other of that name among the Arabs.
سلوى:
The letters sīn, lām and the weak letter are a single root indicating ease and pleasantness of life.

1. fulānun fī salwatin min al-ʿaysh — so-and-so is in the ease of life, meaning in a comfort that eases his cares.
2. salā l-muḥibbu yaslū suluwwan — the lover is consoled, said when what he had of care and passion has left him.
3. al-sulwāna — the [magic] bead; they used to say that whoever drank [water] over it was consoled from what afflicted him and from the one he loved.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
I drank, over a sulwāna-bead, the water of a rain-cloud — yet by the freshness of life, O Mayy, I am not consoled.

4. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: a man says to his companion, "You have given me your salwa and sulwān to drink," meaning: I soothed my own soul and made it forget you.
5. salītu — has the same meaning as salawtu, I was consoled.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Even if I drank the sulwān-draught, I would not be consoled.

And from the chapter:

1. al-salā — the membrane in which the young is held, so named for its softness, delicacy and pliancy.

As for the letters sīn, lām and hamza, they are a single word not to be reasoned on by analogy. One says salaʾa l-samn yaslaʾuhu salʾan, said when he melts the ghee and clarifies it from the milk. He said:
We protected you, Tamīm, though you are but clients — if you do not do well the clarifying, you will be struck.
سم:
The letters sīn and mīm: their regular root points to an entrance into a thing, like a hole and the like, and other things are derived from it.

1. al-samm and al-summ — the hole in a thing. God, mighty is His mention, said: {until the camel passes through the eye of the needle} [al-Aʿrāf: 40].
2. al-samm — the deadly poison, said with either vowel on the sīn. It is named so because it sinks into the body and works its way inside it, unlike other things that are merely tasted.
3. al-sāmma — one's inner circle, named so because they mix in with an intimacy no one else has. The Arabs say: "How are al-sāmma and al-ʿāmma?" [How are your inner circle and the common folk?] — al-sāmma being the inner circle.
4. al-samūm — the hot wind, because it too works its way forcefully into bodies.
5. al-summ — reconciling people, because before this they are separated and do not mix, and when peace is made between them they come together.

Among what is an exception to this chapter: al-samm, something like the cowrie shell that comes out of the sea. Al-samsām, a bird. Al-samsam, the fox. Al-sumsumānī, a light, nimble man. Al-samāsim, red ants, singular "sumsima". Al-simsim, a seed.

It is possible that what we have mentioned as exceptions here belongs to another root, one pointing to lightness of a thing. And among what is an exception to both origin senses is their saying: "mā lahu samm wa lā ḥamm ghayraka" — meaning he has no concern but you.
سمت:
The letters sīn, mīm and tā' are a root indicating a way, a course, a manner. One says samata, said when he took the way.

1. al-samt — some of them used to say it is travelling by conjecture and guesswork. It is the saying of the poet: There is no landmark there for the wayfarer's reckoning to fix on.
2. fulānun ḥasanu l-samt — so-and-so is of good samt, said when he is of upright conduct, given to doing good; the verb from it is samata.
3. samata samtahu — he headed in someone's direction, said when he aimed for what that other aimed for.
سمج:
The letters sīn, mīm and jīm are a root indicating the opposite of beauty. One says huwa samij and samj; plural simāj and samājā.

1. al-samj min al-albān — milk that is foul in taste.
سمح:
The letters sīn, mīm and ḥā' are a root indicating smoothness and ease. One says samaḥa lahu bi-l-shayʾ, he yielded the thing to him readily.

1. rajulun samḥ — a generous man; plural sumaḥāʾ and masāmīḥ.
2. samaḥa fī sayrihi — he quickened his pace, said when he went fast.

He said:
He hastened on and crossed a desolate, trackless waste.

3. al-musāmaḥa fī l-ṭiʿān wa-l-ḍarb — going easy in thrusting and striking, said when it is done leniently.
4. rumḥun musammaḥ — a spear that has been trued and straightened until it grew supple.
سمحاق:
sim ḥāq — a thin membrane on the head; when a head-wound reaches down to it, it is called sim ḥāq. Likewise samāḥīq al-salā — the thin membranes of the afterbirth — and samāḥīq al-saḥāb — the thin, wispy streaks of cloud.

1. From this: iskhankaka al-ẓalām — the darkness thickened and deepened.
2. iskhanfara al-shayʾ — the thing grew long and broad.
3. sanāmun musarhad — a hump cut into pieces.
4. ismaharra al-shawk — the thorn dried out and hardened. And one also says, of darkness when it deepens: ismaharra.
5. al-sarhafa and al-sarʿafa — both meaning: feeding well, good nourishment.
6. al-sakhbar — a kind of shrub.
7. al-samālīkh — the dried stalks of naṣī grass; singular sumlūkh.
8. al-samsaq — jasmine.
9. al-safanj — the male ostrich.
10. al-saljam — tall.
11. al-sarawmaṭ — tall.
12. al-siltim — the ghoul.
13. al-siltim, again — a hard, unrelenting year. As in the line: "and a hard year (sitm) came, giving no way back, no relief in it, so the herdsmen were driven on."
14. al-siltim, again — calamity.
15. al-sabantā — the leopard; and likewise al-sabandāt. As said of the sabantā, in a line of verse: "I never feared that his death would come at the paws of a blue-eyed, watchful leopard (sabantā)."
16. al-sirbāl — the shirt.
17. israndānī al-shayʾ — the thing overpowered me.
18. al-sifsīr — the courier, the attendant.
19. al-sawdhaq, al-sawdhanīq and al-sūdhāniq — the falcon.
20. al-sabārīt — barren, waste land.
21. al-subrūt — a short man.
22. al-sarbakh — wide, open land.
23. al-sindaʾwa — a light, nimble man.
24. al-sajanjal — the mirror.
25. A boy called samahdar — plump, full of flesh.
26. al-musmahirr — even, well-balanced.
27. al-musjahirr — white.
28. al-musmaghidd — swollen.
29. al-muslaḥibb — straight.
30. al-surādiq — dust.
31. al-samḥaj — a she-donkey with a long back.
32. al-sijillāṭ — the cloth covering of a camel-litter; it is said not to be an Arabic word.
33. al-samahdar — far off, distant. In the saying of the rajaz poet: "and short of Laylā lies a far-off land (samahdar)."
34. One says sardajtuhu, so it is musardaj, meaning: I neglected it, so it is a neglected thing. Abū al-Najm said: "Hind has killed, without a qualm, and has left you today like the neglected one (musardaj)."
35. isbakarra al-shayʾ — the thing stretched out, extended.

And God knows best. [Here ends the Book of Sīn.]
سمخ:
The letters sīn, mīm and khāʾ are not a root, being of the substitution kind, its sīn substituted from ṣād. Al-simākh in the ear is its opening.

1. samakhtu fulānan — I struck him in the ear-canal.
2. samakhanī bi-shiddati ṣawtihi — he pierced my ear with the loudness of his voice.
سمد:
The letters sīn, mīm and dāl are a root pointing to going straight onward without turning aside.

1. samadat al-ibilu in their journeying — they press on hard and go straight ahead, heads down.

An unnamed poet said, in a line of verse:
Pressing onward through the night, light of provisions.

He means: there is no fodder in their bellies.

2. al-sumūd — idle diversion, heedlessness; al-sāmid — one who is heedlessly absorbed. From it His saying, exalted and high: {while you are heedlessly diverted} [al-Najm: 61], meaning heedlessly diverted. This fits the pattern of the root, because one who is heedlessly diverted goes on in his state without turning aside or lingering.

They recite, in a line of verse:
It was said: rise and look at them, then leave off your heedless idling.

As for their saying "sammada ra'sahu", when he shaved his head to the roots, that belongs to the category of letter-substitution, for its true root has a bā, not a dāl, and it has already been mentioned under that root.
سمر:
The letters sīn, mīm and rā' are a single root indicating the opposite of whiteness in color. From this is al-sumra among colors; its origin is their saying, "I will not come to you [as long as there is] al-samar and al-qamar" — al-qamar being the moon. Al-samar is the darkness of night, and from this al-sumra is named.

Al-sāmir is the people who stay up at night talking; al-sāmir is also the place where they gather for that talk.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And a night-gathering where their talk lasted long for them.

Al-samrā' is wheat, named for its color. Al-asmar is the spear. Al-asmar is also water. Al-samār is thin, watered-down milk, named so because, being like that, its color has changed. Al-samur is a kind of acacia tree, a single one of which is samura; it may be that it too was named for its color.

Al-Samār is also a place name, in the line of verse:
If he comes to water at al-Samār, we shall surely kill him — no, by your father, he did not come to water at al-Samār.
سمط:
The letters sīn, mīm and ṭā' are a root indicating the joining of a thing to a thing and binding it with it.

1. al-samīṭ — bricks laid one on top of another.
2. al-simṭ — a necklace, because it is strung, its parts gathered one to the other.
3. sammaṭa l-shayʾa ʿalā maʿālīqi l-sarj — he hung the thing on the saddle's hangers.
4. khudh ḥaqqaka musammaṭan — take your due musammaṭ, meaning: take it and hang it on your mount's saddle-straps.
5. al-shiʿr al-musammaṭ — poetry in which the line contains musammaṭ hemistiches bound together by a rhyme, different from the poem's main rhyme yet running throughout, that stays with the whole ode.

As for al-laban al-sāmiṭ, that is, soured milk, it is not from this chapter, being of the substitution kind, its sīn substituted from khāʾ.
سمع:
The letters sīn, mīm and 'ayn are a single root, and it is the taking in of a thing with the ear, in people and in every creature that has an ear. You say: sami'tu al-shay' sam'an - I heard the thing. Al-sim' and al-sam' are fair repute. One says, his repute has gone abroad among people, that is, his fame. And one says samā'i, meaning listen. And one says sammi'tu bi-l-shay', when you spread it about so that it may be talked of. Al-musmi'a is the singing girl. Al-misma' is like an ear for the big leather bucket; it is a loop in the middle of the bucket into which a rope is put so as to balance the pail. The poet said, in a line of verse:
And we set straight the one that leans, if it means to overcome us, as the bucket is balanced by its loop.

Among what strays from the section is al-sim': the offspring of a wolf by a hyena.
سمق: The letters sīn, mīm and qāf hold one word, and perhaps the qāf is substituted from kāf. Samaqa, said when it grew tall.
سمك:
The letters sīn, mīm and kāf are a single root pointing to height.

1. samaka — a thing rose high; al-masmūkāt — the heavens.
2. samaka in ascending — climbing up steps or degrees; "ismuk" — rise, go high.
3. A hump is sāmik, meaning high.
4. al-mismāk — that with which you raise up a tent, a tent-pole.

Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
As though its two legs were two tent-poles of 'ushar wood, two fresh saplings whose bark has not yet been peeled off.

5. al-simāk — a star.

Irregular against this root and differing from it entirely: al-samak, fish.
سمل:
The letters sīn, mīm and lām are a root indicating weakness and scantiness.

1. al-samal — a garment worn to rags.
2. al-samal — the little water left in a trough; plural asmāl.
3. sammaltu l-biʾr — I cleaned out the well.
4. al-ismāl — making peace between people; it is from this last word, as though he had cleared away the enmity that lay between them. And God, most high, knows best.
سمن:
The letters sīn, mīm and nūn are a root indicating the opposite of leanness. From this is al-siman (fatness); one says: he is samīn. Al-samn (clarified butter) comes from this too.

Outside this root is an expression said to belong only to the people of Yemen: they say "sammantu the thing" meaning: you cooled it — al-tasmīn, in this usage, being cooling. It is said that al-Ḥajjāj was once served a fish, and said to the one who had prepared it, "sammin-hā," meaning: cool it.
سمه:
The letters sīn, mīm and hā' are a root indicating bewilderment and falsehood. One says samaha, said when he was dazed; he is sāmih, and a people are summah.

1. samaha l-baʿīr — the camel that shows no sign of exhaustion, said of a camel that did not seem to tire.
2. dhahabat ibiluhum al-summahā — their camels scattered, said when they went their separate ways.
3. al-summahā — falsehood and lying.

As for Ru'ba's saying — "...the running of al-summah" — the quotation is broken off in the source.
سمو:
The letters sīn, mīm and wāw are a root pointing to height. One says samawtu — I rose — when you go up. And samā baṣaruhu — his gaze rose high. And samā lī shakhṣun — a figure rose up to me until I made it out. And samā al-faḥl — the stallion mounted his she-camels, samāwatan. And the samāwa of the new moon and of everything is its shape as it shows, and the plural is samāw. And the Arabs call the cloud samā', and the rain samā'; and when the rain is meant by it, it is made plural as sumiyy. And al-samā'a is the shape, the figure. And al-samā' is the roof of the house. And everything high and overlooking is a samā', so that even the back of the horse is called samā'. And they widen it until they call the plants samā'. He said:
When the sky comes down upon a people's land, we pasture upon it even if they are angry.
And they say: " We did not cease to tread the sky until we came to you ", meaning by it the herbage and the rain.

And it is said that the origin of " ism ", a name, is simw, and it is from height, because it is a raising up and a pointing to the meaning.
سن:
The letters sīn and nūn are a single, regular root: the flowing of a thing and its running smoothly and easily. The origin sense is their saying "sanantu al-mā' ʿalā wajhī asunnuhu sannan" — I let the water pour freely over my face.

From this is derived "rajul masnūn al-wajh" — a man with a smoothly-shaped face, as though the flesh had been drawn smooth over it. And "al-hama' al-masnūn" [dark, molded clay] comes from this too, as though it had been poured out in a continuous pour.

Among what is derived from it is al-sunna, the customary way. The Sunna of the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, is his way. Al-Hudhalī said, in a line of verse:
Do not grieve over a way that you yourself have walked ... for the first to accept a way is the one who walks it.

It is named so because it runs along in a flowing course. From this too is their saying "imḍi ʿalā sananika wa sunanika" — go on along your way, meaning your direction. And "jā'ati al-rīḥ sanā'in" — the wind came steadily, in one continuous course.

Then carried on this: "sanantu al-ḥadīda asunnuhā sannan" — I sharpened the iron, when you pass it over the whetstone, "al-sinān", which means the whetstone.

A poet said:
A whetstone like the edge of a lean, hard stone.

And al-sinān, the spearhead, is from this too, because it is "masnūn" — drawn out thin and sharpened. Likewise al-sanāsin, the projecting tips of the vertebrae of the back, as though they had been sharpened to points.

From this chapter: the "sinn", the tooth, of a human or anything else, likened to the spearhead. Al-sanūn is what one brushes the teeth with, because the teeth are sharpened smooth with it.

As for the bull.

As for their saying "sanna ibilahu" — he pastured his camels — the meaning is that he pastured them until their hides became fine, as though polished smooth, the way iron is sharpened. This is the sense of the phrase, and it goes back to the origin sense established.
سنب:
The letters sīn, nūn and bā' are two distinct words.

1. al-sanba — a stretch of time.
2. al-sanib — a horse of wide, far-reaching stride.
سنت:
The letters sīn, nūn and tā' are not a root that branches from a single meaning. But they say al-sanūt — some said it is honey, others said it is cumin.

The poet said:
They are the ghee and the sanūt, no deceit is in them, and they protect their neighbour from being humbled.
سنج: The letters sīn, nūn and jīm hold one word. They say: al-sinnāj is the mark left by a lamp's smoke on a wall.
سنح:
The letters sīn, nūn and ḥāʾ are a single root, taken to indicate the appearing of a thing from a particular place, though this is disputed.

1. al-sāniḥ — whatever comes to you from your right, whether bird or other; one says sanaḥa sunūḥan.
2. al-sāniḥ and al-sanīḥ — the same thing.

Dhū al-Rumma said:
I remembered you when a mother-gazelle passed by us, ahead of the riding-beasts, stretching her neck and crossing from the right.

3. sanaḥa lī raʾyun fī kadhā — an idea occurred to me about such-and-such: this use was borrowed from the bird-omen sense, meaning it presented itself to me.
سنخ:
The letters sīn, nūn and khāʾ are a single root indicating the base of a thing.

1. al-sinkh — the root, the base of a thing.
2. asnākh al-thanāyā — the roots of the front teeth.
3. sanakha l-rajulu fī l-ʿilm sunūkhan — the man became deeply grounded in knowledge, meaning he learned its foundations.

As for their saying sanikha l-duhn, said when oil turns rancid, that amounts to nothing, is not reliable.
سند:
The letters sīn, nūn and dāl are a single root pointing to one thing leaning onto another.

1. sanadtu ilā al-shay'i asnudu sunūdan — I leaned against the thing; istanadtu istinādan — I leaned back on something; asnadtu ghayrī isnādan — I made someone else lean against something.
2. al-sinād — a strong she-camel, as though her back were braced against something strong.
3. al-musnad — time, because its parts are joined one to another.
4. So-and-so is a sanad, meaning one relied upon.
5. al-sanad — the part of a mountain that faces you, rising up from the foot of it.
6. al-isnād in hadith — that it be traced back to the one who said it; this fits the same sense.

As for al-sinād in poetry, a metrical fault, it is said to be a difference between the vowels of the two letters before the rhyme-consonant in two lines. Abū ʿUbayda said: that is like his saying, in a line of verse:
As though their eyes were the eyes of wild cows.

Then he said, in a line of verse:
And his head became at morning like silver.

This is derived from their saying "the people went out mutasānidīn", when they went out under separate banners — belonging to the root, because each group had leaned onto its own banner.
سنط: The letters sīn, nūn and ṭā' are not anything [not a root] — except al-sinaṭ, which is the one who has no beard.
سنع:
The letters sīn, nūn and ʿayn, if sound, indicate beauty, goodness, and eminence.

1. asnaʿ — said of an eminence (sharaf) that is asnaʿ, meaning lofty and elevated.
2. sanīʿa — a woman is sanīʿa, meaning beautiful.
سنف:
The letters sīn, nūn and fā' are a root indicating the tying of something, or the hanging of something upon something.

1. al-sināf — a cord tied from the camel's flank to its breast-girth, then tied at its neck. Al-Khalīl said: al-sināf for the camel is like the labab (breast-strap) for a riding animal.
2. misnāf — a camel is called misnāf when the rider is set back [on it] and a sināf is made for him.
3. asnaftu — one says asnaftu [the camel], meaning you tied it with the sināf. And one says asnafū amrahum, meaning they made their affair firm and secure.

It is said as a proverb, of one confused about his affair: "He has been baffled by the asnāf [straps]." A poet said, in a line of verse:

When a people are baffled by the asnāf ... over a matter that resembles [another] and might turn out either way.

Some of them related sanaftu al-baʿīr, the same as asanaftu, but al-Aṣmaʿī would accept nothing but asanaftu.

4. al-sinf — the pod that holds the fruit of the markh tree, resembling horses' ears; it belongs to this chapter because it hangs upon a tree. Abū ʿAmr said: al-sinf is the leaf.

Ibn Muqbil said, in a line of verse: the markh-pod rattles loose in an empty quiver.
سنق: The letters sīn, nūn and qāf have one word in them, which is al-sanaq, and it is like bashm [over-fullness, satiety]. One says: the young camel drank until it became saniq [bloated]. Likewise the horse, from fodder. It is like indigestion is among people.
سنم:
The letters sīn, nūn and mīm are a single root pointing to height and elevation.

1. al-sanām, the hump of a camel, is well known.
2. tasannamtu — I climbed up, mounted onto the top.
3. A she-camel is sanima — great of hump.
4. asnamtu al-nāra — I made the fire's flame rise high.
5. Asnuma — a place-name.
سنه:
The letters sīn, nūn and hā are a single root pointing to a span of time.

1. al-sana, the year, is well known, and a hā has been dropped from it — do you not see that you say sunayha, its diminutive, showing the hidden hā?
2. sanahat al-nakhla — years have passed over the palm tree.

His saying, exalted be His mention: {so look at your food and your drink, it has not spoiled with years} [al-Baqara: 259] — meaning, it did not become like a thing that years pass over and so change it.

3. The palm tree is called sanhā', one that a run of years has worn.
سنى:
The letters sīn, nūn and the weak letter are a single root indicating watering, and it also carries a sense of height and elevation. One says sanati l-nāqa, said when the she-camel watered the land, tasnū, she being al-sāniya.

1. al-saḥāba tasnū l-arḍ — the cloud waters the land; and al-qawm yastanūna li-anfusihim, said when people draw water for themselves.

And from the chapter:

1. sānaytu l-rajul — I conciliated the man, usāniyhi, said when you appease him — as though affection had withered and dried, as it comes in the hadith: "Moisten your ties of kinship, even if only with a greeting."

As for the sense that indicates loftiness:

1. al-sanāʾ, with a long final vowel — indicates loftiness; and likewise if you shorten it, sanā, it indicates loftiness too, except that it is for one particular thing: light.

God, glorious is His praise, said: {The flash of its lightning well-nigh takes away the sight} [al-Nūr: 43].
سهب:
The letters sīn, hā' and bā' are a root indicating expansiveness in a thing. The origin is al-sahb, which is the vast open wasteland; then the horse that ranges widely in its running is called sahb.

1. bi'r sahba — a well is called sahba when it is deep at the bottom.
2. ashabū — it is said: the people dug until they ashabū, meaning they reached the sand; and when that happens there is more water, and it is more plentiful and abundant.
3. mushab — the man who talks a great deal is called mushab, with the hā' opened. It has come from the Arabs thus: ashaba, so he is mushab — and this is an unusual form.
سهج:
The letters sīn, hā' and jīm are a root indicating continuance in a thing. One says: the people sahajū their night, meaning they journeyed on continuously.

1. sahajat al-rīḥ — the wind is said to sahaj when it blows continuously; it is called sayhaj and sayhūj.
2. mashajuhā — its path, the course along which it runs.
سهد:
The letters sīn, hā' and dāl are two unrelated words: one indicates the opposite of sleep, the other stillness.

1. al-suhād — the first is al-suhād, which is scantness of sleep.
2. suhud — a man is suhud when he sleeps little. A poet said, in a line of verse:

She bore him tightly wrapped, close of heart ... suhud, [waking] whenever the heedless man's night [still] sleeps.

3. sahhadtu — I sahhadtu so-and-so, meaning I drove his sleep away, kept him from it.

The other word is their saying:

1. sahd mahd — a thing is sahd mahd, meaning still, causing no trouble.
2. sahdatan — one says mā ra'aytu min fulānin sahdatan, meaning: I did not see from so-and-so a matter I could rely on, whether news or speech, or something I could settle my mind to.
سهر:
The letters sīn, hā and rā — most of this root concerns sleeplessness, the loss of sleep.

1. sahara yashharu saharan — he stayed awake.
2. The earth is called al-sāhira, named so because its work in bringing forth plants goes on continuously, night and day.

For that reason it is said: "the best of wealth is a gushing spring, in soft fertile ground, that stays awake when you sleep, and is present when you are away."

Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt said, in a line of verse:
And in it is the flesh of land and sea, and what they have spoken remains for them.

Another poet said, mentioning wild asses, in a line of verse:
They seek out open ground, as though its tall grass and its short new growth were the dark folds of a black night.

Then al-sāhira came to be a name for any tract of land. God, great is His majesty, said: {it will be but one blast, and behold, they are upon the surface of the earth} [al-Nāziʿāt: 13]

3. al-ashharān — two veins inside the nose, which, when a wild donkey is in rut, run with fluid.

Al-Shammākh said, in a line of verse:
She flees from a powerful male, whom the flowing of his two nose-veins has worn out with dripping.

It is as though the two of them were named so because they flow by night just as they flow by day. It is also transmitted as "asharathu", wore him out.

4. A man is suhara — one who sleeps little.
5. al-sāhūr — some said it is the covering of the moon, and it is also said to be the moon itself; whichever it is, it belongs to this root, because it travels on in its orbit unceasingly, night and day.
سهف:
The letters sīn, hā' and fā' — its branches are few.

1. al-sahaf — they say al-sahaf is the writhing and thrashing of a slain man in his blood.
2. al-suhāf — it is said al-suhāf is thirst.
سهق:
The letters sīn, hā' and qāf are a root indicating length and extension, and it is sound.

1. al-sahwaq — the tall man.
2. al-sahwaq — also the liar, so called because he exaggerates the matter and adds to what he says.
3. al-sahwaq — of the winds, the one that weaves up the swirling dust.
4. al-sahwaq — well-watered, from sāq [trunk] of trees, because when it is well-watered it grows tall.
سهك:
The letters sīn, hā' and kāf are two roots: one indicates scraping and pounding, the other a foul smell.

1. sahakat al-rīḥ al-turāb — the wind sahaka'd the dust, that is, when it scraped it off the ground.
2. al-mashaka — the place over which the wind's passing is severe.
3. sahaktu — one says sahaktu the thing, meaning you scraped it; it is less severe than sahq [grinding].
4. sahakat al-dawābb — the mounts sahaka'd, when they ran with a light run.
5. faras mishak — a swift horse; called so because it scrapes (yashaku) the ground with its legs.

The second root is al-sahak. Some said it is the smell of fish on the hand. Others say al-sahak is an unpleasant smell a person notices on himself when he sweats.

1. al-sahak — from this chapter too, the rust of iron.
2. sāhik — as in their saying "bi ʿaynihi sāhik," meaning his eye is sore, inflamed from ophthalmia.

A poet said, of al-sahak, in a line of verse:

Rust-marked from the iron's corrosion ... as though beneath the cauldron they were the cattle-herders' brood.
سهل:
The letters sīn, hā and lām are a single root pointing to softness, the opposite of roughness.

1. al-sahl — the opposite of rugged terrain.
2. The adjectival form for soft, level land is suhlī.
3. ashala al-qawmu — the people rode over level ground.
4. A river is sahil — it contains sihla, sand that is not fine-grained.
5. Suhayl — a star.
سهم:
The letters sīn, hā and mīm are two roots: one points to a change in colour, the other to a share, a portion, and one thing among things.

1. al-suhma — a share. The two men "asham", when they drew lots, from suhma and naṣīb — each obtaining what falls to him. God Most High said: {and he cast lots and was among the losers} [al-Ṣāffāt: 141].
2. From this, the single arrow among arrows, sahm, was named so, as though it were a portion among portions and a share among shares.
3. al-suhma — also kinship, because it is a share in the bond of the womb.
4. Their saying "a striped cloak, musahham" — it was named so because each stripe on it is likened to an arrow.

As for the other root:
5. "a man's face sahuma", when it changes colour — derived from al-suhām, what strikes a person from the summer heat until his colour changes. sahima al-rajulu — the suhām struck him.
6. al-suhām — also a disease that afflicts camels, like a burning thirst.
7. Camels are sawāhim, when travel has changed them.

And God knows best.
سهو:
The letters sīn, hā' and wāw mostly indicate heedlessness and stillness. al-sahw — heedlessness. One says sahawtu fī l-ṣalāti asahū sahwan, I was inattentive during the prayer. From this root: al-musāhāt — good, easy companionship, as though a person overlooks a lapse when it comes from someone else. al-sahw — stillness. One says jā'a sahwan rahwan, he came calmly, at ease.

Among what departs from this root: al-sahwa, which is like a shaded portico standing in front of a house. And further still from the root's sense: their saying "the woman conceived her child sahwan," meaning during menstruation. As for al-suhā [a faint star], it may belong to the first sense after all, because it is so faint that one is inattentive to seeing it.
سوء:
As for the letters sīn, wāw and hamza — that is not from that [preceding matter]; rather it belongs to the chapter of ugliness. You say: a man is aswa', meaning ugly, and a woman is sawʾā', meaning ugly. The Messenger of God, peace and blessings of God be upon him and his family, said: "A sawʾā' [an ugly woman] who bears children is better than a beautiful one who is barren." That is why al-sayyi'a [the evil deed] was named sayyi'a. And the Fire was named sū'ā, for the ugliness of its appearance. God, exalted, said: {Then the end of those who did evil was al-sū'ā [the worst]} [al-Rūm: 10]. Abū Zubayd said:

He did not respect the sanctity of the drinking-companion, and it was owed him ... O my people, for the ugliest of ugly deeds.
سوح: The letters sīn, wāw and ḥā are a single word. One says sāḥat al-dār, the courtyard of the house; its plurals are sāḥāt and sūḥ.
سوخ: The letters sīn, wāw and khā' are one word. One says: sākhat qawā'imuhu fī al-arḍ tasūkh, meaning his legs sank into the ground. And it is said: we were rained on until the ground became suwwākhā, on the pattern fuʿʿālā — that is, when the rain's mire became abundant; and when it is so, the legs of those passing through it sink into it.
سود:
The letters sīn, wāw and dāl are a single root, and it is the opposite of whiteness in colour; then other things are carried onto it and derived from it. Blackness in colour is well known. In the view of some, everything that differs from white, whatever colour it may be, falls within the compass of black. One says iswadda al-shay' and sawādda — the thing turned black. The sawād of anything is its figure, the bulk of it seen from a distance. Al-siwād is talking in secret; one says sāwadahu musāwadatan wa-siwādan when he spoke to him in secret. Abū 'Ubayd said: it is from bringing your own person close to his person, and that is the figure. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Whoever is a man given to women, in secret talk and idle play and infatuation — I am no such man.
Al-asāwid is the plural of al-aswad, and they are snakes. As for the words of Abū Dharr, God's mercy upon him, 'and these asāwid around me', he meant only the shapes of some vessels he had; [and around him] there was nothing but a water jug, a jar and a bowl. Al-sawād is also a great number, so called because the ground turns black with it.

As for lordship: some said al-sayyid is the forbearing man. Others denied that this comes from forbearance, and said: he is called sayyid only because people take refuge in his sawād, his person. This is more in keeping with the analogy than the first, and sounder. One says fulān aswad min fulān — that is, higher in lordship than he. Al-aswadān are dates and water. They said sawād al-qalb and suwaydā'uhu, the black of the heart, and it is its inner grain. One says sāwadanī fulān fa-sudtuhu — he vied with me and I overcame him — from blackness of colour and from lordship alike. The analogy in the whole chapter is one.
سور:
The letters sīn, wāw and rā' are a single root pointing to height and rising up. From it: sāra yasūru when a man is angry and flares up. And inna li-ghaḍabihi la-sawra — his anger has a surge to it. Al-suwar is the plural of sūra, which is every level of a building. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Many a man behind a curtained, guarded enclosure ... I climbed to him along the top of the wall.

As for the other's line:
A drinker, quick to profit by the cup, kept me company ... neither one who holds back nor one who flares up over it —
he means that he is not a man who grows angry. Some of them used to say: it is the one in whose head the drink rises quickly. As for a woman's siwār, a bracelet, and al-iswār, one of the asāwira of the Persians, who are their commanders, I think these two are not Arabic. And sawrat al-khamr is the sharpness of the wine and its seething.
سوس:
The letters sīn, wāw and sīn are two roots: one is corruption in a thing, the other is inborn nature and disposition.

1. sāsa al-taʿām — the food sāsa, or asāsa, meaning it spoiled from something called sūs [weevil].
2. sāsat al-shāh — the ewe sāsat, when its lice multiplied.
3. al-sawas — it is said al-sawas is a disease that afflicts horses in their hindquarters.

The other word is al-sūs, which is inborn nature. One says: hādhā min sūsi fulānin, meaning this is from so-and-so's nature. As for their saying sustuhu asūsuhu, it may well come from this too, as if it points him toward his noble nature and carries him upon it.

1. al-sīsā' — the aligned vertebrae of the back.
2. mā' masūs, kala' masūs — water or pasture is called masūs when it is beneficial to livestock, that is, camels and sheep.

And God knows best what is right.
سوط:
The letters sīn, wāw and ṭā are a root pointing to one thing mixing with another.

1. "suṭtu al-shay'" — I mixed one part of it with another.
2. So-and-so "sawwaṭa" his affair, when he threw it into confusion.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
So stir it up, blameworthy in judgment, unblessed with success — for you shall have no help in stirring it up.

3. al-sawṭ, the whip — because it mixes into the skin (strikes against it); "suṭtuhu bi'l-sawṭ" — I struck him with the whip.
4. Their calling a portion or share a sawṭ is from this root too. God, exalted be His praise, said: {so your Lord poured upon them a portion of punishment} [al-Fajr: 13], meaning, a share of punishment.
سوع: The letters sīn, wāw and ʿayn point to a thing running on and passing. From that al-sāʿa, the hour, was so named. One says jā'anā baʿda sawʿin min al-layl and suwāʿin — he came to us after a stretch of the night, that is, after a still quiet part of it; and that is because it is something that passes and runs on. From that also is their saying ʿāmaltuhu musāwaʿatan — I dealt with him by the hour, as one says muyāwamatan, by the day; and that is from al-sāʿa. And one says asaʿtu al-ibil isāʿatan, and that is when you let the camels go loose so that they wander where they will. And sāʿat fa-hiya tasūʿu — she strayed off, and she strays. From it one says huwa ḍā'iʿ sā'iʿ — he is lost and adrift. And a she-camel is misyāʿ, and she is the one that goes off into the pasture. And al-siyāʿ is clay with straw mixed in it.
سوغ:
The letters sīn, wāw and ghayn are a root indicating the ease of a thing and its going down smoothly, specifically in the throat; other senses are then carried from that.

One says "the drink sāgha in the throat, sawghan" — it went down smoothly. "God, glorious is His majesty, asāgha [it]" — made it go down smoothly.

1. "So-and-so obtained such a thing, and I sawwaghtuhu it to him" — I let him keep it without contest.

As for their saying "this is the sawgh of that," meaning its equal, this may belong to the same root — meaning it runs the same course and continues as the other continues. Or it may be that the sīn stands in for a ṣād, as though it means "it was shaped in the same fashion" — this has already been discussed under its own entry.
سوف:
The letters sīn, wāw and fā' are three roots.

The first is smell. One says: sufta al-shay' asūfuhu sawfan, and asaftuhu — I smelled the thing. Some scholars held that their saying "there is a masāfa [distance] between us and them" comes from this. He said: the guide would sawf [smell] the dust, to know whether the path was straight or crooked. And they cited, in verse:

When the guide has smelled out the character of the roads —

meaning he smelled them.

The second root: al-suwāf is the loss of livestock, and the disease that causes it. One says: the man asāfa, when suwāf befell his wealth. Ḥumayd ibn Thawr said:

They lost, of their inherited wealth, and were left destitute.

As for delay, it is al-taswīf. One says sawwaftuhu, meaning you put him off, when you said "sawfa afʿalu kadhā" [I shall do such-and-such, later].
سوق:
The letters sīn, wāw and qāf are a single root, and it is the driving of a thing. One says sāqahu yasūquhu sawqan — he drove it. Al-sayyiqa is what is driven off from the beasts. And one says suqtu ilā imra'atī ṣadāqahā, and asaqtuhu — I sent my wife her bride-price. Al-sūq, the market, is derived from this, for all the things that are driven to it; the plural is aswāq. Al-sāq is the shank of a man or of anything else, and the plural is sūq; it was named so because the walker is driven along upon it. One says imra'a sawqā' and rajul aswaq of one with a great shank; the verbal noun is al-sawaq. Ru'ba said, in a line of verse:
Short-haired from hard running, long-backed, with fine shanks.

And sūq al-ḥarb is the thick of the fighting, derived from the first chapter.
سوك:
The letters sīn, wāw and kāf are one root, indicating motion and unsteadiness. One says: tasāwaqati al-ibil — the camels' necks shook unsteadily from emaciation and poor condition. And it is also said: jā'ati al-ibilu mā tasāwaku huzālan, meaning they do not even move their heads.

1. al-siwāk — from this the name al-siwāk [the tooth-stick] is derived, being the twig itself.
2. al-siwāk — also, the using of it.

Ibn Durayd said: suktu al-shay' sawkan, meaning you rubbed it; and from this comes the derivation of al-siwāk. One says: sāka fāhu, he rubbed his mouth with it; but if you say istāka, you do not need to mention the mouth — it is understood.
سول:
The letters sīn, wāw and lām are a single root indicating slackness, a looseness in a thing. One says sawila yaswalu sawalan.

A poet of Hudhayl said, in a line of verse:
Like white cloth whose colour has come out clear ... the pouring rush of a cloud sagging low with rain.

As for their saying sawwaltu lahu al-shay' — meaning I made the thing look good to him — it is possible this means "I gave him his su'l", his wish, the hamza having been softened away from su'l.
سوم:
The letters sīn, wāw and mīm are a root pointing to seeking a thing.

One says sumtu al-shay', asūmuhu sawman — I sought the thing. From it is al-sawm, haggling in buying and selling.

And of this section: sāmat al-rāʿiya tasūm — the grazing beasts pastured; and asamtuhā anā — I sent them out to pasture. God, exalted be He, said: {in it you pasture} [al-Naḥl: 10], that is, you graze your beasts. And one says sawwamtu fulānan fī mālī taswīman — when you give him free authority over your property. And sawwamtu ghulāmī — I left my boy to do as he wished. And al-khayl al-musawwama are the horses set loose with their riders upon them. The origin of all of this is one.

And of what falls outside the section is al-sūma, which is the mark that is put upon a thing. And al-sīmā, with a short final vowel, is of this. God, be He glorified, said: {their mark is on their faces from the trace of prostration} [al-Fatḥ: 29]. And when they lengthen it they say al-sīmā'.
سوي:
The letters sīn, wāw and yā' are a root that points to straightness and evenness between two things. One says hādhā lā yusāwī kadhā — this does not equal that, that is, it does not match it. And so-and-so and so-and-so are ʿalā sawiyya in this matter, that is, they are on an equal footing in it. And a makān suwan is a known landmark, a place the people know how to enter and how to leave. One says aswā al-rajul when a man's descendants and his children come out sound and whole.

ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm al-Qaṭṭān related to us, from ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, from Abū ʿUbayd, from al-Kisā'ī, who said: one asks kayfa amsaytum — how have you come to the evening? And the answer is mustawūna ṣāliḥūn — we are even and well. They mean: our children and our livestock are sound and well.

And of this chapter is al-siyy: the open empty stretch of land, in the words of the one who said:
As though the ostriches of the open plain had laid their eggs upon them.

And al-siyy is the like, the equal. And their saying siyyān means two of a kind. From that comes their saying lā siyyamā — that is, there is nothing like what — and it is from sīn, wāw and yā', as one says wa-lā sawā'a. The proof that siyy is the like is al-Ḥuṭay'a's words, in a line of verse:
So beware the snake of the valley floor, biting of fang; for you there is no match for it.

And of this chapter is al-sawā': the middle of a house or of anything else, so called for its being even. God, exalted be His praise, said: {So he looked and saw him in the midst of Hellfire} [al-Ṣāffāt: 55].

As for their saying hādhā siwā dhālika — this is other than that — it is of this chapter, because when one thing is apart from another, each of them is in its own space on an equal footing. The proof of that is their lengthening it as al-siwā' with the meaning of siwā. Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
And she turned aside from her own people to none but you.

And one says qaṣadtu siwā fulān — I made for so-and-so — as one says qaṣadtu qaṣdahu. And al-Farrā' recited, in a line of verse:
I shall surely turn my praise away from Ḥudhayfa, to the young man of the evening and the horseman of al-Ajrāf.
سيب:
The letters sīn, yā and bā are a root pointing to a thing's continuing on and going along freely.

1. sayb al-mā' — the flowing course of water.
2. insābat al-ḥayyatu insiyāban — the snake glided along.
3. "sayyabtu al-dābba" — I let the animal go loose, leaving it wherever it wished.
4. al-sā'iba — a slave who is set free without any bond of clientage, free to put his wealth wherever he wishes.
5. al-sayb — a gift or bestowal, as though it were something set flowing toward him.
6. al-suyūb — buried treasure, as though it were a gift God Most High set flowing for whoever finds it.

Irregular against this root is al-sayāb, unripe green dates; singular sayāba.
سيح:
The letters sīn, yā' and ḥā' are a sound root, following the same pattern as the entry before it.

One says "he sāḥa in the land" — he journeyed, roamed freely. God, exalted be His praise, said: {So journey freely in the land for four months} [al-Tawba: 2].

1. al-sayḥ — flowing water.
2. al-masāyīḥ — in a hadith of ʿAlī, may God ennoble his face: "those are the lamps of the darkness; they are neither spreaders of secrets nor roaming sowers of discord" — for al-madhāyīʿ is the plural of midhyāʿ, one who spreads a secret rather than keeping it, while al-masāyīḥ are those who roam the land spreading slander, evil, and discord among people.

Among what confirms this reasoning is their saying "the shadow sāḥa," when it swings back [as at midday].

3. al-sayḥ — the striped cloak, so named by likening its stripes to a thing that flows.
سيد:
The letters sīn, yā' and dāl are one word, which is al-sīd. Some said: al-sīd is the wolf. Others said: the lion too is sometimes called sīd. And they recite:

Like the sīd, the maned one, fierce and roused to attack.
سير:
The letters sīn, yā' and rā' are a root indicating going on and running, one says sāra yasīru sayran, he journeyed, and that may be by night or by day. And al-sīra is the way followed in a thing, and the customary practice, because it goes on and runs its course. One says sārat, it ran its course, and sirtuhā anā, I set it running.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
So do not shrink from a practice you yourself set going ... for the first to be content with a practice is the one who follows it.

And al-sayr is a strip of leather, well known, and it is from this, so named for its being drawn out, as though it were running along. And sayyartu al-jull ʿan al-dābba, I threw the horse-cloth off the beast. And al-musayyar among garments is the one that has stripes in it, as though they were leather thongs.
سيع:
The letters sīn, yā' and ʿayn are a root indicating the flowing of a thing.

1. al-sayʿ — water flowing over the surface of the ground; one says sāʿa and insāʿa.
2. insāʿa al-jamad — the ice insāʿa'd, meaning it melted.
3. al-sayāʿ — what a wall is plastered with.
4. al-sayāʿ — it is also said to be the grease with which a water-skin (mazāda) is coated; and the woman sayyaʿat her water-skin, meaning she coated it.
سيف:
The letters sīn, yā' and fā' are a root indicating extension and length in a thing.

1. al-sayf — the sword, named for this because of its length.
2. sayfāna — a woman is called sayfāna when she is slender, as if she were a sword's blade. Al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad said: a man is not described by it. But ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm related to me, from ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, from Abū ʿUbayd, from al-Kisā'ī: a man may be called sayfān and a woman sayfāna.
3. sīf al-baḥr — what shows the correctness of this derivation is their saying sīf al-baḥr [the seashore], which is what extends along with its coastline.
4. al-sīf — from this too, what clings to the base of the palm-fronds, of the fibre [līf]; it is the worst kind of it. A poet said:

The sīf and the līf lie upon its fringes.

5. al-sā'ifa — of the land, is from this too, because it is the sand that slants within the firm ground and extends along with it. They said: it is what is called al-ʿadāb. Abū Ziyād said: al-sā'ifa of sand is the softest kind there is. But the first view is more correct, and it is the view of al-Naḍr, because it is more analogically sound and closer to the root sense we have mentioned — and whatever in the language is more analogically sound is more correct. The plural of al-sā'ifa is sawā'if. Dhū al-Rumma said:

She smiles, showing gums the colour of dark honey, as if [her teeth] were the crowns of camomile among the camomile of the sā'if-sands.

He also said:

... as though they were, upon a barren sā'ifa, the backs of striped snakes.

6. asaftu al-kharz — as for their saying asaftu al-kharz, meaning you pierced the stitched beading, it may be an anomaly outside this root, or it may belong to the wāw-family and come from al-suwāf [wasting], already mentioned. One says: huwa musīf, when he pierces the beading. Al-Rāʿī said:

Water-skins, weak-handed, ill-stitched — the two hindmost driven hard and pressed on by them.
سيل:
The letters sīn, yā' and lām are a single root indicating flowing and stretching out.

1. sāla al-mā'u wa-ghayruhu yasīlu saylan wa-sayalānan — water and other things flow.
2. masīl al-mā', the watercourse. If the mīm is taken as an added letter this belongs here; if the mīm is taken as an original letter of the root it belongs to another chapter, already discussed.
3. al-sīlān of a sword or a knife — the iron tang that goes into the handle. I heard 'Alī ibn Ibrāhīm al-Qaṭṭān say: I heard 'Alī ibn 'Abd al-'Azīz say: I heard Abū 'Ubayd say, "al-sīlān — I have heard the word, but not from any scholar."
4. sīyat al-qaws, the tip of the bow — one is said to say the adjective from it is sīyawiyy.

And God knows best.
شأت:
The letters shīn, hamza and tā'. Al-sha'īt, among horses, is the one that stumbles.
A bay horse, neither aḥaqq nor sha'īt.
شأز:
The letters shīn, hamza and zā' are a small root pointing to restlessness and unevenness in a place.

1. al-sha'z (of a place) — the rough, uneven place. Ru'bah said:
A rough, uneven place, whoever camps in it finds it barren, hard to travel through.
2. ash'azahu — a thing ash'aza someone, when it unsettled him.
شأس:
The letters shīn, hamza and sīn are like the chapter before it, and it is not unlikely that this is a case of letter-substitution.

1. Sha's — a man's name.
2. al-sha's — the rough, hard place.
شأف:
The letters shīn, hamza and fā' are a word pointing to hatred.

1. al-shā'afah — hatred. One says: sha'aftuhu sha'afan, I hated him.
2. al-sha'fah — a sore that comes out at the gums, which is cauterised and then goes away. They say: ista'sala Allāhu sha'fatahu, may God root out his sha'fah utterly. One says: shu'ifat rijluhu, his foot was sha'ifat, meaning God removed it just as that sore is removed. It was named sha'fah for the hatred and loathing already mentioned.
شأم:
The letters shīn, hamza and mīm are a single root indicating the left side.

1. al-mash'ama — the opposite of al-maymana [the right side].
2. al-Sha'm [Syria, the Levant] — a land lying to the left of the qibla. One says al-Sha'm and al-Shā'am.
3. rajul shā'am, imra'a shā'amiyya — a Syrian man, a Syrian woman.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
My mother was Syrian, when we had no kin in Iraq — a people we loved, when our own people were fierce.

4. rajul mash'ūm — an ill-omened man, from al-shu'm [ill omen].
شأن:
The letters shīn, hamza and nūn are a single root indicating seeking and pursuing. From this, the Arabs' saying sha'antu sha'nahu, meaning I aimed at what he aimed at. They cited the line:
O seeker of generosity, generosity is a noble trait ... stinginess is not from you, nor is generosity your pursuit.
They said its meaning is: nor is generosity what you seek.

From this also: their saying mā hādhā min sha'nī, meaning this is not my concern, that is, not what I seek and what I aim after. As for al-shu'ūn, these are the sutures between the plates of the skull, one of them a sha'n. They were so named because they are the channels of tears, as though the tears seek them out and make them a course to flow in.
شأو:
The letters shīn, hamza and wāw are two words very far apart from each other.

1. al-sha'w (the first) — outrunning, getting ahead. One says: sha'awtuhu, meaning I outran him.
2. al-sha'w (the second) — what is brought up out of a well when it is cleaned out. The basket used to bring that up is called al-mish'āh.
شأي:
The letters shīn, hamza and yā' are a word belonging to the chapter of substitution [one letter standing for another], with disagreement about it. Some said: shaʾaytu is like shaʾawtu, [used] of racing ahead; one says from it shaʾā and ishtaʾā. [Al-Mufaḍḍal said this] and recited:

A poet said, in a line of verse:
So it was, with Kindīr, the donkey of Ibn Wāqiʿ — he saw you by the forge-fire and shied away, fleeing from ʿUtāʾid.

Some said: ishtaʾā means he rose up, became prominent. But what al-Mufaḍḍal said is more correct and more sound by analogy.
شب:
The letters shīn and bāʾ are a single root indicating the growth of a thing and its strength amid a heat that comes over it. From that: shababtu al-nāra ashubbuhā shabban wa-shubūban (I kindled the fire) — it is the maṣdar of shubbat. Likewise shababtu al-ḥarb, when you set it ablaze. That is the origin.

1. al-shabāb — the opposite of grey hair, derived from that. One says "shabba al-ghulām shabīban wa-shabāban," and "ashabba Allāhu qarnahu" (God let his generation grow young). Al-shabāb is also the plural of shābb (a young man); that is growth and increase through the strength of his body and its heat. Then, to differentiate, one says "shabba al-faras shibāban," with a kasra on the shīn, when it grew lively and reared up on both its legs. And they say: "I disown to you his liveliness (shibāb) and his biting." Al-shabība is the same as al-shabāb.
2. al-shabab — a young one of the wild cattle. Dhū al-Rumma said: "a young bull, shabab, roaming free."
3. From this same reasoning: "ushibba lahu al-shayʾ," when a thing was allotted and made available to him, as though it were raised up and named for him.
شبث:
The letters shīn, bā' and thā' are a small root denoting one thing's clinging to another.

1. tashabbathtu — I clung on, I held fast.
2. al-shabath — a small creeping creature, one of the vermin of the earth, so named because it clings to whatever it crawls over. Its plural is shibthān.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
The crawling-tracks of shibthān, which have a faint rustling.

That is, a creeping motion.
شبح:
The letters shīn, bā' and ḥā' are a sound root denoting a thing's extension in width.

1. al-shabaḥ — a person's shape or figure, so called because there is extension and width in it.
2. al-mashbūḥ — a man of great, broad bones.

Abū Dhu'ayb al-Hudhalī said, in a line of verse:
And that one — broad in the two forearms, big of neck.

3. shabaḥtu al-shay' — I stretched the thing out.
4. shabḥu dhirāʿayhi — his stretching out of his two arms, in supplication and elsewhere.
5. It is said of the chameleon, when it stretches itself out on a branch: qad shabaḥa — it has stretched out.
شبر:
The letters shīn, bā' and rā' are two roots: one is a certain body part, the other is surplus and giving.

The first:
1. al-shibr — a person's hand-span; it is masculine. One says shabartu al-thawb shabran, I measured the garment by hand-spans. Al-shibr is also the thing used to measure. A short, compactly built man is called qaṣīr al-shabr — short of span.
2. al-mashābir — channels that dip low, so that water runs down into them; they seem to be called mashābir because their width is small.

The second root is al-shabar: goodness, surplus, and giving.

ʿAdī said, in a line of verse:
I did not betray him, nor the One who gave the shabar.

1. ashbartuhu bi-kadhā — I singled him out with such a thing.

It is related from some that al-shabar is something Christians give one another in the sense of a communion-offering, but this is nothing [i.e. not sound]. The correct analogy is what we have stated.

2. aʿṭāhā shabrahā — he gave her her due; said of a man's right owed to his wife in marriage, when he gives her what is hers.

It came in the hadith that he [the Prophet] "forbade the shabr of the camel" — that is, its hire, and what is taken for its covering [a stud fee], which is like ʿasb al-faḥl, the fee taken for a stallion's service.

3. shubbira — said of a thing when it is made great, magnified.
شبص: The letters shīn, bā' and ṣād are not a root. Ibn Duraid related: al-shabaṣ is roughness, and this too is not sound. He said: and one says tashabbaṣa al-shajar — the trees became entangled, some growing into others.
شبع:
The letters shīn, bā' and ʿayn are a sound root denoting fullness, in eating and elsewhere.

1. shabiʿa al-rajulu shibaʿan and shibʿan — the man became full, sated; a man in this state is shabʿān.
2. ashbaʿtu al-thawb ṣibghan — I saturated the garment with dye [this is derived from the above].
3. imra'atun shabʿā al-khalkhāl — a woman "full at the anklet," that is, plump, from the abundance of flesh on her shank.

From that is the saying of the Prophet, God bless him and his family and grant him peace: "al-mutashabbiʿ bimā laysa ʿindahu ka-lābisi thawbay zūr" — the one who makes himself appear full with what he does not have is like one wearing two garments of falsehood. He means the one who makes himself appear abundant in what he does not possess; this is a proverb, as though he meant: he shows fullness while he is hungry — just as the Arabs say, "Luqmān belched without being full."

4. thawb shabīʿ al-ghazl — a garment abundant, thick, in its spun thread.

What runs in the manner of a comparison, from this same chapter, is their saying: "shabiʿtu min hādhā al-amr wa rawītu" — I had my fill of this matter and drank my fill of it — said when you have grown weary of and averse to a thing.
شبق: The letters shīn, bā' and qāf are a single word: al-shabaq, which is the desire for intercourse.
شبك:
The letters shīn, bā' and kāf are a sound root denoting one thing's interlocking with another.

1. shabbaka aṣābiʿahu tashbīkan — he interlaced his fingers.
2. bayna al-qawmi shubkatu nasab — among the people there is an interlocking of lineage, that is, an intermingling.
3. al-shabaka — the net, [named] from this.
شبل:
The letters shīn, bā' and lām are a sound root denoting affection and love. Every one who is affectionate toward and loving of a thing is called mushbil.

1. al-shibl — the lion's cub, taken from this, because of its two parents' affection toward it.
2. labu'a mushbil — a lioness said to be so when her cubs are with her.
3. ashbalat al-mar'a — said of a woman when she stood fast for the sake of her children and did not remarry.

Al-Kumayt said:
The one full of tenderness, and the one full of affection.

4. It is related from al-Kisā'ī: shabaltu fī banī fulān — I grew up among the tribe of so-and-so.
5. shabala al-ghulāmu aḥsana al-shubūl — the boy grew up most excellently, said when he reached maturity. This is by way of extension and figurative use, for it is as though affection is extended over him — yushbal ʿalayhi, that is, he is embraced.
شبم:
The letters shīn, bā' and mīm are two words very far apart from one another.

The first is al-shabam: cold; and al-shabim: the cold [thing].

The other is al-shibām: a piece of wood placed crosswise in a kid's mouth so that it cannot suckle. This is then likened to something else, so that al-shibāmān is said of the two cords of the face-veil, which a woman ties behind her neck.
شبه:
The letters shīn, bā' and hā' are a single root, pointing to a thing resembling another and being of the same form as it in colour and description. One says shibh, shabah and shabīh — a likeness. Al-shabah among the metals is the one that resembles gold. Al-mushabbihāt among affairs are the ones that are hard to make out. And ishtabaha al-amrān, when two matters become hard to tell apart.

Of what strays from that is al-shabahān.
شبو:
The letters shīn, bā' and the weak letter are two roots: one denotes an edge and sharpness, the other denotes growth, surplus, and honour.

The first:
1. al-shabāh — the edge of anything is its shabāh; its plural is al-shabā and al-shabawāt.
2. al-shabwa — a name for the scorpion, so named for the sharpness of its sting.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Shabwa began to bristle up.

3. Al-Liḥyānī mentioned that a foul-mouthed girl is called shabwa, likened in this to the scorpion.

The other root:
1. al-ishbā' — honouring; one says atā fulānun fulānan fa-ashbāhu — so-and-so came to so-and-so and he honoured him.
2. ashbaytu al-rajul — said when you raise a man up to glory and honour.

Dhū al-Iṣbaʿ said, in a line of verse:
And they — those to whom they gave birth, they raised to honour, by the pure secret of their lineage.

3. al-mushbī — one to whom an intelligent, able child is born; one says qad ashbā.
4. ashbat al-shajara — the tree grew tall.
5. ashbā fulānan waladuhu — said when a man's child resembles him [ashbahūhu].

And they recited:
I am the son of him who never disgraced me in his lifetime, of old — and whoever resembles his father has done no wrong.

God knows best.
شت:
The letters shīn and tāʾ are a root indicating separation and scattering apart. From that is tashtīt al-shayʾ al-mutafarriq (scattering something already dispersed). You say shatta shaʿbuhum shatātan wa-shattan, meaning their gathering scattered. Al-Ṭirimmāḥ said: "the tribe's gathering scattered after being joined, and the abandoned camp stirred your grief — the camp of dwelling."

1. It is said "the people came ashtātan," scattered, in separate groups.
2. A gapped mouth is called shatīt, meaning well-spaced and handsome; this is from the same root, as though the teeth are not crowded together.
3. "Shattāna mā humā" (how different the two are) — they say this is the more eloquent form, and they recite: "how different my day upon her saddle, and the day of Ḥayyān, brother of Jābir." Sometimes they say "shattāna mā baynahumā," but the first is more eloquent.
شتر:
The letters shīn, tā' and rā' denote a tear or rip in a thing.

1. al-shatar, in the eye — a turning-back in its lower lid together with a tear that occurs there.
2. shattara bihi — derived from this, said when a man diminishes another, finds fault with him, and tears into him.
شتم:
The letters shīn, tā' and mīm denote disgust and hatred.

1. al-asad al-shatīm — the lion of hateful, repellent appearance; likewise al-ḥimār al-shatīm, the donkey of the same description.
2. al-shatm — cursing, abuse — is derived from this, because it is disliked, hateful speech.
شتو:
The letters shīn, tā' and the weak letter are a single root naming a season, and it is winter, the opposite of summer. It is called al-shatwa, with a short vowel after the shīn. The place of wintering is al-mashtāh and al-mashtā.

Ṭarafa said, in a line of verse:
We, at the winter-camp, call everyone to the general feast — you will not see the feast-giver among us being selective.

Al-Khalīl said: winter is well known; its singular is al-shatwa. This follows a good pattern, like shakwa and shikā' [a small water-skin, water-skins]. One says ashtā al-qawm, when the people entered the winter season, and shatū, when winter struck them.
شث: The letters shīn and thāʾ are not a root; it is only al-shathth: a tree.
شثن: The letters shīn, thā' and nūn. Al-shathn is thick-fingered. Anything thickened, in a limb, is shathn. One says shathana and shathina. God knows best.
شج:
The letters shīn and jīm are a single root indicating a splitting of a thing. One says shajajtu raʾsahu ashujjuhu shajjan (I gashed his head). There was among the people shijāj and mushājja, when they gashed one another's heads.

1. al-shajaj — the mark of a gash on the forehead; the descriptive term for it is ashajj.
2. "shajajtu al-mafāza shajjan" — said when you cut across the wasteland in travel.
3. "shajajtu al-sharāb bi-l-mizāj" — I diluted the drink by mixing it.
4. "shajjat al-safīna al-baḥr" — the ship cut through the sea.
5. al-shajīj — that which is gashed (al-mashjūj). A tent-peg is called shajīj.
شجب:
The letters shīn, jīm and bā' are two words: one denotes intermixture, the other denotes passing away and ruin.

The first: the Arabs' saying tashājaba al-amr — the matter became mixed up, and parts of it entered into other parts.

1. al-mishjab — interlocking wooden pieces, bound and set upright, on which clothes are spread out [a clothes-rack]. They said it is derived from this.
2. al-shujūb — poles among the poles of a tent.

A line of verse:
And they stood together, alike, like the shujūb.

3. al-shijāb — a stopping-up, a plug; one says shajabahu bi-shijāb, he stopped it up. This too belongs to the same meaning.

The other root is al-shajib, which is the perishing, dying one. One says qad shajiba — he perished.

A line of verse:
So whoever is in doubt about his killing — indeed Abū Nawfal has perished.

1. Sometimes they called a grieving man shajib.
2. shajabahu — said when a thing grieved him.
3. shajabahu Allāh — meaning God destroyed him.

Ibn al-Sikkīt said: shajabahu yashjubuhu shajban, said when a thing occupied and preoccupied him; the origin of al-shajb is what we have stated, and everything that comes after it is carried upon it, by extension.
شجذ:
The letters shīn, jīm and dhāl are a single word. One says ashjadhat al-samā', said when its rain grows calm and lessens.

Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
It reveals al-Wadd when its rain grows light — and hides it when the rain turns fierce.

Ibn Duraid said: "Al-Wadd is a known mountain, and tashtakir means its rain intensifies, from their saying ishtakara al-ḍarʿ — the udder filled with milk." As for my copy of al-Khalīl's Kitāb al-ʿAyn, in it the letters shīn, jīm, dhāl are left untreated, so I do not know whether that is a gap in what was transmitted to him, or whether the word was simply unknown to the author of the book. The word itself is sound.
شجر:
The letters shīn, jīm and rā' are two roots that run into each other, each close to the other, and their meaning is never free of one thing entering into another, and of height and rising in a thing. We have gathered the branches of these two chapters together because of the overlap we have mentioned.

Al-shajar, trees, is well known; a single one is a shajara, and it is never free of height and of branches running into one another. A valley that is shajir is one with many trees. One says: this land is ashjar than another, that is, it has more trees. Al-shajar is every plant that has a stem. God Most High said: {And the stemless plants and the trees bow down} [al-Rahman: 6]. And shajara bayna al-qawm al-amr, when a matter came between people, that is, when it differed or they differed and quarrelled over it; it is called mushājara, a quarrel, because their words run into one another. And ishtajarū: they disputed. God, glorified and exalted, said: {But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge in what has arisen between them} [al-Nisa': 65].

As for the shajr of a man, some people said it is the opening of the mouth. Al-Asma'ī used to say: the shajr is the chin itself. The two statements are close to each other in our view, because when the two jawbones come together they have run into one another, as we said of the reasoning of the word. One says ishtajara al-rajul, when a man puts his hand on his shajr. A poet said, in a line of verse:
I could not sleep, and passed the night with my hand under my chin, as though my eyes had bitter sāb-juice pressed into them.

And one says shajartu al-shay', when a thing hung down and you raised it. Al-shijār, also read al-shajār, is the wood of a camel-litter. Both meanings are found in it, because there is height in it and things running into one another. Al-mishjar is called mishjar because parts of it run into one another. And tashājara al-qawm bi'l-rimāh: they thrust at one another with spears. Land that is shajrā' or shajira is land with many trees. Ibn Durayd said: one does not say wādin shajrā'.
شجع:
The letters shīn, jīm and ʿayn are a single root denoting boldness and daring — and there may be something of tallness bound up in it too; it is one chapter.

1. al-rajul al-shujāʿ — the bold man, the one who goes forward daringly; its plural is shajʿa and shujaʿā'.

Ibn Duraid said: "Do not heed their saying shujʿān, for it is a mistake. Abū Zayd said: I heard the men of Kilāb say rajul shujāʿ, and a woman is not described by it. This is Abū Zayd's own statement." But it has been related to us, on al-Khalīl's authority by the chain of his book: rajul shujāʿ, imra'a shujāʿa, niswa shujāʿāt — and he also mentioned shujʿān as a further plural of shujāʿ.

2. al-shujāʿ — [also] the snake.

The Messenger of God, God bless him and his family and grant him peace, said: "yajī'u kanzu aḥadihim yawma al-qiyāmati shujāʿan aqraʿ" — the hoarded wealth of one of them will come, on the Day of Resurrection, as a bald snake.

As for al-shajaʿ in camels, some said it is quickness in moving the legs; then one says jamal shajiʿ, nāqa shajiʿa. It is also said to mean length, and he recited:
So we rode it over unfamiliar ground, over hard earth, in which there was shajaʿ.

It is also said that al-shajaʿ is madness, but the people of the language said this is a mistake — for if al-shajaʿ were madness it would not describe legs.

3. al-shajiʿa, of women — the daring one.
4. al-labu'a al-shajʿā' — the daring lioness; likewise the lion is called ashjaʿ. So it is said that the ashjaʿ among men is the one who seems to have a touch of madness in him.
5. al-ashjaʿ — the sinew stretched along the leg above the sulāmā [the small bone of the instep].
شجن:
The letters shīn, jīm and nūn are a single root denoting a thing's connection and its entanglement.

1. al-shijna — entangled, intertwined trees.
2. baynī wa baynahu shijnatu raḥim — between him and me there is an entanglement of kinship, meaning its connection and intertwining.
3. al-shajan — a need, so called for its tangled complexity and for the way the heart becomes attached to it; its plural is shujūn.

A line of verse:
And the soul — scattered are its cares.

4. al-ashjān — the plural of shajan.

A line of verse:
I have two cares: a care in Najd, and a care of mine in the land of India.

5. al-shawājin — deep, hidden valleys, thick with trees, named for the entanglement (tashājun) of their trees.

Al-Ṭirimmāḥ said, in a line of verse:
Like the back of the [hard, level ground] — were water sought there by day, it would prove impossible, in the depths of the shawājin.
شجوى:
The letters shīn, jīm and the weak letter denote intensity and difficulty, and a thing's becoming caught fast in a narrow space.

1. al-shajw — grief and worry; one says shajāhu yashjūhu, it grieved him.
2. shajānī al-shay' — the thing grieved you.
3. al-shajā — what lodges in the throat, the choking lump of worry.
4. mafāza shajwā' — a waterless desert narrow of passage.
شح:
The letters shīn and ḥāʾ — the origin in it is withholding, then it becomes withholding joined with greed. From that is al-shuḥḥ, which is stinginess joined with greed. One says "the two men tashāḥḥā over the matter," when each of them wanted to win it for himself and keep it from his companion. God, exalted be His praise, said: {and whoever is guarded from the greed of his own soul — those are the successful} [al-Ḥashr: 9].

1. al-zand al-shaḥāḥ — the fire-stick that does not strike a spark. Ibn Harma said: "and I, in leaving the generosity of the noble, and my striking with my two hands a stingy fire-stick."

This is the origin in the doubled form. As for the reduplicated form, it is close to this.

2. They call one who is persistent in a thing "shaḥshaḥ" — his persistence in it is only out of withholding it from others.
3. They call the jealous man "shaḥshaḥ," which follows the same reasoning, because when he is jealous he withholds/guards.
4. Likewise al-shujāʿ (the brave one) — he is the one who guards what is behind his back.
5. And the one who presses on eloquently in his speech is called "shaḥshaḥ," as though carried on the analogy of al-shujāʿ, likened to him.
شحب:
The letters shīn, ḥā' and bā' are a sound root denoting a change of colour; its verbal noun is al-shuḥūb.

1. shaḥaba and shaḥuba, yashḥubu — to lose one's colour, grow pale. A pale, faded colour is called shāḥib.

A line of verse:
My daughter says, when she saw me pale: it is as though you, O father, were among us a stranger.

2. It is related, by al-Duraydī: shaḥabtu al-arḍa — I stripped the ground of its surface. If this report is sound, then this is the pattern the word follows.
شحج:
The letters shīn, ḥā' and jīm are a root denoting a sound.

1. shaḥaja al-ghurābu yashḥaju — the crow cawed; and likewise of the mule. Mules are called banāt shāḥij, the daughters of the one that brays.
2. They call the wild donkey mishḥaj and shaḥḥāj.

God knows best what is correct.
شحذ:
The letters shīn, ḥā' and dhāl are a single root denoting lightness and sharpness.

1. shaḥadhtu al-ḥadīd — said when you sharpened the iron.
2. al-mashāḥīdh — mountain peaks, said to be so named for the sharpness just mentioned.
3. al-shaḥdhān — said of a hungry man, from the same sense of lightness. It is also said that al-shaḥdhān is the one light and quick in his going about.
شحر: The letters shīn, ḥā' and rā' are not a root; it is perhaps the name of a place.
شحص: The letters shīn, ḥā' and ṣād are a single word. One says: "al-shaḥaṣ is the ewe that has no milk," and it is also said she is the one that has never once been covered [mated]. In al-Khalīl's book: al-shaḥṣā'.
شحط:
The letters shīn, ḥā' and ṭā' are two roots: one is distance, the other is a mixing-together in a thing and a disturbance.

The first: their saying shaḥaṭat al-dār tashḥaṭu shaḥṭan wa shuḥūṭan — the dwelling grew distant, it is shāḥiṭa, distant.

The other root is al-shaḥṭ, which is a thrashing about in blood.

1. One says of a newborn, when it thrashes about within the amniotic sac: huwa yatashaḥḥaṭu fī damihi — he thrashes about in his own blood.
2. al-laban al-mashḥūṭ — milk that has had water poured onto it, derived from this.
3. al-shaḥṭa — a disease that takes hold of camels, from which they scarcely recover, [belonging] to this chapter.
4. al-mishḥaṭ — a small stick set beside a vine-branch to protect it from the ground, [belonging] to this chapter.

Some said al-shaḥṭ is bird droppings, and they recited:
And many a felted-haired, huge-bodied one, between a waterless waste and a place of destruction, I passed by it, with the loftiness of its build, towering;
As though the shaḥṭ upon the tops of its haunches were strips of fine cloth, of silk and linen.

If this is sound, then it too belongs to the sense of intermixture.
شحم:
The letters shīn, ḥā' and mīm are a root indicating a kind of meat.

1. al-shaḥm — fat, well known.
2. shaḥmat al-udhun — the earlobe, where the earring hangs.
3. rajulun mushḥim — a man with much fat. If he loves fat, he is called shaḥim; if he feeds it to his companions, shāḥim; if he sells it, shaḥḥām.
شحن:
The letters shīn, ḥā' and nūn are two distinct roots: one indicating filling, the other distance.

The first: "shaḥantu the ship," when you filled it.
1. "so-and-so ashḥana for weeping" — he made himself ready for it, as though gathering himself for it.

The second: al-shaḥn — driving away, expelling. "He shaḥanahum" — he drove them off.
2. A thing intensely sour is said "to shaḥan the flies," meaning it drives them away.
3. al-shaḥnā' — enmity.
4. ʿaduww mushāḥin — an estranged, distancing enemy. Enmity is estrangement.
شحوى:
The letters shīn, ḥā' and the weak letter denote an origin, which is the opening of a thing.

1. al-shaḥwa — the space between the two legs when a person takes a stride. A horse wide in its stride is said to be baʿīd al-shaḥwa, far-striding.
2. shaḥā al-rajulu fāhu — the man opened his mouth; shaḥā al-famu nafsuhu — the mouth itself opened. Both al-shaḥy and al-shaḥw serve as its verbal noun.
3. shaḥā al-lijāmu fama al-farasi shaḥyan — the bit forced open the horse's mouth.
4. jā'ati al-khaylu shawāḥiya — the horses came shawāḥiya, that is, with their mouths open.

A line of verse:
