Jaws thrown open, of one with a clattering, rattling bit.
شخ: The letters shīn and khāʾ are not a root. They only say: shakhkha al-ṣabiyyu bi-bawlihi, when the child urinated and it made a sound. And shakhkhat rijluhu daman, meaning it flowed with blood.
شخب:
The letters shīn, khāʾ and bāʾ are a minor root indicating a stretching in something that flows and runs.

1. al-shakhb — the stream of milk that stretches out as it is milked.
2. shakhabat — said of the slain man's throats when they spurted with blood: shakhabat awdāj al-qatlā daman, the throats of the slain spurted blood.
شخت:
The letters shīn, khāʾ and tāʾ are a single word: al-shayʾ al-shakht is the slender thing, of wood or anything else.

He said, in a line of verse:
Can lances that sway in the fray be equal — to seven sticks of slender boxthorn?
شخر:
The letters shīn, khā' and rā'. The sound root denotes a sound. Another word has also been related about it, if it is sound.

The root: al-shakhīr — the repeated sound in the throat [snoring]. It is also said: al-shakhīr is the raising of the voice with a snort. This is the well-known sense.

The other word: their saying that al-shakhīr is what crumbles away from a mountain when feet tread upon it.

The poet said, in a line of verse:
At a pool of Bāriq, atop a towering, lofty peak — below it, of it, was shakhīr [loose scree].
شخز:
The letters shīn, khā' and zā' are a single word denoting hardship and toil. They said: al-shakhz is difficulty and toil.

The rajaz-poet said, in a line of verse:
When matters became given over to hardship.

It is also said that al-shakhz is stabbing, piercing.
شخس:
The letters shīn, khā' and sīn are a sound root denoting crookedness and a turning away from the path of straightness.

1. al-asnān al-mutashākhisa — teeth out of true alignment, meaning some of them lean while others fall out; this happens from old age.

Al-Ṭirimmāḥ said, in a line of verse:
And time skewed his mouth, until it was as though it were...

2. ḍarabahu fa-tashākhasa — he struck him, and he leaned over. Anything leaning is mutashākhis.
شخص: The letters shīn, khā' and ṣād are a single root indicating a rising, an elevation in a thing. From that: al-shakhṣ, the dark form of a person as he appears to you from a distance. It is then extended: shakhaṣa min baladin ilā balad, he set out from one town to another — the same reasoning applies. From it also: shukhūṣ al-baṣar, the eyes staring fixedly upward. One says rajulun shakhīṣ and imra'atun shakhīṣa, meaning large-bodied. From this root: ashkhaṣa l-rāmī, when the archer's arrow passed above the target, and it is called sahmun shākhiṣ, an overshooting arrow. One says, when a matter comes upon someone that unsettles him, shukhiṣa bihi — because when he grew uneasy his place became too narrow for him and he rose up and left it.
شخل: The letters shīn, khā' and lām are not a root. A word has been related about it that I do not take to be genuine Arabic speech, even though it occurs in al-Khalīl's own words. He said: al-shakhl is the boy who befriends the man.
شخم:
The letters shīn, khāʾ and mīm are a word indicating change in something.

1. ashkhama al-labanu — the milk changed, said when its smell turned.
2. shakhima al-ṭaʿāmu — the food went bad.
شد:
The letters shīn and dāl are a single root indicating strength in a thing, and its branches go back to it. From that: shadadtu al-ʿaqda shaddan ashudduhu (I tightened the knot). Al-shadda is the single instance of it. This is also the analogy in war: yashuddu shaddan (he charges). A poet said: "What a charge we charged, not falsely, against Sakhīna — were it not for the night and the sanctuary."

1. al-shadīd and al-mutashaddid — the miser. God, glory be to Him, said: {and indeed, in his love of wealth, he is intense} [al-ʿĀdiyāt: 8]. And Ṭarafa said of the miser: "I see death picking off the noble, and choosing the prized wealth of the stingy, tight-fisted man."
2. It is related from Abū Zayd: "aṣābatnī shuddā," meaning a hardship.
3. It is said "ashadda al-qawm," when their riding beasts were shidād (strong).
4. shadd al-nahār — its climbing, mid-morning.
5. al-ashudd — twenty [years of age], and it is also said forty. Some say it has no singular; others say its singular is shadd.
شدح: The letters shīn, dāl and ḥāʾ are not a root. It is related that al-shawdaḥ is the tall one among she-camels. And it is said: rather, it is the fast one. And inshadaḥa al-rajulu means he lay down on his back. But this too is not sound; it is probably insadaḥa, which we have already mentioned.
شدخ:
The letters shīn, dāl and khāʾ are a word indicating the breaking of something hollow.

1. shadakhtu al-shayʾa shadkhan — I broke the thing, a breaking.
2. al-mushaddakh — unripe dates pressed until they crack open.
3. al-ghurra al-shādikha — the white blaze that covers the face from the base of the forelock to the nose.
شدف:
The letters shīn, dāl and fāʾ indicate height in something.

1. al-shadaf — a figure or silhouette (al-shakhṣ); and we have already said that al-shakhṣ indicates loftiness and elevation. Its plural is shudūf.
2. ashdaf and shundaf — said of a horse.

Some people say al-shadaf is like a leaning to one side, but the first meaning is the correct one, and it is sounder by analogy.

3. al-shadfāʾ — said of a bow, for its crookedness.
شدق:
The letters shīn, dāl and qāf are a root indicating a gap or widening in something.

1. al-shidq — the corner of the mouth, for a person and for others.
2. al-shadaq — the wideness of the shidq.
3. ashdaq — said of a man, and of an eloquent speaker: khaṭīb ashdaq.

The origin of this is shidq al-wādī, the width of a valley. It is said: nazalnā shidqa l-ʿIrāq, we alighted at the shidq of Iraq, meaning its region — and that too is al-shidq.
شدن:
The letters shīn, dāl and nūn are a minor root indicating soundness in a body.

1. shadana — said of a gazelle: shadana l-ẓabyu yashdunu shudūnan, when its body grew sound and well.
2. shadana — said also of a foal.
3. al-shādin — used on its own, means the young of a gazelle.
4. mushdin — said of a gazelle that has such a young one with her.

As for al-shadaniyya, it is said to be named after a place in Yemen. ʿAntara said, in a line of verse:
Will a shadaniyya bring me to her dwelling — a she-camel denied her drink, cursed, her udder bound?
شده: The letters shīn, dāl and hāʾ are a word formed by letter-substitution. One says: shudiha al-rajulu, the man was dazed, the same as dahisha.
شدو:
The letters shīn, dāl and the weak letter are a minor root indicating taking hold of the edge of some knowledge.

1. al-shadw — that a person does well in some branch of knowledge or the like. One says yashdū shayʾan min ʿilm, he has picked up something of knowledge.

Some said: everyone who knows a thing and infers from part of it to another part — that is al-shadw.
شذ:
The letters shīn and dhāl indicate solitariness and separation. Shadhdha al-shayʾu yashiddhu shudhūdhan (the thing became isolated).

1. shudhdhādh al-nās — those who are among a people but are not of their tribes or their dwellings.
2. shudhdhān al-ḥaṣā — the scattered part of it, of gravel. Imruʾ al-Qays said: "scattering the loose gravel with hooves, hard of pastern, their fetlocks unworn, not thin."
شذب:
The letters shīn, dhāl and bāʾ are a root indicating the stripping of a thing from its bark or rind, then that sense is carried further.

1. al-shadhb — trimming flesh, paring it away.
2. shadhabtahu — said of anything you strip or remove from something else.
3. al-tashdhīb — cutting away, pruning.
4. al-shawdhab — the tall one of anything, as though stripped bare in its tallness — for when a thing is stripped of its rind, its length shows more clearly.
5. farasun mushaddhabun — a horse that is tall, like a trimmed tree-trunk.
شذر:
The letters shīn, dhāl and rāʾ are two roots: one indicates the scattering of a thing and its separateness; the other indicates threat and impetuous haste.

The first is the Arabs' saying tafarraqa l-qawmu shadhara madhara, the people scattered when they dispersed through the land.

1. al-shadhra — a piece of gold.

As for the other root, it is al-tashadhdhur, which is like eagerness and haste for a matter.

1. tashadhdhara l-qawmu fī l-ḥarb — they exceeded themselves in the fighting.
2. tashadhdharat al-nāqa — the she-camel tossed her head for joy.
3. al-tashadhdhur — the threat. From it is the hadith of Sulaymān ibn Ṣurad, that word reached him from ʿAlī — peace be upon him — of the saying "he made tashadhdhur in it," that is, he threatened.

As for their saying that al-tashadhdhur is al-istithfār bi-l-thawb — gathering up one's garment and binding it around oneself — that follows the same analogy as the chapter we have mentioned, as though a man showing earnestness about his matter were described this way, so it is said: tashadhdhara.

4. tashadhdharahu — a man came to his horse fa-tashadhdharahu, meaning he mounted it from behind.
شذم:
The letters shīn, dhāl and mīm are not a root. They mentioned regarding it a word said to be formed by transposing its letters. They said: al-shaydhumān, which occurs in the saying of al-Ṭirimmāḥ, in a line of verse:
The shaydhumān tore it open, laying bare the unborn young.
It is said that it is really al-shaymudhān.
شذى:
The letters shīn, dhāl and the weak letter are a single root indicating sharpness and keenness.

1. shadhāh — sharpness, as in inna fīhi shadhāatan, meaning sharpness and boldness.
2. Al-Khalīl said: it is said of the hungry man, when his hunger grows intense, ḍarima shadhāhu — his shadhā has flared up.
3. al-shadhā — harm and evil.
4. al-shadhā — said to be the fly that bites at dogs.
5. al-shadhā — chips or splinters of fragrant wood, which he thinks were named this for the keenness of their scent.

The poet said, in a line of verse:
Whenever she walks, what is in her garments calls out — the scents of shadhā-wood, and mandalī incense carried on the air.

As for what is known among ships as al-shadhā, I do not think it is Arabic.
شر:
The letters shīn and rāʾ are a single root indicating spreading and flying apart.

1. al-sharr — the opposite of al-khayr (good). A man is shirrīr (wicked); this is the origin, on account of its spreading and abundance.
2. al-sharr — also your spreading a thing out in the sun.
3. al-sharāra, plural al-sharār, and al-sharar: what flies off from a fire, singular sharara. God, exalted and glorified, said: {it throws up sparks like castles} [al-Mursalāt: 32].
4. It is said "sharshara al-shayʾ," when he cut/tore it up.
5. al-ishrāra — that upon which a thing is spread out.
6. al-shiwāʾ al-shirshār — roasted meat whose fat drips.
7. al-sharshara — to shake a thing from your mouth after biting it.
8. sharāshir al-adhnāb — the dangling ends of tails. A verse was recited: "They howled, urging it on, and met it, striking it with the dangling tail-ends."

If someone asks: by what analogy in this chapter is al-sharāshir carried, meaning the self (al-nafs)? One says "he threw his sharāshir upon him," meaning he threw himself upon him out of eagerness and love — as in the saying: "and out of an infatuation the sharāshir are thrown upon it." The answer is that the analogy is sound, and by al-sharāshir is not meant the body, but the self. It is an expression for the ambitions and desires within the self. "He threw his sharāshir upon it" means he gathered together what had been scattered of his ambitions for this thing, and occupied all his cares with it. That, then, is the analogy.

9. It is said "asharrartu fulānan," when you attributed him to evil. Ṭarafa said: "and my drinking of wine never ceased until my friend held me to be evil, and until some of that grieved me."
10. It is said "asharrartu al-shayʾ," when you brought it out and made it manifest. A verse: "until the copies of scripture were held up by the palms." And: "if it is said, which of the people is worst in tribe — the fingers point out Kulayb by the palms." And Imruʾ al-Qays said: "I passed by guards over her, and a company eager against me, who — had they had the power — would have made my killing manifest."
شرب:
The letters shīn, rā' and bā' are a single root that can be reasoned upon and runs steady, and it is drinking, which is well known; then what is near to it is carried upon it by figure and likeness. You say sharibtu al-mā'a ashrabuhu sharban - I drank the water; and that is the verbal noun. Al-shurb is the noun. Al-sharb is the people who are drinking. Al-shirb is a share of the water. The poet said of al-sharb - the drinking company, in a line of verse:
So I said to the drinkers at Durnā, when they had grown drunk: look out for the lightning - but how shall a drunken drinker look out?

Al-sharaba is water gathered round a palm tree from which it gets its drink, and the plural is sharab. Al-mashraba is the place from which people drink; and in the hadith: "Cursed is he who walls in a drinking place." Al-mashrab is the way by which one drinks, and it may be a place and it may be a verbal noun. Al-sharīb is the one who drinks along with you. And one says ashrabtanī mā lam ashrab - you charged me with drinking what I did not drink; this is a proverb, said when someone charges another with what he did not do. And mā' sharūb and sharīb is water fit to be drunk with some unpleasantness in it. Al-ishrāb is a colour that has been made to drink in another colour; one says [in it] is shurbat ḥumra - a tinge of red. And one says ushriba fulān ḥubba fulān, when it has mingled with his heart. God - exalted be His praise - said: {And they were made to drink the calf into their hearts} [al-Baqara: 93]; the commentators said: the love of the calf. Al-Shaybānī said: al-sharb is understanding; one says shariba yashrabu sharban, when he understood. And one says: listen, then drink it in. Al-shāriba are the people who live on the bank of a river and have its water for their own. A man's shārib - his moustache - is well known, and it is made plural as shawārib. Al-shawārib are also the veins encircling the windpipe; and a donkey ṣakhib al-shawārib - loud in the throat - is from this, when he brays hard. And al-shārib is a part of the sword.

As for ishra'abba - to crane the neck - it is not far off that it should be of this same reasoning, as though the man were making himself ready to drink and stretching his neck out for it. Then it is reasoned upon further, and one says ishra'abba li-yanẓura shura'bība - he craned his neck to look. The hamza was only added to make a difference between the two meanings. And Sharabba is a place.
شرث: The letters shīn, rāʾ and thāʾ are a single root: al-sharath, which is thickness and coarseness in the fingers and the palms of the hands.
شرج:
The letters shīn, rāʾ and jīm are a sound root, following a consistent pattern, indicating mixing and interpenetration.

1. al-sharaj — the loops or ties of a water-skin, named so because they interlink with one another.
2. sharajtu al-laban — I stacked the milk-curds in layers.
3. sharrajtu al-sharāb — I mixed the drink.
4. al-sharīja — a bow whose wood shows two colours.
5. tasharraja l-laḥmu bi-l-laḥm — flesh became intermixed with flesh.

This is the origin. Their saying "the people became, in this matter, sharjayn" is thought to mean they split into two factions. This is as it is said, and it goes back to the meaning already given, because when people differ, opinion and speech become mixed and repeated argument follows, as Zuhayr said, in a line of verse: the singing-girls turned the tribe's camels back, and they loaded up; by mid-morning a matter still tangled between them.

As for sharaj al-wādī, that is its opening, its outlet, plural ashrāj.
شرح: The letters shīn, rā' and ḥā' are a small root indicating opening up and making clear. From this: sharaḥtu al-kalām wa-ghayrahu sharḥan — I explained the speech and other things, meaning you made it clear. It is derived from tashrīḥ al-laḥm, the cutting-open of meat.
شرخ:
The letters shīn, rāʾ and khāʾ are two roots: one is the first flush of a thing, occurring mostly in offspring; the other indicates an equality between two corresponding things.

The first is sharkh al-shabāb, the beginning of youth, its first flush.

1. sharkh of every year — its offspring, the young born to the livestock that year.
2. sharakha nābu l-baʿīr — said when the camel's canine tooth split through the gum and came out.

The poet said, in a line of verse: indeed the first flush of youth, and black hair — so long as they are not resisted, they are a kind of madness.

The other root:

1. al-sharkhān — the rear-piece and the mid-piece of a camel-saddle, together called by this name.
2. sharkhatā l-sahm — the two notches of the arrow's nock, the bowstring's place lying between them.
شرد: The letters shīn, rā' and dāl are a single root indicating driving off and putting at a distance, and indicating shying away and scattering into the distance. For a single case of this one may say sharada al-baʿīr shurūdan — the camel bolted. Sharradtu al-ibil tashrīdan usharridūhā — I drove the camels off, scattered them. From this is His saying, exalted be His praise: {so by them, strike fear into those who come after them} [al-Anfāl: 57] — meaning: make an example of them, and let it be heard of. And the sense is this: when a wrongdoer sins and is punished for it, others are driven off by that punishment, because each of them fears what happened to the wrongdoer, and so flees from sin and holds back. God knows best.
شرز:
The letters shīn, rāʾ and zāʾ are a root indicating the opposite of good in all its branches — ruin, contention, and the like.

1. ashrazahu Allāh — said to an enemy, meaning: may God destroy him.
2. ramāhu bi-sharzatin — he cast him into ruin.
3. al-mushārazah — like companionship mixed with contention.
4. al-mushāriz — a man of bad character, harsh in constitution.
5. ashraztu al-shayʾa — you cut a thing and did not rejoin it.
شرس:
The letters shīn, rāʾ and sīn are a root close to the one before it.

1. al-sharsu — harsh handling of a thing. One says sharastuhu sharsan, I handled it roughly.
2. al-sharīs — the difficult one, much given to opposition.
3. tashārasa l-qawmu — the people became hostile to one another.
4. al-shirs — a plant bitter to the taste.
5. al-ashras — the man bold in fighting.
6. al-shirās — a tethering rope (al-ribāq).
شرص:
The letters shīn, rāʾ and ṣād — I do not think there is anything sound in it, for I do not see its pattern holding consistently. Yet they say:

1. al-shirṣatān — the two sides of the forelock, where the hair is thin.
2. shirwāṣ — said of anything large and flabby.
3. al-shiraṣ — hard, rough ground.
شرط:
The letters shīn, rā' and ṭā' are a root indicating a mark or a sign, and whatever is close to that sense.

1. al-sharaṭ — the mark, the sign.
2. ashrāṭ al-sāʿa — the signs of the Hour. This is what the hadith means when it mentions ashrāṭ al-sāʿa.
3. al-shuraṭ, the police — named so because they set a mark for themselves by which they would be known.
4. asharaṭa fulānun nafsahu lil-halaka — so-and-so marked himself out for ruin, when he made it a sign of destruction.
5. asharaṭa min ibilihi wa ghanamihi — he set some of his camels or sheep aside for sale.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
So he staked himself in it while holding fast, and cast down his ropes and put his trust in God.

6. sharṭ al-ḥājim — the cupper's incision, well known; because that too is a mark and a trace. Ashrāṭ al-sāʿa are also said to mean its first signs.
7. al-sharīṭ — a cord used to tether young lambs, named so because when they are tied with it a mark is left on them.
8. al-sharaṭ — the small watercourse, about ten cubits wide, named so because it leaves a mark in the ground like the cupper's incision.
9. al-sharaṭān — two stars, said to be the two horns of the Ram, well-known landmarks in the sky.
10. jamalun shirwāṭ — a huge camel, named so because when he is among other camels he stands out as though he were a marker.

Ḥassān said, in a line of verse:
Among companions of bright faces, noble men, roused after the sleep of the ashrāṭ.

There is disagreement about this word. Some said he meant the two sharaṭān stars and the third star before them, and on this basis some called the three of them ashrāṭ. Al-ʿAjjāj said, in a line of verse:
From the early rising of the ashrāṭ, my own ashrāṭ.

Others said he meant by al-ashrāṭ the guards. It is also said al-ashrāṭ are the lowly people. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Scraps of the lowest of the low of Ṭayyi' — their father was named Ashraṭ, son of Ashraṭ.

11. sharaṭ al-miʿzā — the culled, worthless goats, in Jarīr's saying, a line of verse:
You see the worthless goats given as the dowries of their women; and in the worthless goats lies their whole dowry.

Some said al-shuraṭ, the police, take their name from this word because they are lowly; others said they were named so because they set a mark for themselves by which they are known. As for al-sharaṭ meaning the worthless ones, the reasoning is that they are always put forward first for misfortunes, ahead of the rest of the herd — the same sense given above for "he staked himself in it," meaning he made it a mark for ruin.
شرع:
The letters shīn, rā' and ʿayn are a single root: something that is opened up along a stretch it lies within.

1. From this: al-sharīʿa, the approach to water where drinkers come down to it.
2. From this is derived al-shirʿa in religion, and al-sharīʿa, the sacred law.

God Most High said: {To each of you We have given a law and a way} [al-Mā'ida: 48]; and He, glory be to Him, said: {Then We set you upon a clear way in the matter} [al-Jāthiya: 18].

The poet said, about the approach to water, in a line of verse:
and when she saw that the water's approach was her whole concern, and that the white of her flanks was streaked with blood.

3. Also from this root: ashraʿtu al-rumḥ naḥwahu ishrāʿan — I leveled the spear toward him. Sometimes they say sharaʿtu for this as well.
4. al-ibil al-shurūʿ — camels that have come down to water and drunk their fill.
5. One says ashraʿtu ṭarīqan — I opened a road through, when you drove it through and opened it; sharaʿtu is also said.
6. ḥītān shurraʿ — fish that lower their heads to drink [at the surface].
7. sharaʿtu al-ibil — I let the camels come down to the water's approach.

This is the origin sense; then everything that is stretched out, whether raised up or not, is referred back to it.

8. From this: al-shiraʿ, bowstrings, singular shirʿa; al-shirāʿ is the plural of the plural.

The poet said, in a line of verse:
as a singing-girl delighted in the strings.

9. From this too: shirāʿ al-safīna, the ship's sail, stretched out and raised up; the camel's neck is likened to it, so one says sharaʿa al-baʿīr ʿunuqahu, the camel stretched out its neck. He has "spread his sail," when he raises his neck.

It is said in the exegesis of His saying: {when their fish came to them on their Sabbath day, [visible] with raised heads} [al-Aʿrāf: 163], that this means their heads were lifted up. From this too is their saying rumḥ shirāʿī, a long spear, in the saying of the Hudhalī poet.

10. Of the "opening" sense we mentioned first is Ibn al-Sikkīt's report: sharaʿtu al-ihāb — I "opened" the hide, meaning you slit it between its two legs.
شرف:
The letters shīn, rāʾ and fāʾ are a root indicating loftiness and elevation.

1. al-sharaf — loftiness.
2. al-sharīf — the eminent man. A man sharīf, from a people called ashrāf — said to be a rare plural pattern, like ḥabīb/aḥbāb and yatīm/aytām.
3. mashrūf — said of one whom another has surpassed in standing.
4. istashraftu al-shayʾa — said when you raised your gaze to look at something.
5. al-ashrāf — said of the nose-tips, singular sharaf.
6. al-mashraf — the place from which you look down, rising above what is around it.
7. mashārif al-arḍ — the highlands of a land.
8. al-mashrafiyya — swords named for Mashārif al-Shām, the highlands of Syria.
9. al-shurfa — said to be the choicest part of one's property; its derivation is from al-shurfa, the battlement that crowns a palace, plural shuraf.
10. al-mustashrif — said of a horse that is great and tall.
11. Al-Khalīl said: sahmun shārifun, a thin, long arrow; and udhun sharfāʾ, an ear long in the tip.
12. mankib ashraf — a high shoulder.

As for al-nāqa al-shārif, that is the old, worn-out she-camel, and this may come from the sense of advanced age. It is also mentioned from al-Khalīl that al-sahm al-shārif belongs here too — the arrow long kept in store, whose sinew-binding and feathers have grown frayed. Aws said, in a line of verse:
He turns an arrow he had fledged with matched, well-paired feathers — yet it is lean and worn with age.

And they claim that Shurayf is the tallest mountain on earth.
شرق:
The letters shīn, rā' and qāf are a single root pointing to shining and to opening. From it: sharaqat al-shams when it rises; and ashraqat when it gives light. Al-shurūq is its rising. They say lā af'alu dhālika mā dharra shāriq — I will not do that as long as a rising one rises; by this the rising of the sun is meant. The days of al-tashrīq were named so because the flesh of the sacrifices is spread out in the sun in them. And some people say: they were named so from their saying, "Shine forth, Thabīr, that we may hurry away." Al-mashriqān are the sunrise-point of summer and of winter. Al-sharq is the east. And a group said that red meat is called sharq; if that is sound, then it is because in its redness it is as though it were shining.

Following the rule of this chapter: al-shāt al-sharqā', the ewe with a slit ear — and this is from the opening we described.

Among the words that depart from this chapter is their saying shariqa bi-al-mā' when a man chokes on it, sharaqan. 'Adī said, in a line of verse:
If my throat were choked with something other than water ... I could be like one who chokes and clears it by squeezing down water.
شرك:
The letters shīn, rā' and kāf are two roots; one of them points to being paired with and to not being alone, and the other points to stretching out and to straightness.

The first is al-shirka, partnership, which is that a thing is between two people so that neither of them has it alone. And one says: shāraktu fulānan fī al-shay', when you became his partner. And ashraktu fulānan, when you made him a partner of yours. God, exalted be His praise, said in the story of Mūsā: {wa-ashrik-hu fī amrī} [Ṭā Hā: 32]. And one says in supplication: O God, make us share in the prayer of the believers, that is, make us partners with them in it. And sharaktu al-rajula fī al-amr, ashrakuhu.

As for the other root, al-sharak is the main track of the road, and it is also its shirāk. And the thong of a sandal, shirāk al-na'l, is likened to this. And from it is the hunter's snare, sharak al-ṣā'id, so called for its stretching out.
شرم:
The letters shīn, rāʾ and mīm are a single root that never varies, indicating a tearing and rending in a thing.

1. tasharrama al-shayʾu — the thing tore apart. From this comes the hadith that he was brought a copy of the Qur'an whose edges had become torn.
2. al-sharīm — a woman whose two passages have become joined through tearing (mufḍāh).
3. al-sharm — a cut taken from the tip of the nose, or a cut taken from the base of a she-camel's tail.
4. al-shārim — the arrow that tears the side of the target.
5. sharama lahu min mālihi — he cut off for him a small portion of his wealth.
6. al-sharm — said to be a deep place in the sea.

I heard someone say that al-sharm is rather like a breach on the side of the sea, an opening into it — and this is sounder than the first saying. He said, in a line of verse:
Out of my love for Buthaynah I wished that we were together on a raft in the sharm, owning nothing.

7. ʿushbun sharmun — said of a plant whose top has been sharima, eaten away.
شرى:
The letters shīn, rāʾ and the weak letter are three roots: one indicates a reciprocal exchange between two parties in two matters, taking and giving, as an equivalence; the second is a plant; the third is agitation and rising in a thing.

The first is their saying sharaytu al-shayʾa wa-shtaraytuhu, you took a thing from its owner for its price. Sometimes they said sharaytu meaning you sold it. God Almighty said: {and they sold him for a paltry price} [Yūsuf: 20].

1. hādhā sharwā hādhā — this is the like of that; so-and-so is sharwā so-and-so, his equal. From this is the hadith of Shurayḥ, about a bow that a man broke for another, in which Shurayḥ said sharwāhā, its equal.
2. ashrāʾ al-shayʾ — its sides, singular sharan, named so because each side is like the other.
3. al-shirā — one says sharā al-shayʾa shiran.

As for the plant:

1. al-shary — said to be colocynth (al-ḥanẓal).
2. al-sharya — the palm tree that grows from a date-stone. Ruʾba said, in a line of verse: "and a shary-palm in a village."
3. al-sharā — a place thick with undergrowth and lions. He said, in a line of verse: the lions of Sharā met the lions of Khafiyya, and in their fury gave each other the blood of snakes to drink.
4. al-shiryān — a tree used for making bows.

The third root:

1. shariya l-rajulu sharan — he was swept up in anger.
2. shariya l-baʿīru fī sayrihi sharan — the camel quickened its pace.
3. shariya l-barqu — the lightning flashed again and again. The poet said, in a line of verse: O companion, do you see the lightning that never rests — it dies down for a moment, then flares up again for a moment.
4. istashrā l-rajulu — the man persisted stubbornly in a matter.
5. shariya zimāmu l-nāqati yashrā sharan — the she-camel's nose-rein grew more restless, its tugging increased.

And they say: kullu mujrin fī l-khalāʾi yashrā — every loose-running horse in open country runs wild.
شز: The letters shīn and zāy are a single, weak root. They say: al-shazāza is extreme dryness.
شزب: The letters shīn, zāʾ and bāʾ are not a root, for it belongs to the chapter of letter-substitution. It is said of a thing, when it dried out: shazaba — the zāʾ standing in for a sīn, as mentioned in its place. And sometimes they say makānun shāzibun, meaning ground that is rough and hard.
شزر:
The letters shīn, zāʾ and rāʾ are a sound root, following a consistent pattern, indicating a twist in something away from the straight way.

1. naẓara ilayhi shazran — he looked at him from the corner of his eye, out of hatred.
2. al-ṭaʿnu l-shazru — a thrust that does not follow a straight line.
3. al-ḥablu l-mashzūru — a rope twisted leftward, against the usual direction.

As for Abū ʿUbayd, he said: ṭaḥana bi-l-raḥā shazran, when he ground with the hand-mill moving his hand away from his right side; and battan, when he moved it away from his left.
شزغ: The letters shīn, zāʾ and ghayn are not a thing. They say al-shizgh is the frog. And this makes no sense.
شزن:
The letters shīn, zāʾ and nūn are a single root indicating a stretching-out in a thing.

1. shazan — said of rough, hard ground.
2. tashazzana l-shayʾu — the thing stretched out.

As for their saying nazala shazanan min al-dār, meaning to one side of the house, that is close to what has just been said. Ibn Aḥmar said, in a line of verse: so let him not shoot, grieving, from off to one side.

3. al-shazan — said to be the exhaustion that comes from walking barefoot, a thing that is indeed hard on a person.
شس: The letters shīn and sīn are close to the one before it. Al-shass is hard ground, plural shisās and shusūs.
شسب: The letters shīn, sīn and bāʾ belong with the one before it. One says shasibat al-qaws, when a bow was cut down until its shaft dried out.
شسع:
The letters shīn, sīn and ʿayn indicate two things: the first is scarcity, the other is distance.

The first is the Arabs' saying lahu shisʿun min al-māl, he has but a little of wealth. Perhaps shisʿ al-naʿl, the sandal-strap, comes from this, for its smallness. One says shassaʿtu l-naʿla, I fitted the sandal with its strap.

The other: al-shāsiʿ, the far one. One says al-dāru shasaʿat, the house grew distant.

Ibn Durayd mentioned a word which, if sound, fits the pattern. He said: it is said shasiʿa of a horse, when there was a gap between its front teeth.
شسف:
The letters shīn, sīn and fāʾ indicate parchedness and dryness.

1. shāsif — said of a thing that is parched; one says shasafa yashsifu.
2. laḥmun shasīfun — meat that has nearly dried out.
شص:
The letters shīn and ṣād are a single root, applied consistently. It indicates hardship and distress. From that is their saying: shaṣṣat maʿīshatuhum (their livelihood grew hard), and "they are in shaṣāṣāʾ," meaning in hardship. Its origin is from their saying "shaṣṣa the man," when he bit down hard on something with his molars. It is said in a blessing: "may God drive the shaṣāʾiṣ away from you," meaning hardships.

1. al-shiṣṣ — a thing fish are not caught with.
2. shiṣṣ — also said of a thief who leaves nothing he sees untaken.
3. Al-Kisāʾī said: it is said "so-and-so is on shaṣāṣāʾ," meaning in haste.

A poet said, in a line of verse: "We bred the she-camel of al-Ḥajjāj, in haste, in the breeding."
شصب:
The letters shīn, ṣād and bāʾ are a root indicating hardship in livelihood and other things. It is said: al-shaṣāʾib are hardships. It is said "a life is shāṣib," meaning hard, and it has shaṣaba shuṣūban. It is said "ashṣaba Allāhu ʿayshahu" (may God make his life hard).

From this chapter, if it is sound: shaṣabat al-nāqatu ʿalā l-faḥl, said when the stallion covered her repeatedly and she did not conceive by him.

As for what comes after this, their saying that al-shiṣb is "a share," and that al-mashṣūba is "the skinned one" — all of that is doubted, not to be relied upon.
شصر:
The letters shīn, ṣād and rāʾ are a root, if sound, indicating the joining of one thing to another.

1. al-shiṣār — a piece of wood tied through the nostrils of a she-camel. You say shaṣṣartuhā, ushaṣṣiruhā, tashṣīran.
2. Close to this: al-shaṣr — sewing, in which there is some looseness.

As for their saying "shaṣara baṣaru fulān" (so-and-so's eyesight grew fixed), that belongs to the chapter of letter-substitution, the ṣād being substituted for a ṭāʾ, and it has been mentioned in its own place.

And among what departs from this: al-shaṣar, said to be the young gazelle fawn; sometimes they call it al-shāṣir. Jarīr mentioned it.
شط:
The letters shīn and ṭāʾ are two sound roots: one is distance, the other indicates leaning.

As for distance, it is their saying: shaṭṭat al-dār, when the house grew distant, tashuṭṭu shuṭūṭan.

1. al-shaṭāṭ — distance.
2. al-shaṭāṭ — also height/tallness; this follows the same reasoning as distance, because the top of a tall thing is far from the ground.
3. It is said "so-and-so ashaṭṭa in bargaining," when he went to excess and reached al-shaṭaṭ, which is exceeding the fair measure. God, exalted be His praise, said: {and do not exceed the bounds} [Ṣād: 22].
4. It is said "the people ashaṭṭū in pursuit of so-and-so," when they went far and pressed hard.

As for leaning, it is leaning in judgment. It is permissible to bring in as evidence for this chapter God's saying: {and do not exceed the bounds} [Ṣād: 22], meaning: do not lean. One says shaṭṭa and ashaṭṭa, meaning injustice and bias in judgment.

1. In the hadith of Tamīm al-Dārī: "You are truly shāṭṭī, until I place your strength upon my weakness" — shāṭṭī meaning unjust toward me in judgment.
2. al-shaṭṭ — the side of a camel's hump; every hump has two such sides. It is called shaṭṭ because it leans to one side.

A poet said, in a line of verse: "As if beneath her bent coat of mail were a shaṭṭ, upon which you had thrown another shaṭṭ."

3. A she-camel is called shaṭawṭā, from this.
4. The bank of a river is called shaṭṭ for the same reason, because it lies on both sides.
شطأ:
The letters shīn, ṭā' and hamza contain two words. One is al-shaṭ', the shoot of a plant — what comes out around the base of the main stalk, plural ashṭā'. One says shaṭa'at al-shajara, the tree put out shoots. God, exalted be His praise, said: {like a crop that has put forth its shoot} [al-Fatḥ: 29].

The other: shāṭi' al-wādī, the bank of the valley, its side. One says shāṭa'tu l-rajul, I walked along one bank while he walked along the other. The two [words] are distinct from one another.
شطب:
The letters shīn, ṭāʾ and bāʾ are one consistent root, indicating a stretching-out in something soft, and is then said of other things.

1. al-shaṭba — a green palm-frond, plural shaṭb. In the hadith of Umm Zarʿ: "like the drawing of a shaṭba."
2. A tender young girl is called shaṭba.
3. A horse too may be called shaṭba.
4. Carried on the same idea as the palm-frond: al-shaṭba, of the shuṭb of a sword — a line/streak along its flat side, plural shuṭub. One says "a sword mushaṭṭab."
5. It is said the shuṭba, or shiṭba, is the piece cut lengthwise from a camel's hump. One says "shaṭabat al-sanām."
6. al-shawāṭib, of women: those who cut leather lengthwise into strips. A verse: "the weaving of the shawāṭib wove a mat between them." And another: "you see the shafts of the lances thrown down, as though they were the trimmed arrow-shafts in the hands of the shawāṭib." The singular is shāṭiba.
7. al-shawāṭib — also those who split palm-fronds for weaving mats.
8. A fat horse whose back-line is cut off and whose muscles stand apart is called mashṭūb al-matn wa-l-kafal, because upon its back appear streaks like tracks, each streak like a shaṭba.
9. A land is called mushaṭṭaba when the floodwater has cut a streak across it.
شطر:
The letters shīn, ṭā' and rā' are two roots: one indicates the half of a thing, and the other indicates distance and facing toward.

1. The first is their saying shaṭara al-shay' — he halved the thing; and shāṭartu fulānan al-shay' — I shared the thing with so-and-so, when you took half of it and he took the other half.
2. One says shāh shaṭūr — a ewe one of whose two teats is longer than the other.
3. From this root too: shaṭara baṣaruhu shuṭūran wa-shaṭran — his gaze "halved," said of one who looks at you and at another at once. This is counted under the root because, when he is like that, he has given each of the two a half of his look.

In the Arabs' saying "so-and-so has milked time of its halves," the meaning is that various kinds of its good and its bad have passed over him. Its origin is in the she-camel's teats: two front teats and two others, and each pair of teats is a shaṭr, because when there are four teats, two of them are the half of the four.

4. When one of a ewe's two teats has dried up she is shaṭūr; and of camels, [shaṭūr] is one two of whose teats have dried up, since she has four teats, as we have said.
5. As for the other root: al-shaṭīr, the distant one.

They say shaṭarat al-dār — the dwelling grew distant. The rajaz poet says, in a line of verse:
do not leave me among them, a stranger far off.

6. From this: shaṭara fulān ʿalā ahlihi — so-and-so turned away from his people, when he left them defiantly, in opposition.
7. al-shāṭir — one whose wickedness has worn out his family's patience. This fits the pattern, because when he does that he grows distant from their community and their main concerns.
8. From this root too is al-shaṭr said of heading toward a thing, its direction.

God Most High said, concerning the direction of prayer: {...the Sacred [Mosque], and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it} [al-Baqara: 144], meaning toward it.

The poet said, in a line of verse:
I say to Umm Zinbāʿ: keep the she-camels' chests turned toward Banū Tamīm.

Another said, in a line of verse:
and from the direction of your frontier a terror has loomed over you, whose darknesses cover you in patches.

The "direction of your frontier" cannot mean directly facing it unless it is also distant from it, separate from it. And God knows best what is right.
شطن:
The letters shīn, ṭā' and nūn are a root, running steadily and sound, pointing to farness.

One says shaṭanat al-dāru tashṭunu shuṭūnan — when the dwelling goes far off. And nawan shaṭūn, that is, a far-off place of settling. Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
A far destination carried Suʿād away from you; she departed, and the heart is left pledged to her.

And one says bi'run shaṭūn, that is, a well far down in its bottom. And al-shaṭan is the rope, and this follows the reasoning, because what lies between its two ends is far. And a bedouin described a horse and said: "It is as though he were a devil among ropes." Al-Khalīl said: al-shaṭan is the long rope. And of a horse, when it is stubborn with its owner, one says: he leaps between two ropes; and that is because he ties it fast between two ropes.

As for al-shayṭān, a people said: it is from this section, and the nūn in it belongs to the root, and it was named so for its farness from the truth and its rebellion. And that is because every insolent rebel among jinn, men and beasts is a shayṭān. Jarīr said, in a line of verse:
In the days when they called me the devil for my love-verse, and the women loved me because I was a devil.

And on that basis His word, exalted, was explained: {ṭalʿuhā ka-annahu ru'ūsu al-shayāṭīn} [al-Ṣāffāt: 65]. And it is said that he meant snakes, and that is because a snake is called a shayṭān. A poet said:
She plays with a doubled Ḥaḍramī thong, as though it were the winding of a serpent in an empty patch of castor-plants.

And it seems that among the proofs of the one who held this view — that the nūn in shayṭān belongs to the root — is the saying of Umayya:
Whatever rebel disobeyed Him, He bound him and threw him into fetters and chains.

Do you not see that he built it on the pattern fāʿil and made the nūn in it part of the root? So on this view shayṭān is of the pattern fayʿāl. And it is said that the nūn in it is added, [on the pattern] faʿlān, and that it is from shāṭa, which has been mentioned in its own section.
شظ:
The letters shīn and ẓāʾ are a root indicating a stretching-out in something.

1. al-shiẓāẓān — the two sticks placed through the loops of a large sack, to fasten it.

A poet said, in a line of verse: "Where are the two shiẓāẓ-sticks, and where is the middle strap, and where is the load of the well-laden she-camel?"

2. They say "ashaẓẓa the man," when what he had stirred began to move — he grew restless.
3. They say "ashaẓẓa the camel," when it stretched out its tail.
شظف:
The letters shīn, ẓāʾ and fāʾ are a sound root indicating hardship in life and other things. The origin of it: al-shaẓīf, of trees, is that which did not find its watering and so dried out and grew hard.

1. From this: "so-and-so is in shaẓaf of life," meaning constriction and hardship. It came in the hadith: "he never had his fill of bread and meat except amid hardship." Ibn al-Riqāʿ said: "and I have tasted a delight of living, and met from the hardship of affairs its severities."
2. In this chapter, of hardship: a camel is called shaẓafu l-khilāṭ, meaning it mixes roughly with the other camels.
3. shaẓifa al-sahm — said when the arrow lodged between the skin and the flesh.
شظم: The letters shīn, ẓāʾ and mīm are a single word. The tall horse is called shayẓam, and it is then borrowed for a man.
شظي: The letters shīn, ẓāʾ, and the weak letter are a root indicating the splitting apart of a thing from many places, until it becomes scattered splits. From that: al-shaẓiyya of a thing is a splinter. One says tashaẓẓat al-ʿaṣā, when the staff broke into fragments. Farwa bint [Abān ibn] ʿAbd al-Madān said: "O one who felt for my two little sons, who were like two pearls from which the shell split apart."
شع:
The letters shīn and ʿayn, doubled, are a single root indicating scattering and spreading.

1. al-shuʿāʿ — the shuʿāʿ (rays) of the sun, so called for its diffusion and spread. One says ashaʿʿat al-shams tushiʿʿu, when the sun casts its rays.
2. al-shaʿāʿ (with a different vowelling) — scattered blood. Qays ibn al-Khaṭīm said, in a line of verse: "I stabbed Ibn ʿAbd al-Qays with the thrust of an avenger, a stab that passed clean through — had the shuʿāʿ (spurt of blood) not lit it up."
3. shuʿāʿ al-sunbul — its awn, when it dries. Abū al-Najm said: "a shock of thin hair like the shuʿāʿ of ears of grain."
4. It is said "a soul is shaʿāʿ" when its resolves are scattered. A poet said: "I lost you, from a scattered soul — did I not forbid you this, while you were whole?"
5. al-shaʿʿ — a she-camel spraying her urine on her thigh. One says shaʿʿat tashuʿʿu shaʿʿan.
6. It is said "a shade is shaʿshaʿ" when it is not dense. The rajaz poet said, of scattering: "sincere in meeting, not scattered in betrayal." He means: he is whole of resolve, not scattered in it.
7. From this chapter: al-shaʿshāʿ and al-shaʿshaʿān, of people and riding beasts — the tall one. One says a camel is shaʿshāʿ and a she-camel shaʿshāʿa or shaʿshaʿāna. Dhū al-Rumma said: "Far be it, Kharqāʾ, unless the Lord of the Throne brings her near — and the tall, big ones."
8. From this chapter: shaʿshaʿtu al-sharāb — I diluted the drink; that is because the mixture spreads and diffuses through it. A poet said: "A well-diluted drink, as if saffron were in it, when the water mingled with it, growing warm within it."
شعب:
The letters shīn, ʿayn and bā' are two differing roots, one indicating separation and the other togetherness. The people of language then disagreed about this: some said it belongs among the words that carry two opposite meanings, and al-Khalīl stated this plainly. Others said it is not among such words, but is simply different dialect usage. Al-Khalīl said: among the wonders of speech and the breadth of Arabic is that al-shaʿb can mean a scattering and can mean a gathering. Ibn Durayd said: al-shaʿb is separation, and al-shaʿb is gathering, and this is not a case of opposite meanings — it is merely a usage of some people.

What belongs to the sense of separation:
1. A crack in a thing is called shaʿb.
2. al-shaʿb — what branched out from the tribes of the Arabs and non-Arabs, plural shuʿūb. He, exalted be His praise, said: {and We made you into peoples and tribes} [al-Ḥujurāt: 13]. One says al-shaʿb is the great clan. They said mashʿab al-ḥaqq — the path of truth. Al-Kumayt said, in a line of verse:
"I have no loyalty but to the family of Aḥmad, and I have no path but the path of truth as my path."
3. inshaʿabat bihimu l-ṭuruq — the roads branched off from them; inshaʿabat aghṣānu l-shajara — the tree's branches split off.
4. shuʿab al-faras — the horse's rising parts, such as the neck and withers, whatever stands high on it. He said, in a line of verse:
"A fine, high-nosed stallion, its high parts towering."
5. ẓabyun ashʿab — a gazelle whose two horns spread far apart from each other. Abū Du'ād said, in a line of verse:
And the short ribs of a tight-sinewed, loud-crying one, of the branch-horned kind.
6. al-shiʿb — what opens between two mountains, a mountain pass.
7. Shaʿūb — [a name for] death, because it separates people, divides them. One says shaʿibathumu l-maniyya fa-nshaʿabū, death divided them and they scattered.
8. al-shaʿīb — a worn-out waterskin, named so because it lets its water go, does not hold it but lets it run out. He said, in a line of verse:
"What is wrong with my eye, like the leaking, worn-out waterskin?"
Ibn Durayd said: "Shaʿbān was named for their scattering [tashaʿʿub] during it" — that is, their dispersing in search of water.
And in the hadith: "What is this ruling that has divided the people?" — meaning it split them apart.

As for the other root, of gathering: their saying shaʿaba l-ṣadʿ, he mended the crack; and shaʿaba l-ʿuss [a large bowl] and the like of it, when he mended it. The awl used for mending is called al-mishʿab. It may also be that al-shaʿb, in the sense of the tribes, was named for gathering and unity rather than separation. They say: "the shaʿb of such-and-such a clan has scattered," and this shows it means a unity [that then broke apart]. Al-Ṭirimmāḥ said, in a line of verse:
"The unity of the clan scattered, after having been joined."

And from this root, though not derived from it, is Shaʿabʿab, a place. He said, in a line of verse:
"Shall I ever rest my cheek on my hand, at Shaʿabʿab, between the trough and the watering-yard?"
And Shuʿabā — also a place.
شعث: The letters shīn, ʿayn and thā' are a root indicating dishevelment spreading through a thing. They say: lamma Allāhu shaʿathakum, and jamaʿa shaʿathakum — meaning what has become scattered of your affairs. Al-shaʿath is the raggedness at the tip of a tooth-stick (siwāk) or of a tent-peg. They call the tent-peg ashʿath for that reason.
شعذ: The letters shīn, ʿayn and dhāl are not a root. Al-Khalīl said: al-shaʿwadha [sleight of hand] is not from the speech of the desert Arabs; it is nimbleness of the hands, and a charm like sorcery.
شعر:
The letters shīn, ʿayn and rā' are two well-known roots: one points to something fixed and firm, and the other to knowing and to a mark by which a thing is known.

The first is al-shaʿr - hair - which is well known; the plural is ashʿār, and that is a plural of a plural, and the single one is shaʿra. And rajul ashʿar is a man long in the hair of head and body. Al-shaʿār is trees; one says arḍ kathīrat al-shaʿār - land with many trees. What goes round the hoof at the end of the skin, where the hair grows about the hoof, is called ashʿar, and the plural is al-ashāʿir. Al-shaʿrā' among fruits is a kind of peach, so called for something upon it like down. The proof of that is that there is a kind with no down upon it which they call al-qarʿā', the bald one. And al-shaʿrā' is a fly as though it had down upon its forelegs.

Of this chapter is dāhiya shaʿrā' - a hairy calamity, and dāhiya wabrā' - a furry one. Ibn Durayd said: of their speech, when a man has said something thought monstrous: "You have brought it hairy and covered in fur." And rawḍa shaʿrā' - a meadow thick with growth. And ramla shaʿrā' - sand that grows the naṣī grass and its like. Al-shaʿrā' is thick-standing trees.

Among what comes near this is al-shaʿīr - barley - which is well known. As for al-shaʿīra, the iron pin made to hold the blade of a knife when it is set in, it is likened to a grain of barley. Al-shaʿārīr are small cucumbers. Al-shiʿār is the clothing next to the body, because it touches the hair that is on the skin.

The other chapter: al-shiʿār is the watchword the people call out to one another in war so that they may know one another. The origin is their saying shaʿurtu bi-al-shay', when you knew it and were alert to it. And layta shiʿrī - would that I knew. A group said: its origin is from al-shaʿra, like al-durba - practised skill - and al-fiṭna - quickness of mind; one says shaʿara shaʿratan. They said: and the poet is called shāʿir because he is alert to what others are not alert to. They said: and the proof of that is the saying of ʿAntara, in a line of verse:
Have the poets left anything to be patched up, or did you know the dwelling place after doubting?
He means: the poets left nothing without being alert to it. Al-mashāʿir of the pilgrimage are the places of its rites, so called because they are the marks of the ḥajj. Al-shaʿīra is the single one of al-shaʿā'ir, which are the marks of the pilgrimage and its acts. God - great is His majesty - said: {Indeed al-Ṣafā and al-Marwa are among the shaʿā'ir of God} [al-Baqara: 158]. And it is said that al-shuʿayra also is the sacrificial camel that is offered. And its ishʿār is said to be that the base of its hump is cut so that the blood runs and it is known to be an offering. And for this reason they say of a caliph if he is killed: he has been "marked" - a word kept for him alone among all the slain. Al-shiʿrā is a star, and it is famous. And one says ashʿara fulān fulānan sharran, when he covered him over with evil.

And ashʿarahu al-ḥubb maraḍan - love clothed him in sickness: this may fittingly belong to this chapter, if that is set upon him like a mark, and it may fittingly belong to the first, as though it were made an inner garment for him.

As for their saying tafarraqa al-qawm shaʿārīra - the people scattered in all directions - it is with us of the chapter of letter-substitution, and the origin is shaʿālīl, and it has already passed.
شعف:
The letters shīn, ʿayn and fāʾ indicate the upper parts of a thing and its top.

1. al-shaʿafa — the top of a mountain, plural shaʿafāt and shaʿaf. "So-and-so was struck upon the shaʿafāt of his head," meaning the top of his head.
2. shaʿafat al-qalb — its tip, at the place where the aorta attaches. For that reason one says "shaʿafahu l-ḥubb" (love struck the tip of his heart), as though it covered his heart from above. Some read it: "qad shaʿafahā ḥubban," and that is from this. It came in the hadith: "the best of people is a man on a shaʿafa with a small flock of livestock," meaning the top of a mountain.
شعل:
The letters shīn, ʿayn and lām are a sound root pointing to a spreading out and scattering on all sides of one single thing.

1. "ashʿaltu al-nāra fī al-ḥaṭab" — I kindled the fire in the firewood; "ishtaʿalat al-nāru" — the fire blazed up.
2. Gray hair "blazed forth" and spread. God, blessed and exalted, said: {and my head has flared up with grayness} [Maryam: 4].
3. al-shaʿīla — the flame kindled in the wick.
4. "We ashʿalnā the horses in the raid" — we scattered them out.
5. al-shuʿla, of fire, is well known.
6. al-shaʿal — whiteness scattered in the forelock and tail of a horse; a horse is ashʿal, the female shaʿlā'.
7. "The people scattered shaʿālīl", meaning into separate groups, as though they had blazed apart.
8. Shaʿl — a nickname, said also to be a woman's name.

Irregular against this root: al-mishʿal, a thing made of hides with four feet to stand on, in which drink is fermented.

Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
They deliberately let the appointed times of prayer slip, and bound themselves instead to the wineskins and the jars.
شعن: The letters shīn, ʿayn and nūn are one word. They say: huwa mushʿānn al-ra's — he is mushʿānn of head, when his hair stands up unkempt.
شعي:
The letters shīn, ʿayn and the weak letter are a root indicating the like of what the one before it indicated.

1. It is said "ashʿā l-qawmu l-ghāra ishʿāʾan," when they set the raid ablaze/kindled it.
2. ghāra shaʿwāʾ — a raid that spreads widely. Ibn Qays al-Ruqayyāt said: "how is my sleep upon the bed, while not yet has a spreading raid encompassed Syria?"
شغ:
The letters shīn and ghayn are a root indicating scantiness. The people of language said: al-shaghshagha in drinking is al-taṣrīd, which is reducing the amount. Ruʾba said, in a line of verse: "If I could manage you, my drinking would not be curtailed — and the one kept busy is not like the one left free."

This is the origin. And in the chapter is a word whose path is the path of imitation of a sound, which is sometimes carried on the analogy and sometimes not.

1. They say al-shaghshagha is the sound of a spear-thrust, in the saying of the Hudhalī poet: "the thrust is a shaghshagha and the striking a hayqaʿa — like the striker's blow beneath the steady rain, upon the upper arm."
2. al-shaghshagha — also a kind of roaring/bellowing of camels.
شغب: The letters shīn, ghayn and bā' are a sound root indicating the stirring up of trouble, never found in anything good. Al-Khalīl said: al-shaghb is the stirring up of trouble. It is said of a she-donkey, when she is in heat and resists the stallion-ass: 'she has shaghb and rancor (ḍighn).' Abū ʿUbayd said: one says shaghabtu ʿalā l-qawm, and shaghabtuhum, and shaghabtu bihim — I stirred trouble against the people.
شغر:
The letters shīn, ghayn and rā' are one root indicating spreading out and lack of restraint, and then whatever is close to it is attached to it. The Arabs say: ishtagharat al-ibil, when the camels became so numerous that they could hardly be kept in order. And they say: tafarraqū shaghar baghar, when they scattered in every direction. Abū Zayd used to say that this is said only of a group coming together first.

And from this chapter:
1. shaghara l-kalb — the dog raised one of its legs to urinate.
2. hādhihi balda shāghira bi-rijlihā — this is a town that offers no defence with its leg, said when it keeps no one from raiding it.

Al-shighār, which occurs in the hadith as forbidden — that a man should say to another: 'marry me to your sister, on condition that I marry you to my sister, with no dowry between them but that' — belongs to this chapter, because it is a matter fixed by no dowry or valid condition. It is from shaghara l-kalb, when it goes off to one side of the road, far from it.

1. ishtaghara ʿalā fulānin ḥisābuhu — his accounts became confused on him, so that he could not find his way through them.
2. ishtaghara fulānun fī l-falāti — he wandered on and on in the open desert and went far off.
3. Al-Shaybānī reported: shaghartu banī fulānin min mawḍiʿi kadhā — meaning I drove them out.

He said, in a line of verse:
'And we drove out both sons of Nizār, and a dog too, with a blow, terrifying, close together.'

God knows best.
شغف: The letters shīn, ghayn and fā are a single word: al-shaghāf, the membrane covering the heart. God Most High said: {he has pierced her heart with love} [Yūsuf: 30], meaning, he brought love through to the very covering of her heart.
شغل:
The letters shīn, ghayn and lām are a single root indicating the opposite of being free. You say shaghaltu fulānan fa-anā shāghiluhu, wa huwa mashghūl — I occupied so-and-so, I am his occupier, and he is occupied. shughiltu ʿanka bi-kadhā, in the form where the doer is left unnamed. They said one does not say ushghiltu. One says shughlun shāghil. The plural of al-shughl is ashghāl. It has also come from them: ushtughila fulānun bi-l-shay', and he is mushtaghil. He cited, in a line of verse:
"She greeted you, then said: our whole company today, O ʿUrwa, is occupied."
Some related ashghalanī, with the added alif.
شغم:
The letters shīn, ghayn and mīm are a sound root with few branches, indicating beauty.
1. al-shughmūm — the handsome one.
2. al-shughmūm — a beautiful woman.
3. al-shughmūm, of camels — the one good in appearance, complete and full-grown.
شغن: The letters shīn, ghayn and nūn are not a root, and what Ibn Durayd mentioned — that al-shaghna is a bundle (al-kāra) — has no basis and no meaning.
شغو:
The letters shīn, ghayn and the weak letter are a sound root indicating a defect in the natural form of some body part.

They said: al-shughūw, from your saying 'a man ashghā and a woman shaghwā'' — that being when his upper teeth project ahead of the lower. Al-Khalīl said: al-shaghā is irregularity of the teeth, and from it the eagle is called shaghwā', because its upper beak exceeds the lower. Some people claimed that al-shaghā is an excess in the number of the teeth.
شف:
The letters shīn and fāʾ are a single root indicating thinness and scantiness; nothing in the whole chapter departs from this.

1. al-shiff — a thin veil. They say it is so called because what is behind it can be seen through it (yustashaffu). The origin is that the veil itself is thin (yashuffu) because of its thinness, being what it is. And if what the people said is correct, that too follows the same reasoning, because what is seen through it is faint and scattered to the eye's sight.
2. al-shiff — also excess/surplus. One says "so-and-so has a shiff over so-and-so," meaning a surplus. And it is said "you gave one of your children a shiff over another," meaning you favored him. This word is used because that excess is not usually large — if one is given a hundred and another two hundred, one does not say ashfafta but rather afḍalta or aḍʿafta or ḍaʿʿafta, and the like.

And the saying of one who said al-shiff is also deficiency is plausible too, as if it diminishes a thing until it reduces it to shufāfa (a residue).

3. al-shufūf — the wasting of the body. One says "sickness shaffahu, yashuffuhu, shaffan" — it wasted him.
4. al-shafīf — is only the coldness of a breeze with a little moisture; so called for that slight moisture, however little. It is also called al-shaffān. A poet said: "A shaffān with its shafīf drove her to shelter."
5. al-istishfāf, in drinking — to drain what is in the vessel, leaving nothing in it, as if that remainder were shufāfa. When a person drinks it, one says ishtaffahā and tashāffahā. In the hadith of Umm Zarʿ: "if he ate, he ate it all up; if he drank, he drained it (ishtaffa)." And anything that consumes something fully has "ishtaffahu." A poet said: "He has a neck that turns with whatever is bound to it, and two flanks that drain (yashtaffāni) every rope-load." Al-ẓiʿān is the rope; he means: his two sides are broad, so between them they take up the whole rope.
6. As for the saying of al-Farazdaq: "and they undo what the intensely jealous, wasted man supposed" — it is said: the man of intense jealousy. This is correct, except that he is the one whom jealousy has wasted (shaffathu), so that his body grew thin.
شفر:
The letters shīn, fā' and rā' are one root indicating the edge and border of a thing.
1. shafrat al-sayf — the edge of the sword.
2. shafīr al-bi'r and shafīr al-nahr — the rim of a well and the bank of a river, both meaning 'the edge.'
3. al-shufr — the place on the eye where the eyelashes grow, plural ashfār.
4. shufr al-farj — the edges of its rim.
5. mishfar al-baʿīr — like the jaḥfala [lip] of a horse, but of a camel.
6. al-shafra — the well-known [blade].
All of this is one and the same pattern.

As for their saying 'mā bi-l-dāri shufr' [there is nothing in the house with a shufr], and the view of one who said it means 'there is no one in it' — the matter is not so. What is meant by al-shufr is the shufr of the eye, and the meaning is 'there is no one in it with an eyelid,' just as one says 'mā bihā ʿaynun taṭrifu' [there is not in it an eye that blinks], meaning there is no one with an eye in it. And what has been reported from Abū Zayd, that shafrat al-qawm is their youngest, like the servant — this is a comparison, likened to the blade (shafra) that is put to use.
شفع:
The letters shīn, fā' and ʿayn are a sound root indicating the pairing of two things. From this is al-shafʿ, the even, which is the opposite of al-watr, the odd. You say: it was single, and I made it a pair. God, exalted be His praise, said: {And by the even and the odd} [al-Fajr: 3]. The people of commentary said: the odd is God, exalted, and the even is creation. Al-shufʿa, the right of pre-emption in a house, is from this. Ibn Durayd said: it was called shufʿa because by it a man pairs his property. A shāfiʿ ewe is one that has her young with her. And shafaʿa so-and-so for so-and-so when he came as a second to him, seeking his request and helping him.

And from this chapter: a nāqa shafūʿ, a she-camel that fills two milking vessels at one milking. And it is related: so-and-so shafaʿa [against me] with enmity, that is, he helps others against me. This follows the analogy of the chapter, as though he makes the one who is at enmity with him a pair. And of what strays from this chapter, whose soundness we do not know: imra'a mashfūʿa, a woman who has been struck by a shufʿa, which is the evil eye. This has indeed been said, and perhaps it is with an undotted sīn. God knows best.

The Banū Shāfiʿ are of the Banū al-Muṭṭalib b. ʿAbd Manāf; among them is Muḥammad b. Idrīs al-Shāfiʿī. God knows best.
شفق:
The letters shīn, fā' and qāf are a single root pointing to thinness in a thing, and then things are derived from it. Of that is their saying *ashfaqtu min al-amr* — when you grew tender over the matter and were wary of it. And they sometimes said *shafiqtu*. Most of the men of the language said: one only says *ashfaqtu* and *anā mushfiq*, I am anxious. As for the words of the poet:
as the household grudged over the food
the meaning is: she was miserly with it.

Of this chapter is *al-shafaq* among garments. Al-Khalīl said: *al-shafaq* is what is poor among things.

From it comes *al-shafaq*, the glow seen in the sky at the setting of the sun, which is the redness. It was so named for its colour and its thinness.

And ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm al-Qaṭṭān related to us, from al-Maʿdānī, from his father, from Abū Muʿādh, from al-Layth, from al-Khalīl, who said: *al-shafaq* is the redness between the setting of the sun and the time of the last evening prayer.

And Ibn Najīḥ related from Mujāhid, who said: it is the daytime, in His words, whose praise is exalted: {so I swear by the shafaq} [al-Inshiqāq: 16]. And al-ʿAwwām ibn Ḥawshab related from Mujāhid, who said: it is the redness.

And in the commentary of Muqātil he said: *al-shafaq* is the redness. Al-Zajjāj said: *al-shafaq* is the redness that is seen in the west after the sun has gone down.

And ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm told us, from Muḥammad ibn Faraj, who said: Salama related to us, from al-Farrā', who said: *al-shafaq* is the redness.

He said: and Ibn [Abī] Yaḥyā related to me, from Ḥusayn ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ḍumayra, from his father, from his grandfather, tracing it up to the Prophet, who said: "*Al-shafaq* is the redness."

Al-Farrā' said: I have heard some of the Arabs say, "On him is a dyed garment as though it were the *shafaq*" — and it was red. He said: this is a proof for whoever said that it is the redness.
شفن:
The letters shīn, fā' and nūn are a root indicating continuous watching. Its basis is their saying, of the jealous man who never tires of watching: shafūn. Some people say shafana yashfinu, when he looks from the corner of his eye, and also shafina yushfanu shafnan; he is shafūn and shāfin. Al-Khalīl recited, in a line of verse:
'Wary of a watcher who never stops gazing.'
Al-Umawī said: al-shafin is the shrewd, intelligent one. All of this is close, one sense to another.
شفي:
The letters shīn, fā' and the weak letter indicate being on the brink of a thing, overlooking it. Ashfā 'alā al-shay'i, he came to the very brink of the thing, overlooking it. Al-shifā' (healing) is named for its overcoming the illness and bringing it to that brink. Istashfā fulānun, so-and-so sought healing. Shafā kulli shay'in is its edge. This may belong to this chapter, or it may belong to letter-substitution, with the fā' standing in for a yā'.

One says: I gave you the thing so that you might seek relief by it (tastashfī bihi); then it is said ashfaytuka al-shay'a, which is the correct form. Ashfā al-marīḍu 'alā al-mawti, the sick man came to the brink of death; mā baqiya minhu illā shafan, only a little of him remained. As for al-'Ajjāj's line —
I paid it in full before the brink, or right at the brink —
they said he means when the sun was on the brink of setting.

As for al-shafa, the lip, it has been said the missing letter is a wāw, and one says thalāth shafawāt, three lips. A man called ashfā is one whose two lips do not close together, like al-arwaq. Others said the lip has had its final hā' dropped, and its diminutive is shufayha. Al-mushāfaha, speaking face to face, mouth to mouth. A man called shufāhiyy is big-lipped. Both explanations are possible, but the first is better, being closer to the analogy already given, since the two lips overlook the mouth.

What falls outside this chapter is their saying shafahanī fulānun 'an kadhā, so-and-so distracted me from such a thing.
شق:
The letters shīn and qāf are one sound root indicating a splitting in a thing; it is then extended and derived from by way of metaphor. You say shaqaqtu al-shayʾa ashuqquhu shaqqan, when you split it. There are shuqūq (cracks) in a hand, and shiqāq in a riding beast; the origin is the same. Al-shiqqa is a splinter split off from a plank or a piece of wood.

1. al-shiqāq — disagreement/discord; that is when a group splits and separates apart. One says "they shaqqū the staff of the Muslims," and "the staff of the people split (inshaqqat) after being joined," when their affair became divided.
2. al-shiqq — half of a thing.
3. "So-and-so was struck by shiqq and mashaqqa" — a difficult matter, as if from its severity it splits (yashuqqu) a person. God, exalted be His praise, said: {and carry your burdens to a land you could not have reached except with great hardship to yourselves} [al-Naḥl: 7].
4. al-shiqq — also a side of a mountain. In the hadith: "he found me among a small flock of livestock, in a shiqq (region)."
5. al-shiqq — also al-shaqīq, a full brother. One says "this is my brother, my shaqīq, the shiqq of myself." The meaning is that he is likened to a piece of wood split into two halves.
6. Of an angry man they say: "iḥtadda fa-ṭārat minhu shiqqa," as if he split apart from the intensity of his anger. All these are figures of speech.
7. al-shuqqa — a long journey to a distant land. You say "this is a shuqqa shāqqa." God, glory be to Him, said: {but the distance was too far for them} [al-Tawba: 42].
8. al-shuqqa — also, a well-known term for a bolt of cloth.
9. ishtaqqa in speech — to go off to the right and left in a dispute, without keeping to the point, as if he were now on this side, now on that.
10. A horse is ashaqq when it leans to one side as it runs. The reasoning is the same throughout all of this.

al-shaqīqa — a gap between sand-dunes where plants grow. Abū Khayra said: al-shaqīqa is a soft patch amid rough ground, as long as the sand-ridge is long. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: it is rough ground between two ridges of sand. Abū Hishām al-Aʿrābī said: it is what lies between two amīl (sand-ridges); al-amīl and al-ḥabl are the same. Labīd said: "Khansāʾ lost her young one, and its wandering and bleating did not leave the open ground of the shaqāʾiq." Al-Aṣmaʿī also said: rough tracts between every two sand-ridges. In al-Naḍr's account: al-shaqīqa is the land between two mountains, along their line, following whatever course the land follows, hard ground where water collects, its extent a bowshot or two. We say: were it not for the lexicographers' lengthy treatment of these shaqāʾiq, and our following their path in this, it would have been more fitting to occupy ourselves with something more useful — for what use is there in knowing what a thing is, when the use lies only in knowing where people differ about it? Much of what we have mentioned in this book runs the same course, especially with words of more than three letters — but it is the lexicographers' own way and method.

1. al-shiqshiqa — the organ in a camel's mouth, an appendage that looks as though split. For this an eloquent orator is called "a shiqshiqa," likened to a stallion. Al-Aʿshā said: "So be content, for I am sharp, knowing — sharper than the shiqshiqa of the bellowing stallion." In the hadith: "many sermons are the shaqāshiq of Satan."

And among what departs from this chapter: al-shaqīq — they say it is the stallion camel once he has grown strong and vigorous. A poet said: "Your father is a shaqīq, possessed of horns, well-trained."
شقب: The letters shīn, qāf and bā' are a word indicating tallness. From it: al-rajul al-shawqab, a tall man. They also say al-shiqb is like a cave in a mountain.
شقح: The letters shīn, qāf and ḥā' are a minor root indicating an unpleasant color. One says: shaqqaḥa l-nakhl [the palm trees turned that color], that being at their ripening, and it was forbidden to sell them before they shaqqaḥa. Al-shaqīḥ follows al-qabīḥ, as an echo-word intensifying it; one says qabīḥun shaqīḥun, thoroughly ugly.
شقذ:
The letters shīn, qāf and dhāl are a minor root indicating little sleep. They say that al-shaqidh is the eye [the sleepless, watchful eye] — that which scarcely sleeps. They said it is that which afflicts people with the evil eye.

As for their saying ashqadhtu fulānan, when you drove him away, citing as evidence the saying of the poet:
'When they grew angry with me and drove me off ... I became as though I were a startled young wild ass' —
this too, although its meaning is sound, means: they eyed me with hostility, the way an enemy looks at one he does not love.

1. al-shaqdhā' — the eagle intensely hungry, so named because being so makes its gaze sharper. The poets have said much on this that is well known.
2. Some of them reported: fulān yushāqidhu fulānan — meaning he is hostile to him.

As for their saying mā bihi shaqadhun wa-lā naqadhun, its meaning to them is: nothing ails him — he is free to move. This is far from the pattern we have described. If it is sound, then it belongs to the anomalous.
شقر:
The letters shīn, qāf and rā' are a root indicating a color. Al-shuqra, among the colors found in people, is a redness overlying whiteness. Al-shuqra in horses is a pure redness together with which the mane, forelock and mane-crest also redden. It is possible that al-shaqir — the poppy anemones — is derived from this too. Ṭarafa said, in a line of verse:
'And blood like the shaqir covered the horses.'

Three words stand apart from this root:
1. akhbartu fulānan bi-shuqūrī — I told so-and-so my shuqūrī, meaning my state and my affair. Ru'ba said:
'My neighbor-woman, do not think my excuse strange — my journeying, and my care for my camel, and the much talk of my shuqūr.'
2. jā'a bi-l-shuqar wa-l-buqar — said when someone comes with lies.
3. al-mishqar — sand that slopes down into the ground, plural mashāqir.
شقص:
The letters shīn, qāf and ṣād are not a root from which branches are derived or upon which analogy is made. There are words in it:
1. al-shiqṣ — a portion of a thing.
2. al-mishqaṣ — an arrow with a broad head.
3. al-shaqīṣ, if sound, describing a horse — the excellent, fast one.
شقع: The letters shīn, qāf and ʿayn are a single word. One says: shaqaʿa l-rajulu fī l-ināʾ, when he drank straight from the vessel. It is like karaʿa.
شقل: The letters shīn, qāf and lām are not a root. Something has been reported about it that is not worth pursuing.
شقن: The letters shīn, qāf and nūn. They say that al-shiqn is smallness in a gift; you say shaqantu l-ʿaṭiyya, when you make it small.
شقو:
The letters shīn, qāf and the weak letter are a root pointing to hardship and to the opposite of ease and good fortune.

Al-shiqwa is the opposite of good fortune. A man is shaqiyy, clearly marked by al-shaqā', al-shiqwa and al-shaqāwa — wretchedness. And it is said that al-mushāqāt is toiling at a thing and working away at it. The origin of that is that a man takes on hardship and is made wretched by it.

When the word is given a hamza the meaning changes. You say shaqa'a nāb al-ba'īr yashqa'u, when the camel's eye-tooth first shows. He said: al-shāqi' is the eye-tooth that has not yet grown bent.
شك:
The letters shīn and kāf are a single root, derived one part from another, indicating interpenetration. From that is their saying shakaktuhu bi-l-rumḥ, when you pierce someone with the spear so that the spearhead penetrates his body. A poet said: "I pierced with the numbing spear his garments — the noble man is not spared by spears." This comes from the joining of two things when they are locked together (shukkā).

1. al-shakk — the opposite of certainty; so called because the one in doubt (al-shākk) seems as if the two possibilities were locked together for him (shukka lahu) in a single locking, and he is certain of neither of them — that is the derivation of al-shakk. You say shakaktu bayna waraqatayn, when you fix a stick through two leaves, joining them together.
2. al-shikka — the equipment of arms a man wears; one says "he is shākk fī l-silāḥ" (fully armed). Weapons are called shikka because a man is fastened with it, or because part of it is locked into another.

As for the saying of Dhū al-Rumma: "the leap of the branded one, from the wild asses of Maʿqula, as though he were a plain limp or a bruise" — al-shakk here is said to be a slight limp; one says a camel is shākk, and it has shakka shakkan. This is a sound analogy, because that is a pain that penetrates it. Or it is said: rather, al-shakk is the sticking of the upper arm to the side; if this is correct it is even clearer on the analogy.

3. al-shakāʾik — factions of people, singular shakīka; so called because when they split apart, each faction's members interpenetrate one another.
شكد: The letters shīn, kāf and dāl are a root. They say that al-shukd is thanks. I heard ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm al-Qaṭṭān say: I heard ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz say: I heard Abū ʿUbayd say: I heard al-Umawī say: al-shukd is giving, and al-shukm is recompense, and the verbal noun is al-shakd. Al-Kisā'ī said: al-shukm is compensation. And al-Aṣmaʿī says al-shukm and al-shukd are both giving.
شكر:
The letters shīn, kāf and rā' are four separate roots, far apart in their reasoning.

The first is al-shukr, thanks: praise of a person for a kindness he does you. And it is said that the reality of shukr is contentment with little. They say: a faras shakūr is a horse for whose fattening little fodder is enough. And they recite al-A'shā's words, in a line of verse:
And there must be a raid in the hot season, a fearful one that wearies even the hard-hoofed, easily-kept horse.
And it is said in the proverb: 'More thankful than a barwaqa plant', because it turns green from cloud without rain.

The second root is fullness and abundance in a thing. One says ḥalūba shakira, of a milch beast that has got a good share of pasture and so given much milk. And one says ashkara al-qawm, and truly they are milking a shakira, and the milch beast has shakirat. And of this chapter: shakirat al-shajara, when the tree's shade grows thick.

The third root is al-shakīr among plants, which is what grows from the trunk of the tree, tender shoots. And that is also in plants at the first of their growing. He said, in a line of verse:
The chick has blackened, like the curling fresh shoots.

The fourth root is al-shakr, which is sexual intercourse. And it is said, rather, that a woman's shakr is her private part. And Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar said to a man whose wife had brought suit against him: 'If she asks you the price of her shakr and of your shabr, you set about denying her her due and doling her out a mere trickle.'
شكع:
The letters shīn, kāf and ʿayn are a root indicating anger, irritation, and the like. One says shakiʿa l-rajul, when his groaning increased; likewise the angry man, when his anger intensifies: yashkaʿu shakaʿan.

They have also reported two other words whose soundness I do not know:
1. shakaʿa ra'sa baʿīrihi bi-zimāmihi — he raised its head with its halter-rope.
2. shakiʿa l-zarʿ — its grain grew abundant.
شكل:
The letters shīn, kāf and lām mostly indicate resemblance. You say hādhā shiklu hādhā, this is the like of that. From it one says amrun mushkil, as one says amrun mushtabih — this matter resembled/was confused with that one, this entered into the likeness [shikl] of that. It is then extended: shakaltu l-dābbata bi-shikālihi, I hobbled the animal with its hobble, because the hobble joins one of its legs to a matching restraint. Likewise a riding animal has shikāl when one foreleg and one hindleg are white-marked — by the same reasoning, because the white marking took one leg and its match.

1. From this root: al-shukla — a redness mixed into whiteness. ʿaynun shaklā' — an eye with a slight redness in its white.
Ibn Durayd said: blood is called ashkal for the mixed redness and whiteness in it. This is correct, and belongs to the sense of ishkāl [ambiguity] we mentioned — a mingling — since blood is a redness mingled with whiteness.
Al-Kisā'ī said: ashkala l-nakhl, when a palm's ripe dates became good and ready — this too belongs to the root, because the dates come to resemble [shākala] dried dates in their sweetness, moistness and redness.

As for their saying shakaltu l-kitāba ashkuluhu shaklan, when you mark a text with the signs of vowelling, I do not take this to be the speech of the true Arabs — it is something the grammarians introduced, a later-coined term. It may be that they modeled it on what we mentioned, because such marking, even though not a straight line, resembles it.
