Among what departs from this root: shākil al-dābba and shākilatuhu, what rises above the ṭifṭifa [flank] of an animal. Quṭrub said: al-shākil is what lies between the cheek-strap and the ear, of the white part.
Also departing from it: al-shaklā' — need, want; likewise al-ashkala. Banū Shakal — a clan among the Arabs.

And, unrelated to this root though sharing its letters: al-ashkal, the mountain lote-tree. The poet said, in a line of verse:
"Bent, as the measuring-rods of the ashkal-tree bend."
شكم:
The letters shīn, kāf and mīm are two sound roots: one indicates giving, the other indicates intensity and strength in a thing.

The first: al-shakm — that is giving and reward. One says shakamanī shakman, and the noun is al-shukm. It occurs in the hadith that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant him peace, had himself cupped and then said: 'ashkumūhu' — meaning: give him his wage. A poet said:
'Or is there a great man who has wept and not finished his weeping, following the loved ones on the day of parting, rewarded?'
Another said:
'Convey to Qatāda, who asks no one, from him the gift and the ready reward.'

The other root: al-shakīma — that is strength of spirit.
1. shakīmat al-lijām — the bit-piece of the bridle, the iron crosspiece carrying the mouthpiece bar; plural shakā'im.
2. Some people reported: shakamahu, meaning he bit him.
3. al-shakīm — the bite, in Jarīr's saying: 'Its bite struck Ibn Ḥamrā' al-ʿIjān.'
4. shakīm al-qidr — its handles.
شكه: The letters shīn, kāf and hā' are one root indicating resemblance and approximation. One says: shākaha l-shay'u l-shay'a, mushākahatan wa-shikāhan, when it resembled and came close to it. In the proverb: 'shākih, Abā Yasār' — meaning: come close. It is reported from Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlā': ashkaha l-amr, when the matter became doubtful.
شكو:
The letters shīn, kāf, and the weak letter [wāw or yā'] are a single root indicating pained complaint about something.

1. al-shakw — the verbal noun. "shakawtuhu [shakwan, and] shakāh, and shikāyah" — I complained of him.
2. "I complained of so-and-so and ashkānī" — he made amends to me over my complaint. "He ashkānī" also means: he did something to you that makes you need to complain of him.
3. al-shakāh and al-shikāyah mean the same thing.
4. al-shakī — one who complains of a pain.
5. al-shakī is also al-mashkū [the one complained about]: "shakawtuhu," so he is called shakī and mashkū.
شل:
The letters shīn and lām are a single root indicating a moving apart, which then applies to distance, and to the weaving and sewing of cloth, and to what is near that.

1. al-shall — driving away. One says "shallahum shallan," when he drove them off.
2. It is said "the people became shilāl," meaning scattered. A poet said: "By Him whom Quraysh made pilgrimage to as a tribe — scattered, and each has a patron, whether living or dead."
3. al-shalal — that which has been shulla, i.e., driven off. From it: "they do not intend to press hard on the shalal."
4. One says "I shallaltu the garment, ashulluhu," when you sewed it with a light, loose, spaced stitch.

1. al-shalal — the ruin/paralysis of the hand. One says "lā tushlil wa-lā taklil" (may your hand not be paralyzed nor grow dull), and "a man is ashall," and "he has shalla, yashallu."
2. al-shalal — also a stain on a garment that leaves a mark in it.
3. al-shalshala — the trickling of water intermittently.
4. al-shulla — a place of parting, from this chapter, where a group departs. Abū Dhuʾayb said: "and I said: avoid the wrath of a cousin, and the seeking-out of a shulla — that is al-ṭarūḥ, the far-flinging."

As for al-shalīl: some said it is al-ḥils (a saddle-cloth), one not tightly woven. As for the junan (shields), in them is the shalīl; some said it is a garment worn beneath the coat of mail, not weak; others said it is the short coat of mail, plural ashilla. Aws said: "and they came with her, grey, having ashilla, with a side on which death gleams." Whichever of these it is, it is only a likeness and a metaphor.
شلح: The letters shīn, lām and ḥā' are not a root. They say that al-shalḥā' is the sword.
شلو:
The letters shīn, lām and the weak letter are one root indicating a limb among the limbs, and sometimes the body itself is meant by it. The people of language say: al-shilw is the limb. In the hadith from ʿAlī, peace be upon him: 'Bring me its right limb.' It is said that Banū so-and-so are ashlā' among Banū so-and-so, meaning remnants among them. Ibn Durayd used to say: 'al-shilw is a person's shilw, and it is his body after it has decayed.' But what we have mentioned from ʿAlī's hadith, 'bring me its right shilw,' points against this view.

As for ishlā' al-kalb [calling a dog]: they say its ishlā' is calling it. Their evidence is the saying of the poet:
'I called my she-goat and wiped my bowl.'
This is a sound analogy — as though, when you called it, you called it up the way a shilw is drawn up out of the cooking pot, that is, lifted out. Some people say ashlaytuhu bi-l-ṣayd: I set him on to the game, and they cite as evidence the saying of Ziyād al-Aʿjam:
'We came to Abū ʿAmr, and he set his dogs on us, until we very nearly were eaten between his two tents.'
ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm al-Qaṭṭān told us, from Thaʿlab, from Ibn al-Aʿrābī, who said: one says ashlaytuhu, when you incited him.
شم:
The letters shīn and mīm are a single root indicating nearness and closeness. You say shamamtu al-shayʾa, fa-anā ashummuhu (I smelled the thing). Al-mushāmma is the mufāʿala-form from shāmamtuhu, when you drew close and near to him. And ashmamtu fulānan al-ṭīb (I let so-and-so catch the scent of perfume). Al-Khalīl said: you say to a governor "ashmimnī yadaka" (let me touch your hand), which is better than saying "nāwilnī yadaka" (hand me your hand).

As for al-shamam, it is a rise in the nose, and the description from it is al-ashamm; on the surface this seems far from the root we have based it on, but in meaning it is close, because when the bridge of the nose is raised it is nearer to what it wishes to smell. Do you not see that they say [their noses] reach the water before their lips? And since this is so, from it also comes what is related from Abū ʿAmr: "ashamma fulān," when he passed by holding his head up. And "I offered him such-and-such, and he was mushimm" (turning away). And "while they were on a road, ashammū," meaning they turned aside — because when a man distances himself from one thing he draws near another. And when he turns away from a thing (ashamma) he draws near to another; so the reasoning in it is not far-fetched.
شمت:
The letters shīn, mīm and tā are a sound root, and some of what it contains — where there is difficulty and obscurity — falls outside it.

The root sense is an enemy's joy at a misfortune that befalls the one he opposes.

1. shamita bihi yashmatu shamātatan — he gloated over him; "God, mighty and glorious, ashmatahu", made him an object of gloating, through his enemy. In the Book of God Most High: {so let not the enemies gloat over me} [al-Aʿrāf: 150].
2. "So-and-so spent bi-laylat al-shawāmit", a night of misfortune, over which those who gloat would gloat.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
He was startled by the voice of a huntsman, and so spent the night at the mercy of those who would gloat over him, from fear and from cold.

3. "The people came back shamātā or shimātan from where they had set out for", when they returned disappointed, having failed.

Sāʿida said so in his poetry.

What I said contains obscurity and uncertainty is their saying about tashmīt of the one who sneezes — that is, to say when he sneezes: "God have mercy on you." In the hadith: two men sneezed in the presence of the Messenger of God (peace and blessings upon him and his family); he said the prayer to one of them and not to the other. When he was asked about this, he said: "This one praised God, mighty and glorious, and the other did not praise God, mighty and glorious." Al-Khalīl said: tashmīt of the one who sneezes is a prayer for him, and anyone who prays good for another is mushammit for him.

This is the most that has reached us concerning this word, and in my view it belongs to the kind of thing whose knowledge has become hidden; perhaps it was known long ago and then was lost with the passing of those who knew it.

Another word: their naming the legs of an animal "shawāmit". Al-Khalīl said: it is simply a name for them. Abū ʿAmr said: one says "may God not leave him a shāmita", meaning a leg to stand on. This too is among the difficult cases, because there is no clear derivation requiring that the leg of a creature with legs be called shāmita. And God knows best.
شمج: The letters shīn, mīm and jīm are a root indicating mixing and a thing's lack of proper cohesion. One says shamajahu yashmujuhu shamjan, when he mixed it. Mā dhāqa shamājan means: he tasted nothing of food. They say: shamajū, when they baked coarse bread. This is used metaphorically, so that loose, widely-spaced stitching is called shamj; one says shamaja l-thawb shamjan yashmuju, he stitched the garment loosely. The pattern in all of this is one.
شمخ:
The letters shīn, mīm and khā are a sound root pointing to loftiness and rising high.

1. A mountain is shāmikh, meaning high.
2. "So-and-so shamakha with his nose" — said when he holds himself proudly.
3. Shamkh — a man's name.
شمر:
The letters shīn, mīm and rā' are two contrary roots: one indicates drawing up and rising, the other indicates trailing and letting go.

The first: their saying shammara li-l-amri adhyālahu, he tucked up his skirts for the matter.
1. rajul shammarī — a man light in his affair and earnest, who has girded himself for it.
2. shāh shāmir — a ewe whose udder has drawn up close to her belly.
3. nāqa shimmīr — a she-camel girded and swift, in Ḥumayd's poetry.

The other root: one says shamara yashmuru, when he walked with a swaggering gait, and marra yashmuru, he passed by swaggering. From it one says: shammara l-rajulu l-sahm, when he released the arrow.
شمس:
The letters shīn, mīm and sīn are a root pointing to changing and to little settling. Al-shams, the sun, is well known, and it was named so because it does not stay still; it is forever moving. And it is read: and the sun runs, having no fixed place. And one says shamasa yawmunā, and ushmisa, when the sun of the day grows fierce. And al-shamūs of beasts is the one that will hardly stand still. One says shamasa shimāsan. And a woman is shamūs when she shies away from anything suspect and it does not settle with her; the plural is shumus. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Shy ones, refusing on every free woman's night, who disappoint the guess of the foul and jealous man.

And a man is shamūs when he does not hold to one temper, and he is somewhat inclined to difficulty. And one says shamisa lī fulān, when he shows you his enmity. And this is carried upon what we mentioned of the changing of tempers. So this is the reasoning of this name. As for what the Arabs have named with it, Ibn Durayd said: the Arabs have named ʿAbd Shams. He said: and Ibn al-Kalbī said: Shams was an ancient idol. And no one but he mentioned it. He said: and some people said: Shams is a well-known spring of water. And the Arabs have named ʿAbshams, and they are the Banū Tamīm, and to them the name ʿAbshamī is traced.
شمص: The letters shīn, mīm and ṣād are a single word. One says shamaṣtu l-farasa, when you startled the horse to make it move. And one says shammaṣa ibilahu, when he drove his camels harshly.
شمط:
As for the letters shīn, mīm and ṭā', they are a sound pattern indicating mixture. From this is al-shamaṭ, which is the mixing of grey hair with the blackness of youth. Every two mixed things that you blend together are said to be shamaṭtahumā, and they are shamīṭ. It is said the morning was named shamīṭ because of its mixing with the remaining darkness of the night. They reported that Abū ʿAmr said: one says ashmaṭū a discourse at times, and a poem at others.

And from this chapter:
1. al-shamāṭīṭ — scattered groups; one says: the horses came shamāṭīṭ.
2. They say: this pot holds a sheep with its shamṭ or shimṭ — meaning with what is mixed in with it of its spices.
شمع:
The letters shīn, mīm and ʿayn are one root, a consistent pattern for joking, pleasant talk, humor, and what is close to that. Its basis is their saying jāriya shamūʿ, when she is pleasant in speech, good-natured, and much given to joking. In the hadith: 'Whoever pursues levity, God will make him an object of levity.' Some scholars said: al-mashmaʿa is joking and laughter, and the meaning is said of one whose habit and character this is — not that joking and laughter as such are disliked, when they are not in falsehood or mockery. Al-Hudhalī said, describing his guest:
'I will begin with them in jest, and bring, by my effort, of food or a spread.'
He means that he begins with his guests, when they alight, with joking and making them laugh, so as to put them at ease.

And from this chapter:
1. ashmaʿa l-sirāj — the lamp blazed, when its light shone out. A poet said: 'Like the flash of lightning, or a lamp ablaze.'

As for al-shamʿ [wax] — said with the mīm quiescent or vowelled — it is well known, and it is anomalous, departing from the root I have mentioned.
شمق: The letters shīn, mīm and qāf — they say it is a sound root, and under it they mention al-shamaq, which is either liveliness, or being infatuated with a thing.
شمل:
The letters shīn, mīm and lām are two roots that hold good and run true, each of them in its own meaning and its own class.

The first points to a thing going round another and taking it in from its sides. Of that is their saying shamilahum al-amr (also shamalahum), when a matter takes them all in. And this is amr shāmil, a matter that covers everyone. From it is al-shamla, which is a cloak worn wrapped round the waist and drawn about the body. And jama'a Allāh shamlahu, when one prays for a man that his affairs be gathered together; and when they are gathered, each of them takes in the other.

Of this root: shamiltu al-shāt, when you make her a shimāl, which is a bag like a purse that her udder is put into and which closes round it. And likewise shamaltu al-nakhla, when the palm tree was shedding its fruit and its clusters were bound with pieces of cloak.

Of this root: al-mishmal is a small sword that a man wraps his garment about.

The second root points to the side opposite the right. Of that is al-yad al-shimāl, the left hand; and from it the north wind, al-rīḥ al-shimāl, because it comes from the left of the direction of prayer when a man leans toward it from the side of the prayer-direction of Iraq. About al-shamūl, which is wine, there are two views: one of them is that it has a gust like the gust of the north wind; the second view is that it takes hold of the mind. The plural of shimāl is ashmul.

Abū al-Najm said, in a line of verse:
He comes at them from right sides and from left sides.

And it is said a pool is mashmūl when the north wind strikes it until it is cold. For that reason wine is called mashmūla, that is, that it is cold to the taste.

As for the words of Dhū al-Rumma, in a line of verse:
And in the shamā'il, a hunter of Jillān, shabby of clothes, his person hidden, crouched in his hide —
it is said that he meant the hunters' hides, of which the single one is shimāla. If he meant this, it is as though he likened the hide to the shimāla that is made for the udder — and we have already mentioned it. And it is said that he meant the side of the north.

Of what strays from these two roots: al-shamala is what is left on the palm tree of its ripe dates. One says: nothing is left on it but shamālīl. And it is said that al-shamālīl are the branches that spread out. Al-shamlala is speed, and from it the she-camel called shimlāl and shimlīl.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
A lean she-camel whose brother is her father, of crossed stock, and whose paternal uncle is her maternal uncle — long-necked and swift.
شن:
The letters shīn and nūn are a single root indicating wearing out and dryness.

1. al-shann — a dry, worn-out old skin (a waterskin), plural shinān. In the hadith concerning the Qur'an: "lā yatfahu wa-lā yatashānnu," meaning it does not grow trivial nor wear out.
2. al-shanīn — the trickling of water from the shanna (old waterskin). A poet said: "O one who has tears of constant trickling."
3. al-shinshina — a man's inborn nature. In their proverbs: "a shinshina I know from Akhzam," derived from what we mentioned — meaning it is his nature that was born with him and has grown old, as if it were a shanna.

Al-shanūn is disputed: some said it is the emaciated one, citing al-Ṭirimmāḥ's description of the hungry wolf: "like the emaciated wolf." Others said it is the fat one. And it is said it is the one who is neither fat nor thin. When sayings differ, one looks to whichever is closest to the analogy of the chapter and takes that. Al-Khalīl said: al-shanūn is the one who has lost some of his fatness, likened to the shann. He said: it is said of a man when he has grown thin: "qad istashanna."

4. As for ishnān al-ghāra (launching a raid), it is derived from al-shanīn, the trickling of water from the shanna — as if they scattered upon their target, coming at them from every direction.
5. One says "shanantu al-māʾ," when you poured it out scattered. It is the opposite of "sanantu" (poured it in a steady stream).
شنأ:
The letters shīn, nūn and hamza are a root indicating hatred and avoidance of a thing.

1. al-shanū'a — fastidious aversion [to what is impure]; from this comes the name "Azd Shanū'a" [a tribal name].
2. "so-and-so shani'a so-and-so" — he hated him. The verbal noun is al-shana'ān, sometimes lightened to al-shanān.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Life is only what you enjoy and desire — even if the resentful one blames it and finds fault.

3. al-shan' — also means al-shana'ān.
4. rajul mishnā' — a man hated by people.

As for their saying "shani'tu for the matter" and "with it," meaning you assented to it, and their citing the verse:
Had this matter happened in the Age of Ignorance, you would have consented to it, or its drinker would have choked on the water —

[Translator's note: the Arabic text breaks off here with a row of dots in the original, marking a gap or damage; nothing more of this entry was given to me.]
شنب:
The letters shīn, nūn and bā' are a single root pointing to coldness in a thing. They say: shanaba our day, so it is shanib and shānib, when it turned cold.

From this: al-thaghr al-ashnab, the front teeth, meaning cool and pleasant. A poet said, in a line of verse:
O, by my father, you, and your mouth so cool and fresh.
شنث: The letters shīn, nūn and thā' are not a root, though there is one word in it. They say: the lips of the camel shanithat, when they grew coarse and thick from eating thorns.
شنج: The letters shīn, nūn and jīm are a single word, and it is al-shanaj, which is a contracting, a drawing-in, in skin and other things.
شنح: The letters shīn, nūn and ḥā' are a single word, and it is al-shanāḥiyy, which is the tall one. One says: he is shanāḥ, as you see.
شنص:
The letters shīn, nūn and ṣād are a word, if it is sound. They say: a horse is shanāṣiyy, meaning tall. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And a shanāṣiyy horse, when startled, bolted upright.
And it is said: it is really nāshiṣiyy [with the letters reversed]. And it is reported: shaniṣa bihi, meaning attached to it, like sadika.
شنع:
The letters shīn, nūn and ʿayn are a single root pointing to raising talk of a person by means of something bad — defamation.

1. al-shanāʿah — infamy, disgrace.
2. shanuʿa — a thing shanuʿa, became disgraceful; so it is shanīʿ, disgraceful.
3. shanaʿtuhu — I overpowered him with something he dislikes.
4. shanaʿa fulānun fulānan — some people mentioned this phrase, meaning he reviled him.

They cited a line of verse for Kuthayyir:
And Asmā' is not held in disgrace through any weariness of her, in our company... [the line breaks off in the text as printed]

5. tashannaʿat al-ibil — carrying this further, they say the camels tashannaʿat in their gait, when they went hard and fast.

That only happens at the swiftest pace, so the underlying sense returns to the idea of elevation we already gave, even where there is no ugliness in it.
شنف: The letters shīn, nūn and fā' are two separate words. One of them is al-shanf, an ornament worn in the ear. The other word is al-shanaf: hatred. One says: shanifa lahu yashnafu shanafan, he hated him.
شنق:
The letters shīn, nūn and qāf are a sound, well-founded root, pointing to a stretching out while attached to something.

1. al-shināq — the cord with which the mouth of a waterskin is tied shut.
2. shanaqa (of a man, with his she-camel's halter) — he did to her what a horseman does to his horse, curbing it by its bridle.
3. al-shanaq — length of the head, as though it stretches continually upward.
4. mashnūq (of a horse) — tall.
5. al-shanaq (the heart's longing) — also a sound analogy from this chapter: al-shanaq is the heart's longing toward a thing, and that never happens except through an attachment already formed, so the analogy already given may well hold.

As for al-ashnāq, the singular of which is shanaq, it is what falls short of the full blood-price: when the one bearing the payment brings a full blood-price, and along with it there are payments for wounds not amounting to the full sum, those additional payments are the ashnāq — as though hanging on to the greater blood-price. This is what the poet meant by his saying:
A chief to whom the ashnāq of blood-prices are attached, when the heavy loads are bound fast and laid upon him.

And al-shanaq, in the hadith, is what falls short of the two obligatory levels [of zakat], in camels, sheep and cattle. It is his saying, God bless him and his family and grant him peace: "No shināq" — meaning no obligatory payment is taken on the shanaq amount until it reaches the full measure.

1. al-laḥm al-mushannaq — meat that is sliced and cut lengthwise. Al-Umawī said: dough that is cut up and worked with oil is also called mushannaq; that word is never used unless the thing has length to it.
شهب:
The letters shīn, hā' and bā' are a single root, indicating whiteness mixed into something black; shuhba is never pure white.

1. al-shuhba, in a horse — a white mixed with black.
2. katība shahbā' — an army unit "grey," when its upper part shows the white gleam of iron [armor].
3. A day of cold and biting chill is called ashhab; and the night likewise, al-layla al-shahbā'.
4. ishhābba al-zarʿ — the crop dried out but still had some green left amid it.
5. Also from this root: al-shihāb, a blazing flame of fire.
6. "So-and-so is a shihāb of war" — said when he is known and renowned in it, like the fame of gleaming stars.
7. It is said that al-naṣl al-ashhab is an arrowhead lightly filed until its blackness has gone.
8. It is said that al-shihāb is also milk diluted thin with water, so named because its water content has increased until it becomes like a white mixed with another color.
شهد:
The letters shīn, hā' and dāl are a root pointing to presence, knowledge and making known; nothing of its branches goes outside what we have mentioned. Of that is al-shahāda, testimony, which gathers the roots we have mentioned - presence, knowledge and making known. One says shahida, yashhadu, shahādatan. And al-mashhad is the gathering place of people.

Of this section: al-shuhūd, the plural of al-shāhid, and it is the water that comes out on the head of a child when it is born; and it is said, rather it is the membrane. The poet said, in a line of verse:
She came with one like fine Sābirī cloth - they marvelled at him, and the earth was not yet dry of her birth-fluids.

And some people said: the shuhūd of a she-camel are the traces of the place where she gave birth, of blood or afterbirth. Al-shahīd is the one slain in the way of God; some people said he was called that because the angels of mercy attend him, that is, are present with him.

And others said he was called that because he falls to the ground, and the earth is called al-shāhida. And al-shāhid is the tongue, and al-shāhid is the angel. Al-A'shā gathered them both in one line of verse:
Do not think me ungrateful for a favour of yours; by my own tongue - O witness of God, bear witness!

So his shāhid is the tongue, and the shāhid of God, exalted be His praise, is the angel. As for His words, mighty and exalted: {shahida Allāhu annahu lā ilāha illā huwa} [Āl 'Imrān: 18], the people of learning said: its meaning is, God, mighty and exalted, made it known, God made it clear - as one says, so-and-so bore witness before the judge, when he made clear and made known whose the right is and against whom it is.

And a woman is mushhid when her husband is present, as one whose husband is absent is called mughīb. As for their saying ashhada al-rajul, when he emitted the thin fluid, it is as though it were carried onto what we mentioned of the water that comes out on the head of a newborn.

Among what strays from this root: al-shuhd, honey in its wax; and it is pluralised as al-shihād. A poet said, in a line of verse:
To broad bowls of shīzā wood, filled with the finest of the wheat, kneaded up with honeycomb.
شهر:
The letters shīn, hā' and rā' are a sound root pointing to clearness in a matter and to giving light.

From this is al-shahr, which in the speech of the Arabs is the crescent moon. Then every thirty days was called by the name of the crescent, so it was called a shahr, a month. The Arabs and the non-Arabs agree in this, for the non-Arabs call thirty days by the name of the crescent in their own language.

The proof of this is the saying of Dhū al-Rumma, in a line of verse:
He woke clear of eye, nothing adding to his sight; he sees the new moon before the people do, thin as it is.

Al-shuhra is the plainness of a matter. Shahara sayfahu means he drew his sword out. And so-and-so has been shuhira among the people for such a thing, that is, he has become well known for it, so he is mashhūr, famous, and they have made him famous. One says ashharnā bi'l-makān when we stayed a month in a place. And Shahrān is a tribe.
شهق: The letters shīn, hā' and qāf are a single root indicating height. From that: jabalun shāhiq — a lofty mountain. Then from that is derived al-shahīq, the opposite of al-zafīr, because al-shahīq is the drawing of the breath back in, and al-zafīr is letting the breath out. The origin is what we have said. Some said: fulānun dhū shāhiq, when his anger grew intense — and perhaps that came with a [loud] sound too.
شهل:
The letters shīn, hā' and lām are a root to do with certain colours: it is al-shuhlah in the eye, which is when a blueness tinges its blackness.

As for what does not belong to this chapter: a woman is called shahlah — they said she is a woman past her first youth, of sound judgement, and that this name is hers alone, never used to describe a man. So say the language scholars. As for the Arabs, they did in fact name a man Shahl — he is al-Find al-Zimmānī; it is said his name was Shahl ibn Shaybān.

Also strange to this chapter: al-mushāhalah, meaning contention, quarrelling — and I think the shīn here stands in place of a jīm. Likewise their word for need, shahlā', which belongs to the same kind of letter-substitution, the true root letter being kāf: al-shaklā'.
شهم:
The letters shīn, hā' and mīm are a root pointing to sharpness of mind.

1. shahm (of a man) — sharp-witted, shrewd.
2. mashhūm — what they sometimes call a person who has been startled; a sound analogy, because when a person is startled, the sharpness of his mind shows itself.
3. al-shahām — they say this is the siʿlāh [a female demon of legend]; if that is correct, it too comes from the idea of sharpness.
4. al-shayham — the hedgehog; it is not unlikely that this too belongs to the analogy of this chapter.

And of it al-Aʿshā said:
If the causes of enmity between us grow serious, you will surely go from me riding on the back of a shayham.
God knows best.
شهو: The letters shīn, hā' and the weak letter are a single word, and it is al-shahwa, appetite or desire. One says a man is shahwān — full of desire — and a thing is shahiyy — desirable.
شوب:
The letters shīn, wāw and bā' are a single root, and it is mixing.

1. One says shubtu al-shay'a ashūbuhu shawban — I mixed the thing.
2. Honey was named shawb, because among them it was used to mix into other drinks. This is what the people of language said.
3. al-shiyāb — the name for whatever is mixed into a thing.

They say: mā ʿindahu shawbun wa lā rawbun — he has neither shawb nor rawb. Al-shawb is honey, and al-rawb is curdled milk.
شوذ:
The letters shīn, wāw and dhāl contain nothing but al-mishwadh, the turban. Al-Walīd ibn ʿUqbah said:
When I bind my head with a turban... then away with you from me in your folly, Taghlib, daughter of Wā'il.
شور:
The letters shīn, wāw and rā' are two consistent roots: the first is displaying and showing and exposing a thing; the other is taking a thing.

The first: their saying shurtu al-dābbata shawran, meaning I paraded the riding animal for display. The place where riding animals are displayed is al-mishwār. They say: "Beware of speeches, for they are a mishwār full of stumbling." Some philologists said, of their saying shawwara bihi, meaning he shamed him: it is really from al-shuwār, and al-shuwār is a man's private parts. From this: their saying "God laid bare his shuwār." As though shawwara bihi meant he exposed his private parts until he was shamed. He said al-shawār also means the household goods. If that is correct, it is because such things are guarded closely, as a man guards what belongs to him.

The other root: their saying shurtu al-'asala ashūruhu, meaning I drew out the honey. Some allowed asharta al-'asala, citing the line:
And a hearing the old man permits himself ... and talk like strained honey.
(Al-Aṣma'ī said it is rather "strained-honey talk," as a possessive phrase.) He said al-mashār is the hive from which honey is drawn.

Some philologists said this chapter also gives shāwartu fulānan fī amrī, I consulted so-and-so in my affair. He said it is derived from the drawing of honey, as though the one seeking counsel takes the opinion from someone else the way honey is drawn out.

They said what is also derived from this is their calling a camel mustashīr, meaning the camel that can tell a pregnant female from one that is not. And he recited a line of verse:
It startled away from her every mustashīr, and every wanton young bull-camel eager to mount [mi'shīr — sense uncertain].
And it is said mi'shīr instead means the fat one.
شوس: The letters shīn, wāw and sīn are a single root pointing to a look given in anger. From this: al-shawas, looking from the corner of one eye out of anger. A man is ashwas, of a people who are shūs. It is also said he is the one who narrows his eyes and closes his eyelids.
شوص:
The letters shīn, wāw and ṣād are a root pointing to shaking a thing and rubbing it.

1. al-shawṣ — brushing the teeth with the tooth-stick. And in the hadith: "He used to shawṣ his mouth with the tooth-stick." Imru' al-Qays said:
With [hair] black, thickly plaited, hanging down, and with filed teeth she brushes and polishes.
2. al-shawṣ (the rubbing itself) — rubbing; the word is also used of cloth.
3. shāṣṣa — one says shāṣṣa the thing, when he shook it.
4. al-shawṣah — an illness said to knot itself up in the ribs.
شوط:
The letters shīn, wāw and ṭā' are a root pointing to going ahead without settling and without a rightful claim.

1. shawṭ — one says jarā shawṭan, he ran a shawṭ, meaning a single stretch of a race.
2. shawṭ bāṭil — what they call the light that comes into houses through a small window: a "vain streak".

Some jurists disliked it being said, "he circled the House a number of ashwāṭ," and would say instead: shawṭ is an idle word, while circling the House belongs among the everlasting good deeds.
شوظ: The letters shīn, wāw and ẓā' are one sound word. Al-shuwāẓ is the blaze of flame from fire, without smoke accompanying it. God, exalted, said: {a flame of fire} [al-Raḥmān: 35].
شوع:
The letters shīn, wāw and ʿayn are a root pointing to spreading out and scattering.

1. al-shawaʿ — the spreading and scattering of hair.
2. al-shūʿ — a kind of tree, perhaps so named because its growth is scattered.
شوف:
The letters shīn, wāw and fā' are a single root, and it points to appearing and standing out. From this, the saying of the Arabs:

1. tashawwafat (of mountain goats) — they tashawwafat when they climbed up into the strongholds of the mountains.
2. tashawwafa (of a man) — carried on from that and derived from it: so-and-so tashawwafa for a thing, when he reached ambitiously for it.
3. shawf — polishing a thing bright. One says: shuftuhu ashūfuhu shawfan, I polished it.
4. mashūf — the polished thing; the polished, burnished dinar takes its name from this. Of it ʿAntarah said:
The blazing midday heat lay still upon the polished, marked one.
It was called shawf because through it the thing's surface and colour are made to stand out.
5. tashawwafat (of a woman) — she tashawwafat, when she adorned and decorated herself.
6. al-jamal al-mashūf — a camel in rut, excited. As the poet said: like the mashūf [camel] which you smeared with tar. Some said that in this line the word is really al-masūf, with a sīn: the stud camel that the she-camels sūf, meaning sniff at.
7. ishtāfa — one says ishtāfa fulānun, when he stretched himself up and looked out.
8. ashāfa — he ashāfa on a thing, when he came right up to it and looked out over it.
9. al-shayyifah — the lookout, the scout, named from this.
شوق:
The letters shīn, wāw and qāf point to one thing's being attached to another.

1. al-shiyāq — one says shuqtu al-ṭunub, meaning the tent-peg; the cord used for that is named al-shiyāq.
2. al-shawq — like nawṭ, a hanging-attachment; from this shawq was derived, meaning the self's longing toward a thing. One says shāqanī yashūqunī, it stirred longing in me, and that only ever happens through an attachment already formed by love.
شوك:
The letters shīn, wāw and kāf are a single root indicating roughness and a sharp point in a thing.

1. al-shawk — thorns, well known. One says shajaratun shawikatun, shā'ikatun, or mushīkatun for a thorny tree.
2. shākanī al-shawk — the thorn pricked me.
3. ashaktu fulānan — I hurt so-and-so with a thorn.
4. shawwaka al-farkh — said of a young bird when its feathers began to sprout, like thorns.
5. al-shawka — derived from this, meaning strength and fierceness in battle.
6. jā'a bi-l-shawki wa-l-shajar — he came with thorn and tree, meaning in great numbers.
7. burdatun shawkā' — a cloak rough to the touch because it is new; it is also said to mean rough in its weave.
8. shawwaka thadyu al-mar'a — a woman's breast rose and its tip grew pointed.
9. shawwaka al-baʿīr — a camel's canine teeth grew long.
شول:
The letters shīn, wāw and lām are a single root pointing to rising up.

1. shāla al-mīzān — the balance shāla, when one of its two pans rose.
2. ashaltu al-shay' — I raised the thing.
3. al-shawl (of she-camels) — those whose milk yield has risen, meaning gone down toward its end; singular shā'ilah.
4. al-shuwwal — she-camels that raise their tails at the time of mating; singular shā'il. Some claimed that the month Shawwāl was so named because it coincided with the time the she-camels do this.
5. al-shawlah — a star, the tail-star of the Scorpion; the scorpion itself is called shawwālah.
6. tashāwala (of people in a fight) — the people tashāwalū with their weapons in battle, meaning each raised his weapon toward his opponent.
7. shawl (of water) — a small amount of water, so called because once it is reduced it rises and disappears quickly. As the poet said: and its drawers poured out its last remaining shawl.
8. shawil (of a servant) — one quick and light in service, for the speed with which he rises to whatever task he takes up.
شوه:
The letters shīn, wāw and hā' are two roots: one points to ugliness of form, the other to a certain kind of look with the eye.

The first: al-shawah, ugliness of form. One says: shāhat al-wujūh, meaning the faces became ugly. And shawwahahu Allāh, so he is mushawwah, disfigured. And in the hadith, the Prophet, God bless him and his family and grant him peace, threw dust at the polytheists and said: "May the faces be ugly." As for a mare called shawhā', that is one whose head is long.

The second root: they say a man is shā'ih al-baṣar, or shāhī al-baṣar, meaning sharp-sighted — as though by letter-reversal. And al-ashwah is the one who strikes people with the evil eye. They say: lā tashawwah ʿalayya, do not shawwah upon me, said when someone remarks how handsome one is — meaning: do not strike me with your eye.

Strange to this chapter is al-shāh, the ewe. They said its word is in fact built on this root; one says tashawwahtu shāh, meaning I took a ewe.
شوي:
The letters shīn, wāw and yā' indicate the easy, trifling matter. From that: al-shawā, the worthless part of one's livestock/wealth. He said, in a line of verse:
"We ate the poor cuts until, when no poor cut was left, we pointed with our fingers to its best parts."

1. al-shawā — also the plural of shawāh, the skin of the head.
2. al-shawā — the extremities/limbs, everything that is not a vital, fatal spot. Any easy matter is shawā. In the manner of matched reduplication they say ʿayiyyun shawiyy [utterly hapless]. Ibn Durayd said this is from al-shawā, the worthless part.
3. One says ramaytu l-ṣayda fa-ashwaytuhu, when you struck the game in a non-vital spot without killing it.
4. al-shawāyā — the survivors of a people who perished, singular shawiyya, named so for their fewness and lowliness. They said al-shawwāya is a small piece cut from something larger, like a scrap cut from a sheep. One says mā baqiya mina l-māl illā shuwāyatun, only a trifling amount of the wealth remained.

What we do not doubt is that al-shiwā' [roast meat] is derived from this, because when it is roasted it is as though it has been reduced/degraded. If someone asks: then meat that is cut up small and skewered ought also to be called shiwā', since it too has been reduced — the answer is: we explain what the Arabs say only so as to trace it to one consistent, agreed origin; beyond that there is nothing more for us to do.

You say shawaytu l-laḥma shayyan, and ishtawaytuhu, so I am mushtawin. The poet said, in a line of verse:
"So he roasted meat on a windy night, and rendered fat."
One says inshawā l-laḥm, the meat became roasted. He said, in a line of verse:
"Our shredded roast is done — come near to the meal, and eat."
Al-Khalīl said: al-ishwā' is the leaving-over of something, or close to that meaning, so much so that some say fulānun taʿashshā fa-ashwā min ʿashā'ihi, he had supper and left some of it over. He said, in a line of verse:
"There is speech that has nothing left over to it, once its slip has escaped from the tip of the tongue."
Meaning it cannot be taken back or made good again. The sense returns to what we established at the start.
شيأ:
The letters shīn, yā' and hamza are a single word. One says shayya'a Allāhu wajhahu — may God make his face ugly — when one calls down ugliness upon him. And a face is mushayya', made ugly. And he recited:
The sons of Fazāra ibn Dhubyān — their she-camel has given birth in the night to a human being,
misshapen and ugly. How wondrous is the making of the Merciful!
شيب:
The letters shīn, yā' and bā'. This root is close to the root shīn-wāw-bā', and the two are alike in meaning the mixing of one thing with another.

1. al-shayb — the graying of the head. One says "shāba, yashību."

Al-Kisā'ī said: "grief shayyaba his head" and "shayyaba with his head," and "grief ashāba his head" and "ashāba with his head" — all meaning grief turned his hair gray.

2. al-ashyab — a man once he has grayed.
3. al-shīb — mountains upon which snow falls, named from grayness.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Old ones [mountains] that gray when winter strikes them — yet grayness is no blemish upon them,
meaning: the mountains, when they whiten with snow.

It was found in a commentary on a verse of ʿUbayd, in his saying "grayness is a disgrace to one who grays," that al-shayb and al-mashīb are one and the same. It is said Al-Aṣmaʿī held: al-shayb is the whiteness of the hair itself, while al-mashīb is a man's entering the stage of grayness, among men advanced in years and gray-haired.

Also on this point: Ibn al-Sikkīt said, regarding a line of ʿAdī, "and the head — grayness has shābahu [turned it]," that he meant grayness whitened it, not that it merely mixed into it. He cited the verse:
It troubled him, and the like of it troubled him before — grayness fell upon grayness, and so it turned him,
meaning: it whitened his black hair.

4. Shaybān and Milḥān — the two months of qimāḥ [severe winter cold], the harshest of winter for cold; named so for the whiteness the ground takes on from the frost upon it.

Outside this root, they say: "so-and-so spent a shaybā' night," when she was deflowered [on her wedding night], and "she spent a ḥurra night," when she was not.
شيح:
The letters shīn, yā' and ḥā' are two distinct roots: one points to earnestness and wariness, the other to turning away.

The first: the saying of the Arabs, ashāha ʿalā al-shay', he kept persistently at a thing and strove hard in it. A poet of rajaz said:
Lean-flanked ones, obedient to a diligent, watchful herdsman.
Another said:
And you were wary before today, for you are shīḥ, one who is wary.
And al-shiyāḥ is caution, wariness; a man is shā'iḥ. This is meant by his saying:
They grew wary of him, most thoroughly wary.
And al-mashyūḥā' is when people are racing each other to be first in some matter; one says they are in a mashyūḥā'.

The second root: one says ashāha biwajhihi, he turned his face away. And it is said its derivation comes from their saying, the horse ashāha with its tail, when it let it hang loose.

Strange to both roots together: al-shīḥ, which is a plant.
شيخ: The letters shīn, yā' and khā' are a single word, and it is al-shaykh, the old man. You say huwa shaykhun — well known, plainly marked by shaykhūkha, shayakh and tashyīkh. They also used another word: shayyakhtu 'alayhi [I am not fully certain what this idiom means beyond addressing or treating someone as an elder].
شيد: The letters shīn, yā' and dāl are a single root indicating the raising up of a thing. One says shidtu l-qaṣra ashīduhu shaydan, I built up the palace [with plaster]. It is qaṣrun mashīd, meaning built up with al-shīd [plaster/mortar] — named shīd because a building is raised by it. One also says qaṣrun mashīd meaning made tall. al-ishāda — raising the voice, spreading word of something.
شيص: The letters shīn, yā' and ṣād. It is said that al-shīṣ is the worst kind of dates.
شيط:
The letters shīn, yā' and ṭā' are a root pointing to a thing's going, whether by burning or otherwise.

1. al-shayṭ — from shāṭa al-shay', when a thing burned. One says shayyaṭtu al-laḥm, I singed the meat. They also say shayyaṭahu when he smoked it without fully cooking it, though the first sense is more correct and better founded.
2. istashāṭa — a man istashāṭa, when he flared up in anger.
3. mishyāṭ (of a she-camel) — one on which fat builds up and shows quickly.
4. al-shayṭān [the devil] — here the yā' stands close to a wāw. One says shāṭa yashīṭu, when a thing became void. And ashāṭa al-sulṭānu dama fulānin, the ruler ashāṭa someone's blood, when he declared it forfeit. The derivation of the name al-shayṭān has already been discussed elsewhere.
شيع:
The letters shīn, yā' and 'ayn are two roots. One of them points to supporting and helping, and the other to spreading abroad and making known.

The first is their saying shayya'a fulānun fulānan when he escorts him as he sets out. And it is said ātīka ghadan aw shay'ahu, that is, the day after it, as though the second were escorting the first in its passing.

The poet said, in a line of verse:
The travelling companions said: tomorrow is our parting, or the day after it — will you not bid us farewell?

And a brave man is called al-mushayya', as though for his strength he had been strengthened and escorted by another, or escorted with strength.

Some people claimed that al-shay' is the lion's cub, but I have not heard it from a scholar by direct hearing. And some people say that al-shay' is a measure, in their saying aqāma shahran aw shay'ahu — he stayed a month or thereabouts. The correct view is what I have said, that al-mushayyi' is the one who helps another and keeps him company. Al-shī'a are the helpers and supporters.

As for the other root, [it is their saying] shā'a al-ḥadīth, when talk spreads and becomes widely known. And it is said shayya'a al-rā'ī ibilahu, when the herdsman shouts among his camels. The noun is al-shiyā': the reed pipe that the herdsman blows into.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Like the yearning cry of the old she-camels that thrill to the herdsman's reed.

Of this root is their saying about such a thing: he has a sahm shā'i', an undivided share, when it is not portioned off. It is as though the man who has a share and a portion has spread through the whole share until he took it, just as talk spreads among people and reaches the hearing of every one of them.

Of this root too: shayya'tu al-nār fī al-ḥaṭab, when you set the fire blazing in the firewood.
شيق:
The letters shīn, yā' and qāf are one word. It is said that al-shīq is the narrow fissure at the top of a mountain. A poet said:
A crook-beaked bird that nests between the shīq and the nīq [the mountain peak].
شيم:
The letters shīn, yā' and mīm are two distinct roots, and they seem to belong to the class of opposites, since one points to bringing into view, and the other to its opposite.

The first: their saying shimtu al-sayf, when you draw the sword. And the earth dug up and brought out of the ground is called al-shīmah, plural al-shiyam. Also from this: shimtu al-barq ashīmuhu shayman, I shimtu the lightning, meaning I watched it to see where it would head. This is carried on the analogy already given of drawing the sword. Al-Aʿshā said:
I said to the drinking-companions in our dwelling, when they were drunk: shīmū! — but how can a drunk drinker shīm?
As though, when he watched the clouds, he shāma its lightning just as a sword is drawn and watched.

The other root: their saying shimtu al-sayf, when you sheathe it, put it away. From this: al-shīmah, a person's nature and disposition, called shīmah because it is as though tucked away inside him, hidden and settled. And al-inshiyām is entering into a thing; one says: he anshāma into the matter, meaning he entered it. And al-mashīmah is the membrane covering a human infant, called by others al-salā [the afterbirth]; it was named this as though the child had tucked itself away inside it.

As for al-shāmah, a mole, it may well belong to the first root, since it is something that stands out and is visible; from it one says a man is ashyam, meaning one who has a shāmah.
شين: The letters shīn, yā' and nūn are one word pointing to the opposite of adornment. One says: shānahu is the opposite of zānahu [he made it ugly, as opposed to he adorned it]. God knows best what is right.
صأ: The letters ṣād and hamza are a single word. One says: ṣaʾṣaʾa al-jarw, when a puppy moves its eyes trying to open them. In a hadith of one of the Followers: "We opened our eyes, while you were still only stirring yours." One also says ṣaʾṣaʾat al-nakhla, when a palm tree does not take the pollination.
صب:
The letters ṣād and bāʾ are a single root: the pouring out of a thing. Every branch of this chapter goes back to it.

1. ṣababtu al-māʾ aṣubbuhu ṣabban — I poured the water out.
2. al-ṣabab — ground that slopes downward; plural aṣbāb, as though it were something pouring down in its descent. In the hadith: "When he — peace and blessings of God be upon him and his family — walked, it was as though he were walking down a slope." The rājiz-poet said, in a line of verse: "Rather, a land of steep climbs and slopes."
3. al-ṣubba — a troop of horses, as though it pours itself down in a raid; a flock of sheep is likewise called ṣabba, for the same reason.
4. al-ṣabb — the black snakes are called this, because when one means to strike, it pours itself down upon the one it bites.
5. al-ṣabīb — said to be the liquid pressed from sesame leaves; also said instead to be the juice pressed from henna. A poet said, in a line of verse that supports the first view: "I brought them to water, as though its still surface, from long standing, were henna and ṣabīb together." Some said al-ṣabīb is [instead] pure blood, and [also] refined safflower dye.
6. al-ṣubāba — the water left over in a vessel. Al-ṣabāba [passionate longing] comes from "it poured itself toward him."
7. A man is called ṣabb when passion overcomes him — from the heart's "pouring."
8. taṣabbaba al-ḥarr — the heat grew intense, as though it were something poured down onto the ground.
9. taṣabṣaba al-shayʾ — the thing vanished and was wiped away, as though it had been poured out entirely.
10. taṣābabtu al-ināʾ — I drank the last dregs left in the vessel. Likewise taṣābabtu al-shayʾ, when you obtain a thing only a little at a time. Al-Shammākh said, in a line of verse: "People from whom I sipped a meager living, once they were gone, are dearer to me than worn hide-fur that has changed with age."
صبح:
The letters ṣād, bā' and ḥā' are a single root, regular. And it is one of the colours; they said: its root is redness. They said: the dawn was called ṣubḥ for its redness, just as the lamp was called miṣbāḥ for its redness. They said: and for that reason one says a face is ṣabīḥ, bright and handsome. And al-ṣabāḥ is the light of day. This is the root, and then it branches out. So they said, of the morning drink, al-ṣabūḥ, and one has iṣṭabaḥa, he has taken his morning drink; and that is al-jāshiriyya, the drink at daybreak. A poet said, in a line of verse:
When we drink the daybreak draught we care nothing ... for a governor, even if the governor is from Azd.

And one says: "More lying than the captive who has had his morning drink" — they mean the prisoner who has taken the morning draught. And the origin of it is that a people took a man captive and asked him about his tribe, and he lied to them and pointed to a far-off stretch of country; so they stabbed him, and the milk he had drunk that morning came out ahead of the blood; so they said: "More lying than the captive who has had his morning drink." And al-miṣbāḥ is the she-camel that kneels at her resting place and does not rise until morning comes. And al-taṣabbuḥ is sleeping in the early morning. And yawm al-ṣabāḥ is the day of the raid. Al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse:
With him the thousand bleed when they are sent out ... on the morning of the raid, when the dust has risen.

And one says: I came to him at the early morning of every day, and I met him with a morning drink. And al-maṣābīḥ are the cups from which the morning drink is taken. And one says: he came to us at the ṣubḥ of a fifth day and the ṣibḥ of a fifth day.

And from the first word: al-ṣabaḥ is a deep redness in the hair; one says a lion is aṣbaḥ.
صبر:
The letters ṣād, bā' and rā' are three roots: the first is holding back, the second the upper parts of a thing, and the third a kind of stone.

The first: al-ṣabr, and it is holding back. One says ṣabartu nafsī ʿalā dhālika al-amr, that is, I held it back. A poet said, in a line of verse:
So I held to it a soul that knew its duty, a free soul that stands firm when the coward's spirit rises to escape.

And al-maṣbūra is the beast held fast to be killed. And the Messenger of God — God bless him and his family and give him peace — forbade the killing of any beast in that way, tied up.

Of the section: al-ṣabīr, and it is the guarantor, and he was named so only because he bears the payment patiently. One says ṣabartu nafsī bihi aṣburu ṣabran — when you go surety for him — so I am ṣabīr for him. And ṣabartu al-insāna — when you make him swear by God the strongest oath.

As for the second, they said: the ṣubr of everything is its top. They said: and aṣbār al-inā' are its sides, the single one ṣubr. And a poet said:
So I filled it with blood to its very brim.

As for the third root, al-ṣubra of stones is what is hard and thick, and the plural is ṣibār. And in Ibn Durayd's book: "al-ṣubāra is a piece of iron or of stone", in al-A'shā's saying:
Who will carry to ʿAmr that man was not created of stone.

Ibn Durayd said: and the Baghdadis transmitted it as "ṣabāra", and I do not know what they meant by this.

We say: what the Baghdadis meant is what is reported, that al-ṣibār is what is hard and thick. And it is in al-A'shā's saying:
Just before dawn, the sounds of the stones.

This is what the Baghdadis meant, and the hā' comes upon it as a mark of the collective.

Abū ʿUbayd said: al-ṣubr is the ground that has pebbles in it and is not rough; and from it a lava-field was called umm ṣabbār.

And of what is carried onto this is the saying of the Arabs: waqaʿa al-qawmu fī ummi ṣabbūr — when they have fallen into a grave affair.
صبع:
The letters ṣād, bā' and 'ayn are a single root, which is then used metaphorically. The origin is iṣba', a person's finger, one of his aṣābi' (fingers).

1. They said it is feminine. And they said it may also be made masculine. It is related from the Prophet, God bless him and his family and grant him peace, that he said: "Are you but a finger that has bled, and in the path of God is what you have met?" — said this way, in the feminine.
2. One says: ṣaba'a fulānun bi-fulānin, so-and-so "ṣaba'a" at so-and-so, when he pointed at him with his finger, speaking ill of him behind his back.

Al-iṣba' also means: a good, beautiful trace or mark left by someone — this is a metaphorical use. And there is a proverb: "So-and-so has an iṣba' in his wealth," meaning a beautiful mark. And it is said of the shepherd who tends the camels well, whose good effect shows on them: "He has an iṣba' over them." Al-Rā'ī said, describing a shepherd, in a line of verse:
Weak of staff, veins showing plainly, yet you see he has left his mark [iṣba'] on them whenever people suffer drought.

Al-ṣab': your pouring out what is in a vessel from between your two fingers.
صبغ:
The letters ṣād, bā' and ghayn are a single root, and it is the coloring of a thing with some color. You say "ṣabaghtuhu, aṣbughuhu" — I dyed it.

1. A ripening date is said to have "ṣabbaghat" — taken on its color.

As for His words, exalted is He, {the dye of God} [al-Baqara: 138], some said it means His shaping of His creation from birth; others said everything by which one draws near to God is a ṣibgha.

2. al-aṣbagh — a horse with white at the tip of its tail, less white than al-ashkal. The first [al-aṣbagh] is likened to a thing whose tip has been dyed.
صبى:
The letters ṣād, bā' and the weak letter are three sound roots: the first indicates young age, the second is a wind among the winds, and the third is [inclining].

1. al-ṣabī — the singular of al-ṣibya and al-ṣibyān, both plurals meaning children. One says ra'aytuhu fī ṣibāhu, ay ṣighārihi — I saw him in his ṣibā, that is, in his youth.
2. al-muṣbī — one who has many children.
3. al-ṣabā' — the lengthened form of al-ṣibā (childhood); it is also said with a lengthened fatḥa.

Abū 'Amr recited a line of verse:
I awoke, with one part of me no longer able to bear another, as though my youth had been only a loan.

4. ṣabā ilā al-shay' yaṣbū — his heart inclined toward it. The derivation is the same [as ṣibā], and the noun is al-ṣabwa.

Al-'Ajjāj said, concerning al-ṣibā, in a line of verse:
Only the child experiences childhood.

The second is the wind called al-ṣabā, which blows facing the qibla. One says ṣabat taṣbū of it.

The third is the Arabs' saying ṣābaytu al-rumḥ, meaning I tilted the spear.

As for the hamzated form, it indicates going out and emerging.

1. ṣaba'a min dīnin ilā dīn — he went out from one religion to another.
2. ṣaba'a nābu al-ba'īr — the camel's canine tooth emerged.
3. One who goes out from a religion to another is called ṣābi', plural ṣābi'ūn and ṣubbā'.
صت:
The letters ṣād and tāʾ are a root indicating dispute, quarreling, and separation.

1. al-ṣatīt — uproar, clamor.
2. uṣātitu fulānan — I kept disputing with so-and-so.
3. al-ṣatt — said, according to some, to mean a violent collision.
4. al-ṣatīt — [also] a faction, a group of people.
5. al-ṣatt — they say it is [the same as] al-ṣadd, turning away.
صتع:
The letters ṣād, tā' and ʿayn are two words: one of them is disputed in how it is to be understood, and the other is a going back and forth over a matter.

Ibn Durayd said: al-ṣata' is the base form from which al-ṣuntu' is built. Then his account and al-Khalīl's differed: al-ṣata' is the thick-set young man, in al-Khalīl's account. He recited a line of verse:
And what use is there in the company of the sturdy, thickset young man?

Ibn Durayd also said: al-ṣuntu' is the small-headed male ostrich.

The other word: al-taṣattu' — wavering over a matter, going back and forth in it.
صتم:
The letters ṣād, tā' and mīm are a sound root indicating completeness and strength.

1. al-ṣaytama — the rock, according to Ibn Durayd. He also said: a'ṭaytuhu alfan ṣatman — I gave him a full thousand.
2. al-ṣatam — the young man of strong build.
صح:
The letters ṣād and ḥāʾ are a root indicating freedom from sickness and defect, and also evenness.

1. al-ṣiḥḥa — health: the going away of illness, and freedom from every defect. Al-ṣaḥīḥ and al-ṣiḥāḥ [both meaning "healthy"] carry the same sense.
2. al-muṣiḥḥ — one whose household and camels are all healthy and sound. The Messenger of God — peace and blessings of God be upon him and his family — said: "Let no one with a diseased animal bring it in among a healthy herd" — meaning one whose camels are all sound.
3. al-ṣaḥṣaḥ, al-ṣaḥṣaḥān, and al-ṣaḥṣāḥ — level, even ground.
صحب:
The letters ṣād, ḥā' and bā' are one root pointing to a thing being joined to another and kept near it.

Of that is al-ṣāḥib, the companion, and the plural is al-ṣaḥb, as one says rākib (rider) and rakb (a riding party). And of the section: aṣḥaba fulānun — when he submits. And aṣḥaba al-rajul — when his son comes of age. And everything that suits another thing has istaṣḥabahu — taken it as its companion. And a hide left with its hair on it is called muṣḥab. And one says aṣḥaba al-mā' — when the green scum covers it.
صحر:
The letters ṣād, ḥā' and rā' are two roots: one is open, level ground, and the other is a color among colors.

1. al-ṣaḥrā' — the open expanse of land. One says aṣḥara al-qawm, meaning the people came out into the open.
2. laqītuhu ṣaḥrata baḥrata — I met him with no screen between me and him.
3. al-ṣuḥra — the open desert, in the words of Abū Dhu'ayb:
A shaft, from its reed-cane, cast off by a flash-flood swollen by open desert land and shimmering heat.

The other root: al-ṣuḥra is a white color tinged with red.

1. atānun ṣaḥrā' — a she-donkey with this ṣuḥra color in her coat: a dun-grey mixed with white and black.
2. aṣḥārra al-nabt — a plant turned that color as it grew up, its color changing and becoming mixed.
صحف:
The letters ṣād, ḥā' and fā' are a sound root pointing to a spreading out in a thing and to width.

It is said that al-ṣaḥīf is the face of the earth. And al-ṣaḥīfa is the skin of a man's face. Al-Buʿayth said, in a line of verse:
And every man of Kulayb, the page of his face is lowlier to the feet of men than a sandal.

And from the section: al-ṣaḥīfa, the sheet in which one writes; the plural is ṣaḥā'if, and ṣuḥuf as well, as though it were the plural of ṣaḥīf. A poet said, in a line of verse:
When in the morning they saw their foreheads, the ties of kinship and the written sheets yearned toward us.

And al-ṣaḥfa is the wide flat bowl. Al-Shaybānī said: al-ṣiḥāf are small hollows made to hold water; the plural is ṣuḥuf.
صحل:
The letters ṣād, ḥā' and lām are a single word: it is hoarseness in the voice. The hoarse man is called al-aṣḥal, the noun is al-ṣaḥal, and he is [said to be] ṣaḥil. Al-A'shā said:
Hoarse of voice, husky.
صحم:
The letters ṣād, ḥā' and mīm are a small sound root indicating a color.

1. al-aṣḥam — dust-grey shading into black. A land called ṣaḥmā' is dusty grey.
2. iṣḥāmmat al-baqla — the plant turned green. It is called this because when it is well-watered it looks almost black; for the same reason one says idhāmmat [of a very dark green].
صحن:
The letters ṣād, ḥā' and nūn are a small root indicating breadth in a thing.

1. al-ṣaḥn — the courtyard, the middle of a house.
2. al-ṣaḥn — also a hollow that opens up in hard, stony ground; by that resemblance the large bowl was named ṣaḥn.

Deviating from the chapter:
1. ṣaḥantu bayna al-qawm — I made peace between them.
2. ṣaḥantuhu shay'an — I gave him something.
3. ṣaḥanahu ṣaḥanātin — he struck him blow after blow.
4. nāqatun ṣaḥūn — a she-camel that kicks.
صحو:
The letters ṣād, ḥā' and the weak letter are a sound root indicating the clearing away of something.

1. al-ṣaḥw — the opposite of drunkenness. One says ṣaḥā yaṣḥū of the drunk man, when he sobers up; he is then called ṣāḥin.
2. aṣḥat al-samā'u — the sky cleared; it is then called muṣḥiya.

It is related from Abū Ḥātim that he said: common people think ṣaḥw only means the clouds clearing away, but that is not so — ṣaḥw is the cold departing and the clouds scattering.

Deviating from this root is al-miṣḥāh, a cup one drinks from, like a bowl.
صخ:
The letters ṣād and khāʾ are a root indicating a kind of sound.

1. al-ṣākhkha — said to be the deafening blast [that stuns the ears].
2. ḍarabtu al-ṣakhra bi-ḥajar fa-samiʿtu lahā ṣakhkhan — I struck the rock with a stone and heard it make a clacking sound.
3. ṣakhkha al-ghurāb bi-minqārihi fī dabarat al-baʿīr — the crow struck with its beak into the camel's saddle-sore, meaning it jabbed at it.
صخب:
The letters ṣād, khā' and bā' are a sound root indicating a loud voice.

1. al-ṣakhab — noise and clamor. Some said: rajulun ṣakhbān, a man given much to clamor.
2. mā'un ṣakhib al-ādhiyy — water is called this when its waves have a loud sound.
صخد:
The letters ṣād, khā' and dāl are a sound root indicating intensity, in heat and other things.

1. al-ṣaykhad — the intensity of heat. It is also said that al-ṣaykhad is the disk of the sun.
2. iṣṭakhada al-ḥirbā' — the chameleon basked, warming itself in the sun's heat.
3. yawmun ṣakhadān, on the pattern fa'alān — a day of intense heat.
4. ṣakhada al-nahāru yaṣkhadu, and ṣakhida yaṣkhadu — the day grew intensely hot.
5. al-ṣakhra al-ṣaykhūd — the hard, unyielding rock.

Close to this, in the matter of intensity, is their saying ṣakhada al-ṣurad, when the shrike screeched loudly; likewise one says ṣakhada al-rajul, of a man.
صخر: The letters ṣād, khā' and rā' form a sound word, and it is al-ṣakhra — the great rock, the boulder. One says ṣakhra and ṣakhara.
صخم: The letters ṣād, khā' and mīm are a word. One who stands upright and erect is called muṣṭakhim.
صخي: The letters ṣād, khā' and yā' are a word. One says ṣakhiya al-thawb yaṣkhā — the garment became soiled and grimy, so it is ṣakhin; and the noun is al-ṣakhā.
صد:
The letters ṣād and dāl: most of this chapter comes back to turning away and swerving aside. After that come words that deviate from it.

1. al-ṣadd — turning away. One says ṣadda yaṣuddu; it is a leaning toward one of two sides.
2. ṣadadtu fulānan ʿan al-amr — I turned so-and-so away from the matter, when you divert him from it.
3. al-ṣaddān — the two sides of a valley, singular ṣadd; this follows the pattern, since a side inevitably slants away.
4. al-ṣadad — they say it means whatever faces something. One says: "this house is on the ṣadad of that one," meaning facing it, in line with it.
5. al-ṣadad — they also say it means nearness.
6. al-ṣuddād — the path leading to water.
7. al-ṣadd — [also] a mountain.

These words I have listed are not, in my view, part of the [core] root, since they lie too far from the pattern; but if they are sound, they are to be referred back to it by extension.

Among what is sound but does not belong to this chapter is their saying ṣadda yaṣiddu, said when someone cries out in distress. Some read [the Qur'an] as: {when your people cry out at it} [al-Zukhruf: 57] — they explained it as meaning they clamor. Al-ṣadīd is blood mixed with pus; from it one says aṣadda al-jurḥ, the wound discharged such matter.
صدح:
The letters ṣād, dāl and ḥā' are a small root indicating a sound.

1. ṣadaḥa al-dīku wa'l-ghurāb — the rooster crowed and the crow cawed, loudly.
2. innahu la-ṣaydaḥ — al-Liḥyānī used to say this, meaning loud of voice.

They also say — though it does not fit this pattern:
1. al-ṣudḥa — a bead used for [magical] binding-charms.
2. al-ṣadaḥ — hillocks.
And God knows best.
صدر:
The letters ṣād, dāl and rā' are two sound roots: one of them points to the opposite of coming down to water, and the other is the breast of a man and of other things.

The first is their saying ṣadara ʿan al-mā' and ṣadara ʿan al-bilād, when he had come down to it and then went away from it.

And al-Aḥmar said: one says ṣadartu ʿan al-bilād ṣadaran, and that is the noun; but if you mean the verbal noun you make the dāl silent, ṣadr. And he recited:
And many a night whose meeting-time I made the dawn ... the setting out of the riding-beast, until it should know the dark before daybreak.
ṣadr al-maṭiyya here is the verbal noun.

As for the other, al-ṣadr is the breast of a man; the plural is ṣudūr. God, exalted be He, said: {but it is the hearts within the breasts that go blind} [al-Ḥajj: 46]. Then words are derived from it. So al-ṣidār is a garment covering the head and the breast. And al-ṣidār is a brand-mark on the breast of a camel. And al-taṣdīr is a rope with which a camel is girt at the breast so that its load is not pushed back behind it. And al-muṣaddar is the lion, so named for the strength of his chest. And al-maṣdūr is the one who complains of his chest.
صدع:
The letters ṣād, dāl and ʿayn are a sound root, indicating a splitting-open in a thing.

1. One says ṣadaʿtuhu fa-nṣadaʿa wa-taṣaddaʿa — I split it, and it split apart.
2. ṣadaʿtu al-falāt — I crossed the open desert.
3. dalīl hādin miṣdaʿ — a guide who leads truly is called miṣdaʿ.
4. al-ṣadʿ — plant growth, because it splits open the earth. In His saying, Most High: {and the earth that splits open [with sprouting plants]} [al-Ṭāriq: 12].
5. Also from this root: ṣadaʿa bi-l-ḥaqq — he spoke the truth out loud, openly.

He, glory be to Him, said to His prophet, peace be upon him: {So proclaim openly what you are commanded} [al-Ḥijr: 94].

6. One says taṣaddaʿa al-qawm — the people scattered.
7. al-ṣidʿa, of camels — a group of about sixty or so, as though it had split off from a large herd.

What falls outside this root: al-ṣadaʿ, a young mountain-goat.
صدغ:
The letters ṣād, dāl and ghayn are two roots: one is a body part, the other indicates weakness.

1. al-ṣudgh — what lies between the corner of the eye and the base of the ear [the temple]. One says ṣadaghtu al-rajul, meaning I walked level with him, my temple beside his temple.
2. al-ṣidāgh — a brand-mark on the temple.

1. al-ṣadīgh — the weak man. One says mā yaṣdaghu namlatan min ḍa'f — he cannot even kill an ant, from weakness.
2. al-ṣadīgh — it is also said this means a newborn child, up until he completes seven days.

Deviating from both roots is their saying ṣadaghtuhu 'an al-shay', meaning I turned him away from it.
صدف:
The letters ṣād, dāl and fā' are two roots: the first indicates turning aside, and the second is one item among physical objects.

1. The first is their saying ṣadafa ʿan al-shay' — he turned away from the thing, when he inclined away from it and went off.

God Most High said: {We shall repay those who turn away from Our signs} [al-Anʿām: 157].

2. al-ṣadaf, of a camel — that its foot, front or hind, tilts toward the outer side; one says it ṣadifa.
3. Camels that stand behind the hindquarters of other camels at the trough, waiting for the drinking ones to leave so they can come in, are called al-ṣawādif.

He said, in a line of verse:
the watchers for their turn, the ones waiting aside.

4. al-ṣadaf — the side of a mountain, so named for its leaning toward one of two directions.
5. As for the other root: al-ṣadaf, the sea-shell; well known.
صدق:
The letters ṣād, dāl and qāf are a root pointing to strength in a thing, in speech and otherwise. From that is al-ṣidq, truthfulness, the opposite of lying; it was so named for its strength in itself, and because a lie has no strength, being void. The origin of this is their saying shay'un ṣadq — a hard, firm thing — and rumḥun ṣadq, a stout spear. And one says ṣadaqūhum al-qitāl — they fought them in earnest; and the opposite of that, kadhabūhum — they fell short against them. Al-ṣiddīq is the one who never leaves the truth.

Al-ṣadāq is a woman's bride-gift; it was so named for its strength and because it is a right that is binding. And one says ṣadāq, ṣudqa and ṣaduqa. God, exalted be He, said: {wa-ātū al-nisā'a ṣaduqātihinna niḥla} — and give the women their bride-gifts as a free gift [al-Nisā': 4]. It is also read "ṣadaqātihinna".

And [from] this chapter is al-ṣadaqa: what a man gives away as alms out of himself and his wealth.

As for al-muṣaddiq: Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm reported to us, from the commentator, from al-Qutaybī, who said: among the things people put out of their proper place is their saying huwa yataṣaddaqu when a man gives, and yataṣaddaqu when he asks. That is a mistake, because the mutaṣaddiq is the giver. God, exalted be He, said in the story of the one who said: {wa-taṣaddaq ʿalaynā} — and give us charity [Yūsuf: 88].

And this shaykh related to us from al-Maʿdānī, from his father, from Abū Muʿādh, from al-Layth, from al-Khalīl, who said: the one who feeds is a mutaṣaddiq and the one who begs is a mutaṣaddiq, and the two are the same. But the one in the Qur'an is the giver. And al-muṣaddiq is the one who takes the alms due on sheep.

And one says huwa rajulu ṣidq — he is a man of truth. Al-ṣadāqa, friendship, is derived from al-ṣidq — truthfulness in affection. And one says ṣadīq for one, for two, for a group, and for a woman. And sometimes they say aṣdiqā' and aṣādiq.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
May they never cease to be worn out and limping, for having carried her to a far country with few friends.
صدم: The letters ṣād, dāl and mīm are a single word: it is al-ṣadm, the striking of a hard thing against its like.
صدن: The letters ṣād, dāl and nūn are a weak root. They say: al-ṣaydan is the fox.
صدى:
The letters ṣād, dāl and the weak letter contain words far apart in their derivation — scarcely do two of them meet in one root.

1. al-ṣadā — the male owl, plural aṣdā'. A poet said:
After you, people are not worth a date-stone's groove, and they are nothing but owls and skulls.
2. al-ṣadā — the brain itself. It is also said to be the place in the brain where hearing sits, and for that one says aṣamma Allāhu ṣadāhu — may God deafen his ṣadā. It is also said this is rather ṣadā al-ṣawt, the echo, which answers you when you call out near a mountain. He said, describing a dwelling:
Its echo has gone silent and its trace worn away, and it stays mute to the questioner's speech.
3. al-ṣadā — a man who manages his wealth well; one says huwa ṣadā mālin, he is the ṣadā of [his] wealth. It is used only joined to another word.
4. al-ṣadā — thirst. One says rajulun ṣadin wa ṣādin, a thirsty man, and imra'atun ṣādiya, a thirsty woman.
5. taṣaddā fulānun lil-shay' — so-and-so exposed himself to a thing, watching closely for it.
6. al-taṣdiya — clapping the two hands together. God Almighty said: {Their prayer at the House was nothing but whistling and clapping} [al-Anfāl: 35].
7. al-ṣawādī min al-nakhl — tall palm trees.
8. ṣādaytu fulānan — I dealt gently and cunningly with so-and-so.
9. ṣādaytu fulānan muṣādātan — I treated him just as he had treated me.

If a hamza follows the dāl, the meaning changes, and it belongs to al-ṣada', the rust of iron. They say ṣāghirun ṣadi', from the rust of disgrace.
صر:
The letters ṣād and rāʾ are [several] roots.

The first is their saying ṣarra al-darāhima yaṣurruhā ṣarran, he tied up the coins; that cloth [bundle] is a ṣurra. What the Arabs specifically know as al-ṣirār is a cloth tied over a she-camel's teats so that her young cannot suckle her; one says ṣarrahā ṣarran.

1. al-iṣrār — firm resolve on a thing. We have placed this under the same pattern because resolving on a thing and being fully decided on it are one and the same; likewise al-iṣrār is persisting firmly on a thing.
2. "This is my ṣirrī oath," meaning in earnest — that I am firm and fully resolved upon it.
3. al-ṣarra — a group of people. Imruʾ al-Qays said, in a line of verse: "He brought us level with the leading [wild cows], while the stragglers behind him stayed in a tight, unscattered group."
4. ḥāfir maṣrūr — a hoof described this way is contracted, drawn in.
5. al-ṣurṣūr — a huge herd of camels.

As for the second [root] — concerning rising and being high — it is their saying ṣarra al-ḥimār udhunahu, the donkey pricked up its ear. One also says aṣarra when the ear is not named, and if it is named, one says aṣarra bi-udhunihi — though I think this latter form is rare. The origin word here is al-ṣirār: raised ground that water hardly ever climbs over. Ṣirār [without the article] is a proper name, a mountain. A poet said, in a line of verse: "Al-Farazdaq will never part from his baseness, until [the mountain] Ṣirār moves off from the road."

As for the third: cold and heat — it is al-ṣirr.
1. One says the plant was struck by ṣirr, meaning a harmful cold struck it. Al-ṣirr also names the icy chill of a cold wind. Sometimes they put heat in this place instead: some said al-ṣārra is the intensity of heat, the sun's heat.
2. qaṭaʿa al-ḥimār ṣārratahu — the donkey "cut short" its ṣārra, meaning it drank a draught that broke its thirst.
3. al-ṣārra — [also] thirst; plural ṣawārr.
4. al-ṣarīra — thirst; plural ṣarāʾir. A poet said, in a line of verse: "The dun she-camels bolted off, their thirst not yet quenched." Abū ʿUbayd stated that al-ṣārra means thirst with plural ṣarāʾir; this is a mistake — the correct account is what we have given [ṣārra/ṣawārr and ṣarīra/ṣarāʾir are two separate words].

As for the fourth: sound.
1. al-ṣarra — intensity of shouting.
2. ṣarra al-jundab ṣarīran — the locust made its shrill sound.
3. ṣarṣara al-akhṭab ṣarṣaratan — the green woodpecker made its chattering call.
4. al-ṣarārī — the sailor; possibly named so for raising his voice.

Among what deviates from these roots are two words, though perhaps there is a pattern for them whose place has stayed hidden from us. The first is al-ṣārra, meaning need — one says "I have a ṣārra with so-and-so," plural ṣawārr, meaning a need. The other is al-ṣarūra: one who has not made the pilgrimage, and [also] one who has not married; al-ṣarūra is also said of one who forgoes marriage, devoting himself wholly [to worship]. It occurs in the hadith: "There is no ṣarūra in Islam."

Abū Bakr Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan ibn Durayd said: "The origin of al-ṣarūra is that in pre-Islamic times, if a man committed some offense and took refuge at the Kaʿba, he would not be molested; so when the blood-avenger met him within the sanctuary, he would be told, 'He is a ṣarūra, so do not molest him.' This became so common in their speech that they also called the devoted worshipper who kept away from women and fine food a ṣarūra or ṣarūrī. This is what al-Nābigha meant, in a line of verse: 'Had she presented herself, she would have tempted even a gray-haired monk devoted to God, a ṣarūra given wholly to worship' — meaning one withdrawn from women and perfume. Then, when God brought Islam and made establishing the [legal] penalties obligatory in Mecca and elsewhere, the one who had not made the pilgrimage came to be called ṣarūra and ṣarūrī, unlike the pre-Islamic usage — as though they made forgoing the pilgrimage in Islam equivalent to the ascetic's forgoing women and comfort before Islam."

What we have said about the meaning of al-ṣarūra may possibly go back to al-ṣirār, the cloth tied over a she-camel's teats so that her young cannot suckle her. And God knows best what is correct.
صرب:
The letters ṣād, rā' and bā' are a small sound root indicating something like what the previous chapter indicated. Al-Khalīl added another sense to it: he said al-ṣarīb is milk that has been stored up, and the milk-skin holding it is called muṣarrab. Ibn Durayd said: everything smooth is called ṣarab, and what he said fits the pattern better, because they call gum-resin al-ṣarab, and they recite:
A land far off from good things and from power, where the two sweetest things in it are the ṭurthūth-plant and the gum-resin.
And gum has smoothness in it. What al-Khalīl said is rather a branch of this: their saying of a child, when his belly is bound up so that he may fatten — ṣaraba — meaning at the time his fat is knotting together. And al-ṣarb is sour milk.
صرح:
The letters ṣād, rā' and ḥā' are a regular root indicating the appearing and coming forth of a thing. From this: al-shay' al-ṣarīḥ, the pure, plain thing. Al-ṣarīḥ is one of pure lineage, plural ṣuraḥā'. Al-Khalīl said: horses are pluralized as al-ṣarā'iḥ. And he said: everything unmixed is ṣarīḥ. One says huwa bayyinu al-ṣarāḥati wa-l-ṣurūḥa. Ṣarraḥa bimā fī nafsihi means he made plain what was in his mind. One says ka'sun ṣurāḥ for a cup not mixed with anything. Ṣarraḥati al-khamru means the wine cleared, when its foam had gone. Al-A'shā said:
Dark-red, its redness uncovered ... once it clears after its foaming.
One says jā'a bihi ṣurāḥan, meaning he brought it openly. Laqītu fulānan muṣāraḥatan wa-ṣirāḥan means I met so-and-so face to face. One says ṣarraḥa al-ḥaqqu 'an maḥḍihi, meaning the matter became uncovered after having been hidden. Al-ṣarḥa is a place — it is said rather that it is raised, hard ground. One says yawmun muṣarriḥ for a cloudless day, found in al-Ṭirimmāḥ's poetry. Al-ṣarḥ is a single building, built standing alone, huge and tall, rising into the sky, and every tall building is a ṣarḥ.
صرخ:
The letters ṣād, rā' and khā' are a small root indicating a raised, loud sound.

1. From this: al-ṣurākh, crying out. One says ṣarakha yaṣrukhu, said when he makes a loud sound.
2. al-ṣārikh is said to mean both the one crying for help and the one who comes to help; it is also said that the helper is rather called muṣrikh, on account of His saying, Most High, in the story of the one who said: {I am not the one who can help you, nor are you the ones who can help me} [Ibrāhīm: 22].
صرد:
The letters ṣād, rā' and dāl are three roots: one is cold, the second is being pure and free of anything else, and the third is scantiness.

1. al-ṣard — cold. A day is called ṣarid, and a man is said to have felt cold, ṣarida. A man called miṣrād feels the cold badly. The noun is al-ṣarad. The poet said:
An excellent garment for the young man, when the night turns cold before dawn and the cold-stricken man shivers.
2. ṣarida al-qalbu 'an al-shay' — the heart gave up on a thing, meaning it wearies of it, cools toward it, and turns from it; this belongs to this chapter.
3. al-ṣurrād — thin cloud.

1. al-ṣard — pure and unmixed. One says kadhibun ṣard, a bare-faced lie, and uḥibbuka ḥubban ṣardan, I love you with a pure love, and sharābun ṣard, an undiluted drink. The poet said:
Indeed undiluted wine, if drunk alone, on an empty stomach, its hunger pains the liver.
