2. ṣarada al-sahmu min al-ramiyyah — the arrow passed clean through what it struck, its point coming out the other side; a naṣlun ṣārid is an arrowhead that passes clean through, and aṣradtuhu means I made it pass clean through — this is the sense of being free and clear of the target.

The third root is al-taṣrīd: giving [an animal] to drink less than its fill. A drink given in reduced amount is called sharābun muṣarrad, and ṣarrada lahu al-'aṭā' means he reduced what he gave him.

Deviating from the chapter:
1. al-ṣurad — a bird.
2. al-ṣuradān — two veins under the tongue.
صرط:
The letters ṣād, rā' and ṭā': this is of the chapter of letter-substitution, and it has already been mentioned under sīn; and it is the road. A poet said, in a line of verse:
I charge my colt against the Ḥarūrites ... and drive them onto the plain white of the road.
صرع:
The letters ṣād, rā' and ʿayn are a single root indicating the falling of a thing to the ground out of a struggle between two, and other things are then built on that and derived from it. From that: ṣaraʿtu al-rajula ṣarʿan — I threw the man down; ṣāraʿtuhu muṣāraʿatan — I wrestled him; rajulun ṣarīʿ — a thrown-down man. Al-ṣarīʿ, said of branches, is what has drooped and fallen to the ground, plural ṣuruʿ; and if a bow is made from such a fallen branch, it too is called ṣarīʿ.

Built on this is their saying humā ṣirʿān, said to mean the two fall, or happen, together — a comparison and a figure of speech. Likewise miṣrāʿā al-bāb, the two leaves of a door, are taken from this, meaning the two are equal and close together. Al-ṣarʿān are two strings of camels that differ in their pace, so that this one goes as that one comes, on account of how many there are. It was said, in a line of verse:
I relieved him with our two matching shares, for a widow or a wretched man whose need was like his.

Maṣāriʿ al-nās are the places where people fall, meaning where they die. Abū Zayd said: atānā ṣarʿay al-nahār, meaning morning and evening — this too rests on what was said above, that al-ṣarʿān are the matching pair. The reasoning throughout is the same one.
صرف:
The letters ṣād, rā' and fā': the greater part of this chapter indicates the turning back of a thing. From this: ṣaraftu al-qawma ṣarfan and they turned away, when you turned them back and they went back. And al-ṣarīf is milk at the moment it is milked and carried off. And al-ṣarf in the Qur'an is repentance, because by it one is brought back from the rank of sinners. And al-ṣarfa is a star; the people of the language said it was called ṣirfa because the cold turns away when it rises. And al-ṣarfa is a bead by which men are put under a spell, so named as though by it they turn a man's heart away from what he wants of the woman. Al-Khalīl said: al-ṣarf is the excess of one dirham over another in value. And the sense of ṣarf with us is that a thing is turned to a thing, as though the dinar were turned to dirhams, that is, brought back to them, when you take its equivalent. Al-Khalīl said: and from it the name al-ṣayrafī, the money-changer, is derived, for his turning one of the two into the other. He said: and the taṣrīf of dirhams in all buying and selling is the spending of them. Abū ʿUbayd said: the ṣarf of speech is the adorning of it and the adding to it, and it was so called only because, when it is adorned, it turns ears toward listening to it. And an event of time is called ṣarf, the plural being ṣurūf, so named because it turns people about, that is, overturns them and sends them back and forth. As for the heat of sheep, cattle and dogs, it is called al-ṣirāf, and with us it follows the analogy of the chapter, because they turn about in it, that is, go back and forth and return to it. And from the chapter is al-ṣarīf, which is the grating sound of a camel's canine tooth, so named because he repeats it and brings it back again.

As for the saying of the speaker, in a line of verse:
Sons of Ghudāna, you are not gold ... nor ṣarīf, but you are potsherds.

Some people said: by al-ṣarīf he meant silver. If that is sound, it was called ṣarīf from their saying "I exchanged the dinar for dirhams"; it has no other explanation than this.

And of what I reckon strays from this root is al-ṣarafān, which is lead. And al-ṣarafān in the saying, in a line of verse:
Or ṣarafān, cold and hard

is disputed. Some said it is lead; others said al-ṣarafān is a kind of date. And they recited, in a line of verse:
He ate butter along with ṣarafān.

They said: and no rarity used to be given as a gift to al-Zabbā' that was dearer to her than dates. And they recited, in a line of verse:
And when the caravan came to her she said, is it something cool ... of dates, or is this iron and stones?

And of what also strays is al-ṣirf, a dye with which leather is dyed.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
A bay whose colour leaves no room for oaths, but ... like the colour of the ṣirf-dye in which the hide is steeped.

And upon this is carried their saying: he drank the drink ṣirfan, when he did not mix it, as though it were left upon its own colour and redness.
صرم:
The letters ṣād, rā' and mīm are a single, sound, consistent root, and it is cutting.

1. ṣurm al-hijrān — the cutting-off of estrangement.
2. al-ṣarīma — firm resolve upon a thing, which is the cutting of every attachment short of it.
3. al-ṣurām — the last of the milk, after it has increased; when a man needs it he milks it out of necessity.

A poet [Bishr] said, in a line of verse:
Oh, carry word to the Banū Saʿd — and to their ally — the last milk has now been drawn,
a proverb, as though saying: matters have reached their very worst, for the end of a thing comes at its cutting-off.

4. al-ṣayram — the single, main meal one eats, because eating it "cuts off" the rest of the day.
5. "ṣaramtuhu ṣarman," with a fatḥa — the verbal noun; al-ṣurm is the resulting noun.

As for al-ṣarīm, it is said to be a name for both dawn and night — either way it fits the root's reasoning, since each of day and night cuts the other off and is cut off from it.

God, exalted is He, said {so it became like the night} [al-Qalam: 20]. He says: it was scorched and turned black like the night — this for those who take it to mean "night." As for [it meaning] dawn, Bishr said, in a line of verse:
So he spent the night saying "Dawn, O night!" — until the darkness cleared from its ṣarīma.

6. al-ṣarīm — sand cut off from the firm, level ground.
7. al-ṣirām — the season for cutting the palm-clusters. "The palms aṣrama" — their cutting-time arrived.
8. al-ṣirma — a herd of camels, about thirty head.
9. al-ṣiram — patches of cloud, singular ṣirma.

A poet [al-Nābigha] said, in a line of verse:
And the wind blew from the direction of Dhū Urul, driving along, out of the night's chill, patches of cloud.

10. al-ṣirm — a group of people who camp with their camels apart from the main water; they are "people of a ṣirm."
11. rajul ṣārim — a man decisive in his affairs, like a cutting sword.
12. nāqa muṣarrama — a she-camel whose teat has been cut so its milk-duct is ruined and dries up, making her stronger, since no milk drains from her. This cutting [al-taṣrīm] is done by cauterizing two teats.
13. al-ṣarmā' — waterless land.
14. al-ṣarīma — also said to mean land whose crop has been harvested.

As for his line of verse:
And a waterless waste where the eye grows bewildered — when it becomes impassable, the two aṣramān overcome it,
the two aṣramān are the wolf and the crow, so named because they cut themselves off from human company.
صرى:
The letters ṣād, rā' and the weak letter are a single sound root indicating gathering. One says ṣarā al-mā'a yaṣrīhi, meaning he collected it, and water called ṣaran is water that has been collected. A poet said:
She saw a young man in whose spine the water of youth had gathered, in the very prime of his vigor.

1. al-ṣarāt — [a place-name] that appears to be derived, taken from this.
2. al-muṣarrāh — a ewe or she-camel [whose milk is left unmilked], named because the milk gathers in her udders. The Messenger of God, God's blessings and peace upon him, said: "Do not bind up the udders of camels and sheep [to make them look full of milk]. Whoever buys a muṣarrāh has the choice for the next two milkings: if he wishes he may return her, along with a ṣā' of dates."
3. ṣarayta mā baynahum — I set right what was between them; this fits the pattern, because it gathers together scattered words.
4. ṣarayta al-rajul — I kept the man from what he wanted. A poet said:
And nothing that has held him back from remembering her has [truly] held him back.
This too fits the pattern, because when a thing is withheld it is held back and gathered in against it.
5. ṣarāhu Allāh — said just as one says waqāhu Allāh, meaning: may He not let his affairs scatter, but rather gather his wealth together.
6. ṣarā fulānun fī yad fulān — it remained in so-and-so's hand, held as a pledge.

Deviating from the chapter is al-ṣarāya, the colocynth [bitter gourd], in his words:
Or the pulp of a colocynth.
صع:
The letters ṣād and ʿayn are a sound root indicating scattering and movement.

1. taṣaʿṣaʿa al-qawm — the people scattered, when they broke apart and dispersed.
2. ṣaʿāṣiʿ — Al-Khalīl said: one says dhahabat al-ibil ṣaʿāṣiʿa, the camels went off in scattered groups.
3. ṣaʿṣaʿtu al-shayʾa fa-taṣaʿṣaʿa — I shook the thing, and it moved: this is said when you set something moving and it moves.
صعب:
The letters ṣād, ʿayn and bāʾ are a sound, consistent root indicating the opposite of ease.

1. al-amr al-ṣaʿb — a difficult matter, the opposite of an easy, tractable one. One says ṣaʿuba yaṣʿubu ṣuʿūba; one also says aṣʿabtu al-amr, I found the matter difficult.
2. al-muṣʿab — the [untrained, unridden] stud camel, so named for its strength and vigor.
3. aṣʿabnā al-jamal — we left the camel unridden. It is mentioned that they [likewise] say aṣʿabtu al-nāqa, when you leave a she-camel and do not load her; this is a figurative use.

And in the sand [dune country] there are maṣāʿib [difficult stretches].
صعد:
The letters ṣād, ʿayn and dāl are a sound root pointing to rising and to hardship.

From this: al-ṣaʿūd, the going up, the opposite of al-ḥadūr, the going down. One says ṣaʿida yaṣʿadu — he climbed. Al-iṣʿād is to face the downward slope from a higher place. Al-ṣaʿūd is also the steep hard pass, and hardship in an affair. God, exalted be He, said: {I shall burden him with a hard climb} [al-Muddaththir: 17].

A poet said, in a line of verse:
ʿUtba and al-Muʿallā forbade the man of Taym, and they said: the hard climb will drive you back.

As for al-ṣaʿadāt, they are the roads; the single one is ṣaʿīd. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: "Beware of sitting in the roads, except one who gives them their due." One says ṣaʿīd, ṣuʿud and ṣuʿudāt, and that last is a plural of a plural, as one says ṭarīq, ṭuruq and ṭuruqāt — a road, roads, roads.

As for al-ṣaʿīd, some people said it is the face of the earth. Abū Isḥāq al-Zajjāj used to say: it is the face of the earth, and the place, whether there is dust on it or not. Al-Zajjāj said: the people of the language do not differ that al-ṣaʿīd is not dust. This is the position the followers of Mālik ibn Anas hold. Their saying that al-ṣaʿīd is the face of the earth, whether it has dust on it or not, is our own position too — except that the truth has more right to be followed, and the matter is otherwise than what al-Zajjāj said. For Abū ʿUbayd related from al-Aṣmaʿī that al-ṣaʿīd is dust. And in the book known as al-Khalīl's is their saying tayammam bi-l-ṣaʿīd — cleanse yourself with the ṣaʿīd — meaning take of its dust. So this is the opposite of what al-Zajjāj said.

And from this section is al-ṣuʿadā', which is a breathing out with pain; it is a breath that rises, so it follows the sense of the section.

As for al-ṣaʿūd among she-camels, she is the one whose young dies, so she is brought back to her first offspring and gives it milk. That, so it is said, is better for her milk. And it is said: rather she is the one that casts her young. That is the explanation of the line:
Hers is the milk of the khaliyya, the she-camel left to be milked, and of the ṣaʿūd.

One says taṣaʿʿadanī al-amr, when a matter weighs hard on you. ʿUmar said: "The sermon of marriage never weighed hard on me." And some of them said: "The sermon is a hard climb, and on a man of understanding it is heavier still."

Near to this is the saying of Abū ʿAmr: aṣʿada fī al-bilād — he went off through the land, wherever he turned. From it is al-Aʿshā's saying, in a line of verse:
If you ask about me, then many is the questioner, eager for news of al-Aʿshā, wherever he has gone.

And of what is not far from the same sense is al-ṣaʿda among women: the woman straight of stature, as though she were a ṣaʿda, which is the even spear-shaft that grows so, needing no straightening.
صعر:
The letters ṣād, ʿayn and rā' are a regular root indicating a tilt in a thing. From that: al-ṣaʿar, a tilt in the neck. Al-taṣʿīr: turning the cheek away from looking at someone, out of pride. And sometimes a person or an ostrich is aṣʿar [tilt-necked] by nature. God, exalted, said: {and do not turn your cheek away from people in pride} [Luqmān: 18]. This is from al-ṣayʿariyya, a camel's swerving in its gait. Al-ṣayʿariyya is also a brand-mark among the brand-marks placed on she-camels' necks, and perhaps there is a swerve in its shape. Al-Musayyab said, in a line of verse:
Upon a swift one bearing the ṣayʿariyya brand, scarred by the branding.

As for the hadith "laysa fīhim illā aṣʿaru aw abtaru" — its meaning is: there is none among them but one puffed up with conceit and passing away, or one abased and cut off. One says sanāmun ṣayʿariyyun, meaning a huge hump; it was named so because when it grows large it tilts. Among what strays from this root is their saying qarabun muṣʿarrun, meaning a hard, forced night-march to water. It was said, in a line of verse:
And they made a hard, forced march to water.

God knows best what is correct.
صعف: The letters ṣād, ʿayn and fāʾ are not [an established] root. Though they do say al-ṣaʿf is a [kind of] drink.
صعق:
The letters ṣād, ʿayn and qāf are a single root pointing to a crash and a violence of sound. Of that is *al-ṣaʿq*, which is the loud noise. One says *ḥimār ṣaʿiq al-ṣawt* of a donkey whose bray is loud. From it comes *al-ṣāʿiqa*, the thunderbolt, which is the violent fall of the thunder. And it is said that *al-ṣuʿāq* is the loud sound. From it comes their saying *ṣaʿiqa* when a man dies, as though a thunderbolt had struck him.

God, exalted, said: {and the trumpet is blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth falls dead, save whom God wills} [al-Zumar: 68].
صعل:
A small root [ṣād-ʿayn-lām] indicating smallness and being stripped bare.

1. al-ṣaʿl — small-headed, said of men and of ostriches. A poet said, in a line of verse: "Small of head, I said to him..."
2. A donkey is called ṣaʿl when its coat has worn away.
3. One says rajul aṣʿal and imraʾa ṣaʿlāʾ [man and woman so described].
4. al-ṣaʿla, said of a palm tree: crooked and bare at the base of its fronds.
صعن:
A small root [ṣād-ʿayn-nūn] indicating fineness in a thing.

1. "So-and-so is ṣiʿwann al-raʾs," meaning fine, slender of head.
2. A finely-shaped ear is [also] called muṣʿanna. A poet said, in a line of verse: "...and the ear finely-formed, like a reed-pen."
صعو: The letters ṣād, ʿayn and the weak letter form a single word: al-ṣaʿwa, a small bird [a sparrow]; plural ṣiʿāʾ.
صغر:
The letters ṣād, ghayn and rā' are a sound root that points to smallness and lowliness. From that is al-ṣighar, smallness, the opposite of largeness; and al-ṣaghīr, the small one, the opposite of the great one. Al-ṣāghir is the one who accepts being wronged, ṣughran and ṣaghāran.

One says aṣgharat al-nāqa wa akbarat. Al-iṣghār is her low moaning, [and al-ikbār is] the high one. Al-Khansā' said, in a line of verse:
She has two moanings, a low one and a high one.
صغل: The letters ṣād, ghayn and lām are not [an established] root. Al-ṣaghil is simply [someone] poorly nourished; the original form of this word has a sīn — saghil. And God knows best what is correct.
صغوى:
The letters ṣād, ghayn and the weak letter are a sound root indicating leaning.

1. "Ṣighw of so-and-so is with you," meaning his inclination is toward you.
2. ṣaghati al-nujūm — the stars leaned toward setting.
3. aṣghā ilayhi — he leaned his hearing toward it, he listened attentively.
4. aṣghaytu al-ināʾ — I tilted the vessel.
5. Those among a man's companions and kin who lean toward him and take his side are called his ṣāghiya.

It is also reported: ṣaghawtu ilayhi aṣghā ṣaghwan and ṣaghan, the latter with a short final vowel.
صف:
The letters ṣād and fāʾ indicate a single root: evenness in a thing, and two things being level with each other in position.

1. al-ṣaff — a row. One says waqafā ṣaffan, when each of two men stood beside the other. One also says iṣṭaffa al-qawm and taṣāffū, the people lined up together.
2. al-ṣafṣaf — level ground; this is the origin word behind al-ṣaff. From it, the place where people stand lined up for battle is called a maṣaff, plural maṣāff.
3. al-ṣafūf — a she-camel that "lines up," meaning she gives enough at one milking to fill two milk-pails at once. Al-ṣafūf is also said of a she-camel that presses her forelegs together while being milked.

Among what deviates from this chapter — though a case might possibly be sought for it by analogy, except that we dislike a forced and unwelcome analogy — is what we have just mentioned: al-ṣafīf. Some said it is dried, cured meat. Others said it is meat carried on journeys, cooked or roasted, that never finishes cooking through.

A poet said, in a line of verse: "So the meat-cooks spent the day, one of them finishing meat left half-roasted [ṣafīf], another a hastily-made stew."
صفح:
The letters sad, fa and ha are a single sound root, consistently used, and it indicates breadth and width.

1. safh of a thing — its breadth, its width.
2. ra's musaffah — a broad head.
3. al-safiha — any broad sword.
4. safhata l-sayf — the two flat faces of the sword.
5. Any broad stone is called safiha, plural safa'ih.
6. al-suffah — any broad stone.

Al-Nabigha said, in a line of verse:
It cuts through the doubled-weave mail-coat, and with the broad stones they strike fire like the fire-beetle's glow.

From this root too: al-musafaha, shaking hands — as if one had stuck his hand to the flat side of the other's hand. Al-safh is the side (al-janb). Safha of anything: its two sides. As for their saying 'safaha 'anhu' — turning away from someone's offense — it too is from this root, because when he turns from him it is as if he has shown him his flat side and his side (safhatahu wa safhahu), that is his breadth and his flank; it is a figure of speech (a metaphor).

From this root also: 'safahtu l-rajula wa asfahtuhu', when he asked you [for something] and you refused him — this comes from your having shown him your flat side, turning away from him. One says: 'safahtu l-ibila 'ala l-hawd', when you drove the camels across/past the trough — as if you showed the trough their sides (safahatiha), that is their flanks.

An anomaly from this root: their saying 'safahtu l-rajula safhan', when you gave the man a drink — whatever the drink and whenever it was given.
صفد:
The letters ṣād, fā' and dāl are two sound roots: one is giving, the other is binding with something.

The first: al-ṣafad. One says aṣfadtuhu, when you gave to him. He said, in a line of verse:
"This is the praise — if you hear the one who speaks it — I did not offer it seeking a gift, may cursing be spared you."

As for al-ṣafd, it is the shackle/collar; and it is said al-ṣafd is binding fast. al-aṣfād — the fetters. al-ṣifād is also a fetter. He said, in a line of verse:
"Why did you not show mercy to your little brother Maʿbad, while the man of ʿĀmir led him in fetters?"
And in the hadith: "When the month of Ramadan enters, the devils are bound in fetters."
صفر:
The letters ṣād, fā' and rā' have six senses: the first is a color among colors. The second: an empty thing. The third: a substance among the earth's substances. The fourth: a sound. The fifth: a time. The sixth: a plant.

1. The first: al-ṣufra among colors, yellow. Banū al-Aṣfar — the kings of the Byzantines, named for a yellowness that came over their forefather.
2. al-aṣfar can also mean black, as in his saying, in a line of verse:
those are my horses from it, and those my riding-camels; they are dark, their young like raisins.
3. The second sense: a thing that is empty; one says huwa ṣifr, it is empty.
4. In cursing they say: "may his vessel go empty" — meaning may his livestock perish.
5. Also from this root, they say of someone who has madness: "he is in ṣufra / ṣifra" (with ḍamma or kasra), when he is passing through days in which his reason leaves him. The reasoning holds, since he is as though emptied of his reason.
6. The third sense: al-ṣufr, one of the earth's substances, said to be copper. It is also said as al-ṣifr.

ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm al-Qaṭṭān told me, from ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, from Abū ʿUbayd, who said: al-Aṣmaʿī said: nuḥās means the underlying nature and substance [of a thing]; and nuḥās is also the ṣufr from which vessels are made — he said "al-ṣufr," with ḍamma on the ṣād. Abū ʿUbayd said the same, except that he said "al-ṣifr," with kasra on the ṣād.

7. As for the fourth sense: al-ṣafīr, the whistling call of a bird. Their saying "there is not a ṣāfir [whistler] in it" comes from this, as if it means one who makes a sound.
8. As for the time-sense: Ṣafar, the name of this month. Ibn Durayd said: the two Ṣafars are two months of the year; one of them was renamed al-Muḥarram in Islam.
9. al-ṣafarī — a plant that grows at the start of autumn. Al-ṣafarī, in the birthing-season of livestock, comes after al-yaqaẓī.
10. As for the plant-sense: al-ṣafār, a plant said to be the dried-out stalk of būhmā-grass. He said, in a line of verse:
so we spent the night naked, beside our colt, pulling the dry ṣafār-grass from its lips.
صفع: The letters ṣād, fāʾ and ʿayn are a single, well-known word.
صفق:
The letters ṣād, fāʾ and qāf are a sound root indicating a flat-sided thing meeting another like it with force.

1. ṣafaqtu al-shayʾa bi-yadī — I struck the thing with my hand, meaning you hit it forcefully with your palm.
2. al-ṣafqa — the striking of hand upon hand in a sale or a pledge of allegiance, a custom current among those who trade with each other.
3. aṣfaqa al-qawm ʿalā al-amr, meaning they united upon it, comes from this too — they are likened to two parties striking hands together over a sale.
4. al-ṣafaq — the water poured onto freshly tanned hide, which then comes out of it yellowed.
5. al-sharāb al-muṣaffaq — drink poured over from one vessel to another, as though it "struck" the vessel when it met it, and the vessel was "struck" with it.
6. ṣafaqa al-ibil — he moved the camels from one pasture to another.

Then, by extension from this, anything flat and spread out came to be called ṣafq, even if it is not struck against anything.

7. The two sides of the neck are called ṣafqān, and each side [of a thing generally] is a ṣafq.
8. The skin next to the dark part of the belly is [also] called ṣafq.

Among what deviates from this chapter, though a rationale might be found for it, is their saying "a ṣafūq bow," said of one that is supple and springs back [after being drawn].
صفن:
The letters ṣād, fā' and nūn are two sound roots: one is a kind of standing, the other a container.

The first: al-ṣufūn, which is for a horse to stand on three legs and raise the fourth, while still touching the ground with the tip of its hoof. Al-ṣāfin is one who stands with his feet lined up together. In the hadith of al-Barā': "we stood behind the Messenger of God, peace and blessings of God be upon him and his family, standing still (ṣufūnan)." From this comes taṣāfana al-qawm [the water] — when they shared it out by the ṣufn, and al-ṣufn is a hide used to draw water. It was said, in a line of verse:
When we shared out the water-skin between us, the arms of the big-bellied man of ʿAnbar reached eagerly toward me.

It is said that this sharing was measured with a small stone: it was dropped into the vessel, and each man given to drink the amount of water that would cover it.

Among what strays from the two roots: al-ṣāfin, which is a vein.
صفو:
The letters ṣād, fā' and the weak letter are a single root pointing to being free of every impurity. From it is al-ṣafā', clearness, which is the opposite of muddiness; one says ṣafā yaṣfū when a thing becomes pure. One says laka ṣafwu hādhā al-amri wa-ṣifwatuhu — the clear best of this matter is yours. And Muhammad is God Almighty's chosen and best out of His creation, and His elect — may God bless him and his family and grant them peace. Al-ṣafiyy is what the leader picks out of the spoil for himself; it is also said with the hā', al-ṣafiyya, and the plural is al-ṣafāyā. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Yours is the fourth part of it and the choice pickings ... and your ruling, and the extra taken on the way, and the surplus.

Al-ṣafiyya and al-ṣafiyy — and without the hā' it is better known — is the she-camel with much milk and the palm-tree with a heavy crop; the plural is al-ṣafāyā. It was called ṣafiyy only because its owner picks it out for himself.

From this chapter is their saying aṣfat al-dajāja when the hen stops laying, iṣfā'an. That is as though she had become ṣafat, that is, free of eggs; then it was put on the pattern af'alat, to keep it apart from the rest of what belongs in its chapter. And the poet is likened to this when his poetry dries up.

From this chapter is al-ṣafā, which is the smooth rock, and it is al-ṣafwān; the single one is ṣafwāna, and it was called ṣafwāna for that reason, because it is clear of clay and sand. Al-Aṣma'ī said: al-ṣafwān and al-ṣafwā' and al-ṣafā are all one. And he recited, in a line of verse:
As the smooth rock slips beneath the one who comes down it.

And one says yawm ṣafwān of a day with a clear sun and hard cold.
صقب:
The letters ṣād, qāf and bāʾ hardly amount to a [true] root, because the ṣād here sometimes stands for a sīn — the two chapters overlap, sometimes said with sīn and sometimes with ṣād — except that it indicates nearness, and also length together with thinness.

As for nearness:

1. al-ṣaqab — nearness. It occurs in the hadith: "The neighbor has the greater right to what is near him" — meaning [this applies to] the right of pre-emption.
2. al-ṣāqib — the near one.
3. "The two men yataṣāqabān" in the same quarter, when they live close to each other.

As for the other sense: al-ṣaqb is the pole with which a tent is propped up; plural ṣuqūb. Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse: "Two poles from which the bark has not been stripped."

As for their saying ṣaqabtu al-shayʾa, meaning I struck it, this applies only to something solid and dry. It is possible this comes from letter-substitution, as though from ṣaqaʿtuhu, the bāʾ standing in for the ʿayn.
صقر:
A small root [ṣād-qāf-rāʾ] indicating a thing striking down hard.

1. al-ṣaqr — your striking a rock with a pickaxe; the pickaxe is called al-ṣāqūr, and may also be said with a final tāʾ, al-ṣāqūra.
2. al-ṣaqr — this bird [the falcon], so named because it strikes its prey with force.
3. ṣaqarāt al-shams — the intensity of the sun's beating down on the ground. A poet said, in a line of verse: "When the sun blazes fiercely, he shelters from its scorching beat beneath the branches of a tree grown thick from spring rain in the sandy hollow, its leaves stripped for grazing."

It is reported of the Arabs: "so-and-so came with al-ṣuqar wa-l-buqar," said when he comes out with a lie. This deviates from the root just described. Likewise al-ṣāqūra, in the poetry of Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt, is a deviant usage; it is said to mean the third heaven, though I do not think that belongs to sound Arabic speech — there are [other such] things in Umayya's poetry. As for date-syrup, and their calling it ṣaqr, that belongs to the speech of settled townspeople, and is not pure Bedouin Arabic.
صقع:
The letters ṣād, qāf and ʿayn are three roots: one is a thing striking down upon another, such as a blow and the like; another is a sound; and the third is one thing covering another.

The first: al-ṣaqʿ, striking with the flat of the palm. One says ṣaqaʿahu ṣaqʿan.

As for the sound: their saying ṣaqaʿa al-dīk yaṣqaʿu, the rooster crowed.

1. khaṭīb miṣqaʿ — an eloquent orator, as though named for the loudness of his voice.

As for the third root, one thing covering another: it is al-ṣiqāʿ, the cloth a woman wraps over her head to keep oil off her headscarf. Al-ṣaqīʿ — frost that scorches plants — fits here too, as though it were something that covered the plant and burned it, though it also fits under the chapter of striking.

1. al-ʿuqāb al-ṣaqʿāʾ — the eagle white on the head, as though whiteness had covered its head.
2. al-ṣiqāʿ — [also] the face-veil.
3. al-ṣiqāʿ — [also] something tied around a she-camel's nose. Al-Quṭāmī said, in a line of verse: "When I saw a head inclined to unruliness, I bound for it the head-coverings and the nose-strap."
4. al-ṣaqaʿ — a faintness that takes hold of a person from the heat, in the words of Suwayd, in a line of verse: "It seizes the traveler in it, like a swoon."
5. al-ṣāqiʿa [thunderbolt] — possibly named because it envelops, and possibly belonging instead to the chapter of striking. As for the words of Aws, in a line of verse: "O father of Dulayja, who is there for a lone tribe, struck by enemies, in Shawwāl?" — some said what befell him from the enemies is like a thunderbolt.
6. al-ṣawqaʿa — the turban, because it covers the head.

What remains of the chapter belongs to letter-substitution, since al-ṣuqʿ means a region. The origin, as Al-Khalīl stated, has a sīn, as though the original form was "saqaʿa." From this same substituted chapter is their saying "I do not know where he ṣaqaʿa," meaning where he went — to what region he went. And of Aws's words "struck by enemies," it was said this means the one withdrawn to [some] region.
صقل:
A small root [ṣād-qāf-lām] indicating the polishing of a thing; other things are then measured against it by analogy.

1. ṣaqaltu al-sayf aṣquluhu — I polished the sword; the craftsman who does this is al-ṣayqal. Al-ṣaqīl [also] means the sword itself.
2. "The horse is in its ṣiqāl," meaning its careful keeping, said when it is well looked after — as though it is being polished and groomed.
3. al-ṣuql, of a man or a horse, is the flank; the flank is the smoothest part of the body, so it was called ṣaql, as though it had been polished.
4. From this one says "a ṣaqil horse," meaning long in both flanks.
صك:
The letters ṣād and kāf are a root indicating two things meeting with force and violence, as though one of them were striking the other. From this is their saying: ṣakaktu al-shayʾa ṣakkan, I struck the thing forcefully.

1. al-ṣakak — a man's two knees knocking together.
2. ṣakka al-bāb — he shut the door forcefully and hard.
3. miṣakkak — a camel is called miṣakkak when its flesh has become tightly packed and firm on it.
4. miṣakk — a man described as miṣakk is strong. The same word is used of horses, donkeys, and other animals.

As for their saying "I came to him at ṣakkat ʿUmayy," what is meant is that a blind man meets one like himself and the two of them collide, each striking the other. This is an expression they coined specifically for the hottest part of midday, when the heat is at its fiercest.
صكم:
The letters ṣād, kāf and mīm are a single root indicating striking a thing hard.

1. al-ṣakma — a violent collision.
2. ṣakamathum ṣawākim al-dahr — the hard blows of time struck them, the Arabs say.
3. The horse yaṣkumu, when it bites down on its bit, stretching out its head.
4. Al-Farrāʾ said: ṣakamahu, meaning he struck him and shoved him.
صل:
The letters ṣād and lām are two roots: one indicates moisture and a little water, the other a sound.

As for the first: al-ṣalla is the ground, called al-tharā for its moisture — though some Arabs use al-ṣalla to mean the moist soil itself. For that same reason, the water left standing in a pool is called ṣulṣula.

1. ṣilāl al-maṭar — what falls of the rain, a little at a time, one part after another.
2. ṣilāl — said of scattered plants, because they are named after the scattered rain. A poet said, in a line of verse: "...like the stones of Lubn, driving the scattered patches [of herbage] along."
3. ṣalla al-laḥm — the meat, roasted or cooked, went off, when its smell changed. This comes from al-ṣalla [the moist ground], as though it had been buried in that moist ground and so spoiled. The verbal noun of this is al-ṣulūl. A poet said, in a line of verse: "That is a young man who gives away freely what his cooking-pot holds; spoiling [al-ṣulūl] does not ruin the meat kept with him."

As for the sound [root]: one says ṣalla al-lijām, and likewise of other things, when it makes a sound. When this happens repeatedly, one says ṣalṣala. Fired clay is called ṣalṣāl for this reason, because it makes a sound and rattles.

Among what deviates from these two roots: 1. al-ṣill — a calamity; plural aṣlāl. 2. ṣallathum al-ṣālla — the calamity struck them, when disaster befell them.
صلب:
The letters sad, lam and ba are two roots: one indicating hardness and strength, the other a kind of rendered fat.

The first: al-sulb, the hard thing. Likewise the back was called sulb for its strength. It is said that al-salab means al-sulb. A line is recited:
In a back like a well-oiled tanned rein-strap.

From this too: al-salib, the severe stage of fever. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Your sweet water — had I drunk it while the violent chill of fever gripped me, it would surely have healed me.

Al-Kisa'i related: 'salabat 'alayhi l-humma', the fever persisted on him and grew severe, so he is 'maslub 'alayhi' — overcome by it.

From this root: al-sullabiyya, the stones of a whetstone. One says 'sinanun musallab', a sharpened spearhead. From it too: al-tasliib, moist dates reaching full dryness/hardness; one says 'sallaba'. From this root also: al-salib, meaning the standard/banner. Al-Nabigha said:
Herds of penned camels stood all day beside a standard raised at al-Zawra'.

As for the second root, it is al-salib, meaning fat rendered from bone. One says: the man 'istalaba' — he gathered bones and extracted their fat to use as a condiment. A line is recited:
And the old man of the household spent the night rendering fat from bones.

They said: the crucified man (al-maslub) was so named as if fatness runs over his face. [And al-salib means the crucified one.] Then, by association, the thing on which one is crucified was itself called salib. A garment with the image of a cross on it is 'thawbun musallab'. In the hadith concerning the cross-patterned garment: that the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him and his family, 'whenever he saw it on a garment, would cut it out' — that is, remove it.

As for what is said, that al-sawlab is seed scattered over the ground and then ploughed under — this is from the coined, invented speech that has no true root basis.
صلت:
The letters ṣād, lām and tā' are a single root that indicates a thing's standing out and being clear.
1. al-ṣult — a clear, open forehead; one says "ṣalt al-jabīn," clear of brow, and a man is praised for it. Kuthayyir said, in a line of verse: Clear of brow — when he smiles, laughing, the finest of his wealth falls due as pledge to his laughter.
2. al-sayf al-ṣalt and al-iṣlīt — the sword that is polished and bright; from this one says "aṣlata fulānun sayfahu," so-and-so drew his sword, when he bared it from its sheath.
3. al-ṣult — the knife, plural aṣlāt; one says "ḍarabahu bi-l-sayfi ṣaltan wa-ṣultan," he struck him with the sword bare and unsheathed.
4. al-ḥimār al-ṣaltān — the donkey, as if, when it runs, it stands forth (inṣalata), meaning it shows and displays itself.
5. jā'a bi-maraqin yaṣlitu — said of one who brings broth that is thin, low in fat and high in water; so called because its water shows and appears clearly on its surface, from the scantness of fat upon it.
صلج:
The letters ṣād, lām and jīm are not anything, because of how rarely ṣād combines with jīm. Words have been reported for it that have no basis in the old speech of the Arabs.
1. al-ṣawlaj — this, as they claim, is fine silver; one says "hādhihi fiḍḍatun ṣawlaj," this is ṣawlaj-silver.
2. al-ṣawlajān — this word is also from it.
3. al-aṣlaj — hard and very smooth.

And all of that is without real meaning.
صلح:
The letters ṣād, lām and ḥā' are a single root pointing to the opposite of corruption. One says: ṣaluḥa al-shay', yaṣluḥu, ṣalāḥan - the thing was sound. And one says ṣalaḥa with a fatḥa on the lām. And Ibn al-Sikkīt reported both ṣalaḥa and ṣaluḥa. And one says ṣalaḥa ṣulūḥan. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And how shall it be with my kin when you have reviled me? After the reviling of a man's two parents there is no setting right.

And some of the people of learning said that Mecca is called Ṣalāḥ.
صلخ: The letters ṣād, lām and khā' have in them a single word. It is said that al-aṣlakh is the deaf one. Salama said: al-Farrā' said, "al-Kumayt was deaf, al-aṣlakh."
صلد:
The letters ṣād, lām and dāl are a single sound root indicating hardness and dryness. From that: al-ḥajar al-ṣald, the hard rock. Upon this is built their saying ṣalida al-zand — a fire-stick failed to strike fire, and aṣladtuhu — I made it fail. From it: al-ra's al-ṣald, a head that grows no hair, like ground that grows nothing. Ru'ba said, in a line of verse:
Gleaming, in the bare patches of a broad, receding forehead.

A miser is called aṣlad, either from the ground that grows nothing, or from the fire-stick that will not strike. One says nāqatun ṣalūd, a she-camel scant and low in milk, with a thick-skinned udder. From it: al-faras al-ṣalūd, a horse that does not sweat. And when a she-camel gives birth and has no milk, she is called nāqatun miṣlād.
صلع:
The letters ṣād, lām and ʿayn are a sound root indicating smoothness.
1. al-ṣalaʿ — baldness of the head; its origin is taken from al-ṣullāʿ, the broad, smooth rock, singular ṣullāʿa.
2. jabalun ṣalīʿ — a mountain that is smooth and grows nothing. 'Amr ibn Ma'dīkarib said, in a line of verse: And the advance of one troop to meet another, as though its bulk were a bald hilltop.
3. ṣalʿā' — said of the ʿurfuṭa tree [a thorny acacia] when the tips of its branches fall off.
4. ṣalʿā' — also the name given to a great calamity, meaning one that is stark and plain, whose matter cannot be hidden.
5. al-ṣalʿa — the bald spot on the head.
6. al-ṣalʿā' of sands — that which grows no plant and no tree.
7. al-uṣayliʿ — the name for a kind of snake, like the one that came in the hadith: "The hoarded wealth of one of them will come on the Day of Resurrection as a bald serpent" — meaning by that the one whose head-hair has fallen out, from how fat it has grown. The poet said, in a line of verse: It hosted venom until the skin of its head fell away from the bone — a deadly viper, fierce of sting, defiant.
صلغ: The letters ṣād, lām and ghayn are not a root, because it belongs to the category of letter-substitution. The sheep whose tooth is complete in its fifth year is called ṣāligh. One says "ṣalagha ṣulūghan."
صلف:
The letters ṣād, lām and fā' are a sound root indicating hardness and roughness.
1. al-ṣalaf — the scantness of nourishment in food. They say, in proverbs: "Ṣalaf beneath the thundering cloud" — said of one who talks much and praises himself while there is no good in him.
2. ṣalifat al-mar'atu ʿinda zawjihā — said of a woman when she does not find favour with her husband; she is bayyinat al-ṣalaf, plainly so. He said, in a line of verse: And grief and ṣalaf returned to her.
3. aṣlafa Allāhu rufghahā — al-Shaybānī said this is said of a woman: "May God make her rufgh [her intimate flesh] harsh" — meaning by that, God makes her hateful to her husband.
4. al-arḍ al-ṣalfā' — hard ground; and al-makān al-aṣlaf — a hard place. This is the true origin within this chapter.
5. al-ṣalīf — the side of the neck, which is hard.
6. al-ṣalīfān — two pieces of wood that lie crosswise on the camel-saddle, by which the litters are bound. He said, in a line of verse: Lean-bellied, as though its neck were the ṣalīf.
7. al-rajul al-ṣalif — the man who is ṣalif comes from this; it is from harshness and scantness of good.

Al-Khalīl used to say: al-ṣalaf is exceeding one's true measure of refinement, and claiming for oneself beyond that.
صلق:
The letters ṣād, lām and qāf are a single root indicating a loud cry, a striking blow, and the like.
1. al-ṣalq — a loud, harsh cry. The Messenger of God — peace and blessings upon him and his family — said: "He who wails loudly or shaves his head [in mourning] is not of us" — meaning the loud crying out when a calamity befalls.
2. al-ṣallāq and al-miṣlāq — one loud of voice.
3. al-ṣalqa — a collision, a fearsome clash. Labīd said, in a line of verse: We struck against Murād a fierce clash, and against Ṣudā', which brought them down to ruin. Al-Kisā'ī said: al-ṣalqa is crying out, and one says "aṣlaqū iṣlāqan," they cried out; he cited this same line of verse as evidence.
4. ṣalaqahu bi-l-ʿaṣā — Abū Zayd said this means he struck him with the stick.
5. al-ṣalq — the clash of horses in a raid.
6. ṣalaqa banū fulānin banī fulānin — said when one clan struck another and killed them in a swift slaughter.
7. taṣallaqat al-ḥāmil — said of the pregnant [female] when labour pains seize her and she throws herself now on one side, now on the other.
8. al-faḥl yuṣliqu bi-nābihi — the stallion does this with its tusk, which is its grinding.
9. al-ṣalaqāt — the camel-tusks that grind in this way. He said, in a line of verse: Its old she-camels did not weep around you, and its grinding tusks scattered like where trees are planted. [This line is obscure and rendered as best as can be made out.]

As for the round, level plain, it is called al-ṣalaq, but this does not belong here, because it is a case of letter-substitution — one also says al-salaq for it, which has already been mentioned elsewhere. The line of Abū Du'ād is recited with both sīn and ṣād: You see its mouth, when it comes forward, like the barren ṣalaq-plain. And I do not deny that this whole chapter may be carried on the pattern of letter-substitution.
10. al-ṣalā'iq — thin bread, singular ṣalīqa; it may also be said with rā' as al-ṣarīqa, and with sīn as al-salā'iq. Perhaps it belongs to later, non-classical speech.
صلم:
The letters ṣād, lām and mīm are a single root indicating cutting off and uprooting entirely.

1. ṣalama udhunahu — he cut off his ear entirely; the ear is [likewise] said to be uṣṭulimat, cut off. Al-Farrāʾ recited, in a line of verse: "Like the ostrich, which while unharmed had [full] ears — until doom and cowardice lured it on; it came to buy a horn, or trade for one, while in time's dealings there is both profit and loss in trading. So it was said: 'Your ears are already a wrong done to you' — then they were cut off entirely, down to the ear-hole, so that now it has neither horn nor ear."
2. al-ṣaylam — a calamity, a momentous event, as though named because it "cuts off entirely."
3. al-ṣalāma — also said with a kasra, al-ṣilāma — a splinter group of people, so named because it has cut itself off from the larger body. A poet said, in a line of verse: "Woe to your mothers, however you have come — while you are but splinter-groups, many though your number is."
صلى:
The letters ṣād, lām and the weak letter are two roots: one is fire and what resembles it, such as fever; the other is a kind of worship.
As for the first:
1. ṣalaytu al-ʿūda bi-l-nār — I roasted the stick with fire.
2. al-ṣalā — the heat of the fire.
3. iṣṭalaytu bi-l-nār — I warmed myself at the fire.
4. al-ṣilā' — what one warms oneself with, and what is used to kindle and light the fire.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
She makes aloeswood, yalanjūj, and rand into kindling for herself upon the brazier.

As for the second: it is al-ṣalāh, which is supplication. The Messenger of God — peace and blessings upon him and his family — said: "If one of you is invited to a meal, let him accept; if he is not fasting, let him eat, and if he is fasting, let him pray (fal-yuṣalli)" — meaning let him supplicate for them with good and blessing.

Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
My daughter says, as I made ready to depart: O Lord, spare my father ailments and pain.
Upon you be the like of what you have prayed; so close your eyes and sleep, for a man's side has its place to lie.

And he said, describing wine, in a line of verse:
The wind faced it in its jar, and prayed over its jar, and traced a mark.

And al-ṣalāh is that which the sacred law brought, consisting of bowing, prostration, and the rest of the bounds of prayer.

As for al-ṣalāh from God, Exalted is He, it is mercy. From this is the hadith: "O God, bless the family of Abū Awfā" — meaning by that, mercy.

Among what falls outside this chapter is a word that came in the hadith: "Satan has traps and maṣālī" — he said: these are snares, the singular of which is miṣlāh.
صم:
The letters ṣād and mīm are a root indicating a thing drawing tightly together, and the disappearance of any hole or opening.

1. al-ṣamam — deafness in the ear. One says ṣamimtu, anta taṣammu ṣamaman [I became/you become deaf]. Sometimes they say ṣumma with the same meaning as ṣamma. One also says aṣmamtu al-rajul, when you find a man to be deaf. Ibn Aḥmar said, in a line of verse: "Deaf is the call of the woman who blames me — she claims to remember our last, and forgets our first."
2. al-ṣammāʾ — a calamity, as though from deafness, meaning it is a matter with no opening or relief in it. From this too is ishtimāl al-ṣammāʾ: wrapping yourself fully in your garment, then throwing its left side over the right.

The Arabs say, to magnify a matter: "ṣammī ṣamāmi" — go deaf, deafness itself! The origin of this is their saying "a pebble has gone deaf with blood," meaning that on the day of battle blood becomes so abundant on the ground that if a pebble were dropped, no sound of its fall would be heard. This is in the words of Imruʾ al-Qays, in a line of verse: "I have been given, in place of Wāʾil and Kinda, enemies, and Fahm too — go deaf, O daughter of the mountain." He means to magnify what has befallen him and been dealt to him.

1. ṣimām al-qārūra — the stopper of the flask, so named because it seals its opening.

Their saying ṣammama fī al-amr, meaning he pressed ahead in a matter headlong, follows the same pattern just described: as though, once set on doing it, he did not hear the blame of any blamer nor the forbidding of any forbidder — as if he had gone deaf.

1. al-ṣamṣām and al-ṣamṣāma — a sword, derived from this root.
2. ṣammama — [also] means he bit into a thing and sank his teeth firmly into it.
3. al-ṣammān — a [tract of] land. Some said any land bordering a sandy tract is called ṣammāna. This is correct, because sand has gaps in it, while ṣammāna ground does not.
4. al-ṣimṣim — a thickset man, named for what has just been described, as though there were no gap in his flesh.
5. The lion, too, is called ṣimma, as though he cannot be reached from any side.
6. al-ṣimṣima — a group of people, so named because it has gathered so tightly that there is no gap or opening left in it.
صمت:
The letters ṣād, mīm and tā' are a single root indicating vagueness and closing-off. From that: ṣamata al-rajul — a man fell silent; aṣmata means the same. From it their saying "laqītu fulānan bi-baldati iṣmit" — I met so-and-so in the land of iṣmit, meaning the empty wasteland where no one is, as if it were itself silent, holding no speaker. One says "mā lahu ṣāmitun wa lā nāṭiq" — he has neither ṣāmit nor nāṭiq: al-ṣāmit being gold and silver, al-nāṭiq being camels, sheep and horses. Al-ṣamūt is the soft coat of mail that makes no sound when a man puts it on. It was said, in a line of verse:
And every silent coat of mail, a wide one of Tubbaʿ's make, and of Sulaym's weaving, every trailing, well-forged one.

A door that is mubham (muṣmat) has been sealed shut. Al-ṣāmit of milk is the thick, curdled kind, named so because when it is poured into a vessel in that state, no sound is heard from it. One says "bittu ʿalā ṣimāti dhāka," meaning upon its intent. This may be an irregular form, or it may be a case of letter-substitution, as though taken from al-samt, meaning the path. It was said, in a line of verse:
And a need I stayed fixed upon its aim; I came to it alone by its proper way.

One says "ramāhu bi-ṣimātihi," meaning with what silenced him. And "aʿṭā al-ṣabiyya ṣumtatan," meaning he gave the child something to quiet him.
صمج: The letters ṣād, mīm and jīm are not anything, except that they say al-ṣamaj is the [hanging] lamps, singular ṣamaja. And they recite, in a line of verse: And the star is like the Byzantine lamps.
صمح:
The letters ṣād, mīm and ḥā' are a minor root indicating strength in a thing, or length.
1. al-ṣamaḥmaḥ — the tall one.
2. al-ṣumāḥ — they say this is cauterizing.
3. al-ṣumāḥ — [also,] stench.
4. al-ṣimḥā'a — the rough, coarse place.
صمخ: The letters ṣād, mīm and khā' are a single root and a single word: it is al-ṣimākh, the opening of the ear. One says "ṣamakhtuhu," when you strike his ṣimākh.
صمد:
The letters ṣād, mīm and dāl are two roots: one is intent, the other is hardness in a thing.

The first: al-ṣamd, intent. One says ṣamadtuhu ṣamdan — I turned toward it with intent. Fulānun muṣammad — so-and-so is a chief who is sought out in [important] matters; he is also called ṣamad for this. God, exalted be His praise, is al-Ṣamad, because His servants turn to Him (yaṣmidu) with prayer and petition. It was said, of al-Ṣamad, in a line of verse:
I struck him with a sharp sword, then said to him: take this, Ḥudhayf — for you are the chief who is sought out.

Ṭarafa said of al-muṣammad, in a line of verse:
And if the whole tribe should gather, you would find me at the peak of the lofty tent that all seek out.

The other root: al-ṣamd, any hard ground. Abū al-Najm said:
It leaves the hard ground behind, like the back of the rocky ridge.
صمر:
The letters ṣād, mīm and rā' — Ibn Durayd said this is a disused verb, and it is the base from which al-ṣamīr is formed.
1. rajulun ṣamīr — a man whose flesh has dried onto his bones.
2. al-ṣamr — stench.
3. al-mutaṣammir — one who exposes himself to the sun.
4. laqiytuhu bi-l-ṣumayr — I met him at al-ṣumayr, meaning at the time of sunset.

And in all of that there is room for doubt.
صمع:
The letters ṣād, mīm and ʿayn are a single root indicating fineness in a thing and a tight closeness. Al-Khalīl and others said: everything drawn tightly together is mutaṣammiʿ. He said: from this is the derivation of al-ṣawmaʿa, the [monk's] cell. From that: al-ṣamaʿ in the ears. One says huwa aṣmaʿ, when his ears lie close and flat. One says qalbun aṣmaʿ, meaning a fine, sharp mind. Al-buhmā [a wild grass], when it rises without yet splitting open, is called ṣamʿā', because in that state it is bunched close and fine. When a thing is smeared with something and clumps together, like the feathers of an arrow, it is called mutaṣammiʿ. It was said, in a line of verse:
So he shot, and drove clean through a barren wild she-ass a shaft, and it fell, its feathers clumped together.

Meaning smeared with blood and drawn tight. Al-kilāb ṣumʿu al-kuʿūb — dogs fine and small in their leg-joints. Al-Nābigha said:
Fine in their joints, free of any swelling.
صمغ: The letters ṣād, mīm and ghayn are a single word: it is al-ṣamgh, gum [tree resin].
صمك:
The letters ṣād, mīm and kāf are a minor root indicating strength and intensity.
1. al-ṣamakmak — the strong one.
2. al-ṣamkūk — a thing that is hard and intense.
3. al-ṣamkīk — anything sticky, like frankincense-resin and the like.
4. iṣmākka al-rajul — said of a man when he grows angry; this follows the same pattern of meaning.
5. iṣmākka al-laban — said of milk when it thickens until it becomes firm and turns like cheese.
صمل:
The letters ṣād, mīm and lām are a single root indicating hardness and firmness.
1. ṣamala al-shay'u ṣumūlan — said of a thing when it becomes hard and firm.
2. rajulun ṣumull — a man firm of build. Al-Khalīl used to say this is only said of one whose years have come together, that is, who has reached full maturity.
3. iṣma'alla al-nabāt — said of a plant when it grows strong and thick.
4. al-ṣāmil of anything — the dried-up one.
5. ṣamala al-shajar — said of a tree when it does not get enough water and so becomes coarse.
6. ṣamalahu bi-l-ʿaṣā — said when he struck him with the stick.

And God knows best what is correct.
صمى:
The letters ṣād, mīm and the weak letter are a single root indicating swiftness in a thing.
1. ṣamayān — the man who rushes swiftly into battle out of courage is called this; it is from al-ṣamayān, which is leaping and tumbling about.
2. inṣamā al-ṭā'ir — said of the bird when it swoops down.
3. aṣmā al-faras — said of the horse when it goes straight ahead, biting on its bit.
4. ramā al-rajulu al-ṣayda fa-aṣmā — a man shot the game and it "aṣmā," when he killed it on the spot; this is the opposite of "anmā," when it escapes wounded and dies elsewhere.
صن:
The letters ṣād and nūn are two roots: one indicates refusal and a proud turning-away of the face out of arrogance.

1. al-muṣinn — a man so described; they said he is one who holds his head high and turns to no one. They also said he is the silent one. They also said he is the one filled with rage. The rājiz-poet said, in a line of verse: "Is it my camels you take, defiantly?" — meaning: do you take my camels while no rebuke from any rebuker holds you back, and you turn to no one?

The other root indicates a foul smell. From this is al-ṣinn, the urine of the rock-hyrax, in the words of Jarīr: "She smears herself, her bared skin unlovely, with the hyrax's urine, taking it for perfume."

2. al-ṣunān — derived from this: the rank odor of the armpit.

As for their saying that one of the "Days of the Old Woman" [the last cold days of winter] is called al-ṣinn, this is something I have not found anyone to establish precisely or know the truth of, so I have not gone into it here.
صنج: The letters ṣād, nūn and jīm are not anything. And al-ṣanj [the cymbal] is a loanword.
صند:
The letters ṣād, nūn and dāl are a sound root indicating great measure and great bulk.
1. al-ṣindīd — the noble chief, plural ṣanādīd.
2. ṣanādīd al-barad — large lumps of hail.
3. ghaythun ṣindīd — a rainstorm with huge drops.
4. ṣanādīd — said of great calamities. It is related of al-Ḥasan, in his supplication: "We seek refuge in You from the ṣanādīd of fate" — meaning its calamities.
صنر:
The letters ṣād, nūn and rā' are not a root, nor is there anything in it to rely on, because of how rarely rā' combines with nūn.
1. al-ṣinnāra — yet they say this, in the dialect of Yemen, means the ear.
2. al-ṣinnāra — also, a hooked piece of iron in the spindle.

But it is not [a genuine root].
صنع:
The letters ṣād, nūn and 'ayn are one sound root, and it is the making of a thing, ṣun'an.

A woman is ṣanā' and a man is ṣana' when the two of them are skilful in what they make. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Clumsy at good, she does not find her way to it, yet she is skilled at harm among family and neighbour.

Al-ṣanī'a is the good turn you do to someone. Al-taṣannu' is a good bearing and manner. Faras ṣanī' is a horse whose people have made him fine by tending him well. Al-maṣāni' are what is made of wells and the like for watering.

And of this chapter is al-muṣāna'a, which is like a bribe.

And of what stands apart from this root is al-ṣin'; it is said that it is the roasting spit. And al-Marrār said:
صنف:
The letters ṣād, nūn and fā' are a sound root, running consistently in two senses: one is a portion of a thing, the other is distinguishing things from one another.
1. al-ṣinf — the first: al-Khalīl said al-ṣinf is a portion of anything; and "this is a ṣinf among the aṣnāf," meaning a kind.
2. ṣinfat al-thawb — as for the ṣinfa of a garment, some said it is its border; others said, rather, it is the fringed side.
3. al-taṣnīf — the other origin: al-Khalīl said al-taṣnīf is distinguishing things from one another. And perhaps compiling a book (taṣnīf al-kitāb) comes from this. And al-gharīb al-muṣannaf [a classified lexicon of rare words] is from this too, as though its chapters were distinguished and each chapter given its own place.
4. ṣannafat al-shajara — but its origin in the language of the Arabs is from their saying this of a tree when it puts out its leaves. Ibn Qays al-Ruqayyāt said, in a line of verse: Rain upon Ḥulwān of the vineyards, and what has leafed out of its figs and its grapes.
صنق:
The letters ṣād, nūn and qāf are a word, if it is sound.
1. al-ṣanaq — they say this is a foul smell.
2. aṣnaqa al-rajulu fī mālihi — some of them related this, said when he manages his wealth well.
صنم: The letters ṣād, nūn and mīm are a single word with no branch to it: al-ṣanam, the idol. It was a thing made of wood or silver or copper and then worshiped.
صنو:
The letters ṣād, nūn and the weak final letter are a sound root indicating closeness between two things, whether in kinship or in distance.

1. al-ṣinw — the full brother. A man's paternal uncle is the ṣinw of his father. Al-Khalīl said: one says fulānun ṣinwu fulānin, when he is his full brother by the same mother and father. The origin of this is two palm trees growing from a single root — each on its own is called ṣinw, plural ṣinwān. God, exalted be He, said: {and palm trees, joined and not joined} [al-Raʿd: 4]. Abū Zayd said: rikiyyatāni ṣinwān — two wells so close together that no basin lies between them.

Among what departs from this root: al-ṣinw — like a hollow dug in the ground, its diminutive ṣunayy. Laylā said, in a line of verse:
"O one who never rose to prominence, who was never first — you were only a little hollow between two rock-slabs, unknown."
صه: The letters ṣād and hāʾ form a word said to call for silence — it is ṣah — and it follows no [derivational] pattern.
صهب:
The letters ṣād, hā' and bā' are a sound formation; it is a colour among colours.
1. al-ṣuhba — a reddish tinge in the hair; one says "rajulun aṣhab," a man of that colour.
2. al-ṣahbā' — wine, because its colour resembles this.
3. al-muṣahhab of meat — that whose redness is mixed with the whiteness of fat, and which is dry.
4. al-ṣayāhib — as for rocks, they are called this; it is possible this is for that colour, and possible it is for their hardness, or that it is from al-ṣaykhad, in which case it would belong to the category of letter-substitution.
5. aṣhab — they call a day of severe cold this, because of the colours that come over the ground.
صهد:
The letters ṣād, hā' and dāl are a sound formation indicating something close to the chapter before it.
1. ṣahadathu al-shams — they say this, like "ṣaharathu al-shams," the sun scorched him.
2. ṣayhad — then, by association, this is said of the shimmering mirage. Al-Hudhalī said, concerning the fierce heat of summer, in a line of verse: And the blazing heat of the star of al-Furūʿ, from the scorching heat of summer, reminded her of the coolness of the north wind.
صهر:
The letters ṣād, hā' and rā' are two roots: one indicates a closeness of kinship by marriage, and the other indicates the melting of something.

The first: al-ṣihr, meaning the khatan, a relation by marriage.

1. Al-Khalīl said: the people of a man's household are called only akhtān, and the people of a woman's household are called only aṣhār; some Arabs, however, call them all aṣhār.
2. Ibn al-A'rābī said: al-iṣhār is the bond of protection formed through neighborliness, kinship, or marriage.

In all of this is understood the saying of the poet, in a line of verse:
Leading noble horses, marriage-alliance with kings, and patience in situations that would have worn other men down.

The other root: the melting of something.

1. One says ṣahartu al-shaḥma — I melted the fat.
2. Al-ṣuhāra — what has melted from it.
3. Iṣṭahartu al-shaḥma — I melted the fat (a variant form of the verb).

He said, in a line of verse:
You were — when the young ones' time to be rendered came — the one who rendered them, and no renderer rendered as you rendered.

One says ṣaharat-hu al-shams, the sun "melted" him, as though it had melted him. This is said of the chameleon when its back shimmers from the intensity of the heat. And it is said that they say, "la-aṣharannahu bi-yamīnin murratin" — I will surely "melt" him with a bitter oath — as though he meant, I will surely dissolve him.
صهل: The letters ṣād, hā' and lām are a sound root, and its branches are few; perhaps there is nothing in it but "ṣahala al-faras," the horse neighed, and "farasun ṣahhāl," a neighing horse.
صهم: The letters ṣād, hā' and mīm are a sound root with few branches, but they say al-ṣihmīm is the ill-tempered one among camels, and they compare to it the man who does not hold to one opinion. And God knows best.
صهو:
The letters ṣād, hā' and the weak letter are a minor root indicating elevation.
1. al-ṣahwa — the seat of the rider on the horse's back.
2. al-ṣahawāt — the tops of hills; sometimes towers are built upon them, singular ṣahwa.
3. al-ṣihā' — al-Shaybānī said this is pools where water collects, singular ṣahwa. And this, even if it is sound, the expected pattern would be that these are pools in elevated places.
4. ṣahiya yaṣhā — from this chapter too, when a person is struck with a wound that then continually oozes moisture, one says this; it follows the same pattern, since it is a moisture that rises over the wound.
صوب:
The letters ṣād, wāw and bā' are a sound root pointing to a thing coming down and settling in its place. Of that is al-ṣawāb, rightness in word and deed, as though it were a matter that has come down and settled in its place. And it is the opposite of error. And from it is al-ṣawb, which is the falling of rain; and what falls is ṣawb also. And the proof of the soundness of this reasoning is their calling rightness ṣawb. The poet said, in a line of verse:
Leave me be: my error and my rightness are upon me alone, and it is my own wealth that I have spent.

And it is said: al-ṣayyib is the cloud that has ṣawb, rain. God, exalted be He, said: {Or like a rain-cloud from the sky} [al-Baqara: 19]. And al-ṣawb is the coming down. He said, in a line of verse:
You are not for a human being but for an angel, come down descending from the air of heaven.

And of a matter when it has settled in its place they say, in speech that runs as a proverb: 'It has come down cold and settled.' Ṭarafa said, in a line of verse:
Heedless, counting my straying as right guidance; then I came to an end, and it had come down cold and settled.

And al-taṣwīb is a rise within a descent; it can only be so. As for al-ṣuyyāba, it is the choicest of everything, as though it were from al-ṣawb, which is the pure water of the cloud, so it seems derived from that.
صوت: The letters sad, waw and ta are a single sound root: it is sound, a genus for everything that registers in the hearer's ear. One says: this is Zayd's voice (sawtu Zayd). A man is 'sayyit' when he has a strong voice, and 'sa'it' when he cries out. As for their saying, [he was called] and 'so he responded' (fa-nsata) — this too is from the same root, as if he was cried out to (suwwita bihi) and reacted to the sound — that is, when he answers. Al-sit is a good reputation among people. One says: his fame has faded (dhahaba situhu).
صوح:
The letters ṣād, wāw and ḥā' are a minor root indicating a scattering in a thing after it has dried.
1. taṣawwaḥa al-baql — said of green herbage when it withers and scatters after its withering.
2. ṣawwaḥathu al-rīḥ — said of the wind when it dries it out, splits it, and scatters it. Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse: And a gusting wind withered the herbage, brought by a southerly heat-wind that veers off course in its passing.
3. al-ṣuwāḥ — from this chapter too, they name the sweat of horses this; if this is sound, it can only be so once it has dried, and they call it al-yabīs, "the dried water." The poet said, concerning al-ṣuwāḥ, in a line of verse: We drove the horses in, their hooves bleeding, the dried sweat rubbed smooth upon their hooves.
4. taṣawwaḥa al-shaʿr — then one says this of hair, when it splits and falls out.
5. al-ṣūḥ — among what may also be carried on this same pattern: the wall of a wadi, which has two ṣūḥs; it is called ṣūḥ because it is clay that crumbles and scatters until it comes to form something like a wall.
صور:
The letters ṣād, wāw and rā' are many words whose origins fall apart from one another. This chapter is not a chapter of analogy or of derivation. The like of it has already passed in what we have written.

Of what can be brought under an analogy in it is their saying ṣawira yaṣwaru, when a thing leans. And ṣurtu al-shay' aṣūruhu, and aṣartuhu, when you incline it toward you. And its analogy carries on: taṣawwara, said of one who is struck down, as though he leant over and fell. This is what follows the analogy; and apart from that every word stands alone by itself.

Of that is al-ṣūra, the form of every created thing, the plural being ṣuwar, and it is the shape of its making. And God Most High is al-Bāri', the Maker, al-Muṣawwir, the Fashioner. And one says rajul ṣayyir when he is beautiful of form. And of that is al-ṣawr, a stand of palm trees, which is al-ḥā'ish; and al-ṣawr has no singular from its own wording. And of that is al-ṣuwār, and it is a herd of wild cattle, the plural being ṣīrān. A poet said, in a line of verse:
So there went on a growling among the herds of the cut-off thicket, as he thrust at them with the polished Samharī spear.

And of that is al-ṣuwār, the ṣuwār of musk. Some people said: it is its scent; and some people said: it is the vessel that holds it. And they recite a line of verse — and it well deserves to be a made-up one, though the two words are sound:
When the herd came into view I remembered Laylā, and I remember her when the musk breathes out its scent.

And of that is their saying ajidu fī ra'sī ṣawra, I find in my head a ṣawra, that is, an itching. And of that is something al-Khalīl related; he said: 'uṣfūr ṣawwār, which is the sparrow that answers when it is called. And this I do not reckon to be Arabic; and it is possible, if it is sound, that it belongs to the chapter we mentioned first, because it inclines toward the one who calls it. As for the hair of a horse's forelock, it is called ṣawr. And this may be by way of likeness to the ṣawr of palm trees, which has been mentioned. A poet said, in a line of verse:
As though a vein were leaning out of his forelock.

And one says: al-ṣāra is land that has trees on it.
صوع:
The letters ṣād, wāw and ʿayn are a sound root with two branches: one indicates scattering and splitting apart, the other a vessel.

The first: their saying taṣawwaʿū, when they scattered. Dhū al-Rumma said:
The herds keep scattering away from me on account of it.

One says taṣawwaʿa shaʿaruhu, when his hair became tangled and split — so said al-Khalīl. He also said: taṣawwaʿa al-nabt, the plants shot up wildly. One says inṣāʿa al-qawmu sirāʿan, they went past swiftly.

As for the vessel: al-ṣāʿ and al-ṣuwāʿ, a vessel one drinks from. A certain measure among measures is also called a ṣāʿ; it belongs to the wāw-root family, and was named ṣāʿ because it is turned round with whatever is being measured. One says the armed champion "yaṣūʿu" his rivals — comes at them from every side — and a man "yaṣūʿu" the camels, driving them in from all directions.

From this: al-ṣāʿ, a low hollow of ground, in the line:
With the two hands of the striker, in a hollow.

And from it: ṣāʿ ju'ju'i al-naʿāma, the place of an ostrich's breast when she lays it against the ground.
صوغ:
The letters ṣād, wāw and ghayn are a sound root; it is the shaping of a thing according to a straight, regular pattern.
1. ṣāgha al-ḥalya yaṣūghuhu ṣawghan — from this is their saying: he fashioned the jewellery, fashioning it.
2. humā ṣawghān — the two of them are "ṣawghān" when each is in the shape of the other.
3. ṣāgha al-kadhiba ṣawghan — said of the liar, when he fabricates a lie. And on this is based the explanation of the hadith: "A lie which the ṣawwāghūn told" — meaning by that those who fashion hadiths and fabricate them.
صوف:
The letters ṣād, wāw and fā' are a single sound root, and it is wool, well known; the whole chapter goes back to it. One says kabshun aṣwaf, ṣawif, ṣā'if, or ṣwāf, all meaning a ram with much wool. They say akhadha bi-ṣūfati qafāhu, when he took hold of the loose hair hanging at the nape of the neck. Ṣūfa were a people who, before Islam, served the Kaʿba and escorted pilgrims through their rites. Abū ʿUbayda related that they were remnants of various tribes who gathered and became interlocked with one another, as wool becomes interlocked. It was said, in a line of verse:
They do not leave their standing-place at ʿArafa until it is said: let the people of Ṣūfāna pass through.

As for their saying ṣāfin ʿan al-sharr, when someone turns away from wrong, that belongs to a chapter of letter-substitution: one says ṣāba, when he leaned aside — it has been discussed in its own place.
صوك: The letters ṣād, wāw and kāf are a single word. One says laqītuhu awwala ṣawkin — I met him at the first ṣawk — meaning at the very first moment.
صول:
The letters ṣād, wāw and lām are a sound root indicating overpowering and elevation.
1. ṣāla ʿalayhi yaṣūlu ṣawlatan — said when he assails someone, when he acts overbearingly toward him.
2. ṣāla al-ʿayr — said of the wild donkey when it charges at the herd of wild asses.
3. al-miṣwal — something was related from Abū Zayd which, if sound, is irregular; he said this is the vessel in which the colocynth [bitter gourd] is soaked so that its bitterness leaves it.
صوم:
The letters ṣād, wāw and mīm are a root pointing to holding back and to standing still in a place.

From this is the fasting of the faster: it is his holding back from his food and his drink and everything else he is kept from. And holding back from speech may be a fast: they said of His saying, exalted be He, {I have vowed a fast to the Merciful} [Maryam: 26], that it is holding back from speech and keeping silent.

As for standing still, one calls a horse that stands ṣā'im.

Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
Horses standing still and horses not standing still, under the dust, and horses champing at the bits.

And al-ṣawm is the stillness of the wind. And al-ṣawm is the sun's standing level at midday, as though it had come to a stand when it seemed to circle overhead. And so one says ṣāma al-nahār — the day stood still at noon.

Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
When the day stood still at noon and the noon heat came on.

And maṣām al-faras is the horse's standing place, and so also maṣāmatuhu.

Al-Shammākh said, in a line of verse:
When he scented out a standing place from her.
صون:
The letters ṣād, wāw and nūn are a single root, and they are covering and safekeeping.

1. ṣuntu al-shay'a aṣūnuhu ṣawnan wa ṣiyānatan — I kept the thing safe, safeguarding it.
2. al-ṣiwān — the covering of a garment (ṣiwān al-thawb), that which the garment is kept safe in.

As for their saying ṣā'in for a horse that stands still, that may be a case of one letter standing in for another: it is as though ṣā'im (fasting) were meant, and the mīm was then changed to a nūn.

Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
And what did you two achieve, leading horses about, in which the roan and the bay stand still, well-fed and idle.

Deviating from the chapter is al-ṣawwān, a kind of stone, the singular being ṣawwāna.
صوي:
The letters ṣād, wāw and yā' are a sound root indicating hardness, firmness and dryness.
1. ṣawā al-shay' — from Ibn Durayd: said of a thing when it dries up, so it is ṣāwin; one also says ṣawiya yaṣwā.
2. al-ṣawwān — stones that have hardness.
3. ṣawwaytu li-ibilī faḥlan — and sometimes this is borrowed and extended from the above, so one says this when you select a stud for your camels; but selection alone is not "taṣwiya" — rather, the animal is cared for toward that end until it grows strong and firm. He said, in a line of verse: He readied for her one thick-fleshed, hardy stud.
4. taṣwiya in winter — this is derived from taṣwiya in winter, which is drying up the teats of the ewe so that she grows fatter; one says "ṣawwāhā aṣḥābuhā," her owners did this to her.
5. al-ṣuwā — from this chapter too: the stone waymarkers. And the saying of one who said these are set where the winds cross — waymarkers are only ever placed thus. He said, in a line of verse: And a wind blew upon him at the crossing-place of the waymarkers.
صي:
The letters ṣād and yāʾ are a single word carrying one sense: anything one fortifies oneself with.

1. ṣayāṣī — fortresses, so called from this root sense.
2. ṣīṣiya — what a cock fights and defends himself with, his spur, named by likeness to that.
3. A bull's horn is called by the same name [ṣīṣiya], because he defends himself and fights with it.
صيأ: The letters ṣād, yā' and hamza. One says ṣayya'tu ra'sī taṣyī'an, meaning I wetted my head.
صيح:
The letters ṣād, yā' and ḥā' are a sound root, and it is a loud voice. From it is al-ṣiyāḥ, shouting, and the single instance of it is a ṣayḥa, a cry. One says: I met so-and-so before every ṣayḥ and nafr. Al-ṣayḥ is shouting, and al-nafr is scattering apart.

Among what is borrowed from this is their saying ṣāḥat al-shajara and ṣāḥa al-nabt — the tree and the plant cried out — when they grow tall, as though, when it grew tall and rose up, its height was made like a shout that points to the one shouting.

As for al-taṣayyuḥ, which is the splitting of wood, its origin is with a wāw, and it is al-taṣawwuḥ, which has already passed. And from it is inṣāḥa al-barq inṣiyāḥan, when the lightning is cleft and splits open. A poet said:
Between a part of it still closed up and a part split open.
صيخ:
The letters ṣād, yā' and khā' are a single word. One says aṣākha yuṣīkhu, meaning he listened closely.

A poet said:
The intent listening of the one seeking [it], to the one reciting.
صيد:
The letters ṣād, yā' and dāl are a sound root indicating one meaning: a thing riding its own head, going straight on without turning aside or leaning. From this, al-ṣayad, for a person to be looking straight ahead. The people of language said: al-aṣyad is the king, plural al-ṣīd, so named for how seldom he turns his head. Some people are naturally aṣyad, stiff-necked, by birth.

The word al-ṣayd, hunting or game, is derived from this, because the game passes by without swerving; and when it is caught, one says qad ṣīda, it has been "ṣayd-ed" — the verb drawn from its own name, the way one says ra'astu al-rajula when you strike a man's head, or baṭantuhu when you strike his belly. Likewise, when you come upon the game and take it, you say ṣidtuhu, I caught it. What confirms this analogy is Ibn al-Sikkīt's statement that among women, al-ṣaydāna is the bad-tempered woman, named so for how little she turns to others. From this chapter too: al-ṣaydāna, the female ghoul.
صير:
The letters ṣād, yā' and rā' are a sound root, and it is the place a thing comes to and the place it returns to. From this: ṣāra yaṣīru ṣayran and ṣayrūratan, he came to be. And one says: I am upon the ṣīr of a matter, that is, on the point of its being settled, and that is what a thing comes to.

As for the saying of Zuhayr, in a line of verse:
And for eight years I had been, in what came of Salmā ... on the very edge of a matter that neither turned bitter nor turned sweet

the ṣīr of a matter is what it comes to and its outcome. And al-ṣīr are like pens made for cattle, the singular being ṣīra, so named because the cattle come to it. And the ṣayyūr of a matter is its end, so named because it is come to. And one says: so-and-so has no judgement and no ṣayyūr, that is, nothing of firm resolve or anything else that he comes back to. And taṣayyara so-and-so his father, when he took after him in likeness; and it was so called as though he had come to be his father. And of what strays from the chapter is al-ṣīr, which is a crack. And in the hadith: "Whoever looks through the crack of a door without leave, his eye goes for nothing." As for al-ṣīr, which is a thing called al-ṣiḥnāt, a fish paste, I do not reckon it Arabic, and I do not reckon that the Arabs knew it. The people of the language have indeed mentioned it, but it has no sense.
صيف:
The letters ṣād, yā' and fā' are two roots: one indicates a season, the other a leaning or turning aside.

The first: al-ṣayf, the season after the latter part of spring, summer. Rain that falls in it is called al-ṣayyif. One says yawmun ṣā'if, a summer day, and laylatun ṣā'ifa, a summer night. ʿĀmaltuhu muṣāyafatan — I dealt with him for the span of a summer, as one says mushāhara for the span of a month. Al-ṣayfiyyūn are a man's children born after he has grown old. It was said, in a line of verse:
My sons are children born late; fortunate is the one whose sons were born early.

The other: ṣāfa ʿan al-shay', he turned away from it. Ṣāfa al-sahm ʿan al-hadaf yaṣīfu ṣayfan, when an arrow veered off from the target. Abū Zubayd said:
Every day she shoots a volley of arrows at him — some hit, and what veers off does not veer far.

As for ṣā'if in Aws's saying, "tanakkara baʿdī min Umaymata ṣā'ifu," ṣā'if there is the name of a place.
صيق:
The letters ṣād, yā' and qāf.

1. al-ṣayq — dust. Ru'ba opened its yā' and said 'al-ṣayaq.'
2. al-ṣīq — the foul smell that comes off animals.
صيك:
The letters ṣād, yā' and kāf. One says ṣāka yaṣīku, meaning it clung and stuck fast.

Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
And one like you, delighted by youth, on whose bodies the perfume clings and sticks fast.

Al-Khalīl said: he meant ṣa'ika, and softened the hamza. It is also said: ṣa'ika al-damu, meaning the blood congealed.

Know that the alif in this chapter stands in place of another letter:

1. al-ṣāb — a bitter tree, possibly [in its root] from a wāw. A poet said:
Indeed I lay sleepless, spending the night resting on my elbow, as though in my eye the bitter ṣāb-tree, freshly cut, had been poured.
2. al-ṣād — copper cooking-pots, the alif here too standing in place of another letter. Ḥassān said:
You would see the copper cooking-pots around our tents.
ضأ:
The letters ḍād and hamza are a sound word: it is al-ḍiʾḍiʾ, meaning origin or stock. In the hadith: "From the stock (ḍiʾḍiʾ) of this one a people will come out who will pass out of the religion."

As for ḍād with the weak letter [wāw], that indicates shouting and clamor. From this: al-ḍawwa and al-ḍawḍāt — the voices of people and their clamor. One says ḍawḍaw, without a hamza.
ضأد: The letters ḍād, hamza and dāl are a small root with few branches, indicating one of the diseases. They said: al-ḍuʾd is a cold [catarrh], and likewise al-ḍuʾda. Rajulun maḍʾūd — a man afflicted with catarrh. And another word was related from Abū Zayd, if it is sound: they said ḍaʾadtu al-rajula ḍaʾdan — when you disputed with him.
ضأل: The letters ḍād, hamza and lām are a small root indicating weakness and slightness in a body. From this, al-ḍaʾīl, which is the weak. The verb from it is: ḍaʾula yaḍʾulu. And rajulun ḍuʾala — a weak man. And al-ḍaʾīla — the slender snake.
