ضأن: The letters ḍād, hamza and nūn are a small, sound root, and it names one kind of livestock. From that: al-ḍa'n, sheep. One says aḍ'ana al-rajul, when a man's sheep became numerous. Al-ḍā'ina is the single animal of al-ḍa'n. Some related fulānun ḍā'inu al-baṭn, meaning slack and loose of belly.
ضب:
The letters ḍād and bāʾ are a single root, most of it indicating a coming-together. Abū Zayd said: aḍabba al-qawm — the people aḍabbū — when they all spoke at once. Then most of the chapter is referred back to this origin.

1. ḍabbat al-ḥadīd, plural ḍabbāt — an iron clasp, a plate that binds two pieces together.
2. al-ḍabb — rancor held in the heart; one says aḍabba ʿalā ghillin fī ṣadrihi, he 'clasped' rancor, when he gathered it within his chest.
3. al-ḍabāb — mist, which is like dust that gathers and covers things; such a day is called muḍibb.
4. ḍabiba al-balad — the land ḍabiba, meaning its mist grew thick.

And from the chapter:
1. al-taḍabbub — growing fat.
2. al-ḍabība — clarified butter and thickened fruit-syrup mixed together; one says ḍabbibū li-ṣabiyyikum, make ḍabība for your child.
3. al-ḍabb — the well-known land-creature [a spiny-tailed lizard], so named for how compact its body and flesh are; plural ḍibāb. The unopened spathe of the palm is sometimes likened to it.

He said, in a line of verse:
He circled round a male palm-tree, as though its spathes were the bellies of freed men who had eaten their midday meal.
He means: its spathe is huge, as though it were plump lizards; then he likens those lizards to the bellies of freed clients who ate until they were full to the ribs.

4. "waqaʿnā fī maḍābb munkara" — we fell into forbidding maḍābb, meaning stretches of land thick with these lizards.
5. al-ḍubāḍib — a short, fat man.

As for their saying ḍabba al-nāqa, it is like ḍaffahā, when he milks her with the whole hand together. Al-Kisāʾī said: faṭartu al-nāqa, aftiruhā — I milk her — when you milk her with the tips of your fingers; and ḍababtuhā, aḍubbuhā, ḍabban, when you milk her with the whole hand. Al-Farrāʾ said: this [milking with the whole hand] is al-ḍaff. As for al-ḍabb, it is that you put your thumb on the teat and your fingers over the thumb and the teat together.

Among what departs from this origin is their saying nāqa ḍabbāʾ and baʿīr aḍabb — a pain that afflicts them in the firsin, the pad of the foot. As for their saying ḍabbat lithatuhu daman (his gum flowed with blood) and ḍabbat yaduhu (his hand flowed with blood), that does not belong to this chapter; it is [the letters] inverted from baḍḍa, already discussed.
ضبأ:
The letters ḍād, bā' and hamza are one sound root, close to concealment and the like of it — to silence and its like.

1. aḍbaʾa — Abū Zayd said: aḍbaʾa al-rajulu ʿalā al-shayʾ iḍbāʾan, when he kept silent about it and said nothing; he is muḍbiʾ ʿalayhi. And he said: aḍbaʾa ʿalā dāhiya, of a calamity kept quiet about.
2. ḍabaʾtu — I hid. It is also said the word is aḍbā, without the hamza, but the first form [with hamza] is better.
3. Abū Saʿīd said: ḍabaʾa yaḍbaʾu ḍabʾan — he clung close to the ground.
4. al-maḍbaʾ — the place where one hides, that is, conceals himself. Al-Kumayt said: 'when he rose above the middle of the two hiding-places...'

The man was named Ḍābiʾ for this reason.

5. ḍabaʾtu ilayhi — I took refuge with him.
6. al-ḍābiʾ — ash, so named because it 'hides,' as though concealing itself.

If you soften the hamza the meaning changes, and it becomes one of the descriptions of fire. It is said: ḍabathu al-nār, when it roasted him, taḍbūhu ḍabwan. Al-maḍbāh is bread [baked] in hot ashes. God knows best what is right.
ضبث: The letters ḍād, bāʾ and thāʾ are a sound root indicating gripping. One says: ḍabatha, when he gripped a thing. And nāqatun ḍabūth — a she-camel whose fatness is doubted, so she is gripped with the hands [to check]. And they say: ḍubitha, meaning he was struck — and this is close to what we have mentioned.
ضبح:
The letters ḍād, bā' and ḥā' are two sound roots: one is a sound, the other a change of colour caused by fire.

The first: their saying ḍabaḥa al-thaʿlab yaḍbaḥu ḍabḥan, the fox yelped; its sound is al-ḍubāḥ, and it is ḍābiḥ. It was said, in a line of verse:
I called upon my Lord, who does not disappoint — for in it there was a yelping little fox.

As for God's saying, exalted: {and the racers, panting} [al-ʿĀdiyāt: 1], it is said this is the sound of their breath, and that is the sounder reading by analogy; it is also said it instead means a run faster than a canter, and that the word is at root ḍabaʿa, to stretch the forelegs out to their fullest — and if that is so, it is a case of letter-substitution.

As for the second root: al-ḍabḥ, the scorching of the top of a stick with fire. Al-ḍibḥ is ashes. Al-ḥijāra al-maḍbūḥa are fire-striking flints that look as though they have been burnt. It was said:
And the flint-stones, split pieces scorched by the striking of fire.

One says al-inḍibāḥ is a change of colour toward black.
ضبد: The letters ḍād, bāʾ and dāl are not a root, even though what Ibn Duraid mentioned may be sound — that al-ḍabad is al-ḍamad [a grudge] — in which case it belongs to the category of letter-substitution. He said: one says aḍbadtuhu, when you angered him.
ضبر:
The letters ḍād, bāʾ and rāʾ are one sound root indicating gathering and strength.

1. ḍabara al-shayʾa — he gathered the thing.
2. ḍabara al-farasu qawāʾimahu — the horse gathered its legs together, to leap; and farasun ḍibirr is named from this.
3. iḍbāratu al-kutub — a bundle of books, from this.
4. The derivation of Ḍabāra is from this — he is Abū ʿĀmir ibn Ḍabāra.
5. nāqatun muḍabbara and maḍbūratu al-khalq — firm and compact in build. He said, describing a horse:
Firm-built in its build, compactly so ... the long mane splits away from off its face.
6. al-ḍabr — the group, the company [of people]. Al-Hudhalī said:
A company, their garb chain-mail, closely arrayed.
7. As for the mountain pomegranate, it is said that they name it al-ḍabr. And we have already said that plants and places can scarcely be brought under analogy.
ضبز: The letters ḍād, bā' and zā'. They say al-ḍabz is intensity of gaze, but this has no [real] meaning.
ضبس:
The letters ḍād, bā' and sīn form a small root, if it is sound at all — it applies to nothing but something blameworthy, not praised.

1. al-ḍabīs — the greedy man. Al-Khalīl said this.
2. al-ḍabīs — the one of little understanding, who cannot find his way to anything. Al-Khalīl said this too.
3. al-ḍabīs — it is also said this means the coward.
ضبط:
The letters ḍād, bā' and ṭā' are a sound root: ḍabaṭa al-shayʾ ḍabṭan — he took hold of the thing firmly.

1. al-aḍbaṭ — the one who works with both hands equally [ambidextrous].
2. It is said: a she-camel is called ḍabṭāʾ [firm-built].

He said, in a line of verse:
A sturdy she-camel, firm-built, trotting swiftly, as though she were a stud-camel that set out at dawn driving the grazing herds before it.

And in the hadith: he was asked about al-aḍbaṭ.
ضبع:
The letters ḍād, bā' and ʿayn are a sound root indicating three senses: the first, a kind of animal; the second, an organ of the human body; the third, a description of she-camels.

As for the first: al-ḍabuʿ, the hyena, well known; the male is ḍibʿān. In the hadith: 'and there he was, with a mud-caked hyena.' Then this word is carried over and a barren, drought-stricken year is likened to it, so it too is called al-ḍabuʿ. A man came and said, 'O Messenger of God, the ḍabuʿ has eaten us up' — meaning the [drought] year the Arabs call al-ḍabuʿ, as though it eats people the way the hyena eats. He said, in a line of verse: 'O Abū Khurāsha, though you have kinsmen, my own people the hyena has not eaten.'

As for the organ, it is ḍabʿ al-yad [the upper arm], its derivation being from ḍabʿ al-yad meaning extension. The Arabs say: ḍabaʿat al-nāqa and ḍabbaʿat taḍbīʿan, as though she were extending her two upper-arms. Abū ʿUbayd said: al-ḍābiʿ is the she-camel that raises her upper-arm as she goes.

And from this root is derived:
1. al-iḍṭibāʿ bi-l-thawb — wrapping the garment: passing the cloth under the right arm and throwing it over the left shoulder.
2. al-ḍibāʿ — the raising of both hands in supplication. Ruʾba said: 'and hands do not cease, over us, raised in prayer' — meaning they extend their upper-arms in supplication.
3. Ibn al-Sikkīt said: ḍabaʿū lanā min al-ṭarīq — they allotted us a portion of the road, when they set aside a share for us; yaḍbaʿūna ḍabʿan; as though they measured it out, extending their upper-arms over it.
4. ḍabaʿat al-khaylu wa-l-ibil — horses and camels are said to do this when they stretch out their upper-limbs in running. And the saying of a poet: 'there will be no peace until you extend your arms to us and we extend ours' — meaning: you extend your arms toward us with swords, and we extend our arms toward you with them.
5. Abū ʿAmr said: ḍabaʿa al-qawmu li-l-ṣulḥ — the people did this for the sake of peace, when they inclined toward it with their upper-arms.
6. Some have related: kunnā fī ḍabʿi fulān — we were in so-and-so's ḍabʿ, meaning his shelter/protection — because the two flanks are a person's two wings, and his two wings are his two ḍabʿ.
7. And the she-camel is said ḍabaʿat, taḍbaʿu, ḍabʿan and ḍabʿatan, when she desires the stallion.
ضبن:
The letters ḍād, bā' and nūn are a sound root, and it names a part of the body.

1. al-ḍabn — what is between the armpit and the waist.
2. iḍṭabantuhu — I put it under my arm, at my ḍibn.
3. al-ḍabna — a man's household, whom he carries at his side [yaḍṭabinuhā].
4. al-maḍbūn — some people say this means the paralyzed man, but in my view that comes from a switching of the mīm [a misreading].
5. a place described as ḍabn — a narrow place.

This word belongs to the first chapter.
ضج:
The letters ḍād and jīm are a sound root indicating crying out in distress.

1. ḍajja, yaḍijju, ḍajījan — to cry out; and ḍajja al-qawm ḍijājan — the people cried out together.
2. Abū ʿUbayd said: aḍajja al-qawm, when they made a clamor and shouted.
3. But when they grew distressed over something and were overcome, one says: ḍajjū.
4. al-ḍijāj — quarreling and wrangling.
5. Someone else said: al-ḍajūj, among camels, is the one that cries out when she is milked.

Among what departs from this chapter: al-ḍajāj, which is beads.
ضجر: The letters ḍād, jīm and rā' are a sound root indicating distress caused by speech. It is said: ḍajira yaḍjaru ḍajaran. The she-camel is said to ḍajirat when her groaning increased. In poetry they say ḍajr, with the jīm left unvowelled. He said, in a line of verse: 'If I satirize him he will grow irritated, just as a veteran stud-camel grows irritated.'
ضجع:
The letters ḍād, jīm, and ʿayn are a single root pointing to lying flat against the ground on one's side, and other senses are then carried on that. One says: ḍajaʿa ḍujūʿan, he lay down. A single instance of it is al-ḍajʿa. One also says: iḍṭajaʿa yaḍṭajiʿu iḍṭijāʿan (he lay himself down). Your ḍajīʿ is the one who lies beside you. He has a good ḍijʿa, a good manner of lying down, just as one speaks of a good rikba, a manner of riding.

From this chapter: ḍajjaʿa fī al-amr, he fell short in a matter, as though he did not stand up to it and lay down away from it instead. One says a man is ḍajūʿ, meaning weak in judgement. A man is ḍujaʿa: helpless, one who scarcely stirs from his place. Al-ḍajūʿ is also a she-camel that grazes off to one side. One says the clouds taḍajjaʿa, when they settled heavily and lingered over a place — this occurs in the poetry of Hudhayl. One says a hillock is ḍajūʿ when it lies flat against the ground; al-ḍujūʿ is a particular hillock known by that name. Al-ḍawājiʿ is a place, in his words, the line cut off before it reaches us:
... Rākis, then al-Ḍawājiʿ

Al-ḍājiʿa and al-ḍajʿāʾ are many sheep or goats gathered together, and this too belongs to the chapter, because they graze and then lie down. Al-ḍajūʿ is also a she-camel that grazes apart from the herd and lies down alone.
ضجم:
The letters ḍād, jīm and mīm are a sound root indicating crookedness in a thing.

1. al-ḍajam — crookedness.
2. tadājama al-amru bi-l-qawm — the matter differed and was disputed among the people.
3. al-ḍajam — crookedness of the nose, and a leaning of the face to one side.
4. Ḍubayʿat Aḍjam — a tribe of the Arabs, as though their forefather were aḍjam [crooked-nosed].
5. al-ḍajam — it is also said this means crookedness of the shoulders.
ضجن: The letters ḍād, jīm and nūn amount to nothing, except that they say al-ḍajan is a well-known mountain — we have already spoken of this. Al-Aʿshā said: 'like a smooth rock among the hillocks of al-Ḍajan.' And Ḍajnān is a mountain in Tihāma.
ضح:
The letters ḍād and ḥāʾ are a sound root indicating the thinness of a particular thing.

1. al-ḍaḥḍāḥ — water reaching only to the ankles, so named for its shallowness.
2. al-ḍaḥḍaḥa — the shimmering of a drink.
3. al-ḍiḥḥ — the light of the sun when it takes firm hold on the ground. Ibn al-Aʿrābī used to say it is the color of the sun.
4. "So-and-so came bi-al-ḍiḥḥ wa-al-rīḥ" — meaning abundance, i.e. all that the sun rose upon and the wind blew over.

He said: one does not say al-ḍīḥ.
ضحك:
The letters ḍād, ḥā' and kāf are close to the chapter before this one, and they point to uncovering and coming out into view. From that is al-ḍaḥik, a person's laughing. One also says al-ḍaḥk, and the first is the better speech. Al-ḍāḥika is every tooth that shows from among the front teeth and the molars when one laughs.

Ibn al-A'rābī said: al-ḍāḥik among clouds is like al-'āriḍ, the cloud that rises across the sky, except that when it flashes with lightning it is said of it ḍaḥika — it laughed. Al-ḍaḥūk is the plain, open road. One says aḍḥakta ḥawḍaka when you fill your watering trough until it brims over. Ibn Durayd said: al-ḍāḥik is a very bright stone that shows out in a mountain, whatever colour it may be. In the chapter of laughing one says al-uḍḥūka is the thing that is laughed at. A man who is a ḍiḥka is one who is laughed at, and a ḍuḥaka is one who laughs a great deal. As for al-ḍaḥk, it is said to be honey. And this is recited, in a line of verse:
He came with a mixed drink the like of which people had never seen; it is ḍaḥk, save that it is the work of bees.
It is also said to be unripe dates. Al-Shaybānī said: al-ṭal', the palm spathe, is both al-kāfūr and al-ḍaḥk together, at the moment when it splits open.
ضحل:
The letters ḍād, ḥā' and lām are a sound root: it is scant water and the like of it.

1. al-ḍaḥl — scant water; its place is al-maḍḥal, plural maḍāḥil.
2. ḍaḥila al-māʾ — the water thinned and lessened; this is correct, eloquent usage.
3. atān al-ḍaḥl — a rock partly in the water and partly out of it.
ضحى:
The letters ḍād, ḥā' and the weak letter are one sound root indicating the coming-forth of a thing.

1. al-ḍaḥāʾ — the stretching of daytime, that being the time when things are apparent and laid bare.
2. al-ḍaḥāʾ — the same word is then used for the food eaten at that time. He said, in a line of verse: 'you see the bull walking back from his forenoon meal.'
3. ḍaḥiya, ḍaḥā — a man ḍaḥiya yaḍḥā, or ḍaḥā, when he exposes himself to the sun.
4. iḍḥa yā Zayd — come out, O Zayd, meaning: come out into the sun.
5. al-ḍaḥiyya, also al-uḍḥiyya — the well-known sacrificial animal. Al-Aṣmaʿī said there are four dialect forms of this word: uḍḥiyya and iḍḥiyya, plural aḍāḥī; ḍaḥiyya, plural ḍaḥāyā; and aḍḥāh, plural uḍḥan. Al-Farrā' said al-aḍḥā is feminine, though sometimes made masculine, taken to refer to 'the day.' He cited: 'al-Aḍḥā drew near, and the dried meat had grown rank.' It was named this because on that day the sacrifice is offered only once the sun has fully risen.
6. laylatun iḍḥiyāna, ḍaḥyāʾ — a bright, moonlit night, with no cloud in it.
7. hum yataḍaḥḥawna — they take their midday meal; al-ghadāʾ [the midday meal] is also called al-ḍaḥāʾ. From this is the hadith of Salama ibn al-Akwaʿ: 'while we were with the Messenger of God, peace and blessings upon him, natadaḥḥā' — meaning: taking our midday meal.
8. ḍāḥiyat [every town] — its exposed outer edge. It is said: they dwell in al-ḍawāḥī, the outskirts. It is said: he did that ḍāḥiyatan, when he did it openly, plainly. He said, in a line of verse: 'my uncle, who withheld the dinar openly — the dinar owed to Kalb — and it was witnessed.' And he said, in another: 'Banū Dhubyān have already repaid you openly for what you did, like measuring the ṣāʿ against the ṣāʿ.'

As for the line of Jarīr — 'the trees of your stock among Quraysh are not thin of branch, nor exposed' — he means: they are not on the margins, but in the very middle. It is said of the whole sky: al-ḍawāḥī. Ta'abbaṭa Sharran said, in a line of verse: 'and a hilltop like a spearhead, standing out... ḍaḥyāna...' — meaning: exposed to the sun.

9. Abū Zayd said: ḍaḥā al-ṭarīq, yaḍḥū, ḍaḥwan and ḍuḥuwwan, when the road appeared and became visible.

All these branches show the soundness of what we took as the origin sense: the coming-forth of a thing and its being made plain.

As for what is related from Abū Zayd, from the Arabs — ḍaḥḥaytu ʿan al-amr, meaning I was lenient about the matter — in my view this is most likely anomalous, outside the pattern. Zayd al-Khayl said, in a line of verse: 'if Naṣr had set right the relation between them, ʿAmr would gently have let go, little by little, of its concerns.'
ضخ: The letters ḍād and khāʾ are not a root. Even so, they say: al-ḍakhkh is the spurting-out of urine. And al-miḍakhkha is a reed or pipe with which water is shot out so that it stretches into a jet.
ضخم:
The letters ḍād, khā' and mīm are a sound root indicating great bulk in a thing.

1. ḍakhm, ḍukhām — used of something bulky, massive.
2. al-uḍkhūma — something with which a woman pads out her buttocks, to enlarge them.
ضد:
The letters ḍād and dāl are two distinct words, differing from each other in derivation.

The first: al-ḍidd is the opposite of a thing. And al-mutaḍāddān are two things that cannot come together at one time, like night and day.

The other word is al-ḍadd, with the ḍād given a fatḥa, which is filling. One says: ḍadda al-qirba — he filled the waterskin — malaʾahā, ḍaddan.
ضر:
The letters ḍād and rāʾ are three origins: the first is the opposite of benefit; the second is a thing's gathering together; the third is strength.

As for the first: al-ḍurr is the opposite of benefit. One says: ḍarrahu, yaḍurruhu, ḍarran — he harmed him. Then everything akin to or close to this is referred back to it.

1. al-ḍurr — emaciation.
2. al-ḍirr — a woman's being married alongside a co-wife; one says "so-and-so was married ʿalā ḍirr," meaning alongside a woman who was there before her.
3. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: the woman married ʿalā ḍurr or ḍirr; and al-iḍrār is the same, and such a man is called muḍirr.
4. al-ḍarra — a name derived from al-ḍarr, as though she harms the other as the other harms her, i.e. a co-wife.
5. iḍṭarra fulān ilā kadhā — so-and-so was driven to such-a-thing, from al-ḍarūra, necessity.
6. In poetry they say al-ḍārūra, [hardship, poetic necessity].

Ibn al-Dumayna said, in a line of verse:
Requite a man in hardship, for whom even his enemies felt pity, and whose excuses to a friend have grown scant.

7. al-ḍarīr — mutual harming; it is used mostly of jealousy; one says "how intense is his ḍarīr toward her!"
8. The two millstones are likened to two co-wives, so they are called al-ḍarratān.
9. al-ḍarīr — one who has been harmed by the loss of his eyesight, or by the wasting of his body.

As for the second origin: ḍarrat al-ḍarʿ is the flesh of the udder. Abū ʿUbayd said: al-ḍarra is the part of it never without milk, so named for its being gathered together.

1. ḍarrat al-ibhām — the flesh gathered beneath the thumb.
2. al-muḍirr — one who has a ḍarra, an abundant store, of wealth; a description of abundant property.

He said, in a line of verse:
It is enough for you, among the people, that they know you are, among them, a rich man of abundant wealth.

As for the third: al-ḍarīr is strength of spirit. One says: so-and-so is dhū ḍarīr over a thing, when he has patience and endurance for it, in the saying of Jarīr, in a line of verse (only part of it given):
"...boldness and endurance."

And one says of a horse: aḍarra ʿalā faʾs al-lijām — it pressed hard on the crosspiece of the bit — when it clamped down on it.
ضرب:
The letters ḍād, rā' and bā' are one root, then it is used as a figure and other things are carried upon it.

Of that is ḍarabtu ḍarban, when you deal another a blow. And borrowed from it and likened to it is the striking out in the land for trade and other travel. God - exalted - said: {And when you strike out in the land, there is no blame on you that you shorten the prayer} [al-Nisā': 101]. And they say that hastening in travel is also ḍarb. He said, in a line of verse:
For that which you were fearing - spies came to us hastening with it.
And al-ṭayr al-ḍawārib are the birds that go out seeking their food. And one says a man miḍrab: one who strikes hard. Of this section is al-ḍarb: the shaping and casting of a thing. One says this is of the ḍarb of so-and-so, that is, of his shaping, because when he shapes a thing he has struck it.

And al-ḍarīb is the like of a thing, as though the two had been struck one striking and cast in one casting. And al-ḍarīb is hoar frost, as though the sky had struck the earth with it. And the thing the frost has hit is called maḍrūb. He said, in a line of verse:
And a frost-struck one that moans without a blow, tossed from tent to tent.
And al-ḍarīb of milk is fresh milk mixed with curdled milk, as though one of the two had been struck upon the other. And al-ḍarīb is honeycomb, as though the bees had struck it. And a man's nature and disposition is called al-ḍarība, as though the man had been struck upon it a striking and cast in a casting. And the maḍrab and maḍrib of a sword is the place on it with which one strikes. And a sort of a thing is called al-ḍarb, as though it had been struck on the pattern of the rest of that thing. And al-ḍarība is what is levied on a man of tribute and the like. And the measure is one, as though it had been struck upon him. Then they widen it and say ḍaraba fulānun 'alā yadi fulānin, when he restrains him, as though the man wanted to stretch out his hand and the striker struck his hand so that he drew it back. And of this section is the stallion's covering of the she-camel.

And one says aḍrabtu al-nāqa: I brought the stallion up onto her. And aḍraba fulānun 'an al-amr, when he left off, and it is from holding back, as though he had wanted to spread himself in it and then struck, that is, dealt himself a blow and held himself back from what it wanted.

As for what is related of Abū Zayd, that the Arabs say aḍraba al-rajulu fī baytihi, he stayed at home, its measure is the measure of the word before it.

Of this section is al-ḍarab: thick honey, as though it had been struck a striking, as one says nafaḍtu al-shay'a nafḍan, I shook the thing, and the thing shaken is nafaḍ. And the man entrusted with the gaming arrows is called al-ḍarīb. He was called ḍarīb because he is with the one who strikes them, so he was called ḍarīb like qa'īd, the one who sits with you, and jalīs, the one seated beside you.

And among what is borrowed in this section is their saying, of a light-bodied man, ḍarb, likening him in his lightness to the blow that a man strikes. He said, in a line of verse:
I am that lean man you know, slight as the head of a blazing snake.
And al-ḍārib is the broad open place in a valley, as though it were a track that strikes into the valley a striking.
ضرج:
The letters ḍād, rā' and jīm are one sound root indicating the opening-up of a thing. The Arabs say: inḍarajat ʿan al-baql lafāʾifuhu, when the wrappings of the herb opened away from it. All splitting is called inḍirāj. He said: '...and the calyxes opened away from it.'

1. taḍarraja al-barq — the lightning split and flashed repeatedly.
2. ʿaynun maḍrūja — a wide-slit eye.
3. al-iḍrīj — among horses, the one profuse in sweat, generous and swift; it belongs to this root because it is as though it breaks open in sweat.
4. ʿadwun ḍarīj — a violent gallop.
5. taḍarraja bi-l-dam — he was stained with blood.

And among what departs from the root: al-iḍrīj — cloaks made from the finest goat-wool [mirʿizzā], also said to be silk [khazz].
ضرح:
The letters ḍād, rā' and ḥā' are two roots: one is the throwing of a thing, the other a color among colors.

The first:
1. ḍaraḥtu al-shayʾ — you threw the thing away; al-shayʾ al-muḍṭaraḥ is the thing thrown away.
2. al-farasu al-ḍarūḥ — the horse that kicks out with its leg.
3. qawsun ḍarūḥ — a bow forceful in casting the arrow.
4. al-ḍarīḥ — a grave dug without a side-niche, as though the dead man were thrown into it.

As for the other:
1. al-maḍraḥī — the white of everything is called this.
2. al-ṣaqru muḍraḥī, al-sayyidu muḍraḥī — the falcon is called muḍraḥī, and the chief/lord is called muḍraḥī.
ضرز: The letters ḍād, rā' and zā' are a single word. It is said that al-ḍirizza is the short, mean-natured woman.
ضرس:
The letters ḍād, rā' and sīn are a sound root indicating strength and roughness, though a thing may occasionally depart from it.

1. al-ḍirs — among the teeth [a molar], named for its strength over the rest of the teeth.
2. ḍarasahu — he took hold of it with his molar. He said, in a line of verse: 'when you make enemies of men, do not be prey to them — wound with your fang and bite.'
3. al-ḍirs — also, what is rough among the hills.
4. taḍārasa al-bināʾ — the building became uneven.
5. Some have said: ḍarrasathu al-khuṭūb — troubles roughened/hardened him.
6. biʾrun maḍrūsa — a well lined with stones.
7. nāqatun ḍarūs — a she-camel that bites the one who milks her.
8. rajulun ḍaris — a man of difficult temper.
9. aḍrasahu al-amr — the matter troubled him.
10. al-muḍarras — a kind of cloth, so named, it seems, because it carries patterns in it like molars.
11. al-ḍaras — a weakness in the molar.

And among what departs from this root, though a rationale might be found for it: al-ḍirs — scant rain, plural ḍurūs.
ضرع:
The letters dad, ra and 'ayn are a single sound root indicating softness in a thing. From it: the man 'dara'a' with 'dara'a' — he became humble/submissive. A man is 'dara'' — weak. Ibn Wa'la said, in a line of verse:
Patience, forbearance, and waiting for them tomorrow — for I am neither slack nor the raw, inexperienced weakling.

From this root: the udder of a ewe or other animal (dar' al-shah), named for the softness in it. One says 'adra'ati l-naqa', the she-camel's milk descended [into the udder] near the time she is due to give birth. As for al-mudara'a, it means resemblance between two things. Some scholars said its derivation is from al-dar' (the udder), as though the two resembling things had suckled from one udder. A ewe with a large udder is 'dari'', and also 'dari'a'. One calls a person of a wasted/emaciated body 'dari''. The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him and his family, said of the two sons of Ja'far: 'What is it that I see them so wasted (dari'ayn)?'

An anomaly from this root: al-dari', a plant. It is possible to bring it under the root, saying it is so named for its weakness — being that it does not fatten [an animal] nor stave off hunger. A poet said:
They were left in the hollow where the dari' plant grows, every one of them hump-backed, her forelegs bloodied, holding back [her milk] in grief.
ضرف:
The letters ḍād, rā' and fā' name something among plants.

1. al-ḍirf — a kind of mountain tree, the singular being ḍirfa.
2. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: fulānun fī ḍirfati khayr — so-and-so is in an abundance of good.
ضرك: The letters ḍād, rā' and kāf are a single word with no wider pattern to it. It is said: al-ḍarīk is al-ḍarīr — the wretched one, in bad condition.
ضرم:
The letters ḍād, rā' and mīm are a sound root indicating heat and blazing.

1. al-ḍirām — firewood that blazes up quickly. He said, in a line of verse: 'but on that high ground, kindle with thick logs — when you kindle, not with kindling-sticks.'
2. ḍarima al-shayʾ — its heat intensified.
3. farasun ḍarim — a horse of intense running.
4. al-ḍarīm, al-ḍirām — the blazing of fire.

And among what departs from the root, in what they say: al-ḍaram is the chick of the eagle — perhaps it was so named when its hunger intensified, as though it were ablaze.
ضرى:
The letters ḍād, rā' and the weak letter are two roots: one is something like being incited toward a thing and given over to it; the other is something that conceals.

The first: the Arabs say ḍariya bi-l-shayʾ, when he was incited to it until he could scarcely bear to be without it.
1. ḍarāwa — this thing has ḍarāwa, meaning: one can hardly bear to be without it.
2. al-ḍārī — one of the offspring of dogs [a trained hunting dog], plural al-ḍirāʾ, so named because it is given over [ḍarā] to something.
3. al-ḍirw — the same as al-ḍārī.
4. al-ḍārī — also, the flowing vein. It is said ḍarā yaḍrū ḍarwan, as though given over to flowing. Al-Khalīl said: al-ḍarw is the throbbing of the blood as it comes out from the vein.

As for the other root:
1. al-ḍarāʾ — walking amid what conceals, of trees or otherwise. It is said: huwa yamshī lahu al-ḍarāʾa, when he stalks or deceives someone.
2. al-ḍirw — a tree, so named because it conceals with its leaves.
ضز: The letters ḍād and zāy are a single word: it is al-ḍazaz, the sticking of the upper palate to the lower; a man with this is aḍazz.
ضزن:
The letters ḍād, zā' and nūn are one sound root indicating pressing and rivalry.

1. al-ḍayzan — the one who rivals his father over his [father's] wife. Aws said, in a line of verse: 'every one of you is, to his father, a rival co-wife's-son, a co-husband.'
2. al-ḍayzan — it is also said this means the enemy.
3. al-ḍayzan — when the hub of a pulley-wheel becomes too wide and is narrowed with a piece of wood, that piece of wood is called this.
4. al-ḍayzan — the one who crowds and jostles at the drawing and bringing of water.
ضطر:
The letters ḍād, ṭāʾ and rāʾ are a word indicating bulkiness. And they say meanness goes along with it. Abū ʿUbayd said: al-ḍayṭar is the huge man; plural ḍayṭārūn and ḍayāṭira.

He recited, in a line of verse:
The bulky men of Fuʿāla presented themselves before us — and what good is a bulky man turning over a mistaḥ [a date-drying floor]?
ضع:
The letters ḍād and ʿayn, doubled, are a single sound root indicating submission and weakness. One says taḍa'ḍa'a, meaning he was humbled and gave way. Abū Dhu'ayb said, in a line of verse:
And my show of endurance before those who gloat, showing them that against the blows of fate I do not give way.
Every weak thing is called ḍa'ḍā', when it has neither judgment nor strength.
ضعس: The letters ḍād, ʿayn and sīn are not a root. Ibn Durayd mentioned that they call the greedy, gluttonous man ḍaʿwas.
ضعف:
The letters ḍād, ʿayn and fā' are two separate roots. One of them points to the opposite of strength, and the other to a thing being increased by the like of itself.

The first: al-ḍaʿf and al-ḍuʿf, and that is the opposite of strength. One says ḍaʿufa yaḍʿufu — he grew weak; a weak man is ḍaʿīf, and weak people are ḍuʿafā' and ḍiʿāf.

As for the other root, al-Khalīl said: aḍʿaftu al-shay' iḍʿāfan, and ḍaʿʿaftuhu taḍʿīfan, and ḍāʿaftuhu muḍāʿafatan — I doubled the thing; and that is that something is added to the original of a thing so that it is made two of it or more. Someone else said: al-maḍʿūf is the thing that has been doubled. Abū ʿAmr said: al-maḍʿūf comes from aḍʿaftu al-shay'. Abū ʿUbayd mentioned that in the chapter of afʿaltuhu fa-huwa mafʿūl — words whose verb is on the pattern afʿala but whose passive form is mafʿūl. And al-muḍāʿafa is a coat of mail woven of two rings.
ضعو:
The letters ḍād, ʿayn and wāw are a single word: it is al-ḍaʿa, a tree, its wāw dropped; plural ḍaʿawāt.

He said, in a line of verse:
Taking for himself, among the ḍaʿawāt, a den.
ضغ:
The letters ḍād and ghayn are not anything — not a root that other things branch from or are measured against — but they say:

1. al-ḍaghḍagha — the sound of a wolf eating meat. Al-Khalīl said instead: it is chewing with gapped, toothless gums.
2. al-ḍaghghāgha — the fool.
3. al-ḍaghīgha — soft, thin dough.
4. 'ayshun ḍaghīgh — an abundant, fertile life.

None of this amounts to anything, even though it is mentioned.
ضغب: The letters ḍād, ghayn and bāʾ are not a root, but rather one of the [echoed] sounds. They say that al-ḍaghīb is the writhing cry of the hare when it is caught, and likewise al-ḍughāb. And al-ḍāghib is the one who hides in thick cover to frighten people.
ضغت: The letters ḍād, ghayn and tāʾ are not a root.
ضغث:
The letters ḍād, ghayn and thā' are a single root indicating the mingling of a thing, part with part.

1. "You aḍghathta the dream" — said to a dreamer whose dream is a confused jumble.
2. al-aḍghāth — confused, jumbled dreams.
3. al-ḍighth — a handful of twigs or grass. Al-Khalīl said this is itself a single root.
4. nāqa ḍaghūth — said of a she-camel when you are unsure of her fatness and so feel or grope her, to check whether she carries fat [in her hump].
5. al-ḍighth — also like al-mars [kneading, twisting].
ضغز: The letters ḍād, ghayn and zāy are not a sound root, except where poetry brings it. Al-Khalīl did mention that al-ḍighz, among beasts of prey, is the ill-tempered one. God knows best what is correct.
ضغط:
The letters ḍād, ghayn and ṭāʾ are a single sound root indicating pressing hard against something. One says: ḍaghaṭahu, when he pressed him against a wall.

1. al-ḍaghīṭ — a well beside which another well is dug, so that its water diminishes.
2. al-maḍāghiṭ — low-lying tracts of land.
3. A camel with ḍāghiṭ — the upper foreleg sticking to the side of the body through chafing, so that the two press against each other and its skin hangs down. Abū ʿUbayd said: al-ḍāghiṭ and al-ḍabb are the same thing, a splitting-open at the armpit together with excess flesh.
4. One says: "O God, lift this ḍaghṭa from us" — meaning hardship and difficulty.
5. One says: "I sent him as a ḍāghiṭ over so-and-so" — one like a watcher who restrains him from wrongdoing.
ضغم:
The letters ḍād, ghayn and mīm are a small single root indicating biting. One says: ḍaghamahu, he bit him.

1. al-ḍaygham — the lion, derived from this. Abū ʿUbayd said: al-ḍaygham is the one that bites, and the yāʾ in it is an extra letter.
2. al-ḍughāma — what you bite and then spit out, as Ibn Durayd mentioned.
ضغن:
The letters ḍād, ghayn and nūn are a sound root indicating the covering of something along with a leaning and a crookedness, and it does not indicate anything good. From this: al-ḍighn and al-ḍaghan, meaning rancor or a grudge. A horse described as ḍāghin is one that does not give what running it has except by being struck. One says: ḍaghina ṣadru fulānin ḍighnan wa-ḍaghanan, so-and-so's chest harboured rancour. A spear-shaft described as ḍaghinah is crooked. They say: a she-camel is "dhāt ḍighn" when she strains toward her home ground, longing for it.

As for al-Khalīl, he said: it is said of a wild she-ass, when she is pregnant and resists the male donkey: "she has shaghb [contrariness] and ḍighn." One says: ḍaghana fulānun ilā al-dunyā, so-and-so leaned and inclined toward the world. "Ḍighnī ilā fulānin" — my inclination toward so-and-so.

What points to the sense of covering something, which we mentioned, is their saying that al-iḍṭighān is wrapping oneself in a garment. He said, in a line of verse:
As if he were one wrapped up, a child.

And one says: iḍṭaghantu al-shay'a taḥta ḥiḍnī, I tucked the thing under my arm. Ibn Muqbil said, in a line of verse:
When I tucked my weapon in at its narrow flank, and at an elbow-joint like the withered hilt of a sword.
ضف:
The letters ḍād and fā' are a sound root indicating two things: one is gathering, the other is scantiness and weakness.

1. al-ḍafaf — people gathering around a thing. One says mā'un maḍfūf, when many people gather at the water, and ṭa'āmun maḍfūf, likewise of food. In hadith: "He, peace be upon him, never ate his fill of bread and meat except when there was ḍafaf," meaning many hands upon the food. And of water:
None may draw from the crowded, drained well, except by lowering deep, hollow buckets.
2. ḍaffatā al-nahr — the two banks of a river, named because people gather along them.
3. nāqatun ḍafūf — a she-camel giving much milk, according to al-Khalīl, milked only with the whole hand, ḍaffan; al-ḍaff is milking with the whole palm.

1. fī ra'yi fulānin ḍafaf — there is weakness in so-and-so's judgment.
2. laqītuhu 'alā ḍafaf — I met him in haste, without the chance to deal with him properly.
ضفر:
The letters ḍād, fāʾ and rāʾ are a sound root: it is joining one thing broadly to another, whether by weaving or otherwise.

1. ḍafāʾir al-shaʿr — braids of hair: any hair plaited until it becomes a lock.
2. taḍāfarū ʿalayhi — they combined against him, meaning they cooperated. In my view its origin is from the braids of hair: that they draw so close together that each of them seems to have tied his braid to the braid of the other. This is a good pattern of derivation for mutual aid, backing, and the like.
3. al-ḍafir — a curved ridge of sand. What we retain from Abū ʿUbayd's book is that al-ʿaqida and al-ḍafira are sand that has bound together.
4. kinānatun ḍafira — a quiver that is full. Its origin is from the taḍāfur, the crowding-together, of the arrows within it, that is, their being packed together.
5. al-ḍafīra — that which is called al-musannāh, an embankment, so named as though it were plaited together, like something whose parts are joined to each other by weaving or otherwise.
ضفز:
The letters ḍād, fāʾ and zāy are a sound root indicating pushing one thing into another by shoving it into the mouth as a mouthful; other senses are referred back to that.

1. al-ḍafz — feeding a camel a mouthful.
2. al-ḍafar — that you feed it to him as a mouthful even if he dislikes it.
3. The Arabs say: "ḍafaztuhu ḥaqqahu fa-mā qabilahu" — I forced his due upon him but he did not accept it — meaning: I compelled him to it.
4. ḍafaztu al-faras lijāmahu — I forced the bit into the horse's mouth, i.e. put it into its mouth.
5. It is sometimes said: al-ḍafz is sexual intercourse, which is close to the sense of the chapter.
ضفس: The letters ḍād, fāʾ and sīn are not a root, except that Ibn Durayd mentioned that al-ḍafs is like al-ḍafz.
ضفط:
The letters ḍād, fāʾ and ṭāʾ are a small root that they say is sound, and its origin is stupidity and coarseness.

1. The fool is called ḍafīṭ, plainly showing ḍafāṭa.
2. al-ḍaffāṭ — one who hires out camels.
3. al-ḍaffāṭa, as it is said — camels that carry baggage.

I reckon the whole of this chapter is something not to be relied upon.
ضفع: The letters ḍād, fāʾ and ʿayn are not a root. Al-Khalīl did relate that ḍafaʿa means: he defecated. And al-salam — what is meant by this word here is not clear from the text as printed.
ضفن:
The letters ḍād, fāʾ and nūn are a sound root indicating throwing a thing furtively. Its origin is ḍafantu bi-al-rajul al-arḍ — I threw the man to the ground — when you throw him down and strike the ground with him.

1. ḍafana al-baʿīr bi-rijlihi — the camel struck out and kicked with its leg.
2. ḍafana bi-ghāʾiṭihi — he voided his excrement, cast it out.
3. ḍafana al-ḥiml ʿalā nāqatihi — he loaded the burden onto his she-camel, carrying it upon her.
4. ḍafanahu bi-rijlihi — he struck him with his leg, kicked him.

The pattern in all of this is one and the same.

1. ḍafana ilā al-qawm — he threw himself upon the people, when he took refuge with them and sat among them. In my view a further description should be added to this, namely "and they do not want him," as though he had thrown himself upon them uninvited. The proof of this is their calling the uninvited guest who tags along with a true guest ḍayfan; this is the pattern fayʿal from ḍafana. I have heard — though not from a scholar — that the one who tags along with the ḍayfan is called al-ḍayfanān, and I do not know how sound this is, though the derivation allows it.

He said of al-ḍayfan, in a line of verse:
Whenever a guest comes, a ḍayfan comes along with the guest — and so the uninvited hangers-on make away with what is set out to feed the guests.

2. al-ḍifann — a foolish man, along with great bulk of body.
ضفو:
The letters ḍād, fāʾ and the weak letter are a sound root indicating fullness and completeness.

1. thawb ḍāfin — an ample garment.
2. faras ḍāfī al-sabīb — a horse full in the tail-hair, when the hair of its tail is abundant.
3. "So-and-so is fī ḍafw / ḍafwa min ʿayshihi" — in ample ease from his living.

Al-Akhṭal said, in a line of verse:
When the solitary, straggling ram lowers its head, and is pleased by the ample flock of floppy-eared sheep.
al-khuṭl: those with drooping ears.

4. rajul ḍāfī al-raʾs — a man full in the head, abundant in the hair of his head.

He said, in a line of verse (obscure):
"When you cry for help to one full-headed, loud-shouting..."

5. Ḍafwā — a place-name.
ضك: The letters ḍād and kāf are a small sound root holding two words: imra'atun ḍakḍāka and rajulun ḍakḍāk, meaning short and compact of flesh. The other word: al-ḍakḍaka — quickness of walking.
ضكع: The letters ḍād, kāf and ʿayn contain a word with no derivational pattern to it. One says: rajul ḍawkaʿa, when he is heavy with much flesh.
ضكل: The letters ḍād, kāf and lām. They say that al-ḍaykal is: the naked man.
ضل:
The letters ḍād and lām are a sound root indicating a single meaning: a thing's being lost, and its going away not as it should.

1. ḍalla, yaḍillu and yaḍallu — two dialect forms of the same verb, to go astray.
2. Anyone who turns aside from the right course is ḍāll — astray.
3. al-ḍalāl and al-ḍalāla — the same meaning: straying, error.
4. A man is ḍillīl or muḍallal when he is given to error and falsehood.

Among what shows that this is indeed the origin sense of al-ḍalāl is their saying uḍilla al-mayyit — the dead man was 'lost' — meaning he was buried, as though he were a thing that had gone astray. And they say: ḍalla al-laban fī al-mā' — the milk 'went astray' in the water — and then they say it was istuhlika, consumed.

A poet said, of uḍilla al-mayyit, in a line of verse:
Those who buried him came back with clear sight, while resolve and bounty were left behind at al-Jawlān.

Ibn al-Sikkīt said:
1. adlaltu baʿīrī — I lost my camel, said when it has wandered off from you.
2. ḍalaltu al-masjid wa-al-dār — I lost my way to the mosque and the house, said when you cannot find the way to them; and likewise for anything fixed in place that cannot be found.
3. arḍ muḍilla and maḍalla — a land in which one loses one's way.
4. They fell into wādī taḍallul (the valley of losing-the-way), said when they fell into a maḍalla, a place where one loses the way.
ضلع:
The letters ḍād, lām and ʿayn are a single sound root, consistently applied, indicating a leaning and a crookedness. al-ḍilaʿ is the rib of a person or other creature, so named for the curve that is in it.

And a speaker says, describing a woman, in a line of verse:
She is the crooked rib — you will never straighten her; indeed, to straighten ribs is to break them.

Their saying dābba ḍalīʿ majfar al-janbayn — a beast full in the two flanks — is, in my view, from the strength of the ribs; and that was then borrowed for anything, until every strong thing was called ḍalīʿ. In the hadith of ʿUmar, when he wrestled the jinnī, he said to him: "Among them I am indeed ḍalīʿ."

al-rumḥ al-ḍaliʿ — the spear that leans, that is bent.

He said, in a line of verse (obscure):
"Its faliq is smooth, like the leaning spear."

1. ḍalaʿa fulān ʿan al-ḥaqq — so-and-so leaned away from the truth.
2. "kallamtu fulānan fa-kāna ḍalʿuka ʿalayya" — I spoke to so-and-so, and your ḍalʿ (your bias) was against me.
3. Ibn al-Sikkīt said: ḍalaʿta, taḍluʿu — you leaned, when you tilted.

They say in the proverb: "Do not pick out a thorn with a thorn, for its bending goes with it" [a thorn used to remove a thorn shares its crookedness].

As for their saying taḍallaʿa al-rajul — the man filled himself with eating — this too is from this root, meaning that the food, from its abundance, filled his ribs. As for their saying ḥiml muḍliʿ, meaning heavy, this too is from this: its weight reaches to the ribs. And so-and-so is muḍṭaliʿ with this matter, meaning his ribs are strong enough to bear it.

As for the saying of Suwayd, in a line of verse: "breadth of character among us, and al-ḍalaʿ [staying-power]" — its origin is from this; he means strength for handling affairs. Al-Mufaḍḍal said: al-ḍalaʿ is breadth/capacity. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: it is the bearing of weight and strength. And from the chapter, which supports this pattern, their saying "they are against him ḍalʿ wāḥid," one rib, meaning their united leaning against him in enmity. God knows best what is correct.
ضم:
The letters ḍād and mīm are a single root indicating a fitting-together between two things. One says: ḍamamtu al-shay' ilā al-shay' — I joined the thing to the thing — aḍummuhu, ḍamman.

1. iḍmāma of horses — a group of horses.
2. faras sabbāq al-aḍāmīm — a horse that outruns the groups (al-jamāʿāt), that beats the whole herd.
3. iḍmāma of books — like an iḍbāra, a bundle.
4. ḍamḍam and ḍamāḍim — a lion, one that clasps/gathers everything.
ضمج: The letters ḍād, mīm and jīm are not a root, and likewise whatever resembles it. As for al-ḍamkh, with khāʾ, it is sound. One says: taḍammakha bi-l-ṭīb — he smeared himself with perfume, and he is mutaḍammikh, one smeared with perfume.
ضمد:
The letters ḍād, mīm and dāl are a sound root indicating gathering and coming-together.

1. ḍamadtu al-shayʾ, aḍmiduhu — I ḍamadtu the thing, when you gather it together.
2. al-ḍimād — the bandage; one says: ḍamadtu al-jurḥ, I bound the wound.
3. al-ḍamd, with the mīm quiescent — that a woman takes two [male] companions.

Al-Hudhalī said, in a line of verse:
You wish to keep both me and Khālid together as yours — but can two swords, woe to you, be gathered in one sheath?

4. "The camels ate their fill min ḍamd al-arḍ," said when they ate their fill of both moist and dried plants, old growth and new.
5. They say a man says to his debtor: "I will pay you min ḍamd hādhihi al-ghanam," meaning from a mix of the good and the poor among these sheep, the large and the small.
6. aḍmada al-ʿarfaj — the ʿarfaj-plant aḍmada, when the young shoot hollowed into it and did not emerge, that is, it stayed inside it — this too is from the root sense, as though the plant had gathered the shoot within itself.
7. al-ḍamad, with the mīm given a fatḥa — rancor that gathers in the chest and is not dispelled so as to ease.

Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
Whoever disobeys you, punish him with a punishment that restrains the wrongdoer — and do not sit nursing a smoldering grudge.

One says: ḍamida, yaḍmadu, ḍamadan. Abū Bakr said: some distinguished between al-ghayẓ (anger) and al-ḍamad, saying: al-ḍamad is to be enraged at one over whom you have no power, while al-ghayẓ is to be enraged whether or not you have power over him — and they cited as evidence the saying of al-Nābigha. But the derivation of these words is one and the same.

8. al-ḍamad, with the mīm given a fatḥa, is also said of what remains outstanding of a due: "We have a ḍamad owed to us by so-and-so," meaning an outstanding due, whether blood-money or a debt. Its origin is something that has accumulated in their hands and remained unpaid.
ضمر:
The letters ḍād, mīm and rā' are two sound roots: one indicates leanness in a thing, the other indicates absence and concealment.

The first: their saying ḍamara al-faras wa-ghayruhu ḍumūran, from a lightness of flesh, and it may also come from emaciation. The place where horses are trained lean is al-miḍmār. Rajulun ḍamr — a man light of body. Al-lu'lu' al-muḍṭamir — a pearl with some slight indentation in its middle.

The other: al-ḍimār, wealth that is absent and not hoped for. Anything absent from you, that you cannot be sure of, is ḍimār. The poet said, in a line of verse:
And worn-out camels that knelt at Saʿīd's by night, then hastened back at early morning — they praised his hospitality, and received from him a gift that was no unfulfilled promise, no absent thing.

From this chapter: aḍmartu fī ḍamīrī shay'an — I concealed something in my ḍamīr, because it hides it away in the heart and breast.
ضمز:
The letters ḍād, mīm and zāy are a sound root indicating holding back in speech, or holding something in the mouth, and the like.

1. ḍamaza al-baʿīr — the camel held back from chewing its cud.
2. al-ḍāmiz — the silent one.

Bishr said, in a line of verse:
Sulaym held back with their cud ... in fear of us, as the donkey held back.

3. al-ḍamz — a kind of eating, because when a man eats this way he holds the food in his mouth.
4. ḍamaza fulānun ʿalā mālī — so-and-so held fast to my property, meaning he clung to it.

What deviates from this root: al-ḍamza — the low, humbled hillock; its plural is ḍamz.
ضمس: The letters ḍād, mīm and sīn are not a root. Ibn Duraid mentioned a word which, if it is sound, belongs to the category of letter-substitution. He said: al-ḍams is chewing. If that is so, it is from al-ḍamz.
ضمن:
The letters ḍād, mīm and nūn are a sound root, and it is putting a thing inside something that contains it.

1. ḍammantu [al-shayʾ] — you say this when you put the thing into its container.
2. Surety is called ḍamān (a guarantee) from this, because it is as if, when one stands surety for a thing, he has taken it in fully under his own responsibility.
3. al-maḍāmīn — what is in the wombs of pregnant animals. From this comes the hadith in which he forbade the sale of al-malāqīḥ and al-maḍāmīn, for people used to sell what a pregnant animal was carrying, and this was forbidden.
4. As for his saying, "yours is the ḍāmina among the palm trees," he means what their villages enclosed within their boundaries.

This chapter runs consistently throughout.

As for al-ḍamāna, which is chronic illness, and al-ḍamin, the chronically ill person — these, in my view, belong to the category of letter-substitution, as though the ḍād were substituted for a zāy. And in the hadith: "Whoever registers himself as ḍaminan [chronically ill], God the Exalted will raise him up ḍaminan" — meaning whoever wrote himself down among the chronically ill.
ضن:
The letters ḍād and nūn are a sound root indicating stinginess with a thing. One says: ḍanintu bi-al-shay' — I was stingy with the thing — aḍannu bihi, ḍannan and ḍanāna; and a man is ḍanīn, stingy.

1. ʿilq maḍanna / maḍinna — a precious possession one is stingy with, said of something so valuable that people are reluctant to part with it.
2. "So-and-so is my ḍinnī among my brothers" — said when he is the precious one who is jealously guarded.

They sometimes say ḍanantа, with the nūn given a fatḥa instead.
ضنط: The letters ḍād, nūn and ṭāʾ — they say of it: al-ḍināṭ is a great crowding, a crush of people.
ضنك:
The letters ḍād, nūn and kāf are two sound roots, though their branches are few. The first is narrowness, the other an illness.

The first: al-ḍank, narrowness. From this: imra'atun ḍinnāk, a woman firm and compact of flesh, when the flesh presses tightly together.

The other root: al-maḍnūk, one afflicted with a head-cold, and al-ḍinnāk is the head-cold itself. God knows best.
ضنى:
The letters ḍād, nūn and the weak letter [alif] are two sound roots. One indicates illness, and the other wavers between being hamzated and not, and it indicates one of two things: either an origin, or offspring — and origin and offspring are close in meaning.

The first is al-ḍanā, meaning illness. One says: ḍaniya yaḍnā ḍanan shadīdan, when a lingering disease afflicts a man, so that whenever he thinks he has recovered, he relapses. And one says the illness aḍnāhu, yuḍnīhi — it wore him down.

As for the other, one says: ḍanaʾat al-marʾa ḍanʾan — a woman, meaning her children grew many; she is ḍāniʾa, and one also says aḍnaʾat.

1. al-ḍinʾ — origin and source. One says, "So-and-so is of good stock [min ḍinʾi ṣidq]."
2. aḍnaʾa al-qawm — the people's livestock grew numerous.
3. ḍanaʾa al-māl — the property [livestock] multiplied.

ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm told us, from ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, from Abū ʿAmr, that al-ḍanw means "the child" [offspring], and one also says al-ḍinw. Al-Umawī reported from Abū al-Mufaḍḍal of Banū Salāma: al-ḍanw, with fatḥa, is "the child," and al-ḍinʾ, hamzated, is "origin."

What deviates from all of this: aḍnaʾa fulānun min kadhā — so-and-so felt shame because of such a thing.
ضهب:
The letters ḍād, hāʾ and bāʾ are a sound root indicating a thing, and the like of that.

1. al-laḥm al-muḍahhab — meat that is roasted. Some said: it is meat that is roasted but not fully cooked through. Imruʾ al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
We wipe our hands on the manes of the horses ... when we rise from a roasted [muḍahhab] roast.
Some said instead that al-laḥm al-muḍahhab is meat cut into pieces — but this is nothing, unless it is both cut up and roasted, for that is what the analogy requires.
2. al-ḍayhab — the place that is heated so that meat may be roasted upon it.
3. ḍahhabtu al-qawsa [wa] al-rumḥa bi-l-nāri ʿinda al-tathqīf — I heated the bow and the spear over the fire while straightening them.
ضهد: The letters ḍād, hāʾ and dāl are a single word. ḍahadtu fulānan — I overpowered so-and-so; so he is muḍṭahad and maḍhūd — both meaning: overpowered, oppressed.
ضهر: The letters ḍād, hāʾ and rāʾ are not a root, and there is no line of poetry as evidence for it. But they say: al-ḍahr is a natural formation in a mountain, made of rock differing from the rest of its formation.
ضهس: The letters ḍād, hāʾ and sīn are not a root. However Ibn Duraid mentioned that biting with the front of the mouth is called ḍahs; one says from it: ḍahasa ḍahsan. He said: and in the curse said against a person: "may he eat nothing but ḍāhis [gnawed with the front teeth], and drink nothing but qāris [ice-cold]" — meaning he eats nothing that requires effort to chew, but only the scant produce of the earth's plants. And al-qāris is the cold, meaning he drinks nothing but water.
ضهل:
The letters ḍād, hāʾ and lām are two sound roots: one indicates scarcity, and the other, return.

1. ḍahalat al-nāqa — when the she-camel's milk grew scant; she is a nāqa ḍahūl.
2. ʿaynun ḍāhila — a spring scant in water.

And in the hadith of Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmur: "If she asks you the price of her milk-share and your loan-portion, you set about withholding it from her and making it scant."

3. Also from this chapter: ḍahala al-sharāb — the drink grew scant and thin.

The other root: hal ḍahala ilaykum khabarun — did any news come back to you, meaning: did it return. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: ḍahaltu ilā fulānin — I returned to so-and-so, in the sense of going back to fight and overcome him.

What deviates from both roots: aḍhalati al-nakhla — the palm tree ripened into soft ripe dates.
ضهي: The letters ḍād, hāʾ and yāʾ are a sound root indicating one thing's resemblance to another. One says: ḍāhāhu yuḍāhīhi, when it resembled it; and sometimes it is hamzated, so one says yuḍāhiʾu. Al-marʾa al-ḍahyāʾ is the woman who does not menstruate; and it may be said, by a stretch and with some strain, that it is as if she has come to resemble men, in that she does not menstruate.
ضوأ:
The letters ḍād, wāw and hamza are a sound root indicating light. From it, al-ḍaw' and al-ḍū', the same in meaning, which is light and illumination. God Almighty said: {but when it lit up what was around him} [al-Baqara: 17]. Abū 'Ubayd said: one says aḍā'at al-nāru, the fire gave light, and aḍā'at ghayrahā, it lit something else. A verse was recited:
The fire lit up for us a radiant face ... entangled together with the heart.
ضوب: The letters ḍād, wāw and bāʾ are something whose soundness I do not know. Al-ḍūbān — the strong camel; and it is also said: rather al-ḍūbān is the withers of the camel.
ضوج: The letters ḍād, wāw and jīm are a single word, and it is al-ḍawj — the bend of a valley; its plural is aḍwāj.
ضور:
The letters ḍād, wāw and rāʾ are a small sound root, with some letter-substitution in it.

1. al-taḍawwur — crying out and writhing under a blow; it is also said to be turning over from back to belly.
2. al-ḍawr — severe hunger.

As for the substitution, al-Kisāʾī said: lā yaḍūrunī kadhā, in the same sense as lā yaḍīrunī — it does not harm me.
3. rajulun ḍūra — a lowly, abject man, from this.
ضوز:
The letters ḍād, wāw and zāy are two sound roots: one, a kind of eating; the other indicating crookedness.

1. ḍāza al-tamra yaḍūzuhu ḍawzan — when he ate it roughly and forcefully. [A poet] said:
So he kept eating [yaḍūzu] the dates while the dates lay glistening ... with a redness the color of crimson dye, in streaks.
Ibn Duraid said: it is when a man takes the date in his mouth until it softens. The meaning of the line of verse is that he takes the blood-money in dates instead of the blood-payment, whose color is the color of crimson.

The other root: al-qismatu al-ḍīzā — the unjust, crooked division.
ضوض: The letters ḍād, wāw and ḍād: al-ḍawḍāʾ has already been mentioned, and the root is a doubled one.
ضوط: The letters ḍād, wāw and ṭāʾ are a single word, and it is al-ḍawīṭa. It is said of dough, when its water becomes so much that it turns slack: al-ḍawīṭa.
ضوع:
The letters ḍād, wāw and ʿayn are a single word that branches out, and it indicates motion and disturbance.

1. ḍāʿanī laka al-shayʾu yaḍūʿunī — when it stirred me. [A poet] said:
But it is the smell of blood that spreads.
2. taḍawwaʿat rāʾiḥatuhu — its scent wafted and spread. [A poet] said:
Musk spread through the hollow of Nuʿmān when Zaynab passed through it, among a group of perfumed women.
3. ḍāʿati al-rīḥu al-ghuṣna — the wind bent the branch.
4. hādhā al-amru lā yaḍūʿunī — some said this means: it does not weigh on me; though the sounder analogy is that it means: it does not stir me, and I pay it no heed.
5. ḍāʿa yaḍūʿu wa-yanḍāʿu — when he writhed and cried out in pain. [A poet] said:
Two chicks that cry out at dawn ... whenever they sense the sound of the wind or a crow's call.
6. Abū ʿUbayd said, on the authority of Abū ʿAmr: ḍāʿanī al-shayʾu — the thing frightened me. And this is sound, because fright disturbs and unsettles a person.
ضون: The letters ḍād, wāw and nūn are not a root. But they say: al-ḍaywan is a small creature resembling the cat.
ضوي:
The letters ḍād, wāw and yāʾ are a sound root indicating emaciation. One says: ghulāmun ḍāwiyyun — an emaciated boy; its pattern is fāʿūl. And jāriyatun ḍāwiyya — an emaciated girl. The Arabs used to say: when the kinship between the two parents is close, the child is born ḍāwī [frail]. And it came in the hadith: "Marry outsiders, do not become frail." Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
Her brother is her father, and frailty does not harm her ... and her father's leg is her mother, wounded, badly wounded.
One says from it: ḍawiya yaḍwā ḍawan.

1. What is carried on this: their saying aḍwaytu al-amra, when you did not carry out a matter properly; and one also says aḍwaytuhu, when you diminished it and deemed it weak. [A poet] said:
And how should I be belittled, when Bilāl is my ally?
2. al-ḍawāh — something said to come out of a she-camel's birth-passage before her young is born. It is also said that al-ḍawāh is a swelling that afflicts a camel in its head. [A poet] said:
So it became a swelling in the jowls of a tough old she-camel.

What deviates from this root: ḍawaytu ilayhi aḍwī ḍuwiyyan, and awaytu, with the same meaning — I took refuge with him. It may be that this belongs to letter-substitution, the ḍād being put in place of the hamza.
ضيح: The letters ḍād, yāʾ and ḥāʾ are a small sound root, and it is milk mixed [with water], which is al-ḍiyāḥ. One says: ḍiḥtu al-labana ḍayḥan, and ḍayyaḥtu is more [emphatic].
ضير: The letters ḍād, yā' and rā' are one word, and it is from al-ḍayr, harm. "Lā yaḍīrunī kadhā" means it does not harm me. God, exalted, said: {And if you are patient and mindful of God, their scheming will not harm you at all} [Āl ʿImrān: 120].
ضيز:
The letters ḍād, yā' and zā' have been mentioned before; it is said their true origin is a wāw. It has also been said the root belongs to the family of words with a final yā', and so it is mentioned here as well. Al-qisma al-ḍīzā is the unjust, unequal division. One says ḍiztuhu ḥaqqahu, when you deprived him of his right. Some related the form ḍa'azahu, with a hamza, and cited:
So your right is denied, and your nose is brought low.

There is nothing more in this chapter than this.
ضيع:
The letters ḍād, yā' and 'ayn are a sound root pointing to a thing's slipping away, going and perishing. One says ḍā'a al-shay' yaḍī'u ḍayā'an wa-ḍay'atan — the thing was lost — and aḍa'tuhu anā iḍā'atan — I let it go to waste. As for their calling landed property ḍay'a, I do not think it belongs to the original language; I think it is from newly coined speech. I have heard someone say: it is called that only because, if the tending of it is left off, it goes to ruin.

If it is so, that is proof of what we said, that it is from newly coined speech. One says aḍā'a fa-huwa muḍī' when his losses are many. As for the words of al-Shammākh:
O 'Ā'ish, what ails your people that I do not see them
And there remains a word that is not of this chapter but of the chapter of letter-substitution: Ibn al-Sikkīt reported taḍayya'at al-rīḥ, like taḍawwa'at — the scent spread abroad.
ضيف:
The letters ḍād, yā' and fā' are a single, sound root, indicating the leaning of one thing toward another. Aḍaftu al-shay'a ilā al-shay'i, I inclined the thing toward the thing. Ḍāfati al-shamsu taḍīfu, the sun leaned toward setting; likewise taḍayyafat, when it leaned toward its going down. In the hadith: he forbade prayer when the sun has begun to lean toward setting. Imru' al-Qays said:
When we had entered it, we leaned our backs ... against every fresh, striped tent-hide.
Meaning, we rested our backs. One also says ḍāfa al-sahmu 'ani al-hadafi yaḍīfu, the arrow veered away from the target. Abū Zubayd said:
Every day she looses at it a volley of arrows ... some finding their mark, some veering off, not far astray.

1. al-ḍayf — the guest, of this chapter. Ḍiftu al-rajula, I sought the man out so that he would host me. Aḍaftuhu, I took him in as my guest. One also says ḍayyaftuhu, the same as aḍaftuhu, when you lodge him with you. Fulānun yataḍayyafu al-nāsa, so-and-so goes about seeking hospitality from people, following them so they will take him in. This is in al-Farazdaq's line: "and he whose favour the hospitality-seeker hopes for." Al-ḍayf serves for both singular and plural; one also says aḍyāf and ḍīfān.
2. ḍīf — a side of a valley; there are two ḍīfān. Taḍāyafnā al-wādiya, we came at the valley from its two sides; likewise taḍāyafa al-kilābu al-ṣayda, the dogs closed in on the game from its sides. A verse: "A gazelle beset from every side by cringing dogs."
3. al-muḍāf — the one who has been surrounded in battle. A verse: "He protects the surrounded man when he calls for help ... when the shaggy giant of a man turns and flees." This belongs to the same analogy. One also says taḍayyafūhu, when they closed in on him from every side. A verse: "When they closed in on him from every side, he slipped away."

As for the line —
A foundling, whom his mother carried while she was a guest ... and bore, base spawn for a base breed —
ḍayfa there is the familiar sense, from hospitality (ḍiyāfa), a woman being hosted.

Some said ḍāfati al-mar'atu means the woman menstruated; this is not sound, and there is no analogy that supports it, no reason to trouble with it.

As for their saying aḍāfa min al-shay'i, when he was wary of it, this may be an anomaly outside the root already stated, or it might be forced to fit by saying he was wary of it as if he had gone to stand at the ḍīf, the margin, that is, he did not go into the middle of it out of caution. But that is far-fetched, and I think it better simply to call it anomalous. The word is well known. A verse: "and the reproach was that you should show alarm and cry out." Al-Hudhalī said: "when he raids, she grows afraid" — meaning tushfiq, she is anxious. Abū Sa'īd said: ḍāfa al-hammu, the anxiety settled upon its bearer — the reasoning being that when it settles on him, it has leaned toward him.
ضيق:
The letters ḍād, yā' and qāf are a single word that points to the opposite of roominess, and that is al-ḍīq, narrowness. Al-ḍīqa is poverty. One says aḍāqa al-rajul — the man's wealth went from him; and ḍāqa when he was miserly. A thing is ḍayq, that is, ḍayyiq, narrow. The whole chapter runs on one and the same analogy.

As for the saying of the poet:
In a ḍīqa between al-Najm and al-Dabarān.
It is said that al-ḍīqa here is one of the way-stations among the stations of the moon. Abū 'Amr said: al-ḍīqa here is from al-ḍīq, narrowness.
ضيك: The letters ḍād, yāʾ and kāf are a word that does not branch out. They say al-ḍaykān is the walk of a man heavy with flesh in the thighs, so that he perhaps waddles. And one says: these are camels that taḍīku, meaning their thighs spread apart from the largeness of their udders.
ضيل:
The letters ḍād, yāʾ and lām are a single root indicating a known plant.

1. al-ḍāll — the wild lote-tree; its singular is ḍālla.
2. Al-Farrāʾ said: aḍālat al-arḍ, and aḍyalat — when the ḍāll grows in it.
3. And it is said: al-ḍāla is the nose-ring of a she-camel. Ibn Mayyāda said:
I cut through with [a she-camel fitted with] a swift-turning nose-peg, that a nose-ring and a rein turn back, against her will.
ضيم: The letters ḍād, yāʾ and mīm are a sound root, and it is like overpowering and oppression. One says: ḍāmahu yaḍīmuhu ḍayman — it is both a noun and a verbal noun. Al-rajulu al-maḍīm — the wronged man. And there remains in this chapter one word: it is said that al-ḍīm, with kasra on the ḍād, is the side of a mountain. Al-Hudhalī said [the line of verse is not given in the text].
طأ: The letters ṭā' and hamza indicate the sinking-down of a thing. From this, their saying: ṭaʾṭaʾa raʾsahu, he lowered his head. It is taken from al-ṭaʾṭāʾ, a low-lying place in the ground. It occurs in the saying of al-Kumayt.
طب:
The letters ṭā' and bā' are two sound roots: one indicates knowledge of a thing and skill in it, the other indicates extension in a thing and stretching-out.

The first:
1. al-ṭibb — knowledge of a thing. It is said: rajulun ṭabbun wa-ṭabībun, meaning: knowing, skilled. He said, in a line of verse: 'if you ask me about women, then I am, well-versed in the ailments of women, a physician.'
2. faḥlun ṭabbun — a stud-animal skilled at covering [mating].
3. ṭabb — also said of the one who takes care to note where his foot treads.
4. al-ṭibb — sorcery is called by this name; it is said maṭbūb, meaning bewitched. He said, in a line of verse: 'if you have been bewitched, may you remain so; and if enchanted, may the enchantment never be cured.'

As for their saying mā dhāka bi-ṭibbī, meaning that is not my [habitual] practice — this amounts to nothing as a genuine derivation; its meaning is rather: that is not the matter I am skilled at, not the thing I have mastered as knowledge, as in the hadith 'fa-mā ṭahwī idhan' [then what is my roasting-skill, then] — we have already mentioned this in its place.

As for the other root:
1. al-ṭibba — the elongated strip of cloth, plural ṭibab.
2. ṭibab shuʿāʿ al-shams — the extended streaks seen in the sun's rays when it rises.
3. al-ṭibāba — the thong between two stitch-holes in leatherwork.
4. al-ṭibba — also, a long, narrow strip of land, abundant in plants. From this, their saying: talqā fulānan ʿan ṭibabin kathīra, meaning: of many kinds.
طبخ:
The letters ṭāʾ, bāʾ and khāʾ are a single root, and it is the well-known cooking. One says: ṭabakhtu al-shayʾa aṭbukhuhu ṭabkhan — I cooked the thing; I am ṭābikh, a cook; and the thing is maṭbūkh or ṭabīkh.

1. al-ṭubbakh — the plural of al-ṭābikh, cook. Al-ʿAjjāj said, in a line of verse: "By God, were it not that the cooks would stoke the fire..." He meant by it the angels appointed over the Fire.
2. ṭabāʾikh — what the scorching blasts of heat are called.
3. ṭābikha — the nickname of a man among the Arabs, because he did a cooking, and was named for that.
4. al-ṭubākha — what boils up as froth from the pot when it is cooking; the same as al-ṭufāḥa and al-fuwwāra.
5. ṭābikh — what a raging, shivering fever is called.

Among what is carried onto this chapter — and it may be later speech, not classical — is their saying: laysa bihi ṭubākh, there is no ṭubākh in him, said of a thing with no strength in it, as though they mean something not yet finished, not yet cooked through.

And among what falls outside this chapter — though it is sound speech — is their calling the young of the ḍabb lizard muṭabbikh, once it grows strong. They say: it is first a ḥisl, then a muṭabbikh, then a khuḍarim, then a ḍabb.
طبس: The letters ṭāʾ, bāʾ and sīn amount to nothing. Except that they say: al-ṭabasān are two districts. This and the like of it is not worth mentioning, because when everything of similar shape is brought in, what is not truly part of Arab speech gets carried along with it. So too the saying of one who said: al-taṭbīs is al-taṭbīn.
طبع:
The letters ṭā', bā' and ʿayn are a sound root, and it is a figure for an end at which a thing arrives and is sealed off. One says *ṭabaʿtu ʿalā al-shay'i ṭābaʿan* — I set a seal on the thing. Then on this pattern one speaks of *ṭabʿ al-insān*, a man's stamp and inborn nature. Of that is *ṭabaʿa Allāhu ʿalā qalb al-kāfir* — God sealed the unbeliever's heart, as though He set a seal on it so that no guidance and no light reach it, and so he is not granted any good. Of that also is *ṭabʿ al-sayf wa-l-dirham*, the striking of the sword and the coin, and that is when he beats it until he makes it complete. *Al-ṭābaʿ* is the seal with which one seals; *al-ṭābiʿ* is the one who seals. Of this chapter is their word for the filling of a measure: *ṭabʿ*. The rule is one, because it has come to its full and been closed off. And *taṭabbaʿa al-nahar* — the river filled up, and that is the same meaning. And likewise when a she-camel is loaded with her full and complete load she is *muṭabbaʿa*. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Where are the two pack-pins, and where is the lifting-pole, and where is the load of the fully laden she-camel?

Ibn al-Sikkīt said: *al-ṭibʿ* is the river; the plural is *al-ṭibāʿ*. A poet said, in a line of verse:
So they turned away, their walking slack, like the water-camels of the river when they come upon the mire.
And perhaps what they said in describing the river is that it is full, so that it would fit the rule better.

Among what stands apart from this root — though the two may possibly be brought near one another, only that this is forced — is their word for filth: *ṭabaʿ*. One says *rajul ṭabiʿ*, a filthy man. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "Seek refuge with God from a greed that leads to filth." And a poet said, in a line of verse:
It has crowns set with rubies, which its goldsmith spaced out; you see in them no flaw and no tarnish.

And from this same word comes their saying of a man when he does not carry a matter through: *qad ṭabiʿa*.
طبق:
The letters ṭā', bā' and qāf are a single sound root, indicating the laying of one flat thing over its like until it covers it. From this: al-ṭabaq. You say aṭbaqtu al-shay'a 'alā al-shay', I laid the one over the other, and so the first is a ṭabaq, a match, for the second; and the two may taṭābaqā, correspond to one another. From this: their saying aṭbaqa al-nāsu 'alā kadhā, the people were all agreed on such a thing, as though their sayings were so equal that if one were set as a match to the other it would fit exactly.

1. al-ṭabaq — a state or condition, in His words {You shall surely ride stage upon stage} [al-Inshiqāq: 19].
2. iḥdā banāti ṭabaq — the great calamity, called ṭabaq because it covers and encompasses all.
3. ṭabaq al-arḍ — whatever spreads over the earth until it blankets it. From this is Imru' al-Qays's line describing rain:
A steady drizzling rain with a fine mist in it ... covering the whole earth, coming round and pouring.
4. ṭabbaqa al-ḥaqqa, said when he hit upon it — from this, meaning it matched, his purpose falling in agreement with, and matching, the truth. From this too, ṭabbaqa is said of one who strikes a joint exactly, without missing it; and then they say ṭabbaqa 'unuqahu bi-l-sayfi, he severed his neck with the sword, striking the joint exactly.
5. al-muṭābaqa — the gait of a man in fetters, since his two feet fall close together as though matching one another. From this is al-Ja'dī's line:
Dogs treading step for step upon the harāsā-plant.
6. al-ṭabaq — a thin bone separating two vertebrae.
7. yadun ṭabiqah — a hand stuck fast against the side.
8. ṭābaqtu bayna al-shay'ayni, I made the two things match, set them to one pattern. For this we call speech doubled twice over muṭābaq, such as jarjara, ṣalṣala, ṣa'ṣa'a.
9. al-ṭabaq — a swarm of locusts, likened to a ṭabaq that covers the earth.
10. waladati al-ghanamu ṭibqan wa-ṭabaqatan, said of sheep giving birth one after another. The reasoning is one and the same throughout.

As for their calling a slow-witted man al-ṭabāqā', and a camel unable to mate properly ṭabāqā', this too is from the same reasoning, as though a thing were hidden from him until it was shut over him, so that he became as one covered. Jamīl said:
ṭabāqā' — who never stood witness in a dispute, nor led riding-camels to their saddles when they are made to kneel.
طبل:
The letters ṭāʾ, bāʾ and lām are three words that have none of the polish of true Arabic speech, and I do not know how they stand.

1. al-ṭabl — the drum that is beaten.
2. al-ṭabl — they say it also means: physique, bodily form.
3. al-ṭūbāla — and were it not that it came in a piece of poetry, there would be no reason to mention it; I do not know it except in this one line:
His tenderness brought me news of a ṭūbāla,
who browses on dried ʿishriq leaves.
And it is said: it means the ewe.
طبن:
The letters ṭāʾ, bāʾ and nūn are a sound root indicating firmness.

1. iṭbaʾanna — one says this when a thing became firm and settled, like iṭmaʾanna.
2. ṭabantu al-nāra — I buried the fire so that it would not go out, and that place is called al-ṭābūn.
3. ṭābin hādhihi al-ḥafīra — meaning: press this pit down level.
4. "The good in the sons of so-and-so is like a firmly-rooted ṭabn" — meaning: it is inherited, of old standing.

And from this chapter is:
1. al-ṭaban — shrewdness. That fits the pattern of the chapter, because there is in it something like firmness in the knowledge of a thing.
طبى:
The letters ṭāʾ, bāʾ and the weak letter are a minor root indicating the calling in of something.

1. iṭṭabā — one says: iṭṭabā banū fulānin fulānan, when they won him over as kin and took him in. Sometimes they say ṭabāhu and iṭṭabāhu, meaning: he called him.

If al-ṭabyu is taken from aṭbāʾ al-nāqa, the teats of the she-camel, on the idea that the milk is drawn out from it, taking this together with that, it would not be far-fetched. And it is reported that the Arabs say: hādhā khilfun ṭibiyyun, meaning: responsive [to the pull]. If this is sound, it points to the soundness of the analogy we have drawn.
طث: The letters ṭā' and thā' amount to nothing. They claim that al-ṭathth is a game played with a piece of wood called al-miṭathha.
طثر:
The letters ṭāʾ, thāʾ and rāʾ are a minor sound root indicating richness in a thing and abundant moisture.

1. ṭathra — they say: fulānun fī ṭathratin min al-ʿaysh, meaning: he is in richness and ease of life. They say its derivation is from al-laban al-ṭāthir, thickened, curdled milk. Mud is likened to this by the same reasoning and is also called ṭathra. And a man among the Arabs was named Ṭathra.

And among what falls outside this chapter, and we do not know how sound this is, is their saying that al-ṭaythār is the mosquito. God knows best.
طثرج:
In what is said, it is the ant. He said, in a line of verse:
A trace like the traces of young ants.

1. ṭalsama, of a man — he made his face ugly, scowled.
2. al-ṭilkhām — they say it is the elephant.
3. iṭrakhamma — he swelled with pride, grew haughty.
4. al-ṭumrūs — they say it is the liar.
5. al-ṭurmūs — bread baked in hot ashes.
6. al-ṭirmisā' — darkness. It is possible that this word is one where the rā' has been added, as though it were from ṭamasa.
7. ṭarbala, of a man — when he trailed his skirts.

All that we have mentioned is without any consistent pattern, and the mind is doubtful of its soundness, even though we have heard it said. And God knows best what is correct.

(The Book of the Letter Ṭā' is complete.)
طجن: Regarding the letters ṭāʾ, jīm and nūn, they say: al-ṭājin is al-ṭābaq, a flat griddle-pan. This is a reported word. God knows best.
طح:
The letters ṭā' and ḥā' are close to the root before it, in that they say:

1. al-ṭaḥḥ — scraping something with your heel.
2. ṭaḥṭaḥa bihim — he scattered them.
3. ṭaḥṭaḥahum — he overpowered them.
طحر:
The letters ṭāʾ, ḥāʾ and rāʾ are a sound root indicating driving forth, throwing and casting out.

1. ṭaḥarat al-ʿaynu qadhāhā — the eye cast out its speck of dirt, when it threw it out. One also says: ṭaḥarat ʿaynu al-māʾ al-ʿirmiḍ — the spring threw out the algae growing on it.
2. qawsun miṭḥar — a bow that drives its arrow forcefully, shooting it up straight.
3. ḥarbun miṭḥara — a grinding, relentless war.
4. al-ṭaḥīr — the high, labored breath, named so because the one who has it does the action ṭaḥar. Al-Kumayt said, in a line of verse:
With melodies from its songs, harsh,
following them with the sighing, panting breath.
5. al-muṭḥar, among arrowheads, is the long, tapering one. Al-Hudhalī said, in a line of verse:
From the muṭḥarāt of the ilāl.
[The line is cut off in the text as it stands.]
طحل:
The letters ṭāʾ, ḥāʾ and lām are a sound root indicating a color that is neither pure nor bright.

1. al-ṭuḥla — the color of dust-grey.
2. ramādun aṭḥal, sharābun aṭḥal — ash, or a drink, is called aṭḥal when it is not clear.
3. al-ṭiḥāl — the spleen, well known; it is possible it was named for the dullness of its color.
4. ṭaḥila al-māʾ — the water spoiled and changed.
طحلب:
Al-ṭaḥlab [moss, algae] is well known. The bā' in it is extra; it is really from ṭaḥala, which concerns colour, and we have already discussed it.

1. ṭaḥmara — when he leapt. The ḥā' is extra; it is really ṭamara (to leap).
2. ṭarmaḥa the building — he made it tall. From it is the name al-Ṭirimmāḥ. Its origin is al-ṭaraḥ, meaning the far one and the tall one, which we have already explained.
3. ṭarfashat, of an eye — it grew dark. The shīn is extra; its origin is from ṭurifat: something's edge struck it and it welled up with tears, and at that point it darkens — which has already passed.
4. al-ṭalakhf — the severe, the intense. The lām is extra; it is al-ṭakhaf, meaning intensity.
5. al-ṭulkhūm — stagnant, foul water. The mīm is extra; it is really from al-ṭalkh, which we have already mentioned.
6. youth described as al-muṭrahimm — this is a case where the rā' has been added; its origin is muṭahham (well-formed, robust), which has already passed.
7. their saying, there is not a ṭaḥraba in the sky, meaning a cloud. The bā' is extra, as though it were something that drives the rain off, ṭaḥran — that is, pushes it back and casts it away.
8. the dry loaf called al-ṭamallas — this word is carved from two words, ṭalasa and ṭamasa, both of which indicate smoothness in a thing.
