Among what has been set down and can scarcely be put to any consistent pattern:

1. al-ṭafannash — wide across the front of both feet.
2. ṭarsama, of a man — he bowed his head in silence.
3. al-ṭirfisān — a great tract of sand.
طحم:
The letters ṭāʾ, ḥāʾ and mīm are a sound root indicating gathering and density.

1. al-ṭuḥma — a group of people, the dense, crowded gathering.
2. ṭuḥmat al-layl and ṭaḥmatuhu, ṭuḥmat al-sayl and ṭaḥmatuhu — the bulk, the main mass, of the night or the flood.
3. Al-Khalīl said: ṭaḥmat al-fitna is the surging of people at the time of it.
4. It is said, of a man fierce in combat: ṭuḥama.

And the whole chapter is one sense.
طحن:
The letters ṭāʾ, ḥāʾ and nūn are a sound root, and it is the crushing and pounding of a thing by what turns over it from above. One says: ṭaḥanat al-raḥā ṭaḥnan — the millstone ground. Al-ṭiḥn is the ground flour. They say: "I hear the creaking but I see no ṭiḥn" — the creaking being the sound of the millstone.

1. katībatun ṭaḥūn — a troop that grinds down whatever it meets.
2. al-ṭawāḥin — what the back teeth, the molars, are called.
3. al-ṭuḥan — a small creature that buries itself in dust it has smoothed and shaped round.
4. ṭaḥanat al-afʿā — the viper coiled itself, when it twisted round into a circle.
طحو:
The letters ṭā', ḥā' and the weak letter are a sound root indicating spreading and stretching out. From that: al-ṭaḥw, like al-daḥw, a spreading-out. God, exalted, said: {and the earth and what spread it out} [al-Shams: 6], meaning He spread it out; and He said, exalted, elsewhere: {and the earth, after that, He spread it out} [al-Nāziʿāt: 30]. One says ṭaḥā bika hammuka yaṭḥū, when your worry carried you off and stretched out with you in the matter. ʿAlqama said, in a line of verse:
A heart carried you off, delighting in beautiful women, not long after youth, at the time grey hair came.

Al-mudawwima al-ṭawāḥī are the vultures that circle round the slain. Al-Shaybānī said: ṭaḥaytu means I lay down. Al-ṭāḥī is a great multitude, named so because it drags over a thing, as such a host is also called jarrār [a dragging crowd]. It was said:
From the vast throng, the huge multitude, sweeping in upon you.

God knows best.
طخ:
The letters ṭā' and khā' are not, in my view, a root that runs consistently or admits of sound analogy. It has been reported from al-Khalīl:

1. ṭakhṭakha al-saḥāb — the clouds drew together, part joining part.
2. al-ṭakhṭakha — the smoothing or evening out of a thing.

This needs evidence before it can be established as sound. As for the mere report current in this chapter, it is said that al-ṭakhṭakha means laughter — but mere reports of this kind are not grounds for analogy.

Close to this in weakness is their saying:

1. al-mutakhaṭkhikh — one weak of sight.
2. al-ṭukhūkh — bad character and harshness.
طخر:
The letters ṭāʾ, khāʾ and rāʾ are a sound root indicating lightness in a thing.

1. al-ṭakhārīr — the scattered ones; the light, quick-darting man is likened to this.
طخف:
The letters ṭāʾ, khāʾ and fāʾ are a minor root indicating something thin.

1. al-ṭakhāf — the thin cloud.
2. al-ṭakhf — something like the worry that settles over the heart.
طخم:
The letters ṭāʾ, khāʾ and mīm are a sound root indicating blackness in a thing.

1. al-ṭukhma — blackness at the tip of the nose. They say: kabshun aṭkham, asadun aṭkham — a ram or a lion is called aṭkham for this.

God knows best what is correct.
طخى:
The letters ṭāʾ, khāʾ and the weak letter are a sound root indicating darkness and a covering-over.

1. al-ṭakhwa and al-ṭakhya — the thin cloud.
2. al-ṭakhyāʾ — the dark night. They say: ẓalāmun ṭākhin — dark, covering darkness.
3. wajada ʿalā qalbihi ṭakhāʾ — he found upon his heart a ṭakhāʾ, something like distress.
4. kallamanī kalimatan ṭakhyāʾ — he spoke to me a ṭakhyāʾ word, meaning: a foreign, unintelligible one.
طر:
The letters ṭā' and rā' are a sound root indicating sharpness in a thing, elongation, and extension.

1. ṭarra al-sinān — he sharpened the spearhead. This gives sinānun maṭrūr, a sharpened spearhead.
2. al-rajul al-ṭarīr — a man of fine bearing, as though he were something that had been trimmed, polished, and sharpened.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
The fine-looking man pleases you, so you put him to the test... and the fine-looking man disappoints your expectation.

3. fatan ṭārr — a young man whose moustache has begun to grow (ṭarra shāribuhu).
4. al-ṭurra — the border or hem of a garment.
5. ramā fa-aṭarra — he shot, and it went clean through.
6. Anything made fine or finished is said to have "ṭarra" — to the point that they say ṭarra ḥawḍahu, he plastered his trough with clay.
7. ṭurrat al-ghaym — the long, drawn-out streak in a cloud.
8. The black mark on a donkey's back is called ṭurra.
9. ṭurrat al-nahr — the bank or edge of a river.
10. ṭarra al-nabt — the plant sprouted; this comes from ṭarra shāribuhu, his moustache sprouting.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Among us is he whose moustache has not yet sprouted, and the long-unmarried... and among us are the beardless youths and the grey-haired.

As for al-ṭarr in the sense of driving off and expelling, this too belongs to the root, because one who drives a thing off and expels it makes it go sharply, so that it grows keen in its haste and running.

As for the line of al-Ḥuṭay'a:
You grew angry at us because we killed, for Khālid's sake, the sons of Mālik... behold, this is an anger no one can account for.

Abū Zayd said: al-iṭrār is inciting someone to do a thing. This is close in analogy to the root, because when one incites another to a thing he has made him sharp and keen. Others said: al-muṭirr means the boastful, overbearing one. The first explanation is better and closer to sound analogy. It is also said that "al-ghaḍab al-muṭirr" is anger that comes from the aṭrār of the land — that is, anger whose source is not known. This too is sound, because aṭrār al-arḍ means the outer edges of the land, and the ṭaraf, the edge, of anything is its sharp point.
طرب:
The ṭā', rā', and bā' are a genuine small root. They say: al-ṭarab is a lightness that comes over a man from intensity of joy or something else. They recite, in a line of verse:
They said, you have grown excited — and I said, no; does the hardy, steadfast man weep from excitement?
And Nābigha of Banū Jaʿda said, in a line of verse:
And I see myself excited in their wake, the excitement of the love-struck, or like the bewildered.
They said: ṭarraba fī ṣawtihi, when he drew it out at length — and this is from the first meaning. And al-karīm, the generous man, is ṭarūb.
Among what strays from this chapter is al-maṭārib — narrow, scattered paths. I take it to be a case of letter-substitution, as though it were madārib, derived from al-darb, the mountain pass.
As for their saying about al-ṭurṭubb, that it is the sagging breast, and likewise al-ṭarṭaba, the sound a milker makes to the goats — all this, and anything like it, is loose talk not to be relied on.
طرث: The ṭā', rā', and thā' are a genuine word: it is al-ṭurthūth, which is a plant.
طرح:
The letters ṭā', rā' and ḥā' are a sound root indicating the casting away and throwing of a thing. One says ṭaraḥa al-shay' yaṭraḥuhu ṭarḥan. From that: al-ṭaraḥ, a far-off place. Ṭaraḥat al-nawā bi-fulānin kulla maṭraḥ, when distance and fate carried him far away and cast him off. It was said, in a line of verse:
Stop a while by Mayy's dwelling, before separation casts us to some far place, or before a parting takes her from us.

One says faḥlun miṭraḥ, a stallion whose seed lands far within the womb. From this chapter: nakhlatun ṭarūḥ, a palm with long frond-stalks; sanāmun iṭrīḥ, a long hump; qawsun ṭarūḥ, a bow that drives its arrow far and hard. The reasoning throughout is the same one.
طرد:
The letters ṭā', rā' and dāl are a single sound root, indicating driving away and distancing.

1. One says ṭaradtuhu ṭardan — I drove him off. aṭradahu al-sulṭān and ṭarradahu — the ruler exiled him, when he expelled him from his land.
2. al-ṭard — pursuing to catch game.
3. al-ṭarīda — the game, the quarry.
4. muṭārada of matched opponents — their charging one another; so called because this one drives that one off [and is driven off in turn].
5. al-miṭrad — a short spear.
6. The main-trodden part of a road is called maṭrada.
7. One says iṭṭarada al-shay' iṭṭirādan — the thing ran on continuously, when one part followed another; this is said by comparison, as though the first part drives the second one on.

From this is his saying, in a line of verse:
do you recognize traces, like the running lines of pathways, of ʿUmra's camp — deserted now, with no rider halting there.

8. muṭṭarad al-nasīm — the nose, along which the breeze runs continuously.

ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm al-Qaṭṭān recited to us, from Thaʿlab, from Ibn al-Aʿrābī, in a line of verse:
and it is as though the passage of the breeze, when it flows, after weariness, were two hollow wasp-hives.

9. iṭṭarada al-amr — the matter ran smoothly, went straight.

Anything that stretches out follows this same pattern. One says ṭarrid sawṭaka, stretch out your whip.

10. al-ṭarīd — a child born right after his brother; the second is the ṭarīd of the first. This is a comparison, as though he drove him along and followed him; ṭarīd here has the sense of ṭārid, the one driving or following.
طرز:
The letters ṭāʾ, rāʾ and zāʾ are a word thought to be Persian, brought into Arabic. It occurs in the poetry of Ḥassān:
Fair of face, noble of lineage,
high of nose, of the first ṭirāz.
And they say: ṭirzuhu, meaning: his form, his appearance.
طرس: The letters ṭāʾ, rāʾ and sīn have something said of them that may be sound. They say: al-ṭirs is the erased writing, a manuscript scraped clean for reuse. It is said every sheet is a ṭirs. And they say: al-taṭarrus is that a person eats and drinks nothing but what is wholesome.
طرش: The letters ṭāʾ, rāʾ and shīn are a well-known word, and it is al-ṭaraš, deafness, well known. Abū ʿAmr said: taṭarrasha al-nāqih min al-maraḍ — the convalescent grew restless, standing up and sitting down, in his recovery from illness.
طرط: The letters ṭāʾ, rāʾ and ṭāʾ are one word. They say: al-aṭraṭ is the one sparse of eyebrows; and one says: ṭariṭa, he became so.
طرف:
The letters ṭā', rā' and fā' are two roots: the first points to the edge of a thing and its rim, and the second points to a movement in certain of the limbs.

The first is *ṭaraf al-shay'* — the end of a thing, of a garment, of a wall. And one says *nāqa ṭarifa*, a she-camel that grazes the edges of the pasture and does not mix with the other camels.

And their saying *ʿayn maṭrūfa* is from this; that is, that the edge of something — a garment or otherwise — strikes the eye so that it brims with tears. And this is borrowed until one says *ṭarafahā al-ḥuzn*, grief struck her eye.

As for their saying *huwa karīm al-ṭarafayn*, some people said: what is meant by it is his descent on the father's side and the mother's side. And *lā yudrā ayyu al-ṭarafayni aṭwal* — it is not known which of the two ends is the longer — is from this. The plural of *ṭaraf* is *aṭrāf*. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And how is it with my two ends when you revile me? And after the reviling of both parents there is no making peace.

And it is said that *al-ṭirāf* is what is taken from the edges of the standing crop.

Of this chapter are *al-ṭawārif* of the tent, which are the parts of its sides that you lift so as to look out. As for their saying *jā'a fulān bi-ṭārifati ʿayn*, it is from what we mentioned in their saying *ṭurifat al-ʿayn*, when the edge of something strikes it and it brims with tears. And when it is like that one can hardly see. So too their saying *bi-ṭārifati ʿayn*, that is, with something at which the eye is bewildered from the sheer quantity of it.

Of this chapter is their word for a thing newly got: *ṭarīf*, which is the opposite of *al-talīd*, the long-inherited. Its meaning is that it is a thing gained now, at the edge of a time already gone by. From it they say *iṭṭaraftu al-shay'* — I got it new — *aṭṭarifuhu, iṭṭirāfan*.

Of this chapter is *al-rajul al-ṭarif*: the man who does not hold to one wife or one companion. And that is the rule, because he keeps seeking out one edge after another. And *al-mar'a al-maṭrūfa*: they say she is the one who does not hold to one man, but takes the men one after another as fresh acquisitions. That is what al-Ḥuṭay'a said, in a line of verse:
He sought love from a woman whose love roves, whose eye strays.

Of this chapter is *al-ṭirf*, the noble horse, as though its owner had newly acquired it. And what is newly got has an excellence over what is long inherited.

As for the other root, it is *al-ṭarf*, and it is the moving of the eyelids in looking. This is the root; then they call the eye *al-ṭarf* by a figure. For that reason one of the stars is called *al-ṭarfa*, as though it were, as I think, the eye of the Lion. Jarīr said, in a line of verse:
Those eyes with a languor in their glance have killed us, and then have not brought our slain back to life.

As for *al-ṭirāf*, it is a tent of hide, and it stands apart from the two roots we have mentioned.
طرق:
The letters ṭā', rā' and qāf are four roots: one of them is coming in the evening; the second is striking; the third is a kind of slackness in a thing; and the fourth is stitching one thing onto another.

The first is *al-ṭurūq*. It is said that it is coming to the dwelling by night. They said: a man is *ṭuraqa* when he travels on until he comes to his people by night. And it was mentioned that this is said of the daytime too, but the root is the night. The proof that the root is the night is their calling the star *ṭāriq*, because it rises by night. They said: everyone who comes by night has done *ṭaraqa*. A woman said, in a line of verse:
We are the daughters of Ṭāriq — the star.
Those are a woman's words. She means: our father is a star in his nobility and his height. Of this chapter — and God knows best — is *al-ṭarīq*, the road, because it is come upon. And it may be from another root, the one we mentioned of stitching one thing over another.

Of the first chapter is their saying *ataytuhu ṭarqatayn*, that is, twice. From it comes *ṭāriqat al-rajul*, which is the branch of his tribe that he belongs to; it was called *ṭāriqa* because it comes to him and he comes to it. A poet said, in a line of verse:
I complained to him of the going away of my kin, and my kin were off in the reaches of the mountain passes.

The second root is striking. One says *ṭaraqa yaṭruqu ṭarqan*. The thing struck with is *miṭraq* and *miṭraqa*. From it comes *al-ṭarq*, which is striking with pebbles to divine, and it is what the hadith came forbidding; and it was said: "Striking with pebbles, reading omens from birds, and driving them off, are of sorcery." A woman who does this is *ṭāriqa*; the plural is *al-ṭawāriq*. A poet said, in a line of verse:
By your life, the women who strike the pebbles do not know, nor those who drive off birds for omens, what God is going to do.

And *al-ṭarq* is beating wool with a rod, and that rod is a *miṭraqa*. And the soothsayer sometimes does that, so he does *ṭarq*, that is, he mixes cotton with wool when he divines. And they make a proverb of this and say, "He beat and he mixed." A poet said, in a line of verse:
O blamer, you have taken a liking to prettying up talk against me in secret — so beat your wool and mix it in.

And one says *ṭaraqa al-faḥl al-nāqa ṭarqan*, when the stallion covers her. *Ṭarūqat al-faḥl* is his female. And *istaṭraqa fulān fulānan faḥlahu*, when he asked him for his stallion to cover among his camels, and he granted it to him. And one says *hādhā al-nabl ṭarqatu rajulin wāḥid*, that is, the making of one man.

The third root is the slackness of a thing. Of that is *al-ṭaraq*, which is a softness in a bird's feathers. The poet said, in a line of verse:
(the line stands blank in the printed text)
From it comes *aṭraqa fulān fī naẓarihi* — he dropped his gaze. And *al-muṭriq* is the one whose eye is slack. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And I never feared that his death would be at the two hands of a bold blue-eyed man with drooping gaze.
And another said, about lowering the eyes, in a line of verse:
So he lowered his head as the serpent lowers its head; yet if the serpent saw a way in for its fangs it would drive them home.

Of this chapter is *al-ṭirrīqa*, which is softness and yieldingness. They say in the proverb: "Beneath his soft manner there is a stubbornness." That is: in his softness there is at times some hardness. As for *al-ṭaraq*, some people said: it is a crookedness in the shin without the feet turning outward. And others said: *al-ṭaraq* is a weakness in the two knees. This second saying fits the rule better and is more like the rest of what we mentioned of softness and slackness.

The fourth root is stitching one thing onto another. One says *naʿl muṭāraqa*, that is, a sandal sewn in layers. And *khuff muṭāraq*, when two soles have been laid over it. Every stitching-on is *ṭirāq*. And *turs muṭarraq*, a shield when a hide has been laid over it to its own size. Of this chapter is *al-ṭirq*, which is fat and strength, so called because it is a thing that is as though stitched on. They say *mā bihi ṭirq*, that is, there is no strength in him. Abū Muḥammad ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muslim said: the root of *al-ṭirq* is fat, because strength comes mostly from it. Of this chapter is *al-ṭaraq*, the standing pools of water; they were named so by likeness to a thing that lies layer upon layer. So too water, when it stands long, lies in layers. Ru'ba said, in a line of verse:
To the perennial spring, when the water of the standing pools had failed him.

Of this chapter — and we mentioned it at the start, and it is not far-fetched that it should be from this rule — is *al-ṭarīq*, the road; and that is because it is a thing lying over the ground, as though the ground had been layered and stitched with it. And they say *taṭāraqat al-ibil*, when the camels come one following another. So too *al-ṭarīq*, which is the palm trees standing in a single row; and this is a likeness, as though it were likened to the road in its running on and its lying over the ground. Al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse:
And of every dark bay like the trunk of a row-palm, that adorns the courtyard when it stands still.

And from it comes feathers that are *ṭirāq*, when they lie one over another. And *kharaja al-qawm maṭārīq*, when they come on foot with no mounts, as though each one of them were stitching with the print of his feet the print of the one who went before. And one says *jā'at al-ibil ʿalā ṭarqatin wāḥida* and *ʿalā khuffin wāḥid* — the camels came in one track; that is what we mentioned, that they stitch other camels' tracks with their own. And *ikhtaḍabat al-mar'a ṭarqatayn*, when she puts on the dye a second time, as though she stitched the first with the second. Then from *al-ṭarīq* a verb is derived, and they say *ṭarraqat al-mar'a* at childbirth, as though she had made a road for the child. And it is said — and it is that first sense — that one does not say *ṭarraqat* except when half the child has come out and then is held back a while and then comes out. You say: she *ṭarraqat*, then she came clear.

And like this is their saying *ṭarraqat al-qaṭāt*, when the sand-grouse has hard labour with her egg and so scratches the ground with her breast.
طرم:
The letters ṭāʾ, rāʾ and mīm are a minor sound root indicating the piling up of a thing.

1. al-ṭurāma — the green film on the teeth.
2. al-ṭirm — honey.
3. al-ṭiryam — a thick cloud.
طرى:
The ṭā', rā', and the weak letter are a genuine small root indicating freshness and newness. So al-ṭariyy is a soft, fresh thing; its verbal noun is al-ṭarāwa and al-ṭarā'a. From it comes aṭraytu fulānan — that is, when you praise someone with the best that is in him.
If hamzated, one says: ṭara'a fulānun, meaning he appeared, came into view. I take this to be a case of letter-substitution (ibdāl), and the true root is daraʾa, which has already been mentioned.
طس: The letters ṭā' and sīn are not a root. Al-ṭass is a dialect form of al-ṭast, a basin.
طسأ: The ṭā', sīn, and hamza are a single word. They say: ṭasi'at nafsī, my stomach turned queasy — so it is ṭasi'a, queasy.
طست: The ṭā', sīn, and tā' amount to nothing, except al-ṭast, the basin, which is well known.
طسل:
The ṭā', sīn, and lām — several words fall under it, and perhaps they are genuine, except that they follow no consistent pattern.

1. al-ṭasl — the wavering shimmer of a mirage.
2. al-ṭaysal — the abundant; one says mā'un ṭaysal, abundant water.
3. al-ṭaysal — dust.
طسم: The ṭā', sīn, and mīm are a single word. One says: ṭasama, like ṭamasa (to efface, blot out). And Ṭasm is a tribe descended from ʿĀd.
طش:
The letters ṭā' and shīn are a small root indicating scantness of rain; it may also be borrowed for something else.

1. al-ṭashsh — light, weak rain.

Ru'ba said, in a line of verse:
Nor is the wetness of your downpour reduced to a mere drizzle.

God knows best what is correct.
طع: The letters ṭā' and ʿayn amount to nothing. As for what al-Khalīl related, that al-ṭaʿṭaʿa is an imitation of the sound of the one who smacks or licks, that too amounts to nothing.
طعم:
The letters ṭā', ʿayn and mīm are a root, consistent and regular, in the tasting of a thing. One says ṭaʿimtu al-shay' ṭaʿman — I tasted the thing. And al-ṭaʿām is what is eaten. Some of the people of the language used to say: al-ṭaʿām is wheat in particular, and he cited the hadith of Abū Saʿīd: "We used to give out the alms of the fast-breaking in the time of the Messenger of God — may God bless him and his family and grant them peace — a ṣāʿ of ṭaʿām or a ṣāʿ of such and such." Then what is not of the chapter of tasting is carried onto the chapter of food by way of borrowing, so one says istaṭʿamanī fulān al-ḥadīth when he wants you to tell him the talk. And in the hadith: "When the prayer-leader asks you for food, feed him" — he means: when he is stopped in his recitation and seeks the opening, open it for him. And al-iṭʿām, the giving of food, applies to everything that is taken in, even water. God, exalted be He, said: {and whoever does not taste it, he is of me} [al-Baqara: 249]. And he, peace be upon him, said of Zamzam: "It is food that feeds and a cure for sickness." And Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh al-Qasrī was faulted for his saying, "Feed me water", and [someone] composed verse faulting him for that; but in our view that is no fault, for the reason we have mentioned. And one says a man is ṭāʿim: in good condition as to his eating. Al-Ḥuṭay'a said, in a line of verse:
Leave noble deeds, do not travel in search of them ... and sit still, for you are the one who eats and clothes himself.

And a man is miṭʿām — much given to feeding guests. And you say: he is muṭʿam when he is granted provision. And al-ṭuʿma is the thing eaten, the source of a living. And "I made this estate a ṭuʿma for so-and-so" — a living for him. As for the line of Dhū al-Rumma, in a line of verse:
And in the left hand a bow of shiryān wood, muṭʿama ... curved, with a bend and a straightening in its grip —
it is related with a fatḥa on the ʿayn, muṭʿama, meaning that it is a bow granted game. And it is related muṭʿima; whoever relates it so means that it feeds its owner game.

And the thick, foremost toe of the bird of prey is called muṭʿima, because it feeds it when it hunts with it. And they say that al-muṭaʿʿam among camels is the one in whose marrow the taste of fat is found from its fatness. And of the palm, when its fruit ripens, one says: it has aṭʿamat, it has begun to yield food. And al-taṭaʿʿum is tasting. One says "taṭaʿʿam taṭʿam" — taste the food and you will want it and eat it. And one says: so-and-so is khabīth al-ṭuʿma when his earning is base. And one says: come near and eat; and he says: mā bī ṭuʿm — I have no appetite for food, as one says of drink: mā bī shurb — I have no wish to drink. And one says a ewe is ṭaʿūm when there is some fat in her.
طعن:
The letters ṭā', 'ayn and nūn are a sound, consistent root: it is the piercing of a thing with something that goes through it, and from there it is extended and used metaphorically. From this: al-ṭa'n, thrusting with the spear. One says: taṭā'ana al-qawm wa-iṭṭa'anū, the people thrust at one another; they are maṭā'īn [given to spear-thrusting] in war. A man is ṭa''ān fī a'rāḍ al-nās, one who stabs at people's honour, meaning he slanders them. In hadith: "The believer is not one who stabs at others [ṭa''ān]." Some related: ṭa'antu fī al-rajuli ṭa'anānan, and no other form — as though distinguishing this word from thrusting with the spear. He said, in a line of verse:
His open hostility refused anything but reviling [ṭa'anān] and saying what should not be said.

Ṭa'ana fī al-mafāzah: he went off into the waterless desert. Some said: ṭa'ana bi-l-rumḥi yaṭ'unu [with a spear, with the vowel u], and ṭa'ana bi-l-qawli yaṭ'anu [with speech, with the vowel a] — as though the two vowel-patterns keep the two senses apart.
طغم: The letters ṭā', ghayn, and mīm form a word which I do not think belongs to the genuine root-stock of Arabic speech. They call the basest sort of people ṭaghām.
طغى:
The letters ṭā', ghayn, and the weak letter are a sound root that runs by consistent analogy, and it is the overstepping of a limit in disobedience.

1. huwa ṭāghin — he is one who has overstepped the limit, a transgressor.
2. ṭaghā al-sayl — the flood came bringing great volumes of water.

He said, Exalted is He: {When the water rose beyond its limit} [al-Ḥāqqa: 11] — meaning, God knows best, its going out beyond its due measure.

3. ṭaghā al-baḥr — the sea's waves rose up in turmoil.
4. ṭaghā al-dam — the blood surged up (tabayyagha).

Al-Khalīl said: al-ṭughyān and al-ṭughwān are dialect variants of the same word; the verb from it is ṭaghaytu and ṭaghawtu.

One thing that strays from this root: they say al-ṭaghya is a smooth, flat rock.
طف:
The letters ṭā' and fā' indicate scantness of a thing.

1. ṭafīf — a scant thing.
2. ināʾun ṭaffān — a vessel described as full, to the brim.
3. al-taṭfīf — shortchanging the measure or the scale. Some scholars said it is so named because what is taken short from it is ṭafīf, scant.
4. al-ṭafāf, al-ṭufāfa — what is above the vessel, [the overflow at its rim].
5. ṭaffaftu bi-fulān mawḍiʿa kadhā — I raised him up to such a place and brought him level with it. In the hadith: 'the horse brought me level with the mosque of Banū so-and-so' — meaning it leapt until it nearly matched the mosque [in height]. This follows the same pattern as the ṭufāf and ṭufāfa of a vessel.

And among what departs from the root: their saying aṭaffa fulānun bi-fulān, when he was cunning toward him and sought to deceive him. From this: istuṭiffa al-amr, when the matter became possible and was completed — this belongs to the chapter of letter-substitution, already discussed in its place.
طفح:
The letters ṭā', fā', ḥā'. This is close to the chapter before it.

1. al-ṭufāḥa — what rises to the top when something is cooked, whether froth, butter, or the like; from this, anything that rises over another thing and covers it is called ṭāfiḥ.
2. ṭafaḥa al-nahr — the river filled up and overflowed.
3. ṭafaḥa al-sakrān — the drunken man became overcome with drink; he is ṭāfiḥ.
4. ṭaffaḥat al-rīḥ al-quṭna fī al-hawā' — the wind sent the tuft of cotton soaring up into the air.
طفر: The letters ṭā', fā', rā' form a sound word: one says ṭafara, he leapt.
طفس: The letters ṭā', fā', sīn: they say ṭafasa, he died; and al-ṭafas is grime or filth.
طفق: The letters ṭāʾ, fāʾ, and qāf are a sound word. They say: ṭafiqa yafʿalu kadhā, he set about doing such a thing, just as one says ẓalla yafʿalu. God Most High said: {and he set about wiping the legs and necks} [Ṣād: 33], and {and the two of them set about fastening leaves of the Garden over themselves} [al-Aʿrāf: 22].
طفل:
The letters ṭā', fā' and lām are a sound, regular root, then further reasoned upon by analogy; its origin is the small newborn. One says huwa ṭiflun, and the female is ṭiflatun. Al-muṭfil is a gazelle-doe with her young (ṭifl) with her, one lately delivered. One says ṭaffalnā ibilanā taṭfīlan, meaning our camels had their young with them, so we went gently with them on the march — this is the origin. Derived from it: their calling a soft, tender woman ṭaflah, as though she were likened, in her softness and tenderness, to the infant ṭiflah, the two forms then kept apart, one with fatḥa and the first with kasra. From this chapter, or close to it: ṭifl al-ẓalām, the first onset of darkness, called ṭifl for its slightness and fineness, coming before the bulk of the night arrives. Labīd said:
Then I let myself down upon it, returning ... while on the ground lay the last shadows of the early dark.
One says ṭafala al-laylu, meaning its darkness came on. As for the speaker's line —
For a hollow the early setting of the Pleiades had watered
— [the entry as given to me appears to break off here].
طفن: The letters ṭā', fā', nūn amount to nothing, not a real root. Even so, they say al-ṭufāniya is a term of reproach applied to a man or a woman. God knows best what is correct.
طفو:
The letters ṭā', fā', and the weak letter are a sound root, indicating something light that rises above another thing.

1. ṭafā al-shay' fawqa al-mā', yaṭfū ṭafwan wa-ṭufuwwan — a thing floated atop the water, when it rose above it and did not sink — so much so that they even say ṭafā al-thawr fawqa al-ramla, the bull loomed up above the sand.

2. al-ṭufya — the palm-leaf of the wild dwarf-palm, al-muql. It was named this because it grows large until it covers the tree. In al-Khalīl's book: al-ṭufya is a wicked, venomous snake. This, in our view, is a mistake — al-ṭufya is properly the palm-leaf of the muql, plural ṭufyy; the streak on a snake's back is then likened to it. The Messenger of God, may God bless him, his family, and grant him peace, said of snakes: "Kill the one marked with the two ṭufya-streaks, and the short-tailed one." Do you not see that he called it possessor of two ṭufya-streaks, because the two lines on its back were likened to that leaf? Al-Hudhalī said, concerning al-ṭufy, in a line of verse:
The trace of the dwelling is effaced, nothing left to mark it out... and the remnants of palm-leaf mats, effaced now among the strongholds.

As for the saying:
As the ṭufā-marked ones submit to the charmer's charm — he meant by al-ṭufā the snakes themselves. The Arabs sometimes extend a word's use even further than this, as when it was said:
When I load my gear onto 'ʿadas' — meaning: onto the mule that is called by that name, that being a cry used to drive mules on.

3. When the word is pronounced with hamza it carries a different meaning: one says ṭafi'at al-nār taṭfa'u, the fire went out; anā aṭfa'tuhā, I put it out.

As for al-ṭafā' — like al-ṭakhā', a thin cloud — it belongs to the first root, as though it were something that floats.
طل:
The letters ṭā' and lām indicate three roots: one is the freshness and tenderness of a thing; another is looming and rising above; the third is nullifying a thing.

The first: al-ṭall — the weakest, lightest rain, so named because it makes the earth beautiful. For this a man's wife is called his ṭalla; some said she is so named because she is fresh in his eye, as though she were ṭall [light rain]. In the sense of scantness, carried over from al-ṭall, is their saying mā bi-l-nāqati ṭallun, meaning: she has no milk at all, not even a little. The ṭāʾ is given a different vowel [ṭull] to set it apart from [the word for] rain.

The second root: al-ṭalal — what stands up of the traces of dwellings, ruins. A man's stature is called his ṭalal. From this: aṭalla ʿalā al-shayʾ, when he loomed over it. Ṭalal al-safīna — its gunwales, plural aṭlāl. It is said: taṭālaltu, when you stretch your neck to look at something far off. He said, in a line of verse: 'sorrow enough it was that I stretched up to see the peaks of the two waymarks of Damkh, but they did not appear.'

As for nullifying a thing: that is iṭlāl al-dimāʾ, nullifying blood-claims, when [a killing] goes unavenged. It is said: ṭulla damuhu, so it is maṭlūl; and uṭilla, so it is muṭall, when it is voided.

And among what departs from these roots — and I do not know how sound it is — their saying that al-ṭill is the snake. Al-ṭalāṭila is a disease that strikes in the spine.
طلب:
The letters ṭā', lām and bā' are a single root indicating the seeking of a thing. One says ṭalabtu al-shay'a aṭlubuhu ṭalaban. Hādhā maṭlabī, hādhihi ṭalibatī — this is what I seek, this is my object of pursuit. Aṭlabtu fulānan bimā ibtaghāhu means I supplied so-and-so with what he sought, that is, I helped him to it. Sometimes they say aṭlabtuhu meaning I put him in need of seeking. Aṭlaba al-kala' means the pasture grew far from water, until people had to go seeking it, and such water is called mā'un muṭlib. Dhū al-Rumma said:
[He was led astray by two shepherds of Kalbiyya, who turned aside from a distant watering-place whose visitors were scattered bands.]
طلح:
The letters ṭā', lām and ḥā' are two sound roots: one is a kind of tree, the other a chapter about emaciation and the like.

The first: al-ṭalḥ, a well-known tree, singular ṭalḥa. Dhū Ṭulūḥ is a place-name, perhaps having ṭalḥ trees growing there. One says ibilun ṭalāḥā and ṭaliḥa, when camels have sickened from eating ṭalḥ.

The second: their saying nāqatun ṭilḥu asfār, when travel has worn her down and left her thin; she has ṭaliḥat. Al-ṭilḥ is also the emaciated one among ticks. It was said, in a line of verse:
When a bedraggled tick sleeps behind her, her breath and panting guide it to her.

From this chapter: al-ṭalāḥ, the opposite of al-ṣalāḥ [a good, sound state] — as though taken from a bad condition and emaciation.
طلخ:
The letters ṭā', lām, khā' amount to nothing, not a real root. They mention in it a word that looks as though it were formed by transposing the letters of another word. Al-Khalīl said:

1. al-ṭalkh — smearing with filth.
2. al-ṭalkh — also, the silt (al-ghirīn) that remains at the bottom of a watering-trough.
طلس:
The letters ṭā', lām, sīn are a sound root; it seems to indicate smoothness.

1. ṭils — the thigh of a camel, when its hair has fallen away, is called ṭils.
2. ṭalastu al-kitāb — I effaced the writing, as though I had smoothed it over.

As for al-dhi'b al-aṭlas, they say it means the dust-grey wolf; but analogy suggests it is rather the one whose hair has come out in patches — and if what they say is correct, then it is as though, from its dust-grey colour, it seems clothed in a ṭaylasān, a kind of cloak.

3. al-ṭaylasān, with fatḥa on the lām, is a sound word. A poet said, concerning it, in a line of verse:
And a night in which every star that appears to you seems glimpsed through the gaps of a ṭaylasān cloak.
طلع:
The letters ṭā', lām and 'ayn are a single sound root pointing to appearing and coming out into view.

One says ṭala'at al-shams ṭulū'an wa maṭla'an — the sun rose. Al-maṭli' is the place of its rising. God Most High said: {ḥattā maṭla'i al-fajr} — until the rising of the dawn [al-Qadr: 5]. Whoever opens the lām means the verbal noun, and whoever gives it a kasra means the place from which it rises. And one says ṭala'a 'alaynā fulān, when a man comes upon us suddenly. And aṭla'tuka 'alā al-amr iṭlā'an, I let you see into the matter. And qad aṭla'tuka ṭil'ahu, I have shown you the news of it. Al-ṭilā' is the stretch of land that the sun rises upon. And in the hadith: 'If I had the earth's fill of gold.' Nafs ṭula'a is a soul that keeps craning after a thing. And imra'a ṭula'a is a woman who looks out and peers a great deal. Al-ṭal' is the spathe of the palm, which is the thing that has the kāfūr inside it, and the palm has aṭla'at, put out its spathe. And qaws ṭilā' al-kaff is a bow whose grip fills the hand. Aws said, in a line of verse:
Silent, a hand's fill, not less than filling it, nor is its grip wider than the place of the hand.

And of this chapter is istaṭla'tu ra'y fulān, when you look to see what comes out to you from him. And ṭal'at al-insān is the sight of a man, because it comes out into view. And ramā fulān fa-aṭla'a wa ashkhaṣa, when a man shoots and his arrow passes
over the head of the target. And ṭalī'at al-jaysh is the one who spies out the news of the enemy. And al-muṭṭala' is the way a thing is come at; one says ayna muṭṭala'u hādhā al-amr, where is the way into this matter, that is, how it is come at. As for his saying, peace be upon him: 'I would have ransomed myself with it from the terror of al-muṭṭali'.' And of this chapter is al-ṭula'ā', vomit; one says aṭla'a, when a man vomits.
طلف:
The letters ṭā', lām, fā' are a sound root indicating the disparaging of a thing and its being cast aside; other words are then carried on this base.

1. al-ṭalaf — bloodshed for which no restitution is claimed; anything not sought or claimed is likewise called hadar, forfeit.

The poet said, in a line of verse:
Time has ruled against us: whatever it has taken from us is uncompensated loss, unclaimed.

2. al-ṭalaf — carried on this base — a gift, an outright giving-away; a thing is not given away until its loss is of little weight to the giver. One says aṭlafanī and aslafanī: al-ṭalaf is an outright gift, and al-salaf is what is later claimed back, a loan.
3. al-ṭalaf — the trifling, light thing.

The poet said, in a line of verse:
And everything of this world that befalls us, as long as you live among us, is a trifle, even if the calamity is great.

Al-ṭalīf and al-ṭalaf are close in meaning. As for their saying that al-ṭalaf means "surplus," that amounts to nothing, unless what is meant is that it is what is left over from a thing, for the reason already given.
طلق:
The letters ṭā', lām and qāf are a sound root, running straight through, and one; and it points to letting go and setting loose.

One says inṭalaqa al-rajulu yanṭaliqu inṭilāqan — the man went off freely. Then the branches come back to it: you say aṭlaqtuhu iṭlāqan — I set him free. And al-ṭilq is the thing that is lawful, as though it had been let go and not forbidden.

Of this chapter: the horse ran a ṭalaq or two ṭalaqs, a heat or two of running. And a woman is ṭāliq — [her husband has divorced her] — and ṭāliqa tomorrow. And aṭlaqtu al-nāqata min ʿiqālihā and ṭallaqtuhā, so she was set free from her tether. And a man is ṭalq al-wajh and ṭalīquhu, open of face, as though it were let loose; and that is the opposite of al-bāsir, the frowning man, because the frowning man is one who scarcely brightens or opens out with cheerfulness. The people of Yemen say absara al-markabu when the ship came to a stop. And one says ṭalaqa yadahu bi-khayr and aṭlaqa, with the same meaning — he opened his hand with good.

Thaʿlab recited, in a line of verse:
Set your two hands free and they will profit you, man; slowly you water her, not in haste.

And al-ṭāliq is the she-camel let loose to graze where she pleases. And of the gazelle, when it passes on without turning aside for anything, one says: it has taṭallaqa, gone free. And a man is ṭalq al-lisān and ṭalīquhu, loose of tongue. And this is a tongue that is ṭalq dhalq, free and sharp.

And you say: this is a matter my soul does not taṭallaqu for — that is, it does not open out gladly for it. And one says ṭulliqa al-salīm when the pain of the snake-bitten man settles after the watching over him.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
At one time she lets him go free, and at another she comes back to him.

As for the words:
As terrors come over the head of al-muṭallaq —
it is related thus, with a fatḥa on the lām, "al-muṭallaq", and he is the one released from the pain of the venom.

Some people relate it as "al-muṭalliq", with a kasra on the lām; and then its meaning is that they call the man who wants to race with his horse al-muṭalliq, and terrors come over him because he does not know whether he will win or be beaten.

Al-Shaybānī said: al-ṭāliq among [the camels] is the one the herdsman keeps for himself and does not milk at the water. One says istaṭlaqa al-rāʿī li-nafsihi nāqatan — the herdsman kept a she-camel free for himself. And laylat al-ṭalaq is [the night] the herdsman leaves his camels free to go to the water; and along with that he leaves them to graze that night. One says aṭlaqtuhā ḥattā ṭalaqat ṭalaqan and ṭulūqan; and it is before the qarab, the last night's drive to water, and after the taḥwīz.
طلم:
The letters ṭā', lām, mīm are a sound root, and it is the striking of a thing with the flat of something spread out.

1. al-ṭalm — your striking bread baked in hot ashes with your hand, to shake off the ash on it.

How close al-ṭalm is to al-laṭm, slapping! The proof of that is Ḥassān's line of verse:
The women strike them with their head-veils.

Some read the verse this way, and others read it as "they slap them" — proof that the meaning is one and the same.

2. al-ṭalma — a loaf of bread, so named because it is "slapped" (tulṭamu) to shake off the ash.
طله:
The letters ṭā', lām, hā' are not, in my view, a root from which other words branch, nor is that a sound analogy. Still, they say:

1. ṭalaha fī al-bilād, yaṭlahu ṭalhan — he went off, wandered away in the land.
2. al-ṭulha — a small amount of speech.
3. al-ṭulha — worn-out, ragged clothes. One says: taṭalla this worn-out garment, until you get new ones in its place.
طلى:
The letters ṭā', lām, and the weak letter are two sound roots: one indicates smearing a thing with something, the other indicates something small, like the young of a creature.

The first:
1. ṭalaytu al-shay'a bi-l-shay', aṭlīhi — I smeared the thing with the thing; also iṭṭalaytu bihi, I smeared myself with it.
2. al-ṭilā' — a kind of drink, as though it were thickened until it became like the tar that things are smeared with.
3. al-miṭlā' — land that readily brings forth growth, plural al-maṭālī — this too fits the analogy, since it has been "smeared" with moisture until it softened.
4. kalāmun lā ṭalāwata lahu — speech that has no gloss to it, when it is poor and worthless, as though when it is otherwise it has been smeared with something that sweetens it.
5. bi-asnānihi ṭalyun wa-ṭilyān — his teeth have a [yellow] coating — two words for it.
6. ṭaliya fūhu yaṭlā ṭalan — his mouth took on a yellowness, as though it had been smeared with it.

The other root:
7. al-ṭilwa — the young of a wild female animal; the male is called ṭilan.
8. al-ṭilw — the wolf; perhaps because it is likened to its young, for the reason just given.

9. ṭilwa — the rope with which the young animal is tied, so said Ibn Durayd.

But al-Qaṭṭān recited to me, on the authority of Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā Thaʿlab, a line of verse:
Ever since its outer skin was stripped from it, it has had, from baseness, a leash that drags it along.

10. Al-Farrā' said: ṭalaytu al-ṭilā and ṭalawtuhu both mean I tied the young animal by its leg.

There remains in this chapter something that departs from this analogy, though it belongs to another chapter.

11. al-ṭalā — a person's build or figure, so said al-Shaybānī; one says, he is truly of a handsome build.

He cited a line of verse:
A cheek like the back of well-tanned hide, which I unveiled — handsome of build, tinged with the deep yellow of wars-dye, dark-eyed.

If this is sound, then in my view it comes from letter-substitution: as though the speaker meant al-ṭalal, a ruin, and substituted one of its two lāms with a weak letter. This belongs to the pattern known as "the falcon's folding of its wings," and it is not far-fetched.

12. al-ṭulya, plural al-ṭulā — the necks; they were named so because they stand up prominently, the word carried over from al-ṭalā, a person's figure.
طم:
The letters ṭā' and mīm are a sound root indicating the covering of one thing by another until it is made level with it, whether earth or something else.

1. ṭamma al-biʾra bi-l-turāb — he filled the well with earth and made it level.
2. al-ṭimm — the sea is called this, as though the water had covered that basin. They say: 'lahu al-ṭimm wa-l-rimm,' he has everything: al-ṭimm is the sea, al-rimm is the moist earth.
3. ṭamma al-amru — the matter rose up and prevailed; for this the Resurrection is named al-ṭāmma.
4. ṭamma shaʿrahu — he cut some of his hair; this carries the sense of leveling, even without the sense of covering.
5. al-ṭimṭim — the man who cannot speak clearly, as though he had been stopped up, the way a well is filled in.

And among what departs from this root, something Ibn al-Sikkīt mentioned: it is said ṭamma al-farasu, when the horse rose up; and ṭamma al-ṭāʾiru, when the bird rose above the tree.
طمث:
The letters ṭā', mīm and thā' are a sound root indicating the touching of something. Al-Shaybānī said: al-ṭamth, in the speech of the Arabs, is touching, and that applies to anything. One says: mā ṭamatha dhā al-mart'a qablanā aḥad, no one touched this pasture before us. He said: anything can be "yuṭmath," touched.

From this: al-ṭāmith, the menstruating woman — ṭamithat and ṭamathat. One says: ṭamatha al-rajulu al-mar'ata, the man "ṭamatha" the woman, meaning he touched her through intercourse — though here the word is not restricted to intercourse alone. God, Most High, said: {untouched before them by man or jinn} [al-Raḥmān: 56].

Al-Khalīl said: ṭamathtu al-ba'īra ṭamthan, when you hobbled the camel. One says: mā ṭamatha hādhihi al-nāqata ḥablun qaṭṭu, no rope ever touched this she-camel, meaning nothing touched her.

As for the saying of 'Adī, "aw ṭamthi al-'aṭan" [or the touching of the resting-place], some said al-ṭamth here means dirt or filth.
طمح:
The letters ṭā', mīm, ḥā' are a sound root indicating loftiness in a thing.

1. ṭamaḥa bi-baṣarihi ilā al-shay' — he raised his gaze toward the thing; anything raised up is ṭāmiḥ.
2. ṭamaḥa bi-bawlihi — he shot his urine up into the air.

The poet said, in a line of verse:
Tall, his gaze lifted... toward what frightens off the dog.

3. ṭamaḥātu al-dahr — the hardships of fate.
طمر:
The letters ṭā', mīm, rā' are a sound root indicating two senses: one is leaping, and the other, close to the first, is a thing's plunging downward.

The first:
1. ṭamara — he leapt; he is ṭāmir.
2. ṭimirr — said of a horse, as though it were "the leaper."
3. ṭāmir ibn ṭāmir — the flea.

The other sense:
4. ṭamara — he plunged down.
5. al-amr al-muṭammir — the ruinous matter; al-umūr al-muṭammirāt — ruinous matters.
6. ṭamāri — a place to which a person is raised up and then thrown down from.

The poet said, in a line of verse:
Toward a man whose face the sword has maimed, and another falling, slain, from a height.

7. ṭamartu al-shay' — I hid the thing away.
8. al-maṭmūra — a pit dug beneath the ground into which a thing is thrown.
9. ṭamartu al-ghirāra — I filled the sack, as though the thing had been thrown into it.

What strays from this root: al-ṭimr, a worn-out garment. As for their saying that al-miṭmar is a builder's plumb-line, I have already told you there is no point troubling over it — it does not fit this root.
طمس: The letters ṭā', mīm and sīn are a root indicating erasing a thing and wiping it out. One says ṭamastu al-khaṭṭ, I erased the writing; ṭamastu al-athar, I effaced the trace. A thing can itself be ṭāmis, fading away; and it can ṭamasa of itself, fade away on its own.
طمش:
The letters ṭā', mīm, shīn admit of no sound analogy; and were it not that the word occurs in poetry it would be counted among the doubtful, for it does not resemble genuine Arabic speech. Even so, they say:

1. mā adrī ayya al-ṭamsh huwa — I do not know which of the ṭamsh he is, meaning which of mankind and creation he is.

The poet said, in a line of verse:
A wild creature, not one of the ṭumūsh.
طمع: The letters ṭā', mīm and 'ayn are a single sound root pointing to a strong hope in the heart for a thing. One says ṭami'a fī al-shay' ṭama'an wa-ṭamā'atan wa-ṭamā'iyatan — he coveted the thing. And laṭamu'ta yā Zayd — how greedy you are, Zayd! — as they say laqaḍuwa al-qāḍiya, how well the judge judges! This is in expressing wonder. And it is said imra'a miṭmā' of a woman who makes a man hope and does not let him reach her.
طمل:
The letters ṭā', mīm, lām are a small root indicating lowliness and baseness. Its origin is what remains at the bottom of a watering-trough of scant water mixed with mud.

1. al-ṭamla — that residue is called al-ṭamla. One says uṭṭumila mā fī al-ḥawḍ, and he uṭṭumilahu it, when he leaves not a single drop in it.

They then carry the word further:
2. ṭimla — applied to a weak woman.
3. ṭiml — applied to a thieving man.

They also say that al-ṭiml means the shameless one. God knows best what is correct.
طمن:
The letters ṭā', mīm, nūn are a small root, formed with an added hamza.

1. iṭma'anna al-makān, yaṭma'innu, ṭumā'nīna — the place became settled and still.
2. ṭāmantu minhu — I calmed it, stilled it.
طمى:
The letters ṭā', mīm, and the weak letter are a sound root indicating loftiness and rising, in a particular thing.

1. ṭamā al-baḥr, yaṭmū and yaṭmī — two dialect forms — the sea rose, meaning it filled and swelled up; it is described as ṭāmin.
2. ṭamā al-faras — the horse went past swiftly; and that only happens with a raised, rising gait.
طن:
The letters ṭā' and nūn are a root indicating a sound.

1. ṭanna al-dhubābu — the fly buzzed, ṭanīnan.
2. ḍaraba yadahu fa-aṭannahā — he struck his hand and severed it with a sound, as though meaning by it the sound of the cutting.

And among what I do not consider genuine Arabic: their calling a bundle of firewood or the like ṭunn. They say ṭanna, meaning he died — but that is not sound.
طنب:
The letters ṭā', nūn, bā' are a root indicating a thing's fixity and firm hold, drawn out at length.

1. al-ṭunub — the guy-rope of tents, the cords by which they are tied down.
2. ṭannaba bi-l-makān — he settled and stayed at the place.
3. al-iṭnāba — an awning, as though it were an ifʿāla-form from ṭannaba, because it stays fixed over whatever it shades.
4. al-iṭnāba — also, a strap tied at the end of a bow's string.
5. aṭnaba fī al-shay' — he went to excess in the matter, as though he held fast to it out of a wish to press on in it.
6. ṭaniba al-faras — said of a horse, meaning the length and strength of its back, like the ṭunub-cord that is stretched out and by which a thing is held fast.
7. aṭnabat al-ibil — the camels went in a train, each following the other in their pace.
8. aṭnabat al-rīḥ, iṭnāban — the wind grew fierce, raising dust; the sense is that the dust rises up until it becomes like the iṭnāba, which is like an awning.
طنخ: The letters ṭā', nūn, khā' form a word, if it is sound. They say ṭanikha, when someone is sickened from over-eating; and it is also said of one who has grown fat.
طنف:
The letters ṭā', nūn, fā' are a sound root indicating one thing running around, overhanging, another.

1. al-ṭunuf — a jutting ledge on a mountain, overhanging it.
2. al-ṭunuf — also, the cornice or eaves-projection of a wall.
3. al-ṭanaf — leather straps or thongs.

As for al-ṭanaf in the sense of suspicion, it is a transposed form, as though from al-naṭaf, which has already been discussed in its own place.

What strays from this root: something reported from al-Shaybānī, that al-ṭanaf is one who eats little. One says: mā aṭnafahu — how little he eats!
طنى:
The letters ṭā', nūn, and the weak letter form a word indicating a disease among the diseases of camels.

1. ṭaniya al-baʿīr, yaṭnā, ṭanan — the camel's lung stuck to its side and it died of it.
2. mā ṭaniytu bi-hādhā al-amr — I have had no dealings with this matter, as though he were saying: it has not stuck to me, nor have I been smeared by it.

As for the form with hamza, it does not belong to this root in its consonantal shape, but it is close in meaning.

3. al-ṭin' — with hamza — suspicion, a scandalous imputation.

The poet said, in a line of verse:
As though upon the one under suspicion there rested a watching eye, at his seat, or wherever he looks out from.

It was named this because suspicion is among the things that smear, and by which one gets smeared.

What strays from this root: al-ṭan', with hamza, a dwelling — far removed indeed from what has been mentioned. Also straying from it: their saying "I left him at his ṭan'", meaning I left him clinging to the last of his life.
طه: The letters ṭā' and hā' are a single word. The swift horse is called ṭahṭāh.
طهر:
The letters ṭā', hā' and rā' are a single sound root indicating cleanness and the removal of filth. From this is al-ṭuhr, purity, the opposite of filth. And al-taṭahhur is holding oneself clear of blame and of everything ugly. And so-and-so is ṭāhir al-thiyāb, clean of garment, when he is not sullied.

[He said], in a line of verse:
The garments of the Banū ʿAwf are pure and clean ... and their faces, to the traveller who comes upon them, are bright.

And al-ṭahūr is water. God, exalted, said: {And We sent down from the sky purifying water} [al-Furqān: 48]. And I heard Muḥammad b. Hārūn al-Thaqafī say: I heard Aḥmad b. Yaḥyā Thaʿlab say: al-ṭahūr is that which is pure in itself and which purifies what is other than itself.
طهش: The letters ṭā', hā', shīn amount to nothing, not a real root. A word is mentioned concerning which there is question: they say al-ṭahsh is the spoiling of a piece of work.
طهف:
The letters ṭāʾ, hāʾ and fāʾ are like the root before this one. Except that they say:

1. al-ṭahaf — a food made from maize; it is also said to be the tops of ṣilliyān grass.
2. al-ṭuhāfa — the forelock, a tuft of hair.

All of that is reported speech.
طهل: The letters ṭāʾ, hāʾ and lām are a word, if it is sound. They say: ṭahila al-māʾ — the water became foul and stagnant. And al-ṭihliʾa is the mud that flakes off the side of a trough into the water.
طهم: The letters ṭāʾ, hāʾ and mīm are a sound root indicating something in the physical form of a person or other creature. Abū ʿUbayda reported that al-muṭahham is the one complete and handsome in form, among people and horses. Others said: al-muṭahham is the round, full-faced one. This, in our view, is the more correct of the two sayings, because of the hadith reported by ʿAlī — peace be upon him — describing the Messenger of God, God's blessings and peace be upon him and his family: "He was not muṭahham, nor mukaltham." And a word was reported, if it is sound: they say taṭahhamtu al-ṭaʿām — I disliked the food.
طهى:
The letters ṭā', hā', and the weak letter are a sound root indicating two things: either the handling of something, or fineness and thinness.

The first:
1. ʿilāj al-laḥm fī al-ṭabkh — the preparing of meat in cooking; al-ṭāhī is the one who does it, the cook, plural ṭuhāh.

The poet said, in a line of verse:
And the cooks of the meat went on, some roasting thin-sliced grilled meat, others a quickly-made stew.

Abū Hurayra, asked about something, said: "What then is my ṭahwī" — meaning, what is my handling of it, if I have not done it properly.

2. ṭahati al-ibil, taṭhā, ṭahyan — said of camels, when they scattered at night and grazed, as though in that they were "handling" something.

The poet said, in a line of verse:
And we bear no blame for one seeking stray camels, when its scattered ones range at night.

The other root: al-ṭahā' — a thin cloud; and ṭuhayya — a tribe among the Arabs, from which the word is derived; the adjective belonging to them is ṭuhawī and ṭuhwī.
طوب: The letters ṭāʾ, wāw and bāʾ are not a root, because al-ṭūb — as I reckon it — is what is called al-ājurr, the baked brick, and I do not think the Arabs knew it. As for ṭūbā, it is not from this; its true letter is a yāʾ, as though it were the pattern fuʿlā from al-ṭīb, fragrance and goodness, and the yāʾ was turned into a wāw because of the ḍamma before it.
طوح: The letters ṭāʾ, wāw and ḥāʾ are not a root, and it appears to be a case of one letter substituted for another. One says: ṭāḥa yaṭīḥu. Then they also say: ṭāḥa yaṭūḥu, meaning: he perished.
طود: The letters ṭā', wāw and dāl are a sound root holding one word. Al-ṭawd is the great mountain. God, glorified be He, said: {and it split apart, and each part was like the great mountain} [al-Shuʿarā': 63]. They say: "ṭawwada fī al-jabal," when he roamed about the mountain, as though it were a verb derived from al-ṭawd.
طور: The letters ṭā', wāw and rā' are a sound root pointing to one meaning, and it is stretching out in something, of place or of time. Of that is *ṭawār al-dār*, which is the ground that runs along with the house, of its forecourt. And for that reason one says *ʿadā ṭawrahu* — he went beyond the limit that belongs to him from his own house. Then this was borrowed for everything in which a bound is overstepped. And *al-Ṭūr* is a mountain; it may be a proper name simply given, and it may be that it was so called for the stretching out in it in length and in breadth. Of this chapter is their saying *faʿala dhālika ṭawran baʿda ṭawrin* — he did that time after time. This is the part we mentioned that belongs to time, as though he did it for a stretch after a stretch. And their calling the wild ones among birds and other creatures *ṭūriyy* and *ṭūrāniyy* is from this, as though such a creature had gone wild and passed the *ṭawr*, that is, kept far off from the bound of what is tame.
طوس:
The letters ṭāʾ, wāw and sīn are not a root; it contains only the word for what is called al-ṭāwūs, the peacock.

1. muṭawwas — from al-ṭāwūs, a thing that is beautiful is then called this.
2. taṭawwasat al-marʾa — the woman adorned herself. This was reported from al-Aṣmaʿī.
3. al-ṭaws — the covering of a thing; one says ṭustuhu ṭawsan, meaning: I covered it.
4. ṭawās — one of the nights of the moon's waning near its disappearance.
طوط:
The letters ṭāʾ, wāw and ṭāʾ are two words, if they are sound.

1. al-ṭawṭ — cotton.
2. al-ṭawṭ — the tall man.
طوع:
The letters ṭā', wāw and ʿayn are a single sound root pointing to going along with and submitting. One says ṭāʿahu yaṭūʿuhu — when he went along with him and carried out his command. And aṭāʿahu has the sense of ṭāʿa lahu. And of one who agrees with another it is said: qad ṭāwaʿahu.

And al-istiṭāʿa, being able, is derived from al-ṭawʿ, as though it were in origin al-istiṭwāʿ; and when the wāw was dropped, the hā' was put in its place — the same pattern as al-istiʿāna, seeking help, and al-istiʿādha, seeking refuge.

And the Arabs say taṭāwaʿ li-hādhā al-amr ḥattā tastaṭīʿahu — school yourself to this matter until you are able for it. Then they say taṭawwaʿa — that is, he put himself to the trouble of being able for it. As for their saying, of doing a thing freely, qad taṭawwaʿa bihi, it belongs to the chapter, only it was not binding upon him; rather he went along with a good that he wished to do. And this is not said except in the chapter of good and piety. And the fighters who volunteer for jihād are called al-muṭṭawwiʿa, with a shadda on the ṭā' and the wāw; its origin is al-mutaṭawwiʿa, then the tā' was assimilated into the ṭā'. God, exalted be He, said: {alladhīna yalmizūna al-muṭṭawwiʿīna mina al-mu'minīn} — those who find fault with the believers who give freely [al-Tawba: 79] — He meant, and God knows best, al-mutaṭawwiʿīn.
طوف:
The letters ṭā', wāw and fā' are a single sound root pointing to a thing going round about a thing, and to its being encircled by it. Then other things are carried upon it. One says ṭāfa bihi and ṭāfa bi-al-bayt yaṭūfu ṭawfan and ṭawāfan, and iṭṭāfa bihi, and istaṭāfa. Then what goes round things and covers them over of water is called ṭūfān. Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿAjjāj likened the darkness of night to that, and said, in a line of verse:
And the flood of the darkness covered over the ath'ab trees.

And "ghamma" is also read in place of "ʿamma". Of this chapter is al-ṭā'if, who is the one who patrols at night. And al-ṭayf and al-ṭā'if are what goes round a man of the jinn. One says ṭāfa and iṭṭāfa. God - exalted is He - said: When a ṭayf from Satan touches them; and (ṭā'if) as well. Al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse:
And she comes at morning after the night journeying as though a madness from a visitation of the jinn had come upon her.

And they say of a phantom seen in sleep: ṭāfa and aṭāfa. And it is related, in a line of verse:
Whence did the phantom come to you, going round you - and its circling about you is a remembrance and a longing?
And it is also related as: "and its circling for you is a remembrance and a fondness."

As for al-ṭā'ifa of people, it is as though it were a company that goes round about one man or about a thing. The Arabs hardly fix it at a known number, except that the jurists and the commentators say of it at one time that it is four and upwards, and at another that a single one is a ṭā'ifa, and they say it is three, and they have much talk about that. The Arabs on this point are as I have told you: every company that can encircle a thing is with them a ṭā'ifa, and this is hardly the case except with a small number. This is in the language, and God knows best. Then they widen it by way of figurative speech and say akhadhtu ṭā'ifatan min al-thawb - I took a piece of the cloth; and this is on the sense of figure, because a ṭā'ifa of people is like a portion and a piece of them. As for ṭā'if al-qaws - the part of the bow so called - [it is] what lies next to its abhar, the strong part of its limb.
طوق: The letters ṭā', wāw and qāf are a sound root indicating the same thing as the chapter before it. Everything that goes round a thing is a ṭawq. A building was called ṭāq for its curve, once vaulted. Al-ṭaylasān (a cloak worn over the shoulders) is a ṭāq because it goes round its wearer. As for their saying aṭāqa hādhā al-amra iṭāqatan, and huwa fī ṭawqihi, and ṭawwaqtuka al-shay', meaning I laid the thing on you as a duty — all of this belongs to this chapter and its reasoning, because when a man aṭāqahu, is able to bear it, it is as though he has gone round it and encircled it on every side. What departs from this root: their saying ṭāqatun min khayṭin aw baqlin, a single strand of thread or a single stalk of a plant, the lone one of it. It is possible, by stretching the point, to force this back onto the first sense, but it is a distant reach.
طول:
The letters ṭā', wāw and lām are a sound root pointing to excess and stretching out in a thing. From that: ṭāla al-shay' yaṭūlu ṭūlan — the thing was long. Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā Tha'lab said: al-ṭūl is the opposite of breadth. One says ṭāwaltu fulānan fa-ṭultuhu — I matched myself against him for height and was the taller. And ṭāla fulānan fulān — that is, he is taller than he. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Al-Farazdaq is a rock packed hard; it has risen so high that the mountain goats cannot reach it.
This is a rule that runs through everything like it, so a rope is called al-ṭiwal for its length and its stretching out. Ṭarafa said, in a line of verse:
By your life, death, when it misses the young man, is like the tether let out long with its two folds still held in the hand.
They say lā ukallimuhu ṭawāla al-dahr — I shall not speak to him for all time. One says jamal aṭwal when a camel's upper lip is long. And ṭāwalanī fulān fa-ṭultuhu — that is, I was taller than he. Al-ṭuwāl is the tall one. Al-ṭiwāl is the plural of ṭawīl, tall. Some have reported qalānis ṭiyāl, with a yā' — long caps. Amr ghayr ṭā'il is a matter of no worth, when there is no profit in it; it is said so of the masculine and the feminine alike. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And they laid upon me a course of no worth.
Wa-taṭāwaltu fī qiyāmī — I stretched myself up as I stood — when you stretch your legs out to look. Ṭawwil farasaka — that is, let your horse's tether out long in its pasture. Wa-staṭālū 'alayhim — when they killed more of them than had been killed of their own.
طوي:
The letters ṭā', wāw and yā' are a sound root indicating the folding of a thing so that part of it is folded into another part; other things are then referred to it by comparison.

1. One says ṭawaytu al-thawb wa-l-kitāb ṭayyan aṭwīhi — I folded the garment and the letter.
2. One says ṭawā Allāh ʿumr al-mayyit — God "folded up" the dead man's life.
3. al-ṭawiyy — a well lined with stone. He said, in a line of verse:
she said to him: here is the lined well, and its water — while [he was] scorched, parched from dried-out skin.

4. Among what is referred to this root: they say of one who has gone off on his own way: ṭawā kashḥahu, he "folded his side," meaning he turned away and left.

He recited, in a line of verse:
a companion of mine turned his side away, and I said to him: your turning away from me will fold me up in turn.

This fits the pattern, because when he goes off and is hidden from him, it is as if he were folded away.

5. Also from this root: aṭwā' al-nāqa, the folds of fat along the she-camel's sides.
6. al-ṭayyān — one whose belly is "folded," empty from hunger.

One says ṭuwiya, he was "folded," meaning that when he goes hungry and grows lean he becomes like a thing that, if one wanted to fold it, one now could. If he goes hungry deliberately, one says ṭawā yaṭwī ṭayyan; this fits the pattern rightly, because he "folded up" the times [of eating] and did not eat during them.

The poet said, about al-ṭawā (hunger), in a line of verse:
and I have indeed spent the night in hunger, and stayed through the day in it, until through it I attained a noble sort of food.

7. Then they changed this word-pattern slightly, and the meaning shifted to something else: they said al-ṭāya, a sound word indicating flatness in a place. Some said: al-ṭāya is the flat roof. Others said: it is the date-drying yard. Others said: it is a great rock in sandy ground.
طيب:
The letters ṭā', yā' and bā' are a single sound root pointing to the opposite of what is foul. From that is al-ṭayyib, the good and wholesome, the opposite of the foul. One says sabyun ṭība — that is, ṭayyib, captives taken in a good and lawful way.

And al-istiṭāba is cleaning oneself after relieving oneself, because a man makes himself wholesome, yuṭayyib nafsahu, of the filth upon him by that cleaning. "And the Messenger of God — may God bless him and his family — forbade a man to clean himself with his right hand."

And al-aṭyabān, the two most wholesome things, are eating and the marriage act. And Ṭayba is the city of the Messenger — may God bless him and his family. And one says: this is a food that is a maṭyaba li-l-nafs, something that makes the soul feel good. And al-ṭayyib is the lawful. And al-ṭāb is al-ṭīb, sweet fragrance. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Of matched pedigrees, in fragrance upon fragrance ... between Abū al-ʿĀṣ and the family of al-Khaṭṭāb.
طيخ:
The letters ṭāʾ, yāʾ and khāʾ are a sound root indicating being smeared with something unseemly. They said: ṭākha yaṭīkhu and taṭayyakha, when a person was smeared with something foul. And they said: al-ṭīkh is levity, having the meaning of al-ṭaysh, rashness. Al-Ḥārith said, in a line of verse:
So leave off frivolity and transgression; for if
you turn a blind eye to one another's faults, in that turning a blind eye is the sickness.
طير:
The letters ṭā', yā' and rā' are a single root indicating the lightness of a thing in the air. Then that is used by way of borrowing for other things, and for every kind of swiftness. From this is al-ṭayr, the plural of ṭā'ir, a bird, so named for what we have said. One says ṭāra yaṭīru ṭayarānan, it flew. Then it is said of everyone who moves lightly: he has flown. The Messenger of God, God's blessing and peace be upon him and his family, said: "The best of men is a man holding the rein of his horse in the way of God; whenever he hears an alarm he flies to it."

And a poet said, in a line of verse:
So we flew at them with our troops and our spears.

And from this one says taṭāyara al-shay', the thing scattered. And istaṭāra al-fajr, the dawn spread out; and likewise everything that spreads. God, exalted, said: {And they fear a day whose evil is far-spreading} [al-Insān: 7]. As for their saying taṭayyara min al-shay', he took an ill omen from a thing, its derivation is from al-ṭayr, birds, such as the crow and the like. And from the chapter is a man's ṭā'ir, which is his deeds. And a well is muṭāra when it is wide of mouth.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
The rushing of the wind in a wide-mouthed pit.

And from the chapter is al-ṭayra, anger, so named because a man is made to fly up by it. And from the chapter is their saying: take what has flown out of the hair of your head, that is, what has grown long.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And the hair of the tallest hump flew loose.
طيس:
The letters ṭāʾ, yāʾ and sīn are one word. A poet said, in a line of verse:
I counted my people like the count of al-ṭays.
He meant by it a great number.
طيش: The letters ṭāʾ, yāʾ and shīn are one word, and it is al-ṭaysh, meaning lightness and rashness. And ṭāsha al-sahm is from this — the arrow strayed, when it did not hit its mark, as though it grew light, swerved, and flew off.
طين: The letters ṭā', yā' and nūn are a single word, and it is al-ṭīn, clay, which is well known. And it is said ṭayyantu al-bayt — I plastered the house with clay — and ṭintu al-kitāb — I sealed the letter with clay. And it is said ṭānahu Allāh Most High 'alā al-khayr, that is, He formed him upon good. And its meaning seems to be — and God knows best — from ṭintu al-kitāb, that is, I sealed it; as though He stamped him upon good and sealed his affair with it.
ظأب:
The letters ẓā, hamza and bā' are two distinct words. One is *al-ẓa'b*, meaning a man's *silf* — the husband of his wife's sister. The other is speech and clamor.

He said, in a line of verse:
A dark-coated buck, with a wattle at his throat, drives her young kids together — he makes a clamor like the din of a man pressing for his debt.
ظأر:
The letters ẓā, hamza and rā' are a single sound root, meaning an inclining with affection, and a drawing near.

1. *al-ẓi'r* — the wet-nurse. She is named so for her fondness toward the child she raises. One says *aẓ'artu li-waladī ẓi'ran*, I got a wet-nurse for my child, as already passed under the entry *iẓẓalama* with ẓā'.
2. *al-ẓa'ūr*, of she-camels — the one that inclines toward the stuffed calf-skin.
3. *ẓa'aranī* — "so-and-so *ẓa'aranī* on such a matter" means he turned me toward it.
4. *al-ẓu'ār* — a word used to describe the three stones a cooking pot rests on, as if they lean in around the ashes.
5. *al-ẓi'ār* — that a she-camel is treated with a wrap of cloth over her nose so that she will take to and suckle another's young.
6. Their saying, "the spear-thrust *yaẓ'aru*" — meaning it inclines men toward reconciliation.

One says both *ẓi'r* and, as its plural, *ẓu'ār*, which follows the plural pattern *fu'āl* — a rare pattern.
ظأم: The letters ẓā, hamza and mīm belong to the sense of speech and clamor; this is a substitution of letters. So *al-ẓa'm* and *al-ẓa'b* carry the same meaning. And God knows best.
ظب:
The ẓā' and bā' — nothing of it is sound except a single word. One says: mā bihi ẓabẓāb, meaning there is nothing wrong with him. Ibn al-Sikkīt said: mā bihi ẓabẓāb means he has no defect and no ailment. The rājiz-poet said, in a line of verse:
My little daughter has no ailment in her.
And they say: al-ẓabāẓib is the rattling in the insides of camels from thirst — but this is not sound; and it is said it is a scribal error, and the word is really with ṭā' [not ẓā']. As for what is found in al-Khalīl's book, that al-ẓābb means the co-wife — I take this to be an error attributed to al-Khalīl, because what we ourselves have heard is al-ẓa'b, without doubling the letter, and it has already been mentioned in its own place.
ظبى:
The letters ẓā, bā' and the weak letter are two distinct words. One is *al-ẓaby*, the gazelle; the other is *ẓubat al-sayf*, the edge of a sword. Neither of them has a known derivation.

As for al-ẓaby: it is the singular of al-ẓibā', well known; the female is *ẓabya*. It may also be pluralized as *ẓubiyy*. When there are few of them, they are called *aẓbin*.

As for what came in the hadith — "When you come to them, crouch down in their dwelling like a gazelle" — he means: be at ease among them, as though you were a gazelle safe in its covert, seeing no one to trouble it.

They say: "He has the ailment of a gazelle." They said its meaning is that he has no ailment at all, just as the gazelle has none.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Do not scowl at us, Umm 'Amr — we have the ailment of a gazelle, whose legs have never failed it.

By way of metaphor, al-ẓabya names a woman's private parts, and a she-camel's vulva. Al-ẓabya also names a small hide bag with the hair still on it. All of this rests on resemblance to the gazelle.

As for the other word: al-ẓuba is the edge of a sword; its derivation is not known. It is pluralized as ẓubīn and ẓubāt. Some said it belongs among words whose weak letter is a wāw, from our saying *ẓabawtu* — but nothing supports this claim.

And he said, on the plural of *ẓiba* as *ẓibīn*, in a line of verse:
Onlookers see, upon its blade-edges, something like the glow of Abū Ḥubāḥib's fire, and the sword-edges.
ظر:
The ẓā' and rā' are a single sound root indicating a stone with a sharpened edge. They say: al-ẓurar is a hard, sharpened stone, plural ẓirrān. He said, in a line of verse:
With a sturdy, swift she-camel that scatters the sharp stones, when the flint sparks in the desolate waste.

1. aẓarra al-rajul — the man walked on the sharp stones. And they say: aẓirriyya innaki nā'ila — meaning, walk on the sharp stones, for you have sandals on — it is used as a proverb for someone given a task he is well able to bear.
2. al-maẓarra — said to be the flint struck for fire; or, it is said, rather a stone used to cut away something that forms in a she-camel's vulva, like a wart.
3. arḍun maẓarra — land abundant in sharp stones.

Straying from this chapter is their saying iẓrawrā, he swelled up. And God knows best.
ظرب:
The letters ẓā, rā' and bā' are a sound root, meaning something either fixed or not fixed, together with sharpness.

1. *al-ẓirāb* — the plural of *ẓarib*, a stone jutting up with a sharp point at its tip.
2. *al-aẓrāb* — it is said these are the roots of the teeth; it is also said they are rather the four teeth behind the molars.
3. *al-aẓrāb*, in a horse's bit — Ibn Durayd claimed these are the knobs at the ends of the iron piece. He quoted, in a line of verse: his molars showing, over the knobs of the bit.
4. *al-ẓurubb* — a short, fleshy man, by way of resemblance to the stone. He quoted, in a line of verse: do not weigh me equal to a stumpy, close-knit man.
5. *al-ẓarabān* — a small animal.
ظرف: The letters ẓā, rā' and fā' are a word that appears to be sound. They say: this is the container of a thing, its *ẓarf*. They then call skillfulness *ẓarf*, and likewise sharpness of mind — the meaning being that the mind is a container for it. Such a man is *ẓarīf*. A man is said to have *aẓrafa* when he has fathered clever sons. But I do not think any of this belongs to the genuine speech of the Arabs.
ظعن:
The letters ẓā', ʿayn and nūn are a single sound root indicating departure from one place to another. You say ẓaʿana yaẓʿanu ẓaʿnan wa-ẓaʿanan, when he set out. God, glorified be He, said: {and He made for you, from the hides of livestock, tents which you find light to carry on the day you journey and the day you settle} [al-Naḥl: 80]. There is disagreement about al-ẓaʿīna: some said it is the woman herself, others said the ẓaʿā'in are the litters carried on camels, whether or not there were women inside them — and this second view is the sounder of the two, since the word belongs among the tools of travel. Al-ẓaʿūn is the camel set aside for the journey. From this chapter: al-ẓiʿān, the rope that ties the pack-saddle onto the camel, named so because it is one of the tools of travel and departure. It was said, in a line of verse:
It has a neck that twists with whatever is tied to it, and two flanks that wear thin every travel-rope.
ظفر:
The letters ẓā', fā' and rā' are two sound roots: one indicates overcoming, triumph and victory, and the other indicates strength in a thing. Perhaps the two roots are close to one another in their underlying sense.

The first: al-ẓafar, meaning success and attaining a thing. One says: ẓafira yaẓfaru ẓafaran. God, Most High, granted him victory (aẓfarahu). God, Most High, said: {after He gave you victory over them} [al-Fatḥ: 24]. A man is muẓaffar, victorious.

The other root: al-ẓufr, a person's fingernail.

1. One says: ẓaffara fī al-shay'i, when he dug his nail into it.
2. A man is aẓfar, meaning long-nailed, just as one says ashʻar meaning long-haired.
3. Of a lowly man it is said: he is kalīl al-ẓufr [blunt of nail] — this is a proverb. Ṭarafa said, in a line of verse:
Not one worn down and stumbling from old age, fearful of the night, nor blunt of nail.
4. One says: ẓaffara al-nabtu tazfīran, when a plant sprouted, because what comes up from it looks like fingernails pushing up with force.
5. As for their calling the thin film that covers the eye ẓafarah, that is by way of comparison to a nail. One says: ẓufirat al-'aynu, when it has a ẓafarah. Abū 'Ubayd said: this is what is called ẓufr.
6. Also from this chapter: ẓufr al-qaws, the two end-pieces of a bow, at the tips of its curved ends, where the bowstring sits.

Sometimes they said al-ẓafarah is a low, fertile stretch of ground — this too is a comparison. Al-aẓfār: small stars, called this by way of metaphor.

As for Ẓafār, a city in Yemen, it is possible it comes from some of what we have mentioned; the adjective from it is Ẓafārī. God knows best.
ظل:
The ẓā' and lām are a single root indicating one thing's covering of another — this is what is called al-ẓill, shade. And the words of this chapter all trace back to it. So al-ẓill is the shade of a person or anything else, and it falls in the early morning as well as the late afternoon, whereas al-fay' [the other word for shade] falls only in the late afternoon. You say: aẓallatnī al-shajara, the tree gave me shade. And ẓillun ẓalīl is an unbroken, lasting shade. And the night is [itself called] a shade. He said, in a line of verse:
Often I push on through the unknown, far country, its rough going, in the shade of a dark-green night where owl calls to owl.
He means: in the cover of a dark-green night. And aẓallaka fulān, so-and-so sheltered you, as though he protected you with his shade — that is, with his standing and his protection. And al-miẓalla, the awning, is well known. And aẓalla yawmunā, our day stayed shaded, means its shade lasted [it stayed overcast]. And it is said that al-ẓulla is the first cloud that casts shade. And al-ẓulla is also something shaped like a raised shelter. God Almighty said: {And when We raised the mountain over them as though it were a shade} [al-A'rāf: 171]

1. Also from this chapter is their saying ẓalla yafʿalu kadhā, he kept on doing such-and-such — used when he did it by day. We say it belongs to this chapter because that is a thing particular to daytime: a thing has a shadow by day, and one does not say ẓalla yafʿalu kadhā of something done by night, because the night is itself a shade.
2. Also from this chapter, and its derivation is sound: al-aẓall, the underside of a camel's foot-pad. It may be so called either because it covers what lies beneath it, or because it is covered by what lies above it. He said, in a line of verse:
On a rough, worn track, the underside of its pad bloodied.
As for the other poet's saying:
It complains of soreness, from pad-underside and pad-underside —
this is the same word, al-aẓall, but he pronounced the doubled letter in full, by poetic necessity.
ظلع:
