The ẓā', lām, and ʿayn are a genuine small root indicating a leaning, a limp, in walking. One says: a beast has ẓalʿ in it, when it favours a leg and so leans to one side. And they say: huwa ẓāliʿ, meaning leaning away from the straight path. Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
Do you threaten a servant who has never betrayed your trust, yet leave alone a servant who does wrong — while he himself limps?
ظلف:
The ẓā', lām, and fā' are a sound root indicating the least degree of strength and toughness.

1. ẓilf — the [cloven] hoof of a cow or the like, and it is sometimes used, by extension, of the horse. He said, in a line of verse:
And horses that trample you with their hooves.
And when you shoot game and strike its hoof, you say qad ẓalaftuhu, and it is maẓlūf.
2. al-ẓilf and al-ẓalīf — any rough, hard ground. Al-Umawī said: arḍun ẓalifa is rugged ground on which the track of one who walked over it cannot be seen, clearly marked by its ẓalaf, its roughness. And from this is taken al-ẓalaf, used of hardship in one's way of life.
3. people's saying huwa ẓalif ʿan kadhā — strictness and self-restraint in scrupulousness; it follows the same reasoning.
4. the curved side-piece of a pack-saddle — called ẓalifa for its strength and toughness.
5. akhadha al-jazūr bi-ẓalafihā wa-ẓalīfatihā — he took the slaughtered animal whole, all of it.
ظلم:
The letters ẓā', lām and mīm are two sound roots: one of them is the opposite of light and brightness, and the other is the putting of a thing somewhere other than its place, by way of overstepping.

So the first is al-ẓulma, darkness, and the plural is ẓulumāt. And al-ẓalām is a name for darkness; and the place has aẓlama iẓlāman — grown dark. And of this section is what al-Khalīl related of their saying laqītuhu awwala dhī ẓulma — I met him at the first dark shape. He said: and it is the first thing that blocks your sight in seeing, and no verb is derived from it. And of this is their saying laqītuhu adnā ẓalamin, of what is near. And they say it in other wordings as well, put together from ẓā', lām and mīm; and the origin of that is al-ẓulma, darkness, as though they made the figure a darkness by way of likeness — and that is as they call a figure a blackness. So upon this the section is to be carried, and it is one of the strange things upon which their speech is carried.

And the other root: ẓalamahu yaẓlimuhu ẓulman — he wronged him. And the origin is the putting of a thing [in] somewhere other than its place. Do you not see them say: " Whoever resembles [his father] has done no wrong ", that is, he has not put the resemblance out of its place. Kaʿb said:
I am the son of him who never shamed me in his life, of old; and whoever resembles his father has done no wrong.

And one says ẓallamtu fulānan — I ascribed wrongdoing to him. And ẓalamtu fulānan fa-iẓẓalama and inẓalama — I wronged him and he bore the wrong. And he recited the line of Zuhayr:
He is the open-handed one who gives you his gift freely, and who is sometimes wronged, and bears the wrong —
with the ẓā' and with the ṭā'. And the land that is maẓlūma is the one that had never been dug and then was dug; and that soil is ẓalīm. He said:
So he came to be in the dust after striving hard for life, its dug-up soil turned back over him.

And when a camel is slaughtered for no cause, it has been wronged. And of that is his saying:
The lowly came back into a dwelling where once there were men with roaring throats, great slaughterers of camels.

And al-ẓulāma is what you seek back for the wrong done you, at the hands of the wrongdoer. And one says: he gave us good ẓalīma to drink. And qad ẓalama waṭbahu — he wronged his milk-skin, when he gives drink from it before it curdles and yields its butter. And that milk too is called ẓalīm. He said:
And many a woman said, You have wronged my skin for your sake — and can the too-early-drawn milk stay hidden from one who knows it?
And God knows best what is right.
ظما:
The letters ẓā, mīm, and the weak letter — and its hamzated form — are a single root, meaning a withering and a scarcity of water.

1. *al-ẓamā*, without the hamza — a scantiness of blood in the gums. One says a woman is *ẓamyā' al-lithāth*, thin-gummed.
2. *ẓamyā'* — an eye that is thin-lidded.
3. It is then extended further, so that a leg is called *ẓamyā'*, meaning lean of flesh.
4. From the hamzated form: *al-ẓama'* — thirst. You say *ẓami'tu aẓma'u ẓamā*, I thirsted.
5. *al-ẓim'* — the interval between two drinks.

The reasoning behind all of this is one and the same.

1. *rumḥ aẓmā* — a spear that is brown and slender. It became so because its moisture had gone.
ظن:
The ẓā' and nūn are a genuine small root indicating two different meanings: certainty, and doubt.
As for certainty, it is in the saying ẓanantu ẓannan, meaning I was certain. God Almighty said: {Those who are certain they will meet God, said} [al-Baqara: 249] — He meant, and God knows best, they are certain. The Arabs say this and know it in this sense. Their poet said, in a line of verse:
So I said to them: be certain of two thousand armoured men, their nobles among the close-linked Persian mail.
He meant: be certain. And it is frequent in this sense in the Qur'an.

1. From this chapter is maẓinnat al-shay', a thing's known mark, its place. They say: huwa maẓinnatun li-kadhā, he is the [known] place for such-and-such. Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
For the mark of ignorance is youth.

The other origin is doubt. One says ẓanantu al-shay', when you are not certain of it.

1. From this is al-ẓinna, accusation, suspicion.
2. and al-ẓanīn, the accused, the suspected one.
One says: iẓẓannanī fulān, so-and-so suspected me. The poet said, in a line of verse:
Not everyone who suspects me is one I owe an apology to, nor do I repeat everything that is reported against me.
And sometimes it is written with ṭā' [instead of ẓā'], because the ẓā' is assimilated into the tā' of the [verb-form] iftiʿāl.
3. And al-ẓanūn is the one of ill opinion, quick to suspect.
4. And al-taẓannī is the exercising of conjecture; the origin of al-taẓannī is al-taẓannun.
They say: su'tu bihi ẓannan and asa'tu bihi al-ẓann, they bring in the alif when they use the word with al- (the definite article).
5. And al-ẓanūn is [also] a well that no one knows whether it holds water or not. He said, in a line of verse:
The stubborn, uncertain digging was not undertaken — that which was kept clear of the rain-cloud's pouring downpour.
6. And al-dayn al-ẓanūn is a debt of which it is not known whether it will be repaid or not.
The whole chapter is one [meaning].
ظنب:
The letters ẓā, nūn and bā' are a sound word, meaning the dry bone of the shin or elsewhere. It is then used as a figure of speech, so that one says of a person in earnest about a matter: he has struck his shin-bone.

Salāma ibn Jandal said, in a line of verse:
Whenever a frightened crier came to us, the outcry for him was like the striking of shin-bones.

Some said: the shins of horses are struck with whips as they are spurred at a run toward the enemy. Others said: al-ẓunbūb is the pin fitted into the socket of a spearhead — that is, we fit the spearheads onto their shafts with it.
ظهر:
The letters ẓā', hā' and rā' are one sound root pointing to strength and to coming out into the open. Of that is ẓahara al-shay'u yaẓharu ẓuhūran, so it is ẓāhir, when it is uncovered and comes out into view. And for that reason the time of ẓuhr and ẓahīra, noon, was so named, and it is the most open of the times of the day and the brightest of them. And the origin in all of it is the back of a man, which is the opposite of his belly, and it gathers together both coming out into view and strength. And riding-beasts are called al-ẓahr, because what carries a load of them is their backs. And one says a man muẓahhar, that is, strong of back. And a man ẓahir: one who complains of his back.

Of this section is aẓharnā, when we travel at the time of noon. And of it is ẓahartu 'alā kadhā, when you come to know of a thing. And al-ẓahīr is the strong camel. And al-ẓahīr is the helper, as though he set his back against your back. And al-ẓuhūr is overcoming. God - exalted - said: {and they became the ones who overcame} [al-Ṣaff: 14]. And al-ẓāhira is the bulging eye. And al-ẓihār is a man's saying to his wife: you are to me as my mother's back. It is a word they used to say, meaning by it separation. They singled out the back only because of riding; otherwise the rest of her limbs are like the back in being forbidden. And al-ẓuhār of feathers is what shows of them on the wing. And al-ẓihrī is everything you put at your back, that is, you forget it, as though you had put it behind your back, turning away from it and leaving it. God, glory be to Him, said: {and you have put Him behind you, cast away} [Hūd: 92]. And so-and-so has put my need at his back, when he does not turn toward it but puts it behind him. And al-Farazdaq said, in a line of verse:
Tamīm ibn Badr, let my need not be at your back, so that its answer be not hidden from you.
Of this section is: this is a matter whose shame is ẓāhir from you, that is, passing away, as though when it goes it has come to be behind your back. And Abū Dhu'ayb said, in a line of verse:
The slanderers reproached her that I love her; but that is a complaint whose shame passes away from you.
And they say that al-ẓahara is the goods of a house. And I think this too is borrowed from the back, because a man strengthens himself with them, that is, he takes strength and help from them against what comes upon him. And al-ẓāhira is that the camels come to water every day at midday. And they say: we travelled the ẓahr, meaning the road by land, and that is for its being open and out in view. And they say: so-and-so came in his ẓahra and his nāhiḍa, that is, among his people. They were called a ẓahra only because he takes strength from them. And Quraysh al-Ẓawāhir were called that because they camp on the outer side of Mecca. He said:
Quraysh of the valley-bottoms, not Quraysh of the outskirts.
And aqrān al-ẓahr are those who come upon you from behind. And Ibn Durayd related: "taẓāhara al-qawm, when they turn their backs upon one another, and it seems to be one of the words that carry two opposite meanings." And this meaning that Ibn Durayd mentioned is sound, because he meant that each of the two turned away from his fellow and set his back toward him. And God knows best.
عب:
The letters ʿayn and bā' are a single sound root, meaning abundance and a great bulk, in water and elsewhere.

1. *al-ʿabb* — the drinking of water without sipping. One says ʿabba fi'l-inā', yaʿubbu, ʿabban, when he drank in a rough gulping way. In the hadith: "Drink water by sipping, and do not gulp it down — for a disorder of the liver comes from gulping."

He said: when he gulps, in the well, with a rumbling sound.

2. One says: "*ʿabba* the bucket, yaʿubbu, ʿabban," when it made a sound as the water was drawn.
3. *Al-ʿubāb*, in travel — swiftness. Al-Farrā' said: al-ʿubāb is the great bulk of a flood.
4. *Al-yaʿbūb* — a swift, generous horse, much given to running; it is also said to mean tall, or, alternatively, far-reaching in its stride.

He said: harsh of voice, a yaʿbūb, that neighs when the encampment is roused for a raid.

5. *Al-yaʿbūb*, likewise — a river abundant in water, swift in its current.

He said: it steps between two reed-stalks, nourished by a plentiful flow, in the courtyard of a wide, brimming pool.

They also say that al-ʿabʿab, among men, is the one who mumbles in his speech, speaking from deep in his throat. One says thawbun ʿabʿabun and ʿabʿābun, meaning ample or wide. They say: al-ʿabʿāb, among men, also means tall. Al-ʿabʿab is a soft, fine woollen cloak.

He said: you have been given, after nakedness and rough wear, and after your wearing of one ʿabʿab-cloak after another — fine cloaks of silk, so trail your skirts and go free.

Straying from this chapter is al-ʿubab: a plant resembling al-ḥarmal, wild rue, except taller in its growth, that puts out thread-like shoots, and has a pod like that of al-ḥarmal, with dense leaves.

Ibn Mayyāda said:
As though a stand of reed, through which channels surged, dark-green at its watering places, with al-ʿubab all about its edges.

Close to the first chapter, and not far from its pattern, is what al-Khalīl related: that al-ʿabʿab is the freshness of youth, and al-ʿabʿab, among young men, is one in his full prime.
عبأ:
The letters ʿayn, bāʾ, hamza, and the weak letter that is not hamzated are a single root, indicating a gathering-together with heaviness.
1. al-ʿibʾ — any load, whether a debt or a burden one carries, plural al-aʿbāʾ. A poet said, in a line of verse: "The carrying of the burden [al-ʿibʾ] from the necks of my people, and my conduct in hardships, by what has concerned me."
2. mā ʿabaʾtu bihi shayʾan — I did not care about it, when you do not trouble yourself over it, as if you found no weight to it.
3. ʿabaʾtu al-ṭīb — I prepared the perfume. They distinguish between this and preparing an army: they say ʿabbaytu al-katība uʿabbīhā taʿbiyatan, when you made it ready. They also said ʿabbaʾtu al-jaysh with the same sense — Ibn al-Aʿrābī mentioned this. And he said, of preparing perfume, in a line of verse: "As though on his chest and his two shoulders were perfume that a bride had spent the night preparing [taʿbaʾuhu]."
4. al-ʿabāʾa — a kind of cloak. Its derivation is sound, because it wraps around the one wearing it and gathers him in. God knows best what is correct.
عباهل:
The plural of al-ʿabhal, which is camels left untended, coming to water however and whenever they wish. He said:
Untended camels, whom those who come to water leave untended.
Kings over whom no hand stands higher are likened to this. Here the bāʾ has been added; the origin is al-ʿayhal and al-ʿayhala, that which does not settle down. We have already explained it.
عبث:
The letters 'ayn, bā' and thā' are one sound root, indicating mixing. One says: 'abatha al-aqiṭ, and I say a'bithuhu 'abthan, and it is 'ibbīth — meaning the dried curd is mixed and dried in the sun. Al-'abīth: any mixture. One says: fī hādhā al-wādī 'abīthah, meaning a mixing together of two tribes.

Of what is derived by analogy from this: al-'abath, an act done not with evenness and full correctness. You say: 'abitha ya'bathu 'abathan; he is 'ābith, one fooling about with what does not concern him and is not on his mind. In the Qur'an: {Did you then suppose that We created you in vain?} [al-Mu'minūn: 115], meaning as idle play. The underlying pattern in all of this is one.
عبج: The letters ʿayn, bāʾ and jīm — Al-Khalīl says nothing about it. It has been said that al-ʿabaja is the fool.
عبد:
The letters ʿayn, bā' and dāl are two sound roots, as though they were opposites of one another: [the first] of those two roots points to softness and lowliness, and the other to hardness and roughness.

So the first is al-ʿabd, and it is the owned slave; and the group is al-ʿabīd, and three are aʿbud, and they are al-ʿibād. Al-Khalīl said: except that people at large have agreed to put a difference between ʿibād Allāh, the servants of God, and al-ʿabīd, the owned slaves. One says hādhā ʿabdun bayyinu al-ʿubūda — this is plainly a slave. And we have not heard them derive a verb from it; and if a verb were derived, one would say ʿabuda, that is, he became a slave and owned himself a slave; but the verb was let die and not used. He said: as for ʿabada yaʿbudu ʿibādatan, it is said only of one who worships God the Exalted. From it one says ʿabada yaʿbudu ʿibādatan, and taʿabbada yataʿabbadu taʿabbudan. So al-mutaʿabbid is the one who sets himself apart in worship. And istaʿbadtu fulānan — I took him as a slave. As for ʿabd in the sense of serving his master, one does not say ʿabadahu, and one does not say yaʿbudu mawlāhu. And taʿabbada fulānun fulānan — when he makes him like a slave to himself, even if he is a free man. He said:
Nimr ibn Saʿd has made a slave of me, and yet I see that Nimr ibn Saʿd is obedient to me and hurrying at my word.

And one says aʿbada fulānun fulānan, that is, he made him a slave. And of the idolaters one says: ʿabadat al-ṭāghūt wa-l-awthān, the worshippers of the false god and the idols; and of the Muslims: ʿubbād, who worship God the Exalted. And some of them mentioned ʿābid and ʿabad, like khādim and khadam, a servant and servants. And the feminine of ʿabd is ʿabda, as one says mamlūk and mamlūka. Al-Khalīl said: and al-ʿibiddā' is the body of slaves who were born into slavery.

And of the section is the camel that is muʿabbad, that is, the one smeared with tar. And this too points to what we have said, because that lowers him and brings him down. Ṭarafa said:
Until the whole clan kept away from me, and I was set apart as the tarred camel is set apart.
And al-muʿabbad is the tractable one, and the camel is described by it too.

And of the section: al-ṭarīq al-muʿabbad, the beaten road, the one trodden and brought low.

And the other root is al-ʿabada, and it is strength and hardness; one says this is a garment with ʿabda in it, when it is close-woven and strong. And from it is ʿAlqama ibn ʿAbada, with a fatḥa on the bā'.

And of this same reasoning is al-ʿabad, like scorn and hot pride. One says: he is scornful in this matter. And the words of God the Exalted — {Say: if the Merciful had a son, then I am the first of the worshippers} [al-Zukhruf: 81] — were explained as: the first to be angry at this and to scorn saying it. And it is related of ʿAlī — peace be upon him — that he said: " «I was scornful, so I kept silent» ", that is, I scorned it and fell silent. And he said:
And the rough ignorant man rages over their right, after judgement has gone against him, when there is no raging left.
And another said:
And I scorn that Kulayb should be lampooned by Dārim —
that is, I disdain that and am angered by it.
عبر:
The letters ʿayn, bā' and rā' are one sound root pointing to passing through and going on in a thing. One says ʿabartu al-nahra ʿubūran — I crossed the river. And ʿabr al-nahr is its bank. And one says a she-camel ʿubru asfārin — one that never ceases to be travelled upon. Al-Ṭirimmāḥ said, in a line of verse:
I have ridden the belly of a swift bold one, a crosser of journeys, that keeps back its groaning.

And al-maʿbar is the bank of a river made ready for crossing. And al-miʿbar is a boat on which the river is crossed. And a man is ʿābir sabīl — that is, a passer-by. God, exalted be He, said: {nor in a state of major impurity, save as passing along a way} [al-Nisā': 43].

And from the section is al-ʿabra. Al-Khalīl said: ʿabrat al-damʿ is its running. He said: and the tear itself is also an ʿabra. Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
My cure is a flow of tears if I pour it out — but is there at an effaced trace any place to weep?

And this follows the sense, because the tear passes through, that is, it runs. And what al-Khalīl said is sound and points to the soundness of the sense we have mentioned.

And their saying ʿabira fulānun yaʿbaru ʿabaran, of grief, and he is ʿabrān and the woman is ʿabrā and ʿabira — this is only where there is weeping. And one says istaʿbara when his tear runs. And from this one says a woman ʿābir — that is, in her is the grief that brings weeping. And a poet said, in a line of verse:
The man of Jarm says to me: will you take me up behind you? — and how should a routed man ride pillion? Your mother is in tears.

So this is the root that we have mentioned. Then a kind of lote-tree is called ʿubrī, and it is so only when it grows on the banks of the rivers; and the bank is crossed, and it is crossed to. Al-ʿAjjāj said, in a line of verse:
Clinging about it the young palms and the ʿubrī lote.

Al-ashā' is the young palm shoots, the single one ashā'a, and we have already mentioned it. And it is said that the ʿubrī is only tall, and what is smaller than it is the ḍāl. Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
I cut across, when the blowing winds hollowed it out, the kinds of lote, the ʿubrī and the ḍāl.

And it is said: rather the ḍāl is what is in the open country.

And from the section: ʿabara al-ru'yā yaʿburuhā ʿabran and ʿibāratan, and yuʿabbiruhā taʿbīran, when he interprets the dream. And the face of the sense in this is the crossing of the river, because he goes from one bank to another bank. So too the interpreter of the dream takes it from one side to another side, as when he is asked about water and says: it is life. Do you not see that he has crossed in this from one thing to another thing.

And of what is carried upon this is al-ʿibāra. Al-Khalīl said: you say ʿabbarta ʿan fulānin taʿbīran, when he is tongue-tied in his argument and you speak it for him. And this follows the sense we have mentioned, because he could not pass through in his speech, so the other passed through with it in his place.

As for al-iʿtibār and al-ʿibra, they are with us both measured from the ʿibr, the bank of the river, because each one of the two is an ʿibr equal to its fellow: this one is an ʿibr to that, and that one is an ʿibr to this. So when you say iʿtabartu al-shay', it is as though you looked at the thing and made what concerns you an ʿibr to it, so the two became equal in your sight. This, with us, is the derivation of al-iʿtibār. God, exalted be He, said: {so take heed, O you who have eyes} [al-Ḥashr: 2], as though He said: look at the one who did what he did and was punished with what he was punished with, and shun the like of their doing, so that there may not come down upon you the like of what came down upon those. And of the proof of the soundness of this sense we have mentioned is the saying of al-Khalīl: ʿabbarta al-danānīr taʿbīran, when you weigh them dinar by [dinar]. He said: and al-ʿibra is the taking of a lesson from what has passed.

And of what strays from the root: al-muʿbar among camels is the one thick with hair. And al-muʿbar among boys is the one who has not been circumcised. And I do not know what the sense in this is. And Bishr ibn [Abī] Khāzim said, of the muʿbar who has not been circumcised, in a line of verse:
Swollen of ʿafl, uncircumcised.

And of this straying part is al-ʿabīr. Some people said: it is saffron. And some people said: it is a mixture of perfumes. And al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse:
And she is cool as the coolness of the bride's mantle in summer, upon which the ʿabīr has been sprinkled.
عبس:
The letters ʿayn, bāʾ, and sīn are a sound root pointing to a distaste in a thing. Its origin is al-ʿabas, what dries onto the hair of the tail from dung and the like — in camels it is what al-wadhaḥ is in sheep and goats. Abū al-Najm said:
As though on the tails of the milk-she-camels there were, from the summer's dried crust (ʿabas), the horns of a wild mountain goat.
In the hadith: he passed by camels that had crusted [dung] dried on their urine. Jarīr said, describing a shepherdess:
You see the year-old crust (al-ʿabas), dark, on her wrist, worn as bangles — not of ivory, and not of ...
Then from this is derived: al-yawm al-ʿabūs, the harsh, disagreeable day. And from it is derived: ʿabasa al-rajulu yaʿbisu ʿubūsan, he frowned; he is ʿābis al-wajh, scowling in the face, angry. And ʿabbās, said of one in whom this occurs often.
عبسورة:
And al-ʿubsura: the swift she-camel. He said:
I have indeed seen myself, while the days delighted me, with the lent-out, weak-humped swift camels among them.
The sīn in this is added; it is really from a she-camel that is tireless in journeys — its explanation has already passed.

A day described as ʿamarras is a harsh day, full of trouble. Al-Uraqiṭ said:
Harsh, baring its fangs.
This is a blend from 'a harsh day' — meaning severe — and from al-mars, a thing tightly twisted; both have already been explained.
عبط:
The letters ʿayn, bāʾ and ṭāʾ are a sound root indicating a harm that strikes without being deserved. Al-ʿabṭ is that the she-camel is slaughtered while healthy, with no disease and no injury to explain it. They said: al-ʿabīṭ is the fresh, of anything — though what they said about "fresh" is a widening of the sense by them; the true root is what was given above.

1. ʿubiṭat al-nāqa, uʿtubiṭat iʿtibāṭan — said of the she-camel, when she was slaughtered fat and young, with no disease.
2. a man yaʿbiṭu bi-nafsihi in war, ʿabṭan — when he throws himself into it though not compelled to.
3. a man yaʿbiṭu the ground, ʿabṭan — when he digs a spot that had never been dug before. Marrār said:
He stayed atop a high place, planted firmly, digging into the ground as one who digs a fresh spot digs.
4. so-and-so died ʿabṭatan — young and sound; death iʿtabaṭahu, took him suddenly. Umayya said:
Whoever does not die young and sound will die of old age; death has a cup, and every man tastes it.
5. al-dam al-ʿabīṭ — fresh blood. Al-Khalīl (repeating the very phrase already given) said: ʿabaṭat-hu l-dawāhī, misfortunes struck him, when they befell him though he did not deserve it. Ḥumayd said:
in a chaste dwelling, not mixing with the soiled, suspect ones, wrongly struck down.
6. al-ʿabīṭa — the sheep or she-camel slaughtered without cause. A poet said:
and for him there never cease to be fresh-slaughtered, humped she-camels, whether of the slender young ones or the full-grown.
عبق:
The letters ʿayn, bāʾ and qāf are a sound root indicating one thing clinging to another. From this: ʿabiqa al-ṭīb bihi, when perfume clung to him and stayed. He said:
Ambergris and musk clung to her, so she is golden, like the palm-spathe of a ripe cluster.
And Ṭarafa said:
Then they went off in the evening, musk clinging to them, trailing over the ground the fringes of their waist-wraps.

1. "mā baqiya lahum ʿabaqa" — nothing ʿabaqa remains for them, meaning no remainder of wealth is left to them; the sense behind it is the residue of clarified butter left clinging inside its skin container.
2. al-ʿabāqiya — a thorny tree. If this is taken by the same reasoning it is sound, because it clings to a thing, and one is caught by it in turn. He cited:
On the morning of Shuwāḥiṭ you got away at a run, your garment torn in a thorny thicket. (Rendered as best sense allows; the line is obscure.)
3. al-ʿabāqiya — also the residue left of perfume, or of a debt; the reasoning for it has already been given.
4. al-ʿabāqiya, of men — Al-Khalīl said: it is the formidable, cunning man, on the pattern ʿalāniya, named so because he latches onto everything. He cited:
There was destined for her a formidable, bold one, bold of chest, open-handed.
Al-Aṣmaʿī said: "shānahu shaynan ʿabāqiyatan," meaning he disgraced him severely — better said, with a disgrace that clings and does not part. Al-Kisāʾī said it is also said that al-ʿabāqiya is a wound that strikes a man on the fine skin of his face; this too is sound, since it is a lasting blemish that clings.
عبك: The letters ʿayn, bāʾ and kāf make a sound little word, meaning the same as the one before it; it is not unlikely that this is a case of letter-substitution. Al-Khalīl said: "mā dhuqtu ʿabakatan wa lā labakatan" — I did not taste an ʿabaka nor a labaka. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: one says "mā aghnayta ʿannī ʿabakatan wa lā labakatan," meaning you availed me nothing at all. Its root is their name for what remains, of clarified butter, inside its skin container: ʿabaka. It is also said of a lump of mud. What is sound in this chapter is this; other words have been reported in it from unknown Bedouin speakers, with no reliable basis, and we have left them out for that reason.
عبل:
The letters ʿayn, bāʾ and lām are a sound root indicating bulk, extension and firmness. From this: al-ʿabl, of bodies, is the massive one; you say ʿabula yaʿbulu ʿabālatan. He said:
We struck them with every broad-hoofed, sturdy horse, hard as a date-stone-crusher, thick and tough. (Al-araḥḥ is the broad hoof.)

1. al-aʿbal — the hard, white stone. One says jabal aʿbal, a mountain aʿbal, and ṣakhra ʿablāʾ, a rock ʿablāʾ. Abū Kabīr al-Hudhalī said, describing the fang of a she-wolf:
I drew out from it a lean she-wolf, gaunt, her fang gleaming white like al-aʿbal.
2. "huwa ʿablu l-dhirāʿayn" — said of a man, meaning thick and long in the forearms.
3. "alqā ʿalayhi ʿabāllatahu" — he cast his weight upon him.
4. It is possible that al-ʿabal, the fruit of the artā shrub, belongs here too, perhaps having in it a sense of length and extension.
عبم:
The letters ʿayn, bāʾ and mīm are a word indicating coarseness and roughness. From it: al-ʿabām, the man thick in build, with stupidity. One says: ʿabama yaʿbumu ʿabāmatan. A poet said, in a line of verse:
"And I denied it as the noble man denies, and I was not like a dull, stupid man who, asked something, mumbled."
And it is said that al-ʿabām is abundant water; if that is sound then it is close [to the first sense], and if not, then it belongs to the chapter of letter-substitution.
عبن:
The letters ʿayn, bāʾ and nūn are sound, and there is one word in it. They say: al-ʿabann is the huge, massive camel. It is also said al-ʿabann and al-ʿabannā, and the female is ʿabannāʾah. All of that is the same. Sometimes they describe a man with it. Ḥumayd said, describing a camel, in a line of verse:
"Trustworthy, thick of build, of varied tusks — the disputer says: he has long been a stud camel."
عبهر:
The massively built one; anything huge is ʿabhar. A woman is ʿabhara. Al-Aʿshā said:
Full-built, of Lubākh stock ... adorning him with her plain good character.
Here an ʿayn has been added at the start of the word; its origin is from al-bahr, meaning that she overwhelms [onlookers] by her build. We have already explained al-bahr.
عت:
The letters ʿayn and tāʾ are two roots: one is sound, and denotes going back over speech, and quarrelling; the other is something said about a trait of young men, and it may well be sound too.

The first is what al-Khalīl related: one says ʿatta yaʿuttu ʿattan, when a person repeats a saying again and again. And ʿatattu ʿalā fulānin qawlahu — I repeated the saying back to him again and again.

1. al-taʿattut — faltering in speech, not managing to keep going steadily in it. One says taʿattat yataʿattat taʿattutan.

He recited, in a line of verse: 'My two friends, put it to Suhayla for me, and see — is she grieving after I am gone, as I grieve?' He means: they went back and forth putting the words to her.

2. ʿātattu, uʿātituhu, muʿāttatan — to go back and forth with someone in speech, from the same root.

Abū ʿUbayd said: I kept disputing and quarrelling with so-and-so, ʿitāt and ṣitāt — both meaning dispute. The origin of ṣatt is a striking blow.

As for the second root, which may well be sound: they say al-ʿutʿut is a young man.

He said: 'When she saw him short and stunted, she said: I want the tall, strong young man.' Al-dhifirr means the tall one; al-mūdan and al-ʿiẓyarr mean the short one. And they also say al-ʿutʿut is a young goat kid.
عتب:
The letters ʿayn, tā' and bā' are a sound root; all of it goes back to a matter that has some difficulty in it, whether in speech or otherwise.

1. From this: al-ʿataba, the door's threshold, so called for its being raised above the level, easy ground.
2. ʿatabāt al-durja — the steps of a stairway; each step is an ʿataba.
3. By comparison to that, the ledges found in mountains are also called ʿatabāt, singular ʿataba; the plural is also ʿatab.
4. Anything that has become hard and rough has this word derived for it; one says fīhi ʿatab, when something has come over it that changes it away from being smooth.

He said, in a line of verse:
there is no roughness in the goodness of our obedience, nor in our hearing.

He said, describing a sword, in a line of verse:
tested in its strike, with no flaw in it — meaning not turning aside from what it strikes, nor glancing off it.

5. They say: "so-and-so was made to bear a hateful ʿataba" — meaning a hateful roughness, of affliction and harm.

Al-Mutalammis said, in a line of verse:
he is raised up over the hateful hardship, and made to endure it.

6. Of a stallion camel that is hobbled, or one that limps, when it walks on three legs as though hopping, one says ʿataba ʿatabānan. Al-Khalīl said: this is a comparison, as though he were walking on the steps of a stairway, hopping from one step to the next.
7. One says ʿattib lanā ʿataba — make us a threshold, meaning fashion one.
8. Also from this root, and this is the sound pattern: al-ʿatb, reproach. You say ʿatabtu ʿalā fulān ʿatban wa-maʿtaba, meaning I held something against him. From it is derived: aʿtabanī, he gave up what I held against him and came back to what pleased me; he is muʿtib, one turned back from wrongdoing.

He recited, in a line of verse:
I held it against Jumal, though I do not gloat over Jumal, even though her sandal had slipped.

9. They say: "he gave me al-ʿutbā" — meaning he made amends with me. "You have al-ʿutbā" — meaning I have granted you satisfaction.
10. al-taʿattub is when this one and that one, each, speak of their grievance. Likewise al-muʿātaba: when someone blames you and presses you for more, you say ʿātabanī, he remonstrated with me.

He said, in a line of verse:
when reproach is gone, there is no love left; but love remains as long as reproach remains.

11. Of a man, when he asks to be reconciled with, one says: he has istaʿtaba, sought reconciliation.

Abū al-Aswad said, in a line of verse:
so I remonstrated with him, then went back to him again, with gentle reproach and honest speech — and I found him not seeking reconciliation, and hardly remembering God at all.

12. Some of them said: "I saw no ʿutbān from so-and-so," meaning that he made amends with you, but you saw no clear sign of it.
عتد:
The letters ʿayn, tā' and dāl are a single root pointing to being present and close at hand.

Al-Khalīl said: you say ʿatuda al-shay' — the thing was ready — yaʿtudu ʿatādan, so it is ʿatīd, present and to hand. He said: from this the ʿatīda is named, the box in which perfume and oils are kept. Of a thing that has been got ready one says: it is ʿatīd; we have made it ready, aʿtadnāhu, and prepared it for a matter should one press hard upon us. The plural of ʿatād, gear held ready, is ʿutud and aʿtida.

Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
The ready gear of a man whose purpose distance does not break, a hunter of enemies, plain to see and not obscure.

Al-Khalīl said: they say hādhā al-faras ʿatad — this horse is ʿatad, that is, kept ready, so that whenever its owner wishes he rides it; the male and the female are alike in this word.

Salāma ibn Jandal said, in a line of verse:
With every horse bent in the hock like a wolf, deep of chest, and every long-bodied mare, ready, running till she seems to tear apart.

As for al-ʿatūd, al-Khalīl mentioned a sound analogy for it: it is the young goat that has reached the age of covering the females. If it is so, then it is as though it were a thing made ready for covering. The plural is ʿiddān, on the pattern fiʿlān; the original form was ʿitdān, and the tā' was merged into the dāl.

Al-Akhṭal said, in a line of verse:
And mention Ghadāna, young goats marked with the slit ear-flap, of the small ḥabalq breed, with the stone folds built around them.
عتر:
The letters ʿayn, tāʾ and rāʾ are a sound root indicating two meanings: one is the base and the stock, and the other is dispersal.

The first is what al-Khalīl mentioned: that the ʿitr of everything is its stock. He said: the ʿitrah of the spade is its wood, called the spade's handle. He said: from this it is said 'the ʿitrah of so-and-so', meaning his standing. He also said: they are his relatives — his children, his children's children, and his paternal cousins. This is al-Khalīl's account of the derivation of ʿitrah; others said that the true reasoning for ʿitrah is what we shall mention afterward.

The second origin: al-ʿitr — some people said it is what is called marzanjūsh [marjoram], and it does not grow except scattered. They said: the reasoning for a person's ʿitrah is from this, because they are his relatives, scattered in their lineages — this one from his father, this one from his offspring, like his child. And a line of verse was recited about al-ʿitr:
"I was not one to fear that I would stand against them for six households, as al-ʿitr grows [scattered]."
This points to dispersal, and it is a fine way of accounting for ʿitrah.

Close to it is ʿitr al-misk, a pebble-like grain found scattered through musk. Perhaps ʿitr al-misk is sound Arabic, for it is not far from what we have mentioned, though we have not heard it from a scholar.

From this same root is their saying: ʿatara al-rumḥ, fa-huwa yaʿtiru ʿatran wa-ʿatarānan, when it quivers and sways in a shaking motion. He said, in a line of verse:
"And every spear of true wood, when shaken, quivers."
We said it belongs to this chapter only because, when shaken, it appears as though its parts are coming apart. This is something observed. If what we have interpreted here is sound [it stands]; otherwise it belongs to the chapter of letter-substitution, being from ʿ-s-l [ʿasal], with the tāʾ standing in place of the sīn and the rāʾ in place of the lām.

What may rightly be reckoned to this is al-ʿatīrah, because its blood is ʿutira, that is, made to flow until it disperses. Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿātir is the one who sacrifices a ewe by slaughtering it — they used to do this in pre-Islamic times, slaughtering it and then pouring its blood over the head of the idol; that ewe is al-ʿatīrah and al-maʿtūrah, plural ʿatāʾir. Some of them used to say: al-ʿatīr is the idol for which the ʿatāʾir sacrifices were offered in the month of Rajab. And a line of Zuhayr's was recited:
"He slipped away from it and climbed to the top of a lookout, like the place where al-ʿitr stood, its head reddened by the sacrifice."
If this is sound, then it belongs to the first meaning, and the poet made his reasoning plain where he said: "like the place where al-ʿitr stood, its head reddened by the sacrifice."
عترسة:
Overpowering, and seizing from above. A man once brought a debtor of his to ʿUmar, and ʿUmar said, 'Do you ʿatarrasuhu?' — meaning, do you provoke him to anger and overpower him.

1. al-ʿitrīs — among the ghouls, is the male.
2. al-ʿantarīs — the sturdy she-camel; a horse may also be described by it. He said, in a line of verse:
Every well-knit, sturdy steed, long in flank and throat.
Al-ʿantarīs also means a calamity.

All of this has the tā' added into it; it is really from ʿarisa bi-l-shayʾ, when he clings persistently to a thing. The nūn is also added in al-ʿantarīs.
عتق:
The letters 'ayn, tā' and qāf are a sound root joining together the meaning of nobility — whether by nature or by character — and the meaning of oldness. What falls outside this has been mentioned separately.

Al-Khalīl said: 'ataqa al-'abdu ya'tiqu 'atāqan, 'atāqatan, and 'utūqan, the slave became free, and a'taqahu ṣāḥibuhu i'tāqan, his owner set him free. Al-Aṣma'ī said: 'ataqa fulānun ba'da isti'lājin, when a person became refined after having been coarse. One says: ḥalafa bi-l-'atāq, he swore by manumission; he is mawlā 'atāqah, a freedman by manumission. The slave becomes 'atīq. One does not say 'ātiq in place of 'atīq unless intending that the act will happen in future, saying 'ātiq ghadan, to be freed tomorrow.

A woman is 'atīqah, meaning free, of free birth rather than of slave descent. A woman is also 'atīqah meaning beautiful and noble. A horse is 'atīq, outstanding, plainly of fine stock. A soft, fine garment is 'atīq. Al-'atīq also means: the excellent, of anything. And it is said 'ataqa and 'atuqa, of anything that time has passed over.

Al-Khalīl said: a young girl is 'ātiq, meaning newly come of age. Ibn al-A'rābī said: she is called 'ātiq because she has passed beyond childhood ('ataqat) and reached the age of putting on the woman's garment. They said: birds of prey are 'itāq, because they hunt and are not hunted — the noblest of birds, as though they have won their freedom from being hunted, like the falcon and its like. Labīd said:
We competed at shooting while Ibn Salmā sat, like a noble bird of prey — it lowers its gaze, and is held in awe.

Abū 'Ubayd said: a'taqtu al-māla fa-'ataqa, meaning I put the livestock right, and it became sound. One says 'ataqati al-furusu, when the horse won the race. Al-Aṣma'ī said: I was at al-Mirbad and two horses were being raced, and a bedouin said, "This is the moment al-Shaqrā' has won [ʻataqat]!" One says fulānun mi'tāq al-wasīqah, of a man who pursues a herd driven off by raiders, saves it, and gets away safely with it. One says: mā abyana al-'itqa fī wajhi fulānin, how plain the nobility shows in so-and-so's face.

Al-Khalīl said: al-bayt al-'atīq, the Ancient House, is the Ka'bah, because it was the first house set up for people. God, Most High, said: {and let them circle round the Ancient House} [al-Ḥajj: 29]. It is said it was so named because it was freed from the flood in the days of the Deluge and raised up; it is also said it was freed from the Abyssinians in the Year of the Elephant; and it is said it was freed from anyone's claim of ownership, being the House of God, Most High.

Abū 'Ubaydah said: among their proverbs: "Had it not been for its age and nobility, it would surely have worn away" — said of a man who remains firm and lasts.

Al-Khalīl said: al-'ātiq, among birds, is the stage above the fledgling. Al-Aṣma'ī said: one says a young sand-grouse was caught as an 'ātiq, when it had become able to fly on its own. We think this is related to 'ataqati al-furusu, the horse that outran the rest. Abū Ḥātim said: a bird is 'ātiq when it is past the fledgling stage, because it has left the nest behind.

As for al-'ātiq among wineskins, it is the roomy, well-made one — this is by way of comparing it to something noble. Labīd said:
He sold the wine dear, from every dark, well-aged skin, or a dark jar broached, its seal broken.

Al-Khalīl said: shabābun 'ātiq means 'atīq, aged wine. Abū Zubayd said:
Let not the waterskin, cast aside, be lost — it was once, for a time, kept for the aged wine.

The old well is called 'ātiqah. Aged wine, al-khamr al-'atīqah, is that which has been kept a long time until it aged. Al-A'shā said:
And a fine vintage of what Bābil ages, like the blood of a sacrificed beast, whose colour I stripped away.

Some said: al-'ātiq, describing wine, means that which has not been decanted or broached — likening it to the young girl [al-jāriyah al-'ātiq] who has not yet left her parents. It is also said the wine is 'ātiq from its age, and everything old is 'ātiq and 'atīq. Ibn al-A'rābī said: anything that has reached its peak has "'ataqa," and the slave is called 'atīq because he has reached his full worth.

As for the saying of 'Antarah:
Al-'atīq lied, and cold water from a skin — if you are asking me for an evening drink, then go away —
some said this refers to a kind of aged date, and "lied" here means "turn instead to this kind." It is also said al-'atīq here means water, so named because it is the noblest of drinks, and life is in it.

From the sense of oldness already mentioned, their saying: 'atuqat 'alayhi yamīnun, meaning the oath became old and binding. He said, in a line of verse: "Upon me is an oath that became binding long ago; it cannot, however sought, be undone." Anything noble is called 'atīq.

What falls outside these two roots: 'ātiqā al-insān, a person's two shoulders, what lies between the shoulder-joints and the neck, plural al-'awātiq. Al-'ātiq is used for both masculine and feminine. Al-Aṣma'ī said: one says fulānun amyalu al-'ātiqi, when the place where his cloak sits is crooked. And he said, using the feminine of al-'ātiq, in a line of verse:
There will be no peace between me — know it well — and you, for as long as my shoulder has carried my sword, and we were not in Najd, nor did the valley's pale doves coo by the towering height.

Ibn al-A'rābī said: al-'ātiq is a bow whose colour has changed and turned black — this too goes back to the sense of oldness, the first meaning.
عتك:
The letters ʿayn, tāʾ and kāf are a sound root indicating something close to the one before it, and it is not unlikely that it belongs to the chapter of letter-substitution; it is about advancing boldly and about being old.

Al-Khalīl and others said: ʿataka fulān bi-fulān, when he pressed on him with a beating that nothing could restrain. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: it is to charge upon him in a rush of seizing and violence. Al-Khalīl said: ʿataka al-rajul, yaʿtiku ʿatkan wa-ʿutūkan, when he went off travelling in the land.

1. al-qaws al-ʿātikah — a bow so long possessed that it has reddened with age. Al-Hudhalī said, in a line of verse: "And a yellow, pared bow of nabʿ-wood, like an ivory bracelet, its seams reddened."
2. imraʾah ʿātikah — a woman smeared with perfume; and from this too is said ʿatakat al-qaws, the bow reddened.

Al-Khalīl said: every noble, generous man is called ʿātik, meaning old/ancient; and its origin is from ʿatakat al-qaws, the bow reddening.
عتل:
The letters 'ayn, tā' and lām are a sound root indicating force and strength in a thing. From this: al-rajul al-'utull, the strong, powerful, sound-bodied man; its derivation is from al-'atalah, the tool used for digging, a crowbar. Al-'atalah also means a thick wooden club, plural 'atal. He said, in a line of verse:
And wherever you are among the lands, keep clear of the insolence of the drivers, and strike them with the stout crowbars.

From this chapter: al-'atl, taking hold of a man by his collar and dragging him — ta'tiluhu — that is, pulling him toward you with force and violence. God, Most High, said: {Seize him and drag him into the midst of the Blazing Fire} [al-Dukhān: 47]. It is not al-'atl unless done with roughness and force. Some claimed people say "lā an'atilu ma'aka," meaning I will not be led along with you.
عتم:
The letters ʿayn, tāʾ and mīm are a sound root indicating slowness in a thing, or holding back from it. Al-Khalīl said: ʿattama al-rajul, yuʿattimu, when he held back from a thing after having gone ahead in it; also ʿatama, yaʿtimu. And [one says]: ḥamaltu ʿalā fulān fa-mā ʿattamtu an ḍarabtuhu — I bore down on so-and-so and did not hold back from striking him, meaning I did not restrain myself, did not flinch, and did not delay.

And in the hadith: that the Messenger of God — God bless him and his family and grant him peace — planted so many young palm shoots, "and not one of them ʿattamat", meaning not one delayed [in taking root], until it took hold.

And he said, in a line of verse: "the gathering-places of the heads, and none is spared [lā yuʿtam]" — meaning: none is granted respite and none is held back.

And he said, in a line of verse: "And I am not one to hold back when the horses shy away, nor am I, before the champion rider, one who flinches."

He said: al-ʿatamah is the first third of the night after the setting of the sun and the twilight-glow. One says: aʿtama al-qawm, when they came to be at that time. And 'the guest came ʿātiman', that is, muʿtiman, arriving at that hour.

Straying from this chapter is al-ʿatm: the wild olive. Al-Nābighah said: "She runs beside the ḍarw-trees of Barāqish, or Haylān, or a fresh one of al-ʿatm."
عتو:
The letters 'ayn, tā' and the weak letter are a sound root pointing to arrogance. Al-Khalīl and others said: 'atā ya'tū 'utuwwan — he behaved with arrogance. God Almighty said: {and they behaved with great arrogance} [al-Furqān: 21]. Likewise ya'tū 'itiyyan, so he is 'ātin; a tyrant king is 'ātin, and tyrants are 'utāh. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And people rebel against the man who is set over them.
One says ta'attā fulān, of a man, and ta'attat fulāna, of a woman, when she does not obey. Al-'Ajjāj said, in lines of verse:
Praise be to God, by whose command the heaven stands upright, and has settled firm,
and by whose command the earth stands, and it does not rebel.
That is, it did not disobey.
عث:
The letters ʿayn and thāʾ are two sound roots: one denotes a known small creature, which other things are then likened to; the other denotes softness in a thing.

As for the softness, al-Khalīl said:

1. al-ʿathʿath — a soft, easy sand-heap. He said: 'As if, by the sea beyond Hajar, on the farthest soft sand-heap, at daybreak, were cattle.' Some said al-ʿathʿath belongs with al-ʿadhāb and al-labab, both meaning loose, packed sand; and al-ʿathʿath is also counted among the choicest kinds of plant growth. He said: 'As if it were a gleaming white egg-shape, marked out for it in soft sand growing buttercup and colocynth.'
2. ʿithāth — their name for singing, from this chapter or close to it, for its beauty and the smoothness of its wording when spoken. Kuthayyir said: 'A ringing voice — when those departing tasted it, you heard from it, after its low note, a sweet full sound.'
3. ʿathʿath of the hip — the soft part of it. Dhū al-Rumma said: 'She shows you, with locks of hair hanging down, hips whose soft flesh at the hollows is struck black.'

The other root is:

1. al-ʿuthth — the moth grub that gnaws wool. One says ʿathathat al-ṣūfa, when it eats it. The Arabs say, as a proverb for a weak thing straining to make a mark on something it cannot: 'A little moth grub gnawing at smooth skin.'
2. al-ʿuththa, said of women, likened to the moth grub — the obscure, insignificant woman, according to Abū Zayd, whether feeble in body or not; its plural is ʿathāʾith. Someone else said it means the old woman, and recited: 'Do not think me like one who sits beside a moth grub, or who trusts in a slack market.'
3. ʿaththu māl — carried on the same likeness: so-and-so who is the steady companion of wealth, as if he clings to it the way the moth grub clings to wool.
4. ʿathʿatha bi-l-makāni — he stayed on in a place.
5. ʿathʿathtu ilā fulānin — I leaned on him, relied on him.
عثجل:
The wide, capacious one, said of water-skins and vessels. He said:
He waters with it a wide-mouthed, capacious one.
This is a word with the ʿayn added into it; it is really from al-thujla, the wideness of the belly. Al-athjal is the wide belly.
عثر:
The letters 'ayn, thā' and rā' are two sound roots: one indicates coming to know a thing, and the other the raising of dust.

The first: 'athara 'uthūran; a horse "'athara ya'thuru 'ithāran" means it stumbled and fell on its face. Some scholars said it was called 'athara from the sense of coming to know, because anyone who stumbles inevitably looks at the spot where he stumbled. One says: 'athara al-rajulu ya'thuru 'uthūran wa-'atharan, when he came to know of a matter no one else had discovered. Al-Khalīl said this. A'thartu fulānan 'alā kadhā, when you made him aware of it. God, Most High, said: {but if it is found out that the two of them deserved to be suspected of sin} [al-Mā'idah: 107], meaning "if it becomes known." And He said: {and thus We made them discovered by others} [al-Kahf: 21]. Al-'āthūr: a place where one stumbles. He said, in a line of verse: "and a land abounding in stumbling-places" — meaning abounding in places of ruin.

The other root: al-'ithyar and al-'ithyarah, rising dust. He said, in a line of verse: "you see around the hard ground its rising dust." As for their saying, "I saw of him neither a trace nor a puff of dust," they said al-'athyar is what is turned up of dust or clods of earth, and this too goes back to what we have mentioned. He said, in a line of verse: "You have surely startled your bird into flight — had you but read the omen" — meaning, you saw it fly off, as though he meant the sense of "trace."
عثل: They mentioned in it one word, if it is sound. It is said: al-ʿithwall among men is the coarse, rough one. They said: and al-ʿathūl is the coarse, thick palm tree. He said, in a line of verse: "I shook a coarse palm that had drawn up water and moisture for a long while, yet it never thought to bear fruit freely."
عثم:
The letters ʿayn, thāʾ and mīm are a sound root indicating thickness and a swelling protrusion in a thing. They said: al-ʿaythūm is the huge, powerful one of anything. And they said: elephants too are called al-ʿaythūm. He said, describing a she-camel: "And I have journeyed ahead of the tribe, she carrying me — she and the two weaned young ones, firm of flesh, huge [ʿaythūm]." meaning: massive, powerful. And the huge camel is called ʿaythūm. Al-ʿathamtham among camels is the one tall and thick, and [it is said] in the plural ʿathamthamāt. The lion, too, is sometimes described as al-ʿathamtham.

From this chapter is al-ʿathm, which is when a broken bone is set badly so that a crookedness and a swelling like a lump remains in it. One says: he is ʿathim, and there is ʿathm in him, as though it were a bony growth. Al-Khalīl said: and from this ʿUthmān was named, because it is taken from [the idea of] bone-setting. And it is also said, rather, [it is from] al-ʿuthmān...
عثن:
The letters ʿayn, thāʾ and nūn are a sound root indicating a spreading-out in a thing and a puffing-up.

1. al-ʿuthān — smoke; it is so named for its spreading in the air. One says ʿaththana yuʿaththinu, when he made smoke. And the fire ʿathunu and tuʿaththinu. And one says: ʿaththanat al-bayt bi-rīḥ al-dukhnah taʿthīnan — she fumed the house with the smoke of incense. And ʿathana al-bayt, yaʿthunu ʿathnan, when the smell of the incense-smoke clung to it. One says: ʿaththantu al-thawb bi-l-ṭīb taʿthīnan, as you would say dakhkhantuhu tadkhīnan, I fumed the garment.
2. al-ʿuthnūn — the ʿuthnūn of the beard, which is its length and the hair beneath it, named so for the spreading and puffing-out just mentioned.
3. ʿuthnūn al-rīḥ — the trailing edge of the wind at its first onset, when it comes on dragging the dust along; the plural is al-ʿathānīn. Its 'trailing edge' [haydab] is what of it falls upon the ground. Ibn Muqbil said: "Slender ones, ambling at midmorning, easy of shoulder, the evenings clothe them in the trailing dust-clouds."
4. ʿuthnūn al-baʿīr — small hairs at the place where a camel is slaughtered [the throat]; the plural is ʿathānīn.
عثى: The letters ʿayn, thāʾ and the weak letter are a word indicating corruption. One says ʿathā yaʿthū, and it is also said ʿathiya yaʿthī, like ʿātha. God Almighty said: {and do not go about in the land working corruption} [al-Baqara: 60].
عج:
The letters ʿayn and jīm are one sound root, denoting a rising in a thing — in sound, or dust, or the like.

1. al-ʿajj — raising the voice. One says ʿajja al-qawmu yaʿijjūna ʿajjan wa-ʿajījan, and ʿajjū bi-l-duʿāʾ, when they raise their voices. In the hadith: 'The best of the Hajj is al-ʿajj wa-l-thajj' — al-ʿajj is what we have described, and al-thajj is the pouring out of blood. Waraqa said: 'Entering into what Maʿadd disliked, even if it raised its voice loudly at its Mecca.' He means: entering into the religion.
2. ʿajīj al-māʾ — the sound of water; from it comes al-nahr al-ʿajjāj, the roaring river.
3. ʿajja al-baʿīru — the camel bellowed in its rutting-cry, yaʿajju ʿajījan. He said: 'I describe a stallion, bellowing in his rutting-cry.' If he repeats his bellow it is said ʿajʿaja.
4. ʿajjat al-qawsu — the bow twanged, when it made a sound. He said: 'It twangs in the hand when the archer draws taut, like the low hum of an old she-camel among the rest of the herd.'
5. ʿajjat al-rīḥu and aʿajjat — Abū Zayd said this of the wind, when it grew fierce and drove the dust along. A day is miʿajj, meaning one with dust-storms.
6. al-ʿajāj — the dust the wind raises, one cloud of it being ʿajājah. One says ʿajjajat al-rīḥu taʿjījan, and ʿajjajtu al-bayta dukhānan ḥattā taʿajjaj — I filled the tent with smoke until it billowed.

From this chapter also:

7. faras ʿajʿāj — a fast-running horse, so named because it raises the dust-cloud. He said: 'As if he, while the wind struck his cloak, in the tribe, above a hobbled camel, were a dust-raising runner.'
8. al-ʿajājah — a great number of sheep or camels.

Among what runs as a proverb and comparison: so-and-so wraps his dust-cloud around so-and-so, when he raids him, as if that were from the dust-cloud of war and the like. Al-Shanfarā said: 'And I love to wrap my dust-cloud around a man in a cloak, of Salāmān or of fine cloth.'

9. rajulun ʿajʿāj — a great shouter, as al-Liḥyānī related.

And the reasoning of this chapter has run straight throughout.

As for their saying that al-ʿajʿajah is turning a doubled yāʾ into a jīm, and their reciting: 'O Lord, if You have accepted my pilgrimage' — this has no proper connection to be occupied with, and it is not known what it is.
عجب:
The letters 'ayn, jīm and bā' are two sound roots. One of them points to reckoning a thing great and being puffed up over it; the other is a part of an animal's make.

The first is al-'ujb, which is a man's being proud in himself. You say: he is mu'jab bi-nafsihi, pleased with himself. And in the chapter of wonder you say: 'ajiba ya'jabu 'ajaban, he wondered; and amrun 'ajīb, a wonderful matter; and that is when a thing is reckoned great and enormous. They said: al-Khalīl held that there is a difference between 'ajīb and 'ujāb. As for 'ajīb, and 'ajab is like it, it is a matter that is wondered at; but 'ujāb is that which goes beyond the limit of the wonderful. He said: that is like tawīl and tuwāl: the tall, tawīl, are many among people, while tuwāl is the wildly, excessively tall. And they say 'ajabun 'ājib, wonder upon wonder. Al-isti'jāb is intense wonder; one says musta'jib and muta'ajjib, astonished at what he sees. Aws said, in a line of verse:
And one who marvels at what he sees of our patient endurance, though had war shouldered him aside he would not so much as stir.
And qissatun 'ajab, an astonishing tale. And a'jabanī hādhā al-shay', this thing pleased me; and I have been pleased with it, u'jibtu bihi. And shay'un mu'jib is a thing that is very fine.

The other root is al-'ajb, which in every beast is the part that the two haunches close upon, at the base of the tail that is set in the hinder part of the rump. The 'ujūb of sand-hills are called 'ujūb by likeness to that, in that they are the thin trailing ends of the dunes. Labīd said, in a line of verse:
By the tail-ends of sand-drifts, their loose sand slipping down.
And a she-camel that is 'ajbā' is one in whom the 'ajab and the 'ujba are plain, and how greatly she has it; and that is when the top of her hinder part is thin and her two haunch-bones stand out; and it is an ugly make.
عجد: The letters ʿayn, jīm and dāl amount to nothing, except that they say: al-ʿujd is raisins. It is also said to be al-ʿunjud.
عجر:
The letters ʿayn, jīm and rāʾ are a single sound root indicating a knotting-up in a thing, and a swelling together with a twist.

From it: al-ʿajar, the verbal noun of ʿajira yaʿjaru ʿajaran. Al-aʿjar is the descriptive form. Al-ʿujrah is the place of the ʿajar. And it is said: a hoof that is ʿajir is hard and firm. Marrār ibn Munqidh said, in a line of verse: "Whose forelock streams, deep-clefted, sharp of frog, in a firm, knotted pastern."

Al-aʿjar is anything in which you see knots: a ram is aʿjar, and a belly is aʿjar when it is very full. ʿAntarah said: "Sons of Zabībah, what ails your colt, gaunt of flank, while your own bellies are swollen [ʿujr]?" Someone said: I think it is a fabricated line, except that al-Khalīl recited it: "Fine of clothing, he spends the night swollen, well-fed, while the guest, from love of food, is doubled over [with hunger]."

And al-ʿujrah is every knot in a piece of wood or elsewhere, such as the veins of the body; the plural is ʿujar. From this chapter is al-iʿtijār, which is the winding of the turban about the head without passing it beneath the chin. He said: "She came bearing him, wrapped [muʿtajiran] in his cloak, a swift she-camel trotting along with singular weave." It was named iʿtijār only for the twisting and swelling in it.

Straying from this root is al-ʿajīr, which among horses is like the impotent man among men.
عجرد:
The naked one. This too is a word with the ʿayn added into it; it is really from jarada and tajarrada min thiyābihi — he stripped off his clothes.

From this comes al-ʿanjarid, the brazen, sharp-tongued woman; the ʿayn in it is also added. It is really from her tajarrud, her forwardness in quarrelling, and her lack of shame. He said:
A sharp-tongued woman who swears when I swear — a she-devil, like the crested donkey.
عجرفية:
Harshness in speech and clumsiness in work. This is a blend formed from two things: jarafa and ʿajara, as though he sweeps speech along roughly, in a knotted way. Al-ʿajar is knottedness. This word is used figuratively, so that the calamities of time are called ʿajārīf. Qays said:
Umm ʿAmmār did not make me forget her, though the distance of travel was far — nor did the calamities of time, which do not leave me be.
That is: they do not release me — for they come sweeping in violently.
عجرم: The thick, coarse one; the mīm in it is added. The origin is al-aʿjar.
عجز:
The letters 'ayn, jīm and zāy are two sound roots: one of them points to weakness, and the other to the hinder part of a thing.

The first is 'ajiza 'an al-shay' ya'jizu 'ajzan, so he is 'ājiz, that is, weak. And their saying that al-'ajz is the opposite of firm resolve is from this, because his judgement is weak. And they say: "A man will fail, there is no escaping it." And one says: a'jazanī fulān, when I was unable to seek him out and to reach him. And nothing will make God, exalted, unable, that is, God, exalted, is not unable for it whenever He wills. And in the Qur'an: {We shall never be able to escape God in the earth, nor shall we escape Him by flight} [al-Jinn: 12], and He, exalted, said: {And you are not ones to escape in the earth} [al-'Ankabut: 22]. And they say 'ajaza, with a fatha on the jīm. And I heard 'Alī ibn Ibrāhīm al-Qattān say: I heard Tha'lab say: I heard Ibn al-A'rābī say: one does not say 'ajiza except when his buttocks have grown large.

Of this chapter: al-'ajūz, the old woman, and the plural is 'ajā'iz. And the verb is 'ajjazat ta'jīzan. And one says: so-and-so 'ājaza so-and-so, when he went off and could not be reached. And He, exalted, said: {striving against Our signs, trying to escape} [Saba': 38]. And al-'ajūz is also given the plural al-'ujuz; and perhaps they carried this further and called wine 'ajūz, and they named it so only for its age, as though it were an old woman. And al-'ijza, and ibn al-'ijza, is the last child of an old man. And he recited:
The late-born child of two aged parents, named Ma'bad.

As for the other root, al-'ajuz is the hinder part of a thing, and the plural is a'jāz, so much so that they say 'ajuz al-amr and a'jāz al-umūr, the tail ends of affairs. And they say: "Do not busy yourselves with the tail ends of affairs whose fronts have already passed." He said: al-'ajīza is a woman's rump in particular, when it is bulky; one says imra'atun 'ajzā'. And the plural is 'ajīzāt likewise. Al-Khalīl said: one does not say 'ajā'iz, for dislike of the confusion. And Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
Full in the hips, shapely, slender of waist; her belt hangs loose about her, and her body and her limbs are perfect.
And Abū al-Najm said:
Of every full-hipped one,
,
The veil slipping down, guileless: she neither kept watch nor let things go to waste.
And al-'ajaz is a sickness that takes a beast in its hinder part; one says she is 'ajzā', and the male is a'jaz. And of what is likened [in] this chapter: al-'ajzā' of sand is a raised sand-hill as though it were a mountain, and the plural is al-'ujz. And this is on the ground that it is likened to the rump of a woman with a large rump, just as they sometimes liken rumps to sand and to dunes. And al-'ajzā' among eagles is the one light in the rump. Al-A'shā said:
Light-rumped, she provides for her young with the entrails.
And what we have left out here for dislike of repeating goes back to the two roots we have mentioned. And we have heard someone say that al-'ajūz is the blade of a sword. If this is sound, then it is called so for its age, like the old woman, and for the passing of the seasons over it.
عجس:
The letters ʿayn, jīm and sīn are one sound root, indicating a thing's being set back, like the rump, in bulk and thickness and a gathering-together.

From it: al-ʿujs and al-maʿjis, the grip of the bow; its ʿujs and its ʿajz are the same, likened to the rump [ʿajuz] and buttocks of a person. Aws said of the ʿajs, in a line of verse: "A silent bow, filling the whole hand, its grip no less nor more than a hand's measure." He means: its grip matches the grip precisely, evenly. And Muhalhil said of the maʿjis, in a line of verse: "They twanged the grips of the bows and shone out, as the stallions challenge the stallions."

From this chapter: ʿajāsāʾ al-layl, the darkness of the night, that which is in its latter part, likened to the ʿajāsāʾ of camels.

The scholars of language said: al-ʿajāsāʾ among camels are the huge, aged she-camels. Al-Rāʿī said: "When there kneel down of them huge old she-camels, at a bend in the valley, revealing al-ʿIfās and Barwaʿ." [al-ʿIfās and Barwaʿ are two she-camels.] This follows the pattern of what we mentioned about the latter and greater part of a thing. For the scholars of language say: al-taʿajjus is holding-back. They said: it is possible that the derivation of al-ʿajāsāʾ among camels is from this, in that they are the ones that lag behind the other camels at pasture. They said: al-ʿajāsāʾ of clouds are the great masses of them. One says: taʿajjasanī ʿanka kadhā, meaning: such a thing held me back from you. All of this points to the soundness of the analogy we have drawn.

Al-Duraydī said: taʿajjasta al-rajul, when he had given an order and you altered it against him. This is sound, for it belongs to coming-after, which happens only once the first has passed and the next comes on its heels, at its rear. And they mentioned that al-ʿajīsāʾ is a slow gait, and it belongs to this chapter. And what shows the soundness of our reasoning about the end of the night and its ʿajāsāʾ is al-Khalīl's saying: al-ʿajs is the end of the night. And he recited: "And true companions I roused in the depth of the night — but for love of Ẓamyāʾ they would have made camp — so they rose, dragging their garments, while behind them the night's last hour [ʿajs], like the ostrich, hunched."

And Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā mentioned, from Ibn al-Aʿrābī: that al-ʿujsah is the last hour of the night. As for their saying, 'I will not come to you sajīsa ʿujays' — that too is from this, meaning: I will not come to you until the end of time. The proof of this is the saying of Abū Dhuʾayb: "May black rain-clouds, brimming with pouring water, water Umm ʿAmr every latter part of the night." He did not mean the latter parts of the nights as against their earlier parts, but rather he meant forever.
عجف:
The letters 'ayn, jīm and fā' are two sound roots: one indicates emaciation, and the other the restraining of oneself and enduring patiently regarding, or away from, a thing.

The first: al-'ajaf, emaciation and the loss of fatness; the male is a'jaf and the female 'ajfā', plural 'ijāf for both males and females. The verb is 'ajifa ya'jafu. There is no other word in Arabic on the pattern af'al whose plural is on the pattern fi'āl besides this word — they modelled it on the word for "fat ones." And 'ijāf follows the pattern fi'āl. One says a'jafa al-qawm, when their livestock became emaciated; they are mu'jifūn.

Al-Kisā'ī related: shafatān 'ajfāwān, meaning thin, delicate lips. Abū 'Ubayd said: one says 'ajufa when meaning became emaciated, though the expected pattern would be 'ajifa, since anything of the pattern af'al/fa'lā' has a past tense on the pattern fa'ila, like 'arija ya'raju — except for a small number of words that came on the pattern fa'ula: samura, ḥamuqa, ra'una, 'ajufa, and kharuqa.

Al-Aṣma'ī related, of al-a'jam [one who speaks unclearly]: 'ajuma. And sometimes they extended the usage and said arḍun 'ajfā', barren land with no good and no vegetation in it. From this is the scout's saying: "I found a barren land." And they say naṣlun a'jaf, a thin arrowhead. Ibn Abī 'Ā'idh said, in a line of verse:
His two hands find rest with a bundle of gathered arrows, thin-shafted, thin of point.

As for the second root, their saying: 'ajaftu nafsī 'an al-ṭa'ām a'jifuhā 'ajfan, when you hold yourself back from food while craving it. "'Ajaftu ghayrī" [holding someone else back] is rarely used. He said, in a line of verse: "No measure of food nor half-measure nourished her, nor dates, nor deliberate withholding." One says: 'ajaftu nafsī 'alā al-marīḍi a'jifuhā, when you endure patiently and nurse the sick person. He said, in a line of verse: "Though you taunt me for my thinness, I will surely hold myself back for my friend's sake, offering love and generosity."
عجل:
The letters ʿayn, jīm and lām are two sound roots: one of them points to haste, and the other to a certain animal.

The first: al-ʿajala, haste in a matter. One says he is ʿajil and ʿajul, two ways of saying it. Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
As though his legs were the legs of a hurrying man on a short-stepping mount ... when a humming answers back from his two cloaks.

And istaʿjaltu fulānan — I urged him on. And ʿajiltuhu — I got ahead of him. God, exalted be He, said: {Were you hasty about the command of your Lord?} [al-Aʿrāf: 150]. And al-ʿujāla is what is hurried up of a thing. And one says: "The rider's quick fare is dates and parched-barley meal." And it was reported from al-Khalīl that al-ʿajal is food that is hurried and set out before the meal is ready. And he recited:
If you do not help me, O generous one, I shall be a thing snatched ... like a bite fallen into a hungry man's mouth.
But we say: as for the reasoning of the word we have mentioned, it is sound, because the word has no root at all, and the verse is fabricated.

And one says, from al-ʿujāla: ʿajaltu al-qawm — I gave the people a hasty bite, as one says lahhantuhum. And the people of the language said: al-ʿājil is the opposite of al-ājil, what is deferred. And this world is called al-ʿājila, the hastening one, and the next world al-ājila, the deferred one. And al-ʿAjlān is Kaʿb ibn Rabīʿa ibn ʿĀmir; they said he was called al-ʿAjlān for his hurrying his slave along. And they recited:
And al-ʿAjlān was named so only for his saying: Take ... the bowl and milk, slave, and be quick.

And they said that al-muʿajjil and al-muʿjil among she-camels is the one that gives birth before the full time is out and whose young lives.

And of what has been carried upon this is al-ʿajala, the ox-cart. And al-ʿajala is the water-wheel with which water is drawn; the plural is ʿajal and ʿajalāt.

Abū ʿUbayd said: al-ʿajala is a piece of wood laid across the two uprights of the well, with the bucket hung from it; the plural is ʿajal. Abū Zayd said: al-ʿajala is the pulley-wheel. And he recited:
Its master had made ready — heedless as he was ... a red one of teak-wood that the wheel takes up.

And of this chapter: al-ʿijla, the small water-skin; the plural is ʿijal. And al-Aʿshā said:
And the women trailing the skirts of silk at times ... and those swaying with the little water-skins on their haunches.
It was named so only because it is light and its carrier moves quickly with it. And al-Khalīl said: al-ʿajūl among camels is the one distracted with grief that has lost her young; the plural is ʿujul. And he recited:
I yearn for you with the yearning of the bereaved camel ... whenever the dove wails its cooing.

And al-Khansā' said, in a line of verse:
No bereaved camel circling a stuffed calfskin ... helped in her moaning by other nursing mothers —

They said: and sometimes a bereaved woman is called ʿajūl; the plural is ʿujul. Al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse:
Until the chief of the people stays propped on his elbow ... while bereaved women push him back with the palm.

And they explained it no further than this. We say: its explanation is the agitation and haste that come upon the distracted one in her distraction; only, from this ʿajūl no verb was built, so that one might say ʿajilat, as thakilat was built from thukl, bereavement — and the root of it is one; only it did not come from the Arabs.

And the other root is al-ʿijl, the calf, the young of the cow; and in one dialect ʿijjawl; the plural is ʿajājīl, the female is ʿijla and ʿijwala, and by that a man was named ʿIjl.
عجلد: Thickened, curdled milk. This is a word with the ʿayn added into it, as though it were likened to skin (jild) in its thickness.
عجلزة:
The horse of firm build. Al-Khalīl stated something specific about this: he said the derivation of this description is from jalz al-khalq, the firmness of its build. This confirms what we say about this and its like — he has told you that the ʿayn in it is added. He said:
And a firm-built one, on which the felt saddle-pad slips.
عجلط: The same as the one before it, with the ṭā' substituted for the dāl.
عجم:
The letters 'ayn, jīm and mīm are three roots: one indicates silence and muteness, another indicates hardness and firmness, and another indicates biting and tasting.

The first: a man who does not speak clearly is a'jam, and the woman is 'ajmā', plainly marked by 'ujma. Abū al-Najm said, in a line of verse:
Inarticulate to her ears, yet in truth eloquent [sense uncertain].
One says 'ajuma al-rajulu, when he became a'jam, like samura and adumu. One says of a child, as long as he cannot yet speak clearly: ṣabiyyun a'jam. One says ṣalātu al-nahāri 'ajmā', meaning that the recitation in it is not spoken aloud. Their saying al-'ajam for those who are not Arabs is from this same reasoning, as though, because the Arabs did not understand them, they called them 'ajam; they are also called 'ujm. A line says:
The abodes of Mayya, when Mayy still favoured us ... and none her equal is seen, neither 'ajam nor Arab.
They say istaj'amati al-dāru 'an jawābi al-sā'il, the abode gave no answer to the one who asked of it. A line says:
Its echo fell silent and its trace was worn away ... and it gave no answer to the speech of the one who asked.
One says al-a'jamī is one who does not speak clearly, even if he lives among the Arabs of the desert. This, in our view, is a mistake; we know of no one who called a desert-dweller a'jamī, just as they do not call him 'ajamī — perhaps whoever said this meant al-a'jam and said al-a'jamī instead. Al-Aṣma'ī said: one says ba'īrun a'jam when it does not bray. Al-'ajmā' is the dumb beast, called so because it does not speak; likewise everyone unable to speak is a'jam and musta'jim. In hadith: "the injury caused by a dumb beast incurs no liability," meaning the beast.

Al-Khalīl said: ḥurūf al-mu'jam, shortened from al-mu'jama, are the separate letters of the alphabet, because they are 'ajamiyya, inarticulate. Kitābun mu'ajjam — its ta'jīm is its dotting, so that its obscurity is made clear and it is made plain. I think al-Khalīl meant by "'ajamiyya" that so long as letters stand apart, not composed into intelligible speech, they are 'ajamiyya, because they signify nothing. If this is what he meant, it makes sense; if not, I do not know what he meant by it. What we hold is that what is meant by ḥurūf al-mu'jam is the letters of the dotted script, that is, the Arabic script, since we know of no other script that is dotted in this way so as to convey so many meanings. As for the dotting of writing with diacritical shapes, that in our view falls under the sense of "biting into a thing," since it is a mark made into it, and so it is called i'jām because it is an effect made in it that points to the meaning.

As for the speaker's saying yurīdu an yu'riba fa-yu'jimuhu, he means to make it clear but instead renders it obscure — this too belongs to the chapter already given. Its meaning: he intends to make something plain but cannot, and so produces it inarticulate, failing to convey the meaning. That has nothing to do with the dotting of writing.
عجن:
The letters ʿayn, jīm and nūn are a sound root indicating the compacting-together of something soft, not firm.

From it: al-ʿajan, which is the compacting of the flesh of a she-camel's udder, and likewise of a cow's or a ewe's. One says: she is ʿajnāʾ, plainly showing al-ʿajan. And she has ʿajinat, taʿjunu ʿajanan. And the compacted one [al-mutaʿajjin] among camels is packed tight with fat, as though it were flesh without bone.

From this chapter: ʿajana al-khabbāz al-ʿajīn, yaʿjinuhu ʿajnan — the baker kneaded the dough. Close to this is their saying of the foolish man: ʿajjān, and [of a foolish woman] ʿajīnah. He said: its meaning is that they say, 'So-and-so kneads with his elbows out of foolishness,' then they shortened it and simply said ʿajīnah and ʿajjān, meaning 'with his elbows', as it comes in the proverb.

From this chapter: al-ʿijān, which is what the one urinating cleans himself with [i.e. the perineum], and it is soft. Jarīr said: "He pulls the rope, leaning his weight upon it, as though his ʿijān were a fresh bowstring."
عجنجر:
The thick, coarse one; one says 'thick butter' (zubd ʿajanjar). This is a word whose letters have been added for the meaning we have mentioned. It is from taʿajjara, when it clots and thickens. He said:
I churned my milk-skin, and it foamed and gurgled — it brought out from it thick, clotted butter.
عجنس:
The huge camel; the nūn in it is added. It is among what we mentioned in the chapter of al-ʿajas and al-ʿajāsā'. He said:
They follow one with a rumbling gait, huge — when the two ravens have brushed against it.
عجى:
The letters ʿayn, jīm and the weak letter are a sound root indicating a weakness in a thing, whether it comes about newly or is inborn.

From it: al-ʿujāyah, a sinew set with small bone-nodules, found at the fetlock of a riding beast, and it is soft; they claimed that a hungry man would pound that ʿujāyah between two stones and eat it. Its plural is al-ʿujāyāt and al-ʿujā. Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr said: "Dark-sinewed ones, leaving the gravel scattered, whose heads the sandhills' tops did not spare from being shod [with stones]."

What shows the soundness of this reasoning is their saying of a mother: hiya taʿjū waladahā, said when her child's suckling is delayed past its due times, which brings on a weakness in his body. Al-Aʿshā said: "Her heart anxious over him, she nurses him with nothing but a scant sip or a mere mouthful." Al-ʿufāfah is the slight thing, and al-fuwāq is what gathers in the udder before the flow of milk. And 'she taʿjūhu' means: she treats him with feeding until he rises up. The name of that child is al-ʿajiyy, the female al-ʿajiyyah, plural ʿajāyā. He said: "What kept me from visiting you is that my lambs are all ʿajāyā but a few."

And when a child is denied milk and fed instead on food, it is said: he has been ʿūjiya. Dhū al-Iṣbaʿ said: "If you wish, you will see, among their offspring, orphans fed like wolf-cubs [yuʿājūn]." And another said, describing locusts: "When it moved on from a resting-place, it left behind there ʿajāyā, its young ones scraping about in the dust." It is also transmitted: "radhāyā yuʿājā."
عد:
The letters ʿayn and dāl are one single sound root that never strays from al-ʿadd, which is counting, and from al-iʿdād, which is preparing a thing. All the branches of this chapter go back to these two senses.

Al-ʿadd is counting a thing. You say ʿadadtu al-shayʾa aʿudduhu ʿaddan, so I am ʿādd, and the thing is maʿdūd.

1. al-ʿadīd — abundance, great number. Fulānun fī ʿidādi al-ṣāliḥīn, meaning he is counted among them.
2. al-ʿadad — the amount of what is counted. One says mā akthara ʿadīda banī fulānin wa-ʿadadahum, and innahum la-yataʿāddūna wa-yataʿaddadūna ʿalā ʿasharati ālāfin — they exceed ten thousand.

From the other side comes:
