3. al-ʿuddah — what is prepared for something that may happen. One says aʿdadtu al-shayʾa uʿidduhu iʿdādan, and istaʿdadtu li-l-shayʾi, and taʿaddadtu lahu — I got ready for it.

Al-Aṣmaʿī said: among the proverbs is: 'Every man runs with what he has made ready.'

4. al-ʿiddah, from al-ʿadd — a woman's waiting period.
5. al-ʿidd — a standing pool of water, plural aʿdād. We say it belongs to this chapter because water that never runs dry is as if it were something kept perpetually ready. He said: 'And I have crossed, on a she-camel hardy as a stallion, a waterless waste with neither pool nor puddle in it.'

Abū ʿUbayda said: al-ʿidd is an old, plentiful well, and for that reason one says ḥasabun ʿidd, meaning ancient lineage; the plural is aʿdād. He said: and they sometimes call every well an ʿidd. They also say māʾun ʿidd, using it as a description, when it is well-water. He said: 'If you were a well's steady water, you would have brimmed — when the people came to draw, you would not have run thin.'

Abū Ḥātim said: al-ʿidd is water from the ground, just as al-karaʿ is rain-water from the sky. Dhū al-Rumma said: 'There, the wild cows and the white gazelles have neither well-water nor rain-pool by them, only the caves and the low scrub.'

6. al-ʿidād — the recurring pain of a snakebite's sting. Its derivation and reasoning are sound, because it comes at a fixed time, as if that time were being counted off exactly. Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿidād is the recurring pain of the one bitten, because some snakes, when the one they struck grows moist again, the pain comes back on him. One could also correctly say ʿādda-hu, meaning that when a full year has passed since the day he was bitten, the pain flares up in him; he is muʿādd. Its derivation seems to be from reckoning, from the counting of months and days — meaning the pain was counting off what passed of the year, and when it was complete it came back upon the bitten man. Al-Shaybānī said: ʿidād al-maldūgh is his feeling the pain hour after hour. Ibn al-Sikkīt said: ʿidād al-salīm is that seven days are counted for him, and when they pass, they hope for his recovery; if the seven have not passed, he is still fī ʿidād. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: al-ʿidād is the day of giving a stipend, and likewise everything that had a fixed time within the year. From this is his saying, peace be upon him: 'The morsel of Khaybar has kept coming back on me, and now is the time it has cut my aorta,' meaning it comes to me every year at its time. He said: 'What is left of the bond with Suʿād has become an attachment and a recurring sickness.'

7. al-ʿiddān — time itself, so called because every span of time is bounded and counted. Al-Farazdaq said: 'You wept for a harsh, coarse, cursed man, like Chosroes in his time, or like Caesar.' Al-Khalīl said: one says kāna dhālika fī ʿiddāni shabābihi wa-ʿiddāni mulkihi, meaning its greatest, best, and earliest part. He said: 'And the king lies hidden away, safe within his time.' The meaning is that this had been made ready and prepared for him. This is al-Khalīl's account. It is related from al-Shaybānī that al-ʿidād is that a group of people gather and each of them brings out an expense.

As for ʿidād al-qaws, some say it is its twanging sound — this is what they say without qualification. More correct than that is what Ibn al-Aʿrābī said, that ʿidād al-qaws is that it hums, hour after hour — and this fits the pattern better. Al-Hudhalī said of it: 'A yellow bow of nabʿ-wood, whose humming is as if it were a violent gust stripping off garments, sweeping all before it.'

As for the saying of Kuthayyir: 'So leave Suʿdā be — it is only distance from her that eases the ache, coming round like the return of the Pleiades, once, then fading away' — Ibn al-Sikkīt said: one says laqītu fulānan ʿidāda al-thurayyā al-qamar, meaning once a month, for they claim that the moon comes to rest by the Pleiades once every month.

As for Maʿadd, some have mentioned it in this chapter, treating the mīm as extra and weighing it as mafʿal — but this is not so with us, for the analogy does not require it; with us it is faʿall, from mīm, ʿayn and dāl, and we have already discussed it in its place in the chapter on mīm.
عدب: The letters ʿayn, dāl and bāʾ — al-Khalīl claimed it is unused, and perhaps nothing of it simply reached him. As for the form itself, it is sound. Al-ʿadāb is ground that has become sandy/loose. Ibn Aḥmar said: "Like the lone hillock of al-ʿadāb, the dew strikes it, the dew rising over its surface then trickling down." And God knows best.
عدر: The letters ʿayn, dāl and rāʾ amount to nothing. Yet one word has been mentioned in it. They said: al-ʿadr is heavy rain.
عدس: The letters ʿayn, dāl and sīn have no established sense in the language, but they name the well-known grain al-ʿadas (lentils). They also say "ʿadas" as a cry used to drive mules on. A poet said: "ʿAdas! ʿAbbād has no authority over you — you have escaped, and this one you carry is free." And his saying: "When I load my gear onto ʿAdas" — he means the mule, naming her ʿAdas from the cry used to drive her.
عدف:
The letters ʿayn, dāl and fāʾ are a small sound root indicating scarcity, or a little out of much.

From it: al-ʿadf and al-ʿadūf, a scant bit of fodder. One says: 'the horses did not taste even a scant bit [ʿadūfan].' He said: "And [horses] set apart, that taste not a scrap, hurling themselves among the young mares and colts." And al-ʿadf is a meager gift. One says: aṣabnā mālahu ʿadfan — we got only a scant portion of his wealth.

From this chapter: al-ʿidfah, which is like a scrap [ṣanifah] of cloth. As for the saying of al-Ṭirimmāḥ: "Bearer of the heavy loads of blood-money for the wrong done, from the scant remnant [ʿidaf] of the stock and its generous men" — they said: al-ʿidaf means the little [that remains].
عدق: The letters ʿayn, dāl and qāf amount to nothing. And they mentioned that an iron tool with prongs, used to draw a bucket up out of a well, is called an ʿawdaqah. And they related: ʿadaqa bi-ẓannihi, like rajama [he guessed at random]. And I do not know of any sound verse to bear witness to this.
عدك: The letters ʿayn, dāl and kāf amount to nothing, except for one word among Ibn Durayd's oddities: he said, al-ʿadk is the beating of wool with a mallet.
عدل:
The letters al‑ʿayn, dāl and lām are two correct roots, but they are opposite like opposites: one indicates equality and the other indicates curvature.

The first meaning is justice among people: the fair, the level, the straight way. It is said: this is justice, and they are justice. Zuhayr said: When will a people say their paths are ... they are between us and they are content and they are justice.

It also says: they are two just, and they are unequal, and a certain person is justice, clear in justice and equality. Justice means judgment by equality. It is said of a thing that it equals another thing: it is its justice. I exchanged someone for someone, and he is equivalent to him. The polytheist equates with his Lord – exalted – as if he balances another with him.

From the chapter "the two just": the load of a cart, they are called that because they are equal. The adjective al‑ʿadīl: the one who equals you in the load. Justice: the value of a thing and its ransom. Allah says: {and no ransom is accepted from it} [Al‑Baqarah 123], i.e. a ransom. All this is from equivalence, which is equality.

Justice is the opposite of excess. It is said: justice in his pasture. A moderate day is when the heat and cold are equal, and likewise in food. It is said: I made it just until it became moderate, i.e. I established it until it stood straight and level. The poet says: you made the people with it until they held ... the earth balances it so it does not tilt.

From the chapter: the moderate one among the camels, and the good one that matches the parts. As for their saying about a strike from the ships: adawliyya, it may be allowed as an analogy we measured, because it is only a level, moderate thing. The friend claimed it belongs to a place called adawla. Tarafa said: adawliyya or from the ship of Ibn Yamin ... the sailor uses it to turn and to guide.

The other root is said in curvature: adala, and it means to bend. Zu al‑Rummah said: I will turn the side away from its direction ... out of modesty, and even if I obeyed it it would not be equivalent.
عدم:
The letters ʿayn, dāl and mīm are a single root indicating the losing of a thing and its going away.

From it: al-ʿadam. And ʿadima fulān al-shayʾ, when he lost it. And aʿdamahu Allāh — Exalted is He — such a thing, meaning He took it away from him. Al-ʿadīm is the one who has no wealth; and its plural may be al-ʿudamāʾ, as one says faqīr and fuqarāʾ. And aʿdama al-rajul: he came to have want. He said of al-ʿadīm: "Our man without means is one who holds himself back with dignity and generosity, while upon the rich falls the duty of the poor man's due." And Ḥassān ibn Thābit said of al-ʿadam: "Many a forbearance has poverty of wealth destroyed, and an ignorance that plenty has covered over."
عدن:
The letters ʿayn, dāl and nūn are a sound root indicating staying/dwelling. Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿadn is the dwelling of camels specifically among the salt-bushes [ḥamḍ]. One says: ʿadanat al-ibil, taʿdinu ʿadnan. The origin al-Khalīl mentioned is the root sense of this chapter, and every act of dwelling was then measured by it, so that it is said Jannat ʿAdn, meaning the Garden of Dwelling.

From this chapter: al-maʿdin, the mine [source] of gems. And by analogy they say: he is a maʿdin of good and generosity. As for al-ʿidān and al-ʿadān, they are the seashore. It is possible that this too comes from the analogy we mentioned, and it is not far-fetched. Labīd said: "All my companions well know my patience and my forbearance by the sea's shore [ʿadān al-sayf]." And ʿAdan is a town.
عدو:
The letters ʿayn, dāl and the weak letter are one sound root to which all the branches return, and it points to going beyond in a thing and pressing on past what one ought to stop at.

Of that is al-ʿadw, and it is running. You say ʿadā yaʿdū ʿadwan, and he is ʿādin, a runner. Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿuduww is with a ḍamma and a doubled letter, and the two are two forms of the word: one is ʿadw, as you say ghazw (raiding), and the other ʿuduww, as you say ḥuḍūr and quʿūd. Al-Khalīl said: al-taʿaddī is going beyond what one ought to stop at. And this verse is read in two ways: {fa-yasubbū Allāha ʿadwan bi-ghayri ʿilm} [al-Anʿām: 108], and also "ʿuduwwan". Al-ʿādī is the one who runs upon people in wrong and enmity. And one says: so-and-so yaʿdū your affair; and, he did no more than do such a thing. And of the horse's running one says ʿadawān, that is, good at running and much given to it. And a dhi'bun ʿadawān is a wolf that runs at people.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Remember when you were a strong leaper, full in the flank, a great runner at the bound.

And you say mā ra'aytu aḥadan mā ʿadā Zaydan — I saw no one but Zayd. Al-Khalīl said: that is, none went past Zayd. And one says ʿadā fulānun ṭawrahu — so-and-so went beyond his proper limit. From it is al-ʿudwān. He said: and likewise al-ʿadā', al-iʿtidā' and al-taʿaddī.

Abū Nukhayla said, in a line of verse:
The wretched slave never ceased going past his limit, transgressing and transgressing and transgressing.

He said: al-ʿudwān is plain wrongdoing, and al-iʿtidā' is derived from al-ʿudwān.

As for al-ʿadwā, al-Khalīl said: it is your asking a governor or a judge to give you redress against one who has wronged you, that is, to take vengeance on him for his transgression against you. And al-ʿadwā is what is said to be passed on from a scab or a disease. In the hadith: "There is no ʿadwā, and nothing passes anything on to anything." And al-ʿudā' is the same. And this follows the reasoning, that is, if a disease is in him it does not go past him to you.

Al-ʿadwa is the running-up of the thief and the running-up of the raider. One says ʿadā ʿalayhi fa-akhadha mālahu — he set upon him and took his money — and ʿadā ʿalayhi bi-sayfihi, he struck him with his sword; he does not mean by it running on his two feet, but it is from wrongdoing.

As for his saying:
And troubles and calamities came between us —
he means that they went beyond bounds until they took up all attention. And one says kuffa ʿannā ʿādiyataka — hold your ʿādiya off from us. Al-ʿādiya is one of the businesses of time that runs over you away from your affair, that is, keeps you busy. And al-ʿadā' is being kept busy.

Zuhayr said, in a line of verse:
So cut her cord, since she has cut it, and a hindrance turned you from meeting her.

As for al-ʿidā', it is that a horse, or a dog, [or] a hunter should take two quarries in one run, bringing down one right after the other.

Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
He ran a double course between a bull and a ewe, and between a young one like a strip of matting and a thick-horned old buck.

That too is derived from al-ʿadw, as though he ran at this one and ran at the other. And sometimes they said ʿadā', with a fatḥa on the ʿayn, and it is the single heat of a run. A poet said:
He brings down five at a single run, in one heat.

And al-ʿadā' is the length or side of anything, whatever its breadth or its length runs along with. They say lazimtu ʿadā'a al-nahr — I kept to the length of the river — and, this is a road that takes the length of the mountain. And sometimes al-ʿidwa is said in the sense of al-ʿadā'; and sometimes the hā' is dropped and one says ʿidw, and it is given a plural: aʿdā' al-nahr, the banks of the river, and aʿdā' al-ṭarīq, the sides of the road. He said: and al-taʿdā' is on the pattern tafʿāl. And sometimes they called the shifting, unsettled resting-place al-ʿudawā'.

And Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
His heart was mad with the memory of her, and there mingled in him, from her, upon the unsettledness of the dwelling, a sickness.

Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿindā'wa is crookedness and hardness. Al-Khalīl said: and it is from al-ʿadā'.

And we say ʿaddā ʿani al-amri yuʿaddī taʿdiyatan, that is, he passed it by to something else. And ʿaddayta ʿannī al-hamm, that is, you put the care aside from me. And ʿaddi ʿannī ilā ghayrī — turn from me to another. And ʿaddi ʿan hādhā al-amr, that is, go past it and take up another.

Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
So turn away from what you see, since there is no bringing it back, and heap the saddle-frames upon a strong, firm she-camel.

And you say taʿaddaytu al-mafāza, that is, I crossed the waterless waste on to another. And ʿaddaytu al-nāqata uʿaddīhā. A poet said, in a line of verse:
I drove on a great strong she-camel, like the smith's anvil, a bearer of male young.

Of the section is al-ʿaduww, the enemy, derived from what we mentioned before. It is said of one, of two, and of many alike: ʿaduww. God, exalted, said in the story of Abraham: {fa-innahum ʿaduwwun lī illā rabba al-ʿālamīn} [al-Shuʿarā': 77]. And there are al-ʿidā, al-ʿudā, al-ʿādī and al-ʿudāt, all names for enemies.

As for al-ʿudawā', it is dry hard ground, and it was named so only because whoever settles on it passes on from it. Al-Khalīl said: sometimes it comes in the middle of a well when it is dug, and sometimes it is a rock, so that they must veer somewhat aside from it.

Al-ʿAjjāj said, describing the wild bull and his digging of his lair, telling how he came to hard ʿudawā' and could not dig it, so he swerved away from it:
And if he struck hard ground he swerved away from it, and turned his cloven hoofs upon it.

Al-ʿudwa — also ʿidwa — is a firm place on the bank of a valley. It is called ʿudwa because it, as it were, stands against the river, that is, as though the two were a pair set against one another.

Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿadawiyya is of the summer plants, after the spring has gone; it grows green and the camels graze it. You say aṣābat al-ibilu ʿadawiyyatan, and its pattern is faʿaliyya.
عذب:
The letters ʿayn, dhāl and bā' are a sound root, but its words hardly hold to one measure, and they cannot be gathered under one thing. It is like what we mentioned just now in the section of ʿayn, dhāl and rā'. And this shows that the language as a whole is not reasoned measure — but the bulk of it and the greater part of it is.

So of the section: ʿadhuba al-mā' yaʿdhubu ʿudhūbatan, so that it is ʿadhb — sweet and good to drink. And aʿdhaba al-qawm — the people's water became sweet. And istaʿdhabū — they drew and drank sweet water.

And another section that does not resemble the one before it. One says ʿadhaba al-ḥimār yaʿdhibu ʿadhban wa-ʿudhūban, so that it is ʿādhib [and] ʿadhūb: it does not eat, from the hardness of its thirst. And one says aʿdhaba ʿan al-shay' — he turned from the thing, when he leaves off from it and abandons it. And in the hadith: «Leave off the mention of women». He said:
And they took al-Yaʿbūb in exchange for their god, an idol — so flee, O Jadīl, and leave off.
And a horse or another beast is called ʿadhūb when it passes the night eating nothing and drinking nothing, because it holds back from that.

And another section that does not resemble the one before it: al-ʿadhūb is the one between whom and the sky there is no cover, and so also al-ʿādhib. Nābigha al-Jaʿdī said, in a line of verse:
So he passed the night bare to the sky, as though he were Suhayl when the stars leave him alone.
As for the words of the other:
We passed the night uncovered and the gnats kept biting us; where we halted, our welcome was the barking of a dog —
it is possible that he meant: there is no cover between us and the sky; and it is possible that it is from the first sense, when they pass the night neither eating nor drinking.

And al-Khalīl related: ʿadhdhabtuhu taʿdhīban, that is, I weaned him. And this belongs to the section of holding back from food and drink.

And another section that does not resemble the one before it: al-ʿadhāb, torment. From it one says ʿadhdhaba taʿdhīban. And some people say the origin of al-ʿadhāb is beating, and they argued from the words of Zuhayr:
And behind her a driver urging her on; when she fears his beating from him she stretches out her back and her neck.
He said: then that was borrowed for every hardship.

And another section that does not resemble the one before it: the end of the whip is called ʿadhaba, and the plural is ʿadhab. He said:
Flat-eared, wide-jawed, trained to the hunt, like wolves, with the whip-thongs on their necks.
And the ʿadhaba in the camel's member is its tip. And al-ʿUdhayb is a place.
عذر:
The letters 'ayn, dhāl and rā' are a sound structure with many branches, in which God — Most High — has set no way of analogy at all; rather every word of it stands alone in its own manner and its own direction.

Al-'udhr is well known: it is a man's seeking, with words, to set right what has been held against him. From it one says 'adhartuhu fa-anā a'dhiruhu 'adhran — I excused him — and the noun is al-'udhr. And you say 'adhartuhu min fulān, that is, I blamed him and did not blame this other one. It is said man 'adhīrī min fulān and man ya'dhirunī minhu — who will hold me excused against so-and-so?

A poet said, in a line of verse:
I want to give him a gift and he wants to kill me — take your excuse for your friend, the man of Murād.

And it is said that a man's 'adhīr is what he aims at and attempts, of the sort of thing he is held excused for when he does it. Al-Khalīl said: al-'Ajjāj was mending his saddle for a journey he intended, and his wife said: what is this you are mending? And he said, in a line of verse:
My neighbour, do not think strange my 'adhīr —
meaning: do not find fault with what I am attempting. Then he explained it in another line and said:
My travelling, and my care for my camel.

And you say i'tadhara ya'tadhiru i'tidhāran wa-'idhratan min dhanbihi fa-'adhartuhu — he offered an excuse for his sin and I excused him. Al-ma'dhira is the noun. God — Most High — said: {they said: an excuse to your Lord} [al-A'rāf: 164]. And a'dhara fulānun when he does enough to be excused and so is not blamed.

Of this same root is their saying 'adhdhara al-rajul ta'dhīran, when he does not put his whole effort into a matter while showing you that he is putting his whole effort into it. In the Qur'an: {and the makers of excuses among the bedouin came} [al-Tawba: 90], and it is also read "al-mu'dhirūn". The people of Arabic said: al-mu'dhirūn, with the light dhāl, are those who have a real excuse, and al-mu'adhdhirūn are those who have no excuse but force one up. And their calling a man who falls short in a matter mu'adhdhir is, in our view, also from al-'udhr, because he falls short in the matter relying upon the excuse that he does not wish to trouble himself over.

And another class that does not resemble the one before it: they say ta'adhdhara al-amr, when a matter does not go straight. Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
And one day on the back of the sand-hill she was hard with me and swore an oath that was never undone.

And another class that does not resemble the one before it: al-'idhār, the cheek-strap of the bridle. He said: and whatever there is on the two cheeks of a branding or a scratch running lengthwise is 'idhār. From al-'idhār you say 'adhartu al-faras fa-anā a'dhiruhu 'adhran bi-l-'idhār, in the sense of I bridled him. And a'dhartu al-lijām, that is, I made a cheek-strap for it. Then they use this as a figure and say of a man plunging headlong in his error: "he has thrown off the cheek-strap". And from al-'idhār one also says 'adhdhartu al-faras ta'dhīran.

And another class that does not resemble the one before it: al-'idhār, which is food to which people are invited for a happy event. From it one says a'dharū i'dhāran.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Rabī'a craves every kind of food — the birth-feast, the circumcision feast, and the feast for the returning traveller.

And it is said: rather it is the food of the circumcision in particular. One says 'udhira al-ghulām, when the boy is circumcised. And so-and-so and so-and-so are 'idhār of one and the same year.

And another class that does not resemble the one before it: al-'adhawwar. Al-Khalīl said: it is the wide-bellied one that bites hard. The poet said, describing a kingdom as wide and broad, in a line of verse:
God gathered for us prophethood and guidance, and gave through it might and a wide, spreading kingdom.

And like this is the saying of one who praises, in a line of verse:
When guests alight he is 'adhawwar toward the tribe until his cooking pots are set up.

They said: he meant ill-tempered, until the pots are set on the fire. And it is like what al-Khalīl said in describing the ass that bites hard.

And another class that does not resemble the one before it: al-'udhra, the maidenhead of the virgin girl, al-'adhrā'. A girl is 'adhrā' when no man has touched her. This is close to what was mentioned before about the 'udhra of the boy.

And another class that does not resemble the one before it: al-'udhra, a pain that takes hold in the throat. From it one says 'udhira, and he is ma'dhūr. Jarīr said, in a line of verse:
Ibn Murra pressed her, O Farazdaq, as the physician presses the swellings in the throat of the man with the 'udhra.

And another class that does not resemble the one before it: al-'udhra, a star which, when it rises, the heat grows fierce. They say: "when al-'udhra rises, not a half-ripe date is left in 'Umān".

And another class that does not resemble the one before it: al-'udhra, a lock of hair, and the lock of a horse's mane. And its forelock is 'udhra. And he said, in a line of verse:
Sleek of forelock, swinging as he gallops.

And another class that does not resemble the one before it: al-'adhira, the open ground in front of a house. In the hadith: "The Jews are the foulest of God's creation in their 'adhira", that is, in the ground before their houses. Then human filth was called 'adhira, because it used to be thrown out in the open ground before the houses.
عذق:
The letters ʿayn, dhāl and qāf are a single root indicating an extending-out in a thing, and one thing's being attached to another.

From it: al-ʿidhq, the ʿidhq of the palm tree, which is one cluster among its clusters. And al-ʿadhq, the palm tree itself, with the ʿayn opened. All of that belongs among things attached one to another. He said: "It sways with a moist frond, as though it were the hanging bunches of a date-cluster from Sumayḥah, ripening soft." Al-Khalīl said: the ʿidhq of anything is the branch that has offshoots.

From this chapter: ʿudhiqa al-rajul, when he was branded with a mark by which he is known. This is sound, and it comes from their saying: ʿadhaqa shātahu, yaʿdhuquhā ʿadhqan, when he tied onto it a tuft of wool of a different colour.

Among what runs as a metaphor and figure is their saying: 'In the sons of so-and-so there is a mature cluster [ʿidhq kahl]', said when there is might and protection among them. Ibn Muqbil said: "And among Ghaṭafān there is a true, well-defended cluster, ripening, despite the resentment of the people around it."
عذل:
The letters ʿayn, dhāl and lām are a sound root indicating heat and intensity in a thing, and from it what is close to it is then measured. From it: iʿtadhala al-ḥarr, the heat intensified. Abū ʿUbayd said: ayyām muʿtadhilāt, days of intense heat.

What has been measured against this is their saying: ʿadhala fulān fulānan ʿadhlan, and al-ʿadhal is the noun [blame]. A man is ʿadhdhāl and a woman ʿadhdhālah when this occurs much from them. Men [who blame] are al-ʿudhdhāl, women are al-ʿudhdhal. This was called ʿadhl for the intensity and the stinging touch in it. He said: "My two blamers set out at dawn, and I said, gently — is it, over love for Salmā, that you two blame me?"
عذم:
The letters ʿayn, dhāl and mīm are a small sound root indicating biting and the like of it. Al-Khalīl said: the origin of al-ʿadhm is biting; then it is said: ʿadhamahu bi-lisānihi, yaʿdhimuhu ʿadhman, when he seized him with his tongue [rebuked him sharply]. Al-ʿadhīmah is blame/reproach. The rajaz-poet said: "Whoever races against him will remain amid reproaches [ʿadhāʾim], from the very outset of his furious running." meaning reproaches. And a horse is ʿadhūm.

As for al-ʿadhamdham, al-Khalīl mentioned it in this chapter with a dotted ghayn [i.e. ghadhamdham], while others said: rather it is ghadhamdham with a ghayn. Al-Khalīl said: it is the all-sweeping thing. One says: mawt ghadhamdham, a sweeping death that leaves nothing. He said: "Heavy of platters and of forbearance, their generosity like a mill-wheel of water — they measure out a sweeping measure, holding nothing back [ghadhamdhaman]."
عذي:
The letters ʿayn, dhāl and the weak letter are a small sound root indicating the wholesomeness of soil. Al-Khalīl and others said: al-ʿadhāh is wholesome-soiled land, of noble growing-ground. He said: "In a land of pure soil, watered by the early rain, wholesome ground [ʿadhāh], from which the brackish water and the sea have withdrawn."

He said: al-ʿidhy is a place that puts forth growth in winter and summer without a spring of water. And it is said [also] that it is sown land watered only by rain-water, for being far from [other] water-sources. They said: this is also called al-ʿadhā, singular ʿadhāh. And they recited: "In a land of wholesome soil — how good its forenoons, and sweeter still is its night and its late afternoons."
عر:
The letters ʿayn and rāʾ are four sound roots.

The first denotes smearing something with what is not fragrant, and the like; the second denotes a sound; the third denotes height and elevation; and the fourth denotes working at something — on condition that we do not count plant names or place names among what follows this pattern in the speech of the Arabs.

1. al-ʿarr and al-ʿurr — Al-Khalīl said: these are two dialect words meaning mange. Likewise al-ʿurrah. It is so named because it is like a smearing on the body. Al-ʿurrah is also said to mean filth itself. In the hadith: 'God curses the seller of al-ʿurrah and its buyer.'

2. al-ʿarr / al-ʿurr, distinguished — Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: al-ʿarr is mange; al-ʿurr is the peeling of a camel's hide, and cautery is applied for al-ʿarr, not al-ʿurr. Muḥammad ibn Ḥabīb said: a mangy camel is aʿarr, a mangy she-camel ʿarrāʾ. Al-Naḍr said: an afflicted male camel is ʿārr, a female ʿārrah; one does not say maʿrūr for mange, because al-maʿrūrah is the she-camel whose milk and yield have been struck by an evil eye. In a proverb: 'Keep the fully mangy one away from the just-touched one' — al-jarbāʾ is the one mange has covered entirely, al-ʿārrah is the one where it has only begun; a man wanted to move his fully mangy camels away from the one just touched, and his companion rebuked him for it, meaning: why move her away when they are all mangy? One also says nāqatun maʿrūrah, a she-camel whose udder has been touched by filth, spoiling her milk. A foul man is ʿārūrah, meaning filthy. Abū Dhuʾayb said: 'And each I saw had already been struck by its filth.'

3. al-ʿarr, a sore — Al-Aṣmaʿī said: like a pustule, that breaks out on camels' necks, most often striking the young ones. Abū Zayd said: one says uʿirra fulān, when al-ʿurr has struck his camels.

4. al-ʿurrah, filth generally — Al-Khalīl said: one says huwa ʿurratun min al-ʿurar, meaning whoever comes near him is smeared with harm by him. He said: al-ʿurrah is also used for the droppings of birds. Al-Ṭirimmāḥ said: 'Among the mountain-crags, wild goats, among which is the birds' filth, like the fasting-abstinence of the ostrich.' Al-shanāẓī are mountain crags, singular shunẓuwah; the word was heard only in this line.

5. istaʿarrahum al-sharr / al-maʿarrah — one says istaʿarrahum al-sharr, when evil spread among them. One says ʿarrahu bi-sharrin yaʿurruhu ʿarran, when he charged him with it. Al-Khalīl said: al-maʿarrah is what befalls a person by way of sin. God, glory be to Him, said: {so that a sin without knowledge should befall you through them} [al-Fatḥ: 25].

6. ʿarārah, bad character — perhaps belonging to this chapter also is what Abū ʿUbayd related: rajulun fīhi ʿarārah, meaning bad character.

7. al-muʿtarr / al-ʿurʿur — al-muʿtarr, meaning the poor man, the one who importunes you and presents himself to you, to us it belongs here too, as if he were a man who clings and stays close. As for the ʿarārah that Abū ʿUbayd mentioned, meaning bad character, there is another word for it: al-Shaybānī said al-ʿurʿur means bad character. Mālik al-Dubayrī said: 'And I bore her fasting-abstinence and her bad temper, and I could not set her right, nor came near it' — meaning: I could not set right what they had done; al-ṣawm is filth; he means: she persisted in her evil deeds and her blameworthy character.

8. al-miʿrār, of palm trees — Abū Ḥātim said al-miʿrār is al-miḥshāf, a poor variety of dates. It is also said that al-miʿrār is the one struck by something like al-ʿarr, meaning mange.

9. al-ʿarīr, the stranger — he is so named on the analogy already given, as if he had been smeared onto, attached to, those he had come to; it goes back to the chapter of al-muʿtarr. From this is the report of Ḥāṭib, when he was asked, 'Why did you write to the people of Mecca?' and he said: 'I was a stranger among them,' meaning a foreigner with no support.

10. al-maʿarrah, in the sky — which is what lies beyond the Milky Way toward the north pole, so named for the abundance of its stars. He said: the origin of al-maʿarrah is the place of al-ʿarr, meaning mange, and the Arabs call the sky al-jarbāʾ, the mangy one, for the abundance of its stars. A man asked another about his dwelling, and he told him he lived between two great tribes of the Arabs, and he said: 'You have settled between the Milky Way and the Beyond-it.'

The second root is the sound.

1. al-ʿirār — the cry of the male ostrich, its call. Labīd said: 'Its people have moved on, leaving nothing but the ostrich's cry, and the whistle of the wind, after lively encampments.' Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: one says ʿārra al-ẓalīmu yuʿārru, and one does not say ʿarra. Abū ʿAmr said: al-ʿirār is the cry of the male when he wants the female, and al-zimār is the cry of the female when she wants the male. He recited: 'Whenever you wish, you will hear his mating-cry in a bare waste, answering a female cry like a pierced reed-pipe.'

2. taʿārra al-rajulu — Al-Khalīl said: when a man wakes from his sleep. He said: I take the male ostrich's cry to belong here too. In the hadith of Salmān: 'that whenever he woke in the night, he would glorify God.'

3. ʿarʿār, a children's game — a boy goes out, and if he finds no other children, he raises his voice, and the children come out to him. Al-Kumayt said: 'Where the bows do not twang, nor is a startled band of children met with a shout of ʿarʿār.' Al-Nābigha said: 'Sheltering on both sides of the flanks of ʿUkāẓ, each of them calling his young child there with ʿarʿār,' meaning they are safe, and their children play this game. Al-Kumayt means that this bull hears neither the twanging of bows nor children's voices, and no sound startles him. One says ʿaraʿarah and ʿarʿār, as one says qarqarah and qarqār — it is simply the Arab children's own cry.

The third root, denoting height and elevation:

1. al-ʿurʿurah — al-Khalīl said: the ʿurʿurah of anything is its highest point. Al-Farrāʾ said: al-ʿurʿurah is the mane-crest of any mount; al-ʿurʿurah is also the tip of the camel's hump. Abū Zayd said: the ʿurʿurah of the hump is a sinew running along the cartilage-ridges.

2. jamalun ʿurāʿir — a fat camel. Al-Nābigha said: 'For him, in the tent's courtyard, a hollow dark pot swallows the joints of the fat, slaughtered camel.' They broaden this until they call a noble man ʿurāʿir. Muhalhil said: 'He stripped kings of their crowns and marched beneath his banner, the tribal props and the noble men of the peoples.'

3. a donkey called aʿarr — when its fat lies in its chest and neck.
4. al-ʿarārah, lordship — from the same. He said: 'Lordship and abundant hospitality belong to Dārim, and the lightweight among them is their kinsman who bears the burdens.' Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: al-ʿarārah is might; one says huwa fī ʿarārati khayr, and tazawwaja fulānun fī ʿarārati nisāʾ, when he marries among women who bear sons.

5. al-ʿarar, a small hump — as for what al-Khalīl mentioned in this sense, it does not conflict with what we have said, for it goes back to the first chapter, of one thing sticking to another, as if from its smallness it were stuck close to the back. One says jamalun aʿarr and nāqatun ʿarrāʾ, when its hump has not grown large though the animal is fat; the trait is bayyinat al-ʿarar, and its plural is ʿurr. He said: 'They set out humped and came back with small humps.' They also say naʿjatun ʿarrāʾ, when its rump-fat has not grown large, and this follows the same reasoning, as if it were a thing that had been stuck to it, that is, attached.

The fourth root, working at something: you say ʿarʿartu al-laḥma ʿan al-ʿaẓmi, and sharshartuhu, with the same meaning. They said: al-ʿaraʿarah is working hastily at a thing when it is hard to deal with. You say ʿarʿarta raʾsa al-qārūrati, when you worked at it to get it out. It is said that a man of the Arabs slaughtered a ram and invited his people, and said to his wife: 'I have invited these people, so work at this ram and be quick about finishing it,' then went off and invited the people; he said to her, 'What have you done?' and she said, 'I have finished all of it except the shoulder-blade — I am still working it and it is working me.' He said, 'Take it home with you as provisions,' and divorced her. Dhū al-Rumma said: 'And a green one, in two nests, whose head I worked at, to fulfil, when she parted, an excuse in my company.'

As for al-ʿarʿar, it is a tree, and we have said this is not to be reckoned on the pattern, and likewise place-names such as ʿUrāʿir, Maʿarrīn, and others.
عراهم: The soft, plump one. And a cane/reed — [the text breaks off here].
عرب:
The letters ʿayn, rā' and bā' are three roots: one of them is speaking out and making plain, another is liveliness and cheerfulness of soul, and the third is a corruption in a body or a limb.

The first is their saying aʿraba al-rajulu ʿan nafsihi, when he made himself plain and clear. The Messenger of God 0 God bless him and his family and grant them peace - said: "The woman who has been married before, her own tongue speaks out for her; and the virgin is asked about herself."

And it has come in the hadith: "It is liked that when the child first speaks out he should say: there is no god but God, seven times" — that is, when he makes himself plain. And this is not from the iʿrāb of speech, the marking of its endings. The iʿrāb of speech is also from this same rule, because by iʿrāb one tells apart the meanings in the doer and the one done to, in denial, in wonder, in questioning, and in the rest of the chapters of this kind of knowledge.

As for the nation that is called al-ʿArab, it is not far-fetched that they were named ʿArab from this same rule, because their tongue is the plainest of tongues and their clear speech the best of clear speech. What makes this plain is the hadith that has come: "Arabic is not one single chapter, but a speaking tongue." What points to this too is the Arabs' saying: mā bihā ʿarībun — there is no one there — as though they meant: there is no companion there who speaks out for himself. Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿarab al-ʿāriba are the pure Arabs. And al-aʿārīb is the plural of al-aʿrāb, the desert Arabs. And a man is ʿarabī. He said: aʿraba al-rajulu when he spoke clearly, and he is ʿarabāniyy al-lisān, plain of speech. And aʿraba al-farasu: its Arab breeding came out pure and no suspicion about its stock attached to it. And al-ibil al-ʿirāb are the Arabian camels. And al-ʿarab al-mustaʿriba are those who came in afterwards and made themselves Arabs and took on Arab ways.

The other root: al-mar'a al-ʿarūb is the woman who laughs much and is sweet of soul, and they are al-ʿurub. God, exalted be He, said: {So We made them virgins, loving, of equal age} [al-Wāqiʿa: 36]. The people of interpretation said: they are the ones who make themselves beloved to their husbands.

And al-ʿarb, with a sukūn on the rā', is liveliness.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And the horses pull with liveliness against their reins.

And al-ʿarab, with a fatḥa on the rā', is a mark left behind. From it one says ʿariba yaʿrabu ʿaraban.

The third root is their saying: [ʿaribat] miʿdatuhu, when his stomach went bad, taʿrabu ʿaraban. From this one says a woman is ʿarūb, that is, corrupt. ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm al-Qaṭṭān recited to us, saying: Thaʿlab recited to us from Ibn al-Aʿrābī, in a line of verse:
And no replacement for Umm ʿImrān is a coarse-tongued black woman, loose in the rein, corrupt.

As for the day of Friday, it is called al-ʿarūba, and it is a name laid down, in our view, otherwise than by the rule we have described. And they say that in ancient times it used to be called al-ʿarūba. But the Book of God, exalted be He, and the hadith of the Messenger of God, God bless him and his family and grant them peace, have come only with the mention of al-jumuʿa. Even so, they have recited:
The day of al-ʿarūba, waterings upon waterings.

And they have also recited, in a line of verse:
How fine he is before the mighty one when he appears on the day of al-ʿarūba and the pulpit is set in its place.

And all of this, in our view, is not to be relied on as sound.
عربس:
And al-ʿarbasīs: a level stretch of ground. Al-ʿAjjāj said:
And a level tract of it, with a rough going.
And al-Ṭirimmāḥ said:
It travels a barren level stretch of ground, like the back of flowing water, its surface running level.
This is a word with the bā' added into it; it is really from al-muʿarras, that is, it is level and easy for camping upon.
عرت: The letters ʿayn, rā' and tā'. Al-ʿart is rubbing or chafing. And rumḥ ʿarrāt (a quivering spear) is like ʿarrāṣ, that is, one that shakes.
عرث: Abū Bakr said: al-ʿarth is wrenching away. 'ʿarathahu ʿarthan' — he wrenched it away. It belongs to al-Mujmal [Ibn Fāris's shorter dictionary].
عرج:
The letters ʿayn, rā' and jīm are three roots: the first points to a leaning and to lameness, the next to a number, and the next to height and ascent.

The first: al-ʿaraj is the verbal noun of al-aʿraj, the lame man. One says from it ʿarija yaʿraju ʿarajan, when he becomes lame. And they said: ʿarija yaʿraju is by natural make, and ʿaraja yaʿruju is when he walks the walk of the lame. And al-ʿarjā' is the hyena, and that is a natural thing in her, so for that she was called al-ʿarjā'; the plural is ʿurj. And the plural of al-aʿraj among people is al-ʿurjān. And the crow is called aʿraj, because when it walks it hops.

And of this section is al-taʿarruj, which is the holding back of the mounts at a resting place or a halting place, leaning them toward it. Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
O my two neighbours, daughter of Faḍḍāḍ, have you no mind to halt until we may speak to her?

And Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: ʿarrajtu ʿalayhi — that is, I held back my mount for him. And I have no ʿurja and no maʿraja at him — that is, no halting. And of the road, when it bends aside, one says: inʿaraja. And the valley bends; and its munʿaraj is where it turns to the right and to the left. And the people inʿaraja from the road when they turned aside from it. And they say that al-ʿurayjā' is the noonday heat. And if this is sound, it is because everything bends aside toward a place that shields it from the heat. A poet said, in a line of verse:
But Suhayya knows that I am a man, at the ʿurayjā' when the loin-cloths were wet.

And al-Aṣmaʿī used to say that it is that the camels come to water one day in the morning and one day in the evening. And we have watered by the ʿurayjā'. And al-ʿArjā' is a well-known hill. Abū Dhu'ayb said, in a line of verse:
So she, at the bend, the bend of Nubāyiʿ, and the lands of Dhū al-ʿArjā', is a booty gathered.

And it is said that it was called al-ʿArjā' only because the road bends by it. And one says an affair ʿarīj, when it does not go straight but is still crooked.

And the other root is of camels. Some people said: from eighty to ninety; and when they reach a hundred they are hunayda. The plural is ʿurūj and aʿrāj. Ṭarafa said, in a line of verse:
On the day the white women show their legs, and the horses wind about the droves of cattle.

And it is said: al-ʿarj is a hundred and fifty. And this root can be joined to the first, because the owner of it halts by it and is content with it.

And the third root: al-ʿurūj is the ascent. One says ʿaraja yaʿruju ʿurūjan and maʿrajan. And al-maʿraj is the place of ascent. God, exalted be He, said: {the angels and the Spirit ascend to Him} [al-Maʿārij: 4]. As for the saying of the one who said, in a line of verse:
Until, when the sun had a mind to ʿaraj,

they said: he meant the setting of the sun. And this, though it be sound, is not clearly set out in the explanation; the meaning is only that when it set, it was as though it had climbed to the sky, that is, gone up. And of what supports this is the saying of the other, in a line of verse:
And the towers of the sun sent the night climbing.

So this is the sound sense.
عرد:
The letters ʿayn, rā' and dāl are two sound roots: one indicates strength and hardness, the other indicates turning aside and swerving.

The first: al-ʿard is anything hard and strong.

A poet said, in a line of verse: firm-collarboned, thick-set, tightly coiled.

One says: 'ʿarada nābu al-baʿīr yaʿrudu ʿurūdan' — the camel's tusk 'ʿarada,' when it came out, grew strong, and stood upright.

Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse: they [the mounts] raise dappled [tusks] among bow-legged [camels], as though the glass-bright heads of the spears among them were rising and standing tall — 'al-najīm' meaning that which is rising and appearing.

As for the other root, it is al-taʿrīd: abandoning one's intended course. Its basis is their saying 'ʿaradat al-shajaratu taʿrudu ʿurūdan' — the tree shot out [a branch, turning aside from its line].

Labīd said, in a line of verse on turning aside: so he went on and led her forward, and it was his habit, whenever she swerved away (ʿarradat), to press her onward.

Another said, in a line of verse: al-Jawzāʾ [the constellation] meant to turn away.

Among what falls outside these two roots is al-ʿarād, a kind of tree. And al-ʿarāda is said to be the female locust. God knows best what is correct.
عرز:
The letters ʿayn, rāʾ and zāʾ are a sound root indicating stubborn resistance and a drawing-in/contraction. Al-Khalīl said: istaʿraza ʿalayya is like istaṣʿaba, it resisted me stubbornly. What he said is sound, and its proof is the saying of al-Shammākh: "And every friend who does not humble himself for the sake of a friend's bond is either cutting [it off] or drawing back [muʿāriz]." He meant: the one drawing back from him.

The Arabs say: 'al-iʿtirāz is al-iḥtirāz' [drawing-in is caution], meaning: the contraction is the prompting cause of caution. They warn against over-familiarity and excessive exposure of oneself, for that may sometimes lead to something disliked. And it is said al-ʿarz is blame and reproach, in al-Shammākh's line, and it comes back to what we have mentioned.
عرزال:
What the lion gathers in its den, something it spreads out for its cubs, like a nest.

1. The hunter's ʿirzāl — his worn-out garments and their rags, which he spreads out and lies upon in the hunting-blind. He said:
He does not tire of spreading out the lairs.
2. Al-ʿirzāl is also said to be what is gathered of dried meat in his hunting-blind.

This is a blend formed from two words: from ʿazala and ʿaraza — yaʿziluhu wa yaʿrizuhu, meaning he gathers it, just as I have said aʿraza, when it contracted and drew together.
عرس:
The letters ʿayn, rāʾ and sīn are a single sound root to which all its branches return, and it is staying-close/attachment. Al-Khalīl said: ʿarisa bihi, when he clung to it/stayed attached to it.

Among the branches of this root: al-ʿirs, a man's wife, and [also] the lioness of the lion. Imruʾ al-Qays said: "You lied — indeed I may draw a man's own wife [ʿirsahu] to trifle with him, while I guard my own wife [ʿirsī] against any onlooker suspecting her." And it is said that a man and his wife are called ʿirsān; and they cite as evidence ʿAlqamah's line: "a nest for two mates [ʿirsayn], in which the eggs lie heaped."

A man is ʿarūs among men who are ʿurus, and a woman is ʿarūs among women who are ʿarāʾis and ʿurus. He recited: "The tall she-camels dragged with them their trains, veiled all about, as the brides [al-ʿurus] drag the garments of saffron-dyed cloth." Al-Khalīl claimed that al-ʿarūs is a description applying to both man and woman alike, on the pattern faʿūl, and the two are equal in it so long as they remain in their ʿarūs-state for some days, once one of them has consummated the marriage with the other [ʿarrasa]. It is better still to say of the man muʿris, meaning he has taken a bride. The Arabs make al-ʿurs feminine. The rajaz-poet said: "We found the bride [ʿurus] of the grain-seller to be blameworthy, base of guardian." And he said of al-muʿris: "He walks — when the boy takes hold of his head — a walk like the walk of the half-breed muʿris."

Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ said: one says aʿrasa al-rajul bi-ahlihi, when he consummated the marriage with her — yuʿrisu iʿrāsan; and ʿarrasa yuʿarrisu taʿrīsan. And sometimes they broadened it to use for intercourse itself: taʿrīs and iʿrās. And one says: taʿarrasa al-rajul li-imraʾatihi, meaning he showed her affection. Yūnus said: this points to the analogy we have drawn. And ʿarisa al-ṣabiyy bi-ummihi, yaʿrasu, on the pattern ʿalima yaʿlamu, said of a child devoted to and clinging to his mother; and likewise ʿarisa al-rajul bi-ṣāḥibihi. Al-Muʿaqqir said: "And he has grown attached [ʿarisa] to staying put and settling down."

And al-Khalīl mentioned: ʿarisa yaʿrasu ʿarasan, when he grew reckless with pride; it is also said, rather, [it means] he grew weary and gave up. This is only sound if carried on the analogy we have mentioned, namely that he grows attached to one thing away from another. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: ʿarisat al-kilāb ʿan al-thawr, meaning they grew reckless and gave up on the bull. And this, by what we have said, is as though they were occupied with something else and grew attached to it instead.

Yaʿqūb said: al-ʿirs among men is the one who does not leave the fight, like al-ḥils. Others said: a man is ʿaris maris [a fixture in battle]. From this chapter: al-ʿirrīs, the lion's lair, in a thicket of trees and groves, in the most tangled part of it. As for Jarīr's line: "my dense thicket [ajamī] is among them, and my lair [ʿirrīsī]" — he means the place where his own roots are set among his people. It is said ʿirrīs and ʿirrīsah. And the Arabs say, among their proverbs: "like one seeking game in the lion's lair [ʿirrīsat al-asad]."

From this chapter: al-taʿrīs, the halting of travelers on a journey in the last part of the night — they lie down for a stop, then set off again. We said of this: even if their stop is brief, it is still carried on the analogy we mentioned, because they must, of necessity, stay for a while. Zuhayr said: "And they halted [ʿarrasū] a while among the sand-hills of Asnumah, and among them, at al-Qasūmiyyāt, was a battle-place." And Dhū al-Rummah said: "Halting [muʿarrisan] in the whiteness of dawn was his stop, and all the rest of the journey, but for that, was driven straight on."

From this chapter: ʿarastu al-baʿīr, aʿrisuhu ʿarsan, which is to tie its neck together with its two forelegs while it is kneeling. This too goes back to what we have said.

Close to this chapter is al-muʿarras, that for which an ʿars [partition] has been made — a wall set between the two walls of the house, not reaching all the way to its far end, then the roof-beam is laid from the inner edge of that partition to the far end of the house, and the whole house is roofed.

Among their proverbs: "There is no hiding-place for perfume after the bride [ʿarūs]" — its origin is that a man married a woman, and when he consummated the marriage with her he found her unscented, so he said to her, "Where is the perfume?" She said, "I hid it away!" So he said: "There is no hiding-place for perfume after the bride."
عرش:
The letters ʿayn, rā' and shīn are one sound root pointing to height in something built, and then it is borrowed for other things. Of that is al-ʿarsh. Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿarsh is the king's throne. And this is sound. God, exalted is He, said: {And he raised his parents up upon the throne} [Yūsuf: 100].

Then that was borrowed, and a man's affair and the prop of it was called ʿarsh; and when that goes from him it is said thulla ʿarshuhu, his throne has been pulled down. Zuhayr said, in a line of verse:
You two came up with the Aḥlāf when their throne had been pulled down, and with Dhubyān when the sandal slipped from under their feet.

And of the chapter: the trellising of the vine, because it is a raising of it and a making it firm. And al-ʿarīsh is a structure of branches raised and bound fast so that it gives shade. And it was said to the Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, on the day of Badr: Shall we not build you an ʿarīsh? And every building one takes shade under is ʿarsh and ʿarīsh. And the roof of a house is called ʿarsh. God, exalted is He, said: {So it is fallen in upon its roofs} [al-Ḥajj: 45]; and the sense is that the roof falls and then the walls come down crumbling upon it. And of the chapter is al-ʿarīsh, which is something like a camel-litter made for a woman to sit in on her camel. Ru'ba said, describing old age, in a line of verse:
If you see that time has bent me over crooked, as the two craftsmen bend the litter-frame into its curve.

And of what has come about the ʿarīsh also is al-Khansā's words, in a line of verse:
Abū Ḥassān was a shelter, now fallen empty, of what time had built, low-hanging and shady.

As for al-Ṭirimmāḥ's words, in a line of verse:
A little while she follows up an errand, then she was lifted onto every stout beast with trellised sides.

Some people said: he meant the ʿarīsh, which is the litter; and its two ḥaṣīr are its two sides. And it is said that al-maʿrūsh is the camel strong in the flanks.

And of the chapter: ʿarashtu al-karm and ʿarrashtuhu - I trellised the vine. One says iʿtarasha al-ʿinab, when the grapevine climbs up over the trellis. And it is said that al-ʿurūsh are tents of wood, the single one being ʿarīsh. And a poet said, in a line of verse:
Lying close in shelter within the coverts they have gone into.

Al-dawāmij means those that are gone into.

And of the chapter: the ʿarsh of the well is its lining with wood. Some of them said: the well may be crumbly at the bottom and at the top, so it does not hold the lining, because it is sandy; so its top is trellised with wood laid one piece upon another, and then the water-drawers stand on it and draw. And there was recited, in a line of verse:
And nothing is left of the standing-places of the well-frames when the props are drawn out from under the frames.

Al-mathāba is the top of the well where the drawer of water stands. And some of them said: al-ʿarsh is what is over the mouth of the well, on which the water-drawer stands. Al-Shammākh said, in a line of verse:
And when I saw the matter was a frame over a pit, I comforted the heart's needs with Shammar.

Al-huwiyya is the place from which whoever stands upon it falls down. And al-Khalīl said: when the ass mounts the herd of wild asses raising his head and gaping his mouth, it is said ʿarrasha bi-ʿānatihi taʿrīshan. And this is by the reasoning of the chapter, because of his raising his head.

And of the chapter is al-ʿursh, the ʿursh of the neck. There are two ʿurshān with the vertebrae between them, and in them are the two aḥdaʿ veins; and they are two long pieces of flesh along the length of the neck, that is, on the side of the neck. Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
And ʿAbd Yaghūth, with the birds hopping about him, the tempered sword having cut clean through the sides of his neck.

And some people claimed that they are ʿarshān, with a on the ʿayn. And al-ʿarsh in the foot is what lies between the ridge and the toes on the top of the foot, and the plural is ʿirasha. And several close sayings have been said about the two ʿurshān, which we did not care to lengthen this by mentioning. And it is said that the ʿarsh of al-Simāk is four stars below al-ʿAwwā', in the shape of a bier. And it is said they are the hindquarters of the Lion. Ibn Aḥmar said, in a line of verse:
A night of the ʿArsh stars passed over him, pressing hard with rain, and he passed it beside a crumbling sand-hill.

He is describing a wild bull. And his word shariyat means it kept on with the rain.
عرص:
The letters ʿayn, rāʾ and ṣād are two sound roots: one indicates one thing's casting shade over another, and the other indicates agitation/trembling. Al-Khalīl mentioned both analogies together.

Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿarṣ is a piece of wood laid crosswise over a house when it is to be roofed, and then the ends of [other] timbers are laid upon it. One says ʿarraṣtu al-saqf taʿrīṣan. What al-Khalīl said here is sound, except that al-ʿarṣ is really the roof [made] with that piece of wood together with the rest of what completes the roofing.

Al-Khalīl also said: al-ʿarrāṣ among clouds is that which casts shade from above and draws near until it becomes like a roof, and it never occurs without thunder and lightning. So al-Khalīl drew the same analogy we have mentioned, of casting shade, in both the roof and the cloud. And he recited: "He rests slowly in the shade of a shading cloud [ʿarrāṣ], and it is chased off by the rustle of a heavy-laden [cloud] whose trailing edge is pebble-strewn." Do you not see that he gave it a shade?

The other root indicates agitation. Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿarrāṣ is also said of clouds driven this way and that by the wind. He said: the origin of al-taʿrīṣ is agitation, and from it it is said: rumḥ ʿarrāṣ, a spear [described so] for its trembling when shaken. Abū ʿAmr said: it is also said of the sword, for its flashing and gleaming; and 'a spear ʿarrāṣ of shaft', and 'lightning ʿarrāṣ'. He said: "and every flashing one, quivering in its glimmer."

From this chapter: ʿarṣat al-dār, the open courtyard of the house, its middle; plural ʿarṣāt and ʿirāṣ. Jamīl said: "What makes you weep over the courtyards of a house whose time has grown old and whose ruin has drawn near?" It is said it was named ʿarṣah because it was a playground for children and a place where they gathered to run about however they wished. Al-Aṣmaʿī used to say: every open gap with no building in it is an ʿarṣah.

From this chapter: al-ʿaraṣ, which is liveliness. One says ʿariṣa, when he grew skittish/frisky. He said: and one says, ḥalabtuhā ḥalaban ka-ʿaraṣi al-hirrah, meaning her friskiness and liveliness and her playing with her paws. And iʿtaraṣa is like ʿaraṣa. He said: "When you frisk about like the frisking of the cat, you will soon fall into a pit." And Abū Zayd said: ʿaraṣat al-samāʾ, taʿriṣu ʿarṣan, when its lightning kept steady. And 'the sky spent the night ʿarrāṣah'. And one says: ghayth ʿarrāṣ, a downpour whose lightning does not still.

From this chapter: ʿariṣa al-bayt. He said: it is from a foulness of smell. And this, along with its foul smell, is because the smell does not stay fixed in a place, but agitates about. And from this: laḥm muʿarraṣ — some said it is meat that still has some rawness in it, not yet fully cooked. He recited: "A half-raw meat [muʿarraṣ] will spare you the people's blow, and the water of pots, mixed, in the bowls."
عرصاف:
al-ʿarṣāf is the long, drawn-out tendon.

1. al-ʿarāṣīf — pegs that join the heads of the curved wood-pieces of a pack-saddle.

This is a word in which the ʿayn was added; it is really from raṣaftu (I bound together), and from al-riṣāf, which is the tendon-wrapping — and this has already been explained.
عرصم: the strong man, firm of flesh. This is from al-ʿaraṣ, which is liveliness. One also says al-ʿirṣimm, and its derivation is the same.
عرض:
The letters ʿayn, rā' and ḍād are a structure whose branches are many, and for all their number they go back to a single root, which is al-ʿarḍ, breadth, the opposite of length. Whoever looks into it closely and carefully will know the soundness of what we say, and we have explained that with a sufficient explanation.

So al-ʿarḍ is the opposite of length. From it you say ʿaruḍa al-shay' yaʿruḍu ʿiraḍan — the thing was broad — so it is ʿarīḍ, broad.

Abū Zayd said: ʿaruḍa ʿarāḍatan. And he recited, in a line of verse:
When the people race one another to noble deeds, the breadth of Ibn Laylā's character, and its length, overcome them.

And a qaws ʿurāḍa is a broad bow. And aʿraḍat al-mar'a awlādahā — she bore her children broad — as one says aṭālat of length.

And of this chapter: ʿaraḍa al-matāʿ yaʿriḍuhu ʿarḍan — he displayed the goods; and it is as though in doing so he had shown its breadth. And ʿarraḍa al-shay' taʿrīḍan — he made it broad.

And of that is ʿarḍ al-jund, the review of troops: that you make them pass before you, and that is as though you looked at the breadth of their state. And what is reviewed in that way is called ʿaraḍ, with the middle letter vowelled, as one says qabaḍa qabaḍan and, he has thrown it into the qabaḍ. And ʿaraḍūhum ʿalā al-sayf ʿarḍan — they put them to the sword — as though the sword took the whole breadth of the people so that not one of them escaped it. And ʿaraḍtu al-ʿūd ʿalā al-inā' aʿruḍuhu, with u on the rā', when you lay it across it crosswise. And in the hadith: 'Why did you not cover it, even with a stick laid across it?' And in other senses one says ʿaraḍa yaʿriḍu, with i on the rā'. And mā ʿaraḍtu li-fulān, and lā taʿriḍ lahu, do not cross him; and that is that you set your breadth against his breadth. And one says ʿaraḍa al-rumḥ yaʿriḍuhu ʿarḍan, he held the spear crosswise. Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
They have a habit with them that they know well: when they lay the Khaṭṭī spears across the withers.

And ʿaraḍa al-faras fī ʿadwihi ʿarḍan — the horse ran side-on, as though he showed the onlooker his breadth. He said, in a line of verse:
He runs side-on until he stretches out his muzzle.
They said: this is when he runs turning his chest sideways, or with his head leaning over.

And one says ʿaraḍa fulān min silʿatihi, when he bartered with it, gave one thing and took another. And from it, in a line of verse:
Have you a mind to it? For the one who barters with you gets a return from you.
That is: he barters with you, taking something from you and giving you something.

And one says ʿaraḍtu aʿwādan baʿḍahā ʿalā baʿḍ — I laid sticks across one another — and iʿtaraḍat hiya, they lay crosswise. Abū Du'ād said, in a line of verse:
You see the feathers in its hollow floating, like your laying of blade across blade.
He is describing water: some of the feathers lie crosswise over others, as one blade lies across another like a cross.

And one says ʿaraḍtu lahu min ḥaqqihi thawban fa-anā aʿriḍuhu, when a man had a claim on him and he gave him a garment for it, as though he set the breadth of this against the breadth of the right that was his. And one says aʿyā fa-iʿtaraḍa ʿalā al-baʿīr — he grew tired and lay across the camel.

And al-Khalīl mentioned: aʿraḍtu al-shay' — I made it broad. And the Arabs say: 'aʿraḍta al-qirfa'; and some of them used to say 'aʿraḍta al-furqa', and perhaps that is the better. That is said of a man who is asked, whom do you suspect? and he says, I suspect the Banū so-and-so, meaning the whole tribe. So it is said to him: aʿraḍta al-qirfa — that is, you have brought a broad accusation that crosses the whole tribe.

And of this chapter: aʿraḍtu ʿan fulān — I turned away from so-and-so — and aʿraḍtu ʿan hādhā al-amr, and aʿraḍa bi-wajhihi. And this is the sense we mentioned, because when he is so he turns his broad side toward him. And al-ʿāriḍ is derived only from al-ʿarḍ, which is the opposite of length. And one says aʿraḍa laka al-shay' min baʿīd, so it is muʿriḍ, and that is when it appears and shows itself to you; and the sense is that you saw its breadth. ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm said, in a line of verse:
And al-Yamāma showed broad and towered up, like swords in the hands of men drawing them.

[And] you say ʿāraḍtu fulānan fī al-sayr, when you travelled level with him. And ʿāraḍtuhu mithla mā ṣanaʿa, when you do to him the like of what he did to you. And from it muʿāraḍa is derived. And this is the reasoning, as though the breadth of the thing he does were like the breadth of the thing that was done to him. And Ṭufayl said, in a line of verse:
And I rode level with her at an easy pace, on a horse of steady stride, great in the short ribs, outstripping his own stock, curved of hock.

And one says iʿtaraḍa fī al-amr fulān, when he puts himself into it. And ʿāraḍtu fulānan fī al-ṭarīq, and ʿāraḍtuhu bi-l-kitāb, and iʿtaraḍtu uʿṭī man aqbala wa-adbara — I went broadside, giving to whoever came and went. And this is the reasoning. And iʿtaraḍa fulān ʿirḍ fulān yaqaʿu fīhi — he set upon so-and-so's honour, slandering him — that is, he does a deed that takes the breadth of his honour. And iʿtaraḍa al-faras, when he does not go straight for the one leading him. Al-Ṭirimmāḥ said, in a line of verse:
The King has shown me my right way, though once I was a man of rough pride and of swerving aside.

And taʿarraḍa lī fulān with what I hate. And a rajul ʿirrīḍ is one who is always crossing others.

And of this chapter: istaʿraḍa al-Khawārij al-nās, when they did not care whom they killed. And in the hadith: 'Eat cheese ʿurḍan' — that is, take it crosswise however it is and do not ask about it. And this is as we said about the iʿrāḍ of accusation. And al-muʿriḍ is the one who crosses people's path taking loans from whoever he can. And from it is the hadith of ʿUmar: 'Truly the little Usayfiʿ of Juhayna has taken on debt as a muʿriḍ.'

And of this chapter is al-ʿirḍ, a person's honour. Some people said: it is his ancestry. Others said: it is his own self. And whichever of the two it is, it is from the ʿarḍ we have mentioned.

As for their saying that al-ʿirḍ is a person's smell, whether sweet or not sweet, this is by way of extension, because since it came from his ʿirḍ it was called ʿirḍ. And his words, may God bless him and his family and give them peace: 'It is only sweat running from their aʿrāḍ' — that is, their bodies — point to the soundness of this. And they argued that al-ʿirḍ is the self from the words of Ḥassān, praising the Messenger of God, blessing and peace be upon him, in two lines of verse:
You have lampooned Muhammad, and I have answered for him, and with God is the reward for that.
My father and my mother and my own self are a shield for Muhammad's honour against you.

And you say huwa naqiyy al-ʿirḍ — that is, far from being reviled or faulted.

And of this chapter: maʿārīḍ al-kalām, the hinting turns of speech; and that is because it comes out in a wrapping other than its plain wording, so this wrapping is made for it like the wrapping of a slave-girl, which is the dress she is displayed in; and that is derived from al-ʿarḍ. And we have said enough about the reasoning of al-ʿarḍ.

And some people claimed that the Arabs say ʿaraftu dhāka fī ʿarūḍ kalāmihi — that is, in the hinting turns of his speech.

And of this chapter is al-ʿarḍ, the great army; and this is by way of likening it to the ʿarḍ of cloud, which is what blocks the horizon with its breadth. He said, in a line of verse:
We used to, when we led an ʿarḍ against a people —
that is, an army like a mountain or a cloud blocking the horizon. And Durayd said, in a line of verse:
News of death from a raiding-party, or the broad front of an army that the gaps of the earth are too narrow for, thick-massed.

And Ibn al-A'rābī used to say: al-aʿrāḍ are the mountains, the valleys and the clouds; the singular is ʿirḍ. So he said, with i on the ʿayn; and it is related from him also with a. And Abū ʿUbayda said: al-ʿarḍ is the side of the mountain. And he recited, in a line of verse:
Do you not see, on every broad slope that shows itself —
And al-Aṣmaʿī recited, in a line of verse:
As the boulders roll down from the mountain-side.

And al-ʿarīḍ is the kid when it mounts [or] is near to mounting, and that is when it has come of age. And the reasoning of this too is the reasoning of the chapter, and it is from al-ʿarḍ; its plural is ʿurḍān.

As for the ʿarūḍ of poetry, some people said it is derived from al-ʿarūḍ, which is the side or quarter, as though it were a quarter of knowledge. And he recited concerning al-ʿarūḍ, in a line of verse:
Every people of Maʿadd has a clan, a quarter they take refuge in, and a flank.

And others said: al-ʿarīḍ is the difficult road, and that is on the flank of a mountain, so its chapter has come back to the reasoning of the rest of the chapter. They said: and this is from their saying nāqa ʿurḍiyya, when she is difficult. And the meaning of this is that she does not go straight in travelling but goes crosswise. The poet said, in a line of verse:
And I gave her my word while on a wayward, unbroken mare; I soothe her rancour with gentleness.

And of this chapter: ʿurḍ al-ḥā'iṭ, and ʿurḍ al-māl, and ʿurḍ al-nahr, and by it the middle is meant. And that is from al-ʿarḍ also. And Labīd said, in a line of verse:
So the two went down into the middle of the stream and split a brimming water whose qullām plants grew close together.

And ʿurḍ al-māl is of that, and all of it is the middle. And al-Liḥyānī used to say: so-and-so is shadīd al-ʿāriḍa — that is, of the side, the quarter. And al-ʿaraḍ among the happenings of time, such as illness and the like, is called ʿaraḍ because it crosses one — that is, it takes hold of him in whatever part of his body it comes across. And al-ʿaraḍ is the greed of this world, little [or] much. And it was so called because it yuʿriḍ — that is, it shows you its breadth. And he said, in a line of verse:
Whoever hopes for a permanence that has no ending, let not the goods of this world be a grief to him.

And they say: 'This world is a ready ʿaraḍ; the righteous and the wicked both take from it.' As for his words, may God bless him and his family and give them peace: 'Wealth is not in the abundance of al-ʿarḍ' — we heard it only with the rā' unvowelled, and it is everything of property that is not coin; and its plural is ʿurūḍ. As for al-ʿaraḍ, with a on the rā', it is what a person gets of his share of this world. God, exalted be He, said: {And if goods like it come to them, they take them} [al-A'rāf: 169].

And al-Khalīl said: so-and-so is an ʿurḍa for people — they never stop falling upon him. And the sense of that is that they cross his breadth. And al-miʿrāḍ is an arrow with four thin feathers, which when it is shot goes sideways. Al-Khalīl said: it is the arrow that is shot with no feather on it and goes crosswise.

As for their saying shadīd al-ʿāriḍa, we have mentioned what al-Liḥyānī said about it. And al-Khalīl said: he is shadīd al-ʿāriḍa — that is, a man of endurance and resolve. And the two senses are close: that is, what comes at people from him is hard. And ʿāriḍat al-wajh is what shows of the face when one laughs. And he claimed that a woman's teeth are called al-ʿawāriḍ; and the reasoning in all of that is one. ʿAntara said, in a line of verse:
And as though a merchant's musk-pouch in a scented box had gone ahead of her side-teeth to you from her mouth.

And a man khafīf al-ʿāriḍayn, meaning the two sides of the beard. And Abū Laylā said: al-ʿawāriḍ are the laughing teeth, for their place in the breadth of the face. Ibn al-A'rābī said: a man's ʿāriḍān are the hair of his two cheeks; one does not say to a beardless youth, wipe your ʿāriḍayn. As for their saying yamshī al-ʿiraḍnā, the nūn in it is added, and it is of one who goes off in his running crosswise. Al-ʿAjjāj said, in a line of verse:
Their horses run sideways, in bands.

And a woman ʿurḍa is bulky, one whose fat has gone into breadth.

Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿawāriḍ are the broad roof-slats of the camel-litter whose ends rest on the two side-pieces, and all of that together is the roof of the litter. And likewise the ʿawāriḍ of a house-roof, when they are laid crosswise. And he also said: the ʿāriḍa of a door is the beam that holds the two doorposts from above. And al-ʿarḍī is a kind of cloth, and perhaps it has breadth. Abū Nukhayla said, in a line of verse:
She swayed a figure that strains the ʿarḍī cloth, as the south wind shakes the choice palm-tree.

And everything that gives you a chance at its broad side is muʿriḍ to you, with i on the rā'. And one says aʿraḍa laka al-ẓaby fa-irmihi — the gazelle has offered you its flank, so shoot it — when it gives you a chance at its breadth; like afqara and aʿwara.

And of their proverbs: 'so-and-so is ʿarīḍ al-biṭān', broad of belly-girth, when he has grown rich and his wealth is much. And one says ḍaraba al-faḥl al-nāqa ʿirāḍan, when he covers her without being led to her. And this is from our saying iʿtaraḍa al-shay' — he came at it from the side, as though he came upon her crosswise out of the rest of the she-camels. Al-Rāʿī said, in a line of verse:
Choice she-camels that are got with young only by a chance encounter, side-on, and are bought only at a high price.

And al-Liḥyānī said: laqiḥat al-nāqa ʿirāḍan — that is, she went to a stallion she was not led to. And al-ʿāriḍ is the cloud, and the mention of its reasoning has already passed. God, exalted be He, said: {They said: this is a cloud bringing us rain} [al-Aḥqāf: 24]. And the ʿāriḍ of anything is what comes to meet you, like the ʿāriḍ of cloud and the like. And Abū ʿUbayda said: the ʿāriḍ of cloud is that which shows itself in one quarter of the sky in the evening and then in the morning has spread and levelled out. And it is called al-ʿānn, with doubling.

And of what is derived from this is their saying: a ʿāriḍ of locusts passed by me, when it filled the horizon. And so-and-so has ʿurḍiyya against his enemies — that is, hardness. And this is from our saying nāqa ʿurḍiyya, whose reasoning has been mentioned. And it is said that al-taʿrīḍ is what is carried on the backs of camels of provision or food-supply. And this is derived from its being offered to whoever may need it. And one says ʿarriḍū min mīratikum — that is, feed us from it. He said, in a line of verse:
A red one, of those that offer the crows their fill.
He is describing a she-camel of his that carries the provision; she goes ahead of the camels, and what is on her comes open from her speed, so the crows alight on her loads — as though she offered the crows their provision.

And the camels whose tracks show far in the ground are called al-ʿurāḍāt — that is, they take the ground crosswise so that their tracks show plain. And they say: 'When Sirius rises in the hot season and you see no rain in it, then send out the broad-treading camels on the trail; they will seek you out a place to live in the land.'

And one says nāqa ʿurḍa li-l-safar — that is, strong for it. And the sense of this is that for her strength she is always set out for travel. As for al-ʿāriḍa among she-camels or sheep, it is the one slaughtered because of something that befalls her. And he said, in a line of verse:
Of roast meat, not from an ailing beast, in the hands of every open-handed man with spoil to give.

And this, in our view, is of the sort in which the active is put in the place of the passive, because the ʿāriḍa is the one that illness has come upon, as they say sirr kātim. And the meaning of ʿuriḍa lahā is that the illness crossed her; and they widened this until they built the verb attributed to her, so they said ʿaraḍat. The poet said, in a line of verse:
When a fat, full-grown she-camel of them falls sick, give none of her away: cut off strips and store the fat.

And al-ʿirḍ is the valley; and al-ʿIrḍ is a valley in al-Yamāma. Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
Have you not seen that al-ʿIrḍ's floor has become palms and growing crops and lucerne?
And al-Mutalammis said, in a line of verse:
This is the season of al-ʿIrḍ: its flies are alive, its hornets, and the blue one that keeps searching.

And of this chapter: naẓartu ilayhi ʿarḍ ʿayn — that is, I set him crosswise before my eye. And ra'aytu fulānan ʿarḍ ʿayn — that is, a glance. And the sense of this is that he crossed my eye and I saw him. And one says ʿaliqtu fulānan ʿaraḍan — that is, by a crossing, with no preparing for it on my part and no wanting it. And this is on what we mentioned of the chance covering of the camel and the she-camel. And he recited, in a line of verse:
I came to love her by chance, while I kill her people — a claim, by your father's life, that is no claim to be made.

And one says aṣābahu sahm ʿaraḍ — a stray arrow struck him — when it comes to him from where he does not know who shot it. And this too is of the chapter, as though it came to him crosswise from where he was not aimed at, as we mentioned about the miʿrāḍ among arrows.

And al-maʿāriḍ is the plural of maʿraḍ, and they are lands in which livestock are put out to graze. He said, in a line of verse:
I say to my two companions, when we had gone down and left the grazing-grounds and the hill-slopes behind us.
عرف:
The letters ʿayn, rā' and fā' are two sound roots: one of them points to a thing following on, joined part to part, and the other to stillness and calm.

The first is al-ʿurf, the horse's mane. And it was so called for the hair following on one after another upon it. And one says: the sand-grouse came ʿurfan ʿurfan — that is, one behind another.

And of this chapter is al-ʿurfa, whose plural is ʿuraf, and it is a long stretch of raised ground between two soft plains, bearing plants, as though it were a horse's mane. And of the poetry on that . . .

And the other root is al-maʿrifa and al-ʿirfān, knowing. You say ʿarafa fulān fulānan ʿirfānan wa-maʿrifatan. And this is a well-known matter. And this points to what we said of his settling toward it, because whoever does not know a thing shies away from it and turns from it.

And of this chapter is al-ʿarf, which is the sweet smell. And it is the reasoning, because the soul settles toward it. One says: how sweet is his ʿarf. God, glorified and exalted be He, said: {and He will admit them to the Garden, having made it known to them} [Muhammad: 6] — that is, He made it sweet for them. He said, in a line of verse:
How many a day I have spent in play, and a night, with a bright-cheeked woman of sweet scent.
And al-ʿurf is kindness, and it was so called because souls settle toward it. Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
God has refused all but His justice and His faithfulness; so no wrong is counted good, and no kindness is wasted.

As for al-ʿarīf, al-Khalīl said: he is the one who takes charge of a people's affair, having been made ʿarīf over them. He said: and he was called ʿarīf only because he is known by it. And it is said: rather al-ʿirāfa is like a governorship, and it seems he was so called so that he might know their states.

As for ʿArafāt, some people said: it was so named because Adam and Eve, peace be upon them, came to know one another there. And others said: rather it was so named because when Gabriel, peace be upon him, taught Abraham, peace be upon him, the rites of the pilgrimage, he said to him: have you understood? And some people said: rather it was so named because it is a hallowed, honoured place, as though it had been made sweet, as we mentioned about His words, exalted be He: {and He will admit them to the Garden, having made it known to them} [Muhammad: 6]. And the standing at ʿArafāt is a taʿrīf. And al-taʿrīf is the announcing of a stray beast or a found thing, that one says: who knows this? And one says iʿtarafa bi-l-shay', when he confesses, as though he made it known and then admitted it. And one says: the soul is ʿarūf, when it is put to a matter and it accepts it — that is, it grows calm. And he said, in a line of verse:
So they came back with the women mounted behind them, submissive, after seclusion and shelter.
It is from al-wijāḥ, which is the screen.

And al-ʿārif is the patient one. One says: a misfortune struck him and he was found ʿarūf — that is, patient. Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
On mares patient for the thrusting, grim-faced, with wounds upon them, some bleeding and some crusted over.
عرق:
The letters ʿayn, rāʾ and qāf are four sound roots: one, a thing that is generated out of another thing, like dew and seepage and the like of it; the second, a thing that has a root-stock [sinkh], its root-stock being measured by this chapter; the third, the scraping of a thing off another thing, which hardly occurs except with flesh; the fourth, a lining-up and a following-in-succession among things. Derivation is then made from all these origins and from what is close to them.

The first: al-ʿaraq, which is what flows at the roots of the hair from the water of the skin [sweat]. One says: ʿariqa yaʿraqu ʿaraqan. He said: I have not heard a plural for al-ʿaraq, but if it were made plural its analogy would be aʿrāq, like jamal and ajmāl. A man much given to sweating is ʿuraqah. And one says istaʿraqa, when he exposed himself to heat so as to sweat.

From this chapter: the horse ran a ʿaraq or two ʿaraqs, meaning a full course or two full courses [ṭalaq], and that too is from al-ʿaraq. One says: ʿarriq farasaka, meaning run it until it sweats [tataʿarraq].
