Al-Aʿshā said: "The saddlecloth is lifted from him every evening, and he throws off the weariness of the morning and is made to sweat." And it is said: milk is ʿaraq, seeping in the veins until it reaches the udder. Al-Shammākh said: "It goes forth at morning, its udders already laden with sweetness [ʿaraqan], of sweet taste, abundant, untiring." And milk that is ʿariq is milk put into a skin and tied against the camel's flank, so that sweat [ʿaraq] reaches it and it spoils.

As for ʿaraq al-qirbah in the saying 'jashimtu ilayka ʿaraqa al-qirbah' [I strained myself for you the sweat of the waterskin] — its meaning, as Yūnus claimed, is: the gift of the waterskin, that is, its water; as though he were saying: I strained myself for you until I journeyed and had need of the waterskin's water on the road. And one says: ʿariqa lahu bi-kadhā, as though he grew moist/generous toward him and was open-handed. He said: "I shall set it in place of the sword upon me, though I was given for it no waterskin's yielding [ʿaraq al-khilāl]." meaning: I was not given it out of affection, but I took it by force; and al-nūn here is the sword. Some said: jashimtu ilayka ḥattā ʿariqtu ka-ʿaraqi al-qirbah, meaning: the flowing of its water. Others said: ʿaraq al-qirbah means to say, 'I undertook for you what no one else reaches, until I strained myself with what does not [normally] happen' — for the waterskin does not [truly] sweat — going by the way of their saying 'until the crow turns grey [i.e. never].' Al-Aṣmaʿī used to say: ʿaraq al-qirbah is a phrase indicating hardship, and I do not know what its origin is. And Ibn Abī Ṭarafah said: one says 'I met from so-and-so ʿaraq al-qirbah,' meaning hardship. He said: and al-Aḥmar recited: "It is no cause for reproach to be counted, and its pardon is [as light as] the sweat of the waterskin [ʿaraq al-siqāʾ] upon a worn-out riding-camel." He is praising a man who hears the harsh word and does not take its speaker to task for it.

From this chapter: ʿarraqtu fī al-dalw, said when [the water drawn] is less than a full bucket, as though this, for its scantness, were likened to sweat. And a scant giver is said to have ʿarraqa. He said: "Do not fill the bucket, but give sparingly [ʿarriq] in it — do you not see the drought of those it waters?" And one says: kaʾs muʿraqah, a cup not filled, with some left in it; and khamr muʿraqah, wine lightly mixed, that light mixing being likened to sweat. And he said of a lightly mixed cup: "I took hold of his head and warded off from him, with a lightly-mixed cup [muʿraqah], the reproach of any who would reproach."

The second origin: the branching root-stock. From it: al-ʿirq, the root of a tree. The ʿurūq of anything are the cords branching out from its base. The Arabs say: 'May God root out their ʿirqāt [utterly]' — they claim the tāʾ is opened; then they differed over its meaning: some said they meant a single [feminine noun] and gave it the form of siʿlāh; others said, rather, it is the tāʾ of the feminine plural, but lightened with a fatḥah. And one says: aʿraqat al-shajarah, when the tree's roots struck deep and spread through the ground.

From this chapter: ʿaraqa al-rajul, yaʿruqu ʿurūqan, when he went off into the land — this by way of comparison, his going likened to the spreading and reaching of a tree's roots through the ground.

As for his saying — God bless him and his family and grant him peace —: "Whoever revives dead land, it is his, and there is no right for an unjust root [ʿirq ẓālim]" — this is a proverb-like saying. The scholars said: roots are of four kinds: two visible and two hidden. The visible ones are planting and building; the hidden ones are the well and the mine. And the meaning of the 'unjust root' is that a man comes to land already revived by another before him, and plants something in it or brings about some change by which he claims a right to the land.

Al-ʿirq is also a yellow plant. Among their proverbs: 'So-and-so is deep-rooted [muʿriq] in nobility,' meaning he has in it a root and a stock. And his paternal and maternal uncles have been rooted in him [ʿarraqa fīhi taʿrīqan], and aʿraqū fīhi aʿrāqan. And 'the roots of slaves have taken hold in him [aʿraqa fīhi]', when that has mixed into him and he has taken on their character. And one says: taḍārakahu aʿrāq khayrin wa-aʿrāq sharrin, good and bad strains have overtaken him. The poet said: "He ran a clear course, until, when it was said 'a winner!', an ill strain [iʿrāq sawʾ] overtook him and he fell behind."

Al-ʿarīq among horses and men is the one who has a root in nobility. And 'so-and-so yuʿāriqu so-and-so' means he vies with him in boasting, and its meaning is that he says: our root is the nobler. And one says: 'a root among the daughters of Ṣaʿdah' — these being the domestic donkeys. And the saying of ʿIkrāsh ibn Dhuʾayb, 'I brought him camels as though they were the roots of al-arṭā' — he meant that they were red-brown, for the roots of the arṭā-shrub are red-brown, and red-brown camels are the choicest of them. He said: "It stirs up [the ground] and reveals roots as though they were the reins of a hardened [leather-worker], drawn tight and scraped." He is describing a bull digging out a burrow beneath an arṭā-shrub.

The third origin: scraping the flesh off a bone. Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿurāq is a bone from which the flesh has been taken. He said: "So throw to your dog, from it, a stripped bone [ʿurāqan]." When the bone still has its flesh on it, it is ʿarq. It is said al-ʿurāq is the plural of ʿaraq, as one says ẓiʾr and ẓuʾār. And it is said in the proverb: "He is baser than a dog over a bone [ʿarq]." Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: the plural of ʿarq is ʿirāq. And he recited: "My guest spends the night amid smooth bones [ʿirāq], and amid a wine exposed to the ill-wind." Muls means the fat and grease. Al-naḥs is the wind. One says: ʿaraqtu al-ʿaẓm, aʿruquhu, and iʿtaraqtuhu and taʿarraqtuhu, when you ate what flesh was on it. And one says: aʿṭinī ʿarqan ataʿarraquhu, meaning a bone with flesh on it. And so-and-so is muʿtaraq, meaning emaciated, as though his flesh had been stripped away [uʿturiqa]. He said: "A wolf lying in wait for a swift, gaunt one [muʿtariq]." And he said: "I have surely witnessed the wide-flung raid, borne by a lean, firm mare, stripped of flesh at the jaws [maʿrūqatu al-liḥyayn], swift-running." He is describing the horse for the scantness of flesh on its face, which is the more prized in it. Al-Kisāʾī said: a mouth that is muʿraq has little saliva; and a face that is maʿrūq has little flesh.

The fourth origin: extension and succession, in things following one after another. From it: al-ʿaraqah, plural ʿaraqāt, which is anything plaited or lined up in a row. When birds line up in the air they are called ʿaraqah, and likewise horses. Ṭufayl said: "As though it were, after they set off in a line [ʿaraq], a lion, drenched, prowling through the depth of night." And al-ʿaraqah is the woven strip of palm-leaf before it is made into a basket, and the basket itself is called ʿaraq for this reason; it is also said ʿaraqah. Abū Kabīr said: "We go forth at morning and leave in the battle-place whoever has fallen, and we lead on in the tying-cords [al-ʿaraqāt] whoever has not been killed." meaning: we take them captive and bind them with the ʿaraqāt, which are the plaited straps. And the tracks of lined-up horses are called ʿaraqah. Al-ʿaraqah is also a woven border stitched onto a length of cloth, the length of cloth being that of a tent. And Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: al-ʿaraqah is a group of horses or camels standing in a row.

As for ʿirāq al-mazādah and al-rāwiyah [the waterskin], it is the seam-stitching at its bottom, plural ʿuruq; and that, to us, belongs to what we have mentioned of extension and succession. Ibn Aḥmar said: "From one whose seam [ʿirāq] is fastened through its middle, its folding light, its waist drawn tight." And another said: "It laughs, showing something like the seam of an old waterskin [ʿirāq al-shannah]."

From this chapter: al-ʿirāq, which for al-Khalīl is the shore of the sea. And al-ʿIrāq [Iraq] was so named because it lies along the banks of the Tigris and the Euphrates, running continuously until it joins the sea. And al-ʿirāq in the speech of the Arabs is the shore of the sea along its length.

From this chapter too: al-ʿirāq, which is what surrounds the nail of flesh [the cuticle]. Al-Duraydī said: 'Al-ʿIrāq was named so because it hemmed in the land of the Arabs,' that is, it became like a rim around it. And it is related, from Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ, that al-ʿIrāq is taken from the roots of trees, these being the places where trees take root. Al-ʿIrāqān [the Two Iraqs] are Kūfah and Baṣrah. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: al-ʿirāq is every place of fertile pasture-land. Jarīr said: "We long for the moist ground of al-ʿIrq, since after you we found no ground like al-ʿIrq, nor any sands like the Sulān." And one says: aʿraqa al-rajul wa-ashʾama, meaning he went to al-ʿIrāq and to al-Shām. Al-Mumazzaq said: "If you go to Najd in defiance of you, and if you turn toward Yemen bearing evil with you, I shall go to al-ʿIrāq."

As for ʿurqūwat al-dalw, it is the piece of wood laid crosswise over the bucket.
عرقوب:
A sinew drawn taut behind the two ankle-bones. And I say ʿarqabtu al-dābba, I cut the animal's hamstring [ʿurqūb]. Here the rāʾ has been added; the origin is al-ʿaqib, the heel, for a human being alone, and afterward al-ʿurqūb was applied to it and to other creatures too. Al-ʿurqūb is also used figuratively: a sharp bend in a valley, with a hard twist in it, is called an ʿurqūb. He said:
And many a fearsome, deserted watering-place ... with treacherous bends, foul and long stagnant.
Al-Khalīl said: the ʿarāqīb of a matter are its tangles, meaning the confusion introduced into it. And people cite as a proverb: "A day shorter than the hamstring of the sandgrouse."
عرك:
The letters ʿayn, rāʾ and kāf are a single sound root indicating that, and the like of it, from the working of one thing against another, or its rubbing against it. Al-Khalīl said: ʿaraktu al-adīm ʿarkan, when I rubbed the leather with a rubbing. And ʿaraktu al-qawm fī al-ḥarb ʿarkan [I ground down the people in war]. Zuhayr said: "And it will grind you down [taʿruk] as the millstone grinds with its base, and conceive by force and then bear and bring forth twins."

From this chapter: iʿtaraka al-qawm fī al-qitāl, which is the mutual rubbing of some of them against others and the grinding of some against others, and that place is muʿtarak and muʿtarakah. Al-Khalīl said: a man is ʿarik and a people are ʿarikūn, meaning they are fierce in wrestling.

From this chapter too — though it has been augmented in its letters seeking an addition to its meaning — is their saying ʿarakrak, meaning thick, powerful, enduring. He said: "Do not attend the watering-place with just anyone, save one broad of shoulder, sturdy — a thickset one [ʿarakrak] who fills the beholder's eye." And one says: a man is ʿarik, meaning steadfast, never leaving the fight. And the ʿarīkah of the camel is its hump, because the load rubs against it [yaʿrukuhu]. Dhū al-Rummah said: "Light of step, their humps [al-ʿarāʾik] pressed close [to the ground]." Muṭlanfiʾah means clinging close to the ground. And one says: a she-camel is ʿarūk, like al-lamūs, said when it has wool upon it so that its state cannot be seen beneath the wool until it is felt. And ʿaraktu al-shāh also, when I felt/palpated it. He said: a single time or two does not count as ʿark; that is only said when the palpating is thorough. And one says: laqītuhu ʿarakāt, meaning several times, and this is by way of figurative comparison with the repeated palpatings of ʿark.

Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿark is the rubbing of the elbow against the flank, from the chafing that occurs in a camel. Al-Ṭirimmāḥ said: "Scant of chafing [al-ʿark], its elbow-joints unblemished." As for their saying, 'he is lenient of disposition [layyin al-ʿarīkah]' — al-Khalīl said: so-and-so is layyin al-ʿarīkah when he has no stubbornness and is easy-natured. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: al-ʿarīkah is strength of spirit/temper. He said: "Days of hardship have schooled her, until her temperaments [ʿarāʾikuhā] have grown soft." Kharrajahā means: it refined her and trained her, as a person is trained; and all this goes back to what was said before about the ʿarīkah of the hump.

As for the sailors, they are called al-ʿarak; one says ʿarakiyy for a single one and ʿarak for the group, like ʿarabiyy and ʿarab. Zuhayr said: "The drivers cover them, with the roughness of the sand-dune, just as the sailors [al-ʿarak] cover the ships with the surging of the deep sea." They were called al-ʿarak only for their grinding contention [muʿārakah] with the water and the ships.

And one says: land that is maʿrūkah, when grazing animals have grazed it down [ʿarakathā] and eaten its plants.

From this chapter: al-ʿirāk at the watering-place. And one says: water that is maʿrūk, meaning crowded upon; and this fits the analogy, for when the one bringing his camels to water brings them all together they crowd and jostle one another [taʿārakat]. Labīd said: "He brought them to the crowded watering [al-ʿirāk] and did not drive them off, nor was he concerned by the disorder of their crowding-in." And among their proverbs: "Contend [ʿārik] with a yearling, or leave it be."

As for al-ʿārik, it is the menstruating woman, and it is possible that its reasoning is that she is preoccupied, given what she undergoes of her state and her blood — as though she were contending [tuʿāriku] with something. One says a woman is ʿārik, women are ʿawārik. Al-Khansāʾ said: "You will never wash away the disgrace that has overshadowed you, as the menstruating women [al-ʿawārik] wash away their blood after their purity." From this one says: ʿaraket, taʿruku ʿarkan wa-ʿirākan, and she is ʿārik.
عركس:
Al-Khalīl said: ʿarkas is the base form behind iʿrankasa, said of a thing when it piles up, part upon part; one says iʿrankasa. Al-ʿAjjāj said, describing the night:
And its terrors piled up thick, and it piled up thick.
What he said here is a word blended from ʿakasa and ʿaraka, for it describes a thing whose parts press back on one another and recoil, jostling against each other as though wound together.
عرم:
The letters ʿayn, rāʾ and mīm are a single sound root, indicating intensity and sharpness. One says: ʿaruma al-insānu yaʿrumu ʿarāmatan — a man is fierce and sharp-tempered, and he is ʿārim. A poet said, in a line of verse: "I am a man who defends what is sacred to him, with a broad reach of hand and a sharp [ʿārim] tongue."
1. He has ʿurām, when that quality is in him.
2. ʿurām al-jaysh — the army's fierceness, its edge, and its great numbers. A poet said, in a line of verse: "Many a night of terror I journeyed through, with young men I led, and a host of great fierceness [ʿurām], massed together."
For that reason one says jaysh ʿaramram, a mighty army — we have already said that when they wish to make a matter grand they add letters to it. Al-ʿaramram comes from ʿarama and ʿarra. A poet said, in a line of verse: "Two dwelling-places at the frozen ground of al-Naʿām — I knew them once, with abundant livestock and mighty [ʿaramram] strength."
As for sayl al-ʿarim (the flood of al-ʿArim), it is said that al-ʿarima is the dam, plural ʿarim. This is sound, because when water is dammed up it has ʿurām from its great volume. It is also possible that al-ʿarima is the threshed heap of grain not yet winnowed, made in the shape of a vaulted structure — if so, this is because it is dense and abundant, like water with ʿurām.
As for al-ʿurma, it is the white patch on a ewe's mouth; one says shātun ʿarmāʾ — this is an exception from the root we have described — and afʿā ʿarmāʾ, a viper with such markings. It is possible this belongs to letter-substitution, as though the rāʾ stands in place of a lām, as if the word were ʿalmāʾ (from ʿalāma, a mark) — the white patch being like a marking on the animal, and this is not far-fetched. A poet said, in a line of verse (the sense is uncertain in places): "O Abū Maʿqil, let not my hatred fall in step with yours toward the heads of vipers at their speckled [ʿurm] look-out places."
As for their saying that al-ʿarim is the male rat, this has no sense to it and is not worth dwelling on.
عرمرم: the numerous army. This is plain to anyone who considers it, and knows that whatever exceeds the ʿayn, rāʾ and mīm in it is extra. What we have named was added only for emphasis; otherwise its origin is al-ʿurām and al-ʿaram.
عرمس:
A name for the rock, and by it the hard she-camel was named. He said:
A strong-cheeked one, whose hoof-pads are compact, a rock.
This is a word with the mīm added into it; the origin is ʿars, and she was likened to the foundation-stone of a building.
عرن:
The letters ʿayn, rā' and nūn are one sound root indicating fixedness and the fixing of a thing in place, as with something that has been fitted together.

1. al-ʿirnīn — the nose, plural ʿarānīn, named thus as though it had been fitted (ʿurina) onto the face, that is, set in place. A poet said, of al-ʿirnīn, in a line of verse: She folds her headscarf over the ridge of a high, arched nose, its tip touched with musk.
2. Flesh (al-laḥm) is likewise called ʿarīn, because it is fixed and fitted onto the body. A poet said, in a line of verse: tattooed at the extremities, soft, is her ʿarīn (flesh).
3. al-ʿirān — a piece of wood put through a camel's nose. A poet said, in a line of verse: If you let your talk be known, at dawn you will be brought, your head in a halter-rope or a nose-peg.
4. al-ʿarīn — the lion's den, because it is the place where he stays fixed. A poet said, in a line of verse: dark of back, its uppermost colour like the colour of the back of a snake from the den.
5. A spear called muʿarran is one whose head has been riveted fast into it. A poet said, in a line of verse: monuments of pride, not built of clay, but by the thrust of the muʿarran lance of Samhar's making.
6. Their saying, of a man strong and hard to throw in wrestling: 'he is ʿirna, not to be overcome' — meaning he is fixed, unmoving.
عرندد:
the hard, solid one, of anything. He said, in a line of verse: I overtook her at a run, with an ʿarandad gait.

This is a word in which the nūn was added, and the dāl doubled to strengthen the meaning; the origin is al-ʿurudd, which means strong — this has already been mentioned.
عرندس: strong. Everything beyond the ʿayn, rāʾ and dāl in it is extra; its origin is ʿurudd, which means strong — this has already been mentioned.
عرهوم: And a camel that is ʿurāhim is a tall one. Here the rāʾ has been added; the word is really from al-ʿayhāma and al-ʿayhama, which among she-camels means the tall one. This has already passed.
عروى:
The letters ʿayn, rā' and the weak letter are two distinct sound roots. One indicates fixed attachment, clinging, and coming over someone; the other indicates emptiness and separation.

The first is their saying: 'amrun ʿarāhu' — a matter came over him and befell him; and 'al-bardu ʿarāhu' — the cold came over him. They say: 'When [the star] al-Simāk rises, then what has troubled you (mā ʿanāka) comes over you (yaʿrūka), from the cold that overtakes you.' And 'al-hammu ʿarāhu wa-ʿtarāhu' — worry came over him and gripped him. Al-ʿurawāʾ is a shivering chill that seizes a fever patient.

1. al-ʿurwa — the handle or loop of a jug and the like, plural ʿuran.
2. 'ʿarraytu al-shayʾ' — I fitted a handle to the thing.

Labīd said, in a line of verse: stout, strong-scented, fitted with loops (ʿuran) of Kurdish work and of coarse leather like an onion-skin.

Another said: 'By God, even if you fitted my two neck-sinews with a loop, I would not bow to you' — meaning: even if you set two handles on them. It was named ʿurwa because it is held and the finger clings to it.

1. al-ʿurwa — also a kind of plant, a shrub that keeps its greenness through winter, so that camels cling to it until spring comes; it is called both al-ʿurwa and al-ʿulqa.

Muhalhal said, in a line of verse: he slew kings and marched beneath his banner — the ʿurwa-shrub [and its like], and the noblest of tribesmen.

Some said: al-ʿurwa is a tangled, thickly grown tree. Al-Farrāʾ said: al-ʿurwa, among trees, is one that does not shed its leaves. All this comes back to the same reasoning of the root, because livestock cling to it, so it is like the handle and all we have mentioned.

Sometimes they call a precious, valuable thing ʿurwa, as it is also called ʿilq; the reasoning for both is the same. It is said that 'the ʿurwa of Islam' means what remains of it, as one says 'in the land of so-and-so's tribe there is an ʿurwa,' meaning a remainder of pasture. To my mind this is a harsh way of putting it, for Islam — praise be to God — endures forever; rather, the ʿurwas of Islam are its ordinances that one holds fast to, each ordinance being an ʿurwa. God, exalted is He, said, mentioning faith: {he has grasped the firmest handhold, which will never break} [al-Baqara: 256].

As for al-ʿariyy, it is the cold wind, also called ʿariyya. It is so named because it comes over (taʿrū) and befalls (taʿtarī), that is, it covers over.

Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse: shall I gather firewood for the people while it [the wind] is a cold ʿariyya, from the roots of alāʾ-shrubs in moist, packed, curling soil?

They say: 'go to your family, for you have brought the cold wind (aʿrayta),' meaning the sun has set and a cold wind has blown.

As for the other root, it is the emptiness of a thing from a thing.

1. al-ʿuryān — the naked one; one says of it 'ʿariya min al-shayʾ yaʿrā' — he became bare of the thing; the plural of ʿārin is ʿurāh.

Abū Duwād said, in a line of verse: we spent the night bare (ʿurāh) beside our colt, drawing the yellow film from his lips.

That is, stripped down, as one says 'he stripped himself (tajarrada) for the task,' when he applied himself earnestly to it. They also say it is from al-ʿurawāʾ, as though people shudder from the cold. And from the first sense one says: 'how lovely is this girl's ʿuryah,' meaning what shows of her when uncovered, what is bared of her; her ʿuryah is her bareness.

It is said: al-maʿārī are the two hands, the two feet, and the face, because these are always exposed.

Abū Kabīr said, in a line of verse: curled together over their bare limbs (al-maʿārī) between them, a striking like the wringing of a great bulging waterskin.

It is said: 'iʿrawraytu al-faras' — I rode the horse bareback, with nothing between his back and me.

[A poet] said, in a line of verse: the mother of the horsemen mounted the piebald, unbranded [horse] bareback, urging it on at a run and a trot.

One says: faras ʿuriy — a bareback horse, and rajul ʿuryān — a naked man.

Also of this root: al-ʿarāʾ is anything you have stripped (aʿrayta) of its covering. One says: 'shelter [it] from al-ʿarāʾ.' As for al-ʿarā, written short, it is whatever shelters one thing from another; you say: 'we left him in the ʿarā of the wall' [its sheltered side]. This word could equally belong to the first root.

Also of this second root: 'aʿrā al-qawmu ṣāḥibahum' — the people abandoned their companion, when they left him and went off.

Also of this root, al-ʿarāʾ: open, empty land — said to be masculine. You say: 'we came to a wide stretch of open land (ʿarāʾ).' And aʿrāʾ al-arḍ are the exposed high ground and open backs of the land. They call a man's wife 'the naked confidante' (al-najiyy al-ʿuryān), meaning he speaks intimately with her in bed while she is unclothed.

[A poet] said, in a line of verse: the confidant who comes to you clothed is not like the confidant who comes to you naked.

A horse long in the legs is called ʿuryān, and this too belongs to this root, meaning that his legs are bare [of excess flesh] and long.

As for al-ʿariyya, said of palm trees, and what has come in the hadith — that he, peace and blessings of God be upon him and his family, 'forbade al-muzābana and permitted al-ʿarāyā' — its reasoning follows what we described under this second root, namely the emptiness of a thing from a thing. The jurists then disagreed about its exact form. Some said it is a palm tree whose owner grants its use, that year, to a needy man, giving him its fruit for that season; the owner of the palms was then permitted to buy back the fruit of that tree from the needy man with dried dates, on account of his need. Others said: rather, it is a man who owns one palm tree standing amid a great many belonging to someone else; the owner of the single tree would go in among the other man's palms [to tend it], and this would trouble the owner of the many trees by his coming and going, so the owner of the many trees was permitted to buy the fruit of that one tree from its owner, before it was harvested, with dried dates, so as not to be troubled by it.

Abū ʿUbayd said: the first explanation is the better one, for in the second case there is no 'setting free' (iʿrāʾ) at all — it is simply a palm tree owned outright by its owner, so how could it be called ʿariyya? What makes this clear is the saying of the poet of the Anṣār: it is neither a biennial-bearing palm (sanhāʾ) nor a propped-up palm (rujbiyya), but rather ʿarāyā in years of calamity.

And from this too is another hadith: that when he sent out the assessors [of the date-harvest] he would say to them: 'go easy in your assessment, for in the property there is the ʿariyya and the bequest.'

Al-Aṣmaʿī said: 'people helped themselves freely on every side' (istaʿrā al-nāsu fī kulli wajh), when they went about eating fresh ripe dates; he said this is taken from al-ʿarāyā.

As for al-Khalīl, sayings have been reported from him, some belonging to the first root and some to the second; but the sum of what he said points to what we have described — that it follows the reasoning of the rest of the chapter, namely the emptying of a thing from a thing. Al-Khalīl said: the ʿariyya palm is one whose fruit, when offered for sale, you set aside (ʿarrayta) from the transaction, that is, you exclude it from the bargaining; the plural is al-ʿarāyā, and the verbal noun of it is iʿrāʾ, which is the giving of its fruit, for that year, to one in need.
عز:
The letters ʿayn and zāʾ are one sound root, denoting strength and power and what resembles them, of overcoming and subduing. Al-Khalīl said: 'Might belongs to God, glory be to His praise, and it is from al-ʿazīz. One says ʿazza al-shayʾu, when it becomes so that it can hardly be found.' This, though sound, is better put another way: one says of a thing that can hardly be obtained. One says ʿazza al-rajulu after weakness, and aʿzaztuhu anā, I made him mighty; and iʿtazza bī and taʿazzaza. He said: one also says ʿazzahu ʿalā amrin yaʿuzzuhu, when he overcame him in a matter. In the proverb: 'Whoever overcomes, plunders.' They say: 'If your brother is too strong for you, then yield,' meaning, if he deals hard with you, deal gently with him. Al-muʿāzzah is striving to overcome; you say ʿāzzanī fulānun ʿizāzan wa-muʿāzzatan fa-ʿazaztuhu, meaning he strove against me and I overcame him. A poet described old age and youth: 'And when I saw the eagle overcome the young raven, and nest in its two nesting-places, my heart surged for it.' Al-Farrāʾ said: one says ʿazaztu ʿalayhi, aʿizzu ʿizzan wa-ʿazāzatan, and aʿzaztuhu, meaning I made him strong, and ʿazzaztuhu likewise. God, exalted is He, said: 'so We strengthened them with a third.' Al-Khalīl said: you say uʿziztu bimā aṣāba fulānan, meaning it weighed heavily and hard on me.

1. nāqatun ʿazūz — when she is narrow in the teat and gives milk only with effort. One says qad taʿazzazat ʿazāzatan. In the proverb: 'She is only a stubborn she-goat, whose yield is abundant,' said of a rich miser. He said: one also says ʿazzat al-shātu taʿuzzu ʿuzūzan, and ʿazuzat also, ʿuzuzan, so she is ʿazūz, plural ʿuzuz. One says istuʿizza ʿalā al-marīḍ, when his sickness grows severe. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: rajulun miʿzāz, when he is severely ill; and istuʿizza bihi al-maraḍ. In the hadith: that the Prophet, peace and blessings upon him, when he came to Medina, stayed with Kulthūm ibn al-Hidm, who was ailing, and remained with him three days, then Kulthūm was overcome — that is, he died — and he moved to the house of Saʿd ibn Khaythama. Rajulun maʿzūz, meaning his wealth was seized and taken from him. One says istaʿazza ʿalayhi al-shayṭān, meaning he overpowered him and his reason; and istaʿazza ʿalayhi al-amr, when it persisted against him.

2. al-ʿazāzah / al-ʿazāz — al-Khalīl said: hard ground, without stones, that water does not cover. He said: 'Away from the smooth, worn rock, they trample the low ground, its hard patches, and press on through whatever pours down.' One says al-ʿazāz is something like hardship, coarse ground that scarcely grows anything even if rained on, though level. Abū Ḥātim said: al-ʿazāz as ground was then derived from their saying taʿazzaza laḥmu al-nāqati, when the she-camel's meat becomes tough and firm.

Al-Zuhrī said: I used to visit ʿUbaydallāh ibn ʿAbdallāh ibn ʿUtba to take dictation from him, and I would rise for him when he came in or went out, and straighten his clothes when he mounted; then I thought I had exhausted what he had, so one day he went out and I did not rise for him, and he said to me: 'You are still on the hard, outlying ground — so rise.' He meant: you are still at the beginnings and edges of knowledge, and have not reached its heart. Abū Ḥātim said: this is because al-ʿazāz lies at the edges and margins of land, and once you reach the middle you come into the soft ground.

Abū Zayd said: aʿzaznā, we came into hard ground. Al-Farrāʾ said: arḍun ʿazzāʾ means hard, like al-ʿazāz. One says istaʿazza al-ramlu and other things, when it holds firm and does not give way. Ruʾba said: 'He spent the night by a bent hollow of dune, taking of it a screen for shelter, when he saw its firmness, he restrained himself.'

3. al-ʿazzāʾ — a hard year. He said: 'And he slaughters the fat she-camels in the hard year, when it strikes.' Al-ʿizz, of rain, means abundant and violent rain; a land struck by that is arḍun maʿzūzah. Abū ʿAmr said: ʿazza al-maṭaru ʿizāzatan. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: one says aṣābanā ʿizzun min al-maṭar, when it was violent, and he said this is not said of a flood. Al-Khalīl said: ʿazzaza al-maṭaru al-arḍa, meaning it packed it down firm, taʿzīzan. It is also said that al-ʿazāzah is a surge that drives a spear's length up a valley. Ibn al-Sikkīt said: maṭarun ʿizz, meaning violent; and one says hādhā saylun ʿizz, the overpowering flood.

4. al-ʿuzayzāʾ, of a horse — the part between its dock and its haunch. Thaʿlaba al-Asadī said: 'Its haunches were drawn taut and its flanks bound close, to a firm rump and a well-corded back.' Al-kurūm is plural of karmah, the rounded top of the thigh, as if a bowl. Al-ʿuzayzāʾ is properly a long word; the poet perhaps shortened it for the metre, and the proof that it is the long form is that in the dual they say ʿuzayzāwān. It is said the two are the two sides of the hip. Al-ʿuzzā is the feminine of al-aʿazz, plural ʿuzaz. One says al-ʿuzzān is plural of ʿazīz, and al-dhulān is plural of dhalīl — one says atāka al-ʿuzzān. They say, as proverbs: 'More precious than the eggs of the vulture,' and 'more precious than the piebald stallion never mounted,' and 'more precious than the crow with the white foot,' and 'more precious than the marrow of a mosquito.' Al-Farrāʾ said: one says ʿazza ʿalayya kadhā, meaning it grew hard for me. And they say, when asked 'Do you love me?': la-ʿazza mā, meaning, indeed, greatly so.
عزاهيل:
They say: these are camels left to wander untended; the singular is ʿuzhūl. They recite, for al-Shammākh:
Until he cried for help to a dark one marked with streaks above him ... calling Hadīl, [with] the straying, untended ones about him.
This word too, if it is sound, has an added hāʾ, as though it meant that [the camels] were left untended, so they went off and roamed wherever they wished.
عزب:
The letters 'ayn, zāy and bā' are a sound root indicating distance and withdrawal. One says 'azaba ya'zubu 'uzūban. Al-'azab: one who has no family, a bachelor. One says 'azaba ya'zubu 'uzūbatan. Al-'Ajjāj said, describing a wild donkey, in a line of verse:
A month, and two months, he lives on alone, sharpening himself.

They said: al-mi'zābah is one whose bachelorhood has lasted so long that he has no need of a household. One says 'azaba ḥilmu fulānin, meaning it left him, and a'zaba Allāhu ḥilmahu, God took it away from him. Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse: "So my forbearance left me — no, rather today it is most entirely gone."

Al-'āzib, of pasture: that which is far off and hard to reach. Abū al-Najm said, in a line of verse: "and far-off pasture that bloomed in its solitude." Anything that escapes you, that you cannot get hold of, has "'azaba" from you. A'zaba al-qawm: the people reached far-off pasture.
عزر:
The letters ʿayn, zāʾ, and rāʾ are two words: one is honouring and support, and the other word is a kind of striking.

The first is support and reverence, as in His words, Most High: {and support him and honour him} [al-Fatḥ: 9].

The other root is al-taʿzīr, striking that falls short of the fixed penalty (al-ḥadd). A poet said, in a line of verse:
There is no disgrace to me in the governor's chastisement, so long as I am not one under suspicion.
عزف:
The letters ʿayn, zā' and fā' are two sound roots: one indicates turning away from a thing, the other indicates a kind of sound.

The first is the Arabs' saying: 'ʿazaftu ʿan al-shayʾ,' when you turned away from it and left it. Al-ʿazūf is one who scarcely stays faithful to a friend's affection.

[A poet] said, in a line of verse: do you not know that I have turned away from passion, when my companion grows angry over nothing?

Al-Farazdaq said, in a line of verse: you turned away at Aʿshāsh, though you had scarcely meant to turn away.

The second root: al-ʿazīf is the sounds of the jinn. It is said that the origin of this is ʿazf al-riyāḥ, the sound and roar of the winds.

[A poet] said, in a line of verse: I cross the wasteland, and between its stretches are the wailing sounds of jinn and skulls scorched hot.

It is said that a place called Abraq al-ʿAzzāf was named for this, because it is said to harbour jinn. From this too is derived al-ʿazf used for playing and musical entertainments.
عزق:
The letters ʿayn, zā' and qāf: nothing sound-rooted is said of it, but al-Khalīl mentioned that al-ʿazq is dealing with a thing with difficulty. A mutaʿazziq man is one of harsh temper. They say al-miʿzaqa is a tool used for tilling.

[A poet] said, in a line of verse: we raise the dust of [the battle of] al-Kulāb, while you raise the flat ground of the villages with your hoes.

All of this is, in its weakness of attestation, close together. Stranger still is the Yemeni usage that Abū Bakr Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan al-Duraydī — God have mercy on him — passes on without naming its source: his statement that al-ʿazīq is low-lying ground, a Yemeni word. And we say nothing but good of our teachers.
عزل:
The letters 'ayn, zāy and lām are a sound root pointing to putting aside and turning away. You say 'azala al-insān al-shay' ya'ziluhu when he sets it aside to one side. And he is bi-ma'zil and fī ma'zil from his companions, that is, in a place apart from them. Al-'uzla is keeping apart. A man ya'zilu 'an al-mar'a when he does not want a child by her.

Of this chapter: al-a'zal, the man who has no spear with him. Some said al-a'zal is the man who has no weapon at all to fight with, so he keeps out of the war; al-Khalīl mentioned it and recited, in a line of verse:
No weaponless men in the wars, but men stripped for battle who are not to be faced on the day of oppression.
To this was likened the star called al-simāk al-a'zal, the unarmed simāk. It is called a'zal only because there is another simāk called al-rāmiḥ, the lancer, which has a star going before it that they say is its lance. So this one was named a'zal for that reason. It is said that al-mi'zāl among people is [the one] who does not halt with the company on a journey but halts apart. Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
It makes the old man forget his sons, and it carries off the milch camels of the man who pastures alone and camps apart.
Al-a'zal among beasts is the one whose tail leans to one of its sides. As for al-'azlā', it is the mouth of a water-skin. It may be a stray from this root we have described; the two can be brought together only with difficulty, and it is nearer to being a stray. One says arsalat al-samā' 'azāliyahā when the sky comes with pouring rain. And this was recited, in a line of verse:
The hand pours it out as it lies folded, with the pouring of a hide water-skin from its spout.
عزم:
The letters ʿayn, zāy and mīm are one sound root pointing to firm decision and to cutting. One says ʿazamtu aʿzimu ʿazman — I resolved. And they say ʿazamtu ʿalayka illā faʿalta kadhā — that is, I have made it a binding order with no turning back in it. And it is said: they used to hold that the binding order of the caliphs was to be obeyed. Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿazm is what the heart has settled upon of a matter you are going to do — that is, of which you are certain. And one says: so-and-so has no ʿazīma — that is, nothing that he resolves upon, as though he cannot cut the matter through, but is confused in it and wavers.

And from the section is their saying ʿazamtu ʿalā al-jinnī, and that is that you recite over him from the ʿazā'im of the Qur'an, which are the verses by which the cutting away of the affliction from the afflicted is hoped for. And the traveller iʿtazama, when he keeps to the straight way, cutting through it. And the man ʿazama al-ṭarīq — he goes on in it and does not turn aside. Ḥumayd said, in a line of verse:
Pressing straight on along the branching roads.

And those of firm resolve among the messengers, peace be upon them, are those who cut the ties between themselves and whoever did not believe of those to whom they were sent — like Nūḥ, peace be upon him, when he said: {leave not upon the earth any dweller of the disbelievers} [Nūḥ: 26]; and like Muḥammad, may God bless him and his family, when he declared himself quit of the disbelievers and God, exalted be He, declared him quit of them and commanded him to fight them, in His saying: {A quittance from God and His Messenger to those of the idolaters with whom you made a treaty} [al-Tawba: 1], and then He said: {and when the sacred months have passed, kill the idolaters wherever you find them} [al-Tawba: 5].
عزوى:
The letters ʿayn, zā' and the weak letter are one sound root, indicating belonging and connection.

Al-Khalīl said: al-iʿtizāʾ is claiming connection to one's lineage in a war-cry, when there is battle; whoever proclaims his identity in his cry has performed iʿtizāʾ — when he says 'I am so-and-so, son of so-and-so,' he has claimed connection to him. And in the hadith: 'whoever calls out with the war-cry of the Age of Ignorance, make him bite it [in sharp rebuke]' — that is, when he calls out 'O clan of so-and-so!'

[A poet] said, in a line of verse: when our horsemen and their men met, they called out 'O Kaʿb!' and we claimed our kinship to ʿĀmir.

Another said, in a line of verse: how could it be otherwise, when my root is of Tamīm, and its branch reaches to the root of my own branch, and my claimed lineage is theirs?

That is the root. As for their saying 'ʿaziya al-rajulu yaʿzā ʿazāʾan,' and 'he is ʿaziyy,' meaning patient, when he bears calamities well, this too belongs to the root we have described — because the sense of al-taʿazzī (consoling oneself) is to take another as one's example, saying: 'my state is like so-and-so's state.' For this reason one says 'taʾassā,' meaning he made his affair a model (uswa) of another's affair; likewise al-taʿazzī. And your saying 'ʿazzaytuhu' means you said to him: 'look to another, to one who has suffered as you have suffered.' This is the root we have described.
عس:
The letters ʿayn and sīn are two close roots: one is drawing near to a thing and seeking it out, the other is a lightness in a thing.

The first: al-ʿass by night, as though it carried something of seeking. Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿass is shaking out the night against people under suspicion. One says ʿassa yaʿussu ʿassan. From it comes al-ʿasas, the one who patrols by night for the ruler. Al-ʿassās is the wolf, because it prowls by night. One says ʿasʿasa al-laylu, when night comes on. ʿasʿasat al-saḥābatu, when a cloud draws near the ground at night; said only of night, in darkness. A poet described clouds: 'It drew near, until, had we wished, when it came close, we could have kindled a light from its fire.' One says taʿasʿasa al-dhiʾbu, when the wolf draws near a thing to smell it out. He recited: 'Like the nostril of the wolf when it draws near, sniffing.' Al-Farrāʾ said: one says jāʾa fulānun bi-l-māli min ʿassihi wa-bassihi, meaning from his own seeking of it, for he seeks it out, yaʿussuhu; it may also be said with kasra. And yaʿtassuhu also means he seeks it. Al-Akhṭal said: 'And was al-Ṣamʿāʾ ever more than a passing solace for one who used to prowl after unfaithful women?'

As for the other root: al-ʿass is said to be lightness in food.

1. al-ʿass, of food — one says ʿasastu aṣḥābī, when I fed them a light meal. He said: ʿasastuhum, I offered them the least of hospitality.
2. nāqatun ... ʿisāsan / ʿasūs — Abū ʿAmr said: a she-camel that gives milk only grudgingly is nāqatun mā tadurru illā ʿisāsan, and when she is like this her yield is light and scant, and she is ʿasūs. Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿasūs is the one that kicks with her legs and spills the milk. They say fīhā ʿasas wa-ʿisās. Some said al-ʿasūs, of camels, is the one that treats her young tenderly and gives it milk when people keep away from her, but if approached or touched, withholds her milk.

Yūnus said: al-ʿass, the night-patrol, is derived from this, as if it were a wary guardedness by night; likewise the wolf's prowling. In the proverb: 'A dog that prowls is better than a lion that skulks away.'

3. al-ʿasūs, also — al-Khalīl said: the she-camel that still has a little milk left in her, not much.

As for their saying ʿasʿasa al-laylu, meaning it withdrew, this falls outside both these roots. The meaning there is that it is the reversal of saʿsaʿa, meaning it passed on, which we have already discussed; this belongs to the chapter of saʿʿa. A poet said, putting the ʿayn first: 'I escaped with pedigree horses and young men, at dawn's approach, in the fading, waning night.'

And straying from both roots: ʿasʿas, a place-name. Imruʾ al-Qays said: 'Did you not weep for the house on the sand-hill at ʿAsʿas? As if I were calling out, or speaking, to one deaf.'
عسب:
The letters ʿayn, sīn and bā' are three separate words, each with its own distinct meaning, from which almost nothing branches. The first is the covering [of a mare] by a stallion or the like; the second is ʿasīb of the tail; the third is a kind of flying creature.

The first is al-ʿasb: they say it is the covering by a stallion-horse or another animal. Then, by extension, the fee taken for allowing the covering was itself called ʿasb. In the hadith, he — God's blessings and peace be upon him and his family — forbade 'the ʿasb of the stallion,' that is, al-ʿasb as the fee taken for it, named after the act itself by association.

Zuhayr said, in a line of verse: had it not been for his covering-fee (ʿasbuhu) I would have sent him back — and the worst of loans is a borrowed stallion.

And Kathīr said, in a line of verse: they abandon the covering-fee of al-Wāliqī and of Nāṣiḥ, which Umm al-Ṭarīq reserves for her family. He is describing mares, [saying] that from exhaustion they miscarried the foals in their bellies.

The second is ʿasīb of the tail, the bone in which the hair grows. By likeness to it, the ʿasīb of the palm tree is named — the straight palm-frond stalk; the two resemble each other in being long and straight. One says ʿasīb, plural aʿsiba and ʿusub.

[A poet] said, in a line of verse: a channel like an unsheathed sword draws it out among the young palm shoots, the fronds (al-ʿusub) rising round it. And the ʿasīb of a feather-quill is likened to the ʿasīb of the palm frond.

The third word: al-yaʿsūb — the yaʿsūb of the bees is their king [queen bee].

Abū Dhuʾayb said, in a line of verse: the yaʿsūb led it on until he settled it in a wide, sheltered haunt, richly stocked with honey. The plural is yaʿāsīb.

[A poet] said, in a line of verse: blue-tipped spears, red, well-balanced, their points a resting-place for the yaʿāsīb. They also claim that al-yaʿsūb is a kind of partridge, and a kind of locust.

Among what does not belong to this root is ʿAsīb, the name of a mountain, of which Imruʾ al-Qays said, in a line of verse: O our neighbour, the visiting-place is near, and I shall stay as long as ʿAsīb stands.
عسج:
The letters ʿayn, sīn and jīm: a sound word; it is said that al-ʿasj is the stretching of the neck while walking.

Jamīl said, in a line of verse: they stretched their necks like gazelles, with the eyes of fawns, and their hindquarters shook.

Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse: the white camels, at a stretching or a swift trotting pace, driven along their flanks while they slip swiftly on.
عسد: The letters ʿayn, sīn and dāl: nothing in it can be relied on as sound, except that they say 'ʿasada,' meaning he had intercourse. And they say al-ʿiswadda is a small creeping creature. It amounts to nothing.
عسر:
The letters 'ayn, sīn and rā' are a single sound root pointing to difficulty and hardship. Al-'usr is the opposite of al-yusr, ease. Poverty too is 'usra, because the matter is narrow and hard upon a man. God — Most High — said: {and if a man is in difficulty, then a waiting until ease} [al-Baqara: 280]. Al-'asar is contrariness and crookedness. And it is said amr 'asir and 'asīr — a hard matter — and yawm 'asīr, a hard day. And sometimes they said rajul 'asir. Jarīr said, in a line of verse:
Bishr, the father of Marwān: if you deal hard with him he is hard, and in his open-handedness he is easy.

And they say 'asura al-amr 'usran and also 'asaran. And they said: "keep to what is easy and leave what is hard." And a'sara al-rajul, when he goes from ease into hardship. And 'asartuhu anā a'siruhu, when you press a man for your debt while he is straitened and you do not give him time until his ease comes. And it is said 'assartu 'alayhi ta'sīran, when you go against him. Al-'usrā is the opposite of al-yusrā. And ta'assara al-amr — the matter became twisted. And of yarn, when it is tangled and cannot be freed, it is said: it has become ta'assara. I heard Ibn Abī Khālid say: I heard Tha'lab say: ta'assara al-amr is with the undotted 'ayn, and taghassara al-ghazl, of yarn, with the dotted ghayn.

And it is said a'sarat al-mar'a, when her giving birth is hard for her. And it is said against her by way of a curse: a'sarti wa-ānathti — may you bear hard and bear a girl. And it is said for her by way of a prayer: aysarti wa-adhkarti — may you bear easily and bear a boy.

And it is said: al-'asīr is the she-camel that has become barren and hard to get with young, so that she does not carry in her year. Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
And many a barren dark-white camel, full of eye, swinging out her foreleg, strong as a wild ass, swift.

And the she-camel that is ridden before she is broken in is called 'awsarāniyya. This is of the kind we spoke of, that an increase in a word's letters points to an increase in its meaning.

And a man who works with his left hand is called a'sar. Al-'usrā is the left hand, and it is called 'usrā only because what is easy for the right is hard for it. As for their calling it yusrā, the lucky one, that seems to be by way of taking a good omen, as a waterless desert is called mafāza, the place of safety, and as one bitten by a snake is called salīm, the sound one.

Al-'āsir among she-camels is the one that lifts her tail when she runs. And I do not think that is anything but from a hardness in her nature; the plural is 'awāsir. He said, in a line of verse:
It breaks the tails of the young she-camels that raise their tails as they run.
عسف:
The letters ʿayn, sīn and fā' are words close to one another in form that do not indicate anything good; they are rather like confusion and lack of insight.

Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿasf is undertaking a matter without forethought, and crossing a waterless desert without a set course. From it is al-taʿassuf (acting blindly, without guidance).

Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse: I press on through the distant, unknown land whose way is unmarked, in the shade of a green [tract] where the owl calls to its fellow owls.

Al-ʿasīf is the hired worker; it is not far-fetched that this belongs to the same reasoning, because his undertaking of tasks, in what he must endure, differs from that of the one who owns the affair.

Abū Duwād said, in a line of verse: like the hired man kept for the season, who drove on camels gone lame, having no resting-place short of his destination.

He has hinted at the meaning, though I think the line is not soundly transmitted. The Messenger of God — God's blessings and peace be upon him and his family — forbade 'the killing of al-ʿusafāʾ,' who are the hired workers. And in another hadith: 'my son was a hired worker (ʿasīf) for this man.'

It is said that a camel called al-ʿāsif is one in its death-throes, like the death agony (al-nazʿ) in a human. Supporting what we have said about al-ʿasīf is al-Aṣmaʿī's statement: al-ʿasīf is a slave held in contempt, who has been forced (iʿtusifa) into service, that is, subjugated.

[A poet] said, in a line of verse: I obeyed my soul in its desires, until it brought me back a slave's slave, a hired hand.

And ʿUsfān is a place in the Hijaz, of which ʿAntara said, in a line of verse: as though, when she turned away and would not speak to us, she were a gazelle at ʿUsfān, drowsy-eyed, startled.
عسق:
The letters ʿayn, sīn and qāf are a small sound root indicating one thing sticking to another.

Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿasaq is one thing sticking to another; one says 'ʿasaqa bihi ʿasaqan.' And 'ʿasiqat al-nāqatu bi-l-faḥl' — the she-camel stayed close and attached to the stallion.

Ruʾba said, in a line of verse: he kept away from her secrets after the clinging (al-ʿasaq), and did not waste her between estrangement and passion.

1. In his character there is ʿasaq — that is, crookedness and narrowness of temper.

It is said: 'his fee (juʿl) clung to a man' — meaning it stuck fast to him and he could not be rid of it.
عسقول:
A patch of mirage. Here the lām has been added; the origin is al-ʿasaq, said to mean the capacity to bear with a thing, from the clinging sense already mentioned.

Al-ʿasallaq is the male ostrich. It could be from swiftness, with the qāf added, and belong with al-ʿasalān [a swift gait]; or the ʿayn could be the added letter, and it belong with al-salq and al-tasalluq. Both explanations are sound.
عسك:
The letters ʿayn, sīn and kāf are close to the one before it. Al-Khalīl said: 'ʿasika bihi,' when he clung fast to it, like 'sadika bihi.'

Al-Aṣmaʿī cited, in a line of verse: whenever the crossing of the road grew hard for them, they clung close to its side, wary of the hills.
عسل:
The letters ʿayn, sīn and lām — the sound material in this chapter comes to two roots, and after them some further words if they prove sound. The first of the two roots indicates disturbance and agitation; the second is a sweet food, and other words are drawn from it.
The food is al-ʿasal (honey), well known.
1. al-ʿassāla — the place where the bees make their honey, the honeycomb.
2. al-ʿāsil — the owner of the honey, who harvests it from its place and draws it out. A poet said, in a line of verse: "and the honey of the west-wind flowers, harvested by the honey-gathering bees."
3. ʿassala al-naḥlu taʿsīlan — the bees made honey. On the feminine form of ʿasal a poet said, in a line of verse: "It has honey [ʿasal] — sweet and pleasant are the two hands of the one who harvests it."
4. al-ʿusayla — a word carried over from this. In the hadith: "until he tastes her ʿusayla and she tastes his ʿusayla" — by this intercourse is meant.
5. khaliyyatun ʿāsila, jinḥun ʿāsil — meaning rich in honey. Al-jinḥ is a cleft in a mountain. Al-Hudhalī said, in a line of verse: "The queen-bee grew there until she settled it into a wide, honey-rich [ʿāsil] dwelling-place."
6. al-ʿāsil is also said of the one who harvests the honey. In the hadith: "When God intends good for a servant He ʿasalahu" — this is from the same root, meaning He makes his reputation sweet and endears him to people's hearts through good deeds — from your saying ʿasaltu al-ṭaʿām, I put honey in the food.
7. fulānun maʿsūlu al-khuluq — so-and-so is sweet-natured, pleasant.
8. ʿasaltu fulānan — I put honey into so-and-so's provisions. The Arabs say: "fulānun mā yuʿrafu lahu maḍribu ʿasalatin" — so-and-so, no origin is known for him, meaning his lineage is unknown; and likewise "lā yuʿrafu lahu manbiḍu ʿasalatin."
The second root: al-ʿasalān, the violent shaking of a spear when you shake it. One says ʿasala yaʿsilu ʿasalānan, as the wolf ʿasala when it moves off swiftly. The wolf is ʿāsil, plural ʿussal and ʿawāsil. One says rumḥun ʿassāl, a springy spear. A poet said, in a line of verse: "Every springy spear [ʿassāl], when shaken, whips [ʿasal]." And he said, of the wolf, in a line of verse: "The wolf's swift lope [ʿasalān], as evening drew near and the cold settled on him, and so he slunk off."
9. ʿasala al-māʾ — the water rippled, when the wind struck it and it stirred. And he recited: "a trough, as if its water, when it rippled..."
10. al-dalīlu yaʿsilu fī al-mafāza — the guide moves swiftly through the open waste, when he hastens. He said of that, in a line of verse: "I moved swiftly [ʿasaltu] a while after sleep, until its stretches broke apart one by one, and the night grew dark over the people."
Abū ʿUbayda said: one says farasun ʿāsil, of a horse whose mane sways as it moves, whose head bobs, and whose back runs in a steady rhythm. This is what is sound and not in doubt. But among what he said, and we do not know how sound it is — indeed it is closer to being false: al-ʿasīl is the elephant's member. And they claimed that al-ʿasīl is the perfumer's broom, with which he sweeps up the perfume, and they recite: "like one who one day carves a rock with a broom [ʿasīl]."
عسلق: Every beast of prey bold enough to hunt; the plural is ʿasāliq. This word is blended from three words: from ʿasiqa bihi, when it clung fast to a thing; from ʿaliqa; and from salaqa. All of these have already been explained.
عسم:
The letters ʿayn, sīn and mīm are a sound root indicating crookedness and stiffness in a limb or elsewhere.

Al-Khalīl and others said: al-ʿasam is stiffness in the elbow that leaves the hand crooked. One says: 'ʿasima al-rajulu,' so he is aʿsam, and the woman is ʿasmāʾ. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: al-ʿasam also occurs in the palm and the foot — it is when the wrist joint stiffens until the palm or the foot becomes crooked.

[A poet] said, in a line of verse: in his shoulders and in his back there is weakness, and in his joints a soreness from the stiffness (al-ʿasam).

Al-Kilābī said: al-ʿasmāʾ is a hand that is turned inward and stiff. They say al-ʿusūm are pieces of bread; this has been reported from al-Khalīl, but we consider it a mistake — it is more correctly given in the chapter on the letter shīn, and has been mentioned there.

1. 'ʿasama' — he became greedy for a thing. The reasoning is sound, for one who covets a thing leans toward it and pursues it hard.

One also says 'ʿasama yaʿsimu,' from the same word as before, because he does not obtain it except after leaning toward it. Al-Khalīl said: a man 'yaʿsimu' among a crowd of people in battle when he plunges in headlong and throws himself forward, unconcerned. You say: 'ʿasama bi-nafsihi,' meaning he plunged in.
عسن:
The letters ʿayn, sīn and nūn are a small sound root indicating fatness and what comes close to it or resembles it.

Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿasn is fodder and grazing agreeing well with animals; one says 'ʿasanat al-ibilu ʿasnan' — the camels thrived on it. Some people say 'ʿasinat ʿasanan.' It is said that al-ʿusun is old, long-standing fat. Al-Farrāʾ said: when some fat remains on an animal from before, that is al-ʿusun. One says: 'a camel of good iʿsān' [good residual fatness]. And 'aʿsanat al-ibil' — the camels kept up on fat they already had.

Al-Namir said, in a line of verse: many a two-year-old, thick-furred [camel] I have marked for slaughter, when among the fattened ones (al-muʿsināt) you would see none tied up [for lack].

As for their saying 'taʿassana abāhu' [he took after his father], this belongs to the category of sound-substitution; its true origin has the hamza, and it has been mentioned elsewhere. And it is said: 'so-and-so is ʿisnu māl,' when he manages his wealth well; this too is from sound-substitution, as though the true origin were ʿasal, which has been mentioned elsewhere.
عسوي:
The letters ʿayn, sīn and the weak letter are a sound root indicating strength and hardness in a thing. One says: 'ʿasā al-shayʾu yaʿsū,' when it becomes hard and tough.

[A poet] said, in a line of verse: of a hardened, stubborn thing, when it stands rigid and firm. The three words in this line are close in meaning, all denoting hardness and strength.

Also of this root: 'shaykhun ʿāsin' — an old man, from 'ʿasā yaʿsū' or 'ʿasiya yaʿsā,' that is because what was once soft in his skin has thickened and coarsened. Sometimes they extend this so far as to say 'ʿasā al-layl,' when its darkness grows intense — though with the letter ghayn it is better known, I mean for the night. One says: 'ʿasā al-nabātu,' when a plant thickens and toughens.

[A poet] said, describing an old man, in a line of verse: dishevelled, sturdy, grown hard and bent.

As for ʿasā, it is a word of hopeful expectation; you say 'ʿasā yakūnu kadhā' — perhaps it will be so; it denotes nearness and possibility. Scholars say that when 'ʿasā' comes from God, exalted is He, it is a certainty, as in His saying: {It may be that God will place affection between you and those of them you have held as enemies} [al-Mumtaḥana: 7].
عش:
The letters ʿayn and shīn are one sound root, denoting scantness and slightness, and its branches go back to it by sound reasoning.

Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿushsh is thin-boned in the hands and feet, and a woman like this is ʿashshah. He said: 'By your life, Laylā is no clumsy fool, nor is she thin, her anklet rattling loose.' Al-ʿAjjāj said: 'She was given full, plump legs, neither poor and thin, nor overdone.' One says nāqatun ʿashshah, weak-limbed, with a bend in her, marked by ʿashāshah and ʿushūshah. One says fulānun fī khilqatihi ʿashāshah, meaning scant flesh and crooked bones. One says taʿashshasha al-nakhl, when a palm dries out, marked by taʿashshush and taʿshīsh. One says shajaratun ʿashshah, meaning sparse in leaf; arḍun ʿashshah, sparse in trees.

Al-Shaybānī said: al-ʿashsh, of animals and people, is the one thin in flesh; and of trees, one growing on a single stem with sparse branching, even if green. Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿashshah is a tree with thin twigs and scattered branches, plural ʿashshāt. Jarīr said: 'The trees of your thicket among Quraysh are not thin-branched, nor bare.' One says ʿashsha al-rajulu al-qawm, when he gave them something meagre; ʿaṭiyyatun maʿshūshah, a scant gift. He said: 'Ḥārith, your bucketful is not the scant kind, nor is the yield of your rain-shower a mere drizzle.' Another described sand-grouse: 'They are given to drink neither scantly nor thinly measured,' meaning not meagrely.

Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: a woman of Kināna said, 'We lost you, so we grew thin and scant for want of you,' meaning we were struck by humbling and scarcity.

1. al-ʿushsh, the nest — on this same reasoning, the bird's nest, the crow's, on a tree, and likewise other birds', plural ʿishashah. One says iʿtashsha al-ṭāʾiru yaʿtashshu iʿtishāshan. He said: 'Where the laying crow nests.' He described it as laying though it is the male, because the male shares in the egg, on the analogy of wālid, a parent, said of either sex. Abū ʿAmr said: ʿashshasha al-ṭāʾiru, it built a nest, and recited: 'And in the young, unripened palm-shoots is the nest of the little owl and the woodpeckers.' Abū ʿUbayd said the Arabs say: 'This is not your nest, so move along,' as a proverb for one who settles in a place unfit for him. We say this belongs to the chapter's reasoning because a bird builds a nest only from thin twigs and slight branches. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: al-iʿtishāsh is a people foraging for provisions that are not abundant.

2. ʿashshasha al-khubz — as al-Khalīl related, when bread grows a crust. Someone else said ʿashsha, fa-huwa ʿāshsh, when it spoils and dries out. ʿashshasha al-kalaʾ, the pasture dried up; ʿashshashat al-arḍ, the ground dried up.

Straying from this root is their saying aʿashshashta al-qawm, when you settle among people against their will, until they are forced to move because of you. He recited: 'And had she been left alone she would have slept, but a nuisance made her uneasy, young she-camels like a bent bow.'

Among the place-names that are not to be reckoned on this pattern: Aʿshāsh, a place in the desert, of which al-Farazdaq says: 'You made music at Aʿshāsh, though you had scarcely made music before, and you failed to recognise, of Ḥadrāʾ, what you once knew.' Some relate from al-Layth that he heard al-Farazdaq's transmitter recite 'bi-Iʿshāsh' instead, and said: al-iʿshāsh means old age, meaning: you turned, in your old age, from one you love, that is, you turned yourself away from her.
عشب:
The letters ʿayn, shīn and bā' are one sound root indicating dryness in a thing, being parched, and the like.

1. al-ʿushb — they say it is the quick, early growth of pasture-plants in spring, which then dries out (yahīj) and does not last.
2. arḍun ʿashiba — muʿshiba, land abundant in ʿushb; and 'aʿshabat' when its ʿushb grew plentiful.
3. 'aʿshaba al-rajulu' — the man found, or came upon, pasture (ʿushb).

Abū al-Najm said, in a line of verse: they say to the scout: 'you have found pasture (aʿshabta), dismount!'

By extension of this, a shrivelled old man is likened to it, and one says: rajul ʿashab, imraʾa ʿashaba [dried-up, worn out]. This is also said of she-camels. It is said: 'aʿshaba so-and-so so-and-so,' when he gave him a worn-out she-camel.
عشر:
The letters 'ayn, shīn and rā' are two sound roots: one of them is in a known number, and then other things are carried upon it; the other points to entering in and mixing.

The first is al-'ashara, ten, and al-'ashr with the feminine. And you say: 'ashartu al-qawm a'shiruhum, when you become the tenth of them. And kuntu 'āshira 'asharatin, that is, they were nine and I completed them to ten men. And 'ashartu al-qawm, when you take a tenth of their wealth. One also says: 'ashartuhum u'ashshiruhum ta'shīran. And from it the tax-taker, al-'ashshār, is called 'ashshār. Al-'ushr is one part of ten parts, and it is al-'ushayr and al-mi'shār. As for al-'ishr, it is said to be the camels' coming to water on the tenth day. And ibilun 'awāshir: camels that came to the water at an 'ishr. It is made plural and dual, so one says 'ishrān and 'ishrūn, and every 'ishr of that is nine days. Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
I held up for her the necks of thirsty camels, as though they were sand-grouse driven off from it by a bird of the stony ground, coming to water on the fifth.
By "the fifth" he means the sand-grouse that came to the water at a khims, a five-day interval.

Al-Khalīl said: you say jā'a al-qawm 'ushāra 'ushāra and ma'shara ma'shara, that is, ten by ten, as you say jā'ū uhāda uhāda and mathnā mathnā, one by one and two by two. Al-Khalīl did not mention mawhada mawhada, but it is sound. As for the ta'shīr of a donkey, we say nothing about it but what they have said, and it is sound by our reasoning if what is said is true. Al-Khalīl said: al-mu'ashshir is the donkey with a strong bray. He said: it is said he is so described because he does not stop until he reaches [ten] brays and repetitions. A poet said, in a line of verse:
By my life, if I bray ten times from fear of death, like the braying of a donkey, then I am indeed a coward.

He said: and a she-camel that is 'ushrā' is one whose time is near; she is called 'ushrā' for the completing of ten months of her pregnancy. One says 'ashsharat al-nāqa tu'ashsharu ta'shīran, and she is 'ushrā' until she gives birth; the counted plural is 'ushrāwāt, and the plural is 'ishār. And it is said: rather the name 'ishār falls on the she-camels of which some have given birth and some are near, their birth awaited. And a poet said, in a line of verse:
O 'Ām, her milch-camels and her near-birth camels: a lean-limbed slaughterer, a man who marks himself out in battle, has made away with them.
And al-Farazdaq said, in a line of verse:
How many an aunt of yours, Jarīr, and how many a mother's sister with cracked hands, has milked my 'ishār for me!
And he said: the 'ishār have no milk; he called them 'ishār only because they were so lately, being mothers with young at foot that had brought forth their offspring. Al-'ushr is the piece that breaks off a drinking-bowl or a cooking-pot and the like. And a poet said:
As the mender's rivet draws the broken pieces together.
This has been reported. As for al-Khalīl, he reported and said: they hardly ever use al-'ishr by itself. And he mentioned that their saying qudūrun a'shār and a'āshīr means only that the pots are broken into ten pieces. And Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
Your two eyes shed tears only that you might strike with your two arrows into the shattered pieces of a slain heart.
Al-Khalīl also mentioned that a sword's scabbard, when it is broken up, is called a'shār. And he recited:
The Yemeni sword may cut, though its scabbard is splinters and broken pieces mended over a break.
He said: and al-'ushārī is what reaches ten cubits in length. And 'Āshūrā' is the tenth day of Muharram.

As for the other root, which points to mixing and entering in, it is al-'ishra and al-mu'āshara, the keeping of company. And your 'ashīr is the one who keeps company with you. He said: I have not heard a plural for 'ashīr; they hardly say hum 'usharā'uka, and when they make a plural they say hum mu'āshirūka. He said: a man's 'ashīra, his kin, is called so only for their keeping company with one another, so much so that a husband is the 'ashīr of his wife. It came in the hadith, in the mention of women: "You curse much and are ungrateful to the husband." And one says 'āsharahu mu'āsharatan jamīla, he kept fine company with him. And Zuhayr said, in a line of verse:
By your life, and events do change things, in long companionship there is dislike.
He said: al-ma'shar is every group whose affair is one, such as the ma'shar of the Muslims; mankind is a ma'shar and the jinn are a ma'shar, and the plural is ma'āshir. And al-'ushar is a plant.
عشز:
The letters ʿayn, shīn and zā' are two sound words, one recognized by al-Khalīl, the other not recognized by him.

The first: al-ʿashawzan, said of places, is one whose path is hard and rough; the plural is al-ʿashāwiz.

Al-Shammākh said, in a line of verse: the hard, sinewy, well-shod hooves, the rough ground (al-ʿashāwiz).

Some people say it is al-ʿashwaz or al-ʿashawwaz — I am uncertain which. The spear-shaft is called ʿashawzana for its hardness, the nūn being an added letter.

The other word: 'ʿashaza ʿashazānan,' the halting walk of one lame in the leg; Abū ʿUbayd mentioned it.
عشط: The letters ʿayn, shīn and ṭā'.
عشق:
The letters ʿayn, shīn and qāf are a sound root indicating exceeding the limit of love. You say: 'ʿashiqa yaʿshaqu ʿishqan wa-ʿashaqan.'

Ruʾba said, in a line of verse: and did not waste her between estrangement and passion (ʿashaq).

It is said: 'a woman ʿāshiq' too, without the feminine ending — modeled on their saying 'rajul bādin' and 'imraʾa bādin' [both left unmarked]. Some people claim that al-ʿashaqa is the bindweed plant, and that the name al-ʿāshiq [the lover] is derived from it because of how it trails and clings — though this is merely a saying.
عشك: The letters ʿayn, shīn and kāf: there is no sound meaning in it. Sometimes they say 'yaʿshiku' and 'yaḥshiku,' meaning he separates and gathers. It amounts to nothing.
عشم:
The letters ʿayn, shīn and mīm are a root indicating dryness in a thing and being parched. From this, bread called ʿāshim is that which has dried out. They call an old man ʿashama. Outside that reasoning is al-ʿayshūm, a kind of plant.

[A poet] said, in a line of verse: as the ʿayshūm plants sway against each other on a windy day.
عشنزر:
The strong, harsh one. This is a word with the ʿayn and the nūn added into it; its origin is from al-shazr, which has already passed. He said:
Striking and thrusting, splitting open, harsh.
عشنط:
A tall man; the plural is ʿashannaṭūn and ʿashāniṭ. This is a word with the shīn added into it; it is really from ʿanaṭa, on the pattern ʿanaṭnaṭ. Al-ʿanshaṭ is the same. He said, in a line of verse:
There came to you, of the young men, an impressive, noble one — steadfast against whatever befalls him, not ʿanshaṭ.
عشنق: The tall of body. Here the shīn has been added; the word is really from al-ʿanaq [the neck, or a swift pace]. It is not unlikely that the ʿayn too has been added, in which case the word is blended from two words, al-ʿanaq and al-shanaq — both already explained. Al-Khalīl said: a woman is ʿashannaqa, long-necked, and an ostrich is ʿashannaqa. This confirms what we have said.
عشو:
The letters ʿayn, shīn and the weak letter are a sound root pointing to darkness and to little clearness in a thing; then there branches from it what comes near to it.

From this is al-ʿishā', which is the first darkness of the night. And ʿashwā' al-layl is its darkness. And from it: ʿashawtu ilā nārihi — I made for his fire; and that is only when you grope your way to it through the dark.

Al-Ḥuṭay'a said, in a line of verse:
Whenever you come to him, making for the light of his fire, you find the best of fires and beside it the best of fire-lighters.

And al-ʿāshiya is everything that makes its way by night toward the light of a fire. And al-taʿāshī is pretending not to know about a matter.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
She counts pretending not to know a right guidance in her religion; her offerings were not accepted.

And al-ʿashiyy is the end of the day. If you say ʿashiyya, it belongs to one particular day. You say laqītuhu ʿashiyyata yawmi kadhā — I met him on the evening of such a day; and laqītuhu ʿashiyyatan min al-ʿashiyyāt — I met him on one of the evenings. This that is related from al-Khalīl is a view held; but the sounder in our judgment is that ʿashiyy should be treated just as ʿashiyya is. One says laqītuhu ʿashiyya yawmi kadhā just as one says ʿashiyyata yawmi kadhā, since al-ʿashiyy is simply the end of the day. And it has been said: everything after the sun's decline is ʿashiyy. And the diminutive of ʿashiyya is ʿushayshiya. And al-ʿashā', lengthened and with a hamza and with a fatḥa on the ʿayn, is the food eaten at the end of the day and the beginning of the night.

Al-Khalīl said: and al-ʿashā, with a short ending, is the verbal noun of al-aʿshā; the woman is ʿashwā', and men are ʿushw; and it is one who does not see at night while by day he sees. One says ʿashā yaʿshī ʿashan.

Al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse:
Is it because she saw a man whom the changes of time and a treacherous, ruinous age had worn down?

And al-ʿashwā' among she-camels is the one that seems not to see what is in front of her, so she strikes at everything with her forefeet. They said: that only comes from the sharpness of her spirit.

Zuhayr said, in a line of verse:
I have seen the fates as the blind-striking she-camel's blows: whomever they hit they kill, and whomever they miss lives on and grows old.

And you say innahum la-fī ʿashwā' min amrihim — they are in the dark about their affair. Zuhayr likened the fates to a she-camel that strikes at whatever comes before her and kills.
عشوزن:
The twisted thing, difficult in nature, of anything. He said:
When the straightening-press gripped it, it recoiled — and you were left in charge of a rugged, forceful thing.
This is a blend formed from ʿashaza and shazana.

1. al-ʿashazān — the limping man's gait.
2. al-shazan — hard ground.
عص:
The letters ʿayn and ṣād are one root, denoting hardness and firmness in a thing. Ibn Durayd said: ʿaṣṣa al-shayʾu yaʿaṣṣu, when it becomes hard and firm, and this is sound.

1. al-ʿuṣʿuṣ — from this is derived al-ʿuṣʿuṣ, the base of the tail-bone, that is, the coccyx, plural ʿaṣāʿiṣ. Dhū al-Rumma said: 'A kinship traced through Imruʾ al-Qays reaches her, as the tailbones are strung along the length of the backbone.' He said: it is also called al-ʿuṣʿūṣ. Al-Kisāʾī said: al-ʿuṣuṣ is a dialect word for al-ʿuṣʿuṣ. Marrār al-ʿUqaylī said: 'A wolf came to him at the dimming of dusk, along the trodden road and the sides of his tracks, a wild wolf, to keep him from our provisions, crouched on his haunches.' It is also called al-ʿuṣʿūṣ, as al-burquʿ, the veil, is also called burqūʿ. He said: 'What the fair women suffered from the beetle, entering between the tail-root and the tail-bone.'
2. al-ʿuṣʿuṣ, also — a stocky, thickset man, like al-mukattal.
عصب:
The letters ʿayn, ṣād and bā' are a single sound root, indicating the binding of one thing to another, whether lengthwise or in a circle. Many branches come from it, all going back to one single pattern.

1. From this: al-ʿaṣab. Al-Khalīl said: these are the cords of the joints that hold them together; it is not the same as al-ʿaqab, the sinew used for bowstrings.
2. One says laḥm ʿaṣib — meat that is firm, dense, full of sinew.
3. "So-and-so is maʿṣūb al-khalq" — meaning firmly, densely built. He is ḥasan al-ʿaṣb (well-knit); a woman likewise.
4. al-ʿaṣb — tight winding. A man maʿṣūb al-khalq is as though he had been tightly twisted together.

Ḥassān said, in a line of verse:
leave off waddling, and walk with an easy gait; men are men of firm build and manly vigor.

5. al-ʿaṣīb, from the sheep's intestines, is so called because it is bound and coiled together.
6. As for their calling the hungry man maʿṣūb — some said it is one whose intestines nearly dry out. This is worth nothing; rather the maʿṣūb is one who has bound his belly [with a cloth] from hunger. One says ʿaṣabahum — [hunger] made them go hungry.

Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: al-muʿaṣṣab is the needy one, from their saying ʿaṣṣabahu al-jūʿ, hunger "bound" him; it is not [about] one who tied a stone or anything else [to his belly]. Abū ʿUbayd said: al-muʿaṣṣab is one who binds himself with rags against hunger. The correct view is what Abū ʿUbayd said, by the reasoning-pattern we have applied, and because his statement is better known among scholars.

Abū Zayd said: al-muʿaṣṣab is one whom the [drought] years have "bound," meaning they have eaten up his wealth. This is sound; in short, they took away his wealth so that he became like the hungry man who resorts to binding himself with rags.

7. Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿaṣb, a kind of striped cloth, is called ʿaṣb because its yarn is bound together, then dyed, then woven. He said: it has no plural of its own; one only says burd ʿaṣb and burūd ʿaṣb, since it is attached [in construct] to the action-word itself.
8. Also from this root: al-ʿiṣāba, a thing bound round the head against headache. It is only said ʿiṣāba, with the tā' marbūṭa; whatever you bind around something other than the head is ʿiṣāb, without it — they distinguished the two so each would be known apart.
9. One says iʿtaṣaba bi-l-tāj wa-bi-l-ʿimāma — he bound on the crown, or the turban.

The poet said, in a line of verse:
the crown is bound about the parting of his hair, upon a brow as if it were gold.

10. "So-and-so is ḥasan al-ʿiṣba" — meaning good at wrapping the turban.
11. ʿaṣṣabtu ra'sahu bi-l-ʿaṣā wa-l-sayf taʿṣīban — I struck his head repeatedly with the stick or the sword, as though from al-ʿiṣāba.

Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ ibn Umayya used to be called "Dhū al-ʿIṣāba," because when he wound his turban, no other Qurayshī would wind his, out of respect for him. They recite, in a line of verse:
Abū Uḥayḥa — whoever winds a turban like his is struck down, even if he has wealth and numbers.

12. Also from this root: al-ʿaṣṣāb, the spinner, which fits the pattern, because the thread is bound up by him.

He said, in a line of verse:
as al-Qasāmī folds the spinner's woven cloths.

13. A tree has its branches bound so that its leaves will be shaken off. From this is al-Ḥajjāj's saying: "I will surely bind you as the salama-tree is bound [beaten to strip its leaves]."
14. al-ʿiṣāb — the wrappings that bind a tree, wound about it (this last clause is obscure to me and I give it tentatively).

He said, in a line of verse:
generous providers of food, whose bowls go out in the morning with fresh meat, when the cold twists its bands around the thorn-trees.

Ibn Aḥmar said, in a line of verse:
O my people, how my people bear their being far off, when barren clouds and cold have closed in around the people — meaning it gathered them and drew them together.

15. The she-camel's thigh is bound so that she will give milk.

He said, in a line of verse:
our nature is our giving and our refusing; when we refuse, we give no milk for any binder — meaning we do not give under compulsion.

16. al-ʿaṣūb, among camels, is this same kind — a she-camel that will not give milk until her thigh is bound.
17. al-ʿaṣb — that an animal's two testicles are bound tightly until they fall off; it is then maʿṣūb.
18. One says ʿaṣiba al-fam — the mouth "bound up," meaning saliva that gathers on the teeth from dust or severe thirst.

He said, in a line of verse:
the saliva binds up his mouth, such a binding — like the crust of curdled milk binding the lips of the skin-bag.

19. Also from this root: al-ʿuṣba. Al-Khalīl said: they are ten men; fewer than that is not called an ʿuṣba. It is called ʿuṣba because it has been bound, as if part of it were tied to another part. al-ʿuṣba and al-ʿiṣāba are used of people, birds, and horses.

Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
when the two hosts meet, flocks of birds circle above them, each flock guided by another.

20. iʿṣawṣaba al-qawm — the people gathered into a band.
21. al-yawm al-ʿaṣīb — a hard, oppressive day. iʿṣawṣaba al-yawm — the day grew harsh; yawm ʿaṣabṣab, likewise; iʿṣawṣabat — [clouds or troops] massed together.

He said, in a line of verse:
and [the cold] massed early with a biting wind, while amid the dwellings her worn-out, emaciated animals remained.

Abū Zayd said: whatever clings closely to something has ʿaṣaba by it. One says ʿaṣaba al-qawm bi-fulān, the people gathered closely around so-and-so.

22. He said: from this is named al-ʿaṣaba, a man's kin through his father and his paternal cousins; likewise, anything that circles around a thing and gathers close to it has ʿaṣiba by it.

Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: ʿaṣaba bihi and ʿaṣṣaba, when he circled around it and stayed close to it.

He recited, in a line of verse:
do you not see that the watering-crowd has pressed together, and tall, dark [camels] have crowded closely round the water — tadāka'a meaning pressed against one another, and ʿaṣaba al-mā' meaning stayed close by the water.
