Abū Mahdī said: ʿaṣibat al-ibil bi-l-mā' taʿṣabu ʿuṣūban — the camels crowded round the water, when they circled it and hovered close about it.

He said, in a line of verse:
you know indeed that when the watering-crowd presses close... and: I never crowded around that place nor came near it.

Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿaṣaba are those who inherit from a man collaterally, not through a parent or child. As for the fixed shares [of inheritance]: anyone whose share is not fixed by name is ʿaṣaba; if anything remains after the fixed shares, they take it. Al-Khalīl said: from this al-ʿaṣabiyya, tribal partisanship, is derived.

23. Ibn al-Sikkīt said: "that is a man from the ʿaṣab of the people," meaning from their best men. This fits the root's pattern, because affairs are bound up with them.
عصر:
The letters ʿayn, ṣād and rā' are three sound roots: the first is time, an age; the second is pressing something until it drips out; the third is clinging to something and holding fast to it.

The first is al-ʿaṣr, which is time, an age. God said: {By the age, indeed man is in loss} [al-ʿAṣr: 1]. And sometimes they said ʿuṣur.

Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
Good morning, O crumbling ruin — but can one who lived in the vanished ages ever know ease again?

Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿaṣrān (the two ʿaṣrs) are night and day.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
The two ʿaṣrs — day and night — never linger, once they alternate, before reaching what they set their aim on.

They said: from this the ʿaṣr prayer was named, because it is "pressed" — that is, delayed after the noon prayer. Morning and evening are also both called al-ʿaṣrān. Someone said: those who feed the people through the succession of morning and evening.

Ibn al-Aʿrābī: "aʿṣara l-qawmu" and "aqṣarū" (the people entered the time of ʿaṣr, and desisted for the day) — from al-ʿaṣr and al-qaṣr. And it is said: "ʿaṣṣarū" and "they waited, detained, until the ʿaṣr." A hadith is related that the Messenger of God — God's blessings and peace upon him and his family — said to a man: "Keep to the two ʿaṣrs." The man said — and this was not from our dialect — "so I asked: what are the two ʿaṣrs?" He said: "A prayer before sunrise, and a prayer before sunset" — meaning the dawn prayer and the ʿaṣr prayer.

As for al-jāriya al-muʿṣir (a girl who is "muʿṣir"), some have derived it by this same analogy, and what they said about it is not far-fetched. Al-Khalīl and others said: when a girl feels in herself the growing fullness of youth, she has "aʿṣarat," and she is muʿṣir — she has reached the prime (ʿaṣr) of her youth and her maturity. Abū Laylā said: when a girl comes of age and nears her first menstruation, she is muʿṣir.

He quoted, in a line of verse:
A girl whose home is at Safawān — she has come of age, or her coming-of-age has drawn near.

Some said she is called muʿṣir because she has changed from her former time. Others said something different about it, and we have mentioned that elsewhere.

The second root is al-ʿuṣāra: what drips from something you press. Someone said: the ooze of the bread that has drained out — and that is al-ʿaṣīr, the juice.

He said about al-ʿuṣāra, in a line of verse:
The stalk has its water pressed out — every kind of wood has its own ooze.

Ibn al-Sikkīt said: the Arabs say: "I will not do it as long as oil is pressed" (meaning: never). Aws said: "There is no cure from Ḍabbā', while the oil is pressed" [I am not fully sure of the sense of this fragment].

The Arabs make al-ʿuṣāra and al-muʿtaṣar a figure of speech for goodness and giving: "he is generous of ʿuṣāra" and "generous of muʿtaṣar," meaning generous in what he yields. You say "ʿaṣartu l-ʿinab" (I pressed the grapes) when you handled it yourself, and "iʿtaṣartuhu" when it was pressed specifically for you. Al-miʿṣār is something like a sack in which grapes are put and pressed.

From this root also: al-muʿṣirāt, clouds that bring rain. God — exalted is He — said: {and We sent down from the rain-clouds pouring water} [al-Naba': 14]. The people are said to be "uʿṣira" when rain comes to them. And it was recited [as a variant reading]: "in it the people are given rain, and in it they yuʿṣarūn" — meaning rain comes to them. This is derived from the pressing of grapes and other things. As for the winds, and their being called al-muʿṣirāt, it is not far-fetched that this belongs to this root by association — because when they stir up the rain-clouds, they themselves came to be called muʿṣirāt and iʿṣār.

He said about al-muʿṣirāt, in a line of verse:
As if the dust-smell of the rain-winds had clothed her in the dust of the stony plateaus and the valleys, sifted as through a sieve.

Al-iʿṣār: the dust that rises up whirling in a circle; plural al-aʿāṣīr.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
While a man is among the living, rejoicing in his lot, suddenly he is in the grave, the whirlwinds effacing him.

The dust of a dust-storm is also called iʿṣār. God — exalted is He — said: {then a whirlwind with fire in it struck it, and it burned} [al-Baqara: 266]. It is said: so-and-so passed by, and his clothes had an ʿaṣra — a waft of perfume and its rising scent — taken from al-iʿṣār. And in the hadith: "A perfumed woman passed by, her trailing garment giving off an ʿaṣra."

From this root also: al-ʿaṣr and al-iʿtiṣār. Al-Khalīl said: al-iʿtiṣār is for wealth to be extracted from a person, whether as a fine or by some other means. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: it is said, "the sons of so-and-so yaʿtaṣirūn the gift" — they claim it back. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: al-muʿtaṣir is the one who takes from something, getting his share of it.

Ibn Aḥmar said, in a line of verse:
Life is only in its full bloom, and you but take your share from its branches.

The yield of land is called ʿuṣāra. His saying — exalted is He — {and therein they press} [Yūsuf: 49] was explained: it means they draw produce from their lands. This fits the analogy, because it is as if something were pressed out, the way grapes and other things are pressed. Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿaṣr is giving, a gift.

Ṭarafa said, in a line of verse:
If there were among our kinsmen anyone who gave to us as generously as you give.

That is, "you give."

The third root: al-ʿaṣar is a refuge; one says "he took refuge in the place" (iʿtaṣara bi-l-makān).

Abū Duwād said, in a line of verse:
A wide open plain, where the wild ass has no refuge from the blaze of heat.
[I am not fully sure of this line's exact sense.]

It is said: "you have no ʿuṣra from this matter" — on the pattern fuʿla — and "ʿaṣar" on the pattern faʿal — meaning a refuge.

He said about al-ʿuṣra, in a line of verse:
And indeed he was the refuge of the one in distress.

And it is said, regarding the words of a poet, in a line of verse:
Blind one, did you see the spear — or was it the spear that saw — aimed at your backsides, when you cast away al-maʿāṣir?
[This line is obscure to me; I give it as best I can.]

Al-maʿāṣir are said to be turbans. And they said: they are black garments. But the correct view is that al-maʿāṣir are coats of mail, taken from al-ʿaṣr (pressing), because one is pressed by them. And God knows best.
عصف:
The letters ʿayn, ṣād and fāʾ are one sound root pointing to lightness and speed.
1. Al-ʿaṣf: the husks of chaff on grain. Al-ʿaṣf: the dried, crumbled leaf on the stalk of a crop — all of this is al-ʿaṣf. God, Glorified is He, said: {and made them like eaten-out chaff} [al-Fīl: 5]. Some commentators said al-ʿaṣf is any crop whose grain has been eaten, its straw remaining. Ibn al-Aʿrābī used to say al-ʿaṣf is the leaf of every growing plant.
It is said: ʿaṣaftu al-zarʿ, when you cut its tips and ate them, like a vegetable. A place muʿṣif is one abundant in ʿaṣf. A poet said, in a line of verse:

When Jumādā withheld its rain ... my quarter was still adorned by a leafy watering-place

Al-ʿaṣf is also called al-ʿaṣīfa and al-ʿuṣāfa. Al-Farrāʾ said: when you take the ʿaṣīfa off a crop, it has been iʿtuṣifa (stripped).
2. Al-rīḥ al-ʿāṣif: the violent wind. God, Most High, said: {a stormy wind came upon it} [Yūnus: 22]. This is what al-Khalīl mentioned; the sense of the phrase is that it makes things light and sweeps them away. It is also said muʿṣif and muʿṣifa. Al-ʿAjjāj said, in a line of verse:

and the storm-winds, never ceasing to drive the litters along

Some scholars said rīḥun ʿāṣifatun follows the pattern 'she did' (ʿaṣafat), while rīḥun ʿāṣifun (without the tāʾ) means only 'possessed of ʿuṣūf,' following the pattern of words like 'milk-having' and 'date-having.'
3. By the same reasoning: al-nāqa al-ʿaṣūf, the she-camel that sweeps off with her rider as if she were a wind in her speed; also aʿṣafat. War 'sweeps off' a people, carrying them away. Al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse:

in a great, close-packed host ... that sweeps away both the armoured and the unarmoured

An ostrich-hen ʿaṣūf is a swift one. And we have said al-ʿaṣf is lightness and speed.
4. From this chapter too: ʿaṣafa and iʿtaṣafa, meaning he earned a livelihood, because he moves briskly in his toil. A poet said, in a line of verse:

without any striving or toil to earn

He is dhū ʿaṣf, meaning resourceful.
عصفر: A plant [safflower]. If this is an arabicized foreign word, it has no derivational pattern; and if it is Arabic, it is a blend from ʿaṣara and ṣafara, meaning by it its juice and its yellowness.
عصفور:
It is a male bird; the ʿayn in it is extra, and it is really from al-ṣafīr, the whistling sound it makes in its call. Everything that comes after this is metaphor and comparison.

1. al-ʿuṣfūr — the drooping tuft of hair hanging from the blaze on a horse's forehead.
2. al-ʿuṣfūr — a piece of the brain. He said, in a line of verse: "concerning the mother of the skull's young, or its ʿuṣfūr."
3. al-ʿuṣfūr in the howdah — a piece of wood that joins the ends of the sticks within it; the plural is ʿaṣāfīr.

Al-Ṭirimmāḥ said, in a line of verse: everything strung together has its ʿaṣāfīr.
عصل:
The letters ʿayn, ṣād and lām are one sound root indicating a crookedness in a thing, together with hardness and stiffness.

The philologists said: al-ʿaṣl is the crookedness of a tusk together with its hardness.

[A poet] said, in a line of verse: on a tall, sturdy [camel] whose tusk has not grown crooked (yaʿṣil).

1. al-aʿṣal — said of men, one whose shin and forearm have become ʿaṣila, that is, badly bent.
2. al-shajara al-ʿaṣila — a crooked tree that cannot be straightened.
3. sahmun aʿṣal — a crooked arrow.

Labīd said, in a line of verse: I shot at the people with an unerring volley, not of the crooked shafts (al-ʿuṣl) nor hastily made.

[Another] said of trees, in a line of verse: a truthful clan of ʿUqayl, like lions amid dense thicket and gnarled wood (ʿaṣal).

By al-ʿuṣl in the first line he meant crooked arrows; he means: they were not hastily made at the moment of need, but were made beforehand.

4. One says 'ʿaṣala al-sahmu' or 'ʿaṣila' — the arrow wobbled when released, from a crookedness in it or poor drawing.
5. 'ʿaṣila al-kalbu' — the dog, when it chased its quarry, then thrashed and twisted about in despair of it.
6. shajaratun ʿaṣlāʾ — a tree grown tall and crooked; an emaciated [woman] is likened to it.

[A poet] said, in a line of verse: she is not gaunt (ʿaṣlāʾ), her breath offensive to a dog, nor thick-breasted, her breasts knocking together.

7. al-ʿaṣal — a twist in the tail-bone (ʿasīb), such that some of its hairless underside shows. Such a horse is called aʿṣal.
8. al-aʿṣāl — the intestines; this fits the pattern, on account of how they twist along their length.

[A poet] said, in a line of verse: the gulley casts it down toward their twisting coils (aʿṣālihā).

9. al-ʿaṣal — also hardness in meat; from it too, 'ʿaṣṣala yuʿaṣṣilu taʿṣīlan,' when he was slow and lagged behind.

[A poet] said, in a line of verse: so al-ʿAmrī lagged behind (ʿaṣṣala), as a dog lags.
عصلبي:
the strong, enduring one. He said, in a line of verse: the night wrapped it up with an ʿaṣlabī.

It is coined by blending three words — from ʿaṣaba (to bind), ṣalaba (to be hard), and ʿaṣala (to twist) — all of which relate to the strength of a thing, and this has already been explained. Al-Khalīl alluded to some of what we have said: he said, ʿaṣlabatuhu is the firmness of his sinews.
عصم:
The letters 'ayn, ṣād and mīm are a single sound root that points to holding back, preventing, and clinging close. The meaning in all of it is one meaning.

From that is al-'iṣma, that God Almighty guards His servant from an evil he might fall into. And i'taṣama al-'abd bi-llāh Almighty when he takes shelter with Him. And ista'ṣama: he took refuge. The Arabs say a'ṣamtu fulānan, that is, I prepared for him something to hold fast to with whatever his hand could reach, that is, he takes refuge in it and clings to it. Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
Out of fear of it the sailor stays clinging to the rudder-pole, from fear and from thunder.

Al-mu'ṣim among horsemen is the one who is in a bad way in his riding; you see him gripping his horse's mane or something else. A poet said, in a line of verse:
When he goes forth in the morning, terror does not make his spear fall from him, nor does he attend the battle as a feeble man clinging on.

Al-'iṣma is everything you hold fast to. And 'aṣamahu al-ṭa'ām — the food kept him from hunger.

From this chapter is al-'aṣīm, which is the crust of tar and urine that dries on the thigh of a she-camel. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And he became, from their fighting, a slain man, with thongs at his throat like the 'aṣīm.
The trace left by dye is also 'aṣīm. And al-mu'ṣam is a hide whose fur has not been taken off it; rather its hair has been left clinging to it, because it is of no use. One says a'ṣamnā al-ihāb — we left the hide with its hair on.

Al-Aṣma'ī said: al-'uṣm is the trace of anything, of wars dye or saffron or the like. He said: I heard a woman of the Arabs say to another: 'Give me the 'uṣm of your henna', that is, what you have scraped off from it. And one says: on her hand is 'uṣmat khalūq, that is, its trace. We say: this that al-Aṣma'ī reported of the woman's words disagrees with his saying that al-'uṣm is the trace, because she did not ask for the trace. The correct thing in this is to say that al-'uṣm is the henna itself, what clings to the hand of the woman dyeing herself; and its trace after that is 'uṣm, because it stays and clings.

Among what is measured against the 'uṣm of henna is al-'uṣma, the whiteness that is on the pastern of a hoofed or footed animal. From that is the ibex called al-a'ṣam, and its 'uṣma is a whiteness on its pastern; the plural of al-a'ṣam is 'uṣm. And a poet said, in a line of verse:
The measures of men's souls are fixed to their times; they bring the white-footed ibexes down from the top of the high hill.

And al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
Time may leave a breach in a smooth firm-set rock, and bring down from it the white-footed ibex, the young one.

One says a crow is a'ṣam when that place on it is white, and such a crow is seldom found. Ibn al-A'rābī said: al-'uṣma in horses is whiteness, little or much, on the forelegs and not the hind legs, so they say: he is a'ṣam of the two forelegs. All of this has one and the same analogy, as though that white marking were a trace clinging to the leg, as we said about the 'aṣam of henna.

From this chapter is al-'iṣma, the necklace, so called because it clings to the neck. Labīd made its plural a'ṣām, as though he meant the plural of 'uṣm, and said in a line of verse:
Until, when the archers despaired and loosed the floppy-eared trained hounds, their collar-thongs shrunk dry.

From this chapter also is the 'iṣām of a camel-litter, which is its fetter and the binding by which its two sides are tied. And the 'iṣām of a waterskin is a cord about two cubits long, put through the two holes at the mouths of the two skins so that they come together. And I have said a'ṣamtuhumā — I made a 'iṣām for them. Ta'abbaṭa Sharran said, in a line of verse:
And many a waterskin of a people whose carrying-cord I set upon a shoulder of mine, tractable and used to journeying.
He said: and a bucket has no 'iṣām.

From this chapter also is the mi'ṣam of a woman, which is the place of the two bracelets on her forearms. And a poet said, in a line of verse:
Today you have her coquetry and her talk, and tomorrow her hand and her wrist belong to another.
It is called a mi'ṣam only because it holds the bracelet; then it is still a mi'ṣam even when there is no bracelet. And one says a'ṣama bihi wa akhlada when he clings to him and stays with him.

'Iṣām is a man's name. The Arabs say, when asking for news: 'What is behind you, O 'Iṣām?' The origin of it is the line of al-Nābigha:
But what is behind you, O 'Iṣām?

And they say, of the man who becomes a lord by himself and not by his fathers:
'Iṣām's own soul made 'Iṣām a lord.
عصوى:
The letters ʿayn, ṣād and the weak letter are two distinct sound roots: one indicates gathering together, the other indicates separation.

The first: al-ʿaṣā [the staff], so named because the hand of the one who holds it wraps around it; by extension, a group of people was also called ʿaṣā. One says: al-ʿaṣā is the community of Islam, and whoever opposes them has 'split the staff of the Muslims' [broken their unity]. If someone does this and is killed for it, he is called 'the one slain by the staff,' with no blood-money and no retaliation owed for him.

They say: hādhihi ʿaṣā (this staff), ʿaṣawān (two staffs), thalāth aʿṣin (three staffs); the plural without a set number is ʿiṣiyy or ʿuṣiyy. They extend the pattern of al-ʿaṣā and say 'ʿaṣaytu bi-l-sayf' — I struck with the sword, as with a staff.

Jarīr said, in a line of verse: you describe swords, while others than you strike (yaʿṣā) with them, O son of the blacksmith — and that is the swordsmith's craft.

[Another] said, in a line of verse: you know well that the Mashrafī blades are struck with, when the noble men wield them.

[A poet said], on the dual of al-ʿaṣā, in a line of verse: she came with the spider's weave, as though upon her two staffs (ʿaṣawayhā) there hung fine, embroidered silk.

Also of this root: 'ʿaṣawtu al-jurḥa aʿṣūhu' — I bound up the wound; this fits the pattern, because it closes up, that is, comes together.

Among their proverbs: 'so-and-so threw down his staff' — said when a traveler reaches good pasture and resolves to settle, so he throws down his staff.

[A poet] said, in a line of verse: she threw down her staff and the journey's end was settled with her, just as the returning traveler's eye grows cool with homecoming.

Also of this root is his saying — God's blessings and peace be upon him and his family: 'do not lift your staff from your family.' He did not mean the staff one strikes with, nor did he command anyone to strike, but he meant discipline [keeping order in the household].

Abū ʿUbayd said: the root sense of al-ʿaṣā is gathering and coming together in harmony; this confirms what we said of the pattern of this root.

The other root: al-ʿiṣyān (disobedience) and al-maʿṣiya (sin). One says: ʿaṣā — he disobeyed; he is ʿāṣin, plural ʿuṣāh and ʿāṣūn. Al-ʿāṣī is also a young weaned camel when it disobeys its mother by refusing to follow her.
عض:
The letters ʿayn and ḍād are one sound root: holding onto a thing with the teeth. From it is drawn every likeness to it, until a hard, tough, or calamitous thing is called by it.

The first is biting with the teeth. One says ʿaḍiḍtu aʿaḍḍu ʿaḍḍan wa-ʿaḍīḍan, so I am ʿāḍḍ. Kalbun ʿaḍūḍ, a biting dog; farasun ʿaḍūḍ, a biting horse. I disclaim to you any part in al-ʿiḍāḍ. Most faults named in animals come on the pattern al-fiʿāl, like al-khirāṭ and al-nifār, and by that pattern one also says ʿaḍiḍta al-rajula, when you took hold of him with what you should not.

1. al-ʿaḍāḍ — what is bitten on. Al-Naḍr said: one says laysa lanā ʿaḍāḍ, meaning nothing to bite on, as one says maḍāgh for what is chewed. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: mā dhuqtu ʿaḍāḍan, meaning nothing at all to eat.
2. zamanun ʿaḍūḍ — a harsh, fierce time, so the scholars of the language said. He said: 'To you I complain of a harsh, biting time — whoever escapes it turns back cheated.'
3. rakiyyatun ʿaḍūḍ — a well whose bottom is deep and hard for the drawer to draw from. He said: 'I spend the night by the biting-hard well, as though I were a childless man, though no man of seven children is childless.'
4. qawsun ʿaḍūḍ — a bow whose string clings tight to its belly.
5. al-ʿaḍḍ — a man of bad, disreputable character, so al-Khalīl said. He said: 'And I was never a foul-tempered man, blamed among boon-companions.'
6. al-ʿiḍḍ — calamity: huwa ʿiḍḍun mā yuflitu minhu shayʾ, nothing escapes him; and it also means the miser, one in whose hand something falls and he clamps down on it. Innahu la-ʿiḍḍu sharrin, meaning he is its very embodiment. Abū Zayd said: fulānun ʿiḍḍu safarin wa-ʿiḍḍu māl, when he is strong at it, well-tried in it. One says ʿaḍḍa bi-mālihi yaʿaḍḍu bihi ʿuḍūḍan. Al-Farrāʾ said: raʾaytu rajulan ʿiḍḍan, meaning a rebellious one, and imraʾatan ʿiḍḍatan likewise. Hādhā ʿiḍḍu hādhā, meaning his rival and equal match. One says al-ʿiḍḍ is the calamitous man; and it is recited of it: 'Many tales, of ʿĀd and Jurhum, are stirred up by the two calamitous men, Zayd and Daghfal.'

Straying from this root, if it is sound: they say al-ʿuḍḍāḍ is the ridge of the nose. They recite: 'And it bridled him with the bit of humiliation and gnawed him, and he shut his eyes over the ridge of a flattened nose.'

As for what comes on this pattern concerning plants, we have already said what is enough about it, except for one more word:

7. al-ʿuḍḍ, with ḍamma — the fodder of the people of villages and towns: date-stones, dried lucerne, and the like. Al-Aʿshā said: 'Among the noble-born, whom al-ʿuḍḍ has toughened, and the grazing of the protected land, and long endurance.' Al-Shaybānī said: al-ʿuḍḍ is fodder. It is also said that al-ʿuḍḍ is the acacia trees, al-ṭalḥ, al-samur, and al-salam, which are al-ʿiḍāh. Al-Farrāʾ said: aʿaḍḍa al-qawmu, fa-hum muʿiḍḍūn, when they graze their camels on al-ʿiḍāh. He recited: 'I say, while my people rest content and hers graze the thorn-trees — if she journeys on, how can I stay?' This usage was allowed because, since al-ʿiḍāh are trees and not soft herbage, camels that stay grazing on them are, for their owners, like animals fed on date-stones and the like, for al-ʿuḍḍ is the fodder of settled country, of date-stones and lucerne. He said: one may not say muʿiḍḍ of al-ʿiḍāh except on this reasoning. The root sense in al-muʿiḍḍ is one whose camels eat al-ʿuḍḍ. Some said: al-ʿiḍḍ, with kasra, means al-ʿiḍāh. One says baʿīrun ghāḍin, when it is fed on it or grazes it. He said: 'By God, I do not know, though you threaten me, and I have walked between the mottled and the pale-clad — is it a camel fed on ʿuḍḍ, its shoulders swollen, thick-lipped, or a camel fed on ghaḍā?' Abū ʿAmr said: al-ʿuḍḍ is barley and wheat. The meaning of the line is that al-ʿuḍḍ is the fodder of the settled towns and al-ghaḍā the fodder of the desert; he means: I do not know whether he is a true Arab or a half-breed.

Belonging back to the first chapter:

8. al-ʿaḍūḍ, of women — the one whom a man's member can scarcely penetrate. One says innahu la-ʿiḍāḍu ʿaysh, meaning enduring through hardship. One says mā fī hādhā al-amri maʿaḍḍ, meaning nothing to get a grip on.

Al-Aṣmaʿī said: in the proverb: 'You are like the one who cares for the one who bites.' Its origin is that a weaned young camel came to its mother wanting to suckle, and hurt her udder, so she bit it, but that did not stop it from coming back. This is said of a man who is turned away and yet goes back.
عضب:
The letters ʿayn, ḍād and bā' are one sound root indicating cutting or breaking.

Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿaḍb is the sharp, cutting sword; al-ʿaḍb is also cutting itself. You say: 'ʿaḍabahu yaʿḍibuhu,' meaning he cut it. From it, a man is called 'ʿaḍb al-lisān' — sharp-tongued; his tongue has become 'ʿaḍub,' ʿuḍūban and ʿaḍūbatan. This is simply a comparison to the cutting sword.

Ibn Durayd said: 'I ʿaḍabtu a man with my tongue,' when I went after him with it, that is, I insulted him; and a man is ʿaḍḍāb when he is given to insulting. And 'ʿaḍabanī al-waʿku' — the fever cut into me, that is, wore me down.

Also of this root: al-shāh al-ʿaḍbāʾ is a ewe with a broken horn. It is said that al-ʿaḍab occurs in only one of the two horns. Ibn al-Aʿrābī mentioned that al-ʿaḍab in the ear is when half or a third of it is gone, and in the horn, when part of its bony core is gone. It is reported: 'a man aʿḍab,' meaning short of arm. It is said that al-aʿḍab, among men, is one who has no brothers, no helper, no one at all to support him.
عضد:
The letters 'ayn, ḍād and dāl are a sound root indicating a limb among the body's limbs, used metaphorically for the sense of strength and a helper.

Al-'aḍud: what lies between the elbow and the shoulder — one says 'aḍud and 'aḍd; a person has two 'aḍudān, plural a'ḍād; it is feminine. One says fulānun 'aḍudiyy, referring to the strength that is in the 'aḍud. A man is 'aḍudiyy and 'iḍādiyy.

Al-Khalīl said: al-'aḍd is help, support. One says 'aḍadtu fulānan, meaning I helped him. God, Most High, said: {and I would not take the misleaders as a support} [al-Kahf: 51]. Ibn al-A'rābī said: a man's 'aḍud is his people and his clan, and from this one says "yafuttu fī 'aḍudihi," it breaks his strength/support. A bedouin said to a man who had asked his help and was refused: "By God, you are the broken 'aḍud," ascribing weakness to him. When the 'aḍud is short or thin it is called 'aḍidah.

As for al-'aḍad, with a different vowel on the ḍād, it is a disease that afflicts the 'aḍud. Al-Nābighah said, in a line of verse: "He pierced the shoulder-flesh with the horn and made it go through, like the cut of the animal-doctor treating the 'aḍad." Some said al-'aḍad occurs only in camels specifically. A she-camel is 'aḍidah when she complains of her 'aḍud. Camels are mu'aḍḍadah when branded on their 'aḍuds. The armlet is called al-mi'ḍad and al-mi'ḍād, because it is worn on the 'aḍud; it is also called al-'iḍād. The same word is used for what is bound on the 'aḍud to carry money.

Al-Khalīl said: the a'ḍād of anything are what is built up around it, like the a'ḍād of a watering-trough — flat stones set up around its rim, singular 'aḍud. Labīd said, in a line of verse: "firm on its supports, every wind and rain-shower has worn it down." The 'aḍud of the camel-saddle: the two pieces of wood attached to the seat-frame. 'Iḍādat al-bāb: the two door-jambs the door closes against. Al-'aḍīd: a palm tree whose fruit you can reach with your hand — it is possible it was named this because the reach of an arm [al-'aḍud] extends up to it. A man called al-'uḍādiyy is full-fleshed in the two 'aḍuds. He said, in a line of verse: "and she was charmed by one wrapped in a cloak, with a club, a broad-armed youth, fat in the sides of the chest."

He said: al-'āḍid is the one who stays at the side of the camels — they must have two 'āḍids, because the driver is behind them and the two 'āḍids are at their two sides. Ibn al-A'rābī recited, in a line of verse: "Would that I had, instead of my two companions, one companion who, when he walked, would not come at the herd from its flanks" — meaning he would not approach them from the side. Al-'āḍid: an arrow that veers off to one side of the target and misses it. 'Aḍada al-rajulu 'an al-ṭarīq: he turned aside from the road.

Ibn al-Sikkīt said: al-'āḍid, among camels, is the male that comes at the she-camel from the side and mounts her. He said, in a line of verse: "He readied for her a stout, powerful one, obedient to the spear-point, an arm's length and a flank."

The other root: cutting. Al-Khalīl said: al-'aḍd is the cutting of a tree with al-mi'ḍad, a sword used specifically for cutting trees. Al-'āḍid: the cutter. In hadith, regarding the city of the Messenger: "Its trees are not to be cut." And he said, regarding al-mi'ḍad, in a line of verse: "A sharp blade — when I rise seeking victory with it, the first stroke suffices, needing no second — it is no blunt tool." Ibn al-A'rābī said: a sword is mi'ḍad, mi'ḍād, and 'aḍḍād, meaning sharp. One says 'aḍḍadat al-shajarah, the tree was cut, and the name for what is cut from it is al-'aḍīd and al-'aḍad. Al-Hudhalī said, in a line of verse: "The thrusting is a clashing sound and the striking a resounding blow, like the woodcutter's blow beneath the rain-cloud on the cut branch."

What falls outside these two roots: al-thawb al-mu'aḍḍad, the striped garment. He said, in a line of verse: "nor those of fine striped cloth and the striped garment."
عضر: The letters ʿayn, ḍād and rā' have no root in the speech of the Arabs; whatever has been said under it is not sound.
عضل:
The letters 'ayn, ḍād and lām are a single sound root indicating hardness and a twisting, knotted quality in a matter. From this: al-'aḍal. Al-Aṣma'ī said: any hard piece of flesh within a sinew is an 'aḍalah, a muscle. One says 'aḍila al-rajulu ya'ḍalu 'aḍalan, he became muscular. From this chapter: huwa 'uḍlatun min al-'uḍal, meaning a formidable, baffling thing — this too follows the pattern, as though described by hardness. Al-'aḍal, of men, means the powerful one.

From this chapter also: al-dā' al-'uḍāl, the intractable disease; al-amr al-mu'ḍil, the difficult matter that wears out anyone trying to fix or resolve it — one says of this a'ḍala. It is said that Dhū al-Iṣba' married a woman, and went to his people asking for her bride-price, and they did not give it to him, so he said, in a line of verse:
One wife alone has baffled you as to her bride-price — how then if I turned to four?
meaning: you could not manage the bride-price of one, so how would it be if I married four.

One says a'ḍalahu al-amr and a'ḍala bihi. 'Umar said: "The people of Kūfah have baffled me — they are pleased with no governor, nor is any governor pleased with them," meaning their affair has worn him out. Al-mu'ḍilāt: hardships.

One says 'aḍḍaltu 'alayhi, meaning I made things difficult for him. 'Aḍaltu al-mar'ata 'aḍlan, and 'aḍḍaltuhā ta'ḍīlan, when you wrongfully prevent a woman from marrying. God, Most High, said: {do not prevent them from marrying their [former] husbands} [al-Baqarah: 232], meaning "restrain them." One says 'aḍḍalati al-mar'ah, when the child becomes lodged in her womb and cannot easily come out. A ewe is mu'aḍḍilah, and a flock is ma'āḍīl. 'Aḍḍalati al-arḍu bi-ahlihā, meaning it became crowded and constrained by its people, from their great number. Aws said, in a line of verse:
You see the land, because of us, ailing across the open plain, hemmed in by us, a vast massed host.

One says sanatun 'iḍl, a hard year. He said, in a line of verse: "O people, because of the hard year." Al-Farrā' said: mā ya'tīnā khayru fulānin illā mu'ḍilan, meaning tangled and difficult to come by. And 'Aḍal is a tribe, named from this.
عضم:
The letters ʿayn, ḍād and mīm — words have been reported in it from al-Khalīl and others, but I take them to be a mistake of those transmitting from him, for al-Khalīl is too eminent to have confirmed something like this.

He said: al-ʿaḍm is the grip of the bow.

They cited, in a line of verse: many a bow-grip (ʿaḍm) I have seen in the heart of a ḍahr. They said al-ḍahr is a place on a mountainside — all of this is merely reported talk.

Al-ʿiḍām is the tail-bone of a camel. Al-ʿaḍm is a wooden implement with prongs used for winnowing grain. The ʿaḍm of the plough is its broad blade. And al-ʿayḍūm, they say, means the voracious eater.

We have mentioned all of this only to make known that it has no sound root; were it not for that, there would be no reason to mention it.
عضنكة: The woman full and wrapped in the haunches, whose thighs meet so closely, from abundant flesh, that the space between them is narrow. Here the ʿayn has been added; the word is really from al-ḍank, which is narrowness. The explanation of al-ḍināk has already passed.
عضو:
The letters ʿayn, ḍād and the weak letter are a single root indicating the dividing of a thing into parts. From this: al-ʿiḍw and al-ʿuḍw, a limb.
1. al-taʿḍiya — to divide a slaughtered animal into limbs (aʿḍāʾ).
2. al-ʿiḍa — a piece of a thing. You say: ʿaḍḍaytu al-shayʾ, meaning I divided it up. Ruʾba said, in a line of verse: "God's religion is not something to be broken into pieces [muʿaḍḍā]" — meaning divided up.
Al-Khalīl said: as for His — Exalted — saying {those who have made the Qurʾan into portions} [al-Ḥijr: 91], it means piece by piece, so they divided it up, believing in part of it and disbelieving in part. The noun from it is al-taʿḍiya.
From this too is the hadith: "There is no taʿḍiya in an inheritance" — meaning: do not divide up what cannot bear division, such as a sword or a pearl and the like.
عط:
The letters ʿayn and ṭāʾ are a lesser root, denoting a kind of sound.

1. al-ʿaṭʿaṭah — al-Khalīl said: it is the imitation of the sound made by rowdy young men when they call out ʿīṭa ʿīṭ. Al-Durayd said: al-ʿaṭʿaṭah is the imitation of sounds following one after another in battle.
2. al-ʿaṭāṭ — as Abū ʿAmr said, the great, brave one, and the lion is described by it — this too comes from the first, as if his roar were likened to al-ʿaṭʿaṭah. Al-Mutanakhkhil said: 'And that kills young men two by two, and strips the great, brave lion of his mane.'
3. al-ʿaṭṭ — splitting cloth crosswise or lengthwise without fully tearing it apart. One says jadhabtu thawbahu fa-nʿaṭṭa, and ʿaṭṭaṭtuhu ana, I tore it. Al-Mutanakhkhil said: 'With a striking upon helmets, of ready effect, and a thrusting like the tearing of woven mats.' Abū al-Najm said: 'As though, beneath her torn armour, were a strip of shore, struck upon by another strip.'

And the root sense in this too goes back to sound, for when he tears it, there is at least a faint sound in it.
عطب:
The letters ʿayn, ṭā' and bā' are two words not close to one another in meaning.

The first: al-ʿaṭab, which is destruction; one says ʿaṭiba — he perished, and 'aʿṭabahu ghayruhu' — another destroyed him.

The other word: al-ʿuṭb, which is cotton.
عطبول:
The soft, full-bodied woman. He said:
So we journeyed on and left Hubayra behind us, and before him the fair, beautiful, full-bodied women.
This is a word with the ṭā' added into it; it is really from ʿabālat al-jism, fullness of body. It is also possible that it is a blend from ʿaṭala: al-ʿuṭul is the bare body, as though he is saying — her bare figure is full-bodied. This is the better explanation.
عطد:
The letters ʿayn, ṭāʾ and dāl — a word has been reported under them, but analogy does not sanction it. Yet they say: al-ʿaṭawwad is a swift, gruelling journey. And they recite, in a line of verse:
To you I complain of a swift, hard-driving pace.
عطر:
The letters ʿayn, ṭāʾ and rāʾ are a single root, and it may well be sound: it is scent, for things treated with perfume.

1. al-ʿaṭṭār — the perfumer, the one whose craft this is.
2. ʿaṭira — a word for a woman who is fragrant.
3. miʿṭīr — another word for a woman who is fragrant.

And he said, in a line of verse:
They follow a wild ass, like the perfumer's pounding-stone.
عطس:
The letters ʿayn, ṭāʾ and sīn are a single word, then it is used figuratively. It is sneezing; one says ʿaṭasa yaʿṭisu, he sneezed. The nose is called maʿṭis, with the ṭāʾ said either way [with i or a]. This is used figuratively, so one says ʿaṭasa al-ṣubḥ, dawn sneezed, meaning it broke. They have also said that al-ʿuṭās means dawn itself, in his saying:
And I would set out early, before the dawn-sneeze, on a great-bodied mount.
عطش:
The letters ʿayn, ṭāʾ and shīn are a single, sound root: it is thirst. One says ʿaṭisha yaʿṭashu ʿaṭashan, he thirsted. They say al-maʿāṭish are the set times of thirst. Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
She does not complain of any stumble from it, though the spells of thirst have made her dance ... until her back is bowed.
عطف:
The letters ʿayn, ṭāʾ and fāʾ are a single sound root, indicating a bending and a curving. One says: ʿaṭaftu al-shayʾ, when you tilt it. Inʿaṭafa, when it curved. The verbal noun of ʿaṭafa is al-ʿuṭūf. Taʿaṭṭafa bi-l-raḥma taʿaṭṭufan — he was moved with compassion. ʿAṭafa Allāhu taʿālā fulānan ʿalā fulānin ʿaṭfan — God inclined so-and-so favourably toward so-and-so. A man yaʿṭifu al-wisāda — he folds the cushion, ʿaṭfan, when he leans on it for support. Labīd said, in a line of verse: "And one weary from the last dregs of sleep, folding [ʿāṭif] the cushion, true to what is well-worn."
1. al-ʿiṭfān — the two sides of a person, so named because a person leans on them. Do you not see that they say: thanā ʿiṭfahu — he bent his side, when he turned away from you and treated you coldly.
2. rajulun ʿaṭūf — a man generous and gentle in war and in kindness; also ʿaṭṭāf.
3. ẓabyatun ʿāṭif — a gazelle, when she crouches and bends her neck.
4. fulānun yataʿāṭafu fī mishyatihi — so-and-so sways as he walks.
5. al-insān yataʿaṭṭafu bi-thawbihi — a person wraps himself in his garment, which resembles draping a cloak over one shoulder.
6. al-ridāʾ (the cloak) itself is called ʿiṭāf, because it is wrapped (yuʿṭaf). Then they extend the usage and call the sword ʿiṭāf too, because it occupies the place of the cloak.
عطل:
The letters 'ayn, ṭā' and lām are one sound root indicating emptiness and vacancy. We say 'uṭṭilat al-dār, the house was left empty and unattended, a house is mu'aṭṭalah; and whenever camels are left without a herdsman they have been 'uṭṭilat, likewise a well when it is not visited and not drawn from. God, Blessed and Exalted, said: {and an abandoned well} [al-Ḥajj: 45], and He said: {and when the pregnant she-camels are neglected} [al-Takwīr: 4]. Anything left without a keeper has been 'uṭṭila; from this, the leaving unguarded of frontier posts and the like.

From this chapter also: al-'aṭal, that is, al-'uṭūl. A woman is called 'āṭil when she wears no jewellery, plural 'awāṭil. He said, in a line of verse: "They wear costly pearls year after year, and their necks are never without them." A bow with no string is qaws 'uṭul. Horses without collars are khayl a'ṭāl.

What falls outside this root: al-nāqah al-'ayṭal, the she-camel that is tall and beautiful; sometimes a woman is described this way too. Dhū al-Rummah said, of the she-camel, in a line of verse: "I set my back upon the spine of a sturdy, spirited, fair-faced, tall she-camel."
عطن:
The letters ʿayn, ṭā' and nūn are one sound root indicating staying in place and settling firmly.

1. al-ʿaṭan and al-maʿṭin — the resting-place of camels [by water].
2. 'iʿṭānuhā' (letting them settle) is said to mean keeping them by the water after they have drunk.

Labīd said, in a line of verse: the two [camels] shunned the water and we did not let them settle by it — for only one hoping to return is left to settle there.

3. It is said: every place that becomes a habitual haunt for camels is called ʿaṭan, and al-maʿṭin is that very place.

[A poet] said, in a line of verse: let neither my own soul nor my greed burden me with a longing to dwell in a resting-place of disgrace.

Others said: aʿṭān of camels occur only at the water; as for their resting-places out in open country or by the encampment, that is called al-maʾwā, also al-murāḥ. The line we quoted, 'in a resting-place of disgrace,' shows that al-maʿṭin can be wherever the camels are kept at their resting-places, wherever that may be; Labīd's line supports the other view — the matter is close either way.

Also of this root: ʿaṭn al-jild — the steeping of a hide, that is, placing it in the tanning liquid.
عطو:
The letters ʿayn, ṭā' and the weak letter are a single sound root pointing to taking and handing over; the section does not go outside these two.

Al-ʿaṭw is reaching for a thing with the hand.

Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
And she reaches out with soft fingers, not coarse, as though they were the grubs of Ẓabī or the tooth-sticks of the isḥil tree.

He is describing a woman cleaning her teeth. And the gazelle does ʿaṭw, and that is when it lifts its forelegs, stretching up to the tree to reach the leaves.

And a poet said, in a line of verse:
She strips with her two horns the fruit of an arāk tree, and reaches with her two cloven hooves when the branch is too high for her.

Al-Khalīl said: and from it al-iʿṭā', giving, is derived. And al-muʿāṭāt is handing over. And one says ʿāṭā al-ṣabiyy ahlahu — when the boy works and hands over what they wanted. And al-ʿaṭā' is a name for what is given, and it is al-ʿaṭiyya, a gift; the plural is ʿaṭāyā, and the plural of ʿaṭāyā is aʿṭiya.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
She hands him at times, when the night dew has fallen well, saliva like the taste of honeyed ginger.

And they say that al-taʿāṭī is taking what one has no right to; one says so-and-so takes upon himself the wronging of so-and-so. And in the Book of God, exalted be He: {so he took it in hand and hamstrung} [al-Qamar: 29]. And among the proverbs of the Arabs: "one reaching up with nothing to hang on to," that is, he aspires to [a thing] and has no means to it, like one who tries to hang on where there is nothing to hang from.
عظ:
The letters ʿayn and ẓāʾ — something was related in it from al-Khalīl that may well be doubtful. If it is sound, it may perhaps belong to the chapter of letter-substitution. That is his saying: that al-ʿaẓẓ is severity in war; one says ʿaẓẓat-hu al-ḥarbu, like ʿaḍḍat-hu, as if it were from war's biting him. If it is a substitution, it is sound; otherwise there is no ground for it. They sometimes recite: 'Steady in the face of the calamity and in fierce war.'

What may perhaps be sound is their saying that al-ʿaẓʿaẓah is the twisting of an arrow when it is not aimed true at the target and trembles as it flies — ʿaẓʿaẓa yuʿaẓʿiẓu, ʿaẓʿaẓatan wa-ʿiẓʿāẓan. Likewise ʿaẓʿaẓat al-dābbah in its gait, when it moves its tail and walks with laboured breath. The coward is said to ʿaẓʿaẓa away from his opponent, when he flinches back from him, retreats, and turns aside. Al-ʿAjjāj said: 'And the coward and the weakling flinched away.' Abū ʿUbayd said: among their proverbs is: 'Do not preach at me while you yourself flinch.'
عظب: The letters ʿayn, ẓāʾ and bāʾ. They say ʿaẓaba the bird, when it moved the base of its tail. This is a reported usage. Al-ʿunẓub is the large locust; the nūn in it is an added letter.
عظل:
The letters ʿayn, ẓāʾ and lām are a small but sound root.

1. taʿāẓala al-kilāb — said of dogs, when they mated; they are taʿāẓalu.
2. jarād ʿaẓlā — locusts are called ʿaẓlā from this.
3. fulānun lā yuʿāẓilu fī shiʿrihi bayna al-qawāfī — so-and-so does not yuʿāẓilu in his poetry between the rhyme-words, meaning he does not pile one upon another.

You may judge that this is either what is called al-īṭāʾ — not repeating the rhyme-words — or what is called al-tadmīn, which is when the sense of a line is only completed in the line that follows it.
عظم:
The letters ʿayn, ẓā' and mīm are a single sound root pointing to bigness and strength. So al-ʿiẓam is the verbal noun of the thing that is great. You say ʿaẓuma yaʿẓumu ʿiẓaman — it grew great; and ʿaẓẓamtuhu anā — I magnified it. And when it grows great in your eyes you say aʿẓamtuhu and istaʿẓamtuhu. And muʿẓam al-shay' is the greater part of it. And ʿaẓmat al-dhirāʿ is the thick part of the forearm. And al-ʿaẓīma is the calamity that comes down, pressing and hard.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
If you escape from her, you escape from one bringing a great calamity; and if not, then I do not think you a survivor.

And from this chapter is al-ʿaẓm, the bone, which is well known, and it was so named for its strength and hardness.
عف:
The letters ʿayn and fā' are two sound roots: one is restraint from what is foul; the other points to a scantiness of something.

The first: *al-ʿiffa* — restraint from what is not fitting. A man is *ʿaff* and *ʿafīf*. One says *ʿaffa yaʿiffu ʿiffatan* and *ʿafāfatan* and *ʿafāfan*.

The second root: *al-ʿuffa* — the remainder of milk left in the udder. It is also called *al-ʿufāfa*.

Al-A'shā said:
It is not kept from it by day, nor do you turn it away, except for a remaining sip or a single draught.

One says: *taʿāffa nāqataka*, milk your she-camel again after the first milking, and leave her young to take the remainder — as though it were suckling that leftover. And "*ʿaffaftu* so-and-so" means I gave him the *ʿufāfa* to drink.

As for their saying, "he came at the *ʿiffān* of that," meaning its due time — this is a substitution of letters; the true word is "*iffān*," already discussed.
عفاهم:
The tough, strong one; anything strong is ʿufāhim. He said:
From the first vigorous burst of its powerful running.
Here the fāʾ has been added; it too is from al-ʿayhama.
عفت: The letters ʿayn, fāʾ and tāʾ are a word denoting the breaking of a thing. They say ʿafata al-ʿaẓma, he broke the bone. Then they say al-ʿafat, in speech, is breaking it with a stammer, like the speech of an Abyssinian.
عفج:
The letters ʿayn, fāʾ and jīm are two words: one is a bodily organ, the other a kind of striking.

The first: al-aʿfāj, the intestines; they say its singular is ʿifj or ʿafj.

The other:

1. ʿafaja — one says this when he struck.
2. miʿfāj — the piece of wood a washerman beats clothes with.

Everything else said in this chapter has no sound basis.
عفر:
The letters ʿayn, fā' and rā' are a sound root with several senses. The first is a colour, the second a plant, the third strength and power, the fourth a stretch of time, the fifth something belonging to an animal's body.

The first: al-ʿufra among colours is a tending toward a dusty tone within redness, and for that reason soil itself is named al-ʿafar. One says ʿaffartu al-shay' fī al-turāb taʿfīran, I rubbed the thing into the dust. Iʿtafara al-shay' — it fell into the dust. A poet described a woman's plaited hair, that when she let it down it fell to the ground, in a line of verse:
The comb wears out among its edges; and when she lets it loose, it falls into the dust.

Ibn Durayd said: al-ʿafar is the visible surface soil of the ground, spoken either with a short vowel or none after the fā', and the voweled form is the more refined usage. The gazelle is called aʿfar for its colour. It was said:
The Nabataeans say to me, as I lay fallen there: not like the fall of a dust-coloured gazelle in the sand-hollow.

He said it is named after the colour of the soil, and likewise al-raml al-aʿfar, dust-coloured sand. He said al-yaʿfūr is the young gazelle, named so for how closely it presses to the ground. Ibn Durayd said al-ʿafīr is meat dried on the sand in the sun. From this chapter: sharibtu sawīqan ʿafīran, I drank ground-grain gruel that was ʿafīr, meaning it had not been moistened with oil or clarified butter.

As for what Ibn al-Aʿrābī said, of their saying "waqaʿū fī ʿāfūri sharrin," like ʿāthūr, it is possible this comes from al-ʿafar, the dust, and possible that the fā' stands in for a thā'. Ibn al-Aʿrābī also said it is derived from ʿaffarahu, meaning he threw him down and rolled him in the dust, and cited:
It brought a shunned, dust-rolling evil.

As for what Abū ʿUbayda related, that al-ʿafr is people's sowing of seed, so that they say ʿafarū meaning they sowed — this too may come from the dust sense, since seed is thrown into the dust. Al-Aṣmaʿī related, in a hadith from Hilāl ibn Umayya: "I have not gone near my wife since we ʿaffarnā [sowed]."

Built on this is al-ʿafār, the pollinating and fertilising of the palm tree — something further has also been said about ʿafār al-nakhl, mentioned in its own place.

Ibn al-Aʿrābī said al-ʿufr are the bright, moonlit nights; the thirteenth night of the month is called ʿafrā', also called laylat al-sawā' [the night of equal light]. It is also said al-ʿufr are white, bare-skinned sheep, and a people owning such sheep are called muʿfirūn and muḍī'ūn; he said Hudhayl are called muʿfira, and no other tribe is called so. They say "mā ʿalā ʿafari al-arḍi mithluhu," meaning upon the face of the earth there is none like him. From this chapter, it is related that the Messenger of God, peace and blessings of God be upon him and his family, when he prostrated, would hold his upper arms away from his sides until the paleness of his armpits could be seen from behind him.

The second root: al-ʿafār, a tree rich in fire, from which fire-sticks are made, singular ʿafāra. Among their proverbs: "iqdaḥ bi-ʿafārin aw markhin, wa-shdud in shi'ta aw arkhi" — strike fire with ʿafār or markh wood, and tighten if you wish, or loosen. Al-Aʿshā said:
Your fire-sticks are the best fire-sticks of kings, in which markh-wood was mixed with ʿafār.

Perhaps a woman was named ʿAfāra from this. Al-Aʿshā said:
ʿAfāra departed, to leave us grieving — o neighbour, what a neighbour you were.

Likewise ʿUfayra. Some said al-ʿufur is the plural of al-ʿafār, the tree already mentioned, and cited:
There was, among the Hāshim clan, in their purest house, one who kept the fire-sticks in reserve when the ʿufur-wood failed to strike.

They say "fī kulli shajarin nārun, wa-stamjada al-markhu wa-l-ʿafāru" — in every tree there is fire, but markh and ʿafār draw on it most freely — meaning the two of them took more from fire than the rest.

The third root: strength and power. Al-Khalīl said: a man is called ʿifrun bayyinu al-ʿafāra for his devilish cunning. One says shayṭānun ʿifriyatun or ʿifrītun, plural al-ʿufāriya and al-ʿafārīt; it is said to mean the clever, resourceful one. One may also say ʿifrun wa-aʿfār, meaning the insolent, rebellious one — taken from strength and daring. The lion is called ʿifirr and ʿafarnā; the wicked man ʿifirrīn, plural al-ʿifirrūn; a fierce lion is aʿsad ʿafarnā and a fierce lioness laboa ʿafarnāt. It was said, in a line of verse:
With a fierce, twisting one — when she stumbles, ruin is nearer to her than for me to say, up you get.

A certain small creature is called "laythu ʿifirrīn" [lion of ʿifirrīn]; it is said the root here is the first sense, dust, because this creature lives in the soft ground, turning a small hollow and burrowing into its middle, and when disturbed throws the dust upward. Al-Khalīl said a man in full vigour, at fifty years of age, is called "laythu ʿifirrīn." They say: the son of ten plays with knucklebones, the son of twenty seeks women, the son of thirty runs the hardest of runners, the son of forty strikes the hardest of strikers, the son of fifty is a lion of ʿifirrīn, the son of sixty brings comfort to companions, the son of seventy is wisest of judges, the son of eighty is quickest at reckoning, the son of ninety is among the most abject, and the son of a hundred neither comes nor goes — meaning he is fit for nothing, neither man nor woman. Abū ʿUbayd said al-ʿifriya al-nifriya is the wicked, detestable one, like al-ʿifr; one says rajulun ʿifr, imra'atun ʿifra. In the hadith: "God, exalted, detests the ʿifriya al-nifriya, the one never touched by loss in wealth or body" — meaning the one kept perfectly sound, scarcely ever ill.

Some claimed al-ʿafarfar is like al-ʿafarnā among lions, meaning the one that throws down its rival and rolls him in the dust; if that is right, this chapter returns to the first root. It was said, in a line of verse:
When he walks in his narrow-waisted coat of mail, a wide helmet and a helm, he tramples as the ʿafarfar lion tramples.

It is said ʿAfār was the name of a man from whom this word is derived, and arrowheads were attributed to him. It was said:
An ʿAfārī arrowhead, hard its ridge — of the old arrowheads, none remains but it.

Al-ʿifirr is also called ʿufāriya. Jarīr said:
I matched the wrongdoers with a hard, formidable one, before whom the rebellious ʿufāriya submits.

The fourth root, from time: their saying "laqītuhu ʿan ʿufrin," meaning after a month. One says of a man of old nobility, "mā sharafuka ʿan ʿufr," meaning it is ancient, not recent. Kuthayyir said:
Your rise to nobility was not something recent — rather, the inheritance of ancestors settles and tends it.

It is also said, of ʿafār al-nakhl, that after the palm was pollinated it was left forty days without being watered.

They said this chapter also holds al-taʿfīr: when a nursing mother suckles her child for a while, then leaves off for a while. Labīd said:
For a pale fawn whose carcass dust-coloured scavengers fought over, creatures whose feeding is never begrudged.

Al-Farrā' related that al-ʿafīr, said of a woman, is one who gives gifts to no one, taken from the taʿfīr above — though this stretches the comparison; perhaps al-ʿafīr instead names a woman whose gift-giving was once constant but became occasional, which fits the pattern better, as shown by the line al-Farrā' cited, by al-Kumayt:
And when the tender girls turned dusty and grey from hardship, their gift-giving became occasional.

Al-mihdā' is a woman whose way is to give gifts constantly; she then reverted to ʿafīr, no longer keeping the gift-giving up.

The fifth: they say al-ʿifriya and al-ʿifrā are the same, the hair at the crown of the head. It was cited:
Time has climbed to his crown, and shorn it with the two blades of its clippers.

It is a dialect variant of al-ʿifriya, like nāṣiya and nāṣāh. By comparison they also call a cock's comb ʿifriya. It was said:
Like the comb of the jealous one among the hens — meaning the roosters.

Abū Zayd said the hair at the back of a man's neck is called al-ʿifriya.
عفز: The letters ʿayn, fāʾ and zāʾ are nothing — they do not resemble the speech of the Arabs at all. Even so, they say al-ʿafz is a man's playful sport with his wife, and that al-ʿafz means walnuts. There is no point in recording this.
عفس:
The letters ʿayn, fāʾ and sīn are one sound root, denoting handling and working at a thing.

1. yuʿāfisu al-shayʾ — they say huwa yuʿāfisu al-shayʾ, when he handles it.
2. iʿtafasa al-qawm — the people wrestled together.
3. ʿufisa — when he was imprisoned, by way of metaphor, as if being confined made him like one thrown down.
4. al-maʿfūs — the worn, well-used thing.
5. al-ʿafs — driving camels along.

The sense running through all of this is close and consistent.
عفص: The letters ʿayn, fāʾ and ṣād are a lesser root, denoting a twisting or a bending. One says ʿafaṣa yadahu, he twisted his hand. They say al-ʿafaṣ is a twist in the nose.
عفضاج: The fat, flabby one. This is a word with the dād added into it; it belongs to the letters ʿayn, fā', and jīm, as though he were full in his aʿfāj, which are the intestines.
عفط:
The letters ʿayn, fāʾ and ṭāʾ are a lesser, sound root, denoting a small sound, from which other meanings are then drawn.

1. al-ʿafṭah — the snorting sound a ewe makes through her nose.
2. ʿāfiṭah and nāfiṭah — one says: 'He has neither an ʿāfiṭah nor a nāfiṭah,' meaning nothing at all. It is said al-ʿāfiṭah is the slave-woman, and al-nāfiṭah the ewe.
3. al-ʿifṭī — what they call the one who mispronounces his speech.
4. ʿafaṭa bi-ghanamihi — when he called his flock.

And God knows best what is right.
عفق:
The letters ʿayn, fāʾ and qāf are one sound root, denoting a coming and going, and it sometimes denotes a kind of sound.

Al-Khalīl said: ʿafaqa al-rajulu yaʿfiqu ʿafqan, when a man follows his own whim and goes off. One says lā yazālu yaʿfiqu al-ʿafqata thumma yarjiʿ, meaning he is gone for a spell, then comes back. Camels ʿafaqa, ʿafqan wa-ʿufūqan, when they are turned loose to graze and pass on ahead; sometimes they turn from pasture toward water, coming back to it every two days. Every animal that comes and goes is ʿāfiq, and everything that returns irregularly is ʿāfiq. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said, of the saying: 'Until four fell in the place of return,' he meant: in the place they turned back from the water. He said: one says ʿafaqa banū fulānin, meaning they went back to their own people. He recited: 'A quick return, and whoever grazes the sour, salty plants makes a quick return too,' meaning that whoever grazes such plants finds his herd thirsting quickly and has no choice but to turn back fast.

1. ʿafaqahu ʿan ḥājatihi — he turned him and diverted him from it.
2. al-taʿaffuq — a moving about and taking every direction in walking, not going straight, like a snake, drawn from the same.
3. al-ʿafq — Abū ʿAmr said: the quick, repeated stepping of camels' fore and hind legs. He recited: 'They strike hard and quick with their legs.'
4. yuʿaffiqu al-ghanam — Abū ʿAmr said: he turns the flock back from straying.
5. rajulun miʿfāqu al-ziyārah — a man given to constant visiting, always coming and going. It is related of one of the Arabs that he said: 'I linger there over some matters, then I go,' meaning: I finish off what remains of my needs, then leave.
6. taʿaffaqa bi-l-shayʾ — Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: when he keeps coming back to it again and again. He recited: 'Men turned to her again and again by the arẓā tree, wanting her, but she and her tribesman outstripped them with their arrows.'
7. al-ʿifāq — their word for milking. In sum, this means milking her every hour. One says ʿafaqta nāqataka yawmaka ajmaʿ fī al-ḥalab. Dhū al-Khiraq said: 'Upon you falls the sheep, the sheep of Banū Tamīm, so milk them constantly, for you are a man of constant milking.'
8. ʿafaqat al-rīḥu al-turāb — when the wind struck the dust and scattered it. Suwayd said: 'And if there is a fire, it is a fire at the meeting-point of the wind, that stirs it and scatters it, scattering.'
9. ʿafaqa bihā — as for the sound we mentioned: they say this when he broke wind loudly and let out a sound.
10. al-ʿafq — close to this chapter: a striking with a stick, and beating, as if that too were a making of sound.
عفك:
The letters ʿayn, fāʾ and kāf are one sound root, denoting only a disliked trait. Al-Khalīl said: al-aʿfak is the fool. He said: 'Friend, do you not marvel at that gross fool, the clumsy, foolish, left-handed one?' Al-ḍayṭar is the coarse, extreme fool; al-aʿfak likewise, and al-akhraq is the one who has no good in him and does nothing well, the sort of man cast off.

Ibn Durayd said: the Banū Tamīm call the left-handed man al-aʿfak.
عفل:
The letters ʿayn, fāʾ and lām are a word denoting an excess growth in the body.

1. al-ʿafal — al-Khalīl said: it comes out in a she-camel's vulva like a hernia-swelling, and she is ʿaflāʾ.
2. al-ʿafl — it is also said to mean the fat of a ram's testicles. Bishr said: 'Swollen at the ʿafl, well-filled out.'
3. al-ʿafl — al-Kisāʾī said: the place felt on a sheep when they want to judge its fatness.
عفلق: The genitals, when slack and wide. This word is blended from ʿafaqa and al-ʿufāqa, and from falaqa.
عفن: The letters ʿayn, fāʾ and nūn are a word denoting spoiling in a thing from dampness. One says ʿafina al-shayʾu yaʿfanu ʿafanan.
عفو:
The letters ʿayn and fā' with the weak letter are two roots. One of them points to leaving a thing, and the other to seeking it. Then many branches come back to it which do not differ in meaning.

The first: al-ʿafw is God's pardon, exalted is He, of His creation, and that is His leaving them and not punishing them, as a bounty from Him. Al-Khalīl said: everyone who deserves a punishment and you leave him, you have pardoned him. One says ʿafā ʿanhu yaʿfū ʿafwan. And what al-Khalīl said is sound; and it may be that a person pardons a thing in the sense of leaving it, and that is not a matter of desert. Do you not see that the Prophet, upon him be blessing and peace, said: I have pardoned you the alms on horses. The pardon here is not from desert, and its meaning is: I have left off laying upon you the alms on horses.

And of the chapter: al-ʿāfiya is God's defending, exalted is He, of His servant. You say ʿāfāhu Allāh, exalted is He, from a hateful thing, and He gives him health, muʿāfātan. And aʿfāhu Allāh has the same sense as ʿāfāhu. And al-istiʿfā' is that you ask of the one who lays a task upon you that he excuse you from it. Al-Shaybānī said: ʿafā ẓahr al-baʿīr, when the camel's back is left unridden; and aʿfaytuhu anā - I left it so.

And of the chapter: al-ʿifāwa is something set aside from the food and given to a person as a gift. And it is only from al-ʿafw, which is leaving, in that it was left and not eaten. As for al-Kumayt's words, in a line of verse:
The boy of the tribe passed the day empty and starving, and their girl with the budding breasts, she who had the set-aside portion, was hungrier still.

Some people said: she used to give away the surplus of the wealth, and then came to hunger through the hardness of the times. But this is far-fetched; it is rather from al-ʿifāwa. He means: as food used to be set aside for her and given her as a gift, then the times bore hard upon them and they did it no more.

As for al-ʿāfī of the broth, it is what the borrower of the cooking-pot sends back. It is called ʿāfī because it is left and not eaten. A poet said, in a line of verse:
When the one who borrows the pot sends back what is left in it.

And of this chapter: al-ʿafw is the ground that has not been trodden. A poet said, in a line of verse:
A tribe like the thong of a sandal, passing along; if they go down into untrodden ground, no trace of them is found.

That is, from their fewness they leave no mark on the earth.

And you say hādhihi arḍ ʿafw - this is land with no trace on it, land not grazed. And ṭaʿām ʿafw is food no one has touched before you, and that is al-unuf, the untouched.

As for their saying ʿafā meaning it was effaced, that is from this; and that is because it is a thing left, not tended and not lived in, so it fades away as the days pass. Labīd said, in a line of verse:
The dwellings are effaced, her halting place and her long-stay place at Minā; Ghawl and Rijām have gone back to the wild.

Do you not see that he said ta'abbada, and so made it known that a long age had passed over it? And it may be that ta'abbada means the wild beasts, al-awābid, have taken to it.

This then is the sense of al-ʿafw, and to it comes back everything like it.

And the saying of the one who says: ʿafā means it was effaced, and ʿafā means it grew much - so that it is one of the words with two opposite senses - that is nothing. The meaning is only what we have mentioned: when a thing is left and not tended until it fades with the passing of time, it has ʿafā; and when it is left uncut and unclipped, it has ʿafā. The root in all of it is leaving, as we have said.

And of this chapter is their saying ʿalayhi al-ʿafā'. Some people said it is the dust, and it is said in abuse. If that is sound, then it is the left dust in which no mark is made and which is not trodden; because when it is trodden, and not left free of walking upon it, it grows packed and is no longer dust. And if al-ʿafā' is effacement, then it is by the sense we have explained. Zuhayr said, in a line of verse:
Its people took up their loads and were gone; upon the traces of those who have departed be effacement.

One says ʿafat al-dār fa-hiya taʿfū ʿafā'an, and the wind effaces the dwelling, ʿafā'an and ʿafwan. And taʿaffat al-dār taʿaffiyan.

Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: al-ʿafw in a dwelling is that the dust grows thick upon it until it covers it. And the noun is al-ʿafā' and al-ʿafw.

And of the chapter: al-ʿafw and al-ʿufuww, the plural being al-ʿifā', and they are the young asses; the female is ʿafwa and the plural ʿifwa. They were named so because they are left unridden and nothing is loaded upon them. As for al-ʿifawa in this plural, there is not known in the speech of the Arabs any moving wāw after a moving letter at the end of a word except this one, and that is because they disliked to say ʿifāt.

Al-Farrā' said: al-ʿifw and al-ʿufw, and al-ʿify and al-ʿufy, are the young of the ass; the female is ʿifwa and the plural ʿifā'. A poet said, in a line of verse:
With a striking that lifts the skulls from their seats, and a thrusting like the drawn-in breath of the young ass when it is about to bray.

And of the chapter: al-ʿifā' is what is thick of fur and of feather. One says nāqa dhāt ʿifā' - a she-camel with much long fur, near to shedding it. And it is called ʿifā' because it is left from plucking and shearing. And the ʿifā' of the ostrich is the feathers that lie over the small down. And so too the ʿifā' of birds; the single one is ʿifā'a, with a long alif and a hamza. He said: a single feather is not called ʿifā'a until there is thickness in it. And al-Ṭirimmāḥ's words:

O morning, gather up the last of the night, rising with a deep note; and rouse the one with the plumage, the mantled one, who when he crows is not left unanswered, and thin-shanked ones answer his voice, crowing from every crowing place.

So dhū al-ʿifā' is the feathers. He is describing a cock. He says lam yukhdhal, that is, the cocks answer him from every side. And he said of a she-camel's fur, in a line of verse:
Firm and well-knit, as though her fur were the two side-feathers on the flanks of a startled male ostrich.

And al-Khalīl said: al-ʿifā' is cloud like nap upon its face. And this is sound, and it is a likening: it is only likened to what we mentioned of thick fur and feather. And the people of the language all said: of hair one says ʿafawtuhu and ʿafaytuhu, like qalawtuhu and qalaytuhu; and ʿafā so it is ʿāfin, and that is when you leave it until it grows much and long. God, exalted is He, said: {until they grew many} [al-Aʿrāf: 95], that is, they grew and multiplied. And this shows what we said, that the root of the chapter in this sense is leaving.

Al-Khalīl said: ʿafā al-mā' - nothing trod the water to muddy it. And that is ʿafwat al-mā'. And ʿafā al-marʿā of those who camp in it, a long ʿafā'.

Abū Zayd said: ʿafwat al-sharāb is the best and fullest of the drink. And in that it is as though it were left, not lessened and not pilfered from.

The other root, whose meaning is seeking, is in al-Khalīl's saying that al-ʿufāt are the seekers of bounty, and they are also al-muʿtafūn. One says iʿtafaytu fulānan, when you seek his bounty and his favour. And if the bounty is itself the ʿafw, then the two roots come back to one meaning, which is leaving; and that is because the ʿafw is what is freely given, not hoarded and not held back.

Abū ʿAmr said: aʿṭaytuhu al-māl ʿafwan - I gave him the money without his asking.

Al-Aṣmaʿī: iʿtafāhu and ʿafāhu are one and the same; and the ʿufāt are also called al-ʿuffā. A poet said, in a line of verse whose first half is missing:
. . . . . . . . they do not find fault with me, when its butcher shrinks back from the meat and the paunch.

Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿāfiya are the seekers of provision, a name that gathers them all. And in the hadith: whoever brings dead land to life, it is his, and what the ʿāfiya eat of it is alms for him.

Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: one says mā akthara ʿāfiyata hādhā al-mā' - how many are those that come down to this water, of every kind. And he said also: ibil ʿāfiya, camels that come down upon pasture people have trodden, and when they graze it they are not content with it, so they lift their heads from it and seek other.

And al-Naḍr said: istaʿaffat al-ibil this dry herbage with their lips, when they take it up from off the dust.
عق:
The letters ʿayn and qāf are a single root, meaning a splitting; to this, with a little care of thought, every branch of the chapter can be traced back. Al-Khalīl said: the origin of al-ʿaqq is splitting. He said: to this al-ʿuqūq, undutifulness to parents, traces back. He said: likewise hair — the skin splits open for it to emerge. What al-Khalīl, God have mercy on him, established as the root is correct. The chapter's expansion, with its explanation, is what he stated, saying:

1. One says *ʿaqqa* the man about his son, *yaʿuqqu ʿanhu*, when he shaved off his newborn's birth-hair, al-ʿaqīqa, and slaughtered a sheep on his behalf. That sheep is called al-ʿaqīqa. In the hadith: "every person is held pledged by his ʿaqīqa."
2. *al-ʿaqīqa* — the hair a creature is born with, and likewise its down or fur. Once it sheds for the first time, that name leaves it.

Imru' al-Qays said:
O Hind, do not marry a foolish, owl-like man, on whom his birth-hair has turned grey and matted.
He describes him with baseness and stinginess. He means: it is as if his birth-hair was never shaved off in his childhood, so that it simply aged with him until he grew old.

Zuhayr said, describing the wild donkey:
Is that it, or a lean-bellied, ash-grey one, on which there remains, from its birth-coat, a shaggy covering?

3. Ibn al-A'rābī said: hair, wool, and camel-down are all called *ʿaqā'iq* or *ʿiqaq*, singular *ʿiqqa*.

'Adiyy said:
Loud in its bellowing, sleeping through the morning — its birth-coat shedding, like twisted rope.

Ru'ba said:
Grazing has stripped from it the year-old birth-coat.

4. One says *aʿaqqat* the ewe, when her wool has grown abundant; the name for it is al-ʿaqīqa.
5. "*ʿaqaqtu* the sheep" means I sheared its ʿaqīq, its first fleece; likewise camels. Al-ʿaqq is the first shearing.
6. One says: "shear your lambs, for they have *aʿaqqa*" — meaning shear them, for the time has come for it.
7. On this pattern, the first plant growth of the earth is called al-ʿaqīqa.
8. Al-ʿuqūq is the cutting-off of one's parents and of any close blood relative. One says "*ʿaqqa* his father, *yaʿuqquhu*, *ʿaqqan* and *ʿuqūqan*," he was undutiful to him.

Zuhayr said:
So the two of you came, through her, to the best standing — far, in it, from undutifulness and from sin.

In the proverb: "Taste it, undutiful one!" In the hadith, Abū Sufyān said to Ḥamza — God be pleased with him — as he lay slain: "Taste it, undutiful one!" — meaning "O undutiful one." The plural of *ʿāqq* is *ʿaqaqa*.

In the proverb: "Undutifulness is the bereavement of one who has not lost a child" — meaning: whoever's child is undutiful to him is as if he had lost them, even though they are alive. And: "He is more undutiful than a lizard" — because the lizard kills its own young. Al-maʿaqqa means al-ʿuqūq.

Al-Nābigha said:
Minds like those of 'Ād, and bodies kept pure — from undutifulness, from afflictions, and from sin.

9. From this chapter: the lightning *inʿaqqa*, split out.
10. "The wind *ʿaqqat* the rain-cloud," when it drew the rain from it, as though it were splitting it open.

A poet of Hudhayl said:
It stood still, baffled, and the wind split open its rain-cloud, and the wide sky above it settled, unstirred by any north wind.

11. *ʿaqīqat al-barq* — what remains in the cloud of the lightning's gleam; swords are likened to it, and so are called *ʿaqā'iq*.

'Amr ibn Kulthūm said:
With brown, supple spears of al-Khaṭṭ cane, and white swords like flashes of lightning, mowing us down.

12. *al-ʿaqqāqa* — the cloud that splits open with lightning, meaning it cracks open.

Muʿaqqir ibn Ḥimār had gone blind. He heard the sound of thunder and said to his daughter: "What do you see?" She said: "I see a black, lightning-splitting cloud, like a she-camel's afterbirth-sac, its fringe hanging low, moving slowly." He said: "My daughter, take refuge with me by a qaflah-tree, for it grows only where there is safety from the flood."

13. *al-ʿaqūq* — a place from whose top the plants split open as they sprout.
14. One says "the dust *inʿaqqa*," when it rose and lifted high.

Al-'Ajjāj said:
When the flying dust-cloud splits and rises.

15. The watered pattern on a sword-blade is called *ʿaqīqa*.
16. Al-a'iqqa are said to be valleys within the sands. Al-ʿAqīq is a valley in the Ḥijāz.

Jarīr said:
How far, how far is al-ʿAqīq and those who dwell there — how far a friend at al-ʿAqīq whose bond I still keep.

And he said, on al-a'iqqa:
He called out to his people, when what was sacred to him was violated — while between him and them lay the breadth of the valleys, then the sand.

We have already said: the whole chapter goes back to a single root.

17. Among the remaining words on al-ʿaqīqa and pregnancy is their saying: "*aʿaqqat* the pregnant she-camel, *tuʿiqqu*, *iʿqāqan*," and she is *ʿaqūq* — this is when the birth-coat has grown in her belly on the young one; the plural is *ʿuquq*.

He said: secretly, when it had groaned the groan of the pregnant she-camels.

18. It is said al-ʿaqāq is pregnancy itself.

A Hudhalī poet said:
They showed themselves pregnant, then they kick at anyone who wrongs them, in refusal — and in it is both a show of force and a swift, easy pace.
He means: they showed signs of pregnancy.

Another said:
Swift creatures, darting as gazelles dart, that leave no belly without its pregnancy.

19. Ibn al-A'rābī said: al-ʿaqaq also means pregnancy.

'Adiyy said:
And I left the wild donkey with its chest bleeding, and a lean, long-bodied she-donkey carrying young.

As for their saying, "the piebald, pregnant one" — it is a proverb they say for something impossible to achieve. Yūnus said: the piebald is a male, and the pregnant one is a female, and a male cannot be pregnant; that is why they say "you have burdened me with the piebald pregnant one," for an impossible task. They also say "he is more famous than the piebald pregnant one," meaning by it the dawn — because it has both whiteness and blackness in it.

20. Al-ʿaqūq is al-shanaq, a due paid on livestock.

He quoted:
Had they accepted me with the levy, I would have brought them a thousand head of clear-branded property, which I would have paid over.
He means: even had I brought them the piebald pregnant one, the impossible, they would not have accepted me.

21. As for al-ʿawāqq of the palm trees, these are the offshoots, singular *ʿāqq* — young palm shoots that grow amid the green undergrowth. If one grows on the trunk without touching the ground, it is called al-rākiba, the riding one.
22. Al-ʿaqīqa is a small amount of water lying in the bed of a valley.

Kuthayyir said:
When she comes out of her tent, its sheltered fringe of growth delights her eye, and the pools of water in the valley please her.

This pattern holds true: when a pool and its water come into view, it is as though the earth had split open. He means: when she comes out, she sees around her, from the sheltered growth and the pools, what pleases her.

23. Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿaqʿaq is a well-known bird, piebald with black and white, long-tailed, that makes a chattering cry, as though its throat were splitting open with it. They say: "He is more foolish than a magpie" — because it neglects its young.

24. Among the earlier words: "nawā al-ʿaqūq" — a soft, loose date-stone, easy to chew, which an old woman may eat or chew, and which is fed to camels. Al-Khalīl said: this is a word of the people of Basra; the desert Arabs do not know it.

25. Ibn Durayd said: al-ʿaqqa is a pit in the ground when it is deep. It comes from al-ʿaqq, a splitting; from it is derived al-ʿAqīq, the well-known valley.

As for al-Farazdaq's line:
You set up, on the morning of al-Jafr, white ones as though they were flashes of lightning, when the day's sun had risen high.

Al-Aṣma'ī said: al-ʿaqā'iq is what the sun makes gleam on a wall, so that you see it flash like the glint of a mirror. All of this rests on resemblance. It is also possible he meant flashes of lightning — this is like 'Amr's line: "and white swords like flashes of lightning, mowing us down."

As for Ibn al-A'rābī's saying, "*aʿaqqa* the water, *yuʿiqquhu*, *iʿqāqan*" — this does not belong to this chapter, because it is a transposition of *aqaʿʿahu*, meaning he made it flow.

He quoted: Your sea is sweet of water — how your Lord has made it flow! — and deprived is the one who has not reached it.
عقب:
The letters ʿayn, qāf and bā' are two sound roots: one of them points to a thing coming later and following after another, and the other root points to height, hardness and difficulty.

As for the first, al-Khalīl said: everything that follows a thing is its ʿaqīb, as you say khalafa yakhlufu, like night and day: when one of them passes, the other follows it. They are two ʿaqībs, each of them the ʿaqīb of its fellow. And they follow one another in turn: when night comes, day goes; so one says ʿaqaba al-laylu al-nahār and ʿaqaba al-nahāru al-layl. Some of the people of Qur'an interpretation said of His words, exalted be He: {He has muʿaqqibāt before him and behind him} [al-Ra'd: 11] — he said: it means the angels of the night and of the day, because they take turns after one another. And it is said that the ʿaqīb is the one who takes another's turn on a mount; you have aʿqabtahu when you get down so that he may ride. And they say ʿaqiba ʿalayya fī tilka al-silʿa ʿaqab — that is, a claim caught up with me over that piece of goods. And al-taʿqiba is that liability.

And of this chapter: ʿāqabtu al-rajul muʿāqabatan wa-ʿuqūbatan wa-ʿiqāban — I punished the man. And beware al-ʿuqūba and al-ʿaqb, punishment. And he recited, in a line of verse:
How good a governor of judgement and a neighbour is ʿUmar: gentle to the people of right, a man of hard and manly punishment.

And they say this is the speech of the Banū Asad. Punishment was called ʿuqūba only because it comes last and second after the sin. It is related from [Ibn] al-A'rābī: al-muʿāqib is the one who has obtained his blood-vengeance. He was called that for the sense we have mentioned. And he recited, in a line of verse:
And we killed a horseman at al-Mukhāriq, as swift as the blessing after a sneeze; the avenger does not die.

That is: we took his blood-vengeance in the time between a sneeze and the blessing said over it. And like it, in a line of verse:
So a killing for our killed and a shearing for our shorn, as swift as the blessing after a sneeze; he who takes vengeance does not die.

Al-Khalīl said: the ʿāqiba of everything is its end, and likewise al-ʿuqab, the plural of ʿuqba. He said, in a line of verse:
You were my brother in the turns of misfortune.

And one says: so-and-so istaʿqaba good or evil from his deed, and he istaʿqaba regret from his affair, and taʿaqqaba likewise. And taʿaqqabtu what so-and-so did — that is, I followed his trail. And they say: you will find the ʿaqib of the matter to be good or to be evil, and that is the ʿāqiba, the outcome.

And of this chapter is their saying of a man whose speech is cut short: if he had an ʿaqib he would have spoken — that is, if he had an answer. And they said about ʿUmar's line:
There is no wealth but we have taken its recompense, and no blood but we have shed blood for it.
He said: ʿiqābahu — he meant ʿuqbāhu and ʿuqbānahu, its requital. And one says: so-and-so and so-and-so yaʿtaqibān so-and-so, when the two of them help each other against him.

Al-Shaybānī said: ibil muʿāqiba are camels that graze the salt-bush one time and the herbage another. And it is said: al-ʿawāqib among camels are those that were among the thorn-trees and then passed on from them to other trees. Ibn al-A'rābī said: al-ʿawāqib among camels are those that come to the water by turns: they drink, then go back to the resting place, then return to the water. And he recited, describing camels:
Coming on the fourth day, coming on the fifth, coming again in turn.

Abū Ziyād said: al-muʿaqqibāt are the she-camels that stand behind the rumps of the camels jostling at the trough; when one she-camel turns away, another enters her place. The singular is muʿaqqiba. He said, in a line of verse:
Those that look on, the ones that take their turn, the ones that turn aside.

And they said: the ʿuqba of camels is that they graze the salt-bush [one time] and the sweet pasture another. And Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
The ā' fruit and the tannūm plant have kept him busy, and his next turn of grazing is from the gleaming flint-ground; pasture comes to him in turns.

Al-Khalīl said: ʿaqabtu al-rajul — that is, I came after the man, aʿqubuhu ʿaqban.
