From it the Messenger of God, may God bless him and give him peace, was named al-ʿĀqib, because he came after those prophets, peace be upon them, who were before him. And faʿaltu dhālika bi-ʿāqiba — I did that at the last, as one says bi-ākhira. He said, in a line of verse:
The talk of union with Umm Maʿbad wore thin at the last, and she broke every promise.

And it is related from al-Aṣmaʿī: I saw a ʿāqiba of birds — that is, birds following one after another, this one alighting in the place of the one that had flown before it. Abū Zayd said: ji'tu fī ʿuqb al-shahr and ʿuqbānihi — that is, after it had passed, the two ʿayns being vowelled with u. He said: and ji'tu fī ʿaqib al-shahr and ʿuqbihi and fī ʿuqubihi. He said, in a line of verse:
[And] I may go out at evening after the camels are driven back from water, swaggering, with my waist-wrap hanging loose.

Al-Khalīl said: jā'a fī ʿaqib al-shahr means at its end; and fī ʿuqbihi when it has passed and something of the next has begun. And one says: I took an ʿuqba from my captive, and that is that you take a substitute for him. He said, in a line of verse:
No harm in it; I have got hold of a substitute.
And this is an ʿuqba from so-and-so — that is, taken in his place. As for their saying ʿuqbat al-qamar . . . . . . . .

And of this chapter is their saying ʿuqbat al-qidr, and that is that a man borrows a cooking-pot and, when he returns it, leaves something in the bottom of it. The reasoning of that is that it is the last of what is in the pot, or what stays behind after ladling from it. Ibn Durayd said, in a line of verse:
When the leavings of the pots count as wealth, my wife loves other men's wives.

And al-Kumayt said, in a line of verse:
. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . and there was no one to leave anything in the pot for those who borrow it.

And they say: give a charity that has no taʿqiba in it — that is, no reservation. And they sometimes say ʿāqaba bayna rijlayhi, when he shifts from one to the other, leaning once on the right and once on the left.

And of what al-Khalīl mentioned is that al-miʿqāb is the woman who bears a boy after a girl, that being her habit. And Abū Zayd said: so-and-so has no ʿāqiba, meaning no offspring. And one says ʿaqaba li-l-faras jary baʿda jary — the horse had run after run, that is, one thing after another. Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
At the second burst he surges, as though his roaring, when his heat boils up in him, were the bubbling of a cauldron.

And al-Khalīl said: everyone who does a thing a second time is a muʿaqqib. Labīd said, in a line of verse:
Until she pushed on at midday for the evening march, and what stirred her was the wronged man's pursuit of his due from the one who put him off.

Ibn al-Sikkīt said: al-muʿaqqib is the one who puts a creditor off; and here it is the object, because the wronged man is the seeker, as though he said: the wronged man's seeking of his right from the one who puts him off. And al-Khalīl said: the meaning is, as the wronged man seeks the delayer for his right; so he carried al-maẓlūm on the place of al-muʿaqqib and put it in the nominative.

And in the Qur'an: {he turned back and did not yuʿaqqib} [al-Naml: 10] — that is, he did not turn round. And al-taʿqīb is a raid after a raid. Ṭufayl said, in a line of verse:
Its tent-ropes are the halters of short-haired horses, as though they were spear-shafts, of the one who attacks first and the one who follows.

And one says: so-and-so ʿaqqaba in the prayer, when he stays in his place praying after the people have finished the prayer.

And of this chapter is ʿaqib al-qadam, the heel, the back of the foot. And in the proverb: 'Your son is the one who made your two heels bleed.' The origin of that was in the matter of ʿAqīl ibn Mālik: Kabsha bint ʿUrwa al-Raḥḥāl had adopted him, and one day ʿAqīl behaved insolently toward his mother and she beat him; so Kabsha came to hold her off, saying, my son, my son! Then the Qayn woman — a slave-girl of the Banū al-Qayn — said: 'Your son is the one who made your two heels bleed,' meaning: I count your son to be the one you laboured with and bore until the birth-blood made your heels bleed, not this one.

And of their speech about punishment and chastisement, Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
And upon the most wretched fell the punishment.

And one says aʿqaba fulān — that is, he came back; and the sense is that he came right after his going. Labīd said, in a line of verse:
So he wheeled and did not come back with the lop-eared hounds, as though they were slivers of a burning wick racing for their reward.

Al-Duraydī said: al-muʿqib is a star that follows another star — that is, it rises after it. He said, in a line of verse:
As though she, between the curtains, were a star that rises after another.

And of this chapter is their saying: upon him is the ʿuqba of nobility and beauty — that is, its trace. He said: And a people upon whom is the trace of nobility . . . . . And that was only said because the trace of a thing comes after the thing.

And of what they say in the way of proverbs is their saying: 'Where has your heel come from?' — that is, where have you come from. And 'so-and-so is muwaṭṭa' al-ʿaqib' — that is, he has many followers. From it is the hadith of ʿAmmār: 'O God, if he has lied, make him one whose heel is trodden.' He prayed that he be a ruler whose heel people tread — that is, they follow him and walk behind him — or a man of wealth whom they follow for his wealth. He said, in verse:
I knew Qays when they were the best of nations,
they set no foot upon another's foot.
That is: they are leaders whom people follow, not followers treading the feet of those ahead of them.

As for al-Nakhaʿī's words, 'the muʿtaqib is answerable for what he has held back' — the muʿtaqib is the man who sells another something and the buyer does not pay him the price, so the seller refuses to hand the goods over until he is paid, and the goods perish in the seller's keeping. He says: the liability is upon the seller. And he was called muʿtaqib only because he did something after the sale, namely the holding back of the thing.

And they say iʿtaqabtu al-shay' — that is, I held it back.

And of this chapter: al-iʿqāba is a brand-mark like the idbāra; and it is also a piece of skin hanging behind the ear.

As for the other root: al-ʿaqaba is a road up a mountain, and its plural is ʿiqāb. Then everything with height or hardness in it was referred back to this. Ibn al-A'rābī said: a well is lined with stone, and its lower courses are backed up with stones behind them. One says aʿqabtu al-ṭayy. And every road part of which lies above another part is aʿqāb.

Al-Kisā'ī said: al-muʿqib is the one who backs up the lining of the well, which is to put pebbles and small stones into it and into its gaps so as to make the courses of the lining firm. He said, in a line of verse:
Packing tight up to the backing behind it.

Abū ʿAmr said: al-ʿuqāb is the potsherd put in between the baked bricks in lining a well so that it may hold firm.

And al-Khalīl said: al-ʿuqāb is a climbing-place on the flank of a mountain, and it juts out. And it is said: al-ʿuqāb is a stone the water-drawer stands on; and they say it is also the channel down which the water runs to the trough. And it is recited, in a line of verse:
As though the sound of its great bucket when it gushed were a torrent down the back of a rugged rock-ledge.

And of this chapter: al-ʿaqab is the sinew with which spears and arrows are bound. He said: and the difference between it and al-ʿaṣab is that ʿaṣab tends to yellow while ʿaqab tends to white, and it is the harder and tougher of the two; and ʿaṣab is of no use. This points to what we said, that the reasoning of this chapter is hardness.

And of this chapter is what Abū Zayd related: ʿaqiba al-ʿarfaj yaʿqab with the utmost ʿaqab. Its ʿaqab is that its stalk grows thin and its fruit turns yellow, and after that there is nothing but its drying up.

And of this chapter: al-ʿuqāb among birds, the eagle, so called for her fierceness and strength; the plural is aʿqub and ʿiqbān, and she is among the birds of prey. And one says ʿuqāb ʿaqabnāt — that is, swift to snatch. He said, in a line of verse:
An eagle swift to snatch, as though her shank and the upper part of her beak were scorched with fire.
Her khurṭūm is her beak. Her waẓīf is her shank. He meant that the two of them are black.

Then the war-banner was likened to this eagle, as though it flew as she flies.
عقبول: They say: the remnant left by an illness [after recovery]; the lām is an added letter, for it is really an illness that follows on the heels of [yaʿqubu] a serious illness.
عقد:
The letters ʿayn, qāf and dāl are one root pointing to binding and to firmness of a tie, and every branch of this chapter goes back to it.
1. ʿaqd al-bināʾ, the vaulting of a building, plural aʿqād and ʿuqūd. Al-Khalīl said: I have not heard a verb made from it. But if one said ʿaqqada taʿqīdan, meaning he built an arch, that would be allowed. And ʿaqadtu al-ḥabl, aʿqiduhu, ʿaqdan, I tied the rope; it becomes tied (inʿaqada), and that knot is al-ʿuqda.
2. Belonging to the same meaning, but with a letter added to keep the senses apart: aʿqadtu al-ʿasal, I thickened the honey by cooking; it becomes inʿaqada, thickened; honey so thickened is ʿaqīd or munʿaqid. A poet said, in a line of verse (this line is obscure to me and I give only my best sense of it):

As if syrup had flowed, once thickened ... down the firm jowls of some massive, rugged thing

3. ʿāqadtuhu is like ʿāhadtuhu, I made a pact with him; that is al-ʿaqd, plural ʿuqūd. God, Most High, said: {Fulfil your pacts} [al-Māʾida: 1]. Al-ʿaqd is also the binding of an oath, from which His saying, Most High: {But He will call you to account for the oaths you have bound} [al-Māʾida: 89].
4. ʿuqdat al-nikāḥ, and of anything, is its becoming binding and settled. Al-ʿuqda in a sale is its being made binding.
5. Al-ʿuqda is a landed estate, plural ʿuqad. One says fulān iʿtaqada ʿuqdatan, so-and-so acquired an estate; and iʿtaqada an amount of property, or a brother, meaning he came to possess it.
6. He 'tied' his heart on such a thing, so that he does not turn from it. A thing iʿtaqada, became hard. Brotherhood iʿtaqada, became firm.
7. Al-ʿaqīd is food thickened with honey.
8. Al-maʿāqid are the places where a string of beads is knotted. A poet said, in a line of verse (this line looks cut off in the text before me, giving only its first half):

the knots of its string were not joined

9. ʿIqd al-qilāda is what encircles the neck, that is, its measure. Al-Durayd said: al-miʿqād is a thread on which beads are strung.
10. Al-Khalīl said: ʿaqada al-raml is sand that has piled up and gathered, plural aʿqād; it is rarely said ʿaqid and ʿaqidāt, though that is allowed. Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:

Between the day and the night, dunes piled up ... on whose sides grow asbāṭ-plants and drooping foliage

Among their proverbs: 'more foolish than the dust of the sand-heap,' meaning the piled sand, whose foolishness is that dust never stays settled in it but only crumbles away; and 'thirstier than the piled sand,' and 'more absorbent than the piled sand,' meaning it drinks up all the rain and light dew that falls on it.
Al-Khalīl said: a she-camel is ʿāqid when she has 'become firm' (I am not fully sure whether this means she has conceived or grown firm-bodied).
11. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: ʿuqdat al-shajar is trees enough to sustain the livestock for their whole year. Another said: it is trees that have massed together and taken firm root. A place thick with trees is also called ʿuqda. All that is said of the ʿuqda of trees and plants goes back to this same sense; there is no point padding the chapter with repetition.
They say: 'more attached to a place than the crow of the ʿuqda,' whose crow never flies off, meaning it finds there all it wants.
12. One says: the ground iʿtaqadat the rain of its year, that is, when it has been rained on so heavily that a man digging into the moist soil sinks his hand in until, as he digs, his ear touches the ground, the moist soil holding firm and unbroken.
Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: ʿuqad of houses and lands is taken from ʿuqad of pasture, because in both there is sufficiency and provision.
13. ʿaqada al-karm, of a grapevine: when you see its wood has dried of its sap and stopped growing.
14. And ʿaqada al-ifṭ (I do not know what al-ifṭ names here; I give the phrase as it stands rather than guess).
It is said that ʿakad al-lisān, also called ʿaqad, is the thickness in the middle of the tongue. A man is ʿaqid when there is a 'knot' in his tongue; such a man is aʿqad.
15. A gazelle-doe is ʿāqid when she twists her neck back. Al-aʿqad, among he-goats and gazelles, is the one whose horn has a knot in it. Al-Nābigha said, of the twist-necked gazelle-does, in a line of verse:

They strike out with their forelegs, behind the young gazelle-fawns ... fair of face, like the twist-necked does

16. What Ibn al-Sikkīt related: a base man is aʿqad, when he is not easy-natured. Al-Ṭirimmāḥ said, in lines of verse:

And if I wished, I would drive on a saying ... upon its plain, unmistakable marks

against a man crooked, base on both sides ... whose own kinsfolk bring him the disgrace of his life

It is said that al-aʿqad here is the dog, that he likened him to it.
17. A she-camel maʿqūdat al-qarā, meaning firm of back. He recited, in a line of verse:

taut of hock-sinew, firm of back ... pressing steadily on when the noble long-striders tire

18. A camel is ʿaqd, meaning tightly built in its frame. Al-Nābigha said:

How is her dwelling reached, except by a firm bond ... tightly made, that no treachery can undo

19. One says: the clouds taʿaqqada, when they become as if a vault struck up and built.
It is said of a man: 'his knots have come undone,' when his anger has settled.
It is said: 'he has tied up his forelock,' when he has grown angry and readied himself for trouble. A poet said, in a line of verse (again only half the line is before me):

with the whip-lashes of a people, tying up their forelocks

It is said: the dogs taʿāqadat, when they mate.
20. Al-Durayd said: 'so-and-so ʿaqqada his speech,' when he made it obscure and knotted. It is said that al-muʿaqqid is the sorcerer. A poet said, in a line of verse:

Her glance ties the knots of the two Babylonians' magic ... again and again, while she pours us the choicest wine

This was said because the sorcerer ties knots for his spell. It has come in the Book of God, Most High: {and from the evil of the women who blow upon knots} [al-Falaq: 4] — meaning the sorceresses who tie knots into threads and blow on them.
21. It is said, when a flood-valley closes upon a people and destroys them: 'it ʿaqada upon them.'
22. Resembling this root is their calling a short man aʿqad, because he is like a knot; al-ʿuqd are short men. A poet said, in a line of verse (this line describes spearheads, and its exact images are not fully certain to me):

honey-gold spearheads, blue-grey their points ... when they aim them, neither crooked nor bent
عقر:
The letters 'ayn, qaf and ra are two roots, far apart from each other in meaning; each is regular in its sense, gathering together the meanings of its branches.

The first is a wound, or what resembles a wound — a gash or gouge in a thing. The second indicates fixity and permanence.

The first: it is Al-Khalil's statement — al-'aqr is like a wound. One says 'aqartu l-farasa', I hamstrung the horse, that is, I struck its legs with the sword. A horse so struck is 'aqir' and 'ma'qur'; hamstrung horses are 'khaylun 'aqra'. Ziyad said, in a line of verse:
And when you pass by his grave, sacrifice there the humped white she-camels and every swift, well-bred horse.

Labid said:
When Lubad saw the eagles scatter in flight, he raised his flight-feathers like the hamstrung, weaponless one.
He likened the eagle to a hamstrung horse. The she-camel is hamstrung until she falls, and once fallen he slaughters her while he holds her fast. Imru' al-Qays said:
And the day I sacrificed my riding-camel for the young women — how strange was the burden its saddle carried!

Al-'aqqar is one who is harsh with camels, not gentle with them in loading their pack-saddles, so that he galls their backs. 'Aqartu zahra l-dabba' — I galled the riding animal's back. Imru' al-Qays said:
She said, as the litter tilted with the two of us: You have lamed my camel, O Imru' al-Qays — so dismount!

Their saying ''aqarta bi' — you have detained me — is not to be taken literally as its plain wording; rather its meaning is that he held him back as though he had hamstrung his she-camel, so that he cannot travel. Likewise the saying (obscure in the text, rendered as best as can be made out): the mother of al-Khazraj held the people back — when she moved she seemed to flow rather than roll along.

One says 'ta'aqqara l-ghayth' — the rain lingered/stayed, as if it were a thing hamstrung, unable to move on.

From this root: al-'aqir among women — the one who cannot conceive, as though she were 'hamstrung' (ma'qura). Barren women are 'nisa'un 'awaqir'; the verb is 'aqarat ta'qiru 'aqran', though ''aqirat ta'qaru' is the better form. Al-Khalil said this is because it is something that befalls her from outside herself, not from any act of her own. In hadith: 'old, barren women' ('ujuzun 'uqqar').

Abu Zayd said: 'aqarati l-mar'a and 'aqirat [both forms are used], and a barren man is 'aqir'; by strict analogy it should have been ''aqurat', since it is an intransitive verb of state, as one says 'zarufa' and 'karuma' [became refined; became noble].

In the proverb: 'more barren than a mule.' A poet, describing an eagle, said:
She has a fledgling in the nest for which she has made a bed, just as a beautiful but barren woman prepares herself for her husband.
That is because the barren woman is more devoted in adorning herself for her husband and more attentive to him, since she has no child to occupy her or distract her from him.

They say: 'laqihati l-naqa 'an 'uqr', the she-camel conceived after a period of barrenness, just as one says 'after a period of infertility' ('an 'uqm).

Among what is carried on this sense: their calling the compensation owed for violating a woman 'al-'uqr' — when she has been forced. This is something the Arabs do, naming one thing by the name of a nearby thing when the two are close. So the bride-price too was called 'uqr, because it is taken on account of the 'uqr [the act of defloration]. Their saying 'the egg of al-'uqr' is a name for the last egg a hen ever lays, after which she lays no more; it is used as a proverb for anything after which nothing of its kind follows.

Al-Khalil said: I heard a Bedouin of the people of al-Samman say that every gap between two things is 'aqr and 'uqr; he put his hand between the two legs of the dining-table while we were eating and said: what is between them is 'uqr. One says the palm tree is 'cut' ('uqr) — its crown is severed so that nothing ever again grows from its trunk; that is al-'aqr, and such a palm is 'aqira. One says of pasture that harms and kills camels: 'kala'un 'aqar'.

As for their saying 'rafa'a 'aqiratahu', he raised his voice in song or recitation — this too is by association: it comes from [the image of] a man whose one leg had been cut off, so he raised it and rested it on the other and cried out at the top of his voice; then the expression came to be used for anyone who raised his voice. Al-'aqira is the severed leg, and since raising the voice happened in connection with it, the voice itself came to be called by that name.

As for their saying 'I never saw an 'aqira like so-and-so', meaning the eminent/noble man — its origin is that it used to be said of a great, illustrious man who was killed: 'I never saw, as I saw today, an 'aqira among a people!' A poet said (the line is obscure and is rendered as best it can be):
When the horsemen scattered their flock, the best of those who hamstring was hamstrung by a hamstringer.

Al-Khalil said: in cursing one says ''aqran lahu wa jad'an' — may he be hamstrung and maimed. One says to a woman 'halqa 'aqra' — meaning: may God afflict her, that is injure her body, and afflict her throat, that is strike her with pain in the throat. Some said it describes her as ill-omened, meaning she brings ruin and injury upon her people. One says ''aqqartu l-rajula' when you said to him 'aqra halqa' [that curse]. It is related of some Bedouin: 'I neither plucked the patch of matted pasture nor came upon it/exhausted it' — al-ruq'a being matted, tangled pasture-growth; one says its herbage is plucked but not cut down to nothing.

They say: 'the bane of knowledge is forgetting' (on the pattern of a word meaning indigestion) — meaning that forgetting injures it. The mixtures used in medicine are called al-'aqaqir, singular 'aqqar, so named as if it 'wounds' the innards. One says al-'aqar is an ailment that seizes a person at a sudden fright so that he cannot move, and his legs give way beneath him.

Al-Khalil said: a galling saddle is 'sarjun mi'qar', and a biting dog is 'kalbun 'aqur'. Ibn al-Sikkit said: a biting dog is 'kalbun 'aqur', and a galling saddle is 'sarjun 'uqara' and 'mi'qar'. Al-Ba'ith said, in a line of verse:
A galling pack-saddle pressed relentlessly on their shoulders.
One also says a galling saddle is 'mi'qar' and ''aqqar' and 'mi'qar'.

As for the second root: al-'aqr is the stronghold that serves as the refuge the people of a settlement fall back on. Labid said:
Like the stronghold of the man of Hajar, when he built it with uniform bricks shaped to one mould.
Here 'al-ashbah' means fired bricks, because they are all struck to one and the same shape.

Abu 'Ubayd said: al-'aqr is any elevated structure. Al-Khalil said: 'uqr al-dar is the encampment of a people, between the dwelling and the watering-trough, whether or not there was a building there. He cited, for Aws ibn Maghra':
In the time we drove them from the seat of their homeland, until it settled and brought them near Hawran.

He said: al-'uqr is the base/root of anything. 'Uqr al-hawd is where the camels stand at the trough when they come to drink. Dhu al-Rumma said (the line is obscure, rendered as best as can be made out):
At its edges the ticks are wasted, as though they were scattered husks of crushed, dry colocynth seed.
meaning the edges of the trough. And he said, concerning the 'uqr of the trough:
He struck her in the flank-muscles, from opposite the trough, or from its rear.
One calls a she-camel that drinks from the rear of the trough 'aqira, and one that drinks facing it 'aziya.

From this root: 'uqr al-nar, the gathered mass of a fire's embers. A line (obscure, rendered as best as can be made out):
And in the depth of the quiver are keen-edged arrows, as though their heads were the heart of a fire cut open.

Al-Khalil said: al-'aqar is a man's landed estate, plural al-'aqarat. One says: he has neither house nor estate. Ibn al-A'rabi said: al-'aqar is well-guarded property, and a man with abundant property is 'mu'qir'.

Abu Muhammad al-Qutaybi said: al-'uqayra is a name built from ''uqr al-dar' [the seat of the household]. From it comes the hadith of Umm Salama to 'A'isha: 'Stay settled in your home, and do not go out into the open' — meaning: keep to your house.

Among what is likened to al-'aqr in the sense of 'stronghold': al-'aqr is [also] a cloud that rises up from before the sun and covers its disc and what is around it. Humayd said (obscure, rendered as best as can be made out):
And when it rises where it rests, you see it like the stronghold-cloud, set apart by the rain-cloud around it.

It has been said that wine is called al-'uqar because it 'clings to' the wine-jar (i.e. it stays constantly with it, 'aqarat al-dann). Al-'aqir, of sand, is that which grows nothing, as though it were sifted flour. This is the second root.

There remain some place-names that may be derived from some of what we have mentioned. Among them: 'Aqara', a place. Humayd said (a line about wine, obscure, rendered as best as can be made out):
A still, potent draught, whose water was tinged by aged wine from the vineyards of 'Aqara'.

Al-'Aqr is a place in Babylon where Yazid ibn al-Muhallab was killed; that day is called the Day of al-'Aqr. Al-Tirimmah said:
You boasted of the Day of al-'Aqr, east of Babylon, when Tamim showed cowardice there and grew few.

'Aqra is [the name of] a body of water. A line:
Has it not reached Salma that her beloved is by the water of 'Aqra, upon one of the riding-camels?
عقرب: A well-known creature [the scorpion]; the bāʾ in it is an added letter, for the word is really from al-ʿaqr [wounding]. It is then used figuratively, so it is said of one who stings people: his scorpions are crawling. An animal that is muʿaqrab al-khalq is one whose build is compact, tightly knit and firm.
عقز: The letters ʿayn, qāf and zāʾ form no pattern resembling the speech of the Arabs, and likewise ʿayn-qāf-sīn, and qāf-shīn, though they do say al-ʿaqsh is a certain plant or herb. It is nothing.
عقص:
The letters ʿayn, qāf and ṣād are one sound root, denoting a twisting in a thing.

1. al-ʿaqaṣ — al-Khalīl said: a twist in a billy-goat's horn, or any horn; kabshun aʿqaṣ, a ram with such horns, shātun ʿaqṣāʾ, a ewe.
2. al-ʿaqaṣ, also — Ibn Durayd said: stiffness of the hand, withholding it from giving. One says huwa ʿaqiṣu al-yadayn or aʿqaṣu al-yadayn, when he is tight-fisted, miserly.
3. al-ʿaqiṣ, of men — al-Shaybānī said: the twisted, obstinate, difficult one, plural aʿqāṣ. He said: 'I have wrestled with a stubborn, twisted spirit.'
4. al-ʿaqṣ / ʿaqīṣah — al-Khalīl said: taking each lock of hair and twisting it, then knotting it so a twist stays in it, then letting it go. Every such lock is ʿaqīṣah, plural ʿaqāʾiṣ or ʿiqāṣ. One says ʿaqaṣa shaʿrahu, when he plaited and twisted it. It is also said al-ʿaqṣ is twisting the hair on the head and tucking its ends back into its roots, from their saying qarnun aʿqaṣ, a twisted horn. Every such twist is ʿiqṣah or ʿaqīṣah. Imruʾ al-Qays said: 'His braided locks rise upward, the plaits lost among the doubled and the loose.' It is also said al-ʿiqāṣ is the cord with which the ends of tresses are bound.
5. al-ʿaqiṣ, of sands — a stretch of sand with no path through it. He said: 'How did she find her way, with the sand-hills between, and the twisted, confusing dunes of ʿĀlij beyond?'
6. al-miʿqaṣ — Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: an arrow whose head breaks off leaving its tang behind, so it is drawn out, the base of the head hammered out long, and put back in place, yet does not fill the hole it left, being now too thin, taken from the term for the twisted-horned ewe.
7. al-ʿuqayṣāʾ — among the parts of the stomach, one so called.
8. al-ʿaqiṣ, of the tripe — they also say this is the neck of the tripe. He recited: 'Have you anything left, of what you ate yesterday, of tripe or neck-of-tripe or head?'

Al-Khalīl said, on Imruʾ al-Qays's line 'the plaits lost among the doubled and the loose,' it means the woman who sometimes takes a hairpiece from someone else's hair that gets lost among her own on her head. It is also said he means she has so much hair that whatever is plaited does not show clearly amid all that remains.
عقف:
The letters ʿayn, qāf and fāʾ are one sound root, denoting the bending and curving of a thing. Al-Khalīl said: ʿaqaftu al-shayʾa fa-anā aʿqifuhu ʿaqfan, wa-huwa maʿqūf, when I bend and curve it; and inʿaqafa huwa inʿiqāfan, like inʿaṭafa.

1. al-ʿuqqāfah — like a crook-staff.
2. aʿqaf — everything with a curve in it. The poor man is also called aʿqaf, perhaps so named for his stooping and his low state. He said: 'O you crooked one, driving on your mount, seeking neither favour from me nor wealth.'
3. al-ʿuqāf — a disease that seizes a sheep in its legs so that they bend; a sheep with it is ʿāqif or maʿqūfat al-rijlayn. It may afflict any animal, and each is aʿqaf.
4. ʿaqūf — Abū Ḥātim said: among cows' udders there is one so called, whose milk-stream goes crooked when milked.
5. aʿrābiyyun aʿqaf — one says this meaning uncouth and coarse, not yet made gentle, as if he were still bent and had not straightened out. A camel with a stoop in it is likewise aʿqaf.

And God knows best.
عقل:
The letters ʿayn, qāf and lām are a single root, regular and consistent, the greater part of which points to a holding back in a thing, or to what comes near to holding back. From that is al-ʿaql, the mind, and it is what holds a man back from blameworthy speech and deed.

Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿaql is the opposite of ignorance. One says ʿaqala yaʿqilu ʿaqlan when he comes to know what he was ignorant of before, or restrains himself from what he had been doing. Its plural is ʿuqūl. A man of sense is ʿāqil, and a people of sense are ʿuqalā' and ʿāqilūn. A man is ʿaqūl when his understanding is good and his mind is ample. And mā lahu maʿqūl — he has no maʿqūl, that is, no sense; it came out on the pattern of al-majlūd for jalāda, endurance, and al-maysūr for yusr, ease. A poet said, in a line of verse:
It has brought them good sense and a warning ... for whoever has a mind's wit and understanding.

And they say in the proverb: "Many a simpleton has good sense." And they say: "He came to know a slain man and lacked a man of understanding." And they say: so-and-so is ʿaqūl for talk — his hearing lets no word slip away from him.

And of this chapter is al-maʿqil and al-ʿaql, and it is the fortress; its plural is ʿuqūl. Uḥayḥa said, in a line of verse:
I have made ready against the blows of fate a stronghold hard to take ... if only fortresses could profit a man.
He means fortresses.

And of this chapter is al-ʿaql, and it is the blood-money. One says ʿaqaltu al-qatīl aʿqiluhu ʿaqlan when you pay the blood-money for the slain man. A poet said, in a line of verse:
That I should kill Sulayk and then pay his blood-money ... is like the bull beaten when the cows refuse to drink.

Al-Aṣmaʿī: ʿaqaltu al-qatīl — I paid his blood-money. And ʿaqalta ʿan fulān when you pay the fine for his offence. He said: I spoke about that to Abū Yūsuf the judge in the presence of al-Rashīd, and he did not tell apart ʿaqaltuhu and ʿaqaltu ʿanhu until I made him understand it.

And al-ʿāqila are the people among whom the blood-money is shared out from their own wealth when the man was killed by mistake; they are the killer's nearest paternal cousins and his brothers. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: ṣāra damu fulān maʿqulatan ʿalā qawmihi — so-and-so's blood became a blood-debt upon his people, that is, they came to pay his blood-money.

And some of the learned say: a woman is on a par with a man in blood-money up to a third of her blood-money. They mean that her mūḍiḥa, the head wound that lays the bone bare, and his are the same; but when the payment goes beyond a third of the blood-money, the woman's blood-money becomes half the man's.

And "the sons of so-and-so are upon the maʿāqil they were upon in the days before Islam" means their ranks in the payments of blood-money; the singular is maʿqula. They also said: the blood-money was called ʿaql because the camels that used to be taken in blood-money were gathered and tethered, tuʿqal, in the courtyard of the slain man; so the payment was called ʿaql even when it is dirhams and dinars. And it is said it was called ʿaql because it holds back the blood.

Al-Khalīl said: when the alms-collector takes the alms due on camels in full for one year it is said: he took an ʿiqāl; and two ʿiqāls for two years. And "he took no naqd" means he took no price, but took the alms in kind as it stood. And he recited:
He collected one year's alms and left us not a rag ... so how if ʿAmr had collected two years' alms?

And the people of the language say that the alms-tax altogether is ʿiqāl. One says: so-and-so was set over the ʿiqāl of the sons of so-and-so, that is, over their alms-payments. They said: it was called ʿiqāl because it holds back from its owner the demand made for it, and holds back from him the sin as well.

And they explained the saying of Abū Bakr, when the Arabs withheld the alms-tax: "By God, if they withheld from me an ʿiqāl of what they used to pay to the Messenger of God — may God bless him and his family and grant them peace — I would fight them for it." They said: he meant by it one year's alms. And they also said: he meant by al-ʿiqāl the trifling, paltry thing, and made the hobbling-rope with which a camel is tied a byword for that. And it is said that when a man gave the alms due on his camels he gave with them their hobbling-ropes and their watering-cords.

Al-Aṣmaʿī said: ʿaqala al-ẓaby yaʿqilu ʿuqūlan when it takes refuge up in the mountain. And one says ʿaqala al-ṭaʿām baṭnahu when the food binds his belly. And al-ʿaqūl among medicines is what binds the belly. He said: and one says iʿtaqala rumḥahu when he sets his spear between his stirrup and his shin. And iʿtaqala shātahu when he puts the ewe's leg between his thigh and his shin and milks her. And so-and-so has a hold, ʿuqla, by which he locks people up, when he wrestles them and hooks their legs. And one says ʿaqaltu al-baʿīr aʿqiluhu ʿaqlan when you bind the camel's foreleg with its ʿiqāl, which is the tie. And among their proverbs:
The stallion guards his herd even when hobbled.
And uʿtuqila lisān fulān — so-and-so's tongue was tied, when he is held back from speech.

As for their saying "so-and-so is the ʿaqīla of her people", she is the noblest and the choicest of them. A chief is described so too, and one says: he is the ʿaqīla of his people. And the ʿaqīla of anything is the noblest of it. And the pearl is the ʿaqīla of the sea. Ibn Qays al-Ruqayyāt said, in a line of verse:
A pearl of the choice ones of the sea, still unpierced ... unmarred by the drills of the pearl-borers.

And the reasoning of this was reported from Ibn al-Aʿrābī; they said on his authority: she was called ʿaqīla only because she held her companions back from reaching her rank. But al-Khalīl said: rather its meaning is that she was kept back, ʿuqilat, in her curtained chamber. Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
The choicest of her companions, not ugly ... nor of ill make, if you look closely, and coarse.

Abū ʿUbayda said: al-ʿaqīla is the same for the male and the female. A poet said, in a line of verse:
A young camel that outstrips the full-grown and the young ... a choice one of noble Mahrī stock.

And of this chapter is al-ʿaqal in the legs — the knocking together of the knees. One says a camel is aʿqal, and it has ʿaqila ʿaqalan. And he recited:
A man of war, who puts on its trappings ... and is no slinker in among the women, knock-kneed.

And al-ʿuqqāl is a disease that takes riding beasts in the legs, and it is sometimes said light, ʿuqāl. And a beast is maʿqūla and has ʿuqqāl when it walks as though it were pulling its legs out of a rock. Most often that happens among sheep.

Abū ʿUbayda said: a woman is ʿaqlā' when she is slender in the shins and thick in the calves. Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿāqūl of a river, of a valley, and of affairs too, is what is tangled and crooked.

And it was reported from Ibn al-Aʿrābī, though we did not hear it directly, that al-ʿiqāl is the well whose bottom is near; it was called ʿiqāl because its water is close, as though it were drawn up with a hobbling-rope; and that was reported from Abū ʿUbayda as well.

And near to this chapter is al-ʿaqanqal of sand, and it is what is heaped up of it; its plural is ʿaqāqīl. It was named so only for its heaping and gathering together. And from it is ʿaqanqal al-ḍabb, the lizard's gut.

And they say: "Feed your brother from the gut of the lizard" — it is used as a byword, and they say it is good to eat. As for al-Aṣmaʿī, he said that it is thrown away, and that "Feed your brother from the gut of the lizard" is said in mockery. They said: it was called ʿaqanqal only for its coiling and twisting; and everything that coils and twists is ʿaqanqal. And from this the shoots of the vine were called ʿaqāqīl, because they are twisted. A poet said, in a line of verse:
We cut the necks of the people from every side as the vine-shoots are cut by one who knows them.

As for the names that have come from this build, and they may perhaps be regular: ʿĀqil is a particular mountain. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Whose are the dwellings at Rāmatayn and ʿĀqil ... effaced, their traces changed by the rain?

Abū ʿUbayda said: Banū ʿĀqil are the clan of al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥujr; they were named so because they camped at ʿĀqil, and they are kings.

And Maʿqila is a place in the desert. And he recited:
And an eye, as though the two Babylonians had clothed ... your heart with sorcery from it on the day of Maʿqula.

And Aws said, in a line of verse:
The hollow of al-Sulayy, then al-Sikhāl, were emptied ... then Maʿqula on to Muṭār and Wāḥif.

Al-Aṣmaʿī said: in al-Dahnā' there is a clay hollow called Maʿqula.

And Dhū al-ʿUqqāl is a well-known horse. And he recited:
It is as though they had wiped upon their donkey's face ... at al-Raqmatayn the brow of Dhū al-ʿUqqāl.
عقم:
The letters 'ayn, qāf and mīm are a single root indicating obscurity, narrowness and severity.

1. ḥarbun 'aqāmun wa-'uqāmun — a war so severe that no one relents toward another in it.
2. dā'un 'uqāmun — an incurable disease.
3. rajulun 'aqāmun — a man narrow and hard of temper. A line of verse says:
You are 'aqām — no desire of his is ever met, a man of ambition who yet wastes it in delay.
4. 'aqimat al-raḥimu 'uqman — an injury befalling the womb so that it will not accept a child. One says 'aqimat al-mar'atu and 'uqimat, the latter the better form. In hadith: "The spines of the hypocrites will be seized up so that they cannot prostrate," meaning the stiffening of their joints. One says rajulun 'aqīmun, rijālun 'uqamā'u, and niswatun ma'qūmātun and 'aqā'imu and 'uqumun.

Abū 'Amr said: 'uqimati al-mar'atu, said when a woman bears no children. Ibn al-A'rābī said: 'uqimati al-mar'atu 'aqman, she is ma'qūmatun and 'aqīmun, and it is said of a man too: 'uqima, so he is 'aqīmun and ma'qūmun. Sometimes they said 'aqamtu fulānata, meaning I bewitched her so that her womb became ma'qūma, unable to bear children.

Al-Khalīl said: 'aqlun 'aqīmun, an intellect that brings its owner no benefit. It is related that intellect is of two kinds: 'aqlun 'aqīmun, the intellect of the man given to this world, and 'aqlun muthmirun, a fruitful intellect, the intellect of the man given to the next world.

One says al-mulku 'aqīmun, kingship is barren, because a man will kill his own father for the sake of it, meaning that it shuts the door on keeping faith with kinship. Al-dunyā 'aqīmun, worldly life returns no good to the one who has it. Al-rīḥ al-'aqīmu, the wind that fertilizes neither tree nor cloud. God, exalted is He, said: {and in 'Ād, when We sent against them the barren wind} [al-Dhāriyāt: 41] — it is said this was the west wind. Al-Kisā'ī said: one says 'aqimat 'alayhimu al-rīḥu, ta'qamu 'uqman. Al-'aqīm of land is what you break open by digging into it. A line says:
He took, among us, between his two ears, a blow that summoned him to the dusty, barren ground.

Al-Khalīl said: al-i'tiqām is the digging into the sides of a well. Rabī'a ibn Maqrūm said:
And stagnant, deserted pools of water ... whose sides the wild beasts dig into.
It is called i'tiqām because it is done to the side, and that is evidence of the narrowness already mentioned.

From this chapter: al-mu'āqim, one who disputes, the sense being that he closes his opponent in narrowly with words.

Al-Shaybānī used to say: this is 'uqmī speech, meaning speech from the time before Islam, not understood. He claimed he asked a man of Hudhayl known as Abū 'Iyāḍ about an obscure word of Hudhayl's dialect, and the man said: this is 'uqmī speech, from the speech of the pre-Islamic age, not spoken today. They say the barrier set between the straw and the grain, when the grain is winnowed, is called mi'qam.
عقنباة: the formidable one among eagles; the plural is ʿaqanbayāt. This is a word to which extra letters were added for emphasis and magnification. It also illustrates the very method we have followed in these comparisons, for no one doubts that ʿaqanbāh's origin is ʿuqāb (eagle), but letters were added to it for the reason we gave. Understand that.
عقو:
The letters ʿayn, qāf, and the weak final letter make up words that follow no single pattern and are not gathered under one root, though each is sound in itself.

1. al-ʿaqwah — what lies around a dwelling. One says mā yaṭūru bi-ʿaqwati fulānin aḥad, meaning no one comes near his encampment.
2. al-ʿiqy — what comes out of an infant's belly at birth.
3. al-ʿiqyān — said to be gold that grows of itself, not among what is extracted from rock.
4. al-iʿtiqāʾ — like al-iʿtiqām in a well, which we have already discussed.
5. ʿaqqā al-ṭāʾiru — when a bird rises high in its flight; and ʿaqqā bi-sahmihi fī al-hawāʾ. It is recited: 'They shot an arrow high, unnoticed by anyone, then they cried out for help and said, how fine the mark.'
6. aʿqā al-shayʾu — when its bitterness grows intense.
عك:
The letters ʿayn and kāf are three sound roots: one is intensity of heat; another is confinement; and another is a kind of striking.

The first: al-ʿakka is heat, a violent surge of it in the height of summer, which is the most intense heat there is, when the wind lies still. One also says al-akka, with a hamza. Al-Farrā' said: this is called "arḍun ʿakkatun" and "ʿukkatun," a land in a heat-haze. He said: in a land, sticky, damp-heated. Ibn Durayd said: "ʿakka our day" means its wind fell still and its heat grew intense. Ibn al-A'rābī said: al-ʿukka is intensity of heat together with mugginess and a stilled wind. Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿukka also means a stretch of sand that the sun has heated up. Abū Zayd said: al-ʿukka is a dampness found near the sea — dew and moisture that falls by night; this only happens along with heat. The Arabs say: "When al-'Udhra rises, there is early heat-haze upon the people of Basra, and there is no fresh date in Oman, nor any seed for a farmer there." Al-Liḥyānī said: a day that is ʿakk, akk, is intensely hot. The Arabs say, in their rhymed sayings: "When al-Simāk rises, the heat-hazes depart, and the crowding at the water lessens." A day dhū ʿakīk is a hot day.

Ṭarafa said:
It drives off the cold with a burning heat, and the summer's heat-haze, if a chill should come.

As for the other root, al-Farrā' said: camels *maʿkūka* are penned in. And "*ʿukka* so-and-so" means he was detained.

Ru'ba said:
O son of one high in lineage and origin, what do you make of the counsel of a brother now detained?

1. "*ʿakaktuhu bi-kadhā, aʿukkuhu ʿakkan*" — I put him off, delayed him. From it also, "*ʿakkanī fulānun bi'l-qawl*" — so-and-so wore me down, repeating something until he tired me.
2. *Al-ʿukka*, for clarified butter — a vessel smaller than a water-skin, plural *ʿukak* and *ʿikāk*; named so because the butter is gathered and kept in it, just as something is confined.
3. *Al-ʿakawwak* — a short, tightly-built man, that is, a short man.

He said: a short, tightly-built one, when he walks, waddling heavily. He was named this by resemblance to the butter-vessel. Al-ʿakawwakān is like it.

He said: a short, tightly-built one with a broad chest.

4. Al-miʿakk, of horses — one that runs a little, then needs to be struck; this too is from the sense of holding back.

As for the third root, Ibn al-A'rābī said: "*ʿakkahu* with the whip" means he struck him; one also says *ʿakkahu* and *ṣakkahu*, in the same sense. Also from this chapter: "*ʿakkat-hu* al-ḥummā," the fever wracked him.

He said:
And a care that the pangs of grief seize hold of, wracking with a burning fever or with distress.

It is possible this belongs to the first root, as though the fever were named for its heat. One also says, in the sense of striking, "*ʿakkahu* bi'l-ḥujja," he overpowered him with the argument.

It has also been said in this chapter that al-ʿukka of pregnant she-camels is a colour that comes over them, reddish at one time, ash-grey at another. And that so-and-so said: "so-and-so wrapped himself in a wrap, ʿakkā wakkā." All of this has no clear sense and nothing to be built upon.

Something close to this has also been related from al-Khalīl: that al-ʿakankaʿ is the wicked male among the ghouls.

He quoted:
As if she and he, when the two of them traded insults, were a ghoul contending fiercely, wicked, ʿakankaʿ.

This is close, in its weakness, to what came before it. I think al-Khalīl's book grew a little diminished, in the eyes of scholars, on account of such tales as these.
عكب:
The letters ʿayn, kāf and bāʾ are a single sound root, and it is not far from the chapter before it — it too points to gathering together. One says the camels have ʿukūb at the watering trough, meaning crowding.

1. al-ʿakab — thickness in a person's jaw (Al-Khalīl said this).
2. ʿakbāʾ — a slave woman coarse and rough in nature, one of the thick-jawed (ʿukb) slave-women.
3. ʿakabat (of birds) — they gathered around them, so they are called ʿukūb, gathered. A poet said, in a line of verse: vultures from Shamām stay circling above them, gathered together with the eagles, the eagles of Yadhbul.
4. al-ʿakab (a second sense) — a crookedness of the big toe, like al-wakaʿ, a similar defect; this too comes from pressing together.
5. aʿkab — a man whose toes draw close to one another (some people said).
6. al-ʿakūb — the dust that horses raise (Al-Khalīl said this); ʿUkāba ibn Ṣaʿb was named from it. Bishr said: we carried them off the way dogs carry their pups, over every well-trodden track raising its own cloud of dust. Dust is called ʿakūb because it too gathers together. Abū Zayd said: al-ʿukāb is smoke, and that is sound, and fits the same reasoning given.
7. ʿikabb — a short man; every short man is compactly built.

As for al-Shaybānī's saying, "his ʿakūb has stirred up," meaning uproar and fighting — this is only by way of comparing what stirs up to rising dust and smoke. He recited: while we were hoping to catch you at dawn, uproar broke out among you at midnight. The doubling of the letter you see in it is a poetic necessity.
عكبرة:
Of women: the coarse, boorish one. Al-Khalīl said: she is ʿakbāʾ in her build. He said:
Coarse and thick-built, with a swell in her belly ... and a crookedness in the joints of her limbs.
It is plain here that the rāʾ has been added; the origin is al-ʿakab and al-ʿikabb, already mentioned.
عكد:
The letters ʿayn, kāf and dāl are a single sound root, pointing to the same thing as the one before it. Al-ʿukda is the root of the tongue. One says iʿtakada the thing, when he held fast to it.

Ibn al-Aʿrābī said this is derived from ʿakadat al-lisān, the root of the tongue. As for the saying of the poet — "the people meant by it will burn from it, and if not, then it is held ready for us, Umm Jundub" — its meaning is that this is possible for us, prepared, agreed upon. Umm Jundub means wrong and oppression. The root of the heart is also called ʿakda.

1. ʿakada al-ḍabb ʿakdan — the lizard grew fat and its flesh thickened. Al-ʿakd is like al-kidna, which is fatness. In plants, al-ʿakd is said to be thickness and abundance.
2. shajar ʿakid — trees whose dead wood lies dry, packed one part upon another.
3. nāqa ʿakida — a she-camel dense with fat.
4. istaʿkada al-ḍabb — the lizard took refuge, sheltering by a rock or a burrow. Al-Ṭirimmāḥ said: whenever it took refuge from him in every rocky hollow, he was there to meet it at every place it might run.

And ʿukida is like ḥubisa, was confined. Anything prepared and made ready is called maʿkūd.
عكر:
The letters ʿayn, kāf and rāʾ are a single sound root, pointing to the same thing as the one before it: gathering and piling up. One says the night iʿtakara, when its darkness thickened and grew dense. A poet said: the night stretched long over us, and grew thick and dark. One says the rain iʿtakara in a place, when it grew heavy and abundant, and the wind iʿtakara with dust, when it brought it along in masses.

1. al-ʿakir — the dregs of oil. One says the drink ʿakira, yaʿkiru, ʿakaran, grew turbid, and I ʿakkartuhu when I put dregs into it.
2. ʿakara ʿalā qirnihi — he turned back against his opponent, because in doing so he presses close against him. A poet said: O Zamal, if you become my guide, I shall turn back upon you, and if you swerve we shall not race ahead.
3. al-maʿkir — a place to turn back to, a place of return; one says "he has no maʿkir," meaning no refuge, no turning-back. Al-maʿkir is also said to mean the root of a thing — this is the sound reasoning, because everything presses close to its own root. "So-and-so returned to his ʿikr" means his origin. They say, "Lamīs has returned to her ʿikr."
4. al-ʿakar — a huge herd of camels, above five hundred head. A poet said: in it are the neighing horses, the banners, and the ʿakar.
5. ʿakara — a single group of that herd, plural ʿakar. Sometimes people lengthen the word while the meaning stays the same: al-ʿakarkar for thick milk. A poet said: he brought them the thick milk, a mean, low-born wretch both in descent and in glory.

Ibn Durayd mentions: taʿākara al-qawm, the people became mixed up together in a quarrel or the like.
عكركر: Thick milk. Here too the letters have been repeated; the origin is al-ʿakar.
عكز: The letters ʿayn, kāf and zāy are a small root, close to the chapter before it. Al-Duraydī said: al-ʿakz is contracting, drawing in; one says ʿakiza, yaʿkazu, ʿakzan. As for al-ʿukkāza, the walking-staff, I think it is Arabic, and perhaps it was so named because the fingers gather together and close upon it when they grip it. That is not far-fetched.
عكس:
The letters ʿayn, kāf and sīn are a single sound root, pointing to the same thing spoken of before: gathering and collecting.

1. al-ʿakīs, of milk — fresh milk with melted fat poured over it. Al-Khalīl said this. A poet said: when we gave her the ʿakīs to drink, her insides filled and her throat-vein ran wet, bursting with it. Al-madhākhir are the intestines that store up the food.
2. al-ʿaks — Al-Khalīl said it is your turning the end of a thing back onto its beginning, like a fold; one says taʿakkasa in his walking.
3. al-ʿaks — the hobbling of a camel's forelegs, tying them together with its neck, so that it cannot raise its head.
4. The proverb: "min dūni dhālika al-amr ʿikās," short of that there is ʿikās — meaning going back and forth, retreat and return.
عكش:
The letters ʿayn, kāf and shīn are a sound root, pointing to the same thing as the one before it: gathering.

1. ʿakisha shaʿruhu — his hair became matted. Hair that has matted is called mutaʿakkish, and it has taʿakkasha. Durayd said: you wished for me Qays ibn Saʿd, foolishly, though you are a man whom troops of horsemen cannot surround; you are a man stiff-napped, matted-haired, from year-old dried curd, full-bellied and gorged. Ibn al-Aʿrābī recited: when she captivates you with matted black hair, its locks loosened, dark, flowing.
2. In plants: nabāt ʿakish, when it is tangled together; it has ʿakisha, ʿakashan.

What is mentioned under this root all goes back to this same sense. In Al-Khalīl's book it is said that this pattern is unused — but a scholar can sometimes miss a chapter among the chapters, and there is more to say about it than that.
عكص: The letters ʿayn, kāf and ṣād are close to the one before it, except that it adds a further meaning: severity. Al-Farrāʾ said: a man is ʿakiṣ, meaning harsh and bad-natured. ʿakaṣ al-raml is the severity of its looseness, soft sinking sand; one says ramla ʿakiṣa, such sand.
عكف:
The letters ʿayn, kāf and fā' are a sound root pointing to facing a thing and to holding back. One says ʿakafa yaʿkufu and yaʿkifu ʿukūfan, and that is your turning toward a thing and not turning away from it. A poet said, in a line of verse:
So they keep to it when he holds fast, as the Nabaṭ keep to it, playing the fanzaja dance.

And one says ʿakafat al-ṭayr bi-l-qatīl — the birds kept about the slain man. ʿAmr said, in a line of verse:
We left the horses keeping their place over him, their reins slung upon them, standing still.

And al-ʿākif is al-muʿtakif, the one who keeps to a place in retreat. And from the section is their saying of a string when a jewel is strung on it: ʿukkifa taʿkīfan — it was gathered and set upon it. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And it is as if the strings of pearls, which the thread had gathered, lay on the two sides of a long-necked woman, mother of a fawn.

And al-maʿkūf is the one held back. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: one says mā ʿakafaka min kadhā — that is, what held you back from it. God, exalted be He, said: {and the offering held back from reaching its place} [al-Fatḥ: 25].
عكل:
The letters ʿayn, kāf and lām are one sound root, denoting gathering and drawing together. Al-Khalīl said: one says ʿakala al-sāʾiqu al-ibila yaʿkulu ʿaklan, when the herder draws the stragglers together and gathers them. Al-Farazdaq said: 'And, on the height of al-Amīl, they gathered together livestock, driven on to the chief and drawn in.'

1. ʿakaltu al-ibil — I held them back. Everything you gather, you have ʿakaltahu.
2. al-ʿawkal — the ridge of a gathered sand-heap. He said: 'By every coiled dune, or hilltop of clay-ground, and the ridge of every long-stretched sand-hill.'
3. al-ʿawkalah — said to mean a great mass of sand. He said: 'And opposing dunes rose up to meet it.'
4. al-ʿawkal, of women — their saying that it means the foolish woman is carried on the image of gathered, heaped sand, since it is always crumbling down — the woman with little self-restraint is likened to it, just as passed already regarding loose, crumbling soil in the entry on ʿaqd.
5. al-ʿawkal, of men — the short one, this too by the sense of being drawn together. He said: 'He is no shepherd of ewes, that short one.'
6. ibilun maʿkūlah — held back, hobbled, and this follows the sound reasoning. (ʿUkl is a known tribe.)
7. ʿakaltu al-matāʿ — baʿḍahu ʿalā baʿḍ, when I stacked it up together.
عكم:
The letters ʿayn, kāf and mīm are one sound root, denoting gathering and packing a thing into a container. Al-Khalīl said: one says ʿakamtu al-matāʿa aʿkimuhu ʿakman, when I gathered it into a container.

1. al-ʿikmān — the two packs tied to the two sides of a howdah. He said: 'O Lord, marry me to an old, aged woman — no luck, Lord, do I have with the young girls — who will tell me of her youth gone by, and feed me dates from her pack.' It is said in the proverb, of two equal things: 'They fell like the two packs.'
2. aʿkamtu al-rajula — I helped him carry his pack.
3. ʿākamtuhu — I carried a load along with him. Al-Quṭāmī said, of aʿkama: 'When a sand-grouse has filled her water-skin from it, do not load the other one, nor ask her help.' He means she carries water to her chicks in her crop, and once her own crop is full she does not help the other sand-grouse carry hers. You say aʿkimnī, meaning help me carry the pack; if you order him to carry it you say iʿkimnī, with kasra on the alif if you begin the sentence with it, elided if you continue from what precedes, as one says abghinī thawban, meaning help me seek it.
4. ʿakamat al-nāqatu — wa-ghayruhā, when she carries fat upon fat, and fatness upon fatness. Iʿtakama al-shayʾ and irtakama, with the same meaning.
5. ʿakama ʿanhu — when he turned away out of cowardice, this too belongs here, for the frightened man draws in close to something beside him. He said: 'And thirst wasted him after he had come from watering, yet he was never one to turn away from the water's approach,' meaning he did not turn back, did not draw in to one side. As for his saying: 'He wheeled about, not turning away, and saw off his companion, by the broken edge of the soft ground, in a close, paired charge,' his words 'lam yaʿkim' mean he did not turn back, for one who wheels upon a thing draws in close to it.
6. mā ʿakama ʿan shatmī — he did not shrink back. From this is the saying of the Hudhalī poet: 'Zuhayr, is there any turning back from old age, or is there no lasting life for a generous, giving man?' He means by maʿkim, the turning-away.
7. al-ʿakmah — as al-Khalīl said, one says of an animal, when it drinks and its belly fills up: 'no hollow or pocket was left in its insides that did not fill,' meaning by al-ʿakmah the place where water gathers and it is satisfied; the reasoning is the same. He recited: 'Until it had wetted the packed-full places, from the reed-pipes of its insides and its hollows.'
8. rajulun muʿakkam — firm and hard of flesh.
عكمس:
The night, when it grows dark, [is described this way]. He said:
And the night is a dark night, ʿukāmis.
This is from ʿakasa and ʿamasa, for ʿamasa carries something of the sense of concealment, and darkness conceals; one says ʿammasa ʿalayhi al-khabar, he kept the news hidden from him. This has already been explained.
عكن:
The letters ʿayn, kāf and nūn are one sound root, close to the one before it.

1. al-ʿukan / ʿuknah — al-Khalīl said: al-ʿukan is the plural of ʿuknah, the fold in a plump girl's belly from her fatness. It would be permissible to say jāriyatun ʿaknāʾ, but instead they say muʿakkanah.
2. taʿakkana al-shayʾ — taʿakkunan, when it piles up on itself. Al-Aʿshā said: 'To her, and even if he misses a full meal elsewhere, he comes back, to another, of great fatness and full folds.'
3. al-naʿam al-ʿakanān — the many, gathered livestock; one also says ʿaknān with the kāf unvowelled. He said: 'And it came down to the water in a crowded throng.'
4. nāqatun ʿaknāʾ — al-Durayd said: when her udder and teats have grown thick.
عكو:
The letters ʿayn, kāf and the weak final letter are one sound root, denoting gathering together and thickness too, close to the one before it.

1. al-ʿakwah — the base of the tail. One says ʿakawta dhanaba al-dābbah, when you bend the tail back at its base and knot it. The plural of ʿukwat al-dhanab is ʿukā. He said: 'Until its tail-knots have brought you low.'
2. ʿakat al-marʾatu shaʿrahā — meaning she plaited it.
3. ʿakā ʿalā qirnihi — they sometimes say this, like ʿakara and ʿaṭafa, meaning he turned on his match in combat — if sound, this follows the same reasoning.
4. ʿakwāʾ — a ewe whose hindquarters are white and the rest black, so named because the white lies at the tail-base.

As for Ibn Muqbil's saying: 'They do not knot up their waist-wrappers,' its meaning is that they are noble men whose garments are so fine and soft that no bunching shows at the fastenings of their wraps. This is sound, for when a man knots his garment he has gathered and bunched it.

5. ʿakat al-nāqah — meaning she grew thick and stout; nāqatun miʿkāʾ, a thick, sturdy she-camel.
عل:
The letters ʿayn and lām are three sound roots: one is a repeating or a reiterating; another is an obstacle that obstructs; and the third is a weakness in a thing.

The first: al-ʿalal is the second drink, of camels after the first. One says "ʿalalun baʿda nahalin," a second drink after a first. The verb is *yaʿullūna ʿallan wa ʿalalan*; the camels themselves are said to *taʿullu ʿalalan*.

He said:
The two of them shunned the water, so we did not let them settle by it; only one who hopes for a second drink settles.

In the hadith: "If he strikes him repeatedly, retaliation is due" — meaning if he repeats the blow on him. Its origin is in drinking.

Al-Akhṭal said:
When my drinking-companion gave me a second cup, then gave me a second cup again, three glasses that had a gurgling sound.

One says *aʿalla* the people, when their camels drank a second drink, ʿalalan. Ibn al-A'rābī said, in the proverb: "your visiting us is nothing but the bidding of a returning one" — that is, like the camels that *taʿullu*. Also: "he offered him the bidding of a returning one" — this was said because, when the drink is repeated on them, their second drink is less than the first.

1. *Al-ʿulāla* — the remainder of milk. The remainder of anything is called ʿulāla, to the point that the last burst of a horse's running is called ʿulāla.

He said: except for a last burst, or the first eager stretch of a mettled, sturdy-flanked steed.

All of this belongs to the first sense, because that remainder is returned to by milking again. Hence they say "*ʿālaltu* the she-camel," when I milked her, then let her rest a while so she would settle, then milked her again — that second milking is al-muʿālla and al-ʿilāl. The name for the milk itself is al-ʿulāla. It is said that ʿulālat al-sayr, of a journey, is: when you think the she-camel has flagged, so you strike her to spur her onward in the march. One says a she-camel is "karīmat al-ʿulāla," generous in her second effort. They sometimes say of a man praised for generosity: "he is karīm al-ʿulāla" — meaning he repeats his giving even on what remains of his means.

He said: and if there is no requital, then a further gift, given despite hardship, out of what remains of the offspring of the fire-sticks, is a relief.

Manẓūr ibn Marthad said, on a she-camel's repeated effort in travel:
And I have kept spurring the swift pace of the she-camel, with the whip, across a featureless waste like a shield.

The other root: the obstacle that obstructs. Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿilla is an event that occupies its owner, turning him away from his purpose. One says *iʿtallahu* ʿan kadhā, meaning it turned him aside from it.

He said: so time turned him aside — and time has its turnings.

The third root: al-ʿilla is sickness, and the one who has it is *muʿtall*. Ibn al-A'rābī said: *ʿalla* the sick man, *yaʿillu*, ʿillatan, so he is ʿalīl. A man is ʿulala, meaning much afflicted with sickness.

From this chapter too, the chapter of weakness: al-ʿall, of men — the old man whose body has shrunk and grown small.

Al-Mutanakhkhil said:
He is not an old man, feeble, with no strength left in him — but rather Uthayla, clear of complexion, freshly come to strength.

He said: every aged creature is called ʿall. Ibn al-A'rābī said: al-ʿall is the weak one, whether from old age or illness. Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿall is the large tick. Perhaps he meant by this that it is the one on which a long span of time has passed, so that it has become like an aged creature.

There remains in this chapter al-yaʿālīl, over which there has been disagreement. Abū 'Ubayd said: al-yaʿālīl are white clouds. Abū 'Amr said: a well called yaʿālīl is one into which rain and water have gathered time after time. He said: this belongs to the sense of al-ʿalal, repetition. Al-yaʿālīl has no singular. This, which al-Shaybānī said, is more correct, because it is better reasoned.

Among what strays from these roots, if what is said of it is sound, is that al-ʿulʿul is the male of the lark. Al-ʿulʿul is also the top of the cartilage near the flank. Al-ʿulʿul is also a man's member. All of this is disputed talk.

Likewise their saying: "he is ʿallān at riding horses," when he is not skilled at it. They recite on this matter things that are not sound and cannot be relied upon.

As for their saying "laʿalla such a thing will be" — this is a word close to the third root, the one indicating weakness, because it is the opposite of certainty. They say: "laʿalla your brother will visit us" — in this there is an approach and a holding-out of hope, short of certainty and the affirming of a statement. They also say ʿalla in the sense of laʿalla. And they say laʿallanī and laʿallī.

He said:
And I look out from the high, bare hills — perhaps I may see Laylā's fire, or her watchdog may see me.
Al-baṣīr, in the verse, is the dog.

As for laʿalla when it comes in the Book of God, Most High — some said it is a strengthening of hope and longing. Others said its meaning is "so that." And some people took it, in what God, Most High, related, as certain fact, deriving its meaning from the first root we mentioned, that of repetition and reiteration. And God knows best what He meant by it.
علب:
The letters ʿayn, lām and bāʾ are two sound roots: one points to thickness and hardness in a thing, the other to a mark left on something.

The first: their saying ʿaliba al-nabāt, the plant hardened. One says laḥm ʿalib, thick coarse meat, and al-ʿalib, rough hard ground.

1. al-ʿalib — an old lizard.
2. al-ʿilbāʾ — the sinew of the neck, so named for its hardness.
3. ʿaliba al-baʿīr — the camel took a disease in one side of its neck.
4. One says of an aging man: "his ʿilbāʾ has shriveled," meaning his neck-sinew.
5. tays ʿalib — a billy-goat thick in the neck-sinew.
6. ʿallabtu al-sikkīn bi'l-ʿilbāʾ — I bound the knife-handle with the neck-sinew.

The other root: al-ʿalb, which is a scratch, a mark. A well-trodden road is maʿlūb. Bishr said: we carried them off the way dogs carry their pups, over every well-trodden track raising its own cloud of dust.

7. ʿallabta al-shayʾ — you left a mark on it.
8. al-ʿilāb — a brand mark running along the length of the neck; a branded she-camel is muʿallaba.

What falls outside both these roots: al-ʿulba, a small box; and ʿUlayb, a valley.
علث:
The letters ʿayn, lām and thāʾ are a single sound root pointing to the mixing of one thing with another.

1. al-ʿalīth — wheat mixed with barley; anything not pure follows this same reasoning.
2. aʿlāth al-zād — food eaten without being picked over or chosen.
3. qaḍīb muʿtalath — a stick whose wood was not carefully chosen.

The proverb: "innahu la-yaʿtalithu al-zinād," he takes his fire-sticks without choosing, said of a man who does not choose carefully whom he marries.
علج:
The letters ʿayn, lām and jīm are a sound root pointing to strenuous effort and practice, done roughly and coarsely.

1. al-ʿilj — the wild ass, and by it the rough non-Arab man is described. They say it is from al-muʿālaja, effortful handling — this is from Ibn al-Aʿrābī. Al-Khalīl said: he is called ʿilj for the coarseness of his build, meaning his thickness; he said a man whose face grows rough and coarse has istaʿlaja.
2. al-ʿilāj — handling and practicing a thing; one says ʿālajtuhu ʿilājan wa-muʿālajatan.
3. iʿtalaja al-qawm — the people grappled with one another in their wrestling and fighting.
4. iʿtalajat al-amwāj — the waves, when they crashed against each other; a poet said: the surging waves ride one upon another, out of its foam.
5. ʿālajtu fulānan fa-ʿalajtuhu ʿaljan — I contended with so-and-so and overcame him.
6. fulān ʿilj māl — so-and-so tends and manages it.
7. al-ʿullaj — a man fierce and strong in fighting and wrestling. A poet said: from us the leading men, and a fierce, formidable head.
8. nāqa ʿalija — a coarse, strong she-camel. A poet said: he did not measure her against the thick-lipped strong ones. Another said: there among them are strong she-camels with worn teeth, that ate saltbush until their faces turned pale.
9. arḍ muʿtalija — land whose plants have grown thick and tall, one part entering into another.

What falls outside this root, though it too concerns plants: al-ʿalajān, a green tree that, they say, camels eat only when forced to. A poet said: what distracts you from Lubnā, when you remember her, are the sandy tracts where al-ʿalajān has not grown. They also claim al-ʿalaj is the young shoots of the palm. A poet said: if you drink your morning draught, drink it with a toothstick from ʿalaj, if you find no arāk-wood. ʿAbd Banī al-Ḥasḥās said: we spent the night, our two pillows against an ʿalajāna-bush and a sand-ridge that the winds passed gently over, back and forth.
علجوم:
Piled-up darkness. Dhū al-Rumma said:
Or a rain-cloud about to burst, whose crests are lit clear by the flashing of lightning, while the darkness is heaped and roiling.
This is a word with the mīm added into it; it is really from the iʿtilāj of the darknesses, their surging together, one against another.
علد:
The letters ʿayn, lām and dāl are a sound root pointing to strength and hardness.

1. al-ʿald — the hard, firm part of a thing; the sinew of the neck is called ʿald.
2. rajul ʿalwadd — a firm, composed man; one says iʿlawwada from it.

What we have not mentioned of it follows this same reasoning.
علز:
The letters ʿayn, lām and zāy are a small root pointing to restlessness brought on by illness.

1. al-ʿalaz — a trembling, like a shiver, that seizes the sick person.
2. Sometimes they say ʿaliza min al-shayʾ, meaning he grew weary and disgusted of it.

ʿĀliz is a place-name. A poet said: the belly of Qaww has been effaced of Sulaymā, and ʿĀliz too, and then Dhāt al-Ghaḍā... [the line breaks off, unfinished in the text].
علس: The letters ʿayn, lām and sīn are a sound root pointing to hardness and toughness in a thing. One says jamal ʿalasī, a tough, strong camel. A poet said: when the ʿalasī camel sees her, it stands cowed. They also say al-muʿallas is an experienced, seasoned man, and al-ʿalas is a large tick.
علش: The letters ʿayn, lām and shīn are nothing, not a true root — though they do say al-ʿillawsh is the wolf. Its derivation is not sound, because shīn does not properly follow lām.
علص: The letters ʿayn, lām and ṣād are close to the one before it. They say al-ʿillawṣ is indigestion, but this is nothing, with no sound derivation; and they say al-ʿilāṣ is striking with the sword, and this too has no real meaning. Whatever is mentioned under this pattern follows the same course.
علط:
The letters ʿayn, lām and ṭāʾ, in most of their sound sense, point to attaching one thing to another, or hanging it upon it. You say ʿalaṭtuhu bi-sahmin, I struck him with an arrow — for when you strike someone with it you have attached it to him. Al-ʿulṭa is a black mark a woman draws on her face to adorn herself; al-ʿulṭa is also a necklace made of colocynth. One says iʿlawwaṭanī fulān, so-and-so clung fast to me.

1. al-ʿilāṭ — a brand or mark made crosswise on the front of the neck; one says ʿalaṭtu al-baʿīr, aʿliṭuhu, ʿalṭan.
2. ʿilāṭ al-ibra — the thread of a needle.
3. ʿilāṭ al-shams — something that looks like a thread, a streak of sunlight.
4. al-iʿlīṭ — the pod that holds the fruit of al-markh, a desert shrub, hanging in its tree. A poet said: she has an ear, fine and delicate, like the iʿlīṭ-pod of markh when it dries and yellows.
5. al-ʿilāṭān — the two sides of the neck.

As for the camel called ʿuluṭ, and the she-camel ʿuluṭ, meaning one with no halter on its head, this is not from this root; rather it is a transposed word, its true form being ʿuṭul, said of a woman with no jewelry on — the reasoning is the same. Ibn Aḥmar said: and I granted her my word, on an unadorned ground, coaxing away her rancor with kindness.
علطميس:
al-ʿalṭamīs is a plump young woman of fine stature.

1. nāqah ʿalṭamīs — a she-camel, strong and huge.

The origin of this is ʿayṭamūs, the lām standing in place of the yāʾ, and the yāʾ standing in place of the wāw. Everything beyond the ʿayn and ṭāʾ in this word is extra, and its origin is al-ʿayṭāʾ — the tall woman, tall of neck.
علف: The letters ʿayn, lām and fāʾ are not a large root; it is simply al-ʿalaf, fodder. You say ʿalaftu al-dābba, I fed the animal fodder. Sheep that are given fodder are called ʿalūfa. Al-ʿullaf is the fruit of al-ṭalḥ tree.
علق:
The letters ʿayn, lām and qāf are one large, sound root going back to a single meaning: that a thing be hung on something above it. The discussion then broadens, but all of it returns to the origin sense named.
You say ʿallaqtu al-shayʾ, uʿalliquhu, taʿlīqan, I hung the thing up. And it ʿaliqa bihi, it clung to it, when it became attached; the sense-pattern is one.
1. Al-ʿalaq: that by which the water-pulley is hung from its frame. It is also said al-ʿalaq is the whole gear of the pulley. They say: the well needs its ʿalaq. Abū ʿUbayda said: al-ʿalaq is the pulley with all its fittings, apart from the rope and the bucket.
2. Al-ʿalaq: clotted blood — a sound sense-pattern, since it clings to a thing; a single piece of it is ʿalaqa. A poet said, in a line of verse:

leaping upon his ragged garments, from the clotted blood

A man threatens: 'you will do such-and-such, or you will choke on a clot,' meaning blood, as though threatening him with death.
3. Al-ʿalaq: that two camels be yoked with a rope and made to draw water together, when the large bucket is heavy. Aʿlaqtu bi'l-gharb baʿīrayn, I paired two camels by joining them to the end of its rope. Al-Liḥyānī said: so-and-so's well 'stays constant on its ʿalaq,' meaning it never runs dry, when it has two buckets, a frame, and a rope; and 'this frame has no ʿalaq,' meaning no rope to hang a bucket on.
Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿalaq is for a thing to sink its claws into another. Jarīr said, in a line of verse:

When its claws catch fast on a horned foe ... it strikes the heart, or tears open the chest

4. So-and-so ʿaliqa with so-and-so: he quarrelled with him. Al-ʿalaq also means passionate love. In the proverb: 'a glance from one with ʿalaq,' meaning one whose heart has become attached in love to the one he loves. Al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse:

I became attached to her by chance, and she attached herself ... to another man than me, and that man attached himself to another besides her

5. Al-ʿalāq: the little herbage livestock get by on until spring comes. Al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse:

a barren waste, like the back of a shield ... nothing to live on there but the cud they bring back up

meaning the camels find no sustenance there but what they chew over again in their mouths.
6. The gazelle-doe taʿluqu, ʿulūqan, when she takes a tree-branch in her mouth.
In the hadith of the martyrs: 'their spirits are within green birds that browse in Paradise.'
7. Al-ʿulqa: trees that stay green through winter, on which the camels browse and so need nothing else, like al-ʿalāq. It is said: so-and-so eats nothing but an ʿulqa, meaning just enough to keep himself going. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: al-ʿulqa is any small amount of anything, plural ʿulaq.
8. Al-ʿalaqa: a small creature that lives in water, the leech, plural ʿalaq, which fastens onto the throat of one who drinks. A man is maʿlūq when leeches have taken hold of his throat. An animal ʿaliqat ʿalaqan when a leech fastens on it while drinking.
9. By way of metaphor: so-and-so's blood ʿaliqa his garments, meaning he was his killer. They also say: so-and-so's blood is in so-and-so's garment. Abū Dhuʾayb said, in a line of verse:

She disclaims the slain man's blood and his war-gear ... though her waist-wrap has clung with the slain man's blood

They say al-izār is used as both masculine and feminine in the dialect of Hudhayl, and bazzuhu means his weapons. Some said 'her waist-wrap clung with the slain man's blood' is a set phrase, meaning: you carried so-and-so's blood in your garment, that is, you killed him — this rests on two merged statements, meaning first that the woman hung the slain man's blood on herself, then that her waist-wrap clung to it.
10. Al-ʿalāqa: a dispute. Al-Khalīl said: a man is miʿlāq when fierce in disputing. Muhalhil said, in a line of verse:

Beneath the stones lies resolve ... and generosity, and a stubborn, sharp-tongued disputant

Another transmitted the word with a ghayn instead, meaning the disputant with whom his opponent's pledge becomes locked fast, so the opponent cannot redeem it from him, for his stubbornness.
11. Taʿlīq al-bāb: setting a door up on its hinges.
12. Al-maʿālīq and al-aʿālīq: clusters hung up, of grapes and the like; al-aʿālīq has no singular.
13. Al-ʿilāqa: the strap of a whip and the like.
14. Al-ʿalāqa also means love.
15. Al-ʿalāqa: what has been mentioned of al-ʿalāq, that which one relies on for a living or otherwise.
16. Al-ʿalīq: fodder-grain, from aʿlaqtuhu, so it is ʿalīq, as one says aʿqadtu al-ʿasal, so it is ʿaqīd.
It has been related of al-Khalīl that he said drink too is called ʿalīq — though this is something al-Khalīl perhaps did not actually say, especially since this is the line offered as its evidence:

Give this one and that one and that one to drink, and pour on ... we call the drink nothing but al-ʿalīq

17. They call one content with a thing short of its full measure: mutaʿalliq.
Among their proverbs: 'its hooks have caught, and the locust has begun to chirp.' Its origin: a man reached a well and hung his rope onto its rope, then went to the well's owner and claimed his protection as a neighbour. Asked the reason, he said: 'I hung my rope on your rope.' Told to move on, he said: 'its hooks have caught, and the locust has chirped,' meaning the bucket has already caught fast and the heat has come, so leaving now is impossible.
18. The young palm-shoot ʿaliqat, when it has taken root once planted.
19. They say the mother aʿlaqat — pressed up with her finger — on the child's ʿudhra (an ailment near the uvula, causing pain), tuʿliqu, iʿlāqan; it is as if, lifting it, she 'hung' it.
20. It is said, 'this is an ʿilq among precious things,' of something valuable, as though everyone who sees it becomes attached to it. By likeness they also call wine al-ʿilq. They recited (this line is obscure to me in its close detail):

When you taste her mouth, you say: a treasure laid away ... meant for a chief, but left forgotten in its jar

21. A precious thing is also called ʿilq maḍinna, something one is loath to part with.
22. So-and-so is dhū maʿlaqa, a raider who fastens onto everything.
aʿlaqtu: I came upon a precious thing; plural of ʿilq is ʿulūq. Al-Kumayt said, in a line of verse (its precise sense is compressed and not fully certain to me):

If he sells something for youth, then he has sold ... cheap, from among precious things, something dear

23. Al-ʿalāqa: love that clings fast to the heart. They say al-ʿalūq, among women, is the one devoted in love to her husband.
His saying, Most High: {so you leave her as if suspended} [al-Nisāʾ: 129] — she who is neither free to remarry nor truly a kept wife, her state unsettled. Likewise the woman's words in the hadith of Umm Zarʿ: 'If I speak, I am divorced; if I stay silent, I am left suspended.' And their saying, 'the one who makes do is not like the one who picks and chooses,' meaning one of meagre living is not like one who may be particular and choose as he wishes.
24. Al-ʿalāʾiq: goods carried on a journey.
25. They say: so-and-so came with ʿulaq fulaq, meaning with a remarkable feat; one says aʿlaqa wa-aflaqa. Its origin is that it is a calamity that fastens onto everyone.
26. It is said that al-ʿalūq is what grazing animals take with their mouths from trees, leaf or fruit; whatever the animal has browsed on is ʿalūq. A poet said, in a line of verse:

He is the one who gives away the choicest hundred [camels] ... on which the browsing brought out a ruddy glow

meaning they grazed the trees and browsed until they grew fat and reddened; camels grazing on ṭalḥ-acacia and the like, eating its leaves, thrive on it, fatten, and redden.
27. Al-ʿullayq: a small thorn-bush that does not grow large; when a thing catches in it, it can hardly get free for the abundance of its thorn, whose hooks are sharp — hence its name.
28. They say: 'this is a report long of al-ʿawlaq,' meaning long-tailed, drawn-out.
As for al-ʿalūq among she-camels: al-Kisāʾī said al-ʿalūq is the she-camel that refuses to take to her young; al-maʿāliq are the same. He recited (this line's exact force I give only approximately):

Or how does what the withholding mother gives avail ... a mere nuzzling of the nose, when she is stingy with her milk

The sense-pattern is sound: it is as if she has 'clung fast' to her milk, so it can hardly be freed from her.
Abū ʿAmr said: al-ʿalūq is whatever fastens onto a person; death too is called al-ʿalūq. A poet said, in a line of verse:

And a woman asking after Thaʿlaba ibn Sayr ... while death had already fastened onto Thaʿlaba
