29. The gazelle ʿaliqa in the snare, yaʿlaqu, when caught in it; the snare aʿlaqathu. The trapper aʿlaqa, iʿlāqan, when game falls into his snare. A Bedouin said: 'a gazelle came circling the noose, so I caught it.' The trapper is told: 'you have caught it, so go seize it.' Likewise a gazelle caught in the snare is said to be uʿliqa bihi. Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse (the second half is obscure to me):

And a day that drives the gazelle to the farthest of its lair ... while its locusts leap as caught, dangling things leap

30. They say: 'the milker left the she-camel no ʿulqa,' meaning he left nothing in her udder without milking it.
31. The necklaces worn at the throat are al-ʿalāʾiq.
32. Al-ʿalīqa: a riding-animal given to a man to fetch provisions on for its owner, plural ʿalāʾiq. A poet said, in a line of verse:

And a woman said: never ride out on such an errand ... yet among this world's pleasures is riding such errands

Another said, in a line of verse (the last word of this line is unclear to me):

He sent her off on the errand, knowing well ... that those sent on such errands meet with hardship

33. They say: ʿaliqa yafʿalu kadhā, he set about doing such a thing, as though attaching himself to what he wants.
34. Old age has already fastened its hooks into him.
35. Al-maʿālīq of a necklace and of earrings: what is hung on them to make them beautiful.
36. They say: the woman ʿaliqat, meaning she conceived.
A man dhū maʿlaqa is a raider who fastens onto everything. A poet said, in a line of verse:

I fear that one who fastens on everything will fasten on her

37. Al-ʿalāqiya: a man who, once he fastens onto a thing, will hardly let it go.
38. As for al-ʿilqa, Ibn al-Sikkīt said it is a shift reaching to the navel or just past it, also called al-baqīra. He recited:

And she was in nothing but a waist-wrap and a shift ... swift as Ibn Hammām's raid on the tribe of Khathʿam

This fits the pattern, since when a garment is not full and ample it is as if merely a thing hung on another. Abū ʿAmr said: it is a garment with an opening cut, its two sides left unsewn, worn by a young woman down to the waist-band, also called al-shawdhar.
علك:
The letters ʿayn, lām and kāf are a sound root pointing to something like chewing, and gripping a thing.

1. Al-Khalīl's saying: al-ʿalk is chewing. One says ʿalakat al-dābba al-lijām, the animal is chewing the bit, taʿlukuhu ʿalkan. He said gum, al-ʿilk, is so named because it is chewed. Al-Nābigha said: horses fasting, and others not fasting, beneath the dust, and horses chewing at their bits.
2. Al-Duraydī said: ṭaʿām ʿalik, food tough to chew.
3. They say of a man's tongue "ʿawlak," when he chews over and mulls his words.
4. Abū Zayd said: arḍ ʿalika, land close to water; ṭīna ʿilka, clay that is good, moist and green.

God knows best.
علكد:
The strong one. This is from ʿakada, and from al-ʿilwadd, which is the strong one, and from al-lakad, which is a thing's parts pressing into one another. He said:
A pale [camel], firm-backed, sturdy.
علكوم:
The big-bodied, fat she-camel. Labīd said:
Watering the gardens, a mature, big-boned [she-camel].
This is from ʿakama, with the lām added, as though she were packed with flesh the way a load is packed and bound.
علم:
The letters ʿayn, lām and mīm are one sound root, and it points to a mark upon a thing by which it is told apart from anything else.

Of this is al-ʿalāma, the mark, which is well known. One says ʿallamtu ʿalā al-shay'i ʿalāmatan — I set a mark upon the thing. And one says aʿlama al-fāris — the horseman marked himself out, when he has a sign upon him in war. And so-and-so went out muʿliman bi-kadhā — marked out by such and such. Al-ʿalam is the banner, and the plural is aʿlām. Al-ʿalam is also the mountain, and so is everything that serves as a maʿlam — a landmark, the opposite of a maǰhal, a place with no track to guide you. The plural of ʿalam here is aʿlām as well.

Al-Khansā' said, in a line of verse:
And Ṣakhr — the guides take their lead from him, as though he were a mountain with a fire on its head.

Al-ʿalam is also the split in the upper lip, and such a man is aʿlam. The reasoning is one and the same, because it is like a mark upon the person. Al-ʿullām, as is said, is henna; and that is because when a man is dyed with it, it is like a mark. Al-ʿilm, knowledge, is the opposite of ignorance, and its reasoning is the reasoning of ʿalam and ʿalāma. The proof that the two go back to one reasoning is the reading of some of the reciters: " And he is indeed a mark (ʿalam) of the Hour ". They said: what is meant by it is the coming down of Jesus — peace be upon him — and that by that the nearness of the Hour is known. And taʿallamtu al-shay' — I learned the thing, when I take the knowledge of it. And the Arabs say taʿallam annahu kāna kadhā, in the sense of " know that it was so ".

Qays ibn Zuhayr said, in a line of verse:
Know that the best of people as a living tribe is at the pool of al-Habā'a — he does not stir from it.

And the whole section is one reasoning.

And of the section is al-ʿālamūn, the worlds, and that is because every kind of created thing is in itself a landmark and a mark. And some people said: the ʿālam is so named for its being gathered together. God the Exalted said: {And praise be to God, Lord of the worlds} [al-Anʿām: 45]. They said: it means all created things together. And they recited:
I have neither seen nor heard of the like of them among the worlds.

And he said of al-ʿālam, in a line of verse:
Khindif is the head of this world.

And what the speaker said — that in this there is something pointing to gathering and coming together — is not far-fetched, and that is because they give the name al-ʿaylam, and it is said that it is the sea, and it is said that it is the well with much water in it.
علن: The letters 'ayn, lām and nūn are a sound root pointing to making a thing plain, pointing [to it], and its coming out into the open. One says 'alana al-amru ya'lunu — the matter became known. And a'lantuhu anā — I made it known. And al-'ilān is al-mu'ālana, open dealing between two parties.
عله:
The letters ʿayn, lām and hāʾ are a sound root. It may belong to the class where hamza is exchanged for ʿayn, because it runs the same course as al-alah and al-walah [bewilderment, distraction]. These three words come from a single source, taking in confusion, hesitation and looking about, haste, and coming and going — never far from these senses.

Al-Khalīl said: ʿaliha al-rajul, yaʿlahu, ʿalahan, so he is ʿalhān, when his own self pulls him toward a thing, and he is one who stays constantly in that restless craving. A poet said: my forelocks turned fresh and grey and, after a long stretch, the blindness of a heart in constant restless craving lifted from me.

1. ʿaliha — his hunger grew severe; the hungry man is ʿalhān, the woman ʿalhā, plural ʿilāh and ʿalāhā. One says ʿalihta ilā al-shayʾ, when your soul longs intensely for it. Ibn Aḥmar said, in a line of verse: they were bewildered, so we do not hope for the yearning cry of a noble, untouched female, nor do we build a tent for an unmarried woman — as though he means: they were distracted, with no settling in them. They said: al-ʿalhān and al-ʿālih are the male ostrich, and that is not far-fetched from the reasoning.

Among what shows that al-ʿalah is wavering in a matter, like confusion, is Labīd's saying, describing a cow: she wandered, lingering aimlessly in the lowlands of Ṣuʿāʾid, seven whole days, twin-born, her time complete. And from it, Abū al-Najm's saying, describing a horse full of liveliness and excitement: of every restless one tossing in the bridle.

Among the names that may be derived from this root: al-ʿAlhān, the name of a horse belonging to one of the Arabs. Jarīr said: Shabath, of whom I boasted over you, and Maʿqil, and by Mālik, and by the rider of al-ʿAlhān.
علهب:
The billy-goat with long horns; the bull too is described by it. Jarīr said:
When the backs of Banū Tamīm arch back [in flight] ... it shows them for what they are: like the long-horned wild goats.
Here the hāʾ has been added; the word is really from al-ʿulab. Al-ʿulab means tall palm trees. This has already passed.
علو:
The letters ʿayn, lām and the weak letter, be it yā' or wāw or alif, are a single root pointing to loftiness and rising; nothing stands apart from it. And of that is al-ʿalā' and al-ʿuluww. And they say taʿālā al-nahār — that is, the day rose high. And to one who stumbles it is prayed: laʿan laka ʿāliyan — that is, rise up in height and in steadiness. And ʿālaytu al-rajul above the camel: I lifted him up onto it. He said, in a line of verse:
And unless you mount her, they will hoist you above her; and how are you to guard the back of what you are riding?

Al-Khalīl said: the origin of this structure is al-ʿuluww. As for al-ʿalā', it is high rank. And as for al-ʿuluww, it is greatness and overbearing. They say: ʿalā al-malik fī al-arḍ ʿuluwwan kabīran — the king behaved with great high-handedness in the land. God, exalted be He, said: {Truly Pharaoh exalted himself in the land} [al-Qaṣaṣ: 4]. And they say a rajul ʿālī al-kaʿb — that is, noble. He said, in a line of verse:
When your ankle-bone rose high for me, I rose high.

And of everything that rises one says ʿalā yaʿlū. But if it is in rank and nobility one says ʿaliya yaʿlā. And whoever masters a matter has iʿtalāhu and istaʿlā ʿalayhi and bihi, as you say istawlā, he took possession. And the horse, when it runs in a race and reaches the goal, is said to have istaʿlā upon the goal and istawlā. And Ibn al-Sikkīt said: he is muʿtalin with his load — that is, equal to it. And he has iʿtalā bihi. And he recited, in a line of verse:
Truly, when my friend does not keep company with me and she draws far from me, I rise above her keeping away.
He means: I overcame her distance. And I have ʿalawtu ḥājatī aʿlūhā ʿuluwwan, when you get the upper hand of your need.

And al-Aṣmaʿī said about Aws's words, in a line of verse:
The calamity grew great, and the overpowering one —
that is, the great matter that overcomes patience and defeats it. And he said also about the words of Umayya ibn Abī al-Ṣalt, in a line of verse:
To God I complain of what I see of the misfortunes, with what is easy and with what is hard —
that is, with my ease and with my struggle, from your saying ʿalāhu kadhā — that is, it overcame him. And al-ʿāfī is the easy, and al-ʿālī is the hard.

Al-Khalīl said: al-maʿlāt is the winning of nobility, and the plural is al-maʿālī. And so-and-so is of the ʿilya of the people — that is, of the people of nobility. And these are the ʿilya of their people, with i on the ʿayn, on the pattern fiʿla, light. And al-sifl and al-ʿilw are the lowest of a thing and its highest. And they say ʿāli ʿan thawbī and iʿlu ʿan thawbī, when you mean, get up off my garment and rise from my garment; and ʿāli ʿanhā — that is, step aside; and iʿlu ʿan al-wisāda, get off the cushion.

Abū Mahdī said: aʿli ʿalayya and ʿāli ʿalayya — that is, load it upon me.

And they say: so-and-so, the eye rises over him and the eye rises away from him — that is, it does not accept him, it shrinks from him. And the root in all of that is one. And one says ʿalā al-faras yaʿlūhu ʿuluwwan, when he mounts it; and aʿlā ʿanhu, when he gets down from it. And this, though on the face of it far from the reasoning, is sound in meaning, because when a person gets down from a thing he has parted from it and in truth risen away from it — only the Arabs distinguished the two senses by distinguishing the two words.

Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿalyā' is the top of every mountain or high place. Zuhayr said, in a line of verse:
Look well, my friend: do you see any women in litters, setting out from al-ʿAlyā' above Jurthum?

And the top of a spear-shaft is called al-ʿāliya, and its lower part al-sāfila, and the plural is al-ʿawālī. Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿĀliya is one of the dwelling-places of the Arabs, of the Ḥijāz and what adjoins it; and the relative form from it, by the root, is ʿālī, while what is used is ʿulwī.

Abū ʿUbayd said: ʿālā al-rajul, when he comes to al-ʿĀliya. And Ibn Durayd claimed that al-ʿĀliya is called ʿUluww, that being a name for it, and that they say: so-and-so has come from ʿUluww. And he claimed that the relative form from it is ʿulwī.

They said: and al-ʿulliyya is an upper room, on the pattern of ḥurriyya. And in word-formation it is fuʿliyya, and it is also said to be fuʿlūla.

Al-Farrā' said about His words, exalted be He: {Truly the record of the righteous is in ʿIlliyyīn} [al-Muṭaffifīn: 18] — they said: it is only a rising upon a rising, to what has no limit. And it was made plural with wāw and nūn because when the Arabs make a plural in which they do not go by a form built from one and two, they say it so for the masculine and the feminine, as in ʿilliyyīn; for by it only a thing is meant, with no one and no two intended, as the Arabs said: 'Feed us the broth of broths.' And he said, in a line of verse:
Little she-camels and small young camels —
so he made it plural with the nūn when he meant the number that has no limit. And another said in this measure, in a line of verse:
And the tracks came to be scattered by the whirlwinds, after downpour upon downpour.
He meant rain after rain, a thing not fixed in number. And he said also, in a line of verse:
One says the upper of Muḍar and the lower of it; and when you say sufl you say ʿulī.
And the high heavens, al-samāwāt al-ʿulā: the singular is ʿulyā.

As for what is related from Abū Zayd: ji'tu min ʿalayka — that is, from beside you — and his argument for it from the line, in a line of verse:
She went out in the morning from beside him, after her thirst-interval was complete, ringing, and away from a dry salt ground in a trackless waste.

And al-mustaʿlī of the two milkers is the one who has the vessel in his hand and milks with the other hand. And it is said: al-mustaʿlī is the one who milks the she-camel from her left side, and al-bā'in is the one who milks her from her right side. And he recited, in a line of verse:
The one on the right gives the one above good news, of the two milkers, that there is no scanting.

And one says ji'tuka min aʿlā, and min ʿalā, and min ʿālin, and min ʿali. Abū al-Najm said, in a line of verse:
Lean of belly from below, broad from above.
And some of the Arabs put it in the nominative as a final form. Ibn Rawāḥa said, in a line of verse:
I have borne witness, and I did not lie, that Muhammad is the Messenger of Him who is above the heavens, from on high.
And another said, describing a horse, in a line of verse:
Dry-sinewed from below, full-fleshed from above; she is ransomed with the clearest and with the mole-marked.

As for al-A'shā's words, in a line of verse:
A report has come to me that I take no joy in, from on high; there is no wonder in it and no mockery —
the word in it is recited in three ways: with u, with a, and with i.

And another recited, in a line of verse:
So she drinks up the trough with quick draughts from above, draughts by which she cuts across the middles of the wastes.

Ibn al-Sikkīt said: ataytuhu min muʿālin. And he recited, in verse:
The pulling of the nose-rings and the running of the mountains loosed the rings of the fetters from him,
and the shaking of the saddle from on high.

And one says ʿūliyat al-faras, when her build is made lofty. And one says nāqa ʿilyān — that is, tall and big-bodied. And a rajul ʿilyān is tall. And he recited, in verse:
From a soft, generous, tall she-camel that cast down light dew where the sandy tracts meet.

Al-Farrā' said: a jamal ʿilyān and a nāqa ʿilyān. And we have not found a word with i on its first letter come as a descriptive term for both masculine and feminine except these two. And he recited, in verse:
A red one, of those that offer the crows their fill; every anvil-hard, towering one goes before her.

And one who raises his voice is called ʿilyān also. As for Abū ʿAmr, he claimed that ʿilyān is not said of the male; they only say a jamal nabīl. As for their saying taʿāl, come, it is from al-ʿuluww, as though he said: come up to me; then it became common until the one at the bottom said it to the one above him. And one says taʿālayā and taʿālaw. This is used only in the imperative, and it has died out in everything else. And a man's head and neck are called ʿilāwa. And al-ʿilāwa is what is loaded on the camel after the load is complete. And his words, in a line of verse:
O you who go out in the morning, carry a message, light in its loading, great in its reward —
muʿallāhā is the place where it is carried. And one says: he sat in the ʿulāwa of the wind and in its sufāla. And he recited, in a line of verse:
It brings us, whenever it was our upwind side, the scent of khuzāmā flowers, with dew and moisture in it.

Al-Khalīl said: al-muʿallā is the seventh of the gaming arrows, and it is the best of them; when it wins it takes seven shares of the slaughtered camel, and in it are seven notches, which are marks. And al-muʿallī is the one who draws up the bucket when he hauls. He said, in a line of verse:
The plunge of the bucket that the hauler pulled up.

And of a woman when she becomes clean after childbirth one says: she has taʿallat, and she is tataʿallā. And they claimed that this is said only of a woman in childbed and is not used of any other. Jarīr said, in a line of verse:
May no pregnant woman bear a child after al-Farazdaq, and may none with child rise clean from childbed.

Al-Aṣmaʿī said: one says ʿalli rishā'aka — that is, throw your well-rope above all the other ropes. And it is said that al-muʿallā is the one who, when the rope slips off the pulley, climbs up to it and puts it back. Al-ʿUjayr said, in a line of verse:
And I have a water-drawer who never brought water before him, one who climbs up, while the ropes of the deep well are many.

And they say of a man whom [another] has quarrelled with: he has someone to raise him over him.

As for the ʿulwān of a book, some people claimed that it is a mistake and that it is only ʿunwān. But that is not a mistake; the two forms are both sound, though they are both later coinages, not from the root of the speech of the Arabs. As for ʿunwān, it is from ʿanna; and as for ʿulwān, it is from al-ʿuluww, because it is the first of the book and its highest part.

And of this chapter is al-ʿalāt, which is the anvil, and a hard she-camel is likened to it. He said, in a line of verse:
And many a waterless waste between deserts, in a place of death, I crossed on a she-camel of anvil build, towering.

Al-Khalīl said: ʿAlī is on the pattern faʿīl, and the relative form from it is ʿalawī. And the Banū ʿAlī are a clan of Kināna; it is said he is ʿAlī ibn Sūd al-Ghassānī, who married their mother after their father and raised them, so they were traced to him. He said, in a line of verse:
And our lookouts said: Ho, men of ʿĀmir! At the water is a wrapped head from ʿAlī.

And Abū Saʿīd said: one says mā anta illā ʿalā aʿlā wa-arwaḥ — that is, in ease and elevation. And it is said that aʿlā means the heavens; as for arwaḥ, it is the places from which the winds blow from the horizons of the earth. Ibn Harma said, in a line of verse:
Generosity went out in the morning seeking someone to pay it its dues; so it went at evening and travelled by night between the highest and the airiest.
That is: he went at evening and travelled by night between the highest of his wealth and the meanest of it, and so had free rein over all of it.
عم:
The letters ʿayn and mīm are a single sound root, meaning length, abundance, and height. Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿamīm is what is tall among plants. One says nakhlatun ʿamīmatun, a tall palm, plural ʿumm. They say: "the plant stood at its ʿamam," meaning at its full completion. One also says jāriyatun ʿamīmatun, meaning tall; and jismun ʿamamun, a full, ample body.

Ibn Shaʾs said:
Even if 'Irār is not clear, I still love the dark-coated one with the full, broad shoulder.

Ibn al-A'rābī said: a man is ʿamamun and a woman is ʿamamun likewise. One also says ʿushbun ʿamīmun, luxuriant herbage, and it is said *iʿtamma*, it grew full.

The Hudhalī poet said:
They roam a bare open plain, where its dense growth and its low-growing herbage seem like the shadows of a dark night.

Some said: the tall palm-tree is called ʿamma, plural ʿamm, citing Labīd's saying:
Tall palms that the bare rock and its stream sustain — full-grown, graceful ones, with vines among them.

Abū 'Amr said: al-ʿamīm, among palms, is what stands above al-jabbār, a class of tall palm.

He said:
So a tall palm is of use to your tall ones, and a young shoot to your young ones —
meaning: its small ones for your small ones, and its large ones for your large ones.

Abū Duwād said:
Swaying, supple, plump of leg — like a tall shoot of reed amid the scant water.
Al-ʿamīma means the tall one; al-rafḍ is the small remaining water.

1. *Al-ʿimāma* — well known, the turban, plural ʿimāmāt and ʿamā'im. One says taʿammamtu bi'l-ʿimāma and iʿtamamtu, and ʿammamanī ghayrī, someone else wound the turban on me. He is ḥasan al-ʿimma, meaning fine in the winding of his turban.

He said: it escapes, when its harness-straps begin to bleed with wear, and the foaming spray wraps the curved part like a turban.

One also says *ʿummima* the man, meaning he was made chief — because the crowns of a people are their turbans, just as one says, of the non-Arabs, "he was crowned," so one says of the Arabs "he was turbaned."

Al-'Ajjāj said:
And among them, when the turbaned one was turbaned.
Meaning: he was made chief, and so was clothed with the turban of chieftaincy.

One also says shātun muʿammama, when it is black-headed. Abū 'Ubayd said: a horse is muʿammam when the white of its blaze runs down to its root and what surrounds it on the head; and a blaze is muʿammama when it is such. He said: al-taʿmīm in piebald colouring is when the white lies on the crown and does not reach the neck; one says ablaqu muʿammamun.

As for the assembling sense we mentioned at the root of the chapter, al-Khalīl and others said: al-ʿamā'im are the assemblies of people, singular ʿamm. Abū 'Amr said: al-ʿamāyim, with a yā', are the assemblies; one says qawmun ʿamāyimu. He said: I know no singular for it.

Al-'Ajjāj said:
The assemblies streamed toward her from Ḥimyar.

Ibn al-A'rābī said: al-ʿamm is the assembly of people.

He quoted:
The assembly relieves, through him, the need of one man; so we returned with our needs met, though he is not a man of wealth —
meaning the Black Stone.

Another said:
And the running between the two assemblies, when the evening draws close and the crowd calls out to one another.

From the sense of gathering also comes their saying: "ʿammanā this matter, yaʿummunā, ʿumūman," when it befell the whole people together. He said: al-ʿāmma is the opposite of al-khāṣṣa, the common folk against the elite. From this chapter too is their saying: "there is in him ʿummiyya," meaning pride — and if that is so, it belongs to the sense of loftiness.

Al-Naḍr said: they say so-and-so is dhū ʿummiyya, meaning he extends his aid generally to his companions, not singling anyone out.

He said:
So he drove them off, his back teeth showing green with rage, as the proud, valiant man drives off.

Al-Aṣma'ī said: he is drawn from their ʿamīm and their ṣamīm — meaning the pure stock, unmixed with any other.

Also from this chapter, by way of resemblance: *ʿammama* the milk, when it foamed up — and this only happens when it is fresh, straight from milking.

Labīd said:
The milking-groups of al-Ladīd come round to them repeatedly, and the guest's bowls are filled brim-full with pure, foaming milk.

Among what has no derivation except by forcing one is 'Ammān, the name of a town. Abū Wajza said:
The sand-grouse yearned at the gates of 'Ammān, when its companions had already seen to their needs and their wants —
al-Qaṭāh, in the verse, is his she-camel.
عمت:
The letters ʿayn, mīm and tāʾ are a small sound root pointing to the tangling and twisting of a thing, from which whatever resembles it is then derived.

1. Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿamt is when wool ʿamit, is carded and wraps over itself, lengthwise and in circles, the way a wool-spinner does it; one says ʿamata, yaʿmitu.
2. Abū ʿUbayda said: al-ʿimmīt is a blind man, ignorant of affairs — like the mute, the ʿamāmīt.
3. They also say al-ʿimmīt is a drunk man.
4. Al-ʿamt is striking without caring whom the blow falls on.
عمج:
The letters ʿayn, mīm and jīm are a sound root pointing to twisting and crookedness.

1. Al-Khalīl said: al-taʿammuj is a winding in one's gait, not the winding of a road — the way a flood taʿammaja, winds back on itself, when part of it turns over another part.
2. sahm ʿamūj — an arrow that twists as it flies. Al-Hudhalī said: like the back of a wolf, neither weak nor short, so that I outrun it, nor a stiff twisting arrow.
3. taʿammajat al-ḥayya — the snake, when it wound about in its movement. A poet said: playing with a pair of Hadramī [spearheads], as though it were a demon's winding through a lonely patch of khirwaʿ-plant.
4. The snake itself is called al-ʿamaj, because it taʿammaju, twists. A poet said: they follow the way of the winding one.
عمد:
The letters ʿayn, mīm and dāl are a large root with many branches, going back to one meaning: steadiness in a thing, whether standing upright or stretched out, and likewise in opinion and in the intending of a thing.
1. From this: ʿamadtu fulānan, aʿmiduhu, ʿamdan, I made straight for so-and-so, when you intend him. Al-ʿamd is the opposite of error in killing and elsewhere, called ʿamd for the steadiness of your intent toward it. Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿamd is also to prop a thing with a support that holds it up and that it leans on. Ibn Durayd said: ʿamadtu al-shayʾ, I propped it up; the thing propped against is ʿimād, plural ʿumud; also said ʿamūd and ʿamad. Al-ʿamūd is of wood or iron, plural aʿmida, and applies to a tent's poles; those who dwell only in tents are called ahl ʿamūd and ahl ʿimād.
2. Al-Khalīl said: ʿamūd al-sinān is the ridge running along the two edges of a spearhead from its base, bearing the line called khaṭṭ al-ʿayr. The two legs of the male ostrich are called ʿamūdān. ʿAmūd al-amr: the support of a matter, without which it cannot stand straight. ʿAmīd al-qawm: the chief of the people, their mainstay, to whom they turn in alarm when trouble presses them. ʿAmūd al-udhn: the main part of the ear, its support.
As for calling a sick man ʿamīd, the language-scholars said al-ʿamīd is the man who is propped up, unable to sit for his illness until cushions are placed under his sides. They said the 'love-struck heart' (al-qalb al-ʿamīd) is derived from this: a heart propped up, worn down and broken by passion, become like a thing propped against another. Al-Akhṭal said, in a line of verse:

Suʿād departed, and the eye's sleep became sleeplessness ... and the heart, grief-stricken and burning, is propped and broken

One says ʿamīd, maʿmūd, and muʿammad.
Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿamd is to labour at a matter with earnest resolve and certainty. You say: I did that ʿamdan and ʿamda ʿaynin (deliberately, with open eyes), taʿammadtu lahu, and faʿaltuhu muʿtamidan, meaning intentionally.
3. From this chapter too: al-sanām al-ʿamid, of a camel's hump, ʿamida, yaʿmadu, ʿamdan — carried on the pattern of qalb ʿamīd and maʿmūd: when the hump is large and fatty and something is loaded onto it, so it is bruised and its fat dies within it and it never sits right again (al-wārī being the fatty one), just as a wound ʿamida when pressed before its abscess has ripened, so it swells. A he-camel is ʿamid, a she-camel ʿamida, and her hump ʿamid.
As for His saying, Most High: {in extended columns} [al-Humaza: 9], meaning something like tent-shelters of fire, stretched out; it was also read 'in ʿumud,' plural of ʿimād.
Al-Mubarrid said: a man muʿmad means tall; al-ʿimād means tallness. God, Most High, said: {Iram, possessor of lofty pillars} [al-Fajr: 7], meaning of great height. In the hadith: 'he is of high standing, long of sword-strap.' Abū ʿUbayd said: ʿamadtu al-shayʾ, I set it upright, so it is maʿmūd; aʿmadtuhu, with the added letter, iʿmādan, means I put a support under it.
4. From this chapter too: al-ʿumudd, the dāl strong, a young man filled out with vigour, called al-ʿumuddānī, plural al-ʿumuddāniyyūn; a woman ʿumuddāniyya is one of full, ample body.
5. From this chapter too: al-ʿamūd is the vein of the liver that feeds it. Al-watīn is called ʿamūd al-saḥr. ʿAmūd al-baṭn is something like an extended cord running from near the breastbone-cartilage to just below the navel, along its middle, cut open when a sheep's belly is dressed. They also say the two ʿamūds of the belly are the back and the spine, so called because each leans on the other.
6. From this chapter too: tharan ʿamid, moist soil soaked by rains. A poet said, in a line of verse:

And shall I gather firewood for the people, while it lies bare ... the roots of alāʾ-shrubs, in soil moist and firm-clinging

Abū Zayd said: ʿamidat al-arḍ, ʿamdan, meaning the rain sank into the ground to the moist layer, so that when you grip it in your hand it holds together and curls. They say: 'stick to your ʿumda,' meaning your purpose.
This chapter has proceeded soundly in its roots and branches, but one expression remains whose meaning, for us, we do not know, nor from what it is drawn — I suppose it is among the words that faded away with those who once understood them well: their report that Abū Jahl, when struck down, said 'aʿmadu min sayyidin qatalahu qawmuhu' (roughly: '[more?] than a chief killed by his own people') — the report is well known, but this word does not point to that explanation nor come near it, so I do not know how it truly is. They cited a line by Ibn Mayyāda:

And more ... than a people, whom their brother sufficed ... against the enemies' onslaught, when their fangs were broken

said to mean: have we done more than sufficing our brothers? This is what has been said. It has been related from al-Naḍr that its meaning is 'more astonishing than a chief killed by his own people,' and that the Arabs say 'I am aʿmadu than such-and-such,' meaning more astonishing than it — though this is further still from the first explanation. And God knows best how it truly is.
عمر:
The letters 'ayn, mīm and rā' are two sound roots: one of them points to lasting and length of time, and the other to a thing that rises high, of voice or otherwise.

The first is al-'umr, and it is life, and it is al-'amr too. And the Arabs' saying la-'amruka: he swears by his 'amr, that is, his life. As for their saying 'amraka Allāh, its meaning is: I put you in mind of God that you should do such a thing, that is, I remind you of God; you make him swear by God and you ask Him for length of his life. And one says: 'amira al-nās, their lives grew long. And God, great be His praise, gave them long life, ta'mīran.

And of this chapter is the tilling of the land: one says 'ammara al-nās al-ard 'imāratan, and they work it, and it is 'āmira ma'mūra. And their saying 'āmira is carried upon 'amarat al-ard, and al-ma'mūra is from 'umirat. And the noun and the verbal noun is al-'umrān. And God, exalted, set people to till the earth so that they should work it. And the whole chapter goes back to this.

As for the other, al-'awmara is shouting and clamour. And one says i'tamara al-rajul, when he raises the call for his 'umra, the lesser pilgrimage, and that is his raising his voice with the talbiya for the 'umra. As for the words of Ibn Ahmar, in a line of verse:
Its riders raise the cry at the sight of al-Farqad, as the mounted 'umra-pilgrim raises his cry.
some people said: it is what we mentioned of the raising of the voice at the call for the 'umra. And some people said: al-mu'tamir is the one wearing a turban. And whichever of these it was, it is from height and rising, according to what we have said.

The people of the language said: al-'amār is everything you set upon your head, of a turban, or a cap, or a garland, or a crown, or anything else; all of it is 'amār. Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
And when he came to us a little after the first sleep, we bowed down to him and raised the 'amār.
And some people said: the 'amār may be of sweet basil too. Ibn al-Sikkīt said: al-'amār is greeting. One says 'ammaraka Allāh, that is, may He give you life. And it may be that this is for the raising of the voice. And it is possible that the great clan is called an 'imāra for the clamour and shouting that comes of it. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Every folk of Ma'add has a clan, a side to which they resort, and a flank.

And of what falls outside these two roots: al-'amr is a kind of palm tree. And so-and-so used to clean his teeth with the stalks of the 'amr. And they may say al-'umr.

And of this too is al-'amr: what shows of the gums, and they are al-'umūr. And from it the name 'Amr is derived.
عمرد: This is from al-ʿurudd, which means strong; the mīm is extra, and the ṭāʾ is a substitute for the dāl.
عمرس: The harsh-natured, strong one. This is a word with the ʿayn added into it; it is really from a thing that is maris, that is, tightly twisted.
عمرط: the bold, strong one. And it is said —
عمروس: The young ram, once it has reached the age of mating. This is a word with the mīm added into it; it is from ʿarisa bi-l-shayʾ — he clung persistently to a thing and became fond of it. It is also possible that it is a blend from ʿarisa and marisa, because he rubs against the females and clings to them.
عمس:
The letters ʿayn, mīm and sīn are a sound root pointing to intensity mixed with obscurity and confusion in a matter.

1. Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿamās is fierce war; any matter that cannot be settled, or whose direction cannot be found, is ʿamās. A day is ʿamās, one of a set of days called ʿumus. Al-ʿAjjāj said: they camped on open ground after hardship, through the passing of fierce, confused days.
2. ʿumisa yawmunā ʿamāsatan wa-ʿumūsatan, our day grew fierce and obscure. Al-ʿAjjāj said: when the fierce day grew pregnant with trouble and bristled up.
3. Abū ʿAmr said: he brought us muʿammasāt or muʿammisāt matters, meaning tangled, obscure ones.
4. rajul ʿamūs — a man who gropes his way through things like one ignorant of them.
5. Al-Khalīl said: taʿāmastu ʿan al-shayʾ, when you make it appear you do not know a thing while in fact you know it and where it stands.
6. iʿmis-hu — do not make it clear, so that it stays uncertain; iʿmis al-amr, hide the matter.
7. al-ʿamās — calamity, disaster.

Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: al-taʿāmus is to be stubborn and headstrong, so as to wrong others and act arrogantly. Al-Mukhabbal said: she was stubborn and headstrong, until people supposed that she...

Al-Farrāʾ said: ʿamisa al-khabar, the news grew dark and obscure; aʿmasa al-ṭarīq, the road became confused; ʿamisa al-kitāb, the writing faded. Al-Murrār said: you stopped, trying to make out the page, after the writing had faded, though it may sometimes look as if it had not faded.
عمش:
The letters ʿayn, mīm and shīn are two sound words, very distinct from each other: the first is a weakness of eyesight, the other something good for the body.

The first: al-ʿamash is when the eye never stops running with tears, so that the man who has it, al-aʿmash, can hardly see with it; a woman with it is ʿamshāʾ, and the verb is ʿamisha, yaʿmashu, ʿamashan.

The other word: al-ʿamsh, with the mīm left unvoweled, is whatever brings good to the body. They say circumcision is "the ʿamsh of the boy," because afterward you see growth in him. They also say "this food is ʿamsh for you," meaning wholesome and agreeable.

As for ʿayn, mīm and ṣād, there is nothing in it worth mentioning.
عمق:
The letters ʿayn, mīm and qāf are a root mentioned by Ibn al-Aʿrābī, who said: al-ʿumq, said of a road, means distance; said of a well, means the length of its shaft. Al-Khalīl said: bi'run ʿamīqa, a well whose bottom lies far down, and aʿmaqahā ḥāfiruhā, its digger made it deep. They say "mā abʿada ʿamāqata hādhihi al-rakiyya," how far down is the bottom of this well. From this chapter: taʿammaqa al-rajul fī kalāmihi, when he went to excessive, laboured lengths in his speech. Ibn al-Aʿrābī related, from an eloquent Arab: "ra'aytu khalīqatan famā ra'aytu aʿmaqa minhā," I saw a khalīqa and never saw one deeper; he said al-khalīqa is a newly-dug well.

What remains in this chapter are place-names, or a plant-name. We have said that such names rarely follow a regular pattern, but we mention them anyway. ʿAmq is a land belonging to Muzayna. Sāʿida said:
When he saw ʿAmq and turned back across its breadth, roaring as the tethered stud-camel roars.

Al-ʿimqā is a place-name. Abū Dhu'ayb said:
When I remembered the brother of al-ʿImqā, grief returned to me by night, and the towering wormwood-thicket left my back bare.

Al-ʿimqā, in its short form, also names a plant. Yūnus said: jamalun ʿāmiq, a camel that grazes on al-ʿimqā. Uʿāmiq is said to be the name of a place. Al-Akhṭal said:
And there had been, among them, a dwelling-place we delighted in — Uʿāmiq, with its stony flats, where I would ride about.
عمل:
The letters ʿayn, mīm and lām are a single sound root, and it is general in every deed that is done.

Al-Khalīl said: ʿamila yaʿmalu ʿamalan — he worked, working — so he is ʿāmil, a worker; and iʿtamala al-rajul — the man worked with his own hands. He said:
The generous man — by your father — works with his own hands, if he does not one day find someone to lean upon.

And al-ʿimāla is the wage for what has been worked. And al-muʿāmala is the verbal noun of your saying ʿāmaltuhu, and I deal with him, dealing. And al-ʿamala are the people who work with their hands at kinds of work — digging, or walling a well, or the like. And of the section: the ʿāmil of the spear and its ʿāmila, and it is the part a little below the socket, next to the spearhead; it is its foremost part. He said:
I thrust the wide thrust, its wound howling, the shaft of the spear in it bending down heavy.

He said: and a man works for himself, and works for a people, and puts another to work, and puts to work his opinion, or his speech, or his spear. And the builder yastaʿmil the brick — puts it to work — when he builds with it. He said: and al-yaʿmala among camels is a name for them derived from work, and the plural is yaʿmalāt. And it is said only of the female, though al-yaʿāmil may be allowed. Dhū al-Rumma, or another, said, in a line of verse:
And the working she-camels, footsore, cut across desert after desert.
And God knows best.
عملس:
The cunning wolf. One says 'a wolf of night-journeying' (ʿamallas dalajāt). Al-Ṭirimmāḥ said:
He ties up in the leashes every ʿamallas, of the game-catching, laden hunting hounds.
This is a word with the lām added into it. It is possible that it is from two words: from ʿamila and ʿamasa. You say: he is ʿamūl ʿamūs, meaning he follows his own head and presses on in whatever he sets out to do.
عملط:
The strong one, among men, and likewise among camels. He said:
Have you not seen the strong man?
This is a word with the ʿayn added into it; it is really from al-milṭ, which has already been mentioned in its own chapter.
عمن: The letters ʿayn, mīm and nūn are not a true root; among them is ʿUmān, a country. They say aʿmana, when he went to ʿUmān. A poet said: if you go to Tihāma we shall oppose you by going to Najd, and if you go to ʿUmān, laden with harm, we shall go to ʿIrāq.
عمه: The letters ʿayn, mīm and hāʾ are one sound root, pointing to bewilderment and loss of direction. Al-Khalīl said: ʿamiha al-rajul, yaʿmahu, ʿamahan, when he wanders back and forth not knowing which way to turn. God said: {and He leaves them wandering blindly in their transgression} [al-Aʿrāf: 186]. Yaʿqūb said: 'his camels went off al-ʿummayhā,' with the mīm doubled, meaning he did not know where they had gone.
عمي:
The letters ʿayn and mīm with the weak letter are one root pointing to covering and veiling. Of that is al-ʿamā, the going of sight from both eyes. Its verb is ʿamiya yaʿmā ʿaman. And they may say iʿmāyya yaʿmāyyu iʿmiyā'an, like idhhāmma, to turn deep black; they brought it out on the form of the sound verb. A man is aʿmā and a woman ʿamyā'. And this description does not fall upon one eye alone. One says ʿamiyat ʿaynāhu - both his eyes went blind. Among women it is ʿamyā', ʿamyāwān, ʿamyāwāt. And a man is ʿamin when he is blind of heart, and a people are ʿamūna. And in this sense they say mā aʿmāhu, how blind he is; but they do not say mā aʿmāhu of blindness of sight, because that is a plain quality that the eye takes in, and they say mā afʿalahu only of the qualities that are hidden. Al-Khalīl said: because it is ugly to say of a man pointed at, how blind he is, when the one you address already shares with you the knowledge of his blindness.

He said: and al-taʿmiya is that you make a thing dark for a person so that you thoroughly confuse it for him. As for al-ʿAjjāj's words, in a line of verse:
And many a land whose blind wastes efface the traveller.

He made ʿamā a noun and then gathered it as al-aʿmā'. And they say: your love of a thing makes you blind and deaf. And they say: love is blind. And they may say aʿmaytu al-rajul, when you find the man blind. A poet said, in a line of verse:
So I found ʿAmr deaf, and I found him blind to giving and to glory on the day of boasting.

And they may say al-ʿumyān for blindness, bringing it out on the pattern of ṭughyān. And of the chapter: al-ʿummiyya is going astray, and so too al-ʿimmiyya. And in the hadith: God, exalted is He, has taken away from you the ʿimmiyya of the Days of Ignorance. They said: he meant pride. And it is said fulān fī ʿamyā', when he does not know the face of the truth. And qatīl ʿimmiyyan, that is, it is not known who killed him. And al-ʿamāya is being led astray, which is stubborn persistence. And of the chapter: al-ʿamā' is thick, close-packed cloud, and a piece of it is ʿamā'a. And al-Kisā'ī said: he is in a heavy ʿimāya and in ʿamā', that is, in darkness.

And the people of the language said: al-maʿāmī of lands are the neglected ones that have no trace of tilling upon them. And of it is the letter of the Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, to Ukaydir: the maʿāmī and the untilled parts of the land are ours.

And of the chapter: al-ʿamy, on the measure of ramy, and that is the waves' driving of the scum and the foam on their tops. And it is the reasoning, because that covers the face of the water. A poet said, in a line of verse:
It has foam with which the swelling wave covers its face.

And the camel, when he brays, ʿamā with his froth over the top of his head, ʿamyan. A poet said, in a line of verse:
He covers it with the like of teased cotton.

And the Arabs say ataytuhu ẓuhran ṣakkata ʿumayy, when you come to him in the noonday heat. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: the time is meant when the heat all but blinds. And Muḥammad ibn Yazīd al-Mubarrad said: the time when the gazelle comes to his lair and cannot see for the heat. And it is said that al-ʿamā' is the dust. And there is recited, of al-Murrār, in a line of verse:
You see them circling about their caves, while a hot wind full of dust breaks in upon them.
عميثل:
the big, heavy one.

1. al-ʿamaythal — anything in which there is slowness.
2. imraʾatun ʿamaythalah — a woman who is big and heavy.

Abū al-Najm said, in a line of verse: he is not slack-limbed, nor is he ʿamaythal.

This is a word in which the mīm was added; the origin is ʿathal. Al-ʿithwal is the slow, heavy one — this has already been explained.
عن:
The letters ʿayn and nūn are two roots: one points to the appearing of a thing and its presenting itself; the other points to confinement.

The first: the saying of the Arabs, "ʿanna lanā kadhā, yaʿinnu, ʿunūnan," when something appeared before you.

He said:
And there appeared to us a herd, whose does seemed like the maidens of Duwār, in long trailing wraps.

Ibn al-A'rābī said: al-ʿanān is whatever presents itself to you of anything. Al-Khalīl said: ʿanān al-samā', the expanse of the sky, is what presents itself to you of it when you look up at it. As for al-Shammākh's line:
It endured its thirst through the white-hot midday of the summer heat, after the rocky tracts had run beneath the range of the two Shi'rā stars —
some transmitted it, as here, with fatha, ʿanāni; Abū 'Amr transmitted it as ʿinān al-Shi'rayayn, meaning the first rising-time of the two Shi'rā stars.

Abū 'Ubayda said, in the proverb: "one exposed to a matter that did not concern him."

Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿanūn, among riding-beasts and others, is the one that goes ahead in its pace.

He said:
As if the saddle were fastened on a swift, dark she-camel from among the black ones, out ahead, forward-going.

Al-Farrā' said: al-ʿinān is al-muʿānna, meaning opposition and stubborn resistance.

He quoted:
You will know, if the mill of war turns between us, opposing the north wind, who among us proves the weaker.

Ibn al-A'rābī said: so-and-so *shāraka* so-and-so *shirkat ʿinān* — this is when a man presents part of what is in his hand as a share, and so takes another as his partner in it — that is, he offers it.

He quoted:
No substitute for Umm 'Uthmān is a dark, coarse woman, of poor stock, unsound in her offering, corrupt.
He said: ʿarūb, in the verse, means corrupt, from their saying ʿaribat maʿidatuhu, his stomach went bad.

Abū 'Ubayda said: al-miʿann, of horses, is the one that opposes everything it sees, nothing escaping its notice. He said: al-miʿann is also the orator whose gaze grows intent, whose mouth grows moist, whose voice carries far, and whom no branch of speech ever leaves at a loss.

He quoted: an orator, loud-voiced in his speech.

From this chapter too: ʿunwān al-kitāb, the heading of a document, because it is the most prominent and clearest part of it. One says ʿanantu the letter, aʿunnuhu, ʿannan, and ʿanwantuhu, and ʿannantuhu, uʿinnuhu, taʿnīnan. When you give the command, you say ʿannin-hu.

Ibn al-Sikkīt said: one says laqītuhu ʿayna ʿunnatin, meaning suddenly, as if it had presented itself to me without my seeking it.

Ṭufayl said: when it turned back from one encounter after another encounter.

It is said that the mountain-range stretching up into the sky is called ʿānn, plural ʿawānn.

As for the other root, confinement: al-ʿunna is the enclosure for livestock, plural ʿunan. Abū Ziyād said: al-ʿunna is a structure you build of stones, plural ʿunan.

Al-A'shā said:
You see the meat from a withered strip, gone dry, and a fresh one, raised up over the enclosure-walls.

One says: ʿannantu the camel, meaning I confined it in the ʿunna. Sometimes, finding the repetition of the letter nūn heavy on the tongue, they turned the last one into a yā', just as they say: the falcon's turning-back, when the falcon is broken in its stoop. So they say ʿannaytu.

He said:
You have spent the age like a bellowing stud-camel kept from the herd — roaring in Damascus, never settling.
By this is meant al-muʿannan, the confined stud-camel.

Some said: the stud-camel that is not approved among them has a stick tied across against his sheath; then when he tries to mount a she-camel to cover her, the stick prevents him — and that stick is called al-nijāf. So when they want it, they remove it and bring a nobler stud than him and let him cover her, and they name the first one al-muʿannā, the kept-back one.

He quoted:
I have held myself back for death, which is bound to come.
Meaning: I have restrained myself from worldly desires, just as was done to al-muʿannā.

In the proverb: "He is like the one bellowing while confined in the pen." He said: the well-known transmission is taʿannantu, from al-ʿinnīn, the man who cannot come to women.

From this chapter too: ʿinān al-faras, the horse's rein, because it holds it back; plural aʿinna and ʿunun. Al-Kisā'ī said: aʿnantu the horse, meaning I fitted a rein to it; and ʿannantuhu, meaning I restrained it by its rein. As for al-mar'a al-muʿannana, this is by way of resemblance — she is the one slender-waisted, supple, twisted like the twisting of a rein.

He quoted:
And among the tribe are white, house-dwelling women, soft, their wraps twisted like a rein.

Abū Ḥātim said: ʿinān al-matn, of the back, means its two ridges; this too is by way of resemblance.

Ru'ba said: toward the two rein-like ridges of a lean, slender one. The origin, in the sense of al-ʿinān, is what we mentioned under confinement.

The Arabs have proverbial sayings about ʿinān. They say: "His rein grew tame for me," when he yielded. And: "He is hard of rein," when he will not yield. And: "Slacken from his rein," meaning ease off him. And: "I filled the horse's rein," meaning I reached the limit of its effort at a gallop.

He quoted:
A she-camel, remote from the driver's call, when the midday sun has filled the rein of the burning-hot, echoing tract.
He means: when the sun has reached the utmost exertion of the locust, which is called al-abraq.

They also say: "The two of them run in a single rein," when they are equal in some work or excellence. And: "So-and-so ran a rein, or two reins," meaning a lap or two laps.

Al-Ṭirimmāḥ said:
They will all come to know that I am old and experienced, when they lift rein above rein.

Ibn al-Sikkīt said: "so-and-so is ṭarib al-ʿinān," meant for lightness and grace. And "so-and-so is ṭawīl al-ʿinān," meaning he is not turned away from what he wants, on account of his standing or his wealth.

Al-Ḥuṭay'a said: inherited glory, and a long rein.

Some said: thanaytu ʿalā al-faras ʿinānahu, meaning I bridled it; and ithni ʿalā farasika ʿinānahu, meaning bridle it.

Ibn Muqbil said:
And he pressed hard upon me, until I turned back his rein, over one retreating, thick-necked, with drenched shoulders.

As for the poet's saying:
You will know, if the mill of war turns between us, opposing the north wind, who among us proves the weaker —
Abū 'Ubayda said: by his saying ʿinān al-shimāl, he meant the strap by which something is hung at the left side of the ewe, and gave it that name. Others said: the riding-beast can only be turned from its left side; so the meaning is: if it turns its turning in that direction. Some said: ʿinān al-shimāl is an ill-omened thing, just as one says of it: "I read an omen from the birds of the left." And they say, of one who has succeeded in his need: "he came, his rein turned back a second time."
عنابل:
the thick bowstring. He said, in a line of verse: and the bow has upon it a thick ʿunābil string.

This is coined by blending ʿanab and ʿabal, both of which indicate extension and firmness.
عنب:
The letters ʿayn, nūn and *al-bāb* [so printed] are a small root pointing to a well-known fruit, and to one other word.

The fruit is *al-ʿinab*, grapes; a single one is *ʿinaba*. And they say: there is nothing in their speech on the pattern *fiʿala* except *ʿinaba*. And they sometimes called grapes *al-ʿinabā'*. A poet said, in a line of verse:
the picked-over grapes and the figs.
And they sometimes made the plural of *ʿinab* to be *aʿnāb*. And one says *rajul ʿānib*, that is, a man with many grapes, just as one says *tāmir*, a man with many dates, and *lābin*, a man with much milk.

The other word is *al-ʿanabān*, on the pattern *faʿalān*: the mountain goat with long horns. A poet said, in a line of verse:
He charges as the ʿanabān charges, swerving aside.
And the brisk gazelle is called *al-ʿanabān*; and no verb is built from it.
عنبس: One of the names of the lion. Al-Khalīl said: when you describe it you say ʿanbas and ʿunābis, and when you make it a proper name you say ʿAnbasa, without mentioning the lion. This is a word with the nūn added into it; it is on the pattern fanʿal, from al-ʿubūs, a scowling frown.
عنت:
The letters ʿayn, nūn and tā' are a sound root, indicating hardship and the like; it does not indicate soundness or ease.

Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿanat is a hardship that comes upon speech. You say ʿanita fulān, meaning he met with ʿanat, that is, hardship. aʿnatahu fulān iʿnātan — so-and-so put him through ʿanat, when he brought hardship upon him. taʿannatahu taʿannutan — he pressed him hard, when he asked him about something meaning to confuse and trouble him by it.

Ibn Durayd said: al-ʿanat is oppression and forcing someone into what is hateful. aʿnatahu yuʿnituhu iʿnātan.

Referred to this and following its pattern, one who sins is said to ʿanita ʿanatan, when he has incurred a sin.

Al-Farrā' said, concerning His saying, Most High: {that is for those among you who fear sin} [al-Nisā': 25] — meaning: you are permitted to marry slave-women if one of you fears he will fall into fornication.

Al-Zajjāj said: al-ʿanat in the language means severe hardship. One says akama ʿanūt, a hill that is hard [to climb].

Al-Mubarrad said: al-ʿanat here means ruin. Others said: its meaning is, that is for one who fears that desire will drive him to fornication, so that he meets with great sin in the next life.
عنتر: The brave one. This is a word with the nūn added into it; the origin is al-ʿitr, from ʿatara al-rumḥ — the spear quivered. The brave man was named by this for his quickness to engage in battle and the great motion he shows in it.
عنج:
The letters ʿayn, nūn and jīm are a single sound root pointing to pulling one thing by another that stretches out, like a rope and the like. Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿinaj is a strap or cord tied to the bottom of a bucket, then tied to its handle-loop; anything fitted this way is called ʿinaj. If the rope snaps, the ʿinaj keeps the bucket from falling into the well. He said: anything you pull toward yourself, you have ʿanajtahu. A poet said: a people who, when they made a pact for their neighbor, tightened the ʿinaj and tightened the karab above it — the cord that binds the bucket's crossbar. Another said: some talk has no ʿinaj, like flowing water with no yield. Al-itāʾ means increase, yield.

The plural of al-ʿinaj is ʿunuj, and "three aʿnija." A man yaʿnuju his camel's head toward himself, meaning he pulls it by its nose-rein. It is said the ʿinaj is only in the loops of the bucket, not at its bottom. A line was recited: it has two ʿinajs and six loops, wide-mouthed, of two hides.

1. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: ʿanajtu al-dalwa and aʿnajtuhā both mean fitted the bucket with its ʿinaj.
2. Abū Zayd said: al-ʿanj is your pulling its head while you ride it, meaning the she-camel.
3. Abū ʿUbayda said, among their proverbs for one who will not accept training: "an old animal being taught al-ʿanj."

As for what was mentioned in "some talk has no ʿinaj," Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ said: al-ʿinaj in speech is that it should carry weight, so that a man speaks with knowledge and consideration; and if it has no ʿinaj, what comes out of him is not what its speaker intends. The meaning of this saying is that his speech has no halter and no rein, so it goes off wherever, with no sense to it. The Arabs also say "ʿinaj amr fulānin," meaning its rein and the mastery of its affair.

4. Al-ʿunjūj is a fine, excellent horse, plural ʿanājīj. A poet said: we came upon ʿĀmir and ʿAbs at dawn, sleek chestnut horses of fine breed, that outran the sun.

It could be a name coined without derivation, like everything else that stands outside the roots, or it could be so named for its length, or the length of its neck, following the reasoning of the long rope. Abū ʿUbayda said: al-ʿunjūj among horses is the long-necked one, feminine ʿunjūja. Supporting this is their saying "istaqāma ʿunjūj al-qawm," meaning their established course — this confirms it, because a course also stretches out lengthwise. What is carried over to this by comparison is their saying "ʿanājīj al-shabāb," meaning its attractions. Ibn Aḥmar said: and the ʿanājīj of soft youth passed on. They also say "rajul miʿnaj," said of a man who involves himself in affairs, as though he is always being pulled toward something by some tie, and clings to it.
عنجرد: the bold, sharp-tongued woman. This means that she strips herself bare for mischief. The ʿayn and nūn are extra.
عند:
The letters 'ayn, nūn and dāl are one sound root pointing to going past a limit and leaving the straight road. Al-Khalīl said: 'anada al-rajul, and he is 'ānid, ya'nudu 'unūdan, when he becomes insolent and overbearing and goes beyond his measure. From it is al-mu'ānada, obstinacy, which is that a man knows a thing and refuses to accept it. One says: 'anada fulānun 'an al-amr, when he turns aside from it. Al-'anūd among camels is the one that does not mix with the camels but keeps off on one side. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And many a suspicious companion who keeps apart, who has been dull towards me with the worst dullness.

And one says: a man is 'anūd, when he keeps to himself and does not mix with people. And he recited, a line of verse:
And many a client keeping apart whom a crime has caught up with - and crimes do catch up with the client who keeps apart.

He said: as for al-'anīd, it is from tyranny, and for that reason they made a difference between al-'anīd, al-'anūd and al-'ānid. And one says of the stubborn tyrant: he has been obstinate, 'andan and 'unūdan.

Al-Khalīl said: al-'irq al-'ānid is the vein that gushes blood so that it hardly stops. You say: 'anada 'irquhu.

Ibn Durayd said: a road that is 'ānid is one that bends away. And a she-camel is 'anūd when she swerves off the road out of her liveliness and strength. The rajaz poet said, in a line of verse:
When you ride, put me in the middle; I am an old man and cannot bear the ones that swerve aside.

Mā 'anhu 'undad, that is, there is no escaping it - this belongs to the section. The explanation of mā 'anhu 'andad is: there is no turning aside from it and no swerving. Jundal said, in a line of verse:
Death is only a watering place that must be come to; do not feel safe from it, there is no turning aside from it.

And one says: a'nada fī qay'ihi, when his vomiting does not stop. Ya'qūb said: a vein that has 'ānada - its blood has 'anada, ya'nudu, that is, it goes off to one side. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And what thing does not love its own child? - even the bustard, and it flutters at its side.

That is, at a side of it, watching over it. And one says: ista'nada al-ba'īr, when it overpowers the man leading it on the halter and drags him. And of this section is a proverb of theirs: 'Beneath his smoothness there is a rough side.' Al-ṭirrīqa is softness. One says: beneath that softness there is arrogance, going past bounds and overstepping.

As for their saying zaydun 'inda 'amrin, Zayd is beside 'Amr, it is not far-fetched that it should be of this same analogy, as though he had turned away from all people towards him until he came near him and clung to him.
عنز:
The letters ʿayn, nūn and zāy are two sound roots: one points to withdrawing and setting oneself apart, the other is a kind of animal.

The first:
1. iʿtanaza fulān — so-and-so withdrew and kept apart. One says "mā lī ʿanhu muʿtanaz," meaning I have no place to withdraw to from it. A poet said: as though I were Suhayl, whose withdrawal from its place is to appear on the horizon, then vanish.

The second root: al-ʿanz — the female of goats, of mountain-goats, and of gazelles; the female of gazelle young is also called ʿanz, plural "three aʿnuz," and al-ʿināz. Abū Ḥātim said: I have heard "three aʿnuz" only for sheep and goats, and I have heard al-ʿināz only for gazelles. They also say al-ʿanz is a kind of fish, and sometimes they call the female eagle ʿanz; some said al-ʿanz is the eagle. All of this is carried over by comparison from al-ʿanz of the flock.

What falls outside both this root and the first: al-ʿanaza, shaped like a staff, from which a group of Arabs called ʿAnaza take their name.

From the first root also: muʿannaz al-wajh, said of one whose face has little flesh on it, as though compared to the ʿanz of the flock. Among place-names is ʿUnayza, a stretch of land. Muhalhil said: as though we, one morning, and the sons of our father, were beside ʿUnayza a pair of turning millstones.
عنس:
The letters ʿayn, nūn and sīn are a single sound root pointing to hardness and strength in a thing. Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿans is one of the names of the she-camel; she is said to be named ʿans when her age has come to fullness, her strength has firmed up, and her bones and limbs have filled out. Iʿnawnasa dhanabuhā, her tail grew thick with hair; al-iʿnīnās is the abundance and length of its hair. Al-Ṭirimmāḥ, describing a bull, said: he sweeps the ground with his thick-haired tail, like the mourning-woman's plume held upright. Al-ʿAjjāj said: how many a firm, tough, bow-backed she-camel, and another one hard as a rock, have we worn down.

1. ʿanasat al-marʾa, taʿnusu, ʿunūsan — the woman, when she reached middle years while still an unmarried virgin. ʿannasahā ahluhā taʿnīsan — her family kept her from marrying until she had passed the flower of her youth, without yet being elderly. This is sound reasoning, because that is the time of her firmness and strength. One says imraʾa muʿannasa, plural maʿānis and muʿannasāt; she is also ʿānis, plural ʿawānis. A line was recited: and slender-waisted women, like flocks of sandgrouse, whose younger girls, along with the older unmarried women, had begun to show themselves. The plural of ʿānis is ʿunnas. A line was recited: among a fair-formed people who outshine the ʿunnas.

Al-Aṣmaʿī mentioned that ʿānis is also said of men, one who has not married. A line was recited: among us is the one whose mustache has not yet sprouted, and the ʿānis men, and among us the beardless youths and the grey-haired.

Some mentioned that al-ʿans is also a rock, and the tough she-camel is compared to it and so called ʿans. That is not far-fetched.
عنسل: The swift she-camel of sturdy build. This is from two words: from ʿanasa and nasala. ʿAnasa is from the strength of her build — she was named from al-ʿans, which is the rock. And nasala refers to speed and going forth.
عنش:
The letters ʿayn, nūn and shīn are a small root, perhaps sound. If sound, it points to hard engagement, grappling with something. They say fulān yuʿānishu al-nās, meaning he fights them and grapples with them; yuʿānishu also means he wrongs them. They recite: then every armed man would come to him, his forearm grappling on the day of hardship, sturdy.

They also say ʿānashtu al-rajul, meaning I embraced him. They recite, for Sāʿida: the grappling of an enemy that cannot reach a swift man on foot, when the fire of war blazes up.

If this is not a case of letter-substitution, the shīn standing in for a qāf, I do not know how it stands — but we hope it is sound, God willing.

Ibn Durayd said: ʿanashtu al-shayʾ, aʿnishuhu, ʿanshan, when I bent it. This too is close to what has been mentioned.
عنص:
The letters ʿayn, nūn and ṣād are a small sound root concerning hair. Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿanṣuwa is a lock of hair. A poet said: my wife has reproached me for my grey hair, and stroked the locks of my head, marveling at that.

What is compared to this: they say "in the land of the sons of so-and-so there is ʿanāṣ of plant-growth" — and likewise hair, when it is sparse and scattered, singular ʿunṣuwa. Abū al-Najm said: should my head turn grey-streaked in its locks, as though a comb had parted it.

Al-Farrāʾ said: one says "mā baqiya min mālihi illā ʿanāṣ," said when only a little of it remains. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: al-ʿunṣuwa is a small tuft of hair at the side of the head.
عنصر: the root of one's lineage and standing. This is a word in which the nūn was added; it is originally al-ʿaṣr, which is the refuge — we have already explained it — because everyone takes refuge in tracing his lineage back to the origin he comes from.
عنط:
The letters ʿayn, nūn and ṭāʾ are a sound little root indicating length of body and beauty of stature.

Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿanaṭnaṭ — its derivation is from ʿanaṭa, but two letters have been added after it, at its end. Ruʾba said, in a line of verse:
He stretches out on the night journey with a long, ʿanaṭnaṭ neck.

And a woman ʿanaṭnaṭa is one long in the neck, with good stature besides. He said, describing a man and a horse, in a line of verse:
A long-necked one — a long-necked mare runs with him — the water under her belly making a gurgling sound.
عنف:
The letters ʿayn, nūn and fāʾ are a sound root indicating the opposite of gentleness.

Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿunf is the opposite of rifq (gentleness). You say ʿanufa yaʿnufu ʿunfan, so he is ʿanīf, when he is not gentle in his affair. And I made him harsh — aʿnaftuhu.

1. iʿtanafta al-shayʾ — said when you disliked a thing and found it harsh and burdensome for you.
2. al-taʿnīf — severity in blame.

As for al-ʿunfuwān, it is the beginning of a thing — one says ʿunfuwān al-shabāb, the first flush of youth, meaning its beginning. But this does not belong with the first sense; rather it belongs to the chapter of letter-substitution, where the ʿayn stands in for a hamza, and the true root is al-anf, the nose — for the anf of anything is its front, its beginning. He said:
What does her daughter say, feeling her way, when the failing first flush [of her youth], now flecked grey, has called to her?
And another said:
You blame a man in the first flush of his youth, while you leave the followers of error to bide their time.
عنفص:
the woman who is slight/of little worth, and it is said she is the wicked, promiscuous one. Al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse: she is not dark-skinned, nor is she an ʿinfiṣ, stealing glances toward a promiscuous man.

This second account is the sounder one by analogy; it is from ʿafaṣtu al-shayʾ, if I twisted it — as if she is crooked in nature and inclines toward the promiscuous.
عنق:
The letters ʿayn, nūn and qāf are one sound root pointing to extension in a thing, either in height or in spreading out.

The first is al-ʿunuq, the neck, which is the join between the head and the body. It is used as masculine and as feminine, and its plural is aʿnāq. A man aʿnaq is long-necked. A mountain aʿnaq is towering. A highland is aʿnaq, and a hill ʿanqā'. A woman ʿanqā' is long-necked. And a hill is muʿniqa as well. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Long-necked and towering, whose only company is the grey doves, its fresh herbage uneaten.

Al-Aṣmaʿī said: al-muʿanniqāt are like al-muʿniqāt, the towering heights. ʿUmar ibn Laja' said, in a line of verse:
And of the crags of al-Arūm, towering heights.

Abū ʿAmr said: al-muʿanniq is the tall one. And he recited:
On a high hump like the towering sand-hill.

Abū ʿAmr said: al-ʿanqā', so it is said, is a bird of which nothing has remained but its name. It was called ʿanqā' for a whiteness that was on its neck. And in the proverb for a thing not to be found: "The ʿanqā' has flown off with him."

As for their calling a company ʿunuq, its sense is sound, because it is a thing whose parts are joined one to another. God, exalted be He, said: {so their necks stayed bowed before it} [al-Shuʿarā': 4], meaning their company. Do you not see that He said {bowed} [al-Shuʿarā': 4] in the form used for men? Had it been the necks themselves, He would have said khāḍiʿatan or khāḍiʿātin. To this Abū Zayd went. The grammarians said: since the necks were joined to them by possession, He turned the verb back to them and not to the necks.

Muḥammad ibn Yazīd said: since the bowing of their owners is by the bowing of their necks, He told of the owners, because the meaning goes back to them. The Arabs say: my neck has been humbled to so-and-so, and my nape has bowed to him — that is, I bowed to him. That is like what they said of its opposite: he twisted his neck away from me and his temples did not soften to me — that is, he did not bow to me and did not yield.

Al-Duraydī said: aʿnaqtu al-kalba uʿniquhu iʿnāqan, when you put a collar or a cord on the dog's neck. And al-miʿnaqa is the dog's miʿnaqa, which is its collar. And what rises up of the winds is called aʿnāq al-riyāḥ, the necks of the winds. And they say aʿnaqat al-rīḥ bi-l-turāb — the wind carried the dust up. Al-Khalīl said: uʿtuniqat al-dābba fī al-waḥl, when the beast put out its neck in the mire. Ru'ba said, in a line of verse:
Their necks coming out of a muʿtanaq.

Al-muʿtanaq is the place where the necks of the mountains come out of the mirage — that is, they were seized in it and so put out their necks.

And al-iʿtināq is also from al-muʿānaqa, embracing, except that al-muʿānaqa is in affection and al-iʿtināq is in war and the like. You say iʿtanaqū fī al-ḥarb — they grappled in the war — and you do not say taʿānaqū. The sense is one, only they chose al-iʿtināq for war and al-muʿānaqa for affection and the like. And if you single out one of the two by the verb, you say only ʿānaqa fulānun fulānan — so-and-so embraced so-and-so. And sometimes iʿtanaqa is said of one alone. Zuhayr said, in a line of verse:
He kept spearing them while they shot; then when they speared, he smote; and when they smote, he closed and grappled.

Yūnus ibn Ḥabīb said: ʿanaqtu al-baʿīr, when you struck its neck, as one says ra'astuhu — I struck its head. Al-Khalīl said: one says taʿannaqa al-arnab fī al-ʿāniqā'; and the ʿāniqā' is a burrow filled with soft earth belonging to the hare and the jerboa when they are afraid. And sometimes it enters that earth, so one says taʿannaqa, because it thrusts its head and neck into it and goes on until it comes to be beneath it.

Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: al-ʿāniqā' is the earth of the jerboa's lughghayzā and the earth of its run. And its lughghayzā are its two diggings on the two sides of the burrow. Quṭrub said: ʿunuq al-raḥim, the neck of the womb, is the narrow part of it next to the vulva. Abū Ḥātim said: ʿunuq al-kirsh is the lower part of the paunch. He said: al-ʿunuq and al-qibba are one thing. And one says ʿannaqat kawāfīr al-nakhl, when the palm-spathes grow long and do not split open; that is al-taʿnīq. One says busra muʿanniqa, when there is left round its calyx something like a signet-ring, and that is when the ripening has come near to its calyx. And al-Aʿnaq is a man of the Arabs, and he is Qays ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Hammām; he was so named for the length of his neck. A people are traced to him who are called Banū al-Aʿnaq, a clan of Wā'il ibn Qāsiṭ. And another people of the Yemen are called Banū al-ʿAnqā'. Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿAnqā' is Thaʿlaba ibn ʿAmr ibn Mālik, of Khuzāʿa. Some people said: he was so named for the length of his neck, and in the wording he went to the feminine of ʿunuq, as in their saying:
And ʿAntara al-Falḥā'.

He made it feminine when he went to the lip. And a poet said, in a line of verse:
Or al-ʿAnqā', Thaʿlaba son of ʿAmr — the blood of the people is a cure for one mad with rage.

Quṭrub said: the Arabs say of a thing that never parts: he is to you as the ring on the dove's neck, meaning its collar, because it never parts from it.

And from the section: al-ʿanaq, one of the paces of riding beasts; the descriptive words are miʿnāq and ʿanīq. One says a hack ʿanīq, and a pace ʿanīq. A poet said, in a line of verse:
When she saw me, my going was a creeping — yet I have been seen, and my going was long-striding.

Abū ʿUbayda said: al-ʿanaq is the outstretched pace. And this is what we mentioned in the root of the section: that the section is built upon extension. Ibn al-Sikkīt said: aʿnaqa al-faras yuʿniqu iʿnāqan, and it is the light walk. And a hack is miʿnāq. And in the proverb: "I shall surely make its slow one catch up with the swift one." Abū Ḥātim said: al-miʿnāq among camels is the light one that makes for the pasture and does not graze it. And it is said: al-maʿānīq among camels are those that are not content with the pasture, out of their bad nature and their little good; their herdsman is never out of toil. And the meaning of this is that they always stretch their necks toward what is before them. And he recited, in lines of verse:
And he, by God's praise, suffices me the work — the watering, the herding, and the long walking,
and the seeking of the first swift-necked camels.

Some of the people of the language said: aʿnaqat — they wandered about in their pastures and did not graze, seeking other herbage. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said, on the saying of Ibn Aḥmar, in a line of verse:
The daughters of Aʿnaq stay saddled for the sight of her, going out at evening and at morning.

He said: by "the daughters of Aʿnaq" he means every beast that stretched its neck, whether horse or camel; and he is only describing a pearl. He says: the beasts stay saddled in seeking it and in looking at it.

As for al-ʿanqā', it is said that it is calamity, and it was so called to make it ugly and dreadful, as though it were a thing long of neck. A poet said, in a line of verse:
They carry the ʿanqā' and the ʿanqafīr, calamity upon calamity, and the bucket, the Daylam and the groaning.

And it is said that al-muʿniq of the hard ground is what is firm and raised while what is around it is soft, running along in length about a mile or less; and the plural is maʿāniq.

And from the section: al-ʿanāq, the female of the young of goats; the plural is ʿunūq. Jamīl said, in a line of verse:
When a kid of hers fell sick, you would see him with his knife, hovering about her in grief.

And it is said of a man when he moves from high standing to lowness: "Kids after she-camels" — that is, you have become a herder of kids after having been a herder of she-camels. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: al-ʿanāq is so from the time her mother drops her until she becomes a jadhaʿ two months after her weaning, when she is five months old. Abū ʿUbayda said: al-ʿanāq falls upon the female of the young of the flock, from the time she is born until a year passes over her and she becomes a ʿanz, a she-goat. And a ewe is miʿnāq when she gives birth to kids. And he recited, in a line of verse:
An old one of a noble flock, well-bred, of many young, a bearer of kids.

And ʿanāq al-arḍ is a beast smaller than the cheetah.

As for their calling disappointment ʿanāq, that is not a root, as we have said. The face of it, with us, is that the Arabs sometimes give some things a nickname by which they hint at the thing, as they nickname treachery Kaysān, and what is like this. So for that reason they hinted at disappointment by al-ʿanāq. And sometimes they said al-ʿanāqa with the hā'. A poet said, in a line of verse:
They got nothing of us but disappointment — wretched is the gift, of one who presses his demands.

Al-aws is the gift and the recompense. One says ustuhu awsan — I gave him a gift. And another said, on al-ʿanāq, in a line of verse:
Was it for the crying of a sand-grouse that you killed your prisoners and came back with disappointment?

And upon this too is carried what Ibn al-Sikkīt related, that al-ʿanāq is calamity. And he recited, in a line of verse:
When they stretched out over the hilltops, they met from him the two ears of a ʿanāq — that is, calamity.

As for what they relate of their saying: this water of yours is ʿanāq al-arḍ, and that it is the water of lying, and the report that is mentioned in it — that is of the kind by which tales are multiplied and books are stuffed; it has no meaning and no use in it.
عنقفير: a formidable calamity. This too was made to sound formidable by addition. They call a calamity ʿanqāʾ, then add these further letters, as we have said more than once.
عنقود: A well-known thing [a cluster, as of grapes]. It is from al-ʿaqd, as though it were a thing whose parts are bound one to another.
عنك:
The letters ʿayn, nūn and kāf are two roots. One is a color among colors. The other is entanglement in a matter, and being shut and closed upon a thing.

The first: al-ʿānik. Al-Khalīl said it is a shade of red; one says "blood that is ʿānik." A poet said, in a line of verse:
Or one that is ʿānik, like the blood of a sacrificed animal, dark and pooling.
Others transmit this as "or ʿātiq" instead. He also said: sweat is ʿānik when there is redness in its color. Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
Upon a chamomile flower, amid the hollows of virgin sand, a thick, deep-red glow presses at its heart.

The other root: al-muʿtanik, of camels, is the one that, when the sand grows too heavy for it, kneels down and crawls upon it. A poet said:
You have perished, if you do not crawl as the muʿtanik camel crawls.
Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: one says iʿtanaka al-baʿīr, when the camel walks in sand that is ʿānik, meaning deep, so that it cannot walk in it except by crawling — and he cited this line of verse. Its meaning is: if you do not bear for me, on your own back, what this camel bears for itself in the sand, then I have perished.

1. al-ʿink — Al-Khalīl said it is the door. Ibn Durayd said: ʿanaktu al-bāb and aʿnaktuhu both mean I shut it — a Yemeni dialect word. This confirms the analogy we gave for this second root.
2. al-ʿank of the night — a stretch of darkness in it, because the darkness seems to shut the door of light. And the word is sound — I mean that al-ʿink is darkness. He cited, in lines of verse:
And two true-hearted young men I sent out into the murk of the night — had it not been for love of Ẓamyāʾ, they would have made camp.
So they rose, sluggish, groping their way, and behind them a stretch of the night's darkness, hunched like an ostrich.
3. ʿanaka al-laban — said of milk, when it thickened, if what Yūnus reported of it is correct.
عنم:
The letters ʿayn, nūn and mīm are not a root to be reasoned from; rather it names a plant, or something likened to it.

1. al-ʿanam — they said it is a tree among the trees used for tooth-sticks, soft and delicate of branch, as though it were the fingertips of a young woman; its singular is ʿanama.
2. al-ʿanama — likened to that: Al-Khalīl said it is the lizard.

Ruʾba said, in a line of verse:
They show delicate fingertips, its tender twigs, while love of Arwā is his care and his obsession.
(Al-sadam is infatuation with a thing.) God knows best.
عنى:
The letters ʿayn, nūn and the weak final letter cover three roots: the first is aiming at a thing with earnest effort and eagerness for it; the second points to submission and being humbled; the third is a thing's appearing and coming into view.

The first: ʿuniytu bi'l-amr wa-bi'l-ḥāja, I was concerned with the matter and the need. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: ʿaniya bi-ḥājatī and ʿuniya, others said this too; one also says taʿannaytu in the same sense — all said as ʿināya and ʿunīy, so I am maʿnīy bihi and ʿanin bihi. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: one does not say ʿaniya in that form. Al-Farrāʾ said: rajul ʿānin bi-amrī, meaning maʿnīy bihi. He recited: concerned with her farthest reach, long in his preoccupation, with two quivers and every kind of arrow at hand.

1. ʿanānī hādhā al-amr yaʿnīnī ʿināyatan — this matter concerned me, so I am maʿnīy bihi, and iʿtanaytu bihi wa-bi-amrihi, I concerned myself with it and its affair.

The second root: their saying ʿanā, yaʿnū, when he submitted; a captive is ʿānin. Abū ʿAmr said: aʿni hādhā al-asīr, meaning leave him until the leather binding on him sets. Zuhayr said: and were it not that Abū Ṭarīf would suffer capture by a ruler, or hardship.

Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿunūw and al-ʿanāʾ are the verbal noun of al-ʿānī. One says ʿānin aqarra bi'l-ʿunūw, the captive who has submitted to his captivity; al-ʿānī is the submissive, humbled one. God Most High said: {and faces shall be humbled before the Living, the Sustaining} [Ṭāhā: 111]. It is taʿnū ʿunūwan. One also says of the captive, ʿannā yaʿnū. A line was recited: and one does not say, through all of time, "her ʿānī." Sometimes they said aʿnūhu, meaning cast him into captivity.
