The pilgrim-cry of the people of Yemen in the pre-Islamic age was: she has come to You, humbled — Your Yemeni worshippers — that she may make the pilgrimage again, upon swift she-camels.

They also say al-ʿānī is the slave, and al-ʿāniya the slave-woman. Abū ʿAmr said: aʿnaytuhu, when you made him owned, enslaved; he is ʿānin bayyin al-ʿanāʾ. Al-ʿanwa is subjugation; one says akhadhnāhā ʿanwatan, we took it by force, by the sword. One also says jiʾtu ilayka ʿāniyan, meaning submissively. They also say al-ʿanwa is obedience. A line was recited: are you obedient to me, O heart, out of submission...

Al-ʿanāʾ, hardship, is well known and comes from this. Al-Shaybānī said: rubbat ʿanwatin laka min hādhā al-amr, meaning ʿanāʾ, hardship. Al-Qaṭāmī said: and she turned away from our need, and how much hardship you had, from her broken promises. They say the Arabs also say ʿanawtu ʿinda fulānin ʿunūwan, when you were a captive with him; and in cursing a captive they say "lā fakka Allāhu ʿunwatahu," may God never loosen his captivity, with the first letter raised, meaning his bond.

From this same root also — and we hold it a sound piece of reasoning — is al-ʿanīya: because it "humbles," as if it degrades and overpowers, and grows harsh on whoever is smeared with it. Al-ʿanīya is camels' urine left to thicken when set in the sun. They also say al-ʿanīya is urine set and thickened with dung. Aws said: as though congealed kohl, or ʿanīya, were dripping over the turn of her jowl-hollow from the mange-medicine. Abū ʿUbayd, among the proverbs of the Arabs: "ʿanīya cures the mange" — said of one who treats himself by his own judgment and opinion, as mangy camels are treated with ʿanīya. Some said: ʿannaytu al-baʿīr, I smeared the camel with ʿanīya, and recited a line describing camels smeared and left to be treated.

The third root: ʿunyān al-kitāb, and ʿunwānuhu, and ʿunyānuhu, the superscription of a letter. Its explanation, in our view, is that it is what shows plainly on it once it is sealed. From this same root comes maʿnā al-shayʾ, the meaning of a thing. Al-Khalīl said no more than: the maʿnā of everything is its trial and the state its affair comes to.

Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: one says "mā aʿrifu maʿnāhu wa-maʿnātahu," I do not know its meaning. What the reasoning of the language shows is that al-maʿnā is the intent that shows and comes into view in a thing when it is examined. One says "hādhā maʿnā al-kalām wa-maʿnā al-shiʿr," meaning what emerges from what the wording holds hidden within it. Confirming this reasoning is the Arabs' saying "lam taʿni hādhihi al-arḍu shayʾan wa-lam taʿnu ayḍan," said when land did not bring forth plants — as though, being so, it yielded nothing and brought forth no good. Confirming it too is the poet's saying: nothing remained at al-Khulaṣāʾ of what it had put forth in herbage, except its dryness and its scorched remains. Confirming it also is their saying "ʿanati al-qirba taʿnū," said when its water leaked out. Al-Mutanakhkhil said: it leaks, from a pierced skin...

Al-Khalīl said: ʿunwān al-kitāb — one says from it ʿannaytu al-kitāb, ʿannantuhu, and ʿanwantuhu. He said it is, as is mentioned, derived from al-maʿnā. Someone else said: whoever holds al-ʿunwān to be from al-maʿnā says ʿannaytu with an original yāʾ, and ʿunwān has the pattern fuʿwāl, while your saying ʿanwantu has the pattern faʿwaltu. Al-Shaybānī said: one says "mā ʿanā min fulānin khayrun," and "mā yaʿnū min ʿamalika hādhā khayrun ʿanwan."
عهب:
The letters ʿayn, hāʾ and bāʾ make a single word, if it is sound. Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿayhab is the man too weak to pursue vengeance. A poet said:
Through him I settled my blood-debt and achieved my vengeance, when every weak man forgets his own grudge.

As for what is reported from al-Shaybānī: "that was in the ʿihibbā of so-and-so," meaning in his time. He cited:
My memory of Salmā is from when she was unmarried, in the full ease of her untroubled life.
So it has been said — and God knows best whether it is sound.
عهج:
The letters ʿayn, hāʾ and jīm make a sound word with no pattern to be reasoned by, in either direction.

1. al-ʿawhaj — a gazelle of fine color, long in the neck; and a woman is called ʿawhaj, in comparison to it. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: al-ʿawhaj means marked/striped in the neck.
2. al-ʿawhaj is also said of the ostrich, for the length of its neck. Al-ʿAjjāj said, in a line of verse:
Like the Abyssinian wrapped up, or clothed in a cloak — or like a long-necked, downy-feathered one.
3. It is also said of the young she-camel: ʿawhaj.
4. And they say it of the snake too. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Pelting the wayward — the driven-off snake.
(Al-mansūs means the driven off.)
عهد:
The letters ʿayn, hā' and dāl: the root of this chapter, in our view, points to one meaning, which al-Khalīl indicated. He said: its root is the keeping of a thing and the renewing of one's contact with it. And what he mentioned of keeping is the meaning to which the branches of the chapter go back. So from that is their saying ʿahida al-rajul yaʿhadu ʿahdan, and it is from the sense of a testament. It was named so only because a covenant is one of the things that ought to be kept. And from it is derived al-ʿahd, the writ that is written for governors, from the sense of a testament; its plural is ʿuhūd. And al-ʿahd is the binding pledge; its plural is ʿuhūd. And of this chapter is al-ʿahd whose meaning is meeting and visiting: one says he is qarīb al-ʿahd bihi — his contact with him is recent; and that is because his coming to him is a keeping of him and a turning toward him.

And al-ʿahīd is the thing whose time has grown old. And al-ʿahd is the dwelling that a people, whenever they move off from it, keep coming back to. Ru'ba said, in a line of verse:
Do you know the changed abode, whose traces I trace ... whose signs the winds have effaced, and whose age is long?
And al-maʿhad is the like of that; its plural is maʿāhid. And the people of the covenant are al-muʿāhadūn, those with whom a treaty is made; the verbal noun is al-muʿāhada, meaning that a covenant is made with them over the tribute due from them. And the reasoning is one: as though it were a thing kept for them; and when they become Muslims the name of muʿāhada leaves them. And al-Khalīl mentioned that al-iʿtihād is like al-taʿāhud and al-taʿahhud, the attending to a thing. And he recited for al-Ṭirimmāḥ:
And he lets go to waste what God ... has laid upon him as a duty, and does not attend to it.
And he also said: your ʿahīd is the one who makes a covenant with you and with whom you make one. And he recited:
The Turks are truer to their covenant than Nizār ... so let none who has a covenant with her feel safe from treachery one day.

And of this chapter: al-ʿuhda, the document by which security is taken in sales. And they say: there is in this matter an ʿuhda that has not been made firm, the meaning being that there remains in it something that ought to be tied down. And of this chapter is their saying: "A slipping away, and no liability" — the two parties to a sale say it, that is: we have slipped free of any firm undertaking, so nothing remains in the matter that needs attending to and tightening. And they say: "In his affair there is an ʿuhda", pointing to weakness; and what they mean by that is only what we have explained.

Al-Khalīl said: taʿahhada fulān al-shay' and taʿāhada — so-and-so attended to the thing. Abū Ḥātim said: I say taʿahhadtu ḍayʿatī, I looked after my estate, and one does not say taʿāhadtu, because taʿāhud can only be between two. We say: al-Khalīl, in any case, knows the speech of the Arabs better than al-Naḍr. Besides, one says taghāfala ʿan kadhā and tajāwaza ʿan kadhā, and this is not from two. And sometimes they call stipulating istiʿhād; and it was so called only because a stipulation is one of the things that ought to be kept when it is stipulated. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And the people never took a pledge from the husband of a free woman ... among men, except from you or from a warrior.

And in the Book of God, exalted be He: {Did I not enjoin upon you} [Yā Sīn: 60], and its meaning — and God knows best — is: did I not put before you the command whose keeping I made binding upon you?

So this which we have mentioned, from the beginning of the chapter to where we have ended, is regular by the reasoning we have laid down. And there remains in the chapter al-ʿahd of rain, and in our view it is of the reasoning we have mentioned; for al-ʿahd, as al-Khalīl mentioned, is the rain that comes after the wasmī, the first rain, and it is what people call al-walī. And if it is so, its reasoning is the reasoning of our saying "he attends to his affair and his estate", as though the rain marked the earth first and attended to it a second time, that is, kept it, and so came to it and turned toward it. Al-Khalīl said: and that is that the wasmī passes, then the spring follows it with rain after rain, the last of it catching the wetness and softness of the first. He said: and that is al-ʿahd, and the plural is ʿihād. And he said: it is said that every rain that comes after a rain is ʿihād. And ʿuhidat al-rawḍa, and this is a rawḍa maʿhūda: a meadow on which ʿihād of rain has fallen. Al-Ṭirimmāḥ said, in a line of verse:
Choice ones of a sand-tract, they took from it ... the sides of rained-on camomile and dayn.
Al-maʿhūd is the rained-upon. And Ibn al-Aʿrābī recited:
You see the clouds, the ʿahd rain and the futūḥ.
Al-futūḥ is the plural of fatḥ, and it is the wide-spreading rain. And others than these said: al-ʿihād is the beginning of spring before the cold grows hard; the singular is ʿahda. And some of the Arabs used to say: al-ʿihād is of the wasmī, and the first rains are a store laid up in the earth: roots strike down for them, and the earth spreads out with green; then if they have successors and followers, that is al-ḥayā', the life-giving rain; and if not, they are nothing.

And they say: that was in the ʿahd of so-and-so and in his ʿihdān, his times. And they recited:
You are not Sulaymān as in your former times.
عهر:
The letters ʿayn, hāʾ and rāʾ make a single word indicating nothing good; it is sexual immorality. Al-Khalīl and others said: al-ʿahr is immorality, and al-ʿāhir is the immoral one. One says ʿahira and ʿahara, ʿuhran and ʿuhūran, when his coming to her was by night. In the hadith: "The child belongs to the marriage-bed, and for the fornicator is the stone" — he has no share in the lineage. He said:
Never entrust a secret to a traitor, ever, and do not go near the fornicator.
Yaʿqūb said: ʿuhūr occurs with both the slave woman and the free woman, while musāʿāh (paid liaison) occurs only with slave women.

And among what is reported, rarely, in this chapter, is something related from al-Muntajiʿ: he said that anyone who seeks evil by night, whether theft or fornication, is ʿāhir. And they say — though it is a doubted report — that al-ʿāhir is the languid, lazy one.
عهق:
The letters ʿayn, hāʾ and qāf have no consistent pattern to reason by. I have mentioned some words under it that, God knows, may perhaps be sound; had the lexicographers not mentioned them, it would have been better for us to set them aside.

1. Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿawhaq, on the pattern fawʿal, is the huge black raven.
2. It is also said to be the black camel.
3. It is also the color of lapis lazuli.
4. They say: al-ʿawhaq was a stallion in ancient times, to whom the noble riding-camels trace their line. Ruʾba said:
A hollow-backed she-camel, among the daughters of al-ʿawhaq.
5. Al-Khalīl also said: al-ʿawhaq is the bull whose color tends toward black.
6. And al-ʿawhaq is the mountain swallow. He said:
She is ash-grey, the color of the ʿawhaq.
7. One says: a camel ʿawhaq, meaning tall. He said:
Love of the morning graze made him linger, once he had seen the pale skyline, and a lean-shanked, tall camel.
8. Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿawhaqān are two stars beside the two Farqad stars, in a line; their path lies toward the pole. He cited:
Where the two Farqad stars ran level with al-ʿawhaq, by the fixed pole, when they fell into line.
9. He also said: al-ʿayhaqa is the friskiness of energetic play and running loose. He said:
Indeed the first flush of youth has its friskiness.
10. Ibn al-Sikkīt said: al-ʿawhaq is the best and choicest part of the nabʿ wood, from which bows are made. He said:
And every far-shooting, ʿawhaq-wood, tawny bow.
11. And ʿAwhaq is the name of a meadow. Ibn Harma said:
As if she had been struck by the fragrance of a meadow — from the meadow of ʿAwhaq, dewy and lush with grass.
عهل:
The letters ʿayn, hāʾ and lām are a sound root indicating release and departure, and a want of settling down.

1. al-ʿayhal — Al-Khalīl said it is the swift she-camel. He said, in a line of verse:
I drove on through it a swift she-camel, worn lean by travel, sound in gait and full in build.
Ibn al-Aʿrābī said the same, except that he added: and she may also be old and tough.
2. Abū Ḥātim said: one says nāqa ʿayhala and ʿayhal, but one does not say jamal ʿayhal — a male camel is never called this. They cited:
With a full-grown, big-cheeked she-camel, or a restless one.
(They said he doubled the lām only because the metre needed it.)
3. It is also said of a woman: ʿayhal or ʿayhala, when she will not settle, out of restlessness.
4. Sometimes they describe the wind this way too, calling it ʿahīl — which confirms that this pattern is sound.
5. As for their calling the woman who has no husband ʿāhil, plural ʿawāhil — this is sound, and she is named so because she has no husband to restrain her. They cited:
The walk of women going to other women, husbandless, among those who know captivity well.
And a widow whose husband the spears took from her, leaving him lodged in the breast of a straight, well-shaped lance.
And, of the ʿayhal again:
How fine a resting-place for guests and traders, and a place to unload the saddle of a sturdy, restless she-camel.
6. There remains one more word in this chapter, which, if sound, is not far from the pattern we have given: it is reported from Abū ʿUbayda that al-ʿāhil is the king above whom there is none but God, the exalted; the caliph is called ʿāhil. If that is right, it is because he has no one among his people standing over him to restrain him.
عهم:
The letters ʿayn, hāʾ and mīm are close to the one before it, and it is not unlikely that this too is a case of letter-substitution.

1. Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿayhama is the she-camel that presses steadily forward. He cited:
I came to water with a noble, persistent she-camel; she gulped to the right and gulped to the left.
2. It is also said that she is complete and sound in build. He cited:
driven fast by a huge, persistent camel, compact and massive in build, strong of pace.
3. Abū Zayd said: nāqa ʿayhama is one that is noble and swift; they also say she thirsts quickly, and her plural is ʿayāhīm. Dhū al-Rumma said:
Far off is Khaqrāʾ, unless the Lord of the Throne brings her near, and the tall, swift, persistent she-camels bring her near.
Abū ʿAmr cited:
A persistent she-camel, whose foot-pad presses into the ground, as a cobbler's awl presses into raw hide.
4. Abū ʿAmr said: her ʿayhama is her speed. Sometimes it is said ʿuyāhima, on the pattern of ʿuḏāfira.
5. What strays from this root: ʿAyham is the name of a place. He said:
And for the man of Iraq, the passes of ʿAyham.
6. They say al-ʿayhūm is the base of a tree; it is also said to be red-tanned leather. Abū Duwād said:
It faded, after al-Rabāb, for a time, and became a wasteland, as though it were tanned red leather.
7. As for the poet's saying "and I startled up the sleeping ʿayhamān" — they say it names something that does not travel by night, and is made to stand at the roadside. This last is obscure and I give only my best sense of it.
عهن:
The letters 'ayn, hā' and nūn are a sound root indicating softness, ease, and scantiness of nourishment in a thing.

1. Al-Khalīl said: al-'āhin is wealth that comes readily to hand for its owner, that is, what is on hand and present. One says: a'ṭāhu min 'āhini mālihi, he gave him from his readily available wealth. He recited:
Killing answered by our killing, captivity by our captivity, and wealth on hand [ʻāhin] matched with wealth, without discrepancy.
2. Al-Shaybānī said: al-'āhin means the immediate, the quick. One says: mā a'hana mā atāka, how quickly it came to you! And they say: "Did you sell for 'āhin [cash in hand] or on credit?"
3. Ibn al-A'rābī said: one says 'āhin when a thing is in your hand, within your power. And it is said: 'ahina ya'hanu 'uhūnan. He recited for the poet:
The abode of the daughter of al-Ḍamrī — when her bond was firm, and her kindness to you was ready at hand [ʻāhin] — meaning present, constant.
4. Abū Zayd said: 'ahana min fulānin khayrun aw khabarun — I am uncertain of this — ya'hanu 'uhūnan, when it came out from him.
5. Al-Naḍr said: one says i'hin lahu, meaning hurry it for him. And it is said: 'ahana lahu mā arāda, what he wanted came to him promptly.
6. Ibn Ḥabīb said: one says huwa yulqī al-kalāma 'alā 'awāhinihi, of a person who speaks without caring how he speaks. This fits the underlying pattern properly, because he does not speak with care and deliberation. Sometimes they say yarmī al-kalāma 'alā 'awāhinihi, when he says something only on conjecture, without certainty — the same meaning.

Also from this chapter: qaḍīb 'āhin, a broken, bent-down twig. One says: fī al-qaḍībi 'uhnah, meaning a break without full separation — when you look at it you think it whole, but when you shake it, it bends. The poor man is called 'āhin from this too. Sometimes they say 'ahantu al-qaḍība a'hinuhu 'ahnan, I bent it.

As for what is related from Abū al-Jarrāḥ, that he said "'ahanat 'awāhinu al-nakhl," of palm-fronds when they dry out, ya'hinu 'uhūnan — this is a mistake, because the underlying pattern runs the other way. Ibn al-A'rābī said: 'awāhin al-nakhl are the fronds nearest the heart of the palm tree, and this is more correct than the first. It is related from the Prophet, peace and blessings upon him, that he said to one of his companions: "Bring me palm-branches and avoid the 'awāhin," because they are moist. Some scholars of language said the people of the Ḥijāz call the fronds nearest the heart of the tree al-'awāhin, because they are moist and have not yet hardened.

As for their saying that al-'āhin means the one who holds back or restrains, and their citing for al-Nābighah:
I say to her, when she flagged and grew reluctant: press on, for short of the water-hollow there is no restrainer [ʻāhin] to hold you back —
this, in our view, is a mistake. Its meaning, on the pattern we have set out, is rather that what lies short of the water-hollow is accessible and not forbidden — that is, the way to it is easy. And "mā" here functions as a noun.

Also from this chapter, if what Ibn al-Sikkīt related is sound, that al-'awāhin are veins in a she-camel's womb. He recited for Ibn al-Riqā':
It drew a narrow passage from its inner veins [ʻawāhin], just as the flank of the free-born woman holds in the unborn child —
as though he likened those veins to the 'awāhin of the palm tree.

As for al-'ihn, dyed wool, it is not far-fetched that it belongs to this same pattern, because dyeing softens it. God knows best.
عوج:
The letters ʿayn, wāw and jīm are a sound root pointing to a bending in a thing or a leaning, and its branches go back to it.

Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿawj is the turning of the camel's head by the rein or the halter. And the woman turns her head toward the one who lies beside her. Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
My two friends, turn aside — God bless you both — at Mayya's dwelling, off the fronts of the mounts.

And a poet said, in a line of verse:
Until, when they turned their fine necks toward us, as the nose-pegs turn the necks of swift steeds.

He means that the girls bent their necks as the nose-peg bends the she-camel's neck. And of everything you bend you say: ʿujtuhu fa-nʿāja — I bent it and it bent. Ru'ba said, in a line of verse:
And my wood bent like the rough splinter.

Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿawaj is a name fixed to what the eyes see in a rod or in wood or in something else, and you say: there is a plain ʿawaj in it. And al-ʿawaj is the verbal noun of ʿawija yaʿwajju ʿiwajan. And one says iʿwajja yaʿwajju iʿwijājan and ʿawajan. So al-ʿawaj with a fatḥa is in everything standing upright, like a wall or a stick, and al-ʿiwaj is what is in a carpet or in an affair, such as a religion or a way of living. From it one says a stick aʿwaj, plainly bent. The descriptive words are aʿwaj and ʿawjā', and the plural is ʿūj. And al-ʿūj among horses are those that have a curve in their legs. As for the Aʿwajī horses, they are traced to a racing stallion that was in the age before Islam, and the form of relation to him is aʿwajī. And one says: he is of the daughters of Aʿwaj. Ṭufayl said, in a line of verse:
The daughters of al-Wajīh and al-Ghurāb and Lāḥiq, and of Aʿwaj — to them the tracer of pedigrees traces his line.

And it may be that he was so named for a curve that was in him. As for their saying a she-camel ʿāj, and she is the one obedient in going, soft to turn — that too is from the section. Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
An obedient one carried me across the waterless waste, as though before the mounts she were an ostrich when it is startled.

And when they turn her they say: ʿāji, ʿāji.
عود:
The letters 'ayn, wāw and dāl are two sound roots: one of them points to doing a thing a second time, and the other is a kind of wood.

The first is al-'awd. Al-Khalīl said: it is the doing of a matter a second time, a return after a beginning. You say: he began, then he came back. Al-'awda is the single time. And their saying 'āda fulānun bi-ma'rūfihi is when a man does a kindness and then adds to it. Of this section is al-'iyāda, that you visit a sick man. And the family of so-and-so have a ma'āda, that is, a matter for which people come to them. Al-ma'ād is everything to which the return is made. And the next world is a ma'ād for men. And God - exalted - is al-Mubdi' al-Mu'īd, the one who begins and brings back, and that is because He began the creation and then brings them back. And you say: I saw so-and-so neither beginning nor coming back, that is, he speaks neither a first word nor a second. 'Ubayd said, in a line of verse:
'Ubayd is left empty of his people; today he neither begins nor repeats.
Al-'īd is what comes back again of a phantom or a care. And of it is al-mu'āwada, and a man's growing used to a thing, and al-ta'awwud. And 'Antara said, describing a male ostrich that comes back to its eggs every hour, in a line of verse:
A small-headed ostrich returning at Dhū al-'Ushayra to its eggs, like a slave in a long fur cloak with cropped ears.
And they say: he did the prayer again, and the story again. Al-'āda is practice: keeping at a thing until it becomes a nature to a man. And one calls the man who keeps at a thing al-mu'āwid. And in some of their speech: "Keep to the fear of God - exalted - and make a habit of it", that is, grow used to it. And a'āda is used with the meaning of ta'awwada. He said, in verse:
The bucket is a great bucket of ox-hide, huge; the weak ones cannot drag it,
none but the practised she-camels that heave with it.
He means the she-camels that have grown used to heaving up the bucket. And of a brave man one says baṭal mu'āwid, that is, what he has seen of the hardness of war does not keep him from going back to it. And the measure is sound in all of this. As for the old camel, it is called an 'awd. It is possible that it is from this, as though it had gone back to journeys and travels time after time.

And al-Khalīl pointed to another meaning, saying: it is the one that has some strength left in it. If it is so, then it is because its owners have a return in the working of it. Both meanings are good.

The plural of the camel called 'awd is 'iwada. And from it one says 'awwada yu'awwidu ta'wīdan, when it reaches that age. And he said, in a line of verse:
Is glory anything but old lordship, and open-handedness, and the mending of the rent, and steadfastness in the places of battle?
This is by way of a figure, as though he meant lordship that is ancient. And they also call an old road an 'awd. He said, in verse:
An old camel on an old road of peoples long gone; it dies by being left and lives by being used.
By al-'awd he means the camel; "on an 'awd" means on an old road. And likewise the road dies, or is effaced, when it is left, and lives when it is travelled. Of this section is al-'ā'ida, and it is kindness and a gift. You say: how great is so-and-so's kindness to us. And this matter is a'wad than that, that is, easier and more suitable.

Of this section is al-'īd: every day of gathering. Al-Khalīl has mentioned its derivation from 'āda ya'ūdu, as though they returned to it. And it may be said that it is because it comes back every year; and this in our view is the sounder. Another said, and it is close to the two meanings: it was called an 'īd because they have grown used to it. And the yā' in 'īd is originally a wāw, but it was turned into a yā' because of the kasra on the 'ayn. And al-'Ajjāj said, in a line of verse:
He comes back to resting-places that have a tether-stake, as a Christian comes back to his feast.
And they make 'īd plural as a'yād, and its diminutive, with a change, as 'uyayd. And they say a stallion mu'īd, that is, used to covering. And al-'īdiyya are choice riding-camels of a known stock; they said: they are traced to 'Ād. And God knows best.

As for the other root, it is al-'ūd, and it is every piece of wood that is thin. And it is said: rather every piece of wood is an 'ūd. And al-'ūd, the wood with which one perfumes with smoke, is well known.
عوذ:
The letters 'ayn, wāw and dhāl are a sound root pointing to one meaning, and it is taking refuge with a thing; then everything that clings to a thing or keeps close to it is carried back to this.

Al-Khalīl said: you say a'ūdhu bi-Allāh — glorious be His praise — that is, I take refuge with Him, blessed and exalted, 'awdhan or 'iyādhan. He also mentioned that they say fulān 'iyādhun laka — so-and-so is a refuge for you. And their saying ma'ādha Allāh means I take refuge with God; and so too asta'īdhu bi-Allāh. And «the Messenger of God — may God bless him and grant him peace — said to the woman who sought refuge from him: you have taken refuge with a place of refuge». He said: al-'ūdha and al-ma'ādha are what a person is guarded with against fright or madness. And they call every female that has just given birth 'ā'idh; she stays so for seven days. The plural is 'ūdh. Labīd said, in a line of verse:
The wild cows stand still over their young ... newly delivered, their calves spread out in droves over the open ground.

Ta'ajjala means they become ājāl, that is, droves. It was named so only for what we have mentioned, the young one's keeping close to her, or her keeping close to it.
عور:
The letters 'ayn, wāw and rā' are two roots: one indicates a thing passing turn by turn; the other indicates a defect in one of a person's two eyes, and of any creature with two eyes, meaning the lack of sight in it. It is then further extended and derived from.

The first: their saying ta'āwara al-qawmu fulānan wa-i'tawarūhu ḍarban, meaning they took turns striking him together, so that whenever one stopped another struck. Al-Khalīl said al-ta'āwur applies generally to anything. One says ta'āwarati al-riyāḥu rasman ḥattā 'afathu, the winds worked upon a trace by turns until they wore it away, meaning they kept steadily at it. Al-A'shā said:
A deserted, desolate camp, which summer alternated upon ... with two winds, from the east and from the north.
Al-Aṣma'ī or another related: ta'awwarnā al-'awāriyya, we borrowed things by turns from one another.

The other root: al-'awar in the eye. Al-Khalīl said: one says "look at his 'awrā' eye," his defective eye. One does not call either of the two eyes alone 'amyā', blind, because 'awar can only occur in one of the two eyes. One says 'urtu 'aynahu, and 'awwarat, and a'artu — all of these are said. And it is used figuratively: kalimatun 'awrā', a crooked saying. Al-Khalīl said it is a saying that falls without sense or right guidance. A line says:
Do not utter the crooked word among the people heedlessly, for know it has, among the people, one who remembers it.
Some said al-'awrā' is the ugly word that pains and angers a man. And he recited:
A crooked word was said, and I paid it no heed ... the crooked word is not acceptable to me.
From this chapter: al-'awā', a tear or slit in a garment. From this chapter: al-'awra, its derivation from what has already been mentioned, as something carried over from the root — as though al-'awra is a thing that ought to be guarded because it lies exposed. On this His words, exalted is He, were explained: {they say, our houses are exposed, and they are not exposed} [al-Aḥzāb: 13] — they said, meaning, as if they are not secured. The plural of al-'awra is 'awrāt. A poet said:
Among a people who guard all their exposed places ... they do not rush to pursue in flight.
Al-id'āq is hastening; al-shalal is being driven off in retreat. One says of a place that is exposed: it has a'wara, yu'wiru, i'wāran. Al-Khalīl said: were one to say a'āra yu'īru i'āratan it would be allowed by analogy, meaning it became a place of exposure. One says a'wara al-baytu, the house became exposed. Al-Khalīl said: one says 'awira ya'waru 'awaran. So 'awratun, in His words {indeed our houses are exposed} [al-Aḥzāb: 13] — al-Khalīl said it is a description used the same for any number and for masculine and feminine, 'awratun staying fixed in one form for plural and singular, feminine and masculine, as you say "a man ṣawm" and "a woman ṣawm," "men ṣawm" and "women ṣawm."

As for their saying that al-'awar means abandoning the truth, citing al-'Ajjāj's line:
God has mended the faith, so it was mended ... and the Merciful blinded whoever turned away, with blindness.
The reasoning does not actually support the sense given of "abandoning the truth"; rather al-'Ajjāj meant the 'awar that is the defect of the eye, using it as a likeness for one blind to the truth, who is not guided to it.

As for the Arabs' saying that so-and-so has "'ā'irat 'ayn" of wealth, meaning abundance, its sense is the same as already given, as though the eye becomes dazzled looking at abundant wealth, so that it is as if it becomes defective. They say 'awwarta 'ayna al-rakiyyati, you stopped up the spring of the well until the water sank away. Al-makān al-mu'wir is the place where one fears being cut off and attacked.
عوز:
The letters ʿayn, wāw and zāʾ make a single word indicating a bad state.

1. al-ʿawaz — that a person lacks a thing he needs; he seeks it and it is not there for him. One says: ʿāzanī, it eluded me.
2. aʿwaza al-rajul — the man's state grew bad, he fell into need.
3. al-miʿwaz, plural maʿāwiz — worn-out clothes and rags that show their owner's neediness. Al-Shammākh said:
When the dew fell, she was sheltered and clothed in fine striped cloth, and no worn-out rags were wrapped about her.

As for al-ʿizza [strength/might] — [the entry breaks off here in the source and is not completed].
عوس:
The letters ʿayn, wāw and sīn make a word the lexicographers have recorded, whose pattern, though sound, is far-fetched.

1. al-ʿawāsāʾ — the pregnant female among dung beetles. They cited:
a young one, ʿawāsāʾ, drawing near her time, about to give birth.
2. al-ʿawasān and al-ʿaws — roaming about by night.
3. al-aʿwas — the sword-polisher.
4. al-aʿwas — one who describes a thing well.

All of this is such that the heart can hardly settle on its being sound.
عوص:
The letters ʿayn, wāw and ṣād are a little root indicating scant possibility in a thing. One says iʿtāṣa al-shayʾ, when it was not possible. Al-ʿawaṣ is the verbal noun of al-aʿwaṣ and al-ʿawīṣ.

1. kalām ʿawīṣ, kalima ʿawṣāʾ — obscure speech, a difficult saying. He said:
O you who ask about its hard saying.
2. aʿwaṣa fī l-manṭiq, aʿwaṣa bi-l-khaṣm — to speak, or to speak to an opponent, in a way he cannot make sense of. Labīd said:
Indeed I baffle the opponent with hard speech, even while I fill the bowl with the fat of the choicest cuts.
3. iʿtāṣat al-nāqa — said of the she-camel, when the stallion covered her and she did not conceive, with no illness to account for it.
عوض:
The letters ʿayn, wāw and ḍād are two sound words: one indicating a substitute for a thing, the other a span of time.

The first is al-ʿiwaḍ, compensation; its verb is al-ʿawḍ. Al-Khalīl said: ʿāḍa yaʿūḍu ʿawḍan wa ʿiyāḍan; the noun is al-ʿiwaḍ, and the word in common use is al-taʿwīḍ — you say ʿawwaḍtuhu min hibatihi khayran, I gave him something better in return for his gift. Iʿtāḍanī fulān, when someone came asking me for compensation and a gift; istaʿāḍanī, when he asked you for compensation. Ruʾba said:
An excellent young man, and one sought out by him who wants compensation; and God repays the loan with a loan.
You also say iʿtaḍtu mimmā aʿṭaytu fulānan, and ʿuḍtu, meaning I obtained compensation. He said:
O Layla, may the flashing lightning water you — is there, while the suitor from you seeks his exchange, in a hundred camels, one who takes and leaves something over?
Its meaning is that he had asked for her hand for a hundred camels, then said to her: and I who am taking you am the one giving compensation — I have given compensation, meaning the advantage and the compensation now fall to me, in taking you.

The other word is their saying "ʿawḍu," over which there is disagreement. Some said it is a word of oath. It is reported from Al-Khalīl that he said it means time, the age — a man says to his companion, "ʿawḍu that will not happen," meaning never. Then Al-Khalīl said: if ʿawḍu were a noun for time, it would take full declension with tanwīn; but it is a particle meant for oath, just as ajal and naʿam and the like, not being fully declinable words, are given no case-ending. Al-Aʿshā said:
Two who shared the milk of a mother's breast, swearing by a dark, overspreading night: never shall we part.
And God knows best what is correct.
عوي:
The letters ʿayn, wāw and yāʾ are a sound root indicating twisting a thing and bending it.

Al-Khalīl said: ʿawayta al-ḥabl ʿayyan, when you twisted the rope. And ʿawayta raʾs al-nāqa, when you bent the she-camel's head, so that it bent.

1. al-nāqa taʿwī buratahā — the she-camel twists her nose-ring as she moves, when she wrenches it with her muzzle. Ruʾba said, describing the she-camels in their gait:
twisting their nose-rings, hurrying swiftly along.
2. Said of a man, when he calls people to strife: ʿawā qawman, and istaʿwā.
3. ʿuwāʾ al-kalb — the howling of the dog and other beasts of prey — is close to this sense, because it twists the voice away from the path of ordinary barking. One says ʿawati l-sibāʿu taʿwī ʿuwāʾan, the beasts of prey howled.
4. The bitch in heat is called al-muʿāwiya, likewise from al-ʿuwāʾ, as though it were on the pattern mufāʿila from it.
5. al-ʿawwāʾ — a star in the sky, treated as feminine, called "ʿawwāʾ al-bard," the star of the cold: when it rises, cold weather comes with it. They say, in their rhymed sayings: "When al-ʿAwwāʾ rises, winter settles in, and warming by the fire becomes welcome." It is not unlikely that this too comes from al-ʿuwāʾ, since it brings a cold for which the dogs howl.
6. By way of metaphor they also use al-ʿawwāʾ for a person's backside. He cited:
Standing, hiding their own backsides with abuse of me, while their backsides are more exposed than mine.
And also:
Why did you not tie the knot fast, or spend the night hungry, instead of opening up your shame as wells are opened? (al-qulub is the plural of qalīb, a well.)
7. From the chapter of al-ʿuwāʾ is their saying of the shepherd: qad ʿāʿā yuʿāʿī ʿāʿāʾatan, he called out loudly. [A line is cited, broken off:] "and I did not borrow it from a shouter or a caller."
عيب:
The letters ʿayn, yāʾ and bāʾ are a sound root, containing two words: one is al-ʿayb (a fault, a defect) and the other al-ʿayba (a chest for clothes), and the two are far apart from each other in meaning.
As for ʿayb in a thing, it is well known. You say: fulānun ʿāba fulānan yaʿībuhu — so-and-so found fault with so-and-so. Rijlun ʿayyāba — a man who slanders people, speaking ill of them. ʿĀba al-ḥāʾiṭu wa-ghayruhu — the wall or other such thing, when a defect appears in it. Al-ʿāb is another word for al-ʿayb.
The other word is al-ʿayba: the ʿayba of clothes and the like, meaning a traveling-chest — and this is genuine Arabic.
The Messenger of God — peace be upon him and his family — said: "The Anṣār are my karish and my ʿayba" (my belly and my chest) — he gave this as a likeness for them, as if they were the place of his secret and those he trusts with his affairs.
عيث:
The letters ʿayn, yāʾ and thāʾ are two close, sound roots: one is haste in doing harm, the other is seeking a thing without clear sight of it.

The first is their saying: ʿātha yaʿīthu, when he hastened into corruption. They say: he is aʿyath al-nās fī mālihi, the most reckless of people with his wealth. And the wolf yaʿīthu among the sheep, taking nothing from them without killing it. He said:
I said to the wolf, O wicked one — while the wolf ranged destructively among my sheep.

The other root: 1. al-taʿyīth — Al-Khalīl said it is the blind man's search for a thing, and a man's search for something in the dark. 2. al-taʿyīth — also, putting the hand into the quiver, feeling about for an arrow. Abū Dhuʾayb said:
And the flanks of a swerving, hastening quarry appeared to him, so he groped in the quiver, drawing an arrow back.
And Ibn Abī ʿĀʾidh said:
so he groped about, the moment they left him alone, for the bowstring-notch and the shot, or for drawing an arrow out.
عيج:
The letters ʿayn, yāʾ and jīm are a sound little root indicating attention to a thing and concern for it. They say: mā ʿijtu bi-qawli fulānin, meaning I did not believe him and paid him no heed. And: mā aʿīju bi-shayʾin yaʾtīnī min qibalihi, I pay no heed to anything that comes from him. Al-Nābigha said:
And I saw nothing of hers that I cared for, except the thumām grass and the fire's hearth.
عيد: The letters ʿayn, yāʾ and dāl — their discussion has already passed in its proper place, because that is the true root.
عير:
The letters ʿayn, yāʾ, and rāʾ are two sound roots: one points to a thing standing proud and raised up, the other to coming and going.

The first: al-ʿayr is the bone that stands proud in the middle of the shoulder blade, plural ʿuyūra. ʿayyara al-naṣl means to cut a ridge down the middle of an arrowhead, as though it were a splinter. A poet said, in a line of verse:
His arrow met the stones of a rocky plateau, which broke its ridge (al-ʿayr) off it, and its edge.
Al-ghirār is the cutting edge. Al-ʿayr in the foot is the bone that stands proud on the top of the foot. It is related from al-Khalīl [ibn Aḥmad al-Farāhīdī] that al-ʿīr is the chief of a people; if this is sound it fits the pattern, since he is highest among them in standing, most raised up. He said: if you saw a ridge standing proud in a rock, a naturally jutting edge, that too would be called ʿayr.

The other root: al-ʿayr is the donkey, wild or tame, plural al-aʿyār and al-maʿyūrāʾ. It is named ʿayr for its constant coming and going. Al-Khalīl said: words that came from the Arabs on the plural pattern mafʿūlāʾ are al-maʿyūrāʾ, al-maʿlūjāʾ, and al-mashyūkhāʾ. He said: they also say mashyakha on the pattern mafʿala, and they said nothing else like it for any other plural. Among the proverbs about the donkey: "When one donkey goes, [another] donkey stays at the tether." The pupil of the eye is also called ʿayr, named for the coming, going, and restless movement we described. Al-Khalīl said, among their proverbs: "So-and-so came before ʿayr and what ran," meaning speed — that is, before the blink of an eye. He quoted for Taʾabbaṭa Sharran:
And a fire I kindled a while after nightfall, in a place where I wished to make no stay,
Except to loosen a mount, and a donkey I strove against, for fear it should fall asleep.
And al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥillizah said:
They claimed that everyone who strikes at the pupil (al-ʿayr) is bound to us in loyalty — but what is that loyalty worth?
Meaning: everyone whose eyelid blinks over his pupil. Al-ʿiyār is the behaviour of a horse that is ʿāʾir. One says ʿāra yaʿīru — its going off, as though it had broken loose from its owner and wanders to and fro. A qaṣīda that is ʿāʾira is one that travels widely and is much repeated. The Arabs never spoke a line more widely repeated (aʿyar) than his words:
Whoever meets good, people will praise his conduct; whoever strays will never lack for a blamer over his straying.
He means: a widely-travelled line of verse.
عيس:
The letters ʿayn, yāʾ and sīn make two words: one a pale white color, the other the stallion's covering fee.

Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿayas and al-ʿīsa are a white color tinged with a faint darkness beneath its clarity. A camel is jamal aʿyas, a she-camel nāqa ʿaysāʾ; the plural is ʿīs. Abū Duwād said:
and pale camels, worn thin by the pleasure of the procession and the drinking.
And another, describing a bull:
and the pale bull-calf embraced the shade.
He said: and the Arabs reserved al-ʿayas specifically for the pure-bred white camels. Al-ʿīsa, in its original form, is on the pattern fuʿla, like al-ṣuhba and al-kumta, but the ʿayn was given a kasra because of the yāʾ following it. They also say: gazelle aʿyas. But in what he said of the gazelle and of the pale bull-calf there is a contradiction with what he had said, that the Arabs reserved al-ʿīs specifically for the pure-bred white camels.

The other word: al-ʿays is the stallion's fluid. Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿays is ʿasb al-faḥl, the stallion's covering fee, which is its act of mating. One says: do not take a fee for your camel's covering. This second thing that Al-Khalīl mentioned is the more correct.
عيسجور: The swift she-camel. This is a word with the rā' and the yā' added into it; it is really from ʿasajat in her gait — she moved swiftly. The mention of al-ʿāsij has already passed.
عيش:
The letters 'ayn, ya and shin are a single sound root indicating life and continuance. Al-Khalil said: al-'aysh is life. Al-ma'isha is that by which a person lives — food, drink, and whatever else life consists of. Al-ma'isha is [also] a name for the thing one lives by. One says: he is in a good living and livelihood (fi 'aysha wa ma'isha saliha). Al-'aysha is like al-jilsa and al-mishya [nouns denoting a manner of being — a way of sitting, a way of walking]. Al-'aysh is the comprehensive verbal noun. Al-ma'ash runs the same course as al-'aysh; one says 'he lived (a life), living, and a livelihood' ('asha ya'ishu 'ayshan wa ma'ashan'). Anything one lives by, or in, is 'mu'ash'. God, Most High, said: {and We made the day for livelihood} [al-Naba': 11]. The earth is a livelihood for creation, in which they seek their means of living.

Al-Khalil mentioned that al-ma'ish, with the final ha dropped, stands in poetry in place of al-ma'isha, and cited, for Humayd, a line (obscure, rendered as best as can be made out):
A guardian of livelihood, who does not loosen her waist-wrap out of prudence — she has spirit in her though she sits still.
People also transmit it as 'a guardian of livelihood' with the other wording.

Some of them said: so-and-so lived a decent little life ('ayshushatan saliha), and 'they are getting by' (muta'ayyishun) when they have some sufficiency of livelihood. A man in good circumstances is 'a'ish'.
عيص:
The letters ʿayn, yāʾ and ṣād are a sound root, and it is the place where a thing grows. Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿīṣ is the place where the choicest trees grow. He said: the aʿyāṣ of Quraysh are their noble men, who trace their descent to an ʿīṣ; aʿyāṣ and ʿīṣ are both used of one's forefathers. He also mentioned al-maʿīṣ, saying it means the same as manbit, a place of growth. Al-ʿAjjāj said, of al-ʿīṣ:
from the stock of Marwān to a vast, abundant stock.
And Jarīr said:
The trees of your stock among Quraysh are not thin of branch, nor left bare.
عيط:
The letters ʿayn, yāʾ and ṭāʾ are two sound roots: one indicates height, the other the tracking of a thing.

1. al-ʿayaṭ, the verbal noun of al-aʿyaṭ — one long in the head and the neck. One says nāqa ʿayṭāʾ and jamal aʿyaṭ, plural al-ʿīyaṭ. Al-Khalīl said wild donkeys are also described by it. Al-ʿAjjāj said, describing a horse that brings down long-necked game:
He throws the long-necked ones of them down on their chins, in wild spirited energy, or something close to it. (Al-arann is liveliness pushed to the point of seeming madness.)
2. A hill that rises very high into the sky is said to be ʿayṭāʾ.
3. Likewise a towering palace is aʿyaṭ. Umayya said:
We are Thaqīf; our might is unassailable — towering, hard to climb, exalted.
4. And what may also be reasoned on this pattern: the she-camel that has gone years without conceiving, though with no defect in her, is said to have iʿtāṭat — she holds herself too high, as it were, for conceiving. They said her holding back sometimes comes from an excess of fat in her. A woman too is said taʿtāṭu, by the same figure. One says nāqa ʿāʾiṭ, and ʿāṭat taʿīṭu ʿiyāṭan, meaning barren, among nūq ʿīṭ and ʿawāʾiṭ. He cited:
and with the full-grown she-camels, her fat had marked her — and the one that resists conceiving, the barren one.
The verbal noun is also ʿūṭaṭ and ʿūṭa.

The other root: al-taʿayyuṭ is the oozing of a thing from a stone or a stick, from which something like water comes out and either gums up or flows. The camel's poll oozes sweat in this way — taʿayyuṭ. He said:
Her poll oozes with a black sweat, as though it were tar, running dripping down the side of her neck.
عيف:
The letters ʿayn, yāʾ and fāʾ are one sound root indicating aversion. From this: their saying ʿāfa al-shayʾ yaʿāfuhu ʿiyāfan, when he disliked a thing, whether food or drink.

1. al-ʿayūf, of camels — the one that smells the water while thirsty and leaves it, out of distaste for it; though sometimes, if hard pressed, it drinks it after all. Ibn Abī Rabīʿa said:
So she sniffed it and did not refuse it, and murky, churned-up water did not stop her from drinking her fill.
2. ʿiyāfat al-ṭayr — the reading of birds for omens, their driving-off. This too comes from aversion: one sees a crow or some other bird, or some other sign, and takes it as an ill omen from it. Sometimes the soothsayer is called ʿāʾif. Al-Aʿshā said:
What do you read as an omen today, among the birds returning home in the evening — a crow, or a billy-goat crossing your path?
And he said:
You have indeed confounded your omen-bird, if only you knew how to read it. (This last line is obscure and rendered as best it can be.)
عيق:
The letters ʿayn, yāʾ and qāf — Al-Khalīl mentioned nothing under it, yet it is sound. They say: al-ʿayqa is the seashore. The Hudhali poet said:
A leader who spent eight full turns at sea, winding along the shores of the seas, keeping close beside them.
And Al-Khalīl hinted that this pattern is in use, not among the discarded ones, for he said in his book: "ʿAyyūq" is on the pattern fayʿūl; it may be built from ʿawaqa or from ʿayaqa, since yāʾ and wāw are equivalent here. So he made it known that the pattern — ʿayn, yāʾ, qāf — is indeed in use.
عيك: The letters ʿayn, yāʾ and kāf — Al-Khalīl mentioned nothing under it, yet it is a good pattern even though no usage has come down for it. But al-ʿaykatān is a known place in the lands of the Arabs.
عيل: The letters 'ayn, yā' and lām — there is nothing in this root except what is turned from a wāw. Al-'aylah: poverty and need. One says 'āla ya'īlu 'aylatan, when he fell into need. God, Most High, said: {and if you fear poverty} [al-Tawbah: 28]. In hadith: "one who lives moderately never falls into poverty [mā 'āla muqtaṣid]." And he said, in a line of verse: "Whoever among us falls into poverty after her, may he never be made whole again." And 'Aylān is a name.
عيم: The letters ʿayn, yāʾ and mīm make a single sound word: craving for milk. One who craves milk is called ʿaymān, a woman ʿaymā. You say: ʿimtu ilā al-labani ʿaymatan wa ʿayaman shadīdan, I craved milk intensely. Al-Khalīl said: every verbal noun of this kind, belonging to the pattern faʿlān / faʿlā, is said, in its light feminine form, as faʿla, and in its heavier form as faʿal — like al-ḥayar and al-ḥayra. The plural of al-ʿaymān is ʿayāmā and ʿiyām.
عين:
The letters 'ayn, yā' and nūn are one sound root pointing to the limb by which one sees and looks; then words are derived from it, and the origin in all of them is what we have said.

Al-Khalīl said: al-'ayn is the seeing eye of every creature that has sight. And 'ayn is made plural as a'yun, 'uyūn and a'yān. The poet said, in a line of verse:
I do startle the hearts of the fair women with it, until they turn away with their necks and their eyes.
And another said:
It has cooled the eyes of those who gloat, that they -
And sometimes they make a'yun plural again as a'yunāt. He said:
With eyes that no speck has come into.
And the eye of the heart is a figure said by way of likeness. Among the sayings of the Arabs about the eye is: "I will not do it as long as my eye carries water", that is, I will never do it. And they say, of a man with many faults: "an eye with every disease in it". And one says: a man of strong eyelid, when he can bear staying awake. And one says 'intu al-rajula, when you strike him with your eye, so I am a'īnuhu 'aynan, and he is ma'yūn, struck by the eye. He said, in a line of verse:
Your people used to reckon you a lord, and I think you are a lord struck by an eye.
And a man 'ayūn and mi'yān is one with an evil eye. Al-'ā'in is the one who strikes with the eye. And I saw the thing 'iyānan, that is, with my own eyes. And they say laqītuhu 'ayna 'unnatin, that is, face to face. And you did that 'amda 'aynin, when you did it on purpose. The origin of it is the seeing eye, that is, he did it before the eye of everyone who saw him. And he is 'abdu 'aynin, a slave who serves only so long as his master is looking at him. And of a matter that is plain they say: "The morning has shown itself to one who has two eyes."

Of this section is al-'ayn: the man you send to spy out news, as though he were something by which you see what is hidden from you. And one says ra'aytuhum adnā 'ā'inatin, that is, before anybody else; he means - and God knows best - before every soul that looks. And one says idhhab fa-'tan lanā, that is, go and look for us. And one says mā bihā 'ayanun, with the yā' voweled, meaning anyone who has an eye; the yā' was voweled to keep the two apart. He said:
And no seeing soul, only ostriches hurrying away.
As for their saying i'tāna lanā manzilan, that is, he sought out a camping place for us, they did not explain it. The meaning is that he looked at the camping places with his eye and then chose.

Of this section is al-'ayn: the flowing spring, welling up from the springs of water. It was called an 'ayn only by likening it to the seeing eye, for its clearness and its water. And one says qad 'ānat al-ṣakhra, when the rock has a crack out of which water comes. And one says ḥafara fa-a'yana wa-a'āna - he dug and reached water.

Of this section is al-'ayn: the cloud that comes from the direction of the qibla. This is a likeness built on a likeness, because it was likened to the spring of water, which was itself likened to the eye of a man. They say: when the cloud rises from the side of the 'ayn it hardly ever fails.

Ibn al-A'rābī said: one says "this is the rain of the 'ayn", and one does not say "we were rained on by the 'ayn". And the eye of the sun is likened to the eye of a man. Al-Khalīl said: the eye of the sun is its round burning disc.

Of this section is mā' 'ā'in, that is, running water. And of this section is the 'ayn of a waterskin. Al-Khalīl said: of a waterskin, when a place in it wears out and grows thin, one says: it has come to have an eye, qad ta'ayyana. This too is from al-'ayn, because when it grows thin it comes close to tearing, so that the skin is as though one looked through it. Tha'lab recited, in verse:
Sulaymā said a word to her companion: what ails my cousin, coming back from her watering-place, with a limp skin whose eye is at its neck?
He meant a waterskin that had come to have a worn thin place at its neck. And one says a waterskin 'ayyin, when it has in it what are like eyes, which is what we have described. And he recited:
What ails my eye, like a waterskin full of holes?
And they said, about the line of al-Ṭirimmāḥ:
It drenched from it every worn and hole-ridden skin, and the water-camels dried out in the hollow open plain -
that al-'ayyin means "new" in the speech of Ṭayy. This, in our view, has no sense in it. Al-'ayyin is only the one that has eyes in it, the holes of a waterskin that we have described. The people fell into error only because they saw "worn" and "'ayyin" together, so they went to the idea that the poet meant every new thing and every worn thing. That is a mistake, because al-bālī is the one that has worn out, and al-'ayyin is the one that has eyes in it. A new skin may well have eyes in it because of a fault in the hide. The proof of what we say is the line of al-Quṭāmī:
But the hide, when it splits with wear and with holes, defeats the skilled workman.

And of the rest of their speech about the 'ayn is al-'īn: wild cows. A cow is described as being wide of eye, so one says baqara 'aynā', and a man a'yan. Al-Khalīl said: one does not say thawr a'yan, a wide-eyed bull. Another said: one does say thawr a'yan. Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
The mate of a wide-eyed, long-tailed bull that you would liken to a noble stallion drawing aside, not pulled away.
Al-Khalīl said: al-a'yan is a name for the bull, and one says mu'ayyan as well. He said, in a line of verse:
And a mu'ayyan bull gathering the herd of wild cows, as though he were a raging, hungry one when he snarls.
And one says qawāfin 'īn, rhymes that are 'īn. Al-Aṣma'ī was asked to explain it and said: I do not know it. This is from the scruple he used to keep in refusing to explain the Qur'an; it is as though he did not explain al-'īn just as he did not explain al-ḥūr, because they are two words that are in the Qur'an. God - exalted - said: {And wide-eyed maidens like hidden pearls} [al-Wāqi'a: 22]. The meaning in "rhymes that are 'īn" is only that they are piercing, like a thing of piercing sight. Al-Hudhalī said, in a line of verse:
With the speech of an opponent, or the wrangling of a disputer, stubborn and struggling, or with piercing rhymes.

Of this section is their saying a'yān al-qawm, the notables of a people, and they follow the measure of what we have said, as though they were the eyes with which the people see. And so too brothers. Al-Khalīl said: you say of any brothers who are from one father and one mother while they have brothers from different mothers: these are the a'yān of their brothers. This too is measured on what we have said. And the 'īna of anything is the best of it - the word is the same for the male and the female - as one says the 'ayn of a thing and its 'īna, that is, the finest of it; because the clearest thing in a man's face is his eye.

Of this section is ibnā 'iyān, the two sons of plain sight: two lines that the diviner draws, saying: "O two sons of 'iyān, hasten the plain showing!" - as though by them he looked at what he wanted to know. And al-Rā'ī said, describing a gaming arrow:
The two sons of 'iyān ran with the half-roasted meat.
And one says: the land looked with one eye, or with two eyes, when the plants come up. All of this is carried over, borrowed speech and likeness. The poet said, in two lines of verse:
When the lands of Banū Numayr look with an eye, or the lands of Banū Ṣubāḥ,
we pelt them with every lean-bellied, full-chested horse, and with young men of the evening and of the morning.

Of this section is al-'ayn: ready money that is present and at hand. One says huwa 'aynun ghayru daynin, that is, it is wealth present, which eyes can see. And the 'ayn of a thing is the thing itself. You say: take your very dirham. As for their calling the tilt in a balance 'ayyan, that too is from this, because the 'ayn is like the extra weight in the balance.

Al-Khalīl said: al-'īna is a loan on credit. One says ta'ayyana fulānun min fulānin 'īnatan, and 'ayyanahu ta'yīnan. Al-Khalīl said: it is derived from the 'ayn of the balance, which is its excess. And what al-Khalīl has said is sound, because the 'īna must draw an increase with it.

And from al-'īna one says i'tāna. And he recited, in two lines of verse:
How shall we have drink, if we have no dirhams with the wine-seller and no cash,
shall we buy on credit, or take a loan, or will there come forward for us a youth like a sword-blade that the scabbard has laid bare?

Of this section is the 'ayn of a well: they are two 'ayns, like two little hollows in the front of it.

This is the chapter of 'ayn and yā' and what goes with them among the three-letter words. As for 'ayn and alif, the mention of that has already passed, because the alif in it must be turned from a yā' or a wāw, and that has been dealt with. And God knows best.
عيهرة: The unchaste woman. The added letter in it is the yāʾ; it is really from al-ʿahr [illicit union].
غار:
The letters ghayn, alif and rāʾ. The alif in this root is never original — it always stands for something else.

1. al-ghār — a fragrant plant. Someone said, in a line of verse:
Many a fire I spent the night watching, consuming Indian wood and laurel.
2. al-ghār — a dialect word for al-ghayra (jealousy), already explained. Someone said, in a line of verse:
They have a wailing over the boiled meat, as though they were the co-wives of a man of Ḥarīm whose jealousy grew extreme.
3. al-ghār — a great army. From this is the hadith of ʿAlī, peace be upon him: "What do you think of a man who has brought together these two hosts (ghārayn)?"
4. al-ghār — the roof of the mouth.
5. al-ghār — a man's origin and his tribe.
6. al-ghār — the cave.

The reasoning behind all of this has already passed. God knows best.
غب:
The letters ghayn and bāʾ are a sound root indicating a stretch of time with a pause or gap within it.

1. al-ghibb — the camels coming to water one day and staying away the next.
2. al-mughabbabah — the ewe milked one day and left the next.
3. aghbabtu al-ziyārah — I made the visit come every other time, also from al-ghibb.
4. ghabbaba fī al-amr — said when someone does not put full effort into a matter, as if a pause had been set into it.
5. "ruwayda al-shiʿr yaghubb" — take it slow, the poetry will settle — meaning its recitation is set aside until some time has passed over it.
6. ghabba al-amr — said when a matter reaches its final outcome.
7. laḥmun ghābb — meat not eaten right away, but left for a stretch of time.
غبث: The letters ghayn, bāʾ and thāʾ are not a real root. They mentioned of al-Farrāʾ that he said: ghabathtu al-iqiṭ, like ʿabathtuhu — I stirred and worked the dried curd cheese.
غبر:
The letters ghayn, ba and ra are two sound roots: one indicates remaining/persisting, the other a color among colors.

The first: ghabara — it remained. God, Most High, said: {except your wife; she was among those who remained behind} [al-'Ankabut: 33]. One says of a she-camel that 'biha ghubr' — she has something remaining [in her, e.g. of pregnancy]; and 'bihi ghubbar min marad' — he has a remnant of an illness. Ibn Muqbil, or another, said:
If Sulayma asks after me, tell her: he has a remnant of his illness, yet he is well.

From this root: a vein or wound that keeps reopening is ''irqun ghabir', as if it always has some lingering remainder in it. 'Taghabbarati l-mar'atu l-shaykh' — the woman took what remained of the old man's strength [an obscure, euphemistic expression rendered cautiously].

The second root: al-ghubar, dust, named for its dust-color (ghubra), which is its hue. Al-aghbar is anything of the color of dust. Tarafa's saying:
I found the sons of Ghabra' not disowning me, nor [did] the people of that spread-out leather tent.
The 'sons of Ghabra'' are the needy poor, because their complexions are dust-colored, they being people of poverty. Al-ghabra' is the earth. Al-ghubayra' is a fermented drink made from sorghum, perhaps because its color carries a tinge of dust-grey.

As for [the expression] 'the calamity of al-ghabar', I take it to belong to this root as well, meaning it is dust-dark, that is, obscure and murky, such that no way out of it can be seen.

An anomaly from these two roots is what Ibn al-Sikkit related: 'aghbartu fi talab al-haja' — I exerted myself/hastened in pursuit of the need.
غبس:
The letters ghayn, bāʾ and sīn are a word indicating a color among colors.

1. al-ghubsa — a color like the color of ash. One says: farasun aghbasu, a horse of that color. Some said this is what is called "samand" [a dun, isabelline color].
2. Their saying "lā afʿaluhu mā ghabā ghubaysun" — "I will never do it as long as ghubays lasts" — means time itself, al-dahr.

Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: I do not know its origin.
غبش:
The letters ghayn, bāʾ and shīn are a word indicating darkness, being dark.

1. al-ghabash — intense darkness.
2. aghbāsh al-layl — the darknesses of the night.

Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
The darknesses of a full night, whose visitor was the thickening of cloud, until it had no gaps.

Abū ʿUbayd said: al-ghabash is what remains of the night; its plural is aghbāsh.
غبط:
The letters ghayn, bāʾ and ṭāʾ are a sound root with three aspects: the first is a thing's persisting and remaining attached, the other is feeling by hand, and the other is a kind of envy.

The first: their saying aghbaṭat ʿalayhi al-ḥummā — the fever persisted on him, that is, it continued. And aghbaṭtu al-raḥla ʿalā ẓahri al-baʿīr — I kept the saddle continuously on the camel's back and did not lift it off. For that the saddle is called ghabīṭ, plural ghubuṭ. Al-Ḥārith ibn Waʿla said, in a line of verse:
Or have you left the women of the tribe exposed, in the courtyard of the house, kindling fire with the ghubuṭ?
From this is al-ghibṭa — a good state, and the lasting of joy and good.

The other origin is al-ghabṭ. One says ghabaṭtu al-shāh — I felt the sheep with my hand to judge its fatness. Someone said, in a line of verse:
Truly my coming to Bujayr, when I ask him, is like one who feels a dog, hoping for fat in its tail.
From this chapter: al-ghabīṭ — low-lying land, as though it had been pressed down until it settled.

The third is al-ghabṭ, a kind of envy said not to be blameworthy, because in it one wishes for the like without wanting the blessing to leave the other person — unlike ḥasad (envy proper), which is the opposite of this. In the supplication: "O God, ghabṭan lā habṭan" — meaning, O God, [we ask You] that we be envied and not brought low, that is, not cast down.
غبق: The letters ghayn, bāʾ and qāf are a single word: al-ghabūq — the evening drink. One says: ghabaqtu al-qawma ghabqan — I gave the people their evening drink, and ightabaqa ightibāqan — he took the evening drink.
غبن:
The letters ghayn, bāʾ and nūn are a word indicating weakness and being wronged. One says: ghubina al-rajulu fī baiʿihi, fa-huwa yughbanu ghabnan — a man is cheated in his sale, that being when he is wronged in it.
1. ghabana fī raʾyihi — he was mistaken in his judgement, that being when his judgement is weak. The sense of the two words is the same.
2. al-ghabīna, from al-ghabn, is like al-shatīma from al-shatm.
3. al-maghābin — the groin-folds, so named for their softness and their weakness compared to the strength of the rest of the body.
غبي:
The letters ghayn, bāʾ and the weak letter are a sound root indicating a thing's being concealed so that it cannot be found.

1. al-ghabya — the same as al-zubya, a pit-trap; so named because the trapped animal did not perceive it until it fell into it.
2. ghabiya fulānun ghabāwatan — so-and-so was of little perception; he is called ghabiyy.
3. ghabītu ʿan al-khabar — I was unaware of the news, I did not know it.
4. One says: jāʾat ghabyatun min maṭar — a downpour of rain came, meaning it came with darkness, intensity and density.
غت:
The letters ghayn and tāʾ are not [a real root]; it is only the tāʾ standing in place of a ṭāʾ. You say ghaṭaṭtuhu and ghatattuhu, the same word.

1. ghatta fī al-ḍaḥik — he laughed in a stifled way, hidden.
2. ghatta — he followed one utterance right on another, or one draught of drink right on another.

This belongs to the pattern of the imitative words.
غتم:
The letters ghayn, tāʾ and mīm are a root indicating a splitting-open in a thing, and a blocking-up.

1. al-ghutma — foreignness, an impediment in speech.
2. al-ghatm — said of holding in the breath.
3. warada ḥiyāḍa Ghutaym — said of a man when he dies: he came to the pools of Ghutaym. The reasoning is the same, since he comes to a house that is sealed shut.
غث:
The letters ghayn and thāʾ are a sound root indicating corruption in a thing.

1. labistu fulānan ʿalā ghathīthatin fīhi — I dealt with so-and-so despite a corruption in him, meaning a defect of mind and judgement.
2. al-ghathīthah — the matter/pus in a wound.
3. al-laḥm al-ghathth — meat that is not fat, lean meat.
4. aghatha al-ḥadīth — the talk turned worthless and corrupt. He said, in a line of verse: a soft young woman whose talk turns worthless once she falls silent, though from her mouth it is a fresh delight.
5. fulānun lā yaghuthth ʿalayhi shayʾ — said of one who refuses nothing, so that even the poor and worthless seems good to him.

As for al-ghathghathah, it follows the pattern of the imitative words. One says: ghathghathtu al-thawb — I washed the garment and worked it back and forth in my hands. It is said that al-ghathghathah is weak fighting without weapons, likened to the working of a garment as it is washed.
غثر:
The letters ghayn, thāʾ and rāʾ are a small root indicating a gathering of people who are not noble.

1. al-ghathrāʾ — the lowly common people; their gathering is called ghaythara.
2. al-aghthar — clustered algae, the scum on water; this is the origin the word goes back to.
3. al-aghthar (of cloaks) — one whose wool is abundant.
غثم:
The letters ghayn, thāʾ and mīm are two distinct words.

1. al-aghtham (of hair) — hair whose whiteness has overcome its blackness, mostly gray.
Someone said, in a line of verse:
Do you not see an age that has come over me, graying me?
2. The other word: ghathamtu lahu min mālī — I gave him from my wealth.
غثي:
The letters ghayn, thāʾ and the weak letter are a word indicating the rising of something base above something else.

1. al-ghuthāʾ — the debris carried along by a flood. One says: ghathā al-wādī yaghthū, and aghthā yughthī, likewise.
Someone said, in a line of verse:
As though the flood-mark of al-Mujaymir at dawn, from the flood and its debris, were the whorl of a spindle.
(It is also transmitted as al-ghuththāʾ.)
2. al-ghuthāʾ is also said of the lowly common people, by likening them to what has just been described.
3. ghathat nafsuhu taghthī — his stomach churned, as though it welled up with something harmful.
غد: The letters ghayn and dāl are [one] word: it is al-ghuddah, the gland in the flesh, well known. The rajaz poet said: so grant him a wife who is mighdād. They said: she is the one who is angry without end, as if in her throat there were a gland.
غدر:
The letters ghayn, dāl and rā' are a sound root indicating the leaving of a thing. From this: al-ghadr, breaking a covenant and failing to keep faith with it. One says ghadara yaghdiru ghadran. In reproach they say "yā ghudar," O treacherous one, and in the plural "yā la-ghudar." A treacherous night is one plainly marked by ghadr, meaning dark — called this because it "leaves" people behind in their houses, unable to go out, from the intensity of its darkness.

Al-ghadīr, a pool where rainwater collects, is named this because the flood-torrent left it behind. From this chapter: ghadirat al-shāh, when a ewe falls behind from the flock; if the shepherd leaves her, she is called ghadīrah. Al-ghadar: rocky, hoof-hostile ground, hard going, named this because it is hardly ever travelled — it has been "left behind." One says rajulun thabtu al-ghadar, steadfast in speech and in fighting — derived from the word before it, meaning he does not mind crossing the difficult terrain that people have abandoned on account of its ruggedness.

Al-ghadā'ir: braided locks of hair, because they are twisted up and "left" that way for a time. He said, in a line of verse: "His braided locks rise high, coiled toward the crown; the plaits are lost, some doubled, some loose."
غدف:
The letters ghayn, dāl and fāʾ are a sound root indicating covering and concealment.

1. aghdafat al-marʾatu qināʿahā — the woman let down her veil, loosened it.
Someone said, in a line of verse:
If you let your veil down before me, I am still skilled at seizing the armored horseman.
2. aghdafa al-laylu — night let down its curtains.
3. al-ghudāf — the large crow; this is a likening to the letting-down (ighdāf) of the night — its darkening.
غدق:
The letters ghayn, dāl and qāf are a sound root indicating abundance, plenty and ease. From this: al-ghadaq, which is what is abundant and copious. God — Exalted — said: {We would have given them abundant [ghadaqan] water to drink} [al-Jinn: 16].
1. al-ghadaq and al-ghaydāq — what is soft and luxuriant in anything.
2. ghadiqat ʿaynu al-māʾ taghdaqu ghadaqan — the water-spring flowed abundantly.
3. al-ghaydāq — a man generous of nature.
4. Some people claimed that the ḍabb (a large desert lizard) is called ghaydāq, and perhaps that is only because of the fatness and ease found in it.
غدن:
The letters ghayn, dāl and nūn are a small, sound root indicating softness, flowing looseness, and slackness.

1. al-mughdawdin — long, soft, flowing hair.
Ḥassān said, in a line of verse:
And she stood, showing you her hair flowing loose, whenever it bent beneath its own weight, it wearied her.
2. al-shabāb al-ghudāniyy — fresh, tender youth.
Someone said, in a line of verse:
After the fresh, foolish tenderness of youth.

All of that goes back to al-ghadan, which is slackness and languor.
غدو:
The letters ghayn, dāl and the weak letter are a sound root pointing to a time.

From this is al-ghuduww, going out early in the morning; one says ghadā yaghdū — he went out in the morning. And al-ghudwa and al-ghadāt, the early morning; the plural of ghudwa is ghudan and the plural of ghadāt is ghadawāt. Al-ghādiya is a cloud that comes up in the morning. And you say afʿalu dhālika ghadan — I shall do that tomorrow; the original form is ghadwan.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
In them, where they camped, and tomorrow, empty wastes.

And al-ghadā' is that particular meal, so called because it is eaten at that time of day.
غذ: The letters ghayn and dhāl are [one] word: it is ighdhādh al-sayr, hastening one's travel — that is, when there is no slackness or pause in it. From it: ghadhdha al-jurḥ and aghadhdha — said of a wound when it has healed but its moisture has not settled, so that it keeps weeping forever.
غذم:
The letters ghayn, dhāl and mīm are a sound root indicating a kind of eating and drinking.

1. al-ghadhm — eating roughly and forcefully.
2. ightadhama al-faṣīl mā fī ḍarʿi ummihi — the weaned young camel drank up everything in its mother's udder.
غذى:
The letters ghayn, dhāl and the weak letter are a sound root indicating something to do with food, and a kind of movement.

As for the food: al-ghidhāʾ — food and drink. Ghadhiyy al-māl and ghadhawiyyuhu — the young of livestock, such as lambs and the like; called ghadhawiyy because it is nourished (yughdhā).

As for the other: al-ghadhawān — a lively, energetic horse, named for its youth and vigor. One says: ghadhdhā al-baʿīru bi-bawlihi yughadhdhī — the camel voided its urine in intermittent spurts. Ghadhā al-ʿirqu yaghdhū — the vein flowed with blood. Someone said, in a line of verse:
And a thrust like the mouth of a skin, flowing with blood, while the skin was full.
غر:
The letters ghayn and rāʾ are three sound roots: the first is the pattern or model, the second is deficiency, and the third is nobility, whiteness, and generosity.

The first: al-ghirār is the mould on which arrows are shaped. One says: so-and-so bore her children ʿalā ghirārin wāḥid, meaning she brought them one after another, all on one pattern. The origin of this is al-ghurr, the fold pressed into a garment. One says: fold the garment along its ghurr, meaning its crease, its first pattern. Al-ghurrah is a person's habitual bearing, and also his face — and from that the whole body comes to be referred to by it.

1. "in the miscarried child there is a ghurrah: a male or a female slave" — meaning that its blood-money requires a living soul, a male or female slave. He said, in a line of verse: every man slain from [the clan of] Kulayb is a ghurrah owed, until the killing reaches the clan of Murrah.
2. al-gharīr — the guarantor. One says: anā gharīruka min fulān, I am your guarantor against so-and-so. He is called gharīr because he stands as the counterpart of the one he guarantees: he is held to the money just as the one guaranteed for would be held. It is possible that ghirār al-sayf, the edge of a sword, comes from this too — anything with an edge, its edge is called ghirār, because that is the point where the shaping and the pattern of the sword come to their end.

As for deficiency: one says ghārat al-nāqah taghāru ghirāran, said when a she-camel's milk grows less. In the hadith: "there is no ghirār in prayer, nor in the greeting of peace." Al-ghirār in prayer is not completing its bowing or its prostration. Al-ghirār in the greeting is to say "peace be upon you" without waiting, or to answer only "and upon you."

1. al-ghirār — light, broken sleep. The poet said: the calamity from [the tribe of] Thaqīf is a ruinous one; it left the eyes with nothing but broken sleep. And Jarīr said: what ails your sleep in bed, that it is so broken — if your heart were able, it would have flown away.
2. bayʿ al-gharar — a sale carrying risk, where it is not known whether the thing will come to be or not, like selling a runaway slave, or a bird still in the air; this is deficient, and such a sale is never completed.
3. gharra al-ṭāʾir farkhahu — the bird fed its chick by regurgitating into its mouth, because of how little and how short the food was.

The third root: al-ghurrah. The ghurrah of anything is its finest, most noble part. Al-ghurrah is also whiteness — everything white is agharr. The first three nights of the month are called ghurrah.

1. al-gharīr — a fine, generous nature. They say of an old man: "his gharīr has departed and his harīr [snarling ill-temper] has taken its place."

Close to this is al-gharārah, which is like heedlessness — it comes from a generous nature, and may be found in anyone generous. But the blameworthy kind of it belongs to the root before this one, deficiency, since it comes from a want of sharp judgement.

What falls outside these roots, if it is sound, is a thing al-Shaybānī mentioned: that al-ghirghir is the guinea-fowl, singular ghirghirah. He recited: I wrap them round with the sword from every side, just as eagles wrap up partridges and guinea-fowl.
غرب:
The letters ghayn, rā' and bā' are a sound root, and its words do not follow one analogy, but they are of one kind; and for that reason we have written it out as it comes, without seeking an analogy for it.

Al-gharb is the edge of a thing. One says: this is the gharb of the sword, its edge. And they say kafaftu min gharbihi, that is, I blunted his edge. And their saying istaghraba al-rajul, when a man goes to excess in laughing, may be from this, as though he reached the furthest limit of laughter. Al-gharb is also the great bucket. Al-gharbān of the eye are its front corner and its back corner. Ghurūb al-asnān is the water and gloss of the teeth. As for al-ghurūb, it is the channels of the eye. A poet said, in a line of verse:
What ails you that you never mention Umm 'Amr, but your eyes have channels running with tears.

And al-gharb also, with a sukūn on the rā', is in their saying atāhu sahmun gharb, a stray arrow came to him, when it is not known who shot it.

As for al-gharab, with a fatḥa on the rā', it is said that al-gharab is the great water-skin carried on a camel. And al-gharab is water that spills at the well so that its smell changes. Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
And the spilt water was sniffed out.

And al-gharb is a tree. And they say — and God knows best whether it is sound — that al-gharab is a vessel of gold or of silver. And they recite, in a line of verse:
So the two of them made the middle of the well gurgle, as the cupbearer of the foreigners made the gold vessel gurgle.

And al-gharb is a swelling in the inner corner of the eye; from it one says gharibat al-'ayn gharaban. And al-gharb is a vein that keeps running and does not stop. Al-ghurba is being far from one's homeland; one says gharabat al-dār, the dwelling grew distant. And of this chapter is ghurūb al-shams, the setting of the sun, as though it were its going far from the face of the earth. And sha'w mugharrab means a far-off stretch. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Do I still know you from the first days of youth, still seeking, after it has turned its back? Far off! a distant stretch.

And they say hal min mugharribati khabar, meaning news that has come from far away.

And in the book of al-Khalīl: 'When the dogs press hard in the pursuit of game one says gharrabat.' And there is something to look into in that.

Al-ghārib is the top of the back and of the hump. One says alqā ḥablahu 'alā ghāribihi, he threw his rope over his withers, when he lets him go free. Al-ghurāb, the crow, is well known. Al-ghurābān are two hollows beside the two rump-bones of a horse. Al-ghurāb is the head of the axe. Rijl al-ghurāb, the crow's foot, is a kind of tying up of the udder. Al-Kumayt said, in a line of verse:
The crow's-foot knot was tied.

Al-ghirbīb is the black one, as though it were derived from the colour of the crow. Al-mughrab is that which is white in the lashes, in anything. Al-gharbī is the faḍīkh drink made of unripe dates and steeped. And al-gharbī is a red dye.
غرث: The letters ghayn, rāʾ and thāʾ are a sound root indicating hunger. Al-gharath — hunger; a man is gharthān. They borrow this and say jāriyatun gharthā al-wishāḥ — a girl whose sash is "hungry", because she is slender-waisted and her sash is never filled, as though her sash itself were hungry.
غرد:
The letters ghayn, rāʾ and dāl are two words: one a sound, the other a plant.

1. gharrada al-ṭāʾiru fī ṣawtihi yugharridu taghrīdan — the bird trilled in its call.
2. al-gharad — the truffle, singular gharada. Al-maghārīd — a plant, singular mughrūd; they claimed it too is the truffle.
غرز:
The letters ghayn, rāʾ and zāʾ are a sound root indicating the fixing of a thing into a thing.

Gharaztu al-shayʾa aghrizuhu gharzan — I fixed the thing in. Gharaztu rijlahu fī al-ghirz — I put his foot in the stirrup. Gharazat al-jarādatu bi-dhanabihā fī al-arḍ — the locust fixed its tail into the ground, like razzat. Al-ṭabīʿa is called gharīza (instinct), as though it were something fixed into a person.

As for their saying ightaraztu al-shayʾa, and ightaraztu al-sayra ightirāzan when your pace drew near — its meaning is bringing the pace close, as though I had now placed my foot in the ghirz of the saddle.
