As for their saying gharazat al-nāqa, when the she-camel's milk grew scant — its meaning likewise goes back to this, as though her milk were fixed within her body and did not come out.
غرس:
The letters ghayn, rāʾ and sīn are a sound root close to the one before it. One says gharastu al-shajara gharsan — I planted the tree; this is the season of planting, al-ghirās. It is said that al-gharīsa is the palm sapling when it first sprouts.

Anomalous from this is al-ghirs — a thin membrane that comes out on a newborn's head. Someone said, in a line of verse:
Every hairy newborn, in its birth-caul.
غرض:
The letters ghayn, rāʾ and ḍād are one of the roots not built on a single pattern; its words come from divergent origins, and you will see how far apart they are.

1. al-gharḍ and al-ghurḍa — the girth-strap, the belt of the saddle.
2. al-maghriḍ (of a camel) — like the girth-place (maḥzim) on a riding beast.
3. al-ighrīḍ — hail; it is also said to be the palm-spathe.
4. laḥmun gharīḍ — fresh meat.
5. māʾun maghrūḍ — likewise, fresh water.
6. al-gharaḍ — weariness; one says ghariḍtu bihi and ghariḍtu minhu.
7. al-gharaḍ — longing.
Someone said, in a line of verse:
Who is a faithful messenger to convey from me to ʿUlayya, other than the word of a liar —
that I have longed for the meeting of her face, as the lover longs for the absent beloved.
8. gharaḍat al-marʾatu siqāʾahā — the woman churned her waterskin.
9. gharaḍnā al-sakhla naghriḍuhu — we weaned the young goat before its time.
10. al-gharḍ — falling short of being full. One says gharriḍ fī siqāʾika — do not fill your waterskin.
11. warada al-māʾa ghāriḍan — he came to the water early.
12. al-maghāriḍ — the sides of the belly below the ribs, singular maghriḍ.
غرف:
The letters ghayn, rāʾ and fāʾ are a sound root, except that its words do not follow one pattern but diverge. Al-gharf is the verbal noun of gharaftu al-māʾ wa-ghayrahu, aghrifuhu, gharfan, I scooped up the water or other. Al-ghurfa: what is scooped up. Al-gharīf: a thicket, plural ghuruf. A poet said, in a line of verse:

as the wild donkey crouches low in the thickets

Al-ghurfa: an upper room. It is said gharafa nāṣiyata farasihi, when he shaved his horse's forelock right off.
غرق:
The letters ghayn, rā' and qāf are a single sound root pointing to reaching the end in a thing, going to its utmost.

Of this is al-gharaq, drowning in water. And al-ghariqa is land watered to the utmost. And ighrawraqat al-ʿaynu wa-l-arḍ — the eye and the ground brimmed over — is from this too, as though the eye had drowned in its tears.

Of this chapter: aghraqtu fī al-qaws — [I drew] the bow to the utmost of the draw. And ightaraqa al-farasu fī al-khayl, when it mixed in among the horses and then outran them.

Of what has strayed from this chapter is al-ghurqa of milk: about a third of the vessel; the plural is ghuraq.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
She comes into the morning with her udders holding measures of milk, of good taste, sweet, got without labour.
غرل: The letters ghayn, rāʾ and lām are a single word: al-ghurla, which is the foreskin. Al-aghral — the uncircumcised. They say al-ghiral is one who is loose and slack of build.
غرم:
The letters ghayn, rā' and mīm are a sound root indicating persistence and constant attachment. From it, al-gharīm, the one bound by debt, so named for his persistence and pressing insistence. Al-gharām is punishment that never lets go, in His words, Most High: {indeed its punishment is ever persistent} [al-Furqān: 65]. Al-A'shā said:
If he punishes, it is relentless, and if he gives ... generously, he does not care what it costs him.
And ghurm al-māl, a debt or financial loss, is from this too, named because it is the debtor's own burden.
غرن: The letters ghayn, rāʾ and nūn are a single word. They say al-gharīn is what remains in a trough of its water and its mud.
غرو:
The letters ghayn, rā' and a weak final letter are a sound root indicating being struck with admiration and wonder at the beauty of a thing. From this: al-gharī, the beautiful. One says of a man rajulun gharin. Then wonder itself came to be called gharw. From this also: aghraytuhu bi-l-shay', I incited him toward the thing, and the substance by which things are stuck together [glue] is named from this too. One says ghārat al-'aynu bi-l-dam'i ghirā'an, when the eye persists in weeping; and ghariyat bi-l-dam' likewise. The poet said, in a line of verse:
Whenever I say, let me forget, my eye is overcome with weeping, and the flowing tears keep pouring.
غز: The letters ghayn and zā' — there is nothing in it. Ghazza is a town.
غزد: The letters ghayn, zāʾ and dāl do not resemble sound Arabic speech. They have claimed that al-ghizyad means loud-voiced, and that al-ghizyad is soft, tender growth. God knows best.
غزر: The letters ghayn, zāʾ and rāʾ are a single word: their saying ghazurat al-nāqa — the she-camel's milk became abundant, ghuzr and ghazāra. ʿAynun ghazīra — an abundant spring, and maʿrūfun ghazīr — abundant kindness.
غزل:
The letters ghayn, zāy and lām are three distinct words; none is to be measured against another.
1. The first: al-ghazl, spinning. One says ghazalat al-marʾatu ghazlahā — the woman spun her yarn. The wooden implement is mighzal, plural maghāzil.
2. The second: al-ghazal, the talk of young men and young women [courting-talk]. One says ghazila al-kalbu ghazalan — the dog courted, which is that it chases the gazelle until, when it catches up to it, it leaves it and turns away.
3. The second, as the text has it again: al-ghazāl, the gazelle, well known, the female being ghazāla. Perhaps the name of the sun is borrowed from this, for the sun is called al-ghazāla at the rising of mid-morning.
غزو:
The letters ghayn, zāy and the weak letter are two sound roots: one is seeking a thing, the other belongs to the category of conceiving.
The first is al-ghazw, raiding. One says: ghazawtu aghzū. Al-ghāzī — the one who seeks that, plural ghuzāh and also ghaziyy, just as the group of pilgrims is called ḥajīj. Al-mughziya — a woman whose husband has gone raiding. In relation to al-ghazw one says ghazawiyy.
The second: their saying aghzat al-nāqa — the she-camel, when her conceiving became difficult. Some said: al-atān al-mughziya is the she-donkey whose bearing is delayed and then she gives birth. Al-Hudhalī said, in a line of verse whose full sense is not certain: "It rings out over the barren she-donkeys slow to bear, roaming with them the desolate stony wastes."
غس:
The letters ghayn and sīn — there is nothing in it except their saying: a man is ghuss, when he is weak. From this is the saying of Aws, in a line of verse:
Left-behind men, while other people settle their own affairs ... frail in trust, a lone reed-stalk after another.
غسا: The letters ghayn, sīn and the weak letter are a single letter-root indicating an extremity, in largeness or something else. One says ghasā al-laylu and aghsā — the night grew very dark. Shaykhun ghāsin — an old man of great age. It is transmitted that a reciter read: "and I have reached, from old age, ghusiyy" [a variant reading].
غسر:
The letters ghayn, sīn and rā' are a word, if it is valid, indicating mixing. They say: taghassara al-ghazl — the yarn became tangled.

Ibn Duraid said: "al-ghasar is what the wind throws into a pool. Then it became common in use, until they said: taghassara al-amr — the matter became muddled."
غسق: The letters ghayn, sīn and qāf are a sound root indicating darkness. Al-ghasaq is darkness. Al-ghāsiq is the night. One says ghasaqat 'aynuhu, his eye grew dark. Aghsaqa al-mu'adhdhin, said when the caller to prayer delayed the sunset prayer until the darkness of the night had come on. As for al-ghassāq, mentioned in the Qur'an, the commentators said it is what drips from the skins of the people of the Fire.
غسل:
The letters ghayn, sīn and lām are a sound root indicating the purifying and cleansing of a thing. One says ghasaltu al-shay'a ghaslan. Al-ghusl is the noun. Al-ghasūl is what the head is washed with, of khiṭmī (a soap-plant) or other. A line says:
O Layla, the ghisl, so long as you remain unmarried ... is forbidden to me, the ghisl shall not touch me.
One says faḥlun ghusalatun, said of a stallion whose mating is frequent yet does not get with young. Al-ghislīn, mentioned in the Book of God, is said to be what washes off from the bodies of the disbelievers in the Fire.
غسم: The letters ghayn, sīn and mīm amount to nothing. And sometimes they say al-ghasam for darkness.
غسن: The letters ghayn, sīn and nūn are a word. They say that al-ghusan is the locks of hair. And the forelock is called ghusna.
غش:
The letters ghayn and shīn are roots that indicate weakness in a thing and haste in it.

1. al-ghishsh — from this. They say: al-ghishsh is that sincere advice is not given in full.
2. ghishāsh — a scant drink, a little one. One says: he slept only ghishāshan, that is, a little; and I met him ghishāshan — and that is at the fading of the sun, near sunset.
غشم:
The letters ghayn, shīn and mīm are a single root, indicating overpowering, domination and injustice.

1. al-ghashm — injustice.
2. al-ḥarb ghashūm — war is called ghashūm, because it strikes even one who did no wrong.
3. al-ghashamsham — the one whom nothing turns back from his courage. Extra letters were placed in its form to add to its meaning.
غشى:
The letters ghayn, shīn and the weak letter are a sound root, indicating the covering of one thing by another. One says: ghashshaytu al-shay'a ughashshīhi, I covered the thing.

1. al-ghishā' — the cover.
2. al-ghāshiya — the Resurrection, because it overtakes creation with its terror.
3. ghāshiya — it is said: ramāhu Allāhu bi-ghāshiya, God struck him with a ghāshiya, a disease that seizes a man as though it were covering him.
4. al-ghishyān — a man's ghishyān of a woman, meaning intercourse with her.
غص:
The letters ghayn and ṣād — there is nothing in it except al-ghaṣaṣ, choking on food. A man who chokes is called ghaṣṣān. He said, in a line of verse:
If my throat were choked by something other than water ... I would be like the one choking, straining to swallow it with water.
غصن: The letters ghayn, ṣād and nūn are a single word: it is ghuṣn, the branch of a tree, plural ghuṣūn and aghṣān. And one says: ghaṣantu al-ghuṣn, I cut the branch.
غض:
The letters ghayn and ḍād are two sound roots: one indicates restraint and diminishment, the other freshness.

1. al-ghaḍḍ — restraint: the lowering of the gaze. Anything you have held back, you have ghaḍaḍtahu, restrained it. From this comes their saying: such a thing brings ghaḍāḍa upon him, a matter over which he must lower his gaze in shame.
2. al-ghaḍghaḍa — diminishment, a decrease. It is said in the hadith: "He passed from this world with his belly still full, never diminished." And they say: it is a sea that is not diminished. Ghaḍghaḍtu al-siqā' means I lessened the waterskin — and likewise for a right or due owed to someone.

The other root is freshness.

1. al-ghaḍḍ — whatever is fresh of anything.
2. ghaḍīḍ — what the palm-spathe is called when it first emerges.
غضا:
The letters ghayn, ḍād and the weak letter are two words.

The first: al-ighḍā' — the lowering of the eyelids. This is derived from al-layla al-ghāḍiya, the intensely dark night.

The other word: al-ghaḍā, a well-known tree. One says: arḍ ghaḍyā', land abundant in ghaḍā. And one says: ibil ghaḍiya, camels that suffered from eating ghaḍā.
غضب:
The letters ghayn, ḍād and bā' are a sound root pointing to intensity and strength.

It is said that al-ghaḍba is the hard rock. They said: from it al-ghaḍab, anger, is derived, because anger is displeasure grown intense. One says ghaḍiba yaghḍabu ghaḍaban — he became angry — and he is ghaḍbān and ghaḍūb, an angry man. One says ghaḍibtu li-fulān, I was angry for someone, when he is alive; and ghaḍibtu bihi when he is dead.

Durayd said, in a line of verse:
That we are angry over Maʿbad.

And it is said that al-ghaḍūb is the huge snake.
غضر:
The letters ghayn, ḍād and rā' are a sound root, indicating goodness, blessing and freshness.

1. al-ghaḍāra — the pleasantness of life. And they say, in a curse: abāda Allāhu ta'ālā ghaḍrā'ahum, may God Almighty destroy their good and their prosperity.

'Abd Allāh ibn Muslim said: the root of al-ghaḍrā' is a green, sticky clay.

2. anbaṭa bi'rahu fī ghaḍrā' — said of one who struck water for his well in ghaḍrā' clay.
3. dābba ghaḍirat al-nāṣiya — an animal with a ghaḍira forelock, said when it is a blessed animal.
4. al-ghāḍir — the hide that has been well tanned.

Deviating from this root is their saying: lam yaghḍir 'an dhālika, meaning: he did not turn away from it. Ibn Aḥmar said, in a line of verse: and they did not turn away from that, a turning-away.

And al-ghaḍwar is a plant.
غضف:
The letters ghayn, ḍād and fā' are a sound root, indicating slackness, collapse, and being covered over.

1. al-aghḍaf — said of predators, one whose ear hangs slack.
2. layl aghḍaf — a dark night, one that covers with its darkness. A poet, Dhū al-Rumma, said, in a line of verse:
   I roam the far, unknown place through wandering, in the shade of an aghḍaf night, where owls call to its skulls.
3. 'aysh ghāḍif — a soft life, so they say, as though it has covered one over with its goodness and abundance.
4. al-ghuḍf — the dark-grey sandgrouse, named so by comparison with the night and its blackness.
5. taghaḍḍafat al-bi'r — said of a well when its sides collapsed and so covered what lay beneath it.
6. ghaḍafat al-utun taghḍifu — said of she-donkeys when they broke into a hard run, because they cover the ground with their running. A poet said:
   They slacken, then break into a run at the first draught, like a rain-cloud carrying hail and pouring down.
غضل: The letters ghayn, ḍād and lām. One says: aghḍalati al-shajaratu, and ightaḍallat, when a tree's branches grew abundant.
غضن:
The letters ghayn, ḍād and nūn are a sound root, indicating bending and breaking.

1. al-ghuḍūn — the creases of the skin; the creases of anything are also called ghuḍūn.
2. taghaḍḍana jilduhu — said of his skin when it wrinkled.
3. al-mughāḍana — the scrunching together of the two eyes.
4. mā ghaḍanaka 'an kadhā — their saying, meaning: what held you back from it.
5. ghaḍan al-'ayn — the visible skin of the eye, named for the crease that is in it.

Deviating from this root is their saying: ghaḍanat al-nāqa bi-waladihā, said of a she-camel when she miscarried her young before it had grown hair.
غط:
The letters ghayn and ṭā' form a small sound root with two meanings: one is a sound, the other a time among times.

1. ghaṭīṭ — the snoring of a person in his sleep.
2. al-ghaṭāṭ — the sandgrouse (al-qaṭā), named for its sound, ghaṭāṭ. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Their driver startled up crouching sandgrouse ... their sounds like the murmuring speech of the Persians.

The other root is al-ghuṭāṭ. Some said it is the dawn, and they cited a line: he went to a red-hued one at al-ghuṭāṭ. Others said it is the darkness just before dawn. And regarding the line of Ibn Aḥmar [30], "the first of the criers, like the oncoming ghuṭāṭ" — those who read it with a fatḥa compared them to sandgrouse, and those who read it with a ḍamma compared them to the blackness of darkness in its abundance.

As for ghaṭaṭtuhu fī al-mā', I plunged it in the water — it could be from that sound water makes at such a moment, or it could be from the darkness before dawn, as though you concealed it and covered it [ghaṭṭaytahu] with the water.
غطس: The letters ghayn, ṭā' and sīn are a sound root, indicating al-ghaṭṭ, plunging under. One says: ghaṭaṭtuhu fī al-mā'i and ghaṭastuhu, I plunged him into the water. And taghāṭasa al-qawm, the people plunged one another under, meaning taghāṭṭū.
غطش:
The letters ghayn, ṭāʾ and shīn are a single sound root, indicating darkness and what resembles it. From this: al-aghṭash, one whose eye has something like weak, blurred sight; the woman is ghaṭshāʾ.
1. falātun ghaṭshā — a trackless waste through which one cannot find one's way. A poet said, in a line of verse: "And a desolate, dark and pathless [ghaṭshā] waste, where the cry of its horned-owl keeps me company."
2. ghaṭasha al-layl — the night grew dark; God — Exalted — darkened it [aghṭashahu].
3. al-mutaghāṭish — one who feigns blindness to a thing, pretending not to see it. One says: huwa yataghāṭashu.
غطف: The letters ghayn, ṭā' and fā' are a sound root, indicating goodness and abundance in a thing. Its origin is al-ghaṭaf in the eyelashes: their abundance, length, and curving. Then one says: 'aysh aghṭaf, when a life is soft and bends over its owner with good things. The verbal noun is al-ghaṭaf.
غطل:
The letters ghayn, ṭā' and lām are three words.

1. al-ghayṭala — the tree, plural al-ghayṭal. He said:
   And he kept swaying in a ghayṭal, as the gadfly-stricken donkey spins round.
2. al-ghayṭala — the cow.
3. al-ghayṭala — the density of night and its blackness.
غطم:
The letters ghayn, ṭā' and mīm are a sound root, indicating abundance and gathering.

1. al-baḥr al-ghiṭamm — the sea, so called.
2. ghuṭāmiṭ — the term used for the greater part of the sea.
3. rajul ghiṭamm — a man broad of character.
غطو: The letters ghayn, ṭā' and a weak final letter indicate covering and concealment. One says ghaṭaytu al-shay'a and ghaṭṭaytuhu, I covered the thing. Al-ghiṭā': that with which something is covered. Ghaṭā al-laylu yaghṭū, when the night covers everything in its darkness.
غف:
The letters ghayn and fāʾ are a single word that does not branch; it is bare sufficiency, and one calls it a ghuffah of livelihood. He said, in a line of verse: a ghuffah, enough to keep life going, suffices me.

And the horses grazed their fill (ightaffat) of a ghuffah from the spring pasture, when they got enough of it without taking more. He said, in a line of verse: and we were — whenever the horses took their fill of spring grazing — such that seekers of old scores would strip themselves bare and go after them.
غفر:
The letters ghayn, fā' and rā' - the great mass of this section is covering, and then things stray from it that will be mentioned. So al-ghafr is covering. Al-ghufrān and al-ghafr have one meaning. One says: God forgave his sin, ghafran, maghfiratan and ghufrānan. Concerning al-ghafr, a poet said, in a line of verse:
In the shade of him before whom faces have humbled themselves, the king of kings and the owner of forgiveness.

And one says: ghafira al-thawb, when the nap of the cloth rises. It belongs to this section, because the nap covers the face of the cloth. Al-mighfar, the mail hood, is well known. Al-ghifāra is a rag that the man who oils his hair puts on the crown of his head. And it is said that al-ghafīr is the hair that hangs down at the nape. It is reported of a woman of the Arabs that she said to her daughter: 'ighfirī ghafīraki' - meaning, cover it. Al-ghafīra is forgiveness as well. A poet said, in a line of verse:
O my people, there is no forgiveness in them.

Among what strays from this: al-ghufr, the young of the mountain ewe, and its mother is mughfir. And al-ghafr is a relapse in illness. A poet said, in a line of verse:
My two friends, the dwelling place brings a relapse upon the man in love, as the fevered man relapses, or the man with a wound.

As for al-maghfūr, it is something like gum that comes out of the 'urfuṭ tree.
غفص: The letters ghayn, fā', and ṣād are a single word. Ghāfaṣtu al-rajul — I seized the man unawares, taking him off his guard. And God knows best what is correct.
غفق:
The letters ghayn, fā', and qāf are a sound root indicating lightness, speed, and repetition in a thing, with pauses in between.

1. ghafaqa ibilahu — he hastened the bringing of his camels [to water], then did that again and again.
2. yataghaffaq al-sharāb — he keeps sipping the drink, hour after hour.
3. ghafaqa ghafqatan min al-layl — he slept a light sleep during the night.
4. al-ghafq — rain that is not heavy.
5. ghafaqahu bil-sawṭ ghafaqāt — he struck him with the whip, several strikes.
6. al-ghafq — a sudden attack on a thing without prior intent; it is also said of one who returns suddenly from his absence.
7. ghafaqa al-ḥimār al-atān — the donkey mounted the she-donkey, again and again.
غفل: The letters ghayn, fā' and lām are a sound root pointing to leaving a thing out of forgetfulness, and it may be on purpose. Of that: ghafaltu ʿan al-shay' ghaflatan wa-ghufūlan, and that is when you leave it and it has slipped your mind. And aghfaltuhu, when you leave it while it is present in your memory. And they say of everything that has no mark on it: ghufl, as though it had been overlooked. So they say arḍ ghufl - land with no landmark in it. And nāqa ghufl - a she-camel with no brand on her. And rajul ghufl - a man who has not been tried by affairs.
غفوي:
The letters ghayn, fā', and the weak letter form a small root that seems to indicate something like what the previous root indicated, the leaving of a thing, except that this one is specific to a kind of sleep.

1. aghfā — a man dozed off in sleep, yughfī, ighfā'an. Al-ighfā'ah is a single doze. He said, in a line of verse:
If you were water, you would be the water of a rain-cloud ... and if you were sleep, you would be the dawn's brief doze.
2. al-ghafw — the pit-trap [al-zubya], because the one who falls into it is as if he grew heedless and dozed off until he fell.

Anomalous from this is al-ghafā, the worthless part of a thing. One says: the food became aghfā, meaning its worthless part, its ghafā, grew abundant.
غق: The letters ghayn and qāf are not [a real root]; it is only used to imitate the sound of something boiling — one says: it went ghaqq.
غل:
The letters ghayn and lām are a sound root indicating something worked in between another thing, and something held fast, like a thing that is driven in.

1. ghalaltu al-shayʾ fī al-shayʾ — I fixed the thing firmly within the thing, as if I had driven it in. He said, in a line of verse: and an eye of hers, round and full, set to a brow into which the eyelash was fixed.
2. al-ghullah and al-ghalīl — thirst. It is said this is because it is like a thing that works its way into the body with heat. One says: a camel is ghallān, meaning thirsty.
3. al-ghalal — water running among trees.
4. al-ghulūl in war-spoils — concealing something and not returning it for division, as if its holder had hidden it (ghallahu) among his clothes.
5. al-ghill — the rancour that works its way into the chest.

As for the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him, "lā ighlāla wa-lā islāla" — al-ighlāl there is treachery, and the reasoning behind it is plain. Al-Namir said, in a line of verse: may God reward Jamrah, daughter of Nawfal, on our behalf, with the reward of a treacherous man false to a trust.

As for the hadith, "three things toward which a believer's heart does not turn treacherous (lā yughillu / lā yaghillu)" — whoever reads it lā yughillu takes it from al-ighlāl, treachery; whoever reads it lā yaghillu takes it from al-ghill, rancour.

6. al-ghullān — the hidden, low-lying valleys, singular ghāl, because the one who travels through them works his way down into them.
7. al-ghilālah — an undergarment worn beneath the outer garment, and a lining worn beneath a coat of mail.
8. al-ghullah — the strainer-cloth fitted over the mouth of a jug; the plural is ghulal. Labīd said, in a line of verse: she has strainer-cloths of fine linen and cotton, in the hands of foreign servants attending on the chiefs.
9. al-ghalghalah — swiftness in travel. A "mughalghalah" letter is one carried on from land to land — and this fits the reasoning, for it works its way through the lands and threads into them. He said, in a line of verse: carry to Abū Mālik, from me, a far-carried message — for in reproach there is life kept between kinsmen.
10. al-ghalīl — date-stones mixed into chopped fodder to feed the camels. He said, in a line of verse: a thorn like the staff of a man of Nahd, into which was worked a portion of chewed date-stones from Qurrān.
غلب:
The letters ghayn, lām and bā' are a sound root indicating strength, overpowering and severity. From this: ghalaba al-rajul, the man overcame, with the verbal nouns ghalban, ghalaban and ghalabatan. God, exalted, said: {And they, after their being overcome, shall overcome} [al-Rūm: 3]. And al-ghilāb is contending for mastery. And al-aghlab is the man thick of neck; one says ghaliba yaghlabu ghalaban. And a hill may be ghalbā', massive, and a might may be ghalbā', overpowering. And the tribe of Taghlib used to be called al-Ghalbā'.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
The sons of al-Ghalbā' left me as my inheritance a glory ... newly won, after their ancient glory.

And ighlawlaba al-ʿushb: the herbage grew to its utmost. And al-mughallab among poets is the one defeated again and again. And al-mughallab is also the one who has overcome his adversary or his match, as though he had been given the mastery over his adversary, that is, the victory was assigned to him.
غلت: The letters ghayn, lām, and tā' hold one word. They say: al-ghalat in reckoning is like al-ghalaṭ [with the emphatic letter] elsewhere. In one version of a hadith: "There is no ghalat in Islam."
غلث:
The letters ghayn, lām, and thā' are a single sound root, indicating mixing and admixture.

1. ghalathtu al-ṭa'ām — I mixed the food: I mixed wheat and barley. It is called al-ghalīth.
2. rajul ghalith — a man who mixes it with his rivals in combat, sticking fast to what he has set out to do. One says: ghalitha bihi, when he clings to it.
3. ghalitha al-dhi'b bil-ghanam — the wolf clung persistently to the sheep.

As for their saying, ghalitha al-zand, when the fire-stick fails to spark, that is imprecise speech; its meaning is that it is a picked, select fire-stick — but really it is a mixture [khilṭ] of fire-sticks, taken from the surrounding wood mixed in with others. What is meant by al-ghalath is its wood, and when it is of that kind, it does not spark.
غلج:
The letters ghayn, lām, and jīm are a word indicating transgression and domineering insolence. The Arabs say: huwa yataghallaju 'alaynā, meaning he acts insolently toward us.

1. 'ayr mighlaj — a wild donkey that drives off the herd of she-asses.
2. taghalluj can also mean that he drinks and smacks his tongue afterward.
غلس:
The letters ghayn, lām, and sīn are a single word, al-ghalas, the darkness at the end of the night.

1. ghallasnā — we traveled in that darkness before dawn. Al-Akhṭal said, in a line of verse:
Did your eye deceive you, or did you see at Wāsiṭ ... in the darkness before dawn, the phantom form of al-Rabāb?
2. waqa'a fī tughullis — he fell into a calamity, is from this, because he falls into a dark affair he cannot find his way out of.
غلط: The letters ghayn, lām, and ṭā' are a single word, al-ghalaṭ: the opposite of getting something right. One says: ghaliṭa yaghlaṭu ghalaṭan. There is an ughlūṭa between them, meaning something with which they try to trick one another.
غلف: The letters ghayn, lām and fā' are one sound word indicating a covering, and one thing enveloping another. One says ghilāf al-sayf wa-l-sikkīn, the sheath of the sword and the knife. Qalbun aghlaf, a heart as if wrapped in a covering, so that it takes nothing in. God, Most High, said: {and they said, our hearts are wrapped} [al-Baqarah: 88], meaning "they have been covered by something, so they take nothing in." It is also read to mean vessels holding a store of knowledge. The underlying pattern in all of it is one. They also say tughallafu bi-l-ghāliyah, she is perfumed with a scented ointment — this too is not far from what we have mentioned.
غلق:
The letters ghayn, lām and qāf are a single sound root, indicating a thing catching fast in another. From this: al-ghalaq. One says from it: aghlaqtu al-bāb, I locked the door, so it is mughlaq. Ghaliqa al-rahn fī yad murtahinihi — the pledge became stuck fast in the pledgee's hand, when it is not redeemed. The Messenger of God said: "The pledge does not become forfeit [lā yaghlaqu]." The jurists said: this refers to the pledge-giver saying to the creditor, "I grant you a respite for your due until such-and-such a time, and otherwise the pledge is yours" — the Prophet forbade that condition.
1. Anything not redeemed has ghaliqa. Zuhayr said, in a line of verse: "She parted from you with a pledge that has no release, on the day of farewell, so the pledge became forfeit [ghaliqā]."
2. al-mighlaq — the seventh arrow in the game of maysir, because it seizes fast onto something even if small. Labīd said, in a line of verse: "And a slaughter-camel of gamblers, I called for its death with arrows of like appearance [maghāliq]."
3. ghaliqa ẓahru al-baʿīr — the camel's back became fixed with a sore that will not heal from the saddle-gall.
4. From this: ghaliqat al-nakhla — the palm-tree's fronds withered at the base and its fruit was cut off. God knows best what is correct.
غلم:
The letters ghayn, lām and mīm are a sound root that points to youth and to the stirring of desire. From that is al-ghulām, the boy whose moustache is just sprouting. He is clearly in his ghulūmiyya and his ghulūma, his boyhood, and the plural is ghilma and ghilmān.

From its chapter is ightalama al-faḥl ghulmatan — the stallion was stirred with the desire to mate. Al-ghaylam is the young girl. Al-ghaylam is also the young man. And al-ghaylam is the male tortoise. It is not far-fetched that its analogy should be the analogy of the chapter.
غلوي:
The letters ghayn, lām, and the weak letter are a sound root, concerning a matter, indicating a rising and an exceeding of a measure.

1. ghalā al-si'r yaghlū ghalā'an — the price rose; that is its rising.
2. ghalā al-rajul fī al-amr ghuluwwan — the man went to excess in the matter, when he went beyond its due limit.
3. ghalā bi-sahmihi ghalwan — he shot his arrow to its farthest range. He said, in a line of verse:
Like the arrow released from the hand of the one who sends it to its utmost reach.
4. taghālā al-rajulān — the two men vied with each other to outdo one another in that; taghālā is the reciprocal form of it.
5. ghalwa — every distance shot at in such a contest is called a ghalwa.
6. ghalat al-dābba fī sayrihā ghalwan, wa-ightalat ightilā'an, wa-ghālat ghilā'an — the mount went at speed in its gait. Among their proverbs: "the running of seasoned, mature horses is ghilā'."
7. taghālā al-nabt — the plant grew tall and rose up.
8. taghālā laḥm al-dābba — the flesh of the mount grew full and prominent, when its coat receded from it, exposing the muscle beneath; and that only comes from strength, fatness, and excellence.
9. ghalat al-qidr taghlī ghalayānan — the pot boiled.
10. al-ghulawā' — going headlong and heedlessly on one's way. He said, in a line of verse:
She did not turn to look at her playmates ... and went on in her headlong impetuosity.

As for al-ghāliya, the perfume, it is possible that it too is from this, meaning it is of great price, costly. They say taghallaltu and taghallaytu, from al-ghāliya.
غم:
The letters ghayn and mīm are a single sound root indicating covering and closing over. You say: ghamamtu al-shayʾ aghummuhu, meaning I covered it.

1. al-ghamam — when the hair covers the nape and the forehead as it grows. One says: a man is aghamm, and a brow is ghammāʾ. He said, in a line of verse: do not marry, should time part us, one whose nape and face are covered with hair and not receding at the temples.
2. al-ghamām — plural of ghamāmah, cloud; its derivation is plain.
3. al-ghimāmah — the cloth tied over a she-camel's nose so that she cannot catch the scent on the wind. Some said: anything that stops up the nose is a ghimāmah.
4. ghumma al-hilāl — said when the new moon is not seen. In the hadith: "If it is obscured (ghumma) from you, then reckon for it" — meaning the crescent was covered from view.
5. yawmun ghamm, laylatun ghammah — said of a day or a night that is dark and heavy.
6. ghammahu al-amr yaghummuhu ghamman — the matter weighed on him; it is something well known that settles over the heart.

As for al-ghamghamah, it follows the pattern of the imitative words — it is the sound bulls make when startled, and warriors make in the clash of battle. We have already said that such imitative words scarcely follow any settled pattern.
غمج: The letters ghayn, mīm, and jīm are a single root indicating movement, a coming and a going. The weaned young camel is called ghamij: it moves back and forth [yataghāmaju] between its mother's flanks, coming and going. They say of a man whose character is unsteady: ghamaja. Al-ghamaj is the drinking of water, which is close in derivation to the first.
غمد:
The letters ghayn, mīm, and dāl are a single sound root, indicating covering and concealment.

1. al-ghimd, for the sword — its sheath, its covering. One says: ghamadtuhu aghmiduhu ghamdan.
2. taghammadahu Allāhu bi-raḥmatih — God enveloped him in His mercy, as though He covered him with it.
3. taghammadtu fulānan — I placed him beneath me until I had covered him over.

The attributive to Ghāmid is Ghāmidī; it is a tribe of Yemen, and its derivation is from what we have mentioned.
غمر:
The letters ghayn, mīm and rā' are a sound root indicating covering and concealing, with some measure of severity in it.

1. al-ghamr — abundant water, called so because it covers over what lies beneath it. From this a horse is called ghamr, abundant in its running, its running likened in abundance to the ghamr-water.
2. ghamr — a generous, open-handed man, ghamr al-ridā', ample of cloak. Kuthayyir said:
Ample of cloak, when he smiles laughing ... the necks of wealth become bound fast by his laughter.
3. al-ghamra — absorption in vanity and idle amusement, called ghamra because it is a thing that veils the truth from its owner's sight.
4. ghamarāt al-mawt — the hardships of death that overwhelm one. Every hardship is a ghamra, so called because it overwhelms. A line says:
The ghamarāt, and then they clear away.
5. al-ghamīr — green plant growth which the dry, withered growth covers over. This confirms the same reasoning.
6. ghimār al-nās — the press and crush of people, so called because some cover over others; dakhala fī ghimāri al-nās, he entered the throng of people.
7. mughāmir — one who throws himself into affairs, as though he falls into matters that engulf him so that he cannot find a way clear of them.
8. al-ghumr — one with no experience of affairs, as though such things were hidden from him. A line says:
Patience, and forbearance, and waiting for what tomorrow brings them ... I am not the weary one, nor the feeble, untried one.
9. al-ghimr — rancour held in the breast, called so because the breast folds itself over it; one says ghamira 'alayhi ṣadruhu, his breast harboured rancour against him.
10. al-ghimr — thirst, likened to al-ghimr that is rancour, plural al-aghmār. A line says:
Until, when the thirsty ones had drunk their fill.
11. ghamaru al-laḥm — the smell that stays on the hand from meat, as though it covers the hand.

As for al-ghumar, the small drinking-cup, it is not unlikely that it belongs to this same reasoning, as though a small amount of water fills it up; or it may stand outside that root as an exception. A line says:
A cut of the shoulder is enough for him, when he comes upon it, of the roasted meat, and the small cup is enough for his drink.
غمز:
The letters ghayn, mīm and zāʾ are a sound root, and it is like poking at a thing with something, then it is used figuratively. From this: ghamaztu al-shayʾ bi-yadī ghamzan — I poked the thing with my hand.
1. Then one says ghamaza, when he finds fault and speaks of someone unfavourably. Al-maghāmiz — faults.
2. fī ʿaql fulānin ghamīza — in so-and-so's mind there is a weakness, as though it can be taken advantage of.
3. Used figuratively: ghamaza bi-jafnihi — he winked, made a sign with his eyelid.
4. From this: ghamaza al-dābba min rijlihi — the mount favoured its leg [went lame], as though it were poking the ground with its leg.
غمس:
The letters ghayn, mīm, and sīn are a single sound root, indicating the covering of a thing. One says: ghamastu al-thawb wal-yad fī al-mā', I dipped the garment and the hand in water, when you have submerged it in it. In the hadith: "When one of you wakes from his sleep, let him not dip his hand into the vessel."

1. al-ghamīr — fresh green growth: when it lies hidden beneath dry, dead grass, it is called al-ghamīs.
2. al-ghamīs — [also, from the chapter] a small watercourse between the gathering-places of trees.
3. al-mughāmasa — a man's throwing of himself into the thick of war.
4. yamīn ghamūs — an oath. Some said its meaning is that it plunges its swearer into sin; others said al-ghamūs is the one that pierces through. The two meanings, though they differ, share one derivation, because when a thing pierces through it has submerged itself. He said, in a line of verse:
Then I finished him off and gave him relief ... with a piercing oath, or a gashing blow.
5. ghamūs — said also of a severe matter that overwhelms a person with its severity. He said, in a line of verse:
Whenever you come to us or meet us in our lands ... you will find our affair sharp and overwhelming.
غمص:
The letters ghayn, mīm, and ṣād are a small root indicating contempt. One says: ghamaṣtu al-shay', I held the thing in contempt, when you have scorned it. In the hadith: "That is only from one who holds people in contempt," meaning he scorned them.

1. al-ghamaṣ — a discharge in the eye, like al-ramaṣ.
2. al-shi'rā al-ghumayṣā' — [the lesser Sirius], as though it has not the brightness of al-'abūr, the greater one, so it is called al-ghumayṣā', like an eye that has ghamaṣ in it.
غمض:
The letters ghayn, mīm and ḍād are a sound root indicating a sinking-down in a thing and a closing-in upon itself. Al-ghamḍ — what is low-lying of the ground, plural ghumūḍ.
1. ghamaḍa al-shayʾ min al-ʿilm wa-ghayrihi — a matter of knowledge or otherwise became obscure [ghāmiḍ]. dārun ghāmiḍa — a house, when it does not stand out openly onto the road.
2. nasabun ghāmiḍ — an obscure lineage, not known.
3. ghammaḍa ʿaynahu and aghmaḍahā mean the same, and this follows the pattern of the root.
4. mā dhuqtu ghumḍan min al-nawm wa-lā ghimāḍan — I did not taste a wink of sleep, meaning as much as it takes for the eye to close.
5. aghmiḍ lī fīmā biʿtanī — close your eye for me [overlook it] in what you sold me — as though you want more from him because of its poor quality, and a reduction in its price. This too is from the closing of the eye, meaning: leave it, as if you did not see it.
6. al-mughammiḍāt — the sins a man commits while knowing them, but he closes his eyes over them, as if he had not seen them.
7. ghummiḍat al-nāqa — the she-camel, when turned back from the watering-trough, pressed on against the one driving her off, with her eyes closed, and so reached the water. Abū al-Najm said, in a line of verse: "Closing her eyes [al-taghmīḍ] drives her forward, if she is not let go."
8. aghmaḍat ḥadd al-sayf — she thinned the sword's edge, as if, because of its thinness, she had hidden it from sight.
غمط: The letters ghayn, mīm, and ṭā' are a single word. Ghamaṭa al-ni'ma — he held the blessing in contempt. Ghamaṭa al-nās — he held people in contempt. As for their saying, aghmaṭat 'alayhi al-ḥummā, meaning the fever clung to him and persisted, that is not from this: the mīm in it stands in for a bā', the origin being aghbaṭat, which has already been mentioned.
غمق: The letters ghayn, mīm, and qāf are a single word, al-ghamaq: an abundance of dew. One says: arḍ ghamiqa, moist land; nabāt ghamaq, moist plant; layla ghamiqa, a damp night.
غمل:
The letters ghayn, mīm, and lām are a small root indicating narrowness in a thing, and obscurity. What is narrow among valleys is called ghumlūl.

1. ghamaltu al-adīm — derived from this: I wrapped the hide [ghamamtuhu], so that its wool would loosen and come away from it. It is then called ghamīl.
2. al-ghumlūl — anything gathered close together — of trees, or cloud, or darkness — until even a nook or corner is called a ghumlūl.

And God knows best what is correct.
غمن: The letters ghayn, mīm, and nūn are a single word, not to be generalized upon. They say: ghamantu al-jild, meaning I softened the hide, when you have softened it; it is then ghamīn.
غمي:
The letters ghayn, mīm, and the weak letter indicate covering and veiling.

1. ghamaytu al-bayt — I roofed the house, when you have covered it with a roof; the roof is ghimā'.
2. ughmiya 'alā al-marīḍ, fahuwa mughman 'alayhi — the sick person was overcome by unconsciousness, when a covering came over him.
غن:
The letters ghayn and nūn are a small but sound root; it indicates a sound that seems unclear, either because it is mixed with others, or because of some condition accompanying it.

1. qaryah ghannāʾ — said of a village, meaning the massed sound of its people's voices and the mingling of their clamour.
2. wādin aghann — a valley thick with tangled growth, where you see the wind moving through it with a humming sound; that comes from the abundance of flies in it.
3. al-ghunnah in an aghann man — the way his speech comes out as if through his nose.
غنج: The letters ghayn, nūn, and jīm are a single word, al-ghunj: coy allure and flirtatious manner.
غنظ:
The letters ghayn, nūn, and ẓā' are a single word. They say: al-ghanẓ is a persistent, clinging worry. Ghanaẓahu al-amr yaghniẓuhu, the matter oppressed him with worry. He said, in a line of verse:
I have indeed seen horsemen from our people ... who oppressed you as the locust of al-'ayyār oppresses.
غنم: The letters ghayn, nūn and mīm are one sound root pointing to the gaining of a thing that was not owned before; then it is used particularly for what is taken of the property of the idolaters by force and mastery. God, exalted be He, said: {and know that whatever you take as spoil, a fifth of it belongs to God and to the Messenger} [al-Anfāl: 41]. And they say ghunāmāka an tafʿala kadhā — that is, your utmost, and the thing you count as your prize. And Ghanm is a tribe. And perhaps the derivation of al-ghanam, sheep and goats, is from this, and that is not far-fetched.
غني:
The letters ghayn, nūn and the weak letter are two sound roots: one of them points to sufficiency, and the other is a sound.

The first is al-ghinā, wealth. One says ghaniya yaghnā ghinan. And al-ghanā', with a on the ghayn and with lengthening, is sufficiency. One says: so-and-so does not give the ghanā' of so-and-so — that is, he does not suffice as the other suffices. And ghaniya ʿan kadhā, so he is ghānin, free of need of it. And ghaniya al-qawm fī dārihim — they stayed there, as though they had made do with it. And their maghānī are their dwellings. And al-ghāniya is the woman. Some people said: its sense is that she has made do with her parents' home. And others said: she has made do with her husband. And it is said: she has made do with her beauty and needs no jewellery. Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
But he takes no game when he shoots at her, and an ungrateful ghāniya is not to be caught.
And al-ghunyān is wealth. Qays said, in a line of verse:
Has ʿAmra's self-sufficiency grown earnest in her, so that she forsakes us — or is her case our case?
And one says taghannaytu bi-kadhā, and taghānaytu bihi, when you make do with it and need nothing else. Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
And I was a man for a time in Iraq, chaste in my lodging, long in making do.
And he said about making do with one another, in a line of verse:
Each of us can do without his brother while he lives; and when we are dead we shall do without one another still more.

And the other root is al-ghinā', singing, which is of sound. And al-ughniya is one kind of singing.
غهب:
The letters ghayn, hā', and bā' are a sound root indicating darkness and a lack of light, and it is then used figuratively.

1. al-ghayhab — darkness. The horse that is black, intensely dark, is also called ghayhab.
2. ghahab — used figuratively for heedlessness of a thing. One says: ghahiba 'anhu, he was heedless of it, when he neglected it.
غوث: The letters ghayn, wāw and thā' are a single word: al-ghawth, from al-ighātha — which is rescue and aid in time of hardship. And Ghawth is also the name of a tribe.
غوج: The letters ghayn, wāw, and jīm are a single word: it is al-faras al-ghawj, the horse broad in the chest. And sometimes they called anything supple a ghawj.
غود:
The letters ghayn, wāw, and dāl are a small root indicating the suppleness of a thing and its bending.

1. al-aghyad — the drowsy one whose neck leans to one side; the plural is ghīd.
2. al-ghaydā' — the soft, delicate young woman, as though she sways.

The verbal noun is al-ghayad.
غور:
The letters ghayn, wāw and rā' are two sound roots: one is a lowness in a thing, a sinking and settling down; the other root is boldness in seizing wealth by force or in a raid.

The first: their calling the bottom of a thing its ghawr. One says ghāra al-mā'u ghawran, the water sank away, and ghārat 'aynuhu ghu'ūran, his eye sank in. God, exalted is He, said: {Say, have you considered — if your water should sink away} [al-Mulk: 30]. One says ghārati al-shamsu ghiyāran, the sun set. A poet of Hudhayl said:
Is time anything but a night and its day ... and but the sun's rising, then its setting?
Al-ghawr is Tihāma and what borders the Yemen, so named because it is the opposite of Najd, and Najd is the raised part of the land. One says ghāra al-rajulu, when he went down into the ghawr, and aghāra likewise. A line says:
A prophet who sees what you do not see, whose fame ... has spread, by my life, through the lowlands and the highlands of the land.
One says ghawwara al-rajulu, when he stopped for the midday rest, as though he had come down into a low place, for they rarely do so anywhere else. Ghawr al-qurḥa, the depth of a sore, is from this too.

The other root: al-ighāra, raiding. One says aghāra banū fulānin 'alā banī fulānin ighāratan wa-ghāratan, so-and-so's people raided so-and-so's people. Ighārat al-tha'lab, the fox's dashing run, is from this as well.
غوص: The letters ghayn, wāw and ṣād are a sound root indicating a plunging into something that goes down deep. From this: al-ghawṣ, going under water. One who plunges into a thing is ghā'iṣ. Ghāṣa 'alā al-'ilmi al-ghāmiḍ, he dived into obscure knowledge until he drew it out.
غوط: The letters ghayn, wāw and ṭā' are a sound root indicating a settling low and a hollowing. From this: al-ghā'iṭ, low-lying ground, plural ghīṭān and aghwāṭ. Ghūṭat Dimashq, the Ghouta of Damascus, is said to be named from this, as though it were a sunken tract of land. Sometimes they say inghāṭa al-'ūd, when a stick bends — and when it bends it becomes lower, so the underlying pattern holds.
غول:
The letters ghayn, wāw and lām are a sound root indicating deception, and seizing from where it is not perceived. One says: ghālahu yaghūluhu — it seized him from where he did not perceive.
1. al-ghawl — the far stretch of open desert, because it seizes whoever passes through it. A poet said: "By it she stretched forth, through the far reach [ghawl] of every mile."
2. al-ghūl, one of the saʿālī (desert demons), so named because it seizes its victims.
3. al-ghīla — the act of ambush-killing; the yāʾ in it was originally a wāw.
4. al-mighwal — a slender sword with a blunt back edge; I think it is called mighwal because it is kept concealed in a sheath so that what is in it is not known. God knows best.
غوي:
The letters ghayn, wāw and the weak letter after them are two roots: one of them points to the opposite of right guidance and to a matter going dark, and the other to corruption in a thing.

The first is al-ghayy, and it is the opposite of right guidance, and ignorance of a matter, and plunging headlong into falsehood. One says ghawā yaghwī ghayyan.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Whoever meets with good, people praise his conduct; and whoever goes astray will not lack someone to blame him for his straying.

That, in our view, is derived from al-ghayāya, which is the dust and the darkness that cover a man over, as though the one gone astray had been covered by something with which he cannot see the way of truth. And one says taghāyā al-qawmu fawqa ra'si fulānin bi-l-suyūf — the people crowded thick over his head with swords — as though they shaded him with them. And one says the people fell into an aghwiyya, that is, a calamity and a dark affair. And al-taghāwī is gathering together, and that never happens on the way of right guidance. And al-mughawwāt is the hunter's pit, and the plural is mughawwayāt. In the hadith: "they love to be hunters' pits" — what is meant is that they hoard wealth for themselves, like the hunter who catches game.

As for al-ghāya, it is the banner, and it was named so because it shades whoever is under it.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
I passed the night in her company and by a wine-seller's flag; I came when it was raised, and its wine was dear.

Then the end of a thing was called a ghāya. And this is of what is carried over from something else: it was called ghāya only from the ghāya of war, which is the banner, because one comes to a stop at it as a people go back to their banner in war.

The other root: their saying ghawiya al-faṣīl, when the young camel drinks too much milk and his insides go bad. And the verbal noun is al-ghawā.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
One with folded flanks, whose young one neither robs her of her milk nor lies dead of a bellyful.
غي: The letters ghayn and a doubled yāʾ are a sound root indicating one thing casting its shade over another. In the hadith: "al-Baqarah and Āl ʿImrān will come on the Day of Resurrection as if they were two clouds — or — two shade-canopies (ghayāyatān)." The plural is ghayāyāt. Labīd said, in a line of verse: then I let myself down upon him, on my way back, while on the ground lay the shade-shadows of the evening twilight.
غيب: The letters ghayn, yā' and bā' are a sound root pointing to a thing's being veiled from the eyes; then other things are measured on it. Of that is al-ghayb: what is hidden, of what none knows but God. And one says ghābat al-shamsu taghību ghaybatan and ghuyūban and ghayban - the sun set. And a man was absent from his town. And aghābat al-mar'a, so she is mughība, when her husband is away. And we fell into a ghayba and a ghayāba, that is, a dip in the ground in which one is hidden. God - exalted - said, in the story of Joseph, peace be upon him: {and cast him into the depth of the well} [Yūsuf: 10]. And al-ghāba is a thicket, the plural being ghābāt and ghāb. It was so named because one is hidden in it. And al-ghība, speaking ill of people, is from this, because it is only said behind a man's back.
غيث: The letters ghayn, yā' and thā' are a sound root: it is the life-giving rain that falls from the sky. One says jādanā ghaythun, rain came generously to us; hādhihi arḍun maghītha wa-maghyūtha, this is land that has had rain. Ghithnā means the rain fell on us. Dhū al-Rumma said: "I never saw anyone more eloquent than the slave-woman of the family of so-and-so. I said to her, how has the rain been with you? She said: ghithnā mā shīnā" (we were rained on as much as we wished).
غير:
The letters ghayn, yā' and rā' are two sound roots: one of them points to well-being, setting right and benefit, and the other to two things being different.

The first is al-ghīra, the food supply brought home, by which the welfare of a household stands. One says ghirtu ahlī ghīratan wa-ghiyāran — that is, I brought them provisions. And ghārahum Allāh, exalted be He, with rain — yaghīruhum and yaghūruhum — that is, He set their affair right and benefited them. And one says mā yaghīruka kadhā — what does such a thing profit you?

A poet said, in a line of verse:
What does their wailing profit the two daughters of Ribʿ? They do not sleep, and no misery to the one who slept.

And from this chapter is al-ghayra, a man's jealousy over his womenfolk. You say ghirtu ʿalā ahlī ghayratan. In our view this belongs to the chapter, because it is a setting right and a benefit.

The other root is our saying hādhā al-shay'u ghayru dhāka — this thing is other than that, that is, it is apart from it and its opposite. And from this chapter is exception by ghayr: you say ʿasharatun ghayra wāḥidin — ten less one — the one not being of the ten. From it is His saying, exalted be He: {ṣirāṭa alladhīna anʿamta ʿalayhim ghayri al-maghḍūbi ʿalayhim wa-lā al-ḍāllīn} — the path of those You have favoured, not of those who earned anger, nor of those who go astray [al-Fātiḥa: 7].

As for the blood-money, it is called al-ghiyar. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, said to a man who sought retaliation for a kinsman of his who had been killed: «Will you not take the ghiyar?» — meaning, will you not accept the blood-money? This may be from the first root, because in blood-money there is a setting right for the killer, and a sparing of him and of his blood. And it may be from the second root, because it was retaliation and it was changed to blood-money, that is, something other than retaliation was taken, something apart from it.

He said, of the ghiyar, in a line of verse:
We shall surely cut off your noses with our own hands, sons of Umayma, if you do not accept the blood-money.
غيس: The letters ghayn, yā', and sīn — they say: ghaysān al-shabāb is the keenness and prime vigor of youth.
غيض:
The letters ghayn, yā' and ḍād are a small root indicating a decrease in a thing, and obscurity, and scantiness. One says ghāḍa al-mā'u yaghīḍu, the opposite of overflowing — meaning it receded. Ghīḍa, when something else caused it to decrease. God, Most High, said: {and the water was made to subside} [Hūd: 44].

As for the obscurity sense: al-ghayḍah, a thicket, named for its density, because someone walking within it can hardly be seen.
غيظ:
The letters ghayn, yā' and ẓā' are a small root containing a single word, pointing to a distress that comes upon a man from someone else. One says *ghāẓanī yaghīẓunī* — he angered me. And *qad ghiẓtanī yā hādhā* — you have angered me, you there. And a man is *ghā'iẓ* and *ghayyāẓ*. A poet said, in a line of verse:
You were named Ghayyāẓ, the enrager, yet you do not enrage an enemy — it is the friend you enrage.
غيف:
The letters ghayn, yāʾ and fāʾ are a small but sound root, indicating leaning, swaying, and turning away from a thing.

1. taghayyafa — to sway, as when a tree sways its branches right and left.
2. ghayyafa (said of a man) — to be cowardly and turn away from the course of battle.

Al-Qutāmī said, in a line of verse:
So they turn away in cowardice, while we come back swiftly to the fray.
غيق: The letters ghayn, yāʾ and qāf are a single word. They say: ghayyaqa fī raʾyihi taghyīqan — his opinion became confused, mixed up in itself.
غيل:
The letters ghayn, yāʾ and lām are two sound roots: one indicates a gathering, the other a kind of nursing.

1. al-ghīl — trees clustered and tangled together. It is not unlikely that the origin of this word is a wāw, going back to ghālahu yaghūluhu (it destroyed him, overtook him).
2. al-ghayl — the full, well-watered forearm. Someone said, in a line of verse:
A fair woman with two full forearms.
3. al-ghayl — flowing water.

The other origin: a man has intercourse with his wife while she is nursing — this act is called al-ghīla.
In the hadith: "I had considered forbidding al-ghīla." Someone said, in a line of verse:
A woman like you, pregnant, have I visited by night, and a nursing one — I distracted her from an amulet-wearing child conceived through ghīla.
غيم:
The letters ghayn, yāʾ and mīm are a word indicating one thing covering another.

1. al-ghaym — cloud, well known. One says: ghāmat al-samāʾ, taghayyamat, aghāmat — the sky clouded over.
2. al-ghaym — thirst and heat of the belly, because it is something that comes over the heart.
غين:
The letters ghayn, yāʾ and nūn are close to the one before it [ghaym].

1. al-ghayn — cloud. Someone said, in a line of verse:
As if I were between the wing-feathers of an eagle that had struck a dove, on a cloudy day.
2. al-ghayn — thirst.
3. ghīna ʿalā qalbihi — said of the heart, as though something had come over and covered it. In the hadith: "Truly a covering (yughānu) comes over my heart."
4. shajaratun ghaynāʾ — a tree thick with leaves, its branches tangled; plural ghīn.
5. al-ghayna — said to be the meadow.

The reasoning behind all of this is one and the same. God knows best.
فأ:
The letters fā' and hamza, with a weak letter between them, are words indicating returning.

1. fā'a al-fay' — one says this when the shadow returns from the western side to the eastern side. Every return is a fay'. God, Exalted is He, said: {until it returns to the command of God} [al-Ḥujurāt: 9], meaning: returns. A poet said, in a line of verse:
   She made for the spring at Ḍārij, over which the shade returns, its green scum standing thick.
   From this one says: fayya'at al-shajara, the tree cast its returning shade, and tafayya'tu anā fī fay'ihā, I sat in its shade. And a woman tufayyi'u sha'rahā, when she tosses her head out of pride. And it is said her tafayyu' is her turning and bending for her husband. The reasoning is one throughout all of it.
2. al-fay' — spoils taken from the polytheists, which God, Exalted is He, restored (afā'ahā) to them. God, Glorified is He, said: {what God restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns} [al-Ḥashr: 7]. And one says: istafa'tu hādhā al-māl, meaning: I took it as fay'. And so-and-so is quick to fay' — to return — from his anger, and quick to al-fī'a.

As for their saying, yā fay'a mālī, they say it is a word of regret. This, to me, is among the sayings whose true meaning has been lost along with those who understood it well. And he cited:
   O return of my wealth — whoever lives long, time's passing and its turning will wear him down.
فأد:
The letters fā', alif and dāl are a sound root pointing to fever and fierce heat.

From this: fa'adtu al-laḥm — I roasted the meat. And this is fa'īd, that is, roasted. Al-mif'ad is the roasting spit. Al-mufta'ad is the place in which roasting is done.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
As though there were, jutting out from the side of his flank, the spit of a drinking party that they forgot at a roasting place.

And of what belongs to the analogy of this section in our view: al-fu'ād, the heart, so named for its heat. Al-fa'd is the verbal noun of fa'adtuhu — when you strike a man's heart. And they say fa'adtu al-malla — when I baked bread in the hot ashes.
فأر: The letters fā', alif, rā' — and they call the alif in it a hamza. Al-fa'r [mice] is well known; one says from it: makānun fa'ir, a place with many mice. And fa'rat al-misk [the musk-pod] is well known, and it is named by way of resemblance. Likewise fa'rat al-baʿīr, which is a wind that gathers in the camel's fetlock, and which disperses when it walks.
فأس: The letters fā', alif, sīn are one word, and it is used as a metaphor. Al-fa's [the axe] is well known; its counted plural is af'us, and its plural is fu'ūs. And it is used as a metaphor: one says for the back of the crown of the head, fa's. And fa's al-lijām is the upright iron piece in the bit, at the palate.
فأل: The letters fā', alif, lām. Al-fa'l is that by which an omen is taken.
فأم:
The letters fā', alif, mīm are a sound root indicating width in a thing, and abundance.

1. al-fi'ām — for the abundance sense: a crowd of people.
2. al-fi'ām — for the width sense: a cushioned pad placed in the camel litter, and its plural is fu'ūm, on the pattern fuʿul.
3. One says of a camel, when its withers become full of fat: qad fu'ima ḥārikuhu, its withers have filled out, and it is mufa'm.
4. al-mufa'm, among men, is the one broad in the belly. He said, in a line of verse:
They took the waist of the sand dune, then crossed it, each mount fresh from the smith's hand and broad-chested.
فأو:
The letters fā', alif, wāw are a sound root indicating a splitting open in a thing. One says: fa'awtu ra'sahu bi-al-sayfi fa'wan, I split his head open with the sword. And al-fa'w is the gap between two mountains. He said, in a line of verse:
Until the gap had opened over their necks at dawn, they had drunk a little, neither fully quenched nor left maddened by thirst.
فت:
The letters fā' and tā' are a word indicating the crumbling and breaking of a thing. One says: fatattu al-shay' afuttu fattan, so it is mafttūt and fatīt. And al-futta is what is crumbled and placed beneath the fire-drill. And fatta fī 'aḍudihi is said when one has wronged him, as though he has crumbled away something from his arm.

Deviating from this root is al-fatfata: for camels to drink without being satisfied.
فتح:
The letters fā', tā' and ḥā' are a sound root pointing to the opposite of shutting.

One says fataḥtu al-bāb wa-ghayrahu fatḥan - I opened the door and other than it. Then all the rest of what is in this building of letters is carried upon this. Al-fatḥ and al-fitāḥa are judging between people. And God - exalted is He - is al-Fātiḥ, that is, the Judge. The poet said of al-fitāḥa, in a line of verse:
Take word to the Banū ʿAwf, a message, that I have no need of your judging.

Al-fatḥ is water that comes out from a spring or from elsewhere. And al-fatḥ is victory and being given the upper hand. Istaftaḥtu - I sought victory. In the hadith: "That he - may God bless him and grant him peace - used to seek victory through the poor among the Emigrants and the Helpers." Fawātiḥ al-Qur'an are the openings of the sūras. And bāb futuḥ - a door wide and standing open.
فتخ:
The letters fā', tā', khā' are a sound root indicating softness in a thing.

1. al-fatakh — softness in a bird's wing. ʿUqābun fatkhā'u, an eagle whose wing has gone slack in its flight.
2. fatakha aṣābiʿa rijlihi — he loosened the toes of his foot, when sitting. And in the hadith: "He, peace be upon him, when he prostrated, would hold his upper arms away from his sides, and loosen the toes of his feet."
3. it is said that al-fatakh is the broadness of the shoulder and the foot.

And among what diverges from this root: al-fatakh, plural of fatakha, which is like a ring, worn the way a signet ring is worn. He said:
My fatakh-rings fall from it into my sleeve.
فتر:
The letters fāʾ, tāʾ, and rāʾ are a sound root pointing to a weakness in a thing. From this: fatara al-shayʾu yafturu futūran, the thing weakened. Al-ṭarf al-fātir is a glance that is not sharp or piercing. fattartu al-shayʾa and aftartuhu, I weakened the thing. God Most High said: {it is not eased for them} [al-Zukhruf: 75], meaning it is not lessened.

Among what falls outside this root: al-fitr is the span between the tip of the thumb and the tip of the forefinger when the two are opened out. And Fitr is a woman's name, in his words, the line cut off before it reaches us:
Have you cut the cord of affection from Fitr ...
فتش: The letters fā', tā', shīn are one word indicating a searching for something. You say fatashtu fatshan, and fattashtu tafṭīshan.
فتق:
The letters fāʾ, tāʾ and qāf are a sound root indicating an opening in a thing. From this: fataqtu al-shayʾa fatqan — I split the thing open.
1. al-fatq — the splitting of the community's unity.
2. al-fatq — the dawn.
3. aʿwām al-fataq — years of plenty. A poet said: "She did not hope for milk after the years of plenty [al-fataq]."
4. aftaqa al-qamar — the moon, when it met a break in the clouds and rose out through it. aftaqa al-qawm — the people, when the clouds broke open from over them.
5. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: jamalun fatīq — a camel, when it grew so fat it seemed to burst. One says: fatiqa yaftaqu fataqan.
6. al-faytaq — the carpenter, in al-Aʿshā's saying, in a line of verse: "At the door, a carpenter [faytaq]."
فتك:
The letters fā', tā', kāf are a word indicating the opposite of piety and right conduct.

1. al-fatk, also al-fitk — treachery. One says fataka bihi, he assassinated him by treachery. And in the hadith: "Faith is a restraint on treachery." The poet said:
No bride-price dearer than ʿAlī's, however dear it grows, and no assassination but falls short of the assassination of Ibn Muljam.
فتل:
The letters fāʾ, tāʾ, and lām are a sound root pointing to the twisting of a thing. From this: fataltu al-ḥabla, I twisted the rope, and so with other things. Al-fatīl is what is in the slit of a date-stone, as though it had been twisted. A poet said, in a line of verse:
He gathers the army of thousands and goes to war, then takes from the enemy no more than a thread-twist (fatīlan) — that is, next to nothing.
It is also said al-fatīl is what is twisted between the two fingers. Al-fatal is the divergence of the two forearms from the sides of the camel, as though they had been bent and twisted until warped. Ṭarafa said:
She has two forearms turned outward, as though she were passing by Salmā, a water-carrier heavily laden, straining hard.
Among their proverbs: "So-and-so twists (yaftilu) around so-and-so's peak (dhirwa)," meaning he circles behind him with deceit.
فتن:
The letters fā', tā' and nūn are a sound root pointing to trial and testing. Of that is al-fitna. One says fatantu aftinu fatnan. And fatantu al-dhahaba bi-l-nār, when you test the gold by fire. And it is maftūn and fatīn, tested. And al-fattān is Satan. And one says fatanahu and aftanahu. Al-Aṣma'ī denied aftana. And they recited, for aftana, in a line of verse:
If she has tempted me, yesterday she tempted Sa'īd, and he woke hating every Muslim.
And one says qalb fātin, that is, a heart that is tempted. He said, in a line of verse:
Soft of speech, slow to rise - my heart has become smitten with him.
Al-Khalīl said: al-fatn is burning. And a thing fatīn is a thing burnt. And a black stony tract is called fatīn, as though its stones were burnt.

And among what strays from this root is al-fitān: the leather of the saddle. And their saying al-'ayshu fitnān, that is, life is of two colours. And these may be carried back onto the measure of the root, because he says:
And life is of two sorts, sweet and bitter -
and it is possible for the son of Adam to be tested with each one of them.
فتى:
The letters fā', tā', and the weak letter are two roots: one indicates freshness and newness, and the other indicates making a ruling clear.

1. al-fatiyy — the fresh, young one, of camels.
2. al-fatā — of people, one of al-fityān [young men].
3. al-fatā' — youthfulness. One says fatan bayyinu al-fatā', a young man of evident youth. He said, in a line of verse:
If the young man lives two hundred years, then cheerfulness and youth have gone.

The other root is al-futyā. One says aftā al-faqīhu fī al-mas'alati, when the jurist made its ruling clear. And istaftaytu, when you asked about the ruling. God, exalted, said: {They ask you for a ruling; say: God gives you the ruling concerning al-kalāla} [al-Nisā': 176]. And from it one says fatwā and futyā.

And if it takes the hamza, it falls outside both roots. One says mā fati'tu and fata'tu adhkuruhu, meaning I have not ceased. God, exalted, said: {They said, by God, you will not cease [tafta'u] remembering Joseph} [Yūsuf: 85], meaning you will not stop remembering.
فث:
The letters fā' and thā' are words indicating the breaking of a thing, or its scattering, or its uprooting.

1. faththa jullatahu — their saying, meaning: he scattered his palm-leaf basket.
2. infatha al-rajulu min hammin aṣābahu — a man is said to do this from a worry that struck him, meaning: he broke down.
3. al-fathth — said to be the young palm-shoot pulled up from its root.
4. al-fathth — from this chapter: the seeds of the colocynth, because they are scattered.
فثأ:
The letters fā', thā' and hamza indicate the stilling of something that is boiling and seething. One says: fatha'tu l-qidr, meaning I stilled it from its boiling. He said, in a line of verse:
And we still it away from us when its heat boils over.
One also says: ʿadā ḥattā afthaʾa, meaning he ran until he grew exhausted.
فثج: The letters fā', thā', jīm are a small root indicating a cutting off in a thing, of water or otherwise. The man ran until afthaja, meaning he grew exhausted. And one says: bi'run lā tuftathaju, a well that is not drawn dry; and it was said this is for the meaning we gave, so lā tuftathaju means its water does not cut off. And one says: fathajat al-nāqatu, when the she-camel failed to conceive.
فثر: The letters fā', thā', rā' are one word, and it is al-fāthūr, which is a table made of marble or the like. And they say, in some speech: hiya ʿalā fāthūrin wāḥidin, it is upon one fāthūr, as though he meant one spread carpet.
فج:
The letters fā' and jīm are a sound root, indicating opening and parting.

1. al-fajj — the wide road.
2. qaws fajjā' — a bow whose string stands apart from its body.

Al-fajaj is uglier than al-faḥaj. And from it: ḥāfir mufijj, meaning vaulted; when it is so, there is in its underside something like a hollow.

Deviating from this root is al-fijj: a thing not yet ripened that should be ripe.

And one further word deviates, reported by Ibn al-A'rābī: he said: afajja yufijju, when he hurried. And from it: rajul fajfāj, a man of much talk.
فجر:
The letters fā', jīm and rā' are a single root, and it is a thing opening up.

Of this is al-fajr, the dawn: the bursting open of the darkness to let the morning through. From it: infajara al-mā'u infijāran — the water burst out and opened up. And al-fujra is the place where water breaks open.

Then this grew common, until breaking out and opening up into acts of disobedience became fujūr, wickedness. For that reason lying is called fujūr. Then this grew common still, until everyone who swerves from the truth is called fājir; and with them everyone who swerves aside is fājir.

Labīd said, in a line of verse:
If you go forward, you meet a hard rough front of her; and if you hold back, the rump swerves aside.

Of this chapter is al-fajar, which is generosity and bursting open with good. And mafājir al-wādī are the places where the valley pours itself away; perhaps they were called mafājir because the water bursts open in them.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Beside the ʿalandā bushes, where the outpourings lay still.

And munfajar al-raml is a road running through the sand. And yawm al-fijār is a day of the Arabs on which what was sacred was violated.
فجس: The letters fā', jīm and sīn are a word, if it is sound. They say: al-fajs is pride and self-magnification. From it: tafajjasa, he became proud.
فجع: The letters fā', jīm and ʿayn are a single word, and it is al-fajīʿa, which is a calamity, a bereavement. One says: nazalat bi-fulānin fājiʿa, a calamity befell so-and-so. And tafajjaʿa, when he grieved for it.
فجل: The letters fā', jīm and lām are a word that is a plant. Some people said: fajila l-shay', the thing became thick and slack. And anything you widen, you have fajjaltahu.
فجم: The letters fā', jīm and mīm. Ibn Durayd claimed: tafajjama l-wādī and infajama, when the valley widened. And this is fujmat al-wādī, meaning its wide part.
فجن: The letters fā', jīm and nūn. They say: rue [the plant al-sadhāb] is called al-fayjan.
فجو:
The letters fāʾ, jīm and the weak letter indicate a wideness in a thing. Al-fajwa — the open space between two things.
1. qawsun fajwāʾ — a bow whose string stands clear away from its belly.
2. fajwat al-dār — the courtyard of the house.
3. al-fajā — the wide gap between a camel's two hocks.
And if it is given a hamza, you say: fajiʾanī al-amr, yafjaʾunī — the matter took me by surprise [a separate word].
فح:
The letters fā' and ḥā' are a single word: it is al-faḥīḥ, the hissing sound of the viper. He said:
   As though the chirping of the grain in its sack were the hissing of vipers, or the chirping of scorpions.
فحث: The letters fā', ḥā' and thā' are a single word. Al-faḥth is the inside, the belly. One says: mala'a afḥāthahu, meaning he filled his belly.
فحج: The letters fā', ḥā' and jīm are a single word, and it is al-faḥaj, which is the separation between the middles of the two shanks in a person or a beast. The descriptive form is afḥaj and faḥjā', plural fuḥj.
فحس: The letters fā', ḥā' and sīn. They say: al-faḥs is your licking a thing off your hand with your tongue.
فحش:
The letters fā', ḥā' and shīn are a word pointing to ugliness in a thing and to foulness.

Of this are al-fuḥsh, al-faḥshā' and al-fāḥisha — foul speech and the foul deed. They say: everything that goes beyond its proper measure is fāḥish, excessive; and that is said only of what is found repugnant. And afḥasha al-rajulu — the man spoke foully — and faḥasha likewise, and he is faḥḥāsh, foul-mouthed.

And they say: al-fāḥish is the miser. This is by extension, and miserliness is the ugliest of a man's qualities.

Ṭarafa said, in a line of verse:
I see death picking out the noble, and choosing the wealth of the tight-fisted miser.
فحص: The letters fā', ḥā' and ṣād are a sound root, and it is like searching for a thing. One says: faḥaṣtu ʿan al-amr faḥṣan, I searched into the matter. Ufḥūṣ al-qaṭā is the sandgrouse's nesting place in the ground, because it scrapes it out. And in the hadith: "faḥaṣū ʿan ru'ūsihim" — as if they left their heads like the sandgrouse's scraped-out nests, not having shaved them. And faḥaṣa l-maṭaru l-turāb, when the rain turned the soil over.
فحل:
The letters fā', ḥā' and lām are a sound root indicating maleness and strength.
1. al-faḥl — the stud-male of anything, the bold vigorous male. One says: afḥaltuhu faḥlan, when you give someone a stud-male to put among his camels. And faḥaltu ibilī, when I sent a stud-male among my camels. He said, in a line of verse:
We cover them with the white swords, scant of nature.
This is a proverb, meaning: we hamstring them with the swords — he is describing camels that were hamstrung with swords.
2. faḥl (as the name for a mat) — the mat woven from al-fuḥḥāl is called faḥl because it is made from it.
3. al-fuḥḥāl — the male palm-tree that pollinates the female palms, its plural faḥāḥīl.
4. faḥl faḥīl — noble, generous. He said, in a line of verse:
The choice young camels of Mundhir and Muḥarriq ... were their mothers, and their siring was noble.
5. al-faḥl (as a name for the star Suhayl) — the Arabs call Suhayl (Canopus) "al-faḥl", likening it to the stud-camel, because of its standing apart from the [other] stars — for the stud-camel, once he has covered the herd, withdraws from them.
6. imra'atun faḥlatun — by the same likeness, a sharp-tongued, forceful woman.
فحم:
The letters fā', ḥā' and mīm are two roots: one indicates blackness, the other indicates being cut off.
The first is al-faḥm, also said al-faḥam, which is well known [charcoal]. He said, in a line of verse:
Like the smith who stepped aside, blowing on the charcoal.
1. faḥḥama wajhuhu — when he blackened his face.
2. shaʿrun fāḥim — black hair.
3. faḥmat al-ʿishā' — the blackness of the dark at nightfall.
The other root: bakā l-ṣabiyyu ḥattā faḥum, the child cried until his voice was cut off from crying.
1. kallamtuhu ḥattā afḥamtuhu — I spoke to him until I silenced him.
2. shāʿirun mufḥam — a poet who has been cut off from composing verse.
فحو:
The letters fā', ḥā' and the weak letter are a single word.
1. al-faḥā — the seasoning of the cooking pot. One says: faḥḥi qidraka, season your pot.
2. faḥwā l-kalām — what becomes apparent to the understanding from within the folds of speech — like the scent of the seasoning appearing from the pot — the way a blow is understood from someone's cry of pain.
فخ:
The letters fā' and khā' are words that follow no single pattern.

1. al-fakhīkh — like snoring in sleep.
2. al-fakhkha — slackness in the two legs.
3. al-fakhkha — it is also said, a heavily built woman.
4. al-fakhkh — the trap for game, well known.
فخت: The letters fā', khā' and tā' are a word, and it is al-fakht; they say it is the light of the moon when it first appears. From it comes the derivation of al-fākhita [the turtle-dove], for its colour.
فخذ: The letters fā', khā' and dhāl are a single word, and it is al-fakhidh of a person, well known. It was then borrowed by extension, so one says al-fakhidh, with the khā' at rest, for a subdivision below the tribe and above the clan [al-baṭn], plural afkhādh.
فخر:
The letters fā', khā' and rā' are a sound root indicating greatness and long standing. From it, al-fakhr, boasting. They describe boasting as "the recounting of what is ancient" — also called al-fakhar. Abū Zayd said: fakhartu al-rajula 'alā ṣāḥibihi afkharuhu fakhran, I gave the man precedence over his companion in boasting, meaning I set him above him.

1. al-fakhīr — one who competes with you in boasting, on the pattern of al-khaṣīm, the disputant.
2. al-fikhkhīr — one who boasts a great deal.
3. al-fākhir — the fine, excellent thing.
4. al-tafakhkhur — self-aggrandizement.
5. nakhla fakhūr — a palm tree with a thick trunk and heavy fronds.
6. al-nāqa al-fakhūr — a she-camel with a large udder but little milk. So said Ibn Durayd.
7. al-fākhir — among unripe dates, the kind that grows large and has no stone.
8. faras fakhūr — said of a stallion when its member is large.

What falls outside this root: al-fakhkhār, pottery jars — well known.
فخل:
The letters fā', khā' and lām have nothing in them, except that Ibn Durayd claimed one says:
1. tafakhkhala l-rajul — when a man showed dignity and forbearance.
2. tafakhkhala, also — when he made himself ready and put on his finest clothes.
فخم: The letters fā', khā' and mīm are a sound root indicating weightiness and greatness. One says: manṭiqun fakhm, weighty, eloquent speech. And they say: al-fakhm among men is the one whose two cheeks are full of flesh.
فد:
The letters fā' and dāl are a sound root, indicating a sound and clamour. The Messenger of God, God bless him and his family and grant him peace, said: "Harshness and hard-heartedness are found among the faddādīn" — meaning their loud voices over their ploughing and their livestock. A poet said, in a line of verse:
   I was told my maternal uncles, the Banū Yazīd, wronged us, and they raised a clamour, fadīd, against us.

Deviating from this: al-fadfad, the level ground.
فدج:
The letters fā', dāl and jīm.
1. al-fawdaj — they say it is the [camel-borne] litter, al-hawdaj.
2. al-fawdaj — Al-Khalīl said it is a she-camel wide in the flanks.
3. shātun mufawdaja — a ewe whose two horns stand upright with their tips meeting.
فدح: The letters fā', dāl and ḥā' are a word. Fadaḥahu l-amr, when the matter weighed on him and burdened him — fadḥan. And it is amrun fādiḥ, a burdensome matter.
فدخ: The letters fā', dāl and khā' have nothing in them except an oddity of Ibn Durayd: fadakhtu l-shay', like shadakhtuhu, I crushed it.
فدر:
The letters fā', dāl and rā' are a sound root indicating cutting and being cut off.
1. al-fidra — the piece of meat. I do not know whether a verb was built from it or not.
2. fādir — they say: fadara l-faḥl, when the stud-male became incapable of mating, and he is fādir, so named because when he becomes incapable he is cut off [from that function]; the plural of fādir is fawādir. Ibn Durayd said this is among what is anomalous, a fāʿil form whose plural comes as fawāʿil.
3. al-mafdara — the place where the incapable wild goats [al-wuʿūl al-fudr] are found.
فدش: The letters fā', dāl and shīn have nothing before them except an oddity among the oddities of Ibn Durayd. He said: fadashtu l-shay', when I crushed it. And: fadashtu ra'sahu bi-l-ḥajar, I crushed his head with the stone.
فدع: The letters fā', dāl and ʿayn are a root with one word in it, and it is al-fadaʿ: a crookedness in the joints, as if they had shifted from their places. They say: every male ostrich is afdaʿ, because there is a deviation in its joints.
