And it is also said that al-fadaʿ is the turning of the palm toward its inner side; one says from it: fadiʿa yafdaʿu fadaʿan.
فدغ: The letters fā', dāl and ghayn. Ibn Durayd claimed that al-fadgh is crushing. He mentioned the hadith: "idhan tafdaghu Quraysh ra'sī" — "then Quraysh would crush my head" — and this is sound.
فدك: The letters fā', dāl and kāf are a single word, and it is Fadak: a town. And among the oddities of Ibn Durayd: fadaktu l-quṭn, I carded the cotton. He said it is a dialect of the Azd.
فدم:
The letters fā', dāl and mīm are a sound root indicating thickness, turbidity, heaviness, and scarcity of speech through a speech impediment.
1. ṣibghun mufaddam — a thick, saturated dye. This is what they say, from it.
2. al-rajul al-fadm — the man scant in speech through a speech impediment; he is bayyinu l-fudūma wa-l-fadāma. They said this is reasoned by the same analogy.
3. al-fidām — the cloth with which jugs are stoppered to filter what drink is in them. All of this is reasoned from it.
فدن: The letters fā', dāl and nūn are a single word, and it is al-fadan; they say it is the palace.
فدي:
The letters fā', dāl and the weak letter are two words very far apart from each other. The first is that a thing be put in the place of a thing as a protection for it, and the other is a kind of food.

The first is your saying fadaytuhu afdīhi — I ransomed him — as though you were shielding him with yourself or with something given in exchange for him. They say huwa fidā'uka; when you give the fā' an i, you lengthen the word, and when you give it an a, you shorten it, and one says huwa fadāka. A poet said, in a line of verse:
May my mother and my aunt be a ransom for your two feet, on the morning of al-Kulāb, when the hamstrings were being cut.

And he said, using the lengthened form, in a line of verse:
Gently now — all people are a ransom for you, and whatever I gather of wealth and of children.

One says tafādā min al-shay' when he keeps clear of it and draws aside from it. The origin of this word is what we have mentioned, al-tafādī: that people shield themselves one with another, as though a man makes his companion the ransom of himself. A poet said:
The thick-maned lions drew away from him, a real drawing away.

The other word is al-fadā', with a long ending, and it is the drying-floor for dates in the speech of 'Abd al-Qays; Ibn Durayd reported it. Abū 'Amr said: al-fadā' is a heap of food of barley and dates and the like. A poet said, in a line of verse:
As though their heaped grain, when they had stripped it bare and gone round about it, were an orphaned chick.
فذ: The letters fā' and dhāl are a single word, indicating being solitary and separate. From that: al-fadhdh, meaning the single one. One says: shāh mufidhdh, when it gives birth to only one; and if that is its habit, it is mifdhādh. One does not say nāqa mufidhdh, because a she-camel gives birth to only one in any case. And one says: tamr fadhdh, meaning scattered dates. And al-fadhdh is the first of the gambling arrows.
فذح: The letters fā', dhāl and ḥā'. Ibn Durayd mentioned: tafadhdhaḥat al-nāqa and infadhaḥat, when the she-camel spread her legs apart to urinate. And God knows best what is correct.
فر:
The letters fā' and rā' are three roots: the first is uncovering, and what is close to it of revealing a thing; the second is a kind of animal; and the third indicates lightness and rashness.

The first: their saying, farra 'an asnānihi, meaning: he examined its teeth, uncovering them. And iftarra al-insān, when a man smiled. He said, in a line of verse:
   He smiles at you, showing bright teeth, while another's are grimy and gap-toothed.

And they say, in proverbs: huwa al-jawādu 'aynuhu firāruhu, meaning: its very look tells you all you need, sparing you from examining it — as though the sense is that your looking at it spares you from having to farra it, that is, uncover and search its teeth. And they say: afarra al-muhr, when a colt nears the time its teeth are examined as a yearling. And afarrat al-ibil lil-ithnā', when camels shed their milk-teeth and grow their second teeth. And they say: furra fulānan 'ammā fī nafsihi, meaning: search him. And furra 'an al-amr: investigate it.

From this same reasoning, though far apart in meaning: al-firār, which is fleeing, the uncovering of oneself from a place; one says farra yafirru, and al-mafarr is the verbal noun. Al-mafarr is also the place one flees to. Al-farr is the people who flee; one says farr as the plural of fārr, just as ṣaḥb is the plural of ṣāḥib, and sharb the plural of shārib.

The second root: al-farīr, the young of a cow. And al-furār, from the young of goats, is said of one small in body, singular farīr, like rakhl (a lamb) and rukhāl (lambs), or ẓi'r (a wet-nurse) and ẓu'ār (wet-nurses).

The third: al-farfara, rashness and levity. One says: rajul farfār and imra'a farfāra. And al-farfāra is a kind of tree.
فرت: The letters fāʾ, rāʾ, and tāʾ are a single word, and it is al-māʾ al-furāt, sweet water. One says māʾun furāt, and miyāhun furāt, sweet waters.
فرث: The letters fāʾ, rāʾ and thāʾ are a small root indicating something crushed. One says faratha kabidahu — he crushed his liver. Al-farth — what is in the paunch. It is said figuratively: afratha fulānun aṣḥābahu — so-and-so, when he informed against his companions and cast them into calamity.
فرج:
The letters fā', rā' and jīm are a sound root pointing to an opening in a thing. From this is al-furja, the gap in a wall and in other things, the split. One says farajtuhu and farrajtuhu — I opened it. And they say that al-farja is the getting free from a care or a grief. The sense is one, but they distinguish between the two by the fatḥa. A poet said, in a line of verse:
How often souls fret at a matter which has a release like the untying of a hobble.

And al-farj is what is between the horse's legs. Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
She has a tail like the bride's train, with which she covers her farj from behind.

And al-furūj are the frontier gaps that lie between the places of fear; they were called furūj because they need watching and guarding. And it is said that the two frontiers from which fear is felt for Islam are the Turks and the Sudan. And every place of fear is a farj. And a bow furuj, when its two curved ends stand apart. They said: the man afraj is he whose buttocks do not meet; and a woman farjā'. And from it al-furuj: he who does not keep a secret, and al-firj is like it. And al-farij is he whose private part is never out of view. And al-farrūj is the tunic, and it was so named for the slit that is in it.

And of what strays from this root is al-mufraj. They said: he is the slain man whose killer is not known. And it is said he is the foundling who has no clientage to anyone and no lineage. And it is related in one report: "No mufraj is to be left in Islam" — with the jīm.
فرح:
The letters fā', rā' and ḥā' are two roots: one of them points to the opposite of sorrow, and the other is weighing down.

The first is al-faraḥ, gladness. One says fariḥa yafraḥu faraḥan, so he is fariḥ, glad. God, exalted be He, said:
{That is because you used to exult in the earth without right, and because you used to be insolent} [Ghāfir: 75]. And al-mifrāḥ, the man of much gladness, is the opposite of al-miḥzān, the man of much sorrow.

As for the other root, it is al-ifrāḥ, and it is weighing down. And his words, peace and blessing be upon him: "No one weighed down is to be left so in Islam" — they said: this is the man whom debt has weighed down.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
When you never cease discharging one trust and carrying another, the deposits have weighed you down.
فرخ:
The letters fā', rā' and khā' are one word, and it is reasoned from. al-farkh is the young of a bird. One says afrakha al-ṭā'ir, the bird brought forth its young.

1. afrakha al-rawʿ — the fright subsided, reasoned from the same sense.
2. li-yufrikh rawʿuka — let your fright hatch away: they said its meaning is, let your fright leave you and part from you, just as the chick emerges from the egg.
3. afrakha al-amr — the matter became clear after having been doubtful.
4. al-Furaykh — a craftsman who lived before Islam, to whom certain arrowheads or arrows are attributed.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And two well-trimmed shafts, from the paring of al-Furaykh.
فرد:
The letters fā', rā' and dāl are a sound root indicating oneness.

1. Al-fard — that is al-witr, an odd, unpaired thing.
2. Al-fārid and al-fard — a bull that has gone off alone. A gazelle that is fārid has cut itself off from the herd, and likewise al-sidra al-fārida — a lote tree standing alone, apart from the rest of the lote trees.
3. Afrād al-nujūm — the bright stars scattered across the horizons of the sky.
4. Al-farīd — pearls, when strung and spaced apart with something else between them.

And God knows best what is correct.
فرز: The letters fā', rā' and zāy are a small root indicating the setting of a thing apart from something else. One says: faraztu l-shay' farzan, and it is mafrūz, and the separated portion is firza.
فرس: The letters fā', rā' and sīn are a small root indicating the treading on a thing and the crushing of it. They say: farasa ʿunuqahu, when he broke its neck — and this comes from the breaking of the neck in slaughter. Then every killing came to be called fars; one says: farasa l-asadu farīsatahu, the lion killed its prey. Abū Firās is a name for the lion. It is possible that al-faras [the horse] is from this same reasoning, because of its stamping the ground with its legs and treading upon it; then its rider was named fāris. They say: huwa ḥasanu l-furūsiyya wa-l-farāsa, he is skilled at horsemanship and at judging by first sight. And from this chapter: al-tafarrus fī l-shay', the forming of an accurate impression of a thing by looking at it — and its reasoning is sound.
فرش:
The letters fā', rā' and shīn are a sound root indicating the smoothing and spreading out of a thing. Farashtu al-firāsha afrishuhu, I spread the bedding. Al-farsh is the verbal noun; al-farsh is also the thing that has been spread. All the words in this chapter go back to this sense.

Tafarrasha al-ṭā'iru, the bird, when it drew near the ground and beat its wing. From this comes the hadith that some of the Prophet's companions took the two chicks of a small bird called a ḥummara, and its mother came fluttering in distress. Abū Duwād said, describing a lookout:
He came running to us, fluttering like a mother bird over her eggs ... running hard, the day already risen high.

1. al-farsh — among livestock, the kind fit only for slaughter and eating.

His saying, peace be upon him — "the child belongs to the marriage-bed (firāsh)" — some said he meant the husband. They said: al-firāsh in reality is the wife, since she is the one laid with, but the term was extended to the husband too, husband and wife sharing in marriage and in covering one another. Jarīr said:
She spent the night facing him, while her bed-mate ... an old, worn cloak, lay slain in blood.

They say afrasha al-rajulu ṣāḥibahu, the man spoke ill of his companion and slandered him — related by Abū Zakariyyā. This fits the analogy well, as though he had laid him low with bad speech.

2. al-farāsha — the light, nimble man. This too is by comparison, likened to farāshat al-mā', the film of water on the ground just before it dries, as if it were something spread out; anything light is called farāsha. Others said al-farāsha of the ground is what the water has receded from, so that it dried and flaked.

From this chapter too: iftarasha al-sabu'u dhirā'ayhi, the predator lay flat on its forelegs. Iftarasha al-rajulu lisānahu, the man spoke however he pleased, letting his tongue run loose. Farāsh al-ra's is the thin plating next to the skull. Al-farsh is small, broken-up firewood. Al-farsh is also open, level ground.

Ibn Durayd said: so-and-so is noble in his marriage-beds (mafārish), when he marries noble women. Jamal mufarrash is a camel with no hump. He also said akama muftarishat al-ẓahr, a hillock, when its top is flat. They say mā afrasha 'anhu, he did not let up on it. A verse: "it had not yet let up on her, the polishing..." This word sits far from the analogy of this chapter, and I think it belongs instead to letter-substitution, as though it were afraja, he cleared away.

Al-farāsha is also the catch of a lock, and al-farāsh is the flying insect, named for its lightness.

What falls outside this root: al-farīsh, among mares, one that is seven days from foaling.
فرص:
The letters fā', rā' and ṣād are a sound root indicating the cutting off of a piece from something.

1. al-furṣa — a piece of wool or cotton, from faraṣtu al-shay', I cut it.
2. al-mifrāṣ — the iron tool with which silver is cut, so called for the same reason.

Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
And I ward off insult from your honors, and lend you a tongue like the shears of the man of al-Khafaj, keen and cutting.

3. Then an opportunity is called furṣa, because it is a thing snatched, as if it were a swift cutting-off of something.

Also from the root:

4. al-farīṣa — the flesh at the top of the shoulder blade, in the middle of the side. It is said that farīṣ al-ʿunuq, the neck's farīṣ, means its veins. This too belongs to the root, as if the word were furiṣa — set apart, marked off from a thing.
5. al-furāfiṣ, of people — the man of fierce onslaught. It comes from al-furāfiṣa, the lion, as if he cuts things off, that is, seizes them.
6. People are said to yatafāraṣūna the water, when they drink it turn by turn, as if each drink of it were muftaraṣa — cut off, allotted.
7. al-furṣa (in this sense) — the drink, the turn.
8. al-farīṣ — the one who shares this turn with you.
فرض:
The letters fā', rā' and ḍād are a sound root that points to leaving a mark in something, by notching it or otherwise.

So al-farḍ is the notch cut into a thing. One says faraḍtu al-khashaba — I notched the piece of wood. The notch in the curved end of a bow, where the string sits, is a farḍ. Al-farḍ is also the hole in the fire-stick at the spot from which fire is struck. And al-mifraḍ is the iron tool with which the notching is done.

From this chapter comes the derivation of al-farḍ, the duty which God Almighty has imposed; it is called that because it has marks and set limits.

From this chapter is al-furḍa, the watering-place on a river or elsewhere; it was named so by likeness to the notch cut in a thing, because it is like a notch in the bank of the river or the like. And al-farḍ is the shield, called that because it is notched along its sides. A poet said, in a line of verse:
I lay awake for it, like the flash of the bearer of news ... turning in his hand a light shield.

From this chapter is what the judge assigns as maintenance for a wife or for another; it is called that because it is a known amount that shows plainly, like a mark left in a thing. And they say: al-farḍ is what you give freely with no return looked for, and al-qarḍ, a loan, is what is given so as to be repaid. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And no trusty man of mine won her, until she cleared and showed her face ... neither by loan nor by free gift.

Among the words that depart from this origin is al-fāriḍ, the aged cow, in His words, exalted: {neither aged nor young} [al-Baqara: 68]. And al-farḍ is a kind of date. A poet said, in a line of verse:
When I have eaten fish and farḍ-dates ... I have gone off lengthwise and gone off breadthwise.

And al-firyāḍ is the wide.
فرط:
The letters fa, ra and ta are a single sound root indicating the removal of a thing from its place and setting it aside. One says 'farrattu 'anhu ma karihahu' — I removed from him what he disliked, that is, I put it aside for him. A line:
Perhaps your two [being] slow will avert some ill, or your hastening will bring some good ahead of its time.

This is the origin; then one says 'afrata' when someone exceeds the due limit in a matter. They say 'iyyaka wal-farat' — beware of excess, that is, do not go beyond the due measure — and this follows the same reasoning, because when one exceeds the measure he has removed the thing from its proper place. Likewise al-tafrit, falling short, because when one falls short in a matter he has held it back from the rank due to it.

1. al-farat / al-farit — the one who goes ahead in seeking water. From this comes the supplication for a child: 'O God, make him one who goes ahead as a reward for his parents' — that is, a benefit that precedes them [to the next life]. 'Takallama fulanun firatan' — so-and-so spoke rashly, when hasty words rushed ahead of him.
2. afrata fi l-amr — he was hasty/excessive in the matter.
3. afratati l-sahabatu bi-l-wasmi — the cloud hastened with the early-season rain.
4. farrattu 'anhu l-shay' — I removed the thing away from him.
5. farasun furut — a horse that outpaces the other horses.
6. al-ma' al-firat — water belonging to whichever of the encampments reaches it first.
A line about the outpacing horse (obscure, rendered as best as can be made out):
Outpacing was my sash, the day I set out — its bridle...
7. furrat al-qata — the sandgrouse that go ahead of the flock toward the watering-place.
8. furrat al-qawm — those who go ahead of the people. A line:
They hurried on ahead of us, though they were among our own companions, just as those who go on ahead of a party hurry before those coming to draw water.

They say 'afrattu l-qirba' — I filled the waterskin; the sense is that in filling it he has caused it to 'exceed', because the water then runs ahead of it and spills over. A pool filled to overflowing is 'ghadirun mufrat'. 'Afrattu l-qawma' — I went ahead of the people and left them behind me. Concerning His saying, Most High, {and that they are left behind} [al-Nahl: 62], they said it means: postponed, put off till last.

They say: 'laqituhu fi l-farti ba'da l-fart' — I met him now and again, that is, from time to time; its meaning is said to be 'what has passed of time'. Al-fartan are two stars ahead of Banat Na'sh [the Great Bear], so named for going ahead. Afrat al-sabah are the first glimmers of dawn. From this also: al-farat, a landmark of the earth by which one is guided, plural afrat, and this is what the poet meant by his saying (a line, obscure, rendered as best as can be made out):
Or have I attained, with a clamorous army, loud with the neighing of horses, [something] between the multitude and the guiding landmark?
It is also said to be pronounced 'al-farat' with the same reasoning either way.
فرع:
The letters fāʾ, rāʾ and ʿayn are a sound root indicating height, elevation, loftiness and fullness. From this: al-farʿ, the top of a thing. Al-farʿ is also the verbal noun of farraʿtu al-shayʾa farʿan, when you climb over it. One says: afraʿa Banū Fulānin, when they went out first of the people in search of pasture. Al-faraʿ — abundant, ready wealth. Al-afraʿ — a man full of hair; one says fariʿa, he grew full-haired.
1. Ibn Durayd said: imraʾatun farʿāʾ — a woman abundant in hair. They do not call a man afraʿ merely for having a large mane; rather they say rajulun afraʿ as the opposite of al-aṣlaʿ (bald). And the Messenger of God — peace be upon him and his family — was afraʿ.
2. rajulun mufraʿu al-katif — a man whose shoulder juts out; also said to mean broad in the shoulder.
3. From this chapter: iftaraʿtu al-bikr — I deflowered the virgin, that being because he overpowers her and mounts her.
4. afraʿtu al-arḍ — I roamed over the land and came to know its state.
5. farʿatu al-ṭarīq and fāriʿatuhu — the raised part of the road.
6. tafarraʿtu Banī Fulānin — I married the noblest of their women.
7. faraʿtu raʾsahu bi-l-sayf — I struck over the top of his head with the sword.
8. faraʿtu al-jabal — I reached the summit of the mountain.
What is close to this pattern but not quite the same: al-faraʿ, the firstborn young of camels and sheep.
What is anomalous from it: al-faraʿa, a small creature; its diminutive is furayʿa, and by it a woman is named.
Also anomalous: al-faraʿ, something practiced in the pre-Islamic period — the skin of a dead young camel was taken and put on another young camel, so that the mother of the slaughtered or dead one would accept it. In Aws's poetry, in a line of verse: "And the clumsy, dull-witted man among the people was likened to a young camel [saqb] dressed in another's skin [farʿan], in this custom."
As for their saying afraʿtu fī al-wādī — I went down into the valley, this rests on the distinction between faraʿtu (to climb up) and afraʿtu (to go down). A man of the Arabs said: "I met so-and-so fāriʿan mufriʿan" — meaning: one of us was going down and the other going up.
فرغ:
The letters fā', rā' and ghayn are a sound root indicating emptiness and room to spare. From it, al-farāgh, the opposite of being occupied. Faragha farāghan wa furūghan, and also fariġa. From this chapter, al-fargh, the outlet of a bucket from which the water pours. Afraghta al-mā'a, I poured the water out. Iftaraghtu, when you pour water over yourself. Dhahaba damuhu farghan, his blood went for nothing, unclaimed and unavenged. Faras farīgh is a horse of wide stride, so named as though it were emptied of everything, so that its pace and running became light. Ḍarba farīgh is a wide strike, and also a wide thrust. Ḥalqa mufragha is a ring cast whole from molten metal, because it is a thing wholly poured. Ṭarīq farīgh is a wide road. A verse:
I passed it by on a worn-out mount, and would think its track ... a clear path, laid open along a wide, well-travelled way.

As for His words, Most High: {We shall attend fully to you, O you two weighty creations} [al-Raḥmān: 31], this is figurative, for God is never distracted from one matter by another. The exegetes said sanafrughu means "We shall set about it"; one says faraghtu ilā amri kadhā, I set about such a matter.
فرق:
The letters fā', rā' and qāf are a small sound root pointing to distinguishing and separating between two things. Of that is al-farq, the parting of the hair. One says faraqtuhu farqan. And al-firq is a flock of sheep. And al-firaq is the split piece of a thing when it splits. God, exalted be He, said: {and it split, and each piece was like a great mountain} [al-Shu'arā': 63].

And of this chapter is al-farīqa, which is a flock separated from the sheep, as though it were a piece that had parted from the main body of the flock. The poet said, in a line of verse:
And a jaw-bone like the withers of a hyena of al-Khalīf, that fell upon a night-straying flock and wrought havoc.

And of this chapter is the ifrāq of a fevered man from his fever, and it is so only because the fever has parted from him. And some of them used to say: ifrāq is only from an illness that strikes a person once, like smallpox and measles and the like. And a nāqa mufriq is a she-camel whose young has parted from her by death.

And al-Furqān is the Book of God, exalted be He, by which He separated truth from falsehood. And al-furqān is the dawn, so called because by it night is separated from day; and it is said, because the darkness parts from it. And al-afraq is the cock whose comb is parted. And al-faraq in horses is that one of his haunches is higher than the other. And al-faraq in the rams of sheep is the distance between the two testicles, and in the ewe the distance between the two teats. And al-fāriq is the pregnant she-camel that goes off into the land, running away from the pain of labour, and gives birth where her place is not known; and the plural is fawāriq and furraq. And she was so called because she parted from the rest of the she-camels. And a cloud that stands apart from the clouds is likened to this she-camel, so it is called fāriq.

And al-fāriq among people is the one who separates matters, deciding between them. And faraq al-ṣubḥ and falaquhu are one thing.

And of what stands apart from this chapter is al-faraq, a measure among the measures; its fā' is vowelled with a, and it is also left unvowelled. Al-Qutaybī said: it is al-faraq with a on the rā', and it is the one that came in the hadith: 'What a faraq of it intoxicates, a handful of it is forbidden'; and it is said to be sixteen raṭls. And he recited for Khidāsh ibn Zuhayr, in a line of verse:
They take the blood-money for their brothers: a faraq of clarified butter and one ewe out of the flock.
And al-farīqa is dates cooked with fenugreek, taken as a remedy. And al-farūqa is the fat of the two kidneys. He said, in a line of verse:
The fat of the kidney-suet and the kidneys give us light.
And al-Farūq is a place. All of that stands apart from the root we have mentioned.
فرك:
The letters fā', rā' and kāf are a root indicating looseness in a thing, and twisting it.

1. faraktu al-shay' bi-yadī afrukuhu farkan — I rubbed the thing with my hand: your twisting of a thing until it comes apart.
2. thawb mafrūk with saffron — a garment dyed [with it]; the origin in it is what we have mentioned.

Also from the root:

3. farikat al-mar'a zawjahā tafrakuhu — the woman farika'd her husband, when she came to hate him.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And he did not lose her between hatred and passion.

4. rajul mufarrak — a man whom women hate; he is called this because she twists and turns away from him.
5. al-infirāk — the slackening of the shoulder.

As for the saying fāraktu ṣāḥibī, like tāraktuhu — I parted from my companion — this belongs to the chapter of letter-substitution, not to this root's true sense.
فرم:
The letters fā', rā' and mīm are one word — I think it is not [genuine] Arabic — and it is al-istifrām. They say it is for a woman to stuff herself with something that tightens what is beneath her waist-wrap. Al-Khalīl said: this is not from the speech of the desert Arabs. Ibn Durayd said: that thing is called farma.

As for the saying of the rājiz [an unnamed composer of rajaz verse], in a line of verse:
Horses packed tight with gravel, racing headlong.

He means horses: from the force of their running, gravel enters into the gaps beneath them, so he likened the gravel to the farma.

Al-Farmā' is a place.
فره: The letters fāʾ, rāʾ and hāʾ are a word indicating exuberant pride and skill. From this: al-fāriha, one skilled at a thing. Al-farih — the exuberant one. Al-fāriha — a singing-girl. Nāqatun mufrih and mufriha — a she-camel, when she habitually bears offspring that are al-furh, fine and well-bred.
فرى:
The letters fā', rā' and the weak letter — the greater part of the chapter is the cutting of a thing, and from it branches what is close to it.

1. faraytu al-shay' afrīhi faryan — I cut a thing, meaning your cutting of it in order to mend it. Ibn al-Sikkīt said: farā means to stitch [leather]. And afraytuhu means you cut it in order to spoil it.

He said, concerning al-fary:
And indeed you cut skilfully what you have shaped, while some men shape and then do not cut.

2. fulānun yafrī al-farīya — so-and-so does the extraordinary, as if he cuts a thing in an astonishing way.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
You used to do extraordinary things with him — meaning you used to speak much of him and exalt him.

3. farā fulānun kadhiban yafrīhi — so-and-so farā'd a lie, when he invented it.
4. tafarrat al-arḍ bi'l-'uyūn — the earth split open with springs: it gushed forth.
5. al-farā — the coward, so named because he was cut off from boldness, that is, severed from it.
6. al-farā, also — like al-farī, meaning the extraordinary.
7. al-farā — astonishment and bewilderment; one says fariya yafrā faran.

The poet said, in a line of verse:
And I was struck with dread out of fear, so I do not shoot, though I had already bidden a companion farewell.

8. al-farwa — the pelt that is worn.

Some said it was named farwa from a different analogy, that of covering — for the same reason the scalp is called farwat al-ra's, meaning its skin.

9. al-farwa — wealth and riches.
10. al-farwa — any clustered growth of plants once it has dried.

In the hadith: al-Khiḍr sat upon a farwa of the ground, and it turned green. If this is sound, then the chapter rests on two analogies: one is cutting, the other is covering and shielding with something thick.

As for the hamzated form, it does not belong to this sense, and nothing else is measured against it: it is al-fara' — the wild donkey. The Messenger of God, God's blessings and peace upon him and his family, said to Abū Sufyān: All game lies within the belly of the fara'.

The poet said, in a line of verse:
With a blow like the ears of the wild donkeys.
فز:
The letters fā' and zā' are a minor root indicating lightness and what is close to it. You say fazzahu and istafazzahu, when you make someone startled and roused. God, exalted is He, said: {And indeed they were about to scare you off the land} [al-Isrā': 76], meaning they would drive you to be light off it, that is, to leave it. And afazzahu al-khawf and afzaʿahu mean the same: fear startled him. And a man's own ignorance may istafazza him, that is, rouse him to folly.

1. rajul fazz — a light, nimble man.
2. fazza ʿan al-shay' — he turned away from a thing, avoided it.
3. al-fazz — the young of the cow. It may be so named for the lightness of its body.

A poet said, in a line of verse: as the calf of a thicket-dwelling wild cow sought relief with the first thin milk, fearing watching eyes, not waiting for the milk to flow full.
فزر:
The letters fā', zāy and rā' are a small root indicating an opening and a splitting apart.

1. al-ṭarīq al-fāzir — the road that is open and wide.
2. al-fizr — a flock of sheep.
3. fazartu al-shay' — I split it, I cracked it.
4. al-afraz — the one whose back is bowed down; the same analogy applies, as if the two masses of flesh of his back were split apart from each other.

And God knows best.
فزع:
The letters fā', zāy and 'ayn are two sound roots: one is terror, the other is aid.

The first: al-faza', fright. Fazi'a yafza'u faza'an, he was frightened. Afza'tuhu anā, I frightened him. Hādhā mafza'u al-qawm, this is what the people turn to in fright. As for fazza'tu 'anhu, its meaning is I removed the fright from him. God Almighty said: {until, when terror is lifted from their hearts} [Saba': 23]. Al-mafza'a is the place the frightened one takes refuge in. A verse:
Tall, his gaze reaching far ... toward the refuge of the dog.

The other root: al-faza' meaning aid. The Messenger of God, peace and blessing be upon him and his family, said to the Anṣār: "You are many when aid is needed, and few when there is gain to be had." They say afza'tuhu when you have terrified him, and also afza'tahu when you have come to his aid. Fazi'tu ilayhi fa-afza'anī, I turned to him in dread, and he came to my rescue. A poet said, on the theme of rescue:
I said to Kās, "Bridle her, for indeed ... we have alighted at the dune of Zarūd to bring aid."
Another said:
We were such that when a terrified crier came to us ... the outcry for him was met like the striking of shins.
فس: The letters fā' and sīn: there is nothing in it except an arabicized word. They say al-fisfisah: green fodder, alfalfa.
فسأ:
The letters fā', sīn and hamza. One says of it:

1. tafassa'a al-thawb — the garment wore out.
2. fasa'tuhu — I stretched it until it split open (tafazzara).
3. fasa'ahu bi'l-ʿaṣā — he struck him with the staff.
4. tafāsā al-rajul tafāsiyan (in the form without hamza) — he stuck his rump out.
فسج:
The letters fā', sīn and jīm are one word. They say:

1. qalūṣ fāsija — a young she-camel that the stallion covered before the proper time for mating, having hurried her.
2. It is also said to mean rather the fat she-camel that has failed to conceive.
فسح: The letters fāʾ, sīn, and ḥāʾ are a single word pointing to spaciousness and width. From this, al-fasīḥ is the spacious. Tafassaḥtu fī al-majlis, I made room for myself in the gathering, and fassaḥtu al-majlis, I made the gathering wide, made room in it.
فسخ:
The letters fā', sīn and khā' are a word indicating the undoing of a thing.

1. tafassakha al-shay' — it came undone.
2. afsakhtu al-shay' — I forgot it.
3. al-fasīkh — the man who does not attain what he seeks.
فسد: The letters fā', sīn and dāl are one word: fasada al-shay' yafsudu fasādan and fusūdan — the thing went bad and spoiled; and it is fāsid and fasīd, spoilt.
فسر: The letters fāʾ, sīn and rāʾ are a single word indicating the clarifying and explaining of a thing. From this: al-fasr. One says: fasartu al-shayʾa and fassartuhu, I explained the thing. Al-fasr and al-tafsira — the physician's examination of the patient's urine and his judgement upon it. God knows best what is correct.
فسط:
The letters fā', sīn and ṭā' are two distinct words.

al-fasīṭ is the little stalk-cap that joins a date to its bunch, also said to be nail-clippings. al-fusṭāṭ is a gathering of people.

In the hadith: The hand of God, exalted is He, is over the fusṭāṭ. And for this reason [the city] al-Fusṭāṭ was named al-Fusṭāṭ.
فسق: The letters fā', sīn and qāf are one word, and it is al-fisq, and it is going out from obedience. The Arabs say fasaqat al-ruṭaba 'an qishrihā, when the ripe date comes out of its skin - al-Farrā' related it. And they say that the mouse is a fuwaysiqa, a little one that goes out; and this has come in the hadith. Ibn al-A'rābī said: the word fāsiq was never heard at all in the speech of the age before Islam, neither in poetry nor in speech. He said: and this is a wonder - it is Arabic speech, and yet it has not come in any poetry of that age.
فسل:
The letters fā', sīn and lām are a sound root indicating weakness and paucity.

1. al-rajul al-fasl — the worthless one among men.
2. al-fasīl — young palm shoots.
3. fasālat al-ḥadīd — its filings.
فش:
The letters fā' and shīn indicate spreading out and a lack of holding together.

1. nāqah fashūsh — a she-camel, when her milk comes out in a scattered stream.
2. infashsha ʿan al-amr — he grew slack and lazy about the matter.
3. al-fashsh — the seeking out of paltry, petty theft; one who does this is a fashshāsh.
فشا:
The letters fā', shīn and the weak letter are one word, and it is the appearing of a thing. One says fashā al-shay', the thing appeared, spread abroad.

Ibn Durayd related:

1. fasha'a al-maraḍ fīhim fushū'an — the disease spread among them.
2. tafashsha'a tafashshu'an — [it spread] in the same sense.
فشج:
The letters fā', shīn and jīm. They say:

1. fashajat al-nāqa — the she-camel spread her legs apart to urinate.

So it is in the book of al-Khalīl. Ibn Durayd said: [it is] fashaḥt, with ḥā' instead, and he recited:

Had you kept company with us, you would have chafed, and the two saddle-arches would have rubbed you, so that you spread apart.
فشخ: The letters fā', shīn and khā' — in it is a remark of Ibn Durayd. He said: al-fashkh is striking the head with the hand.
فشغ:
The letters fā', shīn and ghayn are a root indicating spreading out.

1. infashagha and tafashshagha — it spread out.
2. al-fashgha — the tuft of cotton inside a reed's hollow.
3. al-fushāgh — a plant that spreads over trees and twines about them.
4. al-nāṣiya al-fashghā' — the forelock that is disheveled, spread out.
5. tafashshagha fīhi al-shayb — grey hair spread through him, appeared.
6. tafashshagha bihi al-dam — the blood spread and coursed through him.
7. afshaghahu sawṭan — he struck him with a whip.
فشق:
The letters fā', shīn and qāf are not, in my view, a [genuine] root, but they say al-fashaq is a sudden surprise.

1. fāshaqa — he took [someone] by surprise.
2. fashaqa Banū fulān al-dunyā — the sons of so-and-so, when worldly wealth grew abundant for them and they grew wanton with it.

And God knows best what is correct.
فشل: The letters fā, shīn, and lām. They say: tafashshala al-māʾ means the water flowed. And al-fashl is a part of the fittings of a howdah (the covered seat carried on a camel).
فص:
The letters fā' and ṣād are a word indicating a separation between two things.

1. al-fuṣūṣ — the joints of all the bones, Abū ʿUbayd said except the fingers; each single one of them is a faṣṣ.
2. afṣaṣtu ilayhi min ḥaqqihi shay'an — I let go to him a part of what was due to me, as though you separated it from yourself over to him.
3. faṣṣa al-jurḥ — the wound ran, oozed fluid.

And close to this:

4. al-faṣṣ — the stone set in a ring. It is so named because it is not part of the ring itself, but is fixed onto it.
5. faṣṣ al-ʿayn — the pupil of the eye; it is called this by way of comparison.
فصح:
The letters fā', ṣād and ḥā' are a root indicating purity in a thing and being free of any mixture. From this: al-lisān al-faṣīḥ, the fluent tongue — unrestrained. al-kalām al-faṣīḥ — clear, correct Arabic speech.

The origin sense: afṣaḥa al-laban — the milk's froth settled. afṣaḥa al-rajul — the man spoke Arabic (correctly). And faṣuḥa — his speech became sound, free of error. In Ibn Durayd's book: "the Arab said afṣaḥa when he spoke fluently, and the non-Arab said faṣuḥa when he spoke Arabic." I think this is a mistake; the first account is the correct one. It is also related: faṣuḥa al-laban, so it is faṣīḥ, when its froth has been taken off it.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And beneath the froth is the clear milk.

They say: afṣaḥa al-ṣubḥ, when the dawn's light appeared clear. They say: everything clear and plain is mufṣiḥ. And it is said that al-aʿjam is what does not speak, and al-faṣīḥ is what does speak.

What does not belong to this chapter is al-fiṣḥ — the feast of the Christians. One says: afṣaḥū, meaning their fiṣḥ has come.
فصد:
The letters fā', ṣād and dāl are a sound word, and it is al-faṣd, the cutting of a vein until it flows.

1. al-faṣīd — blood that used to be put into a gut casing, taken from bleeding the veins of camels, then roasted and eaten; that was done in hard times that befell people.

Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
And do not take up the sharp-tipped arrow to let blood with it.

2. tafaṣṣada al-shay' — the thing oozed, flowed.
فصع:
The letters fā', ṣād and ʿayn indicate a thing's coming out from something.

1. faṣaʿa al-ruṭaba — he peeled the fresh date.
2. al-fuṣʿa — a boy's foreskin, when it has widened until the glans shows through it.
فصل:
The letters fā', ṣād and lām are a sound word pointing to setting one thing apart from another and making it distinct from it. One says faṣaltu al-shay'a faṣlan - I set the thing apart. Al-fayṣal is the judge who decides. Al-faṣīl is the young of a she-camel when it is parted from its mother. Al-mifṣal is the tongue, because by it matters are decided and set apart. Al-Akhṭal said, in a line of verse:
And bones have died, and a tongue.

Al-mafāṣil are the joints of the bones. Al-mafṣil is what lies between two mountains, and the plural is mafāṣil. Abū Dhu'ayb said, in a line of verse:
Mothers of firstborn young whose bearing was recent, mixed with water like the water of the clefts between the mountains.

Al-faṣīl is a wall below the city's rampart. In one hadith: "Whoever spends a spending that is fāṣila - that cuts off - has of reward such and such," and its explanation in the hadith is that it is the spending which separated between his belief and his unbelief.
فصم:
The letters fā', ṣād and mīm are a single root indicating a thing cracking without coming fully apart.

1. al-fasm — for a thing to crack without separating.

Any bent piece of wood or the like is mafṣūm.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
As if it were a gleaming silver bracelet ... cracked, in a playing-place among the tribe's maidens.
فصي:
The letters fā', ṣād and yā' are a sound root indicating a thing's drawing away from something.

1. tafaṣṣā al-laḥm ʿan al-ʿaẓm — the flesh came away from the bone; and tafaṣṣā al-insān min al-baliyya — the man freed himself from misfortune.
2. al-faṣya — the noun [formed] from it.

In the hadith of Qayla: Deliverance, by God — may your standing ever remain high.

3. Afṣā — a man's name.
فض:
The letters fā' and ḍād are a sound root indicating separating and dividing into parts. From this: faḍaḍtu al-shay', when you separated it, and infaḍḍa huwa, it came apart. And infaḍḍa al-qawm: the people dispersed. God, glorified is He, said: {And if you had been harsh and hard of heart, they would have dispersed from around you} [Āl ʿImrān: 159].

1. faḍaḍtu ʿan al-kitāb khatmahu — I broke the seal off a letter; from this same chapter.
2. al-fiḍḍah, silver — it is possible this belongs to this chapter too, as though it faḍḍu, scatters, because of the jewelry made from it.
3. al-fiḍāḍ — what scatters (tafaḍḍaḍa) from a thing when it comes apart.
4. al-fāḍḍah — a calamity, plural fawāḍḍ, as though it disperses, that is, scatters people.
5. al-faḍfaḍah — the looseness of a garment. A garment is called faḍfāḍ and a coat of mail faḍfāḍah, because when they are loose their edges fall apart from each other.
6. al-faḍīḍ — sweet water. It is so named for its looseness (faḍāḍah) and the ease with which it goes down the throat.
فضح:
The letters fā', ḍād and ḥā' are two close words: one indicates a thing becoming uncovered, and is said almost only of something shameful; the other likewise indicates an unpleasant colour.

The first: their saying afḍaḥa al-ṣubḥ and faḍḍaḥa, when the dawn appeared. Then they use al-fuḍūḥ for the tearing-open of a person's cover, their disgrace. They say: iftaḍaḥa al-rajul, when his faults were exposed.

As for the colour, they say al-faḍaḥ is a dustiness within an ashen grey — an ugly colour. afḍaḥa al-busr — when redness appeared in the unripe date. They say al-afḍaḥ is the lion, and likewise the camel, from this faḍaḥ of colour.
فضخ:
The letters fā', ḍād and khā' contain a word indicating crushing.

1. faḍakhtu al-ruṭaba — I crushed the fresh date.
2. al-faḍīkh — fresh dates that are crushed and made into a steeped drink.
فضل:
The letters fā', ḍād and lām are a sound root pointing to an increase in a thing.

Of that is al-faḍl: increase and good. Al-ifḍāl is doing good, and the man is mufḍil. And one says faḍala al-shay'u yafḍulu — the thing was left over — and sometimes they said faḍila yafḍulu, which is rare.

As for al-mutafaḍḍil, it is the one who claims superiority over his likes and his peers. God, exalted, said, telling of the one who said: {mā hādhā illā basharun mithlukum yurīdu an yatafaḍḍala ʿalaykum} [al-Mu'minūn: 24]. And it is said that al-mutafaḍḍil is the one wrapped in his single garment. And they say al-fuḍul is the one who has a shirt and a cloak on him, but no waist-wrapper and no trousers. [And from it] is the saying of Imru' al-Qays, in a line of verse:
The crumbs of musk lie on her bed in the morning; she sleeps late, and does not gird herself, being in her house-dress.
فضى:
The letters fā', ḍād and the weak letter are a sound root indicating openness in a thing and breadth.

1. al-faḍā' — the wide open space.
2. afḍā al-rajul ilā imra'atihi — the man was intimate with his wife.

The meaning in this, in our view, is that the front of his body was likened to an open space, and the front of hers to an open space, as if his open space met her open space. This is not far-fetched given the analogy already given.

And from this, by way of comparison:

3. afḍā ilā fulānin bi-sirrihi ifḍā'an — he confided his secret to so-and-so.
4. afḍā bi-yadihi ilā al-arḍ — he put his hand to the ground, when he touched it with the flat of his palm in his prostration; this belongs to what we mentioned in the analogy of al-faḍā'.
5. al-faḍā, written short — dates and raisins mixed together.

Some of them said: al-faḍā, written short, is the two things that are mixed together in a single container, with neither one of them tied up apart from the other.

He said, in a line of verse:
So I said to her: O my aunt, my she-camel is yours, and mixed dates in my saddlebag, and raisins.

And he said, in a line of verse:
Their food, jumbled and mixed, in their saddle-packs.
فطأ:
The letters fā', ṭā' and hamza are one word indicating a sunken, flattened shape.

1. al-afṭa' — said of a flat-nosed man, [as] al-afṭas.
2. faṭi'a al-baʿīr — the camel's back was, by its natural build, sunken.
فطح:
The letters fā', ṭā' and ḥā' are one word.

1. faṭṭaḥtu al-ʿūd — I flattened a stick or the like, when you widen it flat; it is then mufaṭṭaḥ.
2. ra's mufaṭṭaḥ — a broad, flattened head.
فطر:
The letters fā', ṭā' and rā' are a sound root pointing to the opening of a thing and the bringing of it out.

From this is al-fiṭr, the breaking of the fast. One says afṭara ifṭāran — he broke his fast. And qawm fiṭr, a people who are breaking their fast. And from it is al-faṭr, with a fatḥa on the fā', which is the verbal noun of faṭartu al-shāt faṭran, when you milk the ewe. And they say: al-faṭr is milking with two fingers. And al-fiṭra is the make and constitution a thing is created with.
فطس:
The letters fā', ṭā' and sīn.

1. al-faṭas in the nose — its flatness, its spreading.
2. fiṭṭīsat al-khinzīr — the pig's snout.
3. al-fiṭṭīs — the hammer, perhaps named so because a thing is broken and flattened with it.
4. faṭasa — he died.
5. al-faṭsa — a bead used for a charm.
فطم:
The letters fā', ṭā' and mīm are a sound root indicating the cutting off of one thing from another.

1. faṭamat al-umm waladahā — the mother weaned her child; faṭamtu al-rajul ʿan ʿādatihi — I broke the man of his habit.
2. faṭamtu al-ḥabl — one says this when you cut a rope, as Abū Naṣr, the companion of al-Aṣmaʿī, reported. From this comes the mother's weaning (fiṭām) of her child.
فطن: The letters fā', ṭā' and nūn are one word indicating cleverness and knowledge of a thing. One says rajul faṭin and faṭun; the nouns are al-fiṭna and al-faṭāna.
فظ:
The letters fā' and ẓā' are a word indicating dislike and aversion.

1. al-faẓẓ — the fluid of the rumen. Uftuẓẓa al-kirsh is said when the rumen is pressed to squeeze it out.

A poet said:
They were like the lion's muzzle, never scenting out surrender ... nor did they get at the game's rumen-fluid until it was thrown down in the dust.

Some scholars of language said that al-faẓāẓah comes from this.

2. rajul faẓẓ — a man who is ill-natured, harsh. This is taken from the faẓẓ of the rumen, because it is only taken up out of necessity, with distaste.
3. al-faẓīẓ — the fluid of the stallion.
فظع: The letters fā', ẓā' and ʿayn are one word. afẓaʿa al-amr and faẓuʿa — the matter grew severe, dreadful; it is then mufẓiʿ and faẓīʿ. And God knows best.
فعل:
The letters fā', ʿayn and lām are a sound root pointing to the bringing about of a thing, whether a deed or something else.

Of that: faʿaltu kadhā afʿaluhu faʿlan — I did such a thing. And there was from so-and-so a faʿla, a single deed, fine or ugly. Al-fiʿāl is the plural of fiʿl. And al-faʿāl, with a fatḥa on the fā', is generosity and the fine thing that is done.

And one word remains whose soundness I do not know. They say: al-fiʿāl is the wooden handle of an axe.
فعم:
The letters fā', ʿayn and mīm are a sound root indicating breadth and fullness.

1. al-faʿm — the one who is full; faʿuma yafʿumu faʿāma and fuʿūma.
2. imra'a faʿmat al-sāqayn — a woman whose legs are filled out with flesh.
3. afʿamtu al-shay' — I filled the thing.
فعي: The letters fā', ʿayn and the weak letter are one word, and it is al-afʿā, a snake. Some related: tafaʿʿā al-rajul, when his character turned bad, derived from al-afʿā. And God knows best.
فغ:
The letters fā' and ghayn: there is no genuine word in it, and it is something like the imitation of a sound.

1. al-faghfaghah — the sound made to sheep.
2. al-faghfaghānī — the butcher, or the shepherd; and likewise al-faghfaghī.
3. al-faghfaghān — the light, nimble man.
4. tafaghfagha fī amrihi — he hurried in his affair.

All of this is close, one part to another. God knows best what is correct.
فغر:
The letters fā', ghayn and rā' are a sound root, denoting opening and being open.

1. faghara — one says faghara al-rajulu fāhu, he opened his mouth, meaning fataḥahu (he opened it); and one says faghara fūhu, when his mouth came open.
2. infaghara al-nawru — the blossom opened, meaning tafattaḥa.
3. al-fāghira — a kind of perfume.
4. al-mafghara — they say it means open, wide land.
فغم:
The letters fā', ghayn and mīm are two words. One indicates the opening of a thing, or its opening up, and is never used except of something pleasant. The other indicates being enamored of a thing.

The first:

1. faghama al-ward — the rose opened, bloomed.
2. tafghamu, of a pleasant scent — it reaches the nose, opening the blockage in it.
3. afghama al-misk al-makān — the musk filled the place with its scent.

The other word:

1. faghima bi-kadhā — he became enamored of it, eager for it.

Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
She makes for the dwellings of Banū ʿĀmir, while you are enamored of the family of ʿAqīl.
فغي:
The letters fā', ghayn and the weak letter make up a single word.

1. al-fāghiya — the blossom of the henna plant. One says afghā, when it puts out its blossom.
2. al-faghā — a spoiling that occurs in wheat.
فق: The letters fā' and qāf, in a doubled root, indicate opening and mixing in a matter. One says: infaqqa al-shay', when it split open. And they say: rajul faqfāq, meaning a fool, confused in his speech. And it is also said faqāq.
فقأ:
The letters fā', qāf and hamza indicate the opening of a thing, its splitting open. One says: tafaqqa'at al-saḥābah ʿan mā'ihā, when a cloud let go its water, as though it opened up to release it.

1. al-faq' — the membrane that splits open from the head of a newborn.
2. faqa'tu ʿaynahu afqa'uhā — I gouged out his eye; from this same word.

As for al-fuqā, softened in pronunciation, it is the plural of fūq, the notch of an arrow, which is a transposition of letters and not from this chapter. He said, in a line of verse: my arrows, and their notches, are like the hocks of dusky sandgrouse.
فقح:
The letters fā', qāf and ḥā' indicate something like what we mentioned before it, an opening up.

1. al-fuqqāḥ — the blossom of the idhkhir plant (a fragrant grass), so named for its opening up; and it is also said that it is rather the blossom of every kind of tree, which is called fuqqāḥ.
2. faqqaḥa al-jarw — the puppy opened its eyes.

A poet said:
I will darken your eyes with colocynth-juice, or with kohl ... so open them for that, or close them.
فقد: The letters fāʾ, qāf, and dāl are a slight root pointing to a thing going away and being lost. From this is their saying: faqadtu al-shayʾa faqdan, I lost the thing. Al-fāqid is the woman who has lost her child or her husband, plural fawāqid. As for your saying tafaqqadtu al-shayʾa, when you sought it out, that too comes from this, because you seek a thing at the time you have lost it. God Most High said: {and he sought out the birds and said: why do I not see the hoopoe, or is he among those absent} [al-Naml: 20].
فقر:
The letters fā', qāf and rā' are a sound root pointing to a parting open in something, whether a limb or something else.

From this: al-faqār of the back, the vertebrae, one of them a faqāra, so called for the notches and the divisions between them. And al-faqīr is the man whose backbone is broken. The people of the language said: from this the name faqīr, poor man, is derived, and it is as though his backbone were broken, from his lowness and his neediness.

And from this: faqaratuhum al-fāqira — the calamity broke them; and it is disaster, as though it were a breaker of the backbone.

And some of the men of learning say: al-faqīr is one who has a bare sufficiency of living, and they argue from the saying:
As for the poor man, whose milch camel was just enough for his household, and not even a hair was left him.

He said: so he gave him a milch camel, and made it just enough for his household, that is, food with no surplus in it.

As for al-faqīr, it is the outlet of the water from the water channel, and its analogy is sound, because it has been broken through into the ground and split open. As for their saying afqaraka al-ṣayd, its meaning is that the game has given you its backbone so that you may shoot it. And one says faqartu al-baʿīr — when you notch its muzzle and then set the leading rope on the place of the notch, to make it submit and to break it in. And afqartuka nāqatī — I lent you her back to ride.

And the saying of the poet:
The night of al-Faqīr is nothing but a devil.

Here al-Faqīr is a well-known well. And one says faqartu li-l-fasīl — when you dig for the palm shoot at the time you plant it; and faqartu al-kharaz — when you bore the bead. And sadda Allāhu mafāqirahu — may God stop up his gaps of need, that is, may He make him rich and close up the ways of his poverty.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And truly the One who drove wealth to Ibn ʿĀmir is my Lord, the One I hope in for the stopping up of my needs.
فقس: The letters fā', qāf and sīn. They say: faqasa — he died.
فقص: The letters fā', qāf and ṣād are nothing in themselves, except that they say: fuqiṣat al-bayḍah ʿan al-farkh, the egg was cracked open, freeing the chick.
فقع:
The letters fāʾ, qāf and ʿayn. Know that this chapter and its words are not built on one pattern; they are distinct words.
1. al-faqʿ — a kind of truffle, and by it the lowly man is likened, so one says: "he is more despised than a faqʿ in an open plain."
2. al-faqʿ — a fart. This is from their saying: faqqaʿa bi-aṣābiʿihi, he cracked his fingers, made a sound.
What does not resemble what came before: the description of the colour yellow — one says aṣfar fāqiʿ, a vivid yellow.
3. al-ifqāʿ — they say it means bad circumstances; one says from it afqaʿa, he fell into poverty.
4. fawāqiʿ al-dahr — the calamities of fate.
As for al-fuqqāʿ, it is said to be genuine Arabic. Al-Khalīl said: it is named fuqqāʿ for the foam that rises to its top. He said: al-faqāqīʿ are like little bottles above the water.
فقم:
The letters fā', qāf and mīm are a sound root indicating crookedness and a lack of straightness.

1. al-amr al-afqam — the crooked matter.
2. al-faqam — that the lower front teeth protrude forward so that the upper ones no longer meet them. This is the origin of the chapter.

Abū Bakr claimed that al-faqam is fullness. One says: aṣāba min al-mā' ḥattā faqim, he drank of the water until he was full — he held this to be the origin of the chapter. If this is sound, then it too follows by the same reasoning.
فقه:
The letters fā', qāf and hā' are a single sound root pointing to the grasping of a thing and the knowledge of it.

You say faqihtu al-ḥadīth afqahuhu — I understood the report and I understand it. And every knowledge of a thing is fiqh. They say: lā yafqahu wa lā yanqahu — he neither understands nor takes in. Then this was made special to the knowledge of the sacred law, so that every man who knows the lawful and the forbidden was called a faqīh. And afqahtuka al-shay' means I made the thing clear to you.
فك:
The letters fā' and kāf are a sound root, indicating opening and parting.

1. fakāk al-rahn — the release of a pledge, meaning opening it from being locked away. Al-Kisā'ī reported: al-fikāk, with kasra.
2. fakaktu al-shay' afukkuhu fakkan — one says this, meaning: I released the thing. And when a man falls and his foot gives way, they say: saqaṭa fulānun wa-infakkat qadamuhu, meaning it came apart.
3. lā yanfakku yaf'alu dhālika — their saying, meaning: he does not cease to do that. The meaning is that he and that action are not to be separated; the reasoning holds here.
4. al-fakk — the parting of the shoulder from its joint through weakness.
5. al-fakkān — the place where the two sides of the mouth meet, so named for their parting; this too belongs to the chapter.
فكر: The letters fā', kāf and rā' are the heart going back and forth over a thing. One says tafakkara when a man turns his heart over something, taking a lesson from it. And rajul fikkīr — a man who thinks a great deal.
فكل: The letters fā', kāf and lām are a single word, and it is al-afkal: trembling, shivering. And they say no verb is formed from it.
فكن: The letters fā', kāf and nūn are a single word, and it is regret. One says tanaddama and tafakkana with the same meaning.
فكه:
The letters fā', kāf and hā' are a sound root pointing to pleasantness and to finding a thing pleasant.

From this is al-rajul al-fakih, the man who is pleasant of soul, in good spirits.

And of the chapter is al-fākiha, fruit, because it is found pleasant and is taken as a delicacy.

And of the chapter is al-mufākaha, which is joking and the kind of talk that is found sweet.

And of the chapter is afkahat al-nāqa wa'l-shāt, when the she-camel and the ewe give milk on eating the spring pasture and there is the least thickness in the milk; and that is the best of milk.

As for al-tafakkuh in His saying, exalted be He: {fa-ẓaltum tafakkahūn} [al-Wāqi'a: 65], it is not from this. It belongs to the chapter of letter-substitution, and the original is tafakkanūn, and it is from regretting; and mention of it has already passed.
فل:
The letters fā' and lām are a sound root, indicating breaking and chipping, or something close to that.

1. al-fall — the defeated people who are routed.
2. al-fulūl — the notches in the edge of a sword, singular fall. Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
   There is no fault in them, except that their swords carry notches from clashing with armies.
3. al-falīl — a camel's tooth, when it is chipped.
4. al-fill — land with no plants in it; the reasoning holds here too. He said, in a fragment of verse: fall, set apart from good. One says: aflalnā, meaning: we came to be in the fill.

Deviating from this root is al-falīla: hair gathered together, plural al-falīl. He said:
   And where the blood runs freely, and where, from the plaited hair, is drawn out something like al-falīl.
فلت:
The letters fā', lām and tā' are a sound word indicating breaking free in haste.

1. aflata yuflitu — he broke free, escaped.
2. faltah — a matter was called a faltah when it happened without forethought, without deliberate opinion, and without hesitation.
3. tafallata ilā hādhā al-amr — he strained toward this matter, as though he broke free toward it.
4. faras falatān — a horse that is lively, quick of heart.
5. thawb falūt — a garment whose two ends will not close over its wearer, from its smallness, as though its meaning is that it slips (yuflitu) from the hand.
6. uftulita al-insān — said when a person dies suddenly. And in the hadith: "My mother died suddenly (uftulitat nafsuhā)."
7. al-faltah — the last day of Jumādā al-Ākhirah.
فلج:
The letters fā', lām and jīm are two sound roots: one indicates triumph and victory, and the other a gap between two equal things.

The first: their saying fulija al-rajul ʿalā khaṣmihi, when he triumphed over his opponent. Al-sahm al-fālij is the winning arrow, and a man may likewise be called al-fālij, the winner. The noun is al-fulj. And among the proverbs of the Arabs: "I am, in this matter, Fālij ibn Khalāwah" — they said its meaning is: I am free of it. The explanation is that when a man is free (khalā) of a matter, he has triumphed, that is, escaped it; and khalāwah is from khalā yakhlū, to be free. And ʿAlī, peace be upon him, said: "The Muslim man does not commit a base act that makes him ashamed when it is mentioned to him, and that emboldens base people against him, like the gambler who wins (al-yāsir al-fālij), waiting for a winning throw from his arrows."

The other root: al-falaj in the teeth is the gap between the central incisors and those beside them. Abū Bakr said: "A man is aflaj al-asnān, gap-toothed, and a woman is faljā' al-asnān — the teeth must be named." As for al-falaj in the hands, Abū ʿUbayd said: al-aflaj is one whose crookedness is in his hands; if it is in his legs, he is called faḥaj instead. And this fits the first sense, because when a hand is crooked it must bend outward and grow apart from its fellow.

1. al-fālij — the two-humped camel, so named for the gap between its two humps.
2. faras aflaj — a horse whose two haunches are far apart.
3. kullu shay' shaqaqtahu — anything you split, you have falajtahu falajayn, that is, cut it into two halves.

Ibn Durayd said: "A man is only called fulija because half of him has gone."

4. fulayjah — a strip cut lengthwise from a garment.
5. al-falaj — the stream or channel, so named because it was fulija, split, as though the water cut it open and it became a gap.
6. al-fallūjah — land made ready for cultivation, plural falālīj.

As for the hadith "that the two of them falajā the jizyah," he means that they divided it between themselves; that was called falj because it is a splitting apart.
فلح:
The letters fā', lām and ḥā' are two sound roots: one of them points to splitting, and the other to winning and lasting.

The first: falaḥtu al-arḍ - I split the ground open. The Arabs say: "Iron is split by iron." And for this the ploughman is called fallāḥ. A man whose lower lip is split is called aflaḥ, and it is plain in him, this falaḥa - this cleft. ʿAntara al-ʿAbsī used to be nicknamed "al-Falḥā'" for a cleft lip he had. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And ʿAntara of the cleft lip came clad in mail - as though you were a black crag of ʿAmāya.

The second root is al-falāḥ: lasting and winning. And a man's saying to his wife "istafliḥī bi-amriki" means: win your own affair. Al-falāḥ is also the meal before dawn in the fast. They said: it was called falāḥ because with it a man's strength lasts him for the fasting. In the hadith: "We prayed with the Messenger of God - may God bless him and his family - until we feared that the falāḥ, the pre-dawn meal, would escape us." The poet said, in a line of verse:
For every care among cares there is a room to breathe - but for evening and for morning there is no lasting with them.
فلذ: The letters fā', lām and dhāl are a minor root indicating cutting a piece off a thing. From this: al-fildhah — a piece cut from the liver, plural fildh. He said, in a line of verse: a cut of liver from the roast meat suffices him, if he comes upon it, and a small cup satisfies his drink. So a piece of property is also called a fildhah. One says faladhtu lahu min mālī, that is, I cut off a piece of it for him.
فلز: The letters fā', lām and zā' — there is nothing in it, except that they say: al-filizz — the dross of iron that the bellows of the furnace drives out.
فلس: The letters fā', lām and sīn are a single word, and it is al-fals, well known, plural fulūs. And they say: aflasa al-rajul — they said its meaning is: he became a possessor of fulūs, small copper coins, after having been a possessor of dirhams, silver coins.
فلص: The letters fā', lām and ṣād — there is nothing in it, but they say: al-infilāṣ is slipping free. And I say fallaṣtu al-shay' min al-shay', I freed one thing from another. This, if it is sound, comes only by letter-substitution, the true letter being mīm, one saying mallaṣa. And it is possible that the true letter is khā': khallaṣa.
فلط: The letters fā', lām and ṭā' are not a root, because it belongs to the chapter of letter-substitution, the true letter being rā'. They say: aflaṭahu al-amr, the matter took him by surprise. And so-and-so spoke filāṭan, when he startled people with what he said. The true letter is rā': farraṭa, which has been treated in its own chapter.
فلع: The letters fā', lām and ʿayn are a single word indicating the splitting of a thing. You say: falaʿtu al-shay', I split it. And tafallaʿat al-bayḍah and infalaʿat: the egg split open.
فلق:
The letters fā', lām and qāf are a sound root indicating a gap and a separation opening in a thing, and also the magnifying of a thing.

1. falaqtu al-shay'a aflaquhu falqan, I split the thing.
2. al-falaq — the dawn, because the darkness splits open (yanfaliqu) from it.
3. al-falaq — a low, sunken piece of ground, as though it had split open, plural filqān.
4. al-falaq — all of creation, as though something had split open from it so that it was brought out and made manifest. One says infalaqa al-ḥajaru wa-ghayruhu, and so-and-so spoke to me min filqin fīhi [from an opening in it], following the same reasoning.
5. al-fāliq — an open stretch of ground between two ridges of sand.
6. qawsun filq — a bow made split from a single piece, not a jointed rod.
7. al-falīq — like a gash in the underside of a camel's neck. A line says:
Its scar, smooth, like the bent lance.

The other root: al-fulayqa, the great calamity. The Arabs say "yā lal-fulayqa," oh, what a calamity — the astonishing, great matter. Aflaqa fulānun, he produced something astonishing; likewise a poet is called mufliq. Suwayd said:
When a fearsome, pitch-dark waste stretched before them ... and its driver sang his call, they worked wonders through it.
Al-faylaq also means the astonishing thing.
فلك:
The letters fā', lām and kāf are a sound root pointing to roundness in a thing. Of that is falkat al-mighzal, the whorl of a spindle, with a fatha on the fā'; it is so called for its roundness; and for that reason it is said falaka thady al-mar'a, when a woman's breast becomes round.

And of this reasoning is falak al-samā', the turning course of the sky. And falaktu al-jady bi-qadībin aw hulb: I turned a stick or a hair-loop round upon the kid's tongue so that it would not suck. And al-falak is round pieces of ground raised above what is about them. And it is said that the falka of the tongue is the hard part at its base. And as for the ship, it is called fulk. And it is said that the singular and the plural in this name are the same; and perhaps it is called fulk because it is turned round in the water.
فلم:
The letters fā', lām and mīm are a word. They say al-faylam: a man of great size. And in the mention of al-Dajjāl: "I saw him as a huge man (faylamāniyyan)." A poet said:
He protects the one who calls for help when he calls ... when the long-haired giant of a man flees.
And they say: al-faylam is the comb. But this is not sound.
فلن: The letters fāʾ, lām and nūn stand in for any person — "so-and-so." Abū al-Najm shortened it, saying, in a line of verse: "In the deep of the sea, hold back so-and-so [fulānan] from so-and-so [ful]!" This is used for people; if used for something else, one says: rakibtu al-fulānata wa-l-farasa al-fulān — I rode such-and-such a she-[animal] and such-and-such a horse.
فلو:
The letters fā', lām and the weak letter [wāw] are a sound word holding three distinct words: rearing, searching, and open land.

As for rearing: falawtu al-muhr, when you reared the colt. One says falāhu yaflūhu, and it, the colt, is called a faluww. Al-Ḥuṭay'ah said, in a line of verse: Saʿīd — and whatever Saʿīd does — he is a noble colt, reared while tethered, noble. And their saying falawtuhu ʿan ummihi, that is, I weaned it from its mother, has the same meaning as we mentioned. One also says falawtu al-muhr and iftalaytuhu. He said, in a line of verse: never does a chief of ours perish, but we rear up a young man among us to be chief.

The second word: falaytu al-ra's aflīhi, I picked the lice from the head. Then it is used as a metaphor, so one says: falaytu ra'sahu bi'l-sayf aflīhi, I split his head open with the sword.

The third word: al-falāh, which is open, empty land, plural falawāt and falā.
فم:
The letters fā' and mīm contain nothing but al-fam, the mouth, and this is not the place for it — but fumm, with ḍamma and doubling, has been reported. He said:
   Would that it had come out of his fumm!
فن:
The letters fā' and nūn are two sound roots: one indicates wearying, and the other a kind among the kinds of all things.

The first: al-fann, which is wearying and persistent driving. One says: fanantuhu fannan, when I drove him hard and wearied him.

The other: al-afānīn — the kinds and ways of a thing. From it: al-fanan, the branch, plural afnān. And one says: shajara fanwā', a tree of many branches. Abū 'Ubayd said: as though its underlying form is fannā'.
فنح: The letters fā', nūn and ḥā' are a single word. They say: fanaḥa al-faras min al-mā', when a horse drank without reaching its fill. He said, in a line of verse: and the taking of the evening drink and the morning drink, a coolness for one who drinks much yet is never filled. Al-miq'ab is the one who drinks a great deal of water and milk. Others transmitted it as "li-miṣ'ab", meaning the one who drinks without reaching his fill. God knows best what is correct.
فند:
The letters fāʾ, nūn and dāl are a sound root indicating heaviness and severity, some of its senses built on others. From this: al-find, a jutting peak of a mountain; some said it is the great mountain, and by it a man was named Find.
1. Measured on this pattern: al-tafnīd, which is blame, because it is speech that weighs heavily on the one who hears it and grows severe.
2. al-fanad — senility, and this is on the same pattern, for one is not senile without also losing soundness of mind. One says afnada al-rajulu, fa-huwa mufnid — a man has grown senile, when he has become doting. One does not say ʿajūzun mufnida of an old woman, for in her youth she was not held to be one possessed of judgement [in this old usage].
3. They also say: al-fanad — lying. It is possible it is so named because the one who tells it is yufannad, that is, blamed for it; and it is possible it is so named because it is a grave sin, heavy is its burden.
فنع: The letters fā', nūn and ʿayn are a sound root indicating fragrance, abundance and generosity. Al-fanaʿ is generosity. It is said that the spreading of musk's scent is fanaʿ, and it is also said that it means the spreading of good praise. And one says māl dhū fanaʿ, that is, wealth in abundance. He said, in a line of verse: I may indeed be generous, though my wealth holds no abundance, toward my friend, and my good is never grudged.
فنق:
The letters fā', nūn and qāf are a minor root indicating generosity and comfort.

1. al-faniq — the stallion camel held in honor, never harmed out of respect for it.
2. al-funuq — the pampered young girl.
3. al-mufannaq — the one who is indulged, kept in comfort.
فنك:
The letters fā', nūn and kāf are two words. They said: al-fank is persistence, and it is also said to mean staying put. One says fanaka: he stayed, remained.

The other word: al-fanīk — the end of the two jawbones near the tuft of hair beneath the lower lip. Someone said: I asked Abū ʿAmr al-Shaybānī about al-fanīk, and he said: as for the upper one, it is where the two jawbones meet at the chin; as for the lower one, it is where the two hips meet, at their joining.
فني:
The letters fāʾ, nūn and the weak letter. This is a chapter whose words follow no single pattern, and it is not built on a known rule; we have simply set down what has come regarding it.
1. They said: faniya yafnā fanāʾan — it perished. God — Exalted — afnāhu, caused it to perish, that being when it is cut off; God — Exalted — qaṭaʿahu, meaning He took it away.
2. al-fanā, written with a short vowel — the fox's grape [a berry-bearing plant].
3. al-fināʾ — the open space that extends along a house's sides, plural afniya.
4. They say: huwa min afnāʾi al-ʿArab — he is of the scattered branches of the Arabs, when it is not known which tribe he is from.
5. al-mufānāh — humouring someone, managing them gently. A poet said, in a line of verse: "I make it stand at times and sit at others, as one who leads a headstrong horse manages it gently [yufānī]."
6. al-afānī — a plant, singular afāniya.
7. al-fanāh — the cow, plural fanawāt.
8. shajaratun fanwāʾ — a tree, when its branches spread out on every side; the expected form would be fannāʾ, since it comes from al-fanan, a branch.
فه:
The letters fā' and hā' are a single word, indicating inarticulateness and the like. From that: al-rajul al-fahh, the inarticulate man, and al-mar'a fahha, the inarticulate woman; its verbal noun is al-fahāha. He said, in a line of verse:
   You did not find me inarticulate, nor did you find my argument tangled, so that I sought one to set it right.

And one says: kharajtu li-ḥājatin fa-afahhanī fulānun ḥattā fahihtu, meaning: I went out on an errand, and so-and-so made me forget it, until I was at a loss.
فهج: The letters fā', hā' and jīm are a word. It is said that al-fayhaj is wine. And they recited: come, give us to drink at morning a fayhaj-wine of Jadr ... with the water of a cloud, my truth outrunning my falsehood.
فهد:
The letters fā', hā' and dāl indicate a kind of animal, and the word is then used as a metaphor. Al-fahd, the leopard, is well known, plural fuhūd.

1. fahida al-rajul — the man was heedless, inattentive to his affairs, likened to the fahd.

And in the hadith of Umm Zarʿ: "If he comes in, he is fahid (sleepy, heedless); if he goes out, he is asid (fierce as a lion)." They say this because the fahd is known for sleeping a great deal.

2. al-fahdatān — the two fleshy parts at a horse's chest, used as a metaphor.
3. al-fahd — a peg fixed in the middle of the saddle.
فهر:
The letters fā', hā', rā' — there is nothing of the original language in them except one word, and that is al-fihr, feminine, meaning a stone, one of the stones.

1. They say that al-fahr is when a man has intercourse with a woman and withdraws, ejaculating outside her; this usage has occurred [in speech].
2. tafahhara fī al-māl — he became expansive, well off, in wealth.
3. nāqatun fayharatun — a strong she-camel.

All of this is close together, each of it as weak as the rest.
فهق:
The letters fā', hā', qāf are a sound root indicating width and fullness.

1. al-fahq — fullness. One says afhaqta al-ka's, you filled the cup, when you filled it.
2. al-mutafayhiq — in the hadith: "The most hateful of you to me are the chatterers and the mutafayhiqūn." The singular is mutafayhiq.

Of the one whose speech overflows and fills his mouth with it, al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse:
A bowl comes in the evening to the family of al-Muhallaq ... like the cistern of the Iraqi elder, brimming over.

3. al-fayhaq — Al-Khalīl said: it is anything wide, so much so that one says mafāza fayhaq, a wide, trackless desert.
4. munfahiq al-wādī — he said: it is the widest part of the valley.

And among what diverges from this root: al-fahqa is a bone at the top of the head, overlooking the uvula.
فهم: The letters fāʾ, hāʾ and mīm mean the knowing of a thing — so the people of the language say. And Fahm is the name of a tribe.
فوت:
The letters fā', wāw and tā' are a small sound root indicating the opposite of catching up with a thing and reaching it. One says: "the thing fātahu, fawtan" — it eluded him. "The two things tafāwatā" — the gap between them widened, meaning this one did not catch up with that one.

Al-iftiyāt is the iftiʿāl-form from al-fawt: it is getting ahead to something without taking counsel. One says: "so-and-so lā yuftātu ʿalayhi" — nothing is done without his order.

From this root: al-fawt is the gap between two things, like the gap between two fingers; plural afwāt. It is said: "he died the death of al-fawāt," when he was taken by surprise — as if what he wanted, such as making a bequest, had escaped him. And it is said: "he is from me fawta l-rumḥ" — beyond a spear's reach.

A man cursed another, saying: "May God — exalted is He — put his provision fawta fīhi" — meaning where he can see it but cannot reach it.
فوج:
The letters fā', wāw and jīm are a word indicating a gathering. From this, al-fawj — a group of people; plural afwāj, and the plural of the plural afāwij and afāwīj.

As for "afāja l-rajulu" — when a man hurried — that belongs to a different, weak root, and al-fayj (a fast courier) is from it.
فوح: The letters fā', wāw, ḥā' are a word indicating a rising and a boiling. One says fāḥat al-rīḥu tafūḥu fawḥan, the wind rose and spread. This is said of the wind and other things. Some have related fāḥat al-qidru, the pot boiled. And afaḥtuhā anā, I made it boil.
فود:
The letters fā', wāw, dāl are one word, then it is used as a metaphor. Al-fawd is the greater part of the hair of the forelock, next to the two ears. Then, by metaphor, they say for the two wings of the eagle: fawdān, two fawds.

And what is not from it: their saying fāda yafūdu, when he died — the origin of this is the letter yā', and it has already been mentioned.
فور:
The letters fā', wāw and rā' are a word indicating boiling, and reasoning is then built upon it. Al-fawr is the boiling. One says fārati al-qidru tafūru fawran, the pot boiled. A line says:
Their pot boils over against us, so we pour it back on them ... and we quench it away from us when its heat has boiled fiercely.
Fāra ghaḍabuhu, his anger surged up. From this reasoning also: their saying fa'alahu min fawrihi, he did it at once, at the very outset of the matter, before it had time to settle.
فوز:
The letters fā', wāw and zāy are two words of opposite meaning: the first is deliverance and the other is destruction.

The first is their saying fāza yafūzu, when he escaped safely, and he is fā'iz. And fāza bi-l-amr, when he carried the matter off and got it clear. And a man used to say to his wife when he divorced her: fūzī bi-amrik, take charge of your own affair, as one says: your affair is in your own hand. And it is said of whoever wins some good and carries it off. God, exalted, said: {So whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted into the Garden has indeed won} [Āl ʿImrān: 185].

The other word is their saying fawwaza al-rajul, when the man died. Al-Kumayt said, in a line of verse:
It did her no harm that Kaʿb lay dead ... and that Jarwal perished after him.

Then there is disagreement about al-mafāza, the desert: some people said it was so named as a good omen for the one who rides into it, of safety and deliverance; and al-mafāza is the place of deliverance. God, mighty and exalted, said: {in a place of safety from the punishment} [Āl ʿImrān: 188]. Others said: it is from the second word, fawwaza, when he perished. Then one says fawwaza al-rajul when he rode out into the desert.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
He crossed the desert from Qurāqir to Suwā.
فوص: The letters fā', wāw, ṣād are a word indicating being set free or escaping from something. One says: qabaḍtu ʿalā dhanabi al-ḍabbi fa-afāṣa min yadī, I gripped the lizard's tail and it freed its tail from my hand [and got away]. Al-mufāwaṣa, in hadith, is making plain. And mā yufīṣu bihā lisānuhu means he makes it clear.
فوض:
The letters fāʾ, wāw and ḍād are a sound root indicating relying on another in a matter and referring it back to him, and it then branches out so that whatever resembles this is referred back to it too. From this: fawwaḍa ilayhi amrahu — he entrusted his affair to him, when he handed it back to him. God — Exalted — said, in the story of one who said: {and I entrust my affair to God} [Ghāfir: 44].
1. From this too, their saying: bātū fawḍā — they spent the night fawḍā, meaning mixed together, its meaning being that each entrusted his affair to the other. A poet said, in a line of verse: "Their food lies scattered loose [fawḍā] in their travelling-packs, and they are not careful of a secret except calling out to one another."
2. One says: māluhum fawḍā baynahum — their wealth is held in common among them, when neither of them opposes the other over it.
3. tafāwaḍa al-sharīkān fī al-māl — the two partners entered a full partnership in the wealth, when they joined together, each entrusting his affair to his companion — this one satisfied with what that one does, and that one satisfied with what this one does — being what the Sharia permits.
فوع: The letters fā', wāw, ʿayn indicate a rising in a thing. For the fragrance of perfumed wine and what rises of its scent, one says fawʿa. And for the rise of the daylight, one says fawʿa.
فوغ: The letters fā', wāw, ghayn are a word, if it is sound. They say: al-fawgh is the large, massive one. One says imra'atun fawghā'u, a big woman.
فوف:
The letters fā', wāw, fā' are one word.

1. al-fūf — cotton.
2. al-fūf, also said for the whiteness seen in the fingernails of the young.
3. burdun mufawwaf — a cloak patterned [with that whiteness], named from this.
فوق:
