The letters fā', wāw and qāf are two sound roots: one points to height, and the other to a coming back and returning.

The first is al-fawq, which is height. One says fulān fāqa aṣḥābahu yafūquhum - so-and-so surpassed his companions, when he rose above them. And amr fā'iq - a matter that is raised up and lofty.

As for the other, it is fuwāq al-nāqa, which is the return of the milk into a she-camel's udder after milking. You say mā aqāma ʿindahu illā fuwāqa nāqa - he stayed with him only as long as the milk takes to come back into a camel's udder. The name for what gathers of the milk is fīqa, and its origin letter is the wāw. Al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse:
Until, when a gathering of milk had collected in her udder, she came to suckle the half of her soul, if only it could suckle.

In one hadith, speaking of the Qur'an: "I take it in draughts, as the milk-camel is drawn." It means: I do not read my portion in one go, but a thing after a thing. He likened it to the milk returning to the udder. One says fuwāq and fawāq. God - exalted is He - said: {There is for it no fawāq} [Ṣād: 15], that is, there is for it no returning, no turning back, no going back again. Another said: there is for it no respite. The two meanings are close. And they say afāqa al-sakrān yufīq - the drunken man came to himself, and that is from his mind returning to him. Al-afāwīq are the waters that have gathered in a cloud.

Of this chapter is al-fūq: the notch of an arrow, so called because the bowstring is set into it as though it had been sent back into it; the plural is afwāq. They also say fuqan, which is a reversal of the letters. And one says sahm afwaq, when its notch is broken.

Among what departs from these two roots is their saying huwa yafūqu bi-nafsihi. This belongs to the chapter of letter-substitution: its origin is yasūqu, and the fā' is a substitute for the sīn; it is said when a man is giving up his soul.
فول: The letters fā', wāw, lām are a word, if it is sound. They say: al-fūl is the broad bean.
فوم: The letters fāʾ, wāw and mīm are a sound root disputed in its meaning, and it is al-fūm. Some said it is garlic; others said it is wheat. They say: fawwimū lanā — bake bread for us.
فوه:
The letters fā', wāw and hā' are a sound root that points to an opening in a thing. From that is al-fawah, wideness of the mouth. A man is afwah and a woman fawhā'. The people of Arabic say that the origin of fam, mouth, is fawah, and that is why they said a man is afwah. And fāha al-rajul bi-l-kalām yafūhu bihi when he utters it. Al-mufawwah is the one who has power over speech. Some people claimed that al-fawah is also the jutting out and the length of the upper front teeth.

From this chapter is al-fuwwaha, the mouth of a river; they built it on this pattern only to separate what belongs to the river from what belongs to a human being. And al-fūh is the single one of afwāh al-ṭīb, the aromatic spices, like sūq and aswāq. The analogy is one and the same, as though, when its scent spread out, it spoke it out with a mouth.
فيج:
The letters fā', yā', jīm indicate hastening.

1. al-fayj — this has already been discussed; it is said its origin is the wāw.
2. al-fā'ija — in the land, the wide space between any two elevations, whether of rough ground or of sand.
فيح: The letters fā', yā', ḥā' are one word. Fāḥa yafīḥu, when it rose and spread. This is said of the wind and other things. And in the hadith: "Fever is from the fayḥ [blaze] of Hell." It is said its origin is the wāw, and this has already been mentioned.
فيخ: The letters fā', yā', khā' are a word. They say: afākha yufīkhu bi-rīḥihi, he broke wind. And in the hadith: "Every female that urinates tufīkh [breaks wind]." And they say — though I do not think it sound — that al-faykha is the small dish.
فيد:
The letters fā', yā', dāl are a small, sound root, except that its words did not come by analogy; it is one of the chapters that cannot be extended by analogy.

1. al-fayd — they say it is saffron; by it is named the hair on the muzzle of the horse.
2. al-fayd — swaggering in one's walk. One says rajulun fayyād, a swaggering man. As for al-fayyād in the saying of Abū al-Najm, in a line of verse: "And I am not the fayyāda, the mighty, forceful one" — it is said: he is the one taken with himself, who struts in his walk.
3. al-fayyāda — the great eater.
4. al-fayd — death. [fāda] yafīdu, he dies.
5. al-fayyād — the male owl. He said, in a line of verse:
A vast, pitch-dark waste at night ... the cry of its fayyād [owl] keeps me company.
6. al-fā'ida — the gaining of new wealth or good. One says qad fādat lahu fā'idatun, a benefit came to him. And one says: afadtu ghayrī, I gave benefit to another, and afadtu min ghayrī, I gained benefit from another.
فيش:
The letters fā', yā', shīn are one word. They say: al-fiyāsh is boasting. One says fāyasha, when he boasted. He said, in a line of verse:
Do they still boast, when they have seen their ḥuffāth [a kind of snake] bite one of them, and their bravest then finished it off?
فيص:
The letters fā', yā', ṣād are a small root indicating a flowing in something, of water or the like. One says: fāṣa al-mā'u wa-al-damu, when it dripped.

Al-Aṣmaʿī said, on the saying of Imru' al-Qays, "it is sweet, yafīṣ": I do not know what yafīṣ means, but one says mā fāṣa bi-kalimatin, meaning his tongue did not let it out [he did not utter a word]. And the sense is the same throughout. And from this chapter: mā lahu maḥīṣun wa-lā mafīṣun, meaning no way out through which he might slip free and pass.
فيض:
The letters fā', yā' and ḍād are one sound root pointing to a thing's running easily; then other things are measured upon it. From this: fāḍa al-mā'u yafīḍu — the water overflowed. And one says afāḍa inā'ahu, when he fills it until it overflows. And afāḍa dumūʿahu — he poured out his tears. And from it: afāḍa al-qawm min ʿArafa, when they push on, and that is like the running of a torrent. God, exalted be He, said: {then press on from where the people press on} [al-Baqara: 199]. And afāḍa al-qawm fī al-ḥadīth, when they plunge into it. He, glory be to Him, said: {when you plunge into it} [Yūnus: 61]. And from it: afāḍa bi-l-qidāḥ, when he casts with the divining arrows, as though he set them running from his hand. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And it is as if they were a bundle of arrows, and as if he sets them running upon the shafts and splits them apart.

And one says afāḍa al-baʿīr bi-jirratihi, when he brings up his cud from his chest. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And after their silence they brought up the cud from the man of the valley-beds, when they had grazed Ḥaqīl.

And a land dhāt fuyūḍ, when there is water in it that overflows. And so-and-so gave so-and-so a ghayḍ min fayḍ — that is, a little out of much.

Al-Aṣmaʿī said: the river of Baṣra alone is called al-Fayḍ.

And from the section: fāḍa al-rajul, when he died. A poet said, in a line of verse:
So an eye was put out and a soul flowed away.

He said: and I heard eloquent old men of Rabīʿa ibn Mālik saying fāḍat nafsuhu, with the ḍād; and I heard an old man of them reciting, in a line of verse:
And but for a term put off, my soul had almost flowed out, when their throngs pressed on.
فيظ:
The letters fā', yā', ẓā' are a word. One says fāẓa al-mayyitu fayẓan, the dead man breathed his last; one does not say fāẓat nafsuhu. He said, in a line of verse:
They do not bury, of their own, one who has fāẓa [breathed his last].
فيف: The letters fā', yā', fā' are a word. Al-fayf and al-fayfā' are the open, trackless desert.
فيق: The letters fā', yā', qāf — [al-fayqa] has already been discussed, and its origin is the wāw; it is what gathers of milk in the udder.
فيل:
The letters fāʾ, yāʾ and lām are a root indicating slackness and weakness. One says: rajulun fīlu al-raʾy — a man of weak judgement. Al-Kumayt said, in a line of verse: "Sons of the lord of generosity, do not show weakness [tafīlū] — for whatever you are, we shall excuse you, for it would be weakness [fīl]."
1. It is possible that al-fāʾil belongs to this — it is the flesh over the socket of the hip-bone, named for its softness. Abū ʿUbayd said: some took al-fāʾil to be a vein.
2. What is anomalous, outside this chapter: al-mufāyala, a game. They hide a thing in the sand and divide it into two portions, and ask the player in which of the two it lies. Ṭarafa said, in a line of verse: "Its chest cleaves the ripples of the water, as the player of the sand-game [al-mufāyil] divides the sand with his hand."
فين: The letters fā', yā', nūn are a word. They say: ya'tīhi al-faynata baʿda al-faynati, it comes to him now and again, as though he meant al-ḥīn baʿda al-ḥīn, time after time. God knows best what is correct.
قاب:
The letters qāf, alif and bā'. Al-qāb is the measure, the amount. And in our view the word holds two things: a substitution and a transformation. As for the substitution, the bā' stands in place of a dāl, and the alif is a transformation of a yā', so that the original form is al-qīd. God Almighty said: {and it was the measure of two bow-lengths} [al-Najm: 9]. And it is said: al-qāb is what lies between the grip and the curved tip of a bow — every bow has two qābs.

And among what is not of this chapter, though it too has a hamza, is their saying: qa'iba min al-sharāb — he became full from drink.
قاق: The letters qāf, alif and qāf are a single word, and it is al-qāq: the tall man.
قام:
The letters qāf, alif and mīm — mention of this has already passed, and the original letter throughout it all is a wāw.

And al-qāma is the pulley together with its rigging [used to draw water from a well]. A poet said, in lines of verse:
When I saw that it had no pulley, and that I was on the verge of exhaustion, I pulled with a pull that shook the frame loose.
قاه:
The letters qāf, alif and hā' are a word. They say: al-qāh is obedience and standing. And they recite:
When we saw obedience given to a commander.
قب:
The letters qāf and bā' are a sound root, denoting gathering and coming together.

1. al-qubba — the well-known dome or tent, so named for how it gathers together into its rounded shape.
2. al-qabqab — the belly, because it is the gathering-place of food.
3. al-qabb — a part of the pulley-wheel.
4. al-qabab, said to mean the thinness of the waist — its true meaning is that the waist draws together until it looks slender.
5. khayl qubb — lean, gaunt horses; that is for the loss of flesh and the firmness that remains in them, and not for any other reason.
6. al-qābba — Ibn al-Sikkīt said al-qābba is a drop of rain. He said al-Aṣmaʿī used to misread the word and say it meant thunder; what Ibn al-Sikkīt said is more correct and follows the pattern better, because the rain gathers up the dust.

Among what deviates from this chapter is their naming the third year al-qubāqib, so that they say ʿām [a year], qābil [the year after], qubāqib [the year after that].

Also deviating is their saying iqtabba yadahu, meaning he cut off his hand.
قبح:
The letters qāf, bā' and ḥā' are one word indicating the opposite of beauty, which is ugliness, al-qubḥ. One says qabbaḥahu Allāh — may God make him ugly; this is maqbūḥ and qabīḥ. Some claimed that the sense of qabbaḥahu is: He removed him and cast him far away. From this, His saying, Almighty: "and on the Day of Resurrection they will be among those cast away."

Falling outside the root — and I take it to be from speech whose one who understood it well has passed away — is their saying "kisr qabīḥ": the bone of the forearm, the half nearer the elbow.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Had you been a donkey, you would have been a donkey of abasement ... and had you been a broken piece, you would have been the qabīḥ piece.
قبر:
The letters qaf, ba and ra are a single sound root indicating obscurity/concealment in a thing, and a pressing-low of it.

1. al-qabr — the grave of the dead. One says 'qabartuhu aqburuhu' — I buried him. Al-A'sha said:
Had she propped a dead man against her breast, he would have lived, and never been carried off to a grave-digger.
2. If you provide him a place in which he is buried, you say 'aqbartuhu' — I had him given a grave. God, Most High, said: {then He made him die, and had him buried} [Abasa: 21].

We say: had the scholars not shown such latitude in this matter, we would not think it fitting to join the word of God together with poetry in a single book — let alone on a single sheet or page. But we have followed their example, and God, Most High, forgives us and pardons us and them.

Some scholars of exegesis said, regarding His saying, Most High, {then He made him die, and had him buried} [Abasa: 21]: that he was inspired as to how burial is done.

Ibn Duraid said: low-lying, hidden ground is 'ardun qabur'. A palm tree whose fruit grows hidden among its fronds is 'nakhlatun qabur [and kabus]'. The place of graves is 'maqbara' and 'maqbura'.
قبس:
The letters qāf, bāʾ, and sīn are a sound root pointing to one of the qualities of fire, then used by way of borrowed meaning. From this, al-qabas is a flame taken from a fire. God Most High said, in the story of Moses, peace be upon him: {perhaps I may bring you a firebrand (qabas) from it} [Ṭāhā: 10]. They say: aqbastu al-rajula ʿilman, I gave the man a spark of knowledge, and qabastuhu nāran, I gave him fire. Ibn Durayd said: qabastu min fulānin nāran, I took fire from so-and-so; iqtabastu minhu ʿilman, I acquired knowledge from him; and aqbasanī qabasan, he gave me a firebrand.

From this same reasoning is their saying: faḥlun qabīs, a sire quick to get a female with young, as though likened to a flame of fire. A poet said:
... a mother who is a swift eagle, and a father who is qabīs [the line is cut off before it and cannot be rendered in full]
As for al-qibs, it is said that it is the origin/root.
قبص:
The letters qāf, bā' and ṣād are two roots: one indicates lightness and speed, the other gathering-together.

The first is al-qabaṣ, which is lightness and briskness.

1. al-qabūṣ — a horse that, when it runs, only the tips of its hooves touch the ground.
2. al-qabṣ — taking something with the fingertips, which only happens out of lightness and haste.

And it was read, as a variant: "so I took a handful (qabaṣtu qabṣatan) from the trace of the messenger," with a ṣād. And what is taken that way is called a qabṣa.

The other root is al-qibṣ, which is a great number [of people]. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Yours are the two visited mosques of God, and the gravel [around them] — yours is its great number, from among the wealthy and the poor alike.

1. al-qabaṣ in the head — largeness; one says of it hāma qabṣā', a large head. Abū al-Najm said:
A large head, neither flattened nor tightly balled up.

And among what deviates from these two roots is al-qabṣ, a pain brought on by eating raisins. A poet said:
Companions complaining of gripe and of qabaṣ.
قبض:
The letters qāf, bā' and ḍād are one sound root pointing to a thing taken, and to a gathering in a thing.

You say: qabaḍtu al-shay'a, of money and other things, qabḍan — I took hold of it. And maqbiḍ al-sayf and maqbaḍuhu is where you grip it. And al-qabaḍ, with a fatḥa on the bā', is what is gathered and collected of the spoils. One says: throw this into the qabaḍ — that is, among the rest of what has been taken of the spoil. As for al-qabḍ which is speed, that too is from this, because when he hastens he gathers himself and his limbs together. God, exalted be He, said: {have they not seen the birds above them spreading their wings and drawing them in — nothing holds them up but ...} [al-Mulk: 19]. They said: they hasten in flight. And this word is from their saying a herdsman qubaḍa, when he does not range widely in the pasture of his flock. One says: he is qubaḍa rufaḍa — that is, he gathers them in until, when he reaches the place he is making for, he lets them scatter. And they say of the rough driver: qabbāḍa and qābiḍ. Ru'ba said, in a line of verse:
A hard driver, between the rough and the deft.

And from the section: inqabaḍa ʿan al-amr and taqabbaḍa, when he shrinks from it in disgust.
قبط:
The letters qāf, bā' and ṭā' are a sound root. Ibn Durayd said: al-qabṭ is your gathering something with your hand. One says: qabaṭtuhu aqbiṭuhu qabṭan. He said: from this al-qubbāṭ was named — this is the sweet [confection] — genuine Arabic.

And among what is not of this chapter is al-qibṭ: the people of Egypt, the Copts; the adjective for them is qibṭī. The garments called al-qubṭiyya are perhaps named after them, except that the qāf is pronounced with a ḍamma to keep the two words apart. Zuhayr said, in a line of verse:
There shall come to you from me foul speech, lasting, just as grease stains a qubṭī garment.

Its plural is qabāṭī.
قبع:
The letters qāf, bā' and ʿayn are a sound root indicating something like a person, or something else, hiding itself.

1. qabaʿa — said of the pig and the hedgehog, when it draws its head into its neck.
2. jāriya qubaʿa ṭulaʿa — a girl who hides herself at times and peeks out at other times.
3. al-qubaʿa — a cloth like a hood, which common people call al-qunbuʿa.
4. al-qubāʿ — a large measuring vessel, as though named qubāʿ for what sinks down into it.
5. qabaʿa al-rajul — the man grew exhausted and short of breath; he is called qābiʿ because he draws himself in and stops moving when exhausted.

And among what deviates from this chapter is qabīʿat al-sayf, the piece of iron or silver at the end of a sword's hilt.
قبل:
The letters qāf, bā' and lām are a single sound root, all of whose words point to a thing's facing a thing; and after that it branches out.

So al-qubul of everything is the opposite of its back, and that is because its front part faces the thing. And al-qabīl is what a woman brings forward of her spinning when she twists it, and al-dabīr is what she takes backward. And that is the meaning of their saying: " He does not know qabīl from dabīr ". And al-qibla was named qibla for people's turning to face it in their prayer, and it faces them as well. And one says faʿala dhālika qibalan, that is, face to face. And hādhā min qibali fulān, that is, from him, as though he were the one who turned it towards you. And al-qibāl is the leading-rope of the camel and the thong of the sandal. And qābaltuhā — I made two thongs for it, because each of the two faces the other.

And a ewe that is muqābala is one from whose ear a piece was cut and not severed, and left hanging from the front. [And if it is] from behind, she is mudābara. And al-qābila is the coming night. And al-ʿām al-qābil is the coming year, and no verb is used from it. And al-qābila is the woman who receives the child at the birth. And al-qabūl among the winds is the east wind, because it faces the west wind, or the house. And qabiltu al-shay' qabūlan — I accepted the thing. And al-qabal in the eye is the turning of the black of it towards the inner corner, and it is said: rather it is its turning towards the nose. And al-qabal is the rise of ground that faces you. You say: I saw a figure on that rise. And al-qabīl is the surety; one says qabila bihi qabālatan, and that is because he turns towards the thing to guarantee it. And ifʿal dhālika ilā ʿashrin min dhī qabalin, that is, in the time still to come. And one says aqbalnā ʿalā al-ibil — we drew water at the camels' heads while they were drinking. [And] that is al-qabal. And so-and-so is muqtabal al-shabāb — fresh in his youth: no trace of age has shown in him and his youth has not turned away. And he said:
He is no aged worn-out man with no youth in him; rather a young palm-shoot, clear of colour, fresh in his prime.

And al-qābil is the one who takes the bucket of the watering camel. He said:
And a receiver who sings out whenever his two hands close upon the well-rope, standing, and it pours.

Ibn Durayd said: al-qabala is [a bead like a spindle-whorl, hung on the necks of horses]; and it is said that al-qabala is a thing the sorceress makes, by which she turns one person's face towards another. And qabā'il al-ra's are the pieces of the skull that the sutures join between; and they were so named because each one of them faces the other; and by that the tribes of the Arabs were named. And qabīl al-qawm is their headman; and he was so named because he turns towards them and looks into their affairs. He said:
Is it that whenever a tribe comes to ʿUkāẓ, they send to me their headman to take my measure?

And we are in the qabāla of so-and-so, that is, under his headship. And mā li-fulānin qibla, that is, no direction to turn to and face. And they say: al-qabīl is a body gathered from various tribes, and al-qabīla is the sons of one father. And this, in our view, is merely something that has been said; and the sons of one father may be called qubayl. Labīd said:
And a company from ʿUqayl, true of word.

As for their saying lā qibala lī bihi, that is, I have no strength for it — it is of the section, that is, he is not such that I could face him. As for qablu, which is the opposite of baʿdu, " after ", it may be an oddity falling outside the root we have mentioned; and one may strain to fit it in by saying that it faces the time. And in our view it is nearer to being an oddity.
قبن:
The letters qāf, bā' and nūn. They say:

1. qabana fī al-arḍ — he went off into the land.
2. ḥimār qabbān — a small creature.
قبو:
The letters qāf, bā' and wāw are a sound word, indicating joining and gathering.

1. qabawtu al-shay' — I gathered it and drew it together.
2. al-qabw — what the people of Medina call the raising [ḍamma] in vowel-marking; one says of a letter so marked: it is maqbūw.
3. al-qabā' [the long coat] — said to be derived from this, because a person wraps and gathers it around himself.
قت:
The letters qāf and tā' contain two unrelated words.

1. al-qatt — tale-bearing, carrying talk from one to another. It came in the report: "A tale-bearer [qattāt] will not enter Paradise" — meaning the slanderer, al-nammām. Al-qatt is also the name of a plant.
2. al-taqtīt — perfuming oil with sweet-smelling herbs; al-qatt is used for this too.
قتب:
The letters qāf, tā' and bā' are a sound root indicating an implement among those used for mounts, or something else.

1. al-qatab — for the camel, well known.
2. qatūba — camels on which loads are placed.
3. Ibn Durayd said: al-qatab — a camel is qataba when it is one of those loaded with burdens; but if it belongs to the apparatus of a well-drawing camel, it is called qitb, with the qāf carrying a kasra.
4. al-aqtāb — the intestines; the singular is qatb, and its diminutive is qutayba, this being by way of comparing them to the aqtāb, the pack-saddles of mounts.
قتد:
The letters qāf, tā' and dāl are a sound root, and it is [really] two words:

1. al-qatad — the wood of the camel-saddle frame; its plural is aqtād and qutūd.
2. al-qatād — the other word: a kind of thorny acacia; there is nothing more to it than this.
3. Qatā'id — they say it is a place-name.
قتر:
The letters qāf, tā' and rā' are a sound root indicating gathering together and narrowing.

1. Al-qutra: the hunter's hide, named qutra for its narrowness and because the hunter gathers himself into it; plural qutar.
2. Al-iqtār: stinting in spending. One says "qatara l-rajulu ʿalā ahlihi yaqturu," "aqtara," and "qattara" — he was tight-fisted with his family. God, exalted is He, said: those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy.
3. Al-qatar: what covers the face from anguish. God said: {no darkness or humiliation shall cover their faces} [Yūnus: 26] [Yūnus: 26].
4. Al-qatar: dust.
5. Al-qātir, of riding saddles: the one that sits well on the camel's back — because when it settles well, it presses the hump together.

As for al-qutār, in our view the origin is that the lion-hunter would set out meat little by little in his hide, so the lion would catch its scent and come to the pit-trap; afterward the smell of any roasted meat, whatever it was, came to be called qutār.

Ṭarafa said, in a line of verse:
The people called out to one another in their gathering-place: is that the smell of roasting meat, or the scent of aloeswood?

"She qattarat for the lion" is said when you set out meat for it so it catches the smell of qutār. Ibn al-Sikkīt said: "qatara l-laḥmu, yaqturu" — its smoke rose; it is qātir.

6. Al-qatīr: the heads of the rings in mail-armor. Gray hair is also called qatīr, by comparison to the heads of nails, for their whiteness and gleam.

As for al-qutr, it means "side," and does not belong here — it is a letter-substitution for al-quṭr, which has already been mentioned.

Among what falls outside this root: ibn qitra — a vicious little snake, quite small. So said al-Farrā'. He said: it seems to be named after the headless arrow, which is called qitra; plural qitr.
قتع:
The letters qāf, tā' and ʿayn are a word. It is said that al-qataʿ are red worms that eat wood, the singular being qataʿa. He said:
Timbers in whose insides the qataʿ writhe.

And Ibn Durayd related: qataʿa al-rajul, qutūʿan — when he shrank back out of humiliation.
قتل:
The letters qāf, tā' and lām are a sound root pointing to humbling and to putting to death. One says qatalahu qatlan - he killed him. Al-qitla is the manner in which a man is killed; one says qatalahu qitlata sū'in - he killed him an evil killing. Al-qatla is the single time. Maqātil al-insān are the places in a man which, if they are struck, kill him. And of this: qataltu al-shay' khubran wa-'ilman - I came to know the thing through and through. God, be He praised, said: {wa-mā qatalūhu yaqīnan} [al-Nisā': 157]. [And one says: taqattalat al-jāriya li-l-rajul, the girl made herself killingly sweet to the man, until he loved her, as though she made herself submissive to him. A poet said, in a line of verse:]
You made yourself killingly sweet to me, and then, when you had killed me, you turned devout - this is no deed of devout women.

And aqtaltu fulānan - I exposed him to being killed. And a heart is muqattal when love has killed it. Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
Your two eyes shed tears only that you might strike with your two arrows into the pieces of a slain heart.

The people of the language said: one says qutila al-rajul, the man was killed; but if it is from love one says uqtutila, and likewise if the jinn have killed him. Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
When they set about killing a man, with no rancour between the souls and no blood-debt.

And qutilat al-khamr bi-l-mā', when the wine is mixed with water; and this is of the fine kind of metaphor. A poet said, in a line of verse:
The cup you handed me and I gave back - it was killed. May you be killed! Now bring it unkilled.

Among what strays from this section, though it might be brought into it by a fine consideration: al-qitl, the enemy, and its plural is aqtāl. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And my being far from 'Āmir ibn Lu'ayy, in lands full of enemies.

And the way of its analogy is to make al-qitl the one who fights, like al-sibb, the one [who reviles]. And this is not far-fetched. And their saying humā qitlān, that is, they are two alike, is from this. As for al-qatāl, it is said that it is the self; one says a she-camel is dhātu qatālin when she is firmly built. And some of the people of learning said: this is a substitution of letters, and the origin is al-katāl. And that points to the gathering together of the body; one says takattala al-shay' when it gathered together. And this is a good line of reasoning.
قتم:
The letters qāf, tā' and mīm are a sound root indicating dustiness and blackness.

1. aqtam — every colour overlaid with black.
2. al-qatām — black dust; from it comes [the description] a hawk aqtam al-rīsh, black-feathered.
3. makān qātim — a place that is dusty, dark on its edges.

Ru'ba said, in a line of verse:
And a dust-dark land of deep reaches, hollow where the wind cuts through.
قتن:
The letters qāf, tā' and nūn are a sound word. They say: al-qatīn is a woman who eats little; she has become qatunat qatāna. Al-Shammākh said, in a line of verse:
Her udder-folds had sweated, and so she gave freely, with her flow of milk, sustenance to a puny, thin one.

He meant by it the tick, thin of blood.
قتو:
The letters qāf, tā' and wāw. They say: al-qatw is fine service. And so-and-so yaqtū al-mulūk — he serves kings. He said [the text here has a gap in the edition]:
...I am not good at the service of kings, nor at the ambling gait.

As for al-muqtawī and al-maqtawīn... [the text breaks off here].
قث: The letters qāf and thā' make up one word, denoting gathering. One says: so-and-so came, gathering [yaquththu] wealth and broad worldly goods.
قثا: The letters qāf, thā' and the elongated alif. Al-qiththā' [the cucumber] is well known.
قثد: The letters qāf, thā' and dāl amount to nothing [are not a real root], except that it is said: al-qathad is a plant.
قثم:
The letters qāf, thā' and mīm are a root indicating gathering and giving.

1. qathama min mālihi — he gave from his wealth.
2. rajul quthum — a freely-giving man.
3. al-qathūm — a man who gathers up good [provision] in abundance.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
For the great ones there is eating however they wish, and for the lesser ones there is eating and scraping together what is left.
قح: The letters qāf and ḥā' are not, in our view, a root at all. But they say: al-quḥḥ is the coarse, crude one among people and things — so much so that they call an unripe melon "a quḥḥ."
قحب: The letters qāf, ḥā' and bā' are a word denoting the coughing of horses and camels, and it may sometimes be used of people too.
قحد: The letters qāf, ḥā' and dāl are a single word, it is al-qaḥada: the base of the camel's hump, the plural being qiḥād. And a she-camel [described as] miqḥād has a large hump.
قحر:
The letters qāf, ḥā' and rā' are a single word, and it is al-qaḥr: it is said to be an old stud-camel who still has some vigour and toughness left in him. It may also be said of a man.

1. al-quḥāriya — the same as al-qaḥr.
2. imra'a qaḥra — an elderly woman.
قحز:
The letters qāf, ḥā' and zā' are a single root indicating restlessness, or unsettling and disturbing.

1. al-qaḥz — leaping about, restlessness.
2. al-qāḥizāt — harsh, disturbing matters.
3. Ibn Durayd said: al-qaḥz is for the archer to shoot an arrow and have it fall short, just in front of him; one says qaḥaza al-sahmu qaḥzan. He said:
When the leaping fits of restlessness surge up.
4. al-quḥāz — a disease that afflicts sheep.
قحط:
The letters qāf, ḥā' and ṭā' are a sound root indicating the withholding of good, then it is used figuratively.

1. al-qaḥṭ — the withholding of rain; the people aqḥaṭū, fell into drought.
2. aqḥaṭa al-rajul — said of a man when he had intercourse with his wife but did not ejaculate.
3. Qaḥṭān — the [ancestral] father of Yemen.
قحف:
The letters qāf, ḥā' and fā' are a sound root indicating intensity and hardness in something.

1. al-qaḥf — intense drinking. They say, as a proverb: "Today is heavy drinking, and tomorrow is skull-cracking."
2. al-qāḥif, said of rain — the intense rain that sweeps everything away.
3. al-qiḥf, of this chapter — the bone [the skull-cap] above the brain; its plural is aqḥāf.
4. qaḥaftuhu — I struck his skull-cap.
قحل:
The letters qāf, ḥā' and lām are a sound root indicating dryness in something and aridity.

1. al-qaḥal — dryness.
2. al-qāḥil — the dried-up thing; one says qaḥala yaqḥalu and qaḥila yaqḥalu, both forms being used.
3. qaḥila al-shaykh — the old man's skin dried up on his bones.
4. rajul qaḥl and inqaḥl — [both said of] a withered man.
5. al-quḥāl — a disease that afflicts sheep, causing their skins to dry up.
قحم: The letters qāf, ḥā' and mīm are a sound root indicating entering into a thing with some roughness and boldness. One says qaḥama fī al-umūri quḥūman, he threw himself into matters without prior experience. Quḥam al-ṭarīq: its hard, difficult stretches. It is said al-maqāḥīm, among camels, are those that plunge in among the she-camels without being deliberately let loose to mate. Al-qaḥm: a camel that grows two extra sets of teeth within a single year, so that one age is thrust upon another. Qaḥḥama al-farasu fārisahu 'alā wajhihi, when the horse threw its rider down on his face. They say: "Disputes have their quḥam," meaning they thrust the one caught up in them into what he does not want. Al-quḥmah: the drought-year that forces the bedouin into the fertile lands.
قحو:
The letters qāf, ḥā' and wāw are a single word. They say: al-qaḥw is the base-formation of al-uqḥuwān [the chamomile flower], on the pattern uf'ulān; and were it put into a medicine one would say maqḥūw; its plural is al-aqāḥī.

And al-Uqḥuwāna is a place-name.
قد:
The letters qāf and dāl are a sound root, denoting the cutting of a thing lengthwise; the word is then used more widely by extension.

1. qadadtu al-shay' qaddan, aquddahu — I cut the thing lengthwise. One also says huwa ḥasanu l-qadd, he has a fine build [qadd, his cut], meaning the length of his stature.
2. al-qidd — a strip cut from untanned hide; al-qadīd, dried strips of meat, is derived from it.
3. al-qidda — a way, or a group of people, when each one's inclination differs from the next's. From this they extend the word and say iqtadda fulānun al-umūr, so-and-so sorted through the affairs and told them apart; and qadda al-musāfiru al-mafāza, the traveller cut across the wasteland.
4. al-qaydūd — a she-camel long in the back, close along the ground.
5. al-qadd — the hide of a young kid, the she-goat's young. They say in the proverb: "Your stature is not made to fit your hide."
6. al-qudād — a pain in the belly.
قدح:
The letters qāf, dāl and ḥā' are two sound roots: one indicates something like a dent or hollow in a thing, the other indicates the scooping-out of something.

The first: al-qadḥ — your act when you qadaḥ a thing. al-qadḥ — decay that occurs in trees and in teeth. al-qādiḥa — the worm that eats the tree. From this: qadaḥa fī nasabihi — he attacked his lineage.

He said, of decay in teeth, in a line of verse:
May God cast a mote of dust into Buthayna's eyes ... and decay into the shining front teeth of hers.

1. al-qidḥ — the arrow shaft without head or feathers, seemingly named because fire can be struck (yuqdaḥu) with it.
2. al-qidḥ — one of the arrows used in the game of maysir [gambling by lots], this by resemblance.
3. quddiḥa al-faras taqdīḥan — the horse was made lean and fit until it became like the shaft (qadḥ).
4. qaddaḥat al-ʿayn — the eye became sunken; one also says qadaḥat.
5. qadaḥtu al-nār — I struck fire. qadaḥtu al-ʿayn — I drew the diseased matter out of it.

The other root: al-qadīḥ — what remains at the bottom of the pot, scooped out with effort.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And the slave-women went on racing each other for its dregs ... as [the tribe of] Kalb once raced for the waters of Qurāqir.

qadaḥtu al-qidr — I scooped out what was in the pot. rakiyy qadūḥ — a well drawn from by hand. And al-qadaḥ, among vessels, is from this, because a thing is scooped out with it.
قدر:
The letters qāf, dāl and rā' are a sound root pointing to the extent of a thing, its full measure and its limit. So al-qadr is the extent of everything. One says qadruhu kadhā — that is, its extent is such. And so too al-qadar. And qadartu al-shay' aqdiruhu and aqduruhu, from al-taqdīr, the measuring out; and qaddartuhu uqaddiruhu.

And al-qadr is God's decreeing of things, exalted be He, at the extents and limits that He willed for them; and that is al-qadar as well.

He said, of al-qadar, in a line of verse:
Leave the road to him who builds his landmark upon it, and step out into open ground where fate has forced you.

And he said, of al-qadr with a sukūn on the dāl, in a line of verse:
[And nothing set my leg in the irons of Mujāshiʿ, along with fate, but a need of mine that I was seeking.]

And from this chapter is al-aqdar among horses, which is the one whose hind feet fall in the places of his forefeet, as though something had measured that out exactly.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And a well-measured horse, high in the withers, long-striding, a bay, neither over-long nor short in the hind legs.

And His saying, exalted be He: {wa-mā qadarū Allāha ḥaqqa qadrih} — and they did not measure God with His true measure [al-Anʿām: 91] — the commentators said: they did not magnify God as His greatness deserves. And this is sound; the sum of it is that they did not describe Him with the description that befits Him, exalted be He.

And His saying, exalted be He: {wa-man qudira ʿalayhi rizquh} — and he whose provision is straitened [al-Ṭalāq: 7] — its meaning is that it was made scant. And its pattern is that he was given that by a small measure. And God's power, exalted be He, over His creation is His bringing them to the extent that He wishes and wills; and the pattern in this and in what came before it is the same. And they say rajulun dhū qudratin and dhū maqdiratin — that is, of means. Its meaning is that by his means and his riches he reaches, in affairs, the extent that agrees with his will. And they say al-aqdar among men is the short-necked, and that is the pattern too, as though his neck had been cut to measure.

And of what also strays from this pattern is al-qidr, the cooking-pot, which is well known. And al-qadīr is meat cooked in the pot. And al-qudār, by their account, is the butcher; and it is said the cook, which is the more likely.

And of what also strays is their saying al-qudār: the great serpent — and there is doubt in it.
قدس:
The letters qāf, dāl and sīn are a sound root — and I think it belongs to the language of Islamic law — and it points to purity.

From that, al-arḍ al-muqaddasa, the hallowed land, is the purified land. Paradise is called ḥaẓīrat al-quds, the enclosure of holiness, that is, of purity. And Gabriel, peace be upon him, is rūḥ al-qudus, the spirit of holiness. All of that has one meaning. Among the attributes of God Almighty is al-Quddūs, and it is that same meaning, because He is set far above opposites and equals, and above a consort and a child; God is exalted far above what the wrongdoers say. It is said that al-Qādisiyya was named from this, and that Abraham, peace be upon him, prayed for it that it be holy and be a halting place for the pilgrims. Quds is a mountain. They say that al-qudās is a thing like a pearl, made of silver. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Like a string of qudās beads whose thread is snapped through.
قدع:
The letters qāf, dāl and ʿayn are two distinct sound roots. One denotes holding back from something, and the other denotes falling headlong into something.

The first is explained as follows: al-qadʿ, from qadaʿtuhu ʿan al-shayʾ, I held him back from it.

1. al-qadʿ (restraint) — one also says qadaʿtu al-dhubāb, I drove the fly away from me. A poet said, in a line of verse: standing, driving the flies from itself with tails like the wings of vultures.
2. qadiʿa (a woman so described) — one of few words, shy, as though she had held herself back from speaking.
3. qadaʿtu al-faras bi-l-lijām — I curbed the horse with the bridle.
4. al-miqdaʿa — the stick you fend things off with.

Ibn Durayd said: taqādaʿa al-qawm bi-l-rimāḥ means they thrust spears at one another. The reasoning behind all of this is one and the same.

The other root is falling headlong.

1. al-qadūʿ — that which pours down upon a thing.
2. taqādaʿa al-firāsh fī al-nār — said when moths fall headlong into the fire.
3. taqādaʿa al-qawm baʿḍuhum fī ithri baʿḍ — the people fell one after another.

And in the hadith, speaking of the Bridge over Hell: they fall headlong one after another as moths fall headlong into the fire.
قدف: The letters qāf, dāl and fāʾ. They say: al-qadf is dipping water out of the trough. And it is said that al-qudāf is a jar of pottery.
قدم:
The letters qāf, dāl and mīm are a sound root pointing to going before and precedence, and then what comes near to it is branched off from it. They say: al-qidam is the opposite of coming newly into being. And one says a thing is qadīm, old, when its time is long past. Its origin is their saying maḍā fulān qudum(an) — so-and-so went straight forward; he did not turn aside and did not bend back. And sometimes they make the diminutive of qudḍām: qudaydīm and qudaydīma. Al-Quṭāmī said, in a line of verse:
A little before the trying and the forbearance — truly ... I see the heedless times of life come before the trials.

And one says ḍuriba fa-rakiba maqādīmahu when he falls upon his face. And qādimat al-raḥl is the front of the saddle, the opposite of its rear. And al-qādima of the teats of a she-camel is the one next to the navel. And so-and-so has a qadam ṣidq — that is, something gone before him of good record.

And of this chapter: qadima min safarihi qudūman — he came home from his journey; and aqdama ʿalā al-shay' iqdāman — he pressed forward upon the thing. Ibn Durayd said: the qādim of a man is his head; the plural is qawādim. He said: and they hardly ever speak the singular. And qawādim al-ṭayr are the foremost feathers, ten in each wing; the singular is qādima, and they are al-qudāmā. And muqaddimat al-jaysh is the front of the army. And aqdim is a shout urging on a horse, as though it were commanded to press forward. And "the people went in the war al-yaqdumiyya" when they pushed forward. A poet said:
Those who strike the forward-pressing stroke with the broad Indian blades.

And qaydūm al-jabal is a nose of rock jutting forward from the mountain. And the line:
We strike their heads with the swords ... as the butcher strikes the welcome-feast portion of the qudḍām —
some people said: al-qudḍām is the king. And this is sound reasoning, because the king is the one put in front. And it is said: al-qudḍām are those who come home from a journey. And qadam al-insān, the foot of a man, is well known, and perhaps it was named so because it is the instrument of going forward and going first.

And of what strays from this root is al-qadūm, the iron tool with which one hews, and it is well known. And al-Qadūm is a place. And in the hadith: "Abraham, peace be upon him, was circumcised at al-Qadūm."
قدو:
The letters qāf, dāl and a weak final letter are a sound root indicating drawing guidance from a thing and being rightly directed by it, and a measuring of a thing so as to make it equal to another. From this, their saying: hādhā qidā rumḥin, meaning its length, its measure. So-and-so is qidwah, meaning one to be followed, an example.

They say: al-qadw is the origin from which the branches spread out. From this chapter: fulānun yaqdū bihi farasuhu, when his horse keeps to a steady, measured pace. It is called qadw because it is a measured way of going. Taqaddā fulānun 'alā dābbatihi, when he rode along steadily and directly.

One says: atatnā qādiyatun min al-nās, a first wave of people came to us, the ones who arrive ahead of the rest; one says qadat taqdī. And all of that comes from the measured pace of going.

What falls outside this chapter: al-qadw, the verbal noun of qadā al-laḥmu yaqdū qadwan and yaqdī qadyan, when you catch a pleasant smell from meat. And they say rajulun qinda'w, meaning strong-backed and short-necked.
قذ:
The letters qāf and dhāl are close to the one before, denoting cutting and evening out, whether lengthwise or not.

1. al-qudhadh — the fletching-feathers of an arrow; one feather is a qudhdha. They said al-qadhdh is the cutting of them. One says udhunun maqdhūdha, a clipped ear, as though it had been shaved away. A poet said, in a line of verse: "Clipped of ears, true of eyes."
2. al-qudhādhāt — some claimed these are pieces of gold, and that al-judhādhāt are pieces of silver.
3. al-sahmu l-aqadhdh — the arrow with no fletching on it.
4. al-maqadhdh — the place between the two ears at the back of the head, so named because its hair is clipped away.

Among what deviates from this chapter is their saying that al-qidhdhān means fleas.
قذر:
The letters qāf, dhāl and rā' are a word denoting the opposite of cleanliness.

1. shayʾun qadhirun — a thing plainly filthy.
2. qadhirtu al-shayʾ and istaqdhartuhu — I found the thing filthy; and if you found it to be so, you say aqdhartuhu, I found/declared it filthy.
3. qadhirtu al-shayʾ, meaning karihtuhu qadharan — I loathed the thing, with loathing. A poet said, in a line of verse: my disgust is at what does not deserve disgust.
4. rajulun qādhūra — a man who keeps no company and mixes with no one.
5. nāqatun qadhūr — a proud she-camel that will not graze among the other camels.
6. rajulun maqdhūr — like al-muqdhar, one held in contempt.

Al-Kilābī said: rajulun qudhara is one who shuns whatever is unfitting.
قذع:
The letters qāf, dhāl and ʿayn are a word denoting obscenity.

1. al-qadhaʿ — foul, obscene speech.
2. aqdhaʿa fulānun — so-and-so came out with obscenity. And in the hadith: whoever speaks obscene verse within Islam, his tongue counts for nothing (carries no protection).
3. qadhaʿtu fulānan and aqdhaʿtuhu — I flung obscenity at him.
4. aqdhaʿtu — I came out with obscenity, said of oneself.
قذف:
The letters qāf, dhāl and fā' are a root pointing to throwing and casting. One says qadhafa al-shay'a yaqdhifuhu qadhfan, when he throws it. And a land qadhūf — that is, far-flinging in its distance, tossing the travellers about. And a lodging qadhaf and qadhīf — that is, far off. And a she-camel maqdhūfa with flesh, as though she had been pelted with it.

And al-qidhāf is swiftness of going. And a horse [mutaqādhif] is swift of running, as though he tosses himself about in his running.

And from the section: aqdhāf al-jabal are its sides, the single one qadhaf. And al-qadhīfa is the thing that is thrown. A poet said, in a line of verse:
A missile of a stoned devil, that he flung, and it became a lump in the jaws of an old she-camel.

Al-ḍawāt is a swelling. And al-ḍirzim is the aged she-camel. And qadhafa: he vomited, as though he threw it out.
قذل:
The letters qāf, dhāl and lām are a single word, al-qadhal: the whole of the back of the head.

1. qadhaltuhu — I struck him on the back of the head, his qadhāl.
2. al-qadhl — they also say this means leaning aside, and injustice.
قذم:
The letters qāf, dhāl and mīm are a sound root denoting abundance and plenty.

1. al-qadhm — a generous gift; one says qadhama lahu, he gave generously to him.
2. al-qidhamm — a swift horse.
3. a qudham man — one who takes a great deal of a thing once he has got hold of it.
قذي:
The letters qāf, dhāl and the weak letter [y] are a single word denoting the opposite of clarity and purity.

1. al-qadhā (in a drink) — whatever falls into it and spoils it.
2. al-qadhā (in the eye) — one says qadhat ʿaynuhu taqdhī when the eye casts the qadhā (a speck) out, and qadhiyat taqdhā when the qadhā has got into it.
3. qadhaytuhā — I removed the qadhā from it (the eye).
قر:
The letters qāf and rā' are two sound roots: one denotes cold, the other denotes settledness.

The first is al-qurr, which is cold; a day is described as qārr and qarr. A poet, Imru' al-Qays, said, in a line of verse: "When they mounted their horses and put on their mail, the earth blazed, and the day was cold." A night, too, is qarra and qārra. One says: our day turned cold, yaqurru.

1. al-qirra — the chill of a fever, the point at which one feels from it a slackening and an aching through the limbs. They say: "a burning thirst beneath a chill" — al-ḥirra being thirst, and al-qirra the chill of the fever.

Their saying aqarra Allāhu ʿaynahu (may God settle/cool his eye, i.e. bring him joy) — some claim this too belongs to the chapter of cold, holding that joy brings a cool tear and grief a hot one, and that is why one says of a man who is cursed: asakhana Allāhu ʿaynahu, may God heat his eye.

2. al-qarūr — cold water one washes with. One says from it iqtarartu, I washed myself with cold water.

The other root is settledness: one says qarra and istaqarra.

1. al-qarr — a kind of mount or litter that women ride. A poet said, in a line of verse: "upon a frame like the qarr, my shrouds fluttering."
2. al-qarr — also used for the pouring of water into something; one says qarartu al-mā', I poured the water.
3. al-qarr — the pouring of speech into the ear.
4. al-qarqar — smooth, level open ground.
5. al-qurāra — what sticks to the bottom of the cooking-pot, as though it were something that had settled there.
6. al-iqrār — the opposite of denial; and this, in our view, is a sound analogy, for when a person acknowledges a right he has fixed it firmly in its place.

Some say, of the customary prayer aqarra Allāhu ʿaynahu: it means He gave him enough that his eye settled and did not look longingly at one above him.

7. yawm al-qarr — the day people settle at Minā, the morning after the Day of Sacrifice.

We say: these are sound patterns, as you see, in both chapters together. But to go further and press the word too far, as has reached us from some who said the qārūra [glass vial] was named for the settling of water and other things in it — that is not our position. We have said that the speech of the Arabs is of two kinds: one that follows a pattern, which we have set out, and one that is simply given as it stands, and we have recorded all of that. God knows best.

As for sounds, they may follow a pattern, though most of them are simply imitations. So they say: the dove cooed [qarqarat], a cooing, a qarqarīr.
قرب:
The letters qāf, rā' and bā' are a sound root pointing to the opposite of farness.

One says qaruba yaqrubu qurban. And so-and-so is dhū qarābatī, and he is the one near you in kinship. And so-and-so is my qarīb, and one of my kin. Al-qurba and al-qurbā are kinship. Al-qirāb is coming close to a matter. And you say mā qarubtu hādhā al-amra wa-lā aqrabuhu — when you have not gone near it and have not got mixed up in it.

Of the section is al-qarab, and it is the night on which the camels come down to water; and that is because the people pasture the camels while at the same time they are moving toward the water, and when there is only an evening left between them and the water they hurry toward it — and that night is the night of al-qarab. Al-qārib is the one seeking water by night. Al-Khalīl said: this is not said of the one seeking it by day.

And they have inflected the verb from al-qarab and said qarabtu al-mā'a aqrubuhu qaraban, and that is on the pattern of ṭalabtu aṭlubu ṭalaban (I sought, I seek, a seeking) and ḥalabtu aḥlubu ḥalaban (I milked, I milk, a milking). And they say that al-qārib is a small boat kept with the men of the seagoing ships, made light for their needs; and it is as though it was named so for its nearness to them. Al-qurbān is what is brought near to God, exalted, of a sacrifice or of something else.

Of the section: the king's qurbān and his qarābīn — his ministers and those who sit with him. And a farasun muqraba is the mare that is watched over and kept close and not left to graze at will. Ibn Durayd said: that is only done with the females, so that no base stallion may cover them.

And one says qarraba al-farasu taqrīban, and it is a pace short of the gallop; and it was called taqrīb because when it goes at full gallop its reach is longer. And it has, as they say, two taqrībs: a lower and a higher. And one says aqrabat al-shāt — the ewe's lambing drew near.

Ibn al-Sikkīt said: thawbun muqārib — when it is not good. And this is in the sense that it is middling in its price, neither far off nor dear. And someone else reported: thawbun muqārib — not good; and thawbun muqārib — cheap; and the reasoning in all of it is one.

As for the flank, it is al-qurb, named so for its nearness to the side. And a people said: it was named by likening it to al-qirba, the waterskin. They said: and this is another line of reasoning — it is only from a thing's gathering something in and holding it. They said: and from it is al-qirāb, the sheath of the sword, and the plural is qurub. The poet said, in a line of verse:
O mistress of the house, rise, and no shame to you, gather to yourself the men's saddles and the sword-sheaths.

And the poet said, of al-qurb, which is the flank, in a line of verse:
And whenever the food was brought near I was set upon a dark-red mare, tough, not stripped of her hair,
close-knit in the flanks, not thin, dark-red, as though she were the water-bag of a she-camel that has lost her young.
قرت:
The letters qāf, rā' and tā' are a small but genuine root denoting ugliness in complexion.

1. qarita wajhu al-rajul — the man's face changed, from grief.
2. qarita al-dam — this is the origin of it: the blood dried between the skin and the flesh; such blood is called qārit.
3. qarita al-jild — the skin, when struck, turned black.
قرح:
The letters qāf, rāʾ, and ḥāʾ are three sound roots: one points to pain from a wound or the like, the second to an admixture in a thing, and the third to drawing something up.

1. al-qarḥ — a wound in the skin that has been cut. Al-qarḥ is also what breaks out on the body as sores that cause pain. God Most High said: {if a wound touches you, a wound like it has already touched those people} [Āl ʿImrān: 140]. One says qaraḥahu, when he wounded him; al-qarīḥ is the wounded man; al-qariḥ is the one on whom sores have broken out.
2. al-māʾ al-qarāḥ — water not mixed with anything else. A poet said:
We passed the night unmixed [with others / undiluted — the line is obscure], while the gnats bit at us, ... the pure water, as though no living soul were in the valley.
Al-arḍ al-qarāḥ is land of good soil, whose earth nothing else is mixed into. From this chapter: a man is qurḥān, and a people qurḥānūn, when smallpox or sickness has not touched them — taken from al-māʾ al-qarāḥ and al-arḍ al-qarāḥ. Al-qirwāḥ is like al-qarāḥ. It is also said that al-qirwāḥ means wide/open land, which is close to the first sense, because some roughness is mixed into it.
3. al-qarīḥa — the first water drawn up from a well; for this reason one says so-and-so is jayyid al-qarīḥa, good at drawing out knowledge. From it, iqtaraḥat al-jamal, I rode the camel before it had ever been ridden. And iqtaraḥtu al-shayʾa, I worked the thing out for myself, without having heard it from anyone.

Among what falls outside these three roots: al-qāriḥ, among riding beasts, is the one whose age of teeth has reached its limit. Al-Farrāʾ said: qaraḥa yaqruḥu qurūḥan, said of horses that are qurḥ; every word for [an animal reaching] a stage of teeth takes the form with alif, like athnā and arbaʿa, except qaraḥa.

Also outside the three roots: al-qurḥa, the white mark smaller than a full blaze on a horse's face. He said: a meadow is qarḥāʾ when white blossom is in its middle. Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line whose sense is obscure to me and which I give as best I can:
Dark-green and white-blossomed, of the Ashrāṭ season — the flowers were enough for it, and the buds surrounded it.
They also say: qaraḥa fulānun fulānan bi-l-ḥaqqi, when he confronted him directly with it. This could be a case of one letter standing for another, its origin being qaraʿahu, he struck/confronted him; or it could be as though he wounded him with it.
قرد:
The letters qāf, rāʾ, and dāl are a sound root pointing to a gathering together in a thing along with a breaking into patches. From this: al-saḥāb al-qarid, clouds broken into patches across the regions of the sky, riding one upon another.

1. al-ṣūf al-qarid — wool that is matted, tangled into itself.
2. [al-arḍ] al-qardad — ground that rises up beside a hollow.
3. qurdūdat al-ẓahr — what rises up from the middle of the back.

All of this follows one and the same reasoning. It is possible that al-qurād, the tick, comes from this too, for the way its body is drawn compactly together.

Among what they derive from the word al-qurād: aqrada al-rajulu, the man clung close to the ground out of fear or humiliation; qarida, he fell silent; and from it, qarradtu al-rajula taqrīdan, when you deceived him so as to lead him into trouble.
قرس:
The letters qāf, rā' and sīn are a sound root denoting cold.

1. al-qars — cold.
2. qarisa al-insān qarasan — said when a person cannot use his hands from the severity of the cold. Abū Zubayd said, in a line of verse: I have borne the heat of their war just as one numbed by cold warms himself against the bitter frost.
3. aqrasahu al-bard — one says: the cold benumbed him.

Not from this root is al-qurāsiya: the huge camel.
قرش:
The letters qāf, rā' and shīn are a sound root indicating gathering and coming together. al-qarsh is gathering; one says taqarrashū, when they came together. And they say Quraysh was named from this. al-muqarrisha — the barren, famine year, because in it people draw their livestock together. And they say taqārashat al-rimāḥ fī al-ḥarb, when the spears intermingled with one another in battle. And they say that Quraysh is a beast that dwells in the sea and overpowers all other beasts.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And Quraysh is the one that dwells in the sea ... after it Quraysh was named Quraysh.
قرص:
The letters qāf, rā' and ṣād are a sound root denoting the pinching of something between the fingertips, with a stinging bite to it.

1. qaraṣtuhu aqruṣuhu qarṣan — I pinched him, a pinching.
2. al-qurṣ — the well-known round loaf, because it is dough that is pinched into shape, a qarṣ.
3. qarraṣat al-marʾa al-ʿajīn — the woman divided the dough into rounds, one at a time.
4. labanun qāriṣ — milk that bites the tongue, as though it pinches it.
5. al-qawāriṣ — cutting insults, as though a person's honour is pinched when something unbecoming is said of it. A poet said, in a line of verse: stinging words come to me and you make light of them, yet a vessel may be filled drop by drop until it brims over.

Ibn Durayd said: ḥulī muqarraṣ means jewellery set with gems, as though it were made round in the shape of the qurṣ.

Not from this root is al-qurrāṣ: a plant.
قرض:
The letters qāf, rā' and ḍād are a sound root, and it points to cutting. One says qaraḍtu al-shay' bi-l-miqrāḍ — I cut the thing with the shears.

Al-qarḍ is what you give a person out of your wealth so that it may be repaid to you, and it is as though it were something you had cut off from your wealth. Al-qirāḍ in trade is from this too, and it is as though the owner of the wealth had cut a portion from his wealth and given it to his partner to trade with it.

And they say [al-qarīḍ] is the cud, in their saying 'choking came between him and chewing the cud'; [and what appears is that what was meant by it is] poetry, and that is sounder.

And one says that so-and-so and so-and-so yataqāraḍān al-thanā' — they lend each other praise — when each of them praises his companion. The sense of this is as though each of them had lent his companion praise as one lends money. And it goes back to the analogy we have mentioned.
قرط:
The letters qāf, rā' and ṭā' are three words with no single sense binding them.

1. al-qurṭ — the well-known earring. And qarraṭa fulānun farasahu al-ʿinān means so-and-so threw the bridle-rein onto its head.
2. al-qirṭān and al-qirṭāṭ — [pads] for the saddle, like the walīya-pad for the pack-saddle; sometimes also used for the pack-saddle itself.
3. mā jāda fulānun bi-qirṭīṭa — meaning: so-and-so did not give even the smallest amount.
قرع:
The letters qāf, rā' and ʿayn — most of this root is about striking something. One says "qaraʿtu l-shay'a, aqraʿuhu": I struck it. Muqāraʿat al-abṭāl (the clashing of champions) is their striking one another. Al-qarīʿ: the stud camel, because he covers the she-camel. Al-iqrāʿ and al-muqāraʿa: casting lots, so named because it is something like a striking. "I qāraʿtu so-and-so and I qaraʿtuhu" — the lot fell to me rather than him.

Al-qāriʿa: a calamity, one of the hardships of time, named so because it strikes people, hitting them with its harshness. Al-qāriʿa is also the Resurrection, because it strikes and afflicts people with its striking. Qawāriʿ al-Qur'ān are the verses that, if one recites them, no fright befalls him — it seems, God knows best, they were named so because they strike the jinn. The drinker strikes his forehead with the vessel when he drains all that is in it. It is said "aqraʿa l-dābbata bi-lijāmihi" when he reined it in with its bridle.

From this root: their saying "rajulun qariʿ" — a man is qariʿ when he accepts an advisor's counsel; the meaning is that he was struck with words on the matter and accepted them. If he does not accept it, it is said: "so-and-so lā yuqraʿ." They say: "aqraʿtu ilā l-ḥaqqi iqrāʿan" — I yielded to what is right.

From this root also al-qarīʿ, the chief — named so because he is relied upon in affairs, as if struck upon often, being asked and sought for help; the proof is that they also call him maqrūʿ. Carried further and used figuratively, they said: "aqraʿa so-and-so so-and-so" — he gave him the best of his wealth. The best part of one's wealth is its qurʿa, named so because it is relied on in times of need, as with al-qarīʿ.

Among what they extended the usage to, the root remaining what we mentioned: al-qarīʿa — the best tent in the camp: if it is cold, the best shelter in it; if it is hot, the best shade in it.

Among what falls outside this root: al-qaraʿ, and "faṣīl muqarraʿ" (a weaned young camel that is muqarraʿ).

Aws said, in a line of verse:
By every trench, they leave behind an armored man dragged along, as the weaned young camel al-muqarraʿ is dragged.

Al-qaraʿ also means: hair loss from the head.
قرف:
The letters qāf, rā' and fā' are a sound root indicating mixing with a thing, being enveloped by it, and wearing it as an inner garment.

The origin of this is al-qarf, any kind of peel or crust. From it, qirf al-khubz (the crust of bread); it is called qirf and qarf because it is the "garment" of what lies beneath it.

From this root also al-qarf: something made of hides, in which al-khalʿ is prepared. Al-khalʿ is: meat is taken, cooked, and spices are put in it, then poured into this container.

He said, in a line of verse:
And a woman of Dhubyān charged her sons that the coverlets and the meat-jars had failed them.
[The second half of this line is obscure to me; I give the sense as best I can.]

From this root: "iqtaraftu l-shay'a" — I acquired it, as if I had worn it as an inner garment. Likewise their saying: "so-and-so yuqrafu bi-kadhā" — he is accused of it. The one suspected of a matter is called al-qirfa. A man says, when he has lost something: "so-and-so is my qirfa" — the one I suspect — as if he had clothed him in suspicion. And "the sons of so-and-so are my qirfa" — I think what I am seeking is with them. They say: "ask the sons of so-and-so about your she-camel, for they are a qirfa" — you will find news of it with them; its derivation is what we have mentioned.

The horse al-muqrif: one close to being of mixed stock. They say: al-muqrif is the one whose father is of non-Arab stock and whose mother is a pure Arab mare.

The poet said, in a line of verse:
If she foals a noble colt, that is only to be expected; but if there is any taint of mixed stock, it comes from the sire's side.

"So-and-so qārafa the sin" — he fell into it. "He qārafa his wife" — he had intercourse with her, because each of them is a garment of the other. Al-qaraf: the plague that occurs in a country, as if it were something that becomes an illness clinging to its people like a garment. And in the hadith, a people complained to him of the plague in their land, and he said: "Move away, for from qaraf comes ruin."
قرق:
The letters qāf, rā' and qāf are a single word. They say: al-qariq is smooth, level ground.

A poet said, in a line of verse: as though their hooves upon the level, smooth ground were the hands of girls passing silver coins to one another.
قرم:
The letters qāf, rā' and mīm are a sound root denoting a notch or a cutting into something.

1. al-qarm — the notching of a camel's nose: the cutting of a small piece of skin from it as a mark or a brand; that cut piece is al-qurāma.
2. al-qarm, also al-muqram, meaning the chief or lord — this is the same thing described above: he is so marked, for his nobility among them, until he becomes a stud-stallion, and is then named al-qarm after the mark by which he is known. Aws said, in a line of verse: when a chief among us has the edge of his eyetooth broken off, another chief's tooth grows fierce among us.
3. al-qurāma — a piece cut from the callused pad on a camel's chest, made use of and eaten in times of drought.
4. al-qurāma — also what sticks to the oven from the bread; named so because it is pared away (yuqram) from the oven, that is, removed from it.
5. al-qarm — a lamb's taking of grass, the term for when it first nibbles at the tips of shrubs.
6. al-qirām — a thin curtain, reasoned within this root, as though it were something the doorway is covered with, like the paring taken from a camel's nose.

Straying from this root is al-qaram: a strong craving for meat.
قرن:
The letters qāf, rā' and nūn are two sound roots. One of them points to joining one thing to another, and the other is a thing that juts out with strength and hardness.

The first: qārantu bayna al-shay'ayn - I joined the two things together. Al-qirān is the rope by which two things are tied together. Al-qaran is the rope too. Jarīr said, in a line of verse:
Carry word to our caliph, if you should meet him, that I am at the door like one bound in a rope.

Al-qaran is also a small quiver joined to the big quiver. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And every one of them walks with a bow and a small quiver.

And al-qaran is in the eyebrows, when the two meet. Such a man is maqrūn al-ḥājibayn bayyin al-qaran - plainly joined in the brows. And al-qirn, with i, is your match in courage; and al-qarn, with a, is your equal in age. The reasoning in the two is one, and they were only told apart by the i and the a because the two qualities are different.

Al-qirān is that you pair two dates and eat them together. Al-qirān is also that you join a ḥajj to an ʿumra. Al-qarūn of she-camels is the one whose front and hind teats are set close as a pair. And al-qarūn is the one that, when she runs, puts down her forelegs and her hind legs together. And their saying fulān muqrin li-kadhā means he is strong enough for it. God, exalted is He, said: {Glory to Him who has made this subject to us, and we were not equal to it} [al-Zukhruf: 13]; and that is the reasoning, because its meaning is that he could be a qirn, a match, for it.

Al-qarīna is a person's own self, as though the two had been paired together. And from their speech: fulān idhā jādhabathu qarīna baharahā - when a hardship is coupled to him he masters it. And a man's qarīna is his wife. And they say sāmaḥathu qarīnatuhu and qarūnatuhu and qarūnuhu, that is, his own self was easy with him. Al-qārin is the man who has a sword and arrows with him.

The other root is al-qarn, the horn of a sheep and of other animals, a strong jutting thing; and by way of likeness the long locks of hair are called qurūn. Of that is Abū Sufyān's word about the Byzantines: those of the qurūn. Al-Aṣmaʿī used to say: he meant the locks of their hair; they used to grow them long and were known by them. Muraqqish said, in a line of verse:
Not here! Would that I were the tip of the spear-butt, and my family in Syria, the land of long locks.

And of this chapter: al-qarn is the fleshy growth in a ewe that comes out from her vulva. And al-qarn is a small solitary hill. And they say qad aqrana rumḥahu, when he raised his spear.

And of what strayed from these two chapters: al-qarn is a generation of people, and the plural is qurūn. God, glory be to Him, said: {and many generations in between} [al-Furqān: 38]. And al-qarn is a burst of sweat, and the plural is qurūn. Zuhayr said, in a line of verse:
We school them to the charge, so that every day sweat is poured over their hoofs.

And of plants there is al-qarnuwa; and the hide called al-muqarnā is the one tanned with it.
قره: The letters qāf, rā' and hā' are a word, if it is sound. They say: al-qarah on the skin is like al-qalaḥ (tartar) on the teeth — it is grime. One says: a man is aqrahu and a woman is qarhāʾ, when affected by it.
قري:
The letters qāf, rā' and the weak letter are a sound root pointing to gathering and coming together. Of that is al-qarya, the village; it was called a qarya because people gather in it.

And they say qaraytu al-mā'a fī al-miqrāt: I gathered the water in the basin, and that gathered water is a qarī. And the plural of qarya is quran, which came like kuswa and kusan. And al-miqrāt is the great bowl; it was so named for the guests' gathering about it, or for what is gathered in it of food.

Of this section is al-qarw, and it is like a press for grapes. He said, in a line of verse:
I shoot it out into the wilderness when it turns aside, while you are between the press and the presser.
And al-qarw is a well-known trough drawn out beside the great trough, to which the camels come to drink. And of this section is al-qarw, which is everything that goes upon one way. You say: I saw the people upon one qarw. And their saying that al-qarw is aiming at a thing: you say qarawtu and qaraytu, when you travel a road. And al-Nābigha said:
They travel over the sand-hills of Dhanabān and the hillocks.
And this, in our view, is from the first sense, as though he follows them village by village. And of this section is al-qarā: the back, and it was called a qarā for what is gathered in it of bones. And a she-camel qarwā' is one strong of back. He said:
Firm-jointed, strong of back, tall and well-fleshed.
And one does not say of a he-camel aqrā.

And when this section is given a hamza it is the same as the first. They say: this she-camel has never carried a foetal membrane, as though it were meant that she has never conceived at all. He said, in a line of verse:
The two forelegs of a long-necked, tawny young she-camel, white of colour, that has not conceived a young one.
They said: and of this is al-Qur'an, as though it were named so for its gathering what is in it of rulings and stories and other things. As for aqra'at al-mar'a, it is said that it is from this too. And they mentioned that she is so in the state of her purity, as though she had gathered her blood within her and not let it go. And some people say: her iqrā' is only her going out from purity into menstruation, or from menstruation into purity. They said: and al-qur' is a time, which is once for purity and once for menstruation. And they say: the winds blew at their qāri', that is, at their time. And they recite, in a line of verse:
I have come to hate al-'Aqr, the 'Aqr of Banū Shulayl, when the winds blow at their time.
And the sum of this word is that it is a hard one. And some of the jurists claimed that it is only in the state of purity, and they said: . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . (here the text breaks off).

And of the first section is al-qāri'a, and it is the witness. And they say: people are the qawārī of God - exalted - in the earth, meaning the witnesses. And it is possible that this be carried upon that measure, that is, that they go over things until they gather them up as knowledge and then bear witness to them.

Of this section is al-qira: wealth, of camels and sheep. And al-qira is a man's dependants. And he recited, about al-qurra which is wealth, in a line of verse:
We have never seen a king who raided greater than he in wealth and in dignity.
And among what strays from this section is al-qārriyya, the point of a spearhead. And the edge of anything is its qāriya.
قز:
The letters qāf and zāy are one word, denoting a lack of settling toward a thing.

1. al-qazz — the leap, the jump.
2. al-taqazzuz — fastidiousness, squeamishness.
3. rajulun qazz — a man who does not settle or feel at ease with anything.
قزب: The letters qāf, zāy and bā' — among Ibn Durayd's curiosities on this: al-qazab is hardness and toughness. Qaziba al-shayʾ means the thing became hard.
قزح:
The letters qāf, zāy and ḥā' are a small but genuine root denoting the mingling of different colours, and branching in a thing.

1. al-qazḥ — a spice among the spices of the cooking pot; one says qazziḥ qidraka, season your pot. Ibn Durayd said: from this comes their saying malīḥ qazīḥ, pleasant and well-seasoned.
2. al-quzaḥ — the bands of colour, as in the phrase qawsu quzaḥ, the rainbow; the singular is quzḥa.
3. taqazzaḥa al-nabt — the plant, when it branched out into shoots; likewise shajaratun mutaqazziḥa, a branching tree.
4. qazaḥa al-kalb bi-bawlihi — the dog sprayed with its urine. Ibn Durayd said: it is said that al-qazḥ is the dog's urine. And God knows best.
قزع:
The letters qāf, zāy and ʿayn are a sound root denoting lightness in a thing, and scattering.

1. al-qazaʿ — scattered patches of cloud, the singular being qazaʿa. A poet said, in a line of verse: you see flocks of sandgrouse streaming loose above it, as though their scattered troops were wisps of thin cloud.
2. al-qazaʿ, the forbidden practice — shaving a boy's head and leaving scattered tufts of hair in places on it.
3. rajulun muqazzaʿ — a man on whose head only a few short hairs are seen.
4. farasun muqazzaʿ — a horse whose forelock has thinned.
5. taqazzaʿa al-faras — the horse readied itself to gallop.
6. al-ẓaby yaqzaʿu — said of the gazelle when it moves swiftly.
7. al-qazaʿ — young, small camels.
قزل: The letters qāf, zāy and lām are a single word, al-qazal, which is the worst kind of limp. From it one says qazila yaqzalu.
قزم: The letters qāf, zāy and mīm are a word denoting baseness and meanness. Al-qazam is baseness and meanness. A person is called qazam — the word is used for female and male, singular and plural alike.
قس:
The letters qāf and sīn: most of this chapter is the tracking of a thing, though something close to it in pronunciation deviates from it.

Our scholars said: al-qass is the tracking and seeking of a thing. They said: their saying that al-qass is gossip comes from this too, because the gossip tracks down talk and then spreads it.

1. al-qasqās — the guide who knows the way, so named for his knowledge of the road, his skill in seeking it and following it. One says qassa yaqussu.
2. taqassastu aṣwāt al-qawm bi-l-layl — I listened for the people's voices at night, tracking them.

Their saying qasastu al-qawm, meaning I harmed them with foul speech, is loosely put; its real meaning is what we have mentioned of al-qass, that is, gossip.

3. qurbun qasqās — a relentless, unbroken stretch of road; and sayrun qasīs — constant travel. That follows the pattern, since one tracks the ground and follows it closely.

Among what deviates from this chapter is their saying laylatun qasqāsa, a dark night, and sometimes they call a cold night qasiyya. And Qusās is a place, to which the qusāsiyya swords are attributed.

Some people reported from al-Shaybānī that al-qasqās means hunger, and cited from him a line of verse: "The qasqās brought him to us by night, and short of him lay mounds of sand, between which stretched open ground." If this is sound, it is a deviation; and if it follows the pattern, the poet meant by it only the guide, al-qasqās, and I do not know what "hunger" would mean here.

As for their saying dirhamun qasiyy, meaning a debased coin, some said it is the Arabized form of qāss, a Persian word. The garments called al-thiyāb al-qassiyya are said to be brought from Yemen. And they say qasqastu bi-l-kalb, meaning I shouted at the dog.
قسب:
The letters qāf, sīn and bā' denote the same as the root before it.

1. al-qasb — dry, hard dates. A poet said, in a line of verse: and a tawny spear of khaṭṭī cane, its knots as though they were hard qasb date-stones, quivering, loosened, unfixed from its head.
2. al-qasb — the hard, of anything.
3. al-qasīb — the tall and sturdy.
4. al-qasīb — also the sound of water as it flows; there is no such sound unless it comes with force. ʿUbayd said: beneath it the water has a qasīb, a rushing sound.
قسر: The letters qāf, sīn and rā' indicate subjugation and overpowering by force. From this, al-qasr — overpowering and subjugation. One says qasartuhu qasran, and iqtasartuhu iqtisāran. A camel described as qaysariyy — tough, hardy. And al-qaswara — the lion, for its strength and its dominance.
قسط:
The letters qāf, sīn and tā' are a sound root pointing to two opposite meanings, the form being one. Al-qist is justice. And from it one says aqsata yuqsitu. God Most High said: {Indeed God loves the just} [al-Ma'ida: 42]
[al-Ma'ida 42, al-Hujurat 9, al-Mumtahana 8]. And al-qast, with a fatha on the qāf, is injustice. And al-qusūt is turning aside from the truth. One says qasata, when he acts unjustly, yaqsitu qastan. And al-qasat is a crookedness in the legs, and it is the opposite of al-fahaj, bandiness.

And of the first root is al-qist, a share; and taqassatnā al-shay' baynanā, we divided the thing into shares among ourselves. And al-qistās is the balance. God, glorified, said: And weigh with the true balance. And of what is not of this: al-qust, something used for perfuming with smoke; it is Arabic.
قسم:
The letters qāf, sīn and mīm are two sound roots. One of them points to beauty and comeliness, and the other to dividing a thing into parts.

The first is al-qasām, and it is beauty and comeliness; and fulān muqassam al-wajh, that is, a man of beautiful face. And al-qasima is the face, which is the finest thing in a person. A poet said, in a line of verse:
As though there were gold coins upon their faces, though the meeting had worn the faces thin.

And al-qasām, in al-Nābigha's poetry, is [the fierceness of the heat].

The other root is al-qasm, the verbal noun of qasamtu al-shay' qasman, I divided the thing. And the share is qism, with i on the qāf. As for the oath, that is al-qasam. The people of the language said: the root of that is from al-qasāma, which are the oaths divided among the kin of a slain man when they claim the blood of their dead against people they accuse of it. And amsā fulān mutaqassiman, that is, as though the passing thoughts of care had divided him among themselves.

And of what strayed from this chapter is al-qasāmī, and he is the one who folds the garments at their first folding, and then they are folded upon his fold. A poet said, in a line of verse:
As the folder folds the striped cloths of al-ʿaṣṣāb.

It is said that al-ʿaṣṣāb is the spinner.
قسن:
The letters qāf, sīn and nūn are a word denoting toughness.

1. iqsaʾanna al-layl — the night's darkness intensified.
2. al-muqsaʾinn — a tough, hardy man, one also advanced in age.

A poet said, in a line of verse: if you are supple and soft, then I am, however much you wish, a grizzled, tough old man.
قسي:
The letters qāf, sīn and the weak letter [y] denote severity and hardness.

1. al-ḥajar al-qāsī — the hard stone.
2. al-qaswa — hardness of heart, taken from the hardness (qaswa) of stone. God Almighty said: {Then your hearts hardened after that, so they were like stones, or even harder} [al-Baqara: 74]. [And] al-qāsiya is a cold night.
3. al-muqāsāt — grappling with a hard matter; this too comes from qaswa, because the one doing it shows himself harder than the matter he is dealing with. It follows the pattern of mufāʿala, mutual effort.
قش:
The letters qāf and shīn are words that do not follow a single pattern.

1. al-qashsh — the peel, the rind. One says taqashqasha al-shay', when it peeled.

The two sūras {Qul yā ayyuhā l-kāfirūn — Say: O disbelievers} [al-Kāfirūn: 1] and {Qul huwa Allāhu aḥad — Say: He is God, One} [al-Ikhlāṣ: 1] used to be called al-muqashqishatān, because they bring out their reciter as a believer, cleansed of unbelief by them.

Among what is not of this kind:

2. al-qishsha — a female monkey, and also a little girl.
