3. al-taqashqush — seeking food from here and there; if this is sound, it may belong to the chapter of letter-substitution, its true root having a sīn, which has already been discussed.
4. qashsha al-qawm — said when they were revived after a period of leanness and hardship.
قشب:
The letters qāf, shīn and bā' are two roots: one denotes mixing one thing into another, the other denotes newness in a thing.

The first: al-qashb, mixing something into food, and it is almost always something objectionable.

1. al-qishb — deadly poison. Al-Hudhalī said, in a line of verse: and after a little while he gave them both to drink, a swift, lethal, potent poison.
2. qashaba fulānun fulānan bi-sūʾ — so-and-so smeared so-and-so with evil, speaking of him by it or attributing it to him.
3. qashabahu bi-qabīḥ — he smeared him with something foul.
4. rajulun muqashshab al-ḥasab — a man whose lineage is mixed, tainted.

Ibn Durayd said: al-qishba is a base, contemptible person — a Yemeni word.

The other root: al-qashīb — new, of clothes and the like. Al-qashīb — also a sword newly given its polish.
قشر:
The letters qāf, shīn and rā' are one sound root, denoting the stripping away of something, where that thing is like a garment or the like. From that comes your saying: qashartu al-shayʾ aqshiruhu, I stripped the thing.

1. al-qishra — the peeled-off skin.
2. al-qishr — a person's clothing, his outer covering. The poet said: Ḥanīfa and al-Lahāzim have been denied by you the finery of Iraq, and whatever pleases the throat.

And in a hadith of Qayla: whenever I saw a man of fine bearing and fine dress, my eye would be drawn to him.

3. al-maṭra al-qāshira — a rain that strips the face of the earth.
4. sanatun qāshūra — a barren year that strips people of their wealth. A poet said, in a line of verse: so send upon them a stripping year, that shears away wealth as a depilatory shears away hair.

Everything that does this came to be called qāshūr, so they call ill-omen qāshūr, and they say in the proverb: more ill-omened than Qāshir — a stallion camel with a story of his own. For this reason the horse that comes in last in the race is called al-qāshūr, also al-fiskil. And their saying that al-aqshar means intensely red — that is said of one whose face is so red that it looks as though it is peeling. And Qushayr is the forefather of a tribe of the Arabs.
قشع:
The letters qāf, shīn and ʿayn are one sound root. Abū Bakr [Ibn Durayd] pointed to its underlying sense, saying: anything that becomes light has become qashiʿ; qashaʿa yaqshaʿu qashʿan, like meat when it is dried out. What he said is correct.

1. inqashaʿa al-ghaym, aqshaʿa, taqashshaʿa — all said of clouds clearing away.
2. al-qishʿa — a patch of cloud that remains after the sky has cleared. Some said that al-kunāsa, sweepings, is also called qishʿ.

Al-Kisāʾī said: qashaʿat al-rīḥ al-saḥāb, the wind cleared the clouds away, and inqashaʿa huwa, it (the cloud) cleared.

3. aqshaʿa al-qawm ʿan al-māʾ — the people withdrew from the water, moved on.
4. al-qishaʿ — what is spat out from the chest, phlegm.
5. al-qashʿ — what is stripped from the face of the ground.
6. kalaʾun qashīʿ — scattered pasturage.
7. shātun qashiʿa — a scrawny ewe, as though the fat has been stripped from her.
8. rajulun qashiʿ — a man who does not settle on any one course.

As for al-qashʿ, it is said to be a tent of hide, plural qushūʿ. A poet said, in a line of verse: when the hide-tent rattled in the winter wind. This fits the underlying sense, because when they journeyed they would strip it down. It is also said that al-qashʿ is the leather mat, al-niṭaʿ — and that too fits the same sense.
قشف: The letters qāf, shīn and fāʾ are a single word: their saying qashifa yaqshafu, said when the sun has scorched someone and changed his state. Then it came to be said of anyone who does not trouble to adorn or beautify himself that he is qashif, and that he taqashshafa, lives roughly.
قشم:
The letters qāf, shīn and mīm are a small root, if it is sound, belonging to eating and what resembles food.

1. al-qashm — eating.
2. al-qushām — that which is eaten. Ibn Durayd said: qushām al-māʾida is what is shaken off the table, leftover bread and the like.
3. mā aṣābat al-ibil maqshaman — meaning: the camels found nothing to graze on.

Straying from this root, if it is sound, is their saying qashamtu al-khūṣ, meaning I split the palm-leaf, in order to weave it. Anything split from it is called qushām.
قص:
The letters qāf and ṣād are a sound root, denoting the tracking of a thing.

1. iqtaṣaṣtu al-athar — I tracked the trail, when I followed it closely.
2. al-qiṣāṣ, in wounds — this word too is derived from it, because the same is done to the wrongdoer as he did to the first, as though his trail were being tracked and matched.
3. al-qissa and al-qaṣaṣ — a story, an account; all of that is tracked through and then recounted.
4. al-qaṣṣ — the breastbone, in our view following the pattern of this chapter, because its bones are of even size, as though each bone were tracking, matching, the next.
5. qaṣaṣtu al-shaʿr — I cut the hair; when you trim it you make every hair even with its neighbour, so that each one seems to follow the other, matching it along its length.
6. quṣāṣ al-shaʿr — the line where the hair ends at the front, the hairline; this too follows the pattern.
7. al-quṣṣa — the forelock.
8. al-qaṣīṣiyya, among camels — the camel that follows the tracks of the mounts ahead.

Their saying ḍaraba fulānun fulānan fa-aqaṣṣahu, meaning he struck him and brought him close to death — this means he brought death's track close upon him. And aqaṣṣa fulānan al-sulṭān, when the ruler put him to death in just retribution.

As for their saying aqaṣṣati l-shātu, meaning her pregnancy became visible, that is not from this. Likewise al-qaṣqāṣ, which they say means the lion; al-quṣquṣa, a short man; and al-qaṣīṣ, a plant — all of these deviate from the pattern mentioned.
قصب:
The letters qāf, ṣād and bā' are two sound roots: one indicates the cutting of a thing, and the other indicates an extension in hollow things.

The first is al-qaṣb, cutting; one says qaṣabtuhu qaṣban, I cut it.

1. al-qaṣṣāb — the butcher, named from this.
2. sayf qaṣṣāb — a cutting sword.
3. qaṣabtu l-dābba — said when you cut off the mount's watering before it had drunk its fill.
4. qaṣabtu l-rajul — I found fault with the man; this is by way of metaphor.

The other root is al-aqṣāb, the intestines, singular quṣb.

1. al-qaṣab — the well-known plant [reed or cane], singular qaṣaba.
2. al-qaṣbā' — also a plural of qaṣaba.
3. al-qaṣab — tubes made of gemstone or pearl. In the hadith: "Give Khadīja the glad tidings of a house in Paradise made of qaṣab, in which there is no clamor and no weariness."
4. al-qaṣab — the vessels of the lung.
5. al-qaṣab — the channels through which water runs from springs; this is by way of comparison.
6. al-quṣṣāb — reed-pipes.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Our witness was the rose and the jasmine,
and the singing women with their pipes.

7. al-qaṣā'ib — locks of hair, singular qaṣība.
8. al-quṣṣāba — a lock of hair.
قصد:
The letters qāf, ṣād and dāl are three roots: one indicates coming to a thing and heading straight for it, another indicates being packed tight within a thing, and a third belongs to a she-camel full of flesh.

The first root: qaṣadtuhu qaṣdan wa maqṣadan, I aimed straight for it. From this chapter: aqṣadahu al-sahmu, the arrow struck him dead on the spot — as though named for not swerving from him. Al-A'shā said:
My arrow struck her true, though before her ... he had been a hunter of the like of her, among the women of the tribe.
From it too: aqṣadathu ḥayyatun, a snake struck him dead outright.

The second root: qaṣadtu al-shay'a, I broke it. Al-qiṣda is the broken-off piece of a thing, plural qiṣad — from it, qiṣad al-rimāḥ, broken pieces of spears. Rumḥun qaṣid, a broken spear-shaft, and it has become inqaṣad, snapped. A verse:
You see the broken pieces of the lances flung down, as if they were ... rods measured out in the hands of women splitting palm-fronds.

The third root: the she-camel called al-qaṣīd is the compact one, packed full with flesh. Al-A'shā said:
I crossed the distance, my companion a lean and compact one ... like the shoulder of a mountain-slope, a swift, compact she-camel.
And for this reason the qaṣīda, the ode, is named qaṣīda, for the tight-packing (taqṣīd) of its verses, which are never anything but sound and complete in structure.
قصر:
The letters qāf, ṣād and rā' are two sound roots: one of them points to a thing not reaching its full reach and its end, and the other to holding back. The two roots are close to one another.

The first is *al-qiṣar*, shortness, the opposite of length. One says *huwa qaṣīr bayyin al-qiṣar* — he is plainly short. And one says *qaṣṣartu al-thawba wa-l-ḥabla taqṣīran* — I shortened the garment and the rope. And *al-qaṣr* is the shortening of the prayer, which is not to complete it, on account of travel. God, exalted, said: there is no blame on you that you shorten the prayer. And *al-quṣayrā* is the lowest of the ribs, which is the weak one. And *al-quṣayrā* is a viper, so named for its shortness. And one says *aqṣarat al-shāt*, when the ewe grows old until the tips of her teeth are worn short. And *aqṣarat al-mar'a* — she bore short children. And one says *qaṣṣartu fī al-amri taqṣīran* when I was slack in it; and *qaṣartu ʿanhu qusūran* — I fell short of it, I was unable. And *aqṣartu ʿanhu* when you leave off from it while you are able to do it. A poet said, in a line of verse:
But for the bonds of favours I was caught in, my heart would have left off from it, and what a leaving off.

All of this has one rule, and it is a thing's not reaching its reach and its end. The other root — and we have said that the two are close — is *al-qaṣr*, holding back. One says *qaṣartuhu* when I confined him, and he is *maqṣūr*, that is, held in. God, exalted, said: {maidens confined in the pavilions} [al-Raḥmān: 72]. And a woman *qāṣirat al-ṭarf* is one who does not stretch her glance to any but her husband, as though she held her glance back with a holding. God, glory be to Him, said: in them are maidens restraining their glances. Of this chapter is *quṣārāka an tafʿala kadhā* and *qaṣruka* — your utmost is to do such a thing — as though what were meant is what you limited yourself to and held yourself to. And *al-maqāṣir* is the plural of *maqṣūra*; every quarter of a large house, when a wall is put round it, is a *maqṣūra*. And it is possible that this belongs to the first rule. And they say *faras qaṣīr*: a mare kept close and near, not left to range free, because of her preciousness to her people. A poet said, in a line of verse:
You see her by our tent kept close, and we give her freely when the swift horses run.

And a girl *qaṣīra* and *qaṣūra*, kept at home, is from this. And *al-tiqṣār* is a necklace like a choker, as though it were held in on the neck. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And she has a gazelle that stirs her up, putting a tiqṣār necklace on his throat.

Of this chapter is *qaṣr al-ẓalām*, which is the darkness mingling. And *qad aqbalat maqāṣir al-ẓalām* — the dusks of the darkness have come on; and that is at evening. And it is possible to bring this under the rule and say that the darkness holds a man back from going about. And one says *aqṣarnā* when we entered that hour. That hour is called *al-maqṣara*, and the plural is *maqāṣir*. A poet said, in a line of verse:
So I sent her off cutting short the evening hours, after the life of the fire had all but failed the man seeking its light.

Among what stands apart from this chapter is *al-qaṣar*, the plural of *qaṣara*, and it is the base of the neck, and the base of a tree, and the thick part of it. And it has been read: {it throws up sparks like the qaṣr} [al-Mursalāt: 32]. And *al-qaṣar* is a disease that takes hold in the base of the neck. And God knows best.
قصع:
The letters qāf, ṣād and ʿayn are a sound root denoting a sinking-in of something, or a pressing of it down.

1. al-qaṣʿa — the well-known bowl, named so for the dip in it.
2. al-qāṣiʿāʾ — the first of the burrows of the jerboa; the reasoning is the same as above. One says taqaṣṣaʿa when it enters its qāṣiʿāʾ. A poet said, in a line of verse: Abū Laylā Ṭufayl ibn Mālik wished, at the bend of al-Sūbān, that he could burrow down and vanish.

As for a she-camel's qaṣʿ of her cud, they said it means bringing it back down into her belly.

3. al-māʾ yaqṣaʿu al-ʿaṭash — water quenches thirst, kills it and takes it away. A poet said, in a line of verse: so the tawny she-camels swerved off, their raging thirst not yet quenched.
4. qaṣaʿtu bi-basṭi kaffī hāmatahu — I struck his head with the flat of my hand.
5. qaṣaʿa Allāhu bihi — said when a child remains stunted, neither growing tall nor increasing; he is maqṣūʿ or qaṣīʿ.
قصف:
The letters qāf, ṣād and fā' are a sound root indicating the breaking of a thing, and this pattern never fails to hold. One says qaṣafat al-rīḥ al-safīna fī al-baḥr — the wind broke the ship at sea. A wind described as qāṣif. al-qaṣif — quick to break. al-qaṣīf — broken, dried brushwood of trees. From this: inqaṣafū ʿanhu, when they abandoned him — used here in a borrowed sense. al-aqṣaf — one whose front tooth is broken across the middle. Thunder described as qāṣif, meaning violent — the reasoning being that it seems about to break things with its violence. They say: God Almighty sent against them the violent wind and the crashing thunder. From this: al-qaṣf — the grinding together of a camel's teeth.

As for al-qaṣf in idle amusement and play, Ibn Durayd said he did not think it was Arabic. This al-qaṣf that he doubted is not far from the pattern we have described, for it too belongs among sounds and clamour, on the same reasoning as the crashing thunder and the camel grinding its teeth.
قصل:
The letters qāf, ṣād and lām are one sound root denoting the cutting of something. Al-qaṣl is cutting; one says qaṣalahu when he cut it.

1. al-qaṣīl — the well-known green fodder cut young, named so for how quickly it is cut, being tender.
2. sayfun miqṣal — a sharp-cutting sword; likewise al-qaṣṣāl.
3. lisānun miqṣal — a cutting tongue, by comparison to the sword.
4. al-qiṣl — a weak man, because he is cut off, lacking in strength.

As for al-quṣāla, it is what is set aside from wheat to be threshed a second time; if this is sound, its reasoning is close to the root.
قصم: The letters qāf, ṣād and mīm are a sound root indicating breaking. One says qaṣamtu al-shayʾ qaṣman. al-quṣam — a man who smashes whatever he meets. God Almighty said: {and how many a town We broke, that had been doing wrong} [al-Anbiyāʾ: 11]. He meant — and God knows best — their destruction, and expressed it as breaking. al-qaṣīma and al-qayṣūm are two plants.
قصوى:
The letters qāf, ṣād and the weak letter are a sound root indicating distance and putting at a distance.

1. al-qaṣā — distance. It is used of al-makān al-aqṣā (the farthest place) and al-nāḥiya al-quṣwā (the farthest region). "I went off to so-and-so's qaṣā" means to his direction, his side. It is said: "They surrounded us at a distance (aḥāṭūnā l-qaṣā)" — that is, they stood between far and near, yet encircling us the way a thing encircles another to guard it.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
They surrounded us at a distance, and yet they had seen us
close by, where a whispered word could be heard.

2. aqṣaytuhu — I put it at a distance.
3. al-qaṣiyya, of camels — the treasured, noble she-camel that is not driven hard nor ridden, that is, she is kept at a distance out of honor for her.
4. al-nāqa al-qaṣwā' — the she-camel whose ear is cut off. It may be that this too fits the root, in that her ear was put at a distance from her when it was cut off. They say: qaṣawtu l-baʿīr, fa-huwa maqṣuww — I cut off the camel's ear. One says nāqa qaṣwā', but baʿīr aqṣā is not said.
قض:
The letters qāf and ḍād are three roots: one is the swooping or falling of a thing, another is roughness in a thing, and the third is a hole or perforation in a thing.

The first is their saying inqaḍḍa l-ḥāʾiṭu, the wall fell down; from it comes inqiḍāḍ al-ṭāʾir, the swoop of the bird in its flight.

The second is their saying dirʿun qaḍḍāʾu, a coat of mail rough to the touch, not yet worn smooth. Its origin is al-qiḍḍa, low ground whose soil is sand, with firmer ground beside it.

1. al-qaḍaḍ — broken stone; from it comes al-qaḍqaḍa, the breaking of bones — one says asadun qaḍqāḍ, a lion that crushes bones.
2. al-qaḍḍ — dust that settles over bedding; one says aqaḍḍa ʿalayhi maḍjaʿuhu, his sleeping-place made him restless with grit. Abū Dhuʾayb said, in a line of verse: "Or is it your body that will not settle into any resting-place, without that resting-place turning gritty and restless beneath you?"
3. laḥmun qaḍḍ — meat that has gathered grit when roasted.
4. jāʾū bi-qaḍḍihim wa-qaḍīḍihim — meaning they came in a large, rough-edged company, everyone together. Aws said, in a line of verse: "And a band of young men came, every last one of them, as numerous almost as they had ever been, and they pressed hard."

The third root is their saying qaḍaḍtu l-luʾluʾata aquḍḍuhā qaḍḍan, I bored/pierced the pearl; from it comes iqtiḍāḍ al-bikr, the deflowering of a virgin. Al-Shaybānī said this.
قضب:
The letters qāf, ḍād and bā' are a sound root indicating the cutting of a thing. One says qaḍabtu al-shayʾ qaḍban. "And when the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him and his family, saw a cross-pattern on a garment, he cut it off (qaḍabahu)" — meaning he cut it out. And inqaḍaba al-najm min makānihi — the star shot away from its place.

A poet, Dhū al-Rumma, said, in a line of verse:
As if it were a star, following a demon, marked out, shooting away in the blackness of night.

al-qaḍīb — the branch. al-qaḍb — fresh green fodder, named so because it is cut (tuqḍabu). al-maqāḍib — lands that grow qaḍb. qaḍabtu al-karm — I cut back the vine's branches in the days of spring. A sword described as qāḍib and qaḍīb — sharp-cutting. A man described as qaḍḍāba — decisive in cutting through matters, capable of them. quḍābat al-karm — what falls from the vine's branch-ends when it is pruned.

From this chapter: iqtaḍaba fulānun al-ḥadītha, when he improvised his speech — as if it were words he cut off without forethought. This is used in a borrowed sense so that one says nāqa qaḍīb, of a she-camel ridden before being broken in; and I say iqtaḍabtuhā of doing so. And Qaḍīb is the name of a valley. God knows best.
قضع:
The letters qāf, ḍād and ʿayn are a sound root, and its sense is overpowering and prevailing. They said: al-qaḍʿ is overpowering.

Al-Khalīl said: Quḍāʿa was named from this. Some people mentioned that Quḍāʿa was named so because he broke away (inqaḍaʿa) from his people, that is, he cut himself off. If this is correct, it belongs to the substitution of letters, the ḍād standing in place of a ṭā'. Ibn Duraid said: "The people scattered (taqaḍḍaʿa)." This too is a case of letter-substitution.
قضف:
The letters qāf, ḍād and fā' are a small root indicating thinness and slenderness. Al-qaḍaf is thinness; one says ʿūd qaḍif and qaḍīf, a slender stick, and the plural of qaḍīf is qiḍāf.

1. al-qaḍafa, plural quḍfān — a piece of sand that breaks away from its main body, that is, it crumbles off.
قضم:
The letters qāf, ḍād and mīm are two unrelated words, with no connection between them.

1. al-qaḍm — the beast's nibbling of its barley; one says qaḍimat taqḍamu. They say: mā dhuqtu qaḍāman, I tasted no food at all. It is said: al-qaḍm is eating with the tips of the teeth, while al-khaḍm is eating with the whole mouth.
2. al-qaḍīm — it is said to be white hide, or a white sheet.

Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
It is as though the trailing skirts of the winds that bury every trace,
dragged over it, were a white sheet inscribed by craftsmen's hands.
قضي:
The letters qāf, ḍād and the weak letter are a sound root pointing to the making firm of a matter, the perfecting of it, and the carrying of it through to its end. God - exalted - said: {So He determined them as seven heavens in two days} [Fuṣṣilat: 12], that is, He made their creation firm. Then Abū Dhu'ayb said, in a line of verse:
Upon the two of them are two riveted coats of mail, which David made, or the maker of long mail-coats, Tubba'.
Al-qaḍā' is judgement. God, glory be to Him, said, mentioning the one who said: "So decree what you will decree", that is, do and judge. And for that reason the judge was called a qāḍī, because he makes the rulings firm and carries them out. And death was called qaḍā' because it is a matter carried out upon the son of Adam and upon the rest of created things. Al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥilliza said, in a line of verse:
And eighty men of Tamīm, in their hands spears whose points are al-qaḍā' - that is, death.
And every word in this section runs on the measure we have described. But when it is given a hamza the meaning changes. They say: al-quḍ'a is a fault; one says there is no quḍ'a against you from him, and in his eye there is a quḍ'a, that is, something spoiled.
قط:
The letters qāf and ṭāʾ are a sound root, denoting cutting a thing quickly, crosswise.

1. qaṭaṭtu l-shayʾ aquṭṭuhu qaṭṭan — I cut the thing crosswise.
2. al-qaṭṭāṭ — the turner who makes small cases, as though he were cutting them out. A poet said, in a line of verse: "like the cutting-out of small cases."
3. al-qiṭqiṭ — fine, drizzling rain, so called because there is so little of it that it seems broken into scattered drops.
4. al-shaʿru l-qaṭaṭ — curled hair, the opposite of straight hair, as though it had been sheared into curls. One says qaṭiṭa shaʿruhu; it is one of the rare words that shows its doubled letter openly in this form.
5. al-qiṭṭ — they say it means a written deed, a bond of obligation. If this belongs to the pattern of the chapter, it may be from the sense of cutting found in what is written upon. Al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse: "nor did King al-Nuʿmān, the day I met him, in his pride, give out written bonds [qutūt] and keep his word." On this reading God's word is explained: {and they said: our Lord, hasten for us our qiṭṭ [our written share] before the Day of Reckoning} [Ṣād: 16] — as though they meant the record of the reward they would be given in the next life.

Among what deviates from this chapter is al-qiṭṭa, the cat — said to be a term for the female alone, not the male.

As for qaṭ meaning "enough," that is not from this chapter; it is a case of letter-substitution, its true form being qad. Ṭarafa said, in a line of verse: "a trustworthy brother, who does not turn from a hard task; when told 'enough,' his companion says qad [enough]." But they substituted ṭāʾ for dāl, and say qaṭī, qaṭka, qaṭnī. And they cited: "The trough is full, and he said, 'enough for me [qaṭnī]; that's plenty, slow down, you have filled my belly.'" They also say qaṭāṭi, meaning "enough for me." And their saying mā raʾaytu mithlahu qaṭṭu, meaning "I have never seen the like of it," cuts off the matter entirely by asserting it as fully as possible — and it is said only of something in the past.
قطب:
The letters qāf, ṭā' and bā' are a sound root indicating gathering. One says: jā'at al-ʿarab qāṭibatan, the Arabs came all together.

1. qaṭabtu l-ka's — I mixed the cup, when you blend it.
2. al-qiṭāb — the blend, the mixture.
3. qaṭaba l-rajul mā bayna ʿaynayhi — the man knit his brow between his eyes.
4. al-qaṭība — the mixed colors of camels and sheep, when they are blended together.
5. al-quṭb — the pivot of the millstone, because it gathers its whole working together, its turning being around it.
6. quṭb al-samā' — the pole of the sky; it is said to be a star around which the celestial sphere turns. This is used metaphorically, so one says: so-and-so is the quṭb of the tribe of so-and-so, meaning their chief, the one they take refuge in.

Among what falls outside this root: al-quṭba, a small arrowhead with which targets are shot. As for their saying qaṭabtu l-shay', meaning I cut it, that is not from this root; it belongs to letter-substitution, the original being with ḍād, qaḍabtu, which we have already explained.
قطر:
The letters qāf, ṭā' and rā' — this root is not built on a single analogy; its words come from differing origins, and we have written them out separately.

Al-quṭr: a region, a side. Al-aqṭār: the sides. It is said: "he speared him and qaṭṭarahu" — he threw him down onto one of his two quṭrs, his two sides.

He said, in a line of verse:
Salmā and her neighbors well know: none but I brought the horseman down.

Al-quṭur: aloeswood.

Ṭarafa said, in a line of verse:
The people called out to one another in their gathering-place: is that the smell of roasting meat, or the scent of aloeswood?

Al-qaṭr: the dripping of water and other things. This falls under an analogy at this point, because its meaning is succession, one thing after another. From this, qiṭār al-ibil: a string of camels led one behind the other. "The people taqāṭarū" when they came in successive groups, taken from qiṭār al-ibil. The camel al-qāṭir: one whose urine keeps dripping continuously.

Among their proverbs: "Running short strings out the herd for market" — meaning: when the people's provisions run short, they string their camels in a line and drive them off to sell.

Al-qaṭirān (tar) — it may be so named because it is among things that drip; its pattern is faʿilān. It is said: "qaṭartu l-baʿīra bi-l-hinā'i, aqṭuruhu" — I dripped tar onto the camel to treat it.

He said, in a line:
As the man daubing tar drips it onto the mangy camel being treated.

Among what does not belong to this analogy: al-qiṭr — copper. And their saying "qaṭara fī l-arḍ" — he went away. "The plant iqṭārra" when it neared dryness.
قطع:
The letters qāf, ṭā' and ʿayn are one sound root, pointing to severing and to setting one thing apart from another. One says qaṭaʿtu al-shay' aqṭaʿuhu qaṭʿan - I cut the thing. Al-qaṭīʿa is estrangement. One says taqāṭaʿa al-rajulān, when the two men break with each other. And such a woman sent to such another an uqṭūʿa, which is something she sends her as a token of the breaking off. Al-qiṭʿ, with i on the qāf, is a stretch of the night, as though it were a piece cut off. And one says qaṭaʿtu qaṭʿan. And qaṭaʿat al-ṭayr quṭūʿan, when the birds go out from the lands of [cold to the lands of] heat, or from these to those. Al-qaṭīʿ is the whip. Al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse:
She watches my hand and the whip still stiff and untanned.

And aqṭaʿtu al-rajul iqṭāʿan - I granted the man a holding, as though it were a portion cut out of a country. And they say of the man who despairs of a thing: qad quṭiʿa bihi - as though it were a hope he had entertained and it was cut off. And qaṭaʿtu al-nahr quṭūʿan, when you cross the river. And aqṭaʿtu fulānan quḍbānan min al-karm, when you allow him to cut shoots from the vine. And al-qaḍīb is the qaṭīʿ, the piece cut from a tree from which arrows are shaped, and the plural is aqṭuʿ. The Hudhalī said, in a line of verse:
And a faint sound from a girded hunter, in his hand a light twanging bow and cut shafts.

And this cloth will cut you out a shirt. And it is said that muqaṭṭiʿat al-niyāṭ is the hare; and it is said she was named that because she cuts the heart-strings of the birds of prey that follow her in the chase. And it is said al-niyāṭ is the far reach of the waterless waste. And of the chapter: qaṭṭaʿa al-furs al-khayl taqṭīʿan - the horse left the other horses behind and went on; and this is the explanation of what we mentioned about muqaṭṭiʿat al-niyāṭ, if the heart-strings of the bird of prey are what is meant.

And the word is built out further, so one says jā'at al-khayl muqṭawṭiʿāt - the horses came at speed. And they say jāriya qaṭīʿ al-qiyām, a girl slow to rise, as though her fatness cut her off from rising. And fulān munqaṭiʿ al-qarīn in generosity or in something else - without a match. And in some of the commentary on His words, exalted is He: {then let him stretch a rope to the sky, then let him cut} [al-Ḥajj: 15] - that it is strangling; and the reasoning in it is sound. And munqaṭaʿ al-raml and maqṭaʿuhu are where the sand comes to an end. Al-qaṭīʿ is a flock of sheep. Al-muqaṭṭaʿāt are short garments. And in the hadith: that a man came to him wearing muqaṭṭaʿāt of his. And so too the muqaṭṭaʿāt of lines of poetry, the short pieces. Al-quṭʿ is shortness of breath. And maqāṭiʿ al-awdiya are the lower ends of the valleys. And so-and-so's well was struck by quṭʿ, when its water grows less. Al-qiṭaʿ, with i on the qāf, is the carpet thrown over the camel-saddle; and it seems to have been named so because its weaver cuts it off from the rest of the web when he has finished, just as a garment is called jadīd, new, as though its weaver had just this moment cut it. The plural is quṭūʿ. A poet said, in a line of verse:
The pale camels came to you panting in their nose-cords, the saddle-cloths slipping back off their shoulders.

And al-qiṭʿ is the broad arrowhead, as though when it was shaped it was cut. And of what strayed from this chapter is al-quṭayʿā': [a kind of date. A poet said]:
[They spent the night feeding quṭayʿā' dates to] their guest, while barnī dates were with them in great bulging baskets.
قطف:
The letters qāf, ṭā' and fā' are a sound root indicating taking a fruit from a tree; this is then used figuratively.

1. *qataftu ath-thamarata aqṭifuhā qaṭfan* — I picked the fruit.
2. *al-qiṭf* — the cluster (of grapes).
3. *aqṭafa al-karm* — the vine drew near its picking-time (*qiṭāfuhu*).
4. *al-quṭāfa* — what falls from the pickings.

This is also used figuratively of an animal's gait: *qaṭafa ad-dābbatu yaqṭifu qaṭfan*, and it is *qaṭūf*, as if from the speed with which it moves its legs it were picking something up off the ground. A scratch, too, may be called *qaṭf*; the sense is close to the same.

Someone said, in a line of verse:
But the face of your master, you scratch.
قطل:
The letters qāf, ṭā' and lām are a sound root indicating the cutting of a thing. One says qaṭalahu qaṭlan; it is qaṭīl and maqṭūl.

1. nakhla qaṭīl — a palm tree, when it is cut from its root and falls.
2. al-qaṭīla — a piece of a cloak or garment used to soak up water.
3. al-miqṭala — an iron tool used for cutting, plural maqāṭil.

It is said that Abū Dhu'ayb al-Hudhalī was nicknamed "al-Qaṭīl."
قطم:
The letters qāf, ṭā' and mīm are a sound root indicating the cutting of a thing, and indicating desire.

Cutting is expressed by al-qaṭm. They say: the young camel cropped the grass with the edge of its mouth, yaqṭimuhu. And Qaṭāmi is a name formed on an irregular pattern (ism maʿdūl); they say it comes from al-qaṭm, that is, cutting.

As for desire, it is al-qaṭam.

1. qaṭim — a man eager for meat.
2. al-quṭāmī — the falcon, perhaps named so for its eagerness for meat.
3. faḥl qaṭim — a stallion eager to mate.
قطن:
The letters qāf, ṭā' and nūn are a sound root indicating settling in a place, and stillness. One says qaṭana bi-l-makān, he settled there. The inhabitant of a house is its qaṭīn.

1. qaṭīn al-malik — the king's retinue; it is said they are his followers, because they dwell where he dwells.
2. ḥasham al-rajul, a man's household — also called his qaṭīn.
3. al-quṭn, cotton — in our view derived from this, because it belongs to settled town-dwellers and those who reside in villages.
4. al-qiṭniyya, plural al-qaṭānī — like lentils and the like, belonging only to those settled in houses.
5. qaṭṭana, of a grapevine — said when its buds appear, as though its buds were likened to cotton.
6. al-qaṭina, plural al-qaṭin — flesh between the two hips.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Until he came, his breastbone and haunches bared of flesh.

It was named qaṭina for staying fixed in that place. Likewise al-qaṭina is something resembling a pomegranate inside a cow.
قطو:
The letters qāf, ṭā' and the weak letter are a sound root indicating drawing the steps close together in walking. Al-qaṭw is drawing the stride close together, and from it the sandgrouse, al-qaṭāt, was named, plural qaṭan.

The Arabs say: "Not every qaṭā is like a quṭayy," meaning the great are not like the small.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Not every qaṭā is like a quṭayy,
nor is the shepherded among a people like the shepherd.

It was named qaṭāt because it takes short, close steps (taqṭū) in its gait.

1. iqṭawṭā, of a man in his walk — he turned about, circled.
2. al-qaṭāt, by metaphor from this root — the seat of the one riding behind, on a horse's back.
قع:
The letters qāf and ʿayn are a sound root, denoting the imitation of a sound.

1. al-qaʿqaʿa — the imitation of the sound of shields and the like clashing.
2. al-muqaʿqiʿ — the one who shakes the divination-arrows, which then give off a faint sound.
3. rajulun qaʿqaʿāniyy — a man whose joints you hear clicking as he walks. A poet said, in a line of verse: "like the clicking of the axle's hook-fitting."
4. ḥimārun qaʿqaʿāniyy — a donkey that, when he mounts the female, knocks his jaws together.
5. qarabun qaʿqāʿ — a swift stretch of travel, so named for the movements and the clatter that go with it.
6. ṭarīqun qaʿqāʿ — a road that cannot be travelled without hardship.

As for al-quʿāʿ, that is bitter, thick water; one says aqaʿʿū, when they struck bitter water in digging. This may be a deviation from the root just mentioned, or it may be a reversal of ʿaqqa, already discussed. And they say qaʿqaʿa fī l-arḍ, he went off into the land — this follows the pattern of the chapter, for the movement and clatter that go with his going.
قعث:
The letters qāf, ʿayn and thā' are a small root indicating abundance. They say:

1. al-qaʿīth — heavy rain, and abundant giving.
2. aqʿatha lahu l-ʿaṭiyya — he gave the gift generously.
قعد:
The letters qāf, ʿayn and dāl are a steady root, running to rule and never failing, and it corresponds to sitting (julūs), though it is used in places where julūs is not used. One says: qaʿada al-rajul yaqʿudu quʿūdan, the man sat. And al-qaʿda is the single act of sitting. And al-qiʿda is the manner of sitting, whether good or ugly. And a man may be ḍujaʿa quʿada, much given to sitting and to lying down. And al-qaʿīda: a man's qaʿīda is his wife.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
But she who keeps his house is left neglected ... the bones of her chest standing out, and a stoop upon her.

And a woman is qāʿida if you mean sitting, and qāʿid if you mean one who has ceased from menstruation and from husbands; the plural is qawāʿid. God, exalted, said: {And the women past childbearing who have no hope of marriage} [al-Nūr: 60]. And al-muqʿadāt are frogs. And al-quʿdud is the base man; letters were added to the build of the word for his sitting back from noble deeds. As for al-quʿdad and al-quʿdud, that is the nearest of a people to the eldest forefather. And so-and-so is aqʿad in lineage when he is nearer to the eldest forefather, and its reasoning is sound, because he is sitting alongside the eldest forefather. And al-qaʿīd among wild game is what comes to you from behind you, which is the opposite of al-naṭīḥ, what comes facing you.

And al-qaʿad are people who have no register of pay, as though they had been made to sit back from raiding. And the breast called muqʿad, upon a swelling bosom, is the one that stands up firm, as though it had been seated in that place. And Dhū al-Qaʿda is a month in which the Arabs used to sit back from journeys. And al-quʿda is the beast kept especially to be ridden, and al-qaʿūd among camels is the same. And it is said that al-qaʿīda is the large sack, because it is filled and made to sit. And al-qaʿīd is the locust whose wing has not yet formed evenly. And the qawāʿid of a house are its foundations. And the qawāʿid of a camel-litter are four pieces of wood set crosswise at its bottom. And al-iqʿād and al-quʿād are a disease that takes camels in their haunches and inclines them toward the ground. And a well that is muqʿada is one that was left off and not carried down as far as the water, and abandoned. And al-muqʿad is the young of the vulture. And qaʿadat al-rakhama, the carrion-vulture sat, when it crouched down. And al-maqāʿid are the place where people sit in their markets. And al-quʿudāt are riding-saddles and camel-saddles. As for their saying qaʿīdaka Allāh and qaʿdaka Allāh, in the sense of an oath . . . . . . . . . . . .
قعر: The letters qāf, ʿayn and rā' are one single sound root indicating a hollow in a thing that goes downward. One says: this is qaʿr al-biʾr, the bottom of the well, and qaʿr al-ināʾ, the bottom of the vessel, and this is qaṣʿa qaʿīra, a deep bowl. qaʿʿara al-rajul fī kalāmihi — the man spoke with an affected, mouth-stretching manner. A woman described as qaʿira — a term of reproach in intercourse. inqaʿarat al-shajara min arūmatihā — the tree was torn up from its root.
قعز: The letters qāf, ʿayn and zāy contain nothing but a curious note of Ibn Duraid's. He said: qaʿaztu l-ināʾ means I filled the vessel, and qaʿaztu fī l-mā' means I gulped it down.
قعس:
The letters qāf, ʿayn and sīn are a sound root indicating firmness and strength; they extend this metaphorically, so a man who is unassailable and mighty is called aqʿas.

1. qawʿas — one thick in the neck.
2. al-aqʿasān — two tall mountains.
3. layl aqʿas — a night long and unmoving, as though it would hardly pass.
4. al-iqʿās — wealth and abundance.
5. ʿizza qaʿsā' — might that is firm, never departing.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And might firm-rooted, never to be led by the forelock.

And al-ʿizz al-aqʿas is the same, in the masculine.

6. al-qaʿas — the neck sinking into the chest until it becomes the opposite of a hunch, because the chest then seems to rise. One says taqāʿasa taqāʿusan, and iqʿansasa iqʿinsāsan.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
A bad stand for the old man — "pull, pull!" —
either astride the pulley-block, or let him rear back.
قعش:
The letters qāf, ʿayn and shīn are a small root indicating a bending in a thing. One says qaʿashtu ra's al-khashaba, so that it may be bent toward you.

1. qaʿashtu l-shay' — I gathered the thing together; this fits the same sense, since you bend part of it over another part.
2. taqaʿwasha l-rajul — the man became bent, when he stooped; likewise the trunk, when bent.
3. al-quʿūsh — women's riding-litters, singular qaʿsh.
قعص:
The letters qāf, ʿayn and ṣād are a sound root indicating a disease that brings on death. One says: ḍarabahu fa-aqʿaṣahu, he struck him and killed him on the spot.

1. al-qaʿaṣ — sudden death; one says so-and-so died qaʿaṣan.
2. al-quʿāṣ — a disease that seizes the chest as though it were breaking the neck; one says quʿiṣat, so it is maqʿūṣa.
قعض:
The letters qāf, ʿayn and ḍād are a word indicating the bending and curving of a thing. From this: al-qaʿḍ, your bending the head of a piece of wood, as the shoots of a grapevine are bent.

It is as in his saying:
The two skilled hands bent the trellis-frame with a qaʿḍā-bend.
قعط:
The letters qāf, ʿayn and ṭā' are a sound root indicating binding a thing tightly, and indicating intensity in a thing.

1. al-iqtiʿāṭ — binding a headband or turban tightly; one says iqtaʿaṭtu l-ʿimāma, meaning to bind it on the head without putting a fold under the chin. In the hadith: "He commanded the chin-fold (al-talaḥḥī) and forbade al-iqtiʿāṭ."
2. al-qaʿaṭ — anger and loud shouting.
3. al-qaʿṭ — narrowness; one says qaʿʿaṭa ʿalā gharīmihi, he pressed his debtor hard.
4. al-qaʿṭ, among what falls outside this root — abundant sheep.
قعف:
The letters qāf, ʿayn and fā' are a sound root indicating scooping up a thing and taking all of it.

1. al-qaʿf — heavy treading, scraping up the dust with the hooves.
2. al-qāʿif — violent rain that scrapes away the face of the ground.
3. sayl quʿāf — a torrent like a scouring flood.
4. qaʿaftu l-nakhla — I uprooted the palm tree from its base.
5. al-qaʿf — your draining all that is in the vessel.
قعل:
The letters qāf, ʿayn and lām are three unrelated words, with no common measure among them.

1. al-quʿāl — the blossom that falls scattered from the grapevine.
2. al-qawāʿil — mountain peaks, singular qāʿila.
3. al-qaʿwalā — a gait in which the walker kicks up dust with the fronts of his feet.
قعم:
The letters qāf, ʿayn and mīm are words that do not go back to one common measure, but are distinct from one another.

1. uqʿima l-rajul — said of a man when a disease struck him and killed him.
2. aqʿamathu l-ḥayya — the snake killed him.
3. al-qaʿam — a crookedness in the nose.
4. al-qaʿam, in the buttocks — their being raised, not slack.
5. al-qayʿam — the cat.
قعن: The letters qāf, ʿayn and nūn contain nothing but Quʿayn, a tribe of the Arabs.
قعو:
The letters qāf, ʿayn and the weak letter contain words with no common measure.

1. qaʿā l-faḥl al-nāqa, qaʿuwwan — the stallion mounted the she-camel.
2. al-qaʿw — two pieces of wood in the pulley in which the axle sits.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
A she-camel firm with solid flesh, whose eye-tooth has come through,
gives a creak — the creak of the pulley-block against its rope.

3. aqʿā l-rajul fī majlisihi — the man leaned back in his sitting-place, resting on his haunches as a dog squats (yuqʿī). Squatting (al-iqʿā') in prayer is forbidden.
4. Ibn Duraid mentioned: imra'a qaʿwā' — a woman thin in the shanks.
قف:
The letters qāf and fāʾ are a sound root, denoting gathering, coming together, and shrinking in.

1. al-quffa — a thing shaped like a gourd, made from twigs or palm-leaf strips. One says of an old man shrunk with age: "he is like a quffa." Also istaqaffa, when something shrivels and contracts.
2. aqaffati l-dajājatu — the hen stopped laying.
3. al-qaff — a way of lying in wait to steal, so called, it is said, because he draws the thing to himself.
4. qafqafa l-ṣaridu — the shivering bird trembled; in our view this too is from the contracting that comes over a creature in the cold. A poet said, in a line of verse: "A fine cloak for the young man is this, when the night turns cold toward its last watch, and the shivering bird trembles" — and this is not from trembling alone.
5. al-quff — a raised ridge on the surface of the ground, as though it were gathered up; the plural is qifāf. God knows best.
قفح: The letters qāf, fā' and ḥā' — Ibn Duraid said: qafaḥat nafsuhu ʿan al-shay' means his soul recoiled from the thing, when it found it distasteful. He said this occurs in the poetry of al-Ṭirimmāḥ.
قفخ:
The letters qāf, fā' and khā' are a single word, and it is the striking of a dry thing upon its like. One says qafakha hāmatahu, he struck his skull.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
A striking upon the crowns of heads, and a gash, and a thrust.
قفد:
The letters qāf, fā' and dāl are a root indicating a twist in a thing.

1. al-qafad — a twist in the outer wrist; a man with it is aqfad, a woman qafdā', likewise a horse.
2. al-qafdā' — a manner of wrapping the turban.
قفر:
The letters qāf, fā' and rā' are a root indicating being devoid of good.

1. al-qafr — an empty, barren land.
2. al-qafār — food eaten without any relish. In the hadith: "No house in which there is vinegar is qafr."
3. imra'a qafra — a woman with little flesh.

Among what falls outside this root, by way of letter-substitution, they say: iqtafartu l-athar and iqtafaytuhu, I followed the track, and taqaffara likewise.

Ṣakhr said, in a line of verse:
As for me, I am slow in following after you.

4. al-qaffūr — a plant.

Ibn Aḥmar said, in a line of verse:
The sandgrouse grazes its five-day fast on its qaffūr-plant,
then comes to trouble the water among those who trouble it.

5. From the first sense: their saying "We alighted among the tribe of so-and-so and spent the night al-qafr," meaning they gave us no hospitality.

Ibn Duraid said — and this belongs to neither sense — al-qafar is hair. He cited as evidence:
A young woman well knows, by the hair on her shins,
that the well-ropes will be kept wet, or the well-timbers will wear out.
قفز:
The letters qāf, fā' and zāy are two roots: one indicates something resembling a leap, the other something worn as an ornament.

1. al-qafazān — the verbal noun of qafaza, to leap.
2. al-qawāfiz — a name for frogs.
3. al-quffāz — a kind of ornament a woman wears on her hands and feet.
4. faras muqaffaz — a horse whose white markings encircle its legs without going past the fetlock toward the hoof, by comparison to the quffāz.

As for al-qafīz, it is an Arabized word.
قفس: The letters qāf, fā' and sīn. They say: al-qafas is anger.
قفش: The letters qāf, fā' and shīn. There is a remark of Ibn Duraid on this: qafasha means to gather.
قفص:
The letters qāf, fā' and ṣād are words that point to gathering and coming together.

1. taqaffaṣa — said when something gathers together.
2. qaffaṣtu al-ẓaby — I bound together all four of the gazelle's legs.
3. al-qafṣ — leaping; their saying that al-qafṣ means leaping comes from this same sense, for leaping too is a drawing-together.
قفط: The letters qāf, fā' and ṭā' are a single word. They say: qafaṭa al-ṭā'ir, when the bird mates.
قفع:
The letters qāf, fā' and ʿayn are words that point to a drawing-together in something.

1. udhun qafʿā' — an ear as if struck by fire, so that it shrivelled and curled in.
2. al-rijl al-qafʿā' — a foot whose toes have curled back toward the sole from the cold.
3. al-qafʿa — a thing woven from palm-leaves in which fresh dates are gathered.

And in the hadith, in the mention of locusts: "Would that we had a qafʿa or two of it." God Most High knows best and is most wise.
قفل:
The letters qāf, fā' and lām are a sound root, one sense indicating a return from a journey, the other indicating hardness and toughness in a thing.

The first: al-qufūl — returning from a journey; and those setting out are not called a qāfila [caravan] until they turn back.

The other root: al-qafīl — dry wood. From this: al-qufl, the lock, named so because it involves fastening and firmness. One says aqfaltu al-bāb, so it is muqfal. A miser is called muqfal al-yadayn — locked of hand. qafila al-shayʾ — the thing dried up. Horses described as qawāfil — lean, gaunt. And one says aqfalahu al-ṣawm — fasting dried him out.
قفن:
The letters qāf, fā' and nūn are not a root. But they say:

1. al-qafan — a dialect variant of al-qafā, the back of the head.
2. al-qafīna — a sheep slaughtered from the back of its neck.
3. al-qaffān — the manner of a thing and the final outcome of its work. It came in the hadith of ʿUmar: "Then I will be over its qaffān."
قفي:
The letters qāf, fā' and the weak letter are a sound root indicating one thing following another.

1. al-qafw — following; one says qafawtu atharahu, I followed his track.
2. qaffaytu fulānan bi-fulān — I made so-and-so follow after so-and-so.
3. qāfiyat al-bayt, the rhyme-word of a line of verse — named so because it follows the rest of the speech, that is, it comes after it and follows it.
4. al-qafā — the back of the head and neck, as though it were a thing that follows the face.
5. al-qāfiya — the back of the neck. In the hadith: "The devil sits upon the qāfiya of the head of one of you."

Ibn Duraid said: one says "so-and-so is qifwatī," meaning my object of suspicion, and "qifwatī," meaning my chosen one, my best pick. He said this makes it seem like a word carrying opposite meanings (min al-aḍdād). But the sense is this: when a man suspects someone, he "follows him" (qafāhu), seeking out a fault in him; and when someone is his chosen one, he likewise "follows him" (qafāhu), hoping for good from him. In our view this is not, in any way, an instance of a word carrying opposite meanings.

6. al-qafiyy and al-qafāwa — milk or the like set aside for someone meant to be honored with it. This fits the root, as though the one meant is followed with it when it is given to him as a gift.

Salāma said, in a line of verse:
He is not thin-browed, nor hook-nosed, nor sickly —
he is given to drink the medicine of a well-tended, cherished reserve of milk.

7. qafawtu l-rajul — I accused the man of immorality, as though I followed him with foul speech. In the hadith: "We do not qafū our mother."
قل:
The letters qāf and lām are two sound roots: one denotes the scantness of a thing, the other denotes the opposite of settling, which is being unsettled or disturbed.

The first is their saying qalla al-shay' yaqillu qillatan, so it is qalīl — the thing became little, it becomes little, littleness, so it is little.

1. al-qull — littleness (al-qilla), just as al-dhull is to al-dhilla. And in the hadith about usury: "If it increases, it is heading toward diminishment [qull]."
2. al-qulla, the word that came in the hadith — they say al-qulla is the amount a person can lift of a large jar or vessel, and there is no fixed measure to it among the people of the language. A poet said, in a line of verse: "So we settled in comfort and reclined, and drank what is lawful from its water-jars [qulal]." And our statement that al-qulla is what a person can lift is also from al-qilla, littleness, because the thing becomes little in his hand.
3. istaqalla al-qawm — the people set off, when they went on their way; that too is from al-iqlāl, as if they made the going light for themselves and took it up lightly. The meaning throughout all of this is one and the same.

The other root:
1. taqalqala — a man, or anything else, became unsettled, when it did not stay fixed in a place.
2. taqalqala al-mismār — the nail worked loose in its place.
3. faras qulqul — a swift horse.
4. akhadhahu qillun min al-ghaḍab — a trembling of anger seized him, which is like a shudder.
قلب:
The letters qāf, lām and bā' are two sound roots: one of them points to the pure and noble part of a thing, and the other to the turning of a thing from one direction to another. The first is al-qalb: the heart of a man and of other creatures, so called because it is the purest thing in him and the highest. And the pure and noblest part of everything is its qalb. And they say, an Arab qalb, that is, of pure descent. A poet said, in a line of verse:
[So] do not raise much clamour over her, for I chose her from among them, a Zubayrī woman of pure stock.

Al-qulāb is a disease that strikes a camel so that it suffers in its heart. Al-qulb among bracelets is the one that is a single turn with no other twisted over it. And it is a likening to the qalb, the pith, of the palm tree. Then the snake was likened to the qulb of jewellery and was called qulb. And al-Qalb is a star; they say it is the heart of the Scorpion. [And] qalabtu al-nakhla - I pulled out the pith of the palm tree.

And the other root: qalabtu al-thawb qalban - I turned the garment over. Al-qalab is the turning over of the lip; a woman with it is qalbā' and the man who has it is aqlab. And qalabtu al-shay' - I turned it upside down; and qallabtuhu bi-yadī taqlīban - I turned it about with my hand. And one says aqlabat al-khubza, when it is time for the loaf to be turned. And their saying mā bihi qalba - they said its meaning is, there is no ailment in him for which he would be turned over and looked at. And they recited, a line of verse:
And no farrier has turned over her ground, and there is no mark on her from her two ropes.

That is, no one has turned over her legs because of an ailment in her. And al-qalīb is the well before it is lined with stones; and it was called qalīb only because it is like a thing that is turned from one direction to another, for it was ground, and when it was dug its earth became as though it were turned over. And when it is lined it is al-ṭawiyy. And the word qalīb is masculine. And al-ḥuwwal al-qalb is the man who turns matters over and contrives for them. And the analogy in all that we have mentioned is one.

As for al-qillīb and al-qillawb, it is said that it is the wolf. And it may be carried onto this analogy, so that one says it was named that for its turning about in search of its food. A poet said, in a line of verse:
O my eye, weep for Umm 'Āmir, the prey of a wolf in one of the water-channels.
قلت:
The letters qāf, lām and tāʾ are two sound roots: one denotes a hollow set into a thing, the other denotes the passing away and destruction of a thing.

The first is al-qalt, a hollow in a rock; the plural is qilāt. A poet said, in a line of verse: "and two eyes, like two pools of water, sheltered within the two hollows of the brow-ridges of a hollowed, watered rock." Al-qalt of the eye is its socket; al-qalt of the thumb is the hollow beneath it; al-qalt of the crumbled bread-dish is the dip in its middle.

The other root is al-qalat, meaning destruction. One says qalita, qalatan. It came in the report: "The traveller and his goods are exposed to loss, except what God preserves." Al-miqlāt, among she-camels, is the one whose young does not live; likewise among women, the plural being maqālīt. A poet said, in a line of verse: "the bereaved women [maqālīt] tread on him, saying: will no covering ever be thrown over the man?" And another said: "Do not blame her; she is of a line of women who sleep deep through the summer, bereaved, few in number."
قلح: The letters qāf, lām and ḥāʾ are one word: al-qalaḥ, a yellowing on the teeth; a man is described as aqlaḥ. A poet said, in a line of verse: "Blame has built its house upon them, and, along with the blame, the yellowing of their teeth has spread." They also say al-aqlaḥ means the dung-beetle.
قلخ: The letters qāf, lām and khāʾ are one word: they say al-qalkh is the bellowing roar of a male camel.
قلد:
The letters qāf, lām, and dāl are two sound roots. One indicates hanging something onto something and being tied to it thereby; the other indicates a share and a portion.

The first:
1. al-taqlīd — the garlanding of the sacrificial camel (al-hady): something is hung on its neck so that it is known to be an offering.
2. al-qald — its root sense is twisting. One says qaladtu al-ḥabl aqliduhu qaldan when you twist a rope. A rope is called qalīd or maqlūd, meaning twisted.
3. taqalladtu al-sayf — I slung the sword over my shoulder.
4. muqallad al-rajul — the place on a man's shoulder where the sword-strap (nijād) rests.
5. qallada fulānun fulānan qilādata sawʾin — so-and-so hung a 'necklace of shame' on so-and-so, meaning he satirized him with something whose mark stays on him forever. When they wanted to stress this they said he hung on him 'the collar of the dove' (ṭawq al-ḥamāma), meaning it never leaves him, just as a dove's collar never leaves it.

Bishr said, in a line of verse:
Your patron gave it to you out of deep hatred — and Jaʿfar was hung with the dove's collar.

6. al-miqlad — a stick bent at its tip, used to twist and gather fodder, just as alfalfa is twisted when it is made into ropes.
7. al-qild — the bracelet. This is a sound analogy, because the hand seems to wear it around itself.
8. al-iqlīd — it is said this is the [nose-ring] with which a she-camel's leading-rope is tied.

The other root:
1. al-qild — a share of water. One says: 'we watered our land its qild,' meaning its share. And 'the sky gave us a qild,' likewise meaning a share.

In a hadith: 'The sky gave us a qild's share every week.'

2. al-maqālīd — it is said these are the storehouses.

God Almighty said: {His are the keys of the heavens and the earth} [al-Zumar: 63]. Perhaps they were named this because they secure things, that is, they guard and hold them safe. The Arabs say: 'the sea aqlada over many creatures,' when it seals them within itself.

Straying from this chapter are al-qilda and al-qishda: dates and roasted-grain meal mixed with clarified butter.
قلز: The letters qāf, lām and zāy: they say al-taqalluz is liveliness, briskness.
قلس:
The letters qāf, lām and sīn are two words: one is the cloud casting down dew without rain; from it comes qalasa l-insān, when a person vomits — he is qālis. As for al-taqlīs, they say it is striking on certain instruments of entertainment; this is the other word.

Abū Bakr ibn Durayd said that al-qals is used of ropes, but I do not know how sound this is.
قلص:
The letters qāf, lām and ṣād are a sound root, denoting the drawing together of the parts of a thing.

1. taqallaṣa l-shayʾ — the thing drew together, contracted.
2. shafatun qāliṣa — a lip drawn back, shrunk.
3. ẓillun qāliṣ — a shadow, when it shrinks; as though it too had drawn together. God Most High said: {then We drew it in to Ourselves, a gradual drawing} [al-Furqān: 46].
4. qalaṣatu l-māʾ — the water that gathers and rises in a well, as though it had drawn together from its sides; such water is called māʾun qaliṣ, and the plural of qalaṣa is qalaṣāt.
5. qalaṣat nafsuhu — he felt nausea; this follows a similar pattern.
6. al-qalūṣ — the female of the young ostrich chicks. In my view she is called qalūṣ for the way her body draws together, as though her limbs had contracted in until they gathered close. The female bustard is called this too, and from it the qalūṣ among camels takes its name — the young, firm-bodied she-camel. And one says qalaṣa l-ghadīr, the pool of rain-water shrank, when most of its water was gone.
قلط: The letters qāf, lām and ṭāʾ contain nothing sound, except that Ibn Durayd said: rajulun qulāṭ is a short man — perhaps related to their saying rajulun qalaṭiyy.
قلع:
The letters qāf, lām and ʿayn are a sound root indicating the wrenching of one thing away from another; branches close to this sense are then derived from it. You say qalaʿtu al-shayʾ qalʿan — I pulled the thing out; I am qāliʿ, and it is maqlūʿ.

1. qulʿa — said of a man who is thrown from his saddle, from poor horsemanship.
2. "This is manzil qulʿa" — said when a dwelling is not a place of settling.
3. al-qawm ʿalā qulʿa — the people are ready to move on, on the point of departure.
4. al-maqlūʿ — the ruler or governor who has been deposed.
5. al-qilʿa — a rock that breaks away from a mountain on its own, hard to reach. A great mass of cloud is likened to it and is likewise called qilʿa, plural qalaʿ.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
The travelling clouds burst open above it ... and the khāzibāz [a biting fly] went wild with madness at it.

6. al-qulāʿ — mud that cracks apart when the water has receded from it, named so because it comes apart (yataqallaʿu).
7. aqlaʿa ʿan al-amr — he desisted from the matter.
8. ramāhu bi-qulāʿa — he tore up a piece of ground and threw it at him.
9. al-miqlāʿ — the sling, well known.
10. al-qalāʿ — said to mean the watchman. It is related in a hadith: "Neither a dībūb nor a qalāʿ shall enter Paradise." They said: al-dībūb is the one who creeps about with slander until he divides people against each other.
11. al-qalāʿ (a second sense) — a man who sees another's standing raised in someone's eyes, and keeps slandering between the two until he brings that standing down.
12. aqlaʿat ʿanhu al-ḥummā — the fever left him. They say: taraktu fulānan fī qalaʿin min ḥummā, meaning in a remission from fever. One also says qaliʿa qalaʿan.
13. al-qilʿ — a ship's sail, so called because when it is raised it pulls (qalaʿa) the ship from its place.

Two words fall outside this root. As for al-qalʿ, it is the leather bag a man carries, as in the saying "my fat is in my qalʿ" — meaning I carry my own provision, I need no one. As for al-qilʿ, it is said to be a small vest a man wears over his chest.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Carrying tucked under his arm, in his qilʿ, a knife.
قلف: The letters qāf, lām and fā' are a sound root indicating the stripping of something off something else. One says qalaftu al-shajarata, when I stripped its bark from it. And qalaftu al-danna: I broke away its clay seal. And the circumciser cut away (qalafa) the boy's foreskin — which is al-qulfa — when he cut it off.
قلق: The letters qāf, lām and qāf are a word indicating distress and agitation. One says qaliqa yaqlaqu qalaqan — he grew anxious.
قلم:
The letters qāf, lām, and mīm are a sound root indicating the smoothing of something when it is pared and set right.

1. qalamtu al-ẓufr and qallamtuhu — I pared the nail (both forms are used for trimming it).
2. maqlūm al-aẓfār — said of a weak man: he is 'trimmed of his claws,' meaning he has nothing left to defend himself with.
3. al-qulāma — what falls away from the nail when it is pared, the clippings.
4. al-qalam, the pen — named from this chapter. They said it was so named because it is pared just as the nail is pared; then the arrow-shaft (qidḥ) was likened to it and also called qalam. It is also possible that the arrow-shaft itself was called qalam for the smoothing and paring described.

God Almighty said: {and you were not with them when they cast their pens} [Āl ʿImrān: 44].

5. al-miqlam — the tip of the sheath covering the camel's penis, as if it had been trimmed.
6. maqālim al-rumḥ — it is said these are the joints (kuʿūb) of a spear.

Straying from this root is al-qulām, which is a plant.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
They brought me qulām and told me to eat it as my evening meal — but does anything eat qulām except camels?
قله: The letters qāf, lām and hāʾ — I recall nothing in this, except that Ghadīr Qalahā is a place-name.
قلو:
The letters qāf, lām and the weak letter are a sound root, denoting lightness and speed.

1. al-qilw — the light, swift donkey.
2. qalati l-nāqatu bi-rākibihā qalwan — the she-camel went ahead swiftly with her rider.
3. iqlawlati l-ḥumru — the wild asses went in their swiftness.
4. al-muqlawlī — the one who holds himself apart from his bed, restless upon it; and anything that draws away, averse, from something, is muqlawlin. A poet said, in a line of verse: "I say, when she draws herself up over it and grows still: is there a companion of a sweet life that lasts?" And al-munkamish, the brisk, hurried one, is also called muqlawlin. It came in a report: "Had you seen Ibn ʿUmar you would have seen him muqlūliyyan" — meaning drawn away from the ground, as if to convey how much he prayed.
5. qalā l-ʿayru ātunahu qalwan — the wild donkey drove his females along swiftly.
6. al-qilā — hatred; one says from it qalaytuhu aqlīhi qilan, and they also said qalaytuhu aqlāhu. Al-qilā is a drawing away from a thing and a leaving of it.
7. al-qalyu — the roasting of a thing in the pan; one says qalaytu and qalawtu. Al-qallāʾ is the one who roasts, and this too follows the pattern, because roasting makes the grain light and it becomes lighter too.
قم:
The letters qāf and mīm are a single root, denoting the gathering of a thing.

1. qamqama Allāhu ʿaṣabahu — God drew his sinews together, meaning gathered them.
2. al-qamqām — the sea, because it is a gathering-place for water.
3. al-qamqām — a great number; a chief who gathers up leadership and is ample in good is then likened to it.
4. qumma al-bayt — the house was swept.
5. al-qumāma — what is swept up; it is gathered together.
6. aqamma al-faḥlu al-ibil — the stud camel covered all the she-camels, making every one of them pregnant.
7. miqammat al-shāt — the sheep's mouth-part, so named because with it she gathers up the plants into her mouth.
8. al-qimma — the top of anything, because it is the gathering-point that gives it its support.

Among what deviates from this chapter: al-qamqām — small ticks.
قما:
The letters qāf, mīm and the weak letter are a word indicating lowliness and disgrace. One says huwa qamiyyun bayyinu al-qamā'ah — he is plainly lowly, that is, disgraced. And aqmaytuhu ana: I disgraced him.
When hamzated it has another meaning: that is their saying taqamma'tu al-shay', when you sought it out, taqammu'an. Some people claimed this belongs to the chapter of being pleased (i'jāb); one says aqma'anī al-shay': the thing pleased me. And aqma'ati al-ibil: the camels grew fat. And taqamma'tu al-shay': I gathered it up, bit by bit.
A poet said, in a line of verse:
I have had my fill, so do not mock me foolishly for what I have gathered of pleasure and delight.
قمح:
The letters qāf, mīm and ḥā' are a small root indicating a trait that appears in a drinker while drinking water — the raising of his head.

1. al-qāmiḥ — said of a camel that raises its head at the water, refusing to drink. Camels of this kind are qimāḥ.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And we, sitting at its edges ... lower our gaze, like camels refusing the water.

They say: rawiyat ḥattā inqamaḥat — it drank until it was full and stopped drinking. And shahrā qimāḥ — the two hardest months of cold, named so because when the camels come to the water its cold hurts them, so they qāmaḥat — raised their heads away from it.

Outside this root is al-qamḥ, wheat. And they say — and it may well be sound — iqtamaḥtu al-sawīq and qamaḥtuhu, when you toss the parched-grain meal into your mouth with your palm. Ibn Durayd said: al-qumḥa, of water, is what fills your mouth of it. And al-qummaḥāt are wars [a yellow dye plant], or saffron, or dharīra, a fragrant powder — all these are said.
قمد: The letters qāf, mīm and dāl are a lesser root indicating length, strength and firmness. From that, al-qumudd: the strong, sturdy one. Ibn Duraid said: al-qamd is the base form from which al-qumudd is built. And al-aqmad is the tall one — a man aqmad, a woman qamdā', and also said qumudd and qumuddah.
قمر:
The letters qāf, mīm and rā' are a sound root pointing to whiteness in a thing, and then branches come out from it. Of that is al-qamar, the moon of the sky; it is called qamar for its whiteness. And himārun aqmar, that is, white. And the diminutive of qamar is qumayr. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And a little moon appeared, a child of twenty-five nights, and the two girls said to him: rise!

And one says taqammartuhu: I came to him in the moonlight. And they say qamira al-tamr and aqmara, when the cold strikes the dates so that their sweetness goes before they ripen. And one says taqammara al-asad, when the lion goes out seeking prey in the moonlight. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Evening fell upon a hunter by moonlight, firm of heart, well practised in the thrust.
And qamara al-qawm al-tayr, when they come upon the birds by night and catch them. As for the words of al-A'shā, in a line of verse:
An old man hunted her by moonlight in the evening, and she woke a Qudā'ī woman, going to the diviners, rebellious against her husband.
it was said its meaning is: as the lion hunts prey by moonlight. And others said: taqammarahā, he tricked her, as a bird is come upon by night and caught.

Of this chapter: qamira al-rajul, when a man cannot see in the snow. And this follows their saying qamirat al-qirba, and that is something like a burning that comes upon the waterskin from the moon.

As for their saying qamara yaqmiru qamran, and al-qimār from gambling, some people said it is an odd case out of the root we have mentioned, and others said: rather it is from it. That is because the gambler's wealth increases and does not stay in one state. This is something we have heard. God knows best whether it is sound.

Ibn Durayd said: taqammara al-rajul, when a man seeks someone to gamble with him. And one says qamartu al-rajul aqmuruhu and aqmiruhu, I beat him at gambling.
قمس:
The letters qāf, mīm and sīn are a sound root indicating the dipping of something into water; the water itself is also called by this name.
1. qamastu al-shay' fī al-mā' — I dipped the thing in the water.
2. qāmūs al-baḥr — the main bulk, the depths of the sea. And they said, concerning the ebb and flow of the tide, that an angel is charged over the qāmūs of the sea: whenever he sets down his foot it overflows, and when he lifts it, it recedes.
3. qamasa al-walad fī baṭni ummihi — the child stirred and moved in its mother's womb.
4. al-qammās — the diver.
5. inqamasa al-najm — the star sank down in the west, it set.

And the Arabs say of a man disputing with one bolder than himself: innamā yuqāmisu ḥūtan — he is only diving against a whale.
قمش: The letters qāf, mīm and shīn. They say: al-qamsh is the gathering of something from here and there.
قمص:
The letters qāf, mīm and ṣād are two roots: one indicates wearing a thing and sinking into it, the other indicates leaping and movement.

The first: al-qamīṣ, the shirt, well known. Taqammaṣahu, he put it on. It is then extended figuratively to anything a person enters into, so one says taqammaṣa al-imāra, he took on command, or taqammaṣa al-wilāya, he took on governorship. The plural of qamīṣ is aqmiṣa and qumuṣ.

The other root: al-qamṣ, from their saying qamaṣa al-ba'īru wa yaqmuṣu qamṣan wa qimāṣan, said of a camel raising its forelegs and throwing them down together while kneading with its hind legs, that is, bucking. Al-qāmiṣa, mentioned in the hadith, belongs here. One says qamaṣa al-baḥru bi-l-safīnati, the sea tossed the ship with its waves, as if the ship were a bucking camel.
قمط:
The letters qāf, mīm and ṭā' are a lesser root indicating gathering and coming together.
1. al-qamṭ — the binding of a baby's limbs with its swaddling-wrap (qimāṭ).
2. qamṭ al-asīr — the binding of a captive, when his hands and feet are bound together with a rope.
3. waqaʿat ʿalā qimāṭihi — he grasped the tying of the matter, however it had been tied — that is, when you have fully understood it.
4. marra binā ḥawlun qamīṭ — a whole, complete year passed for us.
5. sifād al-ṭā'ir qamṭ — the mating of a bird is also called qamṭ, because of its gathering its seed into its mate.
قمع:
The letters qāf, mīm and ʿayn are three sound roots: one is a liquid thing descending into a vessel made for it; the second is humbling and overpowering; the third is a kind of animal.

The first: al-qimaʿ, well known — the funnel; one says qimaʿ or qimʿ. In a hadith: "Woe to the funnels of speech" — those who listen but do not retain, as if their ears were funnels that keep nothing in them. They say: iqtamaʿtu what was in the waterskin, when you drank all of it — meaning you became to it like the funnel.

The second root — which can perhaps be joined to the first by a subtle sense — is their saying qamaʿtuhu, I humbled him. From it, qamaʿtuhu, when you struck him with the miqmaʿ, a mace. God Almighty said: {and for them are maces of iron} [al-Ḥajj: 21]. Qamaʿa ibn Ilyās was named so because his father charged him with something and he withdrew into his house, so he was called Qamaʿa. The reasoning here and in the first root is close, for both involve entering into one's house, just as water withdraws down into the funnel.

The third root: al-qamaʿ — the large blue fly. One says: taraknāhu yataqammaʿu al-dhibbān min al-farāgh, meaning he keeps swatting the flies away, as a donkey does. Those flies are themselves called al-qamaʿ.

A poet, Aws, said, in a line of verse:
Have you not seen that God sent down His help ... while the dust-grey gazelles, in their lairs, swat the flies away.

They say: aqmaʿtu al-rajul ʿannī, when you drove him off from you — this too is from this root, as if he were driven away.

Carried by resemblance to this: al-qamaʿ — what is above the ridge-bones at the top of a camel's hump. And from it, al-qamaʿ — a swelling in one of a horse's knees. And al-qamaʿ — a pustule in the inner corner of the eye, from an excess of flesh.

Falling outside these roots is their saying that qamʿat māl al-qawm is the choicest part of people's wealth.
قمل: The letters qāf, mīm and lām are words indicating meanness and lowliness. A qamalī man is a contemptible man. al-qummal — young locusts, not yet grown. And aqmala al-rimth, when the rimth plant's leaves came out small, as if that were likened to the qummal.
قمن: The letters qāf, mīm and nūn are a single word. One says huwa qamanun an yafʿala kadhā — he is likely to do such a thing — and it takes no dual or plural when its mīm carries a fatḥa. But if its mīm carries a kasra, or you say qamīn instead, then it does take a dual and plural. The meaning of qamīn is khaliq — fitting, likely to be so.
قمه:
The letters qāf, mīm and hā' contain words that are not original roots.
They say: qamaha the thing, when it plunged into the water, rising for a time and sinking for a time. And rocky ridges (qifāf) are called qummah when they vanish in the mirage and then appear again. This is a case of sound-substitution; its true origin is qamasa.
And they say: qamaha the camel, like qamaḥa, when it raised its head and did not drink the water — this too is substitution.
And another word, from letter-reversal: Ibn Duraid said, al-qamah is like al-qaham, which is a lack of appetite for food; one says qahima and qamiha.
قن:
The letters qāf and nūn make up a chapter not built on one single pattern; its words are unrelated to one another.

1. al-qinn — the slave whose father, too, was owned as a slave.
2. al-qunna — the top of a mountain.
3. al-qunān — the smell of the armpit at its strongest.
4. al-qunāqin — the guide who knows the way, skilled in finding water underground; the plural is qanāqin.
قنا:
The letters qāf, nūn and the weak letter are two roots: one indicates constant attachment and mingling, the other indicates a rise or elevation in a thing.

The first: their saying qānāhu, when it mingled with it, as one colour mingles with another. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: qānaytu al-shay' — I mixed the thing. Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
Like the first egg [of an ostrich], its whiteness mingled with a tinge of yellow, nourished by abundant water, unfouled.
1. mā yuʿāninī hādhā — it does not agree with me; its meaning is that it recoils from the thing and will not mingle with it.
2. qanā al-shay' wa-qtanāhu — he acquired the thing and kept it for his own use, not for trade.
3. māl qunyān — property taken as a possession (qunya).
4. qanaytu ḥayā'ī — I held fast to my modesty; its derivation is from al-qunya. A poet said, in a line of verse:
So hold fast to your modesty — may you have no father — and know that I am a man who will die unless I am killed.
5. al-qinw — a palm-cluster together with what hangs on it, because it stays attached to its tree.
6. al-maqnāh, among those who do not hamzate it — shade, a place the sun does not reach; it was so named because the shade clings to it and scarcely ever leaves it. And scholars of the Qur'an say the cave of the People of the Cave lay in a maqnāh of a mountain.

The other root: al-qanā — a curve in the nose; the verb is qaniya, qanan. It may be that al-qanāh — the shaft, the cane — comes from this, because it is set upright and raised; its alif is [originally] a wāw, since its plural is qanan and qanawāt. And the water-channel, qanāt al-mā', is likened among us to this qanāh, if qanāt al-mā' is indeed an Arabic word. The likening is not on account of height, but because such channels are underground conduits and wells, so that it is as though it were this qanāh, since it has joints and pipe-lengths.

When hamzated, it departs from this pattern: one says qana'a, when its redness grew intense, and it is qāni'. And sometimes they hamzate maqna'at al-ẓill, though the first, unhamzated form is closer to the pattern we have described.
قنب:
The letters qāf, nūn and bā' are a root indicating gathering and coming together.
1. al-miqnab — a troop of horses, said to number around forty.
2. al-qanīb — a group of people.
3. qannaba al-zarʿ taqnīban — the crop put out its husk-covering. Ibn Duraid said the husk-covering is called al-qunnābah — the gathered leaf-covering in which the ear of grain sits.
4. al-qunb — the sheath of a horse's penis, so named because it gathers what is inside it.

As for al-qunnab [hemp], some people claimed it is an Arabic word. If so, it comes from qanaba al-zarʿ, when the crop put out its husk; though it is a thing not made from any part of that husk.
قنت:
The letters qāf, nūn and tā' are a sound root that points to obedience and to good in religion; it does not go beyond this chapter.

The origin in it is obedience. One says qanata yaqnutu qunūtan. Then every uprightness on the road of religion was called qunūt, and standing long in the prayer was called qunūt, and staying silent in the prayer and turning wholly to it was called qunūt. God Almighty said: {And stand before God devoutly obedient} [al-Baqara: 238].
قنح:
The letters qāf, nūn and ḥā' are not, in our view, an original root. Even so, they say: qanaḥa al-shārib, when the drinker had drunk his fill and raised his head in satisfaction. This comes from qamaḥa, a case of substitution, already mentioned.
And among the curiosities Ibn Duraid records: qanaḥtu al-ʿūd qanḥan — I bent the stick. He said: al-qunnāḥ is the crook-staff, in the dialect of the people of Yemen.
قند: The letters qāf, nūn and dāl are two words they claimed to be genuine. They said: al-qand [cane sugar] is Arabic; one says sawīq maqnūd and muqannad — sweetened with it. And the other word is al-qindaʾwah: they said it means the ill-tempered one.
قنر: The letters qāf, nūn and rā' are one word: al-qanawwar — the big-headed one.
قنس:
The letters qāf, nūn and sīn are a sound lesser root indicating the fixedness of a thing.
1. al-qins — the place where anything grows, its root and base. A poet said, in a line of verse:
In a root of glory that surpasses every root.

They said: whatever is firmly fixed within a thing, that thing is a qins for it.
2. al-qawnas, of a helmet — its topmost part; and the qawnas of a horse's forelock is what rises above it, being firmly set in place. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Drive your cares away, the ones that visit you by night, by striking with the sword the crest of the horse.
قنص:
The letters qāf, nūn and ṣād are a single word indicating hunting, nothing else.
1. al-qāniṣ — the hunter.
2. al-qanaṣ — the game, the hunting itself.
3. al-qanṣ — the act of the hunter.
4. al-qanīṣ, as Ibn Duraid records it — the hunter.

And Banū Qanaṣ ibn Maʿadd were a people who have died out.
قنط: The letters qāf, nūn and ṭā' are a sound word indicating despair of something. One says qanaṭa yaqniṭu, and qaniṭa yaqnaṭu. God Almighty said: {And who despairs of his Lord's mercy except those who are astray} [al-Ḥijr: 56].
قنع:
The letters qāf, nūn and 'ayn are two sound roots: one indicates turning toward and facing a thing, though its meanings then diverge while the underlying pattern stays consistent; the other indicates a roundness in a thing.

The first: al-iqnā', turning the face toward a thing. One says aqna'a lahu yuqni'u iqnā'an. Al-iqnā' also means: raising the hand in supplication, so named because of one's turning toward the direction to which he extends his hand. Al-iqnā' also means: tilting a vessel so the water runs down and pours out.

From this chapter: qana'a al-rajulu yaqna'u qunū'an, when he begged or asked for charity. God, be He glorified, said: {and feed the beggar and the one who asks not} [al-Ḥajj: 36] — al-qāni' is the one who asks; he is called qāni' because of his turning toward the one he asks. He said, in a line of verse: "A man's wealth, when it sets him right and frees him of his want, is worthier than begging."

They say: qani'a qanā'atan, when he was content — it is called qanā'ah, contentment, because he turns toward what is his own, satisfied with it. Al-iqnā' also means: a camel stretching its head toward water to drink. Ibn al-Sikkīt said: qana'ati al-ibilu wa-l-ghanamu li-l-mart'a, when they turned toward the pasture.

So-and-so is a shāhidun maqna' [an acceptable witness] — this is from qani'tu bi-l-shay', when you are satisfied with a thing; its plural is maqāni'. You say: it is a satisfaction one can be content with. He said, in a line of verse: "I made a pact with Laylā in private, and my witnesses over Laylā were not acceptable witnesses."

As for the other root: al-qin', something round made of sand. Al-qin' and al-qinā': a tray-like thing on which a gift is presented. Qinā' al-mar'ah, a woman's veil, is well known, because she wraps it around her head.
