Derived from this qinā' is their saying qanna'a ra'sahu bi-l-sawṭi ḍarban, meaning he struck his head as though covering it like a veil.

What falls outside this root: al-iqnā', the rising of a thing without any downward slope. It could also be made a third root, citing as evidence God's words describing people "straining forward, their heads upraised" — the exegetes said this means with their heads raised.
قنف:
The letters qāf, nūn and fā' are a root indicating a coming-together in a thing.
1. al-qanīf — a group of people.
2. al-qanīf, as Ibn Duraid records it — a portion of the night; one says 'a portion of the night (qanīf) passed.'
3. al-qanaf — smallness and thickness of the two ears, following the same pattern.
4. al-qunāf — the thick-nosed.
قنم: The letters qāf, nūn and mīm are a single word. They say: qanima al-shay' qanaman, when it grew damp and then dust settled on it and it became soiled. This happens in the coats of horses and camels.
قه:
The letters qāf and hā' contain nothing but the imitation of qahqaha — going to excess in laughter.

1. qahh / qahqaha — one says qahhun and qahqahatun, and it may also be said in a lightened form. A poet said, in a line of verse: "So they were in mockery, and in qah [laughter]."
2. al-qahqaha — they also say it means nearness to the watering-place.
قهب:
The letters qāf, hā' and bā' are a lesser root indicating a colour.
1. al-quhba — a whiteness overlaid with a tinge of red.
2. al-qahb, of the young of cattle — the one whose colour is such.
3. al-qahb — the great mountain.
4. al-aqhabān — the elephant and the buffalo.

All of this is close in kind.
قهد: The letters qāf, hā' and dāl are a single word. They say: al-qahd, of the young of sheep, is the one whose colour inclines toward white.
قهر:
The letters qāf, hā' and rā' are a sound word pointing to overcoming and mastery. One says qaharahu yaqharuhu qahran — he overpowered him. Al-qāhir is the victor. Uqhira al-rajul when he is put in a state in which he is humbled. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Ḥuṣayn hoped to be lord over his clan, but Ḥuṣayn ended humbled and overborne.
Quhira — when he is overcome. Of this chapter: quhira al-laḥm — the meat was cooked until its juice ran out. Al-qahqar is said to be the he-goat. If that is sound, it may be from the analogy we have described. Al-qahqar is also hard stone, and that is not far from the root the chapter is built on.

Among what strays from that is their saying [raja'a] al-qahqarā — when he goes back the way he came, walking backwards.
قهز:
The letters qāf, hā' and zāy are a word. They say: al-qihz is cloth of mirʿizzā [soft goat-hair] mixed with silk, to which soft hair is likened. A poet said, in a line of verse:
...of qihz-cloth and qūhī-cloth.
قهس: The letters qāf, hā' and sīn are words, if they are indeed sound. They say: jā'a yataqahwasu, when he came stooping, shaking as he went; it is possible its hā' is extra, as though the word were yataqawwasu — bending like a bow. And they say: al-qahwasa — speed. And al-qahwas — the tall man.
قهل:
The letters qāf, hā' and lām are a word indicating roughness and a bad state.
1. al-qahal — roughness, want of grooming.
2. a man mutaqahhil — one who does not tend to his body with cleanliness.

And from this chapter, or close to it:
3. al-qahl — ingratitude, making little of a favour received.
4. aqhala al-rajulu nafsahu — he defiled himself with what did not concern him.
5. al-taqahhul — complaining of need. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Bold and grasping — whenever he met him, he fell to complaining.
6. inqahala — he collapsed and grew weak.
7. qahaltu al-rajula qahlan — I praised him with a foul, backhanded praise.

Among what falls outside this, and I do not know how sound it is, they say: al-qayhalah is the face. One says ḥayyā Allāhu qayhalatahu — may God preserve his face. It is not a pleasant word.
قهو:
The letters qāf, hā' and the weak letter are a root indicating abundance and plenty. A man whose household or mount is abundantly provided is called qāhin; one says innahu la-fī ʿaysh qāhin — he is in an abundant life.
As for their saying aqhā al-rajulu min ṭaʿāmin, when he found the food distasteful, this is not because he loathed it in itself, but because it was so abundant to him that he had his fill of it and so came to loathe it.
As for al-qahwa, it is wine; they said it was so named because it turns one away (tuqhī) from food — the same reasoning applies.
قوب:
The letters qāf, wāw and bā' are a sound root, and it is a hollow, scooped-out digging into a thing. You say qubtu al-arḍ aqūbuhā qawban, meaning you dug a rounded pit into it; you say qubtuhā fa-inqābat — I dug it and it became hollowed. And qawwabtu al-arḍ, when you left a mark in it. And taqawwaba al-shayʾ — the thing came away from its base.

al-qūbāʾ (ringworm) seems to be from this root, and it is a genuine Arabic word.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
O the wonder of this calamity ... will spittle really drive away the ringworm?

Its wāw may also be left unpronounced, so one says qūbāʾ. And they say, as a proverb: "takhallaṣat qāʾibatun min quwabin" — an egg came free of its chick; it is said of a man who parts from his companion.
قوت:
The letters qāf, wāw and tā' are a sound root indicating a holding-back, a safeguarding, and a power over a thing. From this is His saying, Most High: {and God has power over all things} [al-Nisā': 85], meaning a guardian and witness over it, and capable of what He wills. He said, in a line of verse: "And a rancorous one, I held my soul back from him, and remained, despite his wrongdoing, in full control."

From this chapter: al-qūt, what sustains life and keeps the last breath in the body — it is called qūt because it is the body's sustenance and its strength. Al-qawt: providing for someone. One says quttuhu qawtan, and the noun is al-qūt. One says iqtatt li-nārika qītatan, meaning feed your fire with wood. Dhū al-Rummah said, in a line of verse: "So I said to him: lift it up and revive it with your breath, and feed it a measured feeding."
قود:
The letters qāf, wāw and dāl are a sound root indicating extension in a thing, whether that extension runs along the ground or up into the air.
1. al-qūd — plural of qawdā', the long-necked she-camel.
2. al-qawdā' — the long mountain-pass rising into the sky.
3. afrās qūd — horses long in the neck. Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
Long-necked ones, worn thin by the leading-rein of the mountain pass until they broke down, their heels bleeding, fitted with anklets.
4. qudtu al-farasa qawdan — I led the horse, meaning you draw it toward you; this is the standard sense. From this, horses are collectively named qawd, so one says 'a troop of horses (qawd) passed by us.'
5. faras qaʾūd — a docile, easily-led horse.
6. al-qāʾid, of a mountain — its jutting spur.
7. al-aqwad, of a man — one who, once he sets his face toward a thing, hardly turns away from it.
8. al-qawad — the killing of a killer in retribution for the one he killed; it is called qawad because he is led to it.
قور:
The letters qāf, wāw and rā' are a sound root indicating roundness in a thing.
1. al-shayʾ al-muqawwar — the thing that is rounded, hollowed out.
2. quwwārat al-qamīṣ — the round neck-opening cut in a shirt, well known.
3. al-qūr — plural of qārah, the hillock, so named because it is round.

Some people say that al-dabba [a certain vessel] is also called al-qārah, on the likeness of the round hillock.
4. dār qawrā' — a house [built] with a round [courtyard]; this follows the same pattern, and it was set down according to what the dwellings of the Arabs were like, their tents and domes.
5. iqwarra al-jild — the skin shrivelled and puckered; this belongs to the chapter, because it draws together and rounds one part of it over another.

Among what falls outside this chapter is their saying: laqītu minhu al-aqwarīn wa-l-aqwariyyāt — meaning hardships.
قوز:
The letters qāf, wāw and zāy are a single word: al-qawz — the sand-dune, plural aqwāz and qīzān. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And I looked out from the high sand-dune, hoping that I might see Laylā's fire, or her keen-eyed watcher might see me.
قوس:
The letters qāf, wāw and sīn are a single root indicating the measuring of one thing against another; it is then inflected so that its wāw turns to yāʾ, and the sense throughout stays one.

1. al-qaws — the cubit, the forearm-measure, named so because whatever is measured by the arm's length is measured by it. By this too the qaws that is shot from — the bow — was named.

God Almighty said: {and he was at the distance of two bow-lengths or nearer} [al-Najm: 9]. The exegetes said: He meant two forearm-lengths.

2. al-aqwas — one whose back is bent. And qawwasa al-shaykh — the old man became bent, as if he were a bow.

A poet, Imruʾ al-Qays, said, in a line of verse:
I see that they do not love the one whose wealth has grown little ... nor the one in whom they see grey hair and a bent back.

The wāw is changed to yāʾ for certain reasons, so one says baynī wa-baynahu qīsu rumḥin, meaning the length of a spear between us. From this, al-qiyās — the measuring of one thing against another; the instrument of measure is called miqyās. You say qāyastu al-amrayni muqāyasatan wa-qiyāsan.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
The lowborn are disgraced when the true-born says to them: count the pebbles, then measure by the measures.

The plural of al-qaws is qisiyy, and aqwās, [and qiyās].

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And the horsemen strung their bows.

Some related that al-qaws also means outstripping others, and that al-qiyās comes from this; one says qāsa banū fulān banī fulān, when they outstripped them. And he cited, in a line of verse:
By my life, your father truly outstripped everyone ... so why do you not also outstrip, as he who outstripped did?

The root of all of this is the wāw, as we have already said.

Falling outside this chapter: al-qaws — what is left of the dates in the basket. al-qaws — a constellation. al-miqwas — the place from which horses are run: a rope is stretched across their chests so they are made even, then they are let go. As for al-qūs, it is the monk's cell, and I do not think it is an Arabic word, though it has occurred in poetry.

A poet said, in a line of verse [the opening words are lost]:
... as if it were the staff of a monk in his cell, in its suppleness and its straightness.

And Jarīr said, in a line of verse [the opening words are lost]:
... and had she stopped, she would have tempted me, and the man in the two coarse garments, in his cell.
قوض: The letters qāf, wāw and ḍād are a word indicating the dismantling of a structure. One says: qawwaḍtu al-binā' — I dismantled the building, without demolishing it. And taqawwaḍat al-ṣufūf — the ranks broke apart.
قوط: The letters qāf, wāw and ṭā' are a single word. They say: al-qawṭ is a small flock of sheep, plural aqwāṭ.
قوع:
The letters qāf, wāw and 'ayn are a root indicating a spreading-out and flatness in a place. From this: al-qā', level, smooth ground; the alif was originally a wāw, as the diminutive quwayʻ shows. Ibn Durayd said: al-qaw' is the flat spread of ground where dates are laid out to dry, plural aqwā'. As for al-qaw', the male animal's covering of the she-camel in mating, this does not belong to this chapter, because it is a metathesis; its true form is qa'w, already mentioned elsewhere.

What falls outside this chapter: their saying that al-quwā' is the male hare.
قوف: The letters qāf, wāw and fā' are a word belonging to the chapter of letter-reversal, and not an original root. They say: huwa yaqūfu al-athara wa-yaqtāfuhu, meaning yaqfū — he tracks the footprint. And they say: akhadha bi-qūfati qafāhu — he took hold of the qūfah of his nape, which is the hair hanging down in the hollow of the neck.
قوق: The letters qāf, wāw and qāf form a word. They say: al-qūq is a tall man.
قول: The letters qāf, wāw and lām are a single sound root with few words in it, and it is speech — saying with the tongue. One says qāla yaqūlu qawlan — he said, he says, a saying. Al-miqwal is the tongue. A man who is quwala or qawwāl is one who says a great deal. And as for aqwāl . . . . . . . . . .
قوم:
The letters qāf, wāw and mīm are two sound roots. One of them points to a body of people — and it is sometimes borrowed for others than people — and the other points to standing upright, or to resolve.

The first is al-qawm, the people. They say it is the plural of imru', a man, and it is used only of men. God the Exalted said: Let not a people mock a people [al-Ḥujurāt 11], then He said: nor women other women.

And Zuhayr said, in a line of verse:
I do not know, and I think I shall come to know: are the family of Ḥiṣn men, or women?

And they say qawm and aqwām, and aqāwim is a plural of a plural. As for the borrowed use, it is the saying of the poet:
When the cock comes forward calling some of his household at daybreak — and he is a people without weapons.
So he made them a body and called them a qawm.

As for the other root, it is their saying qāma qiyāman — he stood, standing; and al-qawma is the single time of it, when a man stands upright. And qāma also carries the sense of resolve, as one says qāma bi-hādhā al-amr — he stood to this affair, when he takes it to himself. And they say of the first: qiyām ḥatm — a standing of the body that is fixed; and of the other: qiyām ʿazm — a standing of resolve.

And of the section: qawwamtu al-shay' taqwīman — I set a value on the thing. The root of qīma, value, is the wāw, and its origin is that you set this up in the place of that.

And it has reached us that the people of Mecca say istaqamtu al-matāʿ, that is, I priced the goods. And of the section: hādhā qiwām al-dīn wa-l-ḥaqq — this is what religion and truth stand by, that is, by it they stand. As for al-qawām, it is good tallness. And al-qūmiyya is stature and figure. He said:
In the days when I was of a fine figure.
قوي:
The letters qāf, wāw and yā' are two roots far apart from each other: one points to strength and the opposite of weakness, and the other to the opposite of this and to a scarcity of good.

The first is al-quwwa - strength - and al-qawī is the opposite of the weak. The origin of that is from al-quwā, which is the plural of quwwa, from the strands of a rope. Al-muqwī is the one whose companions and camels are strong. And al-muqwī is also the one who leaves his bowstring slack, when he has not twisted it well, so that its strands ride over one another. And rajul shadīd al-quwā means a man tightly knit in build.

As for their saying aqwā al-rajul fī shiʿrihi - a man made a fault of aqwā in his verse - it is that he falls short of a strand in the measure of his line. As in his saying, in a line of verse:
Is it after the slaying of Mālik ibn Zuhayr that the women hope for happy outcomes of their times of purity?

The other root: al-qawā' is land with no people in it. One says aqwat al-dār - the house was emptied. And aqwā al-qawm - the people came to be in empty, waterless ground. They say bāta fulān al-qawā' and bāta al-qafr, when he passes the night without food. Al-muqwī is the man who has no provisions with him, and it is from this, as though he had come down in an empty land.

Among what departs from this root is a word they say: they say ishtarā al-shurakā' al-shay' thumma iqtawawhu, when the partners bought a thing and then bid one another up for it until it reached the utmost of its price.
قيأ: The letters qāf, yā' and hamza are a single word. Qā'a yaqī'u qay'an — he vomited; and istaqā'a is the istaf'ala-form of vomiting. And they say of a garment saturated with dye: it "vomits" the dye (yaqī'u al-ṣibgh).
قيح: The letters qāf, yā' and ḥā' are a word. Qāḥa [the wound] yaqīḥu — it discharges pus not mixed with blood.
قيد:
The letters qāf, yā' and dāl are a single word, and it is al-qayd, the fetter, which is well known; then it is used figuratively for anything that is confined. One says qayyadtuhū uqayyiduhū taqyīdan — I fettered it. And one says of a horse: it is qayd al-awābid, meaning that, from the swiftness with which it overtakes wild game, the game is as if fettered by it. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And I have set out early, while the birds are still in their nests, on a lean, tall horse, a fetter of the wild game.

1. al-muqayyad — the place of the fetter on the horse.
قيل:
The letters qāf, yā' and lām — the true root-letter of this word is a wāw, written here with a yā' to match the pronunciation. Al-qayl: a king among the kings of Ḥimyar, plural aqyāl. Whoever makes its plural aqwāl, its singular in that scheme is qayyal, with a doubled yā'. Al-qīl wa-l-qāl: Ibn al-Sikkīt said these are two nouns, not verbal nouns. Iqtāla 'alā fulānin, when he ruled over him and imposed his judgement — its meaning, in our view, is that he is being compared to the king who is a qayl. He said, in a line of verse: "and rain-water that brought no fever, and no physician imposed a judgement over me."

What falls outside this root: al-qayl, drinking at midday; al-qā'ilah, sleeping at midday. Their saying taqayyala fulānun abāhu, meaning he resembled his father — its true origin is actually taqayyaḍa, with the lām substituted for a ḍād, meaning the two of them were, in resemblance, exact counterparts of one another.
قين:
The letters qāf, yā' and nūn are a sound root indicating putting right and adorning.

1. al-qayn — the smith, because he mends things and holds them together; its plural is quyūn.
2. qintu al-shay'a aqīnuhu qaynan — I mended it, held it together.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
I have a wounded liver, on which the cracks of love have shown themselves — if only a mender could mend it.

3. al-taqyīn — adorning, decorating.
4. iqtānat al-rawḍa — the meadow took on its finery.
5. muqayyina — said of a woman: one who adorns other women.
6. al-qayna — said to be the slave-girl, whether she is a singer or not.

Some said she is so named because she used to be readied for singing. This is a sound view.

7. al-qayn — [also] the slave, the male servant.

And among what deviates from this chapter is al-qayn: the shin-bone; the two shins are qaynān. Dhū al-Rumma said:
...his two shins, with the softness/plumpness [of flesh] having fallen away from him.
كأب: The letters kāf, hamza and bā' are a word pointing to brokenness and a bad state. From this is al-ka'āba, dejection. One says ka'ba and ka'āba, and a man is ka'īb, dejected.
كأد: The letters kāf, alif and dāl point to intensity and hardship. They say: takā'adahu al-amr, when a matter grew hard for him. And al-'aqaba al-ka'ūd is the difficult mountain pass.
كاذ: The letters kāf, alif and dhāl are a word, and it is al-kādha: the flesh of the upper thighs.
كار: The letters kāf, alif and rā'. They say: al-ka'r is for a man to take from food — that is, to take a portion of it and eat.
كان: The letters kāf, alif and nūn. They say: ka'ana, meaning he became intense or strong, and ka'antu, meaning I became intense or strong.
كب:
The letters kāf and bā' are a sound root pointing to gathering and coming together, and nothing in it falls outside that.

1. kubāb — what has gathered together of sand. A poet said, in a line of verse: It raises the curled kubāb [heaped sand] from the back of the saddle-load.
2. kababtu al-shay' li-wajhihi, akubbuhu kabban — I threw the thing down on its face.
3. akabba fulān ʿalā al-amr yafʿaluhu — so-and-so bent down over the matter, absorbed in doing it.
4. takabbabat al-ibil — said of camels, when they collapsed from emaciation or disease.
5. al-kabkaba — a thing tumbling down when thrown into a pit, until it comes to rest, as though it were repeatedly turned over in the throwing.
6. jā'a mutakabkiban fī thiyābihi — he came wrapped up in his clothes.
7. al-kubba — the ball of spun yarn.
8. kawkab al-mā' — the greater bulk of the water.
9. al-kabkaba — a troop of horses.
10. al-kawkab [star] is so named on this same pattern.

Abū ʿUbayda said: the people went "under every kawkab," when they scattered in every direction. And a boy nearing puberty is called a kawkab, because his build has come together. Al-kabba is a crush of crowding. As for their calling the meadow's blossom a kawkab, that is a comparison, from the sense of brightness. Al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse:

A bright blossom laughing back at the sun within it, girded with luxuriant, full-grown plant-growth.

And likewise they call the gleam of an army's weapons a kawkab.
كبت: The letters kāf, bāʾ, and tāʾ are a single word, belonging to humbling and turning something away. One says: kabata Allāhu al-ʿaduwwa yakbituhu, when He turned the enemy back and humbled him. God Most High said: {those who oppose God and His Messenger are humbled, as those before them were humbled} [al-Mujādala: 5].
كبث:
The letters kāf, bā' and thā' are a word, and it is al-kabāth, said to be the fruit of the arāk tree. And they relate from al-Shaybānī: kabitha al-laḥm, meaning the meat changed and became foul-smelling.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Ammār rose lively and wanton, eating meat left overnight that had gone rank.
كبح: The letters kāf, bā' and ḥā' are a word. One says: kabaḥtu al-farasa bi-lijāmihi akbaḥuhu, I reined in the horse, checking it with its bridle.
كبد:
The letters kāf, bā' and dāl are a sound root indicating severity and strength in a thing. From this, al-kabad — hardship. One says laqiya fulānun min hādhā al-amr kabadan — he met hardship from this matter. God Almighty said: {We have indeed created man in hardship} [al-Balad: 4]. kābadtu al-amr — I endured the matter through hardship.

From this chapter: al-kabid — the liver, well known, named so for its being burdensome. al-akbad — one whose liver protrudes. kabadtu al-rajul — I struck his liver. kabid al-qaws — a name borrowed from the human liver, meaning the bow's grip. A bow described as kabdāʾ — when its grip fills the hand. By further borrowing: kabid al-samāʾ — the middle of the sky. And they say kubaydāʾ al-samāʾ, as though they diminished it, with the plural kubaydāt. One says takabbadat al-shams — the sun reached the middle of the sky. al-kubād — pain of the liver. takabbada al-laban — the milk thickened and curdled.
كبر:
The letters kāf, bā' and rā' are a sound root pointing to the opposite of smallness. One says: he is kabīr, and kubār, and kubbār - great, very great, and greater still. God Most High said: {wa-makarū makran kubbāran} [Nūḥ: 22]. And al-kibr is the greater part of a matter; His words, mighty and exalted: {wa-lladhī tawallā kibrahu} [al-Nūr: 11], that is, the greater part of it. And they say: the greater part of the leadership of a people lies in wealth. As for al-kubr, with a ḍamma on the kāf, it is nearness in descent; one says, al-walā' belongs to al-kubr, by which is meant the nearest of the people in lineage, who is the closest to the eldest forefather.

And of this section is al-kibar, which is old age. And al-kibr is greatness, and so is al-kibriyā'. And one says: they inherited glory kābiran 'an kābirin, that is, great man from great man in honour and might. And a kabra came over so-and-so, when he grew old. And one says: akbartu al-shay' - I thought it great.
كبس:
The letters kāf, bā' and sīn are a sound root: it is a thing being covered over by something heavy, and from this what falls under that meaning is measured by likeness to it.

1. al-kabs — your covering of a pit with soil; the soil used for this is itself called kibs. They extend this usage further and say, kabasa fulānun ra'sahu fī thawbihi, he buried his head in his garment.
2. al-arnaba al-kābisa — the tip of the nose that projects onto the forehead, thick and raised. One says of it, kabasat.
3. al-kibāsa — a date-cluster fully laden with fruit.
4. al-kabīs — dates that are pressed and packed.
5. al-kābūs — what befalls a person at night, a nightmare. Ibn Durayd said: I think it a later coinage, not old Arabic.
6. al-kabīs — a second word of the same form: an ornament cast hollow, then filled with clay.
7. al-kubās and al-akbas — the large-headed one.
كبش:
The letters kāf, bā' and shīn are a single word, and it is al-kabsh, the ram, well known. And kabsh al-katība is the great one and chief of the battalion.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Then they did not take fright, but put forward the ram of the raiding-band, when the clash of horns is met.
كبع:
The letters kāf, bā' and 'ayn. They said — and God knows best whether it is sound — that al-kab' is the testing of a dirham or a dinar for genuineness.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
They said to me, test the coin. I said, I will not be its tester — and I said, I will not go to the ruler in obedience.
كبل:
The letters kāf, bā' and lām are a sound root pointing to confinement and prevention.

1. al-kabl — the heavy shackle. One says kabaltu al-asīra and kabbaltuhu, I shackled the captive.
2. al-kābūl — they say it is the hunter's snare.
3. al-mukābala — this too is from this root: it is delaying payment of a debt. One says kabaltuka daynaka, I deferred your debt from you — that too is from confinement.
4. al-mukābala — also from this chapter: that a house next to yours is sold, and you need it, so you delay buying it so that another buys it, and you then take it from him by the right of pre-emption. This was disapproved of.
كبن:
The letters kāf, bā' and nūn are a sound root pointing to contracting and drawing in.

1. al-kubunna — said of the miser; one says ikba'anna, meaning he drew himself in when asked for something.
2. kabana al-dalw — he folded over the mouth of the bucket and stitched it; this is called al-kabn.
3. kabana 'an al-shay' — he turned away from it; also kanaba, the letters reversed, with the same sense.
4. al-makbūn — of horses, the short-legged one.
5. takabbana — he grew fat, and that happens only where flesh gathers together; this is measured by likeness to the root sense.
6. kabana kubūnan — he ran with a loose, easy gait.
كبو:
The letters kāf, bā' and the weak letter are a sound root pointing to falling and slipping away. One says kabā li-wajhihi yakbū, and he is kābin, when he fell on his face.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
He stumbled as a lean, sturdy stallion stumbles on the open flat — except that this one is the swifter.

1. kabā al-zand yakbū — when the fire-stick failed to strike a flame.
2. kabawtu al-kūz wa ghayrahu — when I poured out what was in it.
3. al-turāb al-kābī — dust that does not settle still on the face of the ground.
4. huwa kābī al-ramād — he has abundant ash, that is, a sign of generosity: it piles up.
5. al-kibā — the sweepings, rubbish; plural al-akbā'.

And of what is anomalous from this root: al-kibā', with a long final vowel, a kind of aloeswood used for incense. One says kabbū thiyābakum, meaning perfume your garments with its smoke.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
... and rose, and lubnā, and the smoking incense-wood.
كت:
The letters kāf and tā' have no genuine root sense in them; the chapter runs along the lines of sound-imitation. Al-katīt is the sound of a young camel, like al-kashīsh. One says katta yakittu, and katta al-rajul, of a man from anger. Katīt al-qidr is the sound of the pot boiling.

And they say: kataattu al-kalām fī udhunihi — I whispered the words into his ear. And katkata fī al-ḍaḥik — he laughed strangely. These are words resembling one another, and how far they are from soundness [as a real root]. As for al-kattān [flax/linen], it is perhaps an arabized foreign word. Al-Aʿshā shortened it and said:

Between silk and between al-katan.
كتب:
The letters Kaf, Ta, and Ba form a correct single root that means to gather something to something else. From this comes the word "the book" and "writing". It is said: I wrote the book, I am writing it, a writing. They also say: I wrote the "baghla" when I gathered the two ribs of its womb with a knot.

He says: Do not trust a Zariy (a kind of person) who has been released with it ... on your palm and write it with bands.

And "the writing" means "the twig"; it was called that because it is a collection of its broken pieces. And "the writings" are "the twigs".

Zul‑Rummah says: And the dust of a cave that has exhausted its kernels ... a clatter that lost its way among them the writings.

From the chapter "the book" is the obligation. Allah says: {It was written upon you the fast} [Al‑Baqara: 183]; and the word is used for a ruling: "the book". The Messenger of Allah said: "I will judge between you by the Book of Allah" meaning his ruling. Allah also says: {He recites purified pages} [Al‑Bayyina: 2]; {in them are valuable books} [Al‑Bayyina: 3], meaning upright rulings. The word is also used for destiny: "the book". Al‑Ja'di says: O daughter of my uncle, the Book of Allah brought me out ... from you and shall I forbid Allah what they did.

From the chapter "the horses' writings", it is said: they wrote down. He says: with an alif it is written or with a qunob.

Ibn al‑Arabiyy says: the writer among the Arabs is the scholar, and he supports his statement with the Qur'an: {Or do they have the unseen so they write} [Al‑Tur: 41]. And "the correspondent" is a servant who writes to his master on his own behalf. They say its root is from "the book", meaning the condition that is written between them.
كتد:
The letters kāf, tā' and dāl are a single word.

1. al-katad — what lies between the withers and the back.
2. al-katad — a star.
كتر:
The letters kāf, tā' and rā'.

1. al-katr — the middle of anything.
2. al-kitr — the hump itself. A poet said, in a line of verse: a hump like the rim of the blacksmith's bellows, close-packed. Al-Aṣma'ī said: I have not heard al-kitr except in this line.
3. al-katr — merit and standing.
كتع:
The letters kāf, tā' and 'ayn are words not laid down on regular pattern, and are not from the original stock of the language.

1. al-kutaʿ — the base, mean man.
2. kataʿa bi-l-shay' — he made off with it.
3. mā bi-l-dāri katīʿ — there is no one in the house.
4. kataʿa fulānun fī amrihi — he girded himself and exerted effort in his affair.
5. jā'a al-qawmu ajma'ūna akta'ūna — the people came, all of them, altogether — akta'ūn here is a reinforcing word that only ever follows ajma'ūn.
كتف:
The letters kāf, tā' and fā' are a sound root pointing to breadth in a piece of iron or in a bone.

1. al-katīfa — an iron plate used to clamp or reinforce something.
2. al-katif — the shoulder-blade, well known, named for the reason just given. One says rajulun aktaf, a man with a large shoulder-blade.
3. katafa al-ba'īru fī al-mashy — a camel's spreading its forelegs strongly in walking, which happens only by the spreading of the places of its two shoulder-blades.
4. al-katf — the binding of the two arches of a saddle to one another with al-kitāf, a strap; this is close to what was said above.
5. kataftu al-laḥm, and likewise katafttu al-thawb — cutting meat, or cloth, as though to the measure of the shoulder-blade or the iron plate.
6. katīfa, said of malice and grudge — this too belongs to the chapter, and is among the strange things of their speech, where a thing is carried on the pattern of something else: they name malice ḍabb, because it clamps (yuḍibbu) upon the heart, and since al-ḍabba on this analogy carries the sense of clamping onto a thing and was also called katīfa, they named malice both ḍabb and katīfa; the plural is katā'if. Someone said, in a line of verse: your brother is the one whose own self cannot govern its feeling, and grudges break loose at what provokes anger.
7. al-kitfān, of locusts — the first stage of it that flies. This is anomalous, outside this root.
كتل: The letters kāf, tā' and lām are a minor root pointing to gathering together. One says: hādhihi kutlatun min shay', this is a gathered lump of something. Ibn Durayd said one also says, alqā fulānun 'alayya katālahu, meaning he threw his burden upon me. This was mentioned in the poetry of Ibn al-Ṭathriyya.
كتم:
The letters kāf, tā' and mīm are a sound root pointing to hiding and covering over.

From this is katamtu al-ḥadīth katman wa kitmānan — I kept the story secret. God Most High said: {wa lā yaktumūna Allāha ḥadīthan} — and they do not hide from God any statement [al-Nisā': 42].

One says nāqa katūm, a she-camel that does not groan when she is ridden, out of strength and endurance. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And she was the remnant of a herd of camels, silent ones.

Saḥāb muktatim is cloud with no thunder in it. Kharz katīm is a stitched seam that does not let water seep through. Qaws katūm is a bow that does not twang. As for al-katam, it is a plant used for dyeing.
كتن:
The letters kāf, tā' and nūn are a root pointing to a staining smear and grime.

1. al-katan — the staining of a house by smoke.
2. katinat jaḥāfilu al-dābba — the beast's muzzle blackened from eating old dry grass.
3. katina al-siqā' — when milk clung to the outside of the waterskin and thickened it.
4. al-kattān — flax, well known; they claimed its nūn is an original root letter. Al-A'shā called it al-katan. Ibn Durayd said: it is a known Arabic word, named so because its fibres are laid one upon another until they become compacted, yaktinu.
كتو: The letters kāf, tā' and wāw. Al-katw is taking short, close steps. One says kata yaktū katwan. Ibn Durayd related this from Abū Mālik.
كث:
The letters kāf and thā' are a sound root pointing to a coming-together, though its branches are few.

1. al-kaththa — a description of a beard that has grown thick and full, the noun being al-kathath and al-kathātha.
2. al-kathkath [also al-kithkith] — fine dust that has gathered together.
كثا:
The letters kāf, thā' and the weak or hamzated letter are a sound root, a quality of milk, afterwards likened to for other things.

1. al-kuthwa — a small amount of fresh milk. From this comes kuthwat al-shā'ir, the poet's small portion.
2. laban mukthin — milk that has a froth on it.

And sometimes they carry the hamzated form onto this same root, so one says:

3. katha'at al-qidr — the pot foamed up as it boiled.
4. katha'a al-nabt — the plant sprouted.
5. katha'at al-liḥya — the beard grew bushy, from this same sense.
كثب:
The letters kāf, thā' and bā' are one single sound root indicating gathering together, and also nearness. From this, al-kuthba — a portion of milk or of dates, said to be named so for its being gathered together. From it, kathīb al-raml — a sand dune. al-kāthib — the one who gathers. al-kāthiba — the raised part of a horse's withers, in front of the saddle; plural kawāthib.

A poet, al-Nābigha, said, in a line of verse:
When they raise the Khaṭṭī spears above the withers.

aktaba al-ṣayd — the quarry came within reach, gave itself up to being caught; this is from al-kathab, nearness.

As for his line:
It would have become crushed, finely pounded gravel ... in the place of the track, at al-Kāthib.

it is said that al-Kāthib is a known mountain. Ibn Durayd and others said al-kuthāb is a small arrow shot by hand, and cited, in a line of verse:
She struck my heart from close range, yet she did not shoot with a kuthāb.

If this is sound, it may be named so for its shortness and the closeness of its two ends.
كثر:
The letters kāf, thā' and rā' are a sound root pointing to the opposite of fewness. Of that is the thing that is kathīr, many, and it has kathura, become many. Then something is added to it for an increase in the description, so one says: al-kawthar is the man who gives much; and it is of the pattern faw'al from kathra, abundance. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And you are a man of much giving, son of Marwān, and good, and your father, son of noble women, was a great giver.

And al-Kawthar is a river in Paradise. God Most High said: {innā a'ṭaynāka al-kawthar} [al-Kawthar: 1]. They said this, and they said: He meant abundant good. And al-kawthar is dust, so called for its abundance and its rising up. A poet said, in a line of verse:
It neighed in dust like horse-cloths.

And one says: the sons of so-and-so contended in numbers with [the sons of so-and-so] and outnumbered them, that is, they were more than they. And a number that is kāthir, that is, many. Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
And you are not the one with more pebbles than they; might belongs only to the one of the greater number.
كثع:
The letters kāf, thā' and 'ayn are close in meaning to the one before it.

1. shafatun kāthi'a — a lip whose blood is abundant, that is, a full lip.
2. kathaʿa al-laban — its cream rose to the top.
3. kaththaʿat liḥyatuhu — his beard grew long and thick.
كثف: The letters kāf, thā' and fā' are a sound root pointing to things being stacked one upon another and gathered together. One says: hādhā shay'un kathīf, this is a dense thing. And saḥābun kathīf, dense cloud, and shajarun kathīf, dense trees.
كثم:
The letters kāf, thā' and mīm are a minor root pointing to fullness and spaciousness.

1. al-aktham — the one who is full/sated.
2. al-aktham — the one with a large belly.
3. akthama qirbatahu — he filled his waterskin.
4. al-aktham — the wide road.
5. akthama famahu — he put a cucumber, or something like it, into his mouth, then bit it off.
كثو: The letters kāf, thā' and wāw are a single word, and it is al-kawthal, the stern of a ship — and sometimes it is doubled, al-kawthall.
كح: The letters kāf and ḥā' amount to nothing. Sometimes they say al-kuḥkuḥ, of sheep, is the old one. And they say: aʿrābiyy kuḥḥ [a pure Bedouin], like quḥḥ.
كحل:
The letters kāf, ḥā' and lām are a single root pointing to a colour among colours. Al-kaḥal is the blackness of the eyelash by nature. One says kaḥilat 'aynuhu kaḥalan, and it is kaḥīl, and the man is akḥal. And the probe used for applying kohl is called al-mikḥāl.

And of what is anomalous from this chapter:

1. al-kuḥayl — the tar-like substance smeared on a mangy camel, built on the diminutive form.
2. al-mikḥālān — the two hip-bones of a horse; it is also said they are rather the two bones of the forearms.
3. al-akḥal — an artery.
4. Kaḥl — a name for a year of drought. Among their proverbs: "'Arār was repaid with Kaḥl", said when a killer is killed in requital for his victim. It is said: they were two cows, one of which killed the other, and so was killed for it.
كد:
The letters kāf and dāl are a sound root pointing to hardship and toughness.

1. al-kadīd — fine dust that has been trodden and pounded by hooves; from this is drawn by analogy:
2. al-kadd — hard effort in work and the seeking of a livelihood, and persistence in seeking.
3. kadadtu fulānan bi-l-mas'ala — I pressed so-and-so persistently with the question, pointing it at him whenever the need arose.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
I held back and did not press you with pointing fingers.

From this chapter:

1. al-kadkada — the sound of a bladesmith's whetstone striking a sword as he polishes it.
2. al-kudāda — what is scraped from the broth at the bottom of a cooking pot.
3. bi'r kadūd — a well whose water is reached only with hard effort.
4. al-kadkada — [also] slowness and heaviness in running.
5. al-kadd — a thing in which things are pounded, like a mortar.
6. al-kudād — a donkey to whom [a certain breed of] donkeys is traced, so that they say "the daughters of Kudād."
كدب: The letters kāf, dāl and bā' — one word is said of it. They said al-kadib is fresh blood. And it is related that some read: and they came upon his shirt with fresh blood.
كدح:
The letters kāf, dāl and hā' are a sound root indicating a mark or effect left on something.

1. *kadaḥahu* and *kaddaḥahu* — he scratched him.
2. *ḥimārun mukaddaḥ* — a donkey the other donkeys have bitten.

From this same reasoning, *kadaḥa* is used of earning a living: *yakdaḥu kadḥan*, so he is *kādiḥ*. God, mighty and exalted, said: {Indeed you are toiling} [al-Inshiqāq: 6], meaning: earning.
كدر:
The letters kāf, dāl and rā' are one root indicating the opposite of clarity, and another indicating motion.

The first: al-kadar — the opposite of clarity. One says kadira al-māʾ and kadura — the water became murky. They say: "take what is clear and leave what is murky." This is used in a borrowed sense, so one says kadaru ʿayshihi — the murkiness of his life. al-kudriyy — the qaṭā bird [sandgrouse], named after the main kind of qaṭā, which are kudr, murky-coloured; this belongs to the first sense, since that colour carries a murkiness. From it, al-kudayrāʾ — fresh milk with dates steeped in it. banāt akdar — wild donkeys named after a particular stallion, that colour perhaps being akdar.

The other root: one says inkadara, when a thing moved swiftly. God Almighty said: {and when the stars are scattered} [al-Takwīr: 2].
كدس:
The letters kāf, dāl and sīn are three words unlike one another.

1. kuds — a stack of grain.
2. al-takaddus — the walking of a horse as though weighed down. A poet said, in a line of verse: horses trudging with the mail-clad riders, like the walk of mountain-goats on the high ground.
3. al-kawādis — the things one takes an omen from, such as a good sign or a sneeze and the like. A poet said, in a line of verse: the omens did not hold you back from me.
كدش:
The letters kāf, dāl and shīn are not a formation resembling the speech of the Arabs; perhaps it is something close to a letter-substitution.

1. kadasa and khadasha — used with the same meaning.
2. kadasha and kadaḥa — meaning he earned his living, toiled.
3. kadasha al-shay' bi-asnānihi — he nipped the thing off with his teeth.

All of this is a single thing, alike in its weakness as Arabic.
كدع: The letters kāf, dāl and ʿayn are not a root. Yet Ibn Durayd mentioned that al-kadʿ is a hard shove.
كدم:
The letters kāf, dāl and mīm are a sound root, with a single word in it. One says kadama, when he bites with the front of his mouth, the way a donkey bites. It is also said that al-kadama is a stirring, a movement. A poet said, in a line of verse:
When I walked out a little after nightfall, I heard, from above the houses, a stirring sound.
كدن:
The letters kāf, dāl and nūn are a sound root indicating the settling of something into a gathered mass.

1. al-kudūn is something a woman uses to pad a seat for herself in the litter.
2. A woman is called kadina when she has abundant flesh.
3. A camel is said to have kudna when its hump has grown large.
4. al-kawdan is drawn from this, because it — a stout, thick-bodied animal — is heavy with flesh and coarse of build. They say, how plain the kadāna is in him, meaning the coarse, mixed breeding.
5. al-kadan is the clinging mud that settles at the bottom of water; this too follows the same pattern.
6. al-kidyawn is said to be fine dust and dung ground and mixed together, used to polish coats of mail.

Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
They were coated above with kidyawn and padded beneath with a covering, so they gleam, their tunics of mail hanging full.
كده: The letters kāf, dāl and hā' are not a root. Yet they say al-kadh is striking with a stone. One says kadaha yakdahu. And a thing fell and takaddaha, meaning it broke.
كدي:
The letters kāf, dāl, and the weak letter, are a sound root indicating hardness in a thing, from which further senses are then measured. al-kudya — a hardness within the ground; one says ḥafara fa-akdā, when the digger reached the hardpan. It is then said of a man who gives a little and then stops: akdā — likened to the digger who digs, then strikes hardpan and holds back.

God Almighty said: {and gave a little, then withheld} [al-Najm: 34]. al-kudāya is the same as al-kudya. One says arḍ kādiya — slow ground, from this same root.

This root sometimes takes a hamza, so it also belongs to the class of words given a hamza though it is not original to them. Al-Khalīl claimed one says aṣābat zurūʿahum kādiʾa, meaning frost. And aṣāba al-zarʿ bardun wa-kaddaʾahu — cold struck the crop and beat it back into the ground. Al-Farrāʾ said: kadiya al-kalb kadan, when the dog drank milk and its stomach was spoiled.

One says akdaytuhu akdīhi ikdāʾan, when you turned him back from a thing — the reasoning through all of this being one. Kadāʾ is a place-name, perhaps from al-kudya.
كذ: The letters kāf and dhāl are a single word: al-kadhdhān — soft, crumbling stones, like clods of earth.
كذب:
The letters kāf, dhāl and bā' are a sound root pointing to the opposite of truthfulness. And to put it briefly, it is that a thing does not reach the utmost of speech in truth. Of that is al-kadhib, lying, the opposite of truth. Kadhaba kadhiban. And kadhdhabtu fulānan — I ascribed lying to him; and akdhabtuhu — I found him a liar. And a man is kadhdhāb and kudhaba, a great liar. Then one says: so-and-so charged, then he kadhaba and kadhdhaba, that is, he did not make his charge good. And Abū Du'ād said:
I said, when the two came out from a hill-top: the wild ass has failed, though he has gone off.

And they claim that one says kadhaba labanu al-nāqa — the she-camel's milk failed. And in that there is something to look into, though its reasoning is sound. And they say mā kadhdhaba fulānun an faʿala kadhā, that is, he did not delay; and all this is from one root. As for the Arabs' saying kadhaba ʿalayka kadhā and kadhdhabaka kadhā, in the sense of urging on — that is, take to it, or it has become binding upon you, as came in the hadith: " «The pilgrimage is binding upon you» ", that is, it has become due — so it has come thus from the Arabs. And they recite much poetry about that, of which is his saying:
And a woman of Dhubyān charged her sons that the woollen cloaks and the hide-vessels were binding upon them.
And the words of the other:
I urged you on — threaten me, and make of me a byword for the land and the peoples, ticks of Mawẓab.

And I do not think there is any summing this up, and I hold it to be nothing [but] of the speech that has passed away, and its people have passed away, and whoever knew it.
كر:
The letters kāf and rā' are a sound root pointing to gathering and repetition.

1. karartu — that is your returning to a thing after the first time; it is the repetition already mentioned.
2. al-karīr — like a rattling in the throat, so named because it repeats itself. A poet said, in a line of verse: My soul be your ransom on the day of battle, when the men's war-cry becomes a death-rattle in the throat.
3. al-karr — a rope, so named for the gathering-together that gives it its strength.
4. al-kurr — a hollow that holds water seeping through sand, plural kirār. A poet said, in a line of verse: Upon one worn thin like coarse cloth, the echo calls out over it — it has ancient stone-linings and water-hollows.
5. al-kirkira — the flat disc of cartilage at a camel's breastbone.
6. al-kirkira — [also] a gathering of people.
7. al-karkara — the winds' driving of the clouds and gathering them together after they had scattered.

As for al-Nābigha's saying:
They were covered with kidyawn and lined beneath with kurra, so they are like lamps, full-robed in their garments —
I take it that this word [kurra] is Persian, which he wove into his verse; poets sometimes do this. And they say that al-kurra is ash used to polish coats of mail; it is also said to be crumbled dung.

8. karkartuhu ʿan al-shay' — I held him back from the thing; the sense is that you turned him away and did not see to his need at the first attempt.
9. karkartu bi-l-dajāja — I shouted at the hen, because you repeat the shouting at her.
10. al-karik — the fool, or the red-faced one — though this is only reported speech.
كرب:
The letters kāf, rā', and bā' are a sound root indicating intensity and strength. One says 'joints mukraba,' meaning strong and firm.

1. al-karab — its root sense: a thick knot tied into a bucket's rope, its end set on the bucket's crossbar, then its folds bound tight. From it one says akrabtu al-dalw, I tied the bucket with a karab.

Al-Ḥuṭayʾa said, in a line of verse:
A people who, when they bind a pact for their neighbour, tie the strap fast and bind the karab-knot above it.

2. al-karb — severe distress.
3. al-kurayba — a severe one among calamities.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Wading toward death through calamities.

4. al-ikrāb — intensity in running; one says akraba, so he is mukrib, running hard.

As for karaba al-shayʾu meaning 'it drew near,' that is not from this chapter — it is a case of one letter standing for another. It really belongs with qurb (nearness): with a qāf they say qaruba, with ḍamma on the rā', and with a kāf they say kariba, with fatḥa on it — the meaning is the same. The angels called al-karūbiyyūn are of the pattern faʿūliyyūn from al-kurūb, and they are those brought near [to God]. One says karabat al-shams, the sun drew near to setting; and a vessel is karbān when it has drawn near to being full.

5. karab al-nakhl — the stub left on a palm-trunk where a frond was cut; it could be called karab for its firmness.
6. al-kurāba — what falls from the palm at the base of these stubs.

As for kirāb al-arḍ, turning the earth over for ploughing, in my view that is not [genuine] Arabic. Their saying 'al-kirāb is upon the cattle' comes from this, but the more correct version, and the one we have heard, is 'the dogs are set upon the cattle' — meaning: leave a task to the one whose craft it is.

7. al-kirāb — they also say these are water-channels, one being a karaba. If this is sound, it is likened to the stubs of the palm for its length and firmness.
كرت: The letters kāf, rā' and tā' — there is nothing in it save their saying ʿām karīt, a complete year.
كرث: The letters kāf, rā' and thā' — there is nothing in it save karathahu l-amr, said when a matter has reached the point of real hardship for someone. And al-kurrāth and al-karāth are two plants.
كرج:
The letters kāf, rā' and jīm are not a root; it is only al-kurraj, the very thing we mentioned under al-kura, the ball. Jarīr mentioned it, saying, in a line of verse:
I put on my weapons, while al-Farazdaq is a plaything, upon him a kurraj's sash and its bells.
كرد:
The letters kāf, rā' and dāl are a sound root indicating driving off and pursuing. One says huwa yakruduhum, meaning he drives them off and chases them away.

1. They claim that al-Kurd, this people, is drawn from al-mukārada, meaning mutual pursuit. Someone said: indeed, the people of treachery are your fathers, the Kurds.
2. As for al-kard, it is the neck; they say it is an arabized word.
3. Among what is said, though its soundness is not known, is that al-kirdīda is a lump of pressed dates. They recite: blessed is he who has a kirdīda, eating from it while his neck is at ease.

How far this, and the like of it, is from being sound. God knows best.
كرز:
The letters kāf, rā' and zāy are a sound root indicating hiding, concealment, and taking refuge. One says kāraza ilā l-makān, when he leaned toward a place and hid himself in it. A poet recited:
Beside the watering-place, hiding.
And kāraza ʿan fulān is said when he fled from someone and hid from him.

1. al-kurz is the sack; it was so named because a thing is hidden away in it. Ru'ba said, in a line of verse — like a kurraz tied between the tent-pegs. This word is Persian, arabized.
2. al-kurraz — they say it is the falcon in its second year.
3. al-karrāz is a ram on which the shepherd hangs his sack, a thing like a jūwāliq (a large sack).

As for al-karīz, which is curdled milk, it does not belong to this chapter, because it comes from letter-substitution — its true letter is ṣād, not zāy.
كرس:
The letters kāf, rā' and sīn are a sound root indicating one thing matting and piling up over another, and its gathering together.

1. *al-kirs* — what has matted, of dung and urine, in a dwelling-place.
2. *al-kurrāsa* (a quire of paper) — taken from this, because it is sheets of paper one on top of another.

Someone said, in a line of verse:
O friend, do you know a trace grown thick and matted? ... He said: yes, I know it — and he fell into despair.

3. *al-karawwas* — the big-headed one, taken from this, as though he were something matted, that is, gathered together thickly.

From this same chapter is *al-karkasa*, the repeated turning-over of a thing. A man born of slave-women is called *mukarkas*, meaning he is passed back and forth among their several bearings of him.
كرش:
The letters kāf, rā' and shīn are a sound root indicating gathering and collecting.

1. al-kirsh, the stomach, is named for its gathering together what is in it.
2. From this it is then extended, and a group of people is called a kirsh. The Messenger of God, God bless him and his family and grant him peace, said: the Anṣār are my kirsh and my inner circle (ʿaybatī).
3. A man's kirsh is his dependents and his young children.
4. A large-flanked she-donkey is called karshā'.
5. A man's face is said to takarrasha, meaning it contracted and became wrinkled like a kirsh.
6. karshā' is also said of a foot that is short with a flat, level arch.
كرص: The letters kāf, rā' and ṣād are a single word. They say al-karīṣ is curdled milk.
كرض:
The letters kāf, rā' and ḍād are one sound word whose meaning is disputed: al-kirāḍ. Some said it is the stallion's fluid which the she-camel expels after having taken it in. One says karaḍat al-nāqa mā'a l-faḥl takruḍuhu, the she-camel expelled the stallion's fluid. Others say al-kirāḍ is a man's semen. Al-Ṭirimmāḥ said, in a line of verse:
A bold, swift she-camel will soon bring you near to Lamīs — one whose urine has shown traces of the kiraḍ-fluid.
Ibn Durayd said al-kirāḍ is the passages of the womb. Al-Aṣmaʿī said it has no singular. Others said its singular is karḍ.
كرع:
The letters kāf, rā' and ʿayn are a sound root indicating slenderness in some part of an animal's limbs.

1. al-kurāʿ, in a human, is what lies below the knee; in animals, what lies below the fetlock joint.
2. Al-Khalīl said: a man is said to takarraʿa when he performs the ablution for prayer, because he washes his lower legs (akāriʿ).
3. He said: the kurāʿ of anything is its outer end.
4. He said: the kurāʿ of a lava-field is the part that stretches out long from it. Muhalhal said, in a line of verse: when their half-breed rider climbed up onto the kurāʿ, I raised the war-cry, seeking vengeance for Jābir or Ṣinbil.

As for their calling horses kurāʿ, the Arabs sometimes name the whole body by one of its parts, just as they say he freed a raqaba (a neck, meaning a slave) and my face is toward you. So it may be that horses were called kurāʿ for their lower legs; and al-karaʿ is slenderness of the legs. As for al-karaʿ meaning rainwater, it was so named because one drinks it by dipping in (yukraʿu fīhi); and it is also said because a person dips his lower legs into it, or takes it up with his two hands, which are then like the two kurāʿs, since each is an outer limb.
كرف: The letters kāf, rā' and fā' are two very different words. The first is al-karf, a donkey sniffing at urine and raising its head. The second is al-kirfi', clouds banked up high, seen layered one above another.
كرم:
The letters kāf, rā' and mīm are a sound root with two chapters. One of them is nobility in a thing in itself, or nobility in one of the traits of character. One says a man is karīm, a horse is karīm, a plant is karīm. And akrama al-rajul when he brings forth noble children. And istakrama — he took for himself a precious possession. And karuma al-saḥāb — the clouds brought the rain. And a land is makruma for plants when it grows them well. And generosity in character is said to be the passing over of the wrongdoer's offence. ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muslim ibn Qutayba said: al-karīm is the much-forgiving. And God, exalted be He, is al-Karīm, who passes over the sins of His believing servants.

And the other root is al-karm, and it is the necklace. A poet said:
Hard-travelling by night, whose throat knows no necklace.
As for al-karm, it is the grapevine too, because its clusters are gathered together and its grapes are set in rows.
كرن:
The letters kāf, rā' and nūn are a single word, to do with instruments of entertainment. It is said that al-kirān is the cymbal. Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse — its opening lost:
...how many a slave-girl, kept in comfort, I have plied to a kirān.
The singing-girl is called karīna.
كره: The letters kāf, rā' and hā' are one sound root pointing to the opposite of contentment and love. One says karihtu al-shay'a akrahuhu karhan - I disliked the thing. Al-kurh is the noun. And it is said: rather al-kurh is hardship, and al-karh is that you be compelled to a thing and do it unwillingly. From al-kurh come al-karāhiya and al-karāhiyya - dislike. Al-karīha is the hard press of war. And a sword that cuts through what it strikes is called dhū al-karīha. And they say that al-karh is the camel hard in the head, as though he disliked being led.
كري:
The letters kāf, rā' and the weak letter are a sound root indicating softness and ease in a thing, and sometimes indicating delay.

1. From the softness and ease comes al-karā, which is drowsiness.
2. From this chapter too is al-sayr al-mukarrī, an easy, gentle pace of travel.
3. From it also is al-mukārī, the shadow that keeps pace with a thing, staying with it and never parting from it; it is the softest and most delicate thing there is. Jarīr said, in a line of verse: I caught up, my companions each on a fine mare, coursing, vying with the Aḥmasī's shadow — meaning she vies with her own shadow, as though racing alongside it.
4. From the chapter too is al-karw: a horse striking out with both forelegs evenly in its gallop, not drawing them in toward its belly.
5. A woman is said to karat in her walking, takrū karwan, doing the same.
6. al-kura, the ball, is a defective word missing a wāw; it was so named because it is set gliding (yukrā) when thrown. One says karā l-kurata yakrūhā karwan.
7. As for al-mukārī, the one who hires out camels and the like, that too is drawn from travel, because he travels alongside the one who hires from him.

They then broadened the usage, and called the fee itself kirā', and carried the word over even to things not traveled with, such as a house and the like — though the origin is what we have described.

As for the sense of delay we mentioned, it is their saying akraytu l-ḥadīth, I put off the story. Al-Ḥuṭay'a said, in a line of verse: I put off the evening meal until Suhayl rose, or al-Shiʿrā, and so the wait grew long for me.

As for al-karawān, it is a bird, whose male is called al-karā. When it is caught, one says, in a chant:
Settle down, karā, settle down, karā — the ostrich is off among the villages.
It is said to have been so named for the slenderness of its legs. And they say a woman is karwā', slender-legged. If this is sound, it is an anomaly outside the pattern we have described.
كز:
The letters kāf and zāy are a sound root pointing to contraction and gripping tightness.

1. al-kazāza — contraction and stiffness.
2. rajul kazz — a stingy man.
3. kazaztu al-shay' — I tightened the thing, so it is makzūz.
4. al-kuzāz — an illness that seizes one from severe cold; I take it to come from the limbs' contracting.
5. bakara kazza — a short pulley-wheel.
كزم: The letters kāf, zāy and mīm are a minor root indicating shortness and meanness of form. al-kazam is shortness in the nose, and likewise in the fingers; one says anfun akzam, a short nose, and yadun kazmā', a short hand. al-kazm is the timid man, so named for his shrinking back from boldness. al-kazūm is a she-camel with no teeth left to her from old age. All of this follows one and the same pattern. It is also mentioned that al-kazm is like al-kadm, biting with the front of the mouth; this belongs to letter-substitution, and God knows best its soundness.
كس:
The letters kāf and sīn are sound, though few in their words. What is sound of it is al-kasas: the lower teeth protruding along with the lower jaw — a man so affected is called akass. So it is in the book of al-Khalīl. Others said: al-kasas is short teeth. What comes after this is [only reported] speech. They say al-kasīs is meat dried on stones then pounded and taken as provisions. Among what is sound in this: al-kasīs, a drink made from durra [sorghum]. And they recite:

If you are given to drink from the plants of Wajj, then we have a spring flowing with kasīs and with sakar.

The verse is sound, but perhaps the word is one of those foreign words the Arabs borrowed into their speech. As for al-kaskasa, it is a coined, later word, used by those who replace kāf with sīn in their speech.
كسب: The letters kāf, sīn and bā' are a sound root, and it points to seeking, wanting, and getting. Earning, al-kasb, is from that. One says kasaba ahlahu khayran - he earned good for his family. And kasabtu al-rajula mālan fa-kasabahu - I got the man wealth and he earned it. This is one of those words that come as fa'altuhu fa-fa'ala, where the same verb is used both for making someone do a thing and for his doing it. And Kasābi is the name of a bitch.
كسح:
The letters kāf, sīn and ḥā' carry two sound meanings: one is the clearing of a thing, the other a defect in bodily form.

As for the first:
1. al-kasḥ — one says kasaḥtu l-bayt, I swept the house, and the wind kasaḥat the ground, scraping the dust off it.
2. al-kusāḥa is what is swept up.
3. One says they raided so-and-so's tribe and iktasaḥūhum, meaning they took all their wealth.

As for the second:
1. al-kasaḥ is lameness.
2. al-aksaḥ is the lame man. Al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse: and one weak in the leg, without lameness.
3. The plural of al-aksaḥ is kusḥān. And in the hadith: charity is [given from] the wealth of the lame and the one-eyed.
كسد:
The letters kāf, sīn and dāl are a sound root indicating something inferior, not sought after. From this, kasada al-shayʾ kasādan, so it is kāsid and kasīd. Anything inferior is kasīd.

A line of verse:
Some noble, some worthless.
كسر:
The letters kāf, sīn and rā' are a sound root indicating the smashing and crushing of a thing. From it comes your saying kasartu l-shay'a aksiruhu kasran, I broke the thing.

1. al-kisra is a fragment of the broken thing.
2. A piece of wood is called ṣulb al-maksir, hard at the break, when its quality is known by breaking it.
3. A bird kasara janāḥayhi, folded its two wings, when it draws them in wanting to alight; from this comes ʿuqāb kāsir, a stooping eagle.
4. al-kisr is a bone with not much flesh left on it. A poet said, in a line of verse: and in her hand a kisr, hoarse-sounding, dripping. And it is said that a thing is never such-and-such unless it is broken.
5. The forearm bone next to the elbow, being half the bone, is called kisr qabīḥ. ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm recited to us, from ʿAlī ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, from Abū ʿUbayd: had you been a donkey, you would have been a donkey of disgrace; and had you been a kisr, you would have been the meager forearm-bone.
6. Land is said to be dhāt kusūr, having rises and dips, as though it had been broken through.
7. al-kisar is the lower panel of a tent, raised at times and let down at others.
8. He is jārī mukāsirī, my neighbor, meaning the panel of his tent lies against the panel of mine.

As for Kisrā, it is a foreign name and not from this root; it is an arabized word. Abū ʿAmr said: the adjective from Kisrā — and he used to pronounce it with the kāf vowelled i — is kisriyy or kisrawiyy. Al-Umawī said: kisriyy, with the same i-vowel, also.
كسع:
The letters kāf, sīn and ʿayn are a sound root indicating a kind of striking. One says kasaʿahu, when he struck him with his foot on his hindquarters, or with his hand. One also says he followed at their backs, kasaʿahum with his sword. And kasaʿtu l-rajula bi-mā sā'ahu is said when one speaks ill of a man behind his back. And kasaʿtu l-nāqata bi-ghubrihā is said when one leaves a remainder of milk in her udder, meaning to build her up again — that is, one lets her be after milking part of her, striking her hindquarters with the hand so that she moves off. A poet said, in a line of verse: do not strike the light-uddered she-camels for what little milk remains — you do not know which of them will bear young.

From this chapter too, a man is called mukassaʿ bi-ghubrihi when he has not married, as though his seed has stayed stored up in him the way the last milk stays stored in a ewe left unmilked. A poet said: by God, none shall draw it up from its depth except a young man left with only his own remainder.

al-kusʿa is donkeys, so named because they are forever struck on their hindquarters when driven.
كسف:
The letters kāf, sīn and fā' are a root indicating a change in the state of a thing to something unwelcome, and also cutting a piece off from something.

From this, kusūf al-qamar (the eclipse of the moon), the departure of its light. It is said: a man is kāsif al-wajh (dark-faced) when he is scowling. He is kāsif al-bāl — meaning in a bad state.

As for the "cutting" sense: it is said the hamstring was severed with the sword, cut through by it. Al-kisfa: a piece cut from a garment; one says "give me a kisfa of your garment." Al-kisfa is also a piece of cloud. God, exalted is He, said: {and if they were to see a piece of the sky falling} [al-Ṭūr: 44].
كسل:
The letters kāf, sīn and lām are a sound root, and it is heaviness about a thing, and holding back from finishing it, or from doing it at all. From this comes *al-kasal*, laziness.

*Al-iksāl* — when a man has intercourse with his wife but does not ejaculate; the same word is used of a stud camel.

A woman who is *miksāl* scarcely ever leaves her house.
كسم:
The letters kāf, sīn and mīm are a minor root indicating matting together and gathering.

1. al-kaysūm is abundant grass.
2. al-akāsim are said to be horses bunched close together, all but climbing atop one another.

A poet said, in a line of verse: O Abū Mālik, al-Ḥuḍayn has crowded in behind us men in close ranks, and horses bunched together.
كش: The letters kāf and shīn amount to nothing; there is a word in it that runs along the lines of sound-imitation — the young camel's braying is called al-kashīsh. Al-kashkasha is a coined, later word, used by those who replace kāf with shīn in their speech.
كشح:
The letters kāf, shīn and ḥā' are a sound root, naming a part of an animal's body.

1. al-kashḥ is the waist, the flank.
2. al-kashaḥ is a disease that strikes a person in the flank. Al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse: every one they cauterize away of the flank-disease — and it is cauterized.
3. From this comes the man known as Makshūḥ al-Murādī.
4. al-kāshiḥ is the one who folds his flank over enmity, hiding hostility within.
5. One says ṭawaytu kashḥī ʿalā l-amr, I folded my flank over the matter, said when one conceals it and keeps it hidden. A line runs: a brother who has folded his flank and made ready to go.

Some said instead that al-kāshiḥ is the one who withdraws from you, from their saying kashaḥa l-qawmu ʿan al-mā', the people withdrew from the water, meaning they scattered from it. A line runs: the carcass of a donkey, from which the other donkeys have withdrawn.

The one who leaves is called kāshiḥ because he goes off showing his flank, turning away from what he is leaving. Do you not see that they say ṭawā kashḥahu for parting and departure — it is common in their poetry.
كشد: The letters kāf, shīn and dāl. It is said that al-kashd is a kind of milking. God knows best what is correct.
كشط: The letters kāf, shīn and ṭā' are a word indicating the removal of a thing and its uncovering. One says kashaṭa al-jild ʿan al-dhabīḥa — he stripped the hide from the slaughtered animal. And they say inkashaṭa rawʿuhu — his fright left him.
كشف:
The letters kāf, shīn and fā' are a sound root pointing to one thing being stripped off another, as a garment is drawn off the body.

One says kashaftu al-thawb wa ghayrahu akshifuhu — I uncovered the garment and other than it. Al-kashaf is a whorl at the edge of the forelock, as though some of that hair were laid bare from where it is set and grows. And that occurs in horses as a twist in the tail-bone. And al-akshaf is
the man who has no shield with him in war. One says takashshafa al-barq, when the lightning fills the sky; and the sense is sound, because what is uncovered is out in the open. Al-kishāf is a conception coming [straight after] a conception. [Ibn Durayd said: al-kishāf is] that the female should stay two years or three without being covered. The poet said: . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
كشم:
The letters kāf, shīn and mīm are a minor root indicating the cutting of a thing, or its shortness.

1. al-aksham is deficient in form, and the word is also used of deficient standing or honor. A line runs: he has one side complete, and another deficient.
2. al-kashm is cutting off the nose entirely, at its root.
كشى:
The letters kāf, shīn and the weak or the hamzated letter. As for the form without hamza, it is a single word: a long strip of fat in the lizard's neck, running down to its thigh; the plural is al-kushā. A poet said, in a line of verse: had you tasted the kushā together with the liver, you would not have let the lizard run off in the valley.

As for the hamzated form, these are words that may perhaps be sound.

1. yatakashsha'u l-laḥm is said of one who eats meat while it is dry.
2. kasha'tu wajhahu bi-l-sayf means I struck his face with the sword.
3. kashi'a min al-ṭaʿām means he became full from food.
كص:
The letters kāf and ṣād are a word pointing to a writhing brought on by exertion.

1. kaṣīṣ — trembling.
2. al-kaṣīṣa — the hunter's snare.
كض: The letters kāf and ḍād. They say: al-kaḍkaḍa is swiftness of gait.
كظ:
The letters kāf and ẓā' are a sound root pointing to hard endurance, severity, and fullness.

1. al-mukāẓẓa in war — fierce, hard grappling.
2. kaẓẓanī hādhā al-amr — this matter weighed heavily on me.
3. al-kaẓkaẓa — the waterskin's being full.
4. al-kiẓẓa — the discomfort that comes over one from too much food.
5. iktaẓẓa al-wādī bi-l-mā' — the valley was choked full with its floodwater.
6. takāẓẓa al-qawm kiẓāẓan — the people went beyond bounds in their fierce contending and rivalry. A poet said, in a line of verse: When Rabīʿa grew weary of the fierce struggle.
كظا: The letters kāf, ẓā' and the weak letter are a word from letter-substitution. They say kaẓā laḥmuhu, his flesh grew firm, the same as khaẓā; one says yakẓū.
كظر: The letters kāf, ẓā' and rā' are a word. They say al-kuẓr is the notch cut at the tip of the bow, where the string catches.
كظم:
The letters kāf, ẓā' and mīm are a sound root indicating one meaning: holding something back and gathering it in. From it, al-kaẓm, swallowing anger and holding back from showing it, as if the one who suppresses it gathers it inside himself. God Almighty said: {and those who hold back their anger} [Āl 'Imrān: 134].

1. al-kuẓūm — silence; also, a camel's holding back from chewing its cud.
2. al-kaẓam — the passage of the breath, the throat. One says akhadha bi-kaẓamihi, he seized him by the throat — this too follows the same reasoning, as if he had stopped his breath from getting out.
3. al-kaẓā'im — channels dug for water to run in from one well to another, named kiẓāma for holding the water in.
4. al-kiẓāma — the ring that gathers the cords of the iron parts of a balance, again from holding things together.
5. al-kiẓāma — a strap attached to the string of the Arab bow and wound around the end of the upper nock.

The reasoning behind all of these is one and the same.
كع:
The letters kāf and ʿayn are a sound root pointing to restraint and holding back.

1. rajul kaʿʿ, kāʿʿ — a coward.
2. akaʿʿahu al-faraq ʿan al-amr — fear made him hold back from the matter. [Ibn Duraid said: one does not say kāʿa, though common people do say it; rather one says kaʿʿa.]

A poet said, in a line of verse:
His bewilderment held him back from the fine, precise things.
كعب:
The letters kāf, ʿayn, and bā' are a sound root indicating a swelling and a rise in something.

1. al-kaʿb — a man's ankle-bone, at the two ends of the shin where the foot and shin meet.
2. al-Kaʿba — the House of God Most High; it is said to be named for standing raised and square.
3. Dhū al-Kaʿabāt — a shrine belonging to [the tribe] Rabīʿa, which they used to circle around. It is also said al-kaʿba means an upper room.
4. kaʿabat al-marʾa, so she is kāʿib — said of a woman whose breast has grown full.
5. thawb mukaʿʿab — a garment folded tight and rolled up firmly.
6. burd mukaʿʿab — a striped cloak with square-patterned ornament on it.
7. al-kaʿb of a reed — the segment between two joints; the kuʿūb of a spear are the same.

ʿAntara said, in a line of verse:
So I thrust with the spear, solid through its segments — the noble man is never forbidden the touch of spears.

8. al-kaʿb of clarified butter — a lump of it.
كعت: The letters kāf, ʿayn and tāʼ. They say: al-kuʿayt is a bird. And they say: akʿata the man akʿātan, when he went off hurrying.
كعد: The letters kāf, ʿayn and dāl. They say: al-kaʿd is the large sack, al-jawāliq.
كعر: The letters kāf, ʿayn and rāʼ. They say: al-kaʿar is for the belly to become full from eating. And akʿara the camel: its hump grew large.
كعس: The letters kāf, ʿayn and sīn. They say: al-kaʿs is a bone in al-sulāmā, the small bones of the finger joints. Its plural is kiʿās.
كعظ: The letters kāf, ʿayn and ẓā'. They say al-kaʿīẓ is a short, thickset man.
كعم:
The letters kāf, ʿayn and mīm are a sound root indicating the stopping of one thing with another, and restraint.

1. al-kiʿām is something put into a camel's mouth so that it cannot bray; one says kaʿamahu, so it is makʿūm.
2. Fear is said to kaʿamahu, muzzle him, so that he cannot speak. Dhū l-Rumma said, in a line of verse: a trackless waste — whoever ventures into it is silenced by fear.
3. From this chapter too, a man kaʿama a woman, when he kissed her, taking her mouth fully with his, as though he had stopped her mouth with his own.
4. al-kiʿm is a kind of container.
كف:
The letters kāf and fā' are a sound root pointing to gripping and contraction.

1. al-kaff — the hand, of a person, so named because it grips things.
2. kafaftu fulānan ʿan al-amr, kafkaftuhu — I restrained so-and-so from the matter.
3. huwa yastakiffu, yatakaffafu — said of a man who begs from people.

This is the origin sense, and then they distinguish between words that differ somewhat in meaning while their pattern is one and the same.

Al-Aṣmaʿī used to say: whatever is elongated is called kuffa, with the kāf given a ḍamma, such as the kuffa [border] of a garment and the like — that is, its edge or hem, called kuffa because it is held in at the edge; likewise the kuffa of sand [its bordering ridge]. He said: whatever is circular is called kiffa, with the kāf given a kasra, such as the kiffa of the scale-pan and the kiffa of the hunter, which is his snare. The two words differ in what al-Aṣmaʿī said, yet their underlying pattern is one.

Al-makfūf is the blind man. As for al-kifaf in tattooing, these are circles found in it. One says: istakaffa al-qawm ḥawla al-shay' — the people ringed around the thing, gazing at it. Ibn Muqbil said, in a line of verse:

He appeared, while the eyes that had gathered around were gazing intently.

As for Ḥumayd's saying, in a line of verse:

Toward mustakiffāt possessing gharūb —

some said these are eyes; others said they are camels gathered together. Al-ghurūb are the shadows. Istakfafta al-shay' is when you put your hand over your eyebrows, like one sheltering himself from the sun to look at something and see whether he can make it out; it is called istikfāf because of his putting his palm over his eyebrow. And they say: laqītuhu kaffatan kaffatan — I met him suddenly, face to face, as though your palm touched his palm. God knows best what is correct.
كفء:
The letters kāf, fāʼ and hamza are two roots. One indicates equality between two things, and the other indicates leaning, tilting, and crookedness.
For the first:
1. kāfaʼtu fulānan — I repaid so-and-so, when I met his deed with the like of it.
2. al-kufʼ — the equal, the match. God Most High said: {and there is none equal to Him} [al-Ikhlāṣ: 4].
3. al-takāfuʼ — equality. The Messenger of God, God bless him and his family and grant him peace, said: "the blood of Muslims is equal [tatakāfaʼu]" — meaning, it is equal.
4. al-kifāʼ — two cloths, one sewn to the other, then let down over the back of the tent.
5. bayt mukfaʼ — a tent covered [with the kifāʼ]; one says akfaʼtuhu, I covered it so.
A poet said, in a line of verse: a tent of dooms, covered and let down.
And it came in the hadith, on the mention of the ʿaqīqa, the sacrifice made for a newborn: "two ewes equal to one another" — they said its meaning is: equal in worth and in age.
As for the other sense, it is their saying: akfaʼtu al-shayʼa, when I tilted it. And so:
1. akfaʼtu al-qaws — I tilted the bow, when you tilt its tip and do not hold it upright as you shoot from it.
2. iktafaʼtu al-ṣaḥfa — I tilted the bowl toward myself. And in the hadith: "a woman may not ask for her sister's divorce, so as to tilt out for herself [li-taktafiʼa] what is on her plate" — that is, take over her share.
3. One says: akfaʼtu al-shayʼa — I overturned it; and kafaʼtu, also, with the same meaning.
4. mukfaʼ al-wajh is said of one downcast in face, as though his face had been tilted away from the cheerfulness it once had.
And of this chapter is al-ikfāʼ in poetry, which is raising one rhyme-letter and lowering another. They claim the Arabs used to recognize this, and that it is not among the terms invented later.
And among what strays from these two roots is al-kufʼa, which is a palm tree's bearing of fruit in its season; the same word is used of the offspring of camels. One says istakfaʼtu fulānan ibilahu, I asked him for a year's offspring of his camels. And one says anā akfīka hādhihi al-nāqata sanatan, I will let you have this she-camel for a year — that is, you milk her, and her offspring is yours. And the saying of Dhū al-Rumma: you see her two kufʼas... [the line breaks off here in the source].
كفا: The letters kāf, fāʼ and the weak letter are a sound root indicating sufficiency, that which needs nothing added to it. One says: kafāka al-shayʼu yakfīka — the thing was enough for you. And one has kafā, kifāyatan, when he saw properly to a matter. Al-kufya is sufficient provision, its plural kufan. And one says ḥasbuka Zaydun min rajulin, Zayd is enough for you as a man, and kāfīka, meaning the same.
كفت:
The letters kāf, fā' and tā' are a sound root indicating gathering and drawing together. From this, their saying kafattu al-shayʾ, when you draw it in to yourself. The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said of the night: "Gather in your children (wakfitū ṣibyānakum)" — meaning draw them to you and keep them within the houses.

God, Mighty and Exalted, said: {Have We not made the earth a gatherer} [al-Mursalāt: 25] {of the living and the dead} [al-Mursalāt: 26] — meaning: they walk upon it while alive, and when they die it draws them into itself.

Ruʾba said, in a line of verse:
From its gathering — tight, like the kindling of a fire.

One says jirāb kafīt — a bag that loses nothing put into it. As for their saying that al-kaft is your turning a thing from its course, so that it yakfitu, meaning turns back — this too is sound, since it draws the thing in from a side.

al-kaft — driving hard, because it gathers the camels together and drives them, as one says yaqbiḍuhā, he grips them. sayr kafīt — swift travel, from this same sense.
كفر:
The letters kāf, fā' and rā' are a sound root pointing to one meaning, and it is covering and concealing. Of a man who covers his coat of mail with a garment one says qad kafara dirʿahu — he has covered his mail. And al-mukaffir is the man covered over by his weapons.

As for the line:
Until, when it had put a hand into a kāfir, and the darkness had hidden away the gaps of the frontiers —
