it is said that al-kāfir is the place where the sun sets. And it is said: rather al-kāfir is the sea. And in the same way the words of another were explained:
And the two remembered a load laid up in store, after the sun had put its right hand into a kāfir.

And the great river is a kāfir, by likeness to the sea. And the sower is called kāfir, because he covers the seed with the soil of the earth. God the Exalted said: {the growth of it pleases the sowers} [al-Ḥadīd: 20]. And ashes that are makfūr are ashes over which the wind has blown dust until it covered them. He said:
Nothing was left, worn away, but ashes covered over.

And al-kufr, unbelief, is the opposite of faith; it is so named because it is a covering over of the truth. And so too kufrān al-niʿma, ingratitude for a blessing: the denying of it and the covering of it. Al-kāfūr is the sheath of the grape before it blossoms. It was called kāfūr because it kafara — covered — the young spathe, that is, it covered it. He said:
Like the vine when it called out from the sheath.
And it is also called al-kufurrā.

As for al-kafirāt and al-kafar, they are the passes of the mountains; and perhaps they were called kafirāt because they lie low, as though the towering mountains had covered them over. He said:
Its sweet scent shows itself out of the mountain passes.

Al-kafr, of land, is what lies far from people, which hardly anyone camps in and nobody passes by. And those who settle in it are ahl al-kufūr. And it is said: rather al-kufūr are the villages. It came in the hadith: " «The Byzantines will surely drive you out of it village by village» ".
كفل:
The letters kāf, fā' and lām are a sound root pointing to one thing holding another within it. From that is al-kifl: a cloth wound round the hump of a camel. It is also said to be a cloth whose two ends are knotted over the camel's rump so that the man riding behind may sit on it. In the hadith: 'Do not drink from the broken place in a vessel, for it is the seat of Satan.' It is called that only for what we mentioned, that it goes round the hump or the rump, as though it had been held within it. As for their calling a coward kifl — and he is the one who is at the rear of the war, whose whole care is to hang back — this was likened to the kifl we described, that is, he is carried and can neither walk nor move; they likened him to the kifl, as the poet said, in a line of verse:
He was worn out, so we slung him as a water-skin is slung, then we bound him fast above with a rope.
The poets have much of this. The plural of this kifl is akfāl. Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
Neither weaponless men nor men carried like baggage.
And of this chapter — and it confirms the analogy we have described — is al-kafīl, the guarantor. You say kafala bihi yakfulu kafālatan — he stood surety for him. Al-kāfil is the one who takes charge of a person and maintains him. God, mighty is His majesty, said: {and Zakariyyā took charge of her} [Āl 'Imrān: 37]. Akfaltuhu al-māl — I made him guarantee the property. Al-kafal is the rump, so named for the flesh it gathers together. Al-kifl in some dialects is a double share of reward, and its origin is what we described first, as though it were something its bearer carries upon the kifl that the camel carries. The same is said of sin. As for al-kāfil, he is the one who does not eat, and it is said he is the one who joins [his fasting] from one day to the next; this is far from what we have described, and I do not know what its origin is, but it is sound in the language. Al-Quṭāmī said, in a line of verse:
They keep to the edges of the watering pools, as though they were Christian women risen in the morning fasting.
كفن: The letters kāf, fāʼ and nūn are a root containing al-kafan, the burial shroud, which is well known. And al-kafn is the spinning of wool; one says kafana, yakfunu. Al-Rāʿī said, in a line of verse: and he spins on through time, save the while he pauses over the preparing of his food.
كل:
The letters kāf and lām are three sound roots. The first points to the opposite of sharpness. The second points to one thing encircling another. The third is a bodily limb.

1. kalla al-sayf yakillu kulūlan wa kallatan — the sword grew dull, growing dull and dullness [being its verbal nouns].
2. al-kalīl — the sword whose edge has grown dull. Sometimes they use kalāla too as its verbal noun; and likewise the tongue and any limb-tip, when they tire, are both called al-kalīlān.
3. akalla al-qawm — said of a people, when their camels have grown weary.
4. kallala fulān, like nakala — so-and-so flinched and turned back. But some say kallala means: he charged and attacked — the opposite of the first sense, and this may be one of the words that carry two opposite meanings.

From this root:

1. al-kall — dependents. God Almighty said: {and he is a burden upon his guardian} [al-Naḥl: 76].
2. al-kall — it is also said to mean the orphan, so named because he is looked after on another's behalf.
3. al-iklīl — a station of the moon [one of its lunar mansions]; this is by way of comparison.
4. al-iklīl — also the cloud that circles around a place. Muḥammad ibn Yazīd said: it is called iklīl because it encircles the head.

As for al-kalāla, Muḥammad said: the kalāla are the male heirs, as a Bedouin said: "My wealth is much, and those who will inherit it from me are kalāla, distant in kinship." He said: it is a verbal noun from takallalahu al-nasab, meaning the kinship curved around him at a remove, and so they named [the heirs] by the verbal noun. The scholars hold views on al-kalāla that are close to one another. They say: al-kalāla are the distant cousins — so said Ibn al-Aʿrābī. As for others among the people of learning, Zuhayr related from Jābir ibn ʿĀmir, who said: when Abū Bakr said, "Whoever dies leaving no child and no father, his heirs are kalāla," ʿAlī objected to it, then came back to his view. Al-Mubarrad said: a child is excluded from being kalāla. He said: the Arabs say, "He did not inherit from him kalāla," meaning he did not inherit from him by a side-line but by nearness and entitlement, as al-Farazdaq said, in a line of verse:

You inherited the spear-shaft of kingship, not through kalāla, from the two sons of Manāf, ʿAbd Shams and Hāshim.

As for the other root: al-kalkal is the chest. It is possible that this is carried over from the sense before it, as though the chest is what curves over what lies beneath it.

Among what falls outside this chapter:

1. al-kulkul — the short man.
2. inkallat al-mar'a, tankallu — said of a woman, when she laughs.

As for kull [meaning "every, all"], it is a word set for encompassing, always joined to what comes after it. Their saying al-kull, and qāma al-kull [using it on its own, without anything following it], is a mistake; the Arabs do not know it that way.
كلأ:
The letters kāf, lām, and the weak letter or the hamza, are a sound root indicating watching and observation; another root indicating a plant; and a third, a bodily organ, later used in a borrowed sense.

Watching and observation: al-kilāʾa — guarding. You say kalaʾahu Allāh — God guarded him. God, Mighty and Exalted, said: {Say: who guards you by night and by day from the Merciful} [al-Anbiyāʾ: 42], meaning who protects you from Him — that is, no one shields you from Him. This belongs to the chapter we named as watching, because to guard a thing is to look at it and keep watch over it.

On this same reasoning, the Arabs' saying takallaʾtu kulʾatan — I asked for a deferral, from delay. From this, the hadith: "He forbade al-kāliʾ bi'l-kāliʾ" — selling a deferred debt for a deferred debt.

And the poet's line:
And his presence is like a deferred, unreliable debt.

meaning that what is present and witnessed of him is like something absent that cannot be counted on. We said this belongs to al-kulʾa because the one owed a debt watches and keeps track of when it falls due — so the reasoning we have drawn holds.

One says iktalaʾtu min al-qawm — I kept watch against them.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
I made my camel kneel, and kept watch with its eye ... and weighed within myself which of my two courses to take.

One says akla'tu baṣarī fī al-shayʾ, when you turned your gaze on it again and again. al-mukallaʾ — a place where ships are moored and sheltered from the wind; and it is said that Kallāʾ of Basra was named from this.

The other root: al-kalaʾ — herbage; one says arḍ mukliʾa, land having herbage, dry or fresh alike. A place is described as kāliʾ, the same as mukliʾ.

The third root: al-kulya, the kidney, well known, later used in a borrowed sense — so that al-kulya of the mazāda [a large waterskin] is a small round piece of leather stitched beneath the carrying-loop. The same word is used of the bow: the two kulyas of a bow are where the strap that carries the arrow is fastened, to the right and left of the arrowhead. kulyat al-saḥāb — the underside of a cloud; plural kulan.
كلب:
The letters kāf, lām and bā' are a single, sound root, indicating one thing's attachment to another with force and a strong pull. From it, al-kalb, the dog, well known, plural kilāb and kalīb.

1. al-kallāb and al-mukallib — one who trains the dog to hunt.
2. al-kalb al-kalib — the dog that turns rabid over human flesh, seized by a kind of madness; when it bites a person, he too becomes kalib, so a man is called kalib and men, kalbā. A verse: "Even if the rabid, ailing dogs drank our blood, it would cure them of that disease, of madness and derangement."

From this chapter too: kulbat al-zamān and kalabuhu, the harshness of the times. Land called kaliba is land whose plants did not get enough moisture and so dried out — named because, once dried, they come to resemble the fangs and claws of dogs.

3. al-kalb — a red strap set between the two edges of a hide when it is being stitched. One says kalabtuhu, I stitched it with it. A verse describes the sheen on the back of a mount, led alongside, as like the strap of a skilled craftsman stitching a hide.
4. al-kalb — a bent iron hook the traveller hangs his provisions on from the saddle.
5. al-kullāb, also called al-kallūb — well known.

As for Ṭufayl's line — "We repaid our dead among the people with their like, and uncounted besides among bound captives" — al-mukallab there means the one who has been shackled (al-mukabbal).

6. al-kalb — the pin in the hilt of a sword, on which the pommel-strap sits.

Al-kullāb is also a place-name, and Ra's Kalb [Dog's Head] is a mountain.
كلت: The letters kāf, lām and tā' are not a genuine root; but they say al-kalt is gathering, and one says imra'a kallūt [a woman marked by this same sense]. And they say al-killīt is a stone with which a hyena's den is blocked up. All of this amounts to nothing.
كلث: The letters kāf, lām and thā' are not a genuine root; but they say: it inclined toward a thing. And sometimes they say: inkalatha fulān — so-and-so went forward.
كلح:
The letters kāf, lām and ḥā' are a root indicating scowling and a grim look in the face. From this, al-kulūḥ — scowling. One says kalaḥa al-rajul, [and] a harsh time is described as kāliḥ.

God Almighty said: "the Fire scorches their faces, and they therein are grinning in torment." And sometimes they call a famine year kalāḥ. "Mā aqbaḥa kalḥatahu" — how ugly is his grimace, meaning: when he scowls, his mouth and what surrounds it become ugly.
كلد:
The letters kāf, lām and dāl are a word pointing to hardness in a thing.

1. al-kalada — a stretch of rough, hard ground; from this comes the name al-Ḥārith ibn Kalada.
2. takallada al-insān — Ibn Duraid said: the man's flesh grew coarse and thick.
كلز: The letters kāf, lām and zāy — they say it is a genuine root, and that al-kalz is gathering. One says kalaztu al-shay' and kallaztuhu, when I gathered it. And a word has been transmitted about it that is sound, not to be doubted: they say iklāzza al-rajul — the man drew in and contracted.
كلس:
The letters kāf, lām and sīn point to fullness in a thing.

1. takallasa takallusan — said when he had drunk his fill. A poet said, in a line of verse: One of vigor and force, who wakes having drunk his fill.
2. kallasa — also said of a hard, serious worker. A poet said, in a line of verse: When the young man is put in charge one day, he strives hard.
كلع:
The letters kāf, lām and ʿayn are words pointing to grime and dirt.

1. kalaʿ — the chapping and dirt of the foot; one says kaliʿat rijluhu, taklaʿu, kalaʿan.
2. inā' kaliʿ — a vessel caked over with dirt.
3. siqā' kaliʿ — a waterskin with dust built up in layers on it.
4. al-kulʿa — a disease that seizes a camel in its hindquarters.

Among what is carried on this same single sense — a build-up of layers, without the dirt:

1. al-kalaʿa, of sheep — so named for their crowding together.
كلف:
The letters kaf, lam and fa are a single sound root indicating being enamored with a thing and attached to it.

1. al-kalaf — one says 'kalifa bi-l-amr yaklafu kalafan', he became infatuated/devoted to the matter. They say: let not your love be an infatuation, nor your hatred a ruin.
2. al-kulfa — a burden one is obliged to bear, whether an unforeseen difficulty or a due obligation.
3. al-mutakallif — one who busies himself with what is not his concern. God, glorified is He, said: {Say: I ask of you no wage for it, and I am not one of the self-imposing pretenders} [Sad: 86].
4. al-kalaf — a mark that comes over the face and changes its complexion.
كلم:
The letters kāf, lām and mīm are two roots: one of them points to speech that makes meaning understood, and the other to wounds.

The first is al-kalām, speech. You say kallamtuhu ukallimuhu taklīman; and he is my kalīm when he speaks to you or you speak to him. Then they widen it, so they call a single meaningful utterance a kalima, and a story a kalima, and a whole long ode a kalima. And they make the plural of kalima kalimāt and kalim. God, exalted be He, said: {They twist the words from their places} [al-Nisā': 46]. And the other root is al-kalm, which is a wound; and al-kilām is wounds; and the plural of kalm is kulūm also. And a rajul kalīm and a qawm kalmā — that is, wounded. As for al-kalām, it is said: it is rough ground. And in that there is something to look into.
كم:
The letters kāf and mīm are a single root pointing to a covering and a veil.

1. al-kumma — the cap; one says from it takammama and takamkama, the man covered his head. From this too comes the hadith: "that ʿUmar saw a girl takamkama [muffled up]."
2. al-kumm — the sleeve of a shirt; one says from it kamamtuhu, meaning I gave it two sleeves.
3. al-kimm — the sheath of the palm-spathe, plural al-akmām. God, Glorified is He, said: {and the palm trees with sheathed clusters} [al-Raḥmān: 11]. Abū ʿUbayd said: it is also pluralised akimma and akāmīm.
4. kamma al-fasīl — said when someone, fearing for a young palm shoot, covers it until it grows strong.
5. al-akāmīm — the coverings of a blossom.
6. al-kamkām — one compact in build.
كمت:
The letters kāf, mīm and tāʾ are a sound word meaning a color, among colors.

1. *al-kumta* — a color that is neither reddish-blond nor black. One says *farasun kumayt*, a bay horse. The word comes only in this diminutive-looking shape.
2. *al-kumayt* — wine that has blackness and redness in it.
كمح:
The letters kāf, mīm and ḥāʾ are words that do not follow the general pattern, and there is doubt about some of them, but we have set down what has been said of them.

1. *akmaḥa al-karm* — said when the grapevine stirred to put out its leaves.
2. *rajulun kawmaḥ* — a man with large buttocks.
3. *kamaḥa al-faras* — said when he reined in, curbed, the horse.
كمر: The letters kāf, mīm and rāʾ are a word. They say: *rajulun makmūr* — a man whose glans (*kamra*) has been nicked at the tip by the circumciser.
كمز: The letters kāf, mīm and zāʾ are not a real root. They say: *al-kumza* is a lump of dates.
كمش:
The letters kāf, mīm and shīn are a sound root meaning fineness and smallness.

1. *kamsha* — said of a ewe with a small udder.
2. *farasun kamīsh* — a horse with a small penis.
3. *kamsh* — said of a resolute, decisive man; he is described this way with reference to fineness and lightness. One says *kamusha kamāshatan*.
4. *kamashahu bi-l-sayf* — said when he cut off its extremities with the sword.
كمع:
The letters kāf, mīm and ʿayn are a sound root meaning settledness and stillness.

1. *al-kimʿ* — a dwelling, so they claimed; one says *huwa fī kimʿihi*, meaning in his house. It is named this because one settles and dwells in it.
2. *al-kamīʿ* — the bed-companion. One says *kāmaʿahā*, said when he shared her bed. *Al-mukāmaʿa*, mentioned in the hadith and forbidden there, is for a man to lie beside another man with no covering between them.

A poet said, in a line of verse, about al-kamīʿ:
The cold north wind blew — and when the girl's bed-companion spent the night wrapped up in a garment.

3. *al-kimʿ* — also, low, settled ground.
كمل: The letters kāf, mīm and lām are a sound root indicating the completeness of a thing. One says: "kamala l-shay'u" and "kamula," so it is kāmil, complete. And "akmaltuhu" — I completed it. God, exalted is He, said: {This day I have completed for you your religion} [al-Mā'ida: 3].
كمن:
The letters kāf, mīm and nūn are a small root meaning to hide oneself away. One says kamana al-shay'u kumūnan, the thing was hidden.

1. *al-kamīn* — the ambush in war is derived from this.
2. *al-nāqa al-kamūn* — some people claimed this is a she-camel that conceals her pregnancy: when she has conceived she does not raise her tail to show it.
3. *muktamin* — grief hidden away in the heart is called this, as though it were concealed.
4. *al-kumna* — a disease in the eye, left over from an inflammation (ramad).
كمه:
The letters kāf, mīm and hā' are a single word, and it is *al-kamah*, blindness a person is born with, though it may also come from an affliction that befalls him.

Suwayd said, in a line of verse:
His two eyes went blind until they turned white ... while he blames himself, now that he has drawn back.
كمي:
The letters kāf, mīm and the weak letter are a root meaning something being hidden. Some hamzated words also enter into it.

1. *kamā fulānun al-shahādata* — said when so-and-so concealed the testimony, meaning he hid it.
2. *al-kamiyy* — the brave warrior is named from this: he is the one who wraps himself (yatakammā) in his weapons, covering himself with them.
3. *takammat al-fitnatu al-nās* — said when strife overwhelms and covers people.
4. *kami'tu ʿan al-akhbāri akmaʾu ʿanhā* — they mentioned that the Arabs say this, meaning I was ignorant of the news.

As for the hamzated form, it is not part of this chapter at all — it is rather a plant. We have already said that most of this does not follow the general pattern.

1. *al-kamʾa* — the truffle, well known; its singular is *kamʾ*. This is unusual: it is rare for the plural to carry a tāʾ marbūṭa while the singular does not.
2. *kamaʾtu al-qawma* — I fed the people truffles.
3. *kami'at rijlī* — my foot cracked open; this can reasonably be reasoned by analogy from the word above.

Perhaps the truffle is named this because the ground cracks open over it.

4. *akmaʾat fulānan al-sinn* — old age made so-and-so an old man.

Among what falls outside this root: *akmaʾa ʿalā al-amr*, said when he resolved firmly upon a matter.
كن:
The letters kāf and nūn are a single root pointing to concealment or protection.

1. kanantu al-shay' fī kinnihi — I put a thing in its shelter and kept it safe there.
2. aknantu al-shay' — I hid it away.
3. al-kināna — the well-known [quiver for arrows] fits this same pattern.
4. al-kunna — like a wing or awning that a man puts out from his wall; it is like a screen.
5. al-kānūn — the hearth, because it conceals what is beneath it. Sometimes they call a tiresome man a kānūn too.

Al-Ḥuṭay'a said, in a line of verse:
Sieves, when entrusted with a secret — and a kānūn [a heavy burden] upon those who talk.

As for al-kanna, it stands outside this root; it is said to mean the son's wife. A poet said, in a line of verse:
We indeed have a kanna — one who listens closely, one who watches closely.
كنب:
The letters kāf, nūn and bāʾ are a single word that does not branch further. They say: *al-kanab* is the hardness and thickening that covers the hands from work, once they have blistered and calloused.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
My hands have grown calloused (aknabat), after being soft.

Al-Aṣmaʿī said: one says *aknabat yaduhu*, his hand grew calloused, and one does not say *kanibat*.

Among what is not from this root: *al-kanab*, a plant. Al-Ṭirimmāḥ said, in a line of verse:
Rising high above the river-valleys, their dwelling is on the edges of Najd, in the land of ṭalḥ trees and kanab.
كنت: The letters kāf, nūn and tāʾ are a word, if it is sound. They say: *kanata* and *iktanata*, said when one clung to a thing and was content with it. And ʿAdiyy said — [the text breaks off here, with no line quoted].
كند:
The letters kāf, nūn and dāl are one sound root indicating cutting. One says kanada al-ḥabl yaknuduhu kandan — he cut the rope. al-kanūd — one ungrateful for a favour, who denies it; this is from the first sense, since he cuts off gratitude. From this: al-arḍ al-kanūd — land that grows nothing.

A poet, al-Aʿshā, said, in a line of verse [obscure]:
Turn aside, turn aside, with a firm heart ... and one who holds to ties, and one who cuts them.

And Kinda was named so, as they claim, because he kanada his father — that is, he parted from him and joined his mother's kinsmen and became their chief, so his father said to him: "you have cut yourself off (kanadta)."
كنر:
The letters kāf, nūn and rāʾ are not, in our view, a root. There are two words in it that we think are Persian.

1. *al-kinnār* — a length of linen cloth.
2. *al-kinnārāt* — lutes, or tambourines; its kāf may be said with either a fatḥa or a kasra.
كنز: The letters kāf, nūn and zāy are a small sound root pointing to a gathering in a thing. From this: a she-camel kināz of flesh — that is, firm-packed. And kanaztu al-tamra fī wiʿā'ihi aknizuhu — I packed the dates into their vessel. And kanaztu al-kanza aknizuhu — I stored the treasure. And they say, of the packing of dates: it is the season of al-kanāz. Ibn al-Sikkīt said: this was heard only with the fatḥa — that is, it is not of what comes in both fiʿāl and faʿāl, like jidād and jadād, the cutting of the date-crop.
كنس:
The letters kāf, nūn and sīn are two sound roots: one indicates the sweeping of a thing off the face of something else, that is, uncovering it; the other indicates concealment.

The first: kans al-bayt — sweeping the house, the removal of dust from the surface of its floor. al-miknasa — the tool for sweeping. al-kunāsa — what is swept up.

The other root: al-kinās — the gazelle's lair. al-kānis — the gazelle entering its lair. al-kunnas — the stars that withdraw into their houses [at setting], just as gazelles withdraw into their lairs. Abū ʿUbayda said: they withdraw at their setting.
كنع:
The letters kāf, nūn and ʿayn are a sound root meaning contracting, drawing in, and gathering together.

1. *al-kanaʿ* — in the fingers, is a contraction and drawing-in. One says *kaniʿat aṣābiʿuhu takanaʿu kanaʿan*, his fingers contracted.
2. *takannaʿa fulānun bi-fulānin* — said when he seized and gripped him tightly.
3. *kanaʿati al-ʿuqāb* — said when the eagle drew in its wing to swoop down.
4. *iktanaʿa al-qawm* — said when the people leaned or inclined.
5. *kanaʿa al-amr* — the matter drew near.
6. *kanaʿa al-rajulu wa-aknaʿa* — said when the man became soft and yielding; this belongs to the root because it is a drawing-in and a gathering-together.

In the hadith: "I seek refuge with You from al-kunūʿ." This is from *kanaʿa*.
كنف:
The letters kāf, nūn and fāʾ are one sound root meaning covering and shelter.

1. *al-kanīf* — that which covers and shelters.
2. Some people claimed that the shield is called *kanīf* because it covers.
3. Every sheltering enclosure, among the Arabs, is called *kanīf*.

ʿUrwa said, in a line of verse:
I say to a people in the *kanīf*: set out in the evening — the evening we spent the night, worn out, by Māwān.

4. *kanaftu fulānan* and *aknaftuhu* — I sheltered so-and-so, I protected him.
5. *kanafā al-ṭāʾir* — a bird's two wings, because they shelter it.
6. *al-kinf* — a bag or pouch, named from this, because it covers what is inside it.

In ʿUmar's saying to ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd, "a little *kinf* filled with knowledge," he meant by it the diminutive of *kinf*.

7. *nāqatun kanūf* — a she-camel affected by the cold, who shelters herself among the rest of the camels.
8. *ḥaẓartu li-l-ibili ḥaẓīratan, wa-kanaftu lahā, wa-kanaftuhā aknufuhā* — I built an enclosure for the camels, and I made a shelter for them, and I sheltered them.

As for their saying *kanaftu ʿan al-shayʾ*, meaning I turned away from it, and their citing:
So that it be known which of us turns away (kānif) from the sale —
that is not fully accounted for by the pattern we have described; rather the meaning is that I turned away from it, hiding and sheltering myself behind something else.
كنه: The letters kāf, nūn and hāʾ are a single word meaning the furthest extent of a thing and the end of its proper time. One says *balaghtu kunha hādhā al-amr*, meaning I reached its full extent, the time that truly belongs to it.
كنو:
The letters kāf, nūn and the weak letter mean speaking of something indirectly, using another name for it. One says *kannaytu ʿan kadhā*, said when you spoke of a thing using another expression by which it could be inferred; one also says *kanawtu*.

What makes this clear is the saying of a poet:
I speak indirectly (aknū) of a shameful thing, using another word for it — and sometimes I speak of it plainly and openly.

Do you not see that he set the indirect expression (kināya) against plain, open speech? For this reason the kunya [a person's byname] is called a kunya, as though it were an indirect way of referring to his own name.

In Al-Khalīl's book it is said that the correct usage is to say "he is given the kunya Abū ʿAbd Allāh," not "he is given the kunya ʿAbd Allāh."

And the *kunā* of a dream are the likenesses which the angel of dreams presents, using them to refer indirectly to the real matters they stand for.
كه:
The letters kāf and hā' have nothing of real language in them, only something close to mimicry of a sound. One says kahha al-sakrān, when you smell the drunk man's breath and he breathes kahh in your face. This is nothing [not a real linguistic root]. And they say kahkaha al-asad, of the lion's roaring. Then they say al-kahkāh, of men, is the weak one. And they recite:

Nor is he a kahkāha [weakling], full of complaint, when the years grow hard.

I see no sense myself in their calling him "the weak one"; this is a loose, figurative use — what is really meant is that he breathes kahh in the face of whoever asks him for something. The whole chapter is one thing.
كها:
The letters kāf, hāʾ and the weak letter are a single word that does not follow the general pattern and nothing branches from it. They call a huge she-camel *kahāt*.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
When a fat *kahāt* [huge she-camel] presents itself among them, do not give any of it away — take your share of it and eat your fill.
كهب: The letters kāf, hāʾ and bāʾ are a word. They call a dusty grey color mixed with black, in camels, *kuhba*.
كهد:
The letters kāf, hāʾ and dāl — they say something of them meaning a moving upward.

1. *kahada al-ḥimār* — said when the donkey pranced and jerked as it walked.
2. *akhadtuhu* — I made it prance; in a line of verse by al-Farazdaq: they make the donkeys prance.
3. *ikwahadda al-farkh* — said when the chick stirred as if to rise up.
كهر:
The letters kāf, hāʾ and rāʾ are two meanings very far apart from each other.

The first is rebuking harshly. One says *kahara yakharu kahran*.
In the hadith: "By my father and mother, he never rebuked me nor cursed me."
Some have recited [the Qur'an]: "As for the orphan, do not rebuke him."

The second meaning: *kahru al-nahār* is the sun's climbing high, its ascent. One says *kahara yakharu*.
He said, in a line of verse:
And when the herd of wild asses is at the height of mid-morning.
كهف: The letters kāf, hā' and fā' are a single word: it is a cave in a mountain, plural kuhūf.
كهل:
The letters kāf, hā' and lām are a root indicating strength in a thing, or a gathering-together of one's build.

1. *al-kāhil* — what is between the two shoulders, named so for its strength.
2. *kahl* — what they call a man whose build has come together, once grey hair has begun to touch him; a woman likewise is *kahla*.

Someone said, in a line of verse:
I will not again be a hired companion ... handling the mature woman and the young girl.

As for their saying of a plant *iktahala*, it is only a likening to the mature man (*al-kahl*). *Iktihāl ar-rawḍa* — when a meadow becomes entirely covered in blossom. Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
Girded with a full covering of plants, in bloom.
كهم:
The letters kāf, hāʾ and mīm are a small root meaning dullness and slowness.

1. *al-faras al-kahām* — the slow horse.
2. *al-sayf al-kahām* — the blunt sword.
3. *al-lisān al-kahām* — the tongue that is slow and inarticulate.
4. *kahkam* — said of an old, aged man.
5. *akhama baṣaruhu* — said when his eyesight grew weak and dim.
كهن: The letters kāf, hā' and nūn are a single word. It is *al-kāhin*, the soothsayer; one also says *takahhana yatakahhanu*, he practised soothsaying. God knows best.
كو:
The letters kāf and the weak letter [wāw] are close to the chapter before it; there is nothing in it besides their saying: kawāhu bi-l-nār, yakwīhi — he cauterized/branded him with fire. They borrow this and say: kawāhu bi-ʿaynihi, when he fixed his gaze sharply on him. And: I warm myself by the closeness of the girl (innī la-atakawwā bi-l-jāriya), meaning I take warmth from her. Al-kūwa [the window] is well known.

Al-ka'ka'a: turning back in retreat; it is also said to mean gathering together.
كوب:
The letters kāf, wāw, and bā are a single word. It is al-kūb: a drinking-cup with no handle; the plural is akwāb.

God Almighty said: {and cups set out} [al-Ghāshiya: 14].

They also say: al-kūba is the drum used for playing.
كود:
The letters kāf, wāw and dāl are a word that seems to point to seeking something with some trouble.

They say kāda yakūdu kawdan and makādan — he sought it with effort. And to one who asks you for a thing you do not wish to give, they say: lā wa-lā makādata — no, and not even the trying for it.

As for their kāda in the sense of coming near, its meaning is: he came close. When kāda stands bare, the thing did not happen: you say kāda yafʿalu — he was about to do it — and this was not done. When it is joined to a negation, the thing did happen: when you say mā kāda yafʿaluhu, he did do it. God, be He glorified, said: {So they slaughtered her, though they were near to not doing it} [al-Baqara: 71].
كور:
The letters kāf, wāw, and rāʾ are a sound root pointing to turning and gathering together. From this, al-kawr is the turning. One says kāra yakūru, when it turned.

1. kawr al-ʿimāma — the winding of the turban round and round.
2. al-kūra — a district, because it turns/circles around the villages within it.

One says ṭaʿanahu fa-kawwarahu, when he struck him and threw him down in a heap. From it is His saying, Most High: {when the sun is wound up} [al-Takwīr: 1], as though it were gathered up entirely.

3. al-kūr — the camel's pack-saddle, because it turns round the withers, plural akwār.

As for their saying "al-ḥawr baʿda al-kawr" [reversal after gathering], the sound version among them is "al-ḥawr baʿda al-kawn" [reversal after having been], meaning he turned back, that is, he reverted and diminished after having been something. Whoever says it with rāʾ is not far wrong either, meaning: his affair had been gathered together, then it turned back and diminished. And His saying, Most High: {He winds the night over the day} [al-Zumar: 5], means He turns this over that and that over this — as it came in the commentary: some of this is added into that, and some of that into this.

4. al-kawr — a group of camels, about a hundred and fifty in number. Its reasoning is not far off, because when camels gather they stand circled together at their resting place.
5. kuwwārat al-naḥl — the beehive, well known.

Among what falls outside this root: their saying iktāra al-farasu, when the horse raised its tail as it galloped.
كوز:
The letters kāf, wāw and zāʾ are a sound root meaning gathering together. Abū Bakr said: *takawwaza al-qawm*, the people gathered together. He said: from this comes the naming of Banū Kūz, of the tribe of Ḍabba.

1. *al-kūz* — the water-jug, from this, because it gathers water.
2. *iktāza al-māʾ* — he scooped up, drew up, the water.
كوس:
The letters kāf, wāw and sīn are a sound root meaning throwing down, felling, or something close to it. One says *kāsahu yakūsuhu*, said when he threw him down.

1. *kāsat al-nāqatu takūsu* — said of a she-camel when she was hamstrung and stood on three legs; she is called this because she has come close to being thrown down.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Had she encamped by Ghassān al-Sulayṭī, a stallion among them would have bellowed, and a hamstrung, wounded one would have cried out too.

2. Sometimes they call a short-legged horse *kawsiyy*.
3. *ʿushbun mutakāwis* — said of herbage when it grows thick and abundant; this fits the pattern of the chapter, because parts of it fall and pile upon one another.

As for *al-kaʾs*, it is said to be the vessel together with the wine in it — it does not belong to this chapter at all.
كوع:
The letters kāf, wāw and ʿayn are a single word: it is *al-kūʿ*, the end of the forearm bone nearest the thumb.

*Al-kawaʿ* is this bone standing out, protruding and large; a man who has it is called *akwaʿ*. It is also said that *al-kawaʿ* is the wrists turning inward toward the shoulders.

*Kawwaʿahu bi-l-sayf* — said when he struck him with the sword; perhaps meaning he struck him on the *kūʿ*, the wrist-bone.
كوف:
The letters kāf, wāw and fāʾ are a small root; they say it means roundness in a thing.

1. *takawwafa al-raml* — said when the sand became rounded, gathered into a mound. They say al-Kūfa was named for this.
2. *waqaʿnā fī kūfān* or *kuwwafān* — we fell into hardship and toil; as though they derived this from the rounded, heaped-up sand, because walking in it wears a person out.
كول: The letters kāf, wāw and lām are a word, if it is sound. They say: *takawwala al-qawmu ʿalā fulān*, said when the people gathered against so-and-so.
كوم:
The letters kāf, wāw and mīm are a sound root meaning a gathering together in something, along with height in it.

1. *al-kawmāʾ* — the she-camel with a tall hump.
2. *al-kawm* — a herd, a portion, of camels.
3. *al-kawma* — a heap of food or of other things.
4. *kāma al-farasu unthāhu yakūmuhā* — said when the stallion horse mounted his mare; that too is simply the same gathering-together.
كون:
The letters kāf, wāw and nūn are a root that points to telling that something has happened, either in time past or in time now present.

They say kāna al-shay'u yakūnu kawnan — the thing came to be — when it takes place and is present. God the Exalted said: {And if there is one in hardship} [al-Baqara: 280], that is, if such a one is present and has come. And they say qad kāna al-shitā' — the winter has come, that is, it has arrived and is here. As for the past, it is our saying kāna Zaydun amīran — Zayd was a commander — meaning that this was so in a time gone by.

Some people said: al-makān, the place, is derived from kāna yakūnu; then, when it grew common, the mīm was imagined to belong to the root, so they said tamakkana — he took a place and settled in it — just as from al-miskīn, the poor man, they said tamaskana.

And in this section there is a word that may well belong to the speech which has passed away with the passing of those who knew it.

They say kuntu ʿalā fulānin akūnu ʿalayhi — I stood for so-and-so — and that is when I go surety for him. And also iktantu iktiyānan, in the same sense. It is a strange word.
كوى: The letters kāf, wāw and yāʾ are a sound root: it is "I cauterized with fire" (*kawaytu bi-l-nār*). We have already spoken of it.
كيت:
The letters kāf, yā' and tā' are a word, if it is sound. They say: al-takyīt is preparing one's gear/equipment.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Prepare your gear, if you are to set off travelling — I fear for your small herd of camels the wild beasts.
كيح:
The letters kāf, yā' and ḥā' are a single word. They say: al-kīḥ is the flank or support of a mountain.

Al-Shanfarā said, in a line of verse:
They run about me at evening as though I were, among the wild mountain-goats, a bandy-legged one who leans toward the mountainside, sure of foot.
كيد: The letters kāf, yā' and dāl are a sound root pointing to handling a thing with force; then the chapter widens, and all of it comes back to this root. The people of the language said: al-kayd is handling. They said: everything you handle, you kīd it. This is the root in the chapter. Then they call trickery kayd. God, exalted is He, said: {Or do they intend a plot} [al-Ṭūr: 42]. And they say huwa yakīdu bi-nafsihi, that is, he is giving up his soul, as though he were handling it to bring it out. And al-kayd is the crow's cawing with strain. And al-kayd is the fire-stick bringing out fire slowly and hard. And al-kayd is vomiting; and they sometimes call menstruation kayd. And al-kayd is war; one says kharajū wa-lam yalqaw kaydan, that is, they went out and met no war.
كير:
The letters kāf, yāʾ and rāʾ are a word: it is *kīr al-ḥaddād*, the blacksmith's bellows. Abū ʿAmr said: *al-kūr* is the furnace built of clay, while *al-kīr* is the bellows made of hide.

Bishr said, in a line of verse:
As though the wheezing of its nostril, when they suppress its panting, were a borrowed bellows.
كيس:
The letters kāf, yāʾ and sīn are a root meaning holding together and gathering.

1. *al-kīs* — the purse, named because it holds a thing together and gathers it.
2. *al-kays* in a person — the opposite of foolishness, because it is a gathering-together of sound judgment and intellect. One says *rajulun kayyis*, *rijālun akyās* — a shrewd man, shrewd men.
3. *akyasa al-rajulu wa-akāsa* — said when children of good sense were born to him.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Had you been born of a shrewd mother, she would have raised you shrewd — for a mother's shrewdness makes her sons the shrewder.

Perhaps *kaysān* is the pattern *faʿlān* from *akyasa*. And Banū Fahm used to call treachery *kaysān*.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
When kaysān is called for, their elders are closer to treachery than their beardless youths.
كيص:
The letters kāf, yāʾ and ṣād, if sound, mean contraction and narrowness. They say: *kāṣa yakīṣu*, like *kāʿa*. They say: *al-kīṣ* is a narrow-tempered, mean-spirited man.

A word has been related that I have my doubts about: they say *kaṣnā ʿinda fulānin mā shiʾnā*, meaning we ate as much as we wanted at so-and-so's.
كيف: The letters kāf, yā' and fā' are one word. They say: al-kīfa is a piece cut from a garment. As for kayfa, it is a word laid down to ask about a person's state; so one says kayfa huwa — how is he? — and the answer is ṣāliḥ, he is well.
كيل:
The letters kāf, yā' and lām are three words, no one of which resembles the others.

The first is al-kayl, measuring: kayyala al-ṭaʿām — he measured out the grain. One says kiltu fulānan — I measured out for so-and-so, that is, I gave to him. And iktaltu ʿalayhi — I took by measure from him. God, be He glorified, said: {Woe to those who give short measure} [al-Muṭaffifīn: 1]. {Those who, when they take by measure from people, take in full} [al-Muṭaffifīn: 2]. {And when they measure out to them or weigh out to them, they give less} [al-Muṭaffifīn: 3]

The second word: kāla al-zand yakīl — when the fire-stick strikes out no fire.

The third word: al-kayyūl, the rear of the line in battle.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
I am a man whose close friend took a pledge from me that I would never, ever stand in the rear of the line.
كين:
The letters kāf, yā' and nūn name a thing they say is in a part of a woman's body, one that narrows around it; the plural is *kuyūn*.

Jarīr said, in a line of verse:
Ibn Murra pressed, O Farazdaq, her *kayn* ... as a doctor presses the throat of the excused man.

As for *al-kīna*, in their saying "so-and-so spent the night in *kīnat* evil," meaning in a bad state — its origin is *al-kawn* (being), a *fi'la*-pattern noun from it.
لأ: As for the letters lām and hamza, they indicate clarity and glitter. From this, taʼallaʼat al-luʼluʼa, the pearl gleamed — and it is named luʼluʼ, pearl, because it gleams. The Arabs say: "I will not do it as long as the wild oryx twinkle with their tails" — meaning, as long as they move them and flash with them.
لأم:
The letters lām, alif and mīm are two origins: one is agreement and coming together, the other is bad character.

The first: their saying la'amtu al-jurḥ, and la'amtu al-ṣad', when I closed it up. And when two things agree, they have become joined (iltama'ā). A poet said:
People imagine of the two kings that they have become united - but if you hear of their union, know that the matter has grown severe.

I think that what Tha'lab recited concerning al-līm belongs to this same word - the poet merely softened the hamza.

1. riyāshun lu'āmun - matched feathers, when the belly-side of one feather-vane meets the back-side of another.
2. al-lu'ma - said to be the collected tools of the plough; and when a saddle is adorned, its whole equipment is called lu'ma.
3. al-la'ma - the coat of mail, plural lu'am, against the usual pattern. It was named la'ma for how closely it fits together (iltiyām). Istal'ama: the man put on a coat of mail.

A poet said:
They put on their armor and girded themselves - girding up is what a raider does.

The other origin is al-lu'm, baseness. They say al-la'īm is the stingy one, base of soul, low of origin; one says la'uma, he became base.

1. al-mil'am - the one who takes up the excuses of the base.

As for al-lām without the hamza, it does not belong to this chapter. They say al-lām is a person's shape or figure. A poet said:
A Mahri she-camel struts on her nose-rein - the journey has left of her nothing but her shape.

They also say al-lām is the arrow, in the saying of Imru' al-Qays:
We pierce them with a straight thrust and a twisting one, like your repeated cast of two arrows upon an archer.
لأو:
The letters lām, hamza and the weak letter are two words: one is hardship, the other is an animal.

The first: al-la'wā' is hardship. In the hadith: "Whoever has three daughters and bears patiently their hardship (la'wā') - they will be a veil for him from the Fire." They say fa'ala dhālika ba'da la'yin, meaning after hardship. Al-ta'ā al-rajul: his life turned bad. From this is the poet's saying:
The worn state of his garments, and hardship, do not change the noble man's nature.
They said he meant al-la'wā', which is hardship of life.

The other: al-la'ā, said to be the wild bull, in the saying of al-Ṭirimmāḥ:
Like the back of the wild bull - were a drink sought by it in daytime, it would appear among the bellies of the ravines.

And God knows best.
لاب: The letters lām, alif and bā'. Al-lāba is the stony black lava tract, plural lūb. And al-luwāb is thirst; one says lāba yalūbu, he wandered from thirst.
لاع: The letters lām, alif and 'ayn. Al-lāʿ is the cowardly man; one says hāʿun lāʿun, and hā'iʿun lā'iʿun, meaning coward.
لاه:
The letters lām, alif and hā'. Lāh is a name of Allah, Most High; then the alif and lām were added for magnification. A poet said:
By God, son of your uncle, you have not excelled me in lineage, nor are you my judge, that you should disgrace me.
لب:
The letters lām and bāʼ are a sound root indicating attachment and steadfastness, and also purity and excellence.
For the first:
1. alabba bi-l-makāni — he "alabba" in a place, when he settled there; yulibbu ilbāban.
2. rajulun labbun bi-hādhā al-amri — a man devoted to this matter, when he clings to it. Al-Farrāʼ related: imraʼatun labbatun, a woman devoted to her husband — meaning, she remains constant in love for him always.
3. al-talbiya — his saying "labbayka", here I am. They said its meaning is: I remain standing in obedience to You. It is put in the accusative as a verbal noun, and doubled in the sense of one answer following another.
4. al-labīb — the one who says "labbayka". The poet said: so I said to her, return to yourself, for I am in the state of pilgrim sanctity, and after that I remain one who answers the call — meaning, in the state of iḥrām, responding.
5. lablaba min al-shayʼi — he showed tender concern over the thing, so he is mulablib. And it was said: among us is the one who shows tender concern, and the one who shelters the young. This too comes from steadfastness in love.
The other sense: al-lubb, well known, of anything, is its pure part, that which is picked out from it; and for that the intellect is called lubb. rajulun labībun, an intelligent man; one has labba, yalubbu. And the pure part of anything is its lubāb.
1. al-labba — the place of the necklace on the chest, that spot being the choicest part; likewise al-labab. One says labbabtu al-rajula, I struck his labba. They call one who has girded himself up mutalabbib, as though he had tied his garment up to his labba, tucked up. Labab al-faras, the horse's breast-strap, is well known. And by comparison, al-labab of sand is what lies close to a mountain, joined to a plain. A poet said, in a line of verse: bright of throat, her breast-hollows plain, as though she were a gazelle whom the sandy slope had opened out onto.
And among what strays from this: they say al-labāb is pasture. And al-lablāb is a plant.
لبأ:
The letters lām, bā' and hamza are two very distinct words. Al-labu'a is the female of lions, the lioness. The other word is al-liba' - the first milk after a birth, which is eaten, written with a short vowel and a hamza. One says alba'ati al-shātu waladahā: she suckled her young the liba', and iltaba'ahā waladuhā: her young drank her liba'. Laba'tu al-qawma: I gave the people liba' to drink. And 'ishārun malābi': pregnant she-camels whose birth has drawn near.

What is irregular here, and rare, is labba'tu, like labbaytu; and it is not an original word of this root.
لبث: The letters lām, bā' and thā' are a word indicating staying on in a place. One says: labitha bi-l-makān, he remained there. God, exalted, said: {They did not stay save an hour of a day} [al-Aḥqāf: 35].
لبج:
The letters lām, bā' and jīm are two words that follow no fixed pattern. The first is their saying lubija bihi, when he was thrown down. Ḥayyun labīj is said of an encampment when it has come down and settled in its place. A poet said:
As if the heavy clouds between Taḍāru' and Shāba were kneeling, settled camels of Judhām.

The other is al-lubja: an iron implement with prongs, as if it were a hand with its fingers.
لبخ:
The letters lām, bā' and khā'. They say al-lubākhiyya is the woman complete and full in form. Al-A'shā said:
Full-figured and complete of form - she adorns him with pure character.
لبد:
The letters lām, bā' and dāl are a sound word indicating one thing matting up on top of another.

1. *al-libd* — felt; well known.
2. *talabbadat al-arḍ*, *labbadahā al-maṭar* — the ground became matted down; the rain matted it down.
3. *ṣāra an-nāsu 'alayhi lubadan* — the people became a crowded mass upon him, when they gathered thickly on him. God, exalted is He, said: {and that when the servant of God stood calling upon Him they well-nigh became a crowding mass (*libadan*) upon him} [al-Jinn: 19]. *Lubadan* is also read on the pattern *fu'al*, from *albada bil-makān*, he stayed in a place.
4. the lion is *dhū libda*, maned, because its shaggy coat mats upon it from the abundance of blood it laps up.

Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
The gnats of the two villages clothed him in a matted cloak ... whenever it touches his hide, it mats down.

They say, as a proverb: "He is more inviolable than the lion's mane (*libdat al-asad*)."

5. *albada bil-makān* — he stayed in the place.
6. *al-lubad* — a man who never leaves his dwelling.

All of that is measured on the first word.

7. *labada bil-arḍ labūdan* — it stayed pressed flat to the ground.
8. *albada al-ba'īr* — the camel struck its tail against its rump after defecating on it, so that its rump comes to look like the matted *libda*.
9. *albadati l-ibl* — the camels became ready to fatten up; it is as though what appeared of that state were likened to the *libda*.
10. *al-labīd* — they say this is the storage-sack (*al-jawāliq*); one says *albadtu al-qirba*, I put it away inside the sack.
لبز:
The letters lām, bā' and zā' are two words close in pattern. Al-labz is the she-camel's striking with the whole of her hoof. A poet said:
Striking with hooves heavy in their blows.
And al-labz is also good eating.
لبس:
The letters lām, bā' and sīn are a sound root, one, pointing to mixing and entering into one another.

Of this is labistu al-thawba albasuhu — I wore the garment — and that is the origin, and from it the branches come out. And al-labs is the confusing of a matter; one says labastu ʿalayhi al-amra ulbisuhu, with a kasra on it — I made the matter obscure to him. God, exalted be He, said: {And We would have confused for them what they confuse} [al-Anʿām: 9]. And in a matter there is labsa, that is, it is not clear. And al-labs is the mixing of darkness. And one says lābastu al-amra ulābisuhu — I mixed myself into the matter.

Of this chapter: al-libās, and it is a man's wife; and the husband is her clothing.

Al-Jaʿdī said, in a line of verse:
When the bedfellow bends her neck, she falls in close and becomes a garment upon him.

And al-labūs is everything that is worn, of clothes [and] mail. And lābastu al-rajula ḥattā ʿaraftu bāṭinahu — I mixed with the man until I knew his inside. And this is used as a figure, so one says: fīhi malbasun — that is, there is enjoyment in him and something left.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Truly, after poverty there is wealth for a man, and after grey hair a long life and something still to enjoy.

And the libs of the litter and of the Kaʿba is the covering upon them, with a kasra on the lām.
لبط:
The letters lām, bā' and ṭā' are a small, sound root indicating falling and being thrown down. One says labaṭa bihi, when he was thrown down; and Labaṭa is a man's name taken from this. Iltabaṭa al-faras: the horse gathered its legs together. Iltabaṭa al-rajulu fī amrihi, and talabbaṭa: he became confused and floundered in his affair. A poet said:
One of ample room, and one of confusion - and my mounts, wherever I direct them, are obedient.
لبق:
The letters lām, bā' and qāf are a sound root indicating the mixing of something to make it pleasant. One says labaqtu al-ṭa'ām and labbaqtuhu, when you soften it and make it pleasant.

1. al-labiq - the one skilled and deft at what he does; one says rajulun labiqun and labīqun, and the verbal noun is al-labāqa.

A poet said:
Deft in the turning of the spear-shaft are my fingers.
لبك:
The letters lām, bā' and kāf are a sound root indicating the mixing of one thing with another. One says labaktu 'alā fulānin al-amra albikuhu, when you mix up the matter for him. A man asked al-Ḥasan about something and he did not make it clear, so he said: "labbakta 'alayya" - you have muddled it for me.

1. labaktu al-ṭa'āma bi-'asalin - when you mix food with honey and the like.

A poet said:
To wide bowls of shīzā-wood, brimming - the best of the wheat mixed with honey.

2. mā dhuqtu 'abakatan wa lā labakatan - they say this means a mouthful of ḥays, a dish of dates, butter and dried curd mixed together.
لبن:
The letters lām, bā' and nūn are a sound root from which words branch out; it is milk, the drink.

1. *labintuhu albinuhu* — I gave him milk to drink.
2. *fulānun lābin* — so-and-so has milk on hand, as one says *tāmir* of a man with dates.

Someone said, in a line of verse:
You deceived me, and claimed that you ... had milk in summer and dates.

3. *al-mulbin* — one with abundant milk.
4. *nāqatun labina* — a copiously milking she-camel.
5. When her milk has come down into her udder she is *mulbin*; if she has any milk at all, copious or scant, she is *labūn*.
6. *rajulun malbūn* — a man made foolish from drinking too much milk.
7. The horse called *malbūn* is the one that is favoured with milk, given it before others.

They say, "How many of your sheep give milk (*lubnu ghanamika* and *libnuhā*)" — meaning: how many of them are milk-givers.

Among what strays outside this chapter: *al-laban* is also used for a pain in the neck from a pillow; one says *rajulun labin* when he has that pain. From it comes *al-labina*, a mud brick.

Ibn al-Sikkīt said: one says "he is his brother by his mother's *libān*," and one does not say "by his mother's *laban*" — for *al-laban* is only the drink. But what Ibn al-Sikkīt rejected is not really to be rejected, because that expression is in fact taken from the drunk milk, as though the two of them had nursed together a nursing (*talābanā libānan*), the way one says *taqātalā qitālan*, they fought a fight. It ought to be said that the phrase comes from *al-laban*, only that one does not say "by his mother's *laban*", but "by his mother's *libān*".

Close to this is *al-labān*, the chest, with fatḥa on the lām. *Al-lubān* is frankincense, as though it were a milk that oozes from a tree; the same reasoning applies to it. From it comes *al-lubāna*, meaning a need or want. It may be possible to carry this back to the chapter by some line of reasoning, though it stands closer to what is anomalous.
لت: The letters lām and tāʼ are a single word. One says: latta al-sawīqa bi-l-samni, yaluttuhu lattan, he mixed the roasted-grain meal with clarified butter; the doer is lātt. It was related, on the authority of Ibn al-Aʿrābī: lutta fulānun bi-fulānin, when he was paired with him. If that is sound, it belongs to the category of letter-substitution, as though the tāʼ were substituted for a zāy.
لتأ:
The letters lām, tā' and hamza are one word, if it is sound. They say lata'ahu bi-sahmin, when he shot him with an arrow; and lata'a al-mar'ata: he had intercourse with the woman.

As for allatī, it is the feminine of alladhī. They say al-latayyā is the grave matter; one says waqa'a fī l-latayyā wa-llatī, he fell into dire straits - a saying for a serious predicament. This is something whose derivation has been lost, and no clear pattern for it is known.
لتب: The letters lām, tā' and bā' are one word indicating attachment and close mixing. One says lataba thawbahu: he put on his garment. Al-lātib is the one who clings to a thing and does not part from it. And they say lataba fī sabalati al-nāqa, when he pierced the fine hair beneath the she-camel's chin.
لتج: The letters lām, tā' and jīm are one word. They say al-latjān is the hungry one; and imra'atun latjā is a hungry woman.
لتخ: The letters lām, tā' and khā'. Ibn Durayd said: al-latkh is like al-laṭkh, a smearing or staining. And God knows best.
لتم: The letters lām, tā' and mīm are one word. One says latamahā, when he struck her, stabbing her at the base of her throat with a blade.
لث:
The letters lām and thāʼ are a sound root indicating staying in place and continuing. One says: althatha al-maṭaru, when the rain continued; al-ilthāth is staying on. And lathlatha has the same meaning as althatha.
A poet said, in a line of verse: there is no good in the love of a wavering man. He means the irresolute one in whom there is no good; he is the one who wavers over keeping to love.
1. lathlathtuhu ʿan ḥājatihi — I held him back from his need.
2. talathlatha al-rajulu fī al-daqʿāʼ — the man rolled about in the fine dust.
لثغ: The letters lām, thā' and ghayn. They say al-luthgha, in the tongue, is to turn the rā' into ghayn and the sīn into thā' - a lisp.
لثق: The letters lām, thā' and qāf are a word indicating water or rain wetting a thing. From this is al-lathaq; one says althaqahu al-maṭar, when the rain soaked it.
لثم:
The letters lām, thā' and mīm are a small, sound root indicating one thing knocking against another, or its close pressing against it.

1. lathama al-ba'īru al-ḥijārata bi-khuffihi - the camel struck the stones with its hoof, when it hit them; and khuffun milthamun is a hoof that strikes stones.
2. al-lithām - the cloth with which the lip is covered. Fulānun ḥasanu al-lithma means so-and-so is good in the way he wears it (al-iltithām).
3. khuffun malthūmun - like marthūmun, when it has bled.
4. lathima al-rajulu al-mar'ata - the man kissed the woman.
لثي:
The letters lām, thā' and the weak letter are words indicating the generation of something.

1. al-lathā - a gum or resin.
2. al-lathā - also said for dirt or filth.
3. al-lathā - the treading of the pads of the feet, when there is with it moisture of water or blood.

A poet said:
On it, from the moist tread of their pads, is fresh blood.
لج:
The letters lām and jīm are a sound root indicating the repeated coming of a thing back upon itself, and the repetition of a thing.
1. al-lajāj — persistence in dispute. One says lajja, yalajju; and one also has lajijtu, ʿalā faʿiltu, giving the verbal nouns lajajan and lajājan.
2. lujju al-baḥr — the sea's depths; likewise lujjatuhu, because it surges back upon itself repeatedly. One says iltajja al-baḥru iltijājan, the sea surged. And in the hadith: "whoever takes to the sea when it surges, the [divine] protection is cleared of him." The sword too is called lujj, by way of comparison, as though its matter were magnified and likened to the lujj of the sea; from this too is the hadith of Ṭalḥa: "so they came forward and set the lujj [the sword] against the back of my neck."
3. lajlaja al-rajulu al-muḍghata fī fīhi — the man rolled the morsel about in his mouth, when he turned it over and would not swallow it. Zuhayr said, in a line of verse: he rolls about a morsel in which is raw, unhealed flesh that has festered — and it lies, beneath the flank, a sickness.
4. al-lajlāj — one who stumbles in his speech, not expressing it clearly.
5. al-lajja — clamor. Abū al-Najm said, in a line of verse: in a clamor, hold so-and-so back from so-and-so.
6. They say: in so-and-so's heart is lajāja, that is, it flutters and will not settle, from hunger; this too is from al-lajāj. And al-lajāj said of darkness is its confusion, likened to the surging of the sea. This is also used as a metaphor, so one says ʿaynun multajjah, an eye of intense blackness.
لجأ:
The letters lām, jīm, and hamza are a single word: al-lajaʾ and al-malja' are the place taken refuge in. One says: lajaʾat and iltajaʾat. And he said of al-lajaʾ:
Winter came, and I had not yet made myself a refuge (lajaʾ) — the burning, oh, of my two hands from digging out shelter-holes.
لجب:
The letters lām, jīm and bā' are two very distinct words.

The first is al-lajab: clamor. One says jayshun dhū lajabin, an army with clamor, and baḥrun dhū lajabin, a sea with clamor, when the tumult of its waves is heard.

The other word: 'anzun lajbatun, plural lijāb - a she-goat whose milk has dried up. A poet said:
Our sons marveled at our deed, when we sold horses for goats gone dry.
لجح: The letters lām, jīm and ḥā' are one word. They say al-lujḥ is a low place in the valley.
لجذ: The letters lām, jīm and dhāl. They say lajidha al-kalbu al-inā'a: the dog licked the vessel clean.
لجف:
The letters lām, jīm and fā' are a word indicating a hollow in a thing. One says talajjafati al-bi'r, when its bottom caved in. Al-lajaf is the hollow at the heart of the valley, and a gaping head-wound is likened to it. A poet said:
It drives deep into a wound that reaches the brain, in whose depth is a hollow.
لجم: The letters lām, jīm and mīm are one word: it is al-lijām, the bridle. One says aljamtu al-farasa: I bridled the horse.
لجن:
The letters lām, jīm and nūn are two words. Al-lujayn is silver. Al-lajīn is fodder that is beaten with stones until it becomes matted, as if it had wrinkled. A poet said:
Many a watering place I came to, to reach Arwā - over it the birds were like the matted, beaten fodder.
لح:
The letters lām and ḥāʼ are a sound root indicating persistent attachment and clinging closeness.
1. alaḥḥa ʿalā al-shayʼi ilḥāḥan — he pressed insistently on the thing, when he kept at it without flagging.
2. laḥiḥat ʿaynuhu — his eye became stuck, when it was glued shut. From this comes their saying: huwa ibnu ʿammihi laḥḥan, he is his cousin closely — meaning, close in lineage.
3. al-milḥāḥ — the saddle-pad that bites into the camel's withers.
4. alaḥḥa al-saḥābu — the cloud kept on, when its rain continued. A poet said, of the saddle-pad, in a line of verse: a worn saddle-pad pressed hard upon their shoulders.
5. talaḥlaḥa al-qawmu — the people stayed put, when they remained where they were and did not move on. A poet said, in a line of verse: they stayed by their baggage and settled in place.
6. makānun lāḥḥ — a narrow, cramped place.
7. raḥan milḥāḥ — a millstone that presses hard on what it grinds.
8. alaḥḥa al-jamalu — the camel balked, just as one says of a she-camel that jibs, or a horse that refuses to move — that is, when it would hardly go forward.
لحج:
The letters lām, ḥā' and jīm are a sound root indicating tightness and getting stuck fast. One says laḥija bi'l-makān, when he got stuck there and clung to it.

1. al-malāḥij — the narrow passes.
2. laḥwajtu al-khabar 'alayhi — I mixed the news up and confused it for him, like laḥḥajtuhu, that being to show someone other than what is really in one's mind.
3. al-multaḥaj — the refuge.

Al-Hudhali said, in a line of verse:
[The destitute man's love of inherited wealth — poverty cut it off, and he took no refuge among people.]
لحد: The letters lām, ḥā' and dāl are a root indicating a leaning away from what is straight. One says alḥada al-rajulu, the man turned away from the path of truth and faith. Al-laḥd, the niche grave, is so named because it leans to one side of the grave-pit. One says laḥadtu al-mayyita and alḥadtu, I buried the dead man in a laḥd. Al-multaḥad is a refuge, so named because the one who seeks refuge leans toward it.
لحز:
The letters lām, ḥā' and zā' are a word indicating narrowness in a thing.

1. al-malāḥiz — the narrow passes.
2. talāḥaza al-qawm fī al-qawl — the people wrangled with each other in speech, when they argued fiercely with one another.
3. al-laḥiz — the man of narrow, stingy character.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
You see the tight-fisted miser — when pressure is twisted upon him over his wealth, he is humbled by it.
لحس:
The letters lām, ḥā' and sīn are a word indicating taking something with the tongue. One says laḥisa al-shay' bi-lisānihi laḥsan, he licked the thing with his tongue.

1. alḥasat al-arḍ — the ground put out its first growth. This only happens with the first growth of plants, which the grazing animal cannot yet cut, so that it seems to lick it instead.
2. rajulun milḥasun — a man who takes everything he can get, out of his greed.

In their speech: "aladdu alyasu milḥasun" — stubborn, bold, and grasping.
They say: "Faster than a dog licking its own nose."
They say: "I left so-and-so at the places where the cows lick their young."
لحص:
The letters lām, ḥā' and ṣād are a single word, it is narrowness in a thing. One says laḥiṣa yalḥaṣu laḥaṣan.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
I have been one who goes out and in, a shrewd turner of affairs — the tangled snare of ḥayṣa bayṣa laḥāṣ did not catch me fast.
That is: I was never caught fast in it. And laḥāṣi is of the pattern fa'āli, from the same word.

One says: iltaḥaṣat al-ibra, when the eye of the needle became blocked.
لحظ:
The letters lām, ḥā' and ẓā' are two unrelated words.

Al-laḥẓ is the glance of the eye; its liḥāẓ is its corner nearest the temple.

The other word is al-liḥāẓ: what comes away with the feathers when they are stripped along with the wing.
لحف:
The letters lām, ḥā' and fā' are a root indicating wrapping and clinging.

1. iltaḥafa bi-l-liḥāf, he wrapped himself in the coverlet.
2. lāḥafahu, he clung persistently to him.
3. alḥafa al-sā'il, the beggar was importunate and pressed hard.
لحق:
The letters lām, ḥā' and qāf are a root indicating catching up with something and reaching it, arriving at another.

1. One says: laḥiqa fulānun fulānan — so-and-so caught up with so-and-so, so he is lāḥiq. Alḥaqa has the same meaning.
2. In the supplication: "Indeed Your punishment is overtaking [mulḥiq] the disbelievers" — they said its meaning is lāḥiq.
3. Sometimes they said: laḥiqtuhu — I followed him; and alḥaqtuhu — I reached him.
4. Al-mulḥaq — one falsely claimed as kin, attached to a family not his own.
5. Al-laḥaq, in dates: [a disease that afflicts it].
لحك: The letters lām, ḥā' and kāf are a root indicating fitting together and interlocking. One says: the vertebrae of the she-camel were lūḥika, made to interlock, so it is mulāḥak, when part of it enters into part of it. The same is said of building and construction.
لحم:
The letters lām, ḥā' and mīm are a sound root pointing to things running into one another, like flesh, one part of which runs into another. Of that is al-laḥm, flesh. War was called malḥama for two reasons: one of them is the running of people into one another, their pressing one into another; the other is that the slain are like flesh thrown down.

Al-laḥīm is the slain man. The Hudhalī poet said, in a line of verse:
They said: we left the people hemmed close about him — there is no doubt that there was a slain man there.

Laḥmat al-bāzī is what the hawk is fed when it catches game, and it is also luḥmatuhu. And luḥmat al-thawb, with u, the weft of the cloth, and laḥmatuhu as well. A man is laḥīm when he has much flesh; and lāḥim when he has meat with him, as one says tāmir of a man who has dates. And alḥamtuka 'irḍa fulān, when you give him power over another's honour by reviling him, as though you had made it a piece of flesh for him to eat. And it is said ḥamtu bayna al-shay'ayn and lā'amtu in the same sense. A man is laḥim when he craves meat, and mulḥim when he feeds people meat. Al-shajja al-mutalāḥima is the head wound that has reached the flesh. And standing corn, when the grain has formed in it, is called mulḥim. And it is said laḥamtu al-laḥm 'an al-'aẓm — I stripped the flesh from the bone. And a rope is mulāḥam when it is hard twisted.
لحن:
The letters lām, ḥā' and nūn have two branches: one indicates the tilting of something away from its direction, and the other indicates perceptiveness and intelligence.

As for al-laḥn, with the ḥā' quiescent, it is the tilting of speech away from its correct direction in Arabic. One says laḥana laḥnan. This, to us, is among the words that arose later, for al-laḥn is a new usage that was not found among the pure Arabs who spoke by their sound natural instinct. From this chapter comes their saying: he is ṭayyib al-laḥn, pleasant in tone, and he recites with alḥān, melodic tones — that is because when he recites in that way he shifts the thing from its correct direction by adding or omitting in his intoning. From this too: al-laḥn is the drift and meaning of speech. God Almighty said: {and you will surely know them by the tenor of their speech} [Muḥammad: 30]. This is speech that is disguised, shifted away from directness and plainness.

The other root is al-laḥan, which is perceptiveness. One says laḥina yalḥanu laḥnan; he is laḥin and lāḥin. And in the hadith: "Perhaps some of you may be more astute in presenting his argument than another."
لحي:
The letters lām, ḥā' and the weak letter [yā'] have two sound roots: one is a bodily part, and the other is the peel or bark of something.

The first:
1. al-laḥy — the bone on which the beard grows, in a person or otherwise; the adjective from it is laḥawī.
2. al-liḥya — the hair of the beard, its plural is liḥan, and the plural of al-laḥy is alḥin.

The other root is al-liḥā', the bark of a tree. One says laḥaytu al-'aṣā, when you peeled its bark, and laḥawtuhā. But in the sense of blame, one says laḥḥaytu — the same pattern, as though he means to strip him with words as one strips bark. Al-mulāḥāh is like mutual reviling.

Aws said, on laḥaytu al-'aṣā, in a line of verse:
We stripped them bare as one strips a stick, and drove them off ... to a year whose ticks had not yet swollen with blood.
لخ:
The letters lām and khāʼ are a sound root indicating confusion and mixing. One says sakrānu multakhkh, thoroughly confused with drink, that is, mixed up. Iltakhkha ʿalā al-qawmi amruhum, their affair became tangled and confused for the people; iltakhkha ʿushbu al-arḍi, the land's herbage grew thick and tangled.
1. lakhkhat ʿaynuhu — his eye kept flowing, when its tears did not stop, which happens from old age. A poet said, in a line of verse: and the flow of his eye streamed and welled up.
2. al-lakhlakhāniyya — thickness of foreign accent in speech.
لخج: The letters lām, khā' and jīm. They say: lakhijat 'aynuhu, when it became crusted shut. Al-lakhaj is the worst kind of eye-rheum. This, in my view, does not resemble the speech of the Arabs.
لخص: The letters lām, khā' and ṣād are a single word, it is al-lakhaṣ, which is the flesh of the eyelid. Al-lakhaṣ is for the upper eyelid to be fleshy. A man is alkhaṣ, and an udder is lakhiṣ, when abundant in flesh. Their saying lakhkhaṣtu al-shay', when you made a thing clear, is from this — as if it were the flesh laid bare, once exposed.
لخع: The letters lām, khā' and 'ayn are a single word. Ibn Durayd said: al-lakha' is a slackness in the body.
لخف: The letters lām, khā' and fā' are two words. One is al-likhāf, which are thin white stones, one of them a lakhfa. The other is their saying lakhafahu bi'l-sayf: he struck him with the sword.
لخم: The letters lām, khā' and mīm are a single word, it is lakhm, a tribe from Yemen. Ibn Durayd said: its derivation is from lakhuma wajh al-rajul, when a man's face grew abundant and thick with flesh. He said: this is a dead verb form they scarcely ever use. Al-lukhm is a fish.
لخن: The letters lām, khā' and nūn are a single word, it is al-lakhan, which is a foul smell. One says lakhina al-siqā', when the waterskin turned foul. From it comes their word for a slave woman: lakhnā'.
لخي:
The letters lām, khā' and the weak letter are a sound root indicating crookedness in a thing, and a tilting.

1. al-alkhā — the crooked.
2. al-lakhā — excessive talk in falsehood. One says rajulun alkhā and imra'atun lakhwā'. One also says lakhiya lakhā, in the shortened form.
3. al-lakhw — the description of a loose, slack vulva.
4. 'uqābun lakhwā' — an eagle whose upper beak is longer than its lower.
5. ba'īrun alkhā and nāqatun lakhwā' — a camel one of whose knees is bigger than the other.
6. al-likhā' — incitement, and that is a leaning toward one of two sides. One says lakhayta bī 'indahu, when he incited someone against you, as if he leaned toward you against you.
7. al-milkhā — the snuff-tube, so named because it sits on one of the two sides of the nose.
8. likhā' — the child's morning meal, which is bread soaked in liquid.
لد:
The letters lām and dāl are two sound roots: one indicates contention, and the other indicates a side or a flank.
For the first:
1. al-ladad — intensity of quarreling. One says rajulun aladdu and qawmun luddun. God Most High said: {and warn thereby a people given to fierce contention} [Maryam: 97].
2. al-ladīdān — the two sides and flat surfaces of the neck.
3. ladīdā al-wādī — the two sides of the valley; and from this one says taladdada, when he turned right and left, bewildered.
4. al-ladūd — medicine poured into one side of a person's mouth. One has ludda, and iltadadtu, I had it poured into my own mouth. Ibn Aḥmar said: I drank the shukāʿā herb, and had the medicine poured into the side of my mouth, and I turned to the mouths of the veins that had been cauterized.
5. Their saying: mā ajidu dūna hādhā al-amri muḥtaddan wa-lā multaddan — I find no turning-place from this matter, meaning: I find no way to swerve from it; and when one swerves from a thing, he comes to be on a side of it.
6. mā ziltu ulāddu ʿanka — I kept on warding off from you, meaning, defending, as though turning evil away to one side, off you.
And straying from this chapter: al-ladd is said to be the large sack, so they said, and they cited, in verse: as though its two sacks lay on the flank of a mountain. It could also be said to belong to this root, because it lies at the side of the thing loaded with it, when the two loads are a matched pair.
لدس:
The letters lām, dāl and sīn are words indicating one thing sticking to another until it takes from it. One says ladasa al-māl al-nabāt, that is, it grazed it.

1. al-ladīs — what first shoots up of a plant, so called because livestock graze it.
2. ludisat al-nāqa — the she-camel put on flesh, as if the fatness, once it clung to her, were like one thing sticking to another.
3. ladastu al-ba'īr — I shod the camel, fitted its foot-pad.
4. al-malādis — the strong stallions, because each of them is worn against the other, chafed.

And God knows best what is correct.
لدغ: The letters lām, dāl and ghayn are a single word. One says ludigha yuldaghu, he is maldūgh and ladīgh, stung, in two forms. Ladaghtuhu bi-kalimatin, when you provoked him with a word.
لدم:
The letters lām, dāl and mīm are a root indicating attaching one thing to another, whether by striking or otherwise. Al-ladm is the striking of stone against stone.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And the heart has a throbbing beneath its great artery — like a boy's striking, out of sight, with a stone.

1. iltadama al-nisā' — the women struck their faces and chests in mourning.
2. al-ladm — your beating of bread baked in hot ashes, to knock the dust off it.
3. al-malādīm — the stones used to crack open date-pits.
4. iltadamat 'alayhi al-ḥummā — the fever clung to him persistently; that is why fever is called umm mildam, the mother of persistent striking.
5. al-muladdam — among men, the fool.

The lām in this word is substituted from a rā', as if the man had become worn through and then patched up, that is, mended.
لدن: The letters lām, dāl and nūn are a single word. A supple twig is called ladn. And ladun means the same as ladā — that is, at, with, in the presence of.
لذ: The letters lām and dhāl are one sound root indicating pleasant taste in a thing. From this: al-ladhdha and al-ladhādha, the pleasant taste of a thing. He said: [words missing here in the source]. And al-ladhdh is sleep, in his saying: and a sleep [ladhdh] like the taste of ṣarkhadī wine. Al-Farrāʼ said: rajulun ladhdh, a man pleasant in conversation.
لذع:
The letters lām, dhāl and 'ayn indicate a single root, it is burning and heat.

1. al-ladh' — the burning of fire, its scorching of a thing. This is used as a metaphor: one says ladha'tuhu bi-lisānī, when you hurt him a little with your tongue.
2. jā'a fulānun yatalaadha'u — so-and-so came looking about right and left, as if something were troubling and burning him.
3. al-lawdha'iyy — the clever, witty man, as if from his quickness and shrewdness he burns.
4. iltadha'at al-qarḥa — the sore gave off its smell, because it burns itself and stings the one who has it.
لذم:
The letters lām, dhāl and mīm are a word indicating one thing's clinging to another. One says ladhimtu al-rajul ladhman: I clung to the man.

1. al-mulzam — the man infatuated with a thing.

Al-Hudhali said, in a line of verse —
لز:
The letters lām and zāʼ are a sound root indicating clinging attachment and adhesion.
1. lazza bihi — he clung to it, when he stuck fast to it; [verbal nouns] lazzan and lazāzan.
2. lāzaztuhu — I clung close to him.
3. rajulun lazāzu khaṣmin — a man who is a tenacious adversary, when he clings to his opponent and does not shrink back from him.
4. al-mulazzaz — one compact and firm in build.
5. al-lazz — thrusting with a spear; this too follows the pattern of the root.
6. al-lazāʼiz — the flesh gathered at the breast, next to the shoulder-blade. A poet said, in a line of verse: one whose elbow stands clear of the lazāʼiz.
And of this chapter: kazzun lazzun; and it is possible that lazz here is merely an echoing word with no meaning of its own.
لزأ: The letters lām, zā' and hamza are two words, which may perhaps both be sound. They say lazza'a al-ibil talzi'atan, when he tended their grazing well. And they say: "God curse a mother who lazza'at with him," that is, who bore him.
لزب:
The letters lām, zā' and bā' indicate a thing's fixedness and its clinging. One says of what clings: lāzib. And this thing became ḍarbata lāzib, meaning it hardly ever parts. Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
They do not think good comes without evil after it ... nor do they think evil is something fixed and lasting.

Al-lazba is a hard year of drought, plural lazbāt, as though the drought had lazaba in it, that is, become fixed there.
لزج: The letters lām, zā' and jīm are close to the chapter before it. One says lazija bihi, when he stuck to it and clung to it. Al-talazzuj is following after scarce herbs and scanty grazing.
لزق: The letters lām, zā' and qāf are not a root, because it belongs to the chapter of letter-substitution. One says lazika al-shay' bi'l-shay' yalzaqu, like laṣiqa.
لزك: The letters lām, zā' and kāf are not, in my view, anything. Yet they say lazika al-jurḥ, when the flesh of a wound grew back evenly but had not yet healed. This does not resemble the speech of the Arabs.
لزم: The letters lām, zā' and mīm are a single sound root indicating one thing's constant attachment to another. It is said: "lazimahu l-shay'u, yalzamuhu" — the thing clung to him permanently. Al-lizām: the punishment that clings permanently to the unbelievers.
لزن:
The letters lām, zā' and nūn indicate narrowness or crowding in a thing. One says 'aysh lazn, that is, straitened. Al-lazan is people gathering crowded together at a well. One says mashrab lazn, when it is crowded upon.

And God knows best what is correct.
لس: The letters lām and sīn are a minor root indicating the licking of a thing. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: al-lass is licking. One says: alassat al-arḍu, when its first plants sprouted up; he said: it is named so because livestock lick it. And lassat al-dābbatu al-khalā bi-lisānihā, talussuhu lassan — the animal licked up the fresh green pasture with its tongue. A poet said, in a line of verse: its muzzle has grown green from licking the fresh young growth. That plant is also called al-lusās. A poet said, in a line of verse: among the low shrubs of al-rimth, and among the lusās.
لسب: The letters lām, sīn and bā' are a root indicating one thing striking another sharply. One says lasabat-hu al-'aqrab, the scorpion stung him. Lasibtu al-'asal, when you licked it up. The pattern is the same for both, and they are told apart only by their vowelling. Abū Zayd said: lasabahu aswāṭan, he struck him with whips. And they say, though this is unrelated: al-lasb is gathering. One also says lasiba bi'l-shay', when it stuck, and that belongs to the first sense.
لسد: The letters lām, sīn and dāl. They say: lasada al-'asal, he licked the honey.
لسع: The letters lām, sīn and 'ayn are a single word. One says lasa'athu al-ḥayya talsa'uhu las'an, the snake stung him. Used as a metaphor: lasa'ahu bi-lisānihi, he stung him with his tongue.
لسق:
The letters lām, sīn and qāf are not a root; its true root has ṣād. Al-lasaq is a twisting pain in the belly. When the lung sticks to the ribcage, one says lasiqa lasaqan. The true form is laṣiqa.

Ru'ba said:
