And the coolness of the water wetted the upper arms of the one gripped by lasaq.
لسم: The letters lām, sīn and mīm are not a root. They say, in the chapter of letter-substitution: alsamtu al-rajula al-ḥujjata: I made the argument binding on the man. Wa alsamtuhu al-ṭarīqa: I made him keep to the road.
لسن:
The letters lām, sīn and nūn are a single sound root pointing to a fine length that does not stick out, in a limb or in something else. Of that is al-lisān, the tongue, which is well known; it is masculine, and the plural is alsun; and when they are many, then they are al-alsina. And one says lasantuhu, when you take him on with your tongue. Tarafa said, in a line of verse:
And when their tongues lash at me, I am no feeble, ignorant man.

And the tongue may be spoken of by way of a message, and then it is made feminine. A poet said, in a line of verse:
There came to me a word I take no joy in, from on high; there is no wonder in it and no jest.

And al-lasan is excellence of tongue and eloquence. And al-lisn is a language; one says: every people has a lisn, that is, a tongue. And some people read: And We sent no messenger but with the lisn of his people. And a sandal that is mulassana is one shaped like a tongue. Kuthayyir said, in a line of verse:
They have wrappers with red borders, which they tread with their feet in the tongue-shaped Hadramī sandals.

And they say: al-malsūn is the liar. And this is taken from the tongue, because when he is known for that he is lusina, that is, tongues have spoken about him, as he said:
And when their tongues lash at me.

And al-talsīn is that a man lend [another man] a young camel so that his she-camel may give milk for it; and when she gives milk the young camel is taken away. And its meaning is that it has tasted the milk with its tongue. And a foot that is mulassana is one that has in it fineness and a slight length.
لص:
The letters lām and ṣād are a minor sound root indicating close clinging and closeness.
1. al-laṣaṣ — the closeness of the two shoulders, so near they almost touch the ears.
2. al-alaṣṣ — also, one whose teeth are set close together.
3. luṣṣiṣa al-bunyānu — the building was tightly packed, like ruṣṣiṣa.
4. It is said a narrow forehead is called al-laṣṣāʼ.
5. al-laṣṣāʼ, of sheep — one whose horn has turned forward onto the face.
6. al-liṣṣ — the thief, named from this, because he sticks close to the thing he means to take. His practice is al-luṣūṣiyya, with the lām opened. One says arḍun malaṣṣa, a land abounding in thieves.
لصب:
The letters lām, ṣād and bā' are a sound root indicating narrowness and constriction.

1. *al-liṣb* — the narrow part of a valley, a defile.
2. *laṣiba al-jild bi'l-laḥm yalṣab* — the skin clings to the flesh, when it sticks fast to it.
3. *fulān laḥiz laṣib* — so-and-so scarcely gives anything away; a miser.
4. *laṣiba al-khātam fī al-iṣbaʿ* — the ring clings tight on the finger; the opposite of *qaliq*, loose.
5. *al-lawāṣib* — narrow wells, deep at the bottom.

Kuthayyir said, in a line of verse:
Deep narrow wells that have dried up and closed in on themselves — the tribe has long since kept its distance from them.
لصغ: The letters lām, ṣād and ghayn are not anything. Yet they say laṣagha al-jild, the skin dried onto the bone from emaciation.
لصف:
The letters lām, ṣād and fā' are a word indicating dryness and gleam. One says laṣifa jildahu laṣafan, when it stuck and dried. Laṣafa yalṣufu, when it gleamed.

What is not from this is al-laṣaf: something that grows at the roots of the caper plant, resembling a cucumber. And Laṣāfi is a mountain.
لصق:
The letters lām, ṣād and qāf are a sound root indicating a thing's clinging to another thing. One says *laṣiqa bihi yalṣaqu luṣūqan* — it clung to it.

1. *al-mulṣaq* — a person falsely attached to a lineage, a claimed son who is not truly one.
2. *fulān bi-liṣqi al-ḥā'iṭ wa bi-lizqihi* — so-and-so is right up against the wall; *liṣq* and *lizq* both mean immediately beside something.
3. *al-laṣaq* in the camel — like *al-lasaq*, an ailment we explained in the line of Ru'ba's poetry.
لض: The letters lām and ḍād — al-Khalīl mentioned that al-liḍlāḍ is the guide. He said: his liḍlāḍa is his looking about and being watchful.
لط:
The letters lām and ṭāʼ are a minor sound root indicating closeness, clinging attachment, and pressing insistence.
1. alaṭṭa al-rajulu — the man pressed hard, when he grew intense over a matter.
2. laṭṭa bihi — he clung to it, stayed attached to it; and anything covered over by another thing is said to be "luṭṭa" by it.
3. laṭṭat al-nāqatu bi-dhanabihā — the she-camel pressed her tail down, when she put it between her thighs as she walked.
4. al-laṭṭ — a necklace of colocynth fruit, named laṭṭ because it clings close to the throat-hollow. Its plural is liṭāṭ.
5. al-liṭāṭ — the edge of a mountain.
6. milṭāṭ of the camel — the ridge in the middle of its head.
7. al-milṭāṭ — the rim of a valley. All of these are so named because each clings close and does not part from what it belongs to.
8. al-liṭliṭ — the very old woman, because she clings to her place and hardly ever leaves it.
لطا:
The letters lām, ṭā' and the weak letter are a single word: *al-milṭāt*, used of head-wounds — it is the *simḥāq* [the layer covering the skull] once it has reached the thin outer skin. Abū ʿUbayd said: al-Wāqidī told me that among them *al-simḥāq* is called *al-milṭā'*. Abū ʿUbayd said: it is also said *al-milṭāt*, with the hā'; if so, then by its form it ends in a shortened alif.

And concerning the hadith that came, 'Truly *al-milṭāt* [is judged] by its blood' — its meaning is: when its owner is wounded, its extent is taken at that hour, and judgment is then given on it, whether retaliation or compensation, with no regard to what happens to it afterward of increase or decrease. He said: this is their view, and not the view of the people of Iraq.

1. *al-laṭāt* — a circular mark on the forehead of a horse.

And if hamzated one says *laṭi'tu alṭa'u*.
لطح: The letters lām, ṭā' and ḥā' are a single word. *al-laṭḥ* is striking with the flat of the hand, not hard. In the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās: 'He began tapping our thighs, saying, my little sons, do not stone the Jamra of al-ʿAqaba until the sun rises.'
لطخ:
The letters lām, ṭā' and khā' are a small sound root indicating the smearing of one thing with another.

1. *laṭakhtu al-shay' bi'l-shay'* — I smeared the thing with the thing.
2. *sakrān mulṭakhkh* — thoroughly drunk, meaning muddled.
3. *fī al-samā' laṭkh min al-saḥāb* — there is a smear of cloud in the sky, meaning a little.
4. *luṭikha fulān bi-shay'* — so-and-so was smeared with something, meaning he was blemished by it. Ibn Duraid said: 'he is smeared with evil,' and 'smeared in reputation.'

God knows best what is correct.
لطع:
The letters lām, ṭā' and ʿayn are a sound root indicating the uncovering of one thing from another, and revealing it. One says *laṭaʿa al-insān al-shay' bi-lisānihi yalṭaʿuhu*, when he licked it.

1. *al-laṭaʿ* — whiteness on the inside of the lip, which is the dark colour of the lip being uncovered from it; this occurs mostly among Black people. Ibn Duraid said, quoting a line: 'An old woman, white-gummed, whose teeth have fallen out.'
2. *al-laṭʿā'* — also a woman with little flesh on the vulva.
لطف:
The letters lam, ta and fa are a root indicating gentleness, and also indicating smallness in a thing. Al-lutf is gentleness in action; one says 'huwa latifun bi-'ibadihi' — He [God] is gentle with His servants, that is, compassionate and kind.

From this root: al-iltaf for a camel — when it does not find [by itself] the place of mating, and it is gently guided to it.
لطم:
The letters lām, ṭā' and mīm are a sound root indicating one thing pressing against another, by a blow or otherwise.

1. *al-laṭm* — striking on the face with the flat of the palm; one says *laṭamahu yalṭimuhu*.
2. *iltaṭamat al-amwāj* — the waves clashed, when they struck one another.
3. *al-laṭīm* of horses — the one whose cheeks are taken by whiteness; some say it is when the whiteness is on one side only of its face, as though it had been struck with that whiteness.
4. *al-laṭīm* — the weaned camel-calf: when the star Suhayl rises, the herdsman takes it and says, 'Do you see Suhayl? By God you shall not taste a drop from me again' — then he strikes it and drives it away, cutting it off from the milk.
5. *al-laṭīm* — also the ninth of the racing horses, as though it had been struck back from taking the lead.
6. *al-mulaṭṭam* — the base, ignoble man, as though he had been struck until turned away from noble deeds.
7. *al-milṭam* — a hide spread beneath the travel-bag so that dust does not reach it. A poet said, in a line of verse (obscure, sense uncertain): 'the tear of al-Muʿayyith, in the leather of the milṭam.'

As for *al-laṭīma*: it is said to mean the market — every market, they said, that is not for grain-trading. Others said *al-laṭīma* is [a load] of perfume. Some said it is derived from *al-laṭm*, because the perfume called *al-ghāliya* is sold there, and it is said to be 'struck' because it is pounded when mixed.
لظ: The letters lām and ẓāʼ are a sound root indicating close attachment. One says: alaẓẓa al-rajulu bi-l-shayʼi, when he kept closely to it. And in the hadith: "keep closely to saying, 'O Possessor of Majesty and Honor'" — meaning, hold fast to this and say it often in your prayers. And one says: alaẓẓa al-maṭaru, the rain continued steadily. They also say: al-ilẓāẓ is anxious concern for a thing; and that is not far in pattern from this root.
لع:
The letters lām and ʿayn are a minor sound root indicating quivering and flickering.
1. al-laʿlaʿ — the mirage; laʿlaʿatuhu is its flickering.
2. talaʿlaʿa al-shayʼu — the thing quivered until it broke apart.
3. laʿlaʿa al-kalbu — the dog let its tongue loll out.
4. imraʼatun laʿʿah — a light, agile woman.
5. talaʿlaʿa min al-jūʿi — he writhed from hunger.
6. al-laʿāʿa — a tender, soft herb.
7. alaʿʿati al-arḍu — the land grew the laʿāʿ herb; talaʿʿaytu, I gathered the laʿāʿ. This last word is anomalous.
لعب:
The letters lām, 'ayn and bā' are two words, and from them words branch out.

One of the two is al-la'ib, play, which is well known. Al-til'āba is one who plays a great deal. Al-mal'ab is the place of play. Al-li'ba is a kind or manner of play. Al-la'ba is a single instance of it, except that they say li-man al-lu'ba — whose turn is the game? And mulā'ib ẓillihi, the one that plays with its own shadow, is a bird.

The other word is al-lu'āb, what runs from a child's mouth. La'aba al-ghulām yal'abu means the boy's spittle ran. Lu'āb al-naḥl, the spittle of bees, is honey. Lu'āb al-shams, the spittle of the sun, is the mirage; and it is said that it is that which is like a spider's weaving. And it is said that the root of the chapter is going along without keeping straight.
لعج:
The letters lām, ʿayn and jīm are a single root: heat in the heart.

1. *al-laʿj* — the heat of love in the heart; one says *laʿaja yalʿaju*.
2. *laʿaja al-ḍarb al-jild* — Abū ʿUbayd said: the blow burned the skin. Al-Hudhalī said, in a line of verse (sense uncertain in part): 'When the mourning-woman bares herself, two rise up with her, striking a painful blow with a leather strap that burns the skin.'
3. *laʿajahu al-amr* — the matter became severe upon him.
لعس:
The letters lām, ʿayn and sīn are two distinct words.

The first:
1. *al-laʿas* — blackness on the inside of the lip; a woman so marked is *laʿsā'*.
2. *nabāt alʿas* — a plant described as abundant, because from its lushness it verges toward black.

The second:
3. *al-laʿwas* — the greedy eater; the wolf is described *laʿwas*. Al-Khalīl said: a man who is *mutalaʿʿis* eats voraciously.
لعص:
The letters lām, ʿayn and ṣād. They say:

1. *al-laʿaṣ* — hardship, difficulty.
2. *fulān talaʿʿaṣa ʿalaynā* — so-and-so grew obstinate and difficult with us.
3. *al-laʿaṣ* — also greed in eating.
لعط:
The letters lām, ʿayn and ṭā'. Its sound sense is a shade among colours. Ibn Duraid said:

1. *al-luʿṭa* — a black stripe or line; and *laʿṭat al-ṣaqr* is the dark patch on a falcon's face.
2. *al-luʿṭa* — also blackness in the neck of a sheep.
3. *laʿaṭahu bi-ḥaqqihi* — mentioned by some as meaning he warded him off with his claim on him (sense uncertain).
4. *marra fulānun lāʿiṭan* — so-and-so passed by, meaning he passed alongside, next to a wall.
لعق:
The letters lām, ʿayn and qāf are a root indicating the licking of a thing with a finger or otherwise. One says *laʿiqtu al-shay' alʿaquhu* — I licked the thing.

1. *laʿaqat al-dam* — a group who swore a pact for war, then slaughtered a camel and licked its blood.
2. *al-laʿūq* — the name for what is licked.
3. *al-luʿqa* — what the spoon takes up, a spoonful.
4. *al-laʿqa* — a single lick.
5. *al-laʿwaqa* — the quickness of a person in whatever work he takes up, with lightness and impetuosity.
6. *rajul laʿwaq* — a light, flighty man, as though likened to a single lick for its quickness and lightness.

Some said: one says 'there is not a lick's-worth of spring grazing on the ground' — meaning except in the moist plants that the livestock lick up.

7. *laʿiqa fulān iṣbaʿahu* — so-and-so licked his finger, said when he died.
8. *al-laʿūq* — also the least of one's provisions; one says 'we have with us only a lick's-worth.'
9. *al-milʿaqa* — what one licks with, the spoon.
10. *al-luʿāq* — Al-Khalīl said this is what remains in the mouth, a remnant of what was swallowed.
لعن:
The letters lām, ʿayn and nūn are a sound root pointing to driving away and putting far off. Laʿana Allāh al-shayṭān - God cursed Satan: He put him far from good and from the Garden. A wolf is called laʿīn, and the outcast man is laʿīn. And rajul luʿna, with a sukūn, is one whom people curse, [and luʿana] is one who curses much. Al-liʿān is the mutual cursing of two. And he said of the outcast, in a line of verse:
I startled the sand-grouse with him, and I drove from him the place of the wolf, like the outcast man.
لعو:
The letters lām, ʿayn and the weak letter are words that do not go back to one single meaning.

1. *al-kalba al-laʿwa* — the greedy bitch.
2. *al-rajul al-laʿw* — the man of bad character.
3. *al-luʿwa* — the blackness around the nipple.
4. *talaʿʿā al-ʿasal* — the honey thickened, congealed.
5. *laʿā laka* — said to one who stumbles, a call for him to rise up again.
6. *mā bihā lāʿī qarw* — there is no one there at all, meaning not even someone to lick out a bowl.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
A sturdy, powerful [she-camel] — if she stumbles, misfortune itself is nearer to her than that I should say 'rise up.'
لغ: The letters lām and ghayn. Some of them mentioned: laghlagha ṭaʿāmahu, he soaked his food thoroughly with fat.
لغب:
The letters lām, ghayn and bā' are one single sound root, indicating weakness and fatigue. One says *rajulun laghbun bayyinu l-laghāba wal-lughūba* — a man plainly weak and worn out.

Al-Aṣma'ī said: Abū 'Amr said: I heard a bedouin say, "So-and-so is *laghūb*: my letter (*kitābī*) came to him and he made light of it." I said: do you say "my *kitābī* came to him"? He said: is it not a sheet (*ṣaḥīfa*, feminine)? I said: what is *al-laghūb*? He said: the fool.

And Ta'abbaṭa Sharran spoke concerning *al-laghb*, in a line of verse:
My mother did not bear, among this people, a weak one ... nor was my feather from the tail-feathers, nor from *laghb*.

Abū Bakr said: an arrow is *laghb* when its feathers are all cut from the belly-side of the bird, and this is a poor arrow. A poet, describing a man who sought a thing and did not attain it, said:
So he got away, and they fitted him out with poor feathers (*laghb*).

*Al-lughūb* is fatigue, exhaustion and hardship. "He came *sāghiban lāghiban*" — hungry and worn out. God, exalted is He, said: {and no weariness (*lughūb*) touched us} [Qāf: 38].
لغد:
The letters lām, ghayn and dāl are a single word.

1. *al-laghādīd* — fleshy folds at the back of the mouth and throat; singular *lughdūd*, also said *lughd*, plural *alghād*.
2. *jā'a fulānun mutalaghghidan* — so-and-so came enraged, as though the anger had reached his throat-flesh.
لغز:
The letters lām, ghayn and zāy are a root indicating a twisting in a thing, and a turning away.

1. *al-lughz* — your turning a thing away from its true direction.
2. *al-lughayzā'* (in the extended form) — the jerboa digging, then veering off in its digging to confuse whoever hunts for it.
3. *al-alghāz* — paths that twist and confuse the one travelling them; singular *laghaz* and *lughz*.
4. *alghaza fulānun fī kalāmihi* — so-and-so spoke in riddles. In the hadith of ʿUmar: he forbade speaking in riddles [*al-lughayzā*] within an oath.
لغم:
The letters lām, ghayn and mīm are a single sound word: *al-malāghim* — what is around the mouth.

1. *talaghghamtu bi'l-ṭīb* — I put perfume there [around the mouth]. Ibn Duraid said: *talaghghama bi'l-ṭīb* means he smeared himself with it.

As for their saying *laghamtu alghamu laghman*, when you tell your companion something he is not certain of — that comes from letter-substitution; it is really *naghamtu*, with a nūn.

2. *laghama al-baʿīr lughāmahu* — Al-Khalīl said: the camel spat out its foam.
لغو:
The letters lām, ghayn and the weak letter are two sound roots: one of them points to the thing that is not counted, and the other to being taken up with a thing and always on about it.

The first is *al-laghw*: what is not counted, of the young of camels, in the blood-price. Al-ʿAbdī said, in a line of verse:
Or a hundred whose young are made no account of, and the pick of the hundred, the hard sturdy ones.
From it one says *laghā yalghū laghwan*. And that is in the *laghw* of oaths. And *al-laghā* is the very same as *al-laghw*. God, exalted, said: {God will not take you to task for the laghw in your oaths} [al-Baqara: 225], that is, for what you did not tie fast with your hearts. The jurists say: it is a man's saying "No, by God" and "Yes indeed, by God." And some people say: it is a man's saying, of a shape coming toward him, "By God, this is so-and-so" — thinking it is he — and then it is not as he thought. They said: his oath is *laghw*, because he did not mean to lie.

The second is their saying *laghiya bi-l-amr*, when he is taken up with it and always on about it. And it is said that the derivation of *al-lugha*, a language, is from this — that is, the one who has it is always on about it.
لف:
The letters lām and fāʼ are a sound root indicating the winding of one thing upon another. One says: lafaftu al-shayʼa bi-l-shayʼi laffan, I wound the thing around the thing. And lafaftu ʿimāmatī ʿalā raʼsī, I wound my turban about my head.
1. Their saying: jāʼa al-qawmu wa-man laffa laffahum — the people came, and whoever wound their winding, meaning whoever attached himself to them, as though he had wound himself in with them. Al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse: Qays, and whoever wound their winding, filled Nubāk, then Qaww, then al-Rajā, then al-Nawāʿiṣ.
2. One says of the tongue-tied man: alaff, as though his tongue had become wound up; and "in his tongue is lafaf."
3. al-alfāf — trees that grow winding, entangled one with another. God Most High said: {and luxuriant gardens} [al-Nabaʼ: 16].
4. al-alaff — one whose thighs draw close together from his fatness, as though wound about each other; this is al-lafaf. A poet said, in a line of verse: the broad-rumped sandgrouse, their haunches close-wound together — and the thighs, wound as they are, do not fail to bear a hobbling-cord.
5. One also calls the heavy, slow man alaff.
6. al-lafīf — a gathering of people out of scattered tribes.
7. alaffa al-rajulu raʼsahu fī thiyābihi — the man wound his head into his garments; alaffa al-ṭāʼiru raʼsahu taḥta janāḥihi — the bird tucked its head beneath its wing.
8. Some of them related: fī al-arḍi talāfīfu min ʿushbin, in the land are winding patches of herbage.
9. laffaftuhu ḥaqqahu — I withheld his due from him.
لفا:
The letters lām, fā' and the weak letter are a sound root indicating the uncovering and revealing of a thing; it occurs both with and without a hamza.

1. *lafa'at al-rīḥ al-saḥāb ʿan wajh al-samā'* — the wind uncovered the clouds from the face of the sky.
2. *lafa'tu al-laḥm ʿan al-ʿaẓm* — I stripped the meat off the bone, scraped it off; also said *lafawtuhu*, both forms related by Abū Bakr.
3. *al-laffā'* — dust and litter on the face of the earth. A proverb says: 'he was content, instead of full payment, with scraps' — meaning he accepted a little in place of his full due.
4. *alfaytuhu* — I met him and found him, verbal noun *ilfā'*.
5. *talāfaytuhu* — I made up for it, caught up with it in time.
لفت:
The letters lām, fāʾ, and tāʾ are a single word pointing to twisting a thing and turning it away from its straight course. From it: lafattu al-shayʾa, I twisted it; lafattu fulānan ʿan raʾyihi, I turned him away from his opinion. Al-alfat is the left-handed man, and this follows the chapter's reasoning.

Al-lafīta is the thick kind of gruel, because it is lafat, twisted/stirred about. A woman is lafūt when she has a husband and also a child by another man, so that she keeps turning toward her child. From this is al-iltifāt, turning your face aside, and likewise al-talaffut. Abū Bakr said: lafattu al-liḥāʾ min al-shajara, I stripped the bark from the tree.
لفج:
The letters lām, fā' and jīm are a single word.

1. *al-mulfaj*, with a fatḥa on the fā' — the poor, destitute man; the past tense of its verb is *alfaja*. It is among rare words.

A verse was cited: 'A girl who grew up tender and youthful, in the lap of one who was never stingy toward her' (sense of the second half uncertain). It was also related, raised to the Prophet in one hadith: 'May a man fondle a woman? He said: Yes, if he is *mulfaj*' — but the sound view is that this saying belongs to al-Ḥasan, not to a hadith.
لفح: The letters lām, fā' and ḥā' are a single word. One says lafaḥathu al-nār bi-ḥarrihā, the fire scorched him with its heat, and likewise the samūm, the hot wind, when its heat struck someone and changed his face. As for their saying lafaḥahu bi-l-sayf lafḥatan, he struck him with the sword a light blow — the root of that is actually with nūn, it is nafaḥahu.
لفظ:
The letters lām, fā' and ẓā' are a sound word indicating the casting out of something, and mostly that is from the mouth. You say lafaẓa bi-l-kalām yalfiẓu lafẓan, he uttered speech, and lafaẓtu al-shay'a min famī, I ejected the thing from my mouth. Al-lāfiẓa is the rooster, and it is also said of the millstone, and the sea. On that is explained his saying, in a line of verse:
As for the one whose bounty is hoped for ... it is more generous in giving than al-lāfiẓa.

It is something malfūẓ and lafīẓ — cast out, uttered.
لفع:
The letters lām, fā' and ʿayn are a small sound root indicating the wrapping and enveloping of a thing.

1. *talaffaʿat al-mar'a bi-mirṭihā* — the woman wrapped herself in her mantle.
2. *laffaʿa al-shayb ra'sahu* — grey hair enveloped his head.
3. *talaffaʿa al-shajar* — the trees clothed themselves, covered themselves in green.
4. *iltafaʿat al-arḍ bi'l-nabāt* — the earth wrapped itself in plants, turned green.
5. *lafaʿtu al-mizāda* — I turned the water-skin over, and put its spouts in the middle.
لفق:
The letters lām, fā' and qāf are a small sound root indicating the fitting together of a matter.

1. *lafaqtu al-thawb bi'l-thawb lafqan* — I fitted the garment together with the garment.
2. *hādhā lifqu hādhā* — this matches that.
3. *talāfaqa amruhum* — their affair became harmonious.
لفك: The letters lām, fā' and kāf. They say: *al-alfak* is the fool, the stupid man.
لفم:
The letters lām, fā' and mīm are a single word.

1. *al-lifām* — the part of the face-veil that reaches the tip of the nose.
2. *talaffamat al-mar'a* — the woman pulled her veil back up over her mouth.
لق:
The letters lām and qāf are a sound root indicating shouting and clamor.
1. al-laqlaqa — shouting; likewise al-laqlāq.
2. al-laqlaq — the tongue. In the hadith: "whoever is guarded against the evil of his laqlaq, his qabqab, and his dhabdhab" — that is, his tongue, his belly, and his private parts — "is guarded against the whole mischief of youth."
3. laqqa ʿaynahu — he struck his eye with his hand, perhaps named so for the sound heard at the blow.
As for al-laqlaqa, it is also used for restlessness, close to the reversed form, as though it were muqalqal — that which does not settle in its place. Imruʼ al-Qays said, in a line of verse: with a glance restlessly darting.
لقب: The letters lām, qāf and bā' are a single word. Al-laqab is al-nabz, a nickname — one and the same thing. Laqqabtuhu talqīban, I gave him a nickname. God Almighty said: {and do not taunt one another with nicknames} [al-Ḥujurāt: 11].
لقح:
The letters lām, qāf and ḥā' are a sound root indicating the impregnation of a female by a male, and then what resembles it is measured against it.

1. liqāḥ al-na'am wa-l-shajar — the impregnating of livestock and of trees. As for livestock, their males impregnate them; as for trees, the winds impregnate them.
2. rīyāḥ lawāqiḥ — winds that impregnate the clouds with water, and impregnate the trees. The origin of lawāqiḥ is mulqiḥa, but they do not impregnate unless they are themselves already lawāqiḥ; the singular is lāqiḥa — this is also what the exegetes say.
3. laqiḥat al-nāqa talqaḥu laqḥan wa-liqāḥan — the she-camel became pregnant; the she-camel is lāqiḥ and laqūḥ.
4. al-laqḥa — a she-camel that is milked, plural liqāḥ and luquḥ.
5. al-malāqiḥ — the females carrying their young in their bellies. Abū Bakr said al-malāqīḥ is also said, though no singular of it was used; al-malāqiḥ are those young that are in the wombs.

Anomalous in this chapter: a people called laqāḥ, with fatḥa on the lām, when they submit to no king and no ruler holds power over them.
لقس:
The letters lām, qāf and sīn are a word indicating an unpleasing trait.

1. *laqisat nafsuhu min al-shay'* — his soul turned in disgust at the thing.
2. *al-laqis* — the man of bad character, greedy and grasping; *al-laqas* is its verbal noun.
3. *al-lāqis* — the faultfinder.
4. *laqastu al-rajul alqusuhu* — I found fault with the man, criticised him.
لقص:
The letters lām, qāf and ṣād are close in meaning to the one before it.

1. *laqiṣa laqaṣan, wa huwa laqiṣ* — he was narrow-tempered, ill-natured.
2. *iltaqaṣa al-shay'* — he seized the thing, taking it up eagerly and greedily.

A line of verse was cited (sense uncertain in part): 'And one who eagerly snatches up what is lost of our slaughtered stock — perhaps the one who gave him respite will yet punish him.'

3. *alqaṣahu al-ḥarr* — sometimes said of the heat: it burned him.
لقط:
The letters lām, qāf and ṭā' are a sound root indicating taking up from the ground something you have suddenly caught sight of and had not sought out, though it may also come by intention and purpose.

1. *laqṭ al-ḥaṣā* — picking up pebbles, and the like.
2. *al-luqṭa* — what a person picks up of lost property.
3. *al-laqīṭ* — the foundling, the abandoned child who is picked up.

Banū al-Laqīṭa were a clan of the Arabs, named so because their mother had been picked up by Ḥudhayfa ibn Badr among a group of slave-girls whom a year of drought had harmed; he took her in, and then, being taken with her, asked her father for her and married her.

4. *al-laqaṭ*, with fatḥa on the qāf — what you have picked up of anything.
5. *al-iltiqāṭ* — to happen suddenly upon something, whether pasture or other than pasture.

Someone said, in a line of verse:
And a watering-place I came to unexpectedly.

Likened to this is *al-laqīṭa* used of a lowly, contemptible man. They say, as a proverb, "For every stray remark, there is someone to pick it up (*lāqiṭa*)" — meaning: any odd thing said has someone who hears it and spreads it about.

6. *al-alqāṭ* of people — the few, scattered ones.
7. *bi'run laqīṭ* — a well come upon by chance, that is, happened upon suddenly.
8. *al-laqaṭ* — pieces of gold or silver found in a mine.
9. A certain part of the stomach is called *lāqiṭat al-ḥaṣā*, the gravel-gatherer.
10. *luqāṭat az-zar'* — what is gleaned of grain after its harvest.
لقع:
The letters lām, qāf and ʿayn are a sound root indicating the throwing of a thing at something and hitting it.

1. *laqaʿtu al-rajul bi'l-ḥaṣāt* — I threw the pebble at the man; likewise *laqaʿahu bi-baʿratin* — he pelted him with a dung-pellet.
2. *laqaʿahu bi-ʿaynihi* — he struck him with his eye, gave him the evil eye.
3. *al-luqqāʿa* — the calamitous man who hurls speech from the depths of his throat; likewise *al-tiliqqāʿa*.
4. *fī kalāmihi luqqāʿāt* — said of one who speaks from the depths of his throat.
لقم:
The letters lām, qāf and mīm are a sound root indicating taking food by hand to the mouth, and then it is measured against that.

1. laqimtu al-ṭa'ām alqamuhu, and talaqqamtuhu and iltaqamtuhu — I took it as a mouthful.
2. a man called tilqāma is one who takes large mouthfuls often.
3. al-laqam, the beaten track of a road, by comparison, as though it takes a mouthful of whoever passes along it — as already mentioned in the chapter of al-sirāṭ.
لقن:
The letters lām, qāf and nūn are a sound word indicating the taking hold of knowledge and understanding it.

1. *laqina al-shay' laqnan* — he took hold of the thing and understood it.
2. *laqqantuhu talqīnan* — I made him understand.
3. *ghulām laqin* — a quick-witted boy, fast to understand, of quick *laqāna*.
لقي:
The letters lām, qāf and the weak letter are three roots: one of them points to crookedness, another to two things meeting, and the other to the throwing away of a thing.

The first is al-laqwa: a disease that takes hold in the face and twists it. A man so struck is malqūw, and luqiya al-insān — the man was struck by it. And al-laqwa is the bucket which, when you send it down into the well and another comes up, is lifted along with it.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
The worst of buckets is the laqwa that clings.

And al-liqwa is the eagle, so named for the crookedness of its beak. And al-laqwa is the she-camel quick to conceive.

The other root is al-liqā': meeting, and the coming together of two who face each other. And laqītuhu laqwatan — I met him one single time — and liqā'atan. And laqītuhu luqyan and luqyānan. And al-luqya is on the pattern fuʿla from al-liqā', and the plural is luqan.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And truly I long for sleep though no drowsiness is on me, hoping that the meeting with you may come about in a dream.

The other root is alqaytuhu — I cast it away, ilqā'an. And a thing flung down is a laqan. The origin of it is that a people among the Arabs, when they came to the House to go round it, would say: we shall not go round in clothes in which we disobeyed God; so they would throw them off, and what was thrown off was called laqan.

Ibn Aḥmar said, describing the chick of the sand-grouse, in a line of verse:
She shelters a castaway thing flung down on bare level ground, which the sun melts and it does not melt.
لك:
The letters lām and kāf are a minor root indicating interlocking within a thing.

1. *al-lakīk* — flesh packed in among the bones.
2. *al-lukālik* — a camel compact with flesh.
3. *iltakka* — one says "the people iltakka" (pressed together) when they crowded together.
4. *al-lukkiyy* — the thickset man, heavy with flesh.

Straying from this chapter is another word also written *al-lakīk*: a frail tree.

Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse, about packed flesh called *al-lakīk*:
So my companions spent the day roasting at their ease, arranging in a pit packed flesh laced with fat.
لكد:
The letters lām, kāf and dāl. They say lakida al-shay' bi'l-shay' — it clung to it and stuck to it.

1. al-milkad — something in which things are pounded.
2. al-lakad — the sticking and clotting of blood; one says, I ate the gum-resin and it stuck in my mouth.
3. al-lakad, Abū Bakr ibn Durayd said — striking with the hand.
4. He walked "yulākidu qaydahu" — when the shackle contested his steps as he walked.
لكع:
The letters lām, kāf and ʿayn are a single root indicating meanness and baseness.

1. lakuʿa al-rajulu — when a man is mean, [the verbal noun is] lakāʿa, and he is alkaʿ. One says to him: yā lukaʿ, and to two: yā dhaway lukaʿ.
2. Banū al-lakīʿa — they say this, and they said the analogy from it gives al-lakaʿ, which is dirt.
3. al-lukaʿ, also — the suckling foal of a donkey.

And what strayed from this chapter is al-lakʿ, which is stinging. He said: "When its sore hindquarters are touched, it stings."
لكم:
The letters lām, kāf and mīm are a single word: *al-lakm* — striking with the closed fist.

They said its analogy is found in *al-khuff al-mulakkam*, the camel's foot-pad grown hard and tough [from repeated pounding].
لكن: The letters lām, kāf and nūn are a single word: *al-lukna* — an impediment, inarticulacy in speech. A man affected by it is *alkan*, a woman *laknā'*; it is also called *al-lakan*.
لكي:
The letters lām, kāf and the weak or hamzated letter indicate staying in a place, and slowness.

1. *lakītu bi-fulān lakan* (shortened form) — I clung to, stayed attached to, so-and-so.
2. *lakiya bi'l-makān* — Abū Bakr said: he stayed in the place; it may be said with or without a hamza.
3. *talakka'a al-rajul talakku'an* — the man lagged, was slow to act on a thing.
4. *lakā'tu al-rajul lak'an* — I whipped the man with the lash.
لم:
The letters lām and mīm are a sound root indicating gathering, drawing near, and pressing close together. One says: lamamtu shaʿathahu, I gathered together [lamamtu] what had been in a dishevelled, scattered state of his affairs.
1. ṣakhratun mulamlamah — a rock that is hard and round; also called mulmūmah. A poet said, in a line of verse: rounded and firm, like the back of the boulder.
2. alamamtu bi-l-rajuli ilmāman — I "came down" upon the man, when I stayed with him and pressed close to him.
3. al-lamam — it is said: this is not the actual committing of a sin, but only coming near to it, then holding back from it. God Most High said: {those who avoid the grave sins and shameful deeds, save the lamam} [al-Najm: 32].
4. al-lamma — so-and-so was struck by a lamma from the jinn, which is like a touch [of madness]. A poet said, in a line of verse: I seek refuge for him from the mishaps of the lamma.
5. al-limma, with the lām vowelled i — hair when it passes beyond the earlobe, named so, it seems, because it draws near the two shoulders and approaches them.
6. katībatun mulmūmah — a troop grown numerous, its squadrons gathered one upon another.
7. al-mulimma — a misfortune, one of the misfortunes of the world.
8. al-ʿaynu al-lāmma, the evil eye — it is said the origin is mulimma, but when it was paired with al-sāmma, the deadly [eye], it was said lāmma; it is the one that strikes with harm. That is the pattern by which it is explained.
As for "lam" [the negating particle], it is said to be a particle whose origin is "lā"; and such particles admit no derivational pattern.
لمأ:
The lām, the mīm, and the hamza are two words indicating enclosing something within.

1. *alma'tu bi-l-shay'* — one says this when a thing enclosed something and made off with it.
2. *talamma'at ʿalayhi al-arḍ* — the ground closed level over him.

As for their saying *iltumi'a lawnuhu* (his color changed), it may be from this, or it may be a case of letter-substitution, as though the hamza stands in place of the ʿayn, the original being *iltumi'a* [with ʿayn].
لما:
The lām, the mīm, and the weak letter are a single word: *al-lamā* — a duskiness on the inside of the lip, which is considered becoming. A woman with this is *lamyā'*.

Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
Dusky-lipped, with a blackish-brown tinge upon her lips, and in her gums and in her eye-teeth a gleaming brightness.

One says a dense, black shade is *ẓillun alma*.

Straying from this is *al-lumma*: the age-mate, also said to mean companions.
لمج:
The letters lām, mīm, and jīm. One says:

1. *al-lamāj* — a bite of food, as in "he tasted not a *lamāj*," meaning: not a mouthful of food.
2. *lamaja al-shay'* — he ate, he tasted the thing.

Labīd said, in a line of verse [only a fragment survives]:
He nibbles the fresh spring herbage.
لمح:
The letters lām, mīm and hā' are a root indicating the gleam of a thing. One says *lamaḥa al-barqu wan-najmu lamḥan* — the lightning and the star flashed.

Someone said, in a line of verse:
I watch for a glimpse of Suhayl, as though ... when it shows itself at the end of the night, it blinks.

"I saw the flash (*lamḥa*) of the lightning." And they say, "I shall show it to you as a clear glimpse (*lamḥan bāṣiran*)", meaning: a plain matter.
لمز:
The letters lām, mīm, and zā' are a single word: al-lamz, which is finding fault. One says lamaza yalmizu lamzan.

God Almighty said: {and among them are those who find fault with you over the alms} [al-Tawba: 58].

A man is called lammāz or lumaza, meaning a fault-finder.
لمس:
The letters lām, mīm and sīn are a single root indicating seeking out a thing, and also touching it. You say: "talammastu l-shay'a" when you sought it out with your hand.

Abū Bakr ibn Durayd said: al-lams originally is with the hand, so the touch of the thing might be known; then this usage grew so widespread that every seeker came to be called multamis. "I lamastu" when you touched — they said: every one who touches is a lāmis. God said: {or you have touched women} [al-Nisā': 43]. Some said sexual intercourse was meant by it. Others held that plain touching is meant, and that lams and mulāmasa can occur without intercourse.

They quoted, in a line of verse:
I touched his hand with my hand, seeking wealth — not knowing that generosity is contagious from his hand.

But this is poetry that cannot be relied on as evidence.

Al-lamāsa: a claim and a need. It is said: "he does not repel the hand of one who reaches out to take," when there is no benefit in him and he has no way to defend what is his.

He said, in a line:
And were it not for them, you would not have repelled the hand of the one who reached out to take.
لمظ:
The letters lām, mīm, and ẓā' are a minor root indicating a fleck of whiteness.

1. *al-lumẓa* — a fleck of whiteness, as in "there is a *lumẓa* on it," meaning: a white fleck. In the hadith: "Faith appears as a *lumẓa* in the heart; the more faith increases, the more the *lumẓa* increases."
2. *al-lumẓa*, of a horse — a whiteness on one of its two lips.
3. *al-talammuẓ* — the putting out of part of the tongue. One says the snake *talammaẓat* when it puts out its tongue, as an eater does when licking his lips. It is called *talammuẓ* because what shows of the tongue in it is slight, like the *lumẓa*.
4. *al-lamāẓ* — as in "he drank the water *lamāẓan*," meaning: he tasted it with the tip of his tongue.
لمع:
The letters lām, mīm, and ʿayn are a sound root indicating the quick shining of a thing; anything that runs the same course is then measured against it.

1. *lamaʿa*, of lightning and the like — it flashed; such a thing is *lāmiʿ*.
2. *lamaʿa*, also of a sword and the like.
3. *yalmaʿu*, said of the mirage — it shimmers, as though named for its movement and glimmer. A lying man is likened to it.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Whenever I complained of love, so that she would reward me with her affection, she said: "You are nothing but a flash."

4. *alma'at al-nāqa* — the she-camel raised her tail, so it was known she was in calf.

Al-Aʿshā said [only the word survives from the verse]: *mulmiʿ*. Some said: every pregnant female whose nipple has darkened is called *mulmiʿ*. This is because her pregnancy is inferred from that, as though she had made her state plain, like a thing that gleams.

5. *al-limāʿ* — the plural of *lumʿa*, a patch of pasture.
6. *al-lumʿa*, said by some, though this is not the sound view — a group of people.
7. *al-lammāʿa* — open wasteland.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
A gleaming waste with no landmark on it, no waymark, and no hollow that holds water.

8. *al-lammāʿa*, also — the eagle, because it flashes with its wings.
9. *iltamaʿtu al-shay'* — I snatched the thing, said when one steals it away; taken from the sense of lightness and speed already given.
10. *alma'at bihi al-maniyya* — death carried him off swiftly.
11. *al-alma'ī* — the man who conjectures and is scarcely ever wrong. The sense is that things hidden from his sight are to him like something gleaming, so that he sees them.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
The *alma'ī* is the one who conjectures the thought for you, as though he had seen and had heard.
لمق:
The letters lām, mīm, and qāf are three words that do not follow one pattern and are not close to one another.

1. *al-lamq* — one says "he *lamaqahu* with his hand" when he struck him.
2. *al-lamq*, a second word — erasing; one says "he *lamaqahu*" when he erased it. Yūnus said: I heard a Bedouin speaking of a tax-collector of theirs, and he said: "he *lamaqahu* after he had *namaqahu*," as though he had erased a document he had written.
3. *al-lamāq* — one says "I tasted not a *lamāq*," meaning: not a scrap of food.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Like a flash of lightning that delights whoever sees it, but affords the thirsty no relief — a mere taste.
لمك:
The letters lām, mīm, and kāf are a single word.

1. *talammaka* — one says this of a thing, like *talammaja*, as though he were tasting it.
2. *lamāk* — one says "I tasted not a *lamāk*," meaning: not a thing, as they also say "I tasted not a *lamāj*."

Its origin is that the camel twists its two jaws.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
When he saw that I had resolved upon his departure, he fretted — as though such fretting could avail him.
لن: The letters lām and nūn form a particle-word, lan, which negates the future-tense verb. It was related, on the authority of al-Khalīl, that the origin of lan is lā an, "not that."
له:
The letters lām and hāʼ are a minor root indicating thinness in a thing and flimsiness.
1. al-lahlah — cloth of poor weave; likewise speech and poetry of poor quality are called so.
2. al-luhluh — a mirage that stretches on continuously.
A poet said, in a line of verse: and many a shimmering stretch of luhluh upon luhluh. Its plural is lahālih.
لهب:
The letters lām, hāʾ, and bāʾ are a sound root, and it is the rising of the tongue of a flame; other things are then measured against it. From this, al-lahab is the flame of fire. You say: iltahabat iltihāban, it flared up. Anything whose glow rises and flashes intensely is spoken of with this word. A poet said, in a line of verse:
I have seen awe-striking men, lions of the thicket, and a crown of kingship blazing in flame.
They say of a thirsty man: lahbān, and this is by way of borrowed meaning, as though the heat inside him were blazing. They also say: al-lahab is billowing dust; if this is sound it too is a borrowed meaning. One says a horse is mulhib, when it raises up dust. For horses there is also ulhūb [a burst of speed], all of it derived from the first sense. Imruʾ al-Qays said:
For the driving-cry there is a burst of speed (ulhūb), for the leg a running sweat, and for the whip upon him the fall of a clean, well-trimmed lash.
Al-lahab and al-luhāb are the blazing-up of fire; al-luhāb is also used for thirst. As for al-lihb, the narrow pass between two mountains, that is not from this chapter — its true letter is ṣād, its origin being liṣb, with the ṣād changed into hāʾ. Banū Lihb are a clan of the Arabs.
لهث: The letters lām, hā' and thā' are a single word: it is a dog letting its tongue loll from thirst. God, exalted is He, said: {If you load it, it pants, or leave it, it pants} [al-A'rāf: 176]. *Al-luhāth* is the heat of thirst. All this is measured on what we have just said of the dog's condition.
لهج:
The letters lām, hā', and jīm are a sound root indicating persistence in a thing and cleaving to it, and another root indicating a mixing-up in a matter.

1. *lahija bi-l-shay'* — one says this when he became enamored of it and persisted at it; such a man is *lahij*.
2. *al-mulhij* — one whose young camels have taken to suckling their mothers, so he makes little pegs which he ties into the udder-teat of the mother, so that the young one cannot suckle, because that hurts its nose.

A poet meant this when he said, in a line of verse:
He grazed on the fresh growth of the early rains, until it seemed, in the awned bristles of the *bahmā* grass, he saw the pegs of a *mulhij*.

3. *al-lahja* / *al-lahaja* — the tongue, in respect of the speech it utters; called *lahja* because everyone persists (*yalhaju*) in his own language and speech.

The other root is their saying:

1. *lahwajtu ʿalayhi amrahu* — I muddled his affair for him. Its origin is from *al-laban al-mulhāj*, thickened milk that is about to curdle.
2. *amruhum mulhāj* — one says this: their affair is in a curdled, muddled state.
3. *lahwajtu al-laḥm* — I did not cook the meat through at all, so that it is, as it were, a mixture of raw and cooked.

As for their saying *lahhajtu al-qawm*, like *lahhantuhum*, it may be a case of letter-substitution, the jīm standing in place of the nūn.
لهد:
The letters lām, hā', and dāl are a sound root indicating humbling and pressing down.

1. *lahadtu al-rajul* — one says this when he pushed the man, so that he is *mulahhad*, humbled.
2. *al-lahīd* — the camel whose side is hurt by a heavy load.
3. *alhadtu al-rajul* — I held the man and set another loose upon him to fight him.
4. *alhadtu bi-l-rajul* — I disparaged the man.
لهز:
The letters lām, hā', and zā' are a sound root indicating a push with the hand or otherwise, or a shot from a bowstring.

1. *lahaztu fulānan* — I pushed so-and-so.
2. *al-lahz* — striking with the clenched fist on the chest.
3. *lahazahu al-qatīr* — grey hair spread through him.
4. *lahaztuhu bi-l-rumḥ fī ṣadrihi* — I struck him with the spear in his chest, I stabbed him.
5. *lahaza al-faṣīl ḍarʿa ummihi* — the young camel butted its mother's udder with its head while suckling.
6. *baʿīr malhūz* — a camel branded on its *lihzima* (the fleshy part beneath the ear).

A poet said, in a line of verse:
She passed by a rider on a branded camel, and he said to her: "Press the udder, and rub it roughly" [this line is obscure].

7. *faras malhūz* — a compactly built horse; sound on the same reasoning, as though its flesh were drawn up from its sides until it interlocked.
8. *dā'irat al-lāhiz* — a whorl of hair on the *lihzima*.
لهس:
The letters lām, hā', and sīn are a word indicating a kind of eating.

1. *lahasa ʿalā al-ṭaʿām* — he crowded eagerly over the food.
2. *lahsa* — one says "you have with me not a *lahsa* of food," meaning: neither much nor little.
3. Ibn Durayd said: *lahasa al-ṣabiyy thadya ummihi* — the child licked at his mother's breast without sucking it.
لهط:
The letters lām, hā', and ṭā' are a word.

1. *lahaṭahu bi-sahm* — he shot him with an arrow.
2. *lahaṭat al-mar'a farjahā bi-l-mā'* — the woman struck her private parts with water.
لهع:
The letters lām, hā', and ʿayn are words that, if sound, indicate slackness and languor.

1. *al-lahiʿ*, of men — one who yields and gives way to everyone; one says *lahiʿa lahāʿatan*. From it comes the name Lahīʿa. He is also called the languid, slack one.
2. Some said: *talahyaʿa fī kalāmihi* — he went to excess in his speech.
لهف:
The letters lām, hā', and fā' are a word indicating regret.

1. *talahhafa ʿalā al-shay'*, or *lahifa* — one says this when he grieved and lamented over the thing.
2. *al-malhūf* — the wronged one who cries for help.
لهق:
The letters lām, hā', and qāf are two unrelated words.

1. *al-lahaq* — white; a white bull is called *lahāq*.

Al-Hudhalī said, in a line of verse [only a fragment survives]:
*Lahāq*, its gleam like the crescent moon.

2. *talahwaqa al-rajul* — the man made a show of generosity though he was not generous.
لهم:
The letters lām, hā' and mīm are a sound root indicating the swallowing of a thing, from which further senses are measured. The Arabs say iltahama al-shayʾ — he swallowed it whole. From this chapter, al-ilhām, inspiration — as though it were a thing cast into the mind, which then swallows it. God Almighty said: {so He inspired it} [al-Shams: 8] with its wickedness and its righteousness.

iltahama al-faṣīl mā fī ḍarʿi ummihi — the weaned young camel drained all that was in its mother's udder. A horse described as lahimm — one that outstrips the rest, as if it were swallowing the ground. al-luhaym — calamity, and likewise umm al-luhaym, named so for its enormity, as though it swallows whatever it meets. A great, sufficient man is called al-lihamm. From this chapter, al-luhmūm — a generous, openhanded man; this too is based on the sense of vastness.
لهن: The letters lām, hā', and nūn are a single word. *Al-luhna* is what a man hastens to eat before his midday meal — one says *talahhana*, he took such a bite. Or, it is said, *al-luhna* is what a man gives as a gift when he arrives back from a journey.
لهو:
The letters lām, hā' and the weak letter are two sound roots: one of them points to being kept busy away from one thing by another, and the other to throwing something from the hand.

The first is al-lahw, diversion, and it is anything that keeps you from something else — it has diverted you, alhāka. And lahawtu, from al-lahw, I amused myself. And lahītu ʿan al-shay' — when you leave a thing for something else. The analogy is one and the same, even if the wording changes a little. And they say: when God, exalted be He, has taken something to Himself alone, then falha ʿanhu — leave it and do not busy yourself with it. In the hadith, about the wetness left after the ablution: "Pay it no mind." And Ibn al-Zubayr, when he heard the sound of thunder, would leave off the talk he was speaking — that is, he left it and turned away from it. And al-lahw is sometimes used as a veiled way of naming something else. God, exalted be He, said: {Had We wished to take to Ourselves a diversion} [al-Anbiyā': 17]. Al-Ḥasan and Qatāda said: by al-lahw He meant a wife. And some people said: by it He meant a child.

As for the other root, it is al-luhwa, which is what the miller throws with his hand into the hole of the millstone; the plural is luhan. From this a gift is called luhwa, and it is said: he is one of many gifts, kathīr al-luhā. As for al-lahāt, it is the far back of the mouth, as though it were likened to the hole of the millstone, and it was called lahāt because of the food that is cast into it.
لو: The letters lām and wāw form a particle-word, law, used to express a wish. The grammarians say: law indicates that a thing did not happen because another thing did not happen, and that it happens because another happens — as in their saying, "law kharaja Zaydun la-kharajtu", had Zayd gone out, I would have gone out. And if you turn law into a noun you double it, saying "aktharta min al-law", you have said "if only" too much. Al-Khalīl cited, in a line of verse: would that I knew — but where from me is "would that"? Indeed "would that" and indeed "if only" are both weariness.
لوب:
The letters lām, wāw, and bā' are two unrelated words, though one may be carried over onto the other.

1. *al-lawb* / *al-luwāb* — thirst; the verb is *lāba yalūbu*, one so afflicted being *lā'ib*.
2. *al-lābba* — a tract of black stones (a *ḥarra*), plural *lūb*.

What joins the two words is that the *ḥarra* is "thirsty," as though it were scorched.
لوت: The letters lām, wāw and tā' — I do not vouch for its soundness, and to me it is not attested in their speech. But some people have claimed that one says lāta yalūtu, when someone reports other than what he was asked about. And they say al-lawt is concealment. There is doubt about both of these.
لوث:
The letters lām, wāw, and thā' are a sound root indicating twisting, slackness, and winding one thing around another.

1. *lātha al-ʿimāma yalūthuhā lawthan* — he wound the turban.
2. *al-lawtha* — slackness; also said to mean a touch of madness.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Then a rough, hardy band would rise to my aid at the moment of zealous defense, even should one slack-limbed man among them grow soft.

3. *al-malāth* — the thing around which a garment is wound.
4. *nāqa dhāt lawtha* — a she-camel that is fleshy and heavy-bodied.
5. *dīma lawthā'* — a steady rain that twists the plants one upon another.
6. *iltātha fī ʿamalihi* — he was slow in his work, from this, as though he grew twisted and crooked.
7. *al-malāth*, also — the eminent man around whom affairs are wound, plural *malāwith*.

A poet said, in a line of verse [only a fragment survives]:
Why did you not weep for the eminent men of the House of ʿAbd Manāf?

8. *al-luwaytha* — a band of people drawn from various tribes, the sense being that they are wound together, that is, inclined toward one another.
لوح:
The letters lām, wāw and ḥā' are a sound root, most of it close to the chapter of gleaming and flashing. One says lāḥa al-shay'u yalūḥu, when a thing gleamed and flashed into view. The verbal noun is al-lawḥ. A verse:
I watch a gleam of Suhayl, as though ... when it showed itself at the end of the night, it were blinking.

One says alāḥa bi-sayfihi, he flashed with his sword; alāḥa al-barqu, the lightning flashed. Al-liyāḥ is white. Ibn Durayd, on the line —
In the evening she is like the gleaming pieces of weaponry, and in the morning ... like the wild cow on a morning after rain —
said that al-alwāḥ are the gleaming pieces of weaponry, most often swords.

From this chapter too: lawwaḥahu al-ḥarr, the heat scorched and blackened him until he could be seen gleaming from far off by anyone looking. From this chapter too: al-lawḥ, the shoulder-blade; al-lawḥ, one plank of a ship's timbers, and indeed any broad bone — named lawḥ because it gleams. From this chapter too: al-lūḥ, with damma, the open air between sky and earth.

What falls outside this chapter: al-lawḥ meaning thirst, and a beast called milwāḥ, one quick to thirst; also outside it, their saying alāḥa min al-shay'i, he was wary of the thing.
لوذ:
The letters lām, wāw and dhāl are a sound root indicating a person's holding close to something, seeking refuge in it and hiding behind it. One says lādha bihi yalūdhu lawdhan, and lādha liyādhan — that is when he takes refuge in it from fear or desire — and lāwadha liwādhan.

God Almighty said: {God already knows those of you who slip away surreptitiously} [al-Nūr: 63]. The hypocrites, when one of them wanted to leave the gathering of the Messenger of God, God's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, would slip behind someone else, concealing himself, then rise and go. He said liwādhan, rather than the expected form, because it is from lāwadha, whose verbal noun is formed regularly; had it been from lādha he would have said liyādhan.

Al-lawdh is what surrounds a mountain, the plural is alwādh.
لوز: The letters lām, wāw, and zā' are a single word: it is *al-lawz*, the almond.
لوس:
The letters lām, wāw, and sīn are a word indicating something of the tasting of food.

1. *al-laws* — for a person to go seeking out food to sample; one says *lāsa yalūsu lawsan*.
2. *al-luwāsa* — a mouthful.
3. Ibn Durayd said: *lustu al-shay' fī famī* — I rolled the thing in my mouth, when you turn it with your tongue.
لوص: The letters lām, wāw, and ṣād. They say *al-lawṣ* is to peer at something through a gap in a curtain or a door. One says *luṣtuhu alūṣuhu lawṣan*.
لوط:
The letters lām, wāw, and ṭā' are a word indicating sticking fast.

1. *lāṭa al-shay' bi-qalbī* — the thing stuck to my heart, said when it clings. In one of the hadiths: "The child clings closer to the heart," meaning: sticks more closely.
2. *hādhā amrun lā yaltāṭu bi-ṣafrī* — this is a matter that does not stick to my heart (*ṣafr*), meaning: it does not cling there.
3. *luṭtu al-ḥawḍ lawṭan* — I plastered the trough with clay.
لوع: The letters lām, wāw, and ʿayn: *al-lawʿa* is love. One also says a man is *lāʿ hāʿ* when he is a coward.
لوغ: The letters lām, wāw, and ghayn. Ibn Durayd mentioned that *al-lawgh* is to turn a thing round in your mouth. One says *lāghahu lawghan*.
لوق:
The letters lām, wāw, and qāf are a word indicating the improving of a thing's flavor.

1. *lawwaqa al-ṭaʿām* — he improved the food's flavor by seasoning it with a relish.
2. *al-lūqa* — butter.
3. *mā lāqat* — said of a woman when she does not find favor with her husband, as though he did not find her company agreeable.
4. *lāqat al-dawāh*, and *alaqtuhā* — [the sense of these two, concerning the inkpot, is not clear from the text as it stands].
لوك: The letters lām, wāw, and kāf are a single word. One says *luktu al-luqma alūkuhā lawkan*, I chewed the morsel. And so-and-so *yalūku aʿrāḍ al-nās*, "chews on people's honor," said when he backbites them.
لوم:
The letters lām, wāw and mīm are two words: one of them points to reproach and blame, and the other to being slow.

The first is al-lawm, which is blame. You say lumtuhu lawman — I blamed him; and the man is malūm, blamed. And al-mulīm is the one who deserves blame. And al-lawmā' is blame. And a man is lūama — one who blames people; and lūma — one who is blamed.

The other word is al-talawwum, and it is waiting and holding back. And it is said that al-lāma is a matter for which a man is blamed.
لون: The letters lām, wāw and nūn are one word, and it is the outward look of a thing. From this is al-lawn, the colour of a thing, such as redness and blackness. And one says talawwana fulānun — his characters became changeable. And al-lawn is a kind of dates. And al-līna is the palm-tree, from it, and the origin of the yā' in it is a wāw. God, exalted be He, said: {whatever palm-tree you cut down} [al-Ḥashr: 5]. And God knows best what is right.
لوي:
The letters lām, wāw and yā' are a sound root indicating the bending of a thing. One says: "lawā yadahu, yalwīhā" — he twisted his hand. "Lawā bi-ra'sihi" — he tilted his head.

Al-lawiyy: withered herbage, called lawiyy because when it wilts it curls and bends. Al-liwā' (the banner) is well known, named so because it is wound around its lance. Al-lawiyya: food set aside for those not present, as if turned away from them toward others. "Alwā bi-l-shay'i" when he signaled with something, such as the hand. "Alwā bi-l-shay'i" also means he made off with it, as if he had bent it toward himself.

Al-alwā: the man who keeps apart and alone, as though he had turned away from companions toward solitude. Al-layyā': land far from water, named so because it is as though it had turned away from the course of water.

"Lawāhu daynahu, yalwīhi, layyan wa-layyānan" — he put him off with his debt; this is the core of the root.

He said, in a line of verse:
You draw out putting me off, though you are well able to pay — while I, O wearer of the sash, press my claim graciously.

Liwā al-raml: where the sand-dune curves and ends. "The people alwaw" when they reached liwā al-raml, named so because the wind bends it however it wishes. They say: "I have said much of al-ḥayy and al-layy." They explained: al-ḥayy is speech that is clear, and al-layy is that which cannot be made sense of.
ليا: The letters lām, yā', and alif: they say it is something of a plant. *Al-liyā'* is something like a chickpea, intensely white. One says of a woman: as though she were a *liyā'a*.
ليت:
The letters lām, yā' and tā' are two words that do not follow one pattern.

1. al-līt — the side of the neck; the two sides together are called lītān.
2. al-layt — diminishment. One says lātahu yalītuhu, he diminished it. God Almighty said: "He will not diminish you anything of your deeds." Al-layt is also turning someone away; one says lātahu yalītuhu.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Many a night full of darkness I traveled through ... and nothing turned me away from journeying through it.

And layta is the word of wishing — would that.
ليث:
The letters lām, yā', and thā' are a sound root indicating strength of build.

1. *al-layth* — the lion, so named for its strength and the force of its seizing.
2. *rajul mulayyith* — a man so called, from this.
3. *al-layth*, also — a spider that hunts flies.
4. *al-līth*, with kasra on the lām — a place name.

Al-Hudhalī said, in a line of verse [obscure]:
Spreading between the valley of al-Līth, on its right, as far as Shamanṣīr — rain sent down, pouring and hastening.
ليغ:
The letters lām, yā', and ghayn are a word.

1. *al-alyagh* — one whose speech is not clear.
2. *sayyigh layyigh* — said of them; this is an *itbāʿ*, a rhyming word added only for emphasis and carrying no meaning of its own, used of something easy to swallow.
ليف: The letters lām, yā' and fā' are one word: it is līf, fiber - an Arabic word.
ليق: The letters lām, yā' and qāf are two words. One is their saying, fulānun lā yulīqu dirhaman, meaning he does not keep a dirham. A poet said: Your two hands are hands that do not keep a dirham. The other is their saying, lā yalīqu bihi kadhā (such-and-such does not suit him), as if it does not fit him and does not cling to him - from lāqa al-dawāta yalīquhā, he worked the ink in the inkpot so that it would take hold.
ليل: The letters lām, yā' and lām are one word, and it is al-layl, the night: the opposite of the day. One says layla and laylāt. As for al-layālī . . . . .
ليم:
The letters lām, yā' and mīm. They say al-līm is reconciliation. 'Alī ibn Ibrāhīm al-Qaṭṭān recited to us; he said Tha'lab recited:

A poet said, in a line of verse:
When Numayr ibn 'Āmir are called upon one day, you see faces whose reconciliation has become plain.
لين: The letters lām, yā' and nūn are a single word: al-līn, the opposite of roughness. It is said: "he is in layān of life" — meaning ease. And "so-and-so is malyana" — meaning gentle-natured.
مأج:
The letters mīm, hamza and jīm are a single word. Al-maʾj is salty water. One says maʾuja yamʾuju, so it is maʾj, clearly salty (bayyin al-muʾūja). He said, in a line of verse:
The salt taste and the sea kept away from it.
مأد:
The letters mīm, hamza and dāl are a word that denotes a thriving state and freshness in a thing.

1. al-maʾd, said of branches — full of sap, soft, supple, swaying.
2. maʾida al-ʿarfaj — the ʿarfaj-plant swayed with its freshness.
3. imtaʾada khayran — by analogy, he acquired good (wealth).
4. Yamʾūd — the name of a place.
مأر:
The letters mīm, hamza and rā' are a word that denotes enmity and severity.

1. al-miʾra — enmity.
2. māʾartuhu muʾāratan, on the pattern of fāʿaltuhu — from this same sense.
3. amrun maʾir — a severe matter.
مأق:
The letters mīm, hamza and qāf are a root that denotes a state that comes over a person after weeping, and also disdain.

The first: al-maʾq is what comes over a person after weeping. One says maʾiqa yamʾaqu, so he is maʾiq. And it is said that al-maʾqa is intense weeping.

The other is their saying amʾaqa: when a person falls into al-maʾqa, that is, disdain. In the hadith: 'as long as you do not harbour al-imāq' — meaning, as long as you do not harbour disdain toward what is due from you in alms.
مأل:
The letters mīm, hamza and lām. Words have been reported for this root that I do not consider sound, but I have written them down so they are known.

1. maʾaltu li-l-amr — I made ready for the matter.
2. imraʾatun maʾla — a fat woman.
3. al-maʾla — a meadow; plural miʾāl.

There is doubt about every one of these.
مأن:
The letters mīm, hamza and nūn are two very distinct words.

The first: al-maʾna is the soft flesh of the flank (ṭifṭifa), plural maʾanāt. He said, in a line of verse:
If you are one who gives gifts, then give
from the flank meat, or cuts of the hump.
Ibn Durayd said: maʾantu al-rajul — I struck him in his flank. And their saying mā maʾantu maʾnahu means: I was not aware of it. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: māʾantu fī al-amr, like māʿantu, meaning I deliberated over it.

As for what came in the hadith, 'a maʾinna of a man's understanding,' that belongs to the chapter of inna, and has already been mentioned there.
مأي:
The letters mīm, hamza and yā' are one word. It is said: al-ma'y is talebearing and stirring up trouble among a people. One says ma'aytu baynahum — I made mischief between them. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And mischief-making among them, a brother of foul deeds.
As for al-mi'a, the hundred, they say am'aytu al-darāhim — I made the dirhams a hundred.
مت:
The letters mīm and tāʾ are a slight root indicating stretching and drawing something out. One says mattatu, the same as madadtu — I pulled.

1. yamuttu bi-kadhā — said when someone claims a connection through kinship or the like.
2. al-matt — drawing water up from a well without a pulley.
متح: The letters mīm, tā' and ḥā' are a minor root that denotes the stretching and lengthening of a thing. Mataḥa al-nahār: the day stretched on. Laylun mattāḥ: a long night. From this comes al-matḥ, which is drawing water: mataḥa yamtaḥu matḥan, and the drawer of water is a mātiḥ or matūḥ. This is said because of the stretching of the rope. Biʾrun matūḥ: a well that is shallow, near at hand to draw from.
متر: The letters mīm, tā' and rā'. They say — and I do not know what it means — matartu al-shayʾ: I cut it, and perhaps this comes from letter-substitution. Ibn Durayd said: matartuhu matran. And imtarra al-ḥabl: the rope stretched taut.
متس: The letters mīm, tā' and sīn have one word reported by Ibn Durayd: mataṣahu yamtiṣuhu matsan — he worked craftily to pull it out from a tent or elsewhere.
متع:
The letters mīm, tā' and ʿayn are a sound root pointing to benefit and the stretching of a span in something good. Of it is istamtaʿtu bi-l-shay', I had the use and enjoyment of the thing. And al-mutʿa and al-matāʿ are benefit, in His words, exalted be He: {houses not lived in, in which there is a benefit for you} [al-Nūr: 29]. And a divorced woman is given something as her mutʿa because she takes benefit from it. And one says amtaʿtu bi-mālī with the meaning of tamattaʿtu, I enjoyed my property. He said, in a line of verse:
Two companions of two different clans, neighbours long ago, and their only enjoyment of one another was parting.
And al-Aṣmaʿī related it as 'bi-l-tafarruq'. He says: neither of them had any enjoyment of his fellow but the separation. And they say: if you buy this boy you will surely enjoy in him a good servant. And they say: a ḥabl mātiʿ is a good rope, and its sense is that the span stretches long with it. And they say: mataʿa al-nahār — the day grew long. And mataʿa al-nabāt mutūʿan. As for al-Nābigha's words, in a line of verse:
To the best religion, whose rites I have known, and his scale in the chapter of righteousness is [full-weighted] —
they said: its meaning is outweighing, exceeding. And mataʿa al-sarāb — the mirage stretched long at the first of the day, mutūʿan also.

Abū Bakr said: al-mutʿa is what you take enjoyment of. And the marriage of mutʿa, which was held hateful, I think is from this. And al-matāʿ among the goods of a house is what a person makes use of for his needs. And mattaʿa Allāh bihi fulānan tamtīʿan, and amtaʿahu bihi imtāʿan, are one in meaning — that is, He kept him alive to enjoy him in what he loves of joy and of benefits.

And some of the people of exact investigation held that the root in the chapter is the taking of pleasure. And mataʿa al-nahār because pleasure is taken in its light. And mattaʿa al-sarāb is likened to the stretching of the day. And al-matāʿ is the enjoying of what has an immediate pleasure in it.

And another of them held that the root is stretching and rising, and that al-matāʿ is a benefit whose time is drawn out. And a sharāb mātiʿ is a red drink — that is, it is enjoyed for its goodness.
متك:
The letters mīm, tā' and kāf.

1. Al-mutk — the citron (utrujj), also called zummāward.
2. Al-mutk — what the woman who performs circumcision leaves in place.
متل: The letters mīm, tā' and lām. They say: matalahu matlan — he shook it.
متن:
The letters mīm, tāʾ, and nūn are one sound root pointing to firmness in a thing together with stretch and length. From it, al-matn is what is firm, raised, and continuous of the ground, plural mitān. "I saw him at that matn." From it, by likeness, the two matnān of a person are named: the two sides flanking the spine, of sinew and flesh. Matantuhu, I struck his matn. They also say matna, meaning the flesh [of the back]. Imruʾ al-Qays said:
She has two firm-fleshed sides to her back, taut, as though a leopard crouched forward upon its forelegs.
Matana qawsahu: he strung his bow with a cord of sinew taken from the sinew of the matn. Matana yawmahu: he travelled the whole day through, by way of borrowed meaning. Matantuhu bi-l-sawṭi amtinuhu: I struck him with the whip — in our view, a strike upon the matn (the back).

Al-mumātana is going to the furthest lengths. Sāra sayran mumātinan: he travelled a long, hard journey. Mātanahu: he put him off, delayed him. From this chapter is al-mumātana between two poets, when one recites a line and the other a line, as though each were stretching out toward a goal he means to reach.

Among what falls outside this root: matantu al-dābbata, I split open its scrotum and drew out its testicle.
مته: The letters mīm, tā' and hā'. They say: al-tamattuh is wandering about in idleness and error. In our view this belongs to the chapter of letter-substitution, the hā' standing for ḥā', as though it were al-tamattuḥ, which we have already mentioned. And matahtu al-dalw means matahtuhā: I drew up the bucket.
متي:
The letters mīm, tā' and the third letter [yā'] hold three words.

The first is used to ask about time. You say: matā yakhruju Zayd? — when will Zayd go out?

The second belongs to the chapter of letter-substitution. They say tamattā in drawing a bow, which comes from tamaṭṭā and tamaṭṭaṭa — to stretch oneself — already mentioned. Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
The wild game came to it, approaching to drink, and he stretched out drawing the bow with his left hand.

The third is a word of Hudhayl. They say: jaʿaltuhu matā kummī, meaning: in the middle of my sleeve. Abū Dhuʾayb said, in a line of verse:
They drank from the water of the sea, then rose up
amid green depths that made a rushing sound for them.
مث:
The letters mīm and thāʾ are two words.

1. maththa yadahu — he wiped his hand.
2. maththa al-shayʾ — said when a thing oozes with grease.
3. maththa shāribuhu, Ibn Durayd said — when he ate something greasy and it remained on his moustache.
مثع:
The letters mīm, thā' and ʿayn are a single word. They say: al-mathʿāʾ is an ugly gait. One says mathaʿati al-ḍabuʿ tamthaʿu — the hyena walked with that gait. A rajaz poet said:
Like the mathʿāʾ hyena, worn out by the stagnant water.
مثل: The letters mīm, thā' and lām are a sound root pointing to one thing matching another. This is the mithl of that, that is, its like; and al-mithl and al-mithāl are in one meaning. And they may say mathīl, like shabīh. The Arabs say: amthala al-sulṭānu fulānan - the ruler put him to death in retaliation; and the sense is that he did to him the like of what he had done. Al-mathal is also al-mithl, the like, as shabah and shibh. And the proverb that is struck is taken from this, because it is mentioned as an indirect way of speaking of what is like it in meaning. And their saying maththala bihi, when he mutilated him as a punishment, is from this too, because the sense in it is that when he is punished in that way, that is made an example for everyone who does that deed or means to do it. And they say maththala bi-l-qatīl - he mutilated the slain man. Al-mathulāt are from this too. God Most High said: {wa-qad khalat min qablihim al-mathulāt} [al-Ra'd: 6], that is, the punishments that hold men back from the like of what they came down for; and the singular of them is mathula, like samura and ṣaduqa. And it may be that they are those that come down upon a man and are made an example by which another is held back and restrained. And mathala al-rajulu qā'iman - he stood upright, and the sense is that, because he is as though he were a figure set up. And the plural of mithāl is amthila. Al-mithāl is the bed, and the plural is muthul, and it is a thing that matches what is under it or over it. And so-and-so is amthal of the sons of so-and-so, that is, the nearest of them to good - meaning that he is a match for the people of soundness and good. And these are the amāthil of the people, that is, their best.
مج:
The letters mīm and jīm are two words: one is confusion in a thing, the other is throwing something quickly.

The first:
1. al-majmaja — confusion in what is written.
2. majmaja fī akhbārihi — he did not make his report clear or state it plainly.

The other: majja al-sharāba min fīhi — he expelled the drink from his mouth.

1. al-sharāb is called mujāj al-ʿinab — the exuded juice of the grape.
2. Rain is called mujāj al-muzn — the exuded water of the rain-clouds.
3. Honey is called mujāj al-naḥl — the exuded product of the bees.
4. huwa harimun mājjun — an old man who dribbles his spit and, from old age, cannot hold it back.
5. amajja fī al-bilādi imjājan — he went off, departed, into the land.
6. amajja al-rajulu — the man hastened in his running.
مجد:
The letters mīm, jīm, and dāl are a sound root indicating reaching the utmost limit, and it is used only of something praiseworthy.

1. al-majd — reaching the utmost limit in nobility.
2. God is al-Mājid and al-Majīd — there is no nobility above His.
3. mājada fulānun fulānan — so-and-so vied with so-and-so in glory.

They say, as a proverb: 'In every tree there is fire, but the marakh and the ʿafār [two trees used for fire-sticks] have taken more of it than their share' — meaning the two of them drew out enough fire to suffice them, reaching the utmost in that, so that fire is even kindled from them [more readily than from other wood].

4. majadat al-ibil mujūdan — they said this means the camels came near to their fill of fresh fodder and the like.
5. amjadtu al-dābba — some said this means: I fed the animal enough to satisfy it. This is closer to the true sense of the chapter.
مجر:
The letters mīm, jīm and rā' are three words that follow no single pattern.

The first: al-majr, a great multitude — dark-coated and numerous.

The second: al-majr, that a thing be sold for what is in a she-camel's womb, unborn. The Messenger of God, peace be upon him and his family, forbade al-majr; the Arabs used to do this in the Age of Ignorance.

The third: al-majar, with the jīm carrying a fatḥa, is a disease found in the bellies of camels and sheep. A ewe is called mumjir or mimjār when she has conceived and grown thin, and can no longer stand without someone to help her up, and rarely escapes the disease unharmed. A man of the Arabs said: 'Sheep are a sound possession, if they escape al-majar.'
مجس: The letters mīm, jīm and sīn are a word for which we know no regular pattern, and I think it is Persian; it is our word al-majūs, the Magians. One says tamajjasa al-rajul, when a man became one of them.
مجع:
The letters mīm, jīm and ʿayn are two distinct words.

The first: al-majʿ is eating dates with milk, and that mixture is called al-majīʿ.

1. al-majjāʿa — one who eats a great deal of it.
2. majāʿat al-tamr wa-l-laban — what remains of it; one says sharaba al-majāʿa, he drank the remainder.

The other denotes the poorness of a thing and its lack of goodness.

1. mijʿ — said of anything poor or inferior.
2. majiʿ — sometimes used for a shameless, impudent person.
3. imraʾatun majiʿa — a woman who speaks obscenely.
4. fī nisāʾ banī fulān majāʿa — 'the women of that tribe have majāʿa,' meaning they speak openly of matters normally only hinted at.
مجل:
The mīm, jīm and lām are a single word: it is majilat yaduhu tamjulu, and majalat tamjulu — his hand blistered. They say: "the camels came as though they were al-majl," meaning full, the way al-majl is full. And tamajjala qayḥan: it filled with pus.

Ibn Durayd erred about this root in two places: he said that al-mājil is a stagnant pool of water — but that belongs to the root (a-j-l); and he said that al-majalla is a written page — but that is from (j-l-l).
مجلنظي:
The one who lies on his back and raises his legs.

And al-majla'ibb is the one who lies stretched out. And a sayl mujla'ibb is a flood heavy with debris.

And al-mujlakhidd is the one who lies on his back.
مجن: The mīm, jīm and nūn are a single word: it is majana. They say: al-mujūn is that a person does not care what he does. They said its analogy from the she-camel is al-mumājin — the one that more than one stallion mounts, so that she barely conceives. And al-majjān is a man's giving something without a price.
مح:
The letters mīm and ḥāʾ are three words that do not reduce to a single root.

The first: maḥḥa al-shayʾ and amaḥḥa — when it grew worn and old. And al-maḥḥ is a worn-out garment.

The second: al-rajul al-maḥḥāḥ — the liar who, by his talk, shows what he does not actually do.

The third: al-muḥḥ — the yolk of the egg. And one says al-māḥ is its white.
محت: The mīm, ḥā' and tā' are not a root; rather it is inverted [from another root]. They say: al-maḥt is what is severe in anything. And yawmun maḥt: a day of severe heat. The origin is al-ḥamt.
محج:
The mīm, ḥā' and jīm.

1. maḥajati al-arḍa al-rīḥ — the wind wiped the dust off the ground.
2. maḥajtu al-laḥma — I scraped it.
3. al-maḥj — as Al-Khalīl said, wiping a thing off a thing.
4. maḥajtu al-adīma wa-l-ḥabla — as Ibn Durayd said, when I rubbed the hide or the rope to soften it.
5. māḥajtuhu muḥājatan wa-miḥājan — also Ibn Durayd, when I put him off and delayed him.

If the root is sound, its origin is wiping.
محز: The mīm, ḥā' and zā' are not a root, except that they say: al-maḥz is intercourse, and maḥazahā maḥzan — he had intercourse with her.
محش:
The mīm, ḥā' and shīn are a sound root indicating fire burning something until its skin is scraped away. One says: maḥashat al-nāru al-shay'a tamḥashuhu — the fire burned the thing. Imtaḥasha al-khubz: the bread burned. Ibn al-Sikkīt related: amḥashahu al-ḥarr — the heat scorched him. And one says imtaḥasha of a man when he grew angry; the meaning is that his anger, from its heat, reached that point, as though it had burned him. And they say of a year of drought: it has amḥashat everything.

As for the saying of al-Nābigha, in a line of verse:
Gather your kinsfolk, O Yazīd, for I have made ready Yarbūʿ and Tamīm against you.
They said its meaning is: gather these tribes — they were tribes that had allied themselves by fire.

And among what was measured by analogy on this:
1. maḥasha wajhahu bi-l-sayfi maḥshatan — he struck someone's face with the sword, a blow that scraped off the skin.
2. marrat ghirāratun fa-maḥashatnī — a sack passed and grazed me, meaning it scraped me.
محص:
The letters mīm, ḥā' and ṣād are a single sound root indicating the freeing and purifying of something.

1. *maḥaṣahu maḥṣan* — he freed it from every flaw.
2. *maḥaṣa Allāhu al-'abda min adh-dhanb* — God cleansed and purified the servant from sin; also *maḥḥaṣahu*. God, exalted is He, said: {that God may purify (*yumaḥḥiṣa*) those who believe} [Āl 'Imrān: 141].
3. *maḥḥaṣtu adh-dhahaba bin-nār* — I purified the gold with fire, freeing it of its impurity.

Their saying "*farasun mumaḥḥaṣ*" — people say it means a horse of strong build, though the reasoning, to our mind, is that it means one free of faults. Likewise *al-maḥiṣ*, said of ropes and bowstrings, is what has been worked over until its nap has gone and it has become smooth and supple.

Al-Hudhalī said, in a line of verse:
It has a smooth, supple cord, not coarse in its strands ... when ridden hard it creaks against a swaying hip.
محض:
The mīm, ḥā' and ḍād are a word indicating the purity of a thing. From it: al-laban al-maḥḍ — pure milk; and ʿarabiyyun maḥḍ — a pure Arab.
