3. *inmalaqa sā'idu r-rajuli* — the man's forearm was chafed raw from carrying loads.

Someone said, in a line of verse:
An old, feeble man whose forearm has been chafed raw ... he says: bent, and how well done, if it is straightened.

4. *al-malaqa* — land on which a track scarcely shows; the plural is *al-malaq* and *al-malaqāt*.
5. *malaqtu th-thawba* — I washed the garment, because you strip it of its dirt.
ملك:
The letters mīm, lām and kāf are a sound root pointing to strength in a thing and to soundness. One says: amlaka 'ajīnahu - he made his kneading strong and firm. And mallaktu al-shay' - I made it strong. A poet said, in a line of verse:
So he made firm with the bark that lies above its skin, like the membrane of an egg that the shell has covered from above.

And this is the origin. Then it was said, a man malaka a thing, yamlikuhu, malkan - he owned it; and the noun is al-milk, because his hand over it is strong and sound. So al-milk is what is owned of property. Al-mamlūk is the slave. And so-and-so is ḥasan al-malaka, that is, good in his treatment of those he owns. And 'abdu mamlakatin is one who was taken captive while his parents were not owned. And so-and-so has no mawlā of ownership other than God Most High, that is, none owns him but He. And we were at the imlāk of so-and-so, that is, we married him to his wife. And amlaknāhu is like mallaknāhu. And al-malak is the water that is carried with a traveller, because when it is with him he is master of his affair.
مله: The letters mīm, lām and hā'. They say: huwa mumtalahu al-ʿaql — he is one whose mind has gone, deranged.
ملو: The letters mīm, lām and the weak letter are a sound root pointing to a stretching out in something, of time or of anything else. Amlaytu al-qayd li-l-ba'īr imlā'an — when you make a camel's hobble roomy. Tamallaytu 'umrī — when I have had long enjoyment of my life. Al-malawān are night and day. Al-milāwa is milāwat al-'aysh, a long stretch of living, that is, he has been given a long rope. Of this chapter is imlā' al-kitāb, dictating a book. And God knows best what is right.
ملي:
The letters mīm, lām and the weak letter are one word: a long stretch of time. Aqāma maliyyan — he stayed a long age.

1. tamallaytu al-shay' — the thing stayed with you a long while [and you enjoyed it].
2. al-malawān — the two extremes of night and day.
3. al-mulāwa — a stretch of time.

And if it is given a hamza, it denotes equality and completeness in a thing.

1. mala'tu al-shay' amla'uhu mal'an — I filled the thing, filling it.
2. al-mil' — the noun for the amount that fills a container; so named because it is equal to its container in quantity. One says: give me its fill, twice its fill, three times its fill.
3. amla'a al-naz' fī al-qaws — he drew the bow to the very limit, when he pressed it to its utmost.
4. al-mala' — the nobles among people, because they are filled with generosity.

As for the poet's saying — they called out, O [tribe of] Buhtha, when they met us, and we said, be fair in your bearing, O Juhayna — some said he meant by 'mala'a' one's character. And it came in the hadith: "Be good in your bearing." The meaning in it is that good character is among the natural traits of the mala', who are the noble and generous.
من:
The letters mīm and nūn are two roots. One indicates cutting and being cut off, and the other indicates doing good.

The first is al-mann: cutting off, and from it one says manantu al-ḥabla — I cut the rope. God Almighty said: {a reward never cut off} [al-Tīn: 6].

1. al-manūn — death, because it diminishes the count [of days] and cuts off the span of life.
2. al-mann — exhaustion, because the exhausted one is cut off from travelling.

He said, in a line of verse: "Young she-camels that do not complain of exhaustion."

The other root is al-mann: you say manna yamunnu mannan, when he did a fine, generous deed.

1. al-munna — the strength by which a person's frame stands.

And sometimes they said "manna bi-yadin asdāhā" — he reproached someone with a favour he had done him. This shows that he had, in effect, cut off his own kindness [by mentioning it], so it belongs to the first root.
منح:
The letters mīm, nūn and ḥāʾ are a sound root indicating a gift. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: one says imtunihtu al-māl, meaning I was granted it as provision.

Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse: "Your eyes turned away from a ruin at Ḥuzwā, which the wind erased, and the streaming rains carried off."

1. al-manīḥa — manīḥat al-laban: a she-camel or ewe that a man gives to another, who milks her and then returns her.
2. al-nāqa al-mumāniḥ — a she-camel whose milk continues after the milk of other camels has gone; also called al-manūḥ.
3. al-manīḥ — the gambling-arrow that has no share in the division, unless it is given something as a gift. Al-manīḥ is also said of one who is not counted, and it was said it is the eighth of the arrows of maysir [the gambling game].
منع: The letters mīm, nūn and 'ayn are a single root, and it is the opposite of giving. One says mana'tuhu al-shay' man'an — I withheld the thing from him; and he is māni' and mannā' (much withholding). And makān manī' — an impregnable place. And huwa fī 'izz wa-man'a — he is in might and in a state of being defended.
مني:
The letters mīm, nūn and the weak letter are a single sound root, pointing to the measuring out of a thing and the carrying through of the decree about it.

Of it is their saying manā lahu al-mānī — the measurer measured it out.

The Hudhalī said, in a line of verse:
Do not feel safe, even if you spend the evening in a sacred place, until you meet what the measurer measures out for you.

And al-manā is what is decreed.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
I shall drive the white camels hard until either wealth suffices me one day, or the measure of the turns of fate does.

And a man's seed is maniyy, because his make-up is measured out from it. And al-maniyya is death, because it is measured out upon everyone. And a man's wishing for such a thing follows the same rule: it is a hope he measures out. Some people said it is the thing he hopes for. And al-umniyya, a wish, is of the pattern ufʿūla from it. And Minā: [Minā] of Mecca — some people said it is named that because of what was decreed to be slaughtered there, from your saying manāhu Allāh, God decreed it for him.

Of what runs along the same way is al-manā, the weight with which things are weighed, because it is a measure that is worked by. And our saying tamannā al-kitāba: he read it. God, exalted be He, said: {except that when he recited, Satan cast into his recitation} [al-Ḥajj: 52] — that is, when he read. And it is that same meaning, because reading is a measuring out and a putting of every verse in its place.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
He read the Book of God at the start of his night; and at the end of it he met the death the decrees appointed.

Of this chapter: mānā yumānī mumānātan, when he matches himself against another. And it is in the poetry of Ibn al-Ṭathriyya, in a line of verse:
Ask about me the drinking companions, when the brother of the cup says to me: match the people in good, and bring them to the water.

And this is from measuring out, because he measures his own act by another's act, wishing to be equal with him. As for the munya of a she-camel, it is the days in which it is found out whether she has conceived or is with young.
مه:
The letters mīm and hāʾ are two words: one indicates a rebuke, the other a sight and a pleasure.

The first is their saying: mah — stop! And mahmaha bihi — he rebuked him by saying that to him. And al-mahmah is smooth, wide open land.

The other is their saying: laysa lahu mahah, when he is not handsome. And they say: "Everything has mahah and mahāh, except women and the mention of them." And al-mahāh is pleasure. Al-Qaṭṭān recited to us, on the authority of Thaʿlab, a line of verse: "Our life has no pleasure left in it, and this world is not our [true] home."
مهج:
The letters mīm, hāʾ and jīm are a word indicating something fluid.

1. al-umhujān — thin milk.
2. labanun māhij — said of milk when it has grown thin.
3. al-muhja, as it is said, is the blood of the heart.
مهد:
The letters mīm, hā' and dāl are a word pointing to making a thing level and easy.

From it is al-mahd, the cradle. And mahhadtu al-amr — I made the matter smooth. And tamahhada — it became smooth and level. Al-mihād is what is level and soft in anything. And imtahada the hump of the camel or of another beast — it rose up.

Abū al-Najm said, in a line of verse:
And the withers rose up the way a boil rises.

That is, it rose and became even and was like a mihād, a levelled bed. The plural of mihād is muhud.
مهر:
The letters mīm, hāʾ and rāʾ are two roots: one indicates a payment in a particular matter, the other something belonging to an animal.

The first: al-mahr — a woman's mahr is her payment. You say mahartuhā, without an alif; but when you marry her to a man for a mahr, you say amhartuhā.

He said, in a line of verse: "Your mother has married Ḍurays — they gave her, as mahr, she-goats and a billy-goat."

And a woman is mahīra, and women are mahāʾir.

The other root: al-mumhir — a mare that has a foal. And al-mahr [also] names a bone in a horse's chest — this too is a figurative use.

He said, in a line of verse: "Rough-handed about the cartilage of the foal."
مهش: The letters mīm, hāʾ and shīn — I do not take it to be a root or a branch, but they say nāqatun mahshāʾ, a she-camel that grows thin quickly. And they say imtahashat al-marʾa — the woman shaved her face with a razor.
مهق: The letters mīm, hāʾ and qāf are a slight root indicating a colour among colours. They said al-amhaq is white. And they say ʿaynun mahqāʾ, which ought to mean an eye of intense whiteness in its white. Ibn Durayd said: it is an unpleasant, ugly whiteness not mixed with yellow or red — except that they also say al-muḥmarra al-māqī — reddened at the corners of the eyes. And they use al-mahaq in Ruʾba's saying: "...they clapped their hands in the mahaq pool" — meaning the intensity of the water's greenness.
مهك: The letters mīm, hāʾ and kāf contain nothing but al-mummahhik, which is the tall, restless one. And they call a soft, supple bow mahūk. And they call a swift horse mummahhik as well, on the same analogy.
مهل:
The letters mīm, hā' and lām are two sound roots. One indicates taking one's time, the other a kind of molten substance.

The first is taking one's time.

1. mahlan yā rajul — "gently, man!" — said the same way to two people and to many. When one says mahlan, they answer: "No mahl [slowness], by God," and "mahl will not spare you anything." A poet said, in a line of verse:
and mahl does not admonish the ignorant one.
2. Abū 'Ubayd said: at-tamahhul means going ahead, advancing — the opposite of the first sense, and perhaps this is one of the words that carries two opposite meanings.
3. amhalahu Allāh — God did not hasten him, gave him respite.
4. He walked ʿalā muhlatihi — at his own leisurely pace.

The other root is al-muhl: they said it is the dregs of oil, and they said it is molten copper.
مهن:
The letters mīm, hā', and nūn are a sound root indicating scorn and lowliness in a thing.

1. mahīn — lowly, contemptible; al-mahāna is lowliness. He is mahīn, clearly so.
2. al-mahn, also al-mihna — service.
3. al-māhin — the servant.
4. mahantu al-thawb — I pulled hard at the garment, wore it hard; a garment worn this way is mamhūn.
5. mahantu al-ibil — sometimes said for: I milked the camels.
مهي:
The letters mīm, hāʾ and the weak letter are a sound root indicating giving free rein, slackening, and ease in a thing.

1. amhaytu al-ḥabl — I slackened the rope. Some transmit Ṭarafa's line of verse this way: "By your life, death does not miss the young man — it is like the loosened tether, its two ends in the hand."
2. amhaytu al-farasa imhāʾan — I slackened the horse's reins.
3. Anything that flows easily is mahw. And labanun mahw is thin milk. And nāqatun mimhāʾ is a she-camel of thin milk. And nuṭfatun mahwa is a thin drop.
4. sayfun mahw — a sword of fine, thin edge, as though it passed through its target the way water flows.

He said, in a line of verse: "A cutting blade whose temper was purified, white and thin, with a faint watered pattern on its body."

5. And of this chapter: amhaytu al-ḥadīda — I tempered the iron [by quenching], meaning the thinness of the water used.
6. al-mahā — the plural of al-mahāt, which is rock-crystal, so named for its clarity, as though it were water.

Al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse: "And she smiles over cool, sound teeth like mahā — when the one who kisses is given more, he wants still more."

The plural is mahawāt and mahayāt. As for the wild cow, it is called mahāh, and I take this to be a comparison to rock-crystal.

And what strayed from the chapter: something al-Khalīl mentioned, that al-mahāʾ, drawn out, is a fault or crookedness that occurs in a gambling-arrow, though it may belong to this chapter too, since that comes close to slackness and the like. And the front teeth, when they turn white and grow moist, are called mahan.

Al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse: "And a gleaming mouth whose front teeth glisten — it heals the love-stricken one who feels the burning [of passion]."

And in the hadith: "a man's body mumahhan," meaning purified, resembling rock-crystal. And in the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās to ʿUtba ibn Abī Sufyān — he had praised him and spoken well of him — "You have amhayta, Abū al-Walīd," meaning: you went to the limit in praise and were thorough. And one says amhā al-ḥāfir and amāha, meaning he dug and struck water.

And perhaps this belongs to the chapter of letter-inversion, and likewise its sister-words in this chapter. And sometimes the stars were called mahan, by the same comparison.
موت:
The letters mīm, wāw and tā' are a sound root pointing to the going away of strength from a thing.

From it is al-mawt, death, the opposite of life. And we said only that its origin is the going away of strength because of what is related from the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace: 'Whoever eats of this foul plant, let him not come near our mosque; and if you must eat it, then kill it by cooking.' Al-mawatān is land not yet brought to life by sowing or by improvement, and likewise al-mawāt. Al-Aṣma'ī said: they say, buy of the mawatān and do not buy of the ḥayawān - buy dead land and not livestock. As for al-mūtān, with a sukūn and a ḍamma on the mīm, it is death; one says, a mūtān has fallen among the people. And one says a she-camel is mumīt and mumīta, of the one whose young dies; and a man is [mawtān al-fu'ād, dead of heart, and a woman] mawtāna. And umītat al-khamr - the wine was cooked. Al-mustamīt for a matter is the one who gives himself up to it. Al-mūta is something like madness that comes over a man. Al-mawta is the single instance of death. Al-mīta is a manner of dying, fair or ugly; and one dies mītatan jāhiliyya, the death of the age of ignorance. Al-mayta is what has died of those creatures whose flesh is eaten, when it has been slaughtered.
موث: The letters mīm, wāw and thā' are a single word: they say muthtu al-shayʾ fī al-māʾ, meaning I rubbed it with my hand in the water — amūthuhu mawthan. And mithtuhu amīthuhu maythan means the same.
موج: The letters mīm, wāw and jīm are one root pointing to turbulence in a thing. Māja al-nās, yamūjūna, when they became agitated. Māja amruhum wa-marija, their affair became disordered. Al-mawj: the wave of the sea, so named for its turbulence. Māja, yamūju, mawjan and mawajānan; and anything that becomes agitated has 'māja.'
مور:
The letters mīm, wāw, and rāʾ are a sound root pointing to constant movement to and fro. Māra al-damu ʿalā wajhi al-arḍi yamūru: the blood poured out over the face of the ground and moved about. Amartu damahu fa-māra, I let his blood flow and it moved. In the hadith: "let the blood flow (amiri al-dama) as you wish" — also transmitted as "amri al-dama," from marā yamrī, which will be discussed elsewhere.

Al-mūr is dust that the wind sets moving. A she-camel māra in her stride, and she is mawwāra, swift-moving. Ṭarafa said, in a line partly obscure to me:
... about the chin, well-formed in the withers, far-striding in the leg, restless-moving in the forehand.
A horse likewise is mawwārat al-ẓahr [restless-backed]. They say: "I do not know whether he went to the lowland or wandered (ghāra am māra)," meaning: I do not know whether he went down to the lowland, or circled round and came back to the highland.

Inmārat ʿaqīqatu al-ḥimār: the young donkey's birth-coat fell away from it in the days of spring, and every piece of it is a mūāra. A poet said:
and the birth-coat's pieces (mūārāt) fell away from them
It was named this because when it fell it moved to and fro (mārat).

Al-mawr is the road, because people move to and fro (yamūrūn) upon it. Al-mawr is also the wave. Their saying "so-and-so does not know sāʾir from māʾir": al-māʾir is the cutting sword that moves to and fro in what it strikes, and al-sāʾir is verse that travels widely, that is widely transmitted.
موس: The letters mīm, wāw and sīn: they say al-maws is shaving the head. [And one says, for the relational adjective formed from Mūsā, Mūsawiyy; and al-Kisā'ī said the relational adjective formed from Mūsā and ʿĪsā and words like them, where the yā' is an extra letter, is Mawsiyy and ʿĪsiyy] — that is because the yā' in it is an extra letter, as al-Kisā'ī said.
موص:
The letters mīm, wāw and ṣād are a single word, it is al-maws: washing a garment. One says muṣtuhu amūṣuhu. And al-muwāṣa is the wash-water.

Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
With black hair, thickly plaited and flowing down, and with finely notched teeth that she brushes and rubs clean.
موع: The letters mīm, wāw and ʿayn: brass and silver melted in the fire — māʿa yamūʿu and yamīʿu — meaning it melted.
موق: The letters mīm, wāw and qāf are two words that do not go back to a single origin. Al-mūq is foolishness joined with dullness. And they say māqa al-bayʿu yamūqu: the sale became cheap.
مول:
The letters mīm, wāw and lām are one word: it is tamawwala al-rajul — the man got property — and māla yamālu — his property became much. And of the saying of the poet:
Brimful of water, like the eye of al-mūla —
they say that al-mūla is the spider; and there is something in this to look into.
موم:
The letters mīm, wāw and mīm are two very distinct words.

1. al-mūm — delirium (birsām, a fever accompanied by raving); a man struck by it is called mamūm.
2. al-mawmāh — a wide, smooth desert waste; its plural is mawāmin.
مون: The letters mīm, wāw and nūn are a single word, and it is al-mawn: that you support your dependents (tamūnu ʿiyālaka) — that is, you see to their needs and bear the burden of maintaining them (maʾūnatahum). As for al-maʾūna, it comes from al-mawn, and its original form is mawūna, without a hamza.
موه:
The letters mīm, wāw and hā' are one sound root, and its words branch out from it. It is al-mawh, the origin of the building of the word al-mā', water, whose diminutive is muwayh. They said: this is proof that the hamza in al-mā' stands in place of a hā'. And one says mawwahtu al-shay'a, as though you gave the thing water to drink; and mawwahtu al-shay'a also means I plated it with silver or gold, as though they put that in the place of what a thing is given to drink. And they said: how fine is the mūha of his face, that is, the shimmer of the water of youth in it.

Of this section is al-māwiyya: crystal stone; and likewise al-māwiyya is the mirror. Ṭarafa said, in a line of verse:
And two eyes like two mirrors, sheltering in the two caves of the brow-bones of a rock, a hollow at a watering-place.
One says māhat al-safīnatu tamūhu and tamāhu - water came into the ship. And amāhat al-arḍ - seeping water showed in the ground. And amāha al-faḥl - the stallion cast his water into the womb of the female. And a man māhu al-qalb, that is, one with much water of the heart. The rajaz poet said:
You, O Jahḍam, are watery of heart.
They said: and the man who is so is dull-witted; māh was brought out on the pattern of māl. And amahtu al-sikkīn and amhaytuhu - I gave the knife its water, that is, I whetted it. And in the relative form, one says of māh: māhī and mā'ī, and of mā': mā'ī and māwī.
ميث: The letters mīm, yā' and thā' are a word that denotes ease in a thing. One says mithtu al-shayʾ fī al-māʾ maythan, when you dissolve it. And al-maythāʾ is soft, level ground.
ميح:
The letters mīm, yā' and ḥā' are a sound root that denotes giving, and its original use is in drawing water.

1. Māḥa yamīḥu — he went down into the well and filled the bucket. He said, in a line of verse:
O drawer of water, my bucket is yours — take it.
2. Miḥtuhu mayḥan — I gave it to him.

As for their saying tamāyaḥa al-sakrān — the drunk man swayed — and that a stick, and likewise a branch, may also 'sway' — that is not part of this chapter.
ميد:
The letters mīm, yā' and dāl are two sound roots: one indicates motion in a thing, the other benefit and giving.

The first: al-mayd is motion, swaying. "Māda, yamīdu" — it swayed. "The branches mādat, tamīdu" — they swayed to and fro. Al-maydān, on the pattern faʿlān: a soft, lush, well-watered life.

Ibn Aḥmar said, in a line of verse [the first half of the line is missing in the source]:
...and it met with comfort and a lush green abundance of life.

The other root: al-mayd. "Māda, yamīdu": he fed and benefited someone. "Mādanī, yamīdunī": he sustained me.

They said: al-mā'ida (the dining-table) was named from this, and likewise al-mā'id follows this analogy.

He said, in a line:
And I was a mā'id (a provider) to those who came seeking pasture.

Abū Bakr said: "he was struck by mayd" — dizziness from riding the sea. "Midtuhu": I gave to him and supplied him with good. "Imtadtuhu": I sought his good.

Some careful scholars held that the root of mayd is motion. Al-mā'ida: the dining-table, because it sways with what is on it — moving it, shifting it from its stacked arrangement. "Mādahum": he fed them at the table.

As for his saying — God's blessings and peace upon him and his family — "mayda annā ūtīnā l-kitāba min baʿdihim" [except that we were given the Book after them] — that is, "except that we" or "given that we" — this is a dialectal variant of bayda annā.
مير: The letters mīm, yā' and rā' are a sound root; it is al-mayr, providing food. Mirtu mayran, I supplied provisions. Al-mīra is food brought to a person's town. And they said: mā 'indahu khayrun wa-lā mayr — he has neither good nor provisions.
ميز:
The letters mīm, yā', and zā' are a sound root indicating the parting of one thing from another and setting it apart. [The exact word for the first of these two verbal nouns is unclear in the copy in front of me — the general sense of the pair is separating and setting apart.]

1. mayyaztuhu tamyīzan, miztuhu mayzan — I separated it, distinguished it (two verb-forms for the same act).
2. imtāzū — they separated, each becoming distinct from the rest.
3. yakādu yatamayyazu ghayẓan — he all but 'separates' with rage, meaning he all but bursts apart.
4. inmāza al-shayʾ — the thing became separated from [another] thing.

A poet said, describing a snake, in a line of verse:
It hoarded venom until the skin of its head split away from the bone — a viper, deadly in its bite, defiant.
ميس:
The letters mīm, yā' and sīn are a word denoting a leaning motion.

1. Māsa mayasānan — he swaggered. A branch too can 'sway' (māsa).
2. Al-mays — a tree said to give the finest wood.
ميش: The letters mīm, yā' and shīn are a root that denotes mixing one thing with another and teasing it apart. A woman 'māshat' the cotton with her hand after it had been carded. From this comes their saying, of a man who tells part of a report and withholds part of it: 'He has māsha, yamīshu.' This is taken from milking a she-camel by the method called maysh: to milk part of what is in the udder and leave part; if the milking goes past the halfway point, it is no longer called maysh.
ميط:
The letters mīm, yā' and ṭā' are a sound word that denotes pushing and repelling. Māṭahu ʿanhu: he pushed it away from him. Miṭtu al-adhā ʿan al-ṭarīq: I removed the harmful thing from the road. One says amāṭahu imāṭatan. That is why they say: 'They are in hiyāṭ and miyāṭ' — al-hiyāṭ is shouting, and al-miyāṭ is pushing away.

Al-Farrāʾ said: tamāyaṭū — they drew apart from one another and the relations between them broke down — tamāyuṭan.
ميع:
The letters mīm, yā' and ʿayn are a sound word that denotes the flowing of a thing, and its agitation and motion.

1. Māʿa al-shayʾ yamīʿu — it flowed over the face of the ground.
2. Al-māʾiʿ — anything liquid or melted.
3. Al-mayʿa — liveliness, so named for the motion in it.
4. Al-mayʿa — the first flush of youth, that is, when a person grows up and becomes active.
ميل:
The letters mīm, yā' and lām are a sound word indicating a thing's leaning to one side. māla yamīlu maylan — he leaned.

1. If it is a natural trait in the thing, it is mayal; one says māla yamīlu mayalan.
2. al-maylā', of sand — a large mound that stands apart and leans off to one side.
3. al-maylā' — a tree with many branches; this fits the pattern of the root.
4. al-amyal, among men, is said to be the one who cannot stay steady on a horse — if so, because he leans off his saddle. It is also said to mean the one with no spear — if so, this use falls outside the pattern of the root. The plural of al-amyal is mīl.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
not unsteady riders, nor cowards in the fray, nor those stripped of weapons, nor stragglers.
مين:
The letters mīm, yā' and nūn are a single word, it is al-mayn: lying. And māna yamīnu means he lied. He said, in a line of verse:
And you claimed that you had killed
our chief men — a lie and a falsehood.
نأ:
The letters nūn and hamza are a root denoting weakness in a thing.

1. al-na'na'a — weakness.
2. rajulun na'nā' — a weak man. Imru' al-Qays said:
By your life, Saʿd is no friend to a wrongdoer, nor weak at the moment of defending honour, nor one who falters.
3. na'na'tu ra'yī — Abū Zayd said, in the Book of the Hamza: I muddled my opinion, when I mixed it up.
نأت: The letters nūn, hamza and tā' are a word indicating the imitation of a sound. One says: na'ata al-rajul na'ītan, like nahata, when he groaned. A man is nā'āt, like nahhāt.
نأج:
The letters nūn, hamza and jīm are a root indicating a sound.

1. na'aja ilā Allāh — he pleaded humbly in supplication to God.
2. nā'ijāt al-hām — the cries of the owls, the ones that call out.
3. al-na'ūj and al-nā'ja — wind that groans (tan'iju) as it blows, meaning it makes a sound. Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse: "A moaning wind withered the herbage, brought by ... a hot Yemeni wind, veering in its course."
4. na'aja al-thawr — the bull cried out.

And in the hadith: "Call on your Lord for us with the most an'aj supplication you can" — meaning with the most humbly pleading form of prayer possible.
نأد: The letters nūn, hamza and dāl are a single word. They say: al-nā'd and al-nā'dā — a calamity. Al-Kumayt said, in a line of verse: "And beware a calamity, a nā'dā ... that has overshadowed you with its threatening storm-cloud."
نأش:
The letters nūn, hamza and shīn are a word indicating seizing and a forceful grasp. A man is na'ūsh: possessed of a forceful grasp.

Another word has been mentioned which, if sound, is not from the pattern of the first: they say of one who arrives among the last of the people, jā'a na'īshan — he came belatedly. Someone said, in a line of verse: "He wished, too late, that he had obeyed me ... but after those affairs, other affairs had come to pass." And what we have heard [as the correct wording] is: "tamannā akhīran" — he wished, at last.
نأف: The letters nūn, hamza and fā'. They say: na'ifa, yan'afu, when he ate.
نأل: The letters nūn, hamza and lām — there is nothing in it but al-na'alān: fast walking, in which the walker jerks his head upward. A man is na'ūl, and a hyena is na'ūl, when it does that.
نأم:
The letters nūn, hamza and mīm are a small root indicating a sound.

1. al-na'īm — a sound with weakness in it, like a moan.
2. na'ama al-asad, yan'imu — the lion made this sound.
3. sami'tu lahu na'matan wāḥidatan — I heard a single na'ma [cry] from him.
4. na'amat al-qaws na'īman — the bow gave a groaning sound.
نأي:
The letters nūn, hamza, and yāʾ are two words: al-nuʾy and al-naʾy.

Al-nuʾy is a trench dug around a tent to turn the rain-water away from it. One says anʾaytu nuʾyan, I dug such a trench. Al-muntaʾā is its place. Al-Khalīl quoted here a poet's line:
When we met, there flowed from our tears streams whose course is turned aside by the fingers.

As for al-naʾy, it is distance. One says naʾā yanʾā naʾyan; and intaʾā is the intensified form of it. Al-muntaʾā is the distant place. A poet said:
For you are like the night, which overtakes me even while I imagine the distant place from you to be wide.
Sometimes they place the hamza at the end and say nāʾin, though its true form is naʾā. A poet said:
He who, seeing you rich, softens toward you; and who, seeing you poor, turns away (nāʾa) and becomes a stranger.
And God knows best what is right.
نب:
The letters nūn and bā' are two words.

1. nabba al-tays nabīban — the billy-goat bellowed at mating.
2. al-unbūb — the segment lying between each two joints of a spear or the like.
نبأ:
The letters nūn, bā' and hamza: their pattern is coming from one place to another. The one who moves from one land to another is called nābi'. A flood is nābi': it came from one country to another; and a man is nābi' in the same way.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
But the mote in her eye is every dishevelled stranger come from afar, whom the fates brought to us from where we do not know.

From this same pattern is al-naba' — a piece of news — because it comes from one place to another. Al-munbi' is the one who brings news. And I say anba'tuhu and nabba'tuhu — I told him the news. And ramā al-rāmī fa-anba'a — the archer shot and his arrow did not tear the mark, as though his arrow turned aside from grazing it and fell somewhere else. Al-nab'a is a sound. And this is the pattern too, because a sound comes from one place to another.

Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
A lonely, keen-eared man in the waste has already caught a faint stirring; at the faint noise of it — there is no lying in his hearing.

And whoever pronounces al-nabī with a hamza does so because he brought news from God, exalted be He. And God knows best what is right.
نبت: The letters nūn, bā' and tā' are a single root pointing to growth in what is sown, and then it is used by transfer. Al-nabt, plants, is well known; one says nabata, it grew. And anbatat al-ard, the land brought forth growth. And nabbattu al-shajar: I planted the trees. And one says: in the sons of so-and-so there is [indeed] a nābitat sharr, a growing crop of evil. And nabatat li-banī fulān nābita, when a fresh growth of little children is born to them. And al-Nabīt is a tribe of Yemen. And how fine is the nibta, the manner of growth, of this tree. And he is fī manbit sidq, that is, of noble stock.
نبث:
The letters nūn, bā' and thā' are a root indicating bringing something out into view. nabatha al-turāb — he brought earth out of a well or a river; what is brought out is a nabītha, plural nabā'ith.

1. al-nābith — the digger.

And their saying khabīth nabīth is simply an itbā' — a rhyming word added for effect, with no meaning of its own.
نبج: The letters nūn, bā' and jīm. They say: al-nabbāj is the one loud of voice; and it is a single word.
نبح: The letters nūn, bā' and ḥā' are a single word: it is nubāḥ al-kalb and nabīḥuhu — the barking of the dog. And sometimes they say of the gazelle that it nabaḥa — made a similar cry. Abū Duwād said, in a line of verse: "and the short rib of one wiry-sinewed ... a crier, from the mountain pass." And in the hadith: "Sit, being manbūḥ [barked at]" — meaning being reviled.
نبخ:
The letters nūn, bā' and khā' are a root indicating swelling and self-aggrandizement. The origin of al-nabkh is what swells up on the hand and comes out like a blister full of water.

1. nābikha — one who is self-important, swollen with pride. The poet said: "He fears for them, from among the kings, a nābikha ... one of the nawābikh, like the strong, weighty one."
2. al-nabkhā' — the hillock, named so for its elevation.
نبذ: The letters nūn, bā' and dhāl are a sound root pointing to throwing and casting. And nabadhtu al-shay' anbidhuhu nabdhan — I threw it from my hand. Al-nabīdh is dates thrown into a vessel with water poured over them. One says nabadhtu anbidhu. The foundling child, al-ṣabiyy al-manbūdh, is the one whose mother casts him away. And it is said: in such-and-such a land there is a nabdh of property, that is, a small amount. And in his head there is a nabdh of grey hair, that is, a little, as though it were the thing thrown away for its smallness and slightness. And likewise al-nabdh of rain.
نبر:
The letters nūn, bā' and rā' are a sound root indicating raising and height.

1. nabara al-ghulām — the boy cried out, as soon as he begins to grow up.
2. nabbār — a man eloquent and loud of voice.
3. al-minbar (the pulpit) — named so because it is raised, and the voice is raised upon it.
4. al-nabr in speech — the hamza-stress, or something close to it.
5. Whoever raises anything has "nabara"-ed it.
6. al-nibr — a small creature, plural anbār, because when it crawls on camels, their skin swells and rises. Someone said, in a line of verse: "As if, from fatness and heaviness ... sharp anbār-creatures had crawled over it."
نبس: The letters nūn, bā' and sīn are a single word. One says: mā nabasa bi-kalima — he did not speak a word. And: mā sami'tu lahum nabsan wa-lā nabsatan — I did not hear a nabs or a nabsa from them.
نبش:
The letters nūn, bā' and shīn are a root, a single word, indicating the exposing of something hidden. nabasha al-qabr — he dug up the grave; he is a nabbāsh, one who nabasha it.

1. anābīsh al-kala' — the scattered patches of vegetation that show on the face of the ground; from the same pattern.
نبص: The letters nūn, bā' and ṣād. They say: nabaṣa al-ghulām bi-al-kalb — the boy made a sound to urge on the dog. And nabaṣa al-ṭā'ir — the bird made a sound.
نبض:
The letters nūn, bā' and ḍād are a small root indicating movement or the causing of movement. nabaḍa al-'irq, yanbiḍu — the vein pulsed; that is its movement.

1. mā bihi ḥabaḍun wa-lā nabaḍ — there is no ḥabaḍ nor nabaḍ in him [nothing stirring left in him].
2. anbaḍtu 'an al-qaws inbāḍan (also nabaḍtu) — I twanged the bowstring.
3. fu'ād nabiḍ — a "pulsing" heart, as if, from its keenness, it stirs. Someone said, in a line of verse: "And when you circled around it, you circled around a broad chest ... pulsing at the flanks, deep in the ribs."
نبط:
The letters nūn, bā' and ṭā' are a word indicating the drawing out of something.

1. istanbaṭtu al-mā', I drew out the water; and the water itself, once drawn out, is called nabaṭ. It is said the Nabaṭ were named for their drawing out of waters.
2. carried on this pattern: al-nubṭa, a whiteness under a horse's armpit; a horse called anbaṭ, as though that whiteness is likened to water that has been drawn out.
نبع:
The letters nūn, bā' and 'ayn are two words.

One of them is the springing-forth of water; the place it springs from is a *yanbū'*, a spring. *An-nawābi'* of a camel are the places from which its sweat flows. *Manābi' al-mā'* are its points of outflow from the ground.

The other is *an-nab'*, a kind of tree.
نبغ:
The letters nūn, bā' and ghayn are a word indicating emergence and appearance.

1. nabagha al-shay' — the thing appeared, emerged.
2. al-nabgh — what scatters from flour when it is ground or sifted.
3. nabagha al-rajul — said of a man who, having no inherited share in poetry, later spoke and did well at it. The poet al-Nābigha was named from this.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
They settled among Banū Qays ibn Jasr ... and matters had newly arisen for us because of them.
نبق:
The letters nūn, bā' and qāf are a word indicating evening out and refining.

1. munabbaq — said of palm trees whose planting is level and evenly set; one says nabbaqahu, its owner set it evenly. The same is said of anything level and refined.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Tell how their loads departed by night ... like palms of the outlying lands, not planted evenly.

Perhaps al-nabiq, the fruit of the lote-tree (sidr), comes from this. And one says — though it is anomalous from this root — anbaqa al-rajul, said when he passed wind gently, without force.
نبك: The letters nūn, bā' and kāf are a word indicating a rise and a fall in the ground. One says nabaka, plural nibāk.
نبل:
The letters nūn, bā' and lām are a sound root indicating excellence and greatness; skill in work is then borrowed from it metaphorically, so that excellence in a person is called nubl.

1. al-nabal — large clods of earth and stones; one says nabal and nubal. It occurs in a hadith: "Prepare the nabal." Some say that here al-nabal means small stones, and that the word is one of the contronyms — a word carrying two opposite meanings.
2. nabbilnī — as in nabbilnī aḥjāran li'l-istinjā', "give me stones to clean myself with," and nabbilnī ʿarqan, "give me a bone with meat on it."

The evidence that it means small ones is the saying of a poet, in a line of verse:
Am I to rejoice at being bereaved of noble men, and left instead with scrawny, hard-used she-camels, small ones (nabalā)?

If the word is indeed one of the contronyms, then the less common sense is the one that departs from the regular pattern.

3. al-nābil — one skilled in a matter; the verbal noun is al-nabāla.
4. fulānun anbalu al-nāsi bi'l-ibil — so-and-so is the most skilled of people with camels, meaning the most knowing of what benefits them.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
He let himself down onto her by ropes, made fast, firm in his instruction — a skilled handler, and son of a skilled handler.

This chapter has another sense too, indicating the throwing and casting-off of a thing, and its being of little weight.

5. al-nabl — Arabian arrows.
6. al-nābil — the owner of the arrows.
7. al-nabbāl — the one who makes them.
8. nabaltuhu — I shot him with an arrow.
9. tanabbala al-baʿīr — the camel died.
10. al-nabīla — a carcass, named so because it is cast off.

Close to this sense: nabala al-ibila yanbuluhā — he drove the camels forcefully.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Do not linger over the she-camels — drive them on.
نبه:
The letters nūn, bā' and hā' are a sound root indicating rising and elevation.

1. al-nubh and al-intibāh — wakefulness, and the rising up out of sleep; one says nabbahtuhu and anbahtuhu, I woke him.
2. rajulun nabīh — a distinguished, noble man.

They say that al-nabah is one of the contronyms: one says nabah for a thing lost and nabah for a thing found. In our view this is sound, because when a thing is lost, attention (intibāh) is drawn to it, and when it is found, attention is likewise drawn to it. The lexicographers said: al-nabah is a stray thing found through inattention — one says "wajadtu hādhā al-shay'a nabahan," I found this thing by chance, and "adlaltuhu nabahan," I lost it without knowing when it strayed. The underlying sense of the chapter is what we have mentioned.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
As though it were a silver bracelet, found by chance, broken, in a playground of the tribe's young women.
نبهرج:
It is not sound Arabic, and for that reason no analogy has been sought for it. Al-bahraj is the poor, inferior thing. One says "a bahraj land," when it has no one to protect it. And "bahraja" a thing, when he took it by other than the proper way. And if there were in it a line of verse as evidence, it would be like their saying "al-samarraj" — and it is nothing.

Among what has an added letter is (al-barzakh), the barrier between two things, as though between them were a barāz, that is, an open expanse of land, then every barrier came to be called a barzakh. So the khā’ is an added letter, for the reason we have mentioned.

And of this chapter is (al-birdis), the wicked man. The bā’ is added, and it is really from al-rads, that is, to plunge headlong into affairs, like al-mirdās, which is the heavy rock. Already explained in its place.

Among this is (balḍhama), when he grew afraid and fell silent. The bā’ is added, and it is really from "laḍhima," when he clung to his place from fear, not moving.

Among this is (birqi‘), the name of the lowest heaven. The bā’ is added, and the root is rā’, qāf and ‘ayn, because every heaven is a raqī‘, and the heavens are arqi‘a.

Among this is (bar‘ama) the plant, when its heads became round. The origin is bara‘a, when it grew tall. And from this...
نبو:
The letters nūn, bā' and the weak letter (wāw) are a sound root indicating a thing's rising above another, or its drawing away from it.

1. nabā baṣaruhu ʿan al-shay' yanbū — his eyesight recoiled from the thing.
2. nabā al-sayfu ʿan al-ḍarība — the sword glanced off the target struck, not cutting into it.
3. nabā bihi manziluhu — his dwelling did not suit him, and likewise his bedding; one also says nabā janbuhu ʿan al-firāsh, his side recoiled from the bedding.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
My side indeed recoils from the bedding ... like the shying-off of a wounded one upon the rocky hillocks.

It is said that the Prophet's (peace and blessings be upon him) name al-Nabī comes from al-nabwa, elevation, as though he were raised above other people by the loftiness of his rank. They also say that al-nabī means the road, the path.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
The fine dust of gravel would have covered it entirely ... in place of the path from al-Kāthib.
نتأ:
The letters nūn, tā' and hamza are a sound root indicating a thing's coming out of its place without fully separating from it.

1. nata'a al-shay' — the thing came out of its place without fully detaching; yanta'u.
2. nata'ati al-jilda — the skin bulged.

They extend the word until they say: nata'tu ʿalā al-qawm — I came upon the people unexpectedly. Nata'ati al-jāriya — the girl reached puberty. Some mention nata'a lī fulānun bi'l-sharr, said when he made himself ready [to do me harm]; that fits the same underlying sense, as though he had risen up from where he lay in wait.

It is among their proverbs: "You belittle him, yet he rises up (yanta'u) against you" — meaning: you look down on him for his stillness, while he in fact rises against you, grappling.
نتب:
The letters nūn, tā' and bā' are nothing — not a real root, because the bā' in it is extra. They say: nataba al-shay', like nahada (it swelled, rose up).

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Her two breasts rose above the chest ... not yet past the budding stage in their swelling (al-nutūb).

He meant al-nutūw [the proper form], but added a letter for the rhyme. God knows best.
نتج:
The letters nūn, tā' and jīm are a single word: al-nitāj, the bringing forth of young.

1. nutijat al-nāqa — the she-camel was delivered of her young; and nataja-hā ahluhā, her owners assisted her delivery.
2. farasun natūj — a mare whose foaling has become apparent.
نتح:
The letters nūn, tā' and ḥā'.

1. nataḥa al-ʿaraq — the sweat oozed out.
2. manātiḥ al-ʿaraq — the places the sweat comes out from.
3. nataḥa al-niḥy — the skin [used for butter] oozed, likewise.
نتخ:
The letters nūn, tā' and khā' are a word indicating the pulling of one thing out of another.

1. nataḵha al-shawkata min al-rijl bi'l-mintākh, that is, bi'l-minqāsh — he pulled the thorn out of his foot with the mintākh, meaning the tweezers.
2. nataḵha al-bāzī al-laḥma bi-minsarihi — the hawk tore the flesh out with its beak.
3. nataḵha ḍirsahu — he pulled out his tooth.

Zuhayr said, in a line of verse:
It leaves its young ones at every stopping-place, their eyes torn at by eagles and vultures.

4. al-mutanattikh — the one who picks the lice off himself.
5. al-bisāṭ al-mantūkh bi'l-dhahab — the carpet woven through with gold thread.
6. al-natkh — weaving, according to Ibn al-A'rābī.
نتر:
The letters nūn, tā' and rā' are a word indicating the pulling of a thing.

1. al-natr — a rough, harsh pull.
2. al-ṭaʿn al-natr — a stabbing thrust like a swift snatch (al-khals).
3. al-nawātir — bows.

They say that al-natar means ruin and loss, and recite:
This affair of yours — guard it well, lest it come to natar.

But the underlying sense is what we have mentioned, as though the affair had been wrenched away from soundness.
نتغ:
The letters nūn, tā' and ghayn are nothing — not a real root, being merely imitative of a sound. 1. antagha al-rajul — said when a man laughed the laugh of one who mocks.
2. nataghtuhu — said when you found fault with him and described him with what was not in him.

Abū Bakr said: a man is mintagh, one much given to that.
نتف:
The letters nūn, tā' and fā' are a root indicating the plucking-out of a thing.

1. nataf al-shaʿr — he plucked the hair, and other things; yantifuhu.
2. al-mintāf — the tweezers.
3. al-nutāfa — what falls from a thing when it is plucked.
4. al-nutfa — what you pluck with your fingers from a plant or other thing.
5. rajulun nutafa — a man who plucks a little from knowledge without mastering it thoroughly.
نتق:
The letters nūn, tā' and qāf are a root indicating the pulling, shaking loose, and uprooting of something from its base.

1. nataqtu al-gharb min al-bi'r, I pulled the bucket up out of the well.
2. when a camel's load shifts loose, its rope-loops natiqa, pulled loose — that being their being pulled so that they slacken.
3. a woman called nātiq has many children. This is the pattern of the chapter, as though children were pulled out from her. A poet said, in a line of verse:
They were not deprived of good nourishment, and their mother ... poured down upon you offspring from a fertile, prolific womb.
And in the hadith: "Take to marrying young virgins, for they are more fertile in their wombs."
4. a fire-stick called nātiq is one that catches fire well — and that is the pattern of the chapter.
نتك: The letters nūn, tā' and kāf. Al-natk — it is among the Yemeni words recorded by Abū Bakr. He said: it resembles al-natf, plucking.
نتل:
The letters nūn, tā' and lām are a sound root indicating going ahead and outstripping.

1. istantala al-rajul — the man went ahead of his companions; a man was named Nātil from this.
2. nataltuhu — I pulled him forward.
3. tanātala al-nabt — the plants did not grow evenly, some taller than others, as though the taller ones had gone ahead of the shorter and outstripped them.

4. al-natal — a huge, powerful servant, explained thus: he is strong enough to go ahead in what others are too weak for. Do you not see the saying of the rājiz-poet:
They circle around a huge one, an agile one (natalin wa-zawāzin).

He described him as zawāz, meaning light and agile.
نث:
The letters nūn and thā' are a sound root denoting the spreading and dissemination of a thing.

1. nathth al-ḥadīth — spreading a report, divulging it.
2. jā'a yanithth siman — he came dripping with fatness, as though oozing it.

And in the hadith: "one of them comes 'nathth'-ing, as the [old, greasy] waterskin oozes."
نثا: The letters nūn, thā' and the weak letter are a word. One says nathā al-kalām yanthū — he made the speech known, spread it about. Al-nathā, they say, is that a person be spoken of unfavorably.
نثر:
The letters nūn, thāʾ, and rāʾ are a sound root pointing to throwing a thing so that it scatters. Nathara al-darāhima, he scattered the coins, and so with other things. Nathharat al-shātu: the ewe cast discharge from its nose. The nose is called al-nathra from this, because it casts out through it whatever is harmful. It came in the hadith: "when you perform ablution, then blow the water out through your nose (fa-ntathir)," or in the other reading "fa-nthir" — meaning: put the water into your nathra, your nostrils.

Al-nathra is also a star, said to be the lion's nose, that the moon passes through. Ṭaʿanahu fa-antharahu: he struck him and threw him down onto his face — this fits the pattern. A poet said:
Upon her is a horseman worth ten — when he sees a rider of some people, he throws him down on his face (antharahu).
It is also said anṭarahu [in another reading]: made him bleed from the nose.

Al-nathra is also a coat of mail, and this may possibly be outside the root we have named.
نثل:
The letters nūn, thā' and lām are a root indicating the extraction of a thing from a thing, or its coming out from it.

1. nathaltu kinānatī — I emptied my quiver, taking out what arrows were in it.
2. nathaltu al-bi'r — I dug out the earth of the well.
3. al-nathīl — dung.
4. al-nathīla — the earth dug out of a well. The underlying sense is one and the same.
نج:
The letters nūn and jīm are a sound root denoting movement, agitation, and the like.

1. al-najnaja — the wheeling about in fright. One says: they 'najnaja'-d.
2. al-najnaja [second sense] — going back and forth over an opinion.
3. tanajnajū — they stayed on where they had settled to graze in spring, then resolved to move on toward water.
4. tanajnaja laḥmuhu — his flesh grew slack.
5. najjat al-qurḥa — the sore discharged.
نجب:
The letters nūn, jīm and bā' are two roots: one indicates the purity and nobility of a thing, the other, weakness.

The first:
1. al-najāba — the verbal noun of al-najīb, the noble man, meaning the generous one.
2. intajaba fulānan — he singled him out and chose him.
3. rajulun munjib — a man who has a noble son.
4. imra'atun munjiba and minjāb — [a woman likewise, whose child is noble].
5. rajulun najb — generous, noble.

The other: al-minjāb, the weak man, plural manājīb.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Since he preferred sleep and warmth — the weak ones (al-manājīb).

1. al-minjāb — an arrow-shaft trimmed but not fledged with feathers.
2. al-najab — what is above the bark, the outer rind of a tree's covering.
3. al-najb — the taking of it.
نجث:
The letters nūn, jīm and thā' are a minor root indicating the bringing-out of a thing, and a shameful matter.

1. al-najītha — what is brought up out of the earth of a well.
2. badā najīth al-qawm — what the people used to conceal of some shameful matter became apparent.
3. al-najīth — a target set up [as a mark]. Al-Khalīl said it is called najīth because it stands erect.

4. huwa yanjuthu banī fulānin — said when he calls on them to come to his aid, appealing to them, meaning that he asks them to come forward in his support.
5. al-istinjāth — dedicating oneself to a matter, setting out for it.

The underlying sense in all of it is one and the same. God knows best.
نجح:
The letters nūn, jīm and ḥā' are a root indicating attainment, truthfulness and good.

1. al-najāḥ fī al-ḥawā'ij — success in one's needs, attaining them.
2. sayrun najīḥ — a swift journey.
3. ra'yun najīḥ — a sound opinion.
4. tanājaḥat aḥlāmuhum — their dreams came true one after another, truly.
5. anjaḥa Allāhu ṭalibataka — God granted you swift attainment of your request.
نجخ:
The letters nūn, jīm and khā' are a word indicating the imitation of a sound.

1. samiʿtu najīkha al-mā'i wa-nājikhatahu — I heard the sound of the water.
2. al-nujākh — the sound of one coughing.
3. Manjakh — a place-name.
نجد:
The letters nūn, jīm and dāl are a single root indicating rising up, strength, and prominence.

1. al-najd — the courageous man. Najuda al-rajul yanjudu najdatan, when a man became courageous; he is najd, najud, najid, and najīd. Courage is najda. Al-munājid is the fighter. Fulānun lāqā najdatan, so-and-so met with hardship, a distressing matter. Ṭarafa said, in a line of verse:
You would think a glance falling upon her brings hardship ... alas, my people, for youth's exuberant vigor!
That is, the onlooker who looks at her is struck by a kind of distress on account of it, as though he meant the softness and delicacy of her body.
2. al-najad — sweat. Najida najadan, he sweated from exertion or distress. A poet said, in a line of verse:
The sailor, from fear of it, remains clinging ... to the steering-oar, after exhaustion and sweat.
Sometimes they say nujida, so he is manjūd. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Thirsting, crying for help, ungranted ... he had indeed been the very refuge of the distressed.
One says: istanjadtuhu fa-anjadanī, I called on him for help and he helped me. In this is a sense of rising above the opponent.
3. al-najūd — the tall, prominent one among wild donkeys.
4. istanjada fulānun, so-and-so grew strong after weakness.
5. najadtu al-rajula anjuduhu, I overcame the man — Ibn al-Sikkīt related this.
6. al-najd — what is elevated of the land; anjada, he rose up from low ground to elevated ground.
7. huwa najdun fī al-ḥāja, he is quick and deft in the matter.
8. al-nijād — the sword's baldric, because it rises up over the shoulder.
9. al-najd — what a house is furnished with of goods.
10. al-tanjīd — adornment, decoration; al-najd — also the elevated road.
11. al-munajjad — one whom time has najjada, seasoned, when he has come to know and have experience, as though it emboldened and strengthened him. And that is the pattern for each one of these senses.
نجذ:
The letters nūn, jīm and dhāl are a single word: al-nājidh, the tooth between the canine and the molars.

1. al-munajjadh — a man metaphorically so called, meaning the experienced one.
2. badat nawājidhuhu fī ḍaḥikihi — his back teeth showed in his laughter.

They say that all the molars are called nawājidh, and this, in our view, is the correct one, on the strength of al-Shammākh's words, in a line of verse:
Their back teeth (nawājidhuhunna), like the swooping kite.

And because they say "ḍaḥika ḥattā badā nājidhuhu," he laughed until his nājidh showed — for if it were only the tooth between the canine and the molars, this would not be said of it, since that tooth shows from the very slightest laugh.
نجر:
The letters nūn, jīm and rā' are two roots: one indicates the evening-out of a thing and the correcting of its measure; the other is a kind of illness.

The first: najr al-khashab, the carpentry of wood, that is, najarahu najran.

1. al-najjār — the carpenter, named from this, as though it were a thing evened out.
2. al-najr — [a person's] natural disposition.
3. najrān al-bāb — the wooden pivot the door turns on (though I do not know how sound this is).

The second root, al-najar:
1. najirat al-ibil — the camels became thirsty (also said majirat) — meaning they drink without being satisfied, which comes from eating al-ḥibba [a certain seed].
2. al-najrān — the thirsty one, as al-Khalīl related.
3. shahru Nājir — the month Nājir is named from this, because the camels become thirsty (tanjuru) in it.
4. al-najar — Ibn al-Sikkīt said it is that a person drinks sour milk and is not satisfied by water afterward.
نجز:
The letters nūn, jīm and zā' are a sound root indicating the completion of a thing swiftly, without delay.

1. najaza al-waʿdu yanjuzu — the promise was fulfilled.
2. anjaztuhu anā — I hastened it, carried it out promptly.
3. aʿṭaytuhu mā ʿindī ḥattā najaza ākhiruhu — I gave him all I had until the last of it was reached.
4. biʿhu nājizan bi-nājizin — sell it cash for cash, as in their saying "yadan bi-yad," promptly for promptly.
5. al-munājaza fī al-ḥarb — in war, that the two horsemen meet in single combat, that is, hasten to fight without holding back.
نجس:
The letters nūn, jīm and sīn are a sound root indicating the opposite of purity. A thing called najis or najas is unclean; al-najas is filth. It is not far-fetched that from this comes their saying: al-nājis is a disease with no cure. Sā'ida al-Hudhalī said, in a line of verse:
Old age is an incurable disease, with no remedy for it ... for a man who was once sound, unerring in his afflictions.
As though when it lingers long with a person, it najisahu, or najjasahu — that is, made him unclean, or rendered him unclean.

As for al-tanjīs, it was something the Arabs used to do: they would hang on a child something to protect him with a charm against the jinn — perhaps a bone or something similar — and for that it was called tanjīs. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And the one who casts charms hung unclean things upon me.
نجش:
The letters nūn, jīm and shīn are a sound root indicating the stirring-up of a thing.

1. al-najsh — that you raise the bid on goods for sale with a high price, so the onlooker notices and is drawn to buy — this is what came in the hadith: "Do not practice najsh with each other," as though al-nājish stirs up that increase.
2. al-nājish — the one who flushes out game.
3. najashtu al-ṣayd — I flushed out the game.
4. najasha al-ibila yanjushuhā — he gathered the camels together after they had scattered.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
[Nothing] but the night-journey and the driver who stirs [them] on (al-najjāsh).

5. al-nijāsha — swiftness of walking; one says marra yanjushu najīshan, he went by moving swiftly, as though it meant he stirs up the dust in his walking.

It is said that the name al-Najāshī is derived from this.
نجع:
The letters nūn, jīm and ʿayn are a sound root indicating the benefit food or medicine has in the body; it is then extended more broadly and reasoned on by analogy.

1. najaʿa al-ṭaʿām — the food agreed with the one who ate it.
2. mā'un najūʿ — like namīr, water that nourishes and builds up the body. Ibn al-Sikkīt said: najaʿa fīhi al-dawā', the medicine took effect in him, and najaʿa fī al-dābba al-ʿalaf, the fodder benefited the animal; one does not say anjaʿa.
3. al-nujʿa — the seeking of pasture, because it is the seeking of what benefits (yanjaʿu); intajaʿahu, he sought its good.
4. al-najīʿ — the pounded leaves (khabaṭ) mixed with flour and water and given to the young camel to drink.
5. najaʿa fī fulānin qawluka — your word took effect on him.

Anomalous to this chapter: al-najīʿ — blood from deep in the body, inclining toward black.
نجف:
The letters nūn, jīm and fā' are two sound roots: one indicates spreading out over a place or other thing, the other the extraction of a thing.

The first: al-najaf, a long, level stretch of ground unreached by water, plural nijāf. It is said to be low-lying tracts of land, level at their bottom, running along the ground, having valleys that drain into softer ground. The flank of a sand dune is called najafat al-kathīb.

1. al-najīf, of arrows — the broad one.
2. najaftu al-sahm — I trimmed the arrow and straightened it accordingly; sahmun manjūf and najīf describe such an arrow.
3. ghārun manjūf — a wide cave.

The second: tays manjūf, a billy-goat whose penis is bound so it cannot mate, as though its fluid had been cut off and drawn out of it.

1. al-intijāf — the drawing-out of the milk in the udder.
2. al-manjūf — one cut off from intercourse.
3. intajafat al-rīḥ al-saḥāb — the wind passed over the clouds and drained them.
نجل:
The letters nūn, jīm and lām are two sound roots: one indicates the throwing of a thing, the other, breadth in a thing.

The first: al-najl, your throwing of a thing; one says najala najlan.

1. al-nāqa tanjulu al-ḥaṣā bi-manāsimihā najlan — the she-camel flings the pebbles with her feet, that is, throws them.
2. najaltu al-rajula najlatan — I struck him with the front of my foot so that he rolled over.

Their saying "man najala al-nāsa najalūhu" means: whoever provokes people, they provoke him back; whoever throws at them, they throw back at him.

3. al-najl — offspring, because the mother, as it were, casts it forth.
4. faḥlun nājil — noble in his offspring; they say "qabbaḥa Allāhu nājilayhi," meaning his two parents.
5. al-najl — seeping moisture, as though it were dew the earth exuded and cast forth.

The second root: al-najal, width of the eye, becomingly.

1. al-nujl — the plural of anjal.
2. al-asadu anjal — the lion is anjal, wide-eyed.
3. ṭaʿnatun najlā' — a wide wound.
4. rumḥun minjal — a spear that makes a wide wound.
5. najaltu al-ihāb — I split the hide open along both hocks together, as hides are flayed; ihābun manjūl.
6. It is said that al-Injīl [the Gospel] is an Arabic word derived from najaltu al-shay', I drew the thing out, as though it were a matter brought forth and made manifest by what is in it.

Anomalous to both these roots: al-najīl, a kind of tree-leaf, of the salt-plants (al-ḥamḍ). Anjalati al-arḍ — the ground turned green.
نجم:
The letters nūn, jīm and mīm are a sound root that points to rising up and coming into view. Najama al-najm — the star rose. Najama al-sinn wa-l-qarn — the tooth and the horn came up. Al-najm is the Pleiades, a name for it; and when they say 'the najm has risen', it is the Pleiades they mean.

And one says: this report has no najm, that is, no origin and no place of rising. Al-najm among plants is what has no stalk, from najama, to come up. Al-minjam in a balance is the crosswise iron in which the tongue of the balance sits; and that is the same analogy.
نجه:
The letters nūn, jīm and hā' are a word indicating aversion to a thing.

1. najahtuhu — said when you confront someone with what he dislikes and repel him from you with it.
2. rajulun nājih — a man who, entering a land, finds it strange and dislikes it.
نجو:
The letters nūn, jīm and the weak letter are two roots: one of them points to stripping off and uncovering, and the other to covering and hiding.

The first: najawtu al-jilda anjūhu — and the hide is najā — when you strip it off. And a poet said, in a line of verse:
So I said: strip yourselves from her as the hide is stripped; her hump and her withers will content you both.

And they say: he is in an arḍun najāt — land from whose trees staves are cut. Branches are called al-najā, the single one najāt; and anjinī ʿaṣan — cut me a stave. And najā al-insānu yanjū najātan, and najā'an in the matter of speed; and that is the sense of going away and getting clear of a place. And a nāqatun nājiya and najāt is a swift she-camel.

And of the section — and it is carried on what we mentioned of al-nijā' — are al-najāt and al-najwa of ground, and it is the ground that no flood rises over. A poet said, in a line of verse:
So he who is on his high ground is like him who is in his own courtyard, and the sheltered one like him who walks on open flat land.

And we said only that it is carried on it because it is as though, when it escaped the flood, it were the thing that escapes from something by going away from it; and this is the sense of what is carried on it.

And their saying baynī wa-baynahum najāwatun mina al-arḍ, that is, a wide space, is of the section, because it is a place in which one goes fast and gets clear. And in the hadith: "When you travel in a barren land, then get clear" — he means: do not go slowly in the march, but get away and pass on.

And of the section is al-najw, the cloud, and the plural is al-nijā'; and it is from its clearing away, because it does not stay. Ibn al-Sikkīt said: anjat al-saḥāba — the cloud turned away. And their saying istanjā fulānun — they said it is from al-najwa, as though a man, when he wants to relieve himself, comes to a rise of ground that screens him; so it was said of the one who wants that, istanjā, just as they said taghawwaṭa, that is, he went to a low hollow.

And of the section is najawtu fulānan — I smelled his breath — as though you wanted to uncover some state in him. A poet said, in a line of verse:
I smelled Mujālid's breath and found in it something like the smell of a dog dead not long since.

The other root: al-najw and al-najwā, the secret between two. And nājaytuhu — I spoke secretly with him — and tanājaw, and intajaw. And he is najiyyu fulān, the one he confides in, and the plural is anjiya. A poet said:
When the people were groups of confiding friends —

He says: the people slept and dreamed in their sleep, so that it was as though they were confiding with their families in sleep. And najawtuhu — I spoke secretly with him. And intajaytuhu — I singled him out for my confiding. A poet said, in a line of verse:
So I passed the night confiding to her a soul that lays on me what the sluggish, cautious man does not trouble himself with.
نح:
The letters nūn and ḥā' are a word imitating a sound.

1. al-tanaḥnuḥ — throat-clearing, well known.
2. al-naḥīḥ — a sound a person repeats within himself.

And a word was reported whose soundness we do not know, and it has no regular derivation: they say, mā anā bi-naḥīḥi al-nafsi ʿan kadhā — meaning, [not] content in myself about such-and-such.
نحب:
The letters nūn, ḥā' and bā' are two roots. One points to a vow, and to what resembles it of risking or staking something; the other to a sound among sounds.

The first: al-naḥb is the vow. "sāra fulānun 'alā naḥbin" is said of a man when he pushes himself hard, as if he had staked something and then applied himself to it. A poet said, in a line of verse:
As the one who staked his hand went forth
meaning al-mukhāṭir, the one who risks. There was among the Arabs a practice called al-tanḥīb, which was like wagering: one would say, if such-and-such happens then you owe me such-and-such, and if not I owe you. Islam came and forbade it. From this comes "nāḥabtuhu ilā fulānin", meaning I brought a dispute with him before so-and-so for judgment. The underlying sense in both is the same. And likewise al-naḥb is death, as if it were a vow a person makes that he must keep, and from which he cannot escape.

The other root is al-naḥīb — the wailing of one who weeps, that is, his weeping together with voice and loud lament. From this comes al-nuḥāb, the coughing of camels; naḥaba al-ba'īru yanḥabu, the camel coughed in this way.
نحت:
The letters nūn, ḥā', and tā' are a word indicating the carving of something and its smoothing with an iron tool.

1. naḥata al-najjāru al-khashaba yanḥituhā naḥtan — the carpenter carved the wood.
2. al-naḥīta — a person's nature, meaning the condition he was 'carved' upon, like the instinct he was formed with.
3. nuḥāta — what falls away from a carved thing, the shavings.
نحر:
The letters nūn, ḥā' and rā' are a single word from which the words of this chapter branch. It is al-naḥr — the throat, of a person or anything else; the plural is nuḥūr.

1. al-naḥr — also the cutting made at the throat. naḥartu al-ba'īr naḥran — I slaughtered the camel by cutting its throat.
2. al-nāḥirān — two veins in a horse's chest.
3. dā'irat al-nāḥir — a whorl of hair that lies on the underside of the neck, below that place.
4. intaḥarū 'alā al-shay' — they competed fiercely over a thing out of greed, as if each of them wanted to cut his companion's throat over it.
5. al-naḥīra — the last day of the month, because it "cuts the throat of" the day that follows and enters — I think the meaning of "cuts its throat" is that it comes right before it.
6. nihrīr — one who knows a thing well through experience. This too, if it follows the same reasoning, is because he has mastered the knowledge thoroughly, as you say "qataltu hādhā al-shay' 'ilman" — I have this thing killed through knowledge, meaning I have mastered it completely.
نحز:
The letters nūn, ḥā' and zā' are two sound roots: one carries the meaning of piercing and pounding, the other the meaning of an extension in a thing.

The first is piercing.

1. al-naḥz — piercing. One says naḥazahu naḥzan, he pierced it. The rider naḥzes with his chest the middle of the saddle. I naḥazed the she-camel with my foot, meaning I kicked her.
2. al-nāḥiz — when the elbow strikes the callus on a camel's chest (al-kirkira); one says the camel has nāḥiz.
3. al-nuḥāz — a disease that takes camels in their lungs.

The reasoning in both is one.

1. naḥaza the thing — he pounded it.
2. al-minḥāz — a thing in which things are pounded.

The other root:

1. al-naḥīza — a stripe of ground that stretches out, about a farsakh long.
2. al-naḥā'iz — woven things like bundles and broad strips, made for pack-saddles.

They also say al-naḥīza is a person's nature. What we say is that al-naḥīza is used by way of comparison: what is meant by it is the state a person is in, as if he had been woven upon it. So they say, huwa ḍaʿīfu l-naḥīza — he is weak in his naḥīza — meaning this state of his is weak.
نحس:
The letters nūn, ḥāʾ, and sīn are a single root pointing to the opposite of good fortune. Nuḥisa huwa, fa-huwa manḥūs: he was made unlucky, so he is unlucky. Al-nuḥās is smoke without flame in it. A poet said:
... devils, whose stray one is pelted with smoke (nuḥās)
And al-nuḥās, copper, among these metals — as though, because it fell short of the noble metals such as gold and silver, it was named nuḥās; this is offered as a possibility. One says yawmun naḥsun and yawmun naḥisun, an inauspicious day. It was recited: {in days of misfortune} [Fuṣṣilat: 16], both as naḥisāt and naḥsāt.

It is also possible that al-nuḥās is the underlying substance, as some have said, and since it was the base of many other metals, the underlying substance of anything came to be called nuḥās.
نحص:
The letters nūn, ḥā' and ṣād are a single word: it is al-naḥūṣ, the barren she-donkey, in a verse of Imru' al-Qays. He said, in a line of verse:
It brayed loudly over him, drawing near, and there leaned toward him — long in the pasterns of her forelegs — a barren she-donkey.
نحض:
The letters nūn, ḥā' and ḍād are a single word: it is flesh. Flesh is called naḥḍ.

1. naḥīḍa — a fleshy woman, abundant in flesh; when her flesh goes she becomes manḥūḍa. This is from their saying naḥaḍtu al-ʿaẓm, I stripped the bone of the flesh on it.
2. naḥaḍtu al-sinān — I thinned the spearhead, as if, in thinning it, you took its naḥḍ away from it.
نحط:
The letters nūn, ḥā' and ṭā' are a word that indicates the imitation of a sound.

1. al-naḥīṭ — like a sigh (al-zafīr).
2. al-naḥḥāṭ — a proud man who naḥīṭs from rage.
3. al-naḥṭa — a disease that takes camels in the chest, from which they naḥīṭ, and they hardly recover from it.
نحف: The letters nūn, ḥā' and fā' are a word that indicates thinness and wasting, as in naḥufa al-rajul, he became thin (naḥāfa), so he is naḥīf — when his flesh grows little and he is emaciated. They are niḥāf.
نحل:
The letters nūn, ḥā' and lām are three words. The first indicates thinness and emaciation, the second giving, and the third laying claim to something.

The first: *naḥala jismuhu nuḥūlan*, so he is *nāḥil*, when it grows thin; *anḥalahu al-hamm*, worry made him thin. *An-nawāḥil* — swords whose cutting-edges have grown thin from much striking.

The second: *naḥaltuhu kadhā*, meaning: I gave it to him; the noun is *an-nuḥl*. Abū Bakr said: the thing given is called *an-nuḥlān*. They say *an-nuḥl* is to give a thing without seeking anything in return. *naḥaltu l-mar'ata mahrahā niḥlatan* — I gave the woman her dowry out of the goodness of my heart, with no claim attached; so the commentators explained His saying, exalted is He: {and give the women their dowries as a *niḥla*, a free gift} [an-Nisā': 4].

The third: their saying *intaḥala kadhā*, when he took a thing up and claimed it as his own. Some said: *intaḥalahu* is when he claims it truthfully, and *tanaḥḥalahu* is when he claims it falsely. This, to our mind, is nothing — the meaning of *intaḥala* and *tanaḥḥala* is, to us, the same. The proof of that is al-A'shā's saying, in a line of verse:
How, then, am I — with my laying claim to verses ... after grey hair? That alone is disgrace enough.
نحو:
The letters nūn, ḥā' and wāw are a word that indicates intent. I naḥawtu his direction (naḥwahu). For that reason the grammar of speech (naḥw al-kalām) is so named, because it aims at the foundations of speech, so one speaks according to how the Arabs used to speak. It is said that Banū Naḥw are a people among the Arabs. As for [the people of] al-manḥāh, it has been said: they are the distant people, not relatives.

From this chapter: intaḥā fulānun li-fulān — so-and-so aimed himself at so-and-so, seeking him and confronting him.
نحي: The letters nūn, ḥā' and yā' are a single word: it is al-niḥy, a skin vessel for clarified butter.
نخ:
The letters nūn and khā' are a sound root, though its meaning is disputed. It is al-nukhkha, in the hadith of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him and his family: "There is no alms-due on al-jabha, nor on al-nukhkha."

1. al-nakhkha — some said: slaves.
2. al-nakhkha [second explanation] — al-Farrā' said: it is the tax-collector taking a dinar for himself once he has finished collecting the alms. But the wording does not require this reading — perhaps what al-Farrā' transmitted was "wa-lā nakhkhata." And he recited: my paternal uncle, who openly refused the dinar — the dinar of the nakhkha of [the tribe of] Kalb, and it is well attested.
3. al-nukhkha [also said] — donkeys, the nūn said either with fatḥa or ḍamma.
4. tanakhnakha al-baʿīr — Abū Bakr said: the camel knelt down, then settled its knee-pads firmly into the ground.
نخب:
The letters nūn, khā' and bā' are a word that indicates a kind of grandness. It is said that one of its two senses concerns the best of a thing, and the other concerns a perforation and a hollow in a thing.

The first:
1. al-nukhba — the best of a thing, also nukhbatuhu; intakhabtuhu means I selected it, and it is muntakhab, chosen. Abū Zayd said: al-nakhba is a huge draught of drink.

The other root:
1. al-nukhba — the opening of al-thafr, the female genital opening.
2. nakhabahā — he had intercourse with her.
3. istankhabat al-mar'a — said of a woman when she desires intercourse.
4. al-nakhb — a man who has no heart.
5. al-nakhīb — one who has lost his mind.

This may be thought to belong to the first sense, as if he were denied the nukhba, the best part of a person.
نخج: The letters nūn, khā' and jīm are a single word. They say: al-nakhj is the flood-water that runs in the bank of the valley until it scours it away. And by analogy with this one says nāḵajahā, meaning he had intercourse with her.
نخر:
The letters nūn, khā' and rā' are a sound root pointing to a sound among sounds, from which further words branch.

1. al-nakhīr — a sound that comes out of the two nostrils; the two nostrils (al-mankhirān) were named from the nakhīr that comes out of them.
2. al-nukhratān — branching from this, the two openings of the nose.
3. al-nakhūr — a she-camel that will not give milk until a finger is put into her nostril.
4. al-nukhra — they also use this for the nose itself, and for a blast of wind.

As for the rotten tree and the rotten bone, they too are called nakhira from this same root, because such wood becomes hollow and the wind enters it, and at that point it makes a nukhra, that is, a sound. They call anything decayed and worn-out al-nakhir. Al-nākhir is that which the wind enters and leaves, and which has a nakhīr. In all of this the underlying sense is one, in our view. "mā bihā nākhir", meaning "there is no one [there]", uses the word to mean one who makes a sound.

Close to this is al-nakhwarī, one wide in the urethra, as if it were something the wind enters, making a nukhra.
نخس:
The letters nūn, khā' and sīn are a word that indicates piercing something with something sharp. One says nakhasahu bi-ʿūdin aw ḥadīdatin nakhsan — he pierced it with a stick or a piece of iron.

1. al-nakhkhās — the livestock dealer, named from this.
2. al-nākhis — mange that appears at a camel's tail or its chest, as if it had been pierced there; a camel affected by it is mankhūs.

What is anomalous to this chapter is al-nakhīsa.
نخش: The letters nūn, khā' and shīn: they say nukhisha, so one is mankhūsh, meaning he became emaciated.
نخط:
The letters nūn, khā' and ṭā': they say intakhaṭa min anfihi, he blew it from his nose, as though it were a substitution and the true letter is mīm.
A poet said, in a line of verse:
They blew it out at the blue flies of high summer.
And I do not know which of the nakhṭ this refers to — meaning, which of the people who did the intikhāṭ.
نخع:
The letters nūn, khā' and ʿayn are a root that indicates the pure inner part of a thing, its core.

1. al-nukhāʿ — a thick white vein that lies within the vertebrae of the neck, that is, the spinal cord. From it a verb branches: one says nakhaʿahu, when the slaughtering cut passes through to the nukhāʿ; an animal so cut is manḵūʿa. In the hadith: "The most nakhaʿ of names before God is that a man name himself with the name of the King of kings" — meaning the most deadly of names for the one who carries it.
2. al-manḵaʿ — the joint of the occipital bone between the neck and the head, on the inside; it too belongs to al-nukhāʿ, because it runs through it.
3. al-nākhiʿ — their word for the learned man, if it is sound, also belongs here, as if he had reached the pure inner part of knowledge. They recite, in a line of verse:
The one who settled her — his affair was secret, but it has now been made plain to al-nākhiʿ.
4. nakhiʿa al-ʿūd — water ran through the wood, as if it had reached its nukhāʿ.
5. nakhaʿa al-naṣīḥa — he made his advice pure and sincere.
6. al-nukhāʿa — the same as al-nukhāma, phlegm.
7. intakhaʿa al-rajul ʿan arḍihi — he grew distant from his land. This too, in our view, belongs to this root, as if he had reached its nukhāʿ on his journey, the way al-nākhiʿ reaches the limit in slaughtering a sheep.
8. nakhaʿa lī fulānun bi-ḥaqqī — so-and-so admitted my right to me, like bakhaʿa. Ibn al-Aʿrābī related this; it runs the course of substitution.
نخف: The letters nūn, khā' and fā' are a word: they say nakhafat al-ʿanzu bi-anfihā, like nafaṭat, the she-goat snorted through her nose. And they say al-nakhf is the raised, audible breath.
نخل:
The letters nūn, khā' and lām are a word pointing to the picking out of a thing and the choosing of it.

And intakhaltuhu means I went to the utmost until I took the best of it. And in our view the date palm, al-nakhl, was named with this because it is the noblest of every tree that has a trunk; the single one is a nakhla. Al-nakhl is also your sifting of the flour with the sieve, al-munkhul, and what falls from it is nukhāla, bran. And al-nakhl is a kind of ornament made in the shape of a palm tree. A poet said, in a line of verse:
She has clothed herself in hare-fur and in palm-shaped ornaments.
نخم: The letters nūn, khā' and mīm are a word: they say al-nukhāma is the same as al-nukhāʿa. And tanakhkhama means he nakhaʿa. Ibn Durayd said: I heard the nakhma of the man, meaning I heard his sound.
ند:
The letters nūn and dāl are a sound root indicating straying and separation. Nadda al-baʿīr naddan wa-nudūdan: the camel went off on its face, straying.

1. al-nidd and al-nadīd — one who opposes another in a matter, that is, brings an opinion different from his companion's.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Lest al-Sandarī become my rival, and I revile uncles — kinsmen upon kinsmen, whole clans of them.

2. al-nadd, as Ibn Durayd mentioned it — the mound that rises up into the sky; this comes close to fitting the root's pattern.

Al-nidd, a kind of perfume, is not an Arabic word.
ندب:
The letters nūn, dāl and bā' are three words: the first is a mark, the second is risk, and the third indicates lightness in a thing.

The first: al-nadab is the scar of a wound, plural andāb — that is when it does not rise above the skin.

The second: al-nadab is risk. Andaba nafsahu means he risked himself.
He said, in a line of verse:
...and I did not stand a day upon a nadab, while I had a risking soul.

The third root: a man who is nadb is light and agile. Al-nadb is the swift, forward-going horse. In our view, al-nadb in a legal command is close to this, because the jurists say al-nadb is what is not obligatory; if this is correct, it is because the weight of the matter is light in it.

What is not from this chapter:

1. nadb al-nādiba — the lamenting woman's eulogy for the dead, praising him well.
2. al-nadb — that you call people to a matter, and they respond (intadabū).
