ندح: The letters nūn, dāl and ḥā' are a word that indicates spaciousness in a thing. From this: al-nadḥ is a wide stretch of land, plural andāḥ. From it too is their saying laka ʿanhu mandūḥa, meaning space and room. Al-Khalīl said: a mandūḥa land is a distant, wide one. And innahu la-fī nudḥatin min al-arḍ means spaciousness and room. God knows best what is right.
ندر:
The letters nūn, dāl and rā' are a sound root that indicates the falling of a thing or the making of it fall. Nadara al-shay' means the thing fell.
Al-Hudhalī said, in a line of verse:
And when the champions traded thrusts at the kidneys, they fell like the young unbroken she-camels fall in an increased blood-price.
That is, their blood was spilled with impunity, just as young she-camels fall as forfeit in blood-money.

I meet so-and-so at al-nadra and al-nadara, meaning: you meet him only now and then across the days, as if that meeting had nadarat, fallen — that is, dropped in rarely. He struck him on his head, and his eye nadarat, meaning it came out of its place.

Their saying al-andarī — we do not think it is Arabic. But they do say:
1. al-andarūn — young men who gather from various places. They recite the saying of ʿAmr, in a line of verse: and does not leave behind the wines of al-andarīn.
2. al-andarīn — some said it is a village.
3. al-andarī — the rope. He recited: as though it were an andarī rope that dampness had touched.
4. al-andar — the threshing floor, so said by al-Khalīl.
ندس:
The letters nūn, dāl and sīn are a sound root that indicates something like nazk, stabbing, and thrusting. They say al-munādasa bi-l-rimāḥ is thrusting at each other with spears. Al-nads is thrusting.
Al-Kumayt said, in a line of verse:
We came upon the family of Najrān at dawn in a raid — Tamīm ibn Murr, and the thrusting spears.

1. al-nadus — the shrewd man, and likewise the one quick to hear a faint sound. The reasoning in these words is close.
2. nadastu bihi al-arḍ — I threw him to the ground.
3. nadastu al-shay' ʿan al-ṭarīq — I pushed the thing off the road.

Otherwise, I had simply struck him.
ندص: The letters nūn, dāl and ṣād are a word, if it is sound. They say: nadaṣat ʿaynuhu, his eye bulged and started out.
ندغ: The letters nūn, dāl and ghayn are a word, if it is sound, that indicates something like thrusting and piercing. One says nadaghahu, he thrust or stung him. Nadaghtu al-ṣabiyya, I tickled the child. And they say al-nudgha is the white mark at the end of the nail, as though something had left its trace on something.
ندف:
The letters nūn, dāl and fā' are a sound word: it is something like fluffing a thing with a tool. Nadaftu al-quṭn bi-l-mindaf, I carded the cotton with the carding-bow.

1. nadafati l-dābbatu fī sayrihā nadfan — the swiftness of the swing of her forelegs in her stride.
2. al-nadf in milking — pressing the udder-quarter with a finger.
3. nadafati l-samā'u bi-maṭarin — like naṭafat, the sky dripped with rain.
4. al-nudfa — a small amount of milk, as though it were a bit of carded cotton.
ندل:
The letters nūn, dāl and lām are a sound root that indicates transferring and disturbance. They say nadaltu al-shay' nadlan, when you transfer it. They said the derivation of al-mindīl [the towel] is from this.

1. al-nadl — pilfering, snatching. A poet said, in a line of verse: so pilfer, Zurayq, the wealth, the pilfering of foxes.
2. al-munawdil — the very old man, named for his unsteadiness.
3. nawdalat khuṣyāhu — his testicles hung slack.

What is anomalous to this chapter, if sound: al-nadl, said to mean dirt; no verb is formed from it.
ندم: The letters nūn, dāl and mīm are a word pointing to distress of mind over something already past — regret. One says nadima ʿalayhi, nadaman and nadāma. A man's drinking-companion is munādimuhu and nadīmuhu. Some said al-munādama is a metathesis of al-mudāmana, habitual indulgence in drink, but this is doubtful. Others say the two drinking-companions were so called because from one of them would come something the other later regretted, and for that they were named nadīmayn.
نده:
The letters nūn, dāl and hā' are a word that indicates driving off and restraint. One says nadahtu al-baʿīr ʿan al-ḥawḍ, I drove the camel from the trough. Nadahtu al-ibil, I drove the camels together. And they say to the divorced woman: Go, I will no longer nadah your flock.

What deviates from this chapter is al-nudha, abundance of wealth. He said: They had no wealth of nudha to benefit me.
ندي:
The letters nūn, dāl and the weak letter point to gathering together, and they may point to wetness in a thing.

The first is al-nādī and al-nadī: the meeting place, about which the people gather; and when they scatter it is no longer a nadī. And of it is Dār al-Nadwa at Mecca, because they used to gather in it, that is, come together. And nādaytuhu: I sat with him in the meeting place. He said, in a line of verse:
A young man who, if he called out to the sun, she would cast off her veil; or to the moon that journeys by night, it would throw down its keys.
And the nadwa of camels is that they go out from the drinking-place to a pasture near it, and then come back to the water the same day or the next. And likewise they go out from the salt-bush to the sweet pasture. And andā ibilahu, he took his camels out so, is from this.

And the other root is al-nadā of wetness, which is well known. One says nadan and andā', and andiya has come too, and it is odd. And sometimes they speak of fat as nadā. And he is andā than so-and-so, that is, more given to good than he. And my hand has not been wetted with anything for so-and-so that he would dislike. Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse:
I have never been wetted with a thing you dislike; and if I were, then may my hand never lift my whip to me again.
And he is yatanaddā upon his companions, that is, he is open-handed to them.

Of this section is nadā al-ṣawt: how far a voice carries. And he is andā of voice than he, that is, further carrying. He said, in a line of verse:
So I said: call you, and I shall call, for the voice that carries furthest is that two callers should call.

When it is given a hamza it changes to something pointing to streaks and marks. And al-nud'a is a streak of fat differing from the colour of the flesh. And al-nud'a is the rainbow, and the redness that comes in the cloud like the evening glow. And nada'tu al-laḥma fī al-malla: I buried the meat in the hot ashes until it was done. Abū Bakr said: and it is al-nadī', like al-ṭabīkh, the cooked thing.
نذر: The letters nūn, dhāl and rā' are a word pointing to frightening or to being afraid. From it is al-indhār, the delivering of a message — and it is hardly ever anything but in frightening. And tanādharū: they made one another afraid. And from it is al-nadhr, a vow, and that is because he fears if he breaks it. Thaʿlab said: nadhirtu bihim — I was warned of them — so I made ready for them and was on my guard against them. And al-nadhīr is the warner, and the plural is al-nudhur. And al-nadhr is also what becomes due, as though it were vowed, that is, made binding. And "the nadhr of a head-wound" in the hadith is from it.
نذل: The letters nūn, dhāl and lām are a word that indicates baseness in a thing. One says nadhl.
نرب: The letters nūn, rā' and bā' do not combine naturally; there may be an intruding letter between them. From this: al-nayrab is slander, tale-bearing; he is nayrab, meaning a slanderer, as if he were a possessor of nayrab. God knows best what is right.
نز:
The letters nūn and zāy are a sound root indicating lightness and scantiness.

1. al-ẓalīm al-nazz — the male ostrich that scarcely settles in one place.
2. al-nazz — the light, quick-witted man; the she-camel of this kind is likewise called al-nazza.
3. al-nazz — water that seeps up out of the ground.

4. anazzat al-arḍ — the land is said to have anazzat when it comes to have such seepage.

It was named nazz for its scantiness and the lightness of its matter.
نزب: The letters nūn, zāy and bā' are a word. One says: nazaba al-ẓaby nazīban — the gazelle gave its cry, and that is its sound at mating.
نزح:
The letters nūn, zāy and ḥā' are a word pointing to distance. Nazaḥat al-dār nuzūḥan — the dwelling grew far away. A land is nāziḥ — distant.

1. nazḥ al-mā' — the drawing-off of water, as though it is carried far from the bottom of the well. One says nazaḥtu al-bi'r, I drew all the water out of a well.
2. bi'run nazūḥ — a well with little water; the plural is ābārun nuzuḥ.
نزر:
The letters nūn, zāy and rā' are a small root pointing to scarcity in a thing. Nazura al-shay' nazāratan — the thing became scarce.

1. shay'un nazr — a thing that is little.
2. 'aṭā'un manzūr — a gift made small.
3. imra'atun nazūr — a woman with few children.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
The lowly baghāth-birds are the commonest of birds in chicks, while the falcon's mother, one who rarely bears, is nazūr — sparse in young.

And their saying, nazartu al-rajul — I pressed him hard — and their saying, 'he does not give until he is pressed,' meaning he is pressed hard, is anomalous from the origin we have named, and has an analogy of its own.
نزع:
The letters nūn, zāy and 'ayn are a sound root pointing to the pulling out of a thing.

And naza'tu al-shay' min makānihi naz'an — I pulled the thing out of its place. Al-minza' is one who pulls hard. Al-minza'a is like a spoon, kept with the man who gathers honey. Naza'a 'an al-amr nuzū'an means he left the matter alone. Sharāb ṭayyib al-manza'a is a drink that is pleasant at the point where the draught ends. Al-naza'a is the place on the head of the anza', the man whose hair has drawn back from the two sides of his forehead, and they are the two naza'as. One does not say imra'a naz'ā' of a woman, but za'rā'. Bi'r nazū' is a well of shallow bottom, drawn from by hand. And 'āda al-amr ilā al-naza'a means the matter went back to what is right; by al-naza'a he meant the plural of nāzi', which is the one who draws at the bow, pulling its string back with the arrow. And fulān qarīb al-manza'a means he is near in his aim and ambition. Manza'at al-rajul is a man's opinion. Nāza'at al-nafs ilā al-amr nizā'an, and naza'at ilayhi, when the soul longs for it. And naza'a ilā abīhi in resemblance, he took after his father. Ba'īr nāzi' is a camel that yearns for its pasture or its home ground. A poet said, in a line of verse:
I said to them: do not blame me, but look at the yearning one held back, and see how he is.

And anza'ū means their camels yearned for their home grounds. Al-nazā'i' among horses are those that have reverted to old strains; and it is said: rather they are those taken away from another people. Al-nazū' is the camel by which water is drawn up on its own. Al-nazā'i' among women are those married outside their own clans; and every stranger is a nazī'.
نزغ: The letters nūn, zā' and ghayn are a word indicating causing discord between two people. nazagha bayna al-qawm — he stirred up trouble among the people, spoiling the bond between them.
نزف:
The letters nūn, zā' and fā' are a root indicating the running-out and cutting-off of something.

1. *nuzifa damuhu* — all his blood ran out.
2. The drunk man is *nazīf*, meaning: his reason has been drained away.

Someone said, in a line of verse:
And when she walks with the walk of the one whose blood has drained ... whom breathlessness fells upon the sand-dune.

3. *an-nazf* — drawing water from a well little by little.
4. *anzafū* — their well's water ran out.
5. *anzafū* — their drink ran out.

God, glorified is He, said: {they are not made to ache from it, nor do they run dry (*yunzifūn*)} [al-Wāqi'a: 19]. *An-nuzfa* is a scoop of water. "It is a sea that is never drained." *nuzifa r-rajulu fī l-khuṣūma* — the man's case ran dry in a dispute, meaning: his argument gave out.
نزق: The letters nūn, zā' and qāf are a word that indicates haste. From this: al-nazaq is lightness and hastiness. Nazzaqtu al-farasa fa-nazaqa, I made the horse impetuous, and it became impetuous. And they say anzaqa fulānun bi-l-ḍaḥik, so-and-so burst out laughing suddenly.
نزك:
The letters nūn, zā' and kāf are a small root that indicates thrusting or something like it.

1. al-nazk — thrusting with the nayzak, a short spear; also bad conduct and speech directed at a person, and a verbal attack on him. In the hadith: "They nazakū Shahr" — meaning they attacked him verbally; the reference is to Shahr ibn Ḥawshab.
2. nizk — compared to this is their word for the male lizard (dhikr al-ḍabb): nizk.
He said, in a line of verse:
A great, fat one, having two nizks that were an excellence over every barefoot and every shod one in the land.
نزل:
The letters nūn, zā' and lām are a sound word pointing to the coming down of a thing and its falling. And nazala ʿan dābbatihi nuzūlan — he came down from his mount. And nazala al-maṭaru min al-samā' nuzūlan — the rain came down from the sky. And al-nāzila is the hard thing among the hardships of time, that comes down. And al-nizāl in war is that the two parties come down against one another. And nazāli is a word put in the place of " come down! ". And a place that is nazil is one much camped in. And wajadtu al-qawma ʿalā nazalātihim, that is, at their camping-places — Ibn al-Aʿrābī said it. And al-nuzul is what is made ready for the one who comes down as a guest. And food that is dhū nuzlin wa-nazalin is food with plenty in it. And they speak of the pilgrimage as " coming down "; and nazala means he made the pilgrimage. He said:
Is Asmā' coming down, or not coming down? Make it plain to us, Asmā' — what is it you will do?
And he said:
And when we came down, the eye was cooled and the hopes that had long been asked of time came to their end.
He said: nazalnā means we came to Minā. And al-nuzāla is a man's seed. And al-nazīl is the guest. He said:
The guest of a people is the greatest of them in rights, and God's right lies in the right of the guest.
And al-tanzīl is the setting of a thing in order and the putting of it in its place.
نزه:
The letters nūn, zā' and hā' are a word that indicates distance, in a place and otherwise.

1. nazīh al-khuluq — a man far removed from base desires.
2. nazihu l-nafs and nāzihu l-nafs — one whose soul keeps clear of impurities, so said Ibn Durayd.
3. kharajnā natanazzahu — we went out roaming, said when people grow distant from water and cultivated land, so said Ibn al-Sikkīt.
4. nazīh — a place that is empty, with no one in it.
نزو:
The letters nūn, zā' and the weak letter are a sound root that goes back to one meaning: leaping, rising, and ascending.

1. al-nazw — nazā yanzū, he leapt.
2. nuzā' al-dhakar ʿalā unthāhu — the mounting of the male upon his female.
3. huwa yanzū ilā kadhā — he strives toward such a thing, as if he had risen toward it.
4. al-tanazzī — the same as al-nazw.

From the hamzated branch:
1. nazi'tu baynahum — I stirred up trouble between them.
2. mā nazaʾaka ʿalā kadhā — what drove you to it, said Ibn al-Aʿrābī.
3. rajulun manzū'un bi-kadhā — a man passionately devoted to such a thing.
نس:
The letters nūn and sīn are a sound root with two meanings: one is a kind of driving, the other is scantiness in a thing, and is specific to water.

The first: nassa ibilahu yanussuhā nassan — he drove his camels.

The second is their saying:
1. nassat al-qaṭā — the sandgrouse grew thirsty.
2. Mecca is called al-nāssa, for the scantiness of water in it.
3. nassat al-khubza nassan — the loaf of bread dried out.
4. nassat al-jumma — the mass of hair on the head grew unkempt and matted, that being from the scantiness of oil in it.
5. al-nasīsa — the moisture found at the tip of a stick when it is kindled; the last remnant of the breath of life is likened to it. He said: it is also called al-nasīs.
نسب:
The letters nūn, sīn, and bāʾ are a single word whose sense is the connection of one thing to another. From this, al-nasab, lineage, is named for its connectedness and for one's connection through it. You say: nasabtu ansubu. He is nasību fulānin, related to so-and-so by descent.

From it also is al-nasīb in poetry, addressed to a woman, as though it were talk that attaches itself to her — and it occurs only concerning women. You say from it: nasabtu ansubu. Al-nasīb is also the straight road, for the way each part of it connects on from the one before.
نسج:
The letters nūn, sīn and jīm are a single root pointing to the joining of one thing to another across a narrow width. One says nasaja al-thawb, yansijuhu — he wove the garment. The wind struck the water and 'wove' tracks upon it. A poet 'weaves' his poetry. Some said: rather, this chapter's true analogy is unsteady motion, not what we have named.

1. al-nāqa al-nasūj — the she-camel whose load sways unsteadily upon her back.
2. minsaj al-faras — likewise derived, because it is always moving; al-minsaj is the withers of a horse.
3. huwa nasīju waḥdihi — 'he is a fabric unto himself,' for his qualities stand apart, unmatched. Ibn Qutayba said this is because a fine, precious garment is not woven a second time on its loom, whereas if a garment is not fine, several garments' warp is worked on the same loom.
نسخ:
The letters nūn, sīn, and khā' are a single root, though there is disagreement over its underlying sense. Some said its sense is removing one thing and setting another in its place. Others said its sense is transferring one thing into another.

1. naskh al-kitāb — copying a document.
2. al-naskh — a ruling that was formerly acted upon and is then abrogated by a new one that comes after it, as when a verse [of the Qurʾan] brings a ruling and is then abrogated by another verse. Anything that replaces something else has 'abrogated' it (intasakhahu) — the sun 'abrogates' the shade, and grey hair 'abrogates' youth.
3. tanāsukh al-warathati — heirs dying one after another while the original estate still stands undivided; from this too comes the term for the succession of ages and generations.

Al-Sijistānī said: al-naskh is transferring what is in one hive of honey and bees into another hive. He said: from this too comes the copying of a book.
نسر:
The letters nūn, sīn and rā' are a sound root pointing to snatching and pilfering. From it comes al-nasr, the taking of a portion of food; nasarahu, he snatched it, as though it were a small thing he took. From this too comes al-nasr, the eagle, as if it snatches its prey. Al-minsar is a body of horsemen between one hundred and two hundred strong, and this follows the same reasoning, as if it came to snatch and pilfer something. It is also said that al-minsar is one that passes by nothing without tearing it up.

By comparison, al-nasr also names two stars in the sky: al-nasr al-ṭā'ir (the Flying Vulture) and al-nasr al-wāqi' (the Falling Vulture). From this too comes nasr al-ḥāfir, what is inside a horse's hoof, resembling date-stones and pebbles.
نسع:
The letters nūn, sīn and 'ayn are a word pointing to the plaiting of a thing.

1. al-nis' — a plaited strap, of the kind used for the reins of mules.
2. nāsi' — said of a long neck, as though it were lengthened and twisted like plaiting.
3. al-minsa'a — land that grows plants quickly, its herbage and its greens growing long.
نسغ:
The letters nūn, sīn and ghayn are a root pointing to the pricking of one thing into another.

1. nasagha al-khubza — he pricked the loaf of bread with a bird's feather; the tool for this is called al-minsagha.
2. nasaghat al-wāshima — the tattooer pricked the hand with the needle.
3. nasaghtu al-dābba bi-rijlī — I prodded the mount with my foot to make it rise.

And they extend the word further, saying:

4. nasaghtu al-laban bi'l-mā' — I diluted the milk with water.
5. nasagha bi'l-'aṣā — he struck him with the stick.
نسف: The letters nūn, sīn and fā' are a sound root indicating the laying bare of something. "The wind intasafat" a thing, like dust and chaff, as though it swept it up off the face of the ground and stripped it away. Nasf al-bunyān (razing a building): its complete uprooting. The foam on milk is called al-nusāfa, because it is skimmed off the surface of the milk. Their saying "his color was intusifa" — drained away — comes from this. A camel nasūf pulls plants up out of the ground with the front of its mouth. Some have related: "the two of them yatanāsafān" — they whisper together; the pattern is the same, as if each draws out what the other has, and the other draws out what this one has.
نسق:
The letters nūn, sīn and qāf are a sound root pointing to succession in a thing.

1. kalāmun nasaq — speech that comes in one order, part following on part.
2. thaghrun nasaq — teeth that are even and set in a row, level with one another; this is the origin of the phrase.
3. kharazun nasaq — beads strung in order.

Abū Zubayd said, in a line of verse:
On the neck of a noble young gazelle, adorned by a string set in order, that the ruby [set in it] all but sets ablaze.
نسك: The letters nūn, sīn and kāf are a sound root pointing to devotion and drawing near to God, Most High. A man is nāsik. The sacrificial animal by which one draws near to God is nasīka. Al-mansak: the place where the sacrificial offerings are slaughtered, occurring only in connection with an offering. Some have claimed al-mansak is simply a place one frequents, but this is doubtful.
نسل:
The letters nūn, sīn, and lām are a sound root indicating the drawing-out of something and its slipping free.

1. al-nasl — offspring, because it slips out from its mother.
2. tanāsalū — they bred, one born from another.
3. al-nasalān — the gait of a wolf when it strides and hastens; a walker 'yansilu' when he hurries.

God Almighty said: {and they will come slipping swiftly down from every rise} [al-Anbiyāʾ: 96].

4. al-nusāla — an animal's hair when it sheds from its body in patches.
5. nusāl al-ṭayr — what falls loose from a bird's feathers.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And it clears away the scattered tufts of shed down.

6. ansalat al-ibil — the camels' time has come for their coat to shed.
7. nasala al-thawbu ʿan al-rajul — the garment fell off the man.
8. al-nasīl — honey once it has melted clear, as if it has slipped free of its wax and parted from it.
9. ansaltu al-qawm — I went ahead of the people, leaving them behind.
نسم:
The letters nūn, sīn and mīm are a sound root pointing to the going-out of breath, or to a wind that does not blow hard.

1. nasīm — a person's breath is called nasīm, and so is a soft-blowing wind.
2. mansim — they say, 'from where is your mansim?', meaning 'from what direction do you come?'; the sense is the same one, because when a thing approaches, its nasīm comes before it.
3. nasama — the soul (al-nafs) is named nasama for this reason.

Anomalous from this is al-mansim — the pad of a camel's foot — though it may be carried on this chapter's analogy, since its pad is what carries its nasama.
نسي:
The letters nūn, sīn and yā' are two sound roots: one of them points to letting a thing slip from the mind, and the second to leaving a thing.

The first: nasītu al-shay' when you do not remember it, nisyānan. And it is possible that al-nisy is from it. Al-nisy is what falls at the camping-places of travellers of the worn-out leavings of their goods; so they say: tatabbaʿū ansā'akum — look after your leavings. Al-Shanfarā said, in a line of verse:
As though she had something dropped on the ground that she is tracking ... towards her mother; and if she speaks to you she falters.
And in that way is explained His saying, exalted be He: {they forgot God, so He forgot them} [al-Tawba: 67], and likewise His saying, glory be to Him: {And We had made a covenant with Adam before, but he forgot, and We found in him no resolve} [Ṭā Hā: 115] — He meant, and God knows best: he abandoned the covenant. And of what strays from the two roots is al-nasā, a vein; the plural is ansā', and the two of them are nasayān. And they say: it is al-nasā, and it is ʿirq al-nasā, the sciatic vein; all of that is said. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And I gave him a gift when he came to me with a water-skin ... like the sciatic vein, given neither belly nor back.

And some of them said: the root in the chapter is al-nisyān, forgetting, and it is the slipping away of a thing from the mind after it had been present to it. And al-nasā is a vein in the thigh, because it lies back away from the upper parts of the body down to the thigh, likened to the thing forgotten, which is put behind and left.

And when it is pronounced with a hamza the meaning changes to the putting off of a thing. And nusi'at al-mar'a — the woman's monthly period came later than its time, so it was hoped that she was with child. And al-nasī'a is your selling a thing on deferment, and that is postponement. You say ansa'tu — I sold on credit. And nasa'a Allāh fī ajalika, and ansa'a ajalaka — God put your term far off and made it distant. And intasa'ū — they drew back and went far off. And nasa'tuhum — I put them back. And nasa'tu nāqatī: some people said, I went gently with her on the journey; and nasa'tuhā — I struck her with the minsa'a, the staff. And this is the better reasoning, because with the staff a thing is, as it were, driven off and pushed away.

And al-nas' is what grows of a she-camel's fur after her fur has fallen; and the reasoning is one, as though this second growth came later. Abū Zayd said: nasa'tu al-ibil fī ẓim'ihā when you add a day or two to the time between their waterings. And al-nasī' in the Book of God is postponement: when they came back from Minā a man of Kināna would stand and say: I am he whose judgement is not rejected. So they would say: put a month back for us — that is, put off from us the sanctity of Muḥarram and set it in Ṣafar. And that was because they hated that three months should follow one upon another in which they made no raids, since their living was from raiding; so Muḥarram was made lawful for them. Then God, exalted be He, said: {The postponement is only an increase in unbelief} [al-Tawba: 37]. And of what strays from the chapter is al-nas': the first coming of fat on riding beasts. Abū Dhu'ayb said, in a line of verse:
On it she recovered through the two months of spring, both of them ... and her fat had come and her filling out.

And al-nasī' is milk on which water is poured. From it you say nasa'tu; and it is al-nas' also, in the verse of ʿUrwa:
They gave me watered milk to drink, then they closed about me ... God's enemies, with lying and falsehood.
نش:
The letters nūn and shīn are not a root at all; the word only represents a sound.

1. al-nashīsh — the hissing sound of water and other things when it boils.
2. arḍ nashīsha — salty land that grows nothing; it is also called arḍ nashshāsha.
3. nashsha al-ghadīr — the pool's water began to recede.
نشأ:
The letters nūn, shīn and hamza are a sound root indicating a rising up in something and a going high. And nasha'a al-saḥāb, the cloud rose up. And ansha'ahu Allāh, God raised it. And from it: {Indeed the rising of the night} [al-Muzzammil: 6], by which is meant, and God knows best, the standing and rising up for prayer.

And from the chapter: al-nash' and al-nasha' are the young among people. And nasha'a so-and-so among the Banū so-and-so, he grew up among them. And al-nāshi' is the young man who has grown up and risen and gone high. And ansha'a so-and-so a piece of talk, and ansha'a reciting and speaking; all of this has one and the same reasoning.

And from the chapter: istansha'tu al-rīḥ, I sniffed the wind, and that is because it is as though you were raising it up to your nose.
نشج:
The letters nūn, shīn and jīm are a word pointing to the representing of a sound.

1. nashaja al-bākī — the weeper choked back tears in his throat without breaking into open sobbing.
2. nashaja al-ḥimār — the donkey brayed, with a sound called nashj.
3. A stab-wound is said to have 'nashajat' when blood comes out of it and a sound is heard from it.
4. The pot 'nashij-es' — gurgles — as it comes to the boil.
5. al-anshāj may come from this: the channels through which water runs, the singular nashaj, perhaps named for the gurgling sound of the water.
نشح:
The letters nūn, shīn and ḥā' are a sound root, but scholars have explained it in opposite ways.

1. Some said: nashaḥa al-shārib — the drinker 'nashaḥa' when he drank until he was full; a full waterskin is called siqā'un nashshāḥ.
2. Others said: al-nushūḥ is drinking short of being fully quenched.
نشد:
The letters nūn, shīn and dāl are a sound root pointing to mentioning and extolling something. Nashada fulānun fulānan — he said, nashadtuka Allāh, meaning 'I ask you by God'; in short, 'I remind you of God, Most High.'

1. inshād al-shā'ir — a poet's 'inshād' is his reciting a poem: mentioning it and extolling it.
2. anshadtu al-ḍālla — this means 'I made the stray beast known,' and that is the true analogy of the word. In the hadith: 'its stray property is not lawful except to a munshid,' meaning one who makes it known.
3. nashadtu al-ḍālla — meaning 'I sought the stray beast,' is named for the raising of one's voice.
نشر:
The letters nūn, shīn and rā' are a sound root pointing to the opening out of a thing and its spreading into branches.

And nashartu al-khashaba bi'l-minshār nashran — I sawed the plank with the saw. Al-nashr is the sweet-smelling wind.

And the falcon clothed itself in rīshan nasharan — feathers that are spread out, wide and long. From this is nashartu al-kitāb, I unrolled the book, the opposite of folding it up. And nashara Allāh al-mawtā fa-nasharū — God raised the dead and they rose. And ansharaAllāh al-mawtā likewise. He, exalted be He, said: thumma idhā shā'a ansharahu — then when He wills He raises him up. Then al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
Until the people say, when they have seen it: what a wonder, a dead man come back to life.

And nasharat al-arḍ means the spring rain fell on the land and it put out growth, and it is nāshira; and that growth is al-nashr, and it is said that it is bad for grazing beasts. It is also said: rather al-nashr is herbage that dries up and then rain falls on it, and there comes out of it something in the shape of ticks, and it is a disease. The veins of the inner side of the forearm are al-nawāshir, so called for their spreading out. Al-intishār is the swelling of a beast's sinew from weariness. Al-nashar is that the sheep scatter at night and graze, and for this reason it is said of a man who has pulled his affair together: 'he has gathered in his scatter'.
نشز: The letters nūn, shīn and zā' are a sound root indicating rising and elevation. Al-nashaz: high, elevated ground. Al-nashz and al-nushūz: rising up; then used figuratively, so it is said "the woman nashazat" — she turned defiant toward her husband; and likewise "her husband nashaza" — he turned cold and harsh toward her, and struck her.
نشس: The letters nūn, shīn and sīn are one word, formed by letter substitution: one says nashasat, the same as nashazat.
نشص:
The letters nūn, shīn and ṣād are a root pointing to rising and height in a thing. Nashaṣa al-saḥāb — the cloud rose.

1. al-nashāṣa — a white, raised cloud; the plural is nashāṣ.

Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
He held back the raised cloud of Dhū al-Qarnayn, until the king's mighty rain-front turned away.

2. nashaṣa al-wabar — the fur/hair stood up, rose.
3. nashaṣnā min balad ilā balad — we journeyed on, up, from one land to another.
4. nashaṣat al-mar'a — said of a woman, the same as nashazat.
5. nashaṣat thaniyyatuhu — his front tooth loosened and rose out of its place.
نشط:
The letters nūn, shīn and ṭā' are a sound root indicating a quivering and a movement. From it comes *an-nashāṭ*, liveliness, well known, so called for the movement, the quivering and the opening-up that is in it.

1. *nashiṭa yanshaṭu* — he became lively.
2. *anshaṭa l-qawmu* — their mounts became lively.
3. The bull is *nāshiṭ*, because it moves briskly from one land to another.

Dhū ar-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
Is that it, or a dappled one, patterned along its legs ... sun-scorched of cheek, a leader, lively, young.

4. *nashaṭtu sh-shay'a* — I peeled the thing, as though, once peeled, it were drawn out of its skin.
5. *ṭarīqun nāshiṭ* — a road that branches off, right and left, from the main road.
6. *nashaṭati n-nāqatu fī sayrihā* — the she-camel quickened her pace.
7. *al-unshūṭa* — a slip-knot, like the knot of a pair of trousers; *nashaṭtuhu bi'unshūṭa*, I tied it with a slip-knot.
8. *anshaṭtu l-'iqāl* — I pulled its slip-knot loose so that it came undone.

Some people said: *al-inshāṭ* is the loosening, and *at-tanshīṭ* is the tying.

9. *bi'run anshāṭ* — a well shallow enough that its bucket comes up with a single pull.
10. *nashaṭtu d-dalwa mina l-bi'ri* — I drew the bucket from the well without need of a pulley.
11. *an-nashīṭa* of camels — livestock come upon and driven off without having been specifically sought out. Some said: it is what a raiding party comes upon before it reaches the encampment it means to raid, and the leader takes it out for himself from among the party's takings.

Someone said, in a line of verse:
Yours is the chief's quarter-share of it, and the pick of the spoils ... and your own judgment, and the *nashīṭa*, and what remains over.
نشع:
The letters nūn, shīn and 'ayn are a single word. Nasha'tu al-ṣabiyya al-wajūr nash'an fa-intasha'ahu — I gave the infant the wajūr [medicine poured into a child's mouth], and he swallowed it down. The verbal noun is al-nushū'.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
I was made to swallow glory into my nose, a swallowing.
نشغ:
The letters nūn, shīn and ghayn are three distinct words, not reducible to one analogy.

1. al-nashgh — a sound like a sigh brought on by longing.
2. al-nāshigh — one who lives on after hardship, who survives exertion.
3. al-nawāshigh — the upper reaches of a valley; the singular is nāshigha.
نشف:
The letters nūn, shīn and fā' are a sound root pointing to moisture entering something that takes it in. From it, al-nashf — the entry of water into cloth or ground until it is absorbed.

1. al-nishfa — a stone, so named because it absorbs dirt away from its place; the plural is al-nishaf.

It is said that nashf in ponds is like nazḥ [drawing-off] in dug wells.

2. minshāf / nashūf — a she-camel that gives milk before she gives birth, and then her milk goes away.
نشق:
The letters nūn, shīn and qāf are a sound root pointing to something catching hold. Nashiqa al-ẓaby fī al-ḥibāla — the gazelle got caught in the snare.

1. al-nashiqa — a rope put around the necks of lambs; it is also called al-nushqa.
2. rajulun nashiq — a man fallen into a matter he can hardly free himself from.

And from this word:

1. anshaqtu al-ṣabiyya al-dawā' — I poured the medicine into the child's nose.
2. al-nashūq — the name for any medicine that is sniffed up the nose; from this, istanshaqtu al-rīḥ — I smelled the wind, sniffed it in; and one says of an unpleasant smell, 'this is a wind of disliked nashaq,' meaning disliked scent.
3. al-mutawaḍḍi' yastanshiqu al-mā' — one performing the ablution sniffs water up into the nose, when he then blows it out.
نشل:
The letters nūn, shīn and lām are a word pointing to lifting a piece of meat out of a pot.

1. nashala al-laḥm min al-qidr — he lifted the meat from the pot with the minshal, the hook used for it, also called al-nashīl.
2. fakhdhun nāshila — a thigh scant of meat.
3. al-minshal / al-minshāl — the implement used to lift meat out of a pot.

They also say — though I do not know how sound it is — that al-manshala is the place where a ring sits on the little finger.
نشم:
The letters nūn, shīn and mīm point to something catching hold.

1. nashshamū fī al-amr — they set about a matter [said only of something bad]. In the hadith: 'when the people set about [nashshama] the matter of 'Uthmān,' meaning they took it up and turned against him.
2. nashshama al-laḥm — the meat began to give off a smell, i.e. it started to spoil.

Anomalous from this: al-nasham — a tree from which bows are made.
نص:
The letters nūn and ṣād are a sound root indicating raising, elevation, and reaching the end or limit of a thing.

1. Their saying naṣṣa al-ḥadīth ilā fulān — he raised, or traced, the report back to so-and-so.
2. al-naṣṣ in traveling is its fastest pace. One says naṣnaṣtu nāqatī, I drove my she-camel at full pace; and a pace is called naṣṣ and naṣīṣ.
3. minaṣṣat al-ʿarūs, the bride's raised seat, is from this too.
4. bāta fulān muntaṣṣan ʿalā baʿīrihi — so-and-so spent the night sitting bolt upright on his camel, meaning muntaṣiban, erect.

The naṣṣ of anything is its utmost limit. In a hadith of ʿAlī, peace be upon him: "When women reach naṣṣ al-ḥiqāq" — meaning when they reach the furthest point of childhood and come to the edge of maturity. Al-ḥiqāq is the verbal noun of al-muḥāqqa, which is when one guardian says "I have more right to her" and another says "I have more right."

5. naṣaṣtu al-rajul — I pressed the man closely in questioning about a matter until I drew out what he knew. This fits the pattern, since you are seeking to reach the furthest point.
6. Also from this word is al-naṣnaṣa: the camel's planting its knees firmly on the ground when it is about to rise.
7. al-naṣnaṣa also means shaking, moving.
8. al-nuṣṣa — the forelock of hair on the head, so called because it sits on a raised place.
نصا:
The letters nūn, ṣād, and the weak letter — mostly wāw here — are a sound root pointing to choosing-out, distinction, and height in a thing.

1. al-naṣiyya — the choice, best part of a people, or of anything. One says intaṣaytu al-shay', I chose it out; and 'this is my naṣiyya,' meaning my chosen one.
2. al-nāṣiya — the forelock, so named for the height of where it grows; al-nāṣiya is also the hairline at the front of the head.

In the inflection of this word one says:

1. naṣawtu fulānan — I seized so-and-so by the forelock.
2. nāṣaytuhu — each of us seized the other by the forelock.
3. mafāzatun tunāṣī ukhrā — one desert tract 'faces' another, as though joined to it, like a hand gripping another's forelock; this is a comparison.
4. intaṣā al-sha'r — the hair grew long.

And 'Ā'isha's words — 'why do you tanṣūna your dead?' — she meant: you comb out his forelock, as though she disliked the combing of a dead person's hair.
نصب:
The letters nūn, ṣād and bā' are a sound root pointing to setting a thing up and making it a mark, standing straight. One says naṣabtu al-rumḥ wa-ghayrahu anṣibuhu naṣban - I set up the spear and other things. And a he-goat is anṣab and a she-goat naṣbā', when its two horns stand up; and a she-camel is naṣbā' when she is high in the chest. And al-naṣb is a stone that used to be set up and worshipped; and it is said it is al-nuṣub, and it is a stone set up before the idol, over which the blood of the beasts sacrificed to the idols was poured. And al-naṣā'ib are stones set up around the lip of the well and made into supports.

And of the chapter: al-naṣab is weariness, and its sense is that a person keeps standing up until he tires. And ghubār muntaṣib is rising dust. And al-naṣīb is the trough built up out of stones. As for the niṣāb of a thing, it is its origin; and it was called niṣāb because its blade is raised up to it and is set and fixed in it, like the haft of a knife and of other things. And al-naṣīb is the share of a thing; one says hādhā naṣībī, that is, my share. And it is from this, as though it were the thing raised up for you and set as a mark. And al-naṣb is a kind of singing, and perhaps it is from what is raised up, that is, the voice is lifted with it. And the wealth reached the niṣāb at which the alms-tax falls due, as though it had reached that amount and risen to it. And the people of Arabic say of the a-vowel that it is al-naṣb, as though the word stood up in the mouth.
نصت: The letters nūn, ṣād and tā' are a single word indicating silence. *anṣata* — he fell silent to listen to speech; *naṣata yanṣitu*. In the Book of God: and be silent, and listen.
نصح:
The letters nūn, ṣād and ḥā' are a root that points to the fitting together of two things and to setting them right. The origin of that is al-nāṣiḥ, the tailor. Al-niṣāḥ is the thread that is sewn with, and the plural is niṣāḥāt; and to these were likened the hides that are stretched out on the ground in tanning. A poet said, in a line of verse:
You see the people all of them drunken, just as the hides of the rubaḥ are stretched out.

From it is al-nuṣḥ and al-naṣīḥa, sincere counsel, the opposite of cheating. And naṣaḥtuhu anṣaḥuhu — I counselled him sincerely. And he is nāṣiḥ al-jayb — sound in the breast of his garment — said as a proverb, when a man is described as pure in his deeds; and al-tawba al-naṣūḥ, sincere repentance, is from it, as though it were sound with no tear and no gap in it.

And one says anṣaḥtu al-ibil when you water the camels until they are full, so that naṣaḥat, that is, they drank their fill. And that belongs to the analogy we have mentioned. And nāṣiḥ al-'asal is its clearest honey, as though it were the pure thing that nothing mixes into. And naṣaḥtu lahu and naṣaḥtuhu have the same meaning. And a shirt is manṣūḥ, that is, sewn.
نصر:
The letters nūn, ṣād and rā' are a sound root pointing to the coming of good and the giving of it. And God granted the Muslims naṣr: He gave them victory over their enemy — yanṣuruhum naṣran. Intaṣara means he took his revenge, and it is from this.

As for the coming, the Arabs say naṣartu balada kadhā — when you came to such and such a town.

The poet said, in a line of verse:
When the sacred month comes in, bid farewell to the lands of Tamīm and come to the land of ʿĀmir.

For that reason rain is called naṣr. And nuṣirat al-arḍ — the land was given rain — so it is manṣūra. And al-naṣr is a gift.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
By me, and by writings that were written line upon line, I am one who says: O Naṣr, a gift, a gift!
نصع:
The letters nūn, ṣād and 'ayn are a root pointing to purity and softness in a thing.

1. al-nāṣi' — bright and beautiful in color, intensely white.
2. al-niṣ' — a kind of cloth, intensely white.
3. naṣa'a al-ḥaqq — the truth became clear.

From the chapter of ease and softness, which is the very analogy we have named:

1. anṣa'at al-nāqa lil-faḥl — the she-camel yielded to the stallion.
2. qabbaḥa Allāhu umman naṣa'at bihi — 'may God disfigure a mother who naṣa'at him,' meaning bore him; related by Ibn al-Sikkīt.
3. al-manāṣi' — gathering-places, so named because they lie in the easiest, most convenient spots.

Anomalous from this is their saying anṣa'a, meaning 'he shivered, broke out in gooseflesh.'

A poet said:
Until his skin broke out in gooseflesh and shivered.
نصف:
The letters nūn, ṣād and fāʾ are two sound roots: one points to the half of a thing, the other to a kind of service and use.
The first: niṣf al-shayʾ and naṣīfuhu, its half. In the hadith: 'not to the amount of one of their mudd-measures, nor its half.' A poet said, in a line of verse:

Neither a mudd nor a half-mudd nourished her ... nor small measures of dates, nor undue stinginess

It is said ināʾun naṣfān, a vessel whose water has reached its halfway point. Al-naṣaf: a woman between full maturity and youth, that is, at the halfway point of her life. Al-inṣāf in dealings is fairness, as though contentment with taking only one's half; al-niṣf also means fairness. Naṣafa al-nahār, yanṣufu, it reached its midpoint. A poet said, in a line of verse:

At midday the water covers it entirely ... while his companion, unseen, does not know

And naṣafa al-izār sāqahu, the waist-wrap reached halfway up his shin. A poet said, in a line of verse:

You see his sword's scabbard-tip not reaching halfway up the shin ... indeed not, though his sword-belts are long
نصل:
The letters nūn, ṣād and lām are a sound root pointing to a thing's emerging from a cover, a screen, or a mount.

1. naṣala al-ḥāfir — the hoof slipped out of its place.
2. naṣala al-khiḍāb — the dye faded away [out of the hair].
3. tanaṣṣala min dhanbihi — he 'emerged' from his sin, that is, he cleared himself of it, as though he had come out of it.
4. al-naṣl — the blade of a sword, or the head of an arrow, so named for how it stands out, for its clarity and its brightness.

In the inflection of this word one says:

1. anṣaltu al-rumḥ — I stripped the spear, I removed its head.
2. naṣaltuhu — I fitted it with a head.
3. al-munṣal — the sword.

He said, on anṣaltu:
He caught up with him in munṣil al-all after he had gone, no great span of days remaining, and he had all but perished.
He means the month Rajab, which used to be called munṣil al-asinna — 'the stripper of spearheads' — because they would not make war during it.

And he said, on al-munṣal:
I am a man of the best lineage of 'Abs by half my descent, and I guard the rest of myself with the sword.

Carried by way of comparison: al-naṣīl is what lies, on the inner side, between the neck and the head, beneath the two jawbones.
نض:
The letters nūn and ḍād are two sound roots. One indicates the making easy of a thing and its becoming apparent; the other, a kind of movement.

The first: the saying of the Arabs, khudh mā naḍḍa laka min dayn — take what has become available to you of a debt owed, meaning what has become easy to obtain.

1. fulān yastanuḍḍu māla fulān — so-and-so seeks to draw off so-and-so's wealth as it becomes available.
2. al-naḍīḍ, of water — the small, scant amount.
3. al-nāḍḍ, of wealth — it is said to be that which has substance and lasting value, and it is also said to be that which is in ready coin. This is the sense the jurists follow for al-nāḍḍ.
نضا:
The letters nūn, ḍād and the weak letter — mostly wāw — are a sound root pointing to a thing's stripping-away, its being made fine, and its being divested.

1. naḍā al-sayf min ghimdihi — he drew the sword from its sheath.
2. naḍā al-sahm — the arrow sped on, went forth.
3. naḍā al-faras al-khayl — the horse outran the other horses, as though it had slipped free of them.
4. naḍā al-ḥinnā' 'an al-yad — the henna faded from the hand.
5. naḍawtu thawbī — I stripped off my garment, cast it from me.

Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
And I came, when she had stripped off her clothes for sleep behind the curtain, all but the loose garment worn at ease.

1. al-niḍw, among camels — the one worn thin by long journeys, as though they had pared it down and stripped it of its flesh.
2. anḍā al-rajul — a man's camel became a niḍw, worn thin.
3. anḍaytu al-shay' — I wore a thing out.
4. niḍw al-lijām — the iron parts of a bridle, without its straps.
5. naḍiyy al-sahm — the shaft of an arrow, what lies between the feathers and the head, so called because it is pared down until it becomes slender.
6. naḍiyy al-rumḥ — the part of a spear above the grip, at its forward end.
7. al-naḍiyy — also, by comparison, an upright neck; the plural is anḍiya.

[A line of verse, apparently cut short in the text:]
And the length of slender necks, and of forelocks.
نضب:
The letters nūn, ḍād and bā' are a word pointing to a thing's laying-bare and its going away.

1. naḍaba al-mā' — the water receded, sank away.
2. naḍabat al-mafāza — the desert-waste 'receded,' as though it had stripped itself bare.
3. kharqun nāḍib — a wide, distant tract of land.

Anomalous from this: al-tanḍub — a tree.
نضج:
The letters nūn, ḍād and jīm are a root pointing to something reaching its completion in cooking, then used by extension for anything that reaches the utmost soundness. naḍija al-tamru wa'l-laḥmu nuḍjan — the dates and the meat became fully cooked, and anḍajtuhu — I cooked it fully. anḍajat-hu al-shamsu — the sun ripened it fully. This is used by extension when one says "huwa naḍīju al-ra'yi", meaning sound and well-considered in his opinion. A she-camel that goes past the time of giving birth without giving birth is said to have naḍḍajat; she is munaḍḍaj, and several of them are munaḍḍijāt.

A poet said:
He is the son of she-camels overdue, that were long ago exceeding their term by nearly a month.
نضح:
The letters nūn, ḍād and ḥā' are a root pointing to something made moist, and to water that is sprinkled. Al-naḍḥ is the sprinkling of water; naḍaḥtuhu, I sprinkled it. The philologists said: naḍḥ is said of anything fine and thin, and this is the very analogy we have named, because a sprinkling is a fine thing.

1. naḍaḥtu al-bayt bi'l-mā' — I sprinkled the house with water.
2. naḍaḥa jildahu bi'l-'araq — his skin broke out with sweat.
3. al-sāniya nāḍiḥ — the watering-camel [that draws water for irrigation] is called nāḍiḥ.
4. naḍaḥūhum bi'l-nabl — they 'sprinkled' them with arrows, by comparison.
5. naḍaḥa 'an nafsihi — he defended himself, as though flinging forth argument in his own defense.

In the hadith: 'sprinkle the horsemen away from us, that we not be come at from behind,' meaning, shoot them with arrows.

6. al-naḍīḥ / al-naḍaḥ — the trough, because it is filled by the sprinkling of water into it.
7. naḍaḥa al-ghaḍā — the ghaḍā-tree broke into blossom, as though the falling of its flowers were likened to the sprinkling of water.

Abū Ṭālib said, in a line of verse:
Blessed be the stranger who has died, as the blossoming of the pomegranate and the olive is blessed.

Ibn al-A'rābī said: the trough is named naḍīḥ because it quenches the thirst of the camels, that is, it wets it. Al-Khalīl said: a man is charged with a matter, and he 'clears himself' — yantaḍiḥu — of it, when he shows his innocence and does his utmost to acquit himself of it.
نضخ: The letters nūn, ḍād and khā' are close to the one before it, except that this one is the greater in degree. They say al-naḍkh is like al-laṭkh, a smear left by a thing that leaves a mark behind. naḍakha thawbahu bi'l-ṭīb — he sprinkled his garment with perfume. ghaythun naḍḍākh — an abundant rain. 'aynun naḍḍākha — a spring copious with water.
نضد:
The letters nūn, ḍād, and dāl are a sound root pointing to the joining of one thing to another in order and gathering, whether standing upright or laid flat. Naḍadtu al-shayʾa baʿḍahu ilā baʿḍin: I stacked the thing part upon part, in order, or one above another.

1. al-naḍad — garments stacked one upon another. Al-Nābigha said, in a line partly obscure to me:
She let loose the course of a stream that had held it back, and raised it up to the two curtains, then to the stack (al-naḍad).
2. al-naḍad — the couch on which goods are stacked.
3. anḍād al-jibāl — boulders piled one upon another.
4. al-naḍad (of clouds) — like al-ṣabīr, layered one against another, plural anḍād.
5. anḍād al-qawm — a people's assembled groups and numbers.
6. naḍad al-rajul — a man's paternal and maternal uncles, who gather to support him.
7. al-naḍad — nobility, eminence.
8. naḍāʾid al-dībāj — plural of naḍīda, the cushion, and whatever is stuffed as furnishing.

Ibn Durayd said: whatever is stacked part upon part is naḍīd.
نضر:
The letters nūn, ḍād, and rāʾ are a sound root pointing to beauty, comeliness, and purity. From this, al-naḍra is beauty of colour. Naḍira yanḍuru. Naḍḍara Allāhu wajhahu: God made his face beautiful and radiant. In the hadith: "May God make radiant a man who heard my words and retained them." Akhḍar nāḍir, vivid green — and this is said of anything shining and beautiful. God Most High said: faces on that day radiant.

Al-naḍīr is gold, for its beauty and purity. A poet said:
When stripped one day, you would think it a fine cloak upon her, and the sheen of pure gold (al-naḍīr), glistening.
A cup [called] nuḍār is one made from athl-wood found in the lowland — and perhaps it was so named for being beautiful.
نضل:
The letters nūn, ḍād and lām are a small root pointing to shooting and contesting in a shooting-match.

1. naḍala fulānan — he contested so-and-so in an archery match and beat him at it.
2. huwa yunāḍilu 'an fulān — he 'contests' on so-and-so's behalf: he speaks up in his defense, as though shooting on his behalf.
3. intaḍaltu sahman min al-kinana — I drew an arrow out of the quiver.
4. By metaphor: intaḍaltu rajulan min al-qawm — I 'picked' a man out from the people, meaning I chose him.
5. intiḍāl al-ibil — the camels' forward casting of their forelegs as they travel.
6. intaḍalū / tanāḍalū — they competed in shooting for precedence.
7. intaḍalnā bi'l-kalām wa al-aḥādīth — we 'shot' one another with talk and sayings, a metaphor from an arrow-contest.

Labīd said, in a line of verse:
So we contested with words, while Ibn Salmā sat — like a noble hawk, lowering his eyes, dignified.
نط:
The letters nūn and ṭāʾ. They say:

1. al-naṭāniṭ, of men — the tall ones; the singular is naṭnāṭ.
2. naṭnaṭtu the thing — I stretched it out.
نطح:
The letters nūn, ṭā' and ḥā' are a single root: it is naṭaḥa, to butt. nataḥa al-kabshu yanṭaḥu — the ram butts. It is used by extension: a wild animal that comes at you facing you is called naṭīḥ and nāṭiḥ. They say it is not taken as a good omen, and for that the ill-fated man is called naṭīḥ. A horse called naṭīḥ is one with whiteness on both sides of its head.

From this same chapter come nawāṭiḥ al-dahr, the hard blows of fate, and "aṣābahu nāṭiḥ", meaning a severe matter struck him — each following the same reasoning. Al-sharaṭān, the two stars, are also called al-naṭḥ and al-nāṭiḥ. Their saying:
The night is dark and the rams are butting
means some of them butting others; this is an expression for the fighting of heroes and the clashing of armored warriors in battle. tanāṭaḥat al-amwāju wa'l-suyūlu wa'l-rijālu fī al-ḥarb — the waves, the floods, and the men in war clashed against one another.
نطس:
The letters nūn, ṭā' and sīn are two distinct words, not reducible to one analogy.

1. al-tanaṭṭus — squeamishness, avoidance of what is unclean. In the hadith of 'Umar: when he came out of the privy, he was asked, 'will you not perform the ablution?', and he said, 'were it not for tanaṭṭus, nothing in the house would stop me from washing my hands.'
2. al-naṭīs / al-niṭāsiyy — the skilled, learned physician. One also says tanaṭṭastu al-akhbār — I pried closely into the news, investigated it.
نطش:
The letters nūn, ṭā' and shīn are a root that indicates motion and strength.

1. *al-naṭsh* — strength of build.
2. *naṭīsh* — used in the phrase "mā bihi naṭīsh," he has no strength in him, meaning power.

Ibn Durayd said: their saying "'aṭshān naṭshān" (thirsty and restless) comes from their saying "mā bihi naṭīsh," meaning motion.
نطع:
The letters nūn, ṭā' and 'ayn are a root pointing to spreading-out in a thing, and smoothness.

1. al-niṭ' / al-naṭ' — a spread-out, smooth [leather mat].
2. al-niṭ' — also, what shows of the roof of the upper mouth, the palate — which fits the same sense.
3. al-tanaṭṭu' fī al-kalām — over-elaborateness in speech, because one 'spreads out' at length in it; this fits the analogy.
4. By metaphor: tanaṭṭa'a al-ṣāni' fī ṣan'atihi — the craftsman 'went deep' in his craft, meaning he displayed his skill.
نطف:
The letters nūn, ṭā' and fā' are two roots. One of them is a kind of ornament, and the other is moisture and wetness, and then it is used as a figure and widened out.

The first is al-naṭaf. It is said that it is pearls, the single one being naṭafa. And it is said: rather al-naṭaf are earrings.

The other root is al-nuṭfa: clear water. And a laylat naṭūf is a night that rained until morning. Al-niṭāf is sweat. Then this is used as a figure, so it is said al-naṭaf is being smeared with something. It is scarcely said except of what is ugly and shameful. And it is said naṭif, that is, faulty. And naṭifa al-shay' — the thing went bad.
نطق:
The letters nūn, ṭā' and qāf are two sound roots: one of them is speech or what resembles it, and the other is a kind of clothing.

The first is al-manṭiq, speech, and naṭaqa yanṭiqu nuṭqan — he spoke. This is also used of what we ourselves do not understand. God Most High said in the story of Solomon: {we have been taught the speech of birds} [al-Naml: 16].

The other is al-niṭāq: a waist-wrapper with a drawstring in it. The flank is called al-nāṭiqa, because it is at the place of the niṭāq. And a ewe that is marked with red at the place of the niṭāq is called munaṭṭaqa. Dhāt al-niṭāq is a hill of theirs. Al-minṭaq is everything with which you bind your middle. Al-minṭaqa is the name of a particular thing, a belt. And jā'a fulānun muntaṭiqan farasahu, when he leads his horse alongside him and does not ride it, as though it were at his niṭāq, since it is at his side.

As for his words, in a line of verse:
I shall not cease, as long as God keeps my people above their enemies, leading a noble horse at my side —
some people said: he meant this by it, and that he never ceases to lead a swift horse beside him. And it is said that it is from the first root, that is, muntaṭiq, one who utters speech in praise of my people. And they say — and this is from the second root — "whoever's father has a long train, let him gird himself with it", which is a proverb, meaning: whoever's father's sons are many, they help him.
نطل:
The letters nūn, ṭā' and lām are a single word. They say: al-nāṭil is a measure among the measures for wine. Or, it is said: al-nāṭil is rather the residue that is left in a vessel from a drink — this fits better with the poet's saying.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Even if what Ibn Bujra has of wine were with her, my uvula would not be wetted by a nāṭil [a mere dreg].

They also say, if it is sound: al-nayṭal is the bucket, and also calamity.
نطي:
The letters nūn, ṭā' and the weak letter are a word pointing to distance and extension in a thing.

1. arḍun naṭiyya — a distant land.

Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
He set off in the evening from one distant land to another, remembering an eggshell around a hatched egg.

2. anṭāhu — he gave to him. Whoever gives someone a thing has thereby made that thing distant from himself; it may also be that this is from the category of letter-substitution, from i'ṭā', giving.

And carried on this sense: 'do not nāṭi men,' meaning, do not grapple with them and prolong enmity against them.
نظر:
The letters nūn, ẓā' and rā' are a sound root whose branches go back to one meaning, and that is looking closely at a thing and seeing it with the eye; then it is used by transfer and widened out. So one says naẓartu ilā al-shay' anẓuru ilayhi — when you saw it with your eye. And ḥayyun ḥilālun naẓar: neighbours settled together who look at one another. And they say naẓartuhu — that is, I waited for him. And that is the same pattern, as though he were looking towards the time at which he would come.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
For if you two would wait for me a single night of time, it would profit me at Umm Jundab's.

And of the chapter of metaphor and widening is their saying naẓarat al-arḍ — the land showed its plants. And this is [the pattern. And] they say naẓarat bi-ʿayn — it looked with an eye. And from it is naẓara al-dahru ilā banī fulānin fa-ahlakahum — time looked at the sons of so-and-so and destroyed them. [And] hādhā naẓīru hādhā — this is the match of that — is from this pattern; that is, if it and its match were looked at, they would be the same. And bihi naẓratun — he has a pallor upon him, as though he were a thing looked at, so that his colour changed. And God knows best what is right.
نظف:
The letters nūn, ẓā' and fā' are a single word: their saying that a thing is *naẓīf* (clean) means it is pure, plainly clean (*naẓāfa*).

1. *naẓufa yanẓufu* — it became clean.
2. *istanẓaftu mā ʿinda fulān* — I took the whole of what so-and-so had, I took all of it.
3. *naẓẓaftuhu* — I cleaned it, a cleaning (*tanẓīfan*).
نظم:
The letters nūn, ẓā' and mīm are a root indicating the stringing and composing of a thing. One says *naẓamtu al-kharaz naẓman* — I strung the beads — and *naẓamtu al-shiʿr wa-ghayrahu* — I composed poetry and other things.

1. *al-niẓām* — the thread that gathers beads together.
2. *al-niẓāmān* of the monitor lizard (*ḍabb*) — two strips on its two sides, strung from the base of the tail to the ear.
3. *anẓamat al-dajāja* — said of a hen when eggs have formed inside her.
4. The stars of Orion (*al-Jawzā'*) are called *naẓm*.
5. *jā'anā naẓm min jarād* — a swarm of locusts came to us, meaning a great many.
نع:
The letters nūn and ʿayn are a sound root indicating leaning and agitation.

1. tanaʿnaʿa — said of a thing when it leans and is agitated.
2. al-nuʿnuʿ — the slack, drooping member.
3. al-nuʿnuʿ — the tall man whose build is loose-jointed and unsteady.
4. tanaʿnaʿa minnā — he grew distant from us.

Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
The one who has gone far off, the one drawing away.
نعب:
The letters nūn, ʿayn and bā' are two sound roots: one indicates a sound, the other a kind of movement.

The first: *naʿaba al-ghurābu* — the crow cawed: *naʿban*, *naʿīban*, *naʿabānan*.

And the other:

1. *faras minʿab* — a swift horse.
2. *nāqa naʿʿāba* — a fast she-camel.
3. *al-naʿb* — a she-camel moving her head forward as she walks; she is also called *nāqa naʿūb*.
نعت: The letters nūn, ʿayn and tā' are a single word, and it is *al-naʿt* — your describing a thing by the good that is in it. Al-Khalīl said this, except when someone strains the usage and says "dhā naʿtu sū'" (this is of bad description). He said: everything good and complete is *naʿt*. And Nāʿitūn is a place.
نعج:
The letters nūn, ʿayn, and jīm are a sound root indicating a particular colour.

1. al-naʿaj — pure white.
2. jamal nāʿij — a camel of fine, excellent colour.
3. al-naʿja — the ewe; the word is also used for wild cattle [oryx] and mountain goats. The females of these kinds are called niʿāj.
4. niʿāj al-raml — [these are] the wild cattle.
5. naʿija al-rajul — the man ate ewe's meat and it upset his stomach.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
As if the people had supped on mutton — so they sit sickened by it, their necks hanging low.

6. anʿajū — their ewes grew fat.

As for nawāʿij al-ibil, it is said these are the swift she-camels; but in our view they are the choice, noble ones, by the analogy already given [of fine colour].

7. imraʾa nāʿija — a woman of fine complexion.
8. al-nāʿija of land — the smooth, level ground, generous to plants, growing rimth [a desert shrub] and the choicest herbage.
نعر:
The letters nūn, ʿayn and rā' are two close roots: one is a sound, the other a kind of movement.

The first: *naʿara al-rajulu* — a sound made from the nose.

1. A wound is called *naʿʿār* or *naʿūr* when its blood makes a sound as it comes out.
2. *al-nāʿūr* — a kind of bucket used for drawing water, named for its sound.

And the second: *naʿara fī al-fitna* — he was active in strife, coming and going.

1. *huwa naʿʿār fī al-fitan* — one who bustles about actively in strife.
2. *naʿara fī al-bilād* — he traveled off through the land.
3. *huwa naʿīr al-hamm* — his worry runs deep.
4. *inna fī ra'sihi naʿra* — meaning arrogance and pride, and a headstrong recklessness that carries him on in his ignorance.
5. *al-naʿra* — a fly that lands in the noses of camels and horses; it may be named for its *naʿīr*, its buzzing sound.
6. *naʿira al-ḥimār* — the donkey is called *naʿir*.

As for his saying, in a line of verse:
The Shadanī she-camels drop the *naʿar*.
He likened the fetuses in their wombs to that fly.

7. *anʿara al-arāk* — the arāk tree bore fruit, as though its fruit was likened to the *naʿar* (fly).

It may be that the origin of all of these is the first sense. And *al-naʿʿār* in matters of strife is one who bustles about in it and stirs people up with his voice.
نعس:
The letters nūn, 'ayn and sīn are a minor root indicating drowsiness. *na'asa yan'asu nu'āsan* — he grew drowsy.

A she-camel that is *na'ūs* is described for her generosity in giving milk, because when she yields milk abundantly she is pictured as growing drowsy from it.

Someone said, in a line of verse:
Drowsy when she gives milk freely, ravenous in the hard season ... a young beast of a single year, or one of six years, like a full-grown one.
نعش:
The letters nūn, ʿayn and shīn are a sound root indicating raising and elevation. Al-Khalīl said: *al-naʿsh* is the bier of the dead — that is how the Arabs know it.

1. *mayyit manʿūsh* — a dead man carried upon the bier.
2. *intaʿasha al-ṭā'ir* — the bird rose up after stumbling. One says *naʿashahu Allāh* and *anʿashahu*, God raised him up. Ibn al-Sikkīt said: one does not say *anʿashahu*.
3. *banāt naʿsh* — stars (the constellation known as "daughters of the bier"). This is a metaphor.

Abū Bakr said: *al-naʿsh* is something like a litter that a king is carried upon when ill; it is not the bier of the dead. And he cited, in a line of verse:
Did you not see that the best of men — his litter in the morning was upon young men who had gone beyond the tribe, journeying on...
Then he goes on to say:
And we are with him, asking God to grant him everlasting life.
This shows that he was not dead.
نعض: The letters nūn, ʿayn and ḍād. They say: *al-naʿḍ* is a plant.
نعط: The letters nūn, ʿayn and ṭā'. They say: Nāʿiṭ is a clan of Hamdān.
نعظ: The letters nūn, ʿayn and ẓā'. They say: *naʿaẓa al-rajulu yanʿaẓu naʿẓan wa-nuʿūẓan* — meaning what he has stirred, became roused.
نعف:
The letters nūn, ʿayn and fā' are a word indicating elevation in a thing.

1. *al-naʿf* — a raised place set crosswise.
2. *al-naʿfa* — the tassel of a saddle, so named because it rises high (*sāmiya*).

*intaʿafa al-rajulu al-shay'* — said when a man leaves a thing for another, as though he raised himself above it.

And from the first word:

1. *nāʿaftu al-rajula* — I opposed, stood level against, the man.
2. *tanaʿʿafa al-rajulu* — the man climbed a ridge (*naʿf*).
نعق: The letters nūn, 'ayn and qāf are a word pointing to a sound. na'aqa al-rā'ī bi'l-ghanami yan'aqu wa-yan'iqu — the shepherd shouted at the sheep, driving them off, idhā ṣāḥa bihi zajran, na'īqan.
نعل:
The letters nūn, 'ayn and lām are a minor root pointing to settledness in a thing and to being low, underneath. From it comes al-na'l, the well-known thing (the sandal), because it is at the bottom of the foot.

1. rajulun nā'ilun — a man who has a sandal on; also munta'il.
2. an'altu al-dābba — I shod the animal; one does not say na'altu.
3. the wild donkey is called nā'il, for the hardness of its hoof.
4. al-na'l of the sword — the piece, of iron or of silver, that is at the bottom of its scabbard.

[A poet] said:
You see his sword, its scabbard-tip does not reach halfway up the shin — yes, even though its straps are long.

5. farasun mun'al — a horse whose whiteness on the lower part of its fetlock stops at the hair-fringe and does not go past it.
6. al-na'l — sinew worn on the back of the bow's tip.
7. al-na'l of land — a place; it is said to be the ḥarra (a black stony tract), and it is said that it grows nothing.

Al-Khalīl said: al-na'l is also an abased man, trodden underfoot as a sandal is trodden.
نعم:
The letters nūn, ʿayn and mīm: its branches are many, and in our view, for all their number, they go back to a single root pointing to ease, good living and well-being. From it is al-niʿma: what God, exalted be He, bestows upon His servant of wealth and living. One says: God, exalted be He, has a blessing upon him. And al-niʿma is a favour, and so is al-naʿmā'. And al-naʿma is enjoyment and good living. God, exalted be He, said: {wa-naʿmatin kānū fīhā fākihīn} — and a comfort in which they took delight [al-Dukhān: 27].

And al-nuʿāmā is the soft wind. And al-naʿam is camels, for the good and blessing in them. Al-Farrā' said: al-naʿam is masculine and is not made feminine, so they say hādhā naʿamun wāridun — this is a herd coming down to water; and it is pluralised anʿām. And al-anʿām are the grazing beasts, and that is the same pattern. And al-naʿāma, the ostrich, is well known — for the softness of its feathers. And by way of likeness there is the naʿāma which is like an awning set up on the heads of a mountain for shade.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
There is nothing on its height but its naʿāma, its shelter — part of it broken down and part of it still standing.

And they say naʿam wa-nuʿmā ʿaynin, and nuʿmata ʿaynin — that is, delight of the eye. And naʿima al-shay' is from al-naʿma. And so-and-so naʿʿama his children: he raised them in ease. And they say ibn al-naʿāma: the front of the foot.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Your mount shall be the young camel and its saddle, while the son of the ostrich is my mount on that day.

And it was so named because it is a soft, smooth place. And tanaʿʿama al-rajul: the man walked barefoot. And a group is spoken of as a naʿāma, so it is said shālat naʿāmatuhum — their ostrich took flight — when they scattered. And this is by way of likeness: that is, as an ostrich flies off, so these people have scattered. And they say ataytu arḍa banī fulānin fa-tanaʿʿamatnī — I came to the land of the sons of so-and-so and it agreed with me. And niʿma is the opposite of bi'sa, how bad. And they say in faʿalta dhāka fa-bihā wa-niʿmat — that is, what a good quality it is.

And from this chapter is their saying naʿam, yes, the answer to what calls for assent, the opposite of lā, no; and it too is from al-niʿma.

And by way of likeness, al-naʿā'im is a star. And al-naʿā'im are also timbers set up over a well from which the pulley-rope is hung, when the well has no wooden frames. And it is said that the anemone, shaqā'iq al-Nuʿmān, was protected by Ibn al-Mundhir, so it was ascribed to him. And it is said: rather al-nuʿmān here is blood. The first is the more likely. Ibn Durayd said: "tanaʿʿamtu Zaydan — I sought Zayd out", as though he meant that he set his naʿāma, the sole of his foot, to work towards him. And they say naʿima Allāhu bika ʿaynan, [and naʿimaka ʿaynan] — may God delight your eye by you — with the same meaning.
نعى:
The letters nūn, ʿayn and the weak letter are a sound root indicating the spreading abroad of something.

1. *al-naʿy* — news of a death; likewise the one who brings news of a death is also called *naʿiyy*.
2. *naʿāʾi fulānan* — announce so-and-so's death, meaning proclaim his death.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Announce the death of Judhām — not by dying or being killed, but a parting from its pillars and its stock.

And of this chapter:

3. *huwa yanʿā ʿalā fulān* — he reproaches so-and-so, as though spreading his misdeeds abroad.
4. *huwa yastanʿī al-ẓibā'* — he calls to the gazelles, going ahead of them so that they follow him.
5. *istanʿaytu al-qawm* — I went ahead of the people so that they would follow me; this rests on the spreading abroad of a call.

One says "his mention spread abroad" (*shāʿa dhikru fulān*) and *istanʿā* in the same sense. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: *istanʿā bihi al-sharr* means the trouble followed him one thing after another. And *istanʿā bihi ḥubbu al-khamr* means the love of wine persisted with him — the sense being that the wine seemed to call him and cry out to him, so he followed it.
نغ:
The letters nūn and ghayn are a word indicating certain parts of the body.

1. al-naghānigh — fleshy growths that form in the throat near the uvula; the singular is nughnugh.

Jarīr said, in a line of verse:
Ibn Murra pressed her secret place, O Farazdaq, as a physician presses the throat-glands of the afflicted.

2. The growths inside the two ears are also called al-naghānigh.
نغب:
The letters nūn, ghayn and bā' are a single word: *al-nughba* — the swallow, the gulp. *Naghabtu* — if you gulped; plural *nughab*. Dhū al-Rumma said, describing donkeys that came to water but did not drink their fill, in a line of verse:
Until, when it had slipped past every throat, down to the burning thirst, and the gulps did not quench it.
نغر:
The letters nūn, ghayn and rā' are a root meaning boiling and rage.

1. *naghirat al-qidr* — the pot boiled.
2. *naghira al-rajul* — the man became enraged.

And from this, the woman's saying in the hadith about ʿAlī (peace upon him): "Return me to my family, not enraged."

3. *naghirat al-nāqa* — the she-camel drew in her hindquarters and went on, as though she had become enraged at something and went her own way.
4. *huwa yatanaghghar ʿalaynā* — he turns hostile toward us. This belongs to the first sense.
5. The chicks of sparrows are called *al-naghar*, perhaps for their continual chirping — singular *naghara*, the male *nughar*, plural *nughrān*.

A poet said, describing bunches of grapes, in a line of verse:
They carry the vessels of wine as though they carried them upon the legs of *nughrān* chicks.
نغش:
The letters nūn, ghayn and shīn are a word indicating agitation and movement.

1. *al-naghashān* — agitation, wriggling.
2. *dār tantaghish* — a house said to swarm, for the abundance of people in it.
3. *al-nughāshī* — a short man.
نغص:
The letters nūn, ghayn and ṣād are a word indicating being cut off from what one intends.

1. *naghiṣa al-rajul* — the man's purpose was not completed for him; *nughghiṣa ʿalayhi* — he was thwarted.
2. *al-naghaṣ* — they say it is bringing your camels to the trough, and when they have drunk, turning them away and bringing others in their place.

And in our view, *al-naghṣ* is not letting them finish drinking.
نغض:
The letters nūn, ghayn and ḍād are a sound root pointing to shaking and movement.

1. al-naghaḍān — the loosening and wobbling of teeth.
2. al-ingḥāḍ — a person's shaking of his head toward his companion, as though astonished at him. God, exalted is He, said: {so they will shake their heads at you} [al-Isrā': 51].
3. al-naghḍ — the male ostrich, for the shaking of its head as it walks. [A poet] said:
And the naghḍ, like the mangy one daubed with tar.
4. al-nāghiḍ and al-nughḍ — the cartilage of the shoulder-blade, named for its movement; the word is also used for that of the ear.
5. al-naghūḍ — a she-camel huge in her hump, which wobbles when it grows large.
6. naghaḍa al-ghaym — the clouds moved on.
نغق: The letters nūn, ghayn and qāf. There is nothing in it except *naghaqa al-ghurābu naghīqan* — the crow croaked. Some report: *nāqa naghīq*, a she-camel that lows softly now and again, that is, once after another.
نغل: The letters nūn, ghayn and lām are a word indicating corruption and corrupting. *Al-naghil* is spoiled, rotten leather. They say: "spoiled leather may yet be patched." It is said that *al-naghal* is sowing discord among people, and slander.
نغم: The letters nūn, ghayn and mīm are nothing but *al-naghma*: the tone of speech and the beauty of the voice in recitation and the like. It is also called *al-naghm*. And *tanaghghama al-insān* — a person hums or intones — in singing and the like.
نغى:
The letters nūn, ghayn and the weak letter are a word indicating pleasant speech.

1. *huwa yunāghī al-ṣabiyya* — he coos to the child: he speaks to him with words that please and delight him.
2. From it: *kallamtuhu fa-mā naghā bi-ḥarf* — I spoke to him and he did not utter a single word.
3. *samiʿtu naghyatan* — I heard a soft word.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
When a soft word like honey came to me.

4. *jabal yunāghī al-samā'* — a mountain that seems to converse with the sky, as though it drew near it and speaks to it. And *al-munāghāh* is flirtatious courtship.
نف:
The letters nūn and fāʾ are a single word: al-nafnaf, the open air. Every gap between two things is a nafnaf.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Our swords hang like pillars, while between them and the ankle lies a deep, open chasm.
نفت:
The letters nūn, fā' and tā'. They say: *nafatat al-qidr* — the pot boiled until its broth dried onto it.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And a companion whose chest seethes against me like a boiling pot.

*nafata ṣadruhu bi-l-ʿadāwa* — his chest boiled with enmity.
نفث:
The letters nūn, fā' and thā' are a sound root pointing to something coming out of a mouth, or elsewhere, with the faintest sound.

1. nafatha al-rāqī rīqahu — the charm-reciter spat out his saliva lightly; it is less than al-tafl, ordinary spitting.
2. al-sāḥira tanfuthu al-summa — the sorceress spits out the poison.
3. "lā budda li'l-maṣdūri an yanfutha" — a proverb: one whose chest is congested must expectorate.
4. "law sa'alanī nufāthata siwākin mā a'ṭaytuhu" — if he asked me for the spat-out scrapings of a toothstick I would not give it to him; that is what is left between the teeth and then spat out.
5. damun nafīth — blood that a wound brings forth, that is, that it shows.
نفج:
The letters nūn, fā' and jīm are a root meaning the springing up of something and its rising.

1. *nafaja al-yarbūʿ* — the jerboa sprang up from its burrow. And *anfajahu ṣā'iduhu* — its hunter flushed it up.
2. *nafajat al-farrūja min bayḍihā* — the chick emerged from its egg.
3. *intafaja janbā al-baʿīr* — the camel's two flanks rose and swelled.
4. *al-nawāfij* — the rear ribs, singular *nāfija*.
5. *al-naffāj* — one who boasts of what he does not have.
6. *nafajat al-rīḥ* — the wind came with force.
7. *al-nafīja* — a strip of *nabʿ* wood taken to make a bow, as though it swells upon the tree.
نفح:
The letters nūn, fā' and ḥā' are a root pointing to the bursting-forth of a thing or its rising up. nafaḥat rā'iḥatu al-ṭībi nafḥan — the scent of perfume spread and burst forth; this perfume has a good nafḥa, a waft.

1. It was then extended by analogy, and one says "nafaḥa bi'l-māli nafḥan", he gave money out freely, as if he released it from his hand.
2. "lā tazālu li-fulānin nafaḥātun min ma'rūf" — so-and-so keeps giving out gusts of kindness.
3. nafaḥat al-rīḥ — the wind blew.
4. qawsun nafūḥ — a bow that sends the arrow far.
5. nafaḥat al-dābba — the animal kicked out and struck with its hoof; likewise nafaḥahu bi'l-sayf, he reached and struck him with the sword.
6. al-nafūḥ among she-camels — one whose milk runs out from her udder-openings without being milked.
نفخ:
The letters nūn, fā' and khā' are a sound root pointing to swelling up and rising high.

From it is intafakha al-shay' intifākhan — the thing swelled. And one says intafakha al-nahār, the day rose high. Nafkhat al-rabī' is the land's putting out of herbage in spring, because the earth rises and swells in it. Al-manfūkh is the fat man. And al-nafkhā' of land is like al-nabkhā'; that has already passed.
نفد: The letters nūn, fā' and dāl are a sound root indicating a thing's running out and coming to an end. "The thing nafida, yanfadu, nafādan" — it ran out. "They anfadū": their provisions ran out. The disputant is called munāfid — when two men argue, each wanting to exhaust the other's argument. And in the hadith: "If you dispute with them, they will dispute with you" — meaning: if you say something to them, they will say something back.
نفذ:
The letters nun, fa' and dhal are a sound root indicating decisiveness in a matter and other things.

1. nafadha as-sahmu ar-ramiyyata nafadhan — the arrow passed clean through the target.
2. anfadhtuhu ana — I made it pass through, I carried it through.
3. huwa nafidh — he is decisive, one who carries a matter through, effective in what he does.
نفر:
The letters nūn, fā' and rā' are a sound root pointing to shying off and drawing away.

From it: nafara al-dābba and other beasts, nifāran — its shying and drawing away from its place and its resting-spot. And nafara jilduhu — his skin swelled. In the hadith: "«that a man picked his teeth with a reed and his mouth swelled»" — that is, it swelled up. Abū 'Ubayd said: it is simply from one thing shying off from another and drawing away from it, because the skin draws off from the flesh on account of the disease that has come between them.

And yawm al-nafr is the day when the people move off from Minā. They say laqītuhu qabla ṣayḥ wa-nafr — I met him before any crier cried or anyone moved off. Al-munāfara is bringing a case before the judge between two men; they said its meaning is that what is sought is the preferring of one man's people over another's.
