And anfartu aḥadahumā 'alā al-ākhar — I gave judgement for one of them over the other. Al-nafar, a body of men, also follows the rule of this chapter, because they move out to bring help. Al-nafīr is al-nafar, and so are al-nafr and al-nafra: all of these run on one and the same rule. Al-Farrā' recited, for al-nafra:
She greeted you, then said: our folk ... today, Ur, are every one of them busy.

And the Arabs say naffartu 'ani al-ṣabiyy — that is, I gave him a nickname; as though in their view this were a driving off of the jinn and of the evil eye from him. A bedouin said: when I was born they said to my father, drive it off from your son! So he named me Qunfudh, hedgehog, and gave me the by-name Abū al-'Addā'.
نفز:
The letters nūn, fā' and zā' are a proper root meaning leaping and something resembling leaping.

1. *nafaza al-ẓaby* — the gazelle leapt as it ran.
2. *al-mar'a tunaffizu waladahā* — the woman dandles her child, as if making it leap.
3. *anfaztu al-sahm ʿalā ẓahri yadī* — I spun the arrow on the back of my hand.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
They fall down when made to leap in the falling dew, even on a day thick with drenching showers.
نفس:
The letters nūn, fā' and sīn are a single root pointing to the going out of a breath of air, however it be, from a wind or from something else; and its branches all come back to it. Of it is al-tanaffus, breathing: the going out of the breath from the inward parts. And naffasa Allāhu kurbatahu — God relieved his distress; and that is because in the going out of the breath there is relief and rest. And al-nafas is everything by which relief is given to one in distress. And in the hadith: " «Do not revile the wind, for it is from the breath of the Merciful» " — meaning that it is a relief by which distress is breathed away from those in distress. And it came in the mention of the Anṣār: " «I find the breath of your Lord coming from the direction of Yemen» " — meaning that through the Anṣār relief was given to those of the believers who were being harmed in Mecca. And the eye is called nafs. And a nafs — an evil eye — struck so-and-so. And al-nafs is blood, and that is sound, because when the blood is lost from a man's body he has lost his life. And the woman in her bleeding is called al-nufasā', because her blood comes out.

And al-nifās is a woman's giving birth; and when she has given birth she is nufasā'. And one says: I inherited this before so-and-so was born. And the child is manfūs, brought forth. And al-nifās is also the plural of nufasā'. And one says karaʿa fī al-inā' nafasan aw nafasayn — he drank from the vessel a draught or two. And one says that water has a nafas; and this is of the sort where a thing is named by the name of another, and because the life stands by it — and the life stands by the breath. He said:
The three black ones pass the night couched over a draught of [the water] of Māwiyya, the sweet.

And of the borrowed uses: tanaffasat al-qaws — the bow split open. And a thing is nafīs, that is, having life and weight in it, a thing men vie for. And al-tanāfus is that each of two who face one another brings out the strength of his own soul. And their saying of tanning that there is a nafas of it — this is the reasoning of the section: that is, a small quantity of it, as much as a hide is tanned with once; he likened it in its smallness to a breath that is drawn. And the reasoning of the section in this, and in what shares its meaning, is one.
نفش:
The letters nūn, fā' and shīn are a sound root indicating a spreading and scattering out.

1. *nafsh aṣ-ṣūf* — the carding of wool, that is, beating it out until it becomes fluffed and spread apart.
2. *nafasha ṭ-ṭā'iru janāḥayhi* — the bird fluffed out its two wings.
3. *nafashati l-ibl* — the camels wandered and scattered without a herdsman; the verb of this is *an-nafsh*, and camels of this kind are *nuffāsh* and *nawāfish*.
نفص:
The letters nūn, fā' and ṣād are words of related meaning, indicating the expelling of something from the body or throwing it out forcefully.

1. *anfaṣa fulān fī ḍaḥikihi* — so-and-so burst into unrestrained laughter.
2. *anfaṣa bi-bawlihi* — like *awzaʿa*, his urine burst out.
3. *al-nufaṣ* — spatters of blood, singular *nufṣa*.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
You see blood in spatters upon their shoulders.

Ibn Durayd said: *al-nufāṣ* is a disease that afflicts sheep, so that the animal urinates until it dies.
نفض:
The letters nūn, fā' and ḍād are a sound root meaning shaking something to clean it of dust or the like, then used metaphorically. One says *nafaḍtu al-thawb wa-ghayrahu nafḍan* — I shook out the garment and the like, a shaking.

1. *al-nafaḍ* — what a tree sheds of its fruit.
2. *imra'a nafūḍ* — a woman said to have shaken her belly free of her child, that is, miscarried.
3. *al-nāfiḍ* — a fever with shivering, because it shakes the body.
4. *anfaḍū* — their provisions ran out; when their provisions were exhausted, they shook out their containers to check what remained.

The Arabs say as a proverb: "the shaking-out drips out the goods for sale" — said when they have run low on provisions and, having little left, bring their camels to be sold.

And used metaphorically from this chapter, one says:

1. *nafaḍtu al-arḍ* — I sent someone to see whether the land held an enemy or not.
2. *nafaḍtu al-layl* — I patrolled by night to search out those under suspicion.
3. *al-nafīḍa* and *al-nafaḍa* — the group of people who do that.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
He comes to the waters in company and as a scout, the way sandgrouse come to water when the shade has shrunk thin.

The Arabs say: "If you speak by night, lower your voice; and if you speak by day, look about you." Meaning: look around you, for perhaps there is someone nearby who should not hear your words.

*al-nifāḍ* — the wrapper of children. It may belong to this chapter.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
A fair-skinned girl in a little wrap.
نفط: The letters nūn, fā' and ṭā' are three words: *al-nifṭ* (naphtha) is well known, with the nūn vowelled with kasra. *Al-nafaṭ* is a blister that comes up on the hand from work. *Nafaṭa al-ṣabiyy nafīṭan* — the child cried out. "He has neither *ʿāfiṭa* nor *nāfiṭa*" (he owns nothing): *al-nāfiṭa* is the sheep that snorts from its nose.
نفع: The letters nūn, fā' and ʿayn are a word pointing to the opposite of harm. And nafaʿahu yanfaʿuhu nafʿan and manfaʿatan — it benefited him, benefit and profit. And intafaʿa bi-kadhā — he drew benefit from such a thing. And God knows best what is right.
نفق:
The letters nūn, fā' and qāf are two sound roots: one of them points to a thing being cut off and going away, and the other to hiding a thing and concealing it. When the discussion of the two is worked out, they come close together.

The first: nafaqat al-dābbatu nufūqan — the beast died. And nafaqa al-siʿru nafāqan — the goods went off briskly, and that is because it passes on and does not stagnate or stand still. Anfaqū — their market became brisk. Al-nafaqa, the spending, is so called because it goes on its way. Nafaqa al-shay' — the thing was used up; one says qad nafiqat nafaqatu al-qawm, the people's provision has run out.

Anfaqa al-rajul — the man became poor, that is, what he had went away.

Ibn al-A'rābī said: and from it is His word, exalted: idhan la-amsaktum khashyata al-infāq — then you would hold back for fear of spending. And a farasun nafiqu al-jary is a horse whose running is quickly cut off.

The other root: al-nafaq is a tunnel in the ground with a way through to some place. Al-nāfiqā' is a spot in the jerboa's burrow which it makes thin, so that when it is come at from the side of the qāṣiʿā' it strikes the nāfiqā' with its head and intafaqa, that is, it comes out. From this is derived al-nifāq, hypocrisy, because the one who has it hides the opposite of what he shows, so that it is as though faith goes out of him, or he goes out of faith, in secret. And it may be that the root in this section is one, and it is going out. Al-nafaq is the passage that goes through, from which coming out is possible.

As for nayfaq al-sarāwīl, the wide part of trousers, Abū Bakr said: it is Persian, taken into Arabic.
نفل:
The letters nūn, fā', and lām are a sound root indicating giving and bestowal.

1. al-nāfila — a voluntary gift, given where none was owed; from it, the voluntary [supererogatory] prayer.
2. al-nawfal — a man who gives abundantly.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
The mighty, generous man refuses to let wrong be done through him.

3. al-nafl — the spoils [of war], plural anfāl; the leader 'yunaffilu' the fighters, meaning he gives them what they have won. One says naffaltuka, I gave you a share of spoils.
4. intafala min al-shayʾ — he disavowed himself of it; this is a case of one letter standing for another, the lām standing in for a yāʾ.

Al-Mutalammis said, in a line of verse:
Did you take me for one who disavows helping Buhtha? No — I am one of them, wherever I may be.
نفه:
The letters nūn, fā' and hā' are a single root meaning exhaustion and weakness.

1. *nafihat al-nafs* — the self grew weary and tired. He is called *nāfih* and *nuffah*.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Upon us are the lean, weary riding-camels.

2. *huwa munaffah* and *manfūh* — weak, cowardly.
نفى:
The letters nūn, fā' and the weak letter are a proper root meaning stripping something away from something and driving it off. One says *nafaytu al-shay' anfīhi nafyan*, and *intafā huwa intifā'an*.

1. *al-nufāya* — the inferior part that gets discarded.
2. *nafiyy al-rīḥ* — what the wind flings off of dust, until it settles at the base of walls.
3. *nafiyy al-maṭar* — what the wind flings off of rain, or sprinkles.
4. *nafiyy al-mā'* — what flies off the rope onto the back of the water-drawer.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Over those wells, from the flung spray.

The hamzated form of it is a single word: *al-nufa'* — scattered patches of pasture apart from the main body of pasture, singular *nufa'a*. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Its night-clouds rained abundantly and its growth was thickened by patches of yellow flowers and *zubbād*.
نق:
The letters nūn and qāf are a minor root indicating a sound among sounds.

1. naqqat al-ḍafādiʿ — the frogs croaked; the frog is al-naqqāqa.
2. The hen is said to tunaqniqu when it clucks for laying; this too may be said of al-naqqāqa.
3. al-niqniq — the male ostrich, so called because it yunaqniqu, makes that sound.

Among what deviates from this root: naqnaqat al-ʿayn — the eye sank in.
نقب:
The letters nun, qaf and ba' are a sound root indicating an opening made in something.

1. naqaba al-ha'ita yanqubuhu naqban — he made a hole through the wall, breached it.
2. the farrier naqaba's the navel of the animal, to let water out of it.
3. that iron tool is called minqab, the piercing-iron.
4. a dog called naqib — its throat is pierced so its bark grows weak; mean people do this so a guest will not hear it bark.
5. an-naqiba — a sore that breaks out on the side and bores inward into the body.
6. naqiba khuffu al-ba'ir — the camel's foot-pad became holed, worn through.
7. an-nuqba — the first mange that shows itself; plural nuqab.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Dressed carelessly, his good features showing — he puts tar on the spots of the mange.

Its derivation is sound, because it is something that pierces the skin.

From this root also: an-naqqab, one who knows affairs thoroughly — as if he probed into them and drew them out; or one who knows them, the munaqqib, the one who searches them out.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Handsome, successful, a companion in the thick of battle — one who probes deeply, telling of what is hidden.

An-naqb and al-manqaba — a path through a mountain; all this is one derivation. naqqabu fi al-bilad — they traveled through the lands; its origin is traveling through the nuqub, the paths. An-naqib, the naqib of a people — their witness and guarantor. Its meaning and the meaning of an-niqab, the learned one, are the same, because he probes into people's affairs, or probes as one probes for secrets. Al-manqaba — a noble deed; its derivation is sound, because it is a fine thing that has become known, as if it were probed out into the open.

What departs from this root: a woman's face-veil, niqab. naqabtu fulanan — I met so-and-so suddenly. An-nuqba — a garment like a waist-wrap with a drawstring, not the same as a girdle.

As for color, it too is called nuqba — one says "good in nuqba", meaning good in color. It is possible this is from the first sense, as if something were probed until something else appeared beneath it.
نقث:
The letters nūn, qāf, and thā' are a sound word indicating the mixing of one thing with another, and its being moved.

1. naqatha mā fī manzilī ajmaʿ — he moved everything that was in my house, all of it.
2. naqqathū ḥadīthahum — they mixed up their talk, as food is mixed (yunaqqath).
3. kharaja yunaqqithu — he went out hurrying, moving his legs quickly.
4. naqathtu al-ʿaẓma anquthuhu — I extracted the marrow that was in the bone.
نقح:
The letters nūn, qāf, and ḥā' are a sound root indicating your pushing something away from something.

1. naqqaḥtu al-ʿaṣā — I trimmed the staff, removing its knots from it.
2. shiʿr munaqqaḥ — refined poetry, that is, gone over and stripped of what does not fit it.
3. naqaḥtu al-ʿaẓma — I extracted its marrow.
نقخ:
The letters nūn, qāf, and khā' are a word indicating the striking of something.

1. mā' nuqākh — cold, sweet water, as if it strikes the thirst with its coldness, that is, knocks it away.
2. al-naqkh — piercing the head down to the brain.
نقد:
The letters nūn, qāf, and dāl are a sound root indicating the bringing out of something and its becoming exposed.

From that:
1. al-naqad in a hoof — its flaking; a flaking hoof is called naqid.
2. al-naqad in a molar — its crumbling, which happens through the outer layer flaking off it.

Also from this chapter:
1. naqd al-dirham — examining a coin, that is, its condition is exposed as to whether it is good or not. A dirham described as naqd is full-weight and good, as if its condition has been examined and made known.
2. al-anqad — the hedgehog. They say "so-and-so spent a night like anqad's night" of one who travels through the whole night; the reasoning is the same, as if it travels until the darkness clears away from it. They also say the porcupine (al-shayham) does not sleep through the whole night.
3. mā zāla fulānun yanqudu al-shay' — so-and-so kept watching the thing closely, said of one who does not stop looking at it.

And falling outside the pattern of this chapter:
1. al-naqad — the young of sheep, small ones, to which the stunted child who barely grows is likened.
نقذ: The letters nūn, qāf and dhāl are a sound root indicating the rescuing of something. "Anqadhtuhu minhu": I rescued him from it. A horse naqīdh is one taken from another people; plural naqā'idh. Anything you rescue is called naqadh.
نقر:
The letters nūn, qāf, and rā' are a sound root indicating striking something until a hollow is beaten into it, after which the sense broadens further.

1. minqār al-ṭāʾir — a bird's beak, because it pecks at something with it until it leaves a mark.
2. naqartu al-raḥā bi-l-minqār — I dressed the millstone with the minqār, that iron tool.
3. naqqartu ʿan al-amri ḥattā ʿalimtuhu — I probed into the matter until I knew it, that is, your investigating something, as if your coming to know it were a pecking into it.
4. naqartu al-rajula — I found fault with him, as if you struck him with something and left a mark.

A woman said to her husband: 'Take me past the sons of Naẓarā, and do not take me past the daughters of Naqarā' — meaning: take me past the men who look at me [admiringly], and not past the women who pick at me [with backbiting].

5. al-nuqra — a low spot where floodwater collects, as if it had been pecked out and dented.
6. al-manāqir, singular minqar — small wells with narrow mouths, as if pecked into the ground.
7. nuqrat al-qafā — the hollow at the back of the neck.
8. al-naqīr — the small mark on the back of a date-stone.
9. al-naqīr — also the hollowed base of a tree-trunk that dates and honey are steeped in; this is the vessel named in the prohibition [in the hadith].
10. fulān karīm al-naqīr — so-and-so is of noble stock, as if it were the place hollowed out around him until he emerged from it.

Their saying 'he called them by al-naqarā' means he invited some and, out of meanness, left others out. This is a sound analogy, because he does not call them all at once, but comes to the gathering and signals to one man as though pecking at him, or nudges him by hand to rise and come along.

11. al-nāqūr — the trumpet the angel blows on the Day of Resurrection; it 'pecks' at all creatures with its blast.
12. naqqartu ʿan al-amr — [as above] to investigate a matter.

Straying from this root is their saying anqara ʿan al-shayʾi inqāran, meaning he desisted.

In a hadith: 'God would never desist from [pursuing] the killer of a believer' — as if He never lets up on punishing him.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And I am not one who lets up on my people's enemies.
نقز:
The letters nūn, qāf, and zāy are a root indicating fineness, lightness, and smallness.

1. al-naqz — leaping.
2. nawāqiz al-ẓaby — the legs of a gazelle.
3. naqaz al-nās — the basest of people.
4. al-naqaz — an inferior man.
5. al-nuqāz — a disease that afflicts sheep, making them restless so that they cannot stay still.
6. al-nuqqāz — small sparrows.
نقس:
The letters nūn, qāf, and sīn are a root indicating the smearing of something with something unpleasant.

1. naqastuhu — I found fault with him, as if you had smeared him with something ugly.
2. Its base word is niqs, meaning ink; plural anqās.
نقش:
The letters nūn, qāf, and shīn are a sound root indicating the extracting of something and taking all of it in so that nothing is left of it; then whatever is close to that is measured by it.

1. naqsh al-shaʿr bi-l-minqāsh — plucking hair with tweezers (al-minqāsh), which is pulling it out.
2. al-munāqasha — going into precise detail in a reckoning so that nothing of it is left out. In the hadith: "Whoever is called to strict account will be punished."
3. shajja manqūsha — a head-wound from which the bone fragments are picked out, that is, extracted.
4. naqashtu marbiḍ al-ghanam — I cleared the sheep's resting-place of thorns.
5. al-naqīsh — scattered goods, as if part of it had been picked apart from the rest, that is, separated from one another.
6. naqsh al-shay' — improving something, as if he carves it, that is, removes its blemishes from it and beautifies it.
7. Then this is used as a metaphor, so one says naqashtu al-ʿidhq — I "carved" the date-cluster, meaning you strike it with a thorn until it ripens.
8. jāda mā intaqashta hādhā — how well you have picked this out, meaning what you chose.
9. hādhā naqīshu hādhā — this is the naqīsh of that, meaning its equal.
10. mā li-llāhi ḍiddun wa-lā naqīsh — God has no opposite and no naqīsh, meaning none resembles Him in His likeness and pattern.
نقص: The letters nūn, qāf and ṣād are a single word, which is al-naqṣ, the opposite of increase. Naqaṣa al-shay' — the thing grew less — and naqaṣtuhu anā — I made it less — and it is manqūṣ. Al-naqīṣa is a fault; one says there is no [naqīṣa in him, that is,] nothing in him that lessens him. The whole chapter goes back to this.
نقض:
The letters nūn, qāf and ḍād are a sound root pointing to the undoing of a thing, and sometimes it points to a meaning among the meanings, to a kind of sound. And naqaḍtu al-ḥabla wa-l-binā' — I undid the rope and pulled down the building. And al-naqīḍ is the undone thing; and for that reason the lean camel is called niqḍ, as though the journeys had undone him; and its plural is anqāḍ. And al-munāqaḍa in poetry is from this, as though he wants to undo what his fellow has knit. And the breaking of a covenant is from it too. And al-niqḍ is the place where the truffle breaks up out of the ground when you want to bring it out. naqaḍtuhā naqḍan — I broke it out. And the sore intaqaḍat, as though it had closed up and then broke open again.

As for the sound: the sound of the joints is called their naqīḍ; and it is near to the first, because they are as though they come undone, so a sound is heard from them at that. And anqaḍat al-dajāja — the hen cried out. And al-inqāḍ is the driving on of the young camel. A poet said, in a line of verse:
How many an old woman of a people, a decrepit hag — I taught her the inqāḍ after the qarqara.

He says: I stole her she-camel that she used to go grumbling along on, and left her a young camel to chirrup at.
نقط:
The letters nūn, qāf, and ṭā' are a root indicating a fine mark in something.

1. A small stand of palm trees is called a nuqṭa.

It is said that this is a comparison, in smallness, to the dot (al-nuqṭa).
نقع:
The letters nūn, qāf and 'ayn are two sound roots: one points to the settling of a thing, like a liquid, in its resting-place; the other to a sound among sounds.

The first: naqa'a al-mā'u fī manqa'ihi — the water settled in its settling-place. istanqa'a al-shay'u fī al-mā'i — the thing became immersed in the water.

1. al-naqū' — what is steeped in water, such as a medicine or a steeped drink.
2. al-minqa' — that vessel; also a small cooking-pot for a child, into which milk is poured and he is fed from it, also called minqa' al-burum, and made of stone.
3. al-naqī' — a drink made from raisins, as if the raisins are steeped for it. Also the trough in which dates are steeped.
4. al-naqī' and al-naq' — settled water. mā'un nāqi' is like nāji', thirst-quenching, as if it has settled in its place and so breaks the thirst; likewise al-naqū'.
5. al-naqī' — a well abundant in water. naq' al-bi'r, which comes in the hadith, is its water, as if the well were a resting-place for it.
6. al-unqū'a — the hollow of the crumbled-bread dish, where the fat gathers.

Their saying "huwa sharrābun bi-anqu'", one who drinks at the pools, means one who returns to a thing again and again. That is what they say, but the true sense, in our view, is that a wary bird does not come to the open watering-places for fear of itself, but comes instead to the settled pools to drink so as to stay safe; likewise the cautious, prudent man does not plunge into a matter except where safety lies.

7. al-naqī'a — pure, unmixed milk.

As for al-naqī'a in the other sense, some said it is what is secured from plunder before it is divided. The poet said:
We strike their heads with swords, the striking of the slaughterer securing the portion of those in front.
Others say al-naqī'a is instead the food prepared for one arriving from a journey, as if once it is made ready for him it has been "naqi'a" — settled, secured. These two explanations are the best said on it, being the most consistent with the underlying sense.

8. al-naqī'a — a slaughter-camel slaughtered on behalf of a group of camel-owners, as al-fara'a is a beast slaughtered on behalf of sheep-owners.

As for the other root: al-naqī' is the outcry, also called al-naq'. naqa'a al-ṣawtu — the voice rose. [A poet] said:
Whenever a true cry rises up, they answer it with clamour and din.
They also say al-naq' is the cry of the ostrich, and al-naqqā' is a man who boasts of having what he does not have, as if he cries out about it.

As for their saying "intuqi'a lawnuhu", his colour drained away, that is by the exchange of one letter for another, the original being "imtuqi'a", which we have already mentioned.
نقل:
The letters nūn, qāf and lām are a sound root meaning moving something from one place to another, and it branches out from there. One says *naqaltuhu anquluhu naqlan*. *Naqala al-farasu qawā'imahu naqlan* — the horse moved its legs.

1. *faras minqal* — a horse quick in the movement of its legs.
2. *al-munaqqila*, of head wounds, is the kind from which fragments of bone are shifted out.
3. *al-nuql* — what the drinker eats alongside his drink. Ibn Durayd used to say it is with *fatḥa* not *ḍamma*, but people say it with *ḍamma*.
4. *al-naqal*, with *fatḥa* on the *qāf* — what remains of small stones when they are dug up, because they get carried off.
5. *al-naqīl* — the road, because only a traveler takes it.

6. *al-manqala* — a stage of a journey.
7. A kind of gait called *naqīl* — that is the same pattern, as though it were a steady keeping-up of travel.
8. *al-munaqqal* — the worn-out sandal, because the walker keeps moving in it until it wears through. Likewise *al-naqal* in a camel is a disease that afflicts its foot-pad so that it tears through. The patches used to mend its foot-pad are called *al-naqā'il*.

And of this chapter:

9. *al-munāqala* — going back and forth over a story or a recitation, as though you passed your account to him and he passed his account to you.
10. *al-niqāl* — camels drinking, then stopping, then returning to the water to drink again, and this is not done to them but is something they do themselves.
11. They say *al-naqla* is the water channel.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
It shakes a bare canal in which is either steeped venom or a worn horn.
And the well-known version of this line is "it shakes a spear-shaft."
نقم: The letters nūn, qāf and mīm are a small root pointing to rejecting something and finding fault with it. And naqamtu 'alayhi anqimu — I rejected his deed and held it against him. Al-niqma belongs to punishment and to taking vengeance, as though one rejected a man's act and then punished him for it. As for their saying naqīma of a man's temper, and huwa maymūn al-naqīma — he is of blessed disposition — that is only a substitution of letters, and the original is naqība.
نقه:
The letters nūn, qāf and hā' are a word meaning recovery from illness, then used metaphorically. *Naqaha min al-maraḍ nuqūhan* — he recovered, so he is called *nāqih*.

They say *naqiha al-ḥadīth*, like *fahima* (understood), with kasra on the *qāf*, to distinguish it from the first. But the underlying sense is one, because when he *naqiha* a thing, he has been cleared of doubt about it.

Al-Liḥyānī said: one says *anqih lī samʿaka* — lend me your ear — as though saying, so that you may understand what I say.

And we have been told that the people of Medina call asking-for-clarification by the name *al-istinqāh*.
نقي:
The letters nūn, qāf, and the weak letter are a single root indicating cleanness and purity.

1. naqqaytu al-shay' — I purified the thing, freeing it from whatever tainted it; the noun is tanqiya.
2. intaqaytu al-shay' — I selected the thing, as if you took its best and purest part.
3. al-nuqāwa — the best part of a thing that you have selected.
4. al-naqāh — as is said, the inferior part of a thing, as if it is what was picked out and thrown away. Some said: the naqāh of everything is its inferior part, except dates — the naqāh of dates is their choicest part.

Also in this chapter:
1. al-niqy — the marrow of bones, named for its purity and cleanness.
2. al-niqy is also said of the fat behind the eye of a fat sheep or other animal.
3. A she-camel described as lā tunqī has no marrow left in her.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
They stood guard over their guests, and roasted for them meat from a marrow-rich beast, and livers.

As for al-Farrā', he claimed that al-anqā' means every bone that has marrow in it. If this is correct, it follows the Arabs' way of naming a thing by the name of something adjacent to it.
نكب:
The letters nūn, kāf and bā' are a sound root indicating a tilt, or a leaning, in a thing.

1. *nakaba 'ani sh-shay'i yankubu* — he turned away from the thing.

God, exalted is He, said: {who are turning away (*nākibūn*) from the path} [al-Mu'minūn: 74].

2. *an-nakbā'* — any wind that veers away from the direction of the four main winds.

Someone said, in a line of verse:
Do not let a chill *nakbā'*-wind turn away travellers ... striking companions on the road as they seek shelter.

3. *al-ankab* — one who seems, in his walk, to lean to one side.
4. *al-mankib* — the joint where the upper arm meets the shoulder; there are two *mankib*s, one on each side.
5. *an-nakab* — a disease that takes hold of camels in their shoulders, so that they limp from it.
6. *al-mankib* — also the assistant of the tribal deputy (*al-'arīf*), likened to a person's shoulder, as though he strengthens the deputy's authority the way a person is braced by his shoulder.
نكت:
The letters nūn, kāf, and tā' are a single root indicating a slight mark left on something, like al-nuktah (a dot) and the like.

Every dot is a nukta.

1. nakata fī al-arḍ bi-qaḍībihi yankutu — he made a mark in the ground with his stick, when he left a trace in it.
2. ruṭaba munakkita — a date that has begun to ripen, as if that early ripening looked like dots.
3. al-nākit in a camel — like a chafing mark, which is when its elbow strikes the edge of its chest-callus (kirkira).
4. nakattuhu — said when you throw someone onto his head, and he intakata, fell headlong; perhaps this too comes from the mark a thing leaves in the ground.
نكث:
The letters nūn, kāf and thāʾ are a sound root pointing to the undoing of a thing. Nakatha al-ʿahd, yankuthuhu, nakthan, he broke the covenant. Intakatha al-shayʾ, it came undone. 'He said a saying with no nakītha in it,' meaning no going back on it. From this too: 'he sought one thing, then intakatha for another,' as though he had undone his first resolve. Al-nikth: when the worn threads of old cloaks are unravelled and respun; a man was named Nikth for this. Al-nakītha: a hard undertaking in which people give way. Ṭarafa said, in a line of verse:

whenever there is a matter testing men for the hard undertaking, I am present
نكح:
The letters nūn, kāf and ḥā' are a single root, and it is sexual union.

And nakaḥa yankiḥu. And a woman is nākiḥ among the sons of so-and-so, that is, she has a husband from among them. And al-nikāḥ may be the marriage contract without the union. One says nakaḥtu: I married. And ankaḥtu ghayrī: I gave someone else in marriage.
نكد: The letters nūn, kāf and dāl are a minor root pointing to a thing coming out to the one who seeks it only with difficulty. hādhā maṭlabun nakid — this is a hard pursuit. rajulun nakidun and nakadun. They say naqada al-ghurābu, the crow strained hard in its cawing, as though it were retching. nāqatun nakdā' — a she-camel with no milk in her.
نكر:
The letters nūn, kāf and rā' are a sound root pointing to the opposite of that knowing in which the heart finds rest. And nakira al-shay'a and ankarahu - his heart did not accept it and his tongue did not acknowledge it. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And she did not know me - and what she failed to know of the happenings was nothing but grey hair and baldness.

The whole chapter goes back to this. Al-nukr is shrewd cunning. Al-nakrā' is the hard, harsh matter. And nakura al-amru nakāratan - the matter became grim. Al-inkār is the opposite of acknowledging. Al-tanakkur is moving from a state that gladdens to another that is disliked. And they call what comes out of the ḥuwalā' - the birth-sac - [of] blood and the like: nakira.
نكز:
The letters nūn, kāf, and zāy are a root indicating the sticking of something long and thin into something.

1. nakaztuhu bi-l-ḥadīd ankuzuhu — I pricked him with iron, which is like piercing.
2. nakazat al-ḥayya bi-anfihā — the snake struck with its snout.
3. nakaza al-mā' — the water sank away, as if it were a thing entering into the ground.
4. bi'r nākiz — a well whose water has sunk down.
5. ankazahā aṣḥābuhā — its owners drew it dry, causing its water to sink.

This follows the same sense — as if, when they drew all its water, it was thought that its water had sunk away and gone down into the ground.

Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
On Ḥimyarī she-camels, as though their eyes were the last remnant of water left in wells, drained dry by those who draw them.
نكس:
The letters nun, kaf and sin are a root indicating turning something upside down.

1. an-naks — your turning something onto its head.
2. al-wilad al-mankus — a reversed birth, when the legs come out before the head.
3. an-niks — an arrow whose notch has broken, so its top is turned to be its bottom.
4. a foolish, stupid man is called niks, by this same comparison.
5. al-munakkis, among horses — one that, when it runs, does not hold its head or its neck up, from weakness.
نكش:
The letters nūn, kāf, and shīn are a word indicating going through the whole of something.

1. They came upon herbage and nakashūhu — went through all of it.
2. They say: "It is a sea that cannot be nukash-ed [gone through to the end]," just as they say "cannot be drained."
نكص:
The letters nūn, kāf and ṣād are a single word. One says *nakaṣa 'alā 'aqibayhi*, he shrank back on his heels, when he drew back from a thing out of fear and cowardice.

Ibn Durayd said: *nakaṣa 'alā 'aqibayhi* — he went back on some good he had been engaged in; the phrase is said only of turning back from good.
نكظ:
The letters nūn, kāf, and ẓā' are a single word. It is said that al-nakẓ is pushing and haste.

He said, in a line of verse:
I passed beyond it in the haste of the mayṭ, when the shimmering mirage ran swiftly.

Ibn Durayd said: ankaẓtuhu inkāẓan, and nakaẓtuhu nakẓan, said when you hurried someone.
نكع:
The letters nūn, kāf, and ʿayn are two roots: one indicates a color, the other restraint and turning back.

The first:
1. al-ankaʿ — red, with a peeling nose; from it one says nakiʿ.
2. nakaʿat al-ṭurthūth — from the top of the ṭurthūth plant to about a finger's length down, it has a red skin on it.
3. shafa nakiʿa — a lip of intense redness.

From the other root:
1. nakaʿahu ḥaqqahu — he withheld his due from him.
2. nakaʿahu ʿanhu — he drove him away from it.
3. nakaʿtuhu bi-l-sayf wa-ghayrihi — I drove him off with the sword and other things.
4. nakaʿtuhu ʿan ḥājatihi — I turned him back from his need.
5. nakaʿtuhu al-shay' — like naqaṣtuhu, as if you drove him off from completing it, whether eating or drinking.
6. al-nakūʿ — a short woman, plural nukuʿ, as if she was restrained from growing tall.
7. rajul hukaʿa nukaʿa — a man who stays fixed in his place, not moving; this too comes from restraint.
نكف:
The letters nun, kaf and fa' are two roots: one indicates cutting something off and setting it aside; the other, a body part, which is then reasoned from by analogy.

The first: an-nakf — your wiping the tears from your cheek with your finger. They say: "we saw rain that no one traveling a day or two could cut across" — meaning: could not get past it. And: "a sea that cannot be nukifa", like "cannot be drained." Al-intikaf — going out from one land to another, or from one matter to another; you say "he intended this, then turned away (intakafa) and intended that instead", as if he had cut off his first resolve. intakafa al-athar — he found the track.

The other root: an-nakaf, plural of nakafa, a gland at the base of the jaw. Camels called munakkifa — their jaw-glands have become swollen and visible.

Then analogy was made from this, and it is said: nakifa min al-amr and istankafa — when he felt too proud for a thing, disdained it. The sense of the analogy here is that when he disdained something he turned away from it and showed the other the base of his jaw — just as one says a'rada, "he turned away", when he turned his cheek to someone and stopped facing him. Al-anaf, disdain, is from this too, as if he raised his nose above the thing. The derivation in all this is one. God knows best what is correct.
نكل:
The letters nūn, kāf and lām are a sound root indicating restraint and holding back, and all its branches return to this. "He nakala ʿanhu, nukūlan, yankilu" — he held back from it.

The origin of this is al-nikl: the fetter, plural ankāl, because it restrains. Al-nikl is also the iron piece of a bridle-bit. "He is nākil regarding matters": too weak to face them. Ibn Durayd said: "May God strike him with His nukl and with a nukla" — meaning He struck him with what would make an example of him.

From this root: "nakkaltu bihi tankīlan," and "nakkaltu bihi nakālan" — this follows the same pattern, meaning one did to him what would keep him from repeating his act and keep others from doing the like. This is the better of the two explanations. Al-mankal is the thing by which a person is made an example of.

He said, in a line:
And strike at the backs of their necks with a mankal.

As for the hadith: "Indeed God — exalted is He — loves al-nakal upon al-nakal," its own explanation given in the hadith is that it means the strong, seasoned man upon the strong, seasoned horse. This is by the explanation that came with it, and is not from the root we have described.
نكه:
The letters nūn, kāf, and hā' are a single word, and it is nakhat al-insān, a person's breath.

1. istankahtuhu — I smelled the odor of his mouth.
2. They say — and I do not know how it is — that al-nukkah among camels are those whose voices have gone from weakness. He said:
After the breaking-down of the weak-voiced, groaning camels.
نم:
The letters nūn and mīm are a sound root with two meanings: one is the showing and revealing of a thing, the other a kind of color.

The first is what al-Farrāʾ related: camels are called nammah when no water is left in their bellies.

1. al-nammām — the talebearer, so called because he does not keep speech inside himself; a man of this kind is nammām.
2. They say: askata Allāhu nāmmatahu — may God silence his nāmma, meaning whatever in his movement betrays him.
3. al-namīma — sound and whispering, because both betray a person.
4. al-nammām — a fragrant plant, sweet basil, so called because its scent betrays it.
5. Their saying mā bihā nummī — there is no one in it — as though they mean: no one whose movement would betray him.

Their calling a small coin nummī is not an Arabic word.

The other root:

1. al-namnama — fine lines set close together.
2. al-numnum — the white marks that appear on fingernails; the singular is numnuma.
نمر:
The letters nūn, mīm, and rā' are two roots: one is a color, the other indicates a drink taking wholesome effect.

The first:
1. al-namir, well-known [the leopard], from the mixing of black and white in its color, though the white is greater.
2. From al-namir is derived the color of clouds called al-numr; likewise livestock called al-numr have black and white in them.
3. al-namira — a striped, multicolored cloak.
4. tanammara lī fulānun — so-and-so threatened me; precisely, he put on the leopard's skin for me.

The other root:
1. al-namīr — sweet water that increases in the body and takes wholesome effect.
2. Then this is used as a metaphor, so one says [a lineage that is] namīr, meaning flourishing.
نمس:
The letters nūn, mīm, and sīn are three words: one indicates the concealing of something, another a color, the third the spoiling of something.

The first:
1. al-nāmūs — the keeper of a person's secret. namasa — he spoke something in secret and concealment.
2. al-nāmūs — the hunter's hiding-place.
3. In the Muṣannaf al-Gharīb: al-nāmūs is Gabriel, peace be upon him.

The origin of all this is one.

4. nāmastu fulānan munāmasatan — I confided secretly in so-and-so and made him the keeper of my secret. Ibn Durayd said: everything with which you conceal something is a nāmūs for it.

The third:
1. al-namas — a dullness in color; the sandgrouse are called al-nums because of a dullness in their color.
2. al-namas — the spoiling of ghee, of perfume, and of any scent.
3. al-nims — a small creature, named for its color.

As for Ḥumayd's saying, "like the bounding of the nims," it is said he meant these creatures. Abū Saʿīd transmitted it as "al-nums," saying: they are the sandgrouse, plural of anmas.
نمش:
The letters nūn, mīm, and shīn are a root indicating the marking of lines on something.

1. al-namash — the lines of a pattern; the adjective is namish.
2. al-namsh — as done by one idly toying, when he picks something up and traces lines with his fingers. He said:
I said to her, as she had grown fond of tracing such marks.
3. namasha al-jarād al-arḍ — the locusts stripped the land bare.
نمص:
The letters nūn, mīm, and ṣād are a root indicating the thinness of hair, or the plucking of it.

1. al-namaṣ — the thinness of hair.
2. al-minmāṣ — tweezers.
3. shaʿr namīṣ, and nabt namīṣ — hair, or a plant, that livestock have plucked out with their mouths.
نمط:
The letters nūn, mīm, and ṭā' are a word indicating a coming-together.

1. al-namaṭ — a group of people. In the hadith: "The best of this community is the middle group; the one falling behind catches up with them, and the one who goes to extremes returns to them."
نمغ:
The letters nūn, mīm, and ghayn are a word indicating the top of something.

1. namaghat al-jabal — the top of the mountain.
2. al-namagha — the part of an infant's soft skull that stirs, when he is first born.
نمق:
The letters nūn, mīm, and qāf are a root indicating the beautifying and improving of something.

1. namaqtu al-kitāb, and nammaqtuhu — I adorned the writing and decorated it.

He said, in a line of verse:
As if the trail the sand-burying winds dragged with their trains were, upon it, a white hide that skilled hands had adorned.
نمل:
The letters nūn, mīm, and lām, in their various words, indicate a clustering-together in a thing, along with smallness and lightness.

1. al-naml — ants, plural of namla.
2. ṭaʿām manmūl — food that ants have gotten into.
3. faras namil al-qawāʾim — a horse light of limb, as if likened to ants.
4. al-namla — a sore that breaks out on the side [of the body], perhaps named for its spreading and creeping, likened to the ant and its crawling.
5. al-anmula — a fingertip, plural anāmil.

They also say, though this is not from the same root, that al-namla is a crack in a horse's hoof, running from the hairline above it to its edge.

Straying from this chapter is al-numla — with ḍamma on the nūn and no vowel on the mīm — which means gossip, tale-bearing; one says namala, when he gossips.
نمى:
The letters nūn, mīm, and the weak letter are a single root indicating rising and increase.

1. namā al-māl yanmī — the wealth increased.
2. namā al-khiḍāb yanmī wa-yanmū — the dye deepened, when it increased in redness and blackness.
3. tanammā al-shay' — the thing rose from one place to another.

He said, in a line of verse:
O love of Laylā, do not fade, but increase — and grow, as the dye deepens on the hand.

4. intamā fulānun ilā ḥasabihi — so-and-so traced himself back to his lineage, that is, claimed descent from it.
5. nammaytu al-ḥadīth — I spread the report; and namaytuhu, in the lightened form — the reasoning behind both is the same.
6. al-nāmiya — creation, because they yanmūna, that is, increase. In the hadith: "Do not mutilate God's creatures."
7. nammaytu al-nār — I built up the fire, when you throw kindling onto it.
8. namat al-ramiyya — the game one has shot namā, when it ran off out of sight and then died; and its hunter is said to have anmāhā, caused it to die unseen. He said, in a line of verse:
So his quarry does not run off to die unseen — may he not be counted among his own kin.
In the hadith: "Eat what you have killed outright, and leave what has died out of your sight."
نه: The letters nūn and hā' are one word. One says: nahnaha fulānun fulānan — so-and-so restrained and rebuked so-and-so.
نهأ: The letters nūn, hāʾ and hamza. Hamzated, it is a single word, and it comes from substitution: one says anhaʾtu al-laḥm, meaning you did not fully cook the meat. In our view this is originally anyaʾtuhu, from al-niyy, rawness, with the yāʾ changed to hāʾ.
نهب:
The letters nūn, hāʾ and bāʾ are a sound root indicating the distribution of something by seizing it, not by equal shares.

1. intihāb al-māl — the plundering of wealth and other things.
2. al-nuhbā — the name for what has been plundered.
3. al-munāhaba — when two riders race each other at full gallop; one says nāhaba al-farasu al-farasa, as though each snatches the gallop and the lead from the other.
4. nahaba al-nāsu fulānan bi-kalāmihim — people set upon so-and-so with their talk, meaning they assailed him with it.

The pattern is the same throughout.
نهت:
The letters nūn, hāʾ and tāʾ are a word indicating the imitation of a sound.

1. al-nahīt — a sound less than a roar; a lion of this kind is nahhāt.
2. nahata al-rajul — the man groaned, strained.
3. A donkey of this kind is nahhāt.
نهج:
The letters nūn, hā' and jīm are two distinct roots: the first is al-nahj, the road.

1. nahaja lī al-amr, he made the matter clear to me; huwa mustaqīm al-minhāj, he is straightforward in his path.
2. al-manhaj — also a road, plural al-manāhij.

The other root is cutting off, breaking off.

1. atānā fulānun yanhaju, when someone came to us panting, out of breath.
2. ḍarabtu fulānan ḥattā unhija, I struck so-and-so until he collapsed breathless.
3. nahaja al-thawb and anhaja, the garment became worn without yet tearing; anhajahu al-balā, wear and age wore it out. Abū 'Ubayd said: one does not say nahaja in this sense.
نهد:
The letters nūn, hāʾ and dāl are a sound root indicating the rising and prominence of a thing.

1. faras nahd — a horse that is prominent and large-bodied.
2. nahada thadyu al-marʾa — the woman's breast rose and grew firm; she is nāhid.
3. nahīda — a large lump of butter.

From this branch: al-munāhada in war, like al-munāhaḍa, because each side rises up toward the other — except, they said, that al-nuhūḍ is rising from a seated position, while al-nuhūd can happen from any state.

4. A man is nahd — noble, one who rises to lofty matters.
5. al-nahdāʾ — a fine stretch of sand that grows the choicest herbs.
6. anhadtu al-ḥawḍ — I filled the trough; it is ḥawḍ nahdān, brimful.
7. al-tanāhud — they say, though I do not know how sound this is, that it is each of a group of companions putting in an expense in proportion to what his companion puts in.
نهر:
The letters nūn, hā' and rā' are a sound root pointing to a thing opening up, or to the opening of it.

Anhartu al-dam — I opened the flow of blood and let it run. The river, al-nahr, is so named because it yanhar the ground, that is, it cleaves it. Al-manhara is an open space between the houses of a people into which they throw their sweepings. The plural of nahr is anhār and nuhur. Istanhara al-nahr — the river took its course. Anhara al-mā' — the water ran. A nahrun nahir is a river with much water.

Abū Dhu'ayb said, in a line of verse:
She stayed there and built herself a tent upon reeds, by sweet water running full.

From it also is al-nahār, the daytime: the opening of the darkness into light, from the rising of dawn to the setting of the sun. And they say that nahār is given the plural nuhur. A rajulun nahir is a man of the daytime, as though he does not stir by night.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
I am no man of the night, but a man of the day.

As for their saying that al-nahār is the chick of a certain bird, that is the sort of thing one does [not] pause over, and it has no sense.
نهز:
The letters nūn, hāʾ and zāy are a sound root indicating movement, rising, and the setting of a thing in motion.

1. al-nahz — rising to take hold of something; from this, intihāz al-furṣa, seizing the opportunity.
2. al-nuhza — anything it becomes possible for you to seize; one says, it has presented itself, so seize it.
3. nahazat al-nāqa bi-ṣadrihā — the she-camel rose with her chest, that is, she rose to set off.
4. nahazat al-dābba bi-raʾsihā — the animal jerked with its head, warding something from itself.

From this branch:

5. nāhaza al-ṣabī al-bulūgh — the boy drew near to puberty, as though he rose toward it and stirred.
6. nahaztu ḍarʿ al-nāqa ʿinda ḥalbihā — I struck the she-camel's udder at milking so it would yield.
7. nahaztu māʾ al-dalw bi-l-māʾ — I struck the water in the bucket with water so the bucket would fill.
نهس:
The letters nūn, hāʾ and sīn are a word indicating biting onto something.

1. nahasa al-laḥm — he gripped the meat and tore at it while eating it.
2. nahasathu al-ḥayya — the snake bit him.
نهش: The letters nūn, hāʾ and shīn are a sound root, and its meaning is the meaning of the one before it. Ibn Durayd said: al-Aṣmaʿī said al-nahs and al-nahsh are the same, meaning taking flesh with the mouth. Abū Zayd disagreed with him and said: al-nahsh is done with the front of the mouth.
نهض:
The letters nūn, hāʾ and ḍād are a root indicating upward movement.

1. nahaḍa min makānihi — he rose from his place, stood up.
2. mā lahu nāhiḍa — he has no nāhiḍa, meaning no people who rise up for his affair and stand by it. They say a man's nāhiḍa are his father's sons, who grow angry on his behalf.
3. nahaḍa al-nabt — the plant stood upright, grew even.
4. al-nāhiḍ — the bird whose two wings have grown full and which is ready to rise and fly.
5. nihāḍ al-ṭuruq — the roads' climbs and steep steps; the singular is nahḍa.
6. anhuḍ al-baʿīr — what lies between the camel's shoulder and its back.
نهط: The letters nūn, hāʾ and ṭāʾ. Ibn Durayd held that al-nahṭ is stabbing. Nahaṭahu bi-l-rumḥ — he pierced him with the spear.
نهع: The letters nūn, hāʾ and ʿayn are not a root at all — except that they say nahaʿa, meaning he retched without bringing anything up.
نهق:
The letters nūn, hāʾ and qāf are a sound root indicating a sound among sounds.

1. al-nahīq and al-nuhāq — the braying of the donkey.
2. nawāhiquhu — the points from which its bray issues out of its throat.
3. nawāhiq al-dābba — veins that flank the animal's nostrils; the singular is nāhiqa.
نهك:
The letters nūn, hāʾ and kāf are a sound root indicating going to an extreme in punishment and harm.

1. nahakathu al-ḥummā — the fever wasted away his flesh.
2. anhakahu al-sulṭān ʿuqūba — the ruler dealt him a punishment that went to the extreme.

From this branch:

3. intihāk al-ḥurma — violating what is sacred, dealing with it in a way that is not lawful.
4. al-nahīk — the lion and the brave man, because both wear down their rivals.
نهل:
The letters nūn, hāʾ and lām are a sound root indicating a kind of drinking.

1. nahila — he drank at the first coming to water.
2. anhaltu al-dawābb — I gave the animals their first drink.
3. al-manhal — the watering place.
4. al-nāhil — the one who has drunk his fill; though they sometimes call the thirsty man nāhil too, perhaps as a kind of good-omen naming, calling him the opposite of what he is.

He said, in a line of verse: the thirsting spear-shafts drink their fill from him — meaning the thirsty spears are given their fill by him.
نهم:
The letters nūn, hāʾ and mīm are two sound roots: one a sound among sounds, the other a craving for something.

The first:

1. al-nahīm — the roar of the lion.
2. al-nahīm — also your driving-cry to camels when you shout at them; you say nahamtuhā when you shout at them to make them go.

He said, in a line of verse: Drive them both on, for they need driving — it is only thirst-driven men who drive them.

3. nahm — the throwing of a stick or of pebbles, said this way because whatever is thrown must make at least some faint sound.

He said, in a line of verse: They pelt at the encampment the pebbles that are pelted.

The other meaning:

1. al-nahma — the reaching of one's full desire in a thing.
2. manhūm — passionately devoted to something; one says from this nuhima yunhamu.

Among what deviates from both roots: al-nahāmī — the blacksmith.
نهي:
The letters nūn, hā' and yā' are a sound root pointing to an end and a reaching. And of it is anhaytu ilayhi al-khabar: I brought the news through to him. And the nihāya of anything is its farthest end. And of it is nahaytuhu 'anhu, I forbade him a thing, and that is for something he is doing. So when I forbid him and he leaves off from you, that is the end of what was and the last of it. And so-and-so is nāhīka min rajulin, and nahyuka, as one says ḥasbuka, he is enough for you; and its sense is that by his earnestness and his sufficiency he forbids you to seek another. And a she-camel nahiyya is one that has reached the end of fatness. And al-nuhya is the mind, because it forbids ugly deeds; and the plural is nuhan.

And he sought his need until nahiya about it, that is, he left it, whether he got it or not, as though he had forbidden himself to seek it. And al-nahy and al-nihy are the pool, because the water comes to its end there. And the tanhiya of a valley is where the floods come to their end. And it is said that nihā' al-nahār is the day's climbing high. If this is sound, then it is because that is the end of its climbing.

And among what strays from this section, if it is sound, is their saying that al-nuhā' are glass flasks; but it is not so in our view. And they recite, in a line of verse:
Their hooves crush the pebbles as though a broken eggshell and glass were being shattered between them.
نوب:
The letters nūn, wāw and bā' are a single word pointing to making a place one's habit and coming back to it. One says nāba yanūbu, and intāba yantābu — to come back again and again. It is said that al-nūb are bees; they said: they were named that for their grazing and their returning to their place. And it has been said that it is the plural of nā'ib, one who comes back in turn. And the line of Abū Dhu'ayb:
I lay sleepless at the thought of him, though no fit had come round to me ... as a newly polished, patterned thing is set stirring.
نوت: The letters nūn, wāw and tāʾ are not, in my view, a root at all — except that they say nāta yanūtu wa-yanītu, meaning he swayed from weakness. If this is sound, then perhaps al-nūtī, the sailor, comes from it.
نوح:
The letters nūn, wāw and ḥāʾ are a root indicating the facing of one thing toward another.

1. tanāwaḥa al-jabalān — the two mountains face each other.
2. tanāwaḥat al-rīḥān — the two winds face each other in their blowing; one wind is nayyiḥa to the other, meaning it faces it.
3. al-nawḥ and al-manāḥa, wailing and the place of mourning, so called for the facing of the women toward each other at the weeping.
نوخ: The letters nūn, wāw and khāʾ are a single word: anakhtu al-jamal, I made the camel kneel down. As for its intransitive form, they said anakhtuhu fa-baraka, I made it kneel and it knelt; others said istanākha, it knelt down of itself. It came in a hadith: "and if it is made to kneel upon a rock, it kneels." Al-Aṣmaʿī said: anakhtuhu fa-tanawwakha — I made it kneel, and it settled down kneeling.
نور:
The letters nūn, wāw and rā' are a sound root pointing to giving light, to unsteadiness and to little fixity. From it are al-nūr, light, and al-nār, fire, both named so from the way of giving light, and because that is unsteady and quick in its movement. And tanawwartu al-nār - I looked out for the fire. Imru' al-Qays said, in a line of verse:
I looked out for her fire from Adhri'āt while her people were at Yathrib - the nearest of her dwelling is a far sight.

And from it al-nawr: the blossom of trees, and its nuwwār. And anārat al-shajara - the tree put out blossom. Al-manāra is of the pattern maf'ala from seeking light, and the origin of it is manwara. And from it manār al-arḍ: the boundaries and marks of land, so called for their clearness and their showing plainly. And what we said about little fixity is: a woman is nawār, that is, chaste, who tanūr, that is, shies away from what is shameful; and the plural is nūr. And nārat: she shied away, nawran. A poet said, in a line of verse:
What, shying away? How quick! What is this, Farūq?

And nurtu fulānan - I made him shy away. And al-niwār is shying away.

Among what strays from this root is al-na'ūr: the smoke of a wick, taken as kohl and as tattoo-dye. And nawwartu al-litha - I pricked the gum with a needle and then put antimony into the pricks.
نوس: The letters nūn, wāw and sīn are a root indicating agitation and swaying. nāsa al-shay' — a thing swayed, yanūsu. Abū Nuwās was named for two locks of hair he had, that used to sway. And they say: nustu al-ibil — I drove the camels.
نوش:
The letters nūn, wāw and shīn are a sound root indicating the taking or reaching for a thing. Nushtuhu nawshan, I reached for it. Tanāwashtu means I took hold of, I reached for. God Almighty said: {but how could they reach it from so far a place} [Saba': 52]. Sometimes they use it without the preposition, saying nushtuhu khayran, when you granted him good. And the words of a speaker, in a line of verse:
She spent the night reaching for the neck, reaching repeatedly.
نوص:
The letters nūn, wāw and ṣād are a sound root indicating wavering back and forth, coming and going.

1. nāṣa 'an qarnihi yanūṣu nawṣan, he swerved away from his match.
2. al-manāṣ — the verbal noun, and also refuge. He, glory be to Him, said: {and it was not a time for escape} [Ṣād: 3].
3. al-nawṣ — the wild donkey, they say, is constantly nā'iṣ, raising its head, wavering like a headstrong, balking animal.
4. nāwaṣa al-jarra, he wrestled with the jar — its explanation has already passed in the chapter of jīm.
نوض:
The letters nūn, wāw and ḍād carry distinct words in it.

1. al-nawḍ — the joint connecting the rump to the back.
2. nāḍa fī al-bilād — he went away, journeyed off through the land. This is their second saying.
3. al-anwāḍ — the valleys, singular nawḍ.
نوط:
The letters nūn, wāw and ṭā' are a sound root indicating the hanging of one thing on another. One says nuṭtuhu bihi — I hung it on it.

1. al-nawṭ — also what is hung on something; plural anwāṭ. In the proverb, "reaching without things hung" — meaning he reaches out and takes hold of something, but has nothing hanging there for him.
2. al-niyāṭ — a vein by which the heart is suspended; plural anwiṭa; also called al-nā'iṭ. Someone said, in a line of verse: like the physician's cutting of the sick man's niyāṭ-vein.
3. niyāṭ al-mafāza — the remoteness of a wasteland, so named because, from its distance, it seems forever tied to something beyond it.
4. al-arnab (the hare) — "cutter of the niyāṭ," because it covers such great distances.
5. al-tunawwiṭ — a bird; this too follows the same pattern, because it hangs [strands] like threads from the tree, making them into a nest.
6. nīṭa fulān — so-and-so was struck by a nawṭa, a swelling in the chest. This, in our view, comes from niyāṭ al-qalb, as if the pain had struck its niyāṭ-vein.
7. nawṭa min ṭalḥ — a cluster of acacia trees, as one says 'īṣ min sidr, a thicket of lote-trees; named so because parts of it hang together, clinging to one another.
8. bi'r nayyiṭ — a well is called this when it is about the depth of a man's height.
نوع:
The letters nūn, wāw and 'ayn are two words: one indicates a portion of a thing resembling the whole, and the second is a kind of movement.

1. al-naw' of a thing — a category of it. "This is not of the same naw' (kind) as that."
2. nā'a al-ghuṣn, yanū'u — a branch swayed; it is nā'i'. Some of them said this is why one says jā'i' nā'i' (hungry and swaying), meaning shaken by the severity of his hunger, swaying. And they curse a person by saying: jū'an lahu wa-nū'an lahu — hunger to him, and swaying to him.
نوف:
The letters nūn, wāw and fā' are a sound root indicating height and elevation. nāfa, yanūfu: it grew tall and rose up.

1. al-nawf — the [camel's] hump; plural anwāf.

It is possible that their saying mi'a wa-nayyif (a hundred and a bit more) comes from this; we have already mentioned it under the chapter n-y-f, for its wording.
نوق: The letters nūn, wāw and qāf are a root pointing to height and elevation. The highest point on a mountain is nīq — its origin is a wāw, changed to a yāʾ because of the kasra before it. It is possible al-nāqa, the she-camel, comes from this same pattern, for the height of her build. One says nāqa, plural nūq. 'The he-camel has turned into a she-camel' is a comparison to her, used as a proverb for one humbled after having been mighty. Al-nāqa also names a constellation shaped like a she-camel. As for their saying tanawwaqa fī al-amr, when he took great pains over a matter, in our view this too comes from the same root: they compare a thing to what they find beautiful, and tanawwaqa is patterned on the word for she-camel, since she is among their finest possessions. Whoever calls this derivation mistaken has himself erred; the pattern is as described. Al-nīqa (fastidious care) can only come from tanawwuq. They say, as a proverb: 'a clumsy woman, yet possessed of nīqa,' said of one ignorant of a thing who claims to know it.
نوك: The letters nūn, wāw and kāf are a single word: al-nawāka and al-nūk, which is foolishness. A man is anwak or mustanwik, and they [as a group] are nawkā.
نول:
The letters nūn, wāw and lām are a sound root indicating giving. nawwaltuhu — I gave to him. al-nawāl — the gift. nultuhu nawlan, like analtuhu.

1. mā nawluka an taf'ala kadhā (it is not your nawl to do such-and-such) — also from this, meaning: it is not fitting that what you give us from your giving should be this.

Labīd said, in a line of verse: "I stopped by them, until my companion said ... you have grown impatient, and that is not al-nawāl." They said: here al-nawāl means what is right; and its sense in summary is: that is not the giving which, had you given it to us, you would have been right to give. And likewise his saying, in a line of verse: "So leave off blame — woe to another than you — for al-nawāl is not the blaming of every noble man." The underlying sense in all of this is one and the same.

1. al-minwāl — though it departs from the pattern of this chapter — the piece of wood on which the weaver winds the cloth.
نوم:
The letters nūn, wāw and mīm are a sound root pointing to stillness and to the quieting of movement. From it is al-nawm, sleep. nāma yanāmu nawman and manāman. And he is na'ūm and nuwama: one who sleeps much.

And a man nawma is one who is obscure and of no account. And from it istanāma lī fulānun, when he is at ease with him and settles to him. And al-manāma is the thick cloak, because one sleeps in it.

And they borrow from it: nāmat al-sūq — the market went slack. And nāma al-thawb — the garment wore out.
نون: The letters nūn, wāw and nūn are a single word. Al-nūn is the fish. And Dhū al-Nūn is a sword belonging to one of the Arabs, as though it was compared to the nūn for its shape.
نوه:
The letters nūn, wāw and hā' are a word indicating loftiness and elevation.

1. nāha al-nabāt — the plant rose up.
2. nāhat al-nāqa — the she-camel raised her head and cried out.
3. nuhtu bi-al-shay' and nawwahtu — I raised mention of it, made it renowned.
4. nāhat nafsuhu — his spirit grew strong.
نوى:
The letters nūn, wāw and the weak letter are a sound root with two meanings: one, aiming at something; the other, the stone of a fruit.

The first: al-nawā. The lexicographers said: al-nawā is moving from one dwelling to another. This is the origin, and the whole chapter was then built upon it, so they said nawā al-amr yanwīhi, he intended the matter, when he purposed it. What confirms this reading is their saying nawāhu Allāh, as though God intends him with protection and care.

He said, in a line of verse: O ʿAmr, may God's intending of you be toward right guidance; and carry my greeting to al-Dhalfāʾ at al-Thamad — meaning He intended you toward right guidance.

Al-niyya — the direction you intend. Your nawiyy — your companion, whose intention is your intention.

The other root: al-nawā, the date-stone. They sometimes used it to express certain weights; it is said that a nawāh weighs five dirhams. He married her for a nawāh of gold, meaning the weight of five dirhams of it.

With the hamza, nāʾa, there is a word indicating rising: nāʾa yanūʾu nawʾan, he rose up.

He said, in a line of verse: We said to them, that then, after a charge, we leave them fallen, their rising feeble — meaning their rising is weak.

Al-nawʾ, one of the star-risings associated with rain, as though it rises bringing the rain with it. Anyone rising under a heavy load is said to nāʾa; the camel nāʾa under its load. A woman: her hips weigh her down, and she rises with difficulty under them — the first sense is that she is weighed down by them, the second that she struggles to rise.

From this branch: al-munāwaʾa, between people; one says nāwaʾahu, he opposed him. This follows the same pattern as what we have said, for it is a mutual confrontation: this one rises against that one and that one rises against him, meaning each rises up against the other.
نيأ: The letters nūn, yā' and hamza are a word: al-nīy of meat — that which has not been cooked. I have anā'tu it [left it raw]. The origin is anya'tuhu. And God knows best what is correct.
نيح:
The letters nūn, yā' and ḥā' are a sound word indicating good and a good state.

1. nayyaḥahu Allāhu bi-khayrin — God granted him good, gave it to him.
2. al-nayḥ — Al-Khalīl said this is the hardening of a bone after its moistness [as it matures]; the verb is nāḥa, yanīḥu, nayḥan.
3. nayyaḥa Allāhu 'iẓāmahu ("may God make his bones firm") — a phrase said as a blessing for someone.

Another word has been mentioned which, if sound, is close to this chapter: they say nāḥa al-ghuṣn, yanīḥu, nayḥan — the branch swayed. Abū Bakr related this from Abū Mālik.
نير:
The letters nūn, yā' and rā' are a word indicating the clarity and prominence of a thing.

1. nīr — said of the clear-cut furrow of a road. Someone said, in a line of verse: "to every one with two nīrs, its markings plain."
2. nīr al-thawb — the woven border of a garment, named so for its prominence and clarity.
3. al-nīr — by the same analogy, the piece of wood [yoke] placed on the neck of the plough-ox along with its fittings; plural nīrān and anyār.
4. dhū nīrayn — a man "of two nīrs," meaning his strength is twice the strength of another.
5. al-nīr — a mountain.

And we do not deny that the origin of all this might be a wāw, so that it goes back to what we mentioned in the chapter of nūr (light) and nār (fire).
نيط: The letters nūn, yā' and ṭā'. They say al-nayṭ: death. Al-Umawī said: "ramāhu Allāhu bi-al-nayṭ" — may God strike him with death.
نيف:
The letters nūn, yā' and fā'. We have already mentioned, in the chapter of nūn-wāw-fā', that it indicates elevation and increase. It is possible that this chapter goes back to that same origin.

1. mi'a wa-nayyif — a hundred and a bit more.
2. anāfat al-darāhim 'alā al-mi'a — the dirhams exceeded a hundred.
3. Abū Zayd said: everything between two tens [between one round number and the next] is a nayyif. Something showing this to be so is the saying of a poet, in a line of verse: "I came to a hill, whose top ... rose above (nayyif) every hill."
4. nāqa niyāf, jamal niyāf — tall, rising high.
5. nayyafa 'alā al-sab'īn — Abū Bakr said: he exceeded seventy, went beyond it.
نيم:
The letters nūn, yā' and mīm are three words, not a single origin sense.

1. al-nīm — the first: the fur cloak.
2. al-nīm — the second: a tree. Sā'ida ibn Ju'ayya al-Hudhalī said, in a line of verse: "Then he reaches out, when the day grows heavy for him ... after watching, from nīm and from katam." And al-katam is also a tree.
3. al-nīm — the third: the rippled track in sand when the wind runs through it. Someone said, in a line of verse: "Until the night cleared from us over a mottled tract ... like tanned leather, with a nīm-ripple in a haze of dust."
هال: Al-hāla: the ring [halo] around the moon.
هام:
The letters hā', alif and mīm are a sound root indicating height in some part of the body, and it is then used metaphorically.

1. *al-hāma* — the head; the plural is hām and hāmāt.
2. *sayyid al-qawm* [the chief of the people] — called hāma, by way of comparison.

As for al-hāma among birds, it is not really a bird; it is something the Arabs used to speak of. They used to say that the spirit of a slain man whose blood has not been avenged becomes a hāma, and it screeches, saying "give me to drink, give me to drink!" And when he is avenged, it flies away. This is what Jarīr meant by his saying:
And among us is the one who wore out Ṣudayy ibn Mālik, and frightened the birds away from Juʿāda's fallen dead.
He means: he killed his killer, and so frightened the hāma away from his grave.
هب:
The letters hā' and bā' — most of this chapter concerns waking, stirring, and movement, and sometimes it indicates the thinness of something.

The first:
1. habbat al-rīḥ tahubbu hubūban — the wind blew.
2. habba al-nā'im yahubbu habban — the sleeper woke.
3. "min ayna hababta yā fulān" — as if saying: from where have you come, from where did you awaken to us. It is related from Yūnus: so-and-so was absent, then habba, turned up.
4. They say: "habba yafʿalu kadhā," he set about doing such-and-such, just as one says "ṭafiqa yafʿalu."
5. hazaztu al-sayf fa-habba habbatan — I brandished the sword and it swung with a stroke. habbatuhu — its swing and its keenness in its stroke. sayf dhū habba — a sword possessing that keen swing.
6. habba al-baʿīr fī al-sayr — the camel grew brisk in its pace, hibāban.

Labīd said, in a line of verse:
It surges briskly against the rein, as though it were a tawny cloud, its rain spent, driven off with the south wind.

7. habba al-tays li-l-sifād habīban, and ihtabba — the billy-goat grew eager to mate; such a goat is mihbāb.
8. habhabtu bihi — I called to it to mount.
9. al-habhabī — the shepherd; and a youth quick in service is also called habhabī.
10. They say: "ʿishnā bi-dhāka hibbatan min al-dahr," we lived through that for a hibba of time, meaning a year, a spell that came upon us (habba lanā).

The other chapter:
1. tahabbaba al-thawb — the garment became worn and frayed.
2. The tattered pieces of a garment are called hibab.
3. habhaba al-sarāb — the mirage shimmered.
4. al-habhāb — the mirage.

How close this is to the first sense!

Among what is unclear to me in meaning is their saying "habhu faʿala kadhā" and "habnī faʿaltuhu" [suppose he did such-and-such, suppose I did it]; I thought this belonged to the chapter of wahaba, to give, since the wording points to that, but even so it remains unclear to me. They say to horses "habī," meaning come forward; this is the imitation of a call.
هبت:
The letters hā', bā' and tā' are a word indicating a continuous striking. One says hubita al-rajulu yuhbatu [the man was struck].

1. *fulānun mahbūt* — so-and-so has no reason/mind.
2. *habīt* — the weak coward is then named this, as if he had been struck [hubita].

Ṭarafa said, in a line of verse:
The habīt has no heart to him ... while the thabīt [the steady one] — his steadiness is his understanding.
هبث: The letters hā', bā' and thā'. They say: al-habth is movement.
هبج:
The letters hā', bā' and jīm are a word indicating swelling and heaviness.

1. *habijat al-nāqa habajan* — the she-camel's udder swelled.
2. *muhabbaj* — for this the heavy-spirited [sluggish] person is called muhabbaj.
3. *habajahu bil-ʿaṣā* — he struck him with the stick.

What is irregular and falls outside this is al-hawbaja: a low ground [khabrāʾ] in a place that is not deep, so its water does not linger long before it dries up.
هبخ: The letters hā', bā' and khā'. Al-habayyakha: the girl who walks with a swagger.
هبد:
The letters hā', bā' and dāl. Al-habīd: the seed of the colocynth [bitter gourd].

Al-tahabbud: gathering it and preparing it. And they went out doing tahabbud [gathering the habīd].
هبذ:
The letters hā', bā' and dhāl are a single word, and its meaning is speed.

1. *al-muhābadha* — speed. Al-Khalīl said this.
2. *al-habdh* — speed in walking. Ibn Durayd said this.

And one says: marra yahbudhu habdhan [he passed by hurrying], and ihtabadha ihtibādhan [likewise].
هبر:
The letters hā', bā' and rā' are two words: one is a cutting and cutting-up of something, and the other describes a place.

As for the first:
1. *al-habr* — the cutting of meat.
2. *al-habra* — a cut piece of it [meat]. One says habartu lahu habratan, I cut off a piece for him.
3. *nāqatun habrāʾ wa habira* — a she-camel plump with much meat.
4. *al-hawbar* — one whose hair has become matted, as if it had been cut into gathered tufts.
5. *al-hibriya* — from this: what is at the base of the hair like bran [dandruff], so named because it is broken up/flaky.
6. *sayfun habbār wa hābir* — a sword that tears off a piece of flesh and throws it aside.

As for the other word: al-habīr is a low, sunken place in the ground. And it is said al-hubūr is the rocks between hillocks, or [just] the rocks — I am not certain of that. And there is a saying they use whose origin I do not know: "lā ātīka hubayrata bni Saʿdin" ["I will not come to you, ever"], meaning "never."
هبز: The letters hā', bā' and zā'. They related from Abū Zayd: habaza — he died.
هبش:
The letters hā', bā' and shīn are a single word.

1. *huwa yatahabbashu* — he earns/gathers a livelihood.
2. *al-hubāsha* — the earning, the gain.

Someone said:
Were it not for gatherings of earning ... for little ones like fledglings in their nests.

And one says: huwa yatahabbashu li-ahlihi, he works to provide for his family.
هبص:
The letters hā', bā' and ṣād are a single word. Al-habaṣ: liveliness, energy. A man is habiṣ [lively].

Someone said:
He passed by and gave me a slippery rope ... like a wolf's tail, hurrying briskly.
هبط: The letters ha, ba and ta are a word indicating descent. 'Habata hubutan' — he descended. Al-habut is the slope/declivity. 'Habattu ana' [I went down] and 'habattu ghayri' [I brought another down]. 'Habata l-maradu lahma l-'alil' — the illness wasted the sick person's flesh away. Al-habit is the emaciated one among camels.
هبع:
The letters hā', bā' and ʿayn are a word indicating a manner of walking. Habaʿa hubūʿan: he walked the walk of a dull, sluggish donkey. And it is said: it is the stretching of the neck while walking.

Al-hubaʿ: the young camel born at the height of summer's heat; it is named hubaʿ because when it walks it does habaʿa, that is, it makes use of its neck [stretching it to help it along].
هبغ: The letters hā', bā' and ghayn. Habagha hubūghan: he slept.
هبل:
The letters hā', bā' and lām hold three words: one indicates bereavement, another heaviness, and the third being deceived and caught unaware.

The first:
1. *al-habal* — bereavement [the loss of a child]. One says of someone, "li-ummihi al-habal" — may his mother be bereaved!

A poet said, in a line of verse:
People — whoever meets with good fortune, they say to him what he desires ... but for the mother of the one who errs, bereavement.

2. *al-habūl*, among women — one whose child does not go on living.

The second:
1. *al-muhabbal* — the heavy man, abundant in flesh.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
One of those they carried while they were tying fast the folds of the waist-wrap ... and he grew up, not muhabbal.

2. *al-hibil* — the very old man, and also the aged male ostrich.

The third: their saying ihtabala al-ghirra — he seized on an unguarded moment, if he took advantage of it. Al-habbāl: the hunter who catches game by lulling it into unwariness; and for that the wolf is named hibill, because he schemes for his prey and stalks it that way.

As for al-mahbil, it is where the child settles in the womb; in our view this belongs to the chapter of letter-substitution, and its true origin there is maḥbil [with ḥā'].
هبو:
The letters hā', bā' and the weak letter are a word indicating dust, and a fineness within it.

1. al-habwa — dust-haze.
2. habā al-ghubār, yahbū, fa-huwa hābin — the dust rose up; it is "hābin", rising.
3. al-habā' — fine particles of dust.

Someone said, in a line of verse:
He carried away from us, between his two temples, a blow ... that called him to the barren, rising dust.
(That is, the blow was fatal — it sent him to the dust of the grave.)

4. habā al-ramād — the ashes "habā": they mixed with the dust and went cold/dead.
5. habā' — the fine scattered matter you see stirring in a shaft of sunlight.
هت:
The letters hā' and tā' indicate the imitation of a sound; there is no original sense in it beyond that.

1. hatta al-bakr fī ṣawtihi — the young camel strained its voice.
2. hatattu al-kalima — I forced out the word.
3. al-hatīt — continuous repetition and overtaking; one says hatta hattan wa-hatītan.
4. They say: rajul mihatt — a man quick at work.
5. al-hathata — a twisting of speech.
6. al-hatt — the tearing of a garment.
7. al-hatt — breaking.
8. They say: "I heard the hatt of the camel's legs as they struck the ground."

The origin of all this is one; and were it not that the scholars mentioned it, I would not have seen a reason to mention it.
هتر:
The letters hā', tā' and rā' are a small root indicating falsehood and bad speech. Uhtira al-rajul: he became senile from old age. The meaning of this is that he speaks al-hitr, which is worthless, discarded speech, and that is the origin of it.

1. *rajulun mustahtir* — one who does not care what is said to him, that is, all speech is worthless to him.
2. *tahātara al-rajulān* — each of the two men falsely accused the other.
3. *hatarahu* — he tore at his honour with falsehood, hatran; and hattarahu tahtīran likewise.
4. *hitr* — their word for a calamity or an astonishing matter; this is from letter-substitution, its origin being hikr, which we have already mentioned.
هتع: The letters hā', tā' and ʿayn. Abū Bakr said: hataʿa al-rajulu ilaynā — he came toward us, approached; like haṭaʿa, when one approaches hurriedly.
هتف:
The letters hā', tā' and fā' are a single word, and it is al-hatf: a sound.

1. *hatafat al-ḥamāma* — the dove made its call, tahtifu.
2. *qawsun hattāfa wa hatfā, hutāfan* — a bow that has a [twanging] sound.

Al-Hudhalī said, in a line of verse:
On a bow-grip with a sounding pair of ends ... curved, drawn aside to the left.
هتك:
The letters hā', tā' and kāf are a root indicating a tear or split in something.

1. *al-hatk* — the tearing of a covering away from what lies behind it.
2. *hutika ʿarshu fulān* — so-and-so's standing was torn down and broken.
3. *al-hutka* — a stretch of the night. One says sirnā hutkatan min al-layl, we travelled a hutka of the night, that is, a portion of it. Hātaknāhā: we travelled through its darkness — the sense being that we cut through the dark.
هتل: The letters hā', tā' and lām are a single word. Hatalat al-samāʾ: haṭalat, the sky rained steadily [the same meaning as haṭalat]. Clouds that do this are called huttal and huṭṭal.
هتم:
The letters hā', tā' and mīm are a word indicating the breaking of something. One says hatamtu al-shayʾ, I broke the thing.

1. *al-hutāma* — what has broken off and crumbled from something.
2. *al-hatm* — the breaking of the front teeth from their root; a man [missing them this way] is ahtam.
هتن: The letters hā', tā' and nūn are a single word. Hatanat al-samāʾ hatnan wa hutūnan — the same meaning as hatalat [it rained steadily].
هتي:
The letters hā', tā' and the weak letter. They say: al-muhātāt is like al-muʿāṭāt [mutual giving and taking]. One says hāti, meaning give!, and you reply mā uhātīka, meaning I will not give you [anything].

But if it is spelled with hamza, the meaning changes. One says tahattaʾa al-thawb: the garment became worn out — and this is the only meaning that stands on its own this way. Abū Bakr said: and hataʾa al-shayʾ yahtaʾu, when he broke it by treading on it with his foot.
هث:
The letters hā' and thā' are close to the one before it; most of it concerns mixing.

1. al-hathhatha — mixing.
2. hathhathat al-saḥāba bi-thaljihā wa-qaṭrihā — the cloud sent down its snow and rain rapidly.
3. hathhatha al-wālī — the governor acted unjustly.

He said:
They did this, so the tumult grew great.
هثم:
The letters hā', thā' and mīm — there is nothing in this chapter, in our view, except al-haytham.

1. *al-haytham* — it is said to be the chick of the eagle.
2. *al-haytham* [a second sense] — it is also said to be the red sand-dune.
