3. *hathama min mālihi* — related from Ibn al-Aʿrābī, meaning the same as qasama [he apportioned from his wealth]; this has already passed.
4. *al-hathm* — Ibn Durayd said: the pounding of a thing until it is crushed; one says hathamtuhu ahthimuhu, I pound it.
هج:
The letters hā' and jīm are a sound root indicating obscurity and confusion in something, and from it also comes something indicating the imitation of a sound.

The first:
1. "hajjat ʿaynuhu" — his eye sank in; this is from the sense of obscurity.
2. al-hajāja — the fool who cannot find his way in matters, as if things had been made obscure to him.
3. Ibn al-Aʿrābī and others said: "rakiba fulānun hajāji," on the pattern faʿāli — he rode headlong into the blind darkness. And he cited:
They rode headlong, heedless of my blame.
4. al-hajīj — the deep valley; this too is from obscurity.

The other chapter:
1. hajhajtu bi-l-sabuʿ — I shouted at the wild beast.
2. hajhaja al-faḥl fī hadīrihi — the stallion camel let out its rumbling bray.
3. "hajj" — a cry used to drive off a dog. He said, in a line of verse:
She unveiled her face, so I said to her "hajj!" and she veiled it again — and when she veiled it, I remembered Ḍabbār.
Ḍabbār is a dog.
4. hajīj al-nār — the same as the roaring of the fire.

As for their saying "mā' hujahij," water neither sweet nor salty, this comes from a substitution of letters, and it has already been mentioned under the letters hā' and zā'.
هجد: The letters hā', jīm and dāl are a minor root pointing to settling and staying still in a place. hajada, idhā nāma, means he slept, hujūd. al-hājid is the sleeper; and if he prays by night he is called mutahajjid, as though by his prayer he had put sleep away from himself. This follows a used pattern, as one says rajulun āthim, a sinning man, and when he dislikes sin and disavows it he is called muta'aththim. The Arabs say ahjada al-ba'īru, meaning the camel laid its breast down on the ground.
هجر:
The letters hā', jīm and rā' are two roots: one of them indicates severance and cutting, and the other the tying and binding of a thing.

The first is al-hajr, the opposite of keeping company; and likewise al-hijrān, estrangement. And a people hājara from one dwelling to another when they left the first for the second, as the Emigrants did when they emigrated from Mecca to Medina. And tahajjara a man, and tamahjara, when he made himself resemble the Emigrants. And in the hadith: "Emigrate, and do not merely play the emigrant", that is, be of them. And [it is said] one does not say tamahjarū; but the first is the sounder in our view. And al-hajr, al-hajīr and al-hājira are midday at the height of the heat. And hajjarū: they journeyed at that hour. And it was called hājira because people take shelter in their houses, as though they had cut themselves off from one another. And al-hajīr is the dried-up growth that the grazing beasts have broken down, so named because the herdsman abandons it.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Nothing was left at al-Khalṣā' of what it had put forth ... of plants, except its dry stalks and its cast-off stubble.

And from the chapter is al-hujr, raving; one says hajara al-rajul, the man raved. And al-hujr is foulness in speech; one says ahjara al-rajul fī manṭiqih, the man spoke foully in his talk.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Like a woman of noble stock, of whom the son of a rival wife spoke ... words in which he went beyond bounds and spoke foully.

And one says: he pelted him with al-hājirāt, which are scandals. All this was named so because it is of what is abandoned, in which there is no good. And they say: this is a thing that is hajr, that is, it has no like, as though, from its excellence and its being set apart from other things, it had cut itself off from them. And they say: this is ahjar than that, that is, more noble; and it may be said of anything.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
And many a Yemeni water, before it a matchless drive to the drinking-place.

They mean: it is a drive to water that has no drive like it.

And al-hajīr is the great watering-trough, so named because it is something cut out for water.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
It cuts its cutting with the wide trough.

And he said, in a line of verse:
They kept turning about, a bowshot off their trough ... as flocks turn about whose hired herdsman has not come.
هجس: The letters hā', jīm and sīn are a single word. One says hajasa al-shayʾ fī al-nafs: it occurred to the mind. Abū Bakr said: al-hajs is the faint sound you hear without making out [what it is].
هجع: The letters hā', jīm and 'ayn are a word pointing to sleep. haja'a hujū'an — he slept at night. laqītuhu ba'da haj'atin — I met him after a nap. Drawn by the same reasoning from this: rajulun huja', a foolish man, one easily lulled into trusting anyone.
هجف: The letters hā', jīm and fā'. They say al-hijfa is a side, a quarter of a place. There is doubt about that. As for al-hijaff, it is the old male ostrich, and I think it belongs to the root in which a hā' was added and its zāy changed to jīm — from al-ziff, which is its down.
هجل:
The letters hā', jīm and lām are two origins: one indicates a mixing-together, the other the throwing of something.

The first:

1. al-hawjal — confused, disordered walking. One says ahjaltu al-ibil — I turned the camels loose, and when left loose they mix together in confusion.
2. al-hajūl — they said: and from this comes al-hajūl, the unchaste woman, because she mixes with everyone. Al-muhājala is like al-musājala [an exchange of boasts]; the pattern in it is the same one.
3. al-hawjal, of land — open desert with no landmarks. It was named this because one cannot find the way across it, so the matter grows confused for travellers.
4. al-hawjal, of men — the slow man whose affairs become tangled and confused on him. A poet said, in a line of verse: she bore him keen of heart, slender-waisted, wakeful, at the hour when the sluggish man's night is asleep.
5. layl hawjal — the long night, so named for the confusion of its darkness. Al-Kumayt said, in a line of verse: a headlong she-camel, whose night is a hawjal-night.
6. al-hajl — a low hollow lying between mountains.

The other origin: hajaltu bi-l-shay' — I threw the thing.
هجم:
The letters hā', jīm and mīm: a single sound root indicating something arriving suddenly, and other things are measured against that. One says: hajamtu ʿalā l-qawmi baghtatan ahjumu hujūman — I came upon the people suddenly.

1. rīḥ hajūm — a fierce wind that flattens houses.
2. hajmat al-shitā' — the severity of winter's cold; it follows that same pattern, because it comes upon one suddenly.
3. hajmat al-ṣayf — the severity of summer's heat.
4. al-hajm — the large drinking-bowl. [He said,] in a line of verse: she fills the great bowl freely while she is untroubled, until the rims of the bowl are almost chipped. It was named hajm because it comes suddenly upon the drinker's thirst and breaks it.
5. al-hajma, of camels — camels numbering between ninety and a hundred, because they come upon the watering-place with force.
6. hajamtu al-bayt — I pulled the tent down, because its top comes crashing suddenly upon its base when it falls.
7. hajamat al-ʿayn — the eye sank in, as though it comes suddenly upon what lies behind it, entering into it.

[A gap in the text here.]

What falls outside this pattern is hijā' al-ḥurūf, the spelling-out of letters; one says tahajjaytu — I spelled it out. And when the word is said with a hamza the meaning changes: they say hajaʾa l-ṭaʿām — he ate the food.
هد:
The letters hā' and dāl are a sound root indicating breaking, crushing, and demolishing. haddadtuhu haddan — I demolished it. The whole chapter goes back to this same pattern.

1. al-hadd among men — the weak man, as if he has been crushed. Men of this kind are called hāddūn.

Al-Aṣmaʿī was contradicted on this: ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm al-Qaṭṭān told me, from Thaʿlab, from Ibn al-Aʿrābī, and from ʿAmr ibn Abī ʿAmr from his father, both of whom said: al-hadd among men is rather the generous, noble man, while the coward is hidd, with a different vowel. They cited:
They are not weaklings in wars, when the belts are girded above the hip-bones.
If this is so, then the coward is hidd, meaning crushed, like dhibḥ for the slaughtered animal.

2. al-hadd — the noble man who freely spends his wealth.
3. al-hadda — the sound of a wall falling.
4. al-hudhud — well-known, the hoopoe.
5. hadhada al-ḥamām — the dove cooed.
6. hadhadat al-mar'a ibnahā — the woman rocked her son to sleep.

What falls outside the chapter, and for which I know no pattern, is their saying: "marartu bi-rajulin haddaka min rajul," I passed by a man enough to overwhelm you, like their saying "ḥasbuka min rajul," enough of a man for you; it is simply an expression said as such. He said, in a line of verse:
And I have a companion in the cave, such a companion as would overwhelm you — he is al-Jawn, except that he cannot be put off with half-measures.
هدب:
The letters hā', dāl and bā' — a sound root indicating the fringe of a thing, or branches that resemble a fringe.

1. al-hudb — the fringe of a garment.
2. al-hadab — the branches of the arṭā shrub, also called al-hudāb. He said, in a line of verse: so the young girls kept tossing pieces of its meat to one another, and fat like the fringes of twisted silk floss.
3. al-hadab, of tree-leaves — leaves that have no central rib.
4. haydab al-saḥāb — what hangs down from a cloud when it is about to rain, as though it were threads.
5. rajul ahdab — a man with abundant eyelashes.
6. hadaba al-thamara — he picked the fruit, yahdibuhā hadban, as though taking the hudb, the fringe, of the tree.
7. This word is also used figuratively: one says hadaba al-nāqa, meaning he milked the she-camel.
هدج:
The letters hā', dāl and jīm — a sound root indicating a kind of walking and movement.

1. al-hadajān — the gait of an old man; one says hadaja, he walked so.
2. ahdaja al-ẓalīm — the male ostrich walked with a trembling gait; he is called haddāj and hadajdaj.
3. tahaddajat al-nāqa — the she-camel walked toward her young one, inclining tenderly over it.
4. hadajat al-rīḥ — the wind blew with a moaning sound.
5. al-hawdaj — in our view, this belongs to the same pattern, because it sways on the camel's back; it is then used as a comparison, so one says hawdajat al-nāqa — the she-camel's hump rose up as though it were the hawdaj.

What departs from this root is al-tahaddoj, the breaking-up of the voice.
هدر:
The letters hā', dāl and rā' indicate the falling of a thing and the causing of it to fall, and also a kind of sound.

1. hadara al-sulṭānu dama fulānin hadran — the ruler declared so-and-so's blood forfeit, permitting his killing.
2. Banū fulānin hadara — meaning fallen, of no account; a man so called is hudara. Some say hadara means fallen. He said, in a line of verse: truly, when the coward — the worthless one — is confounded...
3. hadarat al-ḥamāmatu tahdiru — the dove cooed.
4. hadara al-faḥlu hadīran — the stallion camel rumbled.
5. hadara al-ʿaṣīru fī ghalayānihi — the juice rumbled as it boiled.
6. hadara al-ʿarfaju — its plant grew large, so that when the wind struck it, it made a sound like the hadīr.
هدع: The letters hā', dāl and ʿayn: one word. It is hidaʿ, used to calm young camels when they startle. And al-hawdaʿ is the ostrich.
هدف:
The letters hā', dāl and fā' — a small root indicating uprightness and height.

1. al-hadaf — anything huge and raised up; for that a thickset, coarse-bodied man is also called hadaf. He said, in a line of verse: when the solitary big man lowers his head, delighted by an abundant flock of floppy-eared sheep.
2. al-hadaf — the target, that which is shot at.
3. rakab mustahdif — a broad pubic mound. Al-Nābigha said, in a line of verse: and when you thrust, you thrust into what stands broad...
4. imra'a muhdifa — a fleshy woman.
5. ahdafa laka al-shay' — the thing rose up and stood before you.
6. al-hidfa — a group of people.

As for his saying, in a line of verse: until we heard the faint sound of a white, curly froth falling on the feet of a stooping, standing man — here al-mustahdif is the milker standing over the vessel. He means: we heard the sound of the froth spattering down onto the milker's foot.
هدق: The letters hā', dāl and qāf. Among Ibn Durayd's curiosities on it: al-hadq is breaking.
هدك: The letters hā', dāl and kāf. Ibn Durayd said: inhadaka al-rajulu ʿalaynā bi-kalāmin kathīr — the man burst out upon us with much talk; he set off speaking.
هدل:
The letters hā', dāl and lām are two sound origins: one indicates slackness in a thing, the other a kind of sound.

The first:

1. al-hadal — the slackness of a camel's lip, or of anything; one says hadila, it drooped. Hadaltu al-shay' ahdiluhu — I let a thing hang down.
2. al-hadāl — any branch that grows straight up in an arāk-tree or a ṭalḥ-tree. The correct usage for that, though, is yatahaddal — it hangs down. He said, in a line of verse: he calls out al-hadīl and sāq ḥurr above him, at evening, in valleys full of drooping branches.
3. al-hadīl — they say it is the young of the dove. If so, it seems to have been named for its cry. He said, in a line of verse: I said, does a griever weep, remembering Hadīl — though he had perished, and he was no Tubbaʿ?
هدم:
The letters hā', dāl and mīm are a root pointing to the tearing-down of a building, then extended from that. hadamtu al-ḥā'iṭa ahdimuhu — I tore down the wall. al-hadam, with the dāl vowelled fatḥa, is what has been torn down.

1. al-hidm — a worn-out garment, plural ahdām.
2. "dimā'uhum hadam", meaning hadar, forfeit, as if they have been torn down and no claim is made for them. His saying, peace and blessing upon him: "al-damu al-damu, wa'l-hadamu al-hadam" — it was said its meaning is: our life is your life, and our death is your death.
3. nāqatun hadima — a she-camel intensely in heat, as if she gives way for the stallion.
4. al-hadma — a downpour of rain, as if it comes crashing down in its outpouring.

What falls outside this reasoning: al-mahdūm, said of milk, meaning al-rathī'a, curdled milk mixed with fresh.
هدن:
The letters hā', dāl and nūn — a small root indicating stillness and rectitude. I heard Abū l-Ḥasan ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm al-Qaṭṭān say: I heard Thaʿlab say: tahādana al-amr — the matter became settled and right. Another said: and from this comes the pattern of al-hudna, the truce.

1. al-rajul al-hadān — the sluggish man, with no stir in him. He said, in a line of verse: they do not graze the borders of gentle ease when they camp, nor the land of stillness.
2. haddanat al-mar'a ṣabiyyahā — the woman lulled her infant with her talk, wanting him to sleep.
3. al-tahdīn — slowness; and this follows the pattern of the chapter.
هدي:
The letters hā', dāl and the weak letter are two roots: [one of them] is going in front to guide, and the other is the sending of a kindly gift.

So the first is their saying hadaytuhu al-ṭarīq hidāyatan — I guided him on the road, that is, I went before him to show him the way. And everything that goes in front for that is hādin, a guide. He said:
When the young man's guide through the lands is the head of the spear-shaft, he has obeyed the commander.

And this branches out, so that one says: al-hudā is the opposite of straying. You say hadaytuhu hudan — I guided him with guidance. And one says aqbalat hawādī al-khayl, that is, the necks of the horses; and it is said that its hādī is the first troop of them, because it is what goes in front. And al-hādiya is the staff, because it goes before the one holding it as though it were showing him the way.

And of the section is their saying naẓara fulānun hadya amrihi, that is, its direction; and mā aḥsana hidyatahu, that is, his manner of going. And they say jā'a fulānun yuhādī bayna ithnayn — so-and-so came walking between two men, leaning upon them. And ramaytu bi-sahmin thumma ramaytu bi-ākhara hudayyāhu, that is, on its course, aimed as it was.

And the section in all this reasoning is one.

And the other root is al-hadiyya: what you send as a kindly gift to one who holds you dear. One says ahdaytu uhdī ihdā'an. And al-mihdā is the tray upon which a gift is carried.

And of the section is al-hadiyy, the bride; and she has been hudiyat ilā baʿlihā hidā'an — led to her husband. He said:
If women are kept hidden away, then every chaste one has a right to be led to her husband.

And al-hady and al-hadiyy are what is offered of grazing beasts to the Sacred Precinct, drawing near to God the Exalted. One says hadiyy and hady. He said:
And Ṭurayfa ibn al-ʿAbd was their offering — they struck the very middle of the back of his head with an Indian blade.
And it is said that al-hadiyy is the captive.

As for the form with the hamza, it is not of this reasoning, and most of it points to stillness. Hada'a hudū'an, that is, he grew still. And hada'at al-rijl — the people fell asleep. And ahda'at al-mar'atu ṣabiyyahā bi-yadihā li-yanām — the woman quieted her child with her hand so that he would sleep, that is, she stilled him. And maḍā hud'un min al-layl — a spell of the night passed, after a first sleep, at the first stilling of people. And al-hada'a is a kind of easy running.

And of what falls outside this section: al-hada', and it is the coming forward of the shoulder towards the chest, like al-jana'.
هذ:
The letters hā' and dhāl are a small root indicating cutting.

1. hadhdhahu — he cut it.
2. sikkīn hadhūdh — a knife good for cutting.
3. hadhādhayka, from al-hadhdh — swiftness of cutting; as though one were saying, make the matter firm, and cut it off.
هذب:
The letters hā', dhāl and bā' — a word indicating the cleansing of something from what mars it. One says: shay' muhadhdhab — something purified of its faults.

1. al-ihdhāb — its origin: swiftness in flight and in running, meaning that the swift thing cannot be caught hold of. One says: the horse went by, yuhdhibu — running swiftly.
2. al-haydhabā — walking with a swift, brisk gait.

Likewise al-muhadhdhab, the refined man — no fault can be found to fasten onto him. And God knows best what is correct.
هذر: The letters hā', dhāl and rā': a single word, it is al-hadhar, meaning senseless, rambling talk. A man is called mihdhār, hudhara, and hidhriyān — one who talks excessively and confusedly.
هذف: The letters hā', dhāl and fā'. One says sā'iq hadhdhāf — a driver who is brisk, going about it in earnest.
هذل:
The letters hā', dhāl and lām — a small root indicating smallness, lightness and speed.

1. al-hudhlūl — the light, nimble man.
2. hawdhala al-rajul — the man walked swiftly.
3. hawdhala al-siqā' — the waterskin was churned.
4. al-hadhālīl — small hills, singular hudhlūl, so named for their smallness.

And the pattern of the name Hudhayl is partly drawn from this.
هذم: The letters hā', dhāl and mīm: a sound word indicating the cutting of something. Hadhama l-sayf is the sword's cutting. A sword is called muhdham, hudhām and haydhām. And a brave man is called haydhām, in comparison to this sword.
هذى: The letters hā', dhāl and the weak letter [yā']: a single word — al-hadhayān, speech that makes no sense, like the speech of one deranged. One says hadhā yahdhī, he raved. And Ibn Durayd reported, among the hamzated words: hadha'tu l-laḥma bi-l-sikkīni hadh'an — I cut the meat with the knife.
هر:
The letters hā' and rā' are a sound root, indicating a sound among sounds, and other things are measured by analogy on it.

1. al-hirr — the call used to summon sheep. That is their saying, "He does not know hirr from birr" — birr being the driving of sheep.
2. al-hirra — the cat (al-sinnawra); it seems to have been named for its sound when it growls (harrat). [And a thorn is said to harra when its dryness becomes severe, and it then has a harīr] and a loud noise.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
They grazed on the moist shabriq plant, until, when it dried and its taste turned forbidding.

3. al-hurhūr — abundant water which, when it flows, you hear from it a harhara (murmur).
4. harra fulānun al-ka's — so-and-so disliked the cup. Perhaps this was said because he growls (yahirru) in the face of whoever gives him drink.

What is not from this chapter:
1. al-hurār — a disease that afflicts camels; a she-camel afflicted by it is called mahrūra.
2. Ra's Hirr — a place name.
هرب: The letters hā', rā' and bā' are a single word: it is haraba, meaning he fled. "mā lahu hāribun wa lā qāribun", meaning: neither one going away from the water nor one coming to it — that is, he has nothing.
هرت: The letters hā', rā' and tā': a word indicating wideness in something. Al-hart is the wideness of the mouth-corners. Al-harīt is a woman whose passages have become joined as one [a childbirth injury].
هرج:
The letters hā', rā' and jīm — a sound root indicating mixing and confusion.

1. harraja al-rajulu fī ḥadīthihi — the man rambled confusedly in his talk. By the same pattern, indiscriminate killing is called harj, with the rā' unvowelled. He said, in a line of verse: would that I knew — is this the first of the harj, or a time of turmoil without harj?
2. al-haraj, with the rā' voweled — that a camel's eye darkens from the severity of heat.
3. al-harj — the swift running of a horse; one says marra yahriju, it went by running swiftly.
4. al-arḍ al-mihrāj — land of fine growth, its plants intertwined with one another.

Not far from this, though not strictly of it: harrajtu al-sabuʿ — I shouted at the wild beast.
هرد:
The letters hā', rā' and dāl are words indicating the treating of something with dye or the like.

1. thawb mahrūd — a garment dyed yellow.
2. harradtu al-thawb — I tore the garment.
3. haradtu ʿirḍahu — I disparaged his honour.
4. harradtu al-laḥm — I cooked the meat partway through, tahrīdan.
هرس:
The letters hā', rā' and sīn — a sound root indicating pounding and crushing something.

1. harastu al-shay' — I pounded the thing. From this comes al-harīsa [a pounded dish of wheat and meat].
2. al-mihrās — a hollowed-out stone, perhaps used for pounding things in; sometimes it was long, and one performed ablution from it.
3. al-hars — a worn-out garment, by way of comparison, as though it had been pounded.
4. al-mahārīs — strong camels that crush their fodder heavily as they eat.
5. al-hirs — the powerful lion, as though he crushes whatever he meets. He said, in a line of verse: strong in both forearms, given to pouncing, firm of frame, a crusher, soft of tread.

As for al-harās, it is a thorny tree, and it departs from this pattern. He said, in a line of verse: like the overlapping tracks of dogs, they tread upon the harās.
هرش:
The letters hā', rā' and shīn: a single word, it is muhārashat al-kilāb — the setting of dogs against one another. From this, by the same pattern, comes al-tahrīsh — stirring up trouble between people.

What does not belong to this chapter is Harshā, a well-known hill. He said, in a line of verse: take the front of Harshā, or its rear — for indeed both sides of Harshā have a path for them.
هرص: The letters hā', rā' and ṣād are not a real root, except that they say al-harīṣa is a place where water stands and collects.
هرض: The letters hā', rā' and ḍād follow the same path as the one before [also not a real root], except that Abū Bakr claimed that al-haraḍ is a rash that breaks out on a person from heat. He said: and haraḍtu l-thawb — I tore the garment.
هرط: The letters hā', rā' and ṭā' are something indicating quarrelling and mutual abuse. Tahāraṭa l-rajulān — the two men hurled abuse at one another. Haraṭa fī kalāmihi — he rambled confusedly in his speech.
هرع:
The letters hā', rā' and ʿayn are a sound root indicating motion and agitation.

1. uhriʿa al-rajul — the man "uhriʿa": he trembled from fear.
2. hayraʿ — the fool is named this, for the unsteadiness of his judgement. It is possible the hā' here is an extra letter, in which case the word belongs with the root yā'-rā'-ʿayn.
3. al-hiryāʿ — the litter shed by trees [dead leaves and twigs], because it is unsettled, carried by the wind from place to place.
4. al-haraʿ — flowing tears, or flowing blood; this belongs to the root.
5. tahar'aʿat al-rimāḥ — the spears "tahar'aʿat": they came on, levelled forward.
6. hum yuhraʿūna ilayhi — they "yuhraʿūna" toward him, meaning they are driven, hurried along.

What does not belong to this root: al-harʿa — a small creature; it is also called harīʿ and huryuʿ.
هرف: The letters hā', rā' and fā'. They say: al-harf is like raving, praising a person out of admiration for him. They say: 'Do not harf about what you do not know' [do not rave in praise of what you have no knowledge of]. And they say: harrafat al-nakhla — the palm-tree hastened to bear its fruit early. I do not think this word is genuinely Arabic.
هرل: The letters hā', rā' and lām. They say: al-harwala is a gait between walking and running.
هرم: The letters hā', rā' and mīm are two words. One is al-haram — old age. Al-harima is said to mean the lioness, and ibn hirma is a man's last-born child. The other is al-hurmān — the intellect.
هرو:
The letters hā', rā', the weak letter, and the hamzated one — a chapter not set upon a single pattern; its word-origins are disparate. Among what comes from it:

1. harawtuhu bi-l-hirāwa — I struck him with the club.
2. harraytu l-ʿimāma — I dyed the turban yellow.

Ibn Durayd said: al-harw has no basis in Arabic, except that Abū Mālik brought a word the lexicographers rejected — he said harawtu l-laḥma, I cooked the meat through, but it is really haraʾtuhu, with a hamza.

Among the hamzated words:

1. al-hurā' — corrupt, senseless speech. One says ahra'a l-rajulu fī manṭiqihi — the man spoke nonsense. He said, in a line of verse: she has skin like silk, and speech soft at the edges, neither nonsense nor scanty.
2. taharra'a l-laḥm — the meat was cooked until it fell from the bone.
3. hara'ahu l-bard — the cold's severity struck him; likewise ahra'ahu.
هز:
The letters hā' and zāy are a root indicating agitation and movement in a thing.

1. hazaztu al-qanāta fa-htazzat — I shook the spear-shaft, and it shook.
2. ihtazza al-nabātu, wa hazzat-hu al-rīḥ — the plant swayed, and the wind shook it.
3. hazza al-ḥādī al-ibila bi-ḥidā'ihi wa-htazzat hiya fī sayrihā — the driver urged the camels on with his song, and they swayed as they went.
4. hazīzu al-rīḥ — the movement and sound of the wind.

From this chapter:
1. al-hazāhiz — the turmoils in which people are shaken.
2. sayfun hazhāz and huzhuz — a sword clear and fine in its flexing.
3. mā'un huzahiz — water that trembled as it flowed.

A star (kawkab), too, trembles as it shoots and falls.

4. al-huzahiz — a light, nimble man.

The reasoning is one throughout all of that.
هزأ: The letters hā', zāy and hamza are one word. One says hazi'a and istahza'a, when he mocks.
هزب:
The letters hā', zā' and bā' are a single word.

al-hawzab — the aged camel, in the saying of al-A'shā: and the aged camel (al-hawzab) I mount upon it, and the sturdy, big-humped she-camel, and the camel.
هزج:
The letters hā', zā' and jīm are a sound root, indicating a sound.

1. al-hazaj — the sound of thunder, and by it the hazaj of songs was likened. A poet said, in a line of verse: as though she were a girl trilling in song.
2. tahazzajati al-qaws — the bow made a sound at the release of the bowstring. Al-Kumayt said, in a line of verse: with melodies from its songs, hoarse, followed by sighing and panting.
3. farasun hazijun — a horse with speed in its gait, as though it goes toward what is heard of its rustling sound.
هزر:
The letters hā', zā' and rā' indicate pressing, breaking and striking.

1. hazarahu bi-'aṣāhu hazarātin — he struck him with his stick several blows: he beat him.
2. hazarahu — he pressed and squeezed him.
3. inna fulānan la-dhū hazarātin wa-kasarātin — so-and-so is one who suffers batterings and breakings, said when he is cheated in everything. A poet said, in a line of verse: if you do not give up the beatings you will not give up, your clothes will be stripped from you — neither sheep nor camels will spare you.

And God knows best.
هزع:
The letters hā', zā' and 'ayn are two roots: one indicates dread or desolation, the other agitation and breaking.

The first:
1. hazī' — one says, a hazī' of the night has passed, meaning a portion of it.
2. tahazza'a — so-and-so tahazza'a toward so-and-so, meaning he turned strange and hostile toward him. Al-Khalīl said this is from hazī' al-layl, because that is an hour of dread.

The second:
1. tahazza'ati al-qanāh — the spear-shaft quivered.
2. tahazza'ati al-mar'a — the woman swayed. A poet said, in a line of verse: like the sand-grouse, supple in her swaying.
3. tahazza'a al-sayf — the sword flexed and quivered.
4. tahazza'ati al-ibil fī sayrihā — the camels swayed as they went.
5. hazatu al-'aẓm — I broke the bone.
6. al-mihza' — the crushing lion. A poet said, in a line of verse: as though they feared from you a sharpened point, at Ḥalya, broad-armed, a crushing lion.

Among what falls outside both roots is al-ahza': the arrow that is left remaining in the quiver, because it is the worst of them — though it is also said to be the best of them. And they say: mā lahu ahza', meaning he has nothing at all.
هزف:
The letters hā', zā' and fā' are a single word.

1. al-hizaff — the male ostrich.
2. hazafathu al-rīḥ — the wind carried it off, flying away with it. Ibn Durayd mentioned this.
هزق:
The letters hā', zā' and qāf are words on one pattern.

1. imra'atun hizqatun — a woman who does not settle, is restless.
2. al-mihzāq — likewise, the same meaning.
3. al-hazaq — thunder.
4. ahzaqa al-rajul — the man laughed.
5. ḥimārun hazaqun — a donkey much given to frisking about.
هزل: The letters hā', zā' and lām are two words on one and the same reasoning, pointing to weakness. al-hazl is the opposite of seriousness (al-jidd). al-huzāl is the opposite of fatness. hazaltu dābbatī, and it was huzilat — I made my animal lean, and it was made lean. hazala fī manṭiqihi — he joked in his speech. ahzala — leanness fell upon his livestock.
هزم:
The letters ha', za' and mim are a sound root indicating pressing and breaking.

1. al-hazm — your pressing something with your hand so that it caves inward, like a cucumber or a melon.
2. al-hazima — defeat in war, from this.
3. rain called hazim — pouring heavily.
4. hazim of thunder — its sound, as though it were breaking apart, from their saying "the waterskin tahazzama": it dried out and cracked.
5. ihtazamtu ash-shata — I slaughtered the sheep, from this root.
6. al-hazma — a low, sunken patch of ground.

Not from this derivation: al-mihzam, a stick with fire set at its tip, that Bedouin children play with. Jarir said: "and she plays with the mihzam."
هزن:
The letters hā', zā' and nūn have nothing in them except Hawāzin, a tribe.

1. Hawāzin — a tribe.
2. al-hawzan — dust.
3. al-hawzan — a bird.
هس:
The letters hā' and sīn are a small root indicating sounds and mingling, as in al-hasīs.

1. hasāhis al-jinn — like hathāhith al-jinn, the murmurings of the jinn.
2. rā'in hashās — from the pattern of sound-substitution, like qasqās — said of a shepherd who grazed the sheep all night.
هسم:
The letters hā', sīn and mīm. Abū Bakr said: al-hasm is like al-hashm, breaking.

1. hasamahu yahsimuhu hasman — he broke it.

And God knows best.
هش:
The letters hā' and shīn are a sound root indicating slackness and softness. A thing that is soft and yielding is hashsh.

1. rajulun hashsh — a man of open, cheerful face. One says hashishta, you became cheerful; and dhū hashāsh, a man of cheerfulness.
2. al-faras al-hashsh — a horse that sweats profusely.
3. shātun hashūsh — a ewe rich in milk.

From this chapter:
1. hashashtu al-waraqa hashshan — I beat down the leaves with a stick.
هشر:
The letters hā', shīn and rā' are two words.

1. al-hayshar — a plant.
2. hashara al-nāqa — he milked all that was in her udder.

And God knows best.
هشل:
The letters hā', shīn and lām. They say:

1. al-hashīla — a camel that a man takes without its owner's permission, to reach with it wherever he wants, then returns it. A poet said, in a line of verse: and every hashīla, as long as I live, is forbidden to me, except camels.
هشم:
The letters hā', shīn and mīm are a root indicating the breaking of something hollow, and of something not hollow. hashamtuhu hashman — I broke it.

1. al-hāshima — a head-wound that breaks/crushes the skull-bone.
2. It is agreed that Hāshim was so named because he broke up bread [crumbled it into broth for people to eat]; his given name was ʿAmr.
3. al-hashīm — of plants, that which is dried out and crumbling.
4. hashīm — said of a man weak in body.
5. tahashshama fulān ʿalā fulān — so-and-so "tahashshama" toward so-and-so, meaning he was gentle and inclined kindly toward him; this belongs to the root.
6. ihtashama mā fī ḍarʿ al-nāqa — he "ihtashama" what was in the she-camel's udder, meaning he milked it out; this fits the pattern.
هص:
The letters hā' and ṣād are a word indicating the pressing of a thing.

1. huṣhuṣ — what they call the wolf.
2. haṣhaṣtu al-shay' — I pressed the thing.

They also say — though I do not know how sound it is — that al-hāṣṣa is the eye of the elephant. In my view, this is among what is merely reported, not something established.
هصر:
The letters hā', ṣād and rā' indicate gripping something and bending it.

1. hasartu al-'ūd — said when you take a branch by its top and bend it toward you. A poet said, in a line of verse: I bent down a branch with drooping, swaying clusters.
2. al-haṣūr, al-haysar, al-haṣṣār — the lion, named from this.
هصم:
The letters hā', ṣād and mīm are a word indicating breaking. One says hasamtu al-shay', I broke the thing.

1. al-haysam — the lion, named from this.

And God knows best.
هض:
The letters hā' and ḍād are a word indicating the crushing (raḍḍ) of a thing, or more than that.

1. haḍaḍtu al-shay' and haḍhaḍtuhu — I broke it.
2. al-haḍhāḍ — the stud camel that breaks the necks of other stud camels.
3. al-haḍḍā' — possibly, from this, a group of people.
هضب:
The letters hā', ḍād and bā' indicate expanse, abundance and overflow.

1. al-haḍba — a rain with great drops.
2. al-hiḍabb — a horse profuse in sweat.
3. haḍabāt — tall hills (the plural).
4. al-haḍba — [also] the smooth hillock.

And God knows best what is correct.
هضل: The letters hā', ḍād and lām have nothing in them except al-hayḍala, which is an armed band with a clamour to it. Sometimes they also call a huge she-camel a hayḍala.
هضم:
The letters hā', ḍād and mīm are a sound root indicating breaking, pressing, and one part folding into another.

1. hadamtu al-shay' hadman — I broke a thing.
2. mizmār muhaddam — a reed-pipe so called because, as they claim, it is [made of] broken pieces joined one to another.
3. al-hāḍūm — that which digests food; I take this to be a later, non-classical word.
4. kashḥ muhaddam — a waist/flank [pressed in, slender].
5. imra'a hadīmat al-kashḥayn — a woman slender in both flanks, as though they had been pressed in.
6. al-hadam — the caving-in of the upper belly; in horses this is a fault. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: "No horse with a caved-in belly has ever won a race."
7. al-ṭalʿ al-hadīm — the palm-blossom whose parts fold one into another.
8. hadamtu laka min ḥaqqī ṭā'ifa — I "hadamtu" for you a part of my due, meaning I gave it up.
9. al-mutahaddim — the wrongdoer, one who encroaches on another's due.
10. al-ahḍām — low hollow tracts of valleys, so named for how sunken and hidden they are; the singular is hiḍm.

As for al-ahḍām meaning a kind of perfume — [the text breaks off here].
هطر:
The letters hā', ṭā' and rā'. They say:

1. al-haṭr — striking with wood, and haṭarahu yahṭiruhu haṭran.

And God knows best.
هطع:
The letters ha', ta' and 'ayn are a minor root indicating turning toward a thing and being led, submitting.

1. hata'a ar-rajulu 'ala ash-shay'i bi-basarihi — he turned toward the thing, fixed his gaze on it.
2. ahta'a al-ba'iru — the camel lowered its neck, led submissively.
3. ahta'a — also, he hurried.
هطل:
The letters hā', ṭā' and lām are a word indicating succession, in rain-drops and other things.

1. haṭala al-maṭar haṭalānan — the rain fell in succession, and likewise tears.
2. dīmatun haṭlā' — a continuous rain.
3. ibilun haṭlā — camels coming slowly, one after another; and likewise they call the one among them worn out by this: haṭil.
هعر:
The letters hā', 'ayn and rā' — this cannot occur except with a foreign element in it.

1. al-hay'ara — the reckless, flighty one among women.
2. al-hay'ara — [also] the ghoul.
3. al-hay'arūr — calamity.
هف:
The letters hā' and fā' are a sound root indicating lightness and swiftness, in gait and in sound. al-hafīf is swiftness of gait.

Dhu al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
Whenever we drowsed off, you said, "Sing to us of Khirqā'," and quicken the hafīf of the riding-camels.

1. al-rīḥ al-haffāfa — the wind light in its blowing.
2. al-ẓill al-haffāf — the still shade.
3. qamīṣun hafhāf — a thin shirt.
4. al-hiff — a cloud that has poured out its water and thinned out.
5. al-haffāf — the glittering, bright thing.
6. al-shuhd al-hiff — thin honeycomb with little honey, named for its lightness.
7. al-hiff, of crops — a crop whose harvest is delayed, so its grain scatters.
8. al-mar'a al-muhafhafa — the slender woman, slim of waist.
9. al-yahfūf — the fool, for the lightness of his mind; also said to mean the coward.
هفا:
The letters hā', fā' and the weak letter are a root indicating something going off in lightness and speed.

1. hafā al-shay' fī al-hawā' yahfū — said when a thing goes off in the air, like a wisp of wool and the like.
2. hafā al-ẓalīm — the male ostrich ran.
3. hafā al-qalb fī ithri al-shay' — the heart flutters after a thing, longing for it.
4. hawāfī al-na'am — the strays among the livestock.
5. hafā al-insān yahfū — the person slipped and departed from what is right; and likewise hafā is said when he grew hungry.
6. al-hafwa — the slip.
هفت:
The letters hā', fā' and tā' are a word indicating something falling.

1. tahāfut al-shay' — its falling apart, piece by piece.
2. al-haft — drops of blood falling one after another.
3. tahāfata al-farāsh fī al-nār — the moths fell one after another into the fire.
4. hafata / inhafata — said of everything that sinks down and is lowered.
5. waradat hafītatun min al-nās — a band of people arrived, driven by a year of famine that reduced them to destitution, so that they were the fallen ones.

And God knows best.
هقب:
The letters hā', qāf and bā'. They say:

1. al-hiqabb — the huge, tall one, greedy-bellied. Abū Bakr said: al-hiqabb is [also] the hard, solid one.
2. al-haqab — expanse.
هقع:
The letters hā', qāf and 'ayn. In it are three words:

1. al-haq'a — a star among the mansions of the moon.
2. al-haq'a — [also] a circular marking on a horse's chest. A poet said, in a line of verse: one who is not your equal may ride the marked horse (al-mahqū'), and one paired with a fine stallion may ride the marked horse too.
3. uhtuqi'a lawnuhu — his colour turned pale, like umtuqi'a.
هقل:
The letters hā', qāf and lām have nothing in them except al-hiql, which is the young of the ostrich.

1. al-hiql — the young of the ostrich.
2. al-tahaqqul — walking slowly.
هقم:
The letters hā', qāf and mīm indicate expanse and greatness.

1. al-hiqamm — a name for the sea, for its greatness and the depth of its bottom.
2. hayqam — its sound. A poet said, in a line of verse: like the sea, calling out hayqam, hayqam.
3. al-hiqamm — [also] the man who eats a great deal.
4. al-hayqam — the great male ostrich.
هك:
The letters hā' and kāf are a small root indicating a splitting-open in a thing, or a cleft.

1. inhakka ṣalā al-mar'a inhikākan — the woman's pelvis opened apart at childbirth.
2. hakkahu bi-l-sayf — he struck him with the sword.
3. al-hakk — heavy rain, because it splits open the ground.
4. inhakkat al-bi'r — the well caved in.
هكر:
The letters hā', kāf and rā' are two words.

1. al-hakr — astonishment. A poet said, in a line of verse: so marvel at that turn of fate, and be astonished (ihkar). Al-Khalīl said: one says hakran laka, an exclamation of astonishment addressed to someone.
2. hakira al-rajul — drowsiness overcame the man and he grew weary, and his bones and joints went slack.
هكع:
The letters hā', kāf and 'ayn indicate lowering oneself and submission.

1. hakaʿati al-baqaru taḥta ẓilli al-shajari min shiddati al-ḥarr — the cattle grew still under the shade of the tree from the intensity of the heat.
2. qad haka'a — said of a bone when it breaks again after having been set.
3. ihtaka'a al-rajul — the man humbled himself.
4. haka'a al-layl — the night let down its curtains, settling in.
5. dhahaba fa-mā yudrā ayna haka'a — he went off and it is not known where he went to ground, as though he hid and concealed himself, the way cattle do.
6. al-huk'a — the helpless man who submits to everyone, meaning he humbles himself.
7. al-hukā' — the cough.
8. haka'a yahka'u hukā'an — he coughed.
هكل:
The letters hā', kāf and lām indicate loftiness and height.

1. al-haykal — the tall horse. A poet said, in a line of verse: and I set out early on a swift, tall horse (haykal), full of high spirit, free-flowing in its stride.
هكم:
The letters hā', kāf and mīm indicate rushing recklessly upon something, and collapse.

1. hakama hakman — he rushed recklessly upon people and exposed them to harm.
2. al-tahakkum — mockery.
3. tahakkamati al-bi'r — the well collapsed.
هل:
The letters hā' and lām are a sound root indicating the raising of the voice. It is then broadened, so that the thing at which a sound is made is named by some of the words formed from hā' and lām. Then something else is likened to this named thing, and so named by it.

The origin is their saying ahalla bi-l-hajj — he raised his voice with the talbiya (pilgrim's cry); and istahalla al-ṣabiyyu ṣārikhan — the infant cried out at his birth.

Ibn Aḥmar said, concerning al-ihlāl, in a line of verse:
Its riders raise their cry at the sighting of al-Farqad, just as the pilgrim performing 'umra raises his cry.

One says: inhalla al-maṭaru — the rain poured in the intensity of its downpour and sound, inhilālan.

As for what is carried over to this by nearness and association, it is al-hilāl, the crescent moon in the sky — named so because people raise their voices (yuhillūna) when they look at it, saying takbīr and calling out in prayer. It is called hilāl on the first night, the second, and the third; after that it is simply the moon (qamar). One says ahalla al-hilāl and ustuhilla. Then, by way of likeness, it was said tahallala al-saḥābu bi-barqihi — the cloud gleamed with its lightning — as though the lightning were likened to the crescent.

What is also carried over by likeness:
1. al-hilāl — a spearhead with two prongs.
2. al-hilāl — the small amount of water at the bottom of a well.
3. al-hilāl — a kind of snake.

Dhu al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
To you we drove on every sturdy camel, as though it were a hilāl-snake appearing amid the hot sand, writhing.

4. al-hilāl — the slough, the cast-off skin of a snake.
5. al-hilāl — the tip of the millstone, when it breaks off.
6. thawbun halhal — a garment of flimsy weave, as if its thinness were like the light of the crescent.
7. shi'run halhal — thin, weak poetry.

Imru' al-Qays ibn Rabī'a was named Muhalhil because he was the first to make poetry fine; some said, rather, that he was named Muhalhil for his saying, in a line of verse:
When their base-born rider grew hard-pressed on the rocky ground, I raised my cry, seeking vengeance for Jābir or Ṣinbil.

That is because, when he wished to catch up to someone, he cried out repeatedly.

8. al-hulāhil — abundant water, because it has a sound as it flows; and it is, in origin, hurāhir.
9. al-hilāl — what is fastened between the two arches of a camel-saddle; plural, ahilla.

What deviates from this root: their saying, so-and-so charged his adversary, then halla — meaning, he held back.

As for the saying of the poet:
It has no wind, only sultry stillness, in which the night-traveller keeps crying out and raising dust.

And they say to horses: halā — meaning, stand still — a sound made to them.
هلا:
The letters hā', lām and the weak letter. They say:

1. halā — a word by which females are soothed when the male approaches them to mate. A poet said, in a line of verse: oh, greet Laylā, and say to her, gently now (halā).
2. dhahaba bi-dhī hiliyyān — said of one who has gone off to where none knows, meaning he vanished without trace.
هلب:
The letters hā', lām and bā' are a root indicating copiousness in something, and expanse.

1. al-hulb — what is coarse of hair, like the hair of a tail.
2. 'aysh ahlab — an ample, abundant life, as one also says 'aysh azabb.
3. yawm hallāb — a day whose rain is continuous and gentle.
4. al-hallāba — the cold wind that comes with rain; for this reason the hardship of a time is called hulba.
5. faras mahlūb — a horse is so called because the coarse hair (hulb) of its tail has been clipped.
هلت:
The letters hā', lām and tā' amount to nothing, except that they say:

1. al-halt — the group, the gathering.
2. al-hulāt — slackness, looseness.
هلج: The letters hā', lām and jīm are not a root. They say: halaja — he came out with talk that cannot be trusted.
هلس:
The letters hā', lām and sīn point to concealing something — whether speech or anything else.

1. ahlasa fī l-ḍaḥik — he concealed it, his laughter. A poet said, in a line of verse: "She laughs at me with a laugh that hides itself."
2. hālasa fulānan — he spoke secretly with so-and-so, whispered to him.
3. al-mahlūs — weak of mind; this fits the pattern.
4. al-hulās — [something resembling a wasting sickness, from emaciation], as though his flesh had gone hidden and withdrawn.
5. al-hals — abundant good; this falls outside the chapter.
هلع:
The letters hā', lām and 'ayn point to swiftness and intensity. nāqatun hilwā' — a she-camel sharp and swift; a female ostrich called hāli' likewise. From this comes al-hala' in a person, resembling greed and impatience; a man is called hali' and halū'.

Ibn al-Sikkīt said: a man called hul'a is one who panics and grows anxious quickly. They say "mā lahu hilla'un wa lā hilla'a", meaning he has neither a male kid nor a female kid, the two being named so for their skittishness.
هلف:
The letters hā', lām and fā' are words close in pattern, pointing to bigness and largeness.

1. al-hillawf — a big, heavy old man.
2. hillawfa — a thick, heavy beard.
3. hillawf — a big camel.
هلك:
The letters hā', lām and kāf point to breaking and falling. Of it is al-halāk, perishing, which is a falling; and for that reason of a dead man one says halaka. And ihtalakat al-qaṭāt in fear of the falcon: she threw herself into the places of destruction. As for the Hudhalī's words, in a line of verse:
Nor the ruined ones of the bedding, unarmed —
he says: their mothers are not evil mothers. And a woman is halūk when she gives herself over, breaking herself up, in her coquetry. And one does not say of a man halūk. And al-muhtalik is the one who is forever throwing himself upon whoever will take care of him; and there are people muhtalikūn and hullāk. And al-Ḥuṭay'a's words, in a line of verse:
Pressing hard to the watering, like woven cloth, in which the hands of the riding-beasts have made an old, broad track.
They said: mustahlik means striving hard; but the reasoning points only to what we mentioned about the sand-grouse when she hurls herself in fear of the falcon. And al-arḍ al-halakīn is barren land. And al-halak is the perishing thing. And al-halak is the chasm between two mountains. Dhū al-Rumma said, in a line of verse:
You see her earring in the clear white of her neck, jutting over a chasm, swinging in an empty space.
As for al-Hālikī, it is the blacksmith; they say he is traced to al-Hālik ibn ʿAmr ibn Asad ibn Khuzayma, who used to work iron, and for that the Banū Asad were called the smiths.
هلم:
The letters hā', lām and mīm contain nothing but their word halumma, a word calling someone to something.

They say its origin is hal a'ummu — "shall I go toward [it]?" — the words of one wanting to go to food; then it became so common that anyone summoning another used it, just as they say taʿāla, "come up", originally meaning "rise", which then became so common that even one standing below said it to one standing above him. It is also possible its sense is hal laka fī l-ṭaʿām, umma — "do you want the food? then go to it." What we hold on this is that it belongs to the kind of expression that is hard to settle; the like of it has already come up earlier.
هم:
The letters hā' and mīm are a sound root indicating melting, flowing, creeping, and the like; other things are then measured by analogy on it. From it is the saying of the Arabs, hammanī al-shay' — the thing melted me (with distress). And inhamma al-shahm — the fat melted.

1. al-hāmūm — fat abundant in its rendered grease.
2. al-saḥāb al-hāmūm — a cloud abundant in its downpour.
3. al-hamūm — a well abundant in water.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
It has a deep, generous well.

4. al-hamīma — a light rain-shower.
5. al-rīḥ al-raydāna — the soft, gentle-blowing wind.
6. al-hawāmm — the creeping things of the earth, named for their hamīm, that is, their creeping.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
You see its track on its two flanks, as though it were the crawl-paths of spiders that have a creeping motion.

7. hammama fī ra'sihi — he put his fingers among his hair, moving them back and forth to fall asleep, as though his fingers were creeping through his hair.

From this chapter:
1. al-himm — the aged, elderly man; and the woman is himma — as though the two of them had melted away from old age.

As for al-hamm, meaning grief, we hold it to belong to this same reasoning, for it is as though, from its intensity, it "melts" a person, that is, dissolves him. Al-hamm is also what you set your mind on; likewise al-himma. From al-himma is derived al-humām — a king great in resolve. Muhimm al-amr — a matter that is pressing. Ahammanī — it troubled me. The reasoning is one throughout.

Al-Kumayt said, in a line of verse:
Turning away, in place of all other people, toward them — I have no resolve for it, no resolve.

He means: I will not set my mind on that, nor do it. We have already explained the meaning of al-himma.
همج:
The letters hā', mīm and jīm are a root pointing to mixing and disorder.

Al-hāmij is the abandoned thing, surging together in itself. A poet said, in a line of verse: "Wandering pests surge within it."

And the saying of Abū Dhu'ayb: "Spotted at the two locks, mottled" — so it is said: al-hamīj is any two colours mixed together.

From this chapter:
1. al-hamaj — gnats; and by comparison the base, lowly sort of people are called al-hamaj.
2. al-hamaj — the young of locusts, before they fly.
3. ahmaja l-faras ihmājan — the horse floundered/thrashed about in its running.
4. al-hamaj — hunger, named for the confusion and agitation that comes over the one it afflicts. A poet said: "Our neighbour perished from hunger."
5. hamajat il-ibil — the camels came to the water and drank from it.
6. al-hamaja — the emaciated ewe, as though likened to the gnat.
همد:
The letters hā', mīm and dāl are a root pointing to the dying-down of a thing. hamadati al-nāru — the fire went out completely. arḍun hāmida — land with no vegetation in it. nabātun hāmid — dried-up plant. al-ihmād — staying on in a place.

What falls outside this chapter: the saying of one who held that al-ihmād is speed in walking. [A poet] said:
It was nothing but the swift setting-loose of hurrying.
همذ:
The letters hā', mīm and dhāl point to speed.

1. al-hamādhī — speed.
2. hamādhī l-maṭar — the intensity of the rain.
همر: The letters hā', mīm and rā' are a root pointing to pouring and outpouring. hamara dam'ahu — he poured out his tears; hamara al-dam'u wa-inhamara, sāla, the tears flowed and poured forth. fulānun yuhāmiru al-shay', idhā akhadhahu jarfan — so-and-so takes a thing in one sweeping scoop. hamara fī kalāmihi, akthara — he talked at excessive length; huwa mihmār, ay kathīru al-kalām — he is a great talker. hamara lahu min mālihi, as though he poured it out to him.
همز:
The letters ha', mim and za' are a word indicating pressure and squeezing.

1. hamaztu ash-shay'a fi kaffi — I squeezed the thing in my palm.
2. from this, al-hamz in speech, the glottal catch, as though one presses the letter.
3. hamaza bihi al-ard — they say this of flinging someone down hard onto the ground.
4. a bow called hamza — one that drives the arrow forcefully.
5. al-hammaz — the fault-finder, the slanderer; likewise al-humaza.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
You profess friendship for me falsely when you meet me — but when I am gone, you are the slanderer, the backbiter.

And the hamz — the prodding — of Satan is like a seizure that overcomes a person's heart and carries it away.
همس:
The letters hā', mīm and sīn point to the faintness of a sound or a sensation. From it comes al-hams, the faint sound; hamsu al-aqdām is the very faintest thing that comes from the tread of the foot. As for their saying al-hammās, the fierce lion, this too, in our view, is from the same root, because what is meant by it is its hams, whether in its tread or in its bite. [A poet] said:
Its habit is trampling, and a fierce, faint-sounding bite.
همش:
The letters hā', mīm and shīn are a root pointing to quickness of work or speech.

1. al-hamish — one quick with his fingers at work, so they say.
2. imra'a hamashā l-ḥadīth — a woman quick in her talk, when she rushes through it. A poet said, in a line of verse: "In Zaynab's days she was not shallow of judgement, quick of talk, nor a roaming, brazen woman."
3. al-hamsh — milking quickly.
4. al-hamsh — noise and clamour.
همط: The letters hā', mīm and ṭā' are not a root — except that they say: hamaṭa — he mixed falsehood together with wrongdoing. And ahmaṭa ʿirḍa fulānin — he reviled so-and-so's honour.
همع:
The letters hā', mīm and ʿayn point to something flowing.

1. hamaʿat il-ʿayn — the eye's tears flowed.
2. tahammaʿa l-rajul — the man made as if to weep.
3. saḥābun hamiʿ — a raining cloud.
4. al-himyaʿ — sudden death.
همق: The letters hā', mīm and qāf are a single word. They say: kala'un hamiq — soft, tender pasture.
همك: The letters hā', mīm and kāf are a single word. Inhamaka fī l-amr — he strove hard and persisted in the matter.
همل:
The letters hā', mīm and lām are a single root. Ahmaltu l-shay' — I left the thing to itself, letting it be.

1. al-hamal — that which is left unguarded, unattended.
2. al-hamal — wealth or livestock with no one to guard it.
3. hamalat il-ʿayn — the eye's tears flowed, like hamarat — meaning: poured.

And God knows best what is correct.
هملع:
The one whose gait comes down hard, treading heavily.

1. al-habanqaʿ — the fool who sits on the tips of his fingers, begging. He has sat in that manner, "habanqaʿa".
2. habannaqa — a man proverbial for foolishness. And al-hibnīq — the young servant.
3. al-hirkawla — a heavy-set, large-bodied woman.
4. al-hilkas — what Ibn Durayd related: a man base in character.
5. al-hijris — the fox's cub.
6. al-hayjumāna — the ant.
7. al-hirshaffa — a worn-out old woman, and also a worn-out bucket. And [he has] no halbasīs, meaning: not a thing.
8. al-hirṭāl — the tall one.
9. al-hirdabb — the coward.
10. al-hidamla — a stretch of sand.
11. harthamat al-asad — the lion's nose and muzzle. And when its hair falls out it is called harāmīl.
12. al-hanābith — hard, severe matters.

And God knows best the truth of these matters.

(The Book of Hā' is finished, and God knows best what is correct.)
همن: The letters hā', mīm and nūn are not [a root at all]. As for al-muhaymin, meaning the witness, it does not belong here; rather it belongs to the root hamza-mīm-nūn [amina, safety/trust], with the hā' standing in for a hamza.
همى:
The letters hā', mīm and the weak letter point to a thing going off on its own way.

1. hamā l-mā' — the water flowed.
2. hamati l-māshiya tahmī — the livestock went off on their own way, to graze or otherwise.

And in the hadith: "We come upon the stray camels [hawāmī l-ibil]" — meaning: the strays.

And when it is hamzated the meaning changes: you say tahamma'a l-thawb — the garment wore out.
هن:
The letters hā' and nūn are a sound root indicating a kind of flesh (fat), and there is in it something of what we ascribe to obscurity, even though our scholars have spoken about it.

1. al-hanna — said to be the fat of the inner corner of the eye; so said Abū Bakr.
2. al-hunāna — fat.
3. mā bi-hādhā al-ba'īr hānna — "this camel has no hānna in it," as one says, it has no strength.

As for the other matter, al-Farrā' said: ijlis hāhunā qarīban — sit right here, nearby; and tanaḥḥa hāhunā — meaning, move away.

As for the saying of al-A'shā, a poet said, in a line of verse:
There is no remembering Jubayra here, nor whoever came to me with news of terrors from her.

They said its meaning is: Jubayra is not where you imagined her to be — it disabuses him of hope in her.

Likewise the saying of al-Rā'ī, a poet said, in a line of verse:
Does your eye gaze after the trace of the departing camels? Yes — but this is not the place for it; your heart is unsettled.

They said its meaning is: the matter is not where you supposed.

And the saying of another:
Nawār yearned, but this was not the place for yearning.

He means: this is not a place for such longing.

And his saying:
When I saw her two litters, right here.

He meant, right here.

And Ibn al-Sikkīt said, concerning the saying:
When he saw the house empty, here.

He said it means: he wept. One says hanna, when he wept.

We stop, in such obscure matters, where we have stopped; otherwise, I do not think any of them has fully resolved or explained this yet.
هنأ:
The letters hā', nūn, and hamza indicate obtaining good without hardship.

1. al-hanʾ — the gift; it is a verbal noun, while the true noun is al-hinʾ.
2. al-hanīʾ — something that comes to you without hardship. One says: this food was not hanīʾ [pleasant]; and it did indeed become hanīʾ.
3. haniʾat al-māshiya — the livestock got a good share of herbage; camels in this state are hanʾā.
4. al-hinā' — a kind of tar; hanaʾtu al-baʿīr, I tarred the camel; a tarred she-camel is mahnūʾa. It may be so named for the healing it provides.

Not from this chapter: 'a hinʾ of the night passed,' meaning a portion of it.
هنا:
The letters hā', nūn and the weak letter hold difficult words, things with no fixed pattern.

1. hunā — a word of nearness.
2. hāhunā — a word of distancing.

As for the saying of Imru' al-Qays, in a line of verse: "And the talk of the company, on the day of hunā ... and a tale, however brief it was" — there is disagreement about it. Some said it means the day now past, used for nearness — he means: my time with them was on the day of hunā. Others said it means play. And it is said hunā is a place.

3. han — a word of allusion. You say: atāhu hanun — something came to him; and fī fulānin hanātun — in so-and-so are hanāt, meaning traits of evil; it is not said of good.
هنب: The letters hā', nūn and bā' hold nothing but hinb, a man's name. Ibn Durayd mentioned that al-hanab is heaviness and dullness. They say: imra'atun hanbā' — a foolish woman. He said, in a line of verse: "A madwoman, hunbā', daughter of a madman."
هند:
The letters hā', nūn and dāl are not by analogy; in it are names simply given as names.

1. hind — a woman's name.
2. hunayda — a hundred camels. He said, in a line of verse: "They gave a hundred, driven on by eight men — in their giving there was neither stinting nor excess."
3. hind — said for two hundred.

As for their saying "hannadat fulānatu qalbī" — she carried my heart away, and "hannadat fulānatu fulānan" — she made him fall in love through flirtation — that is talk not to be dwelt on.

And their saying al-tahnīd — the sharpening of the Indian sword, al-sayf al-muhannad — that is only a tempering worked into the swords of India.
هنع:
The letters hā', nūn and ʿayn are a word pointing to a stoop, a bending down, in something.

1. al-hanaʿ — a stoop in the neck.
2. akamatun hanʿā' — a low mound.
3. ẓalīmun ahnaʿ — a male ostrich with a stoop in its neck.
4. al-hanʿa — a mark branded on the lower part of the neck.
5. al-hanʿa — a star.
هنف: The letters hā', nūn and fā' are a single word: al-muhānafa — laughing beyond a smile. They said tahānafa is not said of a man; it describes women's laughter only, as al-Khalīl related. And it is also said that al-tahānuf is the laugh of one who mocks.
هنق: The letters hā', nūn and qāf. Ibn Durayd related: al-hanaq is something like the restlessness that comes over a person. And he cited: "It has vexed me today, and beyond vexing."
هنم: The letters hā', nūn and mīm. The correct view is that al-haynama is a faint, low sound. A poet said, in a line of verse: "I do not witness the improper talk, nor those who speak it, when they mutter it in a low murmur." And among what has been mentioned: al-hinnama — a bead used for charms.
هو:
The letters hā' and wāw do not meet the condition for a true root, yet the word belongs to the Arabic language; its basis is a hā' to which a wāw was joined.

Some of the Arabs double it and say huwwa; others say huw.
هوب: The letters hā', wāw and bā' are not a sound root, but they say: al-hawb is the meddler, one who mixes into things. And Ibn Durayd related, in his Ṭarā'if: aṣābanī hawbu al-nār — the blaze of the fire struck me.
هوت: The letters hā', wāw and tā' are close to the one before it. They say: al-hawta is the path to water. And "ṣabba Allāhu 'alayhi al-hawta wa-l-mawta" — may God pour upon him al-hawta and al-mawta — is a curse; so said al-Khalīl.
هوج:
The letters hā', wāw and jīm are a word indicating rashness and forcing one's way.

1. al-ahwaj — the rash, headlong man.
2. al-hawjā' — a swift she-camel, as though rashness were in her.
3. al-hawjā' — the wind that uproots tents. Abū Bakr said: it blows from one direction in a continuous blast.
4. al-hāja — the frog.
هود: The letters hā', wāw and dāl are a root indicating gentleness and stillness. They say [al-tahwīd] is walking slowly and softly. And they say hawwada when he slept. And the drink hawwada the soul of the drinker when his soul grew heavy with it. And al-hawāda is a state between people in which safety is hoped for. And al-muhāwada is the making of peace. As for al-Yahūd, the Jews, it is from hāda yahūdu, when he repented, the verbal noun being hawd; and they were named by it because they repented of the worship of the calf. And in the Qur'an: {Indeed we have turned back to You} [al-Aʿrāf: 156]; and in repentance there is a gentleness of state and a safety.
هوذ: The letters hā', wāw and dhāl are a single word: hawdha, the sand-grouse; and by it a man was named Hawdha.
هور:
The letters hā', wāw and rā' are a root indicating the collapsing and falling-away of something.

1. *tahawwara l-binā'* — the building collapsed.
2. *tahawwara l-laylu* — the night's darkness broke apart, as though it had collapsed and passed on.
3. *tahawwara sh-shitā'* — the harshest part of winter passed.
4. They call a flock of sheep *hawr*, and this is sound usage, because from its great number some of it tumbles over the rest.

Among what strays outside this chapter: their saying *hurtu fulānan bikadhā, ahūruhu* — I suspected him of such-and-such.

Someone said, in a line of verse:
He saw that I do not credit him with much.
هوس:
The letters hā', wāw and sīn are a word indicating roaming about and coming and going, as in bewilderment. al-haws is roaming about; and any bold pursuit is haws. One says asadun hawwās, a roaming lion; and the camels spent the night roaming (tahūs): travelling by night.

Carried over to this by extension: intensity of eating. One says akūlun hawwās, a voracious eater.

From this chapter:
1. nāqatun hawisa — a weak she-camel; and when she is such, she becomes bewildered.
2. Their saying, bihi hawas — he has madness in him.
هوش:
The letters hā', wāw and shīn are a small root indicating mixing and confusion, and the like.

1. hawwashū — they mixed together, fell into confusion.
2. hāshat al-khaylu fī al-ghāra — the horses surged in confusion during the raid.
3. al-mahāwish, in the hadith, comes from this [root].
4. hawwashat al-rīḥu bi-l-turāb — the wind stirred up the dust, bringing it in different colors.
5. al-hawsh — a great number.
6. tahawwasha al-qawmu 'alā fulānin — the people banded together against so-and-so.

Deviating from this: al-hawash, said to mean smallness of the belly. He said, in a line of verse:
Their bellies grew shrunken and arched up.

And they are mutahāwishūn, meaning, mixed together in confusion.
هوع:
The letters hā', wāw and 'ayn are two words: al-haw' is base greed. One says rajulun hā', a greedy man.

The other word: al-huwā' is vomiting. One says hā'a yahū'u and tahawwa'a. Al-Khalīl said: la-uhawwi'annahu mā akal — I will make him bring up from his throat what he ate.
هوف: The letters hā', wāw and fā' are a single word indicating lightness. al-hūf is the wind that comes from the direction of Yemen. The mother of Ta'abbaṭa Sharran, lamenting him, said: "He was no hulfūf (a big, thick man); the hūf-wind could wrap around him" — meaning he was slight. By this the fool is likened to it, and so he is called hūf. Abū Bakr said: a man is hūf when he is hollow, with no good in him.
هوك: The letters hā', wāw and kāf are a word indicating foolishness and falling into a thing without insight. al-hawak is foolishness. tahawwaka al-rajul — the man blundered blindly into a thing. And in the hadith: "Are you bewildered (mutahawwikūn) as the Jews and Christians were bewildered?"
هول:
The letters hā', wāw and lām are two words: one indicates fear, the other embellishment and adornment.

The first: al-hawl, which is fear. hālanī al-shay' yahūlunī — the thing terrified me. makānun muhāl — a fearsome place.

A poet of Hudhayl said, in a line of verse:
It crossed to us, despite its distance, the terrifying pitfalls of a fearsome, dread wasteland.

al-tahāwīl — whatever has terrified you of anything. hawwalū 'alā al-rajul — they made the man swear an oath beside a fire with which they terrified him.

Aws said, in a line of verse:
As the oath-taker shrank back from the fire of the one making him swear.

The other: their saying, for the ornamentation of an embroidered garment, tahāwīl. And one says hawwalat al-mar'a — the woman adorned herself with her jewelry.
هوم:
The letters hā', wāw and mīm are a word. They say: hawwama al-rajul — the man nodded his head from drowsiness. And we say, hawwamnā, we dozed.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
The eye tastes no sleep, only a nodding-doze.
هون: The letters hā', wāw and nūn are a small root pointing to stillness, or calm, or lowliness. Of that is al-hawn: calm and gravity. God, glorified, said: {who walk upon the earth gently} [al-Furqan: 63]. And al-hūn is disgrace. He, mighty and majestic, said: {shall he keep it in contempt} [al-Nahl: 59]. And al-hāwūn, that with which things are pounded, is sound Arabic, as though it were of the pattern fā'ūl from al-hawn.
هوه:
The letters hā', wāw and hā'.

1. al-hawhā' — the fool.
2. al-hawāhī — falsehood, idle talk.

Ibn Aḥmar said, in a line of verse:
Every day the two of them call physicians to me, and they avail nothing but idle words.

Al-Khalīl said: bi'run hawhā', on the pattern of ḥamrā' — a well abundant in water.
هوي:
The letters hā', wāw and yā' are a sound root pointing to emptiness and to falling. Its origin is al-hawā' - the air between the earth and the sky - so called for its being empty. They said: and everything empty is hawā'. God - exalted is He - said: {And their hearts are hawā'} [Ibrāhīm: 43], that is, empty, holding nothing. Then Zuhayr said, in a line of verse:
As though the saddle upon her were on a small-headed one of the ostriches, its breast hollow.

And one says hawā al-shay'u yahwī - the thing fell. Hāwiya is Hell, because the unbeliever falls into it. Al-hāwiya is every place into which one may fall. Al-huwwa is the deep hollow. And ahwā ilayhi bi-yadihi - he reached out to it with his hand to take it, as though he flung his hand at it when he let it go. And tahāwā al-qawm fī al-mahwāt - the people fell into the pit one after another. And they say: al-hawī is a going down in a descent, and al-huwī is in rising up. Zuhayr said of al-hawī, in a line of verse:
He cuts through the hard stony ground with her, and she goes down as the bucket goes down when the rope lets it go.

And al-Hudhalī said of al-huwī, in a line of verse:
And when you cast him into the mountain passes, you saw him sweeping over their gaps as the falcon sweeps.

And hawat al-ṭaʿna - the spear-thrust opened its mouth wide as it went, and that is from al-hawā', the empty. And hawat ummuhu is an abuse, that is: she has fallen and perished. And "his mother is hāwiya" is said as one says "bereaved". Al-mahwā is the distance between two things standing upright, so that it is even said of the distance between the two shoulders.

As for al-hawā - the desire of the soul - it is from both meanings together, because it is empty of every good and it drops its owner into what he should not do. God - exalted is He - said in describing His Prophet, upon him be blessing and peace: {And he does not speak out of hawā - desire} [al-Najm: 3]; from it one says hawītu ahwā hawan. As for al-muhāwāt, Abū ʿAmr mentioned that it is stubborn wrangling. And Abū ʿUbayd said: it is hard travelling. And he recited, in a line of verse:
Mayy could not keep up with our hard night travelling, nor the night of camels bowed low in their halters.

And what he said is good speech: as for the wrangling, it is because each of the two loves the other's desire to be his own; and as for the travelling, it is for the flinging about of the bodies that goes with it.
هي:
The letters hā' and yā', and hā' and hamza, follow the same course as what came before them.

Yet they say: "mā adrī ayyu hayyi bni bayyin huwa" — I do not know which "hayy son of bayy" he is — meaning: which of the people he is. This, in our view, is among the things whose explanation has been lost. Likewise their saying, "even if that were in al-hay' and al-jay', it would not have helped him" — al-hay' being food, al-jay' being drink, though the two words by themselves do not point to this meaning.

They say: ha'ha'tu bi-l-ibil — when you called the camels to their fodder; this is different from the first. They cited as evidence, in a line of verse:
My praise of you was not for food, nor for drink.

As for hā' — this letter, and hā as a particle, is one of drawing attention. It is their way, when they wish to magnify something, to multiply the particles of attention and pointing used with it. In the Book of God: {Here you are, the very ones} [Āl ʿImrān: 66]. Then the poet said:
Here — this is an excuse; if it does not avail, then its bearer has surely gone astray in the land.

They say in an oath: "No, by God." They say that hā'un can serve as an answering call. He said, in a line of verse:
No, rather he answers you when you call him by his name, saying "here!" — and how long he has answered so.

hā'a yahū'u al-rajulu haw'an [said of a man]; and al-haw' is ambition. Al-Kisā'ī said: "yā hay'a mālī" is an expression of regret.
هيأ:
The letters hā', yā', and alif form a word whose hā' is not part of its true sense. One says hayā, meaning 'oh' [an exclamation].

A poet said:
So he listens closely, hoping he might be alive — and cries out for joy, 'oh, my Lord!'
هيب:
The letters hā', yā' and bā' are a word of reverence and fear.

1. hābahu yahābuhu haybatan — he held him in awe, feared him.
2. rajulun hayyūb — a man who holds everything in awe.
3. hayyūb — also, held in awe, feared by others.

And their saying, "faith is hayyūb" — some said it means held in awe; others said it means the believer shrinks from rushing headlong into what others hasten to.

4. tahayyabtu al-shay' — I feared the thing. tahayyabanī al-shay' — the thing seemed to frighten me.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
The waterless waste I ride does not frighten me.

5. al-hayyabān — the coward.

As for their saying, ahāba bihi, meaning he called out to him — he calls out as a shepherd calls out to his sheep, for them to stop or turn back — this belongs to the same reasoning, as though he startles them.

What is not from this chapter, and I do not know how sound it is: their saying, al-hayyabān is the foam from a camel's mouth.
هيت:
The letters hā', yā' and tā' are a word pointing to a shout. They say hayyata bihi, meaning he called out to him, idhā ṣāḥa, when he shouted. [A poet] said:
Had he been the one meant by it, he would have called out.
They also say, of the meaning of "hayta laka": halumma, come here.
هيج:
The letters hā', yā' and jīm are two sound roots: one indicates something breaking out or stirring up, the other the drying of plants.

The first:
1. hāja al-faḥl, hayjan and hiyājan — the stallion became roused/excited. Blood does likewise (it "hāja" — surges up).
2. al-hayjā' — battle; it is said both stretched (hayjā') and short (hayjā).
3. hijtu al-sharr, and hayyajtuhu — I stirred up trouble, in both forms.
4. hayyajtu al-nāqa fa-inbaʿathat — I roused the she-camel and she set off.
5. mihyāj — said of a she-camel that yearns for her homeland.

The second: they say hāja al-baql — the plants "hāja" when they turned yellow, about to dry out. A "hā'ija" land is one whose plants have dried. ahyaytu al-arḍ — I found the land's plants already dried and withered.

Ru'ba said, in a line of verse:
And he found al-Khalṣā', of Dhāt al-Buraq, [already] withered.
(The line names two places; its exact sense beyond that the land was found parched is not fully clear from the text.)
هيد:
The letters hā', yā' and dāl. The origin from which movement and disturbance are measured by analogy; the rest of it has an unknown analogy.

1. hidtu al-shay' — I moved the thing, haydan.
2. hādanī yahīdunī — it troubled and disturbed me. They say, lā yahīdannaka — let it not disturb you.
3. al-haydān — the coward, as though everything disturbs him.
4. hayd — a word said when driving camels along.
5. hayyada fī al-sayr — he hastened in his going.

As for the hadith mentioning the Messenger of God's mosque, "hidhu" — meaning, repair it; they said this can only be done after demolition. Its meaning is that the ruin was something fallen down, and when it was rebuilt, it was as though it had been brought back to life.

As for what has an obscure analogy, and which we hold to be among the speech whose knowledge has faded — their saying, hayda mālak — most say it means, what is your affair, what is your matter?

They cited, in a line of verse:
O what is it with you — from longing and sleeplessness, and the passing of a phantom, on the terrors, ever knocking.
هيس:
The letters hā', yā' and sīn. They say: al-hays is travelling.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
One of your nights — so go on, go on.
هيش:
The letters hā', yā' and shīn.

1. al-haysh — gentle milking.
2. al-haysh — motion, agitation.

He said: hāsha fī al-qawmi yahīshu — he stirred among the people, causing corruption and mischief.
هيض:
The letters hā', yā' and ḍād are a single word indicating the breaking of a thing, and the like.

1. hāḍa 'aẓmahu — he broke his bone again, after it had been set.
2. hīḍa al-insān — the person relapsed in his illness after recovering.

In the hadith of Abū Bakr: "Indeed, this will set you back."
هيط: The letters hā', yā' and ṭā' are two words: one of them, al-hiyāṭ, is shouting, clamor; the other, a word related by al-Farrā': tahāyaṭa al-qawm — the people gathered to settle their differences.
هيع:
The letters hā', yā' and ʿayn are a single word, and it is al-hayʿa: the sound that one is frightened and afraid of. One says: a man is hāʿ and hāʾiʿ [alarmed]. And in the hadith: "Whenever he heard a hayʿa [an alarm-cry] he flew towards it." And one says hāʿa yahīʿu [he was alarmed].

Al-Ṭirimmāḥ said, in a line of verse:
I am the son of the protectors of glory from the family of Mālik ... when the base men's hearts run to hayʿa.
That is, they turn coward.

It is possible that the origin of this chapter is spreading out and flowing loosely.

1. *al-mahyaʿ* — the wide, clear road.
2. *al-hayʿa* — the flowing of something poured over the face of the ground, that is, it spreads out.
3. *arḍun hayʿa* — wide, spread-out land. Al-Khalīl said this.
4. *mutahayyiʿ* — bewildered, alarmed [like hāʾiʿ].

All of that is from that same origin.
هيغ:
The letters hā', yā' and ghayn are a word that indicates comfort and ease of living.

1. *al-ahyagh* — the most comfortable life, it is said.
2. *al-ahyaghān* — eating and sex, they say.
3. *hayyaghtu al-tharīda* — I made the tharīd [a bread-and-broth dish] rich with fat.

A poet said:
They dip whoever they have dipped into the ahyagh [the rich, comfortable thing].
هيف:
The letters hā', yā' and fā' are a sound root indicating heat and thirst, and it is then used metaphorically.

1. *al-hayf* — a hot wind that comes at the start of summer; it makes the livestock thirsty and dries out anything moist.
2. *rajulun mihyāf* — a man who cannot bear to be without water.
3. *ahāfū* — their camels became thirsty.

And it is used metaphorically: one whose waist is slender is called *ahyaf*, as if there were thirst there [wasting him away]; the plural is *hīf*.

4. *farasun hayfāʾ* — a slender, lean mare.
هيق: The letters hā', yā' and qāf are a single word, and it is al-hayq: the male ostrich. And every long, thin thing is called hayq, by comparison.
هيل: The letters hā', yā' and lām are a single word pointing to letting out something that could be measured, without measuring it. hiltu al-ṭa'āma uhīluhu haylan — I let the food pour out freely. God, glorious is He, said: {and the mountains were like heaped, pouring sand} [al-Muzzammil: 14]. From this comes their saying "jā'a bi'l-hayli wa'l-haylamān", meaning he came with a great abundance of something.
هيم:
The letters hā', yā' and mīm are a word indicating severe thirst.

1. al-hayamān — thirst.
2. al-hīm — thirsty camels.
3. al-hīm — sands that swallow up water.
4. al-huyām — a disease that takes hold of camels when they are thirsty, so that they wander the land, heeding nothing.
5. al-haymān — from this the [love-]struck lover is named, as though he were driven mad by love and went off on his face, without direction.
6. al-haymā' — open waste country with no water in it.
هين: The letters hā', yā' and nūn: al-hayn is al-amr al-hayyin, the easy matter — and it is [really] from wāw, and this has already passed.
وأب:
The letters wāw, hamza and bā' are two words: one indicates the hollowing-out of something, and the other indicates anger.

The first:
1. *al-ḥāfir al-wa'b* — a hoof that is hollowed out, cupped.
2. *al-wa'ba* — a small hollow in a rock that holds water.

The other word:
1. *aw'abtu fulānan* — I angered so-and-so.
2. It is said that *al-iba* comes from this.
وأد:
The letters wāw, hamza and dāl are a word pointing to the weighing-down of one thing by another. It is said of camels, when they walk under their own weight, that they have a wa'īd. [A poet] said:
What ails the camels, that their walk is so heavy?
meaning a walk weighed down. Al-maw'ūda, the girl buried alive, is named from this, because she is buried alive and so weighed down by the earth heaped over her; wa'adahā ya'iduhā wa'dan, he buried her alive. From this comes his saying:
And he kept alive the buried-alive girl, so she was not buried.
وأر:
The letters wāw, hamza and rā'. They say: *istaw'arat al-ibil* — the camels followed one another in succession.

Abū Isḥāq al-Zajjāj held that the origin of this chapter is intensity of heat. He said:
