1. *wa'ira yawmunā* — our day grew intensely hot, a *wa'r*. [And] *yawmun wa'ir* — a hot day.
2. *al-ira* — a pit made for kindling a fire. *Wa'ara al-makān* — he dug a pit in the place for a fire.
3. *al-wa'r* — intensity of terror, as though it were terror that burns from its own severity. *Wa'artuhu, a'iruhu, wa'ran* — I frightened him. *Wu'ira Zaydun* — Zayd was terrified.
وأص: The letters wāw, hamza and ṣād. They say: *mā adrī ayyu l-wa'īṣati huwa* — I do not know which of the people he is. *Al-wa'īṣa*: the group, the gathering of people.
وأق:
The letters wāw, hamza and qāf. They say: *al-wa'q* is the shrike.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
I went out in the morning — though I never used to go out upon a *wa'q* or a *ḥātim* [a raven].
وأل: The letters wāw, hamza and lām are a word pointing to gathering together and taking refuge. istaw'alati al-ibilu — the camels gathered together. al-maw'il — the refuge, from wa'ala ilayhi ya'ilu, he took refuge in it. al-wa'la — the smell of gathered dung.
وأم: The letters wāw, hamza and mīm: a word indicating agreement and closeness. They say: *al-wi'ām* — agreement; *wā'amtuhu* — I agreed with him. Their proverb: 'Were it not for agreement, mankind would have perished.'
وأه: The letters wāw, hamza and hā': a word they say on finding something pleasing: *wāhan lahu* — how excellent it is!
وأي:
The letters wāw, hamza and yā' are two distinct words. The first is the promise: they say *wa'aytuhu, a'īhi, wa'yan*, and he is *ṣādiq al-wa'y* — true to his promise.

The second indicates strength, or gathering and largeness.
1. They say *ḥimārun wa'an* — a strong donkey — and likewise the horse.
2. *Qidrun wa'iyya* — a large pot.
3. It is also said: *al-wa'iyya* is *al-juwāliq* [a large pack or sack], as in the saying of Aws, in a line of verse:
It settled as a merchant's pack settles — its cord loosened, and its bundles fell apart and scattered from it.
And God knows best.
وبأ:
The letters wāw, bā' and hamza are one word: it is *al-wabā'*, plague. *Arḍun wabi'a*, on the pattern *fa'ila* — and it becomes *wabi'at*; and *mawbū'a* — and it becomes *wubi'at*.

Their saying *wa'tu ilayhi* and *awba'tu*, meaning I gestured to him, belongs to the class of substitution [one letter standing in for another]; the true origin is the mīm [i.e. from *awma'tu*]. They have cited, with the bā':
You see the people, whenever we travel, walking behind us; and if we gesture to the people, they stop.
وبخ: The letters wāw, bā' and khā' are one word. *Wabbakhahu*: he blamed him — *tawbīkhan*, reproach.
وبد:
The letters wāw, bā' and dāl: a word indicating a bad state.
1. *Arḍun wabida* — land whose people's condition has gone bad.
2. *Al-wabd* — a small hollow in a rock.
3. *Rajulun mustawbidu l-makān* — a man ignorant of the place.
وبر:
The letters wāw, bā' and rā' are words that do not follow one single reasoning; rather each stands on its own. al-wabar is the well-known thing, camel-hair. al-wabr is an animal. banāt awbar are a kind of small truffle. "mā bi'l-dāri wābir" means there is no one in the house.

Some have related "wabbara fī manzilihi tawbīran", meaning he did not leave it. wabr is also the name of one of "the old woman's days" [a set of bitterly cold days at winter's end].
وبش:
The letters wāw, bā' and shīn: a word indicating mixing.
1. *Jā'a awbāshun min al-nās* — mixed groups of people came.
2. *Awbashat al-arḍ* — its plants grew mixed and varied.
وبص:
The letters wāw, bā' and ṣād: it indicates the appearance of something in a glitter.
1. *Wabaṣa, yabiṣu* — it flashed, glittered.
2. *Awbaṣtu nārī* — I made my fire flare up.
3. *Wabbaṣa l-jirw* — the puppy opened its eyes.
4. *Awbaṣat al-arḍ* — its plants appeared, as though gleaming.

And what stands apart from this: they say, of a man, *innahu la-wābiṣatu samʿin* — when he listens to speech, relies on it, and takes it as true.
وبط:
The letters wāw, bā' and ṭā': a word indicating weakness.
1. *Wabiṭa ra'yuhu* — his judgment weakened.
2. *Al-wābiṭ* — the coward.
3. *Wabaṭanī fulānun ʿan ḥājatī* — so-and-so held me back from my errand.
وبق:
The letters wāw, bā' and qāf are two words. Anything that stands between two other things is called a mawbiq.

The other word: wabaqa — he perished; God "awbaqahu" — destroyed him. It is also said that al-mawbiq is the appointed time or place [for a meeting].
وبل:
The letters waw, ba and lam are a root indicating severity in a thing, and gathering/accumulation. Al-wabl and al-wabil are heavy, violent rain. One says 'wabalati l-sama'' — the sky brought heavy rain. A line (obscure, rendered as best as can be made out):
If they keep at it steadily, he is generous; and if they are generous once, he pours down abundantly.

Wabalatu l-shay' is its heaviness. From this, a harmful/oppressive thing is 'shay'un wabil'. 'Istawbaltu l-balad' — I found the land unwholesome, even though I loved it. Al-wabil is a severe blow. Al-wabil is a man who is a burden in a matter he takes charge of, not managing it well. Al-mawbil is hard, rocky ground. Al-wabil is the fuller's beating-club, with which he beats garments clean. Al-wabil is a bundle of firewood. One says al-wabil is pasture-fodder, whether moist or dry. Al-wabila is the bone of the knee-joint.
وتح:
The letters wāw, tā' and ḥā': a word indicating scantness in something.
1. *Al-watḥ* and *al-watah* — the little, the scant.
2. *Wataḥa l-'aṭiyya* — he made the gift small.
3. *Tawattaḥtu min al-sharāb* — I drank a little of it.
4. *Awtaḥtu ḥaẓẓahu* — I diminished his share.
وتد: The letters waw, ta' and dal are one word: al-watid, the peg. One says watadahu — he drove it in as a peg; watid watidaka — drive your peg in firmly. Watd is also said, in another vocalization. Watid al-udhun — the peg of the ear, the part inside it that resembles a peg. (This root's text is terse and the imperative phrase is unclear beyond what is given here.)
وتر:
The letters waw, ta' and ra' are a chapter whose words do not all follow one single derivation; rather they are separate items unlike one another.

1. al-watira — a round white blaze on a horse's forehead.
2. al-watira — a thing on which spear-thrusting is practiced.
3. al-watira — keeping steadily to a thing; one says "he is on a watira," a settled course.
4. al-watr — a blood-debt, an unavenged wrong; one says watartuhu atiruhu watran, I wronged him, deprived him of his due.
5. al-witr and al-watr — the odd number, opposite of even.
6. watar al-qaws — the bowstring, well known; one says watartuha and awtartuha, I strung it.
7. al-watara — the tip of the nose.

As for al-muwatara, succession in things, al-Lihyani said: it is not muwatara unless a pause falls between the occurrences — otherwise it is mudaraka, unbroken succession. One says: a she-camel is muwatira — she sets down one knee, pauses, then sets down the other.
وتش: The letters wāw, tā' and shīn. *Al-watsh*: the little and worthless of anything. And God knows best what is correct.
وتغ:
The letters wāw, tā' and ghayn: a word indicating sin and affliction.
1. *Al-watagh* — sin.
2. *Awtaghahu* — he cast him into affliction.
3. *Watigha, watagan* — he perished.
4. *Awtaghahu* — he destroyed him.
وتن: The letters wāw, tā' and nūn are a word pointing to steadfastness and constancy. wātana al-amra — he persisted in the matter. mā'un wātin — water that never fails. From this comes al-watīn, a vein attached to the heart that feeds it.
وثأ: The letters wāw, thā' and hamza. It contains nothing but *wuthi'at yaduhu* — his hand was bruised, and it is *mawthū'a*.
وثب:
The letters wāw, thā' and bā' indicate, in the language of the Arabs, attainment and triumph — except in some of the dialects of Ḥimyar, where it is the opposite of this.
1. *Wathaba min makānihi* — he leapt from his place.
2. In the dialect of Ḥimyar, they say of one who has sat down: *qad wathaba* [he has 'leapt' — meaning: he has sat].
3. When they command someone to sit, they say *thib* ['leap' — meaning: sit].
4. They call a king who sits and does not go out to war *al-mawthabān*.
5. *Wathabahu wisādatan* — he threw him a cushion, for him to sit on.
وثج:
The letters wāw, thā' and jīm indicate compactness.
1. *Wathuja l-farasu, wathāja* — its flesh grew firm and compact; it is *wathīj*.
2. *Istawthaja nabtu l-arḍ* — its plants grew thick, clinging to one another.
3. *Arḍun mu'tathija* — land abundant in pasture.
وثر:
The letters wāw, thā' and rā': a word indicating softness in something.
1. *Firāshun wathrun* and *wathīr* — soft, smooth bedding.
2. *Al-mayāthir* — red cloths used on the mounts of foreigners [non-Arabs].
3. Their saying *wathara l-jamalu l-nāqata* — the male camel covered the she-camel, as though she were to him a soft bed.
وثق: The letters wāw, thā' and qāf are a word pointing to binding fast and making firm. And waththaqtu al-shay' - I made the thing firm. And nāqa muwaththaqat al-khalq - a she-camel firmly knit in build. And al-mīthāq is the firmly made covenant. And he is a thiqa, one to be trusted. And I have trusted in him, wathiqtu bihi.
وثل: The letters wāw, thā' and lām, one word. They say: *al-wathīl* — palm fibre, or a rope made from it.
وثم:
The letters wāw, thā' and mīm: a root indicating gathering and collecting. The origin word is *al-wathīma*: the stone. They say: 'he who struck fire out of *al-wathīma*.'

1. Then a bundle of dried grass is also called *wathīma*.
2. One says *thim*, meaning: gather.
3. *Al-wathīm* — compact in flesh.
وثن:
The letters waw, tha' and nun are one word: al-wathan, plural al-awthan — stones that used to be worshipped. Its origin is their saying istawthana ash-shay'u, the thing grew strong.

1. awthana fulanun al-himla — he made the load heavy, increased it.
2. awthantu lahu — I gave to him abundantly.
وج: The letters wāw and jīm are nothing but Wajj — a town of al-Tā'if. And in the hadith: "The last blow that God, exalted, struck was at Wajj" — meaning the campaign against al-Tā'if.
وجب:
The letters wāw, jīm and bā' are a single root pointing to the falling and occurrence of a thing, then it branches out. wajaba al-bay'u wujūban — the sale became binding and took effect. wajaba al-mayyitu — he fell dead, and the slain man is wājib. In the hadith: "fa-idhā wajaba fa-lā tabkiyanna bākiyatun", meaning: when he has fallen [dead], let no wailing woman weep. And God spoke of the sacrificial animals: "fa-idhā wajabat junūbuhā", when their sides have fallen. Qays said, in a line of verse:
The Banū 'Awf obeyed a commander who forbade them peace, until he was the first to fall.

1. wajaba al-ḥā'iṭu — the wall fell, wajba.
2. al-wajība — to make a sale binding by taking part of the price on it each day, so that when he has finished it is said he has "claimed his wajība" in full.
3. al-wajb — the coward, they say. [A poet] said: A seeker-out of enemies, neither weary nor a coward — named so because he is, as it were, one who falls, who gives way.
4. al-muwajjib — a she-camel that cannot move on account of the abundance of her flesh.
5. al-muwajjib among she-camels — also the one in whose udder the beestings has begun to clot.

As for wajīb al-qalb, the throbbing of the heart, that is by the exchange of one letter for another, its origin being al-wajīf, which has already been mentioned.
وجح:
The letters wāw, jīm and ḥā': a word indicating the screening of one thing by another.
1. Anything you shelter behind is a *wijāḥ* or *wajāḥ*.
2. *Al-wijāḥ* — a person, because every person screens what is behind him.
3. From this: *ḥafartu ḥattā awjaḥtu* — I dug until I reached the bedrock; for the bedrock screens and blocks what is beneath it.
وجد:
The letters wāw, jīm and dāl point to one root, and it is the thing one comes upon. And wajadtu al-ḍāllata wijdānan — I found the stray. [And some have reported: wajadtu fī al-ghaḍabi wijdānan — I found, in anger, a finding.]

And he recited:
Each of us turned his companion back in despair, upon rancour and a fierce finding.
وجذ: The letters wāw, jīm and dhāl: a sound word. It is *al-wajdh*, a hollow in a rock, plural *wijādh*. And it has reached us that it is said: *awjadhahu ʿalā l-amr* — he forced him to the matter.
وجر:
The letters wāw, jīm and rā': a word indicating a kind of giving-drink.
1. *Wajartu l-ṣabiyya l-dawā'* and *awjartuhu* — I made the child drink the medicine.
2. They borrow it, saying *awjartuhu l-rumḥa* — when you thrust the spear into his chest.
3. *Al-wijār* — the hyena's den, because she disappears into it as a drink disappears down the throat.
وجز:
The letters wāw, jīm and zā', one word.
1. *Kalāmun wajzun* and *wajīz* — concise speech.
2. Sometimes they say *tawajjaztu l-shay'* — like *tanajjaztu* [I got it done promptly].
وجس:
The letters waw, jim and sin are a word indicating a sensing of something and a listening for it. tawajjasa ash-shay'a — he sensed it and listened for it.

God, Most High, said: {and Musa sensed within himself a fear} [Ta Ha: 67]. Then Dhu ar-Rumma said, in a line of verse: "when he senses..." — the line as given breaks off here.

What departs from this, being obscure speech: their saying "I will never do it, sajisa al-awjas" — meaning: ever, for all time. And "I tasted at his place not a single awjas," meaning: not any food at all.
وجع:
The letters wāw, jīm and ʿayn, one word: it is *al-wajaʿ*, a name covering every sickness.
1. *Huwa yījaʿu* and *yājaʿu*, and *anta tījaʿu min kadhā* — he aches, and you ache from such-and-such. A scout among the scouts said: 'I saw pasture that makes the liver of the herdless man ache [with longing].'
2. *Huwa wajiʿ*, plural *wajāʿā* — in pain.
3. *Anā awjaʿu ra'sī*, and *yūjiʿunī ra'sī* — my head aches me.
4. *Tawajja'tu lahu* — I grieved for him.
5. They say: *al-wajʿā'* is *al-sah* [the backside].
وجم:
The letters wāw, jīm and mīm: it indicates silence out of anxiety.
1. *Wajama min al-amr yakrahuhu* — he fell silent over a matter he disliked. In the hadith: 'What is it, that I see you so silent?'
2. They say *yawmun wajīm* — a day of intense heat, though there is doubt about this. Its verbal noun is *al-wajm* and *al-wujūm*.
وجن:
The letters wāw, jīm and nūn indicate firmness in a thing.

1. *al-wajīn* — a raised strip of ground that runs on evenly, and is firm; by this the she-camel is named *wajnā'*.
2. The human cheekbone, *wajna*, takes its pattern from this, because it has firmness and strength; the plural is *wajanāt*.
3. Sometimes they called the bank of a valley *wajīn* too.
4. *wajana* his garment — he beat it with the *mījana*, the piece of wood used to beat it.
وجه:
The letters wāw, jīm and hā' are a single root pointing to facing something. And the wajh, the face, is what faces you of everything. One says a man's wajh and that of other things. And sometimes the self is expressed by the face. [And] you say wajhī ilayka — my face is toward you. He said, in a line of verse:
I ask God's forgiveness for a sin I cannot count, Lord of servants; to Him is the face and the deed.
And wājahtu fulānan — I set my face opposite his face.

And of this chapter is their saying: he is wajīh, of plain jāh, standing. And al-jāh is the word turned about. And al-wijha is every place you face. God, exalted be He, said: {And for each there is a direction he faces} [al-Baqara: 148]. And wajjahtu al-shay' — I set it on a direction; and the origin of jiha is wijha. And al-tawjīh is that you dig under a cucumber or a melon and then lay it on its side. And tawajjaha al-shaykh — the old man turned away and went off, as though he had turned his face toward the other side. And of a foal, when its forelegs come out of the womb, one says wajīh.
وجى:
The letters wāw, jīm and the weak letter.

1. *taraktuhu wa-mā fī qalbī minhu awjā* — I left him with nothing of him left in my heart, meaning I despaired of him.
2. *sa'altuhu fa-awjā ʿalayya* — I asked him and he was stingy toward me.
وحد:
The letters wāw, ḥā' and dāl are a single root pointing to being alone. Of that is al-waḥda, aloneness. And he is the one of his tribe, when there is none like him among them. He said, in a line of verse:
O one of the Arabs, who has no equal among mankind.
And laqītu al-qawm mawḥada mawḥada, I met the people one by one. And laqītuhu waḥdahu, I met him alone. And it is not put in construct except in their sayings nasīju waḥdihi, and ʿuyayru waḥdihi, and juḥayshu waḥdihi, and nasīju waḥdihi — that is, no other is woven like it, for its excellence; and it is a proverb. And al-wāḥid is the one alone. And ʿUbayd's words, in a line of verse:
By God, had I died it would not have harmed me, and I am not, if I live, in a single thing —
he means: I am not, if I live, in one state that lasts, because everything must come to an end.
وحر: The letters wāw, ḥā and rā' are a single word: it is *al-waḥara* — a small creature like a gecko; when it creeps over meat, the meat becomes *waḥir* [tainted]. Then rancour in the chest was likened to this, so one says *waḥira ṣadruhu* — his chest held rancour. And in the hadith: "the rancour of his chest goes away."
وحش:
The letters wāw, ḥā' and shīn are a word that indicates the opposite of al-uns — human company, familiarity.

1. tawaḥḥasha — he parted from human company.
2. al-waḥsh — the opposite of al-uns; the wild, that which is untamed.
3. arḍun mūḥisha, a desolate land — [named] from al-waḥsh.
4. waḥshī l-qaws — the back of the bow; its insī side is the side that faces you.
5. waḥshī l-dābba, in al-Aṣma'ī's account — the side of a riding animal from which the rider mounts and the milker milks.

He said: this is why they say 'so it swerved on its waḥshī side' and 'its waḥshī side turned away' — because the animal is approached in riding, milking, and handling only from that side, so its fear is from that side alone; al-insī is the other side.

6. laqītu fulānan bi-waḥshi iṣmit — I met so-and-so in an empty, desolate land.
7. waḥasha bi-thawbihi — he threw his garment away.
8. bāta l-waḥsha — he spent the night hungry, as if he were in a wild land where he found nothing to eat.
وحف:
The letters wāw, ḥā and fā' are a word that indicates blackness in a thing.

1. *shaʿrun waḥf* — black, soft hair.
2. *al-waḥfā'* — land that has black stones in it.
3. *ʿushbun waḥf* — abundant plant growth; when it grows abundant it shows black.

And two words fall outside this pattern:

1. *al-muwaḥḥaf* — they say it of the emaciated camel. A poet said, in a line of verse: When I saw the aged, emaciated she-camel.
2. *al-wāḥif* — the large bucket whose two hanging straps have snapped, so that it now hangs by two [replacement] straps.
وحل:
The letters wāw, ḥā and lām are a single word: it is *al-waḥal*, mud.

1. *istawḥala al-makān* — the place became muddy; mud came to be in it.
2. *al-mawḥil* — the place where there is mud.
3. *waḥilat al-dawābb tawḥal* — the animals fell into the mud.
وحم:
The letters wāw, ḥā and mīm: two words, *al-waḥam* and *al-wiḥām*.

*al-waḥam* is a woman's craving for a thing during pregnancy. A woman is called *waḥmā*, and we say *waḥḥamnāhā* — we satisfied her craving. A poet said, in a line of verse: The days of Laylā, the year of Laylā, are my craving — meaning, my desire, my aim, and my pursuit.

From this same derivation, *waḥamtu waḥmahu* — as if you craved what he craved.

As for *al-wiḥām*: it is said that the female, when she conceives, becomes resistant — so one says *waḥimat*.
وحى:
The letters wāw, ḥā and the weak letter are a root that indicates conveying knowledge to someone else, whether concealed or otherwise.

1. *al-waḥy* — the gesture, the sign.
2. *al-waḥy* — the written text and the message.

And whatever you convey to someone else until he comes to know it is *waḥy*, however it happens. One says *awḥā Allāhu taʿālā* and *waḥā*. A poet said, in a line of verse: It gave her a resting place, and she settled.

Everything in the chapter of *waḥy* goes back to this origin sense we have mentioned.

1. *al-waḥiyy* — the swift.
2. *al-waḥā* — the sound, the voice.

And God knows best.
وخ: The letters wāw and khā' point to mixing and disorder. A man wakhwākh — mixed up, weak. He said, in a line of verse: "I was not, among my people, a man wakhwākh."
وخد: The letters wāw, khā and dāl are a single word. One says *wakhadat al-nāqa takhidu wakhadānan* — the she-camel strode, a wideness of stride.
وخز: The letters wāw, khā and zāy are a single word: it is *al-wakhz* — piercing with a spear or the like, when it does not go all the way through.
وخش:
The letters wāw, khā and shīn are a single word: *al-wakhsh* — the lowly among men, and mixed rabble.

They say *awkhashū al-shay'* — they mixed the thing together.

A poet said, in a line of verse: I cast my arrow among them when they mixed together.

Abū Bakr said: *al-wakhsh* is the inferior of anything.
وخض: The letters wāw, khā and ḍād are a word: it is piercing that does not go through. One says *wakhaḍahu bi-l-rumḥ* — he pierced him with the spear, without it passing through.
وخط:
The letters wāw, khā and ṭā' are two words:

1. *wakhaṭa al-shayb fī ra'sihi* — grey hair showed through his head.
2. *al-wakhṭ* — piercing. *wakhaṭahu bi-l-sayf* — he struck at him with the sword, reaching him from a distance.

And they mentioned a third word:

3. *marra yakhiṭu* — he passed by, walking at more than a brisk pace.
وخف: The letters wāw, khā and fā' are a word: it is *al-wakhīf* — your beating of the *khiṭmī* [a mucilaginous mallow plant] in the basin; you beat it, *tūkhifuhu*, so that it blends.
وخم:
The letters wāw, khā and mīm are a single word: *al-wakhim* — the noxious, unwholesome of a thing.

1. *istawkhamtu al-bilād* — I found the land unwholesome; unwholesome lands, *wakhima* and *wakhīma*, do not suit those who live in them.
2. *rajulun wakhim* and *wakhīm* — a heavy, burdensome man.
3. *al-tukhma* [indigestion] comes from this; its *tā'* was originally a *wāw*.
وخى: The letters wāw, khā and the weak letter are a word that indicates travelling with a set course and a destination. One says *wakhat al-nāqa takhī wakhyan* — the she-camel strode toward its course. A poet said, in a line of verse: They follow the course of a tall, towering [she-camel]. And this is so-and-so's *wakhy*, meaning his direction. And I do not know where he *wakhā*, meaning where he headed.
ود:
The letters wāw and dāl are a word pointing to love.

1. wadidtuhu — I loved him.
2. wadidtu anna dhāka kāna — I wished that were so, said when you long for a thing; awuddu is used for both.

In love the noun is al-wudd; in wishing it is al-wadāda. And huwa wadīdu fulānin — meaning: he loves him.

As for al-wadd: it is al-watid, a peg — that has already been mentioned.
ودج:
The letters wāw, dāl and jīm are a single word: *al-wadajān* — the two veins in the two sides of the neck. Then this was used as a likeness, and two brothers were called *wadajān*. A poet said, in a line of verse: disgraced were you both, as arriving envoys chosen to come — and as the two veins of a barren war that flares.

*wadajtu bayna al-qawm* — I made peace between the people; taken from the two veins, as if they came into agreement the way the two veins agree.
ودس:
The letters wāw, dāl and sīn are two words.

1. *al-wadīs* — vegetation, plant growth. One says *awdasat al-arḍ* — the land put forth its plants.
2. *wadasa al-shay'* — he hid the thing. And *mā adrī ayna wadasa* — I do not know where he went, meaning where he disappeared to.
ودص: The letters wāw, dāl and ṣād. They say: *wadaṣa ilayya bi-kalām* — he tossed out a word to me without finishing it.
ودع:
The letters wāw, dāl, and ʿayn are a single root indicating leaving and letting be.

1. wadaʿahu — he left it; from it comes daʿ, 'leave [it]!'

A poet recited, in a line of verse:
I wish I knew about my friend — what was it that ruined him in love, until he gave it up.

2. waddaʿtuhu tawdīʿan — I bade him farewell.
3. al-daʿa — ease, as if a state in which whatever wearies one is set aside.
4. rajul muttadiʿ — a man at rest, one who has obtained something calmly, without effort.
5. al-wadīʿ — the still, calm man.
6. al-muwādaʿa — making peace, a mutual leaving-off of hostility.
7. waddaʿtu al-thawba fī ṣiwānihi — I put the garment away in its storage-wrap; such a garment [or wrap] is a mīdaʿ.
ودف:
The letters wāw, dāl and fā'. They say:

1. *al-wadfa* — the green meadow.
2. *wadafa al-shaḥm* — the fat melted and flowed.
ودق:
The letters wāw, dāl and qāf are a word indicating drawing near and growing at ease with someone.

1. wadaqtu bihi, wadqan — I grew close to and at ease with him.
2. al-mawdiq — the approach; the place where you stand at ease.
3. mawdiq al-ẓaby — the place a gazelle stands when it reaches up to browse a tree.

From this comes the line:
She brushes away [the tracks] with the hem of her wrap, when I come to my place of approach.

4. atān wadīq — a she-donkey is "wadīq" when she wants the male; she has widāq, as though she grows familiar toward him and draws him to familiarity with her.
5. al-wadq — rain, because it "yadiqqu": it comes down from the sky.

What falls outside the root: al-wadaq — red spots that come out in the eye; one is a wadaqa.
ودك:
The letters wāw, dāl and kāf are a single word: *al-wadak* [rendered fat], well known.

1. *dajājatun wadīka* — a fat hen.
2. *rajulun wādik* — a man who has fat on him.
ودن:
The letters wāw, dāl and nūn hold three words that follow no single pattern.

1. *al-wadn* — good attendance given to a bride. One says *akhadhū fī widānihi* — they set about attending to her.
2. *al-mūdan* and *al-mawdūn* — said of someone short and stunted in build. A poet said, in a line of verse: Your mother is black and stunted, as if her fingertips were beetles.
3. *wadantu al-shay'* — I moistened the thing; the command form of it is *din*. And *ittadana* — it became moist.
وده: The letters wāw, dāl and hā' are a single word. *istawdahati al-ibil* and *istaydahat* — the camels moved along in a line, when they gathered and fell into single file. Abū Bakr said: *wadahanī ʿan hādhā* — he turned me away from it.
ودى:
The letters wāw, dāl and the weak letter hold three words that follow no single pattern.

1. *wadā al-faras li-yaḍriba aw yabūla* — the stallion let itself down, to mount or to urinate. From this, *al-wady* — a fluid that comes from a person, like *al-madhy* [a discharge that precedes semen].
2. *wadaytu al-rajula adīhi diyatan* — I paid blood-money for the man.
3. *al-wadiyy* — small palm shoots.

And when it takes a hamza, the meaning changes and shifts to the territory of ruin and loss.

1. *al-muwadda'a* — the place of destruction, in the form of a passive participle.
2. *waddaʾtu ʿalayhi al-arḍ* — I buried the earth over him, meaning I buried him.
3. *wadda'a bi-l-qawm* — he brought the people to ruin.
وذح: The letters wāw, dhāl and ḥā' are a word: *al-wadhaḥ* — what clings to the wool of sheep, of dung. Then a woman is called *wadhāḥ* — unchaste.
وذر:
The letters wāw, dhāl and rā' are two words. One of them is al-wadhara, and it is a lump of meat. And al-tawdhīr is that a wound be scored; one says wadhdhartuhu — I scored it. And in the hadith, that a man said to another: "O son of the woman who sniffs at bits of meat", and he was flogged for it, as though he had made an indecent allusion to her with the parts of men.

And the other is their saying dhar dhā — leave this. The people of the language said: the Arabs killed off the past-tense verb from wadhara, so they do not say wadhartuhu.
وذف: The letters wāw, dhāl and fā' are a single word: *al-tawadhdhuf* — swaggering, strutting. One says *aqbala yatawadhdhafu* — he came forward, swaggering.
وذل:
The letters wāw, dhāl and lām are two words.

1. *al-wadhīla* — well known: it is the mirror.
2. *al-wadhāla* — what the butcher trims from the meat without formal division. One says *tawadhdhalū minhu shay'an* — they each took a scrap of it.
وذم:
The letters wāw, dhāl and mīm are a word that indicates hanging one thing from another.

1. From this comes their saying *waddhamtu al-kalb* — I put a collar on the dog.
2. *al-wadhama* — the piece that hangs from the tripe [the rumen]; the plural is *widhām*.
3. *al-wadham* — the plural of *wadhama* in another sense: the straps tied to the crosspiece of the well-bucket. One says *wadhimat al-dalw* — the bucket's strap snapped.
4. As for *wadhā'im al-amwāl* [pledged property], these are properties over which vows have been made; the reasoning is the same throughout — as if this property is not part of the free wealth a person may dispose of as he likes, but is instead something hung upon the wealth.
5. It is also said that *al-wadhīma* is the offering-animal given for the pilgrimage rite.
6. Their saying *waddhama fulānun ʿalā al-mi'a* — so-and-so added to the hundred — comes from this too, as if the addition were hung upon the hundred.
ورب:
The letters wāw, rā' and bā' are two words.

1. *al-warib* — weakness, slackness.
2. *al-warab* — corruption, decay. One says *ʿirq warib*, meaning a decayed vein.
ورث:
The letters wāw, rā' and thā' are one word, and it is al-wirth, inheritance. And al-mīrāth has wāw for its root. And it is that a thing belongs to a people and then passes to others by kinship or by some cause. A poet said, in a line of verse:
We inherited them from true-born fathers, and we shall pass them on, when we die, to sons.
ورخ:
The letters wāw, rā' and khā' are a single word.

1. *warikha al-ʿajīnu warakhan* — the dough went slack. *awrakhtuhu īrākhan* — I made it slack; the noun for this is *al-warīkha*.

As for *tawrīkh al-kitāb* and *ta'rīkhuhu* — dating a document — we do not consider these to be [genuine] Arabic.
ورد:
The letters wāw, rā' and dāl are two roots: one of them is coming up to a thing, and the second is one of the colours.

The first is *al-wird*, the going down to water, the opposite of *al-ṣadar*, the coming back from it. One says *waradat al-ibil al-mā'a tariduhu wirdan* — the camels came down to the water. And *al-wird* is the onset of a fever when it takes hold of its man at a set time. *Al-mawārid* are the roads, and so too the waters that are come down to, and the villages — Abū ʿUbayda said this. Jarīr said, in a line of verse:
The Commander of the Faithful is on a road that stays straight when the ways to water run crooked.

*Al-warīdān* are two thick veins running down the two sides of the neck, toward the front of it. They too are named from *al-wurūd*, the coming up, as though the two of them came up to meet in that place.

The other root is *al-ward*, the rose. One says *faras ward* and *asad ward*, when its colour is the colour of the rose. And God knows best what is right.
ورس:
The letters wāw, rā' and sīn are a single word: *al-wars* — a plant.

1. *awrasa al-makān* — the place grew *wars*; it is called *wārisun*, an unusual, irregular form.
2. *milḥafatun warīsun* — a cloak dyed with *wars*.
ورش:
The letters wāw, rā' and shīn are two words, close in their reasoning.

1. *al-wārish* — their term for one who joins people at their food without being invited.
2. *al-warisha* — their term for a mount that breaks loose while running, while its rider tries to hold it in.
ورط: The letters wāw, rā' and ṭā' are a word that indicates something like calamity, falling into what has no way out. One says *tawarraṭa fī al-baliyya* — he fell into the affliction. Its origin is *al-waraṭa* of the land, which is land with no path through it. Al-Khalīl said, regarding the hadith "no *khilāṭ* and no *wirāṭ*": *al-wirāṭ* is deception involving livestock — that is, combining what is separate, or separating what is combined.
ورع:
The letters wāw, rā' and ʿayn are a sound root indicating holding back and drawing in.

1. *al-waraʿ* — scrupulousness: holding oneself back from what is not proper. A man who does this is called *wariʿ*.
2. *al-waraʿ* — (also) the cowardly man. One says *waruʿa yawruʿu wurʿan*, "he was cowardly."
3. *warraʿtuhu* / *awraʿtuhu* — I held him back, restrained him. In the hadith: "Restrain the thief, and do not wait for him" — meaning, hasten to hold him back and check him, and do not wait for him.
4. *warraʿtu al-ibila ʿan al-mā'* — I turned the camels back from the water.
5. *al-warīʿa* — the name of a horse, in the saying:

A poet said, in a line of verse:
"And return our friend with a gift given in good faith … and give him after it al-Warīʿa from his due share."
ورف:
The letters wāw, rā' and fā' are a root indicating tenderness and freshness.

1. *nabāt wārif* — a lush, flourishing plant. One says *warafa warīfan* when you see in it, from its being well-watered, a fresh radiance.
2. *ẓill wārif* — an extended, spreading shade.
3. *al-warf* — the thin part at the edges of the liver.
4. *al-rufa* — said to mean straw.

I think the letter missing from the start of this word is a wāw.
ورق:
The letters wāw, rā', and qāf are two roots. One indicates good and wealth, its origin being the leaves of a tree; the other indicates a colour.

The first:
1. al-waraq — the leaves of a tree.
2. al-waraq — also wealth, by the same analogy: when a tree's leaves fall away it is left bare, like a poor man.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
To You I call, so accept my pleading — forgive my sins, and make my wealth grow.

3. al-riqa — silver coin; the same word, distinguished from al-waraq only by its vowelling.

Abū ʿUbayd said: al-wāriqa is a tree green and fine of leaf. He said: al-warāq, however, is the greenness of the ground from grass, and is not from al-waraq [leaves].

A poet said, in a line of verse:
As if their fine horses on the ridge of Zumm were locusts, and the green herbage had yielded itself to them.

4. waraqtu al-shajar — I stripped the tree of its leaves.
5. awraqa al-ṣāʾid — the hunter caught nothing; also from al-waraq, because a hunter sets his snare, stays away from it, then returns after a time to find the ground grown green and leaves fallen over the snare so he cannot find it — hence 'awraqa,' he found leaves covering his snare. The usage then spread until it was said of anyone who sought something and failed to get it.
6. al-warqa (with no vowel on the rā') — a hidden knot in a branch.
7. al-waraqa — a clot of blood, plural waraq, likened to leaves that fall.
8. al-waraq — also weak men, likened in their weakness to the leaves of a tree.

The other root:
1. al-wurqa — a colour resembling ash.
2. baʿīr awraq, ḥamāma warqāʾ — a camel and a dove named for this colour; a man too may be called awraq.
3. ʿām awraq — a drought year, as if the colour of the earth were the colour of ash — this is why 'the Year of Ashes' was so named.
ورك:
The letters wāw, rā' and kāf are a single word: *al-warik* — what lies above the thigh, at the back of a person; the hip.

1. *jalasa mutawarrikan* — he sat pressing his hip to the ground.
2. *tawarraka ʿalā al-dābba* — he sat sideways on the mount, hip to one side, in that same sense.
3. *naʿl mawrika* — a sandal made from the hide of the hindquarters.
4. *al-wirāk* — a cloth woven on its own and used as an ornament, wrapped around the saddle; it is so named because the hip rests on it.

As for the hadith that he forbade a man to prostrate "mutawarrikan," it is said this means raising the hip in prostration until it becomes unseemly. It is also said it means pressing the hip to the heels in prostration.

5. *al-wark* — in a line of verse by the poet of Hudhayl:
"It has a taut bowstring, not slack in its strands … when drawn it hums, with a twisted wark."
He means: it is a bowstring twisted from [the sinew of] the hip.
ورل: The letters wāw, rā' and lām: there is nothing here but *waral*, which is a kind of creature among the animals.
ورم:
The letters wāw, rā' and mīm are a single word: *al-waram* — for the flesh to swell up. One says *warima yarimu*.

1. By way of metaphor: *warima anfuhu* — "his nose swelled" — meaning he became angry.
وره:
The letters wāw, rā' and hā' are a word indicating agitation and foolish clumsiness.

1. *al-warhā'* — the foolish woman.
2. *al-warah* — clumsiness/recklessness; and *rīḥ warhā'* — a wind that, in its blowing, has roughness and violence.
3. *saḥāb warih* — a cloud that does not hold back its water.
4. *al-warih* — some also say it means tender, soft flesh; if that is correct, it was named for its being unsteady.
ورى:
The letters wāw, rā' and the weak letter form a pattern not built on regular analogy, and its words stand apart from one another, unrelated.

1. *al-waryu* — a disease that enters the body. One says *wariya jilduhu yarī waryan*, "his skin was struck with warī"; and *warrāhu ghayruhu yariyahu waryan*, "someone else afflicted him with it." The Messenger of God, peace and blessings upon him and his family, said: "For one of you's belly to be filled with pus until it consumes him with warī is better than for it to be filled with poetry."
ʿAbd Banī al-Ḥasḥās said, in a line of verse:
"May my Lord afflict them just as they have afflicted me … and heat the branding-irons over their livers."
2. *warā al-zand yarī waryan*, and *warāhu* — the fire-stick struck fire, its flame came out. Some report *wariya yarī*, like *waliya yalī*.
3. *al-laḥm al-wārī* — fat meat.
4. *al-warā* — mankind, people. "I do not know which of *al-warā* he is," meaning: I do not know who he is.
5. As for their saying *warā'aka*, "behind you" — it can mean from behind, and it can also mean from in front. God Almighty said: {and there was a king before them} [al-Kahf: 79] — meaning, ahead of them.
6. It is also said that *al-warā'* means a grandchild, a child's child; by that they meant to explain the saying of the Almighty: {and beyond Isaac, Jacob} [Hūd: 71].
وز: The letters wāw and zā' are a letter pointing to lightness and speed. A man wazwāz — light, nimble. Abū Bakr said: al-wazwaza is lightness and speed.
وزا:
The letters wāw, zā' and the weak letter, or the hamzated letter, are a slight root indicating a thing's being compact and tightly packed.

1. *wazan* — said of a donkey compact of build, and of a short man. This form is not hamzated.
2. As for the hamzated form, Abū Zayd said: *wazza'tu al-wiʿā'a tawzī'an* and *tawzi'atan* — I packed the container well and tightly.
وزر:
The letters wāw, zāy and rā' are two sound roots: one of them is refuge, and the other is heaviness in a thing.

The first is al-wazar: refuge. God Most High said: {No indeed! There is no refuge} [al-Qiyama: 11]. And al-Shaybānī reported: awzara fulānun al-shay', so-and-so put the thing in safe keeping. [And] al-wizr is a man's load, when he spreads out his garment, puts goods in it and carries it; and for that reason a sin is called a wizr. So too al-wizr is weapons, and the plural is awzār. Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
And I made ready for war its weapons: long spears and stallion horses.
And al-wazīr, the minister, is called by this because he carries the weight for his master.

And some people have reported, and it may be sound, awzartu mālahu: I made away with it. And wazartuhu: I overcame him. A poet said:
Their colts have overcome their full-grown ones.
وزع:
The letters wāw, zā' and ʿayn: a formation not built on a single analogy. "Wazaʿtuhu ʿani l-amr": I held him back from the matter. God said: {and they are held back, kept in order} [al-Naml: 17] — meaning their front ranks are held for their rear ranks to catch up. The plural of al-wāziʿ (the one who holds back) is wazaʿa. And in a saying: "What the ruler restrains is more than what the Qur'an restrains" — meaning people fear the ruler more.

And another formation: it is said "God awzaʿa so-and-so gratitude" — He inspired it in him. It is said of one "he is of those who are ūziʿa with a thing" when he is made devoted to it — as if God, exalted is He, made him devoted to giving Him thanks. And "in it are awzāʿ of people" — groups, scattered bands.
وزغ:
The letters wāw, zā' and ghayn contain nothing but *al-wazagha* — the small lizard, the gecko.

1. Weak men are called *awzāgh*.
وزف: The letters wāw, zā' and fā': one says *wazafa al-rajulu* — the man hastened in his walking. And it is read: "and they came to him, hastening," in the lightened form.
وزم:
The letters wāw, zā' and mīm are also a pattern not built on regular analogy, and it contains separate, individual words.

1. *al-wazma* — for a man to eat a single time, like *al-wajba* (a single meal eaten once a day). One says *wazamū wazmata shitā'ihim* — they laid in provisions of food sufficient for their winter.
2. *al-wazma* and *al-wazīm* — a bundle of greens.
3. *al-wazīm* — meat that is dried.
4. *al-wazma*, of the spiny-tailed lizards — for their meat to be cooked and then dried.
5. *al-mutawazzim* — one who treads heavily, with force.
وزن:
The letters wāw, zāy and nūn: a building that points to setting straight and to uprightness. And wazantu al-shay'a waznan — I weighed the thing. Al-zina is the measure of the weight of a thing; the origin of it is wazna. And one says qāma mīzān al-nahār when the day reached its middle. And this yuwāzinu that — that is, it is level with it. And wazīn al-ra'y is the man of balanced judgement. And he is rājiḥ al-wazn, of weightier scale, when they ascribe to him soundness of judgement and strength of mind.

Of what has strayed from this chapter is a thing related from al-Khalīl: that al-wazīn is colocynth kneaded into a paste, which used to be made into food. And it is said that al-wazn is a lump of dates.
وس:
The letters wāw and sīn are a word pointing to a sound that is not loud.

1. waswās — the sound of jewellery.
2. waswās — the hunter's faint breathing.
3. waswās — the devil's whispered temptation of the son of Adam.

He said, of the hunter: "And he spent the night troubled by damp, and kept awake by the wind shifting to and fro, and the whisper, and the rugged hills."
وسب:
The letters wāw, sīn and bā'.

1. *awsabat al-arḍ* — the land grew vegetation, they say.
2. *al-nabāt wisb* — the plant [in this state] is called *wisb*.
3. *kabsh muwassab* — a ram thick with wool. Abū Bakr related this.
وسج: The letters wāw, sīn and jīm are a single word: *al-wasīj*, which is a fast, vigorous pace.
وسخ: The letters wāw, sīn and khā' are a word. *Al-wasakh*: grime, filth.
وسد:
The letters wāw, sīn and dāl are a single word: *al-wisāda*, well known [the pillow], its plural *wasā'id*.

1. *tawassadtu yadī* — I made my own hand my pillow.
2. *al-wisād* — what a man rests his head on when he sleeps, its plural *wusud*.

And God knows best.
وسط:
The letters wāw, sīn and ṭā': a sound formation indicating fairness and the middle. The most balanced part of a thing is its awsaṭ and wasaṭ. God said: {a middle, balanced nation} [al-Baqara: 143]. They say: "ḍarabtu wasaṭa ra'sihi," with the middle letter vowelled, and "wasṭ al-qawm," with it silent [two pronunciations for two different senses]. "He is their awsaṭ in standing" when he stands at the center of his people, highest of them in rank.

Al-wasūṭ: a tent of hair-cloth, larger than the miẓalla (a smaller shade-tent). And al-wasūṭ, among she-camels, is like al-ṣafūf — one that fills the vessel with milk.
وسع: The letters wāw, sīn and ʿayn are a word pointing to the opposite of narrowness and hardship. One says wasuʿa al-shay' and ittasaʿa - the thing was wide and grew wide. And al-wusʿ is riches. And God is al-Wāsiʿ, that is, the Rich. And al-wusʿ is means and capacity. And he spends according to the measure of his means. And He said, exalted is He, about saʿa, ample means: {Let the man of ample means spend out of his ample means} [al-Ṭalāq: 7]. And awsaʿa al-rajul - the man had ample means. And the horse of long stride is wasāʿ.
وسف:
The letters wāw, sīn and fā' are a single word.

1. *tawassafat al-ibil* — the camels came into good pasture and grew fat, their old hair fell away and new hair grew in.
وسق:
The letters wāw, sīn and qāf are a word indicating the carrying of a thing. wasaqat al-ʿayn al-mā' — the spring carried the water.

God, exalted is He, said: {and by the night, and what it gathers} [al-Inshiqāq: 17] — meaning it gathered and bore.

And he said, of carrying water, in a line of verse:
I, and they, and a longing for them ... am like one clutching water his fingers cannot hold.

1. al-wasq — sixty ṣāʿs [a measure of grain].
2. awsaqtu al-baʿīr — I loaded the camel with its burden.

A line:
And where now is the load of the heavy-laden she-camel?

What falls outside the root: a bird called mīsāq, one that claps its two wings as it flies; it may also be said with a hamza, and we have already mentioned it.
وسل:
The letters wāw, sīn and lām are two entirely distinct words.

The first is desire and seeking. wasala — he desired. al-wāsil is the one who yearns toward God, mighty and exalted, as in the line of Labīd:
Indeed, everyone who holds to a faith yearns toward God.
From this same pattern comes al-wasīla, the means [of drawing near].

The other word is theft: akhadha ibilahu tawassulan — he took his camels by stealth.
وسم:
The letters wāw, sīn and mīm are a single root indicating a trace and a mark that shows something.

1. wasamtu al-shay' wasman — I left a mark on a thing with a brand.
2. al-wasmī — the first [autumn] rain, because it marks the ground with growing plants. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: tawassama — he went seeking the pasture grown from the wasmī rain.

A line:
And they came, at morning, like the soft, swaying doum-palms, heading toward one who travels, seeking [the marked pasture].

3. mawsim al-ḥājj — the pilgrims' set season was named mawsim because it is a fixed landmark that people gather to.
4. fulān mawsūm bi-l-khayr — so-and-so is marked with good.
5. fulāna dhāt mīsam — so-and-so [a woman] "has a mīsam" when she bears the mark of beauty.
6. al-wasāma — beauty.

A line:
The drinking-troughs of ʿIrāk, which the [pilgrim] seasons have worn down.
It is said he meant the people who come for those seasons, and it is also said he meant branded camels.

7. wassama al-nās — the people "wassamū": they attended the [pilgrim] season, as one says "they kept the feast."

God, exalted is He, said: {Indeed in that are signs for those who read the marks} [al-Ḥijr: 75] — meaning those who look closely at the sign that points to the truth.
وسن:
The letters wāw, sīn and nūn are two close meanings.

1. al-wasan — drowsiness, and likewise al-sina.
2. rajulun wasnān — a drowsy man.
3. tawassana l-faḥlu unthāhu — the stallion came to his mate while she slept.

The other word is their saying: leave this matter, let it not be a wasan for you — meaning do not pursue it, and let it not be among your concerns.
وش: The letters wāw and shīn are a single word: al-washwasha — mixing, confusion. And a man washwāsh.
وشب: The letters wāw, shīn and bā' are a word. One says: *awbāsh min al-nās* and *awshāb* — a mixed rabble of people.
وشج:
The letters wāw, shīn and jīm are a word indicating interlacing and intertwining.

1. *washajat al-aghṣān* — the branches interlaced with one another.
2. Anything interlaced is called *wāshij*.
3. *al-washīj*, among reed-canes — what grows from the ground spreading crosswise; perhaps so named because some of it interlaces with the rest.
وشح:
The letters wāw, shīn and ḥā' are a single word: *al-wishāḥ*, a sash.

1. *tawashshaḥa bi-thawbihi* — he draped his garment over one shoulder as though making it his sash; and likewise *ittashaḥa bihi*, the same.
2. *shāh muwashshaḥa* — a ewe with two streaks along her sides.
وشر:
The letters wāw, shīn and rā' are a single word.

1. *al-washr* / *al-tawshīr* — for a woman to file her teeth to a point.
2. *al-mīshār* — the saw, without a hamza, comes from this.
وشز: The letters wāw, shīn and zā' are a single word: *al-washz* — what rises up from the ground, like *al-nashz* [a hillock]. Then, by analogy with it, hardships and difficult matters were called *awshāz*, singular *washz*.
وشظ:
The letters wāw, shīn and ẓā' are a single principle: attaching a thing to something it is not part of.

1. *al-washīẓ* — a small bone that is an addition to the solid, original bone; for this reason, someone who claims kinship with a people he does not truly belong to is called *washīẓ*.
2. *washaẓtu al-fa'sa ashiẓuhā* — I tightened the axe's socket-hole around a piece that was not [originally] part of its handle.

And God knows best what is correct.
وشع:
The letters wāw, shīn and ʿayn are a single root indicating the weaving of a thing, or its decoration, or the like.

1. *al-washīʿa* — a piece of wood around which yarn of various colours is wound; each wound bundle of it is a *washīʿa*.
2. *awshaʿat al-arḍ* — the land's blossoms appeared.
3. *al-washīʿ* — a mat woven from *thumām* [a desert rush].
4. *al-tawshīʿ* — the patterning of cloth.
5. *al-washā'iʿ* — trails/streaks of dust.
6. *washshaʿahu al-shayb* — grey hair streaked through him.

And not from this chapter: *washaʿtu al-jabala* — I climbed the mountain.
وشق:
The letters wāw, shīn and qāf are a single word: *al-washīqa* — meat that is dried. One says *washaqtu* and *ittashaqtu*.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
"When a fat old she-camel is offered up from it, do not give any of it away — jerk it dry and lay it by."

2. *Wāshiq* — the name of a dog.
وشك:
The letters wāw, shīn and kāf are a single word, from [the sense of] speed.

1. *awshaka fulānun khurūjan* — so-and-so hastened to go out, he made haste.
2. *washkāna mā kāna dhālika* — "how quickly that happened," in the sense of "hastily."
3. *amr washīk* — an imminent, swift matter.
4. *awshaka yūshiku* — its conjugation.

I heard Aḥmad ibn Ṭāhir ibn al-Najm say — [I heard Thaʿlab say] — that *awshaka yūshiku* is the only correct form, and no other.

5. Ibn al-Sikkīt said: *wāshaka wishākan* — he hastened his pace, made speed in travelling.
وشل:
The letters wāw, shīn and lām indicate a little water trickling.

1. *al-washal* — a small amount of water, its plural *awshāl*.
2. *jabal wāshil* — a mountain from which water drips.
3. *huwa wāshil al-ḥaẓẓ* — he is "wāshil of fortune," meaning lacking in it.
4. *al-wushūl* — scarcity of benefit, and weakness.
5. *nāqa washūl* — a she-camel whose udder streams, from the abundance of her milk.
وشم:
The letters wāw, shīn and mīm are a single word indicating leaving a mark on a thing to decorate it.

1. *washm al-yad* — tattooing the hand, when it is pricked and marked with ink.
2. *awshamat al-arḍ* — the land's vegetation began to show.
3. *awshama al-barq* — the lightning gave a faint flash.
4. They extend the usage broadly and say: "no *washma* struck us this year," meaning not a drop of rain fell — because the land is marked, as if tattooed, by raindrops.
5. They sometimes say: "there was a *washīma* between me and him," meaning harsh words; this is used only of the words of enmity. This is a figurative use.
6. *awshama* — he looked closely at a thing, as if he were studying its mark, its pattern.
وشى:
The letters wāw, shīn and the weak letter are two roots: one indicates beautifying and decorating a thing, the other, growth and increase.

The first:
1. *washaytu al-thawba ashīhi washyan* — I decorated, patterned the garment.
2. Of one who lies, slanders, and embellishes his speech, they say: "he has *washā*," and he is a *wāshī*, a slanderer.

The other root:
3. *al-mar'a al-wāshiya* — a woman who bears many children; this is said of anything that gives birth.
4. *al-wāshī* — a man with many offspring.
5. *al-washy* — abundance. *washā banū fulānin* — so-and-so's people multiplied.
6. "*mā washat hādhihi al-māshiya ʿindī*" — "this livestock has not *washat* for me," meaning it has not given birth.
وص:
The letters wāw and ṣād are a word pointing to looking out through a slit, or a slit one looks out through.

1. al-waṣwāṣ — the face-veil.
2. waṣwaṣa l-jarw — the puppy opened its eyes.
3. waṣwaṣa fulānun — so-and-so looked with his eyes narrowed small.
4. waṣāwiṣ — the stones of the level, flat ground, called so by comparison, because they gleam like eyes.

He said, in a line of verse: "With hard stones that wear down the waṣāwiṣ."
وصب:
The letters wāw, ṣād and bā' are a word indicating the constancy of something.

1. waṣaba al-shay', wuṣūban — it persisted.
2. waṣaba al-dīn — the debt/duty became binding.
3. mafāza wāṣiba — a stretch of waterless desert, far-reaching, without end.

In the Book of God, exalted is He: {and for them is an unceasing punishment} [al-Ṣāffāt: 9], meaning everlasting.

4. al-waṣab — a persistent, unrelenting illness.
5. rajul waṣib and muwaṣṣab — a man constantly afflicted with such ailments.
وصد:
The letters waw, sad and dal are a root indicating the joining of one thing to another.

1. awsadtu al-bab — I shut the door.
2. al-wasid — plants growing close together at their roots.
3. al-wasid — the courtyard or threshold of a house, because of its being joined to the dwelling.
4. al-musad — that which is shut tight, sealed.

God, Most High, said: {it is closed in upon them} [al-Humaza: 8].
وصر:
The letters wāw, ṣād and rāʾ: a single word.

1. al-waṣīra — a legal document, a deed. Al-Khalīl said this.
2. al-wiṣr — the register that the king writes for one to whom he grants land.

In one of the traditions: "This man bought land from me and took my wiṣr for it, but he neither returns the wiṣr to me nor gives me the price."
وصع: The letters wāw, ṣād and ʿayn: a single word, it is al-waṣʿ, a small bird. And in the hadith: "Isrāfīl humbles himself before God until he becomes like the waṣʿ."
وصف:
The letters wāw, ṣād and fā' are a single root, and it is the setting out of a thing's qualities.

And waṣaftuhu aṣifuhu waṣfan — I described it. Al-ṣifa is the mark that belongs constantly to a thing, just as one says wazantuhu waznan — I weighed it — and al-zina is the measure of the thing. One says ittaṣafa al-shay' fī ʿayn al-nāẓir — the thing was such that it could bear being described in the eye of the beholder.

As for their saying waṣafat al-nāqa wuṣūfan — when she went well in her pace — that is [from their saying] waṣīf for a manservant and waṣīfa for a maidservant. And one says awṣafat al-jāriya, the girl became fit for service, because the two of them are described at the time of sale.
وصل:
The letters wāw, ṣād and lām are a single root pointing to joining a thing to a thing until it hangs upon it. And waṣaltuhu bihi waṣlan — I joined it to it. Al-waṣl is the opposite of cutting off and shunning. Mawṣil al-ba'īr is what lies between the camel's rump and its thigh. Al-wāṣila in the hadith is the woman who joins her hair to other hair, falsely. And one says waṣaltu al-shay' waṣlan, and the thing joined to it is wiṣl, with i on the wāw.

Of this root is al-waṣīla: settled cultivation and fertility, because it joins people one to another, and when drought strikes them they scatter. Al-waṣīla is also the wide land, as though it had been joined together so that it does not break off. As for al-waṣīla among sheep in His words, Most High: {nor a waṣīla, nor a ḥām} [al-Mā'ida: 103] . . .
وصم:
The letters wāw, ṣād and mīm: a sound root indicating breaking and weakness. He found tawṣīm in his body, that is, breaking, listlessness, and laziness.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
When you intend to travel, then set out — and disobey what the weariness of laziness commands you.

1. al-waṣm — a crack that is not fully split apart. One says: the spear-shaft was struck by a waṣm.
2. waṣm — this is carried further, so it is also said of disgrace and fault.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
If Jarm has a waṣm [a disgrace], we have come against Jarm with one more contemptible than Jarm.
وصى:
The letters wāw, ṣād and the weak letter: a root indicating the joining of one thing to another. I "waṣaytu" the thing: I joined it.

1. "waṭiʾnā arḍan wāṣiya" — we trod land that is wāṣiya, meaning its plants are continuous, having filled it entirely.
2. waṣaytu al-layla bi'l-yawm — I joined the night to the day, in some work being done.
3. al-waṣiyya [the bequest] — from this same reasoning, as though it is speech that is yūṣā, that is, joined on.

One says: waṣṣaytuhu tawṣiya, and awṣaytuhu īṣāʾ.
وضأ: The letters wāw, ḍād and hamza: a single word indicating goodness and cleanliness. "Waḍuʾa" the man, "yawḍuʾu"; and she is "waḍīʾa." Al-waḍūʾ is the water used for ablution. Al-wuḍūʾ is your act when you perform ablution, from al-waḍāʾa, which is goodness and cleanliness — as though the one who washes his face has "waḍḍaʾahu," that is, made it fair.
وضح:
The letters wāw, ḍād and ḥāʾ: a single root indicating the appearance and emergence of a thing. "Waḍaḥa" the thing: it became clear.

1. al-mūḍiḥa — among head-wounds, the one that lays bare the whiteness of the bone.
2. istawḍaḥtu — you put your hand over your eyes to look, to see whether you can make something out.
3. waḍaḥ — light; it comes in the hadith: "Fast from waḍaḥ to waḍaḥ," that is, from light to light.
4. al-waḍḍāḥ — a man fair and white in color, and comely.
5. awḍaḥa — a man to whom fair-skinned children were born.
6. "min ayna awḍaḥta" — from where did you "awḍaḥta," that is, from where did your brightness appear, from where did you rise.
7. waḍaḥ al-ṭarīq — the beaten track of the road.
8. al-wāḍiḥa — the teeth that show when one laughs.

He said, in a line of verse:
Every friend I have taken as a friend — may God leave him no wāḍiḥa [no smile to show].

9. al-awḍāḥ — the remnants of jewelry, and of ṣilliyān [a kind of plant].
10. al-awḍāḥ — jewelry of silver.
وضر:
The letters wāw, ḍād and rāʾ: a single word indicating the smearing of one thing with another. Al-waḍar is like grime and grease.

He said:
Ewers to which no greasy residue of butter clung.

Abū ʿUbayda said: the residue of one thing left upon another is called al-waḍar, like the residue of tar left on a camel.
وضع:
The letters wāw, dād and 'ayn: a single root pointing to the lowering [of a thing] and the setting of it down. And wada'tuhu bi'l-ard wad'an, I set it on the ground; and wada'at al-mar'a waladahā, the woman bore her child. [And] wudi'a fī tijāratihi yūda'u: he lost in his trade. And al-wadā'i' are a people moved from one land to another to settle in it.

Al-wadī' is the low man. And a beast tada'u in its going a wad', and that is an easy pace, unlike the raised pace, al-marfū'. A poet said, in a line of verse:
Her raised pace is a marvel, and her easy pace is like the sweep of a noisy rain-burst in the middle of a wind.
From it one says: she is indeed fine in her easy pace. And her rider has awda'ahā, put her to it. And wada'a al-rajul: the man went at that pace. And it has been mentioned that [al-wādi'āt] are the camels that eat the khalla, the sweet pasture. And they recited:
My companion saw among the wādi'āt a fine she-camel, and others like her among those that go out at morning and plunge onward.
And the man who is muwadda' is the one whose affair is not firmly settled.
وضم:
The letters wāw, ḍād and mīm: a single word, it is al-waḍam, anything of wood or stone that meat is placed upon. I "waḍamtu" the meat: I made a waḍam for it. I "awḍamtuhu": I put it on the waḍam.

1. istawḍamtu al-rajul — I subdued the man, that is, I made him submit to me and put him beneath me like the waḍam.
2. tawaḍḍama al-rajul al-marʾa — the man had intercourse with the woman.
3. al-waḍīma — a group of people, few in number, who come and settle among another people, and that people treats them well.
وط: The letters wāw and ṭā' are a single word: al-waṭwāṭ — the swallow; the coward too is named waṭwāṭ from this. Abū Bakr said: al-waṭwaṭa is weakness.
وطأ:
The letters wāw, ṭā' and hamza are a word indicating smoothing something out and making it easy.

1. waṭṭa'tu lahu al-makān — I made the place smooth and ready for him.
2. al-wiṭā' — the bedding one lays down to lie on.
3. waṭi'tuhu bi-rijlī aṭa'uhu — I trod on it with my foot.

In the hadith: "Make your grip [waṭ'a] harsh upon Muḍar." Al-muwāṭa'a is agreement upon a matter, which each party makes smooth for the other.
وطب:
The letters wāw, ṭāʾ and bāʾ: a single word, it is waṭb al-laban, the skin that milk is kept in.

1. waṭbāʾ — said, by comparison to it, of a woman with large breasts.
2. al-waṭb — a coarse, rough man; this too is by comparison.
وطح:
The letters wāw, ṭāʾ and ḥāʾ: a word indicating crowding and taking turns.

1. tawāṭaḥa ʿalā al-māʾ wirdun kathīr — many came crowding at the water, that is, they pressed in together.
2. tawāṭaḥū ʿalā al-shayʾ — they took turns over the thing.
3. al-waṭaḥ — what clings to hooves and to the talons of birds, of mud and dirt.
وطد:
The letters wāw, ṭāʾ and dāl: a single root, and it is that you fix a thing firm by treading it until it hardens. I "waṭadtuhu, aṭiduhu" to the ground — in the sense of a metaphor, when he has humiliated someone.

1. al-mīṭada — a piece of wood with which a place is tamped down until it hardens.
2. al-waṭāʾid — the three stones a cooking pot stands on over the fire.

Al-Ṭādī appears in a line of verse by al-Qaṭāmī, in his saying:
The remainder of her debt drew to its close, al-ṭādī.
This is al-wāṭid, with the letters turned about [a metathesis].

3. "ʿādatuhu ṭādiya" — his custom is ṭādiya, meaning old, longstanding.
وطر: The letters wāw, ṭā' and rā' are a single word: al-waṭar — a need or a want. No verb is formed from it.
وطس:
The letters wāw, ṭāʾ and sīn: a single word indicating the treading of a thing until it gives way.

1. waṭastu al-arḍa bi-rijlī, aṭisuhā waṭsan — I trod the ground with my foot, that is, I made a hollow, a dent, in it.
2. al-waṭīs — the earth-oven, from this, because it is like a hollow in the ground; and it is used to speak of a severe, dire matter.
وطش:
The letters wāw, ṭāʾ and shīn: two words, if they are sound.

1. waṭasha — they beat him and he did not waṭash against them, that is, he did not defend himself.
2. "waṭṭish lī shayʾan adhkuruhu" — prompt me toward something I may mention; its meaning is "open [the way to it]."
وطف:
The letters wāw, ṭāʾ and fāʾ: a sound root indicating length and slackness in a thing.

1. al-waṭf — length and drooping of the eyelashes.
2. al-waṭf — the pouring down of heavy rain.
3. al-awṭaf — a camel short in the hair of the ears and eyes.

This means only that its waṭaf does not reach the point of being azabb [shaggy-eared], for every azabb animal is skittish; this is a lesser degree than azabb — otherwise its hair is complete. And it is used as a metaphor.

4. "huwa fī ʿaysh awṭaf" — he is in an awṭaf life, that is, one that is wide and easy.
وطن:
The letters wāw, ṭā' and nūn are a sound word.

1. al-waṭan — a person's dwelling place.
2. awṭān al-ghanam — the sheep's resting places.
3. awṭantu l-arḍa — I took the land as a homeland.
4. al-mīṭān — the finish line, the goal [of a race].
وظب:
The letters wāw, ẓāʾ and bāʾ: a word indicating constancy.

1. waẓaba, yaẓibu, waẓban — he persevered.
2. wāẓabtu ʿalā al-shayʾ, muwāẓaba — I kept constantly at the thing; muwāẓaba is constancy.
3. arḍ mawẓūba — thoroughly grazed land: the grazing animals took up all its grazing; this follows the same reasoning already given.

And God knows best what is correct.
وظف:
The letters wāw, ẓāʾ and fāʾ: a word indicating the fixing of an allotted amount of a thing. One says: "waẓẓaftu lahu," when you allot him, at every set time, something of provision or food.

1. al-waẓīf — then this was borrowed for the bone of the shank, as though it were an allotted thing; it is what lies above the pastern of an animal's leg, up to the shank.
2. waẓaftu al-baʿīr — I shortened the hobble for the camel.
3. "marra yaẓifuhum" — he passed by, following close on them, as though he set his shank against their shanks.
وع:
The letters wāw and ʿayn are a word pointing to a sound.

1. waʿwaʿa l-dhi'b — the wolf howled; and by comparison, the sharp, clever man is called waʿwaʿī.
2. al-waʿwāʿ — any mixed, confused sound.

He said, in a line of verse: "And the people fell into an uproar because of him."
وعب:
The letters wāw, ʿayn and bāʾ: a word indicating the taking-up of a thing in full.

1. awʿabtu al-shayʾ — I took the thing up entirely, used the whole of it.
2. "istūʿiba jadʿuhu" — of the nose: if its severing is complete, the full blood-money is due, that is, it was cut off root and branch, nothing of it left.
3. "jāʾa fulānun muʿiban" — so-and-so came, having gathered all he was able to gather.
4. "atā al-farasu bi-rakḍin waʿībin" — the horse came at a waʿīb gallop, that is, it gave the utmost it had.
وعث:
The letters wāw, ʿayn and thāʾ: a word indicating ease and softness in a thing. A place may be "awʿath."

1. al-waʿth — of sand: that in which the feet sink and disappear. Al-Khalīl said this.
2. waʿtha — a fleshy, plump woman.
3. "waʿitha lisānuhu" — his tongue became thick and tangled so that it was not clear, as though it had gone slack and soft.

If it is asked: then how is it said, "I seek refuge in You from the waʿthāʾ of travel," when you have claimed that this indicates ease? It is said: the sense we have given is sound; it is only that sand in which the feet sink calls for hardship, and that is why it is said, "we seek refuge in You from the waʿthāʾ of travel." Both senses are sound.
وعد:
The letters wāw, ʿayn and dāl: a sound word pointing to the holding out of a hope by speech. One says waʿadtuhu aʿiduhu waʿdan — I promised him. And that may be with good or with evil. As for al-waʿīd, threatening, it is only with evil. They say awʿadtuhu bi-kadhā — I threatened him with such a thing.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
He threatened me with prison and with black iron fetters.
. . . .

Al-muwāʿada, making an appointment, is from al-mīʿād, the appointed time. Al-ʿida is a promise, and its plural is ʿidāt; al-waʿd has no plural. And the waʿīd of a stallion is [his roaring] when he means to charge.

A poet said:
It threatens the heart of the unarmed man.

And the land of the sons of so-and-so is wāʿida, promising, when good is hoped of it by way of rain and green growth. And yawmun wāʿid: a day whose beginning promises heat or cold.
وعر:
The letters wāw, ʿayn and rāʾ: a word indicating hardness and roughness.

1. makān waʿr, bayyin al-wuʿūra — a place clearly rugged; one says waʿira, yawʿuru, tawaʿʿara.
2. "fulān waʿr al-maʿrūf" — so-and-so is waʿr in kindness, meaning grudging, stingy with it.
3. "tawaʿʿara ʿalaynā" — we asked him for a favor and he was harsh and difficult with us.
وعز: The letters wāw, ʿayn and zāʾ: a single word about going ahead of someone in a matter. One says: "waʿaztu ilayhi": I went ahead of him in the matter; and "awʿaztu" likewise — that is when you go ahead of him and instruct him in it.
وعس:
The letters wāw, ʿayn and sīn: a root indicating ease and softness in a thing.

1. al-waʿsāʾ — soft ground, having sand in it.
2. al-mīʿās — ground that has not been trodden.
3. al-muwāʿasa — an easy manner of the camels' traveling. One says: "wāʿasnā laylatanā hādhihi": we journeyed through this night of ours. Al-muwāʿasa occurs only at night.
وعظ: The letters wāw, 'ayn and zā': a single word. Al-wa'z is warning by making one afraid. And al-'iza is the noun from it. Al-Khalīl said: it is the reminding of the good, and of that for which a man's heart softens.
وعق:
The letters wāw, ʿayn and qāf: two words.

1. al-waʿīq — a sound that comes out of an animal's sheath.
2. al-waʿqa, and likewise al-waʿq — a man of bad character.
وعك:
The letters wāw, ʿayn and kāf indicate the rubbing and wearing-down of a thing.

1. waʿk al-ḥummā — the malaise of fever, as though it wears the body down by rubbing it.
2. "awʿakat al-kilāb al-ṣayd" — the dogs rolled the game in the dust.
3. al-waʿka — the battleground of the champions.
4. "awʿakat al-ibil" — the camels crowded together; this follows the same reasoning.
وعل:
The letters wāw, ʿayn and lām: two words.

1. al-waʿl — the male of the ibex [al-arwā]. By comparison to it, great men are called wuʿūl. In the hadith: "the lowly (al-tuḥūt) rise while the eminent (al-wuʿūl) depart." Al-tuḥūt means the base, and al-wuʿūl means the noble.
2. "lā waʿl ʿanhu" — the second word: their saying, meaning there is no refuge from it.
وعن:
The letters wāw, ʿayn and nūn are not a root, but they say:

1. al-waʿna — white land.
2. "tawaʿʿanat al-ibil" — fattening began to take hold in the camels.
وعي:
The letters wāw, ʿayn and yāʾ are a word pointing to the holding of a thing together. Waʿaytu al-ʿilm, aʿīhi, waʿyan, I retained the knowledge. Awʿaytu al-matāʿ fī al-wiʿāʾ, ūʿiʿhi, I packed the goods into the container. A poet said, in a line of verse:

and evil is the worst thing you can pack away as provision

As for al-waʿā, it is clamour and noise; in our view this belongs to letter-substitution, its true root being with a ghayn. Al-waʿiyya is the wailing woman, from al-waʿā. They say: 'there is no waʿy about such-and-such.'
وغا:
The letters wāw, ghayn and the weak letter. The sound part of it is al-waghā: clamor and the din of voices.

And a word of which it is said: al-awāghī are the breach-channels of the irrigation beds in cultivated fields.
وغب:
The letters wāw, ghayn and bā' are a word indicating falling and weakness.

1. al-wagb — the cowardly man.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
Not among the troop of the ill-fed is a coward.

2. al-awgāb — the household's discarded odds and ends, like the bowl and the cooking-pot and the like.
وغد:
The letters wāw, ghayn and dāl are a word indicating lowliness. A man is called waghd, meaning the lowly one, from the saying waghadtuhum aghiduhum, meaning I served them. The origin is: al-waghd is a gambling-arrow that has no share.

Among what falls outside this is their saying: al-muwāghada in travel is travel that is not hard or fast.
وغر:
The letters wāw, ghayn and rā' are a word indicating heat, which is then used metaphorically.

1. al-waghra — intense heat.
2. al-waghīr — meat roasted on the hot sand.
3. "wughira ṣadruhu yawghar" — he grew enraged; this follows the same pattern as what we have mentioned.
4. al-īghār — heating stones and then throwing them into water to warm it.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
I knew their place and so I hated them, as the pig hates al-īghār.

5. al-īghār — [also] for the king to grant a man land: he makes it his without land-tax.

And God knows best what is correct.
وغف:
The letters wāw, ghayn and fāʾ: three words.

1. al-waghf — speed in running; also called al-īghāf; one says awghafa, yūghifu.
2. al-waghf — the second word: weakness of eyesight.
3. al-waghf — the third word: a piece of leather tied over a billy-goat's belly, so that it cannot mate.
وغق: The letters wāw, ghayn and qāf. They say: al-waghīq is like al-waʿīq [the sound that comes from an animal's sheath].
وغل:
The letters wāw, ghayn and lām: a word indicating a headlong plunging in travel and the like.

1. awghala al-qawm — the people went deep, far into their journey.
2. al-wāghil — from this same plunging-in: one who comes in upon a people who are drinking, uninvited; that drink [taken uninvited] is called al-waghl.

He said, in a line of verse:
So today let me drink, laden with neither sin from God, nor [the shame of being] a wāghil.

3. "waghala, yaghilu" — he hid himself among the trees.
4. al-waghl — a man good for nothing, as though he is hidden away.
5. al-waghl — one poorly fed, poorly nourished.
وغم:
The letters wāw, ghayn and mīm: a single word, it is al-waghm, rage in the chest, and rancor.

He said, in a line of verse:
He stands over the waghm among his people — forgiving if he wishes, or taking revenge.

As for their saying "waghama bi'l-khabar" [he murmured the news], its origin is naghama [to hum, to intone].
وفد:
The letters wāw, fā' and dāl are a sound root that indicates rising up and coming into prominence.

1. al-wāfid — from it, the people who present themselves [as a delegation]; al-wafd — a delegation.
2. al-wafd — the crest of a ridge of sand that rises up.
3. al-wāfid, of camels — the one that outpaces the rest.
4. al-īfād — hastening.
5. al-wāfidān — two bones that project from the cheeks during chewing. When a man grows old, his wāfid sinks in.

Al-A'shā said, in a line of verse:
She saw a man whose wāfid-bones were sunken, of altered color, dim-sighted, blind.

6. awfada 'alā l-shay', and awfā — he rose above the thing, overlooking it.
وفر:
The letters wāw, fā' and rā' are a word that indicates abundance and completeness.

1. wafara l-shay'u yafiru, and it is mawfūr — the thing was abundant; wafarahu llāhu — God made it abundant.
2. wafrat al-sha'r — hair grown to less than a full jumma [shoulder-length mass].
3. al-wafr — wealth; its name is derived from this.

He said, in a line of verse:
I wished, from my love for Buthayna, that we were on a raft in al-Sharm, having no wealth at all.

4. al-wafrā' — a large waterskin whose leather has not been reduced by anything cut from it.
وفز:
The letters wāw, fā' and zā' are a word indicating haste and lack of settledness.

1. "anā ʿalā wafzin wa-awfāz" — I am in haste. Al-Shaybānī said: one says "huwa ʿalā awfāz", he is in a hurry, but no singular form of it is used.
2. al-wafaz — a raised patch of ground.
3. "jalasa mustawfizan" — he sat mustawfiz, poised as though not settled.
وفض:
The letters wāw, fā' and ḍād are three distinct words.

The first: awfaḍa īfāḍan — he hastened. One says jā'a 'alā wafḍin wa awfāḍin, meaning in haste.

The second: al-awfāḍ — scattered groups of people.

The third: al-wafḍa — the quiver; its plural is wifāḍ.
وفع:
The letters wāw, fā' and ʿayn. They say:

1. al-wafʿa — a rag in which fire is kindled.
2. al-wafīʿa — like a basket, made from palm-branch stalks.
3. al-wafʿa — [also] the stopper of a small glass bottle.
وفق:
The letters wāw, fā', and qāf are a word indicating the matching of two things.

1. al-wafq — agreement.
2. ittafaqa al-shayʾān — the two things drew close and came to match.
3. wāfaqtu fulānan — I befriended him, as if the two of us came together in accord.
وفل:
The letters wāw, fā' and lām are a word indicating hair and roughness. A waterskin is tanned until its wafl goes away, that is, what hair and roughness were on it. Al-wafl [also names] what sheds from a hide's hair.

And God knows best what is correct.
وفى:
The letters wāw, fā' and the weak letter are a word indicating completion and fulfilment.

1. al-wafā' — fulfilling a covenant and completing a condition.
2. wafā means awfā, he fulfilled it fully, so he is called wafiyy, faithful.
3. "awfaytuka al-shay'" — they say this when you paid someone a thing in full, giving it to him complete.
4. "tawaffaytu al-shay'" and "istawfaytuhu" — when you take something entirely, leaving nothing of it.
5. "tawaffāhu Allāh" — said of the dead: God has taken him in full.
وقب:
The letters wāw, qāf and bā' are a word that indicates a thing's disappearance into a hiding place.

1. waqaba l-shay'u — the thing went into a waqba, which is like a hollow in a thing.
2. waqabat 'aynāhu — his eyes sank in.
3. waqaba l-shay' — it came down and fell.

God Almighty said: {and from the evil of a darkness when it settles} [al-Falaq: 3]. They said: it is the night when it comes down.

As for their saying that al-waqb is the fool — that is from letter-substitution; the original is waghb, which we have already mentioned.
وقت: The letters wāw, qāf and tā' are a root that points to the limit of a thing and its full extent, in time and in other things. From it is al-waqt, the known time. Al-mawqūt is the thing that has been given a limit. [And] al-mīqāt is the coming to the appointed time. Waqata lahu kadhā and waqqatahu, that is, he set a limit for it. God, mighty and exalted, said: {Indeed the prayer has been for the believers a decree at appointed times} [al-Nisā': 103].
وقح:
The letters wāw, qāf and ḥā' are a word indicating hardness in a thing.

1. a hard hoof is called waqāḥ; the man of little shame is likened to it, and so he too is called waqāḥ.
2. waqiḥ — clearly marked by shamelessness, impudent.
3. al-tawqīḥ — for a hoof to be treated with melted fat, with which the hairy part above it is cauterized.
4. "istawqaḥa al-ḥāfir" — the hoof grew hard.
5. rajulun muwaqqaḥ — a man who is seasoned, experienced.
وقد: The letters wāw, qāf and dāl are a word pointing to the kindling of fire. *Waqadat al-nār taqidu* — the fire burned — and *ittaqadat* and *tawaqqadat*, and *awqadtuhā anā*, I kindled it. *Al-waqūd* is the firewood. *Al-wuqūd* is the fire's own act when it burns. *Al-waqad* is the fire itself. And *waqdat al-ṣayf* is the hottest part of the summer.
وقذ:
The letters wāw, qāf and dhāl are a word that indicates striking with wood.

1. al-waqdh — causing pain by striking.
2. shātun mawqūdha — a ewe struck with wood until it died.

Something not from this pattern: waqidhati l-nāqa — the she-camel gave milk reluctantly, so her milk grew scant.
وقر:
The letters wāw, qāf and rā' are a root pointing to heaviness in a thing. From it is al-waqr, heaviness in the ear. One says of it waqirat udhunuhu tawqaru waqran. Al-Kisā'ī said: wuqirat udhunuhu, so it is mawqūra — his ear was made heavy, so it is deafened. And al-wiqr is the load. And one says a palm-tree muwaqqara and mūqir — that is, bearing much fruit. And from it is al-waqār, forbearance and gravity. And a man dhū qiratin — that is, grave. One says of it waqara waqāran. And when you give the command you say ūqur, in the speech of him who says ūmur. Al-Aḥmar said of His saying {and stay in your houses} [al-Aḥzāb: 33]: it is not from al-waqār; it is only from sitting. One says of it waqartu aqiru waqran. Abū ʿUbayd said: with me it is from al-waqār. One says qir, as one says ʿid. And a man muwaqqar is one tried by experience.

And of what strays from the section is al-waqīra, a hollow in the rock. As for waqīr, it is a following-word to faqīr, said after it for the sound. And al-waqra is in the bone. And al-waqīr is the flock of sheep.
وقص:
The letters wāw, qāf and ṣād are a word indicating breaking something.

1. al-waqṣ — breaking the neck; "wuqiṣat ʿunuquhu" — his neck was broken, so it is mawqūṣa.

As for the saying of the Hudhalī poet, in a line of verse:
So I sent her treading through the hollows, after the fire's life grew hard for the one seeking to kindle it.

This comes from the mount's "waqṣ" when it travels over the tops of hillocks, treading them down as it goes.

2. al-tawaqquṣ in walking — a heavy tread, as though he breaks what is beneath him.
3. al-waqaṣ — broken bits of wood. One says "waqqiṣ li-nārik", trim wood for your fire; these are the broken pieces of sticks.
4. what falls between two obligatory dues is called waqaṣ; this is the analogy, because it is not a complete due, so it is as if broken.
وقط:
The letters wāw, qāf and ṭā' are a word indicating one thing striking another.

1. "waqaṭa al-dīk al-dajāja" — the rooster mounted the hen.
2. "aṣābatnā samā'un fa-waqaṭat al-arḍ" — rain fell upon us and struck the ground, as though it fell heavily on it; the place where water then collects is called waqṭ, and waqīṭ.
وقع:
The letters wāw, qāf and ʿayn are a single root to which its branches go back; it points to a thing falling.

One says waqaʿa al-shay'u wuqūʿan — the thing fell — so it is wāqiʿ, falling. And al-Wāqiʿa is the Resurrection, because it falls upon creation and covers them over. And al-waqʿa is the shock of battle. And al-waqā'iʿ are scattered pools where water stands, as though the water had fallen into them. And mawāqiʿ al-ghayth are the places where the rain comes down. And al-nasr al-wāqiʿ, the falling eagle, is from the settling of a bird: what is meant is that it has drawn in its two wings, so that it is as if it were coming down on the ground. And mawqaʿat al-ṭā'ir is the place a bird alights on. And kawaytu al-baʿīra waqāʿi — I branded the camel with waqāʿ: a single ring burnt into some part of its hide, wherever it may be, as though the brand had fallen upon it. And waqaʿa fulānun fī fulānin — he fell upon someone with his tongue — and awqaʿa bihi, he fell upon him.

As for waqaʿtu al-ḥadīdata aqiʿuhā waqʿan, when you sharpen the iron, that follows the same rule, because you bring it down on a stone or something else so that it may be drawn out — as though it were of the pattern "the thing did, and I did it to it".
