And a piece of iron is waqīʿ, sharpened. And waqaʿa al-ghaythu: the rain fell scattered. From it is al-tawqīʿ, the mark a galled sore leaves on a camel's back. And from it too al-tawqīʿ: what is added to a letter after it is finished. And tawaqqaʿtu al-shay'a: I waited for it, watching for when it would fall. And al-ḥāfir al-waqīʿ is the hoof that the stones have pared away; it is taken from iron that is waqīʿ, whetted. And al-sayf al-waqīʿ is the sword sharpened with a stone; its rule has already been given. And al-waqaʿ is soreness of the feet, and al-waqiʿ is the footsore one, and it is from this, as though he were a stone that had fallen on a whetting-block and been worn away. And al-waqiʿ is thin scattered cloud, as though it were about to come down with its rain.

As for what Abū ʿAmr related, that al-waqʿ is the high place on a mountain, it seems it was named so because whoever climbs it fears that he may fall from it.
وقف:
The letters wāw, qāf, and fā' are a single root indicating remaining in a place, from which other senses are then drawn by analogy.

1. waqaftu aqifu wuqūfan — I stood, I stopped.
2. waqaftu waqfī — I made my endowment. One does not say awqaftu for this, except that they say of one who has been engaged in something and then withdraws from it: 'he has awqafa.'

Al-Ṭirimmāḥ said, in a line of verse:
Headstrong in my wrongdoing, then I held back, content with piety — and the righteous man is content.

Al-Shaybānī reported the saying: 'I spoke to them, then I awqaftu from them,' meaning I fell silent. He said: whatever you hold yourself back from, you say awqaftu of it.

3. mawqif — the place where a person, or anything else, stands.
4. al-wiqāf — standing opposed to one another [in battle].

Ibn Durayd said: waqīfat al-waʿl is when dogs or hunters corner a mountain-goat on a rock so it cannot climb down, until it is caught.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
So do not take me for a lump of fat from some cornered goat, driven along, from what Salfaʿ hunts down for you.

Salfaʿ is the name of a bitch.

5. al-waqf — a bracelet of ivory, perhaps so named because it stays fixed in its place.
6. ḥimār muwaqqaf — by comparison, said of a donkey with white markings on its fetlocks, as though it wore such a bracelet.
7. mawqifā al-faras — the two hollows in a horse's flanks.

And God knows best what is right.
وقل:
The letters wāw, qāf and lām are a word indicating height, on a mountain.

1. "tawaqqala fī al-jabal" — he climbed up in the mountain, he ascended. Every climber of something is called mutawaqqil.
2. faras waqil — a horse good at moving over mountains.
3. al-waql — the muql tree.
وقم:
The letters wāw, qāf and mīm indicate overpowering and humbling.

1. "waqama Allāhu al-ʿaduwwa waqman" — God humbled the enemy.
2. "tawaqqama fulānun al-ʿilm" — so-and-so mastered the knowledge thoroughly.
3. "tawaqqamtu al-ṣayd" — I stalked the game.
4. al-mawqūm — one intensely grieved. Al-Kisā'ī said this.

And Ḥarrat Wāqim is in Madina.
وقه: The letters wāw, qāf and hā' are a single word. "Istayqaha al-qawm" means the people obeyed, from waqihtu, I obeyed.
وقى:
The letters wāw, qāf and yā' are a single word indicating warding one thing off from another by means of something else.

1. "waqaytuhu aqīhi waqyan" — I shielded him.
2. al-wiqāya — that which protects a thing.
3. "ittaqi Allāh" means tawaqqahu, that is, put something between yourself and Him as a shield. The Prophet, peace be upon him and his family, said: "Guard yourselves from the Fire even with half a date." It is as if he meant: make it a shield between yourselves and it.

Among what falls outside this chapter is al-waqy: they say it is a slight limp.
وكا:
The letters wāw, kāf and the weak letter are a minor root indicating tying something up, and strength.

1. al-wikā' — that with which something is tied. In the hadith: "Guard its wrapping and its tie-string."
2. "sa'altuhu fa-awkā ʿalayya" — I asked him and he tied up toward me, meaning he was stingy, as though he had tied his purse shut. And they say: so-and-so is a wikā' who lets nothing seep out, meaning he is utterly stingy.
3. Abū ʿUbayd said, regarding the hadith of al-Zubayr, that he used to go back and forth between al-Ṣafā and al-Marwa: he meant that he would fill up the space between them with his hurrying, just as a waterskin is tied off after being filled.
4. From this chapter also: "tawakka'tu ʿalā kadhā" — I leaned on such a thing, meaning ittaka'tu, because one braces and strengthens oneself by it.
5. "awka'tu fulānan īkā'an" — I set up a leaning-place for him.
وكب:
The letters wāw, kāf and bā' are two words: one indicates standing upright, the other a kind of gait.

The first: al-wakb — standing upright.

1. al-wākiba — the upright leg among the legs of a bed or something else.
2. "wakaba al-ʿinab" — the grapes began to ripen; that is when they fill with juice and their berries ripen.

The second: al-wakabān — a shuffling gait.

1. ẓabya wakūb — a doe with such a gait.
2. al-mūkib — the bird when it prepares itself to fly.
وكت: The letters wāw, kāf and tā' are a word, which is al-wakta, like a small mark on something. And a fresh date is said to have "wakkatat" when it has begun to develop such marks.
وكح:
The letters wāw, kāf and ḥā' are a word indicating hardness and firmness.

1. al-awkaḥ — stone.
2. "ḥafara ḥattā awkaḥa" — he dug until he awkaḥa, meaning he reached rock that iron could not penetrate.
3. "istawkaḥa al-farkh" — the chick grew firm. And these are called firākh wukaḥ, hardened young birds.
وكد:
The letters wāw, kāf and dāl are a word that indicates tying and making firm.

1. awkid 'aqdaka — make your knot fast, meaning tie it firmly.
2. al-wikād — a rope with which the cow is tied at milking.

They say: wakada wakdahu, meaning he aimed for it and was concerned with it.
وكر:
The letters wāw, kāf and rā' are a sound root, but its words do not follow one single pattern; rather they are individual items.

1. al-wakrā — a kind of running.
2. al-wakkār — a man who runs, a runner.
3. al-wakrā, of women — one heavy of tread when she walks.
4. "wakartu al-ināʾ" — I filled the vessel.
5. "wakara baṭnahu" — it filled his belly.
6. al-wakīra — food prepared for a building [a construction feast].
7. al-wākir — the bird when it enters its nest.
8. al-wukra — the path down to water.
وكز:
The letters wāw, kāf and zāy are a sound formation.

1. wakazahu — he stabbed him.
2. wakazahu — he struck him with the base of his closed fist.
3. wakazahu — he pushed him.
وكس:
The letters wāw, kāf and sīn are a word indicating deficiency and loss.

1. al-waks — deficiency.
2. "wakastuhu" — I shortchanged him.
3. "wukisa al-rajul" and "ūkisa" — the man suffered loss.
4. "bara'at al-shajja ʿalā waksin" — the head-wound healed with a shortfall, meaning its healing was not complete.
وكع:
The letters wāw, kāf and ʿayn are two words: one indicates strength, the other a kind of striking.

The first:

1. siqā' wakīʿ — a waterskin that is wakīʿ, meaning strong, so that nothing leaks from it. They also say: "istawkaʿat miʿidatuhu", his stomach grew strong. The name Wakīʿ is derived along this pattern.
2. al-wakaʿ, in slave-women, comes from this — it is a tilt in the front of the foot toward the little toe; it is found in slave-women only because they labour hard.
3. faras wakīʿ — a horse that is hard, strong.

The second: their saying "wakaʿathu al-ʿaqrab bi-ibratihā", the scorpion wakaʿat him with its stinger, meaning it stung him.

1. "wakaʿa al-nāqa" — he milked the she-camel.
2. "bāta al-faṣīl yakaʿu ummahu al-layla" — the young weaned camel spent the night striking at its mother's udder.
وكف:
The letters wāw, kāf and fā' are a sound root, but its words do not follow one single pattern.

1. al-wakf — the dripping of a house, also called al-wakīf.
2. "istawkafa" — he sought to draw drops out.
3. al-wikāf — a dialect variant of al-ikāf, the pack-saddle.
4. al-wakaf — sin and blemish.
5. al-tawakkuf — expectation; perhaps its origin is waiting for a drip to fall.
6. al-wakaf — a low, settled patch of ground.
7. "wakaf al-jabal" — the lower slopes of the mountain.

He said, in a line of verse:
It rises over the hillocks, and rises over the mountain's foot.

8. al-wakf — the leather mat.
9. "laysa fī hādhā al-amr wakaf" — there is no wakaf in this matter, meaning no corruption or weakness.
وكل:
The letters wāw, kāf and lām are a sound root pointing to relying on another in your affair. Of that is al-wukala, and al-wakal, which is the weak man. They say wukala tukala. And al-tawakkul is from it, and it is the showing of one's inability in a matter and the relying on another. And wākala fulān, when he neglects his affair, relying on someone else. And the wakīl was so called because the matter is entrusted to him. And al-wikāl in a riding-beast is that it always lags behind the other beasts, as though it entrusted the matter of running to another. And in the poetry of Imru' al-Qays, in a line of verse:
He does not lag in her driving on —
that is, he is not slow; and its origin is from mutual reliance. [And] wākaltu al-rajul, when you rely on him and he relies on you. And they say: al-wikāl in a beast is that it goes at the pace of the other.
وكم:
The letters wāw, kāf and mīm are a word. They say:

1. "wukimat al-arḍ" — the ground is said to be wukimat when it is trodden underfoot.
2. "wakamahu al-amr" — the matter grieved him.
3. wukima — he was turned back.
وكن: The letters wāw, kāf and nūn. They call a bird's nest waknun, plural wukunāt. In the hadith: "Leave the birds be in their nests." They also say: tawakkana, in the sense of tamakkana, he settled himself firmly.
ول: The letters wāw and lām. Al-walwala — wailing, the sounds of women weeping.
ولب:
The letters wāw, lām and bā'. They say it has two chapters: one indicates growth, the other departure.

As for the first:

1. al-wāliba — a plant that grows again from the roots of the earlier plant.
2. wālibat al-ibil — the offspring of the camels.
3. "walaba al-shay'" — he joined the thing.

The other is al-wālib. Al-Shaybānī said: it is one who goes off on his own way. One says: "walaba fī dhālika al-wajh", he went off in that direction.

He said, in a line of verse:
I saw Jurayy going off on his own way among their dwellings — and how poor a young man he is, if a grave matter should befall the greater part of his people.
ولث:
The letters wāw, lām and thā' contain two words. One says: between them is a walth, that is, a covenant.

The other: he walatha him with the stick, striking him with it. And the rain-shower walathat the ground, when it beat down upon it.
ولج:
The letters wāw, lām and jīm are a word pointing to a thing's going in.

One says walaja fī manzilihi and walaja al-bayt yaliju wulūjan — he went into his lodging, he entered the house. And al-walīja is the inner circle and the intimates one lets in. And one says rajulun khurajatun wulajatun — a man much given to going out and going in. And al-walija is a pain that goes into a man's inside. And they say al-walaj is the path in the sand, and it belongs to the analogy.
ولح:
The letters wāw, lām and ḥā'. They say: al-walīḥ — the large sacks; the singular is walīḥa.

He said, in a line of verse:
They were draped, over the saddle-cloths, with the large sacks.
ولخ:
The letters wāw, lām and khā' indicate mixing.

1. "i'talakha al-ʿushb i'tilākhan" — the herbage grew large and tall and became intermixed together.
2. "waqaʿa al-qawm fī i'tilākh" — the people fell into confusion.

And some people claim that this belongs to the chapter of hamza, lām and khā', and it has been mentioned there.
ولد:
The letters wāw, lām and dāl are a sound root, and it is the sign of offspring and progeny; then other things are measured against it.

Of that is al-walad, the child, and it is said of one and of many alike; and of the single one wuld is also said. Al-walīda is the female, and the plural is walā'id. And tawallada al-shay'u ʿani al-shay' — one thing came about from another. And al-lida, one born at the same time as another, is short of its wāw, because its origin is wilda.
ولذ: The letters wāw, lām and dhāl. Among the rarities recorded by Ibn Durayd: al-waldh is speed in walking and movement. One says walatha yalidhu.
ولس: The letters wāw, lām and sīn: a word indicating a kind of travel. Al-walasān is a fast, striding pace in walking.
ولع:
The letters wāw, lām and ʿayn: two words. One of them indicates being taken with a thing, the other a kind of color.

The first is their saying: ulitu bi-l-shayʾi walūʿan — I became infatuated with the thing. A man is wulaʿa if he is taken with a thing. By this same pattern one says walaʿa al-ẓabyu, when the gazelle went fast. And walaʿa al-rajulu — the man lied.

The other is their calling a piebald animal muwallaʿ. Al-tawlīʿ is the lengthening of the pied markings. A poet said, in a line of verse:
As though on the hide it were the streaking of vitiligo.
And al-walīʿ is the palm's unopened flower-spathe, still within its sheath.
ولغ:
The letters wāw, lām and ghayn: one word, which is their saying: walagha al-kalbu fī al-ināʾi yalaghu, and yūlaghu when its owner makes it lap (awlagha-hu). ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm al-Qaṭṭān recited to us, saying: Thaʿlab recited to us, in a line of verse:
No day passed but with the two of them was the flesh of men, or they lapped up blood.
A man mustawligh is one who cares nothing for blame or disgrace.
ولق:
The letters wāw, lām and qāf: a word indicating speed and lightness. One says jāʾati al-ibilu taliqu — the camels came hurrying. A poet said, in a line of verse:
A she-camel brought him from Syria, hurrying.
And according to this is the reading of those who recite: idh taliqūnahu bi-alsinatikum — when you were rushing it along with your tongues.

1. nāqatun walaqā — a fast she-camel.
2. al-walq — the lightest kind of thrust; one says walaqahu bi-l-sayfi walaqātin, he struck him with the sword, blow after blow.
3. walaqa yaliqu — he lied.

All of this follows one and the same pattern.

1. al-awlaq — madness. One says akhadhahu al-awlaqu, madness seized him. A man muʾawlaq, on the pattern muʿawlaq, has madness in him.
ولم:
The letters wāw, lām and mīm contain words that resemble one another. They say:

1. al-walm — the girth-strap.
2. al-walm — a rope tied between the breast-girth and the woven strap so that the two do not come loose.
3. al-walm — any cord with which you tie something.

It is not unlikely that the derivation of al-walīma, the wedding feast, comes from this, because the tying takes place at the contracting of marriage. And the people of language say: the food of a wedding is called walīma.
وله:
The letters wāw, lām and hā' are a sound root indicating the distress of something, or its going away. One says: a man is wālih, and a woman is wālih or wāliha.

Al-Aʿshā said, in a line of verse:
So she came forward, distraught, bereaved, in haste — everything overwhelmed her, and everything gathered upon her.

1. al-muwallah — the one whose mind has been thrown into confusion.
2. ʿaynun muwallaha — a spring is muwallaha when its water is let loose and goes off wandering into the deserts.
3. al-tawlīh — separating a woman from her child. In the hadith: "No mother is to be separated in distress from her child."
ولي:
The letters wāw, lām and yā' are a sound root pointing to nearness. Of that is al-waly: nearness. One says: he grew distant after waly, that is, after nearness. And he sat mimmā yalīnī, that is, close beside me. And al-waliyy is the rain that comes after the first autumn rain, so called because it follows the wasmī.

Of this section is al-mawlā: the one who frees a slave and the freed slave, the companion, the confederate, the cousin, the helper, and the neighbour - all of these are from al-waly, which is nearness. And everyone who takes charge of another's affair is his waliyy. And so-and-so is awlā of such a thing, [that is, more fitting for it and worthier of it. As for their saying by way of insult, awlā laka - 'Alī ibn 'Umar related to me, he said: I heard Tha'lab] say: awlā is a threat and a warning. And he recited, a line of verse:
So awlā, then awlā, then awlā - and is there any way back for milk once it is milked?

Al-Aṣma'ī said: its meaning is, what would destroy him has come near him, that is, it has come down upon him. And he recited, a line of verse:
He brought down two of her foremost, one after the other, and came near to going beyond three.

That is, he came near to going beyond. Tha'lab said: no one has said [anything better] than what al-Aṣma'ī said about awlā. Another said: awlā is making him grieve over what he has missed.

Al-walā' is the supporters; one says, these are the walā' of so-and-so. Al-walā' is also the tie of a freed slave, which is that his walā' belongs to the one who freed him, as though that one were nearer to him in inheritance than anyone else when the freer has no blood heir. It is what came in the hadith: 'He forbade the selling of walā' and the giving of it away.' And wālaytu bayna al-shay'ayn, when you set the two one right after the other, in succession. And do this 'alā al-wilā', that is, in order. And the whole section goes back to nearness.
ومأ: The letters wāw, mīm and hamza: one word. One says wamaʾtu ilayhi wamʾan, and awmaʾtu īmāʾan ūmiʾu — I gestured to him. And if you drop the hamza it becomes al-wāmiya, which is a calamity, a disaster.
ومد:
The letters wāw, mīm and dāl: two words.

1. al-wamad — intense heat.
2. wamida — he became angry.
ومض: The letters wāw, mīm and ḍād: a word indicating the flashing of something. One says wamaḍa al-barqu wamīḍan, and awmaḍa īmāḍan — the lightning flashed. And awmaḍa bi-ʿaynihi — he flashed his eye — comes from this.
ومق: The letters wāw, mīm and qāf: one word, which is al-wamaq — love. One says wamiqa yamiqu. Al-miqa is also a noun for it.
ونم: The letters wāw, nūn and mīm. He said: wanama al-dhubābu yanimu wanman wa-wanīman — the fly excreted.
ونى:
The letters wāw, nūn and the weak letter. It indicates weakness. One says wanā yanī wanyan.

1. al-wānī — the weak one. God, Most High, said: {and do not slacken in remembering Me} [Ṭāhā: 42].
2. al-wanā — fatigue; one says awnaytuhu — I wearied him.
3. nāqatun wāniya — a weak, tired she-camel.
4. lā yanī yafʿalu — used exactly as one says lā yazālu, he does not stop doing it.
5. imraʾatun wanātun — a woman is called this when there is languor in her at rising.
وه:
The letters wāw and hā'. It contains nothing but *wahwaha*: the donkey called out around his mares, out of tenderness for them.

A poet said, in a line of verse:
One with power over the estate — his call is tenderness.
وهب: The letters wāw, hā' and bā': words that are not reasoned one from another. You say wahabtu al-shay' ahabuhu hibatan and mawhiban, I gave the thing as a gift. And ittahabtu al-hiba: I accepted the gift. And al-mawhiba is a small hollow in which water settles, and the plural is mawāhib. And one says awhaba ilayya min al-māl kadhā, that is, it rose up for me. And asbaha fulānun mūhaban li-kadhā, that is, made ready for it.
وهت: The letters wāw, hāʾ and tāʾ. One says awhata al-laḥmu, when the meat rots and stinks — yūhitu īhātan.
وهث: The letters wāw, hāʾ and thāʾ. They say: al-wahth is being immersed, absorbed in a thing.
وهج:
The letters wāw, hā' and jīm are a single word, and it is al-wahaj: the heat of fire and its blazing.

That is used figuratively, so one says: tawahhaja l-jawharu, the jewel gleamed and sparkled; tawahhajat rā'iḥatu l-ṭībi, and wahaju l-ṭībi, its fragrance and scent; sirājun wahhāj, a blazing lamp; and likewise najmun wahhāj, a blazing star.
وهد: The letters wāw, hāʾ and dāl: one word, which is al-wahda — a low, settled patch of ground; plural wihād.
وهز: The letters wāw, hāʾ and zāy. They say: al-wahz is one compact and firmly built in body. Wahaztu — I pushed, I shoved. Al-tawahhuz — springing up, leaping forward.
وهس:
The letters wāw, hāʾ and sīn: two words. One is intensity in various matters, the other belongs to secret talk.

1. al-wahs — intensity of travel.
2. al-wahs — intensity of eating.
3. al-wahs — intensity of treading down.

Ḥumayd said, in a line of verse:
In the diminishing of people's honor, and al-wahs.
This belongs to al-tawahhus, which is being harsh and overbearing toward one's own clan.

1. al-wahs — secret talk.
2. al-wahs — slander, carrying tales.
وهص:
The letters wāw, hāʾ and ṣād: closely related words, namely al-wahṣ — pressing hard on a thing with the foot. One says wahaṣa yahiṣu.

1. rajulun mawhūṣ al-khalq — a man whose bones are compacted, overlapping one another.
2. wahaṣtu al-shayʾa — I broke, I crushed the thing.
وهط:
The letters wāw, hāʾ and ṭāʾ. One says awhaṭahu, when he struck him but did not finish him off.

1. wahaṭahu — he broke it.
2. wahaṭahu — he trod on it.

These are close in meaning.

1. al-wahṭ — a low, settled place.
2. al-wahṭ — a thicket of ʿurfuṭ (a thorny acacia).

Al-Rāʿī said, in a line of verse:
Making for Arm, to the left, and for Ḥāra, to the north, and crossing the low grounds, the flowing ones.
وهف:
The letters wāw, hāʾ and fāʾ: two words.

1. awhafa min al-māli kadhā — such an amount of the wealth rose, increased.
2. wahafa al-nabātu — the plant put out leaves and swayed.
وهق:
The letters wāw, hāʾ and qāf: two words. One of them is al-wahaq, which I take to be Persian, brought into Arabic. The other is sound Arabic: al-muwāhaqa — stretching out the necks while travelling. One says tawāhaqati al-rikābu — the mounts stretched their necks level with one another. As for their saying tawahhaqa al-ḥaṣā, when its heat grows intense, that belongs to the substitution of one letter for another — it is really tawahhaja [from blazing heat]. And he recited:
Until, when the heat of the gravel blazed fiercely.
وهل:
The letters wāw, hāʾ and lām: words that do not follow one single pattern — they are separate, individual words. One is al-wahal — terror, fright. One says wahila yawhalu.

1. wahaltu ʿan al-shayʾi — I forgot the thing, said by Abū Zayd.
2. wahaltu ilayhi — my mind turned to it, my thought went to it.
3. laqītuhu awwala wahlatin — I met him at the very first instant, before anything else.
وهم:
The letters wāw, hāʾ and mīm: words that do not follow one pattern, but are separate, individual words. Among them:

1. al-wahm — a huge camel.
2. al-wahm — a road, a path.
3. al-wahm — the mind's notion, its apprehension; one says wahamtu ahimu wahman, when my thought turns to something. From this comes the measure of al-tuhma, an accusation.
4. awhamtu fī al-ḥisābi — I left something out, made an omission, in reckoning.
5. wahimtu — I erred, I was mistaken.
وهن:
The letters wāw, hā' and nūn are two words: one of them points to weakness, and the other to a time.

The first: wahana al-shay'u yahinu wahnan — the thing grew weak; and awhantuhu anā — I weakened it. And from this is al-wāhina, the shortest of the ribs, which is the lowest of them. Abū Bakr said: al-wāhina is a disease that strikes a man in his two neck-veins. And al-wahnāna is the woman of little movement, heavy in rising and in sitting.

And the second word: al-wahn and al-mawhin are an hour that passes of the night. And awhana al-rajul — the man came to be, or travelled, in that hour.

(The book of the letter wāw is finished, and God knows best what is right.)
وهي:
The letters wāw, hā', and the weak letter indicate a slackening in a thing.

1. wahat 'azālī l-saḥābi bi-mā'ihā — the water-spouts of the cloud loosened with their water.
2. Anything whose binding has grown slack is wāhin.
3. al-wahy — the tear or split in a hide or the like.
ويح: The letters wāw, yā' and ḥā'. They say *wayḥa*: a word of mercy for one struck by misfortune. Al-Khalīl said: nothing was heard built this way except *wayḥa*, *ways*, *wayha*, *wayla*, and *wayba*. They are close in meaning.
يأس:
The letters yā', hamza and sīn. They are two words. One of them is al-ya's, the cutting off of hope. It is said that there is no yā' at the beginning of a word with a hamza after it except in this word. From it one says ya'isa yay'asu and yay'isu, on the patterns yaf'alu and yaf'ilu.

The other word is alam tay'as, that is, did you not know. And they said about the saying of God Almighty: {Have those who believe not known} [al-Ra'd: 31], that is, have they not known. And they recited, in a line of verse:
I say to them at the mountain pass, while they were taking me captive: did you not know that I am the son of the horseman of Zahdam?
يا: The letters yāʾ and alif: a particle. It is the yāʾ used for calling out, as in yā Zayd — O Zayd! It may also express wonder and delight, as in their saying yā bardahā ʿalā al-fuʾād — how cool it is upon the heart! And it may express regret, as in the saying of one who says yā ḥasratā ʿalā kadhā — oh, what sorrow over such a thing!
يب:
The letters yāʾ and bāʾ: one word, which is al-yabāb, used to reinforce the word kharāb (ruin), following it as an echo-word. Sometimes they use it on its own, as they said, in a line of verse:
The earth told of his deeds, and made both the desolate waste and the inhabited land speak out from it.
يبس:
The letters yā', bā', and sīn are a sound root indicating dryness.

1. yabisa al-shayʾu, yaybas / yaybis — it dried out (two forms of the verb).
2. al-yabs — dried vegetation; Ibn al-Sikkīt said it is the plural of yābis.
3. al-yabas (with fatḥa on the bā') — a place the water has left, so that it dries out.
4. yabisat al-arḍ — the ground's water and moisture went away; aybasat — its dryness grew widespread.
5. imraʾa yabas — al-Shaybānī said this of a woman who has obtained no good [in life].

A poet said, in a line of verse:
To an old woman, wrinkled of face, and dried up.

6. yabīs al-māʾ — sweat once it has dried.
7. al-aybasān — the parts of the shin and ankle bare of flesh.
يتم:
The letters yā', tā' and mīm. One says: orphanhood among people is on the father's side, and among the rest of animals on the mother's side. And they call everything that stands alone yatīm, so that they even said a line [of poetry] is yatīm, an orphan.

The poet said, describing an archer who struck a wild she-ass and orphaned her young, in a line of verse:
He fixed in her an arrow, hard of edge, and its sinking home orphaned her young.
يتن: The letters yāʾ, tāʾ and nūn: one word, which is al-yatn — the young camel whose legs come out at birth before its head. One says aytanati al-nāqatu wa-l-marʾatu, when the she-camel or the woman gives birth to a yatn.
يد:
The letters yāʾ and dāl: the underlying formation of 'the hand', for a human being and for others, and it is used figuratively for a favor owed, so one says lahu ʿalayhi yad — he has a claim of favor on him. It is pluralized as al-ayādī and al-yudiyy. A poet said: 'Indeed he has with me favors and bounties.'

1. al-yad — strength; pluralized as al-aydī.
2. yudayya — the diminutive form of al-yad.

Some people pluralized 'the hand' of a human being as al-ayādī, and one said, in a line of verse:
It grieved her, what she saw in our favors, and their being drawn close to the necks.

3. Al-Shaybānī reported: imraʾatun yadiyya — a woman skilled with her hands, a craftswoman; and rajulun yadiyy, likewise for a man.
4. mā aydā fulānata — how skilled so-and-so is — an expression of admiration for her skill.
5. yadiya min yadihi, yudʿā ʿalayhi — said of one against whom a curse concerning his hand is invoked.
6. yadaytu ʿalā al-rajuli — I did the man a favor, I showed him kindness. He said, in a line of verse:
I showed a favor to Ibn Ḥashḥās ibn ʿAmr, at the foot of Dhū al-Jadā, the favor of a noble man.
7. yadaytuhu — I struck his hand.
يدع:
The letters yāʾ, dāl and ʿayn are two distinct words.

1. al-aydaʿ — a red dye. From it one says yaddaʿtu al-shayʾ, uyaddiʿuhu, taydīʿan — I dyed the thing, dyeing it.

2. aydaʿa al-ḥajja ʿalā nafsihi — he made the pilgrimage obligatory upon himself. Jarīr said, in a line of verse:
By the Lord of the she-camels racing to the mountain passes, with disheveled pilgrims who made the pilgrimage a complete obligation upon themselves.
ير: The letters yāʾ and rāʾ. They say: al-ḥajaru al-ayarru — the hard stone. The verbal noun is al-yarar. And they say ḥārrun yārrun — yārr being an echo-word reinforcing ḥārr, hot.
يزن: The letters yāʾ, zāy and nūn. There is nothing in this root but Dhū Yazan, one of the kings of Ḥimyar; spears are attributed to him, so one says yazaniyya and azaniyya.
يسر:
The letters yā', sīn and rā' are two roots: one of them points to the opening up of a thing and its lightness, and the other to one of the limbs.

The first: al-yusr, ease, the opposite of hardship. And al-yasarāt are the light legs. And one says a horse is ḥasan al-taysūr, that is, good at moving its legs. A poet said, in a line of verse:
We have tested him for all his faults ... and for his light-footedness and his leanness.

And of this chapter: yassarat al-ghanam, when the sheep's milk and offspring grow many. A poet said, in a line of verse:
They are our two lords, so they claim; but only ... their two flocks' yielding much makes them masters over us.

And one says a man is yasr and yasar, that is, easily led. And al-yasār is wealth. And tayassara al-shay' and istaysara — the thing came easy. And Yusr is a place.

And of this chapter: al-aysār, the people who gather at the game of maysir; the singular is yasar. A poet said, in a line of verse:
And they are the gamblers of Luqmān when ... the winter makes the parts of the slaughtered beasts dear.
And al-maysir is gambling. And of this chapter: al-yasara, the lines of the palm of the hand when they are not joined together.

And the other word: al-yasār for the hand, the left. One says tayāsarū when they take the left-hand side. And one says yāsarū, and that is the better.
يعر:
The letters yāʾ, ʿayn and rāʾ.

1. al-yaʿr — the kid, a young goat. Someone said, in a line of verse:
As the kid was tethered
— that is, as it was tethered — beside the pit-trap set for the wolf.

2. al-yuʿār — the bleating sound of sheep and goats. One says yaʿarat, tayʿaru, yuʿāran — it bleated, it bleats, bleating.
يعط:
The letters yāʾ, ʿayn and ṭāʾ. They say to the wolf, when they drive it off: yaʿāṭ. He said: and one says ayʿaṭtu bihi — I called yaʿāṭ at it. He said, in a line of verse:
It darts off when it is told: yaʿāṭ.
يعفور:
al-khishf, the fawn. Al-Khalīl said: it was named this for how often it presses close to the ground. He said, in a line of verse: she crosses over the people to our mounts, at the end of the night, with a languid fawn.

This is a word in which the yāʾ was added at its start; it is really from al-ʿafar, which is the surface of the ground and the dust on it.
يفع:
The letters yāʾ, fāʾ and ʿayn: a word denoting height.

1. al-yafāʿ — what rises up from the land, high ground.

2. ayfaʿa al-ghulām — said of a boy when his youth has risen up, that is, he has grown up; he is then called yāfiʿ, and mūfiʿ is not said.
يفن: The letters yāʾ, fāʾ and nūn. They say: al-yafan — the very old man.
يقن: The letters yā', qāf and nūn: al-yaqan and al-yaqīn are the passing away of doubt. One says yaqintu, and istayqantu, and ayqantu, all meaning I became certain.
يقه:
The letters yāʾ, qāf and hāʾ. I heard ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm al-Qaṭṭān say: I heard Thaʿlab say: ayqaha, yūqihu, īqāhan — said when he understood. One says ayqih li-hādhā, meaning understand it. And it is said that this is rather related to obedience. He said, in a line of verse:
And they obeyed al-Muḥallim.
يل:
The letters yāʾ and lām: one word, which is al-yalal — shortness of the teeth. He said, in a line of verse:
The one whose teeth jut out grimaces among them, and so does the one whose teeth are short.
يلب:
The letters yāʾ, lām and bāʾ: a single word whose meaning is disputed. It is al-yalab. Some said: al-yalab is helmets made from camel hides. Others said: al-yalab is the shield. And they cited, in a line of verse:
Upon them every ample, smooth coat of mail, and in their hands the round yalab.
Al-Khalīl said: al-yalab is steel. He said:
And an axle wrought pure from the sheen of the yalab.
يلق:
The letters yāʾ, lām and qāf.

1. al-yalaq — the white of anything. They cited, in a line of verse:
And I leave the rival in the dust, and against his two flanks a grey-blue spear whose blade gleams white.

2. al-yalaqa — the white female goat.
يم:
The letters yāʾ and mīm: a word indicating aiming at a thing deliberately and directing oneself toward it. From this is His saying, Most High: {then seek out clean earth} [al-Nisāʾ: 43]. Al-Khalīl said: one says tayammamtu fulānan bi-sahmī wa-rumḥī, when you aim at him with your arrow or your spear, to the exclusion of anyone else. And he recited:
I aimed the spear at him aslant, then said to him: this is valor, not the play of children on a slide.
Al-Khalīl said: whoever, in this line, reads it as amamtuhu has erred, because he said 'aslant', and 'aslant' can only be from one side — he was not aiming straight ahead of himself, so as to say amamtuhu.

1. Al-Shaybānī reported: rajulun muyammam — a man is called this when he attains everything he seeks. And he recited:
We found Aʿṣur ibn Saʿd, one whose house is sought out, of exalted lineage.
This is as though he is sought out for good things. But the word for the sea does not belong to this pattern.
2. Al-Khalīl reported: yumma al-rajulu, fa-huwa maymūm — a man is said to be this when he falls into the yamm, a great body of water, and drowns.
3. al-yamām — a bird; it is said to be the bird that broods and rears its young inside houses.
يمن:
The letters yā', mīm and nūn are words of a single reasoning. So al-yamīn is the right hand. [And] it is said: al-yamīn is strength. And al-Aṣmaʿī said about al-Shammākh's words, in a line of verse:
When a banner is raised for glory, ʿArāba takes it with the right hand —
that he meant the right hand. And al-yumn is blessing, and one is maymūn, blessed. And al-yamīn is an oath, and all of that is from the right hand. And likewise al-Yaman, which is a land. One says a rajul yamān and a sayf yamān.

And an oath was called yamīn because it is as though one of the two who swear strikes his right hand upon his fellow's right hand.
ينف: The letters yāʾ, nūn and fāʾ. Yanūf, in the poetry of Imruʾ al-Qays, is a hill among the two mountains of Ṭayy.
ينم: The letters yāʾ, nūn and mīm. al-yanama — a plant.
يه: The letters yāʾ and hāʾ. They say: yahyaha bi-l-ibili, when he called out to the camels, saying 'yāh, yāh'.
يهر:
The letters yāʾ, hāʾ and rāʾ.

1. al-yahr — persistence, obstinacy.

2. istayhara al-rajul — the man persisted.
يهم:
The letters yāʾ, hāʾ and mīm.

1. al-yahmāʾ — a desert waste with no landmark on it.

2. al-ayhamān — the flood and the fire.

3. al-ayham, of men — the deaf one.

4. ayham, said of the brave man — this too belongs to this root, as if no one can find a way to approach him.
يوح: The letters yāʾ, wāw and ḥāʾ: a single word, and it is Yūḥ — one of the names of the sun.
يوم:
The letters yā', wāw and mīm are a single word: it is al-yawm, one of the days. Then they borrow it for a great affair, and they say niʿma fulānun fī al-yawm — excellent is so-and-so on the day — when it comes down upon them. And he recited:
Excellent is the brother of battle on the day of days.
And some people said: it is turned about; it was fī al-yawim. And the origin of ayyām is aywām, but it was doubled together.

As for what goes beyond the three letters in this section — such as (al-yarbūʿ), which is a small beast, the jerboa; and (Yabrīn), which is a place; and (Yam'ūd) and (Yalamlam), which are two places; and (al-yarandaj), which is black leather, and the like of that — the way of the yā' at the beginning of them is the way of the hamza in the four-letter and five-letter words: both are added letters, and the reckoning goes only by what comes after the yā', just as in the section of the hamza the reckoning goes by what comes after it. And that has already passed in the sections of the book.

The venerable shaykh, the most noble, the blessed, Abū al-Ḥusayn Aḥmad ibn Fāris — the mercy of God be upon him, and may He give him abundant reward — said:

We have set down what we made it our condition at the head of the book to set down, and it is a sound portion of the language. As for encompassing all the speech of the Arabs, [that] is a thing none has power over but God the Exalted, or a prophet from among His prophets — peace be upon them — by the revelation of God, mighty and exalted; that lies with Him. And praise be to God, first and last, inwardly and outwardly. And blessing and peace be upon His messenger Muḥammad and upon all his family, the good and the pure.

The writing of the book Maqāyīs al-Lugha has here come to its end.
